h: Threads and the bugs they cause
x: Threads, races, locks, deadlock, atomics, concurrent collections and synchronizers. By the end of this track you can read concurrent Java and Kotlin code and say what can go wrong: which line races, which pair of locks can freeze each other, which wait can hang forever, and which test proves nothing. You can fix each problem with the smallest tool that works: one atomic library call, a lock around the whole job, a concurrent collection, a synchronizer, or no sharing at all. And you can show that the fix holds, with a test that makes threads collide, and find the cause of a hang or a slowdown with thread dumps and Java Flight Recorder. You need everyday Java or Kotlin and nothing else. The track starts with what a thread is and adds one idea per lesson, each tried on a program you can picture: a shop adding up a year of sales, a mail-room helper that sends letters from a tray, a bank moving money between accounts, a kitchen where waiters pass orders to cooks on a rail, and a slow web service that takes 120 ms to answer. The memory model track comes next and explains why the visibility rules you use here work. Every lesson has a lab in labs/concurrency, in the package workbench.concurrency.lNN. From labs/, run ./gradlew :concurrency:test --tests 'workbench.concurrency.lNN.*': the tests fail on the starting code and pass when your fix is right. Reference answers are in src/solution, and ./gradlew :concurrency:solutionTest runs the same tests against them. The Try-it programs are in src/demo, in Java and Kotlin, and run with ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=<class>. The labs compile for JDK 21 and run on 21 or later; install JDK 25. A race condition is a result that depends on timing. Its two shapes are read-modify-write and check-then-act, and both need the whole compound action made atomic. A race needs state that is shared and changing. Reach for fixes in this order: don't share (immutability, confinement, hand-off), then one atomic library call, then a lock around the whole compound action, reads included. synchronized and ReentrantLock give one thread at a time and visibility. Release explicit locks in finally, lock on private objects, keep locked code short and never call alien code inside it. Waiting for a condition is always while (!condition) wait() or await(). Use notifyAll() with one wait set, or one Condition per kind of waiting thread. Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions. A global lock order removes circular wait; tryLock with a random back-off removes no preemption. jcmd Thread.print finds monitor and ReentrantLock cycles. Atomics are compare-and-set underneath: read, decide, compare-and-set, retry. LongAdder for busy counters, AtomicLong for decisions, AtomicReference plus an immutable object for several fields. Concurrent collections make single calls safe. Use their atomic per-key methods, bound every queue, and don't read size() or an iteration as a snapshot. Latches wait for events once, barriers meet every round, semaphores cap how many run at once, phasers change size. Count down and release in finally, and give every wait a deadline. ThreadLocal values outlive the request on pool threads: remove them in finally, or use scoped values on JDK 25+. Stop consumers with one poison pill each, after the last producer. A concurrency test must make threads collide and check invariants with a timeout. Find hangs with thread dumps and lock waits with JFR.

h: Threads and the bugs they cause: cheat sheet
x: Threads Call What it does t.start() runs t on a new thread; t.run() runs it on the current one t.join() waits for t to end; everything t wrote is visible afterwards t.interrupt() asks t to stop; blocking calls throw InterruptedException and clear the flag setDaemon(true) the JVM may exit while this thread still runs Thread.stop() removed in JDK 26; cancellation is cooperative When you catch InterruptedException: rethrow it, or restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() and stop. The two shapes of race Shape Looks like Fix Read-modify-write count++, balance -= x, put(k, get(k) + 1) an atomic call, or a lock around read and write Check-then-act if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v), setting something up on first use one call that checks and acts: putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, Set.add, a compare-and-set A thread-safe class makes single calls atomic, never two calls in a row. Pick the tool You need Use Picture it A busy counter, read now and then LongAdder visits to a web page One exact value with read-modify-write AtomicLong: updateAndGet, accumulateAndGet, or a compare-and-set loop the largest sale so far Several fields that change together one lock around both, or an AtomicReference to an immutable record a balance and the time it last changed A per-key update in a shared map ConcurrentHashMap.merge, compute, computeIfAbsent sales per item A table replaced as a whole a volatile field holding an immutable map a new price board hung up in one move Read-mostly data updated in place ReentrantReadWriteLock (never upgrade read to write) many readers, one person changing the board A wait that can time out or be cancelled ReentrantLock.tryLock(timeout), lockInterruptibly() a transfer that gives up instead of freezing Two kinds of waiting threads on one lock one Condition each, then signal() is enough waiters wait for room, cooks for tickets Hand work to other threads a bounded BlockingQueue, such as ArrayBlockingQueue(n) the kitchen's order rail Wait for N events, once CountDownLatch the shop opens when three lists have loaded N threads meeting every round CyclicBarrier three tills total each day together At most N at once Semaphore a car park with five spaces A group that changes size between phases Phaser a stocktake helper who goes home early A small list, rarely changed, often read in a loop CopyOnWriteArrayList the listeners of a price board Per-request context ThreadLocal with remove() in finally; ScopedValue on JDK 25+ the user a request runs for Idioms An explicit lock: Java lock.lock(); // before the try try { balance -= cents; } finally { lock.unlock(); // first line of finally } Kotlin lock.withLock { // lock, try, finally unlock balance -= cents } A guarded wait: Java synchronized (lock) { while (items.isEmpty()) lock.wait(); // a while, never an if return items.removeFirst(); } Kotlin lock.withLock { // ReentrantLock + Condition: Any has no wait() while (items.isEmpty()) notEmpty.await() items.removeFirst() } A compare-and-set loop: Java long prev; do { prev = max.get(); if (amount <= prev) return; // decide on what you read } while (!max.compareAndSet(prev, amount)); // write only if nobody changed it Kotlin var prev: Long do { prev = max.get() if (amount <= prev) return // decide on what you read } while (!max.compareAndSet(prev, amount)) // write only if nobody changed it A thread-local on a pool thread: Java USER.set(request.user()); try { handle(request); } finally { USER.remove(); // pool threads are reused } Kotlin USER.set(request.user) try { handle(request) } finally { USER.remove() // pool threads are reused } semaphore.acquire() also goes before the try, and tryAcquire's result must be checked: permits have no owner, so a stray release() adds one. Locks synchronized gives mutual exclusion and visibility, and is reentrant. Lock on a private final object, never on a boxed number or a String literal. Keep the locked code short. Never call alien code, code you don't control (listeners, callbacks, other services), while holding a lock. Every access to shared mutable state, reads included, goes through the same lock or atomic. Deadlock Condition Remove it with Mutual exclusion immutable data, one owner per resource Hold and wait take one lock at a time, or acquire(n) in one step No preemption tryLock(timeout), release and retry with a random back-off Circular wait one global lock order, such as lower id first Livelock: busy threads that make no progress (fix: randomness). Starvation: one thread never gets its turn (fix: fairness, shorter holds). Concurrent collections ConcurrentHashMap: no null keys or values; compute functions run under the bin's lock, so keep them short and never touch the map inside one; size() is an estimate; iterators never throw. ConcurrentModificationException is a fail-fast iterator check. One thread can trip it; concurrent collections never throw it. new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() is unbounded. Always pass a capacity. BlockingQueue Throws Special value Blocks Times out Insert add offer put offer(e, t, unit) Remove remove poll take poll(t, unit) Shut consumers down with one poison pill each, after every producer has finished, compared by identity. Kotlin differences Java Kotlin synchronized method @Synchronized synchronized (lock) { } synchronized(lock) { }, a standard library function volatile @Volatile lock(); try { } finally { unlock(); } lock.withLock { } read and write locks rw.read { }, rw.write { }: write releases read locks first, so re-check new Thread(r).start() thread { } wait() / notify() on any object Any has neither: use ReentrantLock and Condition checked InterruptedException not checked, but you still restore the flag computeIfAbsent getOrPut on a ConcurrentMap may run its default more than once Testing and diagnosis Stress tests: a start latch, more threads than cores, many operations, many rounds, an invariant after join(), and a timeout on every test. A pass is not a proof. No Thread.sleep to wait in tests: use a latch, a future, or polling with a deadline. jcstress: ACCEPTABLE, ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING (allowed, worth seeing), FORBIDDEN (fails the test). Command Shows jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l every thread's state and stack, the java.util.concurrent locks each one owns, Java-level deadlocks jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json f.json the same as JSON; state and lock fields from JDK 25 jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=r.jfr starts a flight recording jfr print --events jdk.JavaMonitorEnter r.jfr waits for synchronized, with duration and previous owner In a dump, BLOCKED means waiting for a monitor; WAITING (parking) means a java.util.concurrent lock, latch, queue or semaphore. Take several dumps a few seconds apart to tell stuck from busy.

h: Threads and the bugs they cause: track quiz
x: What does this print? Java Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName()), "mail-room"); t.run(); Kotlin val t = Thread({ println(Thread.currentThread().name) }, "mail-room") t.run() mail-room main Nothing: a thread must be started first It throws IllegalThreadStateException run() is an ordinary method call, so the lambda runs on the calling thread, main. Only start() creates a new thread that then calls run(). Calling run() by mistake is a classic way to make concurrent code quietly single-threaded. A worker loops while (true) { try { send(queue.take()); } catch (InterruptedException e) { log.warn("interrupted", e); } }. At shutdown, the thread pool's shutdownNow(), which interrupts its threads, doesn't stop it. Why? shutdownNow() never interrupts threads take() ignores interrupts The exception clears the interrupt flag, the catch only logs it, and the loop carries on The worker must be a daemon thread take() throws InterruptedException and clears the flag. Logging isn't handling: the loop goes round and waits again. Restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() and leave the loop, or let the exception travel up to the caller. Four threads record a bank's incoming payments with if (!seen.contains(id)) { credit(p); seen.add(id); }, where seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(). The same payment arrives on two threads at once. What is the smallest correct fix? if (seen.add(id)) credit(p);, removing the id again if the credit fails Make seen a volatile field Switch to Collections.synchronizedSet Add Thread.sleep(10) before the check It's check-then-act: both threads can pass contains before either adds. Set.add checks and inserts in one atomic step and returns false to the thread that lost. volatile and a synchronized wrapper leave the gap between the two calls. Two unrelated classes each declare private static final Integer LOCK = 0; and use synchronized (LOCK). What happens? Each class gets its own lock, because the fields are private It doesn't compile The JVM copies the lock for each class Both share one lock object, because boxing 0 returns the cached Integer; javac warns about synchronizing on a value-based class Integer.valueOf(0) comes from a cache shared by the whole JVM, so both fields point to the same object, and unrelated code waits for, or deadlocks over, one monitor. Lock on a private final Object lock = new Object() instead. A cook does synchronized (rail) { if (rail.isEmpty()) rail.wait(); return rail.remove(); }, with two cooks and notifyAll(). What can go wrong? Nothing: notifyAll() makes if safe A woken cook can find the rail empty again, because the other cook took the ticket or the wake-up was spurious, and remove() throws wait() keeps the monitor, so the waiter can never add a ticket notifyAll() wakes only one cook Waking up only means "something may have changed". The other cook can get the monitor first and take the ticket, and the JVM allows spurious wake-ups, ones with no notify at all. Check again in a while loop. transfer(from, to) locks from, then to. Transfers run in both directions between the same two bank accounts, and the program sometimes freezes. Which fix removes the deadlock? Make the balance fields volatile Use fair locks Always lock the account with the lower id first, whichever way the money moves Add a short sleep between the two locks Opposite orders make a cycle: each thread holds one account and waits for the other. With one global order, nobody can hold the second lock while waiting for the first, so circular wait is gone. Fairness and sleeps only change the odds. Fifty threads update an account's balanceCents and lastUpdated together, and readers must never see one without the other. Which design is correct? One AtomicReference to an immutable record holding both, updated with updateAndGet, or one lock around both Two AtomicLong fields Two volatile fields A LongAdder for the balance and an AtomicLong for the time Each atomic protects one variable, so with two of them a reader can see the new balance with the old time. A compare-and-set on a reference to an immutable pair, or a single lock, makes both fields change as one step. A test checks a counter with 2 threads x 1,000 increments and has passed for a year. Which version of the test could actually catch a lost update? The same test with @RepeatedTest(100) The same test run on a faster machine The same test with Thread.sleep(100) before the assertion 8 threads released together by a start latch, 100,000 increments each, over many rounds, with a timeout With 1,000 increments the first thread often finishes before the second starts, so repeating the same test repeats the same lack of overlap. A start latch, more threads than cores, long runs and many rounds make the threads collide. The timeout keeps a deadlock from hanging the whole test run. The shop's gate in front of the bank's card service does try { permits.acquire(); return bank.check(p); } finally { permits.release(); } with new Semaphore(20). Payments are often cancelled while they wait for a permit. What happens over a day? Nothing: acquire() gives up cleanly Each interrupted wait still releases a permit it never took, so the limit drifts above 20 release() throws once permits pass 20 The semaphore resets itself every hour acquire() throws InterruptedException inside the try, so the finally runs release() anyway. Permits have no owner, so each stray release adds one for good. Call acquire() before the try. A web service's handler calls USER.set(request.user()) on a ThreadLocal only when the request carries a user, and never removes it. What does a request without a user see on a reused pool thread? null, because each request gets a new thread It throws IllegalStateException The user of whichever request that thread served last A random user from another thread Pool threads are reused, and a thread-local value stays on the thread until someone removes it. Set it, then remove() in finally, or use a scoped value on JDK 25 and later.

h: Threads from zero · The threads you already have
x: A thread is a clerk with its own notepad (the stack) and a shared filing cabinet (the heap); run() is a plain call, start() makes a thread, join() waits for it Let's begin with the emptiest program we can write: a main method that only asks the JVM which threads exist. (The JVM, the Java Virtual Machine, is the program that runs your compiled Java and Kotlin code.) Before our code has started a single thread, the list already has six: Reference Handler (daemon) Finalizer (daemon) Common-Cleaner (daemon) Signal Dispatcher (daemon) main Notification Thread (daemon) That list comes from the first Try it below, run on JDK 21. main is the thread that runs your main method. The other five are the JVM's housekeepers, and they were up before your main was. Most of them clean up after objects the program no longer uses, and Signal Dispatcher handles signals, the short messages the operating system sends to a running program. Not every JVM thread makes that list. The garbage collector, which frees the memory of objects nobody uses any more, has threads of its own. So does the JIT compiler, the part of the JVM that turns code that runs often into fast machine code while your program runs. Neither shows up in the list. So you've been writing multithreaded programs all along. Two words will carry us through this track. A process is a running program with its own memory, which other processes can't see. When you run a Java program, the JVM running it is one process. Your web browser is another. A thread is one path of execution inside that process. It runs one statement after another, and it always knows where it is in the code. All the threads of a process live in its memory, and they split it in a simple way. Before computers, our shop would have given this job to people. Picture four clerks in a back room, adding up a year of paper receipts. The receipts sit in one shared filing cabinet. Each clerk, though, keeps a running total on a notepad of their own. In programming terms, each clerk is a thread. The filing cabinet is the heap: every object you create with new and every static field lives there, and any thread with a reference can reach it. The notepad is the thread's stack: its local variables, its parameters and the chain of method calls in progress. Every clerk can open the cabinet but writes only on their own notepad, just as every thread can reach the heap but sees only its own stack. That split explains most of this track. Sharing the heap is what makes threads useful: one thread puts a Sale into a list and another reads it, with no copying. Sharing is also what makes threads dangerous, because two of them can change the same object at the same moment. Lesson 3 of this track (Race conditions: why count++ lies) shows how that quietly loses money. If you go on to write web services, the programs that answer requests from browsers and phone apps, you'll meet the same picture on a larger scale. The framework, the ready-made library your service is built on, starts a whole crowd of threads for you and runs each request on one of them. A busy service often has more than a hundred, all sharing one heap. Locals belong to one thread. The heap belongs to all of them. Code is thread-safe when it still works with several threads running it at once. So when you ask whether some code is thread-safe, start with one question: which of its values live on the heap? Six threads, and we haven't started one yet. Let's start some of our own and put those idle cores to work. Meet the threads you already have Run HelloThreads with the command below, from the labs/ folder. It lists the threads that exist before main starts any, then starts two of its own. Look at the list. Which of these threads are daemons? (A daemon thread is one the JVM doesn't wait for when it exits. The last section of this lesson comes back to that.) Now run it three more times and watch the two hello lines. Does worker-a always speak first? HelloThreads.java package workbench.concurrency.l01; /** Lists the threads the JVM already has, then starts two of your own. Run it a few times. */ public class HelloThreads { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.println("cores the JVM sees: " + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()); System.out.println("Java threads before main starts any:"); for (Thread t : Thread.getAllStackTraces().keySet()) { System.out.println(" " + t.getName() + (t.isDaemon() ? " (daemon)" : "")); } Runnable task = () -> System.out.println("hello from " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); Thread a = new Thread(task, "worker-a"); Thread b = new Thread(task, "worker-b"); a.start(); // try changing these two calls to a.run() and b.run() b.start(); a.join(); // wait for both to finish before main goes on b.join(); System.out.println("main is done"); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l01.HelloThreads labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l01/HelloThreads.java HelloThreads.kt package workbench.concurrency.l01 // Lists the threads the JVM already has, then starts two of your own. Run it a few times. fun main() { println("cores the JVM sees: ${Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()}") println("Java threads before main starts any:") for (t in Thread.getAllStackTraces().keys) { println(" ${t.name}${if (t.isDaemon) " (daemon)" else ""}") } val task = Runnable { println("hello from ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } val a = Thread(task, "worker-a") val b = Thread(task, "worker-b") a.start() // try changing these two calls to a.run() and b.run() b.start() a.join() // wait for both to finish before main goes on b.join() println("main is done") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l01.HelloThreadsKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l01/HelloThreads.kt You'll see main and five daemon helpers, in an order that can change from run to run. The two workers usually print in the order they were started, but not always: in one run on a 4-core Linux machine, worker-b said hello first. Nothing in the code promises an order, so the scheduler is free to pick. Code that depends on that order is a bug waiting for a busy day. Threads in one process share the heap. Each thread has a private stack for its local variables and calls.

h: Threads from zero · Splitting the total across four threads
x: Back to the shop's year of sales. The plan is simple: cut the million amounts into four slices, give each slice to a thread, and add up the four partial sums at the end. Each worker writes only its own slot of a long[] array, so no two threads ever write the same memory. We hand a Thread two things: the work to do, as a Runnable, and a name. Runnable has a single method, void run(), so a lambda fits. (You can also subclass Thread, but I'd avoid it. The thread pools you'll meet later, ready-made groups of threads that run your tasks, take a Runnable.) Here's the first version. It contains the most common first bug with threads, so let's make it once, on purpose: Java // Naive: looks like four threads, runs on one long[] partial = new long[4]; for (int w = 0; w < 4; w++) { int slot = w; Thread t = new Thread(() -> partial[slot] = sumSlice(slot), "sales-worker-" + w); t.run(); } Kotlin // Naive: looks like four threads, runs on one val partial = LongArray(4) for (w in 0 until 4) { val t = Thread({ partial[w] = sumSlice(w) }, "sales-worker-$w") t.run() } Before we run it, make a guess: which thread will sum each slice? Let's print the thread name inside the lambda and run it on a million amounts. Four lines come out, and they all end the same way: slice 0 summed on main, slice 1 summed on main, and so on. The total is right and the tests pass, which is what makes this bug so sneaky. Four threads were created, and not one of them ran. The culprit is the call. run() is an ordinary method call, so the lambda runs on the calling thread, one slice after another, exactly as slowly as before. The call that creates a thread is start(): the JVM asks the operating system for a new thread, and that new thread calls run(). (A thread runs at most once. Call start() a second time and it throws IllegalThreadStateException.) So let's change run() to start(), and add up partial right after the loop. That brings out a second bug. We ran it five times in a row on the same million amounts. The first total came out at about a quarter of the right answer, and the other four at about three quarters. The cause is timing. main added up the slots while the workers were still filling them. Call it the impatient total. You may be tempted to cure the impatience with a Thread.sleep(100) "to give them time". It will pass on your laptop and fail one day on a slower or busier computer, because sleep only lets time pass. The tool for waiting is join(). It blocks, that is, makes the caller wait, until the thread has ended, and it guarantees that the caller then sees everything that thread wrote: Java // Fixed: four real threads, and main waits for all of them Thread[] workers = new Thread[4]; for (int w = 0; w < 4; w++) { int slot = w; workers[w] = new Thread(() -> partial[slot] = sumSlice(slot), "sales-worker-" + w); workers[w].start(); } for (Thread t : workers) t.join(); // only now is partial complete Kotlin // Fixed: four real threads, and main waits for all of them val workers = List(4) { w -> thread(name = "sales-worker-$w") { partial[w] = sumSlice(w) } // created and started } workers.forEach { it.join() } // only now is partial complete Both versions start every worker first and join them afterwards. Joining inside the first loop would wait for worker 0 before starting worker 1, and we'd be back to one slice at a time. The Kotlin version differs in one place: thread { } from kotlin.concurrent builds a java.lang.Thread and calls start() for you, so the run() mistake is hard to make. We also gave every worker a name. When a program misbehaves and you print its list of threads, sales-worker-2 tells you whose job it was. Thread-7 just shrugs. Start every worker, then join every worker. Read nothing before the last join. The total is right now, and the work really is spread over four threads. But is it four times faster? That depends on what sits underneath the threads. Break it with run() In HelloThreads, change a.start() and b.start() to a.run() and b.run(). Before you run it, predict the two "hello from" lines. Run it with the same command as the first Try it. Now put the start() calls back, and add a second a.start(); right after the first one. What do you expect this time? Run it and see. With run(), both lines say hello from main. No new thread was ever created, and the two joins return at once, because a thread that never started has nothing to wait for. With the double start(), main dies with an IllegalThreadStateException, yet worker-a still prints its line, because the first start() worked. A thread runs once, and only start() runs it.

h: Threads from zero · Measuring the speedup, and where it stops
x: Look back at the first line HelloThreads printed. On our test machine it said cores the JVM sees: 4, and that number decides how much our four workers can buy. A core is the part of the processor that carries out instructions, and it runs one thread at a time. (Hyper-threading lets one physical core run two, each a little slower.) Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() tells you how many cores the JVM may use. That can be fewer than the machine has, when the program is only allowed some of them. A program often has far more threads than cores, and the operating system's scheduler, the part that decides which thread runs next, makes that work. It lets a thread run for a short slice of time, then saves its registers and switches to another thread. (Registers are the handful of values a core is working on right now.) That switch is a context switch. It happens thousands of times a second, which is why 200 threads on 4 cores all seem to make progress. Back in the shop's back room, give the clerks calculators, one for each core. Four clerks with four calculators all add at once. With eight clerks and four calculators, the clerks take turns. That's fine while most of them are on the phone waiting for an answer, and pointless when every one of them needs a calculator. Adding at once and taking turns have names, and the names get mixed up. Several tasks in progress at the same time, taking turns if they must, is concurrency, and it works even on one core. Several tasks running at the same instant on different cores is parallelism. Clerks taking turns at one calculator are concurrent; clerks at four calculators are parallel. Our four sales workers are concurrent on any machine. They run fully in parallel only when four cores are free for them. So here's my guess before we time anything. Two threads should take about half the time of one, four threads about a quarter, and eight threads should be no better than four. Now the measurement. Summing a million longs takes a few milliseconds, too quick to time honestly. A real program also does more work per sale (checking it, rounding it, adding the tax). So the ParallelSum demo below stands in for that work with 400 million small sums of pure arithmetic, split over 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads. ParallelSum runs a few warm-up rounds first, so that the JIT compiler has turned the loop into machine code before we time it. On a 4-core Linux machine, one run printed 510 ms, 257 ms, 121 ms and 125 ms. Correctness first: every run printed the same checksum, so splitting the work lost nothing. Then speed. Two threads halved the time, and four threads cut it to about a quarter, as we guessed. (Slightly better than four times, which is just the noise of one short run.) Eight threads were no faster than four, which matched the guess too. The extra four threads had no cores of their own, so they took turns on the same four. That wall is for CPU-bound work, work that keeps a core busy the whole time. Waiting work is different. Picture a thread that asks a slow web service, a program on another computer, for a price, and waits 120 ms for the answer. It uses no core while it waits. So a program that mostly waits can usefully run many more threads than it has cores. CPU-bound work wants one thread per core. Waiting work can use many more. The executors track, on Java's ready-made thread pools, turns that into a sizing formula. So threads can buy real speed, up to the core count. They aren't free, though, and they have one more habit that surprises people when a program ends. Let's look at both. Find the core count by timing Check how many cores your machine has (the first line of HelloThreads tells you). Then write down a guess for 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads. Run ParallelSum with the command below. Every run does the same 400 million additions, split across the threads. Compare the times with your guess. Where does adding threads stop helping? ParallelSum.java package workbench.concurrency.l01; /** Splits a CPU-bound job over 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads and times each run. */ public class ParallelSum { static final int N = 400_000_000; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.println("cores: " + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()); for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) timed(4); // warm-up runs, so the JIT has compiled the loop for (int threads : new int[] {1, 2, 4, 8}) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); long result = timed(threads); System.out.printf("%d thread(s): %4d ms (checksum %d)%n", threads, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, result); } } static long timed(int threads) throws InterruptedException { long[] partial = new long[threads]; Thread[] ts = new Thread[threads]; int chunk = N / threads; for (int w = 0; w < threads; w++) { int slot = w, from = w * chunk, to = (w == threads - 1) ? N : from + chunk; ts[w] = new Thread(() -> { long sum = 0; for (int i = from; i < to; i++) sum += (i * 31L) % 7; // pure CPU work partial[slot] = sum; }); ts[w].start(); } long total = 0; for (int w = 0; w < threads; w++) { ts[w].join(); total += partial[w]; } return total; } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l01.ParallelSum labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l01/ParallelSum.java ParallelSum.kt package workbench.concurrency.l01 private const val N = 400_000_000 // Splits a CPU-bound job over 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads and times each run. fun main() { println("cores: ${Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()}") repeat(3) { timed(4) } // warm-up runs, so the JIT has compiled the loop for (threads in intArrayOf(1, 2, 4, 8)) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() val result = timed(threads) println("%d thread(s): %4d ms (checksum %d)".format(threads, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, result)) } } private fun timed(threads: Int): Long { val partial = LongArray(threads) val chunk = N / threads val workers = List(threads) { w -> val from = w * chunk val to = if (w == threads - 1) N else from + chunk Thread { var sum = 0L for (i in from until to) sum += (i * 31L) % 7 // pure CPU work partial[w] = sum }.apply { start() } } workers.forEach { it.join() } return partial.sum() } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l01.ParallelSumKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l01/ParallelSum.kt The bend in the curve sits at your core count. Each doubling roughly halves the time until the threads outnumber the cores, and after that the extra threads just take turns. If your machine is busy with something else, the curve flattens. On a 4-core machine with other heavy programs running, one run printed 498, 422, 410 and 326 ms. Our threads were now sharing the cores with other programs, and eight threads even came out ahead, because the scheduler shares the cores out thread by thread, so more threads got more turns. Measure on a quiet machine, and run it more than once.

h: Threads from zero · What a thread costs, and who the JVM waits for
x: Every Thread we've created so far is a platform thread: one Java thread backed by one operating system thread. That pairing has a price, in memory and in time. Memory first. Each platform thread gets its own stack, and on 64-bit Linux the JVM reserves 1 MB for it by default. (java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version shows ThreadStackSize = 1024, in KB.) The operating system hands out real memory only as the stack grows, so a thread with shallow calls uses much less. Still, 10,000 threads means 10 GB set aside for stacks, at least on paper, and 10,000 operating system threads sharing the cores. Somewhere along that road, your program dies with an OutOfMemoryError that says it is unable to create a native thread, meaning an operating system thread. Then time. Creating, starting and ending a thread is a round trip to the kernel, the core of the operating system. The ThreadCost demo starts and joins 10,000 empty threads, and on a 4-core Linux machine it printed about 130 microseconds per thread. For one 120 ms call to a slow web service, 130 microseconds is noise. Adding up one sale, though, takes a few nanoseconds. Start a new thread for each of our million sales, and the program spends over two minutes just starting and ending threads. That cost is why the executors track reuses threads in pools, and why the virtual threads track exists at all. Now back to the warm-up question: main starts a worker and returns at once. Does the program end? Not yet. A daemon thread is a background helper that the JVM doesn't wait for. Every other thread is non-daemon, and the JVM exits only when the last non-daemon thread ends, or when something calls System.exit. Returning from main ends the main thread and nothing else, so a worker that's still printing a report keeps the JVM alive until it's done. Threads are non-daemon unless you say otherwise. The housekeepers from the first section are the other kind. All five are daemons: they do their chores in the background, and the JVM never waits for them. Returning from main ends one thread, not the program. That's the whole toolkit of this lesson, so let's be honest about where it stops. A new thread per task suits four long slices. For thousands of short tasks, starting the threads can cost more than the work itself. A worker that fails dies alone. If its run() throws an exception that nothing catches, the thread ends and its stack trace goes to standard error. main isn't told, because join() simply returns. And while we can wait for a thread to finish, we have no way yet to ask a running thread to stop. Measure a thread, then let main go first Run ThreadCost with ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l01.ThreadCost. It starts and joins 10,000 empty threads, three rounds in a row. Note the microseconds per thread. Now read MainEndsFirst below. main starts one worker, which prints a five-page sales report, and returns at once. How many "printing page" lines will print? Commit to a number. Run it with ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l01.MainEndsFirst. MainEndsFirst.java package workbench.concurrency.l01; /** main returns at once. Does the program end? */ public class MainEndsFirst { public static void main(String[] args) { Thread worker = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { System.out.println("worker: printing page " + i + " of the sales report"); try { Thread.sleep(300); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } } System.out.println("worker: report printed"); }, "report-worker"); worker.start(); System.out.println("main: returning from main()"); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l01.MainEndsFirst labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l01/MainEndsFirst.java MainEndsFirst.kt package workbench.concurrency.l01 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // main returns at once. Does the program end? fun main() { thread(name = "report-worker") { // thread {} starts it straight away for (i in 1..5) { println("worker: printing page $i of the sales report") try { Thread.sleep(300) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { return@thread } } println("worker: report printed") } println("main: returning from main()") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l01.MainEndsFirstKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l01/MainEndsFirst.kt ThreadCost prints tens to a couple of hundred microseconds per thread on most machines. Under heavy load it can be far more: with other heavy programs running alongside, a 4-core Linux machine printed 900 to 1,300. MainEndsFirst prints main: returning from main() first, then all five pages and worker: report printed. The JVM waited for the non-daemon worker, long after main was gone.

h: Threads from zero · Java and Kotlin
x: Starting and joining workers in Java and Kotlin Java long[] partial = new long[4]; List<Thread> workers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int w = 0; w < 4; w++) { int slot = w; Thread t = new Thread(() -> partial[slot] = sumSlice(slot), "sales-worker-" + w); t.start(); // nothing runs until start() workers.add(t); } for (Thread t : workers) t.join(); // join() throws the checked InterruptedException KotlinThreads.kt package workbench.concurrency.l01 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // The same slice-and-join idea as LedgerTotals, written with Kotlin's thread {} builder. fun main() { val amounts = LongArray(1_000) { it + 1L } val partial = LongArray(4) val chunk = amounts.size / partial.size val workers = List(partial.size) { w -> thread(name = "sales-worker-$w") { // starts at once: start = true is the default var sum = 0L for (i in w * chunk until (w + 1) * chunk) sum += amounts[i] partial[w] = sum } } workers.forEach { it.join() } // join is the same java.lang.Thread method println("total = ${partial.sum()} on ${workers.map { it.name }}") } Both versions start four named workers and then join them in a second loop. Three things differ. First, Kotlin's thread { } is a small standard-library function: it builds a java.lang.Thread, sets its options and calls start() for you, unless you pass start = false, so forgetting start() mostly stops being a mistake you can make. Second, Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so join() needs no throws InterruptedException. The interruption rules still apply, and lesson 2 of this track covers them. Third, a Java lambda can only use local variables that never change after they're set (Java calls them effectively final), which is why the Java code copies w into slot. The Kotlin lambda captures the w parameter of List(4) { w -> } directly. Java's rule is a quiet safety net here: a lambda running on another thread can never see a captured local change under it. Kotlin lets a lambda capture and change a local var, so with threads, keeping that net is up to you.

h: Threads from zero · Worked example
x: Split the year's sales total across four threads Let's write the fixed version properly, the way the lab wants it. We have the shop's one million sale amounts, in cents, in a List<Long>, and four workers. First, the slices: each worker gets a contiguous range, one unbroken stretch of the list, and the remainder is spread out so that sizes differ by at most one. int slices = Math.min(workers, amounts.size()); // no idle threads int base = amounts.size() / slices; int extra = amounts.size() % slices; // the first `extra` slices get one more val slices = minOf(workers, amounts.size) // no idle threads val base = amounts.size / slices val extra = amounts.size % slices // the first `extra` slices get one more Next, one slot per worker. Worker 2 writes only partial[2], so no two threads ever write the same memory, and there's nothing for them to fight over. long[] partial = new long[slices]; Thread[] threads = new Thread[slices]; val partial = LongArray(slices) val threads = ArrayList<Thread>(slices) Now start every thread. Before you read on, ask yourself: what would happen if you called join() inside this same loop, right after start()? int from = 0; for (int w = 0; w < slices; w++) { int start = from, end = start + base + (w < extra ? 1 : 0), slot = w; // 1. each worker sums its own slice into its own slot threads[w] = new Thread(() -> { long sum = 0; for (int i = start; i < end; i++) sum += amounts.get(i); partial[slot] = sum; }, "sales-worker-" + w); threads[w].start(); from = end; } var from = 0 for (w in 0 until slices) { val start = from val end = start + base + if (w < extra) 1 else 0 // 1. each worker sums its own slice into its own slot threads += thread(name = "sales-worker-$w") { // thread {} also starts it var sum = 0L for (i in start until end) sum += amounts[i] partial[w] = sum } from = end } Joining inside the loop would wait for worker 0 before starting worker 1, and we'd be back to one thread at a time. So start them all, then join them all. Only after the last join is it safe to read partial, because join() makes each worker's write visible to the caller. // 2. wait for every worker for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); // 3. combine on the calling thread long total = 0; for (long p : partial) total += p; // 2. wait for every worker threads.forEach { it.join() } // 3. combine on the calling thread val total = partial.sum()

h: Threads from zero · Quiz
x: What does this print? Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName()), "helper"); t.run(); helper main Thread-0 Nothing, because the thread was never started run() is an ordinary method call, so the lambda runs on the thread that called it, and that's main. No new thread ever exists. You'd see helper only with t.start(). It does print something, though: run() executes the code, just on the wrong thread. A program resizes 10,000 photos. It is pure CPU work, with no waiting for the disk or the network. The laptop has 4 cores. Which thread count finishes the job about the fastest? 1 4 64 400 Pure CPU work keeps a core busy, and each core runs one thread at a time. Four threads keep all four cores working. More threads only take turns on the same cores and add context switches, just as the 8-thread run of ParallelSum showed. Counts like 400 make sense only when most threads spend their time waiting. A worker thread throws a NullPointerException out of its run() method. What happens to main, which started it? main gets the NullPointerException at its next line The JVM shuts down main carries on. The worker ends and its stack trace is printed to standard error main gets it when it calls join() An uncaught exception ends only the thread that threw it. The default handler prints the stack trace to standard error, and nobody else is told: join() simply returns once the worker has ended. Getting the exception back to the caller is a job for Future, in the executors track. What is wrong with this loop? for (Runnable job : jobs) { Thread t = new Thread(job); t.start(); t.join(); } Nothing. It runs the jobs in parallel It runs the jobs one at a time, because each join waits before the next thread starts It deadlocks on the second job join() must be called before start() Each join() blocks until that thread ends, so the next thread starts only after the previous one has finished. You pay for a thread per job and still get one job at a time. Start every thread in one loop, then join them in a second loop. A program asks a slow web service for 12 prices at once, one thread per price, on a laptop with 2 cores. Each thread spends about 120 ms waiting for its answer. Which statement is true? It is concurrent: 12 requests are in progress, at most 2 threads run at any instant, and most are waiting anyway It is parallel: all 12 threads run at the same instant It cannot work, because threads must not outnumber cores It is neither concurrent nor parallel Twelve requests in progress at once is concurrency. With 2 cores, at most 2 threads run at the same instant, and that's the parallel part. Each thread spends most of its time waiting for the web service and uses no core while it waits, so 12 threads on 2 cores is a sensible setup. One thread per core is the rule for CPU-bound work.

h: Threads from zero · Key terms
x: Process A running program with its own memory, such as one JVM. Thread One path of execution inside a process, with its own stack, sharing the process heap. Heap The memory where objects and static fields live. Every thread can reach it. Core A part of the processor that runs one thread at a time. Context switch The operating system pausing one thread and resuming another on the same core. Concurrency Several tasks in progress at once, taking turns or not. Parallelism Several tasks running at the same instant on different cores. Platform thread A Java thread backed one-to-one by an operating system thread. What do threads in one process share, and what does each thread have of its own? They share the heap: objects and static fields. Each thread has its own stack: local variables, parameters and the calls in progress. What happens if you call t.run() instead of t.start()? The code runs on the current thread, like any method call. No new thread is created, and nothing warns you. Concurrency vs parallelism, in one line each. Concurrency: several tasks in progress at the same time (works on one core). Parallelism: several tasks running at the same instant on different cores. When does the JVM exit? When the last non-daemon thread ends, or when something calls System.exit. Returning from main ends only the main thread. How much stack does the JVM reserve for a platform thread on 64-bit Linux by default? 1 MB (ThreadStackSize = 1024 KB). It is set aside up front and filled in as the stack grows. Change it with -Xss. What happens when you call start() twice on the same Thread? The second call throws IllegalThreadStateException. A thread runs at most once. A worker thread throws an uncaught exception. Who finds out? Only that thread dies. The default handler prints the stack trace to standard error. The starting thread is not told.

h: Threads from zero · Go deeper
x: Since JDK 21 there's a builder API for threads. It's worth knowing now, because the virtual threads track uses the same shape: Java Thread t = Thread.ofPlatform() .name("sales-worker-", 0) // sales-worker-0, sales-worker-1, ... .start(task); Kotlin val t = Thread.ofPlatform() .name("sales-worker-", 0) // sales-worker-0, sales-worker-1, ... .start(task) Thread.ofPlatform() gives you the same kind of thread as new Thread(...). Thread.ofVirtual() gives you a virtual thread, which isn't tied to one operating system thread and costs far less. That's a whole track of its own. If you're curious about the threads the JVM keeps for itself, look inside any running Java program with jcmd <pid> Thread.print. jcmd is a tool that comes with the JDK, and <pid> is the process id, the number the operating system gives each running program (jcmd with no arguments lists them). Besides the Java threads from the first Try it, you'll see entries such as VM Thread, the JIT compiler threads and the garbage collector's workers. They live inside the JVM itself, so Thread.getAllStackTraces() doesn't list them, but they use cores and memory like any other thread. One more cost to keep in mind: a context switch isn't free. The kernel saves and restores registers, and the incoming thread often finds the CPU caches, the core's small and fast copies of recently used memory, full of the previous thread's data. That's part of why ParallelSum stops improving past the core count, and why a thousand busy threads can run slower than ten.

h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · The six states a thread lives through
x: A thread's six states as places on a map, the call behind each move, and interrupt as a note the thread must notice and put back A thread is always in one of six states, and t.getState() tells you which. They're the six values of the Thread.State enum. The easiest way to learn them is to follow one thread, the relay, from the line that creates it to the moment it ends. First, the relay in code. The lab class OutboxRelay is our mail-room helper. It takes the next batch of messages from outbox and hands each one to publisher, the code that actually sends it. When the outbox is empty, it naps for idleMillis milliseconds (200 here). It starts life as an ordinary object: Java Thread relay = new Thread(new OutboxRelay(outbox, publisher, 200), "outbox-relay"); System.out.println(relay.getState()); // NEW: only an object so far relay.start(); // now a real OS thread, which calls run() Kotlin val relay = Thread(OutboxRelay(outbox, publisher, 200), "outbox-relay") println(relay.state) // NEW: only an object so far relay.start() // now a real OS thread, which calls run() Before start(), no operating system thread exists and nothing has run, so getState() returns NEW. (Kotlin reads getState() as the property state. Otherwise the two versions are the same.) start() is the call that moves the relay on, as we saw in Threads from zero. The JVM, the program that runs your Java code, asks the operating system for a real thread, and that thread calls run(). The relay checks the outbox and sends what it finds, and getState() now returns RUNNABLE. RUNNABLE covers two cases that the JVM doesn't tell apart. The thread may be running on a core (a part of the processor that runs one thread at a time), or it may be ready to run and waiting for a free core. It covers a third case too, which we'll meet in the next section. Sooner or later the outbox is empty. The relay calls Thread.sleep(idleMillis) and gives up its core until the time is up. A thread that waits with a time limit is TIMED_WAITING. join(ms) leads there too, and so does wait(ms), which we'll meet in a moment. When the time runs out, or an interrupt (another thread's request to stop, more on that soon) wakes it early, the relay is RUNNABLE again and looks once more. Waiting with no time limit is WAITING. Picture a relay fed by a BlockingQueue instead, a JDK queue whose take() method waits until there's something to take. On an empty queue, queue.take() parks the thread, that is, puts it to sleep until another thread wakes it, here by adding a message. join(), which waits for another thread to end, waits the same way, with no time limit. So does Object.wait(), which waits for a signal from another thread (lesson 5 of this track). In fact, the main thread from the opening was WAITING the whole time it sat in relay.join(). The fifth state is about a door. Say the relay writes each sent message into a logbook that other threads share, inside a synchronized (logbook) block. Such a block is a door with one key, called a lock: only the thread holding the lock may be inside (lesson 4 of this track covers it). If another thread is already inside, the relay waits outside the door, BLOCKED. When that thread leaves, the relay gets the lock and is RUNNABLE again. Last, run() returns or throws, and the relay is TERMINATED. That state is final. A second start() throws IllegalThreadStateException, so work that must run again needs a new thread, or better, a thread pool (a group of reusable threads, from a later track). The figure below draws that life as a map. RUNNABLE sits in the middle because the relay keeps coming back to it: it sends, sleeps, wakes up RUNNABLE and sends again. The three waiting states differ in what ends the wait: a lock for BLOCKED, another thread for WAITING, and another thread or the clock for TIMED_WAITING. That's a lot of claims, so let's not take my word for them. The ThreadStates demo in the Try it sends four small threads through the same moves, asks getState() at each stop and prints the answer. On JDK 21 it printed: before start(): NEW inside sleep(2000): TIMED_WAITING in a busy loop: RUNNABLE inside wait(): WAITING entering a held lock: BLOCKED waiter interrupted, flag now false after join(): TERMINATED Each state showed up where the walk said it would, though the demo visits them in its own order. The extra line about the waiter's flag is a clue for later, so hold on to it. getState() only works on a thread you hold a reference to. In a program that won't quit, you hold nothing, but you can still ask every thread at once. Put a thread in every state Read ThreadStates below. Each show(...) call sends a thread somewhere and asks getState(). Match each one to a box in the figure. Run it from the labs/ folder with the command below, and compare with the output in this section. Then find the extra line the waiter prints when it's interrupted out of wait(). It explains the relay's bug, as you'll see in the section on interrupts. Now give the waiter a time limit: change monitor.wait() to monitor.wait(5_000). Predict the inside wait(): line, then run it again.
