Same call plus a time limit, and the thread moves to the other box. The relay's life as a map: it starts NEW, lives in RUNNABLE, steps out to wait for a lock, another thread or the clock, and ends TERMINATED.

h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · Reading the states in a thread dump
x: Back to the program that wouldn't quit. A thread dump is a snapshot of every thread in the JVM, with its state and its stack, the chain of method calls it's in the middle of. jcmd <pid> Thread.print takes one. jcmd is a tool that comes with the JDK, and <pid> is the process id, the number the operating system gives each running program. Here's the relay a moment after it was interrupted, trimmed to the lines that matter: "outbox-relay" #19 prio=5 os_prio=0 ... waiting on condition java.lang.Thread.State: TIMED_WAITING (sleeping) at java.lang.Thread.sleep0(java.base@21.0.12.1/Native Method) at java.lang.Thread.sleep(java.base@21.0.12.1/Thread.java:509) at workbench.concurrency.l02.OutboxRelay.run(OutboxRelay.java:39) The dump says what the relay is doing in two places. The state line says TIMED_WAITING (sleeping), and the stack says where: in Thread.sleep, called from line 39 of OutboxRelay.run. So the relay heard the interrupt, printed that it had heard it, and went straight back to bed. A state is a snapshot, so take two or three dumps a few seconds apart. A thread at the same line in all of them isn't just passing through. Two states need care when you read a dump. The first is RUNNABLE, and here is the third case we put off. The Javadoc, Java's official API documentation, says a RUNNABLE thread is executing in the JVM "but it may be waiting for other resources from the operating system such as processor." So a thread that waits for a slow web service (a program on another computer) to answer over the network often shows RUNNABLE too. The JVM only sees that it's inside native code, code that runs outside Java in the operating system. A dump full of RUNNABLE threads can still be a program that does nothing. The second is BLOCKED, which is only for synchronized. A thread waiting for a ReentrantLock, the JDK's other kind of lock (lesson 7 of this track), is parked by the lock's own Java code. So the dump shows it WAITING, with LockSupport.park near the top of its stack. Search a dump for BLOCKED to find threads stuck behind a lock, and you'll miss every ReentrantLock. A state is a hint. The stack is the evidence. Read both. Our relay spends nearly all of its life in TIMED_WAITING, asleep. So the real question is how one thread can reach into another thread's sleep and ask it to stop.

h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · Weighing the ways to stop a thread
x: We know where the relay spends its time: asleep, or busy sending. Whatever we use to stop it has to reach it in both places. People try four ways, so let's take them in turn, oldest first. The oldest is Thread.stop(). It threw an error inside the target thread, wherever that thread happened to be. The thread unwound, leaving every method it was in, released its locks and left half-updated objects behind. Picture half a batch sent, with those messages not yet marked as sent, so they'd go out a second time. stop() was deprecated, that is, marked as "don't use this", in Java 1.2. It was made to always throw UnsupportedOperationException in JDK 20, and removed in JDK 26. Its partners suspend() and resume() went in JDK 23. In Java, deprecation is a long goodbye. Old code that calls it now fails with NoSuchMethodError. Strike that one. The second is to make the relay a daemon thread, one the JVM doesn't wait for. When the last non-daemon thread ends, the JVM exits, and daemon threads stop wherever they are, without running their finally blocks. A new thread copies the daemon setting of the thread that created it, so you change it yourself, before start(): Java Thread relay = new Thread(outboxRelay, "outbox-relay"); relay.setDaemon(true); // before start(), or you get IllegalThreadStateException relay.start(); Kotlin val relay = Thread(outboxRelay, "outbox-relay") relay.isDaemon = true // before start(), or you get IllegalThreadStateException relay.start() // or: thread(name = "outbox-relay", isDaemon = true) { outboxRelay.run() } A daemon doesn't stop the relay so much as abandon it. The JVM can cut it off between sending a message and marking it sent. Daemons suit work you can afford to lose halfway, such as the metrics-flusher in the Try it below, or the JVM's own housekeepers from Threads from zero. For a mail room that must not lose or repeat messages, strike this one too. The third is a flag of our own, a running field that the owner sets to false and the loop checks on every pass. (It has to be volatile, a keyword that makes other threads see the newest value. The memory model track, on Java's rules for what one thread sees of another's writes, explains why.) A flag works for a busy loop, but it can't wake a sleeping thread. Our relay would notice the flag only when its current sleep ends, and a relay parked in queue.take() would never notice it at all. Thread pools, which you'll meet later, don't know about your flag either. The fourth is interrupt(), and it's the one Java builds on. t.interrupt() sets a flag inside t, called the interrupt flag. If t is blocked, that is, waiting, in sleep, wait, join or a call such as BlockingQueue.take(), that call wakes up and throws InterruptedException. If t is busy instead, nothing happens right away: the interrupt flag stays set until the thread looks at it. When you shut a thread pool down with shutdownNow(), it stops the running tasks this same way. So stopping a thread in Java is cooperative. The interrupt asks. The thread checks, finishes what it's doing, cleans up and returns, at a moment when its data makes sense. Java can't kill a thread. It can only ask, and the thread stops itself. The interrupt is the right tool, then. But our relay was interrupted, and it carried on. Let's find out where the request went. Lose a finally block Run DaemonDemo. Its metrics-flusher thread prints a running count every 200 ms. Count the flushes, and look for the line from the finally block. Change setDaemon(true) to setDaemon(false) (in Kotlin, isDaemon = true to false) and run it again. Stop it with Ctrl+C once you've seen enough. Keep it non-daemon, and add metrics.interrupt(); metrics.join(); just before main's last println. Predict the last two lines, then run it once more. DaemonDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l02; /** A daemon thread does not keep the JVM alive. Its finally block does not run either. */ public class DaemonDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread metrics = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int i = 1; ; i++) { System.out.println("metrics: flush " + i); Thread.sleep(200); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } finally { System.out.println("metrics: finally block ran"); } }, "metrics-flusher"); metrics.setDaemon(true); // must be called before start(); try false metrics.start(); Thread.sleep(700); System.out.println("main: done, returning"); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l02.DaemonDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l02/DaemonDemo.java DaemonDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l02 // A daemon thread does not keep the JVM alive. Its finally block does not run either. fun main() { val metrics = Thread({ try { var i = 1 while (true) { println("metrics: flush ${i++}") Thread.sleep(200) } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } finally { println("metrics: finally block ran") } }, "metrics-flusher") metrics.isDaemon = true // must be set before start(); try false metrics.start() // (or: thread(isDaemon = true) { ... }) Thread.sleep(700) println("main: done, returning") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l02.DaemonDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l02/DaemonDemo.kt As a daemon, you get four flushes and main: done, returning, and no finally block ran: the JVM exited underneath the thread. As a non-daemon, it flushes forever, because nothing asks it to stop. With the interrupt and the join, it stops at once and prints metrics: finally block ran before main: done, returning. That's what a clean shutdown looks like: ask, then wait.

h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · Where the relay's interrupt went
x: Here's the part of the relay that answered the stop request, straight from the lab's starting code: Java // Naive: the interrupt is "handled" by printing it try { Thread.sleep(idleMillis); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.err.println("relay interrupted, carrying on"); } Kotlin // Naive: the interrupt is "handled" by printing it try { Thread.sleep(idleMillis) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { System.err.println("relay interrupted, carrying on") } The catch block looks harmless: the exception was caught, and a line was printed. But methods that throw InterruptedException clear the interrupt flag before they throw. So inside the catch block the flag already reads false, which was the warm-up question. Remember the waiter's line in ThreadStates, flag now false? That was the same clearing, caught in the act. The relay prints, loops round and calls sleep again, and nothing anywhere remembers that someone asked it to stop. Picture the relay as a clerk in the mail room, and the interrupt as a note left on the clerk's desk: "please finish up". If the clerk is napping, the note wakes them. If they're busy sorting letters, they see it the next time they look up. The catch is that waking up tears the note off. The note is the interrupt flag, and sleep tears it off when it throws. Once you've caught the exception, then, you hold the only copy of the request. You have two good options. Let the exception travel up to your caller, by declaring throws InterruptedException. Or stick the note back on, by restoring the flag before you do anything else: Java try { Thread.sleep(backoffMillis); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // put the request back return; // then stop, or throw your own exception } Kotlin try { Thread.sleep(backoffMillis) // Kotlin doesn't force this try, so add it on purpose } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // put the request back return // then stop, or throw your own exception } Never swallow an interrupt. Rethrow it, or restore it. If this feels like an easy mistake, you're in good company. JDK 23 fixed ImageIcon.loadImage to restore the flag, and JDK 24 fixed the same bug in FileSystemPreferences.lockFile(). From JDK 26, the Thread Javadoc has a section on interruption that spells out the rule above. The relay has a second, quieter way to miss the note. When the outbox is full, it sends batch after batch and never reaches sleep, so no InterruptedException ever arrives. A loop like that must look for the note itself, once per batch, with Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted(). Be careful with the static Thread.interrupted(), which looks almost the same. It reads the flag and clears it, so use it only when you mean to take the note down for good. With both fixes in place, the relay stops when it's asked to. The code that asks still has one job left: wait for the relay to finish, and not forever. Watch the flag disappear Run InterruptFlag and read the five numbered lines. Comment out the line me.interrupt() in the catch block. Predict lines 2 to 5, then run it again. Explain to yourself why line 4 prints true with the restore in place, and why line 5 then prints false. InterruptFlag.java package workbench.concurrency.l02; /** Watch the interrupt flag: set by interrupt(), cleared when sleep() throws, restored by you. */ public class InterruptFlag { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread worker = new Thread(() -> { Thread me = Thread.currentThread(); try { Thread.sleep(10_000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("1. caught InterruptedException, flag is now " + me.isInterrupted()); me.interrupt(); // restore it: comment this line out and run again System.out.println("2. after interrupt(), flag is " + me.isInterrupted()); } System.out.println("3. isInterrupted() only reads it: " + me.isInterrupted()); System.out.println("4. Thread.interrupted() reads AND clears: " + Thread.interrupted()); System.out.println("5. so now the flag is " + me.isInterrupted()); }, "worker"); worker.start(); Thread.sleep(200); worker.interrupt(); // a request, not a command worker.join(); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l02.InterruptFlag labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l02/InterruptFlag.java InterruptFlag.kt package workbench.concurrency.l02 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Watch the interrupt flag: set by interrupt(), cleared when sleep() throws, restored by you. fun main() { val worker = thread(name = "worker") { val me = Thread.currentThread() try { Thread.sleep(10_000) // Kotlin doesn't force this try/catch on you } catch (e: InterruptedException) { println("1. caught InterruptedException, flag is now ${me.isInterrupted}") me.interrupt() // restore it: comment this line out and run again println("2. after interrupt(), flag is ${me.isInterrupted}") } println("3. isInterrupted only reads it: ${me.isInterrupted}") println("4. Thread.interrupted() reads AND clears: ${Thread.interrupted()}") println("5. so now the flag is ${me.isInterrupted}") } Thread.sleep(200) worker.interrupt() // a request, not a command worker.join() } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l02.InterruptFlagKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l02/InterruptFlag.kt With the restore: false, true, true, true, false. Line 1 is false because sleep cleared the flag on its way out, and line 2 shows the note stuck back on. Line 4 uses Thread.interrupted(), which reads the flag and clears it, so line 5 is false. Without the restore, every line prints false. The request was lost the moment the exception was caught, exactly as in the relay. Thread.java at jdk-27-ga, with the "Thread Interruption" section docs Interrupts (The Java Tutorials) read

h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · Waiting for the relay to finish
x: Now look at the other side of quitting. The main thread did what the textbooks say: relay.interrupt(), then relay.join(), then close the mailer, the connection the relay sends its messages through. With the old relay, that join() waited until you pressed Ctrl+C. With the fixed relay, it returns as soon as the relay has finished the batch in hand. You may be thinking, "Why wait at all? Interrupt it and close the mailer." Because the relay may still be sending, and closing the mailer under it makes those sends fail. The next idea is usually this one: Java // Naive: hopes two seconds is enough relay.interrupt(); Thread.sleep(2_000); // "should be enough" mailer.close(); Kotlin // Naive: hopes two seconds is enough relay.interrupt() Thread.sleep(2_000) // "should be enough" mailer.close() Thread.sleep(ms) pauses the current thread for at least that long, and it promises nothing about any other thread. On a quiet laptop the relay stops within a few milliseconds, and the code works. On a computer that's busy with other programs, two seconds may not be enough. Even when the relay finishes in time, the main thread isn't promised to see what it wrote. Java's rules give sleep no meaning for other threads. That leaves the JIT compiler free to keep a value in a register, a small storage slot inside the core, or to move a read or a write. (The JIT compiler is the part of the JVM that turns code that runs often into machine code.) The memory model track shows a loop that never ends for exactly this reason. join() fixes both problems. It waits for the thread to end, and when it returns, you're guaranteed to see everything that thread wrote. The java.util.concurrent docs put it this way: "All actions in a thread happen-before any other thread successfully returns from a join on that thread." Happens-before is the memory model's name for that guarantee, and it's why Threads from zero could read the partial array after the joins with no locks at all. Plain join() has one weakness, and our program that wouldn't quit found it: it waits as long as it takes. So give it a limit. join(5_000) waits up to five seconds and returns nothing, so you check relay.isAlive() afterwards. Since JDK 19, join(Duration) returns true if the thread ended: Java // Fixed: ask, then wait, but not forever relay.interrupt(); boolean stopped = relay.join(Duration.ofSeconds(5)); // JDK 19+: true if it ended if (!stopped) System.err.println("relay still running after 5 s"); mailer.close(); Kotlin // Fixed: ask, then wait, but not forever relay.interrupt() val stopped = relay.join(Duration.ofSeconds(5)) // JDK 19+: true if it ended if (!stopped) System.err.println("relay still running after 5 s") mailer.close() A timed join returns as soon as the thread ends, so it costs nothing when the relay behaves. When it returns false, you know the relay is stuck, and can decide what to do. Keep sleep for what it's for: a pause. A back-off, the short wait before you try a slow web service again, is a pause, and so is the relay's nap between looks at the outbox. Wait for the thread, not for the clock. That completes a thread's life: we can start it, read its state, ask it to stop and wait for it to finish. But none of it protects data that two threads change while both are running, and that's where most concurrency bugs live. Give up waiting, then wait properly Read JoinWithTimeout. The worker takes about 500 ms to fetch a price from a slow web service, and main waits for it twice. Predict both printed lines. Run it. Change the timed join to fetch.join(Duration.ofSeconds(2)) and run it again. What does ended say now, and how long did main wait? JoinWithTimeout.java package workbench.concurrency.l02; import java.time.Duration; /** join(timeout) gives up waiting; join() waits for the end and makes the result visible. */ public class JoinWithTimeout { static long priceCents; // plain field: join() is what makes the write visible public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread fetch = new Thread(() -> { sleepQuietly(500); // stands in for a slow web service that answers in 500 ms priceCents = 10_842; }, "price-fetch"); fetch.start(); boolean ended = fetch.join(Duration.ofMillis(100)); // JDK 19+: returns whether it ended System.out.println("after join(100 ms): ended=" + ended + ", alive=" + fetch.isAlive() + ", price=" + priceCents); fetch.join(); // no timeout: wait for the end System.out.println("after join(): alive=" + fetch.isAlive() + ", price=" + priceCents); } static void sleepQuietly(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l02.JoinWithTimeout labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l02/JoinWithTimeout.java JoinWithTimeout.kt package workbench.concurrency.l02 import java.time.Duration import kotlin.concurrent.thread // join(timeout) gives up waiting; join() waits for the end and makes the result visible. private var priceCents = 0L // plain field: join() is what makes the write visible fun main() { val fetch = thread(name = "price-fetch") { try { Thread.sleep(500) // stands in for a slow web service that answers in 500 ms } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } priceCents = 10_842 } val ended = fetch.join(Duration.ofMillis(100)) // JDK 19+: returns whether it ended println("after join(100 ms): ended=$ended, alive=${fetch.isAlive}, price=$priceCents") fetch.join() // no timeout: wait for the end println("after join(): alive=${fetch.isAlive}, price=$priceCents") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l02.JoinWithTimeoutKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l02/JoinWithTimeout.kt First run: ended=false, alive=true, price=0, then alive=false, price=10842. The 100 ms join gave up early, and the plain join waited for the end and saw the price. With a 2-second limit, ended=true and the price is already there after about 500 ms. A timed join returns as soon as the thread ends; it doesn't sit out the full time.

h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · Java and Kotlin
x: An interruptible polling loop in Java and Kotlin Java Thread relay = new Thread(() -> { Thread me = Thread.currentThread(); while (!me.isInterrupted()) { // poll the outbox and publish here try { Thread.sleep(50); // the compiler forces you to handle the checked exception } catch (InterruptedException e) { me.interrupt(); // restore the flag, so the loop condition sees it } } System.out.println("relay stopped, flag = " + me.isInterrupted()); }, "outbox-relay"); relay.start(); KotlinRelay.kt package workbench.concurrency.l02 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A polling loop that follows the interruption protocol, in Kotlin. fun main() { val relay = thread(name = "outbox-relay") { val me = Thread.currentThread() while (!me.isInterrupted) { // property syntax for isInterrupted() // poll the outbox and publish here try { Thread.sleep(50) // no try/catch is forced on you in Kotlin... } catch (e: InterruptedException) { me.interrupt() // ...but the protocol is the same: restore the flag } } println("relay stopped, flag = ${me.isInterrupted}") } Thread.sleep(300) relay.interrupt() relay.join() println("relay alive after join: ${relay.isAlive}") } Both versions follow the same protocol, line for line: loop until the flag is set, sleep, and restore the flag in the catch block. Two things differ. First, Kotlin has no checked exceptions (exceptions the compiler makes you catch or declare), so Thread.sleep(50) compiles with no try at all, and that changes how the bug looks. In Java the usual mistake is a catch that swallows the interrupt. In Kotlin it's often no catch at all: the InterruptedException escapes the lambda, the thread dies with a stack trace on standard error, and any cleanup after the loop never runs. Neither is a clean stop. Here Java's checked exception earns its keep: the compiler won't let you forget that interrupts exist, even if it can't make you handle them well. Second, isInterrupted reads as a property in Kotlin, while the static Thread.interrupted() still reads the flag and clears it.

h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · Worked example
x: Make a retrying send cancellable Here's a retry loop of a kind most programs have somewhere. It hands a letter to a mail server, a program on another computer that delivers it. When the server is too slow and the call times out, the loop waits a little longer each time and tries again. Read it and find the line where a stop request disappears. Receipt send(Letter letter) { for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) { try { return mailServer.send(letter); } catch (MailTimeoutException e) { try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt); } catch (InterruptedException ie) { System.err.println("interrupted while waiting to retry"); // and loop again } } } } fun send(letter: Letter): Receipt { var attempt = 1 while (true) { try { return mailServer.send(letter) } catch (e: MailTimeoutException) { try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt) } catch (ie: InterruptedException) { System.err.println("interrupted while waiting to retry") // and loop again } } attempt++ } } It's the inner catch. sleep cleared the flag before it threw, so after the printed line nothing remembers the request, and the loop has no limit. If the mail server is down when you quit, this thread retries until you press Ctrl+C. It's the relay's bug in a different place. Before you read on, decide what the method should do when it's interrupted. Put the request back first, then stop retrying and tell the caller why. Wrapping the cause in your own exception is fine, as long as the flag is set before you throw. And while we're here, let's give the retries a limit. Receipt send(Letter letter) { for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) { try { return mailServer.send(letter); } catch (MailTimeoutException e) { if (attempt == 3) throw e; // 1. bounded retries try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt); } catch (InterruptedException ie) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // 2. restore the request throw new SendCancelledException(letter.id(), ie); // 3. stop, and say why } } } } fun send(letter: Letter): Receipt { var attempt = 1 while (true) { try { return mailServer.send(letter) } catch (e: MailTimeoutException) { if (attempt == 3) throw e // 1. bounded retries try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt) } catch (ie: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // 2. restore the request throw SendCancelledException(letter.id, ie) // 3. stop, and say why } } attempt++ } } Now the caller, say the relay or a thread pool that is shutting down, finds the interrupt flag still set on its thread, and the letter is reported as cancelled instead of being retried forever. If send could simply declare throws InterruptedException, that would be simpler still: there would be nothing to restore.

h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · Quiz
x: A thread is stuck inside ReentrantLock.lock(), waiting for another thread to release that lock. What does getState() return? BLOCKED WAITING RUNNABLE TIMED_WAITING ReentrantLock parks its waiting threads with LockSupport.park(), and a parked thread is WAITING. BLOCKED is kept for threads trying to enter a synchronized block or method. Remember the difference when you scan a thread dump for threads stuck behind a lock, or you'll miss every ReentrantLock. What does this print? Thread t = new Thread(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(5_000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()); } }); t.start(); t.interrupt(); true Nothing: the thread sleeps for 5 s and ends false It depends on whether interrupt() runs before sleep() starts If the interrupt arrives during the sleep, sleep throws and clears the flag. If it arrives before the sleep starts, sleep sees the flag, clears it and throws at once. Either way the catch block sees false. Timing changes when the exception comes, not what the flag says. A printer thread works through a queue of print jobs. Between jobs it runs try { Thread.sleep(500); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.err.println("interrupted"); } and loops again. To quit, the program calls printer.interrupt() and then printer.join(). What happens? The printer stops, because the exception was printed The printer stops, but prints its last job twice The JVM throws IllegalMonitorStateException The catch clears the request, the loop keeps running, and join() waits until someone kills the program The InterruptedException cleared the flag and the catch didn't put it back, so the loop never learns it should stop, and join() waits for a thread that never ends. It's the relay bug from this lesson in another loop. Printing isn't handling: restore the flag and leave the loop. A daemon thread writes lines to a log file and closes the file in a finally block. The last non-daemon thread ends. What happens to the daemon thread? The JVM waits for it to finish the current line The JVM exits, the daemon stops where it is, and its finally block does not run The JVM interrupts it and waits for the finally block It becomes a non-daemon thread and keeps the JVM alive The JVM doesn't wait for daemon threads, and it doesn't unwind their stacks when it exits, so their finally blocks never run. Log lines can be lost or cut short. Work that must complete belongs on a non-daemon thread that you stop with an interrupt and then join. From Threads from zero: a loop starts each thread and joins it in the same iteration, t.start(); t.join();, for four threads. While the loop runs, how many of those four threads are alive at the same time? At most one All four Two: the current one and the next None, because join() stops them Each join() blocks the loop until that thread is TERMINATED, and only then does the next iteration start a new thread. So at most one of the four is ever alive. Start all four first, then join them in a second loop.

h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · Key terms
x: Thread state What a thread is doing right now, one of the six values of Thread.State. Thread dump A snapshot of every thread in a JVM with its state and stack, taken with jcmd <pid> Thread.print. Lock Something only one thread can hold at a time. A synchronized block waits for one. join Wait for a thread to end. Afterwards you see everything it wrote. Interrupt flag A per-thread true-or-false value that interrupt() sets to ask the thread to stop. InterruptedException Thrown by blocking calls when the thread is interrupted. The flag is cleared when it is thrown. Daemon thread A thread the JVM does not wait for at exit. It can stop mid-work. Cooperative cancellation Stopping a thread by asking it, and letting it check and clean up itself. A thread waits to enter a synchronized block another thread holds. What state is it in? BLOCKED. A thread waits in ReentrantLock.lock(). What state is it in? WAITING (or TIMED_WAITING for a timed tryLock). Explicit locks park the thread; BLOCKED is only for synchronized. Besides waiting, what does t.join() guarantee? Everything t wrote before it ended is visible to the thread whose join() returned. sleep() gives no such guarantee. What happens to the interrupt flag when sleep() throws InterruptedException? It is cleared before the exception is thrown. Inside the catch block, isInterrupted() returns false. What are the two correct ways to handle a caught InterruptedException? Rethrow it (declare throws InterruptedException), or restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() and stop what you're doing. isInterrupted() vs Thread.interrupted()? isInterrupted() only reads the flag. The static Thread.interrupted() reads it and clears it. What is the status of Thread.stop() on JDK 26? Removed. It always threw UnsupportedOperationException from JDK 20, and old programs that call it get NoSuchMethodError on 26+.

h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · Go deeper
x: Not every blocking call listens to interrupts, and it's worth knowing which ones don't before one surprises you. sleep, wait, join, BlockingQueue.take and Lock.lockInterruptibly throw InterruptedException. A thread blocked on an InterruptibleChannel, from java.nio, the JDK's newer library for files and networks, gets different treatment: the Javadoc says the channel is closed, the flag is set and the thread receives a ClosedByInterruptException. So interrupting a thread that is writing to a FileChannel closes the file for everyone who shares that channel. That one surprises people. Plain synchronized doesn't respond at all. A thread that is BLOCKED waiting for a lock stays blocked when you interrupt it; only the flag changes. A platform thread reading a classic java.net.Socket stream may also sit there until data arrives. For those, give the wait a timeout (a socket read timeout, or tryLock with a timeout), so the thread wakes up now and then and can check its flag. Two smaller facts to finish. Interrupts are part of the memory model too: if T1 interrupts T2, everything T1 did before the interrupt is visible to T2 once T2 sees it, by catching the exception or by reading the flag. And the JDK 27 Javadoc for interrupt() notes that interrupting a thread that isn't alive still records the request in the JDK's own implementation, so don't count on an interrupt sent before start() being dropped.

h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · The smallest race: two threads add to one counter
x: Let's shrink the bank down to the smallest program that can go wrong. Two threads share one counter, and each adds one to it a million times. Both versions start the same two threads on the same loop: Java static volatile int count = 0; Runnable work = () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) count++; }; Thread a = new Thread(work), b = new Thread(work); a.start(); b.start(); a.join(); b.join(); System.out.println(count); // 2,000,000? Let's see. Kotlin @Volatile var count = 0 val work = { repeat(1_000_000) { count++ } } val a = thread { work() } val b = thread { work() } a.join(); b.join() println(count) // 2,000,000? Let's see. Two things changed in Kotlin: thread { } creates and starts each thread for us, and @Volatile is an annotation where Java has a keyword. Each version joins both threads before it prints. As A thread's life showed, once join(), which waits for a thread to end, returns, main sees everything that thread wrote, so this prints the counter's real final value. I'd expect 2,000,000. Here's what RaceDemo, the same program in the labs, printed in five runs on a 4-core Linux machine. (A core is a part of the processor that runs one thread at a time.) run 1: expected 2,000,000, got 1,282,924 (lost 717,076) run 2: expected 2,000,000, got 1,288,616 (lost 711,384) run 3: expected 2,000,000, got 1,324,641 (lost 675,359) run 4: expected 2,000,000, got 1,513,931 (lost 486,069) run 5: expected 2,000,000, got 2,000,000 (lost 0) Four wrong answers and one right one, from the same code. Nothing crashed, and there was no exception, no warning and no log line. The program did its arithmetic wrong, by a different amount each time. That's a race condition: a bug where the result depends on how the threads happen to take turns. The fifth run deserves a second look. Sometimes the threads don't collide, and then a racy program prints the right answer. One word in the listing needs explaining. volatile is a keyword that makes every thread see a field's newest value, and it's there only to keep the demo honest. Without it, the JIT compiler may keep count in a register, a tiny storage slot inside the core, for the whole loop, and write it back once at the end. (The JIT compiler is the part of the JVM, the program that runs your Java code, that turns code that runs often into fast machine code.) Then some runs lose almost nothing, which hides the bug without fixing it. And volatile doesn't make count++ safe either: it was on the field for all five runs. Now shrink the loop to 1,000 increments per thread. All five runs print exactly 2,000. The first thread finishes its thousand before the second has even started, so the two never overlap. A race is shy around small numbers. That's why races pass small tests and then fail on a busy day, when many people use the program at once. A test whose threads never collide proves nothing about thread safety. Make them collide. So a line as short as count++ can lose updates. It's short only in Java, though. Let's look at what the JVM actually runs. Watch the counter lose updates Open RaceDemo (or its Kotlin twin) in the labs project. Before you run it, write down the total you expect. Run it from labs/ with the command below, and note how many updates each run loses. Now add -Pargs=1000 to the command. Predict first: will a thousand increments per thread lose any? RaceDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l03; /** Two threads each add 1,000,000 to a shared counter. Watch what comes out. */ public class RaceDemo { // volatile only stops the JIT from keeping count in a register, which would hide the race. // It does NOT make count++ safe. The memory model track explains why. static volatile int count = 0; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int perThread = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 1_000_000; for (int run = 1; run <= 5; run++) { count = 0; Runnable work = () -> { for (int i = 0; i < perThread; i++) count++; }; Thread a = new Thread(work), b = new Thread(work); a.start(); b.start(); a.join(); b.join(); System.out.printf("run %d: expected %,d, got %,d (lost %,d)%n", run, 2 * perThread, count, 2 * perThread - count); } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l03.RaceDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l03/RaceDemo.java RaceDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l03 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // @Volatile only stops the JIT from keeping count in a register, which would hide the race. // It does NOT make count++ safe. The memory model track explains why. @Volatile private var count = 0 /** Two threads each add 1,000,000 to a shared counter. Watch what comes out. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val perThread = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 1_000_000 for (run in 1..5) { count = 0 val work = { repeat(perThread) { count++ } } val a = thread { work() } val b = thread { work() } a.join(); b.join() println("run %d: expected %,d, got %,d (lost %,d)".format(run, 2 * perThread, count, 2 * perThread - count)) } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l03.RaceDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l03/RaceDemo.kt With a million per thread, most runs lose hundreds of thousands of updates, a different number each time, and now and then a run comes out right. With 1,000 per thread you'll almost always get exactly 2,000, because each thread finishes before the other gets going. Same bug, no symptom.

h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · Inside count++: a read, an add and a write
x: Why count++ lies: a read, an add and a write, lost deposits on a thread-safe map, and a payment recorded twice The total came out short because count++ isn't one step, and the bytecode can prove it. Bytecode is the list of simple instructions that javac, the Java compiler, turns your code into, and it's what the JVM runs. Here is the bytecode for the loop body of RaceDemo, as javap -c -p, a JDK tool that prints bytecode, shows it (trimmed): getstatic count // read the current value of count iconst_1 // load the number 1 iadd // add the two putstatic count // write the result back to count Read it aloud: fetch count, add one, store the result back in count. That's a read, an add and a write (loading the 1 only sets up the add). A thread can be paused between any two of those instructions. On a machine with several cores, another thread can run the same instructions at the same moment. So let's trace the smallest case: two threads, one increment each, with count at 41. T1 reads count: 41. T2 reads count: 41. T1 adds one and writes 42. T2 adds one and writes 42. Two increments ran, and the counter moved by one. That's a lost update. A third thread that comes along later reads 42 and carries on, so nothing later in the program ever learns an increment went missing. The pattern behind the lost update has a name: read-modify-write. You read a value, compute a new one from it, and write it back, assuming nobody changed it in between. Kotlin's count++ on a var compiles to the same three steps, so it races in exactly the same way. The cure is to make the read, the add and the write happen as one step that no other thread can split. A step like that is atomic: other threads see it either not started or completely done, never halfway. In the simulator below, you are the scheduler, the part of the operating system that decides which thread runs next. Try to end two increments with count = 1, then try for 2. Getting 2 means letting each thread finish its whole increment before the other starts, which is what an atomic step guarantees. To check the bytecode yourself, run the demo once, then run this from labs/ and look inside lambda$main$0: javap -c -p concurrency/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/concurrency/l03/RaceDemo.class count++ is a toy, though. The bank runs the same three steps on money, and it keeps its balances in a map that calls itself thread-safe. Thread interference (The Java Tutorials) read

h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · Lost deposits in the bank, even on a thread-safe map
x: The bank's deposit is count++ with money in it: Java void deposit(long cents) { balanceCents += cents; // read, add, write } Kotlin fun deposit(cents: Long) { balanceCents += cents // read, add, write } javap shows getfield, ladd and putfield this time: the same three steps for a long field, with the same gaps. The usual next move is to keep the balances in something thread-safe, that is, safe to use from many threads at once. The JDK's ConcurrentHashMap is a map built for exactly that, so let's key the balances by account id and put both ideas through one test. LostDepositDemo plays out payday. It starts eight teller threads (a teller is the bank clerk who takes your deposit), and each one puts 200,000 one-cent deposits into the same account. It does that three times: with a plain field, with a ConcurrentHashMap and a get plus a put, and with the same map and one call: Java balanceCents += 1; // 1. Naive: a plain field balances.put(ACCOUNT, balances.get(ACCOUNT) + 1); // 2. Naive: a thread-safe map, two calls balances.merge(ACCOUNT, 1L, Long::sum); // 3. Fixed: the same map, one call Kotlin balanceCents += 1 // 1. Naive: a plain field balances[ACCOUNT] = balances.getValue(ACCOUNT) + 1 // 2. Naive: a thread-safe map, two calls balances.merge(ACCOUNT, 1L, Long::plus) // 3. Fixed: the same map, one call Before you read the output, guess which of the three come out exact. One run printed: balanceCents += 1 expected 1,600,000 cents, got 440,684 (lost 1,159,316) put(get() + 1) expected 1,600,000 cents, got 329,204 (lost 1,270,796) merge(1, Long::sum) expected 1,600,000 cents, got 1,600,000 (lost 0) The plain field lost more than two thirds of the deposits. With eight threads on four cores, collisions are the normal case. The second line is the setback, and the one that surprises people. ConcurrentHashMap is a fine tool, and every single call on it is thread-safe. The map kept every promise it makes. It never promised anything about two calls in a row. put(get() + 1) is two calls, and the gap between them belongs to nobody. Two tellers get the same old balance, both add a cent, and both put the result back. The third line is the fix. merge(ACCOUNT, 1L, Long::sum) does what the three plain steps do: read the old balance, add the amount, put the result back. But the map runs all three as one atomic step on that key, so no other teller can slip in between. Read it aloud as "add one cent to this balance, whatever it is right now". A thread-safe class makes each call atomic. Two calls in a row are still a race. Read-modify-write hides in arithmetic. The second shape of race hides in an if. Lose deposits three ways Read LostDepositDemo (or its Kotlin twin). For each of the three lines it prints, write down whether you expect it to be exact. Run it with the command below. Then run it twice more and compare the losses. In version 2, replace the put(get() + 1) line with balances.compute(ACCOUNT, (k, v) -> v + 1) (in Kotlin, balances.compute(ACCOUNT) { _, v -> (v ?: 0L) + 1 }). Predict whether it comes out exact, then run it. LostDepositDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l03; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; /** Eight teller threads put one-cent deposits into the same bank account, three ways. */ public class LostDepositDemo { static final int THREADS = 8; static final int DEPOSITS = 200_000; // per thread, one cent each static final String ACCOUNT = "account-42"; // volatile only so the JIT re-reads the field every time, as in RaceDemo. It does NOT make += safe. static volatile long balanceCents; static final Map<String, Long> balances = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { balanceCents = 0; runTellers(() -> balanceCents += 1); // 1. a plain field report("balanceCents += 1", balanceCents); balances.put(ACCOUNT, 0L); runTellers(() -> balances.put(ACCOUNT, balances.get(ACCOUNT) + 1)); // 2. a thread-safe map, two calls report("put(get() + 1)", balances.get(ACCOUNT)); balances.put(ACCOUNT, 0L); runTellers(() -> balances.merge(ACCOUNT, 1L, Long::sum)); // 3. the same map, one call report("merge(1, Long::sum)", balances.get(ACCOUNT)); } static void runTellers(Runnable deposit) throws InterruptedException { Thread[] tellers = new Thread[THREADS]; for (int c = 0; c < THREADS; c++) { tellers[c] = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < DEPOSITS; i++) deposit.run(); }, "teller-" + c); tellers[c].start(); } for (Thread t : tellers) t.join(); } static void report(String how, long cents) { long expected = (long) THREADS * DEPOSITS; System.out.printf("%-20s expected %,d cents, got %,d (lost %,d)%n", how, expected, cents, expected - cents); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l03.LostDepositDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l03/LostDepositDemo.java LostDepositDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l03 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Eight teller threads put one-cent deposits into the same bank account, three ways. private const val TELLERS = 8 private const val DEPOSITS = 200_000 // per thread, one cent each private const val ACCOUNT = "account-42" // @Volatile only so the JIT re-reads the field every time, as in RaceDemo. It does NOT make += safe. @Volatile private var balanceCents = 0L private val balances = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long>() fun main() { balanceCents = 0 runTellers { balanceCents += 1 } // 1. a plain field report("balanceCents += 1", balanceCents) balances[ACCOUNT] = 0L runTellers { balances[ACCOUNT] = balances.getValue(ACCOUNT) + 1 } // 2. a thread-safe map, two calls report("put(get() + 1)", balances.getValue(ACCOUNT)) balances[ACCOUNT] = 0L runTellers { balances.merge(ACCOUNT, 1L, Long::plus) } // 3. the same map, one call report("merge(1, Long::plus)", balances.getValue(ACCOUNT)) } private fun runTellers(deposit: () -> Unit) { val tellers = List(TELLERS) { c -> thread(name = "teller-$c") { repeat(DEPOSITS) { deposit() } } } tellers.forEach { it.join() } } private fun report(how: String, cents: Long) { val expected = TELLERS.toLong() * DEPOSITS println("%-20s expected %,d cents, got %,d (lost %,d)".format(how, expected, cents, expected - cents)) } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l03.LostDepositDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l03/LostDepositDemo.kt The first two lines lose a large share of the 1,600,000 cents, a different amount every run. merge is exact every time. So is compute: like merge, it runs your function inside the map, as one step on that key, so no other teller can change the balance halfway through.

h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · Check-then-act: recording the same payment twice
x: The deposits add up now. The other thing a bank must never do is record the same payment twice. Copies do arrive. Picture a customer who taps Pay in a phone app on a slow network. The app hears nothing back for a few seconds, so it sends the payment again, to be safe. Now two copies of one payment reach the bank, and two threads can handle them at the same moment. So the bank's program keeps a map of the payments it has recorded, and checks it first: Java if (!recordedBy.containsKey(paymentId)) { // check checkPayment(payment); // a slow step recordedBy.put(paymentId, me); // act record(payment); // the money moves } Kotlin if (!recordedBy.containsKey(paymentId)) { // check checkPayment(payment) // a slow step recordedBy[paymentId] = me // act record(payment) // the money moves } recordedBy is a ConcurrentHashMap again, and again every call on it is thread-safe. The code still records payments twice. Two tellers can both check, both see "not recorded yet", and both go on to record it. The second put quietly replaces the first teller's name, and the money moves twice. This shape is check-then-act: you test a condition, then act on it, assuming it still holds. The gap between the check and the act is where the race lives, and the slow step, making sure the payment is genuine, makes that gap wide. The figure shows two tellers inside it at the same time. DoublePostingDemo (to post a payment is bank talk for recording it) exaggerates on purpose, so the gap is easy to see. Eight tellers all receive the same 1,000 payments, as if every payment arrived eight times. A short spin loop, a loop that only burns time, stands in for the slow check. One run printed: payments: 1,000 times recorded: 2,579 duplicates: 1,579 Each customer paid once. The shops they paid got 2,579 payments, which made for a very good evening. The same shape hides in two places you'll meet often. An overdraft check keeps an account from going below zero: if (balanceCents >= cents) balanceCents -= cents;. Yet two withdrawals can both see enough money, and the account goes below zero anyway. Lazy loading, which means creating something only the first time it's needed, if (prices == null) prices = loadPrices();, can load twice. The fix is one call that does both the check and the act, so no gap is left: Java checkPayment(payment); // still slow, but no longer inside a gap if (recordedBy.putIfAbsent(paymentId, me) == null) { // Fixed: check and act in one call record(payment); // only one teller gets here } Kotlin checkPayment(payment) // still slow, but no longer inside a gap if (recordedBy.putIfAbsent(paymentId, me) == null) { // Fixed: the same JDK call from Kotlin record(payment) // only one teller gets here } Read putIfAbsent as "claim this key, unless someone already has". It returns the previous owner, or null if there was none, and only one caller can ever get that null. Inside, the map does the lookup and the insert as one step on that key's slot, as lesson 9 of this track shows. computeIfAbsent, merge and Set.add (which returns false if the element was already there) exist for the same reason. Sometimes several copies of the program run on different computers. Then the same idea moves into the database they all share, the program that keeps their data on disk. Make the payment id a unique key, insert it first, and let the second insert fail. A check is out of date the moment it returns. Make the check and the act one call. Both fixes so far came from the library: one call that does the whole job on one key. Before we meet a job that needs two keys, let's pin down what any fix has to do. Record a payment twice, then once Run DoublePostingDemo with the command below. Eight tellers race through the same 1,000 payments. Note the duplicates. Replace the check and the put with one call: if (recordedBy.putIfAbsent(payment, me) == null) recorded.incrementAndGet(); (in Kotlin, if (recordedBy.putIfAbsent(payment, "teller-$c") == null) recorded.incrementAndGet()). Keep the spin loop just before it. Run it three more times. DoublePostingDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l03; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** * The same 1,000 payments reach eight teller threads, as if every payment arrived eight times. * Each teller records a payment only if nobody has recorded it yet: check-then-act on a ConcurrentHashMap. */ public class DoublePostingDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Map<Integer, String> recordedBy = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // payment id -> the teller that recorded it AtomicInteger recorded = new AtomicInteger(); Thread[] tellers = new Thread[8]; for (int c = 0; c < tellers.length; c++) { String me = "teller-" + c; tellers[c] = new Thread(() -> { for (int payment = 0; payment < 1_000; payment++) { if (!recordedBy.containsKey(payment)) { // check for (int i = 0; i < 300; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); // a slow step: is the payment genuine? recordedBy.put(payment, me); // act recorded.incrementAndGet(); // the money moves } } }, me); } for (Thread t : tellers) t.start(); for (Thread t : tellers) t.join(); System.out.printf("payments: 1,000 times recorded: %,d duplicates: %,d%n", recorded.get(), recorded.get() - 1_000); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l03.DoublePostingDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l03/DoublePostingDemo.java DoublePostingDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l03 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread // The same 1,000 payments reach eight teller threads, as if every payment arrived eight times. // Each teller records a payment only if nobody has recorded it yet: check-then-act on a ConcurrentHashMap. fun main() { val recordedBy = ConcurrentHashMap<Int, String>() // payment id -> the teller that recorded it val recorded = AtomicInteger() val tellers = List(8) { c -> thread(start = false, name = "teller-$c") { for (payment in 0 until 1_000) { if (!recordedBy.containsKey(payment)) { // check repeat(300) { Thread.onSpinWait() } // a slow step: is the payment genuine? recordedBy[payment] = "teller-$c" // act recorded.incrementAndGet() // the money moves } } } } tellers.forEach { it.start() } tellers.forEach { it.join() } println("payments: 1,000 times recorded: %,d duplicates: %,d".format(recorded.get(), recorded.get() - 1_000)) } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l03.DoublePostingDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l03/DoublePostingDemo.kt The first run records hundreds or thousands of payments more than once (one run here: 2,579 times recorded for 1,000 payments). After the change it records exactly 1,000, every run, with the slow step still inside the loop. Every teller still runs the slow check, but only one of them gets to record each payment. Both tellers check before either one records the payment. The gap between check and act is where the race lives.

h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · What every fix has to do, and where one call stops
x: We've met three races and fixed two. Both fixes did the same two jobs, and every fix you write will too. A fix makes the compound action, the group of steps that must happen together, atomic, so no other thread can run in the middle of it. It also makes the result visible, so the next thread to look sees the new value, not an old copy. Visibility gets its own track later, and every tool below gives you both. Here are the options, in the order I reach for them. The first is not to share at all. Give each thread its own counter and add them up after the joins, as the shop's sales total did with its partial array in Threads from zero. Or give every account to exactly one thread, so no other thread ever touches its balance. No sharing, no race. The second is one atomic call that the library already has: merge, putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, Set.add, or an atomic class such as AtomicLong, a number whose updates happen in one step. These calls are fast and hard to get wrong, and lesson 8 of this track opens them up. The third is a lock around the whole compound action. A lock lets one thread at a time into a piece of code, and the others wait at the door until it's free. Mark a method synchronized, and Java puts a lock around it. A lock works for any code, even a change to two balances at once. The price is that every caller waits in line. A lock comes with two conditions. It must cover the reads: a synchronized setter with a plain getter is still broken, because nothing promises the reader the latest value. And it must cover the whole action, since locking containsKey and put separately leaves the same gap between them. Every access to shared state goes through the same lock or the same atomic. Guard the reads too. For the counter, each fix is one line, and the Try it below has you make both. In five runs each on a 4-core machine, both printed 2,000,000 every time. The AtomicInteger version took 41 to 54 ms a run, close to the broken one. The synchronized version took anywhere from 28 to 220 ms. The JIT compiler and the scheduler decide how long each thread keeps the lock before the other gets a turn, and that changes from run to run. So correctness is settled, and speed is something to measure more than once. That brings us to the limit of today's tools. Every fix so far protects one thing: one counter, one key, one balance. A transfer takes money out of one account and puts it into another. No one may see the money in flight, gone from the first account and not yet in the second. No single map call moves money between two keys, and two atomic calls in a row are just a new gap. That job needs a lock, and a lock has rules of its own. Fix RaceDemo two ways In RaceDemo, add static synchronized void inc() { count++; } and call inc() in the loop. (In Kotlin, add a top-level private val lock = Any() and write synchronized(lock) { count++ } in the loop.) Run it. Undo that. Change count to static final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(); (in Kotlin, private val count = AtomicInteger()), call count.incrementAndGet(), reset it with count.set(0) and print count.get(). Run it. Which one felt slower? Add long t0 = System.nanoTime(); before the threads start, print the elapsed milliseconds after the joins, and run each version a few times. Both versions print exactly 2,000,000 on all five runs. The times jump around. On a 4-core Linux machine the atomic version took 41 to 54 ms a run, close to the broken one, and the synchronized one took anywhere from 28 to 220 ms. Get it correct first, then measure the speed, and measure more than once.

h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · Java and Kotlin
x: The same race and fix in Java and Kotlin AccountBalance.java public class AccountBalance { private long balanceCents; // Naive: balanceCents += cents is a read, an add and a write public void depositBroken(long cents) { balanceCents += cents; } // Fixed: one thread at a time, and readers take the same lock public synchronized void deposit(long cents) { balanceCents += cents; } public synchronized long balance() { return balanceCents; } } AccountBalance.kt class AccountBalance { private var balanceCents = 0L // Naive: compiles to the same read, add and write fun depositBroken(cents: Long) { balanceCents += cents } // Fixed: Kotlin has no synchronized modifier; the annotation does the same job @Synchronized fun deposit(cents: Long) { balanceCents += cents } @Synchronized fun balance(): Long = balanceCents } Both classes have the same race and the same fix, and the Kotlin one is a direct translation. Two things differ. Kotlin has no synchronized modifier, so the fix is the @Synchronized annotation, which marks the compiled method as synchronized exactly as Java's modifier does. And += on a Kotlin var property compiles to the same read, add and write as Java's, so it races in exactly the same way. java.util.concurrent.atomic and ConcurrentHashMap.merge work the same from both languages.

h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · Worked example
x: Find and fix the race in the bank's duplicate check The bank's payment desk skips payments it has already recorded, so that a copy sent twice by the phone app is ignored. It runs on four threads, and recording a payment takes about 80 ms. ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() gives a thread-safe set. Read the code and find the shape before you read on. class PaymentDesk { private final Set<String> recorded = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); void handle(Payment p) { if (recorded.contains(p.id())) return; // check bank.record(p); // about 80 ms recorded.add(p.id()); // act } } class PaymentDesk { private val recorded: MutableSet<String> = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() fun handle(p: Payment) { if (p.id in recorded) return // check bank.record(p) // about 80 ms recorded += p.id // act } } It's check-then-act, with an 80 ms gap. Two copies of the same payment, handled by two threads within the same 80 ms, both pass the contains check, and both get recorded. The set being thread-safe doesn't help, because the race is between the calls, not inside them. Claim the id first, in one atomic call. Set.add returns false if the id was already there, so only one thread gets past the first line. If recording fails, release the claim, so that a retry can have another go. void handle(Payment p) { // 1. claim the id: add() returns false if it was already there if (!recorded.add(p.id())) return; try { bank.record(p); // 2. record } catch (RuntimeException ex) { recorded.remove(p.id()); // 3. release on failure throw ex; } } fun handle(p: Payment) { // 1. claim the id: add() returns false if it was already there if (!recorded.add(p.id)) return try { bank.record(p) // 2. record } catch (ex: RuntimeException) { recorded.remove(p.id) // 3. release on failure throw ex } } That closes the race inside one running program. It doesn't survive a restart, and it doesn't cover a second copy of the program running on another computer. For those, the claim belongs in the database that every copy shares, the program that keeps the bank's data on disk. Insert the payment id into a table where ids must be unique, before recording, and treat a duplicate-key error as "already recorded". It's the same idea, one atomic step, moved to the place that every copy can see. INSERT INTO recorded_payment (payment_id, received_at) VALUES (?, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP); -- a second insert with the same id fails

A CountDownLatch is a gate that opens when its count reaches zero: countDown() lowers the count, and await() waits for the gate to open. Create a latch ready of size threads and a latch go of size 1. Each thread calls ready.countDown(), waits on go.await(), then runs the task. The caller waits on ready, calls go.countDown(), then joins every thread. h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · Quiz
x: Two threads run account.balance = account.balance - amount; on the same account at the same time, say for two withdrawals at two cash machines. What can go wrong? Nothing, because one Java statement runs atomically One of the two withdrawals can be lost, because both read the same starting balance The JVM throws an IllegalStateException The balance always goes negative It's read-modify-write. If both threads read 100 and take out 10, both write 90, and one withdrawal is gone. A Java statement isn't atomic just because it fits on one line: javap shows a read, a subtract and a write. counts is a ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer>. Many threads run counts.put(k, counts.getOrDefault(k, 0) + 1). What is the smallest correct fix? Make the map field volatile Wrap the map with Collections.synchronizedMap Use counts.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum) Switch to a HashMap merge reads, computes and writes in one atomic step on that key. volatile on the field only affects the reference to the map. A synchronized wrapper still makes each call atomic on its own, so the gap between get and put stays open. A test runs 2 threads that each call hit() 1,000 times, and checks that the total is 2,000. It passed 100 runs in a row. What does that tell you? The counter is thread-safe Very little: the threads probably never overlapped The JIT compiler fixed the race The test should use 1 thread instead A thread can finish 1,000 increments before the second thread starts. With no overlap, a racy counter gives the right answer every time. Use more threads, more iterations and a start latch, so that they really run at the same time. A cache, a map that keeps results so they needn't be loaded again, does if (cache.get(id) == null) cache.put(id, loadFromDb(id)); on a ConcurrentHashMap. Two threads ask for the same missing id together. What happens? Both may call loadFromDb, and the second put replaces the first value The second thread blocks until the first one finishes The map throws ConcurrentModificationException Only one thread can call get at a time, so it is safe It's check-then-act. Both see null, both load, both put. You pay for two slow database calls, and callers may end up holding different objects. computeIfAbsent(id, this::loadFromDb) runs the loader at most once per key. From the last lesson: main starts thread t, which sets result = 42. When can main safely read result? Right after t.start() returns After t.join() returns After Thread.sleep(100) Any time, because int writes are atomic join waits for t to finish, and everything t wrote before it ended is visible to the thread whose join returned. sleep only makes that likely. An atomic write still says nothing about when another thread will see it.
