h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · Key terms
x: Race condition A bug where the result depends on which thread runs when. Lost update Two threads read the same old value and both write, so one change disappears. Read-modify-write Read a value, compute a new one from it, write it back. Unsafe on shared data unless done atomically. Check-then-act Test a condition, then act on it, assuming it still holds. Unsafe if another thread can act in between. Atomic Happens as one indivisible step. Other threads see it either not started or fully done. Thread-safe Works correctly even when many threads use it at the same time. Critical section A piece of code that only one thread at a time may run, because it touches shared state. What is a race condition? A bug where the result depends on the order in which the threads' steps happen to mix. It usually gives wrong results silently, not an exception. Why is count++ not atomic? It runs as three steps: read count, add one, write it back. Another thread can run between them, so two increments can produce one. Name the two shapes of race condition. Read-modify-write (count++, balance -= x) and check-then-act (if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v)). Is if (!chm.containsKey(k)) chm.put(k, v) safe on a ConcurrentHashMap? No. Each call is atomic, but another thread can put between them. Use chm.putIfAbsent(k, v). Is balances.put(id, balances.get(id) + cents) safe on a ConcurrentHashMap? No. It is read-modify-write across two calls, so deposits get lost. Use balances.merge(id, cents, Long::sum). Why does a 2-thread x 1,000-iteration race test usually pass on broken code? The first thread often finishes before the second starts, so they never overlap. Use a start latch and many iterations.

h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · Go deeper
x: Two terms sound alike and mean different things. A data race is a precise term from the Java Language Specification (JLS), the official rulebook of the language, in chapter 17. Two threads access the same variable, at least one of the accesses is a write, and nothing orders the two accesses by a happens-before relationship, an ordering guarantee such as the one join() gives. A program with a data race can see surprising values, because the compiler and the CPU are allowed to reorder and cache unsynchronized accesses. A race condition is a logic bug: the program is wrong under some interleavings, some orders in which the threads' steps can mix. You can have either one without the other. The fixed payment desk from the worked example has no data race, since every access goes through the thread-safe set. But between the claim and the release on failure, other threads can see a payment that is recorded and then unrecorded again. That's a race condition built entirely from thread-safe calls. Going the other way, String.hashCode() caches its result in a plain field that several threads may write at once. That's a data race, but a harmless one: every thread computes the same value, and an int write can't tear, that is, can't be seen half written. long and double are the exception to that last point. JLS section 17.7 allows a write to a non-volatile long or double to happen as two separate 32-bit writes, so another thread could read half of an old value and half of a new one. 64-bit JVMs write them in one go in practice, but the specification only promises it when the field is volatile. You'll meet happens-before properly in the memory model track. Until then, the rule from the last section holds: every access to shared mutable state, reads included, goes through the same lock or the same atomic variable.

h: synchronized and intrinsic locks · Locking the transfer: what synchronized promises, and to whom
x: One key for the vault: a checker that skips the key sees money in flight, the holder can walk back in, a private key nobody can borrow, and no slow calls while you hold it We'll start where the last lesson stopped. Left alone, a transfer is two read-modify-write steps in a row (read a balance, change it, write it back), and we saw there how two threads lose updates in steps like those. So let's make the pair one step, with a lock. A lock is a guard on a piece of code. A thread takes the lock before it runs the code and gives it back after, and only one thread can hold it at a time. Every Java object carries a built-in lock, and synchronized takes it on the way in and gives it back on the way out: Java private final Object lock = new Object(); private long a = 1_000, b = 1_000; // the two balances void transfer(long amount) { synchronized (lock) { // take lock's monitor, or wait until it is free a -= amount; b += amount; } // give it back, even if the block throws } Kotlin private val lock = Any() private var a = 1_000L // the two balances private var b = 1_000L fun transfer(amount: Long) { synchronized(lock) { // take lock's monitor, or wait until it is free a -= amount b += amount } // give it back, even if the block throws } Both versions say the same thing. In Java synchronized is a keyword, and in Kotlin it's a library function that compiles to the same bytecode, the instructions the JVM runs. The JDK's javap tool prints them: a monitorenter before the two lines, a monitorexit after them, and a second monitorexit on the path an exception takes. The lock every object carries is called its monitor, or intrinsic lock. The code that runs while a thread holds it is called the critical section. Here's a picture from the bank itself. The bank's vault is a room with one door and one key. A thread takes the key and goes in. Every other thread that wants the same key waits outside the door, in the state Java calls BLOCKED: alive, but not allowed to run yet. Inside, the thread updates the balance book. When it hands the key on, the next thread to take it sees every change in the book. The monitor is the key, and the vault is the code that synchronized guards. That picture holds both guarantees that synchronized gives you. Mutual exclusion: while one thread holds a monitor, no other thread can enter a block guarded by the same monitor. So the debit (taking money out) and the credit (putting it in) happen as one step. Visibility: everything a thread wrote before it released a monitor is visible to the next thread that takes the same monitor. The memory model, Java's rules for which writes a thread is sure to see, calls that link a happens-before edge from the release to the next lock. A synchronized instance method is shorthand for synchronized (this) around the whole body. A static synchronized method locks the class object, such as Bank.class. Notice the words both guarantees share: the same monitor. The monitor is strict, and very literal. It keeps out every thread that asks for its key, and it pays no attention to threads that don't ask. The checker from the opening is one of those threads. In AuditDemo it's called the auditor. A transfer thread moves 50 from a to b and back again, 200,000 times, always under the lock. Meanwhile the auditor adds up a + b as fast as it can. Both balances start at 1,000, so every audit should say 2,000. Here are two runs, without and with the lock in the auditor: auditor skipped the lock: 41,004,159 audits, 2,813,398 saw a total other than 2,000 auditor took the lock: 905,017 audits, 0 saw a total other than 2,000 The transfer was correct all along. Without the lock, about one audit in fifteen caught the 50 in flight, in neither account. With the lock, not one of 905,017 audits was wrong. The price shows in the other number: the locked auditor got through far fewer audits, because each one now waits its turn for the key. A lock protects only the threads that take it. Readers take it too. You can play the auditor by hand in the simulator below, where you pick which thread runs next. Step T1 halfway through its transfer, then let T2 read. Then try the same trick on T3. Real classes have more than one synchronized method, though, and the methods call each other. So what happens when a thread that already holds the key asks for it again? Audit with and without the lock Read AuditDemo. A transfer thread moves 50 back and forth 200,000 times, always under the lock. The auditor, the thread that checks the total, adds a + b without it. Run it with the command below and note how many audits were wrong. Predict the count of wrong totals when the auditor takes the lock too. Then run it again with -Pargs=locked. AuditDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l04; /** A transfer thread moves money under a lock. An auditor adds up the two balances, with or without it. */ public class AuditDemo { static final Object lock = new Object(); // volatile only so the JIT re-reads the fields on every pass; it does not make the pair consistent static volatile long a = 1_000, b = 1_000; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean auditorLocks = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("locked"); Thread transfers = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) { synchronized (lock) { // debit and credit as one step a -= 50; b += 50; } synchronized (lock) { // and move it back a += 50; b -= 50; } } }); Thread auditor = new Thread(() -> { long audits = 0, wrong = 0; while (transfers.isAlive()) { long total; if (auditorLocks) { synchronized (lock) { total = a + b; } } else { total = a + b; // reads a, then b, while transfers may run in between } audits++; if (total != 2_000) wrong++; } System.out.printf("auditor %s the lock: %,d audits, %,d saw a total other than 2,000%n", auditorLocks ? "took" : "skipped", audits, wrong); }); transfers.start(); auditor.start(); transfers.join(); auditor.join(); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l04.AuditDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l04/AuditDemo.java AuditDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l04 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A transfer thread moves money under a lock. An auditor adds up the two balances, with or without it. private val lock = Any() // @Volatile only so the JIT re-reads the fields on every pass; it does not make the pair consistent @Volatile private var a = 1_000L @Volatile private var b = 1_000L fun main(args: Array<String>) { val auditorLocks = args.firstOrNull() == "locked" val transfers = thread { repeat(200_000) { synchronized(lock) { // debit and credit as one step a -= 50 b += 50 } synchronized(lock) { // and move it back a += 50 b -= 50 } } } val auditor = thread { var audits = 0L var wrong = 0L while (transfers.isAlive) { val total = if (auditorLocks) { synchronized(lock) { a + b } } else { a + b // reads a, then b, while transfers may run in between } audits++ if (total != 2_000L) wrong++ } println("auditor %s the lock: %,d audits, %,d saw a total other than 2,000" .format(if (auditorLocks) "took" else "skipped", audits, wrong)) } transfers.join() auditor.join() } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l04.AuditDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l04/AuditDemo.kt Without the lock, millions of audits see a total other than 2,000 (one run here: 2,813,398 of 41,004,159). With the lock, zero, every run, though the auditor gets through far fewer audits because it waits for the key. The writer was correct all along. The reader was the bug.

h: synchronized and intrinsic locks · Calling one locked method from another: reentrancy
x: Here's that question in the bank. An account must never go below zero, so its withdraw method first asks canCover: is there enough money? Both methods are synchronized on the same account: Java public synchronized void withdraw(long cents) { if (canCover(cents)) balanceCents -= cents; // canCover takes the same lock } public synchronized boolean canCover(long cents) { return balanceCents >= cents; } Kotlin @Synchronized fun withdraw(cents: Long) { if (canCover(cents)) balanceCents -= cents // canCover takes the same lock } @Synchronized fun canCover(cents: Long): Boolean = balanceCents >= cents This is check-then-act, the shape from the last lesson: check the balance, then act on what you saw. Here it's safe, because the check and the debit sit inside one locked method, so no other withdrawal can get in between. But look at what withdraw does while it holds the account's monitor: it calls canCover, which asks for that same monitor. If a thread had to wait for a key it already holds, it would wait forever. It doesn't wait, because Java monitors are reentrant: a thread that holds a monitor can enter any block guarded by the same monitor without waiting. The JVM keeps a hold count for each monitor. Each entry adds one, each exit takes one away, and the monitor is free again at zero. In the vault picture, the thread with the key can walk back in through a second door. In code, a synchronized method that calls another one on the same object never waits for itself. Subclasses rely on the same rule. In ReentrancyDemo, AuditedAccount is an account that prints a line before each withdrawal. It overrides withdraw with a synchronized method that prints its line and calls super.withdraw, which then calls canCover. One thread enters one monitor three deep, and Thread.holdsLock(this) prints true at every level. Reentrancy has a side effect worth knowing now, because the lab is built on it. The lock lets the same thread back in while your object is halfway through a change. Many classes let other code sign up to hear about changes. Each piece of code that signs up is a listener, and the class calls every listener when something changes. Say a synchronized method publish loops over the listeners, and one listener calls subscribe, which is synchronized too. The lock lets it straight in, because it's the same thread. subscribe adds to the list that publish is walking through, and the loop dies with ConcurrentModificationException, Java's complaint when a list changes under a running loop. The lock did its job. It was never meant to stop the thread that already holds it. So far, every lock in this lesson has been an object we picked without much thought. Which object should hold the key, then? Any object can, and that's the trouble. Enter the same lock three times Read ReentrancyDemo. AuditedAccount.withdraw prints a line and calls super.withdraw, which calls canCover. All three are synchronized on the same object. Predict whether it finishes or hangs, then run it. ReentrancyDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l04; /** A synchronized method calls another synchronized method on the same object. */ public class ReentrancyDemo { static class Account { private long balanceCents = 10_000; public synchronized void withdraw(long cents) { System.out.println("withdraw: holds the lock? " + Thread.holdsLock(this)); if (canCover(cents)) balanceCents -= cents; // takes the same lock again } public synchronized boolean canCover(long cents) { System.out.println("canCover: holds the lock? " + Thread.holdsLock(this)); return balanceCents >= cents; } } static class AuditedAccount extends Account { @Override public synchronized void withdraw(long cents) { System.out.println("audit: about to withdraw " + cents); super.withdraw(cents); // and again, through super } } public static void main(String[] args) { new AuditedAccount().withdraw(2_500); System.out.println("done: no thread waited for a lock it already held"); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l04.ReentrancyDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l04/ReentrancyDemo.java ReentrancyDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l04 // A synchronized method calls another synchronized method on the same object. open class SavingsAccount { private var balanceCents = 10_000L @Synchronized open fun withdraw(cents: Long) { println("withdraw: holds the lock? ${Thread.holdsLock(this)}") if (canCover(cents)) balanceCents -= cents // takes the same lock again } @Synchronized fun canCover(cents: Long): Boolean { println("canCover: holds the lock? ${Thread.holdsLock(this)}") return balanceCents >= cents } } class AuditedSavingsAccount : SavingsAccount() { @Synchronized override fun withdraw(cents: Long) { println("audit: about to withdraw $cents") super.withdraw(cents) // and again, through super } } fun main() { AuditedSavingsAccount().withdraw(2_500) println("done: no thread waited for a lock it already held") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l04.ReentrancyDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l04/ReentrancyDemo.kt It prints holds the lock? true at each level and finishes. One thread entered one monitor three deep, and the hold count went 1, 2, 3 and back to 0.

h: synchronized and intrinsic locks · Choosing the key: lock on a private final object
x: A lock protects state, the fields your threads share. It works only if every thread that touches the state uses the same lock, and no unrelated code uses that lock for something else. The safest choice is the boring one: Java private final Object lock = new Object(); Kotlin private val lock = Any() The lock is private, so no other class can take it and stall you. It's final (a val in Kotlin), so it never changes under you. The other choices go wrong in ways that look harmless when you read the code. A boxed number, an object such as Integer that wraps a plain int, is broken twice. Say the bank counts refused card payments in an Integer field, and locks on that field with synchronized (declines). Then declines++ creates a new Integer and points the field at it, so the next thread locks a different object and nothing is excluded. Small values are also cached and shared: Integer.valueOf(42) returns the same object everywhere in the JVM. javac, the Java compiler, knows this, and prints warning: [synchronization] attempt to synchronize on an instance of a value-based class. The lab's DeclineCounter makes exactly this mistake. A string literal, like synchronized ("lock"), is shared by design. Java keeps one copy of each literal (it interns them), so every class in the JVM that writes "lock" gets the same object. SharedLiteralLock has two classes that know nothing of each other. TokenCache keeps some saved data and takes a second to refresh it, and Metrics records a count for a report. Each one locks on "lock". While the cache spends its second refreshing, the metrics thread sits BLOCKED. The demo reports that it waited about 900 ms for a lock it never shared on purpose. A field that isn't final can be reassigned, and then threads before and after the change lock different objects. this on a public class works, and a synchronized method does exactly that. But any caller can also write synchronized (account) { ... } and hold your key for as long as it likes. A private lock keeps that decision inside your class. synchronized (new Object()) is always wrong. Every thread locks its own fresh object, so nobody ever waits and nobody is promised anything. It's a lock that protects nothing. The opposite mistake is two keys for one piece of state. The classic case is a static field (one copy, shared by every object of the class) updated in a synchronized instance method. Each object locks itself, so two objects update the shared field at the same time. The worked example below fixes one. Give each piece of state one private final lock. Take it everywhere the state is touched. The key is right now, and every reader takes it. A good lock can still make a program slow, though. It depends on what runs while the key is held. Share a lock by accident Read SharedLiteralLock. TokenCache and Metrics never mention each other, and each one locks on "lock". Predict the metrics thread's state after 200 ms, then run it and read how long it waited. In the lab you'll compile DeclineCounter, which locks on an Integer. Look for javac's [synchronization] warning in the Gradle output when you do. SharedLiteralLock.java package workbench.concurrency.l04; /** Two unrelated classes each lock on the string "lock". They are the same object. */ public class SharedLiteralLock { static class TokenCache { void refresh() { synchronized ("lock") { // looks private. It isn't. sleep(1_000); // a slow refresh } } } static class Metrics { void record() { synchronized ("lock") { // a different class, a different "lock"? System.out.println("metrics: recorded"); } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread refresher = new Thread(() -> new TokenCache().refresh(), "token-refresh"); Thread metrics = new Thread(() -> new Metrics().record(), "metrics"); refresher.start(); Thread.sleep(100); // let the refresher take the lock first long t0 = System.nanoTime(); metrics.start(); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println("metrics thread state after 200 ms: " + metrics.getState()); metrics.join(); System.out.printf("metrics waited about %d ms for a lock it never shared on purpose%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); refresher.join(); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l04.SharedLiteralLock labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l04/SharedLiteralLock.java SharedLiteralLock.kt package workbench.concurrency.l04 // Two unrelated classes each lock on the string "lock". They are the same object. private class TokenCache { fun refresh() { synchronized("lock") { // looks private. It isn't. Thread.sleep(1_000) // a slow refresh } } } private class Metrics { fun record() { synchronized("lock") { // a different class, a different "lock"? println("metrics: recorded") } } } fun main() { val refresher = Thread({ TokenCache().refresh() }, "token-refresh") val metrics = Thread({ Metrics().record() }, "metrics") refresher.start() Thread.sleep(100) // let the refresher take the lock first val t0 = System.nanoTime() metrics.start() Thread.sleep(200) println("metrics thread state after 200 ms: ${metrics.state}") metrics.join() println("metrics waited about ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms for a lock it never shared on purpose") refresher.join() } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l04.SharedLiteralLockKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l04/SharedLiteralLock.kt The metrics thread is BLOCKED after 200 ms, and it waits about 900 ms in all, the rest of the refresh. Two classes that never mention each other wait on one lock, because both literals are the same interned String.

h: synchronized and intrinsic locks · Keeping slow calls and alien code out of the lock
x: Before a bank moves money, it often asks a fraud-check service whether the transfer looks suspicious. That service is a web service, a program on another computer, so each question travels over the network. In our demo each answer takes 40 ms, which is slow next to the transfer itself. Everything inside a synchronized block runs one thread at a time, so anything slow in there makes every other thread wait in line. SlowCallUnderLock shows it. Eight threads each make five transfers, and each transfer asks the fraud checker first. Both versions add to the bank's total, movedCents, under the lock. Only one of them also holds the lock while it waits for the fraud checker. My guess before running it: with the check inside the lock, the 40 checks run one after another, about 1,600 ms. With the check outside, they overlap in 5 rounds of 8, about 200 ms. It printed: fraud check inside the lock: 1,618 ms fraud check outside the lock: 201 ms The guess held, and both versions got the total right (the demo checks it). With the check inside the lock, eight threads, forty checks and one key made a very orderly line. The fraud checker takes its 40 ms either way. The only question is whether everyone else waits while it does. So put only the reads and writes of shared state inside the lock. Do the slow work before it or after it: network calls, reading and writing files (together called I/O, for input and output), and heavy computing. A worse form of the same mistake is calling alien code while you hold a lock. Alien code is code you don't control: a listener, a callback (a function someone gave you to call later), a method a subclass can override. It might call a web service that takes 2 seconds to answer. Alien code might also hand work to another thread and wait for it. If that thread needs your lock, the two wait for each other forever. That's a deadlock, the subject of lesson 6 of this track. Or alien code might call back into your object on the same thread, where reentrancy lets it in halfway through your update. The JDK has shipped this bug itself. JDK 25 carries a fix to its logging classes (java.util.logging, or j.u.l) titled "j.u.l.Handler classes create deadlock risk via synchronized publish() method". The fix has the same shape every time. Under the lock, change your own state and take a copy of what you need. Release the lock. Then call out. Here it is in the bank. Say the bank tells a list of listeners, such as a phone app's balance screen, about every new balance. Both versions copy the listeners under the lock and call them outside it: Java List<Listener> toNotify; synchronized (lock) { balances.put(accountId, newBalance); // 1. our state, under the lock toNotify = List.copyOf(listeners); // 2. a snapshot to work from } for (Listener l : toNotify) l.onBalance(accountId, newBalance); // 3. alien code, no lock held Kotlin val toNotify = synchronized(lock) { balances[accountId] = newBalance // 1. our state, under the lock listeners.toList() // 2. a snapshot to work from (the block's value) } for (l in toNotify) l.onBalance(accountId, newBalance) // 3. alien code, no lock held The Kotlin version is one variable shorter, because synchronized is a function and returns its block's value. The cost of the pattern is small: a listener may hear about two balances in a different order than two threads set them. That's almost always a price worth paying. Hold a lock only for your own reads and writes. Call out after you let go. That's the whole toolkit of this lesson, so let's be honest about where it stops. Our bank has one lock for every balance, so two transfers between four different accounts still wait for each other. Give each account its own lock and a transfer must hold two, which is how lesson 6 of this track gets its deadlock. And a transfer that finds too little money can only refuse. While it holds the key, it can't wait for a deposit, because the deposit needs the key too. Move the slow call out of the lock Read SlowCallUnderLock. Both versions add to movedCents under the lock. Only one also holds the lock during the 40 ms fraud check. Predict both times (8 threads x 5 transfers x 40 ms), then run it. SlowCallUnderLock.java package workbench.concurrency.l04; /** Eight threads make transfers. Each one first asks a fraud-check service, which takes 40 ms. Where should the lock go? */ public class SlowCallUnderLock { static final Object lock = new Object(); static long movedCents; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.printf("fraud check inside the lock: %,5d ms%n", run(true)); System.out.printf("fraud check outside the lock: %,5d ms%n", run(false)); } static long run(boolean checkInsideLock) throws InterruptedException { movedCents = 0; Thread[] threads = new Thread[8]; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < threads.length; i++) { threads[i] = new Thread(() -> { for (int p = 0; p < 5; p++) { if (checkInsideLock) { synchronized (lock) { boolean ok = checkForFraud(); // 40 ms while every other thread waits if (ok) movedCents += 1_999; } } else { boolean ok = checkForFraud(); // slow work with no lock held synchronized (lock) { // lock only the shared update if (ok) movedCents += 1_999; } } } }); threads[i].start(); } for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); if (movedCents != 40 * 1_999) throw new AssertionError("lost an update: " + movedCents); return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } /** Stands in for a call to a fraud-check web service: 40 ms, and the answer is "looks fine". */ static boolean checkForFraud() { try { Thread.sleep(40); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return true; } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l04.SlowCallUnderLock labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l04/SlowCallUnderLock.java SlowCallUnderLock.kt package workbench.concurrency.l04 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Eight threads make transfers. Each one first asks a fraud-check service, which takes 40 ms. Where should the lock go? private val transferLock = Any() private var movedCents = 0L // guarded by transferLock fun main() { println("fraud check inside the lock: %,5d ms".format(run(checkInsideLock = true))) println("fraud check outside the lock: %,5d ms".format(run(checkInsideLock = false))) } private fun run(checkInsideLock: Boolean): Long { movedCents = 0 val t0 = System.nanoTime() val threads = List(8) { thread { repeat(5) { if (checkInsideLock) { synchronized(transferLock) { val ok = checkForFraud() // 40 ms while every other thread waits if (ok) movedCents += 1_999 } } else { val ok = checkForFraud() // slow work with no lock held synchronized(transferLock) { // lock only the shared update if (ok) movedCents += 1_999 } } } } } threads.forEach { it.join() } check(movedCents == 40L * 1_999) { "lost an update: $movedCents" } return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 } // Stands in for a call to a fraud-check web service: 40 ms, and the answer is "looks fine". private fun checkForFraud(): Boolean { Thread.sleep(40) return true } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l04.SlowCallUnderLockKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l04/SlowCallUnderLock.kt About 1,600 ms with the check inside the lock (40 checks in a row) and about 200 ms with it outside (5 rounds of 8 checks at once). Both versions get the total right. Only one of them could keep up with a busy bank.

h: synchronized and intrinsic locks · Java and Kotlin
x: Locking in Java and Kotlin Java public class DeclineCounter { private final Object lock = new Object(); private int declines; public void recordDecline() { synchronized (lock) { // a keyword declines++; } } public int total() { synchronized (lock) { return declines; } } } public class HitCounter { private int hits; public synchronized void hit() { hits++; } // locks this public synchronized int total() { return hits; } } KotlinLocks.kt package workbench.concurrency.l04 class DeclineCounterKt { private val lock = Any() // a private lock object, like `new Object()` in Java private var declines = 0 fun recordDecline() { synchronized(lock) { // a standard-library function, not a keyword declines++ } } fun total(): Int = synchronized(lock) { declines } // it returns the block's value } class HitCounterKt { private var hits = 0 @Synchronized fun hit() { hits++ } // like a Java synchronized method: locks `this` @Synchronized fun total() = hits } fun main() { val declines = DeclineCounterKt() val hits = HitCounterKt() val threads = List(8) { Thread { repeat(100_000) { declines.recordDecline() hits.hit() } }.apply { start() } } threads.forEach { it.join() } println("declines = ${declines.total()}, hits = ${hits.total()}") } Both files lock the same way and compile to the same monitor instructions. Three things differ. Kotlin has no synchronized keyword: synchronized(lock) { ... } is an inline standard-library function, and the compiler emits the same monitorenter and monitorexit as a Java block. Because it's a function, it returns its block's value, so total() is one expression. And @Synchronized on a function marks the compiled method as synchronized, exactly like Java's modifier, so it locks this (or, in an object, the object itself). Any() makes a fine private lock. One gap shows up in the next lesson: Any has no wait() or notify(), so Kotlin code that needs them locks on a java.lang.Object or, better, uses the explicit locks from lesson 7 of this track.

h: synchronized and intrinsic locks · Worked example
x: Fix a cash limit with the wrong lock and a slow call inside One program runs all of a bank's cash machines. The bank caps how much cash the machines may pay out in one day, all of them together. The program creates one PayoutLimit object per machine, and the running total is a static field that all of them share. Before each payout, the code asks the fraud-check service, which takes about 300 ms and throws an exception if it refuses. Find every lock problem before you read on. public class PayoutLimit { private static long paidOutCents; // shared by every instance private static final long LIMIT_CENTS = 5_000_000; public synchronized boolean tryPayOut(long cents) { // locks `this` if (paidOutCents + cents > LIMIT_CENTS) return false; fraudCheck.verify(cents); // web service call, about 300 ms paidOutCents += cents; return true; } } class PayoutLimit { companion object { private var paidOutCents = 0L // shared by every instance private const val LIMIT_CENTS = 5_000_000L } @Synchronized fun tryPayOut(cents: Long): Boolean { // locks `this` if (paidOutCents + cents > LIMIT_CENTS) return false fraudCheck.verify(cents) // web service call, about 300 ms paidOutCents += cents return true } } There are two problems. First, the method locks this, but the state is static: two keys for one piece of state. Two machines' objects lock two different monitors and can both pass the limit check at once. Second, a 300 ms web service call runs while the key is held, so every payout waits for the previous one's fraud check. Fix the lock first: one lock object for the one piece of state. private static final Object LOCK = new Object(); // 1. one lock for the static state private val LOCK = Any() // 1. one lock for the shared state, in the companion object Now shrink the critical section, the code that runs under the lock. Reserve the amount under the lock, so the check and the update are one step. Then release the lock and make the call. If the fraud check refuses the payout, give the reservation back, under the lock again. Before you read the last step, ask yourself why the check and the += must stay inside the same block. public boolean tryPayOut(long cents) { synchronized (LOCK) { // 2. check and reserve as one step if (paidOutCents + cents > LIMIT_CENTS) return false; paidOutCents += cents; } try { fraudCheck.verify(cents); // 3. slow call, no lock held return true; } catch (RuntimeException e) { synchronized (LOCK) { paidOutCents -= cents; } // 4. undo the reservation throw e; } } fun tryPayOut(cents: Long): Boolean { synchronized(LOCK) { // 2. check and reserve as one step if (paidOutCents + cents > LIMIT_CENTS) return false paidOutCents += cents } try { fraudCheck.verify(cents) // 3. slow call, no lock held return true } catch (e: RuntimeException) { synchronized(LOCK) { paidOutCents -= cents } // 4. undo the reservation throw e } } Split the check from the += and you're back in Race conditions: why count++ lies, with check-then-act and two threads that both pass the check. The lock has to cover the whole compound action, the check and the update together. What it must not cover is the 300 ms call, and now it doesn't. If the bank ran several copies of this program on different computers, a static field couldn't hold the shared total any more: it would have to live somewhere they all share, such as a database. The shape of the fix would stay the same.

h: synchronized and intrinsic locks · Quiz
x: Which line is the bug? class FeeCounter { private static long feesCents; // line 2 public synchronized void add(long cents) { // line 3 feesCents += cents; // line 4 } } The program creates one FeeCounter for each branch of the bank. Line 2: static fields cannot be locked Line 4: += is not allowed inside synchronized Line 3: it locks this, but the state is static, so different instances don't exclude each other There is no bug, because the method is synchronized Each instance locks its own monitor, while all instances share feesCents. Two branches' counters run += at the same time and lose updates. That's two keys for one piece of state. Static state needs one static lock: private static final Object LOCK, or a static synchronized method. A thread inside synchronized void withdraw() calls canCover(), which is also synchronized on the same object. What happens? It enters at once, because the monitor is reentrant It deadlocks waiting for itself It throws IllegalMonitorStateException It waits until withdraw() returns Java monitors are reentrant. The JVM sees that the current thread already owns the monitor and raises the hold count by one. Without reentrancy, every synchronized method that calls another one on the same object would hang. Which of these is the safest object to lock on for a class's internal state? "bank-lock", a string literal Integer.valueOf(1) this, on a public class that callers also hold references to private final Object lock = new Object() A private final object can't be locked by anyone else and can't change. String literals are interned and shared across the whole JVM. Small Integer values are cached and shared, and javac warns about locking on them. this works, but any caller can lock it too and stall your methods. publish() is synchronized and calls each listener inside the lock. One listener calls a web service that takes 2 seconds to answer. What do other threads notice? Nothing, since each listener runs on its own thread Every thread that needs the same lock, even just to read a value, waits up to 2 seconds The web service call is cancelled because of the lock The JVM detects the slow call and releases the lock Listeners run on the publishing thread, inside its critical section. Anyone who needs that monitor waits in line behind the web service call. Copy the listener list under the lock, release it, then call the listeners. From Race conditions: why count++ lies: setBalance() is synchronized, but getBalance() is a plain getter with no lock. Is the class safe to use from many threads? Yes: only writes need a lock Yes, if the field is a long No: a reader that skips the lock gets no visibility promise and can see an old value No, but only on 32-bit JVMs Visibility comes from unlocking and then locking the same monitor. A reader that never takes the lock has no happens-before edge to the writer, so it may keep seeing an old balance. Guard reads with the same lock, or, for a single value, use a volatile field or an atomic class such as AtomicLong.

h: synchronized and intrinsic locks · Key terms
x: Lock A guard on a piece of code: a thread must take it to run the code, and only one thread can hold it at a time. Monitor (intrinsic lock) The lock every Java object has, taken and released by synchronized. Mutual exclusion Only one thread at a time can run the code guarded by a lock. Visibility Whether one thread is guaranteed to see what another thread wrote. Reentrant A thread can take a lock it already holds without waiting for itself. Critical section The code that runs while a lock is held. Alien code Code you don't control, such as a listener or callback, which can be slow or call back in. Value-based class A class like Integer whose instances may be shared or cached, so its objects are not yours to lock on. What two guarantees does synchronized give? Mutual exclusion (one thread at a time per monitor) and visibility (writes made before releasing a monitor are seen by the next thread that locks it). What does a synchronized instance method lock? A static synchronized method? The instance, this. The static one locks the class object, for example Bank.class. What does it mean that Java monitors are reentrant? A thread that already holds a monitor can enter it again without waiting. The JVM counts the holds and frees the monitor when the count is back to zero. Why is synchronized (count) on an Integer field broken? count++ replaces the field with a new Integer, so threads lock different objects. Small values are also cached and shared JVM-wide. javac warns [synchronization]. Why never lock on a string literal? Literals are interned: every "lock" in the JVM is the same object, so unrelated code shares your lock. What does synchronized (new Object()) { ... } protect? Nothing. Each call locks a fresh object no other thread can see, so there is no exclusion and no visibility. What should you do before calling listeners or callbacks from a locked method? Update your state and copy what you need (for example List.copyOf(listeners)) under the lock, release it, then call them.

h: synchronized and intrinsic locks · Go deeper
x: How does HotSpot, the standard JVM, make synchronized cheap when nobody else wants the lock? It doesn't build a full monitor object for every lock. A lock that no other thread wants at that moment (an uncontended lock) is a small change in the object's header, the few bytes at the start of every object that the JVM uses for bookkeeping. This is called lightweight locking. Only when threads really fight over the lock, or one calls wait(), does the JVM inflate it into a full ObjectMonitor, with a queue of threads waiting to get in and a wait set (the next lesson explains both). The details keep changing between releases, which is a good reason not to depend on them. Lightweight locking became the default LockingMode in JDK 23, the option was deprecated in JDK 24, and its code was removed in JDK 26. JDK 27 switched on, by default, a separate table that maps objects to their monitors, and made compact object headers the default too. None of this changes what synchronized means. It only changes what it costs. If you want to see contention (threads waiting for each other's locks) rather than guess at it, Java Flight Recorder (JFR), an event recorder built into the JVM, records a jdk.JavaMonitorEnter event when a thread has to wait for a monitor, with the monitor's class and the previous owner. JDK 25 added jdk.JavaMonitorNotify and jdk.JavaMonitorStatistics. Lesson 13 of this track uses them. For virtual threads (very light threads that the JVM runs on top of a few ordinary threads, called carrier threads), JEP 491 in JDK 24 is the change to know. Before it, a virtual thread blocked inside synchronized held on to its carrier thread. Since JDK 24 it doesn't, in most cases.

h: wait, notify and guarded blocks · Waiting for the rail without spinning: the guarded block
x: Let's start with one cook and an empty rail. The cook's thread must take the lock (with synchronized, as in the last lesson) every time it looks at the rail, since readers need the lock too. The quickest code just keeps looking: Java // Naive: asks the empty rail again and again String nextOrder() { while (true) { synchronized (lock) { if (!rail.isEmpty()) return rail.removeFirst(); } } } Kotlin // Naive: asks the empty rail again and again fun nextOrder(): String { while (true) { synchronized(lock) { if (rail.isNotEmpty()) return rail.removeFirst() } } } That loop is correct: it never takes an order that isn't there, and it never misses one. But it's a busy wait, or spin: a loop that checks the same thing again and again. The thread stays RUNNABLE (running, or ready to run) and keeps a processor core busy the whole time it waits. The waiters have to fight it for the lock every time they add an order. The Try it below times a simpler spinner, which checks a volatile flag (a field that every thread always reads fresh), against a cook that waits properly. To wait one second, the spinning cook used about a full second of CPU time (time spent running on a processor). The waiting cook used 0 ms. A Thread.sleep(50) between looks saves the CPU, but an order that lands just after a look then sits on the rail for up to 50 ms. A sleep is a guess about when the next order will arrive, and the guess is never quite right. What we want is a cook that sleeps until the rail changes, and a waiter that wakes it when it does. Every Java object can do that, through its monitor, the built-in lock that synchronized takes. Here's the cook's side: Java // Fixed: sleeps until an order arrives String nextOrder() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (rail.isEmpty()) { lock.wait(); // give back the lock, sleep until woken, take it again } return rail.removeFirst(); // the rail has an order, and we hold the lock } } Kotlin // Fixed: sleeps until an order arrives fun nextOrder(): String { synchronized(lock) { // lock is a java.lang.Object: Kotlin's Any has no wait() while (rail.isEmpty()) { lock.wait() // give back the lock, sleep until woken, take it again } return rail.removeFirst() // the rail has an order, and we hold the lock } } wait() does three things, in order. First, it releases the monitor, so a waiter can get in. Then it parks the cook's thread, that is, puts it to sleep in the monitor's wait set, in the WAITING state, using no CPU. Finally, when the thread is woken, it takes the monitor back before wait() returns. So the line after wait() runs with the lock held, like the line before it. A note on names, since this kitchen comes with a pun: here a waiter is always a person who carries orders, and a thread that has called wait() is a waiting thread. A waiter does the other half, holding the same lock: Java void add(String order) { synchronized (lock) { rail.addLast(order); // change the state first lock.notifyAll(); // then wake every thread waiting on lock } } Kotlin fun add(order: String) { synchronized(lock) { rail.addLast(order) // change the state first lock.notifyAll() // then wake every thread waiting on lock } } notifyAll() wakes every thread in the wait set, but it doesn't hand over the lock. Each woken thread moves to the monitor's entry set, the threads lining up to get in. It shows as BLOCKED, the state of a thread waiting for a lock, until the waiter leaves its block. (Its sibling notify() wakes just one waiting thread. Which one it wakes will matter in the third section.) Here's the same thing in the kitchen. The rail has one key, and only the thread holding the key may touch the rail. Threads that want the key stand in a line by the rail: that line is the entry set. A cook who finds the rail empty hangs the key back on its hook and sits on a bench at the back. The bench is the wait set. When a waiter clips a new ticket on, it rings the bell, and everyone on the bench gets up and joins the line for the key again. The bell is notifyAll(). The figure draws the line and the bench. The cook's code is a guarded block. Its guard is a condition, a yes-or-no question about the shared state (here, "is there a ticket on the rail?"), and the thread waits until the answer is yes. Notice that the guard is a while, although with one cook an if looks just as good. We'll come back to that in the next section. The order on the waiter's side matters too: state first, then the signal. If an order arrives before the cook starts waiting, the notifyAll() wakes nobody, and that's fine. The cook checks the rail first, finds the ticket and never calls wait(). Code that waits for a bare signal, with no state to check, sleeps forever when the signal comes first. That's a lost wake-up, and it passes tests because the waiting thread usually gets there first. A notification is only a hint. Wait for a state, never for a signal. One more rule holds it all together. You must hold the monitor of the object you call wait() or notifyAll() on, or you get IllegalMonitorStateException at once. Since the rail can change only under the lock, no order can slip in between the cook's check and its wait. One cook now waits for free and wakes the moment an order lands. A busy evening needs a second one. Spin vs wait Read BusyWaitDemo. Two cooks wait one second for the first order: the spinning cook checks a volatile flag over and over, and the waiting cook sits in a guarded block. Write down your guess for each thread's CPU time. Run it and compare. In the waiting cook, delete the synchronized line around the while loop and its closing brace, so lock.wait() runs without the lock. Predict what happens, run it, then put the lines back. BusyWaitDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l05; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.lang.management.ThreadMXBean; /** Two cooks wait one second for the first order. One spins, one calls wait(). Compare their CPU time. */ public class BusyWaitDemo { static final Object lock = new Object(); static boolean ready; // guarded by lock static volatile boolean readyForSpinner; // the spinner can't use the lock, so it needs volatile public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread spinningCook = new Thread(() -> { while (!readyForSpinner) { } // busy-wait: checks the flag as fast as it can }, "spinning-cook"); Thread waitingCook = new Thread(() -> { synchronized (lock) { while (!ready) { // guarded block: the condition, in a loop try { lock.wait(); // releases lock, parks until notified } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return; } } } }, "waiting-cook"); spinningCook.start(); waitingCook.start(); Thread.sleep(1_000); // the first order arrives a second later ThreadMXBean mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); long spinCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(spinningCook.threadId()) / 1_000_000; // measure while both still wait long waitCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(waitingCook.threadId()) / 1_000_000; readyForSpinner = true; synchronized (lock) { ready = true; lock.notifyAll(); // wake the waiting cook; it runs once we leave this block } spinningCook.join(); waitingCook.join(); System.out.printf("the spinning cook used about %d ms of CPU to wait 1 s%n", spinCpu); System.out.printf("the waiting cook used about %d ms of CPU to wait 1 s%n", waitCpu); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l05.BusyWaitDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l05/BusyWaitDemo.java BusyWaitDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l05 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Two cooks wait one second for the first order. One spins, one calls wait(). Compare their CPU time. @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val lock = Object() // java.lang.Object, because Kotlin's Any has no wait() private var ready = false // guarded by lock @Volatile private var readyForSpinner = false // the spinner can't use the lock, so it needs @Volatile fun main() { val spinningCook = thread(name = "spinning-cook") { while (!readyForSpinner) { } // busy-wait: checks the flag as fast as it can } val waitingCook = thread(name = "waiting-cook") { synchronized(lock) { while (!ready) { // guarded block: the condition, in a loop try { lock.wait() // releases lock, parks until notified } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() return@thread } } } } Thread.sleep(1_000) // the first order arrives a second later val mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() val spinCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(spinningCook.threadId()) / 1_000_000 // measure while both still wait val waitCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(waitingCook.threadId()) / 1_000_000 readyForSpinner = true synchronized(lock) { ready = true lock.notifyAll() // wake the waiting cook; it runs once we leave this block } spinningCook.join() waitingCook.join() println("the spinning cook used about $spinCpu ms of CPU to wait 1 s") println("the waiting cook used about $waitCpu ms of CPU to wait 1 s") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l05.BusyWaitDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l05/BusyWaitDemo.kt The spinning cook uses about a full second of CPU to wait one second (runs here printed 992 to 1,037 ms). The waiting cook uses 0 ms. Without the synchronized block, the waiting cook dies at once with IllegalMonitorStateException: you can only wait on a monitor you hold. wait() moves the owner to the wait set and gives the lock back. notify moves a waiting thread back to the entry set, where it must win the lock again, so it must re-check its condition.

h: wait, notify and guarded blocks · A second cook, and why every wait sits in a while loop
x: Two cooks, one ticket: the bell wakes both, so a woken cook checks the rail again in a while loop, and with two kinds of sleepers on one bench notify() can stall the kitchen Remember the while in the cook's guard? With one cook, an if seems to do the same job: check once, wait if the rail is empty, then take the ticket. Plenty of first versions look exactly like this: Java // Naive: checks once, before waiting synchronized (lock) { if (rail.isEmpty()) lock.wait(); return rail.removeFirst(); } Kotlin // Naive: checks once, before waiting synchronized(lock) { if (rail.isEmpty()) lock.wait() return rail.removeFirst() } With one cook, that passes every test. So let's hire a second cook and send in a single order. The Try it below parks two cook threads in wait(), adds one order and calls notifyAll(). Here's what it printed: cook-2 failed: java.util.NoSuchElementException cook-1 took order-1 notifyAll() woke two cooks for one order, and the second one found the rail empty. NoSuchElementException is what removeFirst() throws when there is nothing to remove. Let's trace it, one thread at a time: Both cooks find the rail empty and call wait(), so both sit in the wait set. A waiter adds order-1 and calls notifyAll(). Both cooks move to the entry set. Cook 1 gets the lock first. Its wait() returns, it takes order-1, and it leaves. Cook 2 gets the lock next, and its wait() returns too. Its if ran long ago, before it waited, so it goes straight to removeFirst() on an empty rail. Which cook wins, and which line prints first, changes from run to run. The ending doesn't. With while, cook 2 checks the rail again after waking, finds it empty and goes back to waiting. It's rare, but it's allowed, and the Javadoc tells you to test the condition again and keep waiting. In the kitchen, nobody gets up from the bench without hearing the bell; a Java thread is allowed to. So even a lone cook needs the loop. A second cook just makes the bug show up on the first busy evening. The loop costs nothing, so use it every time. When you read code, treat an if around wait() as a bug, even in code that has never failed. It just hasn't had two cooks at once yet. Two cooks now share the rail safely. But nothing stops the waiters from adding orders faster than the cooks can cook them. Next, we'll give the rail a limit, and the waiting starts on the other side too. h: wait, notify and guarded blocks · A limit on the rail, and why notify() can stall it
x: So far only the cooks wait. When a big table orders twelve dishes at once, the cooks fall behind and the waiters keep adding tickets. A rail with no limit grows until the heap, the memory where Java keeps its objects, runs out. A real rail holds only so many tickets, so let's give ours a capacity, and make a waiter wait while it's full. At last, a job that suits the name: Java while (rail.size() == capacity) lock.wait(); // the waiter's guard: "not full" Kotlin while (rail.size == capacity) lock.wait() // the waiter's guard: "not full" A thread that puts work in is called a producer, and a thread that takes work out is a consumer: our waiters are producers, and our cooks are consumers. Making a fast producer wait for a slow consumer like this is called backpressure. Backpressure also gives the monitor two kinds of waiting threads. Waiters wait for "not full", and cooks wait for "not empty". A monitor has only one wait set, so they all sit on the same bench. With notifyAll(), that's harmless: everyone wakes, and each while loop sends back the threads that can't go on. With notify(), it isn't. notify() wakes one waiting thread, and it doesn't take requests: the JVM picks which one. Here's what that does to a rail with room for one ticket, two waiters and two cooks, where every signal is a notify(): The rail is empty, so both cooks wait. Waiter 1 clips a ticket on, and its notify() wakes cook 1. Before cook 1 gets the lock, both waiters find the rail full and wait. The bench now holds waiter 1, waiter 2 and cook 2. Cook 1 takes the ticket and calls notify(), which happens to wake cook 2, the wrong kind. Cook 2 finds the rail empty and waits again. Cook 1 loops back, finds it empty too, and waits. Now all four threads wait for a bell nobody is left to ring. No thread holds the lock, so this isn't a deadlock in the textbook sense (the next lesson has those), but the kitchen has stopped just the same. The Try it below gets there fast. One run printed: using notify() after 1 s: 8 orders cooked stalled after 8 orders. Thread states: waiter-0: WAITING waiter-1: WAITING cook-0: WAITING cook-1: WAITING Across runs here it stalled after 1 to 8 orders. With both signals switched to notifyAll(), the same four threads cooked about 136,000 to 139,000 orders in five seconds and never stalled. Each thread of the wrong kind checks its guard and goes back to waiting, so the right kind always gets a turn. The price is some extra wake-ups, which is cheap next to a stalled kitchen. Two kinds of waiting threads on one monitor need notifyAll(). Wake them all, and let each loop decide. notify() is safe only when every waiting thread waits for the same condition and one change lets at most one of them go on. Our rail with no limit, from the first two sections, qualified: only cooks waited, and one order let one cook go. A rail with a limit never does. For a precise wake-up per kind of waiting thread, give each kind its own Condition on a ReentrantLock, as lesson 7 of this track shows. We now have all three pieces: a loop around every wait(), a change of state before every signal, and notifyAll() when the waiting threads differ. Let's put them together. Stall a kitchen with notify() Run NotifyStall. Two waiters and two cooks share a rail with room for one ticket, and every signal is a notify(). When progress stops, read the thread states it prints and match them against the four steps in this section. Predict whether it stalls with notifyAll(). Then run it again with -Pargs=all, which switches both signals to notifyAll(). h: wait, notify and guarded blocks · The bounded buffer, built by hand, and where it stops
x: Put the three pieces together and you get the class you'll write in the lab: a bounded buffer, a queue with a fixed capacity that threads can share. It is our rail, written once for any kind of item. Waiters wait in put() when the cooks fall behind, and cooks wait in take() when there's nothing to cook: Java public class BoundedBuffer<T> { private final Object lock = new Object(); private final Deque<T> items = new ArrayDeque<>(); private final int capacity; public void put(T item) throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (items.size() == capacity) { // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up lock.wait(); } items.addLast(item); // 2. act: condition holds, lock held lock.notifyAll(); // 3. signal: the state changed } } public T take() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (items.isEmpty()) { lock.wait(); } T head = items.removeFirst(); lock.notifyAll(); return head; } } } Kotlin class BoundedBuffer<T>(private val capacity: Int) { @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val lock = Object() // java.lang.Object: Kotlin's Any has no wait() private val items = ArrayDeque<T>() @Throws(InterruptedException::class) // so Java callers see it, as in the Java version fun put(item: T) { synchronized(lock) { while (items.size == capacity) { // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up lock.wait() } items.addLast(item) // 2. act: condition holds, lock held lock.notifyAll() // 3. signal: the state changed } } @Throws(InterruptedException::class) fun take(): T { synchronized(lock) { while (items.isEmpty()) { lock.wait() } val head = items.removeFirst() lock.notifyAll() return head } } } put() and take() have the same three parts. The guard is the while loop that waits until the method can go on. The act changes the rail, safely, because the condition holds and the lock is held. The signal wakes the other side, because the state it waits on just changed. Read put() aloud and it says: while there's no room, wait; add the item; tell everyone something changed. Three smaller choices are deliberate, and each comes from an earlier lesson. The lock is a private object, as synchronized and intrinsic locks recommended, so only the buffer can wait on it or signal it. Both methods signal with notifyAll(), because producers and consumers share one wait set. And both declare throws InterruptedException, the exception a waiting thread gets when another thread interrupts it, that is, asks it to stop. The buffer can't know what its caller wants to do about an interrupt, so it lets the exception propagate, that is, pass up to the caller. That's one of the two good answers from A thread's life. Now the honest part. In real code you won't write this class: ArrayBlockingQueue from the JDK does the same job, with timeouts, and lesson 9 of this track covers it. Our buffer also has a cost built in. With one wait set, every notifyAll() wakes producers and consumers alike, and most of them check their guard and go straight back to waiting. A Condition gives one lock a separate wait set per condition, and lesson 7 of this track builds on that. Why build it, then? Because guarded blocks hide inside many libraries you'll use. If you write programs that use a database, for example, you'll meet a connection pool: a fixed set of open database connections that threads borrow and give back. A pool of 20 makes the 21st thread wait in a guarded block until a connection comes back. In a thread dump, a printout of every thread's state and the method calls it is in the middle of, those threads show WAITING or TIMED_WAITING inside the library's code. Once you've written put() and take() yourself, you can tell which condition they wait for. Check your model before you start the lab. Delete the notifyAll() in take(). Two waiters fill a rail of capacity 2 and then wait in put(). A cook takes one order. What happens next? (The waiters stay in wait(): the take made room, but nothing woke them. The cooks empty the rail and then wait too, until every thread is waiting.)

The idiomatic guarded block uses a Lock and a Condition. class KotlinBuffer<T>(private val capacity: Int) { private val lock = ReentrantLock() private val changed = lock.newCondition() // one wait set, like a monitor's private val items = ArrayDeque<T>() fun put(item: T) = lock.withLock { while (items.size == capacity) changed.await() // same while-loop guard items.addLast(item) changed.signalAll() // same as notifyAll() } fun take(): T = lock.withLock { while (items.isEmpty()) changed.await() items.removeFirst().also { changed.signalAll() } } } fun main() { val buffer = KotlinBuffer<Int>(2) val consumer = thread { repeat(5) { println("took ${buffer.take()}") } } repeat(5) { buffer.put(it) } consumer.join() } Both versions are the same guarded buffer: the same while guard, the same act, and the same signal to every waiting thread. Three things changed in the Kotlin one. lock.withLock { } takes and releases a ReentrantLock where Java writes synchronized. changed.await() stands in for wait(). And changed.signalAll() stands in for notifyAll(). The Java version uses the monitor that every object has carried since Java 1.0, and it needs nothing else. The Kotlin version reaches for a Condition because Kotlin's Any doesn't expose wait(). The rules don't change with the tool: Condition allows spurious wakeups too, so the while stays. What the Condition adds is room to grow, because one lock can have several conditions, so producers and consumers could wait separately. Lesson 7 of this track builds exactly that.

h: wait, notify and guarded blocks · Worked example
x: Wait for a dish, with a deadline A waiter thread waits until the kitchen marks a table's dish as ready. After 30 seconds it gives up, so it can go and tell the table about the delay. Here is the first attempt. Before you read on, find what can go wrong. boolean awaitDish() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { if (!dishReady) lock.wait(30_000); return dishReady; } } fun awaitDish(): Boolean { synchronized(lock) { if (!dishReady) lock.wait(30_000) return dishReady } } It's the if bug in a new shape. wait(30_000) waits at most 30 seconds, but it can return sooner. A spurious wakeup, or a notifyAll() meant for some other condition on the same lock, makes wait() return early with dishReady still false: after 2 seconds, say, instead of 30. Just moving wait(30_000) into a while loop is wrong too, because every wake-up would start a fresh 30 seconds. The cure is to set the deadline once and wait only for what's left of it. The guard loop now checks two things: the condition and the clock. Each pass waits only for the time that's left. boolean awaitDish(Duration timeout) throws InterruptedException { long deadline = System.nanoTime() + timeout.toNanos(); // 1. fix the deadline once synchronized (lock) { while (!dishReady) { // 2. guard on the condition long leftMillis = (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000; if (leftMillis <= 0) return false; // 3. out of time lock.wait(leftMillis); // 4. wait only for what's left } return true; } } fun awaitDish(timeout: Duration): Boolean { val deadline = System.nanoTime() + timeout.toNanos() // 1. fix the deadline once synchronized(lock) { while (!dishReady) { // 2. guard on the condition val leftMillis = (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000 if (leftMillis <= 0) return false // 3. out of time lock.wait(leftMillis) // 4. wait only for what's left } return true } } The cook's thread sets the state before it signals, both under the lock, just as the waiters did with the rail. If it runs before anyone waits, nothing is lost: the waiter thread sees dishReady and never calls wait(). One question before the last step: why does the waiter use System.nanoTime() and not System.currentTimeMillis()? void onDishReady() { synchronized (lock) { dishReady = true; // state first lock.notifyAll(); // then the signal } } fun onDishReady() { synchronized(lock) { dishReady = true // state first lock.notifyAll() // then the signal } } nanoTime() only ever moves forward, so it measures elapsed time. currentTimeMillis() is the wall-clock time, and the computer may move it backwards or forwards when it corrects its clock over the network (with a service called NTP), which would stretch or cut the timeout.

The JVM checks ownership first, so it doesn't matter that nobody is waiting. "Nothing" would be the right answer for the same call made inside the lock. Immediately, in parallel with the notifier After it gets the monitor back, which is at the earliest when the notifier leaves its synchronized block Only after every other woken thread has finished Never: it has to call wait() again notifyAll() doesn't release the lock. Running "immediately" would put two threads inside one monitor, which a monitor never allows. Other woken threads may get the lock first and change the state, which is why the guard checks again. A rail with room for one ticket has 2 waiters (producers) and 2 cooks (consumers), and both put and take call notify(). Each wait() is correctly inside a while. What can happen? Nothing bad, because the while loops make it safe Two cooks take the same ticket IllegalMonitorStateException All four threads end up waiting with nobody left to notify them The while loops stop a thread from acting on a false condition. They can't bring back a signal that went to the wrong thread. If a cook's notify() wakes the other cook instead of a waiter, that wake-up is wasted, and soon every thread waits. notifyAll(), or one Condition per kind of waiting thread, fixes it. A waiter thread calls lock.wait() with no condition, "until the dish is ready". The cook thread calls lock.notifyAll() when the dish is done. Sometimes the waiter thread waits forever. Why? notifyAll() only wakes threads that started waiting before it was called, so a dish that is ready early is a lost wake-up wait() without a timeout is not allowed notifyAll() needs a second call to wake a thread The waiter thread must call notify() itself A notification wakes only threads that are already waiting. If the dish is ready first, the signal goes nowhere, and the waiter thread then waits for a signal that already happened. Wait for a state instead: while (!ready) lock.wait();, with ready = true set before notifyAll(). A timeout would only hide the bug. From A thread's life: a cook thread is parked inside lock.wait() and another thread interrupts it. Which is true? wait() returns normally and the interrupt flag stays set wait() throws InterruptedException at once, without retaking the monitor Nothing happens until someone calls notify() wait() retakes the monitor, then throws InterruptedException with the interrupt flag cleared Like sleep, wait reacts to an interrupt by throwing InterruptedException and clearing the flag. It takes the monitor back first, so your catch or finally block still runs inside the synchronized block. The tempting "at once" answer misses that step: wait() never returns or throws without the lock. Restore the flag or let the exception propagate.
