h: wait, notify and guarded blocks · Key terms
x: Busy wait Waiting by checking a condition over and over in a loop. The thread stays RUNNABLE and keeps a core busy. Guarded block Code that waits, under a lock, until a condition holds: while (!cond) lock.wait();. Wait set The threads parked in wait() on one monitor, waiting to be notified. Entry set The threads waiting to enter a monitor (BLOCKED), including woken threads that must win the lock back. Spurious wakeup A return from wait() with no notify, interrupt or timeout. Allowed by the spec. Lost wake-up A signal sent before anyone waits for it, so the waiting thread never hears it. Producer and consumer A producer is a thread that puts work into a shared queue; a consumer is a thread that takes work out. Backpressure Making a fast producer wait when the consumer can't keep up, instead of buffering without limit. What three things does lock.wait() do? It releases lock's monitor, parks the thread in the wait set (WAITING), and retakes the monitor before it returns. Why must wait() always sit inside while (!condition)? Another woken thread may change the state before you get the lock back, and spurious wakeups are allowed. What happens if you call wait() or notify() without holding that object's monitor? IllegalMonitorStateException, at once. Does notifyAll() release the lock? No. The woken threads compete for the monitor after the notifier leaves its synchronized block. When is notify() safe to use instead of notifyAll()? Only when every waiting thread waits for the same condition and each change lets at most one of them proceed. What is a lost wake-up? A notify that happens before anyone waits. If the waiting thread has no condition to check, it then waits forever. Fix: wait for a state field, set before notifying.

h: wait, notify and guarded blocks · Go deeper
x: Timed waits are the same idea with a clock. wait(millis) returns when it's notified, interrupted, woken spuriously, or when the time is up, and it doesn't tell you which. That's why the worked example tracks its own deadline with System.nanoTime(). The JVM has had bugs here too. JDK 26 carries a fix titled "Notification can be lost due to interrupt in Object.wait". That's one more reason to use the standard library's queues and synchronizers wherever you can: they are tested far harder than any guarded block you or I will write. Two notes on observing waits. Java Flight Recorder (JFR), the event recorder built into the JVM, has a jdk.JavaMonitorWait event, with the monitor's class, the thread that notified, the timeout and whether it timed out, and JDK 25 added a jdk.JavaMonitorNotify event. And on virtual threads (very light threads that the JVM runs on top of a few ordinary carrier threads), Object.wait() used to pin, that is, hold on to, the carrier thread. Since JDK 24 (JEP 491) it no longer does in most cases. Finally, the history. wait and notify have been in Java since 1.0. java.util.concurrent arrived in Java 5 with Condition, BlockingQueue and friends, built by Doug Lea on a framework called AbstractQueuedSynchronizer. Read the source of ArrayBlockingQueue and you'll find the same guard, act and signal as in this lesson, written with a ReentrantLock and two Conditions.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · One lock per account, and two transfers that freeze each other
x: Ana and Ben pay each other at the same moment: two keys taken in opposite orders freeze for good, one lock order breaks the circle, and a lock that gives up needs a random rest Here's the version with one lock per account. A lock, remember, lets only one thread at a time into the code it guards. Here each account object's built-in lock, its monitor, does the job, and synchronized takes it. A transfer locks the account it takes money from, then the account it adds money to, so the two changes still happen as one step: Java // Naive: correct alone, freezes in pairs void transfer(Account from, Account to, long cents) { synchronized (from) { synchronized (to) { from.debit(cents); to.credit(cents); } } } // thread 1: transfer(a, b, 100) thread 2: transfer(b, a, 50) Kotlin // Naive: correct alone, freezes in pairs fun transfer(from: Account, to: Account, cents: Long) { synchronized(from) { synchronized(to) { from.debit(cents) to.credit(cents) } } } // thread 1: transfer(a, b, 100) thread 2: transfer(b, a, 50) Each call is correct on its own, and transfers between different pairs of accounts now run side by side, which was the point. The trouble starts when two transfers touch the same two accounts in opposite directions. Picture two friends who keep paying each other back. Ana's account is a and Ben's is b, and Ana sends Ben 100 for lunch at the same moment Ben sends Ana 50 for the cinema. Let's trace the smallest case. Thread 1 runs transfer(a, b, 100) and locks a. At the same moment, thread 2 runs transfer(b, a, 50) and locks b. Thread 1 now asks for b, which thread 2 holds. Thread 2 asks for a, which thread 1 holds. Each releases its first lock only after it gets its second, so neither ever will. A third transfer that needs a arrives a second later and joins the line behind them, for good. Those two threads will wait for each other forever: that's a deadlock. Nothing throws, and nothing logs. Both threads sit in BLOCKED, the state of a thread waiting for a lock. The processor has nothing to do, and every other transfer that needs either account piles up behind them. The nasty part is timing. Both threads must take their first lock inside the same tiny window, so a test that runs one transfer at a time never sees it. On a busy day, with thousands of transfers a second between the same busy accounts, it's only a matter of when. The simulator below lets you play the scheduler, the part of the system that decides which thread runs next, and find the freeze by hand. The Try it widens the window with a 300 ms sleep, so it freezes every time. Its last lines come from asking the JVM which threads are deadlocked, and the JVM answers with names. When a real program freezes, you'd ask from outside it, before anyone restarts it. That's next. Freeze two transfers Read DeadlockDemo. Each thread takes its first lock, sleeps 300 ms, then asks for the second. Write down what you expect it to print, then run it. After one second, main asks the JVM which threads are deadlocked. Delete the sleep(300) line and run it a few times. Does it still freeze every time? DeadlockDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l06; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.lang.management.ThreadInfo; import java.lang.management.ThreadMXBean; /** Two transfers lock the same two accounts in opposite orders. Run with -Pargs=wait to keep it alive for jcmd. */ public class DeadlockDemo { static final Object accountA = new Object(); static final Object accountB = new Object(); public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean stayAlive = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("wait"); Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> move(accountA, accountB), "transfer-A-to-B"); Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> move(accountB, accountA), "transfer-B-to-A"); t1.setDaemon(true); // daemon, so the JVM can still exit at the end t2.setDaemon(true); t1.start(); t2.start(); Thread.sleep(1_000); ThreadMXBean mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); long[] ids = mx.findDeadlockedThreads(); // what a health check can ask the JVM System.out.println("deadlocked threads: " + (ids == null ? 0 : ids.length)); if (ids != null) { for (ThreadInfo info : mx.getThreadInfo(ids)) { System.out.println(" " + info.getThreadName() + " is " + info.getThreadState() + ", wants a lock held by " + info.getLockOwnerName()); } } if (stayAlive) { System.out.println("pid " + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + ": run jcmd " + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + " Thread.print in another terminal (60 s)"); Thread.sleep(60_000); } } static void move(Object from, Object to) { synchronized (from) { sleep(300); // widen the window: the other thread takes its first lock now synchronized (to) { System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " moved the money"); } } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l06.DeadlockDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l06/DeadlockDemo.java DeadlockDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l06 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory // Two transfers lock the same two accounts in opposite orders. Run with -Pargs=wait to keep it alive for jcmd. private val accountA = Any() private val accountB = Any() fun main(args: Array<String>) { val stayAlive = args.firstOrNull() == "wait" val t1 = Thread({ move(accountA, accountB) }, "transfer-A-to-B").apply { isDaemon = true; start() } val t2 = Thread({ move(accountB, accountA) }, "transfer-B-to-A").apply { isDaemon = true; start() } Thread.sleep(1_000) val mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() val ids = mx.findDeadlockedThreads() // what a health check can ask the JVM println("deadlocked threads: ${ids?.size ?: 0}") ids?.let { mx.getThreadInfo(it) }?.forEach { info -> println(" ${info.threadName} is ${info.threadState}, wants a lock held by ${info.lockOwnerName}") } if (stayAlive) { val pid = ProcessHandle.current().pid() println("pid $pid: run jcmd $pid Thread.print in another terminal (60 s)") Thread.sleep(60_000) } } private fun move(from: Any, to: Any) { synchronized(from) { Thread.sleep(300) // widen the window: the other thread takes its first lock now synchronized(to) { println("${Thread.currentThread().name} moved the money") } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l06.DeadlockDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l06/DeadlockDemo.kt With the sleep: deadlocked threads: 2, both BLOCKED, each wanting a lock held by the other, and no moved the money line. Without the sleep it freezes only sometimes, and often both transfers finish. It's the same bug, now hiding: the sleep only widens a window that is always there.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Asking the JVM: a deadlock in a thread dump
x: A frozen program tempts everyone to restart it. Take a thread dump first. A thread dump is a printout of every thread in a running JVM: its name, its state and its stack (the chain of method calls it is in the middle of). The restart brings the program back, and it throws away the only record of why it stopped. The JDK's jcmd tool sends commands to a running JVM. It finds the program by its PID, the process id that the operating system gives each running program: jcmd # lists Java processes with their PIDs jcmd <pid> Thread.print # every thread's state and stack, plus deadlock detection jstack <pid>, an older tool, prints the same dump. Each thread starts with a header line and its state. Here are our two transfers, from the demo on JDK 21, trimmed: "transfer-A-to-B" #19 ... cpu=1.79ms elapsed=34.69s ... waiting for monitor entry java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor) "transfer-B-to-A" #20 ... cpu=1.40ms elapsed=34.69s ... waiting for monitor entry java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor) Both threads are BLOCKED, and in 35 seconds each one used under 2 ms of CPU time. That's a deadlock seen from outside: threads that exist, hold their locks and do nothing. Asked with jcmd, though, the JVM turns out to be a very precise witness. When it finds a cycle of threads waiting for each other's locks, it says so near the end of the dump: Found one Java-level deadlock: ============================= "transfer-A-to-B": waiting to lock monitor 0x00007fb14c0019a0 (object 0x00000006f794b518, a java.lang.Object), which is held by "transfer-B-to-A" "transfer-B-to-A": waiting to lock monitor 0x00007fb150000fe0 (object 0x00000006f794b508, a java.lang.Object), which is held by "transfer-A-to-B" Java stack information for the threads listed above: =================================================== "transfer-A-to-B": at workbench.concurrency.l06.DeadlockDemo.move(DeadlockDemo.java:42) - waiting to lock <0x00000006f794b518> (a java.lang.Object) - locked <0x00000006f794b508> (a java.lang.Object) ... "transfer-B-to-A": at workbench.concurrency.l06.DeadlockDemo.move(DeadlockDemo.java:42) - waiting to lock <0x00000006f794b508> (a java.lang.Object) - locked <0x00000006f794b518> (a java.lang.Object) ... Found 1 deadlock. Read it from the bottom up. Each thread's stack shows what it holds (- locked <...>) and what it wants (- waiting to lock <...>). The report above the stacks names who holds the lock it wants. Follow the two addresses and you've drawn the cycle: ...b508 is held by the first thread and wanted by the second, and ...b518 the other way round. Both stacks point at DeadlockDemo.java:42, the inner synchronized. The detector finds deadlocks on ReentrantLock too. That's a lock object, used by the lab's accounts, that you take by calling lock() and release by calling unlock(). There the dump says waiting for ownable synchronizer ... which is held by, and the stacks show parking to wait for instead of waiting to lock. Those threads are parked (put to sleep until the lock comes free), so they show WAITING (parking), not BLOCKED. Don't search a dump for BLOCKED alone. Thread.print -l also lists the java.util.concurrent locks each thread owns. Inside the program, the same question is one call to ThreadMXBean, the JDK's window onto the JVM's threads. It's the call the demo made: Java long[] ids = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads(); // null if none Kotlin val ids: LongArray? = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads() // null if none If you write web services, this call makes a cheap health check: a small test the service runs on itself, so whatever watches it can see that it's stuck. Two limits to know. The detector only sees cycles of Java locks. A program that uses a database often keeps a pool of open connections that threads borrow and give back. Twenty threads that each hold one of 20 pooled connections and wait for a second one are deadlocked too, but the dump shows only twenty threads waiting inside the pool. And Java Flight Recorder (JFR), the event recorder built into the JVM, has no deadlock event, so thread dumps and ThreadMXBean are how you find them. The dump tells us what happened: two threads, two locks, one cycle. To stop it happening, we need to know why a cycle can form at all. Take the dump yourself Run ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l06.DeadlockDemo -Pargs=wait. It freezes, prints its PID, and stays alive for 60 seconds. In a second terminal, run jcmd <pid> Thread.print with that PID. Find Found one Java-level deadlock and follow each thread's locked and waiting to lock lines to a line number. Run jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/dump.json and open the file. Which fields does each thread have on your JDK? terminal 2 jcmd # find the PID of DeadlockDemo jcmd <pid> Thread.print jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/dump.json The text dump ends with Found 1 deadlock. and points both threads at DeadlockDemo.java:42. The JSON has tid, name and stack per thread on JDK 21, plus state and lock fields on JDK 25 and later. Thread.dump_to_file refuses to overwrite an existing file unless you add -overwrite. diagnosticCommand.hpp at jdk-27-ga: the jcmd Thread.* commands docs

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Four conditions every deadlock needs, so break one
x: Look back at the dump and you'll find four things true at once. Together they're known as the Coffman conditions, after a 1971 paper. Each one is about a resource, which means anything a thread must hold to get its work done, such as a lock: Mutual exclusion. A resource can be held by only one thread at a time. Each of our locks had one owner. Hold and wait. A thread holds one resource while it waits for another, as each transfer held its first account. No preemption. Nobody can take a resource away from the thread that holds it (taking it away is called preemption), so neither transfer could take the other's lock. Circular wait. There's a cycle: T1 waits for T2, which waits for T1, just as the dump showed. Longer cycles count too. Take away any one of the four, and a deadlock can't form. The figure draws our cycle as a wait-for graph: an arrow from each thread to the lock it wants, and from each lock to the thread that holds it. A deadlock is a loop in that graph, and that loop is what the JVM's detector looks for. A deadlock needs all four conditions. Break any one, and it can't happen. In practice you pick one of three moves. A global lock order breaks circular wait, and the next section builds it. A timed lock breaks no preemption: a thread that can't get its second lock in time gives back the first, and the last section takes that one. Needing only one lock breaks hold and wait, as the one-lock bank we started from did. Mutual exclusion is the one you rarely remove, since it's the reason you took a lock. Data that never changes, or one owning thread per account (lesson 11 of this track), can still design it away. The four conditions apply to any resource, not only Java locks. Test the model on the kitchen from the last lesson, with 20 cooks and 20 pans. Every dish needs two pans, so each cook grabs one pan and then reaches for a second. Which conditions hold, and which move would you pick? (All four hold, and once every pan is taken, every cook waits forever. Taking both pans in one step, or cooking with one, breaks hold and wait. A rule that a cook who can't get a second pan within a minute puts the first one back breaks no preemption.) Of the three moves, a lock order costs the least, so let's start there. A wait-for graph. Each thread holds one lock and waits for the other's. The loop is the deadlock.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · The first fix: every transfer takes the locks in one order
x: Circular wait needs two threads that disagree about which lock comes first. So let's make them agree. Give every account a stable, unique key, and always lock the lower key first, whichever way the money moves: Java // Fixed: every transfer locks the lower id first void transfer(Account from, Account to, long cents) { Account first = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to; // one order for everyone Account second = first == from ? to : from; synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { from.debit(cents); to.credit(cents); } } } Kotlin // Fixed: every transfer locks the lower id first fun transfer(from: Account, to: Account, cents: Long) { val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to // one order for everyone val second = if (first === from) to else from synchronized(first) { synchronized(second) { from.debit(cents) to.credit(cents) } } } Read the two lines that pick the locks as a sentence: the first lock is the account with the lower id, and the second is the other one. Now transfer(a, b) and transfer(b, a) both lock a first. Whoever gets a runs. The other waits for a while holding nothing. That's plain contention, threads taking turns at a lock: it waits its turn, then goes. The Try it below runs the exact traffic that froze the naive version: 200,000 transfers between the same two accounts, half in each direction. Correctness first: the total stayed at 2,000,000. Then time: it finished in 33 to 50 ms on runs here. With the locks put back in argument order (from first, then to), it hung on five runs out of six, anywhere from about 1,500 to 53,000 transfers in. The sixth run finished, which is the same bug, hiding. Three details make or break the fix. The key must be unique and must never change. An account number works. hashCode() doesn't: two different objects can share one, and then two threads may disagree about the order again. The rule must be global, which means all the code follows it. Each method locking in a sensible-looking order isn't enough. One method that locks the account and then the customer, and another that locks the customer and then the account, rebuild the cycle. Put the ordering in one helper method and make every caller use it. A lock order only works if every caller follows it. Write it once, and use it everywhere. The order must also survive calls you don't see. Alien code, meaning code you don't control such as a listener, may take locks of its own, in its own order, if you call it while you hold a lock. That's the alien-code rule from synchronized and intrinsic locks, and the worked example below finds a deadlock hiding exactly there. If you keep accounts in a database, the same rule applies there. Two database transactions that lock the same two account rows in opposite orders deadlock too. (A transaction is a group of changes that succeed or fail together.) Locking rows in account-number order cures it. A lock order works when you know every lock up front. Sometimes you don't, for example when the second account is known only after you've read the first. For that, we need a lock that can give up. Same transfers, one order Read OrderedLocks. It runs 100,000 transfers in each direction between the same two accounts, with the ordering rule above. Predict whether it finishes, then run it. Break it on purpose: change move to lock from first and to second. Run it again a few times, and stop it with Ctrl+C when it hangs. OrderedLocks.java package workbench.concurrency.l06; /** The same opposite transfers, with every thread taking the locks in one global order. */ public class OrderedLocks { record Acct(int id, long[] balance) {} public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Acct a = new Acct(1, new long[] {1_000_000}); Acct b = new Acct(2, new long[] {1_000_000}); Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) move(a, b, 1); }, "A-to-B"); Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) move(b, a, 1); }, "B-to-A"); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); t1.start(); t2.start(); t1.join(); t2.join(); System.out.printf("200,000 opposite transfers in %d ms, total still %,d%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, a.balance()[0] + b.balance()[0]); } static void move(Acct from, Acct to, long cents) { Acct first = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to; // lower id first, whatever the direction Acct second = first == from ? to : from; synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { from.balance()[0] -= cents; to.balance()[0] += cents; } } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l06.OrderedLocks labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l06/OrderedLocks.java OrderedLocks.kt package workbench.concurrency.l06 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // The same opposite transfers, with every thread taking the locks in one global order. private class Acct(val id: Int, var balance: Long) fun main() { val a = Acct(1, 1_000_000) val b = Acct(2, 1_000_000) val t0 = System.nanoTime() val t1 = thread(name = "A-to-B") { repeat(100_000) { move(a, b, 1) } } val t2 = thread(name = "B-to-A") { repeat(100_000) { move(b, a, 1) } } t1.join() t2.join() println("200,000 opposite transfers in %d ms, total still %,d" .format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, a.balance + b.balance)) } private fun move(from: Acct, to: Acct, cents: Long) { val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to // lower id first, whatever the direction val second = if (first === from) to else from synchronized(first) { synchronized(second) { from.balance -= cents to.balance += cents } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l06.OrderedLocksKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l06/OrderedLocks.kt With ordered locks, 200,000 opposite transfers finish in well under a second (33 to 50 ms in runs here), and the total stays 2,000,000. In argument order it usually hangs, often within the first few thousand transfers. With no sleep to widen the window it comes down to luck, so now and then a run survives.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · A lock that gives up: tryLock, livelock and starvation
x: Every lock so far waits as long as it takes, which is the no-preemption condition at work. ReentrantLock, the lock in the lab's Account class, offers a way out. Like synchronized, its lock() waits until the lock is free. Unlike it, tryLock(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) waits at most 10 ms and returns false if the lock is still taken. (The next lesson covers ReentrantLock in full.) So a transfer can try for both locks, and let go if it can't get them: Java if (from.lock().tryLock(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { try { if (to.lock().tryLock(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { try { /* move the money */ return true; } finally { to.lock().unlock(); } } } finally { from.lock().unlock(); // couldn't get both: let go of everything } } Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(1, 10)); // random back-off, then retry Kotlin if (from.lock().tryLock(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { try { if (to.lock().tryLock(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { try { /* move the money */ return true } finally { to.lock().unlock() } } } finally { from.lock().unlock() // couldn't get both: let go of everything } } Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(1, 10)) // random back-off, then retry First we try the account we take money from, for 10 ms. If we get it, we try the other one, for 10 ms more. If both succeed, the money moves and we return. If the second fails, the finally gives back the first, so we hold nothing while we wait to retry. That release is the whole fix: a thread that can't finish lets go of everything. The random back-off on the last line, a short pause before trying again, matters more than it looks. Leave it out, or sleep a fixed time, and two threads can fall into step: both take their first lock, both fail on the second, both release, and both retry at the same moment, over and over. That's livelock. The threads are busy and change state all the time, and nothing gets done. A thread dump looks healthy, which makes livelock harder to spot than deadlock. The Try it shows a livelock with no locks at all. Picture two very polite diners at a table with one spoon. Both are hungry, and each hands the spoon over whenever the other is hungry too. In one second, the demo's diners passed it about 6 million times. Nobody ate. The fix is to break the symmetry: a random back-off, or a rule such as "after three polite turns, eat anyway". With that rule, they passed the spoon 6 times and both diners ate. Two threads that retry in step can retry forever. Back off for a random time. The third failure is starvation: the program makes progress, but one thread never does. A ReentrantLock is non-fair by default, so a thread that just released it can take it again before a waiting thread wakes up. That's faster overall, but one unlucky thread can wait a long time. A fair lock, new ReentrantLock(true), serves the longest-waiting thread first instead, at some cost in throughput, the work done per second. A writer (a thread that changes shared data) that never gets past a crowd of readers (threads that only look at it) starves the same way, and lesson 12 of this track comes back to that. A timeout, a lock that gives up and a fair queue are all things synchronized can't offer. They come from the explicit locks, and the second part of the lab puts tryLock to work. Watch a livelock, then break the symmetry Run LivelockDemo. Both diners are hungry, and both are polite. Read the count of handovers and meals. Predict what a rule of "three polite turns, then eat anyway" will print. Then run it again with -Pargs=fixed. LivelockDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l06; /** Two polite diners share one spoon. Each hands it over while the other is hungry. Try -Pargs=fixed. */ public class LivelockDemo { static volatile int spoonOwner = 0; // diner 0 or diner 1 static final boolean[] hungry = {true, true}; // written by its owner only, read by the other static volatile boolean stop; static final long[] handovers = new long[2]; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean fixed = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("fixed"); Thread d0 = new Thread(() -> dine(0, fixed), "diner-0"); Thread d1 = new Thread(() -> dine(1, fixed), "diner-1"); d0.start(); d1.start(); d0.join(1_000); d1.join(1_000); stop = true; d0.join(); d1.join(); System.out.printf("spoon handed over %,d times; meals eaten: %d%n", handovers[0] + handovers[1], (hungry[0] ? 0 : 1) + (hungry[1] ? 0 : 1)); } static void dine(int me, boolean fixed) { int other = 1 - me; int politeTurns = 0; while (!stop) { if (spoonOwner != me) { // not my spoon: wait for it Thread.onSpinWait(); continue; } boolean otherHungry; synchronized (hungry) { otherHungry = hungry[other]; } if (otherHungry && (!fixed || politeTurns < 3)) { politeTurns++; handovers[me]++; spoonOwner = other; // "you first": both keep saying it continue; } synchronized (hungry) { hungry[me] = false; } // eat spoonOwner = other; // then pass the spoon on return; } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l06.LivelockDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l06/LivelockDemo.java LivelockDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l06 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Two polite diners share one spoon. Each hands it over while the other is hungry. Try -Pargs=fixed. @Volatile private var spoonOwner = 0 // diner 0 or diner 1 private val hungry = booleanArrayOf(true, true) // guarded by synchronized(hungry) @Volatile private var stop = false private val handovers = LongArray(2) fun main(args: Array<String>) { val fixed = args.firstOrNull() == "fixed" val d0 = thread(name = "diner-0") { dine(0, fixed) } val d1 = thread(name = "diner-1") { dine(1, fixed) } d0.join(1_000) d1.join(1_000) stop = true d0.join() d1.join() val meals = (if (hungry[0]) 0 else 1) + (if (hungry[1]) 0 else 1) println("spoon handed over %,d times; meals eaten: %d".format(handovers[0] + handovers[1], meals)) } private fun dine(me: Int, fixed: Boolean) { val other = 1 - me var politeTurns = 0 while (!stop) { if (spoonOwner != me) { // not my spoon: wait for it Thread.onSpinWait() continue } val otherHungry = synchronized(hungry) { hungry[other] } if (otherHungry && (!fixed || politeTurns < 3)) { politeTurns++ handovers[me]++ spoonOwner = other // "you first": both keep saying it continue } synchronized(hungry) { hungry[me] = false } // eat spoonOwner = other // then pass the spoon on return } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l06.LivelockDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l06/LivelockDemo.kt Without the fix: millions of handovers in one second (about 5.7 to 6 million in runs here) and meals eaten: 0. Both threads were RUNNABLE the whole time. With -Pargs=fixed: 6 handovers and 2 meals, done at once.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Java and Kotlin
x: Ordered locking in Java and Kotlin Java void transfer(Account from, Account to, long cents) { Account first = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to; Account second = first == from ? to : from; first.lock().lock(); try { second.lock().lock(); try { from.debit(cents); to.credit(cents); } finally { second.lock().unlock(); } } finally { first.lock().unlock(); } } Kotlin fun transfer(from: Account, to: Account, cents: Long) { val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to val second = if (first === from) to else from first.lock().withLock { // kotlin.concurrent.withLock: lock, try, finally unlock second.lock().withLock { from.debit(cents) to.credit(cents) } } } Both versions take the same two locks in the same order, so both are safe for the same reason. Drop the ordering, and both deadlock the same way: Kotlin adds no protection here. One thing differs. Kotlin's withLock { } extension on Lock writes the lock(), the try and the finally for you, so the release can't go missing. The Java version spells out that discipline by hand, which makes every lock() and its matching finally easy to check line by line when you read it. jcmd is the neutral referee here: both compile to the same ReentrantLock calls, and a deadlock in either one produces the same dump.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Worked example
x: Find a deadlock that hides behind a callback The bank keeps a Ledger, the record of every entry (each amount paid in or out). It also keeps an AuditLog, a file that lists recent entries so someone can check them later. Every time the ledger records an entry, it tells the log. Once a second, a timer thread flushes the log: it writes the waiting entries to the file, along with the ledger's current balance. Each class looks fine on its own. Before you read on, find the cycle. class Ledger { synchronized void post(Entry e) { entries.add(e); auditLog.record(e); // calls AuditLog while holding the Ledger lock } synchronized long balance() { return sum(entries); } } class AuditLog { synchronized void record(Entry e) { pending.add(e); } synchronized void flush() { long b = ledger.balance(); // calls Ledger while holding the AuditLog lock write(pending, b); pending.clear(); } } class Ledger(private val auditLog: AuditLog) { @Synchronized fun post(e: Entry) { entries += e auditLog.record(e) // calls AuditLog while holding the Ledger lock } @Synchronized fun balance(): Long = sum(entries) } class AuditLog { @Synchronized fun record(e: Entry) { pending += e } @Synchronized fun flush() { val b = ledger.balance() // calls Ledger while holding the AuditLog lock write(pending, b) pending.clear() } } A teller thread, one serving a customer, is in post: it holds the Ledger lock and wants the AuditLog lock. The timer thread is in flush: it holds the AuditLog lock and wants the Ledger lock. It's our two transfers again, with the two locks split across two classes. The dump would show it like this: "teller-7": waiting to lock <0x...a0> (a AuditLog), locked <0x...b8> (a Ledger) "log-flusher": waiting to lock <0x...b8> (a Ledger), locked <0x...a0> (a AuditLog) You could impose an order, but the cleaner fix is to stop holding one lock while calling the other class. Each method keeps its own lock only around its own state. Before reading the fix, decide: which call in each method is the alien one, the call into code this class doesn't control? void post(Entry e) { synchronized (this) { entries.add(e); } auditLog.record(e); // 1. no Ledger lock held while calling out } void flush() { long b = ledger.balance(); // 2. read the balance before taking our own lock List<Entry> batch; synchronized (this) { batch = List.copyOf(pending); pending.clear(); } write(batch, b); // 3. slow file writing with no lock at all } fun post(e: Entry) { synchronized(this) { entries += e } auditLog.record(e) // 1. no Ledger lock held while calling out } fun flush() { val b = ledger.balance() // 2. read the balance before taking our own lock val batch = synchronized(this) { pending.toList().also { pending.clear() } } write(batch, b) // 3. slow file writing with no lock at all } Now no thread ever holds one of the two locks while asking for the other, so hold and wait is gone and no cycle can form. The balance written with the batch may be a moment older than the last entry. For an audit log that's fine. If it weren't, you'd need one lock over both, which is the one-lock design we started from.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Lab
x: Fix a transfer deadlock, then add a transfer that gives up labs/concurrency/src/main/java/workbench/concurrency/l06/Transfers.java labs/concurrency/src/main/java/workbench/concurrency/l06/Account.java ./gradlew :concurrency:test --tests 'workbench.concurrency.l06.*' Run the tests. Two transfer tests time out after 10 seconds: they deadlocked. The three tryTransfer tests fail with UnsupportedOperationException. Read Account, a bank account with an id, a balance and its own ReentrantLock. You don't change it. debit (take money out) and credit (put money in) throw unless you hold that account's lock, so a forgotten lock fails loudly. Part 1: fix Transfers.transfer so it always locks the account with the lower id() first. Keep the try/finally around each unlock(). Part 2: write tryTransfer. Loop until the deadline: tryLock the first account for 10 ms, then the second for 10 ms. If you get both, move the money and return true. If not, release what you hold, sleep a random 1 to 10 ms, and loop. Return false when time is up. Run the tests until all five pass, then run them twice more. A transfer from an account to itself (from == to) takes the same ReentrantLock twice. That's fine, because it's reentrant, as long as you release it twice. In part 2, put the from.lock().unlock() in a finally that runs whether or not you got to. The test checks that from is free after a failed attempt. ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(1, 10) gives a random back-off without sharing a Random between threads. All five tests in TransfersTest pass, three runs in a row. By the end you can explain the four conditions for deadlock, remove one with lock ordering or timed tryLock, tell deadlock from livelock and starvation, and find a deadlock in a thread dump.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Quiz
x: Which change makes transfer(from, to) safe from deadlock when transfers run in both directions? Mark the field that holds each balance volatile Always lock the account with the lower id first, then the other Add Thread.sleep(1) between the two locks Make transfer a synchronized instance method on each account One global order means no thread can hold the second lock while waiting for the first, so circular wait can't happen. volatile has nothing to do with locking, and a sleep only changes the odds. The tempting one is the synchronized method: on the source account it is still "lock from, then to", the same broken order. Two threads use tryLock with a fixed 5 ms sleep between attempts. A thread dump shows both RUNNABLE or TIMED_WAITING, their stacks change between dumps, and no deadlock is reported. Nothing has completed in a minute. What is this? A deadlock that the JVM failed to detect Starvation of one thread Livelock: they keep retrying in step and both keep failing A pause for garbage collection The threads are active, they release and retake locks, and neither makes progress. That's livelock, and the fixed sleep keeps them in step; a random back-off breaks the symmetry. It isn't deadlock, because nobody waits forever on a held lock. It isn't starvation either, because starvation needs other threads that do make progress. A program stops answering. You suspect a lock cycle. Which tool tells you for sure? A JFR recording, filtered on the jdk.Deadlock event The garbage collector's log Restarting the program and watching whether it happens again jcmd <pid> Thread.print, which prints "Found one Java-level deadlock" with the threads and locks involved The thread dump's deadlock detector finds cycles on monitors and on ReentrantLock, and names who holds what. JFR has no deadlock event, so the first option sounds right and finds nothing. Restarting destroys the evidence. Take the dump first. A report thread needs a ReentrantLock for 50 ms once a minute. Transfer threads take the same lock thousands of times a second and grab it again the moment they release it. The report sometimes waits for minutes. What is this, and what is one fix? Starvation; a fair lock, new ReentrantLock(true), gives the longest waiter the next turn Deadlock; order the locks Livelock; add random back-off A race condition; make the field volatile Everyone else makes progress and one thread never gets its turn: that's starvation. A non-fair lock lets a running thread take the lock again ahead of waiting threads. A fair lock serves them in order, at some cost in throughput. It isn't deadlock, because the lock keeps changing hands. Making the transfers hold the lock for less time also helps. From wait, notify and guarded blocks: the kitchen's rail with room for one ticket, using notify(), stalls with all four threads WAITING. Will jcmd Thread.print report a Java-level deadlock? Yes, every stall is reported as a deadlock No: no thread holds the monitor, they are all waiting for a notification that will never come Yes, but only with the -l flag No, because jcmd can't see WAITING threads The deadlock detector looks for threads blocked on locks that the others hold. Threads in wait() hold nothing, and the monitor is free. They're stuck because a signal went to the wrong thread, not because of a lock cycle, so the dump shows four WAITING threads and no deadlock section. jcmd sees WAITING threads perfectly well; there's just no cycle to report.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Key terms
x: Deadlock Threads that each wait for a resource another one holds, so none can ever proceed. Livelock Threads that keep reacting to each other, busy but making no progress. Starvation One thread never gets the resource it needs while others keep getting it. Lock ordering A rule that every thread takes locks in the same global order. Wait-for graph A picture of which thread waits for which. A cycle in it is a deadlock. Thread dump A snapshot of every thread's state and stack, from jcmd Thread.print or jstack. Back-off A short pause, ideally of random length, before a thread tries again. Fair lock A lock that serves the longest-waiting thread first, so no thread starves, at some cost in speed. Deadlock condition 1: what is mutual exclusion? A resource can be held by only one thread at a time. Every lock has it. Deadlock condition 2: what is hold and wait? A thread holds one resource while waiting for another. Deadlock condition 3: what is no preemption? Nobody can take a resource away from the thread that holds it; only the holder can release it. Deadlock condition 4: what is circular wait? A cycle of threads, each waiting for a resource the next one holds: T1 waits for T2, T2 waits for T1. How does a global lock order prevent deadlock? Every thread takes locks in the same order (for example lower id first), so no cycle can form. It breaks circular wait. Deadlock vs livelock vs starvation, in one line each. Deadlock: threads wait forever for each other. Livelock: threads stay busy reacting to each other and make no progress. Starvation: others progress, one thread never gets a turn. What does jcmd <pid> Thread.print print when it finds a lock cycle? Found one Java-level deadlock:, then each thread, the lock it waits for and who holds it, then their stacks, ending with Found 1 deadlock.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Go deeper
x: The JVM's detector covers two kinds of lock. ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() looks for cycles on monitors and on ownable synchronizers, locks that one thread owns, such as ReentrantLock and the write lock of ReentrantReadWriteLock (a lock with separate sides for readers and writers, from the next lesson). The older findMonitorDeadlockedThreads() sees monitors only. Neither sees semaphores and latches (the counters and one-time gates of lesson 10 of this track), Object.wait(), futures waiting on each other or pooled connections, because none of those has a single owning thread the JVM could point at. That blind spot covers a common case: two thread pools waiting on each other. A thread pool is a fixed group of threads that runs the tasks you hand it, and a Future is a handle to a task's result that may not be ready yet. Task A runs on pool 1 and waits for a Future from pool 2, while pool 2's only thread waits for a Future from pool 1. No lock is involved, so the detector stays silent. The dump still gives it away if you read the stacks: every pool thread is parked in FutureTask.get or CompletableFuture.join. Java Concurrency in Practice calls this thread-starvation deadlock. For tooling, jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json writes the dump as JSON, and the format keeps improving. On JDK 21 each thread has only tid, name and stack. JDK 25 added per-thread state, parkBlocker, blockedOn, waitingOn, owner and the monitors each thread owns, which is enough to rebuild the wait-for graph. JDK 26 added java.util.concurrent lock information. JDK 27 added a formatVersion field. If you build tooling on these dumps, check that field and the JDK version first. Two smaller notes. Ordering needs a unique key; with none, Java Concurrency in Practice breaks ties with System.identityHashCode and one extra global lock. And a fair ReentrantLock only orders the lock's own queue: its Javadoc warns that fairness of locks doesn't guarantee fairness of thread scheduling. Databases take the opposite approach to the JVM. Oracle, for example, detects deadlocks between sessions (open connections to the database) and breaks them by failing one statement. Your code must be ready to retry that transaction, ideally after ordering its row locks so the retry doesn't deadlock again.

h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · A lock that can give up: ReentrantLock, tryLock and lockInterruptibly
x: The vault with controls on the door: tryLock gives up after 200 ms, lockInterruptibly hears the shutdown, unlock goes in finally, each Condition is its own bench, and a reader who asks for the write lock waits for itself In synchronized and intrinsic locks, we pictured a lock as the key to the bank's vault: one door, one key, and a line of threads outside. synchronized gives that line no choices. A thread that joins it waits until the key comes back, however long that takes. It can't give up after a timeout. An interrupt, another thread's request that it stop, doesn't reach it until it holds the key. ReentrantLock, from java.util.concurrent.locks, is the same vault with controls on the door. Like synchronized, it lets one thread in at a time, and the next owner sees every write the last owner made. It's reentrant too: the owner can take it again, and the lock counts the holds. Unlike synchronized, it gives a waiting thread choices: tryLock() takes the lock only if it's free right now, and returns false otherwise. tryLock(200, MILLISECONDS) waits at most 200 ms. The last lesson used it to break deadlocks, where threads wait for each other forever. lockInterruptibly() waits, but leaves the line with InterruptedException when the thread is interrupted. new ReentrantLock(true) makes a fair lock, which hands the lock to the thread that has waited longest. TryLockDemo plays out the evening from the opening. The interest thread holds the ledger lock for 1.5 seconds. Older code in the bank still guards the ledger with synchronized, so the job also holds that monitor, the built-in lock every Java object has. Three threads want in. The cash-machine waits with tryLock(200 ms), the statement printer with lockInterruptibly(), and an old teller screen with synchronized. After 400 ms, the main thread prints two of their states and interrupts those two, as a shutdown would. Before you read the output, guess which of the three keeps waiting after it's interrupted: cash-machine: gave up after 200 ms, asked the customer to try again states: statement=WAITING, teller=BLOCKED statement: interrupted while waiting, gave up cleanly teller: got the monitor at last, interrupted=true The cash machine waited exactly as long as we allowed, then gave its customer an answer. The statement printer left the line the moment it was interrupted. The teller heard nothing. It got the monitor after the full 1.5 seconds, and only then found out that someone had asked it to stop, more than a second earlier. The two states differ, too. A thread waiting for a ReentrantLock is parked, which means put to sleep until another thread wakes it, so it shows WAITING. A thread waiting for a monitor shows BLOCKED. Expect WAITING (parking) when you read a thread dump (the printout of every thread's state) of code that uses explicit locks. All that control has a price, the one the opening warned about. A synchronized block lets go when it exits, even when it throws. A ReentrantLock lets go only when you call unlock(). So every use follows one pattern. Here it guards the ledger's entries, the amounts paid in and out: Java private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); private final List<Entry> entries = new ArrayList<>(); // the ledger's entries, guarded by lock void post(Entry e) { lock.lock(); // before the try, never inside it try { entries.add(e); } finally { lock.unlock(); // first line of finally: runs even if add throws } } Kotlin private val lock = ReentrantLock() private val entries = mutableListOf<Entry>() // the ledger's entries, guarded by lock fun post(e: Entry) { lock.withLock { // kotlin.concurrent: lock(), try, finally unlock() entries += e } } Read the Java version aloud: take the lock; try the work; finally, whatever happens, give the lock back. In Kotlin, withLock { } writes the lock(), the try and the finally for you. Leave out the finally, and one rare exception, from a bad input say, skips the unlock(). The thread moves on with the lock still taken, and every thread after it parks in lock() for good. A thread dump then shows dozens of threads WAITING, while jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l names an owner that is busy somewhere else entirely. A ReentrantLock lets go only when you tell it to. Put every unlock() in a finally. My rule: use synchronized for a short, simple critical section (the code that runs under the lock), and switch to ReentrantLock when you need one of its controls. For ordinary code, the two cost about the same on current JDKs. One old reason to switch is mostly gone, too. A virtual thread is a very light thread that the JVM runs on top of an ordinary one. Before JDK 24, a virtual thread that blocked inside synchronized held on to that ordinary thread. JDK 24 fixed that in most cases (the change is called JEP 491), and the virtual threads track covers it. The cash machine can give up now. But a lock is also a place to wait for something to change, as the cooks did in wait, notify and guarded blocks. There, too, ReentrantLock has something better. Three ways to wait for a busy lock Read TryLockDemo. The interest thread holds the ledger lock and the old monitor for 1.5 seconds. cash-machine waits with tryLock(200 ms), statement with lockInterruptibly(), and teller with synchronized. Predict the order of the four output lines, and the states printed for statement and teller. Run it. Then let the cash machine wait 2 seconds instead of 200 ms, and run it again. 1.5 s. * Three threads want in, each in a different way. */ public class TryLockDemo { static final ReentrantLock ledger = new ReentrantLock(); static final Object monitor = new Object(); // older code still guards the ledger with this public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread interest = new Thread(() -> { ledger.lock(); try { synchronized (monitor) { // the h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · One waiting room per reason to wait: Condition
x: Remember the kitchen from wait, notify and guarded blocks. Waiters clip order tickets to a rail, and cooks take them off. When the rail is full, waiters wait for a free slot. When it's empty, cooks wait for a ticket. A monitor has only one wait set, the group of threads waiting on it, so both kinds sat on the same bench. A notify() meant for a cook could wake a waiter instead, and that stalled the kitchen. So we woke everyone with notifyAll() and let each while loop decide. A ReentrantLock can have as many benches as you like. Each one is a Condition: a queue of threads waiting for one particular change, made with lock.newCondition(). await() plays the part of wait(). It lets go of the lock, parks, and takes the lock back before it returns. signal() and signalAll() play notify() and notifyAll(). Let's rebuild the rail with two of them: notFull, where waiters wait for a free slot, and notEmpty, where cooks wait for a ticket. Here's the waiter's side, put: Java private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); private final Condition notFull = lock.newCondition(); // waiters wait here for a free slot private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition(); // cooks wait here for a ticket public void put(T ticket) throws InterruptedException { lock.lock(); try { while (items.size() == capacity) notFull.await(); // lets go of the lock while waiting items.addLast(ticket); notEmpty.signal(); // wake one cook } finally { lock.unlock(); } } Kotlin private val lock = ReentrantLock() private val notFull = lock.newCondition() // waiters wait here for a free slot private val notEmpty = lock.newCondition() // cooks wait here for a ticket fun put(ticket: T) = lock.withLock { while (items.size == capacity) notFull.await() // lets go of the lock while waiting items.addLast(ticket) notEmpty.signal() // wake one cook } First we take the lock. While the rail is full, we wait on notFull, which lets go of the lock until a cook signals. Then we clip the ticket on and signal notEmpty. Only cooks ever wait there, and one new ticket lets exactly one cook go on. Those are the two conditions under which the kitchen lesson said a single notify() is safe, and now they hold on each bench. So signal() is enough, and the other waiters sleep on. Is it worth the trouble? WakeupCount measures it. Four waiters and four cooks move 20,000 tickets through a rail with room for one, twice. The first run uses one Condition with signalAll(), the kitchen lesson's design. The second uses two with signal(). Each run counts its wasted wake-ups, the times a thread woke, checked its loop, and had to wait again. One run printed: one condition, signalAll(): wasted wake-ups: 88,340 (2175 ms) notFull + notEmpty, signal(): wasted wake-ups: 375 (676 ms) Both runs moved all 20,000 tickets. With one bench, every signalAll() woke all seven other threads, and most went straight back to sleep: 88,340 times. With two benches, that fell to 375, and the run took a third of the time. The Kotlin twin printed 93,684 against 3,155. The count isn't zero, because of barging: a running thread can grab the lock and the ticket before the signalled thread wakes up. That's why the while loop stays. The rules from the kitchen still hold: Call await() and signal() only while you hold the lock, or you get IllegalMonitorStateException. Wait in a while loop. The Condition Javadoc (the official API documentation) allows spurious wake-ups, wake-ups with no signal at all. And another thread can take the ticket between the signal and your return. Don't call wait() or notify() on a Condition. It's an object like any other, so notFull.wait() compiles. It uses the condition's own monitor, which you don't hold, and throws. A Condition can also wait against a deadline. awaitNanos(n) waits at most n nanoseconds (billionths of a second) and returns the time left, so a loop can keep waiting for whatever remains. The lab's offer(item, timeout) uses it. One kind of waiting thread per Condition lets signal() wake the right one. Keep the while loop anyway. Waiters and cooks both change the rail, so they have to take turns. Many threads only read shared data, though, and readers never get in each other's way. Making them take turns anyway is a waste. Count the wasted wake-ups Read WakeupCount. Four waiters and four cooks move 20,000 tickets through a rail with room for one: once with one Condition and signalAll(), once with two Conditions and signal(). A wake-up is wasted when a thread wakes, checks its while loop, and has to wait again. Predict which version wastes more, and roughly how many more. Run it twice and compare the counts and the times. WakeupCount.java package workbench.concurrency.l07; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** * The kitchen's rail with room for one ticket. 4 waiters (producers) and 4 cooks (consumers) * move 20,000 tickets through it, twice: once with one Condition and signalAll(), once with * notFull/notEmpty and signal(). A wake-up is "wasted" when the thread wakes, re-checks, * and has to wait again. */ public class WakeupCount { static final class Buffer { final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); final Condition notFull; final Condition notEmpty; final boolean shared; final ArrayDeque<Integer> items = new ArrayDeque<>(); long wasted; // guarded by lock Buffer(boolean oneCondition) { shared = oneCondition; notFull = lock.newCondition(); notEmpty = oneCondition ? notFull : lock.newCondition(); // same queue, or two } void put(int x) throws InterruptedException { lock.lock(); try { while (items.size() == 1) { notFull.await(); if (items.size() == 1) wasted++; // woke up for nothing } items.add(x); if (shared) notEmpty.signalAll(); else notEmpty.signal(); } finally { lock.unlock(); } } int take() throws InterruptedException { lock.lock(); try { while (items.isEmpty()) { notEmpty.await(); if (items.isEmpty()) wasted++; } int x = items.remove(); if (shared) notFull.signalAll(); else notFull.signal(); return x; } finally { lock.unlock(); } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (boolean one : new boolean[] {true, false}) { Buffer buffer = new Buffer(one); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { threads.add(new Thread(() -> { try { for (int n = 0; n < 5_000; n++) buffer.put(n); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } })); threads.add(new Thread(() -> { try { for (int n = 0; n < 5_000; n++) buffer.take(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } })); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (Thread t : threads) t.start(); for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); System.out.printf("%-34s wasted wake-ups: %,9d (%d ms)%n", one ? "one condition, signalAll():" : "notFull + notEmpty, signal():", buffer.wasted, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l07.WakeupCount labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l07/WakeupCount.java WakeupCount.kt package workbench.concurrency.l07 import java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock // The kitchen's rail with room for one ticket. 4 waiters (producers) and 4 cooks (consumers) // move 20,000 tickets through it, twice: once with one Condition and signalAll(), once with // notFull/notEmpty and signal(). A wake-up is "wasted" when the thread wakes, re-checks, // and has to wait again. private class CountingBuffer(private val shared: Boolean) { private val lock = ReentrantLock() private val notFull: Condition = lock.newCondition() private val notEmpty: Condition = if (shared) notFull else lock.newCondition() // same queue, or two private val items = ArrayDeque<Int>() var wasted = 0L // guarded by lock private set fun put(x: Int) = lock.withLock { while (items.size == 1) { notFull.await() if (items.size == 1) wasted++ // woke up for nothing } items.addLast(x) if (shared) notEmpty.signalAll() else notEmpty.signal() } fun take(): Int = lock.withLock { while (items.isEmpty()) { notEmpty.await() if (items.isEmpty()) wasted++ } val x = items.removeFirst() if (shared) notFull.signalAll() else notFull.signal() x } } fun main() { for (one in listOf(true, false)) { val buffer = CountingBuffer(one) val t0 = System.nanoTime() val threads = (1..4).flatMap { listOf( thread { repeat(5_000) { n -> buffer.put(n) } }, thread { repeat(5_000) { buffer.take() } }, ) } threads.forEach { it.join() } val label = if (one) "one condition, signalAll():" else "notFull + notEmpty, signal():" println("%-34s wasted wake-ups: %,9d (%d ms)".format(label, buffer.wasted, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l07.WakeupCountKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l07/WakeupCount.kt With one condition, tens of thousands of wake-ups are wasted (88,340 and 93,684 in runs here), because every signalAll() wakes all seven other threads and most of them go back to sleep. With two conditions, the count drops to hundreds or a few thousand, and the run takes about a third or a quarter of the time. It isn't zero, because a running thread can barge in and take the ticket before the signalled thread wakes. That's why the while loop stays. One lock, one line of threads that want it, and a separate waiting room for each condition. await() lets go of the lock and parks in its room; signal() sends one thread from the room back to the line.
