h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · Many readers, one writer: ReadWriteLock, and the upgrade that hangs
x: The bank keeps a table of exchange rates. For each currency pair, such as EURUSD, it says how many dollars one euro costs. Every cash machine and every teller reads it, about 5,000 times a second, and a refresh job replaces the rates every five seconds. Behind a plain lock, each reader waits for every other reader, though reading changes nothing. Picture a reading room in a library. Anyone may come in and read, as many people at once as like. Rearranging the shelves is different: the librarian waits until the room is empty, then works alone with the door shut. A ReentrantReadWriteLock is that room. It has two locks inside. Many threads can hold the read lock together. The write lock is exclusive: it waits until no reader and no writer is inside, and while it's held, nobody else gets in: Java private final ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock(); private final Map<String, BigDecimal> rates = new HashMap<>(); // guarded by rw BigDecimal rate(String pair) { rw.readLock().lock(); // many threads can hold this at once try { return rates.get(pair); } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); } } void refresh(Map<String, BigDecimal> fresh) { rw.writeLock().lock(); // waits until no reader and no writer holds the lock try { rates.clear(); rates.putAll(fresh); } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } } Kotlin private val rw = ReentrantReadWriteLock() private val rates = HashMap<String, BigDecimal>() // guarded by rw fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal? = rw.read { // many threads can hold this at once rates[pair] } fun refresh(fresh: Map<String, BigDecimal>) = rw.write { // waits until no reader and no writer holds the lock rates.clear() rates.putAll(fresh) } Readers share the room, and the refresh works alone. The trap is a missing rate. The table is a cache, a store of answers kept close at hand, and a pair that isn't in it yet is called a cache miss. The natural code checks under the read lock and, if the rate is missing, takes the write lock to load it: Java // Naive: hangs the first time a pair is missing rw.readLock().lock(); try { BigDecimal r = rates.get(pair); if (r != null) return r; rw.writeLock().lock(); // waits for every reader to leave, this thread included: forever try { r = loader.apply(pair); rates.put(pair, r); return r; } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); } Kotlin // Naive: hangs the first time a pair is missing rw.readLock().lock() try { val r = rates[pair] if (r != null) return r rw.writeLock().lock() // waits for every reader to leave, this thread included: forever try { return loader(pair).also { rates[pair] = it } } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock() } } finally { rw.readLock().unlock() } Asking for the write lock while you still hold the read lock is called an upgrade, and ReentrantReadWriteLock doesn't support it. The write lock waits for every reader to leave. This thread is a reader, and it won't leave until it gets the write lock. So it waits, very patiently, for itself. In the reading room, it's a reader who decides to rearrange the shelves and waits inside for the room to empty. Two threads that try it at once wait for each other. The thread dump won't point it out, either. Run UpgradeDeadlock with -Pargs=hang and ask for a dump with jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l. On JDK 21, main looks like this, trimmed: "main" #1 ... waiting on condition java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking) at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(java.base@21.0.12.1/Native Method) - parking to wait for <0x0000000737818bc0> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock$NonfairSync) ... at java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock$WriteLock.lock(java.base@21.0.12.1/ReentrantReadWriteLock.java:959) at workbench.concurrency.l07.UpgradeDeadlock.main(UpgradeDeadlock.java:22) Locked ownable synchronizers: - None There's no Found one Java-level deadlock, and the list of locks that main owns is empty. A read lock has no single owner, so the JVM's deadlock detector has no cycle to find. It's a deadlock with one thread in it, and nobody reports it. The fix has three steps: let go of the read lock, take the write lock, and check again. The check matters, because another thread may have loaded the rate while you held nothing. The lab's FxRateCache needs exactly that. Going the other way, a downgrade, is allowed: while holding the write lock, take the read lock, then let go of the write lock. A read lock never turns into a write lock. Let go first, then check again under the write lock. A read-write lock pays off when reads are frequent and take a while, and writes are rare. For a map lookup that takes 50 nanoseconds, its extra bookkeeping can cost more than it saves. And when the refresh replaces the whole table at once, a map that never changes, held in a volatile field (one whose reads always see the latest write), needs no lock at all. Lesson 11 of this track shows that pattern. The read lock still writes to memory, though: every reader adds one to its count on the way in. On a very busy path, that one write is the next cost to go. Upgrade, then downgrade Run UpgradeDeadlock. It tries the upgrade with tryLock(1, SECONDS) so it can't hang, then does a downgrade. Run the Kotlin twin. Its last line puts write { } inside read { }. Predict: does it hang? Optional: run the Java one with -Pargs=hang. In a second terminal, run jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l with the printed PID and find main. Stop it with Ctrl+C. UpgradeDeadlock.java package workbench.concurrency.l07; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock; /** * One thread, one ReentrantReadWriteLock. Upgrading (read, then write) never succeeds. * Downgrading (write, then read, then release the write) is allowed. * Run with -Pargs=hang to use lock() instead of tryLock() and see the thread wait forever. */ public class UpgradeDeadlock { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock(); boolean hang = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("hang"); // 1. the "upgrade": ask for the write lock while still holding the read lock rw.readLock().lock(); try { System.out.println("holding the read lock, read holds = " + rw.getReadHoldCount()); if (hang) { System.out.println("calling writeLock().lock() ... (pid " + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + ", Ctrl+C to stop)"); rw.writeLock().lock(); // waits for every reader to leave, us included } boolean got = rw.writeLock().tryLock(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // the same wait, with a time limit System.out.println("write lock while holding a read lock, after 1 s: " + got); } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); } // 2. the downgrade: write lock, then read lock, then let go of the write lock rw.writeLock().lock(); try { rw.readLock().lock(); // allowed: we are the only writer } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } try { System.out.println("downgraded: write locked = " + rw.isWriteLocked() + ", read holds = " + rw.getReadHoldCount()); } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l07.UpgradeDeadlock labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l07/UpgradeDeadlock.java UpgradeDeadlock.kt package workbench.concurrency.l07 import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock import kotlin.concurrent.read import kotlin.concurrent.write // One thread, one ReentrantReadWriteLock. Upgrading (read, then write) never succeeds. // Downgrading (write, then read, then release the write) is allowed. // Run with -Pargs=hang to use lock() instead of tryLock() and see the thread wait forever. fun main(args: Array<String>) { val rw = ReentrantReadWriteLock() val hang = args.firstOrNull() == "hang" // 1. the "upgrade": ask for the write lock while still holding the read lock rw.readLock().lock() try { println("holding the read lock, read holds = ${rw.readHoldCount}") if (hang) { println("calling writeLock().lock() ... (pid ${ProcessHandle.current().pid()}, Ctrl+C to stop)") rw.writeLock().lock() // waits for every reader to leave, us included } val got = rw.writeLock().tryLock(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // the same wait, with a time limit println("write lock while holding a read lock, after 1 s: $got") } finally { rw.readLock().unlock() } // 2. the downgrade: write lock, then read lock, then let go of the write lock rw.writeLock().lock() try { rw.readLock().lock() // allowed: we are the only writer } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock() } try { println("downgraded: write locked = ${rw.isWriteLocked}, read holds = ${rw.readHoldCount}") } finally { rw.readLock().unlock() } // 3. Kotlin only: write {} inside read {} does not hang, because write {} first lets go of // this thread's read locks. That makes it a release-then-acquire, not an atomic upgrade. rw.read { rw.write { println("kotlin write {} inside read {}: write locked = ${rw.isWriteLocked}, read holds = ${rw.readHoldCount}") } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l07.UpgradeDeadlockKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l07/UpgradeDeadlock.kt write lock while holding a read lock, after 1 s: false, then downgraded: write locked = false, read holds = 1. The Kotlin write { } inside read { } doesn't hang: it prints write locked = true, read holds = 0, because Kotlin's write lets go of this thread's read locks first. With -Pargs=hang, the dump shows main parked in WriteLock.lock and no deadlock report. ReentrantReadWriteLock (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · Reading with no lock at all: StampedLock and the optimistic read
x: Every reader of a read lock adds one to the lock's count, and takes one away on the way out. On a machine with many cores, that count lives in one cache line. A cache line is the small block of memory that a core copies into its own fast memory, its cache. A core must own the line before it can write to it. So every reader pulls the line over to its own core, and the line bounces from core to core. StampedLock (JDK 8) adds a mode that writes nothing at all, the optimistic read. Read it as "go ahead and read, then check whether anyone wrote while you did". The rate table shows two prices for the euro: the bank buys euros at one price and sells them 2 cents higher. A reader must never see a new buying price with an old selling price: Java long stamp = lock.tryOptimisticRead(); // 1. no lock, just a version number long b = buy, s = sell; // 2. copy both prices into locals if (!lock.validate(stamp)) { // 3. a writer got in: the copies may be torn stamp = lock.readLock(); // 4. fall back to a real read lock try { b = buy; s = sell; } finally { lock.unlockRead(stamp); } } return new EuroPrices(b, s); // 5. use the locals only after validate Kotlin var stamp = lock.tryOptimisticRead() // 1. no lock, just a version number var b = buy; var s = sell // 2. copy both prices into locals if (!lock.validate(stamp)) { // 3. a writer got in: the copies may be torn stamp = lock.readLock() // 4. fall back to a real read lock try { b = buy; s = sell } finally { lock.unlockRead(stamp) } } return EuroPrices(b, s) // 5. use the locals only after validate tryOptimisticRead() returns a stamp, a version number of the lock (or 0 if a writer holds it). We copy both prices into locals with no lock held. Then validate(stamp) asks: did any writer get in since that stamp? If not, the two copies belong together. If one did, we throw them away and read again under a real read lock. Between the stamp and the check, the copies can be torn: half old and half new, such as a new buying price with an old selling price. The Javadoc promises sound values only if a later validate returns true. So the code in between must not act on them: no loops driven by them, no array index, no calls that could throw. An optimistic read can be torn. Copy, validate, and only then use. OptimisticRead checks that promise. A writer keeps moving both prices, and a reader reads them optimistically for one second. One run printed: reads: 843,481 failed validate(): 22,969 torn pairs caught: 12,960 torn pairs that passed validate(): 0 About one read in 37 failed to validate, and more than half of those had really caught a torn pair. Not one torn pair got past validate(). The speed comes without the safety rails of the other locks: StampedLock is not reentrant. A thread that holds the write lock and asks for it again waits for itself, which makes it the second lock in this lesson that can. It has no Conditions. A stamp isn't tied to a thread, and you must pass the right stamp to unlockRead or unlockWrite. Use it for a few fields that are read on a very busy path and written rarely, like these two prices. Even then, wait until a profiler, a tool that measures where a program spends its time, shows that the read-write lock is the cost. For most code, ReentrantReadWriteLock, or no lock at all, is the better choice. That's where this lesson's tools stop. Each one still makes some thread wait for a lock, or fall back to one when its optimism fails. For a single number, such as one balance, there's a way to change it safely with no lock at all. Catch torn reads with validate() Read OptimisticRead. A writer keeps moving the bank's two euro prices, and once a write is done the selling price is always the buying price plus 2. The reader counts the optimistic reads that saw a pair where that isn't true. Predict: will any torn pair get past validate()? Run it. Then delete the validate check (treat every optimistic read as good) and count the torn pairs that would have reached the caller. OptimisticRead.java package workbench.concurrency.l07; import java.util.concurrent.locks.StampedLock; /** * The bank's two prices for the euro: it buys at one price and sells 2 cents higher. * A writer keeps moving both prices. A reader reads them optimistically for one second * and counts how often validate() caught a half-written pair. */ public class OptimisticRead { static final StampedLock lock = new StampedLock(); static long buy = 100, sell = 102; // guarded by lock; sell == buy + 2 when no write is in progress static volatile boolean done; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread writer = new Thread(() -> { long v = 100; while (!done) { long stamp = lock.writeLock(); try { buy = ++v; for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); // widens the half-written moment sell = v + 2; } finally { lock.unlockWrite(stamp); } } }); writer.start(); long reads = 0, failed = 0, tornCaught = 0, tornPassed = 0; long end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { reads++; long stamp = lock.tryOptimisticRead(); // 1. no lock taken, just a version number long b = buy, s = sell; // 2. copy the fields into locals boolean torn = s - b != 2; if (lock.validate(stamp)) { // 3. did a writer get in since step 1? if (torn) tornPassed++; // never happens } else { failed++; if (torn) tornCaught++; stamp = lock.readLock(); // 4. fall back to a real read lock try { b = buy; s = sell; } finally { lock.unlockRead(stamp); } } } done = true; writer.join(); System.out.printf("reads: %,d failed validate(): %,d torn pairs caught: %,d torn pairs that passed validate(): %d%n", reads, failed, tornCaught, tornPassed); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l07.OptimisticRead labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l07/OptimisticRead.java OptimisticRead.kt package workbench.concurrency.l07 import java.util.concurrent.locks.StampedLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread // The bank's two prices for the euro: it buys at one price and sells 2 cents higher. // A writer keeps moving both prices. A reader reads them optimistically for one second // and counts how often validate() caught a half-written pair. private class EuroPrices { val lock = StampedLock() var buy = 100L // guarded by lock; sell == buy + 2 when no write is in progress var sell = 102L } @Volatile private var done = false fun main() { val q = EuroPrices() val writer = thread { var v = 100L while (!done) { val stamp = q.lock.writeLock() try { q.buy = ++v repeat(20) { Thread.onSpinWait() } // widens the half-written moment q.sell = v + 2 } finally { q.lock.unlockWrite(stamp) } } } var reads = 0L; var failed = 0L; var tornCaught = 0L; var tornPassed = 0L val end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L while (System.nanoTime() < end) { reads++ var stamp = q.lock.tryOptimisticRead() // 1. no lock taken, just a version number var b = q.buy; var s = q.sell // 2. copy the fields into locals val torn = s - b != 2L if (q.lock.validate(stamp)) { // 3. did a writer get in since step 1? if (torn) tornPassed++ // never happens } else { failed++ if (torn) tornCaught++ stamp = q.lock.readLock() // 4. fall back to a real read lock try { b = q.buy; s = q.sell } finally { q.lock.unlockRead(stamp) } } } done = true writer.join() println("reads: %,d failed validate(): %,d torn pairs caught: %,d torn pairs that passed validate(): %d" .format(reads, failed, tornCaught, tornPassed)) } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l07.OptimisticReadKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l07/OptimisticRead.kt Tens of thousands of reads fail validation in the second (22,969 of 843,481 in one run here), and more than half of those saw a torn pair, a new buying price with an old selling price. The last number, torn pairs that passed validate(), is always 0. Without the check, every one of those torn pairs would have gone to the caller.

h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · Java and Kotlin
x: A read-mostly cache in Java and Kotlin Java BigDecimal rate(String pair) { rw.readLock().lock(); try { BigDecimal r = rates.get(pair); if (r != null) return r; // 1. fast path under the read lock } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); // 2. let go BEFORE asking for the write lock } rw.writeLock().lock(); try { return rates.computeIfAbsent(pair, loader); // 3. check again under the write lock } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } } Kotlin fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal = rw.read { rates[pair] ?: rw.write { // write {} let go of our read lock first, so another thread may have loaded it: check again rates.getOrPut(pair) { loader(pair) } } } The Java version must let go of the read lock before it takes the write lock, or it hangs. The Kotlin version looks like an upgrade, and it doesn't hang, because the standard library's ReentrantReadWriteLock.write releases every read lock this thread holds, takes the write lock, and takes the read locks back afterwards. Its documentation warns that this is not an atomic upgrade: another thread can write in the gap, so anything you checked before write must be checked again inside it. That's why both versions check again (computeIfAbsent, getOrPut). Kotlin's helpers remove the ceremony of lock, try and finally. They don't remove the reasoning.

h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · Worked example
x: A lock per account that gives up Each account's changes must run one at a time, because each one checks and then updates that account's balance. Changes to different accounts must not wait for each other. And if one thread gets stuck while holding an account, other requests for that account should give up after a short wait and ask the caller to try again, instead of piling up behind it. Read the solution and its subgoal labels. class AccountLocks { private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, ReentrantLock> locks = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); <T> T withAccount(String accountId, Duration maxWait, Supplier<T> action) throws InterruptedException { // 1. one lock per account, created at most once ReentrantLock lock = locks.computeIfAbsent(accountId, id -> new ReentrantLock()); // 2. wait a bounded time; an interrupt also ends the wait if (!lock.tryLock(maxWait.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) { throw new AccountBusyException(accountId); // 3. busy: give up, the caller tries again later } try { return action.get(); // 4. critical section } finally { lock.unlock(); // 5. always release } } } class AccountLocks { private val locks = ConcurrentHashMap<String, ReentrantLock>() fun <T> withAccount(accountId: String, maxWait: Duration, action: () -> T): T { // 1. one lock per account, created at most once val lock = locks.computeIfAbsent(accountId) { ReentrantLock() } // 2. wait a bounded time; an interrupt also ends the wait if (!lock.tryLock(maxWait.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) { throw AccountBusyException(accountId) // 3. busy: give up, the caller tries again later } try { return action() // 4. critical section } finally { lock.unlock() // 5. always release } } } Before reading on, explain to yourself: why does tryLock sit outside the try, when unlock() is inside the finally? Answer: if tryLock returns false or throws InterruptedException, this thread doesn't hold the lock. A finally that called unlock() would throw IllegalMonitorStateException and hide the real result. Only the code that runs while you hold the lock goes inside the try. Why not synchronized (accountId)? Two Strings with the same letters are often different objects, so two requests for the same account could each lock their own string and run together. Interned strings, the single shared copy Java keeps of each string literal, go the other way: unrelated code that locks the same literal shares your lock, as synchronized and intrinsic locks showed. And synchronized has no timeout. A map of real lock objects avoids all three problems. One problem remains: the map gains a lock for every account it ever sees, and never shrinks. With millions of accounts, that's memory you don't get back. Removing entries safely is harder than it looks, because another thread may be about to lock the entry you remove. The usual answer is lock striping: a fixed array of locks, with each account mapped to one of them by its hash. private final ReentrantLock[] stripes = new ReentrantLock[256]; { for (int i = 0; i < stripes.length; i++) stripes[i] = new ReentrantLock(); } ReentrantLock lockFor(String accountId) { return stripes[Math.floorMod(accountId.hashCode(), stripes.length)]; // two accounts may share a stripe: fine } private val stripes = Array(256) { ReentrantLock() } fun lockFor(accountId: String): ReentrantLock = stripes[Math.floorMod(accountId.hashCode(), stripes.size)] // two accounts may share a stripe: fine Two accounts that share a stripe now wait for each other. That costs a little speed and nothing in correctness. If you ever hold two account locks at once, for a transfer, take the stripes in index order, as in Deadlock, livelock and starvation, and skip the second lock when both accounts land on the same stripe.

h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · Lab
x: A rail with two conditions and a rate table that doesn't hang labs/concurrency/src/main/java/workbench/concurrency/l07/LockBuffer.java labs/concurrency/src/main/java/workbench/concurrency/l07/FxRateCache.java ./gradlew :concurrency:test --tests 'workbench.concurrency.l07.*' Run the tests. All eight fail. The five LockBuffer tests hit UnsupportedOperationException. Two FxRateCache tests time out (the upgrade hang), and the snapshot test finds rates from two different refreshes mixed together. Part 1: LockBuffer is the kitchen's rail from the second section, for any kind of item. Write it with one ReentrantLock and two Conditions, notFull and notEmpty. Check the capacity in the constructor. put and take follow the shape in the second section, with signal(). Write offer(item, timeout): the same as put, but wait with notFull.awaitNanos(remaining) and return false when the time runs out. Part 2: FxRateCache is the bank's exchange-rate table from the third section. Fix rate: let go of the read lock, take the write lock, and check again before calling the loader, so the loader runs once per currency pair. Fix snapshot so it reads every pair under one read lock. Run the tests until all eight pass, then twice more. awaitNanos returns the nanoseconds still left (zero or less when time is up). Keep the returned value and pass it to the next awaitNanos in the loop. Use lock.lockInterruptibly() at the top of put, take and offer, so an interrupted thread doesn't wait for the lock either. await() already throws InterruptedException when interrupted. The cache's HashMap is fine as it is: every access to it happens under the read or the write lock. Only the order in which you take the locks is wrong. All eight tests in ExplicitLocksTest pass, three runs in a row. By the end you can use ReentrantLock safely (unlock() in a finally, tryLock, lockInterruptibly), give each kind of waiting thread its own Condition, and use a read-write lock without the upgrade that hangs.

x: A cash machine's request needs the ledger lock, but it must ask the customer to try again if it can't get the lock within 50 ms. Which tool fits? synchronized (ledger) ledger.lockInterruptibly() ledger.tryLock(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) A volatile boolean busy flag checked before lock() tryLock with a timeout waits at most 50 ms and returns false if the lock is still taken. lockInterruptibly waits with no limit unless someone interrupts the thread, and synchronized can't time out at all. The flag is the tempting one, and it's check-then-act: another thread can take the lock between the check and the lock() call. Kotlin code: rw.read { if (cache[k] == null) rw.write { cache[k] = load(k) } }. Two threads ask for the same missing key. What can happen? Both hang, because a read lock can't be upgraded load(k) can run twice, because write { } lets go of the read lock before it takes the write lock Nothing bad: write { } upgrades atomically It throws IllegalMonitorStateException Kotlin's write releases this thread's read locks, takes the write lock, and takes the read locks back afterwards. Both threads can see null, both let go, and each then loads in turn. It doesn't hang, as it would in Java, but it isn't atomic either. Check again inside write, for example with getOrPut. From wait, notify and guarded blocks: a teammate merges notFull and notEmpty into one Condition changed, but keeps changed.signal() in both put and take. With several waiters and cooks, what can happen? Nothing changes: signal() always wakes the right kind of thread Tickets are lost It throws, because two methods can't share one Condition The kitchen can stall: a signal() meant for a cook can wake a waiter, which waits again, and nobody signals the cooks With one queue for both kinds of waiting thread, signal() may pick the wrong kind. That thread checks its loop, waits again, and the signal is gone. It's the same lost wake-up that made the one-monitor rail need notifyAll(). With one condition, use signalAll(); with two, signal() is fine. No ticket is lost, which is why this bug hides in tests. With StampedLock, you call tryOptimisticRead() and copy buy and sell into locals. What must happen before you use them? Call validate(stamp); if it returns false, read them again under readLock() Nothing: the stamp guarantees the two copies match Call unlockRead(stamp) Call tryConvertToWriteLock(stamp) An optimistic read takes no lock, so a writer can change the prices while you copy them. validate tells you whether a writer got in since the stamp, and only after it returns true do the copies belong together. There's nothing to release, because nothing was locked. A dump shows 40 threads WAITING (parking) in ReentrantLock.lock(). Thread.print -l says the lock is owned by interest, the end-of-day job, whose stack shows it asleep in Thread.sleep, waiting for tomorrow's run, outside any code that uses the lock. What is the most likely bug? A deadlock between the 40 threads The lock is unfair, so the 40 threads are starving A code path in the interest job took the lock and left without unlock(), for example on an exception with no finally Thread.sleep gives the lock back, so the dump is out of date The owner isn't waiting for anything that needs the lock, and it isn't in the critical section. It has moved on while still holding the lock, which happens when an exception or an early return skips the release. An unfair lock would still change hands now and then, a deadlock needs the owner to wait for a lock too, and Thread.sleep never gives back a lock.

h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · Explain it back
x: A teammate asks: "Should we replace all our synchronized blocks with ReentrantLock? I heard it's faster." Explain what you would tell them.

h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · Key terms
x: ReentrantLock An explicit lock with the same rules as synchronized, plus tryLock, timeouts, interruptible waits, fairness and conditions. Hold count How many times the owning thread has taken a reentrant lock. It must release it as many times. Condition A waiting room tied to a lock. await() lets go of the lock and waits; signal() wakes one waiting thread. Fair lock A lock that hands over to the longest-waiting thread instead of letting a newly arrived thread barge in. Read-write lock A pair of locks: many threads may hold the read lock together; the write lock is held by one thread alone. Lock upgrade Asking for the write lock while still holding the read lock. ReentrantReadWriteLock waits forever if you try. Optimistic read A StampedLock read that takes no lock and checks afterwards, with validate, that no writer got in. Torn read Copies of several fields that mix old and new values, because a writer ran while they were being read. Where do lock() and unlock() go relative to try and finally? lock() on the line right before try. unlock() as the first statement of finally. In Kotlin, lock.withLock { } does both. What does lock.tryLock(50, MILLISECONDS) do when another thread holds the lock? It waits up to 50 ms. It returns true (and you hold the lock) if it got it in time, false otherwise. It throws InterruptedException if interrupted while waiting. A thread waits in lockInterruptibly() and another thread interrupts it. What happens? And for a thread waiting to enter synchronized? lockInterruptibly() gives up at once with InterruptedException. The synchronized waiter keeps waiting until it gets the monitor, and only sees its interrupt flag afterwards. Why can a bounded buffer with notFull and notEmpty conditions use signal() instead of signalAll()? Each condition has only one kind of waiting thread, and one change (one item in, or one slot free) lets exactly one of them go on. A thread holding the read lock of a ReentrantReadWriteLock calls writeLock().lock(). What happens? It waits forever. The write lock waits for every reader to leave, including this thread. Let go of the read lock first, then check again under the write lock. After long s = lock.tryOptimisticRead() and copying fields into locals, what must you do? Call lock.validate(s). If it returns false, a writer got in: read the fields again under lock.readLock(). In Kotlin, what does rw.write { } do when called inside rw.read { }? It releases this thread's read locks, takes the write lock, and takes the read locks back afterwards. It doesn't hang, but it isn't atomic: check again inside the block.

h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · Go deeper
x: ReentrantLock, ReentrantReadWriteLock, Semaphore and CountDownLatch are all built on one class, AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS). It keeps one int of state and a queue of waiting threads. For ReentrantLock the state is the hold count; for a semaphore it is the number of permits left; for a latch it is the count. A thread that can't go on joins the queue and parks with LockSupport.park. That's why it shows as WAITING in a dump, with a line like parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync). A release unparks the next thread in the queue. In non-fair mode, the default, a thread that arrives just as the lock is released can take it before the queued thread wakes. That's barging, and it's why the two-condition rail in the second Try it still wasted some wake-ups. It's also why non-fair locks get through far more work: waking a parked thread takes microseconds, and a running thread can take and release the lock many times in that gap. Fair mode closes the gap and pays the wake-up cost on every hand-off. Even on a fair lock, the untimed tryLock() barges: its Javadoc says it does not honor the fairness setting. ReentrantReadWriteLock splits its 32-bit state into two 16-bit halves, one for read holds and one for write holds. That's why its Javadoc caps it at 65,535 recursive write locks and 65,535 read locks. StampedLock also has tryConvertToWriteLock(stamp), which upgrades a read or optimistic stamp to a write stamp if no other thread is in the way, and returns 0 if it can't. It's the only upgrade among the JDK's locks, and it can fail, so you still need the fallback path. If you ever build your own synchronizer, subclass AQS and implement tryAcquire and tryRelease; its Javadoc has a small Mutex example. First check java.util.concurrent for one that already exists. Lesson 10 of this track covers the common ones.

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · One step nobody can split: what an atomic variable does
x: Let's start with the balance itself. Here it is as an AtomicLong, with a deposit and a read: Java private final AtomicLong balanceCents = new AtomicLong(); // no lock needed void deposit(long cents) { balanceCents.addAndGet(cents); // read, add, write: one step nobody can split } long balance() { return balanceCents.get(); // like a volatile read: sees the latest value } Kotlin private val balanceCents = AtomicLong() // no lock needed fun deposit(cents: Long) { balanceCents.addAndGet(cents) // read, add, write: one step nobody can split } fun balance(): Long = balanceCents.get() // like a volatile read: sees the latest value An atomic variable holds one value and offers read-modify-write operations (read the value, change it, write it back, as count++ does) that no other thread can split. addAndGet reads, adds and writes as one step. Its get() and set() behave like reads and writes of a volatile field, a field whose reads always see the latest write from any thread. The method names tell you what comes back. incrementAndGet() returns the new value, and getAndIncrement() returns the old one. The same pairs exist for add, update and accumulate. AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicBoolean and AtomicReference cover most needs. How does a library turn three steps into one without a lock? It asks the processor. On x86 processors, the kind in most laptops and servers, HotSpot (the standard JVM) compiles addAndGet to a single lock xadd instruction, and compareAndSet to lock cmpxchg. ARM64 processors have their own equivalents. While that instruction runs, the core keeps the variable's cache line to itself. A cache line is the small block of memory that a core copies into its own fast memory, its cache. A core must own the line before it can write to it. So no other core can get in between the read and the write. No thread ever waits for another. If the operating system pauses a thread, that thread is never in the middle of an atomic update: the instruction either happened or it didn't. So some thread always makes progress, which is what lock-free means. A lock, the guard that lets one thread in at a time, is different. A thread that is paused while it holds a lock stops every thread that needs it, just as the interest job stopped the cash machine in the last lesson. Predict from the mechanism. In the middle of payday, the operating system pauses teller 3 for 50 ms. With the AtomicLong, what do the other seven tellers do in those 50 ms? And with a lock that teller 3 held at that moment? (With the atomic, they keep depositing: teller 3 was paused before or after its instruction, never inside it. With the lock, all seven wait the full 50 ms.) Atomics have one hard limit, and it's the one from the opening. Each atomic protects one variable, one call at a time. Two calls in a row are two steps with a gap between them, and the warm-up's withdrawal lives in that gap. It checks, then acts on what it saw, a shape called check-then-act. To close it, we need the operation underneath all the others.

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · Update it only if nobody beat me to it: compare-and-set and the retry loop
x: It says 41, please make it 42: compare-and-set writes only if nobody beat you to it, the loser reads again and retries, the update function can run twice, and the check belongs inside the request Here's a job that no single method does. The bank's fraud team, the people who look for suspicious payments, watches a screen that shows the largest payment of the day. Many threads report payments, and each one raises the maximum if its payment is bigger. The first version, the lab's MaxTracker, uses a volatile field: Java // Naive: read, decide, then write blindly private volatile long max = Long.MIN_VALUE; void offer(long amount) { if (amount > max) max = amount; // another thread may have raised max since the read } Kotlin // Naive: read, decide, then write blindly @Volatile private var max = Long.MIN_VALUE fun offer(amount: Long) { if (amount > max) max = amount // another thread may have raised max since the read } Let's trace the smallest case. The maximum is 500. Thread 1 reports 900 and thread 2 reports 700, at the same moment. Both read 500, and both decide to raise it. Thread 1 writes 900. A moment later, thread 2 writes 700 over it. The day's biggest payment has vanished from the screen, and volatile made sure every thread saw the wrong answer promptly. The trouble is the blind write at the end. Compare-and-set (CAS) makes it a careful one. compareAndSet(expected, next) does this as one step: if the current value equals expected, store next and return true; otherwise change nothing and return false. Read it as "update it only if nobody beat me to it". Picture a clerk who keeps a tally on a board behind the bank's counter. You may ask her to change it, but you must say what it shows now: "It says 41, please make it 42." If the board still says 41, she writes 42. If someone got there first and it already says 42, she refuses, and you look again. She never makes anyone wait in a line: she either writes the new number or says no. compareAndSet(41, 42) is that request, and the clerk is the processor's compare-and-set instruction. With that one careful step, we can build any read-modify-write. Here's the max tracker again: Java // Fixed: max is now an AtomicLong, and the write happens only if max is still prev long prev; do { prev = max.get(); // 1. read if (amount <= prev) return; // 2. decide: nothing to do } while (!max.compareAndSet(prev, amount)); // 3. write only if max is still prev; else retry Kotlin // Fixed: max is now an AtomicLong, and the write happens only if max is still prev var prev: Long do { prev = max.get() // 1. read if (amount <= prev) return // 2. decide: nothing to do } while (!max.compareAndSet(prev, amount)) // 3. write only if max is still prev; else retry First we read the maximum. Then we decide: if our amount isn't bigger, there's nothing to do. Finally we try the CAS. If another thread changed the maximum since we read it, the CAS fails. Our decision was based on old data, so we start again with the fresh value. The figure shows two threads, T1 and T2, that both read 41. T1's CAS wins. T2's fails, so T2 reads 42 and writes 43. Nothing is lost. A failed CAS costs a retry, not a wait. CasRetries counts the retries. It runs a hand-written CAS increment a million times per thread, on 1, 2, 4 and then 8 threads. One run printed: threads: 1 counter: 1,000,000 failed CAS: 0 (0.00 per increment) threads: 2 counter: 2,000,000 failed CAS: 536,415 (0.27 per increment) threads: 4 counter: 4,000,000 failed CAS: 2,043,130 (0.51 per increment) threads: 8 counter: 8,000,000 failed CAS: 2,805,059 (0.35 per increment) The counter is exact every time. One thread never fails, because nobody else changes the value. With more threads, millions of CAS calls fail and retry. The rate jumps around from run to run: the Kotlin twin gave 0.30 per increment for 4 threads and 0.34 for 8. It stays below one, because a core tends to finish a run of increments before another core takes the cache line away. A CAS loop reads, decides, and writes only if nothing changed. When it fails, it decides again. You'll rarely write that loop by hand, though. The library has it built in, and that brings a surprise of its own. Watch CAS fail and retry Read CasRetries. Its increment() is a hand-written CAS loop that counts its own failures. Predict the failure count for 1 thread, then for 8 threads. Run it twice. Check that counter is exact every time. CasRetries.java package workbench.concurrency.l08; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; /** A hand-written compare-and-set increment. Count how often the CAS fails as threads are added. */ public class CasRetries { static final AtomicLong counter = new AtomicLong(); // returns how many times compareAndSet failed before it worked static long increment() { long failures = 0; while (true) { long seen = counter.get(); // 1. read if (counter.compareAndSet(seen, seen + 1)) { // 2. write only if still `seen` return failures; } failures++; // 3. someone else won: retry } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int perThread = 1_000_000; for (int threads : new int[] {1, 2, 4, 8}) { counter.set(0); AtomicLong failed = new AtomicLong(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); // start them all together List<Thread> ts = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < threads; i++) { ts.add(new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } long mine = 0; for (int n = 0; n < perThread; n++) mine += increment(); failed.addAndGet(mine); })); } for (Thread t : ts) t.start(); go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); System.out.printf("threads: %d counter: %,10d failed CAS: %,10d (%.2f per increment)%n", threads, counter.get(), failed.get(), failed.get() / (double) counter.get()); } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l08.CasRetries labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l08/CasRetries.java CasRetries.kt package workbench.concurrency.l08 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A hand-written compare-and-set increment. Count how often the CAS fails as threads are added. private val counter = AtomicLong() // returns how many times compareAndSet failed before it worked private fun increment(): Long { var failures = 0L while (true) { val seen = counter.get() // 1. read if (counter.compareAndSet(seen, seen + 1)) { // 2. write only if still `seen` return failures } failures++ // 3. someone else won: retry } } fun main() { val perThread = 1_000_000 for (threads in listOf(1, 2, 4, 8)) { counter.set(0) val failed = AtomicLong() val go = CountDownLatch(1) // start them all together val ts = List(threads) { thread { go.await() var mine = 0L repeat(perThread) { mine += increment() } failed.addAndGet(mine) } } go.countDown() ts.forEach { it.join() } println("threads: %d counter: %,10d failed CAS: %,10d (%.2f per increment)" .format(threads, counter.get(), failed.get(), failed.get() / counter.get().toDouble())) } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l08.CasRetriesKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l08/CasRetries.kt One thread never fails: nobody else changes the value. With more threads, failures climb into the hundreds of thousands or millions, and the number changes a lot from run to run (2,805,059 for 8 threads in one run here). The counter is exact every time. Failures stay below one per increment, because a core tends to get a run of increments done before another core takes the cache line away. Both threads read 41. Only one CAS can succeed. The loser reads the new value and tries again, so no update is lost.

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · Letting the library write the loop: updateAndGet, and a function that runs twice
x: updateAndGet(f) and accumulateAndGet(x, f) contain the loop: Java max.accumulateAndGet(amount, Math::max); // the max tracker's loop, written for you balanceCents.updateAndGet(b -> b + 100); // any pure function of the old value Kotlin max.accumulateAndGet(amount, Math::max) // the max tracker's loop, written for you balanceCents.updateAndGet { b -> b + 100 } // any pure function of the old value Inside, they read the value, call your function, and try the CAS. When the CAS fails, they call your function again with the new value. So your function can run more than once for one update, and the results of the extra runs are thrown away. Let's count them. UpdateTwice starts four threads together, and each makes 250,000 one-cent deposits with updateAndGet. The function also counts how often it runs. Guess before you look: exactly 1,000,000 times? updates: 1,000,000 times the function ran: 1,294,839 The balance is exact, and the function ran 294,839 more times than there were deposits. Each extra run was a lost race whose result was thrown away. In six runs here, the extra runs came to between 29 and 99 percent of the deposits, so the number depends on how hard the threads collide. If that function had texted the customer, the bank would have sent close to 300,000 extra texts, for deposits that each happened once. So the function must be pure: it looks only at its input and returns a result. No logging, no counters, no messages, no reads of other shared data that might change. Do any side effects after the call returns, using the value it returned. The update function may run more than once. Keep it pure, and act on the value it returns. The get variants, getAndUpdate and getAndAccumulate, return the value from before the update. Use them when the caller needs to know whether its own update applied. The worked example uses exactly that to build a withdrawal that never overdraws. Every CAS so far fought over one variable. On a busy day, that fight is the cost. Count the calls Read UpdateTwice. Four threads make 250,000 one-cent deposits each with updateAndGet, and the function counts how often it runs. Predict: will the function run exactly 1,000,000 times? Run it two or three times. UpdateTwice.java package workbench.concurrency.l08; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** updateAndGet retries your function when it loses a race. Count how often the function really runs. */ public class UpdateTwice { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { AtomicLong balance = new AtomicLong(); LongAdder calls = new LongAdder(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Runnable deposits = () -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int i = 0; i < 250_000; i++) { balance.updateAndGet(b -> { calls.increment(); // a side effect: imagine this texted the customer return b + 1; }); } }; Thread[] ts = {new Thread(deposits), new Thread(deposits), new Thread(deposits), new Thread(deposits)}; for (Thread t : ts) t.start(); go.countDown(); // all four start together for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); System.out.printf("updates: %,d times the function ran: %,d%n", balance.get(), calls.sum()); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l08.UpdateTwice labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l08/UpdateTwice.java UpdateTwice.kt package workbench.concurrency.l08 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder import kotlin.concurrent.thread // updateAndGet retries your function when it loses a race. Count how often the function really runs. fun main() { val balance = AtomicLong() val calls = LongAdder() val go = CountDownLatch(1) val ts = List(4) { thread { go.await() repeat(250_000) { balance.updateAndGet { b -> calls.increment() // a side effect: imagine this texted the customer b + 1 } } } } go.countDown() // all four start together ts.forEach { it.join() } println("updates: %,d times the function ran: %,d".format(balance.get(), calls.sum())) } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l08.UpdateTwiceKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l08/UpdateTwice.kt The balance is exactly 1,000,000 every time. The function runs more often than that, and how much more changes from run to run (between 1,294,839 and 1,991,780 times in six runs here). Each extra call is a lost compare-and-set whose result was thrown away. If the function had texted the customer, every one of those extra calls would have been an extra text.

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · Counting on a busy day: LongAdder for statistics, AtomicLong for decisions
x: The fight has a name: contention, many threads trying to change the same thing at the same moment. Here's a place it bites. The manager's screen shows how many deposits the bank has taken today. Eight threads add to that count all day, and someone glances at it now and then. On one AtomicLong, that's one cache line that every core wants at once. Each increment pulls the line over to its own core, and the cores spend their time passing it around. LongAdder (JDK 8) spreads the count over several cells, small counters of their own. When threads collide on one cell, it moves them to different cells, so they mostly write to different cache lines. sum() adds the base value and all the cells together: Java private final LongAdder depositsToday = new LongAdder(); void onDeposit() { depositsToday.increment(); } // threads mostly hit different cells long depositsSoFar() { return depositsToday.sum(); } // adds the cells up: not a snapshot Kotlin private val depositsToday = LongAdder() fun onDeposit() = depositsToday.increment() // threads mostly hit different cells fun depositsSoFar(): Long = depositsToday.sum() // adds the cells up: not a snapshot AdderVsAtomic races the two. Eight threads count 2,000,000 deposits each, first on one AtomicLong, then on a LongAdder. I guessed the adder would win by a few times. One run printed: round 1: AtomicLong 16,000,000 in 669 ms LongAdder 16,000,000 in 92 ms round 2: AtomicLong 16,000,000 in 482 ms LongAdder 16,000,000 in 71 ms round 3: AtomicLong 16,000,000 in 578 ms LongAdder 16,000,000 in 53 ms Correctness first: both counted all 16,000,000. Then speed: the LongAdder was 7 to 11 times faster, more than I guessed. With a single thread the gap shrinks or disappears, because there's no contention for the adder to avoid. The price is in sum(). It reads the cells one by one while other threads keep adding. Its Javadoc (the official API documentation) says plainly that the result is not an atomic snapshot: increments made during the sum might not be counted. The adder also uses more memory than one long. That gives a clean rule. Use LongAdder for statistics that many threads update and someone reads now and then: deposits taken, requests served, payments refused. Use AtomicLong when the value drives a decision, such as a balance that must not go below zero, a sequence number, or a limit. A decision needs the exact current value and a compare-and-set against it, and LongAdder has neither. LongAccumulator does the same trick for other functions, such as a maximum, with the same caveat on reads. Count with a LongAdder. Decide with an AtomicLong. One number at a time, then. A transfer changes two. Race an AtomicLong against a LongAdder Read AdderVsAtomic: 8 threads each count 2,000,000 deposits, first on one AtomicLong, then on a LongAdder. Predict which is faster, and by roughly how much. Run it. Then change the thread count in time to 1 and run it again. AdderVsAtomic.java package workbench.concurrency.l08; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** 8 threads each count 2,000,000 events: once on one AtomicLong, once on a LongAdder. */ public class AdderVsAtomic { static long time(Runnable perThreadWork) throws InterruptedException { Thread[] ts = new Thread[8]; for (int i = 0; i < ts.length; i++) ts[i] = new Thread(perThreadWork); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (Thread t : ts) t.start(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int n = 2_000_000; for (int round = 1; round <= 3; round++) { AtomicLong atomic = new AtomicLong(); LongAdder adder = new LongAdder(); long a = time(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) atomic.incrementAndGet(); }); long b = time(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adder.increment(); }); System.out.printf("round %d: AtomicLong %,d in %4d ms LongAdder %,d in %4d ms%n", round, atomic.get(), a, adder.sum(), b); } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l08.AdderVsAtomic labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l08/AdderVsAtomic.java AdderVsAtomic.kt package workbench.concurrency.l08 import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder import kotlin.concurrent.thread // 8 threads each count 2,000,000 events: once on one AtomicLong, once on a LongAdder. private fun time(perThreadWork: () -> Unit): Long { val t0 = System.nanoTime() List(8) { thread { perThreadWork() } }.forEach { it.join() } return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 } fun main() { val n = 2_000_000 for (round in 1..3) { val atomic = AtomicLong() val adder = LongAdder() val a = time { repeat(n) { atomic.incrementAndGet() } } val b = time { repeat(n) { adder.increment() } } println("round %d: AtomicLong %,d in %4d ms LongAdder %,d in %4d ms".format(round, atomic.get(), a, adder.sum(), b)) } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l08.AdderVsAtomicKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l08/AdderVsAtomic.kt Both totals are exactly 16,000,000. With 8 threads, the LongAdder was 7 to 11 times faster in runs here (for example 669 ms against 92 ms). With 1 thread the gap shrinks or disappears, because there's no contention for the adder to avoid. LongAdder.java at jdk-25-ga (when to prefer it over AtomicLong) read

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · Two balances in one swap: AtomicReference, and the ABA trap
x: Remember the checker from synchronized and intrinsic locks? A transfer moved 50 from account A to account B, and a checker that skipped the lock caught the 50 in flight, in neither account. Two AtomicLongs wouldn't help. Each is atomic, but the pair isn't, so the checker could still read A after the transfer and B before it. That lesson promised another way: one object that never changes, swapped in a single step. AtomicReference<V> does compare-and-set on a reference. So put both balances in an immutable record, an object that can't change after it's built. A transfer builds a new record from the old one and swaps the reference: Java record Balances(long a, long b) {} // immutable: a transfer builds a new one private final AtomicReference<Balances> balances = new AtomicReference<>(new Balances(1_000, 1_000)); void transfer(long amount) { balances.updateAndGet(x -> new Balances(x.a() - amount, x.b() + amount)); // both change in one swap } long total() { Balances x = balances.get(); // one read: both balances from the same moment return x.a() + x.b(); // always 2,000 } Kotlin data class Balances(val a: Long, val b: Long) // immutable: a transfer builds a new one private val balances = AtomicReference(Balances(1_000, 1_000)) fun transfer(amount: Long) { balances.updateAndGet { x -> Balances(x.a - amount, x.b + amount) } // both change in one swap } fun total(): Long { val x = balances.get() // one read: both balances from the same moment return x.a + x.b // always 2,000 } The checker reads one reference and gets both balances from the same moment, so the total is always 2,000, with no lock anywhere. In a quick check here, a checker read the total millions of times while 200,000 transfers ran, and it never saw anything else. updateAndGet runs the loop from the last two sections, so the function may run twice. It's pure, so that's fine. The CAS compares references with ==, which asks "is it the same object?", not with equals. That's what we want, because every transfer builds a new object. The lab's TreiberStack, named after R. Kent Treiber, who described it in 1986, uses the same idea on a linked list. A stack is a pile, like a pile of plates: the last item put on (pushed) is the first taken off (popped). Each node holds an item and a link to the node below, and it never changes after it's built. To push, we build a node that points at the current top, then CAS the top from that old node to the new one: Java void push(T item) { Node<T> top, node; do { top = head.get(); node = new Node<>(item, top); // build the new node off to the side } while (!head.compareAndSet(top, node)); // publish it only if head is still top } Kotlin fun push(item: T) { var top: Node<T>? var node: Node<T> do { top = head.get() node = Node(item, top) // build the new node off to the side } while (!head.compareAndSet(top, node)) // publish it only if head is still top } CAS has one blind spot, called ABA. It checks that the value is the same as when you read it, not that it never changed in between. Let's trace it on a stack of A, B and C whose nodes get reused. Thread 1 starts a pop. It reads top = A and next = B, then the operating system pauses it. Thread 2 pops A, pops B, and pushes A back. Thread 1 wakes up and sees A on top, so its CAS from A to B succeeds. But B was already taken off, and the stack now starts with a node that thread 2 owns. In Java, ABA needs reuse: a pool of recycled nodes, array indices, or plain numbers. With freshly built nodes, the garbage collector (the part of the JVM that frees memory nobody uses) never reuses A's memory while thread 1 still holds a reference to A. So the lab's stack is safe. When you do recycle, AtomicStampedReference pairs the reference with an int stamp that you bump on every change, so A with stamp 0 and A with stamp 3 no longer match. That's the honest limit of atomics. One CAS covers one variable. For more, you swap a whole object, and under heavy traffic the retries add up. A whole map of accounts needs something built from these same pieces, and the JDK already has it. Play out ABA by hand Read AbaDemo. It plays both threads on one thread, step by step, so the bad order of events happens every time. Nodes are recycled. Before you run it, predict the stack after T1's compareAndSet. Run it and compare the plain AtomicReference with the AtomicStampedReference. AbaDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l08; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicStampedReference; /** * The ABA problem, played out by hand on one thread so it happens every time. * Nodes are recycled (mutable next), as in a pooled or off-heap structure. */ public class AbaDemo { static final class Node { final String name; Node next; Node(String name, Node next) { this.name = name; this.next = next; } } static String show(Node n) { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); for (; n != null; n = n.next) sb.append(n.name).append(n.next != null ? " -> " : ""); return sb.length() == 0 ? "(empty)" : sb.toString(); } public static void main(String[] args) { Node c = new Node("C", null), b = new Node("B", c), a = new Node("A", b); AtomicReference<Node> head = new AtomicReference<>(a); System.out.println("start: " + show(head.get())); Node top = head.get(), next = top.next; // T1 starts a pop... System.out.println("T1 reads top=A, next=B, then is paused"); head.set(b); // T2 pops A head.set(c); // T2 pops B (B is now T2's) a.next = head.get(); head.set(a); // T2 pushes the recycled A System.out.println("T2 pops A, pops B, pushes A again: " + show(head.get())); boolean ok = head.compareAndSet(top, next); // T1 resumes: head is A again System.out.println("T1 resumes: compareAndSet(A, B) = " + ok); System.out.println("stack now: " + show(head.get()) + " (B was popped by T2: corrupted)"); System.out.println(); a.next = b; b.next = c; AtomicStampedReference<Node> stamped = new AtomicStampedReference<>(a, 0); int[] stampHolder = new int[1]; Node top2 = stamped.get(stampHolder); // T1 reads the node AND the stamp int stamp = stampHolder[0]; Node next2 = top2.next; System.out.println("T1 reads top=A, stamp=" + stamp + ", next=B, then is paused"); stamped.set(b, 1); // every change bumps the stamp stamped.set(c, 2); a.next = c; stamped.set(a, 3); System.out.println("T2 pops A, pops B, pushes A again: stamp is now " + stamped.getStamp()); boolean ok2 = stamped.compareAndSet(top2, next2, stamp, stamp + 1); System.out.println("T1 resumes: compareAndSet(A, B, stamp " + stamp + ") = " + ok2 + ", so T1 re-reads and retries"); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l08.AbaDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l08/AbaDemo.java AbaDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l08 import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicStampedReference // The ABA problem, played out by hand on one thread so it happens every time. // Nodes are recycled (mutable next), as in a pooled or off-heap structure. private class AbaNode(val name: String, var next: AbaNode?) private fun show(start: AbaNode?): String = generateSequence(start) { it.next }.joinToString(" -> ") { it.name }.ifEmpty { "(empty)" } fun main() { val c = AbaNode("C", null) val b = AbaNode("B", c) val a = AbaNode("A", b) val head = AtomicReference(a) println("start: ${show(head.get())}") val top = head.get() val next = top.next // T1 starts a pop... println("T1 reads top=A, next=B, then is paused") head.set(b) // T2 pops A head.set(c) // T2 pops B (B is now T2's) a.next = head.get() head.set(a) // T2 pushes the recycled A println("T2 pops A, pops B, pushes A again: ${show(head.get())}") val ok = head.compareAndSet(top, next) // T1 resumes: head is A again println("T1 resumes: compareAndSet(A, B) = $ok") println("stack now: ${show(head.get())} (B was popped by T2: corrupted)") println() a.next = b; b.next = c val stamped = AtomicStampedReference(a, 0) val stampHolder = IntArray(1) val top2 = stamped.get(stampHolder) // T1 reads the node AND the stamp val stamp = stampHolder[0] val next2 = top2.next println("T1 reads top=A, stamp=$stamp, next=B, then is paused") stamped.set(b, 1) // every change bumps the stamp stamped.set(c, 2) a.next = c stamped.set(a, 3) println("T2 pops A, pops B, pushes A again: stamp is now ${stamped.stamp}") val ok2 = stamped.compareAndSet(top2, next2, stamp, stamp + 1) println("T1 resumes: compareAndSet(A, B, stamp $stamp) = $ok2, so T1 re-reads and retries") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l08.AbaDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l08/AbaDemo.kt With the plain reference, T1's compareAndSet(A, B) returns true and the stack becomes B -> C, although T2 had already popped B: the stack is corrupted. With the stamp, the same CAS returns false, because the stamp moved from 0 to 3, so T1 reads again and retries.

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · Java and Kotlin
x: A max tracker with Java's atomics and Kotlin's Java (java.util.concurrent.atomic) class MaxTracker { private final AtomicLong max = new AtomicLong(Long.MIN_VALUE); void offer(long amount) { max.accumulateAndGet(amount, Math::max); // CAS loop inside } long max() { return max.get(); } } Kotlin (kotlin.concurrent.atomics) @OptIn(ExperimentalAtomicApi::class) class MaxTracker { private val max = AtomicLong(Long.MIN_VALUE) // kotlin.concurrent.atomics, not java.util fun offer(amount: Long) { max.update { prev -> maxOf(prev, amount) } // a CAS loop inside, like updateAndGet } fun max(): Long = max.load() } On the JVM, most Kotlin code simply uses java.util.concurrent.atomic, and everything in this lesson works the same from Kotlin. Kotlin 2.1 added its own atomics in kotlin.concurrent.atomics, mainly for code that must also run outside the JVM. The names differ (load, fetchAndAdd, update), and in the Kotlin 2.4 standard library they are still marked experimental, so they need @OptIn(ExperimentalAtomicApi::class). Underneath, on the JVM, they are the same compare-and-set. One thing doesn't change between the languages: @Volatile var count = 0 followed by count++ compiles happily in Kotlin and loses updates exactly like the Java version.

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · Worked example
x: A withdrawal that never overdraws, without a lock An account must never go below zero. tryWithdraw should take the money only if there's enough, and many threads call it at once. Here's a first attempt with an AtomicLong. Look for the race before reading on. private final AtomicLong balanceCents = new AtomicLong(10_000); boolean tryWithdraw(long cents) { if (balanceCents.get() >= cents) { // check balanceCents.addAndGet(-cents); // act return true; } return false; } private val balanceCents = AtomicLong(10_000) fun tryWithdraw(cents: Long): Boolean { if (balanceCents.get() >= cents) { // check balanceCents.addAndGet(-cents) // act return true } return false } Each call on balanceCents is atomic. The pair isn't: with 100 in the account, two threads can both pass the check for 80, and both take it, ending at -60. Making the variable atomic didn't make the logic atomic. The check has to happen inside the compare-and-set. The CAS loop checks the very value it is about to replace. If another thread changes the balance in between, the CAS fails and the loop decides again on fresh data. boolean tryWithdraw(long cents) { while (true) { long before = balanceCents.get(); // 1. read the balance if (before < cents) return false; // 2. decide on that value if (balanceCents.compareAndSet(before, before - cents)) return true; // 3. commit, if unchanged } // 4. lost the race: read again, decide again } fun tryWithdraw(cents: Long): Boolean { while (true) { val before = balanceCents.get() // 1. read the balance if (before < cents) return false // 2. decide on that value if (balanceCents.compareAndSet(before, before - cents)) return true // 3. commit, if unchanged } // 4. lost the race: read again, decide again } The same thing with getAndUpdate. The function is pure: it looks only at b. Before reading the next step, explain to yourself why the second line checks before >= cents, instead of checking whether the value changed. boolean tryWithdraw(long cents) { long before = balanceCents.getAndUpdate(b -> b >= cents ? b - cents : b); return before >= cents; // did OUR withdrawal apply? } fun tryWithdraw(cents: Long): Boolean { val before = balanceCents.getAndUpdate { b -> if (b >= cents) b - cents else b } return before >= cents // did OUR withdrawal apply? } getAndUpdate returns the value that its last, successful run of the function saw. If that value covered cents, the function took the money, so this caller's withdrawal went through. If it didn't, the function returned b unchanged and nothing was taken. Checking whether the value changed tells you nothing, because other threads change it all the time. This is also why LongAdder is the wrong tool for a balance: it has no compare-and-set, and its sum() isn't exact while others add. If you keep balances in a database, the same idea becomes one statement, UPDATE account SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ? AND balance >= ?, followed by a check that one row changed.

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · Quiz
x: Sixteen threads count every deposit the bank takes. The manager's screen reads the count once a minute. Which is the best fit? A volatile long with count++ A synchronized increment method An AtomicLong with incrementAndGet() A LongAdder with increment() and sum() Many writers and a rare read that may be a little behind is exactly what LongAdder is for: threads mostly update different cells, so they don't fight over one cache line. AtomicLong is correct, but slower under this much contention. synchronized is correct and slower still. volatile with ++ loses deposits. What does this print? Java AtomicInteger n = new AtomicInteger(5); int a = n.getAndIncrement(); int b = n.incrementAndGet(); System.out.println(a + " " + b + " " + n.get()); Kotlin val n = AtomicInteger(5) val a = n.getAndIncrement() val b = n.incrementAndGet() println("$a $b ${n.get()}") 5 7 7 6 7 7 5 6 7 6 6 6 getAndIncrement returns the old value (5) and leaves 6. incrementAndGet makes it 7 and returns the new value (7). The final get() is 7. The name says the order: get, then increment, or increment, then get. balance.updateAndGet(b -> { long next = b - cents; sms.send("New balance: " + next); return next; }) runs on many threads. What can go wrong? Nothing: updateAndGet runs the function exactly once per call The balance can lose a withdrawal Customers can get texts about balances their account never had, because the function runs again whenever its compare-and-set fails It throws IllegalStateException when threads collide When a compare-and-set fails, updateAndGet calls the function again with the fresh value. The failed attempt has already sent its text, with a balance that was never stored. The balance itself is correct, which is why this bug is easy to miss. Keep the function pure, and send the text after the call, with the value it returned. From synchronized and intrinsic locks: to show the average deposit, the bank keeps count and totalCents for today's deposits, and both must always change together. Which is a correct choice? Two AtomicLong fields, each updated with addAndGet One AtomicReference to an immutable record holding both values, or a synchronized method that updates both Two volatile long fields Two LongAdder fields Each atomic protects one variable. With two of them, a reader can see the new count with the old total. One lock around both updates, or one compare-and-set on a reference to an immutable pair, makes the two fields change as one step. When is ABA a real risk for a compare-and-set in Java? On every AtomicReference CAS, even with freshly built nodes Only on ARM processors Never: the JVM prevents it When the same value can come back after changes: recycled nodes, object pools, array indices, plain counters CAS only checks that the value equals what you read, so it's fooled only if the value can return to an earlier one. With new nodes, the garbage collector won't reuse a node's memory while any thread still holds a reference to it, so it can't come back. Pools, indices and numbers can, and AtomicStampedReference adds a version number to catch it.
