h: Atomics and compare-and-set · Key terms
x: Atomic variable A variable whose read-modify-write operations happen as one step that no other thread can split. Compare-and-set (CAS) Write a new value only if the current value is still the one you expected, and report whether it worked. CAS loop Read, decide, try a CAS, and start over if another thread changed the value first. Lock-free Some thread always makes progress, even if others are paused, because nobody holds a lock. Contention Many threads trying to change the same thing at the same moment. Pure function A function that only reads its input and returns a result, with no side effects, so running it twice does no harm. LongAdder A counter spread over several cells so threads rarely collide; its sum is not a snapshot. ABA problem A CAS that succeeds because a value changed and then changed back. What does ref.compareAndSet(expected, next) do? As one indivisible step: if the current value equals expected, it stores next and returns true. Otherwise it changes nothing and returns false. incrementAndGet() vs getAndIncrement(): what does each return? incrementAndGet() returns the new value. getAndIncrement() returns the old value. Both add one atomically. Why must the function passed to updateAndGet have no side effects? When its compare-and-set loses a race, updateAndGet calls the function again with the new value. It can run several times for one update. Busy counter, read rarely: AtomicLong or LongAdder? LongAdder: threads update separate cells, so there is far less contention. Use AtomicLong when the exact value drives a decision. Is LongAdder.sum() an exact snapshot while other threads add? No. It reads the cells one at a time, so increments made during the sum may be missed. What is the ABA problem? A CAS succeeds because the value is back to what you read (A, then B, then A again), though it changed in between. Fix it with a version stamp: AtomicStampedReference. if (n.get() < limit) n.incrementAndGet(); on an AtomicInteger: safe? No. Two atomic calls with a gap between them is check-then-act. Do the check inside a CAS loop or updateAndGet.

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · Go deeper
x: An AtomicLong is a separate object. If you have a million Account objects that each need an atomic balance, that's a million extra objects, each with its own header, the few bytes the JVM keeps at the start of every object. The JDK's own classes avoid this by putting a volatile long field in the class and doing CAS on the field in place. Two tools do that. AtomicLongFieldUpdater (and its Integer and Reference siblings) is the older one. VarHandle, since JDK 9, is the general one: Java private volatile long balanceCents; private static final VarHandle BALANCE; static { try { BALANCE = MethodHandles.lookup().findVarHandle(Account.class, "balanceCents", long.class); } catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) { throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(e); } } boolean swap(long expected, long next) { return BALANCE.compareAndSet(this, expected, next); // CAS on this object's field } Kotlin class Account { @Volatile private var balanceCents = 0L fun swap(expected: Long, next: Long): Boolean = BALANCE.compareAndSet(this, expected, next) // CAS on this object's field companion object { private val BALANCE: VarHandle = MethodHandles.privateLookupIn(Account::class.java, MethodHandles.lookup()) .findVarHandle(Account::class.java, "balanceCents", Long::class.java) } } VarHandle also offers weaker memory orderings (getAcquire, setRelease, plain and opaque access), which the memory model track covers in its last lesson. Two more details. The weakCompareAndSet family may fail even when the value matches. Inside a retry loop that doesn't matter, and on some ARM processors it can be cheaper. And a CAS loop is lock-free but not wait-free: one unlucky thread could, in theory, lose every race forever while others succeed. In practice that almost never happens, but it's why a busy CAS loop under extreme contention can be slower than a lock, which queues threads instead of letting them all retry at once. LongAdder exists because of exactly that case.

h: Concurrent collections · Inside the map: why ConcurrentHashMap is safe one key at a time
x: The card cabinet: ConcurrentHashMap locks one drawer per write, so get then put loses a deposit, while merge reads, adds and writes in one hold of the drawer Let's put three versions of the book through one test. MapShootout has eight tellers record 800,000 deposits across 1,000 accounts, counting one per deposit. It runs three times: on a plain HashMap with merge, on a ConcurrentHashMap with a get followed by a put, and on a ConcurrentHashMap with merge. One run printed: HashMap.merge total 200,410 of 800,000 keys 1,019 of 1,000 threw ConcurrentModificationException ConcurrentHashMap get then put total 797,768 of 800,000 keys 1,000 of 1,000 ConcurrentHashMap.merge total 800,000 of 800,000 keys 1,000 of 1,000 The HashMap kept a quarter of the deposits and found 19 accounts that nobody opened. In other runs it kept between 100,008 and 200,410, and threw every time. It was never built for more than one thread, and it never claimed to be. The concurrent map with get then put lost 2,232 deposits: every call was safe, and the gap between two calls was not, just as in Race conditions. Only merge was exact. So why is one call safe? A hash map keeps an array of slots, called bins. A key's hash code, a number computed from the key, picks its bin, and every key whose hash lands there shares that bin. Picture the bank's old card files: a cabinet of drawers, each holding the cards for some of the account numbers. A clerk who updates a card opens one drawer. Another clerk can work in another drawer at the same time, but two clerks can't work in the same drawer at once. ConcurrentHashMap works like that cabinet. A write locks only the bin its key lands in: while one thread holds a bin's lock, no other thread can write to that bin. So writes to different keys mostly run side by side. A write into an empty bin takes no lock at all: it uses compare-and-set, a write that happens only if nobody changed the slot first, as in the last lesson. And reads never lock. That's where the cabinet picture breaks: in the map, anyone may read any card at any moment, even one that a clerk is busy updating. Every single-key call is atomic, done as one step that no other thread can split, because a write does its whole job inside one bin lock or one compare-and-set. Two calls in a row are two separate steps, and another thread's write can land between them. So the map offers methods that do a whole read-modify-write (read the value, change it, write it back) on one key in one call: putIfAbsent(k, v) inserts only if the key is missing. computeIfAbsent(k, f) computes and inserts only if the key is missing, and runs f at most once. compute(k, f) and computeIfPresent(k, f) replace the value with f of the old one. merge(k, v, f) inserts v, or replaces the old value with f(old, v). replace(k, expected, next) is a compare-and-set on one key. The Javadoc (the official API documentation) of each compute method says "The entire method invocation is performed atomically." That sentence is the reason to use them. Here are two of them at the bank: Java ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long> balances = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); void deposit(String account, long cents) { balances.merge(account, cents, Long::sum); // insert or add, atomically for this key } boolean open(String account) { return balances.putIfAbsent(account, 0L) == null; // true only for the caller that opened it } Kotlin val balances = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long>() fun deposit(account: String, cents: Long) { balances.merge(account, cents, Long::plus) // insert or add, atomically for this key } fun open(account: String): Boolean = balances.putIfAbsent(account, 0L) == null // true only for the caller that opened it The figure shows why this scales. Two tellers who update accounts in different bins never meet. Two tellers who update the same account take turns, which is exactly what we want. One call is atomic for its key. Do the whole read-modify-write in that one call. Two more details. ConcurrentHashMap rejects null keys and values with NullPointerException. That's on purpose. When get(k) returns null, it always means "absent", so you never need a second call to tell "missing" from "mapped to null". A second call would be check-then-act: a check, then an action that assumes the check still holds. And Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>()) is no substitute. It has one lock for the whole map, and the same gap between calls. The function you hand to merge runs inside that bin lock, though. What happens when it's slow? Three maps, one count Read MapShootout. Eight tellers record 800,000 deposits across 1,000 accounts: on a HashMap with merge, on a ConcurrentHashMap with get-then-put, and on a ConcurrentHashMap with merge. Predict the total and the number of keys for each. Run it twice. MapShootout.java package workbench.concurrency.l09; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** 8 tellers count 800,000 deposits over 1,000 accounts, three ways. Only one way is right. */ public class MapShootout { static void run(String label, Map<String, Integer> counts, Consumer<String> countOne) throws InterruptedException { CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] ts = new Thread[8]; String[] error = new String[1]; for (int i = 0; i < ts.length; i++) { ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); for (int n = 0; n < 100_000; n++) countOne.accept("acct-" + (n % 1_000)); } catch (Throwable e) { error[0] = e.getClass().getSimpleName(); } }); ts[i].setDaemon(true); // a corrupted HashMap can even loop forever ts[i].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(5_000); long total = 0; try { for (int v : counts.values()) total += v; } catch (Throwable e) { error[0] = e.getClass().getSimpleName(); } System.out.printf("%-32s total %,9d of 800,000 keys %,5d of 1,000%s%n", label, total, counts.size(), error[0] == null ? "" : " threw " + error[0]); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Map<String, Integer> plain = new HashMap<>(); run("HashMap.merge", plain, k -> plain.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum)); Map<String, Integer> chm1 = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); run("ConcurrentHashMap get then put", chm1, k -> chm1.put(k, chm1.getOrDefault(k, 0) + 1)); Map<String, Integer> chm2 = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); run("ConcurrentHashMap.merge", chm2, k -> chm2.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum)); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l09.MapShootout labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l09/MapShootout.java MapShootout.kt package workbench.concurrency.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import kotlin.concurrent.thread // 8 tellers count 800,000 deposits over 1,000 accounts, three ways. h: Concurrent collections · Keeping the work inside compute short, and never touching the map from it
x: The function you pass to compute, merge or computeIfAbsent runs while the map holds the lock on that key's bin. Three things follow from that. First, other writes to the same bin wait for your whole function. The Javadoc says so: "Some attempted update operations on this map by other threads may be blocked while computation is in progress, so the computation should be short and simple." Remember the exchange-rate table from Explicit locks? On a ConcurrentHashMap, its load-once logic shrinks to one line: Java ConcurrentHashMap<String, BigDecimal> rates = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); BigDecimal rate(String pair) { return rates.computeIfAbsent(pair, rateService::lookup); // 120 ms, with the bin locked } Kotlin val rates = ConcurrentHashMap<String, BigDecimal>() fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal = rates.computeIfAbsent(pair, rateService::lookup) // 120 ms, with the bin locked The read-write lock version had to let go, take the write lock and check again. Here the map does all of that, for one key. The catch is the loader, the function that fetches a missing rate. Say it calls a slow web service, a program on another computer that answers over the network, and the answer takes 120 ms. Then every write that lands in that bin waits 120 ms too. Reads aren't blocked. For a table that loads each pair once, that's often fine. When it isn't, the worked example shows how to keep the slow work outside the map. Second, the function must not change the map. The Javadoc is blunt again: "The mapping function must not modify this map during computation." Memoized recursion is how people break this rule without noticing. That's a function that saves each answer in a map, so it never works out the same answer twice: Java long fib(int n) { if (n < 2) return n; return memo.computeIfAbsent(n, k -> fib(k - 1) + fib(k - 2)); // calls computeIfAbsent again, inside } Kotlin fun fib(n: Int): Long { if (n < 2) return n.toLong() return memo.computeIfAbsent(n) { k -> fib(k - 1) + fib(k - 2) } // calls computeIfAbsent again, inside } On JDK 21, ConcurrentHashMap throws IllegalStateException: Recursive update here, and HashMap throws ConcurrentModificationException. The JDK catches only some of these cases, so don't count on an exception. Compute the value outside the map, or fill the table from the bottom up, smallest first. Third, if the function throws, nothing is stored, and the exception reaches the caller, so the next call tries again. If it returns null, nothing is stored either. The lab relies on that. The function inside compute holds a lock. Keep it short, and leave the map alone. So far, single calls have changed the map. Loops over a collection that others are changing come next, and that's where the exception with the misleading name lives. Break the rule on purpose Run RecursiveUpdate. It works out fib(30) with memoized recursion on a ConcurrentHashMap, then on a HashMap, then from the bottom up. Read the exception messages. Which map tells you what you did wrong? RecursiveUpdate.java package workbench.concurrency.l09; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; /** Memoized Fibonacci where the mapping function calls back into the same map. The Javadoc forbids it. */ public class RecursiveUpdate { static Map<Integer, Long> memo; static long fib(int n) { if (n < 2) return n; return memo.computeIfAbsent(n, k -> fib(k - 1) + fib(k - 2)); // modifies the map from inside compute } public static void main(String[] args) { for (Map<Integer, Long> m : List.<Map<Integer, Long>>of(new ConcurrentHashMap<>(), new HashMap<>())) { memo = m; try { System.out.println(m.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": fib(30) = " + fib(30)); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println(m.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": threw " + e); } } // the fix: build the table bottom-up, outside any compute call Map<Integer, Long> table = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(Map.of(0, 0L, 1, 1L)); for (int n = 2; n <= 30; n++) table.put(n, table.get(n - 1) + table.get(n - 2)); System.out.println("bottom-up: fib(30) = " + table.get(30)); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l09.RecursiveUpdate labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l09/RecursiveUpdate.java RecursiveUpdate.kt package workbench.concurrency.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap // Memoized Fibonacci where the mapping function calls back into the same map. The Javadoc forbids it. private lateinit var memo: MutableMap<Int, Long> private fun fib(n: Int): Long { if (n < 2) return n.toLong() return memo.computeIfAbsent(n) { k -> fib(k - 1) + fib(k - 2) } // modifies the map from inside compute } fun main() { for (m in listOf<MutableMap<Int, Long>>(ConcurrentHashMap(), HashMap())) { memo = m try { println("${m.javaClass.simpleName}: fib(30) = ${fib(30)}") } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println("${m.javaClass.simpleName}: threw $e") } } // the fix: build the table bottom-up, outside any compute call val table = ConcurrentHashMap(mapOf(0 to 0L, 1 to 1L)) for (n in 2..30) table[n] = table.getValue(n - 1) + table.getValue(n - 2) println("bottom-up: fib(30) = ${table[30]}") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l09.RecursiveUpdateKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l09/RecursiveUpdate.kt ConcurrentHashMap: threw java.lang.IllegalStateException: Recursive update, HashMap: threw java.util.ConcurrentModificationException, and bottom-up: fib(30) = 832040. Only the version that fills the table outside any compute call works.

h: Concurrent collections · What ConcurrentModificationException really means: fail-fast and weakly consistent iterators
x: ConcurrentModificationException sounds like "two threads touched my collection". It means something narrower: this collection's own iterator noticed that the collection changed in a way the iterator didn't make. (An iterator is the object a for-each loop uses to step through a collection.) ArrayList and HashMap iterators are fail-fast. They keep a count of changes, and check it at every step. Picture a careful bookkeeper reading down a list of payments. At every line he checks the page count, and if it changed, he stops and complains, even when he made the change himself. That's why one thread is enough to trip the check, as the warm-up showed. And he's careful, not watchful. When two threads really race, the check is only best effort. It may not fire at all, and you get lost entries or a damaged structure instead. Never treat the exception as a race detector. The concurrent collections have weakly consistent iterators instead. They never throw ConcurrentModificationException, and they show the collection as it was at some point at or after the moment the loop began. A change made during the loop may or may not show up. The same goes for size(), isEmpty() and containsValue() on ConcurrentHashMap. While other threads update the map, they describe a moving target. The Javadoc calls them useful for monitoring and estimation, not for program control. So if (balances.size() < 10_000) balances.put(k, v) is check-then-act on an estimate. CopyOnWriteArrayList takes the opposite trade. Every write copies the whole array. Every loop walks the array as it was when the loop started, so a loop never locks and never throws. Remember the listeners from synchronized and intrinsic locks, the pieces of code that ask to hear about every new balance? A list of them changes rarely and is read on every deposit, which suits a copy-on-write list perfectly. It's terrible for a list that grows with traffic, though: adding the 100,000th element copies 100,000 references. Its set cousin is CopyOnWriteArraySet, and ConcurrentSkipListMap is the concurrent map that keeps its keys sorted. The exception is a bookkeeping check, not a race detector. Never count on it to find races. Maps and lists hold data that threads share. The last collection in this lesson moves work from one thread to another, and you've already built it by hand. Trip a fail-fast iterator with one thread Read FailFast. It changes an ArrayList, a ConcurrentHashMap and a CopyOnWriteArrayList while looping over each one, all on the main thread. Predict what each line prints. In the copy-on-write loop, the body adds an item for every item it sees: does the loop ever end? Run it. FailFast.java package workbench.concurrency.l09; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; /** ConcurrentModificationException needs no second thread. And concurrent collections never throw it. */ public class FailFast { public static void main(String[] args) { // 1. one thread, an ArrayList, a remove inside for-each List<String> pending = new ArrayList<>(List.of("pay-1", "pay-2", "pay-3", "pay-4")); try { for (String p : pending) { if (p.equals("pay-2")) pending.remove(p); // changes the list under its own iterator } } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("ArrayList, one thread: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()); } // 2. the same with a ConcurrentHashMap: weakly consistent, never throws Map<String, Integer> open = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(Map.of("pay-1", 1, "pay-2", 2, "pay-3", 3, "pay-4", 4)); for (String k : open.keySet()) { if (k.equals("pay-2")) open.remove(k); if (k.equals("pay-3")) open.put("pay-5", 5); // may or may not show up in this loop } System.out.println("ConcurrentHashMap: no exception, now " + open.size() + " keys"); // 3. CopyOnWriteArrayList: the loop walks a snapshot taken when it started List<String> hooks = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b", "c")); int seen = 0; for (String h : hooks) { hooks.add(h + "+"); // goes into a NEW array seen++; } System.out.println("CopyOnWriteArrayList: loop saw " + seen + " items, list now has " + hooks.size()); // 4. the single-thread fix for case 1: remove through the iterator, or removeIf pending = new ArrayList<>(List.of("pay-1", "pay-2", "pay-3", "pay-4")); pending.removeIf(p -> p.equals("pay-2")); System.out.println("ArrayList.removeIf: " + pending); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l09.FailFast labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l09/FailFast.java FailFast.kt package workbench.concurrency.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList // ConcurrentModificationException needs no second thread. And concurrent collections never throw it. fun main() { // 1. one thread, an ArrayList, a remove inside a for loop var pending = mutableListOf("pay-1", "pay-2", "pay-3", "pay-4") try { for (p in pending) { if (p == "pay-2") pending.remove(p) // changes the list under its own iterator } } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println("ArrayList, one thread: ${e.javaClass.simpleName}") } // 2. the same with a ConcurrentHashMap: weakly consistent, never throws val open = ConcurrentHashMap(mapOf("pay-1" to 1, "pay-2" to 2, "pay-3" to 3, "pay-4" to 4)) for (k in open.keys) { if (k == "pay-2") open.remove(k) if (k == "pay-3") open["pay-5"] = 5 // may or may not show up in this loop } println("ConcurrentHashMap: no exception, now ${open.size} keys") // 3. CopyOnWriteArrayList: the loop walks a snapshot taken when it started val hooks = CopyOnWriteArrayList(listOf("a", "b", "c")) var seen = 0 for (h in hooks) { hooks.add("$h+") // goes into a NEW array seen++ } println("CopyOnWriteArrayList: loop saw $seen items, list now has ${hooks.size}") // 4. the single-thread fix for case 1: remove through the iterator, or removeIf pending = mutableListOf("pay-1", "pay-2", "pay-3", "pay-4") pending.removeIf { it == "pay-2" } println("ArrayList.removeIf: $pending") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l09.FailFastKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l09/FailFast.kt The ArrayList throws ConcurrentModificationException with one thread. The ConcurrentHashMap loop throws nothing and ends with 4 keys. The copy-on-write loop sees 3 items and ends, while the list now has 6, because the loop walks the snapshot it started with. removeIf is the single-thread fix for the first case. h: Concurrent collections · The kitchen's rail, ready-made: BlockingQueue and backpressure
x: In wait, notify and guarded blocks, we built the kitchen's rail by hand. Waiters put order tickets on, cooks take them off, and each side waits when it must. In Explicit locks, we rebuilt it with two Conditions. ArrayBlockingQueue is the version that comes with the JDK. A blocking queue is a queue whose put and take wait when it's full or empty, and every BlockingQueue offers four ways to add and remove: Throws Returns a special value Waits Waits, up to a time limit Insert add(e) offer(e): false if full put(e) offer(e, time, unit) Remove remove() poll(): null if empty take() poll(time, unit) Examine element() peek(): null if empty Pick the column by what the caller should do when the rail is full or empty. A waiter with a customer at the table might use offer and get an answer now. A cook with nothing else to do uses take, and sleeps until a ticket arrives. Queues reject null, because poll uses null to mean "empty". QueueMethods tries each column on a rail with room for two tickets. One run printed: add: throws java.lang.IllegalStateException: Queue full offer: false offer(300 ms): false after 300 ms put: the waiter is WAITING until a slot opens take: ticket-1 (frees a slot) queue now: [ticket-2, ticket-3] offer(null): throws NullPointerException new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() capacity: 2147483647 SynchronousQueue.offer with no taker waiting: false Each of the first five lines matches its column in the table. The last two are the surprises, and the list of implementations explains them: ArrayBlockingQueue has a fixed capacity, backed by one array and one lock. LinkedBlockingQueue takes an optional capacity, and the default is Integer.MAX_VALUE, over two billion. That's unbounded in practice. It uses separate locks for the head and the tail, so waiters and cooks get in each other's way less. SynchronousQueue has no capacity at all. Each put waits for a take, and an offer with no cook waiting returns false. PriorityBlockingQueue orders by priority and is unbounded. DelayQueue releases each element only when its delay has passed. That default capacity is the trap. new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() looks harmless, and its put never waits, so it passes every test. Then one evening the cooks slow down, the waiters keep adding, and the rail grows to millions of tickets. The heap, the memory where Java keeps its objects, fills up, and the program dies, taking every waiting ticket with it. A queue with a capacity gives you backpressure instead, the term from the kitchen lesson. When the cooks fall behind, put makes the waiters wait, or offer tells them to come back later. The program slows down instead of filling memory. Give every queue between threads a capacity. Decide on purpose what a full queue means. drainTo(list, max) moves everything already queued in one call, without waiting, which is how you take work in batches. The lab's Batcher uses exactly that pair: poll with a timeout for the first entry, then drainTo for the rest. The executors track meets the same unbounded queue again, hidden inside Executors.newFixedThreadPool, a ready-made thread pool (a fixed group of threads that runs the tasks you hand it). That's where collections stop. Each one makes a call safe, or moves work between threads. None of them can make a thread wait until five others are ready, or let only three threads in at a time. Fill the rail every way you can Read QueueMethods. It fills an ArrayBlockingQueue with room for 2 tickets, then tries add, offer, timed offer and put on the full rail. Predict each line, including the capacity of a LinkedBlockingQueue built with no arguments. Run it. QueueMethods.java package workbench.concurrency.l09; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** The kitchen's rail as a BlockingQueue: four ways to add to a full one, and two queues that surprise people. */ public class QueueMethods { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { BlockingQueue<String> q = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2); q.put("ticket-1"); q.put("ticket-2"); // now full try { q.add("ticket-3"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("add: throws " + e); } System.out.println("offer: " + q.offer("ticket-3")); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); boolean timed = q.offer("ticket-3", 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); System.out.printf("offer(300 ms): %s after %d ms%n", timed, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); Thread waiter = new Thread(() -> { try { q.put("ticket-3"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); waiter.start(); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println("put: the waiter is " + waiter.getState() + " until a slot opens"); System.out.println("take: " + q.take() + " (frees a slot)"); waiter.join(); System.out.println("queue now: " + q); try { q.offer(null); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("offer(null): throws NullPointerException"); } System.out.println("new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() capacity: " + new LinkedBlockingQueue<String>().remainingCapacity()); System.out.println("SynchronousQueue.offer with no taker waiting: " + new SynchronousQueue<String>().offer("ticket-9")); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l09.QueueMethods labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l09/QueueMethods.java QueueMethods.kt package workbench.concurrency.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import kotlin.concurrent.thread // The kitchen's rail as a BlockingQueue: four ways to add to a full one, and two queues that surprise people. fun main() { val q: BlockingQueue<String> = ArrayBlockingQueue(2) q.put("ticket-1") q.put("ticket-2") // now full try { q.add("ticket-3") } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("add: throws $e") } println("offer: ${q.offer("ticket-3")}") val t0 = System.nanoTime() val timed = q.offer("ticket-3", 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) println("offer(300 ms): $timed after ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms") val waiter = thread { q.put("ticket-3") } Thread.sleep(200) println("put: the waiter is ${waiter.state} until a slot opens") println("take: ${q.take()} (frees a slot)") waiter.join() println("queue now: $q") // Kotlin won't even compile q.offer(null) on a BlockingQueue<String>; the JDK would throw NullPointerException println("LinkedBlockingQueue() capacity: ${LinkedBlockingQueue<String>().remainingCapacity()}") println("SynchronousQueue.offer with no taker waiting: ${SynchronousQueue<String>().offer("ticket-9")}") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l09.QueueMethodsKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l09/QueueMethods.kt add throws IllegalStateException: Queue full, offer returns false at once, the timed offer returns false after about 300 ms, and the waiter in put is WAITING until take frees a slot. h: Concurrent collections · Java and Kotlin
x: Load-once caching in Java and Kotlin Java ConcurrentHashMap<String, BigDecimal> rates = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); BigDecimal rate(String pair) { return rates.computeIfAbsent(pair, rateService::lookup); // lookup runs at most once per pair } Kotlin val rates = ConcurrentHashMap<String, BigDecimal>() fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal = rates.getOrPut(pair) { rateService.lookup(pair) } // atomic put, but lookup may run several times fun rateOnce(pair: String): BigDecimal = rates.computeIfAbsent(pair) { rateService.lookup(it) } // lookup runs at most once per pair Kotlin's usual getOrPut is the trap. The standard library has a special version for ConcurrentMap that uses putIfAbsent, so it never overwrites a value that is already there. But its documentation says the default function "may be invoked even if the key is already in the map". With 8 threads racing for one new key, the lookup ran 8 times in a check here, against once for computeIfAbsent. And if the variable's declared type is plain MutableMap, Kotlin picks the general getOrPut, which is a check followed by a put with no atomicity at all. Use computeIfAbsent when the loader is slow or must run once. Kotlin's types do help in one place: a ConcurrentHashMap<String, BigDecimal> can't be handed a null value, so the NullPointerException that Java callers can hit becomes a compile error.

h: Concurrent collections · Worked example
x: Load once, without holding the bin for 120 ms The rate service takes 120 ms to answer. This table loads each currency pair once, which is good. But while it loads, every other write that lands in the same bin waits, and the Javadoc asks for short functions. The goal: keep the map call tiny and do the slow work outside it, while still loading each pair once. ConcurrentHashMap<String, BigDecimal> rates = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); BigDecimal rate(String pair) { return rates.computeIfAbsent(pair, rateService::lookup); // 120 ms, with the bin locked } val rates = ConcurrentHashMap<String, BigDecimal>() fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal = rates.computeIfAbsent(pair, rateService::lookup) // 120 ms, with the bin locked Store the promise of a value instead of the value. A CompletableFuture is that promise: a box that will hold a result later, and anyone can wait for the result with join(). The function inside computeIfAbsent now only creates the box and starts the lookup on slowCalls, a thread pool kept for slow calls. That takes microseconds, so the bin is free again almost at once. Every caller for the pair gets the same box and waits on it outside the map. private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<BigDecimal>> rates = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); BigDecimal rate(String pair) { // 1. claim the pair: the function only creates a future, so the bin is locked for microseconds CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> f = rates.computeIfAbsent(pair, p -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> rateService.lookup(p), slowCalls)); try { return f.join(); // 2. wait outside the map, with every other caller } catch (CompletionException e) { rates.remove(pair, f); // 3. failed: forget THIS future so a retry loads again throw e; } } private val rates = ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<BigDecimal>>() fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal { // 1. claim the pair: the function only creates a future, so the bin is locked for microseconds val f = rates.computeIfAbsent(pair) { p -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ rateService.lookup(p) }, slowCalls) } try { return f.join() // 2. wait outside the map, with every other caller } catch (e: CompletionException) { rates.remove(pair, f) // 3. failed: forget THIS future so a retry loads again throw e } } Before reading on, explain to yourself: why remove(pair, f) with two arguments, and not remove(pair)? Answer: between the failure and the remove, another thread may already have put a fresh future in place of the failed one. The two-argument remove deletes the entry only if it still maps to the future that failed. It's a compare-and-set on one key, and it keeps you from throwing away someone else's good load. This is the Memoizer from Java Concurrency in Practice, section 5.6, written with CompletableFuture. One gap is left: entries never expire, so yesterday's rate stays in the table until the program restarts. If you write services, a caching library with expiry and loading in the background does all this for you. Writing it once by hand shows you what such a library does, and what to look for when it misbehaves.

h: Concurrent collections · Lab
x: Three concurrent-collection fixes labs/concurrency/src/main/java/workbench/concurrency/l09/BinCache.java labs/concurrency/src/main/java/workbench/concurrency/l09/WebhookRegistry.java labs/concurrency/src/main/java/workbench/concurrency/l09/Batcher.java ./gradlew :concurrency:test --tests 'workbench.concurrency.l09.*' Run the tests. Six of eight fail: BinCache calls its loader 8 times for one key, WebhookRegistry throws ConcurrentModificationException (once even with a single thread), and Batcher throws UnsupportedOperationException. BinCache remembers which bank issued each kind of card. The first six digits of a card number, called the BIN, say which bank issued it, and the loader asks a slow service. Fix issuerFor with one ConcurrentHashMap call, so the loader runs once per BIN. WebhookRegistry keeps the list of listeners that hear about every payment. (It's named after webhooks, the web addresses that shops give a bank so it can tell them about each payment.) Fix it by changing the type of collection it uses. You don't need a lock. Batcher collects entries from many threads and hands them to one writer thread in groups, so the writer can save 100 at a time instead of one. Write it on an ArrayBlockingQueue. submit uses offer. nextBatch waits with poll(timeout) for the first entry, then calls drainTo(batch, max - 1). Run the tests until all eight pass, then twice more. computeIfAbsent takes the loader as it is: issuers.computeIfAbsent(bin, loader). If the loader throws, nothing is stored, which is what the third test checks. Why not Collections.synchronizedList for the registry? Its add and remove are safe, but you must hold its lock for the whole loop while iterating, and a listener that unregisters itself during publish still throws, on the same thread. poll(timeout) returns null when time runs out. drainTo never waits; it moves only what is already there. All eight tests in ConcurrentCollectionsTest pass, three runs in a row. By the end you can pick the right concurrent collection for a job, use ConcurrentHashMap's atomic per-key methods correctly, and explain what weakly consistent iteration and ConcurrentModificationException really mean.

h: Concurrent collections · From memory
x: A per-key counter from memory Close this page. Write DepositCounter with record(String account) and long count(String account), safe for many threads, using a ConcurrentHashMap and one LongAdder per account. Then check: can two threads ever create two adders for the same account?

h: Concurrent collections · Quiz
x: From Atomics and compare-and-set: sixteen threads count deposits per account, and about 200 accounts get most of the traffic. Which is the best fit? HashMap<String, Long> with merge ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> with computeIfAbsent(k, x -> new LongAdder()).increment() ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long> with put(k, get(k) + 1) Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>()) with merge computeIfAbsent creates each adder once, and after that every increment goes to a LongAdder, which spreads a busy account over several cells. merge on a ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long> would also be correct, just with more contention on the busy accounts. A plain HashMap breaks, get-then-put loses updates, and a synchronized map makes every thread wait on one lock. Why does ConcurrentHashMap throw NullPointerException for put(k, null)? So that get(k) == null always means the key is absent, with no second call needed Because nulls would damage its bins It doesn't: only null keys are rejected To save memory If null values were allowed, get returning null would be ambiguous, and telling "absent" from "mapped to null" would need containsKey as well. Two calls is check-then-act, which another thread can break. Banning null removes the question. A cache uses map.computeIfAbsent(id, k -> loadAccount(k)), and loadAccount calls map.computeIfAbsent(parentId, ...) on the same map. What should you expect? It works, because the two keys differ A deadlock every time It breaks the documented contract; ConcurrentHashMap may throw IllegalStateException: Recursive update, or misbehave A ConcurrentModificationException from an iterator The Javadoc says the mapping function must not modify the map. Whether the JDK notices depends on where the keys land, so sometimes it throws Recursive update and sometimes it seems to work. Don't rely on either. Load the parent first, outside the compute call. A list of five listeners, pieces of code that hear about every new balance, changes only when the program is updated. It's looped over on each of 3,000 deposits a second, from many threads. Which collection fits? ArrayList guarded by synchronized around every loop Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>()) ConcurrentLinkedQueue CopyOnWriteArrayList Reads far outnumber writes and the list is tiny, so copying the array on each rare write is cheap, and every loop runs without a lock over a snapshot that can't change. The synchronized options make every deposit take a lock for the whole loop. A queue would work for looping, but it doesn't model a list you add to and remove from as cleanly. Request threads put ledger entries into new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(), and a single writer thread saves them to a database. One evening the database slows down. What happens? put makes the request threads wait once the queue holds 10,000 entries The queue grows without limit, because the default capacity is Integer.MAX_VALUE, until memory runs out put throws IllegalStateException when the queue is full The writer thread speeds up to match With no capacity, the queue never fills, so nothing pushes back on the request threads. Memory grows until the program dies, taking the queued entries with it. Give the queue a capacity, so put makes the producers wait, or offer fails and they can answer "try again later".

h: Concurrent collections · Explain it back
