h: Synchronizers: latch, barrier, semaphore, phaser · Key terms
x: Synchronizer An object that makes threads wait for each other or for events, such as a latch, a barrier or a semaphore. CountDownLatch A one-shot gate that opens when its count reaches zero. CyclicBarrier A meeting point for a fixed number of threads that resets itself after each round. Barrier action Code a CyclicBarrier runs once per round, on the last thread to arrive, before releasing the others. Semaphore A counter of permits that limits how many threads can do something at once. Permit One unit of a semaphore's count. It belongs to nobody. Phaser A reusable barrier whose group of parties can change between phases. A CountDownLatch has reached zero. What do later await() and countDown() calls do? await() returns at once. countDown() does nothing. A latch can't be reset. When does a CyclicBarrier's barrier action run, and on which thread? Once per round, on the last thread to arrive, before any waiting thread is released. What breaks a CyclicBarrier? A waiting thread being interrupted or timing out, the barrier action throwing, or reset(). Then every waiting thread gets BrokenBarrierException. What does release() do on a Semaphore when the caller never acquired a permit? It adds a permit anyway. Permits have no owner, so stray releases silently raise the limit. Where do acquire() and release() go around try and finally? acquire() on the line before try, release() in finally. With tryAcquire, check its result before entering the try. Latch or barrier: "open after 3 lists load" vs "3 tills finish day N before any starts day N+1"? The first is a latch (waiting for events, once). The second is a barrier (a fixed group meeting every round). What can a Phaser do that a CyclicBarrier can't? Change its number of parties between phases: register() to join, arriveAndDeregister() to leave.

h: Synchronizers: latch, barrier, semaphore, phaser · Go deeper
x: CountDownLatch and Semaphore, like ReentrantLock, are thin layers over AbstractQueuedSynchronizer, a JDK class that holds one int of state and a queue of parked threads. For a latch the state is the count, and await parks until it is zero. For a semaphore it is the number of permits left. CyclicBarrier is a ReentrantLock with one Condition, and Phaser and Exchanger keep their own queues of parked threads. All of them park through LockSupport, which is why they look the same in a thread dump: WAITING (parking), with a line like parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.Semaphore$NonfairSync). A few corners of the API are worth knowing. Semaphore.acquire(n) takes several permits in one step, which avoids the hold-one-and-wait-for-another deadlock from the quiz. drainPermits() takes all that are left, which is handy when you want to stop new work during a shutdown. acquireUninterruptibly() ignores interrupts, which you almost never want. CyclicBarrier.await() returns the arrival index (parties minus one for the first to arrive, zero for the last), so you can pick one thread to do extra work without a barrier action. Phaser supports tiering: you can build a tree of phasers so that thousands of parties don't all compete for one. Its Javadoc caps a single phaser at 65,535 registered parties. Virtual threads (JDK 21) are very light threads that the JVM runs on a few ordinary ones. Blocking in any of these tools is cheap there: the virtual thread parks, and the ordinary thread under it runs something else. A Semaphore is in fact the standard way to limit how many calls run at once when you start a virtual thread per task, because there's no pool size to do it for you. The virtual threads track comes back to that. In Kotlin coroutines, the equivalents suspend instead of blocking: kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore, Job.join() or awaitAll() where you'd use a latch, and channels for most of the rest.

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · A race needs two ingredients: take away change with immutable snapshots
x: A race needs state that is shared and changing: a price board swapped in one write takes away change, a ticket handed over on the rail takes away sharing, and a pool thread is a hotel room that needs housekeeping Look back at every race in this track and you'll find the same two ingredients. In Race conditions, eight threads added deposits to one balance: the balance was shared, and it changed. In Deadlock, livelock and starvation, two transfers locked the same two accounts: shared, and changing. A race needs both, so taking away either one leaves nothing to lock. A race needs state that is shared and changing. Take away either one, and there is nothing to lock. This lesson takes them away one at a time, starting with change. Here's the shop's price list. A refresher thread moves every price to a new version now and then, and the tills read prices all day. Most programs start with one map, updated in place: Java // Naive: every call is thread-safe, the refresh as a whole is not private final Map<String, Long> prices = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); void refresh(Map<String, Long> fresh) { prices.putAll(fresh); // one price at a time, while the tills read } Long price(String item) { return prices.get(item); } Kotlin // Naive: every call is thread-safe, the refresh as a whole is not private val prices = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long>() fun refresh(fresh: Map<String, Long>) { prices.putAll(fresh) // one price at a time, while the tills read } fun price(item: String): Long? = prices[item] ConcurrentHashMap, the thread-safe map from Concurrent collections, makes every single put and get safe. But a refresh is four puts, and a till can read between them. The Try it counts how often that happens. Each refresh moves all four prices (bread, milk, eggs and apples) to the same version number, and the main thread reads all four, over and over, for one second. A read that sees two versions at once caught a refresh half done. It printed: reads: 4,702,038 mixed versions, shared mutable map: 981,129 immutable snapshot: 0 About one read in five saw a price list that never existed. Every call was thread-safe, and the answer was still wrong. Now take away change. An object is immutable when nobody can change it after it's built, and then every thread can read it at any time, with no lock. In Java that takes four things. All its fields are final and set in the constructor. It has no setters. Every changing thing it holds is copied in and never handed out. And the constructor doesn't let this escape, that is, it doesn't hand a reference to the half-built object to other code. A record, Java's short form for a class of final fields, gets you most of the way, and so does a Kotlin data class with vals: Java public record Price(String item, long cents) { // fields are final public Price withCents(long newCents) { // "changes" return a new object return new Price(item, newCents); } } Kotlin data class Price(val item: String, val cents: Long) // vals: final fields val cheaper = bread.copy(cents = 230) // "changes" return a new object To "change" an immutable object, you build a new one. That's the price board again: print a new one and swap it. In code, the swap is one write to a volatile field, a field that every thread always reads fresh, so a write to it is seen by every later reader: Java // Fixed: an immutable snapshot, replaced whole private volatile Map<String, Long> prices = Map.of(); void refresh(Map<String, Long> fresh) { prices = Map.copyOf(fresh); // build it completely, then publish it in one write } Long price(String item) { return prices.get(item); // no lock: every map this field ever holds is immutable } Kotlin // Fixed: an immutable snapshot, replaced whole @Volatile private var prices: Map<String, Long> = emptyMap() fun refresh(fresh: Map<String, Long>) { prices = java.util.Map.copyOf(fresh) // build it completely, then publish it in one write } fun price(item: String): Long? = prices[item] // no lock: every map this field ever holds is immutable The refresher builds the new map off to the side, where no till can see it. Map.copyOf makes it unmodifiable, and one volatile write publishes it. A till that reads the field once gets one complete version: the old board or the new one, never half of each. That's the immutable snapshot: 0 in the output, every run. If a till needs several prices from the same version, it copies the field into a local variable first and reads them all from that. final fields carry one more promise, from the Java memory model, the rules for what one thread sees of another thread's writes. A thread that gets a reference to an object after its constructor has finished sees the right values in its final fields, even if nothing else synchronized the hand-over. Non-final fields get no such promise, and the memory model track explains why. The snapshot took away change. Records have a catch, though: they freeze less than they seem to. Half-done refreshes, counted Read SnapshotSwap. A refresher thread moves four prices to a new version over and over. It updates a ConcurrentHashMap in place, and it also publishes an immutable snapshot through a volatile field. For one second, the main thread reads all four prices from each and counts the reads that saw two versions at once. Predict both counts. Run it, then run the Kotlin twin. SnapshotSwap.java package workbench.concurrency.l11; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; /** * A shop's price list, refreshed as a whole while the tills read it. Every refresh moves all * prices to the same new "version". A till that sees two versions in one look saw a half-done refresh. */ public class SnapshotSwap { static final String[] ITEMS = {"bread", "milk", "eggs", "apples"}; // 1. shared mutable map, refreshed in place (each put is thread-safe on its own) static final Map<String, Long> live = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // 2. an immutable map behind a volatile reference, replaced in one write static volatile Map<String, Long> snapshot = Map.of(); static volatile boolean done; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread refresher = new Thread(() -> { for (long version = 1; !done; version++) { for (String p : ITEMS) live.put(p, version); // readers can see a mix Map<String, Long> fresh = new HashMap<>(); for (String p : ITEMS) fresh.put(p, version); snapshot = Map.copyOf(fresh); // build fully, then publish once } }); refresher.start(); long mixedLive = 0, mixedSnapshot = 0, reads = 0; long end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { reads++; if (mixed(live)) mixedLive++; if (mixed(snapshot)) mixedSnapshot++; // one read of the reference: one version } done = true; refresher.join(); System.out.printf("reads: %,d mixed versions, shared mutable map: %,d immutable snapshot: %d%n", reads, mixedLive, mixedSnapshot); } static boolean mixed(Map<String, Long> prices) { Long first = prices.get(ITEMS[0]); for (String p : ITEMS) if (!java.util.Objects.equals(prices.get(p), first)) return true; return false; } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l11.SnapshotSwap labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l11/SnapshotSwap.java SnapshotSwap.kt package workbench.concurrency.l11 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A shop's price list, refreshed as a whole while the tills read it. Every refresh moves all // prices to the same new "version". A till that sees two versions in one look saw a half-done refresh. private val ITEMS = listOf("bread", "milk", "eggs", "apples") // 1. shared mutable map, refreshed in place (each put is thread-safe on its own) private val live = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long>() // 2. an immutable map behind a volatile reference, replaced in one write @Volatile private var snapshot: Map<String, Long> = emptyMap() @Volatile private var done = false private fun mixed(prices: Map<String, Long>): Boolean { val first = prices[ITEMS[0]] return ITEMS.any { prices[it] != first } } fun main() { val refresher = thread { var version = 1L while (!done) { for (p in ITEMS) live[p] = version // readers can see a mix snapshot = java.util.Map.copyOf(ITEMS.associateWith { version }) // build fully, then publish once version++ } } var mixedLive = 0L; var mixedSnapshot = 0L; var reads = 0L val end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L while (System.nanoTime() < end) { reads++ if (mixed(live)) mixedLive++ if (mixed(snapshot)) mixedSnapshot++ // one read of the reference: one version } done = true refresher.join() println("reads: %,d mixed versions, shared mutable map: %,d immutable snapshot: %d".format(reads, mixedLive, mixedSnapshot)) } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l11.SnapshotSwapKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l11/SnapshotSwap.kt The shared mutable map shows mixed versions in hundreds of thousands of reads (981,129 of 4,702,038 in one run here, about one in five), although every single put and get was thread-safe. The immutable snapshot shows 0, every run. Your counts will differ.

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · Records and data classes freeze less than they seem: defensive copies
x: final freezes the reference, not the object it points to. A record that stores a caller's ArrayList or array changes whenever the caller changes that list, and so does anyone you hand the array to. Here's the trap in the shop. A big customer asks for a price quote for bread, with tiers: one price up to 9 loaves, and a lower one for more. The quote also carries a signature, a few bytes that prove who made it. It's a record, so it looks safe: Java // Naive: the fields are final, the list and the array are not record Quote(String item, List<String> tiers, byte[] signature) {} List<String> tiers = new ArrayList<>(List.of("1 to 9 loaves at 2.50")); Quote quote = new Quote("bread", tiers, signature); tiers.add("10 or more at 0.01"); // the caller keeps changing its own list Kotlin // Naive: the vals are final, the list and the array are not data class Quote(val item: String, val tiers: List<String>, val signature: ByteArray) val tiers = mutableListOf("1 to 9 loaves at 2.50") val quote = Quote("bread", tiers, signature) tiers.add("10 or more at 0.01") // the caller keeps changing its own list The Try it builds this quote, then changes the caller's list and array after construction, and also writes into the array it gets back from signature(). It printed: shallow: [1 to 9 loaves at 2.50, 10 or more at 0.01] signature [0, 0, 7] deep: [1 to 9 loaves at 2.50] signature [7, 7, 7] unmodifiableList view: [1 to 9 loaves at 2.50, 10 or more at 0.01] The "immutable" quote now sells bread at a cent a loaf, and its signature changed twice: once through the caller's array, and once through a reader's. Nothing in the record was reassigned. The objects behind its final fields changed. That's shallow immutability: final references to things that can still change. The fix is a defensive copy: copy each changing part on the way in, and for arrays on the way out too. A record's compact constructor, the one with no parameter list, runs before the fields are set, so it can replace each parameter with a copy: Java // Fixed: copy in, and copy the array out record Quote(String item, List<String> tiers, byte[] signature) { Quote { tiers = List.copyOf(tiers); // reassign the parameter: the field gets the copy signature = signature.clone(); } @Override public byte[] signature() { return signature.clone(); // readers get a copy, never our array } } Kotlin // Fixed: copy in, and copy the array out class Quote(val item: String, tiers: List<String>, signature: ByteArray) { val tiers: List<String> = java.util.List.copyOf(tiers) // unmodifiable, even through a cast private val sig = signature.copyOf() val signature: ByteArray get() = sig.copyOf() // readers get a copy, never our array } That's the deep line in the output. A few details decide whether the copy works. List.copyOf makes an unmodifiable copy: later changes to the source don't show, and add on the copy throws. Collections.unmodifiableList(list) is not a copy. It's a read-only view of the caller's list, so the caller's later changes show straight through it, as the third line of the output shows. Arrays can't be made read-only. Clone them in the constructor and again in the accessor, or keep the data in an immutable type instead. The elements must be immutable too. A copied list of changeable objects is a new list of the same shared objects. String, BigDecimal, Instant, LocalDate and the boxed numbers such as Integer are immutable already; arrays, Date and Calendar are not. Kotlin adds one trap of its own. Its List type is a read-only interface, not an immutable list. A data class with val tiers: List<String> stores whatever MutableList the caller passed, and a cast or Java code can still change it. The Kotlin twin of the Try it adds a line to prove it. A data class also can't copy its constructor parameters, because those parameters are its properties. When you need the copy, use a plain class with a separate property, as above. A final field freezes the reference, not the object. Copy what can change. So far we've taken away change. The other ingredient is sharing: state that changes freely is still safe if only one thread can ever reach it. Change a record from outside Read ShallowRecord. ShallowQuote keeps the caller's list and array; DeepQuote copies them in and out. A third reference is an unmodifiableList view of the caller's list. After construction, the caller changes its list and array, and a reader writes into the array it got from signature(). Predict all three lines. Run it, then run the Kotlin twin, which adds one more line. ShallowRecord.java package workbench.concurrency.l11; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; /** A record's fields are final. The objects they point to are not. */ public class ShallowRecord { record ShallowQuote(String item, List<String> tiers, byte[] signature) {} record DeepQuote(String item, List<String> tiers, byte[] signature) { DeepQuote { tiers = List.copyOf(tiers); // copy in signature = signature.clone(); } @Override public byte[] signature() { return signature.clone(); // copy out } } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> tiers = new ArrayList<>(List.of("1 to 9 loaves at 2.50")); byte[] sig = {7, 7, 7}; ShallowQuote shallow = new ShallowQuote("bread", tiers, sig); DeepQuote deep = new DeepQuote("bread", tiers, sig); List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(tiers); // a read-only VIEW, not a copy tiers.add("10 or more at 0.01"); // the caller keeps changing its list... sig[0] = 0; // ...and its array shallow.signature()[1] = 0; // a reader scribbles on what it was given deep.signature()[1] = 0; System.out.println("shallow: " + shallow.tiers() + " signature " + Arrays.toString(shallow.signature())); System.out.println("deep: " + deep.tiers() + " signature " + Arrays.toString(deep.signature())); System.out.println("unmodifiableList view: " + view); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l11.ShallowRecord labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l11/ShallowRecord.java ShallowRecord.kt package workbench.concurrency.l11 // A data class's vals can't be reassigned. The objects they point to can still change. private data class LooseQuote(val item: String, val tiers: List<String>, val signature: ByteArray) private class SealedQuote(val item: String, tiers: List<String>, signature: ByteArray) { val tiers: List<String> = java.util.List.copyOf(tiers) // copy in: unmodifiable even through a cast private val sig = signature.copyOf() val signature: ByteArray get() = sig.copyOf() // copy out } fun main() { val tiers = mutableListOf("1 to 9 loaves at 2.50") val sig = byteArrayOf(7, 7, 7) val loose = LooseQuote("bread", tiers, sig) // List<String> is read-only, not immutable val sealed = SealedQuote("bread", tiers, sig) val view = java.util.Collections.unmodifiableList(tiers) // a read-only VIEW, not a copy tiers.add("10 or more at 0.01") // the caller keeps changing its list... sig[0] = 0 // ...and its array loose.signature[1] = 0 // a reader scribbles on what it was given sealed.signature[1] = 0 println("shallow: ${loose.tiers} signature ${loose.signature.contentToString()}") println("deep: ${sealed.tiers} signature ${sealed.signature.contentToString()}") println("unmodifiableList view: $view") (loose.tiers as MutableList<String>).add("added through a cast") // read-only interface, mutable object println("shallow after a cast: ${loose.tiers}") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l11.ShallowRecordKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l11/ShallowRecord.kt The shallow quote shows the extra tier and a signature of [0, 0, 7]: both the caller and a reader changed it. The deep quote still shows one tier and [7, 7, 7]. The unmodifiableList view shows the extra tier, because it's a view. In Kotlin, a cast to MutableList adds a line to the shallow quote's "read-only" list.

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · Taking away sharing: confinement, and handing objects over
x: Changing state is fine as long as only one thread can reach it. That's confinement, keeping state where only one thread can get at it, and you already use it every day. Stack confinement is the simplest kind. Local variables live on one thread's stack, its private list of method calls in progress, and no other thread can see them. A StringBuilder or ArrayList created inside a method and never stored anywhere else needs no protection at all: Java String receiptLine(Sale s) { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); // local: no other thread can ever see it sb.append(s.item()).append(';').append(s.cents()); return sb.toString(); // only the immutable String leaves } Kotlin fun receiptLine(s: Sale): String = buildString { // the builder is local: no other thread can see it append(s.item).append(';').append(s.cents) } // only the immutable String leaves Thread confinement is the same idea, made bigger. One thread owns some state, and every other thread asks that thread to act on it instead of touching the state itself. The mail-room helper from A thread's life worked this way: other parts of the program dropped messages into its tray, and only the helper ever sent them. Many screen toolkits work the same way, with one thread that is the only one allowed to draw on the screen. When work has to move between threads, move the ownership with it. Back to the kitchen from wait, notify and guarded blocks: a waiter writes a ticket, clips it to the rail and never touches it again. The cook takes it and owns it from then on. In code, the rail is a BlockingQueue, the queue from Concurrent collections whose take() waits until something arrives: Java List<String> ticket = new ArrayList<>(); // owned by the waiter's thread ticket.add("soup"); ticket.add("bread"); rail.put(ticket); // ownership moves to whoever takes it // from here on, the waiter never touches ticket again Kotlin val ticket = ArrayList<String>() // owned by the waiter's thread ticket.add("soup") ticket.add("bread") rail.put(ticket) // ownership moves to whoever takes it // from here on, the waiter never touches ticket again The queue does two jobs. It hands the ticket over, and it makes the hand-over visible. Everything the waiter wrote before put happens-before the cook's take returns, so the cook sees the whole ticket. (Happens-before is the memory model's promise that one thread sees what another wrote first.) The figure shows the moment the owner changes. The whole duty sits on the waiter's side: once you've handed something over, it isn't yours. Picture a waiter who saves paper by erasing a ticket the cook is still reading and writing the next table's order on it. The Try it does exactly that with -Pargs=reuse: the waiter clears one list and fills it again instead of making a new one. Each ticket holds 100 numbered dishes, so the cook can check that nothing is missing or out of order: new ticket each time: 5,000 tickets handed over, 0 damaged one ticket, reused: 5,000 tickets handed over, 447 damaged The reused ticket is a changing object shared by two threads with no synchronization at all, and the cook found 447 half-written tickets. Run it again and the number changes: runs here ranged from 10 to over 3,000. A lucky run could even show 0, which is exactly how this bug gets through testing. A queue hands over the object, not a copy. After put, never touch it again. Confinement keeps state on one thread. The last tool in this lesson does something stranger: it gives every thread its own copy of the same variable. Hand over, or keep using? Read HandOff. A waiter thread writes 5,000 tickets of 100 numbered dishes and puts each one on the rail, a queue with room for 4. A cook thread checks that every ticket it takes is complete and in order. Run it. Then run it with -Pargs=reuse, where the waiter clears and refills one list instead of making a new one. Run the reuse version a few times. Is the damage count the same each time? HandOff.java package workbench.concurrency.l11; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; /** * A waiter writes tickets of 100 numbered dishes and hands each one to a cook through the rail, * a queue. Run with -Pargs=reuse to erase and reuse one ticket instead of handing over a new one. */ public class HandOff { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean reuse = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("reuse"); BlockingQueue<List<Integer>> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(4); int tickets = 5_000; int[] damaged = {0}; Thread cook = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int b = 0; b < tickets; b++) { List<Integer> ticket = queue.take(); // the cook owns this list now try { Object[] entries = ticket.toArray(); boolean ok = entries.length == 100; for (int i = 0; ok && i < 100; i++) ok = entries[i].equals(((Integer) entries[0]) + i); if (!ok) damaged[0]++; } catch (RuntimeException e) { damaged[0]++; // a list changing under you can throw, too } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "cook"); cook.start(); List<Integer> shared = new ArrayList<>(); for (int b = 0; b < tickets; b++) { List<Integer> ticket = reuse ? shared : new ArrayList<>(100); ticket.clear(); // with reuse: erases a ticket the cook may be reading for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) ticket.add(b * 100 + i); queue.put(ticket); // hand it over, and never touch it again } cook.join(); System.out.printf("%s: %,d tickets handed over, %,d damaged%n", reuse ? "one ticket, reused" : "new ticket each time", tickets, damaged[0]); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l11.HandOff labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l11/HandOff.java HandOff.kt package workbench.concurrency.l11 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A waiter writes tickets of 100 numbered dishes and hands each one to a cook through the rail, // a queue. Run with -Pargs=reuse to erase and reuse one ticket instead of handing over a new one. fun main(args: Array<String>) { val reuse = args.firstOrNull() == "reuse" val queue = ArrayBlockingQueue<MutableList<Int>>(4) val tickets = 5_000 var damaged = 0 val cook = thread(name = "cook") { repeat(tickets) { val ticket = queue.take() // the cook owns this list now try { val entries = ticket.toTypedArray() val ok = entries.size == 100 && entries.indices.all { i -> entries[i] == entries[0] + i } if (!ok) damaged++ } catch (e: RuntimeException) { damaged++ // a list changing under you can throw, too } } } val shared = ArrayList<Int>() for (b in 0 until tickets) { val ticket = if (reuse) shared else ArrayList(100) ticket.clear() // with reuse: erases a ticket the cook may be reading for (i in 0 until 100) ticket.add(b * 100 + i) queue.put(ticket) // hand it over, and never touch it again } cook.join() println("%s: %,d tickets handed over, %,d damaged".format(if (reuse) "one ticket, reused" else "new ticket each time", tickets, damaged)) } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l11.HandOffKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l11/HandOff.kt With a new ticket each time: 0 damaged. With reuse: some tickets arrive damaged (from 10 to over 3,000 of the 5,000 in runs here), and the count changes every run. A lucky run could even show 0, which is exactly why this bug survives testing. Ownership moves through the queue. What the waiter wrote before put happens-before the take, and the waiter never touches the ticket again.

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · One copy per thread: ThreadLocal, and why pool threads never forget
x: ThreadLocal<T> gives every thread its own value for the same variable. Web services use it for request context. A web service answers requests from other programs over the network, and it handles each request on a thread. The handler stores the current user once, and code deep in the call chain reads it without passing it through every method. Many logging libraries keep per-request fields the same way, so every log line shows whose request it belongs to. The catch is where the value lives. Each Thread object has its own small map from ThreadLocal to value, and get() looks in the current thread's map. The value stays there as long as the thread is alive. Now add a thread pool, a fixed group of threads that is reused for request after request. A pool thread lives for days, and so does whatever a request left on it. A pool thread is like a hotel room. The next guest finds whatever the last guest left behind, unless housekeeping clears the room between stays. Here's a handler with no housekeeping. It sets the user only when the request carries one: Java // Naive: sets the user, never clears it static final ThreadLocal<String> USER = new ThreadLocal<>(); String handle(String user) { if (user != null) USER.set(user); return "request(" + user + ") ran as " + USER.get(); } Kotlin // Naive: sets the user, never clears it val USER = ThreadLocal<String>() fun handle(user: String?): String { if (user != null) USER.set(user) return "request($user) ran as ${USER.get()}" } The Try it runs six requests on a pool of one thread, so every request lands in the same room: request(alice) ran as alice request(null) ran as alice request(bob) ran as bob request(null) ran as bob request(null) ran as bob request(carol) ran as carol The first anonymous request ran as alice, and the next two ran as bob, whoever that thread served last. In a real service, that's one customer seeing another customer's data. With 200 pool threads instead of one, it happens rarely and at random, which is how it gets past testing and reaches real users. A pool thread keeps its thread-local values for good. Set them, then remove() them in finally. remove() is the housekeeping: Java static final ThreadLocal<String> USER = new ThreadLocal<>(); void handle(Request r) { USER.set(r.user()); try { process(r); // deep code calls USER.get() } finally { USER.remove(); // housekeeping: the pool thread goes back clean } } Kotlin val USER = ThreadLocal<String>() fun handle(r: Request) { USER.set(r.user) try { process(r) // deep code calls USER.get() } finally { USER.remove() // housekeeping: the pool thread goes back clean } } Call remove(), not set(null). remove() deletes the thread's entry, while set(null) keeps an entry that holds null. With the finally in place, the same six requests run as null whenever no user came in. The lab's TenantScope carries the customer company a request works for, and it goes one step further. It puts back the previous value, so a call nested inside another hands the thread back exactly as it found it. ThreadLocal's other common use is a private copy of an object that isn't thread-safe, such as the old SimpleDateFormat. Prefer an immutable replacement there: DateTimeFormatter is immutable, so one shared instance does the job of a copy per thread. Per-thread copies also scale badly with virtual threads, the very light threads from JDK 21 that programs start one per task: every task gets a new thread, and so a new, empty copy. The virtual threads track goes into that. For request context, JDK 25 made scoped values final (JEP 506). A scoped value is bound for one call and everything it calls, and it's gone when that call returns, so there's no housekeeping to forget: Java static final ScopedValue<String> USER = ScopedValue.newInstance(); // JDK 25+ void handle(Request r) { ScopedValue.where(USER, r.user()).run(() -> process(r)); // bound for this call only } Kotlin val USER: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance() // JDK 25+ fun handle(r: Request) { ScopedValue.where(USER, r.user).run { process(r) } // bound for this call only } That code needs JDK 25 or later. On JDK 21 to 24 the API is a preview, a feature you have to switch on with a flag and that may still change. The labs compile for JDK 21, so they use ThreadLocal. Each tool in this lesson took away one ingredient of a race. Immutability took away change, confinement and hand-over took away sharing, and ThreadLocal gave each thread a copy of its own. Their limit is state that is shared and changes by its nature, such as a bank balance. That state still needs the locks and atomics of earlier lessons, and the next lesson puts them to work on three classic problems. Watch one customer's context leak into another's request Read ThreadLocalBleed. Six requests run one after another on a pool of one thread. The handler sets the user only when the request carries one. Predict what each request without a user runs as, in the leaky version and in the clean one. Run it. ThreadLocalBleed.java package workbench.concurrency.l11; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.function.Function; /** * Six requests on a pool of one reused thread. The handler sets the user only when the request * carries one. A pool of 1 makes the bug happen every time; a pool of 200 makes it rare and random. */ public class ThreadLocalBleed { static final ThreadLocal<String> USER = new ThreadLocal<>(); static String leaky(String user) { if (user != null) USER.set(user); return "request(" + user + ") ran as " + USER.get(); } static String clean(String user) { if (user != null) USER.set(user); try { return "request(" + user + ") ran as " + USER.get(); } finally { USER.remove(); // leave the thread as you found it } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String[] requests = {"alice", null, "bob", null, null, "carol"}; for (Function<String, String> handler : java.util.List.<Function<String, String>>of(ThreadLocalBleed::leaky, ThreadLocalBleed::clean)) { ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); System.out.println("---"); for (String user : requests) System.out.println(" " + pool.submit(() -> handler.apply(user)).get()); pool.shutdown(); } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l11.ThreadLocalBleed labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l11/ThreadLocalBleed.java ThreadLocalBleed.kt package workbench.concurrency.l11 import java.util.concurrent.Executors // Six requests on a pool of one reused thread. The handler sets the user only when the request // carries one. A pool of 1 makes the bug happen every time; a pool of 200 makes it rare and random. private val USER = ThreadLocal<String>() private fun leaky(user: String?): String { if (user != null) USER.set(user) return "request($user) ran as ${USER.get()}" } private fun clean(user: String?): String { if (user != null) USER.set(user) try { return "request($user) ran as ${USER.get()}" } finally { USER.remove() // leave the thread as you found it } } fun main() { val requests = listOf("alice", null, "bob", null, null, "carol") for (handler in listOf(::leaky, ::clean)) { val pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor() println("---") for (user in requests) println(" " + pool.submit<String> { handler(user) }.get()) pool.shutdown() } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l11.ThreadLocalBleedKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l11/ThreadLocalBleed.kt Leaky: the first anonymous request runs as alice, and the next two run as bob, whoever that thread served last. Clean: every anonymous request runs as null, because remove() in finally put the thread back as it was. A pool of one makes it happen every time. With 200 threads it happens rarely and at random, which is how it reaches real users. JEP 506: Scoped Values read

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · Java and Kotlin
x: A deeply immutable value in Java and Kotlin Java record public record Receipt(String till, List<Line> lines) { public Receipt { lines = List.copyOf(lines); // reassign the parameter: the field gets the copy } } Kotlin class class Receipt(val till: String, lines: List<Line>) { val lines: List<Line> = java.util.List.copyOf(lines) // a plain parameter, copied into a property } // a data class can't do this: its constructor parameters ARE the properties Both compile to a class with final fields, so both get the memory model's promise for final fields. The difference is where the copy can go. A Java record's compact constructor may reassign its parameters before the fields are set, so lines = List.copyOf(lines) stores the copy; that's Java doing the right thing with very little code. A Kotlin data class can't do the same, because its primary-constructor parameters are its properties. So you use a plain class with a separate property, as here, or a private constructor and a factory function. Kotlin's List type helps less than it looks: it's a read-only interface, and the results of listOf or toList can still be changed through a cast or from Java. java.util.List.copyOf gives you a list that is unmodifiable for everyone. A data class's copy() is shallow too: the copy shares the same list.

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · Worked example
x: A shared constant that someone changed The shop adds a delivery fee to every online order. Money looks like a value, and DELIVERY_FEE looks like a constant. Read it and find what changes, and for whom. public class Money { private long cents; private final Currency currency; public Money(long cents, Currency currency) { this.cents = cents; this.currency = currency; } public Money add(Money other) { // changes this object, then returns it this.cents += other.cents; return this; } public long cents() { return cents; } } static final Money DELIVERY_FEE = new Money(300, EUR); // "a constant" Money total = order.amount().add(DELIVERY_FEE); // also changes order.amount() class Money(private var centsValue: Long, val currency: Currency) { fun add(other: Money): Money { // changes this object, then returns it centsValue += other.centsValue return this } val cents: Long get() = centsValue } val DELIVERY_FEE = Money(300, EUR) // "a constant" val total = order.amount.add(DELIVERY_FEE) // also changes order.amount add changes the object it's called on, so order.amount().add(DELIVERY_FEE) changes the order's own amount. Somewhere else, DELIVERY_FEE.add(surcharge) changes the fee for every order on every thread. And because cents is neither final nor volatile, other threads may see the old fee, the new one, or a mix, at different times. static final on the reference didn't make the object constant. Make Money a value: final fields, and operations that return a new object. Now 200 threads can read DELIVERY_FEE with no lock, and nobody can change it. public record Money(long cents, Currency currency) { public Money { Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency"); } public Money plus(Money other) { // 1. never change this; return a new value if (!currency.equals(other.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch"); return new Money(Math.addExact(cents, other.cents), currency); // 2. overflow fails loudly } } data class Money(val cents: Long, val currency: Currency) { operator fun plus(other: Money): Money { // 1. never change this; return a new value require(currency == other.currency) { "currency mismatch" } return copy(cents = Math.addExact(cents, other.cents)) // 2. overflow fails loudly } } Before reading on, explain to yourself why the record needs no synchronization even though every request thread reads DELIVERY_FEE. Then look at the classic trap with immutable types, which catches everyone moving from changeable ones: calling the operation and throwing the result away. BigDecimal total = BigDecimal.ZERO; for (BigDecimal fee : fees) total.add(fee); // does nothing: the result is thrown away for (BigDecimal fee : fees) total = total.add(fee); // right var total = BigDecimal.ZERO for (fee in fees) total.add(fee) // does nothing: the result is thrown away for (fee in fees) total += fee // right: plus() returns a new BigDecimal Answer: the fields are final, set once in the constructor, and the object never changes, so every thread that can see the reference sees 3.00 EUR. There's nothing to race on. The price is one new object per operation, which the JIT compiler often removes when the object never leaves the method. For money, that's an easy trade.

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · Quiz
x: Which of these can be shared between threads with no synchronization at all? A record whose List<String> component is the caller's ArrayList A class with volatile fields and setters A final class whose private final fields are a String, an Instant and a BigDecimal, with no setters A record with an int[] component and the default accessor All three field types are immutable and the fields are final, so the object can never change, and the promise for final fields makes it visible correctly. The record with the caller's list and the record with an array can both be changed from outside. volatile fields with setters make each write visible, but the object still changes under its readers. A constructor stores this.items = Collections.unmodifiableList(items);. Later the caller adds an item to its own items list. What does the object's list show? The original items only It throws UnsupportedOperationException in the caller The caller's add is ignored The new item too, because unmodifiableList is a view of the caller's list unmodifiableList only stops you from changing the list through that reference. It still reads the caller's list, so the caller's changes show through. List.copyOf makes a copy that nobody can change. From Explicit locks: the shop's price list is replaced as a whole every 5 minutes and read 5,000 times a second. What is the simplest correct design? A ReentrantReadWriteLock around a HashMap A volatile field holding an immutable map, replaced with a freshly built Map.copyOf(...) on each refresh A ConcurrentHashMap refreshed with clear() and putAll() A synchronized getter and setter on a HashMap Readers never wait, and each one sees one complete version, because the new map is built fully before one volatile write publishes it. The read-write lock also works, with more code and some cost on every read. clear plus putAll on a concurrent map lets readers see an empty or half-filled list. A web service's request handler does USER.set(request.user()) on a ThreadLocal when the request carries a user, and never removes it. Its threads come from a pool. What does a later anonymous request on the same thread see? The previous request's user null, because each request gets a fresh thread An IllegalStateException A random user from another thread Pool threads are reused. The value stays on the thread until someone removes it, so the anonymous request runs as whoever that thread served last. Pair every set with remove() in finally. A waiter thread puts an ArrayList ticket into a BlockingQueue, then calls clear() on the same list and fills it again for the next table. What does that do to the cook thread that takes it? Nothing: take() returns a copy of the list Nothing: put made the list thread-safe The cook can see a partly cleared or refilled ticket, because the waiter kept changing an object it had handed over put throws, because the list is already in the queue The queue hands over a reference, not a copy. put happens-before take only for what the waiter did before the put. After that, the two threads share one changing list with no synchronization. Hand over a new list each time.

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · Key terms
x: Immutable object An object whose state can't change after it's built; safe to share without locks. Defensive copy Copying a changeable argument or return value so nobody else can change your object through it. Shallow immutability Final references to objects that can still change, as in a record holding an ArrayList. Snapshot publication Replacing a whole immutable object with one volatile write, so readers see one complete version. Thread confinement Keeping changing state reachable by only one thread. Ownership hand-off Passing an object to another thread, through a queue, and never touching it again. ThreadLocal A variable with a separate value per thread; values live as long as the thread unless removed. Scoped value A value bound for one call and everything it calls, gone when the call returns (final in JDK 25, JEP 506). What does a class need to be immutable? All fields final and set in the constructor, no setters, changing parts copied in and never handed out, and this doesn't escape during construction. What does the memory model promise for final fields? A thread that gets a reference to the object after its constructor finished sees the correct values of its final fields, even without synchronization. Is a record with a List component immutable? Only shallowly. Copy the list in the compact constructor: items = List.copyOf(items);. Collections.unmodifiableList(list) vs List.copyOf(list)? unmodifiableList is a read-only view: the owner's later changes show through. List.copyOf is an unmodifiable copy that nobody can change. How do you share data that changes rarely, without locks? Build a new immutable snapshot, then publish it with one write to a volatile field (or an AtomicReference). Readers read the reference once. A pool thread runs a task that calls ThreadLocal.set and never remove(). What happens next? The value stays on the thread. The next task on that thread sees it if it doesn't set its own. What makes passing a changeable object through a BlockingQueue safe? put happens-before take, so the taker sees everything done before the put, as long as the giver never touches the object again.

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · Go deeper
x: Each Thread object keeps its thread-locals in its own small hash map, called ThreadLocalMap. The keys are weak references to the ThreadLocal objects (references that don't keep an object alive), and the values are ordinary, strong references. When a ThreadLocal itself becomes garbage, its key goes away, but the value stays in the map until a later get, set or remove on that thread happens to clean it up. On a pool thread that lives for days, that can be a long time. Servers that load and unload applications while they run know this as a famous leak. A value whose class came from an unloaded application keeps that application's whole class loader, the object that loaded its classes, alive. remove() avoids all of it. InheritableThreadLocal copies values from a parent thread to a child thread when the child is created. It does nothing useful with pools, because pool threads are created once, long before the request that hands them work. Scoped values (JEP 506, final in JDK 25) fix the design problems rather than the symptoms. A binding is immutable: there is no set, so code deep in the call chain can't change the value under you. It has a clear lifetime: it ends when run or call returns, even on an exception. And it is cheap to share with child tasks. With structured concurrency, still a preview API in JDK 25, threads started inside the scope see the same bindings without copying a map per thread. One immutability trap to know: an object is only safe to share without synchronization if this didn't escape while the constructor was running. A constructor that registers this as a listener, or starts a thread that uses this, hands out the object before its final fields are guaranteed to be visible. Build first, register after. The memory model track's lesson on safe publication covers the full rules.

h: Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers · Closing the kitchen: a bounded queue and one poison pill per cook
x: Closing the kitchen: a bounded rail makes the fast waiter wait, an empty rail can mean late, and one poison pill per cook, after the last waiter, sends every cook home Let's name the parts first. A thread that puts work into a queue is a producer, and a thread that takes work out is a consumer. Our waiters are producers and our cooks are consumers, and the whole shape is called producer-consumer. Most concurrent programs have one somewhere: something makes work at one speed, and something else does it at another. In Java, the rail is a BlockingQueue from Concurrent collections. put adds a ticket, and take removes one, waiting while the queue is empty. Give the queue a limit, as the rail in wait, notify and guarded blocks had. A bounded queue, one with a fixed capacity, makes put wait while it's full, so a fast waiter slows to the cooks' pace instead of piling up tickets until memory runs out. That's backpressure: a full queue pushing back on whoever fills it. The hard part is stopping. A cook waits in take(), and take() never returns from an empty queue. Inside, it parks (sleeps until woken) on the queue's own "not empty" condition, a wait set like the one from guarded blocks, and only a put wakes it. Once the waiters have gone home, nothing ever will. There are three ways out. Interrupting the cooks, that is, asking each thread to stop, is fast. But it drops whatever is still queued: take() checks the interrupt flag before it looks at the queue, so it throws even when tickets are waiting. Polling with a timeout, poll(1, SECONDS) in a loop that checks a stop flag, works too. But every cook can wait up to one timeout before it notices, and every loop has to check the flag correctly. The clean answer is a poison pill: a special item that means "no more work", put on the rail like any other ticket. A cook that takes it stops. Here's the naive version, with one pill for the whole kitchen: Java // Naive: one pill for three cooks for (Thread w : waiters) w.join(); // every order is on the rail rail.put(PILL); // "kitchen closed" for (Thread c : cooks) c.join(); // waits for all three cooks Kotlin // Naive: one pill for three cooks waiters.forEach { it.join() } // every order is on the rail rail.put(PILL) // "kitchen closed" cooks.forEach { it.join() } // waits for all three cooks The Try it runs two waiters, three cooks and a rail with room for four tickets. With -Pargs=onepill it printed: cook-1 got its pill after 1004 orders cooks still waiting: 2 (WAITING in take) A pill is just an item, so the first cook to take it removes it from the rail and goes home. The other two find an empty rail and wait in take(), all night. Anything that waits for them to finish, such as the program's own shutdown, hangs with them. Three rules make pills work: Put the pills only after every producer has finished, so they land behind every real ticket. Put one pill per consumer, because each pill is taken once. Compare against the pill by identity, with ==. A pill made with new String("PILL") is an object of its own, so a real ticket that happens to read PILL is still a ticket. Java // each cook while (true) { String ticket = rail.take(); // waits while the rail is empty if (ticket == PILL) break; // identity: a ticket that reads "PILL" is still a ticket cook(ticket); } // the head chef, after every waiter has finished: for (int i = 0; i < cooks; i++) rail.put(PILL); // one pill per cook Kotlin // each cook while (true) { val ticket = rail.take() // waits while the rail is empty if (ticket === PILL) break // identity: a ticket that reads "PILL" is still a ticket cook(ticket) } // the head chef, after every waiter has finished: repeat(cooks) { rail.put(PILL) } // one pill per cook The same run with one pill per cook printed: cook-1 got its pill after 511 orders cook-2 got its pill after 177 orders cook-0 got its pill after 1312 orders cooks still waiting: 0 The three counts add up to 2,000, every order the waiters put, and no cook was left waiting. The split changes from run to run, because whichever cook is free takes the next ticket. The figure shows the rail at closing time: the last real orders, then the pills. One pill stops one consumer. Put one per consumer, after the last producer. The kitchen now closes without losing an order. The next problem has no queue at all, just five threads, five locks and a table. One pill per cook, or not Read PoisonPills. Two waiters put 1,000 orders each on a rail with room for 4, and three cooks take them. After the waiters finish, main puts the pills. Run it. Note how many orders each cook handled. Run it with -Pargs=onepill. Predict how many cooks are still waiting after one second, and in which thread state. PoisonPills.java package workbench.concurrency.l12; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; /** * Closing time in the kitchen: two waiters (producers), three cooks (consumers), one bounded rail, * shut down with poison pills. Run with -Pargs=onepill to send a single pill instead of one per cook. */ public class PoisonPills { @SuppressWarnings("StringOperationCanBeSimplified") static final String PILL = new String("PILL"); // compared by identity public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean onePill = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("onepill"); BlockingQueue<String> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(4); List<Thread> cooks = new ArrayList<>(); for (int c = 0; c < 3; c++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { int done = 0; try { while (true) { String r = queue.take(); if (r == PILL) break; // this cook stops; the others keep going done++; } System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " got its pill after " + done + " orders"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "cook-" + c); t.setDaemon(true); t.start(); cooks.add(t); } Thread[] waiters = new Thread[2]; for (int p = 0; p < 2; p++) { int me = p; waiters[p] = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) queue.put("order-" + me + "-" + i); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "waiter-" + p); waiters[p].start(); } for (Thread t : waiters) t.join(); // 1. every waiter is done... for (int c = 0; c < (onePill ? 1 : cooks.size()); c++) queue.put(PILL); // 2. ...then one pill each for (Thread t : cooks) t.join(1_000); List<Thread> stuck = cooks.stream().filter(Thread::isAlive).toList(); System.out.println("cooks still waiting: " + stuck.size() + (stuck.isEmpty() ? "" : " (" + stuck.get(0).getState() + " in take)")); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l12.PoisonPills labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l12/PoisonPills.java PoisonPills.kt package workbench.concurrency.l12 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Closing time in the kitchen: two waiters (producers), three cooks (consumers), one bounded rail, // shut down with poison pills. Run with -Pargs=onepill to send a single pill instead of one per cook. private val PILL = String(charArrayOf('P', 'I', 'L', 'L')) // a fresh object: compared by identity fun main(args: Array<String>) { val onePill = args.firstOrNull() == "onepill" val queue = ArrayBlockingQueue<String>(4) val cooks = List(3) { c -> thread(isDaemon = true, name = "cook-$c") { var done = 0 while (true) { val r = queue.take() if (r === PILL) break // this cook stops; the others keep going done++ } println("${Thread.currentThread().name} got its pill after $done orders") } } val waiters = List(2) { me -> thread(name = "waiter-$me") { repeat(1_000) { i -> queue.put("order-$me-$i") } } } waiters.forEach { it.join() } // 1. every waiter is done... repeat(if (onePill) 1 else cooks.size) { queue.put(PILL) } // 2. ...then one pill each cooks.forEach { it.join(1_000) } val stuck = cooks.count { it.isAlive } println("cooks still waiting: $stuck" + if (stuck > 0) " (${cooks.last { it.isAlive }.state} in take)" else "") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l12.PoisonPillsKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l12/PoisonPills.kt With one pill each, all three cooks report their pill, their counts add up to 2,000, and cooks still waiting: 0. The split changes from run to run. With onepill, one cook stops and two are still waiting: cooks still waiting: 2 (WAITING in take). In a real program, that's a shutdown that never finishes. Orders first, pills last, one pill per cook. Each cook stops at its own pill, after every real order has been taken.

h: Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers · Five philosophers, five forks: the table that freezes, and two fixes
x: Here's the most famous puzzle in concurrency, and it needs only a table. Five philosophers sit around a round table, with one fork between each pair of neighbours, so five forks in all. A philosopher thinks for a while, then gets hungry. To eat, each one needs both forks next to them, the one on the left and the one on the right, and each picks up the left fork first. In code, each philosopher is a thread and each fork is a lock, a ReentrantLock from Explicit locks: an object a thread takes with lock() and gives back with unlock(). It works most of the time. Then, one day, all five get hungry at the same moment and each picks up a left fork. Let's trace the smallest version, with three philosophers: Philosopher 0 takes fork 0. At the same moment, philosopher 1 takes fork 1 and philosopher 2 takes fork 2. Philosopher 0 reaches for fork 1, which philosopher 1 holds. Philosopher 1 reaches for fork 2, held by philosopher 2. Philosopher 2 reaches for fork 0, held by philosopher 0. Every fork is in a hand, and nobody can eat. Nobody puts a fork down, because the code never says to. That's the deadlock from Deadlock, livelock and starvation, threads that wait for each other forever, with three locks instead of two. All four of its conditions hold. Each fork has one owner (mutual exclusion). Each philosopher holds one fork while waiting for another (hold and wait). Nobody takes a fork from a neighbour (no preemption). And the waiting goes all the way round the table (circular wait). It's also what the bank's transfers look like when each one locks two of many accounts. The simulator below has three philosophers. First let them eat one at a time. Then reset it and give each philosopher a single step before anyone takes a second. The Try it runs five philosophers, 200 meals each, with a 1 ms pause between the two forks to make the bad moment likely. Left fork first, it printed: naive: 0 of 1,000 meals in 3045 ms, deadlocked philosophers: 5 Zero meals, and the JVM itself, the program that runs your Java code, names all five philosophers as deadlocked, because forks that are ReentrantLocks have owners its deadlock detector can follow. There are two standard fixes, and each removes a different condition. Resource ordering removes the circular wait. Number the forks and always take the lower-numbered one first. Philosophers 0 to 3 still take left, then right. Philosopher 4 needs forks 4 and 0, so it takes fork 0 first: Java int left = seat, right = (seat + 1) % forks.length; ReentrantLock first = forks[Math.min(left, right)]; // philosopher 4 takes fork 0 first ReentrantLock second = forks[Math.max(left, right)]; Kotlin val left = seat val right = (seat + 1) % forks.size val first = forks[minOf(left, right)] // philosopher 4 takes fork 0 first val second = forks[maxOf(left, right)] Now a philosopher who holds a fork and waits always wants a higher-numbered one. A cycle would need someone, somewhere, to wait for a lower number than the one they hold, so the cycle can't close, however many forks or accounts there are. It's the lock order from the bank's transfers, applied to a table. A waiter removes the moment when everyone holds one fork. Only four of the five may sit down at once. Four philosophers share five forks. Even if each seated one holds a fork, one fork is still free, and the seated philosopher next to it can pick it up and eat. A Semaphore(n - 1) from Synchronizers is the waiter, one chair short: Java Semaphore seats = new Semaphore(forks.length - 1); // the waiter: one chair short seats.acquire(); try { eatWithBothForks(); } finally { seats.release(); } Kotlin val seats = Semaphore(forks.size - 1) // the waiter: one chair short seats.acquire() try { eatWithBothForks() } finally { seats.release() } Both fixes served all 1,000 meals in the Try it, in about 1.2 seconds, with no deadlock. A third fix, tryLock on the second fork with a random back-off, removes no preemption, but it brings back the livelock risk of the two polite diners in Deadlock, livelock and starvation. Use ordering when you can number your resources. Use the waiter when you can't, or when you want to cap how many threads compete at all. Any number of locks can freeze in a circle. Take them in one global order. A table of philosophers needs every lock to itself. The last problem is gentler, because most of its threads are happy to share. Freeze the table, then fix it two ways Read Philosophers. Five philosophers try to eat 200 meals each, pausing 1 ms between their two forks. After 3 seconds, the demo asks the JVM which threads are deadlocked. Run it as it is. Then run it with -Pargs=ordered and with -Pargs=waiter. Compare the meal counts, the times and the deadlock counts. Philosophers.java package workbench.concurrency.l12; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** * Five philosophers, five forks, 200 meals each. Run as is (left fork, then right), * with -Pargs=ordered (lower-numbered fork first) or -Pargs=waiter (at most 4 may sit down). */ public class Philosophers { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "naive"; int n = 5; ReentrantLock[] forks = new ReentrantLock[n]; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) forks[i] = new ReentrantLock(); Semaphore seats = new Semaphore(n - 1); // the waiter: one chair short AtomicInteger meals = new AtomicInteger(); Thread[] ps = new Thread[n]; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { int left = i, right = (i + 1) % n; int first = mode.equals("ordered") ? Math.min(left, right) : left; int second = mode.equals("ordered") ? Math.max(left, right) : right; ps[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int m = 0; m < 200; m++) { if (mode.equals("waiter")) seats.acquire(); try { forks[first].lock(); try { Thread.sleep(1); // reach for the other fork forks[second].lock(); try { meals.incrementAndGet(); } finally { forks[second].unlock(); } } finally { forks[first].unlock(); } } finally { if (mode.equals("waiter")) seats.release(); } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "philosopher-" + i); ps[i].setDaemon(true); ps[i].start(); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); long deadline = t0 + 3_000_000_000L; // 3 s for the whole table for (Thread p : ps) p.join(Math.max(1, (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000)); long[] stuck = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads(); System.out.printf("%s: %d of 1,000 meals in %d ms, deadlocked philosophers: %d%n", mode, meals.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, stuck == null ? 0 : stuck.length); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l12.Philosophers labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l12/Philosophers.java Philosophers.kt package workbench.concurrency.l12 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock // Five philosophers, five forks, 200 meals each. Run as is (left fork, then right), // with -Pargs=ordered (lower-numbered fork first) or -Pargs=waiter (at most 4 may sit down). fun main(args: Array<String>) { val mode = args.firstOrNull() ?: "naive" val n = 5 val forks = Array(n) { ReentrantLock() } val seats = Semaphore(n - 1) // the waiter: one chair short val meals = AtomicInteger() val ps = List(n) { i -> val left = i val right = (i + 1) % n val first = if (mode == "ordered") minOf(left, right) else left val second = if (mode == "ordered") maxOf(left, right) else right thread(isDaemon = true, name = "philosopher-$i") { repeat(200) { if (mode == "waiter") seats.acquire() try { forks[first].withLock { Thread.sleep(1) // reach for the other fork forks[second].withLock { meals.incrementAndGet() } } } finally { if (mode == "waiter") seats.release() } } } } val t0 = System.nanoTime() val deadline = t0 + 3_000_000_000L // 3 s for the whole table ps.forEach { it.join(maxOf(1L, (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000)) } val stuck = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads() println("%s: %d of 1,000 meals in %d ms, deadlocked philosophers: %d" .format(mode, meals.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, stuck?.size ?: 0)) } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l12.PhilosophersKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l12/Philosophers.kt As it is: no meals at all in runs here (a lucky run may get one) and deadlocked philosophers: 5, found by ThreadMXBean, the JDK's window onto the JVM's threads, because the forks are ReentrantLocks. Ordered and waiter: all 1,000 meals in about 1.2 seconds, and deadlocked philosophers: 0.

h: Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers · Many readers, one writer: who waits at the price board
x: The last puzzle brings back the price board from Don't share, with one change: this time the shop updates its prices in place, so readers and the writer have to take turns. Many threads at the tills (the cash registers) read prices all day, and readers can share, because two readers never get in each other's way. Now and then the owner changes the prices, and the writer needs the board to itself, so that no reader sees half a change. That's the readers-writers problem. Its real question is what happens when both are waiting, and every answer makes somebody wait longer than they'd like. Readers first lets a new reader in whenever no writer is inside. It looks generous. But with a steady stream of readers that overlap, the reader count never drops to zero, so the writer never gets in. That's starvation: the program makes progress, but one thread never does. Writers first makes new readers wait as soon as a writer is waiting. The owner gets in quickly, but with a stream of writers, the readers starve instead. Fair order serves threads in the order they arrived. Nobody starves, and throughput, the work done per second, drops, because readers that could have shared now wait behind a writer who came first. Let's watch the first policy fail. The Try it has four readers, each holding the read side for 2 ms at a time, overlapping, for one and a half seconds. After 100 ms, the owner asks for the write side. A textbook readers-first lock, written with synchronized and wait(), let the owner in only when the readers stopped on their own: readers-first lock: writer waited 1379 ms ReentrantReadWriteLock: writer waited 2 ms The new prices waited in the owner's hand until the shop went quiet. The second line is Java's own ReentrantReadWriteLock from Explicit locks, a lock with a read side that many threads can hold together and a write side for one. In its default, non-fair mode it promises no order, but a thread asking for the read side waits if the thread at the head of the queue wants to write. In practice, that keeps a stream of new readers from starving a writer. Fair mode gives strict arrival order: Java new ReentrantReadWriteLock(); // non-fair: a new reader waits if a writer is next in line new ReentrantReadWriteLock(true); // fair: strict arrival order, less work done per second Kotlin ReentrantReadWriteLock() // non-fair: a new reader waits if a writer is next in line ReentrantReadWriteLock(true) // fair: strict arrival order, less work done per second A lock that lets new readers pass a waiting writer can starve the writer. Make them queue behind it. Before you choose a policy, ask whether the readers need a lock at all. If the writer replaces the whole board, the snapshot from Don't share lets readers read an immutable map with no lock and no waiting, and the question of who starves goes away. Many databases, the programs that store data for other programs, do something similar, which they call multiversion reads: a reader sees a complete older version while a writer works on the new one. That's also where this lesson's tools stop. A pill, a lock order and a read-write lock each solve one shape of problem. None of them tells you whether your version works on a busy day. For that you need a test that makes threads collide on purpose, and that's where the next lesson goes. Starve a writer Read ReadersWriters. Four readers hold the read side for 2 ms at a time, overlapping, for 1.5 seconds. After 100 ms, one writer asks for the lock. The demo measures how long it waits, first with a hand-written readers-first lock, then with ReentrantReadWriteLock. Predict both waits. Run it. ReadersWriters.java package workbench.concurrency.l12; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock; /** * Four readers keep the shop's price table busy for 1.5 s, overlapping all the time. One writer wants in once. * How long does it wait with a hand-written readers-first lock, and with ReentrantReadWriteLock? */ public class ReadersWriters { interface RW { void readLock() throws InterruptedException; void readUnlock(); void writeLock() throws InterruptedException; void writeUnlock(); } /** The textbook readers-first lock: a reader may enter whenever no writer is INSIDE. */ static final class ReadersFirst implements RW { private int readers; private boolean writing; public synchronized void readLock() throws InterruptedException { while (writing) wait(); readers++; } public synchronized void readUnlock() { if (--readers == 0) notifyAll(); } public synchronized void writeLock() throws InterruptedException { while (writing || readers > 0) wait(); writing = true; } public synchronized void writeUnlock() { writing = false; notifyAll(); } } static final class Jdk implements RW { private final ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock(); public void readLock() { rw.readLock().lock(); } public void readUnlock() { rw.readLock().unlock(); } public void writeLock() { rw.writeLock().lock(); } public void writeUnlock() { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } } static long writerWaitMs(RW lock) throws InterruptedException { long end = System.nanoTime() + 1_500_000_000L; Thread[] readers = new Thread[4]; for (int i = 0; i < readers.length; i++) { readers[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { while (System.nanoTime() < end) { lock.readLock(); try { Thread.sleep(2); } finally { lock.readUnlock(); } // a 2 ms read } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); readers[i].start(); Thread.sleep(1); // stagger them so they overlap } Thread.sleep(100); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); lock.writeLock(); // the owner wants to change the prices long waited = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; lock.writeUnlock(); for (Thread r : readers) r.join(); return waited; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.println("readers-first lock: writer waited " + writerWaitMs(new ReadersFirst()) + " ms"); System.out.println("ReentrantReadWriteLock: writer waited " + writerWaitMs(new Jdk()) + " ms"); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l12.ReadersWriters labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l12/ReadersWriters.java ReadersWriters.kt package workbench.concurrency.l12 import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock // Four readers keep the shop's price table busy for 1.5 s, overlapping all the time. One writer wants in once. // How long does it wait with a hand-written readers-first lock, and with ReentrantReadWriteLock? private interface RwLock { fun readLock(); fun readUnlock(); fun writeLock(); fun writeUnlock() } // The textbook readers-first lock: a reader may enter whenever no writer is INSIDE. private class ReadersFirst : RwLock { private val lock = ReentrantLock() private val changed = lock.newCondition() private var readers = 0 private var writing = false override fun readLock() { lock.withLock { while (writing) changed.await(); readers++ } } override fun readUnlock() { lock.withLock { if (--readers == 0) changed.signalAll() } } override fun writeLock() { lock.withLock { while (writing || readers > 0) changed.await(); writing = true } } override fun writeUnlock() { lock.withLock { writing = false; changed.signalAll() } } } private class Jdk : RwLock { private val rw = ReentrantReadWriteLock() override fun readLock() = rw.readLock().lock() override fun readUnlock() = rw.readLock().unlock() override fun writeLock() = rw.writeLock().lock() override fun writeUnlock() = rw.writeLock().unlock() } private fun writerWaitMs(lock: RwLock): Long { val end = System.nanoTime() + 1_500_000_000L val readers = List(4) { thread { while (System.nanoTime() < end) { lock.readLock() try { Thread.sleep(2) } finally { lock.readUnlock() } // a 2 ms read } }.also { Thread.sleep(1) } // stagger them so they overlap } Thread.sleep(100) val t0 = System.nanoTime() lock.writeLock() // the owner wants to change the prices val waited = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 lock.writeUnlock() readers.forEach { it.join() } return waited } fun main() { println("readers-first lock: writer waited ${writerWaitMs(ReadersFirst())} ms") println("ReentrantReadWriteLock: writer waited ${writerWaitMs(Jdk())} ms") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l12.ReadersWritersKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l12/ReadersWriters.kt Readers-first: the writer waits about 1,400 ms (1,379 and 1,362 ms in runs here), until the readers stop on their own. ReentrantReadWriteLock: 0 to 2 ms, because new readers queue behind the waiting writer instead of passing it. jcstress samples, including Classic_01_DiningPhilosophers and Classic_02_ProducerConsumerProblem read
