x: Stopping consumers: pills in Java, a closed channel in Kotlin coroutines Java, BlockingQueue for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { cooks.add(start(() -> { while (true) { String ticket = rail.take(); if (ticket == PILL) return; // each cook needs its own pill cook(ticket); } })); } for (Thread w : waiters) w.join(); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) rail.put(PILL); // 4 cooks, 4 pills for (Thread c : cooks) c.join(); Kotlin, kotlinx.coroutines Channel // a Channel can be closed, so there are no pills coroutineScope { val rail = Channel<String>(capacity = 8) val waiters = tables.map { table -> launch { for (t in table) rail.send(t) } } repeat(4) { launch { for (t in rail) cook(t) } } // each loop ends when the channel is closed AND empty waiters.joinAll() rail.close() // "no more tickets": cooks finish the rail, then stop } With threads and a BlockingQueue, Kotlin code looks just like the Java version: the queue has no idea of "closed", so you still need one pill per consumer, compared with ===. Java's queue does its job well, and the pill is a small, honest workaround for what it lacks. The real difference comes with coroutines, Kotlin's lightweight tasks that the coroutines track covers. A Channel is a queue for coroutines, and it can be closed: close() means no more items, and every for (t in rail) loop ends once the channel is closed and empty, however many consumers there are. That removes the whole family of pill-counting bugs. coroutineScope also waits for every coroutine it launched, so there is no join loop to forget.

h: Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers · Worked example
x: Close the kitchen without losing an order The kitchen's program has two waiter threads that take orders from the tables and four cook threads, with a bounded rail between them. At closing time, someone wrote this. What happens to the tickets still on the rail, and to the dish a cook is halfway through? // Naive: stop now, whatever is on the rail void closeKitchen() { for (Thread c : cooks) c.interrupt(); for (Thread w : waiters) w.interrupt(); } // Naive: stop now, whatever is on the rail fun closeKitchen() { cooks.forEach { it.interrupt() } waiters.forEach { it.interrupt() } } Interrupting a cook that waits in take() stops it at once, so every ticket still on the rail is dropped. A cook in the middle of a dish may stop halfway and leave it unfinished. And a waiter interrupted inside put loses the order it was holding. Nothing throws, and nothing tells the customers. Here's the orderly version, with a label on each step. open is a volatile flag the waiters check before they take each new order. void closeKitchen() throws InterruptedException { open = false; // 1. waiters stop taking new orders for (Thread w : waiters) w.join(); // 2. wait until no waiter can put again for (int i = 0; i < cooks.size(); i++) { rail.put(PILL); // 3. one pill per cook, behind every real ticket } long deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(30); for (Thread c : cooks) { c.join(Math.max(1, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.toMillis(deadline - System.nanoTime()))); // 4. one deadline for all } for (Thread c : cooks) if (c.isAlive()) c.interrupt(); // 5. still busy: interrupt as a last resort } fun closeKitchen() { open = false // 1. waiters stop taking new orders waiters.forEach { it.join() } // 2. wait until no waiter can put again repeat(cooks.size) { rail.put(PILL) } // 3. one pill per cook, behind every real ticket val deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(30) for (c in cooks) { c.join(maxOf(1L, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.toMillis(deadline - System.nanoTime()))) // 4. one deadline for all } cooks.filter { it.isAlive }.forEach { it.interrupt() } // 5. still busy: interrupt as a last resort } Before reading on, explain to yourself why step 2 must finish before step 3 starts. Answer: a pill put while a waiter is still working can land in front of that waiter's last tickets. A cook that takes the pill goes home. With every cook gone and the rail bounded, the waiter then waits in put forever, and the shutdown hangs in step 2. Joining the waiters first means every real ticket is already ahead of the pills. Step 5 is the safety net. If the oven breaks, the cooks can't finish the rail before the deadline, and interrupting them is then the right call. The orders they didn't finish were never marked as served. A program that records each finished order, as the bank recorded each payment in Race conditions, knows exactly which ones to pick up when it starts again.

h: Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers · Lab
x: A pipeline that stops cleanly, and a table that can't deadlock labs/concurrency/src/main/java/workbench/concurrency/l12/SettlementPipeline.java labs/concurrency/src/main/java/workbench/concurrency/l12/DiningTable.java ./gradlew :concurrency:test --tests 'workbench.concurrency.l12.*' Meet the two classes. SettlementPipeline is this lesson's kitchen in general form: producer threads put records (plain strings) into one bounded queue, and consumer threads take them and call process on each. DiningTable is the philosophers' table: dine(seat, meals, eat) has the philosopher in seat take two forks and eat, meals times. Run the tests. All six fail. The three pipeline tests hit UnsupportedOperationException. The three DiningTable tests time out after 15 seconds each: the philosophers deadlocked. Part 1: write SettlementPipeline.run. Create an ArrayBlockingQueue of capacity and a unique pill (new String("PILL")). Start the consumers: each loops on take(), stops at the pill (compared with ==), and otherwise calls process and counts. Start one producer thread per inner list. Join all producers, then put one pill per consumer, then join all consumers, then return the count. Part 2: fix DiningTable.dine so every philosopher takes the lower-numbered fork first. Keep reachForTheOtherFork() between the two forks. Run the tests until all six pass, then twice more. Count processed records with an AtomicInteger, because several consumers add to it at once. The second pipeline test checks that process is never called after run returns. If it fails, you return before joining every consumer. For the table, compute a = seat and b = (seat + 1) % seats, then lock forks[min(a, b)] before forks[max(a, b)]. Only the last philosopher's order actually changes, and that's enough to break the cycle. All six tests in ClassicProblemsTest pass, three runs in a row. By the end you can stop a producer-consumer pipeline cleanly with poison pills, fix the dining philosophers deadlock two ways, and say who starves under each readers-writers policy.

h: Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers · Quiz
x: The head chef puts the poison pills for 4 cooks right after starting the waiters, without waiting for them to finish. The rail is bounded. What can happen? Nothing: the pills wait at the back of the queue The cooks take the pills early and stop, the rail fills up, and the waiters wait in put forever The pills are rejected because the queue is full Each cook cooks exactly one order Pills are ordinary elements, taken in arrival order. Put early, they sit in front of tickets that the waiters add later. The cooks stop at them, nothing drains the rail any more, and the waiters block once it's full. Join the producers first. Five philosophers each take the left fork, then the right one, and sometimes they all freeze. Which change removes the deadlock? Make every fork a fair ReentrantLock Add a random sleep before picking up the left fork Always take the lower-numbered fork first, so the last philosopher reaches right first Use synchronized instead of ReentrantLock With one global order, no cycle of waiting can form, so circular wait is gone. Fair locks change who gets a free fork next, not the cycle. A random sleep only makes the bad timing rarer. synchronized deadlocks in exactly the same way. A hand-written readers-first lock protects the shop's price table. Readers arrive all the time and overlap. Once an hour, the owner calls writeLock() to change the prices. What happens? The owner waits until the readers stop arriving, which may be never: writer starvation The owner gets in within one read's duration The owner's call throws IllegalStateException Readers and the writer take turns Readers first lets a new reader in whenever no writer is inside, so the reader count never reaches zero while readers overlap. The writer waits for a moment that never comes. ReentrantReadWriteLock makes new readers queue behind a waiting writer, and a snapshot avoids locking reads at all. From Synchronizers: the waiter fix for five philosophers uses a Semaphore. Why new Semaphore(4) and not new Semaphore(5)? To save one thread With at most 4 seated, at least one of them can always pick up both forks, so the cycle can't involve everyone A semaphore can't have more permits than threads Fairness needs one permit fewer than there are threads With five permits, all five can sit, each take a left fork and freeze as before. With four, at most four hold a fork, and five forks between four people means at least one of them can take both. The permits limit how many compete, and that's what breaks the cycle here. A cook checks if (ticket.equals("POISON")) break;, and the pill is the string literal "POISON". What's the risk? equals is too slow for a busy loop None: a real ticket never contains that text The pill might be garbage collected A real ticket with that text stops a cook early and is never cooked A ticket's text can be anything a waiter types, including the pill's text. With equals, such a ticket sends a cook home and is silently dropped. A pill created as a unique object and compared with == (or === in Kotlin) can't be confused with real data.

h: Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers · Key terms
x: Producer-consumer Threads that make work hand it to threads that do it, usually through a queue. Poison pill A special queue item that tells one consumer to stop. Backpressure A full bounded queue making producers wait, so they slow to the consumers' pace. Dining philosophers The classic deadlock: each thread holds one resource and waits for its neighbour's. Resource ordering Taking locks in one global order so that no cycle of waiting can form. Readers-writers Sharing data between many readers and a few writers, and deciding who waits. Writer starvation A writer that never gets in because readers keep holding the lock. Poison pills: how many, and when do you put them? One per consumer, and only after every producer has finished putting. Why compare a poison pill with == rather than equals? So a real item with the same text isn't mistaken for the pill. Make the pill a unique object, such as new String("PILL"). Why bound the queue between producers and consumers? So put makes producers wait when consumers fall behind (backpressure), instead of filling memory. Which deadlock condition does "always take the lower-numbered fork first" remove? Circular wait: with one global order, no cycle of waiting threads can form. How does a Semaphore(n - 1) "waiter" prevent the dining philosophers deadlock? At most n - 1 philosophers compete for n forks, so at least one can always get both. Readers-first lock: who starves? Writers. With overlapping readers the reader count never reaches zero, so the writer never gets in. What does non-fair ReentrantReadWriteLock do when a writer is waiting and a new reader arrives? The reader usually waits if the writer is at the head of the queue, so a stream of readers doesn't starve the writer.

h: Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers · Go deeper
x: Poison pills are one of several ways to stop consumers. Thread pools use interruption: shutdownNow() interrupts every worker, and tasks are expected to stop when interrupted, as A thread's life described. A poll(timeout) loop that checks a volatile flag is simple, but it makes shutdown wait for up to one timeout, and every loop must check the flag. Kotlin channels and reactive streams have completion built in, which is why they need no pills. The dining philosophers problem has more solutions than the two here. Chandy and Misra's solution passes "dirty" and "clean" forks between neighbours on request, which avoids both deadlock and starvation and works across machines, at the cost of messages. A plain tryLock with back-off works too, but it needs randomness to avoid livelock. All of them remove one of the four conditions from Deadlock, livelock and starvation. Readers-writers shows up all over databases. Many of them use multiversion reads: a query reads each row as it was when the query started, so readers don't wait for writers and writers don't wait for readers. That is the immutable-snapshot idea from Don't share applied to storage, and it's why you rarely meet this problem in plain database queries. Writers still wait for other writers on the same rows. If you want to see these problems under a real stress harness, the jcstress samples include Classic_01_DiningPhilosophers and Classic_02_ProducerConsumerProblem. The next lesson shows how to run jcstress and read its results.

h: Testing and debugging concurrent code · Making test threads collide: the stress test
x: Two test threads that never meet catch nothing: a start latch opens the doors at nine, more threads than cores and many rounds make them collide, a latch replaces the sleep, and jcstress counts every outcome Let's start with the smallest form of the problem. In Race conditions, a counter's count++ lost updates when two threads ran it at once, because count++ is three steps: read, add, write. Here's the kind of test most people write for it: Java // Naive: two threads that may never meet Counter c = new Counter(); Thread a = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) c.hit(); }); Thread b = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) c.hit(); }); a.start(); b.start(); a.join(); b.join(); assertThat(c.count).isEqualTo(2_000); Kotlin // Naive: two threads that may never meet val c = Counter() val a = thread { repeat(1_000) { c.hit() } } val b = thread { repeat(1_000) { c.hit() } } a.join(); b.join() assertThat(c.count).isEqualTo(2_000) The Try it runs this test twenty times against that racy counter. Then it runs a stress test, which we'll build in a moment, twenty times against the same counter: naive test (2 threads x 1,000, no start line): failed 1 of 20 runs stress test (8 threads x 100,000, start latch): failed 20 of 20 runs Same code, same bug. The naive test caught it once in twenty runs, and in another run here, not at all. Race conditions put it this way: a race is shy around small numbers. A thousand increments take a few microseconds, about as long as starting a thread, so the first thread is often done before the second begins. On a quiet machine, the scheduler, the part of the system that decides which thread runs when, is kind to small tests. It runs them one after the other, and the bug never gets its chance. A test that doesn't force overlap is really a single-threaded test. Five habits turn it into a stress test, a test that runs code on many threads at once, many times, to make races show up: Hold every thread at a start line and release them together, with the start latch from Synchronizers (a CountDownLatch of 1 that opens for everyone at once). Use more threads than cores, the parts of the processor that each run one thread at a time, so the scheduler has to switch between them. Give each thread many operations, so the threads overlap for a long time. Run many rounds, with fresh state each time. One round is one sample of all the possible timings. When all the threads are done, check an invariant, a fact that must hold whatever the timing: totals that must add up, an amount that must never be passed. Never assert on how long something took. The lab packs these habits into a small harness, a reusable piece of test code, called Stress. You give it a setup that builds fresh state, an actor that every thread runs over and over, and an invariant to check after join(). The figure shows one round. Here's the refund desk from the opening, under stress: Java record Round(RefundLedger ledger, AtomicLong approved) {} int failed = Stress.failingRounds(20, 8, 2_000, () -> new Round(new RefundLedger(Map.of("pay-1", 10_000L)), new AtomicLong()), // fresh state per round r -> { if (r.ledger().refund("pay-1", 1)) r.approved().incrementAndGet(); }, // every thread, over and over r -> r.approved().get() == 10_000 && r.ledger().refunded("pay-1") == 10_000); // must hold at the end assertThat(failed).isZero(); Kotlin class Round(val ledger: RefundLedger, val approved: AtomicLong) val failed = Stress.failingRounds(20, 8, 2_000, { Round(RefundLedger(mapOf("pay-1" to 10_000L)), AtomicLong()) }, // fresh state per round { r -> if (r.ledger.refund("pay-1", 1)) r.approved.incrementAndGet() }, // every thread, over and over { r -> r.approved.get() == 10_000L && r.ledger.refunded("pay-1") == 10_000L }) // must hold at the end assertThat(failed).isZero() Eight threads each try 2,000 one-cent refunds against a sale of 10,000 cents, so a correct ledger, the record that tracks the refunds, approves exactly 10,000. The racy ledger in the lab, which checks the total and then writes it in two separate steps, approves all 16,000. That's the coat refunded 160.00 on a 100.00 sale. Two more rules keep these tests from hurting you. Put a timeout on every one, with @Timeout or assertTimeoutPreemptively from JUnit, the test library the labs use. Then a deadlock fails the test in seconds instead of hanging the whole test run for an hour. And remember what a pass means: this run found no failure. A stress test can prove that a race exists. It can never prove that none does, which is why the design rules from earlier lessons matter more than any test. A passing race test means "not found this time", never "can't happen". A stress test makes threads meet. The next trouble is a test that waits for its threads and guesses how long. The same bug, tested two ways Read NaiveVsStress. It tests the racy counter from Race conditions twenty times the usual way (2 threads, 1,000 hits, no start line), then twenty times as a stress test (8 threads, 100,000 hits, a start latch). Predict how many runs of each fail. Run it two or three times. NaiveVsStress.java package workbench.concurrency.l13; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; /** The same racy counter, tested twice: the way most tests are written, and the way that finds the bug. */ public class NaiveVsStress { static final class Counter { volatile int count; // volatile only stops the JIT from hiding the race (lesson 3) void hit() { count++; } // the bug: read, add, write } // 2 threads, 1,000 hits each, no start line static boolean naiveRound() throws InterruptedException { Counter c = new Counter(); Thread a = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) c.hit(); }); Thread b = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) c.hit(); }); a.start(); b.start(); a.join(); b.join(); return c.count == 2_000; } // 8 threads, 100,000 hits each, released together static boolean stressRound() throws InterruptedException { Counter c = new Counter(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] ts = new Thread[8]; for (int t = 0; t < ts.length; t++) { ts[t] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) c.hit(); }); ts[t].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); return c.count == 800_000; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int naiveFailed = 0, stressFailed = 0; for (int r = 0; r < 20; r++) if (!naiveRound()) naiveFailed++; for (int r = 0; r < 20; r++) if (!stressRound()) stressFailed++; System.out.println("naive test (2 threads x 1,000, no start line): failed " + naiveFailed + " of 20 runs"); System.out.println("stress test (8 threads x 100,000, start latch): failed " + stressFailed + " of 20 runs"); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l13.NaiveVsStress labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l13/NaiveVsStress.java NaiveVsStress.kt package workbench.concurrency.l13 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import kotlin.concurrent.thread // The same racy counter, tested twice: the way most tests are written, and the way that finds the bug. private class RacyCounter { @Volatile var count = 0 // @Volatile only stops the JIT from hiding the race (lesson 3) fun hit() { count++ } // the bug: read, add, write } // 2 threads, 1,000 hits each, no start line private fun naiveRound(): Boolean { val c = RacyCounter() val a = thread { repeat(1_000) { c.hit() } } val b = thread { repeat(1_000) { c.hit() } } a.join(); b.join() return c.count == 2_000 } // 8 threads, 100,000 hits each, released together private fun stressRound(): Boolean { val c = RacyCounter() val go = CountDownLatch(1) val ts = List(8) { thread { go.await(); repeat(100_000) { c.hit() } } } go.countDown() ts.forEach { it.join() } return c.count == 800_000 } fun main() { val naiveFailed = (1..20).count { !naiveRound() } val stressFailed = (1..20).count { !stressRound() } println("naive test (2 threads x 1,000, no start line): failed $naiveFailed of 20 runs") println("stress test (8 threads x 100,000, start latch): failed $stressFailed of 20 runs") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l13.NaiveVsStressKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l13/NaiveVsStress.kt The naive test fails rarely, 0 or 1 of 20 in runs here, and a different number each time. The stress test fails 20 of 20. Same code, same bug. Only the second test is worth keeping. One round of a stress test: fresh state, all actors released together, join, check the invariant. Repeat for many rounds.

h: Testing and debugging concurrent code · Replacing sleeps with latches, and guesses with deadlines
x: Work that happens in the background, such as recording a refund after the customer has left the desk, is hard to test. The test has to wait until the work is done, and the quickest way to wait is a nap: Java // Naive: hopes 50 ms is enough on every machine, and is slow on all of them worker.submit(refund); Thread.sleep(50); assertThat(ledger.status(refund.id())).isEqualTo(RECORDED); Kotlin // Naive: hopes 50 ms is enough on every machine, and is slow on all of them worker.submit(refund) Thread.sleep(50) assertThat(ledger.status(refund.id)).isEqualTo(RECORDED) Thread.sleep in a test is a guess about how long something takes. On your laptop the guess is generous, so the test is slow. On a busy build server, a shared machine that runs everyone's tests, the guess is too short, and the test fails for no reason. A test like that, which passes or fails with no change to the code, is called flaky, and a flaky test teaches the whole team to ignore red builds. The Try it shows how quickly a guess goes wrong. Eight threads keep every core busy, like a build server on a busy afternoon. A background worker records a refund in about 2 ms. One test sleeps 3 ms and then checks; the other waits on a latch for up to 5 seconds. Each runs 100 times: sleep(3) then assert: failed 45 of 100 latch.await(5 s): failed 0 of 100 A nap 50% longer than the work failed almost half the time. Another run here failed 14 of 100; on a busy machine, a guess is a coin toss. The fix is to wait for the event itself, and to keep the timeout only as a deadline far above any real duration: Java // Fixed: wait for the event itself, with a deadline far above any real duration CountDownLatch recorded = new CountDownLatch(1); ledger.onRecorded(id -> recorded.countDown()); worker.submit(refund); assertThat(recorded.await(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue(); assertThat(ledger.status(refund.id())).isEqualTo(RECORDED); Kotlin // Fixed: wait for the event itself, with a deadline far above any real duration val recorded = CountDownLatch(1) ledger.onRecorded { recorded.countDown() } worker.submit(refund) assertThat(recorded.await(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue() assertThat(ledger.status(refund.id)).isEqualTo(RECORDED) The latch version is as fast as the code when the code is fast, and patient when the machine is slow. When it does fail, it fails with a clear message, "not recorded within 10 s", instead of a wrong status. The same tools can hold a thread at a known point, which makes many concurrency tests deterministic: they give the same result on every run. Give the code under test a fake dependency that blocks on a latch, for example a fake bank service: Java class SlowBank implements Bank { final CountDownLatch inCall = new CountDownLatch(1); final CountDownLatch release = new CountDownLatch(1); @Override public Approval check(Payment p) throws InterruptedException { inCall.countDown(); // 1. tell the test: a thread is inside the call release.await(); // 2. hold it here until the test says go return Approval.YES; } } Kotlin class SlowBank : Bank { val inCall = CountDownLatch(1) val release = CountDownLatch(1) override fun check(p: Payment): Approval { inCall.countDown() // 1. tell the test: a thread is inside the call release.await() // 2. hold it here until the test says go return Approval.YES } } Now the test can wait on inCall and know for certain that one thread is inside the call. Plug this fake behind the IssuerGate from Synchronizers, the semaphore that guards the bank's card service, set to one permit. A second caller with a 100 ms limit must then time out. Finally the test opens release and checks that the permit came back. No sleeps, and no luck. When there's no hook to wait on, poll: check the condition, sleep a few milliseconds, and check again, until an overall deadline passes. Checking Thread.getState() until the threads you expect are BLOCKED or WAITING is a common way to know they have queued up, and the worked example uses it. A sleep in a test is a guess. Wait for the event, and keep the timeout as a deadline. Latches and stress tests find the races you can provoke on purpose. Some bugs need millions of tries, and a tool built for exactly that. Make a test flaky on purpose Read SleepVsLatch. Eight threads keep every core busy, like a busy build server. A background worker records a refund in about 2 ms. One test sleeps 3 ms and then checks; the other waits on a latch for up to 5 seconds. Each runs 100 times. Predict the failure counts. Run it. Then change the sleep to 10 ms and run it again. SleepVsLatch.java package workbench.concurrency.l13; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * A test checks that a background worker records a refund. One version sleeps 3 ms and hopes; * the other waits on a latch. Both run 100 times while 8 threads keep every core busy, like a busy build server. */ public class SleepVsLatch { static volatile boolean burn = true; // the code under test: records the refund on another thread, about 2 ms of work static Thread recordAsync(Runnable whenDone) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { long end = System.nanoTime() + 2_000_000; while (System.nanoTime() < end) Thread.onSpinWait(); whenDone.run(); }); t.start(); return t; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread b = new Thread(() -> { while (burn) Thread.onSpinWait(); }); // a busy machine b.setDaemon(true); b.start(); } int sleepFailed = 0, latchFailed = 0; for (int run = 0; run < 100; run++) { boolean[] recorded = {false}; Thread t = recordAsync(() -> recorded[0] = true); Thread.sleep(3); // "should be enough" if (!recorded[0]) sleepFailed++; // (a racy read too, which is the point) t.join(); } for (int run = 0; run < 100; run++) { CountDownLatch recorded = new CountDownLatch(1); recordAsync(recorded::countDown); if (!recorded.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) latchFailed++; // waits exactly as long as needed } burn = false; System.out.println("sleep(3) then assert: failed " + sleepFailed + " of 100"); System.out.println("latch.await(5 s): failed " + latchFailed + " of 100"); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l13.SleepVsLatch labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l13/SleepVsLatch.java SleepVsLatch.kt package workbench.concurrency.l13 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A test checks that a background worker records a refund. One version sleeps 3 ms and hopes; // the other waits on a latch. Both run 100 times while 8 threads keep every core busy, like a busy build server. @Volatile private var burn = true // the code under test: records the refund on another thread, about 2 ms of work private fun recordAsync(whenDone: () -> Unit): Thread = thread { val end = System.nanoTime() + 2_000_000 while (System.nanoTime() < end) Thread.onSpinWait() whenDone() } fun main() { repeat(8) { thread(isDaemon = true) { while (burn) Thread.onSpinWait() } } // a busy machine var sleepFailed = 0 var latchFailed = 0 repeat(100) { var recorded = false val t = recordAsync { recorded = true } Thread.sleep(3) // "should be enough" if (!recorded) sleepFailed++ // (a racy read too, which is the point) t.join() } repeat(100) { val recorded = CountDownLatch(1) recordAsync { recorded.countDown() } if (!recorded.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) latchFailed++ // waits exactly as long as needed } burn = false println("sleep(3) then assert: failed $sleepFailed of 100") println("latch.await(5 s): failed $latchFailed of 100") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l13.SleepVsLatchKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l13/SleepVsLatch.kt The sleep version failed 14 and 45 times out of 100 in two runs here. The latch version failed 0 times. A 10 ms sleep fails less often, but it can still fail, and it makes every run slower.

h: Testing and debugging concurrent code · Letting jcstress search the timings for you
x: Some bugs need millions of attempts to show up at all, and some need a particular kind of processor. ARM processors, such as the ones in Apple Silicon laptops and many cloud servers, may let one core see another core's writes in a different order from how they were made. Intel and AMD processors allow less of that. jcstress is a harness for exactly these bugs, from OpenJDK, the open-source project that builds Java itself. It runs tiny tests millions of times, with careful control over how the threads start and where the state lives, and it counts every outcome it sees. Its latest tagged release is 0.16, from February 2023, and the master branch is 0.17-SNAPSHOT. A jcstress test is a class with shared @State, two or more @Actor methods that run at the same time, and a result object, here II_Result, which holds two int fields. @Outcome annotations list the results you expect and label each one. Here's the race from the first section, as two refund desks bumping one counter: import org.openjdk.jcstress.annotations.*; import org.openjdk.jcstress.infra.results.II_Result; import static org.openjdk.jcstress.annotations.Expect.*; @JCStressTest @Outcome(id = "1, 2", expect = ACCEPTABLE, desc = "actor1 went first") @Outcome(id = "2, 1", expect = ACCEPTABLE, desc = "actor2 went first") @Outcome(id = "1, 1", expect = ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING, desc = "both read 0: one increment lost") @State public class RefundCounterRace { int refunds; // shared state, fresh for every sample @Actor public void actor1(II_Result r) { r.r1 = ++refunds; } @Actor public void actor2(II_Result r) { r.r2 = ++refunds; } } jcstress is a Java-only tool. An annotation processor, a plug-in that runs inside the compiler, turns these classes into test code at build time, so there's no Kotlin twin here. The labels are the part to learn: ACCEPTABLE is a correct result. ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING is allowed but worth seeing, usually the race the test is about. Here, 1, 1 means both actors read 0, so one increment was lost. FORBIDDEN must never happen. If jcstress sees it even once, the test fails. Write down your guess: how often will 1, 1 happen? Here's a real run, on a 4-core x86 Linux machine with JDK 21. It took under two minutes: RESULT SAMPLES FREQ EXPECT DESCRIPTION 1, 1 707,991,481 36.34% Interesting both read 0: one increment lost 1, 2 675,088,320 34.65% Acceptable actor1 went first 2, 1 565,287,693 29.01% Acceptable actor2 went first Almost two billion samples, and the increment was lost in more than a third of them. That's the same bug the naive test caught once in twenty runs. jcstress doesn't hope the threads meet; it arranges for them to meet, two billion times. With an AtomicInteger instead of the plain int, a rerun on the same machine never saw 1, 1 at all, and jcstress listed no interesting results. Had we marked 1, 1 as FORBIDDEN in the racy version, the test would have failed. Results depend on the hardware. x86 processors, the Intel and AMD kind, keep their writes in order, so some surprises that ARM machines show regularly, such as one thread seeing another's writes out of order, may never appear on an Intel laptop. Interesting means allowed, not guaranteed to appear. The README documents a Maven project template and no official Gradle setup, so try it in a separate Maven project. (Maven is a Java build tool, like the Gradle that runs this course's labs.) The jcstress samples on GitHub are a course in themselves. Each one has the outcomes it expects written in its source. Tests find bugs before a program ships. When a running program misbehaves anyway, you need the JVM to tell you what its threads are doing. Run a jcstress test (optional, needs Maven and a network) In a scratch folder outside the labs, make a jcstress project with the template command below, from the jcstress README. Maven downloads what it needs the first time. Add RefundCounterRace from this section to the generated sources, build, and run only that test with -t. A run takes a minute or two and keeps every core busy. Find the line for outcome 1, 1. Then change int refunds to an AtomicInteger and both actors to incrementAndGet(), rebuild and run again. terminal mvn archetype:generate -DinteractiveMode=false -DarchetypeGroupId=org.openjdk.jcstress \ -DarchetypeArtifactId=jcstress-java-test-archetype -DgroupId=org.sample -DartifactId=test -Dversion=1.0 cd test # put RefundCounterRace.java next to the generated sample test, then: mvn clean verify java -jar target/jcstress.jar -t RefundCounterRace The first run reports 1, 2 and 2, 1 as acceptable and 1, 1 as interesting, seen in a large share of the samples (about 36% across all configurations on the 4-core machine here; your share will differ). With AtomicInteger, 1, 1 is never seen, and the run lists no interesting tests. If you mark 1, 1 as FORBIDDEN in the racy version, the test fails. jcstress (README: archetype, running, modes) docs jcstress samples read

h: Testing and debugging concurrent code · When it hangs, take dumps; when it's slow, record JFR
x: Once a program runs for real, you debug it with what the JVM can tell you about itself. Two tools cover most cases, and both come with the JDK, the kit you install to build and run Java. A thread dump answers "where is every thread right now, and what is it waiting for?". It's a printout of every thread's name, state and stack, the chain of method calls the thread is in the middle of. jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l prints one: jcmd is the JDK's tool for sending commands to a running JVM, and the PID is the number the operating system gives each running program. The -l adds the java.util.concurrent locks each thread owns, and the dump ends with a deadlock report if there's a cycle (Deadlock, livelock and starvation). The state line is the first thing to read: What the dump says What the thread is doing RUNNABLE Running, ready to run, or waiting inside the operating system for input, such as data from the network BLOCKED (on object monitor) Waiting to enter a synchronized block that another thread holds WAITING (parking) Parked by java.util.concurrent: a lock, latch, queue or semaphore; the parking to wait for line names it WAITING (on object monitor) Inside Object.wait() TIMED_WAITING The same, with a timeout, or in sleep Here's a trimmed dump of a small program in which till-0 takes a ReentrantLock and then makes a slow call while holding it, and three other tills wait for the lock. It was taken on JDK 25: "till-0" #23 [14677] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=0.24ms elapsed=2.54s ... java.lang.Thread.State: TIMED_WAITING (sleeping) at java.lang.Thread.sleep(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/Thread.java:540) at Stuck.slowCall(Stuck.java:17) ... Locked ownable synchronizers: - <0x000000073781f198> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync) "till-1" #24 [14678] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=0.59ms elapsed=2.34s ... java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking) at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/Native Method) - parking to wait for <0x000000073781f198> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync) ... at java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock.lock(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/ReentrantLock.java:323) at Stuck.lambda$main$1(Stuck.java:12) Read it from the waiting side. till-1 is parked, waiting for the lock at ...f198. The same address appears under till-0's "Locked ownable synchronizers", so till-0 holds it, and its stack says why it's slow: it's asleep in slowCall, still holding the lock. That's the rule from synchronized and intrinsic locks, keep slow calls out of the lock, broken in a real program. One dump is a photo. Take three, a few seconds apart: a thread that shows the same frame every time is stuck, and one whose stack changes is busy. In this program's third dump, four seconds later, till-1 still showed cpu=0.59ms, while elapsed had grown from 2.34 s to 6.58 s. That's a thread that exists, waits and does nothing. For tools of your own, Thread.dump_to_file -format=json writes the same dump as JSON, with state and lock fields from JDK 25. Java Flight Recorder (JFR) answers a different question: "what were the threads waiting for over the last minute, and for how long?". It's an event recorder built into the JVM, cheap enough to leave on in production. jdk.JavaMonitorEnter records each wait to enter a synchronized block that lasts longer than a threshold, with the lock's class, the duration and the previous owner. jdk.JavaMonitorWait covers Object.wait(), and jdk.ThreadPark covers ReentrantLock and the other java.util.concurrent waits. jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l # states, stacks, owned j.u.c locks, deadlocks jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json t.json # JSON; per-thread state and lock fields need JDK 25+ jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=locks.jfr jfr summary locks.jfr # how many events of each type jfr print --events jdk.JavaMonitorEnter locks.jfr # who waited for which monitor, how long, after whom The Try it records one second of six threads fighting, three over a synchronized block and three over a ReentrantLock, each holding its lock for 3 ms at a time. I expected hundreds of short waits for both. The ReentrantLock gave exactly that. The monitor, in most runs here on JDK 21 and JDK 25, gave something else. Here's one run on JDK 25: JavaMonitorEnter on java.lang.Object 3 events, 1975 ms waiting ThreadPark on java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync 326 events, 1728 ms waiting Three waits for the monitor, adding up to almost two seconds. jfr print on the same recording shows one of the two long ones: jdk.JavaMonitorEnter { startTime = 17:45:51.586 (2026-11-16) duration = 986 ms monitorClass = java.lang.Object (classLoader = bootstrap) previousOwner = "ledger-2" (javaThreadId = 28) address = 0x7FB344000F20 eventThread = "ledger-4" (javaThreadId = 30) ... } ledger-4 waited 986 ms to get in, and the thread that held the monitor just before it was ledger-2. In other words, ledger-2 released the monitor and took it straight back, over and over, while the other two threads waited for nearly the whole second. synchronized makes no promise of fairness, and here one thread kept the lock for almost a second: the starvation from Deadlock, livelock and starvation, now with numbers. (One busy run here split the waiting into 94 shorter events instead, so take a few recordings before you decide.) A single thread dump would have shown two BLOCKED threads and nothing more. The recording showed who waited, how long, and for whom. No JFR event reports deadlocks; for those, use a dump or ThreadMXBean, the JDK's window onto the JVM's threads. And if your program runs in a container, a packaged and walled-off environment that many servers use, the JVM is often process 1, so jcmd 1 Thread.print inside the container is the quickest start. Record contention with JFR Read JfrContention. It starts a JFR recording from inside the program, runs six threads for one second (three fight over a synchronized block, three over a ReentrantLock), then reads the recording back. Predict the number of events and the total waiting time for each kind of lock. Then run it. Run jfr summary and then jfr print --events jdk.JavaMonitorEnter on the file the demo printed. Find duration and previousOwner. JfrContention.java package workbench.concurrency.l13; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; import jdk.jfr.Recording; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedEvent; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile; /** * Records one second of lock contention with Java Flight Recorder, from inside the program, * then reads the recording back and summarizes it. The .jfr file is kept for the jfr tool. */ public class JfrContention { static final Object ledgerMonitor = new Object(); static final ReentrantLock batchLock = new ReentrantLock(); static void busy(long micros) { long end = System.nanoTime() + micros * 1_000; while (System.nanoTime() < end) Thread.onSpinWait(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Path file = Files.createTempFile("contention-", ".jfr"); try (Recording rec = new Recording()) { rec.enable("jdk.JavaMonitorEnter").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(1)); // waited > 1 ms for a monitor rec.enable("jdk.ThreadPark").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(1)); // parked > 1 ms (j.u.c locks) rec.start(); long end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L; Thread[] ts = new Thread[6]; for (int i = 0; i < ts.length; i++) { boolean useMonitor = i % 2 == 0; ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { while (System.nanoTime() < end) { if (useMonitor) { synchronized (ledgerMonitor) { busy(3_000); } // hold it 3 ms } else { batchLock.lock(); try { busy(3_000); } finally { batchLock.unlock(); } } } }, (useMonitor ? "ledger-" : "batch-") + i); ts[i].start(); } for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); rec.stop(); rec.dump(file); } Map<String, long[]> byKind = new TreeMap<>(); // count, total ms for (RecordedEvent e : RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) { String what = switch (e.getEventType().getName()) { case "jdk.JavaMonitorEnter" -> "JavaMonitorEnter on " + e.getClass("monitorClass").getName(); case "jdk.ThreadPark" -> "ThreadPark on " + (e.getClass("parkedClass") == null ? "?" : e.getClass("parkedClass").getName()); default -> e.getEventType().getName(); }; long[] agg = byKind.computeIfAbsent(what, k -> new long[2]); agg[0]++; agg[1] += e.getDuration().toMillis(); } byKind.forEach((k, v) -> System.out.printf("%-70s %5d events, %6d ms waiting%n", k, v[0], v[1])); System.out.println("recording kept at " + file); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l13.JfrContention labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l13/JfrContention.java JfrContention.kt package workbench.concurrency.l13 import java.nio.file.Files import java.time.Duration import java.util.TreeMap import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import jdk.jfr.Recording import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock // Records one second of lock contention with Java Flight Recorder, from inside the program, // then reads the recording back and summarizes it. The .jfr file is kept for the jfr tool. private val ledgerMonitor = Any() private val batchLock = ReentrantLock() private fun busy(micros: Long) { val end = System.nanoTime() + micros * 1_000 while (System.nanoTime() < end) Thread.onSpinWait() } fun main() { val file = Files.createTempFile("contention-", ".jfr") Recording().use { rec -> rec.enable("jdk.JavaMonitorEnter").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(1)) // waited > 1 ms for a monitor rec.enable("jdk.ThreadPark").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(1)) // parked > 1 ms (j.u.c locks) rec.start() val end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L val ts = List(6) { i -> val useMonitor = i % 2 == 0 thread(name = (if (useMonitor) "ledger-" else "batch-") + i) { while (System.nanoTime() < end) { if (useMonitor) synchronized(ledgerMonitor) { busy(3_000) } // hold it 3 ms else batchLock.withLock { busy(3_000) } } } } ts.forEach { it.join() } rec.stop() rec.dump(file) } val byKind = TreeMap<String, LongArray>() // count, total ms for (e in RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) { val what = when (e.eventType.name) { "jdk.JavaMonitorEnter" -> "JavaMonitorEnter on " + e.getClass("monitorClass").name "jdk.ThreadPark" -> "ThreadPark on " + (e.getClass("parkedClass")?.name ?: "?") else -> e.eventType.name } val agg = byKind.getOrPut(what) { LongArray(2) } agg[0]++ agg[1] += e.duration.toMillis() } byKind.forEach { (k, v) -> println("%-70s %5d events, %6d ms waiting".format(k, v[0], v[1])) } println("recording kept at $file") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l13.JfrContentionKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l13/JfrContention.kt ThreadPark on java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync with about 320 events and about 1.7 seconds of waiting in total. JavaMonitorEnter on java.lang.Object with only a handful of events (2 to 8 in most runs here), adding up to almost two seconds: one thread kept taking the monitor back while two others waited. A busy machine can split the waiting into many shorter events. jfr print shows each event's duration, monitorClass, previousOwner and the waiting thread's stack.

h: Testing and debugging concurrent code · Java and Kotlin
x: The same stress test in Java and Kotlin Java (JUnit 6) @RepeatedTest(5) // a race test is a sample: take several @Timeout(10) // a deadlock fails the test instead of hanging the build void noRefundIsLost() throws Exception { RefundLedger ledger = new RefundLedger(Map.of("pay-1", 10_000L)); AtomicLong approved = new AtomicLong(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) { // more threads than cores Thread th = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int i = 0; i < 2_000; i++) if (ledger.refund("pay-1", 1)) approved.incrementAndGet(); }); th.start(); threads.add(th); } go.countDown(); // the starting gun for (Thread th : threads) th.join(); assertThat(approved.get()).isEqualTo(10_000); // an invariant, not a timing assertThat(ledger.refunded("pay-1")).isEqualTo(10_000); } Kotlin (JUnit 6) @RepeatedTest(5) // a race test is a sample: take several @Timeout(10) // a deadlock fails the test instead of hanging the build fun `no refund is lost`() { val ledger = RefundLedger(mapOf("pay-1" to 10_000L)) val approved = AtomicLong() val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { // more threads than cores thread { go.await() repeat(2_000) { if (ledger.refund("pay-1", 1)) approved.incrementAndGet() } } } go.countDown() // the starting gun threads.forEach { it.join() } assertThat(approved.get()).isEqualTo(10_000L) // an invariant, not a timing assertThat(ledger.refunded("pay-1")).isEqualTo(10_000L) } JUnit, AssertJ and the latches work the same from both languages, and the Java version is already short for what it does. Kotlin trims the ceremony: thread { } starts a thread in one line, List(8) { ... } collects them, and with no checked exceptions there's no try and catch around go.await(). Two details differ. Backtick test names read like specs. And AssertJ needs 10_000L in Kotlin: assertThat(aLong).isEqualTo(10_000) would pass an Int, which picks the Object overload and fails, because a Long 10,000 isn't equal to an Integer 10,000. For coroutine code, Kotlin has a tool Java lacks: kotlinx-coroutines-test runs suspending code on virtual time, so tests of delays and timeouts run instantly and give the same result every run. The coroutines track covers it.

h: Testing and debugging concurrent code · Worked example
x: Turn a flaky "loads once" test into a deterministic one A cache keeps each answer from a slow web service, so the service is asked only once, like the caches in Concurrent collections. This test is meant to prove that PriceCache loads the price of bread once when eight callers ask together. Read it and decide what it actually tests. // Naive: tests the scheduler, not the cache @Test void loadsOnce() throws Exception { AtomicInteger loads = new AtomicInteger(); PriceCache cache = new PriceCache(item -> { loads.incrementAndGet(); return 250L; }); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) new Thread(() -> cache.priceOf("bread")).start(); Thread.sleep(100); // "they should be done by now" assertThat(loads.get()).isEqualTo(1); } // Naive: tests the scheduler, not the cache @Test fun `loads once`() { val loads = AtomicInteger() val cache = PriceCache { loads.incrementAndGet(); 250L } repeat(8) { thread { cache.priceOf("bread") } } Thread.sleep(100) // "they should be done by now" assertThat(loads.get()).isEqualTo(1) } It tests the scheduler. The loader is so fast that the threads rarely overlap, so a racy cache that checks with get and then stores with put passes too. And on a slow machine the threads might not have run at all within 100 ms, so loads is 0 and a correct cache fails. The fix is to control the timing: hold the first load inside the loader until every caller is known to be waiting, then let it go. Here's the deterministic version, with a label on each step. The loader blocks on a latch, and the test polls the thread states, with a deadline, until all eight callers are waiting. @Test @Timeout(10) void loadsOnceWhileOthersWait() throws Exception { AtomicInteger loads = new AtomicInteger(); CountDownLatch inLoader = new CountDownLatch(1), release = new CountDownLatch(1); PriceCache cache = new PriceCache(item -> { loads.incrementAndGet(); inLoader.countDown(); // 1. a caller is inside the loader try { release.await(); } // and stays there until we say go catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return 250L; }); List<Thread> callers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> cache.priceOf("bread")); When the test opens the latch, all eight loads finish, and loads is 8. With computeIfAbsent, one caller is inside the loader and the other seven are BLOCKED on the part of the map that holds that key, so loads is 1. x: Visibility, reordering, happens-before, volatile, safe publication and VarHandles. By the end of this track you can explain why one thread may never see a value that another thread wrote, and name the rule that makes a read safe. You can choose between volatile, an atomic and a lock for any shared field. You can hand an object to other threads so they never see it half-built, like a letter in a sealed envelope. You can build something on first use exactly once, like a stockroom opened for the first customer. And you can read the lighter memory modes, the labels on single reads and writes, without guessing. This is the rulebook under every concurrent class you use, and the reason "it passed on my machine" means so little. You need the first track, Threads and the bugs they cause: threads, race conditions, synchronized and atomics. Nothing else. Install JDK 25. The memory model, the rules for what one thread sees of another thread's writes, hasn't changed since Java 5 (JSR-133), so everything here holds from JDK 21 to JDK 27. When a lesson mentions a newer feature, it says which JDK. Every lesson has a lab in labs/jmm, in the package workbench.jmm.lNN. The labs are in Java, and every code sample and Try-it program also comes in Kotlin. The JIT may read a plain field once for a whole loop, and a processor's store buffer lets a later read overtake an earlier write. Neither is a bug: the memory model allows both. A read is guaranteed to see a write only through a happens-before edge: the same lock, the same volatile field, start, join, or a java.util.concurrent hand-over. Sleep is not an edge. volatile gives visibility and ordering for one variable, not an atomic read-modify-write. Use atomics or LongAdder for counters, and a lock or an immutable snapshot for several fields. Publishing an object is a write that can race. Seal the envelope: a volatile field, a static initializer, a final field or a java.util.concurrent hand-over. Prefer immutable objects, which survive any race. Final fields are seen as the constructor left them, but only if this didn't escape the constructor. Build first, wire up afterwards. Double-checked locking needs a volatile field. For statics the holder idiom is simpler, and Kotlin's by lazy is the same double check. A failed holder never retries. Access modes form a ladder: plain, opaque, acquire/release, volatile. Release/acquire hands data from one writer through one variable; only volatile gives one total order. Tests can't prove that nothing reorders. Both versions do the same three things: Java static boolean stop; // plain field Thread worker = new Thread(() -> { long spins = 0; while (!stop) { spins++; // stands in for one small job } System.out.println("worker saw stop"); }); worker.start(); Thread.sleep(1_000); stop = true; // main asks the worker to stop Kotlin var stop = false // plain property val worker = thread { var spins = 0L while (!stop) { spins++ // stands in for one small job } println("worker saw stop") } Thread.sleep(1_000) stop = true // main asks the worker to stop In Kotlin, thread { } creates the thread and starts it for us. In the demo, stop is a top-level var, which compiles to a plain static field, just like Java's. Before you read on, decide what you expect. I'd expect worker saw stop a moment after main sets the flag. Here's what StopFlagDemo, the same program in the labs, printed on JDK 25 (JDK 21 does the same): main set stop = true worker still running 3 s later? true The worker never stopped, and it wouldn't have stopped an hour later either. main wrote true, and the worker kept reading false. Nothing crashed and nothing complained. The worker just kept doing laps. Let's change one thing and run the same file with java -Xint. That flag turns off the JIT compiler (the just-in-time compiler). The JIT is the part of the JVM, the program that runs your Java code, that turns code which runs often into fast machine code while the program runs. Without it, the JVM's interpreter carries out the bytecode, the simple instructions that javac turns your code into, one at a time, slowly and literally: main set stop = true worker saw stop after 113,153,939 spins worker still running 3 s later? false The worker stopped at once. Same machine, same processor, same memory. Only the JIT changed, so that's where the bug lives. Here's what the JIT did. Once the loop had run many thousands of times, C2, the optimizing compiler inside HotSpot (the JVM in the standard JDK), compiled it. C2 saw that nothing in the loop writes stop or talks to other threads. So it read stop once, before the loop, kept the value in a register, and ran the rest as while (true). A register is a tiny storage slot inside a core, the part of the processor that runs one thread at a time. It's the fastest place a value can live. A picture helps here, and we'll build on it all lesson. The office whiteboard holds the numbers everyone shares: that's memory. Each clerk also keeps a notepad on the desk. To work with a number, a clerk copies it onto the notepad, because a glance down is quicker than a walk to the wall. A register is that notepad. The compiled loop copied "stop: no" onto its notepad once, and has read only the notepad ever since. Nobody else can write on it, so no change on the board will ever reach it. Whether, and when, one thread sees another thread's write is called visibility. The Java Memory Model (JMM), the part of the Java rules that settles it, promises visibility only when something links the two threads: a volatile field, a lock, Thread.join() and a few more you'll meet in the next lesson. A plain field has no link, so the compiler may assume that no other thread ever changes it. The fix is one word: Java static volatile boolean stop; Kotlin @Volatile var stop = false volatile is a keyword that marks a field as shared between threads. The JIT may not keep a volatile field on the notepad, so every pass of the loop reads it again. And the JMM promises that the write from main becomes visible to the loop. Kotlin's @Volatile annotation marks the compiled field volatile, so the bytecode is the same. A plain field shared between threads comes with no promise. Make it volatile, or link the threads some other way. The fix was easy. The odd part is that the JIT was allowed to break our loop at all, and that one print line would have hidden the damage. h: Why your loop never stops: caches and reordering · What the JIT may change: anything one thread alone can't notice
x: So why was C2 allowed to read stop only once? Every optimizer in the JVM follows one rule, often called as-if-serial: it may change your code in any way it likes, as long as a single thread running that code alone can't tell the difference. A kitchen makes the rule easy to picture. A waiter's ticket for one table says soup, then salad. The cook makes the salad first, because it takes one minute and the soup takes ten, and the table gets both dishes. The people at the table can't tell the difference. Only a waiter watching the pass, the shelf where finished plates wait, sees the salad come out first. The cook promised the dishes on the ticket, not the order in which they're made. In a program, the thread that runs the code is the table, and every other thread is the waiter at the pass. Reading stop once keeps the cook's promise. If no other thread existed, stop couldn't change during the loop, and the loop would behave exactly as written. Here is the change C2 is allowed to make, side by side: // what you wrote // what the compiled code may do while (!stop) { if (!stop) { spins++; while (true) { spins++; } } } Moving a read out of a loop like that is called hoisting. The same rule lets the JIT merge two writes to the same field into one, drop a write that nothing reads, or swap two writes to different fields. The thread that runs the code never notices. Another thread, reading those fields at the same time, can see every one of these changes. The kitchen picture stops at one point. A cook decides plate by plate. The JIT decides once, when it compiles the loop, and the core then repeats that choice billions of times. That's why the hang is permanent, not a delay. Now for the part that lets these bugs survive a code review, where teammates read each other's code before it ships. Put almost any method call inside the loop, and the hang usually goes away: Thread.sleep(10), a log line, Thread.yield(), even Thread.onSpinWait(). With Thread.yield(), a hint that the thread may give up its core for a moment, the demo stopped at once on JDK 25: worker saw stop after 3,603,541 spins C2 can't see inside a call like that, so it assumes the call might have changed any field, and it reads stop again afterwards. That's luck, not a promise. The Java Language Specification (JLS), the official rulebook of the language, says plainly that sleep and yield have no synchronization effect, meaning they link no threads. The compiler needn't even reload the values it keeps in registers after them. A later JDK might see inside more calls, or a teammate might swap the log line for a counter, and the hang comes back. A loop that has worked for two years is still broken. It just hasn't been compiled the wrong way yet. A loop that stops by luck is still broken. Look for the link between the threads, not for the symptom. So the JIT may rearrange our code, as long as one thread can't tell. Surely the processor, at least, runs exactly what it's given? Not quite, and that's where the office picture comes back. Hide the bug without fixing it In StopFlagDemo (either language), take volatile or @Volatile off again, so the flag is plain. Add Thread.yield() as the first line inside the while loop. Predict before you run: will the worker stop? Run the Gradle command from the previous Try it. The worker stops. Thread.yield() ends in a call into the JVM that the JIT can't see inside, so the compiled code reads stop again after each call. The program is still wrong by the JMM: nothing promises that second read. Undo the change and keep volatile.

h: Why your loop never stops: caches and reordering · Where the old value really lives: caches, store buffers and registers
x: Why the stop loop spins: the caches agree, the store buffer drains, the JIT keeps stop in a register The usual story about the stop flag goes like this: each core keeps its own copy of stop in its cache, that copy goes stale, and the worker reads it forever. A cache is a small, fast memory next to each core that keeps copies of recently used data. Main memory, the RAM, is about a hundred times slower. Each core has a small cache of its own, called L1, and the cores usually share a bigger one, often called L3. The cache is where most people look, and the -Xint run already proved it wrong: the caches were the same in both runs, and only one run hung. Let's add caches to the office and see why. Say each desk keeps a photocopy of the part of the whiteboard its clerk uses, so nobody has to walk to the wall. That's a cache. The office also has one strict rule: when anyone changes a number on the board, every photocopy of that number is crossed out at once, and the next look goes back to the board. Processors follow that rule in hardware, and it's called cache coherence. When one core writes a memory location, the other cores' copies are marked invalid or updated, usually within nanoseconds. No cache keeps an old value forever. The notepad has no such rule, which is why the compiled loop hung. The hardware does have one place where a write can wait: the store buffer. Picture an outbox tray on each desk. When a clerk has a new number for the board, she drops the note in her tray and goes on to her next task. A runner carries it to the board a moment later. If her next task is to read a different number from the board, she may read it before her own note arrives. To everyone else, her write and her read look swapped. A store buffer is that tray: a small queue inside each core where writes wait on their way to the cache, so the core can keep running. Here's the classic test for it. Two threads share two fields, x and y, which both start at 0: Java // thread A // thread B x = 1; y = 1; r1 = y; r2 = x; Kotlin // thread A // thread B x = 1 y = 1 r1 = y r2 = x Before you look at the result, play the four lines by hand. Mix the two threads any way you like, but keep each thread's two lines in their order. It's like shuffling two decks of cards together without changing the order inside either deck. Whichever thread reads second runs after the other thread's write, so at least one thread reads a 1. Both reading 0 should be impossible. ReorderDemo runs this test 524,288 times with plain fields, then again with volatile fields. One run on a 4-core machine printed: run 1: both read 0 in 240,989 trials with plain fields, 0 with volatile fields (of 524,288) run 2: both read 0 in 225,261 trials with plain fields, 0 with volatile fields (of 524,288) run 3: both read 0 in 171,281 trials with plain fields, 0 with volatile fields (of 524,288) The impossible result came up in a third to nearly half of the trials. Each thread's write was still in its own tray when it read the other field. With both fields volatile, it never happened. The JMM forbids that result for volatile fields, so on x86 processors HotSpot follows each volatile write with an instruction that empties the store buffer before any later read. So here is the office as it stands. The photocopies, the caches, always agree within nanoseconds. The outbox tray, the store buffer, holds a write for a few nanoseconds and then always delivers it. The notepad, the register, can hold an old value forever, but only because the JIT chose to work from it. The picture breaks in one place: in the office, each clerk decides where to look. In the machine, the JIT chose the notepad once, when it compiled the loop, and the core never looks up again. Processors also differ in how much they reorder. x86 processors, the kind in most laptops and servers, only let a later read pass an earlier write, as in the test above. ARM processors, which run phones, Apple Silicon Macs and many cloud servers, also let reads pass reads and writes pass writes. Code that never fails on an x86 laptop can fail on an ARM server. The JIT and the processor have both rearranged our code now. Do you need to know what each of them does, on every machine, to write correct code? Happily, no. Catch the processor reordering Read ReorderDemo (either language). It runs the two-thread test above 524,288 times with plain fields, then with volatile fields. Run it with the Gradle command below and note the counts. Run the Java file in the interpreter: java -Xint jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l01/ReorderDemo.java (from labs/). Predict first: the JIT is off now, so will the plain count drop to zero? ReorderDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l01; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.IntConsumer; /** * The store-buffering test. Thread A runs {@code x = 1; r1 = y;} and thread B runs {@code y = 1; r2 = x;}. * If the four lines ran in any order that keeps each thread's two lines in program order, * at least one thread would read a 1. Count the trials where both threads read 0. */ public class ReorderDemo { static final class Plain { int x, y; } static final class Volatile { volatile int x, y; } static final int TRIALS = 1 << 19; static final int BATCH = 32; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int run = 1; run <= 3; run++) { System.out.printf("run %d: both read 0 in %,7d trials with plain fields, %,d with volatile fields (of %,d)%n", run, plain(), withVolatile(), TRIALS); } } static int plain() throws InterruptedException { Plain[] s = new Plain[TRIALS]; for (int i = 0; i < TRIALS; i++) s[i] = new Plain(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y; }, i -> { s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x; }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } static int withVolatile() throws InterruptedException { Volatile[] s = new Volatile[TRIALS]; for (int i = 0; i < TRIALS; i++) s[i] = new Volatile(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y; }, i -> { s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x; }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } // Runs a(i) and b(i) for every trial on two threads. A small spin barrier every BATCH trials // keeps the two threads on the same trial at about the same moment. static void race(IntConsumer a, IntConsumer b) throws InterruptedException { AtomicInteger doneA = new AtomicInteger(), doneB = new AtomicInteger(); Thread ta = new Thread(() -> runSide(a, doneA, doneB)); Thread tb = new Thread(() -> runSide(b, doneB, doneA)); ta.start(); tb.start(); ta.join(); tb.join(); } static void runSide(IntConsumer side, AtomicInteger mine, AtomicInteger other) { for (int batch = 0; batch < TRIALS / BATCH; batch++) { mine.set(batch); while (other.get() < batch) Thread.onSpinWait(); // wait for the other thread for (int i = batch * BATCH; i < (batch + 1) * BATCH; i++) side.accept(i); } } static int bothZero(int[] r1, int[] r2) { int n = 0; for (int i = 0; i < r1.length; i++) if (r1[i] == 0 && r2[i] == 0) n++; return n; } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l01.ReorderDemo labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l01/ReorderDemo.java ReorderDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l01 import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.function.IntConsumer import kotlin.concurrent.thread /* * The store-buffering test. Thread A runs `x = 1; r1 = y` and thread B runs `y = 1; r2 = x`. * If the four lines ran in any order that keeps each thread's two lines in program order, * at least one thread would read a 1. Count the trials where both threads read 0. */ private class PlainPair { var x = 0; var y = 0 } private class VolatilePair { @Volatile var x = 0; @Volatile var y = 0 } private const val TRIALS = 1 shl 19 private const val BATCH = 32 fun main() { for (run in 1..3) { println("run %d: both read 0 in %,7d trials with plain fields, %,d with @Volatile fields (of %,d)" .format(run, plain(), withVolatile(), TRIALS)) } } private fun plain(): Int { val s = Array(TRIALS) { PlainPair() } val r1 = IntArray(TRIALS) val r2 = IntArray(TRIALS) race(IntConsumer { i -> s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y }, IntConsumer { i -> s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x }) return bothZero(r1, r2) } private fun withVolatile(): Int { val s = Array(TRIALS) { VolatilePair() } val r1 = IntArray(TRIALS) val r2 = IntArray(TRIALS) race(IntConsumer { i -> s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y }, IntConsumer { i -> s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x }) return bothZero(r1, r2) } // Runs a(i) and b(i) for every trial on two threads. A small spin barrier every BATCH trials // keeps the two threads on the same trial at about the same moment. private fun race(a: IntConsumer, b: IntConsumer) { val doneA = AtomicInteger() val doneB = AtomicInteger() val ta = thread { runSide(a, doneA, doneB) } val tb = thread { runSide(b, doneB, doneA) } ta.join(); tb.join() } private fun runSide(side: IntConsumer, mine: AtomicInteger, other: AtomicInteger) { for (batch in 0 until TRIALS / BATCH) { mine.set(batch) while (other.get() < batch) Thread.onSpinWait() // wait for the other thread for (i in batch * BATCH until (batch + 1) * BATCH) side.accept(i) } } private fun bothZero(r1: IntArray, r2: IntArray): Int = r1.indices.count { r1[it] == 0 && r2[it] == 0 } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l01.ReorderDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l01/ReorderDemo.kt With plain fields, a large share of trials see both reads return 0 (runs here showed between about 150,000 and 290,000 of 524,288, a different number every run). With volatile fields, the count is 0 every time. Under -Xint, the plain count drops but stays well above zero (44,000 to 110,000 here). The interpreter doesn't reorder anything, so those trials come from the store buffer, not the compiler. Coherent caches (the photocopies) carry the write to every core within nanoseconds. The worker still spins, because its compiled loop reads a register, its notepad. The store buffer, the outbox, only delays a write for nanoseconds. jcstress sample BasicJMM_07_Consensus: the store-buffering test with plain, volatile and acquire/release read

h: Why your loop never stops: caches and reordering · Three layers that reorder your code, and the one contract above them
x: Three layers stand between the code you write and what other threads observe: javac, the Java compiler, barely changes the order. It turns statements into bytecode almost one for one. The JIT hoists reads out of loops, merges and drops writes, and swaps independent reads and writes. (HotSpot has two JIT compilers: C1 for code that runs often, and C2 for code that runs very often.) The processor runs ahead through its store buffers, and ARM processors reorder more freely still. Each layer follows the as-if-serial rule, so a single thread never notices. You can't control which layer does what, and you don't need to. The JMM is a contract that sits above all three. Think of it as the office rulebook: it says when a clerk is promised to see a colleague's note, whatever the desks and trays look like. The contract names the operations that link threads: reads and writes of volatile fields, taking and releasing a lock, starting a thread and waiting for it with join(), and the classes in java.util.concurrent, the JDK's package of concurrency tools. Link every read of shared data to the write it needs, and your program behaves as if its lines ran one at a time, in the shuffled-decks order. That property is called sequential consistency, and the next lesson shows how the links work. If you skip the links, you have a data race: two threads use the same variable, at least one of them writes it, and nothing links the two. Then the promises mostly go away. A thread can see an old value forever, or see a write without an earlier write that came before it. For long and double fields, it can even see half of one write and half of another. Data races are why "it works on my machine" means so little here. Your test ran on one kind of processor, with one JIT, on a quiet day. A different JDK, a busier server or an ARM machine can show a reordering your tests never saw. Take a sample from jcstress, the tool from Testing and debugging that runs tiny tests millions of times. One thread writes x and then y, with the compiler told to keep that order, and another thread reads y and then x. On x86, seeing the new y with the old x never happened. On a 64-bit ARM machine, it happened in 0.68% of the samples. Both results obey the same JMM. Write to the contract, and the hardware becomes someone else's problem. Your laptop doesn't decide what's correct; the memory model does. Write to the model. Check yourself: you run StopFlagDemo with -Xint on an ARM laptop, which reorders more than x86. Does the worker stop? It does. The interpreter reads stop from memory on every pass, and coherence brings the new value to the worker's core. ARM's extra freedom only changes the order in which writes to different fields become visible, and each write still arrives. The plain field is still a data race, though, so the fix stays volatile. We've seen one link, volatile, fix one loop. The rulebook has a whole chapter of them, and the next lesson reads it.

h: Why your loop never stops: caches and reordering · Java and Kotlin
x: A stop flag in Java and Kotlin ReceiptPrinter.java public class ReceiptPrinter implements Runnable { private volatile boolean running = true; @Override public void run() { while (running) { printNextReceipt(); } } public void stop() { running = false; } } ReceiptPrinter.kt class ReceiptPrinter : Runnable { @Volatile private var running = true override fun run() { while (running) { printNextReceipt() } } fun stop() { running = false } } Both classes are the same stop flag, and the Kotlin one is a direct translation. Kotlin has no volatile keyword. You put @Volatile on a var property, and the compiler marks its backing field (the JVM field that holds the value) volatile, so the bytecode matches the Java version. A val can't be @Volatile, because it's never written after construction. A plain Kotlin var has exactly the same bug as a plain Java field: while (running) compiles to a field read that the JIT can hoist. AtomicBoolean from java.util.concurrent.atomic works the same from both languages.

h: Why your loop never stops: caches and reordering · Worked example
x: Find the two flags that freeze a backup printer A shop's program has a backup helper that prints receipts only when the main printer breaks. A thread that watches the main printer calls takeOver() when it fails. When the program quits, a shutdown thread calls stop(). In a test, the main printer was unplugged. The backup was told to take over, printed nothing, and then ignored the request to quit as well. Find the shared state before you read on. class BackupPrinter implements Runnable { private boolean onDuty; // 1. written by the thread that watches the main printer private boolean running = true; // 2. written by the shutdown thread @Override public void run() { while (running) { // 3. both flags read in a busy loop if (onDuty) printNext(); } } void takeOver() { onDuty = true; } void stop() { running = false; } } class BackupPrinter : Runnable { private var onDuty = false // 1. written by the thread that watches the main printer private var running = true // 2. written by the shutdown thread override fun run() { while (running) { // 3. both flags read in a busy loop if (onDuty) printNext() } } fun takeOver() { onDuty = true } fun stop() { running = false } } Both flags are written by one thread and read by another, and nothing links them. While the main printer works, onDuty stays false for hours. The JIT keeps a profile, a record of which branches the running code takes. It sees that printNext() never runs, and compiles the loop as if that branch weren't there. What's left is two reads of plain fields that nothing in the loop writes, so it reads each one once. A copy of this class, run for this lesson on JDK 21 and on JDK 25, printed 0 receipts in the second after takeOver(). It was still spinning 3 seconds after stop(). Make both flags volatile. Then stop the backup from spinning: while it has nothing to do, it can sleep between checks and leave the core to other work. class BackupPrinter implements Runnable { private volatile boolean onDuty; // 1. both flags cross threads: both volatile private volatile boolean running = true; @Override public void run() { try { while (running) { // 2. read again on every pass if (onDuty) { printNext(); } else { Thread.sleep(50); // 3. a backup on standby doesn't need a whole core } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // 4. treat an interrupt as a stop, too } } void takeOver() { onDuty = true; } void stop() { running = false; } } class BackupPrinter : Runnable { @Volatile private var onDuty = false // 1. both flags cross threads: both @Volatile @Volatile private var running = true override fun run() { try { while (running) { // 2. read again on every pass if (onDuty) { printNext() } else { Thread.sleep(50) // 3. a backup on standby doesn't need a whole core } } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // 4. treat an interrupt as a stop, too } } fun takeOver() { onDuty = true } fun stop() { running = false } } The sleep alone would also have hidden the hang, because HotSpot reads fields again after it. That's exactly why the volatile stays. The sleep is there to save the processor's time. The volatile is there for correctness, and it keeps working after the next change to the loop.

What's left is the hardware: a write waits in the store buffer while the next read goes ahead. A volatile write empties the buffer first, which is why the volatile count is 0. A stop-flag loop hangs with the JIT on and stops under -Xint. What is the best explanation? The compiled loop read the field once and keeps using a register copy The worker's CPU cache never receives the new value The interpreter runs on a single core, so there is no second cache The main thread's write is still sitting in its store buffer Caches and store buffers are the same in both runs, so they can't explain the difference. Only the JIT changes. C2 hoisted the read out of the loop, which as-if-serial allows for a plain field. A store buffer empties within nanoseconds, so it can't cause a hang.
