h: Why your loop never stops: caches and reordering · Key terms
x: Visibility Whether and when a write by one thread can be seen by a read in another thread. Register A tiny storage slot inside a processor core. Compiled code works on values there; other threads can't see it. Hoisting The JIT moving a read out of a loop because it believes the value can't change inside the loop. Store buffer A per-core queue of pending writes. It lets the core keep running before its writes reach the cache. Cache coherence The hardware rule that keeps every core's cache in agreement about each memory location. As-if-serial Optimizers may change anything that a single thread running alone can't observe. Data race Two threads access the same variable, at least one writes it, and nothing orders the two accesses. volatile A field modifier: every read sees the latest write, and its reads and writes link threads in the memory model. Why can while (!stop) {} spin forever when stop is a plain boolean? The JIT may read stop once, keep it in a register and compile the loop to while (true). Nothing tells it that another thread writes the field. The stop-flag hang disappears under java -Xint. What does that prove? The hang comes from the compiler. The interpreter reads the field on every pass, and the caches are the same in both runs. Can a CPU cache hold an old value forever while another core writes it? No. Caches are coherent: a write invalidates or updates the other cores' copies, usually within nanoseconds. What is a store buffer? A small queue where a core parks its writes on the way to the cache. The core's later reads can finish before those writes are visible to other cores. Thread A: x = 1; r1 = y; Thread B: y = 1; r2 = x; Plain ints, both start at 0. Can r1 == 0 && r2 == 0? Yes, through store buffers or JIT reordering. With both fields volatile, no. Does adding Thread.sleep or a log line to a spin loop fix a plain stop flag? No. It hides the bug on today's HotSpot, because the JIT reads fields again after calls it can't see inside. The JMM promises nothing. Use volatile. What is the as-if-serial rule? Compilers and processors may reorder or remove work as long as a single thread running alone can't tell the difference.

h: Why your loop never stops: caches and reordering · Go deeper
x: volatile is the usual fix, but it does more than this loop needs. The weakest tool that already promises the loop will end is opaque access (getOpaque and setOpaque, JDK 9 and later). It goes through a VarHandle, an object that reads and writes a field with a strength you choose. The jcstress sample BasicJMM_04_Progress makes the point. For the plain spin loop, "Test is stuck" is listed as an allowed result. The volatile spin loop finished in every one of the 17,882 runs the sample records. For the opaque spin loop, getting stuck is marked forbidden. Opaque stops the compiler from keeping the read on its notepad and leaves the rest to the hardware, which makes every write visible sooner or later. It doesn't order other fields, which is why it's rarely what you want. VarHandles and memory ordering modes, the last lesson of this track, covers the modes. The sample BasicJMM_06_Causality is the cleanest look at hardware differences. One thread writes x = 1 then y = 1, and another reads y then x. With plain fields, the sample's recorded run saw y == 1 but x == 0 in 0.09% of samples. With opaque accesses, which keep the compiler from reordering, x86 showed it 0 times, because x86 keeps writes in order. A 64-bit ARM machine still showed it in 0.68% of samples. Make y volatile and that result is forbidden on every platform. If you want the long version of why the JMM is written as a contract about whole runs of a program, read Aleksey Shipilëv's "Java Memory Model Pragmatics". It is long, and worth one slow evening.

h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · Happens-before: a promise about what a read will see, not about when
x: Remember the stop flag. main wrote true one second into the run, and three seconds later the worker was still reading false. On the clock, the write came first by a wide margin, and it made no difference. The memory model answers one question: when is a read in one thread sure to see a write from another? The documentation of java.util.concurrent, the JDK's package of concurrency tools, gives the answer in one sentence: "The results of a write by one thread are guaranteed to be visible to a read by another thread only if the write operation happens-before the read operation." Happens-before is a relation between two actions, such as a write of a field and a read of it. If the write happens-before the read, and no other write to that field races in, the read sees that value. If nothing orders the two, the read may see the new value, an old one, or, as with the stop flag, never the new one at all. Whether a thread sees another thread's write is called visibility, and happens-before is the only thing that promises it. In the bank, happens-before is the promise of the locked cabinet. The cashier's writes come before she locks it, and the night manager's reads come after she opens it with the same key. Locking and opening link the two. The picture breaks in one place: nothing is carried anywhere. Both threads look at the same memory all the time, and without a handover a reader often does see the write. It just has no promise that it will, and the JIT, the part of the JVM that compiles busy code while it runs, is free to make sure it doesn't. The name misleads people, so let's be clear: happens-before is not about the clock. A write can run a full second before a read and still not happen-before it. That was the stop flag. The first rule is one you've always relied on. Inside one thread, each action happens-before every later action of that same thread. This is program order, and it's why code on one thread reads as written. The other rules link different threads, and the next sections take them one at a time. Chain them together and you have a proof that a particular read sees a particular write. When two threads use the same field, at least one of them writes it, and no chain of happens-before orders the two, the program has a data race. Data races are what the JMM, the Java Memory Model, is really about. Its main promise has a clumsy name, DRF-SC, short for "data-race-free programs are sequentially consistent". A program with no data races behaves as if its threads' lines were shuffled together like two decks of cards, each deck keeping its own order: the shuffled-decks order from the last lesson. You can reason about it the way you did in the simulator in Race conditions. A program with a data race gets very few promises beyond that. So the working method is short. For every field that two threads share, name the handover between the write and the read. If you can't name one, you have a race. A later read is not a promised read. Name the handover, or call it a race. Check yourself: T1 sets a plain balance = 12_000 at 10:00:00. T2 reads balance a full second later, with no lock and no volatile on either side. Is T2 sure to see 12,000? No. A second on the clock is not a handover, and you can't name a rule that links the write to the read. That makes it a data race, and the old balance is a legal result. So the promise comes from handovers. The two you'll use most are a lock and a volatile field, and both come with one word in the fine print: same.

h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · The same lock or the same field: the two handovers you'll use most
x: Only the same lock or the same volatile field links two threads: a reader that locks its own object never sees the balance A lock links threads, and so does a volatile field. Both come with a condition. The lock rule first. Every Java object carries a lock, called its monitor, which synchronized takes and releases. The rule: releasing a lock happens-before every later acquisition of the same lock. Leaving a synchronized block or method releases the monitor, and entering one acquires it. Add program order on both sides, and everything T1 did before leaving synchronized (lock) is visible to T2 once it enters synchronized (lock). That's the bank's cabinet: lock it, and whoever opens it with the same key finds everything inside. Now the volatile rule. A volatile field is one whose every read sees the latest write, as the stop flag showed. The rule: a write to a volatile field happens-before every later read of that same field, where "later" means the read sees that write or a newer one. Picture a sign the cashier hangs on the cabinet when she's done: "ledger closed". Anyone who reads the sign and sees "closed" is promised everything she wrote before hanging it. Unlike the key, the sign makes nobody wait, and any number of people can read it at once. A volatile field works like a lock without the waiting. The Java Language Specification (JLS), the official rulebook of the language, calls the start of such a link a release and the end of it an acquire. Leaving a monitor and writing a volatile are releases. Entering a monitor and reading a volatile are acquires. Every class in java.util.concurrent is built on the same pair. Both rules contain the word same, and that's where the bugs are: Java synchronized (ledgerLock) { balance = 12_000; } // T1 releases ledgerLock synchronized (reportLock) { seen = balance; } // T2 acquires reportLock: no link Kotlin synchronized(ledgerLock) { balance = 12_000 } // T1 releases ledgerLock synchronized(reportLock) { seen = balance } // T2 acquires reportLock: no link Two different locks each keep two threads out of the same block, and give no link between those threads. Volatile fields work the same way: a write to a volatile version and a read of a volatile checksum link nothing. That's a sign on one cabinet and a reader looking at another. The most common shape of this bug is the half-locked class: a synchronized setter and a plain getter. The writer releases the lock, and the reader never acquires it, so there's nothing to pair with. LedgerTotals in the lab is that class. One more: synchronized (new Object()) does nothing for other threads. No other thread can ever get hold of that object, so no other thread can take its lock, and no link can form. HotSpot notices too. Its escape analysis, a check that proves an object never leaves the code that made it, removes the lock entirely, and the read inside becomes a plain read. A lock nobody else can take is just ceremony. LockScopeDemo puts both kinds of reader to the test. A writer sets balance inside synchronized (LEDGER_LOCK). By default, the reader locks a brand-new object on every pass; with -Pargs=shared, it locks LEDGER_LOCK, the same lock the writer used. The two runs printed: writer set balance = 12000 inside synchronized (LEDGER_LOCK) reader still spinning 3 s later? true writer set balance = 12000 inside synchronized (LEDGER_LOCK) reader (LEDGER_LOCK) saw balance = 12000 reader still spinning 3 s later? false The reader with its own lock spun forever, just like the stop flag. The reader with the shared lock saw the balance at once. Same field, same loop, and only the lock changed. A lock or a volatile field links only the threads that use the same one. Check both sides. Locks and volatile fields link threads that are already running. Two more handovers link a thread to the thread that started it. Same lock or own lock Read LockScopeDemo (either language). The writer sets balance inside synchronized (LEDGER_LOCK). By default, the reader locks a fresh new Object() (Any() in Kotlin) on every pass. Run it with the Gradle command below, and check that you get the first output above. Run it again with -Pargs=shared added to the command, so the reader locks LEDGER_LOCK too. Now go back to the default reader, but make balance a volatile field (@Volatile in Kotlin). Predict first: will the reader with its own useless lock see the balance now? LockScopeDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l02; /** A writer sets a balance inside a lock. A reader spins until it sees it. Which lock does the reader need? */ public class LockScopeDemo { static final Object LEDGER_LOCK = new Object(); static long balance; // meant to be guarded by LEDGER_LOCK public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean shared = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("shared"); Thread reader = new Thread(shared ? LockScopeDemo::readWithLedgerLock : LockScopeDemo::readWithOwnLock); reader.setDaemon(true); // so the JVM can exit even if the reader never stops reader.start(); Thread.sleep(500); // let the JIT compile the reader's loop synchronized (LEDGER_LOCK) { balance = 12_000; // cents } System.out.println("writer set balance = 12000 inside synchronized (LEDGER_LOCK)"); reader.join(3_000); System.out.println("reader still spinning 3 s later? " + reader.isAlive()); } static void readWithOwnLock() { long seen; do { synchronized (new Object()) { // a lock no other thread can ever take seen = balance; } } while (seen == 0); System.out.println("reader (own lock) saw balance = " + seen); } static void readWithLedgerLock() { long seen; do { synchronized (LEDGER_LOCK) { // the same monitor the writer released seen = balance; } } while (seen == 0); System.out.println("reader (LEDGER_LOCK) saw balance = " + seen); } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l02.LockScopeDemo labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l02/LockScopeDemo.java LockScopeDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l02 import kotlin.concurrent.thread private val LEDGER_LOCK = Any() private var balance = 0L // meant to be guarded by LEDGER_LOCK /** A writer sets a balance inside a lock. A reader spins until it sees it. Which lock does the reader need? */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val shared = args.firstOrNull() == "shared" // daemon, so the JVM can exit even if the reader never stops val reader = thread(isDaemon = true) { if (shared) readWithLedgerLock() else readWithOwnLock() } Thread.sleep(500) // let the JIT compile the reader's loop synchronized(LEDGER_LOCK) { balance = 12_000 // cents } println("writer set balance = 12000 inside synchronized(LEDGER_LOCK)") reader.join(3_000) println("reader still spinning 3 s later? ${reader.isAlive}") } private fun readWithOwnLock() { var seen: Long do { seen = synchronized(Any()) { balance } // a lock no other thread can ever take } while (seen == 0L) println("reader (own lock) saw balance = $seen") } private fun readWithLedgerLock() { var seen: Long do { seen = synchronized(LEDGER_LOCK) { balance } // the same monitor the writer released } while (seen == 0L) println("reader (LEDGER_LOCK) saw balance = $seen") } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l02.LockScopeDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l02/LockScopeDemo.kt With its own lock, the reader is still spinning 3 seconds later: there's no link, the JIT removes the useless lock and reads balance once. With -Pargs=shared, the reader prints balance = 12000 right after the writer, because the writer releases and the reader acquires the same monitor. With a volatile balance, the own-lock reader sees 12000 too. The lock still links nothing, but the volatile write and read of the same field are a handover of their own. Leaving the synchronized block releases LEDGER_LOCK, and entering one in T2 acquires the same lock. Program order on both sides stretches the promise to every write before the release and every read after the acquire.

h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · Starting and joining a thread are handovers; sleeping is not
x: Picture the bank hiring a helper for one evening. Everything the manager tells the helper before the shift starts, the helper knows. And when the manager waits at the door until the helper finishes and walks out, she knows everything the helper did. Threads have the same two handovers. Thread.start() happens-before every action in the started thread. Whatever the parent wrote before calling start() (settings, a list of work, the variables a lambda captured) the new thread sees. Every action in a thread happens-before another thread returns from join() on it. The same holds when another thread sees isAlive() return false. After join() returns, the parent sees every result the worker wrote, even into plain fields and plain arrays. That's why the threads track could read results after join() without a second thought. A third rule matters for stopping threads. When T1 calls t2.interrupt(), that call happens-before any thread notices the interrupt through isInterrupted(), Thread.interrupted() or an InterruptedException. Thread.sleep() has none of this. SleepIsNotJoinDemo starts a worker that adds up the day's sales of 20 shops, one slow call of about 10 ms per shop, and then writes the total. main sleeps 50 ms and reads it: after sleep(50): total = 0 (expected 2,000,000) Fifty milliseconds felt like plenty to main. The worker needed two hundred. So the sleep didn't wait for the worker to finish. Even if the worker had finished in time, the sleep would create no link, so an old value would still be a legal read. A sleep long enough to "always work" passes on your laptop and fails on a busy build server, the shared machine that runs everyone's tests. The fix is to wait for the worker itself: Java Thread worker = new Thread(() -> { /* adds up the 20 shops */ }); worker.start(); worker.join(); // waits for the worker to end, and links its writes to us System.out.println(total); // 2,000,000, every time Kotlin val worker = thread { /* adds up the 20 shops */ } // thread {} calls start() for you worker.join() // waits for the worker to end, and links its writes to us println(total) // 2,000,000, every time The start link covers only the writes made before start(). Here a printer thread reads settings that are loaded one line too late: Java Thread printer = new Thread(() -> print(settings.paperSize())); printer.start(); settings = loadSettings(); // after start(): no link to the printer thread Kotlin val printer = thread { print(settings.paperSize) } // thread {} calls start() for you settings = loadSettings() // after start(): no link to the printer thread The printer thread may see settings as null or as the old value. This case comes back in lesson 4 of this track, where a constructor starts a thread before it has finished setting its own fields. A sleep passes time and promises nothing. Wait with join(), or with another handover. Each handover so far links one write to one read, or so it seems. In fact, one handover can carry a whole bundle of writes. Replace a sleep with a join Read SleepIsNotJoinDemo (either language). The worker makes 20 calls of about 10 ms each, then writes total. Predict what main prints. Run it with the Gradle command below. Replace Thread.sleep(50) with worker.join() and run it again. Think it through: would Thread.sleep(5_000) be a correct fix? Which rule would it be missing? SleepIsNotJoinDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l02; /** main starts a worker that adds up the day's sales of 20 shops, then sleeps and reads the total. */ public class SleepIsNotJoinDemo { static long total; // written by the worker, read by main public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread worker = new Thread(() -> { long sum = 0; for (int shop = 0; shop < 20; shop++) { sum += fetchShopTotal(shop); // each call takes about 10 ms } total = sum; }); worker.start(); Thread.sleep(50); // "plenty of time" System.out.printf("after sleep(50): total = %,d (expected %,d)%n", total, 20 * 100_000L); } // stands in for a slow call that fetches one shop's total for the day static long fetchShopTotal(int shop) { try { Thread.sleep(10); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return 100_000; } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l02.SleepIsNotJoinDemo labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l02/SleepIsNotJoinDemo.java SleepIsNotJoinDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l02 import kotlin.concurrent.thread private var total = 0L // written by the worker, read by main /** main starts a worker that adds up the day's sales of 20 shops, then sleeps and reads the total. */ fun main() { val worker = thread { var sum = 0L for (shop in 0 until 20) { sum += fetchShopTotal(shop) // each call takes about 10 ms } total = sum } Thread.sleep(50) // "plenty of time" println("after sleep(50): total = %,d (expected %,d)".format(total, 20 * 100_000L)) } // stands in for a slow call that fetches one shop's total for the day private fun fetchShopTotal(@Suppress("UNUSED_PARAMETER") shop: Int): Long { Thread.sleep(10) return 100_000 } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l02.SleepIsNotJoinDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l02/SleepIsNotJoinDemo.kt The first run prints total = 0: the worker is only about a quarter of the way through. With join() it prints 2,000,000 every time, because join() waits for the worker to end, and its handover makes the write visible. A 5-second sleep would print the right number on a quiet machine, but it's still a data race: no rule links the worker's write to the read in main.

h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · Promises chain: one handover carries every write made before it
x: The cashier writes many pages before she locks the cabinet, and the night manager can trust every one of them. Happens-before works the same way, because its links chain. If A happens-before B, and B happens-before C, then A happens-before C. That property is called transitivity, and it's why one lock or one volatile field can protect many plain fields. Here's the board of exchange rates from the last lesson's lab, with each step labeled: Java // loader thread // request thread rates = Map.copyOf(loaded); // A while (!ready) { } // C: sees true ready = true; // B Map<String, Long> r = rates; // D Kotlin // loader thread // request thread rates = loaded.toMap() // A while (!ready) { } // C: sees true ready = true // B val r = rates // D ready is volatile and rates is plain. A comes before B in program order. B is a volatile write, and C is a volatile read that sees it. C comes before D in program order. So A happens-before D, and the request thread sees the whole map, though rates is a plain field. This is often called piggybacking: the plain write rides along on the volatile one. Two conditions are easy to miss. The plain writes must come before the release. If the loader wrote rates after setting ready, no link would cover it, just as a page written after the cabinet is locked isn't promised to anyone. And the reader gets the link only when its acquire actually sees the release. If C reads false and the code goes on to read rates anyway, nothing is promised. You rarely need to build these chains by hand. java.util.concurrent writes down its own handovers in its documentation, under "Memory Consistency Properties". Among them: putting an object into any concurrent collection (one built for many threads, such as ConcurrentHashMap or a BlockingQueue) happens-before another thread gets or removes it; handing a task to an executor, an object that runs tasks on threads of its own, happens-before the task starts; whatever a task does happens-before Future.get() returns its result in another thread (a Future stands for the result of a task that may not have finished yet); countDown(), release() and unlock() happen-before a successful await(), acquire() or lock() on the same object in another thread. The kitchen in Don't share relied on the first of these. Everything a waiter wrote on a ticket before put was visible to the cook after take. The ticket needed no volatile fields, as long as the waiter stopped writing on it after put. Prefer these ready-made handovers to flags of your own. A CountDownLatch, the gate from Synchronizers that opens when its count reaches zero, waits without spinning, answers interrupts, and its handover is written down in its documentation. Write everything before the handover, and read it after. Then one handover covers it all. Every handover we've met either makes someone wait (a lock, join(), a latch) or uses a volatile field, which makes nobody wait. That makes volatile look like the cheap tool for every job. How far it really goes is a question for the next lesson. Name the handover For each snippet, name the happens-before handover that makes the last read safe, or write "none". (a) order.setTotal(500); executor.submit(() -> pack(order)); and the task reads order.total(). (b) queue.put(ticket); ticket.setNote("no onions"); and the cook calls queue.take().note(). (c) T1: x = 1; v = 1; T2: if (w == 1) print(x); where v and w are two different volatile fields. (d) T1: synchronized (ledger) { total += 5; } T2: synchronized (ledger) { print(total); }. (a) Handing the task to the executor: writes before submit happen-before the task starts. (b) None for the note: setNote runs after put, so the cook may see the old value. (c) None: the volatile write and the volatile read are on different fields. (d) The lock rule on ledger, as long as T1's block ran first. java.util.concurrent package docs, "Memory Consistency Properties" (JDK 25 source) docs

h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · Java and Kotlin
x: The same lock on both sides, in Java and Kotlin LedgerTotals.java public class LedgerTotals { private long total; // guarded by this public synchronized void add(long cents) { total += cents; } // hb: the release at the end of add() pairs with the acquire here public synchronized long total() { return total; } } LedgerTotals.kt class LedgerTotals { private val lock = Any() private var totalCents = 0L // guarded by lock fun add(cents: Long) { synchronized(lock) { totalCents += cents } } // hb: same lock object on both sides fun total(): Long = synchronized(lock) { totalCents } } Both classes take the same lock to write and to read, so every total() sees every add() that came before it. Kotlin's synchronized(lock) { } is a function from the standard library, not a keyword. It is inlined, which means its body is copied into the caller. It compiles to the same monitor enter and exit bytecode as a Java synchronized block, so it creates exactly the same links. Kotlin code often locks a private val lock = Any() instead of this, which keeps outside code from taking your lock. Both languages offer locked methods on this too: Java's synchronized modifier and Kotlin's @Synchronized. CountDownLatch, executors and Future.get() give the same handovers from either language.

h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · Worked example
x: Find the missing handover when an order goes to a pool A shop's website takes orders. A receiving thread builds an Order object for each one. It hands the order to a pool of packing threads through an executor, an object that runs tasks on threads of its own. Then, for timing, it notes when the order arrived. The packers log how long each order waited, and about one log line in a thousand says receivedAt=null. List each write, each read, and the thread that makes it. void onOrder(String text) { // the receiving thread Order order = Order.parse(text); // 1. build a changeable object packers.submit(() -> pack(order)); // 2. hand it to a pool thread order.setReceivedAt(Instant.now()); // 3. one more write, after the handover } fun onOrder(text: String) { // the receiving thread val order = Order.parse(text) // 1. build a changeable object packers.execute { pack(order) } // 2. hand it to a pool thread order.receivedAt = Instant.now() // 3. one more write, after the handover } Draw the links. The writes in step 1 come before submit in program order, and submit happens-before the task starts, so the packer sees them. The write in step 3 comes after submit, and nothing links it to the packer. The packer's read of receivedAt is a data race. It usually reads the new value, because the task starts a little later, which is why it fails only now and then. Put every write before the release, and stop touching the object after it. Then the one handover covers all of it. void onOrder(String text) { Order order = Order.parse(text); order.setReceivedAt(Instant.now()); // 1. every write happens before the release packers.submit(() -> pack(order)); // 2. submit carries them all to the packer // 3. no writes to order after this line } fun onOrder(text: String) { val order = Order.parse(text) order.receivedAt = Instant.now() // 1. every write happens before the release packers.execute { pack(order) } // 2. the handover carries them all to the packer // 3. no writes to order after this line } If the receiving thread needs the packer's answer, Future.get() is the handover back: everything the task did happens-before get() returns. No field in Order or in the answer needs to be volatile. Better still, build the order once with all its fields, as a record (Java's class for plain data that never changes) or a Kotlin data class with only val properties. Then the question of later writes can't come up. Future<Label> f = packers.submit(() -> pack(order)); Label label = f.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // hb: the task's actions happen-before get() returns val f: Future<Label> = packers.submit(Callable { pack(order) }) val label = f.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // hb: the task's actions happen-before get() returns

h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · Lab
x: Name the handover, then fix three of them labs/jmm/src/main/java/workbench/jmm/l02/LedgerTotals.java labs/jmm/src/main/java/workbench/jmm/l02/IssuerReply.java labs/jmm/src/main/java/workbench/jmm/l02/PartitionReconciler.java ./gradlew :jmm:test --tests 'workbench.jmm.l02.*' Meet the three classes. h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · Quiz
x: setBalance writes inside synchronized (ledgerLock). getBalance reads inside synchronized (reportLock). Is the getter sure to see the latest balance? Yes, because both methods are synchronized No: the link exists only between releasing a lock and a later acquire of the same lock Yes, because entering any synchronized block refreshes all fields from memory No, because a field can't be read inside a synchronized block Two different locks give no link. The idea that any synchronized block refreshes everything comes from picturing locks as memory barriers, instructions that stop reordering across them. The JMM promises the link only for the same lock, and the JIT is allowed to optimize with that in mind. T1 runs x = 1; v = 1; where v is volatile and x is plain. T2 reads v and gets 0, then reads x. What can T2 see for x? Always 0, because T1 hasn't written v yet Always 1, because volatile flushes every earlier write Either 0 or 1: T2's read of v didn't see the write, so no handover covers x It throws, because reading a plain field next to a volatile is illegal The volatile handover forms only when the read sees the write. T2 saw 0, so it has no link to T1's writes, and its read of x races with x = 1. T1 may well have written x already, which is why "always 0" is wrong too. main fills a plain HashMap with 10,000 entries, then calls executor.submit(() -> lookup(map)) and never touches the map again. Is the task's read safe? Yes: handing a task to an executor happens-before the task starts, and nobody writes after that No, because HashMap is not thread-safe Only if the map field is volatile Only if you switch to ConcurrentHashMap HashMap is unsafe when threads write to it at the same time, but here every write comes before the handover and none after. The submit handover makes them visible to the task. Volatile or ConcurrentHashMap would add cost and no safety. A worker thread writes result. Which of these does NOT give main a happens-before link to that write? worker.join() returns future.get() returns, where the worker is the future's task latch.await() returns, after the worker wrote and then called latch.countDown() Thread.sleep(1_000) returns join, Future.get and the latch all document their handovers. sleep only passes time. The worker may not be done, and even if it is, a read after a sleep still races with its write. From lesson 1 of this track: you add Thread.onSpinWait() to a spin loop on a plain flag, and the loop starts noticing the flag. In memory model terms, what changed? The loop now has a happens-before link to the writer Nothing: there is still no link, HotSpot just happens to read the field again onSpinWait makes the next read volatile onSpinWait empties the writer's store buffer onSpinWait is a hint to the processor, with no synchronization effect in the JMM. HotSpot happens to read the field again after it today. The program still has a data race on the flag, and only a volatile, a lock or another real handover fixes it.

h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · Key terms
x: Happens-before The memory model's ordering between two actions. If a write happens-before a read, the read sees it. Program order The order of actions within one thread, as the code is written. Release The sending end of a handover: leaving a lock, writing a volatile, countDown(), put into a concurrent queue. Acquire The receiving end of a handover: entering a lock, reading a volatile, await(), take from a concurrent queue. Data race Conflicting accesses to one variable from two threads with no happens-before link between them. DRF-SC The JMM promise: a program free of data races behaves as if its threads were shuffled together one action at a time. Piggybacking Relying on transitivity, so one volatile or lock handover also publishes the plain writes made before it. When is a write in one thread sure to be visible to a read in another? Only when the write happens-before the read. State the lock rule of happens-before. Releasing a lock happens-before every later acquisition of the same lock. T1 writes inside synchronized (a). T2 reads inside synchronized (b). Is there a link? No. The link needs the same lock on both sides. State the volatile rule of happens-before. A write to a volatile field happens-before every read of that same field that sees it (or a later write). What does Thread.start() promise the new thread? Everything the parent did before calling start() is visible to the new thread. Writes after start() are not covered. Is Thread.sleep(100) a happens-before link? No. Use join(), Future.get() or a latch. What is a data race? Two threads access the same variable, at least one access is a write, and no happens-before link orders them.

h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · Go deeper
x: Two refinements are worth knowing once the basic rules feel natural. First, the JLS builds happens-before from a smaller relation called synchronizes-with. Each synchronizes-with link joins a release in one thread to an acquire in another. Releasing a monitor links to a later acquire of the same monitor, a volatile write to a read that sees it, start() to the first action of the new thread, and a thread's last action to a join() that returns. Happens-before is then program order plus synchronizes-with, chained by transitivity. Apart from a link into finalizers, that's the whole construction. All the synchronization actions in a run also fall into one total order, which is why every thread sees two volatile writes in the same order. Second, a lock is not a memory fence, an instruction that stops the processor and the compiler from moving memory operations across it. It's tempting to picture synchronized as "flush everything on exit, reload everything on entry". The JMM promises less, and the JIT uses the difference. The jcstress sample AdvancedJMM_01_SynchronizedBarriers writes x and y in two back-to-back synchronized (this) blocks, and an observer that takes no lock reads them with volatile reads. On x86 the observer saw the new y with the old x in 207,479 of about four billion samples. The JIT had merged the two blocks into one (lock coarsening) and reordered the writes inside it. That's legal: only a thread that also locks this is owed the order. Aleksey Shipilëv's "Close Encounters of The Java Memory Model Kind" walks through more misreadings like these, each with a jcstress test.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · What volatile gives you: fresh reads, ordered writes and one order for all
x: The museum's door shows what volatile does well. The sign on the door is a volatile field. Every guard reads it at the door itself, every time, and never from a note in a pocket. Declaring a field volatile gets you three things, and you've already used two of them in this track. The first is visibility: a volatile read sees the latest volatile write to that field. The JIT, the part of the JVM that compiles busy code while it runs, can't keep the value on its notepad: a register inside the core, the part of the processor that runs one thread. Nor can it move the read out of a loop. That was the stop flag in lesson 1 of this track. The second is ordering. Before the morning guard turns the sign to OPEN, he switches on the lights and opens the display cases. Whoever reads OPEN may walk in and find everything ready. In code, a volatile write is a release: plain writes that come before it in program order, the order of lines within one thread, can't move after it. A volatile read is an acquire: plain reads that come after it can't move before it. That's the piggybacking from Happens-before, where plain writes ride along on a volatile one: Java config = load(); // plain write: stays before the volatile write version = 42; // volatile write (release) if (version == 42) { // volatile read (acquire), in another thread use(config); // plain read: stays after it, and sees the config } Kotlin config = load() // plain write: stays before the volatile write version = 42 // @Volatile write (release) if (version == 42) { // @Volatile read (acquire), in another thread use(config) // plain read: stays after it, and sees the config } The third is one order for all volatile accesses. Every thread agrees on a single order of all the volatile reads and writes in the program, across every volatile field. That's what forbids the odd result of lesson 1's store-buffer test, in which two threads each write one field, then read the other's, and both read 0. Release and acquire alone don't forbid it, and VarHandles and memory ordering modes, the last lesson of this track, shows the difference. The ordering helps only threads that both use a volatile field. Picture two guards: one reads the door, and the other reads a note in his pocket. The first guard's care does nothing for the second. HalfVolatileDemo runs lesson 1's store-buffer test three ways: with no volatile field, with only x volatile, and with both: run 1: both read 0 in plain: 232,147 only x volatile: 67,837 both volatile: 0 run 2: both read 0 in plain: 193,583 only x volatile: 58,514 both volatile: 0 run 3: both read 0 in plain: 168,073 only x volatile: 26,353 both volatile: 0 With only x volatile, the count dropped and stayed well above zero. Thread A's volatile write empties its store buffer, the core's outbox of pending writes, before its read. But thread B wrote a plain y, and that write can still wait in B's outbox while B reads x. Only when both fields are volatile does the count reach 0. You may wonder what all this costs. Less than people fear. On x86 processors, a volatile read compiles to an ordinary read of memory; the only cost is that the JIT can't optimize around it. A volatile write costs more, because HotSpot follows it with an instruction that empties the store buffer. On ARM processors, HotSpot uses special load-acquire and store-release instructions instead. For a flag read on every request, the price is tiny next to a single call to a slow web service. A volatile field gives fresh reads, ordered writes and one order that every thread agrees on. Both sides must use it. So far the sign on the door has done everything we asked. Let's ask it to count. Make only one side volatile Read HalfVolatileDemo (either language). It runs the store-buffer test three ways: no volatile field, only x volatile, and both volatile. Predict the middle column before you run it: does one volatile field save both threads? Run it with the command below, twice, and compare the columns. HalfVolatileDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l03; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.IntConsumer; /** * The store-buffering test from lesson 1 of this track, three ways: no volatile, only x volatile, * both fields volatile. Thread A runs {@code x = 1; r1 = y;} and thread B runs {@code y = 1; r2 = x;}. * Counts the trials where both threads read 0. */ public class HalfVolatileDemo { static final class Plain { int x, y; } static final class XOnly { volatile int x; int y; } static final class Both { volatile int x, y; } static final int TRIALS = 1 << 19; static final int BATCH = 32; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int run = 1; for (int i = 0; i < TRIALS; i++) s[i] = new Plain(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y; }, i -> { s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x; }); return bothZero(r1, r2); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y; }, i -> { s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x; }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } // Runs a(i) and b(i) for every trial on two threads, in lockstep batches so they overlap. static void race(IntConsumer a, IntConsumer b) throws InterruptedException { AtomicInteger doneA = new AtomicInteger(), doneB = new AtomicInteger(); Thread ta = new Thread(() -> runSide(a, doneA, doneB)); Thread tb = new Thread(() -> runSide(b, doneB, doneA)); ta.start(); tb.start(); ta.join(); tb.join(); } static void runSide(IntConsumer side, AtomicInteger mine, AtomicInteger other) { for (int batch = 0; batch < TRIALS / BATCH; batch++) { mine.set(batch); while (other.get() < batch) Thread.onSpinWait(); for (int i = batch * BATCH; i < (batch + 1) * BATCH; i++) side.accept(i); } } static int bothZero(int[] r1, int[] r2) { int n = 0; With only x volatile, the count drops but stays well above zero (tens of thousands here): thread B's write to the plain y can still wait in its store buffer while B reads x. h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · What volatile doesn't give you: count++ is still three steps
x: volatile keeps every read fresh and every write visible, yet two threads still read 41 and both write 42: the fix is one atomic step Here's the museum's counter, the bug from the warm-up: Java private volatile int visitors; void onVisitor() { visitors++; // read, add one, write: three steps } Kotlin @Volatile private var visitors = 0 fun onVisitor() { visitors++ // read, add one, write: three steps } volatile makes the read fresh and the write visible. It does nothing about the gap between them. Let's trace the smallest case, with the count at 41: The thread for gate 1 reads visitors: 41. The thread for gate 2 reads visitors: 41. Gate 1 adds one and writes 42. Gate 2 adds one and writes 42. Two visitors came in, and the count moved by one. Each of those four accesses was perfectly volatile, and the museum still lost a visitor. A guard who comes along later reads 42 and carries on, so nothing in the program ever learns that someone went missing. That's the lost update from Race conditions, and volatile doesn't touch it. VolatileCounterDemo plays out the busy day. Four threads each add 1,000,000 to four kinds of counter: a plain int, a volatile int, an AtomicInteger and a LongAdder. One run printed: expected 4,000,000 each plain 3,987,596 volatile 3,348,221 atomic 4,000,000 adder 4,000,000 Both the plain and the volatile counters came out short. The plain one looks less wrong in this run, and that proves nothing. The JIT may keep a plain counter on its notepad and add to it there for a while, which changes how often the threads collide. In a run of the Kotlin twin, the plain counter even came out exact while the @Volatile one lost 985,479. Both are broken, just in different patterns. The fix is a single step that reads and writes as one. An atomic operation is one that other threads see either not started or completely done, never halfway: Java private final AtomicInteger visitors = new AtomicInteger(); void onVisitor() { visitors.incrementAndGet(); // one atomic read-modify-write } Kotlin private val visitors = AtomicInteger() fun onVisitor() { visitors.incrementAndGet() // one atomic read-modify-write } For a counter that many threads hit hard and that you only read now and then, such as a statistic, LongAdder is faster still. It spreads the additions over several cells and adds them up when you ask, as Atomics and compare-and-set showed. A lock works too, and it's the only choice once an update touches more than one field. The same trap hides in any compound action on a volatile, any group of steps that must happen together: if (balance >= amount) balance -= amount, max = Math.max(max, x), if (state == OPEN) state = CLOSED. Every one of them reads, decides and writes as separate steps. volatile makes each read and each write visible. It never makes two of them one step. So a volatile counter loses visitors. That doesn't make volatile useless. It means we need to know which fields it's enough for. Count visitors four ways Read VolatileCounterDemo (either language). Four threads each add 1,000,000 to a plain counter, a volatile counter, an AtomicInteger and a LongAdder. Predict which of the four reach 4,000,000, and whether volatile loses fewer updates than plain. Run it twice with the command below and compare the runs. If you can, run the Kotlin twin too. VolatileCounterDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l03; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** Four threads each add 1,000,000 to four kinds of counter. Which ones add up? */ public class VolatileCounterDemo { static int plain; static volatile int vol; static final AtomicInteger atomic = new AtomicInteger(); static final LongAdder adder = new LongAdder(); static final int THREADS = 4, PER_THREAD = 1_000_000; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { run("plain int", () -> plain++); run("volatile int", () -> vol++); run("AtomicInteger", atomic::incrementAndGet); run("LongAdder", adder::increment); System.out.printf("expected %,d each%n", THREADS * PER_THREAD); System.out.printf("plain %,d volatile %,d atomic %,d adder %,d%n", plain, vol, atomic.get(), adder.sum()); } static void run(String name, Runnable increment) throws InterruptedException { Thread[] ts = new Thread[THREADS]; for (int t = 0; t < THREADS; t++) { ts[t] = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < PER_THREAD; i++) increment.run(); }, name + "-" + t); } for (Thread t : ts) t.start(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); // join: the final reads in main see every thread's writes } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l03.VolatileCounterDemo labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l03/VolatileCounterDemo.java VolatileCounterDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l03 import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder import kotlin.concurrent.thread private var plain = 0 @Volatile private var vol = 0 private val atomic = AtomicInteger() private val adder = LongAdder() private const val THREADS = 4 private const val PER_THREAD = 1_000_000 /** Four threads each add 1,000,000 to four kinds of counter. Which ones add up? */ fun main() { hammer("plain Int") { plain++ } hammer("@Volatile Int") { vol++ } hammer("AtomicInteger") { atomic.incrementAndGet() } hammer("LongAdder") { adder.increment() } println("expected %,d each".format(THREADS * PER_THREAD)) println("plain %,d @Volatile %,d atomic %,d adder %,d".format(plain, vol, atomic.get(), adder.sum())) } private fun hammer(name: String, increment: () -> Unit) { val ts = List(THREADS) { t -> thread(name = "$name-$t") { repeat(PER_THREAD) { increment() } } } ts.forEach { it.join() } // join: the final reads in main see every thread's writes } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l03.VolatileCounterDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l03/VolatileCounterDemo.kt The atomic and the adder print exactly 4,000,000 every time. Plain and volatile both come out short, often by hundreds of thousands, and which of the two loses more changes from run to run (the plain one is now and then exact). The volatile counter is not "more correct"; it's wrong in a different pattern.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · When volatile is enough, and when you need an atomic or a lock
x: Make every field volatile, and the museum can still sell its last seat twice. The evening tour has one seat left. The sale code checks that a seat is left, adds one to sold, then marks the tour full. Two threads can both pass the check before either marks the tour full, and every read and write along the way is a correct volatile access. That's check-then-act, the second shape of race from Race conditions: test a condition, then act as if it still holds. volatile doesn't help with it either. The simulator below lets you sell the seat twice by hand. So the useful question is: which fields is volatile enough for? It's the right tool when all three of these hold: Only one thread writes the field, or every write sets a value that doesn't depend on the current one. The field isn't part of a rule that involves other fields. Readers need the latest value, and nothing more. Those three conditions cover more fields than you'd think. The sign on the museum door is one: one guard flips it, and nobody works out OPEN from the old value. So are a stop flag, a status that one thread moves forward, and the time of the last heartbeat (a regular "I'm still alive" signal from one thread). So is a gauge that one thread updates, such as how many jobs wait in the printer's queue. It also covers a reference to an immutable object (one that never changes after it's built) when one thread replaces the whole object, like the shop's price board in Don't share. Readers grab the current board with one volatile read, and the board itself never changes. The moment a decision needs a read and then a write based on what was read, volatile stops being enough. One variable with many writers takes an atomic class: incrementAndGet, compareAndSet, updateAndGet. Several variables that must change together, or a check that spans them, take a lock. Shape of the field Tool One writer, readers need the latest value volatile Many writers, one variable, read-modify-write AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, LongAdder Two or more fields under one rule a lock around every read and write A whole immutable object, replaced now and then a volatile reference or AtomicReference One mixed pattern is worth knowing. If writes are rare and reads are frequent, make the writes synchronized and the field volatile. Writers keep each other out through the lock, so += is safe, and readers pay only for one volatile read: Java private volatile long balance; public long balance() { return balance; } // readers: one volatile read public synchronized void apply(long delta) { balance += delta; } // writers: the lock makes += safe Kotlin @Volatile private var balance = 0L fun balance(): Long = balance // readers: one volatile read @Synchronized fun apply(delta: Long) { balance += delta } // writers: the lock makes += safe One writer, and no read before the write: volatile is enough. Anything more needs an atomic or a lock. Try the simulator now: both fields are volatile, and the last seat still sells twice. After that, one question is left. How much does a single volatile field actually cover? Pick the tool Choose volatile, an atomic or a lock for each field, and say why in one line. (a) boolean closedForCleaning, flipped from the manager's screen, read by every gate thread. (b) int insideNow, one higher when someone enters and one lower when they leave, updated by the gate threads. (c) long dailyLimitCents and long spentTodayCents on a shop's card account, checked together before each payment. (d) Map<String, Long> prices, replaced every minute by a refresher thread with a new map that nobody changes. (a) volatile: one writer, and the new value doesn't depend on the old one. (b) An atomic (AtomicInteger or LongAdder): many writers doing read-modify-write. (c) A lock: one rule spans two fields and needs check-then-act. (d) A volatile reference to an unchangeable map, built with Map.copyOf before it's published.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · What volatile covers: one variable, all 64 bits, and nothing behind it
x: Three details trip people up once the basics are clear, and the museum door explains all three: a sign covers itself, and nothing behind it. First, long and double. The Java Language Specification (JLS), section 17.7, lets the JVM treat a write to a non-volatile long or double as two separate 32-bit writes, one to each half. A racing reader could then see the top half of one value and the bottom half of another: a torn read. Writes and reads of volatile long and double are always atomic, and so are references and every type of 32 bits or less. jcstress, the tool from Testing and debugging that runs tiny tests millions of times, shows torn longs on a 32-bit x86 JVM. A reader saw -4294967296 and 4294967295 when the only values ever written were 0 and -1. 64-bit HotSpot writes a long in one instruction, so you won't see tearing there, but the JLS doesn't promise it. In practice this rarely matters on its own. A long that two threads share needs volatile for visibility anyway, and you get atomicity with it. Second, a volatile reference covers the reference, and nothing inside the object. Think of a sign on the door that says which room today's exhibition is in. Changing the sign is a volatile write. Moving the exhibits around inside the room is not, however volatile the sign. So tours.add(t) on a volatile List<Tour> tours is not a volatile write. It's a call on whatever list the field points to, with no link for readers and no protection for the list. Replace the whole object instead: Java private volatile List<Tour> tours = List.of(); // volatile covers the reference only void replaceTours(List<Tour> fresh) { tours = List.copyOf(fresh); // one volatile write of an unchangeable list } Kotlin @Volatile private var tours: List<Tour> = emptyList() // @Volatile covers the reference only fun replaceTours(fresh: List<Tour>) { tours = fresh.toList() // one write of a copy nobody else holds } The jcstress sample AdvancedJMM_05_MisplacedVolatile shows the price of getting this wrong. A volatile field held a holder object, but the new value went into a plain field inside the holder. On a 64-bit ARM machine, a reader saw the new object's field still at 0 in 553 samples. Third, arrays. A volatile long[] makes the array reference volatile and leaves every element plain: a sign that names a room full of plain lockers. For volatile elements, use AtomicLongArray, AtomicIntegerArray or AtomicReferenceArray: Java class GateCounts { private volatile long[] counts = new long[4]; // volatile reference, plain elements private final AtomicLongArray safe = new AtomicLongArray(4); // each element acts like a volatile void record(int gate, long visitors) { counts[gate] = visitors; // plain element write: no link for readers safe.set(gate, visitors); // volatile element write: readers of safe.get() see it } } Kotlin class GateCounts { @Volatile private var counts = LongArray(4) // volatile reference, plain elements private val safe = AtomicLongArray(4) // each element acts like a volatile fun record(gate: Int, visitors: Long) { counts[gate] = visitors // plain element write: no link for readers safe.set(gate, visitors) // volatile element write: readers of safe.get() see it } } Check yourself: a volatile Map<String, Long> prices holds a HashMap, and refresher threads call prices.put(item, cents). Does a reader that calls prices.get(item) see the new price? Nothing promises it. The only volatile access is the read of the field. The put writes inside the map, and those writes are plain, so no link reaches the reader. Two threads calling put at once can also corrupt the HashMap itself. Use one writer that replaces the whole map with an unchangeable copy, or a ConcurrentHashMap. A volatile field covers one variable. The object behind a volatile reference needs protection of its own. One case is left: an object built in one thread and handed to others through a field, its insides and all. What are the readers promised to see inside it?

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · Java and Kotlin
x: A volatile snapshot reference in Java and Kotlin PriceBoard.java public class PriceBoard { // replaced whole, never changed: one volatile read gives a consistent snapshot private volatile Map<String, Long> prices = Map.of(); // one refresher thread public void refresh(Map<String, Long> fresh) { prices = Map.copyOf(fresh); // build first, then publish with one volatile write } // many till threads public Long priceOf(String item) { return prices.get(item); } } PriceBoard.kt class PriceBoard { // replaced whole, never changed: one volatile read gives a consistent snapshot @Volatile private var prices: Map<String, Long> = emptyMap() // one refresher thread fun refresh(fresh: Map<String, Long>) { prices = fresh.toMap() // a private copy, then publish with one volatile write } // many till threads fun priceOf(item: String): Long? = prices[item] } Both versions follow the same pattern: build a new map, publish it with one volatile write, and never touch it again. The difference is in the copy. Java's Map.copyOf returns a truly unmodifiable map (and rejects nulls). Kotlin's Map type is only a read-only view, so the safety comes from toMap() making a fresh map that no other code holds. If you passed the caller's map straight through, someone holding a MutableMap reference to it could still change it under the readers.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · Worked example
x: Choose the tools for a circuit breaker A program calls a slow web service, and guards each call with a circuit breaker, which works like the fuse box in a house. After 5 failures in a row, the breaker stops calls to the service, and 30 seconds later it lets them through again. Request threads call onFailure and onSuccess, and check allowRequest before each call. Every field is volatile. For each field, ask: who writes it, and does the write depend on a read? class ServiceBreaker { private volatile int consecutiveFailures; // written by request threads private volatile long openedAtMillis; // 0 means closed: calls go through void onFailure(long now) { consecutiveFailures++; // 1. read-modify-write if (consecutiveFailures >= 5 && openedAtMillis == 0) openedAtMillis = now; // 2. check-then-act } void onSuccess() { consecutiveFailures = 0; } boolean allowRequest(long now) { long opened = openedAtMillis; return opened == 0 || now - opened > 30_000; } } class ServiceBreaker { @Volatile private var consecutiveFailures = 0 // written by request threads @Volatile private var openedAtMillis = 0L // 0 means closed: calls go through fun onFailure(now: Long) { consecutiveFailures++ // 1. read-modify-write if (consecutiveFailures >= 5 && openedAtMillis == 0L) openedAtMillis = now // 2. check-then-act } fun onSuccess() { consecutiveFailures = 0 } fun allowRequest(now: Long): Boolean { val opened = openedAtMillis return opened == 0L || now - opened > 30_000 } } consecutiveFailures has many writers, and ++ depends on a read, so increments get lost and the breaker trips late. Line 2 reads the counter again, separately, and then reads and writes openedAtMillis, so two threads can both see 5 and both set the time. openedAtMillis itself is fine as a volatile for the readers in allowRequest, which need one value and nothing else. Make the counter atomic, and decide on the value it returns. Each incrementAndGet returns a different number, so only one thread sees exactly 5 for each run of failures, and only that thread trips the breaker. class ServiceBreaker { private final AtomicInteger consecutiveFailures = new AtomicInteger(); // 1. many writers: atomic private volatile long openedAtMillis; // 2. readers need one value: volatile void onFailure(long now) { int n = consecutiveFailures.incrementAndGet(); // 3. one atomic step, and keep the result if (n == 5) openedAtMillis = now; // 4. only one thread sees n == 5 } void onSuccess() { consecutiveFailures.set(0); } boolean allowRequest(long now) { long opened = openedAtMillis; // 5. read the volatile once return opened == 0 || now - opened > 30_000; } } class ServiceBreaker { private val consecutiveFailures = AtomicInteger() // 1. many writers: atomic @Volatile private var openedAtMillis = 0L // 2. readers need one value: @Volatile fun onFailure(now: Long) { val n = consecutiveFailures.incrementAndGet() // 3. one atomic step, and keep the result if (n == 5) openedAtMillis = now // 4. only one thread sees n == 5 } fun onSuccess() { consecutiveFailures.set(0) } fun allowRequest(now: Long): Boolean { val opened = openedAtMillis // 5. read the volatile once return opened == 0L || now - opened > 30_000 } } Two habits made this work. Use the value the atomic call returns: calling incrementAndGet() and then get() would bring the check-then-act gap back. And read a volatile into a local variable once when you use it twice, as allowRequest does, so both uses see the same value. When the breaker later grows a half-open state, letting exactly one trial call through while it also resets the counter, two fields change together. That's the point to switch to a lock.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · Lab
x: Choose volatile, atomic or lock for a card payment labs/jmm/src/main/java/workbench/jmm/l03/PaymentSession.java ./gradlew :jmm:test --tests 'workbench.jmm.l03.*' Meet PaymentSession. It follows one card payment through its life. First the shop reserves the money on the card (the payment is authorized). Then it takes some or all of it (it captures), and later it may give some back (it refunds). Several threads share the object, and the comment above each field says who writes it and who reads it. Run the tests once. Four of the five fail: two waiting threads never see a write, the attempt counter comes up short, and the money rule breaks. Try the quick fix first: put volatile on every field and run the tests. Two still fail. Before reading on, say which two and why. Now go field by field. Read the comment that says who writes it and who reads it, choose volatile, an atomic or a lock, and add a one-line comment saying why. Keep every public signature as it is. Run the tests until all five pass, then twice more. status and lastHeartbeatMillis each have one writer, and the new value doesn't depend on the old one. attempts++ is read-modify-write with many writers. An AtomicInteger lets attempts() keep returning int. tryRefund reads capturedCents, which tryCapture writes. Guard both fields with one lock, and take it in the two getters too. A pair of AtomicLongs can't keep refunded <= captured. All five tests in PaymentSessionTest pass, three runs in a row. By the end you can say exactly what volatile promises, show why it doesn't make count++ safe, and choose between volatile, an atomic and a lock for any shared field.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · Quiz
x: Many threads run balance += amount on a volatile long balance. What can go wrong? Two threads can read the same balance and both write, so one amount is lost Nothing: volatile makes the whole statement atomic The 64-bit write can tear into two halves Readers may never see the new balance += is a read, an add and a write. Volatile makes each step visible and ordered, but it leaves the gap between them. Tearing is ruled out because the field is volatile, and visibility is fine, which is what makes this bug easy to miss. Which of these fields is correctly protected by volatile alone? A visitor counter that every gate thread increments A reference to an unchangeable PriceList that one refresher thread replaces every minute limit and spent, which are checked together before every card payment A volatile ArrayList<Tour> that several threads add tours to One writer, a whole-object replace, and readers that need only the latest reference: that's exactly volatile's job. The counter needs an atomic, the pair needs a lock, and the volatile list protects only the reference while ArrayList.add races. In HalfVolatileDemo only x is volatile. Why do both threads still sometimes read 0? The volatile write to x is lost Volatile only works between two volatile fields of the same object Thread B's plain write to y can wait in its store buffer while B reads x, so B's own pair of accesses is not ordered The demo's barrier lets the threads run different trials To rule the result out, each thread's write-then-read must stay in order. Thread A's volatile write is followed by an instruction that empties its store buffer, but thread B wrote a plain field, so nothing stops B's read from passing its own write. Make both fields volatile and the count drops to 0. A class has private volatile long[] balances. Thread A runs balances[3] = 500. Thread B later reads balances[3]. What is promised? B sees 500, because the array is volatile B sees 500 or 0, but never a torn value B sees 500 once A releases the array Nothing about the element: only the array reference is volatile, so this is a plain write and a plain read Element accesses of a volatile array are plain accesses. Nothing links A's write to B's read, and a plain long element may even tear under the JLS. Use AtomicLongArray when elements are shared. From lesson 2 of this track: T1 sets a plain fee = 25 and then the volatile ready = true. T2 sees ready == true and then reads fee. Why must T2 see 25? Because fee is an int, and int writes are atomic Program order, then the volatile write-to-read handover, then program order again: the links chain, so the write of fee happens-before its read Because volatile writes flush all CPU caches It doesn't have to; T2 may see 0 This is piggybacking on the volatile. The write of fee comes before the release in T1's program order, and the read comes after the acquire in T2's. Atomicity only rules out half-written values; it says nothing about which value you see.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · Explain it back
