h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · Key terms
x: Visibility Whether a read in one thread sees a write from another. Atomicity An operation happens as one indivisible step that no other thread can split. Read-modify-write Read a value, compute a new one from it, write it back. Needs an atomic or a lock when shared. Compound action A group of steps that must happen together, such as check-then-act or read-modify-write. Torn read Seeing half of one write and half of another, possible for non-volatile long and double under the JLS. Single writer A field that only one thread ever writes. Volatile is enough for it. Snapshot publication Building a new immutable object and publishing it with one volatile write, instead of changing the old one. LongAdder A counter that spreads increments over several cells. Fast when many threads add; its sum is not a snapshot. What does a volatile field promise? Visibility of the latest write, release and acquire ordering around each access, and one order of all volatile accesses that every thread agrees on. Is count++ on a volatile int atomic? No. It's still a read, an add and a write. Use AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() or LongAdder. When is volatile alone enough for a field? When one thread writes it (or writes don't depend on the current value), and the field isn't part of a rule with other fields. Two fields must change together under one rule. Volatile, atomic or lock? A lock, taken around every read and write of both fields. Can a write to a non-volatile long tear? The JLS allows it to be split into two 32-bit writes. A volatile long or double is always written and read atomically. volatile List<Tour> tours; Is tours.add(t) from two threads safe? No. Volatile covers the reference only. Replace the whole list with an unchangeable copy instead, or use a concurrent collection. Are the elements of a volatile long[] volatile? No, only the array reference. Use AtomicLongArray for volatile element access.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · Go deeper
x: Why is the JLS rule for long and double still there, when 64-bit JVMs never tear? Because the JLS is written for every JVM, including 32-bit ones, and dropping the rule would force those JVMs to use more expensive instructions for every 64-bit access. The VarHandle Javadoc states the same rule for its plain mode: plain reads and writes are guaranteed bitwise atomic only for references and for primitive values of at most 32 bits. A related term you may meet is word tearing: a write to one field or array element changing its neighbor, as some processors would do for single bytes. Java forbids it outright. Every field and every array element is its own variable, so a byte[] shared between threads never corrupts the byte next to the one you wrote. Races on that array are still races, of course. The mixed pattern from section 3, with synchronized writes and volatile reads, has a name. Brian Goetz called it "the cheap read-write lock trick" in his article "Managing volatility". The same article lists other safe uses of volatile that this lesson met: status flags, one-time safe publication, and independent observations, such as the time of the last heartbeat. Read his list as a checklist. If a volatile field in your code fits none of those patterns, look at it twice.

h: Safe publication, final fields and escaping this · Handing over an object is a write, and readers can see it half-built
x: Handing an object to another thread is a write: a reader can find the rate card before its fields, unless a seal such as volatile or final fields stops it When a customer pays by card, the card company charges the shop a small fee, say 1.20 euros for a VISA payment. The shop's program keeps these fees in a RateCard: a currency, and a fee for each card brand. A loader thread builds a new rate card whenever the fees change. The request threads, which handle the payments, read the current one. Handing an object to another thread like this is called publishing it: storing a reference to it where another thread can find it, such as a shared field, a static field or a collection. (A reference is the value a variable holds to point at an object.) Here is the loader's side: Java // Naive: publishing through a plain field RateCard card = new RateCard("EUR", fees); // 1. make the object, 2. run the constructor registry.current = card; // 3. publish: store the reference where others look Kotlin // Naive: publishing through a plain field val card = RateCard("EUR", fees) // 1. make the object, 2. run the constructor registry.current = card // 3. publish: store the reference where others look Three things happen. The JVM, the program that runs your Java code, makes the object with every field at its default value: 0, false or null. The constructor writes the real values. Then the reference is stored in current. In the loader thread, they happen in exactly that order. A request thread that reads current gets no such promise. A write is guaranteed visible to a read in another thread only when a happens-before edge links them. A write to a volatile field, a field whose reads always see the latest write, and a later read of that field form one such edge. Happens-before, the rules that matter, lists them all. Here, nothing links the request thread's read to the loader's writes. So two layers are free to change the order. The JIT, the compiler inside the JVM that turns busy code into machine code while it runs, may move the store of the reference ahead of the constructor's stores. And the processor may show its stores to its other cores, the parts of the processor that each run one thread at a time, in a different order. ARM processors, such as the ones in Apple Silicon laptops, do this more than Intel and AMD processors. A request thread can then see current != null and still read a null currency or a fee of 0. That's called a partially constructed object, and no line you wrote creates one. In the letter's terms, the courier delivered the envelope before all the pages were inside. The figure shows it. The picture breaks in one place: a real courier can't carry pages you haven't written yet. Here the reordering happens in layers you never see, and the code gives no hint of it. It isn't only theory. jcstress, a tool from OpenJDK (the open-source project that builds Java), runs tiny tests on several threads at once, millions of times, and counts every result. It has a sample called BasicJMM_08_Finals. One thread publishes an object with four plain int fields, set to 1, 2, 3 and 4, through a plain field. Another thread reads the four fields. Here is the run recorded in the sample, on an x86_64 machine (the Intel and AMD kind), where -1 means the reader didn't see the object yet: RESULT SAMPLES FREQ EXPECT DESCRIPTION -1, -1, -1, -1 115,042,024 52.43% Acceptable Object is not seen yet. 1, 0, 3, 0 3,892 <0.01% Interesting Seeing partially constructed object. 1, 0, 3, 4 14,291 <0.01% Interesting Seeing partially constructed object. 1, 2, 3, 0 123 <0.01% Interesting Seeing partially constructed object. 1, 2, 3, 4 104,365,974 47.56% Acceptable Seen the complete object. About 18,000 of 219 million readers found blank pages. That's rare, but a busy shop takes a lot of card payments. On an AArch64 machine, a 64-bit ARM one, the same sample saw almost every mix of zeros and real values. You may wonder how the x86 machine did it, when Why your loop never stops showed that x86 keeps its stores in order. The sample checks that too. When it asks the JIT to keep those accesses in order, the half-built objects vanish on x86_64 and stay on ARM. On x86, the JIT moved the stores. Publishing through a plain field fails in a second way you met in Why your loop never stops: a reader that loops, waiting for the first card, may read the field once and never again. The lab's RateCardRegistry has exactly that bug. A reader can see a reference before the fields behind it. Never publish through a plain field. So the envelope can arrive with blank pages, or not at all. Next, we'll seal it, so the reference and the fields arrive together. With no edge, a request thread can see the store to current before the constructor's store, and find a real rate card with a null inside. jcstress sample BasicJMM_08_Finals: plain, opaque and final publication, with recorded results read

h: Safe publication, final fields and escaping this · Sealing the envelope: four safe ways to publish
x: An object is safely published when the reference and the state the object had at that moment reach the reader together. In the letter's terms, the envelope is sealed: whoever opens it finds every page that was inside when you sealed it. Java Concurrency in Practice, the classic book on the subject, lists four seals: Build the object in a static initializer, the code that runs once when a class is first used. The JVM runs it under a lock, and every thread that uses the class afterwards sees the result. Store it in a volatile field or an AtomicReference (the holder for one reference from Atomics and compare-and-set). Store it in a final field of an object that is itself properly built (the next section). Store it in a field guarded by a lock, or hand it over through a java.util.concurrent class, such as a concurrent map or queue. Each seal is an edge you have met before. Seal 1 uses the lock the JVM holds while it initializes a class. Seal 2 is a volatile write and a later read of the same field. Seal 4 is a lock released by one thread and taken by another, or a hand-over through a concurrent collection. Seal 3 is new, and it gets the next section. Everything the loader wrote before the seal reaches a reader who breaks the same seal. Here is the registry with three of them: Java // Fixed: three safe ways to publish, in one class class RateCardRegistry { static final RateCard DEFAULT = new RateCard("EUR", Map.of("VISA", 120L)); // 1. static initializer private volatile RateCard current = DEFAULT; // 2. volatile field private final ConcurrentMap<String, RateCard> byCurrency = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // 4. concurrent map void publish(RateCard card) { current = card; // a volatile write seals it byCurrency.put(card.currency(), card); // and so does put } RateCard current() { return current; // a volatile read breaks the same seal } } Kotlin // Fixed: three safe ways to publish, in one class class RateCardRegistry { companion object { val DEFAULT = RateCard("EUR", mapOf("VISA" to 120L)) // 1. static initializer (companion object) } @Volatile private var current: RateCard = DEFAULT // 2. @Volatile property private val byCurrency = ConcurrentHashMap<String, RateCard>() // 4. concurrent map fun publish(card: RateCard) { current = card // a volatile write seals it byCurrency[card.currency] = card // and so does put } fun current(): RateCard = current // a volatile read breaks the same seal } Both versions do the same three things. Kotlin's companion object is initialized together with its class, just like a Java static initializer, so seal 1 works the same way, and @Volatile is Kotlin's volatile. Notice that both sides take part. The loader writes the volatile field, and the reader reads that same field. A seal only the writer uses is no seal. A synchronized publish method with a plain getter, for example, gives the reader no edge at all, because the reader never takes the lock. Which seal should you pick? For something you replace while the program runs, such as the current rate card, use a volatile field or an AtomicReference. For a constant, use static final. Don't add synchronized getters only to publish: a volatile read costs less and says what you mean. Hand an object to another thread through a seal: a volatile field, a static initializer, a lock or a concurrent collection. A seal covers the pages that were inside when you sealed the envelope. If the loader changes the rate card after publishing it, each change needs a seal of its own. That's why the easiest objects to publish are the ones that never change, and Java keeps a special promise for them. Sealed or not? For each line, decide whether a request thread is guaranteed to see the whole RateCard. Name the seal, or the missing edge. (a) static final RateCard DEFAULT = new RateCard(...), read by any thread. (b) private RateCard current;, set by the loader, read by request threads. (c) private volatile RateCard current;, set by the loader, read by request threads. (d) cards.put(id, card) on a ConcurrentHashMap, and request threads call cards.get(id). (a) Sealed: the static initializer runs under the JVM's class-initialization lock. (b) Not sealed: there's no edge, so a reader may see a half-built card, or never see it at all. (c) Sealed: a volatile write, then a volatile read of the same field. (d) Sealed: putting a card into a concurrent map happens-before a get that returns it.

h: Safe publication, final fields and escaping this · Final fields arrive whole, even without a seal
x: final fields get one extra promise from the Java memory model, the rules for what one thread sees of another thread's writes. The Java Language Specification (section 17.5) says, in plain words: a thread that sees a reference to an object only after the object's constructor has finished is guaranteed to see the correct values of its final fields. No volatile and no lock are needed. The promise holds even when the reference reached the reader through a data race, a write and a read of the same field with no edge between them. The promise reaches through the field. If a final field points to a map or an array, the reader also sees its contents as they were when the constructor ended. The specification calls the end of the constructor the freeze: that's when the final fields are frozen. In the letter's terms, final fields are pages glued into the envelope at the factory. However the envelope travels, sealed or not, whoever opens it finds those pages in place. Here's a fee quote with both kinds of field: Java final class Quote { private final String scheme; // final: correct even through a race private final Map<String, Long> fees; // final: and the map's contents as of the freeze private long hits; // plain: a racing reader may see 0 Quote(String scheme, Map<String, Long> fees) { this.scheme = scheme; this.fees = Map.copyOf(fees); } } Kotlin class Quote(scheme: String, fees: Map<String, Long>) { private val scheme = scheme // val: a final field, correct even through a race private val fees = fees.toMap() // val: and the map's contents as of the freeze private var hits = 0L // var: a plain field, a racing reader may see 0 } The Kotlin version is the same class: a val compiles to a final field, and a var to a plain one. The Try it below checks that in the compiled classes. Back to BasicJMM_08_Finals. Its last test makes all four fields final and publishes the object through the same plain field. The recorded results, on x86_64 and on AArch64 alike, show readers seeing either no object or the complete one: not one partial object. The test now marks every other result as forbidden. How does the JVM keep this promise? When a constructor writes a final field, HotSpot, the JVM most people run, puts a barrier at the end of the constructor. Every store before the barrier must be visible before any store after it, and the store that publishes the reference always comes after. On x86 the barrier costs nothing, because the processor keeps stores in order anyway; it only stops the JIT from moving stores past it. On ARM it's a real fence instruction, one that makes the processor finish the earlier stores first. Put the pieces together and you get the immutable object from Don't share: a final class, every field final, changing inputs copied in the constructor, nothing changeable handed out, and no this handed to anyone before the constructor ends. Don't share showed that such an object needs no lock. Here is the reason underneath: thanks to the final-field promise, no reader can see it half-built, however it arrived. Records and Kotlin classes with only val properties get you most of the way. They still keep a caller's list as it is, so copy it, for example in a record's compact constructor, the one with no parameter list: record FeeSchedule(List<Fee> fees) { FeeSchedule { fees = List.copyOf(fees); } }. The promise has two limits. Final fields don't deliver the envelope: a reader that waits on a plain field may still never see the reference at all. That's why the lab's RateCardRegistry needs volatile even after RateCard becomes immutable. And the promise starts at the freeze, so it only holds if nobody got the reference before the constructor finished. Final fields arrive whole through any race, but they don't deliver the reference. Make the data final, and still publish it through a seal. That second limit is easy to break without noticing. Next, we'll see how a constructor hands out its object too early. Find final in the compiled classes Run both demos below once (the Java one, then the Kotlin one), so Gradle compiles them. javap is a JDK tool that prints what's inside a compiled class. Predict first: which fields will say final? From labs/, run javap -p 'jmm/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/jmm/l04/FinalFieldsDemo$Quote.class', then the same for FinalFieldsDemo$MutableQuote.class. Run javap -p jmm/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/jmm/l04/KQuote.class, then the same for KMutableQuote.class. FinalFieldsDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l04; /** Where final fields come from in Java. Run javap on the compiled classes to see them. */ public class FinalFieldsDemo { // a record's components become private final fields record Quote(String scheme, long feeCents) {} // for contrast: plain, non-final fields static final class MutableQuote { String scheme; long feeCents; } public static void main(String[] args) { Quote q = new Quote("VISA", 120); MutableQuote m = new MutableQuote(); m.scheme = "MC"; m.feeCents = 135; System.out.println(q + " and a mutable quote for " + m.scheme); } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l04.FinalFieldsDemo labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l04/FinalFieldsDemo.java FinalFieldsDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l04 /** Where final fields come from in Kotlin. Run javap on the compiled classes to see them. */ class KQuote(val scheme: String, val feeCents: Long) // val: a private final backing field class KMutableQuote(var scheme: String, var feeCents: Long) // var: a private, non-final backing field fun main() { val q = KQuote("VISA", 120) val m = KMutableQuote("MC", 135) m.feeCents = 140 println("${q.scheme} ${q.feeCents} and a mutable quote for ${m.scheme} ${m.feeCents}") } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l04.FinalFieldsDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l04/FinalFieldsDemo.kt The record and KQuote both show private final java.lang.String scheme; and private final long feeCents;. MutableQuote and KMutableQuote show the same fields without final, and the Kotlin one also has setters. A Kotlin val and a Java record component compile to the same thing, a final field, and they get the final-field promise with it.

h: Safe publication, final fields and escaping this · Don't open the house early: keeping this inside the constructor
x: Picture a new house and the agent who will sell it. The builders work first: walls, floor, wiring. When they're done, the agent hands out the address and opens the door to buyers. Now picture an agent who hands out the address on the first morning. A buyer arrives while the floor is still a hole in the ground. A constructor is the builders' work, and this, the reference to the object being built, is the address. Handing this to other code before the constructor ends is called escaping this. The code that receives it is the early buyer: it sees the object with some fields still at their defaults. It doesn't even need another thread. this escapes when a constructor: registers the object as a listener (an object that other code calls when something happens); starts a thread, or hands over a task, that uses the object; creates a lambda or inner class that captures this and hands it out; calls a method that a subclass can override. Here's the first case. An event bus is a notice board inside a program: code pins up events, and every registered listener hears each one. The lab's EventBus also replays its last event to each new listener the moment it registers. This listener texts the shop manager about any sale over a limit: Java // Naive: `this` escapes before the fields are set class BigSaleAlert implements Consumer<SaleEvent> { private final long limitCents; private final Phone manager; BigSaleAlert(EventBus bus, long limitCents, Phone manager) { bus.register(this); // the bus calls accept() right here... this.limitCents = limitCents; // ...before these fields are set this.manager = manager; } public void accept(SaleEvent e) { if (e.amountCents() > limitCents) manager.text("Big sale: " + e); // manager is still null } } Kotlin // Naive: `this` escapes before the properties are set class BigSaleAlert(bus: EventBus, limitCents: Long, manager: Phone) : Consumer<SaleEvent> { init { bus.register(this) // the bus calls accept() right here... } private val limitCents = limitCents // ...before these properties are set private val manager = manager override fun accept(e: SaleEvent) { if (e.amountCents > limitCents) manager.text("Big sale: $e") // manager is still null } } register calls accept at once, to replay the last sale. At that moment limitCents is still 0, so every sale looks big, and manager is still null, so manager.text throws a NullPointerException. No second thread was involved. The buyer came in through a call the constructor made itself. Kotlin runs init blocks and property initializers in the order you write them, so the same bug is one misplaced init away. Kotlin's null safety doesn't save you either: manager is declared non-null, and in the early call it still reads as null. The thread case is in the Try it: a constructor starts a heartbeat thread, which sends a regular "still running" message, and only then looks up the address to send it to. The heartbeat thread is punctual. It reports for work 50 ms before its address exists. The picture breaks here: on a building site, someone would see the buyer and stop them. In Java, nothing does. The early call looks like any other call. You might move register to the last line of the constructor. In this one-thread case it works, but it's still the wrong fix. The final-field promise starts when the constructor returns, so threads that get the object from the bus get no promise at all. And if someone writes a subclass, its constructor runs after yours, while the bus already holds the object. Instead, keep constructors to setting fields, and wire the object up once it's built, in a static factory method or a start() method: Java // Fixed: the constructor only sets fields; a factory wires it up // (the fields and accept() stay as they were) private BigSaleAlert(long limitCents, Phone manager) { this.limitCents = limitCents; this.manager = manager; } static BigSaleAlert listenOn(EventBus bus, long limitCents, Phone manager) { BigSaleAlert alert = new BigSaleAlert(limitCents, manager); // 1. finish building bus.register(alert); // 2. then show it to others return alert; } Kotlin // Fixed: the constructor only sets properties; a factory wires it up class BigSaleAlert private constructor( private val limitCents: Long, private val manager: Phone, ) : Consumer<SaleEvent> { override fun accept(e: SaleEvent) { if (e.amountCents > limitCents) manager.text("Big sale: $e") } companion object { fun listenOn(bus: EventBus, limitCents: Long, manager: Phone): BigSaleAlert { val alert = BigSaleAlert(limitCents, manager) // 1. finish building bus.register(alert) // 2. then show it to others return alert } } } A constructor sets fields and nothing else. Wire the object up after it's built. Every tool in this lesson hands over an object that is already built. None of them helps when several threads ask for an object that doesn't exist yet, and the first one to ask has to build it while the others wait. That's the next lesson's problem. A thread that starts too early Read ThisEscapeDemo. Its constructor starts a heartbeat thread, then looks up the address to send to, which takes about 50 ms. Predict both lines of output, then run it. Fix it: move the thread start out of the constructor into a start() method, and call start() from main after construction. Run it again. ThisEscapeDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l04; /** * A constructor that starts a thread before it has finished setting its fields. * A heartbeat is a short "still running" message that one program sends another every few seconds. */ public class ThisEscapeDemo { static final class HeartbeatSender { private final String endpoint; HeartbeatSender(String endpointName) { Thread beat = new Thread(this::sendHeartbeat, "heartbeat"); beat.start(); // `this` escapes to another thread here... this.endpoint = resolve(endpointName); // ...and this final field is set about 50 ms later } void sendHeartbeat() { System.out.println("heartbeat thread sends to: " + endpoint); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { HeartbeatSender sender = new HeartbeatSender("head-office"); System.out.println("constructor finished, endpoint = " + sender.endpoint); Thread.sleep(100); } // stands in for a slow lookup of the address over the network static String resolve(String name) { try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return "https://" + name + ".example.com"; } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l04.ThisEscapeDemo labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l04/ThisEscapeDemo.java ThisEscapeDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l04 import kotlin.concurrent.thread /** * A constructor that starts a thread before it has finished setting its properties. * A heartbeat is a short "still running" message that one program sends another every few seconds. */ private class HeartbeatClient(endpointName: String) { val endpoint: String init { thread(name = "heartbeat") { sendHeartbeat() } // `this` escapes to another thread here... endpoint = resolve(endpointName) // ...and this val is set about 50 ms later } fun sendHeartbeat() { println("heartbeat thread sends to: $endpoint") // a non-null String that reads as null } } fun main() { val sender = HeartbeatClient("head-office") println("constructor finished, endpoint = ${sender.endpoint}") Thread.sleep(100) } // stands in for a slow lookup of the address over the network private fun resolve(name: String): String { Thread.sleep(50) return "https://$name.example.com" } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l04.ThisEscapeDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l04/ThisEscapeDemo.kt The first run prints heartbeat thread sends to: null, then constructor finished, endpoint = https://head-office.example.com. The heartbeat thread ran while the constructor was still looking up the address. In Kotlin, val endpoint: String is non-null by its type and still reads as null. After the fix, the heartbeat prints the real address: the field was set before start(), and start() happens-before everything the new thread does.

h: Safe publication, final fields and escaping this · Java and Kotlin
x: An immutable rate card in Java and Kotlin RateCard.java public final class RateCard { private final String currency; private final Map<String, Long> feesByScheme; public RateCard(String currency, Map<String, Long> feesByScheme) { this.currency = currency; this.feesByScheme = Map.copyOf(feesByScheme); // our own unmodifiable copy } public String currency() { return currency; } public Map<String, Long> feesByScheme() { return feesByScheme; } // safe to hand out } RateCard.kt class RateCard(val currency: String, feesByScheme: Map<String, Long>) { // our own copy, behind a read-only type val feesByScheme: Map<String, Long> = feesByScheme.toMap() } Both classes have final fields and copy the caller's map, so both get the final-field promise. Kotlin says it in three lines, because Kotlin classes are final by default and a val compiles to a private final field with a getter. The real difference is the map. Java's Map.copyOf returns a map that nobody can change. Kotlin's Map is a read-only interface: toMap() gives you a private LinkedHashMap, and code that casts it to MutableMap could still change it. Inside your own code that's usually fine. If the object travels to code you don't control, build the copy with java.util.Map.copyOf instead, as Don't share did.

h: Safe publication, final fields and escaping this · Worked example
x: Publish the shop's delivery settings safely The shop charges a delivery fee, and delivery is free for orders above a threshold. A helper thread fetches new settings from head office every minute, and every till thread reads them. Now and then a till charges the new fee with the old threshold, a pair head office never set. Find both problems. public class DeliverySettingsHolder { private DeliverySettings settings = new DeliverySettings(); // 1. a changeable object in a plain field void refresh(HeadOffice office) { // the helper thread, every minute Settings s = office.fetch(); settings.setFeeCents(s.feeCents()); // 2. changed in place... settings.setFreeAboveCents(s.freeAboveCents()); // ...one field at a time } public DeliverySettings current() { return settings; } // 3. every till reads it } class DeliverySettingsHolder { private var settings = DeliverySettings() // 1. a changeable object in a plain property fun refresh(office: HeadOffice) { // the helper thread, every minute val s = office.fetch() settings.feeCents = s.feeCents // 2. changed in place... settings.freeAboveCents = s.freeAboveCents // ...one field at a time } fun current(): DeliverySettings = settings // 3. every till reads it } First, the helper changes one shared object in place, field by field, with no lock. A till can read between the two writes and get the new fee next to the old threshold. Second, nothing publishes the settings safely. Their fields are plain, and there's no edge from the helper thread to the tills, so a till may see the writes late or in any order. Even a lock around refresh wouldn't help tills that never take it. Make the settings immutable, build a whole new object on each refresh, and publish it with one volatile write. Each till then gets one complete version. public record DeliverySettings(long feeCents, long freeAboveCents) {} // 1. immutable: final fields, no setters public class DeliverySettingsHolder { private volatile DeliverySettings settings = new DeliverySettings(499, 5_000); void refresh(HeadOffice office) { Settings s = office.fetch(); settings = new DeliverySettings(s.feeCents(), s.freeAboveCents()); // 2. build a new one, 3. publish it } public DeliverySettings current() { return settings; } // 4. one complete version per read } data class DeliverySettings(val feeCents: Long, val freeAboveCents: Long) // 1. immutable: vals only class DeliverySettingsHolder { @Volatile private var settings = DeliverySettings(499, 5_000) fun refresh(office: HeadOffice) { val s = office.fetch() settings = DeliverySettings(s.feeCents, s.freeAboveCents) // 2. build a new one, 3. publish it } fun current(): DeliverySettings = settings // 4. one complete version per read } Why both changes? The record alone makes each version safe to read through any race, thanks to its final fields, but a till might keep reading an old reference for a long time. The volatile field alone delivers the reference, but a changeable object behind it could still change under a till. An immutable object behind a volatile reference fixes both. One habit completes it: a till calls current() once per sale and keeps that version for the whole sale.

h: Safe publication, final fields and escaping this · Quiz
x: registry.current is a plain field. The loader stores a RateCard whose fields are all final. What can a request thread that reads registry.current see? null, or a RateCard with the right field values; it may also keep seeing null for a long time A RateCard whose currency is still null Always the latest RateCard, because its fields are final A ClassCastException, because the object is half-built Final fields promise that whoever sees the reference sees the values the constructor set. They don't deliver the reference, so the reader can see null, an older card, or the new one, but never a half-built one. Option 3 mixes up the two promises: final fields make the pages whole, not the delivery. Which of these publishes a new RateCard safely to request threads that call current()? A plain field, with publish marked synchronized and current() not synchronized A volatile field A HashMap field that publish puts the card into A plain field, written after Thread.sleep(100) The volatile write in publish pairs with the volatile read in current(). The half-synchronized version gives the reader no edge, because the reader never takes the lock. A plain HashMap creates no edge either, and a sleep is not an edge at all. A constructor sets all its final fields and then, as its last line, calls bus.register(this). Is that safe? Yes, all the fields are already set Yes, final fields make any publication safe No: the final-field promise starts when the constructor returns, so threads that get the object from the bus get no such promise, and a subclass constructor hasn't run yet No, register can't accept this inside a constructor The freeze happens at the end of the constructor, and this left before that. It often works in practice, which is why the bug survives review. Build the object first, then register it from a factory method. A final class has private final List<Fee> fees;, set with this.fees = fees; from the caller's ArrayList, and no setters. Is it safe to share between threads? Yes, the field is final Yes, as long as it is published through a volatile field No, because List is an interface No: the caller still holds the ArrayList and can change it after the constructor, racing with every reader Final freezes the reference, and the list's contents as they were at the end of the constructor. Later changes through the caller's reference are ordinary unprotected writes to an ArrayList. Copy it with List.copyOf in the constructor. From volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't: a field is volatile Map<String, Rule> rules. A refresher thread calls rules.put(k, v) on the existing HashMap, and request threads call rules.get(k). Is it safe? Yes, the field is volatile No: put never writes the volatile field, it changes a HashMap that isn't safe to use from several threads at once Yes, if the map has fewer than 16 entries Only on x86 Volatile covers the reference stored in the field. put never writes that field, so there's no edge, and a HashMap can corrupt itself when threads use it at the same time. Build a new map and assign it with one volatile write, or use a ConcurrentHashMap.

h: Safe publication, final fields and escaping this · Key terms
x: Publication Storing a reference to an object where another thread can find it. Safe publication Publishing so the reader gets the reference and the object's state together, through a happens-before edge or final fields. Partially constructed object An object a thread can see before the constructor's writes are visible to it. Data race A write and a read of the same field, in different threads, with no happens-before edge between them. Freeze The end of a constructor, after which final fields carry the memory model's special promise. Immutable object Final class, final fields, copied inputs, nothing changeable handed out, no escaping this. Escaping this A constructor letting other code get a reference to the object before the constructor has finished. Defensive copy Copying a changeable input or output so outside code can't change your object through it. An object is published through a plain field. What can a reader that sees the reference find inside it? Default values (0, false, null) in its non-final fields, because the reference may become visible before the constructor's writes. What do final fields guarantee? A thread that sees the reference after the constructor finished sees the final fields, and what they point to, as the constructor left them, even through a data race. Do final fields make the reference to the object visible to other threads? No. You still need a safe way to publish it, such as a volatile field, for readers to see the reference at all. Name a safe way to publish that needs no volatile and no lock. A static initializer, such as static final RateCard DEFAULT = new RateCard(...). The JVM runs class initialization under a lock. A constructor calls bus.register(this). What's the fix? Let the constructor only set fields. Build the object in a static factory method, then register it, then return it. What does a Kotlin val compile to? A private final field (plus a getter). A var gives a field that isn't final. Is this.fees = fees; enough for an immutable class with a list? No. Copy it (List.copyOf(fees)), or the caller can still change the list under your readers.

h: Safe publication, final fields and escaping this · Go deeper
x: The final-field promise has a few edges worth knowing. It covers what the constructor set, and what the final fields point to, as of the freeze. If you change an object that a final field points to after the constructor, those later changes get no promise. That's why "effectively immutable" objects, objects nobody changes after publishing although nothing stops them, still need a seal, while truly immutable objects don't. Reflection can break final. Reflection is the part of Java that lets code look at and change classes and fields while the program runs. Some frameworks have long used it to write final fields after construction (Field.setAccessible(true), then set), and the memory model gives such writes almost no guarantees. JDK 26 starts closing that door with JEP 500, "Prepare to Make Final Mean Final". By default it prints a warning when reflection changes a final field, and a later release is planned to make that an error unless you allow it. Libraries that turn objects into bytes and back, and tools that build fake objects for tests, are the usual sources of these warnings. The static-initializer seal works because class initialization is itself a careful hand-over. The JVM initializes each class once, under a lock, and any thread that then uses the class is guaranteed to see what the static initializer wrote. The next lesson builds lazy initialization on exactly that. Aleksey Shipilëv's "Safe Publication and Safe Initialization in Java" separates the two ideas this lesson combines: safe publication (the seal) and safe initialization (final fields). It also measures what each one costs.

h: Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders · Checking twice without volatile hands out a half-built table
x: Checking twice without volatile: the lock-free fast path can hand out a table that isn't null and is still empty, until volatile hangs the OPEN sign last Every payment card number starts with six digits, called the BIN, that say which bank issued the card. The shop's program keeps a CardBinTable from those six digits to the bank's name. Loading it means reading a big file, which takes about 50 ms, and some runs of the program never need it at all. So the program builds it on first use. That's called lazy initialization: building something the first time it's needed, instead of at startup. Here's the version most people write first: Java // Naive: check, then act private static CardBinTable instance; static CardBinTable instance() { if (instance == null) { // check: is the stockroom open? instance = new CardBinTable(); // act: two threads can both get here } return instance; } Kotlin // Naive: check, then act private var instance: CardBinTable? = null fun instance(): CardBinTable { if (instance == null) { // check: is the stockroom open? instance = CardBinTable() // act: two threads can both get here } return instance!! } That's the check-then-act race from Race conditions: a check, then an action, with a gap between them that another thread can use. Two threads can both see null, and both build a table. Here that wastes 50 ms. With something that opens a network connection, one connection leaks. There's a second bug, from Safe publication: the table is published through a plain field, so a reader can see the reference before the constructor's writes. Marking the method synchronized fixes both. Its lock, the thing that lets one thread at a time into a piece of code, makes the check and the build one step. It's correct, and often good enough. In the shop, it's one key on a hook by the counter: every assistant takes the key before going near the stockroom, all day, even when the door has stood open since the morning. Every caller takes the lock on every call, for a value that never changes after the first one. So programmers came up with double-checked locking (DCL for short): glance at the door first, and take the key only if it's shut. Java // Broken: double-checked locking without volatile static CardBinTable instance() { if (instance == null) { // 1. first check, no lock synchronized (CardBinTable.class) { if (instance == null) { // 2. second check, under the lock instance = new CardBinTable(); } } } return instance; // a plain read on the fast path } Kotlin // Broken: double-checked locking without @Volatile private val lock = Any() fun instance(): CardBinTable { if (instance == null) { // 1. first check, no lock synchronized(lock) { if (instance == null) { // 2. second check, under the lock instance = CardBinTable() } } } return instance!! // a plain read on the fast path } The lock and the second check do stop two builds: one thread at a time gets past the lock, and whoever comes second finds the table there. The fast path, the first check that takes no lock, is the problem. A thread that finds instance != null never takes the lock. So no happens-before edge, the link that guarantees one thread sees another's writes, connects its read to the builder's writes. As in Safe publication, the JIT (the compiler inside the JVM that turns busy code into machine code) and the processor may let the reference out before the constructor's field writes. That thread can return a table that isn't null and is still empty. The door is open, and the lights are off. jcstress, the OpenJDK tool that runs tiny tests on several threads at once, millions of times, has a sample of exactly this, Singleton_07_BrokenNonVolatileDCL. Two threads ask a non-volatile DCL for a singleton, an object meant to exist once, whose data field isn't final. Here is the run recorded in the sample, on an AArch64 machine, a 64-bit ARM one: RESULT SAMPLES FREQ EXPECT DESCRIPTION data1, data1 1,470,891,960 63.17% Acceptable Trivial. data1, null-data 1,124,329 0.05% Interesting Data races. data2, data2 855,805,003 36.75% Acceptable Trivial. null-data, data2 665,052 0.03% Interesting Data races. About 1.8 million of 2.3 billion callers got a singleton that wasn't null and carried no data. When the sample made the data field final, there were no failures at all, on x86_64 or AArch64, because final fields arrive whole through any race. That's why broken DCL so often seems to work: many such objects happen to have only final fields, and x86 machines (the Intel and AMD kind) rarely show the reordering. The simulator below lets you play the bad order by hand. Checking twice without volatile can hand out an object that looks finished and isn't. The fast path needs an edge. One word gives it one. jcstress sample Singleton_07_BrokenNonVolatileDCL, with its recorded results read

h: Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders · Making the double check correct: one volatile field
x: Make the field volatile, a field whose reads always see the latest write, and double-checked locking is correct. That has been true since Java 5. Java 5 rewrote the memory model, the rules for what one thread sees of another thread's writes (JSR-133), and gave volatile its release and acquire meaning. In the stockroom, volatile turns the door into a sign. The assistant who opens the room hangs up the OPEN sign only after the lights are on and the covers are off. The other assistants trust the sign, not a glance through the door. Where the picture breaks: in a real shop you'd notice a dark room the moment you walked in. In the JVM, a half-built object looks exactly like a finished one. The reference isn't null, and nothing warns you that its fields are still empty. DCL's real job is a lazy field that belongs to one object, so here is that version. For a static field, the next section has something simpler. Java // Fixed: double-checked locking on a volatile field class CardBinTableProvider { private volatile CardBinTable table; CardBinTable table() { CardBinTable t = table; // 1. fast path: one volatile read if (t != null) return t; synchronized (this) { // 2. slow path: one thread at a time t = table; // 3. check again: another thread may have won if (t == null) { t = new CardBinTable(); table = t; // 4. a volatile write publishes the finished table } return t; } } } Kotlin // Fixed: double-checked locking on a @Volatile field class CardBinTableProvider { @Volatile private var table: CardBinTable? = null fun table(): CardBinTable { table?.let { return it } // 1. fast path: one volatile read synchronized(this) { // 2. slow path: one thread at a time table?.let { return it } // 3. check again: another thread may have won val t = CardBinTable() table = t // 4. a volatile write publishes the finished table return t } } } Let's read it in order. First we read the field once, into a local. If the table is there, we're done, and that's what nearly every call does. If not, we take the lock, read the field again, and build the table only if it's still missing. Finally, one volatile write publishes it. The edge is the one from volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't. The volatile write in step 4 is a release: it sends everything written before it along with it. The volatile read in step 1 is an acquire: when it sees that write, it receives all of it. So a thread whose read finds the table sees everything the builder wrote before step 4, including every field the constructor set. The sign goes up last, so whoever sees the sign finds the lights on. Three details matter. Read the field once, into a local. A final return table would be a second volatile read. That's still correct, but the local keeps the fast path to one read. Joshua Bloch's Effective Java (item 83) writes it the same way. Both checks matter. Drop the first and you've rebuilt the synchronized method. Drop the second and every thread that queued at the lock waits politely for its turn, then builds a table of its own. The Try it shows that one. Null needs care. DCL uses null to mean "not built yet", so an initializer that returns null runs again on every call. Kotlin's lazy uses a sentinel instead, a private marker object that only means "not built yet". If the constructor throws, nothing is stored, so the next caller tries again. Keep that in mind, because the holder class in the next section behaves differently. Double-checked locking is correct only on a volatile field. Read it once, and check it twice. That's a lot of care for one field. For a static field, the JVM will take all of it off your hands. Break the double check two ways Run DclDemo (Java or Kotlin) with the command below. Eight threads ask for the card table at the same moment, and loading it takes 50 ms. Delete the line marked try deleting this line. Predict the output, then run it. Put the line back. Remove volatile (@Volatile in Kotlin). Predict, then run. DclDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l05; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Eight threads ask a hand-written double-checked lazy for the same value at the same moment. Edit it and rerun. */ public class DclDemo { static final class LazyCardTable { private volatile Object table; // try: remove volatile private final AtomicInteger loads; LazyCardTable(AtomicInteger loads) { this.loads = loads; } Object get() { Object t = table; // 1. fast path: one volatile read, no lock if (t != null) return t; synchronized (this) { // 2. slow path: one thread at a time t = table; // 3. check again: another thread may have won if (t != null) return t; // (try deleting this line) loads.incrementAndGet(); sleep(50); // reading the card table from a big file t = new Object(); table = t; // 4. volatile write publishes the table return t; } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int round = 1; round <= 3; round++) { AtomicInteger loads = new AtomicInteger(); LazyCardTable lazy = new LazyCardTable(loads); Set<Object> seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); CountDownLatch ready = new CountDownLatch(8), go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { ready.countDown(); try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } seen.add(lazy.get()); }); t.start(); threads.add(t); } ready.await(); go.countDown(); for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); System.out.printf("round %d: table loaded %d time(s), threads saw %d distinct table(s)%n", round, loads.get(), seen.size()); } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l05.DclDemo labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l05/DclDemo.java DclDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l05 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread /** Eight threads ask a hand-written double-checked lazy for the same value at the same moment. Edit it and rerun. */ private class LazyCardTable(private val loads: AtomicInteger) { @Volatile private var table: Any? = null // try: remove @Volatile fun get(): Any { val t = table // 1. fast path: one volatile read, no lock if (t != null) return t synchronized(this) { // 2. slow path: one thread at a time val again = table // 3. check again: another thread may have won if (again != null) return again // (try deleting this line) loads.incrementAndGet() Thread.sleep(50) // reading the card table from a big file val fresh = Any() table = fresh // 4. volatile write publishes the table return fresh } } } fun main() { for (round in 1..3) { val loads = AtomicInteger() val lazy = LazyCardTable(loads) val seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet<Any>() val ready = CountDownLatch(8) val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { thread { ready.countDown() go.await() seen += lazy.get() } } ready.await() go.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } println("round $round: table loaded ${loads.get()} time(s), threads saw ${seen.size} distinct table(s)") } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l05.DclDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l05/DclDemo.kt The correct version loads the table once per round, and all eight threads get the same table. Without the second check, it loads 8 times and hands out 8 different tables: each thread that queued at the lock builds its own. Without volatile, the output doesn't change at all. On an x86 laptop the missing edge almost never shows, so no run of this program can prove the code correct. That's the trap of broken double-checked locking: you need a stress tool like jcstress, ideally on an ARM machine, to see it fail.

h: Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders · Letting the JVM lock for you: the holder class idiom
x: For a static singleton, one object for the whole program, you don't need DCL at all. The JVM already has a lazy, thread-safe, run-once mechanism: class initialization. A class is initialized right before its first active use: creating an instance, calling a static method, or reading a static field that isn't a compile-time constant (Java Language Specification, section 12.4). A compile-time constant is a value the compiler can work out on its own, such as static final int MAX = 3. Initializing it means running its static initializers, once: the assignments to its static fields and its static { } blocks. The JVM does that under a lock of its own, one per class, and every thread that uses the class afterwards sees what the initializer wrote. That's the first seal from Safe publication. In the shop, this is the building's own rule. The landlord holds the only key to each room. The first time anyone asks for a room, the landlord opens it, and everyone else who asks meanwhile waits at the door until it's ready. The JVM is that landlord, a strict doorman: it lets one thread run the initializer and makes the others wait. The holder class idiom puts the instance in a small nested class, so building it waits for the first call that touches that class: Java public final class CardBinTable { private CardBinTable() { /* read the big BIN file */ } private static final class Holder { // not initialized until instance() touches it static final CardBinTable INSTANCE = new CardBinTable(); } public static CardBinTable instance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; // the first call initializes Holder, once, under the JVM's lock } } Kotlin class CardBinTable private constructor() { private object Holder { // an object is initialized on first access val INSTANCE = CardBinTable() } companion object { fun instance(): CardBinTable = Holder.INSTANCE } } Your code has no volatile and no lock. The Kotlin version uses a private nested object, which is initialized on first access, like the Java holder class. The jcstress sample Singleton_09_Holder notes that in hot code the JIT will likely drop the initialization check altogether, so instance() becomes a single field read. The holder has three limits. It only works for statics: one instance per class, never one per object. The constructor can't take arguments you only know while the program runs. And it never retries. If the initializer throws, the first caller gets ExceptionInInitializerError, and every later caller gets NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class CardBinTable$Holder, until the program restarts. The doorman has a long memory: a room that failed to open once stays shut for good. So keep anything that can fail, such as a network connection, out of a holder. An enum gives you the same guarantee: enum CardBinTable { INSTANCE; ... } is built by the enum's own static initializer. Effective Java recommends it for singletons, because serialization (turning objects into bytes and back) and reflection (code that inspects and builds objects while the program runs) can't create a second instance. In Kotlin, an object declaration is the same idea, and the Kotlin docs say its initialization is thread-safe and done on first access. One surprise: lazy here means on first use of the class, not of the instance. A plain static final INSTANCE in a class with other static methods is built the first time any of them runs. A Kotlin companion object is initialized together with its class. The holder exists to separate the two, and the Try it shows exactly when each one is built. For one object per program, let class initialization do the locking. Keep anything that can fail out of it. Statics are covered. For a lazy field on an object, Kotlin has a one-word answer, and it turns out to be an old friend. When is each singleton built? Read HolderIdiomDemo. It has three versions of the card table: an eager static final, a holder, and an enum (an object in Kotlin). Each one prints a line when it's built. Before you run it, write down after which numbered step each built line will appear. Run it, Java first, then Kotlin. HolderIdiomDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l05; /** When does each singleton get built? Watch the order of the lines. */ public class HolderIdiomDemo { // eager: built when the class is initialized, by the first use of anything static in it static final class EagerBins { static final EagerBins INSTANCE = new EagerBins(); private EagerBins() { System.out.println(" EagerBins built"); } static int tableSize() { return 3; } } // holder idiom: built when Holder is initialized, by the first call to instance() static final class LazyBins { private LazyBins() { System.out.println(" LazyBins built"); } private static final class Holder { static final LazyBins INSTANCE = new LazyBins(); } static LazyBins instance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; } static int tableSize() { return 3; } } // enum singleton: built when the enum class is initialized enum EnumBins { INSTANCE; EnumBins() { System.out.println(" EnumBins.INSTANCE built"); } static int tableSize() { return 3; } } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("1. call EagerBins.tableSize()"); EagerBins.tableSize(); System.out.println("2. call LazyBins.tableSize()"); LazyBins.tableSize(); System.out.println("3. call LazyBins.instance()"); LazyBins.instance(); System.out.println("4. call LazyBins.instance() again"); LazyBins.instance(); System.out.println("5. call EnumBins.tableSize()"); EnumBins.tableSize(); } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l05.HolderIdiomDemo labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l05/HolderIdiomDemo.java HolderIdiomDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l05 /** When does each singleton get built? Watch the order of the lines. */ // eager: a companion object is initialized together with its class private class EagerBins private constructor() { init { println(" EagerBins built") } companion object { val INSTANCE = EagerBins() fun tableSize() = 3 } } // holder idiom in Kotlin: a private nested object is initialized on first access private class LazyBins private constructor() { init { println(" LazyBins built") } private object Holder { val INSTANCE = LazyBins() } companion object { fun instance(): LazyBins = Holder.INSTANCE fun tableSize() = 3 } } // Kotlin's own answer: an object declaration, built on first access and thread-safe private object BinTable { init { println(" BinTable built") } fun tableSize() = 3 } fun main() { println("1. call EagerBins.tableSize()") EagerBins.tableSize() println("2. call LazyBins.tableSize()") LazyBins.tableSize() println("3. call LazyBins.instance()") LazyBins.instance() println("4. call LazyBins.instance() again") LazyBins.instance() println("5. call BinTable.tableSize()") BinTable.tableSize() } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l05.HolderIdiomDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l05/HolderIdiomDemo.kt EagerBins built appears right after step 1: calling a static method initialized the class, and that built INSTANCE. LazyBins built appears only after step 3, the first instance() call, because tableSize() in step 2 never touched Holder, and it doesn't appear again in step 4. The enum (or the Kotlin object) is built in step 5, the first time anything in it runs. Class initialization is lazy per class; the holder gives the instance a class of its own. jcstress sample Singleton_09_Holder read

h: Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders · Kotlin's by lazy: the same double check, in three modes
x: val x by lazy { ... } is the double-checked locking from earlier in this lesson, written once in Kotlin's standard library. The property compiles to a private final kotlin.Lazy x$delegate field, and its getter calls getValue() on that delegate, the object that does the work for the property. The default mode is LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED. Its implementation class, SynchronizedLazyImpl, has a volatile value field, a fast path that reads it once, and a synchronized block with a second check. It adds three things to the version you'd write by hand. A sentinel instead of null, so a null result is kept too. A retry: the docs promise that if the initializer throws, it runs again on the next access. And it drops the initializer after the first run, so whatever the lambda captured can be cleaned up by the garbage collector, the part of the JVM that frees memory nobody uses. Here's a Till, one of the shop's cash registers, which several threads share. It connects to its receipt printer on first use, which is slow and can fail, and it reads the list of public holidays, which is cheap: Java // Java has no by lazy: a volatile double check stands in for SYNCHRONIZED, a compareAndSet for PUBLICATION final class Till { private final Shop shop; private volatile ReceiptPrinter printer; private final AtomicReference<Set<LocalDate>> holidays = new AtomicReference<>(); Till(Shop shop) { this.shop = shop; } ReceiptPrinter printer() { ReceiptPrinter p = printer; if (p != null) return p; synchronized (this) { if (printer == null) printer = shop.connectPrinter(); return printer; } } Set<LocalDate> holidays() { Set<LocalDate> h = holidays.get(); if (h != null) return h; holidays.compareAndSet(null, parseHolidays(HOLIDAYS)); // losers throw their result away return holidays.get(); } } Kotlin class Till(private val shop: Shop) { val printer: ReceiptPrinter by lazy { // SYNCHRONIZED: runs once, others wait shop.connectPrinter() // slow, and it can fail } val holidays: Set<LocalDate> by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION) { parseHolidays(HOLIDAYS) // cheap and pure: may run twice, one result wins } } The Kotlin version is two properties. The Java version spells out what each mode does, and it shows that lazy is no magic: a volatile double check, or a compare-and-set, the "update it only if nobody beat me to it" call from Atomics and compare-and-set. There are three modes: Mode The initializer runs Use it for SYNCHRONIZED (default) once; other callers wait on a lock anything slow or with side effects PUBLICATION maybe on several threads at once; one result wins cheap work with no side effects NONE with no synchronization at all values that never leave one thread Keep the default unless you have a reason. PUBLICATION fits a cheap, pure initializer when you'd rather waste a little work than make anyone wait. The losers' results are thrown away without any cleanup, so never use it for work with side effects, changes outside the value itself, such as opening a connection. NONE fits code that only one thread ever runs. Never put it on a property that several threads share: the docs call the result unspecified, and the Try it shows eight threads getting eight different values. SYNCHRONIZED has two traps. The lock is held while the initializer runs, so a 120 ms call to a slow web service inside lazy makes every caller who arrives meanwhile wait up to 120 ms. And by default the lock is the Lazy object itself; the docs warn that synchronizing on it from your own code can cause a deadlock. Keep lazy's default mode unless you have a reason. Never share a NONE lazy between threads. The figure sums up the choice. The simplest answer is often not to be lazy at all: if nearly every call needs the value, build it at startup, and a failure shows up when the program starts instead of in front of a customer. And every tool in this lesson rests on the same pair from volatile: a release write and an acquire read. Next, we'll take that pair apart and see what else it can do. Race the three lazy modes For each mode, predict how many times the 50 ms initializer runs, and how many different values eight threads see. Run the Kotlin demo with the command below, then the Java twin, which builds the three modes by hand. Change the sleep from 50 to 0 and run it a few times. Which numbers move? LazyModesDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l05 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread /** Eight threads read the same lazy value at the same moment, once for each LazyThreadSafetyMode. */ fun main() { for (mode in LazyThreadSafetyMode.entries) { val runs = AtomicInteger() val cardTable: Lazy<Any> = lazy(mode) { runs.incrementAndGet() Thread.sleep(50) // a slow initializer, like reading the card table from a big file Any() } val seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet<Any>() val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { thread { go.await() seen += cardTable.value } } go.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } println("%-12s initializer ran %d time(s), threads saw %d distinct value(s)".format(mode, runs.get(), seen.size)) } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l05.LazyModesDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l05/LazyModesDemo.kt LazyModesDemoJava.java package workbench.jmm.l05; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference; import java.util.function.Supplier; // Java has no `by lazy`. These are the closest Java equivalents of Kotlin's three LazyThreadSafetyMode values. /** Eight threads read the same lazy value at the same moment, once for each kind of lazy. */ public class LazyModesDemoJava { // like SYNCHRONIZED: double-checked locking, so the initializer runs once static Supplier<Object> synchronizedLazy(Supplier<Object> init) { return new Supplier<>() { private volatile Object value; @Override public Object get() { Object v = value; if (v != null) return v; synchronized (this) { if (value == null) value = init.get(); return value; } } }; } // like PUBLICATION: any thread may compute, and the first compareAndSet wins static Supplier<Object> publicationLazy(Supplier<Object> init) { AtomicReference<Object> ref = new AtomicReference<>(); return () -> { Object v = ref.get(); if (v != null) return v; ref.compareAndSet(null, init.get()); return ref.get(); }; } // like NONE: no synchronization at all, only safe on one thread static Supplier<Object> unsafeLazy(Supplier<Object> init) { Object[] box = new Object[1]; return () -> { if (box[0] == null) box[0] = init.get(); return box[0]; }; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { race("SYNCHRONIZED", LazyModesDemoJava::synchronizedLazy); race("PUBLICATION", LazyModesDemoJava::publicationLazy); race("NONE", LazyModesDemoJava::unsafeLazy); } interface LazyFactory { Supplier<Object> make(Supplier<Object> init); } static void race(String name, LazyFactory factory) throws InterruptedException { AtomicInteger runs = new AtomicInteger(); Supplier<Object> cardTable = factory.make(() -> { runs.incrementAndGet(); sleep(50); // a slow initializer, like reading the card table from a big file return new Object(); }); Set<Object> seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } seen.add(cardTable.get()); }); t.start(); threads.add(t); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); System.out.printf("%-12s initializer ran %d time(s), threads saw %d distinct value(s)%n", name, runs.get(), seen.size()); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l05.LazyModesDemoJava labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l05/LazyModesDemoJava.java SYNCHRONIZED: 1 run, 1 value. PUBLICATION: up to 8 runs (here all 8, because every thread started before the first one finished) but 1 value, because the first compare-and-set won and everyone returns its result. NONE: 8 runs and 8 values, each thread keeping its own. With no sleep, PUBLICATION and NONE usually run fewer times, because some threads arrive after the first one has finished. The bug in NONE didn't go away. The window just got smaller. Pick the simplest tool that fits. Many values that are built lazily should simply be built at startup. x: One lazy value per key: computeIfAbsent in Java, and the getOrPut trap in Kotlin IssuerClients.java class IssuerClients { private final ConcurrentMap<String, IssuerClient> clients = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); IssuerClient clientFor(String issuerId) { // connect runs at most once per missing key; other callers for that key wait for it return clients.computeIfAbsent(issuerId, this::connect); } private IssuerClient connect(String issuerId) { return new IssuerClient(issuerId); // opens a connection } } IssuerClients.kt class IssuerClients { private val clients = ConcurrentHashMap<String, IssuerClient>() // looks the same, isn't: two threads can both run connect() for one key fun clientForRacy(issuerId: String): IssuerClient = clients.getOrPut(issuerId) { connect(issuerId) } // the same guarantee as Java: call the JDK method fun clientFor(issuerId: String): IssuerClient = clients.computeIfAbsent(issuerId) { connect(it) } private fun connect(issuerId: String): IssuerClient = IssuerClient(issuerId) // opens a connection } Sometimes you need one lazy value per key, such as one connection per card issuer, the bank that issued a card. Both versions keep the connections in a ConcurrentHashMap. Kotlin's getOrPut reads like computeIfAbsent, and on a concurrent map it never replaces a value that is already there. But its docs say the lambda may run even if the key is already in the map. So two threads can both connect, every caller ends up with the same client, and the losing connection is dropped without being closed. computeIfAbsent is the JDK's atomic version: the function runs at most once per missing key. Its Javadoc asks you to keep that function short, because other updates to the map can wait while it runs. For a slow connect, store a lazy in the map, clients.computeIfAbsent(id) { lazy { connect(id) } }.value, so the map is busy only while the cheap Lazy object is made.

h: Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders · Worked example
x: Make lazily downloaded discount rules safe The shop's program downloads the day's discount rules from head office on first use. The download takes 300 ms, and sometimes it fails. When the shop opens, 200 payments arrive at once. Name the two bugs, then choose a tool before you read on. public class DiscountRulesProvider { private final RulesClient rulesClient; private DiscountRules rules; // a plain field public DiscountRulesProvider(RulesClient rulesClient) { this.rulesClient = rulesClient; } public DiscountRules rules() { // called by every payment thread if (rules == null) { rules = rulesClient.download(); // 300 ms, and it can fail } return rules; } } class DiscountRulesProvider(private val rulesClient: RulesClient) { private var rules: DiscountRules? = null // a plain field fun rules(): DiscountRules { // called by every payment thread if (rules == null) { rules = rulesClient.download() // 300 ms, and it can fail } return rules!! } } First, check-then-act: every payment in the first 300 ms sees null and starts its own download. Second, a plain field: a payment thread can see the reference before the rules' fields. Now the tool. Not the holder: the field belongs to one object, and a failed download must be tried again on the next payment, not turned into NoClassDefFoundError. A volatile double check fits, and in Kotlin by lazy is that double check. Write it with a label on each step. In Kotlin the whole thing is one line, and the retry after a failure comes from the standard library. public class DiscountRulesProvider { private final RulesClient rulesClient; private volatile DiscountRules rules; // 1. volatile: the fast path needs the edge public DiscountRulesProvider(RulesClient rulesClient) { this.rulesClient = rulesClient; } public DiscountRules rules() { DiscountRules r = rules; // 2. fast path: one volatile read if (r != null) return r; synchronized (this) { // 3. slow path: one download at a time r = rules; if (r == null) { // 4. check again: someone may have won r = rulesClient.download(); // if this throws, nothing is stored rules = r; // 5. publish the finished rules } return r; } } } class DiscountRulesProvider(private val rulesClient: RulesClient) { // SYNCHRONIZED by default: steps 1 to 5 of the Java version, plus a retry if download() throws val rules: DiscountRules by lazy { rulesClient.download() } } Ask one more question: does every payment need the rules anyway? Then lazy buys you a slow first payment, and a failure you discover on the first customer instead of at startup. Download the rules when the program starts and publish them through a volatile field, as in Safe publication. Keep lazy for values that some calls never need.
