h: Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders · Key terms
x: Lazy initialization Building a value the first time it's needed instead of at startup. Double-checked locking Check without a lock, then lock and check again before building. Correct only with a volatile field. Fast path The first check in double-checked locking, which reads the field without taking the lock. Holder class idiom Keep the instance in a private nested class, so the JVM builds it on the first call, once, under its class-initialization lock. Class initialization The JVM running a class's static initializers once, before the class's first active use. Enum singleton A one-constant enum used as a singleton; serialization and reflection can't make a second one. Sentinel A private marker object meaning "not set yet", so a real null result can be kept too. LazyThreadSafetyMode Kotlin's choice for lazy: SYNCHRONIZED (once, others wait), PUBLICATION (maybe many runs, one result), NONE (one thread only). Why is double-checked locking without volatile broken? The fast path reads the field without the lock, so it has no happens-before edge to the write. A thread can see the reference before the constructor's writes and use a half-built object. What one change makes double-checked locking correct? Declare the field volatile (@Volatile in Kotlin). The volatile write publishes the finished object; the volatile read on the fast path sees it whole. In the holder class idiom, what does the locking? The JVM's class initialization. Holder is initialized once, under a JVM lock, the first time Holder.INSTANCE is read. A holder's initializer throws on the first call. What does the second call get? NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class ...$Holder. Class initialization never retries; only a restart does. What does val x by lazy { ... } compile to, and which mode does it use? A private final kotlin.Lazy x$delegate field. The default mode is SYNCHRONIZED: double-checked locking on a volatile field. LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION vs SYNCHRONIZED? PUBLICATION may run the initializer on several threads at once and keeps one result. SYNCHRONIZED runs it once while the other callers wait. Kotlin concurrentMap.getOrPut(k) { connect() }: can connect() run twice for one key? Yes. It never replaces a value, but the lambda may run on two threads. computeIfAbsent runs it at most once per missing key.

h: Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders · Go deeper
x: A lazy object can itself reach another thread through a race, and then its own fields matter. Kotlin's SynchronizedLazyImpl keeps its initializer in a field that isn't final, because it sets that field to null after the first run. The jcstress sample Lazy_01_BrokenFactory shows what a non-final factory field costs. On AArch64, the sample handed the lazy object itself to another thread through a plain field. That thread sometimes saw the factory as null and failed with an internal error, and in one sample the factory ran twice. by lazy doesn't hit this in practice, because the compiler keeps the Lazy in a private final x$delegate field, and final fields are safe once the owner's constructor has finished. If you write your own lazy wrapper and also want to drop the initializer, Lazy_05_WrapperOneShot shows the fix: a final field pointing to a small wrapper that holds the factory. Class initialization has one more rule worth knowing. Reading a static final field that is a compile-time constant, such as static final int MAX_BINS = 3, doesn't initialize the class at all: javac copies the value into the caller. That's why a holder only triggers on fields like INSTANCE, whose value is computed while the program runs. The JDK is growing its own answer. JDK 25 previewed stable values (JEP 502). JDK 26 renamed the idea lazy constants (JEP 526, a second preview), and JDK 27 has a third preview (JEP 531). It's a JDK type for a value that is computed at most once and that the JIT may then treat as a constant, which a volatile field never can be. It's a preview API, a feature you switch on with --enable-preview and that may still change, so it stays out of these labs. It's worth following if you write libraries. Finally, the history. "The Double-Checked Locking is Broken" declaration, signed by memory model researchers and JVM engineers before Java 5, explains why no clever trick could save double-checked locking under the old memory model. The JSR-133 memory model of Java 5 fixed it by giving volatile its acquire and release meaning, which is the fix you used today.

h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · A VarHandle puts the memory mode on each access, not on the field
x: First, the parcels in Java terms. A thread is one path of work running beside others in the same program, and each read or write of a shared field is a parcel that one thread sends another. The courier is everything in between. It's the JIT, the compiler inside the JVM that turns busy code into machine code and may move or skip accesses. It's also the processor, whose cores, the parts that each run one thread, may hold writes back for a while. The label on one read or write is called its access mode, and it says what the courier must do for that access. A volatile field puts one label on the field itself: every read and every write of it gets the strongest handling, whether it needs it or not. That's usually right, and it's simple. But some code needs less. Picture a one-item mailbox between two threads that hand over millions of payments a second. The producer, the thread that fills the mailbox, only needs its data to arrive with the item for the consumer, the thread that empties it. Yet on x86, the Intel and AMD kind of processor, every volatile write also waits for the core's store buffer to drain. The store buffer, met in Why your loop never stops, is a small queue where a core parks its writes before other cores can see them. Millions of times a second, that wait adds up. A VarHandle puts the label on each access instead. VarHandles came in JDK 9, with JEP 193. (A JEP, or JDK Enhancement Proposal, is the public design document for one JDK feature.) A VarHandle is a typed handle to one field or array element, with one method per label: get and set (plain), getOpaque and setOpaque, getAcquire and setRelease, getVolatile and setVolatile. It also has atomic updates such as compareAndSet, getAndAdd and getAndSet. Here's one for the lab's SettlementSlot, a one-item mailbox whose item field holds a payment record: Java final class SettlementSlot { private static final VarHandle ITEM; // 1. one handle per field, static final static { try { ITEM = MethodHandles.lookup() // 2. a lookup that can see the private field .findVarHandle(SettlementSlot.class, "item", Settlement.class); } catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) { throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(e); } } private Settlement item; // 3. a plain field: the label goes on each access Settlement peek() { return (Settlement) ITEM.getAcquire(this); // 4. the object first, then cast the result } } Kotlin class SettlementSlot { private var item: Settlement? = null // 3. a plain field: the label goes on each access fun peek(): Settlement? = ITEM.getAcquire(this) as Settlement? // 4. the object first, then cast the result companion object { // 1. one handle per field; 2. looked up inside the class, so it can see the private field private val ITEM: VarHandle = MethodHandles.lookup() .findVarHandle(SettlementSlot::class.java, "item", Settlement::class.java) } } Both versions follow the same four steps. First we look up a handle, once, through MethodHandles.lookup(), which can see the class's private fields. We keep it in a static final field; in Kotlin, a private val in the companion object compiles to exactly that. The field itself stays plain. Every access goes through the handle, which takes the object first and needs a cast on its result. Three details make this work. Keep the handle in a static final field. The JIT treats a static final as a constant, so it can compile ITEM.getAcquire(this) down to one load plus whatever barrier the label needs. A barrier is an instruction that stops the processor from reordering around it. The access methods are signature-polymorphic: the compiler takes the call's real types from the arguments you pass and the cast on the result, and the VarHandle checks them when the call runs. Kotlin does the same and takes the return type from the as cast. Wrong types fail at runtime, with WrongMethodTypeException or ClassCastException. The compiler, usually so keen to complain early, waves these calls straight through. The label at the access wins over the field's declaration. The Javadoc says a plain get reads a field as plain "even if that field is declared volatile", and it warns that mixing modes on one field needs "extreme care". So keep the field plain, and send every access through the handle. You don't need all this setup to use the labels. Since JDK 9, AtomicInteger, AtomicLong and AtomicReference have getPlain, getOpaque, getAcquire, setRelease and friends. The old lazySet, from JDK 6, is setRelease under another name. What a VarHandle saves is the extra object: the label works on a plain field of your own class. Check yourself: a field is declared volatile, and a hot loop reads it through ITEM.get(this). Is that read volatile? No. The label at the access wins, so it's a plain read, and the JIT may lift it out of the loop, exactly as in Why your loop never stops. A VarHandle access gets the label you name, whatever the field says. Keep the field plain, and always go through the handle. We have four labels to choose from. Next, we'll line them up and see what each one promises. JEP 193: Variable Handles read VarHandle (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · Four access modes, from weakest to strongest: plain, opaque, acquire/release, volatile
x: Four access modes as a ladder of parcel labels: each adds one promise, and release/acquire is weaker than volatile, not just cheaper The VarHandle Javadoc defines the modes as a ladder. Each label keeps every promise of the ones below it and adds one more. Plain (get, set) is no label at all: an ordinary field access. It's atomic for references and for values of 32 bits or less, which means a read never sees half of one write and half of another. It promises nothing about what other threads see, or when. The JIT may read it once for a whole loop, which was the hang in Why your loop never stops. Opaque (getOpaque, setOpaque) means "deliver for sure, in order, in one piece". It's atomic for long and double too. And it's coherent for that one variable: the JIT must really perform each read and write, in order, so a thread spinning on it eventually sees a new value. It orders nothing else. Writes to other fields can still show up in any order. Acquire and release (getAcquire, setRelease) add a one-way order. Nothing before a release write may move after it, and nothing after an acquire read may move before it. When an acquire read sees the value that a release write stored, the reader also sees everything the writer did before the release. In parcel terms, a release label says "deliver everything I sent before this one first", and a receiver who signs for it with an acquire has all of it. It's a happens-before edge, the link that guarantees one thread sees another's writes, built from one variable, as in Happens-before, the rules that matter. Volatile (getVolatile, setVolatile, or a volatile field) adds a single total order: every thread agrees on one order of all volatile accesses, like registered mail logged in one central book. That's what forbids the store-buffering result, where each thread writes its own variable, then reads the other's and still gets 0. Label What can still go wrong plain a loop never sees the new value; a long arrives in two halves opaque a reader sees the flag before the data it guards acquire/release two threads each write, then both read the other's old value volatile nothing on this list The jcstress samples show each step. (jcstress is the OpenJDK tool that runs tiny tests on several threads at once, millions of times, and counts every result.) In BasicJMM_04_Progress, a plain spin loop, one that checks a field over and over until it changes, is allowed to hang, and an opaque one is not. In BasicJMM_06_Causality, a reader may see the flag without the data when both sides use opaque (0.68% of samples on AArch64, 0 on x86_64), and never with acquire and release. In BasicJMM_07_Consensus, acquire and release still let both threads read 0 (6.18% of samples in the recorded run), and volatile forbids it. Here the parcel picture breaks. Real labels cost the courier more as they get stronger. On x86, plain, opaque, acquire and release accesses all compile to ordinary loads and stores, so those labels mostly hold back the JIT. Only the volatile write adds an instruction, the one that drains the store buffer. The Try it shows what that instruction buys. Each label adds one promise. Pick the lightest label whose promise your code needs, and never a lighter one. The middle label is the one with a job of its own. Next, we'll use it to hand data from one thread to another. Store buffering with four labels Read ModesDemo. It runs the store-buffering test from Why your loop never stops once per access mode, 262,144 trials each: thread A writes x and reads y, thread B writes y and reads x. Predict, for each mode, whether any trial ends with both threads reading 0. Run it (Java or Kotlin). Then explain the opaque line: opaque stops the JIT from reordering, so who is reordering? Thread A runs * {@code x = 1; r1 = y;} and thread B runs {@code y = 1; r2 = x;}. Count the trials where both read 0. */ public class ModesDemo { static final class Pair { int x, y; } static final VarHandle X, Y; static { try { MethodHandles.Lookup lookup = MethodHandles.lookup(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { X.setRelease(s[i], 1); r1[i] = (int) Y.getAcquire(s[i]); }, i -> { Y.setRelease(s[i], 1); r2[i] = (int) X.getAcquire(s[i]); }); return bothZero(r1, r2); Opaque and release/acquire keep the JIT honest, so what you see is the processor's store buffer: each thread's write is still parked in its own core while it reads the other field. h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · Handing data to another thread with release and acquire
x: Release and acquire have one job: handing data from one thread to another. The writer makes plain writes, then one release write. The reader makes one acquire read, and if it sees the new value, it reads the data. Here a day's report goes from one thread to another: Java // writer thread report.total = 1_250_000; // 1. plain writes of the data report.count = 42; READY.setRelease(report, true); // 2. release: the data can't move after this // reader thread if ((boolean) READY.getAcquire(report)) { // 3. acquire: nothing below moves above this publish(report.total, report.count); // 4. sees the data, because it saw the release } Kotlin // writer thread report.total = 1_250_000 // 1. plain writes of the data report.count = 42 READY.setRelease(report, true) // 2. release: the data can't move after this // reader thread if (READY.getAcquire(report) as Boolean) { // 3. acquire: nothing below moves above this publish(report.total, report.count) // 4. sees the data, because it saw the release } Picture the writer filling a box and then putting the release label on the lid. The reader checks the lid with an acquire. If the label is there, everything that went into the box is there too. Four rules keep it correct. Pair them on the same variable. A release of ready and an acquire of done give you nothing. For the same reason, a volatile write and a volatile read of two different fields gave you nothing in Happens-before, the rules that matter. The promise only holds when the acquire reads the released value, or a later one. A reader that still sees false learns nothing, which is fine: it tries again later. Release and acquire don't make a read-modify-write atomic, that is, an update that reads a value and writes a new one based on it, such as count++. When several threads may write and only the first should win, use compareAndSet, the "update it only if nobody beat me to it" call from Atomics and compare-and-set. The Javadoc says it behaves like volatile: it reads the current value as getVolatile and, if that's the expected value, writes as setVolatile. Weaker variants exist, such as compareAndExchangeAcquire and weakCompareAndSetRelease. The weak ones may fail even when the value matches, so they belong inside retry loops. The lab's KillSwitch uses plain compareAndSet. Don't use them for "I write my flag, then I check yours". That's the store-buffering shape from the last section, and it needs volatile, or better, a lock or one compareAndSet on one shared variable. The Try it runs a one-item mailbox for three seconds, with three kinds of access, and checks every transfer it hands over. Here's a run on an x86 machine: plain: stuck after 3 handoffs. A spinning thread stopped seeing the slot change. opaque: 3,303,358 transfers handed over in 3 s, 0 with wrong fields release: 891,845 transfers handed over in 3 s, 0 with wrong fields The plain slot doesn't crash, and it doesn't complain. Its consumer stands at the mailbox forever, looking at the copy of the slot it read once, because the JIT compiled its spin loop to read the field one time only. The opaque slot kept going, since every opaque read really happens, and on x86 its transfers arrived whole. Nothing promises that, though. Opaque orders nothing but the slot itself, so on ARM a transfer is allowed to arrive with its fields still 0. Only release and acquire promise whole transfers everywhere. The counts also show that a three-second demo is no benchmark: here the opaque run handed over more transfers, and your numbers will differ. Why bother, when a volatile field does all this? Because the write side is cheaper. On x86, a release write is a plain store, while a volatile write also drains the store buffer. For a queue that hands over millions of messages a second from one producer, that difference shows up when you measure it. That's the whole case for this label. Release and acquire hand data from one writer through one variable. Pair them on the same field. You've now seen the labels work. The harder questions are when you should use them, and how you would ever know they're right. Hand over transfers three ways Read HandoffDemo. One producer hands bank transfers to one consumer through a one-item slot, for three seconds. There are three slots: ordinary field access, opaque, and release/acquire. Predict for each one: does it keep going, and does the consumer ever see a transfer with the wrong fields? Run it three times: with -Pargs=plain as below, then with -Pargs=opaque, then with no argument (release/acquire). Try the Kotlin twin too. HandoffDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l06; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles; import java.lang.invoke.VarHandle; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; /** * One producer hands transfers to one consumer through a one-item slot, for three seconds. * The argument picks the slot: plain (ordinary field access), opaque, or release (the default). */ public class HandoffDemo { static final class Transfer { long id; long amountCents; } // plain fields on purpose interface Slot { boolean offer(Transfer t); // producer only: false if the slot is still full Transfer poll(); // consumer only: null if the slot is empty } static class Box { Transfer item; } // null means empty static final VarHandle ITEM; static { try { ITEM = MethodHandles.lookup().findVarHandle(Box.class, "item", Transfer.class); } catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) { throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(e); } } static final class PlainSlot extends Box implements Slot { // what ordinary Java code does public boolean offer(Transfer t) { if (item != null) return false; item = t; return true; } public Transfer poll() { Transfer t = item; if (t != null) item = null; return t; } } static final class OpaqueSlot extends Box implements Slot { public boolean offer(Transfer t) { if (ITEM.getOpaque(this) != null) return false; ITEM.setOpaque(this, t); return true; } public Transfer poll() { Transfer t = (Transfer) ITEM.getOpaque(this); if (t != null) ITEM.setOpaque(this, null); return t; } } static final class ReleaseAcquireSlot extends Box implements Slot { public boolean offer(Transfer t) { if (ITEM.getAcquire(this) != null) return false; ITEM.setRelease(this, t); // release: t's fields were written before this return true; } public Transfer poll() { Transfer t = (Transfer) ITEM.getAcquire(this); // acquire: so the consumer sees them if (t != null) ITEM.setRelease(this, null); return t; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "release"; Slot slot = switch (mode) { case "plain" -> new PlainSlot(); case "opaque" -> new OpaqueSlot(); default -> new ReleaseAcquireSlot(); }; AtomicLong handed = new AtomicLong(); // progress, for main to watch AtomicLong wrong = new AtomicLong(); Thread producer = new Thread(() -> { for (long id = 1; ; id++) { Transfer t = new Transfer(); t.id = id; // 1. fill in the message with plain writes t.amountCents = id * 7; while (!slot.offer(t)) { } // 2. spin until the slot is empty, then hand it over } }); Thread consumer = new Thread(() -> { for (long expected = 1; ; expected++) { Transfer t = slot.poll(); while (t == null) t = slot.poll(); // 3. spin until the slot is full if (t.id != expected || t.amountCents != expected * 7) wrong.incrementAndGet(); handed.set(expected); } }); producer.setDaemon(true); // so the JVM can exit even if they spin forever consumer.setDaemon(true); producer.start(); consumer.start(); long last = -1; for (int tick = 0; tick < 4; tick++) { Thread.sleep(750); long now = handed.get(); if (now == last) { System.out.printf("%s: stuck after %,d handoffs. A spinning thread stopped seeing the slot change.%n", mode, now); return; } last = now; } System.out.printf("%s: %,d transfers handed over in 3 s, %,d with wrong fields%n", mode, handed.get(), wrong.get()); } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l06.HandoffDemo -Pargs=plain labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l06/HandoffDemo.java HandoffDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l06 import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles import java.lang.invoke.VarHandle import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import kotlin.concurrent.thread /* * One producer hands transfers to one consumer through a one-item slot, for three seconds. * The argument picks the slot: plain (ordinary property access), opaque, or release (the default). */ private class Transfer { var id = 0L; var amountCents = 0L } // plain fields on purpose private interface Slot { fun offer(t: Transfer): Boolean // producer only: false if the slot is still full fun poll(): Transfer? A spinning thread stopped seeing the slot change.".format(mode, now)) return } last = now } println("%s: %,d transfers handed over in 3 s, %,d with wrong fields".format(mode, handed.get(), wrong.get())) } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l06.HandoffDemoKt -Pargs=plain labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l06/HandoffDemo.kt Release/acquire hands over around a million transfers with 0 wrong. Opaque usually does the same on x86, but nothing orders the transfer's fields before the slot write, so on ARM it is allowed to deliver a transfer whose fields are still 0. The plain slot usually gets stuck within a second: once the JIT compiles a spin loop, it may read the field once and never again. In runs here, the Java version got stuck after 3 hand-overs and the Kotlin version after 32. A plain run that keeps going is allowed too, which is the point: a plain run that works tells you nothing.

h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · When you need access modes, and why only jcstress can test them
x: Almost never in application code. Prefer, in this order: a java.util.concurrent class, such as a BlockingQueue for hand-overs or a ConcurrentHashMap; then a volatile field or an Atomic class such as AtomicLong; then a lock. Reach for VarHandle labels only when three things are true. You're writing a low-level building block, such as a queue. A measurement shows that the cost of volatile, or of an extra Atomic object, matters. And you will test it with jcstress. That describes the people who write java.util.concurrent itself (FutureTask and ConcurrentLinkedQueue both keep their state behind VarHandles), the authors of fast queue libraries, and almost nobody writing an everyday web service. VarHandles are also the supported way out of sun.misc.Unsafe, an internal JDK class that libraries used for years to reach memory directly. JDK 23 deprecated its memory-access methods for removal (JEP 471), and JDK 24 prints a warning the first time code uses them (JEP 498). A library that still uses them is a library you'll be upgrading soon. The bigger problem is testing. A JUnit test, the kind these labs use, can't prove any of this. Your test ran on one kind of processor, after one JIT warm-up, under one load. A green run says that machine didn't produce the bad result that time. The lab's tests check behavior that is the same on every run once the code is right; they can't catch a missing release on x86. jcstress, which Testing and debugging concurrent code introduced, is the honest test. You write a @State class, two or more @Actor methods that run against each other, and an @Outcome for each result, marked ACCEPTABLE, ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING or FORBIDDEN. jcstress runs the actors on fresh state objects many millions of times, in several JVM configurations, and prints how often each result happened. A forbidden result that appears even once fails the test. Two habits make its results worth having. Read the results table, not just pass or fail: an interesting result at 0.01% is a real bug in a busy program. And run it on ARM if you can, on an Apple Silicon laptop or an ARM cloud server. x86 never lets one store pass another, so many ordering bugs simply can't show there. The Try it puts your lab slot under jcstress and shows exactly that. In application code, use java.util.concurrent, volatile, atomics and locks. Leave the lighter labels to building blocks that jcstress has tested. The labels are the bottom of the stack: below them there's only the hardware. From here, the course climbs back up, to tools that run your tasks on threads you never create yourself. Put your slot under jcstress Optional, and it needs Maven (a Java build tool, like the Gradle that runs these labs) and network access. Finish the lab first. Then create a jcstress project with the template command from the jcstress README: mvn archetype:generate -DinteractiveMode=false -DarchetypeGroupId=org.openjdk.jcstress -DarchetypeArtifactId=jcstress-java-test-archetype -DgroupId=org.sample -DartifactId=test -Dversion=1.0 In test/pom.xml, change <javac.target>1.8</javac.target> to 21. The template targets Java 8, and VarHandle needs JDK 9 or later. Copy Settlement.java and your SettlementSlot.java into test/src/main/java/org/sample/ and change their package line to package org.sample;. Replace ConcurrencyTest.java with the test below. Run mvn clean verify, then java -jar target/jcstress.jar -t SlotHandoffTest -m quick -v. Read the results table. Change your slot's setRelease and getAcquire to setOpaque and getOpaque. Predict, rebuild and run again. SlotHandoffTest.java package org.sample; import org.openjdk.jcstress.annotations.*; import org.openjdk.jcstress.infra.results.J_Result; import static org.openjdk.jcstress.annotations.Expect.*; @JCStressTest @Outcome(id = "-1", expect = ACCEPTABLE, desc = "The slot was still empty") @Outcome(id = "8400", expect = ACCEPTABLE, desc = "Saw the whole settlement") @Outcome(id = "0", expect = FORBIDDEN, desc = "Saw the settlement but not its amount") @State public class SlotHandoffTest { final SettlementSlot slot = new SettlementSlot(); @Actor public void producer() { Settlement s = new Settlement(); s.amountCents = 8400; // a plain write... slot.offer(s); // ...then the release } @Actor public void consumer(J_Result r) { Settlement s = slot.poll(); // the acquire r.r1 = (s == null) ? -1 : s.amountCents; } } java -jar target/jcstress.jar -t SlotHandoffTest -m quick -v jcstress prints a table like the ones in its samples. On an x86_64 machine in quick mode, a run here showed -1 (empty) in about 65% of 199 million samples, 8400 in the other 35%, and 0 (forbidden) in none: the test is OK. The all-opaque version also showed 0 forbidden samples on x86_64, in about 133 million. That doesn't make it correct. x86 never lets one store pass another; ARM does, and there the opaque slot is allowed to fail. jcstress is the tool that would show it, if you run it on the right machine. jcstress tests are written in Java, so this step has no Kotlin twin. jcstress: the OpenJDK concurrency stress tests (README and samples) read JEP 498: Warn upon Use of Memory-Access Methods in sun.misc.Unsafe read

h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · Java and Kotlin
x: The same release/acquire hand-over with AtomicReference, in Java and Kotlin LatestBatch.java final class LatestBatch { private final AtomicReference<Batch> latest = new AtomicReference<>(); // writer: build the batch with plain writes, then release it void publish(Batch b) { latest.setRelease(b); } // readers: an acquire read sees the batch's fields as the writer left them Batch current() { return latest.getAcquire(); } // several writers racing to set the first batch: compareAndSet, volatile semantics boolean publishFirst(Batch b) { return latest.compareAndSet(null, b); } } LatestBatch.kt class LatestBatch { private val latest = AtomicReference<Batch?>(null) // writer: build the batch with plain writes, then release it fun publish(b: Batch) = latest.setRelease(b) // readers: an acquire read sees the batch's fields as the writer left them fun current(): Batch? = latest.getAcquire() // several writers racing to set the first batch: compareAndSet, volatile semantics fun publishFirst(b: Batch): Boolean = latest.compareAndSet(null, b) } A batch here is any group of records that one thread builds and others read. Both versions are the same three calls on the same JDK class. Kotlin has no syntax of its own for memory modes on the JVM: @Volatile gives you volatile, and for every other mode you call the same JDK classes as Java. AtomicReference and friends have had getAcquire, setRelease, getOpaque and getPlain since JDK 9, so this is the readable way to use the modes: no lookup, no casts, one extra object per field. VarHandle calls also work from Kotlin, because the Kotlin compiler (2.4 in these labs) treats VarHandle methods as signature-polymorphic and takes the return type from the as cast. Use a VarHandle only when that extra object per instance matters, as it does for the nodes of a queue with millions of entries.

h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · Worked example
x: Choose the lightest label for a worker's payment counter, then decide whether it's worth it A worker thread counts the payments it has processed. A dashboard thread reads the count every 15 seconds to draw a chart. Right now the count is an AtomicLong. Before reading on, list what the reader actually needs. final class WorkerStats { private final AtomicLong processed = new AtomicLong(); void onPayment() { processed.incrementAndGet(); } // the worker thread, once per payment long processed() { return processed.get(); } // the dashboard thread, every 15 s } class WorkerStats { private val processed = AtomicLong() fun onPayment() { processed.incrementAndGet() } // the worker thread, once per payment fun processed(): Long = processed.get() // the dashboard thread, every 15 s } Only one thread writes, so the increment doesn't have to be one atomic read-modify-write; that was the single-writer case in volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't. The reader needs a long that never arrives in two halves and that moves on eventually. It reads no other data based on the count, so it needs no acquire. That's exactly opaque: atomic for 64 bits, really performed, eventually visible. The lightest correct version uses the modes AtomicLong already has, with a label on each step. final class WorkerStats { private final AtomicLong processed = new AtomicLong(); void onPayment() { long next = processed.getPlain() + 1; // 1. the only writer can read its own value plainly processed.setOpaque(next); // 2. opaque: in one piece, and eventually visible } long processed() { return processed.getOpaque(); // 3. a recent value, in one piece; orders nothing else } } class WorkerStats { private val processed = AtomicLong() fun onPayment() { val next = processed.getPlain() + 1 // 1. the only writer can read its own value plainly processed.setOpaque(next) // 2. opaque: in one piece, and eventually visible } fun processed(): Long = processed.getOpaque() // 3. a recent value, in one piece; orders nothing else } Now decide. On x86 this swaps one atomic processor instruction per payment for a plain store. At 5,000 payments a second you will never see the difference; in a loop doing tens of millions a second, you might. The price is a rule nobody can see in the code: the moment a second thread calls onPayment(), counts are quietly lost. Keep incrementAndGet() until a measurement points at it, and if many threads count, use LongAdder instead.

h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · Quiz
x: When the program shuts down, one thread sets a flag, once. A busy loop on another thread checks the flag and only needs to stop eventually; the flag guards no other data. What is the weakest mode that is guaranteed to work? Plain Opaque Acquire/release Volatile Opaque guarantees that each read really happens, so the loop eventually sees the write (jcstress BasicJMM_04 forbids a stuck opaque spin). Plain may be read once for the whole loop. Acquire/release and volatile also work, but promise more than this loop needs. In application code you'd still write volatile, because it's one keyword and costs nothing extra on an x86 read. Writer: report.total = t; READY.setRelease(this, true);. Reader: if ((boolean) READY.getOpaque(this)) use(report.total);. What can the reader see? The flag as true, but an old total: a release only helps a reader that acquires Always the new total, because the writer used release A WrongMethodTypeException, because the modes don't match Never the flag as true, because opaque reads can't see release writes The ordering is a pair: release on the writer's side, acquire on the reader's. An opaque read does see the flag eventually, but nothing stops the reader's read of total from happening before it. Modes may be mixed without an exception (option 3), and opaque reads do see the value (option 4). Two worker threads decide which of them runs the nightly report: each does MINE.setRelease(this, true), then reads the other's flag with getAcquire, and runs the report if it reads false. What's wrong? Nothing: release/acquire orders the write before the read It only fails on ARM It throws, because each VarHandle may only be used by one thread Both workers can read false and both run the report, even on x86; this shape needs volatile, or better, one compareAndSet or a lock This is store buffering. Release keeps earlier accesses before the write, but it doesn't stop the later read of a different variable from passing it, and an x86 store buffer does exactly that. Volatile forbids it through its single total order. Simpler still: let both workers try one compareAndSet on one shared variable, or take the same lock. Where do VarHandle access modes belong? On every busy volatile field in a web service Instead of synchronized in code that handles requests In low-level building blocks like queues, after a measurement shows the cost, with jcstress tests Nowhere: they were deprecated along with sun.misc.Unsafe VarHandles are the supported replacement for Unsafe, not deprecated with it (option 4). They only pay off in code that hands over millions of values a second, and they need jcstress because ordinary tests can't see reorderings. Code that handles requests gets nothing from them that volatile, an Atomic class or a lock doesn't give it more clearly. From volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't: many threads run balance += amount on a volatile long balance. Someone suggests BALANCE.getAndAdd(this, amount) through a VarHandle instead. Does that fix it? No, a VarHandle has the same problem as volatile Yes: getAndAdd is one atomic read-modify-write, like AtomicLong.getAndAdd Only if a setRelease follows it Only on 64-bit JVMs Volatile makes each read and each write visible, but += is still a read and a write with a gap between them, so updates get lost. getAndAdd is a single atomic update that behaves like volatile. In application code, an AtomicLong or a LongAdder says the same thing more plainly.

h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · Key terms
x: VarHandle A typed handle to a field or array element whose methods read and write it in a chosen access mode (JDK 9). Access mode The memory rules for one read or write: plain, opaque, acquire/release or volatile. This lesson calls it the label. Opaque A mode where each access really happens, in one piece and in order for that variable, with no ordering of other variables. Acquire and release A paired mode: writes before the release are visible to a thread whose acquire read sees the released value. Signature-polymorphic method A method whose real signature comes from the argument types and the result cast at each call, like VarHandle.get. Store buffering Each thread writes one variable, then reads the other's; both may read the old value unless the accesses are volatile. jcstress The OpenJDK tool that runs concurrent actors millions of times and checks every result against acceptable and forbidden ones. What does a VarHandle let you choose that a volatile field doesn't? The access mode of each read and write (plain, opaque, acquire/release, volatile) on a plain field, plus atomic updates such as compareAndSet. What does opaque mode add over plain? Each access really happens, in one piece and in order for that variable, so a spinning reader eventually sees a new value. It orders no other variables. A release write and an acquire read of the same variable: what does the reader get? If its acquire read sees the released value, it also sees every write the writer made before the release. What does volatile add on top of acquire/release? One total order of all volatile accesses. That forbids the store-buffering result where two threads both read the other's variable as 0. Which access mode does VarHandle.compareAndSet behave like? Volatile: it reads the current value as getVolatile and, on success, writes as setVolatile. Why keep a VarHandle in a static final field? The JIT treats a static final as a constant, so each call compiles down to a load or store plus the barrier its mode needs. Why can't a passing JUnit test show that release/acquire code is correct? It only shows one machine didn't produce a bad result that time. jcstress runs the actors millions of times and fails on any forbidden result; x86 can't show many ARM bugs.

h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · Go deeper
x: The VarHandle Javadoc maps the modes onto the memory model of C and C++, which helps when you read papers or C++ and Rust code: volatile is compatible with memory_order_seq_cst, acquire with memory_order_acquire, and release with memory_order_release. There are also static fence methods, VarHandle.fullFence(), acquireFence() and releaseFence(), documented as the matching atomic_thread_fence calls, plus loadLoadFence() and storeStoreFence(). A fence orders a thread's accesses around one point in the code, without tying the order to one variable. Fences are even easier to misuse than modes. The jcstress samples AdvancedJMM_14_SynchronizedAreNotFences and AdvancedJMM_15_VolatilesAreNotFences show that synchronized blocks and volatile accesses don't work as fences either. Their promises hold only between threads that take the same lock, or when a volatile read actually sees the volatile write; you can't use them as free-standing barriers. VarHandles aren't only for fields. MethodHandles.arrayElementVarHandle(String[].class) gives you the modes on array elements, which a volatile array never could, because volatile there applies only to the reference to the array. MethodHandles.byteArrayViewVarHandle reads and writes an int or a long inside a byte[], with a chosen byte order and a chosen mode. If you want the model behind the modes in one sitting, Doug Lea's "Using JDK 9 Memory Order Modes" is the short guide, by the lead author of java.util.concurrent. Aleksey Shipilëv's "Java Memory Model Pragmatics" is the long version.

h: Thread pools and executors
x: ExecutorService, ThreadPoolExecutor internals, sizing, futures, CompletableFuture and ForkJoin. This track runs one restaurant kitchen from opening time to closing time. A thread pool is its team of cooks: a few threads, made once, that take tasks from a queue the way cooks take tickets from a rail. By the end, you can hand work to a pool and close it without losing any. You can predict where ThreadPoolExecutor puts every task in a burst, and give it a queue that says no when the kitchen is full. Its size will come from measurements, not habit, for cooks who chop all day and for cooks who mostly wait for the oven. You can wait for a result with a time limit, cancel a task so that it really stops, and keep a repeating job alive when one run fails. You can chain steps with CompletableFuture, a ticket that carries its own instructions, and ask three suppliers at once without one bad answer spoiling the rest. Then you'll split one big sum among workers who steal from each other. Finally, you'll run it all on a busy night, with named threads, failures you can see, numbers to watch and a calm close. You need the first track, Threads and the bugs they cause: what a thread is, race conditions, synchronized and interruption. The memory model track helps, but isn't required. Each lesson sets up its example in plain words before it puts any weight on it. Besides the kitchen, you'll meet a shop's checkout that asks the bank to charge a card, and a rate service that turns euros into dollars. Later come three flour suppliers and a year of card fees to add up. Install JDK 25. The labs compile for JDK 21, so they also run on 21 or later. A few things changed in JDK 25, such as the pool CompletableFuture uses on a small machine, and ForkJoinPool learning to schedule tasks. Where that happens, the lesson says so and keeps the code out of the labs. Every lesson has a lab in labs/executors, in the package workbench.executors.lNN. The labs run from a tiny pool you build yourself in lesson 1 to a pool ready for production in lesson 9. The labs are in Java, and every code sample and Try-it program also comes in Kotlin. The tests never depend on lucky timing. They hold tasks in place with latches and barriers, count how many tasks run at the same moment, and model a scheduler's timetable in make-believe milliseconds. Their waits have generous time limits, so a wrong answer fails within seconds instead of hanging the build. From labs/, run ./gradlew :executors:test --tests 'workbench.executors.lNN.*' until it passes. ./gradlew :executors:solutionTest runs the same tests against the reference answers, and ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=<class> runs a demo (add Kt to the class name for the Kotlin version). A pool is a few threads made once and a queue in front of them, like cooks and their rail. execute lets a failure reach the thread's handler, and submit keeps it inside the Future. shutdown() locks the door and returns at once, so wait with awaitTermination or close(). shutdownNow() hands back the tasks that never started and interrupts the rest. ThreadPoolExecutor starts core threads, then queues, then grows toward the maximum only when the queue is full, then rejects. With an unbounded queue the maximum never does anything, so give the queue a limit and choose who pays. Size from measurements: about one thread per core for computation, cores x CPU use x (1 + wait / compute) for waiting, and Little's law for traffic. The smallest limit on the path is the real ceiling, and a bulkhead keeps one slow service from taking every thread. A time limit on get ends your wait, not the work. cancel(true) and shutdownNow() only interrupt, so tasks must listen, and code that catches InterruptedException rethrows it or restores the flag. Fixed rate catches up after a slow run, fixed delay moves the later runs, and runs of one task never overlap. One uncaught exception ends a schedule without a word, so catch inside the task. CompletableFuture is a ticket that carries its next step. Start independent calls before you combine them, pass a pool for anything that waits, and wait once, at the edge, with a time limit. A failure skips every stage until a handler, often in a CompletionException envelope. Timeouts and cancel free the caller but not the thread, so give each call its own timeout and its own fallback before allOf. ForkJoinPool is for computation: fork one half, compute the other, then join, while idle workers steal the biggest task left. Parallel streams share its common pool with the whole JVM, so never write shared state or block in them. In production, name the threads and report every failure with its request id, from one wrapper that also carries the context. Watch the queue and the rejections, never let a task wait on its own pool, and shut down in order. The limit: each waiting task still holds a costly platform thread.
