x: The track in one kitchen Each lesson tied its tool to a scene in the same restaurant. The scene is the quickest way back to the rule. Lesson Picture it The rule 1. Why pools a fixed team of cooks takes tickets from one rail Create threads once and reuse them. shutdown() doesn't wait. 2. Inside ThreadPoolExecutor the thrifty manager calls temporary cooks only when the rail is full The pool queues first and grows second. Give the queue a limit. 3. Sizing a pool cooks who chop all day, cooks who wait for the oven, a kitchen with two ovens One thread per core for computing, more for waiting. The smallest limit wins. 4. Futures and cancellation the takeaway ticket, and the manager's note on a cook's station A time limit ends your wait, not the work. Cancelling only asks. 5. Scheduled executors two cleaners: one goes by the clock, one rests after each round Fixed rate catches up, fixed delay doesn't. Catch inside the task. 6. Composing CompletableFuture the ticket for table 4 that carries its own instructions Start independent calls first, then combine. Wait once, at the edge. 7. Errors, timeouts, fan-out the burned steak's note rides to the pass; the kitchen timer; three flour suppliers Recover close to the failure. A timeout frees the caller, not the thread. 8. ForkJoinPool cooks steal from the bottom of a busy cook's stack Fork one half, compute the other, then join. Never block in the common pool. 9. Pools in production a stuck Saturday night: name tags, the pinned note, closing the kitchen in order Name threads, report every failure, carry the context, close in order. Opening and closing a pool Call What it does execute(r) runs r; if it throws, the worker dies and its UncaughtExceptionHandler prints the stack trace submit(c) returns a Future; if the task throws, the exception waits inside it and nothing prints shutdown() the gentle close: rejects new tasks, lets the rest finish, returns at once shutdownNow() the hard close: returns the tasks that never started and interrupts the running ones awaitTermination(t, unit) waits for the end or the timeout, and returns true or false to say which close() (JDK 19+) shutdown(), then waits with no time limit; works with try-with-resources and Kotlin's use Pool threads are not daemon threads, so a pool you never close keeps the JVM running. Inside ThreadPoolExecutor Every execute walks four rules in order. Fewer threads than corePoolSize: start one. Otherwise: queue the task. Queue full: start a thread, up to maximumPoolSize. Still no room: call the rejection handler. Queue Effect Picture it new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() (fixed pool) never full, so the maximum never comes into play and overload hides as memory and waiting a rail with no end SynchronousQueue (cached pool) holds nothing, so every burst becomes new threads a plate passed straight into a free cook's hands new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(n) bounded: a full queue grows the pool, then rejects, so overload pushes back a rail with room for n tickets The rejection handler decides who pays. AbortPolicy (the default) throws at the caller, and CallerRunsPolicy makes the submitting thread run the task, which slows it down. The two discard policies drop work silently. keepAliveTime sends idle threads above core home, and allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true) sends core threads home too. Sizing a pool Work Threads Picture it all computing about availableProcessors() cooks who chop: one per board mostly waiting cores x target CPU use x (1 + wait / compute), both measured cooks who wait for the oven any traffic Little's law: requests inside = arrival rate x time inside; a pool finishes at most threads / latency per second the cinema ticket window any path the smallest limit further along is the ceiling, such as 20 database connections two ovens cap the kitchen several slow services a bulkhead: a separate pool or Semaphore for each a slow pizza oven mustn't hold every cook Futures and cancellation get() throws ExecutionException (the task's exception is its cause), CancellationException or InterruptedException. get(t, unit) adds TimeoutException and ends only your wait. cancel(true) on a submit future interrupts the worker, and the task stops only if it waits in a method that listens (sleep, take, get) or checks isInterrupted(). The future says cancelled at once, either way. Throwing InterruptedException clears the flag, so rethrow it or restore it: Java public void run() { try { rail.put(ticket); // waits while the rail is full } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // put the note back } // and stop } Kotlin override fun run() { try { rail.put(ticket) // waits while the rail is full } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // put the note back } // and stop } JDK 19 added state(), which reads a future without waiting; check it before resultNow() or exceptionNow(). invokeAll waits for every task, and invokeAny returns the first success and cancels the rest. Scheduled executors Method Next run starts Picture it schedule(task, d, unit) once, after d drop a reservation in 15 minutes scheduleAtFixedRate at fixed times (initial delay + n x period); late runs start back to back to catch up the cleaner who goes by the clock scheduleWithFixedDelay delay after the previous run ends the cleaner who rests after each round Runs of one task never overlap. One uncaught exception skips every later run, and nothing is logged, so catch inside the task: Java scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> { try { refreshRate(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { log.warn("rate refresh failed, keeping the last rate", e); // report it, keep the schedule } }, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); Kotlin scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay({ try { refreshRate() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { log.warn("rate refresh failed, keeping the last rate", e) // report it, keep the schedule } }, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) On a scheduler with one thread, a slow task delays all the others. Skip java.util.Timer: one exception stops every task on it. JDK 25: ForkJoinPool, the common pool included, implements ScheduledExecutorService and adds submitWithTimeout. CompletableFuture You have Method T -> U, plain code thenApply T -> CompletableFuture<U>, another async call thenCompose, which flattens it a second future, and (T, U) -> V thenCombine T -> void, a side effect thenAccept Work starts when you call supplyAsync, so start the independent calls first, then combine: Java // both calls start now and run side by side, on the io pool CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> prices.priceEur(cart), io); CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fx.rate("EUR", "USD"), io); CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> usd = price.thenCombine(rate, BigDecimal::multiply); // about 300 ms, not 600 Kotlin // both calls start now and run side by side, on the io pool val price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ prices.priceEur(cart) }, io) val rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ fx.rate("EUR", "USD") }, io) val usd = price.thenCombine(rate) { p, r -> p * r } // about 300 ms, not 600 No pool means ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), shared by the whole JVM. Up to JDK 24, a common pool with fewer than 2 threads meant a new thread per task; JDK 25 always uses the common pool. Pass a pool for anything that waits. A plain step runs on the thread that completed the stage before it, or on the caller if that stage was already done. thenApplyAsync(fn, pool) moves a slow step. join() throws the unchecked CompletionException and has no time limit. Wait once, at the edge, with get(t, unit), and never wait inside a stage. Errors, timeouts and fan-out Handler Runs on Changes the outcome? exceptionally(ex -> value) failure yes: a value instead handle((value, ex) -> result) both yes: any result whenComplete((value, ex) -> ...) both no: it only looks exceptionallyCompose(ex -> future) (JDK 12) failure yes: another future A failure skips every stage until a handler. Recover as close to the failure as you can. An exception thrown inside a stage arrives in a CompletionException envelope; completeExceptionally and orTimeout store it bare. Unwrap with getCause() before you test the type. orTimeout and completeOnTimeout (JDK 9) free the caller while the cook stays on hold, and cancel(true) on a CompletableFuture interrupts nothing. Give each call its own timeout in the client too. allOf waits for all and fails if any failed; anyOf takes the first to finish, failures included. For a fan-out, give each call its own deadline and turn its failure into "no answer" with handle, then allOf. ForkJoinPool and parallel streams Java protected Long compute() { if (to - from <= THRESHOLD) return sumByLoop(); // 1. small enough: just loop int mid = (from + to) >>> 1; SumTask left = new SumTask(a, from, mid), right = new SumTask(a, mid, to); left.fork(); // 2. another worker may take the left half long r = right.compute(); // 3. this thread does the right half return left.join() + r; // 4. then collects the left half } Kotlin override fun compute(): Long { if (to - from <= THRESHOLD) return sumByLoop() // 1. small enough: just loop val mid = (from + to) ushr 1 val left = SumTask(a, from, mid) val right = SumTask(a, mid, to) left.fork() // 2. another worker may take the left half val r = right.compute() // 3. this thread does the right half return left.join() + r // 4. then collects the left half } Fork, compute, join, in that order. fork(); join(); compute() gives the right total, one leaf at a time. Stop splitting at roughly 100 to 10,000 basic steps per leaf, then measure. Each worker works from the top of its own deque, and idle workers steal the oldest, biggest task from the bottom of another's. Parallel streams use the common pool (availableProcessors() - 1 workers plus the caller), shared with every CompletableFuture step that names no pool. Never write to shared state in them, and never block in them. Pools in production Question Answer Picture it Which pool is stuck? name threads: Thread.ofPlatform().name("grill-", 0).factory() (JDK 21+) name tags Did a task fail? wrap execute once: catch what execute tasks throw, read exceptionNow() for submit tasks, report with the request id the grill going out is loud; a negative price is silent Which request? capture a ThreadLocal such as the request id at submission, install it on the worker, restore the old value in finally the note pinned to the wrong jacket Keeping up? queue size, active against max, rejections, time in queue the board by the pass Frozen, CPU idle? a task waits for a task in its own bounded pool: compose, inline, or use a second pool cooks waiting for tickets behind them How to stop? stop intake, then the pool that feeds the others, then the rest, all within one deadline close the kitchen in order The limit of the whole track: every pool here holds one platform thread, one thread of the operating system, for each task that waits. The virtual threads track starts from that wall.

h: Thread pools and executors: track quiz
x: On JDK 21, a method runs try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { pool.submit(this::printSalesReport); }. What happens at the closing brace? Nothing: the pool keeps running until the JVM exits close() calls shutdown() and waits for the report to finish close() calls shutdownNow() and interrupts the report It doesn't compile, because an ExecutorService can't be closed Since JDK 19, ExecutorService is AutoCloseable, so try-with-resources (Kotlin's use) calls close(). It locks the door with shutdown(), then waits with no time limit for every task to finish. It calls shutdownNow() only if the waiting thread itself is interrupted. new ThreadPoolExecutor(4, 32, 60, SECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()) gets a burst of 1,000 slow tasks at once. How many threads does it run? 32, the maximum 4, and 996 tasks wait in the queue 1,000, one per task 4, and 996 tasks are rejected The thrifty manager calls extra threads only when the queue refuses a task, and a LinkedBlockingQueue with no capacity never refuses. So the pool stays at its 4 core threads, the maximum of 32 never comes into play, and nothing is rejected until memory runs out. A program on 8 cores handles requests that each compute for 20 ms and then wait 180 ms for the database. You want the cores about 80% busy, and the database's connection pool has 40 connections. How many threads should the request pool have? 8, one per core 64, from 8 x 0.8 x (1 + 180/20) About 40: the formula says 64, but only 40 requests can use the database at once 200, to be safe in a rush The formula gives 64 threads to keep the cores 80% busy. But every request needs a connection, and only 40 exist, so threads 41 to 64 would just stand in line for one. As in the kitchen with two ovens, the smallest limit on the path is the real ceiling. A task adds up 10 million sales in a loop. It never waits and never checks the interrupt flag. You call future.cancel(true) while it runs. What happens? The thread is stopped at once cancel returns false, because the task is already running cancel returns true and the future says cancelled, but the loop runs to the end The task gets an InterruptedException on the next pass of the loop cancel(true) only sets the interrupt flag, the note on the cook's station. A task that never waits in a method that listens and never checks isInterrupted() doesn't notice, and chops on. The future is marked cancelled at once either way, so the result is thrown away even though the work finishes. A shop refreshes its exchange rate with scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::refreshRate, 0, 30, SECONDS). At 18:12 the rate service doesn't answer, and refreshRate throws. What does the shop show at 21:00? Dollar prices from the last rate fetched before 18:12, and no log line about the failure A fresh rate, because the scheduler tried again 30 seconds later A stack trace in the log every 30 seconds since 18:12 No prices at all, because every task on that scheduler stopped, as with java.util.Timer An exception that escapes a repeating task skips every later run. It waits inside the ScheduledFuture, which nobody reads, and the scheduler's other tasks carry on, which is why nobody notices. Catch RuntimeException inside the task, and let a health page report whether the future is done. price() and rate() each wait 200 ms for another service. Which version takes about 200 ms in total? supplyAsync(() -> price(), io).thenCombine(supplyAsync(() -> rate(), io), BigDecimal::multiply) supplyAsync(() -> price(), io).thenCompose(p -> supplyAsync(() -> rate(), io).thenApply(p::multiply)) supplyAsync(() -> price().multiply(rate()), io) supplyAsync(() -> price(), io).thenApplyAsync(p -> p.multiply(rate()), io) Work starts when you call supplyAsync. Only the first version starts both calls before it waits for either, like the steak and the sauce cooking at once. The others are asynchronous too, but each asks for the rate only after the price has arrived, so they take about 400 ms. A call asks a flour supplier for today's price, with orTimeout(300, MILLISECONDS) on its future. The supplier hangs for 30 seconds. What happens to the thread on the io pool that makes the call? It is interrupted at 300 ms and goes back to the pool It stays busy for the full 30 seconds; only the future completed at 300 ms The pool replaces it with a new thread It is cancelled before the call starts orTimeout is the manager's kitchen timer. It completes the future with a TimeoutException and never touches the cook on the phone. Under load, those abandoned calls fill the pool, so give the call its own timeout in the client, no longer than the future's deadline. A shop's program checks stock with products.parallelStream().map(p -> stock.level(p)).toList(), and each call to the stock service waits 50 ms. Soon, supplyAsync tasks with no executor, in an unrelated part of the program, start to wait for seconds. Why? Parallel streams run on virtual threads, which get stuck on the call toList() locks the list until the other tasks finish The common pool rejects new tasks while a stream is running The stock calls hold the common pool's workers, and supplyAsync with no executor needs the same pool Parallel streams and CompletableFuture steps with no executor share ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), which has one worker fewer than the cores. The waiting calls hold those workers like cooks on the phone, so everyone else's tasks queue behind them. Move the stock calls to a pool built for waiting. A request thread puts the request id req-42 in a ThreadLocal and submits a task to a pool. A wrapper copies the id onto the worker before the task runs, and puts the worker's old value back in finally. Which problem does that finally prevent? The submitting thread losing its own request id The task's exceptions being swallowed A deadlock between the request thread and the worker A later task on the same worker logging with req-42 Pool threads are reused. Without the restore, the worker keeps req-42, like a note left pinned to a cook's jacket, and the next task on that thread logs under the wrong id. The worker never touches the submitting thread's own value, so that one can't go wrong. Pick the tool for each job on JDK 25. (1) Total the year's sales, 20 million amounts already in memory. (2) Make 2,000 calls at once to a slow web service that accepts at most 50 at a time. (3) Send the bank a heartbeat every 30 seconds. (1) virtual threads; (2) a parallel stream; (3) a loop with Thread.sleep(30_000) on the common pool All three on one newFixedThreadPool(200) (1) a parallel stream or a ForkJoinPool; (2) a pool built for waiting, or virtual threads, behind a Semaphore of 50; (3) a ScheduledExecutorService at a fixed rate (1) a single-thread executor; (2) supplyAsync with no executor; (3) java.util.Timer Arithmetic on data in memory splits well across the cores. Thousands of waiting calls want threads that are cheap to keep waiting, capped at what the service accepts, which is a bulkhead. A heartbeat follows the clock, which is what fixed rate is for. Sleeping in the common pool, supplyAsync with no executor for waiting calls, and Timer are each a bug from this track.

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · What a new thread per task costs, and why it has no ceiling
x: A manager who hires a cook for every order: a new thread per tiny task costs more than the task and has no ceiling, a pool hires its cooks once, shutdown only locks the door, and awaitTermination waits Let's put a price on the manager's hiring habit. A task is a piece of work you hand over to be run. In Java it's usually a Runnable, an object with one method, void run(). Our tasks are tiny: a few nanoseconds of arithmetic each, about the size of one side salad. The first version gives every task a brand-new thread, just as Threads from zero did with its workers: Java // Naive: a brand-new thread for every task CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(tasks); for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) { new Thread(() -> { task(); done.countDown(); }).start(); } done.await(); // returns when every task has counted down Kotlin // Naive: a brand-new thread for every task val done = CountDownLatch(tasks) repeat(tasks) { Thread { task(); done.countDown() }.start() } done.await() // returns when every task has counted down done is a CountDownLatch, the one-shot gate from Synchronizers. Each task counts it down once, and await() returns when it reaches zero. The second version runs the same tasks on four threads that are created once and reused: Java // Fixed: four threads, created once and reused for every task try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) pool.execute(ThreadPerTaskDemo::task); } // close() waits for all of them Kotlin // Fixed: four threads, created once and reused for every task Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4).use { pool -> repeat(tasks) { pool.execute(::task) } } // close() waits for all of them For now, read newFixedThreadPool(4) as "four cooks and one rail". The rest of this lesson takes that line apart. My guess before running it: the pool wins, maybe by ten times. ThreadPerTaskDemo, in the Try it below, does 5,000 tasks both ways, twice. It ran on a Linux machine with 4 cores, the parts of the processor that each run one thread at a time. When the machine was quiet, a new thread per task took 0.5 to 1.5 seconds per round, and the pool took 6 to 25 ms. While it was busy with other heavy programs, one run printed: round 1: 5,000 tasks new thread each: 2,635 ms pool of 4: 44 ms round 2: 5,000 tasks new thread each: 2,939 ms pool of 4: 20 ms Correctness first: both versions ran all 5,000 tasks. Then speed. In this run, the pool was 60 to 150 times faster, far beyond my guess. The work was identical, so the difference is the threads. An ordinary Java thread is a platform thread: it wraps one thread of the operating system. Starting one is a trip to the kernel, the core of the operating system. The new thread gets its own stack, the private memory for its local variables and calls in progress. On 64-bit Linux, the JVM (the Java Virtual Machine, the program that runs your compiled code) reserves 1 MB for each stack by default. The thread also gets a place in the scheduler, the part of the operating system that decides which thread runs next. When the thread ends, all of that is torn down again. Threads from zero measured the round trip at about 130 microseconds. A task that runs for nanoseconds pays thousands of times its own cost just to start. The second cost hides until the busiest hour. A thread per task has no ceiling. If 3,000 orders arrive at once, you get 3,000 threads. Something runs out first: the operating system's limit on threads, memory for their stacks, or CPU time spent switching between threads that all want a core. In Java, the first sign is often an OutOfMemoryError that says unable to create native thread. A thread pool fixes both costs. It creates a few threads once and keeps them. Each thread loops: take a task from a queue, run it, take the next one. In the kitchen, the threads are the cooks, the queue is the rail and the pool size is the number of cooks. The pool size also caps how many tasks run at the same moment. So 3,000 orders become 3,000 tickets on the rail, not 3,000 cooks squeezed into a kitchen with four stoves. A thread per tiny task costs more than the task. Create threads once, and reuse them. Virtual threads are much lighter threads that the JVM runs on top of a few platform threads, and the virtual threads track covers them. They make a new thread cheap, so the first cost mostly goes away. The second cost doesn't: you still want a limit on how much work runs at once. With virtual threads, you put that limit on the scarce thing itself, such as the number of calls to a slow service. So we want a pool. Java has one ready-made, behind two interfaces, and the first trap waits in the difference between two of their methods. Pay for 5,000 threads Predict first: for 5,000 tiny tasks, how many times slower is a new thread per task than a pool of 4? Twice? Ten times? A hundred? Run ThreadPerTaskDemo (Java or Kotlin, they do the same thing) with the command below. It runs two rounds. Run it again with -Pargs=10000 added. Does each column double? ThreadPerTaskDemo.java package workbench.executors.l01; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** 5,000 tiny tasks: one new thread per task, then the same tasks on a pool of 4 threads. */ public class ThreadPerTaskDemo { static final LongAdder work = new LongAdder(); static void task() { work.add(Long.toHexString(System.nanoTime()).length()); // a few nanoseconds of real work } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int tasks = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 5_000; for (int round = 1; round <= 2; round++) { // 1. a brand-new platform thread for every task long t0 = System.nanoTime(); CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(tasks); for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) { new Thread(() -> { task(); done.countDown(); }).start(); } done.await(); long perTask = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; // 2. the same tasks on four threads that are created once and reused t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) pool.execute(ThreadPerTaskDemo::task); } // close() waits for all of them long pooled = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("round %d: %,d tasks new thread each: %,d ms pool of 4: %,d ms%n", round, tasks, perTask, pooled); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l01.ThreadPerTaskDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l01/ThreadPerTaskDemo.java ThreadPerTaskDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l01 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder private val work = LongAdder() private fun task() { work.add(System.nanoTime().toString(16).length.toLong()) // a few nanoseconds of real work } /** 5,000 tiny tasks: one new thread per task, then the same tasks on a pool of 4 threads. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val tasks = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 5_000 for (round in 1..2) { // 1. a brand-new platform thread for every task var t0 = System.nanoTime() val done = CountDownLatch(tasks) repeat(tasks) { Thread { task(); done.countDown() }.start() } done.await() val perTask = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 // 2. the same tasks on four threads that are created once and reused t0 = System.nanoTime() Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4).use { pool -> repeat(tasks) { pool.execute(::task) } } // close() waits for all of them val pooled = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println("round %d: %,d tasks new thread each: %,d ms pool of 4: %,d ms".format(round, tasks, perTask, pooled)) } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l01.ThreadPerTaskDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l01/ThreadPerTaskDemo.kt On a quiet 4-core machine, a new thread per task took 0.5 to 1.5 seconds per round and the pool took 6 to 25 ms. A busy machine makes both columns slower. The pool's first round is usually its slowest, because the JIT compiler, the part of the JVM that turns busy code into fast machine code, is still warming up. With 10,000 tasks the first column roughly doubles, because every task pays for its own thread. The pool pays for four threads in all. Thread Pools (The Java Tutorials) read

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · Handing tasks to a pool: Executor, ExecutorService, and where a failure goes
x: java.util.concurrent, the package of concurrency tools in the JDK (the Java Development Kit, Java's standard tools and library), splits a pool's job into two interfaces. Executor has one method, void execute(Runnable task). It promises only that the task will run, at some point, on some thread. That may be the calling thread, a new thread or a pool, and code that takes an Executor doesn't need to know which. It's the rail seen from the dining room: you clip the ticket on, and who cooks it is the kitchen's business. ExecutorService extends Executor with what a real pool needs. submit hands over a task and gives you back a Future, a claim ticket you can later trade for the task's result. invokeAll runs a list of tasks and waits for all of them, and invokeAny returns the result of the first one that succeeds. The lifecycle methods, shutdown, shutdownNow, awaitTermination and (since JDK 19) close, decide when the kitchen closes. Lesson 4 of this track covers Future in depth. You rarely write an ExecutorService yourself. The Executors class is a factory, a class whose static methods build ready-made pools for you: Java ExecutorService fixed = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8); // 8 threads, a queue with no limit ExecutorService single = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); // 1 thread, tasks run in order ExecutorService cached = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(); // grows without limit, idle threads leave after 60 s ExecutorService vts = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); // JDK 21: a new virtual thread per task Kotlin val fixed = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8) // 8 threads, a queue with no limit val single = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor() // 1 thread, tasks run in order val cached = Executors.newCachedThreadPool() // grows without limit, idle threads leave after 60 s val vts = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() // JDK 21: a new virtual thread per task The first three are built on one class, ThreadPoolExecutor, with different settings, and lesson 2 of this track takes it apart. The last one is different. It starts a new virtual thread for every task, so it isn't a pool at all. Now the trap. execute and submit look interchangeable, and they treat a failing task in opposite ways. SwallowDemo, in the Try it below, sends the same task both ways to a pool with one thread. The task prints its thread's name and then throws an exception, because the kitchen is out of eggs. Before you read the output, guess what each half prints: --- execute --- cooking on pool-1-thread-1 Exception in thread "pool-1-thread-1" java.lang.IllegalStateException: out of eggs at workbench.executors.l01.SwallowDemo.lambda$main$0(SwallowDemo.java:14) ... (three more lines of stack trace) --- submit --- cooking on pool-1-thread-2 submit: nothing printed. isDone=true The kitchen ran out of eggs twice, and only the first time did anyone hear about it. With execute, the exception escapes the task and ends the worker thread. Every thread has an UncaughtExceptionHandler, the method the JVM calls when an exception escapes a thread, and the default one prints the stack trace. The pool then starts a new worker to replace the one that died. That's why the second task runs on pool-1-thread-2, in a pool of one. With submit, the pool wraps your task in a FutureTask, a task with a slot for its result. The FutureTask catches the exception and keeps it inside the Future. Nothing is printed. The only way to see the failure is to call get() on the Future, which throws an ExecutionException with your exception as its cause. If nobody ever calls get(), the failure is gone. submit keeps a task's failure inside its Future. Call get(), or use execute. So choose on purpose. Use execute for work that nobody waits for, so that a failure at least reaches the handler. Use submit when some code will call get() and deal with the answer. Lesson 9 of this track shows how to log failures from both. We can hand work to a pool now. What we can't do yet is close it, and closing time has a trap of its own. Lose an exception on purpose Run SwallowDemo below and read the thread name printed for each half. Delete the whole --- get --- part (the println and the try block around f.get()). Predict: will any trace of the second failure remain? Run it again. SwallowDemo.java package workbench.executors.l01; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** The same failing task, sent once with execute and once with submit. Watch where the exception goes. */ public class SwallowDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1)) { Runnable cook = () -> { System.out.println("cooking on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); throw new IllegalStateException("out of eggs"); }; System.out.println("--- execute ---"); pool.execute(cook); Thread.sleep(200); // give the stack trace time to print System.out.println("--- submit ---"); Future<?> f = pool.submit(cook); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println("submit: nothing printed. isDone=" + f.isDone()); System.out.println("--- get ---"); try { f.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { System.out.println("get() threw ExecutionException, cause: " + e.getCause()); } } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l01.SwallowDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l01/SwallowDemo.java SwallowDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l01 import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** The same failing task, sent once with execute and once with submit. Watch where the exception goes. */ fun main() { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1).use { pool -> val cook = Runnable { println("cooking on " + Thread.currentThread().name) throw IllegalStateException("out of eggs") } println("--- execute ---") pool.execute(cook) Thread.sleep(200) // give the stack trace time to print println("--- submit ---") val f = pool.submit(cook) Thread.sleep(200) println("submit: nothing printed. isDone=" + f.isDone) println("--- get ---") try { f.get() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { println("get() threw ExecutionException, cause: " + e.cause) } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l01.SwallowDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l01/SwallowDemo.kt The first run prints a stack trace for the execute failure. Then the submit task runs on pool-1-thread-2, because the first worker died and the pool replaced it. The get() block prints the ExecutionException and its cause, out of eggs. Without that block, the second failure leaves no trace at all: the exception sits inside a Future that nobody reads. Executors (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · Closing time: shutdown(), shutdownNow() and the wait you must ask for
x: A restaurant can close in two ways. The gentle way: lock the front door, but cook every order that is already on the rail. The hard way: lock the door, hand the waiting tickets back to the customers, and tell the cooks to stop what they're doing. Either way, someone has to stay until the last cook leaves before turning off the lights. An ExecutorService has the same choices. It moves through its life one way only: from running, to shutting down or stopping, to terminated. The figure draws the trip. Two methods start it, and neither of them waits. shutdown() is the gentle close. New tasks are rejected with a RejectedExecutionException. Tasks in the queue and tasks already running carry on. The method returns at once. ShutdownDemo, in the Try it below, puts that to the test. Two cooks (a pool of two threads) get six orders, and each order takes 300 ms. Then main calls shutdown(), tries to add a seventh order and waits with awaitTermination, which we'll meet in a moment. My prediction: shutdown() returns within a few milliseconds, long before the first order is cooked. Here's a run (the clock starts with the program, so the first line includes starting the pool): 115 ms shutdown returned. isShutdown=true isTerminated=false 164 ms order 7 rejected: the kitchen is closed 400 ms cooked order 1 403 ms cooked order 2 700 ms cooked order 3 704 ms cooked order 4 1002 ms cooked order 5 1005 ms cooked order 6 1007 ms awaitTermination returned true. isTerminated=true The prediction held. shutdown() returned before a single order was cooked, and the seventh order was turned away. The six orders on the rail were still cooked, two at a time, 300 ms apart. shutdownNow() is the hard close. It takes every task that hasn't started out of the queue and returns them as a List<Runnable>, so you can see what was never done. Then it interrupts the threads that are running tasks. An interrupt is a polite request to stop. It sets a flag on the thread, and a thread blocked in sleep, wait or a queue's take wakes up with an InterruptedException. A task busy in a loop that never checks the flag keeps running. (The lesson A thread's life, in the threads track, covered the flag, and lesson 4 of this track comes back to it.) Here the kitchen picture breaks. A real cook hears "stop!" when you shout it. A Java task hears an interrupt only if it checks for one, or waits in a method that does. Run the demo with now, and it calls shutdownNow() 100 ms in: 130 ms order 2 interrupted 131 ms shutdownNow returned 4 tasks that never started 131 ms order 1 interrupted 217 ms order 7 rejected: the kitchen is closed 223 ms awaitTermination returned true. isTerminated=true Orders 1 and 2 were asleep in their 300 ms of cooking, so the interrupt woke them. The pool handed back the four tickets that never started, and nothing was cooked. The interrupted orders print from their own threads, so their lines can land before or after main's line about shutdownNow. The waiting is a separate call. awaitTermination(timeout, unit) blocks until the pool has terminated or the timeout runs out, and returns true or false to say which. Put the three calls together and you get the shutdown idiom from the ExecutorService documentation (the timeouts are yours to choose): Java pool.shutdown(); // 1. no new work try { if (!pool.awaitTermination(20, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { // 2. let the backlog finish pool.shutdownNow(); // 3. interrupt the stragglers if (!pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) System.err.println("pool did not terminate"); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { pool.shutdownNow(); // we were interrupted: stop now Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // and keep the flag for our caller } Kotlin pool.shutdown() // 1. no new work try { if (!pool.awaitTermination(20, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { // 2. let the backlog finish pool.shutdownNow() // 3. interrupt the stragglers if (!pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) System.err.println("pool did not terminate") } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { pool.shutdownNow() // we were interrupted: stop now Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // and keep the flag for our caller } First we lock the door. Then we give the backlog 20 seconds. If that isn't enough, we interrupt the stragglers and give them 5 more. The catch covers our own thread being interrupted while it waits. Then we stop the pool at once, and set our interrupt flag again so that our caller still sees it. Since JDK 19, ExecutorService is AutoCloseable, so Java's try-with-resources (Kotlin's use) can do the waiting. close() calls shutdown() and then waits until every task has finished. If the waiting thread is interrupted, it calls shutdownNow(), keeps waiting, and sets the interrupt flag again before it returns. There's no timeout, so close() waits forever on a task that never ends. Use close() for a short-lived pool inside one method. Use the idiom for a pool that must stop within a deadline. Forget both, and you meet the most loyal cooks in town. The threads of newFixedThreadPool are not daemon threads, the background helpers that the JVM doesn't wait for. The JVM keeps running until every non-daemon thread has ended. So after main returns, the pool's cooks stand by the empty rail, waiting for orders that will never come, and the program never exits. shutdown() returns before the work is done. Wait with awaitTermination() or close(). We've used the pool from the outside. Inside, it's smaller than you might think: small enough to build in the lab. Watch shutdown not wait ShutdownDemo gives two cooks (a pool of two threads) six orders of 300 ms each, then calls shutdown(). Predict the time on the shutdown returned line, then run it. Run it again with -Pargs=now, which calls shutdownNow() after 100 ms instead. Predict how many orders get cooked. ShutdownDemo.java package workbench.executors.l01; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** shutdown, awaitTermination and shutdownNow on a kitchen of 2 cooks (threads) with 6 orders of 300 ms each. */ public class ShutdownDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg); } static Runnable cook(int id) { return () -> { try { Thread.sleep(300); // 300 ms to cook one order log("cooked order " + id); } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("order " + id + " interrupted"); Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean now = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("now"); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2); for (int i = 1; i <= 6; i++) pool.execute(cook(i)); if (now) { Thread.sleep(100); List<Runnable> neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow(); log("shutdownNow returned " + neverStarted.size() + " tasks that never started"); } else { pool.shutdown(); log("shutdown returned. isShutdown=" + pool.isShutdown() + " isTerminated=" + pool.isTerminated()); } try { pool.execute(cook(7)); } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { log("order 7 rejected: the kitchen is closed"); } boolean done = pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); log("awaitTermination returned " + done + ". isTerminated=" + pool.isTerminated()); } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l01.ShutdownDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l01/ShutdownDemo.java ShutdownDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l01 import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit private val T0 = System.nanoTime() private fun log(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg)) private fun cook(id: Int) = Runnable { try { Thread.sleep(300) // 300 ms to cook one order log("cooked order $id") } catch (e: InterruptedException) { log("order $id interrupted") Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } } /** shutdown, awaitTermination and shutdownNow on a kitchen of 2 cooks (threads) with 6 orders of 300 ms each. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val now = args.firstOrNull() == "now" val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2) for (i in 1..6) pool.execute(cook(i)) if (now) { Thread.sleep(100) val neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow() log("shutdownNow returned ${neverStarted.size} tasks that never started") } else { pool.shutdown() log("shutdown returned. isShutdown=${pool.isShutdown} isTerminated=${pool.isTerminated}") } try { pool.execute(cook(7)) } catch (e: RejectedExecutionException) { log("order 7 rejected: the kitchen is closed") } val done = pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) log("awaitTermination returned $done. isTerminated=${pool.isTerminated}") } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l01.ShutdownDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l01/ShutdownDemo.kt With shutdown(), that line prints a few milliseconds after the pool starts, order 7 is rejected, and the six orders are cooked in pairs, about 300 ms apart. Only then does awaitTermination return true. With now, orders 1 and 2 are interrupted in their sleep, shutdownNow hands back the 4 orders that never started, nothing is cooked, and the pool terminates soon after. The two interrupted lines can come before or after the shutdownNow returned line, because each one prints from its own thread. shutdown() and shutdownNow() only start the trip. awaitTermination() or close() is how you wait for the end. ExecutorService (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · Inside a pool: a queue and a few threads that loop
x: Strip away the options, and a fixed pool is a rail and a few cooks. Each worker thread runs one loop: Java while (true) { Runnable task = queue.take(); // blocks while the queue is empty if (task == POISON) return; // shutdown: time to go home task.run(); } Kotlin while (true) { val task = queue.take() // blocks while the queue is empty if (task === POISON) return // shutdown: time to go home task.run() } execute puts the task on a BlockingQueue, the queue from Concurrent collections whose take() waits while the queue is empty, and the workers take tasks off it. The queue does the hand-off between threads, and the number of workers limits how many tasks run at once. Shutdown is the interesting part. Idle workers are blocked inside take(), so the pool has to wake them somehow. Classic problems closed the kitchen at the end of the threads track with a poison pill: a special ticket that means "go home". One pill per cook goes on the rail, behind every real order, and a worker that takes a pill exits. The queue is first in, first out, so every task submitted before shutdown() runs before any worker sees a pill. shutdownNow() drains the queue instead and puts fresh pills on it. Then it interrupts the workers, so idle ones fall out of take() and busy ones get the request to stop. There's one race to get right. It has the check-then-act shape from Race conditions: why count++ lies, where another thread can change things between the check and the act. execute checks the shutdown flag, then queues the task. Let's trace two threads: A waiter's thread calls execute, reads the flag and finds the kitchen open. Before it queues its ticket, the manager's thread calls shutdown(), sets the flag and puts the pills on the rail. The waiter's thread queues its ticket, behind the pills. The waiter was told the order was accepted, and no cook will ever take it. So execute and shutdown() take the same lock, and the check and the queueing happen as one step. ThreadPoolExecutor solves the same problem another way. It keeps one AtomicInteger called ctl, and packs the run state into its top 3 bits and the worker count into the other 29. That way a single compare-and-set (an update that succeeds only if nobody changed the value first, from Atomics and compare-and-set) can check and change both at once. The lab uses a plain synchronized lock instead. A lock is slower and far easier to read, which is the right trade when the goal is to see the moving parts. Check yourself before the lab. The toy pool has four workers, and shutdown() puts one pill on the rail instead of four. What happens? (One worker takes the pill and exits. The other three stay blocked in take() forever, so awaitTermination returns false. They aren't daemon threads, so the JVM never exits either.) That's all a fixed pool is. Notice what it lacks, though. Its rail has no end, so on a busy evening the tickets pile up without limit. And it has four cooks only because somebody guessed four. The next two lessons deal with both.

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · Java and Kotlin
x: Closing a pool in Java and Kotlin UseDemo.java (sketch) try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { List<Future<Integer>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); for (int n = 1; n <= 10; n++) { int k = n; futures.add(pool.submit(() -> k * k)); } int total = 0; for (Future<Integer> f : futures) { total += f.get(); // must handle InterruptedException and ExecutionException } System.out.println("sum of squares 1..10 = " + total); } // close(): shutdown, then wait for every task UseDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l01 import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** Kotlin's use {} calls ExecutorService.close() (JDK 19+), which waits for the tasks to finish. */ fun main() { val total = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4).use { pool -> val futures = (1..10).map { n -> pool.submit<Int> { n * n } } futures.sumOf { it.get() } // get() can still throw ExecutionException; Kotlin just doesn't force a catch } println("sum of squares 1..10 = $total") } Both versions submit ten small sums and end in ExecutorService.close(), so the waiting is the same. Kotlin's use is its try-with-resources, and it works on a pool because ExecutorService has been AutoCloseable since JDK 19. (On older JDKs, write the shutdown idiom in a finally block.) The real difference is checked exceptions, the ones Java makes you catch or declare. Java makes you deal with InterruptedException and ExecutionException from get(). Kotlin compiles without a catch, so a failed task turns up as an exception you never planned for. Kotlin's coroutines, its own light tasks with a track of their own, can also run on a pool through asCoroutineDispatcher(). That dispatcher needs closing too, and closing it shuts the pool down.

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · Worked example
x: Close the kitchen without losing its order log The kitchen keeps a log file of finished orders. Four cooks (a pool of 4) cook the orders, and each one writes a line to the shared orderLog, a BufferedWriter, when its dish is done. Here is the end of main as first written. Decide what happens to orders that are still cooking when the program reaches orderLog.close(). for (Order o : orders) pool.execute(() -> cookAndLog(o)); pool.shutdown(); orderLog.close(); // close the log file System.out.println("kitchen closed"); for (o in orders) pool.execute { cookAndLog(o) } pool.shutdown() orderLog.close() // close the log file println("kitchen closed") shutdown() returned at once, so orderLog.close() ran while cooks were still cooking. Every order that finishes after that tries to write to a closed file and fails with an IOException that says Stream closed. And "kitchen closed" prints while the kitchen is still busy. Nothing waited for anything. Wait, with a deadline. Say the building closes 10 minutes after the last order, so the cooks get 9 of them. Then we interrupt the stragglers and record what never started. The log is closed only after the pool has terminated. pool.shutdown(); // 1. no new orders try { if (!pool.awaitTermination(9, TimeUnit.MINUTES)) { // 2. let the backlog finish List<Runnable> unstarted = pool.shutdownNow(); // 3. interrupt, collect the rest System.err.println(unstarted.size() + " orders never started"); pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { pool.shutdownNow(); Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } orderLog.close(); // 4. only now pool.shutdown() // 1. no new orders try { if (!pool.awaitTermination(9, TimeUnit.MINUTES)) { // 2. let the backlog finish val unstarted = pool.shutdownNow() // 3. interrupt, collect the rest System.err.println("${unstarted.size} orders never started") pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { pool.shutdownNow() Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } orderLog.close() // 4. only now If there's no deadline, JDK 19's try-with-resources is shorter, and it gets the order right by construction: the block can't end before the pool has terminated. try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { for (Order o : orders) pool.execute(() -> cookAndLog(o)); } // close() waits for every order orderLog.close(); System.out.println("kitchen closed"); Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4).use { pool -> for (o in orders) pool.execute { cookAndLog(o) } } // close() waits for every order orderLog.close() println("kitchen closed")

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · Lab
x: Build a tiny fixed pool labs/executors/src/main/java/workbench/executors/l01/TinyPool.java ./gradlew :executors:test --tests 'workbench.executors.l01.*' Meet the class. TinyPool is this lesson's kitchen in code: a fixed number of worker threads, the cooks, that take tasks from one shared queue, the rail. The constructor and a few small methods are done. Run the tests once: all eight fail with UnsupportedOperationException. Write execute: a null check, then, inside synchronized (lock), throw RejectedExecutionException if shutdown is set, otherwise queue.add(task). Write workerLoop: take() a task, return on POISON or on InterruptedException, run the task, and count a RuntimeException in failed instead of letting it escape. Write shutdown (under the lock: set the flag, add one POISON per worker) and awaitTermination (wait on the terminated latch). Write shutdownNow: under the lock, set the flag, drain the queue into a list, remove the pills from it and add fresh ones. Then interrupt every worker and return the list. Run the tests until all eight pass, then run them twice more. Why add pills in shutdownNow as well? A running task may swallow the interrupt. When it ends, its worker goes back to take(). Without a pill waiting there, that worker blocks forever and awaitTermination never returns true. BlockingQueue.drainTo(list) moves everything in the queue into list in one call, in queue order. The shutdownNow test checks that you return the very same Runnable objects, in the order they were queued. Don't wrap them. All eight tests in TinyPoolTest pass, three runs in a row. By the end you can say what a thread pool saves you, pick execute or submit on purpose, and shut a pool down without losing work or hanging the JVM.
