h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · Quiz
x: A program does pool.submit(() -> saveOrder(order)) and never keeps the Future. One day saveOrder throws an IllegalStateException. What shows up in the program's output? A stack trace from the default UncaughtExceptionHandler Nothing at all A RejectedExecutionException on the next submit A warning that the pool lost a worker submit wraps the task in a FutureTask, which catches the exception and keeps it in the Future. Nobody calls get(), so nobody ever sees it. The stack trace from the default handler is what execute would give you, which is why that option is tempting. main creates Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2), runs three tasks that finish quickly, and returns without calling shutdown(). What happens to the JVM? It exits when main returns It exits once the three tasks are done It keeps running, because the two idle worker threads are not daemon threads It throws IllegalStateException because the pool was never shut down The JVM exits when the last non-daemon thread ends. The pool's workers are non-daemon threads, and they wait in take() for more work, forever. A cached pool would let the JVM exit after 60 idle seconds, because its idle threads leave. A pool runs a task with the loop while (true) { total += next(); }, which never checks the interrupt flag and never blocks. You call shutdownNow() and then awaitTermination(5, SECONDS). What does awaitTermination return? true, because shutdownNow stops the threads true, because the task is removed from the queue It throws InterruptedException false, because the interrupt is only a request and this task ignores it shutdownNow calls interrupt() on the workers. That sets a flag and wakes threads that are blocked in calls such as sleep or take. A loop that never checks the flag and never blocks just runs on, so the pool can't terminate and the wait ends with false. Which code waits until every submitted task has finished, with no timeout, on JDK 21? try (pool) { ... } (try-with-resources, which calls close()) pool.shutdown(); pool.shutdownNow(); pool.isTerminated(); close() (JDK 19 and later) calls shutdown() and then waits until the pool has terminated. shutdown() and shutdownNow() return at once, and isTerminated() only reports the state. From "Race conditions: why count++ lies": four tasks on a fixed pool each run total += amount 100,000 times on a shared long field. What is total after close() returns? Exactly 400,000 times amount, because the pool runs tasks one after another Often less, because the four workers run at the same time and lose updates Exactly right, because each task runs on a single thread Unknown, because the pool throws ConcurrentModificationException A pool of four runs four tasks at once on four threads, so total += amount is the same read-modify-write race as before. The pool changes who creates the threads, not the rules for shared state. Use a LongAdder or an AtomicLong, or give each task its own subtotal.

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · Explain it back
x: A friend asks what shutdown(), shutdownNow() and awaitTermination() each do, and in what order a program should call them when it has 30 seconds to stop. Explain it in your own words.

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · Key terms
x: Task A piece of work handed over to be run, usually a Runnable or a Callable. Thread pool A set of threads created once that run many tasks, taking them from a queue. Executor Anything that can run a Runnable. It has one method, execute. ExecutorService An Executor that also returns Futures and can be shut down and waited for. Future A claim ticket for a task's result: you can wait on it, check it or cancel it. Poison pill A marker item put in a queue to tell the worker that takes it to stop. Daemon thread A background thread that does not keep the JVM alive. Pool threads usually are not daemon threads. Graceful shutdown Stop taking new work, let accepted work finish within a deadline, then release resources. Does shutdown() wait for running tasks to finish? No. It rejects new tasks and returns at once. Queued and running tasks carry on. Wait with awaitTermination or close(). What does shutdownNow() return? A List<Runnable> of the queued tasks that never started. It also interrupts the threads that are running tasks. A task sent with submit() throws. Where does the exception go? Into the Future. Nothing is printed. get() throws ExecutionException with it as the cause. A task sent with execute() throws. What happens? The worker thread dies, its UncaughtExceptionHandler runs (by default it prints the stack trace), and the pool starts a replacement. What does ExecutorService.close() do (JDK 19+)? shutdown(), then waits with no timeout until every task is done. If interrupted while waiting, it calls shutdownNow(), keeps waiting, then sets the interrupt flag again. Why can a forgotten newFixedThreadPool keep the JVM running after main returns? Its worker threads are non-daemon threads, and they wait for new tasks forever.

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · Go deeper
x: ThreadPoolExecutor has five run states, not three: RUNNING, SHUTDOWN, STOP, TIDYING and TERMINATED. shutdown() moves it to SHUTDOWN. shutdownNow() moves it to STOP, from either of the first two. When the queue is empty and the last worker has exited, the pool moves to TIDYING, runs the protected terminated() hook (override it to log something or release a resource), and then becomes TERMINATED. Threads blocked in awaitTermination wake only at that last step. The state and the worker count live together in one AtomicInteger called ctl. The top 3 bits hold the state and the low 29 bits hold the count. That's why the Javadoc caps a pool at about 500 million workers: (2^29) - 1. Packing both into one number lets execute ask "still running?" and "room for one more worker?" and claim the slot with one compare-and-set, the same atomic check-and-act that the lab gets from a lock. One more detail from the Executors Javadoc: newSingleThreadExecutor() is "guaranteed not to be reconfigurable to use additional threads", unlike newFixedThreadPool(1). The fixed pool is a plain ThreadPoolExecutor, so any code holding it can cast it and call setMaximumPoolSize. The single-thread executor is wrapped so that nobody can. If your design depends on tasks running one at a time, in order, say so with newSingleThreadExecutor().

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · Seven orders through four rules: where every task goes
x: The thrifty manager: seven orders through the four rules show a pool queues first and grows second, so an endless rail keeps the maximum of 64 from ever calling a cook Before any code, here are one kitchen's rules in plain words. The kitchen has two permanent cooks. Its rail has room for two tickets. When the rail is full, the manager may phone for temporary cooks, up to two of them. And when every cook is busy and the rail is full, a door policy decides what happens to the next customer. ThreadPoolExecutor has a setting for each part of that picture, and its main constructor takes them in this order: Java new ThreadPoolExecutor( 2, // corePoolSize: the permanent cooks 4, // maximumPoolSize: permanent plus temporary 60, TimeUnit.SECONDS, // keepAliveTime: how long an idle temp stays new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2), // the work queue: a rail with room for 2 new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy()); // the door policy when everything is full Kotlin ThreadPoolExecutor( 2, // corePoolSize: the permanent cooks 4, // maximumPoolSize: permanent plus temporary 60, TimeUnit.SECONDS, // keepAliveTime: how long an idle temp stays ArrayBlockingQueue(2), // the work queue: a rail with room for 2 ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy()) // the door policy when everything is full The core pool size is the number of threads the pool keeps, even when they're idle: the permanent cooks. The maximum pool size is the most threads it may ever run, permanent and temporary together. The keep-alive time is how long a temporary thread may sit idle before it's sent home. The work queue is the rail, a line where tasks join at the back and leave from the front. Here it's an ArrayBlockingQueue with room for two. The rejection handler is the door policy, and AbortPolicy, the default, simply refuses. Every call to execute walks the same four rules, in this order: Fewer threads than the core size? Start a new thread for this task, even if other threads are idle. Otherwise, offer the task to the queue. The queue said no? Start a new thread, if that stays within the maximum. Still no room? Hand the task to the rejection handler. Read rule 3 again, because it surprises almost everyone. The pool grows past its core size only when the queue is full. Most people expect the opposite: use more threads first, and queue when you run out. But the manager is thrifty. A ticket on the rail costs nothing, and a temporary cook costs wages, so temps are called only when the rail has no room left. In code, extra threads are a relief valve for bursts, not the pool's main capacity. Let's run it. Seven orders arrive at once, and each one takes 500 ms to cook. Write down where you think each order goes, then compare with what PoolPuzzleDemo printed. (It calls each order a task, a piece of work handed to the pool.) core=2 max=4 queue=bounded policy=abort task 1 accepted: threads=1 queued=0 task 2 accepted: threads=2 queued=0 task 3 accepted: threads=2 queued=1 task 4 accepted: threads=2 queued=2 task 5 accepted: threads=3 queued=2 task 6 accepted: threads=4 queued=2 task 7 REJECTED: threads=4 queued=2 Tasks 1 and 2 started the two core threads (rule 1). Tasks 3 and 4 waited on the rail (rule 2). Tasks 5 and 6 found the rail full and got temporary threads (rule 3). Task 7 found everything full, and the door policy turned it away with a RejectedExecutionException (rule 4). Now look at who finished first: task 1 done on pool-1-thread-1 task 6 done on pool-1-thread-4 task 2 done on pool-1-thread-2 task 5 done on pool-1-thread-3 task 3 done on pool-1-thread-1 task 4 done on pool-1-thread-4 all done in 1050 ms, completed tasks: 6 Tasks 5 and 6 were cooked before tasks 3 and 4, although they arrived later. A new thread takes the task that made the manager call it, not the oldest ticket on the rail. Here the restaurant picture breaks: a real kitchen would cook the oldest ticket first. So even a pool whose queue is first in, first out doesn't promise to run tasks in the order they arrived. The pool queues first and grows second. Only a full queue brings in extra threads. That rule has a sharp edge. If the queue can never fill, rule 3 never runs at all. Predict a burst, then run it Without running anything, write down where tasks 1 to 7 go for new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, 60, SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2)). Run PoolPuzzleDemo (the Java and Kotlin versions print the same) with the command below, and compare with your notes. Look at the done on lines. Which tasks finished first, and on which threads? PoolPuzzleDemo.java package workbench.executors.l02; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionHandler; import java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * Seven 500 ms tasks into new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, ...). Where does each one go? * Args: queue (bounded | unbounded | handoff) and policy (abort | caller | discard | oldest). */ public class PoolPuzzleDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String queueKind = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "bounded"; String policyKind = args.length > 1 ? args[1] : "abort"; BlockingQueue<Runnable> queue = switch (queueKind) { case "unbounded" -> new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(); case "handoff" -> new SynchronousQueue<>(); default -> new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2); }; RejectedExecutionHandler policy = switch (policyKind) { case "caller" -> new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy(); case "discard" -> new ThreadPoolExecutor.DiscardPolicy(); case "oldest" -> new ThreadPoolExecutor.DiscardOldestPolicy(); default -> new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy(); }; ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, 60, TimeUnit.SECONDS, queue, policy); System.out.printf("core=2 max=4 queue=%s policy=%s%n", queueKind, policyKind); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 1; i <= 7; i++) { int id = i; Runnable task = () -> { try { Thread.sleep(500); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } System.out.printf(" task %d done on %s%n", id, Thread.currentThread().getName()); }; try { pool.execute(task); System.out.printf("task %d accepted: threads=%d queued=%d%n", id, pool.getPoolSize(), pool.getQueue().size()); } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { System.out.printf("task %d REJECTED: threads=%d queued=%d%n", id, pool.getPoolSize(), pool.getQueue().size()); } } pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.printf("all done in %d ms, completed tasks: %d%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, pool.getCompletedTaskCount()); } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l02.PoolPuzzleDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l02/PoolPuzzleDemo.java PoolPuzzleDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l02 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** * Seven 500 ms tasks into ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, ...). Where does each one go? * Args: queue (bounded | unbounded | handoff) and policy (abort | caller | discard | oldest). */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val queueKind = args.getOrElse(0) { "bounded" } val policyKind = args.getOrElse(1) { "abort" } val queue = when (queueKind) { "unbounded" -> LinkedBlockingQueue<Runnable>() "handoff" -> SynchronousQueue<Runnable>() else -> ArrayBlockingQueue<Runnable>(2) } val policy = when (policyKind) { "caller" -> ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy() "discard" -> ThreadPoolExecutor.DiscardPolicy() "oldest" -> ThreadPoolExecutor.DiscardOldestPolicy() else -> ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy() } val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, 60, TimeUnit.SECONDS, queue, policy) println("core=2 max=4 queue=$queueKind policy=$policyKind") val t0 = System.nanoTime() for (id in 1..7) { val task = Runnable { try { Thread.sleep(500) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } println(" task $id done on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } try { pool.execute(task) println("task $id accepted: threads=${pool.poolSize} queued=${pool.queue.size}") } catch (e: RejectedExecutionException) { println("task $id REJECTED: threads=${pool.poolSize} queued=${pool.queue.size}") } } pool.shutdown() pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS) println("all done in ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms, completed tasks: ${pool.completedTaskCount}") } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l02.PoolPuzzleDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l02/PoolPuzzleDemo.kt The same as the output in this section: two core threads, two queued, two extra threads, one rejection. Tasks 1, 2, 5 and 6 finish first, at about 500 ms, in whatever order their threads wake up. Then tasks 3 and 4 run on two of those threads and finish at about 1,000 ms. Task 7 never runs. Every execute() call walks these four checks in order. The pool only grows toward max after the queue refuses a task.

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · A rail with no end: how an unbounded queue makes the maximum dead code
x: Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n), the line from last lesson, is a ThreadPoolExecutor with these settings: Java // what Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) builds new ThreadPoolExecutor(n, n, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()); Kotlin // what Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) builds ThreadPoolExecutor(n, n, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, LinkedBlockingQueue()) The queue is a LinkedBlockingQueue with no capacity given, which means it has no limit: a rail with no end. So rule 2 always succeeds. Rule 3 never runs, so no extra thread is ever started, and rule 4 never runs either, so nothing is ever rejected. Let's put that queue into our seven-order kitchen and keep the maximum of four. Run the demo with unbounded, and the end of the output reads: task 5 accepted: threads=2 queued=3 task 6 accepted: threads=2 queued=4 task 7 accepted: threads=2 queued=5 ... all done in 2019 ms, completed tasks: 7 Every task was accepted, the pool stayed at two threads, and five tasks waited on the rail. All seven finished after about 2,000 ms: four rounds of 500 ms on two cooks. The maximum of four never came into play. That looks safe. It isn't, because an endless rail hides overload instead of reporting it. Say orders arrive at 400 a second, and the pool can finish 300. The rail grows by 100 tasks every second. After ten minutes, 60,000 tasks are waiting, each one holding its order in memory. A new order now waits more than three minutes before a thread even looks at it. The customer gave up long ago, so the kitchen is busy cooking dinners nobody will eat. The first alarm is usually the heap, the memory where Java keeps its objects, running out. Raising the maximum on such a pool changes nothing. new ThreadPoolExecutor(10, 100, 60, SECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()) runs 10 threads, forever. The 100 is dead code: it compiles, and it never does anything. newCachedThreadPool() fails the other way. It's new ThreadPoolExecutor(0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, 60, SECONDS, new SynchronousQueue<>()), and a SynchronousQueue has no room at all. A task gets in only if an idle thread is waiting to take it right then, like a plate passed straight into a free cook's hands. That's called a direct handoff. Under a burst no thread is idle, so every task gets a new thread. Two thousand slow tasks means two thousand threads, which is the manager's hiring habit from last lesson. Run the demo with handoff to see it with our maximum of four. Tasks 1 to 4 each get a thread, nothing ever queues, and tasks 5, 6 and 7 are rejected. There's one shape that pushes back: a bounded queue with a finite maximum. Then rule 4 can fire, and overload turns into a visible event that you choose how to handle. Lesson 3 of this track picks the sizes. This lesson picks the shape. An unbounded queue never says no, so the pool never grows and never rejects. Give the queue a limit. One odd case is worth knowing. With a core size of 0 and an unbounded queue, rule 1 never starts a thread and rule 3 never runs. It looks as if nothing would ever run. The pool handles this as a special case: after it queues a task, if it has no threads at all, it starts one. You get a pool with a single thread. With a limit on the queue, rule 4 can finally fire. The question is what rule 4 should do. Swap the queue Predict the thread count and the total time for the same seven tasks with an unbounded queue. Then run the demo with -Pargs=unbounded. Do the same with -Pargs=handoff, which uses a SynchronousQueue. With unbounded, the pool never goes past 2 threads, all seven tasks are accepted, five of them queue, and the run takes about 2,000 ms (four rounds of 500 ms). With handoff, nothing ever queues: tasks 1 to 4 each get a thread, and tasks 5, 6 and 7 are rejected, because the maximum is 4 and a SynchronousQueue holds nothing. ThreadPoolExecutor (Java SE 25 API), section Queuing docs

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · When everything is full: four rejection policies, and who pays
x: When rule 4 fires, the pool calls its RejectedExecutionHandler, the door policy. The same handler also runs for any task submitted after shutdown(). The JDK, Java's standard library and tools, ships four policies, and each one makes someone different pay: Policy What happens to the task Who notices AbortPolicy (the default) execute throws RejectedExecutionException the caller, at once CallerRunsPolicy the thread that called execute runs the task itself the caller, by being slowed down DiscardPolicy dropped nobody DiscardOldestPolicy the oldest queued task is dropped, then the new one is tried again nobody In the kitchen, AbortPolicy tells the customer at the door, plainly, that the kitchen is full. CallerRunsPolicy sends the waiter who brought the order into the kitchen to cook it himself, and while he cooks, he takes no new orders. DiscardPolicy drops the ticket in the bin. DiscardOldestPolicy bins the oldest ticket on the rail to make room for the new one. AbortPolicy is the right default when a person or a program is waiting for an answer. The caller gets an exception that it can turn into a polite "try again later", and you can count the rejections. CallerRunsPolicy is back-pressure in one line: a full pool pushing back on whoever feeds it. While the submitting thread is busy running a task, it isn't submitting more, so the producer, the thread that feeds the pool, slows down to the pool's speed. Run the demo with "bounded caller" and watch task 7: task 6 accepted: threads=4 queued=2 task 1 done on pool-1-thread-1 task 2 done on pool-1-thread-2 task 5 done on pool-1-thread-3 task 6 done on pool-1-thread-4 task 7 done on main task 7 accepted: threads=4 queued=0 Task 7 ran on main, the thread that called execute. So the line task 7 accepted printed only after task 7 done on main, 500 ms later, and main handed the pool nothing new in the meantime. That suits a job that reads a file and hands out the work. It's a bad idea when the submitting thread has a job of its own that can't wait, such as a thread that reads incoming requests for everyone. Making it cook stalls everyone it serves. And after shutdown(), CallerRunsPolicy drops tasks silently. The two discard policies lose work without a trace, and they have a nastier side with submit. A dropped task never runs, so its Future, the claim ticket that submit returns, never completes. A caller waiting in get() waits forever, like a customer still sitting at the table for a dish that went in the bin. Use them only for work that is truly optional, such as a statistic you can afford to miss. When the pool is full, someone pays. Choose who, on purpose. In real code you usually want a handler of your own. It counts the rejection for a dashboard, then fails fast with a message that says how full the pool was. The interface has one method, rejectedExecution(Runnable task, ThreadPoolExecutor pool), and the lab has you write one. We know now where a task goes when it arrives. What happens to the extra cooks once the rush is over is the last piece. Try the other three policies Run the demo with -Pargs="bounded caller". Find the line for task 7. Which thread ran it, and when was its accepted line printed? Run it with -Pargs="bounded discard" and then -Pargs="bounded oldest". Count the done lines, and work out which task disappeared each time. With caller, task 7 runs on main, so main is stuck for 500 ms and prints "task 7 accepted" only after task 7 done on main. The pool reports 6 completed tasks, because task 7 never ran on it. With discard, task 7 is "accepted" and simply never runs: six done lines, and no error. With oldest, task 3, the oldest task in the queue, vanishes and task 7 runs in its place. Neither discard policy says a word about it.

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · After the rush: keep-alive, core time-out and starting threads early
x: Threads above the core size are temporary. If one sits idle for longer than the keep-alive time, it exits, and the pool shrinks back toward its core size. Core threads stay, even if they're idle for a week. KeepAliveDemo shows the whole cycle. Its pool has core 2, max 4, a rail of 2 and a keep-alive of 300 ms. It gets six orders of 200 ms each, and then prints the pool every 150 ms: before any task: threads=0 0 ms: threads=4 active=4 queued=2 201 ms: threads=4 active=2 queued=0 352 ms: threads=4 active=2 queued=0 507 ms: threads=2 active=0 queued=0 658 ms: threads=2 active=0 queued=0 ... largest pool size seen: 4 The pool starts with no threads at all, because even core threads are created lazily, one per task, the first time tasks arrive. The burst pushes it to 4. At about 200 ms, two threads finish their orders and find the rail empty. Three hundred milliseconds later they're sent home, so by 507 ms the pool is back to two threads, its core size. Two methods change that default. allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true) applies the keep-alive to core threads too, so an idle pool can shrink to zero. That suits a pool used for a report once a night, which then holds no threads for the rest of the day. It needs a keep-alive above zero, or the call throws an IllegalArgumentException. Run the demo with core, and the pool goes from 4 threads to 2, then to 0. prestartAllCoreThreads() goes the other way. It starts all the core threads up front, the way cooks arrive before the doors open. Then the first rush after the program starts doesn't also wait for threads to be created. The Javadoc, the JDK's official documentation of its classes, also recommends it when you build a pool around a queue that already holds tasks. A pool with no threads would never look at them. You can watch the pool through its getters: getPoolSize() (threads alive now), getActiveCount() (threads running a task), getLargestPoolSize() (the highest it has been) and getQueue().size(). They're approximate while the pool is busy, which is fine for a dashboard. Lesson 9 of this track turns them into measurements. For most pools that answer requests, I'd set the core size equal to the maximum, and rely on a bounded queue and a rejection policy. A pool that changes size under load is harder to reason about, and its extra threads arrive exactly when the machine is busiest. I'd keep core below max only when bursts are short and rare, and absorbing them beats turning work away. That's the whole machine: four rules, a queue, a door policy and a clock for idle threads. Every one of those settings is a number, though, and this lesson never said how to choose one. Watch the pool shrink KeepAliveDemo runs a pool with core 2, max 4, a queue of 2 and a 300 ms keep-alive. It submits six 200 ms tasks, then prints the pool every 150 ms. Predict the thread count at the end, then run it. Run it again with -Pargs=core, which also calls allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true). KeepAliveDemo.java package workbench.executors.l02; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * A pool grows to max under a burst, then shrinks back when threads sit idle longer than keepAlive. * Pass "core" to call allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true) as well. */ public class KeepAliveDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2)); if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("core")) pool.allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true); System.out.println("before any task: threads=" + pool.getPoolSize()); for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) { pool.execute(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(200); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int tick = 0; tick <= 8; tick++) { System.out.printf("%4d ms: threads=%d active=%d queued=%d%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, pool.getPoolSize(), pool.getActiveCount(), pool.getQueue().size()); Thread.sleep(150); } System.out.println("largest pool size seen: " + pool.getLargestPoolSize()); pool.shutdown(); } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l02.KeepAliveDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l02/KeepAliveDemo.java KeepAliveDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l02 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** * A pool grows to max under a burst, then shrinks back when threads sit idle longer than keepAlive. * Pass "core" to call allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true) as well. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(2)) if (args.firstOrNull() == "core") pool.allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true) println("before any task: threads=${pool.poolSize}") repeat(6) { pool.execute { try { Thread.sleep(200) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } } } val t0 = System.nanoTime() for (tick in 0..8) { println("%4d ms: threads=%d active=%d queued=%d".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, pool.poolSize, pool.activeCount, pool.queue.size)) Thread.sleep(150) } println("largest pool size seen: ${pool.largestPoolSize}") pool.shutdown() } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l02.KeepAliveDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l02/KeepAliveDemo.kt The pool starts with 0 threads, jumps to 4 during the burst, and drops back to 2 a few hundred milliseconds after the work ends. The largest pool size reported is 4. With core, it drops from 4 to 2 and then to 0, because the core threads now retire too.

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · Java and Kotlin
x: Configuring the same pool from Java and Kotlin AuthPool.java (solution) package workbench.executors.l02; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public final class AuthPool { private AuthPool() {} public static ThreadPoolExecutor create() { ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor( 4, // core: kept even when idle 8, // max: only reached once the queue is full 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS, // idle threads above core retire after 30 s new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(16), // bounded, so max and rejection can ever happen new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy()); // the default, written out so readers see it pool.prestartAllCoreThreads(); // start the 4 core threads now, not on first use return pool; } } AuthPoolConfig.kt package workbench.executors.l02 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong val rejectedAuths = AtomicLong() // Java constructors take no named arguments in Kotlin, so the comments do that job. fun authPool(): ThreadPoolExecutor = ThreadPoolExecutor( 4, 8, // core, max 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS, // keep-alive for threads above core ArrayBlockingQueue(16), // Runnable is inferred from the parameter type ) { _, pool -> // RejectedExecutionHandler, written as a trailing lambda rejectedAuths.incrementAndGet() throw RejectedExecutionException("rejected: queued=${pool.queue.size}") }.apply { prestartAllCoreThreads() } fun main() { val pool = authPool() println("threads before any task: ${pool.poolSize}") pool.shutdown() } Both build the lab's pool: 4 core threads, at most 8, a queue of 16, a 30-second keep-alive, and core threads started early. The Kotlin version also swaps the default policy for a lambda that counts each rejection and then throws. Two things differ when you build the pool from Kotlin. Kotlin doesn't allow named arguments when it calls a Java constructor, so the positional numbers need comments in both languages. And Kotlin turns a lambda into a Java interface with one method, so the RejectedExecutionHandler can be a trailing lambda instead of a class. The getters read as properties (pool.queue, pool.poolSize). In code that uses coroutines, Kotlin's own light tasks, you rarely build a pool at all: Dispatchers.IO is already a shared pool capped at 64 threads (or the number of cores, if that's larger), and limitedParallelism(n) gives you a smaller limit on top of it.

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · Worked example
x: Trace a burst through the checkout's card pool This is the pool from the lab, AuthPool. A shop's checkout uses it for card authorizations: each task asks the customer's bank whether a card payment may go through, and waits about 200 ms for the answer. The pool starts its 4 core threads early, so they're already waiting for work. Then a coach party pays at the same moment, and 30 tasks arrive together. Before reading on, write down how many threads start, how many tasks queue and how many are rejected. ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor( 4, 8, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(16), new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy()); pool.prestartAllCoreThreads(); val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor( 4, 8, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(16), ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy()) pool.prestartAllCoreThreads() Apply the rules in order, and say each core thread grabs its task at once. The four core threads already exist, so tasks 1 to 4 pass through the queue straight into their hands. Tasks 5 to 20 fill the queue of 16 (rule 2). Tasks 21 to 24 find the queue full and start extra threads, up to 8 (rule 3). Tasks 25 to 30 find everything full and are rejected (rule 4). threads = 8, queued = 16, rejected = 6 Six RejectedExecutionExceptions reach the checkout, and six customers are asked to pay again. Decide on purpose instead. Here, a short pause at the checkout beats six failed payments, so let the thread that submits the payments run the overflow itself. ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor( 4, 8, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(16), new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy()); // the submitting thread runs the overflow val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor( 4, 8, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(16), ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy()) // the submitting thread runs the overflow Now tasks 25 to 30 run on the submitting thread, one after another: about 6 x 200 ms = 1.2 s during which it hands the pool nothing new. For a checkout, that's a short pause, and nobody's payment fails. If that thread also had to answer other customers within a deadline, the pause would be the wrong trade. Then you'd keep AbortPolicy and ask the customer to try again.

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · Quiz
x: new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, 60, SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10)) receives 8 tasks that each block for a minute. Where are they? 4 running, 4 queued 2 running, 6 queued 4 running, 2 queued, 2 rejected 8 running Tasks 1 and 2 start core threads. The other 6 fit in a queue of 10, so the queue never refuses and the pool never grows. The tempting answer, 4 running, assumes the pool uses its maximum before it queues. It's the other way round. A job reads 2 million sales from a file and submits one task per 1,000 sales. You want it to go no faster than the pool can keep up, without losing a batch of sales and without writing a retry loop. Which policy fits? AbortPolicy DiscardOldestPolicy CallerRunsPolicy DiscardPolicy CallerRunsPolicy makes the reading thread run the overflow batch itself, so it stops reading while it works. That's back-pressure, and nothing is lost. AbortPolicy would make you write the retry loop, and both discard policies lose batches without telling anyone. A pool uses DiscardPolicy. A thread calls pool.submit(task).get() while the pool is full. What happens? get() throws RejectedExecutionException get() returns null get() throws CancellationException get() blocks forever, because the dropped task never runs and its Future never completes DiscardPolicy drops the FutureTask without running or cancelling it. Nothing will ever complete that Future, so get() without a timeout waits forever. That's why the Javadoc suggests cancelling dropped tasks in a handler of your own. A pool with core 4, max 16 and a bounded queue grew to 16 threads during a rush an hour ago. Things are quiet now. With default settings, how many threads does it have? 4, because idle threads above core retired after keepAliveTime 16, because threads are never removed 0, because idle threads retire 1, the minimum Keep-alive applies to threads above the core size, so the pool shrinks back to 4. It goes down to 0 only if you call allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true). From "Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown": a producer thread keeps calling execute on a ThreadPoolExecutor with the default handler after another thread has called shutdown(). What does the producer see? The tasks run, because shutdown() lets queued work finish A RejectedExecutionException from each execute call Nothing: the tasks are silently dropped An IllegalStateException After shutdown(), new tasks go to the rejection handler, and the default AbortPolicy throws RejectedExecutionException. Only tasks that were already queued still run. With a discard policy or CallerRunsPolicy, they would be dropped silently instead.

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · Explain it back

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · Key terms
x: corePoolSize The number of threads the pool keeps, even when idle. maximumPoolSize The most threads the pool may run, reached only when the queue is full. Work queue The BlockingQueue where tasks wait for a free thread. Direct handoff A SynchronousQueue: no storage, so a task passes straight to an idle thread or not at all. RejectedExecutionHandler The callback that decides what happens to a task the pool cannot take. Back-pressure Slowing the producer down when the consumer can't keep up, instead of piling up work. Keep-alive time How long an idle thread above core waits before it exits. In what order does ThreadPoolExecutor.execute try its options? Start a thread if below core; otherwise queue; if the queue refuses, start a thread if below max; otherwise reject. Why does newFixedThreadPool(8) never run more than 8 threads, whatever max you set? Its LinkedBlockingQueue is unbounded, so the queue never refuses a task, and the pool only grows past core when the queue refuses. What queue does newCachedThreadPool() use, and what is the risk? A SynchronousQueue (no capacity) with max Integer.MAX_VALUE, so every task that finds no idle thread gets a new thread. Threads grow without limit. What does CallerRunsPolicy do with an overflow task? The thread that called execute runs it, which slows that producer down. After shutdown, it drops the task. A pool with DiscardPolicy drops a task sent with submit. What happens to future.get()? It blocks forever. The task never runs, so its Future never completes. What does keepAliveTime apply to by default? Only to threads above corePoolSize. Call allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true) to let core threads retire too. Does a new extra thread pick up the oldest queued task first? No. A thread started by rule 3 runs the task that triggered it, so later tasks can overtake queued ones.

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · Go deeper
x: Why does ThreadPoolExecutor queue before it grows? Its Javadoc lists three ways of queuing and is honest about each. A direct handoff (SynchronousQueue) "avoids lockups when handling sets of requests that might have internal dependencies", because a task never waits in line behind another task that it depends on, but it needs an unbounded maximum. An unbounded queue suits independent tasks and smooths out bursts, but "admits the possibility of unbounded work queue growth". A bounded queue "helps prevent resource exhaustion" but "can be more difficult to tune": a large queue with a small pool keeps CPU use low and can give "artificially low throughput", while a small queue needs a larger pool. That first point comes back in lesson 9 of this track as pool-induced deadlock: tasks that wait for other tasks in the same bounded pool. Two more details for when you read pool code. First, core and max can be changed while the program runs, with setCorePoolSize and setMaximumPoolSize. That's how some frameworks resize pools from their settings without a restart. Second, ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor extends ThreadPoolExecutor but uses its own unbounded queue of delayed tasks, so its max setting has no useful effect: it's a fixed pool of corePoolSize threads. Lesson 5 of this track covers it.

h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · Cooks who chop all day: CPU-bound work wants one thread per core
x: Start with the first kitchen, where all the work is chopping. In a program, that's CPU-bound work: work that keeps a core of the CPU, the processor, busy from start to finish, with nothing to wait for. CpuBoundDemo, in the Try it below, has 32 such tasks. Each one computes a SHA-256 checksum of 16 MB of data. A checksum is a short fingerprint of the data that changes if any byte changes. You'd compute one to check that a big file arrived whole. It's pure arithmetic: no files, no network, no locks. The demo runs the 32 tasks on pools of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 threads. My guess, from Threads from zero: each doubling halves the time until the threads match the cores, and after that nothing improves. On a quiet 4-core machine, it printed: availableProcessors() = 4 1 threads: 359 ms 2 threads: 171 ms 4 threads: 92 ms 8 threads: 96 ms 16 threads: 98 ms (The demo also prints a checksum on each row, left out here. It was the same on every row.) Correctness first: the same checksum on every row means every pool did the same work. Then speed. The guess held. Two threads halved the time, four threads cut it to a quarter, and eight and sixteen threads were no faster than four. A core runs one thread at a time, so a fifth thread on four cores gets CPU time only by taking it from one of the other four. The extra threads add context switches, the operating system pausing one thread to resume another. They give the CPU's caches, its small fast copies of memory, more to juggle. And they get no extra work done. That's the fifth cook, holding a knife. So for CPU-bound work, size the pool to Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors(), the number of cores the JVM (the program that runs your Java code) may use. Brian Goetz's book Java Concurrency in Practice suggests one more than that. The extra thread keeps the cores busy when a thread stops for a moment, for example while the operating system brings some memory in from disk. Either is fine. Fifty threads for checksums is not. Ask the JVM, not the hardware spec. Many programs run in a container, a fenced-off space where the operating system limits how much CPU and memory one program may use. On Linux, the JVM reads that limit, so a container limited to 2 CPUs on a 64-core machine reports 2. That's the number you want, because it's all the CPU your program gets. What else the machine is doing matters too. On the same 4-core machine, while other heavy programs were running, one run printed 457, 282, 339, 434 and 339 ms. The best size was two threads, not four, because the pool only gets the CPU that nobody else is using. CPU-bound work wants about one thread per core. More threads only take turns. Chopping is the easy kitchen. Most programs spend their days in the other one, waiting for the oven. Find where the curve goes flat Check how many cores your machine has. Predict the pool size after which CpuBoundDemo stops getting faster. Run it with the command below, and check that the checksum is the same on every row. CpuBoundDemo.java package workbench.executors.l03; import java.security.MessageDigest; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** The same CPU-bound job (32 hashing tasks) on pools of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 threads. */ public class CpuBoundDemo { // pure computation: a SHA-256 checksum of 16 MB, like fingerprinting a big file. No waiting, no locks. static long hash(long seed) throws Exception { MessageDigest sha = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256"); byte[] block = new byte[16 * 1024]; block[0] = (byte) seed; for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) sha.update(block); return sha.digest()[0]; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("availableProcessors() = " + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()); hash(1); // warm up the JIT once for (int threads : new int[] {1, 2, 4, 8, 16}) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); long sum = 0; try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)) { List<Future<Long>> parts = new ArrayList<>(); for (int task = 0; task < 32; task++) { long seed = task; parts.add(pool.submit(() -> hash(seed))); } for (Future<Long> f : parts) sum += f.get(); } System.out.printf("%2d threads: %,5d ms (checksum %d)%n", threads, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, sum); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l03.CpuBoundDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l03/CpuBoundDemo.java CpuBoundDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l03 import java.security.MessageDigest import java.util.concurrent.Executors // pure computation: a SHA-256 checksum of 16 MB, like fingerprinting a big file. No waiting, no locks. private fun hash(seed: Long): Long { val sha = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256") val block = ByteArray(16 * 1024) block[0] = seed.toByte() repeat(1_000) { sha.update(block) } return sha.digest()[0].toLong() } /** The same CPU-bound job (32 hashing tasks) on pools of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 threads. */ fun main() { println("availableProcessors() = " + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()) hash(1) // warm up the JIT once for (threads in listOf(1, 2, 4, 8, 16)) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() val sum = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads).use { pool -> val parts = (0 until 32).map { task -> pool.submit<Long> { hash(task.toLong()) } } parts.sumOf { it.get() } } println("%2d threads: %,5d ms (checksum %d)".format(threads, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, sum)) } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l03.CpuBoundDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l03/CpuBoundDemo.kt The time roughly halves from 1 to 2 threads and from 2 to the core count, then stays flat or gets a little worse. If other programs are busy on the machine, or the laptop has slower power-saving cores, the curve flattens earlier: the pool only gets the CPU nobody else is using.

h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · Cooks who wait for the oven: how many threads a waiting task needs
x: Now the second kitchen. Most of what programs do looks like the oven, not the chopping board: a little work, then a long wait. Take a shop's website. To build one product page, our program works for 20 ms: it reads the request, finds the product and adds the tax. Then it asks a slow web service for the stock level, how many of the product are left, and waits 180 ms for the answer. A web service is a program on another computer that answers questions over the network. This is the slow one from Threads from zero, which took 120 ms there. Today it's having a slow afternoon. Work like this is I/O-bound, after input and output: it spends most of its time waiting for something outside the processor, such as the network or a disk. A thread that waits uses no core, just as a cook waiting for the oven doesn't need a board. So while one thread waits, another can use the core. Let's work out how many threads by hand, with one core. One page needs the core for 20 ms out of every 200, so the core sits idle nine tenths of the time unless other threads fill the gaps. Ten threads, each waiting nine parts and working one, keep the core busy. With four cores, that's forty. Goetz's book turns that reasoning into a formula: threads = cores x target CPU use x (1 + wait time / compute time) The ratio of waiting to computing does the work. For our page, 180 / 20 = 9, and 1 + 9 gives 10 threads per core, as we found by hand. The target CPU use is how busy you want the cores to be, as a fraction. You rarely want 100 percent, because a core with no spare time makes every burst wait in line. On an 8-core machine at 80 percent, the page needs 8 x 0.8 x 10 = 64 threads. You'll also see the same idea written with the blocking coefficient, the fraction of a task's time spent waiting: threads = cores / (1 - blocking coefficient). Our page waits 180 ms out of 200, a coefficient of 0.9, and 1 / (1 - 0.9) = 10 again. It's the same formula, written another way. Here the kitchen picture breaks, and not in our favor. A real cook would chop onions while the dish bakes. A Java thread can't: it waits for its answer and does nothing else. That's why we need ten threads where one clever cook would do. Virtual threads, much lighter threads that a later track covers, make that waiting cheap. The formula is a starting point, and it can mislead you in three ways. First, you have to measure the waiting and the computing. Put a timer around the call to the web service to get the wait. The rest of the task's time is roughly the compute. A guess like "it's mostly waiting" gives a number that looks precise and isn't. Second, it assumes waiting is free. Waiting for another computer to answer is. Waiting for a lock, which lets one thread at a time into a piece of code, isn't. More threads just make a longer line for the same lock. Third, it sizes for the CPU and knows nothing else. It can't tell that the slow web service accepts only 50 connections (open lines of communication) from you at a time. It can't tell that your database, the program that stores your data, accepts only 20. Those limits often decide the answer, and the last section of this lesson is about them. A task that waits nine parts and works one can share a core with nine others. Measure both parts before you trust the number. The formula starts from the CPU: how many threads keep the cores busy. A busy shop asks from the other side. How many requests arrive, and how many does that put inside our program at once? Size two pools by hand A refund service runs on 4 cores and aims for 50 percent CPU use. Each refund computes for 5 ms and waits 95 ms for the bank. Work out the pool size. A report job on the same machine computes for 40 ms and waits 10 ms per row. Work out its pool size too. Once you've done the lab, check both with PoolSizing.ioBound. Refunds: 4 x 0.5 x (1 + 95/5) = 40 threads. Reports: 4 x 0.5 x (1 + 10/40) = 2.5, rounded up to 3. The report job is mostly computing, so it gets about as many threads as the cores you're willing to give it.

h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · Little's law: how many requests are inside at once
x: Chopping cooks and oven cooks: checksums stop getting faster at one thread per core, a page that waits 180 of 200 ms needs ten threads per core, and 400 requests a second for 250 ms keep 100 inside Picture the ticket window at a cinema. On a busy evening, about 2 people join the line every minute. Each one spends about 5 minutes there, from joining the back of the line to walking away with a ticket. Look at the window at any moment: how many people do you expect to see? About 10. Two arrive each minute and each stays five, so ten are there at once. That multiplication is Little's law. It holds for any stable system, one where on average as many leave as arrive: a ticket window, a supermarket, a thread pool. L = λ x W L is the average number of things inside. λ (the Greek letter lambda) is the arrival rate, how many arrive each second. W is the average time each one spends inside, from arriving to leaving. For a request, that time is its latency. Now take the whole shop website, every kind of page together. At its busiest it gets 400 requests a second, and a request takes 250 ms on average from arrival to answer. So 400 x 0.25 = 100 requests are inside at once, on average. If each one holds a thread for its whole stay, that's 100 busy threads. With fewer threads, the rest wait in the pool's queue, its line of waiting tasks, and that waiting counts as time inside too. Turn the law around, and it tells you what a pool can do. Solve for λ: a pool of 50 threads, where each request holds a thread for 250 ms, finishes at most 50 / 0.25 = 200 requests a second. If 400 arrive, the other 200 a second pile up in the queue. Waiting in the queue adds to W, so the line grows without limit until memory, or the customers' patience, runs out. That's the rail with no end from the last lesson, with numbers. Here the ticket window picture breaks. People who see a long line often walk away. An unbounded queue, one with no limit, never turns anyone away, so it just grows. Let's not take the law's word for it. LittlesLawDemo, in the Try it below, sends 200 requests through pools of 5, 10, 20 and 40 threads. Each request just waits 50 ms, standing in for a call to the slow web service. Little's law predicts the most each pool can finish: its threads divided by 0.05 s. Here's a run: 5 threads: 96 req/s measured, 100 predicted by threads / W 10 threads: 181 req/s measured, 200 predicted by threads / W 20 threads: 389 req/s measured, 400 predicted by threads / W 40 threads: 689 req/s measured, 800 predicted by threads / W The first three rows land within about 10 percent of the prediction. The last falls further short, and the cause is the demo, not the law. For 40 threads, 200 requests are only five rounds, so starting the pool takes a bigger share of the run. When the work is mostly waiting, a pool's throughput, the work it finishes each second, is its thread count divided by the latency. Faster cores wouldn't help at all. More threads would, as long as threads are the scarce thing. JEP 444, the design document behind Java's virtual threads, makes this same argument, and it's why virtual threads exist. The virtual threads track picks it up. Requests inside = arrival rate x time inside. Turned around, threads / latency is the most a pool can finish. "As long as threads are the scarce thing" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. A request needs more than a thread. Check Little's law Read LittlesLawDemo. Predict the throughput for 40 threads before you run it. Run it with the command below, and compare each row with its prediction. LittlesLawDemo.java package workbench.executors.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; /** * 200 requests that each wait 50 ms for a slow web service, on pools of 5, 10, 20 and 40 threads. * Little's law predicts throughput = threads / 0.05 s. Pass "db" to make every request also hold * one of only 10 database connections while it waits. */ public class LittlesLawDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean db = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("db"); Semaphore connections = new Semaphore(10); // a 10-connection pool, when "db" is on int requests = 200; double latencySeconds = 0.050; for (int threads : new int[] {5, 10, 20, 40}) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)) { for (int i = 0; i < requests; i++) { pool.execute(() -> { try { if (db) connections.acquire(); try { Thread.sleep(50); // the call to the slow web service } finally { if (db) connections.release(); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); } } double seconds = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e9; System.out.printf("%2d threads: %4.0f req/s measured, %4.0f predicted by threads / W%n", threads, requests / seconds, threads / latencySeconds); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l03.LittlesLawDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l03/LittlesLawDemo.java LittlesLawDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l03 import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore /** * 200 requests that each wait 50 ms for a slow web service, on pools of 5, 10, 20 and 40 threads. * Little's law predicts throughput = threads / 0.05 s. Pass "db" to make every request also hold * one of only 10 database connections while it waits. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val db = args.firstOrNull() == "db" val connections = Semaphore(10) // a 10-connection pool, when "db" is on val requests = 200 val latencySeconds = 0.050 for (threads in listOf(5, 10, 20, 40)) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads).use { pool -> repeat(requests) { pool.execute { try { if (db) connections.acquire() try { Thread.sleep(50) // the call to the slow web service } finally { if (db) connections.release() } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } } } } val seconds = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e9 println("%2d threads: %4.0f req/s measured, %4.0f predicted by threads / W".format( threads, requests / seconds, threads / latencySeconds)) } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l03.LittlesLawDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l03/LittlesLawDemo.kt 5, 10 and 20 threads land within about 10 percent of 100, 200 and 400 requests a second. 40 threads falls further short of 800 (about 630 to 690 in runs here), because 200 requests are only five rounds for 40 threads, so starting the pool is a large part of the run. Little's law: if 400 requests arrive each second and each stays 250 ms, about 100 are inside at any moment.

h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · The smallest limit wins: connection pools and bulkheads
x: Back in the second kitchen, suppose it has only two ovens. Forty cooks were right for four boards, but a dish can bake only when an oven is free. Each oven holds one dish for nine minutes, so the kitchen bakes at most two dishes every nine minutes, whatever its number of cooks. Extra cooks just stand in line for an oven. Programs have ovens too. Say each page also reads from the shop's database, where its products are stored. A database accepts only so many connections, open lines to it, at once. So a program usually keeps a connection pool: a fixed set of open connections that threads borrow and give back. With 20 connections, each held for 10 ms, the database path tops out at 20 / 0.01 = 2,000 reads a second, whatever your thread count. Threads beyond that line up for a connection instead of a core. LittlesLawDemo can show it. Run it with db, and every request must also hold one of only 10 connections while it waits: 5 threads: 91 req/s measured, 100 predicted by threads / W 10 threads: 195 req/s measured, 200 predicted by threads / W 20 threads: 194 req/s measured, 400 predicted by threads / W 40 threads: 189 req/s measured, 800 predicted by threads / W Up to 10 threads, nothing changed. After that, the curve goes flat at about 200 a second, which is 10 connections divided by 0.05 s. The demo's connection pool is a Semaphore, a counter of permits that threads take and give back. It's the car park from Synchronizers, with 10 spaces, and the extra threads wait at its barrier. So size from the scarcest resource backwards. That may be the database's connection pool, the number of connections the slow web service allows you, or a limit on calls per second. When the bottleneck, the narrowest point, is further along the path, adding threads makes things worse. Picture a team that doubles a slow pool from 64 to 128 threads. The database still has 20 connections, so now 108 threads wait for one instead of 44, each holding a request in memory, and every request takes longer. Thread count is the easiest knob to turn, but here it's the wrong one. Limits also need walls between them. Say the shop's product pages, card payments and order history all share one pool of 64 threads. Card payments ask the bank, which usually answers in 200 ms. One evening the bank slows down to 3 seconds. Little's law fills all 64 threads with waiting payments within seconds, and order history pages, which never call the bank, start to fail because they wait too long. In the kitchen, the pizza oven has gone slow, and every cook is standing in front of it holding a pizza while nobody makes the salads. A bulkhead stops that. It's a separate limit for each slow thing your program calls, named after the walls inside a ship that keep one flooded compartment from sinking the whole ship. A bulkhead can be a separate pool for each one, or a Semaphore around the call, which is what you build in the lab. Give the bank 20 permits. When they're gone, new payments fail fast with a clear message, and the rest of the shop keeps its threads. The smallest limit on the path is the real ceiling. Give each slow service its own wall. We can size a pool from measurements now. But a pool full of waiting threads raises a new question. What if we want one of them to stop waiting, because the customer has gone home, or the bank is taking far too long? Hit the connection ceiling Predict the four rows of LittlesLawDemo when every request also needs one of 10 connections. Run the demo again with -Pargs=db. 5 threads still give about 100 requests a second, and 10 threads about 200. 20 and 40 threads also stay near 200: ten connections at 50 ms each allow 10 / 0.05 = 200 a second, and the extra threads just wait in connections.acquire(). h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · Java and Kotlin
x: A bulkhead in Java and with coroutines Bulkhead.java (solution, core of call) public <T> T call(Callable<T> work) throws Exception { // a waiting caller blocks its platform thread here if (!permits.tryAcquire(maxWait.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) { throw new BulkheadFullException("bulkhead '" + name + "' is full"); } try { return work.call(); } finally { permits.release(); } } Bulkhead.kt (kotlinx.coroutines) import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withPermit class Bulkhead(private val name: String, maxConcurrent: Int) { private val permits = Semaphore(maxConcurrent) // fail fast, like Duration.ZERO in the Java version suspend fun <T> tryCall(work: suspend () -> T): T { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) throw BulkheadFullException("bulkhead '$name' is full") try { return work() } finally { permits.release() } } // wait for a permit: the coroutine suspends and holds no thread while it waits suspend fun <T> call(work: suspend () -> T): T = permits.withPermit { work() } } Both versions protect a slow service the same way: at most N calls at once. The difference is what waiting costs. The Java version blocks a platform thread, an ordinary operating-system thread, in tryAcquire. So a thousand waiting callers are a thousand parked threads, which is why it needs a short maxWait. The Kotlin version runs in coroutines, Kotlin's light tasks, and its Semaphore suspends: the waiting coroutine gives its thread back until a permit is free. So a thousand waiting callers are a thousand small objects. The kotlinx Semaphore has no timed acquire; wrap the waiting call in withTimeout if you need a deadline.

h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · Worked example
x: Size the product-page pool from measurements Measure first. In a test at the expected busiest hour, the product-page path of the shop's website shows these numbers. Before reading on, estimate the pool size. busiest hour 400 requests / s CPU per request 10 ms (read the request, find the product, add tax) wait per request 140 ms (the slow web service) cores 8 the web service allows 50 connections from us at once Little's law gives the number of requests the traffic puts inside: L = 400 x (0.010 + 0.140) = 400 x 0.15 = 60 requests inside at once. If each request holds a thread for its whole stay, that's 60 threads. Check the CPU. 400 requests x 10 ms = 4 CPU-seconds every second, so 4 of the 8 cores are busy: 50 percent. Goetz's formula at that CPU use agrees: 8 x 0.5 x (1 + 140/10) = 60. The machine can carry the load. Now the limit further along the path. The web service allows 50 connections, and each call holds one for 140 ms, so that path tops out at 50 / 0.14 = 357 requests a second. That's below the 400 at the busiest hour. A pool of 60 would leave 10 threads waiting for a connection. So the real answer is: put calls to the web service behind a bulkhead of 50, size the pool near 60 so that the other work keeps moving, and treat 357 a second as the page's real capacity. Getting to 400 is now a question for the web service's owners (more connections) or for a cache that remembers recent answers. It's not a pool setting. Bulkhead stock = new Bulkhead("stock-service", 50, Duration.ofMillis(100)); ExecutorService pages = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(60); val stock = Bulkhead("stock-service", 50, Duration.ofMillis(100)) val pages = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(60)

h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · Quiz
x: A program that resizes photos is pure CPU work, and the JVM sees 8 cores. Someone raises its pool from 8 to 32 threads. What happens to throughput? It roughly quadruples About the same, or a little worse from context switching It doubles It deadlocks Eight cores run eight threads at a time. The other 24 threads only take turns on the same cores, and every switch costs a little. More threads help work that waits, not pure computation. A program receives 300 requests a second, and each one spends 400 ms inside it. How many requests are inside at once, on average? 75 750 120 40 L = λ x W = 300 x 0.4 = 120. Dividing 300 by 4, or multiplying by 2.5, are the tempting slips. Write the units down: requests per second times seconds gives requests. A service runs on 4 cores, aims for full CPU use, and each task computes for 10 ms and then waits 90 ms. What does Goetz's formula give? 40 4 36 400 4 x 1.0 x (1 + 90/10) = 4 x 10 = 40, the second kitchen from the opening. The tempting 36 comes from using wait / compute alone instead of 1 + wait / compute. The 1 counts the time each task spends on the core. A shop's product pages, card payments and order history share one pool of 64 threads. Card payments wait for the bank. When the bank slows down, order history pages, which never call the bank, start timing out. What is the best fix? Double the pool to 128 threads Switch the pool to an unbounded queue Use CallerRunsPolicy Put calls to the bank behind their own limit (a bulkhead), so they can't take every thread Slow calls to the bank fill every shared thread, so unrelated work starves. A bulkhead caps how many threads those calls may hold. Doubling the pool only delays the problem: Little's law fills 128 threads as surely as 64 when each call takes 3 s. From "Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection": a pool is new ThreadPoolExecutor(20, 200, 60, SECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()). Traffic is 400 requests a second at 250 ms each. What happens? It grows to 200 threads, which is plenty It stays at 20 threads, finishes at most 80 a second, and the queue grows without limit It grows to exactly the 100 threads Little's law asks for It rejects the excess requests With an unbounded queue the pool never grows past its core size, so 20 threads at 250 ms finish 20 / 0.25 = 80 a second. Little's law needs 100 inside. The other 320 a second pile up in the queue, which never refuses, so nothing is ever rejected either.

h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · Key terms
x: CPU-bound Work limited by computation. More threads than cores don't help. I/O-bound Work that mostly waits on the network or a disk, so one core can serve many such tasks. Blocking coefficient The fraction of a task's time spent waiting. It decides how many threads one core can keep busy. Little's law Requests inside equal the arrival rate times the time each one spends inside. Throughput Work finished per unit of time, such as requests per second. Latency How long one request takes from arrival to completion. Connection pool A fixed set of open connections to a database that threads borrow and give back. Bulkhead A separate limit for each slow service, so one slow service can't use all the threads. How many threads for a pool doing pure CPU work? About one per core: Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() (Goetz suggests one more). Goetz's pool-size formula for tasks that wait? threads = cores x target CPU use x (1 + wait time / compute time). State Little's law. L = λ x W: requests inside = arrival rate x average time inside. 50 threads, each request holds a thread for 250 ms. Maximum throughput? 50 / 0.25 = 200 requests per second. Why don't threads beyond the size of the database's connection pool make database work faster? Each request needs a connection. The extra threads just wait in line for one. What is a bulkhead? A separate limit on concurrent calls for each slow service (its own pool or a Semaphore), so one slow service can't take every thread. What does availableProcessors() return inside a container limited to 2 CPUs? The JVM reads the container's CPU limit, not the machine's core count.

h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · Go deeper
x: Why aim for 80 percent CPU use and not 100? Queueing theory, the mathematics of waiting lines, has a short answer. In its simplest model, one server with customers arriving at random (called M/M/1), the average time in the system is W = S / (1 - ρ). S is the service time, and ρ (the Greek letter rho) is how busy the server is, as a fraction. At 50 percent busy, a request spends 2 x S in the system. At 80 percent, 5 x S. At 90 percent, 10 x S. At 99 percent, 100 x S. Real systems are not this simple, but the shape holds: latency grows slowly at first and then very fast as you get close to full use. Spare capacity is what keeps the slowest requests reasonable during a burst. Little's law has a subtle side that this lesson only touched. The W in L = λ x W is the measured time in the system, including time spent waiting in line. If you add threads and requests now wait for a database connection instead of for a thread, W grows and throughput doesn't. More threads raise the ceiling only while threads are what requests wait for. Once the narrowest point moves further along the path, that later limit sets λ. Two last tools. You can tell the JVM how many cores to report with -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=N, which helps when a container's limit isn't what you want your pools to see. And you can measure instead of guessing: time each task's wait in the queue and its run time separately (lesson 9 of this track does this with beforeExecute and afterExecute). If the wait in the queue dominates, the pool is too small for its traffic. If the run time grew, look further along the path.

h: Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption · A claim ticket for a result: Callable, Future and a wait with a time limit
x: Start with a shop's website. When a customer pays, the program asks the bank to charge their card. The bank is another computer, so the program sends a request over the network and waits for the answer. On a normal day, that's about 200 ms. (It's the bank from Sizing a pool.) We'd like to hand that call to a thread pool and get the answer back. In Why pools, every task was a Runnable, whose run() method returns nothing. A task that should hand back an answer is a Callable<V> instead. Its call() method returns a value of type V, and it may throw any exception, even a checked one. You give a Callable to the pool with submit, and the pool gives you a Future<V> back at once. A Future is the ticket from the counter: a promise of a result that doesn't exist yet. Here's the smallest one, with a task that just multiplies: Java Future<Integer> answer = pool.submit(() -> 6 * 7); // returns at once, with a ticket int n = answer.get(); // waits for the task: 42 Kotlin val answer: Future<Int> = pool.submit<Int> { 6 * 7 } // returns at once, with a ticket val n = answer.get() // waits for the task: 42 get() is the wait at the counter. It blocks: the calling thread stops and does nothing else until the task has finished. Then get() hands over the value. If the task threw an exception, get() throws an ExecutionException with the task's own exception inside it, as its cause. If someone cancelled the task, it throws CancellationException. And if your own thread is asked to stop while it waits, it throws InterruptedException, which the next two sections are about. (A successful get() also makes everything the task wrote visible to the thread that got the result. The memory model track explains why that matters.) Plain get() waits as long as the task takes. If the bank takes 30 seconds, your customer waits 30 seconds. So real code waits with a time limit, get(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS), which throws TimeoutException if the answer isn't there in time. That's the five minutes before the bus. Now the trap from the counter. TimeoutDemo, in the Try it below, asks a bank that's having a slow day and takes 600 ms, and it waits only 200 ms. Each line shows the time, the thread and what happened. On a busy machine, it printed: 86 ms pool-1-thread-1 asking the bank to charge the card 285 ms main get timed out after 200 ms 771 ms pool-1-thread-1 bank answered: APPROVED (the card was charged) 773 ms main pool closed The main thread gave up at 285 ms. In a real shop, that's the moment the program tells the customer the payment failed. The task didn't know. It kept waiting for the bank, and at 771 ms the bank charged the card. The customer heard "failed" and paid anyway, which is the one combination nobody wants. So the bank call is the burger at minute seven. A time limit on get ends your wait. It says nothing to the task, which keeps going until it's done. A time limit ends your wait, not the work. Decide what happens to the work. You have two choices. Stop the work, or make sure its result is written down somewhere you can find it later. Stopping it means asking the task, and Java's way of asking does less than its name suggests. Give up on a slow bank Run TimeoutDemo in either language. Compare the time on the bank answered line with the time on the get timed out line. Run it again with -Pargs=cancel. That version calls cancel(true) right after the time limit. Before you run it, predict: does the bank still answer? Pass "cancel" to cancel(true) after the timeout. */ public class TimeoutDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%4d ms %-12s %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, Thread.currentThread().getName(), msg); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean cancel = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("cancel"); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1)) { Future<String> auth = pool.submit(() -> { log("asking the bank to charge the card"); try { Thread.sleep(600); // the bank is slow today } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("interrupted: giving up on the bank"); throw e; } log("bank answered: APPROVED (the card was charged)"); return "APPROVED"; }); try { log("result: " + auth.get(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)); } catch (TimeoutException e) { log("get timed out after 200 ms"); if (cancel) log("cancel(true) returned " + auth.cancel(true)); } } // close() waits for the task, which is still running unless we cancelled it log("pool closed"); } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l04.TimeoutDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l04/TimeoutDemo.java TimeoutDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l04 import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException private val T0 = System.nanoTime() private fun log(msg: String) = println("%4d ms %-12s %s".format((System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, Thread.currentThread().name, msg)) /** get(200 ms) on a call that takes 600 ms.
