h: Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption · Asking the kitchen to stop: cancel(true) sends an interrupt, nothing more
x: Ticket 42: a time limit ends the wait, not the work, and cancel(true) only leaves a note, so the cook at the oven stops, the cook who looks up stops, the one who never looks runs on, and every ticket says cancelled at once The cancel run of TimeoutDemo looked easy. We cancelled, and the task stopped within a few milliseconds. Here it is, from the same busy machine: 60 ms pool-1-thread-1 asking the bank to charge the card 257 ms main get timed out after 200 ms 260 ms pool-1-thread-1 interrupted: giving up on the bank 275 ms main cancel(true) returned true 280 ms main pool closed To see why it worked, and when it won't, we need to know what cancel actually does. Future.cancel(boolean mayInterruptIfRunning) has two modes. cancel(false) stops a task that hasn't started yet, so it never runs, and leaves a running task alone. cancel(true) does the same, and if the task is running, it also interrupts the thread that runs it. An interrupt is a request to a thread to stop what it's doing. It sets a true-or-false value inside the thread, called the interrupt flag. If the thread is blocked at that moment, waiting in a method such as Thread.sleep, BlockingQueue.take or Future.get, that method wakes up and throws InterruptedException. If the thread is busy computing, nothing happens to it. The flag stays set until the thread looks at it. Setting the flag is all cancel(true) does. Java has no safe way to kill a thread from outside. Thread.stop() was deprecated, marked as "don't use", for decades, has thrown UnsupportedOperationException since JDK 20, and was removed in JDK 26. So cancelling is cooperative: it works only if the task helps. Picture the interrupt as a note that the manager puts on a cook's station: "please stop order 42". Our kitchen has three cooks. The first is waiting for the oven. The second is chopping onions, and looks up after each one. The third is chopping too, and never looks up. The task in TimeoutDemo was the first cook. It was waiting in Thread.sleep, which stands in for the wait for the bank's answer, so the note woke it at once. CancelDemo builds all three cooks in code. The sleeper sleeps. The checker does 400 slices of arithmetic, a few milliseconds each, and checks Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() before each slice. The ignorer does the same work and never checks. After 100 ms, main calls cancel(true) on all three: after cancel: isCancelled=true/true/true isDone=true/true/true sleeper: InterruptedException, stopping checker: saw the flag after 51 slices, stopping ignorer: finished all 400 slices anyway, 769 ms after the cancel pool closed Read the first line again. All three futures said cancelled and done straight away, before any task had reacted. A Future changes its state the moment you call cancel. It doesn't wait for the task to stop. Then each cook did what that cook does. The sleeper, waiting for the oven, was woken by the note. The checker saw it the next time it looked up. The ignorer chopped on for another 769 ms, as if nobody had said a word. If its work had been charging a card, the card would be charged, under a ticket that says cancelled. Here the kitchen picture breaks in two places. A real cook hears you shout across the room, but a thread hears nothing unless it's waiting or it looks. And a real kitchen can tell you whether the dish was made. A cancelled Future can't. It only knows that nobody will collect a result. Cancelling only asks. The task must listen, and the ticket can't tell you whether it did. So a long computing loop should look up now and then, as the checker does. In the Try it, you'll teach the ignorer that habit. cancel(false) has its own use. When a program shuts down, you may want running tasks to finish but queued ones never to start. Cancel the queued ones with false. And cancel returns false if the task had already finished or was already cancelled, which tells you the request came too late. The sleeper stopped because sleep threw InterruptedException. What a task does with that exception decides whether the stop request survives. Cancel three kinds of task Run CancelDemo and match each line of the output to one of the three cooks. Teach the ignorer to look up: copy the checker's isInterrupted() check, with its return, into the ignorer's loop. Predict how long after the cancel it stops now, then run it. CancelDemo.java package workbench.executors.l04; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** cancel(true) on three tasks: one that sleeps, one that checks the flag, one that never looks. */ public class CancelDemo { static volatile long sink; // keeps each result, so the JIT can't skip the work static volatile long cancelledAt; // when main called cancel, for the ignorer's report // a few milliseconds of CPU work: 400 of them take a second or more static long slice(long x) { for (int i = 0; i < 2_000_000; i++) x = x * 31 + i; return x; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3)) { Future<?> sleeper = pool.submit(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(5_000); System.out.println("sleeper: woke up normally"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("sleeper: InterruptedException, stopping"); } }); Future<?> checker = pool.submit(() -> { long x = 0; for (int s = 0; s < 400; s++) { if (Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) { System.out.println("checker: saw the flag after " + s + " slices, stopping"); return; } x = slice(x); } sink = x; System.out.println("checker: finished all 400 slices"); }); Future<?> ignorer = pool.submit(() -> { long x = 0; for (int s = 0; s < 400; s++) x = slice(x); // never looks at the flag sink = x; long late = (System.nanoTime() - cancelledAt) / 1_000_000; System.out.println("ignorer: finished all 400 slices anyway, " + late + " ms after the cancel"); }); Thread.sleep(100); cancelledAt = System.nanoTime(); for (Future<?> f : new Future<?>[] {sleeper, checker, ignorer}) f.cancel(true); System.out.printf("after cancel: isCancelled=%b/%b/%b isDone=%b/%b/%b%n", sleeper.isCancelled(), checker.isCancelled(), ignorer.isCancelled(), sleeper.isDone(), checker.isDone(), ignorer.isDone()); } // close() waits: the ignorer is still burning CPU System.out.println("pool closed"); } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l04.CancelDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l04/CancelDemo.java CancelDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l04 import java.util.concurrent.Executors @Volatile private var sink = 0L // keeps each result, so the JIT can't skip the work @Volatile private var cancelledAt = 0L // when main called cancel, for the ignorer's report // a few milliseconds of CPU work: 400 of them take a second or more private fun slice(start: Long): Long { var x = start for (i in 0 until 2_000_000) x = x * 31 + i return x } /** cancel(true) on three tasks: one that sleeps, one that checks the flag, one that never looks. */ fun main() { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3).use { pool -> val sleeper = pool.submit { try { Thread.sleep(5_000) println("sleeper: woke up normally") } catch (e: InterruptedException) { println("sleeper: InterruptedException, stopping") } } val checker = pool.submit { var x = 0L for (s in 0 until 400) { if (Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted) { println("checker: saw the flag after $s slices, stopping") return@submit } x = slice(x) } sink = x println("checker: finished all 400 slices") } val ignorer = pool.submit { var x = 0L repeat(400) { x = slice(x) } // never looks at the flag sink = x val late = (System.nanoTime() - cancelledAt) / 1_000_000 println("ignorer: finished all 400 slices anyway, $late ms after the cancel") } Thread.sleep(100) cancelledAt = System.nanoTime() listOf(sleeper, checker, ignorer).forEach { it.cancel(true) } println("after cancel: isCancelled=%b/%b/%b isDone=%b/%b/%b".format( sleeper.isCancelled, checker.isCancelled, ignorer.isCancelled, sleeper.isDone, checker.isDone, ignorer.isDone)) } // close() waits: the ignorer is still burning CPU println("pool closed") } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l04.CancelDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l04/CancelDemo.kt First run: the sleeper and the checker stop within a few milliseconds of the cancel. The ignorer runs on for hundreds of milliseconds (769 ms in the run above, on a busy machine), and close() waits for it, so pool closed comes last. After your change, the ignorer stops after a few dozen slices too, and pool closed follows the cancel almost at once.

h: Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption · Keeping the stop request alive: rethrow InterruptedException or restore the flag
x: Here's a task that does almost everything right. StatementPoller, from this lesson's lab, asks the bank every so often for new lines on an account statement, the list of money in and out of an account. It runs as a task on a pool. It should stop when someone shuts the pool down with shutdownNow(), or cancels the task with cancel(true). Both of those interrupt its thread. Here's its starting code: Java // Naive: the stop request is lost in pause() public void run() { while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) { pollOnce.run(); polls.incrementAndGet(); pause(); } } private void pause() { try { Thread.sleep(interval.toMillis()); } catch (InterruptedException e) { // nothing useful to do here; the loop will carry on } } Kotlin // Naive: the stop request is lost in pause() override fun run() { while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted) { pollOnce.run() polls.incrementAndGet() pause() } } private fun pause() { try { Thread.sleep(interval.toMillis()) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { // nothing useful to do here; the loop will carry on } } (The lab is in Java. The Kotlin version is a translation, so you can read it in either language.) The loop checks the flag on every pass, so it looks right. Yet in the lab's tests, shutdownNow() returns, awaitTermination (which waits for the pool to finish) runs out its full five seconds, and the poller keeps polling. Let's follow one stop request through it, step by step: The poller is asleep in Thread.sleep, where it spends nearly all its time. The test calls shutdownNow() on the pool, which interrupts the poller's thread. sleep wakes up. Before it throws InterruptedException, it clears the interrupt flag. pause() catches the exception, does nothing, and returns. The loop checks isInterrupted(). The flag is clear, so the check reads false, and the poller polls again. Nobody interrupts it a second time, so it never stops. Step 3 is the one people miss. In A thread's life, the interrupt was a note on a clerk's desk, and waking up tore the note off. Inside the catch block, you hold the only copy of the request. If you drop it, no code further up can ever see it. So there are two correct moves. Let the exception travel up to your caller, or put the note back with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() before you go on. Here they are on a task that clips a ticket onto the kitchen's rail, a BlockingQueue whose put waits while the rail is full: Java // 1. propagate: declare it and let it go up void clip(Ticket t) throws InterruptedException { rail.put(t); } // 2. you can't propagate (Runnable.run can't throw it): restore the flag public void run() { try { rail.put(ticket); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // put the request back return; // and stop } } Kotlin // 1. propagate: Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so simply don't catch it fun clip(t: Ticket) { rail.put(t) } // 2. if you do catch it: restore the flag override fun run() { try { rail.put(ticket) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // put the request back return // and stop } } Wrapping it in an exception of your own is fine, as long as you restore the flag first. Logging it and moving on is not. From JDK 26, the Thread Javadoc has a section on interruption that states this same rule. A swallowed interrupt makes shutdownNow() and cancel(true) do nothing. Rethrow it, or restore it. A request can get lost in one more place: a thread waiting for another computer's answer. Whether that thread notices an interrupt depends on how it reads from the network. A read through a channel from java.nio.channels, Java's newer networking classes, does notice: the JDK closes the channel and the read fails. A read from a classic java.net.Socket on a platform thread, an ordinary operating-system thread, doesn't notice and waits on. So give every call to another computer its own time limit, and treat the interrupt as a second line of defense. Check yourself before you go on. A task catches InterruptedException from sleep, logs it, and goes back to sleep. Does the second sleep throw at once? No. The flag was cleared, so it sleeps its full time. Add Thread.currentThread().interrupt() to the catch, and the second sleep throws straight away, because sleep checks the flag before it starts to wait. The stop request survives now. One part of the ticket is still clumsy, though: to find out how a task ended, we call get() and catch every exception it can throw.

h: Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption · Reading the ticket without waiting: Future.state(), invokeAll and invokeAny
x: Before JDK 19, the only way to ask a Future how its task ended was to call get() inside a try, with a catch for each outcome. JDK 19 added state(), the glance at the screen. It never blocks, and it returns one of four values: RUNNING, SUCCESS, FAILED or CANCELLED. Two more methods read a finished ticket without any checked exceptions: Java switch (f.state()) { case RUNNING -> log.info("still waiting for the bank"); case SUCCESS -> record(f.resultNow()); // the value case FAILED -> log.warn("bank call failed", f.exceptionNow()); // the task's own exception case CANCELLED -> log.info("cancelled"); } Kotlin when (f.state()) { Future.State.RUNNING -> log.info("still waiting for the bank") Future.State.SUCCESS -> record(f.resultNow()) // the value Future.State.FAILED -> log.warn("bank call failed", f.exceptionNow()) // the task's own exception Future.State.CANCELLED -> log.info("cancelled") } resultNow() gives you the value, and exceptionNow() gives you the task's own exception, without the ExecutionException around it. Both are for tickets you know are finished. resultNow() throws IllegalStateException if the task isn't done or didn't succeed. exceptionNow() throws it if the task didn't fail, and a cancelled task didn't fail. So check state() first, as the switch does. The lab's Futures.describe is this switch, turned into one line for a log. A pool can also handle a whole list of tickets for you. Picture phoning three shops to ask whether they have an item in stock, and taking the first "yes". ExecutorService, the interface every pool in this track implements, has two methods for jobs like that: invokeAll(tasks) runs every task and returns all their futures once every one has finished. With a time limit, it cancels whatever isn't done by then, so every future it returns is finished. invokeAny(tasks) returns the result of the first task that succeeds. It cancels the rest, and it throws ExecutionException only if every task fails. InvokeAnyDemo asks three exchange-rate services for today's rate from euros to US dollars, that is, how many dollars one euro buys. Alpha takes 300 ms. Beta takes 100 ms and then fails. Gamma takes 200 ms. Before reading on, guess what invokeAny returns: invokeAny -> gamma EUR/USD 1.0842 alpha: interrupted, cancelled invokeAll with a 250 ms deadline: alpha: interrupted, cancelled CANCELLED FAILED: beta is down SUCCESS: gamma EUR/USD 1.0842 Beta answered first, and its answer was that it was down. A failure doesn't count as an answer, so invokeAny waited for gamma, took its rate, and interrupted alpha, which was still on the phone. Then invokeAll, with a 250 ms deadline, returned one ticket of each kind: alpha cancelled at the deadline, beta failed, gamma succeeded. Both methods block the thread that calls them until they return. So call them from a thread that is allowed to wait, never from a task running on the same small pool. Here's why. Picture a pool of 3 threads, running 3 tasks that each call invokeAll with 3 subtasks on that same pool. All three threads now wait for subtasks, and no thread is free to run one. Nothing ever moves again. Lesson 9 of this track calls that pool-induced deadlock, and has you fix one. state() reads a ticket without waiting. Check it before you call resultNow(). We now have the whole ticket: collect it, wait with a limit, cancel it, read it at a glance. What a ticket can't do is come back on its own, every few seconds, all day. First good answer wins Read the three services in InvokeAnyDemo: alpha takes 300 ms, beta fails after 100 ms, gamma takes 200 ms. Predict what invokeAny returns and which service gets interrupted. Predict the three states that invokeAll reports with its 250 ms deadline. Then run the demo. InvokeAnyDemo.java package workbench.executors.l04; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.Callable; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Three FX-rate providers with different speeds: invokeAny takes the first, invokeAll waits with a deadline. */ public class InvokeAnyDemo { static Callable<String> provider(String name, long millis, boolean fails) { return () -> { try { Thread.sleep(millis); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println(" " + name + ": interrupted, cancelled"); throw e; } if (fails) throw new IllegalStateException(name + " is down"); return name + " EUR/USD 1.0842"; }; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { List<Callable<String>> providers = List.of( provider("alpha", 300, false), provider("beta", 100, true), // fastest, but fails provider("gamma", 200, false)); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3)) { System.out.println("invokeAny -> " + pool.invokeAny(providers)); Thread.sleep(50); System.out.println("invokeAll with a 250 ms deadline:"); List<Future<String>> all = pool.invokeAll(providers, 250, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); for (Future<String> f : all) { System.out.println(" " + f.state() + switch (f.state()) { case SUCCESS -> ": " + f.resultNow(); case FAILED -> ": " + f.exceptionNow().getMessage(); default -> ""; }); } } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l04.InvokeAnyDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l04/InvokeAnyDemo.java InvokeAnyDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l04 import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Future import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit private fun provider(name: String, millis: Long, fails: Boolean) = Callable { try { Thread.sleep(millis) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { println(" $name: interrupted, cancelled") throw e } if (fails) throw IllegalStateException("$name is down") "$name EUR/USD 1.0842" } /** Three FX-rate providers with different speeds: invokeAny takes the first, invokeAll waits with a deadline. */ fun main() { val providers = listOf( provider("alpha", 300, false), provider("beta", 100, true), // fastest, but fails provider("gamma", 200, false), ) Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3).use { pool -> println("invokeAny -> " + pool.invokeAny(providers)) Thread.sleep(50) println("invokeAll with a 250 ms deadline:") val all = pool.invokeAll(providers, 250, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) for (f in all) { val detail = when (f.state()) { Future.State.SUCCESS -> ": " + f.resultNow() Future.State.FAILED -> ": " + f.exceptionNow().message else -> "" } println(" ${f.state()}$detail") } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l04.InvokeAnyDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l04/InvokeAnyDemo.kt invokeAny returns gamma's rate. Beta finished first, but it failed, and a failure doesn't count. Alpha prints interrupted, cancelled. With the 250 ms deadline, invokeAll reports alpha CANCELLED (interrupted at the deadline), beta FAILED with beta is down, and gamma SUCCESS. A Future starts RUNNING and ends in one of three states. state() tells you which, without waiting. ExecutorService (Java SE 25 API): invokeAll and invokeAny docs

h: Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption · Java and Kotlin
x: Cancelling work: a Future and an interrupt vs a coroutine CancelOne.java Future<String> f = pool.submit(() -> { Thread.sleep(5_000); // wakes with InterruptedException on cancel(true) return "done"; }); Thread.sleep(100); f.cancel(true); // sends an interrupt to the worker thread // f.isCancelled() is true at once, whatever the task does next CancelOne.kt (kotlinx.coroutines) val job = scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) { delay(5_000) // pauses; resumes with CancellationException on cancel println("done") } delay(100) job.cancel() // no interrupt: delay() notices the cancellation itself // a blocking call ignores job.cancel() unless you wrap it: // runInterruptible { Thread.sleep(5_000) } Both versions ask, and neither can force. Java sends the request as an interrupt, which blocking methods and isInterrupted() checks pick up. Kotlin's coroutines, light tasks that can pause without holding a thread, get it as a CancellationException at the points where they pause, such as delay, await and withContext. No interrupt is involved, so a blocking Java call inside a coroutine doesn't notice the cancel unless you wrap it in runInterruptible. The interrupt rules from this lesson still apply to Kotlin code that runs blocking work on an executor. Watch runCatching there: it catches InterruptedException like any other exception, which makes it an easy way to swallow a stop request. The coroutines track covers cancellation in full.

h: Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption · Worked example
x: Give up on a slow bank without telling the customer something wrong A payment handler hands the bank call to a pool and waits for the answer. On a normal day, this works. Before reading on, decide what happens when the bank starts taking 30 seconds to answer. Future<String> charge = pool.submit(() -> bank.charge(payment)); return charge.get(); // waits as long as the bank does val charge = pool.submit<String> { bank.charge(payment) } return charge.get() // waits as long as the bank does Every request thread ends up stuck in get(). Little's law, from Sizing a pool, does the rest: at 400 payments a second and 30 seconds each, 12,000 requests are inside at once, each holding a thread. The program stops answering anyone. So wait with a time limit, and cancel the work you stopped waiting for. Future<String> charge = pool.submit(() -> bank.charge(payment)); try { return charge.get(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // 1. wait, with a limit } catch (TimeoutException e) { charge.cancel(true); // 2. ask the bank call to stop return "PENDING"; // 3. don't claim it failed } val charge = pool.submit<String> { bank.charge(payment) } return try { charge.get(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // 1. wait, with a limit } catch (e: TimeoutException) { charge.cancel(true) // 2. ask the bank call to stop "PENDING" // 3. don't claim it failed } Why PENDING and not DECLINED? The request may have reached the bank before the interrupt arrived, and a classic socket read may not even notice the interrupt. So the card may still be charged. If we said "declined", the customer would pay again, and then they'd have paid twice. Make the outcome easy to find later. Give every payment a unique ID and send it with the request, so the bank charges each ID at most once, however many times it hears it. On a timeout, add the ID to a list that a small job works through later, asking the bank what happened to each one. (Engineers call an ID like this an idempotency key: sending it twice has the same effect as sending it once.) String paymentId = payment.id(); Future<String> charge = pool.submit(() -> bank.charge(payment, paymentId)); try { return charge.get(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } catch (TimeoutException e) { charge.cancel(true); checkLater.add(paymentId); // 4. a later job asks the bank about it return "PENDING"; } val paymentId = payment.id() val charge = pool.submit<String> { bank.charge(payment, paymentId) } return try { charge.get(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) } catch (e: TimeoutException) { charge.cancel(true) checkLater.add(paymentId) // 4. a later job asks the bank about it "PENDING" }

h: Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption · Quiz
x: A task asks the bank to move money between two accounts. The caller's get(500, MILLISECONDS) throws TimeoutException, and the caller does nothing else. What happens to the transfer? It is cancelled automatically when get() times out It may well still happen, because the task keeps running The pool undoes it The task receives the TimeoutException and stops The time limit is only about the caller's wait. The task doesn't know that anyone gave up, so it carries on, and the transfer goes through. Only cancel(true) sends the task a signal, and even that is just a request. A worker runs while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) { work(); try { Thread.sleep(100); } catch (InterruptedException e) { log.warn("interrupted"); } }. The pool calls shutdownNow() while the worker sleeps. What happens? The worker stops at the next loop check The worker throws, and the pool replaces it The worker logs a warning and keeps looping, because the exception cleared the flag shutdownNow() waits until the worker finishes sleep clears the interrupt flag when it throws. The catch only logs, so the while check sees a clear flag and loops forever. Stopping at the next check is what the code seems to promise, but nothing set the flag again. Restore it in the catch, or return from there. You call cancel(true) on a task that is in a long computing loop and never checks the interrupt flag. What do you see? isCancelled() is true at once, and the loop runs to the end anyway isCancelled() stays false until the loop ends The thread is stopped immediately cancel returns false, because the task is running The Future moves to CANCELLED as soon as cancel succeeds, and cancel returns true for a running task. The interrupt sets a flag that the loop never reads, so the work goes on. Java can't stop a thread from outside. You ask three exchange-rate services for the euro to dollar rate. You want the first successful answer, you want to ignore services that fail, and you want the slower ones cancelled. Which tool fits? Submit each one and call get() on them in order invokeAll, then pick the first SUCCESS A pool with one thread, so they run one at a time invokeAny invokeAny returns the first task that completes successfully and cancels the rest. invokeAll waits for every service, so you pay for the slowest one. Calling get() in order waits for the first service, even if the third is faster. From "A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt": thread t is in Thread.sleep(10_000). Another thread calls t.interrupt(). Inside t's catch block, what does Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() return? true, because the thread was just interrupted false, because throwing InterruptedException cleared the flag It throws IllegalThreadStateException true until sleep's 10 seconds are up Blocking methods clear the interrupt flag when they throw InterruptedException. That's why a catch block that neither rethrows nor calls Thread.currentThread().interrupt() loses the stop request.

h: Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption · Key terms
x: Callable A task that returns a value and may throw any exception, even a checked one. Future A claim ticket for a task's result: wait for it, read its state, or cancel the task. Interrupt A request to a thread to stop what it is doing. It sets a flag, and wakes the thread if it is waiting. Interrupt flag A true-or-false value in each thread. interrupt() sets it, and throwing InterruptedException clears it. Cooperative cancellation Cancelling that works only if the task checks for the request and stops itself. invokeAny Runs several tasks and returns the first successful result, cancelling the rest. What does cancel(true) do to a task that is already running? It calls interrupt() on the task's thread. The task stops only if it responds to the interrupt. You call cancel(true) and the task ignores the interrupt. What does isCancelled() return? true, at once, even though the task keeps running to the end. Does future.get(timeout) stop the task when it throws TimeoutException? No. It only ends your wait. Call cancel(true) if the work should stop. What happens to the interrupt flag when sleep throws InterruptedException? It is cleared. Rethrow the exception, or restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt(). What does invokeAny(tasks) return? The result of the first task that succeeds. It cancels the others, and throws ExecutionException only if all of them fail. What does resultNow() do on a future whose task failed? It throws IllegalStateException. Check state() first, and use exceptionNow() for FAILED.

h: Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption · Go deeper
x: Two methods read the interrupt flag, and they are easy to mix up. Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() reads it and leaves it alone. The static Thread.interrupted() reads it and clears it. Use the second only when you are about to handle the interrupt yourself, for example to throw InterruptedException from a blocking method of your own: Java if (Thread.interrupted()) throw new InterruptedException(); // clear, then report by throwing Kotlin if (Thread.interrupted()) throw InterruptedException() // clear, then report by throwing How does cancel(true) find the thread? submit wraps your task in a FutureTask, and the FutureTask remembers the thread that is running it. cancel(true) moves the task to its cancelled state and then calls interrupt() on that thread. The flag belongs to the thread, not to the task, so a pool has to make sure an interrupt meant for one task doesn't hit the next task on the same thread. ThreadPoolExecutor does that: before each task, its worker clears any leftover interrupt, unless the pool itself is stopping after shutdownNow(). Virtual threads, in the "Virtual threads" track, use the same interrupt mechanism. A virtual thread waiting in sleep or in a BlockingQueue responds exactly as described here, so everything in this lesson carries over.

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · Three ways to ask for later: schedule, fixed rate and fixed delay
x: Programs are full of small jobs that must happen later, or over and over. Our shop shows prices in dollars as well as euros. So it keeps an exchange rate in memory, the number of dollars one euro buys, and fetches a fresh one from a rate service every 5 seconds. It sends the bank a heartbeat every 30 seconds, a short "still here" message that the bank expects on a steady beat. And when a customer reserves a table, the reservation is dropped after 15 minutes unless they confirm it. You could write each job by hand, like the mail-room relay in A thread's life. The relay was a thread that did its job, slept, and looped. That works, and it's easy to read. But it costs a thread for every job, and stopping each one cleanly means getting the interrupt rules from the last lesson right, every time. The first scheduler in the JDK, Java's standard library, was java.util.Timer, from Java 1.3. It runs every task on one thread, and it has a trap. If one task throws, that thread dies and the whole Timer is cancelled. Every other task on it stops too, and the next call to schedule throws IllegalStateException. So skip Timer. JDK 5 replaced it with ScheduledExecutorService. It's a thread pool, a small team of threads that take tasks from a queue, and it can also run tasks later or over and over. You get one from Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(n) or Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(). Three of its methods do nearly all the work: Java ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(2); scheduler.schedule(this::dropReservation, 15, TimeUnit.MINUTES); // once, after a delay scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(this::sendHeartbeat, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // by the clock scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::refreshRate, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // a gap after each run Kotlin val scheduler = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(2) scheduler.schedule(this::dropReservation, 15, TimeUnit.MINUTES) // once, after a delay scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(this::sendHeartbeat, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // by the clock scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::refreshRate, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // a gap after each run Read them as the manager's instructions. schedule says "do this once, in 15 minutes". scheduleAtFixedRate says "start at 0, 30 and 60 seconds and so on, by the clock". scheduleWithFixedDelay says "when you finish, wait 5 seconds, then go again". The first number in the last two is the initial delay, how long to wait before the first run. Each call hands back a ScheduledFuture. It's the ticket from the last lesson, plus one extra: it knows how long until its next run. Cancel it to stop a repeating task. Don't wait on it, though. For a repeating task, get() returns only when the task is cancelled or fails, and that matters in the third section. The scheduler is a pool like any other, so shut it down when you're done. Otherwise its threads keep the JVM, the program that runs your Java code, alive. Not every timetable belongs inside your program, and the aside below says where the others go. For the ones that do, the two repeating methods behave the same until one run is slow. Pick the method For each job, choose schedule, scheduleAtFixedRate, scheduleWithFixedDelay, or "not in this program": (a) drop a table reservation 15 minutes after it was made, unless someone confirmed it; (b) send the bank a heartbeat every 30 seconds, which it expects on a steady beat; (c) refresh the exchange rate from a service whose answers sometimes take 20 seconds; (d) email the day's sales report to the accountant once a night. Write one sentence of reasoning for each before you read the answer. (a) schedule: it happens once, after a delay. (b) Fixed rate: the timing itself is the point. (c) Fixed delay: a slow answer pushes the next fetch later, instead of causing a burst of catch-up calls, as the next section shows. (d) Not in this program: a restart would lose the plan, and every copy of the program would send the report. ScheduledExecutorService (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · When one run is slow: fixed rate catches up, fixed delay moves everything later
x: A cleaner by the clock or one who rests after each round: after one 250 ms run, fixed rate runs the overdue rounds back to back, fixed delay shifts every later one, and a run that throws ends the schedule without a word The two repeating methods measure their period from different places. scheduleAtFixedRate(task, initialDelay, period, unit) follows a timetable fixed in advance, like the cleaner who goes by the clock. Runs are due at initialDelay, then initialDelay + period, then initialDelay + 2 x period, and so on. scheduleWithFixedDelay(task, initialDelay, delay, unit) waits delay after each run ends, then starts the next one, like the cleaner who rests after each round. While every run is short, you can't tell them apart. They split when one run is slow. Let's work one case by hand first. The period is 100 ms, the second run takes 250 ms, and every other run takes 10 ms. The lab's model counts make-believe milliseconds, so no real clock gets in the way, and it gives these start times: fixed rate: 0, 100, 350, 360, 400, 500, 600 fixed delay: 0, 110, 460, 570, 680, 790, 900 Take fixed rate first. Run 2 starts on time at 100 and ends at 350. Run 3 was due at 200, so it's late, and it starts the moment run 2 ends, at 350. Run 4 was due at 300, so it starts as soon as run 3 ends, at 360. Run 5 is due at 400, and by then the timetable is back on track. Fixed delay has no timetable to catch up with. Run 2 starts 100 ms after run 1 ends, at 110, and ends at 360. Run 3 starts 100 ms after that, at 460, and every later run moves along with it. RateVsDelayDemo, in the Try it below, runs the fixed-rate schedule on a real clock. The machine was busy, so every start came a few tens of milliseconds late: scheduleAtFixedRate, 100 ms run 1 started at 42 ms, took 10 ms run 2 started at 139 ms, took 250 ms run 3 started at 395 ms, took 10 ms run 4 started at 413 ms, took 10 ms run 5 started at 442 ms, took 10 ms run 6 started at 555 ms, took 10 ms run 7 started at 639 ms, took 10 ms The shape matches the model. Runs 3 and 4 start 18 ms apart, as the scheduler hurries to catch up, like a cleaner jogging from table to table. From run 5 on, the starts are back on the 100 ms grid, give or take the same 40 or so milliseconds of lateness that run 1 had. That lateness is the busy machine, not the slow run. Both rows come from one thing the executor does. It puts a repeating task back in its queue only when a run returns, with a new due time. For fixed rate, the new due time is the old due time plus the period. For fixed delay, it's the current time plus the delay. A due time that's already in the past means "run as soon as a thread is free". The same rule means a task never runs at the same time as itself, even on a scheduler with many threads. A task that takes 3 minutes on a 1-minute rate doesn't pile up three copies. It just runs late, every time. Here the cleaner picture breaks: a real manager might send a second cleaner to help. A scheduler never will. Fixed rate catches up after a slow run. Fixed delay never does. So pick fixed rate when the timing itself is the point, such as a heartbeat the bank expects every 30 seconds, or a count of sales per minute. Pick fixed delay when the task calls something that can slow down, such as the rate service or a database. A service that has just recovered from a slow spell doesn't need a burst of catch-up calls. A slow run only bends the timetable. A run that throws does something worse. Watch a slow run Run RateVsDelayDemo and compare its start times with the fixed-rate row of the model. Run it again with -Pargs=delay. Before you do, predict when run 3 starts. RateVsDelayDemo.java package workbench.executors.l05; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** A 100 ms schedule whose second run takes 250 ms. Default: fixed rate. Pass "delay" for fixed delay. */ public class RateVsDelayDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean delay = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("delay"); ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(); AtomicInteger runs = new AtomicInteger(); CountDownLatch sevenRuns = new CountDownLatch(7); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); Runnable sync = () -> { int n = runs.incrementAndGet(); long start = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; long work = n == 2 ? 250 : 10; // run 2 is slow: the rate service took its time try { Thread.sleep(work); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } System.out.printf("run %d started at %4d ms, took %3d ms%n", n, start, work); sevenRuns.countDown(); }; ScheduledFuture<?> f = delay ? scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(sync, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) : scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(sync, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); System.out.println(delay ? "scheduleWithFixedDelay, 100 ms" : "scheduleAtFixedRate, 100 ms"); sevenRuns.await(); f.cancel(false); scheduler.shutdown(); } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l05.RateVsDelayDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l05/RateVsDelayDemo.java RateVsDelayDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l05 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** A 100 ms schedule whose second run takes 250 ms. Default: fixed rate. Pass "delay" for fixed delay. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val delay = args.firstOrNull() == "delay" val scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor() val runs = AtomicInteger() val sevenRuns = CountDownLatch(7) val t0 = System.nanoTime() val sync = Runnable { val n = runs.incrementAndGet() val start = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 val work = if (n == 2) 250L else 10L // run 2 is slow: the rate service took its time try { Thread.sleep(work) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } println("run %d started at %4d ms, took %3d ms".format(n, start, work)) sevenRuns.countDown() } val f = if (delay) scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(sync, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) else scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(sync, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) println(if (delay) "scheduleWithFixedDelay, 100 ms" else "scheduleAtFixedRate, 100 ms") sevenRuns.await() f.cancel(false) scheduler.shutdown() } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l05.RateVsDelayDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l05/RateVsDelayDemo.kt With fixed rate, runs 3 and 4 start within about 10 to 20 ms of each other, right after the slow run, and from run 5 the starts are back near the 100 ms grid. With fixed delay, run 3 starts about 100 ms after run 2 ends (around 460 ms, or 529 ms in a run here on a busy machine), and each later run starts about 110 ms after the one before. On a busy machine, every time drifts a little later. The same slow second run under both instructions. Fixed rate catches up with its timetable; fixed delay moves every later run.

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · When one run throws: the schedule stops without a word
x: The ScheduledExecutorService Javadoc has a sentence that surprises most people. A repeating task keeps running until it's cancelled, until the executor shuts down, or until one of its runs throws an exception. After that, "subsequent executions are suppressed." In plain words, every later run is skipped, for good. Nothing is logged, and the cause is the rule from the last section. The task goes back in the queue only when a run returns normally. A run that throws leaves its exception inside the ScheduledFuture, the same way submit hid a failure in Why pools. And the task never goes back in the queue. SilentDeathDemo shows it. A health check, a small task that checks that the program can still reach the bank, runs every 100 ms. On its third run, the bank doesn't answer, and the check throws. After one second, the demo reads the ticket: health check 1 health check 2 health check 3 after 1 s: runs=3 isDone=true get() threw ExecutionException, cause: java.lang.IllegalStateException: bank did not answer Ten periods passed, three checks ran, and the scheduler said nothing. It didn't log, and it didn't retry. It didn't stop its other tasks either, which is exactly why nobody notices. It may be the most discreet class in java.util.concurrent. Only the get() call at the end, which hardly anyone writes for a repeating task, shows what happened. Now picture the same thing in the shop. The exchange-rate refresher throws once, on a day the rate service has a short outage, and it never runs again. The shop keeps showing dollar prices from a rate that's hours old. The first sign is a customer asking why a price looks wrong. That's the cleaner who slipped and went home. The fix is to catch the exception inside the task, so that no exception ever reaches the scheduler: Java scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> { try { refreshRate(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { log.warn("rate refresh failed, keeping the last rate", e); // report it, keep the schedule } }, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); Kotlin scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay({ try { refreshRate() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { log.warn("rate refresh failed, keeping the last rate", e) // report it, keep the schedule } }, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) I'd catch RuntimeException here, or Exception if the body calls code that throws checked exceptions, but not Throwable. An Error, such as OutOfMemoryError, means the JVM itself is in trouble, and a schedule that hides it would keep failing out of sight. Let errors stop the task, and alert on them. The lab wraps this pattern once, as SafeTask.wrap, so every repeating task can use it. A repeating task that throws once never runs again, and nothing logs it. Catch inside the task. For a second line of defense, check the ticket. Many programs serve a health page, a small web page that monitoring tools read to see whether the program is well. Have it report future.isDone(): for a task that should run forever, done means dead. Every schedule so far ran on a scheduler with one thread. What does one thread mean for the tasks that share it? Stop a schedule, then save it Run SilentDeathDemo. Count the health checks before the after 1 s line. Run it with -Pargs=safe, which wraps the check in a try/catch. Predict the number of runs after one second. SilentDeathDemo.java package workbench.executors.l05; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** A health check every 100 ms that throws on its third run. Pass "safe" to catch inside the task. */ public class SilentDeathDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean safe = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("safe"); ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(); AtomicInteger runs = new AtomicInteger(); Runnable check = () -> { int n = runs.incrementAndGet(); System.out.println("health check " + n); if (n == 3) throw new IllegalStateException("bank did not answer"); }; Runnable task = !safe ? check : () -> { try { check.run(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println(" caught and logged: " + e.getMessage()); } }; ScheduledFuture<?> f = scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(task, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); Thread.sleep(1_000); // ten periods System.out.println("after 1 s: runs=" + runs.get() + " isDone=" + f.isDone()); if (f.isDone()) { try { f.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { System.out.println("get() threw ExecutionException, cause: " + e.getCause()); } } scheduler.shutdownNow(); } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l05.SilentDeathDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l05/SilentDeathDemo.java SilentDeathDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l05 import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** A health check every 100 ms that throws on its third run. Pass "safe" to catch inside the task. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val safe = args.firstOrNull() == "safe" val scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor() val runs = AtomicInteger() val check = Runnable { val n = runs.incrementAndGet() println("health check $n") if (n == 3) throw IllegalStateException("bank did not answer") } val task = if (!safe) check else Runnable { try { check.run() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println(" caught and logged: ${e.message}") } } val f = scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(task, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) Thread.sleep(1_000) // ten periods println("after 1 s: runs=${runs.get()} isDone=${f.isDone}") if (f.isDone) { try { f.get() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { println("get() threw ExecutionException, cause: ${e.cause}") } } scheduler.shutdownNow() } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l05.SilentDeathDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l05/SilentDeathDemo.kt The first run prints three health checks and then nothing for the rest of the second. It reports isDone=true, and get() shows the hidden exception. With safe, run 3 prints caught and logged: bank did not answer, and the checks go on to about 10 or 11 in the second, with isDone=false.

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · Inside the scheduler: one fixed pool, and a new scheduler in JDK 25
x: Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(n) returns a ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor. It's a ThreadPoolExecutor, the class from Inside ThreadPoolExecutor, with one change. Its queue is a delay queue, a queue ordered by due time that hands out each task only when it comes due. Its Javadoc says it "acts as a fixed-sized pool using corePoolSize threads and an unbounded queue". You saw in that lesson what an unbounded queue does to the maximum pool size: it never comes into play. Three things follow. First, a scheduler with one thread runs one task at a time. A refresh that hangs for a minute delays every other task on that scheduler by a minute, heartbeats included. So give slow repeating work its own scheduler, or let the scheduled task just hand the real work to another pool. Second, a cancelled task stays in the queue until its due time, by default. If you schedule and cancel a lot, for example one time limit per request, call setRemoveOnCancelPolicy(true) so cancelled tasks don't pile up. Third, after shutdown(), one-time delayed tasks still run when they come due, but repeating tasks stop. Those are the defaults of setExecuteExistingDelayedTasksAfterShutdownPolicy and setContinueExistingPeriodicTasksAfterShutdownPolicy. They matter when a program shuts down with reservations still waiting to be dropped. Check yourself on the first one. One single-thread scheduler sends a heartbeat at a 30-second fixed rate and refreshes the rate with a 5-second fixed delay. A refresh starts just after a heartbeat and hangs for 90 seconds. How many heartbeats go out during the hang, and what happens when it ends? None go out during the hang, because the only thread is busy. When the refresh returns, the three heartbeats that came due in the meantime run back to back, because their due times are all in the past. The next refresh starts 5 seconds after the hung one ended. The bank saw 90 seconds of silence, then three beats at once. JDK 25 adds a second scheduler you already have. ForkJoinPool, the JDK's other big pool, now implements ScheduledExecutorService too (lesson 8 of this track covers ForkJoinPool). So does its common pool, ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), one pool that the whole JVM shares. Fixed rate, fixed delay and the rule about exceptions work the same way there. ForkJoinPool also gains submitWithTimeout, which cancels a task if it hasn't finished in time. Both compile only on JDK 25 or later, so they stay out of the labs: Java // JDK 25+ ForkJoinPool pool = ForkJoinPool.commonPool(); pool.scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::refreshRate, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); ForkJoinTask<BigDecimal> rate = pool.submitWithTimeout(() -> fetchRate("EUR", "USD"), 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, null); // a null timeout action means: cancel(true) if it isn't done after 300 ms Kotlin // JDK 25+ val pool = ForkJoinPool.commonPool() pool.scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::refreshRate, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) val rate: ForkJoinTask<BigDecimal> = pool.submitWithTimeout({ fetchRate("EUR", "USD") }, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, null) // a null timeout action means: cancel(true) if it isn't done after 300 ms Keep work that waits off the common pool, scheduled or not. Every parallel stream in the JVM (a stream that splits its work across threads) shares it, and so does the next lesson's tool when you don't name a pool. A scheduler is a fixed pool. A slow task delays every task that shares its threads. Every tool in this lesson shares one limit: each task runs on its own, start to finish. A refresh can't say "when the rate arrives, convert the price, then charge the card". Steps that follow each other need a different kind of ticket.

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · Java and Kotlin
x: A fixed-delay refresher: a scheduler vs a coroutine loop RateRefresh.java ScheduledFuture<?> refresher = scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> { try { rate = fetchRate(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { log.warn("rate refresh failed, keeping the last rate", e); } }, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // later refresher.cancel(false); // no more runs; a fetch already running finishes RateRefresh.kt (kotlinx.coroutines) val refresher = scope.launch { while (isActive) { try { rate = fetchRate() } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e // let cancellation through } catch (e: Exception) { log.warn("rate refresh failed, keeping the last rate", e) } delay(5.seconds) // the gap starts when the run ends } } // later refresher.cancel() // stops at the next delay() Kotlin's coroutines, light tasks that can pause without holding a thread, have no scheduler API. A loop with delay is a fixed-delay schedule, because the wait starts when the run ends. A fixed rate needs you to work out the next due time yourself. Failures behave differently, in a useful way. An exception that escapes the JDK task disappears into the ScheduledFuture, while one that escapes launch travels up to the parent scope and its exception handler, so it's loud by default. Either way, you catch inside the loop to keep it running. In Kotlin, rethrow CancellationException, or cancel() would be swallowed like any other exception.

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · Worked example
x: Why did the exchange rate stop updating? The shop's dollar prices have used the same exchange rate for six hours. The logs show no errors. Here is the refresher. Find the bug before reading on. scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate( () -> rate = rateService.eurToUsd(), // throws when the rate service has an error 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate( { rate = rateService.eurToUsd() }, // throws when the rate service has an error 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) Six hours ago, the rate service had a short outage and eurToUsd() threw. That run's exception went into the ScheduledFuture, which nobody kept, and every later run was skipped. There's no log line, because nothing ever printed the exception. Fixed rate is a second, smaller problem: when the rate service is slow, overdue runs fire back to back. Catch inside the task, keep the last good rate, and count the failure. Switch to fixed delay, so a slow rate service never gets a burst of catch-up calls. ScheduledFuture<?> refresher = scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> { try { rate = rateService.eurToUsd(); // 1. fetch lastSuccess = Instant.now(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { failures.increment(); // 2. count it log.warn("rate refresh failed, keeping {}", rate, e); // 3. keep the old rate } }, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); val refresher = scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay({ try { rate = rateService.eurToUsd() // 1. fetch lastSuccess = Instant.now() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { failures.increment() // 2. count it log.warn("rate refresh failed, keeping {}", rate, e) // 3. keep the old rate } }, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) Make the next failure visible. A health check that reports whether the schedule is still alive, and how old the rate is, turns six silent hours into one alert. boolean healthy = !refresher.isDone() && Duration.between(lastSuccess, Instant.now()).toMinutes() < 5; val healthy = !refresher.isDone && Duration.between(lastSuccess, Instant.now()).toMinutes() < 5

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · Lab
x: Model the timetable, then build a refresher that survives labs/executors/src/main/java/workbench/executors/l05/Schedules.java labs/executors/src/main/java/workbench/executors/l05/SafeTask.java labs/executors/src/main/java/workbench/executors/l05/FxRateRefresher.java ./gradlew :executors:test --tests 'workbench.executors.l05.*' Run the tests. All eight fail. Write Schedules.startTimes, the model from the second section. Keep the end time of the previous run in a variable. For fixed rate, a run starts at its due time or when the previous run ends, whichever is later. For fixed delay, it starts at that end time plus the period. Write SafeTask.wrap: a lambda that runs the task inside a try/catch for RuntimeException, and hands the exception to onError. Write FxRateRefresher, which keeps the euro to dollar rate fresh. start() calls scheduleWithFixedDelay with an initial delay of 0 and a SafeTask that stores the rate and counts failures. close() cancels the ticket that scheduleWithFixedDelay returned. Run the tests until all eight pass. Run 0 of the model always starts at initialDelay, whatever the mode. Many threads read current() while the scheduler's thread writes the rate. Store it in an AtomicReference<BigDecimal> (or a volatile field), not a plain field, so the readers see each new rate. close() must not shut down the scheduler: it belongs to the caller and may run other tasks. Cancel your own ScheduledFuture with cancel(false). All eight tests in SchedulingTest pass. By the end you can choose between schedule, fixed rate and fixed delay, predict when each run starts, and keep a repeating task alive when one run throws.

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · Quiz
x: A task scheduled with scheduleAtFixedRate(task, 0, 1, SECONDS) takes 3 seconds every time. What happens? Three copies run at once, one starting each second Each run starts as soon as the previous one ends, so it runs back to back The scheduler skips the missed slots and waits for the next whole second The scheduler throws RejectedExecutionException Runs of one repeating task never overlap. Every run is overdue by the time the last one ends, so it starts at once, and the task runs without a break. Missed slots are not skipped; they run late. scheduleWithFixedDelay(task, 0, 10, SECONDS) runs a task that always takes 2 seconds. When do the first three runs start? 0, 10 and 20 seconds 0, 2 and 12 seconds 0, 8 and 16 seconds 0, 12 and 24 seconds The delay counts from the end of each run. Run 1 ends at 2 s, so run 2 starts at 12 s and ends at 14 s, and run 3 starts at 24 s. 0, 10 and 20 is what fixed rate would give. A repeating refresh of a value in memory throws a NullPointerException on its 40th run. Nothing catches it. What do you see? It stops for good, nothing is logged, and its future reports isDone() = true It logs the exception and runs again next period The scheduler's thread dies and is replaced, and the task keeps running The scheduler shuts down Every later run is skipped, and the exception is stored in the ScheduledFuture. Nothing is printed, which is the dangerous part. The scheduler and its other tasks carry on as if nothing happened. A single-thread scheduler sends the bank a heartbeat every 30 seconds and runs a report job that sometimes takes 2 minutes. The bank complains about missing heartbeats. What is the right fix? Raise the scheduler's maximum pool size Switch the heartbeat to fixed delay Give the report job its own scheduler, or have its scheduled task hand the work to another pool Wrap the heartbeat in a try/catch With one thread, the heartbeat can't run while the report is running. The maximum pool size does nothing on a ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor, and neither fixed delay nor a try/catch frees the thread. Keep the slow job away from the one whose timing matters. From "Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption": a repeating task is in the middle of a run when you call cancel(false) on its ScheduledFuture. What happens? The run in progress is interrupted, and no more runs happen The run in progress finishes, and no more runs happen Nothing, because cancel(false) only affects tasks that have not started The run in progress finishes, and the schedule continues cancel(false) doesn't interrupt a running task, so the current run completes. Cancelling still marks the future cancelled, so the scheduler never queues the next run. cancel(true) would also interrupt the current run.

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · Key terms
x: ScheduledExecutorService A thread pool that can run tasks after a delay, or over and over. Fixed rate Runs are due at fixed times (start + n x period), and late runs catch up. Fixed delay A fixed gap between the end of one run and the start of the next. ScheduledFuture The ticket for a scheduled task: cancel it, check isDone, or read the time until its next run. Suppressed execution A run of a repeating task that never happens, because an earlier run threw. Delay queue A queue ordered by due time that hands out each task only when it comes due. scheduleAtFixedRate vs scheduleWithFixedDelay: where is the period measured from? Fixed rate: from a timetable fixed at the start (initialDelay + n x period). Fixed delay: from the end of the previous run. A repeating task throws once, and nothing catches it. What happens to later runs? They are skipped forever. Nothing is logged; the exception sits in the ScheduledFuture. Can two runs of the same repeating task overlap? No. A late run waits for the previous one to finish, however many threads the scheduler has. Why does maximumPoolSize do nothing on a ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor? It's a fixed pool of core threads with an unbounded delay queue, so it never grows past its core size. What did JDK 25 add to ForkJoinPool for scheduling? It implements ScheduledExecutorService (schedule, fixed rate, fixed delay) and adds submitWithTimeout. Why avoid java.util.Timer? It runs all tasks on one thread, and one task that throws kills that thread and cancels every task on the Timer.

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · Go deeper
x: The scheduler's clock is System.nanoTime(), a clock that only moves forward, not the time of day. So a repeating task is not affected when the computer corrects its clock from the network, or when daylight saving time starts, which is what you want for "every 30 seconds". It also means a ScheduledExecutorService can't say "at 02:00 local time". You can come close by working out the delay to the next 02:00 and calling schedule again after each run, but needing that is a sign the job belongs in a scheduler outside the program. CompletableFuture, the subject of the next lesson, has a small scheduling helper of its own: CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(delay, unit) returns an Executor that runs each task after a delay. Lesson 7 of this track uses its relatives, orTimeout and completeOnTimeout.

h: CompletableFuture: composing async steps · A ticket that knows the next step: CompletableFuture, and the pool that runs it
x: Back to the shop's checkout. The shop prices everything in euros, and an American customer pays in dollars. So the checkout needs two answers from two slow services. The cart service knows the cart's price in euros. The rate service knows the exchange rate, how many dollars one euro buys. (The code calls it fx, short for foreign exchange.) Each takes 300 ms. Then the checkout multiplies the two and charges the card. Here's the honest version, with the tickets from Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption. io is a thread pool, a small team of threads that take tasks from a queue: Java Future<BigDecimal> price = io.submit(() -> prices.priceEur(cart)); Future<BigDecimal> rate = io.submit(() -> fx.rate("EUR", "USD")); BigDecimal usd = price.get().multiply(rate.get()); // this thread waits here, doing nothing Kotlin val price = io.submit<BigDecimal> { prices.priceEur(cart) } val rate = io.submit<BigDecimal> { fx.rate("EUR", "USD") } val usd = price.get() * rate.get() // this thread waits here, doing nothing Credit where it's due: it's correct, and both calls run side by side, so the wait is 300 ms, not 600. The catch is the thread that calls get(). It sits there for the whole 300 ms, doing nothing. Little's law, from Sizing a pool, says the number inside equals the arrival rate times the time each one stays. At 400 checkouts a second, that's 400 x 0.3 = 120 threads, all just waiting. A CompletableFuture<T> is a ticket you can clip instructions to. It's still a Future, so get and cancel still work. But it also lets you say "when this is done, do that next", and walk away. Something has to complete the ticket, and usually that's supplyAsync. (Async is short for asynchronous: the work runs while your code moves on.) It takes a Supplier, a function that takes nothing and returns a value. It runs the supplier on the pool you name, and completes the ticket with the result: Java CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> prices.priceEur(cart), io); // starts now, on io CompletableFuture<Void> note = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> orderLog.write(cart), io); // no result Kotlin val price: CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ prices.priceEur(cart) }, io) // starts now, on io val note: CompletableFuture<Void> = CompletableFuture.runAsync({ orderLog.write(cart) }, io) // no result Both calls return at once, while the work runs on io or waits in its queue. runAsync is the same for a task with no result. A ticket can also be completed by hand: a library can hand you a new CompletableFuture<>() and call complete(value) on it when its answer arrives. The payment service in this lesson's lab, the service that charges the card, works that way. The lab calls its client PaymentGateway, and its charge method returns a ticket. The second argument, the pool, matters more than it looks. Leave it out, and the task goes to the default async executor, ForkJoinPool.commonPool(). That's one pool per JVM, the program that runs your Java code. It has one thread fewer than the machine has cores, the parts of the processor that each run one thread at a time. Every parallel stream (a stream that splits its work across threads) uses it, and so does every library that calls supplyAsync without a pool. It's the shared kitchen that everyone borrows and nobody owns. A few 300 ms calls fill it, and everyone else's work waits behind them. WhoRunsItDemo, in the Try it below, prints the thread that runs each supplyAsync, first without a pool and then with a pool named io. On a 4-core machine with JDK 21: JDK 21, common pool parallelism 3 supplyAsync(task) ran on ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1 supplyAsync(task) ran on ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1 supplyAsync(task) ran on ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1 supplyAsync(task, io) ran on io-1 supplyAsync(task, io) ran on io-2 supplyAsync(task, io) ran on io-2 The version of the JDK, Java's standard library and tools, changes the small-machine case. Many programs run in a container, a fenced-off space where the operating system limits how much CPU a program may use. In a container limited to 2 CPUs, the common pool gets just one thread. Up to JDK 24, CompletableFuture noticed that and skipped the pool: it started a brand-new thread for every task. JDK 25 removed that special case. Run the demo with 1cpu, which sizes the common pool as that container would, and the two versions disagree. JDK 21 runs the three calls on Thread-0, Thread-1 and Thread-2, a new thread each time. JDK 25 runs all three on ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1. For a call that waits, both are wrong: one has no limit, and the other has a limit of one. Without a pool, async work runs on threads the whole JVM shares. Pass a pool for anything that waits. The pool you pass can be a fixed pool sized the way Sizing a pool showed. On JDK 21 and later, it can also be Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), which gives each task a virtual thread, a much lighter kind of thread that a later track covers. Keep the default for short computing work. The price and the rate are on their way. Now we clip on the instructions. Find out who runs your task Run WhoRunsItDemo. Note the thread names with and without a pool. Run it again with -Pargs=1cpu, which sizes the common pool as a 2-CPU container would. Predict the names first. Does your JDK version change the answer? WhoRunsItDemo.java package workbench.executors.l06; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool; /** Which thread runs supplyAsync? Pass "1cpu" to size the common pool the way a 2-CPU container does. */ public class WhoRunsItDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("1cpu")) { // must run before anything touches ForkJoinPool: a 2-CPU container gets parallelism 1 System.setProperty("java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism", "1"); } System.out.println("JDK " + Runtime.version().feature() + ", common pool parallelism " + ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism()); for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { String who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()).join(); System.out.println("supplyAsync(task) ran on " + who); } try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { String who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName(), io).join(); System.out.println("supplyAsync(task, io) ran on " + who); } } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l06.WhoRunsItDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l06/WhoRunsItDemo.java WhoRunsItDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l06 import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool /** Which thread runs supplyAsync? Pass "1cpu" to size the common pool the way a 2-CPU container does. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "1cpu") { // must run before anything touches ForkJoinPool: a 2-CPU container gets parallelism 1 System.setProperty("java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism", "1") } println("JDK ${Runtime.version().feature()}, common pool parallelism ${ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism()}") repeat(3) { val who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync { Thread.currentThread().name }.join() println("supplyAsync(task) ran on $who") } Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()).use { io -> repeat(3) { val who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ Thread.currentThread().name }, io).join() println("supplyAsync(task, io) ran on $who") } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l06.WhoRunsItDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l06/WhoRunsItDemo.kt Without a pool, every call runs on ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-N; with io, on io-1 and io-2. With 1cpu on JDK 21 to 24, the calls without a pool run on Thread-0, Thread-1 and Thread-2, a new thread for each task. On JDK 25 or later, they all run on ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1. h: CompletableFuture: composing async steps · Clipping on instructions: thenApply maps, thenCompose flattens, thenCombine waits for two
x: The ticket for table 4: thenApply maps, thenCompose flattens a ticket for a ticket, thenCombine waits for two, and the calls must start first (347 ms side by side, 661 ms chained) Each of these methods takes a ticket, clips on one instruction, and hands back a new ticket for that instruction's result. Here's the smallest one, on a ticket that is already complete: Java CompletableFuture<Integer> six = CompletableFuture.completedFuture(6); CompletableFuture<Integer> answer = six.thenApply(n -> n * 7); // a new ticket, for 42 Kotlin val six = CompletableFuture.completedFuture(6) val answer = six.thenApply { n -> n * 7 } // a new ticket, for 42 Each step is called a stage: a ticket, plus the instruction that completes it from earlier results. Which method you use depends on the shape of the instruction you have: You have Method You get T -> U, plain code thenApply CompletableFuture<U> T -> CompletableFuture<U>, another async call thenCompose CompletableFuture<U> a second ticket, and (T, U) -> V thenCombine CompletableFuture<V> T -> void, a side effect thenAccept CompletableFuture<Void> thenCompose needs a second look. Say a step calls the payment service, which already returns its own ticket. With thenApply, you'd get a CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<String>>: a ticket for a ticket, and nobody collects the inner one. thenCompose flattens it into a single CompletableFuture<String>. (If you know Optional or streams: thenApply is map, and thenCompose is flatMap.) Now the checkout. CombineDemo starts the price and the rate, joins them with thenCombine, and logs each event with its time and thread. Here's the heart of it: Java // both calls start now and run side by side CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::priceEur, io); CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::eurToUsd, io); usd = price.thenCombine(rate, BigDecimal::multiply); Kotlin // both calls start now and run side by side val price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(::priceEur, io) val rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(::eurToUsd, io) price.thenCombine(rate) { p, r -> p * r } Read the last line as the ticket for table 4: when the price and the rate are both ready, multiply them. Each call takes 300 ms, so I expect the charge a little after 300 ms. On a busy machine: 36 ms main pipeline built, nothing has arrived yet 330 ms io-1 price is 100.00 EUR 332 ms io-2 rate is 1.0842 347 ms main charge 108.42 USD The run matched my guess. The main thread built the whole pipeline in 36 ms and walked away. The price and the rate arrived together, on two io threads, and the charge followed. Now a setback. The chain version fetches the rate inside thenCompose, after the price arrives: Java // the rate call starts only when the price has arrived usd = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::priceEur, io) .thenCompose(p -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::eurToUsd, io) .thenApply(p::multiply)); Kotlin // the rate call starts only when the price has arrived CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(::priceEur, io) .thenCompose { p -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(::eurToUsd, io).thenApply { r -> p * r } } The chain is just as asynchronous, and main still walks away at once. But look at the times: 36 ms main pipeline built, nothing has arrived yet 340 ms io-1 price is 100.00 EUR 644 ms io-2 rate is 1.0842 661 ms main charge 108.42 USD The rate arrived at 644 ms, not 332. Nothing warned us. Both versions are asynchronous; only one of them is also fast. The difference is where supplyAsync is called. Work starts when you call supplyAsync, not when you call thenCombine. In the first version, both calls start on the first two lines, before any instruction is clipped on. In the second, the rate call sits inside an instruction, and an instruction runs only when the stage before it completes. Work starts when you call supplyAsync. Start everything independent first, then combine. The figure shows where the lab takes this checkout: the charge clipped on with thenCompose, and the receipt with thenApply. If any step fails, the steps after it are skipped, and the last ticket fails with that exception. That's the next lesson. One question is still open from the first run. The main thread built the pipeline and walked away, so which thread did the multiply? Side by side, or one after the other Run CombineDemo. The price and the rate each take 300 ms. Read the times. Run it with -Pargs=chain, which fetches the rate inside thenCompose, after the price. Predict the total time before you run it. In the chain branch, change thenCompose to thenApply and compile again. Read what the compiler says about the type, then undo the change. Pass "chain" to fetch them one after the other. */ public class CombineDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%4d ms %-6s %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, Thread.currentThread().getName(), msg);
