h: CompletableFuture: composing async steps · Who carries the order to the next station: the thread that runs each step
x: thenApply, thenCompose, thenCombine and thenAccept take no pool. So who runs the instruction? There are two cases. If the stage before it is still running when you clip the instruction on, the instruction runs on the thread that completes that stage. If that stage is already complete, the instruction runs right away, on the thread that called thenApply. Both cases follow from one detail of the class. Each CompletableFuture keeps a stack of the instructions clipped onto it. The thread that completes the ticket, by returning from a supplyAsync task or by calling complete, then takes those instructions off one by one. It runs every one that has no pool of its own. An instruction clipped on after that finds a finished ticket, so thenApply runs it on the spot. The kitchen from the opening works the same way: whichever cook finishes the last part reads the ticket and does the next step. So in CombineDemo, the multiply ran on whichever io thread finished second, not on main. WhichThreadDemo shows both cases, plus the two Async variants you'll meet in a moment. Write down your guess for each line before you read on: 1. thenApply on a finished future: main 2. thenApply attached while running: io-1 3. thenApplyAsync(fn): ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1 4. thenApplyAsync(fn, cpu): cpu-1 Line 1 was clipped onto a finished ticket, so main ran it on the spot. Line 2 was clipped onto a ticket whose task was still sleeping on io-1, so io-1 ran it when the task finished. For cheap steps, that's exactly right, and it's what the plain methods are for. Multiplying a price by a rate takes microseconds. It doesn't matter which thread does it, and skipping a trip to another pool saves a queue and a thread switch. Trouble starts when the step is slow and the completing thread isn't yours. Some client libraries, the code you use to call another service, complete their tickets on a thread of their own that serves many requests at once. (That thread is often called an event loop.) A plain thenApply that blocks there for 50 ms stalls every other request it serves. The same goes for a scheduler's thread, from the last lesson, that completes a ticket at a deadline. Here the kitchen picture breaks. A real cook who finishes the sauce knows to pass a two-hour braise to someone else. A plain thenApply doesn't. The thread that completes the stage does the next step, however slow it is, unless you name a pool. The Async variants fix that. Every method has two of them: thenApplyAsync(fn) always hands the step to the default async executor, the common pool, with the same problems as supplyAsync without a pool. thenApplyAsync(fn, executor) hands it to the pool you name. Use it to move slow or waiting work off a thread you don't own. A plain step runs on whatever thread finished the stage before. Name a pool for any step that is slow. So far, every step completes a ticket and hands on. Sooner or later, though, somebody needs the actual value. Predict four thread names Read WhichThreadDemo and write down the thread you expect for each numbered line. Run it and compare. For line 2, explain why it isn't main, even though main called thenApply. WhichThreadDemo.java package workbench.executors.l06; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** Which thread runs the next stage? It depends on timing, and on the Async suffix. */ public class WhichThreadDemo { static String me() { return Thread.currentThread().getName(); } public static void main(String[] args) { try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()); ExecutorService cpu = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("cpu-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<String> done = CompletableFuture.completedFuture("x"); System.out.println("1. thenApply on a finished future: " + done.thenApply(x -> me()).join()); CompletableFuture<String> slow = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { sleep(200); return "x"; }, io); CompletableFuture<String> attached = slow.thenApply(x -> me()); // attached while slow still runs System.out.println("2. thenApply attached while running: " + attached.join()); System.out.println("3. thenApplyAsync(fn): " + slow.thenApplyAsync(x -> me()).join()); System.out.println("4. thenApplyAsync(fn, cpu): " + slow.thenApplyAsync(x -> me(), cpu).join()); } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l06.WhichThreadDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l06/WhichThreadDemo.java WhichThreadDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l06 import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.Executors private fun me(): String = Thread.currentThread().name /** Which thread runs the next stage? It depends on timing, and on the Async suffix. */ fun main() { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()).use { io -> Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("cpu-", 1).factory()).use { cpu -> val done = CompletableFuture.completedFuture("x") println("1. thenApply on a finished future: " + done.thenApply { me() }.join()) val slow = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ Thread.sleep(200); "x" }, io) val attached = slow.thenApply { me() } // attached while slow still runs println("2. thenApply attached while running: " + attached.join()) println("3. thenApplyAsync(fn): " + slow.thenApplyAsync { me() }.join()) println("4. thenApplyAsync(fn, cpu): " + slow.thenApplyAsync({ me() }, cpu).join()) } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l06.WhichThreadDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l06/WhichThreadDemo.kt main, io-1, ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1 and cpu-1. Line 2 runs on io-1 because the step was clipped on while the task was still sleeping, so the thread that completed it ran the step. If your machine paused main for more than 200 ms between those two lines, you'd see main there instead, which is the whole point: timing decides.

h: CompletableFuture: composing async steps · Getting the value out: join, get, and the one place you may wait
x: Sooner or later, a thread needs the value itself. It might send a web page back to a browser, print a receipt, or check a result in a test. CompletableFuture gives you two ways to wait for it. get() is the Future method from Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption. It throws the checked exceptions InterruptedException and ExecutionException, with the failure as the cause, and get(timeout, unit) adds TimeoutException. join() throws only unchecked exceptions: CompletionException, with the failure as the cause, or CancellationException. That makes it easy to call inside lambdas and streams. But it has no time limit, and it ignores interrupts: a thread stuck in join() stays stuck until the ticket completes. getNow(fallback) and resultNow() (JDK 19) never wait at all. So build the whole pipeline without waiting. Then wait at most once, at the edge, on a thread that is allowed to wait, with a time limit. The edge is where your code meets the outside world, such as a request handler, the main method or a test: Java // a request thread that may wait, but not forever Receipt r = checkout.checkout(cart, "USD").get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); Kotlin // a request thread that may wait, but not forever val r = checkout.checkout(cart, "USD").get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) Never call join() or get() inside a stage, on a ticket that may still be running. (On a ticket you know is complete, join() returns at once.) The stage runs on a pool thread, and that thread now sits idle until another task finishes. Picture a cook who stops cooking and stands at the counter, waiting for a dish that nobody is free to cook. A few of those, and a small pool runs out of threads. If the task being waited for is queued behind them on the same pool, nothing ever finishes. That's the pool-induced deadlock from Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption, and lesson 9 of this track has you fix one. When a stage needs another async result, that's what thenCompose and thenCombine are for. Wait once, at the edge, with a time limit. Never wait inside a stage. The Try it below has a checkout that breaks this rule twice. Find both before you do the lab, which asks you to write it properly. Every pipeline in this lesson has one limit: it assumes that each step succeeds, and none of its steps has a time limit. A rate service that throws, or never answers at all, needs tools we haven't met yet. Spot the waiting calls Read this method. Mark every line that makes a thread wait, and say which thread. Java CompletableFuture<Receipt> checkout(String cart) { BigDecimal price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> prices.priceEur(cart), io).join(); // A CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fx.rate("EUR", "USD"), io); return rate.thenApply(r -> { BigDecimal amount = price.multiply(r); String id = gateway.charge(cart, amount, "USD").join(); // B return new Receipt(cart, amount, "USD", id); }); } Kotlin fun checkout(cart: String): CompletableFuture<Receipt> { val price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ prices.priceEur(cart) }, io).join() // A val rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ fx.rate("EUR", "USD") }, io) return rate.thenApply { r -> val amount = price * r val id = gateway.charge(cart, amount, "USD").join() // B Receipt(cart, amount, "USD", id) } } Sketch the fix with thenCombine and thenCompose. The lab asks you to write it for real. A makes the caller wait for the whole price call, and because the rate call starts only after it, the two calls run one after the other. B makes whichever thread completes rate (an io thread) wait for as long as the payment service takes. The fix starts both supplyAsync calls first, combines them with thenCombine, and calls gateway.charge inside thenCompose, so no thread waits anywhere inside checkout.

h: CompletableFuture: composing async steps · Java and Kotlin
x: Two lookups side by side, then an async call Delivery.java (CompletableFuture) CompletableFuture<String> confirm(String orderId) { CompletableFuture<Address> address = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> customers.address(orderId), io); CompletableFuture<Duration> cooking = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> kitchen.cookTime(orderId), io); return address .thenCombine(cooking, (a, t) -> new RideRequest(a, t)) .thenCompose(riders::book) .thenApply(ride -> "Your food arrives at " + ride.eta()); } Delivery.kt (kotlinx.coroutines) suspend fun confirm(orderId: String): String = coroutineScope { val address = async(Dispatchers.IO) { customers.address(orderId) } // both start now val cooking = async(Dispatchers.IO) { kitchen.cookTime(orderId) } val request = RideRequest(address.await(), cooking.await()) val ride = riders.book(request).await() // pauses on the CompletableFuture, holds no thread "Your food arrives at ${ride.eta}" } The Java version is a chain of instructions: each method clips on a step, and you think about which thread runs each one. The Kotlin version reads top to bottom. It runs in coroutines, Kotlin's light tasks that can pause without holding a thread. async starts the two lookups at once, await() pauses the coroutine until a result is ready, and the await() extension from kotlinx.coroutines.future turns the rider service's CompletableFuture into a pause point. The structure differs too. If the cooking-time lookup fails, coroutineScope cancels the address lookup and rethrows. thenCombine does nothing like that: the address lookup keeps running, and its result is thrown away. The coroutines track covers the details.

h: CompletableFuture: composing async steps · Worked example
x: Turn a waiting delivery order into a pipeline A food-delivery shop confirms each order. It looks up the customer's address (40 ms) and the kitchen's cooking time (60 ms), books a delivery rider with a rider service whose client already returns a CompletableFuture (120 ms), and tells the customer when the food arrives. This version takes 40 + 60 + 120 = 220 ms per order, and holds a thread for all of it. Before reading on, mark which calls depend on which. String confirm(String orderId) { Address address = customers.address(orderId); // 40 ms Duration cooking = kitchen.cookTime(orderId); // 60 ms Ride ride = riders.book(new RideRequest(address, cooking)).join(); // 120 ms return "Your food arrives at " + ride.eta(); } fun confirm(orderId: String): String { val address = customers.address(orderId) // 40 ms val cooking = kitchen.cookTime(orderId) // 60 ms val ride = riders.book(RideRequest(address, cooking)).join() // 120 ms return "Your food arrives at ${ride.eta}" } The address and the cooking time don't depend on each other. The rider needs both, and the message needs the rider. So the best case is max(40, 60) + 120 = 180 ms, and only if the two lookups start together. Start both first, on the io pool, because they wait. // 1. start the independent lookups together CompletableFuture<Address> address = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> customers.address(orderId), io); CompletableFuture<Duration> cooking = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> kitchen.cookTime(orderId), io); // 1. start the independent lookups together val address = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ customers.address(orderId) }, io) val cooking = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ kitchen.cookTime(orderId) }, io) Join the two with thenCombine. Building the request is cheap, so the plain method is right. The rider service returns its own ticket, so flatten it with thenCompose, and finish with a cheap thenApply. return address .thenCombine(cooking, (a, t) -> new RideRequest(a, t)) // 2. wait for both .thenCompose(riders::book) // 3. async call, flattened .thenApply(ride -> "Your food arrives at " + ride.eta()); // 4. cheap mapping return address .thenCombine(cooking) { a, t -> RideRequest(a, t) } // 2. wait for both .thenCompose(riders::book) // 3. async call, flattened .thenApply { ride -> "Your food arrives at ${ride.eta}" } // 4. cheap mapping The method now returns CompletableFuture<String> and waits for nothing. The request handler that calls it waits once, with a time limit. A framework that accepts a CompletionStage gets the ticket itself instead. String message = confirm(orderId).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // 5. wait once, at the edge val message = confirm(orderId).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // 5. wait once, at the edge

h: CompletableFuture: composing async steps · Quiz
x: menu.findAsync(name) returns CompletableFuture<Dish>, and kitchen.cookAsync(dish) returns CompletableFuture<Plate>. What is the type of menu.findAsync(name).thenApply(kitchen::cookAsync)? CompletableFuture<Plate> CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Plate>> Plate It doesn't compile thenApply wraps whatever the function returns, and this function returns a ticket. You get a ticket for a ticket, and nothing waits for the inner one. thenCompose would flatten it to CompletableFuture<Plate>. price() and rate() each wait 200 ms for another service. Which version finishes in about 200 ms? supplyAsync(() -> price(), io).thenCompose(p -> supplyAsync(() -> rate(), io).thenApply(p::multiply)) supplyAsync(() -> price().multiply(rate()), io) supplyAsync(() -> price(), io).thenApply(p -> p.multiply(rate())) supplyAsync(() -> price(), io).thenCombine(supplyAsync(() -> rate(), io), BigDecimal::multiply) Only the last one starts both calls before waiting for either. The other three are all asynchronous, but each runs rate() after price() has returned, so they take about 400 ms. Being asynchronous is not the same as running side by side. Ticket f has already completed. Request thread http-7 calls f.thenApply(this::render). Which thread runs render? http-7, right away A common pool worker The thread that completed f A new thread When the stage before it is already complete, a plain thenApply runs the function at once, on the calling thread. The thread that completed f finished its work earlier and plays no part. Only thenApplyAsync would hand it to a pool. A program on JDK 21 runs in a container with 2 CPUs. It calls supplyAsync(() -> slowLookup()) with no pool, 300 times a second. What happens? The lookups queue up behind a single common pool thread They run on virtual threads They run on the calling threads Each lookup gets a new thread, with no upper limit With 2 CPUs, the common pool has one thread, and before JDK 25 CompletableFuture skipped the common pool when it had fewer than 2 threads. It created a thread per task instead. The first option is what JDK 25 does with the same code. Neither is acceptable for a call that waits: pass a pool. From "Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law": a checkout runs the price call (100 ms) and the rate call (100 ms) side by side on io, and you get 200 checkouts a second. How many io threads are busy on average? 20 40 200 400 Little's law: L = λ x W. Each checkout holds two io threads for 0.1 s, so the pool sees 400 calls a second x 0.1 s = 40 busy threads. Running the calls side by side cuts the time each checkout takes; it doesn't cut the number of threads you need. Size the pool above 40, and check that the services you call accept that many calls at once.

h: CompletableFuture: composing async steps · Key terms
x: CompletableFuture A Future you can complete by hand and clip further steps onto. Stage One step in a pipeline: a ticket, plus the instruction that completes it from earlier results. thenCompose Clips on a step that returns another ticket, and gives you one flat ticket back. thenCombine Waits for two tickets and merges their results with a function. Default async executor Where async methods run when you pass no pool: the common ForkJoinPool. Common pool One ForkJoinPool per JVM, with one thread fewer than the cores, shared by parallel streams and default async tasks. thenApply vs thenCompose? thenApply maps with a plain function (T -> U). thenCompose flattens a function that returns a ticket (T -> CompletableFuture<U>), like flatMap. What does a.thenCombine(b, fn) do? It waits until both a and b complete, then applies fn(aResult, bResult). It starts nothing: a and b must already be running to overlap. Which executor does supplyAsync(task) use on JDK 25? ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), always. Up to JDK 24, it used a new thread per task when the common pool had fewer than 2 threads. Which thread runs a plain thenApply step? The thread that completes the stage before it, or the calling thread if that stage is already complete. join() vs get() on a failed CompletableFuture? get() throws the checked ExecutionException, join() the unchecked CompletionException. Both carry the failure as the cause. Why pass a pool to supplyAsync for calls that wait? Without one, the calls hold common pool threads, which every parallel stream and every default async task in the JVM shares.

h: CompletableFuture: composing async steps · Go deeper
x: The stack of instructions from the third section has one more consequence. One slow plain step delays every other plain step clipped onto the same ticket, because the completing thread runs them one after another. CompletableFuture implements two interfaces. Future gives you get and cancel. CompletionStage has the composing methods, and nothing that completes the ticket or waits for it. When you write an API, return CompletionStage<T>, or call minimalCompletionStage() (JDK 9). Then callers can't call complete or obtrudeValue on your ticket and change a result you already computed. A caller who needs to wait can still call toCompletableFuture().join(), which makes the waiting visible in their code. There are a few other ways to get a ticket. completedFuture(v) and failedFuture(ex) (JDK 9) are handy in tests. new CompletableFuture<>() plus complete(v) connects any library that reports its answer through a callback, a method the library calls when the answer arrives. And completeAsync(supplier, executor) (JDK 9) completes an existing ticket from a task, which helps when you must hand out the ticket before you know which pool will do the work.

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · A dish burns at the grill: how a failure skips every step until a handler
x: When the steak burns: the note skips every station until the pass, arrives in an envelope, a kitchen timer frees the manager but not the cook, and each supplier call must be unable to fail before allOf Let's put the kitchen into code. A future is a claim ticket for a result that isn't ready yet, and a CompletableFuture is one you can attach the next step to. A stage is one such step, such as a thenApply, that runs when the step before it has finished. Our grill runs on kitchen, a thread pool: a few threads, paths of work that run side by side, taking tasks from one queue. Three plain stages follow the grill, one per station. Then come two handlers, which we'll meet in a moment: Java CompletableFuture<String> result = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(ErrorPathDemo::grill, kitchen) .thenApply(s -> step("1. pour the sauce on " + s, s + " with pepper sauce")) .thenApply(s -> step("2. plate " + s, "a plate of " + s)) .thenApply(s -> step("3. carry it to table 4", "table 4 got " + s)) .whenComplete((v, ex) -> System.out.println("whenComplete sees: " + (ex == null ? v : ex))) .exceptionally(ex -> { // the pass System.out.println("exceptionally sees: " + ex); return "table 4 got an apology and the menu"; }); Kotlin val result = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(::grill, kitchen) .thenApply { s -> step("1. pour the sauce on $s", "$s with pepper sauce") } .thenApply { s -> step("2. plate $s", "a plate of $s") } .thenApply { s -> step("3. carry it to table 4", "table 4 got $s") } .whenComplete { v, ex -> println("whenComplete sees: ${ex ?: v}") } .exceptionally { ex -> // the pass println("exceptionally sees: $ex") "table 4 got an apology and the menu" } step prints its text and returns the value, so we can see which stations did any work. And grill always throws an IllegalStateException that says the steak burned. Before you read on, decide which numbered lines will print. ErrorPathDemo, in the Try it below, printed this: whenComplete sees: java.util.concurrent.CompletionException: java.lang.IllegalStateException: the steak burned exceptionally sees: java.util.concurrent.CompletionException: java.lang.IllegalStateException: the steak burned result: table 4 got an apology and the menu Not one numbered line. When a stage throws, its future completes exceptionally: it finishes with an exception instead of a value. Every thenApply, thenCompose and thenCombine after it is then skipped. Its function never runs, and its own future fails with the same cause. That's the note on the ticket, passed from station to station. The failure stops at the first handler, a stage that also runs when the step before it failed. There are four: Method Runs on Changes the outcome? exceptionally(ex -> value) failure only yes, replaces the failure with a value handle((value, ex) -> result) success and failure yes, returns any result whenComplete((value, ex) -> ...) success and failure no, passes the outcome on exceptionallyCompose(ex -> future) failure only yes, with another future (JDK 12) whenComplete is the manager who glances at every ticket on its way past and writes in the log. It sees both outcomes and hands the same one on, so it suits logs and counters. (One detail: if its own action throws after a success, the result becomes that new failure. After a failure, the original failure wins.) exceptionally is the pass. It replaces the failure with a value, and everything after it sees a success. Where you put the handler decides what you can still save. At the end, after the sauce, the plate and the walk to table 4 were all skipped, the only honest thing left is an apology. Move the handler up, right after the grill, and it can swap in a spare steak. Then every station after it works as if nothing had gone wrong. Run the demo with early, and it prints: exceptionally sees: java.util.concurrent.CompletionException: java.lang.IllegalStateException: the steak burned 1. pour the sauce on the spare steak 2. plate the spare steak with pepper sauce 3. carry it to table 4 whenComplete sees: table 4 got a plate of the spare steak with pepper sauce Recover as close to the failure as you can. Every step after the handler then runs as usual. Sometimes the fallback takes time of its own. Cooking a new steak on the second grill returns a future, not a steak. For that case, use exceptionallyCompose, added in JDK 12 (version 12 of Java's development kit). It is to exceptionally what thenCompose is to thenApply: Java CompletableFuture<String> steak = grill.cookAsync(order) .exceptionallyCompose(ex -> spareGrill.cookAsync(order)); // JDK 12+: the fallback is a future too Kotlin val steak: CompletableFuture<String> = grill.cookAsync(order) .exceptionallyCompose { spareGrill.cookAsync(order) } // JDK 12+: the fallback is a future too Look again at what our two handlers printed, though. They didn't get our IllegalStateException. They got a CompletionException with ours inside, like a note sealed in an envelope. Where did the envelope come from? Move the handler Run ErrorPathDemo. The grill throws. Before you run it, write down which of the numbered steps will print. Run it with -Pargs=early, which recovers right after the grill. Predict again, including what whenComplete sees. ErrorPathDemo.java package workbench.executors.l07; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** The steak burns at the grill. Which steps still run? Pass "early" to recover right after the grill. */ public class ErrorPathDemo { static String grill() { throw new IllegalStateException("the steak burned"); } static <T> T step(String what, T value) { System.out.println(what); return value; } public static void main(String[] args) { boolean early = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("early"); try (ExecutorService kitchen = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("cook-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<String> steak = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(ErrorPathDemo::grill, kitchen); if (early) { steak = steak.exceptionally(ex -> { // recover the steak itself System.out.println("exceptionally sees: " + ex); return "the spare steak"; // kept warm for nights like this }); } CompletableFuture<String> result = steak .thenApply(s -> step("1. pour the sauce on " + s, s + " with pepper sauce")) .thenApply(s -> step("2. plate " + s, "a plate of " + s)) .thenApply(s -> step("3. carry it to table 4", "table 4 got " + s)) .whenComplete((v, ex) -> System.out.println("whenComplete sees: " + (ex == null ? v : ex))); if (!early) { result = result.exceptionally(ex -> { // recover at the pass instead System.out.println("exceptionally sees: " + ex); return "table 4 got an apology and the menu"; }); } System.out.println("result: " + result.join()); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l07.ErrorPathDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l07/ErrorPathDemo.java ErrorPathDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l07 import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.Executors private fun grill(): String = throw IllegalStateException("the steak burned") private fun <T> step(what: String, value: T): T { println(what) return value } /** The steak burns at the grill. Which steps still run? Pass "early" to recover right after the grill. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val early = args.firstOrNull() == "early" Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("cook-", 1).factory()).use { kitchen -> var steak = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(::grill, kitchen) if (early) { steak = steak.exceptionally { ex -> // recover the steak itself println("exceptionally sees: $ex") "the spare steak" // kept warm for nights like this } } var result = steak .thenApply { s -> step("1. pour the sauce on $s", "$s with pepper sauce") } .thenApply { s -> step("2. plate $s", "a plate of $s") } .thenApply { s -> step("3. carry it to table 4", "table 4 got $s") } .whenComplete { v, ex -> println("whenComplete sees: ${ex ?: v}") } if (!early) { result = result.exceptionally { ex -> // recover at the pass instead println("exceptionally sees: $ex") "table 4 got an apology and the menu" } } println("result: ${result.join()}") } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l07.ErrorPathDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l07/ErrorPathDemo.kt The default run prints no numbered steps. whenComplete and then exceptionally both see a CompletionException with the burned steak inside, and the result is the apology. With early, exceptionally runs first and returns the spare steak, then steps 1, 2 and 3 run, and whenComplete sees a success: table 4 got a plate of the spare steak with pepper sauce. CompletionStage (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · The note in an envelope: when a handler gets CompletionException, and when it doesn't
x: Handlers don't always get your exception. They get one of two things, by a rule that surprises everyone once. A CompletionException is an unchecked exception, one that Java doesn't make you catch, that CompletableFuture wraps around a failure, with your exception inside as its cause. It's the envelope. If the exception was thrown inside a stage, by a supplyAsync task or a thenApply function, the future stores it in an envelope. A handler on that future, or on any later stage, gets the CompletionException, and getCause() returns your exception. That's what our burned steak did. If somebody completed the future by hand, with completeExceptionally(ex), the future stores ex just as it is. orTimeout, which the next section covers, works that way, and so do many libraries that hand you a future. A handler attached right to that future gets the bare exception. One stage later it's in an envelope again, because the failure crossed a stage boundary on its way. WrapDemo prints every case. Cover the output below, and predict each line before you read it: 1. handle() on the supplyAsync future CompletionException <- IllegalStateException 2. handle() on completeExceptionally IllegalStateException 3. handle() one stage later CompletionException <- IllegalStateException 4. handle() after orTimeout TimeoutException 5. get() throws ExecutionException <- IllegalStateException 6. join() throws CompletionException <- IllegalStateException Lines 2 and 4 are bare, because someone completed those futures by hand. The last two lines are the blocking calls from the last lesson, the ones that make a thread wait for the result: get() throws ExecutionException and join() throws CompletionException, both with the original exception as the cause. So a handler that checks ex instanceof TimeoutException can be right in one place and quietly wrong one stage further down. Open the envelope first, then decide: Java .exceptionally(ex -> { Throwable cause = (ex instanceof CompletionException && ex.getCause() != null) ? ex.getCause() : ex; if (cause instanceof TimeoutException) return lastWeeksPrice; throw new CompletionException(cause); // not ours to handle: keep failing }) Kotlin .exceptionally { ex -> val cause = if (ex is CompletionException && ex.cause != null) ex.cause!! else ex if (cause is TimeoutException) lastWeeksPrice else throw CompletionException(cause) // not ours to handle: keep failing } First we take the cause out, if there is an envelope. Then we handle the one case we know, a timeout, with last week's price. The last line reads as "I opened it, and this one isn't mine, so pass it on." Throwing inside a handler keeps the future failing, so a later handler, or the caller, can deal with it. The lab's unwrap method does the same job in a loop. It also strips the ExecutionException that get() adds, in case one wrapper ends up inside another. And on a future you know has failed, exceptionNow() (JDK 19) hands you the exception with the envelope already removed. Open the envelope before you test the type. Rethrow what isn't yours. Line 4 of the demo came from a timeout. A timeout looks like the cure for a slow call. It is only half of one. Predict the envelope Cover the output in the section. Read WrapDemo and write down, for each numbered line, what you expect it to print. Run it and check. For each line you got wrong, find out whether the exception was thrown inside a stage or passed to completeExceptionally. WrapDemo.java package workbench.executors.l07; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Which exception does each handler see? Predict every line before you run it. */ public class WrapDemo { static String describe(Throwable ex) { String name = ex.getClass().getSimpleName(); return ex.getCause() == null ? name : name + " <- " + ex.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName(); } static void show(String label, CompletableFuture<?> f) { String seen = f.handle((v, ex) -> describe(ex)).join(); System.out.printf("%-42s %s%n", label, seen); } public static void main(String[] args) { IllegalStateException down = new IllegalStateException("the steak burned"); try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<String> supplied = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { throw down; }, io); CompletableFuture<String> completed = new CompletableFuture<>(); completed.completeExceptionally(down); CompletableFuture<String> timedOut = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> sleepThen(1000, "late"), io) .orTimeout(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); show("1. handle() on the supplyAsync future", supplied); show("2. handle() on completeExceptionally", completed); show("3. handle() one stage later", completed.thenApply(String::trim)); show("4. handle() after orTimeout", timedOut); try { supplied.get(); } catch (ExecutionException | InterruptedException e) { System.out.printf("%-42s %s%n", "5. get() throws", describe(e)); } try { supplied.join(); } catch (CompletionException e) { System.out.printf("%-42s %s%n", "6. join() throws", describe(e)); Lines 2 and 4 are bare exceptions, because completeExceptionally and orTimeout store them as they are. Every exception that was thrown inside a stage, or crossed one on its way, arrives as a CompletionException.

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · A kitchen timer for the manager: orTimeout ends the wait, not the work
x: Timeouts need a scene of their own. The restaurant buys flour from a few suppliers, and each supplier has a web service: a program on another computer that answers questions over the network. Ask it for today's price of a sack of flour, and it answers within a few hundred milliseconds. On a bad day, it doesn't answer at all. In code, asking is a blocking call. It holds a thread until the answer comes, just like the slow web service from Sizing a pool. So picture the call as a cook on the phone to the supplier. The manager wants the price, so he starts a kitchen timer. When it rings, he stops waiting and decides without it. Nobody tells the cook, who stays on hold, listening to the supplier's music. JDK 9 gave CompletableFuture two such kitchen timers: Java price.orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // fails with TimeoutException price.completeOnTimeout(lastWeeksPrice, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // completes with a default Kotlin price.orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // fails with TimeoutException price.completeOnTimeout(lastWeeksPrice, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // completes with a default Both change the future you call them on, and return it. If the future hasn't completed when the time is up, a timer thread inside the JDK completes it: orTimeout with a TimeoutException, completeOnTimeout with the value you gave it. The thread's name depends on the JDK. On JDK 21 it's CompletableFutureDelayScheduler, and on JDK 25 it's ForkJoinPool.commonPool-delayScheduler. Plain stages attached to the future, the ones without Async in their name, then run on that thread, so keep them cheap. Now the trap. Neither timer touches the call. KeepsRunningDemo gives a 600 ms call to a slow supplier a deadline of 200 ms. On JDK 21 it printed this: 36 ms io-1 asking the slow supplier for a price 236 ms CompletableFutureDelayScheduler the future completed with TimeoutException 695 ms io-1 the supplier answered, but nobody is listening 702 ms main pool closed The future failed right on time. The call finished anyway, about 600 ms after it started, holding io-1 the whole way, and the pool's close() had to wait for it. The answer went nowhere. Maybe cancel(true) can hang up the phone? Run the demo with cancel: 243 ms main cancel(true) returned true 247 ms main the future completed with CancellationException 773 ms io-1 the supplier answered, but nobody is listening As far as the future knows, the cancel worked. The line interrupted: the call stops here never printed, though, so the call never noticed. The CompletableFuture Javadoc, its official documentation, says the flag mayInterruptIfRunning "has no effect in this implementation because interrupts are not used to control processing." The source code shows why. supplyAsync hands the pool a small task that points to the future. The future keeps no pointer back to that task, or to the thread that runs it. So cancel can only store a CancellationException as the result. There's no thread it could interrupt. The FutureTask that submit returns is the opposite. Its cancel(true) sends an interrupt, the polite request to stop from Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption. Here the kitchen picture breaks. A real manager could walk over and tell the cook to hang up. A CompletableFuture has no line back to its cook at all. Under load, that is how a pool fills up with nothing. Take a pool of 20 threads and a supplier that hangs for 30 seconds. Every request gets its TimeoutException after 300 ms, right on time. But every call holds its thread for 30 seconds. After 20 requests, all 20 cooks are on hold. New calls, even to healthy suppliers, wait in the pool's queue behind them and time out too. So every call to another computer needs two timeouts. The one on the future is the caller's deadline. The one inside the client makes the call itself give up, and that gives the thread back. Java's HTTP client, the JDK's own tool for calling web services, takes it on the request: Java HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)) // the call itself gives up after 300 ms .build(); Kotlin val request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)) // the call itself gives up after 300 ms .build() Set the client's timeout no longer than the future's. And give each supplier a limit of its own, a bulkhead from Sizing a pool, so one hung supplier can't take every thread. (A bulkhead is a separate cap on calls to each slow service.) A timeout on the future frees the caller, not the thread. Give the call its own timeout too. One call with a deadline is under control now. But the manager doesn't want one price. He wants three, and he wants them at the same time. Time out a call, then watch it finish Run KeepsRunningDemo. Read the thread names and the timestamps. Run it with -Pargs=cancel, which calls cancel(true) at 200 ms instead. Predict first: does the call see an interrupt? KeepsRunningDemo.java package workbench.executors.l07; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** A 600 ms call to a slow supplier with orTimeout(200 ms). Pass "cancel" to try cancel(true) at 200 ms instead. */ public class KeepsRunningDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%4d ms %-38s %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, Thread.currentThread().getName(), msg); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean cancel = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("cancel"); try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> quote = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { log("asking the slow supplier for a price"); try { Thread.sleep(600); } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("interrupted: the call stops here"); throw new IllegalStateException(e); } log("the supplier answered, but nobody is listening"); return new BigDecimal("19.80"); }, io); if (cancel) { Thread.sleep(200); log("cancel(true) returned " + quote.cancel(true)); } else { quote.orTimeout(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } quote.handle((v, ex) -> { log("the future completed with " + (ex == null ? v : ex.getClass().getSimpleName())); return null; }).join(); } // close() waits for the supplier call, which is still running log("pool closed"); } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l07.KeepsRunningDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l07/KeepsRunningDemo.java KeepsRunningDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l07 import java.math.BigDecimal import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit private val T0 = System.nanoTime() private fun log(msg: String) = println("%4d ms %-38s %s".format((System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, Thread.currentThread().name, msg)) /** A 600 ms call to a slow supplier with orTimeout(200 ms). Pass "cancel" to try cancel(true) at 200 ms instead. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val cancel = args.firstOrNull() == "cancel" Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()).use { io -> val quote = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ log("asking the slow supplier for a price") try { Thread.sleep(600) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { log("interrupted: the call stops here") throw IllegalStateException(e) } log("the supplier answered, but nobody is listening") BigDecimal("19.80") }, io) if (cancel) { Thread.sleep(200) log("cancel(true) returned ${quote.cancel(true)}") } else { quote.orTimeout(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) } quote.handle { v, ex -> log("the future completed with ${if (ex == null) v else ex.javaClass.simpleName}") }.join() } // close() waits for the supplier call, which is still running log("pool closed") } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l07.KeepsRunningDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l07/KeepsRunningDemo.kt The future completes with TimeoutException at about 200 ms, on the timer thread (CompletableFutureDelayScheduler on JDK 21, ForkJoinPool.commonPool-delayScheduler on JDK 25). The supplier still answers at about 600 ms, and pool closed waits for it. With cancel, cancel(true) returns true and the future completes with CancellationException on main, but the line interrupted never prints: the call runs to the end.

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · Three suppliers at once: allOf, anyOf, and one bad answer that mustn't spoil the rest
x: Back to the flour. Three suppliers sell it: the corner shop, the market and the mill. The manager wants today's price from all three, and he'll buy from the cheapest. Phoning them one after another wastes time, so three cooks phone at once. Sending out several calls at the same time and collecting the answers is called a fan-out. In code, it's three futures, all started before we wait for any of them. FanOutDemo sets up the three suppliers with delays chosen for teaching. The corner shop fails after 50 ms, because it's closed today. The market answers 21.50 after 100 ms, and the mill answers 19.80 after 300 ms. The JDK has two methods that combine many futures, and the demo tries both. allOf(f1, f2, f3) returns a CompletableFuture<Void> that completes when all three have completed. It carries no results of its own. You read them from your own futures with join(), which no longer blocks, because they're all done. Predict what -Pargs=all prints, then compare: 84 ms corner fails 151 ms market answers 21.50 333 ms mill answers 19.80 336 ms all: failed with java.lang.IllegalStateException: corner is closed today Two good prices came back, and the errand failed anyway. If any of its futures fails, allOf fails too, and only after the slowest one has finished. (Every timestamp runs a little late, because the clock starts before the pool does, and the machine was busy with other work.) anyOf(f1, f2, f3) returns a future that completes the same way as the first of them to finish. Here's -Pargs=any: 99 ms corner fails 161 ms any: failed with java.lang.IllegalStateException: corner is closed today 161 ms market answers 21.50 352 ms mill answers 19.80 The corner shop answered first, with the worst possible news, and anyOf took it. The first to finish includes failures. If you want the first successful answer, anyOf can't give it to you. (Go deeper has a ten-line helper for that.) So neither method does the errand on its own. The fix is to make each call unable to fail before we combine them. Give every call its own deadline, then turn any failure into "no answer": Java CompletableFuture<Optional<BigDecimal>> safe = ask(supplier) .orTimeout(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // this supplier's deadline .handle((price, ex) -> ex == null ? Optional.of(price) : Optional.empty()); Kotlin val safe: CompletableFuture<Optional<BigDecimal>> = ask(supplier) .orTimeout(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // this supplier's deadline .handle { price, ex -> if (ex == null) Optional.of(price) else Optional.empty() } handle sees both outcomes and returns a new result either way: the price inside an Optional, or an empty Optional. Now allOf over the safe futures can only succeed, and the step after it picks the lowest price that came back. Here's -Pargs=safe: 91 ms corner fails 170 ms market answers 21.50 340 ms mill answers 19.80 353 ms safe: result 19.80 That's the mill's price, the cheapest, from the slowest supplier. The closed corner shop turned into an empty Optional, and it spoiled nothing. The deadline must sit on each call. Put one orTimeout on the allOf instead, and a single hung supplier throws away the two good answers. Make each call unable to fail before you combine them. Then pick from what came back. That's the lab. Its QuoteAggregator asks every supplier for a quote, a price offer, all at the same time. Each call gets its own deadline, every skipped supplier is reported with its real cause, and the lowest price wins. Notice the limit of the tool before we leave the phones. A CompletableFuture is good at waiting for calls and combining their answers. It can't stop a call it gave up on, and when one call fails, it doesn't cancel the others. It was built for work that waits. For work that is all arithmetic, the JDK has a pool of its own. Three ways to fan out Read FanOutDemo: the corner shop fails at 50 ms, the market answers at 100 ms, the mill at 300 ms. Run it with -Pargs=any, then -Pargs=all, then -Pargs=safe. Before each run, predict the result and when it arrives. FanOutDemo.java package workbench.executors.l07; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.List; import java.util.Optional; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** Three suppliers quote a sack of flour: corner fails at 50 ms, market answers at 100 ms, mill at 300 ms. Pass any, all or safe. */ public class FanOutDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%4d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg); } static CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> ask(String name, long ms, String price, ExecutorService io) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { sleep(ms); if (price == null) { log(name + " fails"); throw new IllegalStateException(name + " is closed today"); } log(name + " answers " + price); return new BigDecimal(price); }, io); } public static void main(String[] args) { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "all"; try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { List<CompletableFuture<BigDecimal>> asks = List.of( ask("corner", 50, null, io), ask("market", 100, "21.50", io), ask("mill", 300, "19.80", io)); CompletableFuture<?> result = switch (mode) { // the first future to complete wins, even when it completes with a failure case "any" -> CompletableFuture.anyOf(asks.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)); // waits for all three, then fails because one of them failed case "all" -> CompletableFuture.allOf(asks.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)) .thenApply(done -> asks.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).min(Comparator.naturalOrder()).orElseThrow()); // turn each failure into an empty Optional first, so allOf can't fail default -> { List<CompletableFuture<Optional<BigDecimal>>> safe = asks.stream() .map(f -> f.handle((price, ex) -> ex == null ? Optional.of(price) : Optional.<BigDecimal>empty())) .toList(); yield CompletableFuture.allOf(safe.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)) .thenApply(done -> safe.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).flatMap(Optional::stream) .min(Comparator.naturalOrder()).orElseThrow()); } }; result.handle((v, ex) -> { log(mode + ": " + (ex == null ? "result " + v : "failed with " + ex.getCause())); return null; }).join(); } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l07.FanOutDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l07/FanOutDemo.java FanOutDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l07 import java.math.BigDecimal import java.util.Optional import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService import java.util.concurrent.Executors private val T0 = System.nanoTime() private fun log(msg: String) = println("%4d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg)) private fun ask(name: String, ms: Long, price: String?, io: ExecutorService): CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ Thread.sleep(ms) if (price == null) { log("$name fails") throw IllegalStateException("$name is closed today") } log("$name answers $price") BigDecimal(price) }, io) /** Three suppliers quote a sack of flour: corner fails at 50 ms, market answers at 100 ms, mill at 300 ms. Pass any, all or safe. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val mode = args.firstOrNull() ?: "all" Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()).use { io -> val asks = listOf(ask("corner", 50, null, io), ask("market", 100, "21.50", io), ask("mill", 300, "19.80", io)) val result: CompletableFuture<*> = when (mode) { // the first future to complete wins, even when it completes with a failure "any" -> CompletableFuture.anyOf(*asks.toTypedArray()) // waits for all three, then fails because one of them failed "all" -> CompletableFuture.allOf(*asks.toTypedArray()) .thenApply { asks.map { it.join() }.min() } // turn each failure into an empty Optional first, so allOf can't fail else -> { val safe = asks.map { f -> f.handle { price, ex -> if (ex == null) Optional.of(price) else Optional.empty() } } CompletableFuture.allOf(*safe.toTypedArray()) .thenApply { safe.mapNotNull { it.join().orElse(null) }.min() } } } result.handle { v, ex -> log("$mode: " + if (ex == null) "result $v" else "failed with ${ex.cause}") }.join() } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l07.FanOutDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l07/FanOutDemo.kt any fails at about 50 ms with the corner shop's closed today, and the market and the mill keep going after the result is printed. all fails with the same exception, but only at about 300 ms, after the mill answers. safe succeeds at about 300 ms with 19.80, the mill's price, because the failure became an empty Optional. On a busy machine, every timestamp runs a little late. Each supplier call gets its own deadline and a handle step, so allOf only ever sees prices or empty results.

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · Java and Kotlin
x: One supplier call with a deadline: CompletableFuture vs coroutines Ask.java (CompletableFuture) CompletableFuture<Optional<Quote>> ask(QuoteProvider p, String item) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> new Quote(p.name(), p.quote(item)), io) .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // the caller stops waiting... .handle((q, ex) -> ex == null ? Optional.of(q) : Optional.empty()); // ...but p.quote keeps running on io until it returns } Ask.kt (kotlinx.coroutines) suspend fun ask(p: QuoteProvider, item: String): Quote? = try { withTimeoutOrNull(300.milliseconds) { // null when time is up runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { // interrupts the thread on cancel Quote(p.name(), p.quote(item)) } } } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e // never swallow cancellation } catch (e: Exception) { null // a failure becomes "no answer" } Both versions have the same shape: a deadline, then a failure turned into "no answer". The difference is what happens to the work. orTimeout only completes the future, and the supplier call runs to its end. Kotlin's coroutines, its own light tasks with a track of their own, can do more. withTimeoutOrNull cancels the block when time is up, and runInterruptible turns that cancellation into Thread.interrupt() on the IO thread. So a blocking call that responds to interrupts stops and gives its thread back. In both languages, a call that ignores interrupts keeps its thread, which is why the client's own timeout still matters. Kotlin has one trap of its own: when you catch Exception, you must rethrow CancellationException by hand, or the coroutine stops responding to cancellation. CompletableFuture has no such trap.

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · Worked example
x: Give the flour price a deadline and a fallback The kitchen gets the flour price from its main supplier through an async client, a library whose methods return a CompletableFuture. When the supplier hangs, everything that needs the price hangs with it. Before reading on, decide what should happen after 300 ms. CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> price(String item) { return supplier.priceAsync(item); // no deadline: a hung supplier hangs the kitchen } fun price(item: String): CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> = supplier.priceAsync(item) // no deadline: a hung supplier hangs the kitchen Give the call a deadline, count failures without changing them, then fall back to a second supplier, which has an async client too. metrics is a small counter that a dashboard reads. The fallback gets a short deadline of its own, because exceptionallyCompose starts a new call that the first timeout doesn't cover. CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> price(String item) { return supplier.priceAsync(item) .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // 1. the main call gets 300 ms .whenComplete((p, ex) -> { // 2. look, don't change if (ex != null) metrics.count("price.failed", unwrap(ex).getClass().getSimpleName()); }) .exceptionallyCompose(ex -> backup.priceAsync(item) // 3. fall back, asynchronously .orTimeout(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)); // 4. the fallback's own deadline } fun price(item: String): CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> = supplier.priceAsync(item) .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // 1. the main call gets 300 ms .whenComplete { _, ex -> // 2. look, don't change if (ex != null) metrics.count("price.failed", unwrap(ex).javaClass.simpleName) } .exceptionallyCompose { // 3. fall back, asynchronously backup.priceAsync(item).orTimeout(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // 4. the fallback's own deadline } Why unwrap in the counter? The supplier's client may complete its future with a bare exception, orTimeout stores a bare TimeoutException, and anything thrown inside a stage arrives in an envelope. Without unwrapping, half the failures would be counted as CompletionException, which tells the person reading the dashboard nothing. One gap is left. After 300 ms the kitchen moves on, but the main call still holds a thread and a network connection. Give the request a timeout of its own, so the client gives up too. With the JDK's HTTP client, it's one line on the request. HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)) // 5. the call stops waiting too .build(); val request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)) // 5. the call stops waiting too .build()

x: A price checker that survives bad suppliers labs/executors/src/main/java/workbench/executors/l07/QuoteAggregator.java labs/executors/src/main/java/workbench/executors/l07/QuoteProvider.java labs/executors/src/main/java/workbench/executors/l07/NoQuoteException.java ./gradlew :executors:test --tests 'workbench.executors.l07.*' Meet the classes. A QuoteProvider is one supplier's price service: quote(item) makes a blocking call and returns today's price, or throws. A Quote is one answer, the supplier's name and its price. QuoteAggregator.best(item) must ask every supplier at once and complete with the lowest Quote. Its Javadoc is the spec. Run the tests: all seven fail. Write unwrap: loop while the throwable is a CompletionException or an ExecutionException and has a cause, moving to the cause each time. Add a private method ask(QuoteProvider p, String item) that returns CompletableFuture<Optional<Quote>>: supplyAsync on io, then orTimeout, then handle. On failure, call onSkip.accept(p.name(), unwrap(ex)) and return Optional.empty(). In best, map every supplier to ask, collect the futures in a list, and pass them to allOf. In the thenApply after it, join each future, keep the quotes that are present, and return the lowest price, or throw NoQuoteException. Run the tests until all seven pass, then once more. orTimeout takes a long and a unit: orTimeout(timeout.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS). allOf takes an array (asks.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)) and returns CompletableFuture<Void>. Read the quotes from your own list. If skipsFailingProvider reports a CompletionException, you passed ex to onSkip without unwrapping it. If skipsSlowProvider times out, the deadline is on the whole call, not on each supplier. Throwing NoQuoteException inside the thenApply is enough: the returned future fails with it as the cause. All seven tests in QuoteAggregatorTest pass. By the end you can recover from a failure at the right stage, unwrap CompletionException, give each call its own timeout, and ask several suppliers at once without one bad answer failing the whole request.

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · Quiz
x: Each step prints its letter: supplyAsync(fails, io).thenApply(A).whenComplete(B).exceptionally(C).thenAccept(D), and the supplier throws. What prints? A, B, C, D B, C, D C, D B and C, then the pipeline fails A is skipped, because its input failed. whenComplete runs on a failure too, but it passes the failure on, so C runs and recovers. Then D runs with the fallback value. After exceptionally recovers, every stage after it sees a success, which is why the last option is wrong. supplyAsync(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("closed today"); }, io).exceptionally(ex -> ...). What is the class of ex? ExecutionException IllegalStateException RuntimeException CompletionException, with the IllegalStateException as its cause The exception was thrown inside a stage, so the future stores it wrapped in a CompletionException. ExecutionException is what get() throws at the blocking edge. You would get the bare IllegalStateException only if someone had called completeExceptionally with it. Supplier calls run on a fixed pool of 20 threads with orTimeout(300, MILLISECONDS). One supplier hangs for 30 s, and 100 requests arrive in one second. What happens? The first 20 time out at 300 ms but keep their threads; later calls queue behind them, so they time out too, even to healthy suppliers Every request times out at 300 ms, and the pool stays free orTimeout interrupts the hung calls, so the threads come back at 300 ms The pool rejects the 21st request orTimeout completes the future but never touches the call, so each hung call holds its thread for 30 s. A fixed pool has a queue with no limit, so nothing is rejected: new calls just wait behind the hung ones until their own deadlines pass. A timeout in the client and a limit per supplier prevent it. You want to count every supplier call as a success or a failure, without changing what the caller receives. Which method fits? exceptionally handle whenComplete thenAccept whenComplete sees both outcomes and passes the original one on. handle sees both too, but you'd have to rebuild the outcome yourself, rethrowing the failure, which is easy to get wrong. exceptionally misses successes, and thenAccept misses failures. From "Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption": the same blocking call, asleep in Thread.sleep, runs twice: once through executor.submit(task) and once through CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(task, executor). You call cancel(true) on both futures. What happens? Both calls are interrupted Only the submit call is interrupted; the CompletableFuture one keeps sleeping Only the CompletableFuture call is interrupted Neither, because cancel only affects tasks that haven't started submit returns a FutureTask, whose cancel(true) interrupts the worker thread. CompletableFuture.cancel ignores the flag: it completes the future with CancellationException and leaves the task alone. Both futures report isCancelled() == true.

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · Explain it back

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · Key terms
x: Stage One step attached to a future, such as a thenApply, that runs when the step before it finishes. CompletionException The unchecked wrapper CompletableFuture puts around an exception thrown inside a stage. exceptionally Runs only on failure and replaces it with a value. handle Runs on success or failure and returns a new result either way. whenComplete Runs on success or failure to look; passes the outcome on unchanged. orTimeout Fails the future with TimeoutException if it isn't done in time. The work keeps running. Fan-out Sending several calls at the same time and collecting their answers. allOf / anyOf Combine many futures: wait for all of them, or take the first to complete. Which CompletableFuture handler sees a failure but can't change the outcome? whenComplete. It passes the original result or failure on. exceptionally and handle can replace it. A handler on a failed supplyAsync future: which exception does it get? A CompletionException, with the exception the task threw as getCause(). Does orTimeout stop the task? No. It completes the future with TimeoutException, and the task keeps running, holding its thread. Does cancel(true) interrupt a CompletableFuture's task? No. The flag has no effect. The future completes with CancellationException, and the task runs on. One of three futures fails at 50 ms, and the slowest takes 300 ms. When does allOf complete? At 300 ms, exceptionally. allOf waits for all of them; it doesn't fail fast. What does anyOf give you if the fastest future fails? A failure. anyOf completes like the first future to complete, success or failure. When do you use exceptionallyCompose instead of exceptionally? When the fallback is itself a future, such as a call to a backup supplier (JDK 12+).

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · Go deeper
x: anyOf gives you the first to finish, not the first to succeed. When you want the first success, complete a future of your own from each success, and fail it only when every call has failed. complete returns false for every caller after the first, so the first success wins without a lock: Java static <T> CompletableFuture<T> firstSuccess(List<CompletableFuture<T>> calls) { // calls must not be empty CompletableFuture<T> first = new CompletableFuture<>(); AtomicInteger failed = new AtomicInteger(); for (CompletableFuture<T> call : calls) { call.whenComplete((value, ex) -> { if (ex == null) first.complete(value); // only the first one counts else if (failed.incrementAndGet() == calls.size()) first.completeExceptionally(ex); }); } return first; } Kotlin fun <T> firstSuccess(calls: List<CompletableFuture<T>>): CompletableFuture<T> { // calls must not be empty val first = CompletableFuture<T>() val failed = AtomicInteger() for (call in calls) { call.whenComplete { value, ex -> if (ex == null) first.complete(value) // only the first one counts else if (failed.incrementAndGet() == calls.size) first.completeExceptionally(ex) } } return first } Two smaller things are worth knowing. orTimeout and completeOnTimeout change the very future you call them on. If a library hands the same cached future to several callers, one caller's timeout fails it for all of them. Call copy() (JDK 9) first, and put the timeout on your copy. And when you need a delay without a timeout, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(500, MILLISECONDS, io) (JDK 9) returns an Executor that runs each task 500 ms after you hand it over. It's handy for a retry that waits a little first: supplyAsync(this::call, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(500, MILLISECONDS, io)).

h: ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams · One big pile, split in half until it's small: a RecursiveTask
x: Let's start with the plain version. The year's payments sit in a long[] called amounts, two million of them, each in cents. One thread, a single path of work through the program, can add them up with a loop, and for the takings, the year's total sales, that loop is the whole program. Our question is how to share such a loop among several threads without a manager handing out the work. A ForkJoinPool, added in JDK 7 (version 7 of Java's development kit), is a thread pool, a few reused threads that run tasks for you, built for one shape of work: a big job of computation that splits itself into smaller jobs of the same kind. To fork a piece is to hand it to the pool, so that another worker can pick it up. To join it is to wait for that piece's answer. The pool's threads are called workers. You describe the job as a RecursiveTask<V>, which returns a value, or a RecursiveAction, which doesn't. Both have one method to write, compute(), and it nearly always has this shape: Java class SumTask extends RecursiveTask<Long> { static final int THRESHOLD = 10_000; final long[] a; final int from, to; SumTask(long[] a, int from, int to) { this.a = a; this.from = from; this.to = to; } @Override protected Long compute() { if (to - from <= THRESHOLD) { // 1. small enough: just loop long sum = 0; for (int i = from; i < to; i++) sum += a[i]; return sum; } int mid = (from + to) >>> 1; // 2. split at the middle SumTask left = new SumTask(a, from, mid), right = new SumTask(a, mid, to); left.fork(); // 3. let another worker take the left half long r = right.compute(); // 4. do the right half here return left.join() + r; // 5. then collect the left half } } long takings = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(new SumTask(amounts, 0, amounts.length)); Kotlin class SumTask(val a: LongArray, val from: Int, val to: Int) : RecursiveTask<Long>() { override fun compute(): Long { if (to - from <= THRESHOLD) { // 1. small enough: just loop var sum = 0L for (i in from until to) sum += a[i] return sum } val mid = (from + to) ushr 1 // 2. split at the middle val left = SumTask(a, from, mid) val right = SumTask(a, mid, to) left.fork() // 3. let another worker take the left half val r = right.compute() // 4. do the right half here return left.join() + r // 5. then collect the left half } companion object { const val THRESHOLD = 10_000 } } val takings = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(SumTask(amounts, 0, amounts.size)) Read compute() from the top. If the range holds at most THRESHOLD amounts, we just loop over it and return the sum. Otherwise we split the range at the middle into two new tasks. We fork the left one, compute the right one ourselves, and then join the left one and add the two halves. ((from + to) >>> 1 is a middle that can't overflow, even for huge arrays.) The order of those last three lines matters more than anything else here, and the next section shows why. The threshold is the one number you have to choose: the size below which a task stops splitting and loops. Too big, and there are only a few pieces, so some workers sit idle at the end. Too small, and the cost of making and scheduling task objects eats the gain. The ForkJoinTask Javadoc, its official documentation, gives a very rough rule: a task should do more than 100 and fewer than 10,000 basic steps of computation. Then measure. WorkStealingDemo, in the Try it below, does a heavier job than adding: it works out the card fee on each of the two million payments and totals the fees. Its fee() method does a hundred rounds of arithmetic per payment, to stand in for real fee rules. It runs once on one thread and once on a ForkJoinPool with 4 workers, and it counts the leaves, the small pieces that each worker looped over. With the default threshold of 50,000, every split halves the range until a leaf holds 31,250 payments, so there are 64 leaves: one thread: 1,021 ms ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1 17 leaves ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2 12 leaves ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3 16 leaves ForkJoinPool-1-worker-4 19 leaves right order, threshold 50,000: 869 ms, 7 steals, same total: true most leaves running at the same moment: 4 Correctness first: same total: true, so the pool did exactly the work of the loop. Then speed, and here I have to be honest. This run was on a machine with 4 cores, the parts of the processor that each run one thread at a time. Other programs were busy on it and kept most of the cores, so the pool was only about 1.2 times faster than one thread. The last line is the neutral referee. It counts how many leaves were running at the same moment, and it said 4. All four workers really did compute side by side. With four cores to itself, the pool could get close to four times faster. I couldn't measure that on this busy machine, so run it on yours and see how close you get. Run it with a threshold of 500 and there are 4,096 leaves, still well spread and still fast. Run it with 1,000,000 and there are only 2 leaves, so only 2 workers ever get work, and the referee says 2. Fork/join is for computation on data you already have in memory: summing, sorting, searching, changing every element of a big array. Its tasks should not wait for a network, a disk or a lock, for reasons the last section shows. The demo printed one more number that deserves a question. Sixty-four leaves ended up spread across four workers, with only 7 steals. Who handed them out? Change the threshold Run WorkStealingDemo. It totals the card fees on 2,000,000 payments, first on one thread, then on a ForkJoinPool with 4 workers. Check same total, then note the speed-up, how many leaves each worker ran, and the last line. Run it with -Pargs="right 500", then with -Pargs="right 1000000". Before each run, predict the number of leaves and the number on the last line. h: ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams · Idle workers steal from the bottom: how work stealing works, and the order that keeps it parallel
x: Four cooks, one pile: each cook splits onto his own stack, an idle cook steals the biggest bundle from the bottom, fork, compute, join keeps four leaves running (the wrong order runs one), and a cook on the phone stalls the shared common pool Nobody did. A ThreadPoolExecutor, the ordinary pool from the first lessons of this track, has one shared queue, the rail that every cook takes tickets from. A ForkJoinPool gives every worker a queue of its own, a deque (say "deck"), short for double-ended queue: a line you can add to or take from at either end. fork() pushes the task onto the top of the current worker's deque. The worker takes its own work from the top as well, so it always runs the task it forked most recently. That's the smallest piece, and its data is still in the worker's cache, the processor's small, fast copy of recently used memory. A worker whose deque is empty becomes a thief. It picks another worker and takes the task at the bottom of that worker's deque. That's the oldest task, the one forked highest up in the splitting, so it's the biggest piece of work there is. The thief splits it on its own deque and stays busy for a long time. That's why the demo needed only 7 steals for 64 leaves. Taking work this way from another worker's deque is work stealing. In the kitchen, each cook's deque is a personal stack of payment slips. Splitting means putting half your pile on top of your own stack and carrying on with the other half. A cook with nothing left takes the bottom bundle from a colleague's stack, the biggest one, so he won't need to come back for a while. The figure shows the same moment in code. join() doesn't simply put the thread to sleep, either. If the forked task is still on the worker's own deque, the worker pops it and runs it right there. If a thief took it, the worker helps by running other waiting tasks until the answer is ready. So a fork/join pool needs no spare thread for each task that waits for another. Now the order. Fork one half, compute the other on this thread, and only then join: Java left.fork(); // the left half becomes stealable long r = right.compute(); // this thread works while a thief can take the left half return left.join() + r; Kotlin left.fork() // the left half becomes stealable val r = right.compute() // this thread works while a thief can take the left half return left.join() + r Swap the last two steps, left.fork(); left.join(); right.compute(), and the worker waits for the left half before it even starts the right one. Run the demo with wrong: one thread: 905 ms ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1 14 leaves ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2 17 leaves ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3 17 leaves ForkJoinPool-1-worker-4 16 leaves wrong order, threshold 50,000: 1,002 ms, 29 steals, same total: true most leaves running at the same moment: 1 It compiles, it gives the right total, and it's a little slower than one cook. The leaves still landed on all four workers, and there were more steals than before, so at a glance the pool looks busy. The referee tells the truth: one leaf at a time. Let's trace a single split. The worker forks the left half, so the left half sits on its deque. Then it joins the left half at once. The right half doesn't exist yet, because right.compute() comes later. So there's nothing else to do. Either the worker runs the left half itself, or a thief steals it and the worker waits. Only when the left half is done does the right half start. That happens at every level of the splitting, so the whole job runs one leaf after another, hopping between workers. left.compute() + right.compute() is the same thing written honestly: plain sequential code with extra objects. All three versions give the right total, which is how this bug gets past code review. invokeAll(left, right) is the library's shortcut for the right order. Fork one half, compute the other, then join. Any other order runs the halves one after the other. You may never write a RecursiveTask yourself. You're much more likely to meet this pool through a single word: parallel. Join too early Run WorkStealingDemo with -Pargs=wrong. It joins the left half before computing the right one. Compare the time with the one-thread line, then read the last line. Why do leaves land on all four workers when only one runs at a time?
