h: ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams · Parallel streams: the same pool, shared with the whole program
x: list.parallelStream(), or .parallel() on any stream, splits its source into pieces and runs them as fork/join tasks. They run on the common pool, ForkJoinPool.commonPool(): one ForkJoinPool that the whole JVM, the Java Virtual Machine that runs your program, shares. It's ready to use without creating anything. The thread that started the stream takes part too. The common pool has availableProcessors() - 1 workers by default, one fewer than the cores the JVM may use, so 3 on our 4-core machine. (You can change that with a setting on the java command line, -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism.) Many users share them. Every parallel stream runs there. So does every CompletableFuture step that names no executor, the object that runs its tasks, as CompletableFuture: composing async steps showed. And since JDK 25, so do tasks scheduled on the common pool, from Scheduled executors. In the kitchen, the common pool is the one team of helpers that every part of the restaurant borrows. Three mistakes cover most parallel stream bugs. The first is writing to shared state. SharedStateDemo sends the numbers 0 to 99,999 through a parallel stream twice. First, it adds each one to a plain ArrayList and to a shared long[] total. Then it lets the stream build the results itself, with toList() and mapToLong().sum(). Predict what the shared versions get. Here is a run of the Java version: shared ArrayList: 50,522 of 100,000 ids, in order: false toList(): 100,000 of 100,000 ids, in order: true shared long[] sum: 4,999,950,000 mapToLong().sum(): 4,999,950,000 threads that ran the first stream: [ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1, ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-2, ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-3, main] Half the ids are gone, and the shared sum came out right by pure luck. The Kotlin run straight after it was less lucky: 4,814,237,001, off by about 185 million. Both are the read-modify-write races of Race conditions: why count++ lies, where threads read a value, change it and write it back at the same moment. Four threads read the list's size, or the total, at the same moment, and some of their writes land on top of each other. Sometimes the ArrayList even throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, because two threads grow its array at once. The fix is to let the stream build the result: toList(), collect(...), sum(), reduce(...). Each thread works on its own piece, and the stream combines the pieces at the end. The last line of the output shows who did the work: the three common pool workers and main. The second mistake is expecting order. forEach on a parallel stream runs in whatever order the threads reach the elements. toList() and forEachOrdered keep the order of the source, at some cost. The third is too little work, or a source that splits badly. Splitting, scheduling and combining all cost time, so a stream of 1,000 cheap elements is faster sequential. How a source splits matters too. An array or an ArrayList splits in half by index, in one step, and each half can go to another worker. A LinkedList has no middle to jump to. Its Spliterator, the object that does the splitting, walks the list from the front and copies the next 1,024 elements into an array, then the next 2,048, each batch a little bigger, all on the one thread that splits. Stream.iterate and BufferedReader.lines() split badly for the same reason. Measure both versions before you keep parallel(). Never write to shared state from a parallel stream. Let the stream build the result. Each of those mistakes stays inside your own stream. The last one reaches every other part of the program. Collect from many threads Run SharedStateDemo. Before you do, predict the size of the shared list, and whether the shared sum is right. Run it twice more. Which numbers change between runs, and which never do? Set<String> threads = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); List<Integer> shared = new ArrayList<>(); try { ids.parallelStream().forEach(id -> { threads.add(Thread.currentThread().getName()); shared.add(id); // many threads, one ArrayList }); System.out.printf("shared ArrayList: %,d of %,d ids, in order: %b%n", shared.size(), ids.size(), shared.equals(ids)); } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) { System.out.println("shared ArrayList: threw " + e); ids.parallelStream().forEach(id -> total[0] += id); // read, add, write from many threads long sum = ids.parallelStream().mapToLong(Integer::longValue).sum(); System.out.printf("shared long[] sum: %,d%n", total[0]); h: ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams · A cook on the phone: how blocking calls starve the common pool
x: A ForkJoinPool tries to keep about parallelism threads running. When one of them blocks, in Thread.sleep, a network read or a database call, the pool normally doesn't know. That worker is simply gone until the call returns. The kitchen picture breaks here, and the break is the bug. In a real kitchen, a cook who spends ten minutes on the phone is easy to spot, and someone would share out his pile. The pool can't see that a worker is waiting. StarvationDemo shows what that costs. It runs 16 lookups in a parallel stream, each one a 300 ms call to the slow stock service from Sizing a pool, which tells you how many of a product are left. That's four rounds of work for the 3 common pool workers plus main. As soon as all four threads are busy, another thread hands the common pool a tiny task, through supplyAsync with no executor. The task does nothing but report its thread's name: 49 ms blocking: common pool parallelism 3, 16 lookups of 300 ms 1331 ms tiny task waited 1202 ms, then ran on ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-3 1335 ms all lookups done A task that takes microseconds waited 1.2 seconds, until the lookups were nearly done. Every helper in the restaurant was on hold with the stock service. In a real program, that tiny task is somebody else's request, from a part of the code that never heard of the stock service. The fix is to keep waiting off the common pool. Run blocking calls on an executor built for waiting, such as a pool with a fixed number of threads, sized for the service you call, as Sizing a pool showed. Then combine the answers with CompletableFuture, as in the last lesson. That's the demo's io mode: 38 ms io: common pool parallelism 3, 16 lookups of 300 ms 109 ms tiny task waited 5 ms, then ran on ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1 419 ms all lookups done All 16 lookups waited at the same time, so together they took little more than one lookup's 300 ms, and the tiny task waited 5 ms. There is also a patch for code you can't move. ForkJoinPool.managedBlock(blocker) tells the pool "this worker is about to block", and the pool may start a spare worker to keep its parallelism up. CompletableFuture uses it internally when a pool thread calls join(). In the demo's managed mode, the tiny task waited 8 ms and ran on ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-16, one of the spares. It is still a patch. Every blocked call costs a whole platform thread, an operating system thread with its own stack, and the number of spares is capped. You may read that a parallel stream started inside customPool.submit(...) runs on customPool. It does today, but that's how the implementation behaves, not something the specification promises. Don't build on it. Keep blocking calls off the common pool. It belongs to the whole program. That is the limit of this lesson's tool. Fork/join shines on computation and has nothing to offer a thread that waits. Waiting is cheap only when threads are cheap, and platform threads are not, a problem the virtual threads track takes on. Starve the common pool Run StarvationDemo. Note how long the tiny task waits, and which thread finally runs it. Run it with -Pargs=io, then with -Pargs=managed. Predict each time: how long do all the lookups take, and how long does the tiny task wait? StarvationDemo.java package workbench.executors.l08; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.stream.IntStream; /** Blocking stock lookups in a parallel stream while a tiny task needs the common pool. Args: [blocking|managed|io]. */ public class StarvationDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static final int PARALLELISM = ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism(); static final AtomicInteger STARTED = new AtomicInteger(); static final CountDownLatch ALL_BUSY = new CountDownLatch(1); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg); } static void lookup() { if (STARTED.incrementAndGet() == PARALLELISM + 1) ALL_BUSY.countDown(); // the common pool and main are all busy sleep(300); // a call to the slow stock service } static void managedLookup() { try { // tells the pool this worker is about to block, so it can start a spare thread ForkJoinPool.managedBlock(new ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker() { boolean done; @Override public boolean block() { lookup(); done = true; return true; } @Override public boolean isReleasable() { return done; } }); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "blocking"; int lookups = (PARALLELISM + 1) * 4; // four rounds of work for the common pool and main log(mode + ": common pool parallelism " + PARALLELISM + ", " + lookups + " lookups of 300 ms"); Thread tiny = new Thread(() -> { try { ALL_BUSY.await(); // start once the lookups are under way } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } long t = System.nanoTime(); String who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()).join(); // a tiny task log("tiny task waited " + (System.nanoTime() - t) / 1_000_000 + " ms, then ran on " + who); }); tiny.start(); if (mode.equals("io")) { try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(lookups)) { List<CompletableFuture<Void>> calls = IntStream.range(0, lookups) .mapToObj(i -> CompletableFuture.runAsync(StarvationDemo::lookup, io)) .toList(); calls.forEach(CompletableFuture::join); } } else { boolean managed = mode.equals("managed"); IntStream.range(0, lookups).parallel().forEach(i -> { if (managed) managedLookup(); else lookup(); }); } log("all lookups done"); tiny.join(); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l08.StarvationDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l08/StarvationDemo.java StarvationDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l08 import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.stream.IntStream import kotlin.concurrent.thread private val T0 = System.nanoTime() private val parallelism = ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism() private val started = AtomicInteger() private val allBusy = CountDownLatch(1) private fun log(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg)) private fun lookup() { if (started.incrementAndGet() == parallelism + 1) allBusy.countDown() // the common pool and main are all busy Thread.sleep(300) // a call to the slow stock service } private fun managedLookup() { // tells the pool this worker is about to block, so it can start a spare thread ForkJoinPool.managedBlock(object : ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker { var done = false override fun block(): Boolean { lookup() done = true return true } override fun isReleasable() = done }) } /** Blocking stock lookups in a parallel stream while a tiny task needs the common pool. Args: [blocking|managed|io]. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val mode = args.firstOrNull() ?: "blocking" val lookups = (parallelism + 1) * 4 // four rounds of work for the common pool and main log("$mode: common pool parallelism $parallelism, $lookups lookups of 300 ms") val tiny = thread { allBusy.await() // start once the lookups are under way val t = System.nanoTime() val who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync { Thread.currentThread().name }.join() // a tiny task log("tiny task waited ${(System.nanoTime() - t) / 1_000_000} ms, then ran on $who") } if (mode == "io") { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(lookups).use { io -> val calls = (0 until lookups).map { CompletableFuture.runAsync(::lookup, io) } calls.forEach { it.join() } } } else { val managed = mode == "managed" IntStream.range(0, lookups).parallel().forEach { if (managed) managedLookup() else lookup() } } log("all lookups done") tiny.join() } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l08.StarvationDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l08/StarvationDemo.kt In the default mode, the lookups take about 1.2 s on a 4-core machine (four rounds of 300 ms for the common pool and main), and the tiny task waits about as long, because every common pool worker is blocked. With io, the lookups take about 300 ms and the tiny task waits a few milliseconds. With managed, the pool adds spare workers, so both numbers drop again, and the tiny task runs on one of the extra threads.

h: ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams · Java and Kotlin
x: Divide and conquer: RecursiveTask vs coroutines CountOver.java (ForkJoinPool) class CountOver extends RecursiveTask<Integer> { final long[] a; final long limit; final int from, to; CountOver(long[] a, long limit, int from, int to) { this.a = a; this.limit = limit; this.from = from; this.to = to; } @Override protected Integer compute() { if (to - from <= 10_000) { int n = 0; for (int i = from; i < to; i++) if (a[i] > limit) n++; return n; } int mid = (from + to) >>> 1; CountOver left = new CountOver(a, limit, from, mid); CountOver right = new CountOver(a, limit, mid, to); left.fork(); // stealable int r = right.compute(); // work here return left.join() + r; // then collect } } // how many payments were over 5,000.00? int big = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(new CountOver(amounts, 500_000, 0, amounts.length)); CountOver.kt (kotlinx.coroutines) suspend fun countOver(a: LongArray, limit: Long, from: Int, to: Int): Int = if (to - from <= 10_000) { (from until to).count { a[it] > limit } } else coroutineScope { val mid = (from + to) ushr 1 val left = async { countOver(a, limit, from, mid) } // like fork() val right = countOver(a, limit, mid, to) // like compute() left.await() + right // like join() } // how many payments were over 5,000.00? val big = runBlocking(Dispatchers.Default) { countOver(amounts, 500_000, 0, amounts.size) } Kotlin can extend RecursiveTask exactly as Java does (the Kotlin WorkStealingDemo does). The coroutine version keeps the same shape and the same order rule: start the left half with async, compute the right half in place, then await. Coroutines are Kotlin's own light tasks, with a track of their own. Two things differ. Dispatchers.Default is the coroutine library's own shared pool of threads, sized to the number of cores (at least two). It isn't the common ForkJoinPool, so it doesn't compete with parallel streams. And await() suspends the coroutine instead of helping with other tasks, so the thread goes back to the dispatcher. Blocking calls are just as wrong on Dispatchers.Default as on the common pool; they belong on Dispatchers.IO.

h: ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams · Worked example
x: Speed up the year's tip report without breaking it The report totals the tips per waiter over the year's 400,000 sales. Someone made it parallel. Before reading on, find what breaks. Map<String, Long> tipsByWaiter = new HashMap<>(); sales.parallelStream().forEach(s -> tipsByWaiter.merge(s.waiter(), s.tipCents(), Long::sum)); // one HashMap, many threads val tipsByWaiter = HashMap<String, Long>() sales.parallelStream().forEach { s -> tipsByWaiter.merge(s.waiter, s.tipCents, Long::plus) // one HashMap, many threads } Many threads call merge on one HashMap. That loses updates, and a resize under several writers can corrupt the map. Let the stream build the result instead: with groupingBy, each thread fills its own small map, and the stream merges them at the end. // 1. computation only, and the stream owns the result Map<String, Long> tipsByWaiter = sales.parallelStream() .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Sale::waiter, Collectors.summingLong(Sale::tipCents))); // 1. computation only, and the stream owns the result val tipsByWaiter: Map<String, Long> = sales.parallelStream() .collect(Collectors.groupingBy({ it.waiter }, Collectors.summingLong { it.tipCents })) Next, someone wants each waiter's full name in the report. The names come from the staff service, a slow web service that takes 20 ms per call. Calling it inside the parallel stream would block the common pool 400,000 times. There are only 40 waiters, so look the names up after adding up, once each, on a pool built for waiting. // 2. waiting goes to a pool built for it, once per waiter Map<String, CompletableFuture<String>> names = tipsByWaiter.keySet().stream() .collect(Collectors.toMap(id -> id, id -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> staff.name(id), io))); // 3. wait at the edge: the report job's own thread may block names.forEach((id, name) -> report.line(name.join(), tipsByWaiter.get(id))); // 2. waiting goes to a pool built for it, once per waiter val names = tipsByWaiter.keys.associateWith { id -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ staff.name(id) }, io) } // 3. wait at the edge: the report job's own thread may block names.forEach { (id, name) -> report.line(name.join(), tipsByWaiter.getValue(id)) } Last question: is parallel() worth keeping? Adding up tips is cheap work, and for cheap work over a few hundred thousand elements, the sequential stream often wins. Time both versions on data of the real size, with a few warm-up runs or with JMH, and keep parallel() only if the numbers say so. Remember, too, that a container's CPU limit sets the size of the common pool, as Sizing a pool showed.

h: ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams · Quiz
x: Which compute() body lets the two halves run at the same time? left.fork(); long l = left.join(); return l + right.compute(); return left.compute() + right.compute(); left.fork(); long r = right.compute(); return left.join() + r; long r = right.compute(); left.fork(); return left.join() + r; Only the third one makes the left half stealable and then keeps this thread busy with the right half, while a thief can run the left. The first and the last both wait for one half before the other is available, and the second never forks at all. All four give the right answer, which is why the bug is easy to miss. An 8-core machine runs products.parallelStream().map(stock::level).toList(), and each call to the stock service takes 120 ms. What is the biggest risk? None: parallel streams run on virtual threads The lookups take the common pool's 7 workers, so other parallel streams and CompletableFuture tasks with no executor wait behind them The stream quietly falls back to running sequentially, because the calls block It throws, because blocking isn't allowed in a ForkJoinPool Parallel streams use the common pool's platform workers, which the whole JVM shares, and the pool can't tell that a worker is blocked. Nothing throws and nothing falls back: everything else that needs the common pool just waits. Run the lookups on an executor built for waiting instead. List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(); payments.parallelStream().forEach(p -> ids.add(p.id())); runs over 100,000 payments. What do you get, most of the time? Fewer than 100,000 ids, or an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException All 100,000 ids, in the original order All 100,000 ids, in a scrambled order A ConcurrentModificationException, every time Several threads call add on one ArrayList, which isn't thread-safe. Their writes race on the size and the backing array, so ids get lost, or the index runs past the end of the array. ConcurrentModificationException comes from changing a list while you iterate over it, not from this race. payments.parallelStream().map(Payment::id).toList() is correct and keeps the order. Pick the tool for each job: (1) total the card fees on 20 million payments already in memory; (2) make 300 calls to the stock service. (1) virtual threads; (2) a parallel stream Both in one parallel stream (1) a single-thread executor; (2) supplyAsync without an executor (1) a parallel stream or a RecursiveTask; (2) a pool built for waiting, or virtual threads, combined with CompletableFuture Computation on data in memory splits well and wants about one thread per core, which is what the common pool gives you. Waiting on a web service wants many threads that are cheap to block, and they must not be the common pool's. supplyAsync without an executor would put those calls right back on the common pool. From "CompletableFuture: composing async steps": one part of a program calls supplyAsync(task) with no executor, and another uses parallelStream(). Do they compete for threads? No: CompletableFuture has its own default pool Yes: both use ForkJoinPool.commonPool() (on JDK 25 always, on JDK 21 whenever its parallelism is at least 2) Only when both run on virtual threads No: every parallel stream creates its own pool The default async executor is the common pool, and so is the pool behind parallel streams. Before JDK 25, the one exception was a common pool with parallelism below 2, where CompletableFuture used a new thread per task instead. Either way, a blocking task in one slows down the other.

h: ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams · Key terms
x: ForkJoinPool A pool where each worker has its own deque, and idle workers steal tasks from busy ones. RecursiveTask A fork/join task that returns a value; RecursiveAction returns nothing. Work stealing An idle worker takes a task from the far end of another worker's deque. Deque A double-ended queue: the owner uses one end, thieves the other. Threshold The size below which a task stops splitting and just loops. Common pool The ForkJoinPool the whole JVM shares, behind parallel streams and async steps with no executor. ManagedBlocker A way to tell a ForkJoinPool a worker will block, so it can add a spare thread. In compute(), what is the right order of fork, compute and join? Fork one half, compute the other half on this thread, then join the forked half. Joining first runs the halves one after the other. Where does a ForkJoinPool worker take its own tasks from, and where does a thief steal from? The owner pushes and pops at the top of its deque (newest first). A thief takes from the bottom (oldest, biggest task). Default parallelism of ForkJoinPool.commonPool()? availableProcessors() - 1 (at least 1). Change it with -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism. Which threads run a parallel stream? Common pool workers, plus the thread that started the stream. Why is a blocking call inside a parallel stream a problem for the whole JVM? It holds a common pool worker, and that pool is shared by every parallel stream and every CompletableFuture step with no executor. What does ForkJoinPool.managedBlock do? It tells the pool that a worker is about to block, so the pool can start a spare thread to keep its parallelism up. How big should a fork/join leaf be, by the ForkJoinTask Javadoc's rough rule? More than about 100 and fewer than about 10,000 basic steps of computation. Then measure.

h: ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams · Go deeper
x: The virtual thread scheduler, which the next track covers, is also a ForkJoinPool, a separate one from the common pool. JEP 444 describes it as a work-stealing ForkJoinPool that operates in FIFO mode, first in, first out. FIFO mode exists for tasks that are handed over and never joined, such as events or messages. You get it with the asyncMode argument of the four-argument ForkJoinPool constructor, and each worker then takes its own tasks oldest first instead of newest first. The common pool has a few more settings, all system properties read once when the pool starts: java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism, .threadFactory, .exceptionHandler and .maximumSpares, which caps the spare threads that managedBlock can add. Calling close() or shutdown() on the common pool does nothing, so library code can't switch it off by accident. Why does availableProcessors() - 1 make sense? Because the thread that calls invoke or starts a parallel stream works too. Seven workers plus the caller keep eight cores busy. It also means that a container limited to 2 CPUs gets a common pool of one worker, and before JDK 25 that was enough for CompletableFuture to stop using it (CompletableFuture: composing async steps). Parallel streams don't use RecursiveTask inside. They use CountedCompleter, a ForkJoinTask that counts its pending subtasks and runs a completion action when the count reaches zero, so no thread ever waits in join(). You rarely need to write one yourself, but it's why a parallel stream can split deep trees without piling up joins.

h: Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown · Name tags and lost failures: naming threads, and catching what submit hides
x: A thread's name, its name tag, shows up in log lines, in profilers (tools that show where a program spends its time) and in thread dumps. A thread dump is a snapshot of every thread in a running JVM, the Java Virtual Machine that runs your program, with its name, its state and the line of code it is on. You can take one with jcmd <pid> Thread.print, where <pid> is the number the operating system gave the program. The ready-made pools from Executors name their threads pool-3-thread-7, the seventh thread of the third pool. In a dump of a program with eight pools, that tells you nothing. A thread factory is the object a pool asks for each new thread. Hand the pool one that names its threads: Java ThreadFactory named = Thread.ofPlatform().name("grill-", 0).factory(); // JDK 21+: grill-0, grill-1, ... ExecutorService grill = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, named); Kotlin val named = Thread.ofPlatform().name("grill-", 0).factory() // JDK 21+: grill-0, grill-1, ... val grill = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, named) Before JDK 21 (version 21 of Java's development kit), you write a small ThreadFactory of your own. Now failures. The first lesson of this track showed that execute and submit treat a failing task in opposite ways. In production, that difference decides whether you ever hear about it. FailureDemo, in the Try it below, makes a pool with one thread. The factory names it grill-0 and gives it an UncaughtExceptionHandler, the method the JVM calls when an exception escapes a thread. This one prints a line. Then it sends one failing task through each method. Predict what each half prints: 1. execute() a task that throws handler: grill-0 died of java.lang.IllegalStateException: the grill went out the next task runs on grill-1 2. submit() a task that throws (nothing printed) the next task runs on grill-1 only get() shows it: java.lang.IllegalStateException: a negative price With execute, the exception escaped the task. The worker grill-0 died, the handler ran, and the pool started grill-1 in its place. With submit, the FutureTask, the wrapper that submit puts around a task, caught the exception and kept it. Nothing printed, and grill-1 carried on. The grill going out at least made some noise. The negative price would have stayed quiet forever if the demo hadn't called get(). In fire-and-forget code, which hands over a task and never looks at its result, nobody does. The default handler prints a stack trace to System.err, outside your logs and with no request id. So a handler on the thread factory covers only half the cases, and that half badly. To cover both, catch failures in one place that every task passes through. submit, invokeAll and CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(task, pool) all end up calling execute. So a ThreadPoolExecutor subclass that overrides execute and wraps each task sees all of them. The wrapper runs the task inside a try. A task from execute throws, and the catch reports it. A task from submit doesn't throw: it's a FutureTask, and after it runs, state() says FAILED and exceptionNow() (both JDK 19) hands over the original exception. Report it with the request id, and don't rethrow. Rethrowing only kills the worker and prints the same stack trace a second time. The lab builds exactly that pool, ProductionPool. submit hides failures and execute kills workers. Report both from one wrapper. That wrapper reports a request id, which raises a fair question: whose request id does a pool thread have? Find out who hears about a failure Read FailureDemo. Its threads are named grill-N and have an UncaughtExceptionHandler. Before you run it, predict for each case: does the handler print, and which thread runs the next task? FailureDemo.java package workbench.executors.l09; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadFactory; /** Named threads with an UncaughtExceptionHandler. Which failures does the handler see? */ public class FailureDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { ThreadFactory factory = Thread.ofPlatform() .name("grill-", 0) // grill-0, grill-1, ... .uncaughtExceptionHandler((t, e) -> System.out.println(" handler: " + t.getName() + " died of " + e)) .factory(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, factory)) { System.out.println("1. execute() a task that throws"); pool.execute(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("the grill went out"); }); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println(" the next task runs on " + pool.submit(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()).get()); System.out.println("2. submit() a task that throws"); Future<?> f = pool.submit(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("a negative price"); }); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println(" (nothing printed) the next task runs on " + pool.submit(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()).get()); try { f.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { System.out.println(" only get() shows it: " + e.getCause()); } } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l09.FailureDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l09/FailureDemo.java FailureDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** Named threads with an UncaughtExceptionHandler. Which failures does the handler see? */ fun main() { val factory = Thread.ofPlatform() .name("grill-", 0) // grill-0, grill-1, ... .uncaughtExceptionHandler { t, e -> println(" handler: ${t.name} died of $e") } .factory() Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, factory).use { pool -> println("1. execute() a task that throws") pool.execute { throw IllegalStateException("the grill went out") } Thread.sleep(200) println(" the next task runs on " + pool.submit<String> { Thread.currentThread().name }.get()) println("2. submit() a task that throws") val f = pool.submit<Unit> { throw IllegalStateException("a negative price") } Thread.sleep(200) println(" (nothing printed) the next task runs on " + pool.submit<String> { Thread.currentThread().name }.get()) try { f.get() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { println(" only get() shows it: ${e.cause}") } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l09.FailureDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l09/FailureDemo.kt For execute, the handler prints grill-0 died of ... the grill went out, and the next task runs on grill-1: the pool replaced the dead worker. For submit, nothing prints, the next task still runs on grill-1, and the exception appears only when get() is called. Thread.Builder (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown · The note pinned to the wrong jacket: carrying request context to the worker
x: A request id is a short label, such as req-42, that a program gives each request it handles and prints on every log line about it. Programs often keep it in a ThreadLocal: a variable that has a separate value for each thread, as Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal showed. Any code on that thread can read it without passing it around. The trouble starts at the hand-off. Picture a note about table 4, "nut allergy", pinned to the jacket of the waiter who took the order instead of clipped to the order itself. The order goes to the grill, and the note stays with the waiter. The grill cook sees no note at all. Or he still has an old note pinned to his own jacket, from the last order he cooked. ContextDemo acts that out with a pool of one thread. main sets the request id to req-42, then submits three tasks. Predict all three lines: 1. plain task sees: null 2. wrapped task sees: req-42 3. next task sees: req-7 (left over from an earlier task) Line 1 is the missing note: the pool's thread never saw req-42. Line 3 is the old note. An earlier task set req-7 on the worker and never removed it, and the next caller had no request id at all. Every log line from that task now blames request 7, which finished long ago and did nothing wrong. Line 2 is the fix, in three steps. Capture the value on the submitting thread, install it on the worker before the task runs, and put the worker's old value back afterwards: Java static Runnable withRequestId(Runnable task) { String captured = RequestContext.get(); // 1. on the submitting thread return () -> { String previous = RequestContext.get(); RequestContext.set(captured); // 2. on the worker try { task.run(); } finally { if (previous == null) RequestContext.clear(); else RequestContext.set(previous); // 3. never leak } }; } Kotlin fun withRequestId(task: Runnable): Runnable { val captured = RequestContext.get() // 1. on the submitting thread return Runnable { val previous = RequestContext.get() RequestContext.set(captured) // 2. on the worker try { task.run() } finally { if (previous == null) RequestContext.clear() else RequestContext.set(previous) // 3. never leak } } } In the kitchen, that is copying the note onto the order ticket, pinning it on whichever cook cooks the dish, and taking it off when the dish leaves. The capture must happen in the method that runs on the submitting thread, which is why it sits outside the lambda. Read the ThreadLocal inside the lambda instead, and you read the worker's value, which is the bug you set out to fix. The finally matters just as much. Pool threads are reused, so whatever a task leaves behind becomes the next task's context. Here the picture breaks. A paper note falls off sooner or later. A ThreadLocal value stays on its thread until some code removes it. Don't make every caller remember: wrap once, in the executor everyone uses, as the lab's ProductionPool does. Virtual threads, the subject of the next track, don't change any of this: a new thread starts with empty ThreadLocals, except inheritable ones, which copy their value from the thread that starts them. Scoped values, final in JDK 25 (JEP 506, the design document behind them), are the newer tool for request context, and that track covers them too. A ThreadLocal belongs to a thread, not to a task. Capture it at the hand-off, and clean up after. Names, failures and context make one task easy to trace. The next question is about all of them at once: is the pool keeping up? Lose a request id, then leak one Read ContextDemo. The main thread sets req-42 and submits three tasks to a pool with one thread. Predict all three lines before you run it. For line 3, find the task that caused it. ContextDemo.java package workbench.executors.l09; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** A request id in a ThreadLocal, handed to a pool three ways. */ public class ContextDemo { static final ThreadLocal<String> REQUEST_ID = new ThreadLocal<>(); // capture on the submitting thread, install on the worker, always clean up static Runnable withContext(Runnable task) { String captured = REQUEST_ID.get(); return () -> { String previous = REQUEST_ID.get(); REQUEST_ID.set(captured); try { task.run(); } finally { if (previous == null) REQUEST_ID.remove(); else REQUEST_ID.set(previous); } }; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1)) { REQUEST_ID.set("req-42"); pool.submit(() -> System.out.println("1. plain task sees: " + REQUEST_ID.get())).get(); pool.submit(withContext(() -> System.out.println("2. wrapped task sees: " + REQUEST_ID.get()))).get(); // a task that sets the ThreadLocal itself and forgets to remove it pool.submit(() -> REQUEST_ID.set("req-7")).get(); REQUEST_ID.remove(); // the next caller has no request pool.submit(() -> System.out.println("3. next task sees: " + REQUEST_ID.get() + " (left over from an earlier task)")).get(); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l09.ContextDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l09/ContextDemo.java ContextDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l09 import java.util.concurrent.Executors private val requestId = ThreadLocal<String?>() // capture on the submitting thread, install on the worker, always clean up private fun withContext(task: () -> Unit): Runnable { val captured = requestId.get() return Runnable { val previous = requestId.get() requestId.set(captured) try { task() } finally { if (previous == null) requestId.remove() else requestId.set(previous) } } } /** A request id in a ThreadLocal, handed to a pool three ways. */ fun main() { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1).use { pool -> requestId.set("req-42") pool.submit { println("1. plain task sees: ${requestId.get()}") }.get() pool.submit(withContext { println("2. wrapped task sees: ${requestId.get()}") }).get() // a task that sets the ThreadLocal itself and forgets to remove it pool.submit { requestId.set("req-7") }.get() requestId.remove() // the next caller has no request pool.submit { println("3. next task sees: ${requestId.get()} (left over from an earlier task)") }.get() } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l09.ContextDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l09/ContextDemo.kt Line 1 prints null: the plain task runs on a pool thread that never saw req-42. Line 2 prints req-42, because the wrapper captured it on main. Line 3 prints req-7, left over from the earlier task that set the ThreadLocal and never removed it, although the new caller had no request at all.

h: Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown · The board by the pass: four numbers that show a pool falling behind
x: A stuck Saturday night: name tags on the cooks, a note left on the waiter's jacket, the board by the pass (2 active, 4 queued, 4 rejected), cooks waiting for tickets behind them, and closing the kitchen in order A pool is a queue in front of a few threads, and it's often the first place a slow service shows up. A good kitchen keeps a board by the pass, and four numbers on a pool's board tell you most of what you need. The queue size, getQueue().size(), is the number of tickets on the rail. A queue that keeps growing means tasks arrive faster than they finish. Little's law, from Sizing a pool (tasks inside = arrival rate x time each one stays), says each task's wait grows with it. The active count, getActiveCount(), compared with the maximum, says how many cooks are busy. A pool stuck at its maximum for minutes has no room left, and it's usually waiting on something further along the path, not working hard. The rejections are the tasks the pool turned away. ThreadPoolExecutor doesn't count them for you. Wrap the RejectedExecutionHandler, the code a pool calls when it refuses a task (Inside ThreadPoolExecutor), in one that adds to a counter and then throws. The time in queue is how long each task waited for a thread. The caller feels that wait, and the task never measures it. Record the time when a task is submitted, in the same wrapper that carries the context, and compare it when the task starts. MetricsDemo sends a burst of 10 tasks of 300 ms each to a pool of 2 threads, named orders-, with a queue of 4 and a counting handler. Then it prints the board every 200 ms. Predict the first row before you read it: ms threads active queued done rejected 0 2 2 4 0 4 244 2 2 4 0 4 446 2 2 2 2 4 647 2 2 0 4 4 849 2 2 0 4 4 1050 2 0 0 6 4 Two tasks run, four wait in the queue, and four are rejected at once, since 2 + 4 = 6 is all the pool can hold. After that, every 300 ms two more finish. The queue goes 4, 2, 0, done climbs 0, 2, 4, 6, and active drops to 0 at about 900 ms. The rejected count stays at 4, and those four callers heard the bad news at once instead of waiting for it. Picture the same burst on newFixedThreadPool(2), whose queue has no limit. The board would show rejected 0 and a queue of 8. Every task is accepted, and the last two wait 1.2 seconds before a thread even picks them up. Only the time in queue would show the trouble. That's why it belongs on the board. The getters are approximate, as their Javadoc, the official documentation, says, because the threads change the numbers while you read them. That's fine for a dashboard and wrong for program logic. If your program already sends numbers to a dashboard, a metrics library such as Micrometer can read most of these from a pool for you. Of the four, time in queue and rejections are what your customers feel. A pool with an empty queue and no rejections is healthy, however busy its threads look. Watch the queue, not just the threads. Count every rejection. Now picture a board where every number has frozen: all threads active, the queue full and not moving, nothing done, and the CPU idle. Read a pool's board MetricsDemo sends 10 tasks of 300 ms to a pool with 2 threads and a queue of 4. Predict how many are rejected, and when the queue empties. Run it, and read the table row by row. MetricsDemo.java package workbench.executors.l09; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** 10 tasks of 300 ms hit a pool of 2 threads with a queue of 4. Watch the numbers a dashboard would show. */ public class MetricsDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { LongAdder rejected = new LongAdder(); ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 2, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(4), Thread.ofPlatform().name("orders-", 0).factory(), (task, executor) -> { rejected.increment(); // count it, then fail like AbortPolicy throw new RejectedExecutionException("orders pool full"); }); for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { try { pool.execute(() -> sleep(300)); } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { // the waiter would say "come back later" here } } System.out.println(" ms threads active queued done rejected"); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) { System.out.printf("%4d %7d %6d %6d %4d %8d%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, pool.getPoolSize(), pool.getActiveCount(), pool.getQueue().size(), pool.getCompletedTaskCount(), rejected.sum()); sleep(200); } pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l09.MetricsDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l09/MetricsDemo.java MetricsDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder /** 10 tasks of 300 ms hit a pool of 2 threads with a queue of 4. Watch the numbers a dashboard would show. */ fun main() { val rejected = LongAdder() val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 2, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(4), Thread.ofPlatform().name("orders-", 0).factory()) { _, _ -> rejected.increment() // count it, then fail like AbortPolicy throw RejectedExecutionException("orders pool full") } repeat(10) { try { pool.execute { Thread.sleep(300) } } catch (e: RejectedExecutionException) { // the waiter would say "come back later" here } } println(" ms threads active queued done rejected") val t0 = System.nanoTime() repeat(6) { println("%4d %7d %6d %6d %4d %8d".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, pool.poolSize, pool.activeCount, pool.queue.size, pool.completedTaskCount, rejected.sum())) Thread.sleep(200) } pool.shutdown() pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l09.MetricsDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l09/MetricsDemo.kt Two tasks run, four wait in the queue, and four are rejected right away (2 + 4 = 6 accepted). Every 300 ms two more finish: the queue goes 4, 2, 0 while done climbs 0, 2, 4, 6, and active drops to 0 after about 900 ms. The rejected count stays at 4. h: Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown · Cooks waiting for tickets behind them: pool-induced deadlock
x: At closing time, a job prints the day's bill for every table. For each table, a task fetches the table's order lines from the order book, a database, and then renders the bill. Someone split the fetch into a task of its own, on the same pool: Java pool.submit(() -> { Future<List<String>> lines = pool.submit(() -> orders.lines(table)); // a task inside a task return render(table, lines.get()); // waits for it }); Kotlin pool.submit<String> { val lines = pool.submit<List<String>> { orders.lines(table) } // a task inside a task render(table, lines.get()) // waits for it } With 20 threads and the 5 tables of a test, it's fine. On a busy Saturday there are 400 tables. Let's trace it with those numbers. The first 20 bill tasks take all 20 threads. Each one submits its fetch, and the 20 fetches join the back of the queue, behind 380 waiting bill tasks. Each bill task then waits in get() for its fetch. Every thread now waits for a task that can only run on a free thread, and no thread will ever be free. In the kitchen, every cook has taken a bill ticket, pinned a "fetch the orders" ticket at the back of the rail, and stands waiting for it. No cook is left to take the fetch tickets. DeadlockDemo builds the smallest case: two bill tasks on a pool of two threads named bills-, where each fetch takes microseconds: after 300 ms: active=2, queued=2, completed=0 no bill after 2 s: both threads wait for fetches that can never start Both threads are active, the two fetches are queued, and nothing has completed. Speed isn't the problem. The demo gives up after 2 seconds, but the pool would wait forever. This is pool-induced deadlock, which Java Concurrency in Practice calls thread starvation deadlock: every thread in a bounded pool, one with a fixed number of threads, waits for a task that is queued in that same pool. Unlike the lock deadlock of Deadlock, livelock and starvation, the CPU drops to zero, nothing throws, and a thread dump has no "deadlock found" line, because no lock is involved: every thread is simply WAITING in FutureTask.get. The figure shows the moment. Here are three fixes, in the order I'd try them: Don't block inside the pool. Compose: supplyAsync(() -> orders.lines(t), pool).thenApply(lines -> render(t, lines)). The render step runs as a callback, code that runs when the fetch completes, so no thread waits. Only the caller joins at the end. The demo's fixed mode does this and prints both bills at once, on the same two threads. Don't split what doesn't need splitting. If the bill task only waits for the fetch, do the fetch inline, in the same task. Give each stage its own pool. Bill tasks may wait for a separate fetch pool, as long as fetch tasks never wait for the bill pool. That's a bulkhead from Sizing a pool, a separate limit for each stage. A cached pool, with no limit on threads, hides the hang by starting a thread for every waiting task, which moves the problem to memory and to the database. Calling join() inside a CompletableFuture stage is the same bug, which is why CompletableFuture: composing async steps warned against it. No task may wait for another task in its own bounded pool. Compose, inline, or use a second pool. Our pools can now run well all day. At night, they have to stop. Hang a pool on purpose Run DeadlockDemo: two bill tasks on a pool of two threads, each waiting for a fast fetch on the same pool. Read the active and queued counts. Run it with -Pargs=fixed, which composes the fetch and the render with CompletableFuture. Predict how long it takes. DeadlockDemo.java package workbench.executors.l09; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; /** Two bill tasks on a 2-thread pool, each waiting for a fetch on the same pool. Pass "fixed" to compose instead. */ public class DeadlockDemo { static List<String> fetchLines(String table) { return List.of(table + "-1", table + "-2"); // fast: the problem isn't speed } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean fixed = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("fixed"); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("bills-", 0).factory()); try { if (fixed) { List<CompletableFuture<String>> bills = List.of("t1", "t2").stream() .map(t -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchLines(t), pool) .thenApply(lines -> t + ": " + lines.size() + " lines")) // nobody waits inside the pool .toList(); bills.forEach(b -> System.out.println(b.join())); return; } List<Future<String>> bills = List.of("t1", "t2").stream() .map(t -> pool.submit(() -> { Future<List<String>> lines = pool.submit(() -> fetchLines(t)); // queued behind us return t + ": " + lines.get().size() + " lines"; // waits for it })) .toList(); Thread.sleep(300); ThreadPoolExecutor tpe = (ThreadPoolExecutor) pool; System.out.printf("after 300 ms: active=%d, queued=%d, completed=%d%n", tpe.getActiveCount(), tpe.getQueue().size(), tpe.getCompletedTaskCount()); try { System.out.println(bills.get(0).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)); } catch (TimeoutException e) { System.out.println("no bill after 2 s: both threads wait for fetches that can never start"); } } finally { pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupts the stuck get() calls } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l09.DeadlockDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l09/DeadlockDemo.java DeadlockDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l09 import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException private fun fetchLines(table: String) = listOf("$table-1", "$table-2") // fast: the problem isn't speed /** Two bill tasks on a 2-thread pool, each waiting for a fetch on the same pool. Pass "fixed" to compose instead. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val fixed = args.firstOrNull() == "fixed" val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("bills-", 0).factory()) try { if (fixed) { val bills = listOf("t1", "t2").map { t -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ fetchLines(t) }, pool) .thenApply { lines -> "$t: ${lines.size} lines" } // nobody waits inside the pool } bills.forEach { println(it.join()) } return } val bills = listOf("t1", "t2").map { t -> pool.submit<String> { val lines = pool.submit<List<String>> { fetchLines(t) } // queued behind us "$t: ${lines.get().size} lines" // waits for it } } Thread.sleep(300) val tpe = pool as ThreadPoolExecutor println("after 300 ms: active=${tpe.activeCount}, queued=${tpe.queue.size}, completed=${tpe.completedTaskCount}") try { println(bills[0].get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) } catch (e: TimeoutException) { println("no bill after 2 s: both threads wait for fetches that can never start") } } finally { pool.shutdownNow() // interrupts the stuck get() calls } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l09.DeadlockDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l09/DeadlockDemo.kt The default run shows active=2, queued=2, completed=0 after 300 ms, then gives up after 2 s with no bill, although each fetch takes microseconds. The fixed run prints both bills at once, on the same two threads. Both threads wait for fetches that sit in the queue behind them. The fetches need a free thread, and none will ever be free.

h: Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown · Closing the kitchen at night: shutting pools down in order, within one deadline
x: A good restaurant closes in a fixed order. First someone locks the front door to new guests. Then the kitchen finishes the orders it has, starting with the stations that feed the others. Only then do the lights go off, and all of it must fit before a deadline. A program stops the same way. As the first lesson of this track described, the system that runs a service usually sends a polite signal first. After a grace period, 30 seconds by a common default, it stops the program by force. Everything in flight has to finish inside that window, or be written down as lost. Here is a stop method for a program with two pools. The kitchen pool's tasks cook dishes, and each finished dish is handed to the billing pool, which adds it to the table's bill: Java void stop() throws InterruptedException { intake.stop(); // 1. no new orders come in long deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(20); // inside the 30 s grace period for (ExecutorService pool : List.of(kitchenPool, billingPool)) { // 2. upstream first: kitchen feeds billing pool.shutdown(); long left = Math.max(0, deadline - System.nanoTime()); if (!pool.awaitTermination(left, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) { List<Runnable> neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow(); // 3. interrupt what is still running log.warn("{} tasks never started", neverStarted.size()); // 4. say what was lost } } } Kotlin fun stop() { intake.stop() // 1. no new orders come in val deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(20) // inside the 30 s grace period for (pool in listOf(kitchenPool, billingPool)) { // 2. upstream first: kitchen feeds billing pool.shutdown() val left = maxOf(0L, deadline - System.nanoTime()) if (!pool.awaitTermination(left, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) { val neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow() // 3. interrupt what is still running log.warn("{} tasks never started", neverStarted.size) // 4. say what was lost } } } First we stop intake. In a web service, that means no longer accepting requests. Otherwise new work keeps arriving at pools that are trying to drain. Then we shut the pools down upstream first: the pool that hands work to the other one goes first. Get it backwards, and shut down billingPool first. The dishes still cooking in kitchenPool then get a RejectedExecutionException when they try to add themselves to the bill. They were cooked and served and never billed, a free dinner nobody planned. The whole sequence gets one deadline, shorter than the grace period, shared between the pools. When a pool misses it, shutdownNow() interrupts what is still running and returns the tasks that never started. Log them, with request ids if your wrapper keeps them, so somebody can run them again. If your program runs inside a framework, it usually offers a hook that runs at shutdown, such as a method marked @PreDestroy, an annotation that means "run me before the program stops". Put this code there. Never leave a pool for the garbage collector, the JVM's memory cleaner, to clean up: its threads keep it alive. Check yourself: why one shared 20-second deadline, instead of 20 seconds for each pool? (The waits add up. Two pools at 20 seconds each can take 40, and the program is stopped by force at 30, before the log.warn line can say what was lost.) Stop intake first, then drain pools upstream first, all within one deadline. Look back over the whole track for its limit. Every pool we sized, named and drained holds one platform thread, the ordinary kind that wraps a thread of the operating system, for each task that waits, and platform threads are costly. A pool of 200 threads stops at 200 waiting requests, however idle the CPU is.

MDCContext() and asContextElement are thread context elements: the dispatcher installs the value each time the coroutine resumes on a thread, and restores the thread's old value when it suspends. It passes every test, then hangs on the busiest day with the CPU near zero. What happened? The queries got slow, so the reports need more time Four report tasks hold all four threads, and each waits for queries queued behind other reports, so nothing can ever finish Two report tasks locked each other's monitors The queue overflowed, and the queries were rejected This is pool-induced deadlock. The awaited tasks need a free thread, and all the threads are busy waiting for them. Slowness wouldn't keep the CPU at zero forever, no monitors are involved, and a fixed pool's queue has no limit, so nothing is rejected. A request thread puts req-42 in a ThreadLocal (such as a logging library's MDC) and submits a task to a fixed pool. The task logs a line. With no context propagation in place, which request id is on that line? req-42, because pool threads inherit the submitter's ThreadLocals None, every time, because pool threads clear their ThreadLocals between tasks Whatever that pool thread last had: often none, sometimes a stale id from an earlier task The logging call throws, because a ThreadLocal isn't thread-safe The value lives on the worker thread. That thread was created long ago and is reused, so it holds nothing, or whatever an earlier task put there and never cleaned up. Nothing clears it between tasks unless your wrapper does. The pool size is fixed in a fixed pool, the completed count only ever rises, and the largest pool size is history. When the queue is full, rejections start. The program's intake hands orders to kitchenPool, whose tasks submit to billingPool. The program is told to stop. In what order do you shut down? Stop intake, shut down kitchenPool and wait for it, then shut down billingPool and wait for it Shut down billingPool, then kitchenPool, then stop intake Call shutdownNow() on both pools at once, to be quick Stop intake, then shut down billingPool first, because it handles the money Upstream first. Shutting it down first makes those submissions fail with RejectedExecutionException, and shutdownNow on both interrupts work that could have finished. h: Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown · Key terms
x: Thread factory The object a pool asks for new threads; it sets their names, daemon flag and exception handler. Thread dump A snapshot of every thread in a running JVM: its name, its state and the code it is running. UncaughtExceptionHandler Code that runs when an exception escapes a thread's run method. ThreadLocal A variable with a separate value for each thread. MDC Mapped Diagnostic Context: a per-thread map of values, such as a request id, that SLF4J adds to log lines. Context propagation Copying thread-local state such as a request id from the submitting thread to the worker. Pool-induced deadlock Every thread in a pool waits for a task that is queued in that same pool. Also called thread starvation deadlock. Graceful shutdown Stopping intake, letting work in progress finish within a deadline, and recording what didn't. How do you name pool threads on JDK 21+? Pass Thread.ofPlatform().name("grill-", 0).factory() to the executor. The threads are named grill-0, grill-1, ... Which pool failures reach an UncaughtExceptionHandler? Only tasks run with execute(). With submit() the exception is stored in the Future, and nothing is printed. Why does a ThreadLocal value, such as a request id, disappear when you hand a task to a pool? The value belongs to the submitting thread, and the task runs on another thread. Capture it at submission and install it in the worker. Why must a context wrapper restore the worker's value in finally? Pool threads are reused. Whatever one task leaves behind becomes the next task's context. What is pool-induced deadlock? Tasks in a bounded pool block waiting for other tasks queued in the same pool. Every thread waits, and the awaited tasks never start. Name two fixes for pool-induced deadlock. Compose instead of blocking (supplyAsync(...).thenApply(...)), or give each stage its own pool, so waits never point back into the same pool. In what order do you shut down chained pools? Stop intake, then shut down the upstream pool and wait, then the downstream one, all within one deadline.

h: Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown · Go deeper
x: Why is the JVM's deadlock detector silent? jcmd <pid> Thread.print (and ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads) look for cycles of threads that each hold a lock another one needs: monitors from synchronized, and ownable synchronizers such as ReentrantLock. A thread waiting in Future.get() parks on the future, which has no owner, so there is no cycle to find. Names and stack traces are your only tools, which is one more reason to name threads. The ThreadPoolExecutor Javadoc shows a second way to catch failures: override the afterExecute hook, which runs on the worker after each task: Java @Override protected void afterExecute(Runnable r, Throwable t) { super.afterExecute(r, t); if (t == null && r instanceof Future<?> f && f.isDone()) { try { f.get(); } catch (CancellationException e) { t = e; } catch (ExecutionException e) { t = e.getCause(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } if (t != null) log.error("task failed on {}", Thread.currentThread().getName(), t); } Kotlin override fun afterExecute(r: Runnable, t: Throwable?) { super.afterExecute(r, t) var failure = t if (failure == null && r is Future<*> && r.isDone) { try { r.get() } catch (e: CancellationException) { failure = e } catch (e: ExecutionException) { failure = e.cause } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } } if (failure != null) log.error("task failed on {}", Thread.currentThread().name, failure) } It works, with two limits. It can't stop an execute failure from killing the worker, because the exception is rethrown after the hook runs. And it doesn't know the submitter's request id unless a wrapper stored it. That's why the lab wraps execute. Its sister hook, beforeExecute(Thread, Runnable), is the natural place to measure time in queue, and terminated() runs once, when the pool has fully stopped.

h: Virtual threads
x: Project Loom from the inside: carriers, pinning, structured concurrency and scoped values. This track follows one restaurant through six lessons. It starts with a personal waiter for every table, who spends most of the evening standing at the kitchen door. Then four waiters learn to carry order slips and clip a waiting slip to a board by the door. After that come 20 tokens on a hook by the grill, a hot pan a waiter can't put down, a head waiter who calls his helpers back, and a note pinned to the order. The last lesson moves an old restaurant over to slips without losing the limit its fixed team gave for free. Underneath runs one program, a shop's checkout of 200 ms: 40 ms at the stock service, 120 ms waiting for the bank, 35 ms in the database and 5 ms of real work. By the end you can explain what a virtual thread is and what happens when it waits, run blocking code with one virtual thread per task, keep a database safe with one shared Semaphore, and find and fix the traps: pinning, ThreadLocal caches and work that only computes. You can also move a pool-based service to virtual threads and measure that it worked. On the way you meet two related features: structured concurrency, still a preview, and scoped values, final in JDK 25. You need the basics from the first track (starting, joining and interrupting threads, locks and semaphores) and from the executors track (ExecutorService, Future, and sizing a pool with Little's law). Install JDK 25, the current long-term-support release. JDK 24 removed most pinning, and the advice changes with it, so the lessons always say which JDK a fact applies to. The labs live in labs/vthreads, one package per lesson (workbench.vthreads.l01 to l06). They compile for JDK 21 and use only final JDK 21 APIs, so they run on 21 and on 25. Lessons 1 to 5 have Java labs, and lesson 6 is in Kotlin. Run ./gradlew :vthreads:test --tests 'workbench.vthreads.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, and use solutionTest to check the reference answers. The Try-it demos run with ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=..., and lesson 5's preview demos live in labs/vthreads/preview/ and run outside Gradle on JDK 25. A platform thread is an operating system thread, so a server gets thousands, not millions. Little's law (in flight = rate × time) says how many a waiting service needs: the personal waiter at the kitchen door. A virtual thread is a Thread that unmounts from its carrier when it waits. Its stack waits on the heap, like a slip on the board, and a few carriers (one per core) run all of them. Virtual threads give scale, not speed: one request is no faster, and work that only computes gains nothing, because there is no time slicing. Use one new virtual thread per task, usually through newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() in try-with-resources. Never pool them. Limit a scarce resource with one shared Semaphore, held only around its calls and sized from what the resource allows: the tokens at the grill. On JDK 21 to 23, blocking inside synchronized pins the carrier, the hot pan. JDK 24 fixed it; on JDK 25 static initializers and native frames still pin. Find pins with JFR's jdk.VirtualThreadPinned. A ThreadLocal cache becomes one object per task, a new pen for every order. Share immutable objects, and move a request's details to arguments or scoped values (final in JDK 25). Structured concurrency ties subtasks to a block, cancels the others on the first failure and waits for all of them, like a head waiter. StructuredTaskScope is a preview until JDK 28. Moving a service means writing down the limits the old pool gave you, keeping connection pools small, giving every wait a deadline, and measuring queues, not thread counts.

h: Virtual threads: track quiz
x: A shop's checkout receives 1,500 requests a second, and each one spends 200 ms, mostly waiting for the bank. With one thread per request, about how many threads are busy at once? About 8 About 300 About 1,500 About 7,500 Little's law: in flight = 1,500/s × 0.2 s = 300. With thread-per-request, that's also the number of threads. 7,500 multiplies by 5 instead of 0.2, and 1,500 forgets the time. Resizing photos and adding numbers only compute, so at most one virtual thread per core works at once, the same as a pool. A single job that runs in order has nothing to overlap. A virtual thread prints Thread.currentThread() before and after Thread.sleep(10). What can differ between the two lines? The thread id, because a new virtual thread carries on with the work Nothing can differ: a virtual thread stays on one carrier for life The carrier worker shown after the @; the virtual thread itself is the same The second print never happens, because sleep throws on a virtual thread currentThread() always returns the virtual thread, so its id stays the same. The sleep unmounts it, and when it wakes, any free carrier can mount it, so the ForkJoinPool-1-worker-N part of toString() can change. 10,000 virtual threads must call the bank's web service, which allows 50 calls at once from the shop. A pool of virtual threads caps the whole request and is the trap from lesson 3. A semaphore per request gives each request its own 50 permits, which limits nothing. On JDK 25, which of these still pins a virtual thread to its carrier? What do you use? -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full, and check that nothing is printed jstack <pid>, looking for blocked carriers A JFR recording with jdk.VirtualThreadPinned, printed with jfr print Thread.getAllStackTraces() from a debug page The JFR event is on by default with a 20 ms threshold and records the stack. -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads was removed in JDK 24, so its silence proves nothing. jstack and getAllStackTraces() don't show parked virtual threads. Which statement about JDK 25 is true? Scoped values are final; StructuredTaskScope is still a preview API Both scoped values and StructuredTaskScope are final StructuredTaskScope is final; scoped values are still a preview Both are still previews and need --enable-preview JEP 506 made scoped values final in JDK 25. Structured concurrency stays a preview through JDK 25, 26 and 27, and JEP 543 makes it final in JDK 28. Inside ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, "ann").run(...), code starts Thread.ofVirtual().start(task). Only subtasks forked in a StructuredTaskScope, which must end before the scope does, see the parent's scoped values. A hand-built fail-fast scope cancels a slow sibling with future.cancel(true) and then calls close() on its newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). On JDK 21, what is the problem? cancel(true) doesn't interrupt virtual threads close() can return while the cancelled task is still running its finally block close() waits forever, because a cancelled task never finishes Nothing: this is exactly how StructuredTaskScope works inside cancel(true) interrupts the thread but marks the future done at once, and the JDK 21 executor counts the task as finished when its future is done. So close() stops waiting while the cleanup still runs. shutdownNow() interrupts without completing the futures. A service ran on a fixed pool of 20 threads with a 20-connection database pool. After moving to one virtual thread per request, the connection pool times out at every busy hour. What is the right fix? Raise the connection pool to 2,000 connections Go back to the fixed pool of 20 threads for all request handling Add a shared Semaphore(20) around the database calls only, with a tryAcquire deadline Raise the pool's connection timeout to several minutes The fixed pool was an unwritten limit on the database. The semaphore puts it back where it belongs, without capping the calls that never needed it, and gives you a queue you can see and a deadline you choose. A huge pool overloads the database, and a long timeout turns overload into very slow requests.

h: The thread-per-request wall · One checkout, one thread: why 200 threads stop at 1,000 a second

Every table keeps its own waiter: a 200 ms checkout waits 195 ms but holds its thread, so 200 threads stop at 1,000 a second on a bored machine, and a slow bank cuts that to 156 Let's give the restaurant a program. A small shop sells online, and its website handles checkouts. To check out one basket, the program reads the request and asks the stock service whether the items are in the warehouse. Then it asks the bank to take the payment, saves the order in the shop's database and writes the reply. A service here is a program on another computer that answers questions over the network. The bank's service is our old friend, the slow web service from Threads from zero, still taking 120 ms. A database is the program that stores the shop's data, such as its orders. Now add up one checkout. Reading the request takes 2 ms, the stock service 40 ms, the bank 120 ms, the database 35 ms and the reply 3 ms. That's 200 ms, and only 5 ms of it runs on the CPU, the processor. The other 195 ms is waiting. The figure below shows the shape. The program gives each checkout one thread from a pool of 200. A pool is a fixed team of threads that take tasks from a queue, a line of waiting tasks, like the kitchen in the executors track. The thread stays with its checkout from the first line to the reply. That style is called thread-per-request, and it's the restaurant's personal waiter. Each of those threads is a platform thread, the kind Java has always had. A platform thread is a Java thread backed by one thread of the operating system, the program that runs every other program and shares out the processor. We'll see what that costs in a moment. While the thread waits for the bank, it is blocked: it can't go on until the answer arrives. A blocked thread does no work, but no other checkout can use it. That one fact sets the wall. One thread finishes a checkout every 0.2 s, so 5 a second. 200 threads finish 1,000 a second, and not one more. At 800 checkouts a second, 160 threads are busy and 40 sit idle. Then traffic rises to 1,500 a second. The idle threads fill at once, and the other 500 checkouts each second wait in the pool's queue. After 10 seconds, 5,000 are waiting, and a new checkout waits 5 seconds before a thread even picks it up. And the processor? Each thread spends one fortieth of its time on the CPU, so at any moment only about 5 of the 200 threads are running code. A server with 16 cores, the parts of the processor that each run one thread at a time, has 11 cores with nothing to do. Anyone watching the server sees a slow shop on a bored machine. Let's watch the wall in a smaller model. WallDemo, in the Try it below, runs 2,000 fake checkouts that each just call Thread.sleep for 100 ms, standing in for the waits. First it runs them on a pool of 100 threads. Predict before you read on: 100 threads at 0.1 s each finish 1,000 a second, so 2,000 checkouts should take about 2 seconds. On this 4-core machine, while other heavy programs were running, the first line said: fixed pool of 100 2,000 requests in 2,229 ms = 897 requests/s That's the prediction, plus a little start-up time. The demo prints a second line too, and we'll come back to it in the last section. The wall comes from two numbers: how many threads there are, and how long each request holds one. That arithmetic has a name, and it works for much more than threads. Predict the wall, then hit it Read WallDemo. It runs 2,000 fake checkouts that each sleep for 100 ms, first on a fixed pool of 100 threads. Write down how long you expect the pool to take. Run it with the command below. Look only at the first line for now. Predict again for a pool of 200, then run with -Pargs='200 2000 100'. Args: pool size, number of requests, latency in ms. Default: 100 2000 100. */ public class WallDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { int poolSize = args.length > 0 ?
