The pool's speed is its thread count divided by the time each checkout holds a thread. The thread is busy for 5 ms and blocked for 195 ms, but it belongs to this one checkout for all 200 ms.

h: The thread-per-request wall · Little's law: how many checkouts are inside at once
x: Sizing a pool met a law from ticket windows. It's worth meeting again, because this whole track leans on it. Little's law says that in any stable system, one where on average as many leave as arrive: L = λ × W inside at once = arrival rate × time each one spends inside L is how many are inside at once. λ (the Greek letter lambda) is the arrival rate, how many arrive each second. W is how long each one stays, from arriving to leaving. For a request, that time is its latency. With thread-per-request, every checkout inside holds one thread, so L is also the number of threads we need. At 1,500 checkouts a second and 0.2 s each: L = 1,500/s × 0.2 s = 300 checkouts inside = 300 threads We have 200. Turn the law around, and it gives the most a pool can finish each second, its throughput: λ max = L / W = 200 / 0.2 s = 1,000 checkouts per second The formula gives the same wall as the last section, and now we can change the numbers in it. Say the bank has a slow afternoon. Its answers take 1.2 seconds instead of 120 ms, so W grows from 0.2 s to 1.28 s. The same 200 threads now finish at most 200 / 1.28 = 156 checkouts a second. Nobody changed a line of our code, and the shop just lost five sixths of its capacity. A slow service elsewhere brings down a thread-per-request program this way. Each waiting checkout holds its thread for longer, so the threads run out sooner, and the CPU has even less to do. WallDemo agrees. With a 300 ms sleep instead of 100 ms (-Pargs='100 2000 300'), the pool's time should triple, to about 6 seconds: fixed pool of 100 2,000 requests in 6,198 ms = 323 requests/s It did. When the work is mostly waiting, a pool's throughput is its threads divided by the latency, and faster cores wouldn't move it at all. A slow service you call makes your own capacity smaller. Measure W on a bad day, not a good one. That leaves two ways out. We can make W smaller, which we often can't, because the bank isn't ours. Or we can make each checkout cheaper to hold while it waits. The quickest-sounding way to do that is to hire more waiters. So why not run 2,000 threads? Size a service by hand, then check the demo A shop's search page gets 600 requests a second, and each one waits 250 ms for a slow service. How many requests are inside at once? The page runs on a pool of 64 threads. What's the most it can finish per second, and how fast does the queue grow? Predict the pool's time in WallDemo with a 300 ms sleep, then run ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l01.WallDemo -Pargs='100 2000 300'. 600 × 0.25 = 150 requests inside at once. 64 / 0.25 = 256 a second, far below 600, so the queue grows by about 344 requests every second. WallDemo with a 300 ms sleep takes about 6 s on the pool (6,198 ms here), three times the 100 ms run. JEP 444: Virtual Threads (see the Little's law discussion in its motivation) read

h: The thread-per-request wall · Why not more threads: what a platform thread costs
x:
If waiting threads are the problem, the obvious fix is more of them. Make the pool 2,000 threads, and even the bank's slow afternoon is covered. The trouble is the kind of thread. Every thread in our pool is a platform thread, and the operating system does real work for each one. When you call start(), Java asks the operating system for a new thread. That's a system call, a request from a program to the operating system, and it isn't cheap. The operating system also reserves the thread's stack, the memory where a thread keeps the method calls it's in the middle of and their local variables. On 64-bit Linux, Java reserves 1 MB for each stack by default (the -Xss setting). The operating system hands out the memory only as the stack really grows, but the reservation and its bookkeeping stay for the thread's whole life. Then the operating system has to share out the cores. With thousands of threads, it spends more and more time switching between them. Each switch also throws away part of the CPU's cache, its small fast copy of recently used memory. The contract, the uniform and the locker from the opening are these costs, and every waiter pays them, even one who only stands at the kitchen door. ThreadCostDemo, in the Try it below, measures them. It starts 4,000 platform threads that all stay alive until it lets them go. Then it does the same with 100,000 virtual threads, the new kind this lesson ends with. Which do you expect to finish first? On this busy machine, one run printed: platform 4,000 threads alive at once: started in 6,644 ms, all finished after 7,454 ms (1863.5 us per thread) virtual 100,000 threads alive at once: started in 585 ms, all finished after 2,571 ms (25.7 us per thread) Twenty-five times as many virtual threads finished in a third of the time. The cost per platform thread swings with how busy the machine is: another run here gave 268 microseconds, not 1,864. It still stayed many times above the virtual threads' 19 to 26 microseconds. So a JVM is comfortable with hundreds of platform threads and survives a few thousand. At tens of thousands, it starts fighting the operating system's limits on threads and memory. A million is out of reach. A platform thread is an operating system thread. You can have thousands, not millions. Here the restaurant picture breaks, and not in our favor. A real waiter at the kitchen door might refill a glass on the way. A blocked platform thread can do nothing else at all until its answer arrives. So more threads can't carry us far. The next idea is older than virtual threads: stop holding a thread while we wait. Count what a thread costs Run ThreadCostDemo with the command below. It starts 4,000 platform threads that all stay alive until it releases them, then 100,000 virtual threads. Before you look at the output, guess which run finishes first: 4,000 platform threads, or 25 times as many virtual threads? Try -Pargs='5000 1000000' for a million virtual threads. Keep the platform count at 5,000 or less on a laptop. ThreadCostDemo.java package workbench.vthreads.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; /** * Starts N threads that all block on one latch, so they exist at the same time, * then releases them. First with platform threads, then with virtual threads. * *

Args: platform count, virtual count. Default: 4000 100000. * Keep the platform count at 5,000 or below on a laptop. */ public class ThreadCostDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int platform = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 4_000; int virtual = args.length > 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[1]) : 100_000; time("platform", platform, Thread.ofPlatform()); time("virtual", virtual, Thread.ofVirtual()); } static void time(String kind, int n, Thread.Builder builder) throws InterruptedException { CountDownLatch release = new CountDownLatch(1); List threads = new ArrayList<>(n); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { threads.add(builder.start(() -> { try { release.await(); // every thread stays alive until we let go } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } })); } long startedMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; release.countDown(); for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); long totalMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%-8s %,7d threads alive at once: started in %,5d ms, all finished after %,5d ms (%.1f us per thread)%n", kind, n, startedMs, totalMs, totalMs * 1000.0 / n); } } ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l01.ThreadCostDemo labs/vthreads/src/demo/java/workbench/vthreads/l01/ThreadCostDemo.java ThreadCostDemo.kt package workbench.vthreads.l01 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch /** * Starts N threads that all block on one latch, so they exist at the same time, * then releases them. First with platform threads, then with virtual threads. * * Args: platform count, virtual count. Default: 4000 100000. * Keep the platform count at 5,000 or below on a laptop. */ fun main(args: Array) { val platform = args.getOrNull(0)?.toInt() ?: 4_000 val virtual = args.getOrNull(1)?.toInt() ?: 100_000 startAndRelease("platform", platform, Thread.ofPlatform()) startAndRelease("virtual", virtual, Thread.ofVirtual()) } private fun startAndRelease(kind: String, n: Int, builder: Thread.Builder) { val release = CountDownLatch(1) val t0 = System.nanoTime() val threads = List(n) { builder.start { try { release.await() // every thread stays alive until we let go } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } } } val startedMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 release.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } val totalMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println("%-8s %,7d threads alive at once: started in %,5d ms, all finished after %,5d ms (%.1f us per thread)" .format(kind, n, startedMs, totalMs, totalMs * 1000.0 / n)) } ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l01.ThreadCostDemoKt labs/vthreads/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/vthreads/l01/ThreadCostDemo.kt Each platform thread costs tens to hundreds of microseconds to start, and more on a busy machine (268 and 1,864 microseconds in two runs here). Each virtual thread costs a few tens of microseconds or less, so 100,000 of them finish sooner than 4,000 platform threads. A million virtual threads take longer and use some heap, but nothing crashes.

h: The thread-per-request wall · Giving the thread back while it waits: async code, and what it costs
x: The first way around the wall was to stop holding a thread during a wait. In the restaurant, that's one waiter running between many tables with a notepad. Table 4's soup is ready, so bring the bread. The bank said yes for table 9, so print the bill. Nobody stands at the door, and a few waiters serve every table. In code, the notepad is a chain of steps to run later. Here's the checkout both ways. Both versions make the same three calls in the same order: Java // blocking: one thread per checkout, held for all 200 ms Receipt checkout(Basket basket) { Stock stock = warehouse.reserve(basket); // 40 ms Payment paid = bank.charge(basket, stock); // 120 ms return orders.save(basket, paid); // 35 ms } // async: the thread goes back to the pool at every wait CompletableFuture<Receipt> checkoutAsync(Basket basket) { return warehouse.reserveAsync(basket) .thenCompose(stock -> bank.chargeAsync(basket, stock)) .thenCompose(paid -> orders.saveAsync(basket, paid)); } Kotlin // blocking: one thread per checkout, held for all 200 ms fun checkout(basket: Basket): Receipt { val stock = warehouse.reserve(basket) // 40 ms val paid = bank.charge(basket, stock) // 120 ms return orders.save(basket, paid) // 35 ms } // async: the thread goes back to the pool at every wait fun checkoutAsync(basket: Basket): CompletableFuture<Receipt> = warehouse.reserveAsync(basket) .thenCompose { stock -> bank.chargeAsync(basket, stock) } .thenCompose { paid -> orders.saveAsync(basket, paid) } A CompletableFuture, from the executors track, is a box for a result that arrives later. Read thenCompose as "when this box is filled, start the next step and hand me its box". No thread waits for the bank. When its answer comes, it starts the next step on whatever thread is free. A program built this way can keep thousands of checkouts going at once on a few threads. Often it has one event loop per core: a thread that runs many requests' small steps in turn and must never block. It works, and it's why async libraries, and the reactive ones built on the same idea (a later track covers them), became popular. The price is paid in the code. Every library on the checkout's path must be async too, including the one that talks to the database. One ordinary blocking call on an event loop stalls every request that shares that loop, and nothing warns you. The call stack stops telling the story. When the bank's step fails, the stack trace lists pool threads and lambdas, which is everything except what happened. A debugger can't step from one stage to the next. Control flow turns into method calls. A try/catch becomes exceptionally, and a loop with an early exit becomes a chain that calls itself. A ThreadLocal is a variable with a separate value for each thread. It doesn't follow the checkout from thread to thread, so anything kept in one, such as the current customer, gets lost on the way. Kotlin coroutines get closest to the blocking style. A suspend function, which the compiler can pause at a wait and resume later on any thread, reads top to bottom like checkout. But coroutines need libraries that suspend instead of block. A blocking database call inside a coroutine blocks a real thread, and we're back to sizing a pool: Dispatchers.IO, the coroutine library's shared pool for blocking calls. If your code is already async and works, keep it. Rewriting plain blocking code as chains just to save threads is a poor trade. Check yourself: an async service runs on 8 event loops, and someone adds a blocking 50 ms database call to one handler. How many of those requests can the service serve per second? At most 160. Each loop is stuck for the whole 50 ms of every call, so Little's law with L = 8 and W = 0.05 s gives 8 / 0.05 = 160, however fast the CPU is. Async code frees the thread by changing the code. What if, instead, threads were so cheap that a waiting one didn't matter?

h: The thread-per-request wall · Virtual threads: cheap threads for the same blocking code
x: JDK 21 took the other way out: it made threads cheap. Virtual threads became a final feature in JDK 21, no longer an experiment you had to switch on. They came through JEP 444, a JDK Enhancement Proposal: the design document for a change to Java. A virtual thread is a normal java.lang.Thread that the JDK schedules instead of the operating system. It runs on a small pool of platform threads, about one per core. When it blocks, for example on a network read or a sleep, the JDK sets it aside. It keeps the thread's stack on the heap, the memory where Java keeps its objects, and lends the platform thread to another virtual thread. The next lesson, How virtual threads work, opens that up. In the restaurant, that's a waiter who costs next to nothing to hire. Every table can keep its personal waiter again, and a waiter standing at the kitchen door is no longer a waste. So we keep the blocking checkout method, and give every checkout its own virtual thread. Both versions start one new virtual thread per basket: Java try (ExecutorService perCheckout = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (Basket basket : incoming) { perCheckout.submit(() -> checkout(basket)); // blocking code, cheap thread } } // close() waits for every task Kotlin Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perCheckout -> for (basket in incoming) { perCheckout.submit(Callable { checkout(basket) }) // blocking code, cheap thread } } // use {} closes the executor, and close() waits for every task The executor starts a brand-new virtual thread for every task and keeps none around. Remember the second line of WallDemo? Here it is, from the same run as the first: fixed pool of 100 2,000 requests in 2,229 ms = 897 requests/s virtual thread per task 2,000 requests in 268 ms = 7,463 requests/s All 2,000 checkouts slept at the same time, so the run took a little over one sleep. With the 300 ms sleep, it took 391 ms. The time follows the latency of one checkout, not the number of checkouts. Little's law still holds. At 1,500 checkouts a second and 0.2 s each, 300 are still inside at once. They just don't cost 300 operating system threads. When the bank slows to 1.2 s, 1,920 are inside, and that's fine too. Be clear about what virtual threads don't change: One checkout is not faster. It still waits 200 ms. Virtual threads give scale (more checkouts waiting at once), not speed. Work that computes gains nothing. With 16 cores, at most 16 threads compute at once, virtual or not. Limits elsewhere stay. The shop's database still accepts 20 connections, open lines to it, at once. With the thread cap gone, 300 checkouts reach it together, and the queue moves there. Lesson 3 of this track puts a limit in front of it. A few kinds of code can also keep a virtual thread from letting go of its platform thread. Lesson 4 of this track covers them. Virtual threads give scale, not speed. Each checkout waits as long as before, but many more can wait at once. The restaurant picture breaks here too: the kitchen is still the kitchen. If the slow part is the cooking itself, or a grill with room for only 20 pans, cheaper waiters don't help. The lab turns the wall into something you can measure: the same blocking handler on a fixed pool, and on one virtual thread per task. Run the same wall on virtual threads Run WallDemo again, and this time read the second line. Run it with -Pargs='100 2000 300'. Predict first: does the virtual-thread time triple, like the pool's did? Run it with -Pargs='100 5000 100'. Predict both lines before you look. The virtual line finishes 2,000 checkouts in a little over 100 ms (148 to 268 ms in busy runs here), because all 2,000 sleep at the same time. With a 300 ms sleep it takes a little over 300 ms (391 ms here): the time follows one checkout's latency, not the number of checkouts. With 5,000 checkouts the pool needs about 5 s (5,134 ms here), and the virtual run still takes well under a second (294 ms).

h: The thread-per-request wall · Java and Kotlin
x: Blocking code that scales: virtual threads and coroutines Java 21+: virtual threads // plain blocking code, one cheap virtual thread per checkout List<Receipt> checkoutAll(List<Basket> baskets) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { List<Future<Receipt>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); for (Basket b : baskets) futures.add(perTask.submit(() -> checkout(b))); List<Receipt> receipts = new ArrayList<>(); for (Future<Receipt> f : futures) receipts.add(f.get()); return receipts; } } Receipt checkout(Basket b) { Stock stock = warehouse.reserve(b); // an ordinary blocking call over the network Payment paid = bank.charge(b, stock); return orders.save(b, paid); // an ordinary database call } Kotlin: kotlinx.coroutines // suspend functions: the compiler turns them into steps it can pause between suspend fun checkoutAll(baskets: List<Basket>): List<Receipt> = coroutineScope { baskets.map { b -> async { checkout(b) } }.awaitAll() } suspend fun checkout(b: Basket): Receipt { val stock = warehouse.reserve(b) // must itself suspend to free the thread val paid = bank.charge(b, stock) return orders.save(b, paid) // a blocking database call here would block a real thread } Both read top to bottom, and both keep thousands of checkouts going at once on a few operating system threads. The difference is where the pausing happens. Kotlin does it in the compiler: only suspend functions can give the thread back, so every waiting call on the path has to be suspend-aware, and a blocking database call needs withContext(Dispatchers.IO), which is a thread pool again. Virtual threads do it in the JDK while the program runs: most blocking JDK calls (network reads, sleep, locks, a BlockingQueue) set the virtual thread aside, so existing database drivers and HTTP clients (libraries that call web services) work unchanged. The two also mix: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher() runs coroutines on virtual threads, which helps when they call blocking libraries.

h: The thread-per-request wall · Key terms
x: Platform thread A Java thread that is one operating system thread. Costly, so you get thousands. Virtual thread A Java thread that the JDK schedules on a few platform threads. Cheap, so you can have millions. Thread-per-request A server style where each request gets one thread for its whole life. Blocked thread A thread that can't go on until something it waits for arrives, such as an answer from another program. Little's law Inside at once = arrival rate × time inside. L = λ × W. Throughput How many requests finish per second. Latency How long one request takes from start to end. Event loop A thread that runs many requests' small steps in turn and must never block. State Little's law. L = λ × W: the number of requests inside equals the arrival rate times the time each request spends inside. 1,500 requests a second, 200 ms each. How many threads does thread-per-request need? 300 (1,500 × 0.2). 200 threads, and each request holds one for 200 ms. What is the most it can finish per second? 1,000 requests a second (200 / 0.2 s). Above that the queue grows, even with idle cores. What is a platform thread? A java.lang.Thread backed one to one by an operating system thread, with its own stack (1 MB reserved by default on 64-bit Linux). Do virtual threads make a single request faster? No. They give scale (more requests waiting at once), not speed. Each request waits just as long. In which JDK did virtual threads become final, and under which JEP? JDK 21, JEP 444. What happens when code on an event loop makes a blocking database call? It blocks the event loop's thread, so every other request on that loop stalls until the call returns.

h: The thread-per-request wall · Go deeper
x: Little's law needs only one assumption: the system is stable, meaning that over the long run requests leave as fast as they arrive. It says nothing about the shape of the traffic or the order of service, which is why it works for a shop's checkout as well as for a supermarket. It doesn't tell you what happens near the limit. As a pool gets close to 100% busy, the queue doesn't grow smoothly. Short bursts above the average rate make requests wait, and the waits add up faster than the load. A pool that is busy 95% of the time has much longer queues than one at 80%, even though it is only a little busier. That's why people who plan capacity leave room to spare. It also explains why thread-per-request lasted so long. If W is 5 ms (a lookup in memory), 200 threads give you 40,000 requests a second, and nobody needs async code. The wall only appears when W is mostly waiting for other programs, which describes most services that call other services. The motivation section of JEP 444 makes this same argument: the number of threads limits throughput long before the CPU or the network do. One honest question remains: why not shrink the stack with -Xss and run 20,000 platform threads? Some teams did. You still pay a system call for every thread you start, the operating system still has to schedule 20,000 threads, and a stack that's too small turns a deep chain of calls into a StackOverflowError. A virtual thread's stack lives on the heap and grows only as deep as the code really goes, so you don't have to guess a size.

h: How virtual threads work: carriers and continuations · What a virtual thread is made of: a Thread plus a continuation
x: Start with what you can see. Thread.ofVirtual().start(task) returns an ordinary java.lang.Thread, and isVirtual() on it returns true. Inside the JDK, the object is a java.lang.VirtualThread, a subclass your code can't use directly. It holds two things that a platform thread, one backed by a thread of the operating system, doesn't have: a continuation and a scheduler. Before we name the first one, do a small job by hand. Suppose you had to stop a method halfway and finish it tomorrow. What would you write down? The line you're on and the values of its local variables. Then the same again for the method that called it, and the one that called that, all the way up. That list already has a name. Each method call that hasn't returned yet has a frame, a small record of its local variables and of the line to go back to. The frames, piled one on another, make the thread's stack. To pause a thread, you save its frames. To resume it, you put them back. A continuation is exactly that: a piece of work that can stop in the middle and carry on later from the same line, with its frames intact. It's the order slip from the opening. The JDK has an internal class for it, jdk.internal.vm.Continuation, with two operations that matter here. In outline (the real class also takes a scope argument, which we skip): cont = new Continuation(() -> { a(); yield(); b(); }) cont.run() // runs a(), stops at yield(), returns here cont.run() // carries on with b() run() starts the work, or resumes it where it stopped. yield(), called from inside the work, stops it and returns to whoever called run(), with the frames kept. The next run() carries on from the line after the yield(). You can't call this class yourself, because Java doesn't export its package. The virtual thread uses it for you. It wraps your task in a continuation, and when the task is about to block, the JDK calls yield(). The task stops, and no thread of the operating system waits for it. The second part, the scheduler, decides which stopped continuation runs next, and on which platform thread. In the restaurant, it's the manager who decides which waiter takes which slip. To your code, a virtual thread is just a thread. Thread.currentThread() returns it, ThreadLocals (variables with a separate value for each thread) work, interrupt() works, and sleep throws InterruptedException the same way. A few things differ, all listed in the Thread Javadoc. Virtual threads are always daemon threads, which the JVM doesn't wait for when the program ends. Their priority is fixed, they have no name unless you give one, and Thread.getAllStackTraces() leaves them out. A slip needs someone to carry it, though. In the JDK, that someone is called a carrier.

h: How virtual threads work: carriers and continuations · Mount, unmount, mount again: how a few carriers run every virtual thread
x:
Four waiters and a board of order slips: a virtual thread is put down at every blocking call with its frames on the heap, and any free carrier picks it up again The default scheduler is a ForkJoinPool, the pool from the executors track whose threads take work from each other's queues. The JDK creates one just for virtual threads, separate from ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), which parallel streams use. It works first in, first out, so ready virtual threads run roughly in the order they became ready. Its workers are platform threads, and they have a name of their own: carrier threads. By default there's one per core, a part of the processor that runs one thread at a time (Runtime.availableProcessors() gives the count, and -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=N changes it). The carriers are the restaurant's four waiters. Two words describe a virtual thread's life on a carrier. To mount is to start running a virtual thread on a carrier. The carrier takes a ready virtual thread and runs its continuation, so the thread's top frames sit on the carrier's own stack. To unmount is the reverse. At a blocking call, the continuation yields and its frames are copied to the heap, the memory where Java keeps its objects. The carrier goes back for the next ready thread. Let's trace the smallest case: two carriers, C1 and C2, and three virtual threads. VT1 and VT2 are ready at the same moment. C1 mounts VT1, and C2 mounts VT2. VT1 calls sleep(50). It unmounts, its frames go to the heap, and C1 is free. VT3 arrives a moment later. C1 mounts it while VT1 sleeps. VT2 finishes, so C2 is free. VT1's 50 ms run out, and it goes back in the queue. C2 mounts VT1, which carries on after sleep. It started on C1 and finishes on C2. That move is normal: a virtual thread that unmounts can come back on any carrier. CarrierDemo, in the Try it below, makes it visible. It starts 8 virtual threads that each print Thread.currentThread(), sleep 50 ms, and print it again. A virtual thread's toString() names its carrier after the @. On this 4-core machine, while other programs were busy, one run printed this (three of the eight rows): before: VirtualThread[#19,checkout-0]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1 after: VirtualThread[#19,checkout-0]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3 before: VirtualThread[#22,checkout-1]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2 after: VirtualThread[#22,checkout-1]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2 before: VirtualThread[#24,checkout-2]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1 after: VirtualThread[#24,checkout-2]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3 8 virtual threads ran on 3 carrier threads [ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1, ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2, ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3] (this machine has 4 cores). 7 of them woke up on a different carrier than the one they slept on. All 8 finished after 109 ms. Seven of the eight woke up on a different carrier, and not one of them was told. The carrier is hidden from your code on purpose. Thread.currentThread() returns the virtual thread, never the carrier, and the carrier's own ThreadLocals are out of reach. If they weren't, a value one checkout left on a carrier would leak into whichever checkout mounted there next. The @ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3 part of toString() is there for debugging only, and its format isn't specified anywhere. So the restaurant holds up: the slip never knows which waiter carries it, and it doesn't need to. A virtual thread can come back on any carrier after every blocking call. Never write code that cares which one. Check yourself: a virtual thread runs a task that sleeps three times and then returns. How many times does its continuation yield, and how many times is it mounted? It yields three times, once per sleep. It's mounted four times: once to start, and once after each sleep. So far our threads only slept. Which other calls let a thread put its slip down, and which don't? Watch virtual threads change carriers Run CarrierDemo with the command below. It starts 8 virtual threads that print Thread.currentThread(), sleep 50 ms, and print it again. Count the carriers in the summary line, and compare that with your number of cores. How many threads woke up on a different carrier? Predict, then run with one carrier: -Pargs='8 1'. Does it take 8 times as long? h: How virtual threads work: carriers and continuations · Where a virtual thread lets go, and where it holds on
x: Unmounting isn't magic inside the JVM. The JDK team rewrote the blocking parts of Java's class library. Each one now checks whether the current thread is virtual and, if it is, yields instead of blocking. Here is parkNanos, the method underneath sleep, from java.lang.VirtualThread, trimmed to its core: // simplified from java.lang.VirtualThread.parkNanos (JDK 25) void parkNanos(long nanos) { timeout = nanos; setState(TIMED_PARKING); boolean yielded = yieldContinuation(); // unmount: frames to the heap, carrier is free if (!yielded) { parkOnCarrierThread(true, nanos); // couldn't unmount: block the carrier instead } } First the method notes the timeout and the thread's new state, and the JDK arranges a timer that will make the thread ready again. Then yieldContinuation() unmounts it. The tricky line is the last one. If the thread can't unmount, it blocks its carrier instead, just as a platform thread would. These operations unmount a virtual thread: Thread.sleep, and LockSupport.park with everything built on it: ReentrantLock, Semaphore, CountDownLatch, BlockingQueue.take and Future.get. Network reads and writes on sockets, including the JDK's HttpClient, its class for calling web services, and database drivers that use plain sockets. The JDK switches the socket to a mode where it never blocks and hands it to a poller, a part of the JDK that watches many sockets at once. Then it parks the virtual thread until data arrives. From JDK 24 (JEP 491), synchronized and Object.wait(). On JDK 21 to 23, these pin the virtual thread instead: it stays mounted, and its carrier blocks with it. Some operations can't unmount. Most file reads and writes block inside the operating system, so the virtual thread keeps its carrier for the whole call. The scheduler adds a temporary extra carrier to make up for it, up to 256 by default. Blocking while a native method (one written in C, say) or a class's static initializer, the code that sets up a class the first time it's used, is on the stack pins the carrier. Lesson 4 of this track is about pinning, and how to find it. The last rule surprises people. Let's replace the sleep in CarrierDemo with 50 ms of busy work, a loop that just watches the clock. Predict first: eight 50 ms loops on one carrier should take about 400 ms, and on four carriers about 100 ms. Here is the end of a one-carrier run, on the busy machine: 0 of them woke up on a different carrier than the one they slept on. All 8 finished after 532 ms. A second one-carrier run took 415 ms, and two runs on four carriers took 172 and 155 ms. The loops ran one after another, with the busy machine adding its share. And no thread changed carrier, because none of them ever blocked, so none of them ever unmounted. There's no time slicing for virtual threads. The operating system takes turns among its threads every few milliseconds, but nothing takes a carrier away from a virtual thread that's computing. The scheduler never taps a busy thread on the shoulder. In the restaurant, it's a waiter chopping onions: the slip stays in his pocket until the chopping is done. Here the picture breaks a little. A real manager would send a second waiter to help. The scheduler doesn't, so four waiters chopping leave every other slip on the rail. Virtual threads make waiting cheap, not computing. A thread that never blocks keeps its carrier. Each time a thread does put its slip down, though, its frames have to go somewhere. Where, and what do they weigh? Replace the sleep with real work In CarrierDemo.java, replace Thread.sleep(50); with a 50 ms busy loop: long end = System.nanoTime() + 50_000_000; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { }. The compiler then complains that nothing in the try can throw InterruptedException, so remove the try and catch too. In CarrierDemo.kt the loop is val end = System.nanoTime() + 50_000_000; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { }, and Kotlin doesn't mind the leftover catch. Predict the total time with one carrier (-Pargs='8 1') and with the default number of carriers. Then run both. Look at the before and after carriers. Did any thread change carrier this time? With one carrier the 8 loops run one after another: about 400 ms on an idle machine (415 and 532 ms in busy runs here). With 4 carriers it takes about 100 ms (155 and 172 ms here), more if other programs are busy. No thread changes carrier, because none of them ever blocks, so none of them ever unmounts. Computing is limited by carriers, which means cores.

h: How virtual threads work: carriers and continuations · Where the saved stack lives, and what it weighs
x:
A platform thread's stack is a fixed block of memory reserved when the thread starts. It's 1 MB by default on 64-bit Linux, whether the thread goes three calls deep or three hundred. A virtual thread's stack works differently. When it unmounts, the JDK copies its frames off the carrier's stack into stack chunk objects on the heap. A chunk is only as big as the frames really there. The garbage collector, the part of the JVM that frees memory nobody uses any more, looks after it like any other object. When the virtual thread mounts again, the JDK doesn't copy the whole stack back. It copies the top few frames, enough to carry on. If the code returns into a frame that's still on the heap, the JDK copies more at that moment. So a thread parked deep inside a library pays for its depth when it parks, not all over again each time it wakes. StackOnHeapDemo, in the Try it below, weighs it. It parks 10,000 virtual threads one call deep, measures the heap, lets them go, and does the same 200 calls deep. Predict: will the deep ones cost 200 times as much? One run printed: depth 1: 10,000 parked virtual threads use about 22 MB of heap (2,344 bytes each) depth 200: 10,000 parked virtual threads use about 95 MB of heap (10,012 bytes each) Not 200 times: about four times. The Thread object and its bookkeeping are a fixed part of every parked thread, and each frame of this small method is small. At 1,000 calls deep, another run gave 27,085 bytes each, still about a fortieth of the megabyte a platform thread reserves up front. Those numbers are what make a million virtual threads possible. On the restaurant's board, a slip with long notes takes more room than a short one, but no slip needs a table of its own. The heap also explains a difference from Kotlin. A coroutine saves only the local variables of its suspend functions, in objects the compiler writes for it. A virtual thread saves the whole real stack, so a blocking call deep inside an old library, written before virtual threads existed, can still unmount. The compare block below shows both side by side. A parked virtual thread costs heap in proportion to its real stack. Nothing is reserved for the worst case. In the lab you build the other half of the machine: a tiny scheduler with a ready queue, a timer queue and one carrier. It mounts and unmounts continuations written by hand. Weigh a parked virtual thread Run StackOnHeapDemo. It parks 10,000 virtual threads at call depth 1, measures the heap, releases them, then does the same at depth 200. Before you look: how many times bigger will the depth-200 number be? Run it with -Pargs=1000 for depth 1,000, and compare with the 1 MB a platform thread reserves. h: How virtual threads work: carriers and continuations · Java and Kotlin
x: Stackful virtual threads and stackless coroutines Java: the JDK saves the real stack // any method can block, even deep inside an old library void checkout(Basket b) throws InterruptedException { Payment paid = bank.charge(b); // a blocking network read: unmounts here Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(30)); // unmounts here too orders.save(b, paid); // a plain database call over a socket: unmounts } // run it on a virtual thread; nothing in checkout() knows Thread.ofVirtual().name("checkout-", 0).start(() -> { try { checkout(basket); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); Kotlin: the compiler builds a state machine // only suspend calls can pause; the compiler rewrites this function suspend fun checkout(b: Basket) { val paid = bank.charge(b) // must be a suspend fun to free the thread delay(30) orders.save(b, paid) // a blocking database call here would block the thread } // roughly what the compiler generates (simplified): // class CheckoutContinuation(var label: Int, var paid: Payment?) // label 0: call charge(b); label = 1; return COROUTINE_SUSPENDED // label 1: paid = result; call delay(30); label = 2; return COROUTINE_SUSPENDED // label 2: orders.save(b, paid) Both pause in the middle of a function and carry on later, possibly on another thread. Kotlin coroutines are stackless: the compiler turns each suspend function into a state machine, a class with a counter that says which step comes next, and keeps its local variables in fields. So only suspend calls can pause. Virtual threads are stackful: the JVM copies the real frames, so any blocking JDK call anywhere on the stack can unmount, even inside a library compiled before virtual threads existed. The fibers in this lesson's lab are written by hand in the Kotlin style, with a counter, so you can see what the JDK saves you from writing.

It puts the virtual thread's continuation in the scheduler's queue as a task, and the caller carries on at once. Mount. A free carrier, worker-2, takes the task and calls run() on the continuation. The network reads inside warehouse.reserve may unmount and mount it again several times on their own. Unmount. sleep reaches parkNanos, which arranges a timer for 50 ms and calls yieldContinuation(). Wake and mount again. The timer fires and makes checkout-1 ready, which puts its continuation back in the queue. Whichever carrier is free next, say worker-4, mounts it and copies the top frames back, and sleep returns. The code calls bank.charge without knowing it moved.

h: How virtual threads work: carriers and continuations · Key terms
x: Continuation Work that can stop at a point and carry on later from the same line, with its stack intact. Carrier thread A platform thread that runs virtual threads, one at a time. Mount / unmount Start running a virtual thread on a carrier / take it off the carrier at a blocking call. Scheduler The ForkJoinPool that decides which ready virtual thread a free carrier runs next. Stack frame The record of one method call that hasn't returned: its local variables and the line to go back to. Stack chunk A heap object holding the saved frames of an unmounted virtual thread. Pinning A virtual thread that blocks but can't unmount, so its carrier blocks with it. Time slicing Taking a running thread off the processor after a short turn. The operating system does it to its threads; nothing does it to virtual threads. What is a carrier thread? A platform thread, a worker of the virtual thread scheduler's ForkJoinPool, that runs a virtual thread while it is mounted. What happens when a virtual thread unmounts? At a blocking call its continuation yields: the frames are copied to the heap, and the carrier goes back to run other virtual threads. How many carrier threads does the default scheduler use? One per core (availableProcessors()), set by jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism. It can add carriers for a while, up to 256 by default. Does the JVM time-slice virtual threads? No. A virtual thread keeps its carrier until it blocks or ends. Where are a parked virtual thread's stack frames? On the Java heap, in stack chunk objects sized to the real stack depth. Is the virtual thread scheduler ForkJoinPool.commonPool()? No. It is a separate ForkJoinPool that works first in, first out. Parallel streams and the default CompletableFuture async methods use the common pool. Name two operations that unmount a virtual thread and one that holds on to the carrier instead. Unmount: Thread.sleep, socket reads, ReentrantLock.lock, BlockingQueue.take. Holds the carrier: most file I/O.

h: How virtual threads work: carriers and continuations · Go deeper
x: Three details of the machinery are worth knowing, because they explain behavior you'll see in real programs. How sockets unmount. A socket used from a virtual thread is put in non-blocking mode, where a read returns at once even when no data has arrived. When a read would have to wait, the JDK hands the socket to its poller and parks the virtual thread. The poller uses the operating system's way of waiting on many sockets at once (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS) and wakes each virtual thread when its socket is ready. One wait covers thousands of connections, which is what event-loop libraries do by hand. Why file I/O is different. Linux has no general non-blocking way to read regular files that the JDK uses here, so a file read really blocks the operating system thread. The JDK lets the virtual thread keep its carrier for the whole call, and asks the scheduler for a temporary extra carrier so the other virtual threads keep running. That's why jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize exists. A program that does heavy file I/O on virtual threads can see the carrier count grow toward 256. Why first in, first out. A ForkJoinPool normally runs a worker's own newest task first, which suits splitting a big job into pieces. For virtual threads the JDK creates it in async mode, which runs tasks first in, first out, so a virtual thread that became ready long ago runs before one that became ready a moment ago. That keeps waits fair across requests. The scheduler itself is not a public API in JDK 21 or 25. You can tune its size with the system properties, but you can't plug in a scheduler of your own. Libraries that need special scheduling still use platform threads.

h: Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores · Five ways to start a virtual thread, and the one you'll use most
x: Before we give every order its own thread, we need a way to make one. A virtual thread is a Java thread that the JDK runs on a few platform threads, called carriers. (A platform thread is one thread of the operating system.) The JDK sets a virtual thread aside whenever it blocks, so it's cheap enough to have one per task. JDK 21 has no new VirtualThread(). You start one through Thread.Builder, a small object that collects settings such as a name and then makes threads, or through an executor. Both lists below show the same five ways: Java // 1. a one-off, no name Thread a = Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> checkout(basket)); // 2. a builder, when you want a name in thread dumps Thread b = Thread.ofVirtual().name("checkout-", 0).start(() -> checkout(basket)); // checkout-0 // 3. created now, started later Thread c = Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted(() -> checkout(basket)); c.start(); // 4. a ThreadFactory, for libraries that ask for one ThreadFactory receipts = Thread.ofVirtual().name("receipt-", 0).factory(); ExecutorService named = Executors.newThreadPerTaskExecutor(receipts); // 5. what you'll use most: one new virtual thread per task ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); Kotlin // 1. a one-off, no name val a = Thread.startVirtualThread { checkout(basket) } // 2. a builder, when you want a name in thread dumps val b = Thread.ofVirtual().name("checkout-", 0).start { checkout(basket) } // checkout-0 // 3. created now, started later val c = Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted { checkout(basket) } c.start() // 4. a ThreadFactory, for libraries that ask for one val receipts = Thread.ofVirtual().name("receipt-", 0).factory() val named = Executors.newThreadPerTaskExecutor(receipts) // 5. what you'll use most: one new virtual thread per task val perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() Read them in order. The first starts a thread at once, with no name. The second gives it a name, and name("checkout-", 0) numbers its threads: the first is checkout-0, the next checkout-1. The third makes the thread now and starts it later. The fourth hands out a ThreadFactory, an object that makes threads on request, for code that wants one. A builder isn't safe to share between threads, so set it up in one place. The factory it returns is safe, so share that. The fifth is the one for normal code. It gives you a Future, a handle on the task's result, for each task. Its close() waits for every task, and most libraries already know how to take an ExecutorService. Use a builder when you start one long-lived thread, such as a helper that emails receipts all day, and want a name you can find in a thread dump, the list of every thread a running program has. Virtual threads have no name by default, which makes a dump of 50,000 of them hard to read. All five give you ordinary Thread objects. join, interrupt and isAlive work as usual, and isVirtual() tells you which kind you have. BuildersDemo, in the Try it below, starts one of each and lets each one print from inside itself. Its run here began: Thread.startVirtualThread name='' virtual=true daemon=true Thread.ofVirtual().name().start name='checkout-7' virtual=true daemon=true Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted name='' virtual=true daemon=true Every line says daemon=true. A daemon thread is one the JVM doesn't wait for when the program ends, and a virtual thread is always one. You can't change that, as the Try it shows. We can make one thread now. The next step is to make one for every order. Start one of each Run BuildersDemo. Each line is printed from inside the new thread. Predict before you look: which ones have a name, and what does isDaemon() say for each? Add .daemon(false) before .start(...) on the Thread.ofVirtual().name("checkout-7") line (in either file) and run again. What happens? the rest print an empty name. Every line says virtual=true daemon=true. The .daemon(false) edit doesn't compile, in Java or in Kotlin: Thread.ofVirtual() returns a Thread.Builder.OfVirtual, which has no daemon method, because virtual threads are always daemon threads.

h: Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores · One order, one virtual thread: a fan-out in one try block
x: newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() starts a brand-new virtual thread for every task you submit. It keeps no threads around and has no queue. Its Javadoc says it plainly: the number of threads it creates is unbounded. Since JDK 19, ExecutorService is AutoCloseable, so it works in try-with-resources. close() shuts the executor down and then waits until every submitted task has finished. So a fan-out, starting many calls at once and then collecting all their results, fits in one block. Both versions save every order on its own virtual thread: Java List<Receipt> saveAll(List<Order> orders) throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException { try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { // 1. fork: start every save before waiting for any List<Future<Receipt>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); for (Order order : orders) futures.add(perTask.submit(() -> database.save(order))); // 2. join: collect the answers in input order List<Receipt> receipts = new ArrayList<>(); for (Future<Receipt> f : futures) receipts.add(f.get()); return receipts; } // 3. close(): waits for any task still running } Kotlin fun saveAll(orders: List<Order>): List<Receipt> = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> // 1. fork: start every save before waiting for any val futures = orders.map { order -> perTask.submit(Callable { database.save(order) }) } // 2. join: collect the answers in input order futures.map { it.get() } } // 3. close(): waits for any task still running Let's walk through it. First we submit every order, so all the saves start before we wait for any of them. Then we call get() on each future in the order we submitted them, so the receipts come back in the same order as the orders. Finally close(), at the end of the block, waits for anything still running. Read aloud, the method says: give every order its own thread, then collect the answers in order. Create the executor where the work starts, and let it end where the work ends. An executor per batch costs almost nothing, because it owns no threads. And when the method returns, no thread it started is still running. That promise gets a name and an API of its own in lesson 5 of this track. Two details trip people up. First, start every task before you call get() on any of them. A loop that submits one order and then waits for it saves the batch one order at a time, on 5,000 threads. With a 35 ms save, that's almost three minutes (5,000 × 0.035 s = 175 s), because only one call is ever in flight, started and not yet finished. Little's law, from The thread-per-request wall, says inside at once = arrival rate × time inside. Here only one order is ever inside, so 5,000 virtual threads didn't help at all. Second, get() reports a failed task as an ExecutionException whose cause is the real exception. The other tasks keep running when one fails, and close() still waits for them. Stopping them is also lesson 5's topic. Now look at what our fan-out does to the database. Nothing in the block limits how many orders are saved at once. A copy of the lab's test, changed to print the count, sent 5,000 orders through it, at 10 ms per save. In one run, 3,069 of them were inside the fake database at the same moment, and in another, 4,772. The real database accepts 20. The executor isn't broken. It does exactly what it promises: one thread per task, no limit. The limit belongs somewhere else, and the first place people put it is the wrong one.

h: Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores · The old habit fails: a pool of 20 virtual threads, and what it costs
x: Thread pools exist for two reasons. Platform threads are costly to start, so a pool reuses them, and a fixed pool caps how much work runs at once. Neither reason survives virtual threads. A virtual thread costs about as much to make as a small object, so reusing one saves almost nothing. And a pool is the wrong place for a cap, because it caps everything the task does, not just the one call that needs a limit. Here's the habit, in code that compiles and runs fine. Each order asks the stock service, which needs no limit, and then saves the order in the database, which accepts 20 at once: Java // Naive: keeps the database at 20, and everything else too ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()); pool.execute(() -> { Stock stock = warehouse.check(order); // 60 ms, needs no limit, but waits for a pool thread anyway database.save(order, stock); // 10 ms, the only call that needs the limit }); Kotlin // Naive: keeps the database at 20, and everything else too val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()) pool.execute { val stock = warehouse.check(order) // 60 ms, needs no limit, but waits for a pool thread anyway database.save(order, stock) // 10 ms, the only call that needs the limit } In the restaurant, this is keeping only 20 slips and making each new table wait for a used one. The grill never holds more than 20 pans. Neither does the coffee machine, or the salad bar. Let's measure the cost. PoolVsSemaphoreDemo, in the Try it below, runs 1,000 such orders. Predict the pool's time first: each task holds a pool thread for 70 ms, so 1,000 tasks take 1,000 / 20 × 70 ms = 3.5 s. One run on this busy machine printed: pool of 20 virtual threads: 3,628 ms The prediction held. To give the pool its due, the database never saw more than 20, and nothing broke. But the stock checks needed no limit, and they waited in line anyway. If only the save were limited, all 1,000 stock checks would overlap. The batch would take about 60 ms plus 1,000 / 20 × 10 ms, about 0.56 s. The demo's second line tries exactly that, and the next section explains how. A reused thread brings one more problem. A ThreadLocal, a variable with a separate value for each thread, survives from one task to the next on a pooled thread. Lesson 4 of this track covers that trap. JEP 444, the design document behind virtual threads, gives the rule in a few words. Never pool virtual threads. Create one per task, and put the limit on the resource. Pools are still the right tool for platform threads that compute. A newFixedThreadPool(cores) for checksums or image resizing keeps that work bounded, and off the virtual thread scheduler. The rule is about virtual threads only. So the limit moves to the database itself. We need something that lets 20 orders in, makes the rest wait, and makes waiting cheap. A pool vs a semaphore, same limit Read PoolVsSemaphoreDemo. Each order makes a 60 ms stock check and a 10 ms save, and the database allows 20 saves at once. Predict both times with the arithmetic above, then run it. Change DB_LIMIT to 50 and predict again. Which version speeds up more? Two ways to respect the database limit: * a pool of 20 virtual threads, or one virtual thread per request plus a Semaphore(20). */ private const val REQUESTS = 1_000 private const val DB_LIMIT = 20 fun main() { // A: the anti-pattern. With a limit of 50, the pool drops to about 1.4 s (1,000 / 50 × 70 ms) and the semaphore version to about 0.26 s (60 ms + 1,000 / 50 × 10 ms). Both keep the database at its limit; only the pool also slows down the work that needs no limit.

h: Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores · Twenty tokens at the grill: one shared Semaphore in front of the database
x:
A 20-pan grill and a hook of 20 tokens: a pool of 20 virtual threads makes the whole order wait (3,628 ms), one shared Semaphore(20) around the save alone does not (604 ms) Back to the restaurant. The grill has room for 20 pans, so a hook beside it holds 20 metal tokens. Before an order goes on the grill, it takes a token, and when it comes off, the token goes back on the hook. An order that finds the hook empty waits on the board, which costs a slip of paper and no waiter. The rest of the kitchen carries on without tokens. In Java, the hook is a Semaphore, the car park from Synchronizers. It holds a number of permits, here 20: the tokens. acquire() takes a permit, and waits if none is left. release() gives one back and wakes one waiting thread. On a virtual thread, waiting in acquire() parks the thread, that is, sets it aside until a permit comes free. So 5,000 waiting orders cost 5,000 small heap objects and no platform threads. The pattern has three rules, numbered in the code: Java final class OrderStore { private final Semaphore connections = new Semaphore(20); // 1. one per resource, shared by all callers private final Database database; OrderStore(Database database) { this.database = database; } Receipt save(Order order) throws InterruptedException { connections.acquire(); // 2. acquire on the line before the try try { return database.save(order); // only the call that needs the limit } finally { connections.release(); // 3. always give it back } } } Kotlin class OrderStore(private val database: Database) { private val connections = Semaphore(20) // 1. one per resource, shared by all callers fun save(order: Order): Receipt { connections.acquire() // 2. acquire on the line before the try try { return database.save(order) // only the call that needs the limit } finally { connections.release() // 3. always give it back } } } First, the semaphore lives with the resource, as one field on the object every order uses. Second, acquire() sits on the line before the try, so a thread that is interrupted while it waits never releases a permit it didn't get. Third, release() sits in the finally, so a save that throws still gives its permit back. PoolVsSemaphoreDemo's second line runs the same 1,000 orders, with one virtual thread each and a Semaphore(20) around the save alone: pool of 20 virtual threads: 3,628 ms virtual thread per task + Semaphore(20): 604 ms Same database limit, six times faster, because all 1,000 stock checks overlapped. Here the restaurant picture breaks, and the break matters. A real token is a thing you can hold; a permit is only a count. The semaphore never checks who hands one back, so a release() from a thread that never acquired adds a 21st permit, as Synchronizers showed. That's why rule two keeps acquire() outside the try. Rule one fails just as quietly. Picture a handler that creates new Semaphore(20) for each request. Every request gets its own hook with 20 tokens, which is generous, and limits nothing: no thread ever waits, and all 5,000 reach the database. Pick the number from the resource's side, such as the database's connection count. Then check it with Little's law. Twenty permits on a 50 ms call allow at most 20 / 0.05 s = 400 calls a second. So 1,000 orders take about 2.5 s, however many threads you start. FanOutKotlin, in the compare block, took 2,639 ms. If orders arrive faster than 400 a second, the line of waiters grows without end. Waiting forever is rarely what a customer wants. tryAcquire(200, MILLISECONDS) returns false if no permit came in time, so the shop can answer "busy, try again" at once instead of after a long wait. That's load shedding, turning work away early when you're over capacity. A limit like this, one per slow thing your program calls, is the bulkhead from Sizing a pool. One last trap: an order that needs two limited things uses two semaphores, one after the other. Don't hold one permit while you wait for another. It ties up the first resource for nothing, and two code paths that take them in opposite orders can deadlock, each waiting forever for the other, exactly like two locks. Threads are cheap, and the database is not. Give every task its own virtual thread, and every scarce resource one shared semaphore. That's the whole pattern. The lab builds it from scratch and proves the limit with 5,000 calls. Shed load instead of queueing forever ShedLoadDemo sends 1,000 requests at once through a Semaphore(20) guarding a 50 ms database call. Each request waits at most 200 ms for a permit, then gives up. Predict how many get served. Hint: in 200 ms each permit can serve about 200 / 50 = 4 calls, plus the first round. Run it, then try -Pargs='20 50 2000' and -Pargs='100 50 200', predicting each first. The database allows 20 calls at once, each takes 50 ms. * A request waits at most 200 ms for a permit, then gives up (a fast "busy, try again" instead of a slow timeout). * *

Args: permits, call ms, max wait ms. Default: 20 50 200. */ public class ShedLoadDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { int permits = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 20; long callMs = args.length > 1 ? Long.parseLong(args[1]) : 50; long maxWaitMs = args.length > 2 ? Long.parseLong(args[2]) : 200; Semaphore db = new Semaphore(permits); AtomicInteger served = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicInteger shed = new AtomicInteger(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) { perTask.execute(() -> { try { if (!db.tryAcquire(maxWaitMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { shed.incrementAndGet(); // no permit in time: fail fast return; } try { Thread.sleep(callMs); // the database call served.incrementAndGet(); } finally { db.release(); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); } } System.out.printf("permits=%d call=%d ms max wait=%d ms: served %d, shed %d, in %d ms%n", permits, callMs, maxWaitMs, served.get(), shed.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } } ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l03.ShedLoadDemo labs/vthreads/src/demo/java/workbench/vthreads/l03/ShedLoadDemo.java ShedLoadDemo.kt package workbench.vthreads.l03 import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** * 1,000 requests arrive at once. A 2 s wait serves about 20 × 41 = 820 on an idle machine (746 on this busy one). With 100 permits and 200 ms, about 500 are served (492 here). Served requests = permits × (max wait / call time + 1), which is Little's law turned around. Thousands of virtual threads park cheaply at the semaphore, like slips waiting for a token. Only 20 at a time reach the database, and Little's law gives the throughput that follows. Semaphore (Java SE 25 API) docs

} public <T> T call(Callable<T> work) throws Exception { permits.acquire(); try { return work.call(); } finally { permits.release(); } } } static final Bulkhead DATABASE = new Bulkhead(20); List<String> saveAll(List<String> ids) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { List<Future<String>> fs = new ArrayList<>(); An inline extension function gives Semaphore a withPermit block, so the try and finally are written once. Callable { ... } picks the submit overload that returns a value; a bare lambda could be read as a Runnable. Watch one name: kotlinx.coroutines has a Semaphore of its own, built for coroutines (see the box in the last section). On virtual threads, use the JDK's. h: Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores · Worked example
x: Send the night's orders to the delivery company, 20 at a time Every night the shop sends 3,000 orders to a delivery company. Its web service allows 20 calls at once from each shop and takes about 150 ms per call. Each order also needs an address lookup in the shop's own data, which has no limit. Start with the limit, as a field on the client that every caller shares. final class DeliveryClient { // one limit for the whole program, from the delivery company's rules private final Semaphore inFlight = new Semaphore(20); } class DeliveryClient { // one limit for the whole program, from the delivery company's rules private val inFlight = Semaphore(20) } Guard only the delivery call. The address lookup happens before acquire(), so 3,000 lookups overlap freely. Booking send(Order order) throws Exception { Address to = addresses.lookup(order.customerId()); // 1. unlimited work first inFlight.acquire(); // 2. wait for a permit (parks a virtual thread) try { return delivery.book(order, to); // 3. the only limited call } finally { inFlight.release(); // 4. always give the permit back } } fun send(order: Order): Booking { val to = addresses.lookup(order.customerId) // 1. unlimited work first inFlight.acquire() // 2. wait for a permit (parks a virtual thread) try { return delivery.book(order, to) // 3. the only limited call } finally { inFlight.release() // 4. always give the permit back } } Fan out one virtual thread per order, and collect in order. The executor block makes sure no order is still being sent when the method returns. List<Booking> sendAll(List<Order> orders) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { List<Future<Booking>> fs = new ArrayList<>(); for (Order o : orders) fs.add(perTask.submit(() -> send(o))); // 5. fork all List<Booking> bookings = new ArrayList<>(); for (Future<Booking> f : fs) bookings.add(f.get()); // 6. join in order return bookings; } } fun sendAll(orders: List<Order>): List<Booking> = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> val fs = orders.map { o -> perTask.submit(Callable { send(o) }) } // 5. fork all fs.map { it.get() } // 6. join in order } Check the timing with Little's law before you rely on it. The delivery step caps you at 20 / 0.15 s = 133 orders a second, so 3,000 orders take about 22.5 s, however many threads you start. If that's too slow, the fix is a higher limit agreed with the delivery company, not more threads.

Which design is right? newFixedThreadPool(50) of platform threads for all checkout handling newFixedThreadPool(50, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()) A virtual thread per checkout, and one shared Semaphore(50) around the stock call A virtual thread per checkout, and a new Semaphore(50) created inside each checkout's handler The limit belongs to the stock service, so put one semaphore on its client and share it. Both pools limit all of the checkout handling, not just the stock call. A semaphore created per checkout gives every checkout its own 50 permits, which limits nothing at all. What does this print? try (var perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) perTask.submit(() -> System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName().isEmpty())); } System.out.println("done"); true three times, then done done first, then true three times false three times, then done, because each thread is named pool-1-thread-N Nothing: the tasks are cancelled when the block ends Virtual threads have no name by default, so getName() is empty. close() at the end of the try block waits for all three tasks before done runs. The pool-1-thread-N names belong to the platform threads of newFixedThreadPool. A Semaphore(20) guards a 50 ms call. 1,000 virtual threads reach acquire() at the same moment. About how long until the last one gets a permit? About 50 ms About 2.5 s About 50 s Never: 980 threads fail with an exception Twenty permits on a 50 ms call serve 400 calls a second, so 1,000 calls need about 2.5 s, and the last thread waits for nearly all of it. Nothing fails: acquire() waits as long as it takes. Use tryAcquire with a timeout if that wait is too long. You submit 1 million tasks to Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). How many threads can it create? As many as there are cores 256, the scheduler's maximum A pool the JVM sizes from the workload Up to 1 million: one new virtual thread per task, with no limit The Javadoc says the number of threads it creates is unbounded. The core count and the 256 cap describe carrier threads, the platform threads that run the virtual threads. They don't limit how many virtual threads exist. From the lesson "Synchronizers: latch, barrier, semaphore, phaser": a developer writes try { sem.acquire(); call(); } finally { sem.release(); }. A thread is interrupted while it waits inside acquire(). What happens to the semaphore? Nothing: release() ignores threads that hold no permit acquire() retries automatically after the interrupt It gains a permit it never handed out, so the limit quietly grows by one release() throws IllegalMonitorStateException A Semaphore doesn't track who holds its permits. release() always adds one, even from a thread that never acquired, so every interrupted waiter raises the limit by one. Put acquire() on the line before the try, so finally runs only after a permit was really taken.
