h: Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores · Key terms
x: Thread.Builder The JDK 21 API that makes threads: Thread.ofVirtual() and Thread.ofPlatform(). Thread-per-task executor An executor that starts a new thread for every task and never reuses one. Fan-out Starting many calls at once, then collecting all their results. Semaphore A counter of permits. acquire takes one or waits, release gives one back. Permit One unit of a semaphore's count: the right for one thread to be inside the guarded code. Bulkhead A limit on how many calls may be inside one slow service at once, so it can't use up everything. Load shedding Turning work away quickly when you're over capacity, instead of letting it queue. Which executor gives every task its own new virtual thread? Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). It has no pool, no queue and no limit. What does close() on an ExecutorService do (JDK 19 and later)? It calls shutdown() and then waits until every submitted task has finished. Should you pool virtual threads? No. Create one per task, and limit the scarce resource with a shared Semaphore. Where does the Semaphore that protects a database belong? One per resource, shared by all callers, for example a field on the object that talks to the database. One per request limits nothing. Semaphore(20) guards a call that takes 100 ms. What is the most calls per second? 200 (20 / 0.1 s). Why put acquire() before the try and release() in finally? So a thread that fails to acquire never releases a permit it didn't get, and a thread whose call throws always gives its permit back. How do you make a wait at a semaphore fail fast? tryAcquire(timeout, unit) returns false if no permit arrives in time, so you can turn the request away.

h: Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores · Go deeper
x: Limits on calls at once and limits on calls per second are different things. A semaphore limits how many calls are in flight. Many web services instead publish a rate, such as 300 requests a second. Little's law connects the two only while the latency stays the same. Twenty in flight at 100 ms is 200 a second, but if the service slows to 400 ms, the same 20 permits give 50 a second, while a rate limiter would happily let 300 a second through and pile them up inside the slow service. If the rule is a rate, use a rate limiter. If it's connections or calls at once, use a semaphore. Some programs use both. Fair or not. new Semaphore(20) is not fair: a thread that calls acquire() just as a permit comes free can take it ahead of threads that have waited longer. That gives a little more throughput. new Semaphore(20, true) hands permits out in arrival order, which keeps the worst wait shorter. For a checkout, where a few very slow customers hurt more than a little lost throughput, fair is often the better choice. Very many waiters. Thousands of virtual threads parked on one semaphore are fine. Each release() wakes one waiter, and each waiter costs one parked virtual thread. With hundreds of thousands of waiters, the bigger problem is time: the last waiter waits for everyone ahead of it. A bounded wait with tryAcquire keeps that under control and turns overload into fast, honest errors. Structured fan-out. The try-with-resources block makes sure that every thread the method started has finished when it returns. What it doesn't do is stop the other tasks when one fails. Lesson 5 of this track builds that behavior with plain executors, and then shows the JDK's own API for it.

h: Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps · A hot pan on JDK 21: how synchronized pinned a virtual thread
x:
A hot pan a waiter can't put down: on JDK 21 to 23 a virtual thread holding a synchronized monitor pins its carrier (a 343 ms gap, 3 pins), a ReentrantLock unmounts, and JDK 24 cooled the pan Let's start with a cache the shop really needs. The shop also sells to customers abroad, so the checkout shows each price in the customer's own money. For that it needs an exchange rate, such as how many dollars one euro buys. A rates service on another computer answers in about 100 ms, and rates change only a few times a day, so the shop keeps each rate after the first lookup. This lesson's lab calls the class FxRateCache (FX is short for foreign exchange). Many virtual threads ask it at once, so it needs a lock. Here is the version most of us would write first: Java // Naive on JDK 21: the slow call runs while the lock is held public synchronized BigDecimal rate(String pair) { // pair: "EURUSD" is euros to dollars BigDecimal r = rates.get(pair); if (r == null) { r = ratesService.apply(pair); // 100 ms over the network, inside the lock rates.put(pair, r); } return r; } Kotlin // Naive on JDK 21: the slow call runs while the lock is held @Synchronized // the same JVM lock as Java's synchronized fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal = // pair: "EURUSD" is euros to dollars rates.getOrPut(pair) { ratesService.apply(pair) } // 100 ms over the network, inside the lock synchronized takes the lock that every Java object has built in, called a monitor: one thread at a time gets in, and the others wait at the door. The code is correct. Each rate loads once, and the lab's first test passes as it stands. The trouble is what a monitor did to a virtual thread on JDK 21 to 23. A virtual thread is a cheap Java thread that runs on a few platform threads, each backed by a thread of the operating system and called a carrier. When a virtual thread waits, it normally unmounts: its saved stack goes to the heap, the memory where Java keeps its objects, and its carrier is free for another. Up to JDK 23, the JVM recorded the owner of a monitor as the carrier, not as the virtual thread. So a virtual thread holding a monitor could not unmount. If it had left, the lock would have seemed to belong to whichever virtual thread mounted on that carrier next. So it stayed, and its carrier blocked with it. That is pinning: a virtual thread reaches a blocking call but can't let go of its carrier. Here is the hot pan, part by part. The pan is the monitor. It's in the waiter's hands, because the JVM records the carrier as its owner. The slip can't go on the board, because the virtual thread can't unmount. And the waiter stands at the stove for the whole wait, because the carrier is blocked. On JDK 21 to 23, a slip waiting to take the pan was pinned too, so the waiters in line for the pan stood still as well. PinningDemo, in the Try it below, runs with one carrier, so a single pin stops everything. A small virtual thread, the ticker, has one modest job: note the time every 50 ms. Three other virtual threads each take a lock and sleep 100 ms inside it, standing in for the slow call. Predict first. If nothing pins, the ticker keeps its rhythm, and the longest gap between ticks stays near 50 ms. On JDK 21, on this busy 4-core machine, it printed: JDK 21.0.12.1, 1 carrier thread synchronized + sleep longest gap between ticks: 343 ms pinned events: 3 ReentrantLock + sleep longest gap between ticks: 102 ms pinned events: 0 The ticker went quiet for 343 ms, about three sleeps in a row. Each sleeper held the only carrier for its whole 100 ms, and the JVM counted three pins. Then a ReentrantLock, the lock class from java.util.concurrent, did the same job, and the gap fell to 102 ms on this busy machine (51 ms on the next run). A ReentrantLock records the virtual thread as its owner and waits by parking, the JDK's way of setting a thread aside until someone wakes it, so it has always unmounted. It's a cool pan. On JDK 21 to 23, blocking while you hold a monitor pins the carrier. There, use a ReentrantLock around slow calls. Slow is the mild case. In 2024, engineers at Netflix described Java 21 services that stopped answering altogether. Every carrier was held by a virtual thread pinned while it waited to enter one synchronized block. The virtual thread that was next in line for that lock was unmounted, and it needed a free carrier to take the lock and let the others through. None was free, and none ever would be. The figure shows the shape. Four waiters stand at the stove waiting for the pan, and the slip that must take it next hangs on the board, waiting for a waiter. That was JDK 21. What does JDK 25 make of the same demo? Pin the only carrier Read PinningDemo. It runs with one carrier. The ticker notes the time every 50 ms, while three virtual threads each block for 100 ms: inside synchronized, inside a ReentrantLock, or inside a class's static initializer. Check your JDK with java -version. For each of the three lines, write down the longest gap between ticks and the number of pinned events you expect on that JDK. Run it. If you have both JDK 21 and JDK 25, run it on both: Gradle uses the JDK that JAVA_HOME points at. PinningDemo.java package workbench.vthreads.l04; import jdk.jfr.Recording; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedEvent; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** * One carrier thread, a ticker virtual thread that wants to tick every 50 ms, and three virtual * threads that each block for 100 ms in a different way. A pinned virtual thread blocks the only * carrier, so the ticker misses its ticks. JFR counts the pins. * *

Args: sync, lock or init to run one scenario (default: all three). */ public class PinningDemo { static final Object MONITOR = new Object(); static final ReentrantLock LOCK = new ReentrantLock(); // a class whose static initializer blocks, like one that loads the shop's price list over the network static class SlowPriceList { static final boolean READY; static { sleep(200); READY = true; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.setProperty("jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism", "1"); // one carrier makes pins easy to see System.out.println("JDK " + Runtime.version() + ", 1 carrier thread"); String only = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "all"; if (only.equals("all") || only.equals("sync")) run("synchronized + sleep", () -> { synchronized (MONITOR) { sleep(100); } }); if (only.equals("all") || only.equals("lock")) run("ReentrantLock + sleep", () -> { LOCK.lock(); try { sleep(100); } finally { LOCK.unlock(); } }); if (only.equals("all") || only.equals("init")) run("class init that sleeps", () -> { boolean ready = SlowPriceList.READY; }); } static void run(String label, Runnable blocker) throws Exception { Path file = Files.createTempFile("pinning", ".jfr"); try (Recording rec = new Recording()) { rec.enable("jdk.VirtualThreadPinned").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(20)); rec.start(); List ticks = new ArrayList<>(); Thread ticker = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { ticks.add(System.nanoTime()); sleep(50); } }); sleep(10); List workers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) workers.add(Thread.ofVirtual().start(blocker)); for (Thread w : workers) w.join(); ticker.join(); rec.stop(); rec.dump(file); long maxGap = 0; for (int i = 1; i < ticks.size(); i++) maxGap = Math.max(maxGap, (ticks.get(i) - ticks.get(i - 1)) / 1_000_000); List pins = RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file).stream() .filter(e -> e.getEventType().getName().equals("jdk.VirtualThreadPinned")) // other recordings may add events .toList(); h: Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps · JDK 24 cools the pan: what still pins on JDK 25, and how JFR shows it
x: JDK 24 changed how monitors work (JEP 491; a JEP, a JDK Enhancement Proposal, is the design document for a change to Java). The JVM now records the virtual thread itself as the owner of a monitor. So a virtual thread can take, hold and release one on any carrier, and synchronized and Object.wait() unmount just as a ReentrantLock does. In the restaurant, JDK 24 hung a hook for hot pans on the board: the pan now travels with its slip. JDK 25 is the first long-term-support release with the fix, the kind of release that gets updates for years. Here is the same demo on JDK 25, on the same busy machine: JDK 25.0.5, 1 carrier thread synchronized + sleep longest gap between ticks: 52 ms pinned events: 0 ReentrantLock + sleep longest gap between ticks: 51 ms pinned events: 0 class init that sleeps longest gap between ticks: 216 ms pinned events: 1 reason: VM call to workbench.vthreads.l04.PinningDemo$SlowPriceList.<clinit> on stack The first line is the fix: no pin, and the ticker kept time. So on JDK 25, leave working synchronized code alone. Rewriting it buys you nothing. The third line shows a pan JEP 491 didn't cool. SlowPriceList has a static initializer, the code that sets up a class the first time anyone uses it. This one sleeps 200 ms, like a class that loads the shop's price list over the network. The JVM runs a static initializer through frames of its own, and it can't move those to the heap. So a virtual thread that blocks inside one is pinned, on JDK 21 and on JDK 25. The ticker lost 216 ms, and the JVM even named the reason: <clinit>, its name for a static initializer, was on the stack. This pin is easy to write by accident: Java class PriceList { // runs inside <clinit>: a network call here pins the first virtual thread that touches PriceList static final Map<String, BigDecimal> PRICES = loadFromPriceService(); } Kotlin object PriceList { // runs inside <clinit>: a network call here pins the first virtual thread that touches PriceList val prices: Map<String, BigDecimal> = loadFromPriceService() } A Kotlin object is set up in a static initializer too, so it pins the same way. Load slow things in a startup step, or lazily into a cache. The other pan that stays hot is a native frame: a call into code written in another language, such as C, through JNI (Java's old bridge to such code) or the newer Foreign Function and Memory API. If that native code calls back into Java and the Java code blocks, the virtual thread is pinned, because the JVM can't copy native frames to the heap. File reads look similar but have a different name. They block inside the operating system, so the virtual thread keeps its carrier, and the scheduler, the part of the JDK that puts virtual threads on carriers, adds a temporary carrier to make up for it. To find pins in a real program, ask JFR, the Java Flight Recorder: a recorder built into the JVM that writes down events while the program runs, cheaply enough for production. Its event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned is on by default for any pin longer than 20 ms, and it keeps the pinned thread's stack. On JDK 25 it also records the reason and the carrier, as the third line above shows: java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=pin.jfr,settings=profile -jar shop.jar jfr print --events jdk.VirtualThreadPinned --stack-depth 20 pin.jfr In a program that is already running, jcmd <pid> JFR.start settings=profile does the same (jcmd comes with the JDK, and <pid> is the number the operating system gives the running program). To catch shorter pins, add jdk.VirtualThreadPinned#threshold=5ms to the recording options. Older articles suggest -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full instead. That property worked on JDK 21 to 23, and JDK 24 removed it. JDK 25 ignores it without a word, like a smoke alarm with no battery: a quiet run proves nothing. On JDK 25, class initializers and native frames still pin. Keep JFR's pinned event on, and fix what it reports. Pins are about carriers. The next trap never touches a carrier, and it hides in code that was right for years: a ThreadLocal. Read a pinned event Run PinningDemo once through Gradle (the previous Try it), so its classes are compiled. From labs/, run the static initializer scenario with a JFR recording, then print the pinned events, with the commands below. Find the frame that names SlowPriceList. On JDK 25, also read the pinnedReason, blockingOperation and carrierThread fields. terminal java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=pin.jfr,settings=profile \ -cp vthreads/build/classes/java/demo workbench.vthreads.l04.PinningDemo init jfr print --events jdk.VirtualThreadPinned --stack-depth 10 pin.jfr One jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event of about 200 ms. On JDK 21 you get the stack, and it shows Thread.sleep called from PinningDemo$SlowPriceList.<clinit>(), which is enough. On JDK 25 the event also says blockingOperation = "LockSupport.park", pinnedReason = "VM call to workbench.vthreads.l04.PinningDemo$SlowPriceList.<clinit> on stack" and carrierThread = "ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1". Without --stack-depth, jfr print shows only the top 5 frames, which stop before the initializer. jdk.jfr.Recording (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps · The apron pocket: a ThreadLocal cache meets a million slips
x: A ThreadLocal is a variable with a separate value for each thread. Each thread that reads it sees its own copy, and no other thread can touch that copy. It works on virtual threads exactly as on platform threads. The trap is one popular use: a ThreadLocal as a cache. The shop prints a timestamp on every receipt. The old class for that, SimpleDateFormat, is not thread-safe: two threads using one formatter at once can print garbage. So for years people kept one per thread: Java // SimpleDateFormat isn't thread-safe, so keep one per thread static final ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> FORMAT = ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSS'Z'")); Kotlin // SimpleDateFormat isn't thread-safe, so keep one per thread val FORMAT: ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> = ThreadLocal.withInitial { SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSS'Z'") } Picture the old restaurant from The thread-per-request wall, with its 200 waiters, each with an apron pocket. On his first order, each waiter puts a pen in his pocket and uses it all evening. That's 200 pens, bought once. The pocket is the ThreadLocal, the pen is the formatter, and withInitial buys a pen whenever a pocket is empty. With slips, the pocket moves to the slip, because each virtual thread has its own thread-local values. Every order is a new slip with an empty pocket. So every order buys a new pen, uses it once and throws it away when the meal ends. A million orders, a million pens. ThreadLocalCostDemo, in the Try it below, counts the pens. It formats 100,000 timestamps three ways. Predict the three counts before you look: ThreadLocal cache, pool of 8 platform threads formatters built: 8 time: 610 ms ThreadLocal cache, virtual thread per task formatters built: 100,000 time: 1,019 ms shared DateTimeFormatter, virtual threads formatters built: 1 time: 633 ms Eight pool threads built eight formatters. One virtual thread per task built 100,000, and nothing failed. The cache did exactly as it was told, a hundred thousand times: build, use once, throw away. It's the busiest cache in the shop, and it never caches anything. You'd only notice it as extra work for the garbage collector, the part of the JVM that frees objects nobody uses. Per-thread buffers are worse, because they hold memory for as long as the thread lives. A 64 KB scratch buffer in a ThreadLocal<byte[]> was 13 MB on 200 threads. On 100,000 live virtual threads it's 6.4 GB. The third line is the fix the lab asks for. DateTimeFormatter, from java.time, is immutable: once built, nothing can change it, so any number of threads can use one at the same moment. Here the picture breaks, in our favor. Two waiters can't write with one pen at once, but a thousand threads can format with one immutable formatter, because formatting changes nothing inside it. So there are three fixes, in order of preference. Share an immutable object when one exists. If the object is costly and not thread-safe, keep a small shared pool of it, not one per thread. And if it's cheap, just create it where you need it. A ThreadLocal also carries a request's details, such as the customer's id for the log. That still works within one virtual thread. But the value doesn't follow the work into threads you start, and it stays until someone calls remove(). Lesson 5 of this track has a better tool for that job. To list every ThreadLocal a program sets on virtual threads, run it with -Djdk.traceVirtualThreadLocals=true. It's an unsupported diagnostic property, present on JDK 21 and 25, that prints a stack trace each time a virtual thread sets one. A ThreadLocal cache builds one object per thread, and with virtual threads that means one per task. Share an immutable object instead. Hot pans and apron pockets are traps you can fix in code. The last trap is a limit, and no code makes it go away. Count the formatters Read ThreadLocalCostDemo. It formats 100,000 receipt timestamps with a ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> on a pool of 8 platform threads, then with the same cache and one virtual thread per task, then with one shared DateTimeFormatter. Write down the three "formatters built" numbers you expect. Run it, and compare the times as well. h: Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps · Chopping onions: work that only computes gains nothing
x:
Virtual threads make waiting cheap. They do nothing for computing. There are as many carriers as cores, so at most that many virtual threads compute at the same moment, which is exactly what a fixed pool of that size gives you. CpuBoundDemo, in the Try it below, checks it. Each of 64 tasks computes a checksum of a 1 MB buffer 20 times. A checksum is a short fingerprint of some data, and computing one is pure work for the processor, with no waiting. The tasks run on a pool of 4 platform threads, then with one virtual thread each. Predict which line wins: fixed pool of 4 platform threads 64 tasks in 655 ms virtual thread per task 64 tasks in 563 ms Nearly a tie, with the virtual line a little ahead. Is that a gain? Not really. Two more runs gave the same small lead, so we swapped the order of the two lines in a copy of the demo. Then the pool won one run and lost the next. On this busy machine, warm-up and noise decide the last 15 percent. Compare that with lesson 1 of this track, where the same switch finished 2,000 sleeping tasks eight times faster. It's worse than no gain, because there is no time slicing: nothing takes a carrier away from a virtual thread that computes. That is the waiter from How virtual threads work who chops onions with his slip in his pocket. Say the shop resizes product photos on virtual threads, and each photo takes 3 seconds of pure computing. Four of those on a 4-core machine hold every carrier for 3 seconds. Every checkout waits behind them, even one that needs a single millisecond of processor time. So keep heavy computing on a bounded pool of platform threads, and let the virtual thread wait for it: Java private final ExecutorService cpu = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()); Photo publish(Photo original) throws Exception { Photo small = cpu.submit(() -> resizer.resize(original)).get(); // heavy computing on a bounded pool return storage.save(small); // blocking I/O stays on the virtual thread } Kotlin private val cpu = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()) fun publish(original: Photo): Photo { val small = cpu.submit(Callable { resizer.resize(original) }).get() // heavy computing on a bounded pool return storage.save(small) // blocking I/O stays on the virtual thread } In the restaurant, the waiter hands the onions to the prep cooks in the back, clips his slip to the board and goes back to his tables. In code, the virtual thread parks in get(), so it holds no carrier while the pool computes. The operating system time-slices those pool threads against the carriers, so checkouts keep moving. The line between waiting and computing is fuzzy for work that does a bit of both. Reading a small request is fine on a virtual thread. Anything that computes for tens of milliseconds without blocking, such as resizing images, compressing files or building a large PDF, belongs on the pool. Virtual threads give scale to waiting, not to computing. Give heavy computing a bounded pool of its own. That's the last trap. In the lab you unpin the rates cache and retire the receipt's ThreadLocal. Compute on virtual threads Read CpuBoundDemo. Each of 64 tasks computes a checksum of a 1 MB buffer 20 times: a fixed amount of pure computing. Predict which line finishes first: a pool sized to your cores, or one virtual thread per task. Run it twice. Then run it with -Pargs='256 20' and predict again: four times the tasks. Args: number of tasks, hash rounds per task. Default: 64 20. */ public class CpuBoundDemo { static final byte[] DATA = new byte[1 << 20]; public static void main(String[] args) { int tasks = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 64; int rounds = args.length > 1 ? With 256 tasks both take about four times as long or more (3,887 and 3,496 ms here). The work is limited by cores, and both setups use all of them.

h: Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps · Java and Kotlin
x: Taking the monitor out of the slow path Java: synchronized becomes ReentrantLock // JDK 21 to 23: this pins for the whole fetch public synchronized BigDecimal rate(String pair) { return rates.computeIfAbsent(pair, ratesService); } // any JDK: a java.util.concurrent lock parks a waiting virtual thread instead private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); public BigDecimal rate(String pair) { lock.lock(); try { return rates.computeIfAbsent(pair, ratesService); // rates is a plain HashMap } finally { lock.unlock(); } } Kotlin: @Synchronized becomes withLock // JDK 21 to 23: @Synchronized and synchronized(lock) {} are monitors, and pin the same way @Synchronized fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal = rates.getOrPut(pair) { ratesService.apply(pair) } // any JDK: kotlin.concurrent.withLock does lock, try, finally and unlock for you private val lock = ReentrantLock() fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal = lock.withLock { rates.getOrPut(pair) { ratesService.apply(pair) } // rates is a plain HashMap } Both versions make the same change: the monitor goes, and a ReentrantLock takes its place around the same lines. Kotlin has no synchronized keyword, but @Synchronized and the synchronized(lock) { } function compile to the same JVM monitor instructions as Java, so they pin on JDK 21 to 23 in exactly the same way. The Kotlin fix is shorter, because the standard library's withLock writes the lock(), the try and the finally { unlock() } for you, and it's inline, so it costs nothing at run time. Notice what neither version does: it doesn't let two different rates load at the same time. That needs one lock per key, and on JDK 25 it's the only reason left to touch this code.

h: Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps · Worked example
x: Find and fix a pin from a JFR recording (JDK 21) The shop's checkout runs on JDK 21, with one virtual thread per checkout. In a load test, the slowest checkouts jump from 200 ms to several seconds, while the processor stays mostly idle. Record two minutes of the test with JFR, then print the pinned events. (jcmd comes with the JDK and talks to a running JVM, and pgrep -f checkout finds the process number of the running checkout program.) jcmd $(pgrep -f checkout) JFR.start name=pins settings=profile duration=120s filename=pins.jfr jfr print --events jdk.VirtualThreadPinned --stack-depth 20 pins.jfr | head -40 Read the stack in one event. The pin lasts as long as one call to the rates service, and above the network read sits a synchronized method of the cache. jdk.VirtualThreadPinned { duration = 103 ms stackTrace = [ java.lang.VirtualThread.parkOnCarrierThread(boolean, long) ... sun.nio.ch.NioSocketImpl.read(byte[], int, int) ... workbench.vthreads.l04.FxRateCache.rate(String) <- synchronized ] } Replace the monitor with a ReentrantLock, and keep the same "load once" behavior. The lock still lets one caller in at a time, but a waiting virtual thread now parks and frees its carrier. private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); public BigDecimal rate(String pair) { lock.lock(); // 1. take the lock (parks, doesn't pin) try { BigDecimal r = rates.get(pair); if (r == null) { r = ratesService.apply(pair); // 2. slow call: the thread can unmount here rates.put(pair, r); } return r; } finally { lock.unlock(); // 3. always release } } private val lock = ReentrantLock() fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal = lock.withLock { // 1. take the lock (parks, doesn't pin) rates[pair] ?: ratesService.apply(pair) // 2. slow call: the thread can unmount here .also { rates[pair] = it } } // 3. withLock always releases Check with the same recording under the same load: no jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events from FxRateCache, and the slowest checkouts back near 200 ms. Then put the move to JDK 25 on the plan, so the next synchronized inside a library doesn't need the same fix.

h: Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps · Quiz
x: A shop's program runs on JDK 25. Its old database code has synchronized blocks around each query. You are moving request handling to virtual threads. What should you do about those blocks? Replace every one with ReentrantLock before the switch, or the program will pin Nothing for pinning: on JDK 24 and later they don't pin. Keep a JFR recording to catch the pins that remain Run with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full and fix what it prints Wrap each query in Thread.ofPlatform().start(...) JEP 491 (JDK 24) lets a virtual thread hold a monitor without pinning, so on JDK 25 these blocks are fine. Rewriting them is the JDK 21 advice, and it's tempting because so many articles still give it. -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads no longer exists on JDK 24 and later, so it would print nothing and prove nothing. Which tool shows you, on JDK 25, that a virtual thread pinned its carrier for 180 ms, and why? jstack <pid> Thread.getAllStackTraces() from a debug page The JFR event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned, printed with jfr print -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short jdk.VirtualThreadPinned is recorded for pins over 20 ms by default and keeps the stack, and on JDK 25 it also records the reason and the carrier. jstack and getAllStackTraces() show platform threads, not parked virtual threads, and the trace property was removed in JDK 24. The shop's checkout computes a checksum of each request with a ThreadLocal<MessageDigest> cache (a MessageDigest computes checksums). It moves from a 200-thread pool to one virtual thread per request and serves 1 million requests. About how many MessageDigest objects does it create? 200, the same as before One per carrier thread, so about the number of cores About 1 million, one per request One, because virtual threads share their ThreadLocal values Each virtual thread has its own thread-local values, and each request runs on a new virtual thread, so withInitial runs once per request. The carriers don't matter: the JDK keeps a virtual thread's thread locals apart from its carrier's. Share a thread-safe object, or create one per call on purpose. An 8-core program resizes 10,000 product photos, and each takes about 50 ms of pure computing. It runs on newFixedThreadPool(8). What happens if you switch it to newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()? It takes about the same time, about 62 s, because only 8 can compute at once either way It finishes in about 50 ms, because all 10,000 run at once It finishes about 8 times faster It deadlocks, because virtual threads can't run computing work There are 8 carriers, so at most 8 virtual threads compute at once: 10,000 × 50 ms / 8 = 62.5 s, the same as the pool. Virtual threads help only when tasks spend their time waiting. With no time slicing, they can also hold up other virtual threads in the same program. From the lesson "Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal": SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe. Which fix works equally well on a platform pool and on one virtual thread per task, with no per-thread state at all? Wrap every format call in synchronized One shared, immutable DateTimeFormatter A ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> A volatile SimpleDateFormat field An immutable object is safe to share with any number of threads, so it needs no copies and no locking. The ThreadLocal works on a pool but becomes one formatter per task on virtual threads. synchronized is correct but makes every caller wait in line. volatile makes the reference visible but leaves the formatter's insides open to races.

h: Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps · Key terms
x: Pinning A virtual thread stuck on its carrier during a blocking call, so the carrier blocks too. Monitor The lock behind synchronized and @Synchronized, built into every Java object. JEP 491 The JDK 24 change that lets virtual threads hold monitors without pinning. Static initializer The code that sets up a class the first time it's used (static {}, static fields, a Kotlin object). The JVM calls it <clinit>. JFR Java Flight Recorder: the JVM's built-in recorder of events, cheap enough for production. jdk.VirtualThreadPinned The JFR event recorded when a virtual thread blocks while pinned for longer than the threshold. ThreadLocal cache Keeping one copy of an object per thread to reuse it. Useless when every task gets a new thread. What does it mean that a virtual thread is pinned? It reaches a blocking call but can't unmount, so it stays on its carrier and the carrier blocks with it. Does blocking inside synchronized pin a virtual thread on JDK 25? No. Since JDK 24 (JEP 491), monitors don't pin. On JDK 21 to 23 they do. What still pins a virtual thread on JDK 25? Blocking while a static initializer (<clinit>) or a native frame (JNI, or a Foreign Function call that calls back into Java) is on its stack. How do you detect pinning on JDK 24 and later? The JFR event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned (on by default, 20 ms threshold). -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads was removed in JDK 24. Why does a ThreadLocal cache stop working with one virtual thread per task? Each task runs on a new virtual thread with empty thread-local values, so the cached object is built once per task and thrown away. Do virtual threads speed up work that only computes? No. At most one virtual thread per carrier (per core) computes at once, and there is no time slicing. Kotlin replacement for @Synchronized around a slow call on JDK 21? private val lock = ReentrantLock() and lock.withLock { ... } from kotlin.concurrent.

h: Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps · Go deeper
x: Why monitors pinned in the first place. Before JDK 24, HotSpot recorded the owner of a monitor as the operating system thread that held it. If a virtual thread could unmount while holding a monitor, another virtual thread mounted on the same carrier would seem to own it too. Rather than redesign monitors for JDK 21, the team behind virtual threads shipped with pinning and a warning. JEP 491 changed the JVM to record the virtual thread as the owner, so the thread can move freely. Object.wait() on JDK 21. A virtual thread in Object.wait() was pinned too, but the scheduler made up for it by adding a temporary carrier, up to jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize. That kept wait-heavy code alive, at the cost of extra operating system threads. Blocking on monitor entry got no such help, which is why the stall in this lesson's figure was possible. Waiting for someone else's class initializer. On JDK 25, a virtual thread that waits for another thread to finish initializing a class is pinned while it waits. JDK 26 changed that case so the waiting thread unmounts. The thread that runs the slow initializer itself still pins, so the advice stays the same: keep slow work out of static initializers. Testing for pins. The lab's JFR test is a pattern you can copy into your own tests: start a jdk.jfr.Recording with jdk.VirtualThreadPinned enabled, run a realistic slice of work on virtual threads, stop and dump the recording, and check that it has no events. Warm up first, so one-time class loading doesn't show up as a pin. On JDK 24 and later, such a test catches static initializer and native pins. On JDK 21, it also catches every synchronized around a slow call. Inheritable thread locals. A new thread copies its parent's InheritableThreadLocal values by default, and that includes virtual threads. Creating a million virtual threads from a thread with large inheritable values copies them a million times. Thread.ofVirtual().inheritInheritableThreadLocals(false) turns the copy off for threads that don't need it.

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · A failed checkout keeps working: what an executor fan-out leaves out
x: Let's set up the example first. A fan-out, from lesson 3 of this track, starts several calls at once and then collects all their answers. Each call is a subtask: a piece of a bigger job that runs on a thread of its own, here a virtual thread, the cheap kind the JDK sets aside whenever it waits. To save time, the shop's checkout now asks two services at the same moment instead of one after the other. The stock service says whether the items are in the warehouse, and the bank says whether the payment is approved. If the items are sold out, the bank's answer is useless. Here is that fan-out in the lesson 3 shape. An executor is an object that runs tasks for you, and submit hands back a Future, a handle on a result that arrives later: Java try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<Approval> bank = perTask.submit(() -> theBank.approve(order)); // 2 s on a bad day Future<Stock> stock = perTask.submit(() -> stockService.check(order)); // fails at 100 ms: sold out return new Receipt(stock.get(), bank.get()); } Kotlin Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> val bank = perTask.submit(Callable { theBank.approve(order) }) // 2 s on a bad day val stock = perTask.submit(Callable { stockService.check(order) }) // fails at 100 ms: sold out Receipt(stock.get(), bank.get()) } Predict when the checkout fails. The stock service says "sold out" after 100 ms, so a careful program would give up at 100 ms. LeakDemo, in the Try it below, runs this exact shape as variant A: A: an executor per checkout, closed by try-with-resources 2,027 ms bank: answered, but nobody needs the answer 2,069 ms checkout failed: stock service: sold out The checkout was doomed at 100 ms, and it failed at 2 seconds. stock.get() threw at 100 ms, as it should. But leaving the try block runs close(), which waits for every task, and nothing told the bank call to stop. The bank, true to form, took its full two seconds to answer a question nobody was asking any more. Many programs keep one long-lived executor in a field instead. LeakDemo tries that too, as variant B: B: one shared executor 102 ms checkout failed: stock service: sold out 2,001 ms bank: answered, but nobody needs the answer Now the checkout fails fast, at 102 ms. But the bank call runs on for another two seconds, for a checkout that is long gone. It's the helper still in the cellar, fetching wine for a table that has left. A call like that holds a connection, and maybe a permit from lesson 3's semaphore. Under load these orphans pile up, and nothing in a thread dump, the list of every thread a program has, says which checkout they belonged to. Three things are missing, and they are the same three in every fan-out: A failure cancels nothing. To stop the others, you'd call cancel(true) on each future, in every fan-out, on every error path. The subtasks' lives aren't tied to the code. A Future is a value you can store anywhere, so nothing promises that the threads a method started have ended when it returns. The order's details don't follow the work. A ThreadLocal is a variable with a separate value for each thread, so one set by the checkout, such as the order id for the log, is empty in the subtasks. Structured concurrency fixes the first two with one rule: a subtask can't outlive the block of code that started it, just as a local variable can't outlive its method. Scoped values, at the end of this lesson, fix the third. Waiting for every subtask is half the job. When one fails, the others must stop too. So we need a head waiter who calls the helpers back. Let's build one. Watch the orphaned call Read LeakDemo. Variant A opens an executor per checkout in try-with-resources. Variant B uses one shared executor. For each, predict when the checkout fails and whether the bank call finishes. Run it with the command below. Fix variant A by hand. Wrap stock.get() in a try, call bank.cancel(true) in the catch (ExecutionException e), then rethrow e. Run it again. LeakDemo.java package workbench.vthreads.l05; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** * A checkout asks two services at the same time: the bank, which takes 2 s on a bad day, * and the stock service, which says "sold out" after 100 ms. Once the stock check has failed, * the bank's answer is useless. Watch what happens to the bank call anyway. */ public class LeakDemo { static volatile long t0; static void log(String what) { System.out.printf("%,7d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, what); } static String bank() throws InterruptedException { try { Thread.sleep(2_000); // the bank, on a bad day log("bank: answered, but nobody needs the answer"); return "approved"; } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("bank: interrupted, stopped early"); throw e; } } static String stock() throws InterruptedException { Thread.sleep(100); throw new IllegalStateException("stock service: sold out"); } // A: an executor per checkout, in try-with-resources static String checkoutA() throws Exception { try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<String> bank = perTask.submit(LeakDemo::bank); Future<String> stock = perTask.submit(LeakDemo::stock); return stock.get() + " " + bank.get(); // throws at 100 ms... } // ...but close() waits for the bank } static final ExecutorService SHARED = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); // B: one long-lived executor for the whole shop static String checkoutB() throws Exception { Future<String> bank = SHARED.submit(LeakDemo::bank); Future<String> stock = SHARED.submit(LeakDemo::stock); return stock.get() + " " + bank.get(); // throws at 100 ms, and returns } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("A: an executor per checkout, closed by try-with-resources"); t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { checkoutA(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { log("checkout failed: " + e.getCause().getMessage()); } System.out.println("B: one shared executor"); t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { checkoutB(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { log("checkout failed: " + e.getCause().getMessage()); } Thread.sleep(2_500); // stay alive to see what B left behind SHARED.close(); } } ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l05.LeakDemo labs/vthreads/src/demo/java/workbench/vthreads/l05/LeakDemo.java LeakDemo.kt package workbench.vthreads.l05 import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** * A checkout asks two services at the same time: the bank, which takes 2 s on a bad day, * and the stock service, which says "sold out" after 100 ms. Once the stock check has failed, * the bank's answer is useless. Watch what happens to the bank call anyway. */ @Volatile private var t0 = 0L private fun log(what: String) = println("%,7d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, what)) private fun bank(): String = try { Thread.sleep(2_000) // the bank, on a bad day log("bank: answered, but nobody needs the answer") "approved" } catch (e: InterruptedException) { log("bank: interrupted, stopped early") throw e } private fun stock(): String { Thread.sleep(100) throw IllegalStateException("stock service: sold out") } // A: an executor per checkout, closed by use {} private fun checkoutA(): String = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> val bank = perTask.submit(Callable { bank() }) val stock = perTask.submit(Callable { stock() }) stock.get() + " " + bank.get() // throws at 100 ms... } // ...but close() waits for the bank private val shared = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() // B: one long-lived executor for the whole shop private fun checkoutB(): String { val bank = shared.submit(Callable { bank() }) val stock = shared.submit(Callable { stock() }) return stock.get() + " " + bank.get() // throws at 100 ms, and returns } fun main() { println("A: an executor per checkout, closed by use {}") t0 = System.nanoTime() try { checkoutA() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { log("checkout failed: ${e.cause?.message}") } println("B: one shared executor") t0 = System.nanoTime() try { checkoutB() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { log("checkout failed: ${e.cause?.message}") } Thread.sleep(2_500) // stay alive to see what B left behind shared.close() } ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l05.LeakDemoKt labs/vthreads/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/vthreads/l05/LeakDemo.kt A: the bank call finishes at about 2,000 ms, and only then does the checkout fail, although the answer was known at 100 ms (2,027 and 2,069 ms in a run here). B: the checkout fails at about 100 ms (102 ms here), and the bank call still finishes at about 2,000 ms, for a checkout that is long gone. After your fix, A prints bank: interrupted, stopped early and fails at about 100 ms (128 ms here). That fixes one fan-out. Every other fan-out in the program needs the same code on every error path. h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · The head waiter: a scope that owns its subtasks
x: A head waiter who calls the helpers back: a scope forks, fails fast so join throws at about 100 ms, and close waits for every subtask; a scoped value is a note pinned to the order Here is the head waiter again, part by part. He is the scope: an object that starts subtasks and owns them. Sending a helper is fork, which starts a subtask on a new virtual thread. Waiting at the table is join, which waits for the subtasks. Calling the others back when one returns with bad news is fail fast: the first failure cancels the rest, and join reports it at once. And not leaving the table until every helper is back is close. When the block ends, every thread the scope started has ended, whether the block returned, threw or was interrupted. In code the shape is always the same. Both versions use this lesson's lab class, FailFastScope, a small scope you build yourself on a plain executor: Java try (var scope = new FailFastScope()) { // the head waiter Supplier<Approval> bank = scope.fork(() -> theBank.approve(order)); Supplier<Stock> stock = scope.fork(() -> stockService.check(order)); scope.join(); // waits, or throws the first failure return new Receipt(stock.get(), bank.get()); } // close(): no subtask is still running Kotlin FailFastScope().use { scope -> // the head waiter val bank = scope.fork { theBank.approve(order) } val stock = scope.fork { stockService.check(order) } scope.join() // waits, or throws the first failure Receipt(stock.get(), bank.get()) } // close(): no subtask is still running Read it aloud: send two helpers, wait for both or for the first bad news, and don't leave until they're back. fork returns a handle, a Supplier whose get() gives the subtask's result after join. Let's trace the smallest case, with the stock check failing and the bank slow: At 0 ms, the scope forks both subtasks, each on a new virtual thread. At 100 ms, the stock subtask throws. Its wrapper records the failure as the first one and cancels the scope. Cancel means interrupt: a signal that wakes a waiting thread with an InterruptedException. The bank subtask, blocked in a network read, wakes up that way. The bank subtask's failure arrives second, so it doesn't replace the first. join() sees the first failure and throws it, at about 100 ms. close() waits until the bank thread has really finished. A subtask forked after the cancel never runs, and its handle throws if you ask for a result. How does the lab do this? Each forked task runs inside a small wrapper. If the task throws, the wrapper records the failure with AtomicReference.compareAndSet(null, failure), read as "store it only if nobody stored one first", so exactly one failure wins. Then it calls shutdownNow() on the executor, which interrupts every running subtask and refuses new ones. An interrupt stops code that waits in sleep, a network read, a lock or a queue, which covers almost all waiting on virtual threads. It doesn't stop a loop that computes and never checks the interrupt flag. In Java, cancelling is a request the code has to cooperate with. Here the head waiter picture breaks: a real helper hears his name called, but a subtask that never waits and never checks hears nothing. One detail looks right and is wrong. You might cancel each sibling with future.cancel(true). That interrupts the thread, but it also marks the future as done at once. On JDK 21, newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor counts a task as finished as soon as its future is done. So close() can return while the cancelled task still runs its finally block, giving back a permit, say. shutdownNow() interrupts without touching the futures, so close() keeps waiting until each thread has truly ended. The lab's close() test catches exactly this bug, which is a good reason to prefer the JDK's own scope once you can use it. A subtask must never outlive the block that forked it. Make the scope wait for threads, not for futures. Check yourself: in your FailFastScope, the stock check fails at 100 ms. The bank call is blocked in a network read, and a third subtask runs a 3-second loop that computes and never checks the interrupt flag. When does join() throw, and when does close() return? join() throws at about 100 ms with the stock failure. close() returns at about 3 seconds: the interrupt stops the network read but not the loop, and close() waits for every thread. We built a head waiter by hand. The JDK has one of its own, still a preview in JDK 25. Let's see what that means. With a shared executor, the failed checkout leaves its bank call running, like a helper still in the cellar. In a scope, the failure cancels it, and close() waits until it has ended.

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · StructuredTaskScope: the JDK's own scope, still a preview in JDK 25
x: StructuredTaskScope, in java.util.concurrent, is the JDK's scope. It's a preview API. An API is the set of classes and methods a library offers, and a preview one is finished and fully specified, and still allowed to change its mind in the next release. The compiler and the JVM refuse it unless you pass --enable-preview. Its current shape arrived in JDK 25 (JEP 505, the fifth preview). It stayed a preview in JDK 26 (JEP 525) and JDK 27 (JEP 533). JEP 543 makes it final in JDK 28, due in March 2027, with the JDK 27 API unchanged. So the Gradle labs, which must run on JDK 21, leave it out, and this lesson's demo lives in labs/vthreads/preview/ as a single-file program for JDK 25. Here is the checkout in the JDK 25 shape: Java Receipt checkout(Order order) throws InterruptedException { try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // fail on the first failure Subtask<Approval> bank = scope.fork(() -> theBank.approve(order)); Subtask<Stock> stock = scope.fork(() -> stockService.check(order)); scope.join(); // JDK 25: throws StructuredTaskScope.FailedException return new Receipt(stock.get(), bank.get()); } // close(): cancels what is left and waits for it } Kotlin fun checkout(order: Order): Receipt = StructuredTaskScope.open<Any>().use { scope -> // fail on the first failure val bank = scope.fork(Callable { theBank.approve(order) }) val stock = scope.fork(Callable { stockService.check(order) }) scope.join() // JDK 25: throws StructuredTaskScope.FailedException Receipt(stock.get(), bank.get()) } // close(): cancels what is left and waits for it It has the same shape as FailFastScope, with stricter rules. Subtasks run on virtual threads. Calling get() before join() throws IllegalStateException. Scopes must nest like blocks, and the JDK checks that you close them in that order. And a thread dump written as JSON, a structured text format (jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json threads.json), groups each scope's threads under it, so you can see which checkout a thread belongs to. ScopeDemo, in the Try it below, is LeakDemo's checkout written this way. Predict the timeline first. On JDK 25, run from labs/, it printed: $ java --enable-preview --source 25 vthreads/preview/ScopeDemo.java 135 ms [order-42] bank: interrupted, stopped early 165 ms [order-42] checkout failed: stock service: sold out 165 ms [-] done: the binding has ended, and no subtask is still running That's the careful head waiter. The stock failure cancelled the bank call, join() threw at once, and nothing was still running when the block ended. The times are a little over 100 ms because the first run also loads the classes it needs. The [order-42] on each line comes from a scoped value, the topic of the next section. Leave out the flag, and javac, the Java compiler, stops at the first line that uses the API: error: StructuredTaskScope is a preview API and is disabled by default. Kotlin's compiler doesn't check for preview APIs, and on JDK 25 the Kotlin jar even ran without the flag here. Don't lean on that: the API can change in the next JDK, flag or no flag. The scope's policy is a joiner, an object you pass to open that decides when join() returns and what it gives back. JDK 25 has four built in: Joiner.awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow(), the default: fail fast, and join() returns null. Joiner.allSuccessfulOrThrow(): fail fast, and join() returns the subtasks as a Stream<Subtask<T>>. Joiner.anySuccessfulResultOrThrow(): the first success wins, and the scope cancels the rest. Joiner.awaitAll(): wait for everything and never throw. You check each subtask's state(). A second argument changes the scope's settings, such as a timeout. Here the shop asks two delivery companies for a price and takes whichever answers first: Java try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.<Price>anySuccessfulResultOrThrow(), cf -> cf.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)))) { scope.fork(() -> fastPost.price(parcel)); scope.fork(() -> cheapPost.price(parcel)); return scope.join(); // the first price back; the slower call is cancelled } Kotlin StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.anySuccessfulResultOrThrow<Price>()) { cf -> cf.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)) }.use { scope -> scope.fork(Callable { fastPost.price(parcel) }) scope.fork(Callable { cheapPost.price(parcel) }) scope.join() // the first price back; the slower call is cancelled } If the 300 ms run out first, the scope cancels both calls, and join() throws StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException. Expect small edits whenever you change JDKs, because that is what preview means. JDK 26 renamed anySuccessfulResultOrThrow to anySuccessfulOrThrow, and allSuccessfulOrThrow now returns a List of results. In JDK 27 the built-in joiners make join() throw the ordinary checked ExecutionException, like Future.get(), instead of FailedException. Your lab scope already behaves that way. And articles from the JDK 21 days show new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure() with throwIfFailed(). That API is gone, and it doesn't compile on JDK 25. A preview API can change in the next release. Pin the JDK version, and keep preview code small and in one place. The scope calls the helpers back. One gap from the first section is left: the order's own details, which a ThreadLocal failed to carry into the subtasks. Run the scope on JDK 25 This one needs JDK 25 exactly, because --enable-preview works only for the JDK's own release. Check with java -version. It runs outside Gradle, as a single-file program, from labs/. Run ScopeDemo and compare its timeline with LeakDemo's. Look at the [order-42] on the bank's line: the subtask can read the checkout's scoped value. Make stock() return "in stock" after its sleep instead of throwing. Predict how long the checkout takes, then run it. Now open the scope with a timeout: StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow(), cf -> cf.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(500))) (in Kotlin, open(Joiner.awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow<Any>()) { cf -> cf.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)) }). Predict, then run. ScopeDemo.java (JDK 25 preview) // JDK 25 only. StructuredTaskScope is a preview API in JDK 25 (JEP 505). From labs/: // java --enable-preview --source 25 vthreads/preview/ScopeDemo.java // The checkout from LeakDemo, written with a scope. Not part of the Gradle build. import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope; import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope.Joiner; // for the Try it import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope.Subtask; public class ScopeDemo { static final ScopedValue<String> ORDER_ID = ScopedValue.newInstance(); static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String what) { System.out.printf("%,7d ms [%s] %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, ORDER_ID.orElse("-"), what); } static String bank() throws InterruptedException { try { Thread.sleep(2_000); // the bank, on a bad day log("bank: answered"); return "approved"; } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("bank: interrupted, stopped early"); throw e; } } static String stock() throws InterruptedException { Thread.sleep(100); throw new IllegalStateException("stock service: sold out"); } static String checkout() throws InterruptedException { try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // default joiner: fail on the first failure Subtask<String> bank = scope.fork(ScopeDemo::bank); Subtask<String> stock = scope.fork(ScopeDemo::stock); scope.join(); // throws FailedException at about 100 ms return stock.get() + " " + bank.get(); } // close(): every subtask has ended } static void handle() { try { log("checkout: " + checkout()); } catch (StructuredTaskScope.FailedException e) { log("checkout failed: " + e.getCause().getMessage()); } catch (StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException e) { log("checkout timed out"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { ScopedValue.where(ORDER_ID, "order-42").run(ScopeDemo::handle); // subtasks see order-42 too log("done: the binding has ended, and no subtask is still running"); } } java --enable-preview --source 25 vthreads/preview/ScopeDemo.java labs/vthreads/preview/ScopeDemo.java ScopeDemo.kt (JDK 25 preview) // JDK 25 only. StructuredTaskScope is a preview API in JDK 25 (JEP 505), called here from Kotlin. // Needs the Kotlin command-line compiler. From labs/: // kotlinc vthreads/preview/ScopeDemo.kt -include-runtime -d vthreads/build/scope-demo.jar // java --enable-preview -jar vthreads/build/scope-demo.jar // Not part of the Gradle build. In Kotlin code you would usually use coroutineScope instead. import java.time.Duration import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope.Joiner // for the Try it private val ORDER_ID: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance() private val t0 = System.nanoTime() private fun log(what: String) = println("%,7d ms [%s] %s".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, ORDER_ID.orElse("-"), what)) private fun bank(): String = try { Thread.sleep(2_000) // the bank, on a bad day log("bank: answered") "approved" } catch (e: InterruptedException) { log("bank: interrupted, stopped early") throw e } private fun stock(): String { Thread.sleep(100) throw IllegalStateException("stock service: sold out") } private fun checkout(): String = StructuredTaskScope.open<Any>().use { scope -> // default joiner: fail on the first failure val bank = scope.fork(Callable { bank() }) val stock = scope.fork(Callable { stock() }) scope.join() // throws FailedException at about 100 ms stock.get() + " " + bank.get() } // close(): every subtask has ended private fun handle() { try { log("checkout: ${checkout()}") } catch (e: StructuredTaskScope.FailedException) { log("checkout failed: ${e.cause?.message}") } catch (e: StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException) { log("checkout timed out") } } fun main() { ScopedValue.where(ORDER_ID, "order-42").run(Runnable { handle() }) // subtasks see order-42 too log("done: the binding has ended, and no subtask is still running") } kotlinc vthreads/preview/ScopeDemo.kt -include-runtime -d vthreads/build/scope-demo.jar && java --enable-preview -jar vthreads/build/scope-demo.jar labs/vthreads/preview/ScopeDemo.kt First run: a little after 100 ms the bank's line says interrupted, stopped early, then checkout failed: stock service: sold out, then the done line with [-], because the binding has ended (135, 165 and 165 ms in a run here; the Kotlin jar printed 144, 172 and 173 ms). When both succeed, the checkout arrives after about 2,000 ms (2,078 ms here), since the default joiner waits for every subtask. With the 500 ms timeout, the bank is interrupted at about 500 ms and the checkout reports checkout timed out (551 ms here). In every case the done line comes last: the scope never leaves a subtask running. JEP 505: Structured Concurrency (Fifth Preview) read JEP 533: Structured Concurrency (Seventh Preview) read

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · A note pinned to the order: scoped values replace request ThreadLocals
x: A checkout carries details that many methods need but few should have to pass along: the order id for the log, or the customer's name for the receipt. The usual tool has been a ThreadLocal, the apron pocket from lesson 4 of this track. For this job the pocket has three problems: Anyone can write in it. Any code can call set(), so the code that reads the value can't tell where it came from. Nobody empties it unless someone calls remove(). On a pooled thread, a value one task forgot is still there for the next. Its inheritance is a copy. An InheritableThreadLocal copies its values into every new thread, so that's one copy per subtask, and a later change in the parent never reaches the children. ScopedValueDemo, in the Try it below, shows the second problem first. A task on a one-thread pool sets the customer to ann and forgets to remove it. Then the next task on the same thread asks who its customer is: 1. next task, same pool thread: ThreadLocal=ann, ScopedValue=unbound That task never set anything, and it believes it's serving Ann. On a receipt, that's a stranger's name. A scoped value is the replacement. Picture a note pinned to the order: everyone who works on the order can read it, nobody can change it, and it comes off when the order closes. In code, you bind a value for the length of one call. Everything that call runs can read it, and nobody can change it. Scoped values are final in JDK 25 (JEP 506), so they need no flag: Java static final ScopedValue<String> CUSTOMER = ScopedValue.newInstance(); void handle(Order order) { ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, order.customer()).run(() -> checkout(order)); // bound only inside run() } static String receiptLine(String item) { return item + " for " + CUSTOMER.get(); // NoSuchElementException if nobody bound it } Kotlin val CUSTOMER: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance() fun handle(order: Order) { ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, order.customer).run(Runnable { checkout(order) }) // bound only inside run() } fun receiptLine(item: String): String = item + " for " + CUSTOMER.get() // NoSuchElementException if nobody bound it Map it back to the note. Pinning the note is where(...), the order being open is the call inside run(), reading the note is get(), and the note comes off when run() returns. There is no set(). To use another value for a nested call, bind again with where(...).run(...), and the outer value comes back when that call returns. isBound() and orElse(...) let code handle the case where nothing is bound, and call(...) is the version that returns a value and may throw. The rest of the demo shows each rule: 2. inside run(): ThreadLocal=null, ScopedValue=ann after run(): ThreadLocal=null, ScopedValue=unbound 3. nested: ThreadLocal=null, ScopedValue=ben outer again: ThreadLocal=null, ScopedValue=ann 4. plain thread: ThreadLocal=null, ScopedValue=unbound The fourth line is the rule to remember. A scoped value flows into subtasks forked in a StructuredTaskScope, as [order-42] did in ScopeDemo. The child doesn't get a copy: it reads the parent's binding, which is safe because nobody can change the binding, and the scope ends before the binding does. A thread you start yourself, or an executor task, could outlive the binding, so it gets nothing. Pass the value as an argument there. Here the note picture breaks a little. A paper note stays on the order for anyone who picks it up, even a helper borrowed from another table. A scoped value is visible only to code inside the call that bound it, and to that call's own scope. On JDK 25 that gives a clear split. Use scoped values for new request details today, with no flag. Their flow into subtasks needs StructuredTaskScope, which is still a preview. Keep ThreadLocal where a library requires it, and clear it in a finally. Details that belong to one call should live as long as that call. Bind them with a scoped value, and let nobody change them. In the lab you build the head waiter itself: FailFastScope, on a plain executor, with JDK 21 APIs only. ThreadLocal and ScopedValue side by side You need JDK 25 or later. Scoped values are final there, so this runs without --enable-preview. Read ScopedValueDemo and predict its six lines of output before you run it. Run it. Then, in part 1, move the first task's work into a try and add CUSTOMER_TL.remove() in a finally. Run it again. ScopedValueDemo.java (JDK 25) // JDK 25 or later. Scoped values are final in JDK 25 (JEP 506), so no flag is needed. From labs/: // java vthreads/preview/ScopedValueDemo.java // Not part of the Gradle build, because the labs compile for JDK 21, where ScopedValue is a preview API. import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class ScopedValueDemo { static final ThreadLocal<String> CUSTOMER_TL = new ThreadLocal<>(); static final ScopedValue<String> CUSTOMER = ScopedValue.newInstance(); // deep in the call chain: reads the context, never sets it static String receiptLine() { return "ThreadLocal=" + CUSTOMER_TL.get() + ", ScopedValue=" + CUSTOMER.orElse("unbound"); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { // 1. a ThreadLocal set on a pooled thread and never removed try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1)) { pool.submit(() -> { CUSTOMER_TL.set("ann"); // forgot CUSTOMER_TL.remove() return receiptLine(); }).get(); System.out.println("1. next task, same pool thread: " + pool.submit(ScopedValueDemo::receiptLine).get()); } // 2. a scoped value is bound for one call, and gone afterwards ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, "ann").run(() -> System.out.println("2. inside run(): " + receiptLine())); System.out.println(" after run(): " + receiptLine()); // 3. rebind for a nested call; the outer binding comes back when it returns ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, "ann").run(() -> { ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, "ben").run(() -> System.out.println("3. nested: " + receiptLine())); System.out.println(" outer again: " + receiptLine()); }); // 4. a thread you start yourself does not inherit the binding ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, "ann").run(() -> { Thread child = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> System.out.println("4. plain thread: " + receiptLine())); try { child.join(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); } } java vthreads/preview/ScopedValueDemo.java labs/vthreads/preview/ScopedValueDemo.java ScopedValueDemo.kt (JDK 25) // JDK 25 or later. Scoped values are final in JDK 25 (JEP 506). Needs the Kotlin command-line // compiler. From labs/: // kotlinc vthreads/preview/ScopedValueDemo.kt -include-runtime -d vthreads/build/sv-demo.jar // java -jar vthreads/build/sv-demo.jar // Not part of the Gradle build, because the labs compile for JDK 21, where ScopedValue is a preview API. import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.Executors private val CUSTOMER_TL = ThreadLocal<String>() private val CUSTOMER: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance() // deep in the call chain: reads the context, never sets it private fun receiptLine() = "ThreadLocal=${CUSTOMER_TL.get()}, ScopedValue=${CUSTOMER.orElse("unbound")}" fun main() { // 1. a ThreadLocal set on a pooled thread and never removed Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1).use { pool -> pool.submit(Callable { CUSTOMER_TL.set("ann") // forgot CUSTOMER_TL.remove() receiptLine() }).get() println("1. next task, same pool thread: " + pool.submit(Callable { receiptLine() }).get()) } // 2. a scoped value is bound for one call, and gone afterwards // Runnable { } is optional; it shows this is the binding's run, not Kotlin's run {} ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, "ann").run(Runnable { println("2. inside run(): " + receiptLine()) }) println(" after run(): " + receiptLine()) // 3. rebind for a nested call; the outer binding comes back when it returns ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, "ann").run(Runnable { ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, "ben").run(Runnable { println("3. nested: " + receiptLine()) }) println(" outer again: " + receiptLine()) }) // 4. a thread you start yourself does not inherit the binding ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, "ann").run(Runnable { val child = Thread.ofVirtual().start { println("4. plain thread: " + receiptLine()) } child.join() }) } kotlinc vthreads/preview/ScopedValueDemo.kt -include-runtime -d vthreads/build/sv-demo.jar && java -jar vthreads/build/sv-demo.jar labs/vthreads/preview/ScopedValueDemo.kt Line 1 shows ThreadLocal=ann in a task that never set it: the value leaked from the previous task on the same pool thread. After your fix it shows ThreadLocal=null. The scoped value is ann inside run() and unbound after it, ben in the nested call and ann again after it. The plain virtual thread prints unbound, because only StructuredTaskScope forks see the parent's binding. The Java and Kotlin versions print the same six lines. JEP 506: Scoped Values read

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · Java and Kotlin
x: Request details that follow the subtasks Java: ScopedValue plus a scope (JDK 25, scope in preview) static final ScopedValue<String> CUSTOMER = ScopedValue.newInstance(); // final in JDK 25 Receipt checkout(Order order) throws Exception { return ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, order.customer()).call(() -> { // bound for this call try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // preview in JDK 25 Subtask<Approval> bank = scope.fork(() -> theBank.approve(order)); Subtask<String> line = scope.fork(() -> receiptLine(order.item())); scope.join(); return new Receipt(line.get(), bank.get()); } }); } static String receiptLine(String item) { return item + " for " + CUSTOMER.get(); // the fork reads the parent's binding } Kotlin: a coroutine context element // the coroutine carries the details, not the thread class Customer(val name: String) : AbstractCoroutineContextElement(Customer) { companion object Key : CoroutineContext.Key<Customer> } suspend fun checkout(order: Order): Receipt = withContext(Customer(order.customer)) { // bound for this block val bank = async { theBank.approve(order) } val line = async { receiptLine(order.item) } // children inherit the context Receipt(line.await(), bank.await()) } suspend fun receiptLine(item: String): String = item + " for " + (currentCoroutineContext()[Customer]?.name ?: error("no customer")) Both are read-only details that children inherit and that end with the block. The difference is what carries them. A scoped value is bound to a thread's call stack, and only StructuredTaskScope forks inherit it. A coroutine context element is bound to the coroutine, so it survives when the coroutine moves to another thread at a suspension point, and every child started with launch or async inherits it. That's why scoped values and ThreadLocals are the wrong tool inside suspending code: a coroutine can resume on a different thread, where the binding isn't there. In Kotlin coroutine code, put the details in the coroutine context. Use ScopedValue from Kotlin only in plain blocking code on threads, as ScopedValueDemo.kt does.

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · Worked example
x: Make the order page fail fast The shop's order page needs two answers: the delivery date from the delivery company's web service (300 ms) and the customer's loyalty points (80 ms). Both are blocking calls. The code runs on a shared executor kept in a field, and the order id lives in a ThreadLocal for the log. Read it, and list what goes wrong when one call fails. OrderPage show(Order o) throws Exception { ORDER_ID.set(o.id()); // a ThreadLocal Future<LocalDate> date = shared.submit(() -> delivery.estimate(o)); // 300 ms Future<Integer> points = shared.submit(() -> loyalty.points(o)); // 80 ms return new OrderPage(date.get(), points.get()); } fun show(o: Order): OrderPage { ORDER_ID.set(o.id) // a ThreadLocal val date = shared.submit(Callable { delivery.estimate(o) }) // 300 ms val points = shared.submit(Callable { loyalty.points(o) }) // 80 ms return OrderPage(date.get(), points.get()) } Three problems. If the points call fails, date.get() still waits up to 300 ms first. If the delivery call fails, the points call keeps running after show has thrown. And both subtasks log without the order id, because ORDER_ID is set on the handler's thread only. On a pooled handler thread it is also never cleared. On JDK 25 without preview, use a scope that owns its threads, like the lab's FailFastScope, and pass the order id as an argument. Every subtask now ends before show returns, and the first failure cancels the other call. OrderPage show(Order o) throws Exception { try (var scope = new FailFastScope()) { // 1. open: owns the subtasks String id = o.id(); // 2. details as a plain argument Supplier<LocalDate> date = scope.fork(() -> delivery.estimate(o, id)); Supplier<Integer> points = scope.fork(() -> loyalty.points(o, id)); scope.join(); // 3. first failure cancels the other return new OrderPage(date.get(), points.get()); } // 4. close: nothing left running } fun show(o: Order): OrderPage = FailFastScope().use { scope -> // 1. open: owns the subtasks val id = o.id // 2. details as a plain argument val date = scope.fork { delivery.estimate(o, id) } val points = scope.fork { loyalty.points(o, id) } scope.join() // 3. first failure cancels the other OrderPage(date.get(), points.get()) } // 4. close: nothing left running On JDK 25 with --enable-preview, the JDK's scope does the same job, and a scoped value carries the order id into both forks. No method signature has to change. static final ScopedValue<String> ORDER_ID = ScopedValue.newInstance(); OrderPage show(Order o) throws Exception { return ScopedValue.where(ORDER_ID, o.id()).call(() -> { // 1. bind the details try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // 2. fail-fast scope Subtask<LocalDate> date = scope.fork(() -> delivery.estimate(o)); // forks read ORDER_ID Subtask<Integer> points = scope.fork(() -> loyalty.points(o)); scope.join(); // 3. FailedException on JDK 25 return new OrderPage(date.get(), points.get()); } // 4. close: nothing left running }); } val ORDER_ID: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance() fun show(o: Order): OrderPage = ScopedValue.where(ORDER_ID, o.id).call<OrderPage, Exception> { // 1. bind the details StructuredTaskScope.open<Any>().use { scope -> // 2. fail-fast scope val date = scope.fork(Callable { delivery.estimate(o) }) // forks read ORDER_ID val points = scope.fork(Callable { loyalty.points(o) }) scope.join() // 3. FailedException on JDK 25 OrderPage(date.get(), points.get()) } // 4. close: nothing left running } When you move to JDK 27 or 28, change the error handling where you call show: catch ExecutionException from join() instead of StructuredTaskScope.FailedException. The fork, join and close lines stay the same.

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · Lab
x: Build a fail-fast scope on an executor labs/vthreads/src/main/java/workbench/vthreads/l05/FailFastScope.java ./gradlew :vthreads:test --tests 'workbench.vthreads.l05.*' Run the tests once. All seven fail with UnsupportedOperationException. Read the class comment in FailFastScope: it lists the rules the tests check. Add the state as fields: an ExecutorService from Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), a CopyOnWriteArrayList<Future<?>>, an AtomicReference<Throwable> for the first failure and a volatile boolean joined. Write fork. Submit a Callable that runs task.call() in a try. In the catch, record the failure with compareAndSet(null, failure), and if that wins, call executor.shutdownNow() to interrupt the siblings. Rethrow. Add the future to the list and return a Supplier that throws IllegalStateException until join() has run, then returns future.resultNow(). Handle a fork after a cancel: once the executor is shut down, submit throws RejectedExecutionException. Catch it and return a handle whose get() always throws IllegalStateException. Write join: call get() on each future in order, ignore ExecutionException and CancellationException, and stop as soon as a failure is recorded. Set joined, then throw new ExecutionException(failure) if there was one. Write close: shutdownNow(), then close() on the executor. Run the tests until all seven pass, then run them twice more. Why compareAndSet? The siblings you interrupt fail too, with InterruptedException. They fail after the real failure is recorded, so their compareAndSet(null, ...) returns false, and they don't replace it. Don't cancel with future.cancel(true). A cancelled future counts as done at once, and on JDK 21 the executor then stops waiting for that thread while its finally block still runs. The close() test catches exactly that. shutdownNow() interrupts the threads and leaves the futures alone. catch (Throwable failure) { ...; throw failure; } compiles inside the submitted lambda: Java's precise rethrow knows that task.call() can only throw an Exception. Future.resultNow() (JDK 19 and later) returns the result of a task that succeeded, and throws IllegalStateException for one that failed or was cancelled, which is what a handle needs after join(). All seven tests in FailFastScopeTest pass, three runs in a row. By the end you can say what structured concurrency guarantees, build fail-fast fork and join on a plain executor, read the JDK 25 StructuredTaskScope API and what changes after it, and use scoped values instead of ThreadLocals for a request's details.
