h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · Quiz
x: You compile on JDK 25 with --enable-preview. Which fan-out compiles and fails fast? try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) { ...; scope.join().throwIfFailed(); } try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { ...; scope.join(); }, with callers catching StructuredTaskScope.FailedException try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { ...; scope.join(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { ... } try (var scope = Executors.newStructuredTaskScope()) { ...; scope.join(); } JDK 25 (JEP 505) uses the static open() factory, and its default joiner makes join() throw the unchecked FailedException. ShutdownOnFailure is the JDK 21 to 24 API and no longer exists, which is why old articles mislead. Catching the checked ExecutionException is the JDK 27 shape: on JDK 25 nothing in the try block throws it, so javac rejects the catch. There is no Executors.newStructuredTaskScope(). What does this print on JDK 25? static final ScopedValue<String> ID = ScopedValue.newInstance(); ScopedValue.where(ID, "a").run(() -> { ScopedValue.where(ID, "b").run(() -> System.out.print(ID.get())); System.out.print(ID.get()); }); System.out.print(ID.orElse("-")); bb- ab- ba- bab The inner where binds ID to b for the nested call only. When it returns, the outer binding a is back, and after the outer run() nothing is bound, so orElse gives -. There is no set() that could leave b behind, which is the difference from a ThreadLocal. Inside ScopedValue.where(CUSTOMER, "ann").run(...), a handler submits a task to Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). What does CUSTOMER.isBound() return inside that task? false: only subtasks forked in a StructuredTaskScope see the parent's binding true: every virtual thread inherits its creator's scoped values true, but only if the task starts before run() returns It throws IllegalStateException, because scoped values can't be read on virtual threads Bindings flow only into threads forked by a StructuredTaskScope, whose lives are sure to end inside the binding. A thread started by an executor could outlive the run() call, so it gets nothing. Pass the value as an argument there. The second option describes InheritableThreadLocal, which copies values into every new thread. The shop asks two delivery companies for a price, wants whichever answers first, and wants the slower call cancelled. On JDK 25, which tool fits? CompletableFuture.anyOf(fast, cheap) StructuredTaskScope.open() with the default joiner StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.allSuccessfulOrThrow()) StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.anySuccessfulResultOrThrow()) anySuccessfulResultOrThrow (renamed anySuccessfulOrThrow in JDK 26) returns the first successful result and cancels the rest. CompletableFuture.anyOf completes with the first result but cancels nothing, so the slower call runs to the end. The default joiner and allSuccessfulOrThrow both wait for every subtask to succeed. From the lesson "Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption": a fail-fast scope cancels a sibling that runs while (true) { total = total.add(nextChunk(buffer)); }, pure computing that never blocks and never checks the interrupt flag. What happens to that sibling? It stops at once, because cancelling a subtask kills its thread It keeps running: cancelling only interrupts, and this loop never looks It stops at its next loop iteration, because virtual threads check the flag automatically The JVM throws InterruptedException inside add Cancelling in Java is cooperative. cancel(true), shutdownNow() and a scope's cancel all just set the interrupt flag. Blocking calls react by throwing InterruptedException, and a loop that never blocks must check Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() itself. A scope's close() would wait for this loop forever.

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · Explain it back
x: A colleague says that try-with-resources around newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() already gives you structured concurrency. Explain what it gives you, what it is missing, and what StructuredTaskScope and scoped values add.

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · Key terms
x: Structured concurrency Subtasks are tied to the block that started them and can't outlive it. Subtask One piece of a bigger job, running on a thread of its own. Scope The object that forks subtasks, joins them, and on close guarantees they have all ended. Fail fast The first failure cancels the remaining subtasks and is reported at once. Joiner The policy you pass to StructuredTaskScope.open: when join() returns, and what it returns or throws. Scoped value A read-only value bound for the length of one call and visible to all the code that call runs. Preview API A complete JDK API that isn't final yet. It needs --enable-preview and can change in the next release. What does structured concurrency guarantee when the block that opened a scope ends? Every subtask forked in the scope has finished. None is still running, whether the block returned, threw or was interrupted. In a fail-fast scope, what happens to the other subtasks when one fails? They are cancelled, which means interrupted. join() throws the first failure. What does join() throw on JDK 25 when a subtask fails in StructuredTaskScope.open()? StructuredTaskScope.FailedException (unchecked), with the subtask's exception as its cause. From JDK 27 the built-in joiners throw ExecutionException. Is StructuredTaskScope final in JDK 25? No. It's a preview API in JDK 25, 26 and 27 and needs --enable-preview. JEP 543 makes it final in JDK 28. Are scoped values final in JDK 25? Yes, since JDK 25 (JEP 506). They need no flag. Which threads can read a scoped value's binding? Code running inside where(...).run(...) or call(...), and subtasks forked in a StructuredTaskScope opened there. Not threads you start yourself, and not executor tasks. Why can't a hand-built scope cancel with future.cancel(true) and rely on executor.close() to wait? A cancelled future is done at once, so on JDK 21 the executor stops waiting for that thread while it still runs its finally. Use shutdownNow(), which interrupts without completing the futures.

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · Go deeper
x: Joiners of your own. A Joiner has two hooks, onFork and onComplete, and a result() method that join() calls at the end. onComplete returns true to cancel the scope. That's enough for policies the built-in joiners don't cover, such as "stop once three of five price services agree" or "collect the successes and ignore the failures". onComplete runs on the thread of the subtask that just finished, so a joiner's state must be thread-safe. Check the Javadoc of the exact JDK you use, because JDK 26 changed the hook signatures slightly. Why CompletableFuture doesn't solve this. allOf waits for everything even after one future fails, and cancel(true) on a CompletableFuture doesn't interrupt the thread doing the work: it only completes the future. The lesson "CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out" builds a fan-out that way. Notice how much code its error handling needs compared with a scope. Kotlin already has this. In coroutine code, coroutineScope { async { } } gives the same guarantees without a preview flag: children can't outlive the scope, the first failure cancels the siblings, and cancelling reaches each child at its next suspension point. The coroutines track covers it. StructuredTaskScope matters most for Java code, and for Kotlin code that blocks on threads. Scoped values and virtual threads. A ThreadLocal costs a map entry per thread, and with a million virtual threads that adds up, as lesson 4 of this track showed. A scoped value's binding belongs to the call, not to each thread, and the scope's forks share it. That makes it a natural fit for one virtual thread per request with many short subtasks. Old articles. Before JDK 25 the API was StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure and ShutdownOnSuccess, subclasses you created with new. Scoped values had static helpers such as ScopedValue.runWhere, which were removed during the previews. If a snippet uses either, it was written for an older preview.

h: Moving a blocking service to virtual threads · The old pool's second job: a database limit nobody wrote down
x: Ten waiters quietly protected ten burners: a fixed pool of 10 also kept the database to 10 callers, a plain swap fails 237 of 300 requests, a Semaphore(10) writes the limit back, and Little's law shows where requests wait Let's meet the service first. Part of the shop answers one question before every checkout: what will this order cost in the customer's own money? The lab calls it QuoteService, since a quote is a price offer. For each request it does two things. It looks up the customer's level, gold or standard, in the shop's database, which takes 5 ms on a borrowed connection, an open line to the database. Then it asks the exchange-rate service from lesson 4 of this track for today's rate, which takes 100 ms. The database sits behind a connection pool: 10 open connections that requests borrow and give back. A request that finds all 10 in use waits, and this pool gives up after 30 ms. Here is the service as it runs today, on a fixed pool: a team of 10 platform threads, the costly kind that each use a thread of the operating system, taking requests from a queue: Java public final class QuoteService implements AutoCloseable { // 10 platform threads, because the database pool has 10 connections private final ExecutorService workers = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10); public Quote quote(QuoteRequest request) throws Exception { String tier = db.tier(request.customerId()); // 5 ms on a borrowed connection BigDecimal rate = fx.rate(request.pair()); // 100 ms call to the exchange-rate service return new Quote(request.customerId(), request.pair(), rate, fee(tier, request.amount())); } } Kotlin class QuoteService(private val db: CustomerDb, private val fx: FxApi) : AutoCloseable { // 10 platform threads, because the database pool has 10 connections private val workers = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10) fun quote(request: QuoteRequest): Quote { val tier = db.tier(request.customerId) // 5 ms on a borrowed connection val rate = fx.rate(request.pair) // 100 ms call to the exchange-rate service return Quote(request.customerId, request.pair, rate, fee(tier, request.amount)) } } A virtual thread is the cheap kind: the JDK sets it aside whenever it waits, so a program can have one per request. The obvious move is one line: replace newFixedThreadPool(10) with newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). MigrationDemo, in the Try it below, sends a burst of 300 requests at once and runs the same handler three ways. Predict line B before you look. On this busy machine it printed: A: fixed pool of 10 3,200 ms ok 300 failed 0 rate calls in flight at peak 10 B: virtual threads 173 ms ok 63 failed 237 rate calls in flight at peak 63 Line A is slow and safe: 300 requests through 10 threads, at about 105 ms each, take 30 rounds, about 3.2 s. Line B is fast and mostly wrong. Four requests in five failed with connection pool: no connection after 30 ms. The pool did two jobs. It ran the requests, and it made sure that no more than 10 of them ever reached the database. Nobody wrote the second job down, but it's the reason the connection pool never had to make anyone wait. Virtual threads take over the first job and quietly drop the second. In the restaurant, the 10 waiters were the pool's threads and the 10 burners are the connections. The slips are the virtual threads, and nothing stops 300 of them from reaching 10 burners. In the burst, all 300 asked for a connection at the same moment. A pool tuned for 10 callers gave each of the others 30 ms and then said no. So write the second job back, on purpose, around the one call that needs it. It's the grill tokens from lesson 3 of this track: a Semaphore, a counter of permits, with one permit per connection: Java private final Semaphore dbPermits = new Semaphore(db.poolSize(), true); // one permit per connection public Quote quote(QuoteRequest request) throws Exception { String tier; dbPermits.acquire(); // outside the try try { tier = db.tier(request.customerId()); // only the database call waits its turn } finally { dbPermits.release(); } BigDecimal rate = fx.rate(request.pair()); // rate calls now overlap freely return new Quote(request.customerId(), request.pair(), rate, fee(tier, request.amount())); } Kotlin private val dbPermits = Semaphore(db.poolSize, true) // one permit per connection fun quote(request: QuoteRequest): Quote { val tier = withDbPermit { db.tier(request.customerId) } // only the database call waits its turn val rate = fx.rate(request.pair) // rate calls now overlap freely return Quote(request.customerId, request.pair, rate, fee(tier, request.amount)) } The Kotlin version wraps acquire, try and release in a small inline function, withDbPermit, which the lab asks you to write. The true makes the semaphore fair: waiting requests get permits in the order they arrived. Line C of the demo runs this version: C: virtual threads + Semaphore(10) 283 ms ok 300 failed 0 rate calls in flight at peak 180 No failures, and eleven times faster than line A. The 300 requests still met the database 10 at a time, but they waited at the semaphore, where waiting is cheap and has no 30 ms limit, not inside the pool. And the rate calls, which never needed a limit, went from 10 at a time to 180. The old pool deserves one word of credit: it was safe. It was also slow, because it held back calls that needed no limit. You may wonder why we don't just raise the pool's 30 ms timeout. You could, and requests would wait inside the pool instead. The semaphore is better for two reasons. Its line is visible: getQueueLength() says how many requests are waiting, a number you can put on a chart. And the policy is yours: wait, or use tryAcquire with a deadline that gives up before any work is done. Removing a pool removes a limit. Write it back as one semaphore per resource, sized from that resource. Ten permits fit ten connections. So why not give the database 300 connections, one per request, and skip the semaphore? Migrate in two steps Read MigrationDemo. 300 requests arrive at once. Each borrows one of 10 connections for a 5 ms query (the pool gives up after 30 ms), then makes a 100 ms call to the exchange-rate service. Predict, for A (the old pool), B (a plain swap to virtual threads) and C (virtual threads plus a Semaphore(10)): the total time, the failed requests, and the most rate calls in flight at once. Run it. Then change C's semaphore to new Semaphore(3, true) (in Kotlin, Semaphore(3, true)) and predict the new time before you run it again. The database part of the request decides the time, and the semaphore is where you choose it. The same burst of 300 requests in three setups. What matters isn't how many threads you have, but where the waiting requests line up.

h: Moving a blocking service to virtual threads · Where the waiting belongs: a small connection pool and a deadline on every wait
x: A database can run only a few queries truly at the same time, roughly a few per processor core of the computer it runs on. Past that point, more connections don't add speed. They add work inside the database, which switches between more sessions and lets them fight over the same data. So a database often runs slower with 300 connections than with 10, not faster. Copies make it worse. A busy shop runs several copies of the same service, each with its own pool. Four copies with 20 connections each are 80 sessions on one database, and the database usually serves other programs as well. So the connection pool stays small, sized from the database, and the waiting moves into your service, in front of the pool. In the restaurant, you don't add burners because you hired cheap waiters. You hang 10 tokens by the burners and let the slips wait on the board. Waiting in your service is cheap, but it isn't free of risk. With a fixed pool, a slow database filled the pool's queue, and the program pushed back on new work. With virtual threads, nothing pushes back. Here the restaurant picture breaks, and the break matters. Real waiters cost wages, so nobody hires 300 by accident, but virtual threads cost almost nothing, so the crowd can grow very large before anyone notices. Parked requests pile up on the heap, the memory where Java keeps its objects, each with its stack, and every one of them is a customer waiting for an answer. So give every wait a deadline: a point after which the request gives up and says so. At the semaphore, tryAcquire with a timeout does that: Java if (!dbPermits.tryAcquire(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { // a deadline, not an endless wait throw new ShopBusyException("database busy, please try again"); // a fast, honest answer } try { tier = db.tier(request.customerId()); } finally { dbPermits.release(); } Kotlin if (!dbPermits.tryAcquire(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { // a deadline, not an endless wait throw ShopBusyException("database busy, please try again") // a fast, honest answer } val tier = try { db.tier(request.customerId) } finally { dbPermits.release() } Turning work away early like this is load shedding, from lesson 3 of this track. The pool's own timeout stays as a safety net, but it fires late, after the request has already done part of its work. A deadline at the semaphore fails before any of that. Calls over the network need deadlines too: give the client that calls the exchange-rate service a timeout, so a bad day there can't hold requests forever. Little's law, from lesson 1, says how long that line can get: requests waiting = arrival rate × time each one waits. At 1,000 requests a second, a 200 ms deadline lets at most about 200 requests wait at once. Pick the deadline from what a customer will accept, and the law tells you what the wait costs in parked requests. Keep the connection pool small, and let requests wait in front of it, with a deadline. The semaphore and the deadline fix one service. A real move touches more than one pool, so it helps to have a list. About Pool Sizing (the HikariCP connection pool's wiki) read

h: Moving a blocking service to virtual threads · A checklist for the move, in the order to do it
x: Most moves to virtual threads need the same handful of changes. Go through them in this order: Run JDK 25 first. On JDK 21 to 23, blocking inside synchronized pins the carrier: the platform thread that runs the virtual thread blocks too. Database drivers, web clients and logging libraries do exactly that. On JDK 25, only static initializers (the code that sets up a class) and native frames (calls into code written in another language) still pin. Lesson 4 of this track has the details. Replace the pools that run blocking work with one virtual thread per task, through newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). Delete the old pool-size setting, so nobody tunes it later by mistake. For each resource the old pool protected, write the limit down: one shared Semaphore per resource, sized from what that resource allows, held only around its calls. Look for resources with no limit at all, too, because now nothing slows the traffic in front of them. Keep the connection pool small, sized from the database and multiplied by the number of copies of the service. Hunt ThreadLocals. A cache becomes one object per request (lesson 4), and a request's details belong in arguments or scoped values (lesson 5). Keep heavy computing on a bounded pool of platform threads. Resizing a photo on a virtual thread holds a carrier for the whole time. Give every wait a deadline: tryAcquire with a timeout, a timeout on every network client, and a fast "busy" answer when you're over budget. Item 3 is the one people skip, because the code still passes every test with light traffic. It fails at the first real rush, exactly as line B did. The three searches in the Try it below find the first candidates for items 1, 2 and 5 in any codebase. In the lab's own code they find a pool, a ThreadLocal and two synchronized methods, all from this track. In a real program, expect more pools than you thought, because many sit inside libraries and their settings, not in your own code. Switching the executor is one line. Writing down the limits it removed is the real move. The checklist gets the move right. To know that it worked, measure it. Audit a codebase From labs/, run the three searches below on the vthreads exercises. Each one looks for one checklist item. For each hit, name the checklist item and the fix. Run the same searches on a program of your own (change the path), and sort the hits: request handling, heavy computing, or a request's details. terminal # 2. pools that run blocking work grep -rnE "newFixedThreadPool|newCachedThreadPool|new ThreadPoolExecutor" --include=*.java --include=*.kt vthreads/src/main # 5. ThreadLocal caches and request details grep -rnE "ThreadLocal" --include=*.java --include=*.kt vthreads/src/main # 1. monitors around slow calls (matters on JDK 21 to 23) grep -rnE "synchronized" --include=*.java --include=*.kt vthreads/src/main Unless you already fixed them, the searches find this lesson's QuoteService with its newFixedThreadPool(10), the ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> in lesson 4's ReceiptStamp, and the synchronized methods in lesson 4's FxRateCache, plus a comment or two that mention them. In a real program, expect more pools than you thought: many of them sit inside libraries and their settings, not in your own code.

h: Moving a blocking service to virtual threads · Measuring the move: Little's law finds the full resource
x:
Measure before you switch, then again after, with the same load test: a program that sends a steady stream of fake requests. You need a baseline of the requests finished per second, the time a typical request takes and the time the slowest one in a hundred takes (often called the p99). Add the error rate, the processor use, the heap and the time spent in garbage collection. Without a baseline, "it feels faster" is all you'll have. After the switch, one number stops meaning anything: the thread count. Fifty thousand virtual threads is normal and tells you nothing. Watch where requests wait instead, with a few gauges, numbers that show a current value and go up and down, like the fuel gauge in a car: the requests in flight in the service the queue length on each semaphore the connection pool's waiting and active counts jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events from a recording of JFR, the JVM's built-in flight recorder, as in lesson 4 of this track Little's law ties these together: requests in flight = throughput × time in the system, where throughput is the requests finished per second. Use it both ways. To predict, multiply. MeasureDemo, in the Try it below, sends 400 requests a second, and each spends about 120 ms inside: 20 ms on the database, holding one of 10 permits, then 100 ms with the exchange-rate service. So about 400 × 0.12 = 48 should be in flight. One run printed a line every 250 ms (two of them here) and a summary: t= 590 ms in flight 48 waiting for a db permit 0 t=1,102 ms in flight 48 waiting for a db permit 0 throughput 378/s, mean time in system 124 ms Little's law: throughput x time = 46.7; measured average in flight = 47.0 The prediction held, and the last two numbers agree, as the law says they must. Both sit a little under 48, because the averages include the start and the end of the run, when fewer requests are inside. To find a bottleneck, divide a limit by the time each request holds it. Ten permits, each held for 20 ms, serve at most 10 / 0.02 s = 500 requests a second. Below that rate the semaphore's line stays near zero. So what happens at 600 a second? Predict both gauges, then look: t= 268 ms in flight 102 waiting for a db permit 45 t= 822 ms in flight 164 waiting for a db permit 104 t=1,336 ms in flight 229 waiting for a db permit 169 t=1,851 ms in flight 281 waiting for a db permit 221 throughput 462/s, mean time in system 380 ms The line at the semaphore grew on every sample, the time in the system tripled, and throughput stayed under 500 however many requests arrived. A rising queue with flat throughput is what a full resource looks like, and it's the alert to set up. The thread count would have said nothing, while the queue gauge named the database. Roll out like any risky change. Switch one copy of the service first, send it real traffic, and compare its numbers with the copies still on the old pool. Look at the slowest requests and the error rate first. Then check that heap and garbage collection didn't jump, because parked virtual threads keep their stacks on the heap. Count where requests wait, not how many threads you have. A growing queue with flat throughput names the full resource. That's the whole move: a new executor, the limits written down, and the numbers that prove it. The lab does it to QuoteService. Watch a resource fill up Read MeasureDemo. Requests arrive at a steady rate. Each holds one of 10 database permits for 20 ms, then makes a 100 ms call to the exchange-rate service. A sampler prints two gauges every 250 ms. Use Little's law to predict the requests in flight at 400 a second. Run it. Work out the database's capacity from the permits and the query time. Then run it at 600 a second with -Pargs='600 2', and predict what the two gauges do first. // 2. the limit the old pool gave you by accident, now written down private final Semaphore dbPermits; public QuoteService(CustomerDb db, FxApi fx) { this.db = db; this.fx = fx; this.dbPermits = new Semaphore(db.poolSize(), true); // one permit per pooled connection } public Quote quote(QuoteRequest r) throws Exception { String tier; dbPermits.acquire(); // outside the try try { tier = db.tier(r.customerId()); // only the database call holds a permit } finally { dbPermits.release(); } BigDecimal rate = fx.rate(r.pair()); // rate calls overlap freely return new Quote(r.customerId(), r.pair(), rate, fee(tier, r.amount())); } // 3. a gauge for the chart public int dbWaiting() { return dbPermits.getQueueLength(); } @Override public void close() { requests.close(); // 4. waits for requests in flight } } QuoteService.kt (the lab's solution) class QuoteService(private val db: CustomerDb, private val fx: FxApi) : AutoCloseable { // 1. one new virtual thread per request: no size to pick private val requests = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() // 2. the limit the old pool gave you by accident, now written down private val dbPermits = Semaphore(db.poolSize, true) // one permit per pooled connection fun quote(r: QuoteRequest): Quote { val tier = withDbPermit { db.tier(r.customerId) } // only the database call holds a permit val rate = fx.rate(r.pair) // rate calls overlap freely return Quote(r.customerId, r.pair, rate, fee(tier, r.amount)) } // 3. a gauge for the chart fun dbWaiting(): Int = dbPermits.queueLength override fun close() = requests.close() // 4. waits for requests in flight private inline fun <T> withDbPermit(block: () -> T): T { dbPermits.acquire() // outside the try try { return block() } finally { dbPermits.release() } } } The move is the same in both: the executor changes, and the limit becomes a semaphore around one call. Kotlin's version reads better, because a small inline function that takes a lambda wraps the acquire, the try and the release, and inlining means the lambda costs nothing at run time. Java has no way to say that without a functional interface, so the try and finally sit in the method. Watch for two Kotlin traps. kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore has a withPermit too, but it suspends a coroutine and isn't the java.util.concurrent.Semaphore your threads need. And Kotlin doesn't check exceptions, so nothing reminds you that acquire() can throw InterruptedException. It still can, and it must still sit outside the try.

h: Moving a blocking service to virtual threads · Worked example
x: Size every limit with Little's law before the switch The shop's checkout runs as 4 copies of the same service behind one address, and each copy gets 200 checkouts a second at the busiest hour. A checkout spends 200 ms in the service: 40 ms asking the stock service, 120 ms waiting for the bank, 35 ms on a database connection and 5 ms computing. The bank allows the shop 150 calls in flight at once, across all copies. Today each copy has a fixed pool of 30 threads and 10 connections. First question: is the thread pool the bottleneck today? time in the service W = 40 + 120 + 35 + 5 ms = 200 ms threads needed L = 200/s x 0.2 s = 40 the pool has 30, so at the busiest hour checkouts queue for a thread pool capacity 30 / 0.2 s = 150 checkouts/s Yes. The pool tops out at 150 checkouts a second, below the 200 that arrive, so checkouts queue at the busiest hour. Virtual threads remove that limit. Now check each resource with the same formula, because nothing caps them any more. database connections busy 200/s x 0.035 s = 7 pool of 10: fine bank calls in flight 200/s x 0.120 s = 24 limit 150 / 4 copies = 37 per copy stock calls in flight 200/s x 0.040 s = 8 no published limit: ask the stock team virtual threads 40 at a time, a little heap Write the limits in code: one shared semaphore per resource, sized per copy, held only around that resource's calls. final class Limits { // 1. the bank: 150 calls in flight for the shop, shared by 4 copies final Semaphore bank = new Semaphore(150 / 4, true); // 2. the database: one permit per pooled connection final Semaphore db = new Semaphore(10, true); // 3. the stock service: no limit yet; add one when its team gives you a number } class Limits { // 1. the bank: 150 calls in flight for the shop, shared by 4 copies val bank = Semaphore(150 / 4, true) // 2. the database: one permit per pooled connection val db = Semaphore(10, true) // 3. the stock service: no limit yet; add one when its team gives you a number } Predict where each limit starts to bite, by dividing the permits by the time each checkout holds one. The bank semaphore starts to queue at 37 / 0.12 s, about 308 checkouts a second per copy, and the database at 10 / 0.035 s, about 285. If one copy stops, the other 3 get about 267 a second each, just under both. So the first alert to set is the queue length of the database semaphore, and each copy can now serve about 285 checkouts a second instead of 150.

h: Moving a blocking service to virtual threads · Lab
x: Migrate the quote service labs/vthreads/src/main/kotlin/workbench/vthreads/l06/QuoteService.kt labs/vthreads/src/main/kotlin/workbench/vthreads/l06/QuoteModel.kt ./gradlew :vthreads:test --tests 'workbench.vthreads.l06.*' This lab is in Kotlin. QuoteService prices an order in the customer's own money: a 5 ms database lookup, then a 100 ms call to the exchange-rate service (FxApi). Run the tests once. Four of five fail. The burst test passes, because the old pool of 10 keeps the database safe by accident. TODO 1: replace Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10) with Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). Run the tests again. Now the burst test fails too, with connection pool: no connection after 30 ms. That's the limit you just removed. TODO 2: add private val dbPermits = Semaphore(db.poolSize, true) and hold a permit around the db.tier(...) call and nothing else: acquire() before a try, release() in its finally. A small private inline fun <T> withDbPermit(block: () -> T): T keeps quote easy to read. TODO 3 and 4: dbWaiting() returns dbPermits.queueLength, and close() calls close() on the new executor. Run the tests until all five pass. Then read the pool-size test: it builds a pool of 3 connections. Explain why Semaphore(10) would fail it. Keep the rate call outside the permit. If the permit covers the whole request, you have rebuilt the old 10-thread limit, and the test about rate calls fails. acquire() goes before the try. If it sat inside, a thread interrupted while waiting would release() a permit it never got, and the limit would quietly grow. h: Moving a blocking service to virtual threads · Quiz
x: After the switch to virtual threads, the slowest requests take twice as long at the busiest hour, while throughput stays flat. Which number tells you whether the database is the bottleneck? The number of live virtual threads The queue length on the database semaphore (or the pool's waiting count), climbing at the busiest hour The processor use of the carrier threads The number of ForkJoinPool worker threads A full resource shows up as a queue that grows while throughput stays flat. The count of virtual threads grows with any slowdown and doesn't say where the time goes, which is why it's tempting and useless. Carrier processor use is low when everybody waits, and the scheduler's worker count stays near the core count. One copy of a service handles 300 requests a second, and each request holds a database connection for 25 ms. On average, about how many connections are busy? About 8 About 25 About 75 About 300 Little's law: busy connections = arrival rate × holding time = 300/s × 0.025 s = 7.5. A pool of 10 is close to its limit at this rate, and 10 / 0.025 s = 400 requests a second is where it fills up. The other options mix up the holding time with a count, or assume every request holds a connection the whole time. After the move, a new Semaphore(10, true) guards the database calls, and the database has 10 connections with a short borrow timeout. To make the service faster, a teammate raises the semaphore to 300 permits. What happens in a burst of 300 requests? It gets faster: 300 requests reach the database at once Nothing changes: the size of a semaphore never matters Most requests time out inside the connection pool again, as before the semaphore The JVM refuses to create more permits than there are connections The semaphore's size is the limit. With 300 permits, 300 callers reach a pool of 10 connections, and those that wait longer than the pool's timeout fail: that's line B of MigrationDemo again. Size the semaphore from the resource, one permit per connection. The JVM doesn't know what the permits stand for, so it allows any number. After the move, the connection pool reports timeouts at every busy hour. Which fix is right? Raise the pool's maximum size to 1,000 connections Go back to a fixed pool of 20 platform threads for all request handling Raise the pool's connection timeout to 5 minutes Put a shared Semaphore sized to the pool around the database work, and use tryAcquire with a deadline that fits the request's time budget The semaphore restores the limit the old pool gave you, only around the database work, with a queue you can see and a deadline you choose. A huge pool overloads the database for every program that shares it. A fixed pool brings back the cap on everything, including calls that never needed it. A 5-minute timeout hides overload as very slow requests. From the lesson "Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps": your service runs on JDK 21, and its database driver (the library that talks to the database) holds a synchronized lock while it reads from the network. You move request handling to virtual threads. What is the main risk, and the simplest fix? Pinning: queries block their carriers, and a few slow ones can stall every virtual thread. Upgrade to JDK 25, or to a driver version that uses ReentrantLock Data races inside the driver, because virtual threads ignore synchronized. Wrap every call in your own lock A ThreadLocal leak in the driver. Call remove() after each query No risk: a database driver never blocks while it holds a lock On JDK 21 to 23, blocking while holding a monitor pins the carrier, and with as many carriers as cores, a few slow queries can hold all of them. JEP 491 fixed this in JDK 24, so JDK 25 is the cleanest fix. synchronized still lets one thread in at a time on virtual threads, so there is no new race.

x: A manager asks why the team can't just flip the virtual threads switch tomorrow. Explain what the switch changes, what can break, and how you would roll it out and measure it.

h: Moving a blocking service to virtual threads · Key terms
x: Implicit limit A cap on how much runs at once that nobody set on purpose, such as a thread pool's size protecting a database. Connection pool A fixed set of open database connections that callers borrow and give back. Callers wait, or time out, when all are in use. Fair semaphore A semaphore that hands out permits in the order the waiters arrived (new Semaphore(n, true)). Deadline A point in time after which a waiting request gives up and says so. Little's law In a stable system, requests in flight = throughput × average time in the system. Load shedding Turning work away quickly, with a "busy" answer, when a limit is full, instead of letting it wait without end. What limit does a fixed thread pool give you without saying so? No more than N requests can reach any resource at once. Moving to virtual threads removes it. Where does the semaphore go when you move to virtual threads? Around the one call that needs the limit, as one object shared by all requests, sized from that resource. Should you grow the connection pool to match the number of virtual threads? No. The database decides how many connections help, roughly a few per database processor core, and every copy of the service multiplies the pool. Queue in front of the pool instead. Why give every semaphore wait a deadline after the move? With virtual threads nothing pushes back, so parked requests pile up. tryAcquire with a timeout turns overload into a fast "busy" answer instead of a long wait. 10 permits, each held for 20 ms. What is the most requests a second they can serve? 500 (10 / 0.02 s). Above that, the semaphore's queue grows while throughput stays flat. Little's law in one line? Requests in flight = throughput × time in the system (L = λW). Which gauge shows a full resource after the move? The queue on its semaphore (or the pool's waiting count) growing while throughput stays flat.

h: Moving a blocking service to virtual threads · Go deeper
x: Admission control at the door. The lab's semaphore waits without a deadline, deep inside the request. In a busy shop it's often better to decide at the start: try to take every permit the request will need, or a single "requests in progress" permit sized with Little's law, with a short tryAcquire deadline, and answer "busy" at once if you can't. Then you never call the bank for a request that would later time out at the database. Pool timeouts and semaphore waits. A pool's borrow timeout and a semaphore's deadline look alike, but they sit in different places. The pool timeout fires after the request has done part of its work and may already hold other resources. A deadline at the semaphore, at the start of the call, fails before any of that. Keep the pool's timeout too, as a safety net for bugs in your own limits. Fairness and the slowest requests. A fair semaphore serves waiters in arrival order. That costs a little throughput and keeps the slowest requests close to the typical ones during a burst. A non-fair one lets a newcomer grab a permit that was just released, which helps the average and hurts the unlucky waiters. For a checkout, the slowest customers matter more. Thread dumps after the move. jstack shows the carriers, not the thousands of parked virtual threads. jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json writes all of them, grouped by the executor or scope that owns them. Before you need it in a hurry, practise finding the stack of one stuck request in such a dump. When not to move. A service that mostly computes, or that already runs fully asynchronous code on a few event-loop threads, gains little. The win is largest for services that block on the network and are limited by their thread pool today. Little's law tells you which kind yours is: compare the threads you need (rate × time) with the threads you have.

h: Capstone: a payment ledger under load
x: Build one ledger in three sittings: correct under contention, on a pool you can reason about, then on virtual threads. In three sittings, you build one working program: a ledger, the bank's book of accounts and of every movement of money between them. Many threads move money at once, and not one cent may be lost or created. By the end, the ledger never deadlocks, closes without dropping a transfer it accepted, shows balances that always add up, and serves 10,000 customers at once on virtual threads, while a slow outside safety service sits behind a shared limit and a deadline. Then you defend the design in a review, and you can name the earlier lesson behind each line of it. The capstone draws on all of Part 1, and calls back its pictures as it goes. Lesson 1 uses the bank's races, the vault key, Ana and Ben's frozen transfers and the stress test from Threads and the bugs they cause, and the sealed envelope from The Java Memory Model. Lesson 2 uses the kitchen with its cooks and order rail, Little's law and closing time from Thread pools and executors, and the cashier's key and the OPEN/CLOSED sign from the memory model. Lesson 3 uses the order slips, the grill tokens and the hot pan from Virtual threads. There is little new theory. Each section shows what breaks if you choose differently, then names the lesson that explains why. The lab lives in labs/ledger, one package per lesson (workbench.ledger.l01 to l03). Each lesson's starter code contains the previous lesson's solution, so you can start any sitting fresh. Lessons 1 and 2 are in Java; lesson 3 adds a Kotlin server on top of the same Java ledger, the way a Kotlin program calls a Java library. From labs/, run ./gradlew :ledger:test --tests 'workbench.ledger.lNN.*' until it passes; solutionTest runs the same tests against the reference answers. The tests check what a real bank cares about (the rules under 8 threads, no lost transfer at shutdown, a limit that holds at 10,000 requests), never timings. The Try-it demos run with ./gradlew :ledger:demo -Pmain=..., and two of them get stuck on purpose so you can read a thread dump. Install JDK 25, and keep jcmd (it comes with the JDK) and jq (a small, free tool for reading JSON) at hand. Start from the rules: money is conserved, no balance goes below zero, a transfer is whole or not at all. Every lock and every happens-before rule in the program protects one of them. One ReentrantLock per account, taken in one global id order, lets transfers on different accounts overlap without deadlock; the balance check lives inside the same critical section as the move. A transfer is a value that can't change, checked when it's built, so any thread sees it whole; a reused, changeable row handed to a pool delivers the wrong data. Stress tests make threads collide behind a start latch and check every rule, at the end and where it can break. A pass is evidence, not proof. The ledger pool is sized by Little's law (8 threads, 80 slots), bounded and named, and it turns overflow away by counting and throwing: a visible "busy, try again", never a lost transfer. Shutdown drains within a deadline, then cancels and hands back what never started. The journal is written before apply, so an interrupt never leaves half a transfer. A whole snapshot holds every account lock in order, copies, and publishes a record that never changes through one volatile field; readers never lock. Requests run on one new virtual thread each, behind written-down limits: a shared semaphore for the safety service, the bounded ledger pool, and one deadline per request with the small-amount rule as its fallback. Fail-fast screening takes answers in the order they finish and ends with shutdownNow() and close(), so no call outlives its request or keeps a permit. Thread dumps find what tests can't: a pool parked on its own futures in Thread.print -l, and 10,000 virtual threads grouped by container and stack in the JSON dump.

h: Capstone: a payment ledger under load: track quiz
x: Two transfers run at once: acc-07 to acc-03, and acc-03 to acc-07. With the ledger's lock order, which lock does each take first? Each takes its from account first Both take acc-03 first Both take acc-07 first Whichever thread starts first decides The order is by id, whichever way the money moves, so both lock acc-03 first. The second thread waits while holding nothing: a short wait, not a deadlock. "from first" is the order that freezes, the way Ana and Ben's transfers did. A stress test of a ledger that checks the balance before taking the locks reports a total of 500,000 and no negative balances at the end. Why did it miss the bug? Accounts went below zero during the run, and later credits topped them up before the final check The race can't happen on Intel and AMD processors The JIT removed the check Eight threads are too few to cause a race Each move was still one step under both locks, so the total held, and the overdrafts healed before the end. Check a rule where it can break as well: debit refusing an overdraft turns the race into an immediate failure. Peak traffic is 3,000 transfers a second, and the journal write takes 4 ms. The disk allows 10 writes at once. What should the ledger pool's thread count be? 12, from Little's law 3,000 10: the journal's limit is lower than what Little's law asks for As many as the machine has cores Little's law asks for 3,000 x 0.004 = 12, but the journal takes only 10 writes at once, so the 11th and 12th threads would only queue inside it. Size from the scarce resource: 10 threads give at most 10 / 0.004 = 2,500 transfers a second, and the counting rejection handles the rest. Which rejection policy can silently lose a transfer that a customer was told was accepted? A counting policy that throws CallerRunsPolicy AbortPolicy DiscardOldestPolicy DiscardOldestPolicy drops the oldest queued task, which a caller already holds a future for, and that future never completes. A throwing policy turns the new transfer away before anyone is told it was accepted, and CallerRunsPolicy runs it on the thread that submitted it. A balances page adds up the accounts one at a time, locking each account while it reads it. Transfers keep running. What can it show? Always the exact total, because every read holds a lock A total that is too high or too low, because a transfer can run between two reads An exception, because two locks are taken A total that is always too low Money can move from an account not yet read to one already read (counted in neither) or the other way (counted twice). Only holding every lock at once, in the global order, gives one moment. A thread dump shows every ledger- thread WAITING (parking) on a FutureTask inside your own statement method, and no deadlock report. What is wrong? Tasks waiting for other tasks queued in the same bounded pool A lock-order deadlock between two accounts The journal is slow The pool's threads are pinned Threads parked on futures of their own pool, with tasks still queued, is pool-induced deadlock: cooks waiting for tickets behind them on the rail. There is no lock cycle, so the JVM's detector reports nothing. Do the work inline, chain the next step instead of waiting, or use a separate pool. Which design caps what the safety service sees when 10,000 requests run on virtual threads? A fixed pool of 20 virtual threads for whole requests A Semaphore(20) created in each request handler newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() on its own One Semaphore(20) field on the safety client, shared by every request One shared semaphore limits only the safety call. A pool of virtual threads caps the whole request, the daily-limit check and the ledger wait included. A semaphore per handler limits nothing, and the per-task executor has no limit at all. On a bad day, each safety call takes 2 s. The request stops waiting at its 300 ms deadline but never cancels the call, and it uses a shared executor. What happens to the bulkhead? Nothing: every request answers in 300 ms It grows to fit the extra calls Its permits stay held by abandoned calls for 2 s each, so most new requests can't get one The calls are interrupted automatically A timeout ends the wait, not the work. Each abandoned call keeps its permit until the safety service answers. Cancel the call at the deadline, so its finally gives the permit back to the next request. The ledger must run on JDK 21 and serve virtual threads. Why are the account locks ReentrantLocks? On JDK 21, a virtual thread waiting to enter, or waiting inside, synchronized pins its carrier; ReentrantLock lets it step off synchronized doesn't make writes visible to other threads ReentrantLock makes the critical section faster Kotlin can't use synchronized JDK 24 (JEP 491) removed that pinning, but on JDK 21 to 23 a waiting synchronized block holds the carrier, like a waiter holding a hot pan. ReentrantLock has always let a waiting virtual thread step off. Either way, nothing slow belongs inside an account lock. jcmd <pid> Thread.print on the server during the safety service's bad day shows no request threads at all. Where are they? They have all finished They are inside the carriers, under the name ForkJoinPool-1-worker-N The garbage collector removed them They are waiting virtual threads, which Thread.print doesn't list; Thread.dump_to_file -format=json does A waiting virtual thread is a stack on the heap, not an operating-system thread. Thread.print lists platform threads (plus virtual threads on a carrier, from JDK 24). The JSON dump lists every thread, grouped by the container that started it.

h: Design the ledger and make it correct · Three rules before any code: what a correct ledger must keep
x: Three rules before any code: a bank that makes and loses money without an error, a surprise auditor who can look at any moment, and the ledger those rules design Over three sittings, we'll build the ledger from the inside out. This sitting builds the core: accounts, locks, transfers and a test. The next one runs the ledger on a thread pool, a small team of threads that takes tasks from a queue. The last one serves thousands of customers at once on virtual threads, threads so light that a program can run thousands of them. Each piece comes from an earlier lesson, and we'll name that lesson when we lean on it. The core starts with the smallest ledger that can be wrong. It keeps 50 balances in an array, in cents, and has no locks at all. A thread, one path of work running beside others in the same program, calls transfer to move money: Java long[] balance = new long[50]; // 10,000 cents each, 500,000 in total void transfer(int from, int to, long cents) { if (balance[from] >= cents) { // check balance[from] -= cents; // read, subtract, write balance[to] += cents; // read, add, write } } Kotlin val balance = LongArray(50) { 10_000L } // 500,000 cents in total fun transfer(from: Int, to: Int, cents: Long) { if (balance[from] >= cents) { // check balance[from] -= cents // read, subtract, write balance[to] += cents // read, add, write } } Every transfer takes out what it puts in, so the total should stay at 500,000 cents forever. Let's run eight threads that each make 100,000 random transfers. One run on the busy machine used for this course printed: run 1: total 1,306,080 cents, expected 500,000, off by 806,080 run 2: total 4,043,302 cents, expected 500,000, off by 3,543,302 run 3: total 4,941,343 cents, expected 500,000, off by 4,441,343 By the third run, the bank holds ten times the money its customers ever paid in. Generous, and very wrong. Race conditions: why count++ lies showed the cause. balance[from] -= cents is three steps: read the balance, subtract, write it back. Say account 3 holds 100. Thread 1 reads 100 to send 20, and at the same moment thread 2 reads 100 to send 30. Thread 1 writes 80. Thread 2 writes 70. Both transfers paid out, but only one debit stuck, so 20 cents now exist twice. That is a lost update, and a lost credit destroys money the same way. Before we fix it, let's decide what fixed means. An invariant is a rule about the data that must be true whenever another thread can look. Our ledger has three: Money is conserved: the sum of all balances never changes. No balance ever goes below zero. A transfer happens whole or not at all: nobody sees the debit without the credit. Each rule decides part of the design. Rules 1 and 3 say the debit and the credit must be one step that no other thread can split, and that step touches two accounts. Rule 2 says the balance check belongs inside that same step. A check in one step and a debit in another is check-then-act, the second shape of race from Race conditions. Another thread can act in the gap between the two. And "whenever another thread can look" tells us when to test: while the threads run, not only at the end. A ledger is correct only against rules you can name. Write them down before the code. The rest of this lesson builds the ledger so that every line points at one of these three rules. We'll start with the thing that moves between threads: the transfer itself. Count what a ledger without locks loses Open BrokenLedgerDemo (or its Kotlin twin). Before you run it, write down the total you expect after each run. Run it with the command below. Note how far off each run is, and in which direction. Run it again with -Pargs=1000, so each thread makes only 1,000 transfers. The threads still wait at a start line and leave together. Predict first: will the total be right now? Count what goes wrong. */ public class BrokenLedgerDemo { static final int ACCOUNTS = 50; static final long OPENING = 10_000; // cents per account: 500,000 in total public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int perThread = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 100_000; for (int run = 1; run <= 3; run++) { long[] balance = new long[ACCOUNTS]; Arrays.fill(balance, OPENING); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> workers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread w = new Thread(() -> { ThreadLocalRandom rnd = ThreadLocalRandom.current(); try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int n = 0; n < perThread; n++) { int from = rnd.nextInt(ACCOUNTS), to = rnd.nextInt(ACCOUNTS); if (from == to) continue; long cents = 1 + rnd.nextLong(5_000); if (balance[from] >= cents) { // check balance[from] -= cents; // act: read, subtract, write balance[to] += cents; // read, add, write } } }); w.start(); workers.add(w); } go.countDown(); for (Thread w : workers) w.join(); long total = 0; for (long b : balance) total += b; System.out.printf("run %d: total %,d cents, expected 500,000, off by %,d%n", run, total, total - ACCOUNTS * OPENING); } } } ./gradlew :ledger:demo -Pmain=workbench.ledger.l01.demo.BrokenLedgerDemo labs/ledger/src/demo/java/workbench/ledger/l01/demo/BrokenLedgerDemo.java BrokenLedgerDemo.kt package workbench.ledger.l01.demo import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom import kotlin.concurrent.thread private const val ACCOUNTS = 50 private const val OPENING = 10_000L // cents per account: 500,000 in total /** A ledger with no locks: 8 threads move money between 50 accounts. Count what goes wrong. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val perThread = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 100_000 for (run in 1..3) { val balance = LongArray(ACCOUNTS) { OPENING } val go = CountDownLatch(1) val workers = List(8) { thread { val rnd = ThreadLocalRandom.current() go.await() repeat(perThread) { val from = rnd.nextInt(ACCOUNTS) val to = rnd.nextInt(ACCOUNTS) if (from != to) { val cents = 1 + rnd.nextLong(5_000) if (balance[from] >= cents) { // check balance[from] -= cents // act: read, subtract, write balance[to] += cents // read, add, write } } } } } go.countDown() workers.forEach { it.join() } val total = balance.sum() println("run %d: total %,d cents, expected 500,000, off by %,d".format(run, total, total - ACCOUNTS * OPENING)) } } ./gradlew :ledger:demo -Pmain=workbench.ledger.l01.demo.BrokenLedgerDemoKt labs/ledger/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/ledger/l01/demo/BrokenLedgerDemo.kt With 100,000 transfers per thread, the total is off by hundreds of thousands or millions of cents, by a different amount every run (from 300,421 to 4,848,480 cents in Java and Kotlin runs here). Once, while the machine was very busy, two runs out of three came out exactly right. That is the most dangerous result of all, because a correct run proves nothing. With 1,000 transfers per thread, most runs are still wrong, by thousands of cents, because the start line releases all eight threads at the same moment. Without a start line, short runs often look correct, because each thread finishes before the next one starts.

h: Design the ledger and make it correct · A transfer travels between threads, so make it a value that can't change
x: A transfer is built in one place and used in others. Say the bank imports a file of transfers each night. One thread reads the file line by line, and a thread pool applies each line to the ledger. Later, a log line prints the same transfer. If anyone can change the transfer after it is built, the others can see two different versions of it. Here is the most common way that goes wrong. The importer reuses one row object for every line, to save memory, and hands the row to the pool: Java TransferRow row = new TransferRow(); // changeable, and reused for every line for (String line : file) { row.parse(line); // overwrites id, from, to, cents pool.execute(() -> ledger.apply(row)); // a pool thread reads row later } Kotlin val row = TransferRow() // changeable, and reused for every line for (line in file) { row.parse(line) // overwrites id, from, to, cents pool.execute { ledger.apply(row) } // a pool thread reads row later } By the time a pool thread reads row, the importer has moved on to later lines. This section's demo imports 100,000 lines this way. One run printed: file: 100,000 lines, 54,910,000 cents applied: 13,920 different lines, 48,394,607 cents, 40 rows mixing two lines The ledger applied 100,000 transfers built from only 13,920 different lines. Forty rows carried the id of one line and the amount of another. In another run, only 15 different lines arrived at all. The bank paid a handful of customers thousands of times and most of them never. Happens-before, the rules that matter, named the cause. Happens-before is the memory model's promise that one thread sees what another wrote before a handover. That lesson pictured the handover as a cashier who locks the cabinet and leaves the key for the night manager. Handing a task to a pool is such a handover, but it covers only what was written before execute. The importer's later writes to the same row have no handover at all. That's a data race: two threads use the same field, at least one of them writes, and no happens-before rule links them. The reader can see any mix of old and new values. The fix is a value that can't change once it's built. A Java record, or a Kotlin data class with only val properties, has final fields and no setters: Java public record Transfer(String id, String from, String to, long cents) { public Transfer { // compact constructor: runs before the fields are set Objects.requireNonNull(id, "id"); Objects.requireNonNull(from, "from"); Objects.requireNonNull(to, "to"); if (cents <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive"); if (from.equals(to)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("two different accounts"); } } Kotlin data class Transfer(val id: String, val from: String, val to: String, val cents: Long) { init { // runs on every construction, copy() included require(cents > 0) { "amount must be positive" } require(from != to) { "two different accounts" } } } The Java version uses a compact constructor, a record constructor without a parameter list. It runs before the fields are set, so it can refuse bad values. Kotlin's init block does the same job, and Kotlin's non-null types make the three null checks unnecessary. Two things come with this design. First, Safe publication, final fields and escaping this compared an object with final fields to a letter in a sealed envelope. Any thread that receives it reads every page, however it got there. Second, the checks run once, when the transfer is built, so a Transfer that exists is a valid one. The ledger never asks whether cents is negative or whether from equals to, and the lock order in the next section relies on two different accounts. One more choice hides in that record: money is a long count of cents. A double can't hold 0.10 exactly. Add 0.10 and 0.20 as doubles and Java prints 0.30000000000000004, so a ledger of doubles drifts away from rule 1 with no thread involved. A value that crosses threads should never change. Make it a record, and check it in the constructor. The transfer is now safe to hand to any thread. The accounts it touches are not, and two transfers can touch the same account at the same moment. Reuse one row, then use a record Run ReusedTransferDemo. It reads 100,000 lines and hands each one to a pool of 4 threads. Predict first: how many different lines reach the ledger? Run it again with -Pargs=record, which builds a new Transfer record for each line. Pass "record" to use an immutable value. */ public class ReusedTransferDemo { // the mutable row a parser fills in for each line, then reuses for the next line static final class TransferRow { String id; long cents; } record Transfer(String id, long cents) {} // immutable: one new value per line public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean immutable = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("record"); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4); LongAdder appliedCents = new LongAdder(); Set<String> appliedLines = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); AtomicInteger mixed = new AtomicInteger(); long fileCents = 0; TransferRow row = new TransferRow(); for (int line = 0; line < 100_000; line++) { long cents = 100 + line % 900; fileCents += cents; if (immutable) { Transfer t = new Transfer("line-" + line, cents); h: Design the ledger and make it correct · One lock per account, always taken in the same order
x: Rules 1 and 3 need the debit and the credit to happen as one step. Synchronized and intrinsic locks gave us the tool. A lock lets one thread at a time into a piece of code, and that lesson pictured it as the key to the bank's vault. A thread takes the key, goes in, changes the balances and hands the key on. Everyone else waits at the door. The code a thread runs while it holds the key is the critical section. The simplest design is one key for the whole ledger. It is correct, and it keeps all three rules. Its cost is that every transfer waits for every other one, even a transfer between two strangers that shares no account with yours. So we give each account its own key. Then a transfer between accounts 3 and 7 and another between 12 and 40 can run at the same time. Two keys per transfer bring back the freeze from Deadlock, livelock and starvation. Ana sends Ben 100 at the same moment Ben sends Ana 50. Ana's transfer takes her key and waits for Ben's. Ben's transfer takes his key and waits for Ana's. Each waits forever for the other: that's a deadlock. The fix from that lesson works here as it is. Give every account a unique id that never changes, and always lock the smaller id first, whichever way the money moves: Java public Outcome apply(Transfer t) { Account from = account(t.from()), to = account(t.to()); Account first = from.id().compareTo(to.id()) < 0 ? from : to; // 1. one order for everyone Account second = first == from ? to : from; first.lock().lock(); try { second.lock().lock(); try { if (from.balance() < t.cents()) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS; // 2. check... from.debit(t.cents()); // 3. ...and act to.credit(t.cents()); return Outcome.APPLIED; } finally { second.lock().unlock(); } } finally { first.lock().unlock(); // 4. on every path } } Kotlin fun apply(t: Transfer): Outcome { val from = account(t.from); val to = account(t.to) val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to // 1. one order for everyone val second = if (first === from) to else from return first.lock.withLock { second.lock.withLock { if (from.balance < t.cents) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS // 2. check... from.debit(t.cents) // 3. ...and act to.credit(t.cents) Outcome.APPLIED } } // 4. withLock releases in a finally } Let's read it in order. First we look up both accounts and decide which one comes first by id (1). Then we take the two locks in that order. Under both locks we check the balance (2), and only then debit and credit (3). Finally, the finally blocks give both locks back on every path (4), including the early return for a refusal. Each line traces back to a rule. Follow the figure below. A transfer from acc-07 to acc-03 and one from acc-03 to acc-07 start at the same moment, and both ask for acc-03 first. One gets it. The other waits for acc-03 while holding nothing, so nobody can be waiting for it, and no cycle can form. A transfer between acc-12 and acc-40 that comes along later needs neither key, and runs straight through. The check sits under both locks, so no other transfer can spend the same money between the check and the debit. And a thread that takes both locks never sees half a transfer. The id is a String, compared with compareTo. It's unique and never changes, and that's all an order needs. hashCode() would not do: two accounts can share a hash code, and then two threads can disagree about which one comes first. Why ReentrantLock, the lock object from the lesson on explicit locks, and not synchronized? For today's code they behave the same. The choice pays off in lesson 3 of this track, where thousands of virtual threads wait for these locks. On JDK 21, a virtual thread waiting at a synchronized block can't let go of the thread that carries it. Keep that promise in mind; we'll come back to it. The lab's Account class is strict about its key. Call debit without holding the account's lock, and it refuses at once: take the lock of account acc-03 first. A missing lock fails loudly in a test, instead of losing money quietly later. What do the extra keys buy? This section's demo counts how many transfers are inside a critical section at once, then times both designs. One run printed: 8 threads x 50,000 transfers, 50 accounts, 50 steps of work inside the lock one ledger lock 294 ms, total 500,000, most transfers in progress at once: 1 per-account locks 336 ms, total 500,000, most transfers in progress at once: 4 The count did what we expected: one at a time with one lock, and about as many as the machine's four cores with a lock per account. The time did not. On this busy machine, the per-account version was no faster. With no work inside the lock, the single lock was often a little quicker, because handing a lock from thread to thread costs more than the few instructions it guards. Both kept the total at 500,000. Count first, then measure, and only then argue. Every path that takes two locks must take them in one order. Lower id first, always. The design is done, and it looks right. But code that looked right has fooled us all through Part 1, so the last step is a test that tries hard to break it. Count the transfers in progress Run LockGranularityDemo. It runs the same 400,000 random transfers under one ledger-wide lock, then under one lock per account, taken in id order. Each transfer does 50 small steps of work inside its locks. Before you read the output, predict the last column, "most transfers in progress at once", for each design. Run it with -Pargs=0 (no work inside the lock) and with -Pargs=200. Compare the times, and explain any surprise. LockGranularityDemo.java package workbench.ledger.l01.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** The same random transfers under one ledger-wide lock, then under per-account locks taken in id order. */ public class LockGranularityDemo { static final int ACCOUNTS = 50; static final class Account { final int id; final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); long balance = 10_000; // guarded by lock (or by the global lock) Account(int id) { this.id = id; } } interface Mover { void move(Account from, Account to, long cents); } static final AtomicInteger inside = new AtomicInteger(); // transfers inside a critical section right now static final AtomicInteger mostInside = new AtomicInteger(); public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int work = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 50; // extra steps inside the lock, per transfer ReentrantLock global = new ReentrantLock(); Mover oneLock = (from, to, cents) -> { global.lock(); // every transfer waits for every other one try { if (from.balance >= cents) { from.balance -= cents; to.balance += cents; } sign(work); // stands in for real work: an entry, a signature } finally { global.unlock(); } }; Mover perAccount = (from, to, cents) -> { Account first = from.id < to.id ? from : to; // lower id first: no cycle can form Account second = first == from ? to : from; first.lock.lock(); try { second.lock.lock(); try { if (from.balance >= cents) { from.balance -= cents; to.balance += cents; } sign(work); } finally { second.lock.unlock(); } } finally { first.lock.unlock(); } }; System.out.printf("8 threads x 50,000 transfers, %d accounts, %d steps of work inside the lock%n", ACCOUNTS, work); for (int round = 0; round < 3; round++) { // round 0 only warms up the JIT time("one ledger lock ", oneLock, round > 0); time("per-account locks", perAccount, round > 0); } } static void sign(int steps) { int now = inside.incrementAndGet(); mostInside.accumulateAndGet(now, Math::max); for (int i = 0; i < steps; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); inside.decrementAndGet(); } static void time(String label, Mover mover, boolean print) throws InterruptedException { Account[] accounts = new Account[ACCOUNTS]; for (int i = 0; i < ACCOUNTS; i++) accounts[i] = new Account(i); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> workers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread w = new Thread(() -> { ThreadLocalRandom rnd = ThreadLocalRandom.current(); try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int n = 0; n < 50_000; n++) { int a = rnd.nextInt(ACCOUNTS), b = rnd.nextInt(ACCOUNTS - 1); if (b >= a) b++; mover.move(accounts[a], accounts[b], 1 + rnd.nextLong(5_000)); } }); w.start(); workers.add(w); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); go.countDown(); for (Thread w : workers) w.join(); long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; long total = 0; for (Account a : accounts) total += a.balance; x: A stress test runs many threads and many operations at once, on purpose, to make bugs show. Testing and debugging concurrent code told the story of a refund test whose two threads never met. On a quiet machine, the first one finished before the second one started. That lesson's habits fix it: a start line so the threads overlap, more threads than cores, many operations, and checks after every thread has finished. The start line is a latch, a counter that threads can wait on. When it reaches zero, every waiting thread goes at once, like runners at the starting gun in Synchronizers. The lab's harness runs 8 threads that each make 100,000 random transfers between 50 accounts: Java CountDownLatch ready = new CountDownLatch(threads), go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> workers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < threads; i++) { int me = i; workers.add(Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { ready.countDown(); try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } // the start line long ok = 0, no = 0; // counted in locals: nothing shared for (int n = 0; n < perThread; n++) { if (ledger.apply(randomTransfer(me, n)) == APPLIED) ok++; else no++; } applied[me] = ok; refused[me] = no; // one slot per thread })); } ready.await(); go.countDown(); // release them together... for (Thread w : workers) w.join(); // ...and wait for all of them Kotlin val ready = CountDownLatch(threads); val go = CountDownLatch(1) val workers = List(threads) { me -> thread { ready.countDown() go.await() // the start line var ok = 0L; var no = 0L // counted in locals: nothing shared repeat(perThread) { n -> if (ledger.apply(randomTransfer(me, n)) == APPLIED) ok++ else no++ } applied[me] = ok; refused[me] = no // one slot per thread } } ready.await(); go.countDown() // release them together... workers.forEach { it.join() } // ...and wait for all of them Let's walk through it. Each worker counts down ready, then waits at go. The main thread waits until every worker is ready, then counts down go, which releases them all together. Each worker counts its own results in local variables, so nothing is shared while it runs, and it writes them into its own slot at the end. Finally, join() waits for every worker, and it is also a handover: after it, the main thread sees every slot. After the joins, the test checks four things. The total is still 500,000. No balance is negative. Applied plus refused is 800,000, so no transfer vanished. And some transfers were refused, which proves the overdraft branch ran at all. That list has a hole, and this section's demo falls right into it. Take a ledger that locks in id order, but checks the balance before it takes the locks. No balance was negative at the end. Yet while it ran, 2,129 debits took an account below zero. Later credits topped those accounts up before anyone looked. A test that checks only the final state sees a healthy ledger. So check each rule where it can break, as well as at the end. The lab's Account.debit throws IllegalStateException when a debit would overdraw, so a race that overdraws fails the stress test at once. The check costs one comparison, and in a real bank it turns a silent loss into an error someone sees. A rule checked only at the end can heal before you look. Check it where it can break. Its withLock is an inline function that calls lock(), runs the block and calls unlock() in a finally, so the two nested try/finally blocks become two nested blocks. Because withLock is inline, return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS inside it returns from apply itself, and both locks are still released. from.id < to.id on strings calls the same compareTo as the Java version. The Transfer differs only in style: a Kotlin data class of vals is exactly as shallow as a Java record. Both make the fields final, and neither copies a changeable list you pass in.

h: Design the ledger and make it correct · Worked example
x: Add a fee without breaking the rules The bank decides to charge a small fee on each transfer, paid into a fee account the bank owns. Money is still conserved: the sender pays cents + fee, the receiver gets cents and the fee account gets fee. Now three accounts change in one step. Here is a first attempt. Read it against the three rules and the lock order before you go on. Outcome applyWithFee(Transfer t, long fee) { Account from = account(t.from()), to = account(t.to()); from.lock().lock(); to.lock().lock(); feeAccount.lock().lock(); try { if (from.balance() < t.cents()) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS; from.debit(t.cents() + fee); to.credit(t.cents()); feeAccount.credit(fee); return Outcome.APPLIED; } finally { feeAccount.lock().unlock(); to.lock().unlock(); from.lock().unlock(); } } fun applyWithFee(t: Transfer, fee: Long): Outcome { val from = account(t.from); val to = account(t.to) from.lock.lock() to.lock.lock() feeAccount.lock.lock() try { if (from.balance < t.cents) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS from.debit(t.cents + fee) to.credit(t.cents) feeAccount.credit(fee) return Outcome.APPLIED } finally { feeAccount.lock.unlock() to.lock.unlock() from.lock.unlock() } } There are two bugs. First, the locks are taken by role, sender first, not by id. A transfer from acc-02 to acc-05 locks 02, then 05, while a transfer from acc-05 to acc-02 locks 05, then 02. That's Ana and Ben again. Second, the check tests cents, but the debit takes cents + fee, so a sender with exactly cents left goes below zero. The lab's debit would throw; a plain field would go negative without a word. Sort every account the operation touches by id, lock them in that order, and release them in reverse. The same code works for two accounts, three, or a batch of fifty. distinct() covers the case where the sender is the fee account itself, because a ReentrantLock taken twice must also be released twice. Outcome applyWithFee(Transfer t, long fee) { Account from = account(t.from()), to = account(t.to()); List<Account> touched = Stream.of(from, to, feeAccount) .distinct() .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Account::id)) // 1. one global order, any number of locks .toList(); touched.forEach(a -> a.lock().lock()); try { if (from.balance() < t.cents() + fee) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS; // 2. check what is debited from.debit(t.cents() + fee); // 3. three changes, one critical section to.credit(t.cents()); feeAccount.credit(fee); return Outcome.APPLIED; } finally { for (int i = touched.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) touched.get(i).lock().unlock(); // 4. reverse order } } fun applyWithFee(t: Transfer, fee: Long): Outcome { val from = account(t.from); val to = account(t.to) val touched = listOf(from, to, feeAccount) .distinct() .sortedBy { it.id } // 1. one global order, any number of locks touched.forEach { it.lock.lock() } try { if (from.balance < t.cents + fee) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS // 2. check what is debited from.debit(t.cents + fee) // 3. three changes, one critical section to.credit(t.cents) feeAccount.credit(fee) return Outcome.APPLIED } finally { touched.asReversed().forEach { it.lock.unlock() } // 4. reverse order } } Check it against the rules. Conservation: the sender loses cents + fee, and the other two gain exactly that. No overdraft: the check and the debit use the same amount, under the same locks. Whole or nothing: all three changes happen inside one set of locks. No deadlock: plain apply locks two accounts in id order and this method locks three in id order, so any two operations agree on which lock comes first. Where the fee account's id sorts among the customers' ids doesn't matter. Only the rule matters.
