h: Design the ledger and make it correct · Key terms
x: Ledger The bank's book of accounts and of every movement of money between them. In the lab, the class that holds the accounts and applies transfers. Invariant A rule about your data that must be true whenever another thread can look, such as "the total never changes". Global lock order One rule, such as "lower account id first", that every piece of code follows when it takes more than one lock. It makes a cycle of waiting threads impossible. Lock granularity How much data one lock guards: the whole ledger, or one account. Finer locks let more work run at once, and they need a lock order. Compact constructor A record constructor without a parameter list. It runs before the fields are set, so it can check or clean up the values. Stress test A test that starts many threads at once, runs many operations, then checks the rules. It can find a race, but never prove there is none. Overdraft A debit that takes a balance below zero. In this ledger it is a bug, so debit refuses it. Ledger rule 1: what must the sum of all balances do? Never change. A transfer moves money between accounts; it never creates or destroys any. Why must the balance check sit inside the same locks as the debit? Otherwise it is check-then-act: another transfer can spend the money between the check and the debit, and the balance goes below zero. What stops transfer(A, B) and transfer(B, A) from deadlocking when each takes two locks? One global lock order: always lock the account with the lower id first, whichever way the money moves. Why not order locks by hashCode()? Two accounts can share a hash code. On a tie, two threads may lock in opposite orders. Use a unique id that never changes. How do you lock N accounts for one operation without deadlock? Sort them by id, lock in that order, release in reverse. Call distinct() first if one account can appear twice. What does a record's compact constructor give a Transfer? Checks that run before the fields are set, so every Transfer that exists is valid. With final fields, any thread sees it whole. A stress test checks only the final state. What can it miss? Broken rules that heal: an account that went below zero and was topped up later. Also check each rule where it can break.

x: Two ways this design grows in a real bank. The first is a busy account. Say one shop's account receives a third of all transfers. Every one of them waits for that account's single lock, whatever the order. A common fix is to split the account into a few smaller accounts, each with its own lock, credit a random one, and add them up when someone asks for the balance. For a single account, you could also drop the lock and use a compare-and-set loop, as Atomics and compare-and-set showed. The check becomes part of the loop: Java boolean debit(AtomicLong balance, long cents) { while (true) { long current = balance.get(); if (current < cents) return false; // the check is inside the loop if (balance.compareAndSet(current, current - cents)) return true; } } Kotlin fun debit(balance: AtomicLong, cents: Long): Boolean { while (true) { val current = balance.get() if (current < cents) return false // the check is inside the loop if (balance.compareAndSet(current, current - cents)) return true } } That works for one account without any lock. A transfer touches two, and two compare-and-sets in a row are not one step: between them, the money is in neither account, which breaks rule 3. That's why locks are the simpler tool for transfers. The second is the database. A ledger kept on disk uses the same ideas with other tools: row locks taken in account id order, a CHECK (balance >= 0) rule on the table, and a unique key on the transfer id, so a transfer that arrives twice is applied once. Many real ledgers never change a balance in place at all. They add entries that never change, one debit and one credit per transfer, and compute each balance by adding up its entries. That's double-entry bookkeeping, a method traders and banks have used for centuries, and rule 1 becomes "the entries of every transfer add up to zero", which you can check one transfer at a time.

h: Run it on a pool you can reason about · Every setting is a decision: sizing the pool from the bank's own numbers
x: Lesson 1's ledger is correct on any number of threads. Now it needs threads to run on. A real transfer does more than change two numbers. It first goes into the journal, a log on disk that the ledger writes before it changes anything in memory. If the program crashes, the journal still says which transfers were accepted, so none of them is lost. Say a journal write takes 5 ms. Thread pools and executors pictured a pool as a kitchen: a team of cooks (the threads) taking tickets off a rail (the queue). The one-line pools each get one part of that kitchen wrong. Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8) has a rail with no end, so a slow disk turns into millions of waiting transfers and, finally, a program that runs out of memory. Executors.newCachedThreadPool() hires a new cook for every ticket, so the same slow disk turns into thousands of threads. So we build the pool ourselves, and write down a reason for every setting: Java PoolPlan plan = PoolPlan.fromLittlesLaw(1_600, Duration.ofMillis(5), Duration.ofMillis(50)); // 8 and 80 ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor( plan.threads(), plan.threads(), // core == max: no extra threads in a rush 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(plan.queueCapacity()), // bounded: a full queue says no Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(), // ledger-0, ledger-1, ... in every dump new CountingAbortPolicy()); // counted, then thrown at the caller pool.prestartAllCoreThreads(); Kotlin val plan = PoolPlan.fromLittlesLaw(1_600, Duration.ofMillis(5), Duration.ofMillis(50)) // 8 and 80 val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor( plan.threads(), plan.threads(), // core == max: no extra threads in a rush 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(plan.queueCapacity()), // bounded: a full queue says no Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(), // ledger-0, ledger-1, ... in every dump CountingAbortPolicy()) // counted, then thrown at the caller pool.prestartAllCoreThreads() The sizes come from Little's law, from Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law. It says the number of things inside a system equals the rate at which they arrive times how long each one stays. At the payday peak of 1,600 transfers a second, each holding a thread for 5 ms, that's 1,600 x 0.005 = 8 transfers in flight, that is, in progress at once. So we need 8 threads. With fewer, the queue grows at every peak. With many more, we only add threads that wait on the same disk. The queue gets the same law. A busy pool finishes 1,600 transfers a second, so 80 queued transfers drain in 80 / 1,600 = 50 ms. If 50 ms is the longest a transfer should wait for a thread, 80 slots is the most the queue should hold. A queue of 10,000 would hide six seconds of waiting, long after the customer's app has given up. A pool has a core size, the threads it keeps, and a maximum size, the most it may ever have. Core equals max here because, as Inside ThreadPoolExecutor showed, a pool adds threads past its core only when the queue is full. Extra threads would only add waiters on the same journal, so the right answer to a full queue is no. That leaves the last decision: what happens to a transfer when the queue is full. That's the rejection policy. DiscardPolicy and DiscardOldestPolicy drop a transfer without telling anyone, so they are never right for money. CallerRunsPolicy makes the thread that submitted the transfer write the journal itself. That suits a nightly import, and it's wrong for a thread serving a customer who is waiting. So the lab counts and throws. The counting policy is the bank's doorman. When the waiting area is full, he turns the next customer away politely and makes a mark on his clipboard. The customer gets a fast "busy, try again in a moment" (web servers send it as status 503) and tries again with the same transfer id. The marks show up on the bank's dashboard, the screen where its staff watch the program's numbers. The thread factory gives each thread a name tag, ledger-0 to ledger-7, as Pools in production did for the kitchen's cooks. Those name tags will matter at the end of this lesson. A pool you can't explain is a pool you can't trust. Write down a reason for every number. The pool can take transfers now. The harder moment comes when it has to stop. Send a burst at the pool Run BurstDemo: 300 transfers of 5 ms each arrive at once at the pool above. Predict how many are accepted, and how long submitting takes. Run it with -Pargs=callerRuns. Predict how many transfers the submitting thread runs itself, and how long submitting takes now. Pass "callerRuns" to swap the counting abort policy for CallerRunsPolicy. */ public class BurstDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean callerRuns = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("callerRuns"); AtomicInteger rejected = new AtomicInteger(); RejectedExecutionHandler policy = callerRuns ? new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy() // the submitting thread runs it itself : (task, pool) -> { // count it, then throw at the caller rejected.incrementAndGet(); throw new RejectedExecutionException("ledger pool full"); }; ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 8, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(80), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(), policy); pool.prestartAllCoreThreads(); AtomicInteger ranOnCaller = new AtomicInteger(); String caller = Thread.currentThread().getName(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); int accepted = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 300; i++) { try { pool.execute(() -> { if (Thread.currentThread().getName().equals(caller)) ranOnCaller.incrementAndGet(); sleep(5); // the journal write }); accepted++; } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { // a web server would answer "busy, try again soon" (status 503) here } } long submitMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); long doneMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%s: accepted %d, rejected %d, run by the submitting thread %d%n", callerRuns ? "CallerRunsPolicy" : "counting abort", accepted, rejected.get(), ranOnCaller.get()); System.out.printf("submitting took %d ms, all done after %d ms%n", submitMs, doneMs); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :ledger:demo -Pmain=workbench.ledger.l02.demo.BurstDemo labs/ledger/src/demo/java/workbench/ledger/l02/demo/BurstDemo.java BurstDemo.kt package workbench.ledger.l02.demo import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionHandler import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** * A burst of 300 transfers hits a pool sized with Little's law: 8 threads, 80 queue slots, 5 ms * per transfer. On a very busy machine you may see 80, if the threads hadn't taken their first tasks before the queue filled. The accepted ones are done after roughly 60 to 70 ms (88 x 5 ms / 8 threads, plus start-up). With CallerRunsPolicy, nothing is turned away, but the submitting thread ran 24 or 25 transfers itself, and submitting took 131 to 141 ms instead of 5 to 8. While that thread writes a journal entry, it can't submit anything, which slows the stream down. If it were serving a customer, that customer would have waited the whole time for other people's transfers. Little's law sizes both halves of the pool: 8 threads for the transfers in flight, 80 slots for 50 ms of waiting. Whatever doesn't fit is turned away and counted. h: Run it on a pool you can reason about · Closing time: shutting down without losing a transfer
x: A new version of the bank's program goes live, and the old one has to stop while transfers are still queued. Each of them belongs to a customer who was told "accepted". So the rule for shutdown is simple to say. When it ends, every accepted transfer has been applied, has failed with an error its caller saw, or has been handed back to us by id. None may vanish. pool.shutdownNow() on its own breaks that rule. It interrupts the running tasks, that is, asks them to stop, and returns the queued ones as a List<Runnable>. Ignore the list, and those transfers are gone. Worse, their futures never complete. A future is the takeaway ticket from Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption: the caller holds it, and waits on it with get() until the result is ready. Here is what this section's demo printed with a bare shutdownNow(): naive, grace 100 ms: accepted 1,000 | applied 0 | interrupted 8 | handed back 0 | lost 992 futures that will never complete: 992 Out of 1,000 accepted transfers, 992 simply vanished, and each one left a ticket that will never be called. A customer waiting on one of them would wait, very patiently, forever. Pools in production closed the kitchen at night in order: stop taking orders, let the cooks finish within a deadline, then stop what's left and write it down. Here is that order for the ledger: Java public ShutdownReport shutdown(Duration grace) throws InterruptedException { pool.shutdown(); // 1. no new transfers; the queue drains if (pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) return new ShutdownReport(true, List.of()); // 2. everything accepted was applied List<Transfer> neverStarted = new ArrayList<>(); for (Runnable r : pool.shutdownNow()) { // 3. interrupt, take back the queue TransferTask task = (TransferTask) r; task.cancel(false); // wakes a caller blocked in get() neverStarted.add(task.transfer()); } pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS); return new ShutdownReport(false, List.copyOf(neverStarted)); // 4. log them, or replay them } Kotlin fun shutdown(grace: Duration): ShutdownReport { pool.shutdown() // 1. no new transfers; the queue drains if (pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) return ShutdownReport(true, emptyList()) // 2. everything accepted was applied val neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow().map { r -> // 3. interrupt, take back the queue val task = r as TransferTask task.cancel(false) // wakes a caller blocked in get() task.transfer } pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) return ShutdownReport(false, neverStarted) // 4. log them, or replay them } First, shutdown() closes the door to new transfers, while the queue keeps draining (1). Then we wait up to the grace period, the time we allow for draining. If the pool finished, everything accepted was applied (2). If not, shutdownNow() interrupts the running transfers and hands back the queue (3). We cancel each queued task, which completes its future, so a caller blocked in get() wakes up with a CancellationException instead of waiting forever. Finally, we wait once more and report the transfers that never started, so someone can log them or run them again later (4). Two details make this work. First, the queue must hold objects that know their transfer. pool.submit(callable) wraps your work in an anonymous FutureTask, so the lab's submit builds a TransferTask, a FutureTask that remembers its transfer, and hands it to execute. Then shutdownNow() gives back transfers, not mystery Runnables. Second, an interrupted task must leave nothing half done. Each task writes the journal first and changes memory second. An interrupt during the journal write means the transfer was never applied: its future fails, and no balance changed. And apply itself never waits for anything, so once it starts, it finishes. The grace period comes from the same numbers as the pool. A full queue of 80 drains in 50 ms, so a few seconds of grace is plenty. The system that stops a program for a new version usually waits about 30 seconds before it stops it by force, and the drain fits easily inside that. With the drain in place, the same demo printed: drain, grace 100 ms: accepted 1,000 | applied 157 | interrupted 8 | handed back 835 | lost 0 futures that will never complete: 0 The arithmetic holds: 100 ms is 20 rounds of 5 ms on 8 threads, about 160 transfers. Eight were stopped in the middle of their journal write, and the other 835 came back by id. Shutdown is part of the program. Drain first, then hand back what never ran. No transfer goes missing at closing time now. But a customer who asks for every balance at once can still see a number that never existed. Lose transfers, then stop losing them Run ShutdownDemo -Pargs=naive: 1,000 accepted transfers, then a bare shutdownNow(). Read the lost column and the last line. Run it with no arguments (drain, 100 ms of grace), then with -Pargs='drain 5000'. Before each run, predict how many transfers are applied. Where does each one end up? * Args: "naive" or "drain" (the default), then the grace period in ms (default 100). */ public class ShutdownDemo { record Transfer(int id) {} // a FutureTask that remembers its transfer, so the queue hands back transfers, not anonymous Runnables static final class TransferTask extends FutureTask<Boolean> { final Transfer transfer; TransferTask(Transfer transfer, Callable<Boolean> work) { super(work); this.transfer = transfer; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "drain"; long graceMs = args.length > 1 ? // not journaled, so not applied throw e; } applied.incrementAndGet(); return true; }); pool.execute(task); accepted.add(task); } int handedBack = 0; if (mode.equals("naive")) { pool.shutdownNow(); // the list of queued tasks it returns is dropped } else { pool.shutdown(); // 1. no new work; the queue keeps draining if (!pool.awaitTermination(graceMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { List<Runnable> neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow(); // 2. interrupt, take back the queue for (Runnable r : neverStarted) ((TransferTask) r).cancel(false); // 3. wake anyone waiting on them handedBack = neverStarted.size(); // 4. log these ids, or replay them on restart } } pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); long neverComplete = accepted.stream().filter(t -> !t.isDone()).count(); System.out.printf("%s, grace %d ms: accepted 1,000 | applied %,d | interrupted %d | handed back %,d | lost %,d%n", mode, graceMs, applied.get(), interrupted.get(), handedBack, 1_000 - applied.get() - interrupted.get() - handedBack); System.out.printf("futures that will never complete: %,d%n", neverComplete); } } ./gradlew :ledger:demo -Pmain=workbench.ledger.l02.demo.ShutdownDemo labs/ledger/src/demo/java/workbench/ledger/l02/demo/ShutdownDemo.java ShutdownDemo.kt package workbench.ledger.l02.demo import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.FutureTask import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger private data class QueuedTransfer(val id: Int) // a FutureTask that remembers its transfer, so the queue hands back transfers, not anonymous Runnables private class QueuedTask(val transfer: QueuedTransfer, work: Callable<Boolean>) : FutureTask<Boolean>(work) /** * 1,000 transfers wait on 8 threads at 5 ms each, then the service stops. Where does each one end up? * Args: "naive" or "drain" (the default), then the grace period in ms (default 100). */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val mode = args.getOrElse(0) { "drain" } val graceMs = args.getOrNull(1)?.toLong() ?: 100 val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 8, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(1_000), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory()) val applied = AtomicInteger() val interrupted = AtomicInteger() val accepted = (0 until 1_000).map { i -> QueuedTask(QueuedTransfer(i)) { try { Thread.sleep(5) // the journal write } catch (e: InterruptedException) { interrupted.incrementAndGet() // not journaled, so not applied throw e } applied.incrementAndGet() true }.also { pool.execute(it) } } var handedBack = 0 if (mode == "naive") { pool.shutdownNow() // the list of queued tasks it returns is dropped } else { pool.shutdown() // 1. no new work; the queue keeps draining if (!pool.awaitTermination(graceMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { val neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow() // 2. interrupt, take back the queue neverStarted.forEach { (it as QueuedTask).cancel(false) } // 3. wake anyone waiting on them handedBack = neverStarted.size // 4. log these ids, or replay them on restart } } pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) val neverComplete = accepted.count { !it.isDone } println("%s, grace %d ms: accepted 1,000 | applied %,d | interrupted %d | handed back %,d | lost %,d".format( mode, graceMs, applied.get(), interrupted.get(), handedBack, 1_000 - applied.get() - interrupted.get() - handedBack)) println("futures that will never complete: %,d".format(neverComplete)) } ./gradlew :ledger:demo -Pmain=workbench.ledger.l02.demo.ShutdownDemoKt labs/ledger/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/ledger/l02/demo/ShutdownDemo.kt Naive: about 990 lost (987 and 992 in runs here), and as many futures that will never complete, so their callers would wait forever. h: Run it on a pool you can reason about · A snapshot of every balance, published so nobody sees it torn
x: Locked reads one account at a time are a panorama, and the sum tears; a snapshot takes every lock in id order, copies into a record that never changes, and publishes it with one volatile write, so readers see old or new, never a mix The bank's app has a page that shows every balance at once, and rule 1 says they must add up to the opening total. Let's try the obvious way on a small ledger: 50 accounts with 1,000 cents each, so 50,000 in total. A reader walks the accounts in id order. It locks one account, reads it, adds it and moves on: Java long sum = 0; for (Account a : accounts) { a.lock().lock(); try { sum += a.balance(); } finally { a.lock().unlock(); } // each read is safe... } // ...the sum is not Kotlin var sum = 0L for (a in accounts) { sum += a.lock.withLock { a.balance } // each read is safe... } // ...the sum is not Trace the smallest case. The reader has already passed account 3. Now a transfer moves 300 cents from account 40 to account 3. The reader goes on and reads the rest, account 40 included, and gets 49,700. It saw account 3 before the money arrived, and account 40 after it left. Every read held a lock, and no transfer broke a rule. The sum still mixes two moments. A sum like that is torn: it matches no state the ledger was ever in. A transfer in the other direction makes the reader count the same money twice. In one Java run of this section's demo, 7,241 of 9,456 sums were torn, some by thousands of cents. Runs on a busier machine tore fewer, 368 to 506 sums out of thousands, but never none. A whole snapshot needs one moment at which no transfer is half done. Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal gave us the picture. The shop owner doesn't erase prices while people read the board; she prints a new board and hangs it up in one move. For the ledger, that means taking every account's lock, in the same id order that apply uses, so a snapshot can never deadlock with a transfer. Then we copy the balances into a new record that never changes, publish it, and let go: Java public BalanceSnapshot snapshot() { for (Account a : inLockOrder) a.lock().lock(); // 1. every lock, in id order try { Map<String, Long> copy = new HashMap<>(); long total = 0; for (Account a : inLockOrder) { copy.put(a.id(), a.balance()); total += a.balance(); } BalanceSnapshot s = new BalanceSnapshot(copy, total, ++version); // 2. a record that never changes latest = s; // 3. one volatile write publishes it return s; } finally { for (int i = inLockOrder.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) inLockOrder.get(i).lock().unlock(); } } Kotlin fun snapshot(): BalanceSnapshot { inLockOrder.forEach { it.lock.lock() } // 1. every lock, in id order try { val copy = inLockOrder.associate { it.id to it.balance } val s = BalanceSnapshot(copy, copy.values.sum(), ++version) // 2. a record that never changes latest = s // 3. one @Volatile write publishes it return s } finally { inLockOrder.asReversed().forEach { it.lock.unlock() } } } First we take every lock, in id order (1). Now no transfer can move money. Then we copy all 50 balances into a new record, with the total and a version number (2). Then one write to latest publishes it (3). The keyword volatile marks a field whose every read sees the latest write, from any thread. Last, the finally releases the locks in reverse order, and any transfer that was waiting runs. Readers stop adding things up. They read one field, latest, which points to the last finished snapshot, and they take no lock at all. A reader who looks just before a new snapshot is published sees all of the old one: old, but whole. A reader who looks just after sees all of the new one. Old or new, never a mix. Happens-before, the rules that matter, asked us to name the rule that makes each shared field safe to read. Here is the list for the whole ledger: Field Why every reader sees it correctly Account.balance the account's lock: each release happens-before the next lock of the same account accounts, inLockOrder final fields, set in the constructor, never changed version written only while every account lock is held latest volatile: its write happens-before every later read a snapshot's balances and total final fields of a record, holding a map that Map.copyOf made unchangeable a Transfer in the pool it never changes, and execute happens-before the task runs a transfer's outcome the task's end happens-before Future.get() returns Three pictures from the memory model track sit in that table. The account locks are the cashier's key: whoever takes the same key next sees everything written before it was handed on. latest is the museum's OPEN/CLOSED sign, a volatile field that every reader checks fresh. And a finished BalanceSnapshot is a letter in a sealed envelope, whole for anyone who receives it. Writing latest before the locks are released keeps snapshots in version order. Two snapshots can't overlap, because each one needs every lock. Build the whole snapshot while no transfer can run, then publish it with one volatile write. Every field now has a named rule behind it. One last kind of failure has no field at all: a pool that waits for itself. Tear a snapshot, then make it whole Run TornSnapshotDemo. Four threads move money while the main thread adds up all 50 balances, one locked account at a time. Predict how many sums come out wrong. Run it with -Pargs=locked, where the reader holds every lock while it adds. TornSnapshotDemo.java package workbench.ledger.l02.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** * Four threads move money between 50 accounts while a reader adds up all the balances. * Pass "locked" to make the reader hold every account lock while it adds. */ public class TornSnapshotDemo { static final class Account { final int id; final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); long balance = 1_000; // guarded by lock: 50,000 in total Account(int id) { this.id = id; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean locked = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("locked"); Account[] accounts = new Account[50]; for (int i = 0; i < accounts.length; i++) accounts[i] = new Account(i); AtomicBoolean writing = new AtomicBoolean(true); List<Thread> writers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int w = 0; w < 4; w++) { writers.add(Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { ThreadLocalRandom rnd = ThreadLocalRandom.current(); for (int n = 0; n < 200_000; n++) { int a = rnd.nextInt(50), b = rnd.nextInt(49); if (b >= a) b++; move(accounts[a], accounts[b], 1 + rnd.nextLong(500)); } })); } long taken = 0, torn = 0, worst = 0; while (writers.stream().anyMatch(Thread::isAlive)) { long sum = locked ? sumAllLocked(accounts) : sumOneByOne(accounts); taken++; if (sum != 50_000) { torn++; worst = Math.max(worst, Math.abs(sum - 50_000)); } } System.out.printf("%s: %,d snapshots, %,d torn (worst off by %,d cents)%n", locked ? "every lock held" : "one account at a time", taken, torn, worst); } // each read is safe on its own; the sum is not, because money moves between reads static long sumOneByOne(Account[] accounts) { long sum = 0; for (Account a : accounts) { a.lock.lock(); try { sum += a.balance; } finally { a.lock.unlock(); } } return sum; } // every lock, in id order: no transfer can run while we add, so the sum is one instant static long sumAllLocked(Account[] accounts) { for (Account a : accounts) a.lock.lock(); try { long sum = 0; for (Account a : accounts) sum += a.balance; return sum; } finally { for (int i = accounts.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) accounts[i].lock.unlock(); } } static void move(Account from, Account to, long cents) { Account first = from.id < to.id ? from : to, second = first == from ? to : from; h: Run it on a pool you can reason about · A stuck pool, found in a thread dump
x: Here is a bug that passes every test with a small batch. At the end of each month, the bank prints a statement for every account, a page that shows its balance. The statement job runs on the ledger pool, and each statement asks the same pool for the balance: Java pool.submit(() -> { Future<Long> balance = pool.submit(() -> balanceOf(account)); // a task inside a task return account + ": " + balance.get(); // waits for it }); Kotlin pool.submit(Callable { val balance = pool.submit(Callable { balanceOf(account) }) // a task inside a task "$account: ${balance.get()}" // waits for it }) With 2 threads and 3 statements, the first two statements take both threads. Each one submits a balance lookup, which joins the queue behind the third statement. Now both threads wait for lookups that need a free thread, and no thread will ever be free. Pools in production called this pool-induced deadlock, and pictured it as cooks waiting for tickets that sit on the rail behind them. This section is about finding it in a running program. The tool is jcmd, which comes with the JDK and sends commands to a running Java program. One of its commands prints a thread dump: every thread's name, state and stack (the chain of method calls it is in the middle of) at one moment. Start PoolHangDemo with a long hang, then run this from a second terminal: jcmd # lists running Java programs and their process ids jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l # -l adds the java.util.concurrent locks each thread holds Here's the part that matters, from a real run on JDK 21, trimmed: "ledger-0" #19 [5741] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=1.33ms elapsed=1.74s ... waiting on condition java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking) at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(java.base@21.0.12.1/Native Method) - parking to wait for <0x00000006f79ef530> (a java.util.concurrent.FutureTask) at java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park(java.base@21.0.12.1/LockSupport.java:221) at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.awaitDone(java.base@21.0.12.1/FutureTask.java:500) at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.get(java.base@21.0.12.1/FutureTask.java:190) at workbench.ledger.l02.demo.PoolHangDemo.statement(PoolHangDemo.java:33) at workbench.ledger.l02.demo.PoolHangDemo.lambda$main$0(PoolHangDemo.java:21) ... at java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor.runWorker(java.base@21.0.12.1/ThreadPoolExecutor.java:1144) ... Locked ownable synchronizers: - <0x00000006f79650b8> (a java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker) "ledger-1" #20 [5742] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=0.83ms elapsed=1.74s ... waiting on condition java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking) at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(java.base@21.0.12.1/Native Method) - parking to wait for <0x00000006f7602c18> (a java.util.concurrent.FutureTask) ... at workbench.ledger.l02.demo.PoolHangDemo.statement(PoolHangDemo.java:33) ... Locked ownable synchronizers: - <0x00000006f79bb838> (a java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker) Read each thread in the same order. The name says which pool: both ledger- threads are stuck, and their name tags tell us so at once. The state, WAITING (parking), means a java.util.concurrent tool put them to sleep; a thread stuck at a synchronized block would say BLOCKED. The parking to wait for line names the object they wait on, a FutureTask, so they are inside get(). The first line from our own code, statement at line 33, is that get() call. And under Locked ownable synchronizers, each thread holds its own ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker, a lock that a pool thread holds while it runs a task. Both threads are busy, and busy waiting. Notice what's missing: the dump never says Found one Java-level deadlock. The JVM's detector looks for threads that hold locks other threads want, in a circle. Here nobody holds a lock that anybody else wants. So learn this signature instead: every thread of one pool parked on a FutureTask from that same pool, with tasks still queued. The fixes come from that lesson. Do the lookup inline, chain the next step with thenApply instead of waiting, or give lookups their own pool. A pool whose tasks wait on the same pool can stop without any lock. Never wait on your own pool from inside it. This pool is right for the journal writes, which are short and few at a time. It would be wrong for the customers' requests themselves. A request spends most of its time waiting on other services, and a pool of platform threads, the ordinary threads the operating system runs, can hold only a few hundred waiting requests. That's the next sitting's job. Take the dump yourself Run PoolHangDemo with -Pargs=60 so it stays stuck for a minute. It prints its process id. In a second terminal, run jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l. For both ledger- threads, find the state, the parking to wait for line, the first line from workbench.ledger, and the Locked ownable synchronizers. Then find main. Scroll to the end of the dump. Is there a deadlock report? Explain why not. Change statement to call balanceOf(account) directly instead of submitting it, and run the demo again. x: Starting the pool and submitting a transfer LedgerService.java public static LedgerService start(Ledger ledger, Journal journal, PoolPlan plan) { CountingAbortPolicy rejections = new CountingAbortPolicy(); ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor( plan.threads(), plan.threads(), 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(plan.queueCapacity()), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(), rejections); pool.prestartAllCoreThreads(); return new LedgerService(ledger, journal, pool, rejections); } public Future<Outcome> submit(Transfer t) { TransferTask task = new TransferTask(t, () -> { journal.append(t); return ledger.apply(t); }); pool.execute(task); return task; } static final class TransferTask extends FutureTask<Outcome> { private final Transfer transfer; TransferTask(Transfer transfer, Callable<Outcome> work) { super(work); this.transfer = transfer; } Transfer transfer() { return transfer; } } LedgerService.kt fun start(ledger: Ledger, journal: Journal, plan: PoolPlan): LedgerService { val rejections = CountingAbortPolicy() val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor( plan.threads, plan.threads, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(plan.queueCapacity), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(), rejections) pool.prestartAllCoreThreads() return LedgerService(ledger, journal, pool, rejections) } fun submit(t: Transfer): Future<Outcome> { val task = TransferTask(t) { journal.append(t) ledger.apply(t) } pool.execute(task) return task } class TransferTask(val transfer: Transfer, work: Callable<Outcome>) : FutureTask<Outcome>(work) Nothing here is special to either language: ThreadPoolExecutor, ArrayBlockingQueue and Thread.ofPlatform() are the same JDK classes, with the same rules. Kotlin shortens the FutureTask subclass to one line, because the constructor parameter work goes straight to the parent class in the class header, and a trailing lambda becomes the Java Callable. One Kotlin detail matters. When you call pool.submit with a bare lambda, Kotlin has to choose between submit(Runnable) and submit(Callable). Writing Callable { ... } says which one you mean, so the future carries your result.

h: Run it on a pool you can reason about · Worked example
x: Size the pool for a busier payday The bank expects a busier payday: 4,000 transfers a second at the peak. Under that load, a journal write takes 4 ms. We want no transfer to wait more than 100 ms for a thread. Start with Little's law, for both halves of the pool. // 1. peak rate, time each transfer holds a thread, longest acceptable wait in the queue PoolPlan plan = PoolPlan.fromLittlesLaw(4_000, Duration.ofMillis(4), Duration.ofMillis(100)); // 2. 4,000/s x 0.004 s = 16 in flight; 4,000/s x 0.1 s = 400 waiting System.out.println(plan); // PoolPlan[threads=16, queueCapacity=400] // 1. peak rate, time each transfer holds a thread, longest acceptable wait in the queue val plan = PoolPlan.fromLittlesLaw(4_000, Duration.ofMillis(4), Duration.ofMillis(100)) // 2. 4,000/s x 0.004 s = 16 in flight; 4,000/s x 0.1 s = 400 waiting println(plan) // PoolPlan[threads=16, queueCapacity=400] Now check what sits behind the pool, as Sizing a pool insisted. The disk that holds the journal handles 12 writes at once before each one slows down. With 16 threads, the extra 4 only queue inside the journal and make every write slower. The real ceiling is the journal's: 12 writes / 0.004 s = 3,000 transfers a second, whatever the forecast says. Size from the scarce resource, and let the rejection policy handle the rest. At 3,000 a second, 100 ms of waiting is 300 slots. Above that rate, the doorman turns transfers away and counts them, and customers get a fast "busy, try again". // 3. the journal takes 12 writes at once: that sets the threads, and the throughput PoolPlan capped = new PoolPlan(12, 300); // 12 / 0.004 s = 3,000 a second; 3,000 x 0.1 s = 300 slots LedgerService service = LedgerService.start(ledger, journal, capped); // 3. the journal takes 12 writes at once: that sets the threads, and the throughput val capped = PoolPlan(12, 300) // 12 / 0.004 s = 3,000 a second; 3,000 x 0.1 s = 300 slots val service = LedgerService.start(ledger, journal, capped) If 3,000 isn't enough, more threads won't help, because the journal is the bottleneck, the narrowest point everything passes through. Make each write carry more instead. Writing a batch of transfers to disk in one go (often called group commit) raises what 12 writes at once can carry. Then check shutdown again: 300 queued transfers on 12 threads at 4 ms drain in 100 ms, so a 5 s grace period still fits well inside the usual 30 s.

h: Run it on a pool you can reason about · Quiz
x: A teammate builds the ledger pool as new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 32, 60, SECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()). The journal slows from 5 ms to 500 ms per write. What happens? The pool grows to 32 threads and keeps up The pool stays at 8 threads and the queue grows without limit Transfers are turned away once 32 are running The pool shrinks back to 8 threads after 60 seconds A pool adds threads past its core size only when the queue refuses a task, and a LinkedBlockingQueue with no size never refuses. So the 32 is dead code, nothing is ever turned away, and every transfer waits behind a queue that only grows. The first option is what most people expect from "max 32". Peak traffic is 1,200 transfers a second, and each holds a ledger thread for 10 ms. How many threads does Little's law ask for? 12 120 1,200 10 In flight = 1,200 a second x 0.010 s = 12. 120 would mean 100 ms per transfer, and 1,200 forgets the time entirely. After that, check that the journal can take 12 writes at once; if not, its limit is your ceiling. The snapshot job writes latest = new BalanceSnapshot(copy, total, v) to a plain field, not a volatile one, and request threads read latest without locks. What can a reader see? Always the newest snapshot, because a reference is written in one step A snapshot with some balances missing, because Map.copyOf copies lazily An exception, because two threads touch the same field An old snapshot, maybe for a long time, because no happens-before rule links the write to the read Without volatile, nothing orders the job's write before the readers' reads, so the JIT, the part of the JVM that compiles busy code while it runs, may keep an old reference in a register, and a reader may not see a newer snapshot for a long time. The record's final fields make whatever snapshot a reader does see complete, so the risk is an old answer, not a half-built map. Map.copyOf copies at once. Make the field volatile. Do the lookup inline in the statement task Chain with supplyAsync(lookup, pool).thenApply(render) and wait only at the caller Give the pool a fifth thread Run the lookups on a separate pool that never waits for the statement pool A fifth thread only moves the hang to the fifth statement running at once, and at the end of the month there are hundreds. The other three remove the wait: inline needs no second task, chaining never holds a thread while it waits, and a separate lookup pool can't be filled up by statements. Which rejection policy fits the ledger pool when the submitting thread serves a customer who is waiting for the answer? DiscardPolicy, because the customer can try again A policy that counts and throws, so the customer gets a fast "busy, try again" DiscardOldestPolicy, because the newest transfer matters most CallerRunsPolicy, so the customer's thread writes the journal itself A counted, thrown rejection tells the caller at once: the customer tries again with the same transfer id, and the count shows the overload on a dashboard. The discard policies drop a transfer without telling anyone, and its future never completes. CallerRunsPolicy suits a nightly import; here it makes one customer wait for other customers' journal writes.

h: Run it on a pool you can reason about · Key terms
x: Journal A log the ledger writes to disk before it changes anything in memory, so a crash can't lose an accepted transfer. Also called a write-ahead log. Bounded queue A queue with a fixed size. When it is full, new work is turned away instead of waiting without limit. Rejection policy What a ThreadPoolExecutor does with a task it can't take: throw, run it on the caller's thread, or drop it. Graceful shutdown Stopping a program so that accepted work finishes, or is handed back, within a deadline. Torn read A result built from reads taken at different moments, matching no state the data was ever in. Pool-induced deadlock Every thread of a pool waits for tasks queued in that same pool, so none can run. No lock is involved. Thread dump Every thread's name, state and stack at one moment, printed by jcmd <pid> Thread.print. Little's law for the ledger pool's thread count? threads = peak rate x time each transfer holds a thread. 1,600 a second x 5 ms = 8. How big should the ledger pool's queue be? Peak rate x the longest queue wait you accept: 1,600 a second x 50 ms = 80 slots. A bigger queue only hides waiting. Why is DiscardPolicy never right for the ledger pool? It silently drops a transfer, and the future of a dropped submit never completes, so a waiting caller waits forever. What does shutdownNow() return, and what must you do with it? The queued tasks that never started. Cancel their futures so waiting callers wake up, then log or replay the transfers. Why is a sum of separately locked balance reads torn? A transfer can run between two reads and move money from an account not yet read to one already read, or back, so the sum mixes two moments. Thread-dump signature of a pool-induced deadlock? Every thread of one pool WAITING (parking) on a FutureTask inside get(), tasks still queued, and no "Found one Java-level deadlock". Why hand a TransferTask to execute and not submit? submit wraps it in another FutureTask, so shutdownNow() would return the wrapper instead of your task and its transfer.

h: Run it on a pool you can reason about · Go deeper
x: Locking every account costs time in proportion to the number of accounts, and it stops every transfer while it copies. At 50 accounts that is microseconds. At five million accounts, it is a pause customers feel. Three designs avoid it. A snapshot per group. Split the accounts into groups, send every transfer to one group, and snapshot each group on its own. The grand total is the sum of the group totals, which stays exact only while no transfer crosses from one group to another. Copy-on-write state. Keep all balances in one map that never changes, behind an AtomicReference, and make every transfer a compare-and-set of a new map. Readers get a whole snapshot for free with get(). Writers pay for the copy and try again when another writer won, so this fits books that are read often and written rarely. It is the printed price board from Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal, used for writes too: Java private final AtomicReference<Map<String, Long>> balances = new AtomicReference<>(Map.of("alice", 100L, "bob", 0L)); boolean transfer(String from, String to, long cents) { while (true) { Map<String, Long> now = balances.get(); // a whole snapshot, for free if (now.get(from) < cents) return false; Map<String, Long> next = new HashMap<>(now); // copy, change two entries next.merge(from, -cents, Long::sum); next.merge(to, cents, Long::sum); if (balances.compareAndSet(now, Map.copyOf(next))) return true; // try again if another writer won } } Kotlin private val balances = AtomicReference(mapOf("alice" to 100L, "bob" to 0L)) fun transfer(from: String, to: String, cents: Long): Boolean { while (true) { val now = balances.get() // a whole snapshot, for free if (now.getValue(from) < cents) return false val next = now + mapOf(from to now.getValue(from) - cents, to to now.getValue(to) + cents) if (balances.compareAndSet(now, next)) return true // try again if another writer won } } Building from the journal. Treat the journal as the truth, and a snapshot as the result of applying it up to some position. That style is called event sourcing. You can build snapshots on another machine that reads the journal, and the live ledger never stops for them. For dumps, jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json <file> writes the same information as JSON, a text format that tools can group and count. Lesson 3 of this track uses it on 10,000 virtual threads.

h: Serve it with virtual threads · One request, one virtual thread, and every limit written down
x: One request, every limit written down: its own virtual thread, 20 grill tokens for the safety service, the 8 + 80 ledger pool, and one 300 ms deadline that interrupts the call and lets small amounts through Let's follow one request through the server. It spends almost all its time waiting: on the safety service, on the daily-limit check, on the ledger pool. The thread-per-request wall gave us the number for that: requests in flight = rate x time. At 2,000 requests a second and 150 ms each, 300 requests are in flight. When the safety service slows to 2 s, 4,000 are. A platform thread is a thread the operating system runs. One per request would mean 4,000 of them, each reserving about 1 MB for its stack (the memory that holds its chain of method calls), created at the worst moment. That lesson's restaurant gave every table a personal waiter, who stood at the kitchen door the whole time. How virtual threads work kept only a few waiters, and clipped each table's order slip to a board while it waited. A virtual thread is that order slip: a thread the JVM manages itself. While it waits on a network call, a lock or a semaphore, it lets go of its carrier, the platform thread that runs it. Its stack waits on the heap, the memory where Java keeps its objects. So 4,000 waiting requests cost 4,000 small objects, not 4,000 operating-system threads. So the server starts one new virtual thread for each request, and never pools them: Java List<Reply> serveAll(List<Transfer> requests) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService perRequest = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { List<Future<Reply>> replies = new ArrayList<>(); for (Transfer t : requests) replies.add(perRequest.submit(() -> handle(t))); // 1. start every request List<Reply> out = new ArrayList<>(); for (Future<Reply> f : replies) out.add(f.get()); // 2. then wait, in order return out; } // 3. close() waits for all } Kotlin fun serveAll(requests: List<Transfer>): List<Reply> = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perRequest -> val replies = requests.map { t -> perRequest.submit(Callable { handle(t) }) } // 1. start every request replies.map { it.get() } // 2. then wait, in order } // 3. close() waits for all First we submit every request, each on its own new virtual thread (1). Then we wait for the replies, in order (2). Leaving the block calls close(), which waits for every request to finish (3). Now the trap from the opening. Moving a blocking service to virtual threads warned that an old pool was also a limit nobody had written down. Take the pool away, and nothing stops 4,000 requests from calling the safety service at once. So every scarce thing gets a limit, written down where we can see it: The safety service (banks call this a fraud check): one shared Semaphore, a counter of permits that threads take and give back, with 20 permits held only during the safety call. These are the 20 grill tokens from Using virtual threads. A limit like this, on one slow outside service, is a bulkhead, named after the walls in a ship that stop one flooded room from sinking the rest. The journal: lesson 2's ledger- pool, 8 threads and 80 slots, which answers "busy" when it's full. Each request: one deadline of 300 ms for all of its checks. The ledger pool stays a pool of platform threads on purpose. It isn't there to save threads; it's a limit with a queue and a rejection rule, around work we want bounded. Request threads wait for its answer with future.get(). A future is the takeaway ticket from Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption: a claim on a result that isn't ready yet. Waiting on one costs a virtual thread a little heap. Threads are free, so every limit sits on a resource. Write each one down. Twenty permits keep the safety service from being flooded. They don't stop a request from waiting as long as the service does on its bad day. That takes a deadline. Do the arithmetic before the load test The safety bulkhead has 20 permits, and a safety call normally takes 20 ms. How many safety checks a second can it pass? Is that enough for 400 requests a second? For 2,000? On a bad day, each safety call takes 2 s, but the request interrupts it at its 300 ms deadline. How many requests a second now get a permit at all, and what happens to the rest? Open TransferServer.handle in the lab. Find the one wait that has no timeout, and explain why it has none. Twenty permits at 20 ms pass at most 20 / 0.02 = 1,000 checks a second: plenty for 400, not enough for 2,000. At 2,000 a second you'd need about 40 permits, if the safety service allows that many. On the bad day, each permit is held for 300 ms, so only about 20 / 0.3 = 67 requests a second get one; the rest wait for a permit until their deadline and fall back. The next section's demo shows exactly that. The wait without a timeout is ledger.submit(t).get(): once the ledger pool has accepted a transfer, the money may move, and a timeout would end the wait but not the transfer. Threads are free, so every limit sits on a resource: 20 permits for the safety service, 8 threads and 80 slots for the journal, and one deadline per request. JEP 444: Virtual Threads read

h: Serve it with virtual threads · A shared limit and one deadline for the slow safety check
x: The safety service is the slow, shared dependency. When it slows down, two things must not follow: every request waiting as long as it does, and every request piling onto it at once. A deadline stops the first, and the bulkhead stops the second. The bulkhead is the shared semaphore from Using virtual threads, with one change: the wait for a permit is bounded by the time the request has left. Java <T> T call(long waitNanos, Callable<T> block) throws Exception { if (!inFlight.tryAcquire(waitNanos, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) // 1. outside the try throw new TimeoutException("no permit in time"); try { return block.call(); // 2. only the slow call holds it } finally { inFlight.release(); // 3. always given back } } Kotlin fun <T> call(waitNanos: Long, block: () -> T): T { if (!inFlight.tryAcquire(waitNanos, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) // 1. outside the try throw TimeoutException("no permit in time") try { return block() // 2. only the slow call holds it } finally { inFlight.release() // 3. always given back } } First, tryAcquire waits for a permit, but no longer than waitNanos (1). It sits outside the try, so a thread that never got a permit never gives one back. Then only the slow call runs while holding the permit (2). Finally, the finally returns the permit on every path: success, failure or interrupt (3). The deadline is one number, computed once per request: System.nanoTime() + budget. Every wait inside the request uses what is left of it: the wait for a permit, and the wait for the safety answer. When it runs out, the request stops waiting and falls back to a plain business rule. Small transfers, up to 50.00 here, go through without the safety answer, and larger ones get a fast "try again". Banks call this kind of fallback stand-in; we'll call it the small-amount rule. Where to draw the line is a decision about risk, not about code. Stopping the wait is not enough, though. Remember the takeaway ticket: you give up and catch your bus, and nobody tells the kitchen. The kitchen timer from CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out ended the wait, not the work. Here, an abandoned safety call keeps running and keeps its permit. On a bad day, abandoned calls fill all 20 permits, and new requests can't get one, even for a call that would succeed. So at the deadline, the request interrupts its own call. An interrupt is Java's polite request to a thread to stop what it's waiting for. Trace the smallest case on a bad day. All 20 permits are held by calls that will take 2 s. A request for 40.00 arrives, and its wait for a permit starts. Meanwhile, another request reaches its deadline. It interrupts its own safety call, and that call's finally hands the permit back. Our request takes it. When our own deadline comes, it does the same: it interrupts its call, the permit goes back, and the small-amount rule lets 40.00 through. Give the safety service's network client its own timeout of the same length as well, so a call that ignores the interrupt still ends. This section's demo sends 400 requests a second for 3 seconds. Here are a normal day and a bad one: safety service takes 20 ms: {approved=1200} most safety calls in flight: 16, slowest reply: 35 ms safety service takes 2000 ms: {let through=312, timed out=888} most safety calls in flight: 20, slowest reply: 326 ms The safety service had a terrible afternoon, and no customer waited longer than a third of a second for an answer. It never saw more than 20 calls at once, and about a quarter of the requests, the small ones, went through anyway. A timeout ends the wait, not the work. Cancel what you stop waiting for. One check now has a limit and a deadline. Each request makes two checks, though, and the order in which we collect their answers decides how fast a no arrives. Give the safety service a bad day Run SafetyOutageDemo (or SafetyOutageDemoJava): 400 requests a second for 3 seconds, and safety calls take 20 ms. Predict the verdicts and the most safety calls in flight. Run it with -Pargs=outage, so every safety call takes 2 s. Amounts are random up to 200.00, and the small-amount rule lets through up to 50.00. Predict the share let through, and the slowest reply. Delete the call.cancel(true) line and run the bad day again. Predict first: what changes, and why? h: Serve it with virtual threads · Two checks at once, and the first no wins
x: Each request runs two checks: the safety service, slow and behind the bulkhead, and the daily-limit check, which is fast. Run them at the same time, and a request costs the slower of the two, not the sum. Starting several pieces of work at once and gathering their answers is called a fan-out. The trap is in how we gather the answers. Structured concurrency and scoped values pictured a head waiter who sends helpers to fetch the parts of one order, and doesn't leave until every helper is back. If he waits for the helpers in the order he sent them, a fast "no" waits behind a slow "yes". In this section's demo, the limit check says no after 10 ms, and the request still answers after about 600 ms: in order: get() the safety check, then the limits check 541 ms safety check answered 592 ms verdict: declined The answer was known at 10 ms. The customer heard it at 592. The fix is to take the answers in the order they finish, and stop at the first no: Java Verdict screen(Transfer t) throws InterruptedException { long deadline = System.nanoTime() + budget.toNanos(); // 1. one deadline for both checks ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); try { CompletionService<Boolean> done = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(perTask); done.submit(() -> safetyBulkhead.call(deadline - System.nanoTime(), () -> safety.passes(t))); // 2. start both done.submit(() -> limits.passes(t)); for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { Future<Boolean> next = done.poll(deadline - System.nanoTime(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS); if (next == null) return fallback(t); // 3. deadline passed: small-amount rule try { if (!next.get()) return Verdict.DECLINED; // 4. a check said no: fail fast } catch (ExecutionException e) { if (e.getCause() instanceof TimeoutException) return fallback(t); // no safety permit in time return Verdict.DECLINED; // 4. a check failed: fail fast } } return Verdict.APPROVED; } finally { perTask.shutdownNow(); // 5. interrupt whatever still runs... perTask.close(); // ...and wait until those threads end } } Kotlin fun screen(t: Transfer): Verdict { val deadline = System.nanoTime() + budget.toNanos() // 1. one deadline for both checks val perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() try { val done = ExecutorCompletionService<Boolean>(perTask) done.submit { safetyBulkhead.call(deadline - System.nanoTime()) { safety.passes(t) } } // 2. start both done.submit { limits.passes(t) } repeat(2) { val next = done.poll(deadline - System.nanoTime(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) ?: return fallback(t) // 3. deadline passed: small-amount rule val passed = try { next.get() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { if (e.cause is TimeoutException) return fallback(t) // no safety permit in time return Verdict.DECLINED // 4. a check failed: fail fast } if (!passed) return Verdict.DECLINED // 4. a check said no: fail fast } return Verdict.APPROVED } finally { perTask.shutdownNow() // 5. interrupt whatever still runs... perTask.close() // ...and wait until those threads end } } ExecutorCompletionService hands us each future as it completes, so the first no is seen at once, and so is the first exception. Either one declines the transfer. The finally is what makes it fail fast, that is, stop all the other work at the first failure. shutdownNow() interrupts the check that is still running, and close() waits until its thread has really ended. That order matters, as Structured concurrency and scoped values showed. On JDK 21, a future cancelled with cancel(true) counts as done at once, so close() could return while its thread is still running. After shutdownNow(), close() waits for the threads themselves, so no check outlives its request. The same demo, collecting in completion order, printed: fail fast: take results as they finish, stop the rest at the first no 12 ms verdict: declined 14 ms safety check interrupted Our screen is that head waiter, built by hand from an executor. JDK 25 has StructuredTaskScope for exactly this job. It's a preview API there, one you must switch on with --enable-preview, so it stays out of the labs. Go deeper shows the same screening with it. One rule binds every check: it has to stop when interrupted. sleep, locks, queues, latches and semaphores all do. A check that computes in a loop and never looks at the interrupt flag keeps running, and close() waits for it, deadline or not. Checks that run side by side pay off only if you collect them as they finish. Stop at the first no. Requests now wait cheaply and stop on time. One place could still hold a carrier thread captive: the account locks from lesson 1. Collect in order, then fail fast Run FailFastDemo. In the fail-fast half, replace done.take() with the futures in submit order: keep the two futures that done.submit returns, and call get() on them in that order. Run it again. h: Serve it with virtual threads · Nothing slow under an account lock: keeping the carriers free
x: Lesson 1 chose ReentrantLock for the accounts and promised a reason. Here it is. A virtual thread is pinned when it waits but can't let go of its carrier, so the carrier waits with it. Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps pictured this as a waiter holding a hot pan. He can't clip his slip to the board, because he can't put the pan down. On JDK 21 to 23, synchronized was that hot pan. A virtual thread that waited inside a synchronized block, or waited to enter one, held on to its carrier. JDK 24 cooled the pan (JEP 491), and JDK 25 is the first long-term-support release with that fix. Our labs compile for JDK 21 and must run there too, so the ledger uses ReentrantLock, which has always let a waiting virtual thread step off its carrier. The lock type is the smaller half of the rule, though. The bigger half is that nothing slow happens while we hold an account lock. Here's what someone might write to make "write the journal and credit the account" one step: Java synchronized (shop) { // or shopLock.lock() journal.append(t); // 20 ms of disk writing while holding the lock shop.credit(t.cents()); } Kotlin synchronized(shop) { // or shopLock.withLock { } journal.append(t) // 20 ms of disk writing while holding the lock shop.credit(t.cents) } This section's demo runs exactly that with one carrier thread. Twenty customers pay into one busy shop's account. Meanwhile a ticker, a small thread that wants to wake every 10 ms, measures how long it really waited. A long gap between ticks means the carrier was stuck. On JDK 21 it printed: JDK 21.0.12.1+1-1-24.04.4-Ubuntu, 1 carrier thread journal inside synchronized 20 transfers in 409 ms, longest gap between ticks: 414 ms journal inside ReentrantLock 20 transfers in 423 ms, longest gap between ticks: 20 ms journal first, then the lock 20 transfers in 22 ms, longest gap between ticks: 12 ms Read the rows one at a time. With synchronized, the ticker missed 414 ms of ticks: the carrier was pinned the whole time, so nothing else ran. With ReentrantLock, the ticker was fine. But the 20 payments still took over 400 ms, one after another, because each held the lock for its whole disk write. That's Little's law again: a lock held for 20 ms lets through at most 50 payments a second. With the journal written first and the lock taken only for the credit, all 20 took 22 ms. Here are the same compiled classes on JDK 25: JDK 25.0.5.0.3+1-1-24.04.1-Ubuntu, 1 carrier thread journal inside synchronized 20 transfers in 411 ms, longest gap between ticks: 16 ms journal inside ReentrantLock 20 transfers in 412 ms, longest gap between ticks: 16 ms journal first, then the lock 20 transfers in 22 ms, longest gap between ticks: 12 ms The pan cooled: the first row's gap dropped to the second row's. Its time didn't move, because the fix removes the pinning, not the line of payments waiting behind a slow lock. So the rule from synchronized and intrinsic locks holds in its strongest form. Inside an account lock, read and write the accounts, and nothing else. The journal write, the safety call and any logging that might wait all happen outside. That's why lesson 2's LedgerService writes the journal before apply takes a single lock. To check a running service, keep JFR's jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event switched on. JFR, the JDK Flight Recorder, is built into the JVM and logs events from a running program. This event records pins longer than 20 ms by default. The old -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads flag was removed in JDK 24. Inside an account lock, touch the accounts and nothing else. Write the journal first. When something does go wrong in a running server, though, we'll need to see 10,000 waiting threads at once. Pin a carrier, then free it Run LockScopeDemo (or LockScopeDemoJava). It forces one carrier thread and runs three versions of the same 20 payments. Predict both columns for each row before you look. Explain the second row: nothing is pinned, so why are the payments still slow? If you have JDK 24 or later installed, point JAVA_HOME at it, run the demo through Gradle again, and compare. JDK 24 added the virtual threads that are on a carrier at that moment, which on a bad day is almost none. A waiting virtual thread is a stack on the heap, not an operating-system thread, so the classic dump never sees it. The dump for virtual threads is Thread.dump_to_file. A container is whatever started them: our executor, with its own entry and list of threads, or <root> for ordinary platform threads such as main. The 10,000 requests are one container, and the carriers are another (ForkJoinPool-1, one carrier per core). On JDK 21, each thread entry has only tid, name and stack. The named factory, Thread.ofVirtual().name("request-", 0), is what gives us request-9999 instead of an empty name, just as the ledger- name tags did in lesson 2. JDK 25 says more about each thread. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so get()'s InterruptedException and ExecutionException need no throws clause, and an interrupted request thread still throws out of handle. A try is an expression in Kotlin, which lets val outcome = try { ... } replace Java's assign-inside-try. use on an ExecutorService is Kotlin's try-with-resources, and both call close(), which waits for every request. Kotlin's default argument (letThrough = false) saves the third constructor argument that the Java record needs every time. In the lab, the Kotlin server calls the Java ledger from lesson 2 directly: same package, same module, and a record's accessors, such as t.id(), work as ordinary methods.

The pool caps the whole task, so on a bad day the limits checks queue behind stuck safety calls: put the limit on the resource, not on a pool. Two timeouts of 300 ms in a row allow 600 ms, so there is no single deadline. A fast no from limits waits behind the safety answer, so it doesn't fail fast. On a timeout nothing is cancelled, so the abandoned calls keep all 20 pool threads busy, and the next requests time out before they even start. And every timeout lets the transfer through, whatever the amount. The fix is the lab's screen. At most 20 calls at once, as before Up to 5,000 calls at once: every request has its own 20 permits At most 1 call at once An IllegalStateException from the second semaphore A semaphore limits only the threads that share it. One per request hands every request a full set of permits, so the limit is gone. Keep one per outside service, in a field that every request uses: one hook of grill tokens for the whole kitchen. The ledger runs on JDK 21, and apply uses synchronized on both accounts, held for microseconds with no disk writing inside. Ten thousand virtual threads pay into the same shop's account. What can happen? Nothing bad: the critical section is too short to matter The JVM throws IllegalMonitorStateException under that much contention Virtual threads waiting to enter the shop's synchronized block pin their carriers, so heavy contention can leave no carrier free for other requests Each virtual thread gets its own copy of the lock On JDK 21 to 23, a virtual thread waiting to enter a synchronized block can't step off its carrier, so with one busy account every carrier can end up waiting there, and requests that never touch the account stop too. JDK 24 fixed it (JEP 491). ReentrantLock frees the carrier while its waiters wait, on every JDK. A short critical section makes each wait short; it doesn't make the pins harmless. call.get(300, MILLISECONDS) throws TimeoutException, the request answers with the small-amount rule, and the code does nothing else. What is the safety call doing now? Still running, and holding its bulkhead permit until the safety service answers Cancelled, because get with a timeout cancels the task Interrupted, because its request thread moved on Finished, because its future is now done A timeout on get ends your wait, nothing more: the takeaway ticket again. Nobody told the task to stop, so it runs on and keeps its permit, and its future is not done. Cancel it with cancel(true), or shutdownNow() on its executor, so the call is interrupted and its finally releases the permit. In a hand-built fail-fast fan-out on JDK 21, you call cancel(true) on the slow check's future, then close() on the virtual-thread executor. Why can close() return while the check is still running its finally block? cancel(true) doesn't interrupt the thread close() never waits for tasks Virtual threads skip finally blocks after an interrupt The executor counts a task as finished once its future is done, and cancel marks the future done at once On JDK 21, the per-task executor tracks tasks by their futures, and cancel(true) completes the future at once while the thread is still finishing. shutdownNow() interrupts the threads and leaves the futures alone, so close() keeps waiting until each thread has really ended. That's why screen calls shutdownNow() and then close(). Why does TransferServer.handle wait for ledger.submit(t).get() with no timeout? Because the ledger pool is so fast that it never matters Because once the pool has accepted the transfer, it may be applied, and a timeout would report a failure for money that moved Because Future.get has no timeout version Because virtual threads can't be interrupted while they wait The wait is already bounded by design: a full queue turns the transfer away at once with BUSY, and 80 queued transfers drain in about 50 ms. A timeout there would end the wait, not the transfer, so the customer would try again for a transfer that already happened. If you need a hard bound, answer "accepted" with the transfer id at once, and let the customer ask for the outcome later.
