h: Serve it with virtual threads · Key terms
x: Virtual thread A thread the JVM manages itself. While it waits, it lets go of its carrier, and its stack waits on the heap. Bulkhead A separate, shared limit on one outside service, so one slow service can't take every thread or connection. Deadline One point in time for the whole request. Every wait inside the request uses whatever is left of it. Small-amount rule This lab's fallback, which banks call stand-in: when a check can't answer in time, small amounts go through unchecked and larger ones are refused. Fail-fast fan-out Running several checks at once and stopping all of them at the first failure or no. Pinning A virtual thread that waits but can't let go of its carrier, so the carrier waits with it. Thread container A group in a JSON thread dump: the executor or scope that started a set of threads. Why one new virtual thread per request, not a pool of virtual threads? Creating one is cheap, and a pool would cap the whole request. Cap the scarce resource with a shared semaphore instead. What must happen to a safety call when its request's deadline passes? Interrupt it (cancel(true) or shutdownNow()), so it stops and its finally releases the bulkhead permit. A timeout alone leaves an abandoned call holding the permit. What makes a fan-out fail fast? Take results in the order they finish, stop at the first no or failure, then shutdownNow() to interrupt the rest and close() to wait for them. What is the small-amount rule (stand-in)? A fallback: when a check can't answer in time, small amounts go through unchecked and larger ones are turned away. On JDK 21, what pins a virtual thread in ledger code? Waiting inside synchronized, or waiting to enter a busy synchronized block. ReentrantLock never pins. JDK 24 removed both cases (JEP 491). Why don't waiting virtual threads appear in jcmd <pid> Thread.print? It lists platform threads, plus virtual threads mounted on a carrier from JDK 24. Use jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json <file>. How do you make 10,000 stacks in a JSON dump readable? Group them: count threads per container, and count stacks by the line where your code starts, with jq ... | sort | uniq -c.

h: Serve it with virtual threads · Go deeper
x: What a production version of this ledger adds, roughly in the order I'd build it: Lasting state: balances and the journal in a database, row locks taken in account id order or one owner per account, a CHECK (balance >= 0) rule, and a unique key on the transfer id. The same answer for a repeated request: store each transfer's outcome by its id, so a customer who tries again after a "busy" reply or a lost connection gets the original answer, not a second transfer. This property is called idempotence. Numbers on every limit: permits in use and the wait for them, how often the small-amount rule fired, the ledger queue's size and rejections, time spent in the queue, journal write times, and JFR's jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events. A circuit breaker in front of the safety service: a switch that stops calling a service that keeps failing, for a while, so that on a bad day requests go straight to the fallback instead of each one waiting out its deadline. Request details, such as the request id, carried in a scoped value (final in JDK 25), the note pinned to the order from Structured concurrency and scoped values, or passed as a parameter, so it reaches every log line on every virtual thread. Load tests with realistic response times, and a test run where the safety service hangs on purpose, checked against the same rules as the lab's tests. Structured concurrency is the JDK's own version of screen: the head waiter, built in. StructuredTaskScope is a preview API in JDK 25 (JEP 505), and still preview in JDK 26 and 27. JEP 543 makes it final in JDK 28, with the JDK 27 API. Here is the screening in the JDK 25 shape. It needs --enable-preview, which is why it isn't in the labs: Java // JDK 25, preview: javac --release 25 --enable-preview ... and java --enable-preview ... Verdict screen(Transfer t) throws InterruptedException { try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.<Boolean>awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow(), cf -> cf.withTimeout(budget))) { scope.fork(() -> { if (!safetyBulkhead.call(budget.toNanos(), () -> safety.passes(t))) throw new Declined(); return true; }); scope.fork(() -> { if (!limits.passes(t)) throw new Declined(); return true; }); scope.join(); // the first failure cancels the other subtask return Verdict.APPROVED; } catch (StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException e) { return fallback(t); // the scope has cancelled both subtasks } catch (StructuredTaskScope.FailedException e) { return e.getCause() instanceof TimeoutException ? fallback(t) : Verdict.DECLINED; } } Kotlin // JDK 25, preview: compile and run with --enable-preview fun screen(t: Transfer): Verdict = try { StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow<Boolean>()) { cf -> cf.withTimeout(budget) }.use { scope -> scope.fork(Callable { if (!safetyBulkhead.call(budget.toNanos()) { safety.passes(t) }) throw Declined(); true }) scope.fork(Callable { if (!limits.passes(t)) throw Declined(); true }) scope.join() // the first failure cancels the other subtask Verdict.APPROVED } } catch (e: StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException) { fallback(t) // the scope has cancelled both subtasks } catch (e: StructuredTaskScope.FailedException) { if (e.cause is TimeoutException) fallback(t) else Verdict.DECLINED } A "no" becomes an exception (Declined, your own small exception class), because this joiner fails fast on exceptions, not on values. The scope's close() cancels and waits for every subtask, which is what your finally did by hand, and the JSON thread dump shows each scope as its own container under the request that opened it. In JDK 27, the built-in joiners throw ExecutionException instead of FailedException, so that catch changes when you move. On JDK 25 here, the Java version answered a small transfer with LET_THROUGH after 322 ms while the safety service hung, and declined in 4 ms when the limits check said no.

h: Reactive programming
x: Reactive Streams, Project Reactor, operators, schedulers, backpressure and testing. By the end of this track you can read and write Project Reactor code with a clear picture of what runs when, on which thread, and how fast. You can explain the Reactive Streams contract and its demand signal, build lazy Mono and Flux chains, and pick the right operators to transform and combine streams. You can make a call to another computer survive failures with timeouts, filtered backoff and fallbacks, move blocking calls off the wrong threads, choose what to lose when a source can't slow down, share one source between many subscribers, and test all of it in milliseconds with StepVerifier and virtual time. The last lesson says plainly when you shouldn't use Reactor at all. One picture runs through all eight lessons: a bakery line, where an oven puts loaves on a belt and a packer at the end sends slips back saying how many more she can take. The bakery's own program, with its cake orders, its flour mill and its oven thermometer, is the running example in the code. You need the first track (threads, races, synchronized), the executors track (pools, CompletableFuture, Little's law) and the virtual threads track, because this one keeps comparing against them. Install JDK 25. The labs use Reactor 3.8.8 and reactor-test 3.8.8 and compile with release 21, so they run on JDK 21 or later. The labs live in labs/reactive, one package per lesson (workbench.reactive.l01 to l08). They are in Java, and every code sample and Try-it demo also comes in Kotlin, with Kotlin Flow and coroutine counterparts where they exist. Timing tests use virtual time, latches and counters of calls in flight rather than sleeps. Run ./gradlew :reactive:test --tests 'workbench.reactive.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, use solutionTest to check the reference answers, and run the demos with ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=.... Reactive Streams is a contract of four interfaces: the subscriber asks for n items, the publisher never sends more, and onError or onComplete ends the stream for good. On the bakery line, that's the packer's slip. Assembly fills in an order form; subscription runs it, once per subscriber for a cold publisher. Mono.just(call()) runs the call at assembly; fromCallable and defer run it per subscription. flatMap runs inners concurrently in completion order (256 at a time by default), concatMap one at a time in order, flatMapSequential concurrently in order, and switchMap keeps only the latest. Mono.zip completes empty, silently, when one source is empty. Say what empty means on each source. For calls to another computer: a lazy source, a per-attempt timeout, retryWhen(Retry.backoff(...).filter(...)) (3 retries means 4 attempts), and a fallback for exhausted retries that admits "we don't know yet". Code runs on the thread that delivered the signal. publishOn moves what follows, subscribeOn moves the source; blocking calls go on boundedElastic, with subscribeOn on each inner. limitRate reshapes demand. For sources that can't slow down, pick a loss policy; onBackpressureBuffer() with no size only hides the backlog. Cap flatMap at the smallest limit of the services you call. share, replay(n).refCount() and cache differ in what late subscribers get and when they disconnect. Sinks need a retrying emit when several threads push. Test with StepVerifier and virtual time: always verify() with a time limit, and build the publisher inside the supplier. Use Reactor for streams and composed concurrency; for one request and one reply over blocking clients, virtual threads and plain code are simpler.

h: Reactive programming: cheat sheet
x: The contract Signal Direction Rule Picture it onSubscribe(s) publisher to subscriber always first, exactly once the oven hands the packer a pad of slips request(n) subscriber to publisher demand; the publisher never sends more than requested the packer's slip: "send me n more" onNext(item) publisher to subscriber zero or more, never null, one at a time a loaf on the belt onError(e) or onComplete() publisher to subscriber at most one, and nothing after it the oven breaks down, or the end-of-day bell cancel() subscriber to publisher the only way a subscriber stops the stream "stop sending" java.util.concurrent.Flow is the same four interfaces in the JDK. Flux is 0 to N items (a tray of loaves), Mono is 0 or 1 (one cake). Nothing happens until you subscribe Picture it: building a chain fills in an order form, and subscribe signs it. Every signature on a cold publisher bakes a fresh cake. You write The work runs Mono.just(call()) once, at assembly, before anyone subscribes Mono.fromCallable(() -> call()) once per subscription Mono.defer(() -> client.call()) once per subscription; client.call() returns a publisher A cold publisher does its work again for each subscriber. retry subscribes again, so it needs a lazy source. Picking an operator You want Use Picture it a quick synchronous change per item map, filter the slicer, the inspector async calls, any order, capped flatMap(call, n) (default n is 256) the icing room async calls, one at a time, in order concatMap(call) one decorator async calls, concurrent, in input order flatMapSequential(call, n) the clerk at the exit only the latest request matters switchMap(call) the customer who changes their mind one result from several independent calls Mono.zip(a, b, c), with switchIfEmpty or defaultIfEmpty on each the gift box two live streams mixed / one after the other Flux.merge / Flux.concat two belts into one / one belt, then the next a value recomputed when any input changes Flux.combineLatest the price board Source 3, 1, 2, item i takes i x 100 ms: flatMap gives 1, 2, 3 at 300 ms, concatMap gives 3, 1, 2 at 600 ms, flatMapSequential gives 3, 1, 2 at 300 ms. Errors, retries, timeouts Picture it: an error is the oven breaking down. Error operators only decide what goes in the box instead, retry bakes the whole order again, and timeout is the kitchen timer on the wait. Java Mono.defer(() -> mill.order(id)) // a fresh call per attempt .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)) // per attempt .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)) // 4 attempts: 0, 100, 300, 700 ms .filter(e -> e instanceof MillBusyException || e instanceof TimeoutException)) .onErrorResume(Exceptions::isRetryExhausted, e -> Mono.just("PENDING:" + id)); Kotlin Mono.defer { mill.order(id) } // a fresh call per attempt .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)) // per attempt .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)) // 4 attempts: 0, 100, 300, 700 ms .filter { e -> e is MillBusyException || e is TimeoutException }) .onErrorResume(Exceptions::isRetryExhausted) { Mono.just("PENDING:$id") } Errors are terminal. retry(n) makes n + 1 immediate attempts and rethrows the original error; Retry.backoff ends with RetryExhaustedException (jitter 0.5 by default). Skip a bad item inside a per-item Mono, not with onErrorContinue. A timeout means you stopped waiting, not that the other side said no: send the same order number on every attempt. Threads Scheduler Threads For Picture it none the thread that subscribed, or the one that delivered the item most operators the worker who brought the loaf carries it on Schedulers.parallel() one per core CPU work and timers; never block a few quick hands who never stand still Schedulers.single() one cheap work that must stay in order one worker Schedulers.boundedElastic() up to 10 x cores, then a queue of 100,000 blocking calls the back room, allowed to wait on the phone publishOn moves the operators after it: a hand-over point on the belt. subscribeOn moves the source, wherever it is written, like the line on the order form that says who starts the oven; the one nearest the source wins. Wrap blocking calls as Mono.fromCallable(...).subscribeOn(boundedElastic()), with subscribeOn on each inner Mono. block() throws on parallel and single threads. -Dreactor.schedulers.defaultBoundedElasticOnVirtualThreads=true (Reactor 3.6+, JDK 21+) runs boundedElastic on virtual threads. Backpressure Between you and the source The source sees subscribe(consumer) or block() alone Long.MAX_VALUE take(3) 3 limitRate(10) 10, 8, 8, ... flatMap(call, 4) 4, 1, 1, ... For a source that can't slow down, choose what to lose at the packer's small table: Operator Picture it onBackpressureBuffer(n) a small pile, and an alarm when it overflows onBackpressureDrop(onDropped) extra loaves go in a bin onBackpressureLatest() one slot, and the newest replaces the old onBackpressureError() stop the line All of them ask the source for everything; none slows it down. Never use onBackpressureBuffer() without a size: it's the doorstep of fourteen loaves. Flux.create buffers without limit by default. Cap the calls you make with flatMap(call, n), set from the smallest limit on the path. Sharing and Sinks Operator A late subscriber gets Disconnects Picture it share() = publish().refCount() only new items when the last one leaves a live radio show replay(n).refCount() the last n, then new ones when the last one leaves a show that repeats its last announcement publish().autoConnect(n) only new items never waits for n listeners, never switches off cache() everything never a recorder that keeps the whole show Mono.cache(ttl) the value until it expires not applicable the price list, loaded again every ttl A sink is a bell anyone can ring. Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort() gives a live bell that survives having no listeners; onBackpressureBuffer() buffers but shuts down when its last subscriber leaves. From several threads, use emitNext(item, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.busyLooping(Duration.ofSeconds(1))); a bare tryEmitNext can return FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED and lose the item. Testing and debugging Picture it: StepVerifier is a quality inspector with a script, and a clock she can wind forward. Java StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> poller.awaitDone("cake-7")) // build it inside the supplier .expectSubscription() // before expectNoEvent .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofSeconds(90)) .expectNext(DONE) .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); // nothing runs without verify() Kotlin StepVerifier.withVirtualTime { poller.awaitDone("cake-7") } // build it inside the supplier .expectSubscription() // before expectNoEvent .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofSeconds(90)) .expectNext(DONE) .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) // nothing runs without verify() TestPublisher drives a source by hand; PublisherProbe proves a branch ran. checkpoint("name") labels errors cheaply, log() prints every signal, Hooks.onOperatorDebug() is a costly last resort. When to use it One request and one reply over databases and services whose clients block: virtual threads and plain code. Streams, demand, cancellation, loss policies, and many calls composed with timeouts and retries: Reactor. Kotlin: coroutines and Flow, bridged by kotlinx-coroutines-reactor.

h: Reactive programming: track quiz
x: A Flow.Subscriber calls request(2) in onSubscribe and never requests again. Its publisher has 100 items ready. What does the subscriber receive? All 100 items, because the publisher pushes what it has 2 items, then nothing until it requests more 2 items, then onComplete 2 items, then onError, because the rest were not requested Rule 1.1: a publisher sends no more onNext signals than were requested. A publisher that still has items to deliver doesn't complete; it waits for more demand. A stream with unmet demand simply stalls, which is what to look for when a chain hangs. Mono<Cake> c = Mono.just(bakeCake(order)); is built, but nothing ever subscribes to c. How many cakes are baked? None: nothing happens until you subscribe One One per subscriber, so none It depends on the scheduler Mono.just takes a value, so Java evaluates bakeCake(order) before just is even called: the cake is baked at assembly. "Nothing happens until you subscribe" is true of the work inside operators and fromCallable, not of arguments you compute yourself. Source 3, 1, 2; each item i is turned into a call that takes i x 100 ms. What does concatMap emit, and when is it done? 1, 2, 3, done at 300 ms 3, 1, 2, done at 300 ms 3, 1, 2, done at 600 ms 1, 2, 3, done at 600 ms concatMap runs one call at a time in source order, so it takes 300 + 100 + 200 = 600 ms. flatMap would give 1, 2, 3 at 300 ms (completion order), and flatMapSequential 3, 1, 2 at 300 ms (concurrent, but put back in order). The cake search box on the bakery's website sends a lookup on every keystroke. Results of an older query must never overwrite newer ones. Which operator fits? flatMap concatMap switchMap flatMapSequential switchMap cancels the previous lookup as soon as a new keystroke arrives, so only the latest query can produce results. flatMap lets a slow old query land after a newer one; concatMap and flatMapSequential would wait for every old query, in order. Mono.zip(price, deliveryFee, discount): discount completes empty because this customer has no discount. What does the zip do? Fails with NoSuchElementException Emits a tuple with null for the discount Waits for a discount that never comes Completes empty, with no error, and cancels the other calls An empty source gives the zip nothing to combine, so it completes empty at once and cancels the rest. Nothing is logged. Put switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(...)) or defaultIfEmpty(...) on each source that can be empty. Mono.defer(() -> mill.order(id)).retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)).jitter(0)) against a mill whose ordering service always fails. What happens? 3 calls, then the mill's exception 4 calls at 0, 100, 300 and 700 ms, then RetryExhaustedException with the mill's exception as its cause 4 calls 100 ms apart, then the mill's exception An endless loop of calls The 3 counts retries, so there are 4 attempts, with waits of 100, 200 and 400 ms. When the retries run out, Retry.backoff signals RetryExhaustedException ("Retries exhausted: 3/3"). Plain retry(3) would also make 4 attempts, with no waits, and rethrow the original error. Flux.fromIterable(shops).flatMap(s -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> stock.loavesLeft(s))).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) asks a blocking stock book about 50 shops, 20 ms each. About how long does it take? About 20 ms: flatMap runs them all at once About 1 second: all 50 run in turn on one thread About 250 ms: one thread per core It fails: blocking is not allowed on boundedElastic subscribeOn on the outer Flux puts the whole subscription on one boundedElastic thread, and each fromCallable runs its call when flatMap subscribes to it, on that same thread. Put subscribeOn(boundedElastic()) on each inner Mono, and cap the fan-out with flatMap's concurrency. Orders arrive from the website over a live connection that can't slow down. No order may be lost silently, and bursts of a few hundred are normal. Which line fits? orders.onBackpressureBuffer() orders.onBackpressureLatest() orders.onBackpressureBuffer(1_000, o -> log.error("overflow at {}", o.id())) orders.limitRate(100) A bounded buffer absorbs the bursts, and if the consumer falls further behind, it cancels the source, logs the overflowing order and fails, so the gap is visible. The unbounded buffer hides the backlog until memory runs out, onBackpressureLatest drops orders silently, and limitRate changes requests that this source ignores. Twelve screens share one connection to the oven thermometer. A screen that switches on late must show the current temperature at once, and the connection must close when nobody watches. Which operator fits? readings.replay(1).refCount() readings.share() readings.cache() readings.publish().autoConnect(1) replay(1) hands a late subscriber the latest reading, and refCount() cancels the source when the last subscriber leaves. share() makes a late screen wait for the next reading; cache() and autoConnect never disconnect, and cache() keeps every reading forever. A test builds Mono<Status> poll = poller.awaitDone("cake-7"); in @BeforeEach, then runs StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> poll).thenAwait(Duration.ofMinutes(5))...verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)). It fails with "VerifySubscriber timed out". Why? Virtual time doesn't work with Mono thenAwait must be replaced with Thread.sleep verify needs a longer timeout, such as 5 minutes The Mono was built before virtual time was installed, so its timers use the real clock Operators such as interval, delay and timeout pick their scheduler when the chain is built. Built in @BeforeEach, the poller's timers run on the real parallel scheduler, and winding the virtual clock forward does nothing. Call poller.awaitDone("cake-7") inside the supplier. A 5-minute real timeout would just make the test slow.

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Pull, push, and a fast oven that drowns a slow packer
x: Every stream of data has two ends. A producer is the code that makes items, and a consumer is the code that uses them. Between the two, something has to decide when the next item moves. In pull, the consumer asks for the next item when it's ready, like walking to the bakery. Iterator.next() works that way, and so does BufferedReader.readLine(). The consumer sets the pace. The cost is waiting: if the next item isn't there yet, the consumer's thread, one path of work in a program, sits and does nothing. In push, the producer hands over each item the moment it exists, like the morning delivery. The consumer gives the producer a callback, a method to call when something arrives, and goes about its day. CompletableFuture.thenAccept works that way. Nobody waits. The cost is that the producer sets the pace, and the consumer has no way to say "slow down". Let's set up the example this track uses from here on. Picture a bakery line. At one end, an oven bakes loaves. A belt carries them, one behind another. At the other end, a packer puts each loaf in a box. The oven is the producer, the packer is the consumer, and the belt is the stream between them. Our oven is fast. It can bake loaves far faster than anyone can box them. Here is plain push in code. The oven hands each loaf to the packer's executor, the JDK object from the executors track that runs tasks on its own thread. Tasks it can't run yet wait in its queue: Java // Naive: the oven never waits, so the packer's queue grows without limit ExecutorService packer = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); for (int i = 0; i < LOAVES; i++) { packer.execute(() -> packLoaf()); // returns at once; the loaf waits in the queue } Kotlin // Naive: the oven never waits, so the packer's queue grows without limit val packer = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor() repeat(LOAVES) { packer.execute { packLoaf() } // returns at once; the loaf waits in the queue } execute puts the task in the queue and returns at once, so the oven never waits. DrowningDemo, in the Try it below, bakes 100,000 loaves this way, with 10 microseconds of packing per loaf. I expected the oven to finish long before the packer. On this 4-core machine, while other programs were busy, one run printed: plain push: oven done in 65 ms, packer boxed 3,193, 96,807 loaves waiting in memory The oven finished in 65 ms and went home happy. The packer had boxed 3,193 loaves, and 96,807 waited in the queue. Each waiting loaf is an object on the heap, the memory where Java keeps its objects. Here they fit, because the demo stops at 100,000. A real oven doesn't stop. With 10,000 loaves a second coming in and 2,000 going out, the heap gains 8,000 objects every second. Nothing fails at first. Then the garbage collector, the part of the JVM that frees memory nobody uses, runs more and more often, everything slows down, and the program dies with OutOfMemoryError. The cure is the note on the doorstep. Backpressure means the consumer tells the producer how much it can take, and the producer never sends more. On the bakery line, the packer sends a slip back up the belt: "send me 10 more". The oven puts 10 loaves on the belt, then waits for the next slip. The second half of DrowningDemo does exactly that, with the JDK's SubmissionPublisher, a ready-made producer we'll meet properly in the third section. This time the packer asks for one loaf at a time. The same run went on: with demand: oven done in 1,521 ms, packer boxed 99,898, never more than 257 waiting Never more than 257 loaves waited, about the 256 that the publisher's buffer holds. The last 102 were still on the belt when the oven finished, and the packer boxed them a moment later. The oven took 1,521 ms instead of 65, because it now works at the packer's pace. That isn't a loss. The packing took that long in both halves; the first half just hid the work in memory. Notice the shape of the slip. If loaves are already waiting, they go to the packer at once, as with pull. If none are ready, the oven sends each one as soon as it's baked, as with push. The documentation of Reactor, the library this track uses from the next lesson on, calls this a push-pull hybrid. When a consumer can't keep up, a program has four honest choices: slow the producer down, buffer up to a limit, drop items, or fail. A queue with no limit is a fifth choice that only looks like one, because it postpones the failure instead of choosing. A queue with no limit only hides a slow consumer. Give the slowness somewhere to go. The belt picture breaks in one place, and the place matters. A real belt keeps rolling whether the packer is ready or not, which is the plain push we just watched fail. On a reactive belt, nothing moves without a slip. So the slip is the whole idea, and it comes with a short contract that says exactly how it works. Drown a packer, then rescue it Read DrowningDemo below. It sends 100,000 loaves to a packer that needs 10 microseconds per loaf, first with plain push, then through a SubmissionPublisher whose subscriber asks for one loaf at a time. Predict for each half: how long will the oven take, and how many loaves will be waiting when it finishes? Run it (the Java and Kotlin versions print the same lines). Then change packLoaf to wait 20,000 nanoseconds instead of 10,000, and run it again. Which number changes in each line? DrowningDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l01; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Flow; import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; /** A fast oven and a slow packer, first with plain push, then with demand. */ public class DrowningDemo { static final int LOAVES = 100_000; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { pushWithoutDemand(); pushWithDemand(); } // Plain push: the oven hands every loaf to the packer's executor. Its queue has no limit. static void pushWithoutDemand() throws Exception { ExecutorService packer = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); AtomicLong boxed = new AtomicLong(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < LOAVES; i++) { packer.execute(() -> { packLoaf(); boxed.incrementAndGet(); }); } long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; long b = boxed.get(); System.out.printf("plain push: oven done in %,5d ms, packer boxed %,7d, %,6d loaves waiting in memory%n", ms, b, LOAVES - b); packer.shutdownNow(); } // With demand: the packer asks for one loaf at a time. submit() blocks when the 256-slot buffer is full. static void pushWithDemand() throws Exception { AtomicLong boxed = new AtomicLong(); long maxLag = 0; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (SubmissionPublisher<Integer> publisher = new SubmissionPublisher<>()) { publisher.subscribe(new Flow.Subscriber<Integer>() { Flow.Subscription s; public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { this.s = s; s.request(1); } public void onNext(Integer loaf) { packLoaf(); boxed.incrementAndGet(); s.request(1); } public void onError(Throwable t) { t.printStackTrace(); } public void onComplete() { } }); for (int i = 0; i < LOAVES; i++) { publisher.submit(i); // waits while the buffer is full maxLag = Math.max(maxLag, publisher.estimateMaximumLag()); } long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; long b = boxed.get(); System.out.printf("with demand: oven done in %,5d ms, packer boxed %,7d, never more than %,d waiting%n", ms, b, maxLag); } TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.sleep(50); } // stands in for 10 microseconds of packing one loaf static void packLoaf() { long until = System.nanoTime() + 10_000; while (System.nanoTime() < until) Thread.onSpinWait(); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l01.DrowningDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l01/DrowningDemo.java DrowningDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l01 import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Flow import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong private const val LOAVES = 100_000 /** A fast oven and a slow packer, first with plain push, then with demand. */ fun main() { pushWithoutDemand() pushWithDemand() } // Plain push: the oven hands every loaf to the packer's executor. Its queue has no limit. private fun pushWithoutDemand() { val packer = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor() val boxed = AtomicLong() val t0 = System.nanoTime() repeat(LOAVES) { packer.execute { packLoaf(); boxed.incrementAndGet() } } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 val b = boxed.get() println("plain push: oven done in %,5d ms, packer boxed %,7d, %,6d loaves waiting in memory".format(ms, b, LOAVES - b)) packer.shutdownNow() } // With demand: the packer asks for one loaf at a time. submit() blocks when the 256-slot buffer is full. private fun pushWithDemand() { val boxed = AtomicLong() var maxLag = 0L val t0 = System.nanoTime() SubmissionPublisher<Int>().use { publisher -> publisher.subscribe(object : Flow.Subscriber<Int> { private lateinit var s: Flow.Subscription override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) { this.s = s; s.request(1) } override fun onNext(loaf: Int) { packLoaf(); boxed.incrementAndGet(); s.request(1) } override fun onError(t: Throwable) = t.printStackTrace() override fun onComplete() {} }) for (i in 0 until LOAVES) { publisher.submit(i) // waits while the buffer is full maxLag = maxOf(maxLag, publisher.estimateMaximumLag().toLong()) } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println("with demand: oven done in %,5d ms, packer boxed %,7d, never more than %,d waiting".format(ms, boxed.get(), maxLag)) } TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.sleep(50) } // stands in for 10 microseconds of packing one loaf private fun packLoaf() { val until = System.nanoTime() + 10_000 while (System.nanoTime() < until) Thread.onSpinWait() } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l01.DrowningDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l01/DrowningDemo.kt With plain push the oven finishes in tens of milliseconds and almost every loaf is still queued (runs here: 32 to 73 ms, with 96,807 to 99,180 loaves waiting). With demand the oven takes as long as the packer needs (1,272 to 1,521 ms here), and never more than about 256 loaves wait, the size of the publisher's buffer. With 20 microseconds of packing, the plain version leaves even more loaves queued, and the demand version simply takes about twice as long. Its memory stays flat.

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Reactive Streams: four interfaces, seven methods and a slip called request(n)
x: Reactive Streams demand: the publisher sends only what the subscriber asked for A slip only works if both ends read it the same way. One library's oven must be able to serve another library's packer. Reactive Streams is that agreement: a short specification, a written contract that libraries promise to follow, with four interfaces, seven methods and a list of numbered rules. Here is the whole API: Java public interface Publisher<T> { void subscribe(Subscriber<? super T> s); } public interface Subscriber<T> { void onSubscribe(Subscription s); void onNext(T item); void onError(Throwable t); void onComplete(); } public interface Subscription { void request(long n); void cancel(); } public interface Processor<T, R> extends Subscriber<T>, Publisher<R> { } Kotlin // the same four interfaces, written as Kotlin declarations interface Publisher<T> { fun subscribe(s: Subscriber<in T>) } interface Subscriber<T> { fun onSubscribe(s: Subscription) fun onNext(item: T) fun onError(t: Throwable) fun onComplete() } interface Subscription { fun request(n: Long); fun cancel() } interface Processor<T, R> : Subscriber<T>, Publisher<R> Each interface has a place on the bakery line. A publisher is the oven, the source of items. A subscriber is the packer, which receives them. A subscription is the pad of slips between one oven and one packer: it carries request(n), "send me n more", and cancel(), "stop sending". A Processor is a station in the middle of the belt, a subscriber to what comes before it and a publisher to what comes after. Every method returns void (Unit in Kotlin), so every call is a one-way message, called a signal: the caller never waits for an answer. Java's Subscriber<? super T> is Kotlin's Subscriber<in T>. Both say that a publisher of rye loaves also accepts a subscriber of any kind of bread, or even a Subscriber<Object> that logs everything. The figure below draws one conversation. The packer calls subscribe on the oven. The oven answers with onSubscribe and hands over the pad of slips. Nothing else happens until the packer writes a slip, say request(2). Then the oven may call onNext twice, once per loaf, and no more. When the oven is out of loaves for good, it calls onComplete, the bell at the end of the day. If it breaks down, it calls onError instead. The spec writes that order as onSubscribe onNext* (onError | onComplete)?. Read it as one onSubscribe, then any number of onNext, then at most one of the two endings. onError and onComplete are terminal signals: after one of them, the stream is over and nothing else arrives. Here are the rules you'll actually meet, each in plain words: 1.1 A publisher never sends more onNext signals than were requested in total. 1.3 Signals to one subscriber never overlap; they come one at a time. So a subscriber needs no locks, the guards from Part 1 that let one thread in at a time, for its own fields. 1.9 onSubscribe comes before any other signal. 2.13 Subscriber methods must return normally. The only exception allowed is a NullPointerException for a null argument. A subscriber that wants to stop must call cancel(), not throw. An exception from onNext lands inside the publisher's delivery code, which can't hand it back. So the spec has the publisher treat the subscription as cancelled and report the problem some other way, such as a log line. 2.8 A subscriber must accept onNext calls that arrive after it cancelled, because loaves it already asked for may still be on the belt. 3.9 request(n) with n <= 0 must produce onError(IllegalArgumentException). 3.17 Demand of Long.MAX_VALUE may be treated as unbounded: a packer saying it wants no backpressure at all. You will rarely write these interfaces by hand. Reactor, RxJava and some database drivers implement them, and the rules are why one library can subscribe to another. Demand is the only permission to send. No slip, no loaf. Rule 3.9 is a good place to see that a spec and a library can differ. RequestZeroDemo, in the Try it below, has a subscriber named Rude that asks for zero items. It subscribes once to the JDK's publisher and once to Flux.range(1, 3) from Reactor: JDK SubmissionPublisher: onError java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: non-positive subscription request Reactor Flux.range: no signal at all, the stream just stalls The JDK complains at once, as the rule says. Reactor only logs the bad request at DEBUG level, which nobody sees by default, and sends nothing. Its stream simply waits. A stream that stalls in silence is a symptom to remember: somewhere, a slip was never written. Here the bakery picture breaks again. A real packer who stopped sending slips would be missed by lunchtime. In code, unmet demand never times out by itself. The contract so far is only interfaces. The JDK carries its own copy of them, and one real publisher you can run today. Break rule 3.9 on purpose RequestZeroDemo has a subscriber that calls request(0) in onSubscribe. It subscribes to a JDK SubmissionPublisher and to a Reactor Flux.range(1, 3). Predict what each publisher sends back. Then run it. Change request(0) to request(2). Predict again: does each stream complete? RequestZeroDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l01; import reactor.adapter.JdkFlowAdapter; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import java.util.concurrent.Flow; import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** A subscriber that breaks rule 3.9 by calling request(0). Two publishers react differently. */ public class RequestZeroDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (SubmissionPublisher<Integer> jdk = new SubmissionPublisher<>()) { jdk.subscribe(new Rude("JDK SubmissionPublisher")); jdk.submit(1); } TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.sleep(300); Flow.Publisher<Integer> reactor = JdkFlowAdapter.publisherToFlowPublisher(Flux.range(1, 3)); Rude rude = new Rude("Reactor Flux.range"); reactor.subscribe(rude); TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.sleep(300); if (!rude.signalled) System.out.println("Reactor Flux.range: no signal at all, the stream just stalls"); } static final class Rude implements Flow.Subscriber<Integer> { final String name; volatile boolean signalled; Rude(String name) { this.name = name; } @Override public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { s.request(0); } // rule 3.9 says: must be > 0 @Override public void onNext(Integer item) { signalled = true; System.out.println(name + ": onNext " + item); } @Override public void onError(Throwable t) { signalled = true; System.out.println(name + ": onError " + t); } @Override public void onComplete() { signalled = true; System.out.println(name + ": onComplete"); } } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l01.RequestZeroDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l01/RequestZeroDemo.java RequestZeroDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l01 import reactor.adapter.JdkFlowAdapter import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import java.util.concurrent.Flow import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** A subscriber that breaks rule 3.9 by calling request(0). Two publishers react differently. */ fun main() { SubmissionPublisher<Int>().use { jdk -> jdk.subscribe(RudeSubscriber("JDK SubmissionPublisher")) jdk.submit(1) } TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.sleep(300) val reactor: Flow.Publisher<Int> = JdkFlowAdapter.publisherToFlowPublisher(Flux.range(1, 3)) val rude = RudeSubscriber("Reactor Flux.range") reactor.subscribe(rude) TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.sleep(300) if (!rude.signalled) println("Reactor Flux.range: no signal at all, the stream just stalls") } private class RudeSubscriber(private val name: String) : Flow.Subscriber<Int> { @Volatile var signalled = false override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) = s.request(0) // rule 3.9 says: must be > 0 override fun onNext(item: Int) { signalled = true; println("$name: onNext $item") } override fun onError(t: Throwable) { signalled = true; println("$name: onError $t") } override fun onComplete() { signalled = true; println("$name: onComplete") } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l01.RequestZeroDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l01/RequestZeroDemo.kt The JDK publisher follows rule 3.9 and prints onError java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: non-positive subscription request. Reactor prints nothing at all: the stream just stalls. With request(2), the JDK publisher sends its one item and then onComplete, because it was closed. Reactor sends 1 and 2 and then stops without completing, because nobody asked for 3. Unmet demand never times out by itself. Demand goes up as request(n), the packer's slip, and loaves come down as onNext. The publisher never sends more than it is owed. Reactive Streams for the JVM: specification and rules docs

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Flow and SubmissionPublisher: the same contract inside the JDK
x: Java 9 copied the four interfaces into the JDK, as nested types of java.util.concurrent.Flow: Flow.Publisher, Flow.Subscriber, Flow.Subscription and Flow.Processor. Same methods, same rules, different package. Reactor works with the org.reactivestreams copies, so you bridge between the two with JdkFlowAdapter (in reactor-core) or FlowAdapters (in the reactive-streams jar). RequestZeroDemo used the first one. The JDK ships one real publisher, SubmissionPublisher. You hand it items from ordinary code, and it delivers them to each subscriber on another thread. Here it is with the lab's BatchingSubscriber, a packer that asks for loaves 32 at a time: Java try (var oven = new SubmissionPublisher<Loaf>()) { oven.subscribe(new BatchingSubscriber<>(32, packer::box)); // asks for 32 at a time for (Loaf loaf : todaysLoaves) { oven.submit(loaf); // waits while this packer is 256 loaves behind } } // close(): each subscriber gets onComplete after the loaves already on its belt Kotlin SubmissionPublisher<Loaf>().use { oven -> oven.subscribe(BatchingSubscriber(32, packer::box)) // asks for 32 at a time for (loaf in todaysLoaves) { oven.submit(loaf) // waits while this packer is 256 loaves behind } } // close(): each subscriber gets onComplete after the loaves already on its belt The parts that matter, mapped onto the belt: Each subscriber gets its own buffer, its own stretch of belt where loaves wait to be delivered. It holds up to Flow.defaultBufferSize() items, which is 256. Delivery runs on an Executor. By default that is ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), a pool of threads the whole JDK shares. Pass your own executor for anything slow. submit(item) blocks the producer's thread while a subscriber's buffer is full: the baker stands at a full belt and waits. This is where backpressure becomes something an ordinary thread can feel. In the first Try it, submit is what slowed the oven to the packer's pace. offer(item, onDrop) never blocks. When a buffer is full, it calls your drop handler and returns a negative number. There is also an offer with a timeout. If a subscriber method throws, the publisher cancels that subscription. close() completes every subscriber, and closeExceptionally(t) sends them onError(t). SaturationDemo, in the Try it, builds a publisher with a belt of just 2 slots and a packer that never writes a slip. Then it offers 10 loaves: offer(1) -> 1 offer(2) -> 2 offer(3) -> -1 ... offer(10) -> -1 dropped 8 of 10, lag 2 The first two offers fill the belt, and offer returns the lag, the number of items waiting. The other eight are dropped, because the belt is full and nobody asked for anything. Not one loaf reached the packer. No slip, no loaf, even with loaves sitting right there. Blocking in submit is fine on a thread of its own, or on a virtual thread from Part 1. It's a bad idea on an event loop, a single thread that serves many connections by never waiting, which the next section explains. There, one blocked submit stalls everything else the loop serves. SubmissionPublisher is a good teaching tool, and a decent way to hand items to several subscribers inside one program. But it has no operators, the methods that add a station to the belt, such as one that slices every loaf. You can't transform, retry or time out a Flow.Publisher without writing that code yourself. Reactor does that job, from the next lesson on. Before we take on a whole library, though, a fair question: why not just block and wait? Fill a two-slot belt SaturationDemo builds a SubmissionPublisher with a buffer of 2 and a subscriber that never calls request. Then it offers 10 items. Predict what each offer returns and how many items are dropped. Run it. Now replace the offer(...) call with publisher.submit(i), and keep the assignment to lag. Predict, then run it. Stop it with Ctrl+C. SaturationDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l01; import java.util.concurrent.Flow; import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool; import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** A SubmissionPublisher with a 2-slot buffer and a subscriber that never asks for anything. */ public class SaturationDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("default buffer: " + Flow.defaultBufferSize()); AtomicInteger dropped = new AtomicInteger(); try (SubmissionPublisher<Integer> publisher = new SubmissionPublisher<>(ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), 2)) { publisher.subscribe(new Flow.Subscriber<Integer>() { public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { } // never calls request(n) public void onNext(Integer item) { System.out.println("got " + item); } public void onError(Throwable t) { } public void onComplete() { } }); for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) { // offer() does not block. When the buffer is full it calls the drop handler instead. int lag = publisher.offer(i, (subscriber, item) -> { dropped.incrementAndGet(); return false; // false: don't retry, drop it }); System.out.printf("offer(%d) -> %d%n", i, lag); } System.out.println("dropped " + dropped.get() + " of 10, lag " + publisher.estimateMaximumLag()); } } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l01.SaturationDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l01/SaturationDemo.java SaturationDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l01 import java.util.concurrent.Flow import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** A SubmissionPublisher with a 2-slot buffer and a subscriber that never asks for anything. */ fun main() { println("default buffer: ${Flow.defaultBufferSize()}") val dropped = AtomicInteger() SubmissionPublisher<Int>(ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), 2).use { publisher -> publisher.subscribe(object : Flow.Subscriber<Int> { override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) {} // never calls request(n) override fun onNext(item: Int) = println("got $item") override fun onError(t: Throwable) {} override fun onComplete() {} }) for (i in 1..10) { // offer() does not block. When the buffer is full it calls the drop handler instead. val lag = publisher.offer(i) { _, _ -> dropped.incrementAndGet() false // false: don't retry, drop it } println("offer($i) -> $lag") } println("dropped ${dropped.get()} of 10, lag ${publisher.estimateMaximumLag()}") } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l01.SaturationDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l01/SaturationDemo.kt The first two offers return a lag of 1 and 2. Offers 3 to 10 each return -1, the drop handler runs eight times, and the last line is dropped 8 of 10, lag 2. Nothing is delivered, because nothing was requested. With submit the program hangs on item 3: the buffer is full, the subscriber never asks for more, and submit waits for space. That hang is backpressure reaching your thread.
