h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · What non-blocking buys you, and what it costs
x: Here is what blocking costs. Say the bakery's program asks a supplier's web service how much flour is left, and the answer takes 120 ms to come back. The thread that makes the call blocks: for 120 ms it holds about a megabyte of memory for its stack, and does no work. So the number of threads caps the number of calls. Little's law says that the calls in flight equal the calls per second times the time each call takes. Turn it around: 200 threads, each holding a call for 0.12 s, finish at most 200 / 0.12 s, about 1,670 calls a second, however idle the processors are. Non-blocking I/O removes the wait. The thread hands the request to the operating system and moves on to other work. When the answer arrives, the operating system tells the program, and a callback carries on where the request left off. An event loop works this way: one thread, many calls in flight, and never a wait. A handful of threads can keep thousands of calls going. Reactive libraries are the way to write code for that world of callbacks without drowning in them. In Reactor, a Mono is the one answer you're waiting for, a Flux is a stream of answers, and demand, the slip, travels with the data. The style has real costs, and its own makers say so. The Spring Framework is a widely used toolkit for building Java web services, and the home of Reactor. Its documentation puts it plainly: "Reactive and non-blocking generally do not make applications run faster." The gain is "the ability to scale with a small, fixed number of threads and less memory", and you only see it when calls take time. You also pay in other ways. Stack traces show library internals instead of your code. Everyone on the team has to learn a new way of thinking. And one rule is strict: nothing on an event loop may block. A single blocking database call on an event-loop thread stalls every request that loop serves. Virtual threads (final in JDK 21) changed the trade. Part 1 showed that a blocked virtual thread lets go of its carrier, the platform thread that runs it. So blocking code no longer ties up a thread of the operating system per call. For a plain request and response, blocking code on virtual threads is now the simpler default. Reactive code still earns its place where the problem really is a stream. Think of backpressure, cancellation that travels back to the source, a cap on how many calls run at once, and retries and timeouts you add like stations on a belt. Lesson 8 of this track comes back to this choice. Quick check: the bakery's program makes 3,000 supplier calls a second, and each takes 120 ms. How many calls are in flight at any moment, and how many threads does each model need? (Little's law gives 3,000 x 0.12 s = 360 calls in flight. Blocking needs 360 threads, one parked per call. An event loop needs a handful, because no thread waits for an answer.) Spring Framework reference: WebFlux overview (applicability and performance) read

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Java and Kotlin
x: A one-at-a-time Flow.Subscriber in Java and Kotlin OneAtATime.java oven.subscribe(new Flow.Subscriber<Loaf>() { private Flow.Subscription s; public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { this.s = s; s.request(1); // the first slip: one loaf } public void onNext(Loaf loaf) { packer.box(loaf); // slow work s.request(1); // only now ask for the next } public void onError(Throwable t) { log.error("the oven stopped", t); } public void onComplete() { log.info("all loaves boxed"); } }); OneAtATime.kt oven.subscribe(object : Flow.Subscriber<Loaf> { private lateinit var s: Flow.Subscription override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) { this.s = s s.request(1) // the first slip: one loaf } override fun onNext(loaf: Loaf) { // non-null type: Kotlin itself throws NPE on null packer.box(loaf) // slow work s.request(1) // only now ask for the next } override fun onError(t: Throwable) = log.error("the oven stopped", t) override fun onComplete() = log.info("all loaves boxed") }) The protocol code is the same in both languages, and three Kotlin details change how it feels. lateinit var s replaces the nullable field you would otherwise check. object : Flow.Subscriber<Loaf> is Kotlin's anonymous class. And because onNext(loaf: Loaf) declares a non-null parameter, the Kotlin compiler adds a null check to it: a publisher that sends null gets a NullPointerException, which is exactly what rule 2.13 asks for, with no code from you. In Java, Objects.requireNonNull(loaf) does the same job by hand. Neither language protects you from the bigger mistake, asking for Long.MAX_VALUE in onSubscribe, which switches backpressure off.

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Worked example
x: Find the broken rules in a hand-written subscriber A teammate wrote this subscriber. It receives the day's cake orders from the order book and writes one line per order to a report file. Read it and look for broken rules before you read on. class ReportSubscriber implements Flow.Subscriber<Order> { private Flow.Subscription s; public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { this.s = s; s.request(Long.MAX_VALUE); } public void onNext(Order order) { if (order.total() == null) throw new IllegalStateException("bad order " + order.id()); file.append(order.toLine()); } public void onError(Throwable t) { s.request(1); } // "try again" public void onComplete() { file.close(); } } class ReportSubscriber : Flow.Subscriber<Order> { private lateinit var s: Flow.Subscription override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) { this.s = s s.request(Long.MAX_VALUE) } override fun onNext(order: Order) { if (order.total == null) throw IllegalStateException("bad order ${order.id}") file.append(order.toLine()) } override fun onError(t: Throwable) = s.request(1) // "try again" override fun onComplete() = file.close() } Three problems. request(Long.MAX_VALUE) turns backpressure off (rule 3.17), so a slow disk makes the publisher pile orders up in memory. Throwing from onNext breaks rule 2.13: the publisher may cancel, log, or do something you didn't expect. And calling request from onError breaks rule 2.3: after a terminal signal the subscription is dead, and talking to it does nothing useful. Fix them one at a time. Ask for one order at a time. Turn a bad order into a cancel plus a recorded error. Treat onError as the end. class ReportSubscriber implements Flow.Subscriber<Order> { private Flow.Subscription s; private boolean stopped; volatile Throwable failure; public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { this.s = s; s.request(1); // 1. bounded demand } public void onNext(Order order) { if (stopped) return; // 2. rule 2.8: late items may still come if (order.total() == null) { stopped = true; failure = new IllegalStateException("bad order " + order.id()); s.cancel(); // 3. stop by cancelling, never by throwing return; } file.append(order.toLine()); s.request(1); // 4. ask for the next one when done } public void onError(Throwable t) { failure = t; file.close(); } // 5. terminal: just clean up public void onComplete() { file.close(); } } class ReportSubscriber : Flow.Subscriber<Order> { private lateinit var s: Flow.Subscription private var stopped = false @Volatile var failure: Throwable? = null override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) { this.s = s s.request(1) // 1. bounded demand } override fun onNext(order: Order) { if (stopped) return // 2. rule 2.8: late items may still come if (order.total == null) { stopped = true failure = IllegalStateException("bad order ${order.id}") s.cancel() // 3. stop by cancelling, never by throwing return } file.append(order.toLine()) s.request(1) // 4. ask for the next one when done } override fun onError(t: Throwable) { failure = t; file.close() } // 5. terminal: just clean up override fun onComplete() = file.close() } This version is correct but chatty: one request(1) per order. Each call crosses into the publisher, and some publishers do real work per request. The lab asks for the same correctness with demand in batches, which is what Reactor's own operators do inside.

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Lab
x: A Flow.Subscriber that asks in batches labs/reactive/src/main/java/workbench/reactive/l01/BatchingSubscriber.java ./gradlew :reactive:test --tests 'workbench.reactive.l01.*' Run the tests once. All five fail. Two show the TODO message. The three that use a real SubmissionPublisher wait 3 seconds and fail on [stream finished], because the TODO exception is thrown on the publisher's thread and never reaches the test. Write onSubscribe: keep the subscription and call request(batchSize). If a subscription is already stored, cancel the new one and return. Write onNext: reject null, pass the item to the handler, count it, and call request(batchSize) again only when a whole batch has been handled. Make a throwing handler safe: catch the exception, cancel the subscription, record the error, count down done, and ignore any later onNext. Write onError and onComplete so that await returns. Run the tests until all five pass. You need two more fields: an int counting the items handled in the current batch, and a boolean that says you have cancelled. Signals never overlap (rule 1.3), so plain fields are safe here. The request test expects exactly [4, 4, 4] for 10 items in batches of 4. If you see eleven requests, you are asking after every item. If you see [4], you never reset the counter. Objects.requireNonNull(item) is all rule 2.13 asks for on null. All five tests in BatchingSubscriberTest pass. By the end you can explain how Reactive Streams demand (request(n)) stops a fast producer from drowning a slow consumer, name the rules a subscriber must follow, and write a Flow.Subscriber that asks for items in batches.

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · From memory
x: Write a one-at-a-time subscriber from memory Close this page. Write a Flow.Subscriber<String> that requests one loaf at a time, prints each one, and cancels the subscription (without throwing) at the first loaf whose name starts with "burnt". Then compare with the answer. Did you guard against loaves that arrive after the cancel?

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Quiz
x: A subscriber calls request(3) in onSubscribe and never calls request again. The publisher has 10 items ready. What does the subscriber receive? All 10 items, because the publisher has them ready 3 items, then onComplete 3 items, and then nothing until it requests more 1 item, because each onNext needs its own request Rule 1.1 caps onNext signals at the total requested. The publisher still has items to send, so it may not complete either: it waits for more demand. Having items ready never lets a publisher send more than it was asked for. Inside onNext, your handler fails on a bad order. What should the subscriber do? Throw the exception so the publisher can call onError Call subscription.cancel(), record the error, and return normally Call request(0) to signal a problem Ignore it and call request(1) to get the next order Rule 2.13 says subscriber methods must return normally, and cancelling is the legal way for a subscriber to stop the stream. Throwing leaves the reaction up to the publisher (SubmissionPublisher cancels; others may only log it), and request(0) breaks rule 3.9 itself. An oven thread calls SubmissionPublisher.submit(loaf) in a loop. One subscriber is slow, and its buffer of 256 is full. What happens? submit blocks until that subscriber has room submit drops the loaf and returns -1 submit throws IllegalStateException The loaf goes to the other subscribers only submit blocks while any subscriber's buffer is full, which slows the producer to the slowest subscriber's pace. offer is the method that drops instead and returns a negative number. Pick offer with a drop handler if the producer must never wait. Which of these is the strongest reason to choose a non-blocking, reactive design for a program? Each request will finish faster It is easier to debug than blocking code It removes the need for timeouts It can keep thousands of slow calls in flight with a few threads and little memory The Spring docs say reactive code generally doesn't run faster. The gain is scale with a small, fixed number of threads, and it shows only when calls really wait. Debugging is harder, not easier, and slow calls still need timeouts. From "How virtual threads work: carriers and continuations": a virtual thread calls a slow web service over a socket and waits 120 ms for the answer. What does its carrier thread do during the wait? It blocks for 120 ms, like a platform thread The JVM creates a new carrier thread for the other virtual threads It unmounts the waiting virtual thread and runs other virtual threads The call throws, because virtual threads cannot block A blocking socket read parks the virtual thread and frees the carrier to run other virtual threads. That's why blocking code on virtual threads scales without a reactive rewrite. The scheduler doesn't add carriers for ordinary network waits.

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Explain it back
x: A friend asks why the bakery's program bothers with request(n) when "a queue in between does the same job". Explain in your own words what demand gives you that a queue with no limit doesn't, and when a queue is fine.

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Key terms
x: Backpressure A way for a slow consumer to tell a fast producer how much it can take, so the producer never sends more. Demand The number of items a subscriber has asked for with request(n) and not yet received. Publisher The source of a stream. It sends items to a subscriber, never more than the subscriber asked for. Subscriber The receiver of a stream. It gets onSubscribe, then onNext items, then onError or onComplete. Subscription The link between one publisher and one subscriber. It carries request(n) and cancel() back to the publisher. Terminal signal onError or onComplete. After one of them the stream is over and nothing else arrives. Non-blocking I/O Input and output where the thread hands the request to the operating system and moves on, and a callback runs when the answer arrives. What does request(n) promise the subscriber? That the publisher will send at most n more onNext signals (rule 1.1). It may send fewer and then complete or fail. In what order can a Reactive Streams subscriber see signals? onSubscribe onNext* (onError | onComplete)?: one onSubscribe, any number of onNext, then at most one terminal signal. How does a subscriber stop a stream when its handler fails? It calls subscription.cancel() and returns normally. Throwing from onNext breaks rule 2.13. What does SubmissionPublisher.submit do when a subscriber's buffer is full? It blocks the calling thread until there is room. offer drops instead and calls your drop handler. What happens if you call request(0) on a Reactor Flux.range subscription? Nothing visible. Reactor only logs it at DEBUG and the stream stalls. Rule 3.9 (and the JDK's SubmissionPublisher) say it must signal onError(IllegalArgumentException). What does request(Long.MAX_VALUE) mean? Unbounded demand: "send everything, no backpressure" (rule 3.17). Is kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow the same as java.util.concurrent.Flow? No. The JDK one is the Reactive Streams protocol with request(n). Kotlin's is a coroutine stream whose backpressure is the suspension of emit.

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Go deeper
x: Four details that will help later. Why request takes a long. Demand adds up. A subscriber may call request(5) and then request(10) before any item arrives, and the publisher then owes 15. Rule 3.17 says a subscription must support demand up to Long.MAX_VALUE, and that a total at or above 2^63 - 1 may be treated as unbounded. Reactor's subscribe(Consumer) uses exactly that: it requests Long.MAX_VALUE. Operators like limitRate and flatMap then turn that unbounded demand into bounded requests upstream, which is lesson 7 of this track. Rule 3.3 and reentrancy. request may be called from inside onNext (rule 3.2), and a publisher that has items ready may answer by calling onNext again from inside that request (rule 3.10). Done naively, a stream of a million items becomes a stack a million calls deep. Rule 3.3 makes publishers bound that recursion, usually with a small loop that hands out items one by one. This is one reason a correct publisher is much harder to write than a subscriber, and why you should use a library's. The TCK. The Reactive Streams project ships a Technology Compatibility Kit: a set of tests that check a publisher or subscriber against the numbered rules. Library authors run it. Reactor's TestPublisher (lesson 8 of this track) borrows the idea for your own tests: you can create a publisher that breaks the rules on purpose, for example one that ignores demand, and check that your code survives it. Processor. A processor is both a subscriber and a publisher, so it can sit in the middle of a chain like a station on the belt. Reactor used to expose processors directly. It has phased them out in favour of Sinks, which you'll meet in lesson 8 of this track.

h: Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe · Flux for many items, Mono for one or none
x: Reactor is a library that implements Reactive Streams, the contract from the last lesson, and adds hundreds of operators: methods that each add one step to a stream, like stations along the bakery belt. It is the engine under the reactive parts of the Spring Framework, but you need nothing from Spring to use it. Reactor has two publisher types, and the type tells you how many items to expect. A Flux<T> emits zero to many items, then maybe onComplete or onError. On the bakery line it's an order for a tray: any number of loaves. All three parts are optional, so a Flux with no terminal signal is endless, like Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(1)), which ticks once a second forever. A Mono<T> emits at most one item and then completes, or emits only an error. It's an order for one cake: you get the cake, or no cake, or a note that says what went wrong. It can never send an item and then an error. Mono<Void> means "tell me when it's done", for a job that returns nothing, such as cleaning the oven. Java Flux<String> loaves = Flux.just("rye-1", "rye-2", "rye-3"); Flux<Integer> trays = Flux.range(1, 3); Mono<String> cake = Mono.just("chocolate cake"); Mono<String> nothing = Mono.empty(); Mono<String> failed = Mono.error(new IllegalStateException("out of flour")); Kotlin val loaves: Flux<String> = Flux.just("rye-1", "rye-2", "rye-3") val trays: Flux<Int> = Flux.range(1, 3) val cake: Mono<String> = Mono.just("chocolate cake") val nothing: Mono<String> = Mono.empty() val failed: Mono<String> = Mono.error(IllegalStateException("out of flour")) Both types implement org.reactivestreams.Publisher, so every rule from the last lesson applies. The split is for readers and for operators. A method that returns Mono<Cake> promises one cake or none, and Mono has operators that only make sense for one value, such as Mono.zip from lesson 4 of this track. Some operators change the type: mono.concatWith(other) gives a Flux, while mono.then(other) gives a Mono. The simplest way to run one is subscribe with up to three lambdas, one for each kind of signal: Java loaves.subscribe( l -> box(l), // onNext e -> log.error("the belt stopped", e), // onError () -> log.info("all loaves boxed")); // onComplete Kotlin loaves.subscribe( { l -> box(l) }, // onNext { e -> log.error("the belt stopped", e) }, // onError { log.info("all loaves boxed") }) // onComplete This form writes one slip for everything, request(Long.MAX_VALUE). FirstFluxDemo, in the Try it, adds log() to the chain, an operator that prints every signal passing through it. The protocol from the last lesson appears line by line: [ INFO] (main) | onSubscribe([Synchronous Fuseable] FluxArray.ArraySubscription) [ INFO] (main) | request(unbounded) [ INFO] (main) | onNext(rye-1) got rye-1 ... [ INFO] (main) | onComplete() done The demo's second subscriber leaves out the error lambda, and its Mono fails with "out of flour". Reactor doesn't throw that to your code. It prints an ERROR log line about ErrorCallbackNotImplemented, and main carries on, cheerfully unaware. So a test that doesn't check for the error passes. The cause is rule 2.13 from the last lesson: onError must return normally, so the subscriber that subscribe builds for you can't throw. With no error lambda, it hands the error to a hook, a method Reactor calls for errors nobody handles, and the default hook only logs it. A subscribe without an error lambda turns failures into log lines. Always pass one. Reactive Streams forbids null items, and Reactor 3.8 enforces it: Mono.just(null) throws a NullPointerException, and so does a map whose function returns null. Use Mono.empty() for "no value". Kotlin catches this even earlier. Reactor 3.8 marks its API with JSpecify annotations, small labels that say whether null is allowed, so a Kotlin map { if (ok) x else null } doesn't even compile. Every subscribe so far ran its chain at once. Let's slow down and look at what happens before the subscribe. Watch the signals go by Read FirstFluxDemo. It subscribes to a Flux of three loaves with log() in the chain, then to a failing Mono with no error callback. Predict the order of the lines, including the log() lines. What happens to the "out of flour" error? Run it. Then add an error lambda to the second subscribe and run it again. FirstFluxDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l02; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; /** A Flux and a Mono, subscribed with the three callbacks, with log() printing every signal. */ public class FirstFluxDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { Flux<String> loaves = Flux.just("rye-1", "rye-2", "rye-3"); loaves .log() // prints each signal that passes this point .subscribe( l -> System.out.println("got " + l), // onNext e -> System.out.println("failed: " + e), // onError () -> System.out.println("done")); // onComplete Mono<String> cake = Mono.error(new IllegalStateException("out of flour")); cake.subscribe(c -> System.out.println("got " + c)); // no error callback: watch what happens System.out.println("main carries on"); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l02.FirstFluxDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l02/FirstFluxDemo.java FirstFluxDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l02 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono /** A Flux and a Mono, subscribed with the three callbacks, with log() printing every signal. */ fun main() { val loaves: Flux<String> = Flux.just("rye-1", "rye-2", "rye-3") loaves .log() // prints each signal that passes this point .subscribe( { l -> println("got $l") }, // onNext { e -> println("failed: $e") }, // onError { println("done") }) // onComplete val cake: Mono<String> = Mono.error(IllegalStateException("out of flour")) cake.subscribe { c -> println("got $c") } // no error callback: watch what happens println("main carries on") } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l02.FirstFluxDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l02/FirstFluxDemo.kt log() prints onSubscribe, then request(unbounded), then each onNext followed by your got ... line, then onComplete() and done: the protocol from the last lesson, live. The failing Mono prints main carries on and an [ERROR] ... Operator called default onErrorDropped - reactor.core.Exceptions$ErrorCallbackNotImplemented: java.lang.IllegalStateException: out of flour log line. The two may appear in either order, since the log goes to a different output stream. Nothing is thrown at main. With an error lambda, your lambda prints the failure and the ERROR line is gone.

h: Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe · Assembly fills in the form, subscribe starts the baking
x: Assembly only builds a chain of objects; subscribe travels up, request follows, data flows down, and a second subscribe runs it all again Here is the most important fact about Reactor: building a chain runs none of your code. Java Flux<Integer> pricesInCents = Flux.range(1, 3) .map(euros -> euros * 100); // nothing has run yet pricesInCents.subscribe(System.out::println); // now range and map run Kotlin val pricesInCents: Flux<Int> = Flux.range(1, 3) .map { euros -> euros * 100 } // nothing has run yet pricesInCents.subscribe { println(it) } // now range and map run Three separate passes happen over that chain, and it helps to keep them apart. The figure below draws them. Assembly is when you call the operators. Each call returns a new Flux that wraps the one before it, so Flux.range(1, 3).map(...) is a FluxMap object holding a FluxRange object. Your lambda is stored, not called. This is filling in the order form. The Reactor docs call the result "an abstract description of your asynchronous process". Subscription is when you call subscribe. Reactor walks the chain backwards, from your end to the source. Your subscriber subscribes to map, and map makes a subscriber of its own and subscribes to range. Then request(n) travels up the same chain to the source. This is signing the form and handing it over. Data comes last. Only now does the source emit. onNext signals flow down through each operator to your lambda, then onComplete or onError. This is the baking. AssemblyDemo, in the Try it, counts how often map runs, before and after subscribe: after assembly: map ran 0 times price 100 cents price 200 cents price 300 cents after subscribe: map ran 3 times Zero, then three. The form was filled in, and nothing was baked until it was signed. Three consequences follow, and each one catches people. First, code inside an operator runs at subscription time: maybe once, maybe once per subscriber, maybe never if nobody subscribes, and possibly on another thread (lesson 6 of this track). Second, operators never change the object you call them on. They return a new one, so a return value you drop is a step that never happens. The second half of AssemblyDemo shows it: Java Flux<Integer> orderSizes = Flux.just(5, 50, 500); orderSizes.filter(loaves -> loaves > 10); // Naive: the new Flux is thrown away orderSizes.subscribe(loaves -> System.out.println("big order: " + loaves + " loaves")); Kotlin val orderSizes: Flux<Int> = Flux.just(5, 50, 500) orderSizes.filter { loaves -> loaves > 10 } // Naive: the new Flux is thrown away orderSizes.subscribe { loaves -> println("big order: $loaves loaves") } It prints all three orders, the 5 included. filter built a new, filtered Flux, and nobody kept it. It compiles, and it filters nothing. The fix is to subscribe to what filter returns. Third, a method that returns a Mono can still do work before it returns, at assembly time. It looks lazy but isn't. That one gets the last section of this lesson. Building a chain runs nothing. Only a subscribe starts the work. A subscription starts the work. So what happens when two of them start it? Count what runs, and when AssemblyDemo counts how often map runs, before and after subscribe. Then it filters a list of order sizes. Predict both counts and the orders printed. Run it. Fix the filter so that only orders above 10 loaves print. AssemblyDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l02; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Building a pipeline runs none of it. Subscribing runs all of it. */ public class AssemblyDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { AtomicInteger mapped = new AtomicInteger(); Flux<Integer> pricesInCents = Flux.range(1, 3) .map(euros -> { mapped.incrementAndGet(); return euros * 100; }); System.out.println("after assembly: map ran " + mapped.get() + " times"); pricesInCents.subscribe(p -> System.out.println("price " + p + " cents")); System.out.println("after subscribe: map ran " + mapped.get() + " times"); // A classic bug: the result of filter() is thrown away, so the filter is never part of the chain. Flux<Integer> orderSizes = Flux.just(5, 50, 500); orderSizes.filter(loaves -> loaves > 10); orderSizes.subscribe(loaves -> System.out.println("big order: " + loaves + " loaves")); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l02.AssemblyDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l02/AssemblyDemo.java AssemblyDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l02 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** Building a pipeline runs none of it. Subscribing runs all of it. */ fun main() { val mapped = AtomicInteger() val pricesInCents: Flux<Int> = Flux.range(1, 3) .map { euros -> mapped.incrementAndGet() euros * 100 } println("after assembly: map ran ${mapped.get()} times") pricesInCents.subscribe { p -> println("price $p cents") } println("after subscribe: map ran ${mapped.get()} times") // A classic bug: the result of filter() is thrown away, so the filter is never part of the chain. val orderSizes: Flux<Int> = Flux.just(5, 50, 500) orderSizes.filter { loaves -> loaves > 10 } orderSizes.subscribe { loaves -> println("big order: $loaves loaves") } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l02.AssemblyDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l02/AssemblyDemo.kt after assembly: map ran 0 times, three prices, then after subscribe: map ran 3 times. All three orders print, 5 included, because orderSizes.filter(...) returned a new Flux that nobody used. The fix is to subscribe to the result: orderSizes.filter(loaves -> loaves > 10).subscribe(...) in Java, orderSizes.filter { it > 10 }.subscribe { ... } in Kotlin. Three passes over the same chain: assembly runs no code of yours, subscription travels up to the source, data travels down to you. Reactor reference: Introduction to reactive programming (source) docs

h: Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe · Cold publishers do their work again for every subscriber
x: Most publishers you meet are cold: each subscriber gets its own run, from the start. Flux.range, Mono.fromCallable, a web client's response, a reactive database query: subscribe twice and the work happens twice. That's often what you want. The retry operator from lesson 5 of this track works by subscribing again, and a cold source gives it a fresh attempt. And two customers who each order a cake should get two cakes. It bites when you subscribe twice without meaning to. In ColdDemo, the work inside the Mono is baking a cake: Java Mono<String> cake = bake("order-42"); // cold: nothing baked yet cake.subscribe(c -> System.out.println("shop log: " + c)); // subscription 1 String handedOver = cake.block(); // subscription 2 Kotlin val cake: Mono<String> = bake("order-42") // cold: nothing baked yet cake.subscribe { c -> println("shop log: $c") } // subscription 1 val handedOver = cake.block() // subscription 2 block() is a subscription too. It subscribes and makes the calling thread wait until the value arrives. The demo printed: oven: baking the cake for order-42 (cake #1) shop log: cake-1 oven: baking the cake for order-42 (cake #2) handed to the customer: cake-2 cakes baked: 2 Two cakes for one order. The shop log recorded cake-1, the customer went home with cake-2, and the flour bill covers both. This is where the order-form picture breaks. A clerk handed the same signed form twice would notice. A cold Mono never does: each subscription is a fresh signature, and the whole order runs again. The same thing happens when code subscribes to a Mono "just to log it" and then returns it to a framework that subscribes again. It happens when a test calls block() twice on the same Mono, too. The fix is one chain, with the side effect inside it. doOnNext runs a side effect for each item and passes the item on unchanged: Java String handedOver = bake("order-42") .doOnNext(c -> System.out.println("shop log: " + c)) // runs inside the one chain .block(); // one subscription, one cake Kotlin val handedOver = bake("order-42") .doOnNext { c -> println("shop log: $c") } // runs inside the one chain .block() // one subscription, one cake If several parts of a program really need one shared result, say so with cache() or share(). Those turn a cold publisher into a hot one, which runs once and hands its items to everyone subscribed. They have sharp edges of their own, so they get lesson 8 of this track. Every subscription to a cold publisher runs it again. Subscribe once, and put side effects inside the chain. Here is a quick test for any Mono you didn't write: count its subscriptions. Wrap it with doOnSubscribe(s -> counter.incrementAndGet()), run your code, and check the number. The lab has you build exactly that helper. Counting finds the cake baked twice. The last trap bakes it too early, before anyone has subscribed at all. Bake one cake twice by accident ColdDemo builds one baking Mono, subscribes once for the shop log, and once with block() for the customer. Predict how many cakes the oven bakes. Run it. Rewrite main as one chain: cake.doOnNext(c -> System.out.println("shop log: " + c)).block() in Java, or cake.doOnNext { println("shop log: $it") }.block() in Kotlin. Run it again. ColdDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l02; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** A cold Mono does its work again for every subscriber. Here the work is baking a cake. */ public class ColdDemo { static final AtomicInteger baked = new AtomicInteger(); static Mono<String> bake(String orderId) { return Mono.fromCallable(() -> { int n = baked.incrementAndGet(); System.out.println(" oven: baking the cake for " + orderId + " (cake #" + n + ")"); return "cake-" + n; }); } public static void main(String[] args) { Mono<String> cake = bake("order-42"); cake.subscribe(c -> System.out.println("shop log: " + c)); // subscriber 1 String handedOver = cake.block(); // subscriber 2 System.out.println("handed to the customer: " + handedOver); System.out.println("cakes baked: " + baked.get()); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l02.ColdDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l02/ColdDemo.java ColdDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l02 import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger private val baked = AtomicInteger() /** A cold Mono does its work again for every subscriber. Here the work is baking a cake. */ private fun bake(orderId: String): Mono<String> = Mono.fromCallable { val n = baked.incrementAndGet() println(" oven: baking the cake for $orderId (cake #$n)") "cake-$n" } fun main() { val cake = bake("order-42") cake.subscribe { c -> println("shop log: $c") } // subscriber 1 val handedOver = cake.block() // subscriber 2 println("handed to the customer: $handedOver") println("cakes baked: ${baked.get()}") } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l02.ColdDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l02/ColdDemo.kt The first run prints two oven: baking the cake for order-42 lines. The shop log shows cake-1, the customer gets cake-2, and the last line is cakes baked: 2. The log and the customer don't even agree on which cake was sold. With one chain there is one cake, and the shop log and the customer see the same one.

h: Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe · Mono.just is eager; fromCallable and defer are lazy
x: Mono.just(x) holds a value you already have. That sounds harmless until x is a method call: Java Mono<String> price = Mono.just(supplier.fetchFlourPrice()); // Naive: the call runs right here Kotlin val price: Mono<String> = Mono.just(supplier.fetchFlourPrice()) // Naive: the call runs right here Java evaluates the argument before just is even called. So the supplier's web service is called at assembly, on the caller's thread, exactly once. This is the cake baked while you were still writing the form. Every later subscriber gets that same captured value, however stale it has become. If the call throws, the exception flies out of the method that builds the Mono, instead of arriving as onError where Reactor's error operators can see it. And a retry can never call the supplier again, because there is nothing left to run again. LazyDemo, in the Try it, builds the same price Mono three ways and subscribes to each one twice: just calls at assembly: 1, after 2 subscriptions: 1 fromCallable calls at assembly: 0, after 2 subscriptions: 2 defer calls at assembly: 0, after 2 subscriptions: 2 just called the supplier once, before anyone subscribed. The other two waited for each subscription. Those two factory methods suit different shapes of work: You have Use When it runs A value already in hand Mono.just(value) at assembly, once A computation that returns a value, often a blocking call Mono.fromCallable(() -> stock.countLoaves(kind)) on each subscription Code that returns a Mono, or reads state at subscribe time Mono.defer(() -> kitchen.book(order, ovens.nextFreeSlot())) on each subscription In Kotlin the same calls read Mono.fromCallable { stock.countLoaves(kind) } and Mono.defer { kitchen.book(order, ovens.nextFreeSlot()) }. fromCallable also turns the awkward cases into signals: a thrown exception becomes onError, and a null result becomes an empty Mono. Mono.fromSupplier does the same for code that throws no checked exceptions. defer is for when building the publisher itself does work: picking the next free oven slot, reading the clock, choosing which kitchen to send to. Wrapping all of that in defer moves it to subscription time. Two look-alikes keep the trap. Mono.justOrEmpty(stock.countLoaves(kind)) handles null, but its argument is still evaluated at once. And Mono.fromFuture(future) takes a CompletableFuture that is already running when you pass it in. Use the Supplier overload, Mono.fromFuture(() -> client.sendAsync(request)), to start a new one for each subscription. Mono.just takes a value, not a job. Give jobs to fromCallable or defer. just, fromCallable, defer LazyDemo builds the same flour-price Mono three ways and subscribes to each twice. Before running, fill in a small table: calls at assembly, and calls after two subscriptions, for each of the three. Run it and compare. Then change the defer line to use Mono.justOrEmpty(fetchFlourPrice()) inside the defer. Does that change anything? LazyDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l02; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Mono.just, fromCallable and defer, each subscribed twice. Count the calls. */ public class LazyDemo { static final AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); static String fetchFlourPrice() { calls.incrementAndGet(); return "flour=1.20/kg"; } public static void main(String[] args) { run("just", () -> Mono.just(fetchFlourPrice())); run("fromCallable", () -> Mono.fromCallable(LazyDemo::fetchFlourPrice)); run("defer", () -> Mono.defer(() -> Mono.just(fetchFlourPrice()))); } static void run(String name, java.util.function.Supplier<Mono<String>> build) { calls.set(0); Mono<String> price = build.get(); int atAssembly = calls.get(); price.block(); price.block(); System.out.printf("%-13s calls at assembly: %d, after 2 subscriptions: %d%n", name, atAssembly, calls.get()); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l02.LazyDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l02/LazyDemo.java LazyDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l02 import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger private val calls = AtomicInteger() private fun fetchFlourPrice(): String { calls.incrementAndGet() return "flour=1.20/kg" } /** Mono.just, fromCallable and defer, each subscribed twice. Count the calls. */ fun main() { run("just") { Mono.just(fetchFlourPrice()) } run("fromCallable") { Mono.fromCallable { fetchFlourPrice() } } run("defer") { Mono.defer { Mono.just(fetchFlourPrice()) } } } private fun run(name: String, build: () -> Mono<String>) { calls.set(0) val price = build() val atAssembly = calls.get() price.block() price.block() println("%-13s calls at assembly: %d, after 2 subscriptions: %d".format(name, atAssembly, calls.get())) } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l02.LazyDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l02/LazyDemo.kt just: 1 call at assembly, still 1 after two subscriptions. fromCallable and defer: 0 at assembly, 2 after two subscriptions. justOrEmpty inside defer is still lazy, because defer delays the whole lambda, argument included. Outside defer, justOrEmpty(fetchFlourPrice()) would be eager like just. Reactor reference: Hot versus cold (source) docs

h: Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe · Java and Kotlin
x: Eager and lazy Monos in Java and Kotlin Prices.java // eager: fetchFlourPrice runs here, once, before just() is called Mono<String> eager = Mono.just(supplier.fetchFlourPrice()); // lazy: the lambda runs on every subscription Mono<String> lazy = Mono.fromCallable(() -> supplier.fetchFlourPrice()); // lazy: build a whole publisher per subscription Mono<Booking> booking = Mono.defer(() -> kitchen.book(order, ovens.nextFreeSlot())); Prices.kt // eager: fetchFlourPrice runs here, once, before just() is called val eager: Mono<String> = Mono.just(supplier.fetchFlourPrice()) // lazy: the lambda runs on every subscription val lazy: Mono<String> = Mono.fromCallable { supplier.fetchFlourPrice() } // lazy: build a whole publisher per subscription val booking: Mono<Booking> = Mono.defer { kitchen.book(order, ovens.nextFreeSlot()) } // lazy, written as a coroutine (kotlinx-coroutines-reactor): the block starts on each subscription val bookingCo: Mono<Booking> = mono { kitchen.bookSuspending(order, ovens.nextFreeSlot()) } The calls are the same Reactor API in both languages, and so is the trap, because it is plain argument evaluation: Kotlin evaluates supplier.fetchFlourPrice() before Mono.just runs, exactly like Java. Kotlin's trailing lambdas make the lazy forms shorter (Mono.fromCallable { ... }). The kotlinx-coroutines-reactor library adds mono { }, a cold Mono whose body is a coroutine: it starts on each subscription, and a null result gives an empty Mono. That's handy when Kotlin code has to hand a Mono to Java code. Kotlin's own Flow has the same trap under other names: flowOf(call()) is eager, and flow { emit(call()) } is lazy.

h: Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe · Worked example
x: Make a booking method lazy This method books a cake order into a slot in the oven schedule and sends the booking to the kitchen's program. It returns a Mono, so it looks lazy. Mark which lines run when book(order) is called, and which run on subscribe. Mono<Booking> book(CakeOrder order) { Slot slot = ovens.nextFreeSlot(); // reads the oven schedule right now log.info("booking {} into {}", order.cake(), slot); return kitchen.book(order, slot); // a cold Mono: books on subscribe } fun book(order: CakeOrder): Mono<Booking> { val slot = ovens.nextFreeSlot() // reads the oven schedule right now log.info("booking {} into {}", order.cake, slot) return kitchen.book(order, slot) // a cold Mono: books on subscribe } The slot lookup and the log line run at call time, once. Only the booking runs on subscribe. Now add .retry(2) at the call site, because the kitchen's program sometimes fails. Say the first attempt fails because another order took that slot a moment earlier. Each retry subscribes again to kitchen.book(order, slot) with the same, already taken slot. All three attempts fail with "slot taken", and the log shows one "booking" line for three attempts. Move the whole body into defer. Now every subscription, every retry included, looks up a fresh slot, logs again and books again. Mono<Booking> book(CakeOrder order) { return Mono.defer(() -> { Slot slot = ovens.nextFreeSlot(); // 1. per attempt log.info("booking {} into {}", order.cake(), slot); // 2. per attempt return kitchen.book(order, slot); // 3. the cold call }); } fun book(order: CakeOrder): Mono<Booking> = Mono.defer { val slot = ovens.nextFreeSlot() // 1. per attempt log.info("booking {} into {}", order.cake, slot) // 2. per attempt kitchen.book(order, slot) // 3. the cold call } Check it with a counter, the way the lab does: build the Mono, check that there were no slot lookups, subscribe twice, and check that there were two. A test like this catches the next person who "simplifies" the method back to the eager version. Mono<Booking> m = bakery.book(order); assertThat(ovens.lookups()).isZero(); // nothing at assembly m.block(); m.block(); assertThat(ovens.lookups()).isEqualTo(2); // once per subscription val m = bakery.book(order) assertThat(ovens.lookups()).isZero() // nothing at assembly m.block() m.block() assertThat(ovens.lookups()).isEqualTo(2) // once per subscription

h: Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe · Quiz
x: What does this print? Flux<String> f = Flux.just("rye", "spelt") .map(s -> { System.out.println("map " + s); return s.toUpperCase(); }); System.out.println("built"); map rye, map spelt, built built only built, map rye, map spelt Nothing Building the chain stores the lambda without calling it. Nobody subscribes to f, so map never runs and only built prints. The tempting first option is how a loop over a list would behave; here nothing ever subscribes. oven.bake(order) returns a cold Mono<Cake> built with fromCallable. A handler does Mono<Cake> c = oven.bake(order); c.subscribe(log::record); return c.block();. How many cakes does the oven bake? Two, one per subscription One, because both use the same Mono object Zero, because subscribe and block cancel each other It depends on which thread runs first A cold publisher runs once per subscriber, and subscribe and block are two subscriptions, so the callable runs twice. Sharing a Mono object shares the order form, not the cake. Put the log in the chain with doOnNext, or use cache() if you really need to share a result. stock.countLoaves(kind) is a blocking call that may return null. Which line gives a lazy Mono that makes the call on each subscription and is empty on null? Mono.just(stock.countLoaves(kind)) Mono.justOrEmpty(stock.countLoaves(kind)) Flux.just(stock.countLoaves(kind)).next() Mono.fromCallable(() -> stock.countLoaves(kind)) fromCallable calls the lambda on each subscription, and turns null into empty and exceptions into onError. justOrEmpty handles null too, but stock.countLoaves(kind) is still an argument evaluated at assembly. Mono.just(null) would throw. You subscribe to Mono.error(new IllegalStateException("out of flour")) with only an onNext lambda. What happens? The exception is thrown out of subscribe to your code Nothing at all: errors without a handler are ignored silently Reactor logs ErrorCallbackNotImplemented at ERROR level, and your code carries on The JVM prints a stack trace and exits With no error callback, Reactor hands the error to its onErrorDropped hook, which logs it at ERROR level. Your thread carries on undisturbed. That's why a test with no check on the error can pass even though the stream failed. From "Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure": you call flux.subscribe(item -> box(item)) with just the one lambda. What demand does that subscriber send to the source? request(1) before each item request(Long.MAX_VALUE): unbounded request(256), then more in batches No request until the first item arrives The lambda form of subscribe requests everything, which log() shows as request(unbounded). That is rule 3.17's unbounded demand: no backpressure from this subscriber. Lesson 7 of this track shows how operators like limitRate turn it back into bounded requests.

h: Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe · Key terms
x: Flux A Reactor publisher of 0 to N items, which may end with complete or error. Mono A Reactor publisher of at most one item. Mono<Void> only signals completion or error. Operator A method like map or filter that wraps a publisher and returns a new one with one more step. Assembly time When you call operators to build the chain. Only wrapper objects are created; none of your lambdas run. Subscription time When subscribe (or block) is called. The chain is linked up, demand goes up, and the source starts. Cold publisher A publisher that does its work again for each subscriber. Hot publisher A publisher that runs once and shares its items with whoever is subscribed (lesson 8 of this track). When does the lambda inside flux.map(...) run? At subscription time, once per item for each subscriber. Never at assembly, and never if nobody subscribes. Mono.just(fetch()) is subscribed three times. How many times does fetch() run? Once, at assembly, before just is even called. All three subscribers get the same value. What does Mono.fromCallable do with a thrown exception and with a null result? The exception becomes onError. null becomes an empty Mono (just onComplete). What is a cold publisher? One that does its work again, from the start, for every subscriber. Most Reactor sources are cold. orderSizes.filter(n -> n > 10); on its own line, then orderSizes.subscribe(...). Is anything filtered? No. Operators return a new Flux. The filtered one was thrown away, so orderSizes is unchanged. When do you pick Mono.defer over Mono.fromCallable? When the code returns a Mono (or another publisher), or must read state at subscription time, such as the next free slot or the clock.

h: Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe · Go deeper
x: Two more eager traps look like the Mono.just one, and one pair of methods is easy to mix up. Flux.fromStream(stream). A Java Stream can only be used once. The first subscriber drains it, and the second gets IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. Use the supplier overload, Flux.fromStream(() -> orders.streamToday()), so each subscription gets a fresh stream. Flux.fromIterable(list) is fine to subscribe to many times, because a List can be walked again. Mono.fromFuture(future). A CompletableFuture stands for work that has already started. Mono.fromFuture(client.sendAsync(request)) sends the request at assembly, and a retry subscribes again to the same finished future. Mono.fromFuture(() -> client.sendAsync(request)) starts a new request for each subscription. This is the bridge you'll use most often from code built with the executors track's CompletableFuture methods. fromCallable and fromSupplier. The first accepts code that throws checked exceptions, because a Callable may throw Exception. The second does not. Both are lazy, and both treat null as empty.

h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · Stations that change one item at a time: map and filter
x: map and filter are the operators you may know from Java's streams in java.util.stream, with one difference: here they run when items arrive, not when you call them. map(f) is the slicer: one item in, one item out, right away, on whatever thread delivered the item. Use it for quick, pure work, which only computes a new value from the item, such as turning a loaf number into a label, or cents into euros. filter(p) is the inspector who lifts burnt loaves off the belt: it keeps only the items that pass a test. filter also keeps the slips honest. A loaf it removes doesn't count against the packer's slip, so filter asks the source for another one. MapFilterDemo, in the Try it, keeps every third loaf, slices it, and takes two: Java Flux.range(1, 10) .doOnRequest(n -> System.out.println(" oven asked for " + n)) .filter(loaf -> loaf % 3 == 0) // only every third loaf has seeds .map(loaf -> "sliced loaf-" + loaf) .take(2) // we only want two .subscribe(s -> System.out.println("got " + s)); Kotlin Flux.range(1, 10) .doOnRequest { n -> println(" oven asked for $n") } .filter { loaf -> loaf % 3 == 0 } // only every third loaf has seeds .map { loaf -> "sliced loaf-$loaf" } .take(2) // we only want two .subscribe { s -> println("got $s") } doOnRequest is an operator that prints each request passing up through it, so we can watch the slip reach the oven: oven asked for 2 got sliced loaf-3 got sliced loaf-6 take(2) wrote one slip for 2, and the oven saw exactly that slip. Yet the oven sent loaves 1 to 6, because filter asked for a replacement each time it threw a loaf away. Now the most common map bug. Say the bakery has a slow icing machine, and icing.ice(cake) returns a Mono<String> that completes when the cake is iced: Java Flux<Mono<String>> iced = cakes.map(cake -> icing.ice(cake)); // Naive: a belt of unsigned forms Kotlin val iced: Flux<Mono<String>> = cakes.map { cake -> icing.ice(cake) } // Naive: a belt of unsigned forms The function returns a Mono, so map gives you a Flux<Mono<String>>: a belt that carries order forms instead of cakes. Remember the last lesson: a Mono that nobody subscribes to does nothing. So not one cake is iced. The compiler is happy, a test that only counts items is happy, and the icing machine never switches on. When your function returns a publisher, you need one of the flattening operators in the next sections. The type is your friend here. If you see Flux<Mono<T>>, you used map where you needed flatMap. Two smaller rules. In Reactor 3.8, a map function may not return null. In Java the stream fails with NullPointerException: The mapper [...] returned a null value., and in Kotlin the lambda doesn't even compile, thanks to Reactor's JSpecify annotations. Filter first, or use handle, which works like a map that may emit zero or one item for each input. And map must stay quick and must not block, because it runs on the thread that delivered the item. A slow database call inside map holds that thread for every single item. Lesson 6 of this track shows where blocking calls belong. map is for quick work that returns a value. If your function returns a Mono, map is the wrong station. So what is the right station, when every cake needs a trip to the icing machine? Count the slips a filter sends MapFilterDemo keeps every third loaf from 1 to 10, slices it, and takes 2. A doOnRequest prints what the oven is asked for. Predict how many requests the oven sees and which loaves print. In Java, predict what the second pipeline does with the null; in Kotlin, read the comment that says why that line can't be written. Run it. Then change take(2) to take(4) and run it again. Watch the demand they send upstream. */ public class MapFilterDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { Flux.range(1, 10) .doOnRequest(n -> System.out.println(" oven asked for " + n)) .filter(loaf -> loaf % 3 == 0) // only every third loaf has seeds .map(loaf -> "sliced loaf-" + loaf) .take(2) // we only want two .subscribe(s -> System.out.println("got " + s)); // Reactor 3.8: a mapper may not return null Flux.just("rye", "spelt") .map(flour -> flour.equals("rye") ? "dark bread" : null) .subscribe(s -> System.out.println("made " + s), e -> System.out.println("error: " + e)); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l03.MapFilterDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l03/MapFilterDemo.java MapFilterDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l03 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux /** map and filter are synchronous and work one item at a time. Watch the demand they send upstream. */ fun main() { Flux.range(1, 10) .doOnRequest { n -> println(" oven asked for $n") } .filter { loaf -> loaf % 3 == 0 } // only every third loaf has seeds .map { loaf -> "sliced loaf-$loaf" } .take(2) // we only want two .subscribe { s -> println("got $s") } // Reactor 3.8 marks its API with JSpecify nullness, so in Kotlin a null-returning mapper doesn't compile: // .map { flour -> if (flour == "rye") "dark bread" else null } // error: Return type mismatch: expected 'Any', actual 'String?'. // handle() is a map and a filter in one: emit when you have a value, skip otherwise. Flux.just("rye", "spelt") .handle<String> { flour, sink -> if (flour == "rye") sink.next("dark bread") } .subscribe({ s -> println("made $s") }, { e -> println("error: $e") }) } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l03.MapFilterDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l03/MapFilterDemo.kt The oven is asked for 2 once, yet it sends loaves 1 to 6, because filter asks for a replacement for each loaf it removes. You get sliced loaf-3 and sliced loaf-6. The Java version's second pipeline prints made dark bread, then error: java.lang.NullPointerException: The mapper [...] returned a null value.. The Kotlin version uses handle, so it prints only made dark bread: the compiler caught the null case instead. With take(4) the oven is asked for 4 and runs to 10, but only three loaves pass the filter, so you get three and the stream completes.

h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · flatMap sends many items out at once, and they come back in any order
x: flatMap emits in completion order; concatMap and flatMapSequential keep input order flatMap(f) takes a function that returns a publisher, called the inner publisher, and does three things with it: For each source item, it calls f and subscribes to the inner right away, without waiting for earlier inners to finish. It keeps up to concurrency inners subscribed at once. The default is 256. It merges all their items into one output, in the order they arrive. In the bakery, flatMap is the hatch to the icing room. Each cake goes through the hatch as soon as it arrives, several decorators work at once, and iced cakes come back out in whatever order they're finished. That last point is the one to remember: the output order follows finishing time, not input order. Reactor's Javadoc, the reference pages built from its source code, says flatMap "does not necessarily preserve original ordering", and with real calls of different speeds, it almost never does. Two facts about flatMap surprise people. First, flatMap does not create threads. This is where the icing-room picture breaks: flatMap hires no decorators. If the inner is synchronous, such as a Mono.fromCallable with nothing to move it elsewhere, the inners run one after another on the calling thread. FlatMapThreadsDemo, in the Try it, shows both cases: 1. synchronous inners: iced cake 1 on main iced cake 2 on main iced cake 3 on main 2. asynchronous inners (Mono.delay runs on Reactor's parallel scheduler): iced cake 3 on parallel-3 iced cake 2 on parallel-2 iced cake 1 on parallel-1 In part 1, everything ran on main, in order. In part 2, each inner was a Mono.delay, which waits on a timer and then finishes on one of Reactor's own threads. Cake 3 had the shortest wait, so it came out first. The concurrency came from the inners themselves: a timer, a non-blocking network call, or a blocking call moved to another thread with subscribeOn (lesson 6 of this track). flatMap only subscribes to several of them before the first one finishes. Second, concurrency is also demand. flatMap(f, 4) writes a first slip for 4 items, then a slip for 1 more each time an inner completes. That makes the concurrency argument a cap on calls in flight: Java Flux<String> iced = cakes.flatMap(cake -> icing.ice(cake), 4); // at most 4 cakes at the machine Kotlin // the lambda stays inside the parentheses when another argument follows it val iced: Flux<String> = cakes.flatMap({ cake -> icing.ice(cake) }, 4) // at most 4 cakes at the machine Part 3 of the demo prints the slips each operator sends to the source: flatMap(f) requests: 256 flatMap(f, 2) requests: 2 1 1 1 1 concatMap(f) requests: 1 1 1 1 1 1 Set the concurrency whenever the inner touches something shared. flatMap is generous by default: unless told otherwise, it sends 256 cakes to an icing machine with four nozzles, or 256 queries to a database that allows 20 connections. Pick the number from what the other side allows, not from a feeling. flatMap's default is 256 calls at once. Set the concurrency to what the other side can take. Each inner also gets a prefetch of 32: if an inner is a Flux, flatMap asks it for 32 items at a time. That rarely matters for Mono inners. One more behavior to know now: if any inner fails, flatMap cancels the others and the whole stream fails. Lesson 5 of this track shows how to keep an error inside one inner. So flatMap is fast, and it has no sense of order. Sometimes order is the whole point. Where does flatMap's concurrency come from? FlatMapThreadsDemo runs flatMap with synchronous inners, then with Mono.delay inners, and prints the thread for each result. Then it prints the slips flatMap and concatMap send to the source. Predict the threads and the order in parts 1 and 2. Predict the request numbers in part 3. Run it. Then change part 3's concurrency from 2 to 3, and predict the new request line. FlatMapThreadsDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l03; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.time.Duration; /** flatMap does not create threads. Its first request upstream is its concurrency. */ public class FlatMapThreadsDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("1. synchronous inners:"); Flux.range(1, 3) .flatMap(i -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> "iced cake " + i + " on " + Thread.currentThread().getName())) .doOnNext(s -> System.out.println(" " + s)) .blockLast(); System.out.println("2. asynchronous inners (Mono.delay runs on Reactor's parallel scheduler):"); Flux.range(1, 3) .flatMap(i -> Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(100L * (4 - i))) .map(t -> "iced cake " + i + " on " + Thread.currentThread().getName())) .doOnNext(s -> System.out.println(" " + s)) .blockLast(); System.out.println("3. what each operator asks the source for (inners take 10 ms each):"); demand("flatMap(f) ", Flux.range(1, 6).doOnRequest(n -> System.out.print(n + " ")).flatMap(FlatMapThreadsDemo::call)); demand("flatMap(f, 2)", Flux.range(1, 6).doOnRequest(n -> System.out.print(n + " ")).flatMap(FlatMapThreadsDemo::call, 2)); demand("concatMap(f) ", Flux.range(1, 6).doOnRequest(n -> System.out.print(n + " ")).concatMap(FlatMapThreadsDemo::call)); } static Mono<Integer> call(int i) { return Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(10)).thenReturn(i); } static void demand(String name, Flux<Integer> flux) { System.out.print(" " + name + " requests: "); flux.blockLast(); System.out.println(); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l03.FlatMapThreadsDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l03/FlatMapThreadsDemo.java FlatMapThreadsDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l03 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import java.time.Duration /** flatMap does not create threads. Part 2 prints cake 3 first (100 ms), then 2, then 1, on parallel-N threads that belong to Mono.delay. Part 3 prints 256 for plain flatMap, 2 1 1 1 1 for concurrency 2, and 1 1 1 1 1 1 for concatMap. With concurrency 3 you get 3 1 1 1: the first request is the cap, then one more per finished inner. Flux Javadoc source, reactor-core 3.8.x (flatMap, concatMap, flatMapSequential, switchMap) docs

h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · Putting the order back: concatMap and flatMapSequential
x: When order matters, you have two choices with very different costs. concatMap(f) is a single decorator who finishes one cake before taking the next. It asks the source for one item, waits for that item's inner to complete, then asks for the next. Output order is input order, and the total time is the sum of all the inner times. In Reactor 3.8, it doesn't fetch ahead from the source at all, which is why the last demo showed its slips of 1. flatMapSequential(f) is the icing room with a clerk at the exit. It subscribes to inners eagerly, like flatMap (concurrency 256, prefetch 32), but the clerk holds back results from later inners until all earlier inners have finished. Output order is input order, and the total time is about the time of the slowest inner. That speed has two costs. One is memory, since cakes that finish early wait in a buffer. The other is head-of-line blocking: one slow cake at the front holds back every cake behind it, even the finished ones. OrderingDemo, in the Try it, runs all three operators on the same input. The source emits 3, 1, 2 at once, and item i takes i x 100 ms. The figure below draws the result: flatMap -> [1, 2, 3] in about 300 ms concatMap -> [3, 1, 2] in about 600 ms flatMapSequential -> [3, 1, 2] in about 300 ms flatMap let the fastest item out first. concatMap kept the order and added up the times: 300, then 100, then 200. flatMapSequential kept the order at flatMap's speed, because items 1 and 2 finished early and waited for 3. Ordered output isn't the only reason to pick concatMap. Pick it when each step must start after the previous one has finished. A tall layer cake is the bakery's case. The second layer may only go on after the first has set, because it sits on top, and after a layer collapses, no more layers go on. flatMapSequential would report the layers in the right order while placing all four at the same moment, which is exactly what the cake can't take. Here is a short guide: You need Use Independent calls, any order flatMap(f, n) Output in input order, calls may overlap flatMapSequential(f, n) One at a time, each after the previous concatMap(f) Only the latest item matters switchMap(f) flatMapSequential orders the results, not the work. When each step must wait for the last, use concatMap. The last row of the table solves a different problem: work that a newer item makes pointless. Measure the three operators OrderingDemo runs the source 3, 1, 2 through all three operators, with real delays. Write down your prediction for each output and time, then run it. Change the source to Flux.just(1, 2, 3). Which operator's output changes, and which timing changes? OrderingDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l03; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.function.Function; /** Source 3, 1, 2. Item i takes i x 100 ms. Same input, three operators. */ public class OrderingDemo { static Mono<Integer> slowCall(int i) { return Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(i * 100L)).thenReturn(i); } public static void main(String[] args) { Flux.just(1).flatMap(i -> Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(1))).blockLast(); // warm up, so timings are fair run("flatMap ", src -> src.flatMap(OrderingDemo::slowCall)); run("concatMap ", src -> src.concatMap(OrderingDemo::slowCall)); run("flatMapSequential", src -> src.flatMapSequential(OrderingDemo::slowCall)); } static void run(String name, Function<Flux<Integer>, Flux<Integer>> operator) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); var out = operator.apply(Flux.just(3, 1, 2)).collectList().block(); long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%s -> %s in about %d ms%n", name, out, Math.round(ms / 100.0) * 100); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l03.OrderingDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l03/OrderingDemo.java OrderingDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l03 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import java.time.Duration import kotlin.math.roundToLong private fun slowCall(i: Int): Mono<Int> = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(i * 100L)).thenReturn(i) /** Source 3, 1, 2. Item i takes i x 100 ms. Same input, three operators. */ fun main() { Flux.just(1).flatMap { Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(1)) }.blockLast() // warm up, so timings are fair run("flatMap ") { src -> src.flatMap { slowCall(it) } } run("concatMap ") { src -> src.concatMap { slowCall(it) } } run("flatMapSequential") { src -> src.flatMapSequential { slowCall(it) } } } private fun run(name: String, operator: (Flux<Int>) -> Flux<Int>) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() val out = operator(Flux.just(3, 1, 2)).collectList().block() val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println("$name -> $out in about ${(ms / 100.0).roundToLong() * 100} ms") } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l03.OrderingDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l03/OrderingDemo.kt flatMap -> [1, 2, 3] in about 300 ms, concatMap -> [3, 1, 2] in about 600 ms, flatMapSequential -> [3, 1, 2] in about 300 ms, as in the figure. With source 1, 2, 3, all three print [1, 2, 3]: the input order now matches the finishing order, so flatMap looks ordered. That's why order bugs hide in tests where every fake call takes the same time. concatMap still takes 600 ms, and the other two still take 300 ms. The same three calls through three operators. Only flatMapSequential is both ordered and fast, and it pays with a buffer.

h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · When only the latest matters: switchMap cancels the old work
x: switchMap(f) is for streams where a new item makes the old work pointless. Each time the source emits, switchMap cancels the inner for the previous item and subscribes to a new one. Picture a customer on the bakery's website, choosing a cake size from a list. Each pick asks a price service for the price. The customer picks small, then medium 50 ms later, while the price for small is still on its way. With flatMap, both prices eventually arrive. If the small one is slower, it arrives last and replaces the medium one on screen, and the customer sees the price of a cake they no longer want. With switchMap, the request for the small price is cancelled the moment medium is picked, and its result can never reach the page: Java Flux<String> prices = sizePicks.switchMap(size -> priceService.priceOf(size)); Kotlin val prices: Flux<String> = sizePicks.switchMap { size -> priceService.priceOf(size) } On the bakery line, it's the customer who keeps changing their mind, and a decorator who bins the half-iced cake each time. SwitchMapDemo, in the Try it, does the same with a search box. The customer types cr, then cro 100 ms later, and each prefix starts a lookup that sends a suggestion every 60 ms: show cr-match0 cancelled lookup for cr show cro-match0 show cro-match1 show cro-match2 all shown: [cr-match0, cro-match0, cro-match1, cro-match2] The cr lookup showed one suggestion and was cancelled when cro arrived. No stale cr suggestion appeared after that. Cancellation travels upstream through the inner, so a reactive web client can abort the request it was making, and a Flux.interval inside stops ticking. Here the bakery picture breaks once more. A decorator who stops icing really stops. A service on another computer may finish its work anyway; cancelling only promises that you stop listening. A few details. switchMap requests an unbounded amount from its source, so it applies no backpressure upstream: every pick is seen, and older ones are dropped by cancelling. The stream completes when the source has completed and the last inner has completed. Search as you type, "recompute when the settings change" and "show the latest stock level" all have this shape. When a newer item makes the older work pointless, switchMap cancels it for you. Kotlin's own Flow has the same operator under another name: flatMapLatest, or mapLatest when the block returns a single value. The comparison below shows how the other three operators map onto Flow. Cancel a stale lookup SwitchMapDemo plays a customer typing in the bakery's search box: cr at 100 ms, then cro at 200 ms. Each prefix starts a lookup that sends a suggestion every 60 ms, three in total. Predict which suggestions are shown, and when the first lookup is cancelled. Run it. Replace switchMap with flatMap and run it again. SwitchMapDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l03; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import java.time.Duration; /** A search box on the bakery's website: each new prefix cancels the lookup for the previous one. */ public class SwitchMapDemo { // a lookup that streams up to three suggestions, one every 60 ms static Flux<String> suggestions(String prefix) { return Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(60)) .map(n -> prefix + "-match" + n) .take(3) .doOnCancel(() -> System.out.println(" cancelled lookup for " + prefix)); } public static void main(String[] args) { Flux<String> typed = Flux.just("cr", "cro").delayElements(Duration.ofMillis(100)); // at 100 ms and 200 ms var shown = typed .switchMap(SwitchMapDemo::suggestions) .doOnNext(s -> System.out.println("show " + s)) .collectList() .block(); System.out.println("all shown: " + shown); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l03.SwitchMapDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l03/SwitchMapDemo.java SwitchMapDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l03 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import java.time.Duration // a lookup that streams up to three suggestions, one every 60 ms private fun suggestions(prefix: String): Flux<String> = Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(60)) .map { n -> "$prefix-match$n" } .take(3) .doOnCancel { println(" cancelled lookup for $prefix") } /** A search box on the bakery's website: each new prefix cancels the lookup for the previous one. */ fun main() { val typed = Flux.just("cr", "cro").delayElements(Duration.ofMillis(100)) // at 100 ms and 200 ms val shown = typed .switchMap { prefix -> suggestions(prefix) } .doOnNext { s -> println("show $s") } .collectList() .block() println("all shown: $shown") } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l03.SwitchMapDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l03/SwitchMapDemo.kt You see show cr-match0 (at about 160 ms), then cancelled lookup for cr when cro arrives at 200 ms, then the three cro suggestions: [cr-match0, cro-match0, cro-match1, cro-match2]. With flatMap nothing is cancelled, and the two lookups interleave: [cr-match0, cr-match1, cro-match0, cr-match2, cro-match1, cro-match2]. A stale cr suggestion shows up after the customer has already typed cro, which is the race that switchMap prevents. Kotlin docs: Asynchronous Flow (flattening flows) docs

h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · Java and Kotlin
x: The four flattening operators in Java and Kotlin BakeryStations.java // any order, at most 4 cakes at the icing machine Flux<String> iced = cakes.flatMap(cake -> icing.ice(cake), 4); // one at a time, each after the previous one completes Flux<String> stacked = layers.concatMap(layer -> stacker.place(layer)); // overlapping calls, output in input order Flux<String> report = ingredients.flatMapSequential(item -> supplier.stockOf(item), 4); // latest wins: a new pick cancels the previous price Flux<String> prices = sizePicks.switchMap(size -> priceService.priceOf(size)); BakeryStations.kt // any order, at most 4 cakes at the icing machine val iced = cakes.flatMap({ cake -> icing.ice(cake) }, 4) // one at a time, each after the previous one completes val stacked = layers.concatMap { layer -> stacker.place(layer) } // overlapping calls, output in input order val report = ingredients.flatMapSequential({ item -> supplier.stockOf(item) }, 4) // latest wins: a new pick cancels the previous price val prices = sizePicks.switchMap { size -> priceService.priceOf(size) } Same operators, two syntax details. In Kotlin a lambda can only trail outside the parentheses when it is the last argument, so flatMap({ ... }, 4) keeps it inside. And Kotlin lambdas adapt to Reactor's Function<? super T, Publisher<? extends V>> parameter without fuss, so the switchMap typing problem the lab hints at in Java doesn't arise. The bigger difference is with Kotlin's own streams. In Kotlin's Flow the default is one at a time: a map whose block suspends waits for each call, so it behaves like concatMap. You ask for concurrency with flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4), whose default is 16 rather than Reactor's 256. flatMapLatest and mapLatest are Flow's switchMap, and there is no flatMapSequential. In kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 those Flow operators still need @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class). FlowOperators.kt in the demo folder runs the same 3, 1, 2 example with Flow (-Pmain=workbench.reactive.l03.FlowOperatorsKt).

h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · Worked example
x: Fix a nightly job that floods the supplier Every night the bakery's program checks the stock of each of its 5,000 ingredients with the supplier's web service. The supplier allows 10 calls at once from each customer. Last night the job got hundreds of answers saying 429 Too Many Requests, the web's way of saying "slow down". Read the pipeline. Flux<StockRow> nightlyCheck(Flux<String> ingredients) { return ingredients .flatMap(item -> supplier.stockOf(item)) // Mono<Stock>, about 120 ms each .map(StockRow::from); } fun nightlyCheck(ingredients: Flux<String>): Flux<StockRow> = ingredients .flatMap { item -> supplier.stockOf(item) } // Mono<Stock>, about 120 ms each .map { StockRow.from(it) } flatMap with no concurrency argument subscribes to up to 256 inners at once, and its first slip to the source asks for 256. With 5,000 ingredients, the job keeps about 256 calls in flight the whole time. The supplier allows 10. Cap the calls in flight at the supplier's limit. By Little's law, which says calls in flight equal calls per second times the time per call, 10 calls at 120 ms each finish at most 10 / 0.12 s, about 83 calls a second. So 5,000 ingredients take about a minute. That's the honest speed this supplier allows. return ingredients .flatMap(item -> supplier.stockOf(item), 10) // 1. never more than 10 in flight .map(StockRow::from); ingredients .flatMap({ item -> supplier.stockOf(item) }, 10) // 1. never more than 10 in flight .map { StockRow.from(it) } The owner then asks for the report in the same order as the ingredient list, so it lines up with yesterday's. Switching to concatMap would cut the speed to one call at a time, about 8 a second, or ten minutes for the list. flatMapSequential keeps the cap of 10 and restores the order, at the cost of buffering results that finish early. return ingredients .flatMapSequential(item -> supplier.stockOf(item), 10) // 2. same cap, list order .map(StockRow::from); ingredients .flatMapSequential({ item -> supplier.stockOf(item) }, 10) // 2. same cap, list order .map { StockRow.from(it) }

h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · Lab
x: Pick the right operator for three bakery stations labs/reactive/src/main/java/workbench/reactive/l03/CakeFlows.java ./gradlew :reactive:test --tests 'workbench.reactive.l03.*' Read the Javadoc on each of the three methods in CakeFlows. Each body is one line. Decide on the operator before you write anything. iceAll: any order, at most 4 cakes at the icing machine, and all 4 nozzles in use. stackLayers: each layer only after the one below it has set, results in stacking order, and nothing placed after a failure. latestPrices: only the most recent pick matters; a price still on its way must be cancelled when the customer picks again. Run the tests. They use StepVerifier.withVirtualTime, a test clock that skips the waits, so the 100 ms delays take no real time. Read CakeFlowsTest to see how it counts calls in flight and cancellations. If a test says Expecting AtomicInteger(12) to have value: 4, you used flatMap without its concurrency argument. flatMapSequential gets the order right for stackLayers, but places all four layers at once; the in-flight check catches it. If sizePicks.switchMap(priceService) doesn't compile, pass a lambda: switchMap(size -> priceService.apply(size)). switchMap declares its parameter as Function<? super T, Publisher<? extends V>>, and a Function<String, Mono<String>> variable is not that type, although a lambda or a method reference can be. All four tests in CakeFlowsTest pass. By the end you can choose between map, flatMap, concatMap, flatMapSequential and switchMap from what a pipeline needs (order, one at a time, a cap on calls in flight, latest wins), and prove the choice with a virtual-time test.
