h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · Quiz
x: You need the delivery time for each of 10,000 orders. The delivery service allows 20 calls at once, and the output order doesn't matter. Which line fits? orders.map(o -> delivery.timeFor(o)) orders.concatMap(o -> delivery.timeFor(o)) orders.flatMap(o -> delivery.timeFor(o), 20) orders.switchMap(o -> delivery.timeFor(o)) flatMap with concurrency 20 keeps exactly as many calls in flight as the service allows. map would give a Flux<Mono<...>> and make no calls. concatMap is correct but makes one call at a time, and switchMap would cancel every lookup but the last. orderBook.status(id) returns Mono<String>. What happens when you subscribe to ids.map(id -> orderBook.status(id))? Each status is fetched, one at a time You receive one Mono<String> per id, and no call is made unless something subscribes to those Monos It doesn't compile All statuses are fetched at once map passes each returned Mono along as an item, giving Flux<Mono<String>>. A Mono is an order form; nobody subscribes to these, so nothing runs. flatMap (or concatMap) is what subscribes to the inner publishers. The layers of a tall cake must be placed one at a time, each after the one below has set. A teammate proposes flatMapSequential because "it keeps the order". What is wrong with that? Nothing, it is the right choice It drops layers that finish out of order It places all the layers at once and only reorders the results It cannot handle errors flatMapSequential subscribes to its inners eagerly, so every layer is placed at the same moment. Only the output is reordered. concatMap is the operator that waits for each inner to complete before subscribing to the next. A switchMap inner is still running when the source emits a new item. What happens to that inner? It is cancelled, and its results never reach the output It finishes, and its results are emitted after the new inner's It is paused until the new inner completes switchMap waits for it before starting the new inner switchMap cancels the current inner and switches to a new one for each source item. That stops a slow, stale result from replacing a newer one, which is what can happen with flatMap. From "CompletableFuture: composing async steps": which CompletableFuture method plays the same role as Reactor's flatMap for one async step? thenApply thenAccept thenCombine thenCompose thenCompose takes a function that returns another CompletableFuture and flattens it, just as flatMap subscribes to the publisher your function returns. thenApply is like map: given a function that returns a future, it produces a CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>>.

h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · Key terms
x: Inner publisher The Mono or Flux your function returns inside flatMap, concatMap or switchMap. Flattening Subscribing to inner publishers and merging their items into one output stream. Concurrency (flatMap) The most inners flatMap keeps subscribed at once, and its first request upstream. Prefetch How many items an operator requests ahead from a source, so they are ready when needed. Head-of-line blocking One slow item at the front holds back items behind it that are already done. Virtual time A fake clock in tests (StepVerifier.withVirtualTime) that you move forward by hand, so delays take no real time. What is flatMap's default concurrency in Reactor? 256 inners at once (and a prefetch of 32 per inner). Its first request to the source is also 256. flatMap(f, 4): what does it request from the source? 4 at first, then 1 more each time an inner completes. So at most 4 inners are in flight. Does flatMap run inners on several threads? No. It only subscribes to several at once. The parallel work comes from inners that are themselves asynchronous (non-blocking I/O, Mono.delay, subscribeOn). Source 3, 1, 2; item i takes i x 100 ms. What does concatMap emit, and when does it finish? [3, 1, 2] at 600 ms: one at a time, in order. What does flatMapSequential trade for ordered output at flatMap speed? Memory: results that finish early wait in a buffer until all earlier inners are done (and a slow first item holds back the rest). When does switchMap cancel an inner? As soon as the source emits a new item. Only the latest item's inner is kept. What is the Kotlin Flow version of Reactor's switchMap? flatMapLatest, or mapLatest when the block returns one value.

h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · Go deeper
x: Order within a group, concurrency across groups. The layers of each cake must be placed in order, but different cakes can be worked on at the same time. The usual shape is groupBy plus concatMap inside a flatMap: Java layers.groupBy(Layer::cakeId) .flatMap(cake -> cake.concatMap(stacker::place), 512) Kotlin layers.groupBy { it.cakeId } .flatMap({ cake -> cake.concatMap { stacker.place(it) } }, 512) There is a trap. Each group stays open until the source completes, and flatMap only drains as many groups as its concurrency allows. The groupBy Javadoc says the concurrency of the subscriber "should be greater than or equal to the number of groups created". In a measured run, Flux.range(0, 1000).groupBy(i -> i % 300).flatMap(g -> g.reduce(0, Integer::sum), 10) simply hung; with concurrency 300 it completed. If the number of cakes has no upper limit, group by cakeId.hashCode() % 32 instead and use concurrency 32, so there are never more than 32 groups. Delaying errors. By default an error in any inner ends the whole stream. flatMapDelayError(f, concurrency, prefetch) and concatMapDelayError(f) let the other inners finish and report the error at the end. Use them for batch jobs where partial results are still useful, then decide what to do with the error. flatMapIterable. When your function returns a List that is already in memory, flatMapIterable(order -> order.items()) flattens it without creating inner publishers. handle. handle((item, sink) -> { if (ok(item)) sink.next(convert(item)); }) is a map and a filter in one step, and it lets you skip an item instead of returning null.

h: Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest · Four ways to join two belts, starting with zip, which pairs by position
x: Two belts, four ways to join them: merge passes items as they arrive, concat starts the next belt after the bell, zip pairs by position and ships nothing when a belt is empty, combineLatest recomputes on every change Every combining operator answers two questions: when does it subscribe to each source, and when does something come out? Here are the four from the opening in those terms. zip subscribes to all its sources at once and emits only when it has one item from each. merge subscribes to all at once and emits each item as it arrives. concat subscribes to the next source only after the previous one has completed. combineLatest subscribes to all at once and emits whenever any source changes. We'll take them in that order, starting with the gift boxes. Flux.zip(a, b) waits until every source has emitted one item, combines those items, and repeats. It pairs by position, first with first and second with second, like one loaf and one jar in each gift box. It completes as soon as any source completes, so the extra items of a longer source are left over. Flux.zip(Flux.just(1, 2, 3), Flux.just("a", "b")) gives [[1,a], [2,b]], and the 3 is never used. In everyday code you'll use Mono.zip far more often, for fan-out: starting several independent calls at once and combining their results. The bakery's order page needs three lookups for a cake quote, each from a different part of the program: Java Mono<Quote> quote = Mono.zip(prices.forCake(cake), delivery.feeTo(address), tax.rateFor(address)) .map(t -> new Quote(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3())); Kotlin val quote: Mono<Quote> = Mono.zip(prices.forCake(cake), delivery.feeTo(address), tax.rateFor(address)) .map { t -> Quote(t.t1, t.t2, t.t3) } Mono.zip subscribes to all of its sources at once. If the price takes 100 ms, the delivery fee 300 ms and the tax rate 200 ms, the quote is ready after 300 ms, not 600. The result is a tuple, a small object that holds one value per source, read with getT1(), getT2() and so on. There are typed versions for up to eight sources. If any source fails, the zip fails and cancels the others. That's usually what you want. The surprise is the other ending. The Mono.zip Javadoc, Reactor's reference page for the method, says it plainly: an "empty completion of any source will cause other sources to be cancelled and the resulting Mono to immediately ... complete". No error, no value. ZipDemo, in the Try it, zips a price, a delivery fee and a discount, for a customer who has no discount. So the discount Mono completes empty: price lookup cancelled Mono.zip result: null The price lookup was cancelled, and doOnSuccess received null, which here means "completed empty". No quote, no error, no complaint. One belt arrived empty, so the quiet packer shipped no box. A web page would show an empty answer, block() would return null, and the logs would show nothing at all. This is where the gift-box picture breaks. A real packer with no jam would say "we're out of jam". Mono.zip just completes. So decide what "empty" means for each source, and say it in code. Either it has a sensible default, as a missing discount means no discount, or it's a real error, as a cake must have a price: Java Mono<BigDecimal> safeDiscount = discount.defaultIfEmpty(BigDecimal.ZERO); // empty means "no discount" Mono<BigDecimal> safePrice = price.switchIfEmpty( Mono.error(() -> new IllegalStateException("missing price"))); // empty is an error Kotlin val safeDiscount = discount.defaultIfEmpty(BigDecimal.ZERO) // empty means "no discount" val safePrice = price.switchIfEmpty( Mono.error { IllegalStateException("missing price") }) // empty is an error The demo runs both, on the discount: with defaultIfEmpty: [24.00,3.50,0.00] price lookup cancelled with switchIfEmpty: missing discount Mono.zip turns one empty source into an empty result. Say what empty means on every source. One more consequence: a Mono<Void> is always empty, so it can never take part in a zip. The last section shows the tool for that. zip waits for one item from each belt. The next two operators either don't wait at all, or wait for a whole belt. Watch a quote disappear ZipDemo zips two Fluxes of different lengths. Then it zips three Monos where the discount is empty, and does it again with defaultIfEmpty and with switchIfEmpty on the discount. Predict each line, including whether the slow price lookup finishes or is cancelled. Run it. Then change the empty discount to Mono.just("2.00") and predict how long the first zip takes. ZipDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l04; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.time.Duration; /** zip pairs by position. Mono.zip with an empty source completes empty, and cancels the others. */ public class ZipDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Flux.zip: " + Flux.zip(Flux.just(1, 2, 3), Flux.just("a", "b")).collectList().block()); Mono<String> price = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(200)).thenReturn("24.00") .doOnCancel(() -> System.out.println(" price lookup cancelled")); Mono<String> deliveryFee = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(100)).thenReturn("3.50"); Mono<String> discount = Mono.empty(); // this customer has no discount Mono.zip(price, deliveryFee, discount) .doOnSuccess(t -> System.out.println("Mono.zip result: " + t)) // null means "completed empty" .block(); Mono.zip(price, deliveryFee, discount.defaultIfEmpty("0.00")) .doOnSuccess(t -> System.out.println("with defaultIfEmpty: " + t)) .block(); try { Mono.zip(price, deliveryFee, discount.switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new IllegalStateException("missing discount")))) .block(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("with switchIfEmpty: " + e.getMessage()); } } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l04.ZipDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l04/ZipDemo.java ZipDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l04 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import java.time.Duration /** zip pairs by position. Mono.zip with an empty source completes empty, and cancels the others. */ fun main() { println("Flux.zip: " + Flux.zip(Flux.just(1, 2, 3), Flux.just("a", "b")).collectList().block()) val price: Mono<String> = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(200)).thenReturn("24.00") .doOnCancel { println(" price lookup cancelled") } val deliveryFee: Mono<String> = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(100)).thenReturn("3.50") val discount: Mono<String> = Mono.empty() // this customer has no discount Mono.zip(price, deliveryFee, discount) .doOnSuccess { t -> println("Mono.zip result: $t") } // null means "completed empty" .block() Mono.zip(price, deliveryFee, discount.defaultIfEmpty("0.00")) .doOnSuccess { t -> println("with defaultIfEmpty: $t") } .block() try { Mono.zip(price, deliveryFee, discount.switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(IllegalStateException("missing discount")))) .block() } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("with switchIfEmpty: ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l04.ZipDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l04/ZipDemo.kt Flux.zip: [[1,a], [2,b]]. The plain Mono.zip prints price lookup cancelled and Mono.zip result: null: doOnSuccess got no value, because the zip completed empty. defaultIfEmpty gives [24.00,3.50,0.00] after about 200 ms, the time of the slowest lookup. switchIfEmpty cancels the price lookup again and prints with switchIfEmpty: missing discount, so now the problem is visible. With a real discount, every zip gets all three values after about 200 ms. The last one then prints nothing, because it only prints when it catches an error. Mono Javadoc source, reactor-core 3.8.x (zip, zipDelayError, when, firstWithValue) docs

h: Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest · Mix or take turns: merge and concat
x: Flux.merge(a, b) subscribes to every source at once and passes items on as they arrive, from whichever source has one. On the bakery line, it's two belts feeding one: loaves join in the order they arrive. It completes when all sources have completed, and by default the first error from any source ends it and cancels the rest. Flux.concat(a, b) subscribes to b only after a has completed. The output is all of a, then all of b: the first belt runs until its end-of-day bell rings, and only then is the second switched on. That makes concat the right tool when the second source must not start early: orders already collected before the slow search for those still waiting, saved results before fresh ones, the first page before the rest. The bakery's kitchen has a screen that shows new orders from two places, the shop counter and the website. At closing time it prints a day sheet. Here are both: Java Flux<String> screen = Flux.merge(counterOrders, webOrders); // both at once, as they arrive Flux<String> daySheet = Flux.concat(collected, waiting); // waiting only after collected completes Kotlin val screen: Flux<String> = Flux.merge(counterOrders, webOrders) // both at once, as they arrive val daySheet: Flux<String> = Flux.concat(collected, waiting) // waiting only after collected completes The trap with concat is a first source that never completes. A live stream of counter orders never sends onComplete, so Flux.concat(counterOrders, webOrders) never subscribes to the web orders at all. They wait for a bell that never rings. If the inputs are endless, you want merge. Flux.mergeSequential(a, b) sits in between. It subscribes to all its sources at once, like merge, but emits them source by source, like concat, and buffers what arrives early. It's the combining twin of flatMapSequential from the last lesson. MergeConcatDemo, in the Try it, makes counter orders every 30 ms and web orders every 40 ms, three of each, and prints when each source is subscribed. One run on this busy machine: merge: [ 8 ms] counter subscribed [ 11 ms] web subscribed [counter-0, web-0, counter-1, web-1, counter-2, web-2], done at about 130 ms concat: [ 0 ms] counter subscribed [ 92 ms] web subscribed [counter-0, counter-1, counter-2, web-0, web-1, web-2], done at about 210 ms mergeSequential: [ 3 ms] counter subscribed [ 3 ms] web subscribed [counter-0, counter-1, counter-2, web-0, web-1, web-2], done at about 120 ms merge subscribed to both at once and mixed them by time. concat subscribed to the web orders only at 92 ms, when the counter source completed. It finished late, because the web source starts its own 40 ms clock only when it is subscribed. mergeSequential gave concat's order at merge's speed. It received web-0 and web-1 early, held them while the counter orders went out, and released both the moment the counter source completed. The figure below draws all three on one clock. concat waits for each source to complete. Behind an endless source, the next one never starts. merge and concat pass items through unchanged. Sometimes you want a new value, made from the latest item on each belt. Three ways to join two order feeds MergeConcatDemo makes counter orders every 30 ms and web orders every 40 ms, three of each, and prints when each source is subscribed. For each combinator, predict when the web source is subscribed, the output order and the total time. Run it. h: Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest · Recompute on every change: combineLatest
x: Flux.combineLatest(a, b, f) waits until every source has emitted at least once. After that, each new item from any source is combined with the most recent item from each of the others. Its Javadoc warns that elements "can and will be passed to the combinator multiple times", because the latest value stays in use until it is replaced. On the bakery wall, it's the price board. The board shows a cake's price, its weight times the price per kilogram. The customer can change the weight on the order page, the owner can change the price per kilogram, and the board shows a new total whenever either one changes: Java Flux<BigDecimal> shown = Flux.combineLatest(weightsInKg, pricesPerKg, BigDecimal::multiply); Flux<Bill> bills = orders.withLatestFrom(pricesPerKg, Order::billAt); // only orders trigger Kotlin val shown: Flux<BigDecimal> = Flux.combineLatest(weightsInKg, pricesPerKg) { w, p -> w.multiply(p) } val bills: Flux<Bill> = orders.withLatestFrom(pricesPerKg) { o, p -> o.billAt(p) } // only orders trigger CombineLatestDemo, in the Try it, runs zip and combineLatest on the same timeline. The weight is 1.5 kg at 0 ms and 2.0 kg at 300 ms. The price per kilogram is 20.00 at 100 ms, 22.00 at 200 ms and 21.00 at 400 ms: zip: [30.000, 44.000] combineLatest: [30.000, 33.000, 44.000, 42.000] zip paired by position, as gift boxes do: the first weight with the first price, and the second weight with the second price. So 2.0 kg was multiplied by 22.00, though the price had moved to 21.00 by the end, and the change at 200 ms never showed. combineLatest showed every state the inputs passed through: 1.5 x 20.00, then 1.5 x 22.00, then 2.0 x 22.00, then 2.0 x 21.00. That's what a price board should do. (The three decimal places come from BigDecimal, which keeps every digit when it multiplies a number with one decimal place by a number with two.) Two details. combineLatest stays silent until every source has emitted once, so an input that might never emit needs a starting value, such as pricesPerKg.startWith(listPrice). And when only one side should trigger output, use withLatestFrom, from the second line above. Each order is billed at the price that is current when the order arrives, and a price change on its own emits nothing. combineLatest shows every change. zip shows only matched pairs. We now have four combinators and a few look-alikes. The last section puts them side by side, and looks at what happens when one source fails. zip versus combineLatest CombineLatestDemo multiplies a cake's weight by the price per kilogram, with zip and with combineLatest, on the timeline from the section. Write down both outputs before you run it. Run it. Then swap combineLatest for weights().withLatestFrom(pricesPerKg(), ...) (keep the multiply) and predict the output. CombineLatestDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l04; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.time.Duration; /** A cake's weight and the price per kilogram change at different times. zip vs combineLatest. */ public class CombineLatestDemo { static Flux<BigDecimal> weights() { // 1.5 kg at 0 ms, 2.0 kg at 300 ms return Flux.concat(Mono.just(new BigDecimal("1.5")), Mono.just(new BigDecimal("2.0")).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(300))); } static Flux<BigDecimal> pricesPerKg() { // 20.00 at 100 ms, 22.00 at 200 ms, 21.00 at 400 ms return Flux.just("20.00", "22.00", "21.00").map(BigDecimal::new) .zipWith(Flux.just(100L, 100L, 200L), (price, wait) -> Mono.just(price).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(wait))) .concatMap(m -> m); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("zip: " + Flux.zip(weights(), pricesPerKg(), BigDecimal::multiply).collectList().block()); System.out.println("combineLatest: " + Flux.combineLatest(weights(), pricesPerKg(), BigDecimal::multiply).collectList().block()); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l04.CombineLatestDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l04/CombineLatestDemo.java CombineLatestDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l04 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import java.math.BigDecimal import java.time.Duration // 1.5 kg at 0 ms, 2.0 kg at 300 ms private fun weights(): Flux<BigDecimal> = Flux.concat(Mono.just(BigDecimal("1.5")), Mono.just(BigDecimal("2.0")).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(300))) // 20.00 at 100 ms, 22.00 at 200 ms, 21.00 at 400 ms private fun pricesPerKg(): Flux<BigDecimal> = Flux.just("20.00", "22.00", "21.00").map { BigDecimal(it) } .zipWith(Flux.just(100L, 100L, 200L)) { price, wait -> Mono.just(price).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(wait)) } .concatMap { it } /** A cake's weight and the price per kilogram change at different times. zip vs combineLatest. */ fun main() { println("zip: " + Flux.zip(weights(), pricesPerKg()) { w, p -> w.multiply(p) }.collectList().block()) println("combineLatest: " + Flux.combineLatest(weights(), pricesPerKg()) { w, p -> w.multiply(p) }.collectList().block()) } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l04.CombineLatestDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l04/CombineLatestDemo.kt zip: [30.000, 44.000] and combineLatest: [30.000, 33.000, 44.000, 42.000]. With withLatestFrom, only the weights trigger output. The first weight arrives at 0 ms, before any price exists, so it is dropped. The second weight (300 ms) uses the latest price, 22.00, which gives [44.000].

h: Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest · Choosing a combinator, and what errors do
x: Most combining questions come down to this table: You want Use One result from several independent lookups Mono.zip, with switchIfEmpty or defaultIfEmpty on each source Items from several streams, as they arrive Flux.merge One stream after another, the next one started late Flux.concat Several streams started together, output stream by stream Flux.mergeSequential Item-by-item pairs Flux.zip A value recomputed from the latest of every input Flux.combineLatest Each item of one stream, with the latest of another withLatestFrom Wait for several jobs that return Mono<Void> Mono.when The first of several sources to produce a value Mono.firstWithValue Mono.when(a, b) exists because Mono.zip and Mono<Void> don't mix: a Mono<Void> always completes empty, so zipping it completes the whole zip empty. Mono.when(orderBook.save(order), receipts.print(order)).then(Mono.just(ticket)) waits for both jobs to finish, then carries on with the ticket. Mono.firstWithValue(millA.flourPrice(), millB.flourPrice()) asks two flour mills for a price, takes the first answer that arrives, and cancels the slower call. Empty sources are skipped. This is called a hedged request. It trades extra work for the mills for a faster answer, so keep it for calls that are cheap for the other side. Every combinator in the table gives up at the first error: the first failure cancels the other sources. Each has a DelayError version, such as Mono.zipDelayError, Flux.mergeDelayError and Flux.concatDelayError, that lets the other sources finish and reports the error at the end. Use those when partial work is still useful, such as a nightly job that should process every file before it reports the bad one. The DelayError versions treat empty differently too: Mono.zipDelayError waits for the other sources to finish before it completes empty, instead of cancelling them. The first error ends every combinator here. Use a DelayError version when the rest is still worth finishing. If a combinator surprises you, ask the two questions from the start of this lesson. When does it subscribe to each source? And what does it do when a source completes early or empty? Those two answers explain every row of the table. Quick check: Mono.zip(orderBook.save(order), prices.forCake(cake)), where the save is a Mono<Void> that completes after 20 ms and the price takes 100 ms. What does the zip emit, when, and what happens to the price lookup? (It completes empty at about 20 ms, because the save completed with no value, and it cancels the price lookup that is still in flight. A run here printed null at 22 ms. orderBook.save(order).then(prices.forCake(cake)) gives you the price after the save.) h: Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest · Java and Kotlin
x: Fan-out with Mono.zip and Mono.when in Java and Kotlin OrderPage.java // three lookups at once; ready when the slowest one is Mono<Quote> quote = Mono.zip( prices.forCake(cake).switchIfEmpty(missing("price")), delivery.feeTo(address).switchIfEmpty(missing("delivery fee")), tax.rateFor(address).switchIfEmpty(missing("tax rate"))) .map(t -> new Quote(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3())); // three jobs that return Mono<Void>: zip would complete empty Mono<String> done = Mono.when(orderBook.save(order), receipts.print(order), screen.show(order)) .then(Mono.just(ticket)); OrderPage.kt // three lookups at once; ready when the slowest one is val quote: Mono<Quote> = Mono.zip( prices.forCake(cake).switchIfEmpty(missing("price")), delivery.feeTo(address).switchIfEmpty(missing("delivery fee")), tax.rateFor(address).switchIfEmpty(missing("tax rate"))) .map { t -> Quote(t.t1, t.t2, t.t3) } // `when` is a Kotlin keyword, so the method name needs backticks val done: Mono<String> = Mono.`when`(orderBook.save(order), receipts.print(order), screen.show(order)) .then(Mono.just(ticket)) The Reactor calls are the same. In Kotlin, tuple getters read as properties (t.t1), and core Reactor has no destructuring for tuples. when is a keyword in Kotlin, so Mono.when has to be written with backticks. Kotlin's own fan-out looks different: inside coroutineScope { } you start each call with async { } and then await() them. The Reactor bridge awaitSingleOrNull() turns an empty Mono into null, which the compiler then makes you handle. That makes the empty case hard to forget, while Mono.zip lets you forget it. The coroutines track covers async.

h: Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest · Quiz
x: Mono.zip(price, deliveryFee): the price lookup fails after 50 ms, and the delivery fee would take 2 seconds. What happens? The zip waits 2 seconds, then fails The zip fails at about 50 ms and cancels the delivery-fee call The zip emits the delivery fee with a null price The zip calls the price lookup again Combinators give up at the first error: it ends the zip and cancels the other sources. Waiting for the others is what Mono.zipDelayError does. Nothing is tried again unless you add retry (lesson 5 of this track). The end-of-day sheet must show collected orders, then waiting ones. The search for waiting orders is slow and must not start until the collected list is complete. Which line fits? Flux.merge(collected, waiting) Flux.mergeSequential(collected, waiting) Flux.concat(collected, waiting) Flux.zip(collected, waiting) concat subscribes to waiting only after collected completes. mergeSequential gives the same output order but subscribes to both at once, so the slow search starts early. merge mixes them, and zip pairs orders that have nothing to do with each other. Counter orders and web orders are two endless streams. The kitchen screen uses Flux.concat(counterOrders, webOrders). What does it show? Only counter orders, forever Counter and web orders, mixed by arrival Nothing until both streams complete Web orders first, because there are fewer of them concat waits for the first source to complete before it subscribes to the second, and an endless stream never completes. The web stream is never subscribed. merge is the combinator for live feeds. Weights: 1.5 kg at 0 ms, 2.0 kg at 300 ms. Prices per kilogram: 20.00 at 100 ms, 22.00 at 200 ms. What does Flux.combineLatest(weights, prices, BigDecimal::multiply) emit? 30, 44 30, 33, 44 30, 33 40, 44 Nothing until both have emitted (100 ms: 1.5 x 20.00 = 30). Then every change from either side emits again with the latest of the other: the price change at 200 ms gives 1.5 x 22.00 = 33, and the weight change at 300 ms gives 2.0 x 22.00 = 44. zip would give only 30, 44. From "CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out": you fan out three calls with CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b, c), and a fails at once. When does the allOf future complete? At once, exceptionally, and it cancels b and c Normally, and you have to check each future yourself Never, because one future failed Exceptionally, but only after b and c have also completed allOf completes when all of the given futures complete, and exceptionally if any of them did. It doesn't cancel the others. That's the opposite of Mono.zip, which fails at the first error and cancels the remaining sources.

h: Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest · Key terms
x: Fan-out Starting several independent calls at once and combining their results. zip Combines one item from each source, position by position; completes when any source completes. merge Subscribes to all sources at once and emits their items in arrival order. concat Subscribes to each source only after the previous one has completed. combineLatest Emits a new combination whenever any source emits, using the latest item of each. DelayError version A version of a combinator that lets the other sources finish before it reports an error. What does Mono.zip do when one of its sources completes empty? It completes empty right away (no value, no error) and cancels the other sources. How do you make an empty source fail inside a Mono.zip? Put .switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(...)) on that source before zipping it (or defaultIfEmpty(x) if there is a sensible default). merge vs concat: when is the second source subscribed? merge: at once, together with the first. concat: only after the first source completes. Flux.concat(endless, other): what happens to other? It is never subscribed, because endless never completes. When does combineLatest emit? Once every source has emitted at least once, and then on every new item from any source, combined with the latest of the others. Why can't you Mono.zip a Mono<Void>? It always completes empty, so the zip completes empty. Use Mono.when(...) to wait for jobs like that, then .then(...).

h: Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest · Go deeper
x: Zip in a chain. mono.zipWith(other) zips two Monos without the static call. Mono.zipWhen(value -> otherCall(value)) runs the second call after the first and gives you both results. That's handy when the second lookup needs the first one's answer, such as fetching a customer and then that customer's discount. It is one after another on purpose, so it takes the sum of both times. Numbering items. flux.index() pairs each item with its position, which is often what people reach for zip with Flux.range to do. Many Monos, number unknown. For a list of calls, Mono.zip(listOfMonos, array -> ...) exists, but it hands you an Object[]. Usually Flux.fromIterable(ids).flatMap(this::lookup, n).collectList() is clearer: it caps how many calls run at once, which Mono.zip cannot, and it returns results in arrival order (use flatMapSequential to keep the input order). Merge and backpressure. merge asks each source for a small batch ahead (a prefetch) and requests more only as items move downstream, so a fast source can't flood a slow subscriber. Lesson 7 of this track looks at demand in detail. switchIfEmpty is lazy, its argument isn't. switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new IllegalStateException(...))) builds the exception object on every call, even when the source has a value. That's cheap but wasteful, and the stack trace points at the place where the chain was built. The supplier form, Mono.error(() -> new IllegalStateException(...)), builds it only when it is needed.

h: Errors, retries and timeouts · An error ends the stream, and error operators can only replace the rest
x: Start with the smallest stream that breaks. The bakery's program shares a tray of 8 loaves equally among some boxes, and the box counts arrive on a stream, one after another: 1, 2, 0 and 4. Zero boxes is a mistake in the data, and 8 / 0 throws. Java Flux<Integer> perBox = Flux.just(1, 2, 0, 4).map(i -> 8 / i); // 8 loaves into i boxes perBox.subscribe(v -> System.out.println("raw: " + v), e -> System.out.println("raw: error " + e)); Kotlin val perBox: Flux<Int> = Flux.just(1, 2, 0, 4).map { i -> 8 / i } // 8 loaves into i boxes perBox.subscribe({ v -> println("raw: $v") }, { e -> println("raw: error $e") }) The Flux is the publisher, the source of the stream: Reactor's type for zero or more items. The two lambdas make up its subscriber, the receiver, one for items and one for errors. ErrorsDemo, in the Try it, printed: raw: 8 raw: 4 raw: error java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero The 4 was never divided. That's the rule from Why reactive: onError is a terminal signal, a signal after which nothing else arrives. On the bakery line, it's the oven breaking down halfway through a tray. The belt stops, a note comes down instead of a loaf, and that tray is over. The packer can't make a broken oven finish the tray. She can only decide what goes in the box instead, and Reactor's error operators, the methods that add a station to the belt, make the same three choices: Java perBox.onErrorReturn(-1) // one loaf from yesterday, then close the box perBox.onErrorResume(e -> backupOven()) // switch to the backup oven's belt perBox.onErrorMap(ArithmeticException.class, e -> new IllegalStateException("bad box count", e)) // a clearer note; still an error Kotlin perBox.onErrorReturn(-1) // one loaf from yesterday, then close the box perBox.onErrorResume { backupOven() } // switch to the backup oven's belt perBox.onErrorMap(ArithmeticException::class.java) { e -> IllegalStateException("bad box count", e) } // a clearer note; still an error onErrorReturn emits one fallback value and completes. onErrorResume switches to a fallback publisher. onErrorMap turns one error into a more useful one, and the stream still fails. The demo runs all three: onErrorReturn: [8, 4, -1] onErrorResume: [8, 4, 100, 200] onErrorMap: java.lang.IllegalStateException: bad box count caused by java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero No line has a result for the 4. Each operator caught the error signal on its way down and replaced the rest of the stream with something else. The source above it had already finished. Each of the three has versions that take an exception class or a test, called a predicate. Use them. onErrorResume(TimeoutException.class, e -> yesterdaysPrice()) recovers from the one failure you planned for and lets the others through. A fallback for every Throwable also hides the NullPointerException in your own code, and the shop shows yesterday's prices for a week before anyone notices. Position matters as well. An error operator only sees errors from the operators above it, the ones nearer the source. Put onErrorReturn(-1) before the map, and the division by zero sails past it. doOnError(e -> log.warn(...)) is the side-effect version: it logs the error and passes it on unchanged. An error ends the stream. Error operators replace what's left; they never resume it. One trap catches tests in particular. Flux.error(e).subscribe(v -> {}) returns normally. With no error handler, Reactor only logs ErrorCallbackNotImplemented, as Mono and Flux showed, and your code never hears about it. Always pass an error handler to subscribe, or test with StepVerifier, a test tool from Reactor that subscribes and checks every signal (lesson 8 of this track). So one bad box count cost us the 4. In a stream of 10,000 order lines, the same mistake would cost us thousands. Four ways to handle zero boxes ErrorsDemo shares 8 loaves among 1, 2, 0, 4 boxes and handles the failure four ways: not at all, onErrorReturn, onErrorResume and onErrorMap. Write down what each line will print. Run it and compare. Does any version ever print a result for the 4? Add one more line: Flux.just(1, 2, 0, 4).onErrorReturn(-1).map(i -> 8 / i) (the error operator before map), collected and blocked like the others. Predict first, then run it. ErrorsDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l05; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; /** An error ends the stream. The error operators replace what is left with something else. */ public class ErrorsDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { Flux<Integer> perBox = Flux.just(1, 2, 0, 4).map(i -> 8 / i); // 8 loaves into i boxes; 0 throws perBox.subscribe(v -> System.out.println("raw: " + v), e -> System.out.println("raw: error " + e)); System.out.println("onErrorReturn: " + perBox.onErrorReturn(-1).collectList().block()); System.out.println("onErrorResume: " + perBox .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.just(100, 200)) // switch to a backup stream .collectList().block()); perBox.onErrorMap(ArithmeticException.class, e -> new IllegalStateException("bad box count", e)) .subscribe(v -> { }, e -> System.out.println("onErrorMap: " + e + " caused by " + e.getCause())); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l05.ErrorsDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l05/ErrorsDemo.java ErrorsDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l05 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux /** An error ends the stream. The error operators replace what is left with something else. */ fun main() { val perBox: Flux<Int> = Flux.just(1, 2, 0, 4).map { i -> 8 / i } // 8 loaves into i boxes; 0 throws perBox.subscribe({ v -> println("raw: $v") }, { e -> println("raw: error $e") }) println("onErrorReturn: " + perBox.onErrorReturn(-1).collectList().block()) println("onErrorResume: " + perBox .onErrorResume { Flux.just(100, 200) } // switch to a backup stream .collectList().block()) perBox.onErrorMap(ArithmeticException::class.java) { e -> IllegalStateException("bad box count", e) } .subscribe({ }, { e -> println("onErrorMap: $e caused by ${e.cause}") }) } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l05.ErrorsDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l05/ErrorsDemo.kt The raw subscriber prints 8 and 4, then the ArithmeticException. onErrorReturn gives [8, 4, -1], onErrorResume gives [8, 4, 100, 200], and onErrorMap reports an IllegalStateException: bad box count caused by the ArithmeticException. No line ever shows a result for 4: the error ended the source. Your extra line throws ArithmeticException from block(), because onErrorReturn only sees errors from operators above it, and the map is below. Reactor reference: Handling errors (source, 3.8.x) docs

h: Errors, retries and timeouts · Skip a bad item inside its own Mono, not on the whole stream
x: Picture a nightly job that reads the day's 10,000 order lines. Line 4,312 says a customer wants zero boxes. You want to log that line, put it on a pile for a person to check, and carry on with the other 5,688. The first idea is onErrorResume(e -> Mono.empty()) on the whole stream. Mono.empty() is a publisher that completes at once with no item. It does stop the error, and it also stops the job. SkipBadItemsDemo tries that idea on our four box counts: onErrorResume on the stream: [8, 4] Everything after the bad item is gone, because the error ended the source before onErrorResume saw it. The fix is to give each item its own small publisher, so that an error ends only that one: Java boxCounts.concatMap(i -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> 8 / i) .doOnError(e -> log.warn("skipping {}", i, e)) .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.empty())) // only this item's Mono ends Kotlin boxCounts.concatMap { i -> Mono.fromCallable { 8 / i } .doOnError { e -> log.warn("skipping {}", i, e) } .onErrorResume { Mono.empty() } // only this item's Mono ends } concatMap, from Transforming streams, runs one inner publisher at a time, in order. Each inner here is a Mono, Reactor's type for one item or none, built with fromCallable, which turns a thrown exception into an error signal. The Mono for the zero fails, and onErrorResume replaces it with an empty one. The outer stream never sees an error: skipping 0: / by zero onErrorResume per item: [8, 4, 2] On the bakery line, that's the inspector lifting one bad loaf off the belt while the oven keeps baking. Use concatMap to keep the order, or flatMap when items may be handled at the same time. For the nightly job, replace Mono.empty() with toCheck.add(line, e).then(Mono.empty()), which puts the line on the pile first. Reactor also has onErrorContinue((e, item) -> ...), and on this input it prints the same [8, 4, 2]. Don't use it. Its own Javadoc calls it "a specialist operator that can make the behaviour of your reactive chain unclear". It doesn't catch anything itself. It leaves a marker that travels up the chain, and the operators above it that know the marker drop the failing item instead of failing. That design has three consequences. It acts on operators above it, never below, so Flux.just(1, 2, 0, 4).onErrorContinue(...).map(i -> 8 / i) still fails. It only works with operators that support it. And it reaches into library code above it that never expected an item to be skipped. Someone adds an operator above it six months later, and the error handling changes with no compile error. The per-item version says what happens in the place where it happens. To skip a bad item, handle the error inside that item's own publisher. Skipping suits a bad line of data, which will be just as bad tomorrow. A mill that is busy right now is a different case: in a moment, the same request may work. Skip the zero three ways SkipBadItemsDemo runs the same four box counts through onErrorResume on the whole stream, onErrorResume inside a per-item Mono, and onErrorContinue. Predict the three lists. Run it. Now move the onErrorContinue line above the map, so it reads boxCounts.onErrorContinue(...).map(i -> 8 / i). Predict what happens, then run it. SkipBadItemsDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l05; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; /** Skipping bad items: handle the error inside each item's own Mono, not on the whole stream. */ public class SkipBadItemsDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { Flux<Integer> boxCounts = Flux.just(1, 2, 0, 4); var whole = boxCounts.map(i -> 8 / i).onErrorResume(e -> Mono.empty()).collectList().block(); System.out.println("onErrorResume on the stream: " + whole); var perItem = boxCounts .concatMap(i -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> 8 / i) .doOnError(e -> System.out.println(" skipping " + i + ": " + e.getMessage())) .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.empty())) // only this item's Mono ends .collectList().block(); System.out.println("onErrorResume per item: " + perItem); var continued = boxCounts.map(i -> 8 / i) .onErrorContinue((e, item) -> System.out.println(" onErrorContinue dropped " + item)) .collectList().block(); System.out.println("onErrorContinue: " + continued); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l05.SkipBadItemsDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l05/SkipBadItemsDemo.java SkipBadItemsDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l05 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono /** Skipping bad items: handle the error inside each item's own Mono, not on the whole stream. */ fun main() { val boxCounts: Flux<Int> = Flux.just(1, 2, 0, 4) val whole = boxCounts.map { i -> 8 / i }.onErrorResume { Mono.empty() }.collectList().block() println("onErrorResume on the stream: $whole") val perItem = boxCounts .concatMap { i -> Mono.fromCallable { 8 / i } .doOnError { e -> println(" skipping $i: ${e.message}") } .onErrorResume { Mono.empty() } // only this item's Mono ends } .collectList().block() println("onErrorResume per item: $perItem") val continued = boxCounts.map { i -> 8 / i } .onErrorContinue { _, item -> println(" onErrorContinue dropped $item") } .collectList().block() println("onErrorContinue: $continued") } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l05.SkipBadItemsDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l05/SkipBadItemsDemo.kt The whole-stream version prints [8, 4]: the 4 is lost. The per-item version prints [8, 4, 2] and logs the skipped zero. onErrorContinue also prints [8, 4, 2] in its original place. Moved above the map, it does nothing and block() throws ArithmeticException, because it only affects operators above it. Flux Javadoc source: onErrorContinue (reactor-core 3.8.x) docs

h: Errors, retries and timeouts · Retrying means subscribing again, so the call has to be lazy
x: An error ends the stream: error operators replace the rest, retry subscribes again from the source (3 retries are 4 attempts), and a timeout turns silence into an error Here is the running example for the rest of this lesson. Every morning, the bakery's program orders flour from the mill. The mill's ordering service is a web service, a program on another computer that answers over the network, and it has three moods. Usually it says CONFIRMED. Sometimes it's busy and fails with MillBusyException, and a minute later the same order goes through. Now and then it refuses with OrderRefusedException, because there's no rye flour this week, and asking again won't change that. The busy case calls for another try. retry doesn't rewind anything, though. When an error reaches it, it subscribes to its source again. That's a new subscription, so a cold publisher, one that does its work again for every subscriber (Mono and Flux), starts over from the beginning. The failed run stays failed. On the bakery line, retry asks for the whole order to be baked again, from the first loaf. Here the picture breaks in a way worth knowing. A repaired oven carries on where it stopped, but a retried Flux starts again from its first item, so the packer may box rye-1 twice. For a Mono with one answer, starting over is exactly what we want. retry(2) on a source that always fails makes three attempts, not two, and then passes on the original exception. It retries at once, with no pause. RetryDemo, in the Try it, shows it: 2. retry(2) on a source that always fails [ 5 ms] attempt 1 [ 6 ms] attempt 2 [ 6 ms] attempt 3 -> java.lang.IllegalStateException: mill down Three calls in about one millisecond. A mill that is already struggling won't feel helped. For a call to another computer, use retryWhen with a Retry spec, a small object that describes the policy: Java Mono.defer(() -> mill.order(orderId)) .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)) // 3 retries, waits double from 100 ms .filter(e -> e instanceof MillBusyException)) // only errors worth another try Kotlin Mono.defer { mill.order(orderId) } .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)) // 3 retries, waits double from 100 ms .filter { e -> e is MillBusyException }) // only errors worth another try Exponential backoff means waiting longer before each retry, usually twice as long each time. Here is the arithmetic people get wrong. Retry.backoff(3, 100ms) means 3 retries, so 4 attempts. With the random part switched off, a source that always fails is called at 0, 100, 300 and 700 ms, as the figure shows. At 700 ms the chain fails with RetryExhaustedException. Its message is Retries exhausted: 3/3, its cause is the last real error, and Exceptions.isRetryExhausted(e) recognises it. An error that the filter rejects, such as a refusal, isn't retried at all and reaches the subscriber unchanged. The demo's third part runs the same policy with a first wait of 50 ms. On this busy machine it printed: 3. backoff exhausted [ 0 ms] attempt 1 [ 53 ms] attempt 2 [155 ms] attempt 3 [356 ms] attempt 4 -> reactor.core.Exceptions$RetryExhaustedException: Retries exhausted: 3/3 cause: java.lang.IllegalStateException: mill down Those are waits of 50, 100 and 200 ms, plus a few milliseconds of a loaded machine. The defaults in Reactor 3.8: the wait doubles each time, the waits run on Schedulers.parallel(), a small set of Reactor's own threads (lesson 6 of this track), and the jitter factor is 0.5. Jitter moves each wait by a random amount of up to half its length, but never below the first wait. Keep it in production. A thousand bakeries that failed together shouldn't all call the mill again in the same millisecond. Turn it off with .jitter(0) in tests that check times. Now the trap, and it's the one from Mono and Flux. retry runs again only what happens at subscription time. Many hand-written clients do the work when you call the method, and wrap the answer they already have: return Mono.just(answer) or Mono.error(e). Retrying that Mono subscribes four times to the same stored answer and never calls the mill again. The demo's last part does exactly that: 4. retry(3) on a Mono built from one eager call [ 0 ms] attempt 1 -> java.lang.IllegalStateException: mill busy after 4 subscriptions Four subscriptions, one call. Wrap the call so that it happens per subscription: Mono.defer(() -> mill.order(orderId)). The reactive WebClient of Spring, the toolkit that Reactor comes from, is lazy already: each subscription sends a new request. Don't assume that of every client. A retry subscribes again. Make the source lazy, and choose which errors deserve another try. Every retry so far had an error to react to. The hardest failure sends none. Count the attempts RetryDemo has four parts: a backoff that succeeds on the third call, retry(2) on a call that always fails, a backoff that runs out, and retry(3) on a Mono built from one eager call. For each part, write down the number of attempts, the times, and the final result. Run it and compare your numbers. In part 3, delete .jitter(0) and run the demo twice. Watch the times of attempts 2 to 4. RetryDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l05; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import reactor.util.retry.Retry; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** retry re-subscribes. What gets re-run depends on how the source was built. */ public class RetryDemo { static final AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); static long t0; // fails on the first two calls, succeeds on the third static String callMill() { int n = calls.incrementAndGet(); System.out.printf(" [%3d ms] attempt %d%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, n); if (n < 3) throw new IllegalStateException("mill busy"); return "CONFIRMED"; } static String alwaysFails() { callMill(); throw new IllegalStateException("mill down"); } // a client that calls the mill when the method is called, and wraps the answer in a Mono static Mono<String> eagerClient() { try { return Mono.just(callMill()); } catch (RuntimeException e) { return Mono.error(e); } } public static void main(String[] args) { // warm up Reactor and the formatter, so the first timings don't include class loading Mono.fromCallable(() -> 1).retryWhen(Retry.backoff(1, Duration.ofMillis(1))).block(); String.format("%3d", 0); start("1. fromCallable + retryWhen(backoff 50 ms, no jitter)"); System.out.println(" -> " + Mono.fromCallable(RetryDemo::callMill) .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(50)).jitter(0)) .block()); start("2. retry(2) on a source that always fails"); try { Mono.fromCallable(RetryDemo::alwaysFails).retry(2).block(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println(" -> " + e); } start("3. backoff exhausted"); try { Mono.fromCallable(RetryDemo::alwaysFails) .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(50)).jitter(0)) .block(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println(" -> " + e + "\n cause: " + e.getCause()); } start("4. retry(3) on a Mono built from one eager call"); AtomicInteger subscriptions = new AtomicInteger(); try { eagerClient().doOnSubscribe(s -> subscriptions.incrementAndGet()).retry(3).block(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println(" -> " + e + " after " + subscriptions.get() + " subscriptions"); } } static void start(String title) { System.out.println(title); calls.set(0); t0 = System.nanoTime(); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l05.RetryDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l05/RetryDemo.java RetryDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l05 import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import reactor.util.retry.Retry import java.time.Duration import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger private val calls = AtomicInteger() private var t0 = 0L // fails on the first two calls, succeeds on the third private fun callMill(): String { val n = calls.incrementAndGet() println(" [%3d ms] attempt %d".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, n)) if (n < 3) throw IllegalStateException("mill busy") return "CONFIRMED" } private fun alwaysFails(): String { callMill() throw IllegalStateException("mill down") } // a client that calls the mill when the function is called, and wraps the answer in a Mono private fun eagerClient(): Mono<String> = try { Mono.just(callMill()) } catch (e: RuntimeException) { Mono.error(e) } private fun start(title: String) { println(title) calls.set(0) t0 = System.nanoTime() } /** retry re-subscribes. What gets re-run depends on how the source was built. */ fun main() { // warm up Reactor and the formatter, so the first timings don't include class loading Mono.fromCallable { 1 }.retryWhen(Retry.backoff(1, Duration.ofMillis(1))).block() "%3d".format(0) start("1. fromCallable + retryWhen(backoff 50 ms, no jitter)") println(" -> " + Mono.fromCallable { callMill() } .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(50)).jitter(0.0)) .block()) start("2. retry(2) on a source that always fails") try { Mono.fromCallable { alwaysFails() }.retry(2).block() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println(" -> $e") } start("3. backoff exhausted") try { Mono.fromCallable { alwaysFails() } .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(50)).jitter(0.0)) .block() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println(" -> $e\n cause: ${e.cause}") } start("4. retry(3) on a Mono built from one eager call") val subscriptions = AtomicInteger() try { eagerClient().doOnSubscribe { subscriptions.incrementAndGet() }.retry(3).block() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println(" -> $e after ${subscriptions.get()} subscriptions") } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l05.RetryDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l05/RetryDemo.kt Part 1 calls at about 0, 50 and 150 ms and prints CONFIRMED (a busy machine adds a little: one run here printed 0, 88 and 194 ms). Part 2 makes 3 attempts in the same millisecond or two and rethrows mill down. Part 3 calls at about 0, 50, 150 and 350 ms, then throws RetryExhaustedException: Retries exhausted: 3/3 with mill down as the cause. Part 4 calls the mill once and fails with mill busy after 4 subscriptions: retry subscribed again to the same stored error. Without jitter the waits are 50, 100 and 200 ms; with the default jitter they change from run to run. Retry.backoff(3, 100 ms) with jitter off, against a mill that always fails: four attempts, waits that double, and an exhausted error at 700 ms that a fallback can catch. Retry and RetryBackoffSpec source (reactor-core 3.8.x) docs

h: Errors, retries and timeouts · A timer on the wait turns silence into an error you can handle
x: Sometimes the mill accepts the connection and then never answers. No item, no error, nothing. That's the most polite failure there is, with no complaint at all, and your code waits along with it. A retry needs an error to react to, so without a timer, nothing ever gives up. timeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)) is the kitchen timer. If no item arrives within 500 ms of subscribing, it signals a TimeoutException and cancels the slow call above it. (For a Flux, the 500 ms count from the previous item.) Its clock runs on Schedulers.parallel() too, which is how a test can fake it. TimeoutDemo, in the Try it, asks for the flour price from a service that takes 300 ms, with a 100 ms timer: slow call cancelled timeout: java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException: Did not observe any item or terminal signal within 100ms in 'peek' (and no fallback has been configured) To swap in a fallback instead, use timeout(Duration, fallbackMono) or onErrorResume(TimeoutException.class, e -> ...). The demo's second run falls back to yesterday's price 0.90. Where you put the timer decides what it limits: Java Mono.defer(() -> mill.order(orderId)) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)) // each attempt gets 500 ms .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)).filter(this::worthRetrying)) .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)); // the caller waits 2 s at most, in total Kotlin Mono.defer { mill.order(orderId) } .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)) // each attempt gets 500 ms .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)).filter(this::worthRetrying)) .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)) // the caller waits 2 s at most, in total Above retryWhen, nearer the source, the timeout applies to each attempt. Its TimeoutException is one more error that the retry handles, if the filter lets it through. Below retryWhen, the timeout is a budget for the whole operation, waits included. With only the budget, one hanging attempt uses up all 2 seconds and is never retried. Most calls to another computer want both. The demo's last run gives each attempt 100 ms inside a 400 ms budget, and the 300 ms call never fits: budget: gave up after 3 attempts and 423 ms: TimeoutException Now the fact that matters more than any operator. A timeout tells you that you stopped waiting. It doesn't tell you that the mill said no. The order may have reached the mill just as your timer rang. The picture breaks here too: when a kitchen timer rings, you can open the oven and look, while timeout can't see the far side at all. That has two consequences for the retry. Every attempt must send the same order number, so the mill can see that the second message is a repeat and deliver one load of flour, not two. And when the retries run out, the honest answer is "we don't know yet". Mark the order pending and check with the mill later. Marking it failed invites someone to order again, and the bakery pays for two loads of flour. A timeout means you stopped waiting, not that the other side said no. That's the whole policy: a lazy call, a timer per attempt, a filtered backoff, and an honest fallback. The lab asks you to build it, and to prove its timing without waiting a single real millisecond. Per attempt or in total TimeoutDemo asks for the flour price from a service that takes 300 ms. It applies a 100 ms timeout, then the same with a fallback, then a 100 ms per-attempt timeout with retries inside a 400 ms budget. Predict each line, and how many attempts fit in the budget. Run it. In the last chain, delete the per-attempt .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(100)) and keep the 400 ms budget. Predict the result and the number of attempts, then run it. TimeoutDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l05; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import reactor.util.retry.Retry; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** timeout turns silence into an error you can handle. Where you put it decides what it limits. */ public class TimeoutDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { Mono<String> slowPrice = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(300)).thenReturn("fresh flour price 0.92") .doOnCancel(() -> System.out.println(" slow call cancelled")); try { slowPrice.timeout(Duration.ofMillis(100)).block(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("timeout: " + e.getCause()); } String price = slowPrice.timeout(Duration.ofMillis(100)) .onErrorResume(TimeoutException.class, e -> Mono.just("yesterday's price 0.90")) .block(); System.out.println("with fallback: " + price); AtomicInteger attempts = new AtomicInteger(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { String r = Mono.defer(() -> { attempts.incrementAndGet(); return slowPrice; }) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(100)) // per attempt .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(5, Duration.ofMillis(50)).jitter(0)) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(400)) // budget for the whole call .block(); System.out.printf("budget: got %s after %d attempts and %d ms%n", r, attempts.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.printf("budget: gave up after %d attempts and %d ms: %s%n", attempts.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName()); } } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l05.TimeoutDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l05/TimeoutDemo.java TimeoutDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l05 import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import reactor.util.retry.Retry import java.time.Duration import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** timeout turns silence into an error you can handle. Where you put it decides what it limits. */ fun main() { val slowPrice: Mono<String> = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(300)).thenReturn("fresh flour price 0.92") .doOnCancel { println(" slow call cancelled") } try { slowPrice.timeout(Duration.ofMillis(100)).block() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println("timeout: ${e.cause}") } val price = slowPrice.timeout(Duration.ofMillis(100)) .onErrorResume(TimeoutException::class.java) { Mono.just("yesterday's price 0.90") } .block() println("with fallback: $price") val attempts = AtomicInteger() val t0 = System.nanoTime() try { val r = Mono.defer { attempts.incrementAndGet(); slowPrice } .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(100)) // per attempt .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(5, Duration.ofMillis(50)).jitter(0.0)) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(400)) // budget for the whole call .block() println("budget: got %s after %d attempts and %d ms".format( r, attempts.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println("budget: gave up after %d attempts and %d ms: %s".format( attempts.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, e.cause?.javaClass?.simpleName)) } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l05.TimeoutDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l05/TimeoutDemo.kt The plain timeout prints TimeoutException: Did not observe any item or terminal signal within 100ms and the slow call is cancelled. The fallback version prints yesterday's price 0.90. The budget run makes 3 attempts (at about 0, 150 and 350 ms) and gives up a little after 400 ms (423 ms in one run here). Without the per-attempt timeout there is no error to retry, the single 300 ms call fits inside the 400 ms budget, and you get fresh flour price 0.92 after 1 attempt.

h: Errors, retries and timeouts · Java and Kotlin
x: One retry policy as a Reactor chain and as a suspend function FlourOrders.java (Reactor) // Reactor: the policy is a chain of operators on a lazy Mono Mono<String> place(String orderId) { return Mono.defer(() -> mill.order(orderId)) // a fresh call per attempt .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)) // per attempt .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)) // waits of 100, 200, 400 ms .filter(e -> e instanceof MillBusyException || e instanceof TimeoutException)) .onErrorResume(Exceptions::isRetryExhausted, e -> Mono.just("PENDING:" + orderId)); } FlourOrders.kt (coroutines) // Kotlin coroutines: the same policy as a plain loop in a suspend function suspend fun place(orderId: String): String { var wait = 100.milliseconds repeat(4) { attempt -> // 1 call + 3 retries try { return withTimeout(500.milliseconds) { mill.order(orderId) } // per attempt } catch (e: MillBusyException) { // worth another try } catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) { // so is a hang; a refusal is not caught, so it reaches the caller } if (attempt < 3) { delay(wait); wait *= 2 } // 100, 200, 400 ms } return "PENDING:$orderId" } Both versions make up to 4 attempts, give each one 500 ms, wait 100, 200 and 400 ms between them, let a refusal through and return PENDING at the end. (In the Kotlin version, mill.order is a suspend function, a function that can pause without holding its thread, and it returns the confirmation itself.) In Reactor the policy is data: operators you can reorder, and a Retry spec you can pass around and reuse, and the result is still a lazy Mono that does nothing until it is subscribed. In the coroutine version the policy is ordinary control flow: a loop, try and catch, delay and withTimeout. That is easier to read and to step through in a debugger, but you write the loop yourself, and you must not swallow CancellationException by catching Exception too broadly (withTimeout throws TimeoutCancellationException, which is one). Kotlin Flow has retry and retryWhen operators too, and the coroutines track covers them.

h: Errors, retries and timeouts · Worked example
x: Make a courier booking safe to retry Every evening a job books a courier van for each cake delivery. The courier's booking service is a web service, and the second argument is a booking number that the courier uses to spot repeats. Someone added retry() after a bad week of timeouts. Read it and list what can go wrong before you read on. Mono<Void> book(Delivery delivery) { return courier.book(delivery, UUID.randomUUID().toString()).retry(); } fun book(delivery: Delivery): Mono<Void> = courier.book(delivery, UUID.randomUUID().toString()).retry() Four problems. retry() with no number retries forever and at once, so one bad delivery stalls the whole job. It retries a refusal, such as an address the courier doesn't serve, as eagerly as a busy answer. Nothing limits how long one attempt may hang. And the booking number is a fresh random one each time book runs. The retries of this one Mono reuse it, but when the job crashes and runs again, book runs again with a new number, and the courier can't tell that the van is already booked. The number has to come from the delivery itself. Rebuild it in the order the lesson used: a lazy call, a per-attempt timeout, a filtered backoff, and a fallback for when the retries run out. CourierErrors.isTemporary returns true for timeouts, busy answers and dropped connections, and toCheck is a list a person goes through in the morning. Mono<Void> book(Delivery delivery) { String number = delivery.bookingNumber(); // 1. the delivery's own number, never a new one return Mono.defer(() -> courier.book(delivery, number)) // 2. a fresh call per attempt .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) // 3. no attempt waits forever .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(200)) // 4. 3 retries, jitter left on .filter(CourierErrors::isTemporary)) // a refusal is final .onErrorResume(Exceptions::isRetryExhausted, // 5. out of retries: a person checks it e -> toCheck.add(delivery, e.getCause())); } fun book(delivery: Delivery): Mono<Void> { val number = delivery.bookingNumber // 1. the delivery's own number, never a new one return Mono.defer { courier.book(delivery, number) } // 2. a fresh call per attempt .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) // 3. no attempt waits forever .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(200)) // 4. 3 retries, jitter left on .filter(CourierErrors::isTemporary)) // a refusal is final .onErrorResume(Exceptions::isRetryExhausted) { e -> // 5. out of retries: a person checks it toCheck.add(delivery, e.cause!!) } } Test the slow path with virtual time, the fake clock from StepVerifier. The jitter is still on, so don't assert exact times: move the clock further than any possible wait, then check the counts. Four attempts, one booking number, one delivery put aside. StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> vans.book(delivery)) // build it inside the supplier .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(10)) // more than any jittered wait .verifyComplete(); // put aside for a person, not failed assertThat(courier.numbersSeen()).hasSize(4).containsOnly(delivery.bookingNumber()); assertThat(toCheck.added()).containsExactly(delivery); StepVerifier.withVirtualTime { vans.book(delivery) } // build it inside the supplier .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(10)) // more than any jittered wait .verifyComplete() // put aside for a person, not failed assertThat(courier.numbersSeen()).hasSize(4).containsOnly(delivery.bookingNumber) assertThat(toCheck.added()).containsExactly(delivery)

Decide what that means for your retry before you write any code. h: Errors, retries and timeouts · Quiz
x: A tray of 100 rolls is shared among boxes, and the box counts arrive as Flux.just(5, 10, 0, 20). What does .map(i -> 100 / i).onErrorReturn(-1).collectList().block() return? [20, 10, -1, 5] [20, 10, -1] [20, 10, 5] It throws ArithmeticException The division by zero ends the source, so the 20 boxes are never handled. onErrorReturn replaces the rest of the stream with one value and completes. The first option assumes the stream carries on after the fallback, and the third is what per-item handling would give. The call for today's flour price sometimes hangs. Which chain retries a hanging attempt? (ofMillis and ofSeconds are Duration factories.) Mono.defer(this::price).retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, ofMillis(100))).timeout(ofSeconds(2)) Mono.defer(this::price).timeout(ofMillis(500)).retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, ofMillis(100))) Mono.defer(this::price).retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, ofMillis(100))) Mono.defer(this::price).retry(3) Only a timeout above retryWhen turns each hanging attempt into an error that the retry can see. In the first option the timeout is a total budget: the first attempt hangs for 2 seconds and is never retried. The last two have no timeout, so a hang produces no error at all and nothing is retried. A nightly job must log and skip order lines whose quantity fails to parse, and keep going. Which is the right shape? lines.map(this::parse).onErrorResume(e -> Mono.empty()) lines.map(this::parse).onErrorContinue((e, l) -> log(l)) lines.concatMap(l -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> parse(l)).onErrorResume(e -> logAndSkip(l, e))) lines.map(this::parse).retry() Handling the error inside each line's own Mono ends only that inner Mono, so the outer stream keeps going. The first option ends the whole stream at the first bad line. onErrorContinue happens to work here, but it acts on operators above it and can leak into library code; its Javadoc recommends the inner-publisher shape. retry() subscribes to the lines again forever and hits the same bad line every time. mill.order(id) always fails with MillBusyException. What does Mono.defer(() -> mill.order(id)).retry(2).block() do? Calls the mill 2 times, then throws RetryExhaustedException Calls the mill 3 times, 100 ms apart, then throws MillBusyException Calls the mill 3 times with no pause, then throws MillBusyException Calls the mill once, because retry re-uses the first result retry(n) means n retries, so 3 attempts, all back to back, and it rethrows the original error. Pauses and RetryExhaustedException come from retryWhen(Retry.backoff(...)). Because of Mono.defer, each attempt really calls the mill; without it, a client that does its work when called would be called once. From "Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe": a teammate writes Mono.just(mill.orderBlocking(id)).retry(3). The call fails on the first try. How many requests reach the mill? One, and the exception is thrown before retry even exists Four Three None, because nothing is subscribed Mono.just takes a value, so Java evaluates orderBlocking(id) first, at assembly time. It throws right there, out of the line that builds the chain, and retry(3) is never even created. Even if it had returned a value, Mono.just would replay that same value to every subscriber. Use Mono.fromCallable or Mono.defer so that each subscription makes the call.
