Who receives what, and what happens with 8 threads? */ public class SinksDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Sinks.Many<Integer> multicast = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(); List<Integer> early = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); List<Integer> late = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); multicast.tryEmitNext(10); // nobody is subscribed yet multicast.asFlux().subscribe(early::add); multicast.tryEmitNext(1); multicast.tryEmitNext(2); multicast.asFlux().subscribe(late::add); multicast.tryEmitNext(3); System.out.println("1. multicast: early=" + early + " late=" + late); afterEveryoneLeft("onBackpressureBuffer()", Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer()); afterEveryoneLeft("directBestEffort()", Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort()); Sinks.Many<Integer> replay = Sinks.many().replay().limit(2); replay.tryEmitNext(1); replay.tryEmitNext(2); replay.tryEmitNext(3); List<Integer> lateReplay = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); replay.asFlux().subscribe(lateReplay::add); System.out.println("3. replay().limit(2): late=" + lateReplay); Sinks.Many<Integer> unicast = Sinks.many().unicast().onBackpressureBuffer(); unicast.asFlux().subscribe(); unicast.asFlux().subscribe(v -> { }, e -> System.out.println("4. unicast, second subscriber: " + e.getMessage())); race("5. tryEmitNext from 8 threads", (sink, i) -> { if (sink.tryEmitNext(i).isFailure()) failures.incrementAndGet(); }); race("6. emitNext + busyLooping", (sink, i) -> sink.emitNext(i, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.busyLooping(Duration.ofSeconds(1)))); } static void afterEveryoneLeft(String flavour, Sinks.Many<Integer> sink) { sink.asFlux().subscribe().dispose(); // the only subscriber leaves List<String> next = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); sink.asFlux().subscribe(v -> next.add("got " + v), e -> next.add("error"), () -> next.add("completed")); sink.tryEmitNext(42); System.out.printf("2. %-22s after everyone left, a new subscriber %s%n", flavour, next); } static final AtomicInteger failures = new AtomicInteger(); static void race(String title, BiConsumer<Sinks.Many<Integer>, Integer> emit) throws InterruptedException { Sinks.Many<Integer> sink = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(); AtomicInteger received = new AtomicInteger(); sink.asFlux().subscribe(v -> received.incrementAndGet()); failures.set(0); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] threads = new Thread[8]; for (int t = 0; t < threads.length; t++) { threads[t] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) emit.accept(sink, i); }); threads[t].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); System.out.printf("%-32s received %,d of 80,000 (%,d emits failed)%n", title, received.get(), failures.get()); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l08.SinksDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l08/SinksDemo.java SinksDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l08 import reactor.core.publisher.Sinks import java.time.Duration import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread private val failures = AtomicInteger() private fun afterEveryoneLeft(flavour: String, sink: Sinks.Many<Int>) { sink.asFlux().subscribe().dispose() // the only subscriber leaves val next = CopyOnWriteArrayList<String>() sink.asFlux().subscribe({ v -> next += "got $v" }, { next += "error" }, { next += "completed" }) sink.tryEmitNext(42) println("2. %-22s after everyone left, a new subscriber %s".format(flavour, next)) } private fun race(title: String, emit: (Sinks.Many<Int>, Int) -> Unit) { val sink = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer<Int>() val received = AtomicInteger() sink.asFlux().subscribe { received.incrementAndGet() } failures.set(0) val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { thread { go.await() repeat(10_000) { i -> emit(sink, i) } } } go.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } println("%-32s received %,d of 80,000 (%,d emits failed)".format(title, received.get(), failures.get())) } /** Sinks push values into Reactor from ordinary code. Who receives what, and what happens with 8 threads? */ fun main() { val multicast = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer<Int>() val early = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Int>() val late = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Int>() multicast.tryEmitNext(10) // nobody is subscribed yet multicast.asFlux().subscribe { early += it } multicast.tryEmitNext(1) multicast.tryEmitNext(2) multicast.asFlux().subscribe { late += it } multicast.tryEmitNext(3) println("1. multicast: early=$early late=$late") afterEveryoneLeft("onBackpressureBuffer()", Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer()) afterEveryoneLeft("directBestEffort()", Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort()) val replay = Sinks.many().replay().limit<Int>(2) replay.tryEmitNext(1) replay.tryEmitNext(2) replay.tryEmitNext(3) val lateReplay = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Int>() replay.asFlux().subscribe { lateReplay += it } println("3. replay().limit(2): late=$lateReplay") val unicast = Sinks.many().unicast().onBackpressureBuffer<Int>() unicast.asFlux().subscribe() unicast.asFlux().subscribe({ }, { e -> println("4. unicast, second subscriber: ${e.message}") }) race("5. tryEmitNext from 8 threads") { sink, i -> if (sink.tryEmitNext(i).isFailure) failures.incrementAndGet() } race("6. emitNext + busyLooping") { sink, i -> sink.emitNext(i, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.busyLooping(Duration.ofSeconds(1))) } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l08.SinksDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l08/SinksDemo.kt Multicast: early=[10, 1, 2, 3] (the 10 waited in the buffer for the first subscriber) and late=[3]. After everyone left, the onBackpressureBuffer() sink only completes the new subscriber, while directBestEffort() delivers got 42. Replay with limit 2: [2, 3]. Unicast: the second subscriber fails with Sinks.many().unicast() sinks only allow a single Subscriber. The tryEmitNext race delivers only a fraction of the 80,000 (11,679 and 15,391 in two runs here), with a different number each run; emitNext with busyLooping delivers all 80,000. h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · StepVerifier checks every signal, and virtual time fakes the clock
x: A reactive test has to subscribe, check each signal in order, and fail when anything else happens. StepVerifier, from the reactor-test library, does exactly that. It's a quality inspector at the end of the belt with a script in her hand: first a loaf named rye-1, then the end-of-day bell, and nothing else. Java StepVerifier.create(orderPage.quote("chocolate", "home")) .expectNext(expectedQuote) .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); Kotlin StepVerifier.create(orderPage.quote("chocolate", "home")) .expectNext(expectedQuote) .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) Four rules, each learned from a test that lied: Nothing runs until verify(), or a shortcut such as verifyComplete() or verifyError(). A test that ends at expectComplete() never subscribes, and passes whatever the code does. It's the most optimistic test you will ever write. verify() has no time limit by default, so a publisher that hangs also hangs the build. Pass a Duration, or set StepVerifier.setDefaultTimeout(...) once. StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> ...) swaps Reactor's schedulers for a virtual clock, a fake clock that the test winds forward, so a one-day delay is checked in milliseconds. Build the publisher inside the supplier lambda. A Mono.delay built earlier has already picked the real clock, and the test times out. expectNoEvent(d) checks that nothing happens during d of virtual time. The subscription counts as an event, so put expectSubscription() first. StepVerifierDemo, in the Try it, breaks the rules on purpose: 1. no verify(): subscriptions=0, wrong expectation unnoticed 2. virtual time: one day took 52 ms of real time 3. expectNoEvent first: expectation failed (expected no event: onSubscribe(reactor.core.publisher.MonoDelay$MonoDelayRunnable@2db7a79b)) 4. built outside the supplier: VerifySubscriber timed out on reactor.core.publisher.MonoIgnoreThen$ThenIgnoreMain@47db50c5 The first test expected burnt from a Mono that says baked, and never noticed, because it never subscribed. The second checked a whole day of waiting in 52 ms. The third and fourth broke rules 4 and 3, and failed as they should. Here the inspector picture breaks in our favour: a real inspector can't wind the clock forward by a day. For a source you drive by hand, there's TestPublisher. Call next(...), complete() or error(...) from the test, then check wasCancelled() or assertMinRequested(n). TestPublisher.create() respects demand like a real source and fails if you push without it; createNoncompliant(...) breaks the spec on purpose (Why reactive). PublisherProbe answers a different question: was this branch subscribed at all? Use it to prove that a switchIfEmpty fallback ran, or didn't. All the virtual-time tests in this track's labs, from the mill's backoff to the courier's limit, are built from these pieces. End every StepVerifier with verify and a time limit, and build timed publishers inside withVirtualTime. A good test tells you that something failed. When a chain fails in a running program, the next question is where. Break four StepVerifier rules StepVerifierDemo runs five small tests: one without verify(), a one-day delay under virtual time, expectNoEvent as the first step, a delay built outside the virtual-time supplier, and a TestPublisher driven by hand. (It runs from src/demo, so the lab's build adds reactor-test to the demo classpath.) Predict which ones pass, which fail, and with what message. Run it. In part 1, add .verify() to the end of the line and run it again. StepVerifierDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l08; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import reactor.test.StepVerifier; import reactor.test.publisher.TestPublisher; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Five StepVerifier habits, most of them shown by breaking them. */ public class StepVerifierDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { AtomicInteger subscriptions = new AtomicInteger(); Mono<String> bake = Mono.fromCallable(() -> "baked").doOnSubscribe(s -> subscriptions.incrementAndGet()); StepVerifier.create(bake).expectNext("burnt").expectComplete(); // no verify(): nothing runs System.out.println("1. no verify(): subscriptions=" + subscriptions.get() + ", wrong expectation unnoticed"); Duration real = StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Mono.delay(Duration.ofDays(1)).thenReturn("stale")) .expectSubscription() .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofDays(1)) .expectNext("stale") .verifyComplete(); System.out.println("2. virtual time: one day took " + real.toMillis() + " ms of real time"); try { StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> Mono.delay(Duration.ofDays(1))) .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofDays(1)) // subscription counts as an event .expectNext(0L) .verifyComplete(); } catch (AssertionError e) { System.out.println("3. expectNoEvent first: " + e.getMessage()); } Mono<String> builtTooEarly = Mono.delay(Duration.ofDays(1)).thenReturn("stale"); // grabs the real clock try { StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> builtTooEarly) .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofDays(1)) .expectNext("stale") .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); } catch (AssertionError e) { System.out.println("4. built outside the supplier: " + e.getMessage()); } TestPublisher<String> readings = TestPublisher.create(); StepVerifier.create(readings.flux().map(r -> r + " C")) .then(() -> readings.next("200", "201")) // push values by hand .expectNext("200 C", "201 C") .then(readings::complete) .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); System.out.println("5. TestPublisher: passed; the map requested " + (readings.wasRequested() ? "some" : "no") + " items"); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l08.StepVerifierDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l08/StepVerifierDemo.java StepVerifierDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l08 import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import reactor.test.StepVerifier import reactor.test.publisher.TestPublisher import java.time.Duration import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** Five StepVerifier habits, most of them shown by breaking them. */ fun main() { val subscriptions = AtomicInteger() val bake = Mono.fromCallable { "baked" }.doOnSubscribe { subscriptions.incrementAndGet() } StepVerifier.create(bake).expectNext("burnt").expectComplete() // no verify(): nothing runs println("1. no verify(): subscriptions=${subscriptions.get()}, wrong expectation unnoticed") val real = StepVerifier.withVirtualTime { Mono.delay(Duration.ofDays(1)).thenReturn("stale") } .expectSubscription() .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofDays(1)) .expectNext("stale") .verifyComplete() println("2. virtual time: one day took ${real.toMillis()} ms of real time") try { StepVerifier.withVirtualTime { Mono.delay(Duration.ofDays(1)) } .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofDays(1)) // subscription counts as an event .expectNext(0L) .verifyComplete() } catch (e: AssertionError) { println("3. expectNoEvent first: ${e.message}") } val builtTooEarly = Mono.delay(Duration.ofDays(1)).thenReturn("stale") // grabs the real clock try { StepVerifier.withVirtualTime { builtTooEarly } .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofDays(1)) .expectNext("stale") .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) } catch (e: AssertionError) { println("4. built outside the supplier: ${e.message}") } val readings = TestPublisher.create<String>() StepVerifier.create(readings.flux().map { r -> "$r C" }) .then { readings.next("200", "201") } // push values by hand .expectNext("200 C", "201 C") .then { readings.complete() } .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) println("5. TestPublisher: passed; the map requested ${if (readings.wasRequested()) "some" else "no"} items") } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l08.StepVerifierDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l08/StepVerifierDemo.kt Part 1 reports subscriptions=0: without verify() nothing ran, and the wrong expectation (burnt) went unnoticed. After you add .verify(), it throws an AssertionError saying it expected burnt and got baked. Part 2 checks a full day in a few dozen milliseconds. Part 3 fails with expected no event: onSubscribe(...). Part 4 fails with VerifySubscriber timed out, because the delay holds the real clock. Part 5 passes. h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · Find the failing operator with checkpoint, and watch the signals with log
x: A stack trace from a reactive chain shows where the error was raised and how the subscription got there. It almost never shows where you wrote the operator that failed. In DebugDemo, a method called priceRow(cake) builds Flux.just(2400, 2600).single(): the cake has two price rows, and the code expects one. single() fails: 1. no help java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException: Source emitted more than one item top frame: reactor.core.publisher.MonoSingle$SingleSubscriber.onNext(MonoSingle.java:135) any frame in priceRow(), where single() was written? false The top frame is Reactor's MonoSingle, and no frame of the trace is in priceRow(). Mono and Flux explains why. priceRow() only filled in the order form and returned. By the time single() sees the second row, the data is flowing, and the frame of priceRow() is long gone. checkpoint("price-row") marks a place in the chain. When an error passes through it, Reactor attaches a suppressed exception, an extra exception carried inside the first one, that names the place: 2. checkpoint("price-row") ... Error has been observed at the following site(s): *__checkpoint -> price-row It's cheap, so put one at the edges of your own chains, named after what they do. checkpoint("price-row", true) also records a stack trace when the chain is built, which points at the line in your code. The cost is capturing that trace every time the chain is built. The demo's third run shows it pointing at the line in main where the checkpoint was written. Hooks.onOperatorDebug() does the same for every operator in the program, and the reference guide calls it a last resort because of the cost. For a program that runs for real, there's the reactor-tools agent (ReactorDebugAgent.init() as the first line of main), which adds the same information by changing your classes as they load. It's a separate dependency, and not in the labs. Java Mono<Integer> price = priceRow(cake).checkpoint("price-row"); // name the place, cheaply Flux<Integer> rows = Flux.range(1, 5).log("rows").take(2); // print every signal at this point Kotlin val price: Mono<Int> = priceRow(cake).checkpoint("price-row") // name the place, cheaply val rows: Flux<Int> = Flux.range(1, 5).log("rows").take(2) // print every signal at this point log("rows") prints every signal that passes that point: [ INFO] (main) | onSubscribe([Synchronous Fuseable] FluxRange.RangeSubscription) [ INFO] (main) | request(2) [ INFO] (main) | onNext(1) [ INFO] (main) | onNext(2) [ INFO] (main) | cancel() It's the quickest way to see this track's ideas in a real chain: the slip that take(2) wrote, the cancel it sent up once it had enough, and the thread each signal arrived on. It logs through SLF4J, a common Java logging front end, when that is on the classpath. When a chain fails far from where it was built, name the place with checkpoint. That completes the toolkit. The last question is when to reach for it at all. Find the operator that failed DebugDemo runs a chain whose single() sees two price rows, three times: plain, with checkpoint("price-row"), and with checkpoint("price-row", true). Then it puts log("rows") between a range and take(2). Run it. For each of the first three runs, find the information that tells you where the failing operator was written. Predict the log output first: which request and which last signal will it show? DebugDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l08; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.util.Arrays; /** Where did it fail? An operator error without help, with checkpoints, and the signals log() shows. */ public class DebugDemo { // assembled here, far away from where it is subscribed: the cake has two price rows, the code expects one static Mono<Integer> priceRow(String cake) { return Flux.just(2400, 2600).single(); } static void show(String title, Mono<Integer> chain) { try { chain.block(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { boolean mentionsPriceRow = Arrays.stream(e.getStackTrace()).anyMatch(f -> f.getMethodName().equals("priceRow")); System.out.println(title); System.out.println(" " + e); System.out.println(" top frame: " + e.getStackTrace()[0]); System.out.println(" any frame in priceRow(), where single() was written? " + mentionsPriceRow); for (Throwable s : e.getSuppressed()) { s.getMessage().lines() .filter(l -> !l.isBlank() && !l.contains("#block")) .limit(4) .map(l -> l.replace("⇢", "->")) // Reactor prints an arrow here .forEach(l -> System.out.println(" " + l.strip())); } } } public static void main(String[] args) { show("1. no help", priceRow("chocolate").map(cents -> cents + 100)); show("2. checkpoint(\"price-row\")", priceRow("chocolate").checkpoint("price-row").map(cents -> cents + 100)); show("3. checkpoint(\"price-row\", true)", priceRow("chocolate").checkpoint("price-row", true).map(cents -> cents + 100)); System.out.println("4. log(\"rows\") between a range and take(2)"); Flux.range(1, 5).log("rows").take(2).blockLast(); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l08.DebugDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l08/DebugDemo.java DebugDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l08 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono // assembled here, far away from where it is subscribed: the cake has two price rows, the code expects one private fun priceRow(cake: String): Mono<Int> = Flux.just(2400, 2600).single() private fun show(title: String, chain: Mono<Int>) { try { chain.block() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { val mentionsPriceRow = e.stackTrace.any { it.methodName.startsWith("priceRow") } println(title) println(" $e") println(" top frame: ${e.stackTrace[0]}") println(" any frame in priceRow(), where single() was written? $mentionsPriceRow") for (s in e.suppressed) { s.message.orEmpty().lines() .filter { it.isNotBlank() && "#block" !in it } .take(4) .map { it.replace("⇢", "->") } // Reactor prints an arrow here .forEach { println(" ${it.trim()}") } } } } /** Where did it fail? An operator error without help, with checkpoints, and the signals log() shows. */ fun main() { show("1. no help", priceRow("chocolate").map { cents -> cents + 100 }) show("2. checkpoint(\"price-row\")", priceRow("chocolate").checkpoint("price-row").map { cents -> cents + 100 }) show("3. checkpoint(\"price-row\", true)", priceRow("chocolate").checkpoint("price-row", true).map { cents -> cents + 100 }) println("4. log(\"rows\") between a range and take(2)") Flux.range(1, 5).log("rows").take(2).blockLast() } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l08.DebugDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l08/DebugDemo.kt All three report IndexOutOfBoundsException: Source emitted more than one item with MonoSingle as the top frame, and no frame in priceRow(). The plain run gives no clue where it came from. The checkpoint run names price-row. The run with true adds an assembly trace pointing at the line in main where the checkpoint was written. The log shows onSubscribe, request(2), onNext(1), onNext(2) and cancel(): take(2) capped the demand and then cancelled the range. Reactor reference: Debugging Reactor (source, 3.8.x) docs

h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · When reactive is still worth it, and when plain code on virtual threads is enough
x: Reactor isn't the default answer for new JVM code, and the Spring team, the home of Reactor, says so itself. The Spring Framework reference compares Spring MVC, its classic style in which each request holds a thread, with the reactive Spring WebFlux. It reads: "If you have a Spring MVC application that works fine, there is no need to change. Imperative programming is the easiest way to write, understand, and debug code." Imperative code is ordinary step-by-step code, one line after another. The reference warns about "the steep learning curve", tells you to "start small and measure the benefits", and adds: "We expect that, for a wide range of applications, the shift is unnecessary." Why reactive quoted the same docs on speed: reactive code doesn't make programs faster; it lets them scale with fewer threads when calls have to wait. Virtual threads (final in JDK 21) took away most of the thread-count argument. Mark Paluch of the Spring team wrote in 2022, while they were still a preview: "The reasons to use asynchronous programming models go away in many cases if we start with the assumption that our code runs on Virtual Threads." The same post keeps a place for reactive. ReactiveX-style APIs "remain a powerful way to compose concurrent logic and a natural way for dealing with streams". They are also "the right approach for concurrent scenarios in which declarative concurrency (such as scatter-gather) matters." ReactiveX is the family of libraries that Reactor's style comes from, and scatter-gather means sending many calls out at once and collecting the answers. So here is the position I'd take for your own programs: For one request and one reply, over databases and services whose clients block, use virtual threads and plain code. Don't rewrite a working service in Reactor. For streams, such as live updates to browsers, a feed that never ends, or anything where demand, cancellation and a loss policy matter, Reactor earns its complexity. For many calls composed with timeouts, retries and fan-out, Reactor's operators are hard to beat. Coroutines, and structured concurrency once it is final (it is a preview in JDK 25), are the alternatives that read from top to bottom. In a program that is already reactive from end to end, stay reactive, and keep the few blocking calls on boundedElastic. In Kotlin, coroutines give code that reads from top to bottom over the same idea. kotlinx-coroutines-reactor bridges both ways (awaitSingle(), mono { }, Flow.asFlux()), and Spring maps Mono to suspend and Flux to Flow. Quick check: the bakery's website has two pages. One reads an order from the database and shows it. The other shows the oven's live temperature to browsers that read at different speeds. Which one needs request(n), and why? (The second. The first waits for one reply, which a virtual thread does cheaply. The second has a fast producer and slow consumers, and only demand or a loss policy stops readings piling up in memory for the slow ones.) That last bullet is where the next track begins. Embracing Virtual Threads (Spring blog, Mark Paluch, 2022) read Spring Framework reference: Spring WebFlux overview, applicability and performance docs

h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · Java and Kotlin
x: A bell for order events and a shared feed in Reactor and Kotlin Kitchen.java (Reactor) // Reactor: a bell that till threads ring, and a shared thermometer feed private final Sinks.Many<OrderEvent> bell = Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort(); void ring(OrderEvent e) { bell.emitNext(e, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.busyLooping(Duration.ofSeconds(1))); } Flux<OrderEvent> live() { return bell.asFlux(); } Flux<Reading> temperature = oven.readings() .replay(1) // late screens get the latest reading .refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5)); // disconnect 5 s after the last one leaves Kitchen.kt (coroutines) // Kotlin coroutines: SharedFlow for events, StateFlow for "the latest value" private val bell = MutableSharedFlow<OrderEvent>(extraBufferCapacity = 1_000) fun ring(e: OrderEvent) { check(bell.tryEmit(e)) { "the screens are too slow" } // thread-safe; suspend emit() waits instead } val live: SharedFlow<OrderEvent> = bell.asSharedFlow() val temperature: StateFlow<Reading?> = oven.readings() .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), null) // latest reading, stop 5 s after the last leaves The shapes match: a multicast sink is close to a MutableSharedFlow, and replay(1).refCount(1, grace) is close to stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), null). The differences are in threads and lifetime. A MutableSharedFlow accepts emissions from any number of threads at once; its tryEmit fails only when the buffer is full, and emit suspends instead. A Reactor sink refuses overlapping emissions unless you retry or serialize them. And stateIn and shareIn need a CoroutineScope: the shared source lives in that scope and is cancelled with it, which is structured concurrency. Reactor's sharing lives as long as subscribers keep it alive. A StateFlow also always has a current value and skips values equal to the last one, which replay(1) does not. The coroutines track covers SharedFlow and StateFlow in detail.

h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · Worked example
x: Test a cake-status poller in milliseconds After a cake goes into the oven, a poller asks the oven's controller for its status every 30 seconds until it says DONE, and gives up after 5 minutes. A real-time test would take 90 seconds for the happy path and 5 minutes for the timeout. Here is the code under test. Mono<Status> awaitDone(String cakeId) { return Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(30)) // ask every 30 s .concatMap(tick -> oven.status(cakeId)) // one call at a time .filter(Status::isDone) .next() // the first DONE, then stop asking .timeout(Duration.ofMinutes(5)); } fun awaitDone(cakeId: String): Mono<Status> = Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(30)) // ask every 30 s .concatMap { oven.status(cakeId) } // one call at a time .filter(Status::isDone) .next() // the first DONE, then stop asking .timeout(Duration.ofMinutes(5)) The happy path: the fake oven answers BAKING twice, then DONE. Under virtual time the questions come at 30, 60 and 90 seconds of fake time. expectNoEvent(90 s) proves nothing came out earlier, and DONE arrives exactly at 90 s. FakeOven oven = new FakeOven(BAKING, BAKING, DONE); StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> new CakePoller(oven).awaitDone("cake-7")) // 1. build it inside the supplier .expectSubscription() // 2. before any expectNoEvent .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofSeconds(90)) // 3. silent until the third question .expectNext(DONE) .verifyComplete(); assertThat(oven.calls()).isEqualTo(3); val oven = FakeOven(BAKING, BAKING, DONE) StepVerifier.withVirtualTime { CakePoller(oven).awaitDone("cake-7") } // 1. build it inside the supplier .expectSubscription() // 2. before any expectNoEvent .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofSeconds(90)) // 3. silent until the third question .expectNext(DONE) .verifyComplete() assertThat(oven.calls()).isEqualTo(3) The timeout path: the cake never finishes. Jump the clock to the deadline and expect the TimeoutException. Keep a real-time limit on verify as well, so a mistake makes the test fail in one second instead of hanging. FakeOven stuck = new FakeOven(BAKING); // baking forever StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> new CakePoller(stuck).awaitDone("cake-8")) .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofMinutes(5)) // 4. jump to the deadline .expectError(TimeoutException.class) .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); // 5. a real-time safety net val stuck = FakeOven(BAKING) // baking forever StepVerifier.withVirtualTime { CakePoller(stuck).awaitDone("cake-8") } .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofMinutes(5)) // 4. jump to the deadline .expectError(TimeoutException::class.java) .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) // 5. a real-time safety net Both tests run in a fraction of a second. If one of them hangs instead, look at where the poller is built. Flux.interval and timeout pick their scheduler when the chain is built, so a poller created before withVirtualTime runs on the real clock. The same goes for a Mono built once in a @BeforeEach method and kept in a field.

h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · Lab
x: An order bell for the kitchen and two shared feeds labs/reactive/src/main/java/workbench/reactive/l08/OrderBell.java labs/reactive/src/main/java/workbench/reactive/l08/SharedFeeds.java labs/reactive/src/main/java/workbench/reactive/l08/OrderEvent.java ./gradlew :reactive:test --tests 'workbench.reactive.l08.*' Run the tests once. All six fail. OrderEvent is one thing that happened to a cake order, OrderBell is the bell the tills ring, and SharedFeeds shares a thermometer feed and caches the price list. OrderBell: choose the sink from the Javadoc of live() (only events rung after you subscribed, nothing kept while nobody listens, and it survives every listener leaving). Then make ring safe for 8 threads at once, and return a read-only view from live(). SharedFeeds.shareWithLatest: one connection to the thermometer, the latest reading for late subscribers, and a disconnect when the last subscriber leaves. SharedFeeds.cacheFor: load at most once per ttl. Read how the test controls the clock with VirtualTimeScheduler.getOrSet() and advanceTimeBy. Run the tests until all six pass, then once more: the 8-thread test must pass every time. If the hot test finds event 0 in the early listener's list, your sink kept events rung before anyone subscribed: multicast().onBackpressureBuffer() does that. The same sink fails the "every listener has left" test with a completion. If the 8-thread test receives fewer than 16,000 events, you ignored the result of tryEmitNext. If it reports crashed threads, you used EmitFailureHandler.FAIL_FAST, which throws on FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED. share() fails the late-subscriber test (no latest value); cache() and replay(1).autoConnect() fail the disconnect test (they never cancel the source). Mono.cache() with no argument never loads again. There is a version that takes a Duration. All six tests in HotPublishersTest pass, twice in a row. By the end you can share one source between many subscribers with the right late-subscriber behaviour, push values in from many threads with Sinks without losing any, test timing with StepVerifier and virtual time, find a failing operator with checkpoint and log, and say when Reactor is still the right tool.

h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · Quiz
x: Two till threads call bell.tryEmitNext(event) on the same Sinks.many().multicast() sink at the same moment, and ignore the return value. What can happen? Both events are emitted, in some order One call returns FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED and its event is never emitted The sink buffers the second event and emits it later The sink throws ConcurrentModificationException Reactor sinks detect overlapping emissions and refuse them instead of blocking or queueing, so one of the two calls gets FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED. Ignoring the result loses that event silently. Use emitNext(event, EmitFailureHandler.busyLooping(...)), which retries, or serialize the calls. A test reads StepVerifier.create(orders.cancel("order-42")).expectNext("CANCELLED").expectComplete(); and passes. The cancel code is in fact broken. Why does the test pass? expectComplete() ignores the value Nothing subscribes until verify() is called, so no expectation is ever checked StepVerifier only fails on errors, not on wrong values The cancel runs on another thread, so its result arrives after the test ends expectComplete() only adds a step to the script. verify(), or a shortcut like verifyComplete(), is what subscribes and runs it. Add .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)), and the test checks the value and fails if it hangs. Screens in the shop share one connection to the oven thermometer. A screen that switches on late must show the current temperature at once, and the connection must close when nobody watches. Which operator fits? readings.share() readings.cache() readings.replay(1).refCount() readings.publish().autoConnect(1) replay(1) gives a late subscriber the latest reading, and refCount() connects on the first subscriber and cancels the source when the last one leaves. share() gives late subscribers nothing until the next reading. cache() and autoConnect never disconnect, and cache() also keeps every reading forever. A team runs a web service written with Spring MVC, the classic style in which each request holds a thread, on a blocking database driver. It meets its speed targets. Someone proposes a rewrite with Spring WebFlux "to make it faster". What do Spring's own docs say? Rewrite it: reactive code is faster for every workload If an MVC application works fine there is no need to change; reactive code doesn't generally make applications faster Rewrite only the database calls with Reactor and keep the rest Switch to WebFlux, but keep the blocking driver on the event loop The Spring reference says a working MVC application has no need to change, that blocking database APIs point to MVC, and that reactive and non-blocking code generally doesn't make applications run faster. With virtual threads, the thread-count argument for this kind of service is mostly gone too. The last option is the worst of both: a blocking driver on an event loop stalls every request that loop serves. From "Errors, retries and timeouts": a retry uses Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(200)) with the default jitter. How should its virtual-time test check the slow path? expectNoEvent for exactly 1,400 ms, then expect the fallback Advance the clock well past the longest possible total wait, then check the result and the number of attempts Use real time with Thread.sleep(2_000) so the jitter is realistic It can't be tested while jitter is on With jitter, each wait moves by up to half its length, so exact times are not fixed. Advancing well past the maximum (the courier example moved the clock 10 seconds) and then checking the outcome and the count is stable. Exact-time checks need jitter(0). Real sleeps make the test slow and still flaky.

h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · Key terms
x: Cold publisher A publisher that does its work again, from the start, for every subscriber. Hot publisher A publisher that produces whether or not anyone subscribes; subscribers see what is produced while they listen. ConnectableFlux What publish() and replay() return: a shared Flux that subscribes to its source when it is connected. refCount Connect on the first subscriber, disconnect when the last one leaves (optionally after a grace period). Sink Reactor's thread-aware way to push values from ordinary code into a Flux or Mono. StepVerifier reactor-test's tool that subscribes to a publisher and checks its signals step by step. Virtual time A fake clock that replaces Reactor's schedulers in a test, so delays pass instantly. checkpoint An operator that labels a place in a chain, so errors passing through it say where they came from. What is share() the same as, and what does a late subscriber get? publish().refCount(). A late subscriber gets only the items emitted after it subscribed. Late subscriber on replay(1).refCount(): what does it get? The most recent item at once, then the live ones. The source is cancelled when the last subscriber leaves. Two threads call tryEmitNext on one sink at the same moment. What can happen? One gets EmitResult.FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED and its item is not emitted. Check the result or use emitNext(item, busyLooping(...)). What happens to Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer() when its last subscriber leaves? By default it shuts down: a later subscriber just receives onComplete. directBestEffort() keeps working. A StepVerifier chain without verify(): what runs? Nothing. verify() (or verifyComplete() and the other shortcuts) is what subscribes and checks the steps. Why must the publisher be built inside the withVirtualTime supplier? Operators like delay, interval and timeout pick their scheduler when the chain is built. Built earlier, they use the real clock and the test hangs. What does checkpoint("price-row") add to an error? A suppressed exception saying the error was observed at the checkpoint named price-row. Cheap; checkpoint(name, true) also captures the stack trace of where the chain was built.

h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · Go deeper
x: Connecting by hand. publish() and replay() return a ConnectableFlux. Besides refCount and autoConnect, you can call connect() yourself once every subscriber is in place, and dispose the returned Disposable to disconnect. That suits a startup sequence that wires several consumers before any data should flow. Context instead of ThreadLocal. Because a chain hops threads, a ThreadLocal, such as the per-request id that a logging library keeps, doesn't follow it. Reactor's Context does: write it at the bottom with contextWrite(Context.of("requestId", id)) and read it upstream with Mono.deferContextual(ctx -> ...). It travels from the subscriber toward the source, so a contextWrite above the reader is invisible to it. With the Micrometer context-propagation library on the classpath, Hooks.enableAutomaticContextPropagation() (Reactor 3.5.3+) restores ThreadLocals around each operator; it isn't in the labs. BlockHound in tests. Calling BlockHound.install() at the start of a test run makes any blocking call on a non-blocking thread throw BlockingOperationError. That catches a blocking database call on a server's event-loop thread, from the Schedulers lesson, before a real user does. On JDK 13+ it needs -XX:+AllowRedefinitionToAddDeleteMethods. Backpressure in tests. StepVerifier.create(flux, 0) starts with no demand, and thenRequest(n) adds it step by step. That's how the lab of Backpressure in practice checked which reading a slow screen receives.

h: Kotlin coroutines
x: Suspend functions, structured concurrency, dispatchers, cancellation, Flow and channels. By the end of this track you can write Kotlin coroutine code that you can trust when many things happen at once. A coroutine is a piece of work that can pause without holding a thread, like a dish a cook leaves to simmer while she starts the next one. You can say what suspend does and doesn't do, start several slow calls together so they take only as long as the slowest, and keep every coroutine inside a scope that waits for it, cancels it and hears about its failures. You can put blocking calls and CPU work on the right dispatcher, make loops and blocking calls hear a cancel, and let independent work fail alone. You can build cold flows, share hot ones with StateFlow and SharedFlow, pass work between coroutines through channels, guard shared state with a Mutex, and test all of it on a fake clock. And you can connect coroutines to CompletableFuture, Reactor and virtual threads, and choose between the three. One picture runs through the whole track: a home cook making a big dinner. The cook is a thread, and each dish on the go is a coroutine. The bookmark in the recipe is what lets a dish pause, a course goes out only when all its dishes are ready, and when the guests call dinner off, the cook hears it only between steps. The cheat sheet below puts each picture next to its code. You need everyday Kotlin; the earlier tracks help, but each lesson explains what it uses. Install JDK 25. The library is kotlinx.coroutines 1.11.0 with Kotlin 2.4.21, and the lessons say which version a fact comes from, because several rules changed recently: passing a Job to a builder is deprecated since 1.11, and explicit backing fields became stable in Kotlin 2.4. The labs live in labs/coroutines, one package per lesson (workbench.coroutines.l01 to l11), all in Kotlin, with one Java test in lesson 11 that calls the Kotlin code from Java. Most starting files are buggy code with a KDoc that says what is wrong; a few are TODO()s. From labs/, run ./gradlew :coroutines:test --tests 'workbench.coroutines.lNN.*' until it passes, and solutionTest to check the reference answers. Nearly every test runs on virtual time with runTest, so a test of a 30-second wait finishes in milliseconds. The Try-it demos run with ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=..., and almost every Kotlin demo has a Java twin with the closest Java equivalent. suspend lets a function pause without blocking its thread, like a bookmark in the recipe; the dispatcher, not suspend, decides which thread runs it. Wrap callbacks with suspendCancellableCoroutine. Every coroutine lives in a tree: parents wait for children, cancellation flows down, failures flow up. Use coroutineScope for work the caller waits for, an owned scope for work that outlives a call, and never GlobalScope. Blocking calls go on Dispatchers.IO (or a limitedParallelism view sized to the resource), CPU work on Default, and withContext switches and comes back. Cancellation is cooperative and travels as CancellationException: check in CPU loops, rethrow it from every catch-all, clean up with NonCancellable, and use runInterruptible for blocking calls. A failed launch or async cancels its parent at once. Supervisors (supervisorScope, SupervisorJob() in a scope's constructor) let children fail alone; handlers only work on roots. Flows are cold and sequential: flowOn moves the upstream, catch handles only upstream errors, onCompletion sees every ending. StateFlow is state (conflated, no repeats); SharedFlow is events (configure its buffer); stateIn with WhileSubscribed shares one upstream. Channels hand each element to one receiver: teams of workers, pipelines and callbackFlow bridges, with select for whichever comes first. Guard compound updates with a Mutex, not a one-thread view, and test timing logic on virtual time with runTest and injected dispatchers. Bridge to Java with future { }, await(), mono { } and awaitSingle(), and choose virtual threads, coroutines or Reactor per part of the program.

h: Kotlin coroutines: track quiz
x: Five coroutines in one runBlocking each call Thread.sleep(100) and print a line. About how long does the program take? About 100 ms, because coroutines run concurrently About 500 ms, because Thread.sleep blocks the one thread they share About 100 ms on a 4-core machine, 125 ms on 2 cores It doesn't compile: Thread.sleep is not allowed in a coroutine runBlocking runs its coroutines on the calling thread, and Thread.sleep blocks that thread, so the five sleeps happen one after another: the cook standing at each pot in turn. delay(100) would suspend instead, and the whole thing would take about 100 ms. What happens here? coroutineScope { launch { delay(100); throw IOException("the oven broke") } launch { delay(1_000); println("salad done") } } salad done prints at 1 s, then the scope throws The exception is logged, and the scope returns normally at 1 s At about 100 ms the second child is cancelled, salad done never prints, and the scope throws IOException Nothing is thrown, because launch swallows exceptions A failed child cancels its parent scope, which cancels the sibling and then rethrows the original exception once every child has stopped. Nothing waits for the full second. A Kotlin program calls a blocking database driver from coroutines, and the database allows 20 connections. Where should the calls run? withContext(Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(20, "db")) inside the code that calls the driver On Dispatchers.Default, because it is the default withContext(Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(20)) Dispatchers.Unconfined, so they start immediately Blocking calls belong on IO, and a view of 20 matches the connections and adds to IO's 64 instead of competing with other blocking work. Default has one thread per core and must never block; a view over Default can't exceed the core count anyway. A poller runs while (true) { runCatching { checkOven(); delay(5_000) } }. When dinner ends, its scope is cancelled. What happens? The loop ends at the next delay The JVM interrupts the thread and the loop ends The loop ends after the current check The loop spins at full speed: every delay throws at once and runCatching swallows it runCatching catches CancellationException like any other Throwable. The coroutine stays cancelled, so each delay throws immediately, gets swallowed, and the loop goes round again. Rethrow CancellationException, or keep the delay outside the catch. To stop a failed thank-you text from cancelling the rest of a dinner, someone writes launch(SupervisorJob()) { texts.send(guest) } inside coroutineScope. What did they get? A supervised child that the scope still waits for A child cut loose from the tree: the scope doesn't wait for it or cancel it, and its failure goes to a handler A compile error The same as supervisorScope A Job in a builder's context replaces the parent, so the coroutine becomes a child of a fresh SupervisorJob outside the dinner's tree. kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 deprecates the pattern. Use supervisorScope { }, or a supervisor scope owned by a long-lived class. orders.map { parse(it) }.catch { emit(FALLBACK) }.collect { pantry.save(it) }. pantry.save throws IOException. What does the caller of collect see? The IOException Nothing: catch emits FALLBACK and the flow continues An IllegalStateException about exception transparency FALLBACK saved in place of the failed order catch only handles exceptions from above it. The save runs in the collector, below catch, so its exception passes straight through. Move the save into onEach above catch if the fallback should cover it. Every change of a dish's status must reach both the kitchen log and the screen in the hall, and none may be lost when a callback that can't suspend publishes a burst of them. Which holder fits?
