It is cancelled, because its future completed It keeps running, and the result is thrown away Its thread is interrupted The whole scope behind the door is cancelled The coroutine started by future { } is cancelled when its future is cancelled or otherwise completed, and orTimeout completes that same future exceptionally. Only that coroutine stops; the scope and its other children carry on.

h: Suspend functions from zero · One cook, five pots: a suspend function waits without holding its thread
x: Start with what a program does while it waits. Picture code that asks a slow web service, a program on another computer that answers over the network, for something. It waits 120 ms for the answer, then asks a second service and waits 30 ms more. Nearly all of its time is waiting. That code runs on a thread, one path of work through the program, with its own stack of method calls. A thread that waits in the usual way is blocked: it holds its memory and does nothing else until the answer comes. That's the cook standing at the pot. The Kotlin docs put the cost plainly: a thread usually needs a few megabytes of memory, and a JVM, the program that runs compiled Kotlin and Java code, typically handles a few thousand of them at once. Kotlin's answer is the suspend function, a function that can pause in the middle and carry on later, without holding its thread while it's paused: Java // Java equivalent: plain blocking calls on a virtual thread (JDK 21+); the JVM does the pausing Soup makeSoup() { Stock stock = boilStock(); // the virtual thread unmounts while it waits return addVegetables(stock); // and here } Kotlin suspend fun makeSoup(): Soup { val stock = boilStock() // may pause here return addVegetables(stock) // and here } When makeSoup pauses inside boilStock, the thread leaves and does other work. When the stock is ready, makeSoup carries on at the next line. The code still reads from top to bottom, with normal try/catch and normal return values. A coroutine is one running piece of such code: work that can be paused and resumed. It's one dish on the go. A suspension point is a call to another suspend function, a place where the coroutine may pause. You start a coroutine with a builder, a function such as runBlocking or launch, which lesson 2 of this track covers. Two rules follow. You can call a suspend function only from another suspend function or from inside a coroutine. Plain code has no bookmark to hand over, so the compiler refuses. (We'll see the bookmark in the third section.) The waiting itself must be a suspending call. delay(200) suspends: the coroutine sets a timer and steps aside, and the thread is free. Thread.sleep(200) blocks: the thread stops, and every other coroutine that needs that thread waits too. The compiler accepts both without a word. Let's watch the difference. SleepVsDelay, in the Try it below, uses runBlocking, which runs coroutines on the one thread that called it, here main. That thread is our cook. It starts five coroutines, the pots, and each one waits 200 ms. Predict first: with delay, the five waits should overlap, so the run should take a little over 200 ms. On this machine, while other programs kept it busy, it printed: pot 0 starts simmering on main pot 1 starts simmering on main pot 2 starts simmering on main pot 3 starts simmering on main pot 4 starts simmering on main 5 pots of 200 ms with delay took 358 ms All five lines appeared at once, and the run took 358 ms: the 200 ms of waiting, plus start-up on a busy machine. Now change one word, and pass sleep: 5 pots of 200 ms with Thread.sleep took 1130 ms Same code, one word changed, and the cook is back at the pot. Each sleep held the only thread, so the five waits ran one after another, and the lines appeared 200 ms apart. A coroutine frees its thread only while it's suspended. Wait with delay, never with Thread.sleep. So suspend lets a function step away from the stove. But who comes back to it, and on which thread? Five pots on one thread Read SleepVsDelay.kt. All five coroutines, the pots, run on main, the one cook. Predict the total time with delay. Run it with the command below. Run it again with -Pargs=sleep added. Predict first, then watch how the five lines appear. SleepVsDelay.kt package workbench.coroutines.l01 import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis /** Five pots share ONE thread, our one cook, and each simmers 200 ms. Pass "sleep" to block instead of suspend. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val blocking = args.firstOrNull() == "sleep" val took = measureTimeMillis { runBlocking { // runs every coroutine below on the main thread repeat(5) { i -> launch { println("pot $i starts simmering on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") if (blocking) Thread.sleep(200) else delay(200) } } } } val how = if (blocking) "Thread.sleep" else "delay" println("5 pots of 200 ms with $how took $took ms") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l01.SleepVsDelayKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l01/SleepVsDelay.kt SleepVsDelayJava.java // Java equivalent of SleepVsDelay.kt: one thread, five pots that simmer 200 ms each. // A non-blocking timer callback plays the role of delay; Thread.sleep blocks the one thread. package workbench.coroutines.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class SleepVsDelayJava { public static void main(String[] args) { boolean blocking = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("sleep"); ExecutorService oneThread = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(r -> new Thread(r, "the-cook")); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<CompletableFuture<Void>> pots = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { int id = i; CompletableFuture<Void> done = new CompletableFuture<>(); oneThread.execute(() -> { System.out.println("pot " + id + " starts simmering on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); if (blocking) { sleep(200); // holds the only thread done.complete(null); } else { // a timer completes it later; the thread is free meanwhile CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, oneThread).execute(() -> done.complete(null)); } }); pots.add(done); } CompletableFuture.allOf(pots.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join(); oneThread.shutdown(); String how = blocking ? "Thread.sleep" : "a timer callback"; System.out.printf("5 pots of 200 ms with %s took %d ms%n", how, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } private static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l01.SleepVsDelayJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l01/SleepVsDelayJava.java With delay the five lines appear at once and the run takes a little over 200 ms on an idle machine (358 and 427 ms in two runs here, on a busy one): the waits overlap on one thread. With Thread.sleep it takes over a second (1,130 ms here), and the lines appear 200 ms apart, because each sleep holds the only thread. Same code, one word changed. The Java twin shows the same two pictures (234 ms and 1,032 ms here): a timer callback on a single-thread executor is the closest Java match for delay.

h: Suspend functions from zero · suspend doesn't choose a thread: the code runs wherever it's called
x: The most common wrong idea about coroutines is that suspend sends work to a background thread. It doesn't. The word adds the ability to pause, and nothing else. Which thread runs the code is decided by the coroutine's dispatcher, the part of the coroutine library that hands coroutines to threads (lesson 4 of this track). Here's a suspend function with nothing to wait for. It scales a recipe written for four people to any number of guests: Java // Java equivalent: the same plain method; in Kotlin the suspend modifier changed nothing int scaleRecipe(List<Integer> gramsForFour, int guests) { int total = 0; for (int g : gramsForFour) total += g * guests / 4; return total; } Kotlin suspend fun scaleRecipe(gramsForFour: List<Int>, guests: Int): Int { var total = 0 for (g in gramsForFour) total += g * guests / 4 return total // no suspension point anywhere } scaleRecipe never suspends, so it runs from start to finish on the caller's thread, exactly like a normal function. IntelliJ IDEA, the editor JetBrains makes for Kotlin, greys out the modifier as redundant. Put a two-second calculation in a suspend function, and the thread that calls it is busy for two seconds. In the kitchen, that's chopping: the cook can't put a bookmark in the middle of slicing an onion. Now the other half of the story. After a real suspension, the coroutine may carry on on a different thread. Picture the kitchen on a busy night, with friends helping. When the soup's timer rings, whichever cook is free opens the book at the bookmark. Dispatchers.Default, the library's ready-made pool of threads, works like that. It has one thread per core, a part of the processor that runs one thread at a time. A coroutine can start on worker-1, pause in delay, and resume on worker-3. WhichThread, in the Try it below, shows both halves. It prints where scaleRecipe ran. Then it starts four dishes on Default, and each one notes its thread, pauses 20 ms, and does that four times. One run printed: main coroutine runs on main scaleRecipe says 2000 g, computed on main dish 1 ran on worker-2 -> worker-4 -> worker-4 -> worker-4 dish 3 ran on worker-4 -> worker-4 -> worker-4 -> worker-4 dish 0 ran on worker-1 -> worker-4 -> worker-4 -> worker-4 dish 2 ran on worker-3 -> worker-4 -> worker-4 -> worker-4 scaleRecipe ran on main, the caller's thread. Three of the four dishes started on one worker and finished on another, and none of them noticed. Two things follow for your code. A ThreadLocal, a variable with a separate value for each thread, isn't safe across a suspension point, because the thread that resumes you may hold someone else's value. It's a note pinned to the cook's apron: when another cook picks up the dish, the note stays with the first cook. Lesson 4 of this track shows the coroutine way to carry such a note. Memory visibility, on the other hand, is taken care of. Values a coroutine wrote before it paused are visible after it resumes, even on another thread, so you don't need @Volatile on its locals. The reason is the hand-off. To resume you on another thread, the dispatcher submits your coroutine to its pool as a task. The JDK's rule for executors, the pools that run submitted tasks, then applies: whatever a thread wrote before it submitted a task is visible to the thread that runs it. The memory model track calls that a happens-before edge. It covers one coroutine's own state. Two coroutines that share a variable still need a lock or an atomic, the tools from the first track, as lesson 10 of this track shows. suspend gives a function the right to pause, not a thread of its own. Move work to another thread on purpose. How can a function stop in the middle on one thread and carry on, with all its local variables, on another? Somebody has to write the bookmark, and that somebody is the compiler. Watch dishes change threads Read WhichThread.kt. Predict which thread runs scaleRecipe. Run it. Look at the dish N ran on lines. Run it twice more. Do the thread sequences repeat? WhichThread.kt package workbench.coroutines.l01 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking private fun where() = Thread.currentThread().name.removePrefix("DefaultDispatcher-") /** A suspend function that never suspends runs on its caller's thread, start to finish. */ suspend fun scaleRecipe(gramsForFour: List<Int>, guests: Int): Int { var total = 0 for (g in gramsForFour) total += g * guests / 4 return total // no suspension point anywhere: plain code with a suspend label on it } fun main() = runBlocking { println("main coroutine runs on ${where()}") println("scaleRecipe says ${scaleRecipe(listOf(400, 250, 120, 30), 10)} g, computed on ${where()}") repeat(4) { id -> launch(Dispatchers.Default) { val seen = mutableListOf<String>() repeat(4) { seen += where() delay(20) // suspends; any free Default thread may resume it } println("dish $id ran on ${seen.joinToString(" -> ")}") } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l01.WhichThreadKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l01/WhichThread.kt WhichThreadJava.java // Java equivalent of WhichThread.kt: virtual threads also move between carrier threads. // A plain method runs on its caller's thread; a virtual thread that sleeps may wake up on another carrier. package workbench.coroutines.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; public class WhichThreadJava { static int scaleRecipe(List<Integer> gramsForFour, int guests) { // the same code as the Kotlin suspend fun: it never pauses int total = 0; for (int g : gramsForFour) total += g * guests / 4; return total; } // a virtual thread prints as VirtualThread[#29]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3; keep the carrier part static String carrier() { String s = Thread.currentThread().toString(); int at = s.indexOf('@'); return at < 0 ? Thread.currentThread().getName() : s.substring(at + 1).replace("ForkJoinPool-1-", ""); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.println("main runs on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); System.out.println("scaleRecipe says " + scaleRecipe(List.of(400, 250, 120, 30), 10) + " g, computed on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); List<Thread> dishes = new ArrayList<>(); for (int id = 0; id < 4; id++) { int dish = id; dishes.add(Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { List<String> seen = new ArrayList<>(); for (int step = 0; step < 4; step++) { seen.add(carrier()); try { Thread.sleep(20); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } // unmounts; any carrier may resume it } System.out.println("dish " + dish + " ran on " + String.join(" -> ", seen)); })); } for (Thread t : dishes) t.join(); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l01.WhichThreadJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l01/WhichThreadJava.java scaleRecipe runs on main, the caller's thread. Each dish shows a sequence such as worker-1 -> worker-4 -> worker-4 -> worker-4: after each delay, any free Default thread may pick it up. The sequences change from run to run. The Java twin shows the same thing for virtual threads: after each Thread.sleep, a virtual thread may carry on on a different carrier, the platform thread that runs it.

h: Suspend functions from zero · The bookmark the compiler writes: a suspend function becomes a state machine
x: The cook's bookmark: a suspend function becomes a state machine, and one small continuation object keeps its step and its local variables Coroutines need no special support from the JVM. They're a compiler feature plus a library, kotlinx.coroutines. Here's the function we'll take apart. It makes a sauce in two steps, and each step waits: Java // Java equivalent: the same steps on a virtual thread (JDK 21+); the JVM saves the whole stack instead String makeSauce(String onions) { String base = fryOnions(onions); // blocks; the virtual thread unmounts String sauce = simmer(base); // and here return sauce; } Kotlin suspend fun makeSauce(onions: String): String { val base = fryOnions(onions) // suspension point 1 val sauce = simmer(base) // suspension point 2 return sauce } The Kotlin compiler rewrites every suspend function in continuation-passing style: it adds one hidden last parameter, a Continuation, and changes the return type to Any?. javap, the JDK tool that prints what's inside a compiled class, shows it: // you write suspend fun makeSauce(onions: String): String // javap shows public static final java.lang.Object makeSauce(java.lang.String, kotlin.coroutines.Continuation<? super java.lang.String>); A continuation is the bookmark: an object that knows how to carry on a paused coroutine. Its interface is short: interface Continuation<in T> { val context: CoroutineContext; fun resumeWith(result: Result<T>) }. The context holds the coroutine's settings, which lesson 4 of this track opens up. resumeWith is how someone says "the wait is over, here's the value". The Object return is either the real result or a marker, COROUTINE_SUSPENDED, which means "I paused; I'll call your continuation later". The body becomes a state machine, a class with a counter that says which step comes next. Each suspension point ends a state. For makeSauce, the compiler generates one small class, StateMachineKt$makeSauce$1. It has an int label for the next state and two fields, L$0 and L$1, where local variables wait while the function is paused. Let's follow it: Label 0: save the locals in the object, set label = 1, and call fryOnions(onions, this). If that returns COROUTINE_SUSPENDED, return the marker straight up the stack. The thread is now free. When the onions are golden, someone calls resumeWith(base). That calls makeSauce again, with the same object. A tableswitch, the JVM's instruction for a switch over a small range of ints, jumps on label to state 1, which picks up base and calls simmer. Label 2: take the sauce and return it to whoever is waiting. If fryOnions doesn't suspend (the onions were fried earlier, say), it returns its value at once and the function carries on. Nothing is scheduled, and no thread changes. The bookmark from the opening is exactly that object. label is the page, and the L$ fields are the sticky note of what's already measured. You met a bigger bookmark in How virtual threads work. There, the JVM copied a virtual thread's whole stack to the heap, the memory where objects live, every frame of it, like a full order slip clipped to the board. A coroutine's bookmark is smaller: one small object for each suspend function still running, holding only that function's own fields. That explains both the cost and the rules. A suspended coroutine is a few small objects, not a thread's stack, so you can have hundreds of thousands. And plain code can't call a suspend function, because it has no continuation to pass in. Here the picture breaks a little. A real cook hears the timer and walks back to the book herself. A paused coroutine does nothing at all until something calls resumeWith: the library's timer, for delay, or the code that got the answer. If nothing ever calls it, the coroutine stays paused for good. A suspended coroutine is a bookmark, not a thread. Something has to call resumeWith to wake it. So who calls resumeWith when the answer comes from someone else's code? Read the state machine with javap Run the demo once, so Gradle compiles it: ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l01.StateMachineKt. From labs/, run the first javap command. Find the Continuation parameter and the Object return type on makeSauce. Run the second command. It prints the generated state class, the bookmark. Find label and the L$ fields. Run the third command. It prints one tableswitch for each of the three suspend functions. Predict first: how many cases will the one for makeSauce, the last of the three, have? terminal javap -p coroutines/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/coroutines/l01/StateMachineKt.class javap -p 'coroutines/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/coroutines/l01/StateMachineKt$makeSauce$1.class' javap -c -p coroutines/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/coroutines/l01/StateMachineKt.class | grep -A4 tableswitch makeSauce(java.lang.String, kotlin.coroutines.Continuation<? super java.lang.String>) returns java.lang.Object, and so do fryOnions and simmer. The state class extends kotlin.coroutines.jvm.internal.ContinuationImpl and has L$0, L$1, result and int label. The first two tableswitches say 0 to 1: they belong to fryOnions and simmer, which pause once each. The third, in makeSauce, says 0 to 2: three states for two suspension points. Each suspension point ends a state. Suspending returns a marker and frees the thread; resuming calls the same function again, and the saved label, the bookmark, says where to carry on. KEEP: Kotlin coroutines design (continuations and state machines) read

h: Suspend functions from zero · Wrapping a callback in a suspend function, so a cancel can reach it
x: Many libraries don't offer suspend functions. They take a callback, a function you pass in that the library calls later with the answer. Picture a bakery with an ordering library. You place an order, the call returns at once, and the library calls you back when the bread is ready. (A library that a company hands out for talking to its service is often called an SDK, a software development kit.) suspendCancellableCoroutine turns such a callback into a suspend function. It suspends the coroutine and hands you its continuation, and you resume it when the callback fires: Java // Java equivalent: complete a CompletableFuture from the callback, and pass cancellation back CompletableFuture<String> orderAsync(BakerySdk bakery, String bread) { CompletableFuture<String> result = new CompletableFuture<>(); Runnable cancel = bakery.order(bread, result::complete); // 1. order; complete on the callback result.whenComplete((v, e) -> { if (e != null) cancel.run(); }); // 2. timed out or cancelled: tell the bakery return result; } Kotlin suspend fun BakerySdk.orderAwait(bread: String): String = suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont -> val cancel = order(bread) { ticket -> cont.resume(ticket) } // 1. order; resume on the callback cont.invokeOnCancellation { cancel() } // 2. we were cancelled: tell the bakery } Read the Kotlin version aloud: "Pause here and place the order. When the bakery calls back, carry on with its ticket. If we're cancelled first, cancel the order." The order call returns a small function that cancels the order, and that's the cancel we keep. Why the long name? The standard library also has a plain suspendCoroutine, and it works fine until someone cancels the caller, that is, asks the coroutine to stop. Our caller uses withTimeout(100), which cancels its block if it isn't done in 100 ms. CallbackBridge, in the Try it below, wraps the bakery with the plain version first. The bakery takes a full second, as bakeries do. Predict: when does withTimeout(100) return? timed out withTimeout(100) returned after 1021 ms Not after 100 ms: after a whole second. The timeout did fire at 100 ms. But a coroutine paused in suspendCoroutine can't react to the cancel. It stays paused until the bakery calls back, and the bakery never hears that anyone gave up. With the cancellable version and invokeOnCancellation, the same run printed: bakery: order for sourdough cancelled timed out withTimeout(100) returned after 135 ms The order was cancelled, and the caller was free after about 100 ms, plus a little for the busy machine. Three rules make a wrapper like this correct. Resume exactly once. Call resume with a value or resumeWithException with an error. A second resume on the same continuation throws IllegalStateException. Use the cancellable version, and tell the library when you give up, in invokeOnCancellation. Expect late replies. If the coroutine is cancelled first, a callback that arrives afterwards is ignored. kotlinx.coroutines calls this the prompt cancellation guarantee: a cancelled coroutine doesn't resume successfully, even if the value was already on its way. If that late value is something you must give back, such as a borrowed pot, pass a cleanup function: cont.resume(pot) { _, late, _ -> late.close() }. The library calls it with the value it couldn't deliver. The worked example below builds exactly that. A callback wrapper must resume once and pass the cancel on. Use suspendCancellableCoroutine. This tool is for callbacks that fire once. Listeners that fire many times need callbackFlow (lesson 9 of this track). A CompletableFuture needs none of this, because future.await() already does it (lesson 11 of this track). Make a timeout reach the bakery Read CallbackBridge.kt. The bakery answers after one second. The caller allows 100 ms. Predict how long withTimeout(100) takes to return. Run it. Change orderAwait to use suspendCancellableCoroutine (import kotlinx.coroutines.suspendCancellableCoroutine). Keep the function the library returns: val cancel = order(bread) { ticket -> cont.resume(ticket) }, then add cont.invokeOnCancellation { cancel() }. Run it again. In the Java twin, run it, then add result.whenComplete((v, e) -> { if (e != null) cancel.run(); }); before return result; and run it again. CallbackBridge.kt package workbench.coroutines.l01 import kotlinx.coroutines.TimeoutCancellationException import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeout import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import kotlin.coroutines.resume import kotlin.coroutines.suspendCoroutine import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis /** A bakery's ordering library with a callback API. It answers after 1 second, on its own thread. */ class BakerySdk { private val pool = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor { r -> Thread(r, "bakery-sdk").apply { isDaemon = true } } fun order(bread: String, onReady: (String) -> Unit): () -> Unit { val task = pool.schedule({ onReady("ticket 17: one $bread") }, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS) return { println(" bakery: order for $bread cancelled"); task.cancel(false) } } } // Wrapped with suspendCoroutine: works, but cancellation cannot reach it. suspend fun BakerySdk.orderAwait(bread: String): String = suspendCoroutine { cont -> order(bread) { ticket -> cont.resume(ticket) } } fun main() = runBlocking { val bakery = BakerySdk() val took = measureTimeMillis { try { withTimeout(100) { bakery.orderAwait("sourdough") } } catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) { println(" timed out") } } println("withTimeout(100) returned after $took ms") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l01.CallbackBridgeKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l01/CallbackBridge.kt CallbackBridgeJava.java // Java equivalent of CallbackBridge.kt: wrap the bakery's callback library in a CompletableFuture. // The bakery answers after 1 second; the caller allows 100 ms. package workbench.coroutines.l01; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; import java.util.function.Consumer; public class CallbackBridgeJava { /** A bakery's ordering library with a callback API. It answers after 1 second, on its own thread. */ static final class BakerySdk { private final ScheduledExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "bakery-sdk"); t.setDaemon(true); return t; }); Runnable order(String bread, Consumer<String> onReady) { ScheduledFuture<?> task = pool.schedule(() -> onReady.accept("ticket 17: one " + bread), 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); return () -> { System.out.println(" bakery: order for " + bread + " cancelled"); task.cancel(false); }; } } // Wrapped as a future: the caller can time out, but nothing tells the bakery yet. static CompletableFuture<String> orderAsync(BakerySdk bakery, String bread) { CompletableFuture<String> result = new CompletableFuture<>(); Runnable cancel = bakery.order(bread, result::complete); return result; } public static void main(String[] args) { BakerySdk bakery = new BakerySdk(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { orderAsync(bakery, "sourdough").orTimeout(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).join(); } catch (CompletionException e) { if (e.getCause() instanceof TimeoutException) System.out.println(" timed out"); } System.out.printf("orTimeout(100) returned after %d ms%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); try { Thread.sleep(1_100); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } // was the bakery told? } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l01.CallbackBridgeJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l01/CallbackBridgeJava.java First run: timed out after about 1,000 ms (1,021 ms here). The timeout did fire at 100 ms, but suspendCoroutine couldn't wake up until the bakery answered, and the bakery was never told. After the change: bakery: order for sourdough cancelled, then timed out after about 100 ms (135 ms here). The Java twin returns at about 100 ms even before your change (114 ms here), because orTimeout completes the future by itself. But the bakery hears about it only once you add the whenComplete hook (123 ms here). suspendCancellableCoroutine (API reference) docs

h: Suspend functions from zero · Java and Kotlin
x: Two waits in a row: CompletableFuture vs suspend Sauce.java CompletableFuture<String> makeSauce(String onions) { return kitchen.fryOnions(onions) // CompletableFuture<String> .thenCompose(base -> kitchen.simmer(base)) // CompletableFuture<String> .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } Sauce.kt suspend fun makeSauce(onions: String): String = withTimeout(2.seconds) { val base = kitchen.fryOnions(onions) // suspend fun kitchen.simmer(base) // suspend fun } Both versions free the thread while they wait. The Java version says "then" with callbacks: each thenCompose registers a function to run later, errors arrive wrapped in CompletionException, and orTimeout only completes the outer future with an error. The two calls underneath keep running, because cancelling a CompletableFuture never interrupts the work behind it. The Kotlin version reads like plain blocking code: locals, try/catch and loops all work, and the compiler builds the callbacks for you. When withTimeout fires, it cancels the coroutine, and the cancel reaches both calls if they're written to cooperate, as in the last section. On JDK 21 and later you can also write the Java version as plain blocking calls on a virtual thread. Lesson 11 of this track helps you choose between the two.

h: Suspend functions from zero · Worked example
x: Wrap a pot-lending library without losing pots A community kitchen lends out big stock pots. Its library's borrow returns a Ticket at once and calls you back later with a pot or an error. Every pot must be given back, which is what its close() does. You want suspend fun PotLender.borrowAwait(): Pot. class Pot(val id: Int) : AutoCloseable { override fun close() { /* back to the shelf */ } } fun interface Ticket { fun cancel() } interface PotLender { fun borrow(onReady: (Pot?, Throwable?) -> Unit): Ticket } // Java equivalent: the same library shape final class Pot implements AutoCloseable { @Override public void close() { /* back to the shelf */ } } interface Ticket { void cancel(); } interface PotLender { Ticket borrow(BiConsumer<Pot, Throwable> onReady); } Ask for the pot inside suspendCancellableCoroutine, and resume exactly once from the callback: a value on success, an exception on error. suspend fun PotLender.borrowAwait(): Pot = suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont -> // 1. ask for a pot; the library calls back on its own thread val ticket = borrow { pot, error -> // 2. resume exactly once, with a value or an error if (error != null) cont.resumeWithException(error) else cont.resume(pot!!) } } // Java equivalent: complete a CompletableFuture from the callback static CompletableFuture<Pot> borrowAsync(PotLender lender) { CompletableFuture<Pot> result = new CompletableFuture<>(); // 1. ask for a pot; the library calls back on its own thread Ticket ticket = lender.borrow((pot, error) -> { // 2. complete exactly once, with a value or an error if (error != null) result.completeExceptionally(error); else result.complete(pot); }); return result; } If the caller gives up, stop waiting for a pot. invokeOnCancellation runs when the coroutine is cancelled while it's suspended here. // 3. our caller gave up: cancel the ticket cont.invokeOnCancellation { ticket.cancel() } // 3. our caller gave up (cancelled the future): cancel the ticket result.whenComplete((p, e) -> { if (result.isCancelled()) ticket.cancel(); }); One gap is left. The kitchen may hand out a pot just after you were cancelled. The continuation ignores that late resume, and the pot never goes back on the shelf. Use the resume overload that takes a cleanup function: the library calls it with the value it couldn't deliver. else cont.resume(pot!!) { _, late, _ -> late.close() } // 4. a late pot: give it back // 4. a late pot: complete() returns false when the future is already done, so give it back else if (!result.complete(pot)) pot.close(); Self-check: why is step 4 needed even though step 3 cancels the ticket? (Cancelling is a request. The kitchen may already be calling you back on another thread, so the pot can still arrive after you were cancelled.)

h: Suspend functions from zero · Quiz
x: This runs on one thread: runBlocking { repeat(3) { launch { Thread.sleep(100) } } }. About how long does it take? About 100 ms, because the three coroutines run concurrently About 300 ms, because each sleep blocks the only thread About 0 ms, because launch returns at once It doesn't compile: Thread.sleep isn't allowed in a coroutine Thread.sleep blocks the thread, and runBlocking gives all three coroutines one thread, so they sleep one after another. With delay(100) they would overlap and finish in about 100 ms. The compiler happily accepts Thread.sleep here, which is why the bug survives code review. suspend fun scaleRecipe(gramsForFour: List<Int>, guests: Int): Int is pure arithmetic with no suspending calls. A coroutine on thread worker-2 calls it. Which thread runs the arithmetic? worker-2, the caller's thread A thread from Dispatchers.IO A new background thread for each call A thread the JVM picks at random A suspend function that never suspends is ordinary code on the caller's thread. suspend doesn't move work anywhere. To run CPU work elsewhere you switch dispatcher on purpose, with withContext(Dispatchers.Default), which lesson 4 of this track covers. How does suspend fun stockOf(item: String): Int look to a Java caller? int stockOf(String item) CompletableFuture<Integer> stockOf(String item) Object stockOf(String item, Continuation<? super Integer> continuation) void stockOf(String item, Consumer<Integer> callback) The compiler adds a Continuation as the last parameter and changes the return type to Object, which holds either the result (boxed) or COROUTINE_SUSPENDED. That's why Java code can't simply call suspend functions; lesson 11 of this track shows the bridges, such as future {}. A callback library is wrapped with suspendCoroutine, not the cancellable version. The caller runs withTimeout(200) { library.callAwait() }, and the library answers after 3 seconds. What happens? TimeoutCancellationException at 200 ms, and the library call is cancelled The call returns the library's value after 3 seconds; the timeout is ignored IllegalStateException, because the continuation was resumed twice The coroutine stays suspended until the library answers at 3 s, then throws TimeoutCancellationException; the library is never told The timeout cancels the coroutine at 200 ms, but a continuation that can't be cancelled can't wake up until it's resumed. When the library answers at 3 s, the coroutine finds itself cancelled and throws. suspendCancellableCoroutine would resume at 200 ms and run invokeOnCancellation, where you cancel the library call. From the virtual threads track: a virtual thread calls Thread.sleep(200). What happens to its carrier thread? The carrier is blocked for the full 200 ms The virtual thread unmounts, and the carrier is free to run other virtual threads The JVM creates a new carrier to replace it sleep throws, because virtual threads can't sleep When a virtual thread blocks in sleep, the JVM saves its stack and unmounts it, so the carrier runs other virtual threads. It's the same idea as a coroutine suspending, done by the JVM for any blocking call instead of by the Kotlin compiler for suspend calls.

h: Suspend functions from zero · Key terms
x: Thread One path of work through a program, with its own stack of method calls. In the kitchen, a pair of hands. Coroutine One running piece of work that can pause and resume later, without holding a thread while it's paused. Suspend function A function marked suspend. It may pause at suspending calls, and it can only be called from a coroutine or another suspend function. Suspension point A call to a suspend function, where the caller may pause. It doesn't always pause, for example when the answer is already there. Continuation The object that knows how to resume a paused coroutine: its context plus resumeWith(result). The bookmark in the recipe. COROUTINE_SUSPENDED The marker a compiled suspend function returns to say it paused and will resume through the continuation. Continuation-passing style Compiling a function so it receives "what to do next" as an extra parameter, instead of returning to a waiting caller. Dispatcher The part of the coroutine library that decides which thread runs a coroutine, and which thread it resumes on. Does suspend run a function on a background thread? No. It only lets the function pause without blocking. The dispatcher decides the thread, and a suspend function that never suspends runs on its caller's thread. Inside a coroutine, what's the difference between delay(200) and Thread.sleep(200)? delay suspends the coroutine and frees the thread for others. Thread.sleep blocks the thread, so every coroutine waiting for that thread waits too. What does the compiler add to a suspend function's signature? A Continuation<T> as the last parameter. The return type becomes Any? (Object in Java). What does a compiled suspend function return when it pauses? The marker COROUTINE_SUSPENDED. The real result arrives later through continuation.resumeWith(...). Where does a suspended coroutine keep its local variables? In fields (L$0, L$1, ...) of a small state-machine object on the heap, next to an int label that says which state runs next. Why wrap a callback with suspendCancellableCoroutine and not suspendCoroutine? Only the cancellable one reacts to cancellation: it resumes the caller at once with CancellationException and runs invokeOnCancellation, where you cancel the underlying call. A callback fires after its coroutine was cancelled. What happens to cont.resume(value)? It's ignored (the prompt cancellation guarantee). If the value must be given back, pass a cleanup function: cont.resume(value) { _, v, _ -> v.close() }.

h: Suspend functions from zero · Go deeper
x: Kotlin coroutines and Java virtual threads both rest on continuations, but they keep them in different places. Kotlin's continuations are stackless. The compiler rewrites each suspend function into a state machine, and a suspended coroutine is a chain of those small state objects, one for each suspend function still in progress. That's why suspend is part of the function's type: every function between the coroutine and the suspending call must be compiled this way, or there's nowhere to save its state. People call this function coloring: suspend functions have a different color, and the color spreads to every caller. It's also why coroutines work on any JVM version, on Android, and on Kotlin/JS and Kotlin/Native, where there are no virtual threads. Virtual threads use stackful continuations inside the JVM. When a virtual thread blocks, the JVM copies its stack frames to the heap and unmounts it from the carrier. Any blocking call, in any library, can pause it, with no change to the code and no coloring. The price is that the JVM decides when to pause, and code that holds a monitor or calls native code could pin the carrier on older JDKs (JDK 24 removed most pinning on synchronized, JEP 491). Neither is free of surprises. A coroutine pauses only where you wrote a suspend call, which makes every pause visible in the code but forces the color on every caller. A virtual thread pauses anywhere the JDK blocks, which keeps old code unchanged but hides where the pauses are. Read the "Implementation details" part of the KEEP (linked in the sources) if you want the pseudo-Java the compiler generates, including how the generated invokeSuspend method re-enters the function.

h: Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope · launch starts a coroutine and hands you a Job
x: A coroutine builder is a plain function that starts a coroutine. A coroutine is a piece of work that can pause and resume without holding its thread, the worker that runs the code. You'll use four every day: launch, async, coroutineScope and runBlocking. They differ in what they give back, and in whether the caller waits. launch starts a coroutine and returns a Job at once. Use it for work whose result you don't need, such as setting the table: Java // Java equivalent: start a virtual thread, keep the handle, join it later Thread table = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> setTable()); // returns at once String sauce = makeSauce("onions"); // carries on meanwhile table.join(); // block until the table is set Kotlin val table: Job = launch { setTable() } // returns at once val sauce = makeSauce("onions") // carries on meanwhile table.join() // suspend until the table is set A Job is a handle to the coroutine's life. You can ask it isActive and isCompleted, wait for it with join(), or stop it with cancel(). It holds no value. And if the coroutine throws, the exception doesn't come back through the Job. It goes to the coroutine's parent, which lessons 3 and 6 of this track cover. launch is an extension function on CoroutineScope, so you can call it only where a scope exists: inside runBlocking, inside coroutineScope, or inside another coroutine. A scope keeps track of the coroutines started in it. That limit is on purpose. The scope becomes the new coroutine's parent, and the parent is what stops work from getting lost. One detail surprises almost everyone. launch doesn't run its block right away. It gives the block to the dispatcher, the part of the library that hands coroutines to threads, and returns. Inside runBlocking, which runs everything on one thread, the new coroutine gets to run only when the current one suspends or finishes. So the line after launch usually runs first. Let's test that. LaunchAndAsync, in the Try it below, prints seven lines, A to G, all on one thread. It launches a job that sets the table, which takes 100 ms, and starts an async that checks the oven, which takes 50 ms. Then it prints a line, waits for the oven's answer and joins the table. Write down your order before you read on. It printed: A: before the builders B: builders returned, table.isActive=true C: table: start setting it D: oven: checking the temperature E: oven is at 180 degrees F: table: set G: table.isCompleted=true B came before C. Both builders only queued their blocks, and the one thread was still busy with the body of main. C and D ran when main paused in await, waiting for the oven. And the Job already said isActive=true for a table nobody had touched yet: a job counts as active from the moment it's created until it finishes. So launch starts work and gives back a handle, but no answer. For the oven's temperature, we needed its partner, async. Predict the order Read LaunchAndAsync.kt. Everything runs on the one thread that runBlocking owns. Write down the order in which the seven lines A to G will print. The letters are not a hint. Run it and compare. For each line you got wrong, find the suspension point that explains it. LaunchAndAsync.kt package workbench.coroutines.l02 import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking /** Predict the order of the lines before you run it. Everything runs on one thread. */ fun main() = runBlocking { println("A: before the builders") val table = launch { println("C: table: start setting it") delay(100) println("F: table: set") } val oven = async { println("D: oven: checking the temperature") delay(50) 180 } println("B: builders returned, table.isActive=${table.isActive}") println("E: oven is at ${oven.await()} degrees") table.join() println("G: table.isCompleted=${table.isCompleted}") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l02.LaunchAndAsyncKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l02/LaunchAndAsync.kt LaunchAndAsyncJava.java // Java equivalent of LaunchAndAsync.kt: one event-loop thread, tasks queue behind the running one. // Java has no suspension, so "await" becomes a callback (thenAccept) instead of a pause. package workbench.coroutines.l02; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class LaunchAndAsyncJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { ScheduledExecutorService loop = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(r -> new Thread(r, "loop")); loop.execute(() -> { System.out.println("A: before the tasks"); CompletableFuture<Void> table = new CompletableFuture<>(); loop.execute(() -> { // like launch: queued behind the running task System.out.println("C: table: start setting it"); loop.schedule(() -> { System.out.println("F: table: set"); table.complete(null); }, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); }); CompletableFuture<Integer> oven = new CompletableFuture<>(); loop.execute(() -> { // like async System.out.println("D: oven: checking the temperature"); loop.schedule(() -> oven.complete(180), 50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); }); System.out.println("B: tasks queued, table.isDone=" + table.isDone()); oven.thenAccept(t -> System.out.println("E: oven is at " + t + " degrees")) // like await, written as a callback .thenCompose(x -> table) // like join .thenRun(() -> { System.out.println("G: table.isDone=" + table.isDone()); loop.shutdown(); }); }); loop.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l02.LaunchAndAsyncJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l02/LaunchAndAsyncJava.java A, B, C, D, E, F, G. B prints before C because launch and async only schedule their blocks, and the thread is still busy with the body of main. The table job already reports isActive=true. C and D run when main suspends in await. E prints at about 50 ms, F at about 100 ms, and G after join. The Java twin prints the same order on a one-thread executor, but look at its shape: with no suspension, every "await" becomes a callback (thenAccept, thenCompose).

h: Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope · async starts work you collect later: start everything, then await
x: async is launch with a result. It starts a coroutine and returns a Deferred<T> at once. A Deferred is a Job that will also hold a value, like a pot with the lid on: the sauce is coming. await() lifts the lid. It suspends until the value is ready and returns it, or rethrows the exception the coroutine failed with. What async buys you is concurrent decomposition: splitting one job into independent calls, starting them all, and then collecting the answers. Here's the cook's tomato question as code. Each Grocer is a shop we can ask, and price(item) suspends until the shop replies: Java // Java equivalent: blocking calls on virtual threads, started together, joined afterwards List<Price> allPrices(String item) { List<CompletableFuture<Price>> pending = grocers.stream() .map(g -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> g.price(item), vthreads)) // 1. text all three .toList(); return pending.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList(); // 2. then read the replies } Kotlin suspend fun allPrices(item: String): List<Price> = coroutineScope { val pending = grocers.map { g -> async { g.price(item) } } // 1. text all three pending.awaitAll() // 2. then read the replies } (coroutineScope gives the function a scope to start children in. It gets its own section next.) Say the greengrocer takes 300 ms to reply, the market 120 ms and the farm stand 200 ms. Asked one after another, that's 620 ms. Asked together, the total should be the slowest reply, about 300 ms. SequentialVsConcurrent, in the Try it below, measures both, on the same busy machine as before: sequential: [greengrocer:300ms, market:120ms, farm-stand:200ms] in 666 ms concurrent: [greengrocer:300ms, market:120ms, farm-stand:200ms] in 321 ms The same answers in the same order, in about half the time. The extra 20 ms or so is the machine, not the code. The texting picture holds because each shop does its own work while the cook waits. It breaks when the work isn't waiting. Three children that each compute for 300 ms on one thread take 900 ms, async or not, because there's only one cook to do the computing. Now the classic mistake, which is to await too early: Java // Java equivalent of the same mistake: join right after starting Price a = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> greengrocer.price(item), vthreads).join(); // waits 300 ms here Price b = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> market.price(item), vthreads).join(); // then starts this one Kotlin // Naive: this looks concurrent, and isn't val a = async { greengrocer.price(item) }.await() // waits 300 ms right here val b = async { market.price(item) }.await() // and only then starts this one That's the cook who texts one shop and stares at her phone until it answers. The code compiles, runs and passes a test that checks the answers. It's also completely sequential. With the await moved inside the map, the demo's concurrent version took 627 ms, the full sum. Concurrency lives in the gap between starting a Deferred and awaiting it. Overlap happens between async and await. Start everything first, then await. Prefer awaitAll() to map { it.await() }. Both return the results in list order. The difference shows on failure: awaitAll fails as soon as any of them fails, while the map version notices only when it reaches the failed one in the list. And don't use async when you don't need the value. An async that nobody awaits hides what you meant, so use launch. We've been leaning on coroutineScope without looking at it. It does more than give async a place to live. Sequential, concurrent, and accidentally sequential Read SequentialVsConcurrent.kt and predict both timings. Run it. In concurrent(), change the body to latencies.map { (g, ms) -> async { price(g, ms) }.await() } and run again. Predict first. In the Java twin, make the same mistake: replace the body of concurrent with return LATENCIES.stream().map(e -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> price(e.getKey(), e.getValue()), vthreads).join()).toList(); and run it. SequentialVsConcurrent.kt package workbench.coroutines.l02 import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.awaitAll import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis private suspend fun price(grocer: String, latencyMs: Long): String { delay(latencyMs) // stands in for a text message and its reply return "$grocer:${latencyMs}ms" } private val latencies = listOf("greengrocer" to 300L, "market" to 120L, "farm-stand" to 200L) suspend fun sequential(): List<String> = latencies.map { (g, ms) -> price(g, ms) } suspend fun concurrent(): List<String> = coroutineScope { latencies.map { (g, ms) -> async { price(g, ms) } }.awaitAll() } fun main() = runBlocking { var result: List<String> val t1 = measureTimeMillis { result = sequential() } println("sequential: $result in $t1 ms") val t2 = measureTimeMillis { result = concurrent() } println("concurrent: $result in $t2 ms") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l02.SequentialVsConcurrentKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l02/SequentialVsConcurrent.kt SequentialVsConcurrentJava.java // Java equivalent of SequentialVsConcurrent.kt: blocking calls on virtual threads, // started together with CompletableFuture and joined afterwards. package workbench.coroutines.l02; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class SequentialVsConcurrentJava { static String price(String grocer, long latencyMs) { try { Thread.sleep(latencyMs); } catch (InterruptedException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } // a message and its reply return grocer + ":" + latencyMs + "ms"; } static final List<Map.Entry<String, Long>> LATENCIES = List.of(Map.entry("greengrocer", 300L), Map.entry("market", 120L), Map.entry("farm-stand", 200L)); static List<String> sequential() { return LATENCIES.stream().map(e -> price(e.getKey(), e.getValue())).toList(); } static List<String> concurrent(ExecutorService vthreads) { List<CompletableFuture<String>> pending = LATENCIES.stream() .map(e -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> price(e.getKey(), e.getValue()), vthreads)) // start all .toList(); return pending.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList(); // then wait } public static void main(String[] args) { try (ExecutorService vthreads = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<String> r1 = sequential(); System.out.printf("sequential: %s in %d ms%n", r1, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); long t1 = System.nanoTime(); List<String> r2 = concurrent(vthreads); System.out.printf("concurrent: %s in %d ms%n", r2, (System.nanoTime() - t1) / 1_000_000); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l02.SequentialVsConcurrentJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l02/SequentialVsConcurrentJava.java About 620 ms for the sequential version (666 ms here, on a busy machine) and about 300 ms for the concurrent one (321 ms here). After your change, concurrent() takes about 620 ms too (627 ms here): each await runs before the next async starts. The Java twin behaves the same way (663 ms and 318 ms here, then 649 ms with join inside the map). Concurrency happens between starting a Deferred and awaiting it. Ask all three grocers, then await: the total is the slowest reply. Composing suspending functions (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope · coroutineScope waits for every child it started
x: A course waits for its dishes: launch and async return at once, and coroutineScope returns only when every child it started has finished coroutineScope is how a suspend function gets a scope to start children in. It creates a scope, runs the block, and then suspends until every coroutine started inside has finished. Only then does it return the block's value. In the kitchen, it's a course: the starters don't go out until every dish in them is ready. Here's a job for launch inside one. callAhead asks every grocer about bread, just so each shop knows we'll order today, and it ignores the answers: Java // Java equivalent: an executor's close() waits for every task it accepted (JDK 19+) void callAhead() { try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { grocers.forEach(g -> executor.submit(() -> g.price("bread"))); } // returns after the slowest grocer has answered } Kotlin suspend fun callAhead() = coroutineScope { grocers.forEach { g -> launch { g.price("bread") } } } // returns after the slowest grocer has answered That gives your callers a strong promise: when a suspend function returns, the work it started is done. Nothing keeps running behind their back, still texting a shop after dinner is over. Failure travels the same path in reverse. If one child fails, coroutineScope cancels the other children, waits for them to stop, and rethrows the exception to its caller. In allPrices, a grocer that fails at 50 ms makes the whole call fail at about 50 ms, and the other two questions are cancelled instead of left running. Lesson 3 of this track draws this tree of parents and children, and lesson 6 of this track is about the exceptions. coroutineScope suspends; it doesn't block. The thread is free while it waits. It's a suspend function itself, so you call it from suspend code, and you can nest it as deep as you like. The lab's priceList puts allPrices inside another coroutineScope. Two items times three grocers is six questions at once, and the list is still ready in 300 ms. A suspend function should return only when its work is done. coroutineScope makes sure of it. Here are the builders so far, side by side. launch and async start a child and return at once. coroutineScope runs a block and suspends until all of its children are done. You'll rarely write launch or async without a coroutineScope around them, or a scope that a class owns (lesson 3 of this track). Quick check: callAhead() asks three grocers who take 300, 120 and 200 ms, and the 120 ms one throws. When does callAhead return, and what happens to the other two questions? (It throws at about 120 ms. The scope cancels the 300 ms and 200 ms questions, waits for them to stop, and then rethrows the failure.) That leaves one builder, the only one of the four that isn't a suspend function at all.

h: Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope · runBlocking belongs at the edges: main and tests
x: runBlocking is the bridge from ordinary code into coroutines. It starts a coroutine, blocks the current thread until that coroutine and all its children finish, and then returns the result. To block is to hold the thread so it can do nothing else. The children run on that same thread, in a small event loop: a queue of coroutines that the thread runs one at a time. Use it at the edges only: fun main(), tests, and the rare library callback that has to be a plain blocking function. For tests, runTest from kotlinx-coroutines-test is better, because it skips delays (lesson 10 of this track). For main, Kotlin also accepts suspend fun main(). Never call runBlocking from suspend code. The kotlinx.coroutines docs call it redundant there, and warn that it blocks the thread. In a real program it does damage. Suspend code usually runs on a small shared pool of threads. runBlocking holds one of them for as long as the inner work takes, which is exactly what suspending was meant to avoid. It's the cook back at the pot, except that this time she's holding the only ladle. It also ignores the caller's coroutine context, so the caller's cancel and timeouts don't reach the work inside. The cause is in its signature. runBlocking is a plain function, not a suspend one, so its caller passes it no continuation and no context. (Suspend functions from zero showed that hidden parameter.) It starts a fresh coroutine with no parent. RunBlockingTrap, in the Try it below, puts numbers on it. It runs eight 200 ms lookups on a pool of two threads: two cooks for eight dishes. With delay, all eight should overlap and take about 200 ms. With runBlocking { delay(200) } hidden inside the suspend function, each lookup holds a thread for its whole 200 ms. Eight lookups on two threads then need four rounds, about 800 ms. On the busy machine: 8 lookups of 200 ms on 2 threads (delay): 292 ms 8 lookups of 200 ms on 2 threads (runBlocking inside): 858 ms Four rounds, as predicted. The Java twin pays the same price for calling join() inside a pool task (226 ms against 854 ms here). runBlocking holds its thread until the work is done. Keep it in main and tests. If you reach for runBlocking inside suspend code to "just call" another suspend function, you don't need it. Call the function directly. If you need several calls at once, that's coroutineScope with async. Starve a pool with runBlocking Read RunBlockingTrap.kt. Eight lookups share a pool of two threads. Run it as it is, the good version. Note the time. Predict the time with runBlocking inside the suspend function, then run it with -Pargs=bad. RunBlockingTrap.kt package workbench.coroutines.l02 import kotlinx.coroutines.asCoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import java.util.concurrent.Executors import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis /** A suspend function that "helpfully" calls runBlocking inside. Pass "bad" to use it. */ suspend fun lookupBad(id: Int): Int { runBlocking { delay(200) } // blocks the calling thread for 200 ms return id } suspend fun lookupGood(id: Int): Int { delay(200) // suspends; the thread serves other coroutines meanwhile return id } fun main(args: Array<String>) { val bad = args.firstOrNull() == "bad" // a pool with only two threads: two cooks for eight dishes Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2).asCoroutineDispatcher().use { pool -> val took = measureTimeMillis { runBlocking { withContext(pool) { repeat(8) { id -> launch { if (bad) lookupBad(id) else lookupGood(id) } } } } } println("8 lookups of 200 ms on 2 threads (${if (bad) "runBlocking inside" else "delay"}): $took ms") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l02.RunBlockingTrapKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l02/RunBlockingTrap.kt RunBlockingTrapJava.java // Java equivalent of RunBlockingTrap.kt: blocking on a future inside a task on a small pool. // Pass "bad" to join inside the task, like calling runBlocking inside suspend code. package workbench.coroutines.l02; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.Executor; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class RunBlockingTrapJava { // a 200 ms lookup that completes from a timer: it holds no thread while it waits. // (If the timer completed on the same two-thread pool, the "bad" version would deadlock: // both threads blocked in join(), waiting for work that needs one of them.) static CompletableFuture<Integer> lookup(int id) { Executor after200ms = CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> id, after200ms); } public static void main(String[] args) { boolean bad = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("bad"); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2); // two cooks for eight dishes long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<CompletableFuture<Integer>> all = new ArrayList<>(); for (int id = 0; id < 8; id++) { int i = id; all.add(bad ? CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> lookup(i).join(), pool) // holds a pool thread for 200 ms : CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> i, pool).thenCompose(RunBlockingTrapJava::lookup)); } CompletableFuture.allOf(all.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join(); System.out.printf("8 lookups of 200 ms on 2 threads (%s): %d ms%n", bad ? "join inside the task" : "thenCompose", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); pool.shutdown(); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l02.RunBlockingTrapJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l02/RunBlockingTrapJava.java About 200 ms with delay (292 ms here, on a busy machine). About 800 ms with runBlocking inside (858 ms here): each lookup holds one of the two threads for 200 ms, so the eight lookups run in four rounds of two. The Java twin shows the same cost for join() inside a pool task (226 ms against 854 ms here). Its comment notes a worse outcome: if the lookup needed the same two threads to finish, both would wait forever. runBlocking (API reference, see the pitfalls) docs

h: Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope · Java and Kotlin
x: Three prices at once: CompletableFuture vs async PriceCheck.java List<Price> allPrices(String item) { List<CompletableFuture<Price>> futures = grocers.stream() .map(g -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> g.price(item), ioPool)) .toList(); return futures.stream() .map(CompletableFuture::join) // blocks until each one is done .toList(); } PriceCheck.kt suspend fun allPrices(item: String): List<Price> = coroutineScope { grocers.map { g -> async { g.price(item) } }.awaitAll() } Both start three questions and collect the answers in order. In Java, each supplyAsync takes a thread from ioPool, a pool of threads kept for waiting work, for the whole call, and join blocks the caller's thread too. In Kotlin, the three children suspend while they wait, so they need no extra threads, and the caller suspends instead of blocking. Failure handling differs most. If one Java future fails, the others keep running to the end, and nobody cancels them (cancelling a CompletableFuture wouldn't interrupt the work anyway). In Kotlin, coroutineScope cancels the remaining children as soon as one fails, and rethrows the original exception. With virtual threads on JDK 21 and later, the Java version can block cheaply, but cancelling the siblings still needs structured concurrency, which is a preview API in JDK 25 (see "Structured concurrency and scoped values" in the virtual threads track).

h: Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope · Worked example
x: Make a dinner planner's screen concurrent A recipe app's "tonight" screen needs three things: the recipe (80 ms), what's in the pantry (150 ms) and the guests' allergies (60 ms). It asks for them one after another. They don't depend on each other, so the 290 ms is all waiting. suspend fun tonight(dinnerId: String): Tonight { val recipe = recipes.load(dinnerId) // 80 ms val stock = pantry.stock(dinnerId) // 150 ms val allergies = guests.allergies(dinnerId) // 60 ms return Tonight(recipe, stock, allergies) } // Java equivalent: three blocking calls in a row Tonight tonight(String dinnerId) { Recipe recipe = recipes.load(dinnerId); // 80 ms Stock stock = pantry.stock(dinnerId); // 150 ms List<Allergy> allergies = guests.allergies(dinnerId); // 60 ms return new Tonight(recipe, stock, allergies); } Open a scope, start all three as children, then await. The function now takes as long as the pantry call, about 150 ms. suspend fun tonight(dinnerId: String): Tonight = coroutineScope { // 1. start every independent call val recipe = async { recipes.load(dinnerId) } val stock = async { pantry.stock(dinnerId) } val allergies = async { guests.allergies(dinnerId) } // 2. collect the answers Tonight(recipe.await(), stock.await(), allergies.await()) } // Java equivalent: start all three on virtual threads, then join Tonight tonight(String dinnerId) { // 1. start every independent call var recipe = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> recipes.load(dinnerId), vthreads); var stock = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> pantry.stock(dinnerId), vthreads); var allergies = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> guests.allergies(dinnerId), vthreads); // 2. collect the answers return new Tonight(recipe.join(), stock.join(), allergies.join()); } A new requirement: the allergy check needs the recipe's ingredients. Keep that one dependency inside its own child, so the pantry call still runs alongside both. val recipe = async { recipes.load(dinnerId) } val stock = async { pantry.stock(dinnerId) } // 3. a dependent call waits for its input inside its own child val allergies = async { guests.allergies(dinnerId, recipe.await().ingredients) } var recipe = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> recipes.load(dinnerId), vthreads); var stock = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> pantry.stock(dinnerId), vthreads); // 3. a dependent call runs once its input is there var allergies = recipe.thenApplyAsync(r -> guests.allergies(dinnerId, r.ingredients()), vthreads); Self-check: the pantry call throws at 40 ms. What happens to the other two calls, and when does tonight fail? (The scope cancels the recipe and allergy children, waits for them to stop, and rethrows the pantry's exception at about 40 ms. Nothing is left running.)

h: Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope · Lab
x: Ask three grocers at once, timed on virtual time labs/coroutines/src/main/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l02/Prices.kt labs/coroutines/src/main/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l02/PriceCheck.kt ./gradlew :coroutines:test --tests 'workbench.coroutines.l02.*' Meet the classes. A Grocer is a shop we can ask: price(item) suspends for 100 to 300 ms, like a text and its reply, and returns a Price (the grocer's name, the item and the price in cents). PriceCheck asks a list of grocers, and its KDoc is the spec. Run the tests. Four of five fail. The order test passes already, and allPrices takes 620 virtual ms instead of 300. Make allPrices concurrent: wrap it in coroutineScope, start one async per grocer, and awaitAll(). Write cheapest on top of allPrices. Write callAhead with one launch per grocer. It must return only after every grocer has answered. Write priceList: one async per item, each calling allPrices, then build the map. Run the tests until all five pass. The tests run in runTest, so delay uses virtual time, a pretend clock that jumps ahead instead of waiting. currentTime reads that clock, and it says exactly 300 when the calls overlap. coroutineScope waits for launch children too. h: Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope · Key terms
x: Coroutine builder A function that starts a coroutine, such as launch, async, runBlocking or coroutineScope. Job A handle to a coroutine's life: check it, join it, cancel it. It holds no value. Deferred A Job that will also hold a result, like a pot with the lid on. await() returns the result or rethrows the failure. CoroutineScope The thing you call launch and async on. It supplies the parent Job and the context for new coroutines. Concurrent decomposition Splitting one task into independent calls, starting them together, and combining their results. Event loop The queue of coroutines that runBlocking runs one at a time on the thread it blocks. What does launch return, and where does its exception go? A Job, with no result. If the coroutine fails, the exception goes to its parent, not to whoever holds the Job. What does async return? A Deferred<T>: a Job that will also hold a value. await() suspends until it's ready, then returns it or rethrows the failure. val a = async { f() }.await(); val b = async { g() }.await(): concurrent or sequential? Sequential. Each await finishes before the next async starts. Start both, then await. awaitAll() vs map { it.await() }? The same results in the same order, but awaitAll fails as soon as any of them fails. The map version notices only when it reaches the failed one. When does coroutineScope { ... } return? After its block and every child started inside it have finished. If a child fails, it cancels the others and rethrows. Where is runBlocking allowed? At blocking edges: main, tests and blocking library callbacks. Never inside suspend code, where it holds the thread and ignores the caller's context.

h: Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope · Go deeper
x: A Job moves through a small set of states. A job created with start = CoroutineStart.LAZY begins in New and starts only when you call start(), join() or await(). Every other job starts in Active. When its block finishes, a job is Completing while it waits for its children, then Completed. If it's cancelled or fails, it goes through Cancelling (its children are being cancelled and finally blocks run) to Cancelled. isActive, isCompleted and isCancelled are views over these states. That's why launch reports isActive = true before its block has run a single line. A lazy async is a coroutine version of Kotlin's lazy {} for suspend work: val prices = async(start = CoroutineStart.LAZY) { loadPrices() } starts nothing until the first await(). Be careful with it inside coroutineScope. A lazy child that nobody starts keeps the scope waiting forever, because the scope waits for all children, including those in the New state. The kotlinx.coroutines guide also has a section on "async-style functions", such as fun priceAsync() = GlobalScope.async { ... }, and strongly discourages them. If the caller fails between starting and awaiting, the work keeps running in the background with nobody to collect it. Expose a suspend function instead, and let the caller decide what runs concurrently.

h: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree · Every coroutine has a parent, and a parent waits for its children
x: Every coroutine you start with launch or async gets a job, a handle to its life that you can wait for or cancel. That job becomes a child of the job in the scope you started it in, and children can have children of their own. The result is a tree, and the tree is the whole idea behind structured concurrency: work that runs at the same time has the same nested shape as the code that started it. Here's the dinner as code, with a name on every coroutine: Java // Java equivalent: StructuredTaskScope (preview in JDK 25, JEP 505; needs --enable-preview) try (var mainCourse = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // a node, like coroutineScope mainCourse.fork(() -> roast()); mainCourse.fork(() -> potatoes()); mainCourse.fork(() -> gravy()); mainCourse.join(); // waits for all three subtasks } Kotlin runBlocking(CoroutineName("dinner")) { // the root launch(CoroutineName("main-course")) { // a child of dinner coroutineScope { // a node of its own async(CoroutineName("roast")) { /* ... */ } async(CoroutineName("potatoes")) { /* ... */ } launch(CoroutineName("gravy")) { /* ... */ } } } } A scope is a coroutine context that holds a job. The context is the small set of settings that travels with a coroutine: its job, its name, its dispatcher (lesson 4 of this track takes it apart). launch reads the job from the scope's context and hangs the new coroutine under it. coroutineScope adds a node of its own, between its caller and the children started inside it. The first rule of the tree is the kitchen's rule: a parent can't complete until all of its children have completed. When a coroutine's body ends, its job waits in a state called "completing" until every child is done. That's why coroutineScope returns only after its slowest child, and why runBlocking doesn't return while anything below it still runs. Finished children leave the tree, so job.children lists only the work still going. JobTree, in the Try it below, prints the tree at 100 ms, while the three dishes are still cooking. Sketch the tree you expect first, then compare: tree at 100 ms, seen from the dinner coroutine: dinner active=true children=1 main-course active=true children=1 main-course active=true children=3 roast active=true children=0 potatoes active=true children=0 gravy active=true children=0 after join: dinner has 0 children main-course shows up twice. The second one is the coroutineScope, a node of its own, which copies its parent's context, name included. Under it sit the three dishes. After join, the dinner has no children left, because finished children leave the tree. The kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 docs spell out four rules for how lives in the tree affect each other. A parent waits for its children. Cancelling a parent cancels its children. A child that fails with an exception cancels its parent, unless the parent is a supervisor (lesson 6 of this track). And a child that ends with CancellationException, the exception a cancelled coroutine throws, counts as cancelled, not failed, so the parent isn't told. The middle two rules are where the kitchen gets busy. Print the tree Read JobTree.kt. Before you run it, sketch the tree you expect to see at 100 ms, with names. Run it and compare it with your sketch. Why does main-course appear twice? (Hint: what does coroutineScope copy from its parent?)
