CoroutineScope)?.coroutineContext?.get(CoroutineName)?.name ?: "(coroutineScope)" println("$indent$name active=$isActive children=${children.count()}") children.forEach { it.printTree("$indent ") } } fun main() = runBlocking(CoroutineName("dinner")) { val course = launch(CoroutineName("main-course")) { coroutineScope { async(CoroutineName("roast")) { delay(300) } async(CoroutineName("potatoes")) { delay(300) } launch(CoroutineName("gravy")) { delay(300) } delay(100) // give the children time to start println("tree at 100 ms, seen from the dinner coroutine:") this@runBlocking.coroutineContext.job.printTree() } } course.join() println("after join: dinner has ${coroutineContext.job.children.count()} children") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l03.JobTreeKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l03/JobTree.kt dinner has one child, main-course. Under it sits a second node, also called main-course: that's the coroutineScope, which copies its parent's context, name included. It has three children: roast, potatoes and gravy. After join, the dinner has 0 children, because finished children leave the tree. coroutineScope (API reference) docs

h: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree · Failure goes up, cancellation goes down
x: One burned roast: in the job tree, a failure goes up and stops the siblings, and a cancel only goes down Take the main course from the last section: roast, potatoes and gravy, three children of one coroutineScope. At 100 ms the roast burns and throws BurnedException, an exception the demo defines for a ruined dish. Here's what the tree does, in order: The roast child fails. It reports the exception to its parent, the scope. The scope's job is cancelled with that exception. A cancelled job cancels all of its children, so the potatoes and the gravy are cancelled, and their finally blocks run. The scope waits until those children have really stopped. coroutineScope rethrows the BurnedException to its caller, which can catch it like any exception. So one failure takes down the whole subtree it belongs to, then comes out as one exception at the place that started the work. The total time is the time to the failure, about 100 ms, not the time of the slowest dish. Nothing is left running in the background. FailureSpreads, in the Try it below, does this with two children: a roast that burns at 100 ms, and potatoes that would take a second. Predict which lines print, and when. On this busy machine it printed: [ 6 ms] scope body finished; the scope now waits for its children [ 161 ms] roast: burned, throwing BurnedException [ 163 ms] potatoes: finally block runs [ 165 ms] caller caught: the roast burned potatoes: done never printed. Two milliseconds after the roast burned, the potatoes were off the heat, and two more later the caller had the exception. (The first delay read 161 ms instead of 100 because a JVM, the program that runs the code, is slow just after it starts. That part is the machine, not the tree.) The Java twin is the honest contrast. An executor, Java's pool that runs submitted tasks, has no tree, so after the roast fails, the potatoes carry on to potatoes: done at about 1,000 ms, and close() waits for them. To stop them, you cancel them by hand, which is the step coroutineScope does for you. Cancellation only travels down. If the caller cancels the dinner, because the guests called it off or a timeout fired, every coroutine below it is cancelled. A child that's cancelled doesn't cancel its parent. A child whose block ends by throwing CancellationException is treated the same way: "cancelled", not "failed", and the parent carries on. A failure goes up the tree and stops the siblings. A cancel goes down and stops there. This is the default because it's almost always what you want. If one of the dishes for a course is ruined, the course is off, so finishing the other two is wasted work. Sometimes you do want siblings to survive each other's failures. Picture a reminder sent by text, by email and by phone, where any one of them is enough. Then you ask for it with a supervisor, the subject of lesson 6 of this track. The picture breaks on timing. A real cook pulls the pans off the heat at once. A coroutine hears the cancel only at its next suspension point, so a child busy with a long calculation or a blocking call finishes that first. Lesson 5 of this track shows how to cooperate. So a failure can't escape the tree. The trouble starts when the work was never in the tree at all. Predict when coroutineScope returns. Run the Java twin, then run it with -Pargs=cancel. Compare what happens to the potatoes. the scope now waits for its children") } log("coroutineScope returned normally") } catch (e: BurnedException) { log("caller caught: ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l03.FailureSpreadsKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l03/FailureSpreads.kt FailureSpreadsJava.java // Java equivalent of FailureSpreads.kt with a virtual-thread executor (JDK 21+, no preview APIs). // An executor has no parent-child tree: a failed task does not cancel its sibling unless you do it. // Pass "cancel" to cancel the sibling by hand, which is what coroutineScope does for you. package workbench.coroutines.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; public class FailureSpreadsJava { /** A dish that went wrong. */ static final class BurnedException extends RuntimeException { BurnedException(String message) { super(message); } } static long t0; static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("[%4d ms] %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, msg); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean cancelByHand = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("cancel"); t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService children = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<?> roast = children.submit(() -> { sleep(100); log("roast: burned, throwing BurnedException"); h: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree · GlobalScope cuts work loose from the tree
x: GlobalScope is a scope with no job. A coroutine launched in it has no parent, so none of the rules above apply. Nothing waits for it, nothing cancels it, and its exception goes to the thread's uncaught exception handler, the code that runs when an exception escapes a thread. That usually means a log line nobody reads. Java // Java equivalent: a task on a shared, app-wide pool; nothing ties it to the dinner void startStock(String pot) { SHARED_POOL.submit(() -> simmerStock(pot)); // returns at once; the stock is an orphan } Kotlin suspend fun startStock(pot: String) { GlobalScope.launch { simmerStock(pot) } // returns at once; the stock is an orphan } The caller of startStock thinks the stock is part of its dinner. It isn't. When the guests call the dinner off and the dinner coroutine is cancelled, the stock keeps simmering. LeakedWork, in the Try it below, cancels the dinner at 250 ms. Predict how many more steps the stock prints: [123 ms] stock pot: still simmering, step 0 [234 ms] stock pot: still simmering, step 1 [266 ms] dinner cancelled (the guests called it off) [335 ms] stock pot: still simmering, step 2 [436 ms] stock pot: still simmering, step 3 [537 ms] stock pot: still simmering, step 4 [637 ms] stock pot: still simmering, step 5 [769 ms] main done Four more steps, in a house where dinner was called off. This is a leaked coroutine: work that outlives everything that knows about it. In a test, it keeps running after the test has finished and may break the next one. When the program shuts down, it can still be writing to a file that's being closed. With coroutineScope { launch { } } instead, the stock is a child of the dinner, and nothing prints after the cancel but main done. kotlinx.coroutines marks GlobalScope with @DelicateCoroutinesApi, so you have to opt in, that is, add an annotation that says you know what you're doing. Its docs still call using it an antipattern, a habit that looks helpful and causes trouble. They also warn about the obvious workaround. CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch { } inside a function creates a brand-new root scope on every call and has every one of the same problems. It just doesn't ask you to opt in. The fix depends on what you meant. If the caller should wait for the work, call it directly, or use coroutineScope { launch { } } when it runs alongside other work. If the work really should outlive the call, something with a longer life has to own it: an object with a scope of its own, which the next section builds. And if the work must survive the program stopping, a coroutine is the wrong home for it. Write it down somewhere that lasts, such as a file or a database, and let a background worker pick it up from there. There's one fair use of GlobalScope: a coroutine that lives exactly as long as the whole program, such as one started in main that reports statistics until the program ends. A coroutine with no parent has no owner. Give every coroutine a scope that waits for it. So who should own work that outlives a single call? Call off the dinner and watch the stock carry on Read LeakedWork.kt. The dinner is cancelled at 250 ms. Predict how many stock steps print after that. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=fixed, which uses the coroutineScope version. Predict first. Run the Java twin both ways. It interrupts the dinner's thread instead of cancelling a coroutine. import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class LeakedWorkJava { static final ExecutorService SHARED = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(r -> { // lives as long as the app Thread t = new Thread(r, "shared-pool"); t.setDaemon(true); return t; }); static long start; static long ms() { return (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000; } static void simmerStock(String pot) throws InterruptedException { for (int step = 0; step < 6; step++) { Thread.sleep(100); System.out.printf(" [%d ms] %s: still simmering, step %d%n", ms(), pot, step); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean structured = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("fixed"); start = System.nanoTime(); Thread dinner = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { try { if (structured) simmerStock("stock pot"); // part of the dinner else SHARED.submit(() -> { simmerStock("stock pot"); return null; }); // an orphan Thread.sleep(10_000); // the dinner goes on } catch (InterruptedException e) { // the dinner was cancelled } }); Thread.sleep(250); dinner.interrupt(); System.out.printf("[%d ms] dinner interrupted (the guests called it off)%n", ms()); Thread.sleep(500); System.out.printf("[%d ms] main done%n", ms()); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l03.LeakedWorkJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l03/LeakedWorkJava.java With GlobalScope, steps 2 to 5 keep printing after dinner cancelled: the stock never heard about it. With -Pargs=fixed, the stock is a child of the dinner, so nothing prints after dinner cancelled except main done. The Java twin leaks the same way: interrupting the dinner's thread doesn't reach a task on a shared pool. Its fixed version simmers the stock on the dinner's own thread, so the interrupt stops it. h: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree · A class that runs background work owns a scope and closes it
x: Some work really does outlive a single call. Picture an oven that bakes trays in the background while the program does other things, until the kitchen closes for the night. Or a loop that checks the pantry every 30 seconds. The structured way to write either one is a class that owns a scope: it creates the scope, launches into it, and cancels it when its own life ends. Java // Java equivalent: the class owns an executor and shuts it down class Oven implements AutoCloseable { private final ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); // 1. the class's own pool private final Consumer<String> bake; Oven(Consumer<String> bake) { this.bake = bake; } Future<?> put(String tray) { return pool.submit(() -> bake.accept(tray)); // 2. every tray runs in it } @Override public void close() throws InterruptedException { pool.shutdownNow(); // 3. interrupt them all pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // and wait } } Kotlin class Oven(context: CoroutineContext, private val bake: suspend (String) -> Unit) { private val scope = CoroutineScope(context + Job()) // 1. the class's own root fun put(tray: String): Job = scope.launch { bake(tray) } // 2. every tray is a child suspend fun switchOff() = scope.coroutineContext.job.cancelAndJoin() // 3. cancel them all, wait } First the class builds its scope from the context it was given plus a fresh Job(). That job is the parent of every tray. Then put launches each tray into the scope and returns at once. Finally, switchOff cancels the parent job, which cancels every tray still baking, and waits for them to stop. One call reaches all of them, and job.children tells you what's still in the oven. The tree still exists. Its root is now the object, not a single call. A few rules keep this honest. Tie the scope to a real end of life: the moment the program shuts down, a window closes, or a test finishes. (JUnit, the usual Java test library, runs a method marked @AfterEach after every test.) An owned scope that nobody cancels is the stock pot from the last section with a nicer name. Create the scope once, as a field. A scope created inside a method is the orphan from the last section. Pass the dispatcher, or the whole context, in. A real program can pass Dispatchers.IO, and a test can pass a test dispatcher that runs on virtual time. The lab does exactly this. Choose cancel or cancelAndJoin on purpose. scope.cancel() isn't a suspend function, and it returns at once, while children may still be running their finally blocks. cancelAndJoin() waits until they've stopped, which is what you want before you close something they still use. CoroutineScope(...) adds a Job() for you if the context has none, but write it out, so readers see it. With a plain Job, one tray that fails cancels the whole oven. Lesson 6 of this track swaps it for a SupervisorJob, so one burned tray doesn't spoil the rest. Work that outlives a call needs an owner with a scope. Close the scope when the owner's life ends. Quick check: you call scope.cancel() and close the oven's log file on the next line, while three trays still have a finally that writes "tray out" to it. What can go wrong, and which one change fixes it? (cancel() returns before those finally blocks run, so they may write to a file that's already closed. cancelAndJoin() waits for them first.)

h: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree · Java and Kotlin
x: Work that can't leak: StructuredTaskScope vs coroutineScope MainCourse.java (preview in JDK 25, JEP 505: compile and run with --enable-preview) Plate mainCourse() throws InterruptedException { try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // default: fail on the first failure Subtask<Roast> roast = scope.fork(() -> kitchen.roast()); Subtask<Potatoes> potatoes = scope.fork(() -> kitchen.potatoes()); scope.join(); // waits; throws StructuredTaskScope.FailedException if a subtask failed return new Plate(roast.get(), potatoes.get()); } // close() cancels unfinished subtasks and waits for them } MainCourse.kt suspend fun mainCourse(): Plate = coroutineScope { val roast = async { kitchen.roast() } val potatoes = async { kitchen.potatoes() } Plate(roast.await(), potatoes.await()) } // returns only when both children are done; a failure cancels the other The idea is the same in both: subtasks can't outlive the block that started them, the first failure cancels the siblings, and the caller gets one exception. In Java each subtask is a virtual thread running blocking code, and cancelling means interrupting it. In Kotlin each child is a coroutine, and a cancel reaches it at its next suspension point. The bigger practical difference is maturity. In JDK 25, StructuredTaskScope is a preview API, one the JDK ships for trying out and may still change, and it needs --enable-preview, and its shape has changed between previews (the JDK 21 to 24 previews used a different API, based on subclasses). In Kotlin, every launch and async already joins the tree, including calls deep inside other suspend functions, and you get the guarantee without asking for it.

h: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree · Worked example
x: Give a pantry checker a scope it owns A small app checks the pantry every 30 seconds and refreshes the shopping list. It was written with GlobalScope. After the app has closed its database, the loop keeps calling it, and in tests one instance's loop runs on into the next test. class PantryWatcher(private val pantry: Pantry) { @OptIn(DelicateCoroutinesApi::class) fun start() { GlobalScope.launch { while (true) { pantry.refresh(); delay(30.seconds) } } } } // Java equivalent of the bug: a static scheduler that nobody shuts down class PantryWatcher { private static final ScheduledExecutorService SHARED = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(1); private final Pantry pantry; void start() { SHARED.scheduleWithFixedDelay(pantry::refresh, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } } Give the class its own scope, created once, with the dispatcher passed in so a test can pass a test dispatcher. A CoroutineName makes the loop easy to spot in debug output. class PantryWatcher( private val pantry: Pantry, dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO, ) : AutoCloseable { // 1. one scope per instance; its Job is the parent of everything we start private val scope = CoroutineScope(dispatcher + Job() + CoroutineName("pantry-watcher")) // Java equivalent: one scheduler per instance, with a named thread class PantryWatcher implements AutoCloseable { private final Pantry pantry; // 1. the instance owns its scheduler private final ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(Thread.ofPlatform().name("pantry-watcher").factory()); Launch into that scope. Catch the failure of a single refresh inside the loop, so that one bad check doesn't end the loop, and, with a plain Job, cancel the whole scope. Rethrow CancellationException (lesson 5 of this track explains why). // 2. the loop is a child of the scope fun start(): Job = scope.launch { while (true) { try { pantry.refresh() } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Exception) { log.warn("pantry check failed", e) } delay(30.seconds) } } // 2. the check belongs to this instance's scheduler ScheduledFuture<?> start() { return scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> { try { pantry.refresh(); } catch (Exception e) { log.warn("pantry check failed", e); } // an escaping exception stops the schedule }, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } Close the scope when the owner's life ends: when the app shuts down, and in @AfterEach in a test. cancel() returns at once; use cancelAndJoin() from suspend code when you must wait for the loop to stop. // 3. tie the scope to a real end of life override fun close() = scope.cancel() } // in a test @AfterEach fun stopWatcher() = watcher.close() // 3. tie the scheduler to a real end of life @Override public void close() { scheduler.shutdownNow(); } } // in a test @AfterEach void stopWatcher() { watcher.close(); } Self-check: a friend suggests fun start() = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch { ... } to get rid of the opt-in annotation. Why is that no better? (Each call makes a new root scope that nothing holds on to. Nobody can cancel it, so it leaks exactly like GlobalScope.)

h: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree · Quiz
x: What happens here? coroutineScope { launch { delay(100); throw IOException("down") } launch { delay(1_000); println("done") } } done prints at 1 s, then the scope throws IOException The IOException is printed by the uncaught handler, and the scope returns normally At about 100 ms the second child is cancelled, done never prints, and the scope throws IOException The scope returns normally at 1 s, because launch swallows exceptions The failed child cancels the scope's job, which cancels its sibling. The scope waits for the sibling to stop, then rethrows the original exception to its caller. Nothing waits for the full second. A child coroutine ends by throwing CancellationException. What happens to its parent and its siblings? Nothing: the child counts as cancelled, and the parent isn't told The parent is cancelled, and so are the siblings The parent rethrows the CancellationException to its caller The siblings are cancelled, but the parent keeps running A CancellationException means "I was cancelled", not "I failed". The child cancels its own children, but the parent keeps going. Only other exceptions travel up. Lesson 5 of this track shows why that makes swallowing it dangerous. A function calls GlobalScope.launch { copyPhotos(album) } and returns. A minute later the program shuts down while the copy is still running. What stops the copy? The caller's scope, which cancels it when the function returns The JVM, which cancels every coroutine politely at shutdown runBlocking at the top of the call stack Nothing in coroutines: it runs until it finishes, or until the JVM exits A GlobalScope coroutine has no parent, so no owner's end of life reaches it. It stops when it finishes, or when the JVM dies, possibly halfway through. If it must be stopped cleanly, it needs an owner with a scope that is cancelled at shutdown. A kitchen timer screen in an app starts a ticking loop when it opens. Where should the loop's coroutine live? In GlobalScope, because it outlives any single button click In a scope owned by the screen, cancelled when the screen closes In runBlocking on the screen's thread In a new CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO) created inside the code that opens the screen The loop lives exactly as long as the screen, so the screen should own the scope and cancel it when it closes. A new scope created in the opening code has no owner and leaks like GlobalScope. runBlocking would freeze the screen's thread. From lesson 2 of this track: what does this return, and when? coroutineScope { launch { delay(200) } 42 } 42, at once, because launch returns immediately 42, after about 200 ms, when the child finishes Unit, because the last expression is launch It never returns, because nobody joins the child The block's value is 42, but coroutineScope returns only after every child has completed. You don't need join: waiting for children is the scope's job.

h: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree · Key terms
x: Structured concurrency Concurrent work forms a tree that matches the code: children can't outlive their parent, and failures and cancels follow the tree. Parent job The job a new coroutine attaches to. It waits for its children, and cancels them when it's cancelled. Child coroutine A coroutine started in a scope. Its failure cancels its parent, unless the parent is a supervisor. Scope A coroutine context that holds a job. New coroutines started in it become that job's children. GlobalScope A scope with no job. Coroutines started there have no parent and belong to no tree. Leaked coroutine A coroutine that keeps running after everything that cared about it has gone, like a pan left on in an empty house. When does a parent coroutine complete? Only after its own block and all of its children have completed. In a regular coroutineScope, one child throws an exception. What happens? The scope is cancelled, which cancels the other children. The scope waits for them to stop, then rethrows the exception to its caller. A child ends with CancellationException. Is its parent cancelled? No. It counts as cancelled, not failed, so the parent isn't told. Which way does cancellation travel in the job tree? Down only. Cancelling a parent cancels all of its children; cancelling a child leaves the parent alone. Why is GlobalScope.launch inside a function a leak? The coroutine has no parent: nothing waits for it, nothing cancels it when the caller is cancelled, and its failure goes to the uncaught exception handler. How should a class that starts background coroutines be built? Own one CoroutineScope(context + Job()) as a field, launch into it, and cancel it (or cancelAndJoin it) when the owner's life ends.

h: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree · Go deeper
x: An owned scope doesn't have to be a separate root. Job(parent) creates a job that is a child of another one, so CoroutineScope(dispatcher + Job(appJob)) gives you a scope for one part of the program that is cancelled when the application's job is cancelled. With a plain Job, the link also works upwards: a failure in that part cancels appJob too. That's usually not what you want for a long-lived part of a program, which is one reason lesson 6 of this track reaches for SupervisorJob(parent). The tree is also how kotlinx.coroutines reports problems. When several children fail, the first exception wins, and the others are attached to it as suppressed exceptions. When you print a stack trace from a failed scope, look at the suppressed list before you decide that only one thing went wrong. The kotlinx-coroutines-debug module can print the live coroutines of a running JVM with their states and where each one was created (DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines()). It isn't on this lab's classpath, but it's the tool to reach for when you suspect a leak in a real program. Without it, the cheap trick from the Try it, walking job.children from a known root, already tells you how much work an object still has in flight. Showing a count like the lab's inOven on a status page is a cheap way to spot work that never finishes.

h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · A dispatcher picks the thread, and withContext moves one step
x: A dispatcher picks the thread: Default is the counter with one cutting board per core, IO the bench by the door for blocking calls, withContext carries one step there and back, and a limitedParallelism view gives the bakery its own 20 seats suspend says nothing about threads, as lesson 1 of this track showed. The dispatcher in a coroutine's context does. It decides which thread runs the coroutine each time it starts or resumes. In the kitchen, it's the station a dish is worked at. kotlinx.coroutines ships four: Dispatchers.Default is a pool, a group of threads kept ready for work. It has one thread per core, a part of the processor that runs one thread at a time, and at least two threads. launch and async use it when the context names no dispatcher. It's the counter, one cutting board per core. Dispatchers.IO is for calls that block a thread. Think of a database driver, the library a program uses to talk to a database, or an old library that waits on the network. Up to 64 of them run at once. It's the bench by the door. Dispatchers.Main is the thread that draws the screen in a desktop or Android app. It needs a module for that kind of app on the classpath, the list of libraries the program runs with (for Android, JavaFX or Swing). A plain program has none, and using it throws IllegalStateException. Dispatchers.Unconfined has no thread of its own. The coroutine starts on the caller's thread, and after its first pause it carries on wherever it was resumed. The docs say it shouldn't be used in general code. runBlocking is the odd one out: it runs its coroutine on the thread that called it. To run one piece of work somewhere else, use withContext. Here a recipe card is printed in two steps, one of each kind. First the steps are read from a recipe book kept in a database, with a driver that blocks. Then they're laid out for printing, which is pure calculation: Java // Java equivalent: CompletableFuture stages, each with its own executor CompletableFuture<byte[]> printCard(String dish) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> book.loadSteps(dish), ioPool) // a blocking database call .thenApplyAsync(printer::render, cpuPool); // CPU-heavy layout } Kotlin suspend fun printCard(dish: String): ByteArray { val steps = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { book.loadSteps(dish) } // a blocking database call return withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { printer.render(steps) } // CPU-heavy layout } withContext suspends the caller, runs the block on the other dispatcher, and then resumes the caller on its own dispatcher with the block's result. Carry this step to the bench, then come back to the counter with the answer. The code still reads from top to bottom. In the Java version, every stage names its executor, the JDK's word for a pool that runs submitted tasks. Whatever you chain next runs where the last stage left off, not back where you started. withContext is also a scope, like coroutineScope in Builders. It waits for any children launched inside the block, and a failure inside it comes out as an exception in the caller. WhereDoesItRun, in the Try it below, prints the thread for each dispatcher. It turns on debug mode, which adds the coroutine's name to thread names: runBlocking Thread[#1,main @dinner#1,5,main] Default Thread[#19,DefaultDispatcher-worker-1 @dinner#1,5,main] IO Thread[#19,DefaultDispatcher-worker-1 @dinner#1,5,main] Unconfined, before Thread[#1,main @dinner#1,5,main] Unconfined, after Thread[#21,kotlinx.coroutines.DefaultExecutor @dinner#1,5,main] Two lines deserve a second look. Default and IO printed the same thread, worker-1: the two share one pool, and the next section explains why that's on purpose. And Unconfined started on main, then woke up on DefaultExecutor, the library's timer thread, because that's the thread that ended the delay. Unconfined goes wherever it's carried, like a dish that ends up with whoever happened to hear the timer. A switch is cheap but not free: the library queues a task on the other dispatcher, and the coroutine's state machine resumes there. Values you wrote before the switch are visible after it, even on another thread, so a coroutine's own locals don't need @Volatile. The dispatcher picks the thread. withContext sends one step elsewhere and brings the answer back. So we can send work to the counter or to the bench. Which one does a blocking call belong on, and what happens when it lands on the wrong one? Print where each step runs Read WhereDoesItRun.kt. It turns on debug mode, which adds the coroutine's name and number to thread names. Predict the thread for each line. Run it. Look closely at the two Unconfined lines. Run it two or three times. Do Default and IO always print different workers? Run the Java twin and match each line to its Kotlin counterpart. WhereDoesItRun.kt package workbench.coroutines.l04 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineName import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.asCoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import java.util.concurrent.Executors private fun here() = Thread.currentThread().toString() fun main() { // debug mode adds " @name#id" to thread names. Set it before any coroutine starts. System.setProperty("kotlinx.coroutines.debug", "on") runBlocking(CoroutineName("dinner")) { println("runBlocking ${here()}") withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { println("Default ${here()}") } withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { println("IO ${here()}") } withContext(Dispatchers.Unconfined) { println("Unconfined, before ${here()}") delay(10) // resumes on whatever thread finishes the delay println("Unconfined, after ${here()}") } Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { r -> Thread(r, "oven") }.asCoroutineDispatcher().use { single -> withContext(single + CoroutineName("roast")) { println("single-thread exec ${here()}") } } Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher().use { vt -> withContext(vt) { println("virtual-thread exec ${here()}") } } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l04.WhereDoesItRunKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l04/WhereDoesItRun.kt WhereDoesItRunJava.java // Java equivalent of WhereDoesItRun.kt: in Java you pick an executor for each step yourself. package workbench.coroutines.l04; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class WhereDoesItRunJava { static String here() { return Thread.currentThread().toString(); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("main " + here()); // the common pool: one thread per core, the closest match for Dispatchers.Default CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println("commonPool " + here()), ForkJoinPool.commonPool()).join(); // a cached pool grows for blocking work, roughly what Dispatchers.IO does (without the cap) ExecutorService cached = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(); CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println("cached pool " + here()), cached).join(); cached.shutdown(); // a non-async stage runs on whichever thread completes the previous stage, like Unconfined CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 1, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) .thenAccept(x -> System.out.println("thenAccept after timer " + here())) .join(); try (ExecutorService single = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(r -> new Thread(r, "oven"))) { CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println("single-thread exec " + here()), single).join(); } try (ExecutorService vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println("virtual-thread exec " + here()), vt).join(); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l04.WhereDoesItRunJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l04/WhereDoesItRunJava.java runBlocking prints main @dinner#1. Default and IO print DefaultDispatcher-worker-N threads, and on many runs IO prints the same worker as Default: the two share one pool. Unconfined starts on main and, after delay, resumes on kotlinx.coroutines.DefaultExecutor, the thread that fired the timer. The single-thread executor prints oven @roast#1 (the new name replaced the old one), and the virtual-thread executor prints a VirtualThread. In the Java twin, the thenAccept stage runs on whichever thread completed the timer stage, which is Java's version of Unconfined. Coroutine context and dispatchers (Kotlin docs) read

h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · Default is for CPU work, IO is for blocking calls
x: Dispatchers.Default has as many threads as the machine has cores. On a 4-core machine, that's 4. Run a 200 ms blocking call there, and you hold one of those 4 threads for 200 ms while it does nothing: the helper at the cutting board, watching the door. Four coroutines doing that at once take every thread, and all the CPU work in the program waits in the queue. BlockingOnDefault, in the Try it below, does it on purpose. It starts 32 blocking calls of 200 ms on Default, then asks Default to run a task that takes a microsecond. Predict how long the tiny task waits to start. On this 4-core machine: 32 blocking calls on Dispatchers.Default (4 cores): 1626 ms a tiny CPU task on Default waited 1570 ms to start A microsecond of work waited a second and a half. The 32 calls ran four at a time, in eight rounds, and the tiny task queued behind all of them. With -Pargs=io, the same calls go to the bench: 32 blocking calls on Dispatchers.IO (4 cores): 255 ms a tiny CPU task on Default waited 4 ms to start All 32 ran at once, and the counter stayed free. A blocking call belongs on Dispatchers.IO. Its limit is 64, or the number of cores if that's larger, and the system property kotlinx.coroutines.io.parallelism, a setting you pass on the command line with -D, changes it. IO threads spend most of their time waiting for something outside the program, a disk or another computer, so 64 of them on 4 cores is fine. IO and Default share one pool of worker threads. When code on Default calls withContext(Dispatchers.IO), the docs say it "typically does not lead to an actual switching to another thread". The same worker keeps going, and the library counts it against IO's limit instead of Default's. That's why WhereDoesItRun printed one worker for both. In the kitchen, the helper stays the same person: she walks from the counter to the bench, and her cutting board is free for somebody else. What the split buys you is two separate budgets. Blocking work can fill the bench, and Default still has a thread for every core. Here the kitchen picture breaks. A helper on the bench could get up and chop for a minute while the doorbell is quiet. A blocked thread can't: it's stuck until the call returns. That's why only blocking calls need the bench at all. A coroutine that suspends gives its thread back at once, wherever it is. Three rules follow. Never block on Default. Put withContext(Dispatchers.IO) around each blocking call at the lowest level, inside the class that makes the call, so callers don't need to know it blocks. Put long CPU work on Default: laying out a whole recipe book for printing, or resizing a hundred photos. A few microseconds of work need no switch at all. Don't wrap calls that already suspend. delay, a suspending network client or a coroutine-aware queue never holds a thread while it waits, so withContext(Dispatchers.IO) around them only adds a hop. Nothing marks a call as blocking. Put each blocking call on IO yourself. Java has the same split under other names. The common ForkJoinPool is sized for CPU work, and blocking in it starves parallelStream() and every CompletableFuture.supplyAsync that names no executor. Sizing a pool, in the executors track, built one pool for each kind of work. Here the library hands you both pools ready-made, and your job is to put each call in the right one. But one bench for every blocking call in the program has a problem of its own, as soon as one shop is slow. Starve Default with blocking calls Read BlockingOnDefault.kt. It starts 32 blocking calls of 200 ms, then asks Default to run a task that takes a microsecond. Predict how long that tiny task waits to start on your machine. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=io, which puts the blocking calls on IO. Predict first. Run the Java twin both ways. BlockingOnDefault.kt package workbench.coroutines.l04 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis /** 32 blocking 200 ms calls, then one tiny CPU task on Default. Pass "io" to run the blocking calls on IO. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val onIo = args.firstOrNull() == "io" val blockingDispatcher = if (onIo) Dispatchers.IO else Dispatchers.Default val cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() var cpuWaitMs = 0L val took = measureTimeMillis { coroutineScope { repeat(32) { launch(blockingDispatcher) { Thread.sleep(200) } } // blocking calls, like waiting at the door delay(20) // let them start val asked = System.nanoTime() val heartbeat = async(Dispatchers.Default) { System.nanoTime() } // 1 microsecond of CPU work cpuWaitMs = (heartbeat.await() - asked) / 1_000_000 } } val where = if (onIo) "Dispatchers.IO" else "Dispatchers.Default" println("32 blocking calls on $where ($cores cores): $took ms") println("a tiny CPU task on Default waited $cpuWaitMs ms to start") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l04.BlockingOnDefaultKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l04/BlockingOnDefault.kt BlockingOnDefaultJava.java // Java equivalent of BlockingOnDefault.kt: blocking calls on the common pool (sized for CPU work) // versus on a separate pool for blocking work. Pass "io" to use the separate pool. package workbench.coroutines.l04; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool; public class BlockingOnDefaultJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean onIo = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("io"); int cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors(); ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(64); // a pool sized like the common pool, so the demo behaves the same on every machine ForkJoinPool cpu = new ForkJoinPool(Math.max(2, cores)); var blockingPool = onIo ? io : cpu; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<CompletableFuture<Void>> calls = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++) { calls.add(CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> sleep(200), blockingPool)); // blocking calls, like waiting at the door } Thread.sleep(20); long asked = System.nanoTime(); long started = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(System::nanoTime, cpu).join(); // tiny CPU task on the CPU pool CompletableFuture.allOf(calls.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join(); System.out.printf("32 blocking calls on %s (%d cores): %d ms%n", onIo ? "a 64-thread pool" : "the CPU pool", cores, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); System.out.printf("a tiny CPU task on the CPU pool waited %d ms to start%n", (started - asked) / 1_000_000); io.shutdown(); cpu.shutdown(); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l04.BlockingOnDefaultJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l04/BlockingOnDefaultJava.java On 4 cores, the 32 calls take about 1,600 ms on Default (8 rounds of 4), and the tiny task waits about 1,500 ms (1,626 and 1,570 ms here), because every Default thread is asleep in Thread.sleep. With -Pargs=io the calls take about 220 ms, all 32 at once (255 ms here), and the tiny task starts within a few milliseconds. Scale the numbers to your core count. The Java twin shows the same starvation with a ForkJoinPool sized like Default (1,628 and 1,588 ms here).

h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · A limitedParallelism view gives one slow resource its own budget
x: IO's 64 is one budget for every blocking call in the JVM, the program that runs your code. That hurts when one resource is slow. Say the bakery from lesson 1 still has an old ordering client that blocks, and the bakery has 20 phone lines. When the bakery slows down, 64 coroutines can pile into bakery calls. Twenty of them get a line, and 44 hold an IO thread while they wait for one. Every other blocking call in the program, such as the recipe book's, queues behind them. limitedParallelism makes a view of a dispatcher, with a limit of its own: Java // Java equivalent: a separate pool per resource, often called a bulkhead ExecutorService bakery = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20, Thread.ofPlatform().name("bakery-", 0).factory()); ExecutorService copier = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(100, Thread.ofPlatform().name("recipe-copy-", 0).factory()); Kotlin val bakery = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(20, "bakery") // at most 20 bakery calls at once val copier = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(100, "recipe-copy") // a nightly copy job with its own budget A view owns no threads and needs no closing. It's a sign over part of the bench that says "bakery calls: 20 seats". At most 20 coroutines from the bakery view run at the same moment, and the rest wait in the view's queue without holding a thread. The name is optional. It arrived in kotlinx.coroutines 1.9, when the API became stable, and it's what toString() returns, which helps in logs. Views over IO are elastic: they don't take a share of IO's 64, they add to it. The library's own docs give an example with a view of 100 for one database and 60 for another. The program, they say, may then run up to 64 + 100 + 60 blocking tasks at peak. So the view protects the bakery both ways. Bakery calls can't take more than 20 threads, and a burst of other blocking work can't starve the bakery either. BlockingBudgets, in the Try it below, runs 400 blocking calls of 200 ms three ways. Predict each before you read on: Dispatchers.IO 1446 ms, peak 64 calls at once IO.limitedParallelism(400) 576 ms, peak 265 calls at once virtual-thread executor 228 ms, peak 400 calls at once Plain IO capped the run at 64 calls at once, so 400 calls took seven rounds. The view of 400 went far past 64, as promised, though not all the way to 400. The shared pool had to create a few hundred new threads, and on this busy machine it couldn't create them fast enough; a second run peaked at 237. The virtual-thread executor, the one from the virtual threads track, ran all 400 at once, because a virtual thread costs almost nothing to start. Views over Default are different. A view can never go beyond its parent's limit, so Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(400) still runs one task per core. Swap it into the demo, and the 400 calls take 20 seconds, four at a time. And limitedParallelism(1) gives a view that runs one task at a time, which is not the same as a lock. Lesson 10 of this track shows why. When you need a dispatcher that isn't one of these, wrap an executor: executor.asCoroutineDispatcher(). That includes Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher(), which the demo used. kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 has no built-in virtual-thread dispatcher, so this is the supported route. A wrapped executor is yours to close: the dispatcher is AutoCloseable, and close() shuts the executor down. A slow resource needs a budget of its own. Give it a view over IO. The dispatcher is only one of the things a coroutine carries with it. Three budgets for 400 blocking calls Read BlockingBudgets.kt. It runs 400 blocking calls of 200 ms on plain IO, on a view of 400 over IO, and on a virtual-thread executor. Predict the time and the peak for each. Run it. Change the view to Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(400) and run it again. Predict first. Run the Java twin. BlockingBudgets.kt package workbench.coroutines.l04 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.asCoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis /** 400 blocking calls of 200 ms each, on three different dispatchers. */ suspend fun runBlockingCalls(label: String, dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher) { val active = AtomicInteger() val peak = AtomicInteger() val took = measureTimeMillis { coroutineScope { repeat(400) { launch(dispatcher) { peak.accumulateAndGet(active.incrementAndGet(), ::maxOf) Thread.sleep(200) // a blocking call, like a phone call on hold active.decrementAndGet() } } } } println("%-32s %5d ms, peak %3d calls at once".format(label, took, peak.get())) } fun main() = runBlocking { runBlockingCalls("Dispatchers.IO", Dispatchers.IO) runBlockingCalls("IO.limitedParallelism(400)", Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(400)) Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher().use { vt -> runBlockingCalls("virtual-thread executor", vt) } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l04.BlockingBudgetsKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l04/BlockingBudgets.kt BlockingBudgetsJava.java // Java equivalent of BlockingBudgets.kt: the same 400 blocking calls on a 64-thread pool, // a pool that grows as needed, and one virtual thread per call. package workbench.coroutines.l04; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; public class BlockingBudgetsJava { static void runBlockingCalls(String label, ExecutorService pool) { AtomicInteger active = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicInteger peak = new AtomicInteger(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (pool) { // close() waits for all 400 calls for (int i = 0; i < 400; i++) { pool.submit(() -> { peak.accumulateAndGet(active.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); try { Thread.sleep(200); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } // a blocking call, like a phone call on hold active.decrementAndGet(); }); } } System.out.printf("%-32s %5d ms, peak %3d calls at once%n", label, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, peak.get()); } public static void main(String[] args) { runBlockingCalls("fixed pool of 64", Executors.newFixedThreadPool(64)); runBlockingCalls("cached pool (grows)", Executors.newCachedThreadPool()); runBlockingCalls("virtual thread per task", Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l04.BlockingBudgetsJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l04/BlockingBudgetsJava.java Plain IO peaks at 64 calls at once, so 400 calls take 7 rounds, about 1,400 ms (1,446 ms here). The view of 400 goes far beyond 64 because it adds to IO's budget instead of sharing it. On an idle machine it gets close to 400 at once in about 300 ms; on this busy one it peaked at 265 and 237 calls in two runs, taking about 600 ms, because the shared pool couldn't create new threads fast enough. The virtual-thread executor peaks at 400 (228 ms here). The view over Default peaks at your core count (at least 2) and takes far longer: 20 seconds on 4 cores, because a view can't exceed its parent. The Java twin shows the same pattern with a fixed pool of 64, a cached pool that grows and a virtual thread per task (1,424, 647 and 225 ms here). Default and IO share one pool of threads but keep separate budgets. Views over IO add their own budgets on top of IO's 64. limitedParallelism (API reference) docs Dispatchers.IO (API reference: the 64 limit and elastic views) docs

h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · The context is a set of elements, and + merges them
x: Picture a note clipped to every dish in the kitchen. It says which station the dish is worked at, what the dish is called and which course it belongs to. It can also hold anything else the cook wants to remember, such as which guest the dish is for. When a dish is split into parts, each part gets a copy of the note. That note is the coroutine context: a small set of elements, with at most one for each key, the label an element is filed under. You've met most of the elements already: the Job, which is the coroutine's place in the tree from Structured concurrency; the dispatcher; CoroutineName; and CoroutineExceptionHandler, which lesson 6 of this track covers. + combines two contexts, and when both have an element with the same key, the right side wins: val ctx = Dispatchers.IO + CoroutineName("soup") val renamed = ctx + CoroutineName("salad") renamed[CoroutineName] // CoroutineName(salad): the right side won renamed[ContinuationInterceptor] // Dispatchers.IO: untouched The picture breaks in one place. A paper note can be scribbled on. A context can't be changed in place: + always makes a new one, and the old one stays as it was. A new coroutine's context is built in three steps: the scope's context, then the context you pass to the builder, which overrides it, then a fresh Job that is a child of the scope's job. So children inherit the dispatcher, the name and anything else you add, but every child gets its own job, its own place in the tree. withContext(ctx) builds the context of its block the same way. Inside a suspend function, read an element with currentCoroutineContext()[Key]. The key is usually the element's companion object, which is why ctx[CoroutineName] reads so naturally. One change in kotlinx.coroutines 1.11: using CoroutineDispatcher as the key is deprecated, and later versions will reject it. Look the dispatcher up with ContinuationInterceptor, as the snippet does. You can define your own element by extending AbstractCoroutineContextElement and giving it a companion Key. The lab does that with ForGuest, a note that says which guest a dish is for, so every coroutine working on that dish can read it. What doesn't follow a coroutine is a plain ThreadLocal, a variable with a separate value for each thread. It's a note pinned to the cook's apron instead of clipped to the dish: when another cook picks up the dish, the note stays with the first cook. A coroutine that resumes on another thread sees that thread's value. asContextElement() turns a ThreadLocal into a context element. The library then sets the value on whichever thread runs the coroutine, and puts the old value back when the coroutine leaves: Java // Java equivalent: copy the ThreadLocal into the task by hand String captured = GUEST.get(); pool.submit(() -> { GUEST.set(captured); try { work(); } finally { GUEST.remove(); } }); Kotlin guest.set("ana") withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { guest.get() } // null: another thread withContext(Dispatchers.Default + guest.asContextElement()) { guest.get() } // ana ContextElements, in the Try it below, prints all three: ana on the main thread, null on Default with the plain ThreadLocal, and ana again with asContextElement. A ThreadLocal stays with the thread, not with the coroutine. Carry it in the context. Real programs need this most for logging. Many logging libraries keep an id for the current piece of work in a ThreadLocal, so that every log line can show it. For the widely used SLF4J library, the kotlinx-coroutines-slf4j module has a ready-made element, MDCContext; it isn't on this lab's classpath. And CoroutineName shows up in thread names when the JVM runs with -Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug (running with -ea, which turns on assertions, does it too). That costs little, and it makes a thread dump, a snapshot of every thread and what it's doing, readable. Merge contexts and lose a ThreadLocal Read ContextElements.kt. Predict the three lines about guest. Run it. Add + CoroutineName("late") to the end of the renamed line and run again. Which name wins now? Run the Java twin, which copies the value by hand, the way a logging library's executor wrapper does. ContextElements.kt package workbench.coroutines.l04 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineName import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.asContextElement import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import kotlin.coroutines.ContinuationInterceptor private val guest = ThreadLocal<String?>() // a note on the cook's apron, not on the dish fun main() = runBlocking { // 1. a context is a set of elements; + combines them, and the right side wins for the same key val ctx = Dispatchers.IO + CoroutineName("soup") val renamed = ctx + CoroutineName("salad") println("ctx[CoroutineName] = ${ctx[CoroutineName]}") println("renamed[CoroutineName] = ${renamed[CoroutineName]}") println("dispatcher by its key = ${renamed[ContinuationInterceptor]}") // 2. a ThreadLocal does not follow a coroutine to another thread guest.set("ana") println("main thread sees ${guest.get()}") withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { println("on Default, plain ThreadLocal ${guest.get()}") } // 3. asContextElement copies the value in and out whenever the coroutine runs on a thread withContext(Dispatchers.Default + guest.asContextElement()) { println("on Default, asContextElement ${guest.get()}") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l04.ContextElementsKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l04/ContextElements.kt ContextElementsJava.java // Java equivalent of ContextElements.kt: a ThreadLocal does not follow a task to a pool thread. // You copy it by hand (this is what logging libraries' executor wrappers do). JDK 25 adds ScopedValue // (final in JDK 25, JEP 506), but the labs compile for Java 21, so this demo copies by hand. package workbench.coroutines.l04; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class ContextElementsJava { static final ThreadLocal<String> GUEST = new ThreadLocal<>(); // a note on the cook's apron // capture the caller's value now, install it around the task later, then restore static Runnable withGuest(Runnable task) { String captured = GUEST.get(); return () -> { String previous = GUEST.get(); GUEST.set(captured); try { task.run(); } finally { GUEST.set(previous); } }; } public static void main(String[] args) { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2)) { GUEST.set("ana"); System.out.println("main thread sees " + GUEST.get()); CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println("pool thread, plain ThreadLocal " + GUEST.get()), pool).join(); CompletableFuture.runAsync(withGuest(() -> System.out.println("pool thread, copied by hand " + GUEST.get())), pool).join(); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l04.ContextElementsJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l04/ContextElementsJava.java The name lookups print CoroutineName(soup), then CoroutineName(salad), and the dispatcher lookup prints Dispatchers.IO. The main thread sees ana, the plain ThreadLocal on Default prints null, and the asContextElement version prints ana. After your change, the rightmost name, late, wins. The Java twin prints the same three guest lines. asContextElement (API reference) docs

h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · Java and Kotlin
x: One job, two kinds of work: executors vs dispatchers RecipeCardService.java class RecipeCardService { private final ExecutorService io; // sized for blocking database calls private final ExecutorService cpu; // sized to the cores RecipeCardService(ExecutorService io, ExecutorService cpu) { this.io = io; this.cpu = cpu; } CompletableFuture<byte[]> printCard(String dish) { return CompletableFuture .supplyAsync(() -> book.loadSteps(dish), io) // 1. block on an IO thread .thenApplyAsync(printer::render, cpu); // 2. lay out on a CPU thread // the caller gets a future; whatever it chains next runs on a cpu thread } } RecipeCardService.kt class RecipeCardService( private val io: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO, private val cpu: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.Default, ) { suspend fun printCard(dish: String): ByteArray { val steps = withContext(io) { book.loadSteps(dish) } // 1. block on an IO thread return withContext(cpu) { printer.render(steps) } // 2. lay out on a CPU thread } // the caller resumes on its own dispatcher with the bytes } Both versions keep the blocking call off the CPU threads, and both take the pools as constructor arguments, so a test can pass its own. The difference is where the caller ends up. With CompletableFuture, the result is delivered on the thread of the last stage, and the caller either blocks on join() or keeps chaining callbacks that run who knows where. With withContext, the caller suspends, and when the block finishes it resumes on its own dispatcher, as if the call had been an ordinary one. You also own less. Dispatchers.IO and Dispatchers.Default are shared pools that live as long as the program and that you never create or shut down, while the Java version needs two executors with a life of their own.

h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · Worked example
x: Give the bakery's blocking client a budget of its own An app orders bread through the bakery's old blocking client, inside launch on Default, on a 4-core machine. When the bakery slows to 2 seconds a call, orders pile up, and unrelated work in the app stalls. class BreadOrders(private val bakery: BlockingBakeryClient, private val scope: CoroutineScope) { fun onOrder(order: BreadOrder) { scope.launch { // scope uses Dispatchers.Default val ticket = bakery.order(order) // blocks a Default thread for up to 2 s pantry.expect(ticket) } } } // Java equivalent of the bug: blocking calls on the common pool, which is sized for CPU work class BreadOrders { void onOrder(BreadOrder order) { CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> bakery.order(order)) // no executor: ForkJoinPool.commonPool() .thenAccept(pantry::expect); } } First, get the blocking call off Default. Put the switch inside a small suspend wrapper around the client, so that no caller can forget it. class SuspendingBakery(private val client: BlockingBakeryClient) { // 1. the only place that knows this client blocks suspend fun order(order: BreadOrder): Ticket = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { client.order(order) } } // Java equivalent: the wrapper picks the executor, so callers can't forget class AsyncBakery { private final ExecutorService io = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(); // 1. the only place that knows this client blocks CompletableFuture<Ticket> order(BreadOrder order) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> client.order(order), io); } } IO allows 64 calls, but the bakery has 20 phone lines. A slow bakery would let 64 coroutines take IO threads, and 44 of them would only be waiting for a line, while other blocking calls queue for IO threads. Give the bakery a view sized to its lines, and pass it in, so a test can pass a test dispatcher. class SuspendingBakery( private val client: BlockingBakeryClient, // 2. a budget sized to the bakery's 20 lines, on top of IO's 64 private val dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(20, "bakery"), ) { suspend fun order(order: BreadOrder): Ticket = withContext(dispatcher) { client.order(order) } } // Java equivalent: a pool of exactly 20 threads for the bakery class AsyncBakery implements AutoCloseable { // 2. a budget sized to the bakery's 20 lines private final ExecutorService bakeryPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20, Thread.ofPlatform().name("bakery-", 0).factory()); CompletableFuture<Ticket> order(BreadOrder order) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> client.order(order), bakeryPool); } @Override public void close() { bakeryPool.shutdown(); } } The app's own code no longer cares where the bakery call runs. Its other work, such as a suspending pantry call, stays on Default. fun onOrder(order: BreadOrder) { scope.launch { val ticket = bakery.order(order) // 3. suspends; no Default thread is held pantry.expect(ticket) // back on Default } } void onOrder(BreadOrder order) { bakery.order(order) // 3. runs on the bakery pool .thenAccept(pantry::expect); // and so does this stage, unless you pass an executor } Self-check: why not Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20).asCoroutineDispatcher() instead of the view? (It works, but it's a pool you must close, with 20 threads that sit idle between rushes. The view has no life of its own to manage, borrows threads from the shared pool only while calls run, and still caps the bakery at 20.)

h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · Lab
x: Put each call on the right dispatcher labs/coroutines/src/main/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l04/RecipeCardService.kt labs/coroutines/src/main/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l04/BakeryDispatcher.kt labs/coroutines/src/main/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l04/GuestContext.kt labs/coroutines/src/main/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l04/KitchenModel.kt ./gradlew :coroutines:test --tests 'workbench.coroutines.l04.*' Read KitchenModel.kt first. BlockingRecipeBook.loadSteps reads a recipe from a database and blocks; CardPrinter.render lays out a printable recipe card, which is pure CPU work; and ForGuest is a context element, a note that says which guest a dish is for. Run the tests: all eight fail. In RecipeCardService.printCard, run loadSteps inside withContext(io) and render inside withContext(cpu). The tests pass two single-thread dispatchers named test-io and test-cpu, so they can see where each call ran. You don't need async, because the two steps depend on each other. limitedParallelism takes an optional second argument, the view's name. The name is what toString() returns. withContext(context, block) accepts the block parameter as it is. h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · Quiz
x: A program handles 10 orders at once on a 4-core machine. Each one runs launch { recipes.load(id) }, a blocking 300 ms database call, in a scope whose dispatcher is Default. At that moment a coroutine on Default needs 1 ms of CPU to resize a photo. When does it run? At once, because Default and IO are separate thread pools Only once a Default thread finishes its blocking call, roughly 300 ms later At once, because kotlinx.coroutines moves blocking calls to IO for you Never: Default throws IllegalStateException when a thread blocks for too long All 4 Default threads are blocked inside database calls, so the photo task waits in the queue until one returns. Nothing moves a blocking call for you, and nothing throws. Wrapping the query in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) keeps Default free. A nightly job makes 300 blocking calls to copy the recipe book into a backup database, whose pool has 100 connections. It must not slow down the program's other blocking calls. Which dispatcher fits? Dispatchers.IO Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(100) Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(100, "recipe-copy") Dispatchers.Unconfined A view over IO caps the copy at 100, and because IO views are elastic, it adds to IO's 64 instead of using them up. Plain IO would let the copy take all 64 threads. A view over Default can't exceed the core count, and Default must never block anyway. What does this print? val ctx = CoroutineName("a") + Dispatchers.IO + CoroutineName("b") println(ctx[CoroutineName]?.name) b a a, b null, because the dispatcher replaced the name A context holds at most one element per key, and + lets the right side win. CoroutineName("b") replaces a. The dispatcher has a different key, so it sits beside the name without touching it. Inside withContext(Dispatchers.IO + CoroutineName("soup")) { ... } you call launch(CoroutineName("salad")) { ... }. What does the child coroutine's context contain? Default and salad, because launch uses Default unless told otherwise IO and soup, because the parent's context always wins IO and salad, and the same Job as the withContext block IO and salad, and a new Job that is a child of the block's job A child starts from its scope's context (IO and soup), then the builder's argument overrides it (salad), then it gets a fresh Job that is a child of the scope's job. The "Default unless told" rule applies only when the context has no dispatcher at all. From the executors track: each bakery call holds one of the bakery's 20 phone lines. You give bakery calls their own pool of 64 threads. How many bakery calls can really make progress at once? 64 20 84 One per core The smallest limit on the path is the real ceiling. The other 44 threads sit waiting for a line. That's why the bakery's dispatcher in this lesson is a view of exactly 20.
