h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · Key terms
x: Dispatcher The context element that decides which thread runs a coroutine each time it starts or resumes. In the kitchen, the station a dish is worked at. Dispatchers.Default The shared pool for CPU work: one thread per core, at least two. Dispatchers.IO The shared pool for blocking calls: up to 64 at once by default, using the same threads as Default. limitedParallelism view A dispatcher in front of another one that lets at most n of its tasks run at the same time. It owns no threads. withContext Runs a block with a changed context, often another dispatcher, and returns its result to the caller. Coroutine context The set of elements a coroutine carries: job, dispatcher, name, exception handler and your own elements. The note clipped to the dish. Context element One entry in a context, found by its key, usually the element class's companion object. How many threads does Dispatchers.Default have? One per CPU core, and at least two. What is Dispatchers.IO's default limit? 64 blocking tasks at once, or the core count if that's larger. The kotlinx.coroutines.io.parallelism property changes it. Does Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(100) take 100 of IO's 64 threads? No. Views over IO are elastic and add to IO's budget: IO and the view together can run 64 + 100 blocking tasks. What does withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { load() } do to the calling coroutine? It suspends the caller, runs load() on IO, then resumes the caller on its own dispatcher with the result. ctx holds CoroutineName("a"). What name does ctx + CoroutineName("b") hold? b. One element per key, and the right side of + wins. Why does a ThreadLocal read null after withContext(Dispatchers.Default)? The block runs on another thread, which has its own value. Pass threadLocal.asContextElement() in the context to carry the value along. In kotlinx.coroutines 1.11, which key looks up the dispatcher in a context? ContinuationInterceptor. Using CoroutineDispatcher as the key is deprecated.

h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · Go deeper
x: Default and IO are two faces of one scheduler. On the JVM, kotlinx.coroutines runs a single pool of worker threads, and each task is marked as CPU work or blocking work. A worker running a blocking task doesn't count against Default's limit, so the scheduler can start another worker for CPU work. That's how a switch from Default to IO can stay on the same thread: the worker just changes which budget it's counted against. IO itself is a view of 64 over an unlimited budget for blocking work, which is why further views over IO can add to it. The docs say Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(n) can safely replace the older newFixedThreadPoolContext(n). The old function creates n threads of its own, which you must close and which sit idle between rushes. If you find it in a code base, a view is almost always the better choice. Dispatchers.Unconfined has one fair niche: code that must react at once, on whatever thread delivered an event, such as some of the library's own operators. To avoid overflowing the stack, nested unconfined coroutines form an event loop instead of calling each other directly, which makes the order of execution surprising. Treat it as a tool for library writers. A virtual-thread dispatcher (Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher()) is an interesting option for code that blocks a lot, because each task gets a cheap virtual thread instead of an IO worker. It isn't a free win. A virtual thread pinned by synchronized on JDK 21 to 23 still holds a carrier (JEP 491 removed most pinning in JDK 24). Each time the coroutine resumes, the executor starts a new virtual thread for it, so you lose the scheduler's habit of keeping a coroutine on the same worker. And cancelling a coroutine that's blocked inside it still needs runInterruptible, which lesson 5 of this track covers. Lesson 11 of this track compares the options for a whole program.

h: Cancellation and timeouts · A cancel is a request, heard only at suspension points and checks
x: A cancel only asks: the cook hears it between steps while a loop with no check sorts the whole sack (2,851 ms), suspending cleanup needs NonCancellable to give the jam pan back, and a timeout is a cancel with a timer that a blocking call hears only through runInterruptible Start with what cancel() really does. A coroutine is a piece of work that can pause and resume without holding its thread, the worker that runs the code. Every coroutine has a job, the handle to its life that you can wait for or cancel; Structured concurrency drew the tree of them. job.cancel() marks that job as cancelling, and that's all it does. It doesn't stop a thread, and it doesn't reach into the middle of your code. The coroutine finds out at its next suspension point, a call to a suspend function where it may pause, such as delay, await, join or withContext. Those library calls look at the job first. When they find it cancelled, they throw CancellationException, the exception that carries a cancel through the code. It unwinds the stack, every finally block runs on the way out, and the job ends as cancelled. A coroutine that is already paused hears it at once: one waiting in delay(10_000) is woken with the exception straight away. In the kitchen, a suspension point is the moment between two steps, when the cook glances at her phone. That's when the news reaches her. Code that never reaches such a point never hears. Here's the helper with the lentils, a loop that is pure CPU work, which means calculation with no waiting in it: Java // Java equivalent: a loop that never reads the interrupt flag int countStones(long[] lentils, LongPredicate isStone) { int stones = 0; for (long lentil : lentils) if (isStone.test(lentil)) stones++; return stones; } Kotlin // Naive: never looks up from the sack suspend fun countStones(lentils: LongArray, isStone: (Long) -> Boolean): Int { var stones = 0 for (lentil in lentils) if (isStone(lentil)) stones++ return stones } Nothing in the loop is a suspension point, so a cancel waits until the loop ends. This is cooperative cancellation: cancelling asks, and the code stops when it next checks. Java works the same way. Future.cancel(true) sets the thread's interrupt flag, a per-thread true-or-false value that asks it to stop (A thread's life, in the first track). A loop that never reads the flag keeps going. CancelABusyLoop, in the Try it below, runs four loops over 60 million lentils on Dispatchers.Default, the pool for CPU work. It has one thread per core, the part of the processor that runs one thread at a time. Each loop is cancelled 100 ms after it starts. Predict how long each takes to stop. On this busy machine it printed: no check stopped 2851 ms after cancel() while (isActive) stopped 4 ms after cancel() ensureActive() every 1,000 stopped 10 ms after cancel() yield() every 1,000 stopped 1 ms after cancel() The loop with no check didn't stop when it was asked. It stopped when the sack was empty, almost three seconds later. (An idle machine sorts the whole sack in about 1.5 s.) The other three looked up now and then, and stopped within a few milliseconds. Those three are the tools a CPU loop has. ensureActive() throws CancellationException if the job is cancelled. isActive returns a boolean, for a loop that wants to stop quietly: while (isActive) { ... }. yield() checks too, and also lets other coroutines waiting for the same thread run first. That matters when a long loop shares a small dispatcher, the part of the library that hands coroutines to threads. A check only reads the job's state, so it costs almost nothing, but once every thousand lentils is plenty: Java // Java equivalent: read the interrupt flag yourself int countStones(long[] lentils, LongPredicate isStone) { int stones = 0; for (int i = 0; i < lentils.length; i++) { if (i % 1_000 == 0 && Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) throw new CancellationException(); if (isStone.test(lentils[i])) stones++; } return stones; } Kotlin // Fixed: looks up every 1,000 lentils suspend fun countStones(lentils: LongArray, isStone: (Long) -> Boolean): Int { val context = currentCoroutineContext() var stones = 0 for ((i, lentil) in lentils.withIndex()) { if (i % 1_000 == 0) context.ensureActive() // throws CancellationException once cancelled if (isStone(lentil)) stones++ } return stones } Watch which job you are checking. Inside launch { }, isActive and ensureActive() belong to the coroutine you launched. A plain suspend function like countStones has no scope to call them on, so it reads its own context with currentCoroutineContext(). A bare isActive in a lambda nested inside another scope can quietly read the outer scope's job. A cancel only asks. Code that never suspends or checks never hears it. So a loop can be taught to look up. The next trap is a loop that looks up, hears the news, and throws it away. Cancel four sorting loops Read CancelABusyLoop.kt. Each loop would sort its sack in about 1.5 s on an idle machine; the demo cancels it after 100 ms. Predict how long each one takes to stop. Run it. In the ensureActive() loop, change 1_000 to 10_000_000 and run it again. Predict first. Run the Java twin, which uses Future.cancel(true) and the interrupt flag. CancelABusyLoop.kt package workbench.coroutines.l05 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.ensureActive import kotlinx.coroutines.isActive import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.yield /** Pure CPU work: looking at one lentil (a little arithmetic stands in for it). 60 million take about 1.5 s. */ private fun inspect(i: Long): Long { var x = i repeat(20) { x = x xor (x ushr 33) x *= -0xae502812aa7333L x = x xor (x ushr 29) } return x } private const val LENTILS = 60_000_000L @Volatile private var sink = 0L // keeps the JIT from deleting loops whose result nobody reads fun main() = runBlocking { // each loop gets the launched coroutine as its receiver, so isActive and ensureActive() look at // that coroutine's job (in a plain lambda they would quietly pick up runBlocking's scope instead) val loops: Map<String, suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Long> = mapOf( "no check" to { var sum = 0L for (i in 0 until LENTILS) sum += inspect(i) sum }, "while (isActive)" to { var sum = 0L var i = 0L while (isActive && i < LENTILS) { sum += inspect(i); i++ } sum }, "ensureActive() every 1,000" to { var sum = 0L for (i in 0 until LENTILS) { if (i % 1_000 == 0L) ensureActive() sum += inspect(i) } sum }, "yield() every 1,000" to { var sum = 0L for (i in 0 until LENTILS) { if (i % 1_000 == 0L) yield() sum += inspect(i) } sum }, ) for ((label, loop) in loops) { val job = launch(Dispatchers.Default) { sink = loop() } delay(100) // let it get going val asked = System.nanoTime() job.cancelAndJoin() println("%-28s stopped %5d ms after cancel()".format(label, (System.nanoTime() - asked) / 1_000_000)) } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l05.CancelABusyLoopKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l05/CancelABusyLoop.kt CancelABusyLoopJava.java // Java equivalent of CancelABusyLoop.kt: Future.cancel(true) only sets the interrupt flag. // A CPU loop stops only if it looks at the flag. package workbench.coroutines.l05; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class CancelABusyLoopJava { static final long LENTILS = 60_000_000L; static volatile long sink; // keeps the JIT from deleting loops whose result nobody reads /** Pure CPU work: looking at one lentil (a little arithmetic stands in for it). 60 million take about 1.5 s. */ static long inspect(long i) { long x = i; for (int k = 0; k < 20; k++) { x ^= x >>> 33; x *= -0xae502812aa7333L; x ^= x >>> 29; } return x; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Map<String, Runnable> loops = new LinkedHashMap<>(); loops.put("no check", () -> { long sum = 0; for (long i = 0; i < LENTILS; i++) sum += inspect(i); sink = sum; }); loops.put("isInterrupted() every 1,000", () -> { long sum = 0; for (long i = 0; i < LENTILS; i++) { if (i % 1_000 == 0 && Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) break; sum += inspect(i); } sink = sum; }); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); // one thread, so the no-op below waits for it for (var e : loops.entrySet()) { Future<?> f = pool.submit(e.getValue()); Thread.sleep(100); // let it get going long asked = System.nanoTime(); f.cancel(true); // sets the interrupt flag; the future reports "cancelled" at once // wait for the thread itself to come back: the no-op runs only once the loop has stopped pool.submit(() -> { }).get(); System.out.printf("%-28s stopped %5d ms after cancel(true)%n", e.getKey(), (System.nanoTime() - asked) / 1_000_000); } pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l05.CancelABusyLoopJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l05/CancelABusyLoopJava.java The loop with no check stops only when its sack is empty: about 1,400 ms after cancel() on an idle machine, and 2,851 ms here on a busy one. The other three stop within a few milliseconds (4, 10 and 1 ms here). With a check only every 10 million lentils, that loop stops late, at its next check, a few hundred milliseconds on. The Java twin shows the same split (1,425 and 0 ms here): cancel(true) reports success at once, but the loop that never reads the flag keeps its thread busy until it ends. The same cancel reaches three coroutines. Only the ones at a suspension point or a check stop, and their finally blocks run. Cancellation and timeouts (Kotlin docs) read ensureActive (API reference) docs

h: Cancellation and timeouts · Never swallow the CancellationException that carries the cancel
x: Cancellation travels as an exception, and that is both its strength and its weak spot. The strength: CancellationException unwinds the stack, runs every finally, and closes every use block (Kotlin's way to close a resource) on the way out. The weak spot: a catch that catches it stops it right there. Picture the evening before the big dinner. The cook phones each supplier in turn to confirm tomorrow's delivery. One busy line shouldn't stop the round, so every call is wrapped in runCatching, the standard function that runs a block and catches whatever it throws: Java // Java equivalent: catching InterruptedException and carrying on for (String order : orders) { try { confirm(order); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("call for " + order + " failed"); failed.add(order); } } Kotlin // Naive: runCatching also catches the cancel for (order in orders) { runCatching { confirm(order) } .onFailure { e -> println("call for $order failed, skipping: $e"); failed += order } } runCatching catches every Throwable. So do catch (e: Exception) and catch (e: Throwable), because on the JVM CancellationException is java.util.concurrent.CancellationException, a subclass of IllegalStateException. Now the dinner is called off during the third call. Predict what the log shows. SwallowedCancellation, in the Try it below, phones the butcher every 100 ms, 20 times, and is cancelled at 250 ms: runCatching, swallowing: calls before cancel: 3, after cancel: 17, cancelAndJoin took 8 ms Seventeen more calls in 8 milliseconds, which is quick work even for a butcher. The coroutine was still cancelled, so every delay threw at once, runCatching caught it, and the loop went round again. Each "failed call" in the log was the cancel in disguise. A while (true) loop written this way is worse: it spins at full speed, forever. That's the part that surprises people. Catching the exception doesn't undo the cancel. The job stays cancelled, so the code after the catch runs in a coroutine whose next suspension point throws again. The Java twin fails differently, and the difference teaches something. Catching InterruptedException clears the thread's interrupt flag, so the next sleep sleeps normally. The swallowing Java loop made the same 17 calls at the usual pace, and shutdown took 1,719 ms. A swallowed interrupt is lost. A swallowed cancellation is still there, and every later suspension point throws it again. The fix is to let it through. With runCatching, rethrow it first: .onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it; ... }. With try, put catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } before the general clause. Better still, catch only the exceptions you expect, such as IOException, and let everything else go up. With the rethrow in place, the same run printed after cancel: 0. A cancel is an exception on its way out. Never catch it without rethrowing it. So the cancel must be free to unwind the stack, finally blocks and all. But what can a finally block still do inside a coroutine that has been cancelled? Swallow a cancel and count the damage Read SwallowedCancellation.kt. The round of calls is cancelled at 250 ms, after 3 calls. Predict how many calls happen after the cancel, and how long cancelAndJoin takes. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=fixed, which rethrows CancellationException. Run the Java twin both ways and compare how long shutdown takes. SwallowedCancellation.kt package workbench.coroutines.l05 import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException /** Phones the butcher 20 times, 100 ms apart, to ask if the order is ready. A failed call is logged and tried again. */ suspend fun phoneButcher(rethrowCancellation: Boolean, onCall: () -> Unit) { repeat(20) { runCatching { onCall() // the phone call to the butcher would go here delay(100) }.onFailure { e -> if (rethrowCancellation && e is CancellationException) throw e // swallowed: logged as a "failed call", and the loop goes round again } } } fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val fixed = args.firstOrNull() == "fixed" var calls = 0 var cancelledAt = -1 val caller = launch { phoneButcher(rethrowCancellation = fixed) { calls++ } } delay(250) cancelledAt = calls val asked = System.nanoTime() caller.cancelAndJoin() val ms = (System.nanoTime() - asked) / 1_000_000 println(if (fixed) "runCatching + rethrow:" else "runCatching, swallowing:") println(" calls before cancel: $cancelledAt, after cancel: ${calls - cancelledAt}, cancelAndJoin took $ms ms") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l05.SwallowedCancellationKt -Pargs=fixed labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l05/SwallowedCancellation.kt SwallowedCancellationJava.java // Java equivalent of SwallowedCancellation.kt: catching InterruptedException and carrying on // swallows the cancel request, just as runCatching swallows CancellationException. package workbench.coroutines.l05; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; public class SwallowedCancellationJava { /** Phones the butcher 20 times, 100 ms apart. A failed call is logged and tried again. */ static void phoneButcher(boolean restoreInterrupt, AtomicInteger calls) { for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) { try { calls.incrementAndGet(); // the phone call to the butcher would go here Thread.sleep(100); } catch (InterruptedException e) { if (restoreInterrupt) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return; // stop: somebody asked us to } // swallowed: the flag is now clear, so the next sleep() sleeps normally } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean fixed = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("fixed"); AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); pool.submit(() -> phoneButcher(fixed, calls)); Thread.sleep(250); int cancelledAt = calls.get(); long asked = System.nanoTime(); pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupts the caller pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); long ms = (System.nanoTime() - asked) / 1_000_000; System.out.println(fixed ? "catch + restore the flag:" : "catch, swallowing:"); System.out.printf(" calls before cancel: %d, after cancel: %d, shutdown took %d ms%n", cancelledAt, calls.get() - cancelledAt, ms); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l05.SwallowedCancellationJava -Pargs=fixed labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l05/SwallowedCancellationJava.java Swallowing: 3 calls before the cancel and 17 after, and cancelAndJoin returns within a few milliseconds (8 ms here), because every remaining delay threw at once. Fixed: 0 calls after the cancel. The swallowing Java twin also makes 17 more calls, but over about 1.7 s (1,719 ms here): catching the interrupt cleared the flag, so the later sleeps were normal sleeps. Restoring the flag and returning stops it at once (1 ms here).

h: Cancellation and timeouts · Cleanup after a cancel: give the pan back inside NonCancellable
x: Picture the cook making jam in a big pan borrowed from the community kitchen down the road. The jam takes a while to set, and the pan must go back afterwards, whatever happens. Giving it back means phoning the lending desk, so giveBack is a suspend function. The natural shape is try and finally: Java // Java equivalent: once the flag is set again, blocking cleanup fails at once String ticket = desk.lend("jam-pan"); try { waitForTheJamToSet(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // keep the cancel request, as you should } finally { desk.giveBack(ticket); // blocks, sees the flag, throws InterruptedException } Kotlin // Naive: after a cancel, the pan stays in our kitchen val ticket = desk.lend("jam-pan") try { waitForTheJamToSet() // cancelled here } finally { desk.giveBack(ticket) // suspends, so it throws at once } The finally block runs, as promised. But it runs inside a coroutine that is still cancelled, and there every suspension point throws CancellationException at once. giveBack never gets past its first one. CleanupAfterCancel, in the Try it below, calls the jam off at 100 ms: borrowed the jam pan on ticket-7 cancel, plain suspend call in finally: giving back failed at once: JobCancellationException jam job finished, cancelled = true JobCancellationException is the library's own subclass of CancellationException. The jam is off, and the pan is still in our kitchen. The community kitchen would like a word. The fix is one wrapper: finally { withContext(NonCancellable) { desk.giveBack(ticket) } }. NonCancellable is a job that is always active. Inside that block, suspension points don't throw, so the call runs to the end. The coroutine itself stays cancelled: when the block finishes, the CancellationException carries on up the stack as before. Run with -Pargs=fixed, the demo printed gave back the pan on ticket-7 about 50 ms after the cancel, and the job still finished as cancelled. Use it in exactly this shape: withContext(NonCancellable), inside a finally, around the cleanup call and nothing else. The docs warn against launch(NonCancellable) or async(NonCancellable). A job passed to a builder replaces the parent, so the new coroutine leaves the tree: nothing waits for it, and nothing can cancel it. Lesson 6 of this track shows the same trap with another job. Keep the cleanup short, too. Nothing will cancel it for you, so a slow call inside it needs its own timeout, which the next section builds. Cleanup that doesn't suspend needs nothing special. Closing a file is an ordinary call, not a suspending one, and it runs fine in a cancelled coroutine. A cancelled coroutine can't suspend. Wrap suspending cleanup in withContext(NonCancellable). So far the guests have phoned to call things off. Often nobody phones. You decide in advance how long you're willing to wait. Keep the pan, then give it back Read CleanupAfterCancel.kt. The jam is called off while it sets. Predict whether gave back the pan prints. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=fixed, which wraps giveBack in withContext(NonCancellable). Run the Java twin both ways. CleanupAfterCancel.kt package workbench.coroutines.l05 import kotlinx.coroutines.NonCancellable import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException private suspend fun giveBack(ticket: String) { delay(50) // the phone call to the lending desk println(" gave back the pan on $ticket") } fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val fixed = args.firstOrNull() == "fixed" val jam = launch { val ticket = "ticket-7" println(" borrowed the jam pan on $ticket") try { delay(10_000) // waiting for the jam to set } finally { try { if (fixed) withContext(NonCancellable) { giveBack(ticket) } else giveBack(ticket) } catch (e: CancellationException) { println(" giving back failed at once: ${e::class.simpleName}") throw e } } } delay(100) println(if (fixed) "cancel, giveBack inside withContext(NonCancellable):" else "cancel, plain suspend call in finally:") jam.cancelAndJoin() println(" jam job finished, cancelled = ${jam.isCancelled}") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l05.CleanupAfterCancelKt -Pargs=fixed labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l05/CleanupAfterCancel.kt CleanupAfterCancelJava.java // Java equivalent of CleanupAfterCancel.kt: a thread that was interrupted can't make a blocking // cleanup call while its interrupt flag is set. Clear the flag for the cleanup, then restore it. package workbench.coroutines.l05; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class CleanupAfterCancelJava { static void giveBack(String ticket) throws InterruptedException { Thread.sleep(50); // the phone call to the lending desk System.out.println(" gave back the pan on " + ticket); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean fixed = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("fixed"); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); pool.submit(() -> { String ticket = "ticket-7"; System.out.println(" borrowed the jam pan on " + ticket); try { Thread.sleep(10_000); // waiting for the jam to set } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // keep the cancel request, as you should } finally { boolean wasInterrupted = fixed && Thread.interrupted(); // fixed: clear the flag for cleanup try { giveBack(ticket); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println(" giving back failed at once: InterruptedException"); Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } if (wasInterrupted) Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // and put it back afterwards } }); Thread.sleep(100); System.out.println(fixed ? "interrupt, flag cleared around giveBack:" : "interrupt, plain blocking call in finally:"); pool.shutdownNow(); pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.println(" task finished"); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l05.CleanupAfterCancelJava -Pargs=fixed labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l05/CleanupAfterCancelJava.java Without the wrapper, giving back failed at once: JobCancellationException prints, and the pan is never returned. With -Pargs=fixed, gave back the pan on ticket-7 prints about 50 ms after the cancel, and the job still finishes as cancelled. The Java twin fails the same way with InterruptedException, and its fix is to clear the flag around the cleanup and restore it afterwards. NonCancellable (API reference) docs

h: Cancellation and timeouts · A timeout is a cancel with a timer, and blocking calls don't hear it
x: Before a big dinner, the cook also sets a kitchen timer on the bread order: if the bakery hasn't answered in a few minutes, she bakes her own. withTimeout(d) { ... } is that timer. It runs the block, and when d runs out, it cancels the block. The cancel is the ordinary kind from the first section: the block stops at its next suspension point, and withTimeout throws TimeoutCancellationException. withTimeoutOrNull(d) { ... } does the same, but returns null instead of throwing: Java // Java equivalent: a fallback value when the future is late String answer = bakery.askAsync("sourdough") .completeOnTimeout("no answer: bake our own", 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) .join(); Kotlin val answer = withTimeoutOrNull(300.milliseconds) { bakery.ask("sourdough") } ?: "no answer: bake our own" Prefer withTimeoutOrNull when a timeout is an outcome you expect, as it is here. TimeoutCancellationException is a subclass of CancellationException, and that has a surprising effect. Inside launch, a timeout looks like an ordinary cancel, so a child that times out inside coroutineScope lets the scope finish normally, and nobody hears about it. If a timeout should fail the caller, turn it into a real error: withTimeoutOrNull(d) { ... } ?: error("the bakery never answered"). A timer is still a cancel, and a cancel still only asks. So what happens when the block is stuck in a blocking call, one that holds its thread until it returns? The bakery from lesson 4 of this track still has an old order line, BakeryHotline, whose ask blocks the thread until somebody picks up. Let's wait 300 ms, and let the bakery take 1.5 s. TimeoutsAndBlocking, in the Try it below, tries four shapes, with Thread.sleep standing in for the call: withTimeout { delay } threw TimeoutCancellationException after 307 ms withTimeoutOrNull { delay } returned null after 304 ms withTimeout { withContext(IO) { sleep } } threw TimeoutCancellationException after 1519 ms withTimeoutOrNull { runInterruptible { sleep } } returned null after 301 ms The two delay lines stopped on time. The third line is the trap. The timer fired at 300 ms, but a thread blocked in Thread.sleep isn't at a suspension point. The thread stayed on the old phone line, listening to it ring, long after the timer had given up. Only when the call ended at 1.5 s did withContext notice the cancel and throw. The Dispatchers.IO thread, from the pool for blocking calls, was stuck the whole time. When the blocking call is the whole block, with no suspension at all, the timeout is ignored entirely, and the late answer comes back as if nothing had happened. The fourth line is the fix. runInterruptible(dispatcher) { ... } runs blocking code on that dispatcher, and when the coroutine is cancelled, it interrupts the thread. It turns the resulting InterruptedException back into a CancellationException, so the caller sees an ordinary cancel: Java // Java equivalent: give up after the timeout and interrupt the worker Future<String> f = io.submit(() -> hotline.ask("sourdough")); try { return f.get(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } catch (TimeoutException e) { f.cancel(true); return null; } // interrupts the blocked thread Kotlin withTimeoutOrNull(300.milliseconds) { runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { hotline.ask("sourdough") } // interrupted on cancel } Here the kitchen picture breaks. A cook can put the phone down whenever she likes. runInterruptible can only interrupt, and that helps only if the blocking call listens for interrupts. Thread.sleep and BlockingQueue.take do. A read from an old-style java.net.Socket network connection doesn't, and database drivers vary, so give such a client its own timeout as well. A timeout is a cancel with a timer. A blocking call hears it only through runInterruptible. That covers the places a cancel can get lost. A cancel, though, is the polite way for a coroutine to end. The next lesson takes the rude one: a coroutine that fails. Time out the bakery four ways Read TimeoutsAndBlocking.kt. The bakery takes 1.5 s to answer and every call waits 300 ms. Predict the outcome and the time for each line. Run it. Delete the withContext(Dispatchers.IO) wrapper in the third case, leaving withTimeout(300) { Thread.sleep(1_500); "bread ready" }. Predict, then run. Run the Java twin and compare orTimeout with get plus cancel(true). TimeoutsAndBlocking.kt package workbench.coroutines.l05 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.TimeoutCancellationException import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.runInterruptible import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeout import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeoutOrNull /** Runs [block] and prints what came out and how long it took. */ private suspend fun timed(label: String, block: suspend () -> Any?) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() val outcome = try { "returned ${block()}" } catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) { "threw TimeoutCancellationException" } println("%-50s %-36s after %5d ms".format(label, outcome, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) } fun main() = runBlocking { // the bakery takes 1.5 s to answer; we wait 300 ms timed("withTimeout { delay }") { withTimeout(300) { delay(1_500); "bread ready" } } timed("withTimeoutOrNull { delay }") { withTimeoutOrNull(300) { delay(1_500); "bread ready" } } timed("withTimeout { withContext(IO) { sleep } }") { withTimeout(300) { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { Thread.sleep(1_500); "bread ready" } } } timed("withTimeoutOrNull { runInterruptible { sleep } }") { withTimeoutOrNull(300) { runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { Thread.sleep(1_500); "bread ready" } } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l05.TimeoutsAndBlockingKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l05/TimeoutsAndBlocking.kt TimeoutsAndBlockingJava.java // Java equivalent of TimeoutsAndBlocking.kt: a timeout on a CompletableFuture gives the caller // an answer on time, but nothing stops the blocking task. Future.cancel(true) interrupts it. package workbench.coroutines.l05; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; public class TimeoutsAndBlockingJava { static long t0; static String callBakery() { try { Thread.sleep(1_500); // the bakery takes 1.5 s to answer System.out.printf(" (the bakery call itself finished at %d ms)%n", ms()); return "bread ready"; } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.printf(" (the bakery call was interrupted at %d ms)%n", ms()); return "interrupted"; } } static long ms() { return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newCachedThreadPool()) { // 1. orTimeout: the caller gets a TimeoutException on time, the task runs on t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(TimeoutsAndBlockingJava::callBakery, io).orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).join(); } catch (CompletionException e) { System.out.printf("orTimeout(300 ms) caller got %s after %d ms%n", e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName(), ms()); } Thread.sleep(1_400); // wait, to see the abandoned task finish anyway // 2. Future.get with a timeout, then cancel(true): the blocked thread is interrupted t0 = System.nanoTime(); Future<String> f = io.submit(TimeoutsAndBlockingJava::callBakery); try { f.get(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } catch (TimeoutException e) { f.cancel(true); System.out.printf("get(300 ms) + cancel(true) caller gave up after %d ms%n", ms()); } Thread.sleep(100); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l05.TimeoutsAndBlockingJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l05/TimeoutsAndBlockingJava.java The two delay cases end at about 300 ms (307 and 304 ms here): one throws, one returns null. The withContext(IO) case throws too, but only after about 1,500 ms (1,519 ms here), when the sleep is over. runInterruptible returns null at about 300 ms. After your change, the bare sleep returns bread ready after 1,500 ms: the block never suspended, so the timeout was ignored. In the Java twin, orTimeout gives the caller its exception on time (320 ms here) while the abandoned call finishes at 1,519 ms anyway, and cancel(true) interrupts the call at about 300 ms. withTimeout (API reference: the pitfalls section) docs runInterruptible (API reference) docs

h: Cancellation and timeouts · Java and Kotlin
x: Stopping a CPU loop: Future.cancel(true) vs Job.cancel() LentilSort.java Future<Integer> f = pool.submit(() -> { int stones = 0; for (int i = 0; i < lentils.length; i++) { if (i % 1_000 == 0 && Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) { throw new CancellationException("sorting stopped at " + i); // 1. look at the flag } if (isStone(lentils[i])) stones++; } return stones; }); f.cancel(true); // 2. sets the worker's interrupt flag; the loop stops at its next check LentilSort.kt val job = scope.async(Dispatchers.Default) { var stones = 0 for ((i, lentil) in lentils.withIndex()) { if (i % 1_000 == 0) ensureActive() // 1. throws CancellationException once cancelled if (isStone(lentil)) stones++ } stones } job.cancel() // 2. marks the job cancelled; the loop stops at its next check Both models are cooperative, and both loops need the same explicit check, once every thousand lentils. The difference is what carries the request. Java's interrupt is a flag on one thread. It doesn't reach other threads the task started, and catching InterruptedException clears it, so a careless catch loses it for good. A coroutine's cancel is a state on its job. It reaches every child in the tree, it stays set whatever you catch, and every suspension point in the library checks it for you, so most coroutine code needs no explicit check at all. Only CPU loops like this one, and blocking calls (which need runInterruptible), have to be taught to look up.

h: Cancellation and timeouts · Worked example
x: Make an oven watcher stop cleanly The community kitchen has shared ovens. This function books one, then checks every 5 seconds whether the bread is done. When the cook calls the evening off, the function seems to hang, and the oven stays booked, so nobody else can use it. Find the three problems before you read on. suspend fun waitForBread(loaf: String): Bread { val booking = ovens.book(loaf) try { while (true) { try { val bread = ovens.check(loaf) if (bread.isDone) return bread delay(5.seconds) } catch (e: Exception) { log.warn("oven check failed for $loaf", e) } } } finally { ovens.release(booking) // suspend: a phone call to the community kitchen } } // Java equivalent of the same bugs Bread waitForBread(String loaf) { Booking booking = ovens.book(loaf); try { while (true) { try { Bread bread = ovens.check(loaf); if (bread.isDone()) return bread; Thread.sleep(5_000); } catch (Exception e) { // also catches InterruptedException log.warn("oven check failed for {}", loaf, e); } } } finally { ovens.release(booking); // fails at once if the flag is set } } Problem 1: catch (e: Exception) swallows the CancellationException from delay, so a cancelled watcher spins. Catch only the oven's own error, and let the cancel through. while (true) { try { val bread = ovens.check(loaf) if (bread.isDone) return bread } catch (e: OvenException) { // 1. only what we expect from the call log.warn("oven check failed for $loaf", e) } delay(5.seconds) // outside the try: a cancel ends the loop } while (true) { try { Bread bread = ovens.check(loaf); if (bread.isDone()) return bread; } catch (OvenException e) { // 1. only what we expect from the call log.warn("oven check failed for {}", loaf, e); } Thread.sleep(5_000); // InterruptedException now propagates } Problem 2: the release suspends in a cancelled coroutine, so it throws before the phone even rings. Wrap it in NonCancellable, with its own short timeout, so a phone nobody answers can't hold up the evening. } finally { // 2. cleanup that suspends must run non-cancellable, and bounded withContext(NonCancellable) { withTimeoutOrNull(2.seconds) { ovens.release(booking) } } } } finally { // 2. clear the flag for the cleanup, then restore it boolean interrupted = Thread.interrupted(); try { ovens.release(booking); } finally { if (interrupted) Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } Problem 3: nothing bounds the whole wait. Give the caller a deadline, and treat running out as an expected outcome rather than an exception. // 3. the caller decides how long the bread may take val bread: Bread? = withTimeoutOrNull(10.minutes) { waitForBread("rye") } if (bread == null) bakeFlatbread() // plan B // 3. the caller decides how long the bread may take Future<Bread> f = pool.submit(() -> waitForBread("rye")); try { serve(f.get(10, TimeUnit.MINUTES)); } catch (TimeoutException e) { f.cancel(true); bakeFlatbread(); } Self-check: the timeout in step 3 cancels waitForBread while it is suspended in delay. Trace what happens. (The delay throws TimeoutCancellationException, which passes the narrow catch. The finally releases the oven under NonCancellable, and withTimeoutOrNull turns the exception into null.)

h: Cancellation and timeouts · Quiz
x: val job = scope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) { while (true) { weigh(nextJar()) } }, where weigh and nextJar are plain functions. You call job.cancelAndJoin(). What happens? It returns at once, because cancel stops the coroutine It returns after the current loop iteration It never returns: the loop has no suspension point and never checks The caller gets a CancellationException thrown from cancelAndJoin Nothing in the loop looks at the job, so the cancel is never noticed, and cancelAndJoin waits forever. Add ensureActive() or yield() to the loop, or loop on while (isActive). The tempting "after the current iteration" would need a check at the top of each iteration, and there is none. A coroutine was cancelled while it waited in delay. Its finally block must call the suspending desk.giveBack(ticket). Which line does that correctly? try { desk.giveBack(ticket) } catch (e: CancellationException) { } withContext(NonCancellable) { desk.giveBack(ticket) } launch(NonCancellable) { desk.giveBack(ticket) } GlobalScope.launch { desk.giveBack(ticket) } Inside withContext(NonCancellable) suspension points don't throw, so giveBack runs to the end, and the cancel carries on afterwards. Catching the exception just loses the call. launch(NonCancellable) and GlobalScope both start a coroutine outside the tree that nothing waits for, so the program can finish before the pan goes back. What does this print? coroutineScope { launch { withTimeout(100) { delay(1_000) } } } println("done") done, after about 100 ms Nothing: coroutineScope throws TimeoutCancellationException done, after about 1,000 ms Nothing: the program hangs TimeoutCancellationException is a CancellationException, so the child counts as cancelled, not failed, and the scope completes normally. If a timeout must fail the caller, write withTimeoutOrNull(100) { ... } ?: error("timed out"). withTimeout(500) { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { Thread.sleep(3_000) } }. How long does the caller wait, and what does it get? About 500 ms, then TimeoutCancellationException About 500 ms, then null About 3 s, then TimeoutCancellationException About 3 s, then the block's result The timer fires at 500 ms and cancels the coroutine, but Thread.sleep doesn't see it. When the sleep ends, withContext checks, finds the job cancelled, and the timeout comes out as the exception. runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) would interrupt the sleep at 500 ms. From the executors track: a task is blocked in Thread.sleep(5_000) when someone calls future.cancel(true) on it. What happens to the task? Nothing until the sleep ends, then it carries on The thread is stopped and the task's finally blocks are skipped The future completes normally with null sleep throws InterruptedException at once, and the task can clean up and stop cancel(true) interrupts the worker thread, and sleep responds to interrupts by throwing. What the task does next is up to its code: restore the flag and stop, or swallow it and carry on. That is the Java version of runInterruptible.

h: Cancellation and timeouts · Key terms
x: Job The handle to a coroutine's life: you can wait for it or cancel it. Cooperative cancellation Cancelling only asks; the code stops when it next checks or reaches a suspension point. Suspension point A call to a suspend function such as delay, await or withContext. Library ones check for cancellation. CancellationException The exception that carries a cancel through the coroutine's code. Catching it without rethrowing breaks cancellation. NonCancellable A job that is always active. withContext(NonCancellable) lets cleanup suspend after a cancel. TimeoutCancellationException What withTimeout throws. It is a CancellationException, so a parent treats it as a cancel, not a failure. runInterruptible Runs blocking code on a dispatcher and interrupts its thread if the coroutine is cancelled. Does job.cancel() stop a CPU loop with no suspend calls? No. Cancellation is cooperative: the loop must call ensureActive() or yield(), or check isActive. What does a suspension point such as delay do in a cancelled coroutine? It throws CancellationException at once, without suspending. Why is runCatching { suspendCall() } risky inside a coroutine? It catches every Throwable, CancellationException included, so the loop carries on in a coroutine that is still cancelled. Rethrow CancellationException. How do you call a suspending cleanup function in finally after a cancel? withContext(NonCancellable) { giveBack() } On timeout, what do withTimeout and withTimeoutOrNull do? withTimeout throws TimeoutCancellationException, a subclass of CancellationException. withTimeoutOrNull returns null. Can withTimeout stop a Thread.sleep(10_000) inside it? No. Blocking calls ignore cancellation. Wrap them in runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { ... } so the thread is interrupted. How does a plain suspend function, with no scope, check for cancellation? currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive().

h: Cancellation and timeouts · Go deeper
x: A CancellationException doesn't always mean "I was cancelled". If you await() a Deferred that someone else cancelled, await throws CancellationException in your coroutine, even though your coroutine is fine. The kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 KDoc calls this a legacy behavior that can't be changed compatibly: your coroutine then ends as "cancelled", so its parent isn't told and the work quietly stops. If you catch it, call currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() in the catch. It throws only if your coroutine was cancelled, so after it you know the exception came from the thing you awaited, and you can turn it into a real error. The library also gives a prompt cancellation guarantee. If a coroutine is cancelled while suspended, it resumes with CancellationException even when the value it was waiting for had already arrived. withContext checks for cancellation both on entry and when its block returns. So val pan = withContext(io) { desk.lendBlocking() } can lose a pan: the block borrowed it, the caller was cancelled in the meantime, and the result is thrown away. Borrow and give back inside the same block, or use the cleanup function of CancellableContinuation.resume when you write the bridge yourself (lesson 1 of this track). Timeouts have one more subtle rule. The KDoc says cancellation on timeout "may happen at any time, even after the block finishes executing but before the caller gets resumed". So never write withTimeout { pan = desk.lend() } and expect pan to be either unset or yours. Borrow outside the timeout, or give it back in the block's own finally. Flows, which lesson 7 of this track introduces, have the same cooperative rule at a smaller scale. A flow { } builder checks for cancellation at every emit, but list.asFlow() and (1..n).asFlow() don't, so add .cancellable() to a long one that must stop on time. Finally, runBlocking bridges in the other direction. If the thread blocked in runBlocking is interrupted, the coroutine is cancelled, and runBlocking throws InterruptedException. That's how coroutine code called from a plain Java worker thread can still be stopped by an executor's shutdownNow().

h: Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers · A burnt dish tells its parent at once, from launch and async alike
x: A coroutine is a piece of work that can pause and resume without holding its thread, the worker that runs the code. A coroutine that ends with an exception other than CancellationException has failed. (CancellationException, from the last lesson, means "cancelled", which is not a failure.) A failed child tells its parent at once. Every coroutine has a job, the handle to its life. With a regular job, the parent then does what Structured concurrency described: it cancels its other children, waits for them to stop, and fails with the same exception. A scope is what hands new coroutines their parent, and coroutineScope { } makes one that waits for every child started in it. That much is true of launch. It surprises people that it's just as true of async. Builders called a Deferred a pot with the lid on, and it's natural to think a burnt dish stays under the lid until somebody lifts it with await. That is how a failed Java CompletableFuture behaves: it waits quietly for join. A coroutine doesn't: Java // Java equivalent: a failed future tells nobody until someone joins it CompletableFuture<Gravy> gravy = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> makeGravy(), pool); CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> roastPotatoes(), pool); Thread.sleep(500); // passed: the potatoes keep roasting too gravy.join(); // the failure shows up only here Kotlin coroutineScope { val gravy = async { makeGravy() } // throws BurnedException at 100 ms launch { roastPotatoes() } // takes a second delay(500) // never passed: the scope is cancelled at 100 ms gravy.await() } Predict what prints, and when. AsyncFailsWithoutAwait, in the Try it below, runs exactly this, with BurnedException, an exception the demos define for a ruined dish: 161 ms potatoes: finally 188 ms caller caught: the gravy burned The gravy burned at 100 ms (161 ms by the clock, on a JVM that had just started), the potatoes came off the heat, and the caller had the exception. The line the body would print at 500 ms never appeared. The smell reached the whole kitchen before anyone lifted the lid. The Java twin is the honest contrast. Nothing reacts at 100 ms. The caller learns about the gravy only when it joins at 500 ms. The potatoes roast on to potatoes: done at 1,056 ms, because a future has no parent to tell. The kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 docs say it directly: async follows the same rules as launch. Only when the parent is a supervisor, or there is no parent, is the exception "only available through the returned Deferred". So a try around await doesn't protect the scope. By the time await would throw, the child has already cancelled everything around it. runCatching { gravy.await() } inside coroutineScope is a common bug, and it's one of the bugs in this lesson's lab. Where do launch and async differ, then? Only when a failure has nobody above it to tell. A root coroutine is one with no parent coroutine above it. A root launch hands its exception to a handler, which the next section covers. A root async keeps it in the Deferred, and await rethrows it. That's the same split as execute and submit on a Java executor, a pool that runs submitted tasks. execute sends a task's exception to the thread's uncaught exception handler, the code that runs when an exception escapes a thread, while submit keeps it in the Future for get. A failed child cancels its parent the moment it fails, from launch or async. Catching at await is too late. So inside a tree, a failure always goes up. At the top of the tree, somebody has to write it down. Burn the gravy that nobody awaits Read AsyncFailsWithoutAwait.kt. The gravy burns at 100 ms, and the body only awaits it at 500 ms. Predict which lines print, and when. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=supervisor, which uses supervisorScope. Predict first: when does the failure come out now, and what happens to the potatoes? Run the Java twin. AsyncFailsWithoutAwait.kt package workbench.coroutines.l06 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.supervisorScope /** The exception the demos of this lesson throw for a ruined dish. */ class BurnedException(message: String) : Exception(message) private var t0 = 0L private fun log(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, msg)) fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { t0 = System.nanoTime() val supervised = args.firstOrNull() == "supervisor" try { val mainCourse: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit = { val gravy = async { delay(100); throw BurnedException("the gravy burned") } // nobody awaits this yet launch { try { delay(1_000); log("potatoes: done") } finally { log("potatoes: finally") } } delay(500) log("body: still running at 500 ms, about to await the gravy") gravy.await() } if (supervised) supervisorScope(mainCourse) else coroutineScope(mainCourse) log("scope returned normally") } catch (e: BurnedException) { log("caller caught: ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l06.AsyncFailsWithoutAwaitKt -Pargs=supervisor labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l06/AsyncFailsWithoutAwait.kt AsyncFailsWithoutAwaitJava.java // Java equivalent of AsyncFailsWithoutAwait.kt: a failed CompletableFuture tells nobody. // The failure sits in the future until someone joins it, and the sibling task runs on. package workbench.coroutines.l06; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class AsyncFailsWithoutAwaitJava { static class BurnedException extends RuntimeException { BurnedException(String message) { super(message); } } static long T0; static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { T0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { CompletableFuture<Void> gravy = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { sleep(100); throw new BurnedException("the gravy burned"); // nobody joins this yet }, pool); CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { try { sleep(1_000); log("potatoes: done"); } finally { log("potatoes: finally"); } }, pool); sleep(500); log("body: still running at 500 ms, about to join the gravy"); try { gravy.join(); } catch (CompletionException e) { log("caller caught: " + e.getCause().getMessage()); } } // close() waits for the potatoes, which nobody cancelled log("pool closed"); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l06.AsyncFailsWithoutAwaitJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l06/AsyncFailsWithoutAwaitJava.java Plain: at about 100 ms, potatoes: finally and caller caught: the gravy burned (161 and 188 ms here, on a JVM that had just started). The body's 500 ms line never prints. With -Pargs=supervisor, the failed async does nothing on its own. The body prints at 500 ms, await rethrows, and because the block itself threw, supervisorScope cancels the potatoes (potatoes: finally) and rethrows. The Java twin is the contrast: nothing reacts at 100 ms, the caller sees the failure only when it joins at 500 ms, and the potatoes roast on to about 1,000 ms. h: Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers · The kitchen notebook: CoroutineExceptionHandler runs only for roots
x: Every kitchen has a notebook by the oven where someone writes down what went wrong: "scones burnt, oven runs hot". It helps next week. It does nothing for this week's scones. CoroutineExceptionHandler is that notebook. It's a context element, one entry in the note clipped to every coroutine from Dispatchers and the coroutine context, and it receives the exceptions nobody else handled. By the time it runs, the coroutine has already finished, so there's nothing left to rescue. Use it to log and to count. The rule that trips people up: only root coroutines use it. A child passes its exception to its parent, all the way to the top, so a handler on a child is never asked. A handler takes effect in two places. One is a coroutine launched straight into a scope you created yourself, such as CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + handler).launch { }, so that no coroutine sits above it. The other is a direct child of a supervisor, which handles its own failure the way a root does (next section). It never takes effect on async, which keeps its exception for await: Java // Java equivalent: the thread's uncaught handler sees execute() failures, never submit() ones Thread.UncaughtExceptionHandler handler = (t, e) -> log.warn("task failed on {}", t.getName(), e); ExecutorService oven = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "oven"); t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler(handler); return t; }); oven.execute(() -> { throw new BurnedException("the tray burned"); }); // the handler gets it Kotlin coroutineScope { launch(handler) { throw BurnedException("the tray burned") } // ignored: this is a child } // coroutineScope throws val oven = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default + handler) oven.launch { throw BurnedException("the tray burned") } // a root: the handler gets it HandlerOnlyAtRoot, in the Try it below, puts one handler in three places. Predict which of them reach the notebook. It printed: 1. handler on a child inside coroutineScope: coroutineScope threw: the tray burned (the child's handler was ignored) 2. handler on a scope with a SupervisorJob, root launch: handler got: the tray burned (from root-launch) 3. the same scope, root async that nobody awaits: nothing printed: the failure waits in the Deferred await threw: the tray burned Only the root launch reached the notebook. The child's handler was skipped, and the root async kept its burnt tray under the lid until await lifted it. With no handler in the context, the library falls back to the JVM's last resort: the thread's uncaught exception handler, which usually prints a stack trace to the error output. A handler also ignores CancellationException, since a cancel isn't a failure. And when several children fail at once, the first exception wins, and the others are attached to it as suppressed exceptions. Read the suppressed list before you decide only one thing went wrong. In practice, put one handler on each long-lived scope you own, at the line where you create the scope. Don't sprinkle handlers on launch calls inside ordinary code, where a failure should reach the caller and a plain try around coroutineScope can deal with it. A handler only records failures, and only for root coroutines. Put it on the scopes you own. Case 2 used something we haven't explained yet: a SupervisorJob, a job that lets its children fail one at a time. Find out where a handler runs Read HandlerOnlyAtRoot.kt. It installs the same handler in three places. Predict which of the three prints handler got. Run it. In case 1, swap coroutineScope for supervisorScope and run it again. Predict first. Run the Java twin, which uses execute and submit on a pool with an uncaught exception handler. h: Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers · A supervisor lets one tray burn without stopping the others
x: A burnt dish tells its parent at once, from launch or async alike; a supervisor keeps one burnt tray from spoiling the rest, the handler is the notebook by the oven for failures at the top, and launch(SupervisorJob()) cuts the child out of the tree Back to the trays by the window. The cookies, scones and muffins for the bake sale share an oven, but they don't need each other: if the scones burn, the other two should still come out. Structured concurrency made a promise about exactly this. Its Oven class had a plain Job, so one burnt tray switched the whole oven off. Lesson 6 was to swap it for a SupervisorJob, "so one burned tray doesn't spoil the rest". It also pictured a reminder sent by text, by email and by phone, where any one of them is enough. Both are supervisor work. A supervisor is a job whose children fail independently. A child's failure doesn't cancel its siblings or the supervisor. Cancellation still flows down, so cancelling the supervisor still cancels every child. There are two ways to get one. supervisorScope { } is the supervisor version of coroutineScope, for work the caller waits for. Here it bakes every tray of one order and reports how each went: Java // Java equivalent: futures are independent, so each one handles its own failure Map<Tray, CompletableFuture<Outcome>> trays = new EnumMap<>(Tray.class); bakers.forEach((tray, baker) -> trays.put(tray, CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> baker.bake(order), pool) .handle((ok, e) -> e == null ? new Baked() : new Failed(e.getMessage())))); CompletableFuture.allOf(trays.values().toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join(); Kotlin suspend fun bakeAll(order: String): Map<Tray, Outcome> = supervisorScope { val trays = bakers.mapValues { (_, baker) -> async { baker.bake(order) } } trays.mapValues { (_, tray) -> try { tray.await(); Outcome.Baked } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Exception) { Outcome.Failed(e.message ?: e.toString()) } } } With async children, each failure stays in its Deferred, and await rethrows it where you can catch it. That's why the try around await works here, when it was too late in the first section. With launch children there's no await, so the failure goes to the handler in the context. supervisorScope doesn't install a handler of its own. SupervisorDemo, in the Try it below, puts three trays in at once. The cookies take 300 ms, the muffins 100 ms, and the scones burn at 50 ms. First under coroutineScope: 100 ms cookies: finally 125 ms muffins: finally 131 ms caller caught: the scones burned One burnt tray, and the oven was emptied. Now with -Pargs=supervisor: 104 ms handler: the scones burned 148 ms muffins baked 148 ms muffins: finally 342 ms cookies baked 343 ms cookies: finally 344 ms scope returned normally The notebook got the scones, and the other two trays came out on time. (Every line is about 50 ms late, because the JVM had just started and the machine was busy.) SupervisorJob() is the supervisor for a scope you own, the long-lived kind from Structured concurrency: CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default + handler). Every launch into that scope is a child that can fail alone, and its failure goes to the scope's handler. The lab gives the Oven exactly that. One rule doesn't change. If the body of supervisorScope itself throws, the whole scope is cancelled, children included. A supervisor protects the children from each other, not from a failing block. That's why the first section's demo, run with -Pargs=supervisor, still took the potatoes off the heat when await rethrew. Here the kitchen picture breaks a little. A real cook decides about each burnt dish as it happens. A scope decides once, when you create it: every child of a supervisor fails alone, and every child of a plain job takes its siblings down. So pick per piece of work. A course that needs all its dishes wants coroutineScope. Trays for a bake sale, reminders on three channels and other independent extras want a supervisor. When siblings need each other, use coroutineScope. When they don't, use a supervisor. So a supervisor goes around the children, or into a scope's constructor. There's a third place people put it, and it's the wrong one. Three trays, one burnt Read SupervisorDemo.kt. The scones burn at 50 ms, the muffins take 100 ms and the cookies 300 ms. Predict the output with coroutineScope. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=supervisor. Predict first: what does the handler print, and when does the scope return? Run the Java twin and compare its default with Kotlin's default. SupervisorDemo.kt package workbench.coroutines.l06 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineExceptionHandler import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.supervisorScope private var started = 0L private fun log(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - started) / 1_000_000, msg)) // supervisorScope installs no handler of its own, so failed launch children need one in the context private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> log("handler: ${e.message}") } fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking(handler) { started = System.nanoTime() val supervised = args.firstOrNull() == "supervisor" // three trays for the bake sale, all in the oven at once val bakeAll: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit = { launch { try { delay(300); log("cookies baked") } finally { log("cookies: finally") } } launch { delay(50); throw BurnedException("the scones burned") } launch { try { delay(100); log("muffins baked") } finally { log("muffins: finally") } } } try { if (supervised) supervisorScope(bakeAll) else coroutineScope(bakeAll) log("scope returned normally") } catch (e: BurnedException) { log("caller caught: ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l06.SupervisorDemoKt -Pargs=supervisor labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l06/SupervisorDemo.kt SupervisorDemoJava.java // Java equivalent of SupervisorDemo.kt: CompletableFutures are independent by default, like // children of a supervisor. Nothing cancels the siblings, so each future handles its own failure. package workbench.coroutines.l06; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class SupervisorDemoJava { static class BurnedException extends RuntimeException { BurnedException(String message) { super(message); } } static long started; static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - started) / 1_000_000, msg); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { started = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { // three trays for the bake sale, all in the oven at once CompletableFuture<Void> cookies = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { sleep(300); log("cookies baked"); }, pool); CompletableFuture<Void> scones = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { sleep(50); throw new BurnedException("the scones burned"); }, pool); CompletableFuture<Void> muffins = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { sleep(100); log("muffins baked"); }, pool); // each failure is handled where it happens; the siblings never hear about it CompletableFuture<Void> sconesHandled = scones.exceptionally(e -> { log("handled: " + e.getCause().getMessage()); return null; }); CompletableFuture.allOf(cookies, sconesHandled, muffins).join(); log("all three trays are out"); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l06.SupervisorDemoJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l06/SupervisorDemoJava.java With coroutineScope, the cookies and muffins are cancelled within about 50 ms of the scones burning (their finally lines) and the caller catches the scones burned. With -Pargs=supervisor, the handler prints at about 50 ms, the muffins are baked at about 100 ms and the cookies at about 300 ms, and the scope returns normally (each line runs some 50 ms late on a busy machine). The Java twin behaves like the supervisor without being asked: futures are independent, so each one has to handle its own failure. Same burnt tray, two parents. A plain Job cancels the whole family; a SupervisorJob keeps the failure with the child that had it. supervisorScope (API reference) docs SupervisorJob (API reference) docs

h: Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers · launch(SupervisorJob()) looks supervised but cuts the child loose
x: Here is the most common wrong fix. A dinner has a dessert in the oven, and every time the dessert burns, it takes the main course down with it. So someone writes: Java // Java equivalent: hand the task to some other, longer-lived executor try (var dinner = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { SHARED_POOL.submit(() -> bakeDessert()); // no longer part of this dinner dinner.submit(() -> cookMainCourse()); } Kotlin coroutineScope { launch(SupervisorJob()) { bakeDessert() } // meant as "make this child supervised" launch { cookMainCourse() } } It reads like "a supervised child", and it is something else. A builder's context argument overrides the scope's, as Dispatchers and the coroutine context showed, and that includes the Job. So the new coroutine becomes the child of that fresh SupervisorJob, which has no parent of its own. The dessert has left the tree. coroutineScope doesn't wait for it, cancelling the dinner doesn't cancel it, and its failure goes to a handler or the uncaught exception handler instead of to the dinner. It's GlobalScope from Structured concurrency, wearing a new apron. SupervisorTrap, in the Try it below, starts one child each way and cancels the dinner at 100 ms: 120 ms normal child: finally 165 ms dinner cancelled and joined 324 ms trap child: still running, nobody cancelled me 566 ms main done The dinner was cancelled and joined. A good 150 ms later, the trap child was still at work. The compiler now says so too. kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 deprecates the overload of launch that takes a Job. Compiling the demo prints a warning that begins: "Passing a Job to coroutine builders breaks structured concurrency, leading to hard-to-diagnose errors." The same rule applies to async and withContext, with one documented exception: withContext(NonCancellable) for cleanup, from the last lesson. Put the supervisor where it belongs. Inside a function, wrap the children in supervisorScope { }. For background work, give the owning class a scope built with SupervisorJob() in its constructor, and launch into it. Then the work is supervised and still owned: the scope waits for it, counts it and cancels it when the owner's life ends. Never pass a Job to a builder. Put the supervisor in a scope instead. When you see launch(SupervisorJob()), launch(Job()) or async(SupervisorJob()) in a review, ask what the author wanted. The answer is almost always one of those two shapes. Cancel the dinner and watch the trap child carry on Read SupervisorTrap.kt. The dinner is cancelled at 100 ms. Predict which of the two children prints after that. Run it. Look for the deprecation warning in the Gradle output when the demo compiles. Delete SupervisorJob() from the first launch and run it again. Run the Java twin, where the detached task lives on a shared executor. SupervisorTrap.kt package workbench.coroutines.l06 import kotlinx.coroutines.SupervisorJob import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking private var since = 0L private fun stamp(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - since) / 1_000_000, msg)) fun main() = runBlocking { since = System.nanoTime() val dinner = launch { // looks like "a supervised child". It is a child of a brand-new SupervisorJob instead, // so it has left the dinner's tree: nobody waits for it and nobody cancels it. launch(SupervisorJob()) { delay(300) stamp("trap child: still running, nobody cancelled me") } launch { try { delay(300); stamp("normal child: done") } finally { stamp("normal child: finally") } } } delay(100) dinner.cancelAndJoin() stamp("dinner cancelled and joined") delay(400) stamp("main done") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l06.SupervisorTrapKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l06/SupervisorTrap.kt SupervisorTrapJava.java // Java equivalent of SupervisorTrap.kt: a task sent to some other executor is not part of the // dinner. Shutting the dinner's executor down interrupts its own tasks, not that one. package workbench.coroutines.l06; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class SupervisorTrapJava { static long since; static void stamp(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - since) / 1_000_000, msg); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { since = System.nanoTime(); ExecutorService shared = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(); // what launch(SupervisorJob()) amounts to ExecutorService dinner = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); shared.submit(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(300); stamp("detached task: still running, nobody cancelled me"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { stamp("detached task: interrupted"); } }); dinner.submit(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(300); stamp("dinner task: done"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { stamp("dinner task: interrupted"); } }); Thread.sleep(100); dinner.shutdownNow(); dinner.awaitTermination(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); stamp("dinner cancelled and joined"); Thread.sleep(400); shared.shutdown(); stamp("main done"); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l06.SupervisorTrapJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l06/SupervisorTrapJava.java The normal child's finally runs at about 100 ms, and the dinner is cancelled and joined. Then, at about 300 ms, trap child: still running, nobody cancelled me prints: it was never part of the dinner's tree. After your change, neither child prints after the cancel. The Java twin shows the same leak with a task on a shared pool. (The warning appears only when the file compiles; once the class is compiled, Gradle doesn't print it again.) launch (API reference: why not to pass a Job) docs
