x: A background sender: pool with an uncaught handler vs supervisor scope with a handler ReminderSender.java class ReminderSender implements AutoCloseable { private final ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "reminders"); // last resort for task failures, like a CoroutineExceptionHandler t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, e) -> log.warn("reminder failed", e)); return t; }); void remind(String guest) { pool.execute(() -> texts.send(guest)); // execute, not submit: failures reach the handler } @Override public void close() { pool.shutdownNow(); } } ReminderSender.kt class ReminderSender(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO) { private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> log.warn("reminder failed", e) } // SupervisorJob: one failed text doesn't cancel the others or the scope private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher + handler) fun remind(guest: String): Job = scope.launch { texts.send(guest) } // a root child: failures reach the handler fun close() = scope.cancel() } The two defaults are opposite. A Java thread pool is a supervisor without being asked: tasks never cancel each other, so your only job is to make sure failures are seen (execute sends them to the uncaught handler, submit hides them in a Future nobody reads). A coroutine scope with a plain Job fails together, which is right for a course of dishes and wrong for a background sender, so you opt in with SupervisorJob(). After that the shapes match: launch is execute and goes to the handler, async is submit and keeps its failure for await. What Kotlin adds is the tree. The scope still knows every child, so close() cancels the texts in flight, and a test that calls remind can wait for them.

h: Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers · Worked example
x: Undo a launch(SupervisorJob()) fix A family recipe app serves a dinner: it marks the dinner as cooked in the recipe book, then posts a photo to the family chat. The chat was down one evening, the photo's failure cancelled the recipe-book entry, and someone fixed it like this. Since then the tests are flaky (photos post after a test has ended), and the app tries to post photos after it has closed. Why? suspend fun serveDinner(menu: Menu) = coroutineScope { val dinner = kitchen.cook(menu) launch { recipeBook.record(dinner) } launch(SupervisorJob()) { chat.postPhoto(dinner.photo) } // the "fix" dinner } // Java equivalent of the same fix: the photo goes to a shared pool nobody owns Dinner serveDinner(Menu menu) throws Exception { Dinner dinner = kitchen.cook(menu); try (var request = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { request.submit(() -> recipeBook.record(dinner)); SHARED_POOL.submit(() -> chat.postPhoto(dinner.photo())); // the "fix" } return dinner; } The SupervisorJob() became the photo's parent, so the photo left the dinner's tree: nothing waits for it and nothing cancels it. Decide what the author wanted. Serving dinner shouldn't wait for the chat, so the photo belongs to a long-lived owner. Give that owner a supervisor scope and a handler. class PhotoPoster(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO) : AutoCloseable { private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { ctx, e -> log.warn("photo ${ctx[CoroutineName]?.name} not posted", e) // 1. log with the dinner's name } // 2. supervised and owned: children fail alone, close() still reaches them private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher + handler) fun post(dinner: Dinner): Job = scope.launch(CoroutineName(dinner.name)) { chat.postPhoto(dinner.photo) } override fun close() = scope.cancel() } // Java equivalent: the poster owns its pool and its failure handler class PhotoPoster implements AutoCloseable { private final ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "photos"); t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, e) -> log.warn("photo not posted", e)); // 1. log return t; }); // 2. owned: close() reaches every task void post(Dinner dinner) { pool.execute(() -> chat.postPhoto(dinner.photo())); } @Override public void close() { pool.shutdownNow(); } } The dinner goes back to plain structured code. The recipe-book entry must succeed or fail with the dinner, so it stays part of the call. The photo is handed to its owner. suspend fun serveDinner(menu: Menu): Dinner { val dinner = kitchen.cook(menu) recipeBook.record(dinner) // 3. part of the dinner: a failure fails the dinner photoPoster.post(dinner) // handed off: the owner deals with failures return dinner } Dinner serveDinner(Menu menu) { Dinner dinner = kitchen.cook(menu); recipeBook.record(dinner); // 3. part of the dinner photoPoster.post(dinner); // handed off to its owner return dinner; } If the app must also show whether the photo got through, the dinner does wait for it, and the right shape is supervisorScope with an outcome for the call instead. suspend fun serveAndShare(menu: Menu): Pair<Dinner, Boolean> = supervisorScope { val dinner = kitchen.cook(menu) recipeBook.record(dinner) // 4. waited for, but allowed to fail alone val photo = async { chat.postPhoto(dinner.photo) } val posted = try { photo.await(); true } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Exception) { false } dinner to posted } Map.Entry<Dinner, Boolean> serveAndShare(Menu menu) { Dinner dinner = kitchen.cook(menu); recipeBook.record(dinner); // 4. waited for, but allowed to fail alone boolean posted = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> chat.postPhoto(dinner.photo()), pool) .handle((ok, e) -> e == null) .join(); return Map.entry(dinner, posted); } Self-check: in step 4, recipeBook.record throws. What happens to the photo? (Nothing: it hasn't started yet. The exception is thrown by the supervisorScope block itself, so the scope is cancelled and rethrows. A supervisor protects siblings from each other, not from a failing block.)

From lesson 5 of this track: a reminder loop goes over three channels with try { sender.send(guest) } catch (e: Exception) { log.warn("send failed", e) }. The dinner is called off, and the loop's coroutine is cancelled while the text is being sent. What happens? The loop stops at the text, because CancellationException is not an Exception The cancel is logged as a failed send, and each remaining channel is tried and "fails" at once The JVM interrupts the thread and the loop exits The scope's handler receives the CancellationException CancellationException extends IllegalStateException, so catch (e: Exception) catches it. The coroutine stays cancelled, so every later send throws at its first suspension point and is logged too. Rethrow CancellationException or catch narrower types. Handlers ignore cancellations.

h: Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers · Key terms
x: Failed coroutine A coroutine that ended with an exception other than CancellationException. It cancels its parent unless the parent is a supervisor. Root coroutine A coroutine with no parent coroutine above it, such as one launched straight into a scope you created. CoroutineExceptionHandler A context element that receives uncaught exceptions from root coroutines, for logging and counting. The notebook by the oven. Supervisor A job whose children fail independently. Cancellation still flows down to all of them. supervisorScope The supervisor version of coroutineScope, for a block of work the caller waits for. Suppressed exception An extra failure attached to the first one, when several children fail together. In a plain coroutineScope, an async child fails and nobody has called await. What happens? The scope is cancelled at once, its other children are cancelled, and the scope rethrows the child's exception. Where does a CoroutineExceptionHandler take effect? On root coroutines and direct children of a supervisor. Never on ordinary children, never on async. What does supervisorScope change compared with coroutineScope? A failed child doesn't cancel its siblings or the scope. Cancelling the scope still cancels every child. A launch child of supervisorScope fails. Where does its exception go? To the CoroutineExceptionHandler in its context, or to the thread's uncaught exception handler if there is none. What does launch(SupervisorJob()) { } inside a scope really do? The new SupervisorJob becomes the parent, so the coroutine leaves the scope's tree: the scope doesn't wait for it or cancel it. Where does SupervisorJob() belong? In the constructor of a scope you own: CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher + handler). Inside a function, use supervisorScope { }. Three children fail at once. Which exception does the parent rethrow? The first one. The other two are attached to it as suppressed exceptions.

h: Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers · Go deeper
x: SupervisorJob(parent) takes an optional parent, and that link works in one direction. If the parent is cancelled or fails, the supervisor is cancelled with it. A failure of one of the supervisor's children doesn't travel up. That makes CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob(appJob) + dispatcher) a good shape for one part of a program that should stop with the whole program but never take it down. supervisorScope and SupervisorJob differ in one detail that bites in tests. supervisorScope waits for all its children, like coroutineScope, and rethrows if its own block throws. A scope built with SupervisorJob() never completes on its own: it's a long-lived container, and you end it with cancel(). That's why the lab's Oven has an explicit switchOff(). The last-resort path on the JVM can be extended. kotlinx.coroutines looks up CoroutineExceptionHandler implementations through ServiceLoader, the JDK's mechanism for finding plug-in implementations on the classpath, and calls each of them before the thread's uncaught exception handler. kotlinx-coroutines-test uses that hook to collect exceptions from coroutines that escape a test, and since 1.7 runTest fails at the end if any were collected, even from coroutines that are not children of the test. That's why the lab's starting code fails loudly instead of printing a stack trace and passing. Finally, CancellationException once more. Since a cancel isn't a failure, it never goes to a handler, and a child that ends with it never cancels its parent. That's the rule that made the runCatching loop in lesson 5 of this track so dangerous, and it's also why withTimeout inside a launch fails quietly. Code that turns a timeout into a real error (withTimeoutOrNull(d) { } ?: error("timed out")) produces an IllegalStateException, which does travel up the tree.

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · A flow is a recipe card that runs once per collector
x: A cold flow is a recipe card: it cooks nothing until someone collects, and each collector cooks it from the top; steps only write on the card, the terminal one cooks, flowOn moves the steps above it, catch handles what falls from above and onCompletion every ending A flow is a stream of values that you receive one at a time, through a suspend call. (A suspend function is one that can pause without holding its thread, the worker that runs the code.) The usual way to make one is the flow { } builder, a block in which you call emit once for each value. Here's a flow of the items in one aisle of a grocer's online shop. The shop's website lists an aisle a page at a time. You ask for the first page, and each page carries a cursor, a small bookmark that says where the next page starts: Java // Java equivalent: a cold Reactor Flux that asks for the next page once the previous one is in Flux<Item> aisleItems(GroceryShop shop, String aisle) { return shop.page(aisle, null) // Mono<ItemPage> .expand(p -> p.nextCursor() == null ? Mono.empty() : shop.page(aisle, p.nextCursor())) .flatMapIterable(ItemPage::items); } Kotlin fun aisleItems(shop: GroceryShop, aisle: String): Flow<Item> = flow { var cursor: String? = null do { val page = shop.page(aisle, cursor) // a suspend call to the shop's website for (item in page.items) emit(item) cursor = page.nextCursor } while (cursor != null) } Calling aisleItems(...) runs nothing. It returns the recipe card, a description of the work. The body runs when someone calls a terminal operator, a suspend function such as collect or toList that reads the flow to the end. It runs again from the top for every collector, every caller doing that reading. A flow that behaves this way is cold. A Reactor Flux, from the reactive track, is cold in the same way: nothing happens until you subscribe. ColdFlow, in the Try it below, checks those claims on a smaller aisle, with two items on each of three pages. It builds the flow, collects it twice, then takes three items. Predict every fetching line first: building the flow built; nothing fetched yet first collect: fetching page 0 of the fruit aisle fetching page 1 of the fruit aisle fetching page 2 of the fruit aisle got [apples, bananas, cherries, dates, figs, grapes] second collect: fetching page 0 of the fruit aisle fetching page 1 of the fruit aisle fetching page 2 of the fruit aisle got [apples, bananas, cherries, dates, figs, grapes] take(3): fetching page 0 of the fruit aisle fetching page 1 of the fruit aisle got [apples, bananas, cherries] Building printed nothing. Each collection fetched all three pages again. And take(3) stopped after page 1, because the third item was on it. The figs and grapes were never fetched, because nobody asked for them. Two properties explain that last line. First, a flow is sequential: emit is a suspend call that returns only when the collector has finished with the value, so the producer never runs ahead of the consumer. That's Flow's backpressure, the way a slow consumer slows the producer down, with no request(n) from the reactive track in sight. Second, a collector that stops early stops the producer. take(3) cancels the flow after the third value, the cancel from Cancellation and timeouts, so the loop never asks for page 2. The other builders are shortcuts. flowOf(a, b, c) emits fixed values, and list.asFlow() or (1..n).asFlow() turn collections and ranges into flows. One caution: flow { } checks for cancellation at every emit, but asFlow() doesn't, so add .cancellable() to a long one that must stop on time. channelFlow and callbackFlow are for producers that aren't plain step-by-step code, and lesson 9 of this track covers them. Here the recipe picture breaks. Two cooks with one card make two cakes, and a real kitchen would notice the waste. A cold flow doesn't: three collectors fetch every page three times, and nothing warns you. Sharing one run is lesson 8 of this track. Building a flow runs nothing. Each collector runs it again, from the top. The card has one step so far: emit each item. Real recipes have more steps, and so do flows. Collect a cold flow three times Read ColdFlow.kt. Predict every fetching page line, including the ones for take(3). Run it. Change take(3) to take(2) and run it again. Predict first: how many pages now? Run the Java twin, a Flux built the same way. ColdFlow.kt package workbench.coroutines.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.take import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.toList import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking private val pages = listOf(listOf("apples", "bananas"), listOf("cherries", "dates"), listOf("figs", "grapes")) /** Three pages of two items each, from the grocer's shop, which takes 20 ms per page. */ fun aisle(name: String): Flow<String> = flow { for ((page, items) in pages.withIndex()) { println(" fetching page $page of the $name aisle") delay(20) for (item in items) emit(item) } } fun main() = runBlocking { println("building the flow") val fruit = aisle("fruit") println("built; nothing fetched yet") println("first collect:") println(" got ${fruit.toList()}") println("second collect:") println(" got ${fruit.toList()}") println("take(3):") println(" got ${fruit.take(3).toList()}") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l07.ColdFlowKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l07/ColdFlow.kt ColdFlowJava.java // Java equivalent of ColdFlow.kt: a Reactor Flux is cold too. Nothing runs until you subscribe, // every subscription starts again, and take(3) cancels the source when it has enough. package workbench.coroutines.l07; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.List; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; public class ColdFlowJava { static final List<List<String>> PAGES = List.of(List.of("apples", "bananas"), List.of("cherries", "dates"), List.of("figs", "grapes")); static Flux<String> aisle(String name) { return Flux.range(0, 3) .concatMap(page -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> { System.out.println(" fetching page " + page + " of the " + name + " aisle"); return PAGES.get(page); }).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(20)), 1) // prefetch 1: ask for one page at a time .flatMapIterable(items -> items); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("building the flux"); Flux<String> fruit = aisle("fruit"); System.out.println("built; nothing fetched yet"); System.out.println("first subscribe:"); System.out.println(" got " + fruit.collectList().block()); System.out.println("second subscribe:"); System.out.println(" got " + fruit.collectList().block()); System.out.println("take(3):"); System.out.println(" got " + fruit.take(3).collectList().block()); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l07.ColdFlowJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l07/ColdFlowJava.java Building prints nothing. Each full collection fetches pages 0, 1 and 2 again. take(3) fetches pages 0 and 1, because the third item, cherries, is on page 1, and the flow is cancelled before page 2. With take(2) only page 0 is fetched. The Java twin prints the same lines, because a Flux is cold too. Asynchronous Flow (Kotlin docs) read

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · Steps on the card: intermediate operators build, terminal operators run
x: Operators are the steps written on the card: wash, peel, chop. They come in two kinds. Intermediate operators such as map, filter, onEach, take and transform take a flow and return a new flow. They're plain functions: they return at once and run nothing, like writing one more line on the card. Terminal operators such as collect, toList, first, fold and count are suspend functions. They start the flow, read it, and return when it ends. That's somebody cooking. Java // Java equivalent: Reactor operators also only build; block() (or subscribe) runs them Flux<String> bargains = aisleItems(shop, "fruit") .filter(i -> i.priceCents() < 200) .map(i -> String.format("%s: %.2f", i.name(), i.priceCents() / 100.0)); List<String> firstTen = bargains.take(10).collectList().block(); Kotlin val bargains: Flow<String> = aisleItems(shop, "fruit") // nothing runs yet .filter { it.priceCents < 200 } .map { "${it.name}: %.2f".format(it.priceCents / 100.0) } val firstTen = bargains.take(10).toList() // now it runs By default all of it runs in one coroutine, one value at a time. Predict the order in which these lines print. OperatorOrder, in the Try it below, sends three weights from the kitchen scale through a filter and a map, and prints at every step. (A negative reading means the scale wasn't set to zero.) pipeline built: no line above has printed yet emit 250 filter passed 250 map -> 0.25 kg collect 0.25 kg emit -40 emit 1200 filter passed 1200 map -> 1.20 kg collect 1.20 kg The first weight went all the way into the collector before the second one was even emitted, and the -40 stopped at the filter. There are no queues between the steps and no extra threads. Each emit, in the end, is a plain call into the next step's code. The few operators that add concurrency on purpose, such as buffer, flowOn and flatMapMerge, say so in their docs. A reusable step is just an extension function, and it reads like a built-in one: Java // Java equivalent: a function from Flux to Flux, applied with transform static Function<Flux<Item>, Flux<Item>> under(long cents) { return items -> items.filter(i -> i.priceCents() < cents); } Flux<Item> cheapFruit = aisleItems(shop, "fruit").transform(under(200)); Kotlin fun Flow<Item>.under(cents: Long): Flow<Item> = filter { it.priceCents < cents } val cheapFruit = aisleItems(shop, "fruit").under(200) transform { value -> ... } is the general form: it can emit zero, one or many values for each value that comes in. Watch for a terminal operator hiding in a function that ought to return a flow. suspend fun bargains(): List<String> = pipeline.toList() cooks the whole recipe at the call and holds every line in memory. fun bargains(): Flow<String> leaves the caller free to stream it, take the first ten, or stop early. Intermediate operators only write steps on the card. A terminal operator cooks. Every step so far ran on the collector's thread. That's fine for a filter. It isn't fine when one of the steps blocks. Watch one value at a time Read OperatorOrder.kt. Predict the order of the emit, filter, map and collect lines. Run it. Add .take(1) just before .collect. Predict how many emit lines print now. Run the Java twin. OperatorOrder.kt package workbench.coroutines.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.filter import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flowOf import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.map import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.onEach import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking fun main() = runBlocking { // weights in grams from the kitchen scale; a negative reading means it wasn't set to zero val pipeline = flowOf(250L, -40L, 1_200L) .onEach { println("emit $it") } .filter { it > 0 }.onEach { println(" filter passed $it") } .map { "%.2f kg".format(it / 1_000.0) }.onEach { println(" map -> $it") } println("pipeline built: no line above has printed yet") pipeline.collect { println(" collect $it") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l07.OperatorOrderKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l07/OperatorOrder.kt OperatorOrderJava.java // Java equivalent of OperatorOrder.kt: a synchronous Flux also moves one item through the whole // chain before the source produces the next one, and nothing runs until subscribe(). package workbench.coroutines.l07; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; public class OperatorOrderJava { public static void main(String[] args) { // weights in grams from the kitchen scale; a negative reading means it wasn't set to zero Flux<String> pipeline = Flux.just(250L, -40L, 1_200L) .doOnNext(g -> System.out.println("emit " + g)) .filter(g -> g > 0).doOnNext(g -> System.out.println(" filter passed " + g)) .map(g -> String.format("%.2f kg", g / 1_000.0)).doOnNext(s -> System.out.println(" map -> " + s)); System.out.println("pipeline built: no line above has printed yet"); pipeline.subscribe(s -> System.out.println(" subscribe " + s)); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l07.OperatorOrderJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l07/OperatorOrderJava.java The pipeline built line comes first. Then each weight goes all the way through before the next one is emitted: emit 250, filter passed, map, collect, then emit -40, which stops at the filter, then the third weight. With take(1) only one emit prints: once the collector has its value, the flow is cancelled. The synchronous Flux in the Java twin prints the same order. Flow (API reference: operators, context, exceptions) docs

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · Move the blocking steps with flowOn, not with withContext around emit
x: A flow runs in the context of the coroutine that collects it. The context is the small set of settings that travels with a coroutine, the note clipped to the dish from lesson 4 of this track. That includes its dispatcher, the part of the library that picks the thread. The docs call this context preservation, and it means the collector never has to wonder which thread its lambda runs on. It also rules out the obvious way to move a blocking source to Dispatchers.IO, the bench by the door from lesson 4 of this track. Say the grocer's deliveries come with a note, a small text file with one line per item, such as flour,2000,g. The kitchen reads it with an old reader whose readLine blocks, so the reading belongs on that bench: Java // Java equivalent: Reactor has no such rule; subscribeOn moves the source to another scheduler Flux.<DeliveryLine>generate(sink -> { String line = reader.readLine(); if (line == null) sink.complete(); else sink.next(parseLine(line)); }) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()); Kotlin // Naive: emit from another context throws IllegalStateException ("Flow invariant is violated") flow { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit(parseLine(reader.readLine()!!)) } } // Fixed: flowOn changes the context of everything above it flow { while (true) emit(parseLine(reader.readLine() ?: break)) }.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) emit must run in the collector's context, and the builder checks every call. It's strict about this, and its error message, "Flow invariant is violated", reads like a court ruling. The reason is in the last section: emit calls the next step's code directly. An emit inside withContext(Dispatchers.IO) would run the collector's lambda on an IO thread that the collector never asked for. flowOn(dispatcher) is the tool. It changes the context of the part of the chain above it, the upstream, and leaves everything below it, the collector included, where it was. To do that, it runs the upstream in a separate coroutine and puts a small queue between the two halves (lesson 9 of this track calls it a channel). So with flowOn, the reading can run ahead of the collector by up to 64 lines, the default buffer size, instead of exactly one. For a file read that's usually what you want. FlowOnDemo, in the Try it below, prints the thread for each step. Predict them first: read on DefaultDispatcher-worker-1 parse on DefaultDispatcher-worker-1 format on main save on main flour: 2000 read on DefaultDispatcher-worker-1 parse on DefaultDispatcher-worker-1 format on main save on main eggs: 12 read and parse sit above flowOn(Dispatchers.IO), so they ran on a worker thread (IO and Default share one pool, as lesson 4 of this track showed). format and save sit below it, and they stayed on main, the collector's thread. Reactor's nearest tools are subscribeOn, which moves the source, and publishOn, which moves what follows it; the reactive track covers both. The difference that matters is the subscriber. With Reactor, unless you add a publishOn, the subscriber runs on the scheduler's thread too. With flowOn, the collector always stays in its own context. So don't reach for flowOn to move the collector. If the collecting side blocks (it writes each line to a file, say), wrap the terminal call instead: withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { flow.collect { writer.write(it) } }. flowOn moves the steps above it. The collector stays where it is. The slow part now runs on the bench by the door. The last question is what happens when a step fails. Print which thread runs each step Read FlowOnDemo.kt. Predict the thread for read, parse, format and save. Run it. Move .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) to just after the second map, before collect. Predict, then run. Run it with -Pargs=wrong to see the invariant check, then run the Java twin. FlowOnDemo.kt package workbench.coroutines.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flowOn import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.map import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext private fun thread() = Thread.currentThread().name fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { if (args.firstOrNull() == "wrong") { try { flow { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit("flour,2000,g") } // emit from another context }.collect { println("collected $it") } } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("IllegalStateException: " + e.message!!.lines().first()) } return@runBlocking } flow { for (line in listOf("flour,2000,g", "eggs,12,pcs")) { Thread.sleep(50) // a blocking read from the delivery note file println("read on ${thread()}") emit(line) } } .map { println("parse on ${thread()}"); parse(it) } .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) // everything above this line runs on IO .map { println("format on ${thread()}"); "${it.first}: ${it.second}" } .collect { println("save on ${thread()} $it") } } private fun parse(line: String): Pair<String, Long> = line.split(",").let { it[0] to it[1].toLong() } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l07.FlowOnDemoKt -Pargs=wrong labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l07/FlowOnDemo.kt FlowOnDemoJava.java // Java equivalent of FlowOnDemo.kt: Reactor's subscribeOn moves the source to another scheduler, // and publishOn moves everything after it. Without a publishOn, the subscriber runs on that // scheduler's thread too, which is the difference from flowOn. package workbench.coroutines.l07; import java.util.List; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; public class FlowOnDemoJava { static String thread() { return Thread.currentThread().getName(); } public static void main(String[] args) { Flux.fromIterable(List.of("flour,2000,g", "eggs,12,pcs")) .doOnNext(line -> { try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } // a blocking file read System.out.println("read on " + thread()); }) .map(line -> { System.out.println("parse on " + thread()); return line.split(","); }) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // the source and the steps above run there .publishOn(Schedulers.single()) // the steps below move to another thread .map(f -> { System.out.println("format on " + thread()); return f[0] + ": " + f[1]; }) .doOnNext(s -> System.out.println("save on " + thread() + " " + s)) .blockLast(); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l07.FlowOnDemoJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l07/FlowOnDemoJava.java read and parse run on a DefaultDispatcher-worker thread, while format and save run on main. After the move, format joins them on the worker, but save stays on main: no flowOn can move the collector. With -Pargs=wrong you get IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated. The Java twin needs subscribeOn for the source and publishOn to move the later steps, which run on single-1. flowOn (API reference) docs

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · Handle errors from above with catch, and every ending with onCompletion
x: Flows make a promise called exception transparency. An exception thrown downstream, by a step below or by the collector, belongs to the downstream, and a flow must not catch it and carry on emitting. The error-handling operators are built around that promise. catch { e -> ... } handles exceptions from the part of the flow above it. It can log, emit a fallback value, or rethrow. Exceptions thrown below it, including inside collect { }, pass straight through to whoever called collect. In the kitchen, catch is the rule for trouble at the stove: if the delivery note is torn halfway, write "aborted" and stop. It has nothing to say about a plate the diner drops. onCompletion { cause -> } is the flow's finally. It runs once, however the flow ends. cause is null after a normal end, the exception after a failure above or below, and a CancellationException when the collector stopped early, as take and first do. Unlike catch, it handles nothing: the exception carries on after it. Here's the delivery note put away into the pantry: Java // Java equivalent: onErrorResume only handles errors from above it; doFinally runs on every exit deliveryLines(reader) .<StockEvent>map(l -> new Stocked(l.item())) .doFinally(signal -> System.out.println("delivery ended: " + signal)) .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.just(new Aborted(e.getMessage()))) .doOnNext(pantry::save) .blockLast(); Kotlin deliveryLines(reader, Dispatchers.IO) // may throw IOException .map<DeliveryLine, StockEvent> { StockEvent.Stocked(it.item) } .onCompletion { cause -> println("delivery ended: $cause") } // sees every way the flow ends .catch { e -> emit(StockEvent.Aborted(e.message ?: "error")) } // failures above it only .collect { pantry.save(it) } // a failure here reaches the caller CatchDemo, in the Try it below, tears the delivery note after two lines: collect flour collect eggs onCompletion: cause = java.io.IOException: delivery note torn catch: java.io.IOException: delivery note torn collect ABORTED collect returned normally Now the same chain with the note intact and a full shelf instead, so saving the eggs throws inside the collector (-Pargs=collector): collect flour collect eggs onCompletion: cause = java.lang.IllegalStateException: pantry shelf full the caller got: java.lang.IllegalStateException: pantry shelf full catch printed nothing. The failure happened below it, so it went straight to the caller, and onCompletion saw it on the way past. The classic way to break the promise is a try and catch around emit inside a builder. emit runs the downstream code, so that catch also catches the collector's exceptions, and if it then emits again, the flow throws IllegalStateException ("Flow exception transparency is violated"). That's one of the bugs in this lesson's lab. Use the catch operator instead, which knows where it sits. Cold flows pay off here once more. retry(3) recovers by collecting the upstream again, and that works only because the recipe can be cooked again from the top. catch covers the steps above it, never the collector. Put the work that may fail above it. When you do want a save failure handled, that's the shape the Kotlin docs show: move the save into onEach above the catch, then call collect() with no lambda. Tear the note, then fill the shelf Read CatchDemo.kt. By default the delivery note tears after two lines. Predict every line of output, including what onCompletion prints. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=collector, where saving the eggs throws instead. Predict first: does catch print anything? Run the Java twin both ways. CatchDemo.kt package workbench.coroutines.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.catch import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.map import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.onCompletion import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.io.IOException fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val failIn = args.firstOrNull() ?: "upstream" // or "collector" val lines = flow { emit("flour,2000,g") emit("eggs,12,pcs") if (failIn == "upstream") throw IOException("delivery note torn") emit("butter,250,g") } try { lines .map { it.substringBefore(",") } .onCompletion { cause -> println("onCompletion: cause = $cause") } .catch { e -> println("catch: $e"); emit("ABORTED") } .collect { item -> println("collect $item") if (failIn == "collector" && item == "eggs") throw IllegalStateException("pantry shelf full") } println("collect returned normally") } catch (e: Exception) { println("the caller got: $e") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l07.CatchDemoKt -Pargs=collector labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l07/CatchDemo.kt CatchDemoJava.java // Java equivalent of CatchDemo.kt: onErrorResume only handles errors from above it, like catch, // and doFinally runs on every way out, like onCompletion. An exception thrown in the subscriber's // own lambda is not an upstream error: no operator above it gets to "handle" it. package workbench.coroutines.l07; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.UncheckedIOException; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; public class CatchDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { String failIn = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "upstream"; // or "collector" Flux<String> lines = Flux.concat( Flux.just("flour,2000,g", "eggs,12,pcs"), failIn.equals("upstream") ? Flux.error(new UncheckedIOException(new IOException("delivery note torn"))) : Flux.just("butter,250,g")); try { lines .map(l -> l.substring(0, l.indexOf(','))) .doFinally(signal -> System.out.println("doFinally: signal = " + signal)) .onErrorResume(e -> { System.out.println("onErrorResume: " + e); return Flux.just("ABORTED"); }) .doOnNext(item -> { System.out.println("consume " + item); if (failIn.equals("collector") && item.equals("eggs")) throw new IllegalStateException("pantry shelf full"); }) .blockLast(); System.out.println("blockLast returned normally"); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("the caller got: " + e); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l07.CatchDemoJava -Pargs=collector labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l07/CatchDemoJava.java Torn note: flour and eggs are collected, onCompletion prints the IOException, catch prints it and emits ABORTED, which is collected, and collect returns normally. Full shelf: onCompletion prints the IllegalStateException, catch prints nothing, and the caller gets pantry shelf full. The Java twin matches: onErrorResume only handles the upstream error, and doFinally reports onError or cancel. catch covers the flow above it, never the collector. onCompletion sees every way the flow can end. catch (API reference) docs onCompletion (API reference) docs

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · Java and Kotlin
x: Putting a delivery away: Flux vs Flow DeliveryImport.java Flux<StockEvent> putAway(LineReader reader) { return Flux.<DeliveryLine>generate(sink -> { // 1. a cold source, pulled on demand String line = reader.readLine(); if (line == null) sink.complete(); else sink.next(parseLine(line)); }) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // 2. the blocking read runs elsewhere .<StockEvent>map(l -> new Stocked(l.item())) .doFinally(signal -> log("delivery ended: " + signal)) // 3. every ending .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.just(new Aborted(e.getMessage()))); // 4. upstream errors only } DeliveryImport.kt fun putAway(reader: LineReader): Flow<StockEvent> = flow { // 1. a cold source, plain step-by-step code while (true) emit(parseLine(reader.readLine() ?: break)) } .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) // 2. the blocking read runs elsewhere .map<DeliveryLine, StockEvent> { StockEvent.Stocked(it.item) } .onCompletion { cause -> log("delivery ended: $cause") } // 3. every ending .catch { e -> emit(StockEvent.Aborted(e.message ?: "error")) } // 4. upstream errors only The shapes line up step for step, and both are cold. The source is where they differ most. Reactor needs a generator callback with an explicit sink, because a Flux source must answer request(n) from its subscribers. A Flow source is an ordinary loop: emit suspends until the collector is ready, so backpressure comes from suspension. Threads differ too. subscribeOn moves the whole chain until a publishOn moves it again, so Reactor subscribers often end up on a scheduler thread. flowOn moves only the upstream, and the collector stays in its own coroutine context. The error operators are nearly identical: catch and onErrorResume both handle only what is above them, and onCompletion and doFinally both run on every ending.

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · Worked example
x: Stream a price list to a file instead of loading it A program writes the grocer's whole price list to a file. It loads every item of every page into a list first, then writes. For a catalogue of two million items the program runs out of memory, and nothing at all is written until the last page is in. suspend fun exportPrices(aisle: String, out: Path) { val all = mutableListOf<Item>() var cursor: String? = null do { val page = shop.page(aisle, cursor) all += page.items // every item held in memory cursor = page.nextCursor } while (cursor != null) withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { Files.write(out, all.filter { it.priceCents > 0 }.map(::format)) } } // Java equivalent of the same design: collect everything, then write void exportPrices(String aisle, Path out) throws IOException { List<Item> all = new ArrayList<>(); String cursor = null; do { ItemPage page = shop.page(aisle, cursor); all.addAll(page.items()); // every item held in memory cursor = page.nextCursor(); } while (cursor != null); Files.write(out, all.stream().filter(i -> i.priceCents() > 0).map(Export::format).toList()); } Make the source a cold flow. Only one page is in memory at a time, and the next page is fetched only when the writer has caught up. // 1. the source: pages on demand fun aisleItems(aisle: String): Flow<Item> = flow { var cursor: String? = null do { val page = shop.page(aisle, cursor) page.items.forEach { emit(it) } cursor = page.nextCursor } while (cursor != null) } // 1. the source: pages on demand Flux<Item> aisleItems(String aisle) { return shop.page(aisle, null) .expand(p -> p.nextCursor() == null ? Mono.empty() : shop.page(aisle, p.nextCursor())) .flatMapIterable(ItemPage::items); } Build the chain with intermediate operators, and write in the collector. The file write blocks, and it's on the collecting side, so it moves with withContext around the terminal call. flowOn wouldn't help: it never moves the collector. suspend fun exportPrices(aisle: String, out: Path) = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { // 3. the collector's blocking writes run on IO Files.newBufferedWriter(out).use { writer -> aisleItems(aisle) .filter { it.priceCents > 0 } // 2. build: nothing runs yet .map(::format) .collect { line -> writer.write(line); writer.newLine() } // runs it, one line at a time } } void exportPrices(String aisle, Path out) throws IOException { try (BufferedWriter writer = Files.newBufferedWriter(out)) { aisleItems(aisle) .filter(i -> i.priceCents() > 0) // 2. build: nothing runs yet .map(Export::format) .publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // 3. the blocking writes run elsewhere .doOnNext(line -> write(writer, line)) .blockLast(); // runs it } } A half-written price list must not look finished. Delete it when the flow ends with an error. onCompletion sees the cause, and the exception still reaches the caller afterwards, which is what an export should do. aisleItems(aisle) .filter { it.priceCents > 0 } .map(::format) .onCompletion { cause -> if (cause != null) Files.deleteIfExists(out) } // 4. no half files .collect { line -> writer.write(line); writer.newLine() } aisleItems(aisle) .filter(i -> i.priceCents() > 0) .map(Export::format) .publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) .doOnNext(line -> write(writer, line)) .doOnError(e -> deleteQuietly(out)) // 4. no half files .blockLast(); Self-check: a caller runs exportPrices(...) inside withTimeout(30.seconds), and the timeout fires halfway. Is the half-written file deleted? (Yes. The timeout cancels the coroutine, so the flow ends with a CancellationException, cause is not null, and onCompletion deletes the file. It runs inside the chain, before use has closed the writer. Linux doesn't mind, but Windows refuses to delete a file that is still open, so a finally around use is the more portable place for the delete.)

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · Lab
x: A grocer's aisle, a delivery reader and a stock report labs/coroutines/src/main/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l07/PantryModel.kt labs/coroutines/src/main/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l07/PantryFlows.kt ./gradlew :coroutines:test --tests 'workbench.coroutines.l07.*' Meet the code. PantryModel.kt holds the grocer's paged shop (GroceryShop), the old blocking reader for delivery notes (LineReader), one parsed line of a note (DeliveryLine) and the events of putting a delivery away (StockEvent). You write three flows in PantryFlows.kt. Run the tests: seven of eight fail. Write aisleItems with flow { }: ask for pages starting with cursor null, emit every item, and stop when nextCursor is null. The three aisle tests check that it is lazy, cold and stops early. Fix deliveryLines: delete the withContext and add .flowOn(io) after the builder. Rewrite stockReport as a chain: map each line to Stocked, then onCompletion { onDone(it) }, then a catch that emits Aborted(message). Run the tests until all eight pass. For aisleItems, a do { ... } while (cursor != null) loop inside flow { } is all you need. emit suspends until the collector is done, so take(3) cancels the loop before the next shop.page call. map needs to know it produces the sealed type, not Stocked, or catch can't emit Aborted into it. Write .map<DeliveryLine, StockEvent> { ... }. Put onCompletion above catch: there it sees the upstream exception itself. Below catch it would see null, because catch turned the failure into a normal end. No try anywhere in stockReport. A try around emit also catches the collector's exceptions, and that breaks exception transparency. All eight tests in FlowBasicsTest pass. By the end you can build a cold Flow with flow { }, tell intermediate operators from terminal ones, move blocking upstream work with flowOn, and handle errors with catch and onCompletion without breaking exception transparency.

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · Quiz
x: What does this print? val f = flow { println("start"); emit(1); emit(2) } println("built") f.collect { println(it) } f.take(1).collect { println(it) } built, start, 1, 2, start, 1 start, built, 1, 2, 1 built, start, 1, 2, 1 start, 1, 2, built, start, 1 Building the flow runs nothing, so built comes first. Each collect runs the body from the top, so start prints twice. take(1) cancels the flow after the first value, so the second run never emits 2. lines.map { parseLine(it) }.catch { emit(FALLBACK) }.collect { pantry.save(it) }, and pantry.save throws on the third line. What happens? catch emits FALLBACK and the import carries on The exception reaches the caller of collect, and catch never sees it The flow retries the third line The exception is swallowed and collect returns normally catch only handles exceptions from the flow above it. save runs in the collector, below catch, so its exception passes through to the caller. Move the save into onEach above catch if the fallback should cover it. In runBlocking on the main thread: flow { A }.map { B }.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO).filter { C }.collect { D }. Where do A, B, C and D run? All four on IO A on IO; B, C and D on main A and B on IO; C and D on main A, B and C on IO; D on main flowOn changes the context of everything above it, the builder and the first map. Operators below it and the collector stay in the collector's context, which here is main. You collect flow { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit(readDeliveryNote()) } }. What happens? It works, and the collector runs on IO too It deadlocks, because emit waits for the IO thread It works, and the collector stays on its own thread It throws IllegalStateException: the flow invariant is violated A flow must emit in its collector's context, and the builder checks every emit. Move the work with flow { emit(readDeliveryNote()) }.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) instead. From the reactive track: Flux<String> f = Flux.just("flour").map(s -> { log(s); return s; }); runs, and nobody ever subscribes to f. What is logged? flour, once, when map is called Nothing flour, once per operator in the chain An error, because a Flux must be subscribed A Flux is cold, like a Flow: putting operators together runs nothing, and the work starts only on subscribe. A Kotlin flow built the same way logs nothing until a terminal operator collects it.

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · Key terms
x: Flow A stream of values received one at a time through a suspend call. Cold flow A flow whose code runs only when collected, from the start, once per collector. A recipe card. Collector The code that reads a flow, by calling a terminal operator such as collect. Intermediate operator An operator that returns a new flow without running anything, such as map or filter. Terminal operator A suspend function that runs the flow and consumes its values, such as collect or toList. Context preservation A flow runs in the collector's context; only flowOn changes the context of the part above it. Exception transparency A flow never catches and hides exceptions thrown by the code downstream of it. Upstream The part of a flow chain above a given operator, closer to the source. When does the body of a flow { } run? Each time a terminal operator collects it, from the top. Building the flow runs nothing. Intermediate vs terminal flow operator: what's the difference? Intermediate ones (map, filter, take) return a new flow and run nothing. Terminal ones (collect, toList, first) are suspend functions that run the flow. How does a flow get backpressure without request(n)? emit suspends until the collector has finished with the value, so the producer can't run ahead. What does .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) move? Everything above it in the chain. Operators below it and the collector stay in the collector's context. What happens if you call emit inside withContext(Dispatchers.IO) in a flow { }? The flow throws IllegalStateException: "Flow invariant is violated". Use flowOn instead. Does .catch { } handle an exception thrown inside collect { }? No. It only handles exceptions from upstream; the collector's exceptions pass through to the caller. What cause does onCompletion get when the collector uses take(1)? A CancellationException: the flow was stopped early. It gets null only after a normal end.

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · Go deeper
x: Why does a flow check emit so strictly? Because the operators rely on it. Every operator in the chain runs in one coroutine and assumes that nothing else calls its downstream at the same time. If emit could be called from another coroutine or thread, map and filter would need locks. The checks for context and for exception transparency are what let ordinary step-by-step code be a correct stream operator. When you need to emit from several coroutines, use channelFlow { }. Its send is safe from any coroutine started inside the builder, because a channel sits between the producers and the collector. callbackFlow { } is the same thing for callback APIs, and it requires awaitClose { unregister() } at the end, or it throws when the block returns. Lesson 9 of this track uses both. The Flow interface itself is "not stable for inheritance", in the words of its KDoc: write flows with the builders, or extend AbstractFlow if you really need a class. That matters if you are tempted to implement Flow on a class of your own. buffer(), conflate() and collectLatest change the sequential model on purpose. With a producer that takes 100 ms per item and a collector that takes 300 ms, three items take about (100 + 300) x 3 = 1,200 ms plain, about 100 + 300 x 3 = 1,000 ms with buffer(), and about 700 to 800 ms with conflate(), which skips the middle item. Lesson 9 of this track runs those numbers. This lesson is the short tour. The Kotlin Flow in depth track, later in the course, builds a flow from two interfaces and a function call, then takes each piece apart: the three checks inside flow { }, flowOn and its buffer, every error operator, and how to test a flow on virtual time.

h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · StateFlow is the board in the hall: one current value, and it skips what you missed
x: The menu board and the house bell: a StateFlow keeps one current value, so a busy collector sees only the last choice; a SharedFlow's buffer decides which rings are lost; stateIn shares one cold flow among many screens; and only the kitchen writes, in one step A StateFlow<T> is a flow that always has a value. You read it with .value at any moment, like glancing at the board. When you collect it, you get the current value first, then each new one. It is hot: it exists and holds its value whether or not anyone collects it, unlike the cold flows of Flow basics. That makes it the natural type for state, a value where only the latest one matters: the status of a dish, the oven's temperature, today's menu. Java // Java equivalent: a Reactor sink that replays its latest value, with repeats filtered out Sinks.Many<Menu> board = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault(new Menu("tomato")); board.tryEmitNext(new Menu("onion")); board.asFlux().distinctUntilChanged().subscribe(this::show); Kotlin val board = MutableStateFlow(Menu(soup = "tomato")) board.value = Menu(soup = "onion") // set from any thread println(board.value) // Menu(soup=onion) board.collect { show(it) } // current value first, then each change; never returns Two rules make a StateFlow cheap, and both surprise people. Updates are conflated: a slow collector doesn't get a queue of the values it missed, it gets the latest one when it's ready. And a StateFlow compares with equals. Setting a value equal to the current one does nothing, and no collector wakes up. With a data class, a new object with the same fields counts as equal. Predict the output before you read on. StateFlowConflation, in the Try it below, has a board in the hall that takes 100 ms to chalk up each menu. The cook changes the soup three times while the first one is being chalked up, then sets the last one again: the board in the hall shows tomato soup the board in the hall shows onion soup setting an equal menu again (a new object, same fields) value is onion; the collector is still waiting, because a StateFlow never completes Leek and pea never reached the board, and the second onion didn't either. Nobody chalks up "still onion". Both rules follow from what StateFlow is underneath. Its KDoc, the documentation written in the library's source, describes MutableStateFlow(initial) as a shared flow (the next section's type) with replay = 1 and DROP_OLDEST. That shared flow starts out holding the initial value, and a distinctUntilChanged() step drops repeats on the way out. So a StateFlow is for state. It's the wrong type for events, values where every single one matters, such as each step a dish goes through for the kitchen log, or "dinner's ready". Conflation would drop some of them without a trace. One more thing to expect: collect on a StateFlow never returns. The KDoc says it plainly, "state flow never completes". Collect it in a coroutine you will cancel, or wait for one particular value with first: status.first { it == DishStatus.SERVED }. A StateFlow keeps only the latest value. Use it for state, never for events. The board shows what's true now. For what just happened, the house needs a bell. Watch the board skip two soups Read StateFlowConflation.kt. Three menus are set while the board is busy, then an equal menu is set again. Predict every the board in the hall shows line. Run it. Change Menu from a data class to a plain class and run it again. Predict first: what changes, and why? Run the Java twin, which needs three Reactor operators for the same behavior. StateFlowConflation.kt package workbench.coroutines.l08 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineStart import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking data class Menu(val soup: String) fun main() = runBlocking { val board = MutableStateFlow(Menu("tomato")) val hall = launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) { board.collect { menu -> println("the board in the hall shows ${menu.soup} soup") delay(100) // chalking up the board is slow } } // the cook changes her mind three times while the board is being chalked up board.value = Menu("leek") board.value = Menu("pea") board.value = Menu("onion") delay(150) println("setting an equal menu again (a new object, same fields)") board.value = Menu("onion") delay(150) println("value is ${board.value.soup}; the collector is still waiting, because a StateFlow never completes") hall.cancel() } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l08.StateFlowConflationKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l08/StateFlowConflation.kt StateFlowConflationJava.java // Java equivalent of StateFlowConflation.kt with Reactor: a sink that replays its latest value, // distinctUntilChanged for the equality rule, and onBackpressureLatest so a slow subscriber only // gets the newest value. StateFlow does all three by itself. package workbench.coroutines.l08; import reactor.core.Disposable; import reactor.core.publisher.Sinks; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; public class StateFlowConflationJava { record Menu(String soup) {} public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Sinks.Many<Menu> board = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault(new Menu("tomato")); Disposable hall = board.asFlux() .distinctUntilChanged() .onBackpressureLatest() .publishOn(Schedulers.single(), 1) // request one value at a time .subscribe(menu -> { System.out.println("the board in the hall shows " + menu.soup() + " soup"); sleep(100); // chalking up the board is slow }); Thread.sleep(20); // the cook changes her mind three times while the board is being chalked up board.tryEmitNext(new Menu("leek")); board.tryEmitNext(new Menu("pea")); board.tryEmitNext(new Menu("onion")); Thread.sleep(250); System.out.println("setting an equal menu again (a new object, same fields)"); board.tryEmitNext(new Menu("onion")); Thread.sleep(150); hall.dispose(); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l08.StateFlowConflationJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l08/StateFlowConflationJava.java The board shows tomato soup, then onion soup: leek and pea are skipped. Setting the equal menu again prints nothing. With a plain class, equality falls back to identity, so the "equal" menu is a new value, and the board shows onion soup a second time. The Java twin prints the same two board lines, using replay().latestOrDefault, distinctUntilChanged and onBackpressureLatest. StateFlow (API reference) docs

h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · SharedFlow is the house bell, and its buffer decides which rings are lost
x: A MutableSharedFlow<T> is the house bell. It sends every value to every current subscriber, each coroutine collecting it at that moment. (A coroutine is a piece of work that can pause without holding a thread.) It has no current value of its own. Three parameters decide what it keeps: Java // Java equivalent: a multicast Reactor sink with a buffer for slow subscribers Sinks.Many<String> bell = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(64, false); Sinks.EmitResult result = bell.tryEmitNext("dinner's ready"); // FAIL_OVERFLOW when full Kotlin val bell = MutableSharedFlow<String>( replay = 0, // late listeners get no history extraBufferCapacity = 64, // room for rings a busy listener hasn't heard yet onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.SUSPEND, // when full: emit waits, tryEmit returns false ) replay is how many recent values a new subscriber gets first. extraBufferCapacity is room beyond that for values that slow subscribers haven't taken yet. onBufferOverflow decides what happens when all of it is full. SUSPEND, the default, makes emit wait for the slowest subscriber. DROP_OLDEST throws away the oldest buffered value, and DROP_LATEST throws away the new one. The two drop policies need some replay or buffer to work with. emit is a suspend function. tryEmit is its twin for code that can't suspend, such as a callback from an older library, and it's the impatient one: it never waits for anybody. If the value doesn't fit, it returns false and walks off. Here's the trap, and it's easy to fall into because the defaults look harmless. With the default parameters there is no buffer at all. So tryEmit fails whenever the flow has a subscriber, even an idle one waiting for a value, and the value is lost unless you check the result. With no buffer, only the suspending emit can hand a value over, and it waits until every subscriber has taken it. With no subscriber at all, tryEmit returns true, and the value goes nowhere. The lab's starting code has exactly this bug. SharedFlowEvents, in the Try it below, rings the bell five times with tryEmit while its one listener needs 50 ms to write each ring in the log. Predict each line: default (no replay, no buffer) tryEmit: [false, false, false, false, false] received: [] extraBufferCapacity = 2 tryEmit: [true, true, false, false, false] received: [e1, e2] extraBufferCapacity = 2, DROP_OLDEST tryEmit: [true, true, true, true, true] received: [e4, e5] extraBufferCapacity = 64 tryEmit: [true, true, true, true, true] received: [e1, e2, e3, e4, e5] a late subscriber to replay = 2 first gets: [e4, e5] The default bell rang five times and reached nobody. A buffer of 2 took two rings and refused the rest. DROP_OLDEST said true five times and quietly threw three rings away. Only the buffer of 64 delivered everything. Here the bell picture breaks. A real bell rings for whoever is in the house, and a listener in the shower simply misses it. A SharedFlow with a buffer keeps each ring for a busy listener until they're ready, and when the buffer is full, SUSPEND makes the ringer wait. In an empty house, though, the two agree: a value emitted while nobody subscribes is gone, apart from the replay cache. If events must survive having no listener, you want something else: a Channel with one consumer (lesson 9 of this track), or a file or a database. Side by side: a StateFlow has a value, replays exactly one, conflates and skips duplicates. A SharedFlow has no value, replays what you configure, and with a buffer and SUSPEND it delivers every event to every subscriber. Both are safe to emit into from many threads, the workers that run code, at once. Reactor's sinks, its objects for pushing values into a Flux, aren't by default: concurrent tryEmitNext calls can fail with FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED. A default MutableSharedFlow() has no buffer. Give it one, and check what tryEmit returns. The board and the bell are hot from the start. Often, though, the values come from a cold flow, and you want many screens to share one run of it. Find out which rings get through Read SharedFlowEvents.kt. Each case calls tryEmit five times while the only subscriber needs 50 ms per value. Predict the five results and what is received, for each of the four set-ups. Run it. Change the last case to MutableSharedFlow(replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 64). Does anything in that line change? Run the Java twin. SharedFlowEvents.kt package workbench.coroutines.l08 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineStart import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.BufferOverflow import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableSharedFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking /** Rings the bell five times with tryEmit while the one listener is busy, and reports what got through. */ suspend fun tryFive(label: String, events: MutableSharedFlow<String>) = kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope { val received = mutableListOf<String>() val listener = launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) { events.collect { delay(50); received += it } // writing each ring in the log takes 50 ms } val accepted = (1..5).map { events.tryEmit("e$it") } delay(400) listener.cancel() println("%-40s tryEmit: %s received: %s".format(label, accepted, received)) } fun main() = runBlocking { tryFive("default (no replay, no buffer)", MutableSharedFlow()) tryFive("extraBufferCapacity = 2", MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 2)) tryFive("extraBufferCapacity = 2, DROP_OLDEST", MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 2, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)) tryFive("extraBufferCapacity = 64", MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 64)) // replay: what a subscriber that arrives later gets first val replayed = MutableSharedFlow<String>(replay = 2) (1..5).forEach { replayed.emit("e$it") } // no subscribers yet println("a late subscriber to replay = 2 first gets: ${replayed.replayCache}") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l08.SharedFlowEventsKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l08/SharedFlowEvents.kt SharedFlowEventsJava.java // Java equivalent of SharedFlowEvents.kt with Reactor sinks: a multicast sink with a bounded // buffer refuses values when a slow subscriber can't keep up (FAIL_OVERFLOW instead of false), // and a replay sink keeps the last N values for late subscribers. Reactor sizes small buffers up // to its own minimum, so this twin sends 20 events instead of 5 to fill one. package workbench.coroutines.l08; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; import reactor.core.Disposable; import reactor.core.publisher.Sinks; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; public class SharedFlowEventsJava { static void tryTwenty(String label, Sinks.Many<String> events) throws InterruptedException { List<String> received = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); Disposable listener = events.asFlux() .publishOn(Schedulers.single(), 1) .subscribe(e -> { sleep(50); received.add(e); }); // writing each ring in the log takes 50 ms List<Sinks.EmitResult> results = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 1; i <= 20; i++) results.add(events.tryEmitNext("e" + i)); Thread.sleep(1_200); listener.dispose(); long ok = results.stream().filter(r -> r == Sinks.EmitResult.OK).count(); System.out.printf("%-26s tryEmitNext OK: %2d, FAIL_OVERFLOW: %2d received %2d events%n", label, ok, results.size() - ok, received.size()); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { tryTwenty("multicast, buffer of 2", Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(2, false)); tryTwenty("multicast, buffer of 64", Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(64, false)); Sinks.Many<String> replayed = Sinks.many().replay().limit(2); for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) replayed.tryEmitNext("e" + i); // no subscribers yet List<String> late = new ArrayList<>(); replayed.asFlux().subscribe(late::add).dispose(); System.out.println("a late subscriber to replay().limit(2) first gets: " + late); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l08.SharedFlowEventsJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l08/SharedFlowEventsJava.java Default: [false, false, false, false, false] and nothing received: with no buffer, tryEmit can't hand anything over while there is a subscriber, busy or not. Buffer of 2: two true, then false, and [e1, e2] received. Buffer of 2 with DROP_OLDEST: every tryEmit returns true, but only [e4, e5] arrive, because the older ones were dropped. Buffer of 64: everything gets through. The late subscriber to replay = 2 gets [e4, e5]. Adding replay = 1 changes nothing in that line, because the subscriber was there from the start. The Java twin reports FAIL_OVERFLOW instead of false, and only after 9 values (it sends 20), because Reactor rounds small buffers up. A SharedFlow keeps replay plus extraBufferCapacity values. The newest are the replay cache; the older ones wait for slow subscribers. MutableSharedFlow (API reference: replay, buffer, overflow) docs

h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · Share one cold flow among many screens with stateIn and shareIn
x: A cold flow runs once per collector, as Flow basics showed. Picture a cold flow that reads the oven thermometer every 100 ms, and three screens around the house that show the temperature. Each screen collects the flow, so the thermometer is read three times as often as it needs to be. stateIn and shareIn run the upstream, the cold flow they read from, just once. They run it in a scope you give them, the owner of coroutines from Structured concurrency, and share its values with every collector: Java // Java equivalent: one shared upstream that starts with the first subscriber // and stops 5 seconds after the last one leaves Flux<Integer> temperature = thermometerReadings .replay(1) .refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5)); Kotlin val temperature: StateFlow<Int> = thermometerReadings // a cold flow .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initialValue = 0) stateIn gives a StateFlow, so it needs an initial value. shareIn(scope, started, replay) gives a SharedFlow. The started argument decides when the shared upstream runs: SharingStarted.Eagerly starts at once, before any subscriber, and runs until the scope is cancelled. SharingStarted.Lazily starts with the first subscriber and then never stops. SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis) starts with the first subscriber and stops once the last one has been gone for stopTimeoutMillis. The default is 0. A few seconds is common, so a screen that restarts doesn't restart the upstream. StateInDemo, in the Try it below, shares the thermometer with WhileSubscribed(300). Two screens subscribe at 200 ms and leave 250 ms later. Predict when reading starts and stops: 79 ms stateIn returned; waiting 200 ms before the first screen 327 ms two screens subscribed 344 ms thermometer: reading started 581 ms both screens left; temperature.value = 182 884 ms thermometer: reading stopped 1081 ms done Reading started once, for both screens, and stopped about 300 ms after they left. Run with -Pargs=eagerly, the same demo started reading at 62 ms, before anyone was watching. The scope owns the shared collection, so make it a long-lived scope you control, like the Oven's scope in Structured concurrency. A scope that belongs to one short call would end the sharing when the call ends, and GlobalScope would never end it. In tests, the test library's backgroundScope plays that part. Sharing doesn't make the upstream any less cold. When WhileSubscribed stops it and a new subscriber arrives later, the upstream runs again from the top. The readings restart, and a running total built with runningFold, the operator that keeps a running total, starts again from its initial value. For a live display that's what you want. For a total that must survive restarts, keep it somewhere durable and use the flow only to show it. stateIn and shareIn run one cold flow for many collectors. Give them a scope you own. Now we can build a class that owns some state and shares it. One question is left: who is allowed to change it? Start and stop a shared thermometer Read StateInDemo.kt. It shares a thermometer flow with WhileSubscribed(300). Predict when reading started and reading stopped print. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=eagerly, then with -Pargs=lazily. Predict each first. Run the Java twin, which uses replay(1).refCount(1, 300 ms).
