h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · Keep the writable flow private, and change it in one step
x: A class that owns some state should let callers read it, and nobody else write it. Picture a tracker for one dish: the board in the hall shows its status (waiting, cooking, served), and only the kitchen may move it on. Before Kotlin 2.4, that took two properties: Java // Java equivalent: a private sink and a public read-only view class DishTracker { private final Sinks.Many<DishStatus> status = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault(DishStatus.WAITING); public Flux<DishStatus> status() { return status.asFlux(); } void startCooking() { status.tryEmitNext(DishStatus.COOKING); } } Kotlin class DishTracker { private val _status = MutableStateFlow(DishStatus.WAITING) val status: StateFlow<DishStatus> = _status.asStateFlow() fun startCooking() { _status.value = DishStatus.COOKING } } A property's backing field is the hidden storage behind it. Kotlin 2.4.0 made explicit backing fields stable: a property can declare its field, with a more specific type than the property itself. They arrived as experimental in 2.3.0, whose release notes used exactly this case as their example: class DishTracker { val status: StateFlow<DishStatus> field = MutableStateFlow(DishStatus.WAITING) fun startCooking() { status.value = DishStatus.COOKING } // smart-cast inside the class } Outside the class, status is a StateFlow with no setter. Inside it, the compiler knows the field is a MutableStateFlow and smart-casts, that is, treats it as the more specific type without a cast. One small difference remains. asStateFlow() returns a wrapper, so a caller can't cast it back to MutableStateFlow. An explicit backing field hides the type only at compile time. Both are fine in application code. In a library other people build on, the wrapper is the stricter choice. Then write every change as one atomic step. count.value = count.value + 1 is a read-modify-write, the race from Race conditions in the first track: two threads both read 41, both write 42, and one plate goes uncounted. StateUpdates, in the Try it below, lets 8 helpers each count 100,000 plates: value = value + 1 expected 800000, got 457636 update { it + 1 } expected 800000, got 800000 Over 340,000 plates were served and never counted. count.update { it + 1 } retries with compare-and-set, an atomic "change it only if nobody beat me to it", until it wins. status.compareAndSet(expected, new) moves only if the value is still expected, and returns whether it did. That's how the lab's tracker makes sure two helpers can't both serve the same dish: the loser's compareAndSet fails, it reads the new status, and the move is no longer allowed. The same habit applies to the bell. Ring it from the method that changes the state, after the change has succeeded, so the kitchen log never describes a move that didn't happen. Expose the read-only type, keep the writable one inside, and change it with update or compareAndSet. Lose plates with value = value + 1 Read StateUpdates.kt. Eight coroutines on Default each add a plate 100,000 times. Predict both totals. Run it twice. Run the Java twin, which does the same with an AtomicReference. StateUpdates.kt package workbench.coroutines.l08 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.update import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking /** 8 helpers on Default each add 1 plate to a shared count 100,000 times. */ suspend fun countPlates(label: String, add: (MutableStateFlow<Long>) -> Unit) { val platesServed = MutableStateFlow(0L) coroutineScope { repeat(8) { launch(Dispatchers.Default) { repeat(100_000) { add(platesServed) } } } } println("%-34s expected 800000, got %d".format(label, platesServed.value)) } fun main() = runBlocking { countPlates("value = value + 1") { it.value = it.value + 1 } // read-modify-write: loses updates countPlates("update { it + 1 }") { it.update { plates -> plates + 1 } } // compare-and-set in a loop } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l08.StateUpdatesKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l08/StateUpdates.kt StateUpdatesJava.java // Java equivalent of StateUpdates.kt: the same read-modify-write race on an AtomicReference, // fixed the same way, with a compare-and-set loop (updateAndGet). package workbench.coroutines.l08; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference; import java.util.function.Consumer; public class StateUpdatesJava { /** 8 helpers each add 1 plate to a shared count 100,000 times. */ static void countPlates(String label, Consumer<AtomicReference<Long>> add) { AtomicReference<Long> platesServed = new AtomicReference<>(0L); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) { for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) pool.submit(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) add.accept(platesServed); }); } System.out.printf("%-34s expected 800000, got %d%n", label, platesServed.get()); } public static void main(String[] args) { countPlates("set(get() + 1)", ref -> ref.set(ref.get() + 1)); // read-modify-write: loses updates countPlates("updateAndGet(c -> c + 1)", ref -> ref.updateAndGet(c -> c + 1)); // compare-and-set in a loop } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l08.StateUpdatesJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l08/StateUpdatesJava.java value = value + 1 comes out far short of 800,000, and the number changes from run to run (457,636 in one run here). update { it + 1 } gives exactly 800,000 every time. The Java twin loses updates with set(get() + 1) (303,507 here) and gets 800,000 with updateAndGet, because it's the same race and the same fix. What's new in Kotlin 2.4.0 (explicit backing fields) read

h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · Java and Kotlin
x: A dish tracker: Reactor sinks vs StateFlow and SharedFlow DishTracker.java class DishTracker { private final AtomicReference<DishStatus> current = new AtomicReference<>(DishStatus.WAITING); private final Sinks.Many<DishStatus> status = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault(DishStatus.WAITING); private final Sinks.Many<Transition> transitions = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(64, false); public DishStatus currentStatus() { return current.get(); } // 1. a synchronous read public Flux<DishStatus> status() { return status.asFlux().distinctUntilChanged(); } public Flux<Transition> transitions() { return transitions.asFlux(); } boolean moveTo(DishStatus next) { DishStatus from = current.get(); if (!from.canMoveTo(next) || !current.compareAndSet(from, next)) return false; // 2. atomic move // 3. sinks reject concurrent emits (FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED), so serialize them synchronized (this) { status.tryEmitNext(next); transitions.tryEmitNext(new Transition(dish, from, next)); } return true; } } DishTracker.kt class DishTracker(private val dish: String) { val status: StateFlow<DishStatus> // 1. .value is a synchronous read field = MutableStateFlow(DishStatus.WAITING) val transitions: SharedFlow<Transition> field = MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 64) fun moveTo(next: DishStatus): Boolean { while (true) { val from = status.value if (!from.canMoveTo(next)) return false if (status.compareAndSet(from, next)) { // 2. atomic move check(transitions.tryEmit(Transition(dish, from, next))) // 3. safe from any thread return true } } } } The Kotlin version needs fewer moving parts, because a StateFlow is both the holder and the stream: .value reads it synchronously, compareAndSet changes it atomically, and collectors see changes with conflation and de-duplication built in. Reactor has no single type for that, so the Java version keeps an AtomicReference for the value and a replaying sink for the stream, and must keep the two in step. The other real difference is concurrency. MutableStateFlow and MutableSharedFlow are documented as safe for emitters on many threads. Reactor's default sinks detect concurrent tryEmitNext calls and fail them with FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED, so the Java tracker serializes its emits with a lock.

h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · Worked example
x: Share one oven reading among every phone in the house A family app shows the oven's temperature on every phone in the house. Each open phone collects temperatures(), a cold flow that asks the smart oven every second. With six phones open, the oven's small web server gets six questions a second and starts refusing some of them. fun temperatures(): Flow<Int> = flow { while (true) { emit(oven.readCelsius()) // one call to the oven per collector per second delay(1.seconds) } } // on each phone's screen temperatures().collect { show(it) } // Java equivalent of the same design: a cold Flux subscribed once per phone Flux<Integer> temperatures() { return Flux.interval(Duration.ZERO, Duration.ofSeconds(1)) .concatMap(tick -> oven.readCelsius()); // one call per subscriber per second } // on each phone's screen temperatures().subscribe(this::show); Decide the type first. A phone wants the latest temperature, and a phone that missed a reading doesn't need it replayed, so this is state: a StateFlow. Share the upstream in a scope that lives as long as the app, and stop it when nobody watches. Five seconds of grace covers a phone that locks its screen for a moment. class OvenFeed(oven: SmartOven) : AutoCloseable { private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO) // 1. the owner of the sharing val celsius: StateFlow<Int?> = flow { while (true) { emit(oven.readCelsius()); delay(1.seconds) } }.stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initialValue = null) // 2. one call for all override fun close() = scope.cancel() // 3. ends with the app } class OvenFeed { // 1. and 2.: one shared upstream, started by the first subscriber, stopped 5 s after the last final Flux<Integer> celsius; OvenFeed(SmartOven oven) { this.celsius = Flux.interval(Duration.ZERO, Duration.ofSeconds(1)) .concatMap(tick -> oven.readCelsius()) .replay(1) .refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5)); } } Each phone now collects the shared StateFlow. A slow phone gets the newest reading rather than a backlog, and a reading equal to the last one isn't sent again at all. // on each phone's screen: no extra call to the oven ovenFeed.celsius.filterNotNull().collect { show(it) } // on each phone's screen: no extra call to the oven ovenFeed.celsius.distinctUntilChanged().onBackpressureLatest().subscribe(this::show); Self-check: why not SharingStarted.Eagerly? (It would ask the oven every second from the moment the app starts, even at night with every phone asleep, and never stop until the app closes. WhileSubscribed asks only while someone is watching.)

h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · Quiz
x: What does the collector print? val s = MutableStateFlow(0) launch { s.collect { println(it); delay(100) } } delay(10) s.value = 1; s.value = 2; s.value = 3 delay(200) s.value = 3 0, 1, 2, 3, 3 0, 1, 2, 3 0, 3 3 The collector prints 0 and is busy for 100 ms while 1, 2 and 3 are set. A StateFlow conflates, so when it's ready it gets only the latest, 3. Setting 3 again is equal to the current value, so nothing is emitted. A kitchen log collects val events = MutableSharedFlow<Transition>() and takes 50 ms to write each line. A callback from an older library, which can't suspend, calls events.tryEmit(t) while the log is busy. What happens? tryEmit blocks the calling thread until the log is ready tryEmit returns false, and the transition is lost unless you check The transition is queued without limit tryEmit throws IllegalStateException With default parameters there is no buffer, so a non-suspending emit has nowhere to put the value while there is any subscriber, busy or not. tryEmit never blocks or throws; it returns false. Use extraBufferCapacity and check the result. Every "dish served" event must reach both the kitchen log and the thank-you texter, which run all the time, and a burst of 50 events must not lose any. Which type fits? MutableStateFlow<Served?>(null) MutableSharedFlow<Served>(extraBufferCapacity = 64) with the default SUSPEND A cold flow { } that each consumer collects MutableSharedFlow<Served>(replay = 1, onBufferOverflow = DROP_OLDEST) Events go to several subscribers, and none may be lost, so a SharedFlow with room for bursts and SUSPEND fits. A StateFlow conflates events away, a cold flow would run once per consumer instead of sending to both, and DROP_OLDEST throws events away when a subscriber falls behind. A screen shows the oven temperature from a flow shared with stateIn. A screen that restarts must not restart the readings, and nothing should read the oven when no screen is on. Which started value fits? SharingStarted.Eagerly SharingStarted.Lazily SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed() SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000) WhileSubscribed(5_000) starts with the first subscriber and stops 5 s after the last one leaves, so a restart within that window keeps it running. The default WhileSubscribed() stops at once, Lazily never stops, and Eagerly reads the oven even before any screen is on. From lesson 7 of this track: three screens each collect the same val readings = flow { while (true) { emit(readOven()); delay(1_000) } }. How many times does readOven() run per second? Three times: a cold flow runs once per collector Once: the flow is shared because it is the same object Once, but only for the first screen; the others get nothing It depends on the dispatcher A cold flow's body runs separately for every collector, even if they all hold the same Flow object. Sharing one upstream takes stateIn or shareIn.

h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · Key terms
x: Hot flow A flow that exists and holds or sends values whether or not anyone collects it. StateFlow A hot flow with one current value; it conflates and skips equal values. The board in the hall. SharedFlow A hot flow that sends every value to every current subscriber. The house bell. Conflation Keeping only the latest value for a slow consumer and dropping the ones in between. Replay cache The last few values a SharedFlow keeps and gives to each new subscriber first. SharingStarted The rule that tells stateIn or shareIn when to start and stop the shared upstream. Explicit backing field A Kotlin property whose hidden field has a different, more specific type than the property itself. A StateFlow collector is busy while three new values are set. What does it see next? Only the latest one. StateFlow conflates: values a slow collector missed are skipped. What happens when you set a MutableStateFlow to a value equal to its current one? Nothing. It compares with equals, and an equal value emits nothing. MutableSharedFlow() with default parameters: what does tryEmit return when the flow has a subscriber? false, even if the subscriber is idle. There is no buffer, so the value is dropped. Add extraBufferCapacity and check the result. replay vs extraBufferCapacity in a MutableSharedFlow? replay: how many recent values a new subscriber gets first. extraBufferCapacity: extra room for values slow subscribers haven't taken yet. What does SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000) do? Starts the shared upstream with the first subscriber and stops it 5 s after the last subscriber leaves. How do you expose a StateFlow read-only with one property in Kotlin 2.4? An explicit backing field: val status: StateFlow<S> followed by field = MutableStateFlow(initial). How do you add 1 to a MutableStateFlow<Int> safely from many threads? flow.update { it + 1 }, which retries with compare-and-set. value = value + 1 loses updates.

h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · Go deeper
x: MutableSharedFlow has a subscriptionCount: StateFlow<Int>. It is deliberately not conflated, so you can react to the first subscriber arriving or the last one leaving, for example to open and close a connection to a slow device. SharingStarted is an interface, and WhileSubscribed is written on top of exactly that count. A custom strategy can start sharing only at certain hours, or only after a warm-up. WhileSubscribed has a second parameter, replayExpirationMillis, which defaults to Long.MAX_VALUE. It decides how long the last value stays in the replay cache after the upstream stops. Set it to 0 if a stale value is worse than none, for instance an oven temperature that must never be shown once the oven has been switched off. stateIn and shareIn keep a coroutine running in the scope you give them, so the scope's life is the sharing's life. If the upstream throws, that coroutine fails, the error goes up into the scope, and the StateFlow simply stops updating. Put a catch or retryWhen on the upstream, above stateIn, and decide what the subscribers should see while it recovers. kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 added two small helpers. SharedFlow.asFlow() returns a view that hides the hot-flow type, so callers can't rely on it being shared. And there is now an onSubscription overload on StateFlow that keeps the StateFlow type. Kotlin 2.1.20 also added common atomics such as AtomicInt in kotlin.concurrent.atomics, marked experimental. For plain counters shared between coroutines they are an alternative to a StateFlow that nobody collects, which lesson 10 of this track compares with Mutex. This lesson is the first look at hot flows. Hot flows in depth, in the Kotlin Flow in depth track, opens up the SharedFlow buffer slot by slot, and shows how stateIn and shareIn decide when to start and stop.

h: Channels, select and pipelines · A channel is the hatch between coroutines, and its shelf sets the pace
x: The hatch between kitchen and dining room: a channel hands each plate to exactly one receiver and its shelf sets the pace, a team of helpers caps the work, select takes whichever answer comes first, and without close the helper waits all night A Channel<T> connects coroutines, pieces of work that can pause without holding a thread, the worker that runs the code. One coroutine calls send to put an element in, and another calls receive to take one out. Each element is received exactly once, by one receiver. That's the difference from the SharedFlow of the last lesson, where every subscriber heard every ring. Java // Java equivalent: a bounded BlockingQueue, with an end marker because a queue can't be closed BlockingQueue<String> hatch = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2); Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { for (String dish : dinner) putQuietly(hatch, dish); // blocks while the queue is full putQuietly(hatch, LAST); }); for (String dish = hatch.take(); !dish.equals(LAST); dish = hatch.take()) serve(dish); Kotlin val hatch = Channel<String>(capacity = 2) launch { for (dish in dinner) hatch.send(dish) // suspends while the shelf is full hatch.close() // the last plate: the receiving loop will end } for (dish in hatch) serve(dish) // receives until the hatch is closed and empty Read the Kotlin aloud: the cook puts each dish through the hatch, then says "that's the last one", and the helper serves plates until the hatch is closed and empty. The Java version is the BlockingQueue from the first track, with one difference that matters. Where a queue blocks a thread, a channel suspends a coroutine, so a helper waiting at an empty hatch holds no thread at all. The capacity is the size of the shelf: how many elements can wait in the channel before send has to suspend. The default, a rendezvous channel, has no shelf at all. The cook holds the plate until a helper's hands take it. Capacity send suspends when Picture it Like Channel.RENDEZVOUS (0, the default) no receiver is waiting no shelf: hand to hand SynchronousQueue Channel(n) n elements are already waiting a shelf with n spots ArrayBlockingQueue(n) Channel.BUFFERED 64 are waiting (a JVM property changes the default) a long shelf ArrayBlockingQueue(64) Channel.UNLIMITED never: memory is the limit a shelf with no end LinkedBlockingQueue Channel.CONFLATED never: a new element replaces the waiting one one spot, and the new plate takes it no JDK equivalent Predict the four lines before you read them. ChannelCapacities, in the Try it below, has a cook who puts five plates through the hatch as fast as she can, and a helper who needs 100 ms per plate: RENDEZVOUS send() returned at [38, 142, 247, 348, 448] ms received [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] capacity 2 send() returned at [0, 0, 0, 101, 201] ms received [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] UNLIMITED send() returned at [0, 0, 0, 0, 0] ms received [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] CONFLATED send() returned at [3, 3, 3, 3, 3] ms received [1, 5] With no shelf, the cook moved in step with the helper, one plate every 100 ms (the first 38 ms is the program warming up). With a shelf for two, three sends returned at once: two plates on the shelf, and one straight into the helper's hands. Then the cook waited. UNLIMITED never waited. CONFLATED never waited either, and only plates 1 and 5 were received, because each new plate replaced the one on the shelf. That waiting has a name. Backpressure is a slow receiver slowing down a fast sender, so work doesn't pile up between them. A rendezvous channel gives it for free, which is why it's the default. Add a small shelf to absorb bursts. Be suspicious of UNLIMITED: with a slow helper, plates pile up until the program runs out of memory, an OutOfMemoryError some hours later. Now the last plate. for (dish in hatch) ends only when the channel is closed and empty. Delete hatch.close() in the Try it, and the program never ends. The helper waits at the hatch, loyal to a fault, for a plate that will never come. Here the picture breaks: a real helper would see the cook take off her apron. A coroutine can't tell "later" from "never" until someone calls close(). The produce { } builder does it for you. It starts a coroutine that sends into a new channel, closes the channel when the block ends or fails, and returns its receiving half, a ReceiveChannel. It is still marked @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi in kotlinx.coroutines 1.11, so it needs an opt-in. A receiver stops only when the channel is closed. Close it, or let produce close it. A channel is hot, like the board and the bell: plates sit on the shelf whether or not anyone takes them, and a coroutine suspended in send waits until someone does. For a stream with one consumer, a cold Flow, the recipe card of Flow basics that runs only when someone collects it, is usually simpler. Channels earn their place when coroutines hand work to each other, and the first job worth handing out is more dishes than one helper can carry. Five plates, four hatches Read ChannelCapacities.kt. The cook sends five plates as fast as she can, and the helper needs 100 ms per plate. For each capacity, predict when each send returns, and what is received. Run it. Delete the hatch.close() line and run it again. Predict first: what happens? Put the line back, and run the Java twin, which uses three BlockingQueues. ChannelCapacities.kt package workbench.coroutines.l09 import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking /** The cook puts 5 plates through the hatch as fast as she can; the helper needs 100 ms per plate. */ suspend fun run(label: String, hatch: Channel<Int>) = coroutineScope { val t0 = System.nanoTime() fun ms() = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 val sendTimes = mutableListOf<Long>() launch { for (plate in 1..5) { hatch.send(plate); sendTimes += ms() } hatch.close() // no more plates: the helper's for loop ends after the last one } val received = mutableListOf<Int>() for (plate in hatch) { delay(100); received += plate } println("%-12s send() returned at %-26s received %s".format(label, sendTimes.toString() + " ms", received)) } fun main() = runBlocking { run("RENDEZVOUS", Channel(Channel.RENDEZVOUS)) run("capacity 2", Channel(2)) run("UNLIMITED", Channel(Channel.UNLIMITED)) run("CONFLATED", Channel(Channel.CONFLATED)) } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l09.ChannelCapacitiesKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l09/ChannelCapacities.kt ChannelCapacitiesJava.java // Java equivalent of ChannelCapacities.kt: blocking queues between two threads. SynchronousQueue // is a rendezvous, ArrayBlockingQueue(2) has capacity 2, LinkedBlockingQueue is unbounded. // The JDK has no conflated queue; Kotlin's CONFLATED channel keeps only the newest element. // A blocking queue has no close(), so the cook sends a marker (-1) at the end instead. package workbench.coroutines.l09; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue; public class ChannelCapacitiesJava { static void run(String label, BlockingQueue<Integer> hatch) throws InterruptedException { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<Long> sendTimes = new ArrayList<>(); Thread cook = Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { try { for (int plate = 1; plate <= 5; plate++) { hatch.put(plate); sendTimes.add((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } hatch.put(-1); // the end marker } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); List<Integer> received = new ArrayList<>(); for (int plate = hatch.take(); plate != -1; plate = hatch.take()) { Thread.sleep(100); received.add(plate); } cook.join(); System.out.printf("%-22s put() returned at %-26s received %s%n", label, sendTimes + " ms", received); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { run("SynchronousQueue", new SynchronousQueue<>()); run("ArrayBlockingQueue(2)", new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2)); run("LinkedBlockingQueue", new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l09.ChannelCapacitiesJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l09/ChannelCapacitiesJava.java Rendezvous: each send returns about 100 ms after the previous one, in step with the helper. Capacity 2: the first three return at once (two on the shelf, one handed straight to the waiting helper), then one every 100 ms. Unlimited: all five at once. Conflated: all five at once, but only [1, 5] is received, because each new plate replaced the waiting one. Without close(), the program never ends: the for loop waits for a plate that will never come (stop it with Ctrl+C). The Java twin's three queues match the first three lines. h: Channels, select and pipelines · Fan out to a team of helpers, and fan in to one table
x: One helper at the hatch carries one plate at a time. Twenty dishes of about 100 ms each take two seconds. The fix in a real kitchen is plain: put more helpers at the same hatch. That's fan-out: several coroutines receive from the same channel. Each element still goes to exactly one of them, and channels are fair: receivers waiting in line are served in the order they asked. So one channel plus N helper coroutines is a team that cooks at most N dishes at once, with no thread pool involved. Fan-in is the reverse: many senders into one channel, read by one receiver, like every helper bringing finished plates to one table. Here is the lab's cookAll, which cooks a list of dishes with a fixed number of helpers and returns what each dish became: Java // Java equivalent: a fixed pool takes tasks from its queue, a CompletionService collects results Map<String, String> cookAll(List<String> dishes, int helpers) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(helpers)) { CompletionService<Map.Entry<String, String>> done = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(pool); for (String dish : dishes) done.submit(() -> Map.entry(dish, cook(dish))); Map<String, String> result = new HashMap<>(); for (int i = 0; i < dishes.size(); i++) { var e = done.take().get(); result.put(e.getKey(), e.getValue()); } return result; } } Kotlin suspend fun cookAll(dishes: List<String>, helpers: Int, cook: suspend (String) -> String): Map<String, String> = coroutineScope { val hatch = produce { dishes.forEach { send(it) } } // fan-out source val done = Channel<Pair<String, String>>() // fan-in val team = List(helpers) { launch { for (dish in hatch) done.send(dish to cook(dish)) } } launch { team.joinAll(); done.close() } // close once every helper is done val result = mutableMapOf<String, String>() for ((dish, plate) in done) result[dish] = plate result } Walk through it in order. produce puts the dishes through a rendezvous hatch, one at a time. List(helpers) { launch { ... } } starts the team. Each helper loops over the hatch, cooks what it gets and sends the result into done. A separate coroutine waits for the whole team with joinAll(), then closes done. Finally, the caller's loop reads done into a map. The tricky line is the closer. Close done too early, and a helper's send throws ClosedSendChannelException. Never close it, and the caller's loop waits all night, like the helper in the last section. A coroutine of its own that calls joinAll() and then close() is the usual answer. FanOutFanIn, in the Try it below, runs the same shape with 20 dishes of 50 to 150 ms each: 4 helpers: {helper 0=5, helper 1=4, helper 2=6, helper 3=5} 20 dishes took 614 ms Twenty dishes of about 100 ms on four helpers should take about 500 ms, and 614 is close on a busy machine. With -Pargs=1 the same run took 2,181 ms, and with -Pargs=10 it took 324 ms, two dishes per helper. Everything sits inside coroutineScope, so the pipeline belongs to its caller's job tree, as in Structured concurrency. If one cook throws, the scope cancels the producer, the other helpers and the closer, then rethrows. No coroutine is left waiting at a hatch. Why not dishes.map { async { cook(it) } }.awaitAll()? Because that starts every call at once. Order 5,000 loaves that way, and the bakery gets 5,000 phone calls in the same second, and it will not thank you. The team caps them at N. It also gives each helper a natural home for its own things, such as one pan per helper. And it grows into a pipeline: stations in a row with a channel between each pair, such as shape, then bake, then pack, each with as many helpers as it needs. The worked example below builds one. A fixed team on one channel caps the work at the team's size. Size the team to what the slow part can take. A team takes whatever comes through the hatch next. Sometimes, though, you are waiting for two different things, and you want whichever comes first. Share 20 dishes among a team Read FanOutFanIn.kt. Twenty dishes take 50 to 150 ms each. Predict the total time with 4 helpers, and how the dishes spread across them. Run it, then run it with -Pargs=1 and -Pargs=10. Run the Java twin, a fixed pool with an ExecutorCompletionService. FanOutFanIn.kt package workbench.coroutines.l09 import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.produce import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.joinAll import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.random.Random @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val helpers = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 4 val t0 = System.nanoTime() coroutineScope { // 1. one cook puts 20 dishes through the hatch, one at a time val hatch = produce { for (i in 1..20) send("dish-$i") } // 2. fan-out: each dish goes to exactly one helper val table = Channel<String>() val team = List(helpers) { h -> launch { for (dish in hatch) { delay(Random.nextLong(50, 150)) // carrying it, serving it table.send("$dish by helper $h") } } } // 3. fan-in: close the table channel when every helper is done launch { team.joinAll(); table.close() } val perHelper = mutableMapOf<String, Int>() for (served in table) perHelper.merge(served.substringAfter("by "), 1, Int::plus) println("$helpers helpers: ${perHelper.toSortedMap()}") } println("20 dishes took ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l09.FanOutFanInKt -Pargs=1 labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l09/FanOutFanIn.kt FanOutFanInJava.java // Java equivalent of FanOutFanIn.kt: a fixed pool takes tasks from its queue (fan-out), and an // ExecutorCompletionService hands back results in the order they finish (fan-in). package workbench.coroutines.l09; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorCompletionService; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom; public class FanOutFanInJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int helpers = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 4; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(helpers)) { ExecutorCompletionService<String> table = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(pool); for (int i = 1; i <= 20; i++) { String dish = "dish-" + i; table.submit(() -> { Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(50, 150)); // carrying it, serving it return dish + " by " + Thread.currentThread().getName(); }); } Map<String, Integer> perHelper = new TreeMap<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) perHelper.merge(table.take().get().split(" by ")[1], 1, Integer::sum); System.out.println(helpers + " helpers: " + perHelper); } System.out.println("20 dishes took " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 + " ms"); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l09.FanOutFanInJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l09/FanOutFanInJava.java With 4 helpers each one serves about 5 dishes, and the run takes roughly 20 x 100 ms / 4, about 500 to 700 ms. With 1 helper it takes about 2 s. With 10 helpers it takes about 300 ms, and each helper serves about 2. The Java twin spreads the work across its four pool threads the same way. One channel feeds four helpers, so at most four dishes cook at once; a second channel brings what they cooked back to one place.

h: Channels, select and pipelines · Take whichever answer comes first with select
x: Picture the cook phoning two bakeries to ask who still has bread tonight. The corner bakery takes 300 ms to answer, and the market bakery 120 ms. She'll take the first answer and hang up on the other. If neither answers within 500 ms, she'll bake her own. select { } is that pair of phone calls. It suspends until the first of several clauses, the things it waits on, can complete. Then it runs that clause and drops the rest. The clauses you'll use are deferred.onAwait (an async result is ready), channel.onReceive (a plate is at the hatch), channel.onSend(value) (there's room on the shelf) and onTimeout(ms), the kitchen timer. Java // Java equivalent: anyOf completes with the first future, completeOnTimeout adds a fallback Object first = CompletableFuture.anyOf(corner, market) .completeOnTimeout("we bake our own", 500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) .join(); corner.cancel(true); market.cancel(true); // only marks the futures; the calls may run on Kotlin val answer = coroutineScope { val corner = async { cornerBakery.ask() } val market = async { marketBakery.ask() } val first = select { corner.onAwait { it } market.onAwait { it } onTimeout(500) { "we bake our own" } // needs @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) } corner.cancel(); market.cancel() // hang up on the others first } Expect the market's answer after about 120 ms. SelectFirst, in the Try it below, printed this: after 213 ms: market bakery: plenty of sourdough The extra 90 ms is a cold program on a busy machine: the clock starts before the coroutine machinery has loaded. With -Pargs=100, a budget of 100 ms, the timer won: nobody answered within 100 ms: we bake our own bread. Three details matter. First, select is biased: if several clauses are ready at the same moment, the first one listed wins, so list the one you prefer first. Second, hanging up is your job, just as with anyOf. The difference is what the hang-up reaches. A coroutine's cancel arrives at the losing call's next suspension point, as Cancellation and timeouts showed. future.cancel(true) only marks a Java future as cancelled, and the work behind it may run on. Third, the status is mixed. In 1.11 the select builder compiles without an opt-in, the guide still calls select expressions experimental, and onTimeout needs @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class). Without the timer, this is the lab's firstOffer, written for a list of shops: select { calls.forEach { c -> c.onAwait { it } } }. The lambda registers one clause per call. select over the onReceive clauses of several channels can merge streams by hand, like a helper at two hatches, one for soup and one for bread, who takes whichever plate shows up first. For most merging, though, Flow operators such as merge and combine are simpler and harder to get wrong. Keep select for "the first of these, then stop", and for the rare loop that must react to whichever of several channels has something. select takes the first clause that's ready, and prefers the first one listed. Cancel the losers yourself. Every channel so far was one we made on purpose. The last two hide inside flows, and one of them rescues an old gadget. Phone two bakeries at once Read SelectFirst.kt. The corner bakery answers in 300 ms, the market bakery in 120 ms, and the budget is 500 ms. Predict the answer and the time. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=100, a budget of 100 ms. Predict first. Run the Java twin both ways. Cancelling the losers is up to you. package workbench.coroutines.l09; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class SelectFirstJava { static String answer(String text, long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return text; } public static void main(String[] args) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); long budgetMs = args.length > 0 ? h: Channels, select and pipelines · Hatches inside flows: callbackFlow and the backpressure operators
x: A flow is sequential: emit may be called only from the flow's own coroutine, as Flow basics showed. Some values come from somewhere else. Picture an older wireless oven probe, a thermometer you push into the roast. Its library has a listener API: you register a function, and the probe calls it on its own thread with every new reading, until you unregister it. Such a function is a callback, code you hand over for someone else to call later. callbackFlow turns that into a Flow by putting a channel inside it. The callback calls trySend on the channel, and the collector receives from it: Java // Java equivalent: Flux.create with a sink, and onDispose for the cleanup Flux<Reading> readings(OvenProbe probe) { return Flux.create(sink -> { Registration registration = probe.register(sink::next); sink.onDispose(registration::unregister); }); } Kotlin fun OvenProbe.readings(): Flow<Reading> = callbackFlow { val registration = register { reading -> trySend(reading) } // called on the probe's thread awaitClose { registration.unregister() } // runs when the collector stops } awaitClose is not optional. It suspends until the collector goes away, then runs the cleanup. Without it, the block returns right after registering, and callbackFlow throws IllegalStateException rather than leave the listener behind. That's the bug in the lab's starting code. From the callback, use trySend: it never blocks the probe's thread, and it fails if the channel's buffer (64 by default) is full. For a callback that fires once, suspendCancellableCoroutine from Suspend functions from zero is the right tool. And channelFlow is the same idea for your own coroutines: launch several producers inside it, and each one can send safely. The other hidden channels sit inside three backpressure operators. Take the guide's numbers, told with our probe: a reading every 100 ms, a screen on the fridge that needs 300 ms to redraw, and three readings. FlowBackpressure, in the Try it below, measured them: Pipeline The screen shows Expected Measured here plain 1, 2, 3 1,200 ms: (100 + 300) x 3 1,246 ms buffer() 1, 2, 3 1,000 ms: the probe runs ahead 1,061 ms conflate() 1, 3 700 ms: a busy screen skips to the latest 720 ms collectLatest { } starts 1, 2 and 3, finishes only 3 600 ms: a new reading cancels the old work 619 ms buffer keeps every reading and lets the probe run ahead into a channel. conflate keeps only the latest, which suits a thermometer and never suits a list of orders. collectLatest cancels and restarts the collector's block for each new value, like a cook who starts the sauce again every time someone changes their order. That suits "work out the time left whenever the temperature changes". It's wrong for anything with side effects you can't take back, because the cancelled run may have done half its work. All three trade memory, completeness and freshness against each other, and the plain flow is the safe default. Reactor makes the same three trades with onBackpressureBuffer, onBackpressureLatest and switchMap, as Backpressure in practice showed in the reactive track, and the Java twin measures them. Pick buffer, conflate or collectLatest by asking which values you can afford to lose. Every hatch in this lesson moved a plate from one coroutine to another, so no two coroutines ever held the same plate. A kitchen also has things that everyone writes on. Time four ways to keep up Read FlowBackpressure.kt. Predict what each of the four lines prints, and roughly how long it takes. Run it. In the conflate() line, change the collector's delay(300) to delay(50). Predict first: does it still skip a reading? Run the Java twin with the Reactor counterparts. h: Channels, select and pipelines · Java and Kotlin
x: A capped team of helpers: ExecutorService vs a channel and coroutines BreadRun.java List<String> orderAll(List<String> loaves) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) { // 1. 8 threads = at most 8 calls CompletionService<String> done = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(pool); for (String loaf : loaves) done.submit(() -> bakery.order(loaf)); // 2. every task queued up front List<String> tickets = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < loaves.size(); i++) tickets.add(done.take().get()); // 3. fan-in, in finish order return tickets; } // a failure surfaces at get(); the other tasks keep running until close() waits for them } BreadRun.kt suspend fun orderAll(loaves: List<String>): List<String> = coroutineScope { val hatch = produce { loaves.forEach { send(it) } } // 2. handed out one at a time val tickets = Channel<String>() val team = List(8) { launch { for (loaf in hatch) tickets.send(bakery.order(loaf)) } } // 1. 8 helpers launch { team.joinAll(); tickets.close() } val result = mutableListOf<String>() for (t in tickets) result += t // 3. fan-in, in finish order result } // a failure cancels the producer and every helper, then rethrows Both keep the bakery's phone line at 8 calls at once and collect the tickets in the order the calls finish. The Java version spends 8 threads, which sit blocked while the bakery answers, and it queues every task up front. The Kotlin version spends 8 coroutines, which suspend while waiting, and the rendezvous channel hands out an order only when a helper is free, so a list of a million loaves never sits in a task queue. The bigger difference is failure. In Java, one failed order shows up at get(), and the other tasks keep running until close() waits for them. In Kotlin, the whole team is one coroutineScope, so the first failure cancels the producer and every helper before the exception reaches the caller.

h: Channels, select and pipelines · Worked example
x: A three-station bake sale The house is baking 600 cookies for a school bake sale. Each one is shaped from the dough (quick), baked (the slow part: 20 ms per cookie in our code, and the oven holds 12 at once), and packed into boxes of 12. In one loop, the oven bakes one cookie at a time: 600 x 20 ms is 12 seconds, with 11 spots in the oven empty the whole time. suspend fun bakeSale(dough: Dough) { val box = mutableListOf<Cookie>() repeat(600) { val ball = dough.shape() // quick val cookie = oven.bake(ball) // 20 ms, one cookie at a time box += cookie if (box.size == 12) { packer.pack(box.toList()); box.clear() } } if (box.isNotEmpty()) packer.pack(box) } // Java equivalent of the same single loop void bakeSale(Dough dough) { List<Cookie> box = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 600; i++) { Ball ball = dough.shape(); // quick Cookie cookie = oven.bake(ball); // 20 ms, one cookie at a time box.add(cookie); if (box.size() == 12) { packer.pack(List.copyOf(box)); box.clear(); } } if (!box.isEmpty()) packer.pack(box); } Station 1 shapes the dough into a small buffer, a little ahead of the oven. produce closes the channel when the dough runs out. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) suspend fun bakeSale(dough: Dough) = coroutineScope { // 1. shape: one helper, a little ahead of the oven val balls = produce(capacity = 24) { repeat(600) { send(dough.shape()) } } void bakeSale(Dough dough) throws Exception { // 1. shape: one thread, a little ahead of the oven BlockingQueue<Ball> balls = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(24); Thread shaper = Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 600; i++) putQuietly(balls, dough.shape()); putQuietly(balls, Ball.LAST); }); Station 2 fans out to 12 bakers, one per spot in the oven. They fan in to one channel, which a coroutine of its own closes when all 12 are done. // 2. bake: 12 helpers, because the oven holds 12 cookies at once val cookies = Channel<Cookie>(capacity = 48) val bakers = List(12) { launch { for (ball in balls) cookies.send(oven.bake(ball)) } } launch { bakers.joinAll(); cookies.close() } // 2. bake: 12 threads, because the oven holds 12 cookies at once BlockingQueue<Cookie> cookies = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(48); ExecutorService bakers = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(12); for (int i = 0; i < 12; i++) bakers.submit(() -> { for (Ball ball = balls.take(); ball != Ball.LAST; ball = balls.take()) cookies.put(oven.bake(ball)); balls.put(Ball.LAST); // pass the end marker on to the next baker return null; }); Station 3 is a single packer, so the boxes stay simple. When cookies is closed and empty, the loop ends, and coroutineScope returns once every station has finished. If any station throws, the scope cancels the others. The oven is now full: 600 x 20 ms / 12 is about one second instead of twelve. // 3. pack: one helper, boxes of 12 val box = mutableListOf<Cookie>() for (c in cookies) { box += c if (box.size == 12) { packer.pack(box.toList()); box.clear() } } if (box.isNotEmpty()) packer.pack(box) } // 3. pack: one thread, boxes of 12 (the end of station 2 needs its own marker or a latch) bakers.shutdown(); List<Cookie> box = new ArrayList<>(); while (!(bakers.isTerminated() && cookies.isEmpty())) { Cookie c = cookies.poll(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); if (c == null) continue; box.add(c); if (box.size() == 12) { packer.pack(List.copyOf(box)); box.clear(); } } if (!box.isEmpty()) packer.pack(box); shaper.join(); } Self-check: the packer runs out of boxes and slows to a crawl. Trace what happens to the counter and the oven. (The packer falls behind, cookies fills up to 48, the bakers suspend in send, balls fills up to 24, and the shaper suspends too. Dough never piles up on the counter, and the oven simply waits. Backpressure travels all the way back to the first station.)

h: Channels, select and pipelines · Quiz
x: val hatch = Channel<String>(). A coroutine runs hatch.send("soup"); println("sent"), and nothing ever receives from hatch. What happens? sent prints at once, because send puts the element in a buffer send suspends forever, so sent never prints send throws IllegalStateException because nobody is receiving The element is dropped and sent prints The default capacity is rendezvous, a hatch with no shelf: send waits until a receiver takes the element. With no receiver it waits forever, and the coroutine never finishes. A buffered channel would accept it at once. Four helpers each run for (dish in hatch) cook(dish) on the same channel. The cook sends 40 dishes and closes it. Which statement is true? Each dish is cooked exactly once, and at most 4 cook calls run at the same time Each dish is cooked four times, once per helper All 40 go to the first helper, because it started first The helpers deadlock, because they compete for the same channel A channel is a queue: each element goes to one receiver, and fair receiving spreads the dishes across the waiting helpers. Four helpers means at most four dishes in progress. That is fan-out. What happens when this flow is collected? callbackFlow { probe.register { trySend(it) } } Readings flow normally until the collector cancels Nothing is ever emitted, but the collector waits forever callbackFlow throws IllegalStateException, because the block returned without awaitClose The listener is unregistered automatically when the block returns callbackFlow requires the block to suspend in awaitClose { } until the collector stops. If the block returns while the channel is still open, it throws IllegalStateException, and the listener it registered is never unregistered. A screen on the fridge shows how many minutes the roast still needs. Working that out from a probe reading takes 300 ms, and readings arrive every 100 ms. Only the latest estimate matters, and a stale calculation should stop at once. Which operator fits? buffer() conflate() Channel.UNLIMITED between the probe and the screen collectLatest { } collectLatest cancels the calculation in progress when a new reading arrives, so only the latest is worked out to the end. conflate skips readings that arrive while busy, but still finishes every calculation it starts. buffer and an unlimited channel work out every stale reading. h: Channels, select and pipelines · Key terms
x: Channel A queue between coroutines: each element is received once, and send and receive suspend instead of blocking. The hatch. Rendezvous A channel with no buffer: the sender waits until a receiver takes the element. Backpressure A slow receiver slowing down a fast sender, so work doesn't pile up between them. Fan-out Several receivers on one channel, so each element is handled by exactly one of them. Fan-in Several senders into one channel, read by one receiver. produce A builder that starts a coroutine sending into a new channel and closes the channel when the block ends. select Waits for whichever of several clauses can complete first, and runs only that one. callbackFlow A flow builder with a channel inside, for turning listener callbacks into a Flow. What is the default capacity of Channel<T>(), and what does it mean for send? RENDEZVOUS (0): send suspends until a receiver takes the element. What does a Channel.CONFLATED channel do with a new element when one is already waiting? It replaces the waiting one. send never suspends, and a slow receiver gets only the newest. Several coroutines receive from one channel. How many of them get each element? Exactly one. That is fan-out, and it caps the work in progress at the number of receivers. When does for (x in channel) stop? When the channel has been closed and every element in it has been received. Why must a callbackFlow block end with awaitClose { ... }? It keeps the flow open until the collector stops, then runs the cleanup. Without it, callbackFlow throws IllegalStateException and the listener is left registered. Two select clauses are ready at the same moment. Which one wins? The one listed first: select is biased toward the first clause. conflate() vs collectLatest { } for a slow collector? conflate skips values that arrived while busy, but finishes each one it starts. collectLatest cancels the block in progress when a new value arrives.

h: Channels, select and pipelines · Go deeper
x: actor { }, which older tutorials use to guard shared state with a channel of messages, is marked @ObsoleteCoroutinesApi: its KDoc says it will become obsolete when "complex actors" arrive. A plain coroutine looping over a channel you create does the same job without the warning, and the next lesson calls that confinement. BroadcastChannel was deprecated in 1.7, and its deprecation level was raised in 1.9. Use a SharedFlow from the last lesson for one-to-many. The BUFFERED default of 64 comes from the JVM system property kotlinx.coroutines.channels.defaultBuffer. It is also the buffer that flowOn, buffer(), channelFlow and callbackFlow use unless you pass a size. When you size a pipeline for memory, count those hidden shelves too. Channels also have trySend and tryReceive, which never suspend and return a ChannelResult. They are for code at the edge that can't suspend, like a listener callback, and trySendBlocking is the blocking variant for a plain thread that may wait. kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 added ReceiveChannel.consumeTo(collection), which drains a channel into a collection. The prime-sieve pipeline in the official channels guide is a fun read: each prime gets its own filtering coroutine, chained by channels, so the pipeline grows as it runs. It shows how cheap coroutines and channels are. It is a poor model for real programs, where a fixed number of stations with a known number of helpers is far easier to watch and to cancel. This lesson is the first look at callbackFlow and the backpressure operators. Bridges and tests, in the Kotlin Flow in depth track, comes back to callbackFlow, and Buffering explains how buffer, conflate and flowOn merge their hidden channels into one.

h: Shared state and testing coroutines · Helpers who share one list race like threads, and the same tools fix them
x: Start with something smaller than a shopping list: a pot of peas. SharedCounter, in the Try it below, starts 100 helpers. Each one is a coroutine, a piece of work that can pause without holding a thread, and each counts 10,000 peas into the same pot. They run on Dispatchers.Default, the dispatcher (the part that picks a thread for each coroutine) with one thread per core. So the helpers really do run at the same moment, on different threads. Here is the pot counted five ways: plain var 982,455 of 1,000,000 in 78 ms @Volatile var 913,871 of 1,000,000 in 61 ms AtomicLong 1,000,000 of 1,000,000 in 43 ms Mutex.withLock 1,000,000 of 1,000,000 in 891 ms withContext(limited(1)) 1,000,000 of 1,000,000 in 1095 ms Some 17,000 peas went into the pot uncounted. count++ is three steps, read, add and write, and two coroutines on two threads can both read 41 and both write 42: the race from Race conditions in the first track. Shared mutable state, a variable that more than one coroutine changes, needs the same care with coroutines as with threads. @Volatile didn't help, and the coroutines guide says so in as many words: "volatiles are of no help". A volatile write is visible to every thread, but read, add and write are still three steps. Pick the tool by the shape of the update. One value, changed in one step: an atomic, a variable whose read-modify-write can't be split by another thread. AtomicLong.incrementAndGet(), AtomicReference.updateAndGet and MutableStateFlow.update { } from lesson 8 of this track never suspend and never block. Kotlin 2.1.20 also added common atomics such as AtomicInt in kotlin.concurrent.atomics, still experimental; on the JVM the java.util.concurrent.atomic classes do the same job. Several steps that must happen together, such as reading the list and writing a new total: a Mutex. State that one coroutine owns: confinement. Keep the list inside one coroutine and send it requests through a channel, the hatch from the last lesson. Nothing else can touch it, so nothing needs a lock. Mutex is the coroutine lock, the pen on a string by the fridge: Java // Java equivalent: a ReentrantLock around the same read-modify-write private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); void add(String item, long grams) { lock.lock(); try { list.put(item, list.getOrDefault(item, 0L) + grams); } finally { lock.unlock(); } } Kotlin private val mutex = Mutex() suspend fun add(item: String, grams: Long) = mutex.withLock { list[item] = (list[item] ?: 0L) + grams } withLock takes the lock, runs the block in a try, and releases the lock in finally, the same idiom as Java's. The difference is what waiting costs. Mutex.lock() suspends the coroutine, so a helper waiting for the pen holds no thread. The KDoc, the documentation in the library's source, gives the Mutex the memory rules of a synchronized block, and makes it fair: waiters get the lock in the order they asked. Two warnings come with it. A Mutex is not reentrant: a coroutine that holds it and calls withLock again suspends forever, waiting for itself. Its KDoc gives it just two states, locked and unlocked, and it keeps no record of who holds it, unless you pass an owner token for debugging. (A ReentrantLock records the thread that holds it, which wouldn't work here, because a coroutine may resume on another thread.) So take the lock once, at the top. And the numbers above show the second warning: a lock or a dispatcher switch around every tiny increment costs about 20 times more than an atomic. Lock around a meaningful piece of work, or use an atomic for a single number. One number: an atomic. Several steps that belong together: a Mutex. The last line of the table looks like a third, cheaper lock. It counted every pea. It fails on the shopping list, and the reason is the heart of this lesson. Count a million peas five ways Read SharedCounter.kt. 100 coroutines on Default each count 10,000 peas. Predict which counters reach 1,000,000, and which is slowest. Run it twice. Run the Java twin, which uses 8 threads and a ReentrantLock. SharedCounter.kt package workbench.coroutines.l10 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withLock import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis private var plain = 0L @Volatile private var volatileCount = 0L /** 100 helpers, coroutines on Dispatchers.Default, each count 10,000 peas into the same pot. */ suspend fun count(label: String, increment: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit, read: () -> Long) { val ms = measureTimeMillis { coroutineScope { repeat(100) { launch(Dispatchers.Default) { repeat(10_000) { increment() } } } } } println("%-28s %,9d of 1,000,000 in %4d ms".format(label, read(), ms)) } fun main() = runBlocking { count("plain var", { plain++ }, { plain }) count("@Volatile var", { volatileCount++ }, { volatileCount }) val atomic = AtomicLong() count("AtomicLong", { atomic.incrementAndGet() }, { atomic.get() }) val mutex = Mutex() var guarded = 0L count("Mutex.withLock", { mutex.withLock { guarded++ } }, { guarded }) val confined = Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1) var onOneThread = 0L count("withContext(limited(1))", { withContext(confined) { onOneThread++ } }, { onOneThread }) } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l10.SharedCounterKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l10/SharedCounter.kt SharedCounterJava.java // Java equivalent of SharedCounter.kt: the same pea counter on 8 platform threads. Coroutines on // Dispatchers.Default run in parallel, so they race exactly like threads do. package workbench.coroutines.l10; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; import java.util.function.LongSupplier; public class SharedCounterJava { static long plain = 0; static volatile long volatileCount = 0; static long guarded = 0; static void count(String label, Runnable increment, LongSupplier read) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) { for (int t = 0; t < 100; t++) pool.submit(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) increment.run(); }); } System.out.printf("%-28s %,9d of 1,000,000 in %4d ms%n", label, read.getAsLong(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } public static void main(String[] args) { count("plain field", () -> plain++, () -> plain); count("volatile field", () -> volatileCount++, () -> volatileCount); AtomicLong atomic = new AtomicLong(); count("AtomicLong", atomic::incrementAndGet, atomic::get); ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); count("ReentrantLock", () -> { lock.lock(); try { guarded++; } finally { lock.unlock(); } }, () -> guarded); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l10.SharedCounterJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l10/SharedCounterJava.java The plain and @Volatile counters come out short, by a different amount each run. AtomicLong, Mutex.withLock and the one-thread view all reach exactly 1,000,000. AtomicLong is fastest by far; the Mutex and the withContext switch for every increment take around a second, because each increment pays for a lock or a dispatch. The Java twin shows the same split, with ReentrantLock much cheaper than a Mutex here, because these threads never suspend.
