h: Shared state and testing coroutines · A one-thread view is not a lock: the pen goes down at every suspension
x: The pen goes down at every suspension: a one-thread view keeps other helpers out only between suspensions, a Mutex holds across them, and runTest skips delays on a virtual clock A view such as Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1) is a slice of a dispatcher that runs at most one of its coroutines at a time. That's the house rule about the pen, and it looks like a lock. The KDoc has a heading of its own to say it isn't one: "limitedParallelism(1) is not a mutex!" The view promises that code between suspension points runs one coroutine at a time. A suspension point is a call where a coroutine may pause, such as delay or a call to another suspend function. Between two of them, each coroutine sees what the one before it wrote, so count++ on the view is safe, which is why it counted every pea. But the moment a coroutine suspends, the view's thread is free, and the next coroutine runs. That's the helper putting the pen down to look up the scoop. Any update that suspends in the middle is open: Java // Java equivalent: one thread, but an async step in the middle CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> grams.getOrDefault(item, 0L), oneThread) .thenCombine(units.toGramsAsync(amount, unit), Long::sum) // another helper runs meanwhile .thenAcceptAsync(after -> grams.put(item, after), oneThread); // writes over the other addition Kotlin withContext(oneAtATime) { val before = grams[item] ?: 0L val more = units.toGrams(amount, unit) // suspends: another helper runs here grams[item] = before + more // writes over the other helper's addition } That is the lab's ShoppingList.add, as the starting code writes it. A critical section is code that must run with nothing else touching the same state in the middle of it, and this one has a middle. Play it out in the simulator: two helpers, one thread, and a suspension in the middle of each. (The simulator lets you switch after any line. On the real view a switch can happen only at the suspending line, and that's enough to lose an addition.) NotAMutex, in the Try it below, runs three helpers on a one-thread view, then the same three under a Mutex: limitedParallelism(1): helper 0: read the list helper 1: read the list helper 2: read the list helper 0: write the list helper 1: write the list helper 2: write the list Mutex.withLock: helper 0: read the list helper 0: write the list helper 2: read the list helper 2: write the list helper 1: read the list helper 1: write the list On the view, all three read before anyone wrote, so two of the three additions are lost. Under the Mutex, each helper reads and writes before the next one starts. The holder still suspends in the middle, but it keeps the pen while it does. There are two fixes. Move the suspension out of the critical part: convert first, then read and write with nothing that suspends between them. Or hold a Mutex across the whole update, which keeps the others out even while the holder is suspended. The first is faster, because the lookups overlap; it's the lab's solution. Use the second when the suspending call really must sit inside, for example a check whose answer must not go stale before you write. The rule is the one you learned for threads, with one word added for coroutines. A critical section is safe only if nothing can run in the middle of it. In a coroutine, every suspension point is a middle, including the ones hidden inside functions you call. The list is safe now. Proving it in a test is another matter: every lookup takes 50 ms, and a test of a retry with long waits takes longer still. We need a faster clock. Interleave three helpers, then lock them Read NotAMutex.kt. Predict the order of the read and write lines for the one-thread view, then for the Mutex. Run it. Look at the last part: why does the nested withLock time out instead of returning inner? Run the Java twin, where a single-thread executor interleaves the same way and ReentrantLock happily locks twice. NotAMutex.kt package workbench.coroutines.l10 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.joinAll import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withLock import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeoutOrNull fun main() = runBlocking { val oneAtATime = Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1) println("limitedParallelism(1):") List(3) { i -> launch(oneAtATime) { println(" helper $i: read the list") delay(20) // the recipe-app lookup suspends: the single thread is free for someone else println(" helper $i: write the list") } }.joinAll() println("Mutex.withLock:") val mutex = Mutex() List(3) { i -> launch(Dispatchers.Default) { mutex.withLock { println(" helper $i: read the list") delay(20) // still suspends, but nobody else can take the lock println(" helper $i: write the list") } } }.joinAll() println("Mutex is not reentrant:") val nested = withTimeoutOrNull(500) { mutex.withLock { withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { mutex.withLock { "inner" } } // the same coroutine tree locks again } } println(" nested withLock -> ${nested ?: "timed out after 500 ms: it waits for itself"}") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l10.NotAMutexKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l10/NotAMutex.kt NotAMutexJava.java // Java equivalent of NotAMutex.kt: a single-thread executor runs one task at a time, but an // async step (a CompletableFuture chain) lets the next helper start before the first one has // written. A ReentrantLock held across the whole read-look-up-write keeps them apart, and unlike // Kotlin's Mutex it IS reentrant. package workbench.coroutines.l10; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; import java.util.stream.IntStream; public class NotAMutexJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { ExecutorService oneThread = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); System.out.println("single-thread executor:"); List<CompletableFuture<Void>> helpers = IntStream.range(0, 3).mapToObj(i -> CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println(" helper " + i + ": read the list"), oneThread) // the recipe-app lookup is async: the thread is free while it waits .thenCompose(v -> CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { }, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(20, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS))) .thenRunAsync(() -> System.out.println(" helper " + i + ": write the list"), oneThread) ).toList(); CompletableFuture.allOf(helpers.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join(); oneThread.shutdown(); System.out.println("ReentrantLock around the whole addition:"); ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3)) { for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { int n = i; pool.submit(() -> { lock.lock(); try { System.out.println(" helper " + n + ": read the list"); Thread.sleep(20); // a blocking lookup, inside the lock System.out.println(" helper " + n + ": write the list"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } finally { lock.unlock(); } }); } } System.out.println("ReentrantLock is reentrant:"); lock.lock(); try { lock.lock(); // the same thread takes it again try { System.out.println(" nested lock -> inner (hold count " + lock.getHoldCount() + ")"); } finally { lock.unlock(); } } finally { lock.unlock(); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l10.NotAMutexJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l10/NotAMutexJava.java On the one-thread view, all three read the list lines print before any write the list: each helper suspended in the middle and let the next one in. With the Mutex, each helper reads and writes before the next one starts (the order of the helpers may vary). The nested withLock times out after 500 ms, because a Mutex is not reentrant: the inner lock waits for the outer one, which waits for the inner one. The Java twin interleaves the same way on one thread, and its ReentrantLock reports a hold count of 2. limitedParallelism (API reference: "not a mutex") docs

h: Shared state and testing coroutines · A rehearsal dinner on a fake clock: runTest skips the delays
x: Tests of code with timers are slow in real time, and they wobble. Take retry with backoff: try again after a wait, and wait longer each time. Waits of 100, 200 and 400 ms cost 700 ms per test. On a busy build machine 700 becomes 1,500, and a timing check becomes a coin toss. A theatre solves the same problem with a rehearsal. Nobody waits three hours for the roast: the stage manager says "the roast is done" and the next scene starts. runTest, from the kotlinx-coroutines-test library, is that rehearsal. Every delay in the test's coroutines is skipped. Instead, a virtual clock, a pretend clock that jumps forward instead of ticking, moves on to the next delay that is due, in the order the delays would have finished. Java // Java equivalent: Reactor's StepVerifier with virtual time (reactor-test) @Test void waitsBetweenAttempts() { StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> bakery.order("rye") .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(2, Duration.ofMillis(100)).jitter(0))) .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofMillis(300)) .expectNext("loaf ordered") .verifyComplete(); } Kotlin @Test fun `waits 100 then 200 ms between attempts`() = runTest { val attempts = mutableListOf<Long>() retryWithBackoff(times = 3, initialDelay = 100.milliseconds, maxDelay = 1.seconds) { attempts += currentTime // virtual milliseconds if (attempts.size < 3) throw IOException("the line is busy") else "loaf ordered" } assertThat(attempts).containsExactly(0L, 100L, 300L) // in a few real milliseconds } retryWithBackoff is the function you write in this lesson's lab. The test reads currentTime, the virtual clock, at every attempt, and checks exact numbers instead of a window of real time. Predict the log of a whole rehearsal dinner. VirtualTime, in the Try it below, calls runTest from a plain main. One coroutine simmers the soup for 1,000 ms, seasons it for 200 and bakes bread for 2,000. Another cooks the roast for 3,000 and rests it for 500: virtual 1000 ms (real 246 ms) soup simmered virtual 1200 ms (real 265 ms) soup seasoned virtual 3000 ms (real 266 ms) roast cooked virtual 3200 ms (real 266 ms) bread baked virtual 3500 ms (real 268 ms) roast rested virtual 3500 ms (real 269 ms) await returned whole runTest took 274 ms of real time withContext(Default) { delay(1_000) }: virtual 0 ms, real 1005 ms Three and a half seconds of dinner took about 20 real milliseconds once the library had loaded, in the right order. runTest runs the body in a TestScope, a scope made for tests, on a single-threaded test dispatcher, a dispatcher tied to the virtual clock. You can also drive the clock by hand: advanceTimeBy(ms) runs everything due before that point, runCurrent() runs what is due now, and advanceUntilIdle() runs everything queued. At the end, runTest waits for every child coroutine, so a test can't pass with work still pending. Now the last line, where the picture breaks. In a rehearsal, the stage manager can skip only the scenes he runs. runTest can skip only delays on its own dispatcher. Code that moves to Dispatchers.IO or Dispatchers.Default waits in real time, and the virtual clock never sees it: one real second, and currentTime stayed at 0. That's why Dispatchers and the coroutine context injected the dispatchers: tests pass StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler), and the program passes the real ones. Two more rules keep the clock honest. withTimeout inside runTest uses virtual time too. Mix it with real work on another dispatcher, and the scheduler, finding nothing of its own to do, can jump the clock forward and fire the timeout while the real work is still running. The tests in Cancellation and timeouts use runBlocking for their blocking call for exactly that reason. And the timeout of runTest itself is real, wall-clock time: 60 seconds by default since kotlinx.coroutines 1.8 (it was 10 s in 1.7). Change it with runTest(timeout = 10.seconds) or the kotlinx.coroutines.test.default_timeout system property. In 1.11 the old dispatchTimeoutMs overloads are errors. Only delays on the test dispatcher are virtual. Inject your dispatchers. The rehearsal has one more question to settle: when a test starts a new coroutine, when does it actually run? Rehearse three and a half seconds of dinner in a blink Read VirtualTime.kt. It calls runTest from a plain main. Predict the virtual time of each log line, and how much real time the first runTest takes. Run it. Look at the last line: why did the clock stay at 0 while a real second went by? VirtualTime.kt package workbench.coroutines.l10 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.test.TestScope import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun main() { val realStart = System.nanoTime() fun real() = (System.nanoTime() - realStart) / 1_000_000 // a rehearsal dinner on a fake clock: runTest is meant for tests, but a plain main can call it too runTest { fun TestScope.log(what: String) = println("virtual %5d ms (real %4d ms) %s".format(currentTime, real(), what)) launch { delay(1_000); log("soup simmered") delay(200); log("soup seasoned") delay(2_000); log("bread baked") } val roast = async { delay(3_000); log("roast cooked") delay(500); log("roast rested") } roast.await() log("await returned") } println("whole runTest took %d ms of real time".format(real())) runTest { val before = real() withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { delay(1_000) } // escapes the test scheduler println("withContext(Default) { delay(1_000) }: virtual $currentTime ms, real ${real() - before} ms") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l10.VirtualTimeKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l10/VirtualTime.kt The lines print at virtual 1,000, 1,200, 3,000, 3,200 and 3,500 ms, in that order, and await returned at 3,500. The real time stays well under a second, and most of it is the test library starting up. The last runTest reports virtual 0 ms and about 1,000 real ms: withContext(Dispatchers.Default) left the test scheduler, so its delay was a real one. runTest (API reference) docs

h: Shared state and testing coroutines · Standard or Unconfined, and backgroundScope for work that never ends
x: runTest uses a StandardTestDispatcher by default. With it, launch only queues the new coroutine, and nothing runs until the test body suspends or moves the clock. Tests stay predictable, because you decide when each child runs. Real dispatchers don't run a new coroutine on the spot either, so this is also the more honest default. UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler) enters a new coroutine at once and runs it up to its first suspension. That's handy for a collector that must be listening before the next line emits. Take the DishTracker from lesson 8 of this track, whose transitions is a SharedFlow with no replay: Java // Java equivalent: StepVerifier subscribes first, then runs the action that emits StepVerifier.create(tracker.transitions()) .then(() -> tracker.moveTo(DishStatus.COOKING)) .expectNextMatches(t -> t.to() == DishStatus.COOKING) .thenCancel() .verify(); Kotlin backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { tracker.transitions.collect { seen += it } // subscribed before the next line runs } tracker.moveTo(DishStatus.COOKING) If you mix dispatchers, give them all the same testScheduler. Two schedulers mean two clocks, and one of them will not move. TestDispatchers, in the Try it below, shows both dispatchers and a third tool: StandardTestDispatcher: [after launch, child ran] UnconfinedTestDispatcher: [child ran, after launch] polls after advanceTimeBy(5_500): 5 polls after advanceUntilIdle(): 5 (background work doesn't keep it busy) The third tool is backgroundScope, for coroutines that never finish on their own: a loop that reads the oven probe every second, a collector of a StateFlow, the sharing scope of a stateIn. runTest waits for every child before it returns, so an endless child in the test body would keep it waiting until the 60-second timeout. Coroutines in backgroundScope are cancelled when the test body ends instead. Two details matter. advanceUntilIdle() stops once only background work is left, otherwise a poller would keep it busy forever, so drive background work with advanceTimeBy. And a failure in backgroundScope doesn't stop the test at once, but it's reported when the test ends, so the test still fails. This lesson's lab is written the way these rules suggest. The retry tests read currentTime to check each wait exactly, and the shopping-list tests count how many lookups overlap instead of timing them. On the starting code, one of those tests reports 0 virtual milliseconds: the lookups ran on a real Default thread, outside the virtual clock. For flows there is also Turbine (app.cash.turbine, not on this lab's classpath), a small test library that adds flow.test { awaitItem() }. Its waits use a 3-second wall-clock timeout, not the virtual clock. Put endless coroutines in backgroundScope, and drive them with advanceTimeBy. A rehearsal proves the order of the scenes and the timing logic. It says nothing about how long the real bakery takes to answer, and that's the limit to keep in mind. Watch the two test dispatchers and a background poller Read TestDispatchers.kt. Predict the order in each of the two lists, and the poll count after each line. Run it. Move the poller from backgroundScope.launch to a plain launch, and add runTest(timeout = 3.seconds) (import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds). Predict, then run. TestDispatchers.kt package workbench.coroutines.l10 import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.test.UnconfinedTestDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.test.advanceTimeBy import kotlinx.coroutines.test.advanceUntilIdle import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runCurrent import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun main() = runTest { // 1. runTest's default, StandardTestDispatcher: launch only queues the child val standard = mutableListOf<String>() launch { standard += "child ran" } standard += "after launch" runCurrent() // run what is due now println("StandardTestDispatcher: $standard") // 2. UnconfinedTestDispatcher: the child starts at once, up to its first suspension val unconfined = mutableListOf<String>() launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { unconfined += "child ran" } unconfined += "after launch" println("UnconfinedTestDispatcher: $unconfined") // 3. backgroundScope: for work that never ends, such as a loop that reads the oven probe every second var polls = 0 backgroundScope.launch { while (true) { delay(1_000); polls++ } } advanceTimeBy(5_500) println("polls after advanceTimeBy(5_500): $polls") advanceUntilIdle() println("polls after advanceUntilIdle(): $polls (background work doesn't keep it busy)") // when the test body ends, runTest cancels everything in backgroundScope } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l10.TestDispatchersKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l10/TestDispatchers.kt StandardTestDispatcher: [after launch, child ran] and UnconfinedTestDispatcher: [child ran, after launch]. The poller has run 5 times after advanceTimeBy(5_500), and still 5 after advanceUntilIdle(), which ignores background work. After your change, advanceUntilIdle() treats the poller as ordinary work and runs it again and again, millions of virtual seconds' worth, until the 3-second wall-clock timeout stops everything with UncompletedCoroutinesError (an AssertionError): the test body did not run to completion.

h: Shared state and testing coroutines · Java and Kotlin
x: A dinner budget: ReentrantLock vs Mutex DinnerBudget.java class DinnerBudget { private final long limitCents; private long spentCents = 0; private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); DinnerBudget(long limitCents) { this.limitCents = limitCents; } boolean buy(String item) { long price = shop.priceOf(item); // 1. the slow call, outside the lock (blocks a thread) lock.lock(); // 2. blocks the thread while waiting try { if (spentCents + price > limitCents) return false; spentCents += price; // 3. check and spend together return true; } finally { lock.unlock(); } } } DinnerBudget.kt class DinnerBudget(private val limitCents: Long) { private var spentCents = 0L private val mutex = Mutex() suspend fun buy(item: String): Boolean { val price = shop.priceOf(item) // 1. the slow call, outside the lock (suspends) return mutex.withLock { // 2. suspends while waiting, holds no thread if (spentCents + price > limitCents) return@withLock false spentCents += price // 3. check and spend together true } } } The shape is the same: ask the shop for the price first, then check and spend under one lock. Two things differ. Waiting for a ReentrantLock blocks a thread, while waiting for a Mutex suspends a coroutine, so a rush of 5,000 purchases doesn't need 5,000 threads. And the Java lock is reentrant while the Mutex isn't, so a helper function that takes the Mutex again from inside withLock hangs instead of nesting. The Kotlin version has one extra trap that Java can't have. If someone later moves shop.priceOf inside withLock, it still works, but it holds the lock across a call to the shop. If they replace the Mutex with a one-thread view, it stops being correct at all.

h: Shared state and testing coroutines · Worked example
x: Test a retry policy without waiting for it Helpers order bread through BakeryOrders.orderWithRetry, which tries again when the bakery's line is busy (an IOException): up to 5 attempts, with waits that start at 200 ms, double each time and never exceed 2 s. The existing test uses real time. It takes 1.4 seconds, and on a busy machine it fails now and then. @Test fun `retries while the line is busy`() = runBlocking { var calls = 0 val started = System.currentTimeMillis() val result = orders.orderWithRetry("rye") { calls++; if (calls < 4) throw IOException("busy") else "ticket 42" } assertThat(result).isEqualTo("ticket 42") assertThat(System.currentTimeMillis() - started).isBetween(1_350L, 1_600L) // 200 + 400 + 800 = 1,400 } // Java equivalent of the shaky test: real sleeps, a timing window @Test void retriesWhileTheLineIsBusy() { AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); long started = System.currentTimeMillis(); String result = orders.orderWithRetry("rye", () -> { if (calls.incrementAndGet() < 4) throw new UncheckedIOException(new IOException("busy")); return "ticket 42"; }); assertThat(result).isEqualTo("ticket 42"); assertThat(System.currentTimeMillis() - started).isBetween(1_350L, 1_600L); } Move to runTest. The waits are delay calls on the test dispatcher, so they become virtual, and the test can check each attempt's exact virtual time instead of a window. @Test fun `waits 200, 400, then 800 ms between attempts`() = runTest { val at = mutableListOf<Long>() val result = orders.orderWithRetry("rye") { at += currentTime // 1. record virtual ms per attempt if (at.size < 4) throw IOException("busy") else "ticket 42" } assertThat(result).isEqualTo("ticket 42") assertThat(at).containsExactly(0L, 200L, 600L, 1_400L) // 2. exact, and instant } // Java equivalent: Reactor's virtual time, if the orders are built on Reactor @Test void waitsBetweenAttempts() { StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> orders.orderWithRetry("rye")) .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofMillis(1_400)) // 1. move the virtual clock .expectNext("ticket 42") // 2. exact, and instant .verifyComplete(); } The test went back to real time when someone added withContext(Dispatchers.IO) around the phone call inside BakeryOrders: its delay calls now ran on IO. Inject the dispatcher, and give the test the one tied to the test scheduler. class BakeryOrders(private val io: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO) { suspend fun <T> orderWithRetry(bread: String, call: suspend () -> T): T = withContext(io) { retryWithBackoff(times = 5, initialDelay = 200.milliseconds, maxDelay = 2.seconds) { call() } } } // 3. in the test val orders = BakeryOrders(io = StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) // Java equivalent: inject the Scheduler, and give the test a virtual one class BakeryOrders { private final Scheduler io; BakeryOrders(Scheduler io) { this.io = io; } <T> Mono<T> orderWithRetry(String bread, Mono<T> call) { return call.subscribeOn(io) .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(4, Duration.ofMillis(200)).maxBackoff(Duration.ofSeconds(2)).jitter(0).scheduler(io)); } } // 3. in the test VirtualTimeScheduler vts = VirtualTimeScheduler.getOrSet(); BakeryOrders orders = new BakeryOrders(vts); Add the case people forget: a cancel during a wait must stop the retries. Virtual time lets you stop exactly between two attempts. @Test fun `a cancel during the backoff stops the retries`() = runTest { var calls = 0 val job = launch { orders.orderWithRetry("rye") { calls++; throw IOException("busy") } } advanceTimeBy(300) // 4. attempts at 0 and 200 ms; now waiting until 600 ms job.cancel() advanceUntilIdle() assertThat(calls).isEqualTo(2) } @Test void cancelDuringBackoffStopsRetries() { AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> orders.orderWithRetry("rye", Mono.<String>fromCallable(() -> { calls.incrementAndGet(); throw new IOException("busy"); }))) .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofMillis(300)) // 4. attempts at 0 and 200 ms .thenCancel() .verify(); assertThat(calls.get()).isEqualTo(2); } Self-check: suppose the helper wrapped both the attempt and the delay in one runCatching and retried on any failure. What would the cancel test report? (calls would be 5, not 2. After the cancel, each delay throws at once, runCatching swallows it as a failed attempt, and the loop races through the remaining attempts. The test catches it because it counts calls instead of timing them. Cancellation and timeouts showed the same trap.)

x: Fix a shared shopping list, then write retry with backoff labs/coroutines/src/main/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l10/ShoppingList.kt labs/coroutines/src/main/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l10/Retry.kt ./gradlew :coroutines:test --tests 'workbench.coroutines.l10.*' Meet the code. Then do the read and the write inside mutex.withLock { }. Replace the one-thread view with the Mutex in total too. Write retryWithBackoff. h: Shared state and testing coroutines · Quiz
x: A dinner budget runs mutex.withLock { if (spent + price <= limit) { spend(price) } }, and spend itself calls mutex.withLock { spent += price }. What happens on the first purchase? It works: a coroutine may take a lock it already holds It throws IllegalStateException: the mutex is already locked It hangs: the inner withLock waits for the outer one, which never finishes The inner withLock is skipped, so spent never changes Mutex is not reentrant. The inner withLock suspends until the lock is free, but the lock is held by the same code that is waiting for it, so it never is. Take the lock once at the top, and have spend assume it is held. Which tool fits a per-dish count of plates served, updated by many coroutines on Default, where each update is just "add one"? A ConcurrentHashMap<String, AtomicLong> and incrementAndGet() A Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1) view around the whole kitchen A Mutex held across each dish's cooking @Volatile on the map field Each update is one step on one value, so an atomic is the cheapest correct tool: it never suspends or blocks. A Mutex held across the cooking makes every dish wait for every other, and @Volatile on the field only covers the reference to the map, not the increments. Inside runTest, the code under test calls withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { delay(2_000) }. What does the test see? currentTime jumps by 2,000 and the test finishes at once The test fails at once, because Dispatchers.IO is forbidden in runTest currentTime jumps by 2,000, but only after advanceUntilIdle() The test waits about 2 real seconds, and currentTime doesn't move Only delays on the test dispatcher are virtual. withContext(Dispatchers.IO) leaves the test scheduler, so that delay is a real one that the virtual clock never sees. Inject the dispatcher, so the test can pass StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler). A test starts launch { while (true) { delay(1_000); poll() } } in the runTest body, checks the poll count after advanceTimeBy(3_500), and ends. What happens? The test passes; the loop is cancelled when the body ends The test hangs until the runTest timeout, because runTest waits for every child The loop never runs, because launch only queues it advanceTimeBy throws, because the loop never ends runTest waits for every child of the test scope before it returns, and this one never ends, so the test fails after the wall-clock timeout (60 s by default). Start endless work in backgroundScope, which runTest cancels when the body ends. From lesson 5 of this track: a retry helper wraps each attempt in runCatching { block() } and retries on any failure. The caller is cancelled while an attempt is suspended in a call to the bakery. What happens? The CancellationException counts as a failed attempt, and the helper goes on to the next one The retries stop at once, because runCatching never catches CancellationException The coroutine is killed and no finally blocks run The helper waits for the call to finish, then stops runCatching catches every Throwable, including CancellationException, so the cancel is handled as a failed attempt. If the backoff delay sits outside the runCatching, it throws at once and ends the loop more or less by luck; if it sits inside, the loop races through every remaining attempt. Rethrow CancellationException before treating anything as worth retrying.

h: Shared state and testing coroutines · Key terms
x: Shared mutable state A variable that more than one coroutine or thread changes. Atomic A variable whose read-modify-write happens as one step that no other thread can split. Mutex A coroutine lock: waiting suspends instead of blocking. Fair, and not reentrant. Critical section Code that must run with nothing else touching the same state in the middle of it. Confinement Keeping changeable state reachable from only one coroutine or thread, so it needs no lock. Virtual time The test scheduler's pretend clock. Delays move it forward at once instead of waiting. StandardTestDispatcher A test dispatcher that queues work until the test lets the scheduler run. backgroundScope A scope inside runTest for endless work; it is cancelled when the test body ends. Does @Volatile make count++ safe across coroutines on Dispatchers.Default? No. It makes each read and write visible, but count++ is still read, add, write. Use an atomic or a Mutex. What does Mutex.withLock do while another coroutine holds the lock? It suspends the caller (no thread is blocked) until the lock is free, and the Mutex hands out the lock in the order coroutines asked. A coroutine holding a Mutex calls withLock on it again. What happens? It suspends forever: Mutex is not reentrant. Why is limitedParallelism(1) not a mutex? It runs one coroutine at a time only between suspension points. When one suspends, another runs, so an update with a suspension in the middle can interleave. What happens to delay(1_000) inside runTest? It is skipped: the virtual clock (currentTime) jumps forward by 1,000 ms, keeping the order of events. StandardTestDispatcher vs UnconfinedTestDispatcher for launch? Standard queues the new coroutine until the test yields or moves the clock. Unconfined starts it at once and runs it to its first suspension. Where do never-ending coroutines go in a runTest test? backgroundScope: they are cancelled when the test body ends, and advanceUntilIdle() doesn't wait for them.

h: Shared state and testing coroutines · Go deeper
x: Semaphore(permits) in kotlinx.coroutines.sync is the counting version of a Mutex: withPermit { } lets at most n coroutines in at once, like the three sinks of the last lesson's drill. It is the coroutine counterpart of the Semaphore from Using virtual threads, in the virtual threads track, and like the Mutex it suspends rather than blocks. Since 1.9 you can no longer cast a Mutex to a Semaphore; they are separate types. Mutex has an optional owner: lock(owner) and withLock(owner) record who holds it, and holdsLock(owner) checks it. Passing an owner turns a reentrant call into an immediate IllegalStateException instead of a silent hang, which is a cheap safety net in code where a helper function might be called with the lock already held. The test library has more knobs than this lesson uses. Several StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler, name = ...) instances can share one scheduler, so code that takes two dispatchers (one for blocking calls, one for CPU work) can get two named test dispatchers with one clock. Dispatchers.setMain(...) and resetMain() swap the Main dispatcher for code written for a user interface. And runTest reports uncaught exceptions from coroutines it doesn't own at the end of the test, which is why a forgotten GlobalScope.launch that throws can fail an unrelated test. Finally, virtual time is not a load test. It proves that the order and the timing logic are right. It says nothing about how long the real recipe app takes, how a real Mutex behaves with 5,000 waiters, or whether the shop keeps up. Keep a few real-time tests, with generous margins, for that.

h: Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads · Cross the fence with futures: await() in, future { } out
x: The neighbour's ticket: get() keeps a thread at the fence and drops the cancel, await() suspends and cancels the future, future { } hands Java a ticket tied to our coroutine, and a cold mono { } runs one coroutine per subscriber Most Java code that waits for something speaks CompletableFuture. A future is an object that stands for a result that isn't ready yet: the neighbour's ticket. kotlinx.coroutines crosses the fence in both directions with nothing extra to add to the build, since the old kotlinx-coroutines-jdk8 artifact was merged into the core library in 1.7. Start with the way in. The bakery has a Java library whose loavesLeft(bread) returns a future at once, and the future completes later with the number of loaves left. Here is the naive bridge, which the lab's starting code uses, and the fixed one: Java // Java equivalent: block a thread on the future, or chain on it int loaves = bakery.loavesLeft("rye").join(); // blocks the caller CompletableFuture<String> note = bakery.loavesLeft("rye").thenApply(n -> n + " left"); // or composes Kotlin // Naive: an IO thread stands at the door for the whole wait, and a cancel never reaches the future withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { bakery.loavesLeft("rye").get() } // Fixed: suspends until the future completes; cancelling this coroutine cancels the future bakery.loavesLeft("rye").await() The naive version "doesn't block the caller", and that's why it ships. But get() blocks an IO thread for the whole wait, the cook standing at the neighbour's door. Worse, if the calling coroutine is cancelled, the future never hears about it. await() suspends instead, so no thread waits. It rethrows the future's exception unwrapped, so you catch the IOException itself rather than an ExecutionException, and it has a fast path for a future that is already done. It also carries the cancel across: if the awaiting coroutine is cancelled, await() calls future.cancel(false). That is usually right, because nobody wants the answer any more. When the future is shared, or must finish anyway (a pie already in the oven), use future.asDeferred().await(), which waits without cancelling it. Now the way out. Our kitchen can hand the neighbour a ticket too: Java // Java equivalent: the Java caller's side, which is plain CompletableFuture code CompletableFuture<String> reply = door.cookAsync(new Order("soup", 4)) .orTimeout(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) .thenApply(outcome -> "soup: " + outcome); Kotlin class KitchenDoor(private val cook: suspend (Order) -> Outcome) : AutoCloseable { private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default) fun cookAsync(order: Order): CompletableFuture<Outcome> = scope.future { cook(order) } override fun close() = scope.cancel() } future { } is a builder like async: it starts a coroutine in the scope and hands its result back as a CompletableFuture. The link runs both ways. The KDoc, the documentation in the library's source, says the coroutine is cancelled when the future "is cancelled or otherwise completed". So a Java caller's cancel(true), or an orTimeout that fires, cancels the Kotlin coroutine. Give the door a scope it owns, as in Structured concurrency, so that closing the door cancels everything still cooking. GlobalScope.future also compiles, and it leaks in exactly the way that lesson described. Predict three lines before you run FutureBridge, in the Try it below: 1. await() on a Java future, then cancel the coroutine: future cancelled: true 2. asDeferred().await(), then cancel the coroutine: future cancelled: false (it still completes: apple pie ready) 3. future { } for a Java caller, who cancels it: [kotlin] cooking leek was cancelled future cancelled: true The cancel crossed the fence both ways. In case 1, cancelling the coroutine cancelled the neighbour's future. In case 3, the Java caller cancelled the future, and the Kotlin coroutine heard it at its next suspension point. Here the picture breaks a little. Cancelling a plain Java future only marks it as cancelled. Whether the work behind it stops depends on the code that made it, just as a real neighbour may or may not read your note. A future from future { } always stops its coroutine. Cross the fence with await() and future { }. get() and runBlocking hold a thread and drop the cancel. The neighbour across the road cooks another way again, with Reactor. Cancel across the fence Read FutureBridge.kt. Predict the three future cancelled lines. Run it. Run the Java twin. It is plain Java calling the Kotlin SoupKitchen from the same file, so watch for the [kotlin] lines. In the Java twin, change orTimeout(50, ...) to orTimeout(500, ...) and run it again. Predict first. FutureBridge.kt package workbench.coroutines.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.SupervisorJob import kotlinx.coroutines.cancel import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.future.asDeferred import kotlinx.coroutines.future.await import kotlinx.coroutines.future.future import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** Kotlin code with a face for Java: the suspend call gets a CompletableFuture twin. */ class SoupKitchen : AutoCloseable { private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default) /** Cooks a pot of [soup] and returns how many bowls it made. */ suspend fun cook(soup: String): Int { try { delay(200) // simmering return soup.length * 7 } catch (e: kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException) { println(" [kotlin] cooking $soup was cancelled") throw e } } fun cookAsync(soup: String): CompletableFuture<Int> = scope.future { cook(soup) } override fun close() = scope.cancel() } /** The neighbour's Java-style future: a pie that takes 500 ms. It reports whether someone cancelled it. */ fun neighboursPie(): CompletableFuture<String> { val f = CompletableFuture<String>() CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).execute { f.complete("apple pie ready") } return f } fun main() = runBlocking { println("1. await() on a Java future, then cancel the coroutine:") val f1 = neighboursPie() launch { f1.await() }.also { delay(100) }.cancelAndJoin() println(" future cancelled: ${f1.isCancelled}") println("2. asDeferred().await(), then cancel the coroutine:") val f2 = neighboursPie() launch { f2.asDeferred().await() }.also { delay(100) }.cancelAndJoin() println(" future cancelled: ${f2.isCancelled} (it still completes: ${f2.get()})") println("3. future { } for a Java caller, who cancels it:") SoupKitchen().use { kitchen -> val f3 = kitchen.cookAsync("leek") delay(50) f3.cancel(true) delay(50) println(" future cancelled: ${f3.isCancelled}") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l11.FutureBridgeKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l11/FutureBridge.kt FutureBridgeJava.java // Java equivalent of FutureBridge.kt, from the Java side: plain Java calling the Kotlin // SoupKitchen through its future {} method. No Continuation, no runBlocking. package workbench.coroutines.l11; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class FutureBridgeJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (SoupKitchen kitchen = new SoupKitchen()) { System.out.println("1. compose two Kotlin calls like any futures:"); CompletableFuture<Integer> bowls = kitchen.cookAsync("leek") .thenCombine(kitchen.cookAsync("tomato"), Integer::sum); System.out.println(" bowls in total: " + bowls.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)); System.out.println("2. a Java timeout cancels the Kotlin coroutine:"); CompletableFuture<Integer> slow = kitchen.cookAsync("onion") .orTimeout(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // fails the future after 50 ms try { slow.join(); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println(" java caller got: " + e.getCause()); } Thread.sleep(50); System.out.println("3. cancel(true) on the future the kitchen returned:"); CompletableFuture<Integer> cancelled = kitchen.cookAsync("pea"); Thread.sleep(50); cancelled.cancel(true); Thread.sleep(50); System.out.println(" future cancelled: " + cancelled.isCancelled()); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l11.FutureBridgeJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l11/FutureBridgeJava.java Case 1 prints future cancelled: true: cancelling the coroutine cancelled the Java future it was awaiting. Case 2 prints false, and the future still completes, because asDeferred().await() only waits. Case 3 prints [kotlin] cooking leek was cancelled, then true. In the Java twin, the two soups make 70 bowls between them, and both the orTimeout and the cancel(true) produce a [kotlin] ... was cancelled line. With a 500 ms timeout the 200 ms soup finishes first, so there is no timeout and no cancel line for it. Each neighbour of the coroutine kitchen has a bridge in and a bridge out, and the bridges that suspend carry cancellation both ways. future (API reference) docs await on CompletionStage (API reference) docs

h: Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads · Cross into Reactor: mono { } out, awaitSingle() and asFlow() in
x: Reactor, the subject of the reactive track, is a Java library for streams of values. A Mono is a recipe for at most one value, a Flux is a recipe for many, and nothing runs until someone subscribes. The kotlinx-coroutines-reactor module, on this lab's classpath, bridges both: Java // Java equivalent: the Reactor side just sees ordinary Mono and Flux values Mono<Recipe> soup = RecipeMonoKt.recipeMono(book, "soup"); // built by mono { } in Kotlin Mono<String> both = Mono.zip(soup, RecipeMonoKt.recipeMono(book, "bread")).map(t -> t.getT1() + " | " + t.getT2()); Flux<Integer> temps = ReactorBridgeKt.temperatureFlux(); // a Kotlin Flow through asFlux() Kotlin fun recipeMono(book: RecipeBook, dish: String): Mono<Recipe> = mono { book.recipe(dish) } // suspend code as a Mono suspend fun recipeNow(dish: String): Recipe = recipeFromReactor(dish).awaitSingle() // a Mono in suspend code fun plates(): Flow<String> = plateFlux().asFlow() // a Flux as a Flow fun temperatureFlux(): Flux<Int> = temperatures().asFlux() // a Flow as a Flux mono { } gives a cold Mono: the coroutine starts on subscription, once per subscriber, which is the contract every Reactor user expects (Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe). It's the recipe card of Flow basics again: each subscriber cooks from it afresh. A null result completes the Mono empty, and disposing the subscription cancels the coroutine. Its context may not contain a Job ("Mono context cannot contain job in it"), because the subscription owns the coroutine's life, not a scope. flux { } does the same for a stream of values, with send inside. In the other direction, awaitSingle() waits for exactly one value, and throws NoSuchElementException for an empty Mono; awaitSingleOrNull() returns null instead. Publisher.asFlow() collects a Flux as a Flow. The Flow's suspension becomes request(n), the Reactive Streams call by which a subscriber asks for n more values, and cancelling the collector cancels the subscription. Flow.asFlux() goes back. The module's README calls the result TCK-compliant: it passes the Reactive Streams test kit (TCK), which checks a publisher against the numbered rules of the specification. ReactorBridge, in the Try it below, looks up a recipe twice through one Mono, then asks for a dish the book doesn't have: 1. mono { } is cold: built the Mono; nothing looked up yet [kotlin] looking up soup awaitSingle() -> soup: 40 minutes [kotlin] looking up soup awaitSingle() again -> soup: 40 minutes 2. an empty Mono: [kotlin] looking up dragon stew awaitSingle() threw NoSuchElementException Building the Mono looked up nothing. Each awaitSingle() subscribed, and each subscription ran the coroutine again. The recipe book, sensibly, has nothing for dragon stew, so that Mono completed empty, and awaitSingle() threw. If one lookup must be shared, .cache() on the Mono does it. Two things need care. Threads first: unless you pass a dispatcher, mono { } starts its coroutine on Dispatchers.Default, while the Reactor operators around it run wherever their schedulers put them. Then context: Reactor's own Context, which a Reactor-based web framework uses for values such as a request id, is visible inside the coroutine as a ReactorContext element. Thread-local values are not, for the reason Dispatchers and the coroutine context gave: a coroutine may resume on another thread. mono { } runs its coroutine once per subscriber, and disposing the subscription cancels it. Futures and Monos are shapes Java code already knows. Plain Java can call our suspend functions too, if we give it a door. Hand a coroutine to Reactor and back Read ReactorBridge.kt. Predict how many [kotlin] looking up soup lines print in part 1. Run it. Run the Java twin, which uses the same Kotlin recipeFor and temperatureFlux functions from plain Reactor code. In the Kotlin file, change awaitSingle() in part 2 to awaitSingleOrNull() and print the result. Predict first. ReactorBridge.kt package workbench.coroutines.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.take import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.toList import kotlinx.coroutines.reactive.asFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.reactive.awaitSingle import kotlinx.coroutines.reactor.asFlux import kotlinx.coroutines.reactor.mono import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import java.time.Duration /** A Kotlin suspend call, handed to Reactor code as a cold Mono. */ fun recipeFor(dish: String): Mono<String> = mono { println(" [kotlin] looking up $dish") delay(50) if (dish == "dragon stew") null else "$dish: 40 minutes" } /** A Kotlin Flow of oven temperatures, handed to Reactor code as a Flux. */ fun temperatures(): Flow<Int> = flow { for (i in 0 until 5) { delay(20); emit(180 + i * 5) } } fun temperatureFlux(): Flux<Int> = temperatures().asFlux() fun main() = runBlocking { println("1. mono { } is cold:") val m = recipeFor("soup") println(" built the Mono; nothing looked up yet") println(" awaitSingle() -> ${m.awaitSingle()}") println(" awaitSingle() again -> ${m.awaitSingle()}") println("2. an empty Mono:") try { recipeFor("dragon stew").awaitSingle() } catch (e: NoSuchElementException) { println(" awaitSingle() threw NoSuchElementException") } println("3. a Flux consumed as a Flow (cancelling the flow cancels the subscription):") val plates = Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(10)).map { "plate-$it" }.doOnCancel { println(" [reactor] subscription cancelled") } println(" ${plates.asFlow().take(3).toList()}") println("4. a Flow handed to Reactor as a Flux:") println(" ${temperatureFlux().map { "$it C" }.collectList().block()}") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l11.ReactorBridgeKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l11/ReactorBridge.kt ReactorBridgeJava.java // Java equivalent of ReactorBridge.kt, from the Java side: Reactor code using the Kotlin // functions through their Mono and Flux faces. The Kotlin side is ReactorBridge.kt. package workbench.coroutines.l11; import java.util.List; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; public class ReactorBridgeJava { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("1. the Kotlin Mono is cold, so each subscription looks it up again:"); Mono<String> soup = ReactorBridgeKt.recipeFor("soup"); System.out.println(" built the Mono; nothing looked up yet"); System.out.println(" block() -> " + soup.block()); System.out.println(" block() again -> " + soup.block()); System.out.println("2. an empty Mono and a default:"); System.out.println(" " + ReactorBridgeKt.recipeFor("dragon stew").defaultIfEmpty("no recipe: make toast").block()); System.out.println("3. zip two Kotlin lookups with Reactor operators:"); System.out.println(" " + Mono.zip(ReactorBridgeKt.recipeFor("soup"), ReactorBridgeKt.recipeFor("bread")) .map(t -> t.getT1() + " | " + t.getT2()).block()); System.out.println("4. a Kotlin Flow as a Flux:"); List<String> temps = ReactorBridgeKt.temperatureFlux().map(c -> c + " C").collectList().block(); System.out.println(" " + temps); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l11.ReactorBridgeJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l11/ReactorBridgeJava.java [kotlin] looking up soup prints twice in part 1, once per awaitSingle(), and not when the Mono is built: mono { } is cold. Part 2 throws NoSuchElementException for the empty Mono, and after your change it prints null. Part 3 prints three plates and [reactor] subscription cancelled, because take(3) stopped the Flow. Part 4 prints five temperatures from 180 C to 200 C. The Java twin shows the same cold Mono from the Reactor side, plus defaultIfEmpty and Mono.zip over two Kotlin lookups. kotlinx-coroutines-reactor (API reference) docs

h: Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads · Give Java callers a door they can use
x: Java can see a suspend function, but it can't call it in any useful way. The compiler adds a Continuation parameter, the bookmark of Suspend functions from zero, and changes the return type to Object. So from Java the signature looks like this: Java // what Java sees for the same function: a Continuation parameter and an Object result public Object cook(Order order, Continuation<? super Outcome> $completion) Kotlin suspend fun cook(order: Order): Outcome You could write a Continuation by hand, but you'd be rebuilding a coroutine builder, badly. Give Java callers one of three doors instead. A CompletableFuture door, built with future { }, like the lab's KitchenDoor. It's the default for Java code that composes its work as futures. A Mono door, built with mono { }, for code that already lives in Reactor. A blocking door that wraps runBlocking { }, for Java callers that block anyway: a command-line tool, a JUnit test, or any code running on a virtual thread. Blocking a virtual thread is cheap, so runBlocking on one is a fair bridge. It's still wrong inside suspend code, as Builders showed. Whichever you choose, name the doors so the difference shows: cook for Kotlin, cookAsync or cookBlocking for Java. Keep the suspend function as the one real implementation, and make the others thin wrappers, so the rules for retries and timeouts live in one place. @JvmOverloads, @JvmStatic and @JvmName take care of the rest of what Java sees: default arguments, functions in a companion object, and names that would clash. A blocking door needs a timeout of its own. runBlocking { withTimeout(2.seconds) { cook(order) } } gives the Java caller an upper bound. And an interrupt of the calling thread, Java's request to stop from the first track, cancels the coroutine and makes runBlocking throw InterruptedException. That's the bridge from Java's way of cancelling to Kotlin's. The lab's Java test, JavaCallerTest.java, shows what a Java caller ends up writing against a future { } door: orTimeout, thenApply and get, with no Kotlin types in sight beyond the data classes. Quick check: two Java callers wait for the kitchen through different doors, and each caller's thread is interrupted while the dish is cooking. Caller A uses cookBlocking, the runBlocking door. Caller B calls cookAsync(order).get(). Whose cooking is cancelled? (Only A's. The interrupt reaches runBlocking, which cancels its coroutine. B's interrupt only makes get() throw InterruptedException. The future isn't complete, so the coroutine behind it keeps cooking until someone cancels the future or closes the door.) Keep one suspend function as the real code, and give Java thin doors: a future, a Mono, or a blocking call with its own timeout. Three neighbours, three ways of cooking. Which one should a new program start with?

h: Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads · Virtual threads, coroutines or Reactor: choosing for a new program
x: All three solve the problem the virtual threads track opened with. A program that answers many requests at once spends most of its time waiting, for a database or for another web service, and an operating-system thread per waiting request is too expensive. They solve it at different layers. Virtual threads, final since JDK 21, are threads so cheap that a waiting one costs almost nothing: a helper at every pot, who simply stands there. Coroutines make waiting explicit with suspend, and add a tree of dishes with cancellation and Flow. Reactor turns a request into a line of stations, with backpressure: a slow consumer slows down a fast producer. ThreeWays, in the Try it below, cooks the same dinner each way: soup in 100 ms, the roast in 300 and the salad in 200, all started at once. Predict the times: coroutines: [soup, roast, salad] took 304 ms on main blocking code on virtual threads: [soup, roast, salad] took 332 ms blocking code on Dispatchers.IO: [soup, roast, salad] took 318 ms Each one takes as long as the slowest dish, and the Java twin's virtual threads and Reactor Mono.zip did the same (309 and 301 ms). Speed doesn't decide between them. The shape of your code does: Virtual threads (JDK 21+) Kotlin coroutines Reactor Picture it a cheap helper standing at every pot one cook, bookmarks and a tree of dishes a line of stations Your code looks like plain blocking Java or Kotlin sequential suspend functions chains of operators Blocking libraries (database drivers, older SDKs) the natural fit withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or a virtual-thread dispatcher wrap them, move them to boundedElastic Several calls with one deadline StructuredTaskScope, preview in JDK 25 coroutineScope, async, withTimeout Mono.zip, timeout Cancellation interrupts, if the code checks them flows down the job tree to every child a cancel signal up the chain Streams with backpressure none built in Flow Flux Debugging ordinary stacks and thread dumps debug mode and coroutine dumps operator traces, harder to read Java callers native through future { } or mono { } native Here is what I would do in a program that answers many requests and talks to a database through a blocking driver. Start with virtual threads for request handling that is mostly blocking calls. Database drivers and many older libraries block anyway. Since JDK 24 (JEP 491), synchronized no longer pins a virtual thread to its carrier, the platform thread that runs it, in most cases, so JDK 25 is a good base. Cap each slow neighbour with a semaphore, a counter of permits, as Using virtual threads showed. Use coroutines in Kotlin code that needs what virtual threads don't give you: several calls with one deadline, a cancel that reaches every child, Flow pipelines, StateFlow-style shared state. Blocking calls inside still go through withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or a virtual-thread dispatcher. Keep Reactor where a reactive stack already exists, or where you stream with backpressure from end to end. Don't start a new program full of blocking calls on it. Mixing them is normal, and cheap with the bridges from this lesson. What to avoid is several models in one call path for no reason: a coroutine that calls runBlocking, which subscribes to a Mono, which blocks on a database. That's three kitchens to boil one egg, and a cancel has to cross every fence on the way. Pick one model for each part of the program, and convert only at its edges. Whichever you pick, the bridges in this lesson keep a cancel from getting lost at the fence. One dinner, three ways Read ThreeWays.kt and its Java twin. Each cooks the same three dishes (100, 300 and 200 ms) at once. Predict every time. Run both. In ThreeWays.kt, wrap the body of dinnerWithCoroutines in withTimeout(250) { ... } and run it again. What happens to the dishes still cooking? ThreeWays.kt package workbench.coroutines.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.asCoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import java.util.concurrent.Executors import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis // one dinner: soup (100 ms), roast (300 ms) and salad (200 ms), all started at once suspend fun dinnerWithCoroutines(): List<String> = coroutineScope { val soup = async { delay(100); "soup" } val roast = async { delay(300); "roast" } val salad = async { delay(200); "salad" } listOf(soup.await(), roast.await(), salad.await()) } /** The same dinner written as BLOCKING code, run on whatever dispatcher you pass. */ suspend fun dinnerBlocking(on: CoroutineDispatcher): List<String> = coroutineScope { val soup = async(on) { Thread.sleep(100); "soup" } val roast = async(on) { Thread.sleep(300); "roast" } val salad = async(on) { Thread.sleep(200); "salad" } listOf(soup.await(), roast.await(), salad.await()) } fun main() = runBlocking { repeat(2) { dinnerWithCoroutines() } // warm up val c = measureTimeMillis { println("coroutines: ${dinnerWithCoroutines()}") } println(" took $c ms on ${Thread.currentThread().name.substringBefore(" @")}") Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher().use { vt -> val v = measureTimeMillis { println("blocking code on virtual threads: ${dinnerBlocking(vt)}") } println(" took $v ms") } val b = measureTimeMillis { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { println("blocking code on Dispatchers.IO: ${dinnerBlocking(Dispatchers.IO)}") } } println(" took $b ms") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l11.ThreeWaysKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l11/ThreeWays.kt ThreeWaysJava.java // Java equivalent of ThreeWays.kt: the same dinner with virtual threads (plain blocking code) // and with Reactor (operators, no blocking). Same total time: the slowest dish. package workbench.coroutines.l11; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; public class ThreeWaysJava { static String cook(String dish, long ms) throws InterruptedException { Thread.sleep(ms); // a blocking call return dish; } static List<String> withVirtualThreads() throws Exception { try (ExecutorService vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<String> soup = vt.submit(() -> cook("soup", 100)); Future<String> roast = vt.submit(() -> cook("roast", 300)); Future<String> salad = vt.submit(() -> cook("salad", 200)); return List.of(soup.get(), roast.get(), salad.get()); } } static List<String> withReactor() { return Mono.zip( Mono.just("soup").delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(100)), Mono.just("roast").delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(300)), Mono.just("salad").delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(200))) .map(t -> List.of(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3())) .block(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { withVirtualThreads(); withReactor(); // warm up long t0 = System.nanoTime(); System.out.println("virtual threads: " + withVirtualThreads()); System.out.println(" took " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 + " ms"); t0 = System.nanoTime(); System.out.println("reactor: " + withReactor()); System.out.println(" took " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 + " ms"); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l11.ThreeWaysJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l11/ThreeWaysJava.java Every version takes about 300 ms: the coroutines, the blocking code on a virtual-thread dispatcher, the blocking code on Dispatchers.IO, the plain virtual threads and the Reactor Mono.zip. With withTimeout(250), the program fails with TimeoutCancellationException at about 250 ms, and the roast and the salad, still cooking, are cancelled with it. Doing that in the Java virtual-thread version would take extra code to cancel the futures yourself. JEP 444: Virtual Threads read Reactor bridges: kotlinx-coroutines-reactor README read

h: Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads · Java and Kotlin
x: Three dishes for one table, with one deadline: virtual threads vs coroutines Dinner.java Dinner dinner(String table) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<Soup> soup = vt.submit(() -> soupPot.serve(table)); // 1. three blocking calls, Future<Roast> roast = vt.submit(() -> oven.carve(table)); // one virtual thread each Future<Salad> salad = vt.submit(() -> salads.toss(table)); long deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.toNanos(800); try { return new Dinner( // 2. one shared deadline soup.get(remaining(deadline), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS), roast.get(remaining(deadline), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS), salad.get(remaining(deadline), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)); } catch (TimeoutException | ExecutionException e) { soup.cancel(true); roast.cancel(true); salad.cancel(true); // 3. cancel by hand throw e; } } // close() waits for every task } Dinner.kt suspend fun dinner(table: String): Dinner = withTimeout(800) { // 2. one shared deadline coroutineScope { val soup = async { soupPot.serve(table) } // 1. three suspending calls, val roast = async { oven.carve(table) } // one coroutine each val salad = async { salads.toss(table) } Dinner(soup.await(), roast.await(), salad.await()) } // 3. a timeout or a failure cancels the other two automatically } Both take as long as the slowest dish, and both are cheap: a virtual thread or a coroutine per call. The difference is how much of the structure you write yourself. In Java with virtual threads, the calls can stay blocking, which is the big win, but the shared deadline, the step that cancels the other dishes on a failure, and the cleanup are your code. JDK 25's StructuredTaskScope covers that, but it is still a preview API (JEP 505). In Kotlin, the deadline is withTimeout, the other dishes are cancelled by coroutineScope, and the calls must suspend, or be wrapped in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or a virtual-thread dispatcher. Pick the model that matches the code you call: blocking libraries favour virtual threads, suspending ones and complex fan-out favour coroutines.

h: Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads · Worked example
x: Give the neighbour's Java program a door into the Kotlin kitchen The kitchen's real work is a Kotlin suspend function with retries: KitchenService.cook(order). The neighbour's Java program must call it from two places: a screen that works with futures and has a Cancel button, and a command-line tool that just waits for the answer. Neither can call the suspend function directly. class KitchenService(private val stove: Stove) { suspend fun cook(order: Order): Outcome = retryWithBackoff(times = 3, initialDelay = 200.milliseconds, maxDelay = 2.seconds) { stove.cook(order) } } // what the Java program sees: a Continuation parameter it can't sensibly supply public final class KitchenService { public final Object cook(Order order, Continuation<? super Outcome> $completion) { /* ... */ } } Add Java doors in a small Kotlin class with its own scope. One returns a future, for Java code that composes; one blocks with its own timeout, for callers that block anyway. class KitchenJavaApi(private val service: KitchenService) : AutoCloseable { private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default) // 1. for Java code that composes futures fun cookAsync(order: Order): CompletableFuture<Outcome> = scope.future { service.cook(order) } // 2. for callers that block anyway, with its own upper bound fun cookBlocking(order: Order): Outcome = runBlocking { withTimeout(10.seconds) { service.cook(order) } } override fun close() = scope.cancel() } // Java equivalent of the same doors, if the service were a Java class returning futures final class KitchenJavaApi implements AutoCloseable { private final KitchenService service; KitchenJavaApi(KitchenService service) { this.service = service; } // 1. for Java code that composes futures CompletableFuture<Outcome> cookAsync(Order order) { return service.cookAsync(order); } // 2. for callers that block anyway, with its own upper bound Outcome cookBlocking(Order order) throws Exception { return service.cookAsync(order).get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } @Override public void close() { } } The screen uses the future door, so its Cancel button can stop the Kotlin work: cancel(true) on the future cancels the coroutine, retries and all. // the screen is Java; this is the Kotlin side it relies on: cancel(true) reaches the coroutine val pending = api.cookAsync(order) pending.cancel(true) // 3. cancels the coroutine inside KitchenService, retries included // 3. the Java screen: show the outcome, or stop the kitchen when Cancel is pressed CompletableFuture<Outcome> pending = api.cookAsync(order); cancelButton.onClick(() -> pending.cancel(true)); // stops the Kotlin coroutine and its retries pending.thenAccept(outcome -> screen.show(order.dish() + ": " + outcome)); A caller written with Reactor gets its own door from the same function, and the retry rules still live in one place. // 4. a cold Mono for Reactor callers fun cookMono(order: Order): Mono<Outcome> = mono { service.cook(order) } // 4. the Reactor caller's side Mono<Outcome> outcome = api.cookMono(order) .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10)) .onErrorReturn(Outcome.REFUSED); Self-check: why not write cookAsync as CompletableFuture.supplyAsync { runBlocking { service.cook(order) } }? (It blocks a pool thread for every order, the future has no link to the coroutine so cancel(true) stops nothing, and the work belongs to no scope, so close() can't stop it either. That is the bug in this lesson's lab.)

h: Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads · Quiz
x: A Java caller holds f = door.cookAsync(order), where cookAsync is scope.future { cook(order) }, and calls f.cancel(true). What happens on the Kotlin side? Nothing: cancel(true) only interrupts Java threads The coroutine is cancelled at its next suspension point The coroutine finishes, and its result is thrown away The whole scope is cancelled, with every other order The future from future { } is tied to its coroutine, and cancelling or completing the future cancels it. Only that coroutine is affected: the scope and its other children carry on, all the more with a SupervisorJob. A coroutine does val n = bakery.loavesLeft("rye").await() and is cancelled while it waits. What happens to the Java future? It is cancelled with cancel(false), because nobody wants the answer any more It keeps running, and its result is thrown away It is completed with null await() blocks until the future finishes, then throws await() cancels the future when the awaiting coroutine is cancelled. If the future must finish anyway (it is shared, or the work is already under way), use future.asDeferred().await(), which waits without cancelling. val r: Mono<Recipe> = mono { book.recipe("soup") } is built, and then two different callers subscribe to r. How many times does book.recipe run? Once, when mono { } is called Once, at the first subscription; the second subscriber gets the cached value Twice: the Mono is cold, so each subscription runs the coroutine Never, unless block() is called mono { } starts the coroutine on subscription, once per subscriber, like any cold Mono. Use .cache() on the Mono if one lookup really should be shared. A Java program answers 2,000 requests at once. Each request makes three database queries through a blocking driver and one call to a slow web service, and the team writes Java. Which model fits best? Rewrite it with Reactor, to avoid blocking Rewrite it in Kotlin with coroutines A pool of 2,000 platform threads Virtual threads, with a semaphore in front of the database The code is blocking and in Java, which is exactly what virtual threads make cheap: one per request, with no rewrite. A semaphore keeps the database's connections from being overrun. Reactor and coroutines would mean rewriting every call for little gain, and 2,000 platform threads cost a lot of memory. From the virtual threads track: on JDK 21, a virtual thread blocks on a socket read while inside a synchronized block. What happens to its carrier thread? It is released, as with any blocking call It is pinned: it stays blocked with the virtual thread until the read returns The JVM throws IllegalStateException The virtual thread is moved to a new carrier On JDK 21 to 23, blocking while holding a monitor pins the virtual thread to its carrier, so the carrier blocks too. JEP 491 in JDK 24 removed most of that pinning, which is one reason to run virtual-thread programs on JDK 25.

h: Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads · Key terms
x: CompletableFuture A Java object for a result that isn't ready yet; it can be completed, chained and cancelled. The neighbour's ticket. future { } A coroutine builder that returns the coroutine's result as a CompletableFuture tied to it. await() Suspends until a CompletableFuture completes, without blocking a thread. mono { } Turns suspend code into a cold Reactor Mono that runs once per subscription. awaitSingle() Suspends until a Mono emits its one value; throws if it completes empty. asFlow / asFlux Convert a Reactive Streams publisher to a Flow, and a Flow to a Flux. Java door A thin wrapper that lets Java call a suspend function, as a future, a Mono or a blocking call. How do you wait for a CompletableFuture inside a coroutine without blocking? future.await() from kotlinx.coroutines.future. It suspends, unwraps the exception, and cancels the future if the coroutine is cancelled. How do you await a CompletableFuture without cancelling it when the coroutine is cancelled? future.asDeferred().await(). How do you hand suspend code to Java as a CompletableFuture? scope.future { suspendCall() }, with a scope the class owns. Cancelling or completing the future cancels the coroutine. When does the coroutine inside mono { } run? On each subscription. The Mono is cold, a null result completes it empty, and disposing the subscription cancels the coroutine. What does awaitSingle() do on an empty Mono? It throws NoSuchElementException. awaitSingleOrNull() returns null instead. What does Java see for suspend fun cook(order: Order): Outcome? Object cook(Order order, Continuation<? super Outcome> completion): give Java a future, Mono or blocking door instead. Virtual threads or coroutines for a Java program full of blocking database calls? Virtual threads: they make the existing blocking code cheap without a rewrite. Coroutines pay off for structured fan-out, cancellation and Flow in Kotlin.

h: Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads · Go deeper
x: kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 has no built-in virtual-thread dispatcher. Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher() is the supported route, and it gives every dispatch a fresh virtual thread. That makes it a good home for blocking calls inside coroutines, with two cautions. A coroutine blocked inside it still ignores cancellation unless the call is wrapped in runInterruptible, which interrupts the virtual thread. And the coroutine scheduler's habit of keeping a coroutine on one worker is lost, so code that relies on per-thread caches gets a new thread every time it resumes. CompletionStage.await() works for any CompletionStage, not just CompletableFuture, and Deferred.asCompletableFuture() goes the other way for a coroutine you already started with async. On the Reactor side, Deferred.asMono() and Job.asMono() give hot Monos for work that is already running, and Scheduler.asCoroutineDispatcher() lets coroutines run on a Reactor scheduler, which keeps all the threads of a Reactor-based program in one place. The structured-concurrency story differs most across the three. Coroutines enforce it by default. Virtual threads get it through StructuredTaskScope, a preview API in JDK 25 (JEP 505) whose shape changed between previews. Reactor has no tree of tasks at all, only operator chains that cancel upstream. When you bridge, the tree ends at the bridge: a future { } coroutine belongs to the door's scope, not to the Java caller, which is exactly why the door must own and close that scope. Bridges and tests, the last lesson of the Kotlin Flow in depth track, comes back to callbackFlow and the Reactor bridges for whole streams.

h: Kotlin Flow in depth
x: How Flow really works: two interfaces, what flow { } checks, flowOn and channels, buffering, flattening and combining, errors and retries, hot flows, bridges and tests. By the end of this track you can explain a Kotlin flow from the inside, and predict what a pipeline you have never seen will do. The whole track takes place in the house kitchen from the coroutines track, seen from inside. A flow is a recipe card, the cook who cooks it is the producer, and the diner at the table is the collector. You'll find that emit is the cook carrying one plate over and standing there while the diner eats, and that this one fact makes a flow cold, one value at a time, and slowed by its collector. From there, each lesson adds one piece of the kitchen. You meet the inspector that flow { } posts at the kitchen door and the three questions it asks, the wall with a hatch and a shelf that flowOn and buffer build, and the overflow policies that decide which plate is lost when the shelf is full. You run sub-recipes on several burners with flatMapMerge and join two flows with zip and combine. You string a net under the cook with catch, cook again with retry, and set an egg timer with timeout. Then you share values with many diners through the house bell and the menu board, SharedFlow and StateFlow, and finish with bridges to an old probe that calls you, to Reactor, and to a rehearsal on a fake clock. This track assumes the Kotlin coroutines track, especially its Flow lessons: lesson 7 (cold flows and operators), lesson 8 (StateFlow, SharedFlow and stateIn), lesson 9 (channels and callbackFlow), lesson 10 (runTest and test dispatchers) and lesson 11 (Reactor bridges). It doesn't repeat them; it goes one level down. Each lesson opens with a small kitchen program whose output surprises, asks you to predict it, and builds the mechanism, often by hand, before it names the API. The numbers come from runs on Kotlin 2.4.21 and kotlinx.coroutines 1.11.0, almost all on virtual time, so they repeat exactly. Install JDK 25; the labs compile with release 21. The labs live in labs/flows, one package per lesson (workbench.flows.l01 to l08), all in Kotlin, with a Java test in lesson 8 that sees only Reactor types. The module has kotlinx-coroutines-core, -reactive and -reactor and Reactor 3.8.8, and for tests kotlinx-coroutines-test, reactor-test and Turbine 1.2.1. Timing tests run on virtual time with injected dispatchers, so they are exact and fast. From labs/, run a lesson's tests with ./gradlew :flows:test --tests 'workbench.flows.l03.*', and the reference answers with ./gradlew :flows:solutionTest. A flow is two interfaces with one suspend function each. The collector runs inside emit, like a cook who stands at the table while the diner eats, and that makes a flow cold, sequential and slowed by its collector. flow { } checks every emit: cancellation, the same context ("Flow invariant is violated") and exception transparency. The library's own operators skip the checks, so flowOf and asFlow need cancellable(), and take stops a producer by throwing through emit. flowOn, buffer, channelFlow and callbackFlow put a second coroutine and a channel into the chain: 64 slots by default, n + 1 emits ahead, fused when adjacent. flowOn moves only what is above it. Choose buffering by what one lost value costs: SUSPEND for plates for the table, conflate() or collectLatest for the newest oven reading. flatMapMerge runs its lambda one value at a time and the returned flows side by side, 16 by default. flatMapLatest cancels the old inner. zip pairs by number; combine keeps the latest of each. catch handles only upstream errors, retry replays the upstream from the top, onCompletion says how the flow ended, and timeout throws a cancellation whose position sets what it limits. A SharedFlow has one buffer for every subscriber, so the slowest sets the pace or the losses; a StateFlow is one slot compared with equals. stateIn and shareIn launch one coroutine in your scope, started and stopped by SharingStarted, and .value is not a subscription. callbackFlow bridges listener APIs: it registers when its producer runs, needs awaitClose, and holds 64 plus one. asFlow and asFlux turn request(n) into suspension and back, and Java gets a Flux. Test on virtual time with injected dispatchers. Know where runCurrent, advanceTimeBy and advanceUntilIdle stop, collect hot flows in backgroundScope, and remember that Turbine shows every value.
