h: Context and threads: flowOn, the invariant, and channelFlow · Key terms
x: flowOn An operator that runs the part of the flow above it in another context, through a channel when the dispatcher changes. Channel A queue between coroutines: send suspends when it is full, receive suspends when it is empty. In the kitchen, the hatch with its shelf. ChannelFlow The internal base class behind flowOn, buffer, channelFlow and produceIn: a flow that can run its upstream in a second coroutine and empty a channel. Operator fusion Adjacent channel-based operators merging into one channel with one combined configuration. channelFlow A builder whose block can launch coroutines that all send into one channel. It completes after all of them. produceIn Launches a coroutine in your scope that collects a flow, and returns its channel: a hot stream you must consume or cancel. ProducerScope The receiver of channelFlow's block: a CoroutineScope and a SendChannel in one. Why does flow { } refuse withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit(x) }? The collector runs inside emit, so it would run on an IO thread it never asked for. Use flowOn on the upstream instead. What does flowOn(io) build when io differs from the collector's dispatcher? A second coroutine that runs the upstream on io and sends into a channel (64 slots by default), plus a loop that emits each value in the collector's coroutine. Which part of a chain does flowOn move? Only the operators above it, up to the previous flowOn. The collector never moves. .flowOn(CoroutineName("x")): is there a channel? No. The dispatcher is unchanged, so the upstream runs inline with the new name. .flowOn(A).flowOn(B) with nothing between them: which dispatcher runs the upstream? A. Adjacent flowOn calls fuse into one, and the first one (nearest the source) wins for each context key. When does a channelFlow complete? When its block and every coroutine launched inside it have finished. The block itself may return much earlier. Why inject the dispatcher you pass to flowOn? flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) inside runTest runs on the real clock: three 1 s delays took about 3.5 s of wall time and 0 ms of virtual time.

h: Context and threads: flowOn, the invariant, and channelFlow · Go deeper
x: Some details of flowOn only show up in real programs. It can lose values in flight on cancellation. Its KDoc says that "flows operating across different dispatchers might lose some in-flight elements when cancelled", and that the operator "ensures that downstream flow does not resume on cancellation even if the element was already emitted by the upstream flow". For the delivery import that means the reader may have read lines that never reached the pantry book. If that matters, track what was stored, not what was read. Whether a channel appears depends on dispatcher objects, not threads. With a collector already on Dispatchers.IO, flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) stays sequential, with no channel. With a collector on Dispatchers.Default, flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) creates one, even though the two dispatchers share threads, because they are different objects. Stability in 1.11.0: flowOn, channelFlow, callbackFlow and produceIn compile with no opt-in. CoroutineScope.produce, which the hand-built myFlowOn uses, is @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi. Use the library's operators in real code and keep myFlowOn as the model in your head. callbackFlow, from lesson 9 of the coroutines track, is a subclass of the same channelFlow builder. The difference is one check: if its block returns while the channel is still open, it throws an IllegalStateException telling you to call awaitClose { ... } at the end. Lesson 8 of this track wraps a listener API with it. buffer() is the same machine as flowOn without the context change, and neighbouring channel operators fuse into one channel. Lesson 4 of this track takes that apart, using toString() as a peek under the hood.

h: Buffering: buffer, conflate, collectLatest and fusion · buffer(n): a second coroutine and a shelf with n spots
x: A shelf in the hatch: buffer(n) lets the cook get n + 1 dumplings ahead, conflate keeps only the newest reading, side-by-side buffers fuse into one shelf, and collectLatest waits for the cancelled drawing's cleanup Here is that lunch as code. The cook is a plain flow { } that counts how many of its emit calls have returned. The diner holds dumpling 1 until the call ends. Put a buffer between them and look at the counter while the diner is on the phone: Java // Closest Java equivalent: a bounded queue between a cook thread and a diner thread BlockingQueue<Integer> shelf = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10); Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { for (int d = 1; d <= 200; d++) { putQuietly(shelf, d); returned.set(d); } }); Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { while (true) diner.eat(takeQuietly(shelf)); }); // stuck on dumpling 1 Kotlin var returned = 0 val cook = flow { for (dumpling in 1..200) { emit(dumpling); returned = dumpling } } launch { cook.buffer(10).collect { d -> diner.eat(d) } } // the phone rings at dumpling 1 delay(100) println(returned) // and with no buffer? buffer(0)? buffer()? Write your four guesses down. The answers are 0 with no buffer, 1 for buffer(0), 11 for buffer(10) and 65 for buffer(). They come out the same on every run. The 0 is lesson 1 of this track: without a buffer, emit calls the diner's code, so it can't return while the diner is stuck. The other three numbers need a mechanism. The buffer KDoc, its documentation in the library's source, sketches it in a few lines, and it is worth writing out once: Java // Closest Java equivalent: a second thread runs the upstream and puts into a queue with n slots static <T> void handMadeBuffer(List<T> upstream, int n, Consumer<T> downstream) throws InterruptedException { BlockingQueue<T> shelf = n == 0 ? new SynchronousQueue<>() : new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(n); Thread producer = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> upstream.forEach(v -> putQuietly(shelf, v))); for (int i = 0; i < upstream.size(); i++) downstream.accept(shelf.take()); producer.join(); } Kotlin fun <T> Flow<T>.handMadeBuffer(n: Int): Flow<T> = flow { coroutineScope { val channel = produce(capacity = n) { collect { send(it) } } // coroutine 2 runs the upstream channel.consumeEach { emit(it) } // our coroutine hands each value on } } Read it as two rooms with a hatch between them and a shelf with n spots in the hatch. buffer(n) moves everything above it into a second coroutine. In there, the cook's emit has become a send into a channel, a queue between coroutines, and send returns as soon as a spot is free. Our own coroutine takes values off the shelf and calls the real emit, which runs the diner. So while the diner holds dumpling 1, dumplings 2 to 11 sit on the shelf. Eleven emits have returned: ten for the dumplings on the shelf, and one for dumpling 1, which left the shelf when the diner picked it up. If this looks like the wall with a hatch from lesson 3 of this track, it is the same machine. flowOn builds it to change the thread, and buffer builds it to change the size of the shelf. buffer(0) has no spots. It's a hand-over where both hands must meet, which channels call a rendezvous. There is still a second coroutine, so exactly one emit returns. That one value of slack is why buffer(0) turns the 1,200 ms of lesson 1's dinner (a 100 ms cook, a 300 ms diner, three dishes) into 1,000 ms, the same as buffer(). buffer() with no argument means Channel.BUFFERED, which is -2 in the code and 64 spots on the JVM. Hence 65. The system property kotlinx.coroutines.channels.defaultBuffer changes that default for every channel in the program. It is @DelicateCoroutinesApi, and its KDoc calls it a "last-ditch effort" for urgent fixes. Write the size at the call site instead. Behind buffer(n) the producer gets n + 1 ahead: n on the shelf, one in the collector's hands. Check yourself before the Try it: what does the probe print for buffer(1)? So far a full shelf made the cook wait. That is only one of the three things it can do. Count the emits that return Open AheadProbe.kt. Before you run it, write down a number for each of the seven lines, including handMadeBuffer(10), the KDoc's sketch. Run it with the command below and compare. Run it again with -Pargs=8 added. That sets kotlinx.coroutines.channels.defaultBuffer to 8 before any channel exists. Which line changes? Run the Java twin, AheadProbeJava. It puts a SynchronousQueue or an ArrayBlockingQueue between two threads. Predict its four numbers first. import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.Supplier; // Closest Java equivalent of Flow's buffer(n): a BlockingQueue between two threads. // Java blocks a thread where Kotlin suspends a coroutine; the counting is the same. public class AheadProbeJava { static void probe(String label, Supplier<BlockingQueue<Integer>> shelf) throws InterruptedException { BlockingQueue<Integer> queue = shelf.get(); AtomicInteger returned = new AtomicInteger(); // put() calls that have returned CountDownLatch callEnds = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread cook = Thread.ofPlatform().daemon().start(() -> { try { for (int dumpling = 1; dumpling <= 200; dumpling++) { queue.put(dumpling); returned.set(dumpling); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); Thread diner = Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { try { queue.take(); h: Buffering: buffer, conflate, collectLatest and fusion · When the shelf is full, the overflow policy decides which value is lost
x: Everything so far used the default overflow policy, which is what a full buffer does with a new value. The default, BufferOverflow.SUSPEND, makes send wait, so the cook waits. Nothing is lost, and the cook is never more than n + 1 ahead. The other two policies never wait. When the shelf is full they throw a value away. Dumplings are the wrong food to throw away, so take something where only the newest value matters. The oven from StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams has a thermometer, and a little screen on the oven door shows its readings. Say the screen is stuck drawing reading 1 while 200 readings arrive. Which ones does it show once it's free? Operator The screen shows What the full shelf did buffer(10) all 200 made the thermometer wait buffer(10, DROP_OLDEST) 1, then 191 to 200 threw the oldest waiting reading in the bin buffer(10, DROP_LATEST) 1 to 11 threw each new reading in the bin conflate() 1 and 200 one spot: each new reading replaces the one on it Reading 1 is in every row because the screen had it in hand before the flood started. conflate() is buffer(CONFLATED), and conflation means keeping only the newest waiting value. The library turns CONFLATED into capacity 0 with DROP_OLDEST. A drop policy can't work with zero spots, so the channel gets exactly one. It's the ruthless shelf: each new value pushes the waiting one into the bin, and it never makes anybody wait. That rule sets a trap. A helper wants "the newest 64 if the table falls behind" and writes buffer(onBufferOverflow = DROP_OLDEST). The capacity defaults to BUFFERED, and the Channel KDoc says what that means with a drop policy: "If a different BufferOverflow is specified, Channel(BUFFERED) creates a channel with a buffer of size 1". So the line is conflate() under another name, and the probe receives [1, 200]. If you mean 64, write buffer(64, DROP_OLDEST). Conflation only loses values that arrive while the collector is busy. A screen that draws in 50 ms, behind a thermometer that reads every 100 ms, shows every reading. So pick the policy by what a lost value costs. A stale temperature is worth nothing once a newer one exists, so the screen may conflate. A dropped plate of dumplings is a guest with no lunch, so plates for the table get SUSPEND, always. Before you pick a drop policy, ask what one lost value costs. If the answer is too much, keep SUSPEND. Reactor makes the same trades under other names, and you used them in Backpressure in practice, in the reactive track: Java // Closest Java equivalent: Reactor's onBackpressure operators readings.onBackpressureLatest(); readings.onBackpressureBuffer(10, r -> {}, BufferOverflowStrategy.DROP_OLDEST); plates.onBackpressureBuffer(10); // full: the stream fails Kotlin readings.conflate() readings.buffer(10, BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST) plates.buffer(10) // full: the cook suspends In the probe the first two match their Flow twins exactly: [1, 200] and [1, 191..200]. The third doesn't. Reactor's bounded buffer with no strategy cancels the source and fails with OverflowException: The receiver is overrun by more signals than expected (bounded queue...). Flow's bounded buffer has no failure mode. It makes the producer wait. Check yourself: what does buffer(0, DROP_LATEST) deliver in the same probe? So far each chain had one buffer. Put two side by side, and they don't stay two. Flood a stuck oven screen Open DropPolicies.kt. For each of the six lines, predict which readings the screen shows after it gets unstuck. Run it. Look hardest at buffer(onBufferOverflow = DROP_OLDEST). Run the Reactor twin, DropPoliciesJava. Find the one line where Reactor and Flow disagree, and the line Flow has no exact twin for. h: Buffering: buffer, conflate, collectLatest and fusion · Buffers side by side fuse into one channel
x: buffer(10).buffer(20) doesn't build two shelves. It builds one shelf with 30 spots, and the probe counts 31 emits. Every operator that is built on a channel (buffer, conflate, flowOn, channelFlow, produceIn) first looks at the flow it was called on. If that is also a channel flow, it adds no coroutine. It merges its settings into the one that is already there. The library calls this fusion. Picture short shelves snapped together into one long shelf with a single label on it. The merge rules are short: Two explicit sizes add up: 10 + 20 is 30. buffer() without a size gives way to an explicit one, so buffer(10).buffer() has 10 spots and buffer().buffer() still has 64. A policy other than SUSPEND replaces everything before it. buffer(10).conflate() is plain conflate(), and the 10 is thrown away. conflate().buffer(10) is a 10-spot shelf that drops the oldest. flowOn shares the channel too. buffer(5).flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) and flowOn(Dispatchers.IO).buffer(5) are both one channel, filled on IO, with 5 spots. You can watch it happen, because these channel flows print their settings in toString(): buffer(10).buffer(20) ChannelFlowOperatorImpl[capacity=30] buffer(10).conflate() ChannelFlowOperatorImpl[capacity=0, onBufferOverflow=DROP_OLDEST] conflate().buffer(10) ChannelFlowOperatorImpl[capacity=10, onBufferOverflow=DROP_OLDEST] buffer(5).flowOn(IO) ChannelFlowOperatorImpl[context=Dispatchers.IO, capacity=5] Treat that string as a peek under the hood. It is a debug aid, not an API, and any release may change it. When it matters, test the behaviour instead: count the emits that return while the collector is stuck, as the lab does. Here the shelf picture breaks. Two real shelves in a row hold the plates of both, and nothing on the second shelf can empty the first. Fused buffers are one shelf with one label, and a drop policy written at the end rewrites the label for everything before it. One line in the docs reads the other way. The conflate KDoc says that if a buffer size was given before it, "the buffer size is unchanged". In 1.11.0, buffer(10).conflate() delivers [1, 200] in the probe, exactly like conflate(), and its toString() shows capacity 0. The buffer KDoc matches the code: a buffer call with a non-SUSPEND policy "overrides all immediately preceding buffering operators". I read the conflate sentence as ambiguous rather than wrong, and I don't rely on it. When I want ten spots that drop the oldest, I write it in one call: buffer(10, DROP_OLDEST). Check yourself: what single channel does buffer(10).buffer(5, DROP_LATEST) become? Every buffer so far threw away values that were still waiting. The Latest operators go one step further: they stop work that has already started. Read the label on the shelf Open Fusion.kt. For each chain, predict the capacity and policy the single channel ends up with, and the emits that return while the collector is stuck. Run it. The middle column is toString(), the right column is the behaviour. Add a line for buffer(10).buffer(5, BufferOverflow.DROP_LATEST) and check your answer to the section's question. h: Buffering: buffer, conflate, collectLatest and fusion · collectLatest: a new value cancels the old block, then waits for its cleanup
x: Back to the screen on the oven door. It moves to collectLatest, so a new reading cancels the drawing in progress. A cancelled drawing must wipe its half-drawn number first, which takes 50 ms that can't be cancelled. (NonCancellable, from Cancellation and timeouts, is the context that lets such cleanup run after a cancel.) Readings arrive every 100 ms and a drawing takes 300 ms. When does the thermometer emit reading 3? Java // Closest Java equivalent: switchMap cancels the inner; a cancel is a signal, so the wipe can only be fired off readings.switchMap(reading -> draw(reading) .doOnCancel(() -> wipeHalfDrawnAsync(reading).subscribe())); Kotlin readings.collectLatest { reading -> try { draw(reading) // 300 ms } catch (e: CancellationException) { withContext(NonCancellable) { wipeHalfDrawn(reading) } // 50 ms throw e } } Most people say 300. The virtual clock says 350, and the run ends at 700 instead of 600 (lines merged for space): t=100 emit 1, start 1 t=200 emit 2, cancelled 1 (ChildCancelledException) t=250 cleanup of 1 finished, start 2 t=350 emit 3, cancelled 2 t=400 cleanup of 2 finished, start 3 t=700 done 3 collectLatest is mapLatest(action).buffer(0).collect(), and mapLatest is a thin wrapper over transformLatest. Its core is a short loop. A producer coroutine collects the upstream, and for each new value it cancels the previous block, joins it (waits for it to finish), and only then launches the new one: flow.collect { value -> previous?.apply { cancel(ChildCancelledException()); join() } // wait until the old block has finished previous = launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) { collector.transform(value) } } The join() is the surprise. Reading 1's wipe must finish before reading 2's drawing starts. And this loop body runs inside the upstream's collect, so the join() also sits inside the thermometer's emit. The thermometer can't start its next delay(100) until the old block has cleaned up. Picture the screen wiping its half-drawn number before it starts the new one, while the thermometer waits at the hatch with the next reading. Reactor's switchMap gives emits at 100, 200 and 300 and ends at 600, because a Reactor cancel is a method call that returns at once, with no suspending cleanup to wait for. Two rules follow. Keep the cancelled path short. And use the Latest family only for work you can throw away. Drawing a number on a screen changes nothing else, so a cancelled drawing costs nothing. Writing each reading into the cooking log is a side effect, a change that stays after the block ends: a cancelled block may have written half a line, and a skipped reading is never written. That pipeline gets buffer(). Use the Latest operators only for work you can throw away, and keep their cleanup short. Cancelling yourself behind a shelf has its own surprise. A collector that never suspends calls cancel() on its own job at value 3. Behind buffer() it still receives 66 values in all, and behind buffer(10) it receives 12. The values already on the shelf keep coming, because receiving from a channel that has elements doesn't suspend, and emitAll checks for cancellation once, before its loop. A collector that waits on a file or calls delay sees the cancel at its next suspension, so this bites only collectors that do nothing but compute. Add .cancellable() after the buffer. It checks before every emit, and the count drops to 3. Every flow in this lesson made one value at a time and handed it on. A value can also start a whole flow of its own, and that is where flows begin to branch. Time the wipe Open LatestJoin.kt. It runs on virtual time. Predict the time of emit 3 and of done 3 before you run it. Run it. Then change the cleanup's delay(50) to delay(150) and predict again. Read the second half of the output: a collector that never suspends cancels itself at 3. Predict each count first. Run LatestJoinJava, the switchMap twin, in real time. A new reading cancels the // drawing in progress. Real time, so expect a few ms of drift. public class LatestJoinJava { static long t0; static boolean quiet; static void log(String msg) { long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; String line = String.format("t=%3d (about %3d) %s", ms, Math.round(ms / 50.0) * 50, msg); if (!quiet) System.out.println(line); } static void run() { t0 = System.nanoTime(); Flux.range(1, 3) .delayElements(Duration.ofMillis(100)) .doOnNext(tick -> log("emit " + tick)) .switchMap(tick -> Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(300)) .doOnSubscribe(s -> log("start " + tick)) .doOnCancel(() -> log("cancelled " + tick)) // a signal: nothing waits for cleanup .thenReturn(tick)) .doOnNext(tick -> log("done " + tick)) .blockLast(); } public static void main(String[] args) { quiet = true; run(); // a silent first run loads the classes, so the timings below are clean quiet = false; run(); } } ./gradlew :flows:demo -Pmain=workbench.flows.l04.LatestJoinJava labs/flows/src/demo/java/workbench/flows/l04/LatestJoinJava.java emit 3 at 350 and done 3 at 700. With a 150 ms cleanup, reading 2 starts at 350, the thermometer emits reading 3 at 450, and reading 3 is done at 900 ms. The collector that only computes gets 0 extra values from flow { }, 9 behind buffer(10), 63 behind buffer(), and 0 once .cancellable() follows the buffer. The Reactor twin emits at about 100, 200 and 300 ms and finishes at about 600 ms: its cancel doesn't wait for anything.

h: Buffering: buffer, conflate, collectLatest and fusion · Java and Kotlin
x: The same loss policies in Kotlin Flow and in Reactor Reactor Flux<Plate> everyPlate = plates.limitRate(64); // demand in batches of 64; nothing is dropped Flux<Reading> newestOnly = readings.onBackpressureLatest(); // one slot, the newest replaces it Flux<Reading> lastTen = readings.onBackpressureBuffer(10, r -> {}, BufferOverflowStrategy.DROP_OLDEST); Flux<Reading> firstTen = readings.onBackpressureBuffer(10, r -> {}, BufferOverflowStrategy.DROP_LATEST); Flux<Reading> failFast = readings.onBackpressureBuffer(10); // full: OverflowException Flux<Shown> shown = readings.switchMap(screen::draw); // a new reading cancels the old drawing Kotlin Flow val everyPlate = plates.buffer(64) // full: the cook suspends val newestOnly = readings.conflate() // one slot, the newest replaces it val lastTen = readings.buffer(10, BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST) val firstTen = readings.buffer(10, BufferOverflow.DROP_LATEST) // no failFast: a bounded Flow buffer never errors, it makes the producer wait @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) val shown = readings.mapLatest { screen.draw(it) } // cancels, joins, then starts the next Both libraries offer the same drop policies, and the probe gives the same lists in both. The machinery underneath differs. Reactor's backpressure is a number sent upstream with request(n), so limitRate reshapes demand and onBackpressureBuffer(n) has to decide what to do when a source ignores it: by default it fails. A cold Kotlin flow can't overflow, because emit doesn't return until the collector is ready. Loss is possible only where something puts a channel between two coroutines, and that is exactly what buffer, conflate and flowOn do. Two more differences show up in this lesson. Adjacent Flow buffers fuse into one channel with combined settings. And mapLatest joins the cancelled block before it starts the next one, while switchMap just sends the cancel.

h: Buffering: buffer, conflate, collectLatest and fusion · Worked example
x: Pick the buffering for three kitchen pipelines The oven-door screen shows the temperature. Readings come every 100 ms, a drawing takes 300 ms, and only the newest reading matters. A drawing that has started may finish. That is conflation. val shown: Flow<Shown> = readings .conflate() // 1. one spot: a busy screen skips to the newest reading .map { screen.draw(it) } // 2. runs below the spot, in the collector's coroutine // Closest Java equivalent: keep the newest reading, draw one at a time Flux<Shown> shown = readings .onBackpressureLatest() // 1. one spot: a busy screen skips to the newest reading .concatMap(screen::draw, 1); // 2. one drawing at a time, asking for one reading at a time The kitchen scale has a display too, and someone is pouring flour. A stale drawing should stop at once, and drawing has no side effects. Cancel it. In virtual time this finishes only the newest of three weights, at 600 ms. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) // mapLatest is experimental in 1.11.0 val display: Flow<Shown> = weights .mapLatest { grams -> scaleScreen.draw(grams) } // a new weight cancels, joins, then starts again // Closest Java equivalent: switchMap cancels the inner drawing when a new weight arrives Flux<Shown> display = weights .switchMap(scaleScreen::draw); The plates for the table: nothing may be lost, and memory must stay bounded when the diner is on the phone. The default policy does both. The cook can get 65 plates ahead, then she waits. cook.plates() .buffer(64) // SUSPEND: a full shelf makes the cook wait .collect { diner.eat(it) } // nothing dropped, at most 64 waiting // Closest Java equivalent: a bounded queue between the cook thread and the diner BlockingQueue<Plate> shelf = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(64); Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> cook.plates().forEach(p -> putQuietly(shelf, p))); // blocks when full while (true) diner.eat(shelf.take()); Review the helper's version of the plates pipeline, which was meant to "keep the newest 64". It keeps one. During a long phone call it serves plate 1 and the last one cooked, and quietly bins the rest. Replace it with step 3. cook.plates() .buffer(onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST) // BUFFERED + a drop policy = ONE spot .collect { diner.eat(it) } // Closest Java equivalent of the bug: Reactor's latest-only buffer cook.platesFlux() .onBackpressureLatest() // one spot, the newest replaces it .concatMap(diner::eat, 1) .blockLast();

Close the channel when the upstream's collect returns, in a finally. mapLatest needs @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) in 1.11.0. Without it the compiler warns but still builds. For towardsTable, the default policy is the right one. You only need the right number of spots. All 11 tests in BufferingTest pass, twice in a row. By the end you can predict how far a producer runs ahead behind any buffer or conflate chain, which values it loses and why, what collectLatest waits for, and pick the right one for values where only the newest matters and for values that must never be lost.

h: Buffering: buffer, conflate, collectLatest and fusion · Quiz
x: Behind buffer(10).buffer(20) with the default policy, the collector is stuck on its first value. How many of the producer's emits have returned? 21: the second buffer wins 32: two coroutines, each holding one 31 11: the first buffer is the one the producer sees Adjacent buffers fuse into one channel, and two explicit sizes add up to 30. One channel means one extra coroutine, so it is 30 on the shelf plus 1 in hand. 32 would be right for two separate shelves, which is what a hand-written buffer without fusion gives you. A helper puts buffer(onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST) between the cook and the table, "to keep the newest 64". The diner is on the phone while 200 plates are cooked. How many reach the table? All 200 Plate 1 and the newest 64 64 2: plate 1 and plate 200 The capacity defaults to BUFFERED, and a BUFFERED channel with a drop policy has one slot, so this is conflate(). The diner eats the plate in hand and the one standing on the shelf at the end. For plates, no drop policy is acceptable: use buffer(64) with the default SUSPEND. Readings every 100 ms go into collectLatest. A drawing takes 300 ms, and a cancelled one runs a 50 ms withContext(NonCancellable) cleanup. When does the thermometer emit reading 3? 300 ms 350 ms 400 ms It never does: collectLatest stops the thermometer transformLatest cancels the old block and then joins it, inside the thermometer's emit. Reading 2 at 200 waits 50 ms for reading 1's cleanup, so the next delay(100) starts at 250 and reading 3 comes at 350. 300 is what you'd get with no cleanup, or with Reactor's switchMap, which doesn't wait. A collector that only computes (no I/O, no delay) reads from flow { for (i in 1..100) emit(i) }.buffer() and calls cancel() on its own job when it sees 3. It receives 66 values. What is the smallest fix? Add .cancellable() after buffer() Add .cancellable() before buffer() Replace flow { } with (1..100).asFlow() Replace cancel() with return@collect The values already on the shelf keep coming because receiving from a channel that has elements doesn't suspend, and nothing checks cancellation per value on the collector's side. .cancellable() after the buffer checks before each emit, and the count drops to 3. Before the buffer it guards the producer, which flow { } already does. asFlow() checks less, not more. And return@collect only ends this one call of the lambda, so all 100 values arrive. From the reactive track: Reactor's onBackpressureBuffer(10) with no strategy and Flow's buffer(10) both sit in front of a stuck subscriber while 200 items arrive. What happens in each? Both drop the newest items once 10 are waiting Both make the source wait Reactor delivers 11 and then fails with an OverflowException; Flow makes the producer suspend and later delivers all 200 Reactor makes the source wait; Flow fails with an exception Reactor's bounded buffer with no strategy cancels the source and signals OverflowException ("The receiver is overrun by more signals than expected") when it overflows. A Flow buffer has no failure mode: with SUSPEND, a full channel makes send wait, so nothing is lost and nothing fails.

h: Buffering: buffer, conflate, collectLatest and fusion · Key terms
x: buffer (Flow operator) Runs everything above it in a second coroutine and puts a channel between that coroutine and the collector. In the kitchen, a shelf in the hatch. Capacity How many values can wait in the channel. With SUSPEND, the producer can get capacity + 1 emits ahead. Overflow policy What a full buffer does with a new value: SUSPEND makes the sender wait, DROP_OLDEST discards the oldest waiting value, DROP_LATEST discards the new one. Conflation Keeping only the newest waiting value. conflate() is a one-slot buffer that drops the oldest. Rendezvous A channel with no slots. A send waits until a receiver takes the value. Fusion Adjacent channel-based operators merging into one channel with combined settings, instead of one coroutine each. ChildCancelledException The cancellation the Latest operators use to stop the previous block. Its message is "Child of the scoped flow was cancelled". With the default policy, how many emits return behind buffer(n) while the collector is stuck on its first value? n + 1: n wait on the shelf (the channel), one is in the collector's hands. What does buffer(0) still create, and how far ahead is the producer? A second coroutine and a rendezvous hand-over. One emit returns: the value that was handed over. How many slots does buffer(onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST) have? One. A BUFFERED channel with a drop policy is a one-slot channel, so it acts like conflate(). Write buffer(64, DROP_OLDEST) if you mean 64. What is buffer(10).conflate()? And conflate().buffer(10)? Plain conflate(): a drop policy overrides the buffers before it. conflate().buffer(10) is one 10-slot channel that drops the oldest. What does buffer(10).buffer(20) build? One fused channel with 30 slots, so the producer gets 31 ahead. In collectLatest, what happens to the old block when a new value arrives? It is cancelled (ChildCancelledException) and joined. Its cleanup finishes before the new block starts, and the producer's emit waits for it too. Flow buffer(10) is full. Reactor onBackpressureBuffer(10) is full. What does each do? Flow suspends the producer. Reactor cancels the source and fails with OverflowException.

h: Buffering: buffer, conflate, collectLatest and fusion · Go deeper
x: The class behind buffer, conflate and flowOn is ChannelFlowOperatorImpl, an internal subclass of ChannelFlow. Its fuse method does the merging. The new context is context + this.context, so for each context key the setting nearest the source wins, which is why two adjacent flowOn calls keep the first one. If the new policy is not SUSPEND, it overwrites the capacity and policy (the source comment says "this additional buffer never suspends => overwrite preceding buffering configuration"). Otherwise the capacities combine: BUFFERED gives way to an explicit size, two explicit sizes add up, and a sum that overflows Int becomes UNLIMITED. buffer checks its arguments with require. buffer(-5) fails with "Buffer size should be non-negative, BUFFERED, or CONFLATED, but was -5", and buffer(Channel.CONFLATED, BufferOverflow.DROP_LATEST) fails with "CONFLATED capacity cannot be used with non-default onBufferOverflow". Other operators are channel flows too, and they fuse with a buffer placed right after them. channelFlow { } prints as ChannelFlowBuilder[capacity=-2], and channelFlow { }.buffer(3) resizes the builder's own channel. mapLatest { } prints as ChannelFlowTransformLatest[capacity=-2], which is why its KDoc says it is "buffered by default". flatMapMerge { } prints as ChannelFlowMerge[concurrency=16, capacity=-2]; the next lesson takes it apart. StateFlow already behaves as if conflate() were applied, and the KDoc says applying conflate to it has no effect. Lesson 7 of this track looks at why. Reactor's limitRate(10) looks like buffer(10) in the probe: the source got 10 ahead, where Flow's count is 11 because the Flow probe counts emits that returned. The mechanism is different: limitRate batches the demand it sends upstream. It asks for 10, then for 8 more each time 75 % of a batch has been used.

h: Flattening and combining: flatMap, zip and combine · The flatMapMerge lambda runs one dish at a time, before a burner is free
x: Start with the ticket in code. A flow is a recipe card for values: it does nothing until a collector, the code that calls collect, asks for them. Each dish name on the ticket is one value of a flow, and stove.cook(dish) is a suspend call that takes 100 ms, a call that pauses its coroutine (a light piece of work that can wait without holding a thread, the worker that runs the code) and lets others run. A helper wrote this to cook the order four dishes at a time: Java // Closest Java equivalent: Reactor's flatMap with a blocking call in the mapper dishes.flatMap(dish -> { Plate plate = stove.cookBlocking(dish); // 100 ms on the calling thread return Mono.just(plate); }, 4); Kotlin dishes.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) { dish -> val plate = stove.cook(dish) // a suspend call, 100 ms flowOf(plate) } flatMapMerge is an operator, a helper on the way from the cook to the diner: a function that takes a flow and returns a new one. It is a flattening operator. For each value of the outer flow (the ticket), your lambda returns an inner flow, a flow of its own, and the operator collects all those inner flows into one stream of plates. concurrency is how many inner flows it collects at the same time: the number of burners. So ten dishes of 100 ms should take 300 ms. The kitchen log says 1,000 ms, with one dish on the stove at a time. To see why, build the operator yourself. It needs three parts: one coroutine that reads the outer flow, a semaphore with one permit per burner (a counter of permits: acquire takes one and waits while none is left, release gives it back), and one coroutine per inner flow. All of them send into one hatch, the small window with a shelf between the kitchen and the dining room. That is channelFlow from lesson 3 of this track, several cooks sharing one hatch: Java // Closest Java equivalent: one loop builds each task, a semaphore caps the lanes, one virtual thread per lane static void mergeLanes(List<String> dishes, int lanes, BlockingQueue<Plate> out) throws InterruptedException { Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(lanes); for (String dish : dishes) { Callable<Plate> inner = () -> stove.cookBlocking(dish); // built here, one dish at a time permits.acquire(); // wait for a free burner Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { try { out.put(inner.call()); } catch (Exception e) { /* omitted */ } finally { permits.release(); } }); } } Kotlin fun <T, R> Flow<T>.mergeLanes(lanes: Int, transform: suspend (T) -> Flow<R>): Flow<R> = channelFlow { val permits = Semaphore(lanes) collect { value -> val inner = transform(value) // runs here, one value at a time permits.acquire() // wait for a free burner launch { try { inner.collect { send(it) } } finally { permits.release() } } } } Read it in order. The collect loop takes one dish, calls transform, waits for a permit, and launches a coroutine, a lane, that collects the inner flow onto the hatch. Then it takes the next dish. The tricky line is the first one in the loop. transform runs inside the one coroutine that reads the outer flow, before it even asks for a permit. That one coroutine is our head cook at the pass. She reads a line, does whatever the lambda says, and only then hands the result to a burner. If the lambda cooks the dish, she cooks it, alone, while the helpers wait. Only the flow the lambda returns gets a burner of its own. So the slow call has to live inside that flow: Java // Closest Java equivalent: the wait lives inside the returned Mono dishes.flatMap(dish -> stove.cook(dish), 4); // cook returns a lazy Mono Kotlin dishes.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) { dish -> flow { emit(stove.cook(dish)) } } The Try it runs a smaller order on two burners: soup 300 ms, salad 100, roast 200, bread 50 and pie 150. The fixed version ends at 450 ms with two dishes on the stove at the busiest moment. The lambda version ends at 800 ms with one, the sum of all five, exactly what a plain map { stove.cook(it) } would take. The library's flatMapMerge is map(transform).flattenMerge(concurrency), and flattenMerge has the same shape as mergeLanes: a producer coroutine, a Semaphore(concurrency), a launch per inner flow, and one output channel, a queue between coroutines, with 64 slots. Its KDoc, the documentation in the library's source, says it "calls transform sequentially". Plates leave in completion order, the order they are ready: salad, soup, roast, bread, pie. The lambda only builds the inner flow. Put the slow work inside it. Without a concurrency argument you get DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY, which is 16, read once from the system property kotlinx.coroutines.flow.defaultConcurrency. Reactor's flatMap defaults to 256. Set the number from what the stove can take, never from the default. In kotlinx.coroutines 1.11.0, flatMapMerge is @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi and DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY is @FlowPreview; without an opt-in you get a compiler warning, not an error. Check yourself: in the fixed version with two burners, when does the lambda run for roast, and when does roast start cooking? flatMapMerge runs inner flows side by side. It's one of three ways to run them, and the other two make different promises about time. Watch the burners fill Open Burners.kt. It runs on virtual time. For the first scenario, predict when lambda called for roast prints and when start cooking roast prints. Run it. Compare the second scenario's total and most on the burners with the first. The third scenario is mergeLanes, the hand-made version from this section. Check that its timeline is the same as the library's, line for line. Run the Reactor twin, BurnersJava, in real time. Find the same trap there. A table keeps changing its mind and sends three orders, 100 ms apart. Each order opens an inner flow in two parts: part a is ready after 50 ms and part b 150 ms later. The run uses virtual time, the fake clock of runTest that skips over waits, so the numbers come out the same on every run. With flatMapConcat, at what time does order 2 come in? Java // Closest Java equivalent: concatMap (and flatMap, switchMap) on the same Flux timeline orders().concatMap(n -> dish(n)); Kotlin orders().flatMapConcat { n -> dish(n) } // also try flatMapMerge and flatMapLatest Most people say 100. It is 300, and the whole run takes 800 ms. flatMapConcat is map(transform).flattenConcat(), and flattenConcat is one line: collect { value -> emitAll(value) }. There is no second coroutine and no channel. The inner flow runs inside the outer's emit, which lesson 1 of this track showed is the cook carrying a plate over and standing there while the diner eats. So the waiter who brings the orders stands at the pass until both parts of the dish are done, and his delay(100) before the next order starts only after that. h: Flattening and combining: flatMap, zip and combine · Pairs by number with zip, the latest of each with combine
x: The oven door has a small screen that shows how far the oven still has to climb. Two flows feed it. The thermometer sends a reading every 100 ms, starting at 100 ms: 150, 152, 154 and so on up to 160 °C. The dial sends a value only when someone turns it: 180 at 250 ms, and 200 at 550 ms. A helper joins them with zip: Java // Closest Java equivalent: the same three Reactor operators Flux.zip(readings, dial, (c, d) -> c + " of " + d); Flux.combineLatest(readings, dial, (c, d) -> c + " of " + d); Flux.merge(tableOrders, takeawayOrders); Kotlin readings.zip(dial) { c, d -> "$c of $d" } // a zipper combine(readings, dial) { c, d -> "$c of $d" } // a slate with the latest of each merge(tableOrders, takeawayOrders) // two queues into one door zip shows two lines: "150 of 180" at 250 ms and "152 of 200" at 550 ms. Then it ends. zip pairs the first value of one flow with the first of the other, the second with the second, and stops at the end of the shorter flow, like the teeth of a zipper. The readings' onCompletion, a hook that runs once when a flow ends (the next lesson takes it apart), reports AbortFlowException: Flow was aborted, no more elements needed, the signed "no more, thanks" note from lesson 2 of this track. Something else happened too: reading 152 came at 350 ms, not 200. zip collects its receiver, readings, in the caller's coroutine with no shelf at all. Only the other flow gets a producer coroutine, with a rendezvous channel between them, a hand-over where both hands must meet. So each reading's emit waits until there is a dial value to pair it with, and the slower side sets the pace. Reactor's zip produced the same two pairs, but its thermometer kept ticking every 100 ms, because Reactor asks its sources for values ahead of time. And Flow has only this two-flow zip. Pairing the second reading with the second turn of the dial is the wrong question. The screen needs each reading against the latest dial setting. That is combine. Picture a slate with one line per flow. combine starts one coroutine per source, and each one writes its newest value on its own line. Nothing comes out until every line has a value. After that, every update produces one output. So the first line is "152 of 180" at 250 ms: reading 150 had already been wiped off the slate by 152 before the dial had a value. Then come 154, 156 and 158 of 180, then "158 of 200" the moment the dial moves at 550, then "160 of 200" at 600. A source that never emits means no output at all, and combine completes when all its sources have completed. merge is the third way to join flows: values come out as they arrive, from either source, like two queues sharing one door. Table orders every 100 ms and takeaway orders every 70 ms come out as takeaway-0 at 70, table-0 at 100, takeaway-1 at 140, and so on. The merged flow ends when the last source ends, and one source that fails cancels the others. Pair by number with zip only when the n-th of one belongs with the n-th of the other. For "the latest of each", use combine. Check yourself: what does combine show if the dial sends 180 at 0 ms, before the first reading? So far the screen drew each line at once. A slow screen changes what combine hands it. Feed the oven screen two ways Open OvenDial.kt. Predict how many lines zip shows, and at what time the thermometer sends its second reading. Run it. Then predict the first line combine shows, and when. Read the third block: a dial that is never turned. Then run the Reactor twin, OvenDialJava, and compare when its thermometer ticks under zip. h: Flattening and combining: flatMap, zip and combine · A slow screen makes combine skip values and slow the thermometer
x: Put a slow screen behind combine. The thermometer ticks every 10 ms, ten times, and is combined with one dial value, 180. The screen needs 100 ms to draw each update. What does it show? Java // Closest Java equivalent: combineLatest in front of a subscriber that takes one at a time Flux.combineLatest(ticks, Flux.just(180), (i, d) -> i + "/" + d) .concatMap(v -> screen.draw(v).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(100)), 1); Kotlin combine(ticks, flowOf(180)) { i, d -> "$i/$d" } .collect { screen.draw(it); delay(100) } // the screen is slow Flow shows 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 10, at 10, 110, 210, 310, 410 and 510 ms. Reactor's combineLatest shows all ten, about 100 ms apart, the last at about 1,050 ms on a busy machine. And there is a second effect in Flow: the thermometer itself slowed down. It needed 330 ms to send its ten readings, not 100. The thermometer has never been slow in its life, and now it waits. The mechanism is a small tray in front of the slate. Each source coroutine puts its update into a channel whose capacity equals the number of flows, here 2, and then calls yield(), a suspension point that lets other coroutines run. The loop that fills the slate takes updates in batches. It reads until it sees a second update from a source it already updated in this batch, rewriting that source's line each time, and then calls your lambda once for the batch. While the screen is busy, updates pile up, and 2 is rewritten by 3 before anyone copies the slate. Once the tray is full, the thermometer's next send suspends: in the log, reading 4 is sent at 40 ms and reading 5 not until 120. So combine skips values and slows its sources, both at once. Reactor's screen keeps every state of the slate in a queue and draws them all. It isn't plain conflation (keeping only the newest waiting value) either. Pure latest-only would show 1 and then 10. If you care, say which one you want: After combine(...) The screen shows nothing 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10, and the thermometer slows .conflate() 1 at 10 ms, then 10 at 110 ms .buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED) all ten, the last at 1,010 ms For a screen, skipping is fine: nobody misses a temperature that was already old. For a cooking log, where every reading must be written next to its dial setting, every combination counts, and an unlimited buffer is a memory bill you size yourself. One more thing not to rely on. Two flows with no waits at all, combine(flowOf("a0", "a1", "a2"), flowOf("b0", "b1", "b2")), give a0b0, a1b1, a2b2 in Flow and a2b0, a2b1, a2b2 in Reactor. With sources that never suspend, which pairs you get depends on scheduling. Check yourself: with the screen at 100 ms per update, would buffer(10) instead of UNLIMITED keep all ten? Every operator in this lesson also shares one weakness: a single failing source or inner flow cancels all the others, and the whole flow ends. Draw from a busy slate Open SlowBoard.kt. Predict which values the slow screen shows in the first block, and when the thermometer sends 5. Run it. Then read the conflate() and buffer(UNLIMITED) blocks. Change Channel.UNLIMITED to 10 and run again, then to 3. Predict each count first. Run SlowBoardJava, the combineLatest twin, in real time. Count its updates. x: Flattening and combining in Kotlin Flow and in Reactor Reactor Flux<Plate> plates = dishes.flatMap(d -> stove.cook(d), 4); // default concurrency 256 Flux<Plate> inOrder = dishes.concatMap(d -> stove.cook(d)); // the source keeps its own timers Flux<Plate> ordered = dishes.flatMapSequential(d -> stove.cook(d), 4); Flux<Hit> hits = letters.switchMap(q -> recipes.search(q)); Flux<Gap> byNumber = Flux.zip(readings, dial, Gap::of); // asks both sides ahead of time Flux<Gap> latest = Flux.combineLatest(readings, dial, Gap::of); // keeps every combination Flux<Order> orders = Flux.merge(tableOrders, takeawayOrders); Kotlin Flow @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun pipelines() { val plates = dishes.flatMapMerge(4) { d -> flow { emit(stove.cook(d)) } } // default 16 val inOrder = dishes.flatMapConcat { d -> flow { emit(stove.cook(d)) } } // outer paused in emit // no flatMapSequential: see the worked example val hits = letters.flatMapLatest { q -> recipes.search(q) } // waits for the old inner val byNumber = readings.zip(dial) { c, d -> Gap.of(c, d) } // the receiver has no shelf val latest = combine(readings, dial) { c, d -> Gap.of(c, d) } // may skip when slow val orders = merge(tableOrders, takeawayOrders) } The operators line up one for one, and the virtual-time demos give the same timelines for flatMap and flatMapMerge, and for switchMap and flatMapLatest. The differences come from how each library moves values. In Flow, a value moves by a suspend call, so whatever is upstream of an emit waits for it: flatMapConcat pauses the outer's code (800 ms against Reactor's 600 on the same timeline), and zip slows its receiver to the other side's pace. Reactor moves values on demand and asks ahead of time, so its sources keep their own timers. The defaults differ too: 16 lanes against 256. And with a slow subscriber, combineLatest queues every state of the slate while combine skips some and makes its sources wait. Flow has no built-in flatMapSequential.

h: Flattening and combining: flatMap, zip and combine · Worked example
x: Cook a ticket on four burners The stove has four burners. Put the cooking inside the returned flow, so each dish gets a lane, and set the cap from the stove. Ten dishes of 100 ms are ready at 300 ms. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun cookAll(dishes: Flow<String>): Flow<Plate> = dishes.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) { dish -> // 1. the lambda only builds the inner flow flow { emit(stove.cook(dish)) } // 2. the slow cooking runs in the lane } // Closest Java equivalent: flatMap with a cap, the wait inside the returned Mono Flux<Plate> cookAll(Flux<String> dishes) { return dishes.flatMap(dish -> stove.cook(dish), 4); // cook returns a lazy Mono } The salad burns. Catch it inside that dish's own inner flow, so only that lane ends with a substitute. With soup at 300 ms, salad at 100 (burnt) and roast at 200, the plates are the salad's substitute at 100, roast at 200 and soup at 300. dishes.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) { dish -> flow { emit(stove.cook(dish)) } .catch { e -> if (e is Burnt) emit(substitute(dish)) else throw e } // 3. per lane } // Closest Java equivalent: handle the error inside each inner Mono dishes.flatMap(dish -> stove.cook(dish) .onErrorResume(Burnt.class, e -> Mono.just(substitute(dish))), 4); Compare a catch placed after flatMapMerge. The burnt lane cancels its siblings first: soup and roast end with a JobCancellationException, and the catch sees Burnt: burnt: salad at 100 ms. A caught error still ends the upstream, so this catch can only send out a stand-in after every other dish was thrown away. dishes.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) { dish -> flow { emit(stove.cook(dish)) } } .catch { emit(Plate("bread basket", "substitute")) } // too late: the other dishes are already off the stove // Closest Java equivalent: onErrorResume after flatMap ends the whole stream dishes.flatMap(dish -> stove.cook(dish), 4) .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(new Plate("bread basket", "substitute"))); The cooking log wants the plates in ticket order. Flow has no flatMapSequential. Start each dish with async, keep up to n of them in flight with a buffer, and wait for them in order. The buffer(n - 2) counts the buffer's slots plus one dish being awaited and one being started, so n must be at least 2. Twenty dishes of 100 ms take 1,000, 700, 500 and 300 ms for n = 2, 3, 4 and 8, always in ticket order. fun <T, R> Flow<T>.mapConcurrentOrdered(n: Int, f: suspend (T) -> R): Flow<R> = flow { coroutineScope { this@mapConcurrentOrdered .map { value -> async { f(value) } } // 4. start cooking .buffer(n - 2) // 5. at most n started and not yet emitted .collect { emit(it.await()) } // 6. emit in ticket order } } // Closest Java equivalent: Reactor has it built in Flux<Plate> ordered = dishes.flatMapSequential(dish -> stove.cook(dish), 4);

h: Flattening and combining: flatMap, zip and combine · Key terms
x: Flattening Turning a flow of flows (one inner flow per outer value) into one flow of values. Inner flow The flow your flatMap* lambda returns for one outer value: a dish's own sub-recipe. Lane One inner flow being collected in its own coroutine. concurrency is the number of lanes, the burners on the stove. Completion order Results leave in the order they are ready, not the order their inputs arrived. zip Pairs the n-th value of one flow with the n-th value of another, and ends with the shorter. combine Keeps the latest value of each flow and emits a combination whenever any of them changes. merge Passes on values from several flows in the order they arrive, and ends when the last one ends. In flatMapMerge, does the lambda run side by side for several values? No. It runs one value at a time, in the one coroutine that reads the outer flow, before a lane is taken. Only the flows it returns run side by side. Default concurrency of flatMapMerge, and of Reactor's flatMap? 16 (DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY, from the property kotlinx.coroutines.flow.defaultConcurrency). Reactor: 256. What happens to the outer flow while a flatMapConcat inner runs? Its code is paused inside emit: there is no extra coroutine or channel. buffer() before flatMapConcat lets it run ahead. flatMapLatest gets a new value while an inner is running. What happens? It cancels the inner with ChildCancelledException, waits for it to finish, then starts the inner for the new value. How does zip pair values, and when does it end? By number: first with first, second with second. It ends when the shorter flow ends and cancels the other. Its receiver has no buffer, so it waits for the other side. When does combine emit its first value? When every source has emitted at least once. After that, once per update of any source. combine with a slow collector: what happens to fast updates? Some are skipped (overwritten on the slate) and the sources are suspended, since the tray holds one update per source. Reactor's combineLatest delivers them all.

h: Flattening and combining: flatMap, zip and combine · Go deeper
x: How far does flatMapMerge run ahead of a slow collector? With 500 one-value inners and a collector stuck on its first value, 82 outer values had been pulled. A likely split (my inference, not measured) is 64 results in the output channel, about 16 inners suspended on a full channel, and a couple in hand. With .buffer(0) after it the count was 18, and with flatMapConcat it was 1. So budget memory for up to 64 finished results plus concurrency inners. A buffer or flowOn after flatMapMerge fuses into the same channel: flatMapMerge(4) { }.buffer(0) prints as ChannelFlowMerge[concurrency=4, capacity=0]. Edge cases: flatMapMerge(1) returns plain flattenConcat(). flatMapMerge(0) throws IllegalArgumentException: Expected positive concurrency level, but had 0 when you build the flow. Setting -Dkotlinx.coroutines.flow.defaultConcurrency=0 makes the first read of DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY throw ExceptionInInitializerError, caused by IllegalStateException: System property 'kotlinx.coroutines.flow.defaultConcurrency' should be in range 1..2147483647, but is '0'. With =4, 40 dishes of 100 ms took 1,000 ms instead of 300. flattenConcat() and flattenMerge() are the same operators for a Flow<Flow<T>> you already have; flatMapX(f) is literally map(f).flattenX(). combineTransform is combine with a FlowCollector receiver, so the lambda can emit zero or several values per update of the slate. Failure works the same way in combine and merge: one source that throws cancels the others (they end with JobCancellationException: Parent job is Cancelling) and the caller gets the original exception.

h: Errors, completion, retries and timeouts · A catch is a net under the upstream, and it checks who threw
x: catch is a net under the cook that asks who threw: an upstream timeout lands in it and becomes crackers, while the diner's dropped plate and the caller's own cancel go past; retry(3) cooks the recipe again from the top, and a backoff rings the bakery at 0, 100, 300 and 700 ms Here is the bread course as a flow, a recipe card for values. The cook, the producer, cooks it only when a diner, the collector, calls collect, and each emit hands one value to the diner. The cook first sends out yesterday's loaf, then fetches a fresh one from the bakery inside withTimeout(50), which cancels the call if it takes longer than 50 ms. A catch below it, an operator (a helper on the way from the cook to the diner), sends out crackers if anything goes wrong. The bakery takes 100 ms today. Most people expect the timeout to fly straight past the catch. The reasoning sounds solid: a timeout is a CancellationException, the exception a coroutine (a light piece of work that can pause without holding a thread) uses to say "stop, you've been called off", and catch doesn't handle cancellation. Run it, and then run a second version where the caller's own job, the handle that can cancel the collecting coroutine, is cancelled instead: Java // Closest Java equivalent: onErrorResume handles what comes from above it; dispose() is a cancel signal Flux.concat(Flux.just(oldLoaf), bakery.fresh().timeout(Duration.ofMillis(50))) .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(crackers)) .subscribe(diner::eat); // case 2: the subscription is disposed meanwhile Kotlin flow { emit(oldLoaf); emit(withTimeout(50) { bakery.fresh() }) } // the call takes 100 ms .catch { e -> emit(crackers) } .collect { diner.eat(it) } // case 2: the caller calls job.cancel() meanwhile Here is what the Try it prints for five ways the bread course can end. (An IOException is Java's usual exception for a failed read, write or call, such as a dropped phone line.) How it ends The catch action runs The caller sees the bakery call throws IOException yes nothing the bakery call throws CancellationException yes nothing withTimeout fires inside the bakery call yes, with TimeoutCancellationException nothing the diner drops a plate no IllegalStateException: the diner dropped the plate the caller's job is cancelled no JobCancellationException The timeout was caught, and the cancelled job was not. To see why, remember lesson 2 of this track. An exception thrown by the collector, the diner, comes back out of emit and up into the cook's code, and the inspector refuses any emit after that. That rule is called exception transparency: an exception from downstream belongs to downstream. So when the upstream's collect throws, catch has to work out who threw. Build it by hand and the rule falls out: Java // Closest Java equivalent: the same bookkeeping around a push-style source and a Consumer static <T> void myCatch(Consumer<Consumer<T>> upstream, Consumer<T> downstream, Function<Throwable, T> action) { RuntimeException[] fromDownstream = {null}; try { upstream.accept(v -> { try { downstream.accept(v); } catch (RuntimeException e) { fromDownstream[0] = e; throw e; } }); } catch (RuntimeException e) { if (e == fromDownstream[0]) throw e; // below the net if (Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) throw e; // our own task was cancelled downstream.accept(action.apply(e)); // an upstream failure } } Kotlin fun <T> Flow<T>.myCatch(action: suspend FlowCollector<T>.(Throwable) -> Unit): Flow<T> = flow { var fromDownstream: Throwable? = null try { collect { value -> try { emit(value) } catch (e: Throwable) { fromDownstream = e; throw e } } } catch (e: Throwable) { if (e === fromDownstream) throw e // below the net if (e is CancellationException && !currentCoroutineContext().isActive) throw e // our job is cancelled action(e) // an upstream failure } } Read it top to bottom. First it wraps the downstream emit and remembers anything that comes out of it. Then, when the whole collect fails, it asks two questions. Did this come from downstream? Rethrow it. Is it the cancellation of our own job? Rethrow that too. Everything else goes to your action. The library's catch keeps the same books. Picture a net strung under the upstream, everything above catch in the chain, while the downstream is everything below it, the collector included. Anything that falls from above lands in the net, even a CancellationException that the upstream throws while the job is still running. The job's own cancellation passes through on purpose. And a plate the diner drops falls below the net, straight to the caller. So catch ignores the cancellation of its collector, not every CancellationException. For a bakery call, that's usually what you want: a timeout becomes crackers. If it isn't, rethrow CancellationException in the action yourself. The net is generous, but it only covers what hangs above it. To put the serving under its protection, move it into onEach above the catch and call collect() with no lambda, or launchIn(scope), which collects in a new coroutine of that scope (the owner of a group of coroutines, which cancels them all when it is cancelled). And a caught error still ends the upstream: flowOf(1, 2, 3).map { fails on 2 }.catch { emit(-1) } gives 1 and -1, and 3 is never made. catch hears only what falls from above it. Put the work it should cover above it. Check yourself: catch sits above map, and map throws. Who handles it? The net can send out crackers. Sometimes you'd rather ring the bakery again. Five ways to end the bread course Open CatchNet.kt. For each of the five cases, predict whether the net catches it and what the caller sees. Run it. Each case runs twice: once with the library's catch, once with myCatch from this section. Check that the two lines always agree. In myCatch, delete the line that rethrows fromDownstream and run again. Which case changes, and what does the caller see now? Run CatchNetJava, the onErrorResume twin. Find the case where moving the serving above the net changes the result. h: Errors, completion, retries and timeouts · A retry cooks the recipe again, from the top
x: The grocer's van is back with the delivery note from Context and threads: flour, eggs and butter, read line by line. On the first attempt the reader loses its connection after line 2, with an IOException. The pantry import wraps the note in retry(3). What does the pantry receive? Java // Closest Java equivalent: retry re-subscribes, so a cold Flux replays from the top too List<String> received = Flux.defer(grocer::note).retry(3).collectList().block(); // [flour, eggs, flour, eggs, butter] Kotlin val received = note.retry(3).toList() // [flour, eggs, flour, eggs, butter] Two lines went into the pantry twice. The flour doesn't mind, but the pantry book now lists it twice. retryWhen, the operator under retry, is a loop around the same books that catch keeps. When the upstream fails with an exception from above the net, it calls your predicate, a function that answers yes or no, with the cause and an attempt number. If the answer is yes, it collects the upstream again. A cold flow is a recipe card, and collecting it again cooks it again from the top. Values that were already emitted are emitted again. The counting follows from the loop. retry(n) is retryWhen { cause, attempt -> attempt < n && predicate(cause) }, so retry(2) on a note that always fails collects it 3 times, and then the third exception comes out. retry(0) fails when you build the flow, with Expected positive amount of retries, but had 0. The default is Long.MAX_VALUE, which retries for ever. attempt is 0 on the first failure, and with retry(n, predicate) the predicate is no longer called once the attempts run out. The cook's longer pause each time is a backoff, and in code it is a delay inside the predicate: Java // Closest Java equivalent: Reactor's backoff spec (jitter off, so the times are exact) bakery.order("sourdough").retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)).jitter(0) .filter(e -> e instanceof IOException)); Kotlin bakery.order("sourdough").retryWhen { cause, attempt -> val retry = cause is IOException && attempt < 3 if (retry) delay(100L shl attempt.toInt()) // 100, 200, 400 ms retry } Against a bakery that never answers, both ring at 0, 100, 300 and 700 ms. Then they differ. Flow gives up by letting the original IOException out. Reactor wraps it in a RetryExhaustedException (Retries exhausted: 3/3, with the real error as its cause), and outside tests it adds jitter, a random spread on each wait so that many callers don't ring at the same moment (0.5 by default, from lesson 5 of the reactive track). Flow has no jitter, no cap and no exhaustion type. You write those yourself, which is what the lab does. Like catch, a retry never fires for an exception the collector threw, or for the caller's own cancellation. It does fire for a TimeoutCancellationException from a timeout() above it, and the last section builds on that. The replay is the part that hurts whenever each value changes something, such as a line in the pantry book. Every consumer after a retry must be idempotent: seeing the same item twice must leave the same result as seeing it once. Skip lines whose id you have seen (one set per collection), or make the source start where it stopped, from a bookmark that a retry can pass back. A retry cooks the recipe again from the top. Make whatever comes after it safe to see an item twice. Check yourself: retry(3) on a note that fails after its second line on every attempt. How many times does the collector see line 1? A retry hides failures well. A tally of how each order ended should hide nothing, and it's easy to get wrong. Read the note twice Open RetryReplay.kt. Predict what the pantry receives in the first block, and how many collections retry(2) makes in the second. Run it on virtual time. Check the backoff block's times against the section. Change the second block to retry(2) { it is IllegalStateException }. Predict the output, then run it. Run RetryReplayJava: the same replay in Reactor, and Retry.backoff on a real clock. h: Errors, completion, retries and timeouts · The onCompletion note is written once, and its cause is not always a failure
x: The kitchen keeps a tally of bread orders: a tick for each one that went well, a cross for each one that failed. The orders go through first(), which takes the first value and stops. At the end of the evening, every order has a cross: Java // Closest Java equivalent: doFinally reports a signal type instead of a cause loaves(kind) .doFinally(signal -> { if (signal == SignalType.ON_COMPLETE) tally.ok(); else tally.failed(signal); }) .next() .block(); Kotlin loaves(kind) .onCompletion { cause -> if (cause == null) tally.ok() else tally.failed(cause) } .first() onCompletion is a try/finally around the upstream, placed exactly where you wrote it. It runs once, when the flow ends, and leaves a note: its cause says what passed through that spot on the way out. How the flow ended cause it completed normally null the upstream threw IOException: line dropped the collector threw IllegalStateException: the diner dropped the plate a map below threw, and a catch below that swallowed it IllegalStateException: map failed above take(1) or first() AbortFlowException: Flow was aborted, no more elements needed below take(1) null the collecting job was cancelled JobCancellationException: StandaloneCoroutine was cancelled first() stops the upstream the way lesson 2 of this track described. It throws AbortFlowException, the signed "no more, thanks" note, out of the upstream's emit. That exception is a CancellationException, and every operator above first() sees it go by, so the tally counts a stopped order as a failed one. Below take(1) the flow simply ended, so the cause there is null. So read the note in order. null means it went well. A CancellationException means it was called off or stopped early, which is not a failure. Anything else is a failure. In code, that is one more branch before the cross: cause is CancellationException -> tally.stopped(). onCompletion can emit, but only on success: flowOf("a", "b").onCompletion { if (it == null) emit("done") } gives a, b, done. After a failure, emit there throws the original cause again. Use catch to send out a replacement. The terminal operators, the calls such as first() and single() that run a flow and return a result, fail in their own words, and they stop the upstream at different points. first() on an empty flow throws NoSuchElementException: Expected at least one element. single() throws NoSuchElementException: Flow is empty, or IllegalArgumentException: Flow has more than one element. On a three-element flow, first() pulls 1 element and single() pulls 2 before it fails. Reactor's single() says Source was a (constant) empty, and throws IndexOutOfBoundsException: Source emitted more than one item instead. Check yourself: onCompletion sits below take(1), and the collector throws on the first element. What is cause? Every failure so far arrived quickly. The worst bakery is the one that never answers. Read the note Open CompletionCauses.kt. Cover the output and write down the cause you expect on each line. Run it. Look at the two lines around take(1), and at above first(). Run CompletionCausesJava. Which doFinally signal does Reactor give above take(1)? x: The corner bakery has stopped answering: each call now rings for 1,000 ms. The chain gives every call 300 ms, retries with backoff and then rings the backup bakery. When does the backup answer? The calls start at 0, 400, 900 and 1,600 ms, and each one is cut at +300. At 1,900 ms the corner bakery gives up with Timed out waiting for 300ms, and the backup answers at 1,930. Reactor's chain prints the same times on a real clock. timeout(d) arrived in kotlinx.coroutines 1.7.0 and is still @FlowPreview in 1.11.0. It takes a Duration only. It runs the upstream in a producer coroutine and arms a timer only while it waits for the next upstream value. Time the downstream spends on a value doesn't count, but the wait for the first value does. Picture the kitchen's egg timer, wound each time the cook starts waiting for the bakery and paused while the diner eats. When it rings, it throws TimeoutCancellationException, and that is a CancellationException. That one fact explains the rest of the chain. The timeout comes from above retryWhen while the job is still running, so retryWhen can retry it, but only if isTransient lists TimeoutCancellationException, because a timeout is not an IOException. Position sets the meaning. Above retryWhen, the timer limits each try. Below it, the timer limits the whole sequence, waits included: a budget. Add .timeout(1.seconds) after the retries, and the same bakery gets calls at 0, 400 and 900, the budget rings at 1,000, and the backup answers at 1,030. The catch at the end filters on isTransient, so moon bread, which nobody bakes, reaches the caller as an IllegalArgumentException at 20 ms, with no retry and no call to the backup. When the backup fails too, the caller sees the backup's error. The corner bakery's error is not attached. Above the retry, a timeout limits one try. Below it, a timeout limits them all. The cancellation nature bites when the flow runs in the background. A timeout that nobody catches inside launch or launchIn just ends that coroutine as cancelled. The scope's CoroutineExceptionHandler, its last-resort handler for failures that nobody caught, never runs, and the parent scope keeps going, because handlers ignore CancellationException. Your bread refresher stops, and nobody hears the egg timer. Translate the timeout at the edge: .catch { e -> if (e is TimeoutCancellationException) throw BakeryTimeout(e) else throw e }, and the handler gets BakeryTimeout with the timeout as its cause. Reactor's timeout signals java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException, an ordinary error, so the trap doesn't exist there. Two notes for tests. Under runTest, withTimeout words its message differently ("Timed out after 50ms of virtual (kotlinx.coroutines.test) time..."), so assert on the exception's type, never its text. And TimeoutCancellationException has no public constructor, so produce one with a real timeout() under virtual time, as the lab does. Check yourself: where does .timeout(1.seconds) go to limit each try instead of the whole sequence? Everything in this lesson acts on one collector and its own cold flow. When many diners share one cooking session, a failure behaves very differently. Time a bakery that won't answer Open FlakyBakery.kt. Before you run it, write down when each of cases A to E ends, and how many calls each bakery gets. Run it on virtual time and compare. Case E is case B with an overall timeout(1.seconds) after the retries. Read the last block: the same timeout inside launchIn, first silent, then translated into BakeryTimeout. h: Errors, completion, retries and timeouts · Java and Kotlin
x: One slow bakery call, as a Reactor chain and as a Flow chain Reactor Mono<Loaf> freshLoaf(String kind) { return Mono.defer(() -> bakery.order(kind)) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)) // TimeoutException: an ordinary error .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)) // jitter 0.5 by default .filter(e -> e instanceof IOException || e instanceof TimeoutException)) .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) // overall budget .onErrorResume(e -> Exceptions.isRetryExhausted(e) || e instanceof TimeoutException, e -> backup.order(kind)); // exhausted: RetryExhaustedException } Kotlin Flow @OptIn(FlowPreview::class) fun freshLoaf(kind: String): Flow<Loaf> = bakery.order(kind) .timeout(300.milliseconds) // TimeoutCancellationException: a cancellation .retryWhen { cause, attempt -> // no jitter, no cap unless you write them val retry = isTransient(cause) && attempt < 3 if (retry) delay(100L shl attempt.toInt()) retry } .timeout(1.seconds) // overall budget .catch { e -> if (!isTransient(e)) throw e; emitAll(backup.order(kind)) } // the original error The two chains have the same shape and, with jitter off, the same timeline. What differs is what the errors are. Reactor's timeout signals TimeoutException, an ordinary error, while Flow's throws TimeoutCancellationException, a CancellationException, so you must list it in isTransient, and a timeout that escapes a launch ends that coroutine silently. Reactor wraps exhausted retries in RetryExhaustedException, while retryWhen lets the original exception out. Reactor's backoff has jitter, a cap and an exhaustion error built in, and in Flow you write the policy yourself. One thing Flow gives you for free: catch and retryWhen never act on the collecting job's own cancellation, so a caller that goes away stops the whole chain without a retry or a call to the backup.

With a bakery that never answers, the backup answers at 1,930 ms; with moon bread, the caller sees the error at 20 ms. val loaf = tries .catch { e -> if (!isTransient(e)) throw e // 3. not ours to hide emitAll(backup.order(kind)) // 4. the backup bakery } // Closest Java equivalent Mono<Loaf> loaf = tries .onErrorResume(e -> Exceptions.isRetryExhausted(e) || isTransient(e), // 3. e -> backup.order(kind)); // 4. Dinner itself has a deadline. Add a budget after the retries. Now the silent bakery gets calls at 0, 400 and 900, the budget rings at 1,000, and the backup answers at 1,030. @OptIn(FlowPreview::class) val loaf = bakery.order(kind) .timeout(300.milliseconds) .retryWithBackoff() .timeout(1.seconds) // 5. the whole sequence, waits included .catch { e -> if (!isTransient(e)) throw e; emitAll(backup.order(kind)) } // Closest Java equivalent Mono<Loaf> loaf = tries .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) // 5. the whole sequence, waits included .onErrorResume(e -> Exceptions.isRetryExhausted(e) || isTransient(e), e -> backup.order(kind)); A background job keeps the bread board up to date with launchIn. If both bakeries time out, the job would end as cancelled and no handler would hear it.
