h: Errors, completion, retries and timeouts · Quiz
x: Which failure does the catch action handle? loaves.map { slice(it) } .catch { emit(crackers) } .collect { diner.eat(it) } diner.eat throws IllegalStateException slice throws IllegalArgumentException the caller's scope is cancelled while it waits for a loaf all three slice runs above the net, so its exception reaches the action. diner.eat runs in the collector, below the net, so its exception goes straight to the caller. The scope's cancellation is the cancellation of the collecting job, which catch always lets pass. A note fails after its second line on every attempt. It is collected through retry(3). How many times does the collector receive line 1? Once: retry carries on after the failure 3 times 4 times It depends on the backoff retry(3) means 3 retries, so 4 collections, and each collection runs the cold flow from the top. Lines 1 and 2 are delivered 4 times each, then the fourth failure comes out. A backoff changes when the retries happen, not how many. A tally hook onCompletion { cause -> if (cause == null) ok() else failed() } sits right above .first(). Every order that went well is counted as a failure. Why? first() stops the upstream by throwing AbortFlowException, a CancellationException, through it first() always fails with NoSuchElementException first and then retries onCompletion runs before the value is emitted, so cause isn't set yet onCompletion sees the collector's exception from first()'s own collect first() throws AbortFlowException ("Flow was aborted, no more elements needed") out of the upstream's emit once it has its value. Operators above it see that as the cause. Below take(1) or after the terminal call, the flow simply completed. Count cause is CancellationException as stopped early, not as a failure. Each bakery call must be limited to 300 ms and retried with backoff, and the caller must get an answer or an error within 1 second overall. Which order? .retryWithBackoff().timeout(300.milliseconds).timeout(1.seconds) .timeout(1.seconds).retryWithBackoff().timeout(300.milliseconds) .retryWithBackoff().timeout(300.milliseconds) .timeout(300.milliseconds).retryWithBackoff().timeout(1.seconds) A timeout above retryWhen covers one try and is retried, so 300 ms goes first. A timeout below the retries covers the whole sequence, waits included, so the 1 s budget goes after them. With the retries first, a 300 ms timeout would cut the whole sequence at 300 ms. From the reactive track: Reactor's timeout signals TimeoutException. In a Flow collected with launchIn(scope), a timeout(50.milliseconds) fires and nothing catches it. What happens? The scope's CoroutineExceptionHandler logs a TimeoutException The launched job ends as cancelled, no handler runs, and the scope keeps running The whole scope is cancelled The flow retries once by default Flow's timeout throws TimeoutCancellationException, a CancellationException, and handlers ignore cancellation. The job just ends cancelled, silently. Translate it in catch into an exception of your own so the handler sees it. In Reactor this trap doesn't exist, because TimeoutException is an ordinary error.

h: Errors, completion, retries and timeouts · Key terms
x: Exception transparency The rule that an exception from downstream belongs to the downstream: once emit has thrown, the flow must not emit again. Upstream and downstream Everything above an operator in the chain, and everything below it, the collector included. catch An operator that handles failures from above it, except the cancellation of the collecting job. retryWhen On an upstream failure, asks a predicate with the cause and attempt number, and collects the upstream again if it says yes. Idempotent consumer A consumer that gives the same result when it sees the same item twice, for example by skipping line ids it has already seen. TimeoutCancellationException What timeout() and withTimeout throw. It is a CancellationException, so handlers ignore it. AbortFlowException The internal CancellationException that take and first throw out of the upstream's emit to stop it: the signed "no more, thanks" note. Does catch handle a CancellationException? Yes, if the upstream throws it while the collecting job is running (a TimeoutCancellationException too). It lets the cancellation of the collecting job pass. How does catch know an exception came from the collector? It wraps the downstream emit and remembers what came out of it. That exception is rethrown, never handled. retry(3): how many collections, and what does the collector see again? Up to 4 collections. Each runs the upstream from the top, so values already emitted are emitted again. In retryWhen { cause, attempt -> }, what is attempt on the first failure? 0. onCompletion placed above first(): what is cause after a lookup that went well? AbortFlowException: Flow was aborted, no more elements needed, a CancellationException. Below take(1) it is null. What does timeout(300.milliseconds) throw, and what is its message? TimeoutCancellationException (a CancellationException): "Timed out waiting for 300ms". A timeout() escapes a launchIn job. What happens? The job ends cancelled, no CoroutineExceptionHandler runs, and the parent scope keeps running. Translate it in catch if someone must hear it.

h: Errors, completion, retries and timeouts · Go deeper
x: When both sides fail, the upstream wins. If the collector throws IllegalStateException("collector failed") and the builder's finally then throws IOException("close() failed"), the caller sees the IOException, with the collector's exception in suppressed, and a catch above does not run its action. The Flow KDoc calls this "a semantic equivalent of throwing from finally block", and notes that the exception-handling operators still treat the downstream exception as the root cause. A failed backup forgets the first bakery. flow { throw IOException("corner bakery closed") }.catch { emitAll(flow { throw IOException("backup bakery closed") }) } gives the caller IOException: backup bakery closed with no cause and nothing suppressed. If you want both in the logs, attach the first one yourself with addSuppressed before you emit from the backup. Don't retry from inside catch with emitAll(sameFlow). The catch KDoc points to retryWhen, which retries "without introducing ever-growing stack of suspending calls". withTimeoutOrNull(250) { flow.toList() } returns null and loses the values that arrived before the deadline. Collect into a list you own (collect { partial += it }) if you need them. Inside runBlocking with a CoroutineName("bread-refresher"), the withTimeout message names the coroutine: Coroutine "bread-refresher" timed out waiting for 50 ms. The exact boundary of timeout(100.milliseconds) depends on how the scheduler orders events at the same instant: under virtual time a 100 ms gap did not time out and a 101 ms gap did. Don't build logic on the equality case. onEmpty { emit(default) } is the counterpart for a flow that completes without a value: a dish with no sauce of its own gets the house sauce, and a dish with one gets its own.

h: Hot flows in depth: SharedFlow, StateFlow and sharing · One slow subscriber decides what the quick one gets
x: One slate by the house bell for every listener: under DROP_LATEST the slow diary keeper makes the quick waiter lose 4, 5 and 6; the menu board (StateFlow) keeps one slot and skips what a busy reader missed; WhileSubscribed(5_000) keeps one cook going until 5 s after the last diner leaves A cold flow is a recipe card: every collector, the code that calls collect to receive its values, cooks it again from the top. A hot flow runs whether or not anyone collects it, and shares each value with whoever is listening at that moment. A MutableSharedFlow is a hot flow that you send values into by hand with emit, and it is the house bell. Each collector of a hot flow is a subscriber. A helper wired up the bell like this, with one coroutine (a light piece of work that can pause without holding a thread) per listener. The waiter is quick. The diary keeper needs a full second per line, so the helper picked DROP_LATEST: when the diary keeper falls behind, the bell should drop announcements while the waiter carries on. Java // Java equivalent: a Reactor multicast sink; the diary subscriber requests one item, then stalls Sinks.Many<Integer> bell = Sinks.many().multicast().directAllOrNothing(); bell.asFlux().subscribe(waiter::add); // quick: unbounded demand bell.asFlux().subscribe(diaryThatRequestsOne); // slow: request(1), then nothing for (int a = 1; a <= 6; a++) bell.tryEmitNext(a); Kotlin val bell = MutableSharedFlow<Int>(extraBufferCapacity = 2, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_LATEST) backgroundScope.launch { bell.collect { waiter += it } } // quick backgroundScope.launch { bell.collect { diary += it; delay(1_000) } } // 1 s per line for (announcement in 1..6) { bell.emit(announcement); delay(10) } extraBufferCapacity = 2 gives the slate room for two announcements, and onBufferOverflow says what to do when it is full. Predict what the waiter receives. Here is the output in virtual time, the fake clock of runTest that skips over waits, with the other two choices for comparison: DROP_LATEST waiter got [1, 2, 3] diary got [1, 2, 3] SUSPEND waiter got [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] diary got [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] emit(4), (5), (6) returned at t=1000, 2000, 3000 DROP_OLDEST waiter got [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] diary got [1, 5, 6] The waiter lost 4, 5 and 6, and he was never slow. To see why, look at the slate. There is one slate beside the bell, and every subscriber reads it at their own pace, keeping their place with a finger. A line can be wiped only when every listener has read it. So the slowest listener decides when the slate is full, for everyone. There is no slate per listener. Walk through it. The diary keeper takes 1 and starts a line that takes a second. Announcements 2 and 3 go onto the slate, which has room for exactly two. The waiter reads them at once, but that wipes nothing, because the diary keeper still needs them. Announcement 4 finds the slate full, and the overflow policy, what a full buffer does with a new value, decides what happens: SUSPEND, the default: emit(4) waits until the diary keeper takes 2, at t=1000. The waiter has nothing new to read, so he waits as well. DROP_LATEST: 4 is never chalked up. Nobody hears it, the waiter included. DROP_OLDEST: 4 is chalked over 2, and the diary keeper's finger is pushed past the wiped line. Only the slow listener skips. That makes the overflow policy a choice about every subscriber at once. When no announcement may be lost and the waiter must not wait, keep SUSPEND and give the slow listener a shelf of its own. bell.buffer(64).collect { ... } puts a channel, a queue between coroutines, between the slate and the slow work (the shelf from Buffering), so the diary keeper copies each line off the slate at once. In the Try it, that version delivers all six to both, and every emit returns by t=50. The shelf has a size: once its 64 spots fill, the diary keeper stops taking from the slate, and everyone waits again. A SharedFlow has one buffer for all its subscribers. Give a slow subscriber a buffer of its own. The picture breaks at the cook's hand. A real cook would just ring louder and carry on. With SUSPEND, she stands with the chalk raised until the slowest listener has read a line. The exact rule behind all this is short enough to fit in two lines, and it also says when tryEmit answers no. Six announcements, two listeners, four setups Read FastAndSlow.kt. h: Hot flows in depth: SharedFlow, StateFlow and sharing · The exact rule: count what the slowest subscriber hasn't taken
x: emit is two steps in the source: if (tryEmit(value)) return, and only then suspend. tryEmit is the version that never waits: it returns true if it handled the value, and false if it would have had to wait. So one rule answers both questions, when emit waits and when tryEmit says no. With no subscribers, every call succeeds. The value goes into the replay cache if replay > 0, the last few values kept for subscribers who arrive later, and nowhere otherwise. extraBufferCapacity plays no part: with replay = 2, extraBufferCapacity = 10, five emits to nobody leave replayCache = [4, 5]. With subscribers, the slate holds replay + extraBufferCapacity values, and it is full when the slowest subscriber has that many values it has not taken yet. Then SUSPEND makes tryEmit return false and emit wait, while the two drop policies return true and drop. "Taken" has an exact meaning. A subscriber takes a value when it reads it off the slate, before your collect lambda runs. A value that a busy subscriber is still working on no longer counts. That is why the diary keeper held only 2 and 3 against the slate in the first section, and not 1. Now the default, MutableSharedFlow(), with no replay and no extra buffer. There is no slate at all, so a value can only pass hand to hand. That is a rendezvous, the hand-over from Buffering where both hands must meet: emit holds the note out until every listener has a hand on it. tryEmit can't wait, so it lets go of the note, and the note falls. It therefore returns false whenever there is a subscriber, even an idle one, as lesson 8 of the coroutines track said. And emit returns the moment the subscriber takes the value, before the subscriber has done anything with it: with 100 ms of work per value, emit(1), emit(2) and emit(3) return at t=0, 100 and 200. Here is the rule at work. One subscriber has subscribed and waits, and then tryEmit(1) to tryEmit(6) run back to back (T is true, f is false): Flow tryEmit(1..6) The subscriber gets MutableSharedFlow(), no subscriber T T T T T T (nobody there) MutableSharedFlow() f f f f f f nothing extraBufferCapacity = 2 T T f f f f 1, 2 replay = 2 T T f f f f 1, 2 replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 2 T T T f f f 1, 2, 3 extraBufferCapacity = 2, DROP_OLDEST T T T T T T 5, 6 extraBufferCapacity = 2, DROP_LATEST T T T T T T 1, 2 Two rows deserve a second look. While someone is subscribed, replay = 2 behaves exactly like extraBufferCapacity = 2: both are lines on the one slate. And three idle subscribers give the same row as one, because they share the slate. The slate also explains a subscriber who arrives late. Someone who walks into the kitchen late reads the lines kept for latecomers, the replay cache, and then hears new announcements. They never see the lines that the slow diary keeper is still working through. With replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 10, a subscriber stuck on value 1 while 1 to 5 are emitted works through all five, and a second subscriber who joins after 5 gets only [5]. Count what the slowest subscriber hasn't taken. That number decides every emit. Check yourself: with extraBufferCapacity = 3, SUSPEND and one waiting subscriber, which call is the first tryEmit to return false? The bell keeps every line until the slowest reader is done. The menu board keeps one. Fill in the tryEmit table Cover the table above. Read OneTape.kt and write down the six results and the received values for each line before you run it. Run it. In the emit timeline, compare when each emit returns with when the subscriber takes the value. Run the Java twin. Predict first: a Reactor subscriber that has called request(1) is idle too. Does the first tryEmitNext succeed? h: Hot flows in depth: SharedFlow, StateFlow and sharing · StateFlow is the menu board in the hall: one slot, compared with equals
x: A StateFlow is a hot flow that always holds exactly one current value, .value. Setting it replaces the old value, and collectors get the new one. It is the menu board in the hall: one slot. Two rules follow, and both compare with equals, the type's own idea of "the same". Pinning up an equal card does nothing. The setter checks the new value against the current one and returns early when they are equal: no collector wakes up, and the old object stays on the board. After board.value = MenuItem("soup of the day", BigDecimal("4.50")) on a board that holds an equal item, board.value === first is still true. Equality is whatever your type says, so BigDecimal("4.500") counts as a new price, because BigDecimal.equals compares the number of decimal places too. Each reader remembers the last card they read. A collector that wakes up reads the slot, and it emits only if the value differs from the one it emitted last. A busy collector skips everything in between, even a value that went away and came back: Java // Java equivalent: Reactor skips repeats and in-between values only when you add both operators Sinks.Many<String> soup = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault("tomato"); soup.asFlux().onBackpressureLatest().distinctUntilChanged().subscribe(busyReader); soup.tryEmitNext("leek"); soup.tryEmitNext("tomato"); // busyReader got [tomato]; without the two operators it gets all three Kotlin val soup = MutableStateFlow("tomato") launch { soup.collect { log += it; delay(100) } } // 100 ms of work per value delay(10); soup.value = "leek" delay(10); soup.value = "tomato" // log is [tomato]: the board changed twice, and the busy reader saw nothing new The busy reader looked up, saw tomato, and concluded that nothing had happened. As far as the board knows, nothing had. A diary built on a StateFlow loses exactly these changes. Use a StateFlow for state, and a SharedFlow for events. Writes go through compare-and-set, an update that succeeds only if nobody changed the value since you read it. update { it + 1 } is a loop: read the value, compute the next one, call compareAndSet(prev, next), and go round again if another writer got in first. With 8 coroutines on Dispatchers.Default, which runs them on real threads, one per core, each adding 1 a hundred thousand times, the value ends at exactly 800,000, and the lambda ran more than that: 807,072 times in one run here, 1,405,098 in another. Any side effect inside update { }, such as a log line or a call, can run more than once. Compute inside the lambda and act after it. compareAndSet compares with equals as well, which gives one odd case: compareAndSet(11, 11) on a board that holds 11 returns true, changes nothing and wakes nobody. Java's AtomicReference.compareAndSet compares references instead, so a fresh BigDecimal("10") fails against the stored one. One counter does not skip anything: subscriptionCount, the number of current subscribers, as a StateFlow of its own. It works like a tally sheet by the hall door that marks every person coming and going. A subscriber that walks in and straight out still leaves +1 and -1 on the sheet. An observer saw [0, 1, 0] for such a visitor, where a plain StateFlow set to 1 and back to 0 showed only [0]. Sharing is built on this count. A StateFlow keeps state, not history. When every change counts, use a SharedFlow. Check yourself: a busy collector last saw tomato, and the soup goes leek, then pea. What does it see when it's free? Both kinds of hot flow so far were filled by hand. Most hot flows in real programs are a cold flow, shared. Read the menu board Read NoticeBoard.kt. Predict each part: which prices the collector sees, what the busy collector logs, the three compareAndSet results, the final value in part D, and the two lists in part E. Run it. Part D runs on real threads, so its lambda count changes from run to run. Run the Java twin, then explain part C: why does Java's compareAndSet fail where Kotlin's would succeed? h: Hot flows in depth: SharedFlow, StateFlow and sharing · One cook for many diners: shareIn, stateIn and when the cook starts and stops
x: stateIn and shareIn read like conversions, but each one launches a coroutine. shareIn(scope, started, replay) creates a MutableSharedFlow with that replay, an extra buffer that brings it up to at least 64 slots, and SUSPEND. Then it launches one coroutine in scope, the owner that cancels all its coroutines when it is cancelled, and that coroutine collects the upstream, the cold flow above it, into the shared flow. stateIn does the same with a MutableStateFlow(initialValue). Picture one cook and many diners. The sharing coroutine is the cook: she cooks the recipe once and serves every diner at the table. started, a SharingStarted value, decides when she works. Eagerly starts her at opening time, diners or not. Lazily lets the first diner get her started, and she never stops. WhileSubscribed(5_000) keeps her cooking while anyone is at the table and stops her 5 s after the last diner leaves, in case someone just stepped out. Inside, WhileSubscribed watches subscriptionCount. When the count drops to 0, it waits for the stop timeout and then sends STOP, which cancels the upstream collection. A subscriber who comes back first cancels that pending wait, so the cook never stopped. The figure shows an exact virtual-time run for the oven thermometer, which sends run * 100 + i every second (made-up readings that show which run sent them). Screen A switches off at 2.5 s and is back at 4 s: it gets 104, from the same run. A goes off again at 6 s, and STOP comes at 11 s. When A comes back at 14 s, it gets the stale 111 first, and then 200 from run #2. Three facts in that run catch people out: The upstream restarts from the top, because it is a cold flow collected again. Run #2 counts from 200, and a running total built with runningFold would start over. The returning subscriber sees the stale value first. replayExpirationMillis = 0 resets the StateFlow to its initial value when the cook stops, so the returning A gets -1 instead of 111. With WhileSubscribed(), whose stop timeout is 0, every flicker of a screen is a STOP and a new START. Java // Java equivalent: connect with the first subscriber, disconnect 5 s after the last. // After a disconnect Reactor reconnects with an empty replay cache, so no stale reading is shown. Flux<Reading> live = thermometer.replay(1).refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5)); Kotlin val live: StateFlow<Reading?> = thermometer.stateIn( houseScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000, replayExpirationMillis = 0), initialValue = null) Reading .value is not a subscription. It is glancing at the hall board from the doorway, and it doesn't call the cook. A hall board built with Lazily or WhileSubscribed and read only through .value never starts: in the Try it, three glances at 3.5 s read [null, null, null], and the thermometer was read 0 times. With Eagerly they read [180, 180, 180] after 4 readings. Pick started by who reads. Code that only reads .value needs Eagerly. Two more ways the sharing goes wrong. If the upstream throws, the sharing coroutine dies, and the exception goes to the scope's handler. The subscribers are not told. They sit at the table and wait for ever, so put retry or retryWhen above shareIn, as in the last lesson. And shareIn inside a function that each request calls starts a new cook per call: 50 calls that each read one value left 50 sharing coroutines and 500 upstream reads after 10 s. Fifty cooks, each one cooking for a diner who left after the first bite. Build the shared flow once, in a field, in a scope that you cancel when the program stops. Check yourself: a screen goes off at 10 s and comes back at 13 s under WhileSubscribed(5_000). Does the thermometer restart? Everything here happens inside one Kotlin program, where every value arrives through emit. The outside world calls you back instead. Watch the cook start, stop and start again Read SharingTimeline.kt. Before running it, write down when upstream START and STOP print, and what A gets each time it comes back. Run it. Then run it with -Pargs=expire and with -Pargs=stop0, predicting each first. Run the Java twin, the same script ten times faster on Reactor's replay(1).refCount. Compare the lines after A's second return. log("A comes back"); a = open(reading); Thread.sleep(150); a.dispose(); log("end, upstream starts=" + starts.get()); } } ./gradlew :flows:demo -Pmain=workbench.flows.l07.SharingTimelineJava labs/flows/src/demo/java/workbench/flows/l07/SharingTimelineJava.java The default run: START #1 at 0, A gets 104 at 4000 with no restart, STOP #1 at 11000, and at 14000 A gets 111, then START #2 and 200, for 2 starts in all. WhileSubscribed(5_000): a return within 5 s cancels the stop timer, so run #1 keeps going; after a real stop, the next subscriber gets the stale value and then a new run from the top. shareIn (kotlinx.coroutines API) docs SharingStarted (kotlinx.coroutines API) docs

h: Hot flows in depth: SharedFlow, StateFlow and sharing · Java and Kotlin
x: One oven thermometer, shared for the hall board and for the kitchen screens OvenBoard.java (Reactor) final class OvenBoard implements AutoCloseable { private final AtomicReference<Reading> latest = new AtomicReference<>(); private final Disposable boardConnection; final Flux<Reading> live; OvenBoard(Flux<Reading> thermometer) { // for the hall board: connect now, retry after a second, keep the latest in a field this.boardConnection = thermometer .retryWhen(Retry.fixedDelay(Long.MAX_VALUE, Duration.ofSeconds(1)) .filter(e -> e instanceof IOException)) .subscribe(latest::set); // for the screens: connect with the first, disconnect 5 s after the last this.live = thermometer.replay(1).refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5)); } Reading current() { return latest.get(); } @Override public void close() { boardConnection.dispose(); } } OvenBoard.kt (StateFlow) class OvenBoard(thermometer: Flow<Reading>, scope: CoroutineScope) { // for the hall board: .value is not a subscription, so start now val board: StateFlow<Reading?> = thermometer .retry { e -> (e is IOException).also { if (it) delay(1_000) } } .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, null) // for the screens: survive a 5 s flicker, then stop and forget the old reading val live: StateFlow<Reading?> = thermometer .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000, replayExpirationMillis = 0), null) fun current(): Reading? = board.value } // cancelling `scope` stops both The Kotlin side needs no AtomicReference, because a StateFlow is both the holder and the stream: .value reads it at once, and collectors get the same value with equality checks built in. Lifetime differs too. Both Kotlin flows live in scope, so cancelling that one scope stops both upstream collections; in Reactor the board lives as long as its Disposable, and the screen connection as long as it has subscribers. The two sides also forget differently. After a disconnect, replay(1).refCount reconnects with an empty cache, and Kotlin needs replayExpirationMillis = 0 for the same effect. Errors are where they differ most. In Reactor an error in the thermometer reaches every subscriber as onError. In Kotlin it ends the sharing coroutine, goes to the scope, and leaves the subscribers waiting, which is why the retry sits above stateIn. Both versions open two connections to the thermometer, one per view.

h: Hot flows in depth: SharedFlow, StateFlow and sharing · Worked example
x: Share one order rail between the grill and the dessert station Orders arrive on a rail and are read off it one by one. Two stations need every order, the grill and the dessert station. Reading the rail twice would take every ticket twice, so the reading is shared with shareIn and replay = 0. The grill starts work at 250 ms and the dessert station at 500 ms. Predict what each has received by 800 ms. var next = 0 val orders = flow { while (true) { delay(100); emit("order-${next++}") } } // stands in for reading the rail val shared = orders.shareIn(houseScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly) // replay = 0 // the grill subscribes at t=250, desserts at t=500 // Java equivalent: one connection, multicast to whoever is subscribed when an order arrives Flux<String> orders = Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(100)).map(i -> "order-" + i); Flux<String> shared = orders.publish().autoConnect(0); // connect now, like Eagerly // the grill subscribes at t=250, desserts at t=500 The virtual-time run. With Eagerly, order-0 and order-1 were read before anyone listened, and the dessert station also missed everything up to order-4. WhileSubscribed() helps the first station and not the second. With replay = 0, the slate keeps nothing for a late subscriber. Eagerly: grill=[order-2, order-3, order-4, order-5, order-6] desserts=[order-5, order-6] WhileSubscribed(): grill=[order-0, order-1, order-2, order-3, order-4] desserts=[order-2, order-3, order-4] Start reading only when both stations are there. SharingStarted is a fun interface that turns the subscriber count into START and STOP commands, so the gate is one line. In the same run, both stations now get [order-0, order-1] by 800 ms. // 1. a strategy built on subscriptionCount val bothStations = SharingStarted { count -> count.map { if (it >= 2) SharingCommand.START else SharingCommand.STOP } } // 2. the same shareIn, gated val shared = orders.shareIn(houseScope, bothStations) // 1. and 2.: connect once two subscribers are there (Reactor's version never disconnects) Flux<String> shared = orders.publish().autoConnect(2); Self-check: the dessert station needs 50 ms per order and the grill needs 5 ms. With shareIn's default SUSPEND, which one sets the pace of reading the rail, and is that what you want here? (The dessert station. The slate is full once the slowest station has 64 orders it hasn't taken, and then emit, the reading, waits. For orders that must all be cooked, that is exactly the waiting you want. A drop policy would lose orders with no error.)

h: Hot flows in depth: SharedFlow, StateFlow and sharing · Quiz
x: Three subscribers have subscribed to MutableSharedFlow<Int>(replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 2) and are waiting. Code calls tryEmit(1) to tryEmit(5) back to back, so no subscriber runs in between. What do the five calls return? true, true, true, false, false true five times: replay keeps values, so the flow never refuses one true, true, false, false, false: only extraBufferCapacity counts true five times: each subscriber has its own three slots, nine in all The buffer has replay + extraBufferCapacity = 3 slots, and all three subscribers share them. None of them can take a value between the calls, so the fourth call finds the slowest subscriber with 3 untaken values, and SUSPEND refuses it. While anyone is subscribed, replay slots are ordinary buffer slots, and there is no queue per subscriber. A dish's StateFlow<Status> goes READY, then SENT_BACK, then READY again within 5 ms, while its only collector is inside a 50 ms write to the kitchen diary that started after it got READY. What does the collector get when the write finishes? SENT_BACK, then READY READY a second time Nothing new: the current value equals the last one it got SENT_BACK only A waking collector reads the one slot and emits only if the value differs from the one it emitted last. The slot holds READY, equal to what it last saw, so nothing is emitted. If every change matters, the stream should be a SharedFlow with a buffer. The kitchen screens share the oven thermometer. A screen that flickers off and on must not reconnect to the thermometer, and a screen switched on after the feed has stopped must never show an old reading. Which started fits stateIn(scope, started, null)? SharingStarted.Eagerly SharingStarted.Lazily SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000) SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000, replayExpirationMillis = 0) The 5 s stop timeout covers the flicker: a subscriber that comes back cancels the pending stop. The second parameter resets the StateFlow to null when the feed stops, so a later screen sees null, then a fresh reading. Plain WhileSubscribed(5_000) shows the stale reading first, and Eagerly and Lazily never stop at all. readings.shareIn(houseScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, replay = 1) has two subscribers. The upstream sends two readings, then throws IOException("thermometer lost"). What happens next? Both subscribers' collect calls throw the IOException The sharing coroutine fails, the scope's handler gets the exception, and the subscribers keep waiting with no error shareIn restarts the upstream on its own Both subscribers' collect calls return normally The upstream runs in the sharing coroutine, not in the subscribers. Its exception ends that coroutine and goes to the scope, and the subscribers are never told: in the measured run the subscriber had [1, 2] and was still waiting a second later. Put retry or retryWhen above shareIn. From lesson 4 of this track: plates.buffer(10).collect { ... }, and the collector is stuck on its first plate. How many of the producer's emit calls have returned? 10 11 1 64 Ten plates wait in the buffer and one is in the collector's hands, so 11 calls returned and the 12th is suspended. shareIn follows the same arithmetic: with its default 64-slot buffer, the upstream ran 65 emits ahead of a stuck subscriber.

h: Hot flows in depth: SharedFlow, StateFlow and sharing · Explain it back
x: A friend asks two things: why did the quick waiter lose announcements under DROP_LATEST when only the diary keeper was slow, and why does tryEmit on a default MutableSharedFlow() fail while the subscriber is idle? Answer both with the slate picture, in a few sentences.

h: Hot flows in depth: SharedFlow, StateFlow and sharing · Key terms
x: Hot flow A flow that runs whether or not anyone collects it, and shares what it produces with whoever is subscribed. SharedFlow and StateFlow are hot. Shared buffer The one slate of replay + extraBufferCapacity slots that every subscriber of a MutableSharedFlow reads from, each at its own place. There is no queue per subscriber. Rendezvous A hand-over with no buffer: the value passes only while the sender waits and the receiver takes it. The default MutableSharedFlow() works this way. Taking a value The moment a subscriber reads a value off the shared buffer, before its collect lambda runs. Only values not yet taken count against the buffer. Equality conflation StateFlow ignores a set that equals the current value, and a waking collector skips a value equal to the last one it emitted. Sharing coroutine The one coroutine that shareIn or stateIn launches in your scope to collect the upstream: the cook who serves every diner. It lives as long as the scope, whatever the subscribers do. Stop timeout How long WhileSubscribed waits after the last subscriber leaves before it cancels the upstream. A subscriber who returns sooner cancels the stop. Default MutableSharedFlow() with one idle subscriber: what does tryEmit return? false. There is no buffer, so a value can only pass from a suspended emit to a subscriber taking it (a rendezvous). With no subscriber at all it returns true and the value goes nowhere. When is a MutableSharedFlow's buffer full? When the slowest subscriber has replay + extraBufferCapacity values it hasn't taken yet. With no subscribers it is never full. One subscriber stalls under DROP_LATEST. Does the quick subscriber lose values too? Yes. The dropped value was never stored, so nobody gets it. Only DROP_OLDEST limits the skipping to the slow subscriber. What does a subscriber that joins a SharedFlow late receive? The replay cache, then live values. Never the backlog that slower subscribers are still working through. A StateFlow goes A, then B, then A while its collector is busy. What does the collector see when it is free? Nothing new. It reads the current value (A), which equals the last one it emitted, so it emits nothing. Does reading stateFlow.value start a Lazily or WhileSubscribed upstream? No. .value is not a subscription. A value that is only read through .value needs Eagerly (or the suspend stateIn(scope)). WhileSubscribed(5_000): the last subscriber leaves and a new one arrives 2 s later. Does the upstream restart? No: the pending stop is cancelled and the same run continues. After more than 5 s it restarts from the top, and the newcomer first sees the stale value unless replayExpirationMillis = 0.

h: Hot flows in depth: SharedFlow, StateFlow and sharing · Go deeper
x: The internals, for a curious day. The field names here are private and may change in any release, so don't build on them. Every collector of a shared flow gets a slot object from an array that starts at size 2 and doubles when full: 2 for one or two subscribers, 4 for three or four, 8 for five. A SharedFlow slot holds the index of the next value its collector will read, plus that collector's suspended continuation. The slate is a ring buffer, also allocated lazily and doubled when needed, and it holds the buffered values followed by the suspended emit calls as placeholder objects. Its start, head, is the smaller of the slowest collector's index and the start of the replay cache. When the slowest collector moves on, head moves, the old cells are cleared, and waiting emitters are resumed as their values move onto the slate. Every change happens under one lock, and the coroutines to resume are collected and resumed after the lock is released. The KDoc puts the cost of an emit at O(N) in the number of subscribers. A StateFlow slot is one atomic field: free, waiting, pending, or a suspended continuation. An update marks every slot pending and copies nothing, which is why the KDoc calls StateFlow allocation-free. Updates that race each other use a sequence number that is odd while an update is being delivered. A second writer that arrives in the middle only bumps it, and the first writer loops round to deliver the newest value. Two APIs in this area are experimental in 1.11.0 and need @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class). resetReplayCache() empties the replay cache for new subscribers, while existing ones keep what they had; on a MutableStateFlow it throws UnsupportedOperationException: MutableStateFlow.resetReplayCache is not supported. SharedFlow.asFlow(), new in 1.11.0, hides the hot type from callers. The suspend overload stateIn(scope) has no started. It launches the upstream in scope, suspends until the first value, and returns a StateFlow holding it: in one run, a settings flow whose first value took 300 ms made stateIn return at t=300. That fits a setting loaded once at start-up. An empty upstream throws NoSuchElementException: Flow is empty. An upstream that fails before its first value rethrows to the caller and also cancels the scope you passed, so choose that scope knowing it goes down with a failed load.

h: Bridges and tests: callbackFlow, Reactor and runTest · A callbackFlow is a hatch between the probe and your flow
x: A hatch fitted to the old oven probe: callbackFlow registers only when its producer runs, so a reading fired at once is lost; trySend fills a 64-spot shelf (65 of a 200 burst get in), awaitClose takes the hatch down, Java gets a Flux, and advanceTimeBy(100) stops just before a task due at 100 Here is a first bridge from the probe's listener to a flow, a recipe card for values that a collector receives by calling collect. The caller starts collecting in a coroutine (a light piece of work that can pause without holding a thread), gives way once with yield(), a pause that lets other coroutines run, and then the probe fires a reading: Java // Java equivalent: Flux.create runs its lambda inside subscribe(), so the listener is there at once Flux<ProbeEvent> events = Flux.create(sink -> { ProbeRegistration registration = probe.register(new ProbeEventListener() { public void onEvent(ProbeEvent e) { sink.next(e); } public void onError(Throwable t) { sink.error(t); } public void onClosed() { sink.complete(); } }); sink.onDispose(registration::unregister); }); events.subscribe(e -> System.out.println("got " + e)); probe.fire(new ProbeEvent(0, 61)); // got ProbeEvent(seq=0, celsius=61) Kotlin fun DemoProbe.events(): Flow<ProbeEvent> = callbackFlow { val registration = register(object : ProbeEventListener { override fun onEvent(event: ProbeEvent) { trySend(event) } // on the probe's thread override fun onError(error: Throwable) { close(error) } override fun onClosed() { close() } }) awaitClose { registration.unregister() } } launch { probe.events().collect { println("got $it") } } yield() probe.fire(ProbeEvent(0, 61)) // fired with listeners=0 callbackFlow is a flow builder for listener APIs. Its block registers a listener that drops each value into a channel, a queue between coroutines, and the collector takes the values out on the other side. The Kotlin reading is lost. collect on a callbackFlow starts a producer coroutine, and your block, with its register call, runs inside that coroutine only when it is first scheduled. launch and one yield() got the collector going, but not its producer. Reactor's Flux.create runs its lambda inside subscribe(), on the calling thread, so the Java version has no gap. In Kotlin, collecting does not mean registered. A test must wait for the registration, and real code must not count on it. Picture the bridge as the hatch with a shelf from Context and threads, fitted to the probe. The probe's thread puts each reading on the shelf with trySend, which never waits. send would wait for room, so it is a suspend function, one that can pause its coroutine, and calling it from a plain listener method doesn't compile: "suspension functions can only be called within coroutine body". awaitClose { } is you standing at the hatch until you're told to leave, and then taking the hatch down. It suspends until the channel closes and runs its block in a finally, so the listener goes away whatever ended the flow: take(2), a cancelled collector, close(error) from onError (the collector's collect throws that error), or close() from onClosed (the flow completes normally). Forget awaitClose, and the library sounds an alarm as soon as the block returns with the channel still open. It is quite insistent: java.lang.IllegalStateException: 'awaitClose { yourCallbackOrListener.cancel() }' should be used in the end of callbackFlow block. Otherwise, a callback/listener may leak in case of external cancellation. See callbackFlow API documentation for the details. Reactor has no such check. A Flux.create without onDispose still has its listener registered after take(1) has finished, and nothing tells you. For your own coroutines feeding one flow, such as two thermometers that you launch yourself, use channelFlow from lesson 3 of this track: the same machinery without the check, and it completes when the block and all its children are done. For a callback that fires only once, use suspendCancellableCoroutine. Collecting is not registering. End every callbackFlow with awaitClose. Check yourself: the collector is cancelled while it waits for a reading. Which line of the bridge runs, and on which ending of the flow would it not run? The listener is now in place and goes away cleanly. The probe's first act on connect is to send everything it stored. Bridge the probe five ways Read ProbeBridge.kt. For parts 0 to 5, predict each [probe] line and what the collector gets. Run it, then run the Java twin, which bridges the same probe with Flux.create. In part 0, replace the first yield() with probe0.awaitRegistered() and run again. Predict first. registration = register(object : ProbeEventListener { override fun onEvent(event: ProbeEvent) { trySend(event) } // never blocks the probe's thread override fun onError(error: Throwable) { 65)); yield() probe3.fail(IOException("probe connection lost")); j3.join() println("== 4. the probe says it is done: close() completes the flow") val probe4 = DemoProbe() val j4 = launch { println(" completed with " + probe4.events().toList()) } probe4.awaitRegistered(); probe4.fire(ProbeEvent(5, 66)); probe4.close(); j4.join() println("== 5. trySend after the channel is closed") val ch = ProbeEventListener() { @Override public void onEvent(ProbeEvent event) { sink.next(event); } @Override public void onError(Throwable error) { sink.error(error); } @Override public void onClosed() { sink.complete(); } })); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("== 0. fire right after subscribe: is the listener there yet?"); DemoProbe probe0 = new DemoProbe(); var d0 = events(probe0).subscribe(e -> System.out.println(" got " + e)); probe0.fire(new ProbeEvent(0, 61)); d0.dispose(); System.out.println("== 1. Flux.create without onDispose: no error, and the listener stays"); DemoProbe probe1 = new DemoProbe(); eventsWithoutOnDispose(probe1).take(1).subscribe(); probe1.fire(new ProbeEvent(1, 62)); System.out.println(" after take(1) finished: listeners=" + probe1.getListeners().size()); System.out.println("== 2. take(2) cancels, and onDispose unregisters"); DemoProbe probe = new DemoProbe(); List<ProbeEvent> two = new ArrayList<>(); events(probe).take(2).subscribe(two::add); probe.fire(new ProbeEvent(1, 62)); probe.fire(new ProbeEvent(2, 63)); probe.fire(new ProbeEvent(3, 64)); System.out.println(" got " + two); System.out.println("== 3. the probe reports an error: sink.error fails the Flux"); DemoProbe probe3 = new DemoProbe(); events(probe3).subscribe(e -> System.out.println(" got " + e), e -> System.out.println(" subscriber got onError " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage())); probe3.fire(new ProbeEvent(4, 65)); probe3.fail(new IOException("probe connection lost")); System.out.println("== 4. the probe says it is done: sink.complete completes the Flux"); DemoProbe probe4 = new DemoProbe(); List<ProbeEvent> all = new ArrayList<>(); events(probe4).subscribe(all::add, e -> {}, () -> System.out.println(" completed with " + all)); probe4.fire(new ProbeEvent(5, 66)); probe4.close(); } } ./gradlew :flows:demo -Pmain=workbench.flows.l08.ProbeBridgeJava labs/flows/src/demo/java/workbench/flows/l08/ProbeBridgeJava.java Part 0 prints fired with listeners=0, and registered only after it, so the collector gets nothing. Part 1 throws the IllegalStateException above, right after registered. Parts 2 to 4 each print unregistered: after take(2) with the first two readings, before the collector catches IOException: probe connection lost, and when the flow completes with the last reading. Part 5 shows trySend on a closed channel: isSuccess=false isClosed=true. With awaitRegistered(), part 0 prints registered, then fired with listeners=1 and got ProbeEvent(seq=0, celsius=61). The Java twin registers inside subscribe(), so its part 0 gets the reading at once, and its part 1 still has listeners=1 after take(1), with no error at all. callbackFlow (kotlinx.coroutines API) docs awaitClose (kotlinx.coroutines API) docs

h: Bridges and tests: callbackFlow, Reactor and runTest · A burst of 200 on connect: 64 spots and one waiting hand
x: The probe keeps its readings while nobody listens, and on connect it replays them in one burst, from its own thread, one callback after another. Fire 200 readings into a default callbackFlow while its collector waits in receive(), and 135 trySend calls fail. The other 65 got through: 64 onto the shelf (Channel.BUFFERED), and one handed straight to the receiver that was already waiting, before the shelf was touched. So a shelf of 64 takes 65 when someone is waiting at the hatch. Better to know that before a test counts it for you. trySend returns a ChannelResult that says whether it worked. Ignore it, and the 135 failures are silent losses. After the channel is closed it fails too, with isClosed=true. The fix is a policy you choose on purpose. A buffer(...) or conflate() right after callbackFlow { } fuses into its one channel (the shelves snapping together from Buffering), so it changes that channel instead of adding a second one: After callbackFlow { } trySend failures The collector got nothing (64, SUSPEND) 135 65 accepted .buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED) 0 all 200 .conflate() 0 [0, 199]: the first went to the waiting receiver, the last stayed in the one spot .buffer(10, DROP_OLDEST) 0 [0, 190, 191, ..., 199] Java // Java equivalent: Flux.create buffers without limit by default (OverflowStrategy.BUFFER); // onBackpressureBuffer(500) caps it and fails with an overflow error past 500 Flux<ProbeReading> readings = Flux.create(sink -> { /* register, sink.next, onDispose */ }) .onBackpressureBuffer(500); Kotlin fun FakeProbe.readings(): Flow<ProbeReading> = callbackFlow { /* register, trySend, awaitClose */ } .buffer(500) // fused: the bridge's own channel now holds the 500 stored readings trySendBlocking(e) looks like the safe version. It is trySend with a fallback of runBlocking { send(e) }, so when the shelf is full it blocks the probe's own thread until there is room. With the probe's thread pushing 200 readings and a collector that takes 2 ms each, trySend let the thread finish in about 1 ms and lost 135, while trySendBlocking lost none and held the probe's thread for about 340 ms. (That run uses the real clock, so your numbers will differ.) Use it only when the library runs your callback on a worker thread of its own, and making that thread wait is how you slow it down. Pick UNLIMITED only when the producer is known to stop. For a feed where only the latest value matters, conflate() drops readings in a way you can explain. A failed trySend is a lost reading. Size the shelf for the burst, or choose what to drop. Check yourself: what does the collector get from the same burst after .buffer(10, DROP_LATEST)? The probe now feeds a flow without losing anything. The neighbour wants the readings too, and her kitchen speaks Reactor. Count what a burst leaves behind Read ProbeBurst.kt. For each of the four buffers in part 1, predict the trySend failures and what the collector gets. Run it. Part 2 runs on real threads, so its numbers change from run to run. Run the Java twin. Which Reactor overflow strategy behaves like conflate(), and what does Reactor do by default? REAL time. private fun probeThread(blocking: Boolean): Flow<Int> = callbackFlow { var failed = 0 val probe = thread(name = "probe-io") { val t0 = System.nanoTime() repeat(200) { if (blocking) trySendBlocking(it) else if (trySend(it).isFailure) failed++ } println(" probe thread done after ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms, trySend failures=$failed") channel.close() } awaitClose { probe.join() } } fun main() = runBlocking { println("== 1. a burst of 200 callbacks before the collector can run") println(" default buffer (64, SUSPEND):"); println(" collector got ${burst(200).take(64).count()}, then cancelled") println(" buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED):"); println(" collector got ${burst(200).buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED).take(200).count()}") println(" conflate():"); println(" collector got ${burst(200).conflate().take(2).toList()}") println(" buffer(10, DROP_OLDEST):"); println(" collector got ${burst(200).buffer(10, BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST).take(11).toList()}") println("== 2. the probe's own thread, collector takes 2 ms per reading (REAL time, numbers vary)") for (blocking in listOf(false, true)) { println(" ${if (blocking) "trySendBlocking" else "trySend"} into the default buffer:") println(" collector received ${probeThread(blocking).onEach { delay(2) }.count()}") } } ./gradlew :flows:demo -Pmain=workbench.flows.l08.ProbeBurstKt labs/flows/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/flows/l08/ProbeBurst.kt ProbeBurstJava.java package workbench.flows.l08; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import org.reactivestreams.Subscription; import reactor.core.publisher.BaseSubscriber; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.FluxSink; // Java equivalent: Flux.create takes an OverflowStrategy instead of a buffer size. // 200 synchronous callbacks arrive while the subscriber has asked for one item. public class ProbeBurstJava { static void burst(String label, FluxSink.OverflowStrategy strategy) { List<Integer> got = new ArrayList<>(); BaseSubscriber<Integer> slow = new BaseSubscriber<>() { @Override protected void hookOnSubscribe(Subscription s) { request(1); } @Override protected void hookOnNext(Integer v) { got.add(v); } @Override protected void hookOnError(Throwable e) { System.out.println(" onError " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()); } }; Flux.<Integer>create(sink -> { for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) sink.next(i); }, strategy).subscribe(slow); slow.request(Long.MAX_VALUE); // the subscriber catches up String shown = got.size() > 6 ? got.size() + " items: " + got.subList(0, 3) + " ... " + got.get(got.size() - 1) : got.toString(); System.out.println(" " + label + ": subscriber got " + shown); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("== 1. a burst of 200 callbacks, the subscriber has requested 1"); burst("BUFFER (the default, unbounded)", FluxSink.OverflowStrategy.BUFFER); burst("LATEST", FluxSink.OverflowStrategy.LATEST); burst("DROP", FluxSink.OverflowStrategy.DROP); burst("ERROR", FluxSink.OverflowStrategy.ERROR); } } ./gradlew :flows:demo -Pmain=workbench.flows.l08.ProbeBurstJava labs/flows/src/demo/java/workbench/flows/l08/ProbeBurstJava.java Part 1 matches the table: 135 failures with 64 collected before take(64) cancels, then 0 failures and 200, then [0, 199], then [0, 190, ..., 199]. In part 2, trySend lets the probe's thread finish almost at once with about 135 failures, and the collector receives about 65. trySendBlocking holds the probe's thread for about 300 ms or more and loses nothing. In the Java twin, BUFFER, the default, keeps all 200 because it has no limit; LATEST gives [0, 199], the same as conflate(); DROP keeps only [0]; and ERROR delivers reading 0 and then fails with OverflowException. trySendBlocking (kotlinx.coroutines API) docs

h: Bridges and tests: callbackFlow, Reactor and runTest · Across the Reactor bridge, demand becomes suspension
x: Reactor follows Reactive Streams, a small standard set of Java interfaces for streams, and it makes the subscriber say how much it can take, with request(n). That number is called demand. A Flow has no such call: it suspends. The bridges in the kotlinx-coroutines-reactive and kotlinx-coroutines-reactor modules translate one into the other. Publisher.asFlow() works like a diner with an order pad, sitting at the end of the neighbour's line of stations. It orders 64, eats them, and orders 64 more after every 64 it has passed on. (A Flux is a Publisher, so flux.asFlow() is this same function.) The items wait in a channel of that size, and buffer sets the size of the order: Flow side Requests sent to a 300-item Flux asFlow() 64 after 0, 64, 128, 192 and 256 asFlow().buffer(10) 10 every 10 asFlow().buffer(0) 1 every 1 asFlow().conflate() or .buffer(UNLIMITED) Long.MAX_VALUE, once asFlow().take(3) 64, then cancel: the 61 extra already in the channel are thrown away That is a refill in batches. Reactor's own operators top up earlier: publishOn asked a Flow-backed Flux for 256 and then 192 at a time, and limitRate(10) for 10 and then 8. Flow.asFlux() and asPublisher() go the other way. Nothing runs until the first request(n). Then each emit calls onNext right there, inside emit, and counts the demand down. When it reaches 0, the flow suspends inside that emit, and a later request resumes it. After request(2) the subscriber had [1, 2], and emit had returned only for 1: the flow was parked inside emit(2). Cancelling the subscription cancels the flow's coroutine, so a callbackFlow underneath runs its awaitClose. Two details bite in real programs. The bridge runs the flow on Dispatchers.Unconfined unless you pass a dispatcher (the part that picks the thread a coroutine runs on), so the flow and every Reactor operator after it run on whichever thread resumed it: the subscriber's thread at first, kotlinx.coroutines.DefaultExecutor after a delay, and the probe's own thread under a probe bridge. Pass asFlux(dispatcher), or add publishOn before anything slow downstream. And Reactor's Context, a small map of values that travels with a subscription, crosses in both directions. Through asFlux(), a table number written with contextWrite was visible inside the flow as a ReactorContext element. The other way, a ReactorContext in the coroutine reaches a publisher collected with asFlow() only when kotlinx-coroutines-reactor is on the classpath, the list of libraries the program can see, because that module supplies the piece that injects it, found with ServiceLoader. Java can't call Flow.collect, which it sees as Object collect(FlowCollector, Continuation). Give Java a face built in Kotlin: Java // Java caller: only Reactor types, no Flow and no Continuation List<ProbeReading> firstTwo = new ProbeApi(probe).readingsFlux().take(2).collectList().block(); Kotlin class ProbeApi(private val probe: FakeProbe) { fun readings(): Flow<ProbeReading> = probe.readings() // for Kotlin callers fun readingsFlux(): Flux<ProbeReading> = readings().asFlux() // for Java and Reactor callers } For a single result, a CompletableFuture built with scope.future { } is the better face, as lesson 11 of the coroutines track showed. Give Java a Flux or a future, never a Flow. Check yourself: how many requests does asFlow().buffer(10) send to a 300-item Flux, and why one more than 30? Every bridge in this lesson has a timing story, and testing timing on a real clock is slow and flaky. So the house rehearses. Watch request(n) cross the bridge Read ReactorDemand.kt. Predict the request lines in part 1 and the two lines of part 2. Run it. Then run the Java twin, which consumes the same Kotlin flows through PlateFaces and sees only Reactor types. In part 3, change asFlux() to asFlux(Dispatchers.IO) (import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers) and predict the thread names. Flux -> Flow: the collector's demand becomes request(n)") demand("asFlow()") { it.asFlow().collect { } } demand("asFlow().buffer(10)") { it.asFlow().buffer(10).collect { } } demand("asFlow().buffer(0)") { it.asFlow().buffer(0).take(3).collect { } } demand("asFlow().conflate()") { it.asFlow().conflate().collect { } } demand("asFlow().buffer(UNLIMITED)") { it.asFlow().buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED).collect { } } demand("asFlow().take(3)") { it.asFlow().take(3).collect { } } println("== 2. Flow -> Flux: the flow suspends inside emit when the demand runs out") val returned = mutableListOf<Int>() val received = mutableListOf<Int>() lateinit var subscription: Subscription PlateFaces.platesTracked(returned).subscribe(object : BaseSubscriber<Int>() { override fun hookOnSubscribe(s: Subscription) { subscription = s; s.request(2) } override fun hookOnNext(v: Int) { received += v } }) println(" after request(2): received=$received, emit() returned for $returned") subscription.request(3) println(" after request(3): received=$received, emit() returned for $returned") subscription.cancel() println("== 3. threads: asFlux() runs the flow on Dispatchers.Unconfined") val threads: Flow<String> = flow { emit("before delay: " + Thread.currentThread().name) delay(10) emit("after delay: " + Thread.currentThread().name) } threads.asFlux().map { "$it | onNext on " + Thread.currentThread().name }.collectList().block()!!.forEach { println(" $it") } println("== 4. context: a Reactor Context reaches the flow as ReactorContext") val table = flow { emit(currentCoroutineContext()[ReactorContext]?.context?.getOrDefault("table", "none") ?: "no ReactorContext") } println(" with contextWrite: " + table.asFlux().contextWrite(Context.of("table", "table-7")).blockFirst()) println(" without: " + table.asFlux().blockFirst()) } ./gradlew :flows:demo -Pmain=workbench.flows.l08.ReactorDemandKt labs/flows/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/flows/l08/ReactorDemand.kt ReactorDemandJava.java package workbench.flows.l08; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.UnaryOperator; import org.reactivestreams.Subscription; import reactor.core.publisher.BaseSubscriber; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; // Java equivalent: a Java caller consumes Kotlin flows through the Flux faces in PlateFaces // (ReactorDemand.kt). It sees only Reactor types. Reactor's own operators decide the demand. public class ReactorDemandJava { static void probe(String label, UnaryOperator<Flux<Integer>> operator) { List<String> requests = new ArrayList<>(); Flux<Integer> source = PlateFaces.plates() // 600 plates from a Kotlin flow .doOnRequest(n -> requests.add(n == Long.MAX_VALUE ? "MAX" : Long.toString(n))); operator.apply(source).blockLast(); String shown = requests.size() > 6 ? requests.subList(0, 6) + " ... h: Bridges and tests: callbackFlow, Reactor and runTest · The test clock has edges: where runCurrent, advanceTimeBy and advanceUntilIdle stop
x: runTest is the rehearsal dinner from lesson 10 of the coroutines track. It replaces the clock with a scheduler that jumps from one due task to the next, so a delay takes no real time: that fake clock is virtual time. Three calls move it along, and each one stops in a different place: runCurrent() runs everything that is due now. advanceTimeBy(n) runs ahead up to, but not including, now + n. With tasks due at 100 and 200, advanceTimeBy(100) leaves the clock at 100 with fired=[]. Only runCurrent() then runs the task at 100. advanceUntilIdle() runs ahead until only background work is left. With nothing but a poller in backgroundScope, it leaves t=0 polls=0, while advanceTimeBy(5000) plus runCurrent() gives t=5000 polls=5. backgroundScope is a scope inside runTest for coroutines that never end on their own; they are cancelled when the test body ends. A test that collects a hot flow there should drive the clock with advanceTimeBy(...) and runCurrent(), as this track's labs do. Reactor's virtual clock puts the edge elsewhere: Java // Java equivalent: Reactor's VirtualTimeScheduler includes the end point @Test void taskDueAt100RunsWithAdvanceTimeBy() { VirtualTimeScheduler clock = VirtualTimeScheduler.create(); List<Long> fired = new ArrayList<>(); clock.schedule(() -> fired.add(100L), 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); clock.advanceTimeBy(Duration.ofMillis(100)); assertThat(fired).containsExactly(100L); // already ran, no extra step } Kotlin @Test fun `the task due at 100 needs runCurrent`() = runTest { val fired = mutableListOf<Long>() launch { delay(100); fired += currentTime } advanceTimeBy(100) assertThat(fired).isEmpty() // runs only what is due BEFORE now + 100 runCurrent() assertThat(fired).containsExactly(100L) // runs what is due now } The test dispatcher decides what a StateFlow collector sees. A dish tracker's cookAndServe() sets COOKING and then SERVED, with no suspension between them. A collector on the default StandardTestDispatcher runs only when the test lets the clock move, so it saw [ORDERED, SERVED]. One launched with UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler), which runs a coroutine at once, inside the call that wakes it, saw all three. That dispatcher is experimental. A real collector on Dispatchers.Default, which runs coroutines on real threads, can see either. So the Unconfined test shows the most a collector can see, and the Standard one shows the menu board skipping a value. Assert on the final state and on the changes that matter. If every change matters, the type shouldn't be a StateFlow. Two failures come with exact messages. async { status.take(3).toList() } waits for a third value that the board skipped, and with runTest(timeout = 500.milliseconds) it ends in UncompletedCoroutinesError: After waiting for 500ms, the test body did not run to completion. (The default timeout is 60 s, and the 20 s JUnit timeout in these labs fires first.) A hot flow collected in the test scope itself, or stateIn(this, WhileSubscribed(), 0), fails with there were active child jobs, followed by the advice to use TestScope.backgroundScope. advanceTimeBy(n) stops just before n. Follow it with runCurrent(). Check yourself: change advanceTimeBy(100) to advanceTimeBy(101) in the first part of the Try it. What does its first line print? Driving the clock by hand is precise and a little tedious. A library can read the flow for you, and its one blind spot is worth knowing. Find the edges of the test clock Read TestClock.kt. Predict every line before you run it, the two error messages included. Run it. Parts 4 and 5 each wait 500 ms of real time for the runTest timeout. In part 1, change advanceTimeBy(100) to advanceTimeBy(101). What does the first line print now? _status.value = "SERVED" } // no suspension between } // The edges of the test clock. runTest is called from main here; in a test it is the body. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun main() { runTest { println("== 1. advanceTimeBy(n) runs what is due BEFORE now + n") val fired = mutableListOf<Long>() launch { delay(100); fired += currentTime } launch { delay(200); fired += currentTime } advanceTimeBy(100); println(" after advanceTimeBy(100): t=$currentTime fired=$fired") runCurrent(); println(" after runCurrent(): t=$currentTime fired=$fired") advanceUntilIdle(); println(" after advanceUntilIdle(): t=$currentTime fired=$fired") } runTest { println("== 2. advanceUntilIdle() stops once only backgroundScope work is left") var polls = 0 backgroundScope.launch { while (true) { delay(1_000); polls++ } } // a poller that never ends, like a thermometer advanceUntilIdle(); println(" after advanceUntilIdle(): t=$currentTime polls=$polls") advanceTimeBy(5_000); runCurrent(); println(" after advanceTimeBy(5000) + runCurrent(): t=$currentTime polls=$polls") } runTest { println("== 3. a StateFlow set twice in a row, collected two ways") val a = DishTracker(); val standard = mutableListOf<String>() backgroundScope.launch { a.status.toList(standard) } runCurrent(); a.cookAndServe(); runCurrent() val b = DishTracker(); val unconfined = mutableListOf<String>() backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { b.status.toList(unconfined) } b.cookAndServe() println(" Standard collector: $standard") println(" Unconfined collector: $unconfined") } println("== 4. take(3) on that StateFlow (runTest timeout 500 ms of REAL time)") try { runTest(timeout = 500.milliseconds) { val t = DishTracker() val three = async { t.status.take(3).toList() } runCurrent() t.cookAndServe() println(" got ${three.await()}") } } catch (e: Throwable) { println(" ${e::class.qualifiedName}: ${e.message?.lines()?.first()}") } println("== 5. stateIn(this, WhileSubscribed()) inside runTest, over flowOf(1, 2, 3)") try { runTest(timeout = 500.milliseconds) { val s = flowOf(1, 2, 3).stateIn(this, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(), 0) println(" saw ${s.first { it == 3 }}, test body done") } println(" test passed") } catch (e: Throwable) { println(" ${e::class.qualifiedName}: ${e.message?.lines()?.first()?.replace(Regex("@[0-9a-f]+"), "@...")}") } } ./gradlew :flows:demo -Pmain=workbench.flows.l08.TestClockKt labs/flows/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/flows/l08/TestClock.kt Part 1: t=100 fired=[], then fired=[100] after runCurrent(), then t=200 fired=[100, 200]. Part 2: t=0 polls=0, then t=5000 polls=5. Part 3: [ORDERED, SERVED] for the Standard collector and [ORDERED, COOKING, SERVED] for the Unconfined one. Part 4: UncompletedCoroutinesError: After waiting for 500ms, the test body did not run to completion. Part 5 prints saw 3, test body done and then fails with there were active child jobs, because the WhileSubscribed sharing coroutine never ends. With advanceTimeBy(101) the clock stops at 101 and the task at 100 has already run, so the first line reads t=101 fired=[100]. (Reactor's virtual clock has no Java twin here: it lives in reactor-test, which only the tests can use.) advanceTimeBy(n) runs what is due before now + n, runCurrent() runs what is due now, and advanceUntilIdle() stops once only backgroundScope work is left. h: Bridges and tests: callbackFlow, Reactor and runTest · Turbine writes down every value, and that is its blind spot
x: Turbine 1.2.1 (app.cash.turbine, a test dependency of this lab module) is a test library that turns a flow into a list of events you read one by one: Java // Java equivalent: StepVerifier subscribes, then runs each step in order StepVerifier.create(api.readingsFlux()) .then(() -> probe.fire(first)) .expectNext(first) .then(() -> probe.fail(new IOException("probe connection lost"))) .expectErrorMessage("probe connection lost") .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(5)); Kotlin probe.readings().test { // collects before the block runs: the listener is registered probe.fire(first) assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo(first) probe.fail(IOException("probe connection lost")) assertThat(awaitError()).hasMessage("probe connection lost") } Picture the rehearsal's note-taker. test { } runs the flow up to its first suspension before your block starts, so a SharedFlow is subscribed and a callbackFlow listener is registered by then, which removes the race from the first section. Every event goes into her notebook, an unlimited channel, in order. You read it with awaitItem(), awaitComplete() and awaitError(), which hands you the error as an event instead of throwing it. An event you never read fails the test with Unconsumed events found, unless you end with cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents(). If no new event arrives within 3 s of real time, the test fails with No value produced in 3s. The flow's own delay calls stay virtual inside runTest; only Turbine's wait is real. To follow two flows at once, call testIn(backgroundScope) inside turbineScope { }. Outside it, testIn compiles and then fails at run time with Turbine can only collect flows within a TurbineContext. The note-taker hears everything, and that is her blind spot. Turbine collects on UnconfinedTestDispatcher, so it takes each value the instant it is sent. It saw COOKING, which the Standard collector of the last section never got. It also took all 500 readings of a burst through a 64-spot callbackFlow, where a Standard collector got 65. She never misses a word, which makes her a poor witness to what a slower listener would miss. So use Turbine to check what a flow emits and in what order. Don't use it to test skipped values, buffer sizes or a slow collector. For those, collect with a Standard collector in backgroundScope and drive the clock yourself, as the lab's burst test does. And on a SharedFlow with no replay, a value emitted before test { } starts is gone, so the test fails with No value produced. Turbine shows what a flow says, not what a slow listener hears. Test buffers with a Standard collector. Check yourself: which test in the lab would still pass with a 64-spot buffer if you rewrote it with Turbine, and why? Every bridge in this lesson sits on top of something that waits: a probe's thread, a Reactor line, a clock. Underneath them all is the place where waiting really happens. A tour of Turbine Read TurbineTourTest.kt. For each of the eight tests, predict the commented line before you run anything. Run the class with the command below. All eight pass; test 6 waits half a second of real time. In test 4, delete the line that awaits SERVED and run again. Predict the failure message first. Read each one, predict the commented line, then run the class. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) // TestScope.runCurrent is experimental in 1.11.0 class TurbineTourTest { @Test fun `1 items and completion are awaited in order`() = runTest { flowOf("COOKING", "SERVED").test { assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo("COOKING") assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo("SERVED") awaitComplete() } } @Test fun `2 an event you did not read fails the test`() = runTest { val failure = runCatching { flowOf("one", "two").test { awaitItem() } }.exceptionOrNull() assertThat(failure).hasMessageContaining("Unconsumed events found") // lists Item(two) and Complete } @Test fun `3 an error arrives as an event, not as a thrown exception`() = runTest { flow { emit(1); throw IOException("probe lost") }.test { assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo(1) assertThat(awaitError()).hasMessage("probe lost") } } @Test fun `4 Turbine sees every StateFlow value, a Standard collector does not`() = runTest { val tracker = TourTracker() tracker.status.test { assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo("ORDERED") tracker.cookAndServe() assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo("COOKING") // Turbine collects on UnconfinedTestDispatcher assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo("SERVED") } val other = TourTracker() val seen = mutableListOf<String>() backgroundScope.launch { other.status.toList(seen) } // StandardTestDispatcher, closer to production runCurrent() other.cookAndServe() runCurrent() assertThat(seen).containsExactly("ORDERED", "SERVED") } @Test fun `5 Turbine never lets a callbackFlow buffer fill`() = runTest { val probe = FakeProbe() val defaultBuffer: Flow<ProbeReading> = callbackFlow { // 64 slots, as callbackFlow has by default val r = probe.register(object : ProbeListener { override fun onReading(reading: ProbeReading) { trySend(reading) } override fun onError(error: Throwable) { close(error) } override fun onClosed() { close() } }) awaitClose { r.unregister() } } defaultBuffer.test { probe.burst(500) repeat(500) { awaitItem() } // all 500 arrive: each one was taken the moment it was sent cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents() } val seen = mutableListOf<ProbeReading>() backgroundScope.launch { defaultBuffer.collect { seen += it } } runCurrent() probe.burst(500) runCurrent() assertThat(seen).hasSize(65) // a Standard collector: 64 buffered plus 1 handed straight over } @Test fun `6 a SharedFlow value emitted before test {} is lost`() = runTest { val events = MutableSharedFlow<String>() events.emit("SERVED") // nobody is subscribed yet, and replay = 0 val failure = runCatching { events.test(timeout = 500.milliseconds) { awaitItem() } }.exceptionOrNull() assertThat(failure).hasMessage("No value produced in 500ms") // after 500 ms of REAL time } @Test fun `7 the flow's delays are virtual, Turbine's timeout is wall-clock`() = runTest { flow { delay(10.seconds); emit("late") }.test(timeout = 200.milliseconds) { assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo("late") awaitComplete() } } @Test fun `8 several flows at once with turbineScope and testIn`() = runTest { turbineScope { val readings = flowOf(180, 181).testIn(backgroundScope, name = "readings") val alerts = flowOf("door open").testIn(backgroundScope, name = "alerts") assertThat(readings.awaitItem()).isEqualTo(180) assertThat(alerts.awaitItem()).isEqualTo("door open") assertThat(readings.awaitItem()).isEqualTo(181) readings.awaitComplete() alerts.awaitComplete() } } } ./gradlew :flows:test --tests Every test passes; read each one and predict before you run the class. class StepVerifierTourTest { @Test @DisplayName("1. items and completion are expected in order") void itemsThenComplete() { StepVerifier.create(Flux.just("COOKING", "SERVED")) .expectNext("COOKING") .expectNext("SERVED") .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1));
