h: Bridges and tests: callbackFlow, Reactor and runTest · Java and Kotlin
x: A probe bridge: Flux.create next to callbackFlow ProbeReadings.java (Reactor) static Flux<ProbeReading> readings(FakeProbe probe) { return Flux.<ProbeReading>create(sink -> { Registration registration = probe.register(new ProbeListener() { @Override public void onReading(ProbeReading r) { sink.next(r); } // runs the subscriber inline @Override public void onError(Throwable t) { sink.error(t); } @Override public void onClosed() { sink.complete(); } }); sink.onDispose(registration::unregister); // optional: nothing complains if it is missing }) .onBackpressureBuffer(500); // the default buffer has no limit } ProbeReadings.kt (callbackFlow) fun FakeProbe.readings(): Flow<ProbeReading> = callbackFlow { val registration = register(object : ProbeListener { override fun onReading(reading: ProbeReading) { trySend(reading) } // never blocks the probe's thread override fun onError(error: Throwable) { close(error) } override fun onClosed() { close() } }) awaitClose { registration.unregister() } // required: collecting throws without it }.buffer(500) // fused into the bridge's channel; the default is 64 The shapes match line for line, and four things differ. Registration time: Flux.create registers inside subscribe(), while callbackFlow registers when its producer coroutine first runs, so a reading fired right after collect starts can be lost. Cleanup: callbackFlow throws when its block returns without awaitClose, and Reactor lets a missing onDispose leak the listener with no message. Buffering: Kotlin's channel holds 64 (65 with a waiting receiver) and makes you look at trySend's result; Reactor buffers without limit unless you add a policy. Threads: sink.next calls the subscriber's onNext on the probe's thread, while the Kotlin collector runs on its own dispatcher and the probe's thread only drops the reading into the channel. That holds until you turn the flow into a Flux with plain asFlux(), whose Unconfined default puts the subscriber back on the probe's thread.

h: Bridges and tests: callbackFlow, Reactor and runTest · Worked example
x: Hand the probe to Java, and test it from both sides Start from the Kotlin bridge, the lab's solution. It registers per collector, never blocks the probe's thread, closes the channel on onError and onClosed, and has room for the 500 stored readings. fun FakeProbe.readings(): Flow<ProbeReading> = callbackFlow { val registration = register(object : ProbeListener { override fun onReading(reading: ProbeReading) { trySend(reading) } // 1. hand over, never block override fun onError(error: Throwable) { close(error) } // 2. fail the flow override fun onClosed() { close() } // 3. complete it }) awaitClose { registration.unregister() } // 4. clean up on any ending }.buffer(500) // Java equivalent of the same four steps static Flux<ProbeReading> readings(FakeProbe probe) { return Flux.<ProbeReading>create(sink -> { Registration registration = probe.register(new ProbeListener() { @Override public void onReading(ProbeReading r) { sink.next(r); } // 1. @Override public void onError(Throwable t) { sink.error(t); } // 2. @Override public void onClosed() { sink.complete(); } // 3. }); sink.onDispose(registration::unregister); // 4. }).onBackpressureBuffer(500); } Give Java a face. asFlux() starts the flow at the first request(n), so registration happens then and not at subscribe(). A cancelled subscription cancels the flow, so awaitClose unregisters. class ProbeApi(private val probe: FakeProbe) { fun readings(): Flow<ProbeReading> = probe.readings() fun readingsFlux(): Flux<ProbeReading> = probe.readings().asFlux() // Unconfined: pass a dispatcher if operators after it are slow } // what the Java caller writes: Reactor types only List<ProbeReading> firstTwo = new ProbeApi(probe).readingsFlux().take(2).collectList().block(); Test the content with Turbine and the buffer with a Standard collector. Turbine registers before its block runs and reads events in order. The burst test needs a collector that can't run during the burst, so it uses the default dispatcher and runCurrent(). @Test fun `a probe error fails the flow`() = runTest { probe.readings().test { probe.fire(first) assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo(first) probe.fail(IOException("probe connection lost")) assertThat(awaitError()).hasMessage("probe connection lost") } } @Test fun `a 500-reading burst arrives in full`() = runTest { val got = mutableListOf<ProbeReading>() backgroundScope.launch { probe.readings().collect { got += it } } runCurrent() // registered and waiting probe.burst(500) // 500 synchronous callbacks runCurrent() assertThat(got).hasSize(500) } // the Java side, with StepVerifier: no demand at first, so nothing is registered yet StepVerifier.create(api.readingsFlux(), 0) .then(() -> assertThat(probe.getListenerCount()).isZero()) .thenRequest(1) .then(() -> probe.fire(first)) .expectNext(first) .thenCancel() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(5)); assertThat(probe.getListenerCount()).isZero(); // cancel reached awaitClose Self-check: why does the burst test avoid Turbine, which would make it shorter? (Turbine collects on UnconfinedTestDispatcher, so every trySend wakes it at once and the reading leaves the channel immediately. The buffer never fills, and a 64-spot version would pass with all 500 readings. In the tour test, a Standard collector got 65.)

Read one failure: it is the awaitClose message from the first section. In ProbeReadings.kt, keep the Registration that register returns, close the channel from onError and onClosed, and end the block with awaitClose. Run ProbeReadingsTest. One test still fails, with a number you have seen in this lesson. Size the bridge's channel for the 500 stored readings that the KDoc promises, without blocking the probe's thread. Then read ProbeReadingsTest and say, for each test, why it uses Turbine, an Unconfined collector or a Standard one. close(error) and close() belong to the ProducerScope the block runs in, so you can call them from inside the listener object. Expected size: 500 but was: 65 is the default 64 spots plus the one reading handed to the waiting collector. A buffer(...) right after callbackFlow { } is fused into its channel. Channel.UNLIMITED passes too; a number states how much memory you allow. Don't reach for trySendBlocking. In the burst test the probe's thread is the test's only thread, the one the collector needs in order to run. asFlux() is in kotlinx.coroutines.reactor. It starts the flow at the first request(n) and cancels it when the subscription is cancelled, which is what the Java tests check. By the end you can wrap a listener API in callbackFlow without leaking the listener or losing values, predict how Reactor demand and Flow suspension map onto each other, give Java callers a Flux, and test flows on virtual time knowing what runCurrent, advanceTimeBy, advanceUntilIdle and Turbine show and hide.

h: Bridges and tests: callbackFlow, Reactor and runTest · Quiz
x: A callbackFlow with the default buffer is followed by .conflate(). Its collector is suspended, waiting for the first value, when the probe fires readings 0 to 199 one after another on its own thread. What does the collector get? [0, 199]: the first went straight to the waiting collector, the last stayed in the one spot [199]: conflate keeps only the latest [0]: the rest were dropped All 200, delivered more slowly conflate() is fused into the callbackFlow's channel and turns it into one spot that a new value overwrites. Reading 0 was handed directly to the receiver that was already waiting, so it never touched the spot; the spot then ended up holding 199. Lesson 4's conflate() works the same way. A test runs backgroundScope.launch { probe.readings().collect { got += it } }, then probe.fire(r) on the next line, then runCurrent(). readings() is a correct callbackFlow with awaitClose. What are got and the listener count afterwards? [r] and 1 [] and 1: the listener registered after the fire [] and 0 [r, r] and 1 The default StandardTestDispatcher only queues the collector. Its producer coroutine, which calls register, runs at runCurrent(), after the fire, so the reading found no listener; from then on one listener is registered. Call runCurrent() before firing, or use Turbine's test { }. Reactor code subscribes to plates.asFlux(), where plates = flow { for (i in 1..10) { emit(i); log += i } }, with a subscriber that calls request(2) and nothing more. What has the subscriber received, and what is in log? [1, 2] and [1, 2] [1..10] in both: asFlux runs 64 ahead Nothing yet: the flow waits for request(64) [1, 2] and [1]: the flow is suspended inside emit(2) asFlux() calls onNext inside emit and then counts the demand down. After the second onNext the demand is 0, so the flow suspends inside emit(2) before log += 2 runs. A later request(n) resumes it. The 64 is the other direction: Publisher.asFlow() requests 64 at a time. cookAndServe() sets a StateFlow to COOKING and then SERVED with no suspension between. Which test setup can show that a collector misses COOKING? Turbine's status.test { } backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { status.toList(seen) } backgroundScope.launch { status.toList(seen) } on the default dispatcher, with runCurrent() before and after async { status.take(3).toList() } Only a Standard collector waits for its turn, so it wakes to SERVED and records [ORDERED, SERVED]. Turbine and the Unconfined collector run inside each set and see all three. take(3) waits for a third value that never comes and fails with UncompletedCoroutinesError. From lesson 7 of this track: people glance at board.value, where board = readings.stateIn(houseScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), null), and nobody ever collects it. What do they read? The latest reading null for ever: reading .value is not a subscription, so the feed never starts The first reading, and never an update An IllegalStateException, because nobody subscribed WhileSubscribed starts the upstream from subscriptionCount, and .value doesn't count as a subscriber. Nothing ever starts the feed. A value that is only read through .value needs Eagerly or the suspend stateIn(scope).

h: Bridges and tests: callbackFlow, Reactor and runTest · Explain it back
x: Explain to a friend why probe.fire(r) right after backgroundScope.launch { probe.readings().collect { ... } } loses the reading in a test, why rewriting the test with Turbine fixes that, and why Turbine would then hide a buffer that is too small.

h: Bridges and tests: callbackFlow, Reactor and runTest · Key terms
x: callbackFlow A flow builder for listener APIs. Its block registers a listener that sends into a channel, and awaitClose removes the listener when the flow ends. awaitClose Suspends the callbackFlow block until its channel is closed, then runs your cleanup, whatever ended the flow. Demand In Reactive Streams, the number of items a subscriber has asked for with request(n) and not yet received. Fusion A buffer, conflate or flowOn placed right after a channel-based flow changes that flow's own channel instead of adding a second one. Virtual time The test scheduler's clock in runTest. It jumps to the next due task, so a delay takes no real time. backgroundScope A scope inside runTest for coroutines that never end. They are cancelled when the test body ends, and advanceUntilIdle() doesn't wait for them. Turbine A test library (app.cash.turbine) that collects a flow into a queue you read with awaitItem, awaitComplete and awaitError. When does a callbackFlow register its listener? When its producer coroutine first runs, after collection starts. A value fired before that is lost. Reactor's Flux.create registers inside subscribe(). What happens when a callbackFlow block returns without awaitClose? Collecting throws IllegalStateException: 'awaitClose { yourCallbackOrListener.cancel() }' should be used in the end of callbackFlow block. A collector waits on a default callbackFlow, and the probe fires 200 readings one after another. How many trySend calls succeed? 65: 64 buffered, plus 1 handed straight to the waiting receiver. The other 135 fail, and are lost unless you check the result. How does Publisher.asFlow() request from the publisher? request(64), then 64 more after every 64 collected. buffer(n) makes it request(n); conflate() and UNLIMITED request Long.MAX_VALUE. With asFlux(), where does the flow suspend when the subscriber's demand runs out? Inside emit, right after the onNext that used the last of the demand. A later request(n) resumes it. Tasks are due at +100 and +200 ms. What does advanceTimeBy(100) run? Nothing: it runs tasks due before now + 100 and leaves the clock at 100. runCurrent() then runs the task at 100. Why can't a Turbine test show a StateFlow skipping a value, or a buffer that is too small? Turbine collects on UnconfinedTestDispatcher and takes every value the instant it is sent, so it sees all values and the buffer never fills.

h: Bridges and tests: callbackFlow, Reactor and runTest · Go deeper
x: The JDK has its own Reactive Streams interfaces, java.util.concurrent.Flow, with Publisher, Subscriber and Subscription. kotlinx.coroutines bridges them in a separate artifact, org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-jdk9:1.11.0. It is a thin wrapper over the reactive module: asFlow(), asPublisher() and collect for the JDK types, with the same demand mapping (a JDK publisher over 150 items saw request(64) three times). You don't need the extra artifact. reactive-streams 1.0.4, already on this lab's classpath through kotlinx-coroutines-reactive, has org.reactivestreams.FlowAdapters, and FlowAdapters.toPublisher(jdkPublisher).asFlow() does the same job. The JDK HttpClient shows why that matters. client.sendAsync(request, BodyHandlers.ofPublisher()) is two bridges in one call. The CompletableFuture completes once, when the headers arrive, so it belongs to await(). The body is a JDK Flow.Publisher<List<ByteBuffer>> that delivers chunks as they come off the socket, so it belongs to asFlow(). In one run against a local server that wrote five lines 50 ms apart, the chunks arrived about 50 ms apart too. Wrapping the future in callbackFlow would be the wrong tool: a single result is a suspendCancellableCoroutine or await() job. A few facts about the Reactor modules themselves. The README of kotlinx-coroutines-reactive calls asPublisher TCK-compliant, meaning it passes the official Reactive Streams compatibility tests. The subscription it creates has no parent job, so its lifetime belongs to the subscription and not to any scope. Element types must be non-null (T : Any), because Reactive Streams forbids null items. And the 1.11.0 reactor module declares reactor-core 3.4.1 in its pom; this course pins 3.8.8, and Gradle picks the higher version.

h: Servers and event loops: NIO, Netty, Vert.x and Jetty
x: Blocking vs non-blocking IO, NIO selectors, Netty pipelines and flow control, Vert.x and Quarkus event loops, Jetty 12, and zero-copy. By the end of this track you can explain what a blocked socket read costs, and why ten thousand idle connections broke servers that give every connection its own thread. You can write a correct java.nio select loop, build and test Netty 4.2 pipelines with codecs, flow control and leak detection, and reason about Vert.x contexts, the event bus and the blocked-thread checker. You can predict which thread runs a Quarkus REST endpoint, set up Jetty 12's thread pool and virtual threads, and choose a server model for a service, down to what the kernel does with epoll, sendfile and io_uring. One picture runs through all eight lessons: a post office, whose clerks, walls of lit boxes, back office and loading dock stand for the threads, selectors, worker pools and kernel calls of a real server. The track assumes no knowledge of NIO, Netty, Vert.x, Quarkus or Jetty. It builds each layer by hand first: a blocking server, then a select loop, then the same ideas in Netty, then the frameworks built on Netty and one that isn't. You need the basics from the first track (threads, locks, races), Little's law from the executors track ("Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law"), and the virtual threads track, which this one connects back to in lessons 1, 6, 7 and 8. Versions are pinned: JDK 21 or newer (install JDK 25, the current long-term support release), Netty 4.2.20.Final, Vert.x 5.2.3, Quarkus 3.40 and Jetty 12.1.14. The labs live in labs/nio, one package per lesson (workbench.nio.l01 to l08). Lessons 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7 have Java labs; lessons 3, 6 and 8 are in Kotlin. Run ./gradlew :nio:test --tests 'workbench.nio.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, and ./gradlew :nio:solutionTest to check the reference answers. Servers in the tests bind 127.0.0.1 on a free port, so nothing clashes with what you have running. The Try-it demos run with ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=..., in Java and Kotlin. A few steps use Linux tools (strace, epoll, io_uring); on macOS the same demos run on kqueue and say so. A blocked read holds its thread, so thread-per-connection needs one thread per open socket, which is why ten thousand idle connections (C10K) broke it. Little's law sizes the threads a blocking design needs. A java.nio server reads and writes partially: keep unsent bytes, compact() instead of clear(), remove selected keys, and arm OP_WRITE only while bytes are pending, because Linux selectors are level-triggered. A Netty event loop is one thread that owns its channels for life. Netty 4.2 builds groups with MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup and an IoHandler factory, and you dispatch blocking work to your own executor by hand. Frame before you decode, release every ByteBuf exactly once (the last owner releases), catch leaks with PARANOID detection in tests, and turn auto-read off while a channel isn't writable. Vert.x puts contexts on Netty's loops: a handler never runs at the same time as itself, the event bus is best effort, the blocked-thread checker only reports after 2 s, and executeBlocking is ordered per context unless you pass false. Quarkus REST picks the thread from the signature: reactive types and suspend run on the IO thread, plain values on a worker. Add @Blocking to JTA endpoints that return Uni, and use @RunOnVirtualThread with explicit limits in front of every downstream. Jetty 12 decides per task from the handler's declared invocation type: non-blocking on the selector thread, blocking with a reserved thread taking over or handed off, optionally to virtual threads. Its pool queue must stay unbounded. Virtual threads hide an event loop inside the JDK's poller. Zero-copy (sendfile) and io_uring are kernel tools to measure, and every server model still needs a concurrency limit somewhere.

h: Servers and event loops: NIO, Netty, Vert.x and Jetty: track quiz
x: A thread-per-connection server keeps 6,000 parcel lockers connected. They send 300 requests a second in total, each taking 100 ms. How many threads does the server hold? 30 300 About 6,000 One per CPU core Little's law gives 300 × 0.1 s = 30 requests in flight, but thread-per-connection keeps a thread on every open socket, busy or idle: about 6,000. That gap is the C10K problem in miniature. An NIO server burns one core at 100% with no traffic. Which change fixes it? Use direct buffers instead of heap buffers Register OP_WRITE only while a connection has unsent bytes Call selectNow() instead of select() Add a second selector thread A socket with free send-buffer space is always writable, and Linux selectors are level-triggered, so a permanent OP_WRITE makes every select() return at once: the light that never goes out. selectNow() would spin even harder. In Netty 4.2, a handler must call a library that looks prices up in a slow database the blocking way. What is the recommended way? pipeline.addLast(new DefaultEventExecutorGroup(8), "prices", handler) Call it in the handler; Netty 4.2 loops are virtual threads Dispatch the call to your own executor and ctx.writeAndFlush the result from there Wrap the call in synchronized Netty 4.2 deprecated the per-handler EventExecutorGroup versions of addLast and says to dispatch by hand. Event loops are platform threads, and writeAndFlush from another thread is queued back onto the channel's loop. A Netty handler extends ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter, logs msg.readableBytes(), and then does nothing else with the ByteBuf. What is wrong? Nothing: the garbage collector frees it It leaks: it neither passes the buffer on nor releases it It releases the buffer twice It blocks the event loop ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter releases nothing. A handler that is the last to touch a buffer must release it (ReferenceCountUtil.release(msg)) or pass it on with ctx.fireChannelRead(msg), as lesson 4's CountingTap does. PARANOID leak detection reports it once the buffer is garbage-collected. A Netty relay forwards from a fast client to a slow central server. The central channel's isWritable() turns false. What should the relay do? Turn off auto-read on the client channel until the central channel is writable again Keep writing; Netty buffers it Close the central channel Sleep in the handler until the central server catches up Writability is Netty's signal that the outbound buffer passed the high water mark. Stopping reads from the producer keeps the backlog in the kernel and TCP, not in your memory; sleeping would block the event loop. A Vert.x consumer wraps a 300 ms database call in vertx.executeBlocking(callable). Six requests arrive at once. Roughly how long until all six are answered? About 300 ms About 600 ms About 1,800 ms, because executeBlocking is ordered per context by default Never: it deadlocks All six messages come from the consumer's one context, and the default executeBlocking runs calls from a context one after another. The event loop is free, but the calls wait in single file. Pass false to let them overlap. In Quarkus 3.40, which endpoint blocks an IO thread? public Price get(...) that calls a database the blocking way @Blocking public Uni<Price> get(...) that calls a database the blocking way @RunOnVirtualThread public Price get(...) that calls a database the blocking way public Uni<Price> get(...) that returns Uni.createFrom().item(db.find(id)) A Uni return type puts the method on the IO thread, and db.find(id) runs while the Uni is being built. The other three run on a worker or a virtual thread. A Jetty 12 health-check handler extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking, and someone adds a database ping to it. What happens under load? Jetty notices and moves it to a worker thread It runs on a selector thread in Produce-Consume mode, so other connections on that selector wait behind each ping It runs on a virtual thread Jetty rejects the handler at startup NonBlocking is a promise Jetty trusts: it runs the handler directly on the selector thread. Blocking there stalls the selector, which Jetty's docs call a risk of server lock-up. Change the superclass to Handler.Abstract. On JDK 21, what happens when a virtual thread calls socket.getInputStream().read() and no data has arrived? Its carrier thread blocks in the kernel until data arrives The JVM creates a new platform thread for the read The read throws, and the virtual thread retries in a loop The JDK does a non-blocking read, registers the socket with its internal poller and parks the virtual thread; a poller thread unparks it when data arrives NioSocketImpl keeps the socket non-blocking, gets EAGAIN, registers the file descriptor with the Poller (epoll, one-shot) and parks. On JDK 21 the pollers are platform threads such as Read-Poller; from JDK 22 on Linux, one platform MasterPoller drives virtual sub-pollers. A service sends 500 MB logbook files to an internal archive over a plain TCP link. Which code sends them most efficiently, and what must it handle? A loop of FileChannel.transferTo calls, because a call may transfer fewer bytes than asked Files.readAllBytes then one write; nothing else Netty with io_uring, because it is always fastest A heap ByteBuffer of 500 MB transferTo to a socket becomes sendfile on Linux, so the bytes never pass through the JVM, and it can return early, so it belongs in a loop. Reading 500 MB into the heap wastes memory, and io_uring was not faster in this track's runs.

h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · One clerk per customer: what a blocked read holds
x: A blocked read parks a whole thread, so ten thousand idle connections hold ten thousand threads; readiness lets one thread watch them all Our running example is the simplest server there is. A server is a program that waits for other programs, its clients, to connect and ask for something. An echo server answers every line a client sends with the same line, like a post office desk that hands each letter straight back: return to sender. Each client talks to the server over a connection, an open line between two programs that TCP, the network's way of delivering bytes in order, keeps alive. Each end of a connection is a socket, the handle a program reads and writes those bytes through. Here is the classic echo server. One thread, a path of work through the program, accepts new connections. Each connection then gets a task of its own, run by a thread pool (a set of threads that run the tasks you hand it): Java try (ServerSocket server = new ServerSocket(8080)) { while (true) { Socket socket = server.accept(); // waits until a client connects pool.execute(() -> echo(socket)); // one task per connection } } static void echo(Socket socket) { try (socket; var in = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(socket.getInputStream(), UTF_8))) { var out = socket.getOutputStream(); String line; while ((line = in.readLine()) != null) { // waits until the client sends a line out.write((line + "\n").getBytes(UTF_8)); } } catch (IOException e) { // the client went away } } Kotlin ServerSocket(8080).use { server -> while (true) { val socket = server.accept() // waits until a client connects pool.execute { echo(socket) } // one task per connection } } fun echo(socket: Socket) { try { socket.use { s -> val reader = s.getInputStream().bufferedReader(UTF_8) val out = s.getOutputStream() while (true) { val line = reader.readLine() ?: break // waits until the client sends a line out.write("$line\n".toByteArray(UTF_8)) } } } catch (e: IOException) { // the client went away } } First, accept() waits for a client and returns its socket. We hand the socket to the pool and go straight back to accept(). Inside echo, readLine() waits for a whole line, and we write it back. The code reads like a recipe, which is its strength. The cost hides in readLine(). Let's go one level down. The operating system's core, the kernel, keeps a receive buffer for every socket: bytes that have arrived from the network but that the program hasn't read yet. read() copies bytes out of that buffer. When the buffer is empty, the kernel takes the calling thread off the processor and parks it on the socket's wait list. When a packet arrives, the kernel adds its bytes to the buffer and wakes the thread. A call that makes its thread wait like this is a blocking call. While the client thinks, the thread waits. Many clients also keep the connection open between requests, so they don't pay to connect again. That's a keep-alive connection, the customer who stays at the counter in case another question comes to mind, and its thread waits for that too. One thread for every open socket, busy or not, is called thread-per-connection. A waiting thread isn't free to keep. Each one here is a platform thread, a thin Java wrapper around one operating system thread, with its own stack, the memory for its method calls. Jetty's documentation (Jetty is a Java web server, lesson 7) puts that at about 1 MiB per thread, and the operating system's scheduler tracks every one. ThreadPerConnectionDemo, in the Try it below, connects 2,000 clients that never send a byte. One run on a busy 4-core machine with JDK 21 printed: platform thread per connection: 2,000 idle clients connected in 1,492 ms platform threads: 6 before, 2007 now a handler blocked in read() reports state RUNNABLE Two thousand customers, two thousand clerks, and not one of them doing anything. Now look at the state. A platform thread blocked in a socket read reports RUNNABLE, because the JVM sees it running native code (SocketDispatcher.read0) and can't tell waiting from working there. That's where the post office picture breaks. In a real post office, you can see a clerk standing still. A thread dump, the JVM's snapshot of every thread and what it's doing, lists each waiting thread of an idle server as RUNNABLE. That's a generous word for a clerk staring at an empty counter. A blocked read holds a whole thread for the whole wait. Count the waits, not the work. So for a blocking server, the question isn't how fast one line comes back. It's how many threads your traffic needs, and arithmetic can answer that. Count the threads Open ThreadPerConnectionDemo.java (or the Kotlin twin, ThreadPerConnectionDemo.kt). It connects 2,000 clients that never send anything: first to a server with a cached thread pool, which makes a new thread whenever none is free, then to one with a virtual thread per connection. Before you run it, write down two predictions: how many platform threads the first server holds, and what getState() returns for a handler stuck in read(). Run it from labs/ with the command below. Then run it again with -Pargs=5000 added. Which number grows, and which one stays put? clients, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); System.out.printf(" platform threads: %d before, %d now%n", before, mx.getThreadCount()); System.out.printf(" a handler blocked in read() reports state * 1_000L); } for (Socket s : open) s.close(); } handlers.shutdown(); handlers.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l01.ThreadPerConnectionDemo h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · Counting the clerks with Little's law
x: Picture a counter on the post office door. If 10 customers come in each minute and each stays 3 minutes, about 30 are inside at any moment. That's Little's law: the number of items in a system equals the rate they arrive times the time each one stays, L = λ × W. You met it in the executors and virtual threads tracks. With thread-per-request, where a pool lends a thread only while a request is being served, L is also the number of threads you need. Take a server that gets 800 requests a second at its busiest. Each request spends 30 ms in our own code and 120 ms waiting for a slow web service, another program it calls over the network. That's 800 × 0.15 s = 120 requests in flight, so 120 busy threads, and a pool of 200 copes. Then the slow service has a bad day and takes 600 ms. The same traffic now needs 800 × 0.63 s = 504 threads. The processor is no busier. The extra threads are all waiting. Thread-per-connection is worse, because it pays for connections, not requests. A connection holds its thread for its whole life, idle time included. Picture 10,000 clients that each keep a connection open and send one request every 10 seconds. That's 1,000 requests a second. At 150 ms each, Little's law says 150 are in flight. The thread-per-connection server still holds 10,000 threads. 9,850 of them sit in read(), waiting for their client's next request. In the post office, 150 customers are being served and 9,850 are standing at the counter, thinking. Servers built for many connections keep those two numbers apart. Tomcat, a widely used Java web server, has two settings for it: maxThreads (200 by default) caps the requests being served at once, and maxConnections (8,192 by default) caps the open connections. One Tomcat thread watches the idle sockets, so a worker thread is needed only while a request is being served. Every extra platform thread costs a stack and a place in the scheduler. When many are ready to run, the operating system also pays for context switches: saving one thread's registers and loading another's, while the processor's caches go cold. A few thousand threads work, as the demo showed. Tens of thousands is where servers fell over in the late 1990s, and it's still a bad place to be. Waiting threads are still threads. Size a blocking server with Little's law, not with the number of cores. Those tens of thousands of connections already have a name. Do the arithmetic before the bad day A server calls a slow web service 300 times a second. Each call spends 40 ms in your own code and 260 ms waiting for the answer. How many threads does thread-per-request need? The slow service has a bad day and takes 2 s per call. Traffic stays the same. How many threads now? Open the lab test fixedPoolCapsConnections. Which of your two numbers would a fixed pool of 100 threads survive, and what would callers see in the other case? 300 × 0.3 s = 90 threads normally, and 300 × 2.04 s = 612 threads on the bad day. A pool of 100 copes with the first. In the second, tasks queue behind busy threads, waits climb past every caller's patience, and the server looks down while its processor sits idle. The pool ran out of threads that were waiting, not threads that were working. Tomcat 11 HTTP connector attributes (docs source) docs

h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · C10K: ten thousand clients at once, and the wall of lights
x: In 1999, Dan Kegel wrote a web page called "The C10K problem". The name is short for ten thousand concurrent clients: ten thousand connections open at the same moment. His point was that the hardware of the day could already serve that many, and the server software couldn't, because of how it used threads. The answer the industry settled on is the one this whole track is about: stop giving each connection a thread. First, put each socket in non-blocking mode, where a read on an empty receive buffer returns 0 bytes at once instead of parking the thread. Then ask the kernel one question: which of these sockets are ready right now? In the post office, that's a new floor plan. Instead of a clerk per customer, each customer gets a box in the wall with a small light above it. A customer drops a form in whenever it's ready, and the box lights up. One clerk watches the wall, serves only the boxes that are lit, and dozes when none are. The next lesson builds that wall in Java. The first answers to "which sockets are ready?" were select and poll, two system calls (requests a program makes to the kernel). Both take the whole list of sockets on every call, which gets slow with thousands of them. It's a clerk who reads out every box number, one by one, to ask whether there's mail. Linux added epoll, and the BSDs and macOS added kqueue. They keep the watched sockets inside the kernel and report only the ones that are ready. That's readiness notification. One thread can then watch thousands of connections and run code only for those with data. That loop (wait for ready sockets, serve each one a little, wait again) is called an event loop. The idea has many names on the JVM, and this track visits each: java.nio's Selector, built on epoll on Linux and kqueue on macOS (lesson 2). Netty, a Java library for network servers, whose event loop is one thread running a selector and your code (lessons 3 and 4). Vert.x, a toolkit built on Netty, and Quarkus, a framework for web services built on Vert.x (lessons 5 and 6). Jetty's selectors (lesson 7). The JDK's own poller, which virtual threads use when they wait on a socket (lesson 8). The price is the way you write code. A thread that serves thousands of sockets must never block on any one of them. Every read returns at once with whatever bytes are there, maybe none, and every write may send only part of the data. Each connection becomes a small record of where it got to, picked up whenever the kernel says something happened. The rest of this track is about writing that well, or choosing a library that writes it for you. A thread that watches many sockets must never wait on one. Ask which are ready, then serve only those. That leaves two ways out of the C10K corner, and the JDK now offers both. See the waiting threads in a thread dump Start the demo with 300 clients and hold the connections for 20 seconds: run the command below. While it holds the platform-thread version, run jcmd workbench.nio.l01.ThreadPerConnectionDemo Thread.print | grep -c NioSocketImpl.implRead in a second terminal. jcmd is a tool that comes with the JDK; Thread.print asks the running program for a thread dump, a snapshot of every thread and what it's doing. jcmd accepts the main class name instead of the process number. Run the same jcmd line again once the demo prints the virtual-thread section. Predict the count first. terminal ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l01.ThreadPerConnectionDemo -Pargs='300 20' The first count is 300: each handler's stack runs through NioSocketImpl.implRead down to SocketDispatcher.read0, and its state line says RUNNABLE. The second count is 0. Thread.print lists platform threads only, and the 300 virtual threads are parked off any thread. Lesson 8 shows how to find them. Thread per connection parks one thread on every socket, a clerk for every customer. An event loop asks the kernel which sockets are ready, like one clerk watching a wall of lights, and runs only those. C10k problem (Wikipedia) read

h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · Two ways out: fewer clerks, or cheaper clerks
x: There are two ways to serve 10,000 connections from one JVM. One uses fewer clerks; the other makes each clerk cheaper. The first is the C10K answer: a few threads, each running an event loop over many non-blocking sockets. Netty and Vert.x work this way. It scales very far, and you pay with code that must never block. Call a database the blocking way from an event loop, and every other connection on that loop stops until the query returns. In the post office, it's the clerk at the wall of lights stepping out for a long lunch. The second arrived in JDK 21: virtual threads (JEP 444). A virtual thread is a thread the JDK runs on a few platform threads, setting it aside whenever it waits. You keep the blocking code from the first section and change one line, the pool: Java // echo() stays exactly as it was ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); Kotlin // echo() stays exactly as it was val pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() The demo showed the effect: the same 2,000 blocked readers on 15 platform threads. You may remember the trick from How virtual threads work, where a waiter clips the order slip to a board and serves another table. For sockets, the JDK runs an event loop for you. When a virtual thread's read would block, the JDK hands the socket to an internal poller built on epoll or kqueue. Then it parks the virtual thread and frees its carrier, the platform thread that was running it. Lesson 8 opens that poller up. In the post office, these are cheap clerks: a clerk leaves a note at a slow customer's counter and serves someone else, and any free clerk comes back when the form is done. Neither way makes a single request faster. A request that waits 120 ms for the slow web service still takes 120 ms. Neither removes the limits behind your server, either. If 10,000 virtual threads all want one of 20 database connections, 9,980 of them wait in line. The virtual threads track showed how to cap that with a semaphore, a counter of permits that lets only so many threads in at once. My default for a new blocking server is virtual threads. I'd move to an event-loop library when measurements say memory per connection is the problem, or when the server already lives on one. Most servers hit the limits of the services they call long before either wall. Event loops and virtual threads make waiting cheap. Neither makes the wait shorter. Swap the pool, keep the code Finish the lab first, so BlockingEchoServer works. Read the test virtualThreadsScale. It passes Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() to the same server class that idleClientsHoldThreads runs on a cached pool. Change its client count from 500 to 1,500 (the loop bound and the isEqualTo(500)) and run only that test with --tests '*virtualThreadsScale'. Predict whether the platform-thread assertion still holds. It still passes. The platform-thread count grows by a few threads (carriers and poller threads) whether 500 or 1,500 connections are open, because a parked virtual thread holds no operating system thread. Put the count back to 500 when you're done. JEP 444: Virtual Threads read

h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · Java and Kotlin
x: One virtual thread per connection, in both languages VirtualEchoServer.java try (ServerSocket server = new ServerSocket(8080); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { while (true) { Socket socket = server.accept(); pool.submit(() -> echo(socket)); // a blocked read parks the virtual thread } } VirtualEchoServer.kt ServerSocket(8080).use { server -> Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { pool -> while (true) { val socket = server.accept() pool.submit { echo(socket) } // a blocked read parks the virtual thread } } } The JDK does the work in both. ExecutorService is AutoCloseable since JDK 19, so Java's try-with-resources and Kotlin's use both shut the pool down and wait for running tasks. The difference worth knowing is coroutines. A Kotlin coroutine that calls the blocking readLine() does not suspend: it holds its dispatcher thread for the whole wait. So launch(Dispatchers.IO) { echo(socket) } is thread-per-connection again, capped by the IO dispatcher's 64 threads. Coroutines free the thread only when the read itself suspends, which is what Kotlin server libraries such as Ktor and Vert.x's Kotlin API provide.

h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · Worked example
x: Size a server for parcel lockers with Little's law A parcel company runs 6,000 lockers, the metal cabinets where people collect their parcels. Each locker keeps one connection open to a server and sends a status line every 20 seconds. Handling a line takes 15 ms of work and 135 ms waiting for a slow tracking service. Today the server runs one platform thread per connection. // 1. today: one platform thread per locker connection ExecutorService pool = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(); while (true) { Socket locker = server.accept(); pool.execute(() -> serveLocker(locker)); // loops: read a status line, call tracking, reply } // 1. today: one platform thread per locker connection val pool = Executors.newCachedThreadPool() while (true) { val locker = server.accept() pool.execute { serveLocker(locker) } // loops: read a status line, call tracking, reply } Apply Little's law to the requests, then compare with the connections. The gap is the cost of idle connections: clerks standing at the counter. arrival rate = 6,000 lockers / 20 s = 300 requests/s time in system = 15 ms + 135 ms = 0.15 s in flight = 300 x 0.15 = 45 requests threads held = one per connection = 6,000 threads idle threads = 6,000 - 45 = 5,955 waiting in read() Make idle connections cheap. A virtual thread parked in read() holds no operating system thread, so the 5,955 idle connections cost a little memory each instead of a platform thread each. The serving code doesn't change. // 2. same serveLocker(), cheap waiting ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); // 2. same serveLocker(), cheap waiting val pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() Now protect the tracking service. It accepts 64 requests at once. The old design limited that by accident, through the number of threads. Virtual threads remove the accident, so put the limit back on purpose, around the call that needs it. // 3. cap the calls to the tracking service, not the number of connections private final Semaphore trackingSlots = new Semaphore(64); StatusReply report(StatusLine line) throws InterruptedException { trackingSlots.acquire(); try { return tracking.send(line); // 135 ms } finally { trackingSlots.release(); } } // 3. cap the calls to the tracking service, not the number of connections private val trackingSlots = Semaphore(64) fun report(line: StatusLine): StatusReply { trackingSlots.acquire() try { return tracking.send(line) // 135 ms } finally { trackingSlots.release() } }

h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · Lab
x: Watch a blocking server run out of threads labs/nio/src/main/java/workbench/nio/l01/BlockingEchoServer.java ./gradlew :nio:test --tests 'workbench.nio.l01.*' Run the tests once. All four fail: the accept loop and the handler are stubs, so the clients give up after 3 seconds. Write acceptLoop(): while the server socket is open, accept() a socket, add it to open, and call handlers.execute(() -> handle(socket)). Return when accept() throws. Write handle(Socket): increment inHandler, wrap the input stream in a UTF-8 BufferedReader, and write every line back with \n and a flush(). In finally, remove the socket from open and decrement inHandler. Run the tests until all four pass. Then read fixedPoolCapsConnections and virtualThreadsScale side by side: the same server code with three different pools gives three very different limits. try (socket; BufferedReader in = ...) closes the socket for you. Since Java 9 you can list an existing, effectively final variable in try-with-resources. accept() throws a SocketException once close() closes the server socket. Treat that as the signal to return. After shutdownNow(), execute throws RejectedExecutionException. Catch it in the accept loop too, so the accepting thread ends quietly. All four tests in BlockingEchoServerTest pass. h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · Quiz
x: A thread-per-connection server has 3,000 clients with open connections. Together they send 600 requests a second, and each request takes 50 ms. How many threads does the server hold? 30 600 About 3,000 8, one per core Little's law gives 600 × 0.05 s = 30 requests in flight, which is what thread-per-request would need. Thread-per-connection keeps a thread on every open socket, so about 3,000. The 30 is the tempting answer, and the difference is the idle time between requests: clerks standing at the counter. A thread dump of a slow server shows 400 threads in SocketDispatcher.read0 with state RUNNABLE, and the processor is 2% busy. What is going on? 400 threads are spinning on the processor 400 threads are waiting for bytes on their sockets; native blocking reads show up as RUNNABLE The JVM is deadlocked The garbage collector has paused them A platform thread blocked in a socket read is inside native code, so the JVM reports it as RUNNABLE. The low processor use confirms they are waiting, not working. A deadlock would show BLOCKED threads waiting on locks. Which change lets the lab's BlockingEchoServer hold 10,000 idle connections without 10,000 platform threads, with no change to handle()? Pass Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10_000) Run handle() inside CompletableFuture.supplyAsync Call socket.setSoTimeout(100) on every connection Pass Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() A virtual thread blocked in read() parks on the JDK's poller and frees its carrier, so idle connections hold no operating system thread. A fixed pool of 10,000 is still 10,000 platform threads. supplyAsync runs on the common pool, which has about one thread per core, so most connections would never be served. A short timeout only makes the reads fail. From the executors track: every thread of a 50-thread pool waits on a slow web service that takes 2 s. What is the most this pool can finish per second, however much traffic arrives? 25 50 100 200 Turn Little's law around: throughput = threads / time per request = 50 / 2 s = 25 requests a second. Extra traffic only makes the queue longer. What do non-blocking IO and virtual threads change for a single request that waits 120 ms for a slow web service? It completes in well under 120 ms Not its waiting time: they let many more such requests wait at the same moment, at a lower cost per wait It no longer needs a database connection It gets retried automatically when the service is slow Both make waiting cheap, so one JVM can keep more requests in flight. The request itself still waits 120 ms for the service. Limits behind the server, such as a pool of database connections, stay exactly where they were.

h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · Key terms
x: Blocking IO A read or write that makes the calling thread wait until the operation can finish. Socket A program's handle on one end of a network connection, kept by the kernel. Thread-per-connection A server design that gives every open socket its own thread for the socket's whole life. Thread-per-request A design where a thread is taken from a pool only while a request is being served. Little's law Items in flight = arrival rate × time each item spends in the system. C10K Ten thousand concurrent clients on one server; the name of the problem Dan Kegel described in 1999. Readiness notification The kernel tells you which sockets can be read or written right now (select, poll, epoll, kqueue). Keep-alive connection A connection the client leaves open between requests, so it is idle most of the time. What does getState() report for a platform thread blocked in a socket read()? RUNNABLE. The wait happens in native code (SocketDispatcher.read0), so idle servers look busy in thread dumps. Little's law, in one line? Requests in the system = arrival rate × time in the system (L = λ × W). With thread-per-request, that's the number of threads you need. Why does thread-per-connection need more threads than thread-per-request? A connection holds its thread while it sits idle between requests. Threads follow open sockets, not requests in flight. What is the C10K problem? Dan Kegel's 1999 name for serving ten thousand concurrent clients from one server. Thread-per-connection didn't scale there; non-blocking sockets with readiness notification did. What does epoll (Linux) or kqueue (macOS) give a server? One call that returns only the sockets that are ready, so one thread can watch thousands of connections. Do virtual threads make a request faster? No. They make waiting cheap, so more requests can wait at once. A 120 ms call to a slow service still takes 120 ms. 2,000 virtual threads blocked in socket reads on a 4-core JDK 21 machine: about how many platform threads? About 15 (this lesson's demo): 4 carriers, a few JDK poller threads, and the JVM's own threads.

h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · Go deeper
x: "About 1 MiB per platform thread" needs one detail to be useful. On 64-bit Linux the default stack size (-Xss) is 1 MB, and the JVM reserves that much address space per thread. The kernel hands out real memory pages only as the stack actually grows, so 2,000 idle threads don't use 2 GB of RAM. They do use real memory for the pages they touched, kernel bookkeeping per thread, and a place in the scheduler each. You can see the JVM's view with Native Memory Tracking. Start a JVM with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary and run jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary, where <pid> is the number the operating system gives the running program. The Thread section shows how many threads exist and their reserved and committed stack memory. Run it on the demo while it holds 2,000 platform threads, and again during the virtual-thread part. The limit a real server hits first is often not memory. Machines and containers (sealed-off boxes that a program runs in) cap the number of processes and threads per user (ulimit -u, or the container's pids.max). When a JVM can't create a thread, it throws OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread, a confusing name for a limit on the number of threads. Kegel's page sorted the ways out of C10K roughly like this: many clients per thread with level-triggered readiness (select, poll), the same with edge-triggered readiness (kqueue, epoll in edge mode), asynchronous IO that reports completion instead of readiness, and one client per thread. Lesson 2 meets level-triggered readiness, and lesson 8 compares readiness with completion (io_uring on Linux).

h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · The tray behind each box: a ByteBuffer's position and limit
x: Start with the tray. Everything in java.nio, Java's package for non-blocking input and output, moves bytes through a ByteBuffer. In the post office, it's the tray behind each box: a fixed number of slots, a cursor that marks the next slot to fill or empty, and a stop line. In Java, those are three numbers. capacity is the tray's size. position is the cursor: where the next put or get happens. limit is the stop line: where reading or writing must stop. Most NIO bugs are one of these three numbers being wrong. A fresh buffer is ready for filling, which we'll call write mode: position at 0 and limit at capacity. Each put moves position forward. Before you can read what you wrote, flip() draws the stop line where filling ended (limit becomes position) and moves the cursor back to the start (position becomes 0). BufferDemo, in the Try it below, walks a 16-byte buffer through the whole cycle: allocate(16) pos=0 lim=16 cap=16 remaining=16 put("hello") pos=5 lim=16 cap=16 remaining=11 flip() pos=0 lim=5 cap=16 remaining=5 get(2) -> "he" pos=2 lim=5 cap=16 remaining=3 compact() pos=3 lim=16 cap=16 remaining=13 put("XY") pos=5 lim=16 cap=16 remaining=11 flip() pos=0 lim=5 cap=16 remaining=5 readable content: "lloXY" After get(2) took he, where should new bytes go? compact() answers that. It slides the unread bytes (llo) to the front of the tray and puts the buffer back in write mode right after them, so new data lands behind what you haven't used yet. That's why the content ends as lloXY. clear() looks similar and does something else: it resets both marks and forgets everything, read or not. Forget flip() and nothing complains. A buffer of 8 with 2 bytes put has remaining() 6, so a write sends the 6 bytes after your data, whatever happens to sit in those slots. The buffer will hand over garbage without a murmur, as long as the numbers say so. There are two kinds of buffer. allocate gives a heap buffer, backed by a byte[] on the Java heap, the memory where Java keeps its objects. allocateDirect gives memory outside the heap. The kernel, the core of the operating system, reads and writes memory by address during a system call (a request a program makes to the kernel), and the garbage collector is allowed to move a byte[] around. So the JDK copies a heap buffer through a temporary direct buffer on every channel read and write (sun.nio.ch.IOUtil does it). Direct buffers skip that copy, but the ByteBuffer Javadoc says they have "somewhat higher allocation and deallocation costs" and recommends them for large, long-lived buffers. So allocate direct buffers once and reuse them. Netty's allocators, lesson 4, do exactly that. A buffer's mode lives in two numbers the compiler can't see. Flip before you read, and compact to keep what's unread. A tray is only half the story. The other half is what the kernel does with it. Predict the marks Open BufferDemo.java (or BufferDemo.kt). Cover the output above and predict pos and lim after compact(). Run it with the command below and check your prediction. Change b.compact() to b.clear() and run it again. What does readable content print now, and which bytes are gone? BufferDemo.java package workbench.nio.l02; import java.nio.ByteBuffer; import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.US_ASCII; /** Walks a ByteBuffer through put, flip, get, compact and clear, printing its cursor after each step. */ public class BufferDemo { static void show(String step, ByteBuffer b) { System.out.printf("%-20s pos=%-2d lim=%-2d cap=%-2d remaining=%d%n", step, b.position(), b.limit(), b.capacity(), b.remaining()); byte[] two = new byte[2]; b.get(two); show("get(2) -> \"" + new String(two, US_ASCII) + "\"", b); b.compact(); // move the unread "llo" to the front, back to write mode show("compact()", b); b.put("XY".getBytes(US_ASCII)); show("put(\"XY\")", b); b.flip(); show("flip()", b); byte[] rest = new byte[b.remaining()]; b.get(rest); System.out.println("readable content: \"" + new String(rest, US_ASCII) + "\""); ByteBuffer forgot = ByteBuffer.allocate(8);
