h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · Non-blocking reads and writes move only what fits
x: A socket is a program's handle on one end of a network connection, and TCP is the protocol that carries its bytes in order. Every TCP socket has two buffers inside the kernel. The receive buffer holds bytes that arrived from the network and that your program hasn't read yet. The send buffer holds bytes your program wrote that the kernel hasn't delivered yet. In the post office, they're the box's street-side slot and its pick-up shelf: letters waiting to come in, and replies waiting to be collected. read and write never touch the network themselves. They copy between your ByteBuffer and these two kernel buffers. A channel is java.nio's handle on something bytes move through, such as a socket or a file. Put a SocketChannel in non-blocking mode with configureBlocking(false), and its copies stop waiting. They do what the kernel buffers allow right now, and return. read(buf) copies whatever sits in the receive buffer. That can be one byte, half a line, three lines, or nothing at all, in which case it returns 0. It returns -1 when the other side has closed its end. write(buf) is the call that bites. Its Javadoc says a socket channel in non-blocking mode "cannot write any more bytes than are free in the socket's output buffer". When the client reads slowly, the send buffer fills up, and write sends part of your buffer, or none of it. That's a partial write, a reply that only half fits on the shelf. So every connection needs its own buffer for the bytes it hasn't sent yet. The pattern that handles both directions is four lines: Java int n = ch.read(buf); // append whatever arrived, maybe 0 bytes; -1 means the client is done buf.flip(); // switch to reading what we hold ch.write(buf); // send what the kernel accepts, maybe only part of it buf.compact(); // keep the unsent tail at the front, back to write mode Kotlin val n = ch.read(buf) // append whatever arrived, maybe 0 bytes; -1 means the client is done buf.flip() // switch to reading what we hold ch.write(buf) // send what the kernel accepts, maybe only part of it buf.compact() // keep the unsent tail at the front, back to write mode First we read, appending to whatever the tray already holds. Then we flip, write what the kernel takes, and compact, so the unsent tail moves to the front. After compact(), buf.position() > 0 means bytes are still waiting to go. One run for this track echoed 8 MiB to a client with a 4 KiB receive buffer and counted 8 partial writes. With clear() in place of compact(), each of them would have dropped bytes. The read side has a twin rule: one read is not one message. TCP is a byte stream. A line sent with one write can arrive in three reads, and two lines can arrive in one. Here the post office picture breaks. A real letter arrives whole, but bytes arrive in whatever pieces the network made. Anything beyond a raw echo needs framing, a way to tell where one message ends, such as a newline at the end or a length at the front. Lessons 3 and 4 let Netty do it. One trap lives in the client, too. If a test client writes 8 MiB and only then starts reading, the echo stalls. The server can't send because the client isn't reading, so the server stops reading, so the client's write blocks. Clients of an echo server must read and write at the same time, and the lab's tests use a writer thread for exactly that reason. Non-blocking calls move only what fits. Keep the rest per connection, and frame what you read. We can read and write without waiting now. What's missing is someone to tell the clerk which boxes to look at. Count the lost bytes Before you fix anything, run the lab tests with the command below. Read the failure for echoesEverything: how many of the 4,194,304 bytes came back? Run it twice more. Predict first: will the number be the same? terminal ./gradlew :nio:test --tests 'workbench.nio.l02.*' The echo comes back short, by a different amount every run: 73,728 bytes in one run on the busy machine here, around 3.4 million in others. How much gets lost depends on timing: how often the send buffer was full when the server wrote, and when the client's half-close arrived. The idle test fails too, with a wakeup count in the hundreds of thousands. WritableByteChannel.write Javadoc (JDK 25 source) docs

h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · The wall of lights: a Selector tells one thread which channels are ready
x: A thread per connection versus one thread asking a Selector what is ready A Selector is the wall of lights. It watches many channels at once. You register each channel with an interest set, the events you want to hear about: OP_ACCEPT (a new client is waiting), OP_READ (bytes arrived) and OP_WRITE (there's room to send). Then select() blocks until at least one of them is ready. Each registration is a SelectionKey. It carries the interest set, the ready set that the selector fills in, and an attachment, a slot where you keep that connection's state, like a card pinned to the box. Here is the clerk's day: Java while (true) { selector.select(); // sleep until something is ready Iterator<SelectionKey> it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator(); while (it.hasNext()) { SelectionKey key = it.next(); it.remove(); // you must remove handled keys yourself if (key.isAcceptable()) { SocketChannel ch = server.accept(); ch.configureBlocking(false); ch.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ, new Conn()); } else { serve(key); // read, write, update the interest set } } } Kotlin while (true) { selector.select() // sleep until something is ready val it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator() while (it.hasNext()) { val key = it.next() it.remove() // you must remove handled keys yourself if (key.isAcceptable) { val ch = server.accept() ch.configureBlocking(false) ch.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ, Conn()) } else { serve(key) // read, write, update the interest set } } } First, select() sleeps until a light comes on. Then we walk the list of lit boxes, selectedKeys(). A lit accept key means a new customer, so we accept the channel, make it non-blocking and give it a box of its own, with a fresh Conn card. Any other key is a box with something to do, and serve handles it. The it.remove() line looks like housekeeping, and it isn't. The selector adds keys to the selected set and never takes them out. Leave a key in, and the next pass handles it again, with its old ready set. It's a list of lit boxes that nobody crosses off. StaleKeyDemo, in the Try it below, sends exactly one 6-byte message and loops for 300 ms: remove handled keys=true loops=7, handled as readable 1 times, bytes read 6 remove handled keys=false loops=7, handled as readable 7 times, bytes read 6 Seven visits to a box that held one letter. For an accept key, the same mistake means calling accept() again and getting null back. The selector comes with a threading rule, too. Its Javadoc says a selector is safe for use by several threads, but its selected-key set is not. The simple way to obey that is the one every library uses: one thread, one path of work through the program, owns a selector, runs its loop, and does all the work for its channels. Netty, in the next lesson, calls that thread an event loop. On Linux, Selector.open() returns sun.nio.ch.EPollSelectorImpl, a wrapper around epoll, the Linux system call from lesson 1 that reports ready sockets. On macOS you get a kqueue selector. The JDK registers sockets with epoll in level-triggered mode: as long as a socket is readable or writable, every select() reports it again, like a light that stays on while there's mail in the box. The other mode, edge-triggered, is more like a bell that rings once when a letter arrives. A light that stays on is forgiving for reads. For writes, it's the bug in the next section. The selector never crosses a box off your list. Remove every key you handle. Forget it.remove() Open StaleKeyDemo.java (or StaleKeyDemo.kt). A client sends exactly one 6-byte message, and the loop runs for 300 ms, once removing handled keys and once not. Predict how many times each version treats the channel as readable. Run it with the command below. StaleKeyDemo.java package workbench.nio.l02; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.InetSocketAddress; import java.nio.ByteBuffer; import java.nio.channels.SelectionKey; import java.nio.channels.Selector; import java.nio.channels.ServerSocketChannel; import java.nio.channels.SocketChannel; import java.util.Iterator; /** One message arrives. How many times does the loop think the channel is readable? */ public class StaleKeyDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { run(true); run(false); } static void run(boolean removeHandledKeys) throws Exception { try (Selector selector = Selector.open(); ServerSocketChannel server = ServerSocketChannel.open()) { server.bind(new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0)); try (SocketChannel client = SocketChannel.open(server.getLocalAddress()); SocketChannel conn = server.accept()) { conn.configureBlocking(false); conn.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ); client.write(ByteBuffer.wrap("letter".getBytes())); // exactly one message ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocate(64); int loops = 0, handled = 0, bytes = 0; long end = System.nanoTime() + 300_000_000L; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { selector.select(50); loops++; Iterator<SelectionKey> it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator(); while (it.hasNext()) { SelectionKey key = it.next(); if (removeHandledKeys) it.remove(); if (key.isReadable()) { // ready set from the last select that added the key handled++; buf.clear(); bytes += Math.max(0, conn.read(buf)); } } } System.out.printf("remove handled keys=%-5s loops=%d, handled as readable %d times, bytes read %d%n", removeHandledKeys, loops, handled, bytes); } } } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l02.StaleKeyDemo labs/nio/src/demo/java/workbench/nio/l02/StaleKeyDemo.java StaleKeyDemo.kt package workbench.nio.l02 import java.net.InetAddress import java.net.InetSocketAddress import java.nio.ByteBuffer import java.nio.channels.SelectionKey import java.nio.channels.Selector import java.nio.channels.ServerSocketChannel import java.nio.channels.SocketChannel /** One message arrives. How many times does the loop think the channel is readable? */ fun main() { staleKeys(removeHandledKeys = true) staleKeys(removeHandledKeys = false) } private fun staleKeys(removeHandledKeys: Boolean) { Selector.open().use { selector -> ServerSocketChannel.open().use { server -> server.bind(InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0)) SocketChannel.open(server.localAddress).use { client -> server.accept().use { conn -> conn.configureBlocking(false) conn.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ) client.write(ByteBuffer.wrap("letter".toByteArray())) // exactly one message val buf = ByteBuffer.allocate(64) var loops = 0 var handled = 0 var bytes = 0 val end = System.nanoTime() + 300_000_000L while (System.nanoTime() < end) { selector.select(50) loops++ val it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator() while (it.hasNext()) { val key = it.next() if (removeHandledKeys) it.remove() if (key.isReadable) { // ready set from the last select that added the key handled++ buf.clear() bytes += maxOf(0, conn.read(buf)) } } } println("remove handled keys=%-5s loops=%d, handled as readable %d times, bytes read %d" .format(removeHandledKeys, loops, handled, bytes)) } } } } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l02.StaleKeyDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l02/StaleKeyDemo.kt With it.remove(): handled once, 6 bytes read. Without it: handled 7 times in 7 loop passes, still 6 bytes in total. The six extra passes each called read and got 0 bytes back, because the key stayed in the selected set and isReadable() kept answering from the old ready set. Selector Javadoc (JDK 25 source) docs

h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · The light that never goes out: arm OP_WRITE only while bytes wait
x: A socket is writable whenever its send buffer has free space, which is nearly always. Put that next to a level-triggered selector, and you get the classic NIO bug. Register OP_WRITE on every connection, and its "room for a reply" light never goes out. select() returns at once, reports every idle connection as writable, and the loop goes around again. SpinDemo measures it on one idle connection for 300 ms. One run on a busy 4-core machine printed: Selector implementation: sun.nio.ch.EPollSelectorImpl idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ : 0 wakeups idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ | OP_WRITE: 374510 wakeups Zero against 374,510, on a connection that sent nothing. That's the clerk walking to a box, finding room for a reply nobody wrote, and walking back, more than a thousand times a millisecond. Under strace, a Linux tool that lists a program's system calls, the shape is just as clear: thousands of epoll_wait calls and a handful of epoll_ctl. On a real server, it shows up as one core at 100% with no traffic at all. The fix is to register OP_READ by default and add OP_WRITE only while the connection has unsent bytes. When a write leaves bytes behind, arm it. When a later write drains them, drop it: Java boolean pending = conn.buf.position() > 0; // after compact(): unsent bytes at the front int ops = 0; if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_READ; // room left: keep reading if (pending) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_WRITE; // only while bytes wait key.interestOps(ops); Kotlin val pending = conn.buf.position() > 0 // after compact(): unsent bytes at the front var ops = 0 if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_READ // room left: keep reading if (pending) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_WRITE // only while bytes wait key.interestOps(ops) The OP_READ line is the other half of the same idea. When the tray is full because the client reads slowly, stop reading from that client. Its bytes pile up in the kernel's receive buffer, and TCP tells the client how much room is left there (the TCP window). As the window shrinks to zero, the client's own writes stop. That's backpressure, a slow receiver slowing the sender down, in two lines. Lesson 4 shows Netty's version of it. In the 8 MiB run from earlier, the server armed OP_WRITE only 4 times in 537 selects. Closing follows the same logic. A client can half-close a connection with shutdownOutput(): it says it will send nothing more, but it keeps reading. Your read then returns -1, the end-of-stream mark (EOF, short for end of file), yet the client still wants the rest of its echo. Close only once nothing is pending. A writable socket is the normal case, not news. Ask for OP_WRITE only while bytes are waiting. Watch the spin Run SpinDemo (or SpinDemoKt) with the command below. Predict both numbers first. On Linux with strace installed, run it outside Gradle to count system calls: strace -f -c -e trace=epoll_wait,epoll_ctl java -cp nio/build/classes/java/demo workbench.nio.l02.SpinDemo. SpinDemo.java package workbench.nio.l02; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.InetSocketAddress; import java.nio.channels.SelectionKey; import java.nio.channels.Selector; import java.nio.channels.ServerSocketChannel; import java.nio.channels.SocketChannel; /** Counts how often select() wakes up on one idle connection, with and without OP_WRITE in the interest set. */ public class SpinDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (Selector probe = Selector.open()) { System.out.println("Selector implementation: " + probe.getClass().getName()); } System.out.println("idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ : " + wakeups(SelectionKey.OP_READ) + " wakeups"); System.out.println("idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ | OP_WRITE: " + wakeups(SelectionKey.OP_READ | SelectionKey.OP_WRITE) + " wakeups"); } static long wakeups(int interest) throws Exception { try (Selector selector = Selector.open(); ServerSocketChannel server = ServerSocketChannel.open()) { server.bind(new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0)); try (SocketChannel client = SocketChannel.open(server.getLocalAddress()); SocketChannel conn = server.accept()) { conn.configureBlocking(false); conn.register(selector, interest); long end = System.nanoTime() + 300_000_000L, count = 0; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { if (selector.select(50) > 0) count++; // nobody sends anything on this connection selector.selectedKeys().clear(); } return count; } } } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l02.SpinDemo labs/nio/src/demo/java/workbench/nio/l02/SpinDemo.java SpinDemo.kt package workbench.nio.l02 import java.net.InetAddress import java.net.InetSocketAddress import java.nio.channels.SelectionKey import java.nio.channels.Selector import java.nio.channels.ServerSocketChannel import java.nio.channels.SocketChannel /** Counts how often select() wakes up on one idle connection, with and without OP_WRITE in the interest set. */ fun main() { Selector.open().use { println("Selector implementation: ${it.javaClass.name}") } println("idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ : ${idleWakeups(SelectionKey.OP_READ)} wakeups") println("idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ | OP_WRITE: ${idleWakeups(SelectionKey.OP_READ or SelectionKey.OP_WRITE)} wakeups") } private fun idleWakeups(interest: Int): Long = Selector.open().use { selector -> ServerSocketChannel.open().use { server -> server.bind(InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0)) SocketChannel.open(server.localAddress).use { _ -> server.accept().use { conn -> conn.configureBlocking(false) conn.register(selector, interest) val end = System.nanoTime() + 300_000_000L var count = 0L while (System.nanoTime() < end) { if (selector.select(50) > 0) count++ // nobody sends anything on this connection selector.selectedKeys().clear() } count } } } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l02.SpinDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l02/SpinDemo.kt 0 wakeups with OP_READ, and hundreds of thousands with OP_WRITE added (374,510 and 421,702 for the Java and Kotlin versions on a busy 4-core Linux machine; the exact number depends on processor speed and load). Under strace the loop slows down a lot, because strace stops the program on every system call, but the table still shows thousands of epoll_wait calls (4,315 in one run) against 5 epoll_ctl. On macOS the first line names the kqueue selector.

h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · Java and Kotlin
x: The serve step in Java and Kotlin serve, Java private void serve(SelectionKey key) throws IOException { SocketChannel ch = (SocketChannel) key.channel(); Conn conn = (Conn) key.attachment(); if (key.isReadable() && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true; conn.buf.flip(); if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf); conn.buf.compact(); boolean pending = conn.buf.position() > 0; if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return; } int ops = 0; if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_READ; if (pending) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_WRITE; key.interestOps(ops); } serve, Kotlin private fun serve(key: SelectionKey) { val ch = key.channel() as SocketChannel val conn = key.attachment() as Conn if (key.isReadable && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true conn.buf.flip() if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf) conn.buf.compact() val pending = conn.buf.position() > 0 if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return } var ops = 0 if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_READ if (pending) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_WRITE key.interestOps(ops) } Both call the same JDK classes, so they behave the same: same partial writes, same level-triggered selector. The differences are on the surface, and they still trip people up. Kotlin has no |= for bit flags, so you write ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_READ. Kotlin reads isReadable() and isAcceptable() as properties (key.isReadable), and the attachment is an untyped Any? that you cast with as Conn, just as Java casts from Object. Neither language helps with the buffer's mode: flip() and compact() change numbers at run time, not types, so neither compiler can stop you from writing a buffer that is still in write mode.

h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · Worked example
x: Trace one connection through a partial write The client sends 20 KiB and reads slowly. The server's tray holds 16 KiB. First select(): readable. The server reads 16 KiB, flips, and the kernel accepts only 6 KiB of the write. read 16384 -> pos=16384 lim=16384 (buffer full) flip() -> pos=0 lim=16384 write -> 6144 -> pos=6144 lim=16384 (10240 bytes not sent) compact() -> pos=10240 lim=16384 (pending: 10240, room: 6144) interest = OP_READ | OP_WRITE Second select(): readable (the other 4 KiB arrived) and writable (the client read some). The server appends 4 KiB behind the pending bytes, then sends everything it holds. read 4096 -> pos=14336 lim=16384 flip() -> pos=0 lim=14336 write -> 14336 -> pos=14336 lim=14336 (all sent) compact() -> pos=0 lim=16384 (pending: 0) interest = OP_READ (OP_WRITE dropped: nothing to send) Now the client half-closes while the server still holds bytes. read returns -1, so stop reading, but keep OP_WRITE until the tail is gone. Close in the pass where pending reaches zero. // 1. remember EOF, don't close yet if (key.isReadable() && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true; // 2. send what we can, keep the rest conn.buf.flip(); if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf); conn.buf.compact(); // 3. close only when drained; otherwise ask for exactly what we need boolean pending = conn.buf.position() > 0; if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return; } key.interestOps((conn.eof ? 0 : SelectionKey.OP_READ) | (pending ? SelectionKey.OP_WRITE : 0)); // 1. remember EOF, don't close yet if (key.isReadable && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true // 2. send what we can, keep the rest conn.buf.flip() if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf) conn.buf.compact() // 3. close only when drained; otherwise ask for exactly what we need val pending = conn.buf.position() > 0 if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return } key.interestOps((if (conn.eof) 0 else SelectionKey.OP_READ) or (if (pending) SelectionKey.OP_WRITE else 0)) The lab's version adds one more condition: drop OP_READ while the tray has no room left. Without it, a full tray and a readable socket make the same spin as a stray OP_WRITE: select() says readable, read() copies 0 bytes into the full buffer, and the loop goes around again.

h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · Lab
x: Fix an NIO echo server that loses bytes and burns a core labs/nio/src/main/java/workbench/nio/l02/NioEchoServer.java ./gradlew :nio:test --tests 'workbench.nio.l02.*' Run the tests. All three fail: the 4 MiB echo comes back short, the half-close test loses its tail, and an idle connection wakes the selector hundreds of thousands of times. In accept(), register the new channel for OP_READ only. In serve(), replace clear() with compact() so unsent bytes stay at the front, and only call write when the flipped buffer hasRemaining(). Close the channel only when conn.eof is true and nothing is pending (buf.position() == 0 after compact()). End serve() by setting the interest set: OP_READ while not at EOF and the buffer has room, OP_WRITE only while bytes are pending. Run the tests three times. After compact(), position() is exactly the number of bytes still waiting to be sent. The tests give the client a 4 KiB receive buffer, and the server's sockets an 8 KiB send buffer, so partial writes happen early and often. Your code must not depend on those sizes. If idleConnectionDoesNotSpin still fails, look for any path through serve() that returns with OP_WRITE still set after the buffer drained. The half-close test reads slowly on purpose. If it fails with a few kilobytes missing, you close on EOF before the pending bytes are written. All three tests in NioEchoServerTest pass, three runs in a row. By the end you can write a single-threaded NIO server that survives partial reads and writes, keeps unsent bytes, and registers OP_WRITE only while it has something to send.

h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · Quiz
x: A buffer of capacity 16 holds hello after five put calls. You call flip(), then get() twice, then compact(). Where are position and limit? position 0, limit 3 position 3, limit 16 position 2, limit 5 position 5, limit 16 compact() moves the 3 unread bytes (llo) to the front, sets position right after them (3) and limit back to capacity (16), ready for more filling. Position 2, limit 5 is the state just before compact(). A non-blocking ch.write(buf) returns 4,096, and buf.remaining() was 16,384 before the call. What should the server do? Call write in a loop until everything is sent Throw an IOException: the client is broken Keep the 12,288 bytes with compact(), arm OP_WRITE, and go back to select() clear() the buffer and read the next message The kernel's send buffer is full. Looping would spin (later writes return 0) and hold up every other connection on this thread. Keep the bytes, ask the selector to say when the socket is writable again, and serve other connections meanwhile. Your NIO server uses one core at 100% with no traffic. Profiles show the loop thread in EPollSelectorImpl.doSelect over and over. What is the most likely cause? OP_WRITE stays in the interest set of idle connections The ByteBuffer is a heap buffer, not a direct one One selector has too many connections The JIT compiled the loop badly A level-triggered selector reports a writable socket on every call, and idle sockets are writable. Heap buffers cost a copy per read or write, not a spin, and a busy selector would show real traffic. From lesson 1: 5,000 parcel lockers keep connections open, and each sends a 100 ms request every 10 s. How many threads sit blocked in read() on a single-selector NIO server, and on a thread-per-connection server? 0 on the NIO server, about 5,000 on the other About 5,000 on both 50 on both: Little's law decides 1 on the NIO server, 50 on the other NIO reads never block: the one loop thread waits in select(), not in read(). Thread-per-connection parks one thread per open socket. Little's law gives 50 requests in flight, but that only sets the thread count for thread-per-request designs. A handler calls ch.read(buf) and then parses one message from buf. Under load, parsing sometimes fails on a cut-off message. What is wrong? The selector is edge-triggered and lost an event The buffer must be direct read must only be called while OP_WRITE is armed It assumes one read returns one whole message; TCP can split or merge messages, so it needs framing TCP delivers a byte stream. One read can hold part of a message or several messages. A delimiter or a length prefix tells the parser when a message is complete; until then, keep the bytes and wait for the next read.

h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · Key terms
x: ByteBuffer A fixed block of memory with a position, a limit and a capacity that NIO reads into and writes from. flip / compact flip() switches a buffer from writing to reading; compact() keeps unread bytes and switches back. Channel NIO's handle on something bytes move through, such as a socket; it can be made non-blocking. Selector An object that waits until one of many registered channels is ready, so one thread can serve them all. SelectionKey One channel's registration with a selector: interest set, ready set and an attachment. Interest set The events you ask the selector to watch for on a channel: accept, read, write. Level-triggered Readiness is reported on every check for as long as it is true, not once when it changes. Partial write A non-blocking write that sends only part of the buffer because the kernel's send buffer is full. What does flip() do to a ByteBuffer? Sets limit to the current position and position to 0: it switches from writing into the buffer to reading out of it. compact() vs clear()? compact() moves unread bytes to the front and continues writing after them. clear() resets both marks and forgets unread bytes. A non-blocking write(buf) sent fewer bytes than buf.remaining(). Why, and what next? The socket's send buffer had less free space. Keep the rest (compact()), arm OP_WRITE, and write again when the selector says the socket is writable. What happens if you never remove keys from selectedKeys()? They stay selected with their old ready set, so the loop handles the same event on every pass: 7 times in 300 ms for one message in this lesson's demo. Why does a permanently registered OP_WRITE make a selector spin? Linux epoll selectors are level-triggered, and a socket with send-buffer space is always writable, so every select() returns at once. How does an NIO server push back on a client that sends faster than it reads? It drops OP_READ while its buffer is full. Unread bytes fill the kernel buffer, the TCP window shrinks, and the client's writes slow down. Heap or direct ByteBuffer for socket IO? Direct, allocated once and reused. The JDK copies a heap buffer through a temporary direct buffer on every channel read or write, and direct buffers are costly to allocate.

h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · Go deeper
x: Level-triggered and edge-triggered are the two ways epoll can report readiness. Level-triggered, the default, reports a socket on every epoll_wait for as long as it is readable or writable: the light that stays on. Edge-triggered (EPOLLET) reports it once, when it changes from not ready to ready, and then stays quiet until the next change: the bell. The JDK's EPollSelectorImpl never sets EPOLLET, so Selector is level-triggered on Linux. That is forgiving for reads (leave bytes unread, and the next select() tells you again) and unforgiving for OP_WRITE. Edge-triggered code has the opposite trap: after a notification you must read until read returns 0, or you never hear about the leftover bytes. The JDK's virtual-thread poller, which lesson 8 looks at, uses a third mode, EPOLLONESHOT: report once, then disarm until the socket is registered again. That fits its job, which is to wake one parked thread once. Two more details from the JDK source. EPollSelectorImpl asks epoll_wait for at most min(fdLimit, 1024) events per call, so a selector with 10,000 ready sockets needs several calls to see them all. And Netty's NIO transport still carries a guard against selectors that return early with nothing selected: after 512 such returns in a row (io.netty.selectorAutoRebuildThreshold), it rebuilds the selector. That is the workaround for the old "epoll spin bug", and the reason Netty counts empty wakeups. To see the system calls yourself on Linux, run any demo that uses only JDK classes outside Gradle with strace -f -c -e trace=epoll_wait,epoll_ctl java -cp nio/build/classes/java/demo <class>. -c prints a count per system call when the program exits.

h: Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline · One clerk per row of boxes: the event loop and its group
x: Netty keeps the shape of the select loop we wrote by hand. Each piece from the last lesson has a Netty name, and each one fixes something we had to get right ourselves: Our loop in lesson 2 Netty What it fixes one thread running select() EventLoop, several in an EventLoopGroup one loop per core instead of one per server the Conn card on each key Channel and its ChannelPipeline of handlers per-connection state and logic in small pieces flip() and compact() by hand ByteBuf, with separate read and write indexes no mode to get wrong (lesson 4) pending bytes and arming OP_WRITE the channel's outbound buffer Netty sets and clears OP_WRITE for you dropping OP_READ when full auto-read and writability backpressure as a setting (lesson 4) nothing: only the loop could touch its keys a task queue on every loop any thread can hand the loop work safely A few names first. A channel is Netty's object for one connection, with its socket (its end of the network connection) and its handlers. A handler is a small object that reacts to that connection's events, such as "a message arrived". An event loop is one thread that runs a selector (the JDK object from lesson 2 that reports which connections are ready) over many channels, plus a queue of tasks that other threads can hand it. It's the clerk, the row of boxes, and the clerk's in-tray. An event loop group is the team of clerks. Our running example in this lesson is the post office's price desk. A client sends a line describing a letter or a parcel, and the server answers with a line of its own. In Netty 4.2 you build each group by naming its IO handler, the part that talks to the operating system: Java EventLoopGroup boss = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()); // accepts connections EventLoopGroup workers = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(NioIoHandler.newFactory()); // serves them Channel server = new ServerBootstrap() .group(boss, workers) .channel(NioServerSocketChannel.class) .childHandler(new ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { @Override protected void initChannel(SocketChannel ch) { ch.pipeline().addLast(new LineBasedFrameDecoder(64), new StringDecoder(UTF_8), new StringEncoder(UTF_8), new QuoteHandler()); } }) .bind(8080).sync().channel(); Kotlin val boss = MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()) // accepts connections val workers = MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(NioIoHandler.newFactory()) // serves them val server = ServerBootstrap() .group(boss, workers) .channel(NioServerSocketChannel::class.java) .childHandler(object : ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { override fun initChannel(ch: SocketChannel) { ch.pipeline().addLast(LineBasedFrameDecoder(64), StringDecoder(UTF_8), StringEncoder(UTF_8), QuoteHandler()) } }) .bind(8080).sync().channel() The boss group only accepts connections and hands each one to a worker loop, so one boss thread is plenty for one port. ServerBootstrap, Netty's helper for starting a server, wires the rest: which groups, which kind of channel, and a ChannelInitializer that sets up the stations for each new connection. We'll walk those stations in the next section. If you learned Netty 4.1, you wrote new NioEventLoopGroup(). Netty 4.2 deprecated it, along with its epoll and kqueue cousins. Ask the compiler (javac -Xlint:deprecation), and it says so without hesitation: warning: [deprecation] NioEventLoopGroup in io.netty.channel.nio has been deprecated. The replacement is always MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup plus a factory: NioIoHandler, EpollIoHandler, KQueueIoHandler or IoUringIoHandler. The bootstrap still names the matching channel class. Small servers often pass one group to .group(group), so the same loops accept and serve. The lab does that, with a single loop, so you can watch a blocked loop clearly. Without a thread count, a group gets two loops per core. EventLoopDemo, in the Try it below, prints 8 on a 4-core machine. Then it connects four clients, one after another, to a group of two worker loops. One run printed (the bytes from lines left out): default loop count: 8 (availableProcessors=4) client port 46484 registered on multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-4-1, inEventLoop=true client port 46488 registered on multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-4-2, inEventLoop=true client port 46490 registered on multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-4-1, inEventLoop=true client port 46498 registered on multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-4-2, inEventLoop=true Each new connection is registered with one loop, in turn, and stays there for life. That lifelong seat is why Netty handlers rarely need locks: every event for a channel runs on its loop's one thread, one after another. It's also why one slow handler hurts. Every other channel on that loop waits behind it, like every box in a row waiting for its one clerk. A channel belongs to one event loop for life. Its handlers never run at once, and they share the loop's one thread. A clerk with a row of boxes still needs a way to handle each letter. That's the pipeline. See which loop owns each connection Open EventLoopDemo.java (or EventLoopDemo.kt). It starts a server with one accepting loop and two worker loops, then connects four clients one after another. Predict the thread name for the third and fourth client, and what inEventLoop() returns inside the handler. Run it. Then change the worker group to new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, ...) and run it again. h: Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline · The sorting line: reads flow in, writes flow out
x:
Netty's event loop and pipeline: reads flow in, writes flow out, never block Every channel has a ChannelPipeline: a list of handlers between a head, next to the socket, and a tail. It's the line of stations each letter passes. Two kinds of traffic move along it, in opposite directions. Each handler gets a ChannelHandlerContext, usually called ctx. It's the handler's own place on the line, with methods to pass an event to the next station or to start a write from there. Inbound events start at the head and move toward the tail. The main ones are channelActive when the connection opens, channelRead for each message, channelReadComplete after a batch of reads, and exceptionCaught when something fails. Inbound handlers change the message on its way. At the price desk, LineBasedFrameDecoder turns the stream of bytes into one ByteBuf (Netty's buffer, lesson 4) per line, and StringDecoder turns that into a String. The last handler only ever sees whole lines. Outbound operations go the other way. write, flush and close start where you call them and move toward the head. StringEncoder sits on that path and turns your String back into bytes. So the order of addLast is the order inbound events see the handlers, and the reverse of the order writes see them. One detail decides which handlers a write passes. ctx.writeAndFlush(msg) starts at the current handler and goes toward the head, skipping everything after it. ctx.channel().writeAndFlush(msg) starts at the tail and passes every outbound handler. Inside a handler, use ctx unless you really want the whole line. PipelineDemo puts taps between the stations, handlers that print whatever passes, and feeds two lines in three pieces. Its last handler is the shout-back desk: it answers each line in upper case. writeInbound("hel") writeInbound("lo
wor") in, after framing : ByteBuf "hello" in, business sees : String "hello" out, to the wire : ByteBuf "HELLO
" writeInbound("ld
") ... 100-byte line -> TooLongFrameException: frame length (100) exceeds the allowed maximum (64) finish() = false The first piece produced nothing. The decoder kept the bytes and waited for the end of the line: last lesson's framing problem, solved once on the line. The 64-byte limit matters as much. Without it, a client that never sends a newline makes the decoder keep its bytes forever. With it, the 100-byte line fails at once. Here the post office picture breaks. On a real sorting line, each station has its own worker, and they all work at the same time. In Netty, one clerk carries each letter through every station, start to finish, before picking up the next. That's exactly why one slow station stops the whole row. The demo runs on an EmbeddedChannel, a channel with no socket and no real event loop. writeInbound pushes bytes in at the head, readOutbound returns what reached the head on the way out, and finish() says whether anything was left over. It's the fastest way to test a handler, and this lesson's lab uses it. Reads flow from head to tail, and writes flow from where you start them toward the head. The order of addLast decides what each handler sees. Every one of those stations runs on the clerk's one thread. So what happens when a station has to wait? Move the tap past the encoder Run PipelineDemo (or PipelineDemoKt) and match each printed line to a station in the figure. In the EmbeddedChannel constructor, move the outbound tap so it comes right after new StringEncoder(UTF_8) instead of before it. Predict what out, to the wire prints now, then run it again. h: Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline · The golden rule: the clerk never makes a phone call
x:
Handlers run on the event loop's thread. A handler that sleeps, waits for a lock, or calls a database the blocking way holds that thread, and every other channel on the loop waits with it. That's the golden rule of event loops: never block the loop. In the post office, it's the clerk who stops to phone the back office about a price while the whole row of boxes fills up. BlockingLoopDemo breaks the rule on purpose, with one event loop and two clients. Client A asks for SLOW, which sleeps 1 s to stand in for a slow call. Client B asks for FAST 50 ms later. FAST needs no work, so it should come back in a few milliseconds. One run on a busy 4-core machine printed: [blocking in the handler] event-loop lag probe: 995 ms FAST reply after 996 ms: FAST on multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-2-1 [dispatch to the back office] event-loop lag probe: 0 ms FAST reply after 3 ms: FAST on back-office With the handler blocking, FAST took 996 ms: it waited for the clerk to hang up. With the slow part handed off, it took 3 ms. The lag probe in that output is a trick worth keeping. Slip an empty task into the loop's in-tray and time how long it waits to run. On a healthy loop, it's close to 0. Netty 4.1 offered a shortcut: pipeline.addLast(executorGroup, "name", handler) ran one handler on a separate group of threads. Netty 4.2 deprecated those versions of addLast, and compiling the old call prints warning: [deprecation] addLast(EventExecutorGroup,String,ChannelHandler) in ChannelPipeline has been deprecated. The commit that did it (d64340b) says per-handler executors caused more problems than they solved, and that it's "much better to dispatch it manually". Manual dispatch is three lines. Hand the slow part to a pool of your own, the back office, and write the reply from there: Java @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) { backOffice.execute(() -> { // 1. leave the event loop String quote = priceBook.lookup(line); // 2. wait here: a database, a slow web service ctx.writeAndFlush(quote + "
"); // 3. safe from any thread }); } Kotlin override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, line: String) { backOffice.execute { // 1. leave the event loop val quote = priceBook.lookup(line) // 2. wait here: a database, a slow web service ctx.writeAndFlush("$quote
") // 3. safe from any thread } } Step 3 works because Netty asks inEventLoop(), "am I on this channel's loop?", on every write. Called from another thread, the write becomes a task in the channel's own in-tray, so the pipeline still runs on one thread. If code in the pool needs the handler's own fields, hop back first with ctx.executor().execute(...), so that state stays with the clerk. Size the back office like any blocking pool: with Little's law and the limits of the service you call, from lesson 1, or with virtual threads. The event loop serves everyone, so it must never wait for anyone. Hand the waiting to another thread. The threading rules are the heart of Netty, and 4.2 left them alone. A few other things did change. Block the loop, then free it Open BlockingLoopDemo.java (or BlockingLoopDemo.kt). Predict the lag probe and the FAST reply time in both runs. Run it with the command below. In the blocking run, which thread produced the SLOW reply? In the dispatch run? Find the line in the code that decides it. h: Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline · What else changed in Netty 4.2
x: Netty 4.2 changed a few things that 4.1 code and older blog posts get wrong. The default allocator, the part that hands out buffers, is new. ByteBufAllocator.DEFAULT is now an AdaptiveByteBufAllocator, and a plain buffer(16) comes back as a direct AdaptiveByteBuf. The migration guide says most workloads should see less memory use, and that it was designed to work well with virtual threads. -Dio.netty.allocator.type=pooled brings back the old pooled allocator if you need it. Lesson 4 looks inside these buffers. io_uring, a newer Linux interface for IO that lesson 8 compares with epoll, graduated from Netty's incubator to a full transport. Its package is now io.netty.channel.uring, its classes start with IoUring, and you use it like the others: MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup with IoUringIoHandler.newFactory() and the IoUring channel classes. TLS clients (TLS is the encryption behind https) now check by default that the server's certificate matches its host name. A test that connected to a server with a mismatched certificate will start failing its handshake. The netty-codec module was split into smaller ones, and the minimum Java version is now 8. And Netty 4.1 and 4.2 can't share a classpath. That one matters in practice. Vert.x 5.2.3 pins Netty 4.2.20.Final, so a library that drags Netty 4.1 jars in next to it fails at run time in confusing ways, instead of with a clear version conflict. Check ./gradlew dependencies for mixed io.netty versions before you debug anything else. What didn't change is the part this lesson is about. A channel still belongs to one loop, handlers still run on it, and blocking it is still the most common way to make a Netty server slow. Switch the transport In EventLoopDemo, change both groups to EpollIoHandler.newFactory() and the channel class to EpollServerSocketChannel.class (on macOS use KQueueIoHandler and KQueueServerSocketChannel). Run it. Predict first: do the thread names or the turn-taking change? Now put the channel class back to NioServerSocketChannel.class but keep the epoll (or kqueue) factory. Predict what happens before you run it. With matching factory and channel class, the output looks the same: same thread names, same turn-taking, because the threading model doesn't depend on the transport. With a mismatch, the bind fails at once with IllegalStateException: incompatible event loop type: io.netty.channel.SingleThreadIoEventLoop: an NIO channel can only register with a loop whose IO handler is NIO. That's why the 4.2 migration guide reminds you to set the channel class as well as the factory.

h: Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline · Java and Kotlin
x: Handing a slow lookup from a Netty handler to the back office QuoteHandler.java final class QuoteHandler extends SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String> { private final Executor backOffice; private final Function<String, String> lookup; QuoteHandler(Executor backOffice, Function<String, String> lookup) { this.backOffice = backOffice; this.lookup = lookup; } @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) { backOffice.execute(() -> ctx.writeAndFlush(lookup.apply(line) + "\n")); } } QuoteHandler.kt class QuoteHandler( private val backOffice: Executor, private val lookup: (String) -> String, ) : SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String>() { override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, line: String) { backOffice.execute { ctx.writeAndFlush(lookup(line) + "\n") } } } At run time these are the same class: Netty sees a SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String>, and the Kotlin lambda becomes a Runnable through SAM conversion. Kotlin saves the constructor boilerplate and takes a function type where Java needs Function<String, String>. One Kotlin-only temptation is worth naming: calling runBlocking { } inside channelRead0 to use a suspend function. That blocks the event loop just like Thread.sleep. If you want coroutines, launch on a scope with its own dispatcher and call ctx.writeAndFlush from the coroutine. That's the same manual dispatch, with a different back office.

h: Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline · Worked example
x: Hand off a slow lookup without racing on the handler's state A handler counts the requests it has served on each connection and looks up each price in a price book that takes 120 ms to answer. It blocks the loop. The field served is safe only because one thread touches it. final class PriceHandler extends SimpleChannelInboundHandler<PriceRequest> { private int served; // per-connection state @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, PriceRequest req) { Price price = priceBook.lookup(req); // 120 ms, on the event loop served++; ctx.writeAndFlush(price.withNumber(served)); } } class PriceHandler : SimpleChannelInboundHandler<PriceRequest>() { private var served = 0 // per-connection state override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, req: PriceRequest) { val price = priceBook.lookup(req) // 120 ms, on the event loop served++ ctx.writeAndFlush(price.withNumber(served)) } } Moving everything into the back office frees the loop but breaks the counter. Two requests on the same connection can now run on two pool threads at once, and served++ is a read-modify-write race on a plain field. backOffice.execute(() -> { Price price = priceBook.lookup(req); served++; // two pool threads, one field: lost updates ctx.writeAndFlush(price.withNumber(served)); }); backOffice.execute { val price = priceBook.lookup(req) served++ // two pool threads, one field: lost updates ctx.writeAndFlush(price.withNumber(served)) } Do only the slow call in the back office, then hop back to the channel's loop for everything that touches the handler's state. The loop is the lock. @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, PriceRequest req) { backOffice.execute(() -> { Price price = priceBook.lookup(req); // 1. wait off the loop ctx.executor().execute(() -> { // 2. back on the channel's loop served++; // 3. confined state, no lock needed ctx.writeAndFlush(price.withNumber(served)); }); }); } override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, req: PriceRequest) { backOffice.execute { val price = priceBook.lookup(req) // 1. wait off the loop ctx.executor().execute { // 2. back on the channel's loop served++ // 3. confined state, no lock needed ctx.writeAndFlush(price.withNumber(served)) } } } One thing the loop no longer gives you is order. Two requests on one connection can finish in either order, so replies can overtake each other. Either give each request a number that the client matches its reply with, or keep one request in flight per connection by turning off auto-read until the reply is written. Lesson 4 shows auto-read.

h: Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline · Quiz

A Netty server's worker group has 2 loops, and 6 clients connect one after another. Client 3's handler calls Thread.sleep(500). Which clients are delayed? Only client 3 Clients 1, 3 and 5, which share an event loop All 6 clients None: Netty gives each read its own thread Channels are handed to the loops in turn and stay on their loop for life, so clients 1, 3 and 5 share one thread. While client 3's handler sleeps, the other two wait. Clients 2, 4 and 6 run on the other loop and are not affected. A pipeline is built with addLast(frameDecoder, stringDecoder, handlerA, stringEncoder, handlerB). handlerA calls ctx.writeAndFlush("ok
") with a String. What happens? The string is encoded and sent The write fails: ctx starts at handlerA and goes toward the head, so it never passes the encoder Netty reorders handlers so encoders always run last handlerB receives the string as an inbound message ctx.writeAndFlush travels from handlerA toward the head, and the encoder sits on the other side of handlerA. The head only accepts ByteBuf and FileRegion, so the write's future fails. ctx.channel().writeAndFlush would start at the tail and pass the encoder. What is the Netty 4.2 way to run a blocking database query (say, through JDBC, Java's standard database API) from a handler? pipeline.addLast(new DefaultEventExecutorGroup(16), "jdbc", handler) Call it directly: Netty 4.2 event loops are virtual threads Hand the query to your own pool and call ctx.writeAndFlush with the result from there Wrap the call in synchronized so only one loop blocks at a time 4.2 deprecated the per-handler executor versions of addLast and recommends dispatching by hand. Netty's loops are platform threads, and a synchronized block still blocks the thread that runs it. From lesson 2: Netty's NIO transport only asks the selector for OP_WRITE while a channel has bytes it couldn't write yet. Why? Linux selectors are level-triggered, so a socket with free send-buffer space would be reported on every select and the loop would spin OP_WRITE is slower than OP_READ Edge-triggered epoll would lose the event The JDK forbids registering OP_WRITE together with OP_READ A socket is writable almost all the time. With level-triggered epoll, a permanent OP_WRITE makes every select() return at once: the light that never goes out. Netty sets it after an incomplete write and clears it when the outbound buffer drains, which is the rule from lesson 2. A test writes "parcel 1kg
parcel 2kg
" in one writeInbound call into an EmbeddedChannel holding LineBasedFrameDecoder, StringDecoder, StringEncoder and a handler that replies once per line. How many messages does readOutbound() return? 1 0 until you call finish() It depends on how the network splits the bytes 2 The frame decoder emits one frame per line, even when both lines arrive in one buffer, and the handler replies to each. EmbeddedChannel runs everything on the calling thread, with no network involved, so the answer is always 2.

h: Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline · Key terms
x: Channel (Netty) Netty's object for one connection: its socket, its pipeline and the event loop it belongs to. EventLoop One thread that runs a selector over its channels plus a queue of tasks. EventLoopGroup A set of event loops; new channels are spread over them in turn. IoHandler Netty 4.2's transport-specific engine inside a loop: NIO, epoll, kqueue or io_uring. ChannelPipeline The ordered list of handlers every event and write of a channel passes through. Inbound handler A handler for events coming from the socket, such as channelRead. Outbound handler A handler for operations going to the socket, such as write and flush. EmbeddedChannel A channel with no socket, for testing a pipeline on the calling thread. Netty 4.2 replacement for new NioEventLoopGroup()? new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(NioIoHandler.newFactory()), optionally with a thread count. The same pattern works with EpollIoHandler, KQueueIoHandler and IoUringIoHandler. Default number of event loops in a Netty group? 2 × available processors (property io.netty.eventLoopThreads): 8 on a 4-core machine. How long does a channel stay on its event loop? For its whole life. All its events run on that one thread, one after another. ctx.writeAndFlush(msg) vs ctx.channel().writeAndFlush(msg)? ctx starts at the current handler and goes toward the head. channel() starts at the tail and passes every outbound handler. Is ctx.writeAndFlush safe to call from a thread that isn't the event loop? Yes. Netty sees inEventLoop() is false and queues the write as a task on the channel's own loop. Why did Netty 4.2 deprecate addLast(EventExecutorGroup, ...)? Per-handler executors caused more problems than they solved. Netty now says to dispatch blocking work by hand to your own pool. What is an event-loop lag probe? Submit an empty task to the loop and time how long it waits to run. Near 0 ms on a healthy loop; about the block time when a handler blocks.

h: Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline · Go deeper
x: Two details make manual dispatch work, and both are worth reading in Netty's source. First, every outbound call checks where it runs. AbstractChannelHandlerContext.write asks executor.inEventLoop(). On the loop, it calls the next handler directly. Off the loop, it wraps the write in a task and puts it in the loop's queue. That's why ctx.writeAndFlush from your pool is safe, and also why it isn't free: each one is a task hand-off and a wake-up of the selector. Second, the loop takes turns between IO and tasks. A Netty 4.2 loop is a SingleThreadIoEventLoop: it runs the IO handler (select, then process the ready channels), then drains its task queue, then selects again. Tasks from other threads, writes from your pool and timers all share the thread with IO. The 4.2 migration guide mentions hooks that measure how long IO processing and task processing take per loop run, for exactly this kind of tuning. When you dispatch, think about the order of replies on a connection, as the worked example showed, and about backpressure: if the pool is slower than the requests arrive, its queue grows without limit unless something stops reading. Lesson 4 covers auto-read and writability, Netty's tools for that. To catch accidental blocking in tests, Netty ships an integration for BlockHound (Hidden$NettyBlockHoundIntegration in netty-common). BlockHound itself is a separate library, a Java agent that watches method calls. Installed in a test, it throws when code on a Netty event-loop thread calls a known blocking method such as Thread.sleep or a socket read.

h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · Envelopes with a page count: framing before decoding
x: A decoder frames bytes that arrive in chunks of any size, writability and auto-read stop a slow client from filling your memory, and a buffer nobody releases never goes back to the pool Start where every protocol starts. A protocol is the set of rules two programs agree on for their bytes. TCP delivers a stream of bytes, not messages (lesson 2), so the first job of any protocol's pipeline is framing: finding where one message ends and the next begins. One whole message on the wire is a frame. This lesson's running example is the post office's letter link. Each letter has a type number and a body of text, and goes on the wire behind its length, like an envelope with the page count written on the front: [ length: int32 ][ type: int8 ][ body: UTF-8 bytes ] length = 1 + body bytes In Netty, each station on a connection's pipeline, its line of stations, is a handler. A decoder is a handler that turns bytes into messages, an encoder does the reverse, and the pair is a codec. Netty's ByteToMessageDecoder is the base class for decoders. It keeps every byte that has arrived so far in one buffer (Netty calls it the cumulation) and calls your decode each time more bytes arrive. Your job is to take out whole frames and leave the rest for later. Here is a frame decoder written by hand: Java class HandMadeFrameDecoder extends ByteToMessageDecoder { @Override protected void decode(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, ByteBuf in, List<Object> out) { if (in.readableBytes() < 4) return; // 1. not even the length yet int length = in.getInt(in.readerIndex()); // 2. peek, don't consume if (length > 1020) throw new TooLongFrameException("frame too long: " + length); if (in.readableBytes() < 4 + length) return; // 3. body incomplete: wait for more in.skipBytes(4); out.add(in.readRetainedSlice(length)); // 4. one whole frame, no copy } } Kotlin class HandMadeFrameDecoder : ByteToMessageDecoder() { override fun decode(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, input: ByteBuf, out: MutableList<Any>) { if (input.readableBytes() < 4) return // 1. not even the length yet val length = input.getInt(input.readerIndex()) // 2. peek, don't consume if (length > 1020) throw TooLongFrameException("frame too long: $length") if (input.readableBytes() < 4 + length) return // 3. body incomplete: wait for more input.skipBytes(4) out += input.readRetainedSlice(length) // 4. one whole frame, no copy } } Read it as the clerk at the first station. If there aren't even 4 bytes, the page count hasn't arrived: wait. Peek at the length without taking it. If the body isn't all there yet, wait again. Only then skip the length and hand on one whole frame. Each line follows a rule from the ByteToMessageDecoder Javadoc. Return without moving the reader index when a frame is incomplete. Use getInt(in.readerIndex()), not getInt(0), because the cumulation can still hold used bytes in front of the reader index. Hand the frame on as a slice, a view of the same memory, because readBytes(n) allocates a new buffer that someone must give back. And never mark a ByteToMessageDecoder @Sharable, Netty's tag for a handler that may sit in many pipelines: it keeps per-channel state. Here the post office picture breaks. A real envelope arrives whole, page count and all. On the wire, even the 4-byte length can arrive in two pieces, which is what the first return is for. You don't have to write it yourself. new LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(1024, 0, 4, 0, 4) does the same job: frames of at most 1024 bytes, a length field at offset 0 that is 4 bytes long, no adjustment (the length counts only what follows it), and strip 4 bytes before passing the frame on. The figure shows each number on the wire. The next decoder sees exactly [type][body] and turns it into a Letter. On the way out, a MessageToByteEncoder<Letter> writes the three fields back. CodecDemo, in the Try it below, encodes two letters, 11 and 13 bytes long, and feeds them to a server pipeline cut at bytes 3, 9 and 14. Its last handler stamps each letter: it sends it back in upper case, with the type plus one. wire: 24 bytes, hex 00000007016e6f74652d31000000090770617263656c2d31 bytes [ 0, 3) -> replies [] bytes [ 3, 9) -> replies [] bytes [ 9,14) -> replies [type=2 NOTE-1] bytes [14,24) -> replies [type=8 PARCEL-1] length 5000 -> TooLongFrameException: Adjusted frame length exceeds 1024: 5004 - discarded The decoder waited through half a page count and half a body, and answered each letter the moment it was whole. The last line is the maximum at work (5,000 plus the 4-byte length field), and it's a safety setting. A client that sends a length of two billion would make a decoder without one hold two gigabytes of bytes while it waits. It's an envelope that claims to hold a million pages, and the first station now turns it away at the door. Frame before you decode, and always set a maximum. A length you didn't limit is memory a stranger can claim. Every one of those frames lives in a ByteBuf. Netty's buffer looks like lesson 2's tray, with two changes. Feed a codec in awkward pieces Open CodecDemo.java (or CodecDemo.kt). It encodes two letters, 11 and 13 bytes long, and feeds them to a server pipeline cut at bytes 3, 9 and 14. Predict which of the four slices produce a reply, and which reply. Run it. Then change the cut at 9 to 11 and predict again. io.netty.handler.codec.LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.MessageToByteEncoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.TooLongFrameException; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8; /** A length-prefixed codec fed in awkward slices: [int length][byte type][UTF-8 text]. */ public class CodecDemo { record Frame(int type, String text) { } static final class FrameEncoder extends MessageToByteEncoder<Frame> { @Override protected void encode(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, Frame f, ByteBuf out) { byte[] text = h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · Trays from a shared stack: a ByteBuf's two indexes and its reference count
x: Netty's ByteBuf fixes the two things that made ByteBuffer painful in lesson 2. It has separate readerIndex and writerIndex, a read line and a fill line, so there's no read mode, no write mode and no flip(). And it's reference-counted, so Netty can lend its memory out and take it back. Lending is the reason for the counting. Netty allocates direct memory, outside the Java heap where objects live, because the kernel can read it without a copy. Direct memory costs a lot to allocate, so Netty's allocator carves buffers out of big chunks and takes them back for reuse. In the post office, the trays come from one shared stack, and every tray must go back on the stack when its letter is done. The garbage collector, the part of the JVM that frees objects nobody uses any more, can't do that hand-back for us. It frees an object at some unknown later time, when memory runs low, while a busy server needs the tray back the moment a letter is done. So every ByteBuf carries a count of its holders. It starts at 1, retain() adds one, release() takes one away, and at 0 the memory goes back to the pool. Touch the buffer after that and Netty throws. RefCountDemo shows each step: buffer(16): AdaptiveByteBuf direct=true readerIndex=0 writerIndex=0 refCnt=1 after writeInt+writeLong: writerIndex=12 readableBytes=12 after readInt: readerIndex=4 readableBytes=8 (no flip) retain(): refCnt=2 release() -> false, refCnt=1 release() -> true, refCnt=0 (memory goes back to the allocator) readLong() after release -> IllegalReferenceCountException: refCnt: 0 AdaptiveByteBuf comes from the adaptive allocator, the default since Netty 4.2. Notice that readInt() moved only the read line: the 8 unread bytes stayed readable, and nobody flipped anything. Who calls release()? Netty's wiki answers in one sentence: the party that accesses a reference-counted object last is responsible for destroying it. On the sorting line, that works out like this: A handler that passes a message on with ctx.fireChannelRead(msg) hands the tray to the next station, and must not release it. A handler that uses a message up and doesn't pass it on must release it. SimpleChannelInboundHandler does that for you after channelRead0 returns. A message you write belongs to Netty, which releases it once it's on the wire. A decoder that turns a buffer into something else releases the input. ByteToMessageDecoder and MessageToMessageDecoder do it for you. Get it wrong one way and you release twice: IllegalReferenceCountException, loud and immediate. Get it wrong the other way and a tray never goes back. Nothing complains, the stack gets shorter, and weeks later the server runs out of direct memory. The last one to touch a buffer gives it back. Passing it on is handing it over. A double release shouts. A missing one whispers, so Netty sends someone to listen. Predict the count Open RefCountDemo.java (or RefCountDemo.kt). Cover the output above and predict refCnt after each line, and what release() returns each time. Run it. Then look at the composite part: addComponents(true, header, body) joins two buffers into one without copying. Predict what body.refCnt() is after frame.release(). h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · Finding the trays nobody handed back: PARANOID leak detection
x: A leaked ByteBuf doesn't throw. Netty finds leaks after the fact with ResourceLeakDetector, the night inspector of this lesson. It attaches a weak reference (one that doesn't keep its object alive) to each buffer it tracks. When the garbage collector sweeps away a tracked buffer whose count never reached 0, the inspector writes a report. Tracking costs time, so by default (the SIMPLE level) Netty tracks about 1 buffer in 128. ADVANCED samples the same way but also records where each buffer was touched. PARANOID tracks every buffer with full records, and the Netty wiki recommends it for tests. Turn it on with -Dio.netty.leakDetection.level=paranoid, or in a test with ResourceLeakDetector.setLevel(Level.PARANOID). LeakDemo has a handler that drops ten buffers without releasing them. Here is the start of the inspector's report: [main] ERROR io.netty.util.ResourceLeakDetector - LEAK: ByteBuf.release() was not called before it's garbage-collected. See https://netty.io/wiki/reference-counted-objects.html for more information. Recent access records: #1: Hint: 'LeakDemo$1#0' will handle the message from this point. ... Created at: io.netty.buffer.AdaptiveByteBufAllocator.newDirectBuffer(AdaptiveByteBufAllocator.java:67) ... 10 buffers leaked; the listener saw 1 report(s): [ByteBuf] Read it from the bottom. Created at is where the buffer was allocated, and the access records show who touched it last: the hint names the handler that received it and never let go. Ten trays were lost, and there is one report, because the inspector reports each distinct path once. Thorough, but never repetitive. Here the tray picture breaks again. In a real post office, a cleaner who finds a lost tray puts it back on the stack. The garbage collector frees only the buffer object. The memory Netty's allocator lent out doesn't go back to the pool, which is why a leak only ever grows. To fail a build on a leak, you need two more pieces. ByteBufUtil.setLeakListener(...) gives you a callback per report, so a test can collect them. And detection needs a garbage collection followed by another allocation, because the inspector checks its list of swept buffers when it tracks the next one. The lab's last test does exactly that: Java for (int i = 0; i < 40 && leaks.isEmpty(); i++) { System.gc(); // collect the leaked ByteBuf objects Thread.sleep(20); ByteBufAllocator.DEFAULT.buffer(8).release(); // the next allocation reports them } assertThat(leaks).isEmpty(); Kotlin var i = 0 while (i++ < 40 && leaks.isEmpty()) { System.gc() // collect the leaked ByteBuf objects Thread.sleep(20) ByteBufAllocator.DEFAULT.buffer(8).release() // the next allocation reports them } assertThat(leaks).isEmpty() When the garbage collector runs is up to the JVM, so this check depends on luck. Pair it with one that doesn't: keep a reference to the buffer you pushed in, and assert refCnt() == 0 after the pipeline ran. The lab does both. A leak is silent until the inspector finds it. Run pipeline tests at PARANOID, and check refCnt() as well. Lost trays are one way to fill your memory. A slow reader is the other. Make a leak, then fix it Run LeakDemo (or LeakDemoKt). Predict first: ten leaked buffers, how many reports? Find the Hint: line in the report and match it to the handler in the code. Fix the handler by adding ReferenceCountUtil.release(msg); to channelRead, and run it again. h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · A full out-tray: writability and auto-read
x: ctx.write(msg) never blocks, and a slow client never makes it fail. Netty puts the message in the channel's outbound buffer, a queue in your own program's memory, and moves it to the socket when the kernel's send buffer has room. In the post office, it's the out-tray behind each box. That's handy, and it's also how a Netty server runs out of memory: if the client reads more slowly than you write, the out-tray grows without limit. Netty tells you when the queue gets long. Each channel has two water marks, 32 KiB low and 64 KiB high by default (WriteBufferWaterMark), like two lines painted on the side of the out-tray. When the bytes waiting pass the high mark, channel.isWritable() turns false and Netty fires channelWritabilityChanged. When they drain below the low mark, isWritable() turns true and the event fires again. Two marks instead of one stop it from flipping on every write. Netty doesn't stop your writes when isWritable() is false. You have to act. For an echo server or a relay, the action is lesson 2's: stop reading from whoever produces the data. setAutoRead(false) tells the event loop, the one thread that serves this channel, to stop reading it, which for the NIO transport means taking OP_READ out of its interest set. The clerk stops taking letters from that box: Java @Override public void channelReadComplete(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) { ctx.flush(); if (!ctx.channel().isWritable()) ctx.channel().config().setAutoRead(false); // stop reading } @Override public void channelWritabilityChanged(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) { if (ctx.channel().isWritable()) ctx.channel().config().setAutoRead(true); // drained: read again ctx.fireChannelWritabilityChanged(); } Kotlin override fun channelReadComplete(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext) { ctx.flush() if (!ctx.channel().isWritable) ctx.channel().config().isAutoRead = false // stop reading } override fun channelWritabilityChanged(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext) { if (ctx.channel().isWritable) ctx.channel().config().isAutoRead = true // drained: read again ctx.fireChannelWritabilityChanged() } BackpressureDemo echoes 8 MiB to a client that writes fast and reads slowly. One run on a busy 4-core machine printed: backpressure=false -> peak bytes waiting in the outbound buffer: 3,620,288 backpressure=true -> peak bytes waiting in the outbound buffer: 129,216 Without those two methods, the peak was 3.6 MB in this run and 2.2 MB in the Kotlin twin's, and an earlier test run for this track saw 16,202,075 bytes: the whole payload, waiting in memory. With them, the peak stayed near 129,000 bytes every time. In a relay, you wire it across two channels: the slow side's writability switches the fast side's auto-read. The post office picture breaks here in your favor. A clerk who stops taking letters leaves customers queueing at the door. Here nobody queues in your memory: the bytes wait in the kernel's buffers and the client's own, and TCP tells the client to slow down. That's backpressure, from one end to the other. Two more traps showed up while measuring this. Calling close() right after the last flush() lost 57,344 bytes that were still in the outbound buffer. Close from the write's future instead: ctx.writeAndFlush(last).addListener(ChannelFutureListener.CLOSE). And channelWritabilityChanged can fire inside your own flush() call, so a handler that writes from that event must cope with being called while it's already writing. Netty queues every write you hand it. Watch isWritable(), and stop reading when it turns false. Measure the queue Run BackpressureDemo (or BackpressureDemoKt) and note both peaks. Lower the water marks: add .childOption(ChannelOption.WRITE_BUFFER_WATER_MARK, new WriteBufferWaterMark(8 * 1024, 16 * 1024)) to the server bootstrap. Predict the new peak with backpressure: about a quarter of the old one? Run it and explain the number. Where in the handler is writability checked?
