ctx.channel().unsafe().outboundBuffer().totalPendingWriteBytes() peak.accumulateAndGet(pending) { a, b -> maxOf(a, b) } } override fun channelReadComplete(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext) { ctx.flush() if (backpressure && !ctx.channel().isWritable) { ctx.channel().config().isAutoRead = false // stop reading from a peer we can't write to } } override fun channelWritabilityChanged(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext) { if (backpressure && ctx.channel().isWritable) { ctx.channel().config().isAutoRead = true // drained below the low water mark } ctx.fireChannelWritabilityChanged() } }) } }) .bind(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0).sync().channel() val total = megabytes shl 20 Socket().use { s -> s.receiveBufferSize = 32 * 1024 s.sendBufferSize = 32 * 1024 s.connect(server.localAddress()) val writer = thread { // the fast writer try { val out = s.getOutputStream() val chunk = ByteArray(64 * 1024) repeat(total / chunk.size) { out.write(chunk) } s.shutdownOutput() } catch (_: IOException) { } } val input = s.getInputStream() // the slow reader: 20 ms pause per 128 KiB val buf = ByteArray(16 * 1024) var got = 0L while (got < total) { val n = input.read(buf) if (n < 0) break got += n if ((got and ((128L shl 10) - 1)) < n) Thread.sleep(20) } writer.join() } server.close().sync() } finally { group.shutdownGracefully(0, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).sync() } return peak.get() } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l04.BackpressureDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l04/BackpressureDemo.kt Without backpressure the peak is in the megabytes and changes every run; with it, about 129,000 bytes. With a 16 KiB high mark, the peak only fell to 113,536 bytes in earlier runs for this track, nowhere near a quarter. The handler checks isWritable() in channelReadComplete, which runs once after a whole batch of reads, so most of the peak is that one batch arriving before auto-read is switched off. Checking in channelRead as well would stop the batch early. WriteBufferWaterMark source, Netty 4.2 docs

h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · Java and Kotlin
x: The letter frame encoder and decoder LetterFrameCodec.java class LetterFrameEncoder extends MessageToByteEncoder<Letter> { @Override protected void encode(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, Letter msg, ByteBuf out) { byte[] body = msg.body().getBytes(UTF_8); out.writeInt(1 + body.length).writeByte(msg.type()).writeBytes(body); } } class LetterFrameDecoder extends ByteToMessageDecoder { @Override protected void decode(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, ByteBuf in, List<Object> out) { int type = in.readByte(); out.add(new Letter(type, in.readCharSequence(in.readableBytes(), UTF_8).toString())); } } LetterFrameCodec.kt class LetterFrameEncoder : MessageToByteEncoder<Letter>() { override fun encode(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, msg: Letter, out: ByteBuf) { val body = msg.body.toByteArray(UTF_8) out.writeInt(1 + body.size).writeByte(msg.type).writeBytes(body) } } class LetterFrameDecoder : ByteToMessageDecoder() { override fun decode(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, input: ByteBuf, out: MutableList<Any>) { val type = input.readByte().toInt() out += Letter(type, input.readCharSequence(input.readableBytes(), UTF_8).toString()) } } They behave the same at run time; the differences are names and types. Java's decoder parameter is called in, which is a keyword in Kotlin, so the Kotlin override renames it (input), which overriding allows. readByte() returns a Byte in Kotlin, and Kotlin never widens it to Int on its own, so you write .toInt() where Java widens silently. The out list is a Java List<Object>, which Kotlin sees as MutableList<Any>. Getters such as isWritable() and isAutoRead() become properties (isWritable, isAutoRead = false) in Kotlin. Reference counting is the same in both: Kotlin's use {} doesn't help, because ByteBuf is not AutoCloseable.

h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · Worked example
x: Frame a link whose length field is 2 bytes The parcel lockers from lesson 1 get a protocol of their own. Each message goes behind a 2-byte big-endian length that counts only the bytes after it, and messages are at most 4,096 bytes. Ask four questions: where is the length, how long is it, what does it count, and do you keep it? wire: 00 08 | 4f 50 45 4e 20 31 31 37 (length 8, then "OPEN 117") offset: 0 the length starts the frame length: 2 bytes counts: what follows lengthAdjustment 0 keep: no initialBytesToStrip 2 That gives the decoder's arguments. LengthFieldPrepender is the matching encoder: it writes the length in front of every outbound buffer, so the business handler never deals with the header. ch.pipeline().addLast( new LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(4096, 0, 2, 0, 2), // 1. frame inbound, strip the header new LengthFieldPrepender(2), // 2. add the header outbound new LockerCodec(), // 3. bytes <-> messages new LockerHandler()); ch.pipeline().addLast( LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(4096, 0, 2, 0, 2), // 1. frame inbound, strip the header LengthFieldPrepender(2), // 2. add the header outbound LockerCodec(), // 3. bytes <-> messages LockerHandler()) A newer locker model counts the 2 header bytes in the length: the same message arrives as 00 0a .... The decoder computes the frame size as the end of the header plus the length value plus lengthAdjustment, so subtract the 2 bytes the value already includes. The prepender has a flag for the same convention. new LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(4096, 0, 2, -2, 2), // 10 - 2 = 8 body bytes new LengthFieldPrepender(2, true) // write 2 + body length LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(4096, 0, 2, -2, 2) // 10 - 2 = 8 body bytes LengthFieldPrepender(2, true) // write 2 + body length Prove it with an EmbeddedChannel before you connect to anything: write one message out, feed the bytes back in split after the first byte, and expect the original. A wrong adjustment shows up here as a frame that never completes, or one that swallows the next message's header. EmbeddedChannel ch = new EmbeddedChannel( new LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(4096, 0, 2, -2, 2), new LengthFieldPrepender(2, true)); ch.writeOutbound(Unpooled.copiedBuffer("OPEN 117", UTF_8)); ByteBuf wire = ch.readOutbound(); // 00 0a 4f 50 45 4e 20 31 31 37 ch.writeInbound(wire.retainedSlice(0, 1)); // half a header: nothing yet ch.writeInbound(wire.retainedSlice(1, wire.readableBytes() - 1)); wire.release(); ByteBuf frame = ch.readInbound(); // "OPEN 117" frame.release(); val ch = EmbeddedChannel( LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(4096, 0, 2, -2, 2), LengthFieldPrepender(2, true)) ch.writeOutbound(Unpooled.copiedBuffer("OPEN 117", UTF_8)) val wire = ch.readOutbound<ByteBuf>() // 00 0a 4f 50 45 4e 20 31 31 37 ch.writeInbound(wire.retainedSlice(0, 1)) // half a header: nothing yet ch.writeInbound(wire.retainedSlice(1, wire.readableBytes() - 1)) wire.release() val frame = ch.readInbound<ByteBuf>() // "OPEN 117" frame.release()

x: Write the letter codec and find a leak labs/nio/src/main/java/workbench/nio/l04/LetterFrameEncoder.java labs/nio/src/main/java/workbench/nio/l04/LetterFrameDecoder.java labs/nio/src/main/java/workbench/nio/l04/LetterCodec.java labs/nio/src/main/java/workbench/nio/l04/CountingTap.java labs/nio/src/main/java/workbench/nio/l04/Letter.java ./gradlew :nio:test --tests 'workbench.nio.l04.*' Run the tests. All five fail. Read Letter.java for the wire format: a record with a type number and a text body. Write LetterFrameEncoder.encode: the length (1 + body bytes) as an int, the type as a byte, then the UTF-8 body. Write LetterFrameDecoder.decode: read the type byte, then the rest as UTF-8 with readCharSequence, and add one Letter to out. Then LetterCodec.handlers. The first three tests should pass. Fix CountingTap, a handler that counts the bytes coming in, so the buffer that arrived is the one that goes on. The last two tests should pass. Now make a leak on purpose: in the decoder, read the body with in.readBytes(in.readableBytes()).toString(UTF_8). Run the tests, see which one fails, and work out why only that one. Put it back. The first test prints the bytes in hexadecimal: 00000007 is the length, 01 the type, and 6e6f74652d31 is note-1 in ASCII. in.readCharSequence(n, UTF_8) decodes in place and moves the reader index. in.readBytes(n) allocates a new ByteBuf, and nobody releases it. The CountingTap test fails with a reference count of 1: the buffer that arrived was never released, because a copy went on in its place. The test class sets PARANOID in @BeforeAll and puts the default back in @AfterAll. The leak test runs last, so it also catches leaks from the earlier tests. All five tests in LetterCodecTest pass, and you have seen the PARANOID test catch the readBytes leak. By the end you can frame and decode a binary protocol with Netty codecs, say who must release each ByteBuf and catch a leak with PARANOID detection in a test, and stop a slow peer from filling your memory with writability and auto-read.

h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · Quiz
x: LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(1024, 0, 4, 0, 4) has received the bytes 00 00 00 03 01 41. What does it pass to the next handler? Nothing yet: the length says 3 bytes follow and only 2 have arrived 01 41 All six bytes It throws, because the frame is shorter than 1024 The length field says 3 bytes follow; only 01 41 are there. The decoder keeps them in its cumulation and waits for one more byte. 1024 is a maximum, not a required size. A handler extends SimpleChannelInboundHandler<ByteBuf>, and inside channelRead0 it calls ctx.fireChannelRead(msg) to pass the buffer on. What happens? It works: ownership moves to the next handler The base class releases the buffer when channelRead0 returns, so the next handler reads freed memory and fails with IllegalReferenceCountException Netty copies the buffer for the next handler The buffer leaks SimpleChannelInboundHandler releases the message after channelRead0, assuming you used it up. Passing it on as well means two owners and one release too many. Call ReferenceCountUtil.retain(msg) before passing it on, or extend ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter. Your pipeline tests run at PARANOID and report no leaks. What does that tell you? The code has no leaks SIMPLE would have found more The allocator must be unpooled No tracked buffer that was garbage-collected during the run had a count above 0; paths the tests never ran stay invisible The detector only sees buffers that were allocated, tracked and collected while the tests ran. A leak on an error path the tests never exercise produces no report. PARANOID tracks more buffers than SIMPLE, not fewer. From lesson 3: on which thread does channelWritabilityChanged run, even when your writes come from a pool of your own? The channel's event loop thread A Netty IO thread from a separate pool The thread that called write Whichever thread is free Every event of a channel runs on the event loop it is registered with. A write from another thread is queued as a task on that loop, so the outbound buffer and its writability only ever change on the loop's thread. A relay server reads messages from many parcel lockers and forwards them to a slower central server over one Netty channel. The central channel's isWritable() turns false. What should the relay do? Keep writing: Netty buffers it Close the central channel and reconnect Turn auto-read off on the locker channels until the central channel is writable again Call Thread.sleep in the handler until it is writable Stop reading from the producers, so the backlog stays in the kernel and in TCP, not in your memory. Writing anyway grows the outbound buffer without limit, and sleeping blocks the event loop for every other channel on it.

h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · Explain it back
x: Explain why Netty's ByteBuf needs release() even though the JVM has a garbage collector, and how you would make sure a pipeline doesn't leak.

h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · Key terms
x: Framing Finding where one message ends and the next begins in a byte stream. Codec A decoder (bytes to messages) and an encoder (messages to bytes) for one protocol. Cumulation The buffer in which a ByteToMessageDecoder keeps bytes until a whole frame has arrived. Reference count A counter on a ByteBuf: retain adds one, release takes one away, and at zero the memory goes back to the pool. Leak detector Netty's ResourceLeakDetector, which reports buffers that were garbage-collected without being released. Outbound buffer The queue in your program where a channel keeps written messages until the socket can take them. Water marks The high and low limits on the outbound buffer that switch isWritable() off and on. Auto-read Whether the event loop keeps reading a channel; turning it off is how Netty stops OP_READ. What do the arguments of LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(1024, 0, 4, 0, 4) mean? Max frame 1024 bytes; the length field is at offset 0 and 4 bytes long; adjustment 0 (it counts only what follows); strip the first 4 bytes before passing the frame on. Who releases a ByteBuf in a Netty pipeline? The party that touches it last. Passing it on with fireChannelRead or write hands it over; using it up means releasing it. Why does ByteBuf need release() when the JVM has a garbage collector? Netty lends out pooled direct memory and must get it back as soon as a message is done. The GC frees objects at an unknown later time and can't return the memory to the pool. SimpleChannelInboundHandler vs ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter: who releases? SimpleChannelInboundHandler releases the message after channelRead0 returns. ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter releases nothing; you pass the message on or release it. Netty's leak detection levels, in one line each? SIMPLE (default): about 1 in 128 buffers, no records. ADVANCED: same sampling, with access records. PARANOID: every buffer, with records; use it in tests. When does channel.isWritable() turn false, and when true again (defaults)? False when the outbound buffer passes the 64 KiB high water mark; true again when it drains below the 32 KiB low mark. How do you close a Netty channel without losing the last bytes? Close from the last write's future: ctx.writeAndFlush(last).addListener(ChannelFutureListener.CLOSE). close() right after flush() can drop bytes still in the outbound buffer.

h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · Go deeper
x: A few ByteToMessageDecoder details explain behavior you will see when you profile a server. The default cumulator, MERGE_CUMULATOR, copies newly read bytes into one growing buffer. COMPOSITE_CUMULATOR adds them as components instead and avoids the copy, but the Javadoc warns it may be slower, because reading across component boundaries costs more. The decoder also compacts the cumulation after 16 reads (discardAfterReads), so a long-lived connection doesn't keep used bytes forever. setSingleDecode(true) makes it produce at most one message per read, which matters when you control reading yourself. That leads to FlowControlHandler. With auto-read off, you call ctx.read() to ask for one more read, but a decoder can still emit many messages from that one read, because one read can contain many frames. Its Javadoc says FlowControlHandler "ensures that only one message per read() is sent downstream". Put it after your decoders when you need strict one-request-at-a-time processing per connection. On allocators: io.netty.allocator.type picks adaptive (the 4.2 default), pooled or unpooled. The adaptive allocator keeps several "magazines" of memory, picks one by thread id, and adds magazines when it sees contention. The older pooled allocator keeps per-thread caches, and its useCacheForAllThreads setting defaults to false, which suggests that buffers allocated on your own pool's threads miss those caches. That last point is an inference from the property's name and default, not something this track measured. Finally, for a server that real users depend on, leave the level at SIMPLE. It samples 1 buffer in 128, so a leak on a busy path still reaches the logs, while the other 127 buffers pay nothing for tracking.

h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · One desk, one clerk: a Vert.x context on Netty's event loop
x: A Vert.x context runs a verticle's handlers on one event-loop thread, so never block it Start with what's underneath. Vert.x 5.2.3, the version this track uses, runs on Netty 4.2.20. When you call Vertx.vertx(), it starts a group of Netty event loops, the clerks from lesson 3. An event loop is one thread, a single line of work inside your program, that watches many connections and runs their code one piece at a time. Vert.x starts two per core by default, 8 on a 4-core machine, named vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 and up. A stack trace later in this lesson ends in io.netty.channel.SingleThreadIoEventLoop.run, the same loop class Netty uses. So what does Vert.x add? Rules about who runs your code. The central one is the context: the home of a piece of code, which decides the thread that runs it. Most contexts are event-loop contexts, each tied to one event loop for life. In the post office, a context is the card on a desk that names its clerk. When you register a handler, Vert.x remembers the current context, and every call of that handler runs there. A handler, in Vert.x, is any piece of your code that Vert.x calls when something happens: a request arrives, a timer fires, a note comes through a tube. The Vert.x docs make a promise about it. A handler is never executed concurrently, and, worker verticles aside, it always runs on the same event loop thread. That promise is lesson 3's Netty rule, one channel and one loop, stretched over all your code: handlers for HTTP (the protocol of the web), timers and event-bus consumers alike. One clerk serves the desk, one job at a time, so nobody needs to lock the drawers. A field that only one context touches needs no synchronized. The promise has a price you already know. While a handler runs, its clerk does nothing else, so every desk and every connection on that loop waits. We'll meet the floor manager who watches for that in the last section. The second change is the API. A future is an object that will hold a result later; you attach code to it, and that code runs when the result arrives. Vert.x 4 offered two styles side by side: callbacks, where you pass a function into the call itself, and futures. Vert.x 5 kept only futures. Every asynchronous method returns an io.vertx.core.Future, and the callback versions are gone: Java // Vert.x 5: listen returns a Future server.listen(8080).onSuccess(s -> System.out.println("listening on " + s.actualPort())); // Vert.x 4 style no longer compiles: // server.listen(8080, ar -> ...) -> error: incompatible types: String is not a functional interface Kotlin // Vert.x 5: listen returns a Future server.listen(8080).onSuccess { s -> println("listening on ${s.actualPort()}") } // Vert.x 4 style no longer compiles: // server.listen(8080) { ar -> ... } the only two-argument listen left is listen(int, String) The Java error looks unrelated. The compiler, trying to help, found the one two-argument listen that's left, listen(int, String), and complained that a String isn't a lambda. The same change replaced executeBlocking(promise -> ...) with a version that takes a Callable and returns a Future, which the last section puts to work. A context is the home of your code. Everything registered on it runs on its thread, one task at a time. A context needs something to belong to. In Vert.x, that something is usually a verticle. Hit the Vert.x 5 API change In ContextsDemo.java, add one line after Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx();: vertx.createHttpServer().listen(8080, ar -> {});. Predict whether it compiles. Then run the demo with the command below. Remove the line again. terminal ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l05.ContextsDemo Compilation fails with error: incompatible types: String is not a functional interface. The callback version of listen no longer exists in Vert.x 5, so javac tries listen(int, String) and can't turn your lambda into a String.

h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · Desks you deploy: verticles and their threading models
x: A verticle is a class you deploy into Vert.x, and deploying it gives each instance its own context. It's a desk: a small, self-contained unit with its own drawers (its fields), its own handlers, and the card that names its clerk. In Vert.x 5 you extend VerticleBase and return a Future from start(), so the deployment finishes only when your setup has. Here is a first weighing desk. It listens at the address desk.weigh and answers every parcel with a JsonObject, Vert.x's map of named values, that says it was accepted. This lesson's lab makes it stricter: Java public class WeighingDesk extends VerticleBase { @Override public Future<?> start() { return vertx.eventBus().<JsonObject>consumer("desk.weigh", msg -> msg.reply(new JsonObject().put("status", "ACCEPTED")) ).completion(); // done when the consumer is registered } } vertx.deployVerticle(WeighingDesk::new, new DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2)); Kotlin class WeighingDesk : VerticleBase() { override fun start(): Future<*> = vertx.eventBus().consumer<JsonObject>("desk.weigh") { msg -> msg.reply(JsonObject().put("status", "ACCEPTED")) }.completion() // done when the consumer is registered } vertx.deployVerticle(::WeighingDesk, DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2)) Read it from the bottom. We deploy two instances, so we pass a factory, a function that makes a new object each time, because each instance must be its own object. In 5.2.3 that factory is a Supplier, though the docs still say Callable. Each instance gets its own event-loop context, usually on different loops, which is how one verticle class uses several cores. Inside one instance, code never runs on two threads at once, so its fields need no locks. Inside start(), the desk registers a consumer, a handler for notes that arrive at one address. Then it returns completion(), a future that completes once the consumer is registered, and Vert.x waits for it before it calls the deployment done. Not every desk wants an event-loop clerk. The threading model in DeploymentOptions decides what kind of context a verticle gets. ContextsDemo deploys one verticle of each kind and prints where its start() runs: [EVENT_LOOP] start() on vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 eventLoopCtx=true workerCtx=false [WORKER] start() on vert.x-worker-thread-0 eventLoopCtx=false workerCtx=true [VIRTUAL_THREAD] start() on vert.x-virtual-thread-0 (virtual) eventLoopCtx=false workerCtx=false EVENT_LOOP, the default, must never block. A WORKER verticle runs on the worker pool, a bounded pool of ordinary threads that are allowed to block, 20 of them by default. It still never runs on two threads at once, but one call can land on a different worker thread from the last. VIRTUAL_THREAD is new in Vert.x 5 and needs Java 21. The verticle runs on virtual threads, cheap threads that the JDK parks while they wait, and future.await() parks the virtual thread until the result arrives. A virtual-thread verticle also runs one task at a time, with one catch from the docs. A field you read before an await() may have changed after it, because another task of the same verticle can run while you wait. Here the desk picture breaks a little. A real desk keeps the same clerk all day. A worker desk can get a different clerk from the pool for each job, though never two at once, so it's single-threaded without being tied to one thread. Each verticle instance is one desk with one context. For more cores, deploy more instances. Desks need a way to talk without opening each other's drawers. That's the event bus. Where does each desk run? Open ContextsDemo.java (or ContextsDemo.kt). It deploys one verticle per threading model, then calls executeBlocking from an event-loop context. Predict the thread name in each line, and on which thread onSuccess runs after executeBlocking. Run it. ContextsDemo.java package workbench.nio.l05; import io.vertx.core.Context; import io.vertx.core.DeploymentOptions; import io.vertx.core.Future; import io.vertx.core.ThreadingModel; import io.vertx.core.VerticleBase; import io.vertx.core.Vertx; import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Where does a verticle's code run? One verticle per threading model, plus executeBlocking. */ public class ContextsDemo { static String where() { Thread t = Thread.currentThread(); Context c = Vertx.currentContext(); return t.getName() + (t.isVirtual() ? " (virtual)" : "") + " eventLoopCtx=" + c.isEventLoopContext() + " workerCtx=" + c.isWorkerContext(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("default event loops: " + VertxOptions.DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP_POOL_SIZE + " (cpus=" + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() + "), default worker pool: " + VertxOptions.DEFAULT_WORKER_POOL_SIZE); Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(); for (ThreadingModel model : List.of(ThreadingModel.EVENT_LOOP, ThreadingModel.WORKER, ThreadingModel.VIRTUAL_THREAD)) { await(vertx.deployVerticle(new VerticleBase() { @Override public Future<?> start() { System.out.println("[" + model + "] start() on " + where()); return Future.succeededFuture(); } }, new DeploymentOptions().setThreadingModel(model))); } vertx.runOnContext(v -> vertx.executeBlocking(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()) .onSuccess(name -> System.out.println("[executeBlocking] callable ran on " + name + ", onSuccess runs on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()))); Thread.sleep(300); await(vertx.close()); } static <T> T await(Future<T> f) throws Exception { return f.toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l05.ContextsDemo labs/nio/src/demo/java/workbench/nio/l05/ContextsDemo.java ContextsDemo.kt package workbench.nio.l05 import io.vertx.core.DeploymentOptions import io.vertx.core.Future import io.vertx.core.ThreadingModel import io.vertx.core.VerticleBase import io.vertx.core.Vertx import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** Where does a verticle's code run? One verticle per threading model, plus executeBlocking. */ private fun where(): String { val t = Thread.currentThread() val c = Vertx.currentContext() return "${t.name}${if (t.isVirtual) " (virtual)" else ""} eventLoopCtx=${c.isEventLoopContext} workerCtx=${c.isWorkerContext}" } private fun <T> Future<T>.awaitIt(): T = toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) fun main() { println("default event loops: ${VertxOptions.DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP_POOL_SIZE} (cpus=${Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()}), " + "default worker pool: ${VertxOptions.DEFAULT_WORKER_POOL_SIZE}") val vertx = Vertx.vertx() for (model in listOf(ThreadingModel.EVENT_LOOP, ThreadingModel.WORKER, ThreadingModel.VIRTUAL_THREAD)) { vertx.deployVerticle(object : VerticleBase() { override fun start(): Future<*> { println("[$model] start() on ${where()}") return Future.succeededFuture<Unit>() } }, DeploymentOptions().setThreadingModel(model)).awaitIt() } // explicit types: an inferred Vert.x Future type carries vertx-codegen's @Nullable, which isn't on the classpath val task = Callable<String> { Thread.currentThread().name } vertx.runOnContext { vertx.executeBlocking(task) .onSuccess { name: String -> println("[executeBlocking] callable ran on $name, onSuccess runs on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } } Thread.sleep(300) vertx.close().awaitIt() } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l05.ContextsDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l05/ContextsDemo.kt The first line reports 8 event loops on 4 CPUs and a worker pool of 20. The three verticles start on vert.x-eventloop-thread-0, vert.x-worker-thread-0 and a virtual thread, vert.x-virtual-thread-0. The executeBlocking callable runs on a worker thread, and onSuccess runs back on an event-loop thread: the context that made the call. Each desk instance has a context on one event loop. Contexts pass notes over the event bus, and blocking work goes to the worker pool and comes back to the same context.

h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · Notes through the tubes: request, reply and publish on the event bus
x: The event bus is how verticles talk without sharing objects. There's one per Vertx instance, and an address is just a string, such as desk.weigh. In the post office, it's the system of mail tubes between desks, each tube labeled with a name. You can send a note in three ways: send(address, msg): to one consumer at that address, chosen in turn (round-robin). request(address, msg): to one consumer, and you get a Future of its reply. publish(address, msg): to every consumer at that address. EventBusDemo deploys two instances of a greeter desk and sends it four requests. Then it tries three addresses: one with nobody behind it, one that fails on purpose, and one that never answers: request greet #0 -> hello dev0 from instance#1 on vert.x-eventloop-thread-1 request greet #1 -> hello dev1 from instance#2 on vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 request greet #2 -> hello dev2 from instance#1 on vert.x-eventloop-thread-1 request nobody -> NO_HANDLERS code=-1 message=No handlers for address nobody request fail -> RECIPIENT_FAILURE code=42 message=boom from instance#1 request silent (timeout 300 ms) -> TIMEOUT after 308 ms The two instances took turns, each on its own loop: the round-robin at work. After them come the three ways a request can fail, each delivered as a ReplyException with a failureType(). NO_HANDLERS means nobody listens at the address, a tube that leads to an empty room. RECIPIENT_FAILURE means the consumer called msg.fail(code, text), and you get its code and text. TIMEOUT means no reply came in time. The silent consumer deserves a second look. It took the note and never wrote back, and the requester only found out because it had set a timeout of 300 ms. The default is 30 seconds, a long time to stand at a tube. Set one on every request with new DeliveryOptions().setSendTimeout(...). The reply comes back on the requester's context, not the consumer's. A worker verticle that sends a request handles the reply on a worker thread, and a virtual-thread verticle resumes on its virtual thread. So the promise of one desk and one clerk holds at both ends of a tube. Two properties keep the event bus from being a message store. First, delivery is best effort: there's no saved copy and no retry, and the docs tell you to write consumers that can safely see the same message twice. Second, inside one JVM a message can be handed over by reference. A codec is the code that turns a message into bytes and back. With a custom local codec whose transform returns its argument, the consumer receives the very object you sent. Here the tube picture breaks. A real tube carries the sheet away, while this one can leave the same sheet in both hands. Never change a message after you send it. Built-in codecs cover strings, numbers, Buffer, JsonObject and JsonArray; other types need a codec you register. The event bus carries quick notes between desks. Set a timeout on every request, and treat delivery as best effort. Notes, timers and requests all run on the clerks. So what happens when one of those jobs doesn't come back? Make every kind of reply happen Open EventBusDemo.java (or EventBusDemo.kt). Predict which instance answers each of the four requests, and how many lines publish prints. Run it. Change the silent request's timeout from 300 to 1,000 ms and run again. What changes, and what doesn't? h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · The golden rule, the floor manager, and a back office that works in single file
x: Vert.x calls it the golden rule: don't block the event loop. Lesson 3 put it as the clerk who never stops to make a phone call. The Vert.x docs list what counts as a phone call: Thread.sleep(), waiting on a lock or a synchronized block, a long database operation, a complex calculation, spinning in a loop. They also give a budget. With one event loop and 10,000 HTTP requests a second, each request can take at most 0.1 ms. Vert.x checks the rule for you, with a floor manager. A separate thread, vertx-blocked-thread-checker, walks past every event loop once a second. Each loop notes when its current task began, and the checker compares that with the clock. If a task has run for more than 2 seconds, it writes a warning in the log. Past 5 seconds, it adds the blocked thread's stack trace, the list of method calls the thread is inside. BlockedThreadDemo makes a clerk sleep for 6 seconds on an event loop: [vertx-blocked-thread-checker] WARN io.vertx.core.impl.BlockedThreadChecker - Thread vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 has been blocked for 2773 ms, time limit is 2000 ms [vertx-blocked-thread-checker] WARN io.vertx.core.impl.BlockedThreadChecker - Thread vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 has been blocked for 3772 ms, time limit is 2000 ms ... io.vertx.core.VertxException: Thread blocked at java.base/java.lang.Thread.sleep(Thread.java:509) at workbench.nio.l05.BlockedThreadDemo.lambda$main$0(BlockedThreadDemo.java:13) ... at io.netty.channel.SingleThreadIoEventLoop.run(SingleThreadIoEventLoop.java:228) The first warning came at 2.8 seconds, not 2.0, because the manager only walks past once a second. Search your logs for has been blocked for; the logger's name is io.vertx.core.impl.BlockedThreadChecker. And notice what the manager never does: interrupt. He writes it down and walks on, and the clerk stays on the phone. The manager has one blind spot. He measures one task at a time, so ten 300 ms calls in a row hold a loop for 3 seconds and never produce a warning. Short blocking calls are the kind that never reach the logs. For blocking work there's executeBlocking, the back office. It runs a Callable, a task that returns a value, on the worker pool, and completes a Future back on your context, so your own clerk writes the reply. ExecuteBlockingDemo tries it on an HTTP server with one event loop. Four requests arrive at once, and each needs a 500 ms lookup. The demo runs it three ways: blocking right on the loop, then executeBlocking with its default, then executeBlocking(callable, false). One run on a busy 4-core machine printed: block-on-event-loop 4 requests x 500 ms -> 2201 ms, ran on [vert.x-eventloop-thread-0] executeBlocking-ordered 4 requests x 500 ms -> 2012 ms, ran on [vert.x-worker-thread-0] executeBlocking-unordered 4 requests x 500 ms -> 511 ms, ran on [vert.x-worker-thread-0, ..., vert.x-worker-thread-3] The first line is the failure we expected: four lookups in a row on the clerk's own time. The second line is the surprise from the opening. The loop was free, so the floor manager had nothing to report, and yet the four lookups still ran one after another, all on vert.x-worker-thread-0. Twenty workers sat in the back office, and one of them did all the work. The cause is one word in the docs: executeBlocking is ordered by default. Calls from the same context go into one queue and run in turn. Every request to one HTTP server shares that server's context, so every request joined the same queue. Pass false when the calls don't depend on each other, and they overlap: 511 ms, on four different workers. Moving a call to the back office frees the clerk. Pass false, or the calls still wait in single file. One last look at the back office itself. Its 20 threads are a bounded pool, like the ones in the executors track, so behind it you have a thread-per-request design again. That's fine, as long as you size it like one, with Little's law from lesson 1. Three ways to make a slow call Open ExecuteBlockingDemo.java (or ExecuteBlockingDemo.kt). Predict the total time and the thread names for each of the three modes. Run it with the command below. Then run ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l05.BlockedThreadDemo and predict when the first warning appears and when the stack trace appears. Run it with -Pargs=2500 too: how many warnings now? ExecuteBlockingDemo.java package workbench.nio.l05; import io.vertx.core.Vertx; import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions; import io.vertx.core.http.HttpServer; import java.net.URI; import java.net.http.HttpRequest; import java.net.http.HttpResponse; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.TreeSet; import java.util.concurrent.Callable; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** One event loop, an HTTP server, 4 concurrent requests that each make a 500 ms blocking lookup. Three ways. */ public class ExecuteBlockingDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { for (String mode : List.of("block-on-event-loop", "executeBlocking-ordered", "executeBlocking-unordered")) { Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(new VertxOptions().setEventLoopPoolSize(1)); Callable<String> slowLookup = () -> { Thread.sleep(500); return Thread.currentThread().getName(); }; HttpServer server = vertx.createHttpServer().requestHandler(req -> { switch (mode) { case "block-on-event-loop" -> { try { req.response().end(slowLookup.call()); // blocks the loop } catch (Exception e) { req.response().setStatusCode(500).end(); } } case "executeBlocking-ordered" -> // the default: ordered = true vertx.executeBlocking(slowLookup).onComplete(ar -> req.response().end(ar.result())); default -> vertx.executeBlocking(slowLookup, false).onComplete(ar -> req.response().end(ar.result())); } }).listen(0, "127.0.0.1").toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(); java.net.http.HttpClient client = java.net.http.HttpClient.newBuilder() .proxy(java.net.http.HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build(); URI uri = URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:" + server.actualPort() + "/"); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>>> calls = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { calls.add(client.sendAsync(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString())); } Set<String> threads = new TreeSet<>(); for (var call : calls) threads.add(call.get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS).body()); System.out.printf("%-26s 4 requests x 500 ms -> %4d ms, ran on %s%n", mode, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, threads); vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(); } } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l05.ExecuteBlockingDemo labs/nio/src/demo/java/workbench/nio/l05/ExecuteBlockingDemo.java ExecuteBlockingDemo.kt package workbench.nio.l05 import io.vertx.core.Vertx import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions import java.net.URI import java.net.http.HttpRequest import java.net.http.HttpResponse import java.util.TreeSet import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.net.http.HttpClient as JdkHttpClient /** One event loop, an HTTP server, 4 concurrent requests that each make a 500 ms blocking lookup. Three ways. */ fun main() { for (mode in listOf("block-on-event-loop", "executeBlocking-ordered", "executeBlocking-unordered")) { val vertx = Vertx.vertx(VertxOptions().setEventLoopPoolSize(1)) val slowLookup = Callable { Thread.sleep(500) Thread.currentThread().name } val server = vertx.createHttpServer().requestHandler { req -> when (mode) { "block-on-event-loop" -> req.response().end(slowLookup.call()) // blocks the loop "executeBlocking-ordered" -> // the default: ordered = true vertx.executeBlocking(slowLookup).onComplete { ar -> req.response().end(ar.result()) } else -> vertx.executeBlocking(slowLookup, false).onComplete { ar -> req.response().end(ar.result()) } } }.listen(0, "127.0.0.1").toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get() val client = JdkHttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(JdkHttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build() val uri = URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:${server.actualPort()}/") val t0 = System.nanoTime() val calls = List(4) { client.sendAsync(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()) } val threads = TreeSet(calls.map { it.get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS).body() }) println("%-26s 4 requests x 500 ms -> %4d ms, ran on %s".format(mode, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, threads)) vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get() } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l05.ExecuteBlockingDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l05/ExecuteBlockingDemo.kt About 2,000 ms on the event loop thread, about 2,000 ms on one worker thread with the ordered default, and about 500 ms across four worker threads with false. Runs for this lesson measured 2,201, 2,012 and 511 ms, and later 2,408, 2,047 and 570 ms on a busier machine. The blocked-thread demo warns between 2 and 3 seconds in, once a second after that, and adds the VertxException: Thread blocked stack trace after 5 seconds. A 2,500 ms sleep gives zero or one warning, depending on when the checker happens to look. Vert.x 5.2.3 core documentation: The Golden Rule (source) docs

h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · Java and Kotlin
x: A desk that sends a blocking lookup to the back office PriceDesk.java public class PriceDesk extends VerticleBase { @Override public Future<?> start() { return vertx.eventBus().<String>consumer("desk.price", msg -> vertx.executeBlocking(() -> PriceBook.postageCents(msg.body()), false) .onSuccess(msg::reply) // back on this desk's context .onFailure(e -> msg.fail(500, e.getMessage())) ).completion(); } } vertx.deployVerticle(PriceDesk::new, new DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2)); PriceDesk.kt class PriceDesk : VerticleBase() { override fun start(): Future<*> = vertx.eventBus().consumer<String>("desk.price") { msg -> val lookup = Callable<Long> { PriceBook.postageCents(msg.body()) } vertx.executeBlocking(lookup, false) .onSuccess { cents: Long -> msg.reply(cents) } // back on this desk's context .onFailure { e -> msg.fail(500, e.message) } }.completion() } vertx.deployVerticle(::PriceDesk, DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2)) Same Vert.x API, same threads at run time. Two Kotlin wrinkles came up while building this lesson's demos. vertx.deployVerticle({ PriceDesk() }, options) does not compile in Kotlin: Deployable is itself a single-method interface, so a bare lambda matches both overloads. Use a constructor reference (::PriceDesk) or Supplier { PriceDesk() }. And some Vert.x 5 signatures carry a @Nullable type annotation from vertx-codegen, which is not on the classpath, so Kotlin can fail with "Type annotation class 'io.vertx.codegen.annotations.Nullable' of the inferred type is inaccessible" when it infers a lambda's type. Giving the Callable and the lambda parameter explicit types, as above, avoids it. Java ignores the annotation.

h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · Worked example
x: Unblock the price desk, step by step The price desk looks postage up in the price book, a database call that takes 300 ms, right on its clerk's time. It works in a demo with one request. Under load, every handler on the same event loop waits behind it, and the floor manager stays silent: he measures one task at a time, and each 300 ms lookup is under his 2-second limit. vertx.eventBus().<String>consumer("desk.price", msg -> { try { msg.reply(PriceBook.postageCents(msg.body())); // 300 ms on the event loop } catch (InterruptedException e) { msg.fail(500, "interrupted"); } }); vertx.eventBus().consumer<String>("desk.price") { msg -> msg.reply(PriceBook.postageCents(msg.body())) // 300 ms on the event loop } First attempt: send the lookup to the back office with the default executeBlocking. The loop is free now, but six requests at once still take about 6 x 300 ms. They all come from this consumer's context, and the default is ordered. vertx.executeBlocking(() -> PriceBook.postageCents(msg.body())) // ordered: one at a time .onSuccess(msg::reply); vertx.executeBlocking(Callable<Long> { PriceBook.postageCents(msg.body()) }) // ordered: one at a time .onSuccess { cents: Long -> msg.reply(cents) } Second attempt: unordered. The lookups now overlap on the worker pool, and the replies still come back on the consumer's context. The lab's test checks both halves: under 1,000 ms in total for six lookups, and an event-loop lag under 150 ms. vertx.executeBlocking(() -> PriceBook.postageCents(msg.body()), false) // independent calls .onSuccess(msg::reply) .onFailure(e -> msg.fail(500, e.getMessage())); vertx.executeBlocking(Callable<Long> { PriceBook.postageCents(msg.body()) }, false) // independent calls .onSuccess { cents: Long -> msg.reply(cents) } .onFailure { e -> msg.fail(500, e.message) } Another design makes the limit visible: turn the whole desk into a worker verticle and deploy as many instances as you want lookups at once. Each instance takes one note at a time on the worker pool, so four instances means at most four lookups in flight, a number you can match to the database's connections. vertx.deployVerticle(BlockingPriceDesk::new, new DeploymentOptions() .setThreadingModel(ThreadingModel.WORKER) // may block .setInstances(4)); // at most 4 lookups at once vertx.deployVerticle(::BlockingPriceDesk, DeploymentOptions() .setThreadingModel(ThreadingModel.WORKER) // may block .setInstances(4)) // at most 4 lookups at once

h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · Quiz
x: The weighing desk is deployed with setInstances(4) and default options. Its consumer adds one to a plain int field on every message. Is that safe? No: four threads can update the same field at once Yes: each instance is its own object with its own context, and a context never runs two handlers at once Only if the field is volatile Only for WORKER verticles The factory creates four separate objects, so there are four separate fields, and each is only touched from its own context, one task at a time. volatile wouldn't make ++ atomic anyway, and worker verticles follow the same one-at-a-time rule. An HTTP handler wraps every database call in vertx.executeBlocking(() -> db.query(...)). Under load, latency climbs while the database is idle and the CPU is low. What is the most likely cause? executeBlocking is ordered by default, so calls from the server's context run one after another The worker pool has only one thread The event loop is blocked Database calls don't work on worker threads All requests to one server share its context, and the default executeBlocking runs calls from a context in single file. The default worker pool has 20 threads, and the event loop is free, which is why there are no blocked-thread warnings. Pass false. A log line says Thread vert.x-eventloop-thread-3 has been blocked for 2412 ms, time limit is 2000 ms. What does Vert.x do to that thread? Interrupts it Replaces the event loop with a new one Nothing: it only logs, and adds a stack trace once the block passes 5 seconds Moves its handlers to another event loop The blocked-thread checker only watches. It logs every second while the block lasts and adds the stack once it passes the warning-exception time (5 s by default). The handlers stay on their loop, so everything on it keeps waiting. From lesson 3: Vert.x event loops are Netty event loops. Which Netty rule explains why a Vert.x handler doesn't need a lock for its own fields? A channel stays on one event-loop thread for life, and that thread runs its events one at a time Netty copies every message before delivering it Netty's event loops are virtual threads ByteBuf is reference-counted Vert.x stretches Netty's one-channel-one-loop rule over contexts: everything registered on a context runs on its thread, one task after another. Keeping the data on one thread is what removes the need for locks. The weighing desk must tell three other desks (tracking, statistics, text messages) about each parcel it accepts, and it needs no answers. Which call fits? eventBus().send("parcel.accepted", parcel) eventBus().request(...) once per listener vertx.executeBlocking(...) around each notice eventBus().publish("parcel.accepted", parcel) publish delivers to every consumer at the address. send would reach only one of them, chosen in turn, and request waits for replies nobody needs. Remember that delivery is best effort: if a notice must never be lost, the event bus is the wrong tool.

h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · Explain it back
x: A colleague wrapped four slow database calls in executeBlocking and is surprised that a burst of four requests still takes four times as long as one. Explain what a Vert.x context is, why their change didn't help, and what to do instead.

h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · Key terms
x: Verticle A class you deploy into Vert.x; each deployed instance gets its own context. Context Where a piece of Vert.x code runs: one event loop, a worker, or a virtual thread, one task at a time. Future An object that will hold a result later; code attached to it runs when the result arrives. Threading model The kind of context a verticle gets: EVENT_LOOP, WORKER or VIRTUAL_THREAD. Event bus Vert.x's messaging inside one program, between verticles, addressed by strings, best effort. Worker pool The pool of threads (20 by default) that runs blocking work and worker verticles. executeBlocking Runs a Callable on the worker pool and completes a Future back on your context. Blocked-thread checker A Vert.x thread that logs a warning when an event loop has been busy with one task for too long. How many event loops does a default Vertx instance create? Two per available processor: 8 on a 4-core machine. What is a Vert.x context? The home of a piece of code: it fixes which thread runs it. A handler registered on a context always runs there, never at the same time as itself. When does Vert.x log a blocked event loop, and when does it add a stack trace (defaults)? A warning once a task has run more than 2 s (checked every 1 s); the stack trace after 5 s. It only logs. Why can executeBlocking(callable) still run your calls one at a time? It is ordered per context by default, so calls from the same context queue behind each other. Use executeBlocking(callable, false) for independent calls. The three failureType() values of a failed event-bus request? NO_HANDLERS (nobody listens), RECIPIENT_FAILURE (the consumer called fail), TIMEOUT (no reply in time; 30 s by default). send vs request vs publish on the event bus? send: one consumer, in turn. request: one consumer, and you get a Future of the reply. publish: every consumer at the address. How do you deploy 4 instances of a verticle in Vert.x 5? vertx.deployVerticle(MyVerticle::new, new DeploymentOptions().setInstances(4)): a Supplier, so each instance is a new object.

h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · Go deeper
x: Testing Vert.x code has its own traps, and the vertx-junit5 library exists because of them. A Vert.x callback runs on an event loop, after your test method has returned. If an assertion fails there, JUnit never sees it. The extension fixes that with VertxTestContext: the test passes only when you call completeNow() (or flag all checkpoints), and fails when you call failNow(...) or when an assertion inside tc.verify(() -> ...) throws. This track's research ran the same failing assertion both ways. Outside verify, the test ran into the timeout after about 2.6 seconds with "The test execution timed out. Make sure your asynchronous code includes calls to either VertxTestContext#completeNow(), VertxTestContext#failNow() or Checkpoint#flag()", and the real AssertionFailedError was only printed to the log. Inside verify, it failed in 0.059 seconds with the actual assertion message. So every assertion in a callback goes inside verify, or inside tc.succeeding(...) and tc.failing(...), which wrap it for you. Other details from the vertx-junit5 docs: the default timeout is 30 seconds, overridden per test with @io.vertx.junit5.Timeout (written in full, to avoid JUnit's @Timeout). A Vertx injected into a @BeforeAll method is shared by the class, one injected into @BeforeEach is shared by that test and its @AfterEach, and injected instances are closed for you. tc.checkpoint(n) gives a counter that must be flagged n times, handy for testing publish to several consumers. And in Vert.x 5, clients rely on Cleaner, the JDK's way to run cleanup when an object becomes unreachable, so a client object you stop referring to can close its pool while a test still uses it. Keep clients in fields during tests. One trap belongs outside tests too: waiting for a result on the event loop itself, with future.toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(). If the result needs that same loop to complete, the clerk waits for himself, and the call never returns. The test helpers in this lesson's lab call get only from the test's own thread, never from inside a handler.

h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · The label on the ticket: how Quarkus picks a thread from the return type
x: Every request arrives on an IO thread; the signature sends it to a worker, keeps it on the event loop, or gives it a virtual thread, and blocking code on the event loop stalls every connection behind it Quarkus is a framework for web services: programs that answer requests sent over HTTP, the protocol behind web pages. Its HTTP layer is a Vert.x server, so every request is first read on a Vert.x event loop, which Quarkus calls an IO thread. That's the counter clerk. Everything in this lesson is pinned to Quarkus 3.40. Quarkus REST, its library for writing web endpoints (formerly called RESTEasy Reactive), then decides who runs your code. An endpoint is a Java method that answers one kind of request, such as GET /prices/P-17. Annotations, the labels that start with @, tell Quarkus which requests it answers. The Quarkus reactive architecture guide describes the choice that follows. Quarkus calls your code right there on the IO thread, which saves a thread switch, or on a worker thread. A worker thread comes from a bounded pool, and it is allowed to block. The decision comes from the method's signature: the label on the ticket. A method that returns Uni, Multi, CompletionStage or Publisher, or a Kotlin suspend function, counts as non-blocking and runs on the IO thread. All of these say "the answer comes later". Uni, from the Mutiny library that Quarkus uses, holds one result, and Multi holds a stream of them. CompletionStage is the JDK's own future, Publisher is the Reactive Streams standard's type for a stream of results, and a suspend function can pause without holding its thread. Anything else, such as a method that returns a Price directly, runs on a worker thread. Here is the price desk as a Quarkus service, with one endpoint of each kind: Java @Path("/prices") public class PriceResource { @Inject PriceBook priceBook; // a database, called the blocking way @Inject LivePrices livePrices; // a non-blocking client that returns Uni @GET @Path("/{parcel}") public Price price(@PathParam("parcel") String parcel) { // plain value: worker thread return priceBook.find(parcel); } @GET @Path("/{parcel}/live") public Uni<Price> live(@PathParam("parcel") String parcel) { // Uni: IO thread return livePrices.find(parcel); } } Kotlin @Path("/prices") class PriceResource( private val priceBook: PriceBook, // a database, called the blocking way private val livePrices: LivePrices, // a non-blocking client that returns Uni ) { @GET @Path("/{parcel}") fun price(@PathParam("parcel") parcel: String): Price = // plain value: worker thread priceBook.find(parcel) @GET @Path("/{parcel}/live") suspend fun live(@PathParam("parcel") parcel: String): Price = // suspend: IO thread livePrices.find(parcel).awaitSuspending() } @Inject asks Quarkus to hand the class the objects it needs; in Kotlin, the constructor does the same job. The first endpoint returns a plain Price, so Quarkus sends it to the back office. The second promises a result later, so it stays at the counter. Read the rule as a promise you make. A Uni return type tells Quarkus "this method won't block", so Quarkus skips the hop to a worker and saves its cost. Quarkus believes that promise completely, and never looks inside the method. Break it with a database call inside, and you're back in lesson 5, with every other connection on that event loop waiting. Here the ticket picture breaks. A real clerk would notice a forty-minute job marked "quick". Quarkus never will. The back office is a bounded pool, like the ones in the executors track. Its size, quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads, defaults to the larger of 8 × CPUs and 200 in 3.40: 200 threads on a 4-core machine. The return type is a promise about blocking, and Quarkus believes it. Return Uni only from code that never waits. When the signature tells the wrong story, you can change the label. Predict the thread Without running anything, write down the thread for each Quarkus 3.40 endpoint: (a) public List<Parcel> recent(), (b) public Uni<Parcel> byId(...), (c) public CompletionStage<Label> printLabel(...), (d) Kotlin suspend fun track(id: String): Status, (e) public Multi<Scan> scans(). Open the lab test DispatcherTest and find the test that encodes the same rules. Check your answers against it. (a) runs on a worker thread; (b), (c), (d) and (e) run on the IO thread. The one people get wrong is (d): Quarkus treats a Kotlin suspend function as non-blocking, so a blocking database call inside it blocks an event loop, exactly like one inside a Uni method. Quarkus REST 3.40's dispatch decision, as this lesson's lab models it. The first rule that matches picks the thread. Quarkus REST guide at 3.40.1: execution model, blocking, non-blocking docs

h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · Changing the label: @Blocking, @NonBlocking, and the @Transactional disagreement
x: Changing the label takes one annotation. @Blocking (from io.smallrye.common.annotation) sends a method to a worker even if it returns Uni. @NonBlocking keeps a method on the IO thread even if it returns a plain value. Both work on a method, on a class, or on your jakarta.ws.rs.core.Application subclass, the class that stands for the whole service, which sets the default for all of it. Filters, small pieces of code that run before or after every endpoint, follow their endpoint: under @Blocking they run on the worker, otherwise on the IO thread. Java @Blocking // returns Uni, but the body blocks: use a worker @GET @Path("/{parcel}/archive") public Uni<Price> archived(@PathParam("parcel") String parcel) { return Uni.createFrom().item(priceBook.find(parcel)); // the database call runs right here } Kotlin @Blocking // returns Uni, but the body blocks: use a worker @GET @Path("/{parcel}/archive") fun archived(@PathParam("parcel") parcel: String): Uni<Price> = Uni.createFrom().item(priceBook.find(parcel)) // the database call runs right here Look at the line inside. Uni.createFrom().item(...) wraps a value that already exists, so priceBook.find(parcel) runs while the method builds the Uni, on whatever thread runs the method. Without @Blocking, that's the counter clerk. Transactions are where the rule book argues with itself. A transaction groups several database changes so that they all happen or none do. JTA, the Jakarta Transactions API, is Java's standard way to run one, and you ask for it with @Transactional. JTA blocks the thread that uses it. The Quarkus REST guide as released with 3.40.1 says a method or class annotated with jakarta.transaction.Transactional "will also be treated as a blocking method", and that an explicit @Blocking or @NonBlocking overrides this. The same guide on Quarkus's main branch, its newest code, says the opposite. Since 3.35, it says, @Transactional no longer makes a method blocking, the return type decides, and a Uni method that uses JTA needs an explicit @Blocking. The research for this track couldn't find the code that settles which is right for 3.40. So don't depend on either reading. Put @Blocking on every endpoint that uses JTA and doesn't return a plain value. It costs nothing when the rule already applies and saves you when it doesn't. When it doesn't, at least the failure is loud. Quarkus's JTA support comes from a library called Narayana, and its interceptor, the code that runs around a @Transactional method, checks whether blocking is allowed before it starts a transaction. In 3.40.1, on an IO thread, it throws BlockingOperationNotAllowedException: "@Transactional cannot start a JTA transaction within a reactive pipeline. If the annotated method is intended to be blocking, ensure it is executed on a worker thread, for example by annotating it with @Blocking. ..." When the signature tells the wrong story, change the label. On a @Transactional endpoint that returns Uni, write @Blocking. That exception is one way Quarkus catches a blocked counter clerk. Lesson 5's floor manager is the other, and Quarkus gives him new instructions. Read the rules both ways Take @Transactional public Uni<Void> record(Parcel p). Where does it run under the 3.40.1 docs? Under the main-branch docs? What does the JTA interceptor do in each case? Now take @Transactional @NonBlocking public Uni<Void> record(Parcel p). Where does it run, and what happens? Check the first answer against the lab test that mentions @Transactional. Under the 3.40.1 docs the first method runs on a worker, and the transaction starts normally. Under the main-branch rule it runs on the IO thread, and the interceptor throws BlockingOperationNotAllowedException before your code runs. The second method runs on the IO thread under both readings, because an explicit annotation wins, so it always throws. In every case @Blocking would have given the same working result, which is why it belongs on the method.

h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · When a counter clerk blocks: Quarkus's settings and its fast failures
x: Quarkus configures its Vert.x differently from plain Vert.x, and the differences change what your logs show: Setting Plain Vert.x 5 Quarkus 3.40 event loops 2 × CPUs CPUs, at least 2, at most one per 10 MB of max heap (the memory for objects) warn about a blocked loop after 2 s 2 s (quarkus.vertx.max-event-loop-execute-time) include the stack trace after 5 s 2 s (quarkus.vertx.warning-exception-time) threads for blocking work worker pool: 20 quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads: max(8 × CPUs, 200) A comment in Quarkus's source explains the first row. Twice the number of cores used to be the recommendation, but matching cores one to one seemed more reasonable, and it saves memory. On a 4-core laptop that means 4 event loops instead of 8, so one blocked loop stalls a quarter of your connections instead of an eighth. The third row is the friendly difference. QuarkusLikeLoopDemo builds a plain Vert.x instance with Quarkus's settings and blocks an event loop for 3 seconds. The first warning already carries the stack trace: plain Vert.x default event loops: 8, Quarkus 3.40 default: max(2, min(3420 MB / 10, 4 cpus)) = 4 [vertx-blocked-thread-checker] WARN io.vertx.core.impl.BlockedThreadChecker - Thread vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 has been blocked for 2681 ms, time limit is 2000 ms io.vertx.core.VertxException: Thread blocked at java.base/java.lang.Thread.sleep(Thread.java:509) at workbench.nio.l06.QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.lambda$main$0(QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.java:30) In the post office, Quarkus's floor manager writes down what the clerk is doing on his very first pass. In a real Quarkus service the line goes through Quarkus's own logging, so the prefix differs, but the message and the stack are Vert.x's. The first frame below Thread.sleep is your endpoint. Some Quarkus APIs don't wait for the floor manager at all. They check where they run and fail at once with BlockingOperationNotAllowedException, which extends IllegalStateException. The JTA interceptor from the previous section is one. Reading a request body as a blocking stream on the IO thread is another, and it fails with "Attempting a blocking read on io thread". Go one level down, and the check is simple. Quarkus asks its IO-thread detectors whether the current thread is an IO thread, and the Vert.x detector in 3.40.1 returns Context.isOnEventLoopThread(), the same call this lesson's lab uses. A fast exception in a test is a better way to find a blocking call than a slow event loop in production. Quarkus reports a blocked IO thread after 2 seconds, stack and all. Read the first frame of your own code below the block. Warnings and exceptions tell you a counter clerk blocked. The last label in the rule book avoids the back office's limit altogether. Block an IO thread with Quarkus settings Open QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.java (or the Kotlin twin). Predict the event-loop count it computes for your machine. Predict whether the first blocked-thread warning comes with a stack trace. Run it. Run it again with -Pargs=1500. How many warnings now, and why? QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.java package workbench.nio.l06; import io.vertx.core.Context; import io.vertx.core.Vertx; import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * A plain Vert.x instance configured the way Quarkus 3.40 configures its own, then blocked for 3 s. * Arg: sleep ms (default 3000). */ public class QuarkusLikeLoopDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { long sleepMs = args.length > 0 ? Long.parseLong(args[0]) : 3_000; int cpus = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors(); long maxHeapMb = Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() / (1024 * 1024); int quarkusLoops = (int) Math.max(2, Math.min(maxHeapMb / 10, cpus)); // VertxCoreRecorder.calculateDefaultIOThreads System.out.println("plain Vert.x default event loops: " + VertxOptions.DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP_POOL_SIZE + ", Quarkus 3.40 default: max(2, min(" + maxHeapMb + " MB / 10, " + cpus + " cpus)) = " + quarkusLoops); Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(new VertxOptions() .setEventLoopPoolSize(quarkusLoops) .setMaxEventLoopExecuteTime(2).setMaxEventLoopExecuteTimeUnit(TimeUnit.SECONDS) // Quarkus: 2 s, like Vert.x .setWarningExceptionTime(2).setWarningExceptionTimeUnit(TimeUnit.SECONDS)); // Quarkus: 2 s, Vert.x: 5 s vertx.runOnContext(v -> { System.out.println("[endpoint] on " + Thread.currentThread().getName() + ", Context.isOnEventLoopThread()=" + Context.isOnEventLoopThread()); try { Thread.sleep(sleepMs); // a database call inside an endpoint that returns Uni } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } }); Thread.sleep(sleepMs + 300); vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(); } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l06.QuarkusLikeLoopDemo labs/nio/src/demo/java/workbench/nio/l06/QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.java QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.kt package workbench.nio.l06 import io.vertx.core.Context import io.vertx.core.Vertx import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** * A plain Vert.x instance configured the way Quarkus 3.40 configures its own, then blocked for 3 s. * Arg: sleep ms (default 3000). */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val sleepMs = args.getOrNull(0)?.toLong() ?: 3_000L val cpus = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() val maxHeapMb = Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() / (1024 * 1024) val quarkusLoops = maxOf(2L, minOf(maxHeapMb / 10, cpus.toLong())).toInt() // VertxCoreRecorder.calculateDefaultIOThreads println("plain Vert.x default event loops: ${VertxOptions.DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP_POOL_SIZE}, " + "Quarkus 3.40 default: max(2, min($maxHeapMb MB / 10, $cpus
