Context.isOnEventLoopThread()=${Context.isOnEventLoopThread()}") Thread.sleep(sleepMs) // a database call inside an endpoint that returns Uni } Thread.sleep(sleepMs + 300) vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get() } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l06.QuarkusLikeLoopDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l06/QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.kt With a few gigabytes of max heap the memory cap doesn't bite, so the count equals your CPUs (4 here, against Vert.x's 8). The first warning, between 2 and 3 seconds in, already includes VertxException: Thread blocked and the stack, because the warning-exception time is 2 s. With a 1,500 ms block there is no warning at all: the checker only reports a task that has run longer than 2 seconds, so short blocks stay out of the logs.

h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · Temporary helpers: @RunOnVirtualThread without the worker-pool cap
x: The back office has a fixed number of workers. @RunOnVirtualThread is the third label in the rule book: it tells Quarkus to run the method on a new virtual thread, instead of the IO thread or a worker. A virtual thread is a thread the JDK manages itself. It runs on a carrier, an ordinary operating system thread, and while it waits it hands the carrier back, so a waiting virtual thread costs a few kilobytes of memory. In the post office, it's the temporary helper, hired for one job, who sits down while the job waits. The code stays blocking style. A database call, or uni.await().atMost(...) on a Mutiny Uni, parks the virtual thread, and the JDK wakes it when the result is ready. VirtualVsWorkerDemo shows what the back office's size costs. 200 requests arrive on one IO context, and each makes a 100 ms blocking call: worker pool (20 threads) 200 calls x 100 ms -> 1,037 ms on 20 distinct threads virtual thread per call 200 calls x 100 ms -> 113 ms on 200 distinct threads Twenty workers needed ten rounds of 100 ms: Little's law from lesson 1, 20 threads / 0.1 s = 200 calls a second. Two hundred helpers needed one. The Quarkus virtual threads guide compares the three models in one table, and its costs column is the part to remember: Model Runs on Main cost plain return value worker thread the pool caps concurrency Uni and friends IO thread more complex code @RunOnVirtualThread a new virtual thread pinning, monopolization, inefficient object pooling Pinning means a virtual thread that can't hand its carrier back while it waits. On Java 21 to 23 that happens when it blocks inside synchronized. JDK 24 removed that case (JEP 491), but native code, code written in C and called from Java, can still pin, and the guide notes that the PostgreSQL driver pgjdbc before 42.6.0 pins often on 21 to 23. Monopolization means CPU-heavy work that never blocks, so it never hands the carrier back: virtual threads are for work that waits, not work that computes. And libraries such as Jackson (which reads and writes JSON) and Netty keep pools of objects per thread, assuming a few long-lived threads. A new virtual thread per request defeats those pools. Two more things stay true. Helpers don't limit anything. 200 virtual threads sharing a 20-connection database pool still queue at the pool, so put a semaphore (a counter of permits that makes extra callers wait) or the pool's own limit in front of anything fragile. And the request still arrives on an IO thread. @RunOnVirtualThread works by moving your code off it. A virtual thread per request removes the back office's cap, and with it the back office's protection. Put the limit back in front of the database. Pool cap versus virtual threads Open VirtualVsWorkerDemo.java (or the Kotlin twin). Predict both times before running. Run it. Give the worker pool 40 threads: change Vertx.vertx() to Vertx.vertx(new VertxOptions().setWorkerPoolSize(40)). Predict the new worker time, then run. VirtualVsWorkerDemo.java package workbench.nio.l06; import io.vertx.core.Context; import io.vertx.core.Future; import io.vertx.core.Promise; import io.vertx.core.Vertx; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** 200 requests arrive on one IO context; each makes a 100 ms blocking call. Worker pool vs a virtual thread each. */ public class VirtualVsWorkerDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(); // default worker pool: 20 threads Context server = vertx.getOrCreateContext(); // where the requests arrive Thread.Builder virtualThreads = Thread.ofVirtual().name("vt-", 0); // used only on the server's thread for (boolean virtual : new boolean[] {false, true}) { Set<String> threads = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); List<Future<Object>> calls = new ArrayList<>(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) { Promise<Object> done = Promise.promise(); server.runOnContext(v -> { Runnable blockingCall = () -> { threads.add(Thread.currentThread().getName()); try { Thread.sleep(100); // a database, a slow web service... } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } done.complete(); }; if (virtual) virtualThreads.start(blockingCall); // like @RunOnVirtualThread else vertx.executeBlocking(() -> { blockingCall.run(); return null; }, false); // like @Blocking }); calls.add(done.future()); } Future.all(calls).toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.printf("%-26s 200 calls x 100 ms -> %,5d ms on %d distinct threads%n", virtual ? "virtual thread per call" : "worker pool (20 threads)", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, threads.size()); } vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(); } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l06.VirtualVsWorkerDemo labs/nio/src/demo/java/workbench/nio/l06/VirtualVsWorkerDemo.java VirtualVsWorkerDemo.kt package workbench.nio.l06 import io.vertx.core.Future import io.vertx.core.Promise import io.vertx.core.Vertx import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** 200 requests arrive on one IO context; each makes a 100 ms blocking call. Worker pool vs a virtual thread each. */ fun main() { val vertx = Vertx.vertx() // default worker pool: 20 threads val server = vertx.getOrCreateContext() // where the requests arrive val virtualThreads = Thread.ofVirtual().name("vt-", 0) // used only on the server's thread for (virtual in listOf(false, true)) { val threads = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet<String>() val t0 = System.nanoTime() val calls = List(200) { val done = Promise.promise<Any>() server.runOnContext { val blockingCall = Runnable { threads += Thread.currentThread().name Thread.sleep(100) // a database, a slow web service... done.complete() } if (virtual) virtualThreads.start(blockingCall) // like @RunOnVirtualThread else vertx.executeBlocking(Callable<Any> { blockingCall.run(); "" }, false) // like @Blocking } done.future() } Future.all(calls).toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) println("%-26s 200 calls x 100 ms -> %,5d ms on %d distinct threads".format( if (virtual) "virtual thread per call" else "worker pool (20 threads)", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, threads.size)) } vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get() } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l06.VirtualVsWorkerDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l06/VirtualVsWorkerDemo.kt About 1,000 ms on 20 worker threads (200 calls / 20 threads x 100 ms) and about 110 to 130 ms on 200 virtual threads; later runs for this lesson measured 1,059 and 132 ms. With 40 workers it drops to about 500 to 600 ms (534 and 598 ms in earlier runs): Little's law again, throughput = threads / time per call. The virtual version has no such cap, which is its strength, and also why you add your own limit in front of a fragile service. Quarkus virtual threads guide docs

h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · Java and Kotlin
x: The lab's dispatch rules in Kotlin and Java DispatchRules.java final class DispatchRules { private static final Set<ReturnKind> NON_BLOCKING_RETURNS = EnumSet.of( ReturnKind.UNI, ReturnKind.MULTI, ReturnKind.COMPLETION_STAGE, ReturnKind.PUBLISHER, ReturnKind.SUSPEND); static Target target(Endpoint e) { Set<Marker> m = e.markers(); if (m.contains(Marker.RUN_ON_VIRTUAL_THREAD)) return Target.VIRTUAL_THREAD; if (m.contains(Marker.BLOCKING)) return Target.WORKER; if (m.contains(Marker.NON_BLOCKING)) return Target.IO_THREAD; if (m.contains(Marker.TRANSACTIONAL)) return Target.WORKER; return NON_BLOCKING_RETURNS.contains(e.returns()) ? Target.IO_THREAD : Target.WORKER; } } DispatchRules.kt object DispatchRules { private val nonBlockingReturns = setOf( ReturnKind.UNI, ReturnKind.MULTI, ReturnKind.COMPLETION_STAGE, ReturnKind.PUBLISHER, ReturnKind.SUSPEND) fun target(e: Endpoint): Target = when { Marker.RUN_ON_VIRTUAL_THREAD in e.markers -> Target.VIRTUAL_THREAD Marker.BLOCKING in e.markers -> Target.WORKER Marker.NON_BLOCKING in e.markers -> Target.IO_THREAD Marker.TRANSACTIONAL in e.markers -> Target.WORKER e.returns in nonBlockingReturns -> Target.IO_THREAD else -> Target.WORKER } } Both encode the same first-match-wins rules; Kotlin's when without a subject reads like the figure, and Java uses early returns. The language difference that matters is in Quarkus itself. Java has no suspend, so a Java endpoint is non-blocking only through its return type, while a Kotlin suspend fun with a plain return type is non-blocking too, and runs on the IO thread. One Kotlin trap from this lesson's lab: Vert.x 5's Future has a member await(), and in Kotlin a member always wins over an extension with the same name, so a test helper fun <T> Future<T>.await() is silently ignored. The lab's test calls its helper awaitResult() for that reason.

h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · Worked example
x: Pick the thread for four post office endpoints A tracking lookup reads the parcel from a database the blocking way. Plain return type, so it runs on a worker. Nothing to add. @GET @Path("/parcels/{id}") public Parcel byId(@PathParam("id") String id) { // worker thread return parcels.findById(id); // blocking database call } @GET @Path("/parcels/{id}") fun byId(@PathParam("id") id: String): Parcel = // worker thread parcels.findById(id) // blocking database call A label-printing endpoint records the label in a JTA transaction and returns Uni because a client library wants one. Under the 3.40.1 docs @Transactional alone would send it to a worker; under the main-branch docs it would run on the IO thread, and the interceptor would throw. Add @Blocking, and both readings agree. @Blocking @Transactional @POST @Path("/parcels/{id}/label") public Uni<Label> printLabel(@PathParam("id") String id) { return Uni.createFrom().item(labels.print(id)); // database writes inside a JTA transaction } @Blocking @Transactional @POST @Path("/parcels/{id}/label") fun printLabel(@PathParam("id") id: String): Uni<Label> = Uni.createFrom().item(labels.print(id)) // database writes inside a JTA transaction A live feed of parcel scans comes from a non-blocking client and never waits. Multi keeps it on the IO thread with no thread switch, which is the case the reactive model is built for. @GET @Path("/scans") public Multi<Scan> scans() { // IO thread return scanFeed.subscribe(); // non-blocking source } @GET @Path("/scans") fun scans(): Multi<Scan> = // IO thread scanFeed.subscribe() // non-blocking source A customs report calls a slow outside web service (2 s) that accepts at most 50 calls at once, and the customs office sends bursts of hundreds of requests. The worker pool would cap the throughput, so give each request a virtual thread, and put the outside service's limit back with a semaphore. private final Semaphore customsSlots = new Semaphore(50); @RunOnVirtualThread @GET @Path("/reports/customs/{day}") public Report customs(@PathParam("day") String day) throws InterruptedException { customsSlots.acquire(); // 1. respect the outside service's limit try { return customsClient.reportFor(day); // 2. blocks: parks the virtual thread } finally { customsSlots.release(); } } private val customsSlots = Semaphore(50) @RunOnVirtualThread @GET @Path("/reports/customs/{day}") fun customs(@PathParam("day") day: String): Report { customsSlots.acquire() // 1. respect the outside service's limit try { return customsClient.reportFor(day) // 2. blocks: parks the virtual thread } finally { customsSlots.release() } }

h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · Lab
x: Simulate Quarkus's rule book on plain Vert.x labs/nio/src/main/kotlin/workbench/nio/l06/Dispatcher.kt labs/nio/src/main/kotlin/workbench/nio/l06/Endpoint.kt ./gradlew :nio:test --tests 'workbench.nio.l06.*' Run the tests. All seven fail with NotImplementedError. Read Endpoint.kt for the types: an endpoint has a name, a return kind and a set of markers (the annotations). Write DispatchRules.target with a when that applies the four rules in its KDoc, first match wins. The four rule tests should pass. Write BlockingGuard.check: throw BlockingNotAllowedException("Attempting $what on an IO thread") when Context.isOnEventLoopThread() is true. Write Dispatcher.invoke: receive the request with server.runOnContext { ... }, then run the body there (IO thread), through vertx.executeBlocking(callable, false) (worker) or on a new virtual thread, and complete a Promise with the result or the failure. Run the tests until all seven pass. Then change false to the default and see which test fails, and why. Marker.BLOCKING in endpoint.markers reads naturally in Kotlin. val p = Promise.promise<T>(), then p.complete(value) or p.fail(e), and return p.future(). For the worker branch, vertx.executeBlocking(task, false).onComplete(p) passes the result straight on. Give the Callable an explicit type (val task: Callable<T> = Callable { body() }); Kotlin can fail to infer Vert.x types whose @Nullable annotation lives in vertx-codegen. Every request goes through the one server context, so an ordered executeBlocking would make the four 300 ms calls queue: that is what the overlap test catches. All seven tests in DispatcherTest pass. h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · Quiz
x: In Quarkus 3.40 with no annotations, which endpoint runs on the IO thread? public Parcel get(@PathParam("id") String id) public List<Parcel> recent() public Uni<Parcel> get(@PathParam("id") String id) public Response cancel(...) Only the Uni return type marks the method as non-blocking. The other three return plain values, so Quarkus runs them on a worker thread. A Kotlin endpoint suspend fun track(id: String): Status = repository.track(id) calls a repository that uses the database the blocking way. What happens under load? Nothing: suspend functions never block a thread It runs on the IO thread, so each database call blocks an event loop; make it a plain function or call a non-blocking client Quarkus notices the database call and moves it to a worker It runs on a new virtual thread Quarkus treats suspend like Uni: non-blocking, so it runs on the IO thread. suspend only frees the thread when the code inside actually suspends, and a blocking database call doesn't. Quarkus can't see inside the method. A Quarkus log shows Thread vert.x-eventloop-thread-2 has been blocked for 2105 ms, time limit is 2000 ms followed at once by a stack trace. Plain Vert.x would print the stack only after 5 s. Why here? Quarkus sets the warning-exception time to 2 s Quarkus lowers the blocked limit to 1 s Vert.x 5 changed its default to 2 s The stack means Quarkus killed the thread Quarkus's quarkus.vertx.warning-exception-time defaults to 2 s, the same as the blocked limit, so the first warning already carries the stack trace. Neither Vert.x nor Quarkus kills or interrupts the thread. From lesson 5: a Vert.x consumer calls vertx.executeBlocking(callable) without the second argument for every message. Six messages arrive at once, each needing 300 ms of blocking work. Roughly how long until all six are answered? About 300 ms About 1,800 ms About 600 ms Never: it deadlocks The default executeBlocking is ordered per context, and all six messages come from the consumer's one context, so they run one after another on the worker pool: 6 x 300 ms. Passing false lets them overlap. A customs report endpoint calls a blocking outside service that takes 2 s and allows 50 calls at once. The customs office sends bursts of 500 requests. Which fits best? Return Uni and call the outside service inside it Plain return type, with the worker pool raised to 500 @NonBlocking, so it doesn't use a worker @RunOnVirtualThread, with a semaphore of 50 around the outside call The call blocks, so it must stay off the IO thread, which rules out Uni and @NonBlocking. Virtual threads make 500 waiting requests cheap, and the semaphore keeps the outside service at its limit of 50. A 500-thread worker pool would work, but it costs 500 platform threads and still sends 500 calls at once to a service that takes 50.

h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · Key terms
x: IO thread Quarkus's name for a Vert.x event-loop thread; it reads requests and writes responses. Worker thread A thread from Quarkus's bounded pool that may block, used for plain return types and @Blocking. Endpoint A method that answers one kind of web request, such as GET /prices/P-17. @Blocking / @NonBlocking Annotations that override the thread Quarkus would pick from the method's signature. @RunOnVirtualThread Runs the endpoint on a new virtual thread instead of the IO thread or a worker. BlockingOperationNotAllowedException Thrown by guarded Quarkus APIs when blocking code runs on an IO thread. Pinning A virtual thread that can't let go of its carrier thread while it waits. Monopolization CPU-heavy work on a virtual thread that never blocks, so it keeps its carrier. Which Quarkus REST return types run on the IO thread by default? Uni, Multi, CompletionStage, Publisher, and Kotlin suspend functions. Everything else runs on a worker thread. Where can you put @Blocking / @NonBlocking in Quarkus REST? On a method, a class, or a jakarta.ws.rs.core.Application subclass (which sets the default for the whole service). Does @Transactional make a Quarkus REST method blocking? The 3.40.1 docs say yes, the main-branch docs say no (since 3.35). Add an explicit @Blocking to JTA endpoints that return Uni. Default number of Vert.x event loops in Quarkus 3.40? One per CPU, at least 2, and at most one per 10 MB of max heap: max(2, min(maxHeapMB / 10, cpus)). Why does a Quarkus blocked-thread warning come with a stack trace at 2 s? Quarkus sets quarkus.vertx.warning-exception-time to 2 s; plain Vert.x uses 5 s. What exception do guarded Quarkus APIs throw on an IO thread? BlockingOperationNotAllowedException (an IllegalStateException), for example from the JTA interceptor or a blocking body read. Three costs of @RunOnVirtualThread named by the Quarkus guide? Pinning (for example synchronized on Java 21 to 23, native code), monopolization by CPU-heavy work, and inefficient per-thread object pools.

h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · Go deeper
x: A few details from the Quarkus 3.40 sources and docs help when you debug thread choices. Filters follow their endpoint. A @ServerRequestFilter runs on the worker for a @Blocking endpoint and on the IO thread otherwise, so a filter that does a blocking lookup (say, checking a key against a database) blocks the event loop for every non-blocking endpoint. @ServerRequestFilter(nonBlocking = true) forces a filter onto the IO thread, which is only safe if it really never blocks. To check which thread runs your code, log Thread.currentThread().getName() or assert io.vertx.core.Context.isOnEventLoopThread() in a @QuarkusTest, Quarkus's annotation for tests that start the whole service. Event-loop threads are named vert.x-eventloop-thread-N, and Quarkus's worker threads usually have executor-thread in their names. The Vert.x settings live under quarkus.vertx.*: event-loops-pool-size, max-event-loop-execute-time, warning-exception-time and max-worker-execute-time (60 s). The old quarkus.vertx.worker-pool-size is deprecated in favor of quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads. Raising the event-loop count rarely helps a service that blocks: it only spreads the damage over more loops. Removing the blocking call is the fix. Finally, a version note on the @Transactional disagreement: the 3.40.1-tagged guide and the main-branch guide were both read for this track, and the code that applies the rule was not found. If you need certainty for your exact Quarkus version, write a @QuarkusTest that calls a @Transactional endpoint returning Uni and asserts which thread it ran on.

h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · Doormen, light-watchers and one staff room: the parts of a Jetty server
x: Jetty's documentation describes a Server as the component that links a collection of Connectors and a collection of Handlers, with threads from one ThreadPool doing all the work. A connector accepts connections and turns their bytes into requests. A handler is your code: the object that answers a request. Every thread you'll see in this lesson comes from that one pool, the staff room. The connector you'll use is the ServerConnector, and it has two kinds of threads. Acceptors, one by default, call accept() and hand each new connection on: they're the doormen. A SelectorManager owns several ManagedSelectors, and each ManagedSelector is one thread running a java.nio Selector. That's the select loop from lesson 2, which uses epoll, Linux's way of watching many connections at once, and each one is a light-watcher with a section of the wall. By default there are max(1, min(cpus / 2, maxThreads / 16)) selectors, and the docs' rule of thumb is that one selector manages 1,000 to 5,000 connections. Inside, each connection becomes an EndPoint that moves bytes and a Connection that understands a protocol, such as HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 or WebSocket. Here is a branch with one connector and the price desk as its handler: Java Server server = new Server(new QueuedThreadPool()); // one pool for everything ServerConnector connector = new ServerConnector(server); connector.setHost("127.0.0.1"); connector.setPort(8080); server.addConnector(connector); server.setHandler(new PriceHandler(300)); server.start(); Kotlin val server = Server(QueuedThreadPool()) // one pool for everything val connector = ServerConnector(server).apply { host = "127.0.0.1"; port = 8080 } server.addConnector(connector) server.handler = PriceHandler(300) server.start() PriceHandler is this lesson's lab class: it answers each request after a 300 ms "database lookup". The default pool is a QueuedThreadPool with at least 8 and at most 200 threads. The connector leases some of them for good, which means it takes them out of the pool for as long as the server runs. JettyThreadsDemo starts a default server on 4 CPUs and counts: cpus=4 acceptors=1 selectors=2 QueuedThreadPool min=8 max=200 started=8 leased=3 One doorman and two light-watchers make three leased threads. The pool must have room for those plus at least one thread for requests. The docs suggest sizing maxThreads as the leased threads plus the threads you want for handlers. Two pool rules surprise people. First, the pool's queue must be unbounded. Jetty sometimes needs to run its own tasks to make progress; HTTP/2, for example, must write in order to read. The docs warn that a rejected task can make the server grind to a halt. Limit load with a QoS handler instead, one of Jetty's handlers that caps how many requests run at once (QoS stands for quality of service). Second, a platform thread, an ordinary thread of the operating system, costs about 1 MiB of memory outside the heap, so a pool of 200 is a real amount of memory. One pool staffs the whole branch. Size it as leased threads plus request threads, and never bound its queue. The staff are in place. The next question is what your handler promises them. Count what a default server starts Open JettyThreadsDemo.java (or JettyThreadsDemo.kt). From the formula above, predict the selector count on your machine with the default pool of 200. Run it and compare. Then predict the selectors for new QueuedThreadPool(12) on 4 CPUs. Leave the last two lines for now; the last section explains them. JettyThreadsDemo.java package workbench.nio.l07; import org.eclipse.jetty.io.Content; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Handler; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Request; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Response; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Server; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.ServerConnector; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.Callback; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.VirtualThreads; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.thread.QueuedThreadPool; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.thread.ThreadPool; import java.net.URI; import java.net.http.HttpClient; import java.net.http.HttpRequest; import java.net.http.HttpResponse; /** What does a default Jetty 12 server start, and which thread runs a blocking vs a non-blocking handler? */ public class JettyThreadsDemo { static final HttpClient CLIENT = HttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build(); static String where() { Thread t = Thread.currentThread(); return t.getName() + " virtual=" + t.isVirtual(); } static class Blocking extends Handler.Abstract { // declares BLOCKING @Override public boolean handle(Request req, Response res, Callback cb) { Content.Sink.write(res, true, where(), cb); return true; } } static class NonBlocking extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking { // declares NON_BLOCKING @Override public boolean handle(Request req, Response res, Callback cb) { Content.Sink.write(res, true, where(), cb); return true; } } static Server start(ThreadPool pool, Handler handler) throws Exception { Server server = new Server(pool); ServerConnector connector = new ServerConnector(server); connector.setHost("127.0.0.1"); connector.setPort(0); server.addConnector(connector); server.setHandler(handler); server.start(); return server; } static String get(Server server) throws Exception { int port = ((ServerConnector) server.getConnectors()[0]).getLocalPort(); return CLIENT.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:" + port + "/")).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { QueuedThreadPool defaults = new QueuedThreadPool(); Server server = start(defaults, new Blocking()); ServerConnector c = (ServerConnector) server.getConnectors()[0]; System.out.println("cpus=" + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() + " acceptors=" + c.getAcceptors() + " selectors=" + c.getSelectorManager().getSelectorCount()); System.out.println("QueuedThreadPool min=" + defaults.getMinThreads() + " max=" + defaults.getMaxThreads() + " started=" + defaults.getThreads() + " leased=" + defaults.getLeasedThreads()); System.out.println("[platform pool] BLOCKING handler -> " + get(server)); server.stop(); server = start(new QueuedThreadPool(), new NonBlocking()); System.out.println("[platform pool] NON_BLOCKING handler -> " + get(server)); server.stop(); for (boolean blocking : new boolean[] {true, false}) { QueuedThreadPool pool = new QueuedThreadPool(); pool.setVirtualThreadsExecutor(VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("jetty-vt-")); server = start(pool, blocking ? new Blocking() : new NonBlocking()); System.out.println("[pool + virtual threads] " + (blocking ? With a 12-thread pool the formula gives max(1, min(2, 12 / 16 = 0)) = 1 selector. Jetty also logs a few INFO lines when servers start and stop. h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · Returning true is a promise: the asynchronous core Handler API
x: Jetty 12 rewrote the API at its center. In Jetty 11 a handler had a blocking signature built on Servlet types, the classic Java web API. In Jetty 12 it is boolean handle(Request request, Response response, Callback callback), and the migration guide spells out the new contract. Return true to say "this request is mine", and then complete the Callback, by succeeding or failing it, possibly long after handle has returned. Return false, and Jetty shrugs and moves on; with no other handler, the client gets a 404 (not found). A callback, here, is the object you complete when the work is done, so Jetty knows the response is finished. A blocking handler is the simple case. Do the work, write the response with Content.Sink.write(response, true, text, callback), which completes the callback once the bytes are written, and return true. A non-blocking handler reads the body without waiting for it. Here is the return-to-sender desk from lesson 1 as a Jetty handler that answers echo: <body>: Java public class EchoHandler extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking { @Override public boolean handle(Request request, Response response, Callback callback) { Content.Source.asStringAsync(request, UTF_8).whenComplete((body, failure) -> { if (failure != null) { Response.writeError(request, response, callback, failure); return; } Content.Sink.write(response, true, "echo: " + body, callback); // completes the callback }); return true; // "this request is mine"; the response finishes later } } Kotlin class EchoHandler : Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking() { override fun handle(request: Request, response: Response, callback: Callback): Boolean { Content.Source.asStringAsync(request, UTF_8).whenComplete { body, failure -> if (failure != null) { Response.writeError(request, response, callback, failure) } else { Content.Sink.write(response, true, "echo: $body", callback) // completes the callback } } return true // "this request is mine"; the response finishes later } } The plan takes three steps. First, ask for the whole body as a future. Then return true at once, before any of the body has arrived. Finally, when the future completes, on whatever thread delivered the last bytes, write the answer or the error; either one completes the callback. No thread waited for the body. The request body is a Content.Source, which you read in Content.Chunks: slices of Jetty's network buffers, passed up without copying. The rule echoes Netty's reference counting from lesson 4. Every chunk you read() must be released, except failure chunks, and a source must be read to the end or failed, or Jetty can leak its buffers. Helpers such as asStringAsync do the reading and the releasing for you. The superclass is a declaration, the label on the job. Handler.Abstract says "I may block", which Jetty calls the BLOCKING invocation type. Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking says "I never block", and Jetty uses that promise to pick a thread, as the next section shows. The Servlet API still exists, as a layer on top of this core. Jetty 12 ships it in separate environments named after versions of Jakarta EE, the family of standard Java server APIs: ee8, ee9, ee10, and since 12.1, ee11, which brings Servlet 6.1. The docs list the core API's strengths as simple, minimal and asynchronous, with low overhead because you only configure what you use. Returning true is a promise to finish the response exactly once. Complete the callback on every path. Finishing is one promise. The other, blocking or not, decides who does the work. Break the handler contract In JettyThreadsDemo, change the Blocking handler's body to just return false; (delete the Content.Sink.write line). Predict what the first GET prints. Put it back. Now think it through without running it: what does a client see if a handler returns true and never completes the callback? With return false the request finds no handler, and Jetty answers with a 404 page, which the demo prints as the body. A handler that returns true and never completes the callback leaves the request open: the client waits until its own timeout or Jetty's idle timeout ends the connection. Returning true is a promise to finish the response exactly once. Jetty 11 to 12 migration guide (Handler API) docs

h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · Who serves the customer: one strategy, three modes
x: Jetty's acceptor, selectors and one thread pool: a ready socket becomes a task, and the handler's declaration picks the thread that runs it When a selector finds a lit box, a readable connection, it produces a task: "run this connection's onFillable", which parses the request and calls your handler. Jetty's AdaptiveExecutionStrategy then decides which thread consumes that task. It has three main modes, named in the Jetty docs: Produce-Consume (PC): the selector thread runs the task itself. There's no hand-off, and the CPU's caches, its small fast memories, still hold the connection's data. But every other connection on that selector waits. The docs say this mode is equivalent to the event loop of Node.js (a JavaScript server) or Netty. Produce-Execute-Consume (PEC): the task goes to the thread pool. Nothing waits behind it, but there's a hand-off, a queue, and cold caches on another core. Execute-Produce-Consume (EPC): the selector thread runs the task, and a reserved thread, one the pool keeps idle and ready, takes over the selecting. Warm caches, and no stall. In the branch, PC is the watcher serving a quick job on the spot. PEC is the watcher handing a long job to the pool. EPC is the watcher waving a standby over to the lights and serving the long job himself. The choice follows the task's invocation type. A NON_BLOCKING task runs in PC mode. A BLOCKING task runs in EPC mode when a reserved thread is available, and in PEC mode when none is. Jetty's source notes that this strategy used to be called "Eat What You Kill": the hunter eats what it caught. StrategyDemo reads the mode from each handler's own stack trace, in four setups: default pool, BLOCKING -> qtp1636182655-25 :: AdaptiveExecutionStrategy.epcRunTask default pool, NON_BLOCKING -> qtp2106165633-37 :: AdaptiveExecutionStrategy.pcRunTask reservedThreads=0, BLOCKING -> qtp1090541608-50 :: no strategy frame: dispatched to the pool virtual threads, BLOCKING -> jetty-vt-1 :: VirtualThread.run qtp threads belong to the QueuedThreadPool. The blocking handler ran in EPC mode, and the non-blocking one in PC mode. With no reserved threads, nobody could take over the lights, so the blocking task went to the pool, and its stack has no strategy frame at all. The fourth line waits for the next section. Now you can see why the handler's declaration matters. NonBlocking is a promise that lets Jetty run your code on the selector thread, exactly like a Netty event loop. Break the promise with a database call, and every connection on that selector stalls; the docs call it a risk of server lock-up. In the branch, the watcher is busy with a long job, and his whole section of the wall goes unwatched. Containers, handlers that hold other handlers, combine their children's types. So one blocking handler anywhere in a handler tree makes the whole tree blocking, which is safe, but it costs the PC fast path. Compare that with the other servers you know. Netty-based servers, including Vert.x and Quarkus, run every handler in PC mode on the event loop, and moving work off it is your job. Tomcat, another widely used Java web server, watches connections with a poller thread and runs each request on its executor's threads, 200 by default. Jetty sits in between: it chooses per task, from what your handler declares. A handler's superclass decides which thread runs it. Declare NonBlocking only for code that never waits. The fourth line of the demo ran on a virtual thread. Jetty 12 offers two ways to get there. Read the mode from the stack Open StrategyDemo.java (or StrategyDemo.kt). For each of the four setups, predict the mode: PC, EPC, PEC, or a virtual thread. Run it with the command below. Explain the third line: why does setReservedThreads(0) change the mode for a blocking handler? StrategyDemo.java package workbench.nio.l07; import org.eclipse.jetty.io.Content; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Handler; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Request; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Response; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Server; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.ServerConnector; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.Callback; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.VirtualThreads; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.thread.QueuedThreadPool; import java.net.URI; import java.net.http.HttpClient; import java.net.http.HttpRequest; import java.net.http.HttpResponse; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.stream.Collectors; /** Which execution-strategy mode ran the handler? Read it from the handler's own stack. */ public class StrategyDemo { static final HttpClient CLIENT = HttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build(); static String mode() { List<String> methods = Arrays.stream(Thread.currentThread().getStackTrace()) .filter(f -> f.getClassName().contains("AdaptiveExecutionStrategy") || f.getClassName().contains("VirtualThread")) .map(f -> f.getClassName().replaceAll(".*\\.", "") + "." + f.getMethodName()) .collect(Collectors.toList()); String strategy = methods.stream().filter(m -> m.contains("RunTask") && !m.equals("AdaptiveExecutionStrategy.runTask")) .findFirst().orElse(methods.isEmpty() ? "no strategy frame: dispatched to the pool" : methods.get(0)); return Thread.currentThread().getName() + " :: " + strategy; } static Handler handler(boolean nonBlocking) { return nonBlocking ? new Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking() { @Override public boolean handle(Request r, Response s, Callback c) { Content.Sink.write(s, true, mode(), c); return true; } } : new Handler.Abstract() { @Override public boolean handle(Request r, Response s, Callback c) { Content.Sink.write(s, true, mode(), c); return true; } }; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { for (String setup : List.of("default pool, BLOCKING", "default pool, NON_BLOCKING", "reservedThreads=0, BLOCKING", "virtual threads, BLOCKING")) { QueuedThreadPool pool = new QueuedThreadPool(); if (setup.startsWith("reservedThreads=0")) pool.setReservedThreads(0); if (setup.startsWith("virtual")) pool.setVirtualThreadsExecutor(VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("jetty-vt-")); Server server = new Server(pool); ServerConnector connector = new ServerConnector(server); connector.setHost("127.0.0.1"); connector.setPort(0); server.addConnector(connector); server.setHandler(handler(setup.endsWith("NON_BLOCKING"))); server.start(); URI uri = URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:" + connector.getLocalPort() + "/"); CLIENT.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()); // warm up the connection System.out.printf("%-28s -> %s%n", setup, CLIENT.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body()); server.stop(); } } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l07.StrategyDemo labs/nio/src/demo/java/workbench/nio/l07/StrategyDemo.java StrategyDemo.kt package workbench.nio.l07 import org.eclipse.jetty.io.Content import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Handler import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Request import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Response import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Server import org.eclipse.jetty.server.ServerConnector import org.eclipse.jetty.util.Callback import org.eclipse.jetty.util.VirtualThreads import org.eclipse.jetty.util.thread.QueuedThreadPool import java.net.URI import java.net.http.HttpClient import java.net.http.HttpRequest import java.net.http.HttpResponse /** Which execution-strategy mode ran the handler? Read it from the handler's own stack. */ private val strategyClient = HttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build() private fun strategyMode(): String { val methods = Thread.currentThread().stackTrace .filter { "AdaptiveExecutionStrategy" in it.className || "VirtualThread" in it.className } .map { it.className.substringAfterLast('.') + "." + it.methodName } val strategy = methods.firstOrNull { "RunTask" in it && it != "AdaptiveExecutionStrategy.runTask" } ?: methods.firstOrNull() ?: "no strategy frame: dispatched to the pool" return "${Thread.currentThread().name} :: $strategy" } private fun modeHandler(nonBlocking: Boolean): Handler = if (nonBlocking) object : Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking() { override fun handle(request: Request, response: Response, callback: Callback): Boolean { Content.Sink.write(response, true, strategyMode(), callback); return true } } else object : Handler.Abstract() { override fun handle(request: Request, response: Response, callback: Callback): Boolean { Content.Sink.write(response, true, strategyMode(), callback); return true } } fun main() { for (setup in listOf("default pool, BLOCKING", "default pool, NON_BLOCKING", "reservedThreads=0, BLOCKING", "virtual threads, BLOCKING")) { val pool = QueuedThreadPool() if (setup.startsWith("reservedThreads=0")) pool.reservedThreads = 0 if (setup.startsWith("virtual")) pool.virtualThreadsExecutor = VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("jetty-vt-") val server = Server(pool) val connector = ServerConnector(server).apply { host = "127.0.0.1"; port = 0 } server.addConnector(connector) server.handler = modeHandler(setup.endsWith("NON_BLOCKING")) server.start() val uri = URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:${connector.localPort}/") strategyClient.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()) // warm up the connection println("%-28s -> %s".format(setup, strategyClient.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body())) server.stop() } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l07.StrategyDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l07/StrategyDemo.kt Blocking on the default pool: epcRunTask. Non-blocking: pcRunTask, on the selector's own thread. With no reserved threads, a blocking task can't use EPC, because nobody could take over selecting, so it is dispatched to the pool and the handler's stack has no strategy frame at all (PEC). With virtual threads, the PEC path hands the task to a virtual thread, jetty-vt-1. A selector produces a task per ready connection; the adaptive strategy runs it in place, runs it in place while a reserved thread selects, or hands it off. Jetty 12.1 programming guide: threading architecture docs

h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · Temporary helpers again: virtual threads in Jetty 12
x: A virtual thread is a cheap thread that the JDK parks while it waits, on top of a few carrier threads from the operating system. In the branch, it's a temporary helper hired for one job. Jetty 12 offers virtual threads in two ways, and they behave very differently. The first way keeps the QueuedThreadPool and gives it a virtual threads executor: Java QueuedThreadPool pool = new QueuedThreadPool(12); pool.setVirtualThreadsExecutor(VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("price-vt-")); Kotlin val pool = QueuedThreadPool(12) pool.virtualThreadsExecutor = VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("price-vt-") When the strategy picks PEC for a blocking task, it now sends the task to a virtual thread instead of a pool thread. Turning this on sets the reserved threads to zero by default, so blocking tasks always take that path. Acceptors, selectors and non-blocking tasks stay on platform threads. JettyThreadsDemo shows it: with the executor set, the blocking handler ran on jetty-vt-0 and the non-blocking one on a qtp thread. The second way is VirtualThreadPool, which replaces the pool. Despite its name, it doesn't pool virtual threads. It starts a new virtual thread for each task, and limits how many tasks run at once with a semaphore, a counter of permits, 200 of them by default. With it there are no qtp threads at all: the acceptor and the selectors run on virtual threads too. JettyLoadDemo sends 40 requests at once to a handler that blocks for 300 ms, on three pools. Before you read on, predict with Little's law how many handlers each pool can run at once. One run on a busy 4-core machine printed: QueuedThreadPool(max=12) 40 x 300 ms -> 1,786 ms, at most 9 in the handler at once QueuedThreadPool(max=12) + virtual 40 x 300 ms -> 410 ms, at most 40 in the handler at once VirtualThreadPool(maxThreads=8) 40 x 300 ms -> 1,853 ms, at most 7 in the handler at once Twelve platform threads, minus the leased ones and a reserved thread, left nine for requests, so 40 requests took five rounds of 300 ms. The virtual executor let all 40 wait at once: one round, plus the cost of starting. The VirtualThreadPool with 8 permits was slowest, because its permits cap concurrency below even the platform pool. Only 7 ever reached the handler at once, so at least one permit was busy with something else. One version note from the Jetty docs. Jetty dedicates a thread to each Selector, and up to Java 23, calling Selector.select() from a virtual thread pins its carrier: the carrier can't run anyone else while the selector waits. From Java 24 it doesn't. On 21 to 23, then, a server that runs everything on virtual threads loses one carrier per selector. That's one more reason to prefer the first way. QueuedThreadPool plus the virtual threads executor keeps the light-watchers on platform threads and gives only the blocking jobs to temporary helpers. And as in every lesson of this track, helpers don't protect what's behind them: 40 handlers at once means 40 database calls at once. Give blocking handlers virtual threads through the QueuedThreadPool's executor. Then put a real limit in front of the database. Three pools, one load Open JettyLoadDemo.java (or JettyLoadDemo.kt). Predict the time and the concurrency for each pool. Use Little's law: 40 requests, 300 ms each, and the number of threads that can run handlers. Run it. Change new VirtualThreadPool(8) to new VirtualThreadPool(64) and predict again before running. With 64 permits, the virtual pool lets all 40 requests run at once and finishes in about the same time as the virtual executor.

h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · Java and Kotlin
x: The return-to-sender desk as an asynchronous Jetty handler EchoHandler.java public class EchoHandler extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking { @Override public boolean handle(Request request, Response response, Callback callback) { Content.Source.asStringAsync(request, UTF_8).whenComplete((body, failure) -> { if (failure != null) { Response.writeError(request, response, callback, failure); return; } Content.Sink.write(response, true, "echo: " + body, callback); // completes the callback }); return true; // "this request is mine"; the response finishes later } } EchoHandler.kt class EchoHandler : Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking() { override fun handle(request: Request, response: Response, callback: Callback): Boolean { Content.Source.asStringAsync(request, UTF_8).whenComplete { body, failure -> if (failure != null) { Response.writeError(request, response, callback, failure) } else { Content.Sink.write(response, true, "echo: $body", callback) // completes the callback } } return true // "this request is mine"; the response finishes later } } The two are the same handler at run time. The Kotlin version shows two small differences. The BiConsumer passed to whenComplete becomes a two-parameter lambda, and if/else replaces the early return, because a bare return inside a Kotlin lambda would return from handle itself and doesn't compile here (you'd need return@whenComplete). Kotlin also lets you write Jetty's setters as properties (server.handler = ..., pool.virtualThreadsExecutor = ...). The threading is identical: the lambda runs on whichever thread completes the body future, which can be a different thread from the one that called handle.

h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · Worked example
x: Move a blocking price service onto virtual threads A Jetty branch serves prices with a 300 ms database lookup per request, on a pool of 50. Under a burst of 400 requests the slowest answers take seconds. Little's law: about 45 threads can run handlers, so 400 requests need 400 / 45 x 0.3 s, about 2.7 s, to drain, while the CPU is nearly idle. QueuedThreadPool pool = new QueuedThreadPool(50); // about 45 left after leasing Server server = new Server(pool); server.setHandler(new PriceHandler(300)); val pool = QueuedThreadPool(50) // about 45 left after leasing val server = Server(pool) server.handler = PriceHandler(300) Keep the handler and give blocking tasks virtual threads. The pool keeps its platform threads for the doorman and the light-watchers; every blocking handler gets a temporary helper, so the burst no longer queues for threads. QueuedThreadPool pool = new QueuedThreadPool(50); pool.setVirtualThreadsExecutor(VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("price-vt-")); val pool = QueuedThreadPool(50) pool.virtualThreadsExecutor = VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("price-vt-") Now the queue has moved to the database. 400 handlers all ask for one of its 20 connections. That's the right place for the wait, but give it a timeout, so a slow database turns into fast errors instead of 400 stuck requests. A database connection pool library has the same two settings, a maximum size and a connection timeout; here they are with a plain Semaphore. private final Semaphore dbSlots = new Semaphore(20); // the database allows 20 connections String lookup(String parcel) throws Exception { if (!dbSlots.tryAcquire(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { // 1. wait for a slot, but not forever throw new IllegalStateException("price book busy"); } try { return priceBook.find(parcel); // 2. blocks: parks the virtual thread } finally { dbSlots.release(); // 3. always give the slot back } } private val dbSlots = Semaphore(20) // the database allows 20 connections fun lookup(parcel: String): String { if (!dbSlots.tryAcquire(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { // 1. wait for a slot, but not forever throw IllegalStateException("price book busy") } try { return priceBook.find(parcel) // 2. blocks: parks the virtual thread } finally { dbSlots.release() // 3. always give the slot back } } Check that the health check is still cheap. It extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking, so it keeps running on platform threads in Produce-Consume mode, which the lab's last test asserts. If someone later adds a database ping to it, change its superclass in the same change.

h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · Quiz
x: A Jetty 12 handler extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking and calls a slow web service that takes 200 ms, the blocking way. What happens under load? Nothing special: Jetty moves it to a worker because the call blocks It runs on a selector thread in Produce-Consume mode, so other connections on that selector wait behind each call Jetty throws an exception because non-blocking handlers can't block It runs on a virtual thread, so blocking is free NonBlocking is a declaration Jetty trusts. It runs the task on the selector thread with no hand-off, like a Netty event loop. Jetty can't see that the call blocks, and only blocking tasks ever go to virtual threads. A team gives Jetty's QueuedThreadPool a bounded queue of 1,000 tasks, so that it rejects work under overload. What do the Jetty docs say? Good practice: a bounded queue protects the heap Fine, as long as the bound is above maxThreads The queue must be unbounded: Jetty needs its own tasks to run to make progress, and rejecting one can stall the server; use a QoS handler instead Only HTTP/1.1 connectors support bounded queues Jetty submits its own tasks to the same pool; for example, HTTP/2 must be able to write in order to read. A rejected internal task can stall connections. Limit load with a QoS handler, which works at the level of requests. On a 4-CPU machine, new Server(new QueuedThreadPool(64)) with one default ServerConnector. How many selector threads? 1 2 4 8 max(1, min(cpus / 2, maxThreads / 16)) = max(1, min(2, 4)) = 2. The selector count follows CPUs and pool size, not the number of connections. From lesson 2: a Jetty ManagedSelector wraps a java.nio.channels.Selector. Why does it run on its own dedicated thread? A selector's selected-key set isn't safe for use by several threads, so one thread owns each selector and its loop Selector.select() must run on the main thread Selectors are faster on platform threads The JDK allows only one selector per thread The Selector Javadoc says the selector itself is thread-safe but its key sets are not. One owner thread per selector is the pattern every framework uses: Netty's event loop, Vert.x's event loop, Jetty's ManagedSelector. You enable QueuedThreadPool.setVirtualThreadsExecutor(...) on JDK 21. Which of these runs on a virtual thread? The acceptor The ManagedSelector loops A Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking health check A Handler.Abstract handler that calls a database Only tasks the strategy runs in PEC mode, which are blocking tasks, go to the virtual threads executor. Acceptors, selectors and non-blocking handlers stay on platform threads, which also keeps selectors from pinning carriers before Java 24.

h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · Explain it back
x: A colleague says "Jetty is just a server that runs every request on a thread from its pool". Explain what Jetty 12 actually does between reading a connection and calling a handler, and why a handler's superclass matters.

h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · Key terms
x: Connector The Jetty component that accepts connections and turns their bytes into requests. Acceptor A thread that calls accept() and hands each new connection to a selector. ManagedSelector Jetty's wrapper around one java.nio Selector, run by one thread. Leased thread A pool thread that a connector takes for good, for an acceptor or a selector. Invocation type A task's or handler's declaration: BLOCKING, NON_BLOCKING or EITHER. Reserved thread An idle pool thread kept ready, so a selector thread can hand off selecting and run a task itself. AdaptiveExecutionStrategy Jetty's per-task choice between running a task in place and handing it off (once called Eat What You Kill). Callback The object a Jetty handler completes, by success or failure, when its response is done. What does a Jetty 12 ServerConnector run on threads? Acceptors (1 by default) that accept connections, and ManagedSelectors, one thread each, each running a java.nio select loop. Default number of selectors in a Jetty 12 ServerConnector? max(1, min(cpus / 2, maxThreads / 16)): 2 on 4 CPUs with the default 200-thread pool. The Jetty 12 core handler contract? boolean handle(Request, Response, Callback): return true if you take the request, then complete the callback exactly once, possibly after handle returns. false means "not mine". PC, EPC, PEC in one line each? PC: the selector thread runs the task. EPC: the selector thread runs it while a reserved thread takes over selecting. PEC: the task is handed to the pool (or a virtual thread). When does Jetty run a task in Produce-Consume mode? When the task is NON_BLOCKING, for example a handler that extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking. QueuedThreadPool.setVirtualThreadsExecutor vs VirtualThreadPool? The first sends only blocking tasks to virtual threads and keeps selectors on platform threads. The second runs everything on new virtual threads with a semaphore cap (200 by default). Why must Jetty's thread pool queue be unbounded? Jetty submits its own tasks to the pool to make progress (HTTP/2 must write to read); rejecting one can stall the server. Use a QoS handler to limit load.

h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · Go deeper
x: Three details from the Jetty 12.1 sources and docs round out the picture. There is a fourth mode. AdaptiveExecutionStrategy's Javadoc names Produce-Invoke-Consume for tasks whose invocation type is EITHER: they are run with Invocable.invokeNonBlocking, which asks the task to proceed in a non-blocking way if it can. The selection order is PC for a non-blocking task, EPC if a reserved thread is available, PIC for EITHER, and PEC otherwise. Strategies also nest: the selector's strategy produces connection tasks, and an HTTP/2 connection runs its own strategy over its streams. Jetty also has the mirror image of a declared handler. Request.demand(Runnable), which asks Jetty to call you back when more body content is available, treats a plain lambda as blocking. If your callback really is non-blocking, pass an Invocable.Task that says so, or Jetty may hand it to another thread for nothing. On sizing: each connector leases a thread per acceptor and per selector, and ReservedThreadExecutor leases its reserved threads, by default max(1, ceilToNextPowerOfTwo(min(cpus, maxThreads / 8))), or 0 once a virtual threads executor is set. The docs suggest maxThreads = leased threads + threads you want for handlers, and remind you that idle threads shrink back according to idleTimeout. Raising maxThreads into the thousands is the old fix for blocking handlers; on JDK 21 or newer, the virtual threads executor is the cheaper one. HTTP/3 shows how far the connector idea stretches. Jetty implements HTTP/3 in Java but uses the native Quiche library for QUIC, the network protocol under HTTP/3, through JNA, with a connector that has zero acceptors and a single selector over a DatagramChannel.

h: Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model · Straight from the loading dock to the van: zero-copy with transferTo
x: Zero-copy with transferTo, then readiness (epoll) versus completion (io_uring) Sending a file over a socket, a program's end of a network connection, the obvious way passes every byte through your process, the running program, twice. read copies bytes from the kernel's page cache, its in-memory copy of recently used file pages, into your buffer. write copies them back into the kernel's send buffer for the socket. With a heap ByteBuffer, the JDK adds another copy through a temporary direct buffer, as lesson 2 showed. Each call is also a system call: a switch from your program into the kernel and back, which costs time of its own. In the post office, that's the sack carried to the counter, unpacked and repacked. FileChannel.transferTo asks the kernel to do the whole move instead, from the dock to the van. On Linux, with a socket as the target, the JDK uses sendfile(2): the kernel sends pages from the page cache straight to the socket, and the bytes never enter your process. That's zero-copy: no copy through your program's memory. ZeroCopyDemo sends a 64 MiB file to a loopback socket, a connection from the machine to itself, twice, first with transferTo and then through a 64 KiB heap buffer. A run for this track counted the system calls with strace, a Linux tool that lists every system call a program makes: transferTo: sendfile 1 call copy through a 64 KiB heap buffer: read 2,119 calls, write 1,037 calls, no sendfile (the reads include the receiving side) One call, against about three thousand. The times, though, were close: 78 ms against 74 ms in one run on a busy 4-core machine, and 56 against 38 ms in the next. With the file already in the page cache and a loopback socket, copying 64 MiB is quick, so one timing proves nothing either way. The system calls are the honest measure here: they count the work that zero-copy removes. Like write on a non-blocking socket, transferTo may move fewer bytes than you asked for. It returns how many it moved, so it belongs in a loop: Java long sent = 0; while (sent < count) { sent += file.transferTo(position + sent, count - sent, socket); // maybe partial } Kotlin var sent = 0L while (sent < count) { sent += file.transferTo(position + sent, count - sent, socket) // maybe partial } Netty wraps the same idea in DefaultFileRegion: write one to a channel, and the transport sends the file. The NIO transport calls FileChannel.transferTo, and Netty's native epoll transport calls sendfile itself. When the socket's buffer fills, sendfile fails with EAGAIN ("try again later"), and Netty waits until the channel is writable and resumes: lesson 2's partial-write logic again. Zero-copy has one condition: the bytes must leave exactly as they sit in the file. Suppose the JVM encrypts them with TLS, the encryption behind https, or compresses them. That work happens in your process, so the bytes have to come up into your memory anyway. The dock picture holds here too: a sack that must be opened on the way can't go straight to the van. Tomcat's connector docs show the trade-off: for static files over 48 KiB it uses sendfile and skips compression. So zero-copy is a tool for bulk files over plain links, or where TLS ends at a proxy in front of the JVM. When bytes leave exactly as they're stored, let the kernel move them. Call transferTo in a loop. Zero-copy saves the copies. The next question is how a server learns which sockets are ready at all. Count the system calls Run ZeroCopyDemo (or ZeroCopyDemoKt) with the command below. It sends a 64 MiB file twice: with transferTo, then through a 64 KiB heap buffer. Before looking at the times, predict how many transferTo calls the first pass makes. On Linux with strace, run it outside Gradle: strace -f -c -e trace=sendfile,read,write java -cp nio/build/classes/java/demo workbench.nio.l08.ZeroCopyDemo, and find the sendfile line. h: Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model · A board of lit boxes, or a drop box for jobs: epoll and io_uring
x: Everything in this track so far uses readiness notification. epoll, the Linux mechanism behind our wall of lights, keeps the list of lit boxes for you. You register each socket once, and epoll_wait returns only the ones that are ready, so asking costs about the same with ten boxes or ten thousand. Then your loop makes the read or write system call itself: one call to wait, and one more per socket to move the bytes. The JDK registers sockets with epoll in level-triggered mode, so a light stays on while there's mail, as lesson 2 showed. io_uring is a newer Linux interface that works by completion instead. Your program and the kernel share two ring buffers in memory, fixed-size queues whose ends wrap around to their starts, like a drop box with two trays. You put requests in the submission ring, such as "read up to 16 KiB from this socket into this buffer". The kernel does the work and puts the results in the completion ring: "done, 4,096 bytes". One system call can submit and collect many operations, and the kernel, not your thread, moves the bytes. In the post office, you leave a whole list of jobs in the drop box and collect the results later, instead of standing at the board waiting for lights. On the JVM you reach io_uring through Netty; the JDK's own selector and poller use epoll. Netty 4.2 moved io_uring out of its incubator into a full transport. Its package is io.netty.channel.uring, and you use it like the other transports: a MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup with IoUringIoHandler.newFactory(), and the IoUring channel classes. Netty checks the kernel when it loads, and IoUring.isAvailable() says whether it can run on this machine. So is the drop box faster? Not reliably. TransportsDemo sends a 32 MiB DefaultFileRegion over every transport this machine offers. One run on a busy 4-core machine printed: nio received 33,554,432 bytes in 137 ms epoll received 33,554,432 bytes in 35 ms kqueue unavailable: java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError io_uring received 33,554,432 bytes in 59 ms kqueue is the macOS and BSD cousin of epoll, so on Linux it reports itself unavailable. Every transport delivered every byte. Epoll beat io_uring in this run, in its Kotlin twin's (40 against 48 ms) and in the research runs for this track (86 against 159 ms), and the gaps moved from run to run. Under strace, io_uring made no sendfile calls at all. The work went through 2,061 io_uring_enter calls, and Netty's history shows that it splices a file region instead. (splice is another kernel call that moves data without copying it into your process.) The transport is also still changing: Netty 4.2.20 itself contains several io_uring fixes. So measure your own workload before you switch. The switch is small, one factory and one channel class, which makes it cheap to try and cheap to undo. A newer kernel interface is a question, not an answer. Measure it on your own workload before you switch. Netty lets you pick the light board. A virtual thread has no such choice: when it waits on a socket, the JDK watches the lights for it. Every transport on your machine Predict which transports your machine supports: Linux has epoll and maybe io_uring; macOS has kqueue. Run TransportsDemo (or TransportsDemoKt). Run it twice and compare the times between runs, not only between transports. h: Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model · The JDK's own light-watcher: what a virtual thread's blocking read really does
x: When a virtual thread calls socket.getInputStream().read() and no bytes have arrived, no operating system thread blocks. A virtual thread runs on a carrier, an ordinary platform thread it borrows. The JDK's sources and a thread dump, a snapshot of every thread's stack, show what happens instead: The JDK's socket code, NioSocketImpl, keeps the socket in non-blocking mode, so the read returns at once with EAGAIN: nothing yet. It registers the socket's file descriptor, the number the kernel uses to name an open socket or file, with an internal Poller. The poller uses epoll with EPOLLONESHOT (report once, then disarm), and the JDK parks the virtual thread, which puts it to sleep until something wakes it. Its carrier moves on to other virtual threads. A poller thread waits in epoll_wait on every registered socket. When data arrives, it unparks (wakes) the virtual thread, which goes back onto a free carrier and tries the read again. In the post office, the temporary helper leaves a ticket with the JDK's light-watcher and takes a seat. When the light comes on, the watcher calls the ticket, and whichever desk is free carries on with the helper's job. A thread dump of a parked reader on JDK 25 shows the path, newest frame first: java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.park(VirtualThread.java:745) ... java.base/java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park(LockSupport.java:367) java.base/sun.nio.ch.Poller.poll(Poller.java:197) ... java.base/sun.nio.ch.NioSocketImpl.park(NioSocketImpl.java:174) ... java.base/sun.nio.ch.NioSocketImpl.implRead(NioSocketImpl.java:307) ... workbench.nio.l08.PollerDemo.lambda$main$0(PollerDemo.java:33) Which threads do the polling depends on the JDK version. PollerDemo blocks 2,000 virtual threads in read() and counts the platform threads. On JDK 21 it printed: 2000 virtual threads blocked in read(); platform threads: 14 4 x ForkJoinPool-N-worker-N 1 x Read-Poller 1 x Read-Updater 1 x Write-Poller 1 x Write-Updater ... wrote 1 byte to each socket: all 2,000 readers woke and finished in 114 ms The four ForkJoinPool workers are the carriers, one per core. The pollers are platform threads named Read-Poller and Write-Poller, with two updater threads beside them on Linux. Two thousand waiting readers cost no extra platform threads at all. From JDK 22, Linux defaults to a mode the JDK source calls VTHREAD_POLLERS: one platform MasterPoller thread plus sub-pollers that are themselves virtual threads, scheduled like any other. The source says it "helps to integrate polling with virtual thread scheduling". The same demo on JDK 25, the current long-term support (LTS) release, printed 12 platform threads, with one MasterPoller and no read or write pollers among them. jcmd <pid> Thread.vthread_pollers, a command added in JDK 24, lists the rest: Master I/O poller: sun.nio.ch.EPollPoller@50062f45 [registered = 5, owner = Thread[#547,MasterPoller,5,InnocuousThreadGroup]] Read I/O pollers: [0] sun.nio.ch.EPollPoller@3f48a9aa [registered = 599, owner = VirtualThread[#1505,SubPoller-0]/waiting] [1] sun.nio.ch.EPollPoller@29c03991 [registered = 411, owner = VirtualThread[#1537,SubPoller-1]/waiting] [2] sun.nio.ch.EPollPoller@309d6a91 [registered = 594, owner = VirtualThread[#1541,SubPoller-2]/waiting] [3] sun.nio.ch.EPollPoller@4b9d1f8b [registered = 396, owner = VirtualThread[#1544,SubPoller-3]/waiting] Four read sub-pollers on four cores, each a virtual thread, share the 2,000 sockets: 599, 411, 594 and 396. On macOS, the JDK keeps platform poller threads. So virtual threads don't make event loops obsolete. They put one inside the JDK, so your code can stay blocking style while an epoll loop does the waiting. A virtual thread's blocking read is a non-blocking read, a ticket at the poller and a park. The event loop is still there, inside the JDK. We've now seen every way of waiting this track covers. The last job is to choose between them. Find the pollers Run PollerDemo (or PollerDemoKt). Predict the number of platform threads before you look. Run it with -Pargs=5000 and predict again: which names grow, if any? If you have JDK 25 installed, run the class with it directly: java -cp nio/build/classes/java/demo workbench.nio.l08.PollerDemo 2000 30, and while it holds, run jcmd <pid> Thread.vthread_pollers with the pid it prints. Which poller names appear, and how many read pollers? Which platform threads exist meanwhile? * Args: [N, default 2000] [seconds to hold before releasing them, default 0] */ public class PollerDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int n = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 2_000; int holdSeconds = args.length > 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[1]) : 0; System.out.println("java " + System.getProperty("java.version") + ", cpus=" + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() + ", pid=" + ProcessHandle.current().pid()); try (ServerSocket server = new ServerSocket(0, n, InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress()); s.getInputStream().read(); // parks this virtual thread on the JDK poller } catch (IOException e) { e.printStackTrace(); } finally { done.countDown(); } }); } List<Socket> accepted = new ArrayList<>(); System.out.println(n + " virtual threads blocked in read(); platform threads: " + platform.values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum()); platform.forEach((name, count) -> System.out.println(" " + count + " x " + name)); if (holdSeconds > 0) { System.out.println("holding " + holdSeconds + " s: try jcmd " + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + " Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json"); Thread.sleep(holdSeconds * 1_000L); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (Socket s : accepted) s.getOutputStream().write(1); // data arrives: the poller unparks each reader done.await(); System.out.printf("wrote 1 byte to each socket: all %,d readers woke and finished in %d ms%n", n, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); platform threads: ${platform.values.sum()}") platform.forEach { (name, count) -> println(" $count x $name") } if (holdSeconds > 0) { println("holding $holdSeconds s: try jcmd ${ProcessHandle.current().pid()} Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json") Thread.sleep(holdSeconds * 1_000L) } val t0 = System.nanoTime() accepted.forEach { it.getOutputStream().write(1) } // data arrives: the poller unparks each reader done.await() println("wrote 1 byte to each socket: all %,d readers woke and finished in %d ms".format(n, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) accepted.forEach { it.close() } } } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l08.PollerDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l08/PollerDemo.kt On JDK 21, about 14 platform threads, the same with 5,000 readers: one carrier per core plus Read-Poller, Write-Poller and the two updaters. All readers wake within about a tenth of a second once data arrives. On JDK 25 on Linux, the platform list shows a MasterPoller instead of the read and write pollers and their updaters (12 platform threads in this lesson's run), because the sub-pollers are virtual threads and getAllStackTraces lists only platform threads. Thread.vthread_pollers shows them all: one read sub-poller per core up to 32, rounded down to a power of 2 (four on four cores), and one write sub-poller. A virtual thread's blocking read is a non-blocking read plus park and unpark, driven by an epoll loop inside the JDK. sun.nio.ch.Poller source (JDK 25) read

h: Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model · Choosing a server model: where the waiting happens, and what limits it
x: After eight lessons, choosing a server model comes down to two questions. Where does the waiting happen, and what limits it? A downstream is anything your service calls in turn, such as a database or another web service, and most waiting happens there: If the service... Choose Watch out for calls its downstreams the blocking way and mostly waits a thread per request on virtual threads: Quarkus @RunOnVirtualThread, Jetty's virtual threads executor a limit per downstream; pinning on JDK 21 to 23; CPU-heavy work has the same blocking code and moderate traffic a bounded worker pool: Quarkus plain endpoints, Jetty's QueuedThreadPool size it with Little's law; the pool caps concurrency is non-blocking end to end (non-blocking database client, async HTTP, streaming) an event loop: Vert.x, Netty, Quarkus Uni endpoints never block the loop; backpressure holds many idle connections that stay open for a long time an event loop, or virtual threads if the work per connection blocks memory per connection; idle timeouts sends large files unchanged zero-copy: transferTo, Netty's DefaultFileRegion no TLS or compression inside the JVM Read the table with the post office in mind. The first two rows are clerks for customers who wait: temporary helpers, or a back office with a fixed staff. The third and fourth are one clerk per row of boxes, who never makes a phone call. The last is the loading dock. Two rules hold in every row. First, concurrency needs a limit somewhere. An event loop limits it by never waiting, and a pool by its size. With virtual threads you have to add one, because 10,000 parked threads will make 10,000 calls to your database the moment they wake. This lesson's lab is exactly that bug. Second, the model doesn't change latency. A 120 ms call to a slow web service takes 120 ms in every row. What changes is how many of those calls you can wait for at once, and what each wait costs you. Here is where I'd start for a new web service that calls a database. Use plain blocking endpoints first. Move to virtual threads when the worker pool becomes the limit, with every database and outside call behind an explicit limit. Event loops and Uni earn their extra complexity when the whole stack is non-blocking, or when the connection counts are very large. Whatever you choose, measure it. Use Little's law for threads, the lag probe and the blocked-thread warnings for loops, and strace -c when you want to know what the kernel is really doing. Choose the model by where your service waits. Then put a limit in front of everything it waits on. Choose for three services The 6,000 parcel lockers from lesson 1 keep TCP connections open all day; each sends one 200-byte message a minute, and the work per message is a 3 ms check in memory. Choose a model. A tracking service: Quarkus, a database it calls the blocking way with JTA transactions, a blocking library for a courier's web service at 400 ms, and 150 requests a second at peak. Choose a model and say where the limits go. A nightly job sends 2 GB logbook files to an archive over a plain internal link. Choose how to send them. The lockers are almost all idle connections with tiny non-blocking work: an event loop (Netty or Vert.x) fits, with an idle timeout and framing as in lesson 4. The tracking service needs 150 x 0.4 = 60 requests in flight: plain blocking endpoints on the worker pool work, or @RunOnVirtualThread; either way, put @Blocking on JTA endpoints that return Uni, cap the courier library with a semaphore, and size the database pool on purpose. The nightly job is zero-copy territory: FileChannel.transferTo in a loop (or Netty's DefaultFileRegion), since nothing has to change the bytes on the way.
