x: A bounded zero-copy export on virtual threads LogbookServer.export, Java private final Semaphore exportSlots = new Semaphore(maxConcurrentExports); // the records database allows 4 void export(String day, SocketChannel out) throws Exception { exportSlots.acquire(); // waiting here parks the virtual thread try { Thread.sleep(QUERY_MILLIS); // the records query try (FileChannel file = FileChannel.open(logbooks.resolve(day + ".csv"))) { FileSender.transferFully(file, 0, file.size(), out); // sendfile on Linux } } finally { exportSlots.release(); } } LogbookServer.export, Kotlin private val exportSlots = Semaphore(maxConcurrentExports) // the records database allows 4 fun export(day: String, out: SocketChannel) { exportSlots.acquire() // waiting here parks the virtual thread try { Thread.sleep(QUERY_MILLIS) // the records query FileChannel.open(logbooks.resolve("$day.csv")).use { file -> FileSender.transferFully(file, 0, file.size(), out) // sendfile on Linux } } finally { exportSlots.release() } } Both use java.util.concurrent.Semaphore, and on a virtual thread acquire() parks without holding a carrier. A Kotlin team might reach for kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore with withPermit { } instead. That one only works inside coroutines, and it suspends rather than parks, so it fits a coroutine-based server, not this server with a thread per connection. FileChannel.transferTo is the same JDK call from both languages; Kotlin's use {} plays the part of Java's try-with-resources for the file channel.

h: Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model · Worked example
x: Design a logbook-download service Requirements: at month end, 600 logbook downloads a minute. Each needs a 1.5 s query to the records database and about 0.5 s to send its file. The database team allows 8 queries at once. Little's law first. arrival rate = 600 / 60 s = 10 requests/s time in system = 1.5 s + 0.5 s = 2 s in flight = 10 x 2 = 20 requests queries at once = capped at 8 -> requests wait for a slot, not for a thread Use one virtual thread per connection, so waiting for the query, for a slot or for a slow client costs no operating system thread. Put the database's limit in a semaphore with a timeout, so an overloaded database turns into a fast error. private final Semaphore querySlots = new Semaphore(8); void export(String day, SocketChannel out) throws Exception { if (!querySlots.tryAcquire(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { // 1. wait for a slot, but not forever throw new IllegalStateException("records database busy"); } try { renderLogbook(day); // 2. 1.5 s query, parks the virtual thread } finally { querySlots.release(); // 3. free the slot before the slow send } sendFile(day, out); } private val querySlots = Semaphore(8) fun export(day: String, out: SocketChannel) { if (!querySlots.tryAcquire(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { // 1. wait for a slot, but not forever throw IllegalStateException("records database busy") } try { renderLogbook(day) // 2. 1.5 s query, parks the virtual thread } finally { querySlots.release() // 3. free the slot before the slow send } sendFile(day, out) } Send the file with zero-copy, in a loop, because transferTo can stop early when the client's socket is full. Releasing the query slot before this step matters: a slow client should hold a cheap virtual thread, not one of the 8 database slots. static int transferFully(FileChannel file, long position, long count, WritableByteChannel target) throws IOException { long sent = 0; int calls = 0; while (sent < count) { sent += file.transferTo(position + sent, count - sent, target); // may be partial calls++; } return calls; } fun transferFully(file: FileChannel, position: Long, count: Long, target: WritableByteChannel): Int { var sent = 0L var calls = 0 while (sent < count) { sent += file.transferTo(position + sent, count - sent, target) // may be partial calls++ } return calls } Check the conditions before you promise zero-copy. If TLS ends inside the JVM, the bytes must be encrypted in your process, and transferTo gives you no zero-copy; send through a buffer and stop worrying about it. If a proxy in front of the JVM handles TLS, the JVM's socket is plain, and sendfile applies. Either way, the design's real limit is the 8 query slots, not the way the file is sent.

h: Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model · Quiz
x: A service sends 200 MB archive files to a partner over HTTPS, with TLS handled by the JVM. Does FileChannel.transferTo give zero-copy here? No: the JVM encrypts the bytes in your process, so they must pass through it Yes: on Linux transferTo always becomes sendfile Only with the io_uring transport Only if the file is read into a direct ByteBuffer first sendfile moves bytes from the page cache to the socket unchanged. TLS has to encrypt them first, and the JDK does that in your process, so the bytes come up into your memory whichever API you call. Zero-copy fits when TLS ends at a proxy in front of the JVM. file.transferTo(0, size, socket) returns a number smaller than size. What does that mean? An error occurred, and the socket should be closed The file is shorter than expected It moved only part of the data, for example because the socket buffer was full; call it again from the new position The kernel doesn't support sendfile Like a non-blocking write, transferTo moves what it can and reports how much. A single call is not a guarantee. Loop until the count is sent, as the lab's transferFully does. On JDK 21, 5,000 virtual threads are blocked in socket reads. Which threads wait in epoll_wait on their behalf? 5,000 platform threads, one per socket The ForkJoinPool carrier threads None: the kernel wakes virtual threads directly The JDK's poller threads (Read-Poller on JDK 21) The JDK registers each socket with its Poller, and the poller thread waits in epoll_wait for all of them. Carriers only run virtual threads that are ready, and the kernel knows nothing about virtual threads. From the virtual threads track: 10,000 requests run on virtual threads, and each calls an outside web service that accepts 100 calls at once. What protects that service? Nothing: virtual threads are cheap A Semaphore(100) around the call A fixed pool of 100 virtual threads Setting jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism to 100 Virtual threads should not be pooled, and the scheduler's parallelism controls carriers, not how many virtual threads make the call. A semaphore around the call is the limit; the other 9,900 virtual threads park cheaply while they wait. A Quarkus web service calls its database the blocking way and uses a blocking library for a slow outside service, at 300 requests a second and 150 ms each. Which model fits best? Non-blocking Uni endpoints on the IO thread The io_uring transport, because it is faster Plain blocking endpoints on the worker pool, or @RunOnVirtualThread, with explicit limits on the database and the outside service A Netty server with blocking handlers on the event loop The code blocks, so it must not run on an event loop, which rules out Uni endpoints and blocking Netty handlers. Little's law gives 300 x 0.15 = 45 requests in flight, easy for a worker pool or virtual threads. The transport doesn't change the threading model.

h: Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model · Key terms
x: Page cache The kernel's in-memory copy of file pages that were read or written recently. System call A switch from your program into the kernel to ask for a service, such as read, write or sendfile. Zero-copy Moving data from a file to a socket without copying it through your process's memory. sendfile The Linux system call that sends file data to a socket inside the kernel. io_uring A Linux interface where programs submit IO requests on a shared ring and collect completions. File descriptor The number the kernel uses to name an open file or socket. Poller The JDK's internal epoll or kqueue loop that wakes virtual threads when their sockets are ready. EPOLLONESHOT An epoll flag: report the socket once, then stop until it is registered again. What does FileChannel.transferTo to a socket become on Linux? sendfile(2): the kernel sends pages from the page cache to the socket; the bytes never enter your process. When can't you use zero-copy for a file transfer? When the JVM must change the bytes on the way: TLS encryption done by the JVM, or compression. transferTo returned fewer bytes than you asked for. What next? Call it again from position + sent with the remaining count, in a loop, until everything is sent. epoll vs io_uring in one line each? epoll: tells you which sockets are ready, then you make the IO call (readiness). io_uring: you submit the IO on a shared ring and collect completions (completion). What happens when a virtual thread's socket read finds no data? NioSocketImpl gets EAGAIN, registers the file descriptor with the JDK Poller (epoll, one-shot) and parks the virtual thread; a poller thread unparks it when data arrives. JDK 21 vs JDK 22+ (Linux) poller threads? JDK 21: platform Read-Poller and Write-Poller (plus updater threads). JDK 22+: one platform MasterPoller plus virtual sub-pollers (VTHREAD_POLLERS). With virtual threads, where must the concurrency limit come from? From you: a semaphore or the client's own pool around each downstream. Virtual threads themselves limit nothing.

h: Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model · Go deeper
x: Dan Kegel's C10K page, from lesson 1, compared ways to serve many clients. This track has now met each family on the JVM: readiness notification with a level-triggered Selector (lesson 2) and Netty's native epoll transport (lessons 3 and 4); completion-based IO with io_uring (this lesson); and one thread per client with blocking IO, which virtual threads made cheap again by running a readiness loop underneath. The JDK's poller has settings, though you should rarely need them. On JDK 21, -Djdk.readPollers sets the number of read pollers (a power of 2, default 1); with 4, a thread dump shows four Read-Poller threads. From JDK 22, -Djdk.pollerMode selects the mode: 1 for SYSTEM_THREADS (platform pollers, the JDK 21 behavior) and 2 for VTHREAD_POLLERS. In VTHREAD_POLLERS mode on Linux, the number of read pollers defaults to the highest power of 2 not above the CPU count, capped at 32, which is why this lesson's JDK 25 run showed four. JDK 27 adds a third mode, POLLER_PER_CARRIER (3), while the Linux default stays VTHREAD_POLLERS. Two smaller facts complete the picture. The JDK's Selector registers sockets level-triggered, while the poller uses one-shot registration: a selector serves the same socket again and again, while the poller wakes exactly one parked thread exactly once. And file IO is different from socket IO: a virtual thread reading a file does not go through the poller. As the virtual threads track explained, file operations hold the carrier while they run, which is one more reason zero-copy file sending is worth knowing about. To check any of this on your own JDK, jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json shows virtual threads and their stacks, and from JDK 24 jcmd <pid> Thread.vthread_pollers shows the pollers.

h: Capstone: a non-blocking quote service
x: A Netty service that fans out to three flaky providers with coroutines and answers inside a deadline. In three sittings, you build one working program: a quote service, a program that gives a price for a job before anyone books it. A customer asks what it costs to send a parcel to Lisbon. The service asks three invented courier companies, Northline, Eastgate and Fjord, at the same time, and within 300 ms it answers with the cheapest price, or with the last good price marked stale. It runs on Netty 4.2 with Kotlin coroutines inside. When a customer hangs up, the calls to the couriers stop. When a crowd arrives, each courier gets only its share of calls, only harmless questions are asked twice, the slow courier gets a second call, customers the service can't serve in time hear "busy" at once, and the service closes at night in order. The tests prove each of those by counting calls, permits, cancellations and virtual milliseconds, never by timing. The capstone draws on all of Part 2, and calls back its pictures as it goes. Lesson 1 is the post office of the Servers track: a clerk who owns a row of boxes and must never stop to make a phone call, the in-tray, and the full out-tray with two painted marks. Lesson 2 is the home cook of the Kotlin coroutines track: texting three shops at once, the kitchen timer, a course that goes out only when all its dishes are ready, the guests calling dinner off, and the neighbour's ticket at the fence. Lesson 3 adds the bakery's slip "send me 10 more" from the Reactive track, the shelf in the hatch from Kotlin Flow in depth, and from Part 1 the grill tokens, Little's law and closing time. There is little new theory. Each section shows what breaks if you choose differently, then names the earlier lesson that explains why. The lab is labs/quotes, one package per lesson (workbench.quotes.l01 to l03). Each lesson's starting code contains the previous lesson's solution, so you can start any sitting fresh. Lesson 1's lab is in Java; lessons 2 and 3 are in Kotlin, with lesson 1's Java server carried along. From labs/, run ./gradlew :quotes:test --tests 'workbench.quotes.lNN.*' until it passes; ./gradlew :quotes:solutionTest runs the same tests against the reference answers. Servers bind 127.0.0.1 on a free port, coroutine tests run on virtual time, and the Try-it demos run with ./gradlew :quotes:demo -Pmain=..., in Kotlin and in Java. Install JDK 25; the labs compile with release 21. The program is a quote service for parcel prices: a Netty shell, a coroutine fan-out to three couriers under a 300 ms deadline, and the guards that keep it standing under load. The event loop never waits, like the clerk who never makes the phone call. Handlers hand futures back and finish in whenCompleteAsync(..., ctx.executor()), and a test proves the loop is free by counting calls and probe tasks. Auto-read is the only tap, the packer's slip at the network's level: read while writable and under 16 in flight, with FlowControlHandler holding lines already decoded. A best-of fan-out uses supervisorScope and withTimeoutOrNull per call, and rethrows only its own cancel. With no answer, it serves a stale price, labelled as such, or fails clearly. scope.future { } in a SupervisorJob scope gives Java a future whose cancel reaches every courier call, so a hang-up stops the work. Each courier gets a bulkhead sized by Little's law. Only idempotent calls are retried, with jitter, and only the slow, idempotent courier is hedged. Turn work away at the door with tryAcquire and a clear ERR busy, and shut down in order: stop accepting, stop admitting, drain, cancelAndJoin, close. Event loop or virtual threads, the limits stay. Pick the model by where the waiting happens and by what the courier clients can do.

Pick When event loop and coroutines (this design) the service lives on Netty, Vert.x or Quarkus; connections in the hundreds of thousands; you need auto-read, decoders and flow control; the courier clients are non-blocking and a cancel must reach them one virtual thread per connection the courier clients only block (JDBC and the like); connections in the thousands; the team prefers plain Java either way bulkheads, deadlines, admission and an ordered shutdown stay. h: Capstone: a non-blocking quote service: track quiz
x: Which line in a Netty handler blocks the event loop? quote.whenCompleteAsync(callback, ctx.executor()) ctx.writeAndFlush(reply) called from a courier's thread source.quote(destination).join() ctx.channel().config().setAutoRead(false) join() holds the loop thread until the price arrives, so every channel on that loop waits. The callback runs later as a task, a write from another thread is queued onto the loop, and changing auto-read returns at once. The handler turns auto-read off after 16 requests, yet it still receives 2,000 more requests from the bytes of one socket read. What is missing? A bigger high water mark A FlowControlHandler between the decoders and the handler A call to ctx.read() in channelRead0 TCP_NODELAY on the channel Auto-read stops the next socket read, not the lines the frame decoder already holds. FlowControlHandler keeps those decoded messages while auto-read is off and releases them as reading resumes. ctx.read() would do the opposite: ask for more. Why does this track's test for a free event loop count calls and probe tasks instead of checking that a probe runs within 300 ms? On a busy build machine a healthy loop can miss a time limit, while a blocked loop's counts are wrong at any speed Netty doesn't let you time tasks on an event loop Counting is faster to run Virtual time doesn't work for Netty, so nothing can be timed Timings depend on the machine's load; counts depend only on what the code did. A loop stuck in join() makes 1 call however fast the machine is, and the test's 5-second wait only bounds how long the failure takes to report. A price needs any one of three couriers' answers. Which scope runs the three calls? coroutineScope, so a failure cancels the rest GlobalScope, so the calls outlive a cancelled request runBlocking, so the event loop waits for the answers supervisorScope, so each call fails alone With supervisorScope, a failed child keeps its exception for await, and the other calls carry on. coroutineScope is right when every answer is needed. GlobalScope leaks the calls, and runBlocking blocks the loop. Each call is async { withTimeout(300) { c.quote(d) } } in a supervisor fan-out, and the await rethrows every CancellationException. A courier is slow. What happens? The slow courier counts as no answer The request ends with TimeoutCancellationException, as if it had been cancelled The request waits for the slow courier The other couriers are cancelled, but the request succeeds withTimeout signals with TimeoutCancellationException, a CancellationException, and the catch passes it up as if the whole request were cancelled. Use withTimeoutOrNull, and check ensureActive() before rethrowing a cancel. Lesson 1's Java handler cancels the future when the client hangs up. Which way of writing QuoteSource.quote turns that cancel into cancelled courier calls? CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> blockingBest(destination), pool) CompletableFuture.completedFuture(runBlocking { best.quote(destination) }) scope.future { best.quote(destination) } in a scope the service owns GlobalScope.async { best.quote(destination) }.asCompletableFuture() with no scope to close The future builder links both ways: cancelling the future cancels the coroutine, and the cancel travels down to the courier calls. supplyAsync's cancel stops nothing, runBlocking blocks the event loop before returning, and GlobalScope work has no owner to close it at shutdown. Which courier may be hedged? Northline: it only looks up a price, so a repeat is harmless, and it has a slow tail worth cutting Fjord: its prices are bookings that hold a place on a van, and it is the slowest Every courier, after the same 80 ms None: hedging always doubles the load A hedge is a duplicate request, so only an idempotent courier qualifies, and it pays off only where the tail hurts. Hedging after about p95 costs about 5% more calls, not double. A booking is never repeated. Where does a courier's bulkhead permit belong? Around the whole retry loop, so a request holds one permit for all its attempts Around each single call, so a pause before a retry holds nothing and a hedge needs its own permit Around the whole fan-out, one permit per request Nowhere: the deadline already limits the calls The permit limits calls in flight to the courier, so it wraps exactly one call. Around the retry loop, it would be held through the pauses; around the fan-out, it would count requests instead of calls; and a deadline limits time, not how many calls run at once. A burst of 500 requests meets a courier that can answer about 60 within the deadline. What does admission with tryAcquire change? It gets live answers to all 500, just later It cuts the live answers to almost none It makes the courier faster The same number of live answers, but the rest hear ERR busy at once instead of failing after the deadline Requests beyond what the courier can serve in time fail either way. Shedding makes them fail in a millisecond, early enough to try another copy of the service, and nothing waits in a queue or on the event loop. In the demo, 50 requests got live answers in both runs. When should this service stay on an event loop instead of moving to one virtual thread per connection? When the courier clients only block When the team prefers plain Java and connections number in the thousands When it already runs on Netty or Vert.x, connections number in the hundreds of thousands, or the courier clients are non-blocking and a cancel must reach them Always: event loops are faster per request The event loop pays off for huge numbers of connections, control over the protocol and non-blocking clients. Blocking clients and plain Java favour virtual threads. Neither model makes a single request faster, and both still need the bulkheads, deadlines and admission.

h: A Netty server that never blocks its loop · The service we'll build, and the one rule it never breaks

The quote service you build, sitting by sitting: a Netty shell, a coroutine fan-out, guards under load, and the earlier lesson behind each part Over three sittings, we'll build one program: the quote service from the opening. A server is a program that waits for other programs to connect and ask it things, and those other programs are its clients. A client opens a TCP connection, a two-way line between two programs over a network, and sends one line of text. The server answers with one line: client: 7 LISBON server: 7 OK LISBON 12.42 northline Read the reply aloud: request 7 went fine, sending the parcel to Lisbon costs 12.42, and Northline offered that price. The 7 is the client's own number for its question, a request id, and the server repeats it on the answer. We'll see in a moment why the client needs it. The three couriers are invented, and like real ones, they're slow on a bad day and sometimes don't answer at all. The three sittings build the program from the outside in, and each one leans on a track of Part 2. This sitting builds the counter on Netty, the Java library for network servers from the Servers track. The next sitting asks the three couriers at once with Kotlin coroutines, the way the home cook from the coroutines track texted three shops. The last sitting keeps the service standing when a crowd arrives, with the slips of the Reactive track, the shelf of the Flow track and the limits of Part 1. Whenever we lean on an earlier lesson, we'll name it. One rule shapes every decision: the event loop never waits. Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline pictured Netty as a post office. Each clerk owns a row of mailboxes for good, and one house rule matters more than the rest: a clerk never stops to make a phone call. In Netty's words, the clerk is an event loop, one thread that serves many connections in turn, and each box is a channel, Netty's object for one open connection. If the code for one channel waits 100 ms for a courier, every channel in that row gets 100 ms of silence. The protocol, the agreed shape of the messages, is lines of text. A client can be nc, a small terminal tool that opens a TCP connection and sends what you type, and tests can write requests as plain strings. A binary protocol would carry a length field instead, as Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks did with its page count on the envelope, and nothing else in the design would change. Two details are there on purpose. The server reads at most 64 bytes per line. Without a limit, a client that sends bytes and never a newline would make the server keep them all, waiting for a line that never ends. A longer line fails with TooLongFrameException. Every request carries an id, and every reply repeats it. A reply leaves when its price arrives, so a quick answer overtakes a slow one, and replies come back out of order. The client matches them by id, the way you match a ticket stub to a coat. Here's the pipeline, the line of stations that every message on a channel passes through. Each station is a handler, a small object that reacts to the channel's events. Each connection gets new instances, because the last handler keeps state for its own connection: Java ChannelHandler[] handlers(QuoteSource source) { return new ChannelHandler[] { new LineBasedFrameDecoder(64), // 1. bytes in, one line out; a longer line fails new StringDecoder(UTF_8), // 2. line bytes to String new StringEncoder(UTF_8), // 3. outbound: String to bytes new FlowControlHandler(), // 4. section 3 explains this one new QuoteHandler(source), // 5. new per connection: it keeps state }; } Kotlin fun handlers(source: QuoteSource): Array<ChannelHandler> = arrayOf( LineBasedFrameDecoder(64), // 1. bytes in, one line out; a longer line fails StringDecoder(UTF_8), // 2. line bytes to String StringEncoder(UTF_8), // 3. outbound: String to bytes FlowControlHandler(), // 4. section 3 explains this one QuoteHandler(source), // 5. new per connection: it keeps state ) Let's walk it in order. The frame decoder cuts the stream of bytes into lines (1), and the string decoder turns each line into a String (2). Replies travel the other way, through the encoder, which turns a String back into bytes (3). FlowControlHandler (4) looks out of place for now; section 3 shows what goes wrong without it. Finally, QuoteHandler (5) answers the request, and it is where the phone call hides. Feed the pipeline by hand Open ProtocolDemo.java (or ProtocolDemo.kt). It pushes bytes into a line pipeline with EmbeddedChannel, Netty's channel for tests, which has no socket at all. Then it completes the two prices by hand, Dublin first. Predict what comes out after each of the five steps, and whether the channel is still open at the end. Run it. Then run it again with -Pargs=6, a 6-byte line limit. Predict first: 7 LISBON is 8 bytes. h: A Netty server that never blocks its loop · Hand the future back instead of waiting on the loop
x:
The handler gets its prices from a QuoteSource. QuoteSource.quote(destination) returns a CompletableFuture<Quote>, the JDK's ticket for an answer that will come later. Coroutines meet Java pictured it as the neighbour's ticket: "come back with this, and the pie will be ready." The first draft of the handler, which is the starting code of this lesson's lab, takes the ticket and waits at the neighbour's door: Java // Naive: this will not work under load @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) { Request r = QuoteProtocol.parse(line); Quote q = source.quote(r.destination()).join(); // the loop waits here ctx.writeAndFlush(QuoteProtocol.ok(r.id(), q)); } Kotlin // Naive: this will not work under load override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, line: String) { val r = QuoteProtocol.parse(line) val q = source.quote(r.destination).join() // the loop waits here ctx.writeAndFlush(QuoteProtocol.ok(r.id, q)) } join() waits until the future has its answer, and it holds the thread while it waits. The draft answers correctly, and it passes a test with one client. This section's demo measures what it costs, with one event loop, ten clients, and a courier that needs 100 ms per price. One run on the busy machine used for this course printed: join 10 replies after 1,163 ms; quotes waiting at the same time: 1 async 10 replies after 146 ms; quotes waiting at the same time: 10 The first line is the draft. The tenth customer waited more than a second, and the courier never saw more than one question at a time. The clerk asked for a price, held the phone until the answer came, and only then opened the next letter. Ten customers, ten phone calls, one after another. The fix hands the ticket back to the loop and finishes later: Java CompletableFuture<Quote> quote = source.quote(r.destination()); // 1. returns at once inFlight.add(quote); quote.whenCompleteAsync((q, e) -> { // 2. later, on this channel's loop inFlight.remove(quote); ctx.writeAndFlush(e == null ? ok(r.id(), q) : error(r.id(), e)); }, ctx.executor()); Kotlin val quote = source.quote(r.destination) // 1. returns at once inFlight += quote quote.whenCompleteAsync({ q, e -> // 2. later, on this channel's loop inFlight -= quote ctx.writeAndFlush(if (e == null) ok(r.id, q) else error(r.id, e)) }, ctx.executor()) Let's read it in order. First we ask for the price, which returns at once (1). We keep the future in inFlight, the set of requests we've read and not yet answered. Then whenCompleteAsync tells the future what to do once the price arrives (2): drop the future from the set and write the reply. channelRead0 now returns in microseconds. The second line of the demo shows the result: all ten customers answered in 146 ms, with ten prices on the way at once. The second argument, ctx.executor(), is the one tricky part. It picks the thread that runs the callback, the piece of code handed over to run later. ctx.executor() is the channel's own event loop, so the callback goes into the clerk's in-tray, the queue of small jobs the loop runs between reads. That matters because the handler keeps state: the set of futures in flight. With plain whenComplete, the callback would run on whatever thread finished the future, a courier's thread, while the loop adds to the same HashSet in channelRead0. That's the lost update from Race conditions: why count++ lies, with a set instead of a counter. When every touch of the handler's state happens on the loop, you need no lock: the loop is the lock. ctx.writeAndFlush would be safe from any thread. The set is not. A handler that waits makes every channel on its loop wait. Hand the future back, and finish on the loop. The interface carries the other half of the rule. quote must return at once and complete the future later, from any thread. Lesson 2 of this track keeps that promise with scope.future { }, which starts a coroutine and returns its ticket at once. A runBlocking { } in its place would block the loop exactly like join(). How do we prove the loop is free? Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline used a lag probe: slip an empty task into the in-tray and time how long it waits. Its lab asserted under 300 ms. That holds on a quiet laptop. On a build machine running eight builds on four cores, a healthy loop can miss 300 ms, and a broken handler can pass when the fake courier answers fast. So this lab's test counts instead of timing. It holds 100 quotes open, checks that the source saw 100 calls, then checks that the loop ran 50 empty tasks. A loop stuck in join() shows 1 call, on any machine and at any load. The worked example builds that test step by step. The loop is free now. It reads as fast as clients send, and some clients send a great deal. Ten customers, one loop, two handlers Open BlockedLoopDemo.java (or the Kotlin twin). One event loop serves ten clients, and the courier answers each price after 100 ms. Predict the time until all ten replies, and the most prices waiting at the same time, for join and for async. Run it. Then change the group to new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(2, ...), two loops, and predict the join numbers again. h: A Netty server that never blocks its loop · Auto-read: the one tap that stops a client who won't listen
x:
A client may pipeline: send many requests without waiting for a single reply. Say one client sends 20,000 requests and doesn't read its replies for half a second. Two things grow in the server's memory. Each request that waits for its price is a future in the in-flight set. And each reply the client hasn't read yet waits in the channel's outbound buffer, the queue of bytes Netty keeps until the network can take them. Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks pictured it as the out-tray behind each box. writeAndFlush never blocks, so the out-tray simply fills. Nothing limits either one. Netty gives you one control, auto-read: whether the loop keeps reading a channel. While it's on, the loop reads the connection whenever bytes arrive. Turn it off, and the clerk stops taking letters from that box. The operating system's buffers for that connection fill up, and TCP makes the client wait before it sends more. It's the packer's slip from the Reactive track, "send me 10 more", carried by the network itself: the server asks for more only when it has room. That's backpressure, a slow receiver slowing down a fast sender. Here the post office picture breaks, in our favour: a clerk who stops taking letters leaves a queue at the door, but a server that stops reading leaves the waiting in the network's buffers and the client's own, not in its memory. The out-tray has two painted marks that say when there's room. They are Netty's water marks, 32 KiB low and 64 KiB high by default. When the bytes waiting pass the high mark, isWritable() turns false. When they drain below the low mark, it turns true again. Our policy is one rule, applied after every new request, after every reply, and whenever writability changes: Java private void updateReading(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) { boolean read = ctx.channel().isWritable() && inFlight.size() < MAX_IN_FLIGHT; ctx.channel().config().setAutoRead(read); } Kotlin private fun updateReading(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext) { val read = ctx.channel().isWritable && inFlight.size < MAX_IN_FLIGHT ctx.channel().config().isAutoRead = read } Read it aloud: read this customer only while their replies can leave and fewer than 16 of their questions are waiting. The cap of 16 bounds the futures one connection can hold. The writability check bounds the out-tray. There's a catch, and the demo shows it. Turning auto-read off stops the next socket read. It doesn't stop the lines the decoder already has. One read can bring 64 KB, a few thousand requests, and LineBasedFrameDecoder hands every one of them to the handler before the loop looks at auto-read again. FlowControlHandler, placed between the decoders and our handler, closes that gap. While auto-read is off, it keeps the decoded lines in a queue of its own, like opened letters left in a tray on the clerk's desk, and passes them on one at a time as reading resumes. The demo pipelines 20,000 requests and reads nothing for 500 ms. The first row moves with the machine's load: how much the server swallows depends on how busy it is, and its queue reached between 1.6 and 2.5 MB in the runs made for this lesson. The last peak is the 64 KiB high water mark (65,536 bytes) plus a few replies. Every client still got all 20,000 replies once it read them. The lab tests the cap directly: 40 pipelined requests against a source that holds every quote must produce exactly 16 calls. Writes never block, so your memory does the waiting. Read only while the client keeps up. We can take requests and pace them now. What's left is how a connection ends, and there are four ways. h: A Netty server that never blocks its loop · Closing on purpose: four ways a connection ends
x: A connection ends in one of four ways, and each has its own code path. The client sends QUIT. The server writes BYE and closes from the write's future, with ctx.writeAndFlush("BYE\n").addListener(ChannelFutureListener.CLOSE). A ChannelFuture is Netty's ticket for a write, and the listener runs once the bytes have left. Closing right after flush() can drop bytes still in the out-tray; Netty in practice lost 57,344 bytes that way. A line is too long. LineBasedFrameDecoder throws TooLongFrameException, and Netty passes it to the handler's exceptionCaught. The server answers ERR line too long and closes the same way. A client that sends 100 bytes where 64 are allowed is broken or hostile, and neither deserves a long conversation. The client hangs up. channelInactive runs on the loop, and the handler cancels every future still in its set, because nobody is left to read those answers. For a plain CompletableFuture, cancel interrupts nothing, as CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out showed: it only marks the ticket as void. It's the guests calling dinner off with nobody passing the news to the kitchen. Lesson 2 of this track turns that cancel into one that reaches all three courier calls. The server shuts down. Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown closed the kitchen in a fixed order, and a server closes the same way: Java @Override public void close() { stopAccepting(); // 1. close the listening socket connections.close().syncUninterruptibly(); // 2. close every open connection group.shutdownGracefully(0, 2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // 3. then stop the loop threads .syncUninterruptibly(); } Kotlin override fun close() { stopAccepting() // 1. close the listening socket connections.close().syncUninterruptibly() // 2. close every open connection group.shutdownGracefully(0, 2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // 3. then stop the loop threads .syncUninterruptibly() } First, stopAccepting() closes the listening socket, the one that takes new connections, so nobody new walks in while the rest shuts down (1). Then we close every open connection (2). connections is a ChannelGroup, a set of channels that drops each one when it closes, and the server adds every new channel to it. Closing the group closes each connection on its own loop, every handler sees channelInactive and cancels its work, and only then does shutdownGracefully stop the loop threads (3). You may wonder why step 2 is needed at all, since shutdownGracefully also closes the channels it still finds. In this track's test runs, that wasn't reliable: in about one run in three, a client still saw its connection open after the loops had stopped. Closing the connections ourselves makes the order plain. Lesson 3 of this track adds one more step between the first two lines: a short grace period in which prices already on their way can still be answered. Check yourself before the lab: a client has two requests pending when close() runs. What does it read from its socket, and what happens to the two futures? (It reads the end of the stream, because its channel was closed. Both futures are cancelled in channelInactive.) The counter is finished, and it still has nothing real to sell: the lab's fake source makes up its prices. Next sitting, the couriers get their phone calls. WriteBufferWaterMark source, Netty 4.2 docs

QuoteProtocol.ok(r.id(), q) : QuoteProtocol.error(r.id(), e)); } updateReading(ctx); }, ctx.executor()); } @Override public void channelInactive(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) { for (CompletableFuture<Quote> f : List.copyOf(inFlight)) f.cancel(true); inFlight.clear(); ctx.fireChannelInactive(); } QuoteHandler.kt (core) override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, line: String) { val r = QuoteProtocol.parse(line) val quote = source.quote(r.destination) inFlight += quote updateReading(ctx) quote.whenCompleteAsync({ q: Quote?, e: Throwable? -> // platform types: say they can be null inFlight -= quote if (ctx.channel().isActive) { ctx.writeAndFlush(if (e == null) QuoteProtocol.ok(r.id, q) else QuoteProtocol.error(r.id, e)) } updateReading(ctx) }, ctx.executor()) } override fun channelInactive(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext) { inFlight.toList().forEach { it.cancel(true) } inFlight.clear() ctx.fireChannelInactive() } Both versions are the same handler at runtime. Hold every price open, so a blocked loop stays blocked for the whole test, and count something the loop can do only while it is free: calls that reach the source. The fake keeps each future until the test releases it. final class FakeSource implements QuoteSource { private final List<CompletableFuture<Quote>> pending = new ArrayList<>(); // guarded by this private int calls; @Override public synchronized CompletableFuture<Quote> quote(String destination) { calls++; // 1. count every call that reaches the source CompletableFuture<Quote> f = new CompletableFuture<>(); pending.add(f); // 2. hold it: a blocked loop stays blocked notifyAll(); return f; } } class FakeSource : QuoteSource { private val pending = mutableListOf<CompletableFuture<Quote>>() // guarded by this private var calls = 0 @Synchronized override fun quote(destination: String): CompletableFuture<Quote> { calls++ // 1. count every call that reaches the source val f = CompletableFuture<Quote>() pending += f // 2. hold it: a blocked loop stays blocked (this as Object).notifyAll() return f } } Add a probe: hand the loop empty tasks and count how many ran. The 5-second wait only bounds how long a failure takes to report. The assertion is on the count, so a slow machine can't fail a healthy loop. static int probe(EventLoopGroup group, int tasks) throws InterruptedException { CountDownLatch ran = new CountDownLatch(tasks); for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) group.next().execute(ran::countDown); // 3. empty tasks ran.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // bounds the failure, it is not the assertion return tasks - (int) ran.getCount(); // 4. the assertion is on this count } fun probe(group: EventLoopGroup, tasks: Int): Int { val ran = CountDownLatch(tasks) repeat(tasks) { group.next().execute(ran::countDown) } // 3. empty tasks ran.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // bounds the failure, it is not the assertion return tasks - ran.count.toInt() // 4. the assertion is on this count } Spread 100 requests over 10 connections. A broken handler is stuck in join(); completing its future wakes the loop, so the server can close and the next test starts clean. h: A Netty server that never blocks its loop · Quiz
x: The server runs 8 event loops with 800 connections, and the first-draft handler calls source.quote(d).join(). One courier stalls for 2 seconds on a single request. Who waits? Only the client whose price stalled All 800 clients: Netty runs one handler at a time for the whole server About 100 clients: every connection registered on the same loop as that request Nobody: join() parks the loop thread and Netty moves its channels to another loop Netty spreads channels over the 8 loops in turn, and each stays where it was registered: about 100 per loop. The loop running join() can't read, decode or write for any of its channels for 2 seconds, while the other 7 loops carry on. Netty never moves a channel to another loop. A handler writes every reply with ctx.writeAndFlush and never looks at writability. A client pipelines thousands of requests and reads its socket slowly. Where do the unread replies pile up? In the client's receive buffer, which grows to fit Nowhere: writeAndFlush blocks the loop until the client reads In the kernel's send buffer, without limit In the channel's outbound buffer, in the server's own memory writeAndFlush never blocks. The kernel's buffers are small and fill first; after that, Netty keeps the bytes in the channel's outbound buffer, in your own memory. In one run of this lesson's demo, that reached 2,084,596 bytes. Only reading less from that client stops it growing. QuoteHandler finishes each price with whenCompleteAsync(callback, ctx.executor()). What goes wrong with plain whenComplete(callback)? The callback runs on the thread that completed the future, so it races the event loop on the in-flight HashSet writeAndFlush throws, because it may only be called on the event loop Nothing: the two behave the same The callback never runs, because the loop doesn't know about it whenComplete runs the callback on whichever thread completes the future, here a courier's thread, while the loop adds to the same set in channelRead0. That's a read-modify-write race on a plain HashSet. writeAndFlush itself is safe from any thread, which is why the bug is easy to miss. In Reactive Streams, a subscriber paces the publisher with request(n), the packer's slip. What plays that part between this server and one client? The 64-byte line limit Auto-read, switched on only while the channel is writable and fewer than 16 requests wait TCP's receive window on its own, with no code in the server The 64 KiB high water mark on its own Auto-read is the server's demand signal: it reads more only when it has room, and TCP carries the pause back to the client. TCP alone does nothing while the server keeps reading, because the bytes just move from the kernel into the server's memory. The water mark only reports a full out-tray; your handler has to act on it. When a client hangs up, channelInactive calls cancel(true) on a pending future from a source that runs blocking calls with supplyAsync on a thread pool. What happens to the courier call? It is interrupted and stops at once The pool thread is stopped It runs to the end, and its result is dropped: cancel only completes the future The cancel fails, because the work has already started CompletableFuture.cancel completes the future with a CancellationException and doesn't interrupt the thread doing the work, whatever you pass. The call finishes, and its result goes nowhere. To stop the work itself, the source has to react to the cancel, which is what lesson 2's coroutines do.

h: A Netty server that never blocks its loop · Explain it back
x: A colleague reviews your handler: "Why all this ceremony? The couriers answer in 5 ms, so join() is fine, and Netty buffers writes for us anyway." Explain what join() costs on an event loop, why the callback runs on ctx.executor(), and why the server needs the auto-read rule.

h: A Netty server that never blocks its loop · Key terms
x: Quote service A program that gives a price for a job before anyone books it; here, the price of sending a parcel. Event loop One thread that reads, decodes and writes for every channel registered with it, plus a queue of tasks. Pipelining A client sends many requests without waiting for the replies. In-flight request A request the server has read but not yet answered. Auto-read Whether the loop keeps reading a channel's socket. Off means the kernel's buffers fill and TCP makes the client wait. FlowControlHandler A Netty handler that holds already-decoded messages while auto-read is off. Request id A number the client puts on a request and the server repeats on the reply, so replies can arrive in any order. Probe task An empty task handed to an event loop to check that it still runs work. What does join() in a Netty handler cost? Every channel on that event loop waits until the future completes, not just the one that asked. Why finish with whenCompleteAsync(callback, ctx.executor())? The callback runs on the channel's own event loop, so the handler's state is only ever touched by one thread. When should the quote server read a connection? Only while the channel is writable and fewer than MAX_IN_FLIGHT (16) of its requests are waiting for a price. What does FlowControlHandler add when auto-read is off? It holds messages the decoder already produced and releases them as reading resumes. Auto-read alone only stops the next socket read. Why count instead of time in a test that proves the loop is free? A healthy loop can miss a time limit on a busy machine. A blocked loop's counts (1 call, 0 probe tasks) don't depend on speed. Why does the quote protocol carry a request id? A reply leaves when its price arrives, so replies can overtake each other. The client matches them by id. In what order does the server shut down? Stop accepting, close every open connection (a ChannelGroup; handlers cancel their work in flight), then shutdownGracefully to stop the loop threads.

h: A Netty server that never blocks its loop · Go deeper
x: Three things a production shell adds to this one. An idle timeout. A client that connects and never sends a line holds a channel forever. IdleStateHandler fires an IdleStateEvent through userEventTriggered after a connection has been quiet for the time you set; close the channel there. TLS, the encryption behind https. An SslHandler goes first in the pipeline, before the frame decoder, and nothing after it changes. That is the payoff of keeping every concern in its own handler. Loop metrics. Every loop of a MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup is a SingleThreadEventExecutor, and pendingTasks() is the length of its task queue, the clerk's in-tray. In this server, every reply is a task, so a queue that keeps growing is a loop that can't keep up. Report it for each loop. Two limits of this lesson's design are worth knowing. The cap of 16 protects the server from one greedy client and does nothing against ten thousand polite ones: lesson 3 of this track adds a limit for the whole service that turns work away with a clear error. And whenCompleteAsync costs a hand-off per reply, even when the price is already there. That is cheap next to a trip across the network, and it buys a handler whose state needs no lock. Finally, the counting probe has a stronger cousin for tests: BlockHound, a separate Java agent library, throws as soon as code on a Netty event-loop thread calls a known blocking method such as CompletableFuture.join or Thread.sleep. Netty ships the integration for it (Hidden$NettyBlockHoundIntegration in netty-common).

h: Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline · One request, three couriers, one deadline
x: One request, three providers, one deadline (Kotlin coroutines): start every call together, give each the deadline, let each fail alone, rethrow only your own cancel, and serve the last good quote marked stale Lesson 1 left the server with a QuoteSource that must return a future at once. This lesson writes that source, in Kotlin. For each request it asks Northline, Eastgate and Fjord for a price, keeps the lowest, and answers by a deadline, whatever the couriers do. The tool is the coroutine. A coroutine is a piece of work that can pause without holding its thread, like a dish the cook leaves to simmer while she starts the next one (Suspend functions from zero). A suspend function is a function that can pause that way. In the lab, each courier is a Provider: a name, and a suspend function quote(destination) that returns that courier's price, or throws. The shape comes from Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope, where the cook texted three shops first and read the replies after. async starts a coroutine that will bring back a result, and hands you a Deferred, the coroutine's own ticket for that result. awaitAll waits until every ticket has its answer. Say the couriers need 120, 300 and 200 ms. Asked one after another, they take 620 ms. Asked together, they take 300 ms, the time of the slowest: Java // Java equivalent with Reactor: Mono.zip subscribes to all three sources at once Mono<List<Quote>> allPrices(String destination) { return Mono.zip(northline.quote(destination), eastgate.quote(destination), fjord.quote(destination)) .map(t -> List.of(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3())); } Kotlin suspend fun allPrices(destination: String): List<Quote> = coroutineScope { providers.map { p -> async { p.quote(destination) } } // 1. text all three .awaitAll() // 2. then read the replies: the slowest decides } coroutineScope gives the three calls a parent that waits for all of them, so none of them can outlive the function. The Java twin uses Reactor from the Reactive track: Mono.zip subscribes to all three sources at once and waits for a value from each, like packing a gift box that closes only when every slot is full. The deadline is the next decision. A price that arrives after two seconds is no use to a customer standing at the counter. So each call gets the kitchen timer: Java // Java equivalent with Reactor: a timeout on each source, turned into "no answer" Mono<Optional<Quote>> inTime(Mono<Quote> call) { return call.timeout(DEADLINE) .map(Optional::of) .onErrorResume(TimeoutException.class, e -> Mono.just(Optional.empty())); } Kotlin providers.map { p -> async { withTimeoutOrNull(deadline) { p.quote(destination) } } // null if p misses the deadline } withTimeoutOrNull is a cancel with a timer, as Cancellation and timeouts called it. At the deadline it cancels the late call, which stops at its next suspension point, the next place where it pauses, and returns null for it. A deadline is the moment by which the request must answer, whatever its couriers are doing. You may wonder why each call gets its own timer, and not one withTimeout around the whole fan-out. Both bound the request. Around the whole fan-out, the timer cancels everything and throws away the answers that did arrive. In the figure, Northline answered at 120 ms and Fjord at 200 ms, and with one timer for everything we would still have nothing to say. With a timer per call, only the late courier drops out. Because all the calls start together, a deadline per call is also a deadline for the request. That's a good day. On a bad day, a courier doesn't just run late. It fails. Three ways to ask three couriers Open FanOutDemo.kt. It runs on virtual time with runTest, so the clock is exact. The Java twin, FanOutDemoJava.java, does the same with Reactor in real time. Predict the three times and the three answer lists: one after another, all at once, and all at once with a 250 ms deadline. Run it. Then set deadline to 100 and predict the last line again. h: Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline · Let one courier fail alone, and tell your cancel from theirs
x: The first draft of BestQuote, the starting code of this lesson's lab, uses coroutineScope and withTimeout. Both are wrong for a price, for reasons earlier lessons gave. coroutineScope treats its children as one unit of work. Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree put it as a kitchen rule: a course goes out only when all of its dishes are ready. So when Northline throws IOException at 50 ms, the scope cancels Eastgate and Fjord and rethrows, as Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers showed with the burnt gravy. That's the right rule when a request needs every answer. A price needs any one of them. supervisorScope is the bake sale from that lesson, where one burnt tray doesn't spoil the others. Each child fails alone. A failed async keeps its exception in its Deferred, and await hands it to you, where you turn it into "no answer". withTimeout has a subtler problem. It signals a late call with TimeoutCancellationException, and that is a kind of CancellationException, the exception that carries a cancel. Cancellation and timeouts gave the rule: never swallow a CancellationException, or you throw away the message that dinner is off. So you rethrow it, and now one courier's timeout looks like a cancel of the whole request, and ends it. withTimeoutOrNull turns our own deadline into a plain null. But a courier can still throw a cancellation from deep inside its own code. Fjord's own client has a short fuse: it gives up after 100 ms, and it says so with a TimeoutCancellationException of its own. So we have to be precise, and rethrow only when our coroutine was cancelled. ensureActive() asks exactly that question: Java // Java equivalent with Reactor: each source handles its own error, so the zip never sees one Mono<Optional<Quote>> alone(Mono<Quote> call) { return call.map(Optional::of) .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(Optional.empty())) // a failure stays with its courier .defaultIfEmpty(Optional.empty()); // and so does an empty answer } Kotlin private suspend fun Deferred<Quote?>.awaitOrNull(): Quote? = try { await() } catch (e: CancellationException) { currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() // 1. were WE cancelled? then this rethrows null // 2. no: only the courier's call ended that way } catch (e: Exception) { null // 3. the courier failed: no answer from it } Let's read the catch in order. If the request itself was cancelled, because the client hung up, ensureActive() throws, and the cancel carries on up (1). If it returns, the cancellation belonged to the courier's call, and that courier simply has no answer (2). Any other exception is a courier that failed, and it counts as no answer too (3). This section's demo runs the same three calls in three scopes. Northline fails at 50 ms, Fjord's client gives up at 100 ms, and Eastgate answers at 300 ms. On virtual time, a fake clock that skips the waiting, it printed: Scope Outcome coroutineScope, awaitAll fails at 50 ms: IOException: northline 503 supervisorScope, rethrow every cancel fails at 100 ms: TimeoutCancellationException supervisorScope, rethrow only our cancel answers eastgate 12.41 at 300 ms The first scope lost two good couriers to one bad one. The second lost Eastgate's price to Fjord's short fuse. Only the third answered. A caught cancellation may belong to someone else. Ask whose it is before you rethrow it. Reactor has no such trap, because there a cancel is not an error signal: you isolate each source with onErrorResume before Mono.zip. The compare block puts the two whole fan-outs side by side. One courier can now fail alone, and a late one drops out. But what if all three do? One failure, one timeout, three scopes Open FailAloneDemo.kt. Northline fails at 50 ms, Fjord's own client gives up at 100 ms, and Eastgate answers at 300 ms. Predict the outcome and the virtual time of each of the three attempts. Run it. Then, in callAll(), move async { fjord() } to the end of the list and predict the second line again. = try { await() } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Exception) { null } private suspend fun Deferred<String>.careful(): String? = try { await() } catch (e: CancellationException) { currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive(); null } catch (e: Exception) { null } private suspend fun TestScope.attempt(what: String, block: suspend () -> List<String?>) { val t0 = currentTime val outcome = try { "answers ${block()}" } catch (e: Exception) { "failed: ${e::class.simpleName}: ${e.message?.substringBefore(" of ")}" } println("%-40s at %3d ms %s".format(what, currentTime - t0, outcome)) } /** The same three calls in three scopes: who survives a failure, and who survives a timeout? h: Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline · When nobody answers, serve the last good price and say it is stale
x: Sometimes no courier answers by the deadline. The network between us and them is down, or every courier is swamped on the busiest morning of the year. The service then has three choices. It can wait longer, fail the request, or serve the last price it saw. Waiting longer breaks the deadline, which is the one promise the service makes. Failing is honest, and no help to a customer who only wants a rough idea of the cost. So BestQuote keeps a cache, a store of recent answers kept close at hand: here, the last live price for each destination. When nobody answers, it serves that price marked as stale, old and labelled so, as 7 STALE LISBON 12.41 eastgate. The customer sees the word and decides whether a slightly old price is good enough: Java // Java equivalent with Reactor: an empty Optional switches to the cache .flatMap(best -> best.map(Mono::just).orElseGet(() -> fromCache(destination))) .doOnNext(q -> { if (!q.stale()) cache.remember(q); }) // only live answers refresh the cache Kotlin val best = answers.minByOrNull { it.price } if (best != null) { cache.remember(best) // only live answers refresh the cache return best } return cache.lastGood(destination)?.asStale() // an old price, marked, beats no price ?: throw NoQuoteException(destination) // the handler writes "7 ERR no quote for LISBON" Two rules keep the cache honest. Only live answers go into it. If a stale answer could refresh the cache, one old price could be served forever, each serving making it look new. And with nothing cached, the request fails with NoQuoteException, which lesson 1's handler turns into 7 ERR no quote for LISBON. A shrug, but at least a quick one. A production cache would also have an age limit, so that a price from a minute ago is served and one from last week is not. Check yourself: after an outage, the couriers recover. On the next request Eastgate answers 12.39 and Fjord 12.42. What does the customer get, and what does the cache hold for Lisbon afterwards? (OK LISBON 12.39 eastgate, and the cache now holds that live price in place of the old one.) The fan-out is complete. It still has to meet lesson 1's Java handler, and the handler holds the one thing we haven't used yet: a cancel.

h: Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline · Tie each request to its connection with scope.future
x: Lesson 1's handler calls quote on the event loop, and it cancels the future when the client hangs up. QuoteService connects that future to a coroutine: Java // Java equivalent with Reactor: toFuture() subscribes, and cancelling the future cancels the subscription final class ReactorQuoteSource implements QuoteSource { @Override public CompletableFuture<Quote> quote(String destination) { return best(destination).toFuture(); // returns at once; cancel() reaches the zip } } Kotlin class QuoteService(context: CoroutineContext, private val best: BestQuote) : QuoteSource, AutoCloseable { private val scope = CoroutineScope(context + SupervisorJob()) // 1. owned; failures stay per request override fun quote(destination: String): CompletableFuture<Quote> = scope.future { best.quote(destination) } // 2. returns at once; cancel() reaches it override fun close() = scope.cancel() // 3. closing the service cancels the rest } The service owns a scope, the object that starts coroutines and keeps track of them (1). scope.future { } starts a coroutine in that scope and returns a CompletableFuture at once (2), so the event loop never waits. Coroutines meet Java pictured this bridge as the neighbour's ticket, and here the ticket is tied to the coroutine in both directions. When the coroutine finishes, the future completes. When someone cancels the future, the coroutine is cancelled. Closing the service cancels whatever is left (3). The second direction is what ties a request to its connection. The client hangs up, channelInactive cancels the future, and the future coroutine is cancelled. The cancel then travels down the job tree, the parent and child links between running coroutines, to the supervisorScope and its three courier calls. The guests have called dinner off, and this time the news reaches every pot on the stove. The picture breaks at the stove, though. A pot comes off the heat the moment the cook lifts it, while a coroutine stops only at its next suspension point, so a courier client stuck in a blocking call keeps going until that call returns (Cancellation and timeouts). Why not give each connection its own scope and cancel it in channelInactive? That works too, and it's the shape to pick when the handler itself is written in Kotlin. Here, the Java handler from lesson 1 already keeps every pending future and cancels them on close, so a scope per connection would track the same requests twice. With future { }, the Java side holds the ticket, the Kotlin side holds the tree, and neither needs to know how the other works. Two choices in the scope matter. The scope uses a SupervisorJob, a parent that lets each child fail alone. With a plain Job, one request that fails with NoQuoteException would cancel its parent, and with it every other request in flight. Every later future would then come back cancelled at once. And the scope takes its dispatcher, the part of a coroutine's context that decides which threads run it, as a parameter. Production passes Dispatchers.Default. The tests pass a StandardTestDispatcher, the rehearsal dinner on a fake clock from Shared state and testing coroutines, so every delay and every deadline runs on virtual time, and a test of a 300 ms deadline takes a few milliseconds. This section's demo starts one request behind scope.future { }, with three courier calls of 300, 400 and 500 ms, and cancels the future after 120 ms, as channelInactive would. All three calls print cancelled within a few milliseconds of the hang-up, and the scope is left with 0 coroutines. The Java twin builds the same request from three supplyAsync calls and cancels it the same way. It prints calls cancelled: 0 of 3, and the three couriers answer later with nobody listening. Cancelling a plain CompletableFuture voided the ticket and stopped nothing. A cancel that can't reach the work only hides it. Tie the ticket to the coroutine with future { }. The service now answers within its deadline and cleans up after a customer who leaves. It still trusts the couriers with as many calls as it likes, and a crowd will test that. Hang up on a request Open HangUpDemo.kt. A request coroutine started with scope.future { } waits for three courier calls of 300, 400 and 500 ms. After 120 ms, the demo cancels the future, as channelInactive would. Predict which calls print answered and which print cancelled, and how many coroutines are left in the scope. Run it, then run the Java twin, which builds the request from three supplyAsync calls. The client hangs up after 120 ms. */ fun main() { val scope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Default + SupervisorJob()) // the service's scope val request = scope.future { // what QuoteService.quote returns supervisorScope { listOf("northline" to 300L, "eastgate" to 400L, "fjord" to 500L) .map { (name, latency) -> async { call(name, latency) } }.awaitAll() } } Thread.sleep(120) println("client hangs up at ${ms()} ms: the handler calls request.cancel(true)") request.cancel(true) Thread.sleep(600) println("at ${ms()} ms: coroutines still running in the scope: ${scope.coroutineContext.job.children.count()}") scope.cancel() } ./gradlew :quotes:demo -Pmain=workbench.quotes.l02.HangUpDemoKt labs/quotes/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/quotes/l02/HangUpDemo.kt HangUpDemoJava.java // Java equivalent with CompletableFuture: cancel() completes the future, but the calls behind it run on package workbench.quotes.l02; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** A request built from three supplyAsync calls. The client hangs up after 120 ms. */ public class HangUpDemoJava { static final long t0 = System.nanoTime(); static long ms() { return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } static String call(String name, long latency) { try { Thread.sleep(latency); System.out.println(" " + name + " answered at " + ms() + " ms, and nobody is listening"); return name; } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println(" " + name + " interrupted at " + ms() + " ms"); return null; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { List<CompletableFuture<String>> calls = List.of( CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> call("northline", 300), pool), CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> call("eastgate", 400), pool), CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> call("fjord", 500), pool)); CompletableFuture<List<String>> request = CompletableFuture.allOf(calls.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)) .thenApply(v -> calls.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList()); Thread.sleep(120); System.out.println("client hangs up at " + ms() + " ms: the handler calls request.cancel(true)"); request.cancel(true); System.out.println("request cancelled: " + request.isCancelled() + ", calls cancelled: " + calls.stream().filter(CompletableFuture::isCancelled).count() + " of 3"); } // close() waits for the three calls, which finish anyway System.out.println("at " + ms() + " ms: all three calls have finished"); } } ./gradlew :quotes:demo -Pmain=workbench.quotes.l02.HangUpDemoJava labs/quotes/src/demo/java/workbench/quotes/l02/HangUpDemoJava.java All three calls print cancelled within a few milliseconds of the hang-up, and the scope has 0 coroutines left: the cancel went from the future to the coroutine and down to its children. The Java twin reports calls cancelled: 0 of 3, and the three couriers answer about 300, 400 and 500 ms after the start, with nobody listening. h: Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline · Java and Kotlin
x: The fan-out with Reactor's Mono.zip and with coroutines BestQuoteReactor.java // Reactor: errors, timeouts and empties become values at each source, then Mono.zip Mono<Quote> best(String destination) { return Mono.zip(inTime(northline.quote(destination)), inTime(eastgate.quote(destination)), inTime(fjord.quote(destination))) .map(t -> Stream.of(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3()) .flatMap(Optional::stream) .min(Comparator.comparing(Quote::price))) .flatMap(best -> best.map(Mono::just).orElseGet(() -> fromCache(destination))) .doOnNext(q -> { if (!q.stale()) cache.remember(q); }); } Mono<Optional<Quote>> inTime(Mono<Quote> call) { return call.timeout(DEADLINE) .map(Optional::of) .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(Optional.empty())) // a failure or a timeout: no answer .defaultIfEmpty(Optional.empty()); // an empty source would empty the zip } Mono<Quote> fromCache(String destination) { Quote last = cache.lastGood(destination); return last != null ? Mono.just(last.asStale()) : Mono.error(new NoQuoteException(destination)); } BestQuote.kt class BestQuote( private val providers: List<Provider>, private val deadline: Duration, private val cache: QuoteCache = QuoteCache(), ) { suspend fun quote(destination: String): Quote { val answers = supervisorScope { // 1. a failed call doesn't cancel the others providers .map { p -> async { withTimeoutOrNull(deadline) { p.quote(destination) } } } // 2. late is null, not an exception .map { it.awaitOrNull() } // 3. failed is null too }.filterNotNull() val best = answers.minByOrNull { it.price } if (best != null) { cache.remember(best) return best } return cache.lastGood(destination)?.asStale() ?: throw NoQuoteException(destination) // 4. stale beats nothing } private suspend fun Deferred<Quote?>.awaitOrNull(): Quote? = try { await() } catch (e: CancellationException) { currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() // we were cancelled ourselves: this rethrows null // only the provider's call ended that way: no answer } catch (e: Exception) { null // the provider failed: no answer from it } } Both start the three calls together, give each its own deadline, turn a failure into "no answer", keep the lowest price and fall back to the cache. In Reactor, every outcome becomes a value at the source. A timeout is an error signal you resume from, and an empty source is a third outcome you must name with defaultIfEmpty, or Mono.zip completes empty (Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest). Nothing runs until something subscribes, and cancelling the subscription cancels the three calls. In Kotlin, the same policy is ordinary control flow: a scope, try and catch, minByOrNull. The scope guarantees that when quote returns, every call is either done or cancelled. The price of that directness is the CancellationException rule, which only coroutines have: a timeout is a cancel, so you must tell your own cancel from a courier's.

h: Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline · Quiz
x: Inside supervisorScope, an async child throws IOException at 50 ms, while its two siblings run until 300 ms. Nobody has called await yet. What happens at 50 ms? The scope is cancelled and rethrows the IOException Nothing visible: the exception waits in that child's Deferred, and the siblings keep running The uncaught exception handler prints it, and the siblings are cancelled The two siblings are cancelled, but the scope itself keeps running In a supervisor, a failed child doesn't cancel its siblings or the scope. A failed async keeps its exception for await, which rethrows it when you get there. A handler is never used for async. In a plain coroutineScope, the first option would be right. Each courier call is async { withTimeout(300) { c.quote(d) } } inside supervisorScope, and the code that awaits it does catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }. One courier takes a second. What does the request get? The best of the other two prices, with null for the slow courier It waits a full second for the slow courier An IOException from the slow courier It ends with TimeoutCancellationException, as if the whole request had been cancelled withTimeout signals a late call with TimeoutCancellationException, a subclass of CancellationException. The catch rethrows it, so one courier's timeout ends the request. Use withTimeoutOrNull for your own deadline, and call currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() before deciding a cancel was yours. In the Reactor version, one courier's Mono completes empty: no value and no error. What does Mono.zip of the three do if that source has no defaultIfEmpty? It emits a tuple with an empty slot It fails with NoSuchElementException It completes empty at once and cancels the other two calls It waits for the other two and emits their pair Mono.zip needs one value from every source. When one completes empty there is nothing to combine, so the zip completes empty, with no error, and cancels the rest. The request would get no price and no error. Mapping each source to Optional with defaultIfEmpty(Optional.empty()) names the empty case. QuoteService.quote returned scope.future { best.quote(destination) } to the handler, and the client hangs up, so channelInactive calls cancel(true) on it. What happens to the three courier calls? They are cancelled at their next suspension point: cancelling the future cancels the coroutine, and the cancel goes down the job tree Nothing: CompletableFuture.cancel never reaches the work behind a future Their threads are interrupted They finish, and their results go into the cache The future builder links both ways: the coroutine completes the future, and cancelling the future cancels the coroutine. From there, cancellation travels down to the supervisorScope and its async children. A future made with supplyAsync is the case where the second option holds. Someone builds QuoteService's scope from context + Job() instead of SupervisorJob(). One request fails with NoQuoteException while 40 others are in flight. What happens? Only that request's future fails The other 40 are cancelled, the scope is cancelled, and every later request's future comes back cancelled at once The other 40 finish, but new requests fail Only requests for the same destination are cancelled A failed child cancels a plain Job parent, and the cancelled parent cancels all its other children. A cancelled scope can't run new coroutines either: each new future completes with JobCancellationException at once. With SupervisorJob, each request's failure stays in its own future.
