h: Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline · Key terms
x: Coroutine A piece of work that can pause without holding its thread, and carry on later where it stopped. Fan-out Starting several independent calls at once and combining what comes back. Deadline The time by which a request must answer, whatever the calls behind it do. Supervisor scope A scope whose children fail alone; cancelling the scope still cancels them all. Stale price The last live price for a destination, served and labelled as old when no courier answers in time. future builder scope.future { }: starts a coroutine and returns a CompletableFuture linked to it both ways. Job tree The parent and child links between running coroutines; cancellation travels down it. Best-of fan-out: coroutineScope or supervisorScope? supervisorScope. Any one answer will do, so a failed call must not cancel the others. Why withTimeoutOrNull inside each async, not one withTimeout around the whole fan-out? Per call, only the late courier drops out. Around everything, the timeout cancels all calls and throws away answers that already arrived. Why is catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } wrong around a courier's await in this fan-out? A courier's own client timeout throws a CancellationException too, so rethrowing it ends the whole request. What does currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() tell you inside a catch? It throws only if your own coroutine was cancelled. If it returns, the cancellation came from the call you awaited. What does cancel(true) on a future from scope.future { } do? It cancels the coroutine, and through the job tree, every child the coroutine started. Why does QuoteService build its scope with SupervisorJob()? With a plain Job, one failed request cancels the scope and every other request, and later futures come back cancelled at once. May a stale price refresh the cache? No. Only live answers go in; otherwise one old price could be served forever.

h: Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline · Go deeper
x: Four refinements a production fan-out often adds. Pass the deadline on. The service knows that a request has, say, 180 ms left; the courier doesn't. Many systems that call each other over a network send the time left along with each call, so that the far side can give up too, instead of finishing work nobody will read. With coroutines you compute it from a start time and pass it down; withTimeoutOrNull then wraps the time that is left, not a fixed number. Answer early when the answer can't get much better. If any price within 10 cents of the lowest seen in the last minute is good enough, the request can return as soon as one such price arrives, and cancel the rest. That is select over the onAwait clauses (Channels, select and pipelines), with the losers cancelled by hand. Put an age on the cache. Store the time with each price, and refuse to serve one older than a few minutes. Then a long outage ends in a clear error, not in a price from last week. Mind the await rule. The kotlinx.coroutines KDoc notes that await() on a Deferred that someone else cancelled throws CancellationException in your coroutine, even though your coroutine is fine. This lesson's ensureActive() check is the documented way to tell the two apart, and it is worth using anywhere you await work you didn't start. Lesson 3 of this track adds what the fan-out still lacks: a limit on how many calls each courier sees at once, retries for the calls that are safe to repeat, a second call for the slowest courier, and turning work away when the whole service is full.

h: Hold up under load · A bulkhead for each courier, sized by Little's law
x: Lesson 2's fan-out sends every request to every courier at once. With a thousand requests in flight, Northline sees a thousand calls at once, and its contract allows 10. Past that, it answers 429, the web's code for "too many requests", or it slows down for everyone. The fix is a bulkhead, named after the walls inside a ship's hull that keep one flooded section from sinking the whole ship. Here, it's a limit on the calls in flight to one courier, so that one courier's limit can't become everybody's outage. Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores pictured it as twenty tokens by the grill: a pan goes on only with a token in hand, and a cook without one waits. A semaphore is that box of tokens, and each token is a permit. In the lab, the guards for one courier live in GuardedProvider, a wrapper that applies them and then passes each call on to the real courier. Its bulkhead is a Semaphore from kotlinx.coroutines.sync: Java // Java equivalent on virtual threads: java.util.concurrent.Semaphore, acquire before the try private Quote once(String destination) throws IOException, InterruptedException { permits.acquire(); // blocks a cheap virtual thread try { return delegate.quote(destination); } finally { permits.release(); } } Kotlin class GuardedProvider(private val delegate: Provider, maxConcurrent: Int /* ... */) : Provider { private val permits = Semaphore(maxConcurrent) // kotlinx.coroutines.sync private suspend fun once(destination: String): Quote = permits.withPermit { delegate.quote(destination) } // suspends while all permits are out } withPermit takes a permit, runs the call and gives the permit back, however the call ends. While no permit is free, it suspends. It holds no thread, and the wait is cancellable, so lesson 2's deadline still applies: a call that waits too long for a permit is cancelled with the rest and counts as no answer. The Java twin does the same with the JDK's Semaphore on a virtual thread, where waiting is cheap too. How many permits? Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law gave the rule: the calls in flight equal the arrival rate times the time per call. If Northline allows 10 calls at once and answers in 50 ms, it serves at most 10 / 0.05 = 200 calls a second. More permits add no speed. They only move the queue to Northline's side, where you can't see it. So take the number from each courier's contract, and give each courier its own: Eastgate allows 40 and Fjord 5, as the figure shows. This section's demo sends 40 requests at once to a courier that answers in 50 ms. With no limit, the courier sees all 40 at once, and every answer arrives after 50 ms. With a limit of 4, it never sees more than 4, and the 40 answers take 10 rounds of 50 ms, 500 ms in all. The limit didn't make anything faster. It made the courier's load a number we chose. Two placement rules matter. The permit goes around each single call, not around a whole retry loop: a call that waits out its pause before a retry shouldn't hold a permit meanwhile, and a hedge, the second call of section 3, needs a permit of its own. And the bulkhead lives in the courier's wrapper, not around the fan-out. A limit on requests can't protect a courier, because each request makes three calls. A courier's limit is a number in its contract. Write it into a semaphore, around every single call. Now each courier sees no more than its share. Some of those calls still fail, and the question is whether to ask again. Forty requests, one courier, two limits Open BulkheadDemo.kt (virtual time) or BulkheadDemoJava.java (virtual threads, real time). Forty requests call a courier that answers in 50 ms. Predict the most calls in flight at once, and the time until all forty are answered, with no limit and with a limit of 4. Run it. Then change the limit to 8 and predict again from Little's law. BulkheadDemo.kt package workbench.quotes.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withPermit import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest /** 40 requests at once to a provider that answers in 50 ms. How many calls does it see at once? */ fun main() = runTest { // virtual time, one thread: plain counters are safe here for (limit in listOf(null, 4)) { val permits = limit?.let { Semaphore(it) } var active = 0 var peak = 0 suspend fun call() { active++ peak = maxOf(peak, active) delay(50) // the provider thinks active-- } val t0 = currentTime coroutineScope { repeat(40) { launch { if (permits == null) call() else permits.withPermit { call() } } } } println("%-9s calls in flight at most: %2d all 40 answered after %3d ms".format( if (limit == null) "no limit" else "limit $limit", peak, currentTime - t0)) } } ./gradlew :quotes:demo -Pmain=workbench.quotes.l03.BulkheadDemoKt labs/quotes/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/quotes/l03/BulkheadDemo.kt BulkheadDemoJava.java // Java equivalent with virtual threads: one per request, and a java.util.concurrent.Semaphore as the bulkhead package workbench.quotes.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 40 requests at once to a provider that answers in 50 ms. How many calls does it see at once? Real time. */ public class BulkheadDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { for (Integer limit : new Integer[] {null, 4}) { Semaphore permits = limit == null ? null : new Semaphore(limit); AtomicInteger active = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicInteger peak = new AtomicInteger(); Runnable call = () -> { peak.accumulateAndGet(active.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } active.decrementAndGet(); }; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService vthreads = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < 40; i++) { vthreads.submit(() -> { if (permits == null) { call.run(); return null; } permits.acquire(); // acquire before the try try { call.run(); } finally { permits.release(); } return null; }); } } // close() waits for all 40 System.out.printf("%-9s calls in flight at most: %2d all 40 answered after %3d ms%n", limit == null ? "no limit" : "limit " + limit, peak.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } } } ./gradlew :quotes:demo -Pmain=workbench.quotes.l03.BulkheadDemoJava labs/quotes/src/demo/java/workbench/quotes/l03/BulkheadDemoJava.java No limit: 40 calls at once, all answered after 50 ms. Limit 4: 4 at once, and 40 / 4 = 10 rounds of 50 ms, 500 ms. With a limit of 8, it is 5 rounds, 250 ms. The Java twin prints the same peaks in real time, with a few extra milliseconds of scheduling (81 and 511 ms in one run on a busy machine). The limit didn't make anything faster; it made the courier's load a number you chose. The finished service: admission at the door, one deadline for the fan-out, and a different set of guards for each courier. Semaphore (kotlinx.coroutines API) docs

h: Hold up under load · Retry only what is safe to repeat, and spread the retries out
x: A transient failure, one that goes away by itself, often succeeds on a second try: a 503, the web's code for "busy, try again later", or a connection that broke halfway. But a retry, asking again after a failure, is a second request, and the courier can't tell it from a new one. That matters more for some couriers than others. Northline and Eastgate only look up a price, so asking twice changes nothing. Fjord's price is a booking: each call holds a place on one of its vans for two minutes and counts against our daily allowance of calls. Ask Fjord twice, and it holds two places. A call is idempotent when repeating it does no harm, like reading a price. So the decision belongs to the courier, as Provider.idempotent, which is false unless the courier says otherwise: Java // Java equivalent with Reactor: the same decision before any retry operator is added Mono<Quote> quote(String destination) { Mono<Quote> once = Mono.defer(() -> delegate.quote(destination)); if (!delegate.idempotent()) return once; // a booking: exactly one call return once.retryWhen(Retry.backoff(2, Duration.ofMillis(50)).jitter(0.5) .filter(e -> e instanceof IOException)); } Kotlin override suspend fun quote(destination: String): Quote { val once: suspend () -> Quote = { permits.withPermit { delegate.quote(destination) } } // 1. a permit per call if (!delegate.idempotent) return once() // 2. a booking: exactly one call val attempt: suspend () -> Quote = if (hedgeAfter == null) once else ({ hedged(hedgeAfter, once) }) return retrying(backoff, random, attempt) // 3. the rest may be asked again } Let's read it in order. Every single call holds a permit (1). A courier that isn't idempotent gets exactly one call (2). The rest go through retrying, with a hedge around each attempt when one is set (3). retrying is the retry loop with growing waits from Shared state and testing coroutines, a backoff, with one change: jitter. When Northline has a bad moment, every request in flight fails in the same millisecond. Without jitter, they all come back one backoff later, punctual to the millisecond, and hit a courier that is still getting back on its feet. Jitter multiplies each wait by a random factor, here between 0.5 and 1.5, which spreads the retries out. Reactor's Retry.backoff does the same by default, as Errors, retries and timeouts showed: Java // Java equivalent on a virtual thread: the same factor, and a sleep that an interrupt ends double factor = 1 + jitter * (ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextDouble() * 2 - 1); Thread.sleep((long) (nominal(n).toMillis() * factor)); Kotlin val factor = 1 + backoff.jitter * (random.nextDouble() * 2 - 1) // 0.5 .. 1.5 for jitter 0.5 delay(backoff.nominal(n) * factor) // cancellable: the deadline still rules It's the broken oven from that lesson, with a crowd of packers. If every packer asks for the tray to be baked again at the same second, the oven that has just been repaired breaks again. This section's demo has 1,000 customers that failed together and retry after a nominal 100 ms. Without jitter, all 1,000 retries land in one millisecond. With a jitter of 0.5, they spread over 50 to 150 ms, and no millisecond gets more than 18. Three more rules keep retries honest. Retry only errors that a later attempt might fix: here an IOException, never an unknown destination. Keep every wait cancellable, so the deadline cuts off retries that can't finish in time; a retry after the deadline is work nobody will read. And count the calls. Two retries means up to three calls per request, and Little's law counts every one of them. A retry is a second request. Send it only when repeating is harmless, and never all at the same moment. Retries help when a call fails. Some calls don't fail at all. They're just slow. A thousand retries in one millisecond Open RetryJitterDemo.kt (or the Java twin, which computes the same waits without sleeping). A thousand customers failed together at 0 ms and retry after a nominal 100 ms. Predict how the retries spread over 25 ms buckets with no jitter and with a jitter of 0.5, and the most retries in any single millisecond. Run it. Then set the jitter to 0.1 and predict the busiest millisecond. RetryJitterDemo.kt package workbench.quotes.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest import kotlin.random.Random import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.milliseconds /** 1,000 clients fail together at 0 ms and retry after a nominal 100 ms. When do the retries land? */ fun main() = runTest { for (jitter in listOf(0.0, 0.5)) { val random = Random(7) val retryAt = IntArray(1_000) val t0 = currentTime coroutineScope { repeat(1_000) { client -> launch { val factor = 1 + jitter * (random.nextDouble() * 2 - 1) // 1 - jitter .. 1 + jitter delay(100.milliseconds * factor) retryAt[client] = (currentTime - t0).toInt() } } } val buckets = retryAt.groupBy { it / 25 * 25 }.toSortedMap() println("jitter $jitter: " + buckets.entries.joinToString(" ") { (from, hits) -> "$from-${from + 24} ms: ${hits.size}" }) println(" most retries in one millisecond: ${retryAt.groupBy { it }.values.maxOf { it.size }}") } } ./gradlew :quotes:demo -Pmain=workbench.quotes.l03.RetryJitterDemoKt labs/quotes/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/quotes/l03/RetryJitterDemo.kt RetryJitterDemoJava.java // Java equivalent: the same jitter formula with java.util.Random; the waits are computed, not slept package workbench.quotes.l03; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Random; import java.util.TreeMap; /** 1,000 clients fail together at 0 ms and retry after a nominal 100 ms. When do the retries land? */ public class RetryJitterDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { for (double jitter : new double[] {0.0, 0.5}) { Random random = new Random(7); Map<Integer, Integer> buckets = new TreeMap<>(); Map<Integer, Integer> perMs = new TreeMap<>(); for (int client = 0; client < 1_000; client++) { double factor = 1 + jitter * (random.nextDouble() * 2 - 1); // 1 - jitter .. 1 + jitter int at = (int) Math.ceil(100 * factor); // delay rounds up to whole ms buckets.merge(at / 25 * 25, 1, Integer::sum); perMs.merge(at, 1, Integer::sum); } StringBuilder line = new StringBuilder("jitter " + jitter + ":"); buckets.forEach((from, hits) -> line.append(String.format(" %d-%d ms: %d", from, from + 24, hits))); System.out.println(line); System.out.println(" most retries in one millisecond: " + perMs.values().stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).max().orElse(0)); } } } ./gradlew :quotes:demo -Pmain=workbench.quotes.l03.RetryJitterDemoJava labs/quotes/src/demo/java/workbench/quotes/l03/RetryJitterDemoJava.java No jitter: all 1,000 retries in the 100 to 124 ms bucket, and all of them in the same millisecond. Jitter 0.5: about 250 in each bucket from 50 to 149 ms (a few land at exactly 150 after rounding up), and the busiest millisecond has 18 (17 in the Java twin, whose random numbers differ). With 0.1, the retries squeeze into 90 to 110 ms, and the busiest millisecond gets about three times as many: less jitter, less spread. Retry and RetryBackoffSpec source (reactor-core 3.8.x) docs

h: Hold up under load · Hedge the slow tail of one courier
x: Hedge the slow tail: when Northbank's first call hasn't answered by 80 ms, send one identical call, take the first answer and cancel the other; p99 falls from 600 to 120 ms for 5% more calls, and only safe-to-repeat calls may be hedged Northline answers in 40 ms most of the time, but one call in twenty takes 600 ms. Nothing failed, so a retry doesn't help. Northline is simply lost in thought now and then. To talk about slow calls, we need one more word. A percentile says how slow the slow ones are: p50 is the time half the calls beat, and p99 is the time 99 calls in 100 beat. The slowest few calls are the tail, and tail latency is what the unluckiest customers see. Northline's p50 is 40 ms. Its p99 is 600 ms. A hedge cuts the tail. If the first call hasn't answered by the time 95 calls in 100 would have (its p95), send one more identical call and take whichever answers first. It's the cook texting a second branch of the same shop when the first hasn't replied by the time shops usually do: Java // Java equivalent with Reactor: the delayed hedge is cancelled before it starts if the first call wins Mono<Quote> hedged(Duration after, Mono<Quote> call) { return Mono.firstWithValue(call, Mono.delay(after).then(call)); } Kotlin suspend fun <T : Any> hedged(after: Duration, call: suspend () -> T): T = coroutineScope { val first = async { call() } // 1. the first call val early = withTimeoutOrNull(after) { first.await() } // 2. stops the waiting, not the call if (early != null) return@coroutineScope early val second = async { call() } // 3. the hedge val winner = select { first.onAwait { it }; second.onAwait { it } } coroutineContext.cancelChildren() // 4. stop the loser winner } Let's read it in order. We start the first call (1). withTimeoutOrNull(after) { first.await() } stops waiting at the hedge time (2), and it doesn't cancel first, which is a child of the coroutineScope, not of the timeout. If nothing came back, we start the hedge (3). select takes whichever deferred completes first, the way Channels, select and pipelines took whichever answer came first. Here the picture breaks in our favour: a dumpling in the bin is gone for good, while a customer who hears "busy" can ask again elsewhere. A request that can't make its deadline fails either way. Fail it at the door, in a millisecond. Shutdown uses the same pieces. Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown closed the kitchen at night in a fixed order, and the post office closes the same way. Lock the front door, stop taking new questions, let the customers at the counter finish, send the rest away, then turn off the lights: Java // Java equivalent for an executor-based service: the same order, from "Pools in production" void shutdown(Duration grace) throws InterruptedException { server.stopAccepting(); // 1. no new connections accepting = false; // 2. stop admitting pool.shutdown(); if (!pool.awaitTermination(grace.toMillis(), MILLISECONDS)) { // 3. drain, up to grace pool.shutdownNow(); // 4. interrupt the rest pool.awaitTermination(5, SECONDS); } server.close(); // 5. close connections, stop the loops } Kotlin suspend fun shutdown(grace: Duration): Int { accepting = false // 2. stop admitting val job = scope.coroutineContext.job withTimeoutOrNull(grace) { job.children.toList().joinAll() } // 3. drain, up to grace val left = job.children.count() job.cancelAndJoin() // 4. cancel the rest, wait for them return left } // QuoteApp: 1. server.stopAccepting(), then the above, then 5. server.close() That order has a name, a graceful shutdown: no new work, a grace period for the work in flight to finish, then cancel the rest and release everything. First, the server stops accepting connections (1). Then the service stops admitting requests, which now get ERR shutting down (2). The requests in flight get the grace period (3). What is left is cancelled, and cancelAndJoin() waits until those coroutines have finished their cleanup, so that no coroutine outlives the service (4). Finally, the server closes the connections and stops its loops (5). Lesson 1's ChannelGroup pays off here: each connection is closed on its own loop, behind the reply that the drain just let through. h: Hold up under load · Design review: would one virtual thread per connection be simpler?
x: Here is the finished design next to the question every reviewer asks about it: wouldn't one virtual thread per connection, with plain blocking calls to the couriers, be simpler? A virtual thread is a thread the JDK makes so cheap that a program can run thousands of them, and blocking means a call that holds its thread until the answer comes. Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem offered the post office two ways out of the crowd: fewer clerks, or cheaper clerks. This service took the first way: a few clerks, each watching a row of boxes, who never wait. Virtual threads take the second: a clerk for every customer, so cheap that most of them can stand and wait. Here are the two side by side: Concern This service One virtual thread per connection idle connections a few loop threads hold thousands one parked virtual thread each, a few KB waiting for couriers suspended coroutines blocked virtual threads deadline and cancel structured: the cancel reaches every courier call interrupts, which some blocking clients ignore limits per courier a Semaphore per courier a Semaphore per courier framing and backpressure Netty's decoders and auto-read your own read loop; TCP does the pacing code shape futures at the Java edge, coroutines inside plain blocking Java Virtual threads make the right-hand column cheap (The thread-per-request wall), and for many services they are the better choice. Switch when the couriers only ship blocking clients, such as JDBC, Java's standard way to talk to a database. This design would then need a pool of blocking threads behind the coroutines, and you'd pay for two models. Switch, too, when the team writes Java and connections number in the thousands. Stay on the event loop when the service already lives on Netty or a framework built on it, such as Vert.x or Quarkus; when connections number in the hundreds of thousands; when you need the control over the protocol that auto-read and decoders give you; or when the courier clients are non-blocking and a cancel must reach them. Either way, the limits stay. Bulkheads, deadlines, admission and an ordered shutdown appear in both columns. Moving to virtual threads removes the pool, and with it the one limit nobody wrote down, as Moving a blocking service to virtual threads found. The question that picks the model is where the waiting happens, as Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model put it. Here it happens in three courier calls per request, under a deadline, and both models can wait well. Pick the model by where the waiting happens. Keep the limits whichever you pick.

What differs is what waiting and stopping cost. In Kotlin, withPermit and delay suspend, so a thousand requests waiting for a permit or a backoff hold no threads, and a cancel (the deadline or a hang-up) reaches them at once through the job tree. On virtual threads, acquire and Thread.sleep block, which is cheap too, and a cancel is an interrupt: it reaches the sleep and the semaphore, but it reaches the courier call only if its client responds to interrupts. The Java version leaves the hedge out. On threads, a hedge takes an ExecutorCompletionService, or JDK 25's StructuredTaskScope, still a preview API there (Structured concurrency and scoped values), and the loser is stopped by an interrupt, which again works only if its client listens. Java code that can block on a virtual thread is shorter to read. Kotlin code gets the hedge and the deadline from the library.

x: In hedged, the first call is still running at 80 ms, so a second starts, and select returns the second call's answer at 110 ms. The author forgot cancelChildren(). When does hedged return? At 110 ms: select cancels the clause that lost When the slow first call finishes, because coroutineScope waits for every child At 110 ms, and the slow call keeps running in the background Never: the two calls deadlock on the permit select only picks the first clause to complete; stopping the losers is your job. The first call is still a child of the coroutineScope, and a scope returns only after all its children are done, so hedged returns when the slow call ends, which undoes the hedge. Nothing runs in the background, because the scope is structured. With Backoff(retries = 2, first = 50 ms, jitter = 0.5), or Reactor's Retry.backoff(2, Duration.ofMillis(50)), a call fails every time with IOException. How many calls does the courier see? 2 It depends on the jitter 3 4 Two retries after the first attempt: three calls, with waits of about 50 and 100 ms between them. Jitter moves when the retries happen, not how many there are. Count them when you size the bulkhead, because Little's law applies to every call. A courier's contract allows 10 calls at once, and it answers in 50 ms. How many calls per second can it serve, and how many permits should its bulkhead have? 200 per second, and 10 permits 500 per second, and 50 permits 10 per second, and 10 permits 200 per second, and 200 permits Little's law: in flight = rate x time, so 10 = rate x 0.05 s gives 200 calls a second. The bulkhead holds the contract's 10. More permits don't add capacity; they move the queue to the courier's side, where it slows everyone and you can't see it. After shutdown, the service must have no coroutines left. Which step guarantees it? scope.cancel(), which returns as soon as the cancel is sent job.cancelAndJoin(), which returns only after every child has finished withTimeoutOrNull(grace) around the drain Setting accepting = false before anything else cancel() only asks for cancellation and returns while children may still be running their finally blocks; cancelAndJoin() waits until they have stopped. The grace period lets well-behaved requests finish, and accepting = false stops new ones from arriving, but neither stops what is already running. The couriers only ship blocking Java clients, the service holds about 2,000 connections, and the team writes Java. A reviewer suggests one virtual thread per connection. What is the strongest argument for switching? Virtual threads make each request faster Virtual threads remove the need for limits per courier Netty can't serve 2,000 connections With blocking clients, this design needs a pool of blocking threads behind the coroutines anyway, while virtual threads run the same calls in plain code, and 2,000 connections are easy for them The model should follow where the waiting happens. Blocking clients put the waiting on threads, so the event loop buys little here and costs a second model. Virtual threads give scale, not speed, and they remove the pool, so the bulkheads must be written down. Netty handles far more than 2,000 connections.

h: Hold up under load · Key terms
x: Bulkhead A limit on the calls in flight to one dependency, so that its limit can't sink the rest of the service. Semaphore A box of permits: a call takes one before it starts and gives it back when it ends, and waits while the box is empty. Idempotent call A call you can repeat without changing the outcome, such as reading a price. Jitter A random change to each retry wait, so clients that failed together don't retry together. Hedged request A second, identical request sent when the first is slower than usual; the first answer wins and the other is cancelled. Tail latency The time of the slowest few percent of requests, such as p99: what the unluckiest customers see. Load shedding Turning work away at the door, at once and with a clear error, when the service can't finish it in time. Graceful shutdown Stopping in order: no new work, a grace period for the work in flight, then cancel the rest and release resources. Where does a bulkhead's permit go? Around each single call to the courier: not around the retry loop (a pause before a retry shouldn't hold a permit), and a hedge takes a permit of its own. How do you size a courier's bulkhead? From its contract's limit on calls at once. Little's law: permits / time per call = the most calls per second it can serve. Which calls may be retried or hedged? Only idempotent ones, where a repeat does no harm. A price that is really a booking is asked for once. Why add jitter to retry waits? Clients that failed together would retry in the same millisecond. A factor between 0.5 and 1.5 spread 1,000 retries so that no millisecond had more than 18. When does a hedge start, and what does it cost? After about the courier's p95 time. It adds about 5% more calls; in the demo it cut p99 from 600 to 120 ms. Why turn work away with tryAcquire instead of queueing it? A request that can't make the deadline fails anyway. Shedding makes it fail in a millisecond with ERR busy, and nothing waits on the event loop. The quote service's shutdown order? Stop accepting, stop admitting, drain within the grace period, cancelAndJoin the rest, then close the connections and the loops.

h: Hold up under load · Go deeper
x: What a production version of this service would add, roughly in the order it would hurt to miss them. Measurements. For each courier: how long calls take (the hedge time comes from the p95), permits in use, calls retried, hedges sent and won, errors by type. For the service: requests admitted, turned away and served stale, and the age of the stale prices. Without them, every number in this track (the 10 permits, the 80 ms hedge, the 50 in flight) is a guess. A circuit breaker. Retries help with short blips; they make a courier that is down worse. A circuit breaker counts recent failures and, past a threshold, stops calling the courier for a while, then lets a few trial calls through. It sits outside the retry loop, so an open breaker fails fast instead of retrying. A retry budget. Cap retries as a share of all calls, for example 10%. During a long outage the budget runs out, and the service stops multiplying its own load. Adaptive limits. Fixed permits are right only for the load they were measured under. Adaptive limits change the number of permits from the response times they observe, the way TCP finds out how much the network can carry: when calls slow down, the limit shrinks before the courier falls over. Deadlines and context passed along. Send the time left with each courier call, so that the courier can give up too, and carry each request's id across the edge between Netty and coroutines (asContextElement or MDCContext, as Dispatchers and the coroutine context showed), so that a slow price can be found in the logs. Fair admission. One heavy client can still take most of the 50 places. A quota per client at the door, on top of the limit for the whole service, keeps a single caller from crowding out the rest. A plan for shutdown on a shared platform. Programs that run as many copies behind a load balancer, a router that spreads customers over the copies, should first tell it to send no more customers, then drain, and keep the grace period shorter than the time the platform waits before it stops the program by force.

h: Kotlin generics, properly
x: Variance from first principles: out, in, projections, star projection, reified, KClass, and Java side by side. Picture a small fruit shop. Boxes come in at the back, pass a clerk at the storeroom door who checks every label, and end up on the shelves and in the glass display case at the front. This track stays in that shop from the first lesson to the last. A type parameter is a box labeled "Box of ___", with a blank each caller fills in. The compiler is the clerk who checks every label at the door and then, when the program runs, tears it off. Each idea gets its own corner of the shop: a box signed "fruit only", a crate of apples that is not a crate of fruit, an apple dispenser with a lever and no slot, a compost bin that makes a fine apple bin, a box whose label wore off and, at the end, a board of bells by the back door. By the end, generics stop being slogans you half remember. You can read any signature, Kotlin or Java, and say what it accepts and why: List<out E>, Comparator<in T>, MutableList<*>, <T extends Comparable<? super T>>. For each type parameter you write, you can decide whether it is out, in or invariant by checking where it appears, instead of guessing. You know what the JVM erases, what inline and reified bring back, and when a KClass is enough or you need a KType, and you can build containers, result types and event buses that need no casts where they're used. You need the syntax of both languages and nothing more: the track starts from zero, and every lesson shows the compiler's error for each wrong move, so you learn what the clerk says when it refuses. Install JDK 25. The labs compile with release 21 and use Kotlin 2.4.21, and the compiler messages in the lessons come from that version. The labs live in labs/generics, one package per lesson (workbench.generics.l01 to l11). Most are Kotlin; lessons 3, 6 and 7 add a small Java exercise about arrays, wildcards or raw types, and lesson 8 has a Java test that calls your Kotlin code with a class token. Some tests check your variance by reading the Java signature Kotlin generates, because out becomes ? extends there. From lesson 8 on, tests reach your inline functions through a Callers.kt file that you don't edit (lesson 8 explains why). Lesson 9's demos run with and without kotlin-reflect: add -Preflect to the demo command. From labs/, run ./gradlew :generics:test --tests 'workbench.generics.lNN.*' until it passes, ./gradlew :generics:solutionTest to see the reference answers pass the same tests, and ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=<class> for the Try-it programs. A type parameter is a blank on the box's label that the caller fills in. It moves a ClassCastException from a far-away read to a compile error at the write. A class is not a type: String backs String and String?, List backs List<String> and List<Int>. Generic types are invariant unless declared otherwise, so a crate of apples is not a crate of fruit. Producer out, consumer in: out T lets C<Apple> stand in for C<Fruit> (the dispenser), in T flips the arrow (the compost bin), and each shuts one side. Java writes ? extends and ? super at every use. Variance limits which types flow, not whether state changes. When intuition stops helping, check the positions with the sign rule. Declare variance on the class when you can; project (MutableList<out T>, MutableList<in T>) when the class both reads and writes; split out a read-only out view when readers need flexibility. * means one unknown type argument, the box whose label wore off: read as Any?, write nothing. It is not Any?, and it is not a raw type. The JVM erases type arguments after checking them. inline + reified brings the outer class back at each call site, a note one word long; Java can't call it, and nested arguments stay erased. KClass and Class describe classes; KType (from typeOf) describes full types. x::class is a KClass<out T>. Describing declarations needs kotlin-reflect. Recursive bounds give base classes a self type; T & Any removes null; @UnsafeVariance promises that a parameter is only compared; Nothing sits below every type and fits every label. Type-safe containers tie the key to the value type (KClass<T>, or Key<T> with a KType), keep the one unchecked cast private, and keep write keys invariant. The limit: they check types, not meaning.

h: Kotlin generics, properly: track quiz
x: fun <T> firstOrDefault(items: List<T>, default: T): T. What does val x = firstOrDefault(listOf(1, 2), "none") do? It doesn't compile: T can't be both Int and String It compiles with T = Any? and prints a warning It compiles: T is inferred as a common supertype of Int and String, so x is 1, typed Comparable<*> & Serializable It compiles and throws ClassCastException when x is used Inference looks for a type that both arguments fit, and Int and String share Comparable<*> and Serializable. That's legal, and usually not what you meant: val y: Int = firstOrDefault(listOf(1, 2), "none") fails with expected 'Int', actual 'Comparable<*> & Serializable'. An explicit type argument, firstOrDefault<Int>(...), turns the mistake into an error at the call. A helper must compare two values with < and also read .length. Which Kotlin signature allows both? fun <T : Comparable<T>> longer(a: T, b: T): T fun <T> longer(a: T, b: T): T where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T> fun <T : CharSequence> longer(a: T, b: T): T fun <T : Any> longer(a: T, b: T): T Two bounds need a where clause, and the caller's type must satisfy both: two signs on one box. Comparable<T> alone gives < but no length; CharSequence alone gives length but no <. Java writes the same thing as <T extends CharSequence & Comparable<T>>. val varieties: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf("Gala"). Which line compiles? val a: MutableList<Any> = varieties val b: List<Any> = varieties val c: MutableList<Any?> = varieties val d: Array<Any> = varieties.toTypedArray() Only the read-only List is declared out E, so only it is covariant: the display case. MutableList and Array are invariant in Kotlin because they can be written to. If they weren't, you could add an Int to a list of strings, which is exactly what Java arrays allow until an ArrayStoreException. Pick the variance for each: interface Feed<T> { fun next(): T }, interface Bin<T> { fun drop(item: T) }, class Slot<T>(var item: T). out, in, invariant in, out, out out, out, out invariant, in, out Feed only returns T: a producer, out. Bin only takes T: a consumer, in, like the compost bin. Slot has a var, which is read and written, so T sits in an invariant position and the class can be neither. What Java signature does Kotlin generate for fun <T> copyInto(from: MutableList<out T>, to: MutableList<in T>)? <T> void copyInto(List<T> from, List<T> to) <T> void copyInto(List<?> from, List<?> to) <T> void copyInto(List<? extends T> from, List<? super T> to) <T> void copyInto(List from, List to) (raw types) Use-site projections are Kotlin's spelling of Java wildcards: out T is ? extends T and in T is ? super T, the same shape as Collections.copy. The lab for that lesson checks exactly this signature through Java reflection. Which function accepts a MutableList<String> and may call clear() on it? fun reset(l: MutableList<Any?>) fun reset(l: MutableList<Any>) fun reset(l: List<*>) fun reset(l: MutableList<*>) A star projection accepts a mutable list of any element type and still allows members that take no element, such as clear(). MutableList<Any?> and MutableList<Any> accept only lists of exactly that element type. List<*> accepts the list but has no clear(). Your Kotlin library offers inline fun <reified T : Any> decode(text: String): T. Java code in the same project needs it. What do you add? @JvmStatic on the reified function Nothing: Java can call it as Decoder.<Apple>decode(text) A version that takes T as a raw Class and returns Object fun <T : Any> decode(text: String, type: Class<T>): T, and make the reified one call it javac can't inline Kotlin code, so the reified function is a synthetic method it ignores. A Class-token overload works for both languages and can do a checked type.cast. Keeping the reified version as a one-line wrapper gives Kotlin callers the short form. Inside inline fun <reified T> describe(), called as describe<List<String>>(), what do T::class and typeOf<T>() keep? T::class is the class List; typeOf<T>() is the full List<String> Both keep List<String> Both give only List T::class doesn't compile for a generic T A KClass can only describe a class, the one-word note, and List<String> and List<Int> share one. typeOf builds a KType at the call site that includes arguments and nullability, and it works without kotlin-reflect. That difference is why a card index holding a Shelf<Apple> and a Shelf<Lemon> needs KType keys. In abstract class Builder<B : Builder<B>>, why write protected abstract fun self(): B instead of return this as B in each setter? Because this as B doesn't compile Because abstract functions are faster Because self() is checked: a subclass that passes the wrong type argument fails to compile, while this as B compiles and throws ClassCastException at a later call Because Java can't call a function that returns B this as B is an unchecked cast; erasure makes it succeed inside the base class, and the failure shows up where a caller uses the result. When each subclass implements self() = this, the compiler checks that this really is a B. Pick the types: (1) a function that only reads fruit from a mutable list and may clear it; (2) a board that stores listeners for Apple and accepts listeners for any Fruit; (3) a key for an order's List<String> of varieties. (1) MutableList<out Fruit>; (2) (Apple) -> Unit listeners stored behind a safeCast adapter, keyed by KClass<out Fruit>; (3) an invariant Key<List<String>> that carries typeOf<List<String>>() (1) MutableList<Fruit>; (2) listeners cast to (Fruit) -> Unit; (3) Key<out List<String>> (1) MutableList<in Fruit>; (2) a Map<String, Any> of listeners; (3) the class List::class as the key (1) MutableList<*>; (2) Consumer<Apple> in a raw list; (3) the string "varieties" Reading while still allowing clear() is an out-projection. Listeners consume, so a general listener fits, but storing a narrow one needs an adapter rather than a cast. A key decides what may be written, so it must be invariant, and a KType keeps List<String> apart from other types with the same name. The other options each repeat a mistake from this track: in for reading, unchecked listener casts, an out write key, class keys for generic types, raw types and string keys.

h: Generics from zero: type parameters · A box with no label: a cast from Any fails far from the bug
x: Java didn't always have generics, the feature this track is about: classes and functions with a blank where a type goes. Before Java 5, a container that could hold anything held Object, and Kotlin's version of that habit is Any. You put a value in, and you cast it back when you take it out. A cast, (String) in Java or as String in Kotlin, tells the compiler "trust me, this is a String". The real check happens later, while the program runs. Here is the storeroom from the opening, written that way. restock is the back room, filling the box before the shop opens. signFor is the counter, reading the box to write the sign for the day's apple: Java class AnyBox { Object value; AnyBox(Object v) { value = v; } } static void restock(AnyBox box) { box.value = 12; // the bug: how many apples, not which variety } static String signFor(AnyBox box) { String variety = (String) box.value; // ClassCastException here return "Today's apple: " + variety; } Kotlin class AnyBox(var value: Any) fun restock(box: AnyBox) { box.value = 12 // the bug: how many apples, not which variety } fun signFor(box: AnyBox): String { val variety = box.value as String // ClassCastException here return "Today's apple: $variety" } The bug is in restock. It stored the count, 12, where the counter expects a name such as "Gala". The compiler accepts it, because an Int is an Any, and restock returns normally. The box didn't complain when the 12 went in. Boxes never do. Before you read the output, decide where you expect the program to fail. Here is what AnyBoxDemo, the same program in the labs, printed: restock() returned. Nothing has failed yet. ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.lang.String (java.lang.Integer and java.lang.String are in module java.base of loader 'bootstrap') thrown in: workbench.generics.l01.demo.AnyBoxDemoKt.signFor(AnyBoxDemo.kt:13) The exception names signFor, line 13: the cast at the counter. The counter did nothing wrong, and the function with the bug isn't in the trace at all. In a bigger program, the read might come hours later, in code another team owns. That is the real cost of Any plus casts. The type check still happens, but it happens late, and in the wrong place. The error shows up where the value is read. The bug is where it was written. Generics move the check to the write. Give the box a type parameter, a name in angle brackets that stands for the type of what goes inside, and say what this box holds: Java class Box<T> { T value; Box(T v) { value = v; } } static void restock(Box<String> box) { box.value = 12; // now a compile error } Kotlin class Box<T>(var value: T) fun restock(box: Box<String>) { box.value = 12 // now a compile error } Both compilers now reject the bad line itself. Think of the compiler as a clerk at the storeroom door who reads every label and turns away anything that doesn't match. javac says incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String. kotlinc says: error: assignment type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'String' was expected. The counter needs no cast any more. box.value is already a String, so signFor can't throw a ClassCastException. A cast checks at the read, far from the bug. Put the type on the label instead. The compiler messages in this track come from kotlinc 2.4.21, the command-line Kotlin compiler. Gradle and IntelliJ print the same text with a capital first letter. So what exactly is that <T>? Let's read the label closely. Watch the cast fail far from the bug Run AnyBoxDemo with the command below (or its Java twin, AnyBoxDemoJava). Note which function the exception names. Make the box generic: change the class to class AnyBox<T>(var value: T), and change both functions to take AnyBox<String>. Leave main alone. (In the Java twin: static class AnyBox<T> with a T value field and a T constructor parameter, and both methods take AnyBox<String>.) Before you run it again, predict which line the compiler will reject. Then run it. Undo the change when you're done. AnyBoxDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l01.demo /** A storeroom box that holds Any. It compiles fine, and it fails far away from the bug. */ class AnyBox(var value: Any) // the back room: restocks the box before the shop opens fun restock(box: AnyBox) { box.value = 12 // the bug: how many apples, not which variety } // the counter: reads the box much later, in another part of the program fun signFor(box: AnyBox): String { val variety = box.value as String // the cast fails HERE, not where 12 went in return "Today's apple: $variety" } fun main() { val box = AnyBox("Gala") restock(box) println("restock() returned. Nothing has failed yet.") try { println(signFor(box)) } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("ClassCastException: ${e.message}") println("thrown in: ${e.stackTrace.first()}") } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l01.demo.AnyBoxDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l01/demo/AnyBoxDemo.kt AnyBoxDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l01.demo; /** Java twin of AnyBoxDemo.kt: a storeroom box that holds Object. It compiles, and fails far from the bug. */ public class AnyBoxDemoJava { static class AnyBox { Object value; AnyBox(Object value) { this.value = value; } } // the back room: restocks the box before the shop opens static void restock(AnyBox box) { box.value = 12; // the bug: how many apples, not which variety } // the counter: reads the box much later, in another part of the program static String signFor(AnyBox box) { String variety = (String) box.value; // the cast fails HERE, not where 12 went in return "Today's apple: " + variety; } public static void main(String[] args) { AnyBox box = new AnyBox("Gala"); restock(box); System.out.println("restock() returned. Nothing has failed yet."); try { System.out.println(signFor(box)); } catch (ClassCastException e) { System.out.println("ClassCastException: " + e.getMessage()); System.out.println("thrown in: " + e.getStackTrace()[0]); } } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l01.demo.AnyBoxDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l01/demo/AnyBoxDemoJava.java The first run prints restock() returned. Nothing has failed yet. and then ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.lang.String, thrown in signFor at line 13. The function with the bug isn't in the trace. After the change, the build stops at compile time on box.value = 12. Kotlin says Assignment type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'String' was expected., and javac says incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String. The check moved from the counter to the back room.

h: Generics from zero: type parameters · Putting a label on the box: a type parameter is a blank the caller fills in
x: A box of Any fails at the read; Box has a blank on its label that each use fills, and the compiler checks every put Picture a box whose label comes printed with a gap: "Box of ________". The person who made the box has no idea what will go in it. Whoever takes the box writes in the gap, "Box of apples", and from then on the clerk at the door turns away anything else. class Box<T> is that printed label. Read it as: "Box has one blank in it, called T. Whoever uses Box fills the blank with a real type." T is the type parameter. The real type you write in, like String in Box<String>, is the type argument. Inside the class, T stands for whatever the caller chose, and the class never finds out which one. Here is the box with one more method. replace puts a new value in and hands back the old one: Java class Box<T> { T value; Box(T value) { this.value = value; } T replace(T newValue) { T old = value; value = newValue; return old; } } Box<String> variety = new Box<>("Gala"); Box<Integer> count = new Box<>(12); variety.replace("Fuji"); // fine count.replace("Fuji"); // error: String cannot be converted to Integer Kotlin class Box<T>(var value: T) { fun replace(newValue: T): T { val old = value value = newValue return old } } val variety = Box("Gala") // Box<String> val count = Box(12) // Box<Int> variety.replace("Fuji") // fine count.replace("Fuji") // error: actual type is 'String', but 'Int' was expected One class gives you many types: Box<String>, Box<Int>, Box<Apple>. To the compiler, Box<String> and Box<Int> are as different as String and Int, and it checks each one on its own. How does it check count.replace("Fuji")? It fills in the blank. count is a Box<Int>, so the compiler reads every T in Box as Int. For that call, replace is replace(newValue: Int): Int, and a String doesn't fit. Fill in the blank, then check the call as if the class had been written for Int all along. Do that in your head, and you can predict any call on a generic class before the compiler does. Functions can have blanks too. In Java, the <T> goes before the return type. In Kotlin, it goes right after fun, before the function name: Java static <T> T firstOrNull(List<T> items) { return items.isEmpty() ? null : items.get(0); } Kotlin fun <T> firstOrNull(items: List<T>): T? = if (items.isEmpty()) null else items[0] <T> declares the blank. List<T> and T? use it, and the two uses are tied together. Pass a List<Apple> and you get an Apple? back, with no cast. Pass a List<String> and you get a String?. A function can have several type parameters, separated by commas: fun <T, K> indexBy(items: List<T>, key: (T) -> K): Map<K, T>. The single-letter names are a habit, not a rule: T for type, E for element, K and V for key and value, R for result. A method can also have a type parameter that its class doesn't have. In fun <C> mapSecond(f: (B) -> C): Duo<A, C> on a class Duo<A, B>, A and B belong to the class. C belongs to this one call, and the lambda you pass decides what it is. You'll write that method in the lab. Here the box picture breaks, and the break matters later. A real label stays on the box, and anyone can read it next week. On the JVM, the program that runs compiled Kotlin and Java code, the compiler checks the label and then tears it off. At run time there is only one Box class, and the <String> part is gone. Lesson 8 of this track, on type erasure, shows what that costs you. Writing every label by hand would get tiring, though. Most of the time, the compiler fills in the blank for you. Fill the blank, then break it Run BoxDemo (or BoxDemoJava) with the command below to see it work. Uncomment the three wrong moves at the bottom of main, one at a time. For each one, write down the error you expect before you run. For the last one, decide how you would fix it without changing firstOrNull. BoxDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l01.demo /** One class with one blank, T. Each use fills the blank with a real type. */ class Box<T>(var value: T) { /** Puts [newValue] in and returns the old value. Both have type T. */ fun replace(newValue: T): T { val old = value value = newValue return old } } /** A generic function: <T> declares the blank, List<T> and T? use it. */ fun <T> firstOrNull(items: List<T>): T? = if (items.isEmpty()) null else items[0] fun main() { val variety = Box("Gala") // Box<String> val count = Box(12) // Box<Int> val old = variety.replace("Fuji") println("variety was $old, now ${variety.value}") println("count is ${count.value}") println("first on the list: ${firstOrNull(listOf("Gala", "Fuji"))}") // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // count.replace("Fuji") // val wrong: Box<String> = Box(42) // val first: String = firstOrNull(listOf("Gala")) } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l01.demo.BoxDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l01/demo/BoxDemo.kt BoxDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l01.demo; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of BoxDemo.kt: one class with one blank, T. */ public class BoxDemoJava { static class Box<T> { private T value; Box(T value) { this.value = value; } T get() { return value; } /** Puts newValue in and returns the old value. Both have type T. */ T replace(T newValue) { T old = value; value = newValue; return old; } } /** A generic method: <T> before the return type declares the blank. */ static <T> T firstOrNull(List<T> items) { return items.isEmpty() ? null : items.get(0); } public static void main(String[] args) { Box<String> variety = new Box<>("Gala"); // diamond: javac infers <String> Box<Integer> count = new Box<>(12); String old = variety.replace("Fuji"); System.out.println("variety was " + old + ", now " + variety.get()); System.out.println("count is " + count.get()); System.out.println("first on the list: " + firstOrNull(List.of("Gala", "Fuji"))); // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // count.replace("Fuji"); // Box<String> wrong = new Box<>(42); // String first = firstOrNull(List.<String>of()); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l01.demo.BoxDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l01/demo/BoxDemoJava.java The demo prints variety was Gala, now Fuji, count is 12 and first on the list: Gala. count.replace("Fuji") gives Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'String', but 'Int' was expected. The Box(42) line gives Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Box<String>', actual 'Box<Int>'. The last one gives expected 'String', actual 'String?': firstOrNull returns T?, so with T = String you get a String?. Declare first as String?, or add a default with ?: "none". In the Java twin, the first two fail (String cannot be converted to Integer, cannot infer type arguments for Box<>), and the third compiles: Java has no T?, so it hands you a null without a word. You write one generic class. The compiler checks each filled-in label as its own type. The JVM runs a single class, with the label torn off.

h: Generics from zero: type parameters · Letting the compiler fill in the label: type inference
x: You rarely write type arguments in Kotlin. The compiler works them out from the values you pass and from the type you expect. That is type inference, and Java does it too, with var and the diamond <>, which the next section explains. Java var weights = List.of(180, 150, 210); // List<Integer> var box = new Box<>("Gala"); // Box<String> var prices = Map.of("apple", 40, "mango", 250L); // Map<String, Number & Comparable<...> & ...> Kotlin val weights = listOf(180, 150, 210) // List<Int> val box = Box("Gala") // Box<String> val prices = mapOf("apple" to 40, "mango" to 250L) // Map<String, Long> Look at the last line in each. Kotlin sees 250L, a Long, in the same map, and makes the literal 40 a Long too, so both prices fit one type. Java never changes a literal's type: 40 stays an Integer, so javac infers a long type for the values, one you couldn't write yourself. When the values really have different types, the compiler picks the closest type they share: Java var mixed = List.of(180, 2.5); // List<Number & Comparable<...> & Constable & ConstantDesc> var odd = List.of(1, "a"); // another intersection, of Serializable, Comparable and more Kotlin val mixed = listOf(180, 2.5) // List<Number & Comparable<*>> val odd = listOf(1, "a") // List<Comparable<*> & Serializable> Number & Comparable<*> is an intersection type: a type that is two types at once, here something that is both a Number and a Comparable. You can't write that type in your own code, but the compiler uses it. When you see one, you have usually mixed types by accident, a whole number and a decimal in one list, say. Sometimes there is nothing to infer from. emptyList() gets no values, so Kotlin has no clue what T should be: error: cannot infer type for type parameter 'T'. Specify it explicitly. Java doesn't complain here. var none = Collections.emptyList(); quietly becomes a List<Object>, which is rarely what you meant: javac shrugs and picks the widest type there is. In both languages, the fix is the same. Write the type argument at the call, or give the variable a type and let the compiler work backwards from it: Java var none = Collections.<String>emptyList(); List<String> alsoNone = Collections.emptyList(); Kotlin val none = emptyList<String>() val alsoNone: List<String> = emptyList() Each pair means the same thing. I use the first form inside expressions and the second for properties, where the declared type documents the code anyway. Kotlin builders infer too. buildList { add("Gala"); add("Fuji") } is a List<String>, worked out from the add calls inside the lambda. Java has no such builder, so there you name the type up front: new ArrayList<String>(). Here is a trick you'll use for the rest of this track. When you're not sure what the compiler inferred, assign the value to a type you know is wrong, such as val probe: Int = mixed in Kotlin or int probe = mixed; in Java. The error message prints the real type. Everything so far works the same in Java, with different punctuation. Let's line the two up, and meet the one box Java kept with no label at all. Make the compiler tell you the type Open InferenceDemo.kt. For each of the six values, write down the type you think the compiler inferred. Uncomment probe1 only and run the demo. The build fails, and the message prints the inferred type. Comment it out again. Repeat for probe2 to probe6, one at a time. Count how many you predicted right. InferenceDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l01.demo /** * Make the compiler tell you what it inferred. Each probe assigns a value to an Int, * which is wrong on purpose. The error message prints the real, inferred type. * Uncomment ONE probe at a time, run, read the message, comment it out again. */ fun main() { val weights = listOf(180, 150, 210) val mixed = listOf(180, 2.5) val tags = listOf("ripe", null) val prices = mapOf("apple" to 40, "mango" to 250L) val varieties = buildList { add("Gala"); add("Fuji") } val none = emptyList<String>() // val probe1: Int = weights // val probe2: Int = mixed // val probe3: Int = tags // val probe4: Int = prices // val probe5: Int = varieties // val probe6 = emptyList() println("compiled: ${weights.size + mixed.size + tags.size + prices.size + varieties.size + none.size} values") } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l01.demo.InferenceDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l01/demo/InferenceDemo.kt InferenceDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l01.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * Java twin of InferenceDemo.kt. Make javac tell you what `var` inferred: assign the value to an int, * which is wrong on purpose. Uncomment ONE probe at a time, run, read the message, comment it out again. */ public class InferenceDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { var weights = List.of(180, 150, 210); var mixed = List.of(180, 2.5); var tags = Arrays.asList("ripe", null); var prices = Map.of("apple", 40, "mango", 250L); var varieties = new ArrayList<String>(); // Java has no buildList: say the type up front varieties.add("Gala"); varieties.add("Fuji"); var none = Collections.emptyList(); // no error in Java: what did it pick? // int probe1 = weights; // int probe2 = mixed; // int probe3 = tags; // int probe4 = prices; // int probe5 = varieties; // int probe6 = none; System.out.println("compiled: " + (weights.size() + mixed.size() + tags.size() + prices.size() + varieties.size() + none.size()) + " values"); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l01.demo.InferenceDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l01/demo/InferenceDemoJava.java The messages say actual 'List<Int>', 'List<Number & Comparable<*>>', 'List<String?>', 'Map<String, Long>' and 'List<String>'. probe6 gives Cannot infer type for type parameter 'T'. Specify it explicitly. Most people miss Map<String, Long> and the intersection type on the first try. The Java twin prints List<Integer>, List<INT#1> (javac's name for an intersection), List<String>, Map<String,INT#1> and ArrayList<String>, and probe6 shows List<Object>: Java picked Object for the empty list without a word.

h: Generics from zero: type parameters · The same box in Java: the diamond, raw types and Integer
x: Java has had generics since Java 5, and Kotlin compiles to the same JVM machinery. The ideas map one to one. Only the punctuation moves: Java class Box<T> { private T value; Box(T value) { this.value = value; } T get() { return value; } } static <T> T firstOrNull(List<T> items) { return items.isEmpty() ? null : items.get(0); } Box<String> box = new Box<>("Gala"); // diamond List<String> none = Collections.emptyList(); // inferred from the target List<String> same = Collections.<String>emptyList(); // explicit type argument Kotlin class Box<T>(private var value: T) { fun get(): T = value } fun <T> firstOrNull(items: List<T>): T? = if (items.isEmpty()) null else items[0] val box = Box("Gala") // no diamond, no new val none: List<String> = emptyList() // inferred from the target val same = emptyList<String>() // explicit type argument Three differences matter in practice. In a Java method, <T> comes before the return type: static <T> T firstOrNull(...). In Kotlin it comes before the function name. The meaning is the same. Java also has no nullable types, so its firstOrNull returns a plain T that may be null, while Kotlin's says T? out loud. Java needs the diamond, the empty <> in new Box<>("Gala"), which asks javac to infer the type argument. Leave it out, and new Box("Gala") is a raw type: Box with its generics switched off. Kotlin has no new and no raw types, so Box("Gala") is always a Box<String>. Java type arguments must be reference types, that is, classes, never the primitive types such as int or double. List<int> is an error (unexpected type, required: reference, found: int), so you write List<Integer>. In Kotlin you write List<Int>, and the compiler stores boxed java.lang.Integer objects for you, each number wrapped in a small object. Raw types are the unlabeled boxes Java kept, so that code from before Java 5 still compiles. A raw List accepts anything, and javac only warns. Here is a helper written the old way, from RawTypeDemo in the labs, with its Kotlin twin: Java static void addOldStock(List names) { // raw: no <...> names.add(42); // compiles, with a warning } List<String> varieties = new ArrayList<>(); varieties.add("Gala"); addOldStock(varieties); for (String variety : varieties) { // throws on the second element System.out.println(variety.toUpperCase()); } Kotlin // Kotlin has no raw types: an unchecked cast is the closest way to switch the check off private fun addOldStock(names: MutableList<*>) { @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") (names as MutableList<Any?>).add(42) } val varieties: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf("Gala") addOldStock(varieties) for (variety in varieties) { // throws on the second element println(variety.uppercase()) } javac's warning is easy to miss. By default, it's a single Note: line near the top of the build output, the kind people scroll past: Note: .../RawTypeDemo.java uses unchecked or unsafe operations. Then the program runs, and fails on the way out: size = 2, nothing failed yet GALA ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.lang.String (...) Why does the read fail and not the add? At run time the list holds plain Object references, so add(42) has nothing to check against. Where your code reads an element as a String, javac adds a hidden cast to String, and that cast is what throws. Lesson 8 of this track shows that cast in the bytecode, the instructions the compilers write into class files. It is the AnyBox failure again, hidden inside a type that claims to be safe. So when a Kotlin program gets a ClassCastException on a line with no cast in it, look for a raw type or an unchecked cast in the code underneath. Our labels have one limit left. A plain T promises nothing about what goes in, so the code inside Box can't ask its value for anything beyond what every type has. Telling the compiler more is the next step. Let a raw type smuggle in an Integer Run RawTypeDemo with the command below. Look for javac's Note: line near the top of the Gradle output. Predict: does names.add(42) fail, or does something later fail? Change the parameter of addOldStock from List names to List<String> names and run it again. Then undo it. (The Kotlin twin has no raw type to remove: it switches the check off with an unchecked cast instead, and fails the same way.) RawTypeDemo.java package workbench.generics.l01.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** A raw type switches the checks off. The bad value goes in quietly and fails on the way out. */ public class RawTypeDemo { // an old helper, written as if Java had no generics: "List" with no <...> is a raw type static void addOldStock(List names) { names.add(42); // compiles, with an unchecked warning } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> varieties = new ArrayList<>(); // diamond: javac infers ArrayList<String> varieties.add("Gala"); addOldStock(varieties); System.out.println("size = " + varieties.size() + ", nothing failed yet"); try { for (String variety : varieties) { // javac inserted a (String) cast here System.out.println(variety.toUpperCase()); } } catch (ClassCastException e) { System.out.println("ClassCastException: " + e.getMessage()); } } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l01.demo.RawTypeDemo labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l01/demo/RawTypeDemo.java RawTypeDemo.kt // Kotlin twin of RawTypeDemo.java. Kotlin has no raw types; the closest way to switch the checks off // is an unchecked cast. The bad value goes in quietly and fails on the way out, exactly as in Java. package workbench.generics.l01.demo // MutableList<*> means "a list of something"; the cast pretends it is a list of anything private fun addOldStock(names: MutableList<*>) { @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") (names as MutableList<Any?>).add(42) // compiles; without @Suppress Kotlin warns } fun main() { val varieties: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf() // the type is declared, nothing to infer varieties.add("Gala") addOldStock(varieties) println("size = ${varieties.size}, nothing failed yet") try { for (variety in varieties) { // the compiler inserted a cast to String here println(variety.uppercase()) } } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("ClassCastException: ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l01.demo.RawTypeDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l01/demo/RawTypeDemo.kt Gradle prints Note: ... RawTypeDemo.java uses unchecked or unsafe operations. The program prints size = 2, nothing failed yet and GALA, then a ClassCastException for the Integer. The add worked. The failure comes in the loop, where javac inserted a hidden cast to String. With List<String> names, the build fails at names.add(42) with incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String. h: Generics from zero: type parameters · Java and Kotlin
x: One generic box and one generic function, in both languages Box.java import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; class Box<T> { private T value; Box(T value) { this.value = value; } T get() { return value; } T replace(T newValue) { T old = value; value = newValue; return old; } // <T> before the return type static <T> T firstOrNull(List<T> items) { return items.isEmpty() ? null : items.get(0); } static void use() { Box<String> box = new Box<>("Gala"); // diamond infers <String> Box raw = new Box("Gala"); // raw type: checks off List<String> none = Collections.<String>emptyList(); List<Integer> weights = List.of(180, 150); // no List<int> } } Box.kt class Box<T>(var value: T) { fun replace(newValue: T): T { val old = value value = newValue return old } } // <T> before the function name fun <T> firstOrNull(items: List<T>): T? = if (items.isEmpty()) null else items[0] fun use() { val box = Box("Gala") // Box<String>, no diamond needed // there is no raw Box: Box without <...> must be inferable or it does not compile val none = emptyList<String>() val weights: List<Int> = listOf(180, 150) // Int works; stored as java.lang.Integer } The model is the same: one class, type parameters checked at compile time, one class at run time. Kotlin infers the type argument from constructor arguments without a diamond, and it has no raw types, so the unchecked escape hatch that Java keeps for old code doesn't exist. Kotlin also accepts Int as a type argument, while Java makes you write Integer. Both compile to boxed objects. One more difference shows in firstOrNull: Kotlin's return type says T?, so callers must handle null. Java's T can be null without saying so.

h: Generics from zero: type parameters · Worked example
x: Make the storeroom generic The shop's storeroom keeps boxes by label, such as "shelf 2" or "back corner". Apple and Lemon are small data classes with a variety and a weight in grams. The first version stores Any, and every caller casts. Find the two places where a wrong type could get in or out. class Storeroom { private val boxes = HashMap<String, Any>() fun put(label: String, item: Any) { boxes[label] = item } fun get(label: String): Any? = boxes[label] } // caller val gala = room.get("shelf 2") as Apple? // a cast on every read class Storeroom { private final Map<String, Object> boxes = new HashMap<>(); void put(String label, Object item) { boxes.put(label, item); } Object get(String label) { return boxes.get(label); } } // caller Apple gala = (Apple) room.get("shelf 2"); // a cast on every read Decide what varies. The label is always a String. What sits in the boxes changes from one storeroom to the next: apples in one, lemons in another. So the item type becomes the type parameter, and the label stays a plain String. class Storeroom<T> { private val boxes = HashMap<String, T>() fun put(label: String, item: T) { boxes[label] = item } fun get(label: String): T? = boxes[label] } class Storeroom<T> { private final Map<String, T> boxes = new HashMap<>(); void put(String label, T item) { boxes.put(label, item); } T get(String label) { return boxes.get(label); } // null when absent } Fill the blank where you use it. Each storeroom gets its own type. The cast is gone, and a wrong put is now a compile error on the line that makes it. val apples = Storeroom<Apple>() val gala: Apple? = apples.get("shelf 2") // no cast apples.put("shelf 2", Lemon("Eureka", 120)) // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Lemon', // but 'Apple' was expected. var apples = new Storeroom<Apple>(); Apple gala = apples.get("shelf 2"); // no cast apples.put("shelf 2", new Lemon("Eureka", 120)); // error: incompatible types: Lemon cannot be converted to Apple Add a helper that fills a box on a miss. It uses the class's T, so it needs no <T> of its own. Stop and answer: what would go wrong if you wrote fun <T> getOrPut(...) here? (A new T on the function would hide the class's T, and boxes[label] = item would no longer type-check. The same happens in Java with <T> T getOrPut(...).) fun getOrPut(label: String, fill: () -> T): T { boxes[label]?.let { return it } val item = fill() boxes[label] = item return item } T getOrPut(String label, Supplier<T> fill) { T stored = boxes.get(label); if (stored != null) return stored; T item = fill.get(); boxes.put(label, item); return item; }

h: Generics from zero: type parameters · Quiz
x: The shop keeps its settings in a MutableMap<String, Any>. One function stores settings["openingHour"] = "9". A report later runs val hour = settings["openingHour"] as Int. What happens? A compile error on the line that stores "9" A ClassCastException on the line that stores "9" A ClassCastException on the as Int line, when the report runs hour is 9, because Kotlin converts the string A String is an Any, so the store compiles and runs. The cast in the report is the first check, and it fails there. Casts never convert values. A typed setting such as openingHour: Int would have made the store a compile error. Given fun <T> firstOrNull(items: List<T>): T?, what does the compiler say about val name: String? = firstOrNull(listOf(1, 2))? Initializer type mismatch: expected 'String?', actual 'Int?' It compiles, and name is null It compiles, and name is "1" It compiles, then throws ClassCastException T is inferred from the argument as Int, so the call returns Int?. That doesn't fit in a String?. The type parameter ties the input and the output together, which is the whole point. Nothing is converted at run time. val none = emptyList() does not compile. Which line fixes it? val none = emptyList<String>() val none: List<String> = emptyList() Either of the two above Neither: emptyList needs an argument The compiler needs to know T. You can give the type argument at the call, or give the variable a type and let inference work backwards from it. Both produce a List<String>. Java: List raw = new ArrayList(); raw.add(7); List<String> names = raw; String s = names.get(0); What happens? A compile error on raw.add(7) It compiles with unchecked warnings, then throws ClassCastException on the names.get(0) line It compiles, and s is "7" ArrayStoreException on raw.add(7) Raw types turn the checks off, so javac only warns. The Integer sits in the list until the read, where javac inserted a cast to String. The failure appears far from the line that caused it, the same as with Any. From the race conditions lesson: two threads take orders off a queue, and each runs if (!seen.contains(id)) { ship(order); seen.add(id) }, where seen is ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet<String>(). The same order arrives twice, once on each thread. What is the smallest fix? Make the field seen volatile Replace seen with a Collections.synchronizedSet Make seen a MutableSet<Any> so both copies fit Ship only after seen.add(id) returned true: if (seen.add(id)) ship(order) This is check-then-act. Each set call is atomic on its own, but two calls in a row are not. add checks and inserts in one step and returns false for the second copy, so only one thread ships. volatile and a synchronized wrapper leave the gap between the two calls open.
