h: Generics from zero: type parameters · Key terms
x: Cast as String or (String): telling the compiler to trust you about a type, with the real check at run time. Type parameter The placeholder in a declaration, like T in class Box<T>: a blank on the label. Type argument The real type that fills a type parameter, like String in Box<String>. Generic function A function with its own type parameters, such as fun <T> firstOrNull(items: List<T>): T?. Type inference The compiler working out type arguments from the values you pass and the type you expect. Intersection type A type that is two types at once, like Number & Comparable<*>. Inferred by the compiler; you can't write it yourself. Diamond Java's <> on new, asking javac to infer the type arguments. Raw type A Java generic type used without type arguments, like plain List. The compiler stops checking it. In class Box<T>, what is T? A type parameter: a blank on the label that each user of Box fills with a real type, such as Box<String>. Where does a bad value stored in an Any field get caught? At the cast in the code that reads it, at run time. The stack trace points at the reader, not at the writer with the bug. val e = emptyList() gives what error? cannot infer type for type parameter 'T'. Specify it explicitly. Fix: emptyList<String>() or val e: List<String> = emptyList(). Where does <T> go in a Kotlin generic function, and in a Java one? Kotlin: before the name, fun <T> first(xs: List<T>): T. Java: before the return type, static <T> T first(List<T> xs). What does Java's diamond in new ArrayList<>() do? It tells javac to infer the type argument from the target type. Without it, new ArrayList() is a raw type. What does listOf(1, 2.5) infer to? List<Number & Comparable<*>>, an intersection type: the closest type that both Int and Double share. How do you see the type Kotlin inferred for x? Write val probe: Int = x. The compile error prints the actual type.

h: Generics from zero: type parameters · Go deeper
x: Two inference tools are worth knowing. A _ type argument lets you give some type arguments and let the compiler infer the rest. Take fun <K, V> emptyShelf(firstKey: K): MutableMap<K, V>. The compiler can work out K from the argument, but nothing tells it V. Write emptyShelf<_, Int>("Gala"), and you get a MutableMap<String, Int>. The Kotlin generics page has a longer example. You can also widen a type on purpose. listOf(1, "a") infers an intersection type that you can't name. If you really want a list of anything, say so: listOf<Any>(1, "a"). Now the type is List<Any>, and it reads honestly to the next person. One Java detail: the explicit type argument goes after the dot, Collections.<String>emptyList(), and it needs something in front of the dot. Inside the same class you must write this.<String>helper() or MyClass.<String>helper(). In Java 8 and later you rarely need it, because target typing infers the argument from the variable you assign to. Finally, Kotlin's List<Int> holds java.lang.Integer objects, so a list of a million weights costs a million small objects. When that matters, use IntArray, which is a real int[].

h: Bounds and constraints: upper bounds, where, T : Any · What a T with no bound can do: only what Any? can do
x: Start with a plain type parameter, one with no sign on it at all. It means "some type, I don't know which", so inside the function, T can do only what every type can do. In Java, the type that every object belongs to is Object. In Kotlin, "every type" includes the nullable ones, such as String?, so a T with no bound is held to Any?. Java static <T> String describe(T x) { return "value=" + x + ", hash=" + Objects.hashCode(x); } describe("Gala"); // fine describe(180); // fine describe(null); // fine: any Java T accepts null Kotlin fun <T> describe(x: T): String = "value=$x, hash=${x.hashCode()}" describe("Gala") // fine describe(180) // fine describe(null) // also fine: T is inferred as Nothing? toString(), hashCode() and == work, because they exist on Any?. The demo prints value=Gala, hash=2211823, value=180, hash=180 and value=null, hash=0. Anything more specific fails, even when every caller you have in mind would pass a String: Java static <T> int lengthOf(T x) { return x.length(); } // error: cannot find symbol: method length() Kotlin fun <T> lengthOf(x: T) = x.length // error: unresolved reference 'length'. The compiler isn't being fussy. Someone could call lengthOf(42), and an Int has no length. A generic function must work for every type the caller is allowed to pick, so it can only use what all of them share. Comparison fails the same way. Java says cannot find symbol: method compareTo(T). Kotlin gives a stranger message: Java static <T> T bigger(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; } // error: cannot find symbol: method compareTo(T) Kotlin fun <T> bigger(a: T, b: T): T = if (a > b) a else b // error: candidate 'fun String.compareTo(other: String, ignoreCase: Boolean = ...): Int' // is inapplicable because of a receiver type mismatch. In Kotlin, a > b means a.compareTo(b). The compiler goes looking for any compareTo it could use on a T, finds only the one on String, and reports that this one doesn't fit. It's a roundabout way of saying no. When an error mentions some unrelated type's method, read it as "this operation isn't defined for T". The null case surprises people coming from Java, where every T accepts null anyway and nobody thinks about it. In Kotlin, fun <T> f(x: T) accepts null too, because T may be String? or Nothing?. (Nothing? is the type Kotlin gives a bare null. Write val x = null, then val y: Int = x, and the error says actual 'Nothing?'.) If your function must not see null, you have to say so. The last section shows how. That is the job of a bound: a sign on the type parameter that promises more about T. The caller can pick from fewer types, and in return your code can do more with the one they pick. Find the edge of an unbounded T Run UnboundedDemo (or UnboundedDemoJava). Note what describe(null) prints. Uncomment lengthOf, run, and read the error. Comment it out again. Uncomment bigger and run. Before you read the message, guess which type it will mention. UnboundedDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l02.demo /** An unbounded T is "some type, maybe nullable". You may only use what every type has. */ fun <T> describe(x: T): String = "value=$x, hash=${x.hashCode()}" // toString and hashCode work on Any? // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // fun <T> lengthOf(x: T) = x.length // fun <T> bigger(a: T, b: T): T = if (a > b) a else b fun main() { println(describe("Gala")) println(describe(180)) println(describe(null)) // T is inferred as Nothing?, and null is allowed } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l02.demo.UnboundedDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l02/demo/UnboundedDemo.kt UnboundedDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l02.demo; /** Java twin of UnboundedDemo.kt. An unbounded T is "some type": only Object's methods are available. */ public class UnboundedDemoJava { static <T> String describe(T x) { return "value=" + x + ", hash=" + java.util.Objects.hashCode(x); // Object's methods only } // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // static <T> int lengthOf(T x) { return x.length(); } // static <T> T bigger(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(describe("Gala")); System.out.println(describe(180)); System.out.println(describe(null)); // any Java T accepts null } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l02.demo.UnboundedDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l02/demo/UnboundedDemoJava.java describe(null) prints value=null, hash=0: null is a legal T. lengthOf fails with Unresolved reference 'length'. bigger fails with a message about String.compareTo being inapplicable, because the only compareTo the compiler could find is String's. Neither error is about your callers. Both say T promises nothing beyond Any?. The Java twin fails both with cannot find symbol: Java's T promises nothing beyond Object.

h: Bounds and constraints: upper bounds, where, T : Any · A box that only takes fruit: upper bounds
x: A bound is a gate at the call site: T : Comparable shuts Payment out and hands the body compareTo, and a where clause adds a second gate Here is the sign from the opening, written in code. The shop's fruit share an interface, Fruit, with a name and a weight in grams, and Apple is a small data class that implements it. An upper bound says "T must be this type or a subtype of it". For now, read subtype as a class that inherits from it, the way Apple inherits from Fruit; the next lesson gives the word its exact meaning. Java writes the bound with extends, even for interfaces. Kotlin writes it after a colon: Java interface Fruit { String name(); int grams(); } record Apple(String name, int grams) implements Fruit {} static <T extends Fruit> T heavier(T a, T b) { return a.grams() >= b.grams() ? a : b; // grams() comes from the bound } Apple apple = heavier(new Apple("Gala", 180), new Apple("Fuji", 150)); Kotlin interface Fruit { val name: String; val grams: Int } data class Apple(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit fun <T : Fruit> heavier(a: T, b: T): T = if (a.grams >= b.grams) a else b // .grams comes from the bound val apple: Apple = heavier(Apple("Gala", 180), Apple("Fuji", 150)) The bound does two jobs. Inside the function, a.grams compiles, because every T is now some kind of Fruit. At each call, the sign turns everything else away: heavier("Gala", "Fuji") fails with argument type mismatch: actual type is 'String', but 'Fruit' was expected. You may wonder why heavier needs a T at all. Why not take two Fruit parameters and return a Fruit? Because then two apples in would give a Fruit out. To get your Apple back, you'd need a cast, the very thing lesson 1 of this track removed. With T, two apples in give an Apple out. The most common bound in practice isn't a class you wrote. It's Comparable<T>: Java static <T extends Comparable<T>> T maxOf2(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; } maxOf2(180, 150); // 180 maxOf2("Gala", "Fuji"); // Gala Kotlin fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T): T = if (a > b) a else b maxOf2(180, 150) // 180 maxOf2("Gala", "Fuji") // Gala maxOf2(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 30)) // 2026-11-02 Read T : Comparable<T> aloud as "T is something that can be compared with another T". Int is a Comparable<Int>, String is a Comparable<String>, and LocalDate, the JDK's class for a calendar date, is a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate>. Kotlin accepts that last one because Comparable is declared in T, which lesson 5 of this track explains. Inside the function, a > b now compiles, because the bound guarantees a compareTo. The T appears twice in T : Comparable<T>, and that's on purpose. Comparable<T> says what T can be compared with. A bound that mentions its own type parameter is called a recursive bound. You'll meet it again in Enum<E : Enum<E>>, and in builder classes in lesson 10 of this track. Now hand the comparing function two apples: Java maxOf2(new Apple("Gala", 180), new Apple("Fuji", 150)); // error: method maxOf2 ... cannot be applied to given types // reason: inference variable T has incompatible bounds // upper bounds: Comparable<T> lower bounds: Apple Kotlin maxOf2(Apple("Gala", 180), Apple("Fuji", 150)) // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Apple', // but 'Comparable<uninferred T (of fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2)>' was expected. Apple has no natural order. Should two apples compare by weight, by name or by price? The compiler won't guess, and it's right not to. Make Apple implement Comparable<Apple>, and the call compiles. Or, usually better, keep Apple plain and pass a Comparator where you need an order. The sign picture breaks in one place. A real "fruit only" sign is checked by a person, who looks at the item. The compiler can only trust what the types declare. A class with a grams property that doesn't say : Fruit is still turned away. One real difference between the languages shows up with LocalDate. In Java, LocalDate later = maxOf2(day1, day2) fails, because the strict bound forces T to be ChronoLocalDate. The JDK writes <T extends Comparable<? super T>> to fix that. Kotlin's plain T : Comparable<T> already returns a LocalDate. A bound shuts some callers out and lets the body do more. Ask for exactly what the body uses. One bound per type parameter covers most code. Sometimes, though, the body needs two abilities at once. Bound T, then make Apple fit Run MaxDemo (or MaxDemoJava) and check the four results. Uncomment the heavier("Gala", "Fuji") line, run, read the error, and comment it out. Do the same with maxOf2(1, "a"). Uncomment the two-apples line for maxOf2 and run it. Then make Apple implement Comparable<Apple> by weight (: Fruit, Comparable<Apple> and override fun compareTo(other: Apple) = grams.compareTo(other.grams)) and run again. Bonus, in Kotlin: what type does heavier(Apple("Gala", 180), Lemon("Eureka", 120)) return? Use the probe trick from lesson 1 of this track, val probe: Int = heavier(...), to find out. MaxDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l02.demo import java.time.LocalDate interface Fruit { val name: String; val grams: Int } data class Apple(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit data class Lemon(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit /** The bound T : Fruit means "T is Fruit or a subtype of it", so .grams is allowed. */ fun <T : Fruit> heavier(a: T, b: T): T = if (a.grams >= b.grams) a else b /** The bound T : Comparable<T> means "T can be compared with another T", so > is allowed. */ fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T): T = if (a > b) a else b fun main() { val apple: Apple = heavier(Apple("Gala", 180), Apple("Fuji", 150)) // two apples in, an Apple out println(apple) println(maxOf2(180, 150)) println(maxOf2("Gala", "Fuji")) println(maxOf2(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 30))) // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // println(heavier("Gala", "Fuji")) // println(maxOf2(1, "a")) // println(maxOf2(Apple("Gala", 180), Apple("Fuji", 150))) } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l02.demo.MaxDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l02/demo/MaxDemo.kt MaxDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l02.demo; import java.time.LocalDate; /** Java twin of MaxDemo.kt. A bound written with extends makes the bound's methods available. */ public class MaxDemoJava { interface Fruit { String name(); int grams(); } record Apple(String name, int grams) implements Fruit {} static <T extends Fruit> T heavier(T a, T b) { return a.grams() >= b.grams() ? a : b; } static <T extends Comparable<T>> T maxOf2(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; } // the JDK's own style: LocalDate is a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate>, not a Comparable<LocalDate>, // so only this version can return a LocalDate static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> T maxOf2Flexible(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; } public static void main(String[] args) { Apple apple = heavier(new Apple("Gala", 180), new Apple("Fuji", 150)); // two apples in, an Apple out System.out.println(apple); System.out.println(maxOf2(180, 150)); System.out.println(maxOf2("Gala", "Fuji")); System.out.println(maxOf2Flexible(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 30))); // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // System.out.println(heavier("Gala", "Fuji")); // System.out.println(maxOf2(1, "a")); // System.out.println(maxOf2(new Apple("Gala", 180), new Apple("Fuji", 150))); // LocalDate later = maxOf2(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 30)); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l02.demo.MaxDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l02/demo/MaxDemoJava.java The demo prints Apple(name=Gala, grams=180), 180, Gala and 2026-11-02. heavier("Gala", "Fuji") fails twice with Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'String', but 'Fruit' was expected. The mixed maxOf2 call fails with actual type is 'String', but 'Int' was expected. The two-apples call fails with Cannot infer type for type parameter 'T' and actual type is 'Apple', but 'Comparable<uninferred T ...>' was expected. Once Apple is comparable, it prints Apple(name=Gala, grams=180). The bonus probe says actual 'Fruit': the closest type an apple and a lemon share. In the Java twin, every bad call fails with method ... cannot be applied to given types, and its extra wrong move shows why the JDK writes Comparable<? super T>: LocalDate later = maxOf2(...) fails with inference variable T has incompatible bounds.

h: Bounds and constraints: upper bounds, where, T : Any · Two requirements at once: the where clause
x: A type parameter can have more than one bound. The angle brackets hold only one, so the rest go into a where clause after the signature. Java joins the bounds with &. Here is a function that picks the shortest name from a list, and uses alphabetical order to break a tie: Java static <T extends CharSequence & Comparable<T>> T shortestLabel(List<T> items) { T best = items.get(0); for (T item : items) { if (item.length() < best.length()) best = item; // CharSequence gives length() else if (item.length() == best.length() && item.compareTo(best) < 0) best = item; } return best; } Kotlin fun <T> shortestLabel(items: List<T>): T where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T> { var best = items[0] for (item in items) { if (item.length < best.length) best = item // CharSequence gives .length else if (item.length == best.length && item < best) best = item // Comparable gives < } return best } T must meet every bound at once. A String is both a CharSequence, the JDK's interface for anything made of characters, and a Comparable<String>, so it fits. An Int is comparable but has no characters: error: cannot infer type for type parameter 'T'. Specify it explicitly. error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'CharSequence' was expected. You get two errors for one mistake. The first says the compiler gave up looking for a T. The second says why: an Int isn't a CharSequence, so no T can meet both bounds. When "cannot infer type" appears next to a mismatch, read the mismatch first. It's the real reason. Here is one that surprises people: shortestLabel(listOf(StringBuilder("plum"), StringBuilder("lime"))) compiles. StringBuilder became a Comparable<StringBuilder> in JDK 11, so it sits in the overlap too. At most one bound may be a class. The others must be interfaces, because a class can extend only one other class. Java also wants the class first: Java static <T extends Number & Exception> void numberOrError(T t) {} // error: interface expected here static <T extends Number & Comparable<T>> T clampToZero(T x) { ... } // fine: class first static <T extends Comparable<T> & Number> T wrong(T x) { ... } // error: interface expected here Kotlin fun <T> numberOrError(t: T) where T : Number, T : Exception {} // error: only one of the upper bounds can be a class. fun <T> clampToZero(x: T): T where T : Number, T : Comparable<T> = x // fine fun <T> anyOrder(x: T): T where T : Comparable<T>, T : Number = x // also fine Kotlin has no ordering rule. It just counts classes. The figure draws each bound as a fence around the types a caller may pick. Each new bound moves a fence in, and a where clause with two bounds leaves only the overlap. Use where when the function needs two abilities that no single type in your code names. If you find yourself writing the same pair of bounds in five places, that pair probably wants to be one interface of your own. So far, every bound has asked for more abilities. The last one asks for less: it takes null away. Predict which calls fit both bounds Before running WhereDemo (or WhereDemoJava), decide whether the StringBuilder line compiles. Run it. Then uncomment sortedLabel(42, 7) and run again. Comment that out and uncomment numberOrError. Run, read the error, and comment it out again. WhereDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l02.demo /** Two bounds at once: T must be a CharSequence AND Comparable to itself. */ fun <T> sortedLabel(a: T, b: T): String where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T> = if (a < b) "$a (${a.length}) then $b (${b.length})" else "$b (${b.length}) then $a (${a.length})" fun main() { println(sortedLabel("kiwi", "fig")) println(sortedLabel(StringBuilder("plum"), StringBuilder("lime"))) // does this compile? predict first // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // println(sortedLabel(42, 7)) // fun <T> numberOrError(t: T) where T : Number, T : Exception {} } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l02.demo.WhereDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l02/demo/WhereDemo.kt WhereDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l02.demo; /** Java twin of WhereDemo.kt. Two bounds at once, written with &. */ public class WhereDemoJava { static <T extends CharSequence & Comparable<T>> String sortedLabel(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) < 0 ? a + " (" + a.length() + ") then " + b + " (" + b.length() + ")" : b + " (" + b.length() + ") then " + a + " (" + a.length() + ")"; } // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // static <T extends Comparable<T> & CharSequence & Number> void tooMany(T t) {} // static <T extends Number & Exception> void numberOrError(T t) {} public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(sortedLabel("kiwi", "fig")); System.out.println(sortedLabel(new StringBuilder("plum"), new StringBuilder("lime"))); // compiles? predict first // System.out.println(sortedLabel(42, 7)); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l02.demo.WhereDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l02/demo/WhereDemoJava.java The demo prints fig (3) then kiwi (4) and lime (4) then plum (4): StringBuilder is both a CharSequence and a Comparable<StringBuilder> on JDK 11 and later. sortedLabel(42, 7) fails with Cannot infer type for type parameter 'T' and actual type is 'Int', but 'CharSequence' was expected. numberOrError fails with Only one of the upper bounds can be a class. In the Java twin, sortedLabel(42, 7) fails with cannot be applied to given types, and both bad bound lists fail with interface expected here. Each bound moves a fence in around the types a caller may pick. A where clause with two bounds allows only the overlap.

h: Bounds and constraints: upper bounds, where, T : Any · Keeping null out of the box: T : Any
x: The default bound is Any?, so T may be a nullable type. Most of the time that's what you want: a Box<String?> is a fine thing to have. Sometimes it quietly breaks your API, the functions and classes that other code calls. Here is a small cache that notes any problem found with each crate in the storeroom. The Java version has the same problem, because HashMap happily stores null values: Java class Cache<K, V> { private final Map<K, V> entries = new HashMap<>(); void put(K key, V value) { entries.put(key, value); } V get(K key) { return entries.get(key); } // null means "no entry"... usually } Cache<String, String> problems = new Cache<>(); problems.put("apples", null); // "checked: no problem" problems.get("apples"); // null problems.get("figs"); // null, but never checked Kotlin class Cache<K, V> { private val entries = HashMap<K, V>() fun put(key: K, value: V) { entries[key] = value } fun get(key: K): V? = entries[key] // null means "no entry"... usually } val problems = Cache<String, String?>() problems.put("apples", null) // "checked: no problem" problems.get("apples") // null problems.get("figs") // null, but never checked With V = String?, get returns null for two different reasons: "we checked the apples and found no problem", and "nobody ever checked the figs". The demo prints apples -> null and figs -> null, then its last line: Can you tell those two apart? Neither can the caller. The fix is the bound T : Any, which means "any type, but not a nullable one". Java has no such bound, so the closest it gets is a check at run time: Java void put(K key, V value) { entries.put(key, Objects.requireNonNull(value, "no null values")); // fails at run time } Kotlin class Cache<K : Any, V : Any> { ... } Cache<String, String?>() // error: type argument is not within its bounds: type parameter 'V (of class Cache<K : Any, V : Any>)' // must be subtype of 'Any', but actual: 'String?'. Now V? in get always means "absent", because a stored value can never be null. The same bound helps functions that must return a real value: Java @SafeVarargs static <T> T coalesce(T... values) { for (T v : values) if (v != null) return v; throw new IllegalArgumentException("all values were null"); } String variety = coalesce(null, "Gala", "Fuji"); // the type says nothing about null Kotlin fun <T : Any> coalesce(vararg values: T?): T { for (v in values) if (v != null) return v throw IllegalArgumentException("all values were null") } val variety: String = coalesce(null, "Gala", "Fuji") // String, not String? The parameters are T? and the return type is T, and that difference only means something because T itself can't be nullable. Pass a bare null to a plain T : Any parameter, and you get null cannot be a value of a non-null type. When null already has a job in your API, such as "not found", a nullable T gives it two. Write T : Any. Leave the default when holding a nullable value is fine, as in a Box<String?>. Java types carry no nullability. A Java <T> always allows null. The best you can do is a run-time check, or an annotation such as @NonNull, which Kotlin reads when it calls the Java code. Lesson 10 of this track shows a related Kotlin tool, T & Any. It's for the rare case where one signature needs both a nullable T and a non-null version of it. That's also where bounds stop. A bound says what one T may be. It says nothing about how two generic types relate to each other. Whether a crate of apples may stand in for a crate of fruit is a different question, and the next lesson's. Make a null mean one thing Run NullBoundDemo (or NullBoundDemoJava). Look at the two lines it prints for apples and figs. Change the Kotlin class header to class Cache<K : Any, V : Any> and run again. Java has no such bound: in the Java twin, uncomment the requireNonNull line instead, and see that it fails only when it runs. Fix main so it compiles. How would you now record "checked: no problem"? (One answer: store an empty string. A better one: a small sealed interface CheckResult with a NoProblem object.) NullBoundDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l02.demo /** A tiny cache. get() returns null for "no entry". Is that always true? */ class Cache<K, V> { private val entries = HashMap<K, V>() fun put(key: K, value: V) { entries[key] = value } fun get(key: K): V? = entries[key] } fun main() { // V = String? is allowed, because the default bound of V is Any? val problems = Cache<String, String?>() problems.put("apples", null) // "we checked the apples: no problem" println("apples -> ${problems.get("apples")}") // stored null println("figs -> ${problems.get("figs")}") // never checked println("Can you tell those two apart? Neither can the caller.") } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l02.demo.NullBoundDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l02/demo/NullBoundDemo.kt NullBoundDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l02.demo; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Objects; /** Java twin of NullBoundDemo.kt. Java has no T : Any, so null stays ambiguous unless you check at run time. */ public class NullBoundDemoJava { static class Cache<K, V> { private final Map<K, V> entries = new HashMap<>(); void put(K key, V value) { entries.put(key, value); } // HashMap accepts null values V get(K key) { return entries.get(key); } // null: absent, or a stored null? } public static void main(String[] args) { Cache<String, String> problems = new Cache<>(); problems.put("apples", null); // "we checked the apples: no problem" System.out.println("apples -> " + problems.get("apples")); // stored null System.out.println("figs -> " + problems.get("figs")); // never checked System.out.println("Can you tell those two apart? Neither can the caller."); // Java's closest fix is a run-time check. Uncomment, run, and see where it fails. // Objects.requireNonNull(null, "stored values must not be null"); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l02.demo.NullBoundDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l02/demo/NullBoundDemoJava.java The first run prints apples -> null and figs -> null: a stored null and a missing entry look the same. With the bound, Cache<String, String?>() no longer compiles: Type argument is not within its bounds: type parameter 'V (of class Cache<K : Any, V : Any>)' must be subtype of 'Any', but actual: 'String?'. From then on, get returning null can only mean "not there". The Java twin's requireNonNull compiles and throws a NullPointerException with your message, but only when that line runs.

h: Bounds and constraints: upper bounds, where, T : Any · Java and Kotlin
x: Bounds in Java and Kotlin Bounds.java import java.util.List; class Bounds { // one bound: extends, even for an interface static <T extends Comparable<T>> T maxOf2(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; } // two bounds with &: the class (if any) must come first static <T extends CharSequence & Comparable<T>> T shortest(List<T> items) { T best = items.get(0); for (T item : items) { if (item.length() < best.length()) best = item; } return best; } // no way to say "not null": T may always be null static <T> T firstOrThrow(List<T> items) { return items.get(0); // could be null } } Bounds.kt // one bound: a colon fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T): T = if (a >= b) a else b // two bounds: a where clause, in any order, at most one class fun <T> shortest(items: List<T>): T where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T> { var best = items[0] for (item in items) { if (item.length < best.length) best = item } return best } // T : Any rules out nullable type arguments fun <T : Any> firstOrThrow(items: List<T>): T = items[0] // never null The bounds mean the same thing in both languages and compile to the same JVM bounds. Kotlin uses a colon and a where clause and doesn't care about order. Java uses extends and & and wants the class first. The real difference is nullability. Kotlin's default bound is Any?, so you can opt out of null with T : Any. Java has no nullable types, so every Java T allows null, and only annotations can say otherwise. One small surprise: javap, the JDK tool that prints what a class file contains, shows Kotlin's T : Comparable<T> as <T extends Comparable<? super T>>, because Kotlin's Comparable is declared in T. Lesson 5 of this track explains that ? super.

h: Bounds and constraints: upper bounds, where, T : Any · Worked example
x: Build a size window that works for any comparable type The shop puts apples between 150 g and 250 g on the front shelf, and it runs a sale from 2 to 6 November. You want one class for both ranges: a window with a start and an end, both included. Start without a bound, and see what breaks. class Window<T>(val start: T, val endInclusive: T) { operator fun contains(value: T) = start <= value && value <= endInclusive // error: candidate 'fun String.compareTo(...)' is inapplicable // because of a receiver type mismatch. } class Window<T> { final T start, endInclusive; Window(T start, T endInclusive) { this.start = start; this.endInclusive = endInclusive; } boolean contains(T value) { return start.compareTo(value) <= 0 && value.compareTo(endInclusive) <= 0; // error: cannot find symbol: method compareTo(T) } } Ask for exactly the ability you use. The body only compares, so the bound is T : Comparable<T>. Now <= resolves to compareTo. class Window<T : Comparable<T>>(val start: T, val endInclusive: T) { init { require(start <= endInclusive) { "start $start is after end $endInclusive" } } operator fun contains(value: T): Boolean = start <= value && value <= endInclusive } class Window<T extends Comparable<? super T>> { final T start, endInclusive; Window(T start, T endInclusive) { if (start.compareTo(endInclusive) > 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("start is after end"); this.start = start; this.endInclusive = endInclusive; } boolean contains(T value) { return start.compareTo(value) <= 0 && value.compareTo(endInclusive) <= 0; } } Use it with types that already fit the bound. Int and LocalDate are comparable out of the box. Self-check: why does Window(1, "z") fail? (Both values must be the same T. Kotlin settles on Int from the first one, then reports actual type is 'String', but 'Int' was expected.) val frontShelf = Window(150, 250) 180 in frontShelf // true val sale = Window(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 6)) LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 4) in sale // true var frontShelf = new Window<>(150, 250); frontShelf.contains(180); // true var sale = new Window<>(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 6)); sale.contains(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 4)); // true (needs the ? super T form for LocalDate) Make your own type fit. A plain Int doesn't say what it measures. A Grams value with an explicit order does, and the window needs no change at all. data class Grams(val value: Int) : Comparable<Grams> { override fun compareTo(other: Grams): Int = value.compareTo(other.value) } val frontShelf = Window(Grams(150), Grams(250)) Grams(270) in frontShelf // false record Grams(int value) implements Comparable<Grams> { public int compareTo(Grams other) { return Integer.compare(value, other.value); } } var frontShelf = new Window<>(new Grams(150), new Grams(250)); frontShelf.contains(new Grams(270)); // false

h: Bounds and constraints: upper bounds, where, T : Any · Key terms
x: Bound A limit on a type parameter that promises more about T, so the body can do more with it. Upper bound "T must be this type or a subtype of it", written T : Fruit or T : Comparable<T>. Default bound Any?, the bound a Kotlin type parameter has when you write none. where clause The place for extra bounds on a type parameter: where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T>. Recursive bound A bound that mentions the parameter itself, like T : Comparable<T>: T can be compared with another T. T : Any A bound that rules out nullable type arguments. Multiple bounds (Java) Java's <T extends A & B>; the class, if any, must come first. What is the default upper bound of a Kotlin type parameter? Any?. So an unbounded T accepts nullable types, and fun <T> f(x: T) can be called with null. Why write fun <T : Fruit> heavier(a: T, b: T): T instead of taking two Fruit parameters? Two apples in give an Apple out. With plain Fruit parameters, you'd get a Fruit back and need a cast. How do you say "T can be compared with another T"? <T : Comparable<T>> in Kotlin, <T extends Comparable<T>> in Java. How do you give one type parameter two bounds in Kotlin? A where clause: fun <T> f(x: T) where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T>. Why does where T : Number, T : Exception fail? only one of the upper bounds can be a class. A JVM type has one superclass; the other bounds must be interfaces. What does class Cache<K : Any, V : Any> buy you? Neither type argument can be nullable, so get(): V? returning null always means "no entry". In Java's <T extends A & B>, which must come first? The class, if there is one. Interfaces follow after &. Otherwise javac says interface expected here.

h: Bounds and constraints: upper bounds, where, T : Any · Go deeper
x: Why does javap show Kotlin's fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T) as <T extends Comparable<? super T>> T maxOf2(T, T)? Because Kotlin declares Comparable<in T>, and when Kotlin writes a Java signature for a parameter of an in type, it adds ? super. That is also why Kotlin accepts LocalDate, which is a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate> and not a Comparable<LocalDate>. Java's own Collections.max shows how messy this gets without declaration-site variance: Java public static <T extends Object & Comparable<? super T>> T max(Collection<? extends T> coll) Kotlin fun <T : Comparable<T>> Iterable<T>.max(): T The Object & part is there for backward compatibility: it keeps the erased signature returning Object, as it did before Java 5. The ? super T lets a List<LocalDate> through. The ? extends T lets a collection of a subtype through. Kotlin's version gets the same flexibility from in and out, declared once on Comparable and Iterable. Lessons 4 to 6 of this track build up to reading that Java signature with ease. One more bound rule: a type parameter bounded by another type parameter can't have extra bounds. fun <T, U> f(u: U) where U : T, U : Comparable<U> gives type parameter cannot have any other bounds if it's bounded by another type parameter.

h: Subtyping, and why List is not List · One class, many types: why a class is not a type
x: Start with two words that sound alike. A class is code: a declaration such as String or ArrayList that exists at run time, and that the JVM, the program that runs your code, loads. A type is what the compiler checks: it says which values a variable may hold, and which calls are allowed on it. Every class gives you at least two types, the plain one and the nullable one. A generic class gives you as many types as there are type arguments, the real types you fill its blank with: List<String>, List<Int>, List<Apple?>, List<List<String>>. The two words come with two relations, and they aren't the same. Subclassing is about classes. class Apple : Fruit means the class Apple inherits from Fruit. It's a fact about declarations. Subtyping is about types. A type A is a subtype of B when a value of type A can be used anywhere a B is expected, and nothing can go wrong. The compiler checks that with the substitution test on every assignment and every argument: "if I secretly hand over an A where a B is expected, can any allowed move go wrong?" Usually the two relations agree. Apple is a subclass of Fruit, and the type Apple is a subtype of the type Fruit. Here are two places where they come apart. The first exists only in Kotlin, because Java's types say nothing about null: Java String sure = "Fuji"; String maybe = sure; // Java has no String?: every String may be null String back = maybe; // compiles, and may hand you a null later Kotlin val sure: String = "Fuji" val maybe: String? = sure // fine: String is a subtype of String? val back: String = maybe // error: expected 'String', actual 'String?' There is only one class here, yet one type is a subtype of the other. A String can stand in for a String?, because a String? variable is allowed to hold a string. The reverse fails, because the value might be null. The second place is the classic one. MutableList<String> and MutableList<Int> share a class, and the JVM can't tell them apart. ClassVsTypeDemo in the labs compares a list of variety names with a list of weights, and prints: same runtime class: true (java.util.ArrayList) MutableList::class == List::class: true MutableList::class.java: interface java.util.List Both lists are a plain java.util.ArrayList at run time. Even Kotlin's read-only List and its MutableList are one JVM interface, java.util.List. Those differences live only in the compiler. The next section shows that the compiler has a very good reason to keep them apart. One class, many types Run ClassVsTypeDemo (or ClassVsTypeDemoJava) with the command below, and read the comparisons. Uncomment val narrowed: String = maybe. Predict the error, then run. Comment it out, and uncomment String?::class. Why can't a class literal be nullable? ClassVsTypeDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l03.demo /** Classes are what exists at run time. Types are what the compiler checks. They are not the same thing. */ fun main() { val varieties: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf("Gala") val weights: MutableList<Int> = mutableListOf(180) // the JVM sees one class for both lists println("same runtime class: ${varieties.javaClass == weights.javaClass} (${varieties.javaClass.name})") // Kotlin's List and MutableList are one JVM interface, java.util.List println("MutableList::class == List::class: ${MutableList::class == List::class}") println("MutableList::class.java: ${MutableList::class.java}") // String and String? are two types of one class val maybe: String? = varieties.firstOrNull() val sure: String = "Fuji" val widened: String? = sure // String is a subtype of String?: always fine println("String? holds '$maybe', widened from String holds '$widened'") // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // val narrowed: String = maybe // val k = String?::class } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l03.demo.ClassVsTypeDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l03/demo/ClassVsTypeDemo.kt ClassVsTypeDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l03.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of ClassVsTypeDemo.kt. Classes exist at run time; types are what javac checks. */ public class ClassVsTypeDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> varieties = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Gala")); List<Integer> weights = new ArrayList<>(List.of(180)); // the JVM sees one class for both lists System.out.println("same runtime class: " + (varieties.getClass() == weights.getClass()) + " (" + varieties.getClass().getName() + ")"); // Java has one List interface; there is no read-only List type to compare it with System.out.println("List.class: " + List.class); // Java types carry no nullability: every String variable may hold null String maybe = varieties.isEmpty() ? null : varieties.get(0); String sure = "Fuji"; String widened = sure; System.out.println("maybe holds '" + maybe + "', widened holds '" + widened + "'"); // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // String narrowed = maybe; // Class<List<String>> k = List.class; } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l03.demo.ClassVsTypeDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l03/demo/ClassVsTypeDemoJava.java It prints same runtime class: true (java.util.ArrayList), MutableList::class == List::class: true and interface java.util.List. The narrowing fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected 'String', actual 'String?'. The class literal fails with Type in a class literal cannot be nullable.: the ? belongs to the type, and a class literal names a class. In the Java twin, the narrowing compiles (Java has no String?), and Class<List<String>> k = List.class fails with Class<List> cannot be converted to Class<List<String>>: a class literal never carries type arguments.

h: Subtyping, and why List is not List · Why a crate of apples is not a crate of fruit: invariance
x: MutableList is not a MutableList : one list, two names, a crash on the read Here is the opening's crate in code, with the shop's fruit: a Fruit interface, and Apple and Lemon as two data classes that implement it. Run the substitution test. If the compiler let you use a MutableList<Apple> where a MutableList<Fruit> is expected, could anything go wrong? Java List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Apple("Gala"))); List<Fruit> anyFruit = apples; // suppose this compiled anyFruit.add(new Lemon("Eureka")); // legal on a List<Fruit> Apple second = apples.get(1); // ClassCastException Kotlin val apples: MutableList<Apple> = mutableListOf(Apple("Gala")) val anyFruit: MutableList<Fruit> = apples // suppose this compiled anyFruit.add(Lemon("Eureka")) // legal on a MutableList<Fruit> val second: Apple = apples[1] // ClassCastException anyFruit and apples are two names for one list object: one crate with two labels. Through the "fruit" label, you may add a lemon. Through the "apples" label, someone reads it back as an apple. So both compilers refuse the second line. javac says incompatible types: List<Apple> cannot be converted to List<Fruit>, and kotlinc says: error: initializer type mismatch: expected 'MutableList<Fruit>', actual 'MutableList<Apple>'. The lesson's title is the same story with the widest types there are. Swap Apple for String and Fruit for Object, and the lemon becomes an Integer: through a List<Object> view, you could add 42 to a list of strings. That is why Java won't let a List<String> pass as a List<Object>, and Kotlin won't let a MutableList<String> pass as a MutableList<Any>. This rule is called invariance. MutableList<A> is a subtype of MutableList<B> only when A and B are the same type. It doesn't matter that Apple is a subtype of Fruit: the subtype arrow between the elements doesn't carry over to the lists. Every Java generic type is invariant in the same way. You can force the assignment anyway, with an unchecked cast: a cast the compiler can't check, because the type argument is gone at run time. In Kotlin, apples as MutableList<Fruit> does it, with a warning: unchecked cast of 'MutableList<Apple>' to 'MutableList<Fruit>'. In Java, a cast through List<?>, a list of some unknown type, does it: (List<Fruit>) (List<?>) apples. Then the compiler does exactly what you asked. InvarianceDemo in the labs forces it and adds the lemon: the apple crate holds 2 items, and nothing failed yet ClassCastException: class workbench.generics.l03.demo.Lemon cannot be cast to class workbench.generics.l03.demo.Apple (...) The lemon went in without a sound. The failure turned up later, on a read, as a ClassCastException on a line with no cast in it. It's the late failure from lesson 1 of this track, with the compiler switched off on purpose. The crate picture breaks in one place, and it's the important one. A real crate holds its apples in plain sight, and you'd spot the lemon when you opened it. At run time, the JVM spots nothing: the list doesn't know it was meant for apples, so nothing checks the lemon until someone reads it as an apple. A list you can write to must match its element type exactly. Don't cast your way past it. Invariance annoys people in practice. You have a MutableList<Apple> and a function that takes a MutableList<Fruit>, and the call doesn't compile. The fix is never the cast. Ask what the function does with the list. If it only reads, it should take a read-only List<Fruit>, and the last section shows why that works. If it adds, the compiler just caught a bug: the function could have dropped a lemon into your crate of apples. Java didn't always say no to this kind of hand-over, though. Its arrays said yes. Switch off the check and watch it fail Uncomment the step 1 line in InvarianceDemo (or InvarianceDemoJava) and run. Read the error, then comment it out again. Run the demo as it is. It forces the same assignment with an unchecked cast, then adds a lemon. Find the line that throws. Is it the line that added the lemon? Bypass the check and see. */ fun main() { val apples: MutableList<Apple> = mutableListOf(Apple("Gala")) // Step 1: uncomment this line and run. h: Subtyping, and why List is not List · Java arrays said yes, so the JVM checks every store
x: Java made the other choice for arrays, back in Java 1.0. An Apple[] is a Fruit[], and a String[] is an Object[]: Java Apple[] crate = { new Apple("Gala"), new Apple("Fuji") }; Fruit[] anyFruit = crate; // compiles: arrays are covariant anyFruit[0] = new Lemon("Eureka"); // compiles too: a Lemon is a Fruit // java.lang.ArrayStoreException: ...Lemon Kotlin val crate: Array<Apple> = arrayOf(Apple("Gala"), Apple("Fuji")) val anyFruit: Array<Fruit> = crate // error: initializer type mismatch: expected 'Array<Fruit>', actual 'Array<Apple>'. val forced = crate as Array<Fruit> // an unchecked cast gets you there... forced[0] = Lemon("Eureka") // ...and to the same ArrayStoreException Arrays whose subtype arrow follows their element type, as here, are called covariant. The last section explains the word properly. This is exactly the substitution the previous section showed to be unsafe, and Java allows it anyway, then pays at run time. Every array remembers its element type, and the JVM checks every store into an array of objects. Picture a guard posted at every array, who looks at each item that goes in. When the value doesn't fit, the guard shouts: the JVM throws ArrayStoreException. ArrayStoreDemo printed: ArrayStoreException: workbench.generics.l03.demo.ArrayStoreDemo$Lemon crate[0] is still Gala The guard costs a little on every store. And the error still comes at run time, maybe in a library far from the code that passed the Apple[] on as a Fruit[]. Java arrays said yes in 1996, and the JVM has checked every store ever since. That is why the rule for generics is the way it is. An array knows its element type at run time, so the JVM can check late. A List<Apple> doesn't know its type argument at run time (lesson 8 of this track shows why), so nothing could check a late store. Java's generics had to be invariant, and so are Kotlin's. Kotlin goes one step further and makes arrays invariant too, as its half of the snippet shows. Array<T> is a generic class like any other. So the ArrayStoreException can't happen in Kotlin code that uses Array<T>, unless you cast your way to it. If you really need to read an Array<Int> through an Array<Any> view, Kotlin has a safe way to say "read only", Array<out Any>, which lesson 6 of this track covers. You still meet covariant arrays from Kotlin, because Java APIs pass them around. Arrays.asList, varargs and toArray all hand out arrays whose real element type may be narrower than their declared type. If a library writes into an Object[] you gave it, give it a real Object[]. So far, the answer has been "no" for lists you can write to, and "yes, with a guard" for Java arrays. There is one more answer. Store a lemon in an apple array Run ArrayStoreDemo. Before it runs, predict whether anyFruit[0] = new Lemon("Eureka") compiles, and whether it runs. Uncomment List<Fruit> fruitList = apples; and run again. Compare the two answers Java gives. x: After two sections of "no", here is a "yes" that seems to break the rule. Picture the shop window. The apples sit in a glass display case: customers can see every one of them, but there's no way to put anything in. Calling it "a display of fruit" is honest, because everything you can see in it is fruit. Kotlin's read-only List is that display case. Java has no read-only List type, so it needs a wildcard to say the same thing: a ? in the angle brackets, which means "some type I don't name". ? extends Fruit reads as "some subtype of Fruit": Java List<Apple> crate = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Apple("Gala"))); List<? extends Fruit> display = crate; // compiles: a read-only view, written where it is used Kotlin val crate: MutableList<Apple> = mutableListOf(Apple("Gala")) val display: List<Fruit> = crate // compiles Run the substitution test again, on the read-only List. What can a caller do with a List<Fruit>? Read items, as Fruit. Ask the size. Go through them in a loop. There is no add and no set. Every item of a List<Apple> really is a Fruit, so every read through the Fruit view tells the truth. Nothing can go wrong, so the compiler allows it. That is the whole idea behind covariance: when a type only hands values out and never takes them in, its subtype arrow can follow the element type. Apple is a subtype of Fruit, so List<Apple> is a subtype of List<Fruit>, and List<String> is a subtype of List<Any>. Kotlin's List is declared as List<out E>, and the out is the promise that E only comes out. The next lesson is about writing that promise yourself. Notice what display doesn't let you do. Kotlin's List has no add at all: display.add(Lemon("Eureka")) // error: unresolved reference 'add' on receiver of type 'List<Fruit>'. javac rejects display.add(new Lemon("Eureka")) with Lemon cannot be converted to CAP#1. CAP#1 is javac's name for the unknown type behind the ?, and no lemon is known to fit it. The arrow also points one way only. val back: List<Apple> = display fails with expected 'List<Apple>', actual 'List<Fruit>', because a display of fruit might hold a lemon. Here the display case picture breaks. A glass case is closed to customers, but the shopkeeper, who has the key, can still change what's inside. The list object is still the mutable crate: crate.add(Apple("Fuji")) works, and display sees the new apple. The List<Fruit> type only removes the ways to write through this reference. Read-only isn't the same as unchanging. At run time, List and MutableList are the same java.util.List, so all of this is checked at compile time and costs nothing. Java writes List<? extends Fruit> at each use instead, and lesson 6 of this track maps those wildcards onto Kotlin. You now have the three answers a generic type can give to "is C<Apple> a C<Fruit>?". Yes, for a type that only hands values out, like List. No, for a type you can write to, like MutableList and every Java generic. And "yes, then a guard checks every store", for Java arrays. Here is today's limit. The compiler knows List is safe to widen only because the standard library declared it out. For a type of your own, a dispenser, say, it can't tell, so it plays safe and says no. h: Subtyping, and why List is not List · Java and Kotlin
x: Invariance and arrays in Java and Kotlin Variance.java import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; class Variance { static void demo() { List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); // List<Object> objects = names; // error: invariant List<? extends Object> view = names; // OK: a read-only view, written at the use site Object first = view.isEmpty() ? null : view.get(0); String[] varieties = { "Gala" }; Object[] objects = varieties; // OK: arrays are covariant objects[0] = 42; // compiles, throws ArrayStoreException } } Variance.kt fun demo() { val names: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf() // val objects: MutableList<Any> = names // error: invariant val view: List<Any> = names // OK: List is declared List<out E> val first: Any? = view.firstOrNull() val varieties: Array<String> = arrayOf("Gala") // val objects: Array<Any> = varieties // error: Kotlin arrays are invariant val readOnly: Array<out Any> = varieties // OK: you can read, not write } Both languages make generic types invariant, for the same reason: the type argument is gone at run time, so a bad write could not be caught later. The differences are in the exceptions to that rule. Java made arrays covariant and checks each store at run time. Kotlin makes arrays invariant like everything else. For the safe read-only case, Java asks you to write a wildcard (List<? extends Object>) at every use, while Kotlin's List declares out once, so a plain List<Any> parameter already accepts a List<String>. Kotlin's List and MutableList are the same java.util.List at run time; the split exists only for the compiler.

h: Subtyping, and why List is not List · Key terms
x: Class A declaration that exists at run time, such as String or ArrayList. Type What the compiler checks: a class plus its type arguments and nullability, such as List<String>?. Subtype A is a subtype of B when an A can be used anywhere a B is expected. Substitution test Ask: if I secretly hand over a C<A> where a C<B> is expected, can any allowed call go wrong? Invariant C<A> is a subtype of C<B> only when A and B are the same. MutableList and all Java generics. Covariant C<A> is a subtype of C<B> whenever A is a subtype of B. Kotlin's List, Java arrays. Wildcard Java's ? in angle brackets: a type it doesn't name. ? extends Fruit means some subtype of Fruit. ArrayStoreException What the JVM throws when you store a value into an array whose real element type doesn't accept it. What is the difference between subclassing and subtyping? Subclassing is about classes: one declaration inherits from another. Subtyping is about types: an A can be used wherever a B is expected. Is String a subtype of String?, or the reverse? String is a subtype of String?. A String? might be null, so it can't stand in for a String. Why can't a MutableList<Apple> be used as a MutableList<Fruit>? Through the MutableList<Fruit> reference you could add a Lemon, and a reader of the original list would get a ClassCastException. What does Object[] o = new String[1]; o[0] = 1; do? Compiles (arrays are covariant), then throws ArrayStoreException: java.lang.Integer at the store. Is a Kotlin Array<Int> an Array<Any>? No. Kotlin arrays are invariant: initializer type mismatch: expected 'Array<Any>', actual 'Array<Int>'. Why is a Kotlin List<String> a List<Any>? Read-only List has no add or set, so reading strings as Any can never go wrong. It is declared List<out E>. MutableList::class == List::class? true. Both are the JVM interface java.util.List; the read-only and mutable split exists only at compile time.

h: Subtyping, and why List is not List · Go deeper
x: Why could Java afford covariant arrays but not covariant generics? Arrays are reified: every array object carries its element type, so the JVM can check each store. Generic types are erased: an ArrayList<String> is just an ArrayList at run time, so no check is possible after compilation. Lesson 8 of this track is about erasure. Array covariance is also why Java has the odd "generic array creation" error. new List<String>[10] is rejected, because the array would remember only List, and its store check could not stop a List<Integer> from going in. In the lab's toy model, a generic class hands its arguments straight to its supertypes. Real Kotlin is more flexible: class StringMap<V> : HashMap<String, V>() fixes one argument and passes the other, and the compiler tracks that mapping for every supertype. The rules in the lab still hold; the real checker just does more bookkeeping. One more pair to keep apart: Nothing is a subtype of every type, and Any? is a supertype of every type. Lesson 10 of this track uses Nothing to explain why emptyList() fits every List<T>.

h: Covariance with out: producers · A dispenser only hands values out: covariance with out
x: A producer only hands values out, so the subtype arrow keeps its direction A producer is a type whose values of T only ever come out of it. The apple dispenser is one. So are an iterator, a page of search results, and a Java Supplier, the JDK interface whose get() hands you a value. You call it, and it hands you a T. Nothing about it takes a T in. Here is the dispenser in code. next() hands out the next item, or null when the dispenser is empty. The shop's fruit are the same as before: a Fruit interface with a name and a weight, and Apple and Lemon as data classes that implement it. gala and fuji below are two apples, of 180 g and 150 g. Run the substitution test from lesson 3 of this track on the dispenser: ask whether a secret swap could make any allowed call go wrong. Suppose some code expects a dispenser of Fruit, and you hand it a dispenser of Apple. Every call it can make returns an Apple, and every Apple is a Fruit. Nothing can go wrong. So it's safe to treat a Dispenser<Apple> as a Dispenser<Fruit>. The compiler can't see that by itself. Generic types are invariant unless you say otherwise: a Dispenser<Apple> and a Dispenser<Fruit> are simply unrelated types. In Kotlin, you say otherwise on the declaration, once, with out. Java has no such keyword, so it says it at every use, with the wildcard ? extends, Java's way of writing "some subtype of": Java interface Dispenser<T> { T next(); // null when it is empty } static int totalGrams(Dispenser<? extends Fruit> dispenser) { ... } Dispenser<Apple> apples = listDispenser(List.of(gala, fuji)); totalGrams(apples); // fine: the parameter says ? extends Dispenser<Fruit> plain = apples; // error: Dispenser<Apple> cannot be converted to Dispenser<Fruit> Kotlin interface Dispenser<out T> { fun next(): T? // null when it is empty } fun totalGrams(dispenser: Dispenser<Fruit>): Int { ... } val apples: Dispenser<Apple> = ListDispenser(listOf(gala, fuji)) totalGrams(apples) // fine: Dispenser is declared out val plain: Dispenser<Fruit> = apples // also fine ProducerDemo in the labs runs both versions, and both print apple total: 330 g. Remove the out, and Kotlin behaves like Java's plain Dispenser<T>: error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Dispenser<Apple>', but 'Dispenser<Fruit>' was expected. This property is called covariance: the subtype arrow between the element types carries over, in the same direction, to the generic type. Apple is a subtype of Fruit, so Dispenser<Apple> is a subtype of Dispenser<Fruit>. The figure shows the two arrows side by side. In short, an apple dispenser is a fruit dispenser, because only apples come out. Where you write out matters. Kotlin's out on the declaration is called declaration-site variance: you think about it once, when you write Dispenser, and every user gets the flexible behavior for free. Java's ? extends is use-site variance: every method that takes a dispenser must remember to write it, and the ones that forget are stricter than they need to be. Lesson 6 of this track shows that Kotlin has the use-site form too, for types that can't be out everywhere. A type that only hands T out can stand in for a dispenser of any supertype. Say so with out. That raises the obvious question: what stops someone from adding a slot? Take out away and watch the call break Run ProducerDemo (or ProducerDemoJava) with the command below. Both print the same total. In ProducerDemo.kt, remove out from both interface Dispenser<out T> and class ListDispenser<out T>. Predict which line fails, then run. Put out back. In the Java twin, uncomment the wrong move. Why does Java need ? extends on totalGrams, while Kotlin needs nothing there? ProducerDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l04.demo // The shop's fruit, used by every demo of this lesson (the Java twins use these Kotlin types too) interface Fruit { val name: String; val grams: Int } data class Apple(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit data class Lemon(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit /** A producer: T only comes out. `out` tells the compiler so. */ interface Dispenser<out T> { fun next(): T? // null when it is empty } class ListDispenser<out T>(items: List<T>) : Dispenser<T> { private val it = items.iterator() override fun next(): T? = if (it.hasNext()) it.next() else null } /** Needs a Dispenser<Fruit>. Because Dispenser is `out`, a Dispenser<Apple> fits. */ fun totalGrams(dispenser: Dispenser<Fruit>): Int { var sum = 0 while (true) { val fruit = dispenser.next() ?: break sum += fruit.grams } return sum } fun main() { val apples: Dispenser<Apple> = ListDispenser(listOf(Apple("Gala", 180), Apple("Fuji", 150))) println("apple total: ${totalGrams(apples)} g") // a Dispenser<Apple> used as a Dispenser<Fruit> val anything: Dispenser<Any> = ListDispenser(listOf("a paper bag")) // Dispenser<String> used as Dispenser<Any> println("first from anything: ${anything.next()}") } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l04.demo.ProducerDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l04/demo/ProducerDemo.kt ProducerDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l04.demo; import java.util.Iterator; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of ProducerDemo.kt. Java has no `out` on a declaration, so Dispenser<T> stays invariant * and every method that wants "a dispenser of some kind of Fruit" says so at the use site: ? extends. * Fruit and Apple are the Kotlin types from ProducerDemo.kt. */ public class ProducerDemoJava { interface Dispenser<T> { T next(); // null when it is empty } static <T> Dispenser<T> listDispenser(List<T> items) { Iterator<T> it = items.iterator(); return () -> it.hasNext() ? it.next() : null; } // ? extends Fruit: "a Dispenser of Fruit or of some subtype". Without it, a Dispenser<Apple> would not fit. static int totalGrams(Dispenser<? extends Fruit> dispenser) { int sum = 0; for (Fruit f = dispenser.next(); f != null; f = dispenser.next()) sum += f.getGrams(); return sum; } public static void main(String[] args) { Dispenser<Apple> apples = listDispenser(List.of(new Apple("Gala", 180), new Apple("Fuji", 150))); System.out.println("apple total: " + totalGrams(apples) + " g"); Dispenser<? extends Object> anything = listDispenser(List.of("a paper bag")); System.out.println("first from anything: " + anything.next()); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // Dispenser<Fruit> plain = apples; } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l04.demo.ProducerDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l04/demo/ProducerDemoJava.java Both versions print apple total: 330 g and first from anything: a paper bag. Without out, Kotlin fails on totalGrams(apples) with Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Dispenser<Apple>', but 'Dispenser<Fruit>' was expected. The Dispenser<Any> line still compiles, because Kotlin infers T = Any for that new dispenser. The Java wrong move fails with incompatible types: Dispenser<Apple> cannot be converted to Dispenser<Fruit>. Java's Dispenser<T> is invariant, so each method that wants flexibility writes ? extends. Kotlin wrote out once, on the interface. Covariance keeps the arrow: a Dispenser of Apple is a Dispenser of Fruit, because a producer only hands values out.

h: Covariance with out: producers · Where T may appear: in, out and invariant positions
x: A Dispenser<out T> can't also have a fun refill(item: T), and the substitution test shows why. out lets you pass apples, a Dispenser<Apple>, where a Dispenser<Fruit> is expected. Through that view, refill(Lemon("Eureka", 120)) type-checks, because a lemon is a Fruit. Now a dispenser that hands out apples holds a lemon, and the next next() gives it to code that reads it as an Apple: a ClassCastException, far from the refill. An apple dispenser with a slot for any fruit stops being an apple dispenser. It becomes a surprise machine. The compiler can't allow both things: treating a Dispenser<Apple> as a Dispenser<Fruit>, and a parameter of type T. With out, it keeps the first and rejects the parameter. out is a promise: "values of T only come out of this type". The compiler holds you to it by checking every member that outside code can call for a hidden slot. Each place where T appears has a position: A return type is an out-position. The value flows out to the caller. A parameter type is an in-position. The value flows in from the caller. A var property is both at once, because it has a getter and a setter. That is an invariant position. In a class declared out T, T may appear only in out-positions. Try to break the rule, and the error names the position: Java // Java has no `out` on the declaration, so it checks the same rule where you USE the type: interface Producer<T> { T produce(); void consume(T item); } Producer<? extends Object> view = strings; // strings is a Producer<String> Object out = view.produce(); // fine: T comes out view.consume("Fuji"); // error: String cannot be converted to CAP#1 Kotlin interface Producer<out T> { fun produce(): T // fine val latest: T // fine: a val only has a getter fun consume(item: T) // error: ... declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position var current: T // error: ... declared as 'out' but occurs in 'invariant' position } The full Kotlin message reads type parameter 'T' is declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position in type 'T (of interface Producer<out T>)'. Java's CAP#1 is javac's name for "the unknown subtype behind ? extends". Java can't promise that any String fits it, so it refuses the call. Three special cases come up all the time in Kotlin. First, constructor parameters are fine, as long as they are plain parameters or val properties. class Holder<out T>(val item: T, plain: T) compiles. Building the object puts a T in, but only once, while the real type is still known. A var constructor property is a var, so class Mutable<out T>(var item: T) fails with the invariant-position error. Second, private members are exempt. private var hidden: T and private fun replace(t: T) are allowed, because no outside code can call them with the wrong type. protected and internal members are checked like public ones. Third, private set is not enough. var lastServed: T? = null with private set still fails, with occurs in 'invariant' position, because the property is still a var. The fix is to split it into a private var for the class and a public val that reads it. The lab makes you do exactly that. These rules can feel strict on a dispenser you wrote yourself. They feel obvious on a type you have used for years. Find the positions the compiler rejects Open PositionsDemo.kt. For the four numbered lines, predict the position the error will name: in or invariant. Uncomment each line on its own and run. Comment it out again before the next. Run PositionsDemoJava and uncomment its view.consume line. Where does Java report the same rule? PositionsDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l04.demo /** Which members may mention T in a class declared `out T`? Uncomment ONE line at a time and run. */ interface Producer<out T> { fun produce(): T // return type: out-position, fine val latest: T // val: out-position, fine // fun consume(item: T) // 1 // var current: T // 2 } class Holder<out T>(val item: T, plain: T, private var hidden: T) { // all three are fine private fun replace(t: T) { hidden = t } // private: exempt fun first(): T = item // protected fun keep(t: T) {} // 3 } // class Mutable<out T>(var item: T) // 4 fun main() { val h: Holder<Any> = Holder("Gala", "x", "y") println("Holder<String> used as Holder<Any>: ${h.first()}") } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l04.demo.PositionsDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l04/demo/PositionsDemo.kt PositionsDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l04.demo; /** * Java twin of PositionsDemo.kt. Java cannot mark a declaration `out`, so the same rule shows up * where you USE the type: through a `? extends` reference you may call methods that return T, * and javac refuses calls that pass a T in. */ public class PositionsDemoJava { interface Producer<T> { T produce(); void consume(T item); // allowed in the declaration: Java checks the use site } public static void main(String[] args) { Producer<String> strings = new Producer<>() { String last = "Gala"; public String produce() { return last; } public void consume(String item) { last = item; } }; Producer<? extends Object> view = strings; // the Java spelling of "used as Producer<out Any>" Object out = view.produce(); // fine: out-position System.out.println("produced " + out); // Wrong move. The demo itself prints Holder<String> used as Holder<Any>: Gala. Java reports the rule at the call: String cannot be converted to CAP#1, because Java checks variance where you use a type, not where you declare it.

h: Covariance with out: producers · List is the dispenser you already use, and Java's ? extends
x: You have used a covariant type every day: Kotlin's read-only List. Its declaration is public interface List<out E> : Collection<E>. That out is why a List<Apple> goes into any function that takes a List<Fruit>, with no ceremony at all: Java static int totalWeight(List<? extends Fruit> fruit) { // the wildcard is the flexible part int sum = 0; for (Fruit f : fruit) sum += f.getGrams(); return sum; } static int totalWeightInvariant(List<Fruit> fruit) { ... } List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(gala, fuji)); totalWeight(apples); // fine totalWeightInvariant(apples); // error: List<Apple> cannot be converted to List<Fruit> Kotlin fun totalWeight(fruit: List<Fruit>): Int = fruit.sumOf { it.grams } fun totalWeightMutable(fruit: MutableList<Fruit>): Int = fruit.sumOf { it.grams } val apples: MutableList<Apple> = mutableListOf(gala, fuji) totalWeight(apples) // fine: List is out totalWeightMutable(apples) // error: actual type is 'MutableList<Apple>', but 'MutableList<Fruit>' was expected The two snippets line up exactly. Java's List<? extends Fruit> and Kotlin's List<Fruit> are the same contract: "a list I will only read from, of Fruit or any subtype". Java's plain List<Fruit> and Kotlin's MutableList<Fruit> are the strict, invariant version. Kotlin keeps this promise when Java code calls it. When a parameter's type is declared out, Kotlin writes a ? extends into the Java signature. javap, the JDK tool that prints what a class file contains, shows it for ListOutDemo: public static final int totalWeight(java.util.List<? extends workbench.generics.l04.demo.Fruit>); public static final int totalWeightMutable(java.util.List<workbench.generics.l04.demo.Fruit>); So Java callers can pass a List<Apple> to totalWeight too. The demo's Java twin does exactly that, and prints Kotlin's totalWeight(apples) from Java = 330. Kotlin leaves the wildcard out in two places. One is return types, so Java callers don't have to handle wildcards. The other is a final type argument, a class like String that nothing can extend, where ? extends String would mean nothing. The lab's tests use this rule to check your out: they read the Java signature of your function and look for ? extends. So out is cheap, checked by the compiler, and visible from Java. What it isn't is a lock. Call a Kotlin function from Java Run ListOutDemo, then ListOutDemoJava. The Java one calls the Kotlin function totalWeight with a List<Apple>. h: Covariance with out: producers · out does not mean immutable: the dispenser can still be emptied
x: The most common wrong idea about covariance is that out means read-only, or immutable. It doesn't. out only limits which types can flow in. State can still change. Here the dispenser picture breaks, in a useful way. A real dispenser has no slot for customers, but the shop assistant can still open it, empty it or refill it. out says nothing about any of that. Shelf below keeps its items in a private MutableList<T>, which is allowed, because private members are exempt. take() removes an item and still only hands a T out, the way an assistant can eat the last apple without ever using the slot. clear() mentions no T at all. Both are legal in an out class. Java's ? extends view behaves the same way, and so does Kotlin's MutableList<out Fruit>, the same idea written where the type is used (lesson 6 of this track covers it): Java List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(gala, fuji)); List<? extends Fruit> view = apples; // "read-only" for the type only Fruit taken = view.remove(0); // fine: remove hands a value out view.clear(); // fine: no T involved view.add(new Apple("Pink Lady", 170)); // error: Apple cannot be converted to CAP#1 Kotlin class Shelf<out T>(private val items: MutableList<T>) { fun take(): T = items.removeAt(0) // changes state, only hands T out fun clear() = items.clear() // changes state, no T at all } val view: MutableList<out Fruit> = mutableListOf(Apple("Braeburn", 200)) view.removeAt(0) // fine view.clear() // fine view.add(Apple("Pink Lady", 170)) // error: contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E)' ImmutableMythDemo prints took Gala, 1 left, then after clear: 0 left. The MutableList<out Fruit> view loses its only apple too: view after removeAt: 0 left. Only the add is refused. The Kotlin docs say it plainly: the only thing variance guarantees is type safety, and immutability is a different story. So when you need a class to be covariant, but it also seems to need a method that takes a T, you have three honest options: Move the method out of the class as an extension function, a function declared outside the class that you call as if it were a member. fun <T> Dispenser<T>.nextOr(fallback: T): T declares its own T, so the class's variance rules don't apply. The standard library does this: plus(element: T) and getOrElse on List are extensions. Give the method its own type parameter, such as fun <R> map(f: (T) -> R): Tray<R>. Here T sits inside the parameter of a function parameter, and two in-positions cancel out. Lesson 5 of this track shows why. Split the type in two: a covariant read interface and an invariant read-write one, like List and MutableList. There is also @UnsafeVariance, which switches the check off for one position. List.contains(element: @UnsafeVariance E) uses it, because contains only compares. It's a promise you make by hand, and lesson 10 of this track shows how to break it. That is also where out stops. It only fits a type whose T never goes in. Some types are the exact opposite: a bin you only drop things into never hands a T back. For those, out is the wrong promise, and the next lesson writes the other one. Empty a covariant shelf Run ImmutableMythDemo (or ImmutableMythDemoJava). Before it runs, predict whether take() and clear() compile in a class declared out T. Uncomment the view.add line and run. Read which rule stops it. ImmutableMythDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l04.demo /** `out` limits which TYPES flow in. It does not stop state from changing. */ class Shelf<out T>(private val items: MutableList<T>) { // a private MutableList<T> is fine in an out class fun take(): T = items.removeAt(0) // changes state, still only hands T out fun clear() = items.clear() // changes state, mentions no T at all val size: Int get() = items.size } fun main() { val shelf: Shelf<Fruit> = Shelf(mutableListOf(Apple("Gala", 180), Apple("Fuji", 150))) println("took ${shelf.take().name}, ${shelf.size} left") shelf.clear() println("after clear: ${shelf.size} left") // The same is true of a use-site out projection: no add, but clear and removeAt still work. val view: MutableList<out Fruit> = mutableListOf(Apple("Braeburn", 200)) view.removeAt(0) println("view after removeAt: ${view.size} left") // view.add(Apple("Pink Lady", 170)) // uncomment: which rule stops this? } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l04.demo.ImmutableMythDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l04/demo/ImmutableMythDemo.kt ImmutableMythDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l04.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of ImmutableMythDemo.kt. A ? extends view stops adds, not changes. Fruit and Apple come from ProducerDemo.kt. */ public class ImmutableMythDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Apple("Gala", 180), new Apple("Fuji", 150))); List<? extends Fruit> view = apples; // read-only for the TYPE, not for the state Fruit taken = view.remove(0); // compiles: remove hands a value out System.out.println("took " + taken.getName() + ", " + view.size() + " left"); view.clear(); // compiles: no T involved System.out.println("after clear: " + view.size() + " left, and apples has " + apples.size()); // view.add(new Apple("Pink Lady", 170)); // uncomment: which rule stops this? } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l04.demo.ImmutableMythDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l04/demo/ImmutableMythDemoJava.java It prints took Gala, 1 left, after clear: 0 left and, in Kotlin, view after removeAt: 0 left. Variance never stopped the state from changing. The add fails with Receiver type 'MutableList<out Fruit>' contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E): Boolean'. in Kotlin, and with Apple cannot be converted to CAP#1 in Java: only the in-position is blocked.
