h: Covariance with out: producers · Java and Kotlin
x: A producer, declared once in Kotlin, spelled at each use in Java Dispensers.java import java.util.List; interface Fruit { int grams(); } record Apple(int grams) implements Fruit {} // Java can't say "T only comes out" on the declaration interface Dispenser<T> { T next(); } class Dispensers { // every method that should accept subtypes must remember ? extends static int total(Dispenser<? extends Fruit> dispenser, int n) { int sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += dispenser.next().grams(); return sum; } static int sum(List<? extends Fruit> fruit) { return fruit.stream().mapToInt(Fruit::grams).sum(); } // forget it once, and the method is stricter than it needs to be static int strict(Dispenser<Fruit> dispenser) { return dispenser.next().grams(); } } Dispensers.kt interface Fruit { val grams: Int } data class Apple(override val grams: Int) : Fruit // say it once, on the declaration interface Dispenser<out T> { fun next(): T } // plain types in every signature: Dispenser and List are both covariant fun total(dispenser: Dispenser<Fruit>, n: Int): Int { var sum = 0 repeat(n) { sum += dispenser.next().grams } return sum } fun sum(fruit: List<Fruit>): Int = fruit.sumOf { it.grams } // the compiler enforces the promise inside Dispenser: // fun refill(t: T) would fail with "declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position" The safety rule is the same in both languages: through a covariant view you may take values out, but not put them in. The difference is who carries the burden. In Java, the type stays invariant, and every method signature has to say ? extends, so the flexibility depends on each author remembering. In Kotlin, the author of Dispenser says out once, the compiler checks every member of Dispenser against it, and every signature that mentions Dispenser<Fruit> is flexible without extra work. When Java calls that Kotlin code, Kotlin writes the ? extends into the parameter types for it.

h: Covariance with out: producers · Worked example
x: Make the shop's Dispenser covariant without losing a feature The shop's weighing report takes a Dispenser<Fruit>, but the apple dispenser is a Dispenser<Apple>. The dispenser only hands items out, so it should be covariant. Here it is before the change. lastServed remembers the last item handed out, and nextOr gives a fallback when the dispenser is empty. class Dispenser<T>(items: List<T>) { private val queue = ArrayDeque(items) var lastServed: T? = null private set fun hasNext(): Boolean = queue.isNotEmpty() fun next(): T { val item = queue.removeFirst(); lastServed = item; return item } fun nextOr(fallback: T): T = if (queue.isEmpty()) fallback else next() } class Dispenser<T> { private final ArrayDeque<T> queue; private T lastServed; Dispenser(List<T> items) { queue = new ArrayDeque<>(items); } boolean hasNext() { return !queue.isEmpty(); } T next() { T item = queue.removeFirst(); lastServed = item; return item; } T nextOr(T fallback) { return queue.isEmpty() ? fallback : next(); } T lastServed() { return lastServed; } } Add out and read the errors. The compiler names two members. nextOr takes a T, an in-position. lastServed is a var, so its type is in an invariant position, even with a private setter. In Java there is nothing to add to the class; each caller writes Dispenser<? extends Fruit> instead. class Dispenser<out T>(items: List<T>) { // error: ... declared as 'out' but occurs in 'invariant' position in type 'T?' var lastServed: T? = null private set // error: ... declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position in type 'T' fun nextOr(fallback: T): T = ... } // Java checks at the use site instead: static List<Fruit> drainAll(Dispenser<? extends Fruit> dispenser) { ... } Dispenser<? extends Fruit> view = appleDispenser; Fruit f = view.next(); // fine view.nextOr(new Lemon("Eureka", 120)); // error: cannot be converted to CAP#1 Fix the property by splitting it: a private var (exempt) and a public val (an out-position). Callers still read lastServed, and nobody outside could set it before either. private var last: T? = null val lastServed: T? get() = last private T last; T lastServed() { return last; } // Java: a getter with no setter Fix nextOr by moving it out of the class as an extension. The extension declares its own T, so the class's out doesn't constrain it. Self-check: why is this safe? (At the call apples.nextOr(x), the compiler picks a T that fits both the dispenser and x. For a Dispenser<Apple> and a Lemon fallback, that T is Fruit, and the result is typed Fruit.) fun <T> Dispenser<T>.nextOr(fallback: T): T = if (hasNext()) next() else fallback val apples: Dispenser<Apple> = Dispenser(listOf(Apple("Gala", 180))) val f: Fruit = apples.nextOr(Lemon("Eureka", 120)) // T = Fruit // Java: a static helper with its own <T> does the same job static <T> T nextOr(Dispenser<? extends T> dispenser, T fallback) { return dispenser.hasNext() ? dispenser.next() : fallback; } Fruit f = nextOr(appleDispenser, new Lemon("Eureka", 120));

h: Covariance with out: producers · Quiz
x: Which member compiles inside class Dispenser<out T>? fun refill(item: T) var current: T? = null with private set fun peek(): T? protected fun replay(item: T) A return type is an out-position, so peek(): T? is fine. refill takes a T (an in-position), and so does the protected replay: only private members are exempt. A var is an invariant position, even when its setter is private. Kotlin: interface Dispenser<out T> { fun next(): T }, interface Fruit, and fun total(d: Dispenser<Fruit>). What does Java see as the parameter type of total? Dispenser<Fruit> Dispenser<? extends Fruit> Dispenser<? super Fruit> The raw type Dispenser Kotlin turns a parameter of an out-declared type into ? extends, so Java callers can pass a Dispenser<Apple> as well. It would skip the wildcard if Fruit were a final class, and it never adds one to a return type. class Shelf<out T>(private val items: MutableList<T>) { fun clear() = items.clear() }. Does it compile, and what does it say about out? Yes: private members are exempt, and out restricts types, not state changes No: an out class can't hold a MutableList<T> No: clear() changes state, and out means immutable Yes, but only with @UnsafeVariance on items The MutableList<T> is private, so the variance check skips it, and clear() doesn't mention T at all. out guarantees that no wrongly typed value gets in through the public members. It says nothing about whether the object can change: a dispenser can still be emptied. Java: static int sum(List<? extends Number> xs) is called with a List<Integer>. Which line compiles inside sum? xs.add(5); Integer first = xs.get(0); xs.set(0, 5); Number first = xs.get(0); Through ? extends Number, you can read elements as Number. You can't add or set an Integer, because the list might really be a List<Double> (javac: cannot be converted to CAP#1). Reading as Integer fails for the same reason: the compiler only knows the elements are some kind of Number. From "Subtyping, and why List is not List ": why does val x: MutableList<Any> = mutableListOf<String>() fail, while val y: List<Any> = mutableListOf<String>() compiles? MutableList is a different class from List at run time Through x you could add an Int to a list of strings; List has no add, so y can only read Kotlin forbids Any as a type argument of mutable types mutableListOf returns a Java type that Kotlin can't widen That is the substitution test. A mutable view of the wider type could write a wrong value into the narrower list, like a lemon into a crate of apples. A read-only view can't, which is exactly what List<out E> declares. At run time both are the same java.util.List.

h: Covariance with out: producers · Key terms
x: Producer A type whose T values only come out: dispensers, iterators, read-only lists. Covariant C<Sub> is a subtype of C<Super>: the arrow keeps its direction. out Kotlin's keyword on a type parameter: "T only comes out of this type". Out-position A place where a value of T flows out: return types and val types. In-position A place where a value of T flows in: parameter types. Invariant position A place where T flows both ways, such as the type of a var. Declaration-site variance Variance written once on the class (interface Dispenser<out T>), as Kotlin does. Use-site variance Variance written where the type is used (Dispenser<? extends Fruit>), as Java does. What makes a generic type safe to declare out T? It only hands values of T out (return types, vals). It never takes a T in through a public member. With Dispenser<out T>, is Dispenser<Apple> a subtype of Dispenser<Fruit>? Yes. Covariance keeps the direction of the subtype arrow. Kotlin's out T on a declaration corresponds to what in Java? ? extends T, written at each use site, such as List<? extends Fruit>. Why does var x: T fail in a class declared out T? A var has a setter, so T is in an invariant position. Even private set doesn't help; split it into a private var and a public val. Are constructor parameters allowed in a class declared out T? Plain parameters and val properties: yes. A var constructor property: no (invariant position). Does out make a type immutable? No. It only blocks T from flowing in. MutableList<out T> still has clear() and removeAt(). How do you keep a method like nextOr(fallback: T) on a covariant type? Make it an extension function with its own type parameter: fun <T> Dispenser<T>.nextOr(fallback: T): T.

h: Covariance with out: producers · Go deeper
x: The rule "parameters are in-positions" has a twist when the parameter is itself a function. In fun <R> map(f: (T) -> R), T is the input of f. The tray calls f and passes it a T, so the value flows out of the tray into the caller's lambda. Two in-positions cancel out. That is why map is legal in Tray<out T>, while fun replay(): (T) -> Unit (a function returned to the caller, which the caller will feed a T) is not. Lesson 5 of this track turns this into a sign rule. Kotlin is strict about inferred types too. In class E<in T> { private fun produce(): T? = null; fun use() = produce() }, the private produce is fine, but the public use() has the inferred return type T?, and fails. Give public members of variant classes explicit types. Private members get one more rule, called private-to-this. Inside class C<out T>(private var t: T), the method fun copyFrom(o: C<@UnsafeVariance T>) { t = o.t } fails with cannot access 'var t: T': it is private/*private to this*/. A private member is only exempt when you reach it through this, because another instance o might really be a C<Subtype> seen as a C<T>. Finally, Kotlin leaves the wildcard out of Java signatures when the type argument is final. fun f(x: List<String>) is f(List<String>) in Java, because nothing can extend String. Use @JvmWildcard to force one, or @JvmSuppressWildcards to drop them.

h: Contravariance with in: consumers · A bin only takes fruit in, so the subtype arrow flips
x: A consumer only takes values in, so the subtype arrow flips A consumer is a type whose values of T only ever go in. (T is the type parameter, the blank on the label that each user of the type fills in.) The compost bin is a consumer. So is a Comparator, which takes two values and says which comes first. You hand a consumer a T, and it hands nothing typed T back. Here is the bin in code. drop puts an item in. The shop's fruit are the same as in the last lesson: a Fruit interface with a name and a weight in grams, and Apple and Lemon as data classes that implement it. throwOut is the helper's job. It needs a bin for apples, and drops each bruised apple into it: Java interface Bin<T> { void drop(T item); } static void throwOut(List<Apple> apples, Bin<? super Apple> into) { ... } Bin<Fruit> compost = f -> System.out.println("compost: " + f + ", " + f.getGrams() + " g"); throwOut(bruised, compost); // fine: the parameter says ? super Bin<Apple> strict = compost; // error: Bin<Fruit> cannot be converted to Bin<Apple> Kotlin interface Bin<in T> { fun drop(item: T) } fun throwOut(apples: List<Apple>, into: Bin<Apple>) { ... } val compost: Bin<Fruit> = CompostBin() throwOut(bruised, compost) // fine: Bin is declared in val appleBin: Bin<Apple> = compost // also fine Run the substitution test from lesson 3 of this track, the question the compiler asks on every assignment: if I secretly hand over one type where another is expected, can any allowed call go wrong? A type that passes is a subtype of the other. throwOut expects a bin for apples, and you hand it the compost bin. Every call throwOut can make drops an Apple, and the compost bin takes every Fruit, so nothing can go wrong. BinDemo in the labs prints compost: Gala, 180 g and compost: Fuji, 150 g. So for a consumer, the more general type is the one that stands in. The subtype arrow flips: Apple is a subtype of Fruit, but Bin<Fruit> is a subtype of Bin<Apple>. This is contravariance, the mirror image of lesson 4's covariance, where the arrow kept its direction. Kotlin declares it on the type parameter with in. Java has no such keyword, so it writes it at each use with a wildcard, a ? that stands for a type it doesn't name. ? super Apple reads "Apple, or a type above it, such as Fruit or Object". The figure puts the two cases side by side. The other direction fails, and it should. A Bin<Apple> might be the pot for apple sauce, where the cook treats every item as an apple. Through a Bin<Fruit> view, someone could drop a lemon into the sauce. A lemon in the apple sauce is a mistake a kitchen only makes once: val back: Bin<Fruit> = appleBin error: initializer type mismatch: expected 'Bin<Fruit>', actual 'Bin<Apple>'. The rules for where T may appear are the mirror image of out, too. In a type declared in T, T may appear in parameters, which are in-positions, and not in return types or vals, which are out-positions. Add fun last(): T to Bin, and the compiler says type parameter 'T' is declared as 'in' but occurs in 'out' position. The reason mirrors lesson 4. Through a Bin<Apple> view of the compost bin, last() would promise an Apple, and the bin may be holding a lemon. That's also where the bin picture breaks. A real compost bin gets tipped out every week, and anyone can see what's inside. A Bin<in T> gives you no typed way to look: through in, values only travel one way. A type that only takes T in can stand in wherever a narrower T is wanted. Say so with in. A bin you write yourself is the easy case. The consumer you'll meet most often was written by someone else, a long time ago. Hand the compost bin to the apple job Run BinDemo (or BinDemoJava) with the command below. Every bruised apple lands in the compost bin. Predict: does the wrong move at the bottom compile? Uncomment it and run. Comment it out again. In BinDemo.kt, remove in from interface Bin<in T>. Predict which lines break, then run. Put in back. BinDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l05.demo // The shop's fruit, used by every demo of this lesson (the Java twins use these Kotlin types too) interface Fruit { val name: String; val grams: Int } data class Apple(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit { override fun toString() = name // prints as "Gala", not "Apple(name=Gala, grams=180)" } data class Lemon(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit { override fun toString() = name } /** A consumer: T only goes in. `in` tells the compiler so. */ interface Bin<in T> { fun drop(item: T) } /** The compost bin takes ANY fruit, and never hands anything back. */ class CompostBin : Bin<Fruit> { override fun drop(item: Fruit) = println("compost: $item, ${item.grams} g") } /** Needs somewhere to put bruised apples. Any bin that takes apples will do. */ fun throwOut(apples: List<Apple>, into: Bin<Apple>) { for (a in apples) into.drop(a) } fun main() { val compost: Bin<Fruit> = CompostBin() throwOut(listOf(Apple("Gala", 180), Apple("Fuji", 150)), compost) // a Bin<Fruit> used as a Bin<Apple> val appleBin: Bin<Apple> = compost // a Bin<Fruit> IS a Bin<Apple> appleBin.drop(Apple("Fuji", 140)) // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // val back: Bin<Fruit> = appleBin } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l05.demo.BinDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l05/demo/BinDemo.kt BinDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l05.demo; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of BinDemo.kt. Without it, the compost bin would not fit. static void throwOut(List<Apple> apples, Bin<? super Apple> into) { for (Apple a : apples) into.drop(a); } public static void main(String[] args) { throwOut(List.of(new Apple("Gala", 180), new Apple("Fuji", 150)), COMPOST); Bin<? super Apple> appleBin = COMPOST; // the Java spelling of Kotlin's Bin<Apple> appleBin.drop(new Apple("Fuji", 140)); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // Bin<Apple> strict = COMPOST; } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l05.demo.BinDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l05/demo/BinDemoJava.java Both print compost: Gala, 180 g, compost: Fuji, 150 g and compost: Fuji, 140 g. The Kotlin wrong move tries the reverse direction and fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Bin<Fruit>', actual 'Bin<Apple>'. The Java wrong move leaves out the ? super and fails with incompatible types: Bin<Fruit> cannot be converted to Bin<Apple>, because Java's Bin<T> is invariant. Without in, Kotlin rejects two lines: throwOut(..., compost) with Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Bin<Fruit>', but 'Bin<Apple>' was expected., and val appleBin: Bin<Apple> = compost. A dispenser keeps the subtype arrow (out). A bin flips it (in): the bin for all fruit stands in for the bin for apples.

h: Contravariance with in: consumers · One comparator for all fruit: a Comparator takes values in
x: You already use the most common consumer: a comparator, an object whose compare(a, b) says which of two values comes first. It only takes values, two at a time, and hands back an Int. So a comparator written for all fruit works for apples, for lemons, for any subtype. Here is one that orders fruit by weight, used on a list of apples: Java Comparator<Fruit> byWeight = Comparator.comparingInt(Fruit::getGrams); List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(gala, fuji)); apples.sort(byWeight); // List<E>.sort(Comparator<? super E>) Comparator<? super Apple> forApples = byWeight; // fine Comparator<Apple> strict = byWeight; // error: Comparator<Fruit> cannot be converted to Comparator<Apple> Kotlin val byWeight: Comparator<Fruit> = compareBy { it.grams } val apples = listOf(gala, fuji) apples.sortedWith(byWeight) // sortedWith(comparator: Comparator<in T>) val forApples: Comparator<in Apple> = byWeight // fine val strict: Comparator<Apple> = byWeight // error: expected 'Comparator<Apple>', actual 'Comparator<Fruit>' ComparatorDemo sorts two apples and two lemons with the one byWeight, and prints [Fuji 150 g, Gala 180 g] and [Eureka 95 g, Eureka 120 g]. The last Kotlin line surprises people. If a comparator is a consumer, why isn't a Comparator<Fruit> simply a Comparator<Apple>, the way the compost bin was an apple bin? Because on the JVM, the machine that runs both Java and Kotlin code, Kotlin's Comparator is java.util.Comparator, a Java interface. Java has nowhere to write variance on a declaration, so Java interfaces have none. Kotlin treats Comparator as invariant, exactly as Java does: a Comparator<Fruit> and a Comparator<Apple> are simply unrelated types. It isn't Kotlin being stubborn. Nobody ever wrote the in down. So the flexibility comes from the use site, the place where the type is used. The standard library declares sortedWith(comparator: Comparator<in T>). That in inside the angle brackets of one parameter is Kotlin's spelling of Java's ? super T, for that parameter only. Lesson 6 of this track calls it a type projection, and gives it a full lesson. The JDK, Java's standard library, made the same choice everywhere. List.sort, Collections.sort, Stream.sorted and the TreeMap constructor all take a Comparator<? super E>. If you write your own ranking helper and forget the ? super (or the in), it accepts only a comparator of the exact element type. The shop's shared byWeight no longer fits a list of apples, and the next person writes a second comparator that does the same thing. Kotlin's own Comparable is different. It's the interface for types with a natural order, such as Int and String, and it's declared interface Comparable<in T>, with the in on the declaration. That is why lesson 2 of this track could call maxOf2 on two LocalDates: a LocalDate is a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate>, and so it also counts as a Comparable<LocalDate>. A parameter that only receives your values is a consumer. Give it in, or ? super in Java. The lab's highest(items: List<T>, comparator: Comparator<in T>) is the shape to copy. A comparator takes two values and returns a number. A plain function takes values too, and the same flip hides inside its type. Sort apples and lemons with one comparator Run ComparatorDemo (or ComparatorDemoJava). One Comparator<Fruit> sorts both lists. Uncomment the strict line and run. Then change its type to Comparator<in Apple> (Java: Comparator<? super Apple>) and run again. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // val strict: Comparator<Apple> = byWeight println("forApples compares Gala with Fuji: ${forApples.compare(apples[0], apples[1])}") } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l05.demo.ComparatorDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l05/demo/ComparatorDemo.kt ComparatorDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l05.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of ComparatorDemo.kt. List.sort takes a Comparator<? super E>. */ public class ComparatorDemoJava { static final Comparator<Fruit> BY_WEIGHT = Comparator.comparingInt(Fruit::getGrams); static List<String> show(List<? extends Fruit> fruit) { return fruit.stream().map(f -> f.getName() + " " + f.getGrams() + " g").toList(); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Apple("Gala", 180), new Apple("Fuji", 150))); List<Lemon> lemons = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Lemon("Eureka", 120), new Lemon("Eureka", 95))); List<Apple> sortedApples = new ArrayList<>(apples); sortedApples.sort(BY_WEIGHT); // List<E>.sort(Comparator<? super E>) List<Lemon> sortedLemons = new ArrayList<>(lemons); sortedLemons.sort(BY_WEIGHT); System.out.println(show(sortedApples)); System.out.println(show(sortedLemons)); Comparator<? super Apple> forApples = BY_WEIGHT; // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // Comparator<Apple> strict = BY_WEIGHT; System.out.println("forApples compares Gala with Fuji: " + forApples.compare(apples.get(0), apples.get(1))); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l05.demo.ComparatorDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l05/demo/ComparatorDemoJava.java Both print [Fuji 150 g, Gala 180 g], [Eureka 95 g, Eureka 120 g] and forApples compares Gala with Fuji: 1, a positive number because the Gala is heavier. The strict line fails in both languages: Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Comparator<Apple>', actual 'Comparator<Fruit>'. and incompatible types: Comparator<Fruit> cannot be converted to Comparator<Apple>. java.util.Comparator is invariant on the JVM, even in Kotlin, and the in (or ? super) at the use site fixes it.

h: Contravariance with in: consumers · Function types: in on the left of the arrow, out on the right
x: A function type such as (Fruit) -> String is the type of a function value: a lambda you can store in a variable and call later. Behind the arrow notation, Kotlin writes it as Function1<in P, out R>. The function takes its parameter in, so it's a consumer of P. It hands its result out, so it's a producer of R. A function type is contravariant on the left of the arrow and covariant on the right. Picture the shop's scale. A scale that weighs any fruit can stand in for a scale that only weighs apples. A function that writes a price card for any fruit can stand in for one that writes cards for apples. The String it returns is certainly an Any, too: Java // Java's Consumer and Function are plain invariant interfaces, so say it at the use site: Consumer<Fruit> weighAny = f -> System.out.println("scale: " + f + ", " + f.getGrams() + " g"); Function<Fruit, String> label = f -> "price card for " + f; Consumer<? super Apple> weighApple = weighAny; // fine Function<? super Apple, ? extends Object> appleLabel = label; // fine Consumer<Apple> strict = weighAny; // error: Consumer<Fruit> cannot be converted to Consumer<Apple> Kotlin val weighAny: (Fruit) -> Unit = { println("scale: $it, ${it.grams} g") } val label: (Fruit) -> String = { "price card for $it" } val weighApple: (Apple) -> Unit = weighAny // fine: takes more general input val appleLabel: (Apple) -> Any = label // fine: in on the left, out on the right val tooBroad: (Fruit) -> Unit = weighApple // error: expected '(Fruit) -> Unit', actual '(Apple) -> Unit' HandlerDemo prints scale: Gala, 180 g and price card for Fuji. The last line fails for the apple-sauce reason: a scale for apples only, used as a scale for any fruit, could be handed a lemon. The flip is also why the lab's DeliveryBell<Apple> accepts a listener written for every Fruit, with no extra work. Function types explain the odd cases from lesson 4 of this track, too: the ones where a T inside a parameter was allowed in an out type. Follow the value. In fun each(f: (T) -> Unit), the class calls f and hands it a T, so the T travels out of the class, even though it sits inside a parameter. In fun handler(): (T) -> Unit, the class hands a function to the caller, and the caller feeds it a T, so the T travels in. To get the same answer without tracing, give each position a sign. An out-position is +, and an in-position is −. When one type sits inside another, multiply the signs. A plain parameter is −. The parameter of a function that is itself a parameter is − times −, which is +: Member in class C<…T> Where T sits Sign Legal under out T Legal under in T fun get(): T return + yes no fun put(t: T) parameter − no yes fun each(f: (T) -> Unit) parameter of a parameter − × − = + yes no fun handler(): (T) -> Unit parameter of the result + × − = − no yes fun putAll(xs: List<T>) List<out E> in a parameter − × + = − no yes You won't need the table often. Use it when an error points at a lambda parameter and your intuition runs out. The SortingBin interface in the demo has three members to try it on. The table is the full theory. Java programmers carry a shorter version of it around, in four letters. Swap scales, then test the sign rule Run HandlerDemo (or HandlerDemoJava). Uncomment the wrong move (Java: the two wrong moves, one at a time) and read the errors. In HandlerDemo.kt, look at the SortingBin<in T> interface. Use the sign table to predict which of the three numbered members compile. Uncomment them one at a time and run to check your predictions. HandlerDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l05.demo /** Function types: in on the parameter, out on the result. (P) -> R is Function1<in P, out R>. */ fun main() { val weighAny: (Fruit) -> Unit = { println("scale: $it, ${it.grams} g") } val label: (Fruit) -> String = { "price card for $it" } val weighApple: (Apple) -> Unit = weighAny // takes more general input: fine val appleLabel: (Apple) -> Any = label // in on the left, out on the right: fine weighApple(Apple("Gala", 180)) println(appleLabel(Apple("Fuji", 150))) // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // val tooBroad: (Fruit) -> Unit = weighApple } /** The sign rule: uncomment ONE member at a time. Which are legal in a type declared `in T`? */ interface SortingBin<in T> { fun drop(item: T) // in-position: fine fun dropAll(items: List<T>) // List<out E> inside a parameter: in x out = in, fine // fun peek(): T // 1 // fun forEachInside(f: (T) -> Unit) // 2 // fun keepIf(p: (T) -> Boolean): SortingBin<T> // 3 } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l05.demo.HandlerDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l05/demo/HandlerDemo.kt HandlerDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l05.demo; import java.util.function.Consumer; import java.util.function.Function; /** * Java twin of HandlerDemo.kt. Java's Consumer and Function are ordinary invariant interfaces, * so the flexibility has to be spelled at the use site: ? super for the input, ? extends for the output. */ public class HandlerDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Consumer<Fruit> weighAny = f -> System.out.println("scale: " + f + ", " + f.getGrams() + " g"); Function<Fruit, String> label = f -> "price card for " + f; Consumer<? super Apple> weighApple = weighAny; Function<? super Apple, ? extends Object> appleLabel = label; weighApple.accept(new Apple("Gala", 180)); System.out.println(appleLabel.apply(new Apple("Fuji", 150))); // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // Consumer<Apple> strict = weighAny; // Function<Apple, Object> strictFn = label; } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l05.demo.HandlerDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l05/demo/HandlerDemoJava.java The demo prints scale: Gala, 180 g and price card for Fuji. tooBroad fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected '(Fruit) -> Unit', actual '(Apple) -> Unit'. The Java twin's lines fail with Consumer<Fruit> cannot be converted to Consumer<Apple> and Function<Fruit,String> cannot be converted to Function<Apple,Object>. All three SortingBin members fail with declared as 'in' but occurs in 'out' position: peek(): T is a return (+), and the T inside the (T) -> Unit and (T) -> Boolean parameters is − × − = +.

h: Contravariance with in: consumers · PECS: Java's four-letter name for out and in
x: Java programmers learn variance as PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. It comes from Joshua Bloch's book Effective Java (Item 31), and the Kotlin docs cite it as the background for out and in. A producer parameter gives you values, so it gets ? extends. A consumer parameter takes your values, so it gets ? super. The mapping onto Kotlin is one to one: Role of the parameter Java Kotlin gives you T values (producer) ? extends T out T takes T values from you (consumer) ? super T in T both T T Here is a copy helper with one of each. from is a list the helper only reads, a producer. to is a list the helper only adds to, a consumer. The test copies the morning's apples onto the shop shelf, which already holds a lemon, and into a list of anything, which already holds a paper bag: Java // java.util.Collections: // public static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) static <T> void copyInto(List<? extends T> from, List<? super T> to) { for (T x : from) to.add(x); } copyInto(apples, shelf); // a List<Apple> into a List<Fruit> copyInto(shelf, new ArrayList<Apple>()); // error: method copyInto ... cannot be applied to given types Kotlin fun <T> copyInto(from: List<T>, to: MutableList<in T>) { for (x in from) to.add(x) } copyInto(apples, shelf) // a List<Apple> into a MutableList<Fruit> copyInto(shelf, mutableListOf<Apple>()) // error: actual type is 'MutableList<Apple>', but 'MutableList<in Fruit>' was expected PecsDemo prints shelf = [Eureka, Gala, Fuji], anything = [a paper bag, Gala, Fuji]. The last line fails, and it's the crate of lesson 3 again. Copying a shelf of mixed fruit into a crate of apples would drop the lemon into the crate. The Kotlin version needs only one in, on to. from is a read-only List, which is already declared out, so writing List<out T> would only earn a warning that the out is redundant. Java needs both wildcards, because none of its types carries its own variance. When you design a signature, ask one question per parameter. Does this parameter give me values of T, take values of T from me, or both? Give: out, or ? extends. Take: in, or ? super. Both: plain T. Ask each parameter whether it gives you T, takes T, or both. The answer picks out, in or plain T. A wrong answer is rarely a compile error in your own code, and your own tests pass. It shows up later, as a caller who can't pass a perfectly good Comparator<Fruit>, and writes a cast to get around you. The question has a limit, and copyInto has just met it. A MutableList both gives and takes, so it can't be declared out or in. The MutableList<in T> on to is a use-site projection: MutableList itself stays invariant, and this one parameter asks for a drop-only view of it. The next lesson is about those views. Copy from a producer into a consumer Run PecsDemo (or PecsDemoJava). Both copy a list of apples onto a shelf of fruit and into a list of anything. Uncomment the wrong move and run. Say in one sentence why copying the shelf into a list of apples must fail. PecsDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l05.demo /** Copy from a producer into a consumer: `from` only gives T, `to` only takes T. */ fun <T> copyInto(from: List<T>, to: MutableList<in T>) { // List is already out; MutableList gets a use-site in for (x in from) to.add(x) } fun main() { val apples: List<Apple> = listOf(Apple("Gala", 180), Apple("Fuji", 150)) val shelf: MutableList<Fruit> = mutableListOf(Lemon("Eureka", 120)) val anything: MutableList<Any> = mutableListOf("a paper bag") copyInto(apples, shelf) // T = Apple; a MutableList<Fruit> accepts apples copyInto(apples, anything) println("shelf = $shelf, anything = $anything") // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // copyInto(shelf, mutableListOf<Apple>()) } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l05.demo.PecsDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l05/demo/PecsDemo.kt PecsDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l05.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of PecsDemo.kt. Producer extends, consumer super: the JDK's own copy has both. */ public class PecsDemoJava { // the same shape as java.util.Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) static <T> void copyInto(List<? extends T> from, List<? super T> to) { for (T x : from) to.add(x); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Apple> apples = List.of(new Apple("Gala", 180), new Apple("Fuji", 150)); List<Fruit> shelf = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Lemon("Eureka", 120))); List<Object> anything = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a paper bag")); copyInto(apples, shelf); // T = Apple, or Fruit: both work copyInto(apples, anything); System.out.println("shelf = " + shelf + ", anything = " + anything); List<Fruit> slots = new ArrayList<>(Collections.nCopies(2, new Lemon("Eureka", 95))); Collections.copy(slots, apples); // the JDK version overwrites the slots in place System.out.println("slots = " + slots); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // copyInto(shelf, new ArrayList<Apple>()); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l05.demo.PecsDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l05/demo/PecsDemoJava.java Both print shelf = [Eureka, Gala, Fuji], anything = [a paper bag, Gala, Fuji], and Java also prints slots = [Gala, Fuji] from the JDK's Collections.copy. The wrong move fails with Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'MutableList<Apple>', but 'MutableList<in Fruit>' was expected. h: Contravariance with in: consumers · Java and Kotlin
x: A consumer, declared once in Kotlin, spelled at each use in Java Bins.java import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Consumer; interface Bin<T> { // no declaration-site variance in Java void drop(T item); } class Bins { // every consumer parameter must remember ? super static <T> void dropAll(List<? extends T> items, Bin<? super T> bin) { for (T item : items) bin.drop(item); } static <T> T highest(List<? extends T> items, Comparator<? super T> order) { T best = items.get(0); for (T item : items) if (order.compare(item, best) > 0) best = item; return best; } static <E> void listen(Consumer<? super E> listener) { /* store it */ } } Bins.kt interface Bin<in T> { // say it once fun drop(item: T) } // Bin and List carry their variance, so these signatures stay plain fun <T> dropAll(items: List<T>, bin: Bin<T>) { for (item in items) bin.drop(item) } // java.util.Comparator is a Java interface: invariant, so project it here fun <T> highest(items: List<T>, order: Comparator<in T>): T { var best = items[0] for (item in items) if (order.compare(item, best) > 0) best = item return best } // function types are already Function1<in P, out R> fun <E> listen(listener: (E) -> Unit) { /* store it */ } The rule is the same in both languages: through a contravariant view you may put values in, but you get nothing typed back out. Java puts ? super on every consumer parameter. Kotlin puts in on the consumer's declaration once, and its function types are contravariant in their parameters from the start. The one trap is a Java interface used from Kotlin. Comparator, Consumer and every other Java interface have no declared variance, so Kotlin treats them as invariant, and you need a use-site in (Comparator<in T>) exactly where Java needs ? super T. When Java calls Kotlin, a parameter of type Bin<Fruit> shows up as Bin<? super Fruit>.

h: Contravariance with in: consumers · Worked example
x: Build a delivery bell that accepts general listeners The shop has a bell by the back door. When a delivery arrives, the bell calls everyone who asked to be told, once for each item. The sign-writer listens for apples, to write a card for each variety. The stock-keeper counts every fruit, whatever it is. You want both of them on the bell for apple deliveries. Start by naming the roles: the bell hands each item out, and each listener takes it in. interface Fruit { val name: String; val grams: Int } data class Apple(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit val appleSign: (Apple) -> Unit = { println("sign: ${it.name}, ${it.grams} g") } val stockCount: (Fruit) -> Unit = { println("stock: ${it.name}") } interface Fruit { String name(); int grams(); } record Apple(String name, int grams) implements Fruit {} Consumer<Apple> appleSign = a -> System.out.println("sign: " + a.name() + ", " + a.grams() + " g"); Consumer<Fruit> stockCount = f -> System.out.println("stock: " + f.name()); Write listen with the listener as a consumer of E. In Kotlin, a function type already has in on its parameter, so (E) -> Unit is enough. In Java, a plain Consumer<E> would turn the stock-keeper away, so write Consumer<? super E>. class DeliveryBell<E> { private val listeners = ArrayList<(E) -> Unit>() fun listen(listener: (E) -> Unit) { listeners.add(listener) } fun ring(item: E): Int { for (l in listeners) l(item) return listeners.size } } class DeliveryBell<E> { private final List<Consumer<? super E>> listeners = new ArrayList<>(); void listen(Consumer<? super E> listener) { listeners.add(listener); } int ring(E item) { for (Consumer<? super E> l : listeners) l.accept(item); return listeners.size(); } } Wire it up. Both listeners join the bell for apples. Self-check before reading on: why can't the sign-writer listen to a DeliveryBell<Fruit>? (That bell may ring with a lemon, and appleSign was written for apples only.) val apples = DeliveryBell<Apple>() apples.listen(appleSign) apples.listen(stockCount) // fine: a (Fruit) -> Unit is an (Apple) -> Unit apples.ring(Apple("Gala", 180)) // 2 val allFruit = DeliveryBell<Fruit>() allFruit.listen(appleSign) // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is '(Apple) -> Unit', // but '(Fruit) -> Unit' was expected. var apples = new DeliveryBell<Apple>(); apples.listen(appleSign); apples.listen(stockCount); // fine thanks to ? super E apples.ring(new Apple("Gala", 180)); // 2 var allFruit = new DeliveryBell<Fruit>(); allFruit.listen(appleSign); // error: incompatible types: Consumer<Apple> cannot be converted to Consumer<? super Fruit>

h: Contravariance with in: consumers · Key terms
x: Consumer A type whose T values only go in: bins, comparators, listeners. Contravariant C<Super> is a subtype of C<Sub>: the arrow flips. in Kotlin's keyword on a type parameter: "T only goes into this type". ? super T Java's use-site wildcard for a consumer: "T or any supertype of T". PECS Producer Extends, Consumer Super: the Java rule for choosing wildcards. Function1 The type behind (P) -> R: contravariant in the parameter, covariant in the result. Sign rule Out-positions are +, in-positions are −; multiply through nesting to find where T really sits. What makes a generic type safe to declare in T? It only takes values of T in, through parameters. No public member returns a T. With Bin<in T>, which way does the arrow go between Bin<Fruit> and Bin<Apple>? Bin<Fruit> is a subtype of Bin<Apple>: the arrow flips. Kotlin's in T corresponds to what in Java? ? super T, written at the use site, such as Consumer<? super Apple>. Is (Fruit) -> Unit a subtype of (Apple) -> Unit? Yes. Function types are Function1<in P, out R>, so a function for the general type fits where one for the specific type is expected. Why must Kotlin code write Comparator<in T> instead of plain Comparator<T>? On the JVM, Comparator is the Java interface java.util.Comparator, which has no declared variance, so Kotlin treats it as invariant. What does PECS stand for? Producer Extends, Consumer Super (Effective Java, Item 31). In Kotlin: producer out, consumer in. Sign rule: where does T sit in fun each(f: (T) -> Unit)? Parameter of a parameter: − × − = +, an out-position. Legal under out T, illegal under in T.

h: Contravariance with in: consumers · Go deeper
x: Contravariance explains a detail of Kotlin's Comparable. It is declared public interface Comparable<in T>. So when Kotlin writes a Java signature for fun <T : Comparable<T>> max(a: T, b: T), the bound becomes <T extends Comparable<? super T>>, the same bound the JDK writes by hand in Collections.max. That is how LocalDate, a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate>, gets through a bound that says Comparable<LocalDate>. The sign rule also covers type arguments of variant classes. Inside class C<out T>, a parameter of type Comparable<T> is allowed: the parameter is −, and Comparable's in is −, so T ends up in a + position. A parameter of type MutableList<T> is not allowed in either kind of class. An invariant argument counts as 0, and anything times 0 stays 0, which is neither in nor out. C# uses the same keywords, in and out, for interfaces and delegates, which is where Kotlin borrowed them. Scala writes +T and -T, the signs from the table. One caution for Java callers. When Java calls a Kotlin function with a parameter listener: (Fruit) -> Unit, it sees Function1<? super Fruit, Unit>. A Java lambda fits that type, but it must return Unit.INSTANCE. Kotlin APIs meant for Java callers often take a Java functional interface instead, or declare a fun interface of their own.

h: Use-site variance and type projections · A crate can't pick a side, so you project it for one job
x: A use-site projection shuts one door of an invariant MutableList: out reads and refuses add, in writes and reads only Any? Lessons 4 and 5 of this track put the variance on the class. Variance is the rule that decides whether a C<Apple> may stand in for a C<Fruit>, that is, whether it's a subtype. A Dispenser<out T> only hands values out, and a Bin<in T> only takes them in. Many types can't do that. MutableList<E> has get(): E and add(element: E), and Array<T> has get and set. T sits in both positions, so the class must stay invariant: a MutableList<Apple> is a MutableList<Fruit> only if Apple and Fruit are the same type. Lesson 3 showed what goes wrong when Java arrays pretend otherwise. The trouble is that one function rarely uses both sides. Here is the copy example from the Kotlin docs, set in the shop. It puts the apples from one array into the shop window, an Array<Fruit> that holds two lemons. First, with no variance at all: fun copyRow(from: Array<Fruit>, to: Array<Fruit>) { for (i in from.indices) to[i] = from[i] } copyRow(apples, window) // apples is an Array<Apple> error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Array<Apple>', but 'Array<Fruit>' was expected. Kotlin refuses for a good reason. If copyRow could see an Array<Apple> as an Array<Fruit>, it could write a lemon into it. But copyRow never writes to from. It only takes items out. So you tell the compiler that, right where the type is used, the way the clerk tells the helper at the door: Java // Java arrays are covariant, so a Fruit[] parameter already accepts an Apple[] static void copyRow(Fruit[] from, Fruit[] to) { for (int i = 0; i < from.length; i++) to[i] = from[i]; // the JVM checks each store } copyRow(apples, window); // fine copyRow(apples, new Lemon[2]); // compiles, then throws ArrayStoreException Kotlin fun copyRow(from: Array<out Fruit>, to: Array<Fruit>) { for (i in from.indices) to[i] = from[i] // get() on Array<out Fruit> returns Fruit } copyRow(apples, window) // fine: Array<Apple> fits Array<out Fruit> copyRow(apples, arrayOfNulls<Lemon>(2)) // compile error: Array<Lemon?> is not an Array<Fruit> Array<out Fruit> is a type projection: an out or in written on one use of a type, instead of on its declaration. You haven't changed Array. You've asked for a narrower view of it, for one parameter: "an array of Fruit or of some subtype, which this function will only take items out of". Through that view, get returns Fruit, and set is gone: from[0] = Lemon("Eureka", 95) error: receiver type 'Array<out Fruit>' contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun set(index: Int, value: T): Unit'. Writing variance where a type is used is called use-site variance. Java's wildcards, the ? in ? extends and ? super, are the same idea, and they are the only kind of variance Java has. Arrays are the odd case on the Java side. Java has no wildcards for arrays, because every Java array has been covariant since Java 1.0: an Apple[] passes as a Fruit[]. Instead, the JVM, the machine that runs the code, checks each store at run time. Java arrays never got the clerk's instruction. They got a guard. ArrayCopyDemoJava shows the guard at work: its second copy compiles, then prints ArrayStoreException: workbench.generics.l06.demo.Apple. Kotlin's Array<out Fruit> compiles to a plain Fruit[], so the projection costs nothing at run time. The figure shows the three ways to look at one invariant type: the plain view takes out and puts in, the out-projection only takes out, and the in-projection only puts in. Arrays are rare in everyday Kotlin. The same instruction on a MutableList is one you'll write often. Copy apples into the shop window Run ArrayCopyDemo and its twin ArrayCopyDemoJava. The JDK, Java's standard library, writes its utility methods this way, and calling them from Kotlin is a good way to learn the mapping. Here are two of them from java.util.Collections, with the same contracts written in Kotlin: Java public static <T> void fill(List<? super T> list, T obj) { /* ... */ } public static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) { /* ... */ } Kotlin fun <T> fill(list: MutableList<in T>, obj: T) { /* ... */ } fun <T> copy(dest: MutableList<in T>, src: List<T>) { /* ... */ } Pass the wrong thing to the real Collections.copy from Kotlin, and the error shows how Kotlin reads Java's wildcards: java.util.Collections.copy(apples, listOf("Gala")) error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'List<String>', but '(Mutable)List<out Apple!>!' was expected. Java's ? extends became out. The rule in the Kotlin docs is that Foo<? extends Bar> becomes Foo<out Bar!>!, and Foo<? super Bar> becomes Foo<in Bar!>!. The ! marks a platform type, a type from Java whose nullability Kotlin doesn't know. (Mutable)List means Kotlin can't tell whether Java will change the list. The mapping works the other way too: a Kotlin parameter MutableList<in T> compiles to Java's List<? super T>, and this lesson's lab checks exactly that. So there are two places to write out and in: on the class, or on one use of it. Which one should you reach for? Restock three crates with one helper Run WriteViewDemo (or WriteViewDemoJava). h: Use-site variance and type projections · Declare variance once when you can, project when you must
x: The rule for choosing is short. If every public member of a class only hands T out, declare out T on the class. If every member only takes T in, declare in T. You do it once, and every caller benefits: nobody writes a projection, and a List<Apple> simply is a List<Fruit>. This is declaration-site variance, and it's why Kotlin code has far fewer wildcards than Java code. If the class both takes and gives T, it stays invariant. MutableList and Array are like that, and so is any crate, cache or store with a put and a get. Then each function that uses only one side asks for a projection. Here is a crate class of our own, with one function of each kind: Java static final class Crate<T> { // takes and gives T: invariant private final List<T> items = new ArrayList<>(); void put(T item) { items.add(item); } T top() { return items.get(items.size() - 1); } } static String topName(Crate<? extends Fruit> crate) { return crate.top().getName(); } static void putApple(Crate<? super Apple> crate, String name, int grams) { crate.put(new Apple(name, grams)); } Kotlin class Crate<T> { // takes and gives T: invariant private val items = mutableListOf<T>() fun put(item: T) { items += item } fun top(): T = items.last() } fun topName(crate: Crate<out Fruit>): String = crate.top().name fun putApple(crate: Crate<in Apple>, name: String, grams: Int) = crate.put(Apple(name, grams)) ChooseDemo puts a Gala into a crate of apples and a Fuji into a mixed crate that holds a lemon, and prints Gala Fuji. The plain types still don't mix: val strict: Crate<Fruit> = apples fails, because the projections live on the two functions, not on the class. Java has no declaration-site variance, so every Java class works like Crate. Each method that only reads or only writes must remember its wildcard, and the JDK has hundreds of them. Forget one, and your own tests still pass. The first caller with a List<Apple> finds out. The Kotlin compiler also guards the line between the two kinds of variance: You write The compiler says List<out Fruit> warning: projection is redundant: the corresponding type parameter of 'List<out Fruit>' has the same variance. List<in Fruit> error: projection conflicts with variance of the corresponding type parameter of 'List<in Fruit>'. Remove the projection or replace it with '*'. fun <out T> onFunction(t: T) error: variance annotations are only allowed for type parameters of classes and interfaces. The last one catches people. Variance says when a C<A> can stand in for a C<B>. A generic function is not a type that one thing can stand in for, so out on its own type parameter has nothing to describe. Put the projection on a parameter's type instead, as copyInto does in this lesson's lab. Declare variance on the class when every member uses one side. Project at the use site when the class uses both. A projection still names a type, though: out Fruit, in Apple. The '*' in the second message is for the case where you can't name one at all, a crate whose label has worn off. That's the next lesson. Take from one crate, put into another Run ChooseDemo (or ChooseDemoJava). topName only takes from a crate; putApple only puts into one. Uncomment the wrong move in main, predict, run. At the bottom of ChooseDemo.kt, predict which of lines 1 to 3 is a warning and which are errors. Uncomment them one at a time to check. ChooseDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l06.demo /** Takes T in AND hands T out, so it can't be declared out or in. It stays invariant. */ class Crate<T> { private val items = mutableListOf<T>() fun put(item: T) { items += item } fun top(): T = items.last() } // Only takes out: ask for a take-only view. A Crate<Apple> fits. fun topName(crate: Crate<out Fruit>): String = crate.top().name // Only puts apples in: ask for a drop-only view. A Crate<Fruit> fits. fun putApple(crate: Crate<in Apple>, name: String, grams: Int) = crate.put(Apple(name, grams)) fun main() { val apples = Crate<Apple>() val mixed = Crate<Fruit>() mixed.put(Lemon("Eureka", 120)) putApple(apples, "Gala", 180) putApple(mixed, "Fuji", 150) println("${topName(apples)} ${topName(mixed)}") // Wrong move: the class is invariant, so the plain type still doesn't fit. // val strict: Crate<Fruit> = apples } // Predict each line, then uncomment it alone and run. // fun redundant(fruit: List<out Fruit>) {} // 1 // fun conflicting(fruit: List<in Fruit>) {} // 2 // fun <out T> onFunction(t: T) {} // 3 ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l06.demo.ChooseDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l06/demo/ChooseDemo.kt ChooseDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l06.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of ChooseDemo.kt. Java has only use-site variance, so every class is like Crate: * invariant, with ? extends or ? super written by each method that only reads or only writes. */ public class ChooseDemoJava { static final class Crate<T> { private final List<T> items = new ArrayList<>(); void put(T item) { items.add(item); } T top() { return items.get(items.size() - 1); } } // only takes out: ? extends static String topName(Crate<? extends Fruit> crate) { return crate.top().getName(); } // only puts apples in: ? super static void putApple(Crate<? super Apple> crate, String name, int grams) { crate.put(new Apple(name, grams)); } public static void main(String[] args) { Crate<Apple> apples = new Crate<>(); Crate<Fruit> mixed = new Crate<>(); mixed.put(new Lemon("Eureka", 120)); putApple(apples, "Gala", 180); putApple(mixed, "Fuji", 150); System.out.println(topName(apples) + " " + topName(mixed)); // Wrong move: the class is invariant, so the plain type still doesn't fit. // Crate<Fruit> strict = apples; } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l06.demo.ChooseDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l06/demo/ChooseDemoJava.java Both print Gala Fuji. h: Use-site variance and type projections · Java and Kotlin
x: The same copy and fill contracts with wildcards and with projections Transfers.java import java.util.List; final class Transfers { // dest only takes T, src only gives T: the shape of Collections.copy static <T> int copyInto(List<? extends T> from, List<? super T> to) { for (T x : from) to.add(x); return from.size(); } // only writes: ? super static <T> void fillWith(List<? super T> target, T value, int count) { for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) target.add(value); } // a read-only parameter still needs ? extends in Java static double sumAll(List<? extends Number> amounts) { double sum = 0; for (Number a : amounts) sum += a.doubleValue(); return sum; } } Projections.kt // MutableList is invariant, so each function projects it at the use site fun <T> copyInto(from: MutableList<out T>, to: MutableList<in T>): Int { for (x in from) to.add(x) return from.size } fun <T> fillWith(target: MutableList<in T>, value: T, count: Int) { repeat(count) { target.add(value) } } // List is declared List<out E>: no projection needed (one would only earn a warning) fun sumAll(amounts: List<Number>): Double { var sum = 0.0 for (a in amounts) sum += a.toDouble() return sum } For MutableList, the two versions say exactly the same thing. Kotlin's MutableList<out T> compiles to Java's List<? extends T>, MutableList<in T> compiles to List<? super T>, and Kotlin shows Java's wildcards back to you as out and in. The real difference is sumAll. Java has no read-only list type with declared variance, so every reading parameter needs ? extends. Kotlin's List carries out E on its declaration, so the plain type is already flexible, and a projection on it is redundant. Arrays differ too: Java arrays are covariant, with a run-time check on every store and no wildcards, while Kotlin's Array<out T> is a compile-time projection that compiles down to a plain Java array.

h: Use-site variance and type projections · Worked example
x: Unpack the delivery crate onto the shop floor The morning delivery comes in a crate of apples. A helper moves every apple onto the shop floor, adds up the weight, and empties the delivery crate. The first draft uses plain types. The shop floor is a MutableList<Fruit>, because it also holds lemons. Read the error. fun unpack(delivery: MutableList<Apple>, floor: MutableList<Apple>): Int { var grams = 0 for (a in delivery) { floor.add(a); grams += a.grams } delivery.clear() return grams } val delivery = mutableListOf(Apple("Gala", 180), Apple("Fuji", 150)) val floor = mutableListOf<Fruit>(Lemon("Eureka", 120)) unpack(delivery, floor) // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'MutableList<Fruit>', // but 'MutableList<Apple>' was expected. static int unpack(List<Apple> delivery, List<Apple> floor) { int grams = 0; for (Apple a : delivery) { floor.add(a); grams += a.grams(); } delivery.clear(); return grams; } List<Apple> delivery = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Apple("Gala", 180), new Apple("Fuji", 150))); List<Fruit> floor = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Lemon("Eureka", 120))); unpack(delivery, floor); // error: incompatible types: List<Fruit> cannot be converted to List<Apple> Name what each parameter does with apples. delivery gives them to you, and is cleared at the end, which takes no element. floor only receives them. So for this one function, delivery is a producer and floor is a consumer. Both are MutableList, which can't be declared out or in, so the variance goes on the parameters. Project each parameter. Self-check before reading the comments: why does delivery.clear() still compile through an out-projection? (It takes no element, so it can't let a wrong type in.) fun unpack(delivery: MutableList<out Apple>, floor: MutableList<in Apple>): Int { var grams = 0 for (a in delivery) { // 1. take out: each a is an Apple floor.add(a) // 2. put in: the floor takes Apple or anything above it grams += a.grams } delivery.clear() // 3. no element in clear(), so the take-only view allows it return grams } unpack(delivery, floor) // compiles: 330, and the floor holds the lemon and both apples static int unpack(List<? extends Apple> delivery, List<? super Apple> floor) { int grams = 0; for (Apple a : delivery) { // 1. take out: producer extends floor.add(a); // 2. put in: consumer super grams += a.grams(); } delivery.clear(); // 3. no T in clear() return grams; } unpack(delivery, floor); // compiles Check it from the caller's side. The floor can now be a MutableList<Apple>, a MutableList<Fruit> or a MutableList<Any>. If you later need unpack to read back from the floor (say, to skip a variety that's already on display), that read returns Any? through the in-projection, and the compiler tells you so. At that point the parameter really is read and write, and it should go back to the plain type.

h: Use-site variance and type projections · Key terms
x: Type projection out or in written on one use of a type, giving a take-only or drop-only view of it. Use-site variance Variance written where a type is used, in a parameter or a variable. Java's wildcards and Kotlin's projections. Declaration-site variance Variance written once on the class (interface List<out E>), so every use gets it. Out-projection C<out T>: you can take T values out; calls that take a T are refused. In-projection C<in T>: you can put T values in; reads come back as Any?. Captured type The compiler's placeholder for the one unknown real type behind a projection or wildcard (CAP#1, CapturedType(out Fruit)). Platform type A type from Java whose nullability Kotlin doesn't know, shown as T! (and (Mutable)List for Java lists). What is a type projection? Variance written where a type is used, such as MutableList<out Fruit> in a parameter. It narrows that one use to taking out or to putting in; the class itself stays invariant. Through MutableList<out Fruit>, what do get and add do? get returns Fruit. add is refused: the real list might be a MutableList<Lemon>. Through MutableList<in Apple>, what type does get return? Any?. The list may be a MutableList<Fruit> or a MutableList<Any?>, so nothing more specific is safe. Does clear() compile on a MutableList<out Fruit>? Yes. clear() takes no element, so a projection doesn't block it. Projections limit types, not changes. How does Kotlin show Java's List<? extends Apple> and List<? super Apple>? As (Mutable)List<out Apple!>! and MutableList<in Apple!>!: ? extends becomes out, and ? super becomes in. Declaration-site or use-site variance: how do you choose? If every member only produces T (or only consumes it), declare out (or in) on the class. If the class both takes and gives T, keep it invariant and project in each function that uses one side. What does fun f(l: List<in String>) give? An error: the projection conflicts with List's declared out E. (List<out String> gives only a warning: the projection is redundant.)

h: Use-site variance and type projections · Go deeper
x: Both compilers turn a wildcard or projection into a fresh captured type each time they check an expression: "the one specific type this list really has". That's why CAP#1 shows up in javac messages. Java can also capture a wildcard for a method call, which gives a well-known trick. You can't write l.set(i, l.get(j)) on a List<?>, but you can pass the List<?> to a private generic helper <T> void swapHelper(List<T> l, int i, int j), and inside the helper the element type has a name. The JDK chose not to bother. Collections.swap(List<?> list, int i, int j) assigns the list to a raw List and calls l.set(i, l.set(j, l.get(i))) under @SuppressWarnings, with a source comment saying that capturing the wildcard would need a supplementary private method. Kotlin captures projected arguments for calls too. Given fun <T> swap(l: MutableList<T>, i: Int, j: Int), the calls swap(star, 0, 1) with star: MutableList<*> and swap(view, 0, 1) with view: MutableList<out Fruit> both compile with kotlinc 2.4.21. Inside swap, T is the captured type, so values read from the list may be written back into the same list. You'll meet MutableList<*> properly in the next lesson. Arrays have one more twist. Because Java arrays carry no wildcards, Kotlin compiles Array<out Fruit> and Array<Fruit> both to Fruit[], and Array<in Fruit> to Object[]. From Java, those differences are invisible; the projection exists only for the Kotlin compiler. The door opens the other way too. Kotlin shows a Java Object[] parameter as Array<(out) Any!>!, so you may pass an Array<String> to it, as Java code could. That brings Java's covariance back: java.util.Arrays.fill(names, 42) with names: Array<String> compiles in Kotlin and throws ArrayStoreException: java.lang.Integer at run time.

h: Star projection: when you don't know the type · A box with a worn-off label: List<*> is a list of some type you don't know
x: List<*> is a list of one type you don't know: reads give Any?, nothing goes in, and the star follows the declared variance The shop keeps a daily log, a running record of what happened. The helper that prints lists into it has to accept every list in the shop: a List<String> of variety names, a List<Int> of weights, a List<Apple> from the storeroom. It never needs to know the element type. Kotlin's way to say that is a star projection, a * in place of the type argument, the real type that normally goes in the angle brackets: Java static void printAll(List<?> items) { for (Object item : items) System.out.println(" " + item); // each item is an Object } printAll(varieties); // a List<String> printAll(weights); // a List<Integer> Kotlin fun printAll(items: List<*>) { for (item in items) println(" $item") // each item is Any? } printAll(varieties) // a List<String> printAll(weights) // a List<Int> Read List<*> as "a list of some specific type, and I don't know which". The list really does have one element type, the way the worn box really does hold one kind of thing. You've only lost the label. Java writes the same idea as List<?>, the unbounded wildcard: a ? with no extends or super after it. What can you do with a list of an unknown type? Ask the same two questions as in the last lesson. Taking things out is safe, but all you know about each element is that it's something, so it comes out as Any? (in Java, Object). Putting things in is not safe. The list might be a MutableList<Int> of weights, so no String may go in. Kotlin doesn't even let null in, because the unknown type might be one that never holds null: unlabeled.add("Eureka") error: receiver type 'MutableList<*>' contains star projection which prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E): Boolean'. unlabeled.add(null) error: null cannot be a value of a non-null type 'CapturedType(*)'. val name: String = unlabeled[0] error: initializer type mismatch: expected 'String', actual 'CapturedType(*)'. CapturedType(*) is the captured type from lesson 6, the compiler's placeholder for "the one real element type of this list". Java is more relaxed about one of these errors. add(null) compiles on a List<?>, because every Java reference type allows null, and StarListDemoJava prints after add(null): [null]. add("Eureka") fails in Java too, with String cannot be converted to CAP#1. Java waves null through. Kotlin doesn't even let that in. Everything that doesn't take an element still works: size, isEmpty(), removeAt(0) and clear(). So a function that empties any crate can take a MutableList<*>: Java static int empty(List<?> crate) { int n = crate.size(); crate.clear(); return n; } Kotlin fun empty(crate: MutableList<*>): Int { val n = crate.size; crate.clear(); return n } StarListDemo empties a list of names and a list of weights with it, and prints first = Gala, emptied 2 names and 3 weights. This is the drain function in this lesson's lab. When a function doesn't care about the element type, say so with *. It may take out Any?, and put nothing in. So far, the star has always meant Any? on the way out. That's because List's type parameter has no bound. Give a type parameter a sign that says "fruit only", and the star remembers it. h: Star projection: when you don't know the type · What the star stands for depends on how the type parameter is declared
x: Here are three old friends from this track, each with a star. The Dispenser from lesson 4 hands fruit out. This time its type parameter carries the "fruit only" bound from lesson 2, a limit on which types T may be. The Bin from lesson 5 takes items in. The Box from lesson 1 does both, so it's invariant, declared neither out nor in. What can you do with a Dispenser<*>, a Bin<*> and a Box<*>? Take the dispenser first. A Dispenser<*> might be a Dispenser<Apple> or a Dispenser<Lemon>. Whichever it is, next() returns some Fruit, because the bound says so, and Fruit is the most the compiler can promise. The label is gone, but the "fruit only" sign was painted on the box itself, and it survives. Now take the bin. A Bin<*> might be a Bin<Fruit>, a Bin<Apple> or a Bin<String>. No value is accepted by every one of them, so the compiler allows none. Nothing is Kotlin's name for a type with no values at all, which is exactly that answer. Both answers come from the substitution test, asked about every type the star could stand for. So a * is shorthand for the safest projection that the declaration allows, and what it means depends on the declared variance. The Kotlin docs give three rules: For Dispenser<out T : Fruit>, Dispenser<*> means Dispenser<out Fruit>. You can take items out, and reads keep the bound: you get a Fruit, not an Any?. For Bin<in T>, Bin<*> means Bin<in Nothing>. No value has type Nothing, so you can't drop anything in at all. For an invariant Box<T>, Box<*> means Box<out Any?> when you read, and Box<in Nothing> when you write. (With a bound, Box<T : Fruit>, reads would give Fruit.) Java interface Dispenser<T extends Fruit> { T next(); } interface Bin<T> { void drop(T item); } static Fruit peek(Dispenser<?> dispenser) { return dispenser.next(); } // the bound survives the ? Bin<?> someBin = compost; someBin.drop(new Apple("Fuji", 150)); // error: Apple cannot be converted to CAP#1 someBin.drop(null); // compiles in Java Kotlin interface Dispenser<out T : Fruit> { fun next(): T } interface Bin<in T> { fun drop(item: T) } fun peek(dispenser: Dispenser<*>): Fruit = dispenser.next() // the bound survives the * val someBin: Bin<*> = compost someBin.drop(Apple("Fuji", 150)) // error: receiver type 'Bin<*>' contains star projection which prohibits ... StarRulesDemo prints peek(dispenser) = Gala, peek(box) = 180. The box case shows the Nothing plainly. Assign to the item of a Box<*>, and the compiler says what it expected: assignment type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'Nothing' was expected. With several type parameters, each star is projected on its own. Map<*, *> reads keys and values as Any?. A function type (Int) -> String is Function1<in P, out R>, so Function1<*, String> means Function1<in Nothing, String>. You can't call it, because no argument fits, but you know any result would be a String. Function1<Int, *> is the opposite: you can call it with an Int, and the result is Any?. The same reasoning rules out comparing through a Comparable<*>: receiver type 'Comparable<*>' contains star projection which prohibits the use of 'fun compareTo(other: T): Int'. The figure puts the three rules side by side. A star is about not knowing. Two other types look as if they say the same thing, and neither does. Take from a Dispenser<>, try to fill a Bin<> Before running StarRulesDemo, predict the static type of peek(apples): Any?, Fruit or Apple? Run it (or StarRulesDemoJava). h: Star projection: when you don't know the type · A worn-off label is not an "anything" label, and not a raw type
x: MutableList<Any?> is a list whose element type is exactly Any?, like the shop's drawer of odds and ends: a pencil, a number, nothing in particular. You can add anything to it. But MutableList is invariant, so a MutableList<String> is not a MutableList<Any?>, and a function that takes one won't accept the other: Java static void addPriceTag(List<Object> list) { list.add("price tag"); } static int countItems(List<?> list) { return list.size(); } addPriceTag(drawer); // a List<Object>: fine countItems(varieties); // a List<String>: fine addPriceTag(varieties); // error: List<String> cannot be converted to List<Object> Kotlin fun addPriceTag(list: MutableList<Any?>) { list.add("price tag") } fun countItems(list: MutableList<*>): Int = list.size addPriceTag(drawer) // a MutableList<Any?>: fine countItems(varieties) // a MutableList<String>: fine addPriceTag(varieties) // error: actual type is 'MutableList<String>', but 'MutableList<Any?>' was expected. The worn-off label and the "anything" label are different boxes. The drawer says what it holds, anything at all, so anything may go in. The worn box holds one kind of thing that nobody remembers, so nothing may go in. So choose by what the function does. If it adds arbitrary values, it needs a real MutableList<Any?>, and it can take only that. If it doesn't care about the element type, it takes MutableList<*>, and accepts every mutable list. For the read-only List, the difference disappears. List is covariant (declared out), so List<Any?> and List<*> accept the same arguments, and StarVsAnyDemo prints a = [Gala], b = [Gala]. Java has a third option that Kotlin doesn't: the raw type, a generic type used with no type arguments at all. A raw List switches generic checking off. It exists so that code written before Java 5 added generics still compiles, and lesson 1 of this track watched one fail: Java @SuppressWarnings({"rawtypes", "unchecked"}) static void addRaw(List list) { list.add(42); } addRaw(varieties); // compiles: an Integer goes into a List<String> String last = varieties.get(1); // ClassCastException here, far from the bug Kotlin // Kotlin has no raw types. A Java raw List arrives in Kotlin as List<*>, // so the same write is refused at compile time: fun addRaw(list: MutableList<*>) { list.add(42) } // error: ... prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E): Boolean' A raw type isn't a worn-off label. It's a box with the clerk sent home. StarVsAnyDemoJava prints varieties = [Gala, 42] (looks fine so far), and then the ClassCastException at the read. The Kotlin docs describe star projections as "very much like Java's raw types, but safe". In Java, write List<?> instead of a raw List whenever you mean "I don't know the type". It reads the same, and it keeps the clerk at the door. A list of anything and a list of something are different types. Write Any? only when the function really stores arbitrary values. So far, the star has been about parameters you declare. It earns its keep when a value arrives from outside, and you have to find out what it is. h: Star projection: when you don't know the type · Checking an unknown value: is List<*> first, then each element
x: Some values arrive with no useful type at all. Picture a supplier's delivery note, read from a text file by a general-purpose reader. The reader knows nothing about apples. It hands back nested maps and lists, typed Any?, and you find out what they are. (JSON, the common text format for notes like this, works exactly this way, and so do many older Java APIs.) The first check most people write doesn't compile: if (weights is List<Int>) println("a list of weights") error: cannot check for instance of erased type 'List<Int>'. At run time, a List<Int> and a List<String> are the same kind of ArrayList object. So the JVM, the machine that runs the code, can check the class and nothing more. That's the torn-off label that lesson 1 warned about, and lesson 8 of this track explains it in full. Here the worn-label picture breaks. In the storeroom, you could open the box, look at one apple, and know what the whole box holds. The JVM can look at each element, but the elements can't tell it the list's type: an empty list, or one that starts with an apple, says nothing about the rest. So the rule is: check with a star, then check each element you use: Java static List<Integer> weightsIn(Object note) { List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>(); if (note instanceof List<?> list) { for (Object e : list) if (e instanceof Integer i) out.add(i); // check every element } return out; } Kotlin fun weightsIn(note: Any?): List<Int> { if (note !is List<*>) return emptyList() return note.mapNotNull { it as? Int } // note is now a List<*>; check each element } The note in IsCheckDemo has a stray word in its list of weights, listOf(180, "bruised", 150): somebody wrote down what they saw instead of what they weighed. weightsIn skips the word and prints weights = [180, 150]. After the !is List<*> line returns early, the compiler smart-casts note to List<*> for the rest of the function: it treats note as a List<*> without an explicit cast, because it has just checked. A when with is List<*> and is Map<*, *> branches does the same in each branch, and the demo's shape function uses one. Java's instanceof List<?> list, pattern matching for instanceof (final since Java 16), gives you the same kind of typed variable. Java's error for the bad check is Object cannot be safely cast to List<Integer>. One full check does compile: when the compiler already knows the type argument. With c: Collection<String>, c is List<String> is fine, because only the class part needs checking at run time. The shortcut to avoid is note as List<Int>. It compiles with an unchecked-cast warning, and it succeeds for any list at all. The ClassCastException comes later, at whichever line first reads "bruised" as an Int. Checking the elements costs one line, and it fails in the right place. Better still, avoid the untyped route when you can. Many readers can fill a class of your own directly, such as a DeliveryNote with a weights: List<Int> property, so the checking happens once, inside the library.
