h: Star projection: when you don't know the type · Java and Kotlin
x: Unknown type arguments: Kotlin's * and Java's ? ShopLog.java import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.stream.Collectors; final class ShopLog { static String describe(Object value) { if (value == null) return "nothing"; if (value instanceof String s) return "text " + s; if (value instanceof List<?> l) return "list of " + l.size(); // List<String> would not compile if (value instanceof Map<?, ?> m) return "map of " + m.size(); return "other"; } static String render(Map<?, ?> map) { // keys and values are Object return map.entrySet().stream() .sorted(Comparator.comparing(e -> String.valueOf(e.getKey()))) .map(e -> e.getKey() + "=" + (e.getValue() instanceof Map<?, ?> m ? render(m) : e.getValue())) .collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "{", "}")); } static int drain(List<?> crate) { // not a raw List: checks stay on int n = crate.size(); crate.clear(); return n; } } ShopLog.kt fun describe(value: Any?): String = when (value) { null -> "nothing" is String -> "text $value" is List<*> -> "list of ${value.size}" // List<String> would not compile is Map<*, *> -> "map of ${value.size}" else -> "other" } fun render(map: Map<*, *>): String = // keys and values are Any? map.entries .sortedBy { it.key.toString() } .joinToString(", ", "{", "}") { (k, v) -> "$k=${if (v is Map<*, *>) render(v) else v}" } fun drain(crate: MutableList<*>): Int { // Kotlin has no raw types val n = crate.size crate.clear() return n } Kotlin's MutableList<*> compiles to Java's List<?>, and the two behave almost the same: reads give Any? or Object, writes of real values are refused, and members that take no element still work. Three things differ. Java lets you pass null through a ?; Kotlin refuses, because the unknown type might be non-nullable. Java still has raw types, which switch checking off; Kotlin has none, and shows a Java raw List as List<*>. And Kotlin works out what * means from the declaration's variance, so a star on an in parameter becomes in Nothing, and a star on an out T : Fruit keeps the Fruit bound, while Java applies the same capture rules to every wildcard.

h: Star projection: when you don't know the type · Worked example
x: Render an untyped delivery note for the shop log A supplier's delivery note is read into a map whose types you don't control. The first draft of the log renderer asks for Map<Any?, Any?>, to be "as general as possible". In a test, the note is a Map<String, Int>. Read the error. fun render(map: Map<Any?, Any?>): String = map.toString() val note: Map<String, Int> = mapOf("crates" to 4) render(note) // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Map<String, Int>', but 'Map<Any?, Any?>' was expected. static String render(Map<Object, Object> map) { return map.toString(); } Map<String, Integer> note = Map.of("crates", 4); render(note); // error: incompatible types: Map<String,Integer> cannot be converted to Map<Object,Object> Map<K, out V> is covariant in V but invariant in K, so a Map<String, Int> is not a Map<Any?, Any?>. The renderer never puts anything into the map; it only reads. So it doesn't need to name either type. Use one star per type parameter. fun render(map: Map<*, *>): String = map.entries .sortedBy { it.key.toString() } // 1. keys are Any?: toString() works, even on null .joinToString(", ", "{", "}") { (k, v) -> "$k=$v" } static String render(Map<?, ?> map) { return map.entrySet().stream() .sorted(Comparator.comparing(e -> String.valueOf(e.getKey()))) // 1. keys are Object .map(e -> e.getKey() + "=" + e.getValue()) .collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "{", "}")); } Notes nest: the apple field is itself a map. Check the value's shape with a star, and the smart cast gives you a Map<*, *> to render the same way. Self-check before reading the comment: why not v is Map<String, Any?>? (Type arguments are erased, so the compiler refuses that check.) fun render(map: Map<*, *>): String = map.entries .sortedBy { it.key.toString() } .joinToString(", ", "{", "}") { (k, v) -> val shown = if (v is Map<*, *>) render(v) else v.toString() // 2. smart cast to Map<*, *> "$k=$shown" } render(mapOf("crates" to 4, "apple" to mapOf("name" to "Gala", "grams" to 180))) // {apple={grams=180, name=Gala}, crates=4} static String render(Map<?, ?> map) { return map.entrySet().stream() .sorted(Comparator.comparing(e -> String.valueOf(e.getKey()))) .map(e -> e.getKey() + "=" + (e.getValue() instanceof Map<?, ?> m ? render(m) : e.getValue())) // 2. pattern match .collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "{", "}")); } Now any map fits: a Map<String, Int>, a Map<String, Any?>, the Map<*, *> that a file reader returns, or a map with Int keys. The renderer is honest about what it knows. This is the render function in the lab, and the tests check exactly this output.

Which line compiles? unlabeled.add("Fuji") unlabeled.add(null) unlabeled.removeAt(0) val s: String = unlabeled[0] removeAt takes an index, not an element, so the star doesn't block it. Both add calls put an element of the unknown type in, which Kotlin refuses, even null, since the type might be non-nullable. A read gives only CapturedType(*), which is not known to be a String. interface Dispenser<out T : Fruit> { fun next(): T } and fun f(d: Dispenser<*>). What is the static type of d.next() inside f? Fruit Any? Nothing It doesn't compile: you can't call anything on a star projection For an out type parameter with a bound, Dispenser<*> means Dispenser<out Fruit>, so reads keep the bound. Any? is what you'd get with no bound. Nothing is what a star gives on the putting-in side of an in or invariant type parameter. You need a function that adds a "price tag" string to whatever list a caller passes: a MutableList<String>, a MutableList<Any> or a MutableList<CharSequence>. Which parameter type fits? MutableList<*> MutableList<Any?> List<Any?> MutableList<in String> The function puts Strings in and never reads, so it is a consumer: MutableList<in String> accepts lists of String or of any supertype. A star forbids add. MutableList<Any?> accepts only lists of exactly Any?. List has no add at all. Use * when you neither read typed values nor write, and in when you write. The cast that javac inserted at varieties.get(1) fails, far from the bad write. ArrayStoreException is the array version of this check, which lists don't have. h: Star projection: when you don't know the type · Key terms
x: Star projection C<*>: a C of some type argument you don't know. Kotlin picks the safest projection for it. Unbounded wildcard Java's ? with no bound, as in List<?>: the Java twin of *. Raw type A Java generic type used with no type arguments at all (List). Generic checks are off for it. in Nothing What a star means on the putting-in side: only a Nothing could go in, and no such value exists. Smart cast After if (x is List<*>), the compiler treats x as a List<*> without an explicit cast. Erased type A type argument that exists only at compile time. At run time a List<String> is just a List. What does List<*> mean? A list of one specific element type that you don't know or don't care about. Reads come out as Any?. Java's spelling is List<?>. Can you call add(null) on a MutableList<*>? Not in Kotlin: Null cannot be a value of a non-null type 'CapturedType(*)'. Java's List<?> does allow add(null). For interface Bin<in T>, what does Bin<*> mean? Bin<in Nothing>: no value fits, so you can't call drop at all. For interface Dispenser<out T : Fruit>, what does Dispenser<*> mean? Dispenser<out Fruit>: reads give Fruit, because the bound survives the star. Why does fun f(l: MutableList<Any?>) reject a MutableList<String>? MutableList is invariant, and Any? is one specific type argument. Use MutableList<*> if f doesn't need to add. How does Kotlin see a Java parameter of raw type List? As a star projection, List<*>, so Kotlin code can't write unchecked elements into it. note: Any?. Why note is List<*> and not note is List<Int>? Type arguments are erased at run time, so the JVM can only check the class. Check with a star, then check each element.

h: Star projection: when you don't know the type · Go deeper
x: Kotlin can still call a generic function with a star-projected argument. Given fun <T> swap(l: MutableList<T>, i: Int, j: Int), the call swap(unlabeled, 0, 1) with unlabeled: MutableList<*> compiles with kotlinc 2.4.21 and swaps the two elements. The compiler captures the unknown element type as T for that one call, so inside swap a value read from the list may be written back into the same list. Java does the same with a private helper method, the "capture helper" pattern; the JDK's Collections.swap(List<?> list, int i, int j) skips it and uses a raw type under @SuppressWarnings. The Map interface has a detail worth knowing. It is declared Map<K, out V>, invariant in K. So on a Map<*, *>, the member get(key: K) would take in Nothing, and you could never look anything up. The standard library adds an extension, Map<out K, V>.get(key: K), so note["weights"] on a Map<*, *> still compiles and returns Any?. Stars also appear in class literals: Map::class.java is a Class<Map<*, *>>, and listOf(1)::class is a KClass<out List<Int>>. The class object of a generic class exists once for all type arguments, so it can't carry them. Lesson 9 of this track is about exactly that. And in Kotlin's own reflection, typeOf<List<*>>().arguments prints [*]: the star is part of the type, not an absence of one.

h: Type erasure and reified type parameters · The label comes off after the check: type erasure
x: The last lesson hit a wall: is List<Int> doesn't compile. Here is why. Both compilers check type arguments, the real types in the angle brackets, and then remove them. At run time, a list of variety names and a list of weights are the same kind of object: Java List<String> varieties = new ArrayList<>(); List<Integer> weights = new ArrayList<>(); System.out.println(varieties.getClass() == weights.getClass()); // true: both are java.util.ArrayList Kotlin val varieties = ArrayList<String>() val weights = ArrayList<Int>() println(varieties.javaClass == weights.javaClass) // true: both are java.util.ArrayList This is type erasure: the compiler checks each type argument, then leaves it out of the compiled code, so objects carry no record of it. It's the torn-off label. Kotlin compiles to the same JVM as Java, the machine that runs both, and inherits the rule. In both languages, the ArrayList object has no field that says String. Here is what both compilers leave in the class file, the compiled form of a class that the JVM loads. Each type parameter becomes its bound, the limit from lesson 2: a plain T becomes Object, and T : Comparable<T> becomes Comparable. So List.get returns an Object. Where your code needs a String, the compiler inserts a checkcast right after the call: an instruction in the class file (its bytecode) that checks the object's class at run time, and throws ClassCastException if it's wrong. Run javap -c, the JDK tool that prints a class file's instructions, on any class that reads from a List<String>, and you'll see one. That inserted cast is the line that throws in the last example below. Three things follow, and each has an error you'll meet: A type check can test only the class. x is List<String> fails with cannot check for instance of erased type 'List<String>'., and is T fails the same way. Java says Object cannot be safely cast to List<String>. You can't create a T. Kotlin's T() gives type parameter 'T' is not an expression., and Java's new T() gives unexpected type. A cast to a generic type checks only the class. This one compiles, with a warning, and it's the dangerous one: Java @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") List<String> lies = (List<String>) (Object) List.of(180, 150); lies.size(); // 2: the cast "worked" String first = lies.get(0); // ClassCastException: Integer cannot be cast to String Kotlin @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") val lies = listOf(180, 150) as Any as List<String> lies.size // 2: the cast "worked" val first: String = lies[0] // ClassCastException: Integer cannot be cast to String ErasureDemo prints the cast worked, size = 2, then ClassCastException at the read: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.lang.String. The cast worked. It just didn't check anything. The list now claims to hold names and holds weights, a state called heap pollution. The exception appears at the first read that needs a String, which may be in another class, written much later. Here the torn-label picture breaks a little, because not every label comes off. The signatures of declarations (a field's type, a method's parameters, a class's superclass) stay in the class file. Reflection, the API that lets code inspect classes while it runs, can read them: Field.getGenericType() on a List<String> field returns java.util.List<java.lang.String>. What erasure removes is the type argument of each object. Lesson 9 of this track puts the surviving part to work. A cast to a generic type checks only the class. Don't trust it to check the elements. So by the time an ordinary generic function runs, its T is gone. Kotlin has one way to bring it back. Watch a cast succeed and a read fail Before you run ErasureDemo and ErasureDemoJava, predict which of the three numbered steps throws. Run them. Then uncomment wrong move 1 in either file, predict the error, run. Uncomment wrong move 2 (a top-level function) and run. Put both back. h: Type erasure and reified type parameters · A clerk who copies the label onto a note: inline and reified
x: Erasure removes T, and inline with reified writes the real class into each call site Picture a second clerk at the door. This one knows the labels are about to come off. So before a label goes, the clerk copies it onto a note and pins the note to the job: "this job: apples". When the job reaches the shop floor, whoever does it can read the note. Kotlin's version of that clerk has two parts. Mark a function inline, and the compiler doesn't build one shared body that every caller jumps to. It copies the function's body into each place that calls it. At each of those places, the type argument is known, because a call like isA<Apple>() is being compiled right there, with Apple in plain sight. Then mark the type parameter reified, from a word that means "made into a real thing". The compiler writes that real class into the copied body: Java // Java has no reified type parameters. The closest equivalent: pass the Class yourself. static boolean isA(Object x, Class<?> type) { return type.isInstance(x); } static <T> List<T> filterIsInstance(List<?> items, Class<T> type) { return items.stream().filter(type::isInstance).map(type::cast).toList(); } isA(gala, Apple.class); // true filterIsInstance(delivery, Apple.class); // [Gala, Fuji] Kotlin inline fun <reified T> Any?.isA(): Boolean = this is T // a real instanceof after inlining gala.isA<Apple>() // true delivery.filterIsInstance<Apple>() // [Gala, Fuji]: the standard library's reified filter ReifiedDemo sorts a mixed delivery of two apples, a lemon, a paper bag and a null, and prints apples: [Gala, Fuji] and lemons: [Eureka]. The figure shows what happened. After inlining, gala.isA<Apple>() isn't a call any more. In the caller's own bytecode, it has become gala instanceof Apple. Inside a reified function, you get back what erasure took away: x is T, x as T and x as? T with a real check, plus T::class and T::class.java. The standard library relies on this for filterIsInstance<T>(), emptyArray<T>() and typeOf<T>(), which lesson 9 covers. The rules follow from how it works: You write Kotlin says fun <reified T> notInline(x: Any) = x is T only type parameters of inline functions can be reified. fun <T> forward(x: Any) = x.isA<T>() cannot use 'T' as reified type parameter. Use a class instead. classOf<Nothing>(TODO()) cannot use 'Nothing' as reified type parameter. The first row is a clerk with no job to pin the note to. Without inline there is one shared body, compiled once for every caller, so there's nowhere to write the class. The second row matters most in practice. A reified function can only be called with a type the caller knows. If the caller is itself generic, with an ordinary T, its own label is already gone, so there is nothing to copy onto the note. The requirement spreads upward: the caller must be inline with a reified T too, or it must pass a real class. Inside an ordinary generic function, T is gone. Make the function inline and T reified when you need its class. Java has no such clerk. It has been passing the class by hand since Java 5. Sort a mixed delivery with a reified T Run ReifiedDemo (or ReifiedDemoJava, which passes Class objects instead). Uncomment the two wrong moves at the bottom of ReifiedDemo.kt one at a time. Predict, run. Remove reified from isA, but keep inline. Run again: does inline alone help? ReifiedDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l08.demo // The shop's fruit, used by the demos of this lesson (the Java twins use these Kotlin types too) interface Fruit { val name: String; val grams: Int } data class Apple(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit { override fun toString() = name // prints as "Gala", not "Apple(name=Gala, grams=180)" } data class Lemon(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit { override fun toString() = name } /** inline copies the body into each caller; reified copies the caller's real T in with it. */ inline fun <reified T> Any?.isA(): Boolean = this is T inline fun <reified T : Any> nameOf(): String = T::class.java.simpleName fun main() { val delivery: List<Any?> = listOf(Apple("Gala", 180), "a paper bag", null, Lemon("Eureka", 120), Apple("Fuji", 150)) println("Gala isA<Apple>() = ${delivery[0].isA<Apple>()}, the bag isA<Apple>() = ${delivery[1].isA<Apple>()}") println("apples: ${delivery.filterIsInstance<Apple>()}") // the standard library's reified filter println("lemons: ${delivery.filterIsInstance<Lemon>()}") println("nameOf<Lemon>() = ${nameOf<Lemon>()}") } // Wrong moves. h: Type erasure and reified type parameters · Java hands over the class itself: Class tokens
x: Before reified, the standard answer was a class token: pass the Class<T> object as an argument, and let it do the run-time work that the erased T can't. Java never got the note, so it carries the label around by hand. Many Java libraries still look like this, such as a database library's find(Apple.class, id) or a text reader's read(text, Apple.class). type.isInstance(x) is a checked is T, and type.cast(x) is a checked as T, with no warning. Kotlin writes the same token as Apple::class.java. Good Kotlin libraries offer both. A core function takes a Class<T> (or a KClass<T>, Kotlin's own class object, which lesson 9 covers) and works for everyone. A one-line reified wrapper on top keeps Kotlin call sites short. ClassTokenDemo does that for the shop's standard items: ask for "an apple" without saying which, and you get a Gala: Java // Java calling the Kotlin functions in ClassTokenDemo.kt: Apple apple = ClassTokenDemoKt.defaultOf(Apple.class); // the Class-token core: fine Apple viaReified = ClassTokenDemoKt.<Apple>defaultOf(); // error: method defaultOf ... cannot be applied to given types Kotlin fun <T : Any> defaultOf(type: Class<T>): T = type.cast(defaults[type] ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("no default for ${type.simpleName}")) inline fun <reified T : Any> defaultOf(): T = defaultOf(T::class.java) val apple: Apple = defaultOf() // T inferred from the expected type Both versions print apple = Gala, lemon = Eureka, blank = ''. Why can't Java call the wrapper? javac, the Java compiler, can't inline Kotlin code, so it has no way to fill in T. Kotlin still writes a method for the wrapper into the class file, but marks it synthetic, a flag that means "made by the compiler, not for callers". javac ignores synthetic methods. Read the error again. javac says defaultOf needs an argument, because the only defaultOf it can see is the Class-token one. A reified function with no Class-token version beside it gives cannot find symbol. If Java code will call your API, give it a Class<T> version. Make the reified one a one-line wrapper. One trap with tokens: Int::class.java is the primitive class int, but T::class.java for a reified Int is java.lang.Integer, the boxed class. A table filled with one and asked for the other finds nothing, and the Try-it's last step ends with no default for Integer. Use Int::class.javaObjectType when you need the boxed class. Java has the same split: int.class and Integer.class are different objects. A class token and a reified T both carry a class. Neither one carries more than that. Call one API from both languages Run ClassTokenDemo, then ClassTokenDemoJava, which calls the Kotlin functions directly. In the Java file, uncomment the wrong move and run. Read the required: line of the error. In ClassTokenDemo.kt, add Int::class.java to 0, to defaults and println(defaultOf<Int>()) to main. Predict, run, then fix it with Int::class.javaObjectType. ClassTokenDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l08.demo /** The shop's standard item of each kind: ask for "an apple" without saying which, and you get a Gala. */ private val defaults: Map<Class<*>, Any> = mapOf( Apple::class.java to Apple("Gala", 180), Lemon::class.java to Lemon("Eureka", 120), String::class.java to "", ) /** The core takes a Class token, so it works for Java callers too. */ fun <T : Any> defaultOf(type: Class<T>): T = type.cast(defaults[type] ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("no default for ${type.simpleName}")) /** The Kotlin wrapper: the compiler writes T::class.java into each call site. */ inline fun <reified T : Any> defaultOf(): T = defaultOf(T::class.java) fun main() { val apple: Apple = defaultOf() // T inferred from the expected type val lemon = defaultOf<Lemon>() val blank = defaultOf(String::class.java) // the Java-style call, from Kotlin println("apple = $apple, lemon = $lemon, blank = '$blank'") // A trap with primitives: Int::class.java is the primitive int, but a reified Int is boxed. println("Int::class.java = ${Int::class.java}, javaObjectType = ${Int::class.javaObjectType}") } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l08.demo.ClassTokenDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l08/demo/ClassTokenDemo.kt ClassTokenDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l08.demo; /** * Java twin of ClassTokenDemo.kt. It calls the Kotlin functions in ClassTokenDemo.kt directly: * the Class-token version works from Java, and the reified one does not exist for javac. */ public class ClassTokenDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Apple apple = ClassTokenDemoKt.defaultOf(Apple.class); Lemon lemon = ClassTokenDemoKt.defaultOf(Lemon.class); String blank = ClassTokenDemoKt.defaultOf(String.class); System.out.println("apple = " + apple + ", lemon = " + lemon + ", blank = '" + blank + "'"); // Java has the same primitive trap: int.class and Integer.class are different Class objects. System.out.println("int.class = " + int.class + ", Integer.class = " + Integer.class); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // Apple viaReified = ClassTokenDemoKt.<Apple>defaultOf(); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l08.demo.ClassTokenDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l08/demo/ClassTokenDemoJava.java Both print apple = Gala, lemon = Eureka, blank = '', then the primitive and boxed classes: int and class java.lang.Integer. The Java wrong move fails with method defaultOf in class ClassTokenDemoKt cannot be applied to given types, and says it requires a Class<T>: javac can't see the synthetic reified version. defaultOf<Int>() throws IllegalArgumentException: no default for Integer, because the table's key is int and the reified lookup uses Integer. With javaObjectType, it prints 0.

h: Type erasure and reified type parameters · What the note can't hold: the limits of reified
x: Reified brings back the class at the call site, and only the class. The note has room for one word. Three limits are worth knowing. First, the type arguments of T itself are still erased. filterIsInstance<List<String>>() compiles without a single warning, and it keeps every list: Java // the Java version passes List.class: there is no List<String>.class List<List<String>> nameLists = filterIsInstance(boxes, List.class); System.out.println(nameLists); // [[180, 150], [Gala]] String n = nameLists.get(0).get(0); // ClassCastException Kotlin val boxes: List<Any> = listOf(listOf(180, 150), listOf("Gala"), "Fuji") val nameLists = boxes.filterIsInstance<List<String>>() // no warning println(nameLists) // [[180, 150], [Gala]] val n: String = nameLists[0][0] // ClassCastException The list of weights got through. The note said "List", and had no room for "of names". The Kotlin docs say the same about their own asPairOf<String, List<String>>() example: it "compiles but breaks type safety". After inlining, is List<String> is only instanceof List. Second, Nothing and erased type parameters can't be reified, as the table in the second section showed. Third, Kotlin 2.4 added an error about null. In inline fun <reified T> klassOf(x: T) = x::class, T may be a nullable type, so x may be null, and null has no class. Kotlin 2.3 warned about this, and 2.4 refuses: expression in class literal has nullable type 'T (of fun <T> klassOf)'. Use '!!' to make the type non-nullable. The fix is to say what you mean with <reified T : Any>, the bound from lesson 2 that keeps null out, so callers can't pass null at all. T::class, the class of the type rather than of a value, is still allowed with a nullable bound. Java has no such check: x.getClass() on a null x throws NullPointerException at run time, as LimitsDemoJava shows. So treat reified as a tool for the outer class of a type: instance checks, casts and class tokens. When the full type matters, List<Apple> and not just List, you need something that keeps the type arguments. That's KType, in the next lesson. Find the edges of reified Run LimitsDemo (or LimitsDemoJava). Is the first line what filterIsInstance<List<String>>() promised? Uncomment wrong move 1 and run. Then uncomment wrong move 2: it compiles, so predict what happens when it runs. Uncomment the klassOf function at the bottom (3), read the Kotlin 2.4 error, then fix it by changing <reified T> to <reified T : Any>. LimitsDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l08.demo inline fun <reified T : Any> classOf(x: T) = x::class // T : Any, so x can't be null fun main() { // 1. Reified T is the outer class only. Nested type arguments are still erased. val boxes: List<Any> = listOf(listOf(180, 150), listOf("Gala"), "Fuji") val nameLists = boxes.filterIsInstance<List<String>>() // compiles with no warning at all println("lists of names? $nameLists") // 2. With a non-null bound, x::class is fine. println("classOf(\"Gala\") = ${classOf("Gala").simpleName}") // Wrong moves. Uncomment one at a time, predict the error, then run. // val nothing = classOf<Nothing>(TODO()) // 1 // val n: String = nameLists[0][0] // 2 (compiles: what happens at run time?) } // 3. Kotlin 2.4 turned this into an error: T may be nullable, and null has no class. // inline fun <reified T> klassOf(x: T) = x::class ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l08.demo.LimitsDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l08/demo/LimitsDemo.kt LimitsDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l08.demo; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of LimitsDemo.kt. The closest Java equivalent passes a Class token, and a Class token * has the same limit as a reified T: List.class stands for every List, whatever its elements. */ public class LimitsDemoJava { @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") static <T> List<T> filterIsInstance(List<?> items, Class<?> type) { return (List<T>) items.stream().filter(type::isInstance).toList(); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Object> boxes = List.of(List.of(180, 150), List.of("Gala"), "Fuji"); List<List<String>> nameLists = filterIsInstance(boxes, List.class); // there is no List<String>.class System.out.println("lists of names? " + nameLists); // getClass() on a value: a null receiver is only found at run time. Object maybe = null; try { System.out.println(maybe.getClass()); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("NullPointerException from getClass() on null"); } // Uncomment, predict, then run: it compiles, so what happens at run time? // String n = nameLists.get(0).get(0); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l08.demo.LimitsDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l08/demo/LimitsDemoJava.java Both print lists of names? [[180, 150], [Gala]]: the list of weights got through. Kotlin then prints classOf("Gala") = String, and Java prints NullPointerException from getClass() on null. Wrong move 1: Cannot use 'Nothing' as reified type parameter. Wrong move 2 compiles and throws ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.lang.String (the same happens in the Java twin). Function 3: Expression in class literal has nullable type 'T (of fun <T> klassOf)'. Use '!!' to make the type non-nullable. With T : Any, it compiles. Kotlin 2.4 compatibility guide (KTLC-370) docs

h: Type erasure and reified type parameters · Java and Kotlin
x: A parser table: Class tokens in Java, Class tokens plus reified in Kotlin Parsers.java import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.function.Function; final class Parsers { private final Map<Class<?>, Function<String, ?>> byType = new HashMap<>(); <T> void register(Class<T> type, Function<String, ? extends T> parser) { byType.put(type, parser); } // T is erased in here, so the caller hands over the Class <T> T parse(String text, Class<T> type) { Function<String, ?> parser = byType.get(type); if (parser == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("no parser for " + type.getSimpleName()); return type.cast(parser.apply(text)); // a checked cast: no warning } } // call site: Weight w = parsers.parse("1.25 kg", Weight.class); Parsers.kt class Parsers { private val byType = HashMap<Class<*>, (String) -> Any>() fun <T : Any> register(type: Class<T>, parser: (String) -> T) { byType[type] = parser } // the same Class-token core, callable from Java fun <T : Any> parse(text: String, type: Class<T>): T { val parser = byType[type] ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("no parser for " + type.simpleName) return type.cast(parser(text)) } // the Kotlin wrapper: the compiler writes Weight::class.java into each call site inline fun <reified T : Any> parse(text: String): T = parse(text, T::class.java) } // call site: val w = parsers.parse<Weight>("1.25 kg") Both languages erase T inside parse, so both cores need the Class<T> argument, and both use Class.cast for a cast that really checks. The difference is at the call site. Kotlin can add an inline wrapper with a reified T, and the compiler fills in Weight::class.java for the caller. Java can't use that wrapper: it is a synthetic method in the class file, and javac can't inline it. Note also that the wrapper calls only public members. A public inline function is copied into other modules, so it may not touch byType directly (public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API property).

h: Type erasure and reified type parameters · Worked example
x: Give a text reader a real type The shop reads its delivery notes with a text reader that, like many Java libraries, wants a class token: fun <T : Any> read(text: String, type: Class<T>): T. The first draft tries to hide the token behind a generic function. Read the error that names T. fun <T : Any> load(text: String): T = reader.read(text, T::class.java) // error: cannot use 'T' as reified type parameter. Use a class instead. static <T> T load(String text) { return reader.read(text, T.class); } // error: cannot select from a type variable Make the token explicit. This version works from Kotlin and from Java, and the reader does a checked conversion. fun <T : Any> load(text: String, type: Class<T>): T = reader.read(text, type) val a = load(text, Apple::class.java) static <T> T load(String text, Class<T> type) { return reader.read(text, type); } Apple a = load(text, Apple.class); Add the Kotlin convenience on top. Self-check before reading the comment: why must the wrapper be inline? (Only an inlined body is compiled at the call site, where T is known.) inline fun <reified T : Any> load(text: String): T = load(text, T::class.java) val a: Apple = load(text) // T inferred from the expected type val l = load<Lemon>(text) // Java can't call the reified wrapper; it keeps using the token version: Lemon l = load(text, Lemon.class); Check the limit before you rely on it. load<List<Apple>>(text) compiles, but it passes List::class.java. The reader has no element type to fill the list with (a library for JSON, the common text format, such as Jackson, fills it with maps), and the first for (a: Apple in apples) throws ClassCastException. For generic targets you need a token that keeps type arguments: typeOf<List<Apple>>() or a super type token, both in lesson 9.

h: Type erasure and reified type parameters · Key terms
x: Type erasure Removing type arguments after compile-time checking, so objects carry no <String> at run time. Unchecked cast A cast to a generic type that can check only the class. The compiler warns; the failure comes later. Heap pollution A variable of a generic type that refers to an object of the wrong type, such as a List<String> holding ints. inline function A function whose body the compiler copies into each call site. Reified type parameter A type parameter of an inline function whose real class is available in the copied body. Class token A Class<T> passed as an argument, so code can check and cast to T at run time. Synthetic method A method the compiler writes into the class file but hides from javac, as Kotlin does with reified functions. What is type erasure? The compiler checks type arguments and then removes them. At run time a List<String> is just a List, with no record of String. Where does val l = listOf(180) as Any as List<String> fail? Not at the cast. It fails at the first read that needs a String, such as val s: String = l[0]. What do inline and reified do together? inline copies the function body into each call site. reified writes the caller's real class for T into that copy, so is T, as? T and T::class work. Can Java call inline fun <reified T : Any> parse(text: String): T? No. It is a synthetic method, and javac can't inline it. Provide parse(text, type: Class<T>) as well. Does filterIsInstance<List<String>>() check the elements? No. Reified covers only the outer class; after inlining it is instanceof List, so a list of ints passes. Why is inline fun <reified T> klassOf(x: T) = x::class an error in Kotlin 2.4? T may be nullable, and null has no class. Write <reified T : Any>. Int::class.java vs T::class.java with a reified T = Int? The first is the primitive int; the second is java.lang.Integer. Use Int::class.javaObjectType for the boxed class.

h: Type erasure and reified type parameters · Go deeper
x: You can see the copy mechanism in the bytecode. Run javap -c -p on ClassTokenDemoKt.class (it is under generics/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/generics/l08/demo/ after you run the demo). The method kept in the class for defaultOf() has the flags ACC_PUBLIC, ACC_STATIC, ACC_FINAL, ACC_SYNTHETIC, and where T::class.java should be, it loads Object.class next to a call to kotlin/jvm/internal/Intrinsics.reifiedOperationMarker. That marker tells the compiler where to write the real class when it copies the body into a caller. In main, the call defaultOf<Lemon>() has no call to defaultOf() at all: you'll find ldc class workbench/generics/l08/demo/Lemon followed by a call to the Class-token defaultOf. This is also why the lab routes test calls through Callers.kt. The inlined copy is fixed when the caller is compiled. Tests compiled once against src/main would keep a copy of your TODO stub forever, even when run next to the reference solution. Two more rules come from copying. A public inline function is copied into other modules, so it may only touch public API: reading a private field gives public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API property. That is the deep reason for the "Class-token core plus one-line reified wrapper" shape. And a lambda passed to an inline function is normally inlined too, so it can't be stored. If the function needs to keep it, say in a table of listeners, that parameter must be marked noinline. Lesson 11 of this track uses that for a typed event bus. Java's own answer to erasure for arrays is different: arrays are reified. Every String[] knows its element type at run time, which is why new T[1] is a compile error (generic array creation), and why Kotlin's arrayOf<T>() needs a reified T.

h: KClass, Class and type tokens · The one-word note and the whole label: KClass, Class and KType
x: An object carries only its class: KClass and Class are two views of it, and only a KType, written by the compiler at a call site, keeps the type arguments Start with what a running program can ask. Lesson 3 of this track pulled classes and types apart. The class String backs two types, String and String?, and the class List backs List<String>, List<Int> and List<Apple>?. Lesson 8 added erasure: the compiler checks each type argument (the real type in the angle brackets, such as String in List<String>) and then drops it, so at run time each object keeps its class and nothing more. A box on the shelf still knows it's a box. It no longer knows what its label said. Kotlin's reflection API, the part of the library that lets code inspect classes while the program runs, gives each idea its own object. Most confusion about KClass comes from mixing them up: A KClass describes a class: String::class, Apple::class, List::class. It has no type arguments and is never nullable. This is the one-word note. A Class is Java's object for the same class: String.class in Java, String::class.java in Kotlin. It's the same note, written on Java's paper. A KType describes a full type: the class, its type arguments, and whether it may be null. typeOf<List<String>?>() gives you one. This is the whole label: "a list of strings, or nothing". Java Class<String> c = String.class; // Java's class object boolean same = new ArrayList<String>().getClass() == new ArrayList<Integer>().getClass(); // true // Java has no KType. The closest thing is a Type read from a declaration, such as a field: Type t = Shop.class.getDeclaredField("varieties").getGenericType(); // java.util.List<java.lang.String> Kotlin val k: KClass<String> = String::class // Kotlin's class object val c: Class<String> = String::class.java // the Java one, for Java code val t: KType = typeOf<List<String>?>() // List, with argument String, nullable val same = ArrayList<String>()::class == ArrayList<Int>()::class // true To pick the right one, ask what you want to know. "What kind of thing is this?" is a question about a class, and a KClass or a Class answers it. "A list of what?" and "may it be null?" are questions about a type, and only a KType can answer them. In the figure, the arrows from the object at run time reach only the class objects. A KType comes from code: the compiler writes it down at a call site. Here the clerk picture breaks a little. A real clerk could copy the full label onto every note. Kotlin writes a KType only where you ask for one with typeOf, and never stores it inside the object. One warning before you run anything. Without the kotlin-reflect library on the classpath (the list of jars and folders a program loads its classes from), Kotlin prints these objects with a little apology attached: class java.lang.String (Kotlin reflection is not available) java.util.List<java.lang.String>? (Kotlin reflection is not available) Nothing is broken. To print Kotlin names such as kotlin.String, toString() needs that library, so it falls back to Java names and says so. A Gradle project doesn't include kotlin-reflect unless you ask for it, while the kotlinc command-line compiler adds it by default, so the same code can print differently in the two. The fourth section of this lesson shows what else the library adds. Objects know their class. Only code knows full types. We've named the three objects. Next, we'll ask a piece of fruit for its own note, and see what type the compiler gives the answer. Meet the three objects Run ClassVsTypeDemo and read each line. Which of the three objects are printed with Java names and the apology? Run it again with -Preflect added to the end of the command, and compare the first and third lines. Run ClassVsTypeDemoJava. Which Kotlin line has no Java twin at all? ClassVsTypeDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l09.demo import kotlin.reflect.KClass import kotlin.reflect.KType import kotlin.reflect.typeOf fun main() { // 1. Three different objects. val k: KClass<String> = String::class // Kotlin's object for a class val c: Class<String> = String::class.java // Java's object for the same class val t: KType = typeOf<List<String>?>() // a full type: class, arguments, nullability println("KClass: $k") println("Class: $c") println("KType: $t") // 2. Different types, one class. println("ArrayList<String> and ArrayList<Int> share a class: ${ArrayList<String>()::class == ArrayList<Int>()::class}") println("String? is backed by the class String: ${typeOf<String?>().classifier == String::class}") println("but the types differ: ${typeOf<String>() == typeOf<String?>()}, ${typeOf<List<String>>() == typeOf<List<Int>>()}") // 3. What a KType knows that a KClass doesn't. println("classifier is List::class: ${t.classifier == List::class}, arguments: ${t.arguments.size}, nullable: ${t.isMarkedNullable}") } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l09.demo.ClassVsTypeDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l09/demo/ClassVsTypeDemo.kt ClassVsTypeDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l09.demo; import java.lang.reflect.ParameterizedType; import java.lang.reflect.Type; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of ClassVsTypeDemo.kt. Java has Class but no KType. The closest thing is * java.lang.reflect.Type, which you can read from a declaration (here, a field). */ public class ClassVsTypeDemoJava { static List<String> varieties = List.of("Gala"); // a declaration keeps its generic type public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Class<String> c = String.class; Type t = ClassVsTypeDemoJava.class.getDeclaredField("varieties").getGenericType(); System.out.println("Class: " + c); System.out.println("Type: " + t + " (read from the field declaration)"); System.out.println("ArrayList<String> and ArrayList<Integer> share a class: " + (new ArrayList<String>().getClass() == new ArrayList<Integer>().getClass())); System.out.println("the field's Type keeps its argument: " + ((ParameterizedType) t).getActualTypeArguments()[0]); // Java types carry no nullability, so there is no twin of typeOf<String?>(). } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l09.demo.ClassVsTypeDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l09/demo/ClassVsTypeDemoJava.java Kotlin prints KClass: class java.lang.String (Kotlin reflection is not available), Class: class java.lang.String and KType: java.util.List<java.lang.String>? (Kotlin reflection is not available), then true, true, false, false and classifier is List::class: true, arguments: 1, nullable: true. With -Preflect the first line becomes class kotlin.String and the third kotlin.collections.List<kotlin.String>?. Java prints the class, the field's type java.util.List<java.lang.String>, true, and the argument class java.lang.String. Java has no twin for the nullable type: its types carry no nullability. A KType is the whole label: class, arguments and nullability. Its classifier is a KClass, the one-word note, which converts to and from Java's Class. An object can give you only its class. Reflection: class references and KType (Kotlin docs) docs

h: KClass, Class and type tokens · Asking a fruit what it is: x::class gives a KClass
x: There are two ways to get a KClass. A class literal, Apple::class, names a class you know while you write the code, and its type is exact: KClass<Apple>. A bound class reference, fruit::class, asks a value for its class while the program runs. Its type has an out in it: Java Fruit fruit = new Apple("Gala", 180); Class<? extends Fruit> c = fruit.getClass(); // what getClass() is declared to return Class<Fruit> strict = fruit.getClass(); // error: Class<CAP#1> cannot be converted to Class<Fruit> Kotlin val fruit: Fruit = Apple("Gala", 180) val k: KClass<out Fruit> = fruit::class // the class of SOME Fruit val strict: KClass<Fruit> = fruit::class // error: expected 'KClass<Fruit>', actual 'KClass<out Fruit>' Why the out? The compiler knows only that fruit is some Fruit. When the program runs, it turns out to be an Apple, but it could have been a Lemon. So the most the compiler can promise is "the class of some subtype of Fruit". That is what out meant in lesson 4: the apple dispenser, which hands out some kind of fruit and takes nothing in. Java says the same with ? extends. Java's documentation for Object.getClass() says the result is Class<? extends |X|>, where |X| is the erased type of the expression. The out doesn't stop you from using the answer. Everything that hands information out still works: fruit::class.simpleName, fruit::class == Apple::class, and cast, which hands back a Fruit. What you can't do is pass it where an exact KClass<Fruit> is required. The compiler makes no exception for final classes either: "Gala"::class is a KClass<out String>. The other half of KClass<T : Any> is its bound, the "no nulls" sign from lesson 2. There is no class for a nullable type, because String? is backed by the class String. So KClass<String?> is an error, and so is asking a value that may be null for its class: val kn: KClass<String?>? = null Type argument is not within its bounds: type parameter 'T (of interface KClass<T : Any>)' must be subtype of 'Any', but actual: 'String?'. val note: String? = ... note::class Expression in class literal has nullable type 'String?'. Use '!!' to make the type non-nullable. Write note?.let { it::class } instead, and you get a KClass<out String>?, which is null when there's no value to ask. Java has no such check at compile time: note.getClass() throws NullPointerException when note is null. A value can tell you only the class of some subtype. Use a class literal when you need an exact KClass<T>. Kotlin's note and Java's note describe the same class. Next, we'll move between them, and put them to work. Ask values for their class Run ClassOfValueDemo (or ClassOfValueDemoJava). The loop variable is declared Fruit. What does simpleName print for each piece? Uncomment the three wrong moves one at a time. Predict each error first. In the Java twin, uncomment the wrong move. Find the captured type in the message. ClassOfValueDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l09.demo import kotlin.reflect.KClass // The shop's fruit, used by the demos of this lesson (the Java twins use these Kotlin types too). // Sealed, so that ReflectDemo can ask Fruit for its subclasses. sealed interface Fruit { val name: String; val grams: Int } data class Apple(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit data class Lemon(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit fun main() { val delivery: List<Fruit> = listOf(Apple("Gala", 180), Lemon("Eureka", 120)) for (fruit in delivery) { val k: KClass<out Fruit> = fruit::class // the class of SOME Fruit println("${fruit.name}: ${k.simpleName}, is an apple: ${k == Apple::class}") } val exact: KClass<Apple> = Apple::class // a class literal is exact val note: String? = delivery.firstOrNull()?.name val noteClass: KClass<out String>? = note?.let { it::class } // no value, no class println("exact = ${exact.simpleName}, noteClass = ${noteClass?.simpleName}") // Wrong moves. Uncomment one at a time, predict the error, then run. // val strict: KClass<Fruit> = delivery[0]::class // 1 // val nullable = note::class // 2 // val kn: KClass<String?>? = null // 3 } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l09.demo.ClassOfValueDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l09/demo/ClassOfValueDemo.kt ClassOfValueDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l09.demo; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of ClassOfValueDemo.kt. getClass() is declared to return Class<? extends |X|>. */ public class ClassOfValueDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { List<Fruit> delivery = List.of(new Apple("Gala", 180), new Lemon("Eureka", 120)); for (Fruit fruit : delivery) { Class<? extends Fruit> c = fruit.getClass(); // the class of SOME Fruit System.out.println(fruit.getName() + ": " + c.getSimpleName() + ", is an apple: " + (c == Apple.class)); } Class<Apple> exact = Apple.class; // a class literal is exact String note = null; // a value that turns out to be null try { System.out.println(note.getClass()); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("exact = " + exact.getSimpleName() + ", getClass() on null: NullPointerException"); } // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // Class<Fruit> strict = delivery.get(0).getClass(); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l09.demo.ClassOfValueDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l09/demo/ClassOfValueDemoJava.java Both print Gala: Apple, is an apple: true and Eureka: Lemon, is an apple: false: the run-time class, not the declared type. Kotlin ends with exact = Apple, noteClass = String; Java ends with exact = Apple, getClass() on null: NullPointerException. Kotlin's errors: (1) Initializer type mismatch: expected 'KClass<Fruit>', actual 'KClass<out Fruit>'., (2) Expression in class literal has nullable type 'String?'. Use '!!' to make the type non-nullable., (3) Type argument is not within its bounds: type parameter 'T (of interface KClass<T : Any>)' must be subtype of 'Any', but actual: 'String?'. Java's: incompatible types: Class<CAP#1> cannot be converted to Class<Fruit>, where CAP#1 is the unknown subtype. Object.getClass (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: KClass, Class and type tokens · One note on two kinds of paper: converting, checking and casting
x: On the JVM, every KClass wraps a java.lang.Class, and two properties move you between them. You'll do it often at the edge of your code, where it calls a Java library: Java Class<Apple> c = Apple.class; boolean isApple = c.isInstance(fruit); // true Apple gala = c.cast(fruit); // checked: ClassCastException if not String name = c.getSimpleName(); // "Apple" Class<?> runtime = fruit.getClass(); // the object's class Kotlin val k: KClass<Apple> = Apple::class val c: Class<Apple> = k.java // KClass to Class, for Java code val back: KClass<Apple> = c.kotlin // Class to KClass k.isInstance(fruit) // true val gala: Apple = k.cast(fruit) // checked: ClassCastException if not val lemon: Lemon? = Lemon::class.safeCast(fruit) // null instead of throwing k.simpleName // "Apple" fruit.javaClass // the object's Class, like Java's getClass() These are lesson 8's class-token tools, in Kotlin's spelling. isInstance is a checked is, cast is a checked as, and safeCast is a checked as?. (cast and safeCast are extension functions, functions added to KClass from outside it, in the package kotlin.reflect, so they need an import.) A failed cast throws ClassCastException: Value cannot be cast to workbench.generics.l09.demo.Lemon. Names work out of the box, simpleName and qualifiedName, and so does equality: fruit::class == Apple::class is true. These checks are real, unlike the as T of lesson 8, because the KClass object exists while the program runs and knows what to compare against. The card index's get will rely on exactly that. Two traps wait here. The first is from lesson 8: Int::class.java is the primitive class int, and Int::class.javaObjectType is java.lang.Integer, the boxed class whose objects wrap a number. The second is javaClass. On a value, fruit.javaClass is the object's Class. On a KClass, it would be the class of the KClass object itself, an internal Kotlin class. Kotlin 2.4.21 rejects it with a deprecation error that says what you meant: k.javaClass 'val <T : Any> KClass<T>.javaClass: Class<KClass<T>>' is deprecated. Use 'java' property to get Java class corresponding to this Kotlin class ... Which one should your code hold? Inside Kotlin code, prefer the KClass. It has safeCast, it's what other Kotlin APIs hand you, and it's what this lesson's card index files its cards under. At the edge, pass .java to the Java library and keep the KClass on your side. Inside Kotlin, keep a KClass. Hand .java to Java code at the edge. A note can name a class, check a value against it and cast. Can it also describe the class: its properties, its subclasses? Check, cast and name a class Run ClassApiDemo and ClassApiDemoJava. Compare the two cast failed: messages. Uncomment the wrong move in ClassApiDemo.kt and read the whole deprecation message. Replace Lemon::class.safeCast(fruit) with Lemon::class.cast(fruit) in the second println. Predict what changes, then run. ClassApiDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l09.demo import kotlin.reflect.KClass import kotlin.reflect.cast import kotlin.reflect.safeCast fun main() { val fruit: Fruit = Apple("Gala", 180) // 1. KClass <-> Class val k: KClass<Apple> = Apple::class val c: Class<Apple> = k.java println("k.java = ${c.simpleName}, c.kotlin == k: ${c.kotlin == k}, fruit.javaClass == c: ${fruit.javaClass == c}") // 2. checked is / as / as? println("isInstance: ${k.isInstance(fruit)}, cast(...).grams: ${k.cast(fruit).grams}, safeCast to Lemon: ${Lemon::class.safeCast(fruit)}") try { Lemon::class.cast(fruit) } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("cast failed: ${e.message}") } // 3. names println("simpleName = ${k.simpleName}, qualifiedName = ${k.qualifiedName}") // 4. the primitive trap from lesson 8 println("Int::class.java = ${Int::class.java}, Int::class.javaObjectType = ${Int::class.javaObjectType}") // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // println(k.javaClass) } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l09.demo.ClassApiDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l09/demo/ClassApiDemo.kt ClassApiDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l09.demo; /** Java twin of ClassApiDemo.kt: the same checks and names, on java.lang.Class. */ public class ClassApiDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Fruit fruit = new Apple("Gala", 180); Class<Apple> c = Apple.class; System.out.println("c.getSimpleName() = " + c.getSimpleName() + ", fruit.getClass() == c: " + (fruit.getClass() == c)); System.out.println("isInstance: " + c.isInstance(fruit) + ", cast(...).getGrams(): " + c.cast(fruit).getGrams() + ", no safeCast in Java: " + (Lemon.class.isInstance(fruit) ? Lemon.class.cast(fruit) : null)); try { Lemon.class.cast(fruit); } catch (ClassCastException e) { System.out.println("cast failed: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("getSimpleName = " + c.getSimpleName() + ", getName = " + c.getName()); System.out.println("int.class = " + int.class + ", Integer.class = " + Integer.class); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l09.demo.ClassApiDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l09/demo/ClassApiDemoJava.java Kotlin prints k.java = Apple, c.kotlin == k: true, fruit.javaClass == c: true, then isInstance: true, cast(...).grams: 180, safeCast to Lemon: null, cast failed: Value cannot be cast to workbench.generics.l09.demo.Lemon, the two names and int / class java.lang.Integer. Java's cast message is Cannot cast workbench.generics.l09.demo.Apple to workbench.generics.l09.demo.Lemon. The wrong move fails with 'val <T : Any> KClass<T>.javaClass: Class<KClass<T>>' is deprecated. Use 'java' property .... With cast instead of safeCast, the program stops with a ClassCastException on that line, before it reaches the try block.

h: KClass, Class and type tokens · The reference book in the other room: what needs kotlin-reflect
x: A KClass offers many more members: objectInstance, sealedSubclasses, isData, members, constructors, supertypes. Your code compiles against all of them, because the standard library declares them. But the code that answers them lives in a separate jar, kotlin-reflect, about 3.8 MB in 2.4.21. Think of it as a thick reference book about every class, kept in another room. A Gradle project doesn't fetch the book unless you add it, and without it these calls fail while the program runs: Storeroom::class.objectInstance KotlinReflectionNotSupportedError: Kotlin reflection implementation is not found at runtime. Make sure you have kotlin-reflect.jar in the classpath Storeroom in the demo is a Kotlin object, a class with exactly one instance, and objectInstance asks for that instance. A rule of thumb holds up well: names, identity, instance checks, casts and typeOf are free; anything that lists or describes declarations needs kotlin-reflect. A declaration is a piece of code that introduces a name, such as a class, a property or a function. Works with the standard library alone Needs kotlin-reflect simpleName, qualifiedName, ==, .java, .kotlin objectInstance, sealedSubclasses, isData, isSealed isInstance, cast, safeCast members, constructors, typeParameters, supertypes typeOf<T>() with classifier, arguments, isMarkedNullable kotlin.reflect.full extensions such as createInstance() The kotlin.reflect.full extensions fail differently, with NoClassDefFoundError: kotlin/reflect/full/KClasses, because that class isn't in the standard library at all. Java reflection needs no extra jar, and it works on Kotlin classes too: Java Apple.class.getDeclaredFields(); // [grams, name] Storeroom.class.getField("INSTANCE").get(null); // a Kotlin object is a static INSTANCE field Kotlin Apple::class.java.declaredFields // the same Java reflection, from Kotlin Storeroom::class.objectInstance // the Kotlin way: needs kotlin-reflect So when a Java-level answer is enough (fields, methods, annotations), go through .java and skip the dependency. When you need Kotlin-level facts, such as whether a class is a data class, which subclasses a sealed interface has, or whether a property may be null, add kotlin-reflect, and add it on purpose. Whatever you add, a KClass still has no room for "of apples". Back to the card index and its two shelves. Run one demo with and without kotlin-reflect Run ReflectDemo with the command below. Every line under -- needs kotlin-reflect fails. Note which error each one gives. Run it again with -Preflect at the end of the command. That flag adds kotlin-reflect to the demo's runtime classpath (see labs/generics/build.gradle.kts). Run ReflectDemoJava. Which of the Kotlin answers can Java reflection give too? ReflectDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l09.demo import kotlin.reflect.full.createInstance import kotlin.reflect.typeOf /** A Kotlin object: exactly one instance. The shop has one storeroom. */ object Storeroom { override fun toString() = "Storeroom" } class PaperBag { override fun toString() = "PaperBag()" } private fun attempt(label: String, block: () -> Any?) { val result = try { block().toString() } catch (e: Throwable) { // KotlinReflectionNotSupportedError is an Error "${e::class.java.simpleName}: ${e.message?.substringBefore(". ")}" } println("%-24s %s".format(label, result)) } /** * Run it twice: * ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l09.demo.ReflectDemoKt (without kotlin-reflect) * ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l09.demo.ReflectDemoKt -Preflect (with it) */ fun main() { println("-- standard library only") attempt("simpleName") { Fruit::class.simpleName } attempt("isInstance") { Apple::class.isInstance(Apple("Gala", 180)) } attempt("== and .java") { Apple::class.java == Apple("Gala", 180).javaClass } attempt("typeOf arguments") { typeOf<List<String>>().arguments.size } attempt("toString()") { String::class } println("-- needs kotlin-reflect") attempt("objectInstance") { Storeroom::class.objectInstance } attempt("sealedSubclasses") { Fruit::class.sealedSubclasses.map { it.simpleName } } attempt("isData") { Apple::class.isData } attempt("members") { Apple::class.members.map { it.name }.sorted() } attempt("createInstance()") { PaperBag::class.createInstance() } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l09.demo.ReflectDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l09/demo/ReflectDemo.kt ReflectDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l09.demo; import java.lang.reflect.Field; import java.lang.reflect.Method; import java.util.Arrays; /** * Java twin of ReflectDemo.kt. Java reflection needs no extra jar: it answers Java-level questions * (fields, methods) about Kotlin classes too. It doesn't know Kotlin ideas like data classes. */ public class ReflectDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("fields: " + Arrays.stream(Apple.class.getDeclaredFields()).map(Field::getName).sorted().toList()); System.out.println("methods: " + Arrays.stream(Apple.class.getDeclaredMethods()).map(Method::getName).sorted().toList()); // A Kotlin object is a class with a static INSTANCE field: Java's way to get objectInstance. System.out.println("Storeroom.INSTANCE: " + Storeroom.class.getField("INSTANCE").get(null).getClass().getSimpleName()); System.out.println("is it a data class? Java reflection can't say: it has no such idea."); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l09.demo.ReflectDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l09/demo/ReflectDemoJava.java Without the jar, the first five lines work (Fruit, true, true, 1, and class java.lang.String (Kotlin reflection is not available)). Then four lines show KotlinReflectionNotSupportedError: Kotlin reflection implementation is not found at runtime, and createInstance() shows NoClassDefFoundError: kotlin/reflect/full/KClasses. With -Preflect: class kotlin.String, Storeroom, [Apple, Lemon], true, [component1, component2, copy, equals, grams, hashCode, name, toString] and PaperBag(). Java prints the fields [grams, name], the methods (with getters such as getGrams and the hidden copy$default), and Storeroom.INSTANCE: Storeroom. It has no notion of a data class.

h: KClass, Class and type tokens · Filing the shelves under their whole labels: typeOf and super type tokens
x: Now the problem from the opening. A card index keyed by KClass works for the scale and the label printer, because neither has a type argument. It can't hold a Shelf<Apple> and a Shelf<Lemon> at the same time. Both have the class Shelf, so the second card silently replaces the first, and nothing fails until someone asks for apples and gets lemons. You can't even write the class of the type you mean: val k = Shelf<Apple>::class Only classes are allowed on the left-hand side of a class literal. A KType keeps the type arguments and the nullability, and in Kotlin typeOf<T>() makes one. Java's answer is older, and cleverer than it looks: Java // A super type token. An anonymous subclass's superclass keeps its type arguments. abstract class TypeRef<T> { final Type type; protected TypeRef() { type = ((ParameterizedType) getClass().getGenericSuperclass()).getActualTypeArguments()[0]; } } Type t = new TypeRef<Map<String, List<Integer>>>() {}.type; // java.util.Map<java.lang.String, java.util.List<java.lang.Integer>> Kotlin val t: KType = typeOf<Map<String, List<Int>>>() t.classifier == Map::class // true t.arguments.size // 2: String and List<Int> typeOf<List<String>>() == typeOf<List<Int>>() // false typeOf<List<String>>() == typeOf<List<String>?>() // false: nullability counts The Java version is the idea Neal Gafter named super type tokens. Lesson 8 said that erasure removes type arguments from objects but not from declarations, and a class's declared superclass is a declaration. So you create a throwaway anonymous subclass, a class with no name written right where it's used, new TypeRef<...>() {}, and read its superclass back with reflection. It's the label carved into a shelf's frame, where the clerk's hands never reach. The {} is the whole trick: two characters that do more work than any others in this lesson. Without them there's no subclass, and javac says TypeRef is abstract; cannot be instantiated. The trick has one well-known hole. Inside a generic method, new TypeRef<List<T>>() {} records the type variable itself, and prints java.util.List<T>. typeOf has no such hole. Through a reified type parameter, one whose real type an inline function receives at each call site, it keeps everything: inline fun <reified T> tokenOf() = typeOf<T>(), called as tokenOf<List<String>>(), gives the full List<String>. That's the difference from lesson 8, where T::class kept only List. typeOf works without kotlin-reflect, apart from the apology in toString(), and KType equality is all a map key needs. File the shelves under typeOf<Shelf<Apple>>() and typeOf<Shelf<Lemon>>(), and the two cards sit side by side. That's the second half of the lab. When a Java library wants a java.lang.reflect.Type, convert with typeOf<List<Apple>>().javaType, which in 2.4.21 still needs @OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class). A super type token written in Kotlin works too, with a twist: it picks up Kotlin's declaration-site variance (the out and in written on a class) as Java wildcards. object : TypeRef<Map<String, List<Int>>>() {} prints java.util.Map<java.lang.String, ? extends java.util.List<? extends java.lang.Integer>>, because Map's V and List's E are declared out. javaType gives the plain form. Key a container by KClass for plain types, and by KType for generic ones. Know the limit, too. A KType exists only where the compiler wrote it, at a call site with a known or reified type. A box pulled off the shelf can still tell you only its class. Capture a full type two ways Run TypeTokenDemo and TypeTokenDemoJava. Compare the two super type token: lines. Find the line in the Java output where the token failed to capture the real type. Uncomment the wrong move in each file. Predict, then run. TypeTokenDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l09.demo import java.lang.reflect.ParameterizedType import java.lang.reflect.Type import kotlin.reflect.KType import kotlin.reflect.javaType import kotlin.reflect.typeOf /** A super type token written in Kotlin: the anonymous subclass remembers its superclass's type argument. */ abstract class TypeRef<T> { val type: Type = (javaClass.genericSuperclass as ParameterizedType).actualTypeArguments[0] } /** typeOf through a reified T keeps the whole type. T::class here would keep only the class. */ inline fun <reified T> tokenOf(): KType = typeOf<T>() @OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class) // KType.javaType still needs the opt-in in 2.4.21 fun main() { val t = typeOf<Map<String, List<Int>>>() // each variety's name, and the grams of each piece println("typeOf: $t") println("arguments: ${t.arguments.size}, second is ${t.arguments[1]}") println("javaType: ${t.javaType}") println("tokenOf<List<String>>() == typeOf<List<String>>(): ${tokenOf<List<String>>() == typeOf<List<String>>()}") println("List<String> == List<Int> as KTypes: ${typeOf<List<String>>() == typeOf<List<Int>>()}") println("super type token: ${object : TypeRef<Map<String, List<Int>>>() {}.type}") // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // val k = List<String>::class } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l09.demo.TypeTokenDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l09/demo/TypeTokenDemo.kt TypeTokenDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l09.demo; import java.lang.reflect.ParameterizedType; import java.lang.reflect.Type; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** Java twin of TypeTokenDemo.kt: the super type token, the trick behind Jackson's TypeReference. */ public class TypeTokenDemoJava { static abstract class TypeRef<T> { final Type type; protected TypeRef() { // getClass() is the anonymous subclass; its generic superclass is TypeRef<the type you wrote> type = ((ParameterizedType) getClass().getGenericSuperclass()).getActualTypeArguments()[0]; } } // the well-known hole: inside a generic method, the token captures the type VARIABLE static <T> Type listOf() { return new TypeRef<List<T>>() {}.type; } public static void main(String[] args) { Type t = new TypeRef<Map<String, List<Integer>>>() {}.type; // each variety's name, and the grams of each piece System.out.println("super type token: " + t); System.out.println("arguments: " + Arrays.toString(((ParameterizedType) t).getActualTypeArguments())); System.out.println("inside a generic method: " + TypeTokenDemoJava.<String>listOf()); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // Type k = new TypeRef<String>().type; } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l09.demo.TypeTokenDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l09/demo/TypeTokenDemoJava.java Kotlin prints the typeOf result java.util.Map<java.lang.String, java.util.List<java.lang.Integer>> (Kotlin reflection is not available), arguments: 2, ..., the same type from javaType without the apology, true, false, and the Kotlin-written token java.util.Map<java.lang.String, ? extends java.util.List<? extends java.lang.Integer>>. Java prints its token as java.util.Map<java.lang.String, java.util.List<java.lang.Integer>>, its two arguments, and inside a generic method: java.util.List<T>: the hole. The wrong moves fail with Only classes are allowed on the left-hand side of a class literal. and TypeRef is abstract; cannot be instantiated. typeOf (Kotlin stdlib API) docs KClass (Kotlin stdlib API) docs

h: KClass, Class and type tokens · Java and Kotlin
x: A type-safe card index in Java and Kotlin CardIndex.java import java.lang.reflect.Type; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; final class CardIndex { private final Map<Class<?>, Object> byClass = new HashMap<>(); private final Map<Type, Object> byType = new HashMap<>(); // Class<T> and T tied together: the compiler checks the pair <T> void register(Class<T> type, T impl) { byClass.put(type, impl); } <T> T get(Class<T> type) { Object impl = byClass.get(type); if (impl == null) throw new NoSuchElementException("no card for " + type.getSimpleName()); return type.cast(impl); // checked } // generic tools: a super type token supplies the full type <T> void registerTyped(TypeRef<T> type, T impl) { byType.put(type.type, impl); } @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") // safe: only registerTyped puts values in <T> T getTyped(TypeRef<T> type) { return (T) byType.get(type.type); } } // index.register(Scale.class, scale); // index.registerTyped(new TypeRef<Shelf<Apple>>() {}, apples); CardIndex.kt class CardIndex { private val byClass = HashMap<KClass<*>, Any>() private val byType = HashMap<KType, Any>() // KClass<T> and T tied together: the compiler checks the pair fun <T : Any> register(type: KClass<T>, impl: T) { byClass[type] = impl } fun <T : Any> get(type: KClass<T>): T { val impl = byClass[type] ?: throw NoSuchElementException("no card for " + type.simpleName) return type.cast(impl) // checked, no kotlin-reflect needed } inline fun <reified T : Any> get(): T = get(T::class) // generic tools: typeOf supplies the full type fun registerTyped(type: KType, impl: Any) { byType[type] = impl } fun getTyped(type: KType): Any = byType[type] ?: throw NoSuchElementException("no card for $type") inline fun <reified T : Any> registerTyped(impl: T) = registerTyped(typeOf<T>(), impl) @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") // safe: only registerTyped<T> puts values in inline fun <reified T : Any> getTyped(): T = getTyped(typeOf<T>()) as T } // index.register(Scale::class, scale); index.get<Scale>() // index.registerTyped<Shelf<Apple>>(apples) Both are what Joshua Bloch calls a typesafe heterogeneous container (Effective Java, Item 33): one map holds values of many types, and the key carries the type, so get can return a T with a checked cast. The KClass half is a direct translation: KClass<T> for Class<T>, type.cast in both. The differences show at the call site and for generic types. Kotlin adds reified wrappers, so callers write get<Scale>() and registerTyped<Shelf<Apple>>(apples). For generic types Java needs a super type token object at each call (new TypeRef<Shelf<Apple>>() {}), while Kotlin's typeOf<T>() is computed from the reified T, with no subclass and no hole for type variables. In both, the full-type half needs one unchecked cast. It is safe because the map is private and filled only through the typed registerTyped.

h: KClass, Class and type tokens · Worked example
x: Build the card index's KClass half, then find where it stops A first draft files cards by class and hands back Any. It compiles, but every caller has to cast, and nothing stops a card being filed under the wrong note. class CardIndex { private val byClass = HashMap<KClass<*>, Any>() fun register(type: KClass<*>, impl: Any) { byClass[type] = impl } fun get(type: KClass<*>): Any? = byClass[type] } index.register(Scale::class, PlainLabels()) // compiles: a label printer filed as the scale val scale = index.get(Scale::class) as Scale // ClassCastException here final class CardIndex { private final Map<Class<?>, Object> byClass = new HashMap<>(); void register(Class<?> type, Object impl) { byClass.put(type, impl); } Object get(Class<?> type) { return byClass.get(type); } } index.register(Scale.class, new PlainLabels()); // compiles: a label printer filed as the scale Scale scale = (Scale) index.get(Scale.class); // ClassCastException here Tie the note and the tool together with one type parameter. Now Scale::class is a KClass<Scale>, so T is Scale, and the tool must be one. 2. Hand back a T with a checked cast. Self-check before reading on: why is type.cast safe here when as T in lesson 8 was not? (The KClass is a real object at run time, so cast has something to check against.) fun <T : Any> register(type: KClass<T>, impl: T) { byClass[type] = impl } fun <T : Any> get(type: KClass<T>): T { val impl = byClass[type] ?: throw NoSuchElementException("no card for " + type.simpleName) return type.cast(impl) } index.register(Scale::class, PlainLabels()) // error: Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'PlainLabels', but 'Scale' was expected. <T> void register(Class<T> type, T impl) { byClass.put(type, impl); } <T> T get(Class<T> type) { Object impl = byClass.get(type); if (impl == null) throw new NoSuchElementException("no card for " + type.getSimpleName()); return type.cast(impl); } index.register(Scale.class, new PlainLabels()); // error: method register in class CardIndex cannot be applied to given types; // reason: inference variable T has incompatible bounds Add the reified wrapper for Kotlin callers. It touches only the public get(type), as lesson 8 required of public inline functions. inline fun <reified T : Any> get(): T = get(T::class) val scale: Scale = index.get() // T from the expected type val labels = index.get<LabelPrinter>() // Java keeps passing the class: Scale scale = index.get(Scale.class); LabelPrinter labels = index.get(LabelPrinter.class); Now file a generic tool. Shelf::class is a KClass<Shelf<*>>, so the best get can hand back is a Shelf<*>, and a second register(Shelf::class, lemons) replaces the apple shelf without a word. Asking for Shelf<Apple> fails at compile time. That's the point where the key has to become a KType, which is the second half of the lab. index.register(Shelf::class, apples) index.register(Shelf::class, lemons) // replaces the apples: same class val any: Shelf<*> = index.get(Shelf::class) val p: Shelf<Apple> = index.get(Shelf::class) // error: Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Shelf<Apple>', actual 'Shelf<*>'. index.register(Shelf.class, apples); // raw Class: Shelf.class has no <Apple> index.register(Shelf.class, lemons); // replaces the apples Shelf<?> any = index.get(Shelf.class);
