h: KClass, Class and type tokens · Quiz
x: val fruit: Fruit = pickFruit(). Which line compiles? val k: KClass<Fruit> = fruit::class val k: KClass<Apple> = fruit::class val k: KClass<out Fruit> = fruit::class val k: KClass<Fruit?> = fruit::class A bound class reference gives the class of some subtype of the declared type: KClass<out Fruit>. The exact KClass<Fruit> is what the class literal Fruit::class gives. KClass<Apple> would need the compiler to know the run-time class, and KClass<Fruit?> breaks the T : Any bound. A Gradle project without kotlin-reflect runs four lines. Which one throws? Apple::class.simpleName Apple::class.isInstance(fruit) typeOf<List<String>>().arguments Storeroom::class.objectInstance objectInstance describes a declaration, so it needs kotlin-reflect and throws KotlinReflectionNotSupportedError. The standard library handles names, instance checks and typeOf on its own. Printing a KClass or KType also works, just with the (Kotlin reflection is not available) apology. A card index must hold a Shelf<Apple> and a Shelf<Lemon> at the same time. Which key type do you use? KClass<*>, from Shelf::class KType, from typeOf<Shelf<Apple>>() Class<*>, from Shelf::class.java The class's simpleName Both shelves have the same class, so every class-based key (a KClass, a Class or a name) collides, and the second card replaces the first. A KType includes the type argument, so the two keys differ. In Java, a super type token's Type plays the same role. Java: static <T> Type listOf() { return new TypeRef<List<T>>() {}.type; }, with the usual TypeRef super type token. What does Tokens.<String>listOf() return? java.util.List<T>: the token records the type variable, not String java.util.List<java.lang.String> The raw java.util.List It throws ClassCastException, because T is not a ParameterizedType The anonymous subclass is compiled once, inside the generic method, and its declared superclass is literally TypeRef<List<T>>. The caller's String never reaches it. Kotlin's typeOf<T>() with a reified T doesn't have this hole, because the compiler writes the real type at each call site. From "Type erasure and reified type parameters": fun <T : Any> lookup(index: CardIndex): T = index.get<T>(), where get<T>() is inline with a reified T. What happens? It compiles and returns the tool for whatever T the caller picks It compiles, but always returns the first tool filed It doesn't compile: Cannot use 'T' as reified type parameter. Use a class instead. It compiles and throws ClassCastException at run time lookup's own T is an ordinary, erased type parameter, so there's no class to copy into the inlined get: its label is already gone. Make lookup itself inline with a reified T, or give it a type: KClass<T> parameter and call index.get(type).

h: KClass, Class and type tokens · Explain it back
x: A teammate asks: "Why do we need typeOf at all? T::class already tells us the type." Explain the difference between a KClass and a KType in your own words, using the Shelf<Apple> and Shelf<Lemon> example, and say what Java uses instead.

h: KClass, Class and type tokens · Key terms
x: KClass Kotlin's run-time object for a class, such as Apple::class. No type arguments, never nullable. Class Java's run-time object for a class: Apple.class, or Apple::class.java from Kotlin. KType A full type at run time: class, type arguments and nullability. Made by typeOf<T>(). Class literal Name::class: the class you name in code. Its type is exact, KClass<Name>. Bound class reference value::class: the run-time class of a value, typed KClass<out DeclaredType>. kotlin-reflect The separate jar that answers questions about declarations: members, sealed subclasses, data classes. Super type token A Java trick that captures a full generic type through an anonymous subclass's declared superclass. Typesafe heterogeneous container One map holding values of many types, with the type as the key, so get can return a T safely. KClass or KType: which one knows that a value is a List<String>? and not just a List? KType (from typeOf<List<String>?>()). A KClass describes only the class: no type arguments, never nullable. Why is fruit::class a KClass<out Fruit> when fruit: Fruit? The real class is some unknown subtype of Fruit, and out means exactly that. Java's getClass() returns Class<? extends Fruit> for the same reason. Why is KClass declared KClass<T : Any>? There is no class for a nullable type: String? is backed by the class String. So KClass<String?> and nullableValue::class don't compile. How do you convert between KClass and Java's Class? k.java gives the Class; c.kotlin gives the KClass. A value's Class is x.javaClass. Without kotlin-reflect, what does Storeroom::class.objectInstance do? It throws KotlinReflectionNotSupportedError. Anything that describes declarations needs kotlin-reflect; names, checks, casts and typeOf don't. How do you get a run-time object for the full type Shelf<Apple> in Kotlin? typeOf<Shelf<Apple>>(), a KType. Shelf<Apple>::class doesn't compile: only classes are allowed on the left of ::class. What is a super type token? An anonymous subclass, new TypeRef<List<String>>() {}, whose generic superclass is read back with reflection. It's how Jackson's TypeReference works.

h: KClass, Class and type tokens · Go deeper
x: Why doesn't a KType need kotlin-reflect, when so much else does? Because the compiler builds most of typeOf<T>(). At each call site it emits code that constructs the type from parts it already knows: the classifier (List::class), the arguments, the variance of each argument and the nullability flag. The standard library holds a small implementation of KType for that. Answering sealedSubclasses is different: it means reading Kotlin's own metadata out of the class file, and the reader for that metadata is what kotlin-reflect contains. KType also records variance and stars. typeOf<MutableList<out Number>>().arguments.single().variance is OUT, and typeOf<List<*>>().arguments prints [*]. So a card index keyed by KType treats MutableList<out Number> and MutableList<Number> as different keys. That's correct, but it can surprise you: the key must be written with exactly the same type on both sides. The docs page on reflection mentions that the kotlinc command-line compiler adds kotlin-reflect by default (you can opt out with -no-reflect). That's why a snippet that prints class kotlin.String in a quick command-line experiment prints class java.lang.String (Kotlin reflection is not available) inside your Gradle project. If you add kotlin-reflect to a program, add it on purpose: it's a 3.8 MB jar, and its first use loads and parses metadata, which costs a little time once per class. Last, the javaClass rule from the third section has a reason. javaClass is an extension property on every type, and a KClass is a value like any other, so k.javaClass would mean the class that implements the KClass object, not the class it describes. The standard library declares a deprecated overload for exactly that receiver, and in 2.4.21 using it is an error. x.javaClass on ordinary values is unaffected.

h: Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance · A form that names itself: a recursive bound keeps the builder chain typed
x: A base-class setter forgets the subclass; with B : Builder each subclass writes its own name into the blank, so amount returns it and the chain keeps cardToken A builder is an object you fill in one setting at a time and then ask to build the finished thing. Each setter returns the builder, so the calls can follow each other on one line, a style called a fluent chain. Put the shared setters in a base class, add a subclass with a setter of its own, and the chain breaks as soon as a base setter runs: Java class PlainBuilder { protected int grams; PlainBuilder grams(int grams) { this.grams = grams; return this; } } class PlainGiftBoxBuilder extends PlainBuilder { PlainGiftBoxBuilder ribbon(String colour) { ... } } new PlainGiftBoxBuilder().grams(1_200).ribbon("red"); // error: cannot find symbol Kotlin open class PlainBuilder { protected var grams = 0 fun grams(grams: Int): PlainBuilder { this.grams = grams; return this } } class PlainGiftBoxBuilder : PlainBuilder() { fun ribbon(colour: String): PlainGiftBoxBuilder { ... } } PlainGiftBoxBuilder().grams(1_200).ribbon("red") // error: Unresolved reference 'ribbon' on receiver of type 'PlainBuilder'. grams returns a PlainBuilder, because that's all the base class knows about itself. The object is still a PlainGiftBoxBuilder, and the demo prints that run-time class. But the static type, the one the compiler goes by, has lost it. The form has forgotten what kind of form it is. The base class needs a way to say "I return whatever subclass I really am". The answer is a self type, a type parameter that stands for "my own subclass", written with a recursive bound, a bound that mentions the type parameter itself: Java abstract class Builder<B extends Builder<B>> { protected int grams; B grams(int grams) { this.grams = grams; return self(); } protected abstract B self(); } final class GiftBoxBuilder extends Builder<GiftBoxBuilder> { GiftBoxBuilder ribbon(String colour) { ...; return this; } @Override protected GiftBoxBuilder self() { return this; } } Kotlin abstract class Builder<B : Builder<B>> { protected var grams = 0 fun grams(grams: Int): B { this.grams = grams; return self() } protected abstract fun self(): B } class GiftBoxBuilder : Builder<GiftBoxBuilder>() { fun ribbon(colour: String): GiftBoxBuilder { ...; return this } override fun self() = this } Read B : Builder<B> as "B is a builder whose own B is B". It's the blank at the top of the base form: "this is a ___ form". The only types that fit are subclasses that write their own name in it, as GiftBoxBuilder : Builder<GiftBoxBuilder>() does. Then substitute, as in lesson 1 of this track: for a GiftBoxBuilder, every B in the base class reads as GiftBoxBuilder. So GiftBoxBuilder().grams(1_200) has the static type GiftBoxBuilder, and .ribbon("red") is in reach again. You've met the shape before. Lesson 2's T : Comparable<T>, "a T that compares with its own kind", is a recursive bound, and so is Java's own Enum<E extends Enum<E>>. Two details matter. The abstract self() keeps the code checked: each subclass returns this, and the compiler verifies that it is a B. The tempting shortcut, return this as B in the base class, is an unchecked cast, and erasure turns it into no check at all. And the bound can't force honesty. class Liar : Builder<GiftBoxBuilder>() compiles, because the blank only asks for the name of some builder. Here the form picture breaks just as the code does: anyone can write another form's name in the blank. With an abstract self(), the liar must hand back a GiftBoxBuilder it doesn't have, which is where you notice. A recursive bound lets a base class return its subclass. Fill the blank with the subclass's own name. In pure Kotlin code you often don't need a builder at all: a data class with default arguments and copy covers most cases. Reach for self types when Java callers need a builder, or when you extend a Java class that already uses one. Next, a smaller tool with a big promise: this box is never empty. Break a builder chain, then fix it with B : Builder Run SelfTypeDemo (or SelfTypeDemoJava). Compare the static type and the run-time class on the first line. Uncomment wrong move 1. Predict, then run. Uncomment wrong move 2, the Liar class. It compiles. Add println(Liar().grams(5)::class.simpleName) below it and predict what prints. SelfTypeDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l10.demo // 1. Without a self type: the base setters return the base class, and the chain loses the subclass. open class PlainBuilder { protected var grams = 0 fun grams(grams: Int): PlainBuilder { this.grams = grams; return this } } class PlainGiftBoxBuilder : PlainBuilder() { private var ribbon = "" fun ribbon(colour: String): PlainGiftBoxBuilder { ribbon = colour; return this } fun build() = "gift box, $grams g, $ribbon ribbon" } // 2. With a self type: B names "my own subclass", so the base setters return it. abstract class Builder<B : Builder<B>> { protected var grams = 0 fun grams(grams: Int): B { this.grams = grams; return self() } protected abstract fun self(): B } class GiftBoxBuilder : Builder<GiftBoxBuilder>() { private var ribbon = "" fun ribbon(colour: String): GiftBoxBuilder { ribbon = colour; return this } override fun self() = this fun build() = "gift box, $grams g, $ribbon ribbon" } fun main() { val lost: PlainBuilder = PlainGiftBoxBuilder().ribbon("red").grams(1_200) // grams() returns a PlainBuilder println("after grams(): static type PlainBuilder, run-time class ${lost::class.simpleName}") println(GiftBoxBuilder().grams(1_200).ribbon("red").build()) // the chain keeps GiftBoxBuilder // Wrong moves. Uncomment one at a time, predict the error, then run. // println(PlainGiftBoxBuilder().grams(1_200).ribbon("red").build()) // 1 // class Liar : Builder<GiftBoxBuilder>() { override fun self() = GiftBoxBuilder() } // 2 (compiles: what does it break?) } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l10.demo.SelfTypeDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l10/demo/SelfTypeDemo.kt SelfTypeDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l10.demo; /** Java twin of SelfTypeDemo.kt. The same recursive bound that java.lang.Enum uses: Enum<E extends Enum<E>>. */ public class SelfTypeDemoJava { static class PlainBuilder { protected int grams; PlainBuilder grams(int grams) { this.grams = grams; return this; } } static final class PlainGiftBoxBuilder extends PlainBuilder { private String ribbon = ""; PlainGiftBoxBuilder ribbon(String colour) { ribbon = colour; return this; } String build() { return "gift box, " + grams + " g, " + ribbon + " ribbon"; } } static abstract class Builder<B extends Builder<B>> { protected int grams; B grams(int grams) { this.grams = grams; return self(); } protected abstract B self(); } static final class GiftBoxBuilder extends Builder<GiftBoxBuilder> { private String ribbon = ""; GiftBoxBuilder ribbon(String colour) { ribbon = colour; return this; } @Override protected GiftBoxBuilder self() { return this; } String build() { return "gift box, " + grams + " g, " + ribbon + " ribbon"; } } public static void main(String[] args) { PlainBuilder lost = new PlainGiftBoxBuilder().ribbon("red").grams(1_200); // grams() returns a PlainBuilder System.out.println("after grams(): static type PlainBuilder, run-time class " + lost.getClass().getSimpleName()); System.out.println(new GiftBoxBuilder().grams(1_200).ribbon("red").build()); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // System.out.println(new PlainGiftBoxBuilder().grams(1_200).ribbon("red").build()); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l10.demo.SelfTypeDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l10/demo/SelfTypeDemoJava.java Both print after grams(): static type PlainBuilder, run-time class PlainGiftBoxBuilder and gift box, 1200 g, red ribbon. Wrong move 1 fails with Unresolved reference 'ribbon' on receiver of type 'PlainBuilder'. (Java: cannot find symbol). The Liar compiles because the bound only asks for some builder, and Liar().grams(5) prints GiftBoxBuilder: a fresh object, not the liar you filled in. Nothing forces a subclass to write its own name in the blank. A recursive bound lets the base class return its own subclass, so a chain keeps the subclass's setters in reach. Each subclass writes its own name into the blank. Generics: upper bounds (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance · This box always holds a real fruit: T & Any takes null out of a type
x: A plain T may stand for a nullable type, because its default bound is Any? (lesson 2). On a label, that's "Box of ___", where the caller may write "apples, or nothing". Sometimes you know that one particular value is not null, and you want its type to say so: whatever the label allows, this box holds a real fruit. Kotlin writes that as T & Any, a definitely non-nullable type: "T, with null taken out". Java // Java's types say nothing about null. The best you can do is a comment and a check at run time. static <T> T firstNotNullValue(List<T> items) { for (T item : items) if (item != null) return item; throw new NoSuchElementException("no non-null element"); } String first = firstNotNullValue(Arrays.asList(null, "Gala", "Fuji")); Kotlin fun <T> List<T>.firstNotNullValue(): T & Any { for (item in this) if (item != null) return item // smart cast: item is T & Any here throw NoSuchElementException("no non-null element") } val first: String = listOf(null, "Gala", "Fuji").firstNotNullValue() // T = String?, result String With T = String?, T & Any is String. With T = Apple, it's just Apple. Inside the loop, the check item != null is what makes item fit: a smart cast, Kotlin's narrowing of a value's type after a check, turns T into T & Any. The compiler holds you to the promise. Return a plain T, and it says Return type mismatch: expected 'T (of fun <T> forget) & Any', actual 'T (of fun <T> forget)'. The Kotlin docs name the main use: overriding Java methods whose generic parameters are annotated @NotNull, a marker that tells tools a value is never null. Kotlin reads @NotNull T in a Java interface as T & Any: Java public interface NotNullTransformer<T> { @NotNull T transform(@NotNull T value); } Kotlin class UpperCaser<T : CharSequence?> : NotNullTransformer<T> { override fun transform(value: T & Any): T & Any = ... } Two rules come with it. The left side must be a type parameter with a nullable bound. With T : Any there is no null to take out, and the compiler says Intersection types are supported only for definitely non-nullable types: left part must be a type parameter with nullable bounds. And the promise is Kotlin's alone: Java sees <T> T firstNotNullValue(List<T>), with no trace of & Any. The docs add that when you work only with Kotlin, you'll rarely need to write it, because inference handles it. Expect to type T & Any at the Java boundary and in small helpers like this one, which turns an optional field into a value the rest of the code can use without !!, Kotlin's "trust me, it isn't null" operator: Java // Java: the null check happens, but the type can't record it static <T> T requireValue(T value, String name) { if (value == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException(name + " is required"); return value; } Kotlin fun <T> T.requireValue(name: String): T & Any = this ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("$name is required") val ribbon: String = order.ribbon.requireValue("ribbon") // order.ribbon is a String? T & Any is T with null taken out. Use it where a nullable T is known to hold a value. That was a type with one door closed. Next, a type with one door opened on purpose. Take null out of a type Run NonNullDemo (or NonNullDemoJava). Open NotNullTransformer.java next to it: a Java interface marked with @NotNull. Uncomment wrong moves 1 and 2 in NonNullDemo.kt one at a time. Predict each error first. Uncomment function 3 at the bottom. In the Java twin, uncomment the oops line and run: what does Java catch, and when? NonNullDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l10.demo /** T may be nullable (String?), but the result is "T, definitely not null". */ fun <T> List<T>.firstNotNullValue(): T & Any { for (item in this) if (item != null) return item // smart cast: item is T & Any here throw NoSuchElementException("no non-null element") } /** The docs' example: fall back to a value that is known not to be null. */ fun <T> elvis(x: T, y: T & Any): T & Any = x ?: y /** Implements the Java interface in NotNullTransformer.java, whose methods are annotated @NotNull. */ class UpperCaser<T : CharSequence?> : NotNullTransformer<T> { @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") override fun transform(value: T & Any): T & Any = value.toString().uppercase() as (T & Any) } fun main() { val varieties: List<String?> = listOf(null, "Gala", "Fuji") // the first order form left it blank val first: String = varieties.firstNotNullValue() // T = String?, result String val note: String? = null val shown: String = elvis(note, "no note") println("first = $first, shown = $shown") println("transformed = ${UpperCaser<String?>().transform("Gala")}") // Wrong moves. Uncomment one at a time, predict the error, then run. // fun <T> forget(x: T): T & Any = x // 1 // val n: String = UpperCaser<String?>().transform(null) // 2 } // 3. & Any needs a type parameter whose bound is nullable. // fun <T : Any> pointless(x: T & Any) {} ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l10.demo.NonNullDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l10/demo/NonNullDemo.kt NonNullDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l10.demo; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; import java.util.Objects; /** * Java twin of NonNullDemo.kt. Java types say nothing about null, so "T, but not null" can only be * a convention (or an annotation such as @NotNull), checked at run time. */ public class NonNullDemoJava { static <T> T firstNotNullValue(List<T> items) { for (T item : items) if (item != null) return item; throw new NoSuchElementException("no non-null element"); } static <T> T elvis(T x, T y) { return x != null ? x : Objects.requireNonNull(y); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> varieties = Arrays.asList(null, "Gala", "Fuji"); String first = firstNotNullValue(varieties); String shown = elvis(null, "no note"); System.out.println("first = " + first + ", shown = " + shown); System.out.println("transformed = " + new UpperCaser<String>().transform("Gala")); // Uncomment and run: it compiles in Java. What happens at run time? // String oops = elvis(null, null); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l10.demo.NonNullDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l10/demo/NonNullDemoJava.java Both print first = Gala, shown = no note and transformed = GALA. Kotlin's wrong moves: (1) Return type mismatch: expected 'T (of fun <T> forget) & Any', actual 'T (of fun <T> forget)'., (2) Null cannot be a value of a non-null type 'String'., because for T = String?, T & Any is String. Function 3: Intersection types are supported only for definitely non-nullable types: left part must be a type parameter with nullable bounds. The Java oops line compiles, and throws NullPointerException from Objects.requireNonNull when it runs.

h: Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance · A display case you can ask but not fill: @UnsafeVariance and List.contains
x: Here's a puzzle left over from lesson 4. List is declared interface List<out E>: it's the glass display case of lesson 3, where things come out and nothing goes in. An out type parameter can't appear as a parameter. Yet you call list.contains(x) every day, and hand it an E. The standard library's source (2.4.21) shows how: public operator fun contains(element: @UnsafeVariance E): Boolean public fun indexOf(element: @UnsafeVariance E): Int @UnsafeVariance "suppresses errors about variance conflict" for one use of the type. Think of it as a note the author tapes to the glass: "this opening is only for pointing". contains compares the element with what's inside and never keeps it. So a List<Int> seen as a List<Number> can't be damaged by it, and contains(2.5) just returns false. The clerk reads the note, nods, and stops checking that one spot. Why take an E at all, when Any? would need no annotation? Because the E lets the compiler catch a question that makes no sense. Java chose Object, and pays for it: Java Set<Long> crateIds = Set.of(42L); crateIds.contains(42); // false: 42 is boxed to an Integer, and Integer(42) != Long(42) List.of(180, 150).contains("180"); // compiles, always false Kotlin val crateIds: Set<Long> = setOf(42L) crateIds.contains(42) // true: the literal 42 is typed as a Long here listOf(180, 150).contains("180") // error: Type inference failed. The value of the type parameter 'T' must be mentioned in input types ... That first Java line is a real kind of bug: an int id looked up in a set of Longs, false every time, with no warning. The annotation is called unsafe for a reason. It switches the check off, and the compiler believes you. Here is a display case with a secret slot cut into the glass: Java // Java's way to break a ? extends view on purpose is an unchecked cast: List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Apple("Gala", 180))); List<? extends Fruit> view = apples; ((List<Fruit>) view).add(new Lemon("Eureka", 120)); Apple last = apples.get(apples.size() - 1); // ClassCastException Kotlin class DisplayCase<out T>(first: T) { private val items = mutableListOf(first) fun add(item: @UnsafeVariance T) { items.add(item) } // keeps it: a broken promise fun last(): T = items.last() } val apples: DisplayCase<Apple> = DisplayCase(Apple("Gala", 180)) val anyFruit: DisplayCase<Fruit> = apples // fine: DisplayCase is out T anyFruit.add(Lemon("Eureka", 120)) // compiles val last: Apple = apples.last() // ClassCastException It's lesson 3's lemon in the crate of apples, back again. The demo prints ClassCastException: class workbench.generics.l10.demo.Lemon cannot be cast to class workbench.generics.l10.demo.Apple. Use @UnsafeVariance only on parameters that are read and compared, such as those of contains, indexOf or an equality check, never on ones that are kept. To check that a use is honest, follow the parameter through the body. If it only reaches ==, equals or hashCode, the promise holds. If it reaches a field, a collection or a callback that keeps it, remove the annotation and make the type invariant, or split it into a read view and a write view, as lesson 11 of this track does. @UnsafeVariance is a promise, not a check. Put it only on parameters that are compared, never kept. Three more tools sit at the edges of the type system, and one of them is a box that can never hold anything. Use the annotation well, then badly Run UnsafeVarianceDemo and UnsafeVarianceDemoJava. Find the line that compiles in Java and is refused in Kotlin. Uncomment wrong move 1 in the Kotlin file. Predict, then run. Uncomment wrong move 2 (DisplayCase2) and read the error. That's the check @UnsafeVariance switched off in DisplayCase. UnsafeVarianceDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l10.demo // The shop's fruit, used by the demos of this lesson (the Java twins use these Kotlin types too) interface Fruit { val name: String; val grams: Int } data class Apple(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit { override fun toString() = name } data class Lemon(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit { override fun toString() = name } /** Declared out, like a glass display case. Then someone cut a slot in the glass for add(). It compiles. */ class DisplayCase<out T>(first: T) { private val items = mutableListOf(first) fun add(item: @UnsafeVariance T) { items.add(item) } fun last(): T = items.last() } fun main() { // 1. The standard library uses @UnsafeVariance safely: contains only compares, it never stores. val weights: List<Number> = listOf(180, 150) // List<Int> seen as List<Number> println("contains(150): ${weights.contains(150)}, contains(2.5): ${weights.contains(2.5)}") // 2. And because contains takes an E, the compiler can catch a nonsense check. // println(listOf(180, 150).contains("180")) // wrong move 1 // 3. Used carelessly, the same annotation breaks type safety. val apples: DisplayCase<Apple> = DisplayCase(Apple("Gala", 180)) val anyFruit: DisplayCase<Fruit> = apples // fine: DisplayCase is out T anyFruit.add(Lemon("Eureka", 120)) // compiles, thanks to @UnsafeVariance try { val last: Apple = apples.last() println(last) } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("ClassCastException: ${e.message?.substringBefore(" (")}") } } // Wrong move 2: remove @UnsafeVariance from a copy of DisplayCase and read the error. // class DisplayCase2<out T> { fun add(item: T) {} } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l10.demo.UnsafeVarianceDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l10/demo/UnsafeVarianceDemo.kt UnsafeVarianceDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l10.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of UnsafeVarianceDemo.kt. Java's contains takes an Object, so it never needed the * annotation, and it can't catch a nonsense check. Java's way to break a ? extends view on purpose * is an unchecked cast. */ public class UnsafeVarianceDemoJava { @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") public static void main(String[] args) { List<? extends Number> weights = List.of(180, 150); System.out.println("contains(150): " + weights.contains(150) + ", contains(2.5): " + weights.contains(2.5)); System.out.println("contains(\"180\") compiles in Java: " + List.of(180, 150).contains("180")); List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Apple("Gala", 180))); List<? extends Fruit> view = apples; ((List<Fruit>) view).add(new Lemon("Eureka", 120)); // the unchecked cast is the Java "unsafe variance" try { Apple last = apples.get(apples.size() - 1); System.out.println(last); } catch (ClassCastException e) { System.out.println("ClassCastException: " + e.getMessage().split(" \\(")[0]); } } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l10.demo.UnsafeVarianceDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l10/demo/UnsafeVarianceDemoJava.java Both print contains(150): true, contains(2.5): false and ClassCastException: class workbench.generics.l10.demo.Lemon cannot be cast to class workbench.generics.l10.demo.Apple. Java also prints contains("180") compiles in Java: false. In Kotlin, wrong move 1 fails with Type inference failed. The value of the type parameter 'T' must be mentioned in input types ..., and DisplayCase2 fails with Type parameter 'T' is declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position in type 'T (of class DisplayCase2<out T>)'. UnsafeVariance (Kotlin stdlib API) docs

h: Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance · Three more tools at the edges: function types, Nothing and type aliases
x: Function types carry variance on both ends. (P) -> R is Function1<in P, out R> (lesson 5): a function takes its parameter in and hands its result out. So a helper that joins two steps accepts a more general second step, and its result can be used as something more general: Java // Function<T, R> is invariant, so the JDK writes the variance into the signature: // default <V> Function<T, V> andThen(Function<? super R, ? extends V> after) Function<String, Long> toGrams = s -> new BigDecimal(s).movePointRight(3).longValueExact(); // kilograms to grams Function<Object, String> describe = x -> "<" + x + ">"; Function<String, String> pipeline = toGrams.andThen(describe); // <1250> for "1.25" Kotlin fun <A, B, C> andThen(first: (A) -> B, second: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> second(first(a)) } val toGrams: (String) -> Long = { BigDecimal(it).movePointRight(3).longValueExact() } // kilograms to grams val describe: (Any) -> String = { "<$it>" } // takes Any, not just Long val pipeline: (String) -> CharSequence = andThen(toGrams, describe) // <1250> for "1.25" Nothing is the bottom type: a subtype of every type, with no values at all. It's the one box that can never hold anything, so it fits every label. throw and TODO() have the type Nothing, which is why val strict: Long = text.toLongOrNull() ?: fail("not a number") type-checks when fun fail(reason: String): Nothing. It also explains emptyList(). One shared, empty List<Nothing> fits every List<Apple>, because List is out E and Nothing sits below Apple: an empty display case is a fine apple display. Lesson 11 uses the same trick for Either. Java has no bottom type. Collections.emptyList() is a generic method whose T is inferred at each call, and a Kotlin List<Nothing> reaches Java as a raw List. A type alias gives an existing type a shorter name, and it can be generic: Java // Java has no type aliases. The nearest thing, a functional interface, is a new, separate type. @FunctionalInterface interface Listener<E> { void hear(E item); } Kotlin typealias Listener<E> = (E) -> Unit // just a name: a Listener<E> IS an (E) -> Unit typealias Index<K> = MutableMap<K, MutableList<K>> val signWriter: Listener<Apple> = { println("sign for ${it.name}") } val plain: (Apple) -> Unit = signWriter // same type, no conversion An alias is a nickname written on the label, not a new kind of box. So it has the variance of what it stands for: a Listener<Fruit> is a Listener<Apple>, exactly as with the function type. That's how lesson 5's delivery bell took a stock-keeper who counts every fruit. Aliases nested inside a class became Stable in Kotlin 2.3, with one limit: they can't mention the outer class's type parameters. All the tools in this lesson share one limit, and it's worth saying plainly: each is a promise the compiler partly takes on trust. A recursive bound can't stop a liar, T & Any means nothing to Java, and @UnsafeVariance is believed without a second look. The lab puts the first and the last of them to work on the shop's order forms. Compose with variance, fail with Nothing Run FunctionTypesDemo (or FunctionTypesDemoJava, which also calls the JDK's own andThen). Uncomment the wrong move and read which type the compiler found for the pipeline. Change fail's return type from Nothing to Unit. Which line breaks, and why? FunctionTypesDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l10.demo import java.math.BigDecimal /** A new name for a function type. Not a new type: a Listener<E> IS an (E) -> Unit. */ typealias Listener<E> = (E) -> Unit fun <A, B, C> andThen(first: (A) -> B, second: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> second(first(a)) } fun fail(reason: String): Nothing = throw IllegalArgumentException(reason) fun main() { // 1. Function1<in P, out R>: a more general second function fits. val toGrams: (String) -> Long = { BigDecimal(it).movePointRight(3).longValueExact() } // kilograms to grams val describe: (Any) -> String = { "<$it>" } val pipeline: (String) -> CharSequence = andThen(toGrams, describe) println("pipeline(\"1.25\") = ${pipeline("1.25")}") // 2. Nothing is a subtype of every type. val none: List<Apple> = emptyList() // emptyList() is a List<Nothing> here val grams: Long = "x".toLongOrNull() ?: 0L val strict: Long = "180".toLongOrNull() ?: fail("not a number") // fail returns Nothing, so this is a Long println("none = $none, grams = $grams, strict = $strict") // 3. A type alias is only a name. val signWriter: Listener<Apple> = { println("sign for ${it.name}") } val plain: (Apple) -> Unit = signWriter // same type, no conversion plain(Apple("Gala", 180)) // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // val tooStrict: (Any) -> String = andThen(toGrams, describe) } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l10.demo.FunctionTypesDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l10/demo/FunctionTypesDemo.kt FunctionTypesDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l10.demo; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Consumer; import java.util.function.Function; /** * Java twin of FunctionTypesDemo.kt. Java's Function<T, R> is invariant, so the JDK writes the * variance into andThen's signature: andThen(Function<? super R, ? extends V> after). */ public class FunctionTypesDemoJava { static <A, B, C> Function<A, C> andThen(Function<A, ? extends B> first, Function<? super B, ? extends C> second) { return a -> second.apply(first.apply(a)); } static <T> T fail(String reason) { throw new IllegalArgumentException(reason); } // no Nothing: fake it with T public static void main(String[] args) { Function<String, Long> toGrams = s -> new BigDecimal(s).movePointRight(3).longValueExact(); // kilograms to grams Function<Object, String> describe = x -> "<" + x + ">"; Function<String, CharSequence> pipeline = andThen(toGrams, describe); System.out.println("pipeline(\"1.25\") = " + pipeline.apply("1.25")); System.out.println("JDK andThen: " + toGrams.andThen(describe).apply("0.35")); List<Apple> none = Collections.emptyList(); // generic method: T inferred as Apple long strict = Long.parseLong("180"); System.out.println("none = " + none + ", strict = " + strict); Consumer<Apple> signWriter = a -> System.out.println("sign for " + a.getName()); // no type aliases in Java signWriter.accept(new Apple("Gala", 180)); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l10.demo.FunctionTypesDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l10/demo/FunctionTypesDemoJava.java Kotlin prints pipeline("1.25") = <1250>, none = [], grams = 0, strict = 180 and sign for Gala. Java prints the pipeline line, JDK andThen: <350>, none = [], strict = 180 and sign for Gala. The wrong move fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected '(Any) -> String', actual '(String) -> String'.: a function that needs a String input can't stand in for one that takes Any. With Unit, the strict line fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Long', actual 'Any'., because the type of the ?: expression becomes the common supertype of Long and Unit. Nothing fits there because it is a subtype of Long. Type aliases (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance · Java and Kotlin
x: A self-typed order builder in Java and Kotlin OrderBuilder.java abstract class OrderBuilder<B extends OrderBuilder<B>> { protected int grams; protected String variety; B grams(int grams) { this.grams = grams; return self(); } B variety(String name) { this.variety = name; return self(); } protected abstract B self(); } final class GiftBoxBuilder extends OrderBuilder<GiftBoxBuilder> { private String ribbon; GiftBoxBuilder ribbon(String colour) { this.ribbon = colour; return this; } @Override protected GiftBoxBuilder self() { return this; } GiftBox build() { if (grams <= 0) throw new IllegalStateException("weight must be positive"); return new GiftBox(grams, variety, "", ribbon); } } // new GiftBoxBuilder().grams(1_200).variety("Gala").ribbon("red").build(); OrderBuilder.kt abstract class OrderBuilder<B : OrderBuilder<B>> { protected var grams: Int = 0 protected var variety: String? = null fun grams(grams: Int): B { this.grams = grams; return self() } fun variety(name: String): B { variety = name; return self() } protected abstract fun self(): B } class GiftBoxBuilder : OrderBuilder<GiftBoxBuilder>() { private var ribbon: String? = null fun ribbon(colour: String): GiftBoxBuilder { ribbon = colour; return this } override fun self() = this fun build(): GiftBox { check(grams > 0) { "weight must be positive" } return GiftBox(grams, variety!!, "", checkNotNull(ribbon)) } } // GiftBoxBuilder().grams(1_200).variety("Gala").ribbon("red").build() The recursive bound is the same idea in both languages: B extends OrderBuilder<B> and B : OrderBuilder<B>, with each subclass passing itself and an abstract self() in place of an unchecked cast. Kotlin adds checks Java can't express. variety and ribbon are String?, so build() must deal with a missing value, and check and checkNotNull throw IllegalStateException with your message. Java's build() happily passes a null ribbon along. The other three tools of this lesson have no Java twin: T & Any (Java types carry no nullability), @UnsafeVariance (Java has no declaration-site variance to suppress) and Nothing (Java has no bottom type). Java has no type aliases either. And in Kotlin you can often skip the builder entirely with a data class, default arguments and copy.

h: Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance · Worked example
x: Add a pickup order to the builder hierarchy The lab's hierarchy has gift boxes and deliveries. The shop wants pickup orders too, collected at the counter at a set time. The quickest path is to copy GiftBoxBuilder and edit it, and that's how the classic bug gets in: the type argument still says GiftBoxBuilder. class PickupBuilder : OrderBuilder<GiftBoxBuilder>() { // copied, not changed private var time: String? = null fun pickupAt(time: String): PickupBuilder { this.time = time; return this } override fun self(): GiftBoxBuilder = this } // error: Return type mismatch: expected 'GiftBoxBuilder', actual 'PickupBuilder'. final class PickupBuilder extends OrderBuilder<GiftBoxBuilder> { // copied, not changed private String time; PickupBuilder pickupAt(String time) { this.time = time; return this; } @Override protected GiftBoxBuilder self() { return this; } } // error: incompatible types: PickupBuilder cannot be converted to GiftBoxBuilder The abstract self() caught it at compile time. With return this as B in the base class, the same slip would compile, and PickupBuilder().grams(500) would throw ClassCastException: class PickupBuilder cannot be cast to class GiftBoxBuilder at the call. Fix the declaration: the subclass writes its own name in the blank. class PickupBuilder : OrderBuilder<PickupBuilder>() { private var time: String? = null fun pickupAt(time: String): PickupBuilder { this.time = time; return this } override fun self() = this // B is PickupBuilder: no cast final class PickupBuilder extends OrderBuilder<PickupBuilder> { private String time; PickupBuilder pickupAt(String time) { this.time = time; return this; } @Override protected PickupBuilder self() { return this; } // no cast Build: check the shared fields with the base class's checkCommon(), then the pickup's own field. Self-check before reading the comment: why does grams(...) in the chain below return a PickupBuilder, with no change to the base class? (Because the declaration fills B with PickupBuilder, and grams returns B.) fun build(): Pickup { checkCommon() val t = checkNotNull(time) { "pickup time is required" } return Pickup(grams, variety!!, note, t) } } val p = PickupBuilder().grams(2_500).variety("Fuji").pickupAt("17:30").build() Pickup build() { checkCommon(); if (time == null) throw new IllegalStateException("pickup time is required"); return new Pickup(grams, variety, note, time); } } Pickup p = new PickupBuilder().grams(2_500).variety("Fuji").pickupAt("17:30").build();

h: Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance · Quiz
x: abstract class Builder<B : Builder<B>> { fun grams(n: Int): B; ... } and class GiftBoxBuilder : Builder<GiftBoxBuilder>(). What is the static type of GiftBoxBuilder().grams(1_200)? Builder<GiftBoxBuilder> GiftBoxBuilder Builder<*> B, which the compiler can't resolve outside the class grams returns B, and the subclass declaration fills B with GiftBoxBuilder. So at the call site the result is a GiftBoxBuilder, and its own methods, such as ribbon, are still in reach. That is the whole point of the recursive bound. fun <T> List<T>.firstNotNullValue(): T & Any. What is the type of listOf<String?>(null, "Gala").firstNotNullValue()? String String? Any String & Any? T is String?, and & Any removes the null: String? minus null is String. With T = Apple it would be Apple. That's why the result can go straight into a val variety: String. Why can interface List<out E> declare fun contains(element: @UnsafeVariance E): Boolean without risk? Because the annotation moves the check to run time Because List is immutable, so nothing can be stored Because contains only compares the argument and never stores it, so a List<Int> seen as a List<Number> can't be damaged Because E is erased, so variance doesn't apply at run time Variance protects against storing a wrong value. contains stores nothing; asking a list of ints whether it contains 2.5 just returns false. The annotation is a promise about that, not a check at run time. And "immutable" isn't the reason: @UnsafeVariance on a storing method breaks a class however read-only it looks, as the DisplayCase demo shows. val toGrams: (String) -> Long and val describe: (Any) -> String. With fun <A, B, C> andThen(first: (A) -> B, second: (B) -> C): (A) -> C, does val p: (String) -> CharSequence = andThen(toGrams, describe) compile? No: describe must be exactly (Long) -> String No: the result would be (String) -> String, which is not a (String) -> CharSequence Only with an explicit cast Yes: (Any) -> String is a (Long) -> String (in on the parameter), and (String) -> String is a (String) -> CharSequence (out on the result) Function types are Function1<in P, out R>. A function that accepts any value can stand in for one that accepts a Long, and a function that returns a String can stand in for one that returns a CharSequence. It's the "pick the right variance" check from lesson 5, applied twice in one call. From "Covariance with out: producers": class DisplayCase<out T> { fun add(item: T) {} } doesn't compile. What does the compiler object to? T appears in an in-position (a parameter) in a class that declared it out add is public; it would compile if it were protected Classes declared out can't have functions with parameters DisplayCase needs a constructor that takes a T An out type parameter may appear only in out-positions, such as return types; a parameter is an in-position, a slot in the dispenser. protected members are checked too; only private ones are exempt. @UnsafeVariance would silence the error, and this lesson's demo shows what that costs when add keeps the value.

h: Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance · Key terms
x: Recursive bound A bound that mentions the type parameter itself: T : Comparable<T>, B : Builder<B>. Self type A type parameter that stands for "my own subclass", so methods in the base class can return it. Definitely non-nullable type T & Any: the type parameter T with null taken out. @UnsafeVariance An annotation that switches off the variance check for one use of a type. A promise, not a check. Nothing Kotlin's bottom type: a subtype of every type, with no values. The type of throw and TODO(). Type alias A new name for an existing type, such as typealias Listener<E> = (E) -> Unit. Not a new type. What problem does abstract class Builder<B : Builder<B>> solve? Shared setters in the base class can return B, the concrete subclass, so a chain like GiftBoxBuilder().grams(1_200).ribbon("red") keeps the subclass's methods. Why an abstract self(): B instead of return this as B? this as B is unchecked and fails late if a subclass passes the wrong type argument. An overridden self() = this is checked by the compiler. What does T & Any mean? T with null removed: a definitely non-nullable type. For T = String? it is String. What is the main use of T & Any? Overriding Java generic methods whose parameters or results are annotated @NotNull. How does List<out E> get away with contains(element: E)? The parameter is marked @UnsafeVariance. It's safe because contains only compares the element and never stores it. Why does val none: List<Apple> = emptyList() compile? emptyList() gives a List<Nothing>. Nothing is a subtype of every type, and List is out E, so it is a List<Apple>. Is typealias Listener<E> = (E) -> Unit a new type? No. It's only a name: a Listener<Apple> is an (Apple) -> Unit, with the same variance.

h: Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance · Go deeper
x: Recursive bounds go further than builders. java.lang.Enum is declared Enum<E extends Enum<E>> so that compareTo takes the same enum type, and EnumSet.noneOf(Class<E>) is bounded <E extends Enum<E>>. Kotlin's Enum<E : Enum<E>> is the same declaration. Lesson 2's fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T) is the most common recursive bound of all; the Java signature Kotlin generates for it is <T extends Comparable<? super T>>, because Kotlin's Comparable is declared in T. The standard library's use of @UnsafeVariance is easy to check. In the 2.4.21 sources (kotlin-stdlib-sources.jar, file Collections.kt) it appears on contains, containsAll and indexOf of List, and on AbstractCollection.contains. The contains("180") error you saw comes from a second safety net. When the member contains(element: Int) doesn't accept a String, the compiler tries the extension Iterable<T>.contains(element: T), whose T is marked so that it must match the receiver's element type, and inference fails with the message you read. Two small facts about Nothing. The type of the literal null is Nothing?, which is why null fits every nullable type. And when a Kotlin function returns List<Nothing>, Java sees a raw List, because Java has no bottom type to write there. Type aliases can't create the separate types people sometimes want from them. typealias CrateId = String lets you pass any String where a CrateId is expected. If you want the compiler to keep crate ids and supplier ids apart, use a value class, @JvmInline value class CrateId(val value: String), which is a real type with no wrapper object at run time in most uses.

h: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus · A problem or a fruit: Either, with two out parameters and Nothing
x: The first design comes from the back door too. Each delivery note is read and checked, and the check has two possible outcomes: a problem ("no weight written") or a good value. A result type that holds exactly one of two kinds of value is often called Either, with a Left for the problem and a Right for the value: Java // Java 21: a sealed interface and records. Java has no Nothing, so Left carries an R it never uses. sealed interface Either<L, R> permits Left, Right {} record Left<L, R>(L value) implements Either<L, R> {} record Right<L, R>(R value) implements Either<L, R> {} static <L, R, R2> Either<L, R2> map(Either<L, R> e, Function<? super R, ? extends R2> f) { return switch (e) { case Left<L, R> l -> new Left<>(l.value()); // must rebuild: a Left<L, R> is not a Left<L, R2> case Right<L, R> r -> new Right<>(f.apply(r.value())); }; } Kotlin sealed interface Either<out L, out R> { data class Left<out L>(val value: L) : Either<L, Nothing> data class Right<out R>(val value: R) : Either<Nothing, R> } fun <L, R, R2> Either<L, R>.map(f: (R) -> R2): Either<L, R2> = when (this) { is Either.Left -> this // no rebuild needed is Either.Right -> Either.Right(f(value)) } Two tools from this track meet here. An Either only hands its values out, so both parameters are out (lesson 4): a dispenser with one of two things inside. And Left fills the unused side with Nothing, lesson 10's box that can never hold anything and so fits every label. Put together, a Left<String> is an Either<String, Nothing>. Because Nothing is a subtype of every type and R is out, it is also an Either<String, R2> for any R2. That's why is Either.Left -> this type-checks: the same problem slip is a valid result for any kind of success. Java has neither tool, so its map must build a new Left every time. The interface is sealed, which means all its subclasses are declared in the same file. So the compiler knows Left and Right are the only cases, and a when that forgets one is an error. A caller can map the value, fall back with getOrElse, or handle both cases. Unlike an exception, the problem is part of the signature, where every reader sees it. Covariance makes results combine, too: an Either<String, Long> is an Either<Any, Number>, so a function that reports any problem and any number accepts it. Remove the outs and almost everything breaks at once, including the Left and Right declarations themselves: Type parameter 'L' is declared as 'out' but occurs in 'invariant' position in type 'Either<L (of class Left<out L>), Nothing>'. A supertype is a position too. The demo counts six errors. With out and Nothing, one Left fits every success type. Return it as it is. Either only hands values out. The next design hands values out from a type that also takes them in. Fold, mapLeft, then remove out Run EitherDemo and EitherDemoJava. Compare how mapLeft handles the Right branch in each. In EitherDemo.kt, remove both outs from sealed interface Either (keep the ones on Left and Right). Predict how many lines break, then run. Put the outs back. EitherDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l11.demo /** Both parameters are out: an Either only hands values out. Left and Right fill the other side with Nothing. */ sealed interface Either<out L, out R> { data class Left<out L>(val value: L) : Either<L, Nothing> data class Right<out R>(val value: R) : Either<Nothing, R> } /** Maps the failure side. `is Right -> this` type-checks because a Right<R> is an Either<Nothing, R>. */ fun <L, R, L2> Either<L, R>.mapLeft(f: (L) -> L2): Either<L2, R> = when (this) { is Either.Left -> Either.Left(f(value)) is Either.Right -> this } fun <L, R, T> Either<L, R>.fold(onLeft: (L) -> T, onRight: (R) -> T): T = when (this) { is Either.Left -> onLeft(value) is Either.Right -> onRight(value) } fun parseGrams(text: String): Either<String, Long> = text.toLongOrNull()?.let { Either.Right(it) } ?: Either.Left("not a number: $text") fun main() { val ok = parseGrams("180") val bad = parseGrams("a handful") println(ok.fold({ "error: $it" }, { "grams: $it" })) println(bad.mapLeft { it.uppercase() }) val wider: Either<Any, Number> = ok // out on both sides: String -> Any, Long -> Number println("wider = $wider") // Break it: remove both `out`s from `sealed interface Either` (keep them on Left and Right), // run, and read the errors in mapLeft and on the `wider` line. } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l11.demo.EitherDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l11/demo/EitherDemo.kt EitherDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l11.demo; import java.util.function.Function; /** * Java twin of EitherDemo.kt, with a sealed interface and records (Java 21 pattern matching). * Java has no Nothing, so Left must carry an R it never uses, and mapLeft must build a new Right. */ public class EitherDemoJava { sealed interface Either<L, R> permits Left, Right {} record Left<L, R>(L value) implements Either<L, R> {} record Right<L, R>(R value) implements Either<L, R> {} static <L, R, L2> Either<L2, R> mapLeft(Either<L, R> e, Function<? super L, ? extends L2> f) { return switch (e) { case Left<L, R> l -> new Left<>(f.apply(l.value())); case Right<L, R> r -> new Right<>(r.value()); // can't reuse r: it is an Either<L, R> }; } static <L, R, T> T fold(Either<L, R> e, Function<? super L, ? extends T> onLeft, Function<? super R, ? extends T> onRight) { return switch (e) { case Left<L, R> l -> onLeft.apply(l.value()); case Right<L, R> r -> onRight.apply(r.value()); }; } static Either<String, Long> parseGrams(String text) { try { return new Right<>(Long.parseLong(text)); } catch (NumberFormatException ex) { return new Left<>("not a number: " + text); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Either<String, Long> ok = parseGrams("180"); Either<String, Long> bad = parseGrams("a handful"); System.out.println(EitherDemoJava.<String, Long, String>fold(ok, l -> "error: " + l, r -> "grams: " + r)); System.out.println(mapLeft(bad, String::toUpperCase)); Either<? extends Object, ? extends Number> wider = ok; // Java: wildcards at the use site System.out.println("wider = " + wider); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l11.demo.EitherDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l11/demo/EitherDemoJava.java Both print grams: 180, the problem in capitals (Left(value=NOT A NUMBER: A HANDFUL) in Kotlin, Left[value=NOT A NUMBER: A HANDFUL] for the Java record) and wider = Right(value=180). Kotlin's mapLeft returns this for a Right; Java builds a new Right. Without the outs you get six errors: Left and Right themselves (Type parameter 'L' is declared as 'out' but occurs in 'invariant' position ...), mapLeft's when, two in parseGrams, and Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Either<Any, Number>', actual 'Either<String, Long>'. h: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus · Reading behind glass: a covariant display case on an invariant storeroom
x: The second design is the storeroom itself. The shop keeps records of its suppliers (the farms that deliver) and its crates, each with an id. A storeroom object can save an item, find one by id and list them all. Because it both takes items in (save) and hands them out (findAll), it must be invariant, like the crate of apples in lesson 3. That hurts the readers. A stock check that wants to list items of any kind can't accept a Storeroom<Supplier, Long> as a Storeroom<Item<Long>, Long>. The fix is to put the reading half behind glass, as an interface of its own: lesson 3's display case. Java interface DisplayCase<T> { List<T> findAll(); } // Java: invariant, so... static void printAll(DisplayCase<? extends Item<?>> display) { // ...each reader writes ? extends for (Item<?> item : display.findAll()) System.out.println("item " + item.getId()); } Kotlin interface Item<ID : Comparable<ID>> { val id: ID } interface DisplayCase<out T> { fun findAll(): List<T> } // only hands T out interface Storeroom<T : Item<ID>, ID : Comparable<ID>> : DisplayCase<T> { fun save(item: T): T // takes T in: invariant fun findById(id: ID): T? } fun printAll(display: DisplayCase<Item<*>>) { for (item in display.findAll()) println("item ${item.id}") } Now printAll accepts the suppliers and the crates, because each storeroom is a DisplayCase of its item type, and the display case is covariant. Unlike lesson 10's display case, this one has no secret slot. The full storeroom is still invariant, and the compiler still refuses val anyItem: Storeroom<Item<Long>, Long> = suppliers with Initializer type mismatch. Nothing was weakened. The safe half simply got its own name. The bounds are lesson 2's tools. ID : Comparable<ID> lets the lab's storeroom keep its items in a TreeMap, a map that keeps its keys in sorted order. T : Item<ID> ties each item to the type of its id: a Long for suppliers, and a String such as "c-1" for crates. The Kotlin docs give the same advice for any type that both reads and writes: split the interface instead of casting. You'll also hear this called interface segregation, here done by variance. Notice where the variance came from. You didn't decide that DisplayCase is covariant. You looked at its members, saw that each one only returns T, and the compiler agreed. That's the habit this track has built: read the positions, and let them tell you. When a type both reads and writes T, give the reading half its own out interface. Values flow out of the display case. In the third design, values flow out of one side and into the other. List any storeroom through its display case Run StoreroomDemo (or StoreroomDemoJava). One printAll reads suppliers, crates and a writable storeroom. Uncomment the wrong move in each file. Predict, then run. Remove out from DisplayCase in the Kotlin file. Which calls to printAll still compile? StoreroomDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l11.demo interface Item<ID : Comparable<ID>> { val id: ID } data class Supplier(override val id: Long, val name: String) : Item<Long> data class Crate(override val id: String, val grams: Int) : Item<String> /** The read side only hands T out, so it can be covariant: a glass display case. */ interface DisplayCase<out T> { fun findAll(): List<T> } /** The full storeroom takes a T in save, so it stays invariant. */ interface Storeroom<T : Item<ID>, ID : Comparable<ID>> : DisplayCase<T> { fun save(item: T): T } /** A stock check that reads items of ANY kind. */ fun printAll(display: DisplayCase<Item<*>>) { for (item in display.findAll()) println(" item ${item.id}") } fun main() { val suppliers: DisplayCase<Supplier> = object : DisplayCase<Supplier> { override fun findAll() = listOf(Supplier(2, "Hill Farm"), Supplier(7, "Orchard Lane")) } val crates: DisplayCase<Crate> = object : DisplayCase<Crate> { override fun findAll() = listOf(Crate("c-1", 12_000)) } println("suppliers:"); printAll(suppliers) // a DisplayCase<Supplier> IS a DisplayCase<Item<*>> println("crates:"); printAll(crates) val storeroom: Storeroom<Supplier, Long> = object : Storeroom<Supplier, Long> { override fun save(item: Supplier) = item override fun findAll() = listOf(Supplier(9, "River Fields")) } println("the storeroom, through its display case:"); printAll(storeroom) // the read side is still covariant // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // val anyItem: Storeroom<Item<Long>, Long> = storeroom } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l11.demo.StoreroomDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l11/demo/StoreroomDemo.kt StoreroomDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l11.demo; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of StoreroomDemo.kt. Java's interfaces are invariant, so the reader writes ? extends. */ public class StoreroomDemoJava { interface DisplayCase<T> { List<T> findAll(); } static void printAll(DisplayCase<? extends Item<?>> display) { // every use must say ? extends for (Item<?> item : display.findAll()) System.out.println(" item " + item.getId()); } public static void main(String[] args) { DisplayCase<Supplier> suppliers = () -> List.of(new Supplier(2, "Hill Farm"), new Supplier(7, "Orchard Lane")); DisplayCase<Crate> crates = () -> List.of(new Crate("c-1", 12_000)); System.out.println("suppliers:"); printAll(suppliers); System.out.println("crates:"); printAll(crates); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // DisplayCase<Item<?>> strict = suppliers; } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l11.demo.StoreroomDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l11/demo/StoreroomDemoJava.java Both print the items 2, 7 and c-1; Kotlin also prints item 9 from the writable storeroom. The wrong moves fail with Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Storeroom<Item<Long>, Long>', actual 'Storeroom<Supplier, Long>'. (the full storeroom is invariant) and, in Java, incompatible types: DisplayCase<Supplier> cannot be converted to DisplayCase<Item<?>> (no wildcard on the variable). Without out, none of the three printAll calls compile.

h: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus · The board of bells: deliveries flow out, listeners take them in
x: The third design is the board from the opening, and the figure shows it. In code it's an event bus: an object that passes each event, a message that something happened, to everyone who asked to hear that kind of event. Here each delivery is the event. Deliveries flow out of the back door, and listeners take them in. That's lessons 4 and 5 in one class: Java final class Bells { private final List<Consumer<Fruit>> adapters = new ArrayList<>(); <E extends Fruit> void listen(Class<E> type, Consumer<? super E> listener) { // Consumer Super adapters.add(item -> { if (type.isInstance(item)) listener.accept(type.cast(item)); }); } } Kotlin class BellBoard { private val bells = HashMap<KClass<out Fruit>, MutableList<(Fruit) -> Unit>>() fun <E : Fruit> listen(type: KClass<E>, listener: (E) -> Unit) { bells.getOrPut(type) { mutableListOf() } .add { item -> type.safeCast(item)?.let(listener) } // the adapter } fun ring(item: Fruit) { bells[item::class]?.forEach { it(item) } } } Every piece has a reason. The map's keys are KClass<out Fruit>, because that's the type of item::class, lesson 9's note asked of a value. The listener can't go into the list as it is, and the compiler explains why: Argument type mismatch: actual type is '(E (of fun <E : Fruit> listen)) -> Unit', but '(Fruit) -> Unit' was expected. A listener that only takes apples can't be handed a lemon, because function parameters are in. So the board stores an adapter, a small wrapper that turns one function type into another. It takes any Fruit, checks it with safeCast, and passes on only an E, like a doorman at each bell who reads every delivery note before calling anyone. The same in helps at the call site: the stock-keeper, a (Fruit) -> Unit, can listen under Apple::class. The shortcut from the opening is to cast the listener instead, .add(listener as (Fruit) -> Unit) under @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST"). It compiles, and erasure makes the cast itself succeed. Then the first lemon that reaches that list throws ClassCastException from inside the sign-writer's own code, far from the line that caused it. The adapter costs one line and turns the wrong delivery into nothing at all. For Kotlin callers, add the reified wrapper from lesson 8, with one new word: Java // Java callers pass the class to the Java board: bells.listen(Apple.class, a -> writeSign(a)); // There is no Java equivalent of the reified, noinline wrapper. Kotlin inline fun <reified E : Fruit> listen(noinline listener: (E) -> Unit) = listen(E::class, listener) board.listen<Apple> { writeSign(it) } A lambda passed to an inline function is normally inlined too, so it never exists as an object. This one gets stored in the map, so it must stay an object, and noinline says so. One limit to know: this board rings by the exact class. A listener under Fruit::class never hears anything, because no delivery's run-time class is the interface itself. The "Go deeper" part shows how to walk the supertypes when you need that. Store a narrow listener behind a checking adapter, never behind a cast. The last design keeps many kinds of values in one place, and it's the most delicate of the four. Route deliveries to typed listeners Run BellBoardDemo (or BellBoardDemoJava). The stock-keeper takes every Fruit but listens under Apple::class. Inside Bells.listen, uncomment wrong move 1 and comment out the adapter line below it. Read the error. Restore it, then uncomment wrong move 2 in main. Why is a listener for one kind refused for the supertype? BellBoardDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l11.demo import kotlin.reflect.KClass import kotlin.reflect.safeCast // The shop's fruit, used by the demos of this lesson (the Java twins use these Kotlin types too) interface Fruit { val name: String; val grams: Int } data class Apple(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit data class Lemon(override val name: String, override val grams: Int) : Fruit /** The smallest typed bell board: one list of adapters, each of which checks the item's class. */ class Bells { private val adapters = mutableListOf<(Fruit) -> Unit>() fun <E : Fruit> listen(type: KClass<E>, listener: (E) -> Unit) { // adapters.add(listener) // wrong move 1 adapters.add { item -> type.safeCast(item)?.let(listener) } // takes any fruit, passes on only an E } fun ring(item: Fruit) = adapters.forEach { it(item) } } fun main() { val bells = Bells() val stockCount: (Fruit) -> Unit = { println("stock: one more ${it.name}") } bells.listen(Apple::class) { println("sign for ${it.name}, ${it.grams} g") } bells.listen(Apple::class, stockCount) // a listener for the supertype fits: in P bells.listen(Lemon::class) { println("lemon tray: ${it.name}") } bells.ring(Apple("Gala", 180)) // items flow out of the delivery... bells.ring(Lemon("Eureka", 120)) // ...and into the listeners that accept them // Wrong move 2. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // bells.listen(Fruit::class) { a: Apple -> println(a.name) } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l11.demo.BellBoardDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l11/demo/BellBoardDemo.kt BellBoardDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l11.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** Java twin of BellBoardDemo.kt. The listener parameter says ? super E: Consumer Super. */ public class BellBoardDemoJava { static final class Bells { private final List<Consumer<Fruit>> adapters = new ArrayList<>(); <E extends Fruit> void listen(Class<E> type, Consumer<? super E> listener) { adapters.add(item -> { // takes any fruit... if (type.isInstance(item)) listener.accept(type.cast(item)); // ...passes on only an E }); } void ring(Fruit item) { adapters.forEach(a -> a.accept(item)); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Bells bells = new Bells(); Consumer<Fruit> stockCount = f -> System.out.println("stock: one more " + f.getName()); bells.listen(Apple.class, a -> System.out.println("sign for " + a.getName() + ", " + a.getGrams() + " g")); bells.listen(Apple.class, stockCount); bells.listen(Lemon.class, l -> System.out.println("lemon tray: " + l.getName())); bells.ring(new Apple("Gala", 180)); bells.ring(new Lemon("Eureka", 120)); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l11.demo.BellBoardDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l11/demo/BellBoardDemoJava.java Both print sign for Gala, 180 g, stock: one more Gala and lemon tray: Eureka. Wrong move 1: Argument type mismatch: actual type is '(E (of fun <E : Fruit> listen)) -> Unit', but '(Fruit) -> Unit' was expected. Wrong move 2: Argument type mismatch: actual type is '(Apple) -> Unit', but '(Fruit) -> Unit' was expected., because listening under Fruit::class would hand a lemon to a listener that only takes apples. Deliveries are produced, listeners consume them. The board keys its adapters by the item's class and checks each item before handing it over.

h: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus · Keys that carry their value's type: one container, many types, no casts
x: Typed keys: the key carries its value's type, so a read needs no cast and same-named keys don't collide, and the key stays invariant because it writes too The last design is a container for values of many types: the facts the shop keeps about one order, such as the varieties chosen, the weight of each piece and the total weight. Lesson 9's card index used the type as the whole key. Here the key is a small object that carries a name and the full type of its value, like a tab on a card that says both "weights" and "a list of grams": Java record Key<T>(String name, Type type) { // Type from a super type token static <T> Key<T> of(String name, TypeRef<T> ref) { return new Key<>(name, ref.type); } } static final Key<List<String>> VARIETIES = Key.of("varieties", new TypeRef<List<String>>() {}); <T> void set(Key<T> key, T value) { values.put(key, value); } @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") <T> T get(Key<T> key) { return (T) values.get(key); } // safe: only set puts values in Kotlin data class Key<T>(val name: String, val type: KType) inline fun <reified T> key(name: String) = Key<T>(name, typeOf<T>()) val VARIETIES = key<List<String>>("varieties") operator fun <T> set(key: Key<T>, value: T) { values[key] = value } @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") operator fun <T> get(key: Key<T>): T? = values[key] as T? // safe: only set puts values in val varieties: List<String>? = attributes[VARIETIES] // no cast, no type argument at the call site The key's type parameter does the typing. attributes[VARIETIES] is a List<String>?, with no cast at the call site, and attributes[VARIETIES] = 42 is a compile error: Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'List<String>' was expected. The KType inside the key makes key<List<Int>>("weights") and key<Int>("weights") different keys. So when two helpers both pick the name "weights", one for the weight of each piece and one for the total, the two values don't land in the same slot. Key<T> is invariant on purpose, and this is the last variance decision of the track. Declare it out T, and a Key<List<String>> becomes a Key<Any>. Then attributes[VARIETIES] = 42 would compile, with T inferred as Any, and the next read of the varieties throws ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.util.List. The demo's LeakyKey does exactly that. A key is used to write as well as to read, so it can't be a producer, however few members it has. The one unchecked cast in get stays safe only while that holds. It's safe by construction: the only way in is set(key: Key<T>, value: T), and the key can't pretend to be another type. A key that decides what may be written must be invariant. This is also a good place to stop adding generics. Four designs, two commented casts, one deliberately invariant key: if a design needs much more than that, a plainer one with a sealed class and a when is usually easier for the next person to read. And know the limit of all four. They check types, not meaning: the compiler will happily file a weight of minus 50 grams under exactly the right key. Store typed attributes, then break the key Run TypedKeysDemo and TypedKeysDemoJava. Neither call site has a cast. Read LeakyKey in the Kotlin file: the same key with out T. Find the line where the bad value goes in, and the line where it fails. Uncomment the wrong move in each file. The invariant key stops at compile time what the leaky key let through. TypedKeysDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l11.demo import kotlin.reflect.KType import kotlin.reflect.typeOf /** Invariant on purpose: a Key<List<String>> is not a Key<Any>. */ data class Key<T>(val name: String, val type: KType) inline fun <reified T> key(name: String) = Key<T>(name, typeOf<T>()) class Attributes { private val values = HashMap<Key<*>, Any?>() operator fun <T> set(key: Key<T>, value: T) { values[key] = value } @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") // safe: only set(Key<T>, T) puts values in operator fun <T> get(key: Key<T>): T? = values[key] as T? } /** The same thing with `out T`: it compiles, and it is broken. */ data class LeakyKey<out T>(val name: String, val type: KType) inline fun <reified T> leakyKey(name: String) = LeakyKey<T>(name, typeOf<T>()) class LeakyAttributes { private val values = HashMap<LeakyKey<*>, Any?>() operator fun <T> set(key: LeakyKey<T>, value: T) { values[key] = value } @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") operator fun <T> get(key: LeakyKey<T>): T? = values[key] as T? } val VARIETIES = key<List<String>>("varieties") val TOTAL = key<Int>("total grams") fun main() { val attrs = Attributes() attrs[VARIETIES] = listOf("Gala", "Fuji") attrs[TOTAL] = 330 val varieties: List<String>? = attrs[VARIETIES] // typed by the key: no cast here println("varieties = $varieties, total = ${attrs[TOTAL]} g") val leaky = LeakyAttributes() val leakyVarieties = leakyKey<List<String>>("varieties") leaky[leakyVarieties] = 42 // compiles: T is inferred as Any try { val first: String? = leaky[leakyVarieties]?.first() println(first) } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("ClassCastException: ${e.message?.substringBefore(" (")}") } // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // attrs[VARIETIES] = 42 } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l11.demo.TypedKeysDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l11/demo/TypedKeysDemo.kt TypedKeysDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l11.demo; import java.lang.reflect.ParameterizedType; import java.lang.reflect.Type; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** Java twin of TypedKeysDemo.kt. The key's type comes from a super type token; Java generics are invariant. */ public class TypedKeysDemoJava { static abstract class TypeRef<T> { final Type type = ((ParameterizedType) getClass().getGenericSuperclass()).getActualTypeArguments()[0]; } record Key<T>(String name, Type type) { static <T> Key<T> of(String name, TypeRef<T> ref) { return new Key<>(name, ref.type); } } static final class Attributes { private final Map<Key<?>, Object> values = new HashMap<>(); <T> void set(Key<T> key, T value) { values.put(key, value); } @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") // safe: only set(Key<T>, T) puts values in <T> T get(Key<T> key) { return (T) values.get(key); } } static final Key<List<String>> VARIETIES = Key.of("varieties", new TypeRef<List<String>>() {}); static final Key<Integer> TOTAL = Key.of("total grams", new TypeRef<Integer>() {}); public static void main(String[] args) { Attributes attrs = new Attributes(); attrs.set(VARIETIES, List.of("Gala", "Fuji")); attrs.set(TOTAL, 330); List<String> varieties = attrs.get(VARIETIES); // typed by the key: no cast here System.out.println("varieties = " + varieties + ", total = " + attrs.get(TOTAL) + " g"); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // attrs.set(VARIETIES, 42); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l11.demo.TypedKeysDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l11/demo/TypedKeysDemoJava.java Both print varieties = [Gala, Fuji], total = 330 g. Kotlin then prints ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.util.List: leaky[leakyVarieties] = 42 compiled because out T let T be inferred as Any, and the read failed later. The wrong move fails with Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'List<String>' was expected. in Kotlin, and method set in class Attributes cannot be applied to given types in Java.
