h: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus · Java and Kotlin
x: The board of bells in Java and Kotlin BellBoard.java import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.function.Consumer; final class BellBoard { private final Map<Class<? extends Fruit>, List<Consumer<Fruit>>> bells = new HashMap<>(); // Consumer<? super E>: a listener for E or for any supertype of E <E extends Fruit> void listen(Class<E> type, Consumer<? super E> listener) { bells.computeIfAbsent(type, t -> new ArrayList<>()).add(item -> { if (type.isInstance(item)) listener.accept(type.cast(item)); // the adapter }); } int ring(Fruit item) { List<Consumer<Fruit>> listeners = bells.getOrDefault(item.getClass(), List.of()); listeners.forEach(l -> l.accept(item)); return listeners.size(); } } // board.listen(Apple.class, a -> writeSign(a)); BellBoard.kt class BellBoard { private val bells = HashMap<KClass<out Fruit>, MutableList<(Fruit) -> Unit>>() // (E) -> Unit is already Function1<in E, ...>: a listener for any supertype of E fits fun <E : Fruit> listen(type: KClass<E>, listener: (E) -> Unit) { bells.getOrPut(type) { mutableListOf() } .add { item -> type.safeCast(item)?.let(listener) } // the adapter } inline fun <reified E : Fruit> listen(noinline listener: (E) -> Unit) = listen(E::class, listener) fun ring(item: Fruit): Int { val listeners = bells[item::class] ?: return 0 for (l in listeners) l(item) return listeners.size } } // board.listen<Apple> { writeSign(it) } The design is the same in both languages: keys from the item's run-time class, listeners stored behind an adapter that checks the class and casts, and a listener parameter that accepts supertypes. Where Java writes the variance at each use (Class<? extends Fruit> keys, Consumer<? super E> listeners), Kotlin gets it from declarations: item::class is already a KClass<out Fruit>, and a function type is already in on its parameter, so (E) -> Unit needs no projection. Kotlin also adds the reified wrapper, which needs noinline because the lambda is stored. Java callers can reach the KClass version only through JvmClassMappingKt.getKotlinClass(Apple.class), so a board meant for Java code should also offer a Class<E> overload.

h: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus · Worked example
x: Receive a delivery note through all four designs A delivery note arrives as a map of text fields, read from a paper form. 1. Parse it into an Either instead of throwing, so the caller decides what a bad note means. fun parseDelivery(note: Map<*, *>): Either<String, Fruit> { val name = note["name"] as? String ?: return Either.Left("missing name") val grams = (note["grams"] as? Number)?.toInt() ?: return Either.Left("missing weight") return when (note["kind"]) { "apple" -> Either.Right(Apple(name, grams)) "lemon" -> Either.Right(Lemon(name, grams)) else -> Either.Left("unknown kind ${note["kind"]}") } } static Either<String, Fruit> parseDelivery(Map<?, ?> note) { if (!(note.get("name") instanceof String name)) return new Left<>("missing name"); if (!(note.get("grams") instanceof Number n)) return new Left<>("missing weight"); int grams = n.intValue(); Object kind = note.get("kind"); if ("apple".equals(kind)) return new Right<>(new Apple(name, grams)); if ("lemon".equals(kind)) return new Right<>(new Lemon(name, grams)); return new Left<>("unknown kind " + kind); } Ring the bell for each good delivery. 3. Record each problem in the day's typed attributes. Self-check before reading the comment: why can Either.Right(Apple(name, grams)) be returned where Either<String, Fruit> is expected? (Right<Apple> is an Either<Nothing, Apple>, and both parameters are out.) val LAST_PROBLEM = key<String>("delivery.lastProblem") fun receive(note: Map<*, *>, board: BellBoard, today: Attributes): Int = when (val parsed = parseDelivery(note)) { is Either.Right -> board.ring(parsed.value) // the item flows out to the listeners is Either.Left -> { today[LAST_PROBLEM] = parsed.value; 0 } } static final Key<String> LAST_PROBLEM = Key.of("delivery.lastProblem", new TypeRef<String>() {}); static int receive(Map<?, ?> note, BellBoard board, Attributes today) { return switch (parseDelivery(note)) { case Right<String, Fruit> r -> board.ring(r.value()); case Left<String, Fruit> l -> { today.set(LAST_PROBLEM, l.value()); yield 0; } }; } Wire the listeners once, when the shop opens. The stock-keeper is a (Fruit) -> Unit and listens under both kinds; the sign-writer only understands apples. A nightly report lists the suppliers through the covariant DisplayCase<Item<*>>. Every type parameter in this flow has the variance its role demands, and the only casts are the two that are safe by construction: safeCast in the board's adapter, and the unchecked cast inside Attributes.get. val stockCount: (Fruit) -> Unit = { stock.add(it.name, it.grams) } board.listen(Apple::class, stockCount) board.listen(Lemon::class, stockCount) board.listen<Apple> { signs.write(it.name) } receive(mapOf("kind" to "apple", "name" to "Gala", "grams" to 180), board, today) // 2 listeners ran receive(mapOf("kind" to "apple", "name" to "Fuji"), board, today) // today[LAST_PROBLEM] == "missing weight" Consumer<Fruit> stockCount = f -> stock.add(f.getName(), f.getGrams()); board.listen(Apple.class, stockCount); board.listen(Lemon.class, stockCount); board.listen(Apple.class, a -> signs.write(a.getName())); receive(Map.of("kind", "apple", "name", "Gala", "grams", 180), board, today); // 2 listeners ran receive(Map.of("kind", "apple", "name", "Fuji"), board, today); // LAST_PROBLEM is "missing weight"

h: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus · Quiz
x: Which interface can safely be declared with out T? interface Storeroom<T> { fun save(item: T): T } interface Slot<T> { var current: T } interface DisplayCase<T> { fun findAll(): List<T> } interface Key<T> { val name: String }, used as set(key: Key<T>, value: T) DisplayCase only hands T out. save takes a T, and a var is both read and written, so those must be invariant. The key is the subtle one: it has no T member at all, so out T would compile, but it is used to choose what may be written, and out would let set(key, 42) through. On the board of bells, why can't listen simply do bells[type]!!.add(listener) with listener: (E) -> Unit and a list of (Fruit) -> Unit? Because lambdas can't be stored in a map Because (E) -> Unit is not a (Fruit) -> Unit: function parameters are in, and a listener for apples can't take a lemon Because E is erased, so the list can't hold it It can; the adapter is only there for speed A (Fruit) -> Unit must accept every fruit. A listener that only takes Apple doesn't, so the compiler refuses the add. The adapter takes any fruit and passes on only those that safeCast to E. The other direction works: a (Fruit) -> Unit listener is an (Apple) -> Unit. Why does the reified listen need noinline on its listener parameter? Because reified functions can't take lambdas Because Java callers need it Because the listener is stored in the map, so it must exist as an object instead of being inlined Because noinline makes the type parameter reified Lambdas passed to an inline function are inlined too, so they don't exist as values. A lambda you store, return or pass on to a function that isn't inline must stay an object, which noinline asks for. It has nothing to do with reified, which is about the type parameter. data class Key<T>(val name: String, val type: KType). Why include the KType when the key already has a name? So that key<List<Int>>("weights") and key<Int>("weights") are different keys and can't collide Because a data class needs at least two properties So that get can cast without an unchecked warning Because a KType makes the key covariant With the name alone, two keys with the same name and different value types would share one slot, and reading one would return the other's value. The KType from typeOf<T>() makes them unequal. The cast in get is still unchecked; it is safe because only set puts values in. From "Star projection: when you don't know the type": a helper reports the size of any in-memory list, a MutableList<Apple>, a MutableList<String> or anything else, and may clear it. Which parameter type fits best? MutableList<Any?> MutableList<in Any> MutableList<Fruit> MutableList<*> The helper neither reads typed elements nor writes any, so a star projection says exactly that and accepts every mutable list, while still allowing size and clear(). MutableList<Any?> accepts only lists whose element type is exactly Any?, and in Any accepts only lists of Any or Any?. MutableList<Fruit> turns away both the apple list and the string list.

h: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus · Key terms
x: Either A result that is a problem (Left) or a value (Right), declared out in both. Interface segregation by variance Splitting a type's reading half into its own covariant interface, so readers get flexibility the full type can't have. Event bus An object that passes each event, a message that something happened, to everyone who asked for that kind of event. Adapter A small wrapper that turns one function type into another, here by checking the item's class first. noinline Marks a lambda parameter of an inline function that must stay an object, because it is stored. Typed key A key object that carries the type of its value, so a container can return that type without casts. Safe by construction An unchecked cast that can't fail, because a private rule guarantees what was stored. Why is Left declared Left<out L>(val value: L) : Either<L, Nothing>? So one Left fits Either<L, R> for every R: Nothing is a subtype of every type, and Either is out in R. A storeroom both saves and returns T. How do you let read-only code accept a storeroom of any item? Split out interface DisplayCase<out T> { fun findAll(): List<T> } and have the full Storeroom extend it. Readers take DisplayCase<Item<*>>. What type do the keys of a class-keyed board of bells have, and why? KClass<out Fruit>, because item::class on a Fruit has exactly that type. How do you store an (Apple) -> Unit in a list of (Fruit) -> Unit? Wrap it: { item -> Apple::class.safeCast(item)?.let(listener) }. The adapter takes any fruit and passes on only an Apple. When does a lambda parameter of an inline function need noinline? When the function stores it, returns it or passes it to code that isn't inline, as listen does with its map of listeners. Why must a typed Key<T> be invariant? It decides what may be written. With out T, a Key<List<String>> could act as a Key<Any>, set(key, 42) would compile, and the next read would throw ClassCastException.

h: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus · Go deeper
x: Each design has a natural next step. The board rings only for the item's exact class. To ring a listener under Fruit::class for an apple too, ring must walk the item's supertypes. Without kotlin-reflect you can do that through Java reflection: item.javaClass.interfaces and item.javaClass.superclass, converted with .kotlin. With kotlin-reflect, KClass.allSuperclasses lists them directly. Cache the result per class, since the walk is the same every time. Either gets more useful with flatMap, which chains steps that can each fail: fun <L, R, R2> Either<L, R>.flatMap(f: (R) -> Either<L, R2>): Either<L, R2>. Its Left branch returns this for the same reason map can. The standard library's own Result<out T> is declared out too, but its failure side is always a Throwable; Either lets the problem be a type of your own, such as a DeliveryProblem. Libraries such as Arrow ship a full Either. The storeroom can grow a write-only view as well: interface Intake<in T> { fun save(item: T) }. A loader that writes Suppliers can then accept an Intake<Item<Long>>. With both views, the invariant Storeroom is simply the type that is both. The typed keys can carry a default: class Key<T>(val name: String, val type: KType, val default: T), with get returning T instead of T?. Keep Key invariant when you do: default is read, but set still writes through the key.

h: Functional programming in Kotlin
x: Pure functions, function types, higher-order functions, collections and sequences, scope functions, errors as values and immutable data. By the end of this track you can write Kotlin in a functional style on purpose. You'll pull decisions out of code that reads the clock or a store into pure functions you test with plain values, like a recipe card that gives the same pancakes every time. You'll hold rules as values, replace loops with collection operations, and send one item at a time down a lazy pipeline when that saves work. You'll pick let, run, with, apply or also for a reason, return expected failures as values with sealed types and Arrow's Either, and keep your data truly immutable. The last lesson puts it together: a shopping job split into a pure core that decides and a thin shell that does the errands. You need no functional programming background, only the Kotlin and Java you can already read. The whole track follows one home cook's recipe app: a flour shopping helper, dish checks for dinner guests, a converter from the measuring jug to the kitchen scale, a baking-day report, a recipe search, a meal planner, an ingredient form and a morning shopping job. Each lesson starts from a small program in that app that hurts (hard to test, broken by shared state, a loop nobody wants to read) and names an idea only after you have felt why it exists. Then it shows what the Kotlin feature compiles to. Every sample comes in Kotlin and in the equivalent Java, with streams, Function, Optional and records, so you see what Kotlin changes. The compiler messages and outputs in the lessons are copied from runs on Kotlin 2.4.21. Install JDK 25; the labs compile with release 21. The labs live in labs/functional, one package per lesson (workbench.functional.l01 to l08), all in Kotlin. The module already has arrow-core 2.3.0 for lesson 7, kotlinx-collections-immutable 0.5.2 for lesson 8, and kotlinx-coroutines with its test library. From labs/, run ./gradlew :functional:test --tests 'workbench.functional.lNN.*' until it passes, ./gradlew :functional:solutionTest to see the reference answers pass the same tests, and ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=<class> for the Try-it programs. A pure function depends only on its arguments and changes nothing, like a recipe card that gives the same pancakes every time; only then can a call be replaced by its value. Put decisions in a pure core and the errands in a thin shell. Functions are values with types like (Dish) -> Problem?. Kotlin 2.x lambdas compile through invokedynamic; a captured var is one shared Ref box that loses updates across threads. Higher-order functions keep the shape of a computation (retry, timing, remembering answers, composition) apart from the work; inline makes the lambdas of map, filter and let free. List operations are eager and inlined; fold is the general loop. Watch the empty-input and duplicate-key traps: reduce, first() and associateBy. A sequence sends one item at a time down the whole chain and only runs at a terminal operation. It pays when the last step stops early or items are made on demand; a Java stream adds parallelism and is single-use. Scope functions differ on two axes: this or it, the value or the block's result. ?.let { } ?: run { }, also { copy() }, nested receivers and nested it all compile without a warning. Nullable types replace Optional: ?., ?: (which can return or throw), takeIf, and requireNotNull/checkNotNull with smart casts. Expected failures are values: sealed types with an exhaustive when, Arrow's fail-fast either { } and collecting zipOrAccumulate. kotlin.Result is for code that throws, and runCatching swallows cancellation. Read-only isn't immutable, copy() is shallow, and BigDecimal equality counts the scale. Persistent collections make new versions cheaply; tailrec is a loop only in true tail position.

h: Functional programming in Kotlin: track quiz
x: val portion = portionFor(guest) is used twice in a method. When can you replace both uses with two direct calls to portionFor(guest) without changing what the program does? Always: it's the same expression Only if portionFor is pure: no hidden inputs and no side effects Only if portionFor is inline Only if portion is a val, not a var Replacing a value with the call that produced it is safe only for a pure function. If portionFor reads the clock, it could return two different portions; if it writes to the shopping list, it now does that twice. inline and val don't change what the function does. Four threads share a lambda that runs repeat(250_000) { total += 1 } on a captured var total = 0L. What does total hold when all four finish? Exactly 1,000,000, because each lambda has its own copy of total It doesn't compile: lambdas can't change captured variables Sometimes less than 1,000,000: the captured var lives in one shared box with a plain field, and += is a read, an add and a write Exactly 1,000,000, because Kotlin makes captured variables volatile Kotlin compiles a captured var into a Ref object with a plain field, shared by every closure that captured it. Four threads doing read-add-write on that field lose updates. Return a value from each task and add them up, or use an atomic held in a val. Why does cookies.filter { it.status == GOLDEN }.map { it.grams } create no lambda objects at run time? filter and map on a List are inline: the compiler pastes the loops and lambda bodies into the caller The JIT removes them with escape analysis Kotlin caches every lambda in a static field Lambdas on the JVM are free inline functions are expanded at the call site, together with the lambdas passed to them, so no Function1 exists. The cost of the chain is elsewhere: one new ArrayList per step. On a sequence the same lambdas do become objects. Someone wrote a tray down twice, so two cookies share the id c3. What does cookies.associateBy { it.id } do? Throws IllegalStateException: Duplicate key c3 Keeps both in a list under c3 Keeps the first cookie for c3 Keeps the last cookie for c3, silently associateBy keeps the last element for a repeated key and says nothing. Java's Collectors.toMap throws on the duplicate instead. When keys should be unique, check first with groupingBy { it.id }.eachCount().filterValues { it > 1 }, or use groupBy to keep all of them. A recipe website shows its search results one page at a time, and the app needs only the first recipe under 20 minutes. Which fits best? Fetch every page into a List, then first { } sequence { while (true) { val page = site.page(n++); if (page.isEmpty()) break; yieldAll(page) } }.first { ... } pages.parallelStream() over all page numbers (0..100).map { site.page(it) }.flatten().first { ... } A sequence { } fetches a page only when someone asks for its next item, so first { } stops the fetching as soon as it finds a match. Fetching into a List, or mapping over a range of page numbers, calls the site for every page before looking. A parallel stream would fetch pages you never need, in parallel. val r = OvenProgram().also { it.minutes = 12 }.let { oven.start(it) }. What is r? The OvenProgram Unit Whatever oven.start returns 12 also hands back the program itself, so the chain continues with it. let hands back its block's result, which is the return value of oven.start. Change let to also and r would be the program, with the result of start thrown away. fun planDish(open: Dish?) = open?.let { menu.add(it) } ?: run { menu.add(suggest()) }. menu.add returns null for a dish that is on the menu already. What happens when the open dish is on the menu already? run also runs: it downloads a suggestion and adds that too Only the let branch runs, and planDish returns null It doesn't compile It throws a NullPointerException ?: tests the result of the let block, not open. The block gives null for the dish on the menu already, so the right side runs too: a download and a second add. Decide the value first (val dish = open ?: suggest()), then add it once. An ingredient form has four independent fields, and the cook should see every problem at once. Which Arrow tool fits? either { } with four ensure calls zipOrAccumulate over four checks, returning Either<NonEmptyList<KitchenError>, Ingredient> runCatching around the four checks Either.catch { } around each field either { } is fail-fast: the first failing ensure ends the block, so the cook learns about one problem per try. zipOrAccumulate runs every check and collects all the failures. runCatching and Either.catch are for exceptions from code that throws, not for checking a form. A coroutine wraps a call to a Java library that throws. Which wrapper turns the library's exceptions into values but still lets the coroutine's cancellation through? runCatching { library.call() } try { library.call() } catch (e: Throwable) { null } Result.success(library.call()) Either.catch { library.call() } Arrow's Either.catch captures ordinary exceptions as a Left and rethrows CancellationException and fatal errors. runCatching and catch (e: Throwable) both catch the CancellationException, so a cancelled coroutine keeps running. Result.success(...) doesn't catch anything. You are splitting the morning shopping job into a pure core and an imperative shell. Which of these belongs in the shell? Rounding the discount HALF_EVEN to two decimals Deciding that an item needed in ten days is still waiting LocalDate.now(clock) Grouping the items due today by shop Reading the clock is a hidden input, so it belongs in the shell, which passes today to the core as a plain value. Rounding, the waiting rule and the grouping are decisions: they go in the pure core, where a test can call them with fixed values and no fakes.

h: Pure functions: the idea everything else builds on · A shopping helper with three inputs, and only one is a parameter
x: Here's a small piece of a recipe app. Before you cook, it looks in the cupboard and tells you how much flour to buy. A Bag holds three facts: the size the shop sells (1 kg), how much is left at home, and the best-before date printed on it. The shop only sells whole bags, so the helper rounds up, and then it writes a line on the shopping list: Java static int flourToBuy(int neededGrams) { Bag bag = Cupboard.flour; // a global: whoever cooked last may have changed it LocalDate today = LocalDate.now(); // the calendar int usable = today.isAfter(bag.bestBefore()) ? 0 : bag.leftGrams(); int missing = Math.max(neededGrams - usable, 0); int toBuy = (missing + bag.sizeGrams() - 1) / bag.sizeGrams() * bag.sizeGrams(); // whole bags only ShoppingList.lines.add(today + ": buy " + toBuy + " g flour"); return toBuy; } Kotlin fun flourToBuy(neededGrams: Int): Int { val bag = Cupboard.flour // a global: whoever cooked last may have changed it val today = LocalDate.now() // the calendar val usable = if (today.isAfter(bag.bestBefore)) 0 else bag.leftGrams val missing = maxOf(neededGrams - usable, 0) val toBuy = (missing + bag.sizeGrams - 1) / bag.sizeGrams * bag.sizeGrams // whole bags only ShoppingList.lines.add("$today: buy $toBuy g flour") return toBuy } Read it top to bottom. First it takes the bag from Cupboard, a global object that any part of the program can change. Then it asks the calendar for today's date, and a bag past its best-before date counts as empty. The missing grams round up to whole bags. The one tricky line, (missing + size - 1) / size * size, is integer division that rounds up instead of down. Finally it writes the line and returns the grams. The signature says it takes the grams you need and returns the grams to buy. That isn't the whole truth. It also takes today's date and whatever bag is in the cupboard at that moment, and it writes to the shopping list. Those two inputs and that one output are hidden. You can't see them where the function is called, and a test can't pass them in. So every test of it is fragile. Say the bag holds 700 g and is good until 31 March. assertEquals(1000, flourToBuy(1500)) passes all through March. On the first of April it fails with 2000, and nobody touched the code. The test didn't break. Its flour went off. Order matters too. Another test puts a fresh bag into Cupboard.flour and forgets to take it out. Now your test fails only when JUnit, the tool that runs the tests, happens to run that one first. And every call writes a real line on the shopping list, so a test that wants to check the line has to go and read the global list. The usual fixes add machinery. You pass in a Clock and use Clock.fixed(...) in tests, a clock that always says the same time. You reset Cupboard in a @BeforeEach method, which JUnit runs before every test. You clear the list after every test. All of that works. All of it exists only because the function reaches outside its own parameters. There's a simpler fix. Make every input a parameter, and make the return value the only output. That kind of function has a name, and the rest of this lesson shows why it pays off so much. Two tests, one cupboard Open OrderDependentTests.kt (or its Java twin, OrderDependentTestsJava.java). It runs two little tests that share one global, Cupboard.flourLeft. Both pass in the order they are written. Predict what happens if you swap the order. Run it with the command below. Then run it again with -Pargs=reverse added. Find the line that makes halfBagTest fail. Notice that it isn't in halfBagTest. OrderDependentTests.kt package workbench.functional.l01.demo // A global the shopping helper reads. Whoever cooked last, or a test, can change it at any time. object Cupboard { var flourLeft = 700 // grams still in the bag } // Looks harmless. But its answer depends on something that is not in its parameter list. fun flourMissing(neededGrams: Int): Int = maxOf(neededGrams - Cupboard.flourLeft, 0) // Two little "tests". The second puts a new bag in the cupboard and never takes it out again. fun halfBagTest(): String { val missing = flourMissing(1_500) return if (missing == 800) "pass" else "FAIL (expected 800, got $missing)" } fun newBagTest(): String { Cupboard.flourLeft = 1_700 // a new 1 kg bag next to the old one val missing = flourMissing(1_500) return if (missing == 0) "pass" else "FAIL (expected 0, got $missing)" } fun main(args: Array<String>) { val tests = listOf("halfBag" to ::halfBagTest, "newBag" to ::newBagTest) val order = if (args.firstOrNull() == "reverse") tests.reversed() else tests for ((name, test) in order) println("$name: ${test()}") } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l01.demo.OrderDependentTestsKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l01/demo/OrderDependentTests.kt OrderDependentTestsJava.java package workbench.functional.l01.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** Java twin of OrderDependentTests.kt: two tests share a static field, so their order decides the result. */ public class OrderDependentTestsJava { // A global the shopping helper reads. Whoever cooked last, or a test, can change it at any time. static int flourLeft = 700; // grams still in the bag // Looks harmless. But its answer depends on something that is not in its parameter list. static int flourMissing(int neededGrams) { return Math.max(neededGrams - flourLeft, 0); } static String halfBagTest() { int missing = flourMissing(1_500); return missing == 800 ? "pass" : "FAIL (expected 800, got " + missing + ")"; } // Puts a new bag in the cupboard and never takes it out again. static String newBagTest() { flourLeft = 1_700; // a new 1 kg bag next to the old one int missing = flourMissing(1_500); return missing == 0 ? "pass" : "FAIL (expected 0, got " + missing + ")"; } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Map.Entry<String, Supplier<String>>> tests = new ArrayList<>(List.of( Map.entry("halfBag", OrderDependentTestsJava::halfBagTest), Map.entry("newBag", OrderDependentTestsJava::newBagTest))); if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("reverse")) Collections.reverse(tests); for (var t : tests) System.out.println(t.getKey() + ": " + t.getValue().get()); } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l01.demo.OrderDependentTestsJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l01/demo/OrderDependentTestsJava.java In the written order both tests print pass. Reversed, newBag still passes, but halfBag prints FAIL (expected 800, got 0). The cause is in the other test, which set Cupboard.flourLeft to 1,700 g and never put it back. flourMissing can't protect itself, because what's in the cupboard is not one of its inputs.

h: Pure functions: the idea everything else builds on · What makes a function pure: it depends only on its arguments and changes nothing
x: A fee function with a hidden clock and a log line is impure; a pure one depends only on its arguments, so a call can be swapped for its value A pure function follows two rules. Its result depends only on its arguments, so two calls with the same values give the same answer. And calling it changes nothing outside it. Break either rule and the function is impure. That's the recipe card from the opening. The same ingredients give the same pancakes, and following the card leaves the kitchen as you found it. The second cook broke both rules: they used things that weren't on the card, and they changed the kitchen on the way. Anything a call does besides hand back its value is a side effect: writing a file, sending a message, printing, changing a field or the contents of a parameter. Eating the batter was a side effect, and so is writing the shopping list. The first rule has a half that people forget. Reading something that can change also breaks purity: LocalDate.now(), Random.nextInt(), a mutable global like Cupboard, or a cache (a store of saved answers) that some other code fills. These are hidden inputs. The answer depends on them, so the same arguments can give different answers. The clock and the scale left on ounces were the cook's hidden inputs. Here is the shopping rule with every input moved into the parameter list: Java static int gramsToBuy(int neededGrams, Bag bag, LocalDate today) { int usable = today.isAfter(bag.bestBefore()) ? 0 : bag.leftGrams(); int missing = Math.max(neededGrams - usable, 0); int bags = (missing + bag.sizeGrams() - 1) / bag.sizeGrams(); return bags * bag.sizeGrams(); } Kotlin fun gramsToBuy(neededGrams: Int, bag: Bag, today: LocalDate): Int { val usable = if (today.isAfter(bag.bestBefore)) 0 else bag.leftGrams val missing = maxOf(neededGrams - usable, 0) val bags = (missing + bag.sizeGrams - 1) / bag.sizeGrams return bags * bag.sizeGrams } Two things changed. The bag and the date arrive as arguments, so nothing is read from outside. And nothing is written: the grams come back as the return value, and that's all. Bag is a record in Java and a data class with vals in Kotlin, so it's a plain value that can't change under you. Now the test: Java assertEquals(2000, gramsToBuy(1500, bag, LocalDate.of(2026, 4, 1))); Kotlin assertEquals(2000, gramsToBuy(1500, bag, LocalDate.of(2026, 4, 1))) No fake clock, no reset, no clean-up. You can test 31 March and 1 April in two lines, run the tests in any order, and run them on eight threads at once. (A thread is one path of work running through a program, and several can run at the same moment.) Nothing is shared, so nothing can race, which means no two threads can change the same data at once and get a wrong answer. A function that reads only its arguments is tested with plain values. Pass everything in. The recipe card picture breaks in one place, and it's worth knowing where. A real recipe never gives exactly the same pancakes twice, because eggs and pans differ. A pure function gives exactly the same value every time, to the last digit. That's stronger than any kitchen. Purity is a property of what a function does, not of the language. Kotlin has no pure keyword, and neither compiler checks it. The clues are in the signature: plain value parameters, a real return type instead of Unit or void, and no clock, file or logger among the things it uses. So the rule is easy to test now. Pure functions also let you do things with the code itself that the first version would not survive. Pure or not? For each function, decide pure or impure. For the impure ones, name the hidden input or the side effect. Write your answers down before you read the expected result. 1: fun gramsFor(cups: Int) = cups * FLOUR_GRAMS_PER_CUP, where FLOUR_GRAMS_PER_CUP is a const val. 2: fun isFresh(bag: Bag) = !LocalDate.now().isAfter(bag.bestBefore). 3: fun totalGrams(items: MutableList<Item>): Int { items.sortBy { it.name }; return items.sumOf { it.grams } }. 4: fun newJarLabel() = UUID.randomUUID().toString(). 5: fun shortName(recipe: String) = recipe.take(12). 6: fun portion(grams: Int): Int { stats.portions++; return grams / 4 }, where stats is a shared object. Pure: 1 (a const val can never change) and 5. Impure: 2 reads the calendar, a hidden input. 3 sorts the caller's list in place, a side effect the caller can see, even though the total is right. 4 reads a random source, so two calls never agree. 6 returns the right portion but bumps a shared counter on every call, a side effect. If you hesitated on 3, that's the one that bites in practice: the caller's list comes back reordered.

h: Pure functions: the idea everything else builds on · Swapping a call for its value: referential transparency
x: Pure functions have a property with a long name and a simple meaning. Referential transparency means you can replace a call with the value it returns, and the program does exactly the same thing. In the kitchen, it's a bowl of batter. If you've already made batter from the card, you can use that bowl instead of making it again, and nobody can tell. Here's the same move in code. batterGrams(pancakes) says how much batter a batch needs, 55 g a pancake: Java int total = batterGrams(8) + batterGrams(8); int b = batterGrams(8); int same = b + b; // always equal to total Kotlin val total = batterGrams(8) + batterGrams(8) val b = batterGrams(8) val same = b + b // always equal to total You make this kind of change every day without thinking about it: extract a variable, inline a variable, move a call out of a loop. It's only safe when the call is pure. Try the same move on a call with a side effect. fridge.takeEgg() takes one egg out of the fridge and returns its label: Java String e = fridge.takeEgg(); List<String> eggs = List.of(e, e); // one egg List<String> inlined = List.of(fridge.takeEgg(), fridge.takeEgg()); // two eggs Kotlin val e = fridge.takeEgg() val eggs = listOf(e, e) // one egg val inlined = listOf(fridge.takeEgg(), fridge.takeEgg()) // two eggs The demo below runs both halves and counts the eggs that leave the fridge: batterGrams(8) + batterGrams(8) = 880 val b = batterGrams(8); b + b = 880 val e = takeEgg(); listOf(e, e) -> [egg_1, egg_1], eggs taken: 1 listOf(takeEgg(), takeEgg()) -> [egg_1, egg_2], eggs taken: 2 The batter came to 880 g both ways. Inlining the egg variable, though, took a second egg out of the fridge. Nothing in the syntax warned you. Both versions look like the same expression, and only what you know about takeEgg tells them apart. That's what purity buys you in practice: the call site tells you everything. You can reorder pure calls, because no call depends on another one's effects. You can cache the result, because the same arguments always give the same answer (lesson 3 of this track builds memoize on exactly this). You can retry after a failure, because a second call can't do anything twice. You can run it on many threads at once, because it touches nothing shared. With an impure function, each of those moves first needs you to read its body, and often the bodies of everything it calls. A pure call can be swapped for its value. An impure call can't. Know which one you hold before you refactor. Pure code works with values rather than changing variables, and Kotlin has a feature that pushes you that way. One egg or two Run ReplaceTheCall (or ReplaceTheCallJava). Before you read the output, predict how many eggs leave the fridge in each half. Add println("weighing batter") as the first line of batterGrams (in Java, System.out.println(...)). Predict how many times it prints, then run again. Is batterGrams still pure? Decide before you read the expected result. ReplaceTheCall.kt package workbench.functional.l01.demo // Pure: the result depends only on the argument, and calling it changes nothing. fun batterGrams(pancakes: Int): Int = pancakes * 55 // Impure: taking an egg out of the fridge is the whole point of the call. This fake fridge counts them. object FakeFridge { var taken = 0 fun takeEgg(): String { taken++ return "egg_$taken" } } fun main() { // 1. With a pure function, a call and its value are interchangeable. val b = batterGrams(8) println("batterGrams(8) + batterGrams(8) = ${batterGrams(8) + batterGrams(8)}") println("val b = batterGrams(8); b + b = ${b + b}") // 2. The same "harmless" refactoring on an impure call changes what the program does. val e = FakeFridge.takeEgg() println("val e = takeEgg(); listOf(e, e) -> ${listOf(e, e)}, eggs taken: ${FakeFridge.taken}") FakeFridge.taken = 0 val both = listOf(FakeFridge.takeEgg(), FakeFridge.takeEgg()) println("listOf(takeEgg(), takeEgg()) -> $both, eggs taken: ${FakeFridge.taken}") } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l01.demo.ReplaceTheCallKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l01/demo/ReplaceTheCall.kt ReplaceTheCallJava.java package workbench.functional.l01.demo; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of ReplaceTheCall.kt: swapping a call for its value is safe only when the call is pure. */ public class ReplaceTheCallJava { // Pure: the result depends only on the argument, and calling it changes nothing. static int batterGrams(int pancakes) { return pancakes * 55; } // Impure: taking an egg out of the fridge is the whole point of the call. This fake fridge counts them. static int taken = 0; static String takeEgg() { taken++; return "egg_" + taken; } public static void main(String[] args) { // 1. With a pure function, a call and its value are interchangeable. int b = batterGrams(8); System.out.println("batterGrams(8) + batterGrams(8) = " + (batterGrams(8) + batterGrams(8))); System.out.println("int b = batterGrams(8); b + b = " + (b + b)); // 2. The same "harmless" refactoring on an impure call changes what the program does. String e = takeEgg(); System.out.println("String e = takeEgg(); List.of(e, e) -> " + List.of(e, e) + ", eggs taken: " + taken); taken = 0; List<String> both = List.of(takeEgg(), takeEgg()); System.out.println("List.of(takeEgg(), takeEgg()) -> " + both + ", eggs taken: " + taken); } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l01.demo.ReplaceTheCallJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l01/demo/ReplaceTheCallJava.java The pure half prints 880 twice. The egg half takes one egg for listOf(e, e), which holds the same label twice, and two eggs for the inlined version, [egg_1, egg_2]. After you add the print, weighing batter appears three times: once for val b, twice for batterGrams(8) + batterGrams(8). Printing is a side effect, so batterGrams is no longer strictly pure: inlining b would now change the output. A debug print is harmless, but it is the same mechanism as the second egg.

h: Pure functions: the idea everything else builds on · Computing values instead of changing variables: if, when and try as expressions
x: Pure code computes values instead of changing variables. Kotlin helps more than Java here, because if, when and try are expressions: code that produces a value you can assign or return. In Java, if and try are statements: they do something, and produce nothing. Our recipe book marks each recipe with one, two or three stars for how hard it is. Here's the habit both languages allow, a variable declared first and assigned in branches: Java Difficulty level; if (stars == 1) level = Difficulty.EASY; else if (stars == 2) level = Difficulty.MEDIUM; else level = Difficulty.HARD; Kotlin var level: Difficulty if (stars == 1) level = Difficulty.EASY else if (stars == 2) level = Difficulty.MEDIUM else level = Difficulty.HARD And this is the expression form: Java Difficulty level = switch (stars) { // switch expression, JDK 14 case 1 -> Difficulty.EASY; case 2 -> Difficulty.MEDIUM; default -> Difficulty.HARD; }; Kotlin val level = when (stars) { 1 -> Difficulty.EASY 2 -> Difficulty.MEDIUM else -> Difficulty.HARD } The expression version is a val, so nothing can reassign it later. It also can't be left without a value. Delete the else branch and Kotlin refuses to compile it: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add an 'else' branch. When the subject is an enum or a sealed type (a type whose subtypes are all listed in one place), you can name every case and leave out else. Then adding a new case to the type breaks every when that doesn't handle it yet, which is exactly the reminder you want. try works the same way in Kotlin. Its value is the last expression of the try block, or of the catch block that ran. Here it reads a weight that someone typed into the app: Java int grams; try { grams = Integer.parseInt(raw); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { grams = -1; } Kotlin val grams = try { raw.toInt() } catch (e: NumberFormatException) { -1 } Java has no try expression, so you assign in each block or return from each block. The demo feeds it "25O", typed with a letter O where the zero should be, and gets -1. (Returning -1 for bad input only keeps the example short. Lesson 7 of this track shows better ways to return a failure.) You can't write a whole program as expressions, and you shouldn't try. Inside the rules, though, expressions push you toward pure code: each line computes one value from the values before it. The rest, reading the cupboard and writing the list, still has to live somewhere. That's the last step. Let the compiler catch the missing branch Run Expressions (or ExpressionsJava). Check that the statement and expression versions agree for one, two and three stars. In difficultyOf, delete the else -> line (in Java, the default -> line). Run the demo again and read the compiler error. Put the line back. In difficultyStatement, delete the last else level = ... line and run once more. Predict first: will the statement version compile? Expressions.kt package workbench.functional.l01.demo // A recipe book marks each recipe with one, two or three stars. enum class Difficulty { EASY, MEDIUM, HARD } // Statement style: declare a var, then assign it in every branch and hope you didn't miss one. fun difficultyStatement(stars: Int): Difficulty { var level: Difficulty if (stars == 1) level = Difficulty.EASY else if (stars == 2) level = Difficulty.MEDIUM else level = Difficulty.HARD return level } // Expression style: the when IS the value. No var, nothing to forget, nothing to reassign later. fun difficultyOf(stars: Int): Difficulty = when (stars) { 1 -> Difficulty.EASY 2 -> Difficulty.MEDIUM else -> Difficulty.HARD } // try is an expression too: the value of the try block, or the value of the catch block. fun parseGrams(raw: String): Int = try { raw.toInt() } catch (e: NumberFormatException) { -1 } fun main() { for (stars in listOf(1, 2, 3)) { println("$stars stars -> ${difficultyOf(stars)} (statement version: ${difficultyStatement(stars)})") } println("parseGrams(\"250\") = ${parseGrams("250")}") println("parseGrams(\"25O\") = ${parseGrams("25O")}") // typed with a letter O } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l01.demo.ExpressionsKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l01/demo/Expressions.kt ExpressionsJava.java package workbench.functional.l01.demo; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of Expressions.kt. Java's if and try are statements; the switch expression (JDK 14) is the expression form. */ public class ExpressionsJava { // A recipe book marks each recipe with one, two or three stars. enum Difficulty { EASY, MEDIUM, HARD } // Statement style: declare a variable, then assign it in every branch. static Difficulty difficultyStatement(int stars) { Difficulty level; if (stars == 1) level = Difficulty.EASY; else if (stars == 2) level = Difficulty.MEDIUM; else level = Difficulty.HARD; return level; } // Expression style: the switch expression IS the value. static Difficulty difficultyOf(int stars) { return switch (stars) { case 1 -> Difficulty.EASY; case 2 -> Difficulty.MEDIUM; default -> Difficulty.HARD; }; } // Java's try is a statement, so the value has to leave through a return in each block. static int parseGrams(String raw) { try { return Integer.parseInt(raw); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { return -1; } } public static void main(String[] args) { for (int stars : List.of(1, 2, 3)) { System.out.println(stars + " stars -> " + difficultyOf(stars) + " (statement version: " + difficultyStatement(stars) + ")"); } System.out.println("parseGrams(\"250\") = " + parseGrams("250")); System.out.println("parseGrams(\"25O\") = " + parseGrams("25O")); // typed with a letter O } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l01.demo.ExpressionsJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l01/demo/ExpressionsJava.java Step 2 fails to compile in both languages. Kotlin: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add an 'else' branch. javac: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values. Step 3 fails too: Kotlin says variable 'level' must be initialized., javac says variable level might not have been initialized. Both compilers track the missing value either way. The expression form reports it where you made the mistake, and leaves you a val that nobody can reassign afterwards. h: Pure functions: the idea everything else builds on · Keeping the effects at the edge: functional core, imperative shell
x: A real app can't be pure. It has to read the calendar, look in the cupboard and write the shopping list. Pure functions don't remove those effects. They let you push them to the edges. Think of the kitchen again. The recipe card decides: how much flour, how long in the pan. The cook does the errands: opens the cupboard, reads the date on the bag, writes the list. Keep the card free of errands, and keep the cook free of decisions. The shape has a name, functional core, imperative shell, usually credited to Gary Bernhardt's Destroy All Software screencasts. The core holds the decisions and is pure. The shell does the input and output, and stays so thin that it has almost no decisions left in it. (Imperative code works by doing things in order: read this, then write that.) For the shopping helper, the shell is three steps: Java static int flourToBuy(int neededGrams, Clock clock) { Bag bag = Cupboard.flour; // 1. gather the inputs LocalDate today = LocalDate.now(clock); int grams = gramsToBuy(neededGrams, bag, today); // 2. decide, purely ShoppingList.lines.add(shoppingLine("flour", grams, today)); // 3. do the effect return grams; } Kotlin fun flourToBuy(neededGrams: Int, clock: Clock): Int { val bag = Cupboard.flour // 1. gather the inputs val today = LocalDate.now(clock) val grams = gramsToBuy(neededGrams, bag, today) // 2. decide, purely ShoppingList.lines.add(shoppingLine("flour", grams, today)) // 3. do the effect return grams } Look at shoppingLine. Deciding what to write is a decision, so it moves into the core as a pure function that returns a String. Writing the line is an effect, so it stays in the shell. The payoff shows in where the tests go. The core has all the branches: the best-before date, the never-below-zero rule, the rounding, and every rule you add later. It gets many fast unit tests with plain values. The shell has no branches, so two tests with Clock.fixed cover it. You still need a fixed clock, but in two tests instead of twenty. Decide in the core, act in the shell. Keep the shell too thin to hide a bug. This is the target shape for the whole track. Function values, higher-order functions, collection pipelines and errors as values are all tools for making the core bigger and the shell smaller. The last lesson of the track puts a whole program into this shape. The shape has a limit, and it's best said plainly. A pure core can't do anything on its own: no file, no screen, no network. The shell still reads and writes, it's still the part that's hard to test, and no compiler checks that the core stayed pure. Purity makes a rule easy to test. It doesn't make the rule right. So far, every rule was a function we called by name. Rules can also be things you hold, store and hand to other code, and that's where the track goes next. The shell, like the cook, gathers the inputs, hands them to the pure core as values, and performs whatever the core decided.

h: Pure functions: the idea everything else builds on · Java and Kotlin
x: The same core and shell in Java and Kotlin Shopping.java record Bag(int sizeGrams, int leftGrams, LocalDate bestBefore) {} final class Shopping { // core: static, every input is a parameter, the result is the only output static int gramsToBuy(int neededGrams, Bag bag, LocalDate today) { int usable = today.isAfter(bag.bestBefore()) ? 0 : bag.leftGrams(); int missing = Math.max(neededGrams - usable, 0); int bags = (missing + bag.sizeGrams() - 1) / bag.sizeGrams(); return bags * bag.sizeGrams(); } static String shoppingLine(String ingredient, int grams, LocalDate today) { return today + ": buy " + grams + " g " + ingredient; } // shell: gather, decide, act static int flourToBuy(int neededGrams, Clock clock, List<String> list) { Bag bag = Cupboard.flour; LocalDate today = LocalDate.now(clock); int grams = gramsToBuy(neededGrams, bag, today); list.add(shoppingLine("flour", grams, today)); return grams; } } Shopping.kt data class Bag(val sizeGrams: Int, val leftGrams: Int, val bestBefore: LocalDate) // core: a top-level function, every input is a parameter, the result is the only output fun gramsToBuy(neededGrams: Int, bag: Bag, today: LocalDate): Int { val usable = if (today.isAfter(bag.bestBefore)) 0 else bag.leftGrams val missing = maxOf(neededGrams - usable, 0) val bags = (missing + bag.sizeGrams - 1) / bag.sizeGrams return bags * bag.sizeGrams } fun shoppingLine(ingredient: String, grams: Int, today: LocalDate) = "$today: buy $grams g $ingredient" // shell: gather, decide, act fun flourToBuy(neededGrams: Int, clock: Clock, list: MutableList<String>): Int { val bag = Cupboard.flour val today = LocalDate.now(clock) val grams = gramsToBuy(neededGrams, bag, today) list.add(shoppingLine("flour", grams, today)) return grams } The idea is the same in both languages, and so is the risk: neither compiler checks purity, so a Java method or a Kotlin function can call LocalDate.now() and nothing complains. Kotlin makes pure code a little easier to write. val and data classes make values the default, top-level functions need no holder class, and if, when and try produce values, so you rarely need a temporary var. Java gets close with records (JDK 16), switch expressions (JDK 14) and the ?: ternary operator, which covers the simple if but not a block with several lines, and try stays a statement.

h: Pure functions: the idea everything else builds on · Worked example
x: Pull a pure decision out of a 'cook it tonight' button The recipe app has a 'cook it tonight' button. Its handler loads the recipe, checks two rules and starts cooking: it sets a timer and marks the ingredients as used. Before reading on, list every hidden input and every side effect in it. fun cookTonight(recipeName: String) { val recipe = book.load(recipeName) val now = LocalTime.now() if (now.plusMinutes(recipe.minutes.toLong()).isAfter(DINNER_TIME)) { log.warn("$recipeName: not enough time"); return } if (!cupboard.hasAll(recipe.ingredients)) { log.warn("$recipeName: something is missing"); return } timer.start(recipe.minutes) cupboard.use(recipe.ingredients) } void cookTonight(String recipeName) { Recipe recipe = book.load(recipeName); LocalTime now = LocalTime.now(); if (now.plusMinutes(recipe.minutes()).isAfter(DINNER_TIME)) { log.warn(recipeName + ": not enough time"); return; } if (!cupboard.hasAll(recipe.ingredients())) { log.warn(recipeName + ": something is missing"); return; } timer.start(recipe.minutes()); cupboard.use(recipe.ingredients()); } Hidden inputs: book.load, LocalTime.now() and cupboard.hasAll, which reads what's in the cupboard right now. Side effects: two log.warn calls, timer.start and cupboard.use. The decision is tangled with all of them. 1. Give the decision a type, so the core can return it as a value instead of acting on it. sealed interface Plan { data class Cook(val recipe: String, val minutes: Int, val ingredients: Set<String>) : Plan data class Skip(val recipe: String, val reason: String) : Plan } sealed interface Plan { record Cook(String recipe, int minutes, Set<String> ingredients) implements Plan {} record Skip(String recipe, String reason) implements Plan {} } Write the core. The recipe, the time and the cupboard's contents come in as values, and the decision goes out as a value. Self-check: how many tests does it need, and which fakes? (Three, one per branch, and no fakes at all.) fun decide(recipe: Recipe, now: LocalTime, inCupboard: Set<String>): Plan = when { now.plusMinutes(recipe.minutes.toLong()).isAfter(DINNER_TIME) -> Plan.Skip(recipe.name, "not enough time") !inCupboard.containsAll(recipe.ingredients) -> Plan.Skip(recipe.name, "something is missing") else -> Plan.Cook(recipe.name, recipe.minutes, recipe.ingredients) } static Plan decide(Recipe recipe, LocalTime now, Set<String> inCupboard) { if (now.plusMinutes(recipe.minutes()).isAfter(DINNER_TIME)) return new Plan.Skip(recipe.name(), "not enough time"); if (!inCupboard.containsAll(recipe.ingredients())) return new Plan.Skip(recipe.name(), "something is missing"); return new Plan.Cook(recipe.name(), recipe.minutes(), recipe.ingredients()); } The shell gathers, calls the core and carries out the decision. Its when has no rules of its own, only one branch per kind of decision, and because Plan is sealed the compiler checks that every kind is handled. fun cookTonight(recipeName: String) { val recipe = book.load(recipeName) // 1. gather when (val plan = decide(recipe, LocalTime.now(clock), cupboard.contents())) { // 2. decide is Plan.Cook -> { // 3. act timer.start(plan.minutes) cupboard.use(plan.ingredients) } is Plan.Skip -> log.warn("${plan.recipe}: ${plan.reason}") } } void cookTonight(String recipeName) { Recipe recipe = book.load(recipeName); // 1. gather switch (decide(recipe, LocalTime.now(clock), cupboard.contents())) { // 2. decide case Plan.Cook c -> { // 3. act timer.start(c.minutes()); cupboard.use(c.ingredients()); } case Plan.Skip s -> log.warn(s.recipe() + ": " + s.reason()); } }

h: Pure functions: the idea everything else builds on · Quiz
x: Which of these functions is pure? fun grams(cups: Int) = cups * densityCache.current(), where a background thread refreshes densityCache fun grams(cups: Int, gramsPerCup: Int) = cups * gramsPerCup fun grams(cups: Int): Int { log.debug("grams for $cups"); return cups * 120 } fun portion(grams: Int) = if (LocalTime.now().hour >= 18) grams * 2 else grams Only the second depends on nothing but its arguments and changes nothing. The first reads a hidden input that another thread changes. The third returns the right number but writes a log line on every call, which is a side effect. The fourth reads the clock, so the same grams give two different portions in one day. val label = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); val labels = listOf(label, label). A teammate inlines the variable: listOf(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), UUID.randomUUID().toString()). What changed? Nothing: inlining a val never changes behaviour Nothing, because UUID objects are immutable The list used to hold one label twice; now it holds two different labels It no longer compiles, because randomUUID can't be called twice in one expression randomUUID reads a random source, so it isn't referentially transparent: the call and its value are not interchangeable. Inlining is only safe for pure calls. The tempting answer is the first one, which is true only when the call is pure. Immutability of the result doesn't help; the call itself gives a different value each time. What does g hold? val g = try { "25O".toInt() } catch (e: NumberFormatException) { -1 } finally { println("done") } (the string has a letter O at the end) -1, and it prints done Unit, because finally runs last It doesn't compile: try is a statement 25, because toInt stops at the first bad character In Kotlin, try is an expression. Its value is the last expression of the try block, or of the catch block that ran, here -1. finally always runs, but it doesn't change the value. toInt doesn't stop early: any bad character makes it throw. In Java the same code would need a variable assigned in each block, because Java's try is a statement. A meal-planning app has 14 rules and talks to three outside systems: a recipe website, an online shop and a calendar. With functional core, imperative shell, where do most of the unit tests go? In the shell, with a fake for each outside system Split evenly between the shell and the core Neither: only end-to-end tests catch real bugs In the pure core, called with plain values and no fakes The core holds all 14 rules, so it holds almost all the branches, and pure functions are tested with plain values in a line each. The shell gathers inputs and carries out decisions with almost no branches, so a couple of tests with fakes cover it. Testing the rules through the shell is what makes test suites full of fakes. From Race conditions: why count++ lies: eight threads call gramsToBuy(needed, bag, today) at the same time, each with its own arguments. Bag is a data class with only vals of immutable types. What do you need to make the calls thread-safe? A synchronized block around each call Nothing: the function reads only its arguments and writes nothing shared An AtomicReference to hold the result A ThreadLocal copy of the bag for each thread A race needs shared state that at least one thread writes: read-modify-write or check-then-act on something both threads can see. A pure function writes nothing outside itself, and the immutable Bag can't change under a reader, so there is nothing to race on. A lock would only make the threads wait in line for no reason.

h: Pure functions: the idea everything else builds on · Key terms
x: Pure function A function whose result depends only on its arguments, and whose call changes nothing outside it. Side effect Anything a call does besides return its value: writing, sending, printing, changing shared state. Hidden input Something a function reads that isn't a parameter: the clock, a random source, a mutable global. Referential transparency A call can be replaced by its value without changing the program. Expression Code that produces a value. In Kotlin, if, when and try are expressions. Functional core, imperative shell A design where pure functions make the decisions and a thin outer layer does the reading and writing. What two rules make a function pure? Its result depends only on its arguments, and calling it changes nothing outside it: no writing, no printing, no changes to shared state. Why does calling LocalDate.now() make a function impure? The calendar is a hidden input. The same arguments can give a different answer on a different day. What is referential transparency? You can replace a call with the value it returns without changing what the program does. Only pure calls have it. val e = takeEgg(); listOf(e, e) vs listOf(takeEgg(), takeEgg()): how many eggs does each take? One, then two. Inlining a variable is only safe when the call is pure. What does Kotlin 2.4 say about val d = when (stars) { 1 -> EASY; 2 -> MEDIUM } with an Int subject? It won't compile: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add an 'else' branch. What is the value of a Kotlin try { ... } catch (...) { ... } expression? The last expression of the try block, or of the catch block that ran. finally runs but doesn't change the value. In functional core, imperative shell, what belongs in the shell? Reading inputs (clock, files, globals) and performing effects (writes, calls, logs), with as few decisions as possible.

h: Pure functions: the idea everything else builds on · Go deeper
x: Purity has fuzzy edges, and it helps to know where they are. Creating an object changes the heap, the memory where objects live, but nobody calls a function impure because it creates a String. What counts is whether a caller can observe the change. The same goes for a cache inside a function: memoize in lesson 3 stores results in a map, yet from the outside the function still returns the same answer for the same arguments, so callers can treat it as pure. Throwing is the contested case. require(neededGrams >= 0) makes a function partial: it has no answer for some inputs. Many people still call it pure, because the same bad input always throws the same way. What hurts is using exceptions for expected outcomes, like a recipe that can't be cooked tonight, because the signature no longer tells you what can come back. Lesson 7 of this track returns those outcomes as values. Kotlin can't check purity, but it can catch the most common bug with pure functions: calling one and dropping the result. Compile with -Xreturn-value-checker=full and Kotlin 2.4.21 warns on a call like plusExtra(grams, 50) on a line of its own: Java static int plusExtra(int grams, int extra) { return grams + extra; } static int total(int grams) { plusExtra(grams, 50); // javac says nothing return grams; } Kotlin fun plusExtra(grams: Int, extra: Int): Int = grams + extra fun total(grams: Int): Int { plusExtra(grams, 50) // warning: unused return value of 'plusExtra'. return grams } In a quick test the warning covered Kotlin functions, including stdlib ones like map, but not Java methods: a dropped call to BigDecimal.add got no warning. That one stays a code-review catch.

h: Function types, lambdas and closures · Making a check a value you can hold: function types
x: Here's a dinner party in code. The host has a few dishes in mind and a few guests to please. A Dish knows its name, how many minutes it takes, its diet (vegan, vegetarian or meat), its main ingredient and whether it has nuts. Before cooking, one method checks a dish against a guest's needs: Java static String check(Dish d, Guest g) { if (d.minutes() > 60) return "too-slow"; if (!AUTUMN.contains(d.main())) return "out-of-season"; if (g.vegetarian() && d.diet().equals("meat")) return "has-meat"; if (g.nutAllergy() && d.nuts()) return "has-nuts"; // ...one more line for every guest with a need of their own return null; } Kotlin fun check(d: Dish, g: Guest): String? { if (d.minutes > 60) return "too-slow" if (d.main !in AUTUMN) return "out-of-season" if (g.vegetarian && d.diet == "meat") return "has-meat" if (g.nutAllergy && d.nuts) return "has-nuts" // ...one more line for every guest with a need of their own return null } Every new need means editing this method, and every guest with a need of their own adds another flag. You can't test one check on its own, reorder them, or let a guest's settings pick which ones apply, because the checks aren't things you can hold. They're lines of code. And the guest list only ever grows. So make each check a value, like a card in the drawer. In Kotlin a function has a type, written with an arrow: (Dish) -> Problem? means "a function that takes a Dish and returns a Problem, or null". Problem is a small data class that says which check said no, and about which dish. You can keep such a function in a val or a list, pass it as an argument, and return it from another function, just as you'd handle an Int. That's what people mean by functions as values. Java // Java has no function types; it uses an interface with one method Function<Dish, Problem> readyInAnHour = d -> d.minutes() > 60 ? new Problem("too-slow", d.name()) : null; List<Function<Dish, Problem>> everyone = List.of(readyInAnHour, autumnOnly); Problem p = readyInAnHour.apply(dish); Kotlin typealias Check = (Dish) -> Problem? val readyInAnHour: Check = { d -> if (d.minutes > 60) Problem("too-slow", d.name) else null } val everyone: List<Check> = listOf(readyInAnHour, autumnOnly) val p = readyInAnHour(dish) The { d -> ... } part is a lambda: a function written right where you need it, with no name, its parameters before the arrow and its body after. Now the code that checks a dish doesn't know any check. It runs a list: checks.firstNotNullOfOrNull { check -> check(dish) }, which calls each check in turn and stops at the first one that returns a problem. Sam is vegetarian, so Sam's list is everyone + meatFree. The demo runs four dishes past both lists: pumpkin soup: everyone=ok, Sam=ok slow roast: everyone=too-slow, Sam=too-slow leek and bacon tart: everyone=ok, Sam=has-meat strawberry cake: everyone=out-of-season, Sam=out-of-season The tart is fine for everyone except Sam, and adding Sam's check changed no other line. The strawberry cake fails because this kitchen cooks in autumn, and the strawberries are five months late. The two languages spell all this differently. Java has no function types, so it uses a functional interface, an interface with one abstract method: Function<T, R>, Predicate<T>, Supplier<T>, or one of your own. You call it by its method name, apply or test. Kotlin has real function types, and you call a value of one like a function: readyInAnHour(dish). On the JVM, Kotlin's (Dish) -> Problem? is the interface kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1<Dish, Problem>, and the call goes to its invoke method. The typealias only gives the type a short name. It creates nothing new. A check you can hold can be tested, reordered and chosen per guest. Make it a value. The card in the drawer holds up well so far: store it, lend it, line it up. The picture breaks in one place, and we'll reach it in the last section. First, a lambda is only one of the ways to make a card. Add a check without touching the others Run ChecksAsValues (or ChecksAsValuesJava). Predict first: which dish gets a different answer for Sam? Alex can't eat nuts. Add a check, val noNuts: Check = { d -> if (d.nuts) Problem("has-nuts", d.name) else null }, and a list, val forAlex = listOf(noNuts) + everyone. Print the answer for the strawberry cake under forAlex. (Java: a NO_NUTS field, and Stream.concat(Stream.of(NO_NUTS), EVERYONE.stream()).toList() for the list.) Note what you didn't touch: firstProblem and every other check. ChecksAsValues.kt package workbench.functional.l02.demo data class Dish(val name: String, val minutes: Int, val diet: String, val main: String, val nuts: Boolean = false) data class Problem(val check: String, val dish: String) // A check is a function from a dish to a problem, or null when the dish passes. typealias Check = (Dish) -> Problem? // Each check is a value: a lambda stored in a val, ready to go into a list. val readyInAnHour: Check = { d -> if (d.minutes > 60) Problem("too-slow", d.name) else null } val autumnOnly: Check = { d -> if (d.main in setOf("pumpkin", "leek", "apple", "mushroom")) null else Problem("out-of-season", d.name) } val meatFree: Check = { d -> if (d.diet == "meat") Problem("has-meat", d.name) else null } // Different guests get different lists. Adding a check for one guest changes nothing above. val everyone: List<Check> = listOf(readyInAnHour, autumnOnly) val forSam: List<Check> = everyone + meatFree // Sam is vegetarian // Run the checks in order and stop at the first problem. fun firstProblem(d: Dish, checks: List<Check>): Problem? = checks.firstNotNullOfOrNull { check -> check(d) } fun main() { val dishes = listOf( Dish("pumpkin soup", 40, "vegan", "pumpkin"), Dish("slow roast", 180, "meat", "beef"), Dish("leek and bacon tart", 50, "meat", "leek"), Dish("strawberry cake", 45, "vegetarian", "strawberry", nuts = true), ) for (d in dishes) { val all = firstProblem(d, everyone)?.check ?: "ok" val sam = firstProblem(d, forSam)?.check ?: "ok" println("${d.name}: everyone=$all, Sam=$sam") } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l02.demo.ChecksAsValuesKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l02/demo/ChecksAsValues.kt ChecksAsValuesJava.java package workbench.functional.l02.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.function.Function; /** Java twin of ChecksAsValues.kt. A check is a Function<Dish, Problem> that returns null when the dish passes. */ public class ChecksAsValuesJava { record Dish(String name, int minutes, String diet, String main, boolean nuts) {} record Problem(String check, String dish) {} // Each check is a value: a lambda stored in a field, ready to go into a list. static final Function<Dish, Problem> READY_IN_AN_HOUR = d -> d.minutes() > 60 ? new Problem("too-slow", d.name()) : null; static final Function<Dish, Problem> AUTUMN_ONLY = d -> Set.of("pumpkin", "leek", "apple", "mushroom").contains(d.main()) ? null : new Problem("out-of-season", d.name()); static final Function<Dish, Problem> MEAT_FREE = d -> d.diet().equals("meat") ? new Problem("has-meat", d.name()) : null; // Different guests get different lists. Adding a check for one guest changes nothing above. static final List<Function<Dish, Problem>> EVERYONE = List.of(READY_IN_AN_HOUR, AUTUMN_ONLY); static final List<Function<Dish, Problem>> FOR_SAM = plus(EVERYONE, MEAT_FREE); // Sam is vegetarian static <T> List<T> plus(List<T> list, T extra) { List<T> copy = new ArrayList<>(list); copy.add(extra); return List.copyOf(copy); } // Run the checks in order and stop at the first problem. A check is called with apply. static Problem firstProblem(Dish d, List<Function<Dish, Problem>> checks) { for (Function<Dish, Problem> check : checks) { Problem p = check.apply(d); if (p != null) return p; } return null; } static String name(Problem p) { return p == null ? "ok" : p.check(); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Dish> dishes = List.of( new Dish("pumpkin soup", 40, "vegan", "pumpkin", false), new Dish("slow roast", 180, "meat", "beef", false), new Dish("leek and bacon tart", 50, "meat", "leek", false), new Dish("strawberry cake", 45, "vegetarian", "strawberry", true)); for (Dish d : dishes) { System.out.println(d.name() + ": everyone=" + name(firstProblem(d, EVERYONE)) + ", Sam=" + name(firstProblem(d, FOR_SAM))); } } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l02.demo.ChecksAsValuesJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l02/demo/ChecksAsValuesJava.java The leek and bacon tart passes for everyone and gets has-meat for Sam. Under forAlex, the strawberry cake gets has-nuts instead of out-of-season: the order of the list is the order of the checks, and the first problem wins. firstProblem didn't change, because it never knew any check. h: Function types, lambdas and closures · Four ways to write a function value: lambdas, references and the rest
x: A lambda is the most common way to write a function value, but it's one of four. All four below have the same type, and all four ask the same question: does this dish take more than an hour? Java Predicate<Integer> lambda = minutes -> minutes > 60; Predicate<Integer> anon = new Predicate<>() { // anonymous class public boolean test(Integer minutes) { return minutes > 60; } }; Predicate<Integer> ref = Timing::isTooSlow; // method reference Predicate<Integer> obj = new TooSlow(60); // class implementing Predicate Kotlin val lambda: (Int) -> Boolean = { minutes -> minutes > 60 } val anon: (Int) -> Boolean = fun(minutes: Int): Boolean { return minutes > 60 } val ref: (Int) -> Boolean = ::isTooSlow // function reference val obj: (Int) -> Boolean = TooSlow(60) // class TooSlow : (Int) -> Boolean A lambda with one parameter can leave it unnamed and use it: { it > 60 }. Its value is its last expression. That's also why a bare return inside a lambda doesn't compile ('return' is prohibited here.): return belongs to the enclosing fun, not to the lambda. If you want early exits, write an anonymous function, the fun(minutes: Int) form above, where return means what it means everywhere else. Or use a labelled return, return@label, which leaves only the lambda. The demo's anonymous function uses its early exit to flag negative times, because a dish that takes minus five minutes is a typo, not a miracle. A function reference turns a named function into a value. ::isTooSlow points at a top-level function. Dish::isVegan is unbound: its type takes the receiver as the first parameter, (Dish) -> Boolean. oven::adjust is bound to one oven object, so its type has only the remaining parameters. ::Problem points at the constructor. Two more shapes show up in Kotlin APIs. A function type can be nullable: ((Problem) -> Unit)? is an optional callback, a function the caller may pass to hear about a problem, or leave out. Mind the parentheses. Without them, (Problem) -> Unit? is a function that returns Unit?. You call a nullable one with onProblem?.invoke(p). And a function type can have a receiver, a value the lambda sees as this. In Int.() -> Boolean, the body sees the Int as this, so { this % 15 == 0 } asks "is this a whole quarter of an hour?". Receivers are how apply and buildList work. Lesson 6 of this track covers the scope functions, and the Advanced Kotlin track has a lesson on type-safe DSLs. Java has neither: a Consumer<Problem> parameter may simply be null by convention, and there is no receiver. Four spellings, one type. They don't cost the same, though, and the next question is what each one becomes when it runs. Four ways, one type Open FourWays.kt (or FourWaysJava.java). Predict the four booleans it prints for 45, 90 and -5 minutes. Run it. In tooSlowLambda, add the same early exit the anonymous function has: if (minutes < 0) return true on its own line before minutes > 60. Run it and read the error. Then fix it with a label: write slow@{ minutes -> ... } and return@slow true. FourWays.kt package workbench.functional.l02.demo // The same "does this dish take too long?" check, written four ways. All four have the type (Int) -> Boolean. // 1. A lambda. val tooSlowLambda: (Int) -> Boolean = { minutes -> minutes > 60 } // 2. An anonymous function. Same type, but `return` means "return from this function". val tooSlowAnon: (Int) -> Boolean = fun(minutes: Int): Boolean { if (minutes < 0) return true // a negative time is a typo, so flag it too return minutes > 60 } // 3. A reference to an ordinary function. fun isTooSlow(minutes: Int): Boolean = minutes > 60 val tooSlowRef: (Int) -> Boolean = ::isTooSlow // 4. A class that implements the function type. class TooSlow(private val maxMinutes: Int) : (Int) -> Boolean { override fun invoke(minutes: Int): Boolean = minutes > maxMinutes } // A function type with a receiver: inside the lambda, `this` is the Int. val isQuarterHour: Int.() -> Boolean = { this % 15 == 0 } // A nullable function type: the caller may pass no callback at all. fun check(minutes: Int, rule: (Int) -> Boolean, onHit: ((Int) -> Unit)? = null): Boolean { val hit = rule(minutes) if (hit) onHit?.invoke(minutes) return hit } fun main() { val rules = listOf(tooSlowLambda, tooSlowAnon, tooSlowRef, TooSlow(60)) for (minutes in listOf(45, 90, -5)) println("$minutes -> ${rules.map { rule -> rule(minutes) }}") println("45.isQuarterHour() = ${45.isQuarterHour()}, 50.isQuarterHour() = ${50.isQuarterHour()}") check(90, tooSlowRef) { println("callback: $it minutes is too slow") } println("no callback given: ${check(90, tooSlowRef)}") } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l02.demo.FourWaysKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l02/demo/FourWays.kt FourWaysJava.java package workbench.functional.l02.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.IntConsumer; import java.util.function.Predicate; /** * Java twin of FourWays.kt. Java has no function types, so each value is an instance of a functional * interface, here Predicate<Integer>. Java has no receiver types either: Kotlin's Int.() -> Boolean has no twin. */ public class FourWaysJava { // 1. A lambda. static final Predicate<Integer> TOO_SLOW_LAMBDA = minutes -> minutes > 60; // 2. An anonymous class: the closest Java has to an anonymous function. `return` leaves test(). static final Predicate<Integer> TOO_SLOW_ANON = new Predicate<>() { @Override public boolean test(Integer minutes) { if (minutes < 0) return true; // a negative time is a typo, so flag it too return minutes > 60; } }; // 3. A method reference to an ordinary method. static boolean isTooSlow(Integer minutes) { return minutes > 60; } static final Predicate<Integer> TOO_SLOW_REF = FourWaysJava::isTooSlow; // 4. A class that implements the interface. static final class TooSlow implements Predicate<Integer> { private final int maxMinutes; TooSlow(int maxMinutes) { this.maxMinutes = maxMinutes; } @Override public boolean test(Integer minutes) { return minutes > maxMinutes; } } // An optional callback: Java can't say "nullable" in the type, so null is just allowed by convention. static boolean check(int minutes, Predicate<Integer> rule, IntConsumer onHit) { boolean hit = rule.test(minutes); if (hit && onHit != null) onHit.accept(minutes); return hit; } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Predicate<Integer>> rules = List.of(TOO_SLOW_LAMBDA, TOO_SLOW_ANON, TOO_SLOW_REF, new TooSlow(60)); for (int minutes : new int[] {45, 90, -5}) { System.out.println(minutes + " -> " + rules.stream().map(rule -> rule.test(minutes)).toList()); } check(90, TOO_SLOW_REF, m -> System.out.println("callback: " + m + " minutes is too slow")); System.out.println("no callback given: " + check(90, TOO_SLOW_REF, null)); } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l02.demo.FourWaysJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l02/demo/FourWaysJava.java 45 prints four false, 90 four true.
