h: Function types, lambdas and closures · What a lambda turns into on the JVM, and what it costs
x: A function value is an object, so something has to create it. What that costs depends on how you wrote it, and Kotlin and Java don't agree on every case. Since Kotlin 2.0, lambdas compile to invokedynamic by default, the mechanism Java has used for lambdas since Java 8. invokedynamic is a bytecode instruction (one step of the JVM's own machine language) that asks a helper method, the first time it runs, how to do its job. The compiler moves the lambda body into a private static method, such as nonCapturing$lambda$0. Where the lambda is created, it emits an invokedynamic whose helper is LambdaMetafactory.metafactory. The first time that instruction runs, the JVM spins up a hidden class that implements Function1 and calls the private method. No .class file for the lambda shows up in your build output. (Kotlin 1.x generated one class per lambda, and the compiler flag -Xlambdas=class still brings that back.) How many objects you get depends on what the lambda captures, that is, which variables from outside its body it uses. The demo's capturing(extra) returns { it + extra }, a card with a note pinned to it, while nonCapturing() returns { it + 10 }, which needs nothing from outside: Java nonCapturing() == nonCapturing(); // true on HotSpot: one shared instance capturing(5) == capturing(5); // false: a new object per evaluation Kotlin nonCapturing() === nonCapturing() // true: one shared instance capturing(5) === capturing(5) // false: a new object per evaluation capturing(5) == capturing(5) // false: lambdas have no equals A non-capturing lambda uses nothing from outside its body, so one instance serves every call. A capturing lambda holds the values it uses (extra here), so each evaluation allocates a new object with those values inside. On JDK 21, the demo printed this for Kotlin (the number after 0x changes from run to run): non-capturing lambda: same object every time? true capturing lambda: same object every time? false capturing lambdas equal with == ? false unbound reference ::addRest: same object? true bound reference oven::adjust: same object? false lambda class: workbench.functional.l02.demo.LambdaShapesKt$$Lambda/0x00000007c0001800 (hidden: true) reference class: workbench.functional.l02.demo.LambdaShapesKt$topLevelRef$1 (hidden: false, extends FunctionReferenceImpl) The shared instance for a non-capturing lambda is what HotSpot does today, not a promise. Don't write code that depends on it. The last line is where Kotlin differs from Java. In Kotlin 2.4.21, function references such as ::addRest and oven::adjust still compile to real classes, LambdaShapesKt$topLevelRef$1 and LambdaShapesKt$boundRef$1, which extend kotlin.jvm.internal.FunctionReferenceImpl. An unbound reference is a singleton held in a static INSTANCE field. A bound one is a new object each time, holding its receiver. Java method references go through invokedynamic like lambdas do, and leave no class file behind. One more cost hides in the types. (Long) -> Long is Function1<Long, Long>, which is generic, so a call through it boxes the long: it wraps the number in a java.lang.Long object and unwraps it again. Java avoids that with primitive interfaces like LongUnaryOperator. Kotlin has no primitive function interfaces. It avoids the box another way, with inline functions, which the next lesson covers. None of this is a reason to avoid lambdas. A capturing lambda costs one small object per evaluation, which the JVM allocates cheaply. It starts to matter in two places: a capturing lambda created inside a hot loop, and code that compares function values with ==, which never works for lambdas. Objects are cheap. The surprise is what happens to a captured variable that changes. Count the objects and the class files Run LambdaShapes (or LambdaShapesJava). Before you look, predict the five true or false answers. From labs/, list the compiled demo classes: ls functional/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/functional/l02/demo/. Look for a class per lambda and a class per reference. Run javap -c -p functional/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/functional/l02/demo/LambdaShapesKt.class and find the first instruction of nonCapturing and of topLevelRef. Compare the last two lines with the Kotlin version. */ public class LambdaShapesJava { static long addRest(long minutes) { return minutes + 10; } // let it rest 10 minutes static LongUnaryOperator nonCapturing() { return m -> m + 10; } // uses nothing from outside static LongUnaryOperator capturing(long extra) { return m -> m + extra; } // captures extra static LongUnaryOperator staticRef() { return LambdaShapesJava::addRest; } // a method reference static final class ColdOven { // this oven runs a little cold private final long extraMinutes; ColdOven(long extraMinutes) { this.extraMinutes = extraMinutes; } long adjust(long minutes) { return minutes + extraMinutes; } } static LongUnaryOperator boundRef(ColdOven o) { return o::adjust; } // bound to one object public static void main(String[] args) { ColdOven oven = new ColdOven(5); System.out.println("non-capturing lambda: same object every time? h: Function types, lambdas and closures · A closure keeps its variables, and a captured var becomes one shared box
x: A lambda is a value that keeps the variables it uses, and a captured var becomes one shared Ref box where two threads lose an update A lambda can use variables from the function that created it, and it keeps them after that function has returned. Code plus the variables it captured is called a closure. It's the recipe card with a note pinned to it: "my oven runs hot, take five minutes off". The note was written where the card was made, and it goes wherever the card goes. Java static IntSupplier makeCounter() { int[] count = {0}; // Java makes you build the box yourself return () -> ++count[0]; } Kotlin fun makeCounter(): () -> Int { var count = 0 return { ++count } // the lambda keeps count alive } Call makeCounter() twice and you get two counters, each with its own count. Each one returns 1, 2, 3 and so on. Look at what the Java version needed. Java refuses to capture a local variable that changes: local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final. The reason is mechanical. A local variable lives in the method's stack frame, the memory one method call uses for its locals, and that frame is gone once makeCounter returns. The lambda outlives the frame, so all it can take is a copy of the value, and copying a variable that keeps changing would be confusing. Java programmers work around it with a one-element array or an AtomicInteger. Either one is an object on the heap, the memory where objects live for as long as something points at them, and both sides can share it. Kotlin builds that object for you, silently. When a lambda captures a var, the compiler moves the variable into a small heap object, a kotlin.jvm.internal.Ref$IntRef (or LongRef, ObjectRef and so on). Both the function and the lambda use its field. The field is a plain public int element, with no volatile and no lock. Java refuses the capture; the Kotlin compiler shrugs and builds the box. Here the recipe card picture breaks, and it breaks in a way that matters. Lend a paper card and your friend gets their own copy of the note. Hand out a closure and everyone holds the same box. That's fine on one thread. It's a bug as soon as two threads share the closure. A thread is one path of work through a program, and several can run at the same moment. ++count becomes "read element, add one, write element", the same read-modify-write as count++ in the race conditions lesson. When two threads read the same old value, one of the two additions is lost. Nothing in the Kotlin source looks shared. The sharing comes from the box the compiler made. The CapturedRace demo shares one captured var total between four tasks on a thread pool (a fixed group of threads that take tasks from a queue). Each task adds 1 a quarter of a million times, and the whole thing runs ten times. One try on this busy 4-core machine began like this: run 1: expected 1,000,000, got 250,956 (lost 749,044) run 2: expected 1,000,000, got 1,000,000 (lost 0) run 3: expected 1,000,000, got 1,000,000 (lost 0) Runs 4 to 10 were correct too. A second try lost 202,126 in run 1, and a third lost nothing in all ten. The Java twin, with its hand-made array box, lost exactly 500,000 in one run. Most losses land in the first run, while the JVM is still interpreting the loop. Then the JIT compiler, the part of the JVM that turns busy code into machine code, compiles it. From then on each task keeps the count in a register, a slot inside the processor, and writes it back once at the end. Then a loss wipes out whole tasks, which is why 500,000 is such a round number. The memory model track explains why the JIT may do that to a plain field. A race that shows up once in ten runs is still a race, and the worst kind, because it passes most tests. A captured var is one box that everyone holding the closure shares. Never change it from two threads. There are two fixes. Share a thread-safe object instead of a var: capture val total = AtomicLong() and call total.incrementAndGet(). Or, better, don't share at all. Let each task count its own work and combine the results at the end with a sum or a fold. The second fix is the functional one, and it keeps working when the tasks move to other machines. That second fix needs functions that take other functions and combine their results. Writing our own is where the next lesson starts. Lose updates, then fix it two ways Run CapturedRace (or CapturedRaceJava). Four pool threads each add 1 to a captured total 250,000 times, ten runs in a row. If all ten runs print 1,000,000, run it once more: the losses come and go. Fix it by sharing a thread-safe object: make it val total = AtomicLong() (Java: AtomicLong total = new AtomicLong()), call total.incrementAndGet() in the loop, and print total.get(). Run it. Undo that, and fix it by not sharing: make each task return its own count, pool.submit(Callable { go.await(); var mine = 0L; repeat(250_000) { mine += 1 }; mine }), then add up tasks.sumOf { it.get() }. (Java: return mine from the lambda and add up the Future<Long> results.) Run it. CapturedRace.kt package workbench.functional.l02.demo import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.Executors // Four pool threads add to one captured var. The var lives in a Ref.LongRef box with a plain field. fun main() { val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4) repeat(10) { run -> var total = 0L // captured below, so it becomes a Ref.LongRef val go = CountDownLatch(1) // start all four tasks at the same moment val tasks = List(4) { pool.submit { go.await() repeat(250_000) { total += 1 } // read element, add 1, write element } } go.countDown() tasks.forEach { it.get() } println("run %2d: expected 1,000,000, got %,9d (lost %,d)".format(run + 1, total, 1_000_000 - total)) } pool.shutdown() } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l02.demo.CapturedRaceKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l02/demo/CapturedRace.kt CapturedRaceJava.java package workbench.functional.l02.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** * Java twin of CapturedRace.kt. Java refuses to capture a local that changes: * long total = 0; ... () -> total += 1 * error: local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final * So Java programmers write the box by hand, a one-element array. That is what Kotlin's Ref.LongRef is. */ public class CapturedRaceJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4); for (int run = 1; run <= 10; run++) { long[] total = {0}; // the hand-made box: a plain array slot CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); // start all four tasks at the same moment List<Future<?>> tasks = new ArrayList<>(); for (int t = 0; t < 4; t++) { tasks.add(pool.submit(() -> { go.await(); for (int i = 0; i < 250_000; i++) total[0] += 1; // read, add 1, write return null; })); } go.countDown(); for (Future<?> f : tasks) f.get(); System.out.printf("run %2d: expected 1,000,000, got %,9d (lost %,d)%n", run, total[0], 1_000_000 - total[0]); } pool.shutdown(); } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l02.demo.CapturedRaceJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l02/demo/CapturedRaceJava.java The broken version loses updates in some runs, by different amounts each time, most often in run 1. Here one try lost 749,044 in run 1 and nothing after, and another lost nothing in all ten runs. Both fixes print exactly 1,000,000 in every run, every try. The don't-share version has no contention at all: mine is only ever touched by one thread, so the compiler keeps it a plain local (repeat is inline, so no lambda captures it). A captured var moves into a Ref box on the heap, a note pinned to the card. The function, the lambda and every thread that calls the lambda share its plain field. h: Function types, lambdas and closures · Java and Kotlin
x: Checks and closures with functional interfaces and with function types Checks.java import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Function; import java.util.function.IntSupplier; record Dish(String name, int minutes, String diet) {} record Problem(String check, String dish) {} final class Checks { // a function value is an instance of a functional interface static Function<Dish, Problem> readyWithin(int maxMinutes) { return d -> d.minutes() > maxMinutes ? new Problem("too-slow", d.name()) : null; // captures maxMinutes } static Problem firstProblem(Dish d, List<Function<Dish, Problem>> checks) { return checks.stream() .map(check -> check.apply(d)) // called by its method name .filter(p -> p != null) .findFirst() .orElse(null); } // a captured local that changes is a compile error; the array is the box, built by hand static IntSupplier makeCounter() { int[] count = {0}; return () -> ++count[0]; } } Checks.kt data class Dish(val name: String, val minutes: Int, val diet: String) data class Problem(val check: String, val dish: String) typealias Check = (Dish) -> Problem? // a real function type: Function1 on the JVM fun readyWithin(maxMinutes: Int): Check = { d -> // captures maxMinutes if (d.minutes > maxMinutes) Problem("too-slow", d.name) else null } fun firstProblem(d: Dish, checks: List<Check>): Problem? = checks.firstNotNullOfOrNull { check -> check(d) } // called like a function // capturing a var is allowed; the compiler builds the Ref box for you fun makeCounter(): () -> Int { var count = 0 return { ++count } } Kotlin has function types; Java has functional interfaces. That changes three things you notice every day. Kotlin calls a function value with f(x), where Java needs the interface's method name (apply, test, getAsInt), and Kotlin has one family of types, (A) -> B, where Java has dozens of interfaces, primitive ones included. Kotlin's types can say "may be null" (Problem?, ((Problem) -> Unit)?), so a check that returns null shows it in its type. And Kotlin lets a lambda capture a var by moving it into a Ref box, where Java insists on effectively final locals and makes you write the box. Under the hood both compile lambdas with invokedynamic; only Kotlin's function references still compile to classes.

h: Function types, lambdas and closures · Worked example
x: Find the hidden shared box in a recipe import A recipe app imports a big file of recipes. It splits the list into chunks of 500 with chunked(500), saves each chunk on a thread pool, and counts how many recipes it saved. Under load the count comes out a little low, and only sometimes. Find the shared state before reading on. fun importAll(recipes: List<Recipe>, pool: ExecutorService): Int { var saved = 0 val futures = recipes.chunked(500).map { chunk -> pool.submit { chunk.forEach { r -> if (book.save(r)) saved += 1 } } } futures.forEach { it.get() } return saved } // The Java version doesn't compile as written: static int importAll(List<Recipe> recipes, ExecutorService pool) throws Exception { int saved = 0; List<Future<?>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); for (List<Recipe> chunk : chunks(recipes, 500)) { futures.add(pool.submit(() -> { for (Recipe r : chunk) if (book.save(r)) saved += 1; // error: local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final })); } for (Future<?> f : futures) f.get(); return saved; } Find the box. saved is a var captured by the lambda passed to submit, which runs on pool threads. The compiler turned it into one Ref$IntRef, and every chunk task does read, add, write on its plain element field. (forEach is inline, so its lambda doesn't count; the submit lambda is the one that captures.) Java refused the same code, and the usual Java workaround is the same box written by hand. // roughly what the compiler made of it val saved = Ref.IntRef() // one box on the heap pool.submit { ...; saved.element += 1 } // every task, on every thread int[] saved = {0}; // the box Java makes you write pool.submit(() -> { ...; saved[0] += 1; }); // the same race Don't share. Make each task count its own saves in a local, return that count, and add the counts up on the calling thread. Each task's lambda now captures only its chunk, which nobody changes. Self-check: why is the var mine inside the task safe? (It's a local of that one task, used on one thread, and no other lambda captures it, so it never becomes a box.) fun importAll(recipes: List<Recipe>, pool: ExecutorService): Int { val futures = recipes.chunked(500).map { chunk -> pool.submit(Callable { // 1. each task returns a value var mine = 0 // a local: only this task touches it for (r in chunk) if (book.save(r)) mine++ mine }) } return futures.sumOf { it.get() } // 2. combine on one thread } static int importAll(List<Recipe> recipes, ExecutorService pool) throws Exception { List<Future<Integer>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); for (List<Recipe> chunk : chunks(recipes, 500)) { futures.add(pool.submit(() -> { // 1. each task returns a value int mine = 0; // a local: only this task touches it for (Recipe r : chunk) if (book.save(r)) mine++; return mine; })); } int total = 0; for (Future<Integer> f : futures) total += f.get(); // 2. combine on one thread return total; } If you do need a live shared number, say a progress bar while the import runs, share a thread-safe object through a val, never a var. LongAdder spreads the work over several cells and is cheaper than AtomicLong when many threads add at once. val savedSoFar = LongAdder() // a val: the reference never changes pool.submit { chunk.forEach { r -> if (book.save(r)) savedSoFar.increment() } } LongAdder savedSoFar = new LongAdder(); // effectively final, so Java is happy too pool.submit(() -> { for (Recipe r : chunk) if (book.save(r)) savedSoFar.increment(); });

What do println(withExtra(5) === withExtra(5)) and println(withExtra(5)(30) == withExtra(5)(30)) print? true and true false and true false and false true and false The lambda captures extra, so every evaluation creates a new object, and === compares objects. Without them, (Problem) -> Unit? is a required function that returns Unit?. The second takes a nullable argument, and the third is a function with a receiver. In Kotlin 2.4.21, which of these leaves a .class file of its own in your build output? ::isTooSlow, a reference to a top-level function { d: Dish -> d.minutes > 0 } { it + extra }, which captures extra Runnable { println("done") } Function references still compile to a class extending FunctionReferenceImpl; an unbound one is a singleton. Capturing changes how many objects you get, not whether a class file exists. A pool of four threads imports recipes. Each task's lambda does saved++ on a captured var saved = 0. What happens to saved? It's exact, because Kotlin makes captured vars thread-safe It doesn't compile, just like in Java It can end up lower than the number of recipes saved, because all four threads share one plain field in a Ref box Each thread gets its own copy, so it counts only one thread's recipes Kotlin allows the capture and moves the variable into one Ref$IntRef on the heap. All four threads run read, add, write on its non-volatile element field, so increments get lost. Java would reject the code; Kotlin compiles it. Yes: a function that accepts any object can certainly accept a Dish No: Any is not Dish, so the types don't match Only after an unchecked cast Only if Problem is declared out The parameter type of a function is an in-position, and Function1 is contravariant in it: (Any) -> R is a subtype of (Dish) -> R because every Dish is an Any. The return type is covariant. The tempting "no" applies the subtype arrow the wrong way round, which is exactly what in fixes.

h: Function types, lambdas and closures · Key terms
x: Function type A type for functions, like (Dish) -> Problem?. Its values can be stored, passed and returned. Lambda A function value written inline, with no name: { d -> d.minutes > 60 }. Function reference A named function used as a value: ::isTooSlow, Dish::isVegan, oven::adjust. Functional interface Java's stand-in for a function type: an interface with one abstract method, like Function<T, R>. Closure A function value together with the variables it captured from the place it was created. Capturing lambda A lambda that uses values from outside its body, so each evaluation creates a new object that holds them. Ref box The small heap object (Ref$IntRef and friends) that the Kotlin compiler puts a captured var into. What JVM interface does Kotlin's (Dish) -> Problem? compile to? kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1<Dish, Problem>. Calling the value calls its invoke method. How do you declare an optional callback that takes a Problem? onProblem: ((Problem) -> Unit)? = null, with the parentheses, and call it with onProblem?.invoke(p). In Kotlin 2.x, is nonCapturing() === nonCapturing() true for a lambda that captures nothing? Yes, on HotSpot today. The invokedynamic call site hands out one shared instance. A capturing lambda is a new object each time. Does ::addRest compile to invokedynamic in Kotlin 2.4.21? No. Function references still compile to a class that extends FunctionReferenceImpl; an unbound one is a singleton INSTANCE. What does a var captured by a lambda become? A kotlin.jvm.internal.Ref box (IntRef, LongRef, ObjectRef) with a plain, non-volatile element field. Why won't { minutes -> if (minutes < 0) return true; minutes > 60 } compile? A bare return returns from the enclosing fun, which is only allowed when the lambda is inlined: 'return' is prohibited here. Use return@label or an anonymous function. What does javac say when a lambda changes a captured local? local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final.

h: Function types, lambdas and closures · Go deeper
x: javap -v shows how invokedynamic is wired. Each lambda site has an entry in the class's BootstrapMethods table pointing at LambdaMetafactory.metafactory, with three arguments: the erased method type of invoke, (Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/lang/Object;, a handle to the private static method holding the body, and the instantiated type, (Ljava/lang/Long;)Ljava/lang/Long; for a (Long) -> Long. The erased signature is why a call through Function1 boxes: invoke takes and returns Object. Kotlin 2.0's switch to invokedynamic changed three visible things, according to its release notes. These lambdas aren't serializable, the experimental reflect() API doesn't support them, and toString() prints the hidden class name, something like LambdaShapesKt$$Lambda/0x...@1b6d3586, instead of a readable description of the function type. A test or log that matched on the old text breaks after the upgrade. Annotate a single lambda with @JvmSerializableLambda, or compile the module with -Xlambdas=class, to get the old class-per-lambda behaviour. SAM conversions went to invokedynamic earlier, in Kotlin 1.5. A SAM conversion turns a lambda into an instance of an interface with a Single Abstract Method: a Kotlin lambda passed where Java expects a Runnable or Comparator, or a lambda for your own fun interface: Java @FunctionalInterface interface Rest { int minutesFor(int grams); } Rest flat = grams -> 10; // Java lambdas have always worked this way Runnable task = () -> System.out.println("timer done"); Kotlin fun interface Rest { fun minutesFor(grams: Int): Int } val flat = Rest { 10 } // a SAM conversion: invokedynamic, no class file val task = Runnable { println("timer done") } // the same for a Java interface A fun interface is worth using when a function type needs a name in a public API, or when Java callers will implement it, since Java code can't write a lambda for Function1 as naturally as for an interface named after its job.

h: Higher-order functions: functions in, functions out · Passing in the part that changes: retry and timed take a function
x: retry takes the call as a function, feeFor hands back a fee function, and three small functions compose into one price where the order matters Look at three places in a recipe app that call something flaky. A flaky call is one that fails now and then for reasons outside your code, like a website that is slow to answer and times out: Java // fetch a recipe page from the website for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) { try { page = site.fetch("pancakes"); break; } catch (SiteTimeoutException e) { if (attempt == 3) throw e; } } // the same loop around shop.prices(basket) // the same loop around weather.today() Kotlin // fetch a recipe page from the website var attempt = 1 while (true) { try { page = site.fetch("pancakes"); break } catch (e: SiteTimeoutException) { if (attempt++ == 3) throw e } } // the same loop around shop.prices(basket) // the same loop around weather.today() The three loops are identical except for one call. An ordinary helper method can't pull that call out, because a method's parameters are values, and the call has to happen inside the loop, up to three times. What you need to pass in is the work itself. A higher-order function is a function that takes a function as a parameter, returns one, or both. It's the friend from the opening: hand it a card, and it does something with the card. Here is retry written as one: Java static <T> T retry(int times, Supplier<T> block) { RuntimeException last = null; for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= times; attempt++) { try { return block.get(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; } } throw new IllegalStateException("gave up after " + times + " attempts", last); } String page = retry(3, () -> site.fetch("pancakes")); Kotlin fun <T> retry(times: Int, block: () -> T): T { var last: Exception? = null repeat(times) { try { return block() } catch (e: Exception) { last = e } } throw IllegalStateException("gave up after $times attempts", last) } val page = retry(3) { site.fetch("pancakes") } The loop is written once. The part that varies, the call, arrives as block, and retry decides when and how often to run it. That's the whole idea of this lesson: keep the shape of a computation (retry it, time it, remember it) apart from the work inside it. (The return inside repeat leaves retry itself. That only works because repeat is inline, which the last section explains.) The demo's fake website times out twice, then answers. It also wraps the call in timed, a second higher-order function that runs any block and reports how long it took: attempt 1 failed: site timeout on call 1 attempt 2 failed: site timeout on call 2 fetch with retry took 41.14 ms result: page:pancakes after 3 calls Three calls, one page, and neither function knows what a recipe is. (The 41 ms is from a busy machine, and most of it is the JVM running brand-new code for the first time.) Kotlin makes the call site read like a language feature. When the last parameter is a function, you can write the lambda after the parentheses. That's a trailing lambda, and if it's the only argument, you drop the parentheses too: retry(3) { ... }, timed("fetch") { ... }. That's why repeat, synchronized, use and buildList look built in. They're ordinary library functions. Java needs an interface for the parameter, and checked exceptions get in the way. Those are exceptions the compiler makes you catch or declare, like IOException. Supplier.get() can't throw one, so retrying file or network code needs a Callable<T> and a throws Exception on retry. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so () -> T fits every call. When code differs by one call, pass the call in. Write the loop once. That's functions in. The friend can also hand back a new card. One retry loop for every flaky call Run Retry (or RetryJava). Predict first: how many calls reach the website in each half? Wrap the second retry in timed("gave up") { ... } as well. Predict whether its timing line prints, even though the block throws. Change the first retry(3) to retry(1) and run again. Retry.kt package workbench.functional.l03.demo // A fake recipe website that times out a few times, then answers. class FlakySite(private var failuresLeft: Int) { var calls = 0 fun fetch(recipe: String): String { calls++ if (failuresLeft-- > 0) throw IllegalStateException("site timeout on call $calls") return "page:$recipe" } } // A higher-order function: the loop is written once, and the work comes in as a function. fun <T> retry(times: Int, block: () -> T): T { var last: Exception? = null repeat(times) { attempt -> try { return block() // returns from retry: repeat is inline } catch (e: Exception) { last = e println(" attempt ${attempt + 1} failed: ${e.message}") } } throw IllegalStateException("gave up after $times attempts", last) } // Another one: run any block, report how long it took, hand back its result unchanged. fun <T> timed(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println(" $label took %.2f ms".format((System.nanoTime() - start) / 1e6)) } } fun main() { val site = FlakySite(failuresLeft = 2) val page = timed("fetch with retry") { retry(3) { site.fetch("pancakes") } } println("result: $page after ${site.calls} calls") val down = FlakySite(failuresLeft = 5) try { retry(3) { down.fetch("waffles") } } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("result: ${e.message} (last cause: ${e.cause?.message})") } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l03.demo.RetryKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l03/demo/Retry.kt RetryJava.java package workbench.functional.l03.demo; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** * Java twin of Retry.kt. The work comes in as a Supplier<T>. Supplier.get() can't throw checked * exceptions, so code that throws IOException needs Callable<T> and a `throws Exception` on retry. */ public class RetryJava { // A fake recipe website that times out a few times, then answers. static final class FlakySite { private int failuresLeft; int calls = 0; FlakySite(int failuresLeft) { this.failuresLeft = failuresLeft; } String fetch(String recipe) { calls++; if (failuresLeft-- > 0) throw new IllegalStateException("site timeout on call " + calls); return "page:" + recipe; } } // A higher-order method: the loop is written once, and the work comes in as a function. static <T> T retry(int times, Supplier<T> block) { RuntimeException last = null; for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= times; attempt++) { try { return block.get(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; System.out.println(" attempt " + attempt + " failed: " + e.getMessage()); } } throw new IllegalStateException("gave up after " + times + " attempts", last); } // Another one: run any block, report how long it took, hand back its result unchanged. static <T> T timed(String label, Supplier<T> block) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return block.get(); } finally { System.out.printf(" %s took %.2f ms%n", label, (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1e6); } } public static void main(String[] args) { FlakySite site = new FlakySite(2); String page = timed("fetch with retry", () -> retry(3, () -> site.fetch("pancakes"))); System.out.println("result: " + page + " after " + site.calls + " calls"); FlakySite down = new FlakySite(5); try { retry(3, () -> down.fetch("waffles")); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("result: " + e.getMessage() + " (last cause: " + e.getCause().getMessage() + ")"); } } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l03.demo.RetryJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l03/demo/RetryJava.java The first half takes three calls: two timeouts, then page:pancakes. The second gives up after three: gave up after 3 attempts (last cause: site timeout on call 3). timed prints its line even when the block throws, because the print is in a finally. With retry(1), the program stops with IllegalStateException: gave up after 1 attempts, a message that never expected to be used with one attempt. retry never changed in any of these runs; only the function you handed it did.

h: Higher-order functions: functions in, functions out · Handing back a function: set up the converter once
x: Higher-order works in the other direction too. A function can build another function and hand it back. Here's a kitchen problem that needs it. Some recipes measure in millilitres, with a jug, but your scale wants grams. A litre of honey weighs roughly 1,420 g, and a litre of loosely spooned flour roughly 530 g. So the grams depend on two things: which ingredient, and how many millilitres. A plain function grams(ingredient, ml) takes both at once. This one takes the ingredient and returns a function that waits for the millilitres: Java static Function<Integer, Integer> gramsFor(String ingredient) { int perLitre = WEIGHT_PER_LITRE.get(ingredient); // looked up once return ml -> ml * perLitre / 1_000; } Function<Integer, Integer> honey = gramsFor("honey"); honey.apply(250); // 355 Kotlin fun gramsFor(ingredient: String): (Int) -> Int { val perLitre = WEIGHT_PER_LITRE.getValue(ingredient) // looked up once return { ml -> ml * perLitre / 1_000 } } val honey = gramsFor("honey") honey(250) // 355 Fixing some of a function's arguments and getting back a function of the rest is called partial application. In the kitchen, it's a card with one blank already filled in: "honey", so only the amount is left to write. It pays off when the first argument is known early and the second arrives many times. Baking a honey cake, you know the ingredient once and measure many times. gramsFor looks the weight up once, and the closure it returns (lesson 2 of this track) keeps only the number it needs. It also moves failure to the right moment. An unknown ingredient fails when you build the function, not halfway through the cake. Ask for gramsFor("sand") and you hear about it at once, before a single gram is weighed. Currying takes the same idea all the way: every function takes exactly one argument and returns a function for the next. A curried converter has the type (String) -> (Int) -> Int. The arrows group to the right, so read it as (String) -> ((Int) -> Int). Java Function<String, Function<Integer, Integer>> curriedGrams = ingredient -> ml -> grams(ingredient, ml); curriedGrams.apply("flour").apply(500); // 265 Kotlin val curriedGrams: (String) -> (Int) -> Int = { ingredient -> { ml -> grams(ingredient, ml) } } curriedGrams("flour")(500) // 265 Some languages, Haskell for one, curry every function. In Kotlin, don't. The signatures get hard to read and the IDE hints get noisy. And Kotlin already covers what currying is for: a lambda that fixes one argument ({ ml: Int -> grams("milk", ml) }), default and named arguments, and bound references like oven::adjust from the last lesson. Return a function when you mean "set up now, run many times". That's the case that earns its keep. One card at a time is useful. Clipping several cards together is where real recipes come from. When does a bad ingredient fail? Run GramsFor (or GramsForJava) and check one number: 250 ml of honey at 1,420 g a litre is 355 g. Add val broken = gramsFor("sand") as the first line of main, without calling broken. Predict whether the program fails, and where. Move the lookup into the returned lambda: return { ml -> ml * WEIGHT_PER_LITRE.getValue(ingredient) / 1_000 } (Java: WEIGHT_PER_LITRE.get(ingredient) inside the lambda). Run again. Now when does it fail? GramsFor.kt package workbench.functional.l03.demo // Roughly what one litre weighs, in grams. The jug measures millilitres; the scale wants grams. val WEIGHT_PER_LITRE = mapOf("flour" to 530, "milk" to 1_030, "honey" to 1_420) // Both arguments at once. fun grams(ingredient: String, ml: Int): Int = ml * WEIGHT_PER_LITRE.getValue(ingredient) / 1_000 // Partial application: fix the ingredient now, get back a function of the volume. fun gramsFor(ingredient: String): (Int) -> Int { val perLitre = WEIGHT_PER_LITRE.getValue(ingredient) // looked up once, right here return { ml -> ml * perLitre / 1_000 } } // Currying by hand: take one argument, return a function that takes the next one. val curriedGrams: (String) -> (Int) -> Int = { ingredient -> { ml -> grams(ingredient, ml) } } fun main() { val honey = gramsFor("honey") println("gramsFor(\"honey\")(250) = ${honey(250)}") println("curriedGrams(\"flour\")(500) = ${curriedGrams("flour")(500)}") // Kotlin idioms that usually read better than a curried signature: val milkGrams = { ml: Int -> grams("milk", ml) } // a lambda that fixes one argument println("lambda that fixes milk = ${milkGrams(250)}") println("named arguments = ${grams(ml = 250, ingredient = "honey")}") val jugs = listOf(100, 250, 1_000) println("jugs.map(honey) = ${jugs.map(honey)}") } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l03.demo.GramsForKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l03/demo/GramsFor.kt GramsForJava.java package workbench.functional.l03.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.function.Function; /** Java twin of GramsFor.kt. Partial application and currying with java.util.function.Function. */ public class GramsForJava { // Roughly what one litre weighs, in grams. The jug measures millilitres; the scale wants grams. static final Map<String, Integer> WEIGHT_PER_LITRE = Map.of("flour", 530, "milk", 1_030, "honey", 1_420); // Both arguments at once. static int grams(String ingredient, int ml) { return ml * WEIGHT_PER_LITRE.get(ingredient) / 1_000; } // Partial application: fix the ingredient now, get back a function of the volume. static Function<Integer, Integer> gramsFor(String ingredient) { int perLitre = WEIGHT_PER_LITRE.get(ingredient); // looked up once, right here return ml -> ml * perLitre / 1_000; } // Currying by hand: the type says it all. static final Function<String, Function<Integer, Integer>> CURRIED_GRAMS = ingredient -> ml -> grams(ingredient, ml); public static void main(String[] args) { Function<Integer, Integer> honey = gramsFor("honey"); System.out.println("gramsFor(\"honey\").apply(250) = " + honey.apply(250)); System.out.println("CURRIED_GRAMS.apply(\"flour\").apply(500) = " + CURRIED_GRAMS.apply("flour").apply(500)); // A lambda that fixes one argument. (Java has no named arguments.) Function<Integer, Integer> milkGrams = ml -> grams("milk", ml); System.out.println("lambda that fixes milk = " + milkGrams.apply(250)); List<Integer> jugs = List.of(100, 250, 1_000); System.out.println("jugs.stream().map(honey) = " + jugs.stream().map(honey).toList()); } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l03.demo.GramsForJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l03/demo/GramsForJava.java With the lookup outside the lambda, gramsFor("sand") fails right away: Kotlin throws NoSuchElementException: Key sand is missing in the map., and Java throws a NullPointerException when it unboxes the missing weight. With the lookup inside the lambda, gramsFor("sand") succeeds and returns a function that fails on its first call, which could be much later. Same code, different moment of failure. You want the first one.

h: Higher-order functions: functions in, functions out · Clipping small functions together: composition, where order matters
x: Adjustments to a recipe come in small pieces. Scale it from four people to six. Use 10 % less sugar, as plenty of cooks do. Never use more than the 250 g left in the bag. Each piece is an (Int) -> Int on grams. The amount you actually weigh out is some of those pieces run one after another, and every cook has a different set. Running one function on the result of another is called composition. Java's Function interface has it built in, as two default methods, andThen and compose: Java Function<Integer, Integer> sugar = FOR_SIX_GUESTS.andThen(TEN_PERCENT_LESS).andThen(AT_MOST_THE_BAG); sugar.apply(200); // 250 Kotlin infix fun <A, B, C> ((A) -> B).andThen(next: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> next(this(a)) } val sugar = forSixGuests andThen tenPercentLess andThen atMostTheBag sugar(200) // 250 Kotlin's standard library has no andThen or compose for function types. Without the one-line extension above, forSixGuests andThen tenPercentLess fails with unresolved reference 'andThen' on receiver of type '(Int) -> Int'. Arrow, the best-known functional library for Kotlin, ships andThen, compose and curried in a separate arrow-functions module. This track's lab doesn't depend on it. One line is all you need, and writing it shows there's no magic: this is the first function, this(a) calls it, and next gets the result. infix lets you write it without dots and parentheses, so the steps read left to right in the order they run. compose is the same with the arguments swapped, (g compose f)(x) == g(f(x)), as mathematicians write it. Pick one and stay with it. andThen matches the way people read. Two things about composition matter in practice. The first is that the order is part of the result. The demo runs the same three steps both ways: recipe says 100 g -> 135 g (cap first: 135 g) recipe says 200 g -> 250 g (cap first: 270 g) For 100 g the cap never bites, so the order doesn't show. For 200 g, scaling gives 300 g, 10 % less gives 270 g, and the cap brings it down to the 250 g you have. Cap first, and you check the bag before you've scaled: the recipe then asks for 270 g of sugar you don't own. It's the same with mixing, baking and icing. Ice before you bake and you still get something, just not a cake. The second is that a list of steps folds into one function, starting from the function that returns its input unchanged: Java Function<Integer, Integer> fromList = steps.stream() .reduce(Function.identity(), (acc, step) -> acc.andThen(step)); Kotlin val fromList = steps.fold({ x: Int -> x }) { acc, step -> acc andThen step } That's how saved settings become code. Read a cook's adjustments when the app starts, turn each one into a function, fold them into one (Int) -> Int, and call it for every ingredient. Every piece stays small, pure and testable on its own. (Lesson 4 of this track covers fold properly.) The order of the steps is part of the function. Test them in the order you'll run them. Composition builds new functions out of old ones. The next higher-order function improves a function without changing a single one of its answers. Compose, reorder, extend Run Compose (or ComposeJava). Predict both amounts for 100 g and for 200 g before you look. Delete the andThen extension at the top of Compose.kt and run again. Read the error, then put the line back. Add a fourth step, val roundToTen: (Int) -> Int = { it / 10 * 10 }, at the end of steps, and print fromList(130). Predict it first. Compose.kt package workbench.functional.l03.demo // The stdlib has no andThen for function types, so here it is. Remove it and the file stops compiling. infix fun <A, B, C> ((A) -> B).andThen(next: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> next(this(a)) } val forSixGuests: (Int) -> Int = { it * 6 / 4 } // the recipe serves four val tenPercentLess: (Int) -> Int = { it * 90 / 100 } // less sugar, rounded down val atMostTheBag: (Int) -> Int = { minOf(it, 250) } // only 250 g left in the bag fun main() { val sugar = forSixGuests andThen tenPercentLess andThen atMostTheBag val capFirst = atMostTheBag andThen forSixGuests andThen tenPercentLess for (grams in listOf(100, 200)) { println("recipe says $grams g -> ${sugar(grams)} g (cap first: ${capFirst(grams)} g)") } // Built from a list, the way a saved set of adjustments would build it. val steps = listOf(forSixGuests, tenPercentLess, atMostTheBag) val fromList = steps.fold({ x: Int -> x }) { acc, step -> acc andThen step } println("fromList(200) = ${fromList(200)}") } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l03.demo.ComposeKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l03/demo/Compose.kt ComposeJava.java package workbench.functional.l03.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Function; /** Java twin of Compose.kt. java.util.function.Function has andThen and compose built in, as default methods. */ public class ComposeJava { static final Function<Integer, Integer> FOR_SIX_GUESTS = g -> g * 6 / 4; // the recipe serves four static final Function<Integer, Integer> TEN_PERCENT_LESS = g -> g * 90 / 100; // less sugar, rounded down static final Function<Integer, Integer> AT_MOST_THE_BAG = g -> Math.min(g, 250); // only 250 g left in the bag public static void main(String[] args) { Function<Integer, Integer> sugar = FOR_SIX_GUESTS.andThen(TEN_PERCENT_LESS).andThen(AT_MOST_THE_BAG); Function<Integer, Integer> capFirst = AT_MOST_THE_BAG.andThen(FOR_SIX_GUESTS).andThen(TEN_PERCENT_LESS); for (int grams : new int[] {100, 200}) { System.out.println("recipe says " + grams + " g -> " + sugar.apply(grams) + " g (cap first: " + capFirst.apply(grams) + " g)"); } // Built from a list, the way a saved set of adjustments would build it. List<Function<Integer, Integer>> steps = List.of(FOR_SIX_GUESTS, TEN_PERCENT_LESS, AT_MOST_THE_BAG); Function<Integer, Integer> fromList = steps.stream() .reduce(Function.identity(), (acc, step) -> acc.andThen(step)); System.out.println("fromList(200) = " + fromList.apply(200)); } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l03.demo.ComposeJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l03/demo/ComposeJava.java 100 g gives 135 g both ways, because the cap never bites. 200 g gives 250 g with the cap last and 270 g with the cap first. Without the extension, Kotlin reports unresolved reference 'andThen' on receiver of type '(Int) -> Int'. The Java version has nothing to delete: andThen is a default method on Function. With roundToTen, fromList(130) goes 195, then 175, then 175 again (under the cap), then 170. Composition turns three small steps into one. The order is part of the function: capping last gives the 250 g in the bag, capping first asks for 270 g. Function: andThen, compose, identity (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Higher-order functions: functions in, functions out · memoize: a function that remembers its answers, and when that lies
x: A higher-order function can also take a function and return an improved version of it. memoize returns a function that gives the same answers as the original but works each one out only once. Picture the friend writing the answer on the back of the card the first time, and reading it off after that. Java static <A, R> Function<A, R> memoize(Function<A, R> f) { Map<A, R> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); return a -> cache.computeIfAbsent(a, f); } Function<String, Integer> kcal = memoize(Foods::kcalPer100g); Kotlin fun <A : Any, R : Any> memoize(f: (A) -> R): (A) -> R { val cache = ConcurrentHashMap<A, R>() return { a -> cache.computeIfAbsent(a) { f(it) } } } val kcal = memoize(::kcalPer100g) Everything from the last lesson is in those few lines. memoize takes a function and returns one. The returned lambda is a closure over cache, so each memoized function gets its own map that nobody else can reach. It's safe on many threads because the captured state is a ConcurrentHashMap, a map built to be shared by threads, held in a val rather than a var. computeIfAbsent runs f at most once per key, even when two threads ask for the same key at the same moment, as the concurrent collections lesson showed. The A : Any, R : Any bounds are there because ConcurrentHashMap can't store null. The demo's food table is slow on purpose, 50 ms a lookup, like a long table searched from the top every time. Five calls for oats and honey: [389, 304, 389, 389, 304] lookups: 2 for 5 calls, 129 ms Two lookups instead of five, and the same answers. Memoizing is only correct for pure functions. Referential transparency, from lesson 1, says a pure call can be replaced by its value, and a cache does exactly that replacement for you. Memoize something impure and you get stale answers. The demo also memoizes eggsIn("fridge"), which reads how many eggs are left: eggs in the fridge now: 6 eggs after someone's omelette: 6 (really: 2) The memo says six. The fridge holds two, and the memo will keep saying six until the program restarts. Here the friend picture breaks: a real cook can open the fridge and look, but a memo has no way to tell that its answer went stale. Calories per 100 g of oats from a fixed table is a good fit. How many eggs are left, today's price of butter, or anything you read from a file or a database is not. Memoize only pure functions. A saved answer is right only if the function would have given it again. Two practical limits. The cache never forgets, so only memoize over a small, known set of keys (ingredients, units, recipe names), never over something that keeps growing, like timestamps. When you need expiry or a size limit, use a real cache library such as Caffeine, which is the same idea plus eviction, throwing old entries out. And the function you pass to computeIfAbsent must not change the same map, so this memoize can't wrap a recursive function that calls its own memoized version. Each of these higher-order functions takes a lambda, and a lambda is an object. So what do all those objects cost? A memo that helps, and one that lies Run Memoize (or MemoizeJava). Predict the number of lookups for the five foods, and roughly how long they take (each real lookup sleeps 50 ms). Replace memoize(::kcalPer100g) with plain ::kcalPer100g and run again. Explain the last line of the output to yourself before you read the expected result. Why is the memoized egg count wrong? Memoize.kt package workbench.functional.l03.demo import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap // A higher-order function that returns a function: same answers as f, but each one computed once. fun <A : Any, R : Any> memoize(f: (A) -> R): (A) -> R { val cache = ConcurrentHashMap<A, R>() // captured: one cache per memoized function return { a -> cache.computeIfAbsent(a) { f(it) } } } // Pure but slow: imagine it searches a long food table on every call. var tableLookups = 0 fun kcalPer100g(food: String): Int { tableLookups++ Thread.sleep(50) return if (food == "oats") 389 else 304 } // Impure: the number of eggs changes whenever someone cooks. var fridgeEggs = 6 fun eggsIn(place: String): Int = if (place == "fridge") fridgeEggs else 0 fun main() { val kcal = memoize(::kcalPer100g) val foods = listOf("oats", "honey", "oats", "oats", "honey") val start = System.nanoTime() println(foods.map(kcal)) println("lookups: $tableLookups for ${foods.size} calls, %d ms".format((System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000)) val eggs = memoize(::eggsIn) println("eggs in the fridge now: ${eggs("fridge")}") fridgeEggs = 2 // someone makes an omelette println("eggs after someone's omelette: ${eggs("fridge")} (really: ${eggsIn("fridge")})") } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l03.demo.MemoizeKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l03/demo/Memoize.kt MemoizeJava.java package workbench.functional.l03.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.function.Function; /** Java twin of Memoize.kt. */ public class MemoizeJava { // A higher-order method that returns a function: same answers as f, but each one computed once. static <A, R> Function<A, R> memoize(Function<A, R> f) { Map<A, R> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // captured: one cache per memoized function return a -> cache.computeIfAbsent(a, f); } // Pure but slow: imagine it searches a long food table on every call. static int tableLookups = 0; static int kcalPer100g(String food) { tableLookups++; try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return food.equals("oats") ? 389 : 304; } // Impure: the number of eggs changes whenever someone cooks. static int fridgeEggs = 6; static int eggsIn(String place) { return place.equals("fridge") ? fridgeEggs : 0; } public static void main(String[] args) { Function<String, Integer> kcal = memoize(MemoizeJava::kcalPer100g); List<String> foods = List.of("oats", "honey", "oats", "oats", "honey"); long start = System.nanoTime(); System.out.println(foods.stream().map(kcal).toList()); System.out.printf("lookups: %d for %d calls, %d ms%n", tableLookups, foods.size(), (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000); Function<String, Integer> eggs = memoize(MemoizeJava::eggsIn); System.out.println("eggs in the fridge now: " + eggs.apply("fridge")); fridgeEggs = 2; // someone makes an omelette System.out.println("eggs after someone's omelette: " + eggs.apply("fridge") + " (really: " + eggsIn("fridge") + ")"); } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l03.demo.MemoizeJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l03/demo/MemoizeJava.java Memoized: 2 lookups for 5 calls, a little over 100 ms. Without memoize: 5 lookups, about 250 ms, and the same answers. The egg line prints 6 after the fridge dropped to 2. eggsIn reads a mutable global, so it is impure, and the memo froze its first answer. A cache is only invisible when the function it wraps is pure. h: Higher-order functions: functions in, functions out · inline: why map and filter create no lambdas
x: Every lambda you pass to retry or memoize is an object (lesson 2), and a var it changes becomes a Ref box. So you might expect recipes.filter { ... }.map { ... } to create two lambda objects on every call. It creates none, because filter, map, forEach, fold, sumOf and almost every other collection function on Iterable are declared inline. When you call an inline function, the compiler doesn't emit a call. It copies the function's body into the call site, and the lambda's body with it. The lambda never exists as an object. Java // Java has no inline functions. The method reference is a lambda object // (shared, since it captures nothing), and only the JIT may inline it at runtime. long total = grams.stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum(); Kotlin inline fun <T> measuredInline(block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() val result = block() lastNanos = System.nanoTime() - start return result } var total = 0L measuredInline { grams.forEach { total += it } } // becomes a plain loop; total stays a local The InlineCost demo compiles two versions of the same code and adds up 500 g, 250 g and 1,000 g, the flour, sugar and milk for one cake. With a non-inline measured, the bytecode (the instructions the JVM actually runs) has new Ref$LongRef, a box for total. It also has an invokedynamic, the instruction that creates the lambda object, and a call through Function0.invoke. With measuredInline it has none of them: the System.nanoTime() calls, the iterator loop and an ladd on a local variable are pasted straight into totalInlined. (ladd is the bytecode instruction that adds two long values.) The JIT compiler, the part of the JVM that turns busy code into machine code while the program runs, may inline Java's lambda later. Kotlin's inline does it before the program ever starts. That's also why return inside repeat worked in retry. After inlining, the lambda body is part of retry, so return leaves retry. This is called a non-local return, and it's only allowed when the lambda is inlined. Inline a small higher-order function that calls its lambda right away. Leave the rest alone. So mark your own small higher-order functions inline when they take a lambda and call it straight away, as measuredInline and retry do. Don't mark everything inline. The body is copied into every call site, so a big inline function bloats the code. And a lambda you keep for later, like the f that memoize stores in its closure, can't be inlined: the compiler needs a real object to keep. The Advanced Kotlin track, later in this part of the course, has a whole lesson on inline, noinline, crossinline and non-local returns. inline removes the lambda objects, not the work. Each filter or map on a list still builds a whole new list, and that's the cost the next lesson puts on the table. Find the missing lambda in the bytecode Run InlineCost. Both totals print 1750. (Java has no inline functions, so this demo has no Java twin.) From labs/, run javap -c -p functional/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/functional/l03/demo/InlineCostKt.class. Compare totalWithLambda with totalInlined: look for Ref$LongRef, invokedynamic and System.nanoTime. Predict what changes in totalInlined if you delete the word inline from measuredInline. Then try it. InlineCost.kt package workbench.functional.l03.demo var lastNanos = 0L // Not inline: the lambda becomes an object, and a var it changes becomes a Ref box. fun <T> measured(block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() val result = block() lastNanos = System.nanoTime() - start return result } // Inline: the compiler pastes this body, and the lambda's body, into every caller. inline fun <T> measuredInline(block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() val result = block() lastNanos = System.nanoTime() - start return result } fun totalWithLambda(grams: List<Long>): Long { var total = 0L measured { for (g in grams) total += g } return total } fun totalInlined(grams: List<Long>): Long { var total = 0L measuredInline { grams.forEach { total += it } } return total } fun main() { val grams = listOf(500L, 250L, 1_000L) // flour, sugar and milk for one cake println("with a lambda object: ${totalWithLambda(grams)}") println("inlined: ${totalInlined(grams)}") } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l03.demo.InlineCostKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l03/demo/InlineCost.kt totalWithLambda has new kotlin/jvm/internal/Ref$LongRef, an invokedynamic that makes a Function0, and a call to measured. totalInlined has none of them: it calls System.nanoTime itself and adds into a local with ladd. Without inline, totalInlined looks like totalWithLambda: a Ref$LongRef, an invokedynamic and a call to measuredInline. measuredInline also exists as an ordinary method in the class, for callers such as Java code that can't inline it. Inline functions (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Higher-order functions: functions in, functions out · Java and Kotlin
x: Functions in, functions out, functions combined Kitchen.java import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.function.Function; import java.util.function.Supplier; final class Kitchen { // functions in static <T> T retry(int times, Supplier<T> block) { RuntimeException last = null; for (int i = 0; i < times; i++) { try { return block.get(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; } } throw new IllegalStateException("gave up after " + times + " attempts", last); } // functions out: partial application static Function<Integer, Integer> gramsFor(int perLitre) { return ml -> ml * perLitre / 1_000; } // composition is built into Function static Function<Integer, Integer> sugarToWeigh(int perLitre) { return gramsFor(perLitre).andThen(g -> g * 90 / 100).andThen(g -> Math.min(g, 250)); } static <A, R> Function<A, R> memoize(Function<A, R> f) { Map<A, R> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); return a -> cache.computeIfAbsent(a, f); } } Kitchen.kt import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap // functions in; inline, so the lambda is pasted into the caller inline fun <T> retry(times: Int, block: () -> T): T { var last: Exception? = null repeat(times) { try { return block() } catch (e: Exception) { last = e } } throw IllegalStateException("gave up after $times attempts", last) } // functions out: partial application fun gramsFor(perLitre: Int): (Int) -> Int = { ml -> ml * perLitre / 1_000 } // composition is not in the stdlib: one line of your own infix fun <A, B, C> ((A) -> B).andThen(next: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> next(this(a)) } fun sugarToWeigh(perLitre: Int): (Int) -> Int = gramsFor(perLitre) andThen { g -> g * 90 / 100 } andThen { g -> minOf(g, 250) } fun <A : Any, R : Any> memoize(f: (A) -> R): (A) -> R { val cache = ConcurrentHashMap<A, R>() return { a -> cache.computeIfAbsent(a) { f(it) } } } Both languages make the same three moves: functions in, functions out, functions combined. The differences are in the plumbing. Java's Function comes with andThen and compose, and Kotlin's function types don't, so you write the extension yourself or use Arrow's arrow-functions module. Java needs a different interface per shape (Supplier, Function, Callable once checked exceptions appear), while Kotlin uses () -> T and (A) -> R everywhere. And Kotlin can declare a higher-order function inline, so the lambda passed to retry is pasted into the caller and never allocated. Java leaves that to the JIT, which may or may not inline at runtime.

h: Higher-order functions: functions in, functions out · Worked example
x: Turn a cook's saved adjustments into one function A cook's adjustments are saved as rows: a kind of adjustment and a number. We want one (Int) -> Int per ingredient, built once when the app starts and called for every measurement. The base step is the jug-to-scale converter, gramsFor(ingredient), from the second section. data class AdjustmentRow(val kind: String, val value: Int) val myRows = listOf( AdjustmentRow("less", 10), // 10 % less AdjustmentRow("atLeast", 50), // at least 50 g AdjustmentRow("atMost", 300), // at most 300 g ) record AdjustmentRow(String kind, int value) {} List<AdjustmentRow> myRows = List.of( new AdjustmentRow("less", 10), // 10 % less new AdjustmentRow("atLeast", 50), // at least 50 g new AdjustmentRow("atMost", 300)); // at most 300 g Turn each row into a function with a when expression. Each branch returns a function, and nothing is computed yet. An unknown kind is a bug in the saved settings, so it throws here. fun toAdjust(row: AdjustmentRow): (Int) -> Int = when (row.kind) { "add" -> { g -> g + row.value } "less" -> { g -> g * (100 - row.value) / 100 } "atLeast" -> { g -> maxOf(g, row.value) } "atMost" -> { g -> minOf(g, row.value) } else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown adjustment ${row.kind}") } static Function<Integer, Integer> toAdjust(AdjustmentRow row) { return switch (row.kind()) { case "add" -> g -> g + row.value(); case "less" -> g -> g * (100 - row.value()) / 100; case "atLeast" -> g -> Math.max(g, row.value()); case "atMost" -> g -> Math.min(g, row.value()); default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown adjustment " + row.kind()); }; } Fold the adjustments onto the ingredient's converter. Self-check: when does a row with an unknown kind fail, at startup or at the first measurement? (At startup: toAdjust runs inside map, while the function is being built.) fun measure(ingredient: String, rows: List<AdjustmentRow>): (Int) -> Int = rows.map(::toAdjust) // 1. rows to functions .fold(gramsFor(ingredient)) { acc, f -> acc andThen f } // 2. one function, converter first static Function<Integer, Integer> measure(String ingredient, List<AdjustmentRow> rows) { return rows.stream() .map(Kitchen::toAdjust) // 1. rows to functions .reduce(gramsFor(ingredient), Function::andThen); // 2. one function, converter first } Build once per ingredient, call per measurement. Each measurement now costs four small calls and no lookups, and every adjustment can be tested on its own with plain numbers. val sugar = measure("sugar", myRows) sugar(500) // 425 -> 382 -> 382 -> 300 sugar(50) // 42 -> 37 -> 50 -> 50 Function<Integer, Integer> sugar = measure("sugar", myRows); sugar.apply(500); // 425 -> 382 -> 382 -> 300 sugar.apply(50); // 42 -> 37 -> 50 -> 50

h: Higher-order functions: functions in, functions out · Quiz
x: val a = atMost(250) andThen add(25) and val b = add(25) andThen atMost(250). What are a(240) and b(240)? 265 and 250 250 and 265 265 and 265 250 and 250 andThen runs the left function first. a caps 240 (no change) and then adds 25, giving 265. b adds 25 (265) and then caps at 250. Composition is not commutative: the order of the steps is part of the function. fun gramsFor(ingredient: String): (Int) -> Int { val perLitre = weights.getValue(ingredient); return { it * perLitre / 1000 } }. A recipe typo passes "hony". When does it fail? At the first measurement that uses the function When gramsFor("hony") is called, before anything is weighed Never: the weight comes out as 0 At compile time The lookup sits outside the returned lambda, so it runs when the function is built, and getValue throws NoSuchElementException: Key hony is missing in the map. Building converters when the app starts turns typos into startup failures. If the lookup were inside the lambda, the first measurement would fail instead. Which of these functions is safe to memoize? fun eggsLeft(fridge: String): Int, which counts what's in the fridge now fun butterPrice(shop: String): Int, which asks the shop's website fun gramsPerCup(ingredient: String): Int, which reads a fixed table printed in the recipe book fun nextJarNumber(shelf: String): Int Only gramsPerCup is pure: the same ingredient always gives the same weight, so a saved answer is always right. The eggs and the price change over time, so a memoized version would freeze them. nextJarNumber is supposed to return a new value on every call, so memoizing it would hand out the same number forever. fun <T> timed(block: () -> T): T is not inline. You call it as var n = 0; timed { n++ }. What does the compiler create at that call site? Nothing extra: Kotlin inlines small lambdas on its own A new .class file for the lambda A compile error: a lambda can't change a captured var A lambda object through invokedynamic, and a Ref$IntRef box for n Without inline, the lambda is a real object, created with invokedynamic (no class file in Kotlin 2.x), and the captured var n moves into a Ref$IntRef. Kotlin never inlines a function you didn't mark inline. Mark timed inline and both disappear: the body and the lambda are pasted into the caller, and n stays a local. From Concurrent collections: two threads call a memoized function with the same new key at the same moment. The cache is a ConcurrentHashMap and uses computeIfAbsent(key) { f(it) }. How many times does f run for that key? Exactly once: the second thread waits and gets the first one's result Twice, once per thread Once or twice, depending on timing Zero: the second thread throws ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent is atomic per key: it runs the mapping function at most once, and a second caller for the same key waits for that result. A HashMap with getOrPut, or get followed by put, is check-then-act and can run f twice.

h: Higher-order functions: functions in, functions out · Key terms
x: Higher-order function A function that takes a function as a parameter, returns one, or both. Trailing lambda A lambda written after the parentheses when it is the last argument: retry(3) { ... }. Partial application Fixing some arguments now and getting back a function of the rest. Currying Turning (A, B) -> C into (A) -> (B) -> C: one argument at a time. Composition Running one function on another's result: f andThen g is { x -> g(f(x)) }. Memoization Remembering a pure function's results so each one is worked out only once. Inline function A function whose body, and the bodies of the lambdas passed to it, the compiler copies into each call site. What makes a function higher-order? It takes a function as a parameter, returns a function, or both. What is partial application? Fixing some of a function's arguments now and getting back a function of the rest. gramsFor("honey") returns an (Int) -> Int. Does Kotlin's stdlib have andThen for function types? No: f andThen g gives unresolved reference 'andThen'. Write infix fun <A, B, C> ((A) -> B).andThen(next: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> next(this(a)) }. What do you start a fold from to compose a list of (T) -> T steps? The identity function, { x: T -> x }. An empty pipeline is exactly that function. When is it safe to memoize a function? When it's pure: the same argument always gives the same answer. Otherwise the cache keeps a stale answer. What does inline do to measuredInline { total += x }? The compiler copies the function's body and the lambda's body into the caller. No lambda object is created, and total stays a local instead of a Ref box. Why can return inside repeat { } leave the enclosing function? repeat is inline, so the lambda's body becomes part of the enclosing function. That non-local return is only allowed for inlined lambdas.

h: Higher-order functions: functions in, functions out · Go deeper
x: Kotlin gives you partial application in a few forms besides returning a lambda. A bound reference fixes the receiver, which is often all you need: Java final class Oven { private final int extraMinutes; Oven(int extraMinutes) { this.extraMinutes = extraMinutes; } int adjust(int minutes) { return minutes + extraMinutes; } } Oven myOven = new Oven(5); Function<Integer, Integer> bake = myOven::adjust; // a bound method reference List.of(20, 35).stream().map(bake).toList(); // [25, 40] Kotlin class Oven(private val extraMinutes: Int) { fun adjust(minutes: Int): Int = minutes + extraMinutes } val myOven = Oven(extraMinutes = 5) // this oven runs a little cold val bake: (Int) -> Int = myOven::adjust // a bound reference: the receiver is fixed listOf(20, 35).map(bake) // [25, 40] This is the strategy pattern with the ceremony removed: an object with one behaviour, passed around as a function. Remember lesson 2's detail, though: in Kotlin 2.4.21 a bound reference compiles to a small class and allocates one object each time the expression runs. Arrow 2.3.0 puts its function utilities in the io.arrow-kt:arrow-functions artifact, separate from arrow-core. Its jar contains andThen and compose, curried and uncurried with overloads up to 22 parameters, partially1 and its siblings, and memoize. If your codebase already uses Arrow, use those rather than your own. If it doesn't, the one-line versions in this lesson are not a reason to add a dependency. One more look at inline and return. Inside an inline higher-order function's lambda, a bare return leaves the enclosing function, and return@forEach (or any label) leaves only the lambda, acting like continue. Java developers moving to Kotlin trip on this in forEach, because a return in a Java Stream.forEach lambda only ends that one call. The Advanced Kotlin track's inline lesson goes through noinline and crossinline, the two modifiers that control which lambdas get pasted and where return may go.

h: Collections without loops: map, filter, fold and friends · A baking-day report written as one loop, and the two bugs it hides
x: Here is the end-of-day report the way most of us first write it. A Cookie has an id, a flavor, its weight in grams from the kitchen scale, a status (GOLDEN, RAW or BURNT) and nibbledGrams, which is null unless someone took a bite. One pass over the cookies builds four results: Java int golden = 0; Map<String, Integer> net = new LinkedHashMap<>(); List<String> burnt = new ArrayList<>(); Cookie largest = cookies.get(0); for (Cookie c : cookies) { switch (c.status()) { case GOLDEN -> { golden += c.grams(); net.merge(c.flavor(), c.grams() - biteOf(c), Integer::sum); if (c.grams() > largest.grams()) largest = c; } case BURNT -> burnt.add(c.id()); case RAW -> { } } } Kotlin var golden = 0 val net = LinkedHashMap<String, Int>() val burnt = ArrayList<String>() var largest = cookies.first() for (c in cookies) { when (c.status) { Status.GOLDEN -> { golden += c.grams net[c.flavor] = (net[c.flavor] ?: 0) + c.grams - (c.nibbledGrams ?: 0) if (c.grams > largest.grams) largest = c } Status.BURNT -> burnt.add(c.id) Status.RAW -> {} } } It works on a normal day. It's also hard to read, for a reason you can name: four results are being built at the same time, interleaved, and every line changes one of them. To check how largest is worked out, you have to read the whole loop, because any line might touch it. And it has two bugs that a normal day never shows. On a day with no cookies, cookies.first() throws NoSuchElementException: List is empty. (Java's get(0) throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException). And say the first cookie of the day is a raw one of 99 g. largest starts there, no golden cookie beats it, and the report proudly names a cookie that is still dough. Here is the same report written with collection operations. Each one is a function from the standard library that takes a lambda and does one job over the whole list: Java List<Cookie> goldenCookies = cookies.stream().filter(c -> c.status() == GOLDEN).toList(); int golden = goldenCookies.stream().mapToInt(Cookie::grams).sum(); Map<String, Integer> net = goldenCookies.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy( Cookie::flavor, LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.summingInt(c -> c.grams() - biteOf(c)))); List<String> burnt = cookies.stream().filter(c -> c.status() == BURNT).map(Cookie::id).toList(); Optional<Cookie> largest = goldenCookies.stream().max(Comparator.comparingInt(Cookie::grams)); Kotlin val goldenCookies = cookies.filter { it.status == Status.GOLDEN } val golden = goldenCookies.sumOf { it.grams } val net = goldenCookies.groupBy { it.flavor } .mapValues { (_, cs) -> cs.sumOf { it.grams - (it.nibbledGrams ?: 0) } } val burnt = cookies.filter { it.status == Status.BURNT }.map { it.id } val largest = goldenCookies.maxByOrNull { it.grams } Each result is one val, computed from the list, and each line says what it computes rather than how to walk the list. The ReportLoop demo prints both versions: chain: golden=125 net={oat=85, chocolate=30} burnt=[c4] largest=c3 loop: golden=125 net={oat=85, chocolate=30} burnt=[c4] largest=c3 Same answers on a normal day. Both bugs are gone without anyone hunting for them: maxByOrNull only ever sees golden cookies and returns null for an empty list, and nothing assumes there is a first element. Give each result its own chain. A loop that fills four piles at once makes every line a suspect. The rest of this lesson takes those operations one at a time, with the trap that comes with each. Break the loop with an empty day Run ReportLoop (or ReportLoopJava). Check that the loop and the chain agree on the sample day. Run it again with -Pargs=empty added. Predict first: which version survives a day with no cookies? Put a raw cookie of 99 g at the front of the sample day, Cookie("c0", "oat", 99, Status.RAW) in sampleDay in SampleDay.kt (Java: new Cookie("c0", "oat", 99, Status.RAW, null) in DAY), and run once more. Compare the two largest values. h: Collections without loops: map, filter, fold and friends · One job per step: map, filter, mapNotNull and flatMap
x: Each collection operation does one job and returns a new collection, so you read a chain top to bottom, one job per line. In the kitchen: weigh every cookie, set aside the burnt ones, tip both trays onto one rack. map transforms every element: cookies.map { it.grams } gives one weight per cookie, in the same order. filter keeps the elements that pass a test: cookies.filter { it.status == GOLDEN }. mapNotNull transforms and drops the nulls in one step. cookies.mapNotNull { it.nibbledGrams } gives just the bites, [10] on the sample day. It replaces map { ... }.filterNotNull() and builds one list instead of two. flatMap turns each element into a list and joins the lists: trays.flatMap { it.cookies } turns a day of trays into one list of cookies. Then come the operations that boil a list down to one answer: sumOf, count { }, any { }, all { }, none { }, first { } and maxByOrNull { }. Several of them take a predicate, a function that answers true or false. Those stop at the first element that decides the answer, so any stops at its first match. Java has the same operations on streams. A stream is Java's pipeline object: you make one from a collection with .stream(), add steps, and finish with an operation such as toList() or sum(). Side by side: Java List<Integer> bites = cookies.stream() .map(Cookie::nibbledGrams) .filter(Objects::nonNull) .toList(); // [10] List<String> ids = trays.stream() .flatMap(t -> t.cookies().stream()) .map(Cookie::id) .toList(); boolean anyBig = cookies.stream().anyMatch(c -> c.grams() > 75); Kotlin val bites = cookies.mapNotNull { it.nibbledGrams } // [10] val ids = trays.flatMap { it.cookies }.map { it.id } val anyBig = cookies.any { it.grams > 75 } The difference that matters isn't the syntax. A Java stream is lazy: nothing runs until the last operation, and then each element travels through the whole pipeline. Kotlin's operations on a List are eager: filter runs over the whole list and returns a new ArrayList, then map runs over that one and returns another. Every step builds a full list in between. As the last lesson showed, the lambdas cost nothing, because these functions are inline. The lists are the cost. For a day of a few hundred cookies that's nothing. For a million rows and five steps it starts to matter, and the next lesson's sequences are the fix. This is also where the tray picture breaks. In a kitchen, cookies move along one at a time: you weigh one and pass it on. Kotlin's list operations finish the whole tray before the next step starts, onto a fresh tray each time. One rule keeps a chain honest: no side effects inside it. A map that also writes to a file, or a filter that bumps a counter, brings back exactly the hidden state that lesson 1 removed. Effects go at the end, in a forEach, or better, in the shell from lesson 1. A chain computes and the shell acts. Keep side effects out of map and filter. Most of these operations are named versions of one general loop. The next section gives it its name. Predict each line Open Operations.kt (or OperationsJava.java) and the sample day in SampleDay.kt. Predict every line of output, then run it. Replace mapNotNull { it.nibbledGrams } with map { it.nibbledGrams } and run. What changed? Then add .sum() after it and read the compiler's answer. Look at the last line. What class does each step return?
