h: Collections without loops: map, filter, fold and friends · The loop you were writing is a fold
x: fold carries one accumulator down the list from a start value with a step; map and filter are the same walk, and reduce throws on an empty day Every loop that builds one result has the same two parts: a starting value, and a step that combines the result so far with the next element. fold is that loop with both parts passed in. Our example is the cookie jar. It already holds 200 g. At the end of the day each golden cookie goes in, minus any bite, and the raw and burnt ones stay out: Java int jar = cookies.stream().reduce(200, (acc, c) -> c.status() == GOLDEN ? acc + c.grams() - biteOf(c) : acc, Integer::sum); // the third argument only matters for parallel streams Kotlin val jar = cookies.fold(200) { jar, c -> when (c.status) { Status.GOLDEN -> jar + c.grams - (c.nibbledGrams ?: 0) Status.RAW, Status.BURNT -> jar } } The value carried from one step to the next is the accumulator, jar here. Picture yourself at the jar with the kitchen scale. You carry one number, the jar's weight, past each cookie in turn, and each cookie either changes it or doesn't. The figure below walks it from 200 g to 315 g. The standard library's fold is the loop you'd write by hand: var accumulator = initial; for (element in this) accumulator = operation(accumulator, element); return accumulator. It's inline, so your lambda is pasted into that loop. The var still exists, but it lives inside fold where nothing else can touch it, and your own code has only vals. sumOf, count, maxByOrNull and joinToString are all special cases of fold, already written and named. Prefer them when they fit, because sumOf { it.grams } says more than fold(0) { acc, c -> acc + c.grams }. Reach for fold when the step needs a when, as the jar does, or when the accumulator is something richer than a number. reduce looks like fold without the starting value. It uses the first element as the start instead, and that's the trap: an empty list has no first element. Here's what Kotlin 2.4.21 does with an empty list of weights, from the EmptyTraps demo: fold(0) { a, b -> a + b } 0 sum() 0 reduceOrNull { a, b -> a + b } null reduce { a, b -> a + b } throws java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException: Empty collection can't be reduced. first() throws java.util.NoSuchElementException: List is empty. firstOrNull() null maxOf { it } throws java.util.NoSuchElementException maxOrNull() null Java chose differently. Stream.reduce without a starting value returns an Optional, a box that may be empty, so the type makes you handle the empty case. Kotlin gives you two names instead, a throwing one and an OrNull one. An empty list is a normal day. Use fold, sumOf or an OrNull function when the input can be empty. Keep reduce and first() for the places where an empty list is a bug you want to hear about loudly. Folding gives one answer. Reports usually want an answer per flavor or per tray, and that means a map. Empty-list traps, both languages Run EmptyTraps (or EmptyTrapsJava). Before you look, mark each line: a value, or an exception? Change none to listOf(45, 50) (Java: List.of(45, 50)) and predict each line again before running. In your own code, search for .first() and .reduce {. For each hit, ask whether that list can be empty on a quiet day. h: Collections without loops: map, filter, fold and friends · From a list to a map: groupBy, associateBy and partition
x: Reports are mostly maps: grams per flavor, cookies by id, counts per status. A map is a lookup table from keys to values. Three operations build one from a list, and each has a behaviour worth knowing before it surprises you. groupBy puts every element into a list under its key, like sorting cookies into jars by flavor: Java Map<String, List<String>> byFlavor = cookies.stream().collect( Collectors.groupingBy(Cookie::flavor, Collectors.mapping(Cookie::id, Collectors.toList()))); // {oat=[c1, c3], ginger=[c4], chocolate=[c2, c5]} a HashMap: no order promised Kotlin val byFlavor = cookies.groupBy({ it.flavor }, { it.id }) // {oat=[c1, c3], chocolate=[c2, c5], ginger=[c4]} a LinkedHashMap: first-seen order Kotlin's groupBy returns a LinkedHashMap, a map that remembers the order its keys arrived in. Its documentation promises that keys keep the order in which they were first seen. Java's groupingBy promises nothing about the map it returns. On JDK 21 it was a plain HashMap, which keeps keys in an order of its own, and it put ginger before chocolate. If a report must list flavors in the order they came out of the oven, Kotlin does that for you, and in Java you pass LinkedHashMap::new. When you only need a number per group, groupingBy { it.flavor }.eachCount() computes it in one pass. So does groupingBy { it.flavor }.fold(0) { acc, c -> acc + c.grams }, and neither builds a list for each group. associateBy builds a map with one element per key. Here the two languages part ways: Java Map<String, String> oneEach = cookies.stream() .collect(Collectors.toMap(Cookie::flavor, Cookie::id)); // throws IllegalStateException: Duplicate key oat (attempted merging values c1 and c3) Kotlin val oneEach = cookies.associateBy({ it.flavor }, { it.id }) // {oat=c3, chocolate=c5, ginger=c4} c1 and c2 are gone, without a word When two elements share a key, associateBy keeps the last one and says nothing. Java's toMap throws. For cookies keyed by an id that should be unique, Java's behaviour is the one you want. Say someone writes the second tray down twice. The same cookies arrive twice, associateBy quietly keeps one copy of each, and nobody hears about the mistake. So check before you index. cookies.groupingBy { it.id }.eachCount().filterValues { it > 1 } lists every repeated id, and the lab's indexById refuses a day that has any. associateBy keeps the last value for a repeated key, without a word. Check for repeats first. partition splits a list in two by a predicate, and destructuring (unpacking a pair into two vals) makes it read well: val (golden, rest) = cookies.partition { it.status == GOLDEN }. Java's version is Collectors.partitioningBy, which returns a Map<Boolean, List<Cookie>>. With these, the report from the first section is complete, and the lab builds it. Every one of these operations shares the limit from the second section, though: each step builds a whole new list or map before the next one starts. Find the line that loses data Run DuplicateKeys (or DuplicateKeysJava). Compare the key order of Kotlin's groupBy with Java's groupingBy. Find the line that loses data without telling you. Which cookies are missing from it? In the Java version, give toMap a third argument, (a, b) -> b, and run. In the Kotlin version, add a line that prints the repeated flavors: groupingBy { it.flavor }.eachCount().filterValues { it > 1 }.keys. Which ones survive? println("associateBy: ${sampleDay.associateBy({ it.flavor }, { it.id })}") // Counting per key in one pass, with no list per group. println("eachCount: ${sampleDay.groupingBy { it.flavor }.eachCount()}") } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l04.demo.DuplicateKeysKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l04/demo/DuplicateKeys.kt DuplicateKeysJava.java package workbench.functional.l04.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.stream.Collectors; /** Java twin of DuplicateKeys.kt. h: Collections without loops: map, filter, fold and friends · Java and Kotlin
x: The baking-day report with streams and with Kotlin collection functions Report.java static BakeReport report(List<Tray> trays) { List<Cookie> cookies = trays.stream().flatMap(t -> t.cookies().stream()).toList(); Map<String, Cookie> byId = cookies.stream() .collect(Collectors.toMap(Cookie::id, c -> c)); // throws on a repeated id List<Cookie> golden = cookies.stream().filter(c -> c.status() == GOLDEN).toList(); return new BakeReport( cookies.size(), golden.stream().mapToInt(Cookie::grams).sum(), cookies.stream().map(Cookie::nibbledGrams).filter(Objects::nonNull) .mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum(), golden.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Cookie::flavor, LinkedHashMap::new, // or no order is promised Collectors.summingInt(c -> c.grams() - biteOf(c)))), cookies.stream().filter(c -> c.status() == BURNT).map(Cookie::id).toList(), golden.stream().max(Comparator.comparingInt(Cookie::grams))); // Optional<Cookie> } Report.kt fun report(trays: List<Tray>): BakeReport { val cookies = trays.flatMap { it.cookies } val repeated = cookies.groupingBy { it.id }.eachCount().filterValues { it > 1 }.keys require(repeated.isEmpty()) { "duplicate cookie ids: ${repeated.joinToString()}" } // associateBy would not val golden = cookies.filter { it.status == GOLDEN } return BakeReport( cookieCount = cookies.size, goldenGrams = golden.sumOf { it.grams }, nibbledGrams = cookies.mapNotNull { it.nibbledGrams }.sum(), netByFlavor = golden.groupBy { it.flavor } // first-seen order .mapValues { (_, cs) -> cs.sumOf { it.grams - (it.nibbledGrams ?: 0) } }, burntIds = cookies.filter { it.status == BURNT }.map { it.id }, largestGolden = golden.maxByOrNull { it.grams }, // Cookie?, null when none ) } The vocabulary is nearly the same, and the defaults are not. Java streams are lazy and single-use and finish with a collector; Kotlin's list functions are eager, return ordinary lists and maps, and can be called again on the same list. Java says "maybe nothing" with Optional, Kotlin with a nullable type and the OrNull functions. Java's groupingBy promises no key order unless you pass a map factory, while Kotlin's groupBy keeps first-seen order. And the duplicate-key defaults are opposite: Java's toMap throws, Kotlin's associateBy keeps the last value, so in Kotlin the duplicate check is your job.

h: Collections without loops: map, filter, fold and friends · Worked example
x: Rewrite a nested-loop match of reviews to recipes A recipe site matches each review to the recipe it belongs to, by recipeId. Here is a direct translation of two nested loops into a chain. Before reading on, estimate how many comparisons it makes for 10,000 recipes and 2,000 reviews. val matched = recipes.flatMap { r -> reviews.filter { it.recipeId == r.id }.map { rv -> r to rv } } List<Map.Entry<Recipe, Review>> matched = recipes.stream() .flatMap(r -> reviews.stream() .filter(rv -> rv.recipeId().equals(r.id())) .map(rv -> Map.entry(r, rv))) .toList(); Count the work. The inner filter runs over every review for every recipe: 10,000 x 2,000 = 20 million comparisons, plus one small list per recipe. A chain is no faster than the loop it replaced; it only reads better. 2. Index once instead: build a map from id to recipe, then look each review up. (?.let runs its lambda only when the lookup found something; lesson 6 covers it.) val recipesById = recipes.associateBy { it.id } // 1. one pass: 10,000 entries val matched = reviews.mapNotNull { rv -> // 2. one pass: 2,000 lookups recipesById[rv.recipeId]?.let { r -> r to rv } } Map<String, Recipe> recipesById = recipes.stream() .collect(Collectors.toMap(Recipe::id, r -> r)); // 1. one pass; throws on a repeated id List<Map.Entry<Recipe, Review>> matched = reviews.stream() // 2. one lookup per review .filter(rv -> recipesById.containsKey(rv.recipeId())) .map(rv -> Map.entry(recipesById.get(rv.recipeId()), rv)) .toList(); Decide what duplicates and orphans mean. associateBy keeps the last recipe for a repeated id, so check for repeats first, as the lab does. And mapNotNull silently drops reviews whose recipe isn't in the list, say because it was deleted. Self-check: is dropping them right? (Usually not. An orphan review is worth reporting, so split them out with partition and keep both lists.) val (known, orphans) = reviews.partition { it.recipeId in recipesById } val matched = known.map { rv -> recipesById.getValue(rv.recipeId) to rv } // orphans goes into the report instead of disappearing Map<Boolean, List<Review>> split = reviews.stream() .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(rv -> recipesById.containsKey(rv.recipeId()))); List<Review> orphans = split.get(false); // goes into the report instead of disappearing List<Map.Entry<Recipe, Review>> matched = split.get(true).stream() .map(rv -> Map.entry(recipesById.get(rv.recipeId()), rv)) .toList();

h: Collections without loops: map, filter, fold and friends · Quiz
x: On a day with no cookies, what does cookies.filter { it.status == GOLDEN }.sumOf { it.grams } return? 0 It throws NoSuchElementException null It throws UnsupportedOperationException sumOf is a fold that starts from zero, so an empty list sums to 0. filter on an empty list returns an empty list without complaint. The exceptions belong to first(), maxOf and reduce, which have no starting value to fall back on. listOf(c1, c3).associateBy { it.flavor }, where both cookies (ids c1 and c3) are oat. What do you get? IllegalStateException: Duplicate key oat A map with only oat -> c3, and no warning oat -> [c1, c3] A map with only oat -> c1 associateBy keeps the last element for a repeated key and says nothing. The exception is what Java's Collectors.toMap does, which is why the first option is tempting. If you want every cookie per key, use groupBy; if a repeat is a bug, check with groupingBy { }.eachCount() first. Which operation gives you "the bites that were taken, for the cookies that have one" as a List<Int>? map { it.nibbledGrams } filter { it.nibbledGrams != null } mapNotNull { it.nibbledGrams } flatMap { it.nibbledGrams } mapNotNull transforms each cookie and drops the null results in one step. map gives a List<Int?> with nulls in it, filter gives cookies rather than bites, and flatMap needs a lambda that returns a collection, so it doesn't compile here. Cookies come out in the flavors ginger, oat, ginger, chocolate, in that order. In what order does groupBy { it.flavor } return the keys? Alphabetical: chocolate, ginger, oat Hash order, as Java's groupingBy gives Last-seen order: oat, ginger, chocolate First-seen order: ginger, oat, chocolate Kotlin's groupBy builds a LinkedHashMap and documents that keys keep the order in which they were first produced. Java's groupingBy promises no particular map, and on JDK 21 it gave a HashMap in hash order. Nothing in either sorts the keys. From Higher-order functions: functions in, functions out: cookies.filter { it.grams > minGrams } on a List creates no lambda object, even though the lambda captures minGrams. Why? filter is inline, so the lambda's body is pasted into the loop inside the calling function Kotlin caches capturing lambdas, one per call site The JIT removes the object at runtime Capturing a val never needs an object An inline function's lambda never becomes an object: the compiler copies filter's loop and the lambda's body into your method, and minGrams is just a local it reads. Without inline a capturing lambda is a new object per evaluation (lesson 2), whether it captures a val or a var. Caching only applies to lambdas that capture nothing.

h: Collections without loops: map, filter, fold and friends · Key terms
x: map Transform every element: the same number of elements comes out, in the same order. filter Keep the elements that pass a test. flatMap Turn each element into a collection and join them all into one list. fold Combine all elements into one result, starting from a given value. The general loop. Accumulator The value fold carries from one element to the next, and finally returns. Eager operation One that runs over the whole collection at once and returns a new collection. associateBy Build a map with one element per key. For a repeated key, the last element wins. What does reduce do on an empty list? It throws UnsupportedOperationException: Empty collection can't be reduced. Use fold with a starting value, or reduceOrNull. What does emptyList<Int>().first() throw? NoSuchElementException: List is empty. firstOrNull() returns null instead. associateBy meets a repeated key. What happens? The last element wins, silently. Java's Collectors.toMap throws IllegalStateException: Duplicate key ... instead. In what key order does Kotlin's groupBy return its map? First-seen order: it returns a LinkedHashMap. Java's groupingBy promises no order (it was a HashMap on JDK 21). What does mapNotNull { it.nibbledGrams } replace? map { it.nibbledGrams }.filterNotNull(), building one list instead of two. How do you find repeated ids before indexing a list? cookies.groupingBy { it.id }.eachCount().filterValues { it > 1 }.keys Is cookies.filter { }.map { } on a List lazy? No. Each step runs over the whole list and returns a new ArrayList. Sequences, in the next lesson, are lazy.

x: A few more operations earn a place in collection code. runningFold (also called scan) is fold that keeps every value along the way, which is exactly a running total. Over the weights [45, 90, 50, 80, 30], runningFold(0) { acc, x -> acc + x } gives [0, 45, 135, 185, 265, 295]: one more element than the input, because it includes the starting value. runningReduce leaves the starting value out. Java // JDK 21 streams have no running fold; a loop is the plain answer. List<Integer> totals = new ArrayList<>(List.of(0)); for (int x : grams) totals.add(totals.get(totals.size() - 1) + x); // JDK 24 added java.util.stream.Gatherers, with scan(...) and windowFixed(...) as intermediate operations. Kotlin val totals = grams.runningFold(0) { acc, x -> acc + x } // [0, 45, 135, 185, 265, 295] val firstOver200 = totals.indexOfFirst { it > 200 } // 4: the tray passes 200 g after the fourth cookie chunked(12) splits cookies into boxes of twelve, and the last box may hold fewer: listOf(1, 2, 3, 4, 5).chunked(2) is [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]. windowed(7) gives sliding windows, for a seven-day average of how much you baked. zip pairs two lists element by element and quietly stops at the shorter one, so zipping 10 planned bakes with 9 actual ones loses the 10th without a word: compare the sizes first. One caution from the other direction. Kotlin's forEach is inline, so a return inside its lambda returns from the enclosing function and skips every remaining element. Java developers expect continue-like behaviour from Stream.forEach. Use return@forEach to skip one element, or better, express the skip with filter.

h: Sequences: lazy pipelines, and where Java Streams fit · A list chain finishes the whole tray before the next step starts
x: The recipe app keeps a big recipe book: a million recipes that its users have shared. Each evening it suggests one. To pick it, the app asks a matching service, a program on another computer that rates from 0 to 100 how well a recipe fits what's in your fridge. Each question takes about 2 ms, and the app pays for every one. Here's the search, written the way the last lesson taught us: Java Recipe firstMatch(List<Recipe> book, ToIntFunction<Recipe> matchScore) { List<Scored> scored = book.stream() .map(r -> new Scored(r, matchScore.applyAsInt(r))) // about 2 ms per recipe .toList(); List<Recipe> good = scored.stream().filter(s -> s.score() >= 90).map(Scored::recipe).toList(); return good.isEmpty() ? null : good.get(0); } Kotlin fun firstMatch(book: List<Recipe>, matchScore: (Recipe) -> Int): Recipe? = book.map { it to matchScore(it) } // about 2 ms per recipe .filter { (_, score) -> score >= 90 } .map { (recipe, _) -> recipe } .firstOrNull() it to matchScore(it) builds a pair: the recipe and its score, side by side. The chain reads well and gives the right answer. But say the first good match is recipe number 518. The chain still asks about all million recipes: 1,000,000 times 2 ms is 2,000 seconds, about 33 minutes of waiting for an answer that was ready after one second. The cause is the tray from the last lesson. map and filter on a Kotlin List are eager: each one does its whole job at once. It loops over its whole input, writes every result into a brand-new list, and only then does the next step start. So the first map scores all million recipes and builds a list of a million pairs. filter builds a second list. Only then does firstOrNull look at element 0. Java's collections have no eager chain, so the Java version above collects into a list after every step to do the same thing. Kotlin's List operations do exactly that for you. The lambdas aren't the cost. As "Higher-order functions: functions in, functions out" showed, these functions are inline: the compiler pastes the loop and your lambda into the caller, so no lambda objects exist while the program runs. The cost is the lists. Every step allocates a new ArrayList, and a list of numbers holds each number as a separate boxed object. In a JMH run made for this course (JMH is a tool for timing small pieces of JVM code), a two-step filter { }.map { }.sum() over a million items allocated 26.5 MB per call. For a short chain over a few hundred items, none of this matters, and the eager chain is the easiest to debug: you can stop after any step and look at a real list. It starts to matter when the input is big, a step is slow, or you only need the first few results. A list chain runs every step on every item. Ask how many items you really need. Let's watch the order of the work on one small tray first, then fix the search. Watch the order of the lambdas Open OrderDemo.kt (or OrderDemoJava.java). h: Sequences: lazy pipelines, and where Java Streams fit · A sequence sends one item at a time down the whole line
x: A List runs each step over every payment; a Sequence pulls one payment through the whole chain and stops early, but sorted() still reads everything Put asSequence() in front of the same chain and the order of the work changes. A sequence is a lazy chain of steps. Lazy means it does no work until a result is wanted, and then only as much as that result needs. Picture a kitchen line with two helpers: one checks each cookie's color, the next one weighs it. With a list, the checker goes through the whole tray before the weigher starts. With a sequence, the first cookie walks down the whole line, checked and then weighed, before the second cookie leaves the tray. When the lunchbox is full, the line stops, and the cookies still on the tray are never touched. The figure shows both orders for the lunchbox you just packed. The work starts at a terminal operation, a step such as toList(), first(), sum() or count() that asks for items. Steps like map and filter are intermediate operations: on a sequence they only add a step to the plan. That's why the lunchbox program printed built TakeSequence, nothing has run yet before any cookie was checked. The sequence is in no hurry at all. It has written down the plan and will wait as long as you like for someone to ask. Now the search. book.asSequence().map { ... }.filter { ... }.map { ... }.firstOrNull() asks the matching service 518 times and stops. This is short-circuiting: stopping as soon as the answer is known. first, firstOrNull, any, find and take(n) can do it, and in a lazy chain they stop every step above them too. For a single test you don't even need a sequence. book.firstOrNull { matchScore(it) >= 90 } is one inlined loop, and it also stops at 518. How does it work underneath? Each intermediate operation on a sequence is an ordinary function, not inline, that wraps the sequence before it. map returns a TransformingSequence that holds your lambda, filter a FilteringSequence, take a TakeSequence. When the terminal operation asks the last wrapper for an item, that wrapper asks the one before it, and so on back to the list. Here is the heart of TransformingSequence in the Kotlin 2.4.21 standard library, next to the same idea written by hand in Java: Java Iterator<R> mapped = new Iterator<>() { public boolean hasNext() { return source.hasNext(); } public R next() { return transformer.apply(source.next()); } }; Kotlin override fun next(): R = transformer(iterator.next()) override fun hasNext(): Boolean = iterator.hasNext() So a sequence trades the lists in between for one small wrapper object per step. The price is that the lambdas become real objects again, of the Function1 interface (created through invokedynamic, as "Function types, lambdas and closures" showed), and a number that passes through map is boxed on its way. One kind of step breaks the line. sorted() and sortedBy { } can't hand out the smallest item until they've seen every item, so the first request makes them pull the whole input into a list and sort it. The kitchen picture breaks here too: no cook can say which cookie is the lightest by looking at one cookie. In the Try it, a sortedBy before firstOrNull { } pulls all 1,000,000 recipes, though the service still runs only 518 times. If you only need the smallest item, minByOrNull { } reads the input once and sorts nothing. A sequence moves one item through every step and stops when the answer is known. Put the step that can stop at the end. So far every item came from a list we already had. A sequence doesn't need one. Count the work on a million recipes Read ScanCount.kt. Every line looks for the same recipe, number 518 of a million. For each line, predict how many times match runs and how many recipes the onEach counter pulls. Run it. In the Sequence chain line, add .toList() just before .firstOrNull(). Predict the counts, then run it again. Run the Java twin and compare findFirst on one stream with collecting first. h: Sequences: lazy pipelines, and where Java Streams fit · Making items on demand: generateSequence and sequence { yield }
x: A sequence can make its items as it goes. Two builders produce an item only when someone asks for the next one. generateSequence(seed) { next } starts from the seed and works out each item from the one before. It ends when the lambda returns null. The app's serving buttons, for 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 servings, are one line: Java List<Integer> servings = Stream.iterate(1, n -> n <= 16, n -> n * 2).toList(); // [1, 2, 4, 8, 16] Kotlin val servings = generateSequence(1) { (it * 2).takeIf { next -> next <= 16 } } servings.toList() // [1, 2, 4, 8, 16] takeIf returns the value when the test passes and null when it doesn't (lesson 6 covers it). Without the takeIf, the sequence never ends. That's fine as long as something downstream stops it, such as take(5) or first { }. sequence { } is for items that take real code to make, like a recipe website that shows its search results one page at a time. Inside the block, yield(x) hands out one item and yieldAll(list) hands out many: Java Stream<SearchResult> results = Stream.iterate(1, page -> page <= 3, page -> page + 1) .flatMap(page -> fetchPage(page).stream()); // fetchPage is a web request results.filter(r -> r.minutes() < 30).findFirst(); // also skips page 3 on JDK 21 Kotlin val results = sequence { for (page in 1..3) yieldAll(fetchPage(page)) // fetchPage is a web request } results.first { it.minutes < 30 } // fetches page 1 and page 2, never page 3 You may wonder how a for loop can stop halfway and wait. The block is a suspend lambda: its type is suspend SequenceScope<T>.() -> Unit. A suspend function is one that can pause in the middle and carry on later, and the coroutines track covers them. The compiler turns the block into a small state machine, code that remembers which step it reached. Each yield saves where the block is and hands control back to whoever asked for an item. When they ask for the next one, the block carries on right after that yield. No second thread is involved: it all runs on the caller's thread, one step at a time. When nobody asks again, the block never carries on, so page 3 is never requested. The block is restricted. Only yield and yieldAll may pause it. Call delay inside sequence { } and Kotlin 2.4.21 refuses: Restricted suspending functions can invoke member or extension suspending functions only on their restricted coroutine scope. For pages you must wait for without blocking a thread, use a Flow (the coroutines track). The lab's version has one more rule: it doesn't know how many pages exist, and an empty page means the end. In Kotlin that's a while (true) loop with a break. In Java it's Stream.iterate(0, p -> p + 1).map(site::page).takeWhile(p -> !p.isEmpty()).flatMap(List::stream). We now have three lazy pipelines: a list turned into a sequence, a generated one and a paging one. Java has a lazy pipeline of its own, and the two part ways at the edges. Fetch only the pages you read Read Paging.kt. Each page holds three recipes, and later pages hold quicker ones. Predict which pages are fetched before the first recipe under 30 minutes prints. Run it. Change first to firstOrNull and < 30 to < 1. Predict which pages are fetched and what prints, then run it. Paging.kt package workbench.functional.l05.demo data class SearchResult(val title: String, val minutes: Int) /** Stands for one web request to the recipe site: three results per page, quicker recipes on later pages. */ private fun fetchPage(page: Int): List<SearchResult> { println(" fetching page $page") return List(3) { i -> SearchResult("R$page-$i", 60 - (page * 3 + i) * 5) } } fun main() { // 1. a paging source: the block runs only as far as the consumer pulls val results = sequence { for (page in 1..3) yieldAll(fetchPage(page)) } println("first recipe under 30 minutes:") println(" ${results.first { it.minutes < 30 }}") // 2. the app's serving buttons: start at 1, double, and stop when the lambda returns null val servings = generateSequence(1) { (it * 2).takeIf { next -> next <= 16 } } println("servings: ${servings.toList()}") } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l05.demo.PagingKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l05/demo/Paging.kt PagingJava.java package workbench.functional.l05.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.stream.IntStream; import java.util.stream.Stream; /** The same paging source and serving buttons with Java streams (JDK 9+ for the three-argument iterate). */ public class PagingJava { record SearchResult(String title, int minutes) {} /** Stands for one web request to the recipe site: three results per page. */ static List<SearchResult> fetchPage(int page) { System.out.println(" fetching page " + page); return IntStream.range(0, 3).mapToObj(i -> new SearchResult("R" + page + "-" + i, 60 - (page * 3 + i) * 5)).toList(); } public static void main(String[] args) { // 1. a paging source: a stream of page numbers, flattened into results Stream<SearchResult> results = Stream.iterate(1, page -> page <= 3, page -> page + 1) .flatMap(page -> fetchPage(page).stream()); h: Sequences: lazy pipelines, and where Java Streams fit · Sequence or Stream, and when you need neither
x: A Java stream is Java's lazy pipeline: you make one from a collection with .stream(), add steps, and finish with a terminal operation. It runs in the same order as a sequence, one item at a time down the whole line, and the Java twins in this lesson print the same order and the same counts. The differences are practical. A sequence is a recipe, not a tray of cookies. Each terminal operation follows the recipe again from the top, side effects included: call sum() and then count() on the same sequence and every map lambda runs twice. A few sequences refuse a second run. iterator().asSequence() and generateSequence { } without a seed throw IllegalStateException: This sequence can be consumed only once. A stream is always single-use, like a disposable piping bag: squeeze it once and it's spent. A second terminal operation throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. Streams can do things sequences can't. parallelStream() splits the work over several threads (paths of work that run at the same time), taken from a shared pool called the common ForkJoinPool. Sequences have no parallel mode at all. IntStream, LongStream and mapToLong keep numbers unboxed, and Kotlin has no LongSequence. On JDK 24 and later, gatherers add windows and running totals to streams (Go deeper has them). Here are the numbers from the JMH run behind this course. The machine was a 4-core virtual machine shared with other work, so treat the times as rough, order-of-magnitude figures. The bytes allocated per call barely move between runs, so you can trust those. Each variant took a list of 1,000,000 items, kept the ones that passed a test (about 60% of them) and summed one Long from each: Variant Time per call Allocated per call for loop 5.2 ms about 0 filter { }.map { }.sum() on a List 148 ms 26,507,194 B sumOf { if (passes) n else 0L } 2.6 ms about 0 asSequence().filter { }.map { }.sum() 9.0 ms 189 B stream().filter().mapToLong().sum() 8.9 ms 428 B stream().filter().map().reduce(0L, ...) 14 ms 28,782,178 B The fastest line is neither a list chain nor a sequence. It's one fused sumOf, which is the hand-written loop. The sequence allocated almost nothing only because the JIT (the compiler inside the JVM that speeds up hot code while it runs) removed the boxes in this tiny benchmark. Don't count on that in a big program, where one call site sees many different lambdas. When the terminal operation could stop early (the first match was at index 101), the gap was huge: 141 ns for the sequence, 4.4 ms for the list chain. So here's the rule I use. Use list operations by default. Switch to asSequence() when the end of the chain can stop early, or when a long chain runs over a big input. Use sequence { } or generateSequence for items made on demand, such as pages. Use a stream when you need parallel(), a primitive stream or a gatherer, or when a Java library hands you one. Laziness saves work only when something stops early. When nothing does, one fused pass beats both. That fused pass is sumOf, count { } or firstOrNull { }, and it's usually the shortest line too. Read a sequence twice, and a stream twice Read Reuse.kt. Predict how many weigh lines print, and what the second read of once does. Run it, then run ReuseJava. In Reuse.kt, delete .asSequence() from weights. Predict how many weigh lines print now. Reuse.kt package workbench.functional.l05.demo data class Item(val name: String, val grams: Int) private val basket = listOf(Item("flour", 500), Item("sugar", 200), Item("butter", 250)) fun main() { // 1. a sequence is a recipe: every terminal operation runs the whole chain again val weights = basket.asSequence().map { println(" weigh ${it.name}"); it.grams } println("sum = ${weights.sum()}") println("count = ${weights.count()}") // 2. some sequences can be read only once val once = basket.iterator().asSequence() println("first read: ${once.map { it.name }.toList()}") try { once.toList() } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("second read: ${e::class.simpleName}: ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l05.demo.ReuseKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l05/demo/Reuse.kt ReuseJava.java package workbench.functional.l05.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.stream.Stream; /** A Java Stream is always single-use: the second terminal operation throws. */ public class ReuseJava { record Item(String name, int grams) {} public static void main(String[] args) { List<Item> basket = List.of(new Item("flour", 500), new Item("sugar", 200), new Item("butter", 250)); Stream<Integer> weights = basket.stream().map(i -> { System.out.println(" weigh " + i.name()); return i.grams(); }); System.out.println("sum = " + weights.mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum()); try { System.out.println("count = " + weights.count()); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("count again: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage()); } // to run it again, build a new stream from the source System.out.println("count = " + basket.stream().count()); } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l05.demo.ReuseJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l05/demo/ReuseJava.java Six weigh lines: three for sum() and three more for count(), because each terminal operation follows the recipe again. The sum is 950 and the count 3. The iterator-backed sequence fails on its second read with IllegalStateException: This sequence can be consumed only once. Java's stream fails on the second terminal operation with IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. Without asSequence(), weights is a List built once, so weigh prints three lines in total. java.util.stream package summary (Java SE 21 API) docs

h: Sequences: lazy pipelines, and where Java Streams fit · Java and Kotlin
x: The first matches for a vegetarian guest: Sequence vs Stream RecipeSearch.java List<Long> firstMatchesFor(List<Recipe> book, ToIntFunction<Recipe> matchScore, int n) { return book.stream() .filter(Recipe::vegetarian) // the quick look first .filter(r -> matchScore.applyAsInt(r) >= 90) .map(Recipe::id) // boxed Long, as in Kotlin .limit(n) // stops early, like take(n) .toList(); // unmodifiable on JDK 16+ } RecipeSearch.kt fun firstMatchesFor(book: List<Recipe>, matchScore: (Recipe) -> Int, n: Int): List<Long> = book.asSequence() .filter { it.vegetarian } // the quick look first .filter { matchScore(it) >= 90 } .map { it.id } // boxed Long at the Function1 boundary .take(n) // stops early, like limit(n) .toList() Both pipelines are lazy and run in the same order, one recipe at a time, so both ask the matching service exactly as often. The real differences are at the edges. The stream can be used once; the sequence can be read again and will run the whole chain again. The stream could go parallel(); the sequence can't. Kotlin's terminal operations mirror the List API (firstOrNull returns null, and groupBy and sumOf are there), while the stream returns Optional from findFirst and needs Collectors for grouping. And on the Kotlin side you can drop asSequence() and get an eager List chain with the same code, which is often the better choice for small inputs.

h: Sequences: lazy pipelines, and where Java Streams fit · Worked example
x: Decide whether a nutrition check should be lazy The app checks the 2 million ingredient lines in its recipe book against a nutrition table, and shows the first 20 lines whose ingredient the table doesn't know, so someone can add them. Here's the first version. Before reading on, find the step that makes laziness pay off. fun firstUnknown(lines: List<Line>, kcalPer100g: Map<String, Int>): List<Check> = lines.map { line -> Check(line.recipeId, line.ingredient, kcalPer100g[line.ingredient]) } .filter { it.kcal == null } .take(20) List<Check> firstUnknown(List<Line> lines, Map<String, Integer> kcalPer100g) { List<Check> all = lines.stream() .map(l -> new Check(l.recipeId(), l.ingredient(), kcalPer100g.get(l.ingredient()))) .toList(); // 2 million objects return all.stream().filter(c -> c.kcal() == null).limit(20).toList(); } take(20) can stop early, so this chain should be lazy. 1. Ask the question: does the last step stop before the end? Here, yes. 2. Put asSequence() at the front. Now the chain builds 20 checks plus the known lines it read on the way, and no 2-million-item lists. fun firstUnknown(lines: List<Line>, kcalPer100g: Map<String, Int>): List<Check> = lines.asSequence() // 2. lazy from here on .map { line -> Check(line.recipeId, line.ingredient, kcalPer100g[line.ingredient]) } .filter { it.kcal == null } .take(20) // 1. stops early .toList() List<Check> firstUnknown(List<Line> lines, Map<String, Integer> kcalPer100g) { return lines.stream() // 2. one lazy pipeline .map(l -> new Check(l.recipeId(), l.ingredient(), kcalPer100g.get(l.ingredient()))) .filter(c -> c.kcal() == null) .limit(20) // 1. stops early .toList(); } Move the cheap test before the work. Building a Check for every line is wasted effort; test first and build the object only for real unknowns. lines.asSequence() .filter { it.ingredient !in kcalPer100g } // 3. cheap test, no object built .map { Check(it.recipeId, it.ingredient, null) } .take(20) .toList() lines.stream() .filter(l -> !kcalPer100g.containsKey(l.ingredient())) // 3. cheap test .map(l -> new Check(l.recipeId(), l.ingredient(), null)) .limit(20) .toList(); Look for a barrier. Now someone asks for the 20 heaviest unknown lines, so the biggest gaps come first. That needs sortedByDescending { } before take(20), and the sort must read all 2 million lines first, so the sequence saves nothing over a List here. Keep whichever reads better, and know that the cost is the full pass plus the sort. lines.asSequence() .filter { it.ingredient !in kcalPer100g } .sortedByDescending { it.grams } // 4. reads everything .take(20) .map { Check(it.recipeId, it.ingredient, null) } .toList() lines.stream() .filter(l -> !kcalPer100g.containsKey(l.ingredient())) .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(Line::grams).reversed()) // 4. reads everything .limit(20) .map(l -> new Check(l.recipeId(), l.ingredient(), null)) .toList();

x: score is a slow call. Which line calls it only until the first recipe that scores 90 or more? book.map { score(it) }.first { it >= 90 } book.asSequence().map { score(it) }.toList().first { it >= 90 } book.asSequence().map { score(it) }.first { it >= 90 } book.asSequence().map { score(it) }.sorted().first { it >= 90 } Only the third line is lazy all the way to a terminal step that stops early. The first is eager and scores everything before first looks. In the second, toList() is a terminal operation that pulls every item. In the fourth, sorted() must read every score before it can hand out the smallest. val weights = basket.asSequence().map { log(it.name); it.grams } runs over a basket of 5 items, then the code calls weights.sum() and weights.max(). How many times does log run? 5 10 0, because sequences are lazy 5, then max() throws IllegalStateException A sequence is a recipe, and each terminal operation follows it again: five calls for sum(), five more for max(). Only a few sequences are once-only (for example iterator().asSequence()). If you need the values twice, call toList() once and reuse the list. The app's server adds up the grams of 40 million logged bakes on a 16-core machine, and should use all the cores. What fits best? grams.asSequence().sum() sequence { yieldAll(grams) }.sum() A List chain with sumOf grams.parallelStream().mapToLong { it }.sum() Only Java streams have a parallel mode, and mapToLong keeps the numbers unboxed. Kotlin sequences run on one thread and have no parallel API. sumOf is the fastest single-threaded option, but it still uses one core. From the collections lesson: today's shopping basket can be empty. What does basket.asSequence().map { it.grams }.reduce { a, b -> a + b } do on an empty basket? Throws UnsupportedOperationException: Empty sequence can't be reduced. Returns 0 Returns null Returns an empty sequence reduce has no starting value, so with no items it has nothing to return, and it throws. That holds for sequences as it does for lists. Use fold(0) { a, b -> a + b } or sum(), which return 0, or reduceOrNull. sequence { for (p in 1..10) yieldAll(site.page(p)) }.take(5).toList(). Every page holds 3 recipes. How many pages are fetched? 1 2 10 0, until the result is printed Page 1 gives three recipes and page 2 gives the fourth and fifth. take(5) is then full and stops asking, so the block never carries on to fetch page 3. toList() is the terminal operation, so the fetching happens right there, not when you print.

h: Sequences: lazy pipelines, and where Java Streams fit · Key terms
x: Eager Does all the work for a step right away and stores the result, before the next step starts. Lazy Does no work until a result is asked for, and then only as much as needed. Sequence Kotlin's lazy chain of steps: each item goes through every step, and nothing runs until a terminal operation asks. Intermediate operation A step such as map or filter that returns another sequence or stream and runs nothing by itself. Terminal operation A step such as toList, first or sum that asks for items and so makes the chain run. Short-circuiting Stopping as soon as the answer is known, as first, any and take do. Stateful operation A step like sorted that must remember many items, often all of them, before it can hand out one. What does list.filter { }.map { } allocate? A new ArrayList per step, plus a box for every number in a List<Long>. The lambdas are inlined, so no function objects. When does a sequence chain run its lambdas? Only when a terminal operation (toList, first, sum, count, ...) asks for items. map and filter on a sequence only add a step to the plan. In what order does asSequence().filter { }.map { } run? Item by item: filter 1, map 1, filter 2, ... Each item goes through every step before the next one is read. Why does sortedBy { } in a sequence read everything? It can't hand out the smallest item until it has seen all of them, so the first request pulls the whole input into a list and sorts it. What happens when you read a sequence twice? The whole chain runs again, side effects included. iterator().asSequence() and seedless generateSequence { } throw IllegalStateException instead. What happens when you use a Java stream twice? IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. Streams are single-use. How does sequence { } pause between items? The block is a suspend lambda. Each yield pauses it until someone asks for the next item. No second thread is involved.

h: Sequences: lazy pipelines, and where Java Streams fit · Go deeper
x: Three details matter once you write sequences in hot code, the code that runs most often. Boxing. A sequence of Long is a sequence of java.lang.Long objects, because each step calls a Function1 whose invoke takes and returns Object. In bytecode, the lambda of map { it.grams.toLong() } is a Function1 whose invokedynamic signature returns Ljava/lang/Long;. Java's mapToLong takes a ToLongFunction that returns a primitive long. In the JMH run above, the sequence still allocated only 189 bytes per call, because the JIT's escape analysis saw that the boxes never left the method and removed them. That worked because the benchmark had one call site and one lambda type. In a big program the same FilteringSequence code runs with dozens of different lambdas, the call site becomes megamorphic (it sees too many types for the JIT to inline them), and the boxes come back. IntelliJ's hint. The Kotlin plugin has an inspection that suggests turning a call chain on a collection into a sequence. It is on by default as a weak warning and fires for chains of five or more calls. Treat it as a prompt to ask this lesson's question (does the end of the chain stop early, and is the input big?), not as a rule. Gatherers. Since JDK 24, streams have Stream.gather, with built-ins in java.util.stream.Gatherers: windowFixed, windowSliding, fold, scan and mapConcurrent. Kotlin has had the equivalents on both List and Sequence for years: chunked, windowed, fold and runningFold (also called scan). So a seven-day average of grams baked is days.windowed(7) { it.average() } in Kotlin, a hand-written loop in Java on JDK 21, and stream.gather(Gatherers.windowSliding(7)) on JDK 24 and later. The labs compile with release 21, so they use none of this.

h: Scope functions: let, run, with, apply and also, on purpose · A scope function is a two-line function you could write yourself
x: Here's code from the recipe app that sets up a program for the oven and writes a line to the app's log, its running record of what it did. It's how most of us write it on day one: Java OvenProgram program = new OvenProgram(); program.setTemperatureC(180); program.setMinutes(12); program.setName("Oat cookies"); log.info("baking {}", program); Kotlin val program = OvenProgram() program.temperatureC = 180 program.minutes = 12 program.name = "Oat cookies" log.info("baking {}", program) Nothing is wrong with it. It repeats program. on every line, and nothing marks where the setup ends. Kotlin code often says the same thing like this: Java // Java equivalent: a helper that takes a Consumer and returns the object OvenProgram program = apply(new OvenProgram(), p -> { p.setTemperatureC(180); p.setMinutes(12); p.setName("Oat cookies"); }); log.info("baking {}", program); Kotlin val program = OvenProgram().apply { temperatureC = 180 minutes = 12 name = "Oat cookies" }.also { log.info("baking {}", it) } Those are the first two habits from the opening. apply sets up a new tray and hands back the same tray. also notes something in passing and lets the value go on unchanged. apply and also look like keywords. They're ordinary functions in the standard library, a couple of lines each. Here are let and apply written by hand: Java static <T, R> R let(T value, Function<T, R> block) { return block.apply(value); } static <T> T apply(T value, Consumer<T> block) { block.accept(value); return value; } Kotlin fun <T, R> T.myLet(block: (T) -> R): R = block(this) // value in as `it`, block's result out fun <T> T.myApply(block: T.() -> Unit): T { block(); return this } // value is `this` inside, value out Both are extension functions: functions you can call on a value of any type T as if they were its own methods. The difference is the type of block. (T) -> R is a plain function type: the value arrives as the lambda's parameter, it. T.() -> Unit is a lambda with a receiver, which "Function types, lambdas and closures" showed briefly: inside the lambda the value is this, so minutes = 12 means this.minutes = 12. Java has no lambdas with a receiver, which is why the Java helper needs p. on every line. The real let in the Kotlin 2.4.21 standard library is that same line plus two things: @kotlin.internal.InlineOnly public inline fun <T, R> T.let(block: (T) -> R): R { contract { callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) } return block(this) } inline makes the compiler paste the block into your code, so no lambda object exists at run time ("Higher-order functions: functions in, functions out" explained why). The contract line is the next section's business. So a scope function is one of these five small inline functions that run a block with one value in hand, the context object. They differ in exactly two ways: whether the block sees the value as this or as it, and whether the call hands back the value itself or the block's result. Two differences make a small grid, and two questions pick a cell. One block, five functions, two answers Open ScopeReturns.kt. The same block, servings * 2, runs through all five scope functions. Write down what each line prints before you run it. Run it. On the also line, change also to let. Predict the output, then run it. Read ScopeReturnsJava.java: what does Java write for each one? ScopeReturns.kt package workbench.functional.l06.demo data class Recipe(val name: String, val servings: Int, val grams: Int) class TraySetup { var paper: Boolean = false var cookies: Int = 0 override fun toString() = "TraySetup(paper=$paper, cookies=$cookies)" } // The two shapes, written by hand. A scope function is nothing more than this. fun <T, R> T.myLet(block: (T) -> R): R = block(this) // object as `it`, returns the block's result fun <T> T.myApply(block: T.() -> Unit): T { block(); return this } // object as `this`, returns the object fun main() { val recipe = Recipe("pancakes", 4, 200) // the same block, five ways: what comes back? println("let -> ${recipe.let { it.servings * 2 }}") println("run -> ${recipe.run { servings * 2 }}") println("with -> ${with(recipe) { servings * 2 }}") println("also -> ${recipe.also { it.servings * 2 }}") println("apply -> ${recipe.apply { servings * 2 }}") // the hand-written versions behave the same way println("myLet -> ${recipe.myLet { it.servings * 2 }}") println("myApply -> ${TraySetup().myApply { paper = true; cookies = 12 }}") } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l06.demo.ScopeReturnsKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l06/demo/ScopeReturns.kt ScopeReturnsJava.java package workbench.functional.l06.demo; import java.util.function.Consumer; import java.util.function.Function; /** * Java has no scope functions and no lambdas with a receiver. This is what each one stands in for, * plus the two shapes written as static methods. */ public class ScopeReturnsJava { record Recipe(String name, int servings, int grams) {} static class TraySetup { boolean paper; int cookies; @Override public String toString() { return "TraySetup(paper=" + paper + ", cookies=" + cookies + ")"; } } // let: hand the value to a function, return what it returns static <T, R> R let(T value, Function<T, R> block) { return block.apply(value); } // apply/also: hand the value to a block, return the value itself static <T> T apply(T value, Consumer<T> block) { block.accept(value); return value; } public static void main(String[] args) { Recipe recipe = new Recipe("pancakes", 4, 200); // let, run and with all compute something from the object System.out.println("computed -> " + recipe.servings() * 2); // also and apply keep the object, whatever the block did System.out.println("kept -> " + recipe); System.out.println("let -> " + let(recipe, r -> r.servings() * 2)); // no receiver: the block must name its parameter and write t. on every line System.out.println("apply -> " + apply(new TraySetup(), t -> { t.paper = true; t.cookies = 12; })); } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l06.demo.ScopeReturnsJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l06/demo/ScopeReturnsJava.java let, run and with print 8, because they hand back the block's result. also and apply print Recipe(name=pancakes, servings=4, grams=200): they run the block and drop its result. myLet and myApply behave the same, because that's all the real ones do, and myApply prints TraySetup(paper=true, cookies=12). Changing also to let changes the value of the whole expression from the recipe to 8. In Java, "compute something" is a plain expression and "keep the object" needs a helper that takes a Consumer.

h: Scope functions: let, run, with, apply and also, on purpose · Two questions pick the function: this or it, the value or the block's result
x: Two questions pick a scope function: this or it, the object or the block's result, and why ?.let { } ?: run { } can run both blocks Because the five differ in only two ways, two questions pick one. First, what should the call hand back? If you want the same value (to keep chaining it, return it or store it), use apply or also. If you want something new, a computed value or a different object, use let, run or with. Second, how does the block use the value? If it mostly sets or calls the value's own members, a receiver (the value as this) reads best: apply, run, with. If it passes the value to other functions, or it also needs the this of the class around it, use an argument (the value as it): also, let. The figure puts the answers in a grid. The Kotlin docs give the same advice as a list of purposes, and each purpose lands in one cell. Here they are with the kitchen habit that matches: You want to Use In the kitchen In the recipe app set up an object apply set up a new tray OvenProgram().apply { minutes = 12; name = title } do something extra and keep the value also note it in passing menu.add(dish).also { log.info("added {}", it) } run code on a non-null value, or compute from it let taste with a spoon guest.favorite?.let { recipes.find(it) } use an object's members to compute a result run read the oven's own dials oven.run { preheat(); minutesLeft() } run statements where an expression is needed run { } val grams = run { val base = recipe.grams(); base + extra } group calls on a value you already hold with read off the card in your hand with(recipe) { "$name for $servings" } run and with do the same job. with(x) { } reads well on a line of its own; x.run { } is the one that fits in a chain and after ?.. There's no ?.with. The picture breaks in one place. A real kitchen habit can only do its own job: a note in the notebook can't change the soup. Kotlin doesn't hold a block to the job its function's name promises. An also block can change the object, and a run block can change it and return something else besides. The name tells the reader what you meant, and the compiler checks none of it. The five share one more property, and it explains code that looks as if it shouldn't compile: Java // Java equivalent: a lambda can't assign a local at all, so this is a plain statement Jar jar = fillJar(450); final String label = jar.label(); Kotlin val label: String val jar = fillJar(450).also { label = it.label } // compiles A val may be assigned only once, and here the assignment sits inside a lambda. The compiler accepts it because also declares a contract, callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE): a promise to the compiler that the block runs right here, exactly one time. All five scope functions declare it. Write your own also without the contract and the same line fails with Captured values cannot be initialized because of possible reassignments. Contracts are an Experimental API that the compiler trusts and never checks; the Advanced Kotlin track covers them in "Contracts and context parameters". Because the five are inline, a bare return inside the block returns from the function around it, not just from the block. In dish?.let { if (it.stage == SKIPPED) return; menu.add(it) }, a skipped dish leaves the whole function. One caution before we go on. The pair x?.let { ... } ?: run { ... } looks like an if/else built from these pieces. It isn't always one, and the next section shows when both halves run. Assign a val inside a block Run ValInit.kt. Both vals are assigned inside a block. Uncomment the two plainAlso lines at the end of main and run it again. Read the compiler error, then comment them out again. In contractAlso, delete the contract { ... } line but keep inline. Predict: is inline enough on its own? Run it. Uncomment the two lines in ValInitJava.java and run it. Read javac's error. ValInit.kt package workbench.functional.l06.demo import kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts import kotlin.contracts.InvocationKind import kotlin.contracts.contract data class Jar(val label: String, val grams: Int) /** Fills a jam jar and prints a label for it. */ fun fillJar(grams: Int) = Jar("J-${grams % 97}", grams) // a hand-written also: not inline, no contract fun <T> T.plainAlso(block: (T) -> Unit): T { block(this); return this } // the same plus what the stdlib adds: inline and an EXACTLY_ONCE contract @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) inline fun <T> T.contractAlso(block: (T) -> Unit): T { contract { callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) } block(this) return this } fun main() { val label1: String val jar1 = fillJar(450).also { label1 = it.label } // the stdlib's also: compiles println("also: $label1 for ${jar1.grams} g") val label2: String val jar2 = fillJar(300).contractAlso { label2 = it.label } // yours, with the contract: compiles println("contractAlso: $label2 for ${jar2.grams} g") // Uncomment the next two lines and run again. The compiler can't know how often plainAlso calls the block. // val label3: String // fillJar(250).plainAlso { label3 = it.label } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l06.demo.ValInitKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l06/demo/ValInit.kt ValInitJava.java package workbench.functional.l06.demo; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** Java equivalent: a Java lambda can't assign a local variable at all, so the assignment is a plain statement. */ public class ValInitJava { record Jar(String label, int grams) {} static Jar fillJar(int grams) { return new Jar("J-" + grams % 97, grams); } public static void main(String[] args) { final String label1; Jar jar1 = fillJar(450); label1 = jar1.label(); // a statement, outside any lambda System.out.println("statement: " + label1 + " for " + jar1.grams() + " g"); // Uncomment the next two lines and run again. javac rejects any assignment to a local inside a lambda. // String label3; // Consumer<Jar> keep = j -> label3 = j.label(); } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l06.demo.ValInitJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l06/demo/ValInitJava.java The first run prints also: J-62 for 450 g and contractAlso: J-9 for 300 g. With plainAlso, the build fails with Captured values cannot be initialized because of possible reassignments., because the compiler can't see how often the block runs. Without the contract, inline is not enough: the errors are 'val' cannot be reassigned. and Variable 'label2' must be initialized. The contract is what carries the promise. javac says local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final: Java never lets a lambda assign a local. Two questions: is the value this or it inside the block, and does the call hand back the block's result or the value? Scope functions (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Scope functions: let, run, with, apply and also, on purpose · Four bugs that compile without a warning
x: Scope functions are inlined, so they cost nothing while the program runs. Their cost is in reading. Each of these four compiles on Kotlin 2.4.21 without a warning, and each looks fine at a glance. The first is ?.let { } ?: run { } used as if/else. Here it plans dinner. If a dish is open in the app, add it to the week's menu; if none is, download a suggestion and add that. menu.add returns the new slot id, or null when the dish is on the menu already: Java String planDish(Dish open, WeekMenu menu, Supplier<Dish> suggest) { return Optional.ofNullable(open).map(menu::add) // map turns a null result into empty .orElseGet(() -> menu.add(suggest.get())); } Kotlin fun planDish(open: Dish?, menu: WeekMenu, suggest: () -> Dish): String? = open?.let { menu.add(it) } // add returns null for a dish on the menu already ?: run { menu.add(suggest()) } It reads as "if a dish is open, add it, else download one and add that". But ?:, the Elvis operator, only looks at the value directly to its left: a ?: b gives a unless a is null, and then b. Here that value is the result of the let block, not open. The Elvis operator doesn't know or care where the null came from. So when the open dish is on the menu already, add returns null, and the planner downloads a suggestion and adds that too: both branches run. Java's Optional.map(...).orElseGet(...) has exactly the same trap. ?: tests the value on its left, not the value you started with. When the left side can be null, write if or when. Or decide the value first: val dish = open ?: suggest(), then add it once. The second is also or apply used to compute. dish.also { it.copy(stage = COOKING) } returns the original dish, because the block's type is (T) -> Unit and the copy is thrown away. dishes.apply { sumOf { it.servings } } returns the list, not the total. A declared type catches the second one: val total: Int = ... fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Int', actual 'List<Dish>'. Nothing catches the first. When you want the block's result, use let or run. The third is nested receivers. In tray.apply { timer.apply { minutes = 12 } }, the bare minutes binds to the innermost receiver that has one, timer. Delete minutes from Timer a year later and the same line still compiles, and now it sets tray.minutes. A change in one class has changed code in another. Java's double-brace initialization (an anonymous subclass with a block that sets fields) follows the same rule and has the same trap. Don't nest apply; name the target, as in timer.minutes = 12. The fourth is a nested it. In cakes[id]?.let { tins[it.tinId]?.let { "${it.name}: ${it.sizeCm} cm tin" } }, the second it.name is the tin's name, not the cake's. Java can't make this mistake: it makes you name both lambda parameters and refuses to reuse a name. In Kotlin, name them, or better, flatten the chain: Java Cake cake = cakes.get(id); if (cake == null) return id + ": no tin"; Tin tin = tins.get(cake.tinId()); if (tin == null) return id + ": no tin"; return cake.name() + ": " + tin.sizeCm() + " cm tin"; Kotlin val cake = cakes[id] ?: return "$id: no tin" val tin = tins[cake.tinId] ?: return "$id: no tin" return "${cake.name}: ${tin.sizeCm} cm tin" Each of the four hides behind a null or a nested block. Nulls, then, deserve a closer look. Run the four bugs Read ScopeBugs.kt. For each of the four numbered parts, predict what it prints. Run it. In class Timer, delete var minutes: Int = 0 (leave class Timer). In part 3, change the println to print only tray.minutes. Predict the value, then run. Run ScopeBugsJava.java. Which of the four bugs does Java share, and which can't it have? ScopeBugs.kt package workbench.functional.l06.demo enum class DishStage { PLANNED, COOKING } data class Plate(val id: String, val servings: Int, val stage: DishStage) class MiniMenu { private val onMenu = mutableSetOf<String>() /** Returns a slot id, or null when this dish is on the menu already. */ fun add(p: Plate): String? = if (onMenu.add(p.id)) "slot-${p.id}" else null } fun planOpen(open: Plate?, menu: MiniMenu, suggest: () -> Plate): String? = open?.let { menu.add(it) } ?: run { println(" no dish open, downloading a suggestion") menu.add(suggest()) } class Timer { var minutes: Int = 0 } class Tray { var minutes: Int = 0; val timer = Timer() } data class Cake(val name: String, val tinId: String) data class Tin(val name: String, val sizeCm: Int) fun main() { val soup = Plate("d1", 4, DishStage.PLANNED) println("1. ?.let { } ?: run { }") val menu = MiniMenu() println(" first plan: ${planOpen(soup, menu) { soup }}") println(" second plan: ${planOpen(soup, menu) { soup }}") println("2. also and apply drop the block's result") val cooking = soup.also { it.copy(stage = DishStage.COOKING) } println(" stage after also { copy }: ${cooking.stage}") val total = listOf(soup, soup).apply { sumOf { it.servings } } println(" total from apply { sumOf }: $total") println("3. nested apply") val tray = Tray().apply { timer.apply { minutes = 12 } } println(" tray.minutes = ${tray.minutes}, tray.timer.minutes = ${tray.timer.minutes}") println("4. nested it") val cakes = mapOf("k-1" to Cake("Lemon drizzle", "round-23")) val tins = mapOf("round-23" to Tin("springform", 23)) val label = cakes["k-1"]?.let { tins[it.tinId]?.let { "${it.name}: ${it.sizeCm} cm tin" } } println(" label: $label") } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l06.demo.ScopeBugsKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l06/demo/ScopeBugs.kt ScopeBugsJava.java package workbench.functional.l06.demo; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Optional; import java.util.Set; import java.util.function.Supplier; import java.util.stream.Stream; /** The same four bugs, as close as Java gets. Three of them exist in Java too; one Java's compiler prevents. */ public class ScopeBugsJava { enum Stage { PLANNED, COOKING } record Plate(String id, int servings, Stage stage) { Plate withStage(Stage s) { return new Plate(id, servings, s); } } static class MiniMenu { private final Set<String> onMenu = new HashSet<>(); /** Returns a slot id, or null when this dish is on the menu already. */ String add(Plate p) { return onMenu.add(p.id()) ? "slot-" + p.id() : null; } } static String planOpen(Plate open, MiniMenu menu, Supplier<Plate> suggest) { // Optional.map turns a null result into empty, so orElseGet runs: the same trap as ?.let ?: run return Optional.ofNullable(open).map(menu::add).orElseGet(() -> { System.out.println(" no dish open, downloading a suggestion"); return menu.add(suggest.get()); }); } static class Timer { int minutes; } static class Tray { int minutes; Timer timer = new Timer(); } record Cake(String name, String tinId) {} record Tin(String name, int sizeCm) {} public static void main(String[] args) { Plate soup = new Plate("d1", 4, Stage.PLANNED); System.out.println("1. Optional.map(...).orElseGet(...)"); MiniMenu menu = new MiniMenu(); System.out.println(" first plan: " + planOpen(soup, menu, () -> soup)); System.out.println(" second plan: " + planOpen(soup, menu, () -> soup)); System.out.println("2. peek drops the block's result, like also"); Plate cooking = Stream.of(soup).peek(p -> p.withStage(Stage.COOKING)).findFirst().orElseThrow(); System.out.println(" stage after peek { withStage }: " + cooking.stage()); System.out.println("3. double-brace initialization, Java's nested apply"); Tray tray = new Tray() {{ timer = new Timer() {{ minutes = 12; }}; }}; System.out.println(" tray.minutes = " + tray.minutes + ", tray.timer.minutes = " + tray.timer.minutes); System.out.println("4. Java makes you name both lambda parameters, and refuses to reuse a name"); Map<String, Cake> cakes = Map.of("k-1", new Cake("Lemon drizzle", "round-23")); Map<String, Tin> tins = Map.of("round-23", new Tin("springform", 23)); String label = Optional.ofNullable(cakes.get("k-1")) .flatMap(cake -> Optional.ofNullable(tins.get(cake.tinId())) .map(tin -> cake.name() + ": " + tin.sizeCm() + " cm tin")) .orElse(null); System.out.println(" label: " + label); } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l06.demo.ScopeBugsJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l06/demo/ScopeBugsJava.java The second plan prints no dish open, downloading a suggestion and then null, although a dish was open: the let block returned null, so run ran too. also { copy } leaves the stage PLANNED, and apply { sumOf } prints the list. The nested apply gives tray.minutes = 0, tray.timer.minutes = 12; after you delete Timer.minutes, the unchanged line sets tray.minutes = 12 and the compiler says nothing. The label is springform: 23 cm tin, the tin's name. Java shares the first three (orElseGet, peek, double-brace initialization) and gets the label right, Lemon drizzle: 23 cm tin, because both parameters have names. h: Scope functions: let, run, with, apply and also, on purpose · Nulls are values: ?., ?:, takeIf and requireNotNull
x: A Java developer new to Kotlin often reaches for Optional, Java's box that holds one value or nothing. You don't need it. A nullable type such as String?, a type whose values may be null, is not a box. In the words of the Kotlin docs, "at runtime, objects of nullable types and objects of non-nullable types are treated the same": the checks all happen at compile time. The operators do what Optional's methods do, with no extra object: Java Optional Kotlin opt.map(f) x?.let(f) or x?.f() opt.orElse(d) x ?: d opt.orElseGet(() -> ...) x ?: run { ... }, also lazy opt.orElseThrow() x ?: throw ... or requireNotNull(x) opt.filter(p) x?.takeIf(p) opt.ifPresent(c) x?.let(c) or x?.also(c) The right side of ?: can return or throw, because both are expressions in Kotlin. That turns a guard clause into one line, and every line after it works with a non-null value: Java String favorite = guest == null ? null : guest.favorite(); if (favorite == null) return "no favorite known: serve soup"; Kotlin val favorite = guest?.favorite ?: return "no favorite known: serve soup" takeIf { } is a filter for one value: the value if the test holds, null if not. It earns its place inside a chain, as in grams.takeIf { it > 0 }?.let(::weighOut). As a guard on its own, a plain if reads better. The test always runs, so keep side effects out of it. For collections, mapNotNull { } maps and drops the nulls in one pass. When a null means somebody broke a rule, fail loudly and say why. requireNotNull(x) { "..." } throws IllegalArgumentException, for bad input from a caller. checkNotNull(x) { "..." } throws IllegalStateException, for our own broken state. Both carry a contract that tells the compiler x isn't null afterwards, so x is smart-cast from the next line on: the compiler treats it as the non-null type, because it can prove nothing changed in between. !! throws a NullPointerException with no message at all. Java's Objects.requireNonNull(x, "...") takes a message but still throws NullPointerException. A null that means a broken rule should fail loudly. Use requireNotNull or checkNotNull, with a message, not !!. Smart casts have one limit you'll hit. A var property is never smart-cast, because other code could change it between the check and the use. In the app's Scale class, if (lastReading != null) show(lastReading) fails with Smart cast to 'Int' is impossible, because 'lastReading' is a mutable property that could be mutated concurrently. This is where ?.let is the right tool: lastReading?.let(show) reads the property once. val reading = lastReading ?: return works too. Arrow, the library in the next lesson, gives the same advice about its own Option type: "Typically, when working in Kotlin, you should prefer working with nullable types over Option as it is more idiomatic." It keeps Option for nested nullability in generic code and for libraries that don't allow null values. That's the whole toolbox. The last section folds it into a checklist. Four null tools, two languages Run NullTools.kt, then NullToolsJava.java. Compare the exception each null check throws. In Scale.report, uncomment the if line and run. Read the error, then comment it out again. Change the first line of starterFor to val favorite = requireNotNull(guest?.favorite) { "no favorite" }. Predict what happens to the second call in main. Is that better or worse here? NullTools.kt package workbench.functional.l06.demo data class Guest(val name: String, val favorite: String?) data class ShoppingLine(val item: String, val grams: Int?, val note: String?) class Scale { var lastReading: Int? = null fun report(show: (Int) -> Unit) { // Uncomment the next line and run: a var property is never smart-cast, even right after the check. // if (lastReading != null) show(lastReading) lastReading?.let(show) // reads the property once, then works with that value } } fun starterFor(guest: Guest?): String { val favorite = guest?.favorite ?: return "no favorite known: serve soup" // ?. chains, ?: can return return "start with ${favorite.lowercase()}" } fun main() { println(starterFor(Guest("Ana", "Tomato salad"))) println(starterFor(Guest("Ben", null))) println(starterFor(null)) // takeIf: a filter for one value; the result is nullable val grams = 250 println("takeIf positive: ${grams.takeIf { it > 0 }}, takeIf over 1,000: ${grams.takeIf { it > 1_000 }}") // requireNotNull and checkNotNull: a message, the right exception, and a smart cast afterwards val line = ShoppingLine("flour", null, "the strong kind") try { val g = requireNotNull(line.grams) { "shopping line ${line.item} has no amount" } println(g) } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("requireNotNull: ${e::class.simpleName}: ${e.message}") } val scaleUnit: String? = null try { checkNotNull(scaleUnit) { "scale not switched on" } } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("checkNotNull: ${e::class.simpleName}: ${e.message}") } // mapNotNull: transform and drop the nulls in one step val lines = listOf(line, ShoppingLine("sugar", 200, null), ShoppingLine("eggs", null, "free range")) println("notes: ${lines.mapNotNull { it.note }}") val scale = Scale().apply { lastReading = 450 } scale.report { println("the scale says $it g") } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l06.demo.NullToolsKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l06/demo/NullTools.kt NullToolsJava.java package workbench.functional.l06.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.Objects; import java.util.Optional; /** The same null handling with Optional and Objects. Note which exception each check throws. */ public class NullToolsJava { record Guest(String name, String favorite) {} record ShoppingLine(String item, Integer grams, String note) {} static String starterFor(Guest guest) { Optional<String> favorite = Optional.ofNullable(guest).map(Guest::favorite); if (favorite.isEmpty()) return "no favorite known: serve soup"; return "start with " + favorite.get().toLowerCase(); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(starterFor(new Guest("Ana", "Tomato salad"))); System.out.println(starterFor(new Guest("Ben", null))); System.out.println(starterFor(null)); // Optional.filter is the closest thing to takeIf int grams = 250; System.out.println("filter positive: " + Optional.of(grams).filter(g -> g > 0).orElse(null) + ", filter over 1,000: " + Optional.of(grams).filter(g -> g > 1_000).orElse(null)); // Objects.requireNonNull throws NullPointerException; Kotlin's requireNotNull throws IllegalArgumentException ShoppingLine line = new ShoppingLine("flour", null, "the strong kind"); try { Objects.requireNonNull(line.grams(), "shopping line " + line.item() + " has no amount"); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("requireNonNull: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage()); } // mapNotNull: map, then drop the nulls List<ShoppingLine> lines = List.of(line, new ShoppingLine("sugar", 200, null), new ShoppingLine("eggs", null, "free range")); System.out.println("notes: " + lines.stream().map(ShoppingLine::note).filter(Objects::nonNull).toList()); } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l06.demo.NullToolsJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l06/demo/NullToolsJava.java Kotlin prints IllegalArgumentException: shopping line flour has no amount and IllegalStateException: scale not switched on; Java's Objects.requireNonNull prints NullPointerException: shopping line flour has no amount. The if line fails with the smart-cast error, because lastReading is a var property. With requireNotNull, the second call stops main with IllegalArgumentException: no favorite. That's worse here: a guest without a favorite dish is an everyday case, not a bug, so the answer belongs in the return value. The next lesson makes that idea its whole topic.
