h: Scope functions: let, run, with, apply and also, on purpose · A checklist you can run in five seconds
x: When your fingers are about to type a scope function, run down this list and stop at the first line that settles it. Do you need one at all? A plain call, a?.b(), an if on a local val, or val x = y ?: return is often clearer. A scope function with one line inside is often a plain call in costume. Detekt, a tool that checks Kotlin code for style problems, ships UnnecessaryLet and UnnecessaryApply rules for exactly this case. What should the call hand back? The same value: apply or also. Something new: let, run or with. How does the block use the value? Its own members: apply, run, with. Passed to other functions, or the outer this must stay visible: also, let. Is the value nullable? Use ?.let, ?.run, ?.also or ?.apply, never with. If you add ?: something, make sure the block on the left can never produce null. If it can, write if or when. Is the block nested, longer than about five lines, or the third link in a chain? Extract a function or use named vals. The Kotlin docs ask you not to nest scope functions, because "it's easy to get confused about the current context object and value of this or it". Try the list on one line: OvenProgram().apply { name = title }.also { log.info("baking {}", it) }. Line 1 has something to say about the apply: a block with a single assignment is exactly what detekt's UnnecessaryApply flags. Line 2 approves of the also: it's a side step, and the program flows on unchanged, like a note in the kitchen notebook.

h: Scope functions: let, run, with, apply and also, on purpose · Java and Kotlin
x: Set up, log and compute: scope functions vs plain Java Bake.java OvenProgram program = new OvenProgram(); // set up: a variable and setters program.setTemperatureC(bake.temperatureC()); program.setMinutes(bake.minutes()); program.setName(bake.recipe()); log.info("baking {}", program); // a side step is just a statement LocalTime doneAt = start.plusMinutes(program.getMinutes()); // compute String favorite = Optional.ofNullable(guest).map(Guest::favorite) // null check with a message .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("no favorite")); Bake.kt val program = OvenProgram().apply { // set up: this, hands back the program temperatureC = bake.temperatureC minutes = bake.minutes name = bake.recipe }.also { log.info("baking {}", it) } // side step: it, hands back the program val doneAt = program.run { start.plusMinutes(minutes.toLong()) } // compute: this, hands back the time val favorite = requireNotNull(guest?.favorite) { "no favorite" } // null check with a message When the program runs, the two are the same. Every scope function is inlined, so the bytecode is the same local variable, setter calls and statements the Java version has. What differs is what the code tells the reader and what the compiler can check. apply puts the whole setup in one block, so the program is finished when the block ends, and also marks the log line as a side step that hands the value on unchanged. Java needs an Optional object to chain a null check; Kotlin's ?. and requireNotNull exist only at compile time, and requireNotNull smart-casts what follows. Java lambdas have no receiver and can't assign locals. That's why Java has no apply and no val inside also, and also why it can't have the nested-receiver bug.

h: Scope functions: let, run, with, apply and also, on purpose · Worked example
x: Untangle a "cook it again" button The app's "cook it again" button orders the ingredients of a recipe you've made before. shop.order returns null when the shop refuses the order. Here it is written as one expression. Before reading on, find every outcome that ends up in the wrong place. fun cookAgain(cmd: CookAgain): Outcome = recipes.find(cmd.recipeId)?.let { it.takeIf { it.cookedBefore }?.let { shop.order(it.ingredients, cmd.servings) }?.let { Outcome.Ordered(it) } } ?: run { Outcome.NotAvailable(cmd.recipeId) } Outcome cookAgain(CookAgain cmd) { return recipes.find(cmd.recipeId()) // Optional<Recipe> .filter(Recipe::cookedBefore) .map(r -> shop.order(r.ingredients(), cmd.servings())) // null when refused: map makes it empty .<Outcome>map(Outcome.Ordered::new) .orElseGet(() -> new Outcome.NotAvailable(cmd.recipeId())); } Three different failures come out as one. A recipe that doesn't exist, a recipe you've never cooked, and an order the shop refused all become null somewhere in the chain, so ?: run reports all three as NotAvailable. The app tells you the recipe is missing when the shop was only out of eggs. And there are four its with three meanings. Rewrite it top to bottom. 1. Load, and leave early if it's missing. 2. Check the rule. 3. Do the work, and name its failure. 4. Put the happy path last. Each failure now has its own outcome, and no line depends on which it is in scope. fun cookAgain(cmd: CookAgain): Outcome { val recipe = recipes.find(cmd.recipeId) // 1. load ?: return Outcome.NotFound(cmd.recipeId) if (!recipe.cookedBefore) // 2. check the rule return Outcome.NeverCooked(recipe.id) val orderId = shop.order(recipe.ingredients, cmd.servings) // 3. act ?: return Outcome.Refused(recipe.id) return Outcome.Ordered(orderId) // 4. the happy path, last } Outcome cookAgain(CookAgain cmd) { Recipe recipe = recipes.find(cmd.recipeId()).orElse(null); // 1. load if (recipe == null) return new Outcome.NotFound(cmd.recipeId()); if (!recipe.cookedBefore()) // 2. check the rule return new Outcome.NeverCooked(recipe.id()); String orderId = shop.order(recipe.ingredients(), cmd.servings()); // 3. act if (orderId == null) return new Outcome.Refused(recipe.id()); return new Outcome.Ordered(orderId); // 4. the happy path, last } A scope function still has a place here: a side step that must not change the result. also logs the outcome and hands it on unchanged, which is what the reader expects from the word. return Outcome.Ordered(orderId) .also { log.info("cook again: {}", it) } // side step: the value flows through Outcome outcome = new Outcome.Ordered(orderId); log.info("cook again: {}", outcome); // Java: just a statement return outcome;

h: Scope functions: let, run, with, apply and also, on purpose · Lab
x: Fix four scope-function bugs in the meal planner labs/functional/src/main/kotlin/workbench/functional/l06/Planner.kt labs/functional/src/main/kotlin/workbench/functional/l06/Model.kt ./gradlew :functional:test --tests 'workbench.functional.l06.*' Run the tests. Four of ten fail, one for each function in Planner.kt. Read each failure message before you read the code. Model.kt holds the types and needs no changes. planDish: an open dish that is on the menu already must not trigger a download or a second add. Rewrite it without ?: run. startCooking: return the copy marked COOKING. ovenProgram: the recipe's name belongs on program.name, the oven's screen, not on program.timer.name. tinLabel: show the cake's name, not the tin's. Use named values instead of it. Run the tests until all ten pass. Then run the five-second checklist over your four functions. For planDish, decide the dish first (open ?: suggest()), then add it once. ?: return handles the dish that is on the menu already. startCooking is a two-branch if expression. It needs no scope function. In ovenProgram, a nested apply with one line inside can become timer.beep = "long". In tinLabel, two vals, each with ?: return "...", read top to bottom and can't mix up the cake and the tin. All ten tests in ScopeFunctionsTest pass. By the end you can pick let, run, with, apply or also by answering two questions, spot the four scope-function bugs that compile without a warning, and handle nulls with ?., ?:, takeIf and requireNotNull instead of reaching for Optional.

h: Scope functions: let, run, with, apply and also, on purpose · Quiz
x: You set up a new Tray, line it with paper, put twelve cookies on it, and pass the tray on in the same chain. Which scope function fits? let apply run with You want the same tray back, so the chain continues, and the block works on the tray's own members: that's the this, hands-back-the-value cell. let and run would hand back whatever the last line of the block gave. with can't sit in a chain. val size = cake?.let { tins[it.tinId]?.sizeCm } ?: DEFAULT_SIZE. The cake exists, but its tin is missing from the map. What is size? DEFAULT_SIZE null It throws a NullPointerException It doesn't compile, because let can't give null ?: checks the result of the let block, which is null because the tin is missing, so you get DEFAULT_SIZE. Here that's what you want. It's the same mechanism that makes ?.let { } ?: run { } run both branches when the left block gives null for a reason you didn't mean. What does val total: Int = dishes.apply { sumOf { it.servings } } do? Sets total to the sum of the servings Sets total to 0 Throws ClassCastException at run time Fails to compile: Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Int', actual 'List<Dish>'. apply hands back the value it was called on, the list, and drops the block's result. The declared Int type makes the compiler catch it. Without the type, total would quietly be the list. run { sumOf { ... } }, or just sumOf { }, gives the sum. A Scale class has var lastReading: Int?. Which line compiles and uses the reading you checked? if (scale.lastReading != null) show(scale.lastReading) with(scale.lastReading) { show(this) } scale.lastReading?.let { show(it) } scale.lastReading.takeIf { it != null }.let { show(it) } ?.let reads the property once and gives the block a non-null it. The if version fails: a var property is never smart-cast. Inside with, this is still Int?. takeIf returns Int?, and the plain .let hands that nullable value to show, which doesn't compile either. From the sequences lesson: val all = allResults(site) is a sequence { } that fetches pages. The code runs all.also { println("${it.count()} results") }.first { it.minutes < 30 }. What does the site see? Only the pages first needs Every page for count(), then the pages from page 0 again for first Nothing, because also doesn't run on a sequence One pass, then an IllegalStateException on the second read also runs its block right away, and count() is a terminal operation that reads the whole sequence. Then also hands back the same sequence, a recipe, and first runs it again from page 0. A sequence { } can be read twice, so nothing throws; it just fetches twice.

h: Scope functions: let, run, with, apply and also, on purpose · Key terms
x: Scope function One of let, run, with, apply, also: a small inline function that runs a block with one value in hand. Context object The value a scope function is called on. Inside the block it is this or it. Extension function A function you call on a value as if it were one of the value's own methods, written outside its class. Lambda with receiver A lambda of type T.() -> R. Inside it, the T value is this, so its members need no prefix. Contract A promise a function makes to the compiler, such as "I call this block exactly once". The compiler trusts it and doesn't check it. Smart cast The compiler treating a value as a narrower type (for example non-null) after a check, when it can prove nothing changed in between. Elvis operator a ?: b: the value of a if it isn't null, otherwise b. b can be return or throw. Which scope functions hand back the value itself? apply and also. let, run and with hand back the block's result. In which scope functions is the value this? run, with and apply, whose blocks are lambdas with a receiver. In let and also it is it. x?.let { f(it) } ?: g(): x is not null but f(x) returns null. Does g() run? Yes. ?: tests the result of the let block, not x. Why does val label: String; jar.also { label = it.label } compile? also declares the contract callsInPlace(block, EXACTLY_ONCE), so the compiler knows the block runs exactly once, right there. inline alone isn't enough. What does dish.also { it.copy(stage = COOKING) } give back? The original dish. The block's type is (T) -> Unit, so the copy is thrown away. requireNotNull, checkNotNull or !!? requireNotNull: IllegalArgumentException with your message (bad input). checkNotNull: IllegalStateException (bad state). !!: NullPointerException, no message. The first two smart-cast afterwards. Why does if (prop != null) use(prop) fail when prop is a var property? A var property is never smart-cast: it could change between the check and the use. Use prop?.let(::use) or copy it into a local val.

h: Scope functions: let, run, with, apply and also, on purpose · Go deeper
x: Two things are changing around scope functions, and one tool can enforce the checklist for you. The return-value checker. Kotlin 2.3.0 added an Experimental checker that warns when you ignore a function's result. It's off by default; -Xreturn-value-checker=check reports ignored results of functions the standard library marks, and full treats every function as marked. In Kotlin 2.4.21, all six scope functions (the five plus non-extension run) carry @IgnorableReturnValue, so dish.let { it.copy(stage = COOKING) } as a bare statement is not reported. takeIf and takeUnless don't carry it. On the standard library's main branch, after 2.4.21, let, run and with have dropped @IgnorableReturnValue for a new returnsResultOf(block) contract, which Kotlin 2.4.0 introduced as Experimental. With it, the checker can tell x?.let { builder.append(it) } (fine to ignore) from x?.let { "kotlin.$it" } (a value you computed and dropped). Which release will ship that change isn't known yet. apply and also keep @IgnorableReturnValue, so the also { it.copy() } bug stays invisible to the checker. Labels for nested receivers. When you can't avoid a nested receiver, this@label says which one you mean. Two nested apply blocks share the implicit label @apply, so you need your own: tray.apply outer@{ timer.apply { this@outer.minutes = 12 } }. If you need a label, that's usually a sign to flatten the code instead. Detekt. Detekt 1.23.8, the current stable release, has rules for most of the checklist: UnnecessaryLet, UnnecessaryApply (active by default since 1.16.0), AlsoCouldBeApply and UseLet in the style rule set, and NestedScopeFunctions in the complexity rule set. Apart from UnnecessaryApply, they're off until you enable them. UseLet pulls the other way from UnnecessaryLet: it wants if (x != null) f(x) else null written as x?.let { f(it) }. A rule of thumb that satisfies both: use ?.let when the non-null value flows into an expression, and use if on a local val for control flow and for branches with more than one statement.

h: Errors as values: sealed results, Result and Either · Exceptions hide the failures your caller has to handle
x: Here's the recipe app's helper that takes flour from the jar, in both languages: Java int takeFlour(int grams) throws NotEnoughFlourException, PastBestBeforeException; Kotlin fun takeFlour(grams: Int): Int // throws NotEnoughFlourException, PastBestBeforeException Java has checked exceptions: exceptions a method must list in its signature, so the compiler makes every caller deal with them. Kotlin has none. In the words of its docs, "Kotlin treats all exceptions as unchecked by default." So the Kotlin signature says only Int, and nothing tells the caller that the jar runs short every few weeks. A new screen forgets the try. The exception flies up past every caller, and the cook sees "Something went wrong" because the flour ran out. The real problem is that two kinds of failure share one mechanism. An empty jar, an old bag or an amount of -5 is expected: it happens in normal use, and the caller must decide what to do. A null pointer, a broken rule inside our own code or a full disk is a bug or a broken machine, and no caller can do anything useful about it on the spot. The Kotlin team draws the same line. The design notes for kotlin.Result say: "Use nullable types or domain-specific classes to represent failures that need specific handling." The newer rich-errors proposal, KEEP-0441, says exceptions "should be used for unrecoverable cases." So put the expected failures in the return type, as values: Java sealed interface TakeResult {} record Taken(int leftGrams) implements TakeResult {} record Refused(JarFailure reason) implements TakeResult {} TakeResult takeFlour(int grams, int leftGrams, LocalDate bestBefore, LocalDate today); Kotlin sealed interface TakeResult { data class Taken(val leftGrams: Int) : TakeResult data class Refused(val reason: JarFailure) : TakeResult } fun takeFlour(grams: Int, leftGrams: Int, bestBefore: LocalDate, today: LocalDate): TakeResult The jar's contents and today's date are parameters now, as the first lesson of this track taught: a pure function takes its inputs as arguments. And sealed means the compiler knows every subtype, so a when over them needs no else. That pays off when someone adds a case. Add JarMissing to JarFailure, and every when that doesn't handle it stops compiling: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'JarMissing' branch or an 'else' branch. Java 21's sealed interfaces and pattern switch give the same check: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values. That error is the whole point. A sealed result lists every expected failure, and the compiler checks each when. Never add else to a when over a sealed type. Exceptions keep their job for bugs. require, check and error() still belong wherever one of your own rules breaks. A sealed type for one step works well. Chain three of them, and every step needs a when to look at the step before. Add a failure and let the compiler find the gaps Run Exhaustive.kt. Four attempts to take flour come out as four lines of advice. Uncomment JarMissing in JarFailure and run it again. Read the error and note which when it points at. Add a branch for it to advice ("look in the other cupboard" will do) and run again. Do the same in ExhaustiveJava.java. Exhaustive.kt package workbench.functional.l07.demo import java.time.LocalDate /** The expected ways taking flour from the jar can fail. A closed set: the compiler knows every case. */ sealed interface JarFailure { data class InvalidAmount(val grams: Int) : JarFailure data object PastBestBefore : JarFailure data class NotEnough(val shortByGrams: Int) : JarFailure // Uncomment the next line and run again. // data object JarMissing : JarFailure } sealed interface TakeResult { data class Taken(val leftGrams: Int) : TakeResult data class Refused(val reason: JarFailure) : TakeResult } /** The signature now says it can fail, and how. Nothing is thrown for a short jar. */ fun takeFlour(grams: Int, leftGrams: Int, bestBefore: LocalDate, today: LocalDate): TakeResult = when { grams <= 0 -> TakeResult.Refused(JarFailure.InvalidAmount(grams)) today.isAfter(bestBefore) -> TakeResult.Refused(JarFailure.PastBestBefore) grams > leftGrams -> TakeResult.Refused(JarFailure.NotEnough(grams - leftGrams)) else -> TakeResult.Taken(leftGrams - grams) } /** The one place that knows what to tell the cook: an exhaustive when with no else branch. */ fun advice(failure: JarFailure): String = when (failure) { is JarFailure.InvalidAmount -> "check the amount" JarFailure.PastBestBefore -> "open a new bag" is JarFailure.NotEnough -> "buy more flour" } fun main() { val today = LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 10) val fresh = LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 31) val old = LocalDate.of(2026, 2, 28) val attempts = listOf(200 to fresh, -5 to fresh, 200 to old, 1_000 to fresh) for ((grams, bestBefore) in attempts) { val line = when (val result = takeFlour(grams, leftGrams = 700, bestBefore, today)) { is TakeResult.Taken -> "ok: ${result.leftGrams} g left" is TakeResult.Refused -> "${advice(result.reason)}: ${result.reason}" } println(line) } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l07.demo.ExhaustiveKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l07/demo/Exhaustive.kt ExhaustiveJava.java package workbench.functional.l07.demo; import java.time.LocalDate; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** The same closed set of failures with Java 21 sealed interfaces, records and an exhaustive switch. */ public class ExhaustiveJava { sealed interface JarFailure {} record InvalidAmount(int grams) implements JarFailure {} record PastBestBefore() implements JarFailure {} record NotEnough(int shortByGrams) implements JarFailure {} // Uncomment the next line and run again. // record JarMissing() implements JarFailure {} sealed interface TakeResult {} record Taken(int leftGrams) implements TakeResult {} record Refused(JarFailure reason) implements TakeResult {} static TakeResult takeFlour(int grams, int leftGrams, LocalDate bestBefore, LocalDate today) { if (grams <= 0) return new Refused(new InvalidAmount(grams)); if (today.isAfter(bestBefore)) return new Refused(new PastBestBefore()); if (grams > leftGrams) return new Refused(new NotEnough(grams - leftGrams)); return new Taken(leftGrams - grams); } /** The one place that knows what to tell the cook: an exhaustive switch with no default branch. */ static String advice(JarFailure failure) { return switch (failure) { case InvalidAmount a -> "check the amount"; case PastBestBefore p -> "open a new bag"; case NotEnough n -> "buy more flour"; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { LocalDate today = LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 10); LocalDate fresh = LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 31); LocalDate old = LocalDate.of(2026, 2, 28); List<Map.Entry<Integer, LocalDate>> attempts = List.of(Map.entry(200, fresh), Map.entry(-5, fresh), Map.entry(200, old), Map.entry(1_000, fresh)); for (var a : attempts) { String line = switch (takeFlour(a.getKey(), 700, a.getValue(), today)) { case Taken t -> "ok: " + t.leftGrams() + " g left"; case Refused r -> advice(r.reason()) + ": " + r.reason(); }; System.out.println(line); } } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l07.demo.ExhaustiveJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l07/demo/ExhaustiveJava.java The first run prints ok: 500 g left, check the amount: InvalidAmount(grams=-5), open a new bag: PastBestBefore and buy more flour: NotEnough(shortByGrams=300). With the new case, Kotlin stops at advice with 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'JarMissing' branch or an 'else' branch. The when in main still compiles, because it only looks at TakeResult. javac reports the switch expression does not cover all possible input values at the same spot. After you add the branch, both run again. Sealed classes and interfaces (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Errors as values: sealed results, Result and Either · A result type you can write in ten lines
x: One generic type can cover every step. It holds either a success with a value or a failure with an error: Java sealed interface Outcome<E, A> { default <B> Outcome<E, B> andThen(Function<? super A, Outcome<E, B>> f) { return switch (this) { case Ok<E, A> ok -> f.apply(ok.value()); case Err<E, A> err -> new Err<>(err.error()); }; } } record Ok<E, A>(A value) implements Outcome<E, A> {} record Err<E, A>(E error) implements Outcome<E, A> {} Kotlin sealed interface Outcome<out E, out A> { data class Ok<A>(val value: A) : Outcome<Nothing, A> data class Err<E>(val error: E) : Outcome<E, Nothing> } inline fun <E, A, B> Outcome<E, A>.andThen(f: (A) -> Outcome<E, B>): Outcome<E, B> = when (this) { is Outcome.Ok -> f(value); is Outcome.Err -> this } andThen runs the next step only if this one succeeded. An Err skips every later step and comes out at the end unchanged. Its sibling map, in the Try it, does the same for a plain function that can't fail, such as uppercase(). Making a loaf becomes one line: checkBatter(b).andThen(::mix).andThen(::bake).map { it.uppercase() }. Picture the kitchen line from the sequences lesson, with a side door. A good batter walks down the line, step by step. When a step fails, the batter leaves through the side door with a note pinned to it, and the note walks straight to the end of the line, past every step still waiting. Programmers draw the same idea as a railway with two tracks, success on top and failure below, which is why the style is called railway-oriented programming. The figure shows it. Look at the variance. Outcome<out E, out A> is covariant in both parameters: an Outcome of a subtype counts as an Outcome of its supertype ("Covariance with out: producers" in the generics track). And Err is an Outcome<E, Nothing>. Nothing is the type with no values at all, and it's a subtype of every type. So an Err<BakeErr> already is an Outcome<BakeErr, String>, an Outcome<BakeErr, Loaf>, an Outcome<BakeErr, X> for any X. That's why is Outcome.Err -> this compiles without building a new object. Java has no declaration-site variance (variance written once, on the type itself) and no Nothing, so the Java version builds a new Err at every step. The kitchen picture breaks at one point. A cook who gets a note can still decide to carry on with a second-best dish; this line never does. Once a value is an Err, nothing after it runs, unless you write a step that looks for errors on purpose. Arrow, later in this lesson, calls that step recover. That's all an Either is at heart: a value that holds one of two things, an error or a result. Libraries add more helpers, and a block syntax that makes chains read like straight-line code. Before we get there, the standard library ships one result type of its own, and it was built for a different job. Walk a batter down the line Read Outcome.kt. Each step prints its name when it runs. For each of the three batters, predict which names print and what comes out. Run it, then run OutcomeJava.java. In Outcome.kt, change is Outcome.Err -> this in map to is Outcome.Err -> Outcome.Err(error). Does it still compile? Why was this allowed? Outcome.kt package workbench.functional.l07.demo /** A hand-written result type: a success holding a value, or a failure holding an error. */ sealed interface Outcome<out E, out A> { data class Ok<A>(val value: A) : Outcome<Nothing, A> data class Err<E>(val error: E) : Outcome<E, Nothing> } /** Change the value on the success track; a failure passes through untouched. */ inline fun <E, A, B> Outcome<E, A>.map(f: (A) -> B): Outcome<E, B> = when (this) { is Outcome.Ok -> Outcome.Ok(f(value)); is Outcome.Err -> this } /** Run the next step that can fail, only on the success track. */ inline fun <E, A, B> Outcome<E, A>.andThen(f: (A) -> Outcome<E, B>): Outcome<E, B> = when (this) { is Outcome.Ok -> f(value); is Outcome.Err -> this } sealed interface BakeErr { data class Invalid(val why: String) : BakeErr data object BowlTooSmall : BakeErr } data class Batter(val flourGrams: Int) fun checkBatter(b: Batter): Outcome<BakeErr, Batter> { println(" check") return if (b.flourGrams > 0) Outcome.Ok(b) else Outcome.Err(BakeErr.Invalid("flour<=0")) } fun mix(b: Batter): Outcome<BakeErr, String> { println(" mix") return if (b.flourGrams <= 1_000) Outcome.Ok("dough") else Outcome.Err(BakeErr.BowlTooSmall) } fun bake(dough: String): Outcome<BakeErr, String> { println(" bake") return Outcome.Ok("loaf from $dough") } fun makeLoaf(b: Batter) = checkBatter(b).andThen(::mix).andThen(::bake).map { it.uppercase() } fun main() { for (b in listOf(Batter(500), Batter(-1), Batter(5_000))) { println("$b:") println(" -> ${makeLoaf(b)}") } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l07.demo.OutcomeKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l07/demo/Outcome.kt OutcomeJava.java package workbench.functional.l07.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Function; /** The same result type in Java 21. Without declaration-site variance and Nothing, Err must be rebuilt each step. */ public class OutcomeJava { sealed interface Outcome<E, A> { default <B> Outcome<E, B> map(Function<? super A, ? extends B> f) { return switch (this) { case Ok<E, A> ok -> new Ok<>(f.apply(ok.value())); case Err<E, A> err -> new Err<>(err.error()); // a new Err with a new type }; } default <B> Outcome<E, B> andThen(Function<? super A, Outcome<E, B>> f) { return switch (this) { case Ok<E, A> ok -> f.apply(ok.value()); case Err<E, A> err -> new Err<>(err.error()); }; } } record Ok<E, A>(A value) implements Outcome<E, A> {} record Err<E, A>(E error) implements Outcome<E, A> {} sealed interface BakeErr {} record Invalid(String why) implements BakeErr {} record BowlTooSmall() implements BakeErr {} record Batter(int flourGrams) {} static Outcome<BakeErr, Batter> check(Batter b) { System.out.println(" check"); return b.flourGrams() > 0 ? new Ok<>(b) : new Err<>(new Invalid("flour<=0")); } static Outcome<BakeErr, String> mix(Batter b) { System.out.println(" mix"); return b.flourGrams() <= 1_000 ? new Ok<>("dough") : new Err<>(new BowlTooSmall()); } static Outcome<BakeErr, String> bake(String dough) { System.out.println(" bake"); return new Ok<>("loaf from " + dough); } static Outcome<BakeErr, String> makeLoaf(Batter b) { return check(b).andThen(OutcomeJava::mix).andThen(OutcomeJava::bake).map(String::toUpperCase); } public static void main(String[] args) { for (Batter b : List.of(new Batter(500), new Batter(-1), new Batter(5_000))) { System.out.println(b + ":"); System.out.println(" -> " + makeLoaf(b)); } } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l07.demo.OutcomeJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l07/demo/OutcomeJava.java Batter(flourGrams=500) runs all three steps and gives Ok(value=LOAF FROM DOUGH). Batter(flourGrams=-1) prints only check and gives Err(error=Invalid(why=flour<=0)). Batter(flourGrams=5000) prints check and mix and gives Err(error=BowlTooSmall): bake never runs. Java prints the same steps. Both versions of the Err branch compile; this works because an Outcome<E, Nothing> is already an Outcome<E, B> for every B, so there's no need to build a new object. Each step either keeps the batter on the success track or switches it to the failure track, where its note rides to the end untouched.

h: Errors as values: sealed results, Result and Either · kotlin.Result wraps code that throws, and swallows cancellation
x: The standard library has one result type, kotlin.Result<T>, and runCatching { } makes one: it runs the block and catches whatever the block throws. Result isn't an Either. It has a single type parameter, and the failure is always a Throwable, the parent class of every exception and error on the JVM. Its design notes are blunt: "The Result class is not designed to represent domain-specific error conditions." It was built mainly for the coroutine machinery: Continuation.resumeWith takes a Result. Use it at the edge, around code that throws when you'd rather have a value. Here the app reads a recipe file that a user imported, and falls back to an empty recipe when the file is broken: Java Recipe recipe; try { recipe = importer.parse(file); } // a Java library that throws catch (Exception e) { recipe = Recipe.EMPTY; } Kotlin val recipe = runCatching { importer.parse(file) } // a Java library that throws .getOrElse { Recipe.EMPTY } Two traps come with it. The first is that runCatching catches every Throwable. It catches everything you throw at it, including the message that tells it to stop. That covers OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError, and inside a coroutine it covers CancellationException, the exception that carries a cancel. A coroutine is a light task that can pause while it waits, without holding on to a thread, and you cancel one to say "stop, nobody wants the answer any more" ("Cancellation and timeouts" in the coroutines track). The Try it cancels a coroutine while it waits for the shop inside runCatching. The cancel turns into a failed Result. The coroutine runs on until its next suspension point, the next place where it could pause, and the line that places the order runs. An issue asking kotlinx.coroutines for a runCatching that rethrows CancellationException (#1814) has been open since February 2020. Until something ships, rethrow it yourself, as the lab asks: Java // Java equivalent: never swallow the interrupt that carries a stop request try { return shop.ask(item); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); throw new CancellationException(); } Kotlin runCatching { shop.ask(item) } // a suspend call that waits for the shop .onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it } // a cancel keeps travelling The second trap is that map doesn't catch. runCatching { "12".toInt() }.map { error("boom") } throws IllegalStateException: boom straight out of map. Only mapCatching turns it into Failure(java.lang.IllegalStateException: boom). The library pairs recover and recoverCatching the same way. If a chain should be safe from end to end, every step that can throw needs the Catching variant. So Result answers one question: did this throwing call work? It can't say which kitchen failure happened. fun order(item: Ingredient): Result<Delivery> tells the caller less than the sealed type from the first section. Keep runCatching at the edge, around code that throws. Let CancellationException through. For our own failures we want the railway back, with a nicer shape. That's Arrow's Either, and it brings a second mode the railway never had. Cancel an order inside runCatching Read part 1 of RunCatchingTrap.kt. The coroutine is cancelled after 50 ms, while it waits for the shop inside runCatching. Predict: does placing the order anyway print, and what's in orders? Run it and compare part 1 with part 2. Read part 3 and predict which line throws. Run RunCatchingTrapJava.java, which makes the same mistake with a thread and catch (Exception e). RunCatchingTrap.kt package workbench.functional.l07.demo import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.isActive import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException fun main() = runBlocking<Unit> { println("1. runCatching around a suspend call, cancelled after 50 ms:") val placed = mutableListOf<String>() val swallowing = launch { val r = runCatching { delay(1_000); "basket-1" } // waiting for the shop to answer println(" runCatching returned: isFailure=${r.isFailure} ex=${r.exceptionOrNull()?.javaClass?.simpleName}") println(" isActive after swallow = $isActive") placed += "placed the order" println(" placing the order anyway (code with no suspension point keeps running)") try { delay(1) } catch (e: CancellationException) { println(" next suspension point throws: ${e.javaClass.simpleName}") throw e } } delay(50) swallowing.cancelAndJoin() println(" orders: $placed") println("2. the same, with CancellationException rethrown:") val placed2 = mutableListOf<String>() val rethrowing = launch { val r = runCatching { delay(1_000); "basket-1" }.onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it } placed2 += "placed the order ($r)" } delay(50) rethrowing.cancelAndJoin() println(" cancelled=${rethrowing.isCancelled}, orders: $placed2") println("3. map rethrows, mapCatching captures:") val parsed = runCatching { "12".toInt() } println(" mapCatching: ${parsed.mapCatching { error("boom") }}") try { parsed.map { error("boom") } } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println(" map threw: IllegalStateException: ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l07.demo.RunCatchingTrapKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l07/demo/RunCatchingTrap.kt RunCatchingTrapJava.java package workbench.functional.l07.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; /** * Java equivalent of RunCatchingTrap.kt: a catch-everything block around a blocking call swallows the * interrupt, the thread's stop signal, and the code after it places the order anyway. */ public class RunCatchingTrapJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.println("1. catch (Exception e) around sleep, interrupted after 50 ms:"); List<String> placed = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); Thread swallowing = new Thread(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(1_000); // waiting for the shop } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println(" caught " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ", carrying on"); } placed.add("placed the order"); }); swallowing.start(); Thread.sleep(50); swallowing.interrupt(); swallowing.join(); System.out.println(" orders: " + placed); System.out.println("2. the same, with the interrupt restored and the work stopped:"); List<String> placed2 = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); Thread stopping = new Thread(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(1_000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // keep the signal return; // and stop } placed2.add("placed the order"); }); stopping.start(); Thread.sleep(50); stopping.interrupt(); stopping.join(); System.out.println(" orders: " + placed2); } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l07.demo.RunCatchingTrapJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l07/demo/RunCatchingTrapJava.java Part 1 prints runCatching returned: isFailure=true ex=JobCancellationException, isActive after swallow = false, then placing the order anyway, and only the next delay throws. orders holds placed the order: work ran after the cancel. h: Errors as values: sealed results, Result and Either · Arrow's Either: stop at the first error, or collect every one
x: Errors as values: fail fast stops at the first error, collecting runs every check, and runCatching swallows the cancel Arrow is a functional programming library for Kotlin, and the lab uses arrow-core 2.3.0. Its Either<E, A> is the Outcome from earlier, Left(error) or Right(value), plus an either { } block that replaces chains of andThen. Here's the lab's grocery order: reserve the ingredient at the shop, check that the delivery arrives in time, then book it: Java // Java equivalent: the hand-written Outcome from earlier, chained with andThen Outcome<KitchenError, Delivery> order(Ingredient ingredient, Shop shop) { return shop.reserve(ingredient).andThen(basketId -> { int minutes = shop.deliveryMinutes(basketId); if (minutes >= LATEST_MINUTES) return new Err<>(new TooLate(minutes)); return shop.book(basketId).map(slotId -> new Delivery(basketId, slotId)); }); } Kotlin fun order(ingredient: Ingredient, shop: Shop): Either<KitchenError, Delivery> = either { val basketId = shop.reserve(ingredient).bind() // a Left ends the block here val minutes = shop.deliveryMinutes(basketId) ensure(minutes < LATEST_MINUTES) { KitchenError.TooLate(minutes) } val slotId = shop.book(basketId).bind() Delivery(basketId, slotId) } Inside either { }, .bind() unwraps a Right. On a Left it stops the block, and that Left becomes the result. ensure(condition) { error } stops the block when the condition is false. The code reads top to bottom like the happy path, and it is fail-fast: the first failure wins, and nothing after it runs. Fail-fast is right for a line of steps where each needs the one before. It's wrong for a form. A cook who types an amount of -5 with the unit oz (the scale was left on ounces again) should hear about both at once, not one per try. zipOrAccumulate runs independent checks, collects every failure into a NonEmptyList, a list that always holds at least one item, and calls its last lambda only if all of them passed: Java // Java equivalent: run every check and collect the errors by hand Validated<Amount> accumulate(int a, String u) { List<FormError> errors = new ArrayList<>(); if (a <= 0) errors.add(new InvalidAmount(a)); if (!UNITS.contains(u)) errors.add(new UnsupportedUnit(u)); return errors.isEmpty() ? new Valid<>(new Amount(a, u)) : new Invalid<>(List.copyOf(errors)); } Kotlin fun accumulate(a: Int, u: String): Either<NonEmptyList<FormError>, Amount> = either { zipOrAccumulate({ validAmount(a) }, { validUnit(u) }) { amount, unit -> Amount(amount, unit) } } // accumulate(-5, "oz") is Either.Left([InvalidAmount(amount=-5), UnsupportedUnit(unit=oz)]) validAmount and validUnit are functions with a Raise<FormError> receiver, so the ensure inside them can stop whichever block called them. The same input through a plain either { Amount(validAmount(-5), validUnit("oz")) } gives only Either.Left(InvalidAmount(amount=-5)). Stop at the first error when each step needs the one before. Collect every error when the checks don't depend on each other. For code that throws, Either.catch { } is the safer cousin of runCatching. It turns an ordinary exception into a Left, but it rethrows CancellationException and fatal errors such as OutOfMemoryError. You may have read that Kotlin is getting error unions, fun load(): Recipe | NotFound. That's a real proposal (KEEP-0441, with the detailed design in KEEP-0462), but it isn't in Kotlin 2.4.21: the compiler rejects error class NotFound with Syntax error: Expecting a top level declaration. Today the picker is short. Use a nullable type when absence needs no reason. Use a sealed type for a few outcomes of one function. Use Either when many steps chain or errors must be collected. Keep Result for code that throws, and exceptions for bugs. Fail fast, then collect everything Read EitherDemo.kt. Predict what failFast(-5, "oz") and accumulate(-5, "oz") print. Run it. Change accumulate(-5, "oz") to accumulate(250, "oz"). Predict the result, then run it. Run EitherDemoJava.java and compare how much code the Java version needs per rule. EitherDemo.kt package workbench.functional.l07.demo import arrow.core.Either import arrow.core.NonEmptyList import arrow.core.raise.Raise import arrow.core.raise.either import arrow.core.raise.ensure import arrow.core.raise.zipOrAccumulate import kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException sealed interface FormError { data class InvalidAmount(val amount: Int) : FormError data class UnsupportedUnit(val unit: String) : FormError } data class Amount(val amount: Int, val unit: String) fun Raise<FormError>.validAmount(a: Int): Int { ensure(a > 0) { FormError.InvalidAmount(a) } return a } fun Raise<FormError>.validUnit(u: String): String { ensure(u in setOf("g", "ml", "pcs")) { FormError.UnsupportedUnit(u) } return u } /** Stops at the first failure: the second check never runs. */ fun failFast(a: Int, u: String): Either<FormError, Amount> = either { Amount(validAmount(a), validUnit(u)) } /** Runs every check and collects every failure. */ fun accumulate(a: Int, u: String): Either<NonEmptyList<FormError>, Amount> = either { zipOrAccumulate({ validAmount(a) }, { validUnit(u) }) { amount, unit -> Amount(amount, unit) } } fun main() { println("fail fast: ${failFast(-5, "oz")}") println("accumulate: ${accumulate(-5, "oz")}") println("all good: ${accumulate(250, "g")}") println("Either.catch around code that throws:") println(" ${Either.catch { "2OO".toInt() }.mapLeft { it::class.simpleName }}") // the letter O, twice try { Either.catch { throw CancellationException("shopping cancelled") } } catch (e: CancellationException) { println(" CancellationException rethrown, not captured") } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l07.demo.EitherDemoKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l07/demo/EitherDemo.kt EitherDemoJava.java package workbench.functional.l07.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; /** Java equivalent: the JDK has no Either. A small sealed result and a list of errors do both jobs by hand. */ public class EitherDemoJava { sealed interface FormError {} record InvalidAmount(int amount) implements FormError {} record UnsupportedUnit(String unit) implements FormError {} record Amount(int amount, String unit) {} sealed interface Validated<A> {} record Valid<A>(A value) implements Validated<A> {} record Invalid<A>(List<FormError> errors) implements Validated<A> {} static final Set<String> UNITS = Set.of("g", "ml", "pcs"); /** Stops at the first failure: the second check never runs. */ static Validated<Amount> failFast(int a, String u) { if (a <= 0) return new Invalid<>(List.of(new InvalidAmount(a))); if (!UNITS.contains(u)) return new Invalid<>(List.of(new UnsupportedUnit(u))); return new Valid<>(new Amount(a, u)); } /** Runs every check and collects every failure. */ static Validated<Amount> accumulate(int a, String u) { List<FormError> errors = new ArrayList<>(); if (a <= 0) errors.add(new InvalidAmount(a)); if (!UNITS.contains(u)) errors.add(new UnsupportedUnit(u)); return errors.isEmpty() ? new Valid<>(new Amount(a, u)) : new Invalid<>(List.copyOf(errors)); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("fail fast: " + failFast(-5, "oz")); System.out.println("accumulate: " + accumulate(-5, "oz")); System.out.println("all good: " + accumulate(250, "g")); } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l07.demo.EitherDemoJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l07/demo/EitherDemoJava.java fail fast: Either.Left(InvalidAmount(amount=-5)): the unit check never ran. accumulate: Either.Left([InvalidAmount(amount=-5), UnsupportedUnit(unit=oz)]). With a good amount, only Either.Left([UnsupportedUnit(unit=oz)]) remains: still a list, now with one item. Either.catch turns "2OO".toInt(), typed with two letter Os, into Either.Left(NumberFormatException) and lets the CancellationException through. Java prints the same results with a hand-built list. h: Errors as values: sealed results, Result and Either · Java and Kotlin
x: A fail-fast grocery order: Java sealed result vs Kotlin either { } Order.java sealed interface Outcome<E, A> { /* map and andThen as in section 2 */ } record Ok<E, A>(A value) implements Outcome<E, A> {} record Err<E, A>(E error) implements Outcome<E, A> {} Outcome<KitchenError, Delivery> order(Ingredient ingredient, Shop shop) { return shop.reserve(ingredient).andThen(basketId -> { // 1. reserve int minutes = shop.deliveryMinutes(basketId); // 2. check the time if (minutes >= LATEST_MINUTES) return new Err<>(new TooLate(minutes)); return shop.book(basketId) // 3. book .map(slotId -> new Delivery(basketId, slotId)); }); } Order.kt fun order(ingredient: Ingredient, shop: Shop): Either<KitchenError, Delivery> = either { val basketId = shop.reserve(ingredient).bind() // 1. reserve val minutes = shop.deliveryMinutes(basketId) // 2. check the time ensure(minutes < LATEST_MINUTES) { KitchenError.TooLate(minutes) } val slotId = shop.book(basketId).bind() // 3. book Delivery(basketId, slotId) } Both are the same railway: the first Err or Left ends the pipeline and comes back unchanged, and the sealed error type keeps every when or switch over it exhaustive. The differences are in how it reads and what the library brings. Java nests a lambda per step, so a five-step pipeline drifts to the right, and every Err has to be rebuilt because Java has no Nothing and no declaration-site variance. Kotlin's either { } keeps the steps flat: bind() and ensure stop the block with the error, so the code reads like the happy path. Arrow also brings what the hand-written version lacks: zipOrAccumulate and mapOrAccumulate for collecting errors, Either.catch that lets cancellation through, and mapLeft and recover for translating errors between layers.

h: Errors as values: sealed results, Result and Either · Worked example
x: Layer the "order it" button: check everything, then stop at the first failure The cook types an ingredient line and taps "order it". 1. Check the line at the edge and collect every problem, so the cook fixes the whole line at once. The lab's validate returns Either<NonEmptyList<KitchenError>, Ingredient>. val checked: Either<NonEmptyList<KitchenError>, Ingredient> = validate(form) // IngredientForm("fl0ur", -5, "oz", "") gives Left([InvalidName(name=fl0ur), InvalidAmount(amount=-5), UnsupportedUnit(unit=oz)]) Validated<Ingredient> checked = validate(form); // every rule runs; the errors are collected if (checked instanceof Invalid<Ingredient> invalid) return showProblems(invalid.errors()); Run the shop steps fail-fast, and give the two kinds of error one type so the button can show either. mapLeft changes the error side and leaves a Right alone. sealed interface ScreenError { data class Invalid(val errors: NonEmptyList<KitchenError>) : ScreenError data class Failed(val error: KitchenError) : ScreenError } fun orderIt(form: IngredientForm, shop: Shop): Either<ScreenError, Delivery> = either { val ingredient = validate(form).mapLeft(ScreenError::Invalid).bind() // every line error at once order(ingredient, shop).mapLeft(ScreenError::Failed).bind() // the first shop failure } sealed interface ScreenError {} record InvalidLine(List<KitchenError> errors) implements ScreenError {} record Failed(KitchenError error) implements ScreenError {} Outcome<ScreenError, Delivery> orderIt(IngredientForm form, Shop shop) { return switch (validate(form)) { case Invalid<Ingredient> invalid -> new Err<>(new InvalidLine(invalid.errors())); // every line error case Valid<Ingredient> valid -> switch (order(valid.value(), shop)) { // the first shop failure case Ok<KitchenError, Delivery> ok -> new Ok<>(ok.value()); case Err<KitchenError, Delivery> err -> new Err<>(new Failed(err.error())); }; }; } At the outer edge, the shop's own client library throws when the network gives up. Turn the one failure that means something to the cook into a value, and let everything else fly. A SocketTimeoutException (the network call gave up waiting) becomes ShopClosed, which the screen can show; an IllegalStateException is a bug and must stay an exception. fun ShopClient.reserveSafely(body: String): Either<KitchenError, String> = Either.catch { post(body) } // rethrows CancellationException and fatal errors .mapLeft { e -> if (e is SocketTimeoutException) KitchenError.ShopClosed else throw e } Outcome<KitchenError, String> reserveSafely(ShopClient client, String body) throws IOException { try { return new Ok<>(client.post(body)); } catch (SocketTimeoutException e) { return new Err<>(new ShopClosed()); // the one failure that means something to the cook } // other exceptions fly on: a bug stays a bug } Turn errors into screen messages in exactly one place, with an exhaustive when and no else. When someone adds a KitchenError case next year, this function stops compiling until they decide what the cook should read. fun message(error: ScreenError): String = when (error) { is ScreenError.Invalid -> "Please fix ${error.errors.size} things in this line" is ScreenError.Failed -> when (error.error) { KitchenError.OutOfStock -> "The shop is out of it" is KitchenError.TooLate -> "It would arrive after your guests" KitchenError.ShopClosed -> "The shop isn't answering, try later" is KitchenError.InvalidName, is KitchenError.InvalidAmount, is KitchenError.UnsupportedUnit, is KitchenError.NoteTooLong -> "Please check this line" } } String message(ScreenError error) { return switch (error) { case InvalidLine i -> "Please fix " + i.errors().size() + " things in this line"; case Failed f -> switch (f.error()) { case OutOfStock o -> "The shop is out of it"; case TooLate t -> "It would arrive after your guests"; case ShopClosed c -> "The shop isn't answering, try later"; case InvalidName n -> "Please check this line"; case InvalidAmount a -> "Please check this line"; case UnsupportedUnit u -> "Please check this line"; case NoteTooLong l -> "Please check this line"; }; }; }

h: Errors as values: sealed results, Result and Either · Quiz
x: Running out of flour must be handled by every caller of takeFlour. Which signature says so in a way the compiler can check? fun takeFlour(grams: Int): Int, with a KDoc saying it throws NotEnoughFlourException fun takeFlour(grams: Int): Result<Int> fun takeFlour(grams: Int): Int? fun takeFlour(grams: Int): Either<JarFailure, Int>, where JarFailure is sealed Only the Either with a sealed error type names the possible failures, and a when over JarFailure is checked for every case. The exception is invisible to the compiler. Result's failure is any Throwable, so it says nothing about flour. A nullable return drops the reason entirely. Inside launch, a coroutine runs val r = runCatching { shop.ask(item) } (a suspend call) and then orders.add(entry), which doesn't suspend. The job is cancelled while ask waits. What happens? add never runs: cancellation stops the coroutine at once r is a failure holding a CancellationException, and add runs runCatching rethrows CancellationException by itself The cancel is ignored until ask returns its value runCatching catches every Throwable, so the cancel becomes a failed Result. The coroutine is still cancelled, but code without a suspension point keeps running, so the order is added after the cancel. Rethrow CancellationException, or use Either.catch, which does it for you. runCatching { parse(text) }.map { toRecipe(it) }. parse succeeds, but toRecipe throws IllegalArgumentException for a bad field. What does the expression do? Throws the IllegalArgumentException out of map Returns a Failure holding the IllegalArgumentException Returns the original Success Returns Success(null) map changes a success but doesn't catch exceptions from its lambda. Only mapCatching captures them as a Failure. A chain that should be safe from end to end needs the Catching variant on every step that can throw. A form line has an amount of -5 and the unit oz. What does either { Amount(validAmount(a), validUnit(u)) } return? Left with both errors It throws on the first error Left(InvalidAmount(...)) only Left(UnsupportedUnit(...)) only either { } is fail-fast. Arguments are evaluated left to right, validAmount raises first, the block stops, and validUnit never runs. To report both, use zipOrAccumulate, which runs every check and returns Left with a NonEmptyList of all the errors. From the scope functions lesson: open?.let { menu.add(it) } ?: run { menu.add(suggest()) } ran both branches when add returned null for a dish on the menu already. Now add returns Either<MenuError, SlotId>. Can both branches still run? Yes, whenever add returns a Left No: an Either is never null, so run runs only when open is null It no longer compiles Only when add throws ?: fires only on null. An Either is always a value, Left or Right, so the left side is null only when no dish is open. Errors as values removed the accidental overlap between "no result" and "nothing there". The dish on the menu already is now a Left the caller can see and handle.

h: Errors as values: sealed results, Result and Either · Key terms
x: Exception An object a function throws to say something failed. It travels up through the callers until some code catches it. Checked exception In Java, an exception a method must list in its signature, so the compiler makes callers handle it. Kotlin has none. Error as a value A failure returned in the result type, like any other value, instead of thrown. Exhaustive when A when over a sealed type that covers every subtype, so it needs no else and breaks when a subtype is added. Railway-oriented programming Chaining steps on a success track and a failure track: after the first failure, the later steps are skipped. Either Arrow's two-case type: Left(error) or Right(value), with a typed error side. Fail fast Stop at the first error and return it; the remaining steps don't run. Error accumulation Run every independent check and return all the errors together, in Arrow as a NonEmptyList. Exception or value: the jar is out of flour? A value. It's expected, and the caller must decide what to do. Keep exceptions for bugs and failures nobody can handle on the spot. What does a sealed type plus a when with no else buy you? Adding a case breaks every when that doesn't handle it: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'X' branch or an 'else' branch. What does runCatching catch? Every Throwable: ordinary exceptions, OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError, and CancellationException, which breaks coroutine cancellation. Result.map vs Result.mapCatching? map lets an exception from its lambda escape. mapCatching turns it into a Failure. Two ensure calls inside either { } would both fail. What comes back? Only the first error: either { } is fail-fast. Use zipOrAccumulate to collect all of them. Does Arrow's Either.catch capture a CancellationException? No. It rethrows CancellationException and fatal errors such as OutOfMemoryError, and captures ordinary exceptions as a Left. Does Kotlin 2.4.21 compile fun load(): Recipe | NotFound? No. Rich errors are a proposal (KEEP-0441, KEEP-0462); 2.4.21 reports a syntax error.

h: Errors as values: sealed results, Result and Either · Go deeper
x: Three parts of Arrow are worth knowing once either { } feels natural. Raise without Either. The lab's checks are functions with a Raise<KitchenError> receiver: they don't return an Either, they raise inside whatever block calls them. Kotlin 2.4.0 made context parameters Stable, and Arrow 2.3.0 ships matching versions of ensure, raise and bind in the arrow.core.raise.context package, so the same check can be written as context(_: Raise<KitchenError>) fun checkUnit(unit: String): String. With Kotlin 2.4.21 that compiles without any compiler flag. Arrow's own docs still show the extension-receiver style and describe context parameters as a future option, so expect both styles in code you read. Collections and the experimental block. mapOrAccumulate checks every element of a list and collects the failures: running it over the amounts [10, -1, 20, -2] gives Either.Left([InvalidAmount(amount=-1), InvalidAmount(amount=-2)]). There is also an accumulate { ensureOrAccumulate(...) } block that reads like a list of checks. In Arrow 2.3.0 it is still marked @ExperimentalRaiseAccumulateApi, so you opt in with @OptIn(ExperimentalRaiseAccumulateApi::class); zipOrAccumulate is the stable choice. Translating errors between layers. mapLeft changes the error value and leaves a Right alone, as in the worked example. recover is more general: inside it you can run any computation that may itself raise, for example trying a second shop when the first returns ShopClosed. Use mapLeft to rename errors at a boundary, and recover to handle them.

h: Immutable data and a functional core · Read-only is not immutable: what val and List really promise
x: Here's the app's weekly menu. The planner screen builds a Menu from the list of dishes the cook is editing, saves it, and then clears the list for next week: Java record Menu(String id, List<String> dishes) {} Menu menu = new Menu("week-7", editing); // editing is the screen's ArrayList saved.add(menu); editing.clear(); // menu.dishes() is now empty too Kotlin data class Menu(val id: String, val dishes: List<String>) val menu = Menu("week-7", editing) // editing is the screen's MutableList saved.add(menu) editing.clear() // menu.dishes is now empty too Everything in Menu looks printed: a data class, val properties, a read-only List. But val only means the property can't point at a different list. List only means you can't call add through that reference. Neither one freezes the object behind them, and here both sides hold the same ArrayList. A read-only List is a shop window: you can't touch the cakes, but the baker behind the glass can. The Kotlin docs put it plainly: a read-only interface "prevents accidental modification through that interface. By contrast, an immutable collection doesn't allow you to change its elements after creation." And the read-only part is checked only at compile time. On the JVM, listOf("soup", "pie") is a java.util.Arrays$ArrayList; cast it to MutableList and set(0, "stew") works, while add throws UnsupportedOperationException. Data classes add two traps of their own. copy() is shallow: in the docs' words, "it doesn't copy components recursively". A shallow copy is a new object whose properties point at the same objects as the original's. card.copy(recipe = "waffles") makes a new card but staples the same page of notes to both, so a note added through the copy shows up on the original too. And equals compares every property with its own equals. For BigDecimal, Java's exact decimal number, that includes the scale, the count of digits after the point. Price("butter", BigDecimal("2.50")) == Price("butter", BigDecimal("2.5")) is false, although compareTo says the amounts are equal. Read 2.5 from one shop's website, compute 2.50 yourself, and your "same price as last week?" check says no: Java BigDecimal price = new BigDecimal(text).setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY); // same fix Kotlin val price = BigDecimal(text).setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY) // one scale for every price UNNECESSARY throws if rounding would be needed, so a third decimal fails loudly instead of being rounded away. Storing prices as a whole number of cents avoids the question entirely. So an immutable value, one nobody can change after it's built, needs three layers. Its properties are val. Their types are immutable all the way down: String, BigDecimal, LocalDate, other immutable data classes, immutable collections. And nothing mutable leaks in or out, which at a boundary means a copy: toList() for a snapshot, or toImmutableList() from the next section when you want the type to promise it. val and List stop you from changing a value, not everyone else. Copy at the boundary. Copying at every change is the price of a printed page. The next section makes that price small. Five ways a printed-looking value changes Read ReadOnly.kt and predict each of the five numbered lines before you run it. Run it, then run ReadOnlyJava.java, where List.copyOf takes a real snapshot. In ReadOnly.kt, change Menu("week-7", backing) to Menu("week-7", backing.toList()). Predict lines 1 and 2 now. ReadOnly.kt package workbench.functional.l08.demo import java.math.BigDecimal data class Menu(val id: String, val dishes: List<String>) data class Price(val item: String, val amount: BigDecimal) data class Card(val recipe: String, val notes: MutableList<String>) fun main() { // 1. a read-only List can be a view of a list someone else still changes val backing = mutableListOf("soup") val menu = Menu("week-7", backing) backing += "pie" println("1. menu after the caller adds pie: ${menu.dishes}") // 2. read-only is a compile-time view: a cast gets around it (menu.dishes as MutableList<String>) += "cake" println("2. after a cast and an add: ${menu.dishes}") // 3. listOf gives a fixed-size view of an array on the JVM val fixed = listOf("soup", "pie") println("3. listOf's class: ${fixed.javaClass.name}") (fixed as MutableList<String>)[0] = "stew" println(" after set(0, \"stew\"): $fixed") try { fixed.add("cake") } catch (e: UnsupportedOperationException) { println(" add: UnsupportedOperationException") } // 4. copy() is shallow: both copies share one list val a = Card("pancakes", mutableListOf("use buttermilk")) val b = a.copy(recipe = "waffles") b.notes += "double the sugar" println("4. a.notes = ${a.notes}, same list: ${a.notes === b.notes}") // 5. BigDecimal.equals compares the scale too, and data class equals uses it println("5.
