h: Immutable data and a functional core · Persistent collections: a new edition instead of crossing out
x: Immutable values pay you back in three ways. You can share them between threads (paths of work that run at the same time) with no lock, because nobody can write ("Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal" in the first track). You can keep the old version, the way an old edition stays on the shelf. And a test can hold the "before" and "after" side by side. The price is that every change makes a new value. Copying a whole list to add one step is what Java does in the Try it, and it costs time and memory in proportion to the list's size, on every change. Persistent collections avoid most of that copy. A new version shares most of its insides with the old one, the way a new edition of a cookbook reuses most of its pages and reprints only the ones that changed. Adding a step builds a few new pieces of the list's inner tree and reuses the rest. The library is kotlinx-collections-immutable, version 0.5.2 in the lab. Its README still says "the library is experimental and the API is subject to change", so treat it as a dependency that hasn't reached 1.0. ImmutableList promises that nobody can change the list; PersistentList adds the operations that return a new version: Java // Java equivalent: no persistent collections in the JDK, so copy the whole list per version List<String> v1 = List.of("preheat the oven"); List<String> v2 = Stream.concat(v1.stream(), Stream.of("cream butter and sugar")).toList(); List<String> tmp = new ArrayList<>(v2); tmp.addAll(List.of("beat in the eggs", "fold in the flour")); List<String> v3 = List.copyOf(tmp); Kotlin val v1 = persistentListOf("preheat the oven") val v2 = v1.adding("cream butter and sugar") // a new list; v1 is untouched val v3 = v2.addingAll(listOf("beat in the eggs", "fold in the flour")) val v4 = v3.mutate { it.removeAt(0); it += "bake for 25 minutes" } // several changes in one go The picture breaks in one place. A publisher prints a whole new book, while a persistent list really does share its pages between versions, in memory. That sharing is safe only because no version can ever change. Notice the names. Until 0.5.0 these methods were called add, remove, put and set, like the changing methods on MutableList. That invited a quiet bug: budget.entries.add(entry) as a statement builds a new list and throws it away, and the budget never changes. Version 0.5.0 renamed the copy-returning methods to adding, removing, putting, replacingAt and removingAt. It follows a naming proposal (KEEP-0459, still a draft) where a verb like add changes the object and a participle like adding returns a copy, as sorted() does next to sort(). The old names still compile, with a warning: 'fun add(element: String): PersistentList<String>' is deprecated. Use adding() instead. A persistent collection makes a new version and leaves the old one alone. Keep the result, or the change is lost. In the lab, the household budget book is a data class around a PersistentList<Entry>, and posting returns a new budget with copy(entries = entries.addingAll(...)). The budget you posted to is still there, unchanged, for the test to compare against. Immutable data changes how functional code loops, too. Instead of a var that changes, a function often calls itself. Four editions of one recipe Run Persistent.kt. Predict what v1 and v3 print at the end. Uncomment v1.add("lost") and run again. Read the build warning and the last line. Run PersistentJava.java and count how many times it copies the whole list. Persistent.kt package workbench.functional.l08.demo import kotlinx.collections.immutable.mutate import kotlinx.collections.immutable.persistentListOf fun main() { // the steps of a recipe, one edition at a time val v1 = persistentListOf("preheat the oven") val v2 = v1.adding("cream butter and sugar") // a new list; v1 is untouched val v3 = v2.addingAll(listOf("beat in the eggs", "fold in the flour")) println("v1 = $v1") println("v2 = $v2") println("v3 = $v3") println("v1 is a ${v1.javaClass.simpleName}") // several changes at once, through a short-lived mutable builder val v4 = v3.mutate { steps -> steps.removeAt(0) steps += "bake for 25 minutes" } println("v4 = $v4") println("v3 = $v3 (unchanged)") // Uncomment the next line and run: the old name compiles with a deprecation warning, // returns a new list like adding, and here the new list is thrown away. // v1.add("lost") println("v1 = $v1 at the end") } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l08.demo.PersistentKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l08/demo/Persistent.kt PersistentJava.java package workbench.functional.l08.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Java equivalent: the JDK has no persistent collections. A new edition means copying the old one * (every element, on every change) into an unmodifiable list. Sharing structure needs a library. */ public class PersistentJava { static List<String> adding(List<String> list, String element) { List<String> copy = new ArrayList<>(list); // copies every element copy.add(element); return List.copyOf(copy); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> v1 = List.of("preheat the oven"); List<String> v2 = adding(v1, "cream butter and sugar"); List<String> v3 = adding(adding(v2, "beat in the eggs"), "fold in the flour"); System.out.println("v1 = " + v1); System.out.println("v2 = " + v2); System.out.println("v3 = " + v3); List<String> builder = new ArrayList<>(v3); // several changes: copy once, change, freeze builder.remove(0); builder.add("bake for 25 minutes"); List<String> v4 = List.copyOf(builder); System.out.println("v4 = " + v4); System.out.println("v3 = " + v3 + " (unchanged)"); } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l08.demo.PersistentJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l08/demo/PersistentJava.java v1 stays [preheat the oven] and v3 stays four steps long, even after v4 is built from it with mutate. v1 is a SmallPersistentVector. With v1.add("lost"), the build warns 'fun add(element: String): PersistentList<String>' is deprecated. Use adding() instead. and the last line still shows [preheat the oven]: add returned a new list that nobody kept. The Java version copies the full list for every version it makes. kotlinx.collections.immutable (GitHub) read

h: Immutable data and a functional core · Recursion: tailrec is a loop, everything else uses the stack
x: Functional code often recurses where Java code loops: a function calls itself on a smaller problem. On the JVM that has a hard limit. Every call takes a stack frame, a slot that holds the call's local variables until it returns, on the thread's stack: the memory that holds the calls in progress. The stack has room for only so many. The JVM never removes a frame early, even for the last call in a method. Sum the numbers 1 to 1,000,000 by recursion and you get a StackOverflowError, in both languages. In Java it overflows even when the recursive call is the last thing the method does. Kotlin's tailrec moves the fix into the compiler. "When a function is marked with the tailrec modifier and meets the required formal conditions, the compiler optimizes out the recursion, leaving behind a fast and efficient loop based version instead." A tail call is a call that is the very last thing a function does. The trick is an accumulator, an extra parameter that carries the result so far. The work still pending becomes an argument, so the recursive call can come last: Java // Java has no tailrec: write the loop the Kotlin compiler would write static long sumTo(long n) { long acc = 0; while (n > 0) { acc += n; n--; } return acc; } Kotlin tailrec fun sumTo(n: Long, acc: Long = 0): Long = if (n == 0L) acc else sumTo(n - 1, acc + n) // sumTo(1_000_000) == 500000500000, no stack growth javap -c, the JDK tool that prints a class's bytecode, shows what the compiler did. sumTo stores the new values into its own parameter slots and ends with goto 0, a jump back to its first instruction. There's no invokestatic sumTo left. The conditions are strict. The function must call itself as its very last operation, not inside try, catch or finally, and it can't be open. Get it wrong and the compiler takes your word for it, mutters a warning and compiles ordinary recursion anyway: A function is marked as tail-recursive but no tail calls are found. and Recursive call is not a tail call. The code still overflows, so read the warnings. Here's recursion that fits tailrec naturally. A sourdough starter is fed from a spoonful of another starter, which came from another, and friends pass them on for years. Walking back to the very first one makes one call per generation, always as the last thing the function does, so the demo walks 100,000 generations without growing the stack. Some recursion has no tail form. Counting the parts of a recipe made of parts, each made of more parts, makes several recursive calls per part. DeepRecursiveFunction from the standard library runs such a function with its "stack" on the heap, the big memory area where objects live, using coroutine machinery. In the Try it, it counts a recipe nested 100,001 levels deep, where the same code as a plain function overflows. Most of the time you need neither. Adding up a basket or a budget is a fold or a sumOf (the collections lesson), which says what it means in one line and compiles to the same kind of loop. Recursion that walks a list with first() and drop(1) is worse than either, because drop(1) copies the rest of the list at every step. Reach for fold or sumOf first. Keep tailrec for problems that are recursive by nature, and read its warnings. We now have every piece of the track: pure functions, function values, collections, errors as values and data that can't change. The last section puts them into one shape. Watch tailrec become a goto Run Recursion.kt. Predict which lines print a number and which print StackOverflowError. From labs/, run javap -c -p -cp functional/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.functional.l08.demo.RecursionKt and find sumTo and sumNaive. Which one calls itself? Add tailrec in front of fun sumNaive and run again. Read the warnings in the build output. Run RecursionJava.java. Does sumTail, with its call in tail position, survive? Recursion.kt package workbench.functional.l08.demo /** Sums 1..n with recursion that is NOT in tail position: one stack frame per number. */ fun sumNaive(n: Long): Long = if (n == 0L) 0 else n + sumNaive(n - 1) /** The same sum with an accumulator: the recursive call is the last thing it does. */ tailrec fun sumTo(n: Long, acc: Long = 0): Long = if (n == 0L) acc else sumTo(n - 1, acc + n) /** A sourdough starter is fed from a spoonful of another starter. Walk back to the very first one. */ data class Starter(val id: String, val parentId: String?) tailrec fun originOf(id: String, byId: Map<String, Starter>): String { val parent = byId.getValue(id).parentId ?: return id return originOf(parent, byId) } /** A recipe made of parts, each part made of parts: counting them is recursion that can't be put in tail form. */ class Part(val parts: List<Part>) val countParts = DeepRecursiveFunction<Part, Long> { part -> var total = 1L for (child in part.parts) total += callRecursive(child) // the "stack" lives on the heap total } fun main() { println("tailrec sumTo(1,000,000) = ${sumTo(1_000_000)}") try { println("sumNaive(1,000,000) = ${sumNaive(1_000_000)}") } catch (e: StackOverflowError) { println("sumNaive(1,000,000): StackOverflowError") } println("fold over 1..1,000,000 = ${(1L..1_000_000L).fold(0L) { acc, n -> acc + n }}") val family = (1..100_000).associate { i -> "s$i" to Starter("s$i", if (i == 1) null else "s${i - 1}") } println("origin of s100000 = ${originOf("s100000", family)}") var deep = Part(emptyList()) repeat(100_000) { deep = Part(listOf(deep)) } // absurdly deep, to make the point println("parts in a recipe nested 100,001 levels deep = ${countParts(deep)}") } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l08.demo.RecursionKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l08/demo/Recursion.kt RecursionJava.java package workbench.functional.l08.demo; import java.util.stream.LongStream; /** Java has no tailrec, and the JVM doesn't remove tail calls: a call in tail position still uses a frame. */ public class RecursionJava { static long sumNaive(long n) { return n == 0 ? 0 : n + sumNaive(n - 1); } static long sumTail(long n, long acc) { return n == 0 ? acc : sumTail(n - 1, acc + n); } // tail position, still a call static long sumLoop(long n) { // what tailrec writes for you long acc = 0; while (n > 0) { acc += n; n--; } return acc; } public static void main(String[] args) { try { System.out.println("sumTail(1,000,000) = " + sumTail(1_000_000, 0)); } catch (StackOverflowError e) { System.out.println("sumTail(1,000,000): StackOverflowError"); } try { System.out.println("sumNaive(1,000,000) = " + sumNaive(1_000_000)); } catch (StackOverflowError e) { System.out.println("sumNaive(1,000,000): StackOverflowError"); } System.out.println("loop = " + sumLoop(1_000_000)); System.out.println("LongStream.sum = " + LongStream.rangeClosed(1, 1_000_000).sum()); } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l08.demo.RecursionJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l08/demo/RecursionJava.java sumTo and fold both print 500000500000; sumNaive overflows; originOf walks 100,000 starters back to s1; countParts returns 100001. In javap, sumTo ends with goto 0 and never calls itself, while sumNaive has invokestatic sumNaive. Marking sumNaive as tailrec gives A function is marked as tail-recursive but no tail calls are found. and Recursive call is not a tail call., and it still overflows. In Java, sumTail overflows too: the JVM doesn't remove tail calls, so only a loop helps. Functions: tail recursive functions (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Immutable data and a functional core · A functional core decides, a thin shell does the errands
x: A pure core decides from plain values, a thin shell does the I/O, and its inputs must not change underneath it Here's the track's last step: put the pieces into one shape. The lab's LegacyShoppingJob runs every morning in the recipe app. In one loop it reads the clock and loads the shopping list. It skips crossed-off items, holds back items it's too early to order, adds up a total per shop and works out each shop's member discount. Then it sends the orders, writes each one into the household budget book and saves the book, with println in between. It works. But to test one discount rule you need a fake store, a fake shop, a fixed clock, and checks on what the fakes recorded. The fix is the shape from the first lesson of this track: the recipe card decides and the cook does the errands. Its usual name is functional core, imperative shell. The functional core is a pure function. It takes plain values, today's date included, and returns a value that describes what should happen: Java static ShoppingPlan planShopping(List<Item> items, Map<String, Shop> shops, LocalDate today) Kotlin fun planShopping(items: List<Item>, shops: Map<String, Shop>, today: LocalDate): ShoppingPlan Everything from this track fits in there. filterNot, partition, groupBy and sumOf from the collections lesson do the work. Data classes of vals, with prices as BigDecimal at scale 2, carry it. Expected outcomes, like an item from a shop the app doesn't know, come back as values in the plan instead of exceptions or log lines, as the errors lesson taught. The imperative shell is the thin outer part, the only code that touches the world, and it has almost no branches: Java ShoppingPlan run() { LocalDate today = LocalDate.now(clock); // 1. read ShoppingPlan plan = planShopping(store.shoppingList(), store.shops(), today); // 2. decide plan.orders().forEach(shopApi::send); // 3. act store.saveBudget(posting(store.loadBudget(), plan.orders(), "shopping-" + today)); return plan; } Kotlin fun run(): ShoppingPlan { val today = LocalDate.now(clock) // 1. read val plan = planShopping(store.shoppingList(), store.shops(), today) // 2. decide plan.orders.forEach(shopApi::send) // 3. act store.saveBudget(store.loadBudget().posting(plan.orders, "shopping-$today")) return plan } The tests change shape with the code. The core gets many small tests that build a list, call a function and compare the result with equals: no fakes, no clock, milliseconds each. Because the date is a parameter, "an item needed in ten days is still waiting" and "the same item is ordered three days later" are two lines. The shell gets one test with fakes that checks the wiring. The shell isn't pure and doesn't try to be. The program still does all its errands. What moved is the decisions: each one now lives where you can test it with a value, like a recipe card you can read without lighting the oven. Decide in the core, with every input passed in. Let the shell read, call the core and act, and nothing more. Run a core and its shell Read CoreShell.kt. decideFridge is the core and FridgeJob is the shell. Predict the two decisions and the one reminder. Run it, then run CoreShellJava.java. Change now to one day later, 2026-03-11T09:00:00Z. Without running anything, which decision changes? Then run it to check. CoreShell.kt package workbench.functional.l08.demo import java.time.Clock import java.time.Duration import java.time.Instant import java.time.ZoneOffset data class Leftover(val id: String, val dish: String, val cookedAt: Instant) sealed interface FridgeDecision { data class ThrowOut(val id: String) : FridgeDecision data class Keep(val id: String, val goodFor: Duration) : FridgeDecision } val KEEPS_FOR: Duration = Duration.ofDays(3) /** The core: leftovers older than three days go. Pure: the time is a parameter. */ fun decideFridge(leftovers: List<Leftover>, now: Instant): List<FridgeDecision> = leftovers.map { l -> val age = Duration.between(l.cookedAt, now) if (age >= KEEPS_FOR) FridgeDecision.ThrowOut(l.id) else FridgeDecision.Keep(l.id, KEEPS_FOR - age) } /** The shell: reads, calls the core, carries out the decisions. No rules in here. */ class FridgeJob(private val load: () -> List<Leftover>, private val remind: (String) -> Unit, private val clock: Clock) { fun run() { val decisions = decideFridge(load(), clock.instant()) // read, then decide decisions.filterIsInstance<FridgeDecision.ThrowOut>().forEach { remind(it.id) } // act } } fun main() { val now = Instant.parse("2026-03-10T09:00:00Z") val leftovers = listOf( Leftover("l1", "soup", Instant.parse("2026-03-06T09:00:00Z")), // cooked 4 days before now Leftover("l2", "rice", Instant.parse("2026-03-09T03:00:00Z")), // cooked 30 hours before now ) println("core, called with plain values:") decideFridge(leftovers, now).forEach { println(" $it") } println("shell, with a fixed clock and a fake phone:") FridgeJob({ leftovers }, { println(" reminder: throw out leftover $it") }, Clock.fixed(now, ZoneOffset.UTC)).run() } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l08.demo.CoreShellKt labs/functional/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/functional/l08/demo/CoreShell.kt CoreShellJava.java package workbench.functional.l08.demo; import java.time.Clock; import java.time.Duration; import java.time.Instant; import java.time.ZoneOffset; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Consumer; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** The same core and shell in Java: records for the values, a static method for the pure core. */ public class CoreShellJava { record Leftover(String id, String dish, Instant cookedAt) {} sealed interface FridgeDecision {} record ThrowOut(String id) implements FridgeDecision {} record Keep(String id, Duration goodFor) implements FridgeDecision {} static final Duration KEEPS_FOR = Duration.ofDays(3); /** The core: leftovers older than three days go. Pure: the time is a parameter. */ static List<FridgeDecision> decideFridge(List<Leftover> leftovers, Instant now) { return leftovers.stream().<FridgeDecision>map(l -> { Duration age = Duration.between(l.cookedAt(), now); return age.compareTo(KEEPS_FOR) >= 0 ? new ThrowOut(l.id()) : new Keep(l.id(), KEEPS_FOR.minus(age)); }).toList(); } /** The shell: reads, calls the core, carries out the decisions. */ record FridgeJob(Supplier<List<Leftover>> load, Consumer<String> remind, Clock clock) { void run() { for (FridgeDecision d : decideFridge(load.get(), clock.instant())) { if (d instanceof ThrowOut t) remind.accept(t.id()); } } } public static void main(String[] args) { Instant now = Instant.parse("2026-03-10T09:00:00Z"); List<Leftover> leftovers = List.of( new Leftover("l1", "soup", Instant.parse("2026-03-06T09:00:00Z")), // cooked 4 days before now new Leftover("l2", "rice", Instant.parse("2026-03-09T03:00:00Z"))); // cooked 30 hours before now System.out.println("core, called with plain values:"); decideFridge(leftovers, now).forEach(d -> System.out.println(" " + d)); System.out.println("shell, with a fixed clock and a fake phone:"); new FridgeJob(() -> leftovers, id -> System.out.println(" reminder: throw out leftover " + id), Clock.fixed(now, ZoneOffset.UTC)).run(); } } ./gradlew :functional:demo -Pmain=workbench.functional.l08.demo.CoreShellJava labs/functional/src/demo/java/workbench/functional/l08/demo/CoreShellJava.java The core prints ThrowOut(id=l1) (4 days old) and Keep(id=l2, goodFor=PT42H) (30 hours old, 42 hours left). The shell sends one reminder: reminder: throw out leftover l1. One day later, l2 is still kept with PT18H left, and l1 goes as before. You could check that from the core alone, with no clock and no phone, which is the point. The shell reads the world, hands plain values to the pure core, and carries out the plan the core returns.

h: Immutable data and a functional core · Java and Kotlin
x: Immutable values and a pure core: Java records vs Kotlin data classes Shopping.java record Order(String shopId, BigDecimal total, BigDecimal discount, BigDecimal toPay) {} record Budget(List<Entry> entries) { Budget { entries = List.copyOf(entries); } // snapshot: nobody can change it later Budget posting(List<Entry> more) { // a new version, by copying everything List<Entry> all = new ArrayList<>(entries); all.addAll(more); return new Budget(all); } } static BigDecimal discount(BigDecimal total, BigDecimal rate) { // pure: same inputs, same output return total.multiply(rate).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN); } Shopping.kt data class Order(val shopId: String, val total: BigDecimal, val discount: BigDecimal, val toPay: BigDecimal) data class Budget(val entries: PersistentList<Entry>) // the type promises it can't change fun Budget.posting(more: List<Entry>): Budget = copy(entries = entries.addingAll(more)) // a new version that shares structure fun discount(total: BigDecimal, rate: BigDecimal): BigDecimal = // pure: same inputs, same output (total * rate).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN) Both languages give you a value type whose equals compares contents, and in both equals uses BigDecimal.equals, so the scale counts. Kotlin's data class adds copy(), which Java records lack (you write "wither" methods by hand), and both are shallow. The real difference is in collections. Java's List.copyOf makes a snapshot that refuses changes at run time, but every new version copies the whole list. Kotlin's List is only a compile-time read-only view, so you need toList() for a snapshot, or kotlinx.collections.immutable for a real promise; its PersistentList makes new versions cheaply by sharing structure. The pure functions themselves look the same in both languages. Purity is a habit, not a keyword: neither compiler checks it.

h: Immutable data and a functional core · Worked example
x: Pull the decisions out of a pantry check Each night the app checks the opened jars in the pantry. A jar past its use-by date goes; a jar within two days of it goes on the shopping list, unless it's on there already; anything else waits. Before reading on, label every line as read, decide or act. fun checkPantry() { for (jar in pantry.openJars()) { // read val daysLeft = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(LocalDate.now(), jar.useBy) // read (the clock!) if (daysLeft < 0) { // decide pantry.remove(jar.id) // act phone.notify("throw out the ${jar.name}") // act } else if (daysLeft <= 2 && !jar.onShoppingList) { // decide shoppingList.add(jar.name, "use within $daysLeft days") // act } } } void checkPantry() { for (Jar jar : pantry.openJars()) { // read long daysLeft = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(LocalDate.now(), jar.useBy()); // read (the clock!) if (daysLeft < 0) { // decide pantry.remove(jar.id()); // act phone.notify("throw out the " + jar.name()); // act } else if (daysLeft <= 2 && !jar.onShoppingList()) { // decide shoppingList.add(jar.name(), "use within " + daysLeft + " days"); // act } } } Name the decisions as values. A sealed type makes the plan explicit and lets the shell's when be exhaustive. sealed interface JarAction { data class ThrowOut(val jarId: String, val name: String) : JarAction data class Restock(val jarId: String, val name: String, val daysLeft: Long) : JarAction data class Wait(val jarId: String) : JarAction } sealed interface JarAction {} record ThrowOut(String jarId, String name) implements JarAction {} record Restock(String jarId, String name, long daysLeft) implements JarAction {} record Wait(String jarId) implements JarAction {} Write the core as a pure function. The clock becomes a parameter, today, and the result is a list of decisions. Every rule is now testable with one line: decide(listOf(jar), LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 10)). fun decide(jars: List<Jar>, today: LocalDate): List<JarAction> = jars.map { jar -> val daysLeft = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(today, jar.useBy) when { daysLeft < 0 -> JarAction.ThrowOut(jar.id, jar.name) daysLeft <= 2 && !jar.onShoppingList -> JarAction.Restock(jar.id, jar.name, daysLeft) else -> JarAction.Wait(jar.id) } } static List<JarAction> decide(List<Jar> jars, LocalDate today) { return jars.stream().<JarAction>map(jar -> { long daysLeft = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(today, jar.useBy()); if (daysLeft < 0) return new ThrowOut(jar.id(), jar.name()); if (daysLeft <= 2 && !jar.onShoppingList()) return new Restock(jar.id(), jar.name(), daysLeft); return new Wait(jar.id()); }).toList(); } The shell reads, calls the core and carries out each action with an exhaustive when. It has no rules left, so one test with fakes covers it. The many rule tests go against decide with plain values. fun checkPantry() { val actions = decide(pantry.openJars(), LocalDate.now(clock)) // read, then decide for (action in actions) when (action) { // act is JarAction.ThrowOut -> { pantry.remove(action.jarId); phone.notify("throw out the ${action.name}") } is JarAction.Restock -> shoppingList.add(action.name, "use within ${action.daysLeft} days") is JarAction.Wait -> Unit } } void checkPantry() { List<JarAction> actions = decide(pantry.openJars(), LocalDate.now(clock)); // read, then decide for (JarAction action : actions) { // act switch (action) { case ThrowOut t -> { pantry.remove(t.jarId()); phone.notify("throw out the " + t.name()); } case Restock r -> shoppingList.add(r.name(), "use within " + r.daysLeft() + " days"); case Wait w -> { } } } }

h: Immutable data and a functional core · Quiz
x: The planner screen builds Menu("week-9", editing) from its MutableList, hands the menu to a background task on another thread that prints it, then calls editing.clear() for next week. What can the printout show? Always the dishes at the moment the menu was built An empty list, or next week's dishes, depending on timing UnsupportedOperationException, because List is read-only A compile error, because dishes is a val The menu holds the screen's list, not a copy, so clearing and refilling it changes what the menu shows. On another thread it's also a data race. Menu("week-9", editing.toList()) takes a snapshot at the boundary; toImmutableList() puts the promise in the type. data class Price(val item: String, val amount: BigDecimal). What is setOf(Price("butter", BigDecimal("2.5")), Price("butter", BigDecimal("2.50"))).size? 1 It depends on the JVM 2 It throws ArithmeticException Data class equals compares each property with equals, and BigDecimal.equals treats 2.5 and 2.50 as different because their scales differ. compareTo would say they're equal. Bring every price to setScale(2, ...) when you read it, or store whole cents. val steps = persistentListOf<String>(), then steps.adding("preheat") and steps.adding("mix") as two statements. What is steps.size? 0 2 1 It doesn't compile, because steps is a val adding returns a new list and leaves the receiver alone, and both results were thrown away. You need val v2 = steps.adding("preheat").adding("mix"). This is the exact bug the 0.5 rename from add to adding makes easier to spot. tailrec fun depth(s: Starter?): Int = if (s == null) 0 else 1 + depth(s.parent), called on a chain of 1,000,000 starters. What happens? It compiles to a loop and returns 1,000,000 It doesn't compile, because tailrec needs an accumulator It returns 0 It compiles with warnings, stays ordinary recursion, and throws StackOverflowError 1 + depth(...) still has work to do after the call, so the call isn't in tail position. Kotlin only warns (A function is marked as tail-recursive but no tail calls are found., Recursive call is not a tail call.) and compiles normal recursion. Make the pending work an argument: tailrec fun depth(s: Starter?, acc: Int = 0): Int = if (s == null) acc else depth(s.parent, acc + 1). From the errors lesson: inside planShopping, an item names a shop that isn't in the map. What should the pure core do? shops.getValue(id), and let NoSuchElementException stop the run shops[id]!! Return it as a value in the plan, such as an unknownShops list or a sealed error Log a warning and skip it An unknown shop is an expected outcome that someone must handle, so it belongs in the result. h: Immutable data and a functional core · Key terms
x: Read-only You can't change it through this reference. Someone else may still change it. Immutable Nobody can change it after it is built, through any reference. Shallow copy A copy whose properties point at the same objects as the original's. Persistent collection An immutable collection whose "change" operations return a new version that shares most of its structure with the old one. Tail call A call that is the very last thing a function does, with no work left after it returns. Accumulator An extra parameter that carries the result so far, which turns pending work into an argument. Functional core The pure part of a program: it decides from plain values and returns a value. Imperative shell The thin outer part that reads inputs, calls the core and carries out the result. Does val dishes: List<String> make the list immutable? No. val stops reassigning the reference and List stops writes through it. The list can still change through another reference or a cast. Is a data class copy() deep or shallow? Shallow. Properties are copied as references, so a nested MutableList is shared between the original and the copy. Price("butter", BigDecimal("2.50")) == Price("butter", BigDecimal("2.5"))? false. Data class equals uses BigDecimal.equals, which compares the scale. compareTo returns 0. What did kotlinx.collections.immutable 0.5 rename, and why? The copy-returning methods: add to adding, put to putting, set to replacingAt and so on, so a call whose result is dropped looks wrong. The old names are deprecated. What does tailrec compile to? A loop: the self-call in tail position becomes stores into the parameter slots and a goto back to the start. No new stack frame. What if a tailrec function isn't really tail-recursive? Only a warning, such as Recursive call is not a tail call. It compiles to ordinary recursion and can still overflow. Functional core vs imperative shell? Core: pure decisions from plain values, with the clock passed in, and many fast tests. Shell: reads inputs, calls the core, does the I/O, with few branches and one wiring test.

h: Immutable data and a functional core · Go deeper
x: Immutability is also a concurrency tool, and the memory model track explains why. A val property compiles to a final field, and the Java memory model gives final fields a special promise: once the constructor has finished, any thread that sees the object sees those fields fully set, without a lock, as long as the constructor didn't let this escape ("Safe publication, final fields and escaping this"). So an object whose state is all vals of immutable types can be handed to another thread with no synchronization at all. A persistent collection extends that: one thread builds a new version with adding while other threads keep reading the old one, and neither can disturb the other. The catch is the same as in the first section. A val holding a MutableList gets the promise only for the reference, not for the list's contents. The naming change in kotlinx.collections.immutable came with a compiler feature. The 0.5.0 line builds the library itself with Kotlin's Experimental return-value checker in its strictest mode, -Xreturn-value-checker=full. The checker arrived in Kotlin 2.3.0, is off by default, and warns when a call's result is ignored. Both changes go after the same bug: a new version computed and then dropped. On recursion, arrow-core 2.3.0 also contains a MemoizedDeepRecursiveFunction, a variant of the standard library's DeepRecursiveFunction that remembers its answers. Reach for either only after a plain fold or a loop has been ruled out.

h: Design patterns in Java and Kotlin
x: Creational, structural and behavioral patterns, what Kotlin makes unnecessary, and concurrency patterns. This track builds one small program from start to finish: the order program of a corner shop in a small town, which delivers by bike with Pedal Post or by van with Big Blue Vans. Along the way you meet the classic design patterns, named designs from a famous 1994 book that programmers still use to talk about code. Each one arrives with a scene from the town: the town hall for Singleton, the bakery counter for Factory Method, gift paper around a teapot for Decorator, the "ring me when the bread arrives" sheet for Observer, the fuse box in the back room for the circuit breaker. By the end you can name the patterns in the code you read, and you know which ones modern Java and Kotlin have turned into a few lines: Strategy and Command into lambdas, State and Visitor into sealed types with an exhaustive switch or when, Builder into named arguments, Decorator into Kotlin's by. You can also tell when a pattern still earns its own class: an adapter at the edge of your program, a facade over a job with several steps, a proxy with rules of its own, and the concurrency patterns that keep a busy program working when a service it calls goes quiet. The last lesson builds a circuit breaker and a bulkhead by hand, out of State, Decorator and compare-and-set. You need to read basic Java and Kotlin, including Kotlin data classes and lambdas. Records, sealed interfaces and pattern matching are explained where they first appear, and the modern Java data modeling track right after this one covers them in depth. The concurrency and memory model tracks help with lessons 1 and 11. Install JDK 25; the labs compile with release 21, so they also run on JDK 21. Kotlin samples use 2.4.21, and guards in when need Kotlin 2.2 or later. The labs live in labs/patterns, one package per lesson (workbench.patterns.l01 to l11). About half are in Java and half in Kotlin, and every code sample and Try-it demo in the lessons comes in both languages. Most labs are refactors: the tests pin the behavior, and you change the shape. From labs/, run ./gradlew :patterns:test --tests 'workbench.patterns.lNN.*' until it passes, and ./gradlew :patterns:solutionTest to run the same tests against the reference answers. The tests that use threads rely on latches, counters and a fake clock, so they pass or fail the same way on every run. Patterns are names for designs you keep meeting. In Java 21 and Kotlin, many of them are now a language feature: lambdas, sealed types with an exhaustive switch or when, records and data classes, named arguments and by delegation. Creational: pass shared objects in instead of hand-rolling singletons, give constructors names with validating factories, use named arguments or a record plus a builder, and remember that every copy (copy(), withers) is shallow. Structural: adapters translate an old program's codes and errors at the edge, facades own jobs with several steps, decorators add behavior behind the same interface (the order of the layers matters), and proxies carry framework behavior with rules of their own, calls to this above all. Composite, State and Visitor become sealed types plus pure functions. Leave the default off the switch over your own types, and the compiler lists every place a new case needs a rule. Strategy, Command, Template Method and Chain of Responsibility become functions: lambdas, comparators, execute-around helpers and folded lists of handlers. Observer: return a handle to leave by and keep listener failures apart; use SharedFlow for events and StateFlow for state. Memento and Command both give undo, by snapshot or by opposite. Iterator and Mediator: a sequence {} walks pages lazily but runs again for every walk, and a mediator routes messages between parts that shouldn't know each other, and does nothing else. Concurrency patterns answer who owns the state and who waits: bounded producer-consumer queues, balking with compare-and-set, guarded suspension with futures, and one owner for each piece of changeable state. Cheap threads don't make services cheap: put a fail-fast bulkhead in front of each service, a circuit breaker that stops calling a failing one, and one retry layer around calls that are safe to repeat.

h: Design patterns in Java and Kotlin: track quiz
x: The shop's program needs one shared PriceList. A teammate writes object PriceList { ... } and calls it directly from twelve classes. What is the main cost? It isn't thread-safe: two threads can create two instances Tests can't swap it for a pretend one, and its state leaks from one test to the next Kotlin creates a new instance for each class that uses it It can't hold changeable state A Kotlin object is created once, safely, on first use, so thread safety isn't the problem. The cost is the hidden dependency: twelve classes reach for a global, so a test can't hand them a pretend price list, and anything one test changes is still there for the next. Pass the price list in through each class's constructor instead. A Kotlin 2.4 data class Email private constructor(val value: String) is meant to be created only through a validating factory, Email.of. What does email.copy(value = "not-an-email") do? It doesn't compile, because copy() is private like the constructor It deep-copies the email and rejects the bad value It compiles, with a warning: copy() stays public and skips the factory, though checks in init still run copy() isn't generated for a private constructor In Kotlin 2.4, a private primary constructor doesn't make the generated copy() private; you get a warning unless you add @ConsistentCopyVisibility. So copy() goes around the factory, and only the rules in init still apply. That is why validation belongs in init. Name these four wrappers, in order: (1) a class that makes the old warehouse program's item numbers and two-digit codes look like the shop's own stock interface; (2) a DeliveryFee that wraps another one and adds 3.00 for heavy parcels; (3) the stand-in object a framework hands out so that an annotation such as @Transactional works; (4) one placeOrder() call that reserves stock, writes the order down and emails the customer. Adapter, Decorator, Proxy, Facade Decorator, Proxy, Adapter, Facade Adapter, Proxy, Decorator, Bridge Facade, Decorator, Proxy, Adapter An adapter changes another program's interface into yours. A decorator keeps the interface and adds behavior. A proxy keeps the interface and controls access, here by running calls inside a database transaction. A facade puts one simple front door in front of several objects. Structure alone can't tell them apart; the intent does. The shop's notices come in four kinds ("on its way", "sold out" and two more) and go out by three channels, and both lists will grow. Which pattern keeps the code at N + M pieces instead of N x M classes? Composite Flyweight Adapter Bridge Bridge splits two sides that vary on their own: each notice holds a Channel and calls it, like a remote that works with any TV, so a new channel works with every notice. Composite is for trees, Flyweight for sharing unchanging objects, and Adapter for fitting one existing class to your interface. Every call to a courier must be timed and logged the same way, around a different call each time. What is the modern replacement for a Template Method base class here? A higher-order function, timed("courier.book", timings) { ... }, inline in Kotlin A Strategy map from call name to Runnable A Singleton that every call registers with A dynamic proxy around every lambda The skeleton is fixed and only the middle changes, which is execute around: one function that does the before and after and takes the changing step as a lambda. It needs no subclass per call site, and it can't fall into the trap of a constructor calling a hook. In Kotlin, inline removes the lambda object too. The shop's program offers "an order was placed" events and the number of items sold today as Kotlin flows. Which pairing is right? StateFlow for both SharedFlow for both SharedFlow for the orders, StateFlow for the count StateFlow for the orders, SharedFlow for the count Orders are events: two equal orders in a row, such as Ana's two rye loaves, are two real orders, and a StateFlow would drop the second because it compares values with equals. The count is state: whoever looks only needs the latest number, which is exactly what a StateFlow gives, including to late collectors. A Java switch over a sealed OrderState covers all five states with no default. A new WaitingAtShop state is added in a separately compiled jar, and a WaitingAtShop value reaches the old switch when the program runs. What happens? It falls into the first case It returns null The JVM throws MatchException Nothing: the compiler rejected the old jar Exhaustiveness is checked at compile time against the subtypes known then. A subtype added later, in separately compiled code, is part of the remainder, and Java throws MatchException for it (Kotlin throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException; a null state throws NullPointerException). Recompiling the switch turns it back into a compile error. When does the classic Visitor pattern still make sense in modern Java or Kotlin? Whenever a hierarchy has more than five subtypes For any sealed hierarchy you own Never: pattern matching replaced it completely For hierarchies open to code you don't compile, or libraries that hand you one, such as annotation processing or tools that read compiled classes For a closed hierarchy you own, a sealed type plus switch or when gives Visitor's benefit (cheap new jobs) without accept methods. Visitor still fits when the hierarchy isn't sealed or isn't yours, as in Java's annotation processing API or the ASM library. Big Blue Vans' booking service is down, and every call hangs until a 2-second timeout. Which tool stops the shop's threads from each waiting those 2 seconds? A bulkhead of 50 A circuit breaker A retry with three attempts A bigger thread pool Once its failure threshold is reached, the breaker opens and turns calls away at once, without calling the service. A bulkhead only caps how many calls wait at the same time, so 50 of them still wait 2 seconds each. Retries multiply the waiting, and a bigger pool just lets more threads wait. Parcel.parse(input) is a factory that returns a sealed ParcelResult with Valid and Invalid. What should the caller's when (or switch) look like? One branch per subtype and no else, so a new result type breaks the build here A single else branch, to be safe A try/catch around the call instead of a when An is Valid branch only, because bad input throws A sealed result is a promise that the caller handles every outcome, and the compiler checks it only if there is no else. Add a TooHeavy result later, and every caller that needs to decide fails to compile. parse never throws for bad input; that's what Invalid is for.

h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · A pattern is a name for a problem you keep meeting
x: A design pattern is a named solution to a design problem that keeps coming back. Think of the town again. Every town needs a way to show strangers where things are, and most towns solve it the same way: a map by the station. Nobody invented that map for your town. The idea was already there, with a name, and your town filled in its own streets. Software has the same kind of ideas. In 1994, four authors, often called the Gang of Four (GoF), wrote down 23 of them in a book called Design Patterns. Each one has a name, the problem it solves, the shape of the solution and what it costs. The names are the part that lasts. When a teammate says "put an adapter around the old warehouse program", five words carry a whole design. So a pattern is a word in a shared vocabulary. It isn't a class you copy and paste. The book was written for C++ and Smalltalk. Java at the time had no lambdas (small functions you can pass around as values), no records (classes that only carry data) and no sealed types. A sealed type lists all of its subtypes in one place, so the compiler knows every case. Many of the 23 patterns were workarounds for exactly those missing features. In Java 21 and later, and in Kotlin 2, the 23 sort into three groups, as the figure shows. The language absorbed some of them. A strategy, an algorithm you plug into other code, used to be an interface and three classes. Now it's a lambda. State and Visitor become a sealed type plus a switch or when that the compiler checks covers every case. Builder mostly becomes Kotlin's named and default arguments, and Singleton becomes an enum or a Kotlin object. Libraries absorbed others. Observer, which tells interested code when something changes, is Kotlin's Flow or the Reactor library, both from earlier tracks. Proxy, a stand-in that controls access to another object, is something the JDK (the kit of tools and libraries that comes with Java) can generate for you while the program runs. You still design the rest by hand. Adapter, Facade, Composite, Bridge, Mediator and Flyweight are about how you cut up your own program, and no language feature does that for you. The intent of an absorbed pattern survives. Strategy still means "swap the algorithm without touching the caller". What changed is the price. When a strategy costs one lambda instead of four classes, you use it ten times as often and stop calling it a pattern. Brian Goetz, Java's language architect, gave the strongest version of this in a 2018 design note on pattern matching. With powerful enough pattern matching, he wrote, "the Visitor pattern is almost completely unnecessary". The same note says this doesn't make inheritance, and methods that subclasses override, wrong. That's the position of this track too. Learn the intent, then reach for the cheapest feature that delivers it. To keep that promise honest, every pattern in this track gets two things: an everyday picture from one small town, and a job in one small program. The program is the order system of the town's corner shop. The shop sells groceries and household things, takes orders by phone and online, and delivers them around town by bike or by van. Its first job is small. Every part of the program needs to know what things cost, so the shop needs one price list that everybody shares. Find five patterns in the JDK Read main in PatternsYouAlreadyUse below (Java or Kotlin, they print the same). Write down what each of the six lines will print before you run anything. Run it from the labs/ folder with the command below. Name the pattern behind each line: singleton, flyweight (one shared object for every equal value), a read-through view (a kind of proxy) or strategy. Which line surprised you? PatternsYouAlreadyUse.java package workbench.patterns.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.Currency; import java.util.List; import java.util.Collections; /** Five patterns hiding in the JDK. Predict each line before you run it. */ public class PatternsYouAlreadyUse { record Order(String id, long totalCents) {} public static void main(String[] args) { // Singleton: one Runtime per JVM, no public constructor System.out.println("1. Runtime is a singleton: " + (Runtime.getRuntime() == Runtime.getRuntime())); // Flyweight: Integer.valueOf caches -128..127, Currency keeps one instance per code Integer a = 127, b = 127, c = 128, d = 128; System.out.println("2. 127 == 127 (boxed): " + (a == b)); System.out.println("3. 128 == 128 (boxed): " + (c == d)); System.out.println("4. EUR == EUR (Currency): " + (Currency.getInstance("EUR") == Currency.getInstance("EUR"))); // Proxy/decorator view: unmodifiableList reads through to the list it wraps List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(List.of("o-1")); List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(ids); ids.add("o-2"); System.out.println("5. view after ids.add(\"o-2\"): " + view); // Strategy: a Comparator is an algorithm you pass in, and a lambda is enough to make one List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Order("o-9", 500), new Order("o-3", 12_000))); orders.sort(Comparator.comparing(Order::totalCents).reversed()); System.out.println("6. sorted by total, desc: " + orders.stream().map(Order::id).toList()); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l01.PatternsYouAlreadyUse labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l01/PatternsYouAlreadyUse.java PatternsYouAlreadyUse.kt package workbench.patterns.l01 import java.util.Collections import java.util.Currency // Five patterns hiding in the JDK and the Kotlin standard library. Predict each line before you run it. private data class Order(val id: String, val totalCents: Long) fun main() { // Singleton: one Runtime per JVM, no public constructor println("1. Runtime is a singleton: " + (Runtime.getRuntime() === Runtime.getRuntime())) // Flyweight: a nullable Int is a boxed java.lang.Integer, and Integer.valueOf caches -128..127 val a: Int? = 127; val b: Int? = 127; val c: Int? = 128; val d: Int? = 128 println("2. 127 === 127 (boxed): " + (a as Any === b as Any)) println("3. 128 === 128 (boxed): " + (c as Any === d as Any)) println("4. EUR === EUR (Currency): " + (Currency.getInstance("EUR") === Currency.getInstance("EUR"))) // Proxy/decorator view: unmodifiableList reads through to the list it wraps val ids = mutableListOf("o-1") val view: List<String> = Collections.unmodifiableList(ids) ids += "o-2" println("5. view after ids += \"o-2\": $view") // Strategy: a Comparator is an algorithm you pass in; compareByDescending builds one from a lambda val orders = listOf(Order("o-9", 500), Order("o-3", 12_000)) println("6. sorted by total, desc: " + orders.sortedWith(compareByDescending { it.totalCents }).map { it.id }) } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l01.PatternsYouAlreadyUseKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l01/PatternsYouAlreadyUse.kt It prints true, true, false, true, [o-1, o-2] and [o-3, o-9]. Line 3 surprises most people: Integer.valueOf only caches the numbers from -128 to 127, so two boxed 128s are two different objects. Line 5 shows that unmodifiableList is a view that reads through to the list it wraps: it blocks writes through the view, and it isn't a copy. Line 6 is a strategy in one line: the comparator decides the order, and sort does the rest. Most of the 23 patterns still have a job. What changed is who writes them: the language, a library, or you.
