h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · Building exactly one price list in Java: enum, holder and double-checked locking
x: Two threads that check a null field both build an FxRates; the holder idiom lets the JVM's class-init lock build exactly one, and a class that needs it takes it through its constructor so a test can pass a fake A singleton is a class with exactly one instance and one place to get it. The JDK has its own: the Runtime Javadoc, Java's official documentation, says every Java application has a single instance of Runtime, and an application can't create its own. In the town, it's the town hall. In the shop's program, it's the price list: every part of the program asks it what a loaf of bread costs, and there should be only one. Making one is easy. Making one lazily, that is, only when somebody first asks, is where people slip. Loading the price list means reading the supplier's price file, which is slow, so we'd like to wait until we need it. Here's the version most of us write first: Java // Naive: this will not work when threads race static PriceList instance; static PriceList getInstance() { if (instance == null) instance = new PriceList(); // two threads can both see null return instance; } Kotlin // Naive: this will not work when threads race private var instance: PriceList? = null fun priceList(): PriceList { if (instance == null) instance = PriceList() // the same race in Kotlin return instance!! } A thread is a path of work that runs alongside others in the same program. The shop's program has several, one for each customer order it's handling, so several can ask for the price list at once. Let's trace the smallest case. Thread A reads instance and sees null. Before A has finished building, thread B reads instance and sees null too. Both build a price list. A third thread that arrives a moment later gets one of the two, and nobody can say which. That's the check-then-act race from Race conditions: why count++ lies. The check and the act are two separate steps, and another thread can slip in between them. Here the town picture breaks for the first time. Two builders who turned up at the empty plot for the town hall would see each other and agree. Threads can't see each other at all. Each one sees only the field. LazyRaceDemo, in the Try it, lets eight threads ask at the same moment, with a constructor that takes 20 ms, like a slow file read. It printed: racy check-then-act: constructor ran 8 time(s), callers saw 8 instance(s) holder idiom : constructor ran 1 time(s), callers saw 1 instance(s) Eight threads asked for the one price list and got eight. So much for one. The second line is a fix, and there are three good ones. Here are the first two, in the order I reach for them: Java enum OrderNumbers { // 1. enum: the JVM makes exactly one INSTANCE INSTANCE; private final AtomicLong last = new AtomicLong(); long next() { return last.incrementAndGet(); } } final class PriceList { // 2. holder: lazy, no lock on the fast path private PriceList() { } private static final class Holder { static final PriceList INSTANCE = new PriceList(); } static PriceList getInstance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; } } Kotlin enum class OrderNumbers { // 1. enum works the same in Kotlin INSTANCE; private val last = AtomicLong() fun next() = last.incrementAndGet() } class PriceList private constructor() { // 2. holder: a private object nested in the companion companion object { private object Holder { val INSTANCE = PriceList() } fun getInstance(): PriceList = Holder.INSTANCE } } The first is an enum with one constant. Effective Java (item 3), the best-known book of Java advice, calls it the preferred approach. The JVM, the program that runs your Java and Kotlin code, creates the constant once. Neither serialization (turning an object into bytes and back) nor reflection (code that inspects and calls classes while the program runs) can make a second. Use it when the object is cheap, or needed at startup anyway, like the counter that hands out order numbers. The second is the holder idiom, for an expensive object you want lazily. The JVM initializes a class, which means running the setup code of its static fields, the first time anyone uses it, and it does that exactly once. So Holder is set up on the first call to getInstance(), not before. The JVM is a strict doorkeeper here: the first thread in runs the setup, and every other thread waits politely at the door until it's done. After that, every call is a plain read of a static field. The third is double-checked locking, from Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders in the memory model track. The holder only works for static fields. When the lazy value is an instance field, one per object, you check it once without a lock. Only if it's still null do you take a lock and check again: Java private volatile Map<String, Long> prices; Map<String, Long> prices() { Map<String, Long> p = prices; // one volatile read on the fast path if (p == null) { synchronized (lock) { p = prices; // check again: another thread may have won if (p == null) prices = p = load(); } } return p; } Kotlin @Volatile private var prices: Map<String, Long>? = null fun prices(): Map<String, Long> { prices?.let { return it } // one volatile read on the fast path synchronized(lock) { prices?.let { return it } // check again: another thread may have won return load().also { prices = it } } } synchronized (lock) lets only one thread at a time into the block. volatile (@Volatile in Kotlin) makes a write to the field visible to every thread that reads the field afterwards. Leave volatile out, and another thread can see a non-null reference to a map whose contents it can't see yet. That's the bug the lab asks you to fix. A plain null check can't promise one instance. Let the JVM or a lock promise it. Java gives us three tools, then, and each needs a little care. Kotlin moves two of them into the language. Build eight singletons by accident Predict: when eight threads call the racy getter together, how many price lists get built? And with the holder? Run LazyRaceDemo with the command below. Delete the Thread.sleep(20) line in the constructor (PriceList in Java, SlowPriceList in Kotlin) and run it three more times. Did the race go away? LazyRaceDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l01; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.IdentityHashMap; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** Eight threads ask for a "singleton" at the same moment. How many get built? */ public class LazyRaceDemo { static final AtomicInteger built = new AtomicInteger(); static final class PriceList { PriceList() { built.incrementAndGet(); try { Thread.sleep(20); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } // a slow load: reading the price file } } // broken: check-then-act on a plain static field static PriceList racy; static PriceList racyGet() { if (racy == null) racy = new PriceList(); return racy; } // initialization-on-demand holder: the JVM runs Holder's static init once, under its class-init lock static final class Holder { static final PriceList INSTANCE = new PriceList(); } static PriceList holderGet() { return Holder.INSTANCE; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { report("racy check-then-act", LazyRaceDemo::racyGet); report("holder idiom ", LazyRaceDemo::holderGet); } static void report(String name, Supplier<PriceList> get) throws InterruptedException { built.set(0); Set<Object> seen = Collections.synchronizedSet(Collections.newSetFromMap(new IdentityHashMap<>())); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] ts = new Thread[8]; for (int i = 0; i < ts.length; i++) { ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } seen.add(get.get()); }); ts[i].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); System.out.printf("%s: constructor ran %d time(s), callers saw %d instance(s)%n", name, built.get(), seen.size()); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l01.LazyRaceDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l01/LazyRaceDemo.java LazyRaceDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l01 import java.util.Collections import java.util.IdentityHashMap import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Eight threads ask for a "singleton" at the same moment. How many get built? private val built = AtomicInteger() private class SlowPriceList { init { built.incrementAndGet() Thread.sleep(20) // a slow load: reading the price file } } // broken: check-then-act on a plain top-level var private var racy: SlowPriceList? = null private fun racyGet(): SlowPriceList { if (racy == null) racy = SlowPriceList() return racy!! } // an object declaration: the JVM runs its static initializer once, under the class-init lock private object PriceListHolder { val instance = SlowPriceList() } private fun holderGet(): SlowPriceList = PriceListHolder.instance private fun report(name: String, get: () -> SlowPriceList) { built.set(0) val seen = Collections.synchronizedSet(Collections.newSetFromMap(IdentityHashMap<Any, Boolean>())) val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { thread { go.await(); seen += get() } } go.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } println("$name: constructor ran ${built.get()} time(s), callers saw ${seen.size} instance(s)") } fun main() { report("racy check-then-act", ::racyGet) report("object holder ", ::holderGet) } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l01.LazyRaceDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l01/LazyRaceDemo.kt With the slow constructor, the racy version builds 8 price lists and callers see 8 different objects. The holder (an object in the Kotlin twin) builds 1. Without the sleep, three runs in a row on a busy four-core machine printed constructor ran 1 time(s). The race didn't go away. The gap between the check and the act shrank to a few microseconds, too small for eight threads to hit often. A real price file is slow, which is why this shows up when the shop is busy and not in your unit test. Runtime (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · Kotlin's object and lazy do the locking for you
x: Kotlin builds the singleton into the language. An object declaration defines a class and its one instance in a single step: Java // what the Kotlin compiler writes for that object, give or take public final class OrderNumbers { public static final OrderNumbers INSTANCE = new OrderNumbers(); private final AtomicLong last = new AtomicLong(); private OrderNumbers() { } public long next() { return last.incrementAndGet(); } } Kotlin object OrderNumbers { private val last = AtomicLong() fun next() = last.incrementAndGet() } The Kotlin docs say the initialization of an object declaration is thread-safe and done on first access. The Java twin shows why. The compiler writes a class with a static INSTANCE field, set when the class is initialized, so the doorkeeper from the holder idiom does the same job here. From Java, you call it as OrderNumbers.INSTANCE.next(). Two details trip people up. A companion object, the object inside a class that holds what Java would make static, is initialized when its outer class is loaded, like a Java static initializer. And companion members aren't really static. They're members of the companion object, so Java callers write PriceList.Companion.getInstance() unless you mark the function @JvmStatic. For a lazy value inside a class, Kotlin has by lazy. You hand it a function, and it runs the function on the first read and keeps the result. It has three modes, and they behave very differently when threads race: Mode What it does Use it for SYNCHRONIZED (default) takes a lock; the function runs once anything with side effects PUBLICATION no lock; racing threads may each run the function, and the first stored value wins cheap, pure computations NONE no lock and no promise across threads values only one thread ever touches LazyModes, in the Try it, sends eight threads at the first two modes at once: SYNCHRONIZED initializer ran 1 time(s), callers saw 1 instance(s) PUBLICATION initializer ran 8 time(s), callers saw 1 instance(s) That second line answers the warm-up. Every caller saw the same map, so the program looks fine. But the function ran eight times. A side effect is anything a function does besides returning its value, such as opening a file or a network connection. If the function opens a connection to the warehouse, eight first reads open eight connections. Seven results are thrown away, and nobody closes their connections. The default lazy is double-checked locking, written once and correctly in the standard library. It does one more thing: if the function throws, the next read runs it again. In Kotlin, never write double-checked locking by hand. Write by lazy. So both languages can make one of something safely. The harder question is whether you should. Count the lazy function's runs Read LazyModes.kt. The Java twin writes each mode by hand, which shows what the modes really do. Predict both lines of output: how many runs of the function, and how many distinct maps, for each mode? Run it with the command below. Add trial(LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE) at the end of main (in Java: trial("NONE", UnsafeLazy::new);) and run it again. Predict first. LazyModes.kt package workbench.patterns.l01 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Eight threads touch a lazy property for the first time, together. Count the initializer runs. class Shop(mode: LazyThreadSafetyMode, private val runs: AtomicInteger) { val prices: Map<String, Long> by lazy(mode) { runs.incrementAndGet() Thread.sleep(20) // pretend to read a slow price file mapOf("BREAD" to 450L) } } fun trial(mode: LazyThreadSafetyMode) { val runs = AtomicInteger() val shop = Shop(mode, runs) val seen = java.util.Collections.synchronizedSet(java.util.Collections.newSetFromMap(java.util.IdentityHashMap<Any, Boolean>())) val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { thread { go.await(); seen += shop.prices } } go.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } println("%-12s initializer ran %d time(s), callers saw %d instance(s)".format(mode, runs.get(), seen.size)) } fun main() { trial(LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED) trial(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION) } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l01.LazyModesKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l01/LazyModes.kt LazyModesJava.java package workbench.patterns.l01; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.IdentityHashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** * Java has no `by lazy`, so here are the three Kotlin modes written by hand. * Eight threads read the value for the first time, together. Count the initializer runs. */ public class LazyModesJava { interface Lazy<T> { T get(); } // SYNCHRONIZED: double-checked locking; the initializer runs once static final class SynchronizedLazy<T> implements Lazy<T> { private final Supplier<T> init; private volatile T value; SynchronizedLazy(Supplier<T> init) { this.init = init; } public T get() { T v = value; if (v == null) { synchronized (this) { v = value; if (v == null) value = v = init.get(); } } return v; } } // PUBLICATION: no lock; every racer computes, compareAndSet keeps the first stored value static final class PublicationLazy<T> implements Lazy<T> { private final Supplier<T> init; private final AtomicReference<T> value = new AtomicReference<>(); PublicationLazy(Supplier<T> init) { this.init = init; } public T get() { T v = value.get(); if (v != null) return v; value.compareAndSet(null, init.get()); return value.get(); } } // NONE: a plain field, no guarantees across threads static final class UnsafeLazy<T> implements Lazy<T> { private final Supplier<T> init; private T value; UnsafeLazy(Supplier<T> init) { this.init = init; } public T get() { if (value == null) value = init.get(); return value; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { trial("SYNCHRONIZED", SynchronizedLazy::new); trial("PUBLICATION", PublicationLazy::new); } static void trial(String mode, java.util.function.Function<Supplier<Map<String, Long>>, Lazy<Map<String, Long>>> make) throws InterruptedException { AtomicInteger runs = new AtomicInteger(); Lazy<Map<String, Long>> prices = make.apply(() -> { runs.incrementAndGet(); try { Thread.sleep(20); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return Map.of("BREAD", 450L); // pretend to read a slow price file }); Set<Object> seen = Collections.synchronizedSet(Collections.newSetFromMap(new IdentityHashMap<>())); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] ts = new Thread[8]; for (int i = 0; i < ts.length; i++) { ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } seen.add(prices.get()); }); ts[i].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); System.out.printf("%-12s initializer ran %d time(s), callers saw %d instance(s)%n", mode, runs.get(), seen.size()); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l01.LazyModesJava labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l01/LazyModesJava.java SYNCHRONIZED runs the function once, and callers see 1 instance. PUBLICATION runs it 8 times, yet callers still see 1 instance, because only the first stored value is kept. The new line reads NONE initializer ran 8 time(s), callers saw 8 instance(s): each thread kept the map it built. No warning, no exception. Object declarations and expressions (Kotlin docs) docs LazyThreadSafetyMode (Kotlin API) docs

h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · Why one shared object causes trouble, and how passing it in helps
x: Back to the town hall for a moment. Everybody depends on it, which is handy, and also the trouble. A note pinned to its board for one visitor is read by the next. And when new staff need to practice, there's no pretend town hall to practice in. Programs have both problems. Here's the shop's code that adds up a basket, fetching the price list the singleton way: Java class OrderPricer { long totalCents(Map<String, Integer> basket) { // product code -> how many long total = 0; for (var line : basket.entrySet()) total += PriceList.getInstance().priceOf(line.getKey()) * line.getValue(); // hidden, global return total; } } Kotlin class OrderPricer { fun totalCents(basket: Map<String, Int>): Long = // product code -> how many basket.entries.sumOf { (code, count) -> PriceList.priceOf(code) * count // PriceList is an object: hidden, global } } To test totalCents with bread at 450 cents, you need to control the price list, and you can't. The instance is global, built once per JVM, and it reads the real price file. A test that changes its state leaks into the next test, so the suite passes or fails depending on the order the tests run in. That's the note on the town hall's board. And nothing in OrderPricer's constructor even tells a reader that it needs a price list. The fix is to pass the dependency in, typed as an interface. This is called dependency injection: an object receives what it needs through its constructor, instead of reaching out for it. Java interface Prices { long priceOf(String code); } class OrderPricer { private final Prices prices; OrderPricer(Prices prices) { this.prices = prices; } long totalCents(Map<String, Integer> basket) { long total = 0; for (var line : basket.entrySet()) total += prices.priceOf(line.getKey()) * line.getValue(); return total; } } // in a test: new OrderPricer(code -> 450) Kotlin fun interface Prices { fun priceOf(code: String): Long } class OrderPricer(private val prices: Prices) { fun totalCents(basket: Map<String, Int>): Long = basket.entries.sumOf { (code, count) -> prices.priceOf(code) * count } } // in a test: OrderPricer { 450 } Now the test has its pretend town hall: one lambda that says every product costs 450 cents. The real program still wants exactly one price list. So make one where the program is put together, in main for example, and pass the same object to everyone who needs it. You get one instance, and nobody calls getInstance(). One instance is a decision for the code that wires the program together. Pass it in. A hand-written singleton still fits in a few places. Stateless objects, such as a comparator that decides which of two values comes first, are safe to share, because there's nothing to pin on their board. So are values with no data at all, such as a Kotlin data object in a sealed hierarchy (lesson 9 of this track). So is state the JVM itself owns, like Runtime. Anything that reads files, talks over the network or holds settings gets passed in. The lab's PriceList follows that rule. It isn't a static singleton: its loader comes in through the constructor, so the tests can pass a slow pretend loader and count how often it runs. The program makes one PriceList, and double-checked locking inside keeps the lazy load safe when eight threads ask at once. Check yourself. Suppose the Kotlin object PriceList had a test helper, PriceList.override("BREAD", 1), and one test called it and never reset it. A test in another class runs later in the same JVM and prices a loaf. What does it get, and why? (1 cent. The object is one static INSTANCE for the whole JVM, so its state outlives the test that set it. A fake that was passed in goes away with its test.)

h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · Java and Kotlin
x: One instance, and one lazy field, in Java and Kotlin Prices.java // one instance: the JVM's class setup does the work enum OrderNumbers { INSTANCE; private final AtomicLong last = new AtomicLong(); long next() { return last.incrementAndGet(); } } // one lazy field per object: double-checked locking final class Prices { private final Supplier<Map<String, Long>> loader; private final Object lock = new Object(); private volatile Map<String, Long> table; Prices(Supplier<Map<String, Long>> loader) { this.loader = loader; } Map<String, Long> table() { Map<String, Long> t = table; if (t == null) { synchronized (lock) { t = table; if (t == null) table = t = Map.copyOf(loader.get()); } } return t; } } Prices.kt // one instance: the language makes it object OrderNumbers { private val last = AtomicLong() fun next() = last.incrementAndGet() } // one lazy field per object: the standard library does the locking class Prices(loader: () -> Map<String, Long>) { val table: Map<String, Long> by lazy { loader().toMap() } // SYNCHRONIZED by default } A Kotlin object compiles to the same thing as a Java holder: a class with a static INSTANCE field set while the class is initialized, so the JVM guarantees one instance. by lazy replaces the whole double-checked block (the volatile field, the lock object and the second check), and it runs the function again on the next read if the first run threw. So Kotlin makes hand-written singletons and hand-written double-checked locking unnecessary. It doesn't fix the design problem: a global object that reads files is as hard to test as a Java static singleton, and the answer in both languages is to pass the instance in.

h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · Worked example
x: Turn a global singleton into a passed-in dependency, then make its lazy load safe The shop charges for delivery by district, and the charge per parcel lives in a zones file read through a global singleton. Before reading on, find what stops you from unit-testing chargeCents. class DeliveryCharge { long chargeCents(String district, int parcels) { long perParcel = Zones.getInstance().centsFor(district); // global; reads the zones file return perParcel * parcels; } } class DeliveryCharge { fun chargeCents(district: String, parcels: Int): Long { val perParcel = Zones.centsFor(district) // an object: global; reads the zones file return perParcel * parcels } } The dependency is hidden and global. A test can't pass its own charges, and anything the singleton keeps leaks into the next test. Make the dependency visible: an interface, passed through the constructor. Now the test is one line. interface Zones { long centsFor(String district); } class DeliveryCharge { private final Zones zones; // 1. the dependency is in the signature DeliveryCharge(Zones zones) { this.zones = zones; } long chargeCents(String district, int parcels) { return zones.centsFor(district) * parcels; } } // test: new DeliveryCharge(d -> 300).chargeCents("HARBOUR", 2) == 600 fun interface Zones { fun centsFor(district: String): Long } class DeliveryCharge(private val zones: Zones) { // 1. the dependency is in the signature fun chargeCents(district: String, parcels: Int): Long = zones.centsFor(district) * parcels } // test: DeliveryCharge { 300 }.chargeCents("HARBOUR", 2) == 600L The real program still wants one zones table, read on first use. main makes one FileZones and passes it to everyone. Inside it the table is an instance field, so the holder idiom can't help, and Java uses double-checked locking. Why must the field be volatile? Answer before you read the comment on it. The Kotlin class is four lines, because by lazy is the whole double-checked block. final class FileZones implements Zones { private final Object lock = new Object(); private volatile Map<String, Long> table; // 2. volatile: readers see the whole map public long centsFor(String district) { Map<String, Long> t = table; // 3. fast path: one read, no lock if (t == null) { synchronized (lock) { t = table; // 4. check again under the lock if (t == null) table = t = loadFromFile(); } } return t.getOrDefault(district, 400L); } private Map<String, Long> loadFromFile() { return Map.of("HARBOUR", 300L, "OLD TOWN", 250L); // the real one reads zones.txt } } class FileZones(private val file: ZoneFile) : Zones { // 2-4. by lazy (SYNCHRONIZED) is the volatile field, the lock and the second check in one line private val table: Map<String, Long> by lazy { file.load() } override fun centsFor(district: String) = table[district] ?: 400L }

h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · Lab
x: A lazy price list that loads once, and a harness that proves it labs/patterns/src/main/java/workbench/patterns/l01/PriceList.java labs/patterns/src/main/java/workbench/patterns/l01/Contention.java ./gradlew :patterns:test --tests 'workbench.patterns.l01.*' Open PriceList, the shop's price list from this lesson. Its loader is a Supplier that reads the prices, priceOf looks one up, and an unknown product, such as CAVIAR (the corner shop doesn't stock it), throws IllegalArgumentException. Run the tests. Seven of ten fail: the harness is a stub, and the price list runs its slow loader eight times when eight threads look up a price together. Write Contention.distinctInstances. Start the threads behind two latches, ready and go, as in Race conditions: why count++ lies. A latch (CountDownLatch) is a gate that opens when its count reaches zero. Store each result in its own array slot, join every thread, then count the results in a set that compares with ==. Fix PriceList.prices() with double-checked locking: a volatile field, a private lock object, and a second check inside synchronized. Keep the Map.copyOf around the loader's result. Run the tests until all ten pass, then twice more. Collections.newSetFromMap(new IdentityHashMap<>()) is a Set that compares with ==. A HashSet would count eight empty lists as one. Read the volatile field into a local variable once at the top, and return the local. The fast path then costs one volatile read. If the loader throws inside the synchronized block, the field is still null and the next caller tries again. You get that for free, as long as you assign the field only after loader.get() returns. All ten tests in SingletonTest pass, three runs in a row. By the end you can say what a design pattern is and which ones modern Java and Kotlin absorbed, pick the right singleton form in each language, prove a lazy instance is built once under contention, and explain why passing an instance in usually beats fetching a global one.

h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · Quiz
x: The shop's Kotlin code has val warehouse by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION) { openConnection() }, and openConnection() opens a network connection to the warehouse. What can go wrong when eight orders arrive at once? Nothing, because the property is lazy Several threads can each open a connection; one is kept and the others are never closed Threads can see a half-built connection The first caller deadlocks PUBLICATION lets every racing thread run the function and keeps the first stored result. Opening a connection is a side effect, so the discarded results leave open connections behind. Drop the mode argument: the default SYNCHRONIZED runs the function once. A half-built value isn't the risk here, because the store itself is safe; only the side effects repeat. You need one counter that hands out order numbers for the whole Java program, and it's fine to create it at startup. Which form is simplest and still correct? An enum with one constant, INSTANCE Double-checked locking on a volatile static field A static field set inside getInstance() behind if (instance == null) A synchronized static getInstance() method An enum gives you exactly one instance, created when the class is initialized, and serialization or reflection can't make another. Double-checked locking is for lazy instance fields and is more than this needs. The plain if version races, and a synchronized getter is correct but takes a lock on every call for nothing. Java code calls a Kotlin factory declared as class Price { companion object { fun of(cents: Long) = Price() } }. What does the Java caller write? Price.of(100) Price.INSTANCE.of(100) Price.Companion.of(100) new Price().of(100) Companion members belong to the companion object, which Java sees as a static field called Companion. Mark of with @JvmStatic if you want Price.of(100) to work from Java. INSTANCE is the field for an object declaration, not for a companion. A test passes alone and fails in the full suite. The class under test reads MessageCounter.INSTANCE.count("sent"). What is the likely cause and fix? JUnit runs tests in parallel, so add synchronized The enum gets created twice, so switch to the holder idiom The JIT caches the count, so make the field volatile The singleton keeps counts from earlier tests, so pass the counter in and give each test its own A global singleton lives as long as the JVM, so one test's counts leak into the next, and the result depends on the order the tests run in. Passing the counter through the constructor lets each test make a fresh one. An enum is never created twice, and visibility isn't the problem when the tests run on one thread. From Lazy init done right in the memory model track: in double-checked locking, what goes wrong if the instance field is not volatile? Two instances can be created The synchronized block can deadlock Another thread can see a non-null reference to an object whose fields it can't see yet Nothing on x86, so it is safe in practice The second check under the lock still prevents a second instance. The problem is the fast path, which reads the field without a lock. Without volatile there's no happens-before edge from the constructor's writes to that read, so a thread can see the reference before the fields. The JIT compiler may reorder those writes on any CPU, x86 included, and the memory model allows it.

h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · Key terms
x: Design pattern A named, reusable shape for solving a design problem that keeps coming back. Singleton A class with exactly one instance and one way to get it. Holder idiom A nested static class whose static field holds the instance. The JVM creates it once, on first use. Double-checked locking Read a volatile field without a lock, and only lock, and check again, when it is still null. Object declaration Kotlin's built-in singleton: a class and its one instance, created thread-safely on first access. Lazy thread-safety mode How by lazy handles racing first reads: SYNCHRONIZED runs once, PUBLICATION may run many times, NONE promises nothing. Dependency injection Giving an object what it needs through its constructor, instead of letting it fetch a global. What is a design pattern, in one sentence? A name for a design problem that keeps coming back, with the shape of its solution and its trade-offs. Vocabulary, not a class template. Which Java singleton form does Effective Java call the preferred approach? A single-element enum: enum OrderNumbers { INSTANCE; ... }. The JVM guarantees one instance, even across serialization and reflection. Why is the holder idiom lazy and thread-safe without a lock in your code? The JVM initializes the nested Holder class on the first read of Holder.INSTANCE, exactly once, under its own class-initialization lock. When do you need double-checked locking instead of the holder idiom? When the lazy value is an instance field, one per object. The holder idiom only works for statics. by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION) { init() }: how many times can init() run? Once per racing thread. The first stored value wins and every caller sees it, but the side effects repeat. Are Kotlin companion object members static on the JVM? No. They belong to the companion object (Price.Companion.of() from Java) unless you mark them @JvmStatic. Why does passing an instance in usually beat getInstance()? The dependency shows in the constructor, a test can pass a fake, and no global state leaks between tests. The program still makes only one.

h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · Go deeper
x: The JDK is getting its own lazy constant, slowly. JDK 25 shipped StableValue as a preview API (JEP 502), that is, a feature you can only try with --enable-preview. JDK 26 renamed it LazyConstant (JEP 526, second preview), and JDK 27 still has it in preview (JEP 531). LazyConstant.of(() -> load()) promises that when several threads race, only one runs the computation. It can't hold null, and a failed computation is remembered: later calls throw without running it again. That's the opposite of Kotlin's lazy, which tries again. Because it's a preview API that has already changed its name once, it stays out of this course's labs. Serialization can break a class-based singleton. Serialization turns an object into bytes and back, and turning the bytes back creates a new object, unless the class defines readResolve() to return the existing instance. The JVM handles enums specially, which is one reason Effective Java prefers them. Kotlin's data object gives a singleton a readable toString() and value-style equals. The Kotlin docs warn that serialization or reflection can still produce a second instance, so compare data objects with ==, never with ===. You'll use data object for states that carry no data, such as Delivered in an order's life, in State and Chain of Responsibility (lesson 9 of this track).

h: Factory Method and Abstract Factory · Static factory methods: constructors with names
x: Start with the counter at the bakery. You say what you want, and the baker hands over something that fits. You never see the kitchen. A static factory method is that counter in code: a static method that returns an instance of its class, or of some class behind an interface. Effective Java, the best-known book of Java advice, opens with it (item 1: consider static factory methods instead of constructors). The JDK, the libraries that come with Java, is full of them: List.of, Duration.ofMinutes, Integer.valueOf, Thread.ofVirtual. A constructor can do one thing: make a new object of exactly its own class. A static factory can do four things a constructor can't. It has a name. Duration.ofMinutes(2) and Duration.ofSeconds(2) both take a long. Two constructors with the same parameter types can't exist, and new Duration(2) would say nothing anyway. It can return an object it made earlier. Integer.valueOf(100) hands back the same cached object every time. It can return any subtype, chosen from the input. List.of(1) and List.of(1, 2, 3) return two different private classes. EnumSet.noneOf picks a set backed by a single long when the enum has 64 constants or fewer, and a bigger one otherwise. The class it returns doesn't have to exist when the factory is written. JDBC, in java.sql, is Java's standard way to talk to a database, and each database company ships its own driver. DriverManager.getConnection(url) returns a connection from whichever driver on the classpath (the list of places the JVM loads classes from) accepts the URL, and those drivers were written long after java.sql. The warm-up was the third point. FactoriesInTheJdk, in the Try it, asks each factory what it handed back. On JDK 21 it printed: List.of(1) -> List12 List.of(1, 2, 3) -> ListN EnumSet of TimeUnit -> RegularEnumSet (7 constants) EnumSet of scripts -> JumboEnumSet (164 constants) Same method, different classes, and you can't write any of those class names in your own code. The factory is the only door. The downsides are small. A class with only private constructors can't have subclasses, which pushes you toward composition (building a class out of other objects instead of extending one) and costs little. Factories are also harder to spot than constructors, so stick to the usual names: of, from, valueOf, parse, newX, create. For the shop's own value types, make this the default. Picture a Price with a private constructor and two doors, Price.ofCents(450) and Price.parse("4.50"). With the constructor private, every Price in the program went through your checks. The compare block at the end of this lesson writes it out in both languages. A constructor can only say new. A factory can say what you mean, and choose. A static factory makes its choice inside its own class. The next step moves the choice out, away from the code that uses the object. Watch the JDK's factories choose Read FactoriesInTheJdk. For each of the first four lines, predict the class name you'll see. The Kotlin twin adds three lines for Kotlin's own listOf. Run it from the labs/ folder with the command below. Type RegularEnumSet in your editor, as if you wanted to use it. Can you? FactoriesInTheJdk.java package workbench.patterns.l02; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.EnumSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Static factories in the JDK pick the class for you. Predict each class name before you run this. */ public class FactoriesInTheJdk { public static void main(String[] args) { // the factory picks an implementation based on the input System.out.println("List.of(1) -> " + List.of(1).getClass().getSimpleName()); System.out.println("List.of(1, 2, 3) -> " + List.of(1, 2, 3).getClass().getSimpleName()); System.out.println("EnumSet of TimeUnit -> " + EnumSet.noneOf(TimeUnit.class).getClass().getSimpleName() + " (" + TimeUnit.values().length + " constants)"); System.out.println("EnumSet of scripts -> " + EnumSet.noneOf(Character.UnicodeScript.class).getClass().getSimpleName() + " (" + Character.UnicodeScript.values().length + " constants)"); // the factory can hand back a cached instance instead of a new one System.out.println("valueOf(100) twice -> same object? " + (Integer.valueOf(100) == Integer.valueOf(100))); System.out.println("Duration.ofSeconds(0) -> same as ZERO? " + (Duration.ofSeconds(0) == Duration.ZERO)); // and its name says what you get, which a constructor can't System.out.println("Duration.ofMinutes(2) -> " + Duration.ofMinutes(2)); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l02.FactoriesInTheJdk labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l02/FactoriesInTheJdk.java FactoriesInTheJdk.kt package workbench.patterns.l02 import java.time.Duration import java.util.EnumSet import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit // The same JDK factories called from Kotlin, plus Kotlin's own. Predict each class name first. fun main() { // JDK static factories pick an implementation from the input println("List.of(1) -> " + java.util.List.of(1).javaClass.simpleName) println("List.of(1, 2, 3) -> " + java.util.List.of(1, 2, 3).javaClass.simpleName) println("EnumSet of TimeUnit -> " + EnumSet.noneOf(TimeUnit::class.java).javaClass.simpleName + " (" + TimeUnit.entries.size + " constants)") println("EnumSet of scripts -> " + EnumSet.noneOf(Character.UnicodeScript::class.java).javaClass.simpleName + " (" + Character.UnicodeScript.entries.size + " constants)") // Kotlin's factory functions do the same (full names, since two of these are nested classes) println("listOf() -> " + listOf<Int>().javaClass.name) println("listOf(1) -> " + listOf(1).javaClass.name) println("listOf(1, 2, 3) -> " + listOf(1, 2, 3).javaClass.name) // a factory can hand back a cached instance, and its name says what you get println("Currency EUR twice -> same object? " + (java.util.Currency.getInstance("EUR") === java.util.Currency.getInstance("EUR"))) println("Duration.ofMinutes(2) -> " + Duration.ofMinutes(2)) } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l02.FactoriesInTheJdkKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l02/FactoriesInTheJdk.kt List12 for one element and ListN for three. RegularEnumSet for TimeUnit (7 constants) and JumboEnumSet for Character.UnicodeScript (164 constants on JDK 21). Both same object? lines print true, because the factories handed back cached objects. None of these classes is public, so your editor won't let you name them: the factory is the only door. Kotlin's listOf plays the same game, returning EmptyList, Collections$SingletonList or Arrays$ArrayList depending on how many elements you pass. DriverManager (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Factory Method and Abstract Factory · Factory Method: let someone else choose the class
x: Checkout asks a factory for a gateway and never names the class; when an authorizer and a refunder must match, one call picks the whole card-network family Here's the problem in the shop. When an order leaves, the shop tells the customer, by text message (SMS) or by email. Tests use a fake messenger that sends nothing. The code that writes the notice shouldn't decide which messenger it gets, or every test run would text real customers. The Factory Method from the Gang of Four (GoF) book on design patterns is the classic answer. A class needs to create something, but it doesn't pick the concrete class. In the book's version, an abstract class declares a creation hook, the factory method, and subclasses override it: Java abstract class OrderNotices { protected abstract Messenger createMessenger(); // the factory method final String orderLeft(String customer) { return createMessenger().send(customer, "your order is on its way"); } } class SmsNotices extends OrderNotices { protected Messenger createMessenger() { return new SmsMessenger(); } } Kotlin abstract class OrderNotices { protected abstract fun createMessenger(): Messenger // the factory method fun orderLeft(customer: String) = createMessenger().send(customer, "your order is on its way") } class SmsNotices : OrderNotices() { override fun createMessenger(): Messenger = SmsMessenger() } That works, and it's still a fair design when the subclass has other reasons to exist. But here it costs one subclass per product, just to pick a constructor. Since Java 8, a function does the same job. A Supplier<Messenger> (in Kotlin, a () -> Messenger) is a factory: call it, and you get a messenger. A constructor reference such as FakeMessenger::new, read as "call this constructor", is the shortest way to write one: Java record OrderNotices(Supplier<? extends Messenger> messengers) { String orderLeft(String customer) { return messengers.get().send(customer, "your order is on its way"); } } new OrderNotices(SmsMessenger::new); // the real program new OrderNotices(FakeMessenger::new); // a test Kotlin class OrderNotices(private val messengers: () -> Messenger) { fun orderLeft(customer: String) = messengers().send(customer, "your order is on its way") } OrderNotices(::SmsMessenger) // the real program OrderNotices(::FakeMessenger) // a test That's the bakery counter in code: OrderNotices asks for "a messenger" and never names a class. The real program and the test each hand in their own way to make one. When the choice depends on data, such as a setting or the customer's preference, put it in one static factory over a sealed family. A sealed interface lists every class that may implement it, so the compiler knows them all: Java static Messenger of(Channel c) { return switch (c) { // no default branch, on purpose case SMS -> new SmsMessenger(); case EMAIL -> new EmailMessenger(); case FAKE -> new FakeMessenger(); }; } Kotlin fun messengerOf(c: Channel): Messenger = when (c) { // no else branch, on purpose Channel.SMS -> SmsMessenger() Channel.EMAIL -> EmailMessenger() Channel.FAKE -> FakeMessenger() } Leave out default (else in Kotlin). Say the shop, in a burst of nostalgia, adds PIGEON to the enum. The switch stops compiling, and the compiler points at the one place that needs a new messenger: MessengerFactory.java:14: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values The compiler is a strict foreman here: it won't build the program until every case has a product. Now add a catch-all branch that returns FakeMessenger, and the build stays green while every pigeon notice goes to the fake. Nothing warns you. That's where the bakery picture breaks. A baker improvises when you ask for something new, and a factory with a default branch improvises too, badly. A factory's switch gets no default. Let the compiler find the new case. People mix up the two names, so let's keep them apart. A static factory is about how one class hands out its own instances. Factory Method is about who decides the concrete class: not the code that uses the object. Kotlin has no static keyword at all, though. So where do its factories live? Break a factory on purpose Run MessengerFactory with the command below. Add PIGEON to the Channel enum and run it again. Read the compiler error. Now add a catch-all as the last branch (default -> new FakeMessenger(); in Java, else -> FakeMessenger() in Kotlin), keep PIGEON, and run again. Where does the pigeon notice go? Undo both changes. MessengerFactory.java package workbench.patterns.l02; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** A factory method over a sealed family, and the same factory passed around as a function. */ public class MessengerFactory { enum Channel { SMS, EMAIL, FAKE } sealed interface Messenger permits SmsMessenger, EmailMessenger, FakeMessenger { String send(String to, String text); // the static factory: an exhaustive switch over the enum, with no default branch static Messenger of(Channel c) { return switch (c) { case SMS -> new SmsMessenger(); case EMAIL -> new EmailMessenger(); case FAKE -> new FakeMessenger(); }; } } record SmsMessenger() implements Messenger { public String send(String to, String text) { return "sms to " + to + ": " + text; } } record EmailMessenger() implements Messenger { public String send(String to, String text) { return "email to " + to + ": " + text; } } record FakeMessenger() implements Messenger { public String send(String to, String text) { return "fake: nothing sent"; } } // the modern "factory method": the caller hands in how to make the product record OrderNotices(Supplier<? extends Messenger> messengers) { String orderLeft(String customer) { return messengers.get().send(customer, "your order is on its way"); } } public static void main(String[] args) { for (Channel c : Channel.values()) { System.out.println(c + " -> " + Messenger.of(c).send("anna", "your order is on its way")); } System.out.println("test notices -> " + new OrderNotices(FakeMessenger::new).orderLeft("anna")); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l02.MessengerFactory labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l02/MessengerFactory.java MessengerFactory.kt package workbench.patterns.l02 // A factory over a sealed family, and the same factory passed around as a function. enum class Channel { SMS, EMAIL, FAKE } sealed interface Messenger { fun send(to: String, text: String): String companion object { // the factory: an exhaustive when over the enum, with no else branch fun of(c: Channel): Messenger = when (c) { Channel.SMS -> SmsMessenger() Channel.EMAIL -> EmailMessenger() Channel.FAKE -> FakeMessenger() } } } class SmsMessenger : Messenger { override fun send(to: String, text: String) = "sms to $to: $text" } class EmailMessenger : Messenger { override fun send(to: String, text: String) = "email to $to: $text" } class FakeMessenger : Messenger { override fun send(to: String, text: String) = "fake: nothing sent" } // the modern "factory method": the caller hands in how to make the product class OrderNotices(private val messengers: () -> Messenger) { fun orderLeft(customer: String) = messengers().send(customer, "your order is on its way") } fun main() { for (c in Channel.entries) { println("$c -> ${Messenger.of(c).send("anna", "your order is on its way")}") } println("test notices -> ${OrderNotices(::FakeMessenger).orderLeft("anna")}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l02.MessengerFactoryKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l02/MessengerFactory.kt The first run prints one line per channel, then test notices -> fake: nothing sent. With PIGEON added, the build fails at the factory: javac says error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values, and kotlinc says 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'PIGEON' branch or an 'else' branch. With a catch-all branch it compiles and prints PIGEON -> fake: nothing sent. A real customer's notice would go to the fake, and nothing warns you.

h: Factory Method and Abstract Factory · Kotlin factories: companion objects, invoke and sealed results
x: Kotlin's factories live in three other places. The companion object is the direct translation of a Java static factory: make the constructor private, and put the factory next to it. Here's the lab's Parcel. The shop sends light parcels with a bike courier and heavy ones by van, so a parcel knows its weight and which courier can carry it: Java public final class Parcel { private final Courier courier; private final int grams; private Parcel(Courier courier, int grams) { this.courier = courier; this.grams = grams; } public static ParcelResult parse(String raw) { /* check, then new Parcel(courier, grams) */ } } Kotlin class Parcel private constructor(val courier: Courier, val grams: Int) { companion object { fun parse(raw: String): ParcelResult { /* check, then Parcel(courier, grams) */ } } } Parcel.parse("2.5 kg") both checks the text and picks the courier. That's the bakery again: you say the weight, and the factory decides who carries it. An operator fun invoke on the companion lets callers write what looks like a constructor call, Fee(250). Behind it runs a factory that can check the value or return a cached one. invoke is the function Kotlin calls when you put parentheses after an object. Use it sparingly, because readers expect Fee(250) to make a new object. The third shape is a top-level function named like the type. Kotlin's coding conventions allow a factory function to share the name of the abstract type it returns, and the kotlinx.coroutines library does exactly that: Job() and MutableStateFlow(0) are functions that return a private class. What a factory returns matters as much as where it lives. A parser that throws makes every caller remember a try. A factory that returns a sealed result, a sealed set of possible answers, makes the compiler remember for them: Java public sealed interface ParcelResult { record Valid(Parcel parcel) implements ParcelResult {} record Invalid(String reason) implements ParcelResult {} } switch (Parcel.parse(input)) { // no default case ParcelResult.Valid v -> book(v.parcel()); case ParcelResult.Invalid i -> askAgain(i.reason()); } Kotlin sealed interface ParcelResult { data class Valid(val parcel: Parcel) : ParcelResult data class Invalid(val reason: String) : ParcelResult } when (val r = Parcel.parse(input)) { // no else is ParcelResult.Valid -> book(r.parcel) is ParcelResult.Invalid -> askAgain(r.reason) } CompanionFactories, in the Try it, uses all three shapes on a delivery slot, a day and an hour. Its parser returns one of three results, and it printed: parse("sat 10") -> ok: SAT 10:00 parse("FRI 23") -> we deliver from 8 to 19, not at 23 parse("MOON 9") -> no such day 'MOON' Add a fourth result later, say Closed for a day the shop doesn't deliver, and every when without an else stops compiling until it handles it. Java 21 gives the same check with a sealed interface, records (classes that only carry data) and a switch whose cases match on the type, as the Java twin shows. Throw for bugs and broken machinery. Return a sealed result for answers the caller must handle. A mistyped weight is an answer, not a bug, so Parcel.parse returns one. We now have a factory that picks a courier for each parcel. But a courier is more than a booking: the shop also has to ask where the parcel is. Let the compiler find the missing case Run CompanionFactories (Kotlin, or its Java twin) with the command below, and read the three parse lines. Add a fourth result: data class Closed(val day: String) : SlotResult in Kotlin, or record Closed(String day) implements SlotResult {} in Java. Predict what happens, then run. Fix it by adding a branch for Closed to describe, not an else or default. CompanionFactories.kt package workbench.patterns.l02 // Three Kotlin factory shapes, and a factory that returns a sealed result instead of throwing. class Slot private constructor(val day: String, val hour: Int) { override fun toString() = "$day $hour:00" companion object { private val days = listOf("MON", "TUE", "WED", "THU", "FRI", "SAT", "SUN") // 1. a named factory in the companion: Slot.parse("SAT 10") fun parse(raw: String): SlotResult { val day = raw.trim().substringBefore(" ").uppercase() val hour = raw.trim().substringAfter(" ").toIntOrNull() ?: -1 return when { day !in days -> SlotResult.BadDay(day) hour !in 8..19 -> SlotResult.BadHour(hour) else -> SlotResult.Ok(Slot(day, hour)) } } } } sealed interface SlotResult { data class Ok(val slot: Slot) : SlotResult data class BadDay(val text: String) : SlotResult data class BadHour(val hour: Int) : SlotResult } class Fee private constructor(val cents: Int) { override fun toString() = "Fee($cents cents)" companion object { private val standard = Fee(250) // 2. operator invoke: callers write Fee(250) and get the cached instance operator fun invoke(cents: Int): Fee = if (cents == 250) standard else Fee(cents) } } interface OrderBook { fun record(entry: String) } // 3. a top-level function named like the interface, as kotlinx.coroutines does with Job() and CoroutineScope() fun OrderBook(): OrderBook = object : OrderBook { override fun record(entry: String) = println(" order book <- $entry") } fun describe(r: SlotResult): String = when (r) { // no else: the compiler checks every case is here is SlotResult.Ok -> "ok: ${r.slot}" is SlotResult.BadDay -> "no such day '${r.text}'" is SlotResult.BadHour -> "we deliver from 8 to 19, not at ${r.hour}" } fun main() { listOf("sat 10", "FRI 23", "MOON 9").forEach { println("parse(\"$it\") -> ${describe(Slot.parse(it))}") } println("Fee(250) === Fee(250)? ${Fee(250) === Fee(250)}") println("Fee(400) === Fee(400)? ${Fee(400) === Fee(400)}") OrderBook().record("o-17 booked for SAT 10:00") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l02.CompanionFactoriesKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l02/CompanionFactories.kt CompanionFactoriesJava.java package workbench.patterns.l02; import java.util.List; /** The Java twin of CompanionFactories.kt: static factories, a cached instance, and a sealed result. */ public class CompanionFactoriesJava { static final class Slot { private static final List<String> DAYS = List.of("MON", "TUE", "WED", "THU", "FRI", "SAT", "SUN"); final String day; final int hour; private Slot(String day, int hour) { this.day = day; this.hour = hour; } @Override public String toString() { return day + " " + hour + ":00"; } // 1. a named static factory: Slot.parse("SAT 10") static SlotResult parse(String raw) { String[] parts = raw.trim().split(" ", 2); String day = parts[0].toUpperCase(); int hour; try { hour = parts.length == 2 ? Integer.parseInt(parts[1].trim()) : -1; } catch (NumberFormatException e) { hour = -1; } if (!DAYS.contains(day)) return new BadDay(day); if (hour < 8 || hour > 19) return new BadHour(hour); return new Ok(new Slot(day, hour)); } } sealed interface SlotResult {} // permitted subtypes: the records in this file record Ok(Slot slot) implements SlotResult {} record BadDay(String text) implements SlotResult {} record BadHour(int hour) implements SlotResult {} static final class Fee { private static final Fee STANDARD = new Fee(250); final int cents; private Fee(int cents) { this.cents = cents; } // 2. Java has no operator invoke, so the cached-instance factory needs a name static Fee of(int cents) { return cents == 250 ? STANDARD : new Fee(cents); } } interface OrderBook { void record(String entry); // 3. a static factory on the interface returns a hidden implementation static OrderBook create() { return entry -> System.out.println(" order book <- " + entry); } } static String describe(SlotResult r) { return switch (r) { // no default: the compiler checks every case is here case Ok ok -> "ok: " + ok.slot(); case BadDay b -> "no such day '" + b.text() + "'"; case BadHour h -> "we deliver from 8 to 19, not at " + h.hour(); }; } public static void main(String[] args) { for (String raw : List.of("sat 10", "FRI 23", "MOON 9")) { System.out.println("parse(\"" + raw + "\") -> " + describe(Slot.parse(raw))); } System.out.println("Fee.of(250) == Fee.of(250)? " + (Fee.of(250) == Fee.of(250))); System.out.println("Fee.of(400) == Fee.of(400)? " + (Fee.of(400) == Fee.of(400))); OrderBook.create().record("o-17 booked for SAT 10:00"); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l02.CompanionFactoriesJava labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l02/CompanionFactoriesJava.java The first run prints ok: SAT 10:00, we deliver from 8 to 19, not at 23 and no such day 'MOON', then true for the cached Fee of 250 cents and false for 400. Java has no operator invoke, so its twin needs a named factory, Fee.of(250). After adding Closed, the build stops: kotlinc says 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is Closed' branch or an 'else' branch., and javac says the switch expression does not cover all possible input values. The compiler found the one place that needs the new case. h: Factory Method and Abstract Factory · Abstract Factory: one choice for a whole matching set
x: Back to the furniture maker. You order a dining set in oak, and one workshop makes the table and the chairs, so they match. Nobody pairs an oak table with pine chairs from the shop down the road. The shop's couriers need the same care. Each courier company gives the shop two services: one books a pickup, and one tells you where a parcel is. Pedal Post carries light parcels by bike, and Big Blue Vans carries heavy ones. A Pedal Post booking reference means nothing to Big Blue Vans. Let every part of the program pick its own booker and tracker, and sooner or later some rarely used path books with the bike courier. Then it asks the van company where the parcel went. Abstract Factory puts that choice in one place. One interface creates every product of the family, and there's one implementation per family: Java public interface CourierServices { Courier courier(); Booker booker(); Tracker tracker(); static CourierServices forCourier(Courier courier) { return switch (courier) { case BIKE -> new PretendServices(Courier.BIKE, "Pedal Post", "PP"); case VAN -> new PretendServices(Courier.VAN, "Big Blue Vans", "BB"); }; } } Kotlin interface CourierServices { val courier: Courier fun booker(): Booker fun tracker(): Tracker companion object { fun forCourier(courier: Courier): CourierServices = when (courier) { Courier.BIKE -> PretendServices(Courier.BIKE, "Pedal Post", "PP") Courier.VAN -> PretendServices(Courier.VAN, "Big Blue Vans", "BB") } } } Callers ask for the family once and take both products from it, as the figure shows. In the lab, Shipping is handed the factory as a function called servicesFor, and asks servicesFor(parcel.courier). Callers can't mix families, because they never pick a product directly. That's the furniture maker in code: one order, one workshop, a matching set. Each family here is one small class built from settings (the courier, the company's name and the prefix of its references), not a PedalPostBooker plus a PedalPostTracker. When the products are interfaces with one method, a family is just a class, or a Java record, of functions. The GoF diagram with two parallel class hierarchies is the worst case, not a requirement. The weakness runs the other way, and it's where the furniture picture breaks too. A new family is cheap: one more implementation, like one more workshop. A new product, say a Canceller that cancels a booking, changes the interface and every family. In the town, every workshop would have to learn to make sideboards before anyone could order one. Make the family the unit of choice. Then a mismatch can't be written. You may not need a factory at all when the whole program uses one family. A test setup and a real setup, chosen once when the program starts, are a single if in main. Write the factory yourself when the choice depends on data that changes from call to call, such as the weight of this parcel. Check yourself. The shop buys a cargo bike and adds CARGO_BIKE to Courier. Where does the build fail, and which callers change? (It fails in forCourier, because its when and switch have no else or default, so you add a branch with the new family's settings. No caller changes: callers only ask for a family and never name a product class.) Shipping asks for a family once. Both products come from that family, so a Pedal Post booking is never tracked at Big Blue Vans.

h: Factory Method and Abstract Factory · Java and Kotlin
x: A checking factory that returns a sealed result Price.java public final class Price { private final long cents; private Price(long cents) { this.cents = cents; } public static Price ofCents(long cents) { // named, and it checks if (cents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative price"); return new Price(cents); } public sealed interface Parsed permits Ok, Bad {} public record Ok(Price price) implements Parsed {} public record Bad(String reason) implements Parsed {} public static Parsed parse(String text) { // "4.50" try { long cents = new BigDecimal(text.trim()).movePointRight(2).longValueExact(); return cents < 0 ? new Bad("negative price") : new Ok(new Price(cents)); } catch (ArithmeticException | NumberFormatException e) { return new Bad("not a price: " + text); } } } // caller: the compiler checks both cases are handled String shown = switch (Price.parse(input)) { case Price.Ok(Price p) -> "saved " + p; case Price.Bad(String why) -> "try again: " + why; }; Price.kt class Price private constructor(val cents: Long) { companion object { @JvmStatic fun ofCents(cents: Long): Price { require(cents >= 0) { "negative price" } return Price(cents) } @JvmStatic fun parse(text: String): Parsed { // "4.50" val cents = text.trim().toBigDecimalOrNull() ?.movePointRight(2) ?.runCatching { longValueExact() }?.getOrNull() ?: return Parsed.Bad("not a price: $text") return if (cents < 0) Parsed.Bad("negative price") else Parsed.Ok(Price(cents)) } } } sealed interface Parsed { data class Ok(val price: Price) : Parsed data class Bad(val reason: String) : Parsed } // caller val shown = when (val p = Price.parse(input)) { is Parsed.Ok -> "saved ${p.price}" is Parsed.Bad -> "try again: ${p.reason}" } The shape is the same in both: a private constructor, named factories, a sealed result and an exhaustive switch or when at the call site. Java 21 takes the result apart with record patterns (case Price.Ok(Price p)), and Kotlin smart-casts it, treating it as that type once is has checked it. The real difference is where the factory lives. Kotlin has no static: ofCents is a function on the companion object, so Java callers would write Price.Companion.ofCents(...) without @JvmStatic. Kotlin also gives you operator fun invoke and top-level factory functions, and its named arguments remove a lot of the constructor confusion that pushes Java code toward factories in the first place.

h: Factory Method and Abstract Factory · Worked example
x: Replace look-alike constructors with named factories The shop's Delivery class grew four constructors: an order can go to the door or be collected in the shop, with or without a note. Look at the last line and decide what it creates before reading on. public class Delivery { public Delivery(String orderId, int grams) { ... } // to the door public Delivery(String orderId) { ... } // collect in the shop public Delivery(String orderId, int grams, String note) { ... } // to the door, with a note public Delivery(String orderId, String note) { ... } // collect, with a note } new Delivery("o-1", "after 5pm"); // ? class Delivery { constructor(orderId: String, grams: Int) { ... } // to the door constructor(orderId: String) { ... } // collect in the shop constructor(orderId: String, grams: Int, note: String) { ... } // to the door, with a note constructor(orderId: String, note: String) { ... } // collect, with a note } Delivery("o-1", "after 5pm") // ? It's a collection with a note, but only the parameter types say so. Adding delivery to a neighbor would mean a fifth constructor with yet another mix of types. Give each kind a name, check there, and make the constructor private so every Delivery goes through a factory. public final class Delivery { private final String orderId; private final OptionalInt grams; // empty = collected in the shop private final String note; private Delivery(String orderId, OptionalInt grams, String note) { this.orderId = orderId; this.grams = grams; this.note = note; } public static Delivery collect(String orderId, String note) { // 1. the name says what you get return new Delivery(orderId, OptionalInt.empty(), note); } public static Delivery toDoor(String orderId, int grams, String note) { if (grams <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("a parcel needs a weight"); // 2. check per kind return new Delivery(orderId, OptionalInt.of(grams), note); } } Delivery.collect("o-1", "after 5pm"); Delivery.toDoor("o-2", 2_500, "blue gate"); class Delivery private constructor( val orderId: String, val grams: Int?, // null = collected in the shop val note: String, ) { companion object { fun collect(orderId: String, note: String) = Delivery(orderId, null, note) // 1. the name says what you get fun toDoor(orderId: String, grams: Int, note: String): Delivery { require(grams > 0) { "a parcel needs a weight" } // 2. check per kind return Delivery(orderId, grams, note) } } } Delivery.collect("o-1", "after 5pm") Delivery.toDoor("o-2", 2_500, "blue gate") Later in the day, a parcel for the door needs a van and a collection needs a shelf behind the till. When the kinds behave differently, let the same factories return different records (or data classes) behind a sealed interface. Callers don't change, and code that handles deliveries can switch over the two cases with the compiler checking it covers both. In Kotlin, @JvmStatic keeps Delivery.collect(...) working for Java callers, and Kotlin callers could also write Delivery.ToDoor(orderId = "o-2", grams = 2_500, note = "blue gate"): named arguments already remove the confusion that started this. public sealed interface Delivery permits Collect, ToDoor { String orderId(); static Delivery collect(String orderId, String note) { return new Collect(orderId, note); } static Delivery toDoor(String orderId, int grams, String note) { return new ToDoor(orderId, grams, note); // 3. the factory picks the record } } record Collect(String orderId, String note) implements Delivery {} record ToDoor(String orderId, int grams, String note) implements Delivery { ToDoor { // 4. the rule lives in the record if (grams <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("a parcel needs a weight"); } } sealed interface Delivery { val orderId: String data class Collect(override val orderId: String, val note: String) : Delivery data class ToDoor(override val orderId: String, val grams: Int, val note: String) : Delivery { init { require(grams > 0) { "a parcel needs a weight" } } // 4. the rule lives in the class } companion object { @JvmStatic fun collect(orderId: String, note: String): Delivery = Collect(orderId, note) @JvmStatic fun toDoor(orderId: String, grams: Int, note: String): Delivery = ToDoor(orderId, grams, note) // 3. the factory picks the class } }

h: Factory Method and Abstract Factory · Quiz
x: Which of these can a static factory do that a constructor can never do? Return an instance of a subtype chosen from its arguments Check its arguments Be called from another package Throw a checked exception Constructors can check their arguments, be public and throw checked exceptions too. Only a factory can return a cached object or a different class, like List.of returning List12 or ListN depending on how many elements you pass. A factory has switch (channel) { case SMS -> ...; case EMAIL -> ...; default -> new FakeMessenger(); }. A teammate adds POST, for letters by post, to the enum. What happens? A compile error in the factory A MatchException at run time Notices by post silently go to the fake messenger The switch throws NullPointerException The default branch catches every new constant, so the build stays green and letters by post go to the fake. Without default, a switch expression over an enum must cover every constant, and adding POST would be a compile error at exactly this line. Which Kotlin shape lets callers write Fee(250) while you return a cached instance? A secondary constructor operator fun invoke in the companion object An init block A data class with a default argument A constructor always makes a new object, primary or secondary. operator fun invoke(cents: Int): Fee on the companion turns Fee(250) into a function call that can return anything, including a cached instance. Readers expect a new object from that syntax, so use it with care. You have interface CourierServices { Booker booker(); Tracker tracker(); } with a bike family and a van family. Now you need a Canceller product too. What does that cost? Nothing: add one new class Only the van family changes You have to switch to Factory Method The interface and every existing family change Abstract Factory makes new families cheap and new products expensive: every family must now produce a canceller, including any fake family your tests use. Weigh that before you add a product to the interface. From lesson 1 of this track: a Kotlin companion object holds a factory of(...) and val cache = loadPrices(). When does loadPrices() run? When the outer class is loaded, like a Java static initializer Lazily, the first time cache is read, under a lock Every time of is called At program startup, for every class on the classpath A companion object is initialized when its outer class is loaded, which matches a Java static initializer, so loadPrices() runs then even if nobody reads cache. If you want it on first read, write val cache by lazy { loadPrices() }.
