h: Factory Method and Abstract Factory · Key terms
x: Static factory method A static method that returns an instance, used instead of a public constructor. Factory Method (GoF) A creation hook that lets something other than the caller pick the concrete class. Now often a Supplier<T> or () -> T. Abstract Factory An interface that creates a whole family of matching objects, with one implementation per family. Product family Objects that must be used together, such as one courier company's booker and tracker. Sealed result A sealed set of answers (Valid, Invalid) returned instead of throwing. A switch or when must handle every case. Companion object A Kotlin object tied to a class, and the usual home for that class's factories. Name two things a static factory can do that a constructor can't. Return a cached instance, and return a subtype chosen from its arguments (List.of gives List12 or ListN). It also has a name. Why leave out default in a factory's switch over a sealed type or enum? So adding a new case is a compile error at the factory. With default, the new case silently takes the default branch. What replaced the GoF Factory Method's creator subclass in modern Java? A function: a Supplier<Messenger>, usually written as a constructor reference such as SmsMessenger::new. Kotlin has no static. Where does a class's named factory usually live? In its companion object: companion object { fun parse(raw: String): ParcelResult }. What name may a Kotlin factory function have, by the coding conventions? The same name as the abstract type it returns, like fun Job(): Job or MutableStateFlow(0). When should a factory return a sealed result instead of throwing? When the failure is an answer the caller is expected to handle, like a mistyped weight. Keep exceptions for bugs and broken machinery. Abstract Factory: what is cheap to add, and what is expensive? A new family is cheap (one implementation). A new product is expensive (the interface and every family change).

h: Factory Method and Abstract Factory · Go deeper
x: DriverManager is a factory whose products didn't exist when it was written. On first use, it asks ServiceLoader for every java.sql.Driver that a JAR on the classpath lists in a META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver file. getConnection(url) then offers the URL to each driver until one accepts it. You can build the same plug-in mechanism yourself: define an interface, list the implementations in META-INF/services/<interface name>, and call ServiceLoader.load(YourInterface.class). The module system adds provides ... with ... and uses ... declarations for the same thing. Effective Java lists the usual factory names, and sticking to them makes factories easy to find: from for a one-argument conversion (Date.from(instant)), of for gathering several values (EnumSet.of(...)), valueOf, getInstance or instance, create or newInstance when each call returns a new object, getType and newType when the factory lives in another class (Files.newBufferedReader), and a bare type (Collections.list). From Java, a Kotlin companion factory is Price.Companion.parse(...). Mark it with @JvmStatic and Java callers can write Price.parse(...). If Java code uses your Kotlin library, do it for every public factory. The same goes for @JvmOverloads on functions with default arguments, which you'll meet in Builder and Prototype (lesson 3 of this track).

h: Builder and Prototype · Named and default arguments replace most builders
x: Here's how the shop prints a parcel label today: Java new Label("12 Mill Lane", "Anna", true, false, true, 2, null); // which true is fragile? Kotlin Label("12 Mill Lane", "Anna", true, false, true, 2, null) // Kotlin allows the same mess Seven arguments, three of them true or false, and only their positions say what they mean. Even the author of Label has to count. Java classes like this often grow a telescoping constructor: one constructor per combination of optional parameters, each calling the next with one more default. That's the sandwich ordered in one breath. The Java fix is the builder from Effective Java (item 2), the best-known book of Java advice: a helper object with one method per field and a build() at the end, as in Label.builder("12 Mill Lane", "Anna").fragile(true).copies(2).build(). It's the sandwich counter. You add one part at a time, and build() hands over the finished object. It works, and it costs a second class that repeats every field. Kotlin removes most of the problem in the language. Parameters can have defaults, and callers can name them. Here's the label as a data class, a Kotlin class that gets equals, toString and copy for free. Its Java twin is a record, a class that only carries data: Java // Java has no named or default arguments: the record keeps the rules, a builder supplies the defaults record Label(String address, String name, boolean fragile, boolean thisWayUp, boolean express, int copies, String note) { Label { if (copies < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("copies must be >= 1"); } Label withExpress(boolean e) { return new Label(address, name, fragile, thisWayUp, e, copies, note); } } var label = Label.builder("12 Mill Lane", "Anna").fragile(true).copies(2).build(); // the builder: next section var rushed = label.withExpress(true); Kotlin data class Label( val address: String, val name: String, val fragile: Boolean = false, val thisWayUp: Boolean = false, val express: Boolean = false, val copies: Int = 1, val note: String? = null, ) { init { require(copies >= 1) { "copies must be >= 1" } } } val label = Label(address = "12 Mill Lane", name = "Anna", fragile = true, copies = 2) val rushed = label.copy(express = true) In the Kotlin version, every argument at the call site says what it is. Optional ones can be left out, in any order. copy gives you a changed copy for free (copies get their own section at the end of this lesson). And the init block, which runs whenever an object is constructed, runs for copy too, so nobody can skip the check. That covers what most Java builders do. Named arguments are the sandwich you can order in one breath after all, because each part comes with its name. Java callers are the gap. Java has no named arguments, so it sees one constructor with seven parameters. @JvmOverloads on the Kotlin constructor generates overloads for Java, one for each trailing default, which is better than nothing and worse than a builder. If Java code will call the class a lot, give it a real builder. Name the arguments and default the rest. Most builders disappear. A rule of thumb for porting Java to Kotlin: if every call site of a Java builder sets two or three fields and leaves the rest alone, the Kotlin version is a data class with defaults and nothing else. If call sites build the object across a loop or an if, keep a builder, as the next section explains. Check yourself. In the Kotlin Label, what does label.copy(copies = 0) do, and why? (It throws IllegalArgumentException. copy builds the new object through the primary constructor, the one in the class header, so the init block runs again.) Named arguments cover the flat, simple cases. A builder is still the better tool in a few others, and the next section names them. Functions: named and default arguments (Kotlin docs) docs Effective Java 3e source, item 2: the Builder read

h: Builder and Prototype · When a builder still earns its place
x: Builders still win in four cases. The first is Java callers, as we just saw. The second is a check that needs the whole object: "a this-way-up arrow only goes on a fragile label" relates two fields. The third is an object built across several steps, such as notes added in a loop, or a neighbor's name added only when nobody is home. Kotlin's buildList { } and buildString { } are standard-library builders for exactly this. The fourth is nested data, which gets its own section next. The modern Java shape is a record that checks plus a small builder that only collects. Here's the shop's request to its courier: Java record DeliveryRequest(String address, String speed, Map<String, String> notes, Duration window, int retries) { DeliveryRequest { // compact constructor: runs on every path Objects.requireNonNull(address, "address"); notes = Map.copyOf(notes); // unmodifiable, and a copy if (retries < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("retries must be >= 0"); } DeliveryRequest withWindow(Duration w) { return new DeliveryRequest(address, speed, notes, w, retries); } static Builder builder(String address) { return new Builder(address); } // Builder: fields with defaults, one setter each, and build() calls the constructor } Kotlin data class DeliveryRequest( val address: String, val speed: String = "STANDARD", val notes: Map<String, String> = emptyMap(), val window: Duration = Duration.ofHours(2), val retries: Int = 0, ) { init { require(retries >= 0) { "retries must be >= 0" } } // runs on every path, copy() too } // no builder and no withers: named arguments and copy(window = ...) do both jobs retries is how many more times the driver comes back when nobody is home, and window is how long the customer will wait in. The builder holds no rules. The rules live in the record's compact constructor, which build(), the method withWindow and a direct new DeliveryRequest(...) all go through. A compact constructor is a record constructor written without a parameter list. Its body runs first, and Java assigns the fields from the parameters after it, which is why notes = Map.copyOf(notes) changes what gets stored. A wither is a method like withWindow that returns a copy with one field changed. Java has no with syntax for records yet, so you write one small wither per field you want to change. The Kotlin twin needs neither builder nor withers, and its init block plays the part of the compact constructor. RecordBuilderDemo, in the Try it, builds one request and pokes at it: built: DeliveryRequest[address=12 Mill Lane, speed=EXPRESS, notes={door=blue gate}, window=PT2H, retries=2] narrower: PT30M notes: unmodifiable wither: retries must be >= 0, was -1 The wither couldn't sneak past the check either. The JDK's newer APIs follow the same idea, a builder that produces an object nobody can change: HttpClient.newBuilder(), and Thread.ofVirtual(), which returns a Thread.Builder. One builder bug deserves a name. If build() checks but the class also has a public constructor that doesn't, half the program skips the rules. That's a sandwich counter with a side door into the kitchen. Put the rules in the type, never only in the builder. The builders so far make flat things. An order has a list of items inside it and notes beside them, and for nested data Kotlin has a neater tool. Find where the rules live Run RecordBuilderDemo with the command below, and read the four lines. In the Java main, change .retries(2) to .retries(-1) (in Kotlin, retries = 2 to retries = -1). Predict: which line throws, and from where? Run it. Undo the change. RecordBuilderDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l03; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Objects; /** A record with a small builder: the record checks, the builder only collects. */ public class RecordBuilderDemo { record DeliveryRequest(String address, String speed, Map<String, String> notes, Duration window, int retries) { DeliveryRequest { // every path to a DeliveryRequest runs this Objects.requireNonNull(address, "address"); notes = Map.copyOf(notes); // really unmodifiable if (retries < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("retries must be >= 0, was " + retries); } DeliveryRequest withWindow(Duration w) { // a hand-written "wither" return new DeliveryRequest(address, speed, notes, w, retries); } DeliveryRequest withRetries(int n) { return new DeliveryRequest(address, speed, notes, window, n); } static Builder builder(String address) { return new Builder(address); } static final class Builder { private final String address; private String speed = "STANDARD"; private final Map<String, String> notes = new LinkedHashMap<>(); private Duration window = Duration.ofHours(2); private int retries = 0; private Builder(String address) { this.address = address; } Builder speed(String s) { speed = s; return this; } Builder note(String k, String v) { notes.put(k, v); return this; } Builder window(Duration w) { window = w; return this; } Builder retries(int n) { retries = n; return this; } DeliveryRequest build() { return new DeliveryRequest(address, speed, notes, window, retries); } } } public static void main(String[] args) { DeliveryRequest req = DeliveryRequest.builder("12 Mill Lane") .speed("EXPRESS") .note("door", "blue gate") .retries(2) .build(); System.out.println("built: " + req); System.out.println("narrower: " + req.withWindow(Duration.ofMinutes(30)).window()); try { req.notes().put("dog", "friendly"); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("notes: unmodifiable"); } try { req.withRetries(-1); // the wither can't skip the check either } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("wither: " + e.getMessage()); } } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l03.RecordBuilderDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l03/RecordBuilderDemo.java RecordBuilderDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l03 import java.time.Duration // The Kotlin twin of RecordBuilderDemo.java: no builder and no withers, because named arguments, // defaults and copy() do both jobs. The rules still live in one place: init. data class DeliveryRequest( val address: String, val speed: String = "STANDARD", val notes: Map<String, String> = emptyMap(), val window: Duration = Duration.ofHours(2), val retries: Int = 0, ) { init { // runs for every construction, copy() included require(retries >= 0) { "retries must be >= 0, was $retries" } } } fun main() { val req = DeliveryRequest( address = "12 Mill Lane", speed = "EXPRESS", notes = mapOf("door" to "blue gate"), retries = 2, ) println("built: $req") println("narrower: ${req.copy(window = Duration.ofMinutes(30)).window}") // Map is a read-only type, so there is no put(). Force a cast and the map behind it refuses too: val write = runCatching { (req.notes as MutableMap<String, String>)["dog"] = "friendly" } println("notes: ${if (write.isFailure) "unmodifiable" else "writable!"}") try { req.copy(retries = -1) // copy() can't skip the check either } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("copy(): ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l03.RecordBuilderDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l03/RecordBuilderDemo.kt The first run prints the built request, PT30M for the narrower copy, notes: unmodifiable and wither: retries must be >= 0, was -1. With .retries(-1) the program stops in build() with IllegalArgumentException: retries must be >= 0, was -1, and the stack trace's top line is the record's compact constructor, RecordBuilderDemo$DeliveryRequest.<init>, called from Builder.build. The builder has no rules of its own, so it can't forget any. The Kotlin twin fails in the same place, its init block, and in a normal run prints copy(): retries must be >= 0, was -1. h: Builder and Prototype · Type-safe builders: lambdas with receivers and @DslMarker
x: For nested data, Kotlin lets you write a builder that reads like a filled-in form. Here's an order in the lab's DSL, a domain-specific language: a small language for one job, written inside Kotlin. Java // Java has no lambdas with receivers; the closest is a Consumer that receives the builder Order o = order(b -> { b.customer("anna@example.com"); b.items(items -> { items.item("rye bread", 450); items.item("oat milk", 220); }); b.note("door", "blue gate"); }); Kotlin val o = order { customer = "anna@example.com" items { item("rye bread", 450) item("oat milk", 220) } note("door", "blue gate") } That's the sandwich counter again, with a smaller counter inside it for the items. The trick is a lambda with receiver. order takes an OrderBuilder.() -> Unit: a function that runs with a builder as this. Inside the braces, customer and items are members of that builder, so you call them with no prefix: Java static Order order(Consumer<OrderBuilder> block) { OrderBuilder b = new OrderBuilder(); block.accept(b); // the block gets the builder as a parameter return b.build(); } final class OrderBuilder { private String customer; private final List<Item> items = new ArrayList<>(); void customer(String c) { customer = c; } void items(Consumer<ItemsBuilder> block) { ItemsBuilder b = new ItemsBuilder(); block.accept(b); items.addAll(b.build()); } Order build() { /* check, then copy into the order */ } } Kotlin fun order(block: OrderBuilder.() -> Unit): Order = OrderBuilder().apply(block).build() class OrderBuilder { var customer: String? = null private val items = mutableListOf<Item>() fun items(block: ItemsBuilder.() -> Unit) { items += ItemsBuilder().apply(block).build() } fun build(): Order { /* check, then copy into the order */ } } Read OrderBuilder().apply(block) as "make a builder, run the block with it as this, and hand the builder back". Gradle's Kotlin build files (the files that build this course's labs) and the kotlinx.html library, for writing web pages in Kotlin, are built the same way. The builder is still a builder: build() is the one place that sees every field, so it checks them there. There's one trap. Inside items { }, two receivers, objects that this can refer to, are in scope: the ItemsBuilder and the outer OrderBuilder. So customer = "x" written inside the inner block compiles, and quietly sets the outer field. The demo in the Try it shows this on a delivery round, a driver and a list of stops. Without protection, one innocent-looking line inside the stops block changed the driver: Round(driver=oops, stops=[Stop(orderId=o-101, parcels=2), Stop(orderId=o-102, parcels=3)]) @DslMarker closes that hole. It's an annotation for annotations: you mark your own annotation with it, then put yours on every builder class. Java // Java needs no marker: each block names its builder, so reaching the outer one means typing b b.items(items -> { items.item("rye bread", 450); b.customer("x"); // compiles, but you can see it in review }); Kotlin @DslMarker annotation class OrderDsl @OrderDsl class OrderBuilder { ... } @OrderDsl class ItemsBuilder { ... } With both builders marked, the compiler only lets you call members of the nearest receiver without a prefix. Reaching the outer one needs an explicit label, this@order.customer, which nobody writes by accident. Mark every builder in a DSL. Then an inner block can't reach outside by accident. Build a DSL only when the data nests. A flat label with seven fields is clearer with named arguments, and a DSL would add two classes for nothing. The payoff comes with structure, like items inside an order or stops on a delivery round. It also helps when many people write the same kind of thing, because inside each block the editor offers only that builder's methods. Building is half of this lesson. The other half starts from an object you already have. Make the inner block reach outside Run DslScope.kt with the command below. Uncomment the line driver = "oops" inside the stops { } block. Predict, then run. Now delete both @RoundDsl lines above the two builder classes (keep the annotation class itself) and run again. Who is driving the round now? Restore the file. Then open the Java twin and uncomment rb.driver("oops"): it compiles, but notice that you had to type the outer builder's name. DslScope.kt package workbench.patterns.l03 // A tiny delivery-round DSL. @DslMarker stops an inner block from reaching the outer builder by accident. @DslMarker annotation class RoundDsl data class Stop(val orderId: String, val parcels: Int) data class Round(val driver: String, val stops: List<Stop>) @RoundDsl class StopsBuilder { private val stops = mutableListOf<Stop>() fun stop(orderId: String, parcels: Int) { stops += Stop(orderId, parcels) } fun build() = stops.toList() } @RoundDsl class RoundBuilder { var driver: String = "unassigned" private var stops: List<Stop> = emptyList() fun stops(block: StopsBuilder.() -> Unit) { stops = StopsBuilder().apply(block).build() } fun build() = Round(driver, stops) } fun round(block: RoundBuilder.() -> Unit): Round = RoundBuilder().apply(block).build() fun main() { val r = round { driver = "Sam" stops { stop("o-101", 2) stop("o-102", 3) // driver = "oops" // step 2 of the Try it: uncomment this line } } println(r) println("parcels on the van: ${r.stops.sumOf { it.parcels }}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l03.DslScopeKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l03/DslScope.kt DslScopeJava.java package workbench.patterns.l03; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** * The Java twin of DslScope.kt. Java has no lambdas with receivers, so each block is a Consumer * that gets its builder as a named parameter. */ public class DslScopeJava { record Stop(String orderId, int parcels) {} record Round(String driver, List<Stop> stops) {} static final class StopsBuilder { private final List<Stop> stops = new ArrayList<>(); StopsBuilder stop(String orderId, int parcels) { stops.add(new Stop(orderId, parcels)); return this; } List<Stop> build() { return List.copyOf(stops); } } static final class RoundBuilder { private String driver = "unassigned"; private List<Stop> stops = List.of(); RoundBuilder driver(String d) { driver = d; return this; } RoundBuilder stops(Consumer<StopsBuilder> block) { StopsBuilder b = new StopsBuilder(); block.accept(b); stops = b.build(); return this; } Round build() { return new Round(driver, stops); } } static Round round(Consumer<RoundBuilder> block) { RoundBuilder b = new RoundBuilder(); block.accept(b); return b.build(); } public static void main(String[] args) { Round r = round(rb -> { rb.driver("Sam"); rb.stops(s -> { s.stop("o-101", 2); s.stop("o-102", 3); // rb.driver("oops"); // step 4 of the Try it: this compiles, but you have to name rb }); }); System.out.println(r); System.out.println("parcels on the van: " + r.stops().stream().mapToInt(Stop::parcels).sum()); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l03.DslScopeJava labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l03/DslScopeJava.java The first run prints a round with driver=Sam and parcels on the van: 5. With the line uncommented, the build fails: 'var driver: String' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver. Use an explicit receiver if necessary. Without the marker it compiles and prints driver=oops: the inner block quietly rewrote the outer round. The Java twin prints driver=oops too, but the line that did it says rb. in plain sight. h: Builder and Prototype · Prototype: every copy is shallow until you make it safe
x: A copy copies the arrow, not the object: two carts share one list until the list can't change and a change builds a new one; named and default arguments replace most builders Now the photocopier. Prototype means making a new object by copying an existing one and changing a few fields. The shop does this every week: the Saturday breakfast box is set up once, and each customer gets a copy with their own name and notes. Tests do it too, with one sample order copied and changed in each test. Java's original tool for this, Cloneable, is broken by design. The interface has no clone method, so implementing it gives callers nothing to call. Object.clone() is protected, and it makes a shallow copy (more on that in a moment). To use it, you override clone, call super.clone(), catch a CloneNotSupportedException that can't happen, and then fix every changeable field by hand. Skip it. Use a copy constructor, a static copy factory, or a wither on a record. Records make withers easy to write, and Kotlin data classes generate copy(). Neither copies deeply. The Kotlin docs say it plainly: copy() creates a shallow copy, and references to other objects are shared. A shallow copy copies each field's value, and when the value is a reference to another object, such as a list, it copies the reference, not the list: Java record Cart(String id, List<String> items) { Cart withId(String newId) { return new Cart(newId, items); } // a wither: shares the list } var c1 = new Cart("c1", new ArrayList<>(List.of("bread"))); var c2 = c1.withId("c2"); c2.items().add("milk"); // c1.items() is now [bread, milk] Kotlin data class Cart(val id: String, val items: MutableList<String>) val c1 = Cart("c1", mutableListOf("bread")) val c2 = c1.copy(id = "c2") c2.items += "milk" // c1.items is now [bread, milk] That was the warm-up. copy() is very obliging: it copies exactly what you asked for, the reference, and not one thing more. Here the photocopier picture breaks. A photocopy is a separate piece of paper, and writing on it never changes the original. But picture a form with a shopping list clipped to it. copy() gives you a new form with the same shopping list clipped on, so writing on the copy's list writes on the original's. The figure shows both carts holding one list. The fix is the same in both languages. Store collections that can't change, List.copyOf in a compact constructor in Java and a read-only List in Kotlin, and let withers build a new collection: copy(items = items + "milk"). Then sharing is harmless, because nobody can write on the shared sheet. A copy is only as safe as the parts it shares. Share only parts that can't change. Kotlin has a second trap. data class Email private constructor(val value: String) still gets a public copy(), so Email.of("anna@example.com").copy(value = "not-an-email") compiles and skips your factory. Kotlin 2.4 only warns, at the line that calls copy: w: CopyTrap.kt:29:24 This 'copy()' exposes the non-public primary constructor of a 'data class'. ... This will become an error in language version 2.5. Add @ConsistentCopyVisibility to make copy() as private as the constructor today. A check in an init block is safer still, because copy() runs it. Java records never had this illusion. A record's canonical constructor, the one that takes every component, can't be less visible than the record itself, so the rules belong in the compact constructor from the start. Check yourself. The shop's breakfast box template is a data class with val tags: MutableList<String>. Anna's copy gets the tag "no nuts" through annasBox.tags += "no nuts". What do Ben's box and the template now say? (Both say no nuts too, because all three share one list. With a read-only List and copy(tags = tags + "no nuts"), only Anna's box changes.) Trigger both copy traps Read CopyTrap.kt (or its Java twin) and predict the three lines it prints. Run it. If Gradle compiles the file again, read the w: warnings too. Add @ConsistentCopyVisibility on the line above data class Email, and run again. CopyTrap.kt package workbench.patterns.l03 // Two traps in data class copy(): it is shallow, and it ignores a private constructor. data class Cart(val id: String, val items: MutableList<String>) data class Email private constructor(val value: String) { companion object { fun of(raw: String): Email { require("@" in raw) { "not an email: $raw" } return Email(raw) } } } data class Price(val cents: Long) { init { require(cents >= 0) { "negative price: $cents" } } } fun main() { // trap 1: copy() copies the reference to the list, not the list val c1 = Cart("c1", mutableListOf("bread")) val c2 = c1.copy(id = "c2") c2.items += "milk" println("c1.items after changing c2: ${c1.items}") // trap 2: the private constructor does not cover the generated copy() val email = Email.of("anna@example.com") val broken = email.copy(value = "not-an-email") println("copy() skipped the factory: $broken") // init blocks DO run on copy() val result = runCatching { Price(5).copy(cents = -1) } println("Price(5).copy(cents = -1): ${result.exceptionOrNull()?.message}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l03.CopyTrapKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l03/CopyTrap.kt CopyTrapJava.java package workbench.patterns.l03; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** The Java twin of CopyTrap.kt: record copies are shallow, and a factory can't hide a record's constructor. */ public class CopyTrapJava { record Cart(String id, List<String> items) { Cart withId(String newId) { return new Cart(newId, items); } // a hand-written wither: shares the list } record Email(String value) { // a record's canonical constructor is never more private than the record itself, // so this factory can always be bypassed with new Email(...) static Email of(String raw) { if (!raw.contains("@")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("not an email: " + raw); return new Email(raw); } } record Price(long cents) { Price { // compact constructor: every path runs it if (cents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative price: " + cents); } Price withCents(long c) { return new Price(c); } } public static void main(String[] args) { // trap 1: the wither copies the reference to the list, not the list Cart c1 = new Cart("c1", new ArrayList<>(List.of("bread"))); Cart c2 = c1.withId("c2"); c2.items().add("milk"); System.out.println("c1.items after changing c2: " + c1.items()); // trap 2: the factory checks, the canonical constructor doesn't Email broken = new Email("not-an-email"); System.out.println("new skipped the factory: " + broken); // the compact constructor DOES run on withers try { new Price(5).withCents(-1); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("new Price(5).withCents(-1): " + e.getMessage()); } } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l03.CopyTrapJava labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l03/CopyTrapJava.java It prints c1.items after changing c2: [bread, milk] (the copy shared the list), copy() skipped the factory: Email(value=not-an-email), and Price(5).copy(cents = -1): negative price: -1, because init runs on copy(). The compiler warns twice: Non-public primary constructor is exposed via the generated 'copy()' method of the 'data' class. on the class, and a second warning at the copy call that says it will become an error in language version 2.5. With @ConsistentCopyVisibility, the build stops with Cannot access 'fun copy(value: String = ...): Email': it is private in 'workbench.patterns.l03.Email'. The Java twin tells the same story: the wither shares the list, new Email("not-an-email") skips the factory, and the compact constructor rejects -1. A shallow copy shares the list, so changing one cart changes both. Build a new list in the copy instead. Data classes: copying (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Builder and Prototype · Java and Kotlin
x: A prototype that copies safely DeliveryPlan.java record DeliveryPlan(String district, List<String> days, Map<String, Long> feeCents) { DeliveryPlan { // every copy passes through here days = List.copyOf(days); feeCents = Map.copyOf(feeCents); } DeliveryPlan forDistrict(String d) { // safe to share: nothing can change return new DeliveryPlan(d, days, feeCents); } DeliveryPlan withDay(String day) { // copy, change the copy, wrap again var copy = new ArrayList<>(days); copy.add(day); return new DeliveryPlan(district, copy, feeCents); } } var base = new DeliveryPlan("town center", List.of("MON", "THU"), Map.of("BIKE", 250L)); var harbour = base.forDistrict("harbour").withDay("SAT"); DeliveryPlan.kt data class DeliveryPlan( val district: String, val days: List<String>, // read-only types val feeCents: Map<String, Long>, ) val base = DeliveryPlan("town center", listOf("MON", "THU"), mapOf("BIKE" to 250L)) val harbour = base.copy( district = "harbour", days = base.days + "SAT", // + builds a new list ) Kotlin generates copy() with named arguments, so it needs no withers, and + on a read-only List or Map returns a new collection. Java needs one hand-written wither per field. Both copies are shallow, and the safety comes from the parts, not from the copy. There's one real difference. Java's compact constructor can replace the incoming list with List.copyOf, while a Kotlin data class property can't be reassigned in init. A Kotlin List parameter is only read-only, so a caller who passes a MutableList and keeps a reference to it can still change it. If that matters, take the list as a plain constructor parameter and store toList() in a property.

h: Builder and Prototype · Worked example
x: From a telescoping constructor to a record and builder, and to a Kotlin class Here's the label call from the first section, with all seven arguments. Before reading on, say which argument is the note, and which rules you'd expect Label to enforce. new Label("12 Mill Lane", "Anna", true, true, false, 1, "ring twice"); Label("12 Mill Lane", "Anna", true, true, false, 1, "ring twice") Put every rule in one place that all paths go through: the record's compact constructor in Java, the init block in Kotlin. The rule that relates two fields (a this-way-up arrow only goes on a fragile label) can only be checked where all the fields are known. Kotlin also gets its defaults here, which is half of what a builder does. record Label(String address, String name, boolean fragile, boolean thisWayUp, boolean express, int copies, String note) { Label { if (copies < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("copies must be >= 1"); // 1. one-field rules if (note != null && note.length() > 30) throw new IllegalArgumentException("note is too long"); if (thisWayUp && !fragile) // 2. a rule across fields throw new IllegalArgumentException("this-way-up arrows only go on fragile labels"); } } data class Label @JvmOverloads constructor( val address: String, val name: String, val fragile: Boolean = false, // 3. defaults live in the signature val thisWayUp: Boolean = false, val express: Boolean = false, val copies: Int = 1, val note: String? = null, ) { init { require(copies >= 1) { "copies must be >= 1" } // 1. one-field rules require(note == null || note.length <= 30) { "note is too long" } require(!thisWayUp || fragile) { // 2. a rule across fields "this-way-up arrows only go on fragile labels" } } } Java needs a builder that only collects and supplies defaults. Its build() calls the record's constructor, so the rules run there. Kotlin needs no builder: named arguments do the job, and @JvmOverloads gives Java callers some overloads. If Java code calls the Kotlin class often, add a builder for it too. // inside record Label static Builder builder(String address, String name) { return new Builder(address, name); } static final class Builder { private final String address; private final String name; private boolean fragile, thisWayUp, express; private int copies = 1; private String note; // 3. defaults Builder(String address, String name) { this.address = address; this.name = name; } // 4. required up front Builder fragile(boolean f) { fragile = f; return this; } Builder thisWayUp(boolean t) { thisWayUp = t; return this; } Builder copies(int n) { copies = n; return this; } Builder note(String n) { note = n; return this; } Label build() { return new Label(address, name, fragile, thisWayUp, express, copies, note); } } var label = Label.builder("12 Mill Lane", "Anna").fragile(true).thisWayUp(true).note("ring twice").build(); // 4. required values have no default, so the compiler insists on them val label = Label("12 Mill Lane", "Anna", fragile = true, thisWayUp = true, note = "ring twice") val rushed = label.copy(express = true) // the "wither" is generated

x: A checking order DSL, and a prototype that stops leaking labs/patterns/src/main/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l03/OrderDsl.kt labs/patterns/src/main/java/workbench/patterns/l03/OrderTemplate.java ./gradlew :patterns:test --tests 'workbench.patterns.l03.*' Open the two files. OrderDsl.kt is the order DSL from this lesson, and OrderTemplate is the shop's prototype for regular orders such as the Saturday breakfast box. Run the tests. Twelve of thirteen fail: the DSL is all TODO, and OrderTemplate leaks tags and notes between copies. In OrderDsl.kt, write ItemsBuilder: keep a private MutableList, and return toList() from build(). Write OrderBuilder: items runs the block on a fresh ItemsBuilder and keeps its items, note puts into a private map, and build() checks with require and copies the collections into the Order. Then write order. Put @OrderDsl on both builder classes. Fix OrderTemplate.java: add a compact constructor that stores List.copyOf and Map.copyOf, and make the withers copy the collection, change the copy, and build a new template. Run the tests until all thirteen pass. require(condition) { "customer is required" } throws IllegalArgumentException with that message when the condition is false. currency.matches(Regex("[A-Z]{3}")) checks for three capital letters. ItemsBuilder().apply(block).build(): apply runs the lambda with the builder as this and returns the builder. In a record's compact constructor, tags = List.copyOf(tags); replaces the parameter before the field is set. You don't write this.tags = .... All thirteen tests in OrderDslTest and OrderTemplateTest pass. By the end you can choose between named arguments, a Java record with a builder, and a Kotlin DSL builder, and make copies of templates that never share changeable parts with the original.

h: Builder and Prototype · Quiz
x: data class Fee(val cents: Int) { init { require(cents in 0..1_000) } }. What does Fee(250).copy(cents = 5_000) do? Returns Fee(5000), because copy() skips init Throws IllegalArgumentException, because copy() runs init Doesn't compile Returns Fee(250) unchanged copy() calls the primary constructor with the new values, so every init block runs again and require throws. That's why init is the safest place for a data class's rules. What copy() does skip is a checking factory, when the constructor is private. Java code will call your Kotlin Label(address, name, fragile = false, thisWayUp = false, express = false, copies = 1) constructor from many places. What helps that code most? Nothing; Java 21 supports named arguments Mark the class data Put @JvmStatic on the constructor Add @JvmOverloads, or give Java a builder Java has no named or default arguments, so it sees one six-parameter constructor. @JvmOverloads generates overloads that drop trailing defaults, and a builder lets Java code set any mix of fields by name. @JvmStatic applies to companion members, not constructors, and data changes nothing for Java callers here. A DSL has no @DslMarker. Inside items { }, someone writes currency = "USD". ItemsBuilder has no currency, but the outer OrderBuilder does. What happens? It sets the outer builder's currency Compile error: unresolved reference An exception at run time It declares a local variable Both receivers are in scope inside the inner lambda, so the compiler finds currency on the outer builder and sets it. Nothing fails. With @DslMarker on both builders, that line becomes a compile error unless you write this@order.currency. record Cart(String id, List<String> items) {}. c1 was built with new ArrayList<>(List.of("bread")). Then Cart c2 = new Cart("c2", c1.items()); c2.items().add("milk");. What happens? c1 is unchanged, because records can't change The add throws UnsupportedOperationException c1.items() now contains milk too It doesn't compile A record only stops its fields from pointing somewhere else. The ArrayList a field points to can still change, and c2 shares it. A compact constructor with items = List.copyOf(items); would give each record its own unmodifiable list, and the add would then throw. From Factory Method and Abstract Factory: you hide a data class's constructor (data class Email private constructor(val value: String)) and offer a checking Email.of(raw). In Kotlin 2.4, which line still creates an unchecked Email? Email("x") in another file Email.of("a@b.example").copy(value = "x") Email.of("x") None: a private constructor covers every path The generated copy() stays public even when the constructor is private; Kotlin 2.4 only warns about it. So copy creates an Email your factory never saw. @ConsistentCopyVisibility makes copy() private, and a check in init would run on copy() too. A direct constructor call from outside doesn't compile.

h: Builder and Prototype · Explain it back
x: A colleague says: "Kotlin data classes can't change, so copy() gives us safe, independent order templates." Explain where that's wrong, and how you'd make templates safe in Kotlin and in Java.

h: Builder and Prototype · Key terms
x: Telescoping constructor A chain of constructors, each adding one more optional parameter. Builder A helper that collects values step by step and makes the finished object in build(). Lambda with receiver A lambda whose this is a given object, written T.() -> R. DslMarker An annotation for your DSL's own marker annotation; it limits calls without a prefix to the nearest receiver. Prototype Making a new object by copying an existing one and changing a few fields. Wither A method like withWindow(w) that returns a copy with one field changed. Shallow copy A copy that shares the objects its fields point to, instead of copying them too. Does a Kotlin data class's init block run on copy()? Yes. copy() calls the primary constructor, so the require checks in init run again. What is a lambda with receiver? A function type like Builder.() -> Unit. Inside the lambda, this is the Builder, so you call its members without a prefix. What does @DslMarker prevent? Calling a member of an outer DSL receiver without a prefix from inside an inner block. Reaching it then needs an explicit this@label. Why is Cloneable considered broken? It declares no clone method, and Object.clone() is protected, shallow and throws a checked exception. Use copy constructors or withers. Is a Kotlin data class copy() deep or shallow? Shallow. A property that holds a changeable object, such as a MutableList, is shared by the original and the copy. Where do the checks go for a Java record that has a builder? In the record's compact constructor, so build(), withers and direct new calls all run them. data class Email private constructor(...): is its copy() private in Kotlin 2.4? No. It stays public, with a warning. Add @ConsistentCopyVisibility to make it private.

h: Builder and Prototype · Go deeper
x: Effective Java's hierarchical builder solves a problem you may meet in a shared Java library: a Pizza.Builder that subclasses (NyPizza.Builder, Calzone.Builder) extend without losing the subclass's type in a chain of calls. It uses a recursive type parameter, Builder<T extends Builder<T>>, and an abstract self() method that each subclass implements as return this;. Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance in the generics track showed why that recursive bound works. In Kotlin you almost never need it, because named arguments and copy() remove the chain. Java has no with syntax for records yet. Project Amber, the OpenJDK project for smaller language features, has proposed one, derived record creation (JEP 468), where you would write something like point with { x = 3; }. Check its status on the JEP page before you plan around it. Until then, write withers for the fields that really change. People sometimes copy a whole tree of objects deeply by turning it into bytes and back (serialization), or with a reflection library. It works, it's slow, and it copies things you didn't mean to copy, such as a shared clock or an open connection. If you need a deep copy, the cleaner fix is usually to make the parts unchangeable, so a shallow copy is enough. Kotlin's buildList { add(...) }, buildMap { } and buildString { } are small standard-library builders with receivers. Use them when you build a collection with loops or conditions; the result is read-only once the block returns.

h: Adapter and Facade · Adapter: make their interface fit your port
x: An adapter has your port's shape on one side and the SDK's on the other and translates calls, answers and errors; a facade is one front door that owns the order of the steps and the undo An adapter makes a class you can't change fit the interface your code expects. That's the travel plug: the hotel's socket is the class you can't change, your charger is your own code, and the adapter sits between them. The first thing the shop has to fit is a courier company's old client library. It speaks XML, a text format of tags in angle brackets, and it throws IOException when the courier's office is closed. IOException is a checked exception, one the Java compiler makes you catch or declare. The shop's code should see none of that. It should see its own port: an interface, in the shop's own words, that the rest of the code depends on. Java interface Courier { String book(String address, int grams); } Kotlin fun interface Courier { fun book(address: String, grams: Int): String } The adapter implements the port and holds the old client. All the translation happens inside it, in both directions: the shop's words into the client's on the way in, and the client's answers and errors into the shop's on the way out. Java record OldCourierAdapter(OldCourierClient old) implements Courier { public String book(String address, int grams) { String xml = "<parcel grams='" + grams + "' to='" + address + "'/>"; try { String answer = old.submit(xml); return answer.substring(answer.indexOf("ref='") + 5, answer.lastIndexOf("'")); // their format ends here } catch (IOException e) { throw new CourierUnavailable("courier unreachable", e); // our exception, not theirs } } } Kotlin class OldCourierAdapter(private val old: OldCourierClient) : Courier { override fun book(address: String, grams: Int): String { val xml = "<parcel grams='$grams' to='$address'/>" try { val answer = old.submit(xml) return answer.substringAfter("ref='").substringBefore("'") // their format ends here } catch (e: IOException) { throw CourierUnavailable("courier unreachable", e) // our exception, not theirs } } } First we write the request in their format, then we call them, then we cut our booking reference out of their answer. The tricky line is the catch. Their IOException stops there, and the caller gets the shop's own CourierUnavailable instead. XmlAdapterDemo, in the Try it, books one parcel and then tries an address the courier can't reach: booked, ref R-2500 caller sees CourierUnavailable: courier unreachable lambda adapter: QUICK-990 The most common adapter bug is a leaky one. If IOException, the old client's codes or its classes show up in the shop's other classes, every caller now depends on that courier. Switching couriers then means changing all of them. That's where the travel plug picture breaks. A plug either fits or it doesn't, but a software adapter must also translate failures. A leaky one passes the foreign voltage straight through. Java's checked exceptions help here, almost by accident. The port doesn't declare IOException, so the Java compiler won't let the client's exception escape the adapter. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so the same leak compiles without a word. In Kotlin, the discipline is yours. Translate at the edge, in both directions. Let nothing foreign through. When the port has one method, as Courier does, you don't even need a class. A lambda or a method reference is the adapter, in both languages, and that's the third line of the output. For plain data, Kotlin has a lighter adapter still. Let the old client's exception leak Run XmlAdapterDemo in either language with the command below. Read the three lines. In the Java version, delete the try/catch in OldCourierAdapter.book, keeping the two lines inside the try. Predict, then run. Do the same in the Kotlin version. Predict, then run. Restore both files. XmlAdapterDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l04; import java.io.IOException; import java.util.function.BiFunction; /** An old courier client adapted to our port, plus a lambda adapter for a one-method port. */ public class XmlAdapterDemo { // the port our shop code depends on interface Courier { String book(String address, int grams); } // a client we can't change: XML text in, XML text out, checked IOException on failure static final class OldCourierClient { String submit(String xml) throws IOException { if (xml.contains("Nowhere")) throw new IOException("courier office closed: 503"); String grams = xml.substring(xml.indexOf("grams='") + 7, xml.indexOf("' to=")); return "<ok ref='R-" + grams + "'/>"; } } static final class CourierUnavailable extends RuntimeException { CourierUnavailable(String message, Throwable cause) { super(message, cause); } } // the adapter: implements our port, holds the old client, translates both ways record OldCourierAdapter(OldCourierClient old) implements Courier { public String book(String address, int grams) { String xml = "<parcel grams='" + grams + "' to='" + address + "'/>"; try { String answer = old.submit(xml); return answer.substring(answer.indexOf("ref='") + 5, answer.lastIndexOf("'")); // their format ends here } catch (IOException e) { throw new CourierUnavailable("courier unreachable", e); // our exception, not theirs } } } // for a one-method port, a lambda is the adapter static Courier fromFunction(BiFunction<String, Integer, String> oldBook) { return (address, grams) -> oldBook.apply(address, grams); } public static void main(String[] args) { Courier courier = new OldCourierAdapter(new OldCourierClient()); System.out.println("booked, ref " + courier.book("12 Mill Lane", 2_500)); try { courier.book("1 Nowhere Road", 2_500); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("caller sees " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage()); } Courier quick = fromFunction((address, grams) -> "QUICK-" + grams); System.out.println("lambda adapter: " + quick.book("3 Pier Street", 990)); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l04.XmlAdapterDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l04/XmlAdapterDemo.java XmlAdapterDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l04 import java.io.IOException // An old courier client adapted to our port, plus a lambda adapter for a one-method port. // the port our shop code depends on fun interface Courier { fun book(address: String, grams: Int): String } // a client we can't change: XML text in, XML text out, IOException on failure class OldCourierClient { @Throws(IOException::class) fun submit(xml: String): String { if ("Nowhere" in xml) throw IOException("courier office closed: 503") val grams = xml.substringAfter("grams='").substringBefore("' to=") return "<ok ref='R-$grams'/>" } } class CourierUnavailable(message: String, cause: Throwable) : RuntimeException(message, cause) // the adapter: implements our port, holds the old client, translates both ways class OldCourierAdapter(private val old: OldCourierClient) : Courier { override fun book(address: String, grams: Int): String { val xml = "<parcel grams='$grams' to='$address'/>" try { val answer = old.submit(xml) return answer.substringAfter("ref='").substringBefore("'") // their format ends here } catch (e: IOException) { throw CourierUnavailable("courier unreachable", e) // our exception, not theirs } } } fun main() { val courier: Courier = OldCourierAdapter(OldCourierClient()) println("booked, ref " + courier.book("12 Mill Lane", 2_500)) try { courier.book("1 Nowhere Road", 2_500) } catch (e: Exception) { println("caller sees ${e.javaClass.simpleName}: ${e.message}") } // for a fun interface, a lambda is the adapter (SAM conversion) val quick = Courier { _, grams -> "QUICK-$grams" } println("lambda adapter: " + quick.book("3 Pier Street", 990)) } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l04.XmlAdapterDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l04/XmlAdapterDemo.kt Both versions print booked, ref R-2500, caller sees CourierUnavailable: courier unreachable and lambda adapter: QUICK-990. Without the catch, Java refuses to compile: unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown. Kotlin compiles and prints caller sees IOException: courier office closed: 503: the old client's exception walked straight through your port. Functional (SAM) interfaces (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Adapter and Facade · Extension functions are Kotlin's light adapters
x: The shop buys tea and spices from a supplier abroad. The supplier's price list arrives as rows with the supplier's own names: qty, unit and avail. One of its units is the pound (LB), while the shop weighs everything in grams. We want our own Product. Write the mapping once, as an extension on the supplier's type: Java // Java has no extension functions: the same adapter is a static method static Product toProduct(SupplierItem item) { double perUnit = switch (item.unit()) { case "KG" -> 1_000.0; case "LB" -> 453.59237; // the supplier abroad still weighs in pounds default -> throw new IllegalStateException("unknown unit " + item.unit()); }; return new Product(item.code(), Math.round(Double.parseDouble(item.qty()) * perUnit), item.avail().equals("Y")); } List<Product> products = fromSupplier.stream().map(Adapters::toProduct).toList(); Kotlin fun SupplierItem.toProduct(): Product { val perUnit = when (unit) { "KG" -> 1_000.0 "LB" -> 453.59237 // the supplier abroad still weighs in pounds else -> error("unknown unit $unit") } return Product( code = code, grams = (qty.toDouble() * perUnit).roundToLong(), inStock = avail == "Y", ) } val products = fromSupplier.map { it.toProduct() } An extension function lets you call a function as if it were a method of a type you don't own. It isn't part of the class. It compiles to a static method that takes the receiver, the object before the dot, as its first parameter, which is exactly the Java twin. What changes is how the call reads, item.toProduct(), and where the editor offers it: type item. and it appears next to the supplier's own properties. The demo printed: Product(code=T-1001, grams=2500, inStock=true) Product(code=T-1002, grams=680, inStock=true) Product(code=T-1003, grams=10000, inStock=false) The 1.5 pounds came in as 680 grams, and the rest of the shop never has to know that pounds exist. That's the plug adapter at its simplest: the same thing in a different shape, translated once, at the edge. Two rules keep these adapters honest. Keep them next to the code that talks to the supplier, not in a shared utils file, because they're part of the translation layer. And use them for data, not for behavior. An extension can't hold state, can't implement your port, and can't be swapped for a fake in a test. When you need something your code depends on, write a port and a class. Extensions translate data. Ports and classes carry behavior. The other light adapter in Kotlin is the fun interface, an interface with one method that a lambda can implement. Courier { _, grams -> "QUICK-$grams" } built the third line of the first section's output, the same way a Java lambda implements an interface with one method. So far each adapter wraps one thing. Placing an order touches several. Turn a supplier's rows into products Read ExtensionAdapters.kt (or its Java twin). Predict the three products, and look hard at the one in pounds. Run it with the command below. Add SupplierItem("T-1004", "0.5", "LB", "N") to the list (new SupplierItem(...) in Java) and predict its grams and inStock before you run. ExtensionAdapters.kt package workbench.patterns.l04 import kotlin.math.roundToLong // A row from a supplier's price list, with the supplier's names and units. class SupplierItem(val code: String, val qty: String, val unit: String, val avail: String) // Our own type. data class Product(val code: String, val grams: Long, val inStock: Boolean) // An extension function is a light adapter: it reads like a method on the supplier's type, // lives in our code, and keeps the mapping in one place. fun SupplierItem.toProduct(): Product { val perUnit = when (unit) { "KG" -> 1_000.0 "LB" -> 453.59237 // the supplier abroad still weighs in pounds else -> error("unknown unit $unit") } return Product( code = code, grams = (qty.toDouble() * perUnit).roundToLong(), inStock = avail == "Y", ) } fun main() { val fromSupplier = listOf( SupplierItem("T-1001", "2.5", "KG", "Y"), SupplierItem("T-1002", "1.5", "LB", "Y"), SupplierItem("T-1003", "10", "KG", "N"), ) fromSupplier.map { it.toProduct() }.forEach(::println) } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l04.ExtensionAdaptersKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l04/ExtensionAdapters.kt ExtensionAdaptersJava.java package workbench.patterns.l04; import java.util.List; /** The Java twin of ExtensionAdapters.kt. Java has no extension functions, so the adapter is a static method. */ public class ExtensionAdaptersJava { // a row from a supplier's price list, with the supplier's names and units record SupplierItem(String code, String qty, String unit, String avail) {} // our own type record Product(String code, long grams, boolean inStock) {} // callers write toProduct(item), not item.toProduct(); the mapping still lives in one place static Product toProduct(SupplierItem item) { double perUnit = switch (item.unit()) { case "KG" -> 1_000.0; case "LB" -> 453.59237; // the supplier abroad still weighs in pounds default -> throw new IllegalStateException("unknown unit " + item.unit()); }; return new Product( item.code(), Math.round(Double.parseDouble(item.qty()) * perUnit), item.avail().equals("Y")); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<SupplierItem> fromSupplier = List.of( new SupplierItem("T-1001", "2.5", "KG", "Y"), new SupplierItem("T-1002", "1.5", "LB", "Y"), new SupplierItem("T-1003", "10", "KG", "N")); fromSupplier.stream().map(ExtensionAdaptersJava::toProduct).forEach(System.out::println); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l04.ExtensionAdaptersJava labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l04/ExtensionAdaptersJava.java 2,500 g in stock, 680 g in stock (1.5 pounds is 680.4 grams, rounded), and 10,000 g not in stock. The new row is grams=227, inStock=false: half a pound is 226.8 grams. The Kotlin call site reads it.toProduct(), and the Java one reads toProduct(item). Underneath, both are the same static method.
