h: Adapter and Facade · Facade: one front desk for a job with several steps
x: Back at the hotel, you asked the reception desk for breakfast at seven, and the desk did the rest. A facade is that desk in code: one simple entry point to a job that takes several parts of the program. Placing an order at the corner shop takes three steps: reserve the stock, book a van, and tell the customer. If every caller (the website, the phone line, the shop counter) makes those calls itself, each one gets the order of the steps and the failure handling slightly different. Put the sequence in one class: Java record FrontDesk(Stock stock, Vans vans, Notifier notifier) { String order(String product, String address, String email) { if (!stock.reserve(product)) throw new IllegalStateException("out of stock: " + product); // 1. reserve String booking; try { booking = vans.book(product, address); // 2. book a van } catch (RuntimeException e) { stock.release(product); // 3. undo the reservation throw e; } notifier.send(email, "on its way, booking " + booking); // 4. tell the customer return booking; } } Kotlin class FrontDesk( private val stock: Stock, private val vans: Vans, private val notifier: Notifier, ) { fun order(product: String, address: String, email: String): String { check(stock.reserve(product)) { "out of stock: $product" } // 1. reserve val booking = try { vans.book(product, address) // 2. book a van } catch (e: RuntimeException) { stock.release(product) // 3. undo the reservation throw e } notifier.send(email, "on its way, booking $booking") // 4. tell the customer return booking } } The desk owns two decisions: the order of the steps, and what a failure at each step means. Booking a van before reserving would send a van for flour the shop doesn't have. A van that can't go somewhere must give the stock back. FrontDeskDemo, in the Try it, places one order to Mill Lane and one to Gull Island, where no van goes: booking: V-flour failed: no van goes to Gull Island; still reserved: [flour] The sugar for Gull Island went back on the shelf. Those rules now live in one tested place, and each caller is one line. Nothing in either language replaces Facade. Records and constructor parameters only make it shorter. The risk is growth. A facade should orchestrate, that is, call the parts in the right order, and nothing else: no unit math and no warehouse codes. A front desk that also cooks, cleans and does the laundry is no longer a desk. It's the whole hotel with one door. That's also where the picture breaks. A clerk can improvise when something new comes up, and a facade only knows the steps it was written with. When one grows to forty methods, split it by job, such as an OrderDesk and a ReturnsDesk. A facade owns the order of the steps and the undo. Nothing else. One Java gotcha showed up while writing this example. A record component can't be called notify. The Java compiler says "illegal record component name", because the accessor method notify() would clash with Object.notify(). The same goes for wait, hashCode, toString, getClass and the other Object methods that take no arguments. A Kotlin property named notify compiles to getNotify() and is fine. We have adapters on the edge and a desk at the front. Let's put them on one picture. Break the desk's undo rule Run FrontDeskDemo in either language, and read the still reserved line. Remove the try/catch around the van booking, so a failed booking no longer gives the stock back. Predict the still reserved line, then run. Restore it. In the Java version only, rename the record component notifier to notify (and its use inside order). Compile. FrontDeskDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l04; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.Set; /** A facade over stock, vans and messages: one call, the right order, cleanup on failure. */ public class FrontDeskDemo { interface Stock { boolean reserve(String product); void release(String product); } interface Vans { String book(String product, String address); } interface Notifier { void send(String to, String message); } record FrontDesk(Stock stock, Vans vans, Notifier notifier) { String order(String product, String address, String email) { if (!stock.reserve(product)) throw new IllegalStateException("out of stock: " + product); // 1. reserve String booking; try { booking = vans.book(product, address); // 2. book a van } catch (RuntimeException e) { stock.release(product); // 3. undo the reservation throw e; } notifier.send(email, "on its way, booking " + booking); // 4. tell the customer return booking; } } public static void main(String[] args) { Set<String> reserved = new HashSet<>(); Stock stock = new Stock() { public boolean reserve(String product) { return reserved.add(product); } public void release(String product) { reserved.remove(product); } }; Vans vans = (product, address) -> { if (address.contains("Island")) throw new IllegalStateException("no van goes to " + address); return "V-" + product; }; Notifier notifier = (to, message) -> System.out.println(" mail to " + to + ": " + message); FrontDesk desk = new FrontDesk(stock, vans, notifier); System.out.println("booking: " + desk.order("flour", "12 Mill Lane", "anna@example.com")); try { desk.order("sugar", "Gull Island", "ben@example.com"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("failed: " + e.getMessage() + "; still reserved: " + reserved); } } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l04.FrontDeskDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l04/FrontDeskDemo.java FrontDeskDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l04 // A facade over stock, vans and messages: one call, the right order, cleanup on failure. interface Stock { fun reserve(product: String): Boolean; fun release(product: String) } fun interface Vans { fun book(product: String, address: String): String } fun interface Notifier { fun send(to: String, message: String) } class FrontDesk( private val stock: Stock, private val vans: Vans, private val notifier: Notifier, ) { fun order(product: String, address: String, email: String): String { check(stock.reserve(product)) { "out of stock: $product" } // 1. reserve val booking = try { vans.book(product, address) // 2. book a van } catch (e: RuntimeException) { stock.release(product) // 3. undo the reservation throw e } notifier.send(email, "on its way, booking $booking") // 4. tell the customer return booking } } fun main() { val reserved = mutableSetOf<String>() val stock = object : Stock { override fun reserve(product: String) = reserved.add(product) override fun release(product: String) { reserved.remove(product) } } val vans = Vans { product, address -> check("Island" !in address) { "no van goes to $address" } "V-$product" } val notifier = Notifier { to, message -> println(" mail to $to: $message") } val desk = FrontDesk(stock, vans, notifier) println("booking: " + desk.order("flour", "12 Mill Lane", "anna@example.com")) try { desk.order("sugar", "Gull Island", "ben@example.com") } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("failed: ${e.message}; still reserved: $reserved") } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l04.FrontDeskDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l04/FrontDeskDemo.kt The first run mails a confirmation for the flour, then prints failed: no van goes to Gull Island; still reserved: [flour]: the failed order gave the sugar back. Without the catch, the line ends [flour, sugar], so a failed booking holds stock until someone notices. The rename gives error: illegal record component name notify. The Kotlin class can have a property called notify. JLS chapter 8.10: Record classes docs

h: Adapter and Facade · Ports and adapters: where the translation lives
x: Adapter and Facade both wrap something, and so do Decorator, Proxy and Bridge, which you'll meet in the next two lessons. Their structure looks much the same, so intent tells them apart: Pattern Wraps Offers Why Adapter one object you can't change a different interface: yours make it fit your port Facade several objects a new, simpler interface hide a sequence of calls Decorator one object the same interface add behavior (Decorator and Proxy, lesson 5 of this track) Proxy one object the same interface control access (lesson 5 of this track) Bridge an implementation you pick your abstraction vary two things separately (lesson 6 of this track) In a program built with ports and adapters, a layout often called hexagonal architecture, you see Adapter and Facade on one picture. The shop's own logic sits in the middle and talks only to ports: Warehouse, OrderBook, Notifier. Adapters sit on the edge, one for each outside system: the old warehouse program, a database, a mail server. The facade is the front door, where the website or the phone line makes one call. The figure shows the lab laid out this way. That layout pays off twice. Switching warehouses means writing one new adapter, and nothing in the middle changes. And the middle can be tested with lambdas: new OrderDesk((product, grams) -> new Reserved("H1"), orderBook, notifier) needs no warehouse, no database and no mail server. Domain-driven design, a well-known way of organizing business software, calls a thick layer of adapters an anti-corruption layer: the place where an outside system's model is translated into yours, so it never spreads. The shop's old warehouse program needs one. It answers every request with a two-digit code and a pipe (|), like a clerk who stopped speaking in full sentences years ago. 00|H4711 means "held, and here's the hold id", and 51| means "out of stock". If you find "51" anywhere outside the adapter, the layer has a hole. The lab is that layer in miniature. WarehouseAdapter keeps the old program's item numbers, kilograms and codes to itself, and OrderDesk lets the website place an order without knowing the steps. Keep foreign words at the edge. The middle speaks only your own. Check yourself. The shop replaces its warehouse, and the new program throws TimeoutException where the old one threw WarehouseException. In a program laid out this way, which files change? (Only the new warehouse adapter, which catches the new exception and returns the same Unavailable. The desk, the shop's logic and their tests don't change, because they never saw WarehouseException either.) Callers make one call to the desk. The shop's own code talks only to ports, and adapters on the edge translate for each outside system.

h: Adapter and Facade · Java and Kotlin
x: An anti-corruption adapter for the courier's status messages CourierUpdateAdapter.java // the courier's status message, with the courier's names record CourierUpdate(String type, String ref, String info) {} // our model of what happened sealed interface DeliveryEvent { record Delivered(String bookingRef) implements DeliveryEvent {} record Missed(String bookingRef, String reason) implements DeliveryEvent {} record Ignored(String why) implements DeliveryEvent {} } final class CourierUpdateAdapter { private CourierUpdateAdapter() {} static DeliveryEvent toEvent(CourierUpdate u) { return switch (u.type()) { // their strings are an open set, so a default is right here case "parcel.delivered" -> new DeliveryEvent.Delivered(u.ref()); case "parcel.missed" -> new DeliveryEvent.Missed(u.ref(), u.info().toLowerCase()); default -> new DeliveryEvent.Ignored("unhandled courier update " + u.type()); }; } } CourierUpdateAdapter.kt // the courier's status message, with the courier's names data class CourierUpdate(val type: String, val ref: String, val info: String) // our model of what happened sealed interface DeliveryEvent { data class Delivered(val bookingRef: String) : DeliveryEvent data class Missed(val bookingRef: String, val reason: String) : DeliveryEvent data class Ignored(val why: String) : DeliveryEvent } // the adapter as an extension: reads like a method on the courier's type fun CourierUpdate.toEvent(): DeliveryEvent = when (type) { // an open set of their strings: else is right "parcel.delivered" -> DeliveryEvent.Delivered(ref) "parcel.missed" -> DeliveryEvent.Missed(ref, info.lowercase()) else -> DeliveryEvent.Ignored("unhandled courier update $type") } The courier's system sends a short status message whenever a parcel's state changes, in the courier's words. The translation is the same in both languages: their strings in, a sealed event of our own out. Kotlin writes it as an extension on their type, so call sites read update.toEvent(). Java needs a static method on a holder class, so call sites read CourierUpdateAdapter.toEvent(update), and in bytecode, the compiled form the JVM runs, the two are the same static method. Both use a catch-all branch on purpose. The courier's message types are an open set you don't control, unlike your own sealed types, where a missing case should break the build. Code that uses DeliveryEvent then switches over it with no default. Neither language makes Adapter unnecessary; Kotlin just makes the data-mapping kind cheaper to write.

h: Adapter and Facade · Worked example
x: Wrap a map service behind a port, then test without it The shop prices a delivery by distance: 2.00 plus 0.50 for every kilometer. Its pricer calls an outside map service directly. The service answers with text like "dist=4.2km;eta=11min" and throws a checked RouteException. Before reading on, list every detail of the map service that leaks into priceCents. class DeliveryPricer { private final RouteClient routes = new RouteClient("https://maps.vendor.example"); long priceCents(String address) throws RouteException { String raw = routes.distance("SHOP", address); // their format: "dist=4.2km;eta=11min" double km = Double.parseDouble(raw.substring(raw.indexOf('=') + 1, raw.indexOf("km"))); return 200 + Math.round(km * 50); } } class DeliveryPricer { private val routes = RouteClient("https://maps.vendor.example") fun priceCents(address: String): Long { val raw = routes.distance("SHOP", address) // their format; RouteException leaks unseen val km = raw.substringAfter('=').substringBefore("km").toDouble() return 200 + (km * 50).roundToLong() } } Four leaks: the "SHOP" name the service wants, its answer format, its checked exception, and its hard-wired address. Define the port in the shop's words first. It says nothing about text formats or vendors, and an empty answer means "no distance right now". interface Distances { OptionalDouble km(String from, String to); // 1. our words: places in, kilometers or nothing out } class DeliveryPricer { private final Distances distances; DeliveryPricer(Distances distances) { this.distances = distances; } OptionalLong priceCents(String address) { OptionalDouble km = distances.km("SHOP", address); return km.isPresent() ? OptionalLong.of(200 + Math.round(km.getAsDouble() * 50)) : OptionalLong.empty(); } } fun interface Distances { fun km(from: String, to: String): Double? // 1. our words: places in, kilometers or null out } class DeliveryPricer(private val distances: Distances) { fun priceCents(address: String): Long? = distances.km("SHOP", address)?.let { 200 + (it * 50).roundToLong() } } Now the adapter. Everything the map service knows lives here: how it wants places named, how it packs its answers, and which exception it throws. Why return empty instead of rethrowing on RouteException? Because the port promised "kilometers or nothing", and the pricer decides what nothing means. final class MapDistances implements Distances { private final RouteClient routes; MapDistances(RouteClient routes) { this.routes = routes; } public OptionalDouble km(String from, String to) { try { String raw = routes.distance(from, to); // 2. our places, their format return OptionalDouble.of(Double.parseDouble(raw.substring(raw.indexOf('=') + 1, raw.indexOf("km")))); } catch (RouteException | RuntimeException e) { // 3. their failure, our answer return OptionalDouble.empty(); } } } class MapDistances(private val routes: RouteClient) : Distances { override fun km(from: String, to: String): Double? = try { val raw = routes.distance(from, to) // 2. our places, their format raw.substringAfter('=').substringBefore("km").toDouble() } catch (e: RouteException) { // 3. their failure, our answer null } catch (e: RuntimeException) { null } } Test the two halves separately. The pricer gets a lambda. The adapter gets a fake map service, a subclass of the client that returns a canned answer, which is how the lab tests its warehouse adapter. // 4. the shop's logic, with no map service at all assertThat(new DeliveryPricer((from, to) -> OptionalDouble.of(4.0)).priceCents("12 Mill Lane")).hasValue(400); // 5. the adapter, against a fake of the client class RouteClient fake = new RouteClient("unused") { @Override public String distance(String from, String to) { return "dist=4.2km;eta=11min"; } }; assertThat(new MapDistances(fake).km("SHOP", "12 Mill Lane")).hasValue(4.2); // 4. the shop's logic, with no map service at all assertThat(DeliveryPricer { _, _ -> 4.0 }.priceCents("12 Mill Lane")).isEqualTo(400L) // 5. the adapter, against a fake of the client class (open in the library, or use an interface) val fake = object : RouteClient("unused") { override fun distance(from: String, to: String) = "dist=4.2km;eta=11min" } assertThat(MapDistances(fake).km("SHOP", "12 Mill Lane")).isEqualTo(4.2)

h: Adapter and Facade · Lab
x: A warehouse adapter and an order desk labs/patterns/src/main/java/workbench/patterns/l04/WarehouseAdapter.java labs/patterns/src/main/java/workbench/patterns/l04/OrderDesk.java ./gradlew :patterns:test --tests 'workbench.patterns.l04.*' Read OldWarehouseSystem.java (the old program you can't change), Warehouse.java (the shop's port) and Units.java (two helpers). They're given; don't edit them. Run the tests: all ten fail. Write WarehouseAdapter.reserve. Call old.hold with Units.itemNumber and Units.toKilos, catch WarehouseException and return Unavailable(e.getMessage()), then split the answer on | and map the code with a switch. Write OrderDesk.place as a switch over the StockResult. Reserved: write it in the order book, send the confirmation (catching a failing notifier), and return Placed. Refused: send the sorry note and return Refused. Unavailable: return RetryLater. Run the tests until all ten pass. raw.split("\\|", -1) splits on a real | and keeps the empty hold id in "51|". The pipe must be escaped, because split takes a regular expression. A switch over the sealed StockResult with case StockResult.Reserved ok -> ... needs no default: the compiler checks all three cases. In a switch expression, use yield to return a value from a block. Wrap only the notifier call in try/catch. If the order book throws, let it travel up: a reserved order that isn't written down is a problem someone must see, not one to hide. All ten tests in AdapterFacadeTest pass. By the end you can wrap an outside program in an adapter that keeps its types, codes and exceptions to itself, use Kotlin extension functions as light adapters for data, and put a multi-step order behind a facade that owns the order of the steps and the failure rules.

h: Adapter and Facade · From memory
x: An adapter from memory Close this page. An outside PostcodeClient has String lookup(String postcode) throws LookupException, returning text like "Mill Lane;OLD TOWN". Your port is interface DistrictOf { Optional<String> district(String postcode); } (in Kotlin, fun interface DistrictOf { fun district(postcode: String): String? }). Write the adapter so the client's exception never escapes, and an empty or malformed answer gives no district.

h: Adapter and Facade · Quiz
x: The warehouse adapter catches WarehouseException and rethrows it wrapped in a RuntimeException. The order desk catches that and checks getCause() instanceof WarehouseException to decide whether to retry. What's wrong? Nothing, since the exception is unchecked now The foreign type still leaks: the desk depends on the old program, so replacing the warehouse breaks it A RuntimeException can't wrap a checked exception Retry decisions belong inside the old warehouse program Wrapping changed the exception's type, not who depends on it. The desk still imports WarehouseException, so it's tied to this one warehouse program. Translate inside the adapter into your own result (Unavailable) or your own exception type that says whether a retry makes sense. A RuntimeException can wrap anything, so that option is simply false. Which statement about an adapter written in Kotlin is true? An IOException thrown inside it can pass through your port without any compile error The compiler forces you to catch the old client's checked exceptions Extension functions can implement your port interface fun interface ports can't be implemented with a lambda Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so nothing stops the client's IOException from reaching callers of your port. Java would refuse to compile the same adapter. Extensions can't implement interfaces, and a fun interface exists precisely so that a lambda can implement it. Three parts of the shop's program (the website, the phone line and the shop counter) each reserve stock, book a van, write the order book and send an email, each with slightly different failure handling. Which pattern fits? Adapter Decorator Facade Singleton A facade puts the sequence and its failure rules in one place, and each caller makes one call. An adapter changes one object's interface, a decorator adds behavior behind the same interface, and a singleton is about how many instances exist, not about running steps in order. Which is the best use of a Kotlin extension function as an adapter? fun OldWarehouseSystem.reserve(...), which callers use instead of a Warehouse port A global fun Any.toJson() in a shared utils file An extension that caches the supplier's rows in a top-level map fun SupplierItem.toProduct(): Product, kept next to the code that talks to the supplier Turning a supplier's row into your own type is pure data translation, which is what extensions are good at, and keeping it next to the supplier code keeps the supplier's model contained. An extension on the old program makes callers depend on that program and can't be swapped in a test. A global utils extension spreads everywhere, and caching in a top-level map is hidden shared state. From Factory Method and Abstract Factory: the shop now has one adapter for Pedal Post's old client and one for Big Blue Vans'. Where should the choice between them live? In each caller, with an if on the parcel's weight In one factory, a switch or when over the courier with no default, passed into the desk Inside the desk's place, as string checks on the address In the adapters: each checks whether the parcel belongs to it Choosing which product to make is a factory's job: one exhaustive switch or when over a sealed or enum Courier, so adding a courier is a compile error in one place. Spreading weight checks over callers or the desk copies the rule, and adapters checking ownership turns every call into a guessing game.

h: Adapter and Facade · Key terms
x: Adapter A wrapper that makes an existing object fit the interface your code expects. Port An interface in your own words that your core code depends on, such as Warehouse. Checked exception An exception the Java compiler makes you catch or declare, such as IOException. Kotlin has none. Anti-corruption layer The adapters where an outside system's model is translated into yours, so it never spreads into your code. Facade One simple entry point that runs a job with several steps across several parts of the program. Extension function A Kotlin function called like a method on a type it doesn't belong to; a static method underneath. Ports and adapters A layout where core logic talks only to ports, and adapters on the edge connect each port to one outside system. Also called hexagonal architecture. What does an adapter do? Makes an object you can't change fit the interface (port) your code expects, translating arguments, answers and errors. What is a leaky adapter? One that lets the outside system's types, codes or exceptions (a WarehouseException, the code "51") reach your own code. A Kotlin adapter calls a method that throws IOException and has no catch. Does it compile? Yes. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so the IOException passes through your port silently. Java would refuse. What does a Kotlin extension function compile to? A static method whose first parameter is the receiver. item.toProduct() is toProduct(item) in bytecode. What does a facade own? The order of the steps in a job with several steps, and what a failure at each step means. Not math, codes or database queries. Can a Java record component be named notify? No: "illegal record component name". Its accessor would clash with Object.notify(). The same goes for wait, hashCode, toString and the other no-argument Object methods. Adapter vs Facade, one line each? Adapter: one object, given a different interface (yours). Facade: several objects behind one new, simpler interface.

h: Adapter and Facade · Go deeper
x: The JDK has adapters you use every day. InputStreamReader adapts a stream of bytes into a stream of characters; its Javadoc calls it a bridge from byte streams to character streams, which shows how loosely the pattern names get used. Arrays.asList adapts an array into a fixed-size List that writes through to the array. Collections.enumeration and Enumeration.asIterator() (Java 9) adapt between the old and new ways of walking through a collection. The GoF book describes two kinds of adapter. An object adapter holds the foreign object and delegates to it, as in this lesson. A class adapter inherits from the foreign class and implements your interface at the same time. Java and Kotlin allow the second only when the foreign class is open to subclassing, and it's usually worse: your adapter inherits every public method of the foreign class, so callers can go around your translation. Prefer the object adapter. Kotlin's by delegation (in Decorator and Proxy, lesson 5 of this track) can build an adapter that forwards most of an interface unchanged and overrides the few methods that need translating. That works when the two interfaces are almost the same, such as two versions of your own API. For an outside system with a different model, write the translation out; it's the part that deserves a careful review. Facades and slow calls mix badly in one way. Suppose a facade starts a database transaction, a group of database changes that succeed or fail together, and then calls a slow outside system inside it. The transaction holds a database connection for as long as the outside system takes. With a pool of 20 connections and a courier service that takes 120 ms to answer, a busy afternoon runs out of connections. Call the slow system first, outside the transaction, then write to the database in a short one.

h: Decorator and Proxy · Decorators: wrap a delivery price and keep its shape
x: A decorator wraps the same interface: the call goes in layer by layer, and the order of the layers changes the fee The corner shop charges for every parcel it sends. The rules are simple: 0.50 for each kilometer, 2.00 to start, 3.00 more for a parcel over 5 kg, and never more than 8.00 in all. The rules also change often, so we'd like each one to be a piece we can add, remove or move. Here's a way to do that. Give each rule its own small object that wraps the rule before it. Each wrapper is still a delivery fee, with the same one method, so whoever asks for the price can't tell how many layers there are. A decorator is exactly that: an object with the same interface as the object it wraps, which does one extra thing and passes the call on. It's the gift wrap. The parcel inside doesn't change, the paper adds one thing, and the courier still handles one parcel. In Java, DeliveryFee is a functional interface: an interface with one abstract method, which a lambda can implement. Each rule is a default method, a method with a body inside the interface. In Kotlin, each rule is an extension function, a function you call like a method on a type, and fun interface is Kotlin's interface for lambdas. Either way, each call returns a new fee and leaves the one it wraps alone: Java @FunctionalInterface interface DeliveryFee { long cents(Delivery d); static DeliveryFee perKm(long centsPerKm) { return d -> d.km() * centsPerKm; } default DeliveryFee plusFixed(long fixed) { return d -> cents(d) + fixed; } default DeliveryFee heavySurcharge(int overGrams, long extra) { return d -> cents(d) + (d.grams() > overGrams ? extra : 0); } default DeliveryFee cappedAt(long max) { return d -> Math.min(cents(d), max); } } DeliveryFee standard = DeliveryFee.perKm(50).plusFixed(200).heavySurcharge(5_000, 300).cappedAt(800); Kotlin fun interface DeliveryFee { fun cents(d: Delivery): Long } fun perKm(centsPerKm: Long) = DeliveryFee { d -> d.km * centsPerKm } fun DeliveryFee.plusFixed(fixed: Long) = DeliveryFee { d -> cents(d) + fixed } fun DeliveryFee.heavySurcharge(overGrams: Int, extra: Long) = DeliveryFee { d -> cents(d) + if (d.grams > overGrams) extra else 0L } fun DeliveryFee.cappedAt(max: Long) = DeliveryFee { d -> minOf(cents(d), max) } val standard = perKm(50).plusFixed(200).heavySurcharge(5_000, 300).cappedAt(800) Read the chain from the inside out. perKm(50) is the parcel. Each method around it adds one layer, a lambda that first asks the fee it wraps, cents(d), and then applies one rule. The tricky part is that bare cents(d). Inside a default method it means this.cents(d), the fee being decorated, and the lambda captures it. Now predict three prices. A 2 kg parcel going 4 km costs 2.00 plus 4 times 0.50, so 4.00. A 12 kg parcel going 4 km pays the surcharge: 7.00. And a 12 kg parcel going 20 km would cost 15.00, so the cap brings it down to 8.00. The lab's tests check all three. Then move cappedAt(800) one place to the left, before the surcharge. Both chains compile, and both read sensibly. For the heavy parcel going 20 km, they disagree: ...heavySurcharge(5_000, 300).cappedAt(800) -> 800 cents ...cappedAt(800).heavySurcharge(5_000, 300) -> 1,100 cents In the second chain, the cap brings 12.00 down to 8.00, and then the surcharge lands on top. The gift-wrap picture predicts this: a ribbon tied under the paper is hidden, and the outer layer has the last word. The picture breaks in one place, though. Paper can only add. A decorator can also take away, as the cap does, or decide not to call the object inside at all. The order of the layers is part of the behavior. Pin it in a test. The JDK has stacked decorators for decades. new DataOutputStream(new BufferedOutputStream(new GZIPOutputStream(out))) is three wrappers around one stream, a destination for bytes such as a file. Each wrapper is an OutputStream too, and each adds one thing: typed writes, buffering, compression. The FilterInputStream Javadoc says such a stream "wraps some other input stream, which it uses as its basic source of data, possibly transforming the data along the way". Behavior stacks the same way as arithmetic. The Try it puts a logging decorator and a retrying decorator around a busy courier line, in both orders. Before you run it, guess whether the order matters there too. Stack two decorators in both orders Open DecoratorStack.java (or DecoratorStack.kt). Big Blue Vans' booking line is busy twice, then it books, as booking lines tend to be. Logging writes down each call it sees; Retrying tries up to three times. Before you run it, write down how many log lines each of the two stacks writes. Run it with the command below. Then decide: if the log fed a chart of how many bookings the shop makes, which order would you want? DecoratorStack.java package workbench.patterns.l05; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Two decorators around a busy courier line. Same pieces, two orders, two different behaviors. */ public class DecoratorStack { interface Booker { String book(int grams); } // the real line: busy twice, then it books the parcel static final class BusyLine implements Booker { private int calls; public String book(int grams) { if (++calls <= 2) throw new IllegalStateException("line busy, try #" + calls); return "BB-" + grams; } } // decorator 1: logs every call that passes through it record Logging(Booker inner, List<String> log) implements Booker { public String book(int grams) { log.add("book " + grams); return inner.book(grams); } } // decorator 2: tries up to `attempts` times record Retrying(Booker inner, int attempts) implements Booker { public String book(int grams) { RuntimeException last = null; for (int i = 1; i <= attempts; i++) { try { return inner.book(grams); } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; } } throw last; } } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> log = new ArrayList<>(); Booker retryOutside = new Retrying(new Logging(new BusyLine(), log), 3); System.out.println("Retrying(Logging(line)): " + retryOutside.book(1_250) + ", log lines: " + log.size()); log.clear(); Booker logOutside = new Logging(new Retrying(new BusyLine(), 3), log); System.out.println("Logging(Retrying(line)): " + logOutside.book(1_250) + ", log lines: " + log.size()); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l05.DecoratorStack labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l05/DecoratorStack.java DecoratorStack.kt package workbench.patterns.l05 // Two decorators around a busy courier line. Same pieces, two orders, two different behaviors. fun interface Booker { fun book(grams: Int): String } // the real line: busy twice, then it books the parcel class BusyLine : Booker { private var calls = 0 override fun book(grams: Int): String { check(++calls > 2) { "line busy, try #$calls" } return "BB-$grams" } } // decorator 1: logs every call that passes through it class Logging(private val inner: Booker, private val log: MutableList<String>) : Booker { override fun book(grams: Int): String { log += "book $grams" return inner.book(grams) } } // decorator 2: tries up to `attempts` times class Retrying(private val inner: Booker, private val attempts: Int) : Booker { override fun book(grams: Int): String { var last: RuntimeException? = null repeat(attempts) { try { return inner.book(grams) } catch (e: RuntimeException) { last = e } } throw last!! } } fun main() { val log = mutableListOf<String>() val retryOutside = Retrying(Logging(BusyLine(), log), 3) println("Retrying(Logging(line)): ${retryOutside.book(1_250)}, log lines: ${log.size}") log.clear() val logOutside = Logging(Retrying(BusyLine(), 3), log) println("Logging(Retrying(line)): ${logOutside.book(1_250)}, log lines: ${log.size}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l05.DecoratorStackKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l05/DecoratorStack.kt Retrying(Logging(line)): BB-1250, log lines: 3 and Logging(Retrying(line)): BB-1250, log lines: 1. The inner decorator sees every attempt; the outer one sees one booking. For a chart of bookings, put the logging outside: one line per booking. To see how often the line is busy, put it inside, where both busy signals show up. FilterInputStream (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Decorator and Proxy · Kotlin's by writes the forwarding, and never calls you back
x: A delivery fee has one method, so a lambda can decorate it. Most interfaces have more. A hand-written decorator for Map in Java must pass on every method (get, put, remove, size, entrySet and a dozen more) just to change one. That passing-on is called forwarding, and it's most of the code. Kotlin's class delegation writes the forwarding for you. Say we want a map that counts how often something is put into it: Java // Java has no `by`. The short way is inheritance, and HashMap's insides decide what you count. class CountingMap<K, V> extends HashMap<K, V> { int puts; @Override public V put(K key, V value) { puts++; return super.put(key, value); } } Kotlin class CountingMap<K, V>(private val inner: MutableMap<K, V> = HashMap()) : MutableMap<K, V> by inner { var puts = 0 override fun put(key: K, value: V): V? { puts++; return inner.put(key, value) } } Read : MutableMap<K, V> by inner as "for every method of MutableMap I don't write myself, call the same method on inner". The object by forwards to is called the delegate. The Kotlin docs call delegation "a good alternative to implementation inheritance", where inheritance means taking a parent class's code with extends. Now predict. We call put("tea", 1) and then putAll with two more entries. What is puts? The CountingMapDemo in the Try it prints: CountingMap: puts=1, size=3 One, while the map holds three. The compiler forwarded putAll to inner.putAll, and inner is a plain HashMap that has never heard of our put. The docs say so: overridden members "do not get called from the members of the delegate object". The delegate never calls you back. To count every insertion, override putAll too, and putIfAbsent, compute and merge. That surprise is also the benefit. With inheritance, the count depends on how the parent class is written today. HashMap.putAll happens not to call put, so the Java version also prints 1. But HashSet.addAll does call add, so a set that counts in both methods counts each item twice, and the Java twin prints added=6 for three items. Effective Java, the well-known book of Java advice, builds its item 18, "Favor composition over inheritance", on that very bug. With by, the delegate never calls back into your code, so a JDK update can't change your numbers. The delegate never calls your overrides. Override every method that should behave differently. The JDK has a read-only decorator you meet often: Collections.unmodifiableList. It forwards reads and throws on writes. It's a view, which means it reads through to the list it wraps, so later changes to that list show up in it. For a frozen copy, use List.copyOf. Kotlin's List is weaker still: a read-only type on the same object, with no wrapper at all: Java List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(shopping); shopping.add("jam"); // the view shows it too view.add("tea"); // UnsupportedOperationException Kotlin val view: List<String> = shopping // the same object, with a read-only type shopping += "jam" // the view shows it too (view as MutableList).add("tea") // works: nothing guards it A decorator works when we know the interface and want one extra behavior. Sometimes we want the same extra behavior, such as timing, on every method of every interface, without writing a class for each one. Count what the delegate does behind your back Read CountingMapDemo.kt. Predict puts after one put and a putAll of two entries, and added after an addAll of three items. Run it with the command below. Now run the Java twin, CountingMapDemoJava, which uses extends HashMap and extends HashSet with the same overrides. Predict first: will the Java numbers match? CountingMapDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l05 // Decorators built with `by`: the compiler writes every forwarding method for you. class CountingMap<K, V>(private val inner: MutableMap<K, V> = HashMap()) : MutableMap<K, V> by inner { var puts = 0 private set override fun put(key: K, value: V): V? { puts++ return inner.put(key, value) } } class CountingSet<E>(private val inner: MutableSet<E> = HashSet()) : MutableSet<E> by inner { var added = 0 private set override fun add(element: E): Boolean { added++ return inner.add(element) } override fun addAll(elements: Collection<E>): Boolean { added += elements.size return inner.addAll(elements) // inner's addAll calls inner's add, never ours } } fun main() { val m = CountingMap<String, Int>() m["tea"] = 1 // goes through our put m.putAll(mapOf("jam" to 2, "rye" to 3)) // forwarded to inner.putAll, which never calls our put println("CountingMap: puts=${m.puts}, size=${m.size}") val s = CountingSet<String>() s.addAll(listOf("tea", "jam", "rye")) println("CountingSet: added=${s.added}, size=${s.size}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l05.CountingMapDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l05/CountingMapDemo.kt CountingMapDemoJava.java package workbench.patterns.l05; import java.util.Collection; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * The Java twin of CountingMapDemo.kt. Java has no `by`, so the short way is inheritance, * and then the result depends on how the parent class happens to be written. */ public class CountingMapDemoJava { static final class CountingMap<K, V> extends HashMap<K, V> { int puts; @Override public V put(K key, V value) { puts++; return super.put(key, value); } } // Effective Java item 18: HashSet.addAll calls add for each element, so this counts twice static final class CountingSet<E> extends HashSet<E> { int added; @Override public boolean add(E e) { added++; return super.add(e); } @Override public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) { added += c.size(); return super.addAll(c); } } public static void main(String[] args) { CountingMap<String, Integer> m = new CountingMap<>(); m.put("tea", 1); m.putAll(Map.of("jam", 2, "rye", 3)); // HashMap.putAll doesn't call put, today System.out.println("CountingMap: puts=" + m.puts + ", size=" + m.size()); CountingSet<String> s = new CountingSet<>(); s.addAll(List.of("tea", "jam", "rye")); System.out.println("CountingSet: added=" + s.added + ", size=" + s.size()); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l05.CountingMapDemoJava labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l05/CountingMapDemoJava.java Kotlin prints CountingMap: puts=1, size=3 and CountingSet: added=3, size=3: the delegate never calls your overrides, so you count exactly what you wrote. Java prints puts=1, size=3 but added=6, size=3, because HashSet.addAll calls add for each item and the override counts them a second time. With inheritance, your count depends on the parent's insides. Delegation (Kotlin docs) docs Collections.unmodifiableList (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Decorator and Proxy · Proxies: one stand-in for every method of an interface
x: Back to the receptionist. Callers dial the manager's number, but the receptionist answers. She may put the call through, take a message, or try again later when the line is busy. A proxy is that receptionist in code: a stand-in with the same interface as the real object, which controls whether and how each call reaches it. A decorator is written for one interface. A dynamic proxy is written once and works for any interface. java.lang.reflect.Proxy creates a class while the program runs, one that implements the interfaces you name and sends every call to a single invocation handler, one method that receives each call as data. Here is a proxy that retries any method of any interface: Java @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") static <T> T retrying(Class<T> iface, T target, int maxAttempts) { InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> { Throwable last = null; for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) { try { return method.invoke(target, args); } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { last = e.getCause(); // unwrap: the target's own exception } } throw last; }; return (T) Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, handler); } Kotlin inline fun <reified T : Any> retrying(target: T, maxAttempts: Int): T = Proxy.newProxyInstance(T::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(T::class.java)) { _, method, args -> var last: Throwable? = null repeat(maxAttempts) { try { return@newProxyInstance method.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { last = e.cause // unwrap: the target's own exception } } throw last!! } as T The handler gets the proxy, the Method being called (an object that describes one method of the interface), and its arguments. First it asks the real object, the target, with method.invoke(target, args). If that throws, it remembers the exception and tries again, and after the last attempt it throws what it remembered. A retry, a timer or a check of who's calling is written once and covers every method of every interface you wrap. The tricky line is the catch. method.invoke is an eager gift wrapper: whatever the target throws, it wraps in an InvocationTargetException. Unwrap it with getCause() and rethrow that. If you rethrow the wrapper instead, the proxy is throwing a checked exception, one the Java compiler makes you catch or declare, that the interface's book method never declared. So Java wraps it once more. RetryingProxyDemo, in the Try it, does exactly that when you remove the unwrap: Exception in thread "main" java.lang.reflect.UndeclaredThrowableException Caused by: java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException Caused by: java.lang.IllegalStateException: line busy That's three layers of paper around one small line busy. Worse, no catch (IllegalStateException e) in the caller will match it. A handler must unwrap what method.invoke throws. Rethrow getCause(). JDK proxies have one more limit: they implement interfaces only, and can't extend a class. Tools that must proxy a class generate a subclass instead, and a subclass can't override final methods. The Kotlin version is shorter for one reason: reified T, which keeps the type parameter available while an inline function runs, lets the function read T::class.java itself, so callers write retrying(busy, 3) and pass no Class object. Before you wrap the shop's order line in this proxy, notice that it retries everything. A check of an order's status is safe to repeat. Placing an order isn't: if the first attempt timed out after the warehouse had already taken it, the second attempt orders the bread again. The worked example fixes that. There's also a quieter gap, and the demo's third line shows it: calls the proxy saw: [pickBoth]. Two more calls happened that the proxy never saw. Break the retry proxy two ways Run RetryingProxyDemo (Java or Kotlin) and read the three lines. In main, change retrying(CourierLine.class, busy, 3) to 2 attempts (retrying(busy, 2) in Kotlin). Predict what the caller sees, then run. Keep 2 attempts. In retrying, replace last = e.getCause() with last = e (in Kotlin, last = e.cause becomes last = e). Predict the exception, then run. Undo both changes. RetryingProxyDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l05; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Dynamic proxies: a retrying proxy for any interface, and a tracing proxy that shows self-invocation. */ public class RetryingProxyDemo { interface CourierLine { String book(String address, int grams); } interface Stockroom { void pick(String item); void pickBoth(String first, String second); } static <T> T retrying(Class<T> iface, T target, int maxAttempts) { InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> { Throwable last = null; for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) { try { return method.invoke(target, args); } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { // unwrap, or callers see a reflective wrapper last = e.getCause(); } } throw last; }; return iface.cast(Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, handler)); } static <T> T tracing(Class<T> iface, T target, List<String> trace) { InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> { trace.add(method.getName()); try { return method.invoke(target, args); } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); } }; return iface.cast(Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, handler)); } public static void main(String[] args) { int[] calls = {0}; CourierLine busy = (address, grams) -> { if (++calls[0] < 3) throw new IllegalStateException("line busy"); return "BB-" + grams; }; CourierLine line = retrying(CourierLine.class, busy, 3); System.out.println("book -> " + line.book("12 Mill Lane", 1_250) + " after " + calls[0] + " target calls"); System.out.println("proxy class: " + Proxy.isProxyClass(line.getClass())); List<String> trace = new ArrayList<>(); Stockroom real = new Stockroom() { public void pick(String item) { } public void pickBoth(String first, String second) { pick(first); pick(second); } // this.pick(): skips the proxy }; tracing(Stockroom.class, real, trace).pickBoth("tea", "jam"); System.out.println("calls the proxy saw: " + trace); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l05.RetryingProxyDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l05/RetryingProxyDemo.java RetryingProxyDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l05 import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException import java.lang.reflect.Proxy // Dynamic proxies: a retrying proxy for any interface, and a tracing proxy that shows self-invocation. fun interface CourierLine { fun book(address: String, grams: Int): String } interface Stockroom { fun pick(item: String); fun pickBoth(first: String, second: String) } // reified T replaces the Class<T> parameter the Java version needs inline fun <reified T : Any> retrying(target: T, maxAttempts: Int): T = Proxy.newProxyInstance(T::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(T::class.java)) { _, method, args -> var last: Throwable? = null repeat(maxAttempts) { try { return@newProxyInstance method.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { // unwrap, or callers see a reflective wrapper last = e.cause } } throw last!! } as T inline fun <reified T : Any> tracing(target: T, trace: MutableList<String>): T = Proxy.newProxyInstance(T::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(T::class.java)) { _, method, args -> trace += method.name try { method.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { throw e.cause!! } } as T fun main() { var calls = 0 val busy = CourierLine { _, grams -> check(++calls >= 3) { "line busy" } "BB-$grams" } val line = retrying(busy, 3) println("book -> ${line.book("12 Mill Lane", 1_250)} after $calls target calls") println("proxy class: ${Proxy.isProxyClass(line.javaClass)}") val trace = mutableListOf<String>() val real = object : Stockroom { override fun pick(item: String) {} override fun pickBoth(first: String, second: String) { pick(first); pick(second) } // this.pick(): skips the proxy } tracing<Stockroom>(real, trace).pickBoth("tea", "jam") println("calls the proxy saw: $trace") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l05.RetryingProxyDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l05/RetryingProxyDemo.kt The first run prints book -> BB-1250 after 3 target calls, proxy class: true and calls the proxy saw: [pickBoth]. h: Decorator and Proxy · The calls a proxy never sees
x: Here is the stockroom from the demo. A tracing proxy, one that writes down the name of every call it handles, stands in front of it: Java class RealStockroom implements Stockroom { public void pick(String item) { /* walk to the shelf */ } public void pickBoth(String first, String second) { pick(first); // really this.pick(first): the real object, not the proxy pick(second); } } Kotlin class RealStockroom : Stockroom { override fun pick(item: String) { /* walk to the shelf */ } override fun pickBoth(first: String, second: String) { pick(first) // really this.pick(first): the real object, not the proxy pick(second) } } The shop's code calls pickBoth("tea", "jam") on the proxy. The proxy writes down pickBoth and forwards the call to the real stockroom. Inside, pick(first) is a plain call on this, and this is the real stockroom, not the proxy. So the trace reads [pickBoth], and the two walks to the shelf go unrecorded. A call that an object makes on itself is called self-invocation, and it never passes the proxy. The figure shows the two paths. The receptionist picture holds here. She hears every call that comes in through the switchboard. When the manager walks to the next office herself, nobody at the front desk hears a thing. The lab's timing proxy has the same gap, and a test pins it. bookTwice on the courier calls its own book twice, the timing sink records one line, CourierBooking.bookTwice 7ms, and the real courier counts two bookings. That isn't a bug in the proxy. A proxy is a separate object, and it can only handle calls that are made on it. There are two ways to get the inner calls handled. Let the caller make them through the proxy, so pick is called twice from outside. Or move pick to its own object, behind its own proxy, and let pickBoth call that object. Either way, each call you care about crosses a proxy. The picture breaks on judgment. A receptionist notices when the same caller has rung three times in a minute. A proxy sees only a method's name and its arguments, so it retries placing an order as happily as a status check, unless the method carries a mark that tells it otherwise. A proxy sees only the calls made on it. Calls through this go straight past. Decorator and Proxy have the same shape: an object with the same interface, holding the real one. What tells them apart is intent. A decorator adds behavior the caller asked for, such as a surcharge or compression. A proxy controls access to the real object: when, whether and how it gets called, as with retries, timing or a check of who's calling. Collections.unmodifiableList sits on the line, which is a good sign that the names are for talking about designs, not for sorting classes into boxes. Check yourself. The timing proxy wraps the courier, and the shop's code calls bookTwice three times. How many lines does the timing sink record, and how many bookings does the real courier make? (Three lines, all named bookTwice, and six bookings. Each outside call passes the proxy once; each inner book goes straight to the real courier.) Calls from outside go through the proxy. A call through this inside the real object goes straight to the target, so the proxy never handles it. h: Decorator and Proxy · Java and Kotlin
x: A timing decorator for a three-method courier desk TimedCourierDesk.java interface CourierDesk { String book(String address, int grams); String track(String ref); void cancel(String ref); } // one method changes; the other two are forwarded by hand final class TimedCourierDesk implements CourierDesk { private final CourierDesk inner; private final Map<String, Long> nanos; TimedCourierDesk(CourierDesk inner, Map<String, Long> nanos) { this.inner = inner; this.nanos = nanos; } @Override public String book(String address, int grams) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return inner.book(address, grams); } finally { nanos.merge("book", System.nanoTime() - start, Long::sum); } } @Override public String track(String ref) { return inner.track(ref); } @Override public void cancel(String ref) { inner.cancel(ref); } } TimedCourierDesk.kt interface CourierDesk { fun book(address: String, grams: Int): String fun track(ref: String): String fun cancel(ref: String) } // `by inner` generates track and cancel; you write only what changes class TimedCourierDesk( private val inner: CourierDesk, private val nanos: MutableMap<String, Long>, ) : CourierDesk by inner { override fun book(address: String, grams: Int): String { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return inner.book(address, grams) } finally { nanos.merge("book", System.nanoTime() - start) { a, b -> a + b } } } } The behavior is the same: time book, pass track and cancel straight on. What differs is who writes the passing-on. Java makes you type track and cancel, and Kotlin's by inner generates them. That matters again when the interface grows. Add void reschedule(String ref) to CourierDesk and the Java decorator stops compiling until someone decides what it should do with the new method. The Kotlin one forwards it without a word, untimed. Neither is wrong, but know which one you have. And remember that by never calls you back: if the real desk's track calls its own book, that inner booking isn't timed. Kotlin makes the hand-written forwarding class unnecessary; it doesn't make Decorator unnecessary.

h: Decorator and Proxy · Worked example
x: Make a retry proxy safe for orders A teammate wrapped the shop's order line in the retrying proxy from this lesson, with three attempts. The warehouse sometimes takes 2 seconds to answer, and the shop's code gives up after 1.5 seconds. Before reading on, say what the customer gets on a slow afternoon. interface OrderLine { String place(String item, int grams); String status(String orderNo); } OrderLine line = retrying(OrderLine.class, new WarehouseOrderLine(), 3); line.place("rye bread", 800); // attempt 1 gives up after 1.5 s, but the warehouse finishes it interface OrderLine { fun place(item: String, grams: Int): String fun status(orderNo: String): String } val line = retrying<OrderLine>(WarehouseOrderLine(), 3) line.place("rye bread", 800) // attempt 1 gives up after 1.5 s, but the warehouse finishes it Attempt one gave up on our side, but the warehouse took the order anyway. Attempts two and three are new orders, so the customer gets two or three loaves. A retry is safe only for a call you can repeat without changing the result: the usual word for that is idempotent. Make that visible in the interface by marking the methods that are safe to repeat. @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) // 1. keep the mark while the program runs, so the handler can read it @Target(ElementType.METHOD) @interface SafeToRepeat {} interface OrderLine { String place(String item, int grams); // not marked: one attempt only @SafeToRepeat String status(String orderNo); // a read: safe to repeat } @Target(AnnotationTarget.FUNCTION) @Retention(AnnotationRetention.RUNTIME) // 1. keep the mark while the program runs, so the handler can read it annotation class SafeToRepeat interface OrderLine { fun place(item: String, grams: Int): String // not marked: one attempt only @SafeToRepeat fun status(orderNo: String): String // a read: safe to repeat } The handler reads the mark before its loop, and unmarked methods get exactly one attempt. Why does method.isAnnotationPresent work here, even though the mark sits on the interface and not on WarehouseOrderLine? Because the Method the proxy receives is the interface's method. InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> { int attempts = method.isAnnotationPresent(SafeToRepeat.class) ? maxAttempts : 1; // 2. ask the method Throwable last = null; for (int i = 1; i <= attempts; i++) { try { return method.invoke(target, args); } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { last = e.getCause(); // 3. unwrap } } throw last; }; val handler = InvocationHandler { _, method, args -> val attempts = if (method.isAnnotationPresent(SafeToRepeat::class.java)) maxAttempts else 1 // 2. ask the method var last: Throwable? = null repeat(attempts) { try { return@InvocationHandler method.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { last = e.cause // 3. unwrap } } throw last!! } Now make placing an order safe to repeat. The caller picks an order number once and sends it with every attempt. The warehouse keeps its first answer for each number and hands it back for a repeat, instead of taking a second order. The number must come from the caller: one made up inside the retry loop would be new on each attempt and protect nothing. interface OrderLine { @SafeToRepeat String place(String orderNo, String item, int grams); // 4. the warehouse remembers order numbers @SafeToRepeat String status(String orderNo); } line.place("7781", "rye bread", 800); // 5. the same number on every attempt interface OrderLine { @SafeToRepeat fun place(orderNo: String, item: String, grams: Int): String // 4. the warehouse remembers order numbers @SafeToRepeat fun status(orderNo: String): String } line.place("7781", "rye bread", 800) // 5. the same number on every attempt

h: Decorator and Proxy · Key terms
x: Decorator A wrapper with the same interface as the object inside it, adding one behavior. Proxy A stand-in with the same interface that controls whether and how the real object is called: retrying, timing, checking. Dynamic proxy A class made while the program runs by java.lang.reflect.Proxy, which implements interfaces and routes every call to one handler. InvocationHandler The one method, invoke(proxy, method, args), that a dynamic proxy calls for every interface method. Class delegation (by) Kotlin syntax that generates the forwarding methods of an interface, sending each call to a delegate object. Self-invocation An object calling its own method through this, which skips any proxy in front of it. View A wrapper that reads through to the collection it wraps, so later changes to that collection show up in it. What makes a wrapper a decorator? It has the same interface as the object it wraps, adds one behavior, and passes the call on. Callers can't tell it's there. Retry decorator outside a logging decorator, and the line is busy twice before it books: how many log lines? Three. The inner decorator sees every attempt; the outer one sees one booking. CountingMap : MutableMap by inner overrides put. After put once and putAll of two entries, what is puts? putAll is forwarded to inner, which never calls your override. What does Collections.unmodifiableList(list) give you? A read-through view: writes throw, but later changes to list show up. Use List.copyOf for a frozen copy. In an InvocationHandler, why rethrow e.getCause() from InvocationTargetException? method.invoke wraps the target's exception. If the wrapper escapes, callers get UndeclaredThrowableException instead of the real error. A proxied object calls its own method through this. Does the proxy handle that call? No. Self-invocation goes straight to the real object; a proxy only sees calls made on it. Decorator and Proxy have the same shape. What tells them apart? Intent. A decorator adds behavior the caller wants; a proxy controls whether, when and how the real object is called.

h: Decorator and Proxy · Go deeper
x: JDK proxy classes are final, extend java.lang.reflect.Proxy, and can be detected with Proxy.isProxyClass. Their names aren't specified, but names starting with $Proxy are reserved for them, which is why stack traces show $Proxy0.book, as the demo's did. A proxy also sends equals, hashCode and toString to the handler, so a proxy and its target are different objects to a HashSet unless the handler forwards those methods. The lab's timing proxy forwards them on purpose. Resilience4j, a widely used Java library for calls that may fail, is a decorator library by design. Its README says it provides "higher-order functions (decorators)" for any functional interface, lambda or method reference, and that you can stack more than one. You wrap a Supplier in a retry, wrap the result in a circuit breaker (a switch that stops calling a service that keeps failing), and so on. The order question from this lesson comes back: a retry outside the breaker retries calls the breaker refused, and a retry inside it counts every attempt as a call. Lesson 11 of this track, Concurrency patterns that tie it all together, builds a breaker by hand. Design Patterns, the 1994 book that named these patterns, lists several kinds of proxy by job. A virtual proxy creates the expensive real object only on the first call, like the lazy price list in lesson 1 of this track. A remote proxy makes an object in another program look local. A protection proxy checks who is calling. All three have the same structure as a decorator, which is why intent, not shape, is how people tell them apart.

h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Composite: a box of boxes priced like one item
x: A group answers the same question as a single rule by asking its children, so one recursive function prices the whole fee plan Here's the Saturday breakfast box from the order template in Builder and Prototype: a loaf of bread, a jar of jam, and a small box of tea packed inside the big box. Ask the big box what it costs, and it asks each thing it holds. The bread says 2.50 and the jam says 3.00. The small box asks its own tea, which says 4.50. The big box adds them up: 10.00. That's Composite: single items and groups of items share one interface, and a group answers by asking what it holds. The code that prices a box never checks whether it holds one jar or a crate of boxes. In tree words, an item with nothing inside is a leaf, and a box is a node with children. Design Patterns, the 1994 book that named these patterns, builds Composite from an abstract Component class with add and remove methods that leaves must implement somehow. Since Java 21, and in Kotlin from the start, a sealed type and one exhaustive switch, a switch that must cover every case, replace it. A sealed type lists all its subtypes up front, so the compiler knows every case: Java sealed interface Goods permits Item, Box {} record Item(String name, long cents) implements Goods {} record Box(List<Goods> contents) implements Goods { Box { contents = List.copyOf(contents); } // immutable: copy what the caller passed } static long price(Goods g) { return switch (g) { // no default case Item i -> i.cents(); case Box b -> b.contents().stream().mapToLong(x -> price(x)).sum(); }; } Goods breakfast = new Box(List.of(new Item("bread", 250), new Item("jam", 300), new Box(List.of(new Item("tea", 450))))); Kotlin sealed interface Goods { data class Item(val name: String, val cents: Long) : Goods class Box(contents: List<Goods>) : Goods { val contents: List<Goods> = contents.toList() // immutable: copy what the caller passed } } fun price(g: Goods): Long = when (g) { // no else is Goods.Item -> g.cents is Goods.Box -> g.contents.sumOf { price(it) } } val breakfast = Goods.Box(listOf(Goods.Item("bread", 250), Goods.Item("jam", 300), Goods.Box(listOf(Goods.Item("tea", 450))))) price(breakfast) is 1,000 cents, as in the figure. price calls itself for each thing a box holds, which is called recursion, and the recursion follows the tree: a Box adds up whatever its contents return, and the contents don't care who asked. A box of two breakfast boxes costs 2,000, with no new code. The sealed type buys two things. The switch has no default, so adding a third kind of node, say a Deal, makes javac report "the switch expression does not cover all possible input values" (kotlinc says "'when' expression must be exhaustive") at every place that prices or prints goods. And a second operation over the same tree, such as describe for the receipt, is just another function. The node classes don't change. The box picture breaks in one place. A cardboard box can't change once it's taped shut, but a Java list can. Build a box from a list that someone else still holds, and the box changes when they edit the list. CompositeDemo, in the Try it, does exactly that once you delete the copy: box: (bread 2.50 + jam 3.00 + (tea 4.50)) after editing the source list: (bread 2.50 + jam 3.00 + (tea 4.50 + champagne 30.00)) A breakfast box already promised to a customer quietly gained a bottle of champagne, and its price went up by 30.00. List.copyOf in the compact constructor, the short record constructor that can adjust values before they are stored, stops that. Kotlin's List is only a read-only view, so the Kotlin box copies with toList(). An immutable tree can't grow a loop either, and threads can share it safely, which the last section relies on. Build the tree from copies. Then it can't change behind your back. One tree, several operations. Next, two things in the program that change on their own. Price a box, then let someone edit its list Open CompositeDemo.java (or CompositeDemo.kt). Before you run it, work out both prices in your head. Run it with the command below and check your numbers. Note the last line. Remove the copy: in Java delete the compact constructor Box { contents = List.copyOf(contents); }; in Kotlin change = contents.toList() to = contents. Predict the last line, then run. CompositeDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l06; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** The Saturday breakfast box as a tree. Items and boxes share one sealed type, so one switch prices them all. */ public class CompositeDemo { sealed interface Goods permits Item, Box {} record Item(String name, long cents) implements Goods {} record Box(List<Goods> contents) implements Goods { Box { contents = List.copyOf(contents); } // copy what we were given: the tree stays immutable } static long price(Goods g) { return switch (g) { // no default: a new node type breaks the build case Item i -> i.cents(); case Box b -> b.contents().stream().mapToLong(CompositeDemo::price).sum(); }; } static String describe(Goods g) { return switch (g) { case Item i -> i.name() + " " + String.format("%d.%02d", i.cents() / 100, i.cents() % 100); case Box b -> "(" + String.join(" + ", b.contents().stream().map(CompositeDemo::describe).toList()) + ")"; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Goods> extras = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Item("tea", 450))); Goods breakfast = new Box(List.of(new Item("bread", 250), new Item("jam", 300), new Box(extras))); System.out.println("box: " + describe(breakfast)); System.out.println("price: " + price(breakfast) + " cents"); System.out.println("a box of two breakfast boxes: " + price(new Box(List.of(breakfast, breakfast))) + " cents"); extras.add(new Item("champagne", 3_000)); // someone edits the list they passed in System.out.println("after editing the source list: " + describe(breakfast)); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l06.CompositeDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l06/CompositeDemo.java CompositeDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l06 // The Saturday breakfast box as a tree. Items and boxes share one sealed type, so one `when` prices them all. sealed interface ShopGoods { data class Item(val name: String, val cents: Long) : ShopGoods class Box(contents: List<ShopGoods>) : ShopGoods { val contents: List<ShopGoods> = contents.toList() // copy what we were given: the tree stays immutable } } private fun price(g: ShopGoods): Long = when (g) { // no else: a new node type breaks the build is ShopGoods.Item -> g.cents is ShopGoods.Box -> g.contents.sumOf { price(it) } } private fun describe(g: ShopGoods): String = when (g) { is ShopGoods.Item -> "${g.name} %d.%02d".format(g.cents / 100, g.cents % 100) is ShopGoods.Box -> g.contents.joinToString(" + ", "(", ")") { describe(it) } } fun main() { val extras = mutableListOf<ShopGoods>(ShopGoods.Item("tea", 450)) val breakfast = ShopGoods.Box(listOf(ShopGoods.Item("bread", 250), ShopGoods.Item("jam", 300), ShopGoods.Box(extras))) println("box: ${describe(breakfast)}") println("price: ${price(breakfast)} cents") println("a box of two breakfast boxes: ${price(ShopGoods.Box(listOf(breakfast, breakfast)))} cents") extras += ShopGoods.Item("champagne", 3_000) // someone edits the list they passed in println("after editing the source list: ${describe(breakfast)}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l06.CompositeDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l06/CompositeDemo.kt box: (bread 2.50 + jam 3.00 + (tea 4.50)), price: 1000 cents, a box of two breakfast boxes: 2000 cents, and the last line unchanged. Without the copy, the last line becomes (bread 2.50 + jam 3.00 + (tea 4.50 + champagne 30.00)): a box already in use changed because someone edited the list they built it from. The big box adds up what its contents return. The small box answers the same question, so one recursive function prices any box. Sealed classes and interfaces (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Bridge: notices and channels that vary on their own
x: The shop sends customers short notices: "order 7781 is on its way", "rye bread is sold out, back in 2 days". Each can go by SMS, a text message to a phone, or by email. Model that with inheritance (OnItsWaySms, OnItsWayEmail, SoldOutSms, SoldOutEmail) and you write four classes. A third channel costs two more, a third notice costs three more, and each one is a near copy of its neighbors. Now think of a TV remote and the TV. The remote's buttons say what you want: louder, next channel. The TV decides how to do it. One remote works with any brand of TV that understands its signal, so nobody builds a separate remote for every model. Bridge splits code the same way, into two sides that vary on their own. The abstraction says what you want: the notice and its words. The implementor says how it gets done: the channel that carries the words. Each notice holds a channel and calls it: Java interface Channel { void deliver(String to, String body); } // implementor: how it travels sealed interface Notice permits OnItsWay, SoldOut { // abstraction: what to say void send(String to); } record OnItsWay(Channel channel, String orderNo) implements Notice { public void send(String to) { channel.deliver(to, "order " + orderNo + " is on its way"); } } record SoldOut(Channel channel, String item, int days) implements Notice { public void send(String to) { channel.deliver(to, item + " is sold out, back in " + days + " days"); } } new OnItsWay(sms, "7781").send("Ana"); new OnItsWay(email, "7781").send("Ana"); // same notice, other channel: no new class Kotlin fun interface Channel { fun deliver(to: String, body: String) } // implementor: how it travels sealed interface Notice { fun send(to: String) } // abstraction: what to say data class OnItsWay(val channel: Channel, val orderNo: String) : Notice { override fun send(to: String) = channel.deliver(to, "order $orderNo is on its way") } data class SoldOut(val channel: Channel, val item: String, val days: Int) : Notice { override fun send(to: String) = channel.deliver(to, "$item is sold out, back in $days days") } OnItsWay(sms, "7781").send("Ana") OnItsWay(email, "7781").send("Ana") // same notice, other channel: no new class Two notices and two channels are now four small pieces, and a new channel is one more. Every notice works with it, because notices only know Channel. Tests pass a recording lambda as the channel and check the words, with no phone in sight. In Kotlin, the implementor side often shrinks to a function: with fun interface Channel, the lambda Channel { to, body -> println("$to: $body") } is a whole channel. The picture breaks in one place. A universal remote learns each brand's signals, so it bends to fit the TV. In a bridge, every channel is written to fit our Channel interface. When a channel wraps someone else's code, such as a text-message service with its own method names, that wrapper is an adapter, as in Adapter and Facade. That's also how to tell Bridge from Adapter. Both put an interface between two pieces of code. You design a bridge up front, because you know two things will vary. You write an adapter afterwards, because a class you can't change has the wrong shape. They often meet: each channel is usually an adapter around someone's service. Two things that vary on their own get two sides and one interface between them. Skip the bridge when only one side varies. If every notice goes by email, a notice with a MailServer field is plain composition, and calling it a pattern adds nothing. Composite and Bridge arrange objects. The next pattern asks how many of them we need at all. Add a channel without touching a notice Run BridgeDemo in either language and count the lines: 2 notices times 2 channels. Add a postcard channel. Java: record Postcard() implements Channel { public String deliver(String to, String body) { return "CARD to " + to + ": " + body; } }, then add new Postcard() to the list. Kotlin: private val postcard = NoticeChannel { to, body -> "CARD to $to: $body" }, then add postcard to the list. Predict how many lines print and how many notice types you had to edit. Run it. BridgeDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l06; import java.util.List; /** Notices (what to say) and channels (how it travels) vary on their own: 2 + 2 classes, not 2 x 2. */ public class BridgeDemo { // the implementor side: how a message travels interface Channel { String deliver(String to, String body); } record Sms() implements Channel { public String deliver(String to, String body) { return "SMS to " + to + ": " + body; } } record Email() implements Channel { public String deliver(String to, String body) { return "EMAIL to " + to + ": " + body; } } // the abstraction side: what to say. Each notice HOLDS a channel instead of being one. sealed interface Notice permits OnItsWay, SoldOut { Channel channel(); String send(String to); } record OnItsWay(Channel channel, String orderNo, String courier) implements Notice { public String send(String to) { return channel.deliver(to, "order " + orderNo + " is on its way with " + courier); } } record SoldOut(Channel channel, String item, int days) implements Notice { public String send(String to) { return channel.deliver(to, item + " is sold out, back in " + days + " days"); } } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Channel> channels = List.of(new Sms(), new Email()); for (Channel ch : channels) { System.out.println(new OnItsWay(ch, "7781", "Pedal Post").send("Ana")); System.out.println(new SoldOut(ch, "rye bread", 2).send("Ben")); } } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l06.BridgeDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l06/BridgeDemo.java BridgeDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l06 // Notices (what to say) and channels (how it travels) vary on their own: 2 + 2 pieces, not 2 x 2. // the implementor side: one method, so a lambda is enough fun interface NoticeChannel { fun deliver(to: String, body: String): String } private val sms = NoticeChannel { to, body -> "SMS to $to: $body" } private val email = NoticeChannel { to, body -> "EMAIL to $to: $body" } // the abstraction side: what to say. Each notice HOLDS a channel instead of being one. sealed interface ShopNotice { val channel: NoticeChannel fun send(to: String): String data class OnItsWay(override val channel: NoticeChannel, val orderNo: String, val courier: String) : ShopNotice { override fun send(to: String) = channel.deliver(to, "order $orderNo is on its way with $courier") } data class SoldOut(override val channel: NoticeChannel, val item: String, val days: Int) : ShopNotice { override fun send(to: String) = channel.deliver(to, "$item is sold out, back in $days days") } } fun main() { val channels = listOf(sms, email) for (ch in channels) { println(ShopNotice.OnItsWay(ch, "7781", "Pedal Post").send("Ana")) println(ShopNotice.SoldOut(ch, "rye bread", 2).send("Ben")) } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l06.BridgeDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l06/BridgeDemo.kt Four lines before, starting SMS to Ana: order 7781 is on its way with Pedal Post. Six after, the last two starting CARD to Ana and CARD to Ben. You edited zero notice types. In Kotlin the new channel was one lambda; in Java it was one small record.
