h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Flyweight: share one unchanging object instead of building new ones
x: The sign shop across the street paints SALE banners. The painter has one stencil for the letter A and uses it every time an A appears; BANANA takes the same stencil three times. The stencil holds the shape. Where each letter goes, and in what color, belongs to each use. A flyweight is that stencil in code: one small object that never changes, shared by many users instead of copied for each. Java has several built in, and one of them surprises everyone once: Java Integer a = 127, b = 127; Integer c = 128, d = 128; System.out.println(a == b); // true System.out.println(c == d); // false Kotlin val a: Any = 127; val b: Any = 127 // typed Any, so Kotlin boxes them as Java does val c: Any = 128; val d: Any = 128 println(a === b) // true: === asks "the same object?" println(c === d) // false == on objects asks "the same object?", not "the same value?". Autoboxing, Java's automatic wrapping of an int in an Integer object, calls Integer.valueOf, which "will always cache values in the range -128 to 127, inclusive". So 127 comes from a shared drawer of ready-made objects, and 128 is a new object every time. That drawer is a flyweight. The JDK has more. The JVM interns string literals, which means it keeps one String object per literal, and s.intern() returns the pooled copy of any string. Currency "is designed so that there's never more than one Currency instance for any given currency", which is why you call Currency.getInstance("EUR") instead of new. Enums are flyweights by definition, and so are Kotlin's object and data object. The drawer also explains an old Java bug: Java Long onShelf = stockGrams.get("coffee"); // 2,500, boxed when it went into the map Long ordered = orderGrams.get("coffee"); // 2,500, boxed separately if (onShelf == ordered) { ... } // false: two different Long objects if (onShelf.equals(ordered)) { ... } // true Kotlin val onShelf: Long? = stockGrams["coffee"] // 2,500 val ordered: Long? = orderGrams["coffee"] // 2,500 if (onShelf == ordered) { /* ... */ } // true: == calls equals() if (onShelf === ordered) { /* ... */ } // false, and the compiler warns Test data such as 100 g sits inside the drawer, so the check passes. Real stock like 2,500 g doesn't, so it fails. The drawer stops at 127, which is about where test data stops and real stock begins. Kotlin's == calls equals, so you meet this bug only with ===, and on Long? kotlinc warns: "Identity equality for arguments of types 'Long?' and 'Long?' is prohibited." You build your own flyweight with a canonicalizing factory: a private constructor, and an of method that returns the one pooled instance for a key. Keep the pool in a ConcurrentHashMap and use computeIfAbsent, which checks and inserts in one atomic step, a step no other thread can cut into. Eight threads asking for a new product code at the same moment still get one instance. A get followed by a put on a miss is check-then-act: another thread can slip in between the check and the act, so under load it builds duplicates. The stencil picture breaks on sharing. Only one painter at a time can hold a stencil. A flyweight can be used by many threads at the same instant, because nothing in it ever changes. That's the first rule: flyweights must be immutable, because every holder sees every change. The second is that the pool must be bounded. Pool the shop's catalog, a few hundred known codes, and never every customer name typed into an order form. Share only what never changes, and only from a set you know. We now have shared boxes and shared products. Let's see what may live inside a shared object, and what must stay outside it. Find out which objects are shared Read FlyweightDemo.java (or FlyweightDemo.kt) and predict all five lines before you run it. Run it with the command below. Break the pool: make Product.of return new Product(code) (Kotlin: make CatalogProduct.of return CatalogProduct(code)). Predict the last line, then run. FlyweightDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l06; import java.util.Currency; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Four flyweights: three from the JDK, one of our own. `==` asks "the same object?" */ public class FlyweightDemo { // our own: one shared instance per product code in the shop's catalog static final class Product { private static final Map<String, Product> POOL = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private static final AtomicInteger BUILT = new AtomicInteger(); final String code; private Product(String code) { this.code = code; BUILT.incrementAndGet(); } static Product of(String code) { return POOL.computeIfAbsent(code, Product::new); } static int built() { return BUILT.get(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Integer a = 127, b = 127; Integer c = 128, d = 128; System.out.println("Integer 127 == 127: " + (a == b)); System.out.println("Integer 128 == 128: " + (c == d) + " equals: " + c.equals(d)); String parsed = new String("T-1001"); // a fresh object, like a code read from an order form System.out.println("parsed == \"T-1001\": " + (parsed == "T-1001") + " after intern(): " + (parsed.intern() == "T-1001")); System.out.println("Currency EUR == EUR: " + (Currency.getInstance("EUR") == Currency.getInstance("EUR"))); Product first = Product.of("T-1001"), second = Product.of("T-1001"); System.out.println("Product T-1001 == T-1001: " + (first == second) + " instances built: " + Product.built()); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l06.FlyweightDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l06/FlyweightDemo.java FlyweightDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l06 import java.util.Currency import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger // Four flyweights: three from the JDK, one of our own. In Kotlin, `==` is equals(); `===` asks "the same object?" // our own: one shared instance per product code in the shop's catalog class CatalogProduct private constructor(val code: String) { init { built.incrementAndGet() } companion object { private val pool = ConcurrentHashMap<String, CatalogProduct>() private val built = AtomicInteger() fun of(code: String): CatalogProduct = pool.computeIfAbsent(code) { CatalogProduct(it) } val instancesBuilt: Int get() = built.get() } } fun main() { // typed as Any so Kotlin boxes them, as Java does for Integer; === on Int? gets a compiler warning val a: Any = 127 val b: Any = 127 val c: Any = 128 val d: Any = 128 println("Integer 127 === 127: ${a === b}") println("Integer 128 === 128: ${c === d} ==: ${c == d}") val parsed = String("T-1001".toCharArray()) // a fresh object, like a code read from an order form println("parsed === \"T-1001\": ${parsed === "T-1001"} after intern(): ${parsed.intern() === "T-1001"}") println("Currency EUR === EUR: ${Currency.getInstance("EUR") === Currency.getInstance("EUR")}") val first = CatalogProduct.of("T-1001") val second = CatalogProduct.of("T-1001") println("Product T-1001 === T-1001: ${first === second} instances built: ${CatalogProduct.instancesBuilt}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l06.FlyweightDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l06/FlyweightDemo.kt 127 is shared (true), 128 is not (false, though equals is true), a code read as "T-1001" is a different object until you call intern(), Currency hands out one EUR, and the pool gives one product with instances built: 1. Without the pool, the last line reads false instances built: 2. Integer.valueOf(int) (Java SE 25 API) docs Currency (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Share the box, keep each order's details outside it
x: Composite and Flyweight work well together. The shop sells the Saturday breakfast box hundreds of times. It doesn't need hundreds of box trees: it builds the tree once and lets every order point at it, as every A on a banner uses the same stencil. Design Patterns names the split that makes this work. Intrinsic state lives inside the shared object and is the same for every user: what the box holds and what each item costs. Extrinsic state belongs to one use, so the order keeps it or the caller passes it in: who ordered the box, where it goes, how many boxes. A breakfast box with a customer field could not be shared, by two orders or by two threads. Sharing across threads costs nothing here, because the trees never change. Records have final fields, List.copyOf returns a list nobody can modify, and an object that never changes can be read by 200 threads at once with no lock, once it has been published safely: stored where other threads are guaranteed to see it fully built, such as a static final field, or set before the threads start. Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal in the concurrency track showed why that holds. The same thinking fits the small values that appear on every order line: delivery methods, units, product codes. If the set is closed and known when you compile, an enum (Java) or enum class (Kotlin) is the flyweight, with no pool to write. Reach for a pooled factory only when the set is open but bounded, such as product codes loaded from the catalog. Keep the shared object's state the same for everyone. Each use brings its own details. In the lab you build both halves. Goods is a five-node composite: items, goods sold by weight, boxes, a percentage off and a deal with a maximum price, priced and described by two functions. Product is a catalog flyweight that stays correct when eight threads ask for the same code at once. Check yourself. The shop wants each breakfast box to show who ordered it, and a teammate adds var orderedBy to the shared box tree. What goes wrong, and where should the name live? (Every order of the breakfast box points at that one tree, so every order shows whoever ordered last, and two threads writing the name at once can mix them up. The name is extrinsic state: keep it on the order, outside the tree.)

h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Java and Kotlin
x: A flyweight that callers can't go around Product.java // Not a record: a record's canonical constructor can't be private, // so `new Product(...)` would always go around the pool. public final class Product { private static final Map<String, Product> POOL = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private final String code; // the catalog code, such as "T-1001" private final String name; private Product(String code, String name) { this.code = code; this.name = name; } public static Product of(String code, Function<String, String> nameLookup) { return POOL.computeIfAbsent(code, c -> new Product(c, nameLookup.apply(c))); // built once per code } public String code() { return code; } public String name() { return name; } } Product.kt // A plain class: a private constructor holds, and there is no generated copy() to go around it. class Product private constructor(val code: String, val name: String) { companion object { private val pool = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Product>() fun of(code: String, nameLookup: (String) -> String): Product = pool.computeIfAbsent(code) { Product(it, nameLookup(it)) } // built once per code } } Both use computeIfAbsent, so the lookup runs at most once per code even when many threads ask at once. The real difference is what each language lets you hide. A Java record would be the natural value type, but javac rejects a private canonical constructor ("attempting to assign stronger access privileges; was public"), so anyone could call new and skip the pool: use a final class. In Kotlin, a data class with a private constructor still exposes a public copy() in 2.4 unless you add @ConsistentCopyVisibility, as Builder and Prototype showed, so a plain class is the safe choice there too. Kotlin also makes the flyweight's identity matter less: == calls equals, so the pool is about memory and one place to check codes, not about making comparisons work. For a closed set, skip the pool and use an enum in either language.

h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Worked example
x: Turn a notice class explosion into a bridge The shop's notice code grew by inheritance. Count the classes, then count what a voice-message channel would cost. abstract class Notice { abstract void send(); } class OnItsWaySms extends Notice { void send() { texts.send(phone, "order " + orderNo + " is on its way"); } } class OnItsWayEmail extends Notice { void send() { mail.send(address, "Your order", "order " + orderNo + " is on its way"); } } class SoldOutSms extends Notice { void send() { /* the SMS code again */ } } class SoldOutEmail extends Notice { void send() { /* the email code again */ } } // voice messages: OnItsWayVoice, SoldOutVoice, and one more per future notice abstract class Notice { abstract fun send() } class OnItsWaySms : Notice() { override fun send() = texts.send(phone, "order $orderNo is on its way") } class OnItsWayEmail : Notice() { override fun send() = mail.send(address, "Your order", "order $orderNo is on its way") } class SoldOutSms : Notice() { override fun send() { /* the SMS code again */ } } class SoldOutEmail : Notice() { override fun send() { /* the email code again */ } } // voice messages: OnItsWayVoice, SoldOutVoice, and one more per future notice Four classes for two notices and two channels, and voice messages add two more. Name the two dimensions: the notice decides the words, the channel decides how they travel. Pull the travel out behind one interface, the implementor. interface Channel { void deliver(String to, String body); } // 1. the implementor side record SmsChannel(TextService texts) implements Channel { // 2. one class per channel, public void deliver(String to, String body) { texts.send(to, body); } // usually an adapter } record EmailChannel(MailServer mail) implements Channel { public void deliver(String to, String body) { mail.send(to, "Your order", body); } } fun interface Channel { fun deliver(to: String, body: String) } // 1. the implementor side class SmsChannel(private val texts: TextService) : Channel { // 2. one class per channel, override fun deliver(to: String, body: String) = texts.send(to, body) // usually an adapter } class EmailChannel(private val mail: MailServer) : Channel { override fun deliver(to: String, body: String) = mail.send(to, "Your order", body) } Each notice now holds a channel and builds only its words. Ask yourself: which notice would change if the text-message service changed its method names? None. Only SmsChannel would. sealed interface Notice permits OnItsWay, SoldOut { void send(String to); } // 3. the abstraction side record OnItsWay(Channel channel, String orderNo) implements Notice { public void send(String to) { channel.deliver(to, "order " + orderNo + " is on its way"); } } record SoldOut(Channel channel, String item, int days) implements Notice { public void send(String to) { channel.deliver(to, item + " is sold out, back in " + days + " days"); } } sealed interface Notice { fun send(to: String) } // 3. the abstraction side data class OnItsWay(val channel: Channel, val orderNo: String) : Notice { override fun send(to: String) = channel.deliver(to, "order $orderNo is on its way") } data class SoldOut(val channel: Channel, val item: String, val days: Int) : Notice { override fun send(to: String) = channel.deliver(to, "$item is sold out, back in $days days") } Test each side alone. A recording lambda is a complete channel, so notice tests need no phone and no mail server. Voice messages are now one class, and no notice changes. List<String> sent = new ArrayList<>(); Channel recording = (to, body) -> sent.add(to + ": " + body); // 4. a fake channel in one line new OnItsWay(recording, "7781").send("Ana"); assertThat(sent).containsExactly("Ana: order 7781 is on its way"); val sent = mutableListOf<String>() val recording = Channel { to, body -> sent += "$to: $body" } // 4. a fake channel in one line OnItsWay(recording, "7781").send("Ana") assertThat(sent).containsExactly("Ana: order 7781 is on its way")

Run the tests: all eight fail. Write price as one when (this) with five branches and no else. Leaves compute (ByWeight is grams * centsPerKg / 1_000); Box adds up its contents; PercentOff is inside.price() * (100 - percent) / 100; Deal is minOf(inside.price(), maxCents). Write describe the same way, following the formats in its KDoc. In Product, add a private pool to the companion object and write of: reject unknown codes first, then return the pooled instance. Run the tests until all eight pass. Then add data class Free(val name: String) : Goods to the sealed interface, read the two compiler errors, and delete it again. contents.sumOf { it.price() } returns a Long when the lambda does, and an empty list sums to 0. joinToString(" + ", "(", ")") { it.describe() } takes a separator, a prefix and a postfix, and gives () for an empty list. "%d.%02d".format(cents / 100, cents % 100) turns 5 into 0.05. requireNotNull(CATALOG[code]) { "unknown product: $code" } throws IllegalArgumentException. By the end you can model a box of goods as an immutable sealed tree priced by one exhaustive switch, split two independent dimensions with a bridge, and share immutable values through a thread-safe flyweight factory without falling for boxed ==.

h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Quiz
x: In Java, two weights are read from two maps: Long onShelf = stockGrams.get("coffee"); Long ordered = orderGrams.get("coffee");. Each holds 2,500, boxed separately. What does onShelf == ordered return on a standard JVM? true, because the values are equal false, because they are two different Long objects It doesn't compile It throws NullPointerException == on objects compares which object, not which value. Long.valueOf shares instances only for -128 to 127, so two separately boxed 2,500s are different objects. With a test value of 100 the cache makes it pass, which is how this bug reaches real stock. Use equals, or primitive long. What does Box(Item("card", 100), Deal(PercentOff(Item("cake", 1_200), 25), 850)).price() return, in cents? 1,300 1,000 950 850 25% off 1,200 is 900. The deal caps that at 850, and the box adds the card's 100: 950. The tempting 1,000 takes the percentage off and forgets the deal's maximum. You're designing the shop's notices: four kinds today, three channels (SMS, email, postcard), and both lists will grow. Which structure fits? Notices that hold a Channel interface, with one class or lambda per channel Twelve classes, one per notice and channel pair An adapter per notice kind A singleton per channel that every notice extends Two things that vary on their own are the case for Bridge: 4 + 3 pieces, and a new channel works with every notice. Twelve classes become fifteen with the next notice. An adapter fixes one mismatched interface, and extending a singleton puts the channel back into the class hierarchy. To save memory, the shop's program puts every customer name typed into an order form into a static ConcurrentHashMap pool and reuses the pooled string. What goes wrong over time? Two threads can get different instances for the same name Nothing: ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe The pool grows with every new name and never shrinks: a slow memory leak Pooled strings can't be compared with equals any more A flyweight pool must be bounded. Names typed by customers are an open set, so the map keeps every name ever seen for as long as the program runs. Pool a known set, such as the catalog's product codes, or use a cache that forgets old entries. Thread safety isn't the issue here; computeIfAbsent handles that. From Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal: the breakfast box tree is built once at startup from records whose lists go through List.copyOf, kept in a static final field, and read by 200 threads. What do the reads need? A synchronized block around each price call The read side of a ReadWriteLock volatile on every record field Nothing: the tree is immutable and safely published Record fields are final, List.copyOf returns a list nobody can modify, and a static final field is published safely when the class is set up. Nothing ever writes after that, so there is nothing to race on, and locks would only make threads wait.

h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Explain it back
x: Explain to a teammate why the customer's name and address live on the order, not inside the shared breakfast box, and why that lets hundreds of orders and many threads share one box object safely.

h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Key terms
x: Composite A tree where groups and single items share one interface, so you handle both the same way. Leaf A node in a composite with nothing inside it, such as Item("jam", 300). Bridge Splitting two things that vary on their own, so one side holds the other through an interface. Implementor In a bridge, the side that does the low-level work, such as a Channel that carries messages. Flyweight A small object that never changes, shared by many users instead of copied for each. Intrinsic and extrinsic state Intrinsic state lives in the shared object; extrinsic state belongs to each use and stays outside it. Canonicalizing factory A factory that returns the one pooled instance for a key, such as Currency.getInstance("EUR"). What does Composite let you do? Treat a single item and a group of items through one interface. A group answers by asking what it holds, so callers never check which one they have. Why leave default out of the switch that walks a sealed composite? So adding a node type is a compile error at every operation that handles the tree, instead of a silent fallback. What problem does Bridge solve? Two things that vary on their own (notice and channel) without N x M classes: the abstraction holds an implementor and calls it. Bridge or Adapter: which one is designed up front? Bridge. An adapter is written afterwards, to make a class you can't change fit your interface. Java: Integer a = 128, b = 128; What is a == b? false with default settings. Integer.valueOf caches only -128 to 127; 128 gives two different objects. Why must a flyweight be immutable? Every holder shares the same instance, so a change made by one would show up for all of them, on every thread. Why does a flyweight factory use computeIfAbsent instead of get then put? computeIfAbsent checks and inserts in one atomic step, so callers at the same moment get one instance. get then put is check-then-act and can build duplicates.

h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Go deeper
x: Design Patterns spends pages on Composite's "transparency versus safety" choice: should add and remove live on the shared Component type, so leaves must throw, or only on groups, so callers must cast? A sealed type with immutable records ends the debate. There are no methods for managing children at all: you build a new tree. Pattern matching gives each operation exact access to each node type, with no casts. Recursion over a tree is fine for a box a few levels deep. A tree built from outside input, such as a gift-box design a customer uploads, could be thousands of levels deep and throw StackOverflowError. Check the depth when you build the tree, or walk it with your own stack. Composite also pairs with Visitor; lesson 10 of this track, Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento, shows why sealed types and pattern matching usually replace it. The Integer cache bounds are part of the contract: valueOf "will always cache values in the range -128 to 127, inclusive, and may cache other values outside of this range". The upper bound can be raised with the java.lang.Integer.IntegerCache.high system property. That can make a boxed == bug disappear on one JVM and show up on another, which is one more reason never to rely on it. String interning has a cousin in the garbage collector, the part of the JVM that frees memory nobody uses. G1's -XX:+UseStringDeduplication lets the collector make equal String objects share one array of characters underneath, with no code change. It saves memory for programs that hold many equal strings, such as product codes and unit names, but doesn't make == work, because the String objects themselves stay distinct.

h: Strategy and Template Method · Strategy: the one decision you pass in
x: A strategy is the one decision you plug in: sort keeps the loop, and the comparator decides which quote goes first Back to the shop counter. The routine for sending a parcel stays the same, and one decision inside it is swapped: which courier to use. The rule for that decision can change from order to order without touching the rest of the routine. Java's sort works the same way. It owns the routine for putting a list in order and leaves one decision to you, passed in as an object: which of two items goes first. That object is a comparator, and it's the Strategy pattern in one line. A strategy is one interchangeable algorithm, passed in by the caller and used by the code that needs the decision. That code is called the context. In Design Patterns, the 1994 book that named these patterns, a strategy meant an interface and a class for every algorithm. Since Java 8, a lambda or a method reference is the class. Here the shop ranks courier quotes, each with a price and a delivery time: Java record Quote(String courier, long priceCents, long minutes) {} Comparator<Quote> cheapest = Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::priceCents); Comparator<Quote> cheapestThenFastest = cheapest.thenComparingLong(Quote::minutes); quotes.sort(cheapestThenFastest); // sort is the context; the comparator is the strategy Kotlin data class Quote(val courier: String, val priceCents: Long, val minutes: Long) val cheapest = compareBy<Quote> { it.priceCents } val cheapestThenFastest = cheapest.thenBy { it.minutes } val ordered = quotes.sortedWith(cheapestThenFastest) // sortedWith is the context; the comparator is the strategy Comparator.comparing "accepts a function that extracts a Comparable sort key" and returns a comparator. thenComparing chains a second comparator behind it, used only when the first one ties. Nobody writes a class called PriceThenTimeComparator any more. Kotlin's compareBy and thenBy do the same with function types, and any (Parcel) -> Long already is a pricing strategy, with no interface to declare. StrategyDemo, in the Try it, ranks three quotes three ways. They come from Pedal Post, Big Blue Vans and Kestrel, a new courier in town: cheapest: [Big Blue Vans, Pedal Post, Kestrel] fastest: [Kestrel, Pedal Post, Big Blue Vans] cheapest, then fastest: [Big Blue Vans, Kestrel, Pedal Post] Look at the first line. Pedal Post and Kestrel both cost 4.50, and they stay in the order they came in, because the JDK's sort is stable: it never swaps two items that compare equal. The third strategy breaks that tie by time, so Kestrel's 20 minutes beat Pedal Post's 30. The JDK hands you strategies in more places than sorting. A ThreadPoolExecutor, the JDK's pool of worker threads, takes a RejectedExecutionHandler that decides what happens when its queue is full. Collectors.groupingBy takes the function that decides which group each element joins. Each time, the library owns the loop and asks you for one decision. A named type still helps in two cases. When the strategy has more than one method, such as a courier client with book and track, you have an interface with implementations, which is ordinary polymorphism: one interface, several classes, one of them chosen while the program runs. And a one-line @FunctionalInterface interface PriceStrategy { long priceCents(Parcel p); } says more than a bare ToLongFunction<Parcel>, and reads better in stack traces, the list of calls an exception prints. The counter picture breaks on memory. The shopkeeper remembers that yesterday's van was late. A strategy shouldn't remember anything. A lambda that captures and changes a field is a strategy with hidden memory, a shopkeeper still holding a grudge, and two threads sorting with it at once will corrupt each other's results. A strategy is one decision, passed in. Keep it pure: input in, answer out. A comparator is a strategy for a context someone else wrote. Next, a context of our own that grew the old way. Rank couriers three ways Read StrategyDemo.java (or StrategyDemo.kt) and predict the three lines. Remember that equal prices keep their original order, because the JDK's sort is stable. Run it with the command below. Add a fourth quote at the end of the list, new Quote("Gull Express", 350, 60) (CourierQuote("Gull Express", 350, 60) in Kotlin). Predict all three lines again, then run. StrategyDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l07; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** Three strategies for one decision: which courier does the shop ask first? */ public class StrategyDemo { record Quote(String courier, long priceCents, long minutes) {} public static void main(String[] args) { List<Quote> quotes = List.of( new Quote("Pedal Post", 450, 30), new Quote("Big Blue Vans", 350, 90), new Quote("Kestrel", 450, 20)); // each value is a complete strategy: no class per algorithm Map<String, Comparator<Quote>> policies = new LinkedHashMap<>(); policies.put("cheapest", Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::priceCents)); policies.put("fastest", Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::minutes)); policies.put("cheapest, then fastest", Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::priceCents).thenComparingLong(Quote::minutes)); // sorted() is the context: it owns the algorithm and asks the strategy one question policies.forEach((name, order) -> System.out.println(name + ": " + quotes.stream().sorted(order).map(Quote::courier).toList())); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l07.StrategyDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l07/StrategyDemo.java StrategyDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l07 // Three strategies for one decision: which courier does the shop ask first? data class CourierQuote(val courier: String, val priceCents: Long, val minutes: Long) fun main() { val quotes = listOf( CourierQuote("Pedal Post", 450, 30), CourierQuote("Big Blue Vans", 350, 90), CourierQuote("Kestrel", 450, 20), ) // each value is a complete strategy: no class per algorithm val policies: Map<String, Comparator<CourierQuote>> = mapOf( "cheapest" to compareBy<CourierQuote> { it.priceCents }, "fastest" to compareBy<CourierQuote> { it.minutes }, "cheapest, then fastest" to compareBy<CourierQuote> { it.priceCents }.thenBy { it.minutes }, ) // sortedWith is the context: it owns the algorithm and asks the strategy one question policies.forEach { (name, order) -> println("$name: ${quotes.sortedWith(order).map { it.courier }}") } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l07.StrategyDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l07/StrategyDemo.kt cheapest: [Big Blue Vans, Pedal Post, Kestrel], fastest: [Kestrel, Pedal Post, Big Blue Vans], cheapest, then fastest: [Big Blue Vans, Kestrel, Pedal Post]. With Gull Express: [Big Blue Vans, Gull Express, Pedal Post, Kestrel], [Kestrel, Pedal Post, Gull Express, Big Blue Vans] and [Gull Express, Big Blue Vans, Kestrel, Pedal Post]. Three algorithms, zero classes: each strategy is one expression. Comparator (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Strategy and Template Method · Refactor the if/else pricer, after pinning what it does
x: The shop's delivery pricer grew the way most do: one if/else if chain on the delivery method, with a special case added every year. LegacyPricer, in the lab, is that method. A bike costs 2.00 plus 0.30 per kg, and 0.10 more per kg outside the Old Town, where the hills are. A van costs 4.50, whatever the weight. Picking the parcel up at the counter is free. Before you touch a method like that, pin what it does. Write a test that runs the old code and the new code over a grid of inputs and asserts that they agree. Michael Feathers, in his book Working Effectively with Legacy Code, calls this a characterization test. It records today's behavior, bugs included, so the refactor can't change it by accident. Choose the grid for its edges, not its size: weight 0, weight 1, the Old Town and two districts outside it, and every enum constant. Integer division rounds down, and that's where a tidied-up rule drifts by a cent. The legacy code rounds the per-kg price and the hill surcharge separately, so 999 g outside the Old Town costs 2.38. A refactor that "simplifies" the two into grams * 40 / 1_000 charges 2.39, and the grid catches it. Then pick one of two shapes: Java static long bike(Parcel p) { // two divisions, rounded separately, as the legacy code does return 200 + p.grams() * 30 / 1_000 + (p.district().equals("Old Town") ? 0 : p.grams() * 10 / 1_000); } // open set: one lambda per method, in a map that settings or plug-ins could fill static final Map<DeliveryMethod, PriceStrategy> STRATEGIES = new EnumMap<>(Map.of( BIKE, p -> bike(p), VAN, p -> 450, PICKUP, p -> 0)); // closed set: one switch, checked by the compiler static long priceCents(Parcel p) { return switch (p.method()) { case BIKE -> bike(p); case VAN -> 450; case PICKUP -> 0; }; } Kotlin fun bike(p: Parcel): Long = // two divisions, rounded separately, as the legacy code does 200L + p.grams * 30 / 1_000 + if (p.district == "Old Town") 0 else p.grams * 10 / 1_000 // open set: one function per method, in a map that settings or plug-ins could fill val strategies: Map<DeliveryMethod, (Parcel) -> Long> = mapOf( BIKE to ::bike, VAN to { _ -> 450L }, PICKUP to { _ -> 0L }, ) // closed set: one when, checked by the compiler fun priceCents(p: Parcel): Long = when (p.method) { BIKE -> bike(p) VAN -> 450 PICKUP -> 0 } A map of strategies suits an open set: methods read from settings, plug-ins, rules a customer can switch on. A switch or when with no default suits a closed set you own, like the DeliveryMethod enum. You see the difference on the day the town's first delivery drone arrives, and someone adds DRONE to the enum. The switch stops compiling, right where the rule is missing. javac says "the switch expression does not cover all possible input values", and kotlinc says "'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'DRONE' branch or an 'else' branch." The map compiles, ships, and fails on the first drone parcel: a NullPointerException in Java, because Map.get returned null, and NoSuchElementException: Key DRONE is missing in the map. from Kotlin's getValue. The Try it shows all four messages. If you do choose a map for a closed set, add a check at startup that every constant has an entry. The failure then moves from the first drone parcel to the moment the program starts. For a closed set you own, let the compiler check every case. Use a map when the set is open. Neither shape needs a class per delivery method: the lambdas are the strategies. A strategy swaps a whole decision. Sometimes the routine is what stays fixed, and one step inside it changes. Add a way to deliver and see who notices Run RouterDemo in either language: the map and the switch agree on all three ways to deliver. Add DRONE to the Way enum. Predict which part fails, and when, then run. Add the missing branch, case DRONE -> 990; in Java or Way.DRONE -> 990 in Kotlin. Predict, then run again. Remove DRONE when you're done. RouterDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l07; import java.util.EnumMap; import java.util.Map; /** The same delivery prices as a map of strategies and as a switch. Add a way to deliver and watch which one tells you. */ public class RouterDemo { enum Way { BIKE, VAN, PICKUP } record Job(Way way, int grams) {} interface PriceStrategy { long priceCents(Job j); } // open set: one lambda per way, in a map that settings or plug-ins could fill static final Map<Way, PriceStrategy> STRATEGIES = new EnumMap<>(Map.of( Way.BIKE, j -> 200 + j.grams() * 30 / 1_000, Way.VAN, j -> 450, Way.PICKUP, j -> 0)); // closed set: one switch, checked by the compiler static long priceSwitch(Job j) { return switch (j.way()) { case BIKE -> 200 + j.grams() * 30 / 1_000; case VAN -> 450; case PICKUP -> 0; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { for (Way w : Way.values()) { Job j = new Job(w, 2_500); System.out.printf("%-7s switch=%d", w, priceSwitch(j)); System.out.printf(" map=%d%n", STRATEGIES.get(w).priceCents(j)); } } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l07.RouterDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l07/RouterDemo.java RouterDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l07 // The same delivery prices as a map of strategies and as a when. Add a way to deliver and watch which one tells you. enum class Way { BIKE, VAN, PICKUP } data class Job(val way: Way, val grams: Int) // open set: one function per way, in a map that settings or plug-ins could fill private val strategies: Map<Way, (Job) -> Long> = mapOf( Way.BIKE to { j -> 200L + j.grams * 30 / 1_000 }, Way.VAN to { _ -> 450L }, Way.PICKUP to { _ -> 0L }, ) // closed set: one when, checked by the compiler private fun priceWhen(j: Job): Long = when (j.way) { Way.BIKE -> 200L + j.grams * 30 / 1_000 Way.VAN -> 450 Way.PICKUP -> 0 } fun main() { for (w in Way.entries) { val j = Job(w, 2_500) print("%-7s when=%d".format(w, priceWhen(j))) println(" map=%d".format(strategies.getValue(w)(j))) } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l07.RouterDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l07/RouterDemo.kt With DRONE added, the build fails: javac says the switch expression does not cover all possible input values, and kotlinc says 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'DRONE' branch or an 'else' branch. After you add the branch, the three lines print, and then the drone line fails: Java throws NullPointerException because Map.get returned null, and Kotlin throws NoSuchElementException: Key DRONE is missing in the map. The compiler found one gap; only a crash found the other. Conditions and loops: when (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Strategy and Template Method · Template Method: a recipe with a blank for subclasses
x: Back to the bakery's recipe card: mix, knead, shape, bake, cool. Only the shaping changes from loaf to loaf, and the card leaves a blank for it. Nobody rewrites the card for a new loaf. They fill in the blank. Every call the shop's program makes to a courier company needs the same steps around it: start a timer, make the call, write down how long it took. Template Method puts those steps in a base class as one final method, which subclasses can't override, called the template, and leaves blanks called hooks for subclasses to fill. The base class is abstract, which means it has methods left for its subclasses to write: Java abstract class OutboundCall<T> { public final T execute() { // the recipe: subclasses can't change it long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return doCall(); // hook 1: the step that changes } finally { timings.record(name(), System.nanoTime() - start); } } protected abstract String name(); // hook 2 protected abstract T doCall(); } final class BookingCall extends OutboundCall<String> { protected String name() { return "courier.book"; } protected String doCall() { return courier.book(address, grams); } } Kotlin abstract class OutboundCall<T> { fun execute(): T { // final by default in Kotlin: subclasses can't change it val start = System.nanoTime() try { return doCall() // hook 1: the step that changes } finally { timings.record(name(), System.nanoTime() - start) } } protected abstract fun name(): String // hook 2 protected abstract fun doCall(): T } class BookingCall(private val address: String, private val grams: Int) : OutboundCall<String>() { override fun name() = "courier.book" override fun doCall() = courier.book(address, grams) } The base class owns the order of the steps, and because execute is final, no subclass can skip the timer. The JDK uses this shape too. To build a read-only list, you extend AbstractList and write only get and size; the rest of List is a recipe built on those two hooks. Inheritance is the cost. A subclass depends on every detail of its parent, and a parent that changes when it calls its hooks can break subclasses it has never seen. That is the fragile base class problem. The sharpest edge is a base-class constructor that calls a hook. Java and Kotlin run the base constructor first, and a subclass assigns its own fields only after that returns. So the hook runs on a half-built object. TemplateHookDemo, in the Try it, builds a log label in the base constructor by calling name(), and BookingCall builds its name from its courier field: start outbound booking via null The courier field hadn't been assigned yet, so the label names a courier nobody in town has heard of: null. In Java, a field that hasn't been assigned reads as null. In Kotlin, the same code reads null from private val courier: String, a property the type system promises is never null, and kotlinc compiles it without a warning. JDK 25 gives Java one way out. With flexible constructor bodies (JEP 513), a constructor may assign its own fields before it calls super(), so this.courier = courier; super(); makes the label read booking via Pedal Post. The labs compile for Java 21, where javac answers "flexible constructors is not supported in -source 21", and Kotlin has no such option. That's where the recipe picture breaks. A baker can't be asked for the shape before anyone has said which loaf it is. A base-class constructor can ask, and it gets back whatever an empty field holds. Never call an overridable method from a constructor. Compute such values when they're first needed, or pass them up to the base constructor as arguments. Template Method gives the recipe to a base class and the blank to a subclass. What if we could fill the blank without writing a subclass at all? Watch a hook run too early Read TemplateHookDemo.java (or .kt). The base constructor builds label by calling name(). Predict the label the template version prints. Run it with the command below and compare the two versions. Fix the template without changing BookingCall: delete the label field and build the label inside execute() instead. Run again. TemplateHookDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l07; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** Template Method's sharpest edge, and the execute-around function that avoids it. */ public class TemplateHookDemo { // classic Template Method: a final skeleton with hooks for subclasses abstract static class OutboundCall { private final String label; OutboundCall() { label = "outbound " + name(); // calls a hook before the subclass has set its fields } final String execute() { // the skeleton System.out.println(" start " + label); try { return doCall(); } finally { System.out.println(" end " + label); } } abstract String name(); // hook abstract String doCall(); // hook } static final class BookingCall extends OutboundCall { private final String courier; BookingCall(String courier) { this.courier = courier; } // runs AFTER OutboundCall() has called name() String name() { return "booking via " + courier; } String doCall() { return "PP-1250"; } } // execute around: the same skeleton as a function; the varying step is a parameter static <T> T outbound(String name, Supplier<T> body) { System.out.println(" start " + name); try { return body.get(); } finally { System.out.println(" end " + name); } } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("template: " + new BookingCall("Pedal Post").execute()); System.out.println("function: " + outbound("outbound booking via Pedal Post", () -> "PP-1250")); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l07.TemplateHookDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l07/TemplateHookDemo.java TemplateHookDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l07 // Template Method's sharpest edge, and the execute-around function that avoids it. // classic Template Method: a skeleton with hooks for subclasses (Kotlin members are final unless open) abstract class OutboundCall { private val label = "outbound " + name() // calls a hook before the subclass has set its fields fun execute(): String { // the skeleton println(" start $label") try { return doCall() } finally { println(" end $label") } } abstract fun name(): String // hook abstract fun doCall(): String // hook } class BookingCall(private val courier: String) : OutboundCall() { // courier is a non-null String... override fun name() = "booking via $courier" // ...and still reads as null here override fun doCall() = "PP-1250" } // execute around: the same skeleton as an inline function; the varying step is a lambda inline fun <T> outbound(name: String, body: () -> T): T { println(" start $name") try { return body() } finally { println(" end $name") } } fun main() { println("template: ${BookingCall("Pedal Post").execute()}") println("function: ${outbound("outbound booking via Pedal Post") { "PP-1250" }}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l07.TemplateHookDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l07/TemplateHookDemo.kt The template prints start outbound booking via null: name() ran inside the base constructor, before BookingCall had assigned courier. Kotlin prints the same null from a property declared as a non-null String, with no compiler warning. The function version prints start outbound booking via Pedal Post. After the fix, the template prints that too, because name() now runs only when the object is complete. AbstractList (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Strategy and Template Method · Execute around: pass the blank in as a function
x: The modern answer keeps the recipe and drops the subclass. Write the recipe as a function, and take the step that changes as a lambda. The blank on the card becomes a parameter: you hand over the shaping together with the card. Java static <T> T timed(String name, Timings timings, Supplier<T> body) { long start = System.nanoTime(); // before try { return body.get(); // the caller's step } finally { timings.record(name, System.nanoTime() - start); // after, always } } String ref = timed("courier.book", timings, () -> courier.book(address, grams)); Kotlin inline fun <T> timed(name: String, timings: Timings, body: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() // before try { return body() // the caller's step, inlined: no lambda object } finally { timings.record(name, System.nanoTime() - start) // after, always } } val ref = timed("courier.book", timings) { courier.book(address, grams) } This shape is called execute around: a function runs the steps before and after, and calls your code in the middle. You already use it every day. try-with-resources is execute around built into Java: the language opens the resource, runs your block, and closes the resource whatever happens. Kotlin's standard library is full of it. use {} closes a resource, synchronized(lock) {} takes and releases a lock, and measureTimeMillis {} times a block. Kotlin makes the function version cheaper than Java's. The compiler copies the body of an inline function, lambda included, into each place that calls it. So no lambda object is created, and a return inside the block returns from the function that called timed. Java's Supplier has a different limit: its get method can't throw checked exceptions, the ones the Java compiler makes you catch or declare, so wrapping a courier library that throws IOException needs your own functional interface with a throws clause. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so timed("courier.book", timings) { client.book(address) } just works. The compare block below shows both. Prefer the function. It composes: timed("courier.book", timings) { retrying(3) { courier.book(address, grams) } } times the whole booking, retries included. It needs no class per call site. And it can't hit the constructor trap, because there is no constructor. Keep Template Method for recipes with many hooks, such as AbstractList, and make the template method final. When only one step changes, pass that step in as a function. The figure puts the two shapes side by side. They run the same steps in the same order; only the way the blank gets filled is different. Check yourself. courier.book(address, grams) throws inside timed. Does the call still show up in the timings, and does the caller see the exception? (Yes to both. The finally block records the time, and then the exception carries on to the caller as if timed weren't there.) The same recipe both ways. Template Method fills the blank with a subclass; execute around takes it as a lambda from the call site. Inline functions (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Strategy and Template Method · Java and Kotlin
x: An execute-around timer for a courier library Couriers.java // Supplier can't throw checked exceptions, so a wrapper for library calls needs its own interface @FunctionalInterface interface IoCall<T> { T call() throws IOException; } final class Couriers { static <T> T timed(String name, Map<String, Long> timings, IoCall<T> body) throws IOException { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return body.call(); } finally { timings.merge(name, System.nanoTime() - start, Long::sum); } } static String bookOrNull(Map<String, Long> timings, CourierLibrary lib, String address) throws IOException { String ref = timed("courier.book", timings, () -> lib.book(address)); return ref.isEmpty() ? null : ref; // a lambda can't return from bookOrNull itself } } Couriers.kt // inline: the block is pasted into the caller, so no lambda object and no checked-exception plumbing inline fun <T> timed(name: String, timings: MutableMap<String, Long>, body: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return body() } finally { timings.merge(name, System.nanoTime() - start) { a, b -> a + b } } } fun bookOrNull(timings: MutableMap<String, Long>, lib: CourierLibrary, address: String): String? { val ref = timed("courier.book", timings) { lib.book(address).ifEmpty { return null } // non-local return: leaves bookOrNull, the finally still records } return ref } The recipe is identical: read the clock, run the caller's block, record in finally. Three things differ. Java's standard functional interfaces can't throw checked exceptions, so a library that throws IOException forces you to declare IoCall with a throws clause; Kotlin has no checked exceptions. Kotlin's inline copies timed and the block into each call site, so there is no lambda object, and return null inside the block returns from bookOrNull itself while the finally still runs. And an inline block may call suspend functions when the caller is a suspend function, which a Java lambda can't do. Neither language needs Template Method for this; the function is the whole pattern.

h: Strategy and Template Method · Worked example
x: Turn a back-off if/else into strategies, without changing behavior When a courier's line is busy, the shop's retry helper waits a little before trying again; that wait is called the back-off. The helper reads the back-off rule's name from the settings file and decides the wait on every attempt. Spot two problems before reading on. // settings: courier.backoff=doubling (or "fixed", "none") Duration waitBeforeRetry(String policy, int attempt) { if (policy.equals("fixed")) { return Duration.ofMillis(200); } else if (policy.equals("doubling")) { long ms = 100L << (attempt - 1); // 100, 200, 400, ... return Duration.ofMillis(Math.min(ms, 5_000)); } else if (policy.equals("none")) { return Duration.ZERO; } return Duration.ofMillis(200); // a typo in the settings silently means "fixed" } // settings: courier.backoff=doubling (or "fixed", "none") fun waitBeforeRetry(policy: String, attempt: Int): Duration = if (policy == "fixed") { Duration.ofMillis(200) } else if (policy == "doubling") { val ms = 100L shl (attempt - 1) // 100, 200, 400, ... Duration.ofMillis(minOf(ms, 5_000)) } else if (policy == "none") { Duration.ZERO } else { Duration.ofMillis(200) // a typo in the settings silently means "fixed" } The rule is chosen again on every attempt, and a typo like doubeling quietly becomes "fixed". Fix neither yet. First pin today's behavior with a characterization test, so the refactor can't change a wait by accident. @ParameterizedTest @CsvSource({"fixed,1,200", "fixed,4,200", "doubling,1,100", "doubling,3,400", "doubling,9,5000", "none,2,0"}) void pinned(String policy, int attempt, long expectedMs) { assertThat(waitBeforeRetry(policy, attempt)).isEqualTo(Duration.ofMillis(expectedMs)); } @ParameterizedTest @CsvSource("fixed,1,200", "fixed,4,200", "doubling,1,100", "doubling,3,400", "doubling,9,5000", "none,2,0") fun pinned(policy: String, attempt: Int, expectedMs: Long) { assertThat(waitBeforeRetry(policy, attempt)).isEqualTo(Duration.ofMillis(expectedMs)) } Now give the decision a type with one method, and a factory for each rule. Each factory returns a lambda: a complete strategy. @FunctionalInterface interface Backoff { Duration delay(int attempt); // 1. one decision, one method static Backoff fixed(Duration d) { return attempt -> d; } static Backoff doubling(Duration base, Duration max) { return attempt -> { Duration d = base.multipliedBy(1L << (attempt - 1)); return d.compareTo(max) > 0 ? max : d; }; } Backoff NONE = attempt -> Duration.ZERO; } fun interface Backoff { fun delay(attempt: Int): Duration // 1. one decision, one method companion object { fun fixed(d: Duration) = Backoff { d } fun doubling(base: Duration, max: Duration) = Backoff { attempt -> minOf(base.multipliedBy(1L shl (attempt - 1)), max) } val NONE = Backoff { Duration.ZERO } } } Choose the strategy once, at startup. Here a default is right, because names in a settings file are an open set you don't control, and it throws, so a typo stops the program the moment it starts. Point the pinned test at fromSettings(policy).delay(attempt): it still passes. static Backoff fromSettings(String name) { // 2. choose once, at startup return switch (name) { case "fixed" -> Backoff.fixed(Duration.ofMillis(200)); case "doubling" -> Backoff.doubling(Duration.ofMillis(100), Duration.ofSeconds(5)); case "none" -> Backoff.NONE; default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown courier.backoff: " + name); // 3. a typo stops the start }; } Backoff backoff = fromSettings(settings.backoff()); // 4. the retry loop calls backoff.delay(n) fun fromSettings(name: String): Backoff = when (name) { // 2. choose once, at startup "fixed" -> Backoff.fixed(Duration.ofMillis(200)) "doubling" -> Backoff.doubling(Duration.ofMillis(100), Duration.ofSeconds(5)) "none" -> Backoff.NONE else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown courier.backoff: $name") // 3. a typo stops the start } val backoff = fromSettings(settings.backoff) // 4. the retry loop calls backoff.delay(n)

h: Strategy and Template Method · Quiz
x: A team prices with Map<DeliveryMethod, PriceStrategy> built from settings, and also has a switch over DeliveryMethod with no default in the receipt code. Someone adds DRONE to DeliveryMethod. Which statement is true? The map fails to compile; the switch throws at runtime The switch fails to compile; the map compiles and fails on the first drone parcel Both fail to compile Both compile, and drone parcels cost 0 Only the switch tells the compiler which constants must be handled, so only the switch breaks the build. The map has no idea DRONE should be a key, so get returns null when the program runs. With a map over a closed set, add a check at startup that every constant has an entry. Quotes: Hilltop Couriers (price 300, 40 minutes), Gull Express (price 250, 75 minutes), Riverside Bikes (price 300, 25 minutes), in that order. In what order does Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::priceCents).thenComparingLong(Quote::minutes) sort them? Gull Express, Riverside Bikes, Hilltop Couriers Gull Express, Hilltop Couriers, Riverside Bikes Riverside Bikes, Hilltop Couriers, Gull Express Hilltop Couriers, Riverside Bikes, Gull Express The first comparator puts the 250 price first: Gull Express. Hilltop and Riverside tie on price, so the second comparator breaks the tie by time: Riverside's 25 minutes before Hilltop's 40. The tempting "Gull Express, Hilltop Couriers, Riverside Bikes" ignores the tie-breaker and keeps the original order. A base class sets label = "outbound " + name(); in its constructor. The subclass BookingCall(String courier) assigns this.courier = courier and implements name() as "booking via " + courier. What is the label of new BookingCall("Pedal Post")? It throws NullPointerException outbound booking via Pedal Post outbound booking via null It doesn't compile The base constructor runs first and calls the overridden name() before BookingCall has assigned courier, so courier is still null, and string concatenation turns null into "null". Nothing throws, which makes the bug easy to miss. Kotlin behaves the same even for a non-null val courier: String. At 30 places, the shop's code calls different courier services, and every call must be timed and logged in the same way. Which shape fits best? An abstract base class with a final execute() and one subclass per call site A Map<String, Runnable> holding all 30 calls A singleton that every call registers with A higher-order function, timed("courier.book") { ... }, inline in Kotlin, wrapped around each call The steps around the call are fixed and the middle changes per call site, which is execute around: one function, and each call site passes its own block. Thirty subclasses is Template Method's ceremony with its inheritance problems, and a map or a singleton doesn't wrap anything. From Decorator and Proxy: each delivery method's base rule is a DeliveryFee stored in a Map<DeliveryMethod, DeliveryFee>. The shop now wants every delivery capped at 8.00. Where does the cap go with the least code? Edit every lambda in the map to call Math.min(..., 800) Decorate each fee once when you build the map: fees.replaceAll((m, f) -> f.cappedAt(800)) Add a default -> 800 branch to the switch Make each strategy extend a CappedFee base class Strategies and decorators combine: the map picks the rule, and wrapping each rule in cappedAt(800) adds the cap once, in one place. Editing every lambda copies the rule into each strategy, a default branch changes nothing for known methods, and a base class brings back the inheritance this lesson moves away from.
