h: Strategy and Template Method · Key terms
x: Strategy One interchangeable algorithm, passed in by the caller and used by the code that needs a decision. Characterization test A test that pins down what old code does now, so a refactor can't change it unnoticed. Template Method A base-class method that fixes the steps and lets subclasses fill in some of them. Hook An overridable method a template calls at a fixed point in its recipe. Fragile base class When a change inside a parent class breaks subclasses that relied on how it worked. Execute around A function that wraps the caller's code with steps before and after, taking that code as a lambda. Inline function A Kotlin function whose body, with its lambda arguments, is copied into each place that calls it. In modern Java or Kotlin, what is a strategy usually written as? A lambda or method reference for a functional interface (Comparator, PriceStrategy), or a Kotlin function type such as (Parcel) -> Long. You add a constant to an enum. What happens to a switch over it with no default, and to an EnumMap of strategies? The switch fails to compile. The map compiles, and get returns null for the new key when the program runs. Map of strategies or exhaustive switch: which for a closed set you own? The switch (or when) with no default, so a new case is a compile error. Use the map for open sets: settings, plug-ins. What is a characterization test? A test that records what existing code does today, bugs included, so a refactor can prove it changed nothing. What is Template Method? A final recipe method in a base class that calls hook methods subclasses override. A base-class constructor calls an overridden method that reads a subclass field. What does it see? The field's default: null or 0, because the subclass constructor hasn't run yet. In Kotlin even a non-null val reads as null. What is execute around? A function that runs the steps before and after, and takes the changing step as a lambda: try-with-resources, use {}, synchronized(lock) {}.

h: Strategy and Template Method · Go deeper
x: Strategy and State have the same structure: an object holds an interface and hands the decision to it. The difference is who chooses. The caller picks a strategy, and it stays put. A state object picks the next state itself as things happen to it. Lesson 9 of this track, State and Chain of Responsibility, builds that kind of object. Java can do execute around without lambdas. Make the step before a constructor and the step after close(), and try-with-resources does the rest: try (var t = timings.start("courier.book")) { return courier.book(address, grams); }. This form lets checked exceptions pass through untouched and needs no functional interface, which is why many timing and logging libraries offer a closeable timer. The cost is that the caller must remember the try. Kotlin's inline has limits worth knowing. An inlined lambda can't be stored or passed to a function that isn't inline, because it doesn't exist as an object; mark such a parameter noinline. If the lambda runs somewhere else, such as on another thread or in a callback, mark it crossinline, which forbids a return from the outer function inside it. And large inline functions grow every place that calls them, so keep them small: the recipe inline, the heavy lifting in a normal function it calls. Strategies hide in Kotlin's collection functions too. sortedWith, maxByOrNull { it.priceCents }, groupBy { it.method } and partition { it.grams > 5_000 } each own the loop and take one decision from you as a lambda.

h: Observer and Command · Observer: tell everyone who signed up, then stay out of the way
x: The ledger tells a list of listeners, each in its own try; a command is an object on an undo stack, pushed only after it worked An order arrives at the corner shop, and several parts of the program care. The stock view shows what's left on the shelves, the confirmation email tells the customer, and the sales chart in the back office counts the day's orders. If place calls all three directly, the order code depends on every one of them. A broken chart then makes orders fail, and adding a fourth part means editing place again. Observer turns that around. The object that knows what happened, called the subject, keeps a list of listeners and tells each one, without knowing who they are. It's the sign-up sheet by the shop door: when the bread arrives, the shopkeeper rings every name on it. Anyone can add a name, and anyone can cross theirs off. Here is a small subject that any part of the program can use. It's called an event bus, because it carries events, values that say what happened, to everyone who subscribed: Java final class EventBus<E> { private final List<Consumer<? super E>> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); AutoCloseable subscribe(Consumer<? super E> listener) { listeners.add(listener); return () -> listeners.remove(listener); // the handle: a way to leave } void publish(E event) { for (Consumer<? super E> l : listeners) { try { l.accept(event); } catch (RuntimeException e) { log.warn("listener failed", e); // one bad listener must not starve the rest } } } } Kotlin class EventBus<E> { private val listeners = CopyOnWriteArrayList<(E) -> Unit>() fun subscribe(listener: (E) -> Unit): AutoCloseable { listeners += listener return AutoCloseable { listeners -= listener } // the handle: a way to leave } fun publish(event: E) { for (l in listeners) { try { l(event) } catch (e: RuntimeException) { log.warn("listener failed", e) // one bad listener must not starve the rest } } } } There is no OrderListener interface. Consumer<E> in Java and (E) -> Unit in Kotlin already say "something that takes an event". Each line prevents a real bug. subscribe returns a handle, because a listener nobody removes is a lapsed listener. The bus holds a reference to it forever, so the garbage collector, the part of the JVM that frees objects nobody uses, can't free it. It keeps reacting long after its owner is gone. The try/catch stops one failing listener from cancelling delivery to the ones after it. EventBusDemo, in the Try it, subscribes three listeners, and the second one always throws: stock view got Ordered[customer=Ana, item=rye bread] (a listener failed: the sales chart is down) email sender got Ordered[customer=Ana, item=rye bread] Delete the try/catch and the program stops after the first line, with IllegalStateException: the sales chart is down. The email sender never hears a thing, and in the real shop the order itself would fail. CopyOnWriteArrayList loops over a snapshot, a copy of the list taken when the loop starts, so a listener may unsubscribe while it's being called. With an ArrayList, that throws ConcurrentModificationException. Copy-on-write makes every subscribe expensive and every publish cheap, which suits listener lists: people sign up rarely, and the bell rings all day. The sign-up sheet picture breaks in two places. The shopkeeper rings one number at a time and waits on each call, and so does publish: every listener runs on the publishing thread, inside place. A 300 ms email makes every order 300 ms slower. And a customer who moved away stops answering, but a listener nobody removed answers forever. Give every listener a way out, and never let one listener break the others. Keeping that list safe took care. Kotlin's coroutine library ships subjects that do the bookkeeping for us. Break a listener, then remove the safety net Read EventBusDemo.java (or EventBusDemo.kt). Three listeners subscribe; the second always throws. Predict the five lines it prints. Run it with the command below. Delete the try/catch in publish, keeping the l.accept(event) (l(event) in Kotlin) line. Predict, then run. Put it back. EventBusDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l08; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** A hand-rolled Observer: subscribe returns a handle, and one bad listener can't starve the rest. */ public class EventBusDemo { static final class EventBus<E> { private final List<Consumer<? super E>> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); AutoCloseable subscribe(Consumer<? super E> listener) { listeners.add(listener); return () -> listeners.remove(listener); // the handle that prevents leaks } void publish(E event) { for (Consumer<? super E> l : listeners) { try { l.accept(event); } catch (RuntimeException e) { // isolate each listener System.out.println(" (a listener failed: " + e.getMessage() + ")"); } } } } record Ordered(String customer, String item) {} public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { EventBus<Ordered> bus = new EventBus<>(); bus.subscribe(e -> System.out.println("stock view got " + e)); bus.subscribe(e -> { throw new IllegalStateException("the sales chart is down"); }); AutoCloseable email = bus.subscribe(e -> System.out.println("email sender got " + e)); bus.publish(new Ordered("Ana", "rye bread")); email.close(); // unsubscribe bus.publish(new Ordered("Ben", "jam")); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l08.EventBusDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l08/EventBusDemo.java EventBusDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l08 import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList // A hand-rolled Observer: subscribe returns a handle, and one bad listener can't starve the rest. class EventBus<E> { private val listeners = CopyOnWriteArrayList<(E) -> Unit>() fun subscribe(listener: (E) -> Unit): AutoCloseable { listeners += listener return AutoCloseable { listeners -= listener } // the handle that prevents leaks } fun publish(event: E) { for (l in listeners) { try { l(event) } catch (e: RuntimeException) { // isolate each listener println(" (a listener failed: ${e.message})") } } } } data class OrderedEvent(val customer: String, val item: String) fun main() { val bus = EventBus<OrderedEvent>() bus.subscribe { println("stock view got $it") } bus.subscribe { throw IllegalStateException("the sales chart is down") } val email = bus.subscribe { println("email sender got $it") } bus.publish(OrderedEvent("Ana", "rye bread")) email.close() // unsubscribe bus.publish(OrderedEvent("Ben", "jam")) } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l08.EventBusDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l08/EventBusDemo.kt The stock view and the email sender both get Ana's order, with (a listener failed: the sales chart is down) between them. After email.close(), only the stock view gets Ben's order, followed by the chart's failure again. Without the try/catch, the program prints the first stock line and stops with IllegalStateException: the sales chart is down: the email sender never hears anything, and in the real shop the order itself would fail. CopyOnWriteArrayList (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Observer and Command · Flows are observers with the bookkeeping done
x: A coroutine is a Kotlin task that can pause while it waits without holding on to a thread, and a flow is a stream of values that a coroutine collects one by one. The coroutine library ships two ready-made subjects, and both are hot: they emit whether or not anyone is collecting. A SharedFlow hands every emitted value to every active collector. A StateFlow holds one current value. Its docs call it "a hot flow" that "never completes", and each new collector gets the current value first, then every change. Both are thread-safe, and both do the last section's bookkeeping for you. There is no list to guard. Cancelling the collecting coroutine unsubscribes it, and each collector runs in its own coroutine, so one that fails doesn't stop the others: Java // Closest Java equivalent: the JDK's java.util.concurrent.Flow, with SubmissionPublisher as a hot publisher SubmissionPublisher<String> sales = new SubmissionPublisher<>(); CompletableFuture<Void> done = sales.consume(item -> System.out.println("sold " + item)); // one subscriber sales.submit("rye bread"); sales.submit("rye bread"); // delivered again: a publisher has no idea of "same as last time" sales.close(); // ends the stream; done completes after the last item Kotlin class Counter { private val _lastSold = MutableStateFlow("nothing yet") val lastSold: StateFlow<String> = _lastSold.asStateFlow() // state: the latest value private val _sales = MutableSharedFlow<String>() val sales: SharedFlow<String> = _sales.asSharedFlow() // events: every one, to every collector suspend fun sell(item: String) { _sales.emit(item) // with no buffer, waits until every current collector has taken it _lastSold.value = item } } Keep the mutable flow private and expose the read-only type, as above. When the new value depends on the old one, use update, as in _itemsToday.update { it + quantity } in the lab, because it reads and writes in one atomic step. The rule that matters most is in the StateFlow docs: values "are conflated using Any.equals comparison in a similar way to distinctUntilChanged", and "a slow collector skips fast updates". Conflation means keeping only the latest value. A StateFlow is the chalkboard by the counter that shows the last thing sold. Whoever glances at it sees the latest, and writing "rye bread" over "rye bread" changes nothing. StateVsShared, in the Try it, sells two loaves and a jar of jam: StateFlow collector saw: [nothing yet, rye bread, jam] SharedFlow collector saw: [rye bread, rye bread, jam] That's right for state. A screen showing the last sale needs only the latest one. It's wrong for events. Ana orders a rye loaf, and ten minutes later she orders another, so Ordered("Ana", "rye bread", 1) arrives twice. A StateFlow passes on one of them, and the bakery bakes one loaf. A slow collector also misses the values in between. State goes in a StateFlow. Events, where each one counts, go in a SharedFlow. Use a Channel instead when each item must go to exactly one consumer, like a queue of jobs. Java has the interfaces but few implementations. java.util.concurrent.Flow holds the Reactive Streams interfaces, a shared standard for streams of events (Publisher, Subscriber, Subscription), and SubmissionPublisher is the one hot publisher in the JDK. Reactor, a library for streams of events, has the same idea in its Flux, and Sinks.many().multicast() plays the role of a MutableSharedFlow. None of them drops equal values unless you ask with distinctUntilChanged(). An event says what happened. The next pattern turns what we want to happen into a value. Watch StateFlow drop a sale Read StateVsShared.kt (or the Java twin, StateVsSharedJava.java). The same three sales go to a state holder and an event stream. Predict both lines. Run it with the command below. Kotlin: change val events = MutableSharedFlow<String>() to val events = MutableStateFlow("nothing yet") and run. Java: delete the if (Objects.equals(value, next)) return; line and run. Predict each first. StateVsShared.kt package workbench.patterns.l08 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineStart import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableSharedFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.yield // The same three sales at the counter, observed through a StateFlow and through a SharedFlow. fun main() = runBlocking { val state = MutableStateFlow("nothing yet") // state: the latest value; equal values are dropped val events = MutableSharedFlow<String>() // events: every value, to every collector val fromState = mutableListOf<String>() val fromEvents = mutableListOf<String>() val collectors = listOf( launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) { state.collect { fromState += it } }, launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) { events.collect { fromEvents += it } }, ) for (update in listOf("rye bread", "rye bread", "jam")) { // two loaves sold, then a jar of jam state.value = update events.emit(update) // suspends until every collector has taken it yield() } collectors.forEach { it.cancel() } println("StateFlow collector saw: $fromState") println("SharedFlow collector saw: $fromEvents") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l08.StateVsSharedKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l08/StateVsShared.kt StateVsSharedJava.java // Closest Java equivalent: the JDK's Flow API, where SubmissionPublisher delivers every event, plus a tiny // "latest value" holder that drops equal values the way Kotlin's StateFlow does. The JDK has no StateFlow. package workbench.patterns.l08; import java.util.List; import java.util.Objects; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.function.Consumer; public class StateVsSharedJava { /** Holds one current value and tells observers about changes; equal values are dropped. */ static final class LatestValue<T> { private final List<Consumer<T>> observers = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); private T value; LatestValue(T initial) { value = initial; } synchronized void set(T next) { if (Objects.equals(value, next)) return; // StateFlow-style conflation by equals() value = next; observers.forEach(o -> o.accept(next)); } synchronized void observe(Consumer<T> o) { observers.add(o); o.accept(value); // new observers get the current value first } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { LatestValue<String> state = new LatestValue<>("nothing yet"); List<String> fromState = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); state.observe(fromState::add); List<String> fromEvents = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); CompletableFuture<Void> done; try (SubmissionPublisher<String> events = new SubmissionPublisher<>()) { done = events.consume(fromEvents::add); // a subscriber that gets every item for (String update : List.of("rye bread", "rye bread", "jam")) { // two loaves sold, then a jar of jam state.set(update); events.submit(update); } } // close() completes the stream done.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.println("state holder saw: " + fromState); System.out.println("event publisher saw: " + fromEvents); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l08.StateVsSharedJava labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l08/StateVsSharedJava.java The state side prints [nothing yet, rye bread, jam]: the starting value, then only real changes. The event side prints [rye bread, rye bread, jam]: every sale. With a StateFlow for events, the Kotlin event line becomes [nothing yet, rye bread, jam], so the second loaf is gone and a sale of "nothing yet" appeared. Without the equality check, the Java state holder prints [nothing yet, rye bread, rye bread, jam]: that one check is the whole difference. StateFlow (kotlinx.coroutines API) docs SubmissionPublisher (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Observer and Command · Command: a request on a slip you can keep, undo and replay
x: Back behind the counter, the spike holds order slips. Each slip says what to do and with what: "restock rye bread, 12 loaves". A slip can wait on the spike, be done now, be crossed out, or be copied and done again. Command turns a request into that kind of slip: an object that holds what to do and with which arguments, a value you can keep. Once a request is a value, you can queue it, log it, retry it and undo it. For a shelf in the shop, a sealed interface of records is the natural shape: Java sealed interface Command permits Restock, Sell { void apply(Shelf s); void undo(Shelf s); } record Restock(int units) implements Command { public void apply(Shelf s) { s.units += units; } public void undo(Shelf s) { s.units -= units; } } record Sell(int units) implements Command { public void apply(Shelf s) { if (s.units < units) throw new IllegalStateException("not enough on the shelf"); s.units -= units; } public void undo(Shelf s) { s.units += units; } } final class CommandLog { private final Deque<Command> history = new ArrayDeque<>(); void run(Command c, Shelf s) { c.apply(s); history.push(c); } // record only after success void undoLast(Shelf s) { Command c = history.poll(); if (c != null) c.undo(s); } } Kotlin sealed interface Command { fun apply(s: Shelf) fun undo(s: Shelf) } data class Restock(val units: Int) : Command { override fun apply(s: Shelf) { s.units += units } override fun undo(s: Shelf) { s.units -= units } } data class Sell(val units: Int) : Command { override fun apply(s: Shelf) { check(s.units >= units) { "not enough on the shelf" } s.units -= units } override fun undo(s: Shelf) { s.units += units } } class CommandLog { private val history = ArrayDeque<Command>() fun run(c: Command, s: Shelf) { c.apply(s); history.addFirst(c) } // record only after success fun undoLast(s: Shelf) { history.removeFirstOrNull()?.undo(s) } } Two details carry the pattern. First, run records the command only after apply succeeds. UndoDemo, in the Try it, restocks 12 loaves, sells 5, and then tries to sell 40: rejected: not enough on the shelf units 7, history [Sell[units=5], Restock[units=12]] after one undo: units 12, history [Restock[units=12]] Swap the two calls in run, so the command is recorded before it's applied, and the rejected sale of 40 sits on top of the history. The next undo puts back 40 loaves that never left, and the shelf shows 47. The baker will want to know where they came from. Second, the commands are data. Sell[units=5] prints well, compares by value, and can be written to a file or a table and read back later. The slip picture holds up well, and it breaks where the paper ends. Crossing out a slip is easy. Crossing out a sale is only safe while everything stays inside the program; the next section shows why. Record a command for undo only after it has succeeded. When a command needs no undo and no data, the class disappears. Runnable, Callable and () -> Unit are commands, and executor.submit(() -> printLabel(orderNo)) hands one to an executor, the JDK's pool of worker threads, which works through its queue. Keep a named class when you need what a lambda can't give: equality, a readable log line, a way to store it, or a second method such as undo. Record the command too early Run UndoDemo in either language and read the three lines. In CommandLog.run, swap the two lines so the command is recorded before it is applied. Predict the history and the units after one undo, then run. Swap them back. UndoDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l08; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Deque; /** Commands as records, an undo log, and the one rule that keeps undo honest. */ public class UndoDemo { static final class Shelf { int units; } sealed interface Command permits Restock, Sell { void apply(Shelf s); void undo(Shelf s); } record Restock(int units) implements Command { public void apply(Shelf s) { s.units += units; } public void undo(Shelf s) { s.units -= units; } } record Sell(int units) implements Command { public void apply(Shelf s) { if (s.units < units) throw new IllegalStateException("not enough on the shelf"); s.units -= units; } public void undo(Shelf s) { s.units += units; } } static final class CommandLog { final Deque<Command> history = new ArrayDeque<>(); void run(Command c, Shelf s) { c.apply(s); // 1. apply first history.push(c); // 2. record only after it worked } void undoLast(Shelf s) { Command c = history.poll(); if (c != null) c.undo(s); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Shelf rye = new Shelf(); CommandLog log = new CommandLog(); log.run(new Restock(12), rye); log.run(new Sell(5), rye); try { log.run(new Sell(40), rye); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("units " + rye.units + ", history " + log.history); log.undoLast(rye); System.out.println("after one undo: units " + rye.units + ", history " + log.history); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l08.UndoDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l08/UndoDemo.java UndoDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l08 // Commands as data classes, an undo log, and the one rule that keeps undo honest. class StockShelf { var units = 0 } sealed interface StockCommand { fun apply(s: StockShelf) fun undo(s: StockShelf) data class Restock(val units: Int) : StockCommand { override fun apply(s: StockShelf) { s.units += units } override fun undo(s: StockShelf) { s.units -= units } } data class Sell(val units: Int) : StockCommand { override fun apply(s: StockShelf) { check(s.units >= units) { "not enough on the shelf" } s.units -= units } override fun undo(s: StockShelf) { s.units += units } } } class CommandLog { val history = ArrayDeque<StockCommand>() fun run(c: StockCommand, s: StockShelf) { c.apply(s) // 1. apply first history.addFirst(c) // 2. record only after it worked } fun undoLast(s: StockShelf) { history.removeFirstOrNull()?.undo(s) } } fun main() { val rye = StockShelf() val log = CommandLog() log.run(StockCommand.Restock(12), rye) log.run(StockCommand.Sell(5), rye) try { log.run(StockCommand.Sell(40), rye) } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("rejected: ${e.message}") } println("units ${rye.units}, history ${log.history}") log.undoLast(rye) println("after one undo: units ${rye.units}, history ${log.history}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l08.UndoDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l08/UndoDemo.kt rejected: not enough on the shelf, then units 7 with a history of Sell 5 and Restock 12, then after one undo: units 12. With the lines swapped, the rejected Sell of 40 sits on top of the history, and the undo puts back 40 loaves that never left: after one undo: units 47.

h: Observer and Command · Commands that leave the program
x: Once a command is a record, it can leave the program: written to a file, saved as a row in a database table, or sent to another program that runs it later. Picture the shop's program saving the slip "tell the bakery: 2 rye loaves for order 7781" in the same database write that saves the order. A database transaction is a group of writes that are all saved or all thrown away, so either the order and the slip are both saved, or neither is. A separate job reads new slips and sends them on, and a crash between the two can't lose the bakery's slip. Stored slips bring two new rules. The first is about duplicates. A stored command is delivered at least once, never exactly once. The job might send the slip and crash before it marks the slip as sent; when it restarts, it sends it again. So every command that leaves the program must be safe to run twice. The bakery keeps the order numbers it has already baked for and skips a repeat, as the warehouse did with order numbers in Decorator and Proxy. The second rule is about undo. Inside the program, undo puts the old state back. Across programs, you can't put a delivered parcel back on the shelf by popping a stack. You send a new command, a collection slip, with its own record, its own courier and its own ways to fail. A new command that reverses an earlier one is called a compensation. When a later step of a long job fails, you run the compensations for the earlier steps, in reverse order. A command that leaves the program must be safe to run twice. Reverse it with a new command, never with undo. The figure shows the two paths: run now, with undo on a stack, or stored and run later, perhaps twice. Check yourself. The job sends "tell the bakery: 2 rye loaves for order 7781", then crashes before it marks the slip as sent. It restarts. How many loaves does the bakery bake if it bakes whatever each slip says, and what fixes it? (Four: the job sends the slip again, and the bakery bakes it twice. The bakery must remember which order numbers it has already baked for, and skip a repeat.) A command is data. Run now, it goes on an undo stack; stored, it goes to a file, a table or another program, and may run more than once.

h: Observer and Command · Java and Kotlin
x: A command queue worked through by one worker StockWorker.java sealed interface StockCommand permits Restock, Sell, Stop {} record Restock(String item, int units) implements StockCommand {} record Sell(String item, int units) implements StockCommand {} record Stop() implements StockCommand {} // a "poison pill": a Java queue can't be closed final class StockWorker implements Runnable { private final BlockingQueue<StockCommand> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1_000); // bounded: put waits when full private final Map<String, Integer> shelves = new HashMap<>(); // touched only by the thread running run() void submit(StockCommand c) throws InterruptedException { queue.put(c); } void stop() throws InterruptedException { queue.put(new Stop()); } @Override public void run() { try { while (true) { switch (queue.take()) { // commands are data: switch on them case Restock r -> shelves.merge(r.item(), r.units(), Integer::sum); case Sell s -> shelves.merge(s.item(), -s.units(), Integer::sum); case Stop s -> { return; } } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } // start it after construction, never from the constructor: // Thread.ofVirtual().start(worker); StockWorker.kt sealed interface StockCommand { data class Restock(val item: String, val units: Int) : StockCommand data class Sell(val item: String, val units: Int) : StockCommand } class StockWorker { private val queue = Channel<StockCommand>(capacity = 1_000) // bounded: send pauses when full private val shelves = mutableMapOf<String, Int>() // touched only by the coroutine in start() fun start(scope: CoroutineScope): Job = scope.launch { for (c in queue) { // ends after stop(), once the queue is empty when (c) { // commands are data: when on them is StockCommand.Restock -> shelves.merge(c.item, c.units) { a, b -> a + b } is StockCommand.Sell -> shelves.merge(c.item, -c.units) { a, b -> a + b } } } } suspend fun submit(c: StockCommand) = queue.send(c) fun stop() = queue.close() // a closed channel is the poison pill } The shape is the same: commands are sealed data, a bounded queue holds them, and one worker applies them in turn, so the shelves map needs no lock because only one thread or coroutine ever touches it. Two things differ. A Kotlin Channel can be closed, and for (c in queue) ends after the last queued command, so the Stop command that Java needs as a poison pill (a special item that tells the worker to finish) disappears. And send pauses the coroutine when the queue is full, where Java's put blocks a thread; with virtual threads that blocking is cheap too, so the real gain is the built-in close. Neither language needs a Command class hierarchy with an execute() method: a sealed type plus an exhaustive switch or when in the worker does that job.

h: Observer and Command · Worked example
x: Take the side effects out of the order desk's place method The order desk's place grew one call at a time. Before reading on, list what happens to an order when the sales chart is down. void place(Order o) { orderBook.write(o); stock.reserve(o.item(), o.quantity()); email.sendConfirmation(o); // a 300 ms call to the mail server salesChart.count(o); // throws when the chart is down bakery.bake(o.item(), o.quantity()); } fun place(o: Order) { orderBook.write(o) stock.reserve(o.item, o.quantity) email.sendConfirmation(o) // a 300 ms call to the mail server salesChart.count(o) // throws when the chart is down bakery.bake(o.item, o.quantity) } The order is already written down, but place throws, so the website tries again and may place it twice. The bakery is never told, and every order waits for the mail server. First split the work by what it is: writing the order and reserving the stock are the order itself; the rest are reactions to it. void place(Order o) { orderBook.write(o); // 1. the order itself stock.reserve(o.item(), o.quantity()); bus.publish(new Ordered(o.customer(), o.item(), o.quantity())); // 2. everything else is a reaction } fun place(o: Order) { orderBook.write(o) // 1. the order itself stock.reserve(o.item, o.quantity) bus.publish(Ordered(o.customer, o.item, o.quantity)) // 2. everything else is a reaction } Wire the reactions in one place, when the program starts. The bus keeps failures apart, so a broken chart costs one log line. Which of these listeners can we afford to lose if the program crashes right after the order is written? bus.subscribe(e -> stockView.refresh()); // 3. fast and losable: fine as listeners bus.subscribe(e -> salesChart.count(e)); // a missed order is a blip on a chart // the email and the bakery are NOT subscribed here: see the next step bus.subscribe { stockView.refresh() } // 3. fast and losable: fine as listeners bus.subscribe { salesChart.count(it) } // a missed order is a blip on a chart // the email and the bakery are NOT subscribed here: see the next step The bakery's slip and the confirmation email must survive a crash, so they become stored commands, saved in the same transaction as the order. A separate job sends them on, at least once, so the bakery and the mailer must each skip a slip they've already handled. void place(Order o) { db.inTransaction(() -> { // 4. all saved, or none orderBook.write(o); stock.reserve(o.item(), o.quantity()); slips.save(new Slip("bakery.bake", o.orderNo())); slips.save(new Slip("email.confirm", o.orderNo())); }); bus.publish(new Ordered(o.customer(), o.item(), o.quantity())); // 5. listeners: best effort only } fun place(o: Order) { db.inTransaction { // 4. all saved, or none orderBook.write(o) stock.reserve(o.item, o.quantity) slips.save(Slip("bakery.bake", o.orderNo)) slips.save(Slip("email.confirm", o.orderNo)) } bus.publish(Ordered(o.customer, o.item, o.quantity)) // 5. listeners: best effort only }

h: Observer and Command · Quiz
x: A Kotlin program publishes order events through a MutableStateFlow. The bakery needs every Ordered event to plan its baking. What will it miss? Nothing: StateFlow delivers every value An order equal to the previous one, and orders a slow collector didn't get to in time Only orders placed before it started collecting, like any hot flow Orders placed from another thread StateFlow conflates by equals, so an order equal to the current value is never delivered, and a collector that falls behind only sees the latest value. Missing orders from before you started collecting is true of a SharedFlow with no replay too, but it isn't what makes StateFlow wrong here. StateFlow is thread-safe, so threads don't matter. A CommandLog.run pushes the command onto the history first and then applies it. The shelf holds 7 loaves. Sell(40) fails with "not enough on the shelf". The shopkeeper presses undo once. How many loaves does the shelf show? 7 12 47 40 The failed sale was recorded before it threw, so it's on top of the history. Undoing it adds back 40 loaves that never left: 7 + 40 = 47. Recording only after apply succeeds keeps undo honest. Each visit to the shop's website creates a small object that subscribes a listener to the program's one shared EventBus in its constructor, and never closes the handle. What happens over a busy day? Memory grows, and every old visit's listener keeps reacting to every order Nothing: listeners are removed when the visit ends The bus throws once it has too many listeners The listeners stop receiving events after a garbage collection The shared bus's list holds a strong reference to each listener, and each listener's lambda captures its visit object, so none of them can be freed, and all of them keep running on every order. That is the lapsed-listener leak. Return a handle from subscribe and close it when the owner's life ends. The bakery must hear about every order, even if the program crashes a moment after the order is saved. Which design fits? A listener on the in-memory EventBus A StateFlow the bakery collects A MutableSharedFlow with replay = 1 A slip saved in the same database transaction as the order, which a separate job sends on Anything in memory dies with the program, so the bus and both flows lose orders made just before a crash. A slip saved in the order's transaction is saved with the order or not at all, and the job delivers it at least once, so the bakery must skip repeats. From StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams: a MutableSharedFlow<Ordered>() (no replay, no buffer) emits three orders, and only then does a new collector start. What does the new collector see? All three orders None of the three; only orders emitted after it starts Only the last order The first order, then it waits A SharedFlow with replay = 0 keeps nothing for late collectors: each emission goes to the collectors present at that moment. A StateFlow would hand the newcomer the latest value, and replay = 1 would replay the last order.

h: Observer and Command · Key terms
x: Observer A subject keeps a list of listeners and tells each one when something happens. Lapsed listener A listener nobody removed: it holds memory and keeps reacting after its owner is gone. Hot flow A flow that exists and emits whether or not anyone collects, such as SharedFlow and StateFlow. Conflation Keeping only the latest value and dropping ones a collector didn't get to, or equal repeats. Command A request turned into a value: what to do, with which arguments, ready to store or queue. At-least-once delivery A promise that a stored message arrives, possibly more than once, so the receiver must skip repeats. Compensation A new action that reverses the effect of an earlier one, such as a collection slip for a delivery. Why should subscribe return an AutoCloseable (or a similar handle)? So the subscriber can leave. A forgotten listener stays referenced by the subject forever: the lapsed-listener leak. Why use CopyOnWriteArrayList for a listener list? It loops over a snapshot, so a listener can unsubscribe during delivery without a ConcurrentModificationException. Writes are rare, reads happen all the time. What does a publish loop need around each listener call? A try/catch, so one throwing listener doesn't stop delivery to the others or fail the publisher. StateFlow or SharedFlow for order events? SharedFlow (or a Channel). StateFlow drops a value equal to the current one, and slow collectors skip updates. When does a command go on the undo history? Only after apply succeeds. Recorded earlier, a failed command gets "undone" and corrupts the state. Is a collection slip the undo of a delivery? No. Work that left the program can't be popped off a stack; a collection slip is a new compensating command with its own record and its own ways to fail. Why must a command that is stored and run later be safe to run twice? Delivery is at least once: a crash after sending but before marking it sent makes it go out again.

h: Observer and Command · Go deeper
x: StateFlow is a special case of SharedFlow. Its docs describe it as a MutableSharedFlow(replay = 1, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST) combined with distinctUntilChanged(). Knowing the knobs helps when neither default fits. replay sets how many past values a new collector gets. extraBufferCapacity lets emit run ahead of slow collectors without pausing. onBufferOverflow decides what happens when that buffer is full: pause the emitter, drop the oldest value or drop the newest. For order events, the default (pause) is the safe choice, because dropping is silent. Kotlin also has an observer for a single property: var status by Delegates.observable("PLACED") { _, old, new -> log("$old -> $new") } calls the handler after every assignment, and Delegates.vetoable runs before the assignment and can reject it. They are handy for state inside one object, and they run on the assigning thread, like a hand-rolled listener list. Java has a history here. java.util.Observable and java.util.Observer shipped in Java 1.0 and were deprecated in Java 9. Observable is a class you must extend, the order in which it notifies observers is unspecified, and it isn't a good fit for code that runs on several threads. Use a Consumer list, SubmissionPublisher or a library for event streams instead. Undo for operations that can't be reversed step by step, such as "apply the weekend discount to every price", doesn't fit the apply/undo pair. There, save a snapshot of the state before the command and restore it on undo. That is the Memento pattern, in lesson 10 of this track, Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento.

h: State and Chain of Responsibility · State: an order's life in one function instead of four buttons
x: The shop's first order screen kept track of an order with a status field: an enum (a type with a fixed list of values) holding PLACED, PACKED, OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, DELIVERED or CANCELLED. Each button changes the status, and each one checks what its author remembered: Java // Naive: each button guards only what its author thought of void pack() { if (status == Status.PLACED) status = Status.PACKED; } void ship() { if (status == Status.PACKED) status = Status.OUT_FOR_DELIVERY; } void deliver() { status = Status.DELIVERED; } // no check: surely the driver knows void cancel() { if (status != Status.DELIVERED) status = Status.CANCELLED; } // forgot: the van may have left Kotlin // Naive: each button guards only what its author thought of fun pack() { if (status == Status.PLACED) status = Status.PACKED } fun ship() { if (status == Status.PACKED) status = Status.OUT_FOR_DELIVERY } fun deliver() { status = Status.DELIVERED } // no check: surely the driver knows fun cancel() { if (status != Status.DELIVERED) status = Status.CANCELLED } // forgot: the van may have left OrderButtonsDemo, in the Try it, presses Pack, Ship, Cancel, Deliver, and then Pack once more by mistake: pack -> PACKED ship -> OUT_FOR_DELIVERY cancel -> CANCELLED deliver -> DELIVERED pack -> DELIVERED The customer cancelled while the parcel was on the road, and the driver delivered it anyway. The shop now has a teapot that was cancelled and delivered, in that order. The last click did nothing at all, and nobody said so. The cause isn't one careless line. The rules for an order live in four places, and each button knows a different part of them. A fifth button means remembering every rule again. State is the pattern for this: an object's behavior depends on the state it's in, so each state should say which moves it allows. The 1994 book of design patterns gives each state its own class. Modern Java and Kotlin let us write it smaller. A state is where the order is in its life, holding exactly the data that state needs. An event is something that happens to the order, such as a button press. A transition function takes the current state and an event, and returns the next state. The states and events below are records, small classes that just hold their data, and each set is sealed: its interface lists every type allowed to implement it, so the compiler knows the whole set: Java sealed interface OrderState permits Placed, Packed, OutForDelivery, Delivered, Cancelled {} record Placed(String orderNo) implements OrderState {} record Packed(String orderNo, int parcels) implements OrderState {} record OutForDelivery(String orderNo, int parcels, String courier) implements OrderState {} record Delivered(String orderNo, String signedBy) implements OrderState {} record Cancelled(String orderNo, String reason) implements OrderState {} sealed interface OrderEvent permits Pack, Ship, Deliver, Cancel {} record Pack(int parcels) implements OrderEvent {} record Ship(String courier) implements OrderEvent {} record Deliver(String signedBy) implements OrderEvent {} record Cancel(String reason) implements OrderEvent {} static OrderState transition(OrderState s, OrderEvent e) { return switch (s) { // no default: a new state breaks the build case Placed p -> switch (e) { case Pack(var parcels) when parcels > 0 -> new Packed(p.orderNo(), parcels); case Cancel(var reason) -> new Cancelled(p.orderNo(), reason); default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case Packed(var no, var parcels) -> switch (e) { case Ship(var courier) -> new OutForDelivery(no, parcels, courier); case Cancel(var reason) -> new Cancelled(no, reason); default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case OutForDelivery o -> switch (e) { case Deliver(var who) when !who.isBlank() -> new Delivered(o.orderNo(), who); default -> throw illegal(s, e); // Cancel lands here: the van has left }; case Delivered d -> throw illegal(s, e); // final case Cancelled c -> throw illegal(s, e); // final }; } Kotlin sealed interface OrderState { data class Placed(val orderNo: String) : OrderState data class Packed(val orderNo: String, val parcels: Int) : OrderState data class OutForDelivery(val orderNo: String, val parcels: Int, val courier: String) : OrderState data class Delivered(val orderNo: String, val signedBy: String) : OrderState data class Cancelled(val orderNo: String, val reason: String) : OrderState } sealed interface OrderEvent { data class Pack(val parcels: Int) : OrderEvent data class Ship(val courier: String) : OrderEvent data class Deliver(val signedBy: String) : OrderEvent data class Cancel(val reason: String) : OrderEvent } fun transition(s: OrderState, e: OrderEvent): OrderState = when (s) { // no else: a new state breaks the build is OrderState.Placed -> when (e) { is OrderEvent.Pack if e.parcels > 0 -> OrderState.Packed(s.orderNo, e.parcels) is OrderEvent.Cancel -> OrderState.Cancelled(s.orderNo, e.reason) else -> throw illegal(s, e) } is OrderState.Packed -> when (e) { is OrderEvent.Ship -> OrderState.OutForDelivery(s.orderNo, s.parcels, e.courier) is OrderEvent.Cancel -> OrderState.Cancelled(s.orderNo, e.reason) else -> throw illegal(s, e) } is OrderState.OutForDelivery -> when (e) { is OrderEvent.Deliver if e.signedBy.isNotBlank() -> OrderState.Delivered(s.orderNo, e.signedBy) else -> throw illegal(s, e) // Cancel lands here: the van has left } is OrderState.Delivered, is OrderState.Cancelled -> throw illegal(s, e) // final } Read it as a table. Each outer case is a state, each inner case is an event that state accepts, and everything else throws. A record pattern such as Packed(var no, var parcels) takes the record's fields out as it matches. A guard, the when parcels > 0 part, adds a condition: if it's false, the case doesn't match. Kotlin's guards in when (is Pack if ...) became stable in Kotlin 2.2.0. Picture the order board in the back room. It has five columns, one per state, and a card for each order. A rule card pinned above the board says which moves are allowed. The transition function is that rule card, kept in one place and checked by the compiler. The picture breaks in a useful spot. On a real board, every card looks the same. In code, each column has its own kind of card: an OutForDelivery card has a space for the courier, and a Placed card has none, so a placed order can't carry a courier by mistake. The function is pure: an old state and an event go in, a new state comes out, and nothing else is touched. You can test it without any fake objects, and replaying an order's history is one loop, as the lab's replay shows. Keep the side effects, such as booking the van, outside it: book first, then feed the answer in as an event. Rules spread over buttons drift apart. Put them in one transition function, and let the buttons only send events. One function holds the rules now. Next, we'll add a sixth state and let the compiler find every place it touches. Press the buttons in the wrong order Read OrderButtonsDemo.java (or OrderButtonsDemo.kt). Predict the five lines it prints. Run it with the command below. h: State and Chain of Responsibility · Add a state, and let the compiler list every place it touches
x: Some deliveries fail because nobody is home. The shop decides to keep those parcels at the counter until the customer collects, so an order needs a sixth state, WaitingAtShop. Add the record to the sealed interface and build, before you write a single rule: javac: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values kotlinc: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is WaitingAtShop' branch or an 'else' branch. Every switch over the state type fails, and each error points at one place that needs a decision: the transition function, the label on the shop's screen, the count of orders on the evening report. A switch the compiler has checked against every subtype is called an exhaustive switch. The compiler, strict as ever, has written your to-do list. Work through it, and the feature is done when the build is green. That only works if you leave room for it. A default (or else) on a switch over your own sealed type means "and anything else", and the compiler believes you: WaitingAtShop falls into the default without a word. The inner switches in transition do use default, on purpose. Most (state, event) pairs aren't allowed, and listing each one adds nothing. So the rule is narrower than "never write default": never write it on the side you expect to grow. States grow. The events one state accepts mostly don't. A default on the switch over states hides every state you add later. Leave it off. The check happens when the code is compiled, so a small gap is left for run time. The design notes for Java's pattern matching, by Brian Goetz and Gavin Bierman, call it the remainder: the values a checked switch can still meet. One is null, and a switch on a null state throws NullPointerException. The other is a subtype (a type that implements the sealed interface) added after the switch was compiled, in a separately compiled jar (a file of compiled classes). Java throws MatchException for it, and Kotlin throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException. You don't write code for those cases, but a program that mixes old and new jars can meet them. State looks a lot like Strategy, from Strategy and Template Method: an object holds a value, and behavior depends on it. The difference is who chooses. The shopkeeper picks a strategy, such as "cheapest courier", and it stays put. A state machine picks its own next state as events arrive. A state machine decides what one order may do. Next, we'll look at a request that several people could answer. Walk a return, then add a state Open ReturnStateDemo.java (or .kt). A customer returns a teapot, and the return has a life of its own, with the same shape as an order. Predict the five lines it prints, then run it. Change the approver from "dana" to " " (a blank name). Predict where the program stops and what it prints, run it, then change it back. Add a state. Java: add record OnHold(String id, String item) implements ReturnState {} and add OnHold to the permits list. Kotlin: add data class OnHold(val id: String, val item: String) : ReturnState inside the sealed interface. Before you build with the demo command, predict how many errors you'll get, and where. Fix them: in next, a return on hold accepts nothing yet (throw illegal(s, e)); in label, return "on hold". Build again, then remove OnHold. ReturnState {} record Binned(String id, String reason) implements ReturnState {} sealed interface ReturnEvent permits Approve, Collect, PutBack, Damaged {} record Approve(String approver) implements ReturnEvent {} record Collect(String label) implements ReturnEvent {} record PutBack() implements ReturnEvent {} record Damaged(String reason) implements ReturnEvent {} static ReturnState next(ReturnState s, ReturnEvent e) { return switch (s) { // no default: a new state breaks the build case Requested(var id, var item) -> switch (e) { case Approve(var who) when !who.isBlank() -> new IllegalStateException(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " not allowed in " + s.getClass().getSimpleName()); } public static void main(String[] args) { ReturnState s = new Requested("rt-31", "teapot"); h: State and Chain of Responsibility · Chain of Responsibility: answer the complaint, or pass it on
x: A request runs along a chain of checks until one answers, and the order of the list is behavior; then a payment's state decides which event is legal A customer comes to the counter: the teapot from the gift box arrived cracked. The shop assistant can sort out anything worth up to 5.00 herself, from the shelf. Anything bigger goes to the manager, who can sort out up to 50.00. The rest goes to head office, which answers everything, eventually. Nobody needs to know who sits further down the line. Each person either answers or passes the complaint on. That is Chain of Responsibility: a request travels along a list of handlers, and each handler either answers it or passes it to the next one. In code, each link is a function of the complaint and next, the rest of the chain: Java Handler assistant = (c, next) -> c.worthCents() <= 500 ? new Reply("assistant", "sorted") // answer now: the rest never runs : next.passOn(c); // pass it on Handler book = (c, next) -> { Reply r = next.passOn(c); // what follows runs on the way back System.out.println(" book: " + c.orderNo() + " " + c.about() + " -> " + r.from()); return r; }; Chain desk = chain(List.of(book, receipt, oncePerOrder, assistant, manager), headOffice); Kotlin val assistant = Handler { c, next -> if (c.worthCents <= 500) Reply("assistant", "sorted") // answer now: the rest never runs else next(c) // pass it on } val book = Handler { c, next -> next(c).also { println(" book: ${c.orderNo} ${c.about} -> ${it.from}") } // runs on the way back } val shopDesk = desk(listOf(book, receipt, oncePerOrder, assistant, manager), headOffice) Each Complaint record says which order it's about, what went wrong, what putting it right is worth in cents, and whether the customer brought the receipt. receipt turns away a complaint without one, and oncePerOrder turns away a second complaint about an order that's already been sorted. The complaints book on the counter is the first link, and it shows the shape of every handler. Code before next runs on the way in, code after it runs on the way back with the reply, and not calling next at all ends the trip early. So the book sees every complaint and every answer, while the receipt check can turn a customer away before the assistant even looks. The 1994 book links handler objects with a setNext() method. You don't need that. A list of functions and a fold make the chain. A fold walks a list and builds one result from it, step by step: here, start from the last stop and wrap it in each handler, from the last one to the first. The result can't change, so one desk can serve every complaint on every thread (a path of work that runs side by side with others). The lab's ComplaintDesk.build copies the list it's given for the same reason: a later edit to the caller's list must not change a chain that's already in use. The picture breaks on the way back. In the shop, an assistant who passes a complaint to the manager may never hear how it ended. In code, the reply travels back through every link that passed it on, and each one can still read it, write it down or change it. The figure shows both directions. The chain is short and easy to build. Next, we'll see the four ways it goes wrong. Swap two handlers Read ComplaintDeskDemo.java (or .kt). The third complaint has no receipt; the fourth is the same customer coming back with it. Predict the four replies and the complaints sorted count. Run it with the command below. Swap receipt and oncePerOrder in the list, so it reads book, oncePerOrder, receipt, assistant, manager. Predict the last reply and the count, then run. ComplaintDeskDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l09; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; /** A complaint passes along the shop's desk: each handler answers it or passes it on. The order of the list is behavior. */ public class ComplaintDeskDemo { record Complaint(String orderNo, String about, int worthCents, boolean hasReceipt) {} record Reply(String from, String says) {} interface Chain { Reply passOn(Complaint c); } interface Handler { Reply handle(Complaint c, Chain next); } // fold the handlers into one chain, from the last to the first static Chain chain(List<Handler> handlers, Chain lastStop) { Chain next = lastStop; for (int i = handlers.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { Handler h = handlers.get(i); Chain rest = next; next = c -> h.handle(c, rest); } return next; } static int sorted = 0; static Reply sort(String who) { sorted++; return new Reply(who, "sorted"); } public static void main(String[] args) { Set<String> handled = new HashSet<>(); Handler book = (c, next) -> { Reply r = next.passOn(c); // in: nothing; out: write it in the book System.out.println(" book: " + c.orderNo() + " " + c.about() + " -> " + r.from()); return r; }; Handler receipt = (c, next) -> c.hasReceipt() ? next.passOn(c) : new Reply("assistant", "please bring the receipt"); // answer now: the rest never runs Handler oncePerOrder = (c, next) -> handled.add(c.orderNo()) ? next.passOn(c) : new Reply("assistant", "we sorted this one already"); Handler assistant = (c, next) -> c.worthCents() <= 500 ? sort("assistant") : next.passOn(c); Handler manager = (c, next) -> c.worthCents() <= 5_000 ? sort("manager") : next.passOn(c); Chain headOffice = c -> sort("head office"); // the last stop answers everything Chain desk = chain(List.of(book, receipt, oncePerOrder, assistant, manager), headOffice); for (Complaint c : List.of( new Complaint("7781", "cracked teapot", 1_800, true), new Complaint("7781", "cracked teapot", 1_800, true), // the same complaint again new Complaint("7782", "stale bread", 250, false), // receipt left at home new Complaint("7782", "stale bread", 250, true))) { // back with the receipt Reply r = desk.passOn(c); System.out.println(r.from() + ": " + r.says()); } System.out.println("complaints sorted: " + sorted); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l09.ComplaintDeskDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l09/ComplaintDeskDemo.java ComplaintDeskDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l09 // A complaint passes along the shop's desk: each handler answers it or passes it on. The order of the list is behavior. data class Complaint(val orderNo: String, val about: String, val worthCents: Int, val hasReceipt: Boolean) data class Reply(val from: String, val says: String) fun interface Handler { fun handle(c: Complaint, next: (Complaint) -> Reply): Reply } // fold the handlers into one function, from the last to the first fun desk(handlers: List<Handler>, lastStop: (Complaint) -> Reply): (Complaint) -> Reply = handlers.foldRight(lastStop) { h, next -> { c -> h.handle(c, next) } } fun main() { var sorted = 0 fun sort(who: String): Reply { sorted++; return Reply(who, "sorted") } val handled = mutableSetOf<String>() val book = Handler { c, next -> next(c).also { println(" book: ${c.orderNo} ${c.about} -> ${it.from}") } // in: nothing; out: write it in the book } val receipt = Handler { c, next -> if (c.hasReceipt) next(c) else Reply("assistant", "please bring the receipt") // answer now: the rest never runs } val oncePerOrder = Handler { c, next -> if (handled.add(c.orderNo)) next(c) else Reply("assistant", "we sorted this one already") } val assistant = Handler { c, next -> if (c.worthCents <= 500) sort("assistant") else next(c) } val manager = Handler { c, next -> if (c.worthCents <= 5_000) sort("manager") else next(c) } val headOffice = { _: Complaint -> sort("head office") } // the last stop answers everything val shopDesk = desk(listOf(book, receipt, oncePerOrder, assistant, manager), headOffice) for (c in listOf( Complaint("7781", "cracked teapot", 1_800, true), Complaint("7781", "cracked teapot", 1_800, true), // the same complaint again Complaint("7782", "stale bread", 250, false), // receipt left at home Complaint("7782", "stale bread", 250, true), // back with the receipt )) { val r = shopDesk(c) println("${r.from}: ${r.says}") } println("complaints sorted: $sorted") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l09.ComplaintDeskDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l09/ComplaintDeskDemo.kt In order: manager: sorted (the cracked teapot is worth 18.00, too much for the assistant), assistant: we sorted this one already, assistant: please bring the receipt, assistant: sorted, and complaints sorted: 2. The book writes a line for every complaint, the turned-away ones included. After the swap, the complaint without a receipt is marked as handled before the receipt check turns it away, so the customer who comes back with the receipt hears we sorted this one already, and the count drops to 1. Nobody sorted out the stale bread. Each handler either answers the complaint or passes it on. The reply comes back out through every handler it passed, so the book sees all of them.

h: State and Chain of Responsibility · Four ways a chain of handlers goes wrong
x: Chains fail in four ways, and each one looks like a bug somewhere else. The order is wrong. Handlers run in list order, so the order of the list is behavior. Put the once-per-order check before the receipt check, as the Try it did, and a customer turned away for a missing receipt has already used up their one complaint. Put the book after the receipt check, and turned-away customers never reach the book. Pin the order with a test. A handler forgets next. A handler that neither answers nor calls next has nothing to return. In Java it's tempting to return null, and the complaint simply disappears, until a caller trips over the null with a NullPointerException. Every path through a handler must either call next or return a real reply. A handler calls next twice. A "try again" step that wraps next.passOn(c) near the front of the chain repeats everything after it. If the assistant's step posts a new teapot, two teapots go out. Put a retry as close as possible to the one call it repeats, never around the rest of the chain. A later handler throws an exception. Then the code after next.passOn(c) in the earlier handlers never runs, so the book never writes its line. Anything that must happen on the way back, such as the book's line or stopping a timer, belongs in a finally block. Every path through a handler answers or calls next, exactly once. Put the work for the way back in finally. Check yourself. In the desk from the last section, the manager's step throws for one complaint. Does that complaint get a line in the book, which is first in the list? (No. The book writes its line after next.passOn(c) returns, and that call never returns. Wrap it in try/finally, write the line in the finally, and the complaint shows up in the book, with the exception still on its way out.) h: State and Chain of Responsibility · Java and Kotlin
x: Building the chain: an index walker and a fold RealChain.java // OkHttp's shape: a chain object that can't change and knows its position interface Chain { Reply passOn(Complaint c); } interface Handler { Reply handle(Complaint c, Chain next); } record RealChain(List<Handler> handlers, int index, Function<Complaint, Reply> lastStop) implements Chain { RealChain { handlers = List.copyOf(handlers); // cheap after the first time: copyOf keeps an unmodifiable list } public Reply passOn(Complaint c) { if (index == handlers.size()) return lastStop.apply(c); // past the last link return handlers.get(index).handle(c, new RealChain(handlers, index + 1, lastStop)); } } Chain desk = new RealChain(List.of(book, receipt, assistant), 0, headOffice); Desk.kt // a function type replaces the Chain interface: the chain is just (Complaint) -> Reply fun interface Handler { fun handle(c: Complaint, next: (Complaint) -> Reply): Reply } fun desk(handlers: List<Handler>, lastStop: (Complaint) -> Reply): (Complaint) -> Reply = handlers.foldRight(lastStop) { h, next -> { c -> h.handle(c, next) } } // wrap from the last to the first val shopDesk = desk(listOf(book, receipt, assistant), headOffice) Both call the handlers in the same order, and neither can change after it's built. The Java record walks an index and creates a small chain object per step, for every complaint. That object is a natural place to carry more, which is why OkHttp (a library for making web requests) builds its real chain this way and lets it carry the call and its timeouts. The Kotlin fold builds the nested functions once, and next is a plain function, so no Chain interface is needed. Java can fold too, with a loop from the last handler to the first, as the lab's ComplaintDesk.build does. What both languages make unnecessary is the 1994 book's handler base class, with a setNext() link that anyone can change.

Note the choice in step 5: a waiting parcel is back in the shop, so cancelling is fine again. case OutForDelivery o -> switch (e) { case Deliver(var who) when !who.isBlank() -> new Delivered(o.orderNo(), who); case NobodyHome() -> new WaitingAtShop(o.orderNo(), o.parcels()); // 3. the parcel comes back default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case WaitingAtShop(var no, var parcels) -> switch (e) { case Ship(var courier) -> new OutForDelivery(no, parcels, courier); // 4. a second try case Deliver(var who) when !who.isBlank() -> new Delivered(no, who); // or collected at the counter case Cancel(var reason) -> new Cancelled(no, reason); // 5. it's in the shop: cancel is fine default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case Delivered d -> throw illegal(s, e); case Cancelled c -> throw illegal(s, e); is OrderState.OutForDelivery -> when (e) { is OrderEvent.Deliver if e.signedBy.isNotBlank() -> OrderState.Delivered(s.orderNo, e.signedBy) OrderEvent.NobodyHome -> OrderState.WaitingAtShop(s.orderNo, s.parcels) // 3. the parcel comes back else -> throw illegal(s, e) } is OrderState.WaitingAtShop -> when (e) { is OrderEvent.Ship -> OrderState.OutForDelivery(s.orderNo, s.parcels, e.courier) // 4. a second try is OrderEvent.Deliver if e.signedBy.isNotBlank() -> OrderState.Delivered(s.orderNo, e.signedBy) // or collected is OrderEvent.Cancel -> OrderState.Cancelled(s.orderNo, e.reason) // 5. it's in the shop: cancel is fine else -> throw illegal(s, e) } is OrderState.Delivered, is OrderState.Cancelled -> throw illegal(s, e) Fix the screen label and the evening report the same way, then pin the new paths in tests. Because transition is pure, a whole failed delivery is one replay call, with no courier and no database. @Test void nobodyHomeThenCollectedAtTheCounter() { var events = List.<OrderEvent>of(new Pack(1), new Ship("Big Blue Vans"), new NobodyHome(), new Deliver("Ben")); assertThat(replay("7790", events)).isEqualTo(new Delivered("7790", "Ben")); } @Test void cancelIsAllowedAgainOnceTheParcelIsBack() { assertThat(transition(new WaitingAtShop("7790", 1), new Cancel("moved away"))) .isEqualTo(new Cancelled("7790", "moved away")); } @Test fun `nobody home, then collected at the counter`() { val events = listOf(OrderEvent.Pack(1), OrderEvent.Ship("Big Blue Vans"), OrderEvent.NobodyHome, OrderEvent.Deliver("Ben")) val end: OrderState = events.fold(OrderState.Placed("7790"), ::transition) assertThat(end).isEqualTo(OrderState.Delivered("7790", "Ben")) } @Test fun `cancel is allowed again once the parcel is back`() { assertThat(transition(OrderState.WaitingAtShop("7790", 1), OrderEvent.Cancel("moved away"))) .isEqualTo(OrderState.Cancelled("7790", "moved away")) }

h: State and Chain of Responsibility · Quiz
x: In transition, the outer switch (s) lists Placed, Packed and OutForDelivery, then ends with default -> throw illegal(s, e) instead of listing Delivered and Cancelled. Someone adds WaitingAtShop. What happens? The build fails at that switch It compiles, and every event on a waiting order throws when the program runs Waiting orders throw NullPointerException Waiting orders throw MatchException The default covers every state not listed, including ones that don't exist yet, so the compiler has nothing to report. WaitingAtShop falls into the default and rejects every event, so a parcel at the counter can never be collected, and nobody notices until a customer asks. MatchException is only for subtypes the compiler couldn't know about; this one it could have flagged. The rule is case Deliver(var who) when !who.isBlank() -> new Delivered(o.orderNo(), who); followed by default -> throw illegal(s, e);. A Deliver(" ") arrives for an order that is out for delivery. What happens? It returns Delivered("7781", " ") It returns the same OutForDelivery state It throws IllegalStateException("Deliver not allowed in OutForDelivery") It doesn't compile, because the guard can be false When a guard is false, that case doesn't match, and the switch tries the next case: here the default, which throws. A guard is part of the pattern, so an unsigned delivery is one more move that isn't allowed. Nothing fills in a signature for you, and nothing quietly keeps the old state. A complaint desk is [book, oncePerOrder, receipt, assistant]. A customer complains about order 7782 without a receipt, then comes back with the receipt. What does the second visit get? sorted, from the assistant please bring the receipt An exception we sorted this one already The once-per-order check runs before the receipt check, so the first visit marks 7782 as handled and only then gets turned away. The second visit finds 7782 already marked and is stopped, although nothing was sorted. With the receipt check first, the first visit never reaches the once-per-order check, and the second goes through. Someone puts a "try again" handler at the front of the desk. It calls next.passOn(c) a second time whenever the first reply looks like an error. Further down, the assistant's step posts the customer a new teapot. What is the risk? Every later step runs again, so a second teapot can go out Nothing: running a chain twice is always safe The second call can't reach the last stop Only the book writes its line twice next is the whole rest of the chain, so calling it again repeats every step after the retry handler, the new teapot included. Put a retry around the one call it should repeat, close to that call, and make that call safe to run twice. From Strategy and Template Method: an order's OrderState and the shop's choose-a-courier strategy both hold behavior behind a type. What actually differs? Only strategies can be lambdas The caller chooses a strategy and it stays; a state machine chooses its own next state as events arrive States must be classes, strategies must be functions A strategy can't depend on data In structure they're the same: an object holds a value, and behavior depends on it. The difference is control. The shopkeeper picks "cheapest courier" for the day, and it doesn't change itself. An order's state moves on its own, from Packed to OutForDelivery, as the transition function handles events.
