h: State and Chain of Responsibility · Key terms
x: State machine A set of states and the events that move between them; any move not listed isn't allowed. Transition function A pure function from the current state and an event to the next state. Guard An extra condition on a pattern case, such as when parcels > 0; if it's false, the case doesn't match. Exhaustive switch A switch the compiler has checked covers every possible subtype or constant. Remainder The values an exhaustive switch can still meet at run time: null, and subtypes compiled later. Chain of Responsibility A request passes along a list of handlers; each one answers it or passes it on. Handler One link in a chain: it gets the request and the rest of the chain, and can act on the way in and on the way back. What replaces the 1994 State pattern's class per state in Java 21 and Kotlin? Sealed states and events as records or data classes, plus one pure transition(state, event) function with an exhaustive switch or when. Why leave default off the switch over a sealed state type? So a new state fails to compile at every switch that needs a rule. A default would quietly swallow it. When is default fine inside a state machine? On the inner switch over events, where most (state, event) pairs aren't allowed. Never on the side you expect to grow. An exhaustive Java switch meets a sealed subtype compiled after it. What happens? And in Kotlin? Java throws MatchException; Kotlin throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException. A null state throws NullPointerException. Why keep the transition function pure? It's tested without fakes, and history becomes a loop: replaying the events rebuilds the state. Side effects run outside it. In a chain of responsibility, what are a handler's two choices? Answer now (return a reply), or pass the request on by calling next. Handlers [a, b, c]: the order on the way in, and on the way back? In: a, b, c, then the last stop. Back: c, b, a.

h: State and Chain of Responsibility · Go deeper
x: Pattern matching for switch (JEP 441) and record patterns (JEP 440) both became final in JDK 21, so everything in this lesson compiles with --release 21 and no preview flags. In Kotlin, the subclasses of a sealed type must live in the same package and module as the type itself, and guards in when with a subject became stable in 2.2.0. Keeping the transition pure doesn't mean the order does nothing. A common shape returns the next state together with a list of things to do, such as "book the van", "text the customer" or "print the label", written as sealed records. A thin outer layer does them and feeds the results back in as events. Tests then check the returned list, with no fake courier at all. Event sourcing takes replay to its end: store the events, not the state, and compute the state with a loop over them. A long history gets slow to replay, so programs that work this way save a snapshot every few hundred events and replay only what came after it. That snapshot is a memento, from the next lesson, Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento. Chains of handlers also wrap single methods, not only whole requests. Many frameworks let you put an interceptor around a method: it gets an object describing the call and calls proceed() to go on to the next interceptor or the method itself. Those interceptors live in proxies, so the rules from Decorator and Proxy apply to them: a method that calls another method on this skips them.

h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Visitor: an inspector with a different check for each kind of goods
x: Visitor stores the type-by-job grid by column and reaches a cell in two hops; a sealed switch does it in one The breakfast box from Composite, Bridge and Flyweight now holds three kinds of goods: a packet with a price (an Item), fresh food that also knows how many days it has left (a Fresh item), and a smaller Box. The shop keeps adding jobs that treat each kind differently: the price (fresh food is half price on its last day), the inspector's check, the label printer, the weight for the courier. Visitor is the 1994 book's answer: put each job in a class of its own, called a visitor, with one method per kind of goods. Each kind gets one small accept method that calls the right one. The goods are records, small classes that just hold their data, and GoodsVisitor<R> is generic: R is what the job returns, a Long for the price: Java interface GoodsVisitor<R> { R visitItem(Item i); R visitFresh(Fresh f); R visitBox(Box b); } sealed interface Goods permits Item, Fresh, Box { <R> R accept(GoodsVisitor<R> v); } record Item(String name, long cents) implements Goods { public <R> R accept(GoodsVisitor<R> v) { return v.visitItem(this); } } record Fresh(String name, long cents, int daysLeft) implements Goods { public <R> R accept(GoodsVisitor<R> v) { return v.visitFresh(this); } } record Box(List<Goods> contents) implements Goods { public <R> R accept(GoodsVisitor<R> v) { return v.visitBox(this); } } final class Price implements GoodsVisitor<Long> { // one job, one method per kind of goods public Long visitItem(Item i) { return i.cents(); } public Long visitFresh(Fresh f) { return f.daysLeft() == 0 ? f.cents() / 2 : f.cents(); } public Long visitBox(Box b) { long sum = 0; for (Goods g : b.contents()) sum += g.accept(this); return sum; } } long total = breakfast.accept(new Price()); // two hops: accept picks the kind, visit picks the job Kotlin interface GoodsVisitor<R> { fun visitItem(i: Item): R; fun visitFresh(f: Fresh): R; fun visitBox(b: Box): R } sealed interface Goods { fun <R> accept(v: GoodsVisitor<R>): R } data class Item(val name: String, val cents: Long) : Goods { override fun <R> accept(v: GoodsVisitor<R>) = v.visitItem(this) } data class Fresh(val name: String, val cents: Long, val daysLeft: Int) : Goods { override fun <R> accept(v: GoodsVisitor<R>) = v.visitFresh(this) } data class Box(val contents: List<Goods>) : Goods { override fun <R> accept(v: GoodsVisitor<R>) = v.visitBox(this) } object Price : GoodsVisitor<Long> { // one job, one method per kind of goods override fun visitItem(i: Item) = i.cents override fun visitFresh(f: Fresh) = if (f.daysLeft == 0) f.cents / 2 else f.cents override fun visitBox(b: Box) = b.contents.sumOf { it.accept(this) } } val total = breakfast.accept(Price) // two hops: accept picks the kind, visit picks the job Read breakfast.accept(new Price()) as two hops. First accept runs on the box, so the box's own version is chosen, and it calls visitBox. Then visitBox asks each thing inside to accept the same visitor. Choosing the code by two types at once, the kind of goods and the job, is called double dispatch. The inspector is the picture: she visits each kind of goods and does a different check for each. A new checklist is one new visitor class, and nothing in the box changes. A new kind of goods, say Frozen, costs a method on the visitor interface, an accept on Frozen, and an edit in every visitor anyone ever wrote. That's a lot of paperwork for a bag of frozen peas. That trade-off is called the expression problem. With ordinary methods, a price() on each record, a new kind is cheap and a new job touches every class. With Visitor it's the other way round. Plain Java and Kotlin can't make both cheap, so you pick the side you expect to grow. In the shop, the kinds of goods change rarely and new jobs arrive every month, which favors Visitor's side. Sealed types and pattern matching give you that side without the machinery. A sealed interface lists every type allowed to implement it, so the compiler knows the whole set. Pattern matching lets a switch or when test which of those types a value is, and take its fields out as it matches. Together they give one function per job, with no accept and no visitor interface, over the same records: Java static long price(Goods g) { return switch (g) { case Item(var name, var cents) -> cents; case Fresh(var name, var cents, var days) when days == 0 -> cents / 2; // last day: half price case Fresh(var name, var cents, var days) -> cents; case Box(var contents) -> contents.stream().mapToLong(VisitorVsSwitch::price).sum(); }; } static List<String> inspect(Goods g) { // a new job: one new function, no class touched return switch (g) { case Item i -> i.cents() > 0 ? List.of() : List.of(i.name() + ": no price label"); case Fresh f -> f.daysLeft() > 0 ? List.of() : List.of(f.name() + ": last day"); case Box b -> b.contents().stream().flatMap(x -> inspect(x).stream()).toList(); }; } Kotlin fun price(g: Goods): Long = when (g) { is Item -> g.cents is Fresh if g.daysLeft == 0 -> g.cents / 2 // last day: half price is Fresh -> g.cents is Box -> g.contents.sumOf { price(it) } } fun inspect(g: Goods): List<String> = when (g) { // a new job: one new function, no class touched is Item -> if (g.cents > 0) emptyList() else listOf("${g.name}: no price label") is Fresh -> if (g.daysLeft > 0) emptyList() else listOf("${g.name}: last day") is Box -> g.contents.flatMap { inspect(it) } } VisitorVsSwitch, in the Try it, prices the box both ways and sends the inspector through it: breakfast box: 1060 cents (visitor) = 1060 cents (switch) inspector found: [milk: last day] The two prices agree. The switch version is one function per job, and the guard when days == 0, an extra condition on a case, states the last-day rule right where it applies. The design notes for Java's pattern matching put it plainly: "if your language has sufficiently powerful pattern matching, the Visitor pattern is almost completely unnecessary". The same notes say ordinary methods are still fine where they fit. The inspector picture breaks at a new kind of goods. A real inspector who meets something new can improvise. A visitor can't: it has no method for a kind it was never told about. With sealed types that's the point, because the compiler lists every job that needs a new branch. For a closed set of kinds you own, a sealed switch does Visitor's job. Keep Visitor for sets you can't close. Visitor still fits when the set of kinds is open to code you don't compile, or when a library hands you one, such as the visitors in Java's annotation processing API or in ASM, a library for reading and writing compiled classes. Next, we'll walk along a list that arrives in pages. Add a kind of goods in both styles Run VisitorVsSwitch (Java or Kotlin) and check that both prices agree. Add a Frozen kind. Java: add Frozen to permits and add record Frozen(String name, long cents) implements Goods { public <R> R accept(GoodsVisitor<R> v) { return v.visitFrozen(this); } }. Kotlin: add data class Frozen(val name: String, val cents: Long) : Goods { override fun <R> accept(v: GoodsVisitor<R>) = v.visitFrozen(this) }. Build with the demo command. Fix each error the compiler gives you, build again, and count the places you edited. List.of() : List.of(f.name() + ": last day"); case Box b -> b.contents().stream().flatMap(x -> inspect(x).stream()).toList(); }; } public static void main(String[] args) { Goods breakfast = new h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Iterator: walk the warehouse's stock list one item at a time
x: The old warehouse program from Adapter and Facade lists its stock a page at a time. Ask for page 0, and it sends a few items plus a cursor, a bookmark that says where the next page starts. Follow the cursors until one comes back empty (null), and you've seen everything. Loading every page into a list first wastes memory, and it makes the first item wait for the last page. An iterator is an object that hands out items one at a time without saying how they're stored. It's walking along a shelf: look at one item, then step to the next. In Java you write its bookkeeping by hand: Java static Iterator<String> stock(Function<Integer, StockPage> fetch) { return new Iterator<>() { private Iterator<String> current = Collections.emptyIterator(); private Integer cursor = 0; // null = no more pages public boolean hasNext() { while (!current.hasNext() && cursor != null) { // while, not if: skip empty pages StockPage page = fetch.apply(cursor); current = page.items().iterator(); cursor = page.next(); } return current.hasNext(); } public String next() { if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException(); return current.next(); } }; } Kotlin fun stock(fetch: (Int) -> StockPage): Sequence<String> = sequence { var cursor: Int? = 0 while (cursor != null) { val page = fetch(cursor) // runs only when the consumer needs more yieldAll(page.items) cursor = page.next } } The Java version keeps two fields of state, and hasNext holds a classic bug: write if instead of while, and an empty page in the middle ends the walk early. Kotlin's sequence {} builder lets you write the loop you'd write for a list. yield and yieldAll pause the block until the consumer, the code reading the items, asks for the next one, and the compiler writes the bookkeeping. Nothing runs until someone starts walking. PagingDemo, in the Try it, takes the first two items and then all of them: warehouse: sending page 0 first two: [rye bread, jam] warehouse: sending page 0 warehouse: sending page 1 warehouse: sending page 2 all: [rye bread, jam, tea] take(2) needed one page, and the warehouse program, which does exactly what it's asked and nothing more, sent one. The full walk needed all three pages, the empty one included. Two properties surprise people. A sequence built this way is cold: each new walk runs the block again from the top, so walking twice fetches every page twice. And if the consumer stops early, the rest of the block never runs. The iterator {} docs warn that "finally blocks may be left unexecuted". So don't open a connection inside the block and close it in finally; open it where you call the sequence, with use {}, which closes it when its own block ends. The shelf picture breaks right there. A real shelf is there whether you look or not, and walking it twice shows the same items. A cold sequence builds the shelf again for every walk. A sequence does its work again for every walk. Collect it with toList() when you need the items twice. When you want your own type to work in a for loop, make it Iterable, the interface for anything a for loop can walk, and build its iterator with iterator {}, the sibling of sequence {}: class Shelf(...) : Iterable<String> { override fun iterator() = iterator { yieldAll(...) } }. Java has no such builder. Stream.iterate(seed, hasNext, next) covers simple cases, but for pages like these the hand-written iterator is still the clearest Java. The iterator reads the shelf. Next, we'll take a photo of it before a change. Count the pages the warehouse sends Open PagingDemo.kt (or its Java twin, PagingDemoJava). Before you run it, predict how many warehouse: lines each of the two calls prints. Kotlin: change take(2) to take(3) and predict the number of pages sent. Java: in hasNext, change while to if and predict the all: line. Run, then undo the change. PagingDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l10 // Walk the warehouse program's stock list lazily. The sequence builder writes the iterator's state machine. data class StockPage(val items: List<String>, val next: Int?) private val stockPages = mapOf( 0 to StockPage(listOf("rye bread", "jam"), 1), 1 to StockPage(emptyList(), 2), // an empty page in the middle 2 to StockPage(listOf("tea"), null), ) fun stock(fetch: (Int) -> StockPage): Sequence<String> = sequence { var cursor: Int? = 0 while (cursor != null) { val page = fetch(cursor) // runs only when the consumer needs more yieldAll(page.items) cursor = page.next } } fun main() { val fetchPage = { cursor: Int -> println(" warehouse: sending page $cursor"); stockPages.getValue(cursor) } println("first two: ${stock(fetchPage).take(2).toList()}") println("all: ${stock(fetchPage).toList()}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l10.PagingDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l10/PagingDemo.kt PagingDemoJava.java package workbench.patterns.l10; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.Iterator; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; import java.util.function.Function; /** Walk the warehouse program's stock list lazily. Java has no generators, so the iterator's state is written by hand. */ public class PagingDemoJava { record StockPage(List<String> items, Integer next) {} static final Map<Integer, StockPage> PAGES = Map.of( 0, new StockPage(List.of("rye bread", "jam"), 1), 1, new StockPage(List.of(), 2), // an empty page in the middle 2, new StockPage(List.of("tea"), null)); static Iterator<String> stock(Function<Integer, StockPage> fetch) { return new Iterator<>() { private Iterator<String> current = Collections.emptyIterator(); private Integer cursor = 0; // null = no more pages @Override public boolean hasNext() { while (!current.hasNext() && cursor != null) { // while, not if: skip empty pages StockPage page = fetch.apply(cursor); current = page.items().iterator(); cursor = page.next(); } return current.hasNext(); } @Override public String next() { if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException(); return current.next(); } }; } static List<String> take(Iterator<String> it, int n) { List<String> out = new ArrayList<>(); while (out.size() < n && it.hasNext()) out.add(it.next()); return out; } public static void main(String[] args) { Function<Integer, StockPage> fetchPage = cursor -> { System.out.println(" warehouse: sending page " + cursor); return PAGES.get(cursor); }; System.out.println("first two: " + take(stock(fetchPage), 2)); System.out.println("all: " + take(stock(fetchPage), Integer.MAX_VALUE)); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l10.PagingDemoJava labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l10/PagingDemoJava.java first two: needs only page 0; all: fetches pages 0, 1 and 2 and prints [rye bread, jam, tea]. With take(3), three pages go out, because the third item sits behind the empty page (the line still says first two:, since only the number changed). With if in Java, the iterator fetches the empty page, finds nothing and gives up: all: [rye bread, jam] after two pages, and the tea is silently lost. h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Memento: a photo of the shelf you can put back
x: Before the shopkeeper rearranges the front shelf, she takes a photo of it. If the new layout is a mess, she puts everything back exactly as in the photo. Observer and Command undid a change by running its opposite, and that works for "restock 12 loaves". It doesn't work for "rearrange the whole shelf for the autumn sale", which has no clean opposite. Memento is the photo. An object saves a snapshot, a copy of its state at one moment, before a change, and puts it back on undo. The object that takes and restores the snapshot is called the originator; the snapshot itself is the memento: Java final class Shelf { private final List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(); private String sign = ""; interface Memento {} // what callers hold: opaque private record Photo(List<String> items, String sign) implements Memento {} Memento save() { return new Photo(List.copyOf(items), sign); } // copy: later changes must not leak in void restore(Memento m) { Photo p = (Photo) m; items.clear(); items.addAll(p.items()); // copy back in: the photo stays as it was sign = p.sign(); } } Kotlin class Shelf { private val items = mutableListOf<String>() private var sign = "" interface Memento // what callers hold: opaque private data class Photo(val items: List<String>, val sign: String) : Memento fun save(): Memento = Photo(items.toList(), sign) // copy: later changes must not leak in fun restore(m: Memento) { val p = m as Photo items.clear() items += p.items // copy back in: the photo stays as it was sign = p.sign } } MementoDemo, in the Try it, puts rye bread on the shelf, takes the photo, adds jam and an autumn sign, then restores: changed: [rye bread, jam] sign=Autumn sale restored: [rye bread] sign= Three rules make it work. The snapshot must not share anything changeable with the live object: copy the list with List.copyOf or toList(), or later changes leak into the photo. Restore must copy back in rather than point at the photo's list, so the same photo can be restored twice. And only the originator reads it. Callers get an opaque Memento, something to keep and hand back, while the record with the data is private, so nothing else depends on how the shelf stores things. The photo picture breaks exactly where the first rule guards. A real photo can't change after you take it. A memento that shares a list with the live shelf changes with every edit: a window, not a photo. The Try it shows what that costs. A snapshot that shares a changeable list is no snapshot. Copy every changeable part, on save and on restore. Records and data classes make the rest easy. When the whole state is already an immutable record, one that can't change after it's made, the pattern almost disappears: the state is its own memento, and an undo history is a list of old states. That's a strong argument for immutable data. There are two costs. History grows with every checkpoint, so bound it; the lab keeps the newest few. And a snapshot of a big object takes memory, which is why programs with long histories save one now and then and replay the changes made after it. Next, a pattern for parts of a program that keep reacting to each other. Let the photo share the list Run MementoDemo in either language and read both lines. In save(), store the live list instead of a copy: new Photo(items, sign) in Java, Photo(items, sign) in Kotlin. Predict the restored: line, then run. Put the copy back. MementoDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l10; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** A shelf that can hand out a photo of itself and later be put back exactly as in the photo. */ public class MementoDemo { static final class Shelf { private final List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(); private String sign = ""; void add(String item) { items.add(item); } void sign(String text) { sign = text; } @Override public String toString() { return items + " sign=" + sign; } // callers see an opaque Memento; only Shelf can read the Photo inside it interface Memento {} private record Photo(List<String> items, String sign) implements Memento {} Memento save() { return new Photo(List.copyOf(items), sign); // copy: later changes must not leak in } void restore(Memento m) { Photo p = (Photo) m; items.clear(); items.addAll(p.items()); // copy back in: the photo stays as it was sign = p.sign(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Shelf shelf = new Shelf(); shelf.add("rye bread"); Shelf.Memento before = shelf.save(); shelf.add("jam"); shelf.sign("Autumn sale"); System.out.println("changed: " + shelf); shelf.restore(before); System.out.println("restored: " + shelf); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l10.MementoDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l10/MementoDemo.java MementoDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l10 // A shelf that can hand out a photo of itself and later be put back exactly as in the photo. class Shelf { private val items = mutableListOf<String>() private var sign = "" fun add(item: String) { items += item } fun sign(text: String) { sign = text } override fun toString() = "$items sign=$sign" // callers see an opaque Memento; only Shelf can read the Photo inside it interface Memento private data class Photo(val items: List<String>, val sign: String) : Memento fun save(): Memento = Photo(items.toList(), sign) // copy: later changes must not leak in fun restore(m: Memento) { val p = m as Photo items.clear() items += p.items // copy back in: the photo stays as it was sign = p.sign } } fun main() { val shelf = Shelf() shelf.add("rye bread") val before = shelf.save() shelf.add("jam") shelf.sign("Autumn sale") println("changed: $shelf") shelf.restore(before) println("restored: $shelf") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l10.MementoDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l10/MementoDemo.kt changed: [rye bread, jam] sign=Autumn sale, then restored: [rye bread] sign=. Without the copy, the photo and the shelf share one list. The jam lands in the "saved" state too, and restore then clears that shared list before copying from it, so you get restored: [] sign=: an empty shelf, which is worse than no undo at all.

h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Mediator: one dispatcher, so bikes and vans never phone each other
x: The town's couriers used to phone each other. A bike rider who found a parcel too heavy rang the van driver, the stock room rang the bike when an item ran out, and the counter rang everyone when an order was cancelled. Four parties need six phone lines, and every new rule means teaching two of them a new call. So the town hired a dispatcher. Everyone phones the dispatcher, and the dispatcher knows who needs to hear what. A mediator is that dispatcher: an object that holds the rules for how several parts of a program react to each other, so the parts, called colleagues, never call each other directly: Java interface Colleague { void receive(String message); } final class Dispatcher { private final Map<String, List<Colleague>> routes = new HashMap<>(); void on(String message, Colleague c) { routes.computeIfAbsent(message, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(c); } void send(String message) { routes.getOrDefault(message, List.of()).forEach(c -> c.receive(message)); } } dispatcher.on("parcel.packed", bike); dispatcher.on("parcel.packed", counter); // the counter texts the customer dispatcher.on("parcel.tooHeavy", van); // the bike never calls the van directly Kotlin fun interface Colleague { fun receive(message: String) } class Dispatcher { private val routes = mutableMapOf<String, MutableList<Colleague>>() fun on(message: String, c: Colleague) { routes.getOrPut(message) { mutableListOf() } += c } fun send(message: String) { routes[message].orEmpty().forEach { it.receive(message) } } } dispatcher.on("parcel.packed", bike) dispatcher.on("parcel.packed", counter) // the counter texts the customer dispatcher.on("parcel.tooHeavy", van) // the bike never calls the van directly When the bike finds a parcel too heavy, it calls dispatcher.send("parcel.tooHeavy") and goes back to riding. It doesn't know the van exists. The figure counts the lines: six without the dispatcher, four with it. Mediator and Observer look alike. An observer, from Observer and Command, is one subject telling its listeners about itself. A mediator sits between many parties and holds the rules about who reacts to what. In coroutine code (Kotlin's light tasks that can pause without holding a thread), one MutableSharedFlow, a stream that hands every message to everyone listening, makes a natural mediator when every colleague shares it. The dispatcher picture holds up well, and it breaks where dispatchers get ambitious. A real dispatcher who starts weighing parcels and planning routes is one person doing two jobs. A mediator that starts working out delivery fees or checking addresses becomes a god object, a class that knows everything and that everything depends on. A mediator routes messages. When it starts doing the work, move the work back to the colleague that owns it. Check yourself. A new rule arrives: when stock runs out, the bike must cancel its pickup. With the dispatcher above, what do you change? (One registration, dispatcher.on("stock.missing", bike), plus the bike's own handling of that message. The stock room doesn't change, and it still knows nothing about bikes.) Without a dispatcher, every party phones the others. With one, each knows only the dispatcher, and the rules about who hears what live in one place.

h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Java and Kotlin
x: Replacing a visitor: nested record patterns in Java, guards in Kotlin GoodsJobs.java sealed interface Goods permits Item, Fresh, Box, Gift {} record Item(String name, long cents) implements Goods {} record Fresh(String name, long cents, int daysLeft) implements Goods {} record Box(List<Goods> contents) implements Goods {} record Gift(Goods inside, String paper) implements Goods {} // gift paper around anything static long price(Goods g) { return switch (g) { case Item(var name, var cents) -> cents; case Fresh(var name, var cents, var days) when days == 0 -> cents / 2; case Fresh(var name, var cents, var days) -> cents; case Box(var contents) -> contents.stream().mapToLong(GoodsJobs::price).sum(); case Gift(Fresh f, var paper) -> price(f); // nested pattern: food is wrapped for free case Gift(var inside, var paper) -> price(inside) + 150; // wrapping anything else costs 1.50 }; } static String label(Goods g) { // a new job: one new function, no class touched return switch (g) { case Item i -> i.name(); case Fresh f -> f.name() + " (" + f.daysLeft() + " days left)"; case Box b -> "box of " + b.contents().size(); case Gift(var inside, var paper) -> label(inside) + " in " + paper + " paper"; }; } GoodsJobs.kt sealed interface Goods data class Item(val name: String, val cents: Long) : Goods data class Fresh(val name: String, val cents: Long, val daysLeft: Int) : Goods data class Box(val contents: List<Goods>) : Goods data class Gift(val inside: Goods, val paper: String) : Goods // gift paper around anything fun price(g: Goods): Long = when (g) { is Item -> g.cents is Fresh if g.daysLeft == 0 -> g.cents / 2 is Fresh -> g.cents is Box -> g.contents.sumOf { price(it) } is Gift if g.inside is Fresh -> price(g.inside) // no nested patterns: a guard says it is Gift -> price(g.inside) + 150 // wrapping anything else costs 1.50 } fun label(g: Goods): String = when (g) { // a new job: one new function, no class touched is Item -> g.name is Fresh -> "${g.name} (${g.daysLeft} days left)" is Box -> "box of ${g.contents.size}" is Gift -> "${label(g.inside)} in ${g.paper} paper" } Both delete the visitor interface and every accept method, and both make a new job a single function. The difference is how far the patterns reach. Java 21 record patterns nest, so Gift(Fresh f, var paper) matches "a gift with fresh food inside" in one case and takes the parts out as it goes. Kotlin's when matches on the type and smart-casts (after is Gift, the compiler treats g as a Gift), but it has no patterns that take a record apart, so the same rule is a guard: is Gift if g.inside is Fresh. Guards in when are stable since Kotlin 2.2.0. In both, adding a kind such as Frozen breaks every function that switches over Goods, which is the compiler listing your work.

h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Worked example
x: Retire a visitor in four steps The shop prices and labels its goods with a classic visitor. Now it sells gift-wrapped goods too: a Gift holds any other goods and the paper around them. Before reading on, list every file a Gift touches in this design. interface GoodsVisitor<R> { R visitItem(Item i); R visitFresh(Fresh f); R visitBox(Box b); } sealed interface Goods permits Item, Fresh, Box { <R> R accept(GoodsVisitor<R> v); } // Item, Fresh, Box: each record implements accept(v) by calling its own visitXxx(this) final class Price implements GoodsVisitor<Long> { /* three visit methods */ } final class Label implements GoodsVisitor<String> { /* three visit methods */ } // ...and any visitor someone else wrote against GoodsVisitor interface GoodsVisitor<R> { fun visitItem(i: Item): R; fun visitFresh(f: Fresh): R; fun visitBox(b: Box): R } sealed interface Goods { fun <R> accept(v: GoodsVisitor<R>): R } // Item, Fresh, Box: each data class implements accept(v) by calling its own visitXxx(this) object Price : GoodsVisitor<Long> { /* three visit methods */ } object Label : GoodsVisitor<String> { /* three visit methods */ } // ...and any visitor someone else wrote against GoodsVisitor Gift needs a visitGift on the interface, an accept on itself, and a new method in Price, Label and every other visitor. The set of kinds is closed and ours, so retire the machinery first: drop accept and the interface, and write each job as a switch. Behavior doesn't change, so the old tests still pass. sealed interface Goods permits Item, Fresh, Box {} // 1. no accept, no visitor interface record Item(String name, long cents) implements Goods {} record Fresh(String name, long cents, int daysLeft) implements Goods {} record Box(List<Goods> contents) implements Goods {} static String label(Goods g) { // 2. each visitor becomes one function return switch (g) { case Item i -> i.name(); case Fresh f -> f.name() + " (" + f.daysLeft() + " days left)"; case Box b -> "box of " + b.contents().size(); }; } sealed interface Goods // 1. no accept, no visitor interface data class Item(val name: String, val cents: Long) : Goods data class Fresh(val name: String, val cents: Long, val daysLeft: Int) : Goods data class Box(val contents: List<Goods>) : Goods fun label(g: Goods): String = when (g) { // 2. each visitor becomes one function is Item -> g.name is Fresh -> "${g.name} (${g.daysLeft} days left)" is Box -> "box of ${g.contents.size}" } Now add the kind, and compile before writing any logic. The errors are the to-do list: one per function that switches over Goods. sealed interface Goods permits Item, Fresh, Box, Gift {} record Gift(Goods inside, String paper) implements Goods {} // 3. the new kind // javac: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values (price) // javac: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values (label) data class Gift(val inside: Goods, val paper: String) : Goods // 3. the new kind // kotlinc: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is Gift' branch or an 'else' branch. (price) // kotlinc: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is Gift' branch or an 'else' branch. (label) Fill in one branch per function. A brand-new job, counting how many things the inspector must check, is one more function, and no type changes at all. case Gift(var inside, var paper) -> price(inside) + 150; // 4. in price case Gift(var inside, var paper) -> label(inside) + " in " + paper + " paper"; // in label static int count(Goods g) { // 5. a new job: one function return switch (g) { case Item i -> 1; case Fresh f -> 1; case Box b -> b.contents().stream().mapToInt(GoodsJobs::count).sum(); case Gift(var inside, var paper) -> count(inside); }; } is Gift -> price(g.inside) + 150 // 4. in price is Gift -> "${label(g.inside)} in ${g.paper} paper" // in label fun count(g: Goods): Int = when (g) { // 5. a new job: one function is Item, is Fresh -> 1 is Box -> g.contents.sumOf { count(it) } is Gift -> count(g.inside) }

h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Quiz
x: Your team owns a sealed Goods hierarchy with four kinds, and keeps adding jobs: price, label, weigh, inspect. Which design makes each new job cheapest? A classic Visitor with an accept method on each record An abstract method per job on the sealed interface One function per job with an exhaustive switch or when instanceof chains with a final else that throws Jobs are the side that grows, so you want each job to be a single function: a sealed switch gives that, with the compiler checking that each one covers all four kinds. A Visitor makes the same trade with more machinery. Abstract methods make each new job touch all four records, and an instanceof chain loses the compiler's check. A Java paging iterator has if (!current.hasNext() && cursor != null) in hasNext. The pages are [rye bread, jam], then an empty page, then [tea]. What does a full walk return? [rye bread, jam] [rye bread, jam, tea] It throws NoSuchElementException It loops forever After the jam, hasNext fetches the empty page once, finds nothing, and returns false, because if doesn't try again. The walk ends early and the tea is never seen, with no error. while keeps fetching until it finds an item or runs out of pages. val stock = pagedSequence(fetch) uses the sequence {} builder. The code calls stock.count() and then stock.first(). How many times is page 0 fetched? Once: a sequence keeps the pages it fetched Twice: each walk runs the block again from the top Never: sequences are lazy Once, but only if the pages are small A sequence from sequence {} is cold: every new walk starts the block over. count() walks all the pages, and first() starts again from page 0. If you need the items twice, collect them once with toList(), or accept the second round of fetches. Shelf.save() returns new Photo(items, sign), where items is the shelf's own ArrayList. The shopkeeper saves, adds jam, and restores. What does she get? The shelf as it was at save time An UnsupportedOperationException A ConcurrentModificationException Not the old shelf: the photo shares the live list, so the jam is in the "saved" state too The record holds a reference to the same list the shelf keeps changing, so the jam is in the photo too. Depending on how restore copies, you get the present back, or even an empty shelf. Copy every changeable part on save (List.copyOf) and on restore. From Observer and Command: the shelf needs undo both for "restock 12 loaves" and for "rearrange the shelf for the autumn sale", which has no simple opposite. Which approach handles both? A command stack where every command implements undo() A memento saved before each change, restored on undo A StateFlow of the shelf that collectors can rewind A chain of undo handlers Undo by command needs an opposite for every command, and "rearrange the shelf" doesn't have a clean one. A snapshot taken before any change can always be restored, whatever the change did. The two combine well: commands for the log, mementos for the undo. A StateFlow keeps only the latest value, so there is nothing to rewind to.

h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Explain it back
x: A teammate wants to add a Visitor to the sealed Goods hierarchy "so we can add jobs without touching the classes". Explain what you would do instead, and when you would agree with them.

h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Key terms
x: Visitor One class per job, with a method per kind of element, called through accept on each element. Double dispatch Choosing code by two runtime types at once: accept picks the kind, visit picks the job. Expression problem No plain design makes both new kinds and new jobs cheap; you pick the side that grows. Iterator An object that hands out a collection's items one at a time without showing how they are stored. Cold sequence A sequence whose work runs again, from the start, every time someone walks it. Memento An opaque snapshot of an object's state that only that object can read and restore. Mediator A hub that holds the rules for how several parts react to each other, so they don't call each other. What is the expression problem, in one line each? Ordinary methods: new kinds are cheap, new jobs touch every class. Visitor (or sealed + switch): new jobs are cheap, new kinds touch every job. When does Visitor still fit in modern Java or Kotlin? For hierarchies open to code you don't compile, or when a library hands you one, such as annotation processing or tools that read compiled classes. Java pattern for "a gift with fresh food inside"? And Kotlin? Java 21: case Gift(Fresh f, var paper), a nested record pattern. Kotlin: is Gift if g.inside is Fresh, a guard (no nested patterns). Why while, not if, in a paging iterator's hasNext? An empty page must not end the walk; while keeps fetching until it finds an item or runs out of pages. Walking a sequence {} twice: what happens to the work inside it? It runs again from the top: sequences built that way are cold. Collect them with toList() if you need the items twice. Why can a finally inside sequence {} or iterator {} fail to run? If the consumer stops early, the rest of the block never runs. Open resources where you call the sequence, with use {}. What makes a memento safe? It copies every changeable part on save, restore copies back in, only the originator can read it, and the history is bounded.

h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Go deeper
x: Kotlin's sequence {} is built on the same machinery as coroutines, but with limits. Its block runs on a SequenceScope, which allows only yield and yieldAll to pause, so you can't call delay or another suspending function inside it. For pages that arrive over the network, where each fetch should wait without holding a thread, use flow {} and emit instead: a Flow is the suspending cousin of a sequence, cold in the same way, as in Flow basics: cold streams and operators in the coroutines track. Java's Iterator has an optional remove(), and its Javadoc says iterators "allow the caller to remove elements from the underlying collection during the iteration with well-defined semantics". That's why iterator.remove() is safe inside a loop where list.remove(x) throws ConcurrentModificationException. For paging iterators, leave remove() unsupported, which is the default. Visitor and Composite often travel together: a visitor walks a composite tree. With sealed types, the walk is plain recursion in each function, as in Composite, Bridge and Flyweight. If a tree gets deep enough to overflow the stack, an explicit stack in an iterator (or a sequence {} that pushes children) turns the recursion into a loop. Memento meets long histories in snapshots. When an object's state is rebuilt by replaying every change since the start, as in the deeper notes of State and Chain of Responsibility, replaying ten thousand changes on every load is slow. So the program saves a snapshot every few hundred changes, and loading means restoring the newest snapshot and replaying what came after it. The snapshot's format then becomes a promise between versions of your program, so give it a version number from the start.

h: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together · The packing rail: producer-consumer and a team of packers
x: The safest way to share work between threads is to share a queue and nothing else. A queue is a line of items that leave in the order they joined. In producer-consumer, producers put work into a queue, consumers take it out, and the queue does all the locking (letting one thread in at a time) and waiting. At the shop, the counter is the producer, the packers are the consumers, and the rail of order slips is the queue: the kitchen rail from wait, notify and guarded blocks, moved to the back room. Java's BlockingQueue is that kind of queue for threads, and team below is a pool of threads that runs each packer. Kotlin's Channel is the same queue for coroutines, light tasks that can pause without holding a thread: Java BlockingQueue<Card> rail = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(16); // bounded: a full rail makes the counter wait for (int p = 0; p < 4; p++) { team.submit(() -> { while (true) { if (rail.take() instanceof Closed) return null; // the poison pill: this packer goes home packed.incrementAndGet(); } }); } for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) rail.put(new Slip(i)); for (int p = 0; p < 4; p++) rail.put(new Closed()); // one card PER packer Kotlin val rail = Channel<Int>(capacity = 16) // bounded: send waits when the rail is full val packers = List(4) { launch(Dispatchers.Default) { for (slip in rail) packed.incrementAndGet() // ends when the rail is closed and empty } } repeat(1_000) { rail.send(it) } rail.close() // one call sends every packer home ProducerConsumerDemo, in the Try it, clips 1,000 slips onto a rail that holds 16, with four packers taking them off: packed 1000 of 1000, all packers finished: true Three rules from Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers still hold. Bound the queue: a full ArrayBlockingQueue(16) makes a fast counter wait, which is called backpressure, while an unbounded queue hides a pile-up until memory runs out. Send one poison pill, a special item that tells one consumer to stop, for each consumer, because each take() removes exactly one. And don't swallow InterruptedException: it's how a pool tells its threads to stop. Kotlin's channel needs no pill: close() ends every for (slip in rail) loop once the rail is empty. Use a for loop in each packer, not consumeEach, which cancels the whole channel when its own loop ends. The rail picture holds until closing time. A packer can see the lights go off; a thread waiting in take() sees nothing until an item arrives, so you must send it one. Forget a card, and three packers wait by the empty rail all night. A worker pool, or thread pool, is the same picture with the rail inside an ExecutorService: the team of cooks from Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown, hired once. A fixed pool of ordinary threads still suits work that keeps the processor busy. For work that mostly waits, Java 21 brought back thread-per-message: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() starts a virtual thread, a cheap thread the JVM manages itself, for every task, and in Kotlin you launch a coroutine per message. Both make it easy to send ten thousand bookings at once to a courier who takes twenty. Share a bounded queue and nothing else. Close it, or send one pill per consumer. So thread-per-message always comes with a limit, and that limit is the bulkhead, two sections down. First, the patterns that keep state apart. Forget a closed card Run ProducerConsumerDemo (Java or Kotlin) with the command below. Java: replace the card loop with a single rail.put(new Closed());. Kotlin: delete rail.close(). Predict both parts of the output line, then run. Put it back. ProducerConsumerDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l11; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** The packing rail: the counter clips order slips on, four packers take them off, and each packer needs its own "closed" card. */ public class ProducerConsumerDemo { sealed interface Card permits Slip, Closed {} record Slip(int orderNo) implements Card {} record Closed() implements Card {} // the poison pill: "the shop is closed, go home" public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int packers = 4, orders = 1_000; BlockingQueue<Card> rail = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(16); // bounded: a full rail makes the counter wait AtomicInteger packed = new AtomicInteger(); ExecutorService team = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); for (int p = 0; p < packers; p++) { team.submit(() -> { while (true) { Card c = rail.take(); if (c instanceof Closed) return null; // this packer goes home packed.incrementAndGet(); } }); } for (int i = 0; i < orders; i++) rail.put(new Slip(i)); for (int p = 0; p < packers; p++) rail.put(new Closed()); // one card PER packer team.shutdown(); boolean finished = team.awaitTermination(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.println("packed " + packed + " of " + orders + ", all packers finished: " + finished); if (!finished) { team.shutdownNow(); // interrupt the ones still waiting in take() System.out.println("some packers never got a card and were still waiting at the rail"); } } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l11.ProducerConsumerDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l11/ProducerConsumerDemo.java ProducerConsumerDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel import kotlinx.coroutines.joinAll import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeoutOrNull import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds // The packing rail: the counter sends order slips, four packers take them, and close() sends every packer home. fun main() = runBlocking { val orders = 1_000 val rail = Channel<Int>(capacity = 16) // bounded: send suspends when the rail is full val packed = AtomicInteger() val packers = List(4) { launch(Dispatchers.Default) { for (slip in rail) packed.incrementAndGet() // ends when the rail is closed and empty } } repeat(orders) { rail.send(it) } rail.close() // one call sends every packer home val finished = withTimeoutOrNull(2.seconds) { packers.joinAll() } != null println("packed $packed of $orders, all packers finished: $finished") if (!finished) { packers.forEach { it.cancel() } println("the packers were still waiting at the rail: nobody closed it") } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l11.ProducerConsumerDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l11/ProducerConsumerDemo.kt packed 1000 of 1000, all packers finished: true. With one card, all 1,000 slips are still packed, but after the two-second wait the line reads all packers finished: false, and the demo reports that packers were still waiting at the rail: three of the four never got a card. In Kotlin without close(), the packers wait for a slip that never comes, and you get all packers finished: false too. In a real program, that is a shutdown that hangs. h: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together · Who owns the state: the patterns you already know, and balking
x: Most of the other concurrency patterns answer one question: who owns this state, and what happens to a thread that arrives at the wrong moment? You've met them all in earlier tracks. Each row names a pattern, what it solves, and where you saw it: Pattern What it solves Java 21+ Kotlin Taught in Immutable object share state with no locks, like the price board nobody writes on records with List.copyOf data class with vals and copied lists Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal Active object one owner for changeable state, like the stock worker that alone touches the shelves a single-thread executor as a mailbox; methods return CompletableFuture a coroutine that owns the state and reads commands from a Channel Observer and Command Guarded suspension wait until a condition holds, like a cook waiting for the next ticket wait() in a while loop, or better CompletableFuture, CountDownLatch, Condition CompletableDeferred.await(), which suspends wait, notify and guarded blocks Balking don't start a job that's already running AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet(false, true) the same, or Mutex.tryLock() Atomics and compare-and-set Read-write lock many readers, rare writers ReentrantReadWriteLock (no read-to-write upgrade), or an AtomicReference to an immutable snapshot the same Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock Future a result that arrives later, like the ticket that says what to do when the steak is ready CompletableFuture with your own executor async and await inside coroutineScope CompletableFuture: composing async steps Balking means returning at once, instead of waiting, when the object isn't ready for the job, and it's the one people get wrong most often. The shop's stock count walks every shelf and counts what's left. It runs at closing time, again after a failure, and whenever the manager presses a button, and it must never run twice at once. If a count is already running, the right answer is to return at once: Java final class StockCount { private final AtomicBoolean running = new AtomicBoolean(); boolean runIfIdle(Runnable count) { if (!running.compareAndSet(false, true)) return false; // balk: a count is already running try { count.run(); return true; } finally { running.set(false); } } } Kotlin class StockCount { private val mutex = Mutex() // kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex suspend fun runIfIdle(count: suspend () -> Unit): Boolean { if (!mutex.tryLock()) return false // balk: a count is already running try { count() return true } finally { mutex.unlock() } } } The Kotlin version uses a Mutex, a lock for coroutines, whose tryLock() gives up at once instead of waiting; the Kotlin twin of the demo keeps the AtomicBoolean, exactly as Java does. StockCountDemo, in the Try it, fires eight triggers at the same moment: ran 1, balked 7, most counts at once: 1 The plain-boolean version, if (running) return; running = true;, is check-then-act, the race from Race conditions: why count++ lies: two threads can both see false before either one sets true, and two counts walk the same shelves at once. And an AtomicBoolean protects one program only. If the shop runs its program on two computers, each has its own flag, so a count that must be unique everywhere needs a shared lock, such as a row locked in the shop's database. Balk with one atomic step, compareAndSet, never with a check and then a set. Balking protects a job from itself. Next, we'll protect the services the shop calls from the shop. Turn the balk into check-then-act Run StockCountDemo in either language: eight triggers fire at the same moment. Read the line. Replace the compareAndSet line with three lines: if (running.get()) return false;, then for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); (Kotlin: repeat(1_000) { Thread.onSpinWait() }), then running.set(true);. Run it four or five times and watch most counts at once. Then put the compareAndSet back. StockCountDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l11; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Balking: eight triggers fire at once, and the stock count refuses to start while one is already running. */ public class StockCountDemo { static final class StockCount { private final AtomicBoolean running = new AtomicBoolean(); boolean runIfIdle(Runnable count) { if (!running.compareAndSet(false, true)) return false; // balk: a count is already running try { count.run(); return true; } finally { running.set(false); } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { StockCount stockCount = new StockCount(); AtomicInteger inside = new AtomicInteger(), mostAtOnce = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicInteger ran = new AtomicInteger(), balked = new AtomicInteger(); Runnable count = () -> { mostAtOnce.accumulateAndGet(inside.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); for (int i = 0; i < 2_000_000; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); // counting the shelves takes a moment inside.decrementAndGet(); }; CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] triggers = new Thread[8]; // the closing-time timer, the manager's button, a retry... for (int t = 0; t < triggers.length; t++) { triggers[t] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } if (stockCount.runIfIdle(count)) ran.incrementAndGet(); else balked.incrementAndGet(); }); triggers[t].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : triggers) t.join(); System.out.println("ran " + ran + ", balked " + balked + ", most counts at once: " + mostAtOnce); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l11.StockCountDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l11/StockCountDemo.java StockCountDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l11 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Balking: eight triggers fire at once, and the stock count refuses to start while one is already running. class StockCount { private val running = AtomicBoolean() fun runIfIdle(count: () -> Unit): Boolean { if (!running.compareAndSet(false, true)) return false // balk: a count is already running try { count() return true } finally { running.set(false) } } } fun main() { val stockCount = StockCount() val inside = AtomicInteger() val mostAtOnce = AtomicInteger() val ran = AtomicInteger() val balked = AtomicInteger() val count = { mostAtOnce.accumulateAndGet(inside.incrementAndGet(), ::maxOf) repeat(2_000_000) { Thread.onSpinWait() } // counting the shelves takes a moment inside.decrementAndGet() Unit } val go = CountDownLatch(1) val triggers = List(8) { // the closing-time timer, the manager's button, a retry... thread { go.await() if (stockCount.runIfIdle(count)) ran.incrementAndGet() else balked.incrementAndGet() } } go.countDown() triggers.forEach { it.join() } println("ran $ran, balked $balked, most counts at once: $mostAtOnce") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l11.StockCountDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l11/StockCountDemo.kt With compareAndSet, most counts at once is always 1, and usually ran 1, balked 7. With check-then-act, several triggers pass the check before any of them sets the flag, so most runs print 2 or 3 for most counts at once: two stock counts walking the same shelves at the same time. It is the race from the concurrency track, inside a pattern. ReentrantReadWriteLock.java at jdk-25-ga (no read-to-write upgrade) read

h: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together · Bulkhead: a fixed number of phone lines for each service
x: Virtual threads make threads cheap. They don't make the services the shop calls any bigger. A service here is another program the shop's program calls over the network, such as a courier's booking line or the shop's database. Pedal Post's booking line takes 20 calls at once, the database accepts 20 connections, and Big Blue Vans slows to a crawl above 50. A bulkhead caps how many calls run against one service at once, so a slow service can use up its own share and nothing else. The name comes from ships, where watertight walls keep one leak from flooding the whole hull. The shop's picture is a switchboard. Pedal Post has 20 phone lines. When all 20 are busy, a caller hears the busy tone at once and can try something else, instead of waiting on hold with the music. In code, the lines are the permits of a semaphore, a counter of permits that threads take and give back: Java final class Bulkhead { private final Semaphore permits; Bulkhead(int maxConcurrent) { permits = new Semaphore(maxConcurrent); } <T> T call(Supplier<T> op) { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) throw new BulkheadFull("all lines busy"); // busy tone: fail fast try { return op.get(); } finally { permits.release(); // always, or the shop loses a line for good } } } Kotlin class Bulkhead(maxConcurrent: Int) { private val permits = Semaphore(maxConcurrent) // kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore suspend fun <T> call(op: suspend () -> T): T { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) throw BulkheadFull("all lines busy") // busy tone: fail fast try { return op() } finally { permits.release() // always, or the shop loses a line for good } } } BulkheadDemo, in the Try it, sends 200 bookings that each take 20 ms through 20 lines, first waiting on hold (acquire()), then with the busy tone (tryAcquire()). One run, on a busy machine, printed: wait done 200, rejected 0, most at once 20, about 288 ms fail fast done 20, rejected 180, most at once 20, about 26 ms Correctness first: neither mode ever had more than 20 calls on the line. Then time. Waiting served all 200 in about ten rounds of 20, close to 300 ms. Failing fast answered every caller within about 26 ms, and 180 of them heard the busy tone. Your numbers will differ a little; the shape won't. tryAcquire() makes the bulkhead fail fast: a call over the limit gets an error at once instead of waiting behind the slow ones. acquire() waits, which turns the bulkhead into a limiter. That's fine for a job that runs at night, and risky for a customer at the counter, where waiting calls pile up until someone gives up. Size each bulkhead to its service, not to your threads. A bulkhead of 30 in front of a database with 20 connections still makes ten callers wait inside. With virtual threads, a semaphore is the natural limit, as in Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores, where the grill had room for 20 pans. The switchboard picture breaks when the call ends. A phone line frees itself when the caller hangs up. A permit comes back only if your code gives it back, which is why release() sits in finally: miss it once on an exception, and the shop has 19 lines for good. Give each service its own bulkhead, sized to what that service can take, and release in finally. A bulkhead limits how much a slow service can hurt the shop. A service that's down needs something stronger. Wait on hold, or hear the busy tone Run BulkheadDemo (Java or Kotlin). It sends 200 bookings that each take 20 ms through a 20-permit semaphore, first with acquire() (wait), then with tryAcquire() (fail fast). Predict both lines first. Change the semaphore from 20 permits to 200 and run again. Predict most at once before you look. Put it back to 20. BulkheadDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l11; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 200 virtual threads book a courier whose booking line takes at most 20 calls at once: wait for a free line, or fail fast. */ public class BulkheadDemo { static void run(String mode, boolean failFast) throws InterruptedException { Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(20); AtomicInteger onLine = new AtomicInteger(), mostOnLine = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicInteger done = new AtomicInteger(), rejected = new AtomicInteger(); long start = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) { ex.submit(() -> { if (failFast) { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) { rejected.incrementAndGet(); return null; } // bulkhead: busy tone, at once } else { permits.acquire(); // limiter: wait on hold } try { mostOnLine.accumulateAndGet(onLine.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); Thread.sleep(20); // a booking takes 20 ms onLine.decrementAndGet(); done.incrementAndGet(); } finally { permits.release(); } return null; }); } } // close() waits for all tasks long ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%-10s done %3d, rejected %3d, most at once %2d, about %d ms%n", mode, done.get(), rejected.get(), mostOnLine.get(), ms); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { run("wait", false); run("fail fast", true); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l11.BulkheadDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l11/BulkheadDemo.java BulkheadDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger // 200 coroutines book a courier whose booking line takes at most 20 calls at once: wait for a free line, or fail fast. suspend fun runBulkhead(mode: String, failFast: Boolean) { val permits = Semaphore(20) val onLine = AtomicInteger() val mostOnLine = AtomicInteger() val done = AtomicInteger() val rejected = AtomicInteger() val start = System.nanoTime() coroutineScope { // waits for all 200 children repeat(200) { launch { if (failFast) { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) { rejected.incrementAndGet(); return@launch } // bulkhead: busy tone, at once } else { permits.acquire() // limiter: wait on hold } try { mostOnLine.accumulateAndGet(onLine.incrementAndGet(), ::maxOf) delay(20) // a booking takes 20 ms onLine.decrementAndGet() done.incrementAndGet() } finally { permits.release() } } } } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000 println("%-10s done %3d, rejected %3d, most at once %2d, about %d ms".format(mode, done.get(), rejected.get(), mostOnLine.get(), ms)) } fun main() = runBlocking { runBulkhead("wait", failFast = false) runBulkhead("fail fast", failFast = true) } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l11.BulkheadDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l11/BulkheadDemo.kt Waiting: done 200, rejected 0, most at once 20, in a bit over 200 ms (ten rounds of 20). Fail fast: about done 20, rejected 180, in 20 to 30 ms. The exact split can vary slightly between runs. With 200 permits, most at once jumps to 200 in both modes: nothing protects the courier. Your times will differ a little from these. Resilience4j BulkheadConfig.java (defaults) read

h: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together · Circuit breaker: State, Decorator and compare-and-set in one class
x: A circuit breaker's three states live in one AtomicReference, and compare-and-set picks the single probe At ten o'clock, the Big Blue Vans booking service goes quiet. Every call hangs for two seconds and then fails, and the customers at the counter wait each time. The shop's back room has a fuse box with a circuit breaker: when something goes wrong in the wiring, it trips and cuts the power, so the fault can't do more damage. The software circuit breaker borrows the name. After a run of failures it opens, and calls fail at once without even trying the van company. After a cool-down, it goes half-open and lets one test call through, called a probe. Success closes it again; failure opens it for another cool-down. The breaker is this track's capstone, because it is three earlier patterns in one class. Its states are sealed records with a transition, as in State and Chain of Responsibility. Its call(op) wraps any operation and keeps its shape, as a decorator does in Decorator and Proxy. And its state lives in an AtomicReference, a holder for one object that threads can swap safely, and changes by compare-and-set, read as "update it only if nobody beat me to it", so a thousand threads can share it without a lock: Java sealed interface State permits Closed, Open, HalfOpen {} record Closed(int consecutiveFailures) implements State {} record Open(Instant until) implements State {} record HalfOpen() implements State {} private final AtomicReference<State> state = new AtomicReference<>(new Closed(0)); // after a failed call: one pure transition, applied atomically state.updateAndGet(cur -> switch (cur) { case HalfOpen h -> new Open(clock.instant().plus(openFor)); // the probe failed case Closed(var n) when n + 1 >= threshold -> new Open(clock.instant().plus(openFor)); // trip case Closed(var n) -> new Closed(n + 1); case Open o -> o; // already open }); Kotlin sealed interface State { data class Closed(val consecutiveFailures: Int) : State data class Open(val until: Instant) : State data object HalfOpen : State } private val state = AtomicReference<State>(State.Closed(0)) // after a failed call: one pure transition, applied atomically state.updateAndGet { cur -> when (cur) { State.HalfOpen -> State.Open(clock.instant() + openFor) // the probe failed is State.Closed if cur.consecutiveFailures + 1 >= threshold -> State.Open(clock.instant() + openFor) // trip is State.Closed -> State.Closed(cur.consecutiveFailures + 1) is State.Open -> cur // already open } } Two choices make it testable and correct. Time comes from a Clock passed in through the constructor, so a test can hand it a fake clock and move time forward 31 seconds at once instead of sleeping. And the move from open to half-open is a compareAndSet: when the cool-down ends and many threads arrive together, exactly one wins the right to probe, and the rest are still turned away. The figure shows the three states and the moves between them. The fuse box picture breaks in two places. A real breaker stays off until a person resets it; the software one tries again by itself after the cool-down. And a real breaker reacts to the current in the wire, while the software one only counts failures, so you must tell it which errors mean "the service is sick". A courier who answers "no vans free in your area" is working perfectly, and must not trip the breaker. Count only the failures that mean the service is sick, and let one probe, chosen by compare-and-set, decide when it has recovered. Check yourself. The breaker opened at 10:00:00 with a 30-second cool-down. A test moves the fake clock to 10:00:31, and eight threads call at the same moment. How many calls reach the van company, and what picks them? (One. Each thread tries the compareAndSet from Open to HalfOpen; exactly one succeeds and runs the probe. The other seven find the state already changed and are turned away.) The breaker's three states. Only one probe runs in half-open; its result decides whether the breaker closes or opens again. h: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together · Java and Kotlin
x: Guarded suspension: waiting for the courier to confirm a pickup PickupConfirmations.java // the counter's thread waits until the courier confirms the pickup, or gives up after a timeout final class PickupConfirmations { private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<String>> pending = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); String awaitConfirmation(String orderNo, Duration timeout) throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException, TimeoutException { CompletableFuture<String> slot = pending.computeIfAbsent(orderNo, no -> new CompletableFuture<>()); try { return slot.get(timeout.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // blocks this thread until completed } finally { pending.remove(orderNo); } } // the courier's message arrives on another thread; one that comes first is kept for the waiter void onConfirmation(String orderNo, String pickupRef) { pending.computeIfAbsent(orderNo, no -> new CompletableFuture<>()).complete(pickupRef); } } PickupConfirmations.kt // the counter's coroutine waits until the courier confirms the pickup, or gives up after a timeout class PickupConfirmations { private val pending = ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableDeferred<String>>() suspend fun awaitConfirmation(orderNo: String, timeout: Duration): String { val slot = pending.computeIfAbsent(orderNo) { CompletableDeferred() } try { return withTimeout(timeout) { slot.await() } // suspends: no thread is held while waiting } finally { pending.remove(orderNo) } } // the courier's message arrives elsewhere; one that comes first is kept for the waiter fun onConfirmation(orderNo: String, pickupRef: String) { pending.computeIfAbsent(orderNo) { CompletableDeferred() }.complete(pickupRef) } } Both replace the hand-written wait() in a while loop with a one-shot promise, which can't miss a signal or wake up by accident: complete happens once, and get or await returns as soon as it has. The difference is what waiting costs. CompletableFuture.get blocks a thread; on a virtual thread that is cheap, but it is still a thread per waiting order. CompletableDeferred.await suspends the coroutine and holds no thread at all, and withTimeout cancels the wait cleanly. Java needs three checked exceptions in the signature; Kotlin needs none, and the timeout arrives as a TimeoutCancellationException. One gap is shared: a confirmation that arrives after the waiter gave up leaves an entry in the map, so a real version also clears out old entries.

h: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together · Worked example
x: Put retry, breaker and bulkhead in the right order Three pieces from this lesson wrap one van booking. The order of the wrappers decides what happens on a bad morning. Before reading on: with the retry on the outside, what does each attempt do while the breaker is open? Supplier<String> book = () -> vans.book("order-7781", 2); // safe to repeat: the van company skips a second booking for 7781 Supplier<String> limited = () -> bulkhead.call(book); // innermost: caps the calls on the line Supplier<String> guarded = () -> breaker.call(limited); // then: stop calling a service that keeps failing String ref = retrying(3, guarded); // outermost: try again after a passing failure val book = Supplier { vans.book("order-7781", 2) } // safe to repeat: the van company skips a second booking for 7781 val limited = Supplier { bulkhead.call(book) } // innermost: caps the calls on the line val guarded = Supplier { breaker.call(limited) } // then: stop calling a service that keeps failing val ref = retrying(3) { guarded.get() } // outermost: try again after a passing failure Each attempt hits the open breaker and gets CallNotPermitted in microseconds, which costs the van company nothing. But a rejection isn't a passing failure, and retrying it is noise. Teach the retry to let the fail-fast signals through untouched. static <T> T retrying(int attempts, Supplier<T> body) { RuntimeException last = null; for (int i = 1; i <= attempts; i++) { try { return body.get(); } catch (CircuitBreaker.CallNotPermitted | Bulkhead.BulkheadFull e) { throw e; // 1. fail-fast signals: never retry them } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; // 2. a timeout or a dropped line: worth another try } } throw last; } inline fun <T> retrying(attempts: Int, body: () -> T): T { var last: RuntimeException? = null repeat(attempts) { try { return body() } catch (e: CircuitBreaker.CallNotPermitted) { throw e // 1. fail-fast signals: never retry them } catch (e: Bulkhead.BulkheadFull) { throw e } catch (e: RuntimeException) { last = e // 2. a timeout or a dropped line: worth another try } } throw last!! } Why is the bulkhead inside the breaker? An open breaker turns calls away before they reach the bulkhead, so a dead service never holds a line. Why is the retry outside? Each attempt is a separate breaker call, so three failed attempts count as three failures, and a van company that is really down trips the breaker within one or two bookings. A retry inside the breaker would hide those failures from it. what each layer sees for one booking while the van company is down: retry attempt 1 attempt 2 attempt 3 breaker Closed(0) -> (1) Closed(1) -> (2) Closed(2) -> Open (three failures trip it) bulkhead line, given back line, given back line, given back next booking: retry -> breaker turns it away at once (CallNotPermitted) -> no call, no line used Pin it in a test, with a fake van service that always fails and the lab's classes. The second booking must never reach the van company. AtomicInteger vanCalls = new AtomicInteger(); Supplier<String> failing = () -> { vanCalls.incrementAndGet(); throw new IllegalStateException("vans booking line down"); }; CircuitBreaker breaker = new CircuitBreaker(3, Duration.ofSeconds(30), clock); Bulkhead bulkhead = new Bulkhead(20); Supplier<String> pipeline = () -> breaker.call(() -> bulkhead.call(failing)); assertThatThrownBy(() -> retrying(3, pipeline)).hasMessage("vans booking line down"); // 3. first booking: 3 attempts assertThat(breaker.state()).isInstanceOf(CircuitBreaker.Open.class); assertThatThrownBy(() -> retrying(3, pipeline)).isInstanceOf(CircuitBreaker.CallNotPermitted.class); assertThat(vanCalls.get()).isEqualTo(3); // 4. the second never left val vanCalls = AtomicInteger() val failing = Supplier<String> { vanCalls.incrementAndGet(); throw IllegalStateException("vans booking line down") } val breaker = CircuitBreaker(3, Duration.ofSeconds(30), clock) val bulkhead = Bulkhead(20) val pipeline = { breaker.call { bulkhead.call(failing) } } assertThatThrownBy { retrying(3, pipeline) }.hasMessage("vans booking line down") // 3. first booking: 3 attempts assertThat(breaker.state()).isInstanceOf(CircuitBreaker.Open::class.java) assertThatThrownBy { retrying(3, pipeline) }.isInstanceOf(CircuitBreaker.CallNotPermitted::class.java) assertThat(vanCalls.get()).isEqualTo(3) // 4. the second never left

h: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together · Quiz
x: A Java program has four packer threads reading a BlockingQueue. After the last slip, the counter puts a single Closed card on the rail, then calls close() on the executor. What happens? All four packers stop, because they all see the card One packer stops and the other three keep packing new slips One packer stops, three wait in take() forever, and close() never returns The queue throws because a card was taken twice take() removes the card, so exactly one packer sees it. The other three wait for the next item, which never comes, and ExecutorService.close() waits for them. Put one card per packer, or in Kotlin close the channel, which ends every for loop. The shop's program runs on virtual threads and calls a courier whose booking line takes 50 calls at once. Which limit fits best? A semaphore of 50 around the courier call, with tryAcquire so extra calls fail fast A fixed pool of 50 ordinary threads for the whole program No limit: virtual threads are cheap A new CompletableFuture per call The limit belongs to the service, not to the program's threads, and with virtual threads a semaphore is the natural way to say it. A fixed pool of 50 throttles everything the program does, not just the bookings. "Virtual threads are cheap" is exactly how you send 5,000 calls to a courier who takes 50. In a unit test, a Resilience4j 2.4.0 circuit breaker built with the default settings fails five calls in a row, yet it stays CLOSED. Why? Resilience4j only counts checked exceptions as failures The default minimumNumberOfCalls is 100, so the failure rate isn't worked out yet Breakers only open after waitDurationInOpenState has passed The test needs a real clock With the defaults, the breaker needs at least 100 recorded calls before it works out a failure rate, so five failures change nothing. Set minimumNumberOfCalls and slidingWindowSize to small numbers in tests. All exceptions count as failures by default, and waitDurationInOpenState controls how long the breaker stays open, not when it opens. The shop's stock count runs at closing time and can also be started by the manager. If a count is already running, a second trigger should simply return. Which pattern is this? Guarded suspension Read-write lock Producer-consumer Balking Balking means: if the object isn't ready for the job, return at once instead of waiting. Guarded suspension is the opposite, waiting until the condition holds, which here would line up a second count behind the first. Build it with compareAndSet on an AtomicBoolean, and with a shared lock, such as one in the database, if it must be unique across copies of the program. From Atomics and compare-and-set: when the cool-down ends, many threads find the breaker Open with an expired until at the same moment. Why must the move to HalfOpen be a compareAndSet rather than a plain set? set is slower than compareAndSet So exactly one thread wins the right to probe; with set, every thread that saw the expired state would call the service AtomicReference doesn't allow set on records compareAndSet makes the call to the service atomic Each thread read the same Open state. compareAndSet(open, halfOpen) succeeds for the first thread only, because after that the state is no longer the Open object the others read, so their compare-and-set fails and they're turned away. A plain set lets all of them through to a service that may still be down. Compare-and-set makes the state change atomic, not the call itself.
