h: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together · Key terms
x: Producer-consumer Producers put work on a shared queue and consumers take it off; the queue does the locking and waiting. Poison pill A special item on a queue that tells one consumer to stop. Active object An object whose method calls become messages, run one at a time by its own thread or coroutine. Balking Returning at once, instead of waiting, when the object isn't ready, such as "already running". Guarded suspension Waiting until a condition holds, then going on: wait in a loop, or a future. Bulkhead A cap on the calls running against one service at once, so one slow service can't use up everything. Circuit breaker A wrapper that stops calling a failing service for a while, then probes to see if it has recovered. Half-open The breaker's state after the cool-down, where one probe call decides whether it closes or opens again. Why bound a producer-consumer queue? A full bounded queue makes producers wait, which is backpressure. An unbounded one hides a pile-up until memory runs out. N consumers stop on poison pills. How many pills? N, one per consumer: each take() removes one pill. In Kotlin, close() the channel instead. Balking or guarded suspension: which returns at once? Balking returns immediately if the object is busy. Guarded suspension waits until the condition holds. Bulkhead: tryAcquire or acquire? tryAcquire, so a call over the limit fails fast. acquire waits in line, which makes it a limiter. Release in finally either way. Circuit breaker: what happens in each state? Closed: calls pass and failures are counted. Open: calls are turned away at once. HalfOpen: one probe runs; success closes, failure opens again. Resilience4j 2.4.0 default minimumNumberOfCalls? A default breaker in a unit test that fails a handful of calls never opens. Which exceptions should a retry wrapper never retry? Fail-fast signals, such as CallNotPermitted and a full bulkhead, and any call that isn't safe to run twice.

h: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together · Go deeper
x: Resilience4j's breaker defaults, read from its source and printed by version 2.4.0: failureRateThreshold 50%, slowCallRateThreshold 100%, slowCallDurationThreshold 60 s, waitDurationInOpenState 60 s, permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState 10, minimumNumberOfCalls 100, and a count-based sliding window of 100 calls. Every exception counts as a failure unless you configure recordExceptions or ignoreExceptions. The project's README says Resilience4j 3 will require Java 21 and adds virtual-thread schedulers; it wasn't on Maven Central when this course was written, so the labs build the breaker by hand. Spring Framework 7, a widely used framework for Java web services, added @Retryable and @ConcurrencyLimit to its core, switched on with @EnableResilientMethods. @Retryable defaults to maxRetries = 3 after the first failure, so four attempts in total, with a one-second delay. Both work through proxies, so the self-call rule from Decorator and Proxy applies: a method that calls another method on this skips them. Structured concurrency is the future pattern with a lifetime. StructuredTaskScope starts subtasks, waits for them, and cancels the rest when one fails, so no subtask outlives the method that started it. It is still a preview API in JDK 25, 26 and 27 (run with --enable-preview), which is why it stays out of the labs. Kotlin's coroutineScope has worked this way from the start: an async that fails cancels its siblings, and the scope waits for every child. The patterns in this lesson have cousins that span several programs. A lock held in a shared database is balking across copies of a program. A queue server, a separate program that holds messages until other programs take them, is producer-consumer between programs. The questions stay the same: who owns the state, what waits, and what fails fast.

h: Modern Java data modeling
x: Records, sealed types, pattern matching and data-oriented programming, and where Project Valhalla is heading. By the end of this track you can model data the way modern Java intends. Picture the paperwork at a small town library: a loan slip in a clear sleeve, a request form with a fixed set of boxes to tick, a clerk who reads each form in one look, and a clerk at the door who checks everything that arrives from outside. Records, sealed types, pattern switches and data-oriented design are those four pictures in code. You'll know where each promise stops (shallow immutability, null, a subtype added after compilation), and you can say, with versions, what Project Valhalla has and hasn't shipped. Every lesson sets the Java feature next to its Kotlin counterpart, from data classes and sealed interfaces to when with guards and @JvmInline value class, and says plainly which side is better at what. You need only the syntax of both languages; the track starts from zero on records and sealed types. Install JDK 25. Records, sealed types, pattern switches and record patterns are all final in JDK 21, so the labs compile with --release 21. Anything newer is marked with its JDK: unnamed patterns (_) need JDK 22, flexible constructor bodies JDK 25, primitive patterns are still a preview, and value objects exist only as a preview in early-access builds of JDK 28. The labs live in labs/modernjava, one package per lesson (workbench.modernjava.l01 to l04), and they all use the library: its forms as records, its items as a sealed type, its loan rules as one switch, and a reply from the regional catalogue parsed into a closed model. Lessons 1 to 3 are in Java and lesson 4 is in Kotlin. Two of the lesson 2 tests run javac inside the test through javax.tools, so Gradle must run on a full JDK. Run ./gradlew :modernjava:test --tests 'workbench.modernjava.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, and ./gradlew :modernjava:solutionTest to run the same tests on the reference answers. Demos for newer JDKs sit in labs/modernjava/preview (run them with java preview/File.java), and two compile-it-yourself experiments sit in labs/modernjava/javac. A record is a final, transparent carrier, like a form in a clear sleeve: javac generates fields, accessors, one canonical constructor and the Object methods from the header, so they can't drift apart. The compact constructor is the counter every instance passes: new, factories, other constructors, withers and Java deserialization all go through it. Kotlin's init is the twin, but it can't tidy a parameter, and Java deserialization skips it. Records are only shallowly immutable and their generated methods read fields: copy collections with copyOf, and mask secrets in toString, not in the accessor. A sealed type names its permitted subtypes, like a form with a fixed set of boxes; each one is final, sealed or non-sealed. On the class path they must share a package. A concrete sealed parent is a value of its own. A switch over a sealed type with no default is checked by the compiler, so adding a subtype turns every forgotten switch into a compile error. A default hides it. Record patterns read several boxes in one look. Cases run in order, guards don't count toward exhaustiveness, and javac rejects dominated cases, which kotlinc doesn't. Exhaustive is a compile-time promise: null needs case null, and a subtype added after compilation makes an old switch throw MatchException. Data-oriented code models closed data as records and sealed types, checks outside data at the edge, and writes the rules as functions. New operations are cheap and new types are loud. Project Valhalla's value objects are a preview in JDK 28, not in 25 to 27. Records are identity objects; JEP 468 withers are on hold; null-restricted types are still drafts.

And with value objects, the JVM, not you, decides what gets printed onto the page, and only small forms qualify. Records Java public record Shelfmark(String section, int shelf) { public Shelfmark { // compact canonical constructor Objects.requireNonNull(section, "section"); section = section.trim().toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT); // reassign the parameter if (shelf < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("shelf must be 1 or more"); } // javac assigns the fields here public Shelfmark withShelf(int s) { return new Shelfmark(section, s); } // a wither } record Crate(String branch, List<String> titles) { Crate { titles = List.copyOf(titles); } } // defensive copy Kotlin data class Shelfmark(val section: String, val shelf: Int) { init { require(shelf >= 1) { "shelf must be 1 or more" } } // runs on every construction and copy() companion object { fun of(section: String, shelf: Int) = Shelfmark(section.trim().uppercase(), shelf) } // tidy here } val next = mark.copy(shelf = 13) // generated, shallow, runs init Generated: private final fields, accessors (section(), no get), one canonical constructor, equals, hashCode and toString. No instance fields in the body, no extends. Static members, methods and nested types are fine. Eight component names are forbidden, wait among them. equals compares every component: Objects.equals for references, compare for primitives (NaN equals NaN, 0.0 doesn't equal -0.0). Arrays compare by reference. Shallow: copy List, Set and Map components with copyOf, or a changed list loses its record in a HashSet. The generated methods read fields, not accessors. To hide a phone number, override toString. Java deserialization runs a record's canonical constructor. It skips a Kotlin data class's init, unless the class is @JvmRecord. Records are identity objects: == compares references, synchronized works. Sealed types Subtype modifier Meaning final (records and enums already are) no subtypes sealed ... permits ... a closed list one level down non-sealed open again; one case still covers the branch Rule Java Kotlin Where subtypes live same module; on the class path, same package same package and same module The list permits, or inferred from one source file whatever is declared in that package and module Concrete parent possible, and it's a value of its own: make it abstract a sealed class is always abstract Enforced by javac, and the JVM at load time (PermittedSubclasses) kotlinc; with a JDK 17+ target, the same class-file attribute Pattern switch Java return switch (loan) { case Loan(var m, Book(var format, var isNew), var b) when format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42; case Loan(var m, Book book, var b) -> 21; // unguarded: closes the Book family case Loan(var m, Disc disc, var b) -> 7; case Loan(Member member, Magazine mag, var b) -> 7; }; // no default over a sealed type Kotlin return when (val item = loan.item) { is Book if item.format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42 // guard: Kotlin 2.2+ is Book -> 21 is Disc -> 7 is Magazine -> 7 } Cases run top to bottom; the first match wins. Guards never count toward exhaustiveness. A null selector throws NullPointerException unless there is case null. default doesn't catch null. A nested type pattern (Point p) matches a null component; a nested record pattern (Point(var x, var y)) doesn't. An old program meeting a subtype or enum constant added later throws MatchException (Kotlin: NoWhenBranchMatchedException). Several patterns in one arm only with _: case Return _, Renew _ -> (JDK 22+). Kotlin destructuring val (a, b) = x goes by position and swaps silently. kotlinc has no dominance check. javac says It means the switch expression does not cover all possible input values a permitted subtype (or combination) has no unguarded case this case label is dominated by a preceding case label an earlier unguarded case already matches everything this one could illegal fall-through from a pattern several patterns with bindings in one arm class is not allowed to extend sealed class: X (as it is not listed in its 'permits' clause) a subtype missing from permits sealed, non-sealed or final modifiers expected a permitted subtype without its modifier class X in unnamed module cannot extend a sealed class in a different package split packages on the class path Data-oriented design checklist One record per valid combination, under a sealed interface. No shared bag of nullable fields. Constructors refuse bad values; the type system refuses bad shapes. Parse untrusted input once, at the edge, into the model or a rejection. Trust the types behind the edge. The rules are functions with one exhaustive switch each. Keep methods for open, plug-in hierarchies and for behavior about the value itself. Don't depend on record identity, so value (JDK 28 preview) can be a one-word change later.

h: Records: transparent carriers for data · A record is its components, and javac writes the rest
x: A record is its components and javac writes the rest; the canonical constructor is the one door every instance passes, and immutability stops at the list a field points to Start with a shelfmark, the label on a book's spine that says where the book lives: a three-letter section and a shelf number, such as FIC 12. Here it is the way Java classes were written for years, by hand. The shelf number was added later: Java public final class Shelfmark { private final String section; private final int shelf; // added later public Shelfmark(String section, int shelf) { this.section = section; this.shelf = shelf; } public String section() { return section; } public int shelf() { return shelf; } @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof Shelfmark s && s.section.equals(section); // nobody updated this } @Override public int hashCode() { return section.hashCode(); } @Override public String toString() { return "Shelfmark[section=" + section + "]"; } } Kotlin class Shelfmark(val section: String, val shelf: Int) { // shelf added later override fun equals(other: Any?) = other is Shelfmark && other.section == section // nobody updated this override fun hashCode() = section.hashCode() override fun toString() = "Shelfmark(section=$section)" } It compiles. The RecordAnatomy demo in the Try it keeps this class as OldShelfmark and runs it on two books on different shelves: by hand: OldShelfmark[section=FIC] equals OldShelfmark[section=FIC]: true Shelf 12 and shelf 40 now count as the same place, and the log line can't even say which shelf it meant. The class states "these fields are the data" in five places: the fields, the constructor, equals, hashCode and toString. Five copies of one list drifted apart, the way paperwork does when nobody owns it. A record states it once. A record is a class whose header lists its components, the values that make up its data, and javac, the Java compiler, writes everything else from that list: Java public record Shelfmark(String section, int shelf) {} Kotlin data class Shelfmark(val section: String, val shelf: Int) Here is the picture we'll use for the whole track: library paperwork. A record is a filled-in form in a clear sleeve. Each component is one box on the form, and what you see through the sleeve is all there is: no notes on the back, no hidden boxes. Comparing two forms means comparing them box by box. Reading a form aloud means reading every box, in order. javac turns that one line into the parts we used to type. Each component gets a private final field and a public accessor, a method named after the component that returns it: section() and shelf(), with no get. The canonical constructor takes every component, in header order. equals, hashCode and toString use every component, so they can't drift. The class is final and extends java.lang.Record. Records have been a final feature, that is, finished and switched on, since JDK 16 (JEP 395, the JDK Enhancement Proposal that describes them). So all of this works on the JDK 21 the labs compile for. Five copies of one list drift apart. Write the list once, in the header. The Record Javadoc calls a record "a shallowly immutable, transparent carrier for a fixed set of values", and each word is a rule. Fixed: you can't add instance fields, and private int cache; in the body fails with field declaration must be static. Static fields, methods and nested types are fine. Transparent: the state is the API, so every component is public through its accessor. A record can implement interfaces, but it can't extend a class, because it already extends Record. Shallowly immutable gets its own section below. The generated methods aren't what you would write by hand, and you can see that one level down. javap, the JDK's class-file reader, shows that equals, hashCode and toString are each one invokedynamic instruction. That is a call whose target the JVM, the program that runs your Java code, picks the first time the call runs, by asking a bootstrap method, here ObjectMethods.bootstrap. javac hands it the component names as one string, section;shelf, and a getter for each private field, and the JDK builds the method bodies from that list. That's why the Javadoc says the toString format may change: never parse it. kotlinc, the Kotlin compiler, does it the older way and writes the bodies into your class. A record is still an ordinary object with its own identity: every new makes a separate one. Two forms with the same boxes are still two sheets of paper, so new Shelfmark("FIC", 12) == new Shelfmark("FIC", 12) is false, and synchronized on a record works. Objects without identity are what Project Valhalla adds, as a preview in JDK 28 (a preview feature is switched off unless you ask for it, and may still change). Lesson 4 of this track covers it. javac now prints every box on the form. It doesn't yet check what anybody writes in them. Look inside a record Run RecordAnatomy (or its Kotlin twin) with the command below. Predict the == line before you look. From labs/, print the bytecode of the nested record: javap -p -c 'modernjava/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/modernjava/l01/demo/RecordAnatomy$Shelfmark.class'. Find the three invokedynamic lines. Run javap -v on the same file and look for BootstrapMethods. Then run javap -p modernjava/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/modernjava/l01/demo/Shelfmark.class and compare what kotlinc generated. RecordAnatomy.java package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo; import java.util.Arrays; /** What javac gives a one-line record, seen from the outside. */ public class RecordAnatomy { // Naive: written by hand. The shelf was added later, and not to every method. static final class OldShelfmark { private final String section; private final int shelf; // added later OldShelfmark(String section, int shelf) { this.section = section; this.shelf = shelf; } String section() { return section; } int shelf() { return shelf; } @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof OldShelfmark s && s.section.equals(section); // nobody updated this } @Override public int hashCode() { return section.hashCode(); } @Override public String toString() { return "OldShelfmark[section=" + section + "]"; } } record Shelfmark(String section, int shelf) {} public static void main(String[] args) { OldShelfmark old12 = new OldShelfmark("FIC", 12), old40 = new OldShelfmark("FIC", 40); System.out.println("by hand: " + old12 + " equals " + old40 + ": " + old12.equals(old40)); Shelfmark a = new Shelfmark("FIC", 12); Shelfmark b = new Shelfmark("FIC", 12); System.out.println("toString: " + a); System.out.println("accessors: section()=" + a.section() + " shelf()=" + a.shelf()); System.out.println("equals: " + a.equals(b) + ", same hashCode: " + (a.hashCode() == b.hashCode())); System.out.println("==: " + (a == b) + " (two objects, each with its own identity)"); System.out.println("isRecord: " + Shelfmark.class.isRecord()); System.out.println("components: " + Arrays.toString(Shelfmark.class.getRecordComponents())); System.out.println("superclass: " + Shelfmark.class.getSuperclass().getName()); synchronized (a) { // compiles and runs: a record is an ordinary identity object System.out.println("locked on a record"); } } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l01.demo.RecordAnatomy labs/modernjava/src/demo/java/workbench/modernjava/l01/demo/RecordAnatomy.java RecordAnatomy.kt package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo // Naive: written by hand. h: Records: transparent carriers for data · The compact constructor: one counter every instance passes
x: A form is only as good as the counter that checks it. Suppose the checks live in a static factory, Shelfmark.of(...). It can check the section all it likes, and new Shelfmark("fiction!", -3) walks straight past it, through the side door. A record gives you a counter with no side door. Every other constructor must call the canonical constructor first, with this(...), and so does every factory and every wither. That makes the canonical constructor the one place to check and tidy every instance. You write it in the compact form, with no parameter list: Java record Shelfmark(String section, int shelf) { Shelfmark { // the compact canonical constructor Objects.requireNonNull(section, "section"); if (shelf < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("shelf must be 1 or more: " + shelf); section = section.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT); // reassign the parameter } // javac assigns the fields here Shelfmark(String section) { this(section, 1); } // any other constructor calls it first } Kotlin data class Shelfmark(val section: String, val shelf: Int) { init { // runs on every construction, and on copy() require(shelf >= 1) { "shelf must be 1 or more: $shelf" } require(section == section.uppercase()) { "section must be upper case: $section" } } constructor(section: String) : this(section, 1) // any other constructor calls it first } Read the compact constructor as the clerk at the counter. First it rejects a missing section, then it checks the shelf, and finally it tidies the writing, so "fic" becomes "FIC". In the compact form the parameters are ordinary local variables. You may reassign them, and javac copies their final values into the fields after your code runs. The clerk can't stamp the fields directly: this.shelf = shelf; fails with cannot assign a value to final variable shelf. The second constructor shows the rule for side doors: it must start with this(section, 1). On JDK 21, any statement before that line fails with constructor is not canonical, so its first statement must invoke another constructor of class Shelfmark. JDK 25 made flexible constructor bodies final (JEP 513), so there you may run plain statements first, such as splitting the label "fic 12" in two, as long as they don't touch the fields. The Kotlin twin shows a real difference. init runs on every construction, including copy(). But a data class can't change a constructor parameter before it becomes a property. It can reject "fic", but it can't turn it into "FIC". Tidying moves into a factory function, and the public constructor still accepts the raw value. The last door is deserialization, which rebuilds an object from bytes, for example bytes read back from a file. The Record Javadoc says the canonical constructor runs during deserialization, so a record gets its checks there for free. An ordinary class needs a hand-written readObject method to check itself again, and most classes don't have one. A Kotlin data class doesn't run its init there at all, unless it's marked @JvmRecord, which compiles it to a real record. The demo in the Try it swaps two numbers inside the bytes of a PageRange, a request to photocopy pages 1 to 5, and reads it back. The Java record prints tampered stream rejected: first > last: 5 > 1. The Kotlin twin prints: tampered stream gave: PageRangeK(first=5, last=1) tampered stream rejected: first > last: 5 > 1 The plain data class climbed in through a window: it came back as a range its own init forbids. The @JvmRecord version went past the clerk like everyone else. A check that some paths skip is only a suggestion. Put it in the canonical constructor. The clerk checks what's written in every box. The clerk can't see a sheet stapled to the form that somebody is still writing on. Go through every door Run CompactConstructorDemo. Read the last line of output before you read the code that produced it. Run the Kotlin twin, CompactConstructorDemoKt. Which tampered page range got through? In the Java demo, add this.shelf = shelf; inside the compact constructor of Shelfmark and run again. Read the compiler error, then undo the change. If you have JDK 25, run java preview/FlexibleConstructor.java from labs/modernjava. Then run the same file with JDK 21 and read the two errors. Shelfmark(String section) { this(section, 1); } // non-canonical: must delegate static Shelfmark parse(String label) { // a factory: still goes through it String[] parts = label.trim().split(" "); return new Shelfmark(parts[0], Integer.parseInt(parts[1])); } } // a request to photocopy pages first to last of a book record PageRange(int first, int last) implements Serializable { PageRange { if (first > last) throw new IllegalArgumentException("first > last: " + first + " > " + last); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println(new Shelfmark("fic", 12)); System.out.println(new Shelfmark("bio")); System.out.println(Shelfmark.parse("ref 7")); try { new Shelfmark("FIC", 0); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("IAE: " + h: Records: transparent carriers for data · Equality and immutability go one level deep
x: Start with what equals compares. Two records are equal when they're the same record class and every component is equal. For a reference component that means Objects.equals. For a primitive it means the wrapper's compare method returns 0, which holds two surprises for a double. A record holding NaN, the "not a number" value, equals another one holding NaN, though NaN == NaN is false. And records holding 0.0 and -0.0 aren't equal, though 0.0 == -0.0 is true. Kotlin data classes behave the same way. Arrays are worse. An int[] component compares by reference, so two records with equal arrays aren't equal, and toString prints something like [I@1b6d3586. Use a List instead. A List component brings the real trap. Picture a form with a box that says "see attached list", and a list stapled behind it. The form is checked and stamped, but whoever kept a copy of the attached sheet can still write on it. A record holds a reference to whatever list the caller passed in. Here a crate of books is on its way to the North branch, and the program keeps the crates it sent in a set: Java // a crate of books on its way to a branch library record Crate(String branch, List<String> titles) {} var titles = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Dune", "Emma")); var crate = new Crate("NORTH", titles); var sent = new HashSet<>(Set.of(crate)); titles.add("Ulysses"); // someone reuses their list sent.contains(crate); // false: the hashCode changed under the set Kotlin // a crate of books on its way to a branch library data class Crate(val branch: String, val titles: List<String>) val titles = mutableListOf("Dune", "Emma") val crate = Crate("NORTH", titles) val sent = hashSetOf(crate) titles += "Ulysses" // someone reuses their list crate in sent // false: the hashCode changed under the set The ShallowDemo in the Try it prints: crate now: Crate[branch=NORTH, titles=[Dune, Emma, Ulysses]] hashCode changed: true sent.contains: false The crate is still in the set. The set just looks for it in the wrong place: a HashSet files each element under its hashCode, and that number changed after the crate was filed. Nothing threw. The fix is one line in the compact constructor: Java record SafeCrate(String branch, List<String> titles) { SafeCrate { titles = List.copyOf(titles); } // an unmodifiable copy of the caller's list } Kotlin data class SafeCrate(val branch: String, val titles: List<String>) { companion object { // Kotlin can't reassign the parameter fun of(branch: String, titles: List<String>) = SafeCrate(branch, java.util.List.copyOf(titles)) } } List.copyOf makes an unmodifiable copy, and it throws NullPointerException for a null element, which is what you want for library data. Kotlin's List<String> is a read-only view, not an immutable list: the caller may still hold the same object as a MutableList. So a data class needs the same copy, made in a factory. Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal in the concurrency track made this point about threads. Here the cost is a lost crate, even with one thread. A record is only as immutable as its components. Copy collections on the way in. The last trap looks like a fix. To keep a member's phone number out of the logs, someone overrides the accessor, so phone() returns ****0123. The demo prints accessor: ****0123 and then toString: Masked[phone=01614960123]. The generated toString reads the field directly (those were the getters in the bootstrap arguments), so the logs never ask the accessor. The override breaks a promise in the Record Javadoc too: a copy built from the accessors, new Masked(m.phone()), should equal m, and the demo prints false. To hide a component, override toString itself, as the lab does. Every slip is now checked at the counter and safe from other people's pens. Which leaves a fair question: how do you change one? Lose a crate, leak a phone number Predict the sent.contains line, then run ShallowDemo. Give Crate a compact constructor that copies its list, as SafeCrate does. Run it again. Run the Kotlin twin and look at the copy shares list line. Did copy() copy the list? } // unmodifiable copy } record Masked(String phone) { @Override public String phone() { return "****" + phone.substring(phone.length() - 4); } } record Rating(double stars) {} public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> titles = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Dune", "Emma")); Crate crate = new Crate("NORTH", titles); Set<Crate> sent = new HashSet<>(Set.of(crate)); int before = crate.hashCode(); titles.add("Ulysses"); // someone reuses their list System.out.println("crate now: " + crate); System.out.println("hashCode changed: " + (before != crate.hashCode())); System.out.println("sent.contains: " + sent.contains(crate)); List<String> titles2 = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Dune", "Emma")); SafeCrate safe = new SafeCrate("SOUTH", titles2); titles2.add("Ulysses"); System.out.println("safe crate: " + safe); Masked m = new Masked("01614960123"); System.out.println("accessor: " + m.phone()); System.out.println("toString: " + m); System.out.println("copy equals orig: " + new Masked(m.phone()).equals(m)); System.out.println("NaN record equals: " + new Rating(Double.NaN).equals(new Rating(Double.NaN)) + " (but NaN == NaN is " + (Double.NaN == Double.NaN) + ")"); System.out.println("0.0 vs -0.0 equals: " + new Rating(0.0).equals(new Rating(-0.0)) + " (but 0.0 == -0.0 is " + (0.0 == -0.0) + ")"); } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l01.demo.ShallowDemo labs/modernjava/src/demo/java/workbench/modernjava/l01/demo/ShallowDemo.java ShallowDemo.kt package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo // List<String> is a read-only view in Kotlin, not an immutable list: the caller may still hold a MutableList data class Crate(val branch: String, val titles: List<String>) // Kotlin can't reassign a constructor parameter, so the defensive copy goes in a factory data class SafeCrate(val branch: String, val titles: List<String>) { companion object { fun of(branch: String, titles: List<String>) = SafeCrate(branch, java.util.List.copyOf(titles)) } } data class Rating(val stars: Double) /** Equality, hashCode and toString are only as deep as the properties. */ fun main() { val titles = mutableListOf("Dune", "Emma") val crate = Crate("NORTH", titles) val sent = hashSetOf(crate) val before = crate.hashCode() titles += "Ulysses" // someone reuses their list println("crate now: $crate") println("hashCode changed: ${before != crate.hashCode()}") println("sent.contains: ${crate in sent}") val copy = crate.copy(branch = "SOUTH") // copy() is shallow too titles += "Persuasion" println("copy shares list: $copy") val titles2 = mutableListOf("Dune", "Emma") val safe = SafeCrate.of("SOUTH", titles2) titles2 += "Ulysses" println("safe crate: $safe") println("NaN data class ==: ${Rating(Double.NaN) == Rating(Double.NaN)} (but NaN == NaN is ${Double.NaN == Double.NaN})") println("0.0 vs -0.0 ==: ${Rating(0.0) == Rating(-0.0)} (but 0.0 == -0.0 is ${0.0 == -0.0})") } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l01.demo.ShallowDemoKt labs/modernjava/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/modernjava/l01/demo/ShallowDemo.kt hashCode changed: true and sent.contains: false. After your fix the crate keeps its two titles, the hash code stays the same, and the set finds it. The masked record prints accessor: ****0123 but toString: Masked[phone=01614960123], and copy equals orig: false. The NaN records are equal and the 0.0 and -0.0 ones are not. In Kotlin, the copy shows Persuasion, which was added after the copy was made: copy() copies references, not the objects behind them.

h: Records: transparent carriers for data · Changing a record: withers in Java, copy() in Kotlin
x: You don't change a stamped form. You fill in a new one, and it goes past the counter again. A renewal is exactly that: the same loan, with a new number of days. Kotlin generates copy() for this, with a named parameter for each property. Java generates nothing, so you write a wither, a method that returns a copy of the record with one component changed: Java record Loan(String memberId, int days, List<String> titles) { Loan { if (days <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("days must be positive: " + days); titles = List.copyOf(titles); } Loan withDays(int newDays) { // a wither, written by hand return new Loan(memberId, newDays, titles); // through the canonical constructor } } Loan renewed = first.withDays(35); Kotlin data class LoanRequest(val memberId: String, val days: Int, val titles: List<String>) { init { require(days > 0) { "days must be positive: $days" } } } val renewed = first.copy(days = 35) // generated, and it runs init Both go through the checks, and that's the point. The WitherDemo ends with wither ran the checks: days must be positive: -1, and its Kotlin twin with the same message from copy(), so there's no path to an invalid loan. Both also print same titles list object: true: a wither and copy() reuse the component references. That's safe here only because the record made its own unmodifiable copy at the counter. The cost on the Java side is typing, and it grows with the record. In a 2020 design draft, Brian Goetz, Java's language architect, noted that a class has one getter per component but "could conceivably have O(2^n) withers". He asked that hand-written withers not become a best practice. Write withers only for the changes your domain really makes. A loan earns withDays; a shelfmark probably needs none. A language fix exists on paper. JEP 468, derived record creation, proposes loan with { days = 35; }. It would take the record apart, run the block, and call the canonical constructor with the result. It's a Candidate JEP, no JDK has it, and in January 2026 Goetz wrote that it "has been 'on hold' for a while". Don't plan around it. The other differences between the two languages matter more day to day. A data class may declare properties in its body, and Kotlin leaves those out of equals, hashCode, toString and copy(), so two objects that differ only there are equal. A record can't have body state at all. A data class can't be open, abstract or sealed, and a record is always final. Kotlin takes a data class apart with val (section, shelf) = mark, through generated componentN() functions. Java takes a record apart with record patterns, which lesson 3 of this track covers. Where the two languages meet, Kotlin reads a Java record's accessors as properties, mark.section. @JvmRecord on a data class emits a real java.lang.Record, which Java code sees as one. The Kotlin docs warn that adding @JvmRecord to an existing class isn't a binary-compatible change, so decide when you create the class. Records have one honest limit. A record can't hide its representation or keep any state beyond its components. A class that needs one private cache, or an inside different from its outside, falls back to writing all five places by hand. Goetz's design note on carrier classes, in Go deeper, sketches a way back. Wither versus copy() Run WitherDemo and its twin WitherDemoKt. Compare the four lines each prints. Add a withMemberId(String id) wither to the Java record and call it with " ". Should that be rejected? Add the check where every wither will get it. In WitherDemo.kt, add var note = "" to the body of LoanRequest, set first.note = "renewed by phone", and print first == first.copy() and first.copy().note. titles = List.copyOf(titles); } Loan withDays(int newDays) { return new Loan(memberId, newDays, titles); } Loan withTitle(String extra) { var more = new ArrayList<>(titles); more.add(extra); return new Loan(memberId, days, more); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Loan first = new Loan("M-1042", 21, List.of("Dune")); Loan renewed = first.withDays(35).withTitle("Emma"); System.out.println("original: " + first); System.out.println("changed: " + renewed); System.out.println("same titles list object: " + (first.titles() == first.withDays(14).titles())); try { first.withDays(-1); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("wither ran the checks: " + e.getMessage()); } } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l01.demo.WitherDemo labs/modernjava/src/demo/java/workbench/modernjava/l01/demo/WitherDemo.java WitherDemo.kt package workbench.modernjava.l01.demo // Kotlin generates copy(): one "wither" with a named, defaulted parameter per property data class LoanRequest(val memberId: String, val days: Int, val titles: List<String>) { init { require(days > 0) { "days must be positive: $days" } } } /** copy() runs init, and like a Java wither it copies references, not what they point to. */ fun main() { val first = LoanRequest("M-1042", 21, listOf("Dune")) val renewed = first.copy(days = 35, titles = first.titles + "Emma") println("original: $first") println("changed: $renewed") println("same titles list object: ${first.titles === first.copy(days = 14).titles}") try { first.copy(days = -1) } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("copy ran the checks: ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l01.demo.WitherDemoKt labs/modernjava/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/modernjava/l01/demo/WitherDemo.kt Both versions print the original loan, the renewed one with 35 days and two titles, same titles list object: true, and a rejected days must be positive: -1. h: Records: transparent carriers for data · Java and Kotlin
x: A checked shelfmark in Java and Kotlin Shelfmark.java public record Shelfmark(String section, int shelf) { private static final Pattern SECTION = Pattern.compile("[A-Z]{3}"); public Shelfmark { Objects.requireNonNull(section, "section"); section = section.trim().toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT); // tidy in place if (!SECTION.matcher(section).matches()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad section: " + section); if (shelf < 1 || shelf > 999) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad shelf: " + shelf); } public Shelfmark next() { return new Shelfmark(section, shelf + 1); // past the counter again } } Shelfmark.kt data class Shelfmark(val section: String, val shelf: Int) { init { require(SECTION.matches(section)) { "bad section: $section" } // can reject, can't tidy require(shelf in 1..999) { "bad shelf: $shelf" } } fun next() = Shelfmark(section, shelf + 1) // past init again companion object { private val SECTION = Regex("[A-Z]{3}") fun of(section: String, shelf: Int) = Shelfmark(section.trim().uppercase(), shelf) } } Both give you equals, hashCode and toString over all components, final fields, and a check that every construction goes through, including Kotlin's copy(). Three things differ. Java's compact constructor can tidy a parameter before it becomes a field; a data class can only reject it, so tidying lives in a factory and the public constructor stays open to raw input. Java deserialization rebuilds a record through its canonical constructor but skips a data class's init (@JvmRecord closes that gap). And Kotlin has copy() with named arguments, while Java has hand-written withers until JEP 468 ships, which it hasn't.

h: Records: transparent carriers for data · Worked example
x: Turn a hand-written membership form into a record When someone joins the library, the program fills in a membership form. Here it is as a JavaBean, a class with a getter and a setter for every field. It hands out its live list of branches, and its hand-written equals and toString weren't updated when the phone number was added. Any code can change a form after it was checked. public class MembershipForm { private String name; private String phone; private List<String> branches = new ArrayList<>(); public void setPhone(String phone) { this.phone = phone; } public List<String> getBranches() { return branches; } // hands out the live list // ... more setters and getters, and equals, hashCode, toString by hand } class MembershipForm { var name: String? = null var phone: String? = null val branches: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf() // hands out the live list } Write the header. The components are the whole state, and every setter is gone. Recompile: each place that called a setter is now a compile error, which is your list of code that changed a form after it was filled in. // 1. the components are the state public record MembershipForm(String name, PhoneNumber phone, List<String> branches) {} // 1. the properties are the state data class MembershipForm(val name: String, val phone: PhoneNumber, val branches: List<String>) Add the compact constructor. Reject what can't be valid, then copy the list so the caller can't change it later. phone is a PhoneNumber, the lab's record that checks itself, so the form doesn't repeat those checks. public record MembershipForm(String name, PhoneNumber phone, List<String> branches) { public MembershipForm { Objects.requireNonNull(name, "name"); // 2. reject Objects.requireNonNull(phone, "phone"); if (name.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("blank name"); branches = List.copyOf(branches); // 3. copy if (branches.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("no home branch"); } } data class MembershipForm(val name: String, val phone: PhoneNumber, val branches: List<String>) { init { require(name.isNotBlank()) { "blank name" } // 2. reject require(branches.isNotEmpty()) { "no home branch" } } companion object { fun of(name: String, phone: PhoneNumber, branches: List<String>) = MembershipForm(name, phone, java.util.List.copyOf(branches)) // 3. copy } } Add only the wither the library needs. Members do change their phone numbers, so withPhone earns its place. It calls the canonical constructor, so a changed form can't skip the checks. In Kotlin, copy(phone = ...) already exists and runs init. // 4. one wither, through the canonical constructor public MembershipForm withPhone(PhoneNumber newPhone) { return new MembershipForm(name, newPhone, branches); } // 4. no wither to write: copy() is generated and runs init val updated = form.copy(phone = PhoneNumber("0161 496 0999"))

h: Records: transparent carriers for data · Quiz
x: record Crate(String branch, List<String> titles) is a key in a HashMap<Crate, String> that records where each crate is. The code that built the crate later calls titles.add("Persuasion") on its own list. What does map.get(crate) most likely return now? The location, because records are immutable null, because the key's hashCode changed and the map looks in the wrong bucket It throws ConcurrentModificationException The location, because HashMap compares record keys with == The record's fields are final, but the list they point to is the caller's list. hashCode includes the list, so it changes, and the map searches a bucket where the entry isn't. Nothing throws. Copying the list in the compact constructor prevents it. Which of these makes new Shelfmark("fic", 12) equal to new Shelfmark("FIC", 12)? public Shelfmark { this.section = section.toUpperCase(); } public String section() { return section.toUpperCase(); } public Shelfmark { section = section.toUpperCase(); } public Shelfmark(String section, int shelf) { section = section.toUpperCase(); } In the compact form you reassign the parameter and javac assigns the field afterwards. Assigning this.section there doesn't compile. The accessor override leaves the fields different, and equals compares fields. The full canonical constructor in the last option never assigns the fields, so it doesn't compile either. A Kotlin data class PageRange(val first: Int, val last: Int) : Serializable checks first <= last in init. A program deserializes a tampered stream that says first = 5, last = 1. What happens? You get PageRange(first=5, last=1): Java deserialization doesn't run init InvalidObjectException, because init runs during deserialization IllegalArgumentException from require ClassCastException, because the stream no longer matches the class Java deserialization builds a plain serializable class without calling its constructor, so init never runs and the invalid object comes back. A Java record, or the same data class marked @JvmRecord, is rebuilt through its canonical constructor, and the stream is rejected with InvalidObjectException. From the memory model track: record OpeningHours(Map<String, String> days) copies the map with Map.copyOf in its compact constructor. A new OpeningHours is published through a plain, non-volatile field. What is guaranteed for a thread that reads the new reference? Nothing: without volatile it may see a null map It may see a half-built map Nothing, because records have no final fields It sees the map as the constructor left it, because record fields are final, though it may keep reading the old reference for a while Record fields are private final, so final-field rules apply: a thread that sees the reference sees the fields, and the map built in the constructor, as the constructor left them. A plain field doesn't promise when the new reference becomes visible. Publish it through a volatile field if readers must see updates promptly. data class Copy(val isbn: String) { var shelf = "FIC 12" }. Copy a sits on shelf FIC 12. Copy b has the same ISBN and sits on REF 3. What is a == b? false, because the shelves differ true It doesn't compile: data classes can't have body properties It depends on which object was created first Only primary-constructor properties take part in a data class's equals, hashCode, toString and copy(). shelf lives in the body, so Kotlin ignores it. A Java record can't have body state at all, so the question can't arise there.

h: Records: transparent carriers for data · Key terms
x: Record component One of the values in a record's header, like one box on a form. Each one gets a private final field and a public accessor. Canonical constructor The constructor whose parameters match the components in order. Every other way of making the record goes through it. Compact constructor The canonical constructor written without a parameter list. Its parameters are locals you can check and reassign; javac assigns the fields at the end. Accessor The generated public method that returns a component. It's named after the component: section(), not getSection(). Shallow immutability The fields can't be reassigned, but the objects they point to may still change. Wither A method that returns a copy of a record with one component changed. Java has no generated ones. @JvmRecord A Kotlin annotation that compiles a data class to a real java.lang.Record. What does javac generate for record Shelfmark(String section, int shelf)? Private final fields, accessors section() and shelf(), a canonical constructor Shelfmark(String, int), and equals, hashCode and toString. The class is final and extends java.lang.Record. In a compact constructor, how do you tidy a component? Reassign the parameter: section = section.trim();. javac assigns the fields after the body. this.section = ... doesn't compile. A record overrides its accessor to mask a phone number. What does toString print? The full number. The generated toString, equals and hashCode read the fields, not the accessors. Override toString instead. record R(double d): is new R(Double.NaN).equals(new R(Double.NaN)) true? Yes. Primitive components compare with Double.compare, which treats NaN as equal to itself. And 0.0 doesn't equal -0.0. How do you make a record with a List component safe as a map key? Copy it in the compact constructor: titles = List.copyOf(titles);. The copy is unmodifiable and rejects null elements. Does Java deserialization run a Kotlin data class's init block? No, so a tampered stream can build an invalid object. A Java record, or a data class marked @JvmRecord, is rebuilt through its canonical constructor. Can you write loan with { days = 35; } in Java today? No. Derived record creation (JEP 468) is a Candidate JEP, on hold since at least January 2026, and in no JDK. Write withers by hand.

h: Records: transparent carriers for data · Go deeper
x: Two details round out the picture. A Java record can't hide its canonical constructor. The Record Javadoc says it "must provide at least as much access as the record class", and javac enforces it: Java public record Key(String v) { private Key { } } // error: invalid canonical constructor in record Key // (attempting to assign stronger access privileges; was public) Kotlin data class Key private constructor(val v: String) { companion object { fun of(raw: String) = Key(raw.trim()) } } // warning (Kotlin 2.4): non-public primary constructor is exposed via the generated 'copy()' method So in Java, the checks must live inside the constructor, where nobody can bypass them. Kotlin lets you make a data class constructor private and send callers through a factory that tidies, but copy() still exposes it. Kotlin 2.4.21 warns about this, says the warning becomes an error in language version 2.5, and offers @ConsistentCopyVisibility to make copy() as private as the constructor. The second detail is about what comes after records. In a January 2026 design note, "Data-Oriented Programming for Java: Beyond Records", Brian Goetz describes the cliff you fall off when a class is almost a record: one derived field or one private cache, and you're back to writing everything by hand. The note sketches carrier classes, written like class Point(int x, int y) { ... }: a normal class with a record-style state description. The language would require the canonical constructor and the accessors and give the class a deconstruction pattern, while the class declares its own fields and need not be final. It's a design note, and no JEP exists yet, so treat it as a direction for now.

h: Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check · A sealed type closes the list of direct subtypes
x: A sealed type puts its list of subtypes into the type, so javac checks every switch, and a new subtype breaks each one without a default Start with the requests a member can make at the desk: borrow a book, renew a loan, return it. Written as an ordinary interface, Request has three implementations today. Any class in any package can add a fourth, say a Donate next week, and it compiles. Every if/else chain that handles requests skips the newcomer without a word and lands in its final else. Before JDK 17, the only fix was a trick: an abstract class with a package-private constructor, so that only classes in its own package can extend it. That closes the list, but the compiler still doesn't know what's on it, so it can't check a switch against it. A sealed type is a class or interface that names its permitted subtypes, the only classes allowed to extend it directly. Add sealed and a permits clause, and the list becomes part of the type: Java public sealed interface Request permits Borrow, Renew, Return {} public record Borrow(String isbn, int days) implements Request {} public record Renew(int extraDays) implements Request {} public record Return() implements Request {} Kotlin sealed interface Request { data class Borrow(val isbn: String, val days: Int) : Request data class Renew(val extraDays: Int) : Request data object Return : Request } In the paperwork picture, a sealed type is a form with a fixed set of boxes to tick. The boxes are printed on the form, so the clerk knows every possible answer. Sealed classes and interfaces have been a standard feature since JDK 17 (JEP 409, the JDK Enhancement Proposal that added them). javac, the Java compiler, checks the list from both sides. Uncomment Donate in the SealedBasics demo without adding it to the list, and javac stops: error: class is not allowed to extend sealed class: Request (as it is not listed in its 'permits' clause) javac also writes the list into the class file, as a PermittedSubclasses attribute, a small table the JVM (the program that runs Java code) reads when it loads a class. So the JVM checks it too: a class compiled against an older, unsealed Request fails to load with IncompatibleClassChangeError next to the sealed one. Nobody gets to scribble a fifth box in the margin. You can leave permits out when every subtype is declared in the same source file. javac then takes the subtypes it finds there. Reflection, the API a program uses to look at its own classes, shows the result: Request.class.isSealed() is true, and getPermittedSubclasses() returns the three records. Kotlin has no permits clause. Its rule is location: any class in the same package and the same module may extend a sealed type. So class Donate : Request in that package compiles, and the list grows by itself. The same line in another package fails with a class can only extend a sealed class or interface declared in the same package. With the JDK 21 target these labs use, kotlinc 2.4, the Kotlin compiler, writes the same PermittedSubclasses attribute as javac. Java code therefore sees a Kotlin sealed interface as sealed: a Java switch over it needs no default, and javac rejects a Java class that tries to implement it. Sealing restricts direct subtypes only. Renew.class.isSealed() is false. What may sit below each permitted subtype is the next question. Break the list on purpose Run SealedBasics (or SealedBasicsKt) with the command below. In the Java demo, uncomment static final class Donate implements Request {} and run again. Read the error. Add Donate to the permits clause and delete final from it. Run again. Then put final back. Now delete the whole permits ... clause and run. What does getPermittedSubclasses() print? In the Kotlin twin, uncomment class Donate : Request. Does it compile? Why is that different from Java? SealedBasics.java package workbench.modernjava.l02.demo; import java.lang.reflect.Modifier; /** A sealed interface names its direct subtypes, and the JVM keeps that list. */ public class SealedBasics { // the three things a member can ask for at the desk sealed interface Request permits Borrow, Renew, Return {} record Borrow(String isbn, int days) implements Request {} // records are final record Renew(int extraDays) implements Request {} record Return() implements Request {} // Step 2: uncomment this line and compile. // static final class Donate implements Request {} public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Request.isSealed(): " + Request.class.isSealed()); for (Class<?> c : Request.class.getPermittedSubclasses()) { System.out.println("permits: " + c.getSimpleName() + (Modifier.isFinal(c.getModifiers()) ? " (final)" : "")); } System.out.println("Renew.isSealed(): " + Renew.class.isSealed()); } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l02.demo.SealedBasics labs/modernjava/src/demo/java/workbench/modernjava/l02/demo/SealedBasics.java SealedBasics.kt package workbench.modernjava.l02.demo import java.lang.reflect.Modifier // Kotlin has no permits clause: the direct subtypes are the ones declared in this package and module sealed interface Request { data class Borrow(val isbn: String, val days: Int) : Request // final by default data class Renew(val extraDays: Int) : Request data object Return : Request } // Step 2: uncomment this line and compile. Then try it in another package. // class Donate : Request /** kotlinc writes the same PermittedSubclasses attribute that javac does. */ fun main() { println("Request.isSealed(): ${Request::class.java.isSealed}") for (c in Request::class.java.permittedSubclasses) { println("permits: ${c.simpleName}" + if (Modifier.isFinal(c.modifiers)) " (final)" else "") } println("Renew.isSealed(): ${Request.Renew::class.java.isSealed}") } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l02.demo.SealedBasicsKt labs/modernjava/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/modernjava/l02/demo/SealedBasics.kt The first run prints Request.isSealed(): true, the three records marked (final), and Renew.isSealed(): false. The unlisted class fails with class is not allowed to extend sealed class: Request (as it is not listed in its 'permits' clause). Listed but without a modifier, it fails with sealed, non-sealed or final modifiers expected. With no permits clause, javac infers all four from the file and prints Donate (final) too. In Kotlin, class Donate : Request compiles: the list is whatever sits in the same package and module. JEP 409: Sealed Classes read

h: Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check · final, sealed or non-sealed: every branch has to choose
x: Every permitted subtype of a sealed type must say how its own branch ends, with exactly one of three modifiers. A class that says nothing stops javac with sealed, non-sealed or final modifiers expected. An interface can't be final, so for one the message is sealed or non-sealed modifiers expected. final ends the branch. Records and enums are final already, so a record needs no modifier, which is one reason sealed interfaces and records fit together so well. sealed continues the closed list one level down, with its own permits. non-sealed reopens the branch on purpose: anyone may extend it, in any package. The library's own list uses all three. Books and magazines are records. Discs are a sealed branch with exactly two kinds, DVDs and audio CDs. And some items are lent to us by partner libraries, which describe them in their own code: Java public sealed interface LibraryItem permits Book, Disc, Magazine, PartnerItem {} public record Book(String isbn, String title) implements LibraryItem {} // final public sealed interface Disc extends LibraryItem permits Dvd, AudioCd {} // closed below public record Magazine(String title, int issue) implements LibraryItem {} // final public non-sealed interface PartnerItem extends LibraryItem { // open below String partnerId(); } Kotlin sealed interface LibraryItem { data class Book(val isbn: String, val title: String) : LibraryItem // final by default sealed interface Disc : LibraryItem // closed below data class Magazine(val title: String, val issue: Int) : LibraryItem interface PartnerItem : LibraryItem { val partnerId: String } // open below } On the form, non-sealed is the box marked "From another library: ______", with a blank line after it. The clerk can't list every partner's items, but one instruction covers them all: send it back to the library named on the line. non-sealed sounds as if it defeats the point. It doesn't, because the compiler still knows the shape of the tree. A switch covers the open branch with one case PartnerItem p, and that case matches every partner's class, including ones a partner writes next year. Your switch stays complete, and the partners stay free. Kotlin has no non-sealed keyword: a plain interface, or an open class, under a sealed parent plays the same role. So "sealed means final" is wrong: a sealed type has subtypes by definition, and a non-sealed branch can have any number. The trap that catches people in code review is a third one. A sealed class that isn't abstract is itself a possible value. The NonSealedDemo has a sealed class Extension, the rule for how many days a renewal adds, with two final subclasses, FixedDays and SameAgain. Delete abstract, and new Extension() becomes legal. The switch with one case per subclass then fails with the switch expression does not cover all possible input values, because a plain Extension matches neither case. Make the parent abstract, or make it an interface. Kotlin avoids the trap entirely: its docs say a sealed class is always abstract. Every branch of a sealed tree ends in final, sealed or non-sealed. Choose each one on purpose. We know how each branch ends. The next question is where the branches may be written down. Reopen one branch, close the trap Run NonSealedDemo. ArchiveBox is a partner library's code: which modifier lets it exist? Delete non-sealed from PartnerItem, leaving a plain interface, and run. Read the error, then put it back. Delete abstract from sealed abstract static class Extension and run again. NonSealedDemo.java package workbench.modernjava.l02.demo; /** Each branch of a sealed hierarchy ends as final, sealed or non-sealed. */ public class NonSealedDemo { sealed interface LibraryItem permits Book, Disc, PartnerItem {} record Book(String title) implements LibraryItem {} // final: a leaf sealed interface Disc extends LibraryItem permits Dvd, AudioCd {} // sealed: closed below record Dvd(String title) implements Disc {} record AudioCd(String title) implements Disc {} non-sealed interface PartnerItem extends LibraryItem { // non-sealed: open below String partnerId(); } // a partner library's code: allowed, because PartnerItem is non-sealed record ArchiveBox(String partnerId, String contents) implements PartnerItem {} // Step 3: delete "abstract" here and compile. sealed abstract static class Extension permits FixedDays, SameAgain {} static final class FixedDays extends Extension { final int days; FixedDays(int days) { this.days = days; } } static final class SameAgain extends Extension {} static String describe(LibraryItem item) { return switch (item) { case Book b -> "book " + b.title(); case Disc d -> "disc " + d; // one case for the sealed branch case PartnerItem p -> "partner " + p.partnerId(); // one case for the open branch }; } // how many days a renewal adds to a loan static int extraDays(Extension e, int loanDays) { return switch (e) { case FixedDays f -> f.days; case SameAgain s -> loanDays; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(describe(new Book("Dune"))); System.out.println(describe(new Dvd("Paddington"))); System.out.println(describe(new ArchiveBox("city-archive", "old maps"))); System.out.println("PartnerItem.isSealed(): " + PartnerItem.class.isSealed()); System.out.println("renewal: " + extraDays(new FixedDays(7), 21) + " and " + extraDays(new SameAgain(), 21) + " extra days"); } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l02.demo.NonSealedDemo labs/modernjava/src/demo/java/workbench/modernjava/l02/demo/NonSealedDemo.java NonSealedDemo.kt package workbench.modernjava.l02.demo // Kotlin subtypes are final unless you open them, and there is no non-sealed keyword: // a plain interface (or an open class) under a sealed parent is the open branch. sealed interface LibraryItem { data class Book(val title: String) : LibraryItem // final: a leaf sealed interface Disc : LibraryItem // sealed: closed below data class Dvd(val title: String) : Disc data class AudioCd(val title: String) : Disc interface PartnerItem : LibraryItem { // open below val partnerId: String } } // a partner library's code, which could live in any package: PartnerItem is an ordinary interface data class ArchiveBox(override val partnerId: String, val contents: String) : LibraryItem.PartnerItem // A Kotlin sealed class is always abstract, so the trap in step 3 of the Java demo can't happen here. sealed class Extension { class FixedDays(val days: Int) : Extension() object SameAgain : Extension() } fun describe(item: LibraryItem): String = when (item) { is LibraryItem.Book -> "book ${item.title}" is LibraryItem.Disc -> "disc $item" // one branch for the sealed branch is LibraryItem.PartnerItem -> "partner ${item.partnerId}" // one branch for the open branch } // how many days a renewal adds to a loan fun extraDays(e: Extension, loanDays: Int): Int = when (e) { is Extension.FixedDays -> e.days Extension.SameAgain -> loanDays } /** Each branch of a sealed hierarchy ends closed, sealed again, or open. */ fun main() { println(describe(LibraryItem.Book("Dune"))) println(describe(LibraryItem.Dvd("Paddington"))) println(describe(ArchiveBox("city-archive", "old maps"))) println("PartnerItem.isSealed(): h: Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check · Where the subtypes may live: one package, or one module
x: Sealing ties a hierarchy to one place, and Java and Kotlin draw the boundary slightly differently. In Java, the permitted subtypes must be in the same module as the sealed type. A module here is a named group of packages, described by a module-info.java file. If your code isn't in a named module, the subtypes must be in the same package. Split the sealed interface and its record across two packages, library.api and library.book, and javac refuses: error: class LibraryItem in unnamed module cannot extend a sealed class in a different package public sealed interface LibraryItem permits library.book.Book {} The wording is clumsy, since it names the sealed interface as the class doing the extending, but the rule is clear. Add a module-info.java that puts both packages in one module, and the same files compile. Kotlin's rule is the same package and the same module, whether or not you use Java modules. So for most code the two languages agree: keep a sealed hierarchy in one package. That's rarely a burden. The subtypes are usually small records or data classes that read best next to each other, often nested inside the sealed type itself, which also lets Java infer permits. The rule makes sense once you see what sealing promises. The author of a sealed type says "this is the complete list", and the compiler can only hold everyone to that if the whole list is compiled and shipped together. In the picture, the form and all its boxes come from one print shop. A box printed somewhere else could be reprinted on its own schedule, and every instruction sheet checked against the old form would quietly go stale. A sealed list must be compiled together. Keep it in one package. With the list closed and kept in one place, the compiler can finally put it to work. Split a hierarchy across packages The folder labs/modernjava/javac/sealed-packages holds a sealed LibraryItem in library.api, a Book record in library.book, and a module-info.java. Gradle doesn't compile it; you run javac yourself. Run the first command. Read the error and the line it points at. Run the second command, which adds the module descriptor. Predict, then check: move Book.java into library/api/, change its package line to library.api, change the permits clause to permits Book, and run the first command again (with library/api/Book.java in place of the old path). terminal cd labs/modernjava/javac/sealed-packages # 1. class path, unnamed module: two packages are not allowed javac -d ../../build/sealed-packages library/api/LibraryItem.java library/book/Book.java # 2. one named module: two packages are fine javac -d ../../build/sealed-packages module-info.java library/api/LibraryItem.java library/book/Book.java The first command fails with class LibraryItem in unnamed module cannot extend a sealed class in a different package, pointing at library.book.Book in the permits clause. The second compiles with no output, because both packages belong to the module library. After the move, the first command compiles too: on the class path, one package is enough.

h: Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check · Let the compiler find every switch, and keep default out
x: Sealing pays off in a switch. Over a sealed type, javac knows every possible subtype, so a switch with one case per subtype is exhaustive: its cases cover every possible value, and it needs no default. javac checks that the cases really do cover every subtype. The StatusSwitches demo has three switches over CopyStatus, where one copy of a book is right now: on the shelf, on loan, on hold for a member, or missing. Here is one of them: Java static boolean canLendToday(CopyStatus s) { return switch (s) { // no default case OnShelf shelf -> true; case OnLoan loan -> false; case OnHold hold -> false; case Missing missing -> false; }; } Kotlin fun canLendToday(s: CopyStatus): Boolean = when (s) { // no else is CopyStatus.OnShelf -> true is CopyStatus.OnLoan -> false is CopyStatus.OnHold -> false is CopyStatus.Missing -> false } Now the library starts sending damaged books away to be repaired, and someone adds InRepair to CopyStatus. Every switch over CopyStatus without a default stops compiling. On JDK 21 to 26 the error is the bare one, pointing at the switch: StatusSwitches.java:30: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values return switch (s) { ^ JDK 27's javac adds the cases you're missing, under a missing patterns: line, here InRepair _. kotlinc has always been specific: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is InRepair' branch or an 'else' branch. Either way, the build hands you a to-do list: every switch that has to learn about repairs. The third switch isn't on that list. reminderDays ends with default -> 0, which means "and anything else", and the compiler takes it at its word. InRepair drops into the default without a sound and gets 0 reminder days, though the repair has a due date too. A default on your own sealed type throws away the one check sealing gives you. The OpenJDK team's 2026 guide to switching over sealed types has a section called "By default, avoid default", because a default "sweeps errors, both present and future, under the rug". A default on a list that grows hides the next item. Leave it out. Keep default for switches where "everything else" really is one answer, such as the illegal (state, event) pairs of a state machine in State and Chain of Responsibility. The same guide asks authors to say in the Javadoc why a type is sealed. Maybe it models a closed set, like the statuses of a copy. Or maybe the author only wants to control who implements it. Say which, and whether you expect to add subtypes, so the people switching over it know what's coming. Exhaustive has one limit, and it's about time. javac checks a switch against the list it can see when it compiles. A program compiled against the old list can still meet an InRepair from a newer library at run time, and lesson 3 of this track shows what happens then. Sealing also fits only lists you own: a plug-in point that other people extend should stay open. Send a copy away for repair Run StatusSwitches once and look at the three functions: label, canLendToday and reminderDays. Which one has a default? Add InRepair to the permits clause and uncomment the InRepair record. Before you run, predict which functions javac will report. Run it, then make it compile again by handling InRepair where javac asked. What does reminderDays return for a copy in repair now? Is that right? Do the same in the Kotlin twin, StatusSwitchesKt. h: Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check · Java and Kotlin
x: The copy statuses in Java and Kotlin CopyStatus.java public sealed interface CopyStatus permits OnShelf, OnLoan, OnHold, Missing {} record OnShelf(String shelfmark) implements CopyStatus {} record OnLoan(String memberId, int daysLeft) implements CopyStatus {} record OnHold(String memberId) implements CopyStatus {} record Missing(int daysMissing) implements CopyStatus {} static String label(CopyStatus s) { return switch (s) { // no default case OnShelf shelf -> "on shelf"; case OnLoan loan -> "on loan"; case OnHold hold -> "on hold"; case Missing missing -> "missing"; }; } CopyStatus.kt sealed interface CopyStatus { data class OnShelf(val shelfmark: String) : CopyStatus data class OnLoan(val memberId: String, val daysLeft: Int) : CopyStatus data class OnHold(val memberId: String) : CopyStatus data class Missing(val daysMissing: Int) : CopyStatus } fun label(s: CopyStatus): String = when (s) { // no else is CopyStatus.OnShelf -> "on shelf" is CopyStatus.OnLoan -> "on loan" is CopyStatus.OnHold -> "on hold" is CopyStatus.Missing -> "missing" } The idea is the same and so is the bytecode: both compilers write a PermittedSubclasses attribute, so each language sees the other's sealed types as sealed. Three things differ. Java names the subtypes in permits (or infers them from one source file) and makes every subtype choose final, sealed or non-sealed; Kotlin's list is whatever is declared in the same package and module, and subtypes are final unless you open them. Java's location rule is the module, or the package on the class path; Kotlin's is always the package and the module. And Kotlin has data object for a case with no fields, where Java uses a record with no components or an enum.

h: Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check · Worked example
x: Seal the events from the self-service machine The self-service machine by the door sends the library's program an event each time someone uses it. Today there are two kinds, and a handler sorts them with an instanceof chain. Someone adds a third kind to the machine, Renewed. This compiles with no warning, and the handler starts throwing on every renewal. public interface MachineEvent {} void handle(MachineEvent e) { if (e instanceof CheckedOut c) lend(c); else if (e instanceof CheckedIn c) takeBack(c); else throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown event " + e); // Renewed lands here } interface MachineEvent fun handle(e: MachineEvent) { if (e is CheckedOut) lend(e) else if (e is CheckedIn) takeBack(e) else throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown event $e") // Renewed lands here } Seal the event type and make each event a record in the same package. Records are final, so they need no modifier. // 1. close the list public sealed interface MachineEvent permits CheckedOut, CheckedIn, Renewed {} public record CheckedOut(String memberId, String isbn) implements MachineEvent {} public record CheckedIn(String isbn) implements MachineEvent {} public record Renewed(String memberId, String isbn, int extraDays) implements MachineEvent {} // 1. close the list sealed interface MachineEvent { data class CheckedOut(val memberId: String, val isbn: String) : MachineEvent data class CheckedIn(val isbn: String) : MachineEvent data class Renewed(val memberId: String, val isbn: String, val extraDays: Int) : MachineEvent } Replace the chain with a switch that has no default. The chain could never be checked; the switch is checked on every build, and the else throw disappears because there is no "else" left. // 2. one case per event, no default void handle(MachineEvent e) { switch (e) { case CheckedOut c -> lend(c); case CheckedIn c -> takeBack(c); case Renewed r -> extend(r); } } // 2. one branch per event, no else fun handle(e: MachineEvent) = when (e) { is MachineEvent.CheckedOut -> lend(e) is MachineEvent.CheckedIn -> takeBack(e) is MachineEvent.Renewed -> extend(e) } A switch statement with patterns must be exhaustive too, so the void version is checked just like an expression. Last, write down why the type is sealed, so the next person knows that new events will come and that handlers must be updated, not given a default. /** * Every event the self-service machine sends. Sealed because handlers must deal with each one. * New events will be added: expect your switch to stop compiling, and handle the new case. */ public sealed interface MachineEvent permits CheckedOut, CheckedIn, Renewed {} // 3. say why /** * Every event the self-service machine sends. Sealed because handlers must deal with each one. * New events will be added: expect your when to stop compiling, and handle the new case. */ sealed interface MachineEvent // 3. say why
