h: Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check · Key terms
x: Sealed type A class or interface that lists which classes may extend it directly, like a form with a fixed set of boxes to tick. Permitted subtype A class on a sealed type's list. It must be final, sealed or non-sealed. non-sealed The modifier that reopens one branch of a sealed hierarchy to any subclass. Exhaustive switch A switch whose cases cover every possible value of its selector, so it needs no default. PermittedSubclasses The class-file attribute that records a sealed type's list. The JVM checks it when a class loads. Unnamed module Where code on the class path lives when it has no module-info.java. Most applications run here. Which modifiers can a permitted subtype of a sealed type have? Exactly one of final, sealed or non-sealed. Records and enums are implicitly final, so they need none. What does non-sealed do? It reopens that branch: anyone may extend it. A switch still covers the whole branch with one case for the non-sealed type. Why don't case FixedDays and case SameAgain cover sealed class Extension permits FixedDays, SameAgain when Extension isn't abstract? new Extension() is a possible value too. Make Extension abstract or an interface. Where may a Java sealed type's permitted subtypes live? In the same module. On the class path (the unnamed module), in the same package. Where may a Kotlin sealed type's direct subtypes live? In the same package and the same module. When can you leave out permits? When every subtype is declared in the same source file as the sealed type. javac infers the list. Why avoid default in a switch over your own sealed type? It stops the compiler from reporting the switch when a subtype is added. The new subtype silently takes the default branch.

h: Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check · Go deeper
x: Sealing is enforced in three places, and it helps to know which one you're looking at. javac enforces it at compile time, with the errors in this lesson. The JVM enforces it at load time, from the PermittedSubclasses attribute. Compile final class B implements S against an old, unsealed S, then run it next to a newer S that is sealed and doesn't list B, and class loading fails with java.lang.IncompatibleClassChangeError: class B cannot implement sealed interface S. That stops a stray jar from smuggling a subtype into your hierarchy. And reflection reports it: Class.isSealed() and Class.getPermittedSubclasses(), both added with sealed classes, are what the tests in this lesson's lab use. None of the three stops you from adding a subtype yourself, and that's on purpose. The 2026 Amber guide calls adding a permitted subtype "a permissible and compatible evolution" of a sealed API. Programs compiled against the old list keep loading and running; only their switches change behavior. Recompiled, those switches fail to build. Not recompiled, they meet the new subtype at run time and throw MatchException. The guide describes this as how Java balances "safety with resilience": you find out either at build time or loudly at run time, never silently. Lesson 3 runs that experiment, and shows that the same thing happens for an enum constant added after the switch was compiled. For Kotlin interop, one detail is worth checking in your own build. The PermittedSubclasses attribute only exists in class files for JDK 17 and later, so Java sees a Kotlin sealed type as sealed only when kotlinc targets 17 or higher. With the JDK 21 target the labs use, kotlinc 2.4 writes it, and javac rejects final class Bad implements Status {} against a Kotlin sealed Status with the usual not listed in its 'permits' clause error.

h: Pattern matching with switch and record patterns · A pattern switch is checked, an instanceof chain is not
x: Add a subtype: the pattern switch stops compiling, the instanceof chain stays silent A pattern is a test with a binding. Book b asks "is this value a Book?" and, if it is, gives you a new variable b of type Book. Pattern matching came to Java in steps. JDK 16 made instanceof patterns a standard feature (JEP 394, the JDK Enhancement Proposal that describes them). The type test and the cast become one, and the binding is in scope wherever the test is known to have passed: Java if (!(o instanceof Book b)) return "not a book"; return "by " + b.author(); // b is in scope: the test can't have failed here Kotlin if (o !is Item.Book) return "not a book" return "by ${o.author}" // smart cast: o is a Book from here on JDK 21 made pattern switch standard (JEP 441), together with record patterns (JEP 440). Here are two ways to describe an item at the desk, both from the PatternBasics demo: Java // an if-chain: javac never checks that it covers every Item if (i instanceof Book b) return "book " + b.title() + " by " + b.author(); else if (i instanceof Disc d) return "disc " + d.title() + ", " + d.minutes() + " min"; else if (i instanceof Magazine m) return "magazine " + m.title() + " #" + m.issue(); else throw new IllegalStateException("unreachable?"); // a pattern switch: javac checks that every Item is covered return switch (i) { case Book b -> "book " + b.title() + " by " + b.author(); case Disc d -> "disc " + d.title() + ", " + d.minutes() + " min"; case Magazine m -> "magazine " + m.title() + " #" + m.issue(); }; Kotlin // an if-chain: kotlinc never checks that it covers every Item if (i is Item.Book) "book ${i.title} by ${i.author}" else if (i is Item.Disc) "disc ${i.title}, ${i.minutes} min" else if (i is Item.Magazine) "magazine ${i.title} #${i.issue}" else throw IllegalStateException("unreachable?") // when with a subject: kotlinc checks that every Item is covered when (i) { is Item.Book -> "book ${i.title} by ${i.author}" is Item.Disc -> "disc ${i.title}, ${i.minutes} min" is Item.Magazine -> "magazine ${i.title} #${i.issue}" } Both print the same three lines, starting with book Emma by Jane Austen. It's tempting to read the switch as a tidier chain, but the differences are the reason to prefer it. Delete the Magazine line from the chain, and it still compiles; the run reaches the magazine and dies in the chain's IllegalStateException. Delete the Magazine case from the switch, and javac, the Java compiler, refuses: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values. A pattern switch used as a statement must be exhaustive too. javac checks two more things the chain never gets: dominance, that is, whether each case can ever be reached (the third section), and fixed rules for null (the fourth). One level down, javac compiles the switch to one invokedynamic call, a call whose target the JVM picks the first time the call runs, to SwitchBootstraps.typeSwitch. That method works out the first matching case. javac also adds a hidden last arm that throws MatchException if nothing matches at run time. Hold on to that hidden arm; it comes back at the end of the lesson. Kotlin has had most of this for years. A when with a subject checks exhaustiveness over a sealed type, whether you use it as an expression or a statement, and a smart cast merges the is check with the cast. javap, the JDK's class-file reader, shows that kotlinc 2.4 (the Kotlin compiler), with the JDK 21 target, compiles that when to the same typeSwitch call; its hidden arm throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException instead. In the paperwork picture, the switch is a clerk whose printed sheet lists every kind of item the library has. The chain is a clerk who remembers the kinds. Mostly. A chain of instanceof checks can't be checked. Switch over the sealed type instead. What Kotlin doesn't have is the subject of the next section: reading the boxes inside the item, in the same look. See which one the compiler catches Run PatternBasics (or PatternBasicsKt) with the command below. Delete the Magazine line from viaChain and run. Put it back, then delete the Magazine case from viaSwitch and run again. Which mistake did the compiler catch? From labs/, run javap -c -p modernjava/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/PatternBasics.class and find typeSwitch and MatchException in viaSwitch. Run the same javap on modernjava/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/PatternBasicsKt.class and look at viaWhen. PatternBasics.java package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo; /** The same sorting three ways: an instanceof chain, an early return, and a pattern switch. */ public class PatternBasics { sealed interface Item permits Book, Disc, Magazine {} record Book(String title, String author) implements Item {} record Disc(String title, int minutes) implements Item {} record Magazine(String title, int issue) implements Item {} // an if-chain: javac never checks that it covers every Item static String viaChain(Item i) { if (i instanceof Book b) return "book " + b.title() + " by " + b.author(); else if (i instanceof Disc d) return "disc " + d.title() + ", " + d.minutes() + " min"; else if (i instanceof Magazine m) return "magazine " + m.title() + " #" + m.issue(); else throw new IllegalStateException("unreachable?"); } // a pattern switch: javac checks that every Item is covered static String viaSwitch(Item i) { return switch (i) { case Book b -> "book " + b.title() + " by " + b.author(); case Disc d -> "disc " + d.title() + ", " + d.minutes() + " min"; return "by " + b.author(); } public static void main(String[] args) { Item[] returns = { new Book("Emma", "Jane Austen"), new Disc("Paddington", 95), new Magazine("Garden Monthly", 214) }; for (Item i : returns) { System.out.println(viaChain(i) + " | " + viaSwitch(i)); } System.out.println(author(returns[0]) + ", " + author("Emma")); } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l03.demo.PatternBasics labs/modernjava/src/demo/java/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/PatternBasics.java PatternBasics.kt package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo sealed interface Item { data class Book(val title: String, val author: String) : Item data class Disc(val title: String, val minutes: Int) : Item data class Magazine(val title: String, val issue: Int) : Item } // an if-chain: kotlinc never checks that it covers every Item fun viaChain(i: Item): String = if (i is Item.Book) "book ${i.title} by ${i.author}" // smart cast: i is a Book here else if (i is Item.Disc) "disc ${i.title}, ${i.minutes} min" else if (i is Item.Magazine) "magazine ${i.title} #${i.issue}" else throw IllegalStateException("unreachable?") // when with a subject: kotlinc checks that every Item is covered fun viaWhen(i: Item): String = when (i) { is Item.Book -> "book ${i.title} by ${i.author}" is Item.Disc -> "disc ${i.title}, ${i.minutes} min" is Item.Magazine -> "magazine ${i.title} #${i.issue}" } // a smart cast lasts for the rest of the function after a negated check returns fun author(o: Any): String { if (o !is Item.Book) return "not a book" return "by ${o.author}" } /** The same sorting three ways: an if-chain, an early return, and a when. */ fun main() { val returns = listOf(Item.Book("Emma", "Jane Austen"), Item.Disc("Paddington", 95), Item.Magazine("Garden Monthly", 214)) for (i in returns) { println(viaChain(i) + " | " + viaWhen(i)) } println(author(returns[0]) + ", " + author("Emma")) } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l03.demo.PatternBasicsKt labs/modernjava/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/PatternBasics.kt Both versions print the same three lines and by Jane Austen, not a book. h: Pattern matching with switch and record patterns · Record patterns read several boxes in one look
x: A type pattern tests a type and binds one variable. A record pattern also takes a record apart, through its accessors, and each part can be a pattern too. In the picture, the clerk reads several boxes in one look, including the boxes on a smaller form clipped inside the first. The lab's loan rules show it. A Loan records who borrows (a Member), what (an Item), and from which branch (a Branch, where BUS is the library bus that comes back every four weeks). Here are the first rules, next to the closest Kotlin. The when after each pattern is a guard, an extra condition that the next section covers: Java return switch (loan) { case Loan(var m, Book(var format, var isNew), var b) when format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42; case Loan(var m, Book(var format, var isNew), var b) when isNew -> 7; case Loan(var m, Book book, var b) when b == Branch.BUS -> 28; // ... }; Kotlin val item = loan.item // pick the nested part out first return when (item) { is Book if item.format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42 is Book if item.newRelease -> 7 is Book if loan.branch == Branch.BUS -> 28 // ... } Read the Java label from the outside in. The selector, the value in switch (...), must be a Loan. Its member() binds to m. Its item() must match Book(var format, var isNew), which binds the book's two boxes. Its branch() binds to b. With var, javac infers each type from the record's components. The figure shows one pattern that reads every box at once, three levels deep. Patterns are positional and type-checked. Put String x2 where a record has an int, as the Try it does, and javac stops with incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String. Generic records work too: over sealed interface Result<T>, the case Ok<T>(var v) binds v as a T. Record patterns also work in instanceof, as in if (o instanceof Line(Point(var x, var y), var to) && x == 0). Kotlin has no record patterns. The closest tools are smart casts on nested properties, as in the twin above, and positional destructuring, val (from, to) = line, through component1() and component2(). Destructuring has a trap that Java's patterns mostly avoid: it goes by position, not by name. With data class Book(val title: String, val pages: Int), the line val (pages, title) = book compiles without a warning. The demo prints swapped names: pages=Dune title=412, a very long book with a very short title. Kotlin 2.3.20 added name-based destructuring as an Experimental feature, behind -Xname-based-destructuring; its name-mismatch mode warns about exactly that line. Java's record patterns are positional too, but every component is type-checked, so most swaps fail to compile. Two var bindings of the same type can still be swapped silently, so keep the record header in front of you. One look now reads every box. The clerk still needs to know which line of the sheet to try first. Take a line apart Predict the third line of output, then run RecordPatterns. In describe, change Point(int x2, int y2) to Point(String x2, int y2) and run. Read the first error, then undo it. Run the Kotlin twin, RecordPatternsKt, and read its last line. RecordPatterns.java package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo; import java.util.List; /** Record patterns: take a record apart in the case label, nested as deep as you like. */ public class RecordPatterns { record Point(int x, int y) {} record Line(Point from, Point to) {} sealed interface Result<T> permits Ok, Err {} record Ok<T>(T value) implements Result<T> {} record Err<T>(String message, Throwable cause) implements Result<T> {} static String describe(Line line) { return switch (line) { case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(int x2, int y2)) when x1 == x2 -> "vertical at x=" + x1 + " len " + Math.abs(y2 - y1); case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2)) when y1 == y2 -> "horizontal at y=" + y1; case Line(Point from, Point to) -> "diagonal " + from + "->" + to; }; } static <T> String show(Result<T> r) { return switch (r) { case Ok<T>(var v) -> "ok " + v; // T inferred for v case Err<T>(var msg, var cause) when cause != null -> "err " + msg + " caused by " + cause.getClass().getSimpleName(); case Err<T>(var msg, var cause) -> "err " + msg; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(describe(new Line(new Point(1, 0), new Point(1, 5)))); System.out.println(describe(new Line(new Point(0, 3), new Point(7, 3)))); System.out.println(describe(new Line(new Point(0, 0), new Point(2, 2)))); System.out.println(show(new Ok<>(List.of(1, 2)))); System.out.println(show(new Err<>("boom", new RuntimeException()))); Object o = new Line(new Point(0, 0), new Point(9, 9)); if (o instanceof Line(Point(var x, var y), var to) && x == 0 && y == 0) { // patterns in instanceof too System.out.println("from origin to " + to); } } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l03.demo.RecordPatterns labs/modernjava/src/demo/java/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/RecordPatterns.java RecordPatterns.kt package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int) data class Line(val from: Point, val to: Point) sealed interface Outcome<out T> { data class Ok<T>(val value: T) : Outcome<T> data class Err(val message: String, val cause: Throwable?) : Outcome<Nothing> } data class Book(val title: String, val pages: Int) // Kotlin can't take records apart in a when branch: match the outer type, then read the properties fun describe(line: Line): String { val (from, to) = line // positional destructuring via component1/2 return when { from.x == to.x -> "vertical at x=${from.x} len ${kotlin.math.abs(to.y - from.y)}" from.y == to.y -> "horizontal at y=${from.y}" else -> "diagonal $from->$to" } } fun <T> show(r: Outcome<T>): String = when (r) { is Outcome.Ok -> "ok ${r.value}" is Outcome.Err if r.cause != null -> "err ${r.message} caused by ${r.cause::class.simpleName}" // guard: Kotlin 2.2+ is Outcome.Err -> "err ${r.message}" } /** The Kotlin side: smart casts and positional destructuring instead of record patterns. */ fun main() { println(describe(Line(Point(1, 0), Point(1, 5)))) println(describe(Line(Point(0, 3), Point(7, 3)))) println(describe(Line(Point(0, 0), Point(2, 2)))) println(show(Outcome.Ok(listOf(1, 2)))) println(show(Outcome.Err("boom", RuntimeException()))) val o: Any = Line(Point(0, 0), Point(9, 9)) if (o is Line && o.from.x == 0 && o.from.y == 0) { // smart cast after the is check println("from origin to ${o.to}") } // destructuring goes by position, not by name: this compiles, with no warning, and swaps the values val (pages, title) = Book("Dune", 412) println("swapped names: pages=$pages title=$title") } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l03.demo.RecordPatternsKt labs/modernjava/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/RecordPatterns.kt vertical at x=1 len 5, horizontal at y=3, diagonal Point[x=0, y=0]->Point[x=2, y=2], then ok [1, 2], err boom caused by RuntimeException and from origin to Point[x=9, y=9]. The String change fails with incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String (and a second error, because x1 == x2 now compares an int with a String). The Kotlin twin prints the same results with smart casts, and then swapped names: pages=Dune title=412: positional destructuring put the title into pages without a warning. One record pattern, three levels deep: the loan, its components, and the parts of each component, all bound in the case label. h: Pattern matching with switch and record patterns · Guards, order and dominance: the sheet is read from the top
x: Cases are tried from the top, and the first one whose pattern matches and whose guard is true wins. The guard is the when clause after a pattern (if in Kotlin). That makes order part of the meaning, exactly as on the clerk's sheet. A new large-print book matches both of the first two lines of the GuardsDemo, so whichever comes first sets its loan: Java case Book(var format, var isNew) when format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42; // 1 case Book(var format, var isNew) when isNew -> 7; // 2 case Book(var format, var isNew) -> 21; // 3 Kotlin is LoanItem.Book if i.format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42 // 1 is LoanItem.Book if i.newRelease -> 7 // 2 is LoanItem.Book -> 21 // 3 The demo prints 42 days for it. Swap lines // 1 and // 2, and it prints 7 days, and nothing else changes. javac accepts both orders, because a guarded case never dominates another. Only a test that sends a new large-print book through the switch can tell you which order you meant. Guards don't count toward exhaustiveness, in either language. The compiler can't prove that a set of guards covers every value, so a family of guarded cases must end with an unguarded case of the same pattern. Delete line // 3, and javac says the switch doesn't cover all possible input values, while kotlinc asks you to Add the 'is Book' branch. You can predict javac's verdict yourself. List the permitted subtypes of the selector's type, and cross off each one that has an unguarded case, or that sits under a sealed parent with one. Inside record patterns, check combinations, not columns. With Pair(Red a, Red b) and Pair(Green a, Light b), the Red cases cover only Red in second place, so Pair(Red, Green) is missing. Whatever is left over is what JDK 27 prints under missing patterns:. javac also rejects a case that can never be reached, with this case label is dominated by a preceding case label. That happens when an earlier unguarded case already matches everything the later one could. Move line // 3 above line // 1, and javac rejects both guarded lines. Other examples are case String s after case CharSequence cs, and a constant case 1 after an unguarded case Integer i. kotlinc has no dominance check at all. Put the unguarded is LoanItem.Book first, and it compiles without a warning; every book then gets 21 days, large print and new releases included. Here kotlinc shrugs where javac objects. Kotlin guards (is T if condition) have been stable since Kotlin 2.2. The sheet is read from the top. Put the most specific rule first, and end each family with an unguarded case. Several patterns can share one arm only if they bind nothing. On JDK 21 that makes such arms awkward: case Return ret, Renew ren -> fails with illegal fall-through from a pattern, so you write two arms. JDK 22 made unnamed patterns standard, and case Return _, Renew _ -> is legal. _ also stands in for a component you don't need, as in case Borrow(var member, _). On JDK 21 it's a preview feature, one that is switched off unless you pass --enable-preview, and javac stops with unnamed variables are a preview feature and are disabled by default. The sheet now has the right lines in the right order. What happens when the clerk is handed a blank sheet, or a form that didn't exist when the sheet was printed? Reorder the loan rules Run GuardsDemo and note the loan for the new large-print book, Book[format=LARGE_PRINT, newRelease=true]. Swap the lines marked // 1 and // 2. Predict which loan changes, then run. Undo. Move line // 3 above line // 1 and run. Do the same in GuardsDemoKt. Undo. Delete line // 3 and run both versions. If you have JDK 22 or newer, run java preview/UnnamedPatterns.java from labs/modernjava, then try the same file on JDK 21. GuardsDemo.java package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo; /** Cases are tried from the top, and the first one that matches wins. Guards decide the order. */ public class GuardsDemo { enum Format { HARDBACK, PAPERBACK, LARGE_PRINT } sealed interface Item permits Book, Disc {} record Book(Format format, boolean newRelease) implements Item {} record Disc(boolean boxSet) implements Item {} static int loanDays(Item item) { return switch (item) { case Book(var format, var isNew) when format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42; // 1 case Book(var format, var isNew) when isNew -> 7; // 2 case Book(var format, var isNew) -> 21; // 3 case Disc(var boxSet) when boxSet -> 14; case Disc d -> 7; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { Item[] items = { new Book(Format.LARGE_PRINT, false), new Book(Format.LARGE_PRINT, true), new Book(Format.HARDBACK, true), new Book(Format.PAPERBACK, false), new Disc(true), }; for (Item i : items) { System.out.printf("%-42s %d days%n", i, loanDays(i)); } } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l03.demo.GuardsDemo labs/modernjava/src/demo/java/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/GuardsDemo.java GuardsDemo.kt package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo enum class Format { HARDBACK, PAPERBACK, LARGE_PRINT } sealed interface LoanItem { data class Book(val format: Format, val newRelease: Boolean) : LoanItem data class Disc(val boxSet: Boolean) : LoanItem } // guards in when branches (`is T if condition`) are stable since Kotlin 2.2 fun loanDays(i: LoanItem): Int = when (i) { is LoanItem.Book if i.format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42 // 1 is LoanItem.Book if i.newRelease -> 7 // 2 is LoanItem.Book -> 21 // 3 is LoanItem.Disc if i.boxSet -> 14 is LoanItem.Disc -> 7 } /** Branches are tried from the top, and the first one that matches wins. Guards decide the order. */ fun main() { val items = listOf( LoanItem.Book(Format.LARGE_PRINT, false), LoanItem.Book(Format.LARGE_PRINT, true), LoanItem.Book(Format.HARDBACK, true), LoanItem.Book(Format.PAPERBACK, false), LoanItem.Disc(true), ) for (i in items) { println("%-42s %d days".format(i, loanDays(i))) } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l03.demo.GuardsDemoKt labs/modernjava/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/GuardsDemo.kt The new large-print book gets 42 days. After the swap it gets 7, and nothing else changes: the new-release rule now matches it first. With line 3 on top, javac rejects lines 1 and 2 with this case label is dominated by a preceding case label, while the Kotlin version compiles and gives every book 21 days. Without line 3, javac reports the switch expression does not cover all possible input values and kotlinc asks for the 'is Book' branch. h: Pattern matching with switch and record patterns · Null, default and the remainder
x: switch has always thrown NullPointerException on a null selector, and a pattern switch keeps that rule unless you opt in with case null. In the picture, a blank sheet handed over the counter stops the clerk, unless the instruction sheet has a line for blank sheets: Java return switch (section) { case null -> "missing"; case "FIC" -> "fiction"; default -> "other"; // default alone does not catch null }; Kotlin return when (section) { // section is a String? null -> "missing" "FIC" -> "fiction" else -> "other" // without the null branch, null lands here } default alone doesn't catch null, and case null, default -> handles both in one arm. For most code, the OpenJDK guide on sealed switches prefers something simpler: reject null before the switch, with Objects.requireNonNull, because a null that reaches the rules is a bug somewhere upstream. Kotlin settles the question in the type system. A when over a nullable subject must handle null somewhere (kotlinc says Add the 'null' branch or an 'else' branch. if it doesn't), and nothing throws. So the NullDemo prints plain(null): NullPointerException in Java and plainWhen(null): other in Kotlin. Inside a record pattern, null follows a rule that surprises everyone once. A nested record pattern never matches null, but a nested type pattern that covers the whole component type does. Take case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2)) when x1 == x2 first and case Line(Point from, Point to) second. A Line whose start is null skips the first case and lands in the second, with from bound to null. Change the second case to Line(Point(var a, var b), Point to), and javac still calls the switch exhaustive. But that Line now matches nothing, and the switch throws MatchException. That points at the bigger limit: exhaustive is a compile-time promise. javac checks the switch against the subtypes it can see when it compiles. The values it can't see, which the Amber design notes call the remainder, are left to that hidden last arm at run time. The javac/remainder experiment compiles a client against Status permits Active, Closed, a member's account status. Then it recompiles only the hierarchy, with a third status, Frozen, and runs the old client: active, priority 1 sealed switch: java.lang.MatchException enum switch: java.lang.MatchException The old switch met a status it had never heard of, and the hidden arm threw. An enum switch with no default does the same when it meets a constant added later, and an old Kotlin when throws kotlin.NoWhenBranchMatchedException. You don't write code for the remainder, but in a program that mixes old and new jars, this is the exception you'll see. Recompile the client, and javac turns it back into a compile error, the switch expression does not cover all possible input values, twice. Exhaustive means exhaustive for the list javac saw. Recompile when the list changes. In the picture, this is a new kind of form printed after the clerk's sheet was written. Here the picture breaks: a real clerk would ask a colleague. The switch can't ask anyone, so it stops loudly, which beats guessing quietly. Feed a switch null, then a stranger Run NullDemo and NullDemoKt and compare their first lines. In the Java describe, change case Line(Point from, Point to) to case Line(Point(var a, var b), Point to) (and use a and b in the text). Predict: does it compile? What happens to the line with a null start? Run the separate-compilation experiment in labs/modernjava/javac/remainder. The five commands are at the top of Client.java. NullDemo.java package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo; /** What a switch does with null: at the top level, and inside a nested pattern. */ public class NullDemo { record Point(int x, int y) {} record Line(Point from, Point to) {} static String plain(String section) { return switch (section) { // the old rule: a null selector throws case "FIC" -> "fiction"; default -> "other"; }; } static String withNull(String section) { return switch (section) { case null -> "missing"; // opt in to null case "FIC" -> "fiction"; default -> "other"; }; } static String nullOrDefault(Object o) { return switch (o) { case String s -> "text " + s; case null, default -> "null or other"; // one arm for both }; } static String describe(Line line) { return switch (line) { case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2)) when x1 == x2 -> "vertical"; case Line(Point from, Point to) -> "other line " + from + " -> " + to; // Point from also matches null }; } public static void main(String[] args) { try { System.out.println(plain(null)); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("plain(null): NullPointerException"); } System.out.println("withNull(null): " + withNull(null)); System.out.println("nullOrDefault: " + nullOrDefault(null) + " / " + nullOrDefault(42)); System.out.println("line, null start: " + describe(new Line(null, new Point(1, 1)))); } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l03.demo.NullDemo labs/modernjava/src/demo/java/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/NullDemo.java NullDemo.kt package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo data class Spot(val x: Int, val y: Int) data class Segment(val from: Spot?, val to: Spot?) // in Kotlin the type says whether null can arrive, and when compares with equals: null never throws fun plainWhen(section: String?): String = when (section) { "FIC" -> "fiction" else -> "other" // null lands here } fun withNullWhen(section: String?): String = when (section) { null -> "missing" "FIC" -> "fiction" else -> "other" } fun nullOrElse(o: Any?): String = when (o) { is String -> "text $o" else -> "null or other" } fun describeSegment(s: Segment): String { val from = s.from val to = s.to return when { from != null && to != null && from.x == to.x -> "vertical" else -> "other line $from -> $to" // you write the null case yourself } } /** What when does with null: the nullable type decides, and nothing throws. */ fun main() { println("plainWhen(null): ${plainWhen(null)}") println("withNullWhen(null): ${withNullWhen(null)}") println("nullOrElse: ${nullOrElse(null)} / ${nullOrElse(42)}") println("line, null start: ${describeSegment(Segment(null, Spot(1, 1)))}") } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l03.demo.NullDemoKt labs/modernjava/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/NullDemo.kt Java prints plain(null): NullPointerException; Kotlin prints plainWhen(null): other, because its when compares with equals and the type allowed null. Both print missing, then null or other twice, then a line whose start is null. After the change in step 2 the switch still compiles, and the null-start line throws java.lang.MatchException. In the experiment, the first run prints active, priority 1, sealed switch: closed and enum switch: priority 2. After only the hierarchy is recompiled, the same old client prints active, priority 1, then sealed switch: java.lang.MatchException and enum switch: java.lang.MatchException. Recompiling the client gives two does not cover all possible input values errors. MatchException (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Pattern matching with switch and record patterns · Java and Kotlin
x: The loan rules in Java and Kotlin LoanRules.java static int loanDays(Loan loan) { return switch (loan) { case Loan(var m, Book(var format, var isNew), var b) when format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42; case Loan(var m, Book(var format, var isNew), var b) when isNew -> 7; case Loan(var m, Book book, var b) when b == Branch.BUS -> 28; case Loan(var m, Book book, var b) -> 21; case Loan(var m, Disc(var boxSet), var b) when boxSet -> 14; case Loan(var m, Disc disc, var b) -> 7; case Loan(Member(var id, int age), Magazine mag, var b) when age < 12 -> 14; case Loan(Member member, Magazine mag, var b) -> 7; }; } LoanRules.kt fun loanDays(loan: Loan): Int { val age = loan.member.age return when (val item = loan.item) { is Book if item.format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42 is Book if item.newRelease -> 7 is Book if loan.branch == Branch.BUS -> 28 is Book -> 21 is Disc if item.boxSet -> 14 is Disc -> 7 is Magazine if age < 12 -> 14 is Magazine -> 7 } } The rules, the order and the exhaustiveness check are the same in both: the first matching branch wins, guards don't count toward exhaustiveness, and neither version needs a default. The difference is where the data comes apart. Java's record patterns reach into Loan, Member and Book in the label and bind the parts. Kotlin can only test the type of the value it switches on, so the twin pulls item out first, switches on that, and reads loan.member.age and loan.branch by hand. javac also checks dominance, which kotlinc doesn't, and Java's switch has explicit null rules, where Kotlin leaves null to the type system.

h: Pattern matching with switch and record patterns · Worked example
x: Rewrite the shelving rules as one switch When an item comes back, this code decides where it goes next. It compiles, it has tests, and it has a bug the compiler can't see. Read it and look for a kind of item it forgets. static String shelveTo(DeskEvent event) { if (event instanceof Returned r) { if (r.item() instanceof Book b) { if (b.newRelease()) return "reservations desk"; return "book trolley"; } if (r.item() instanceof Disc) return "disc shelf"; } return "nowhere"; } fun shelveTo(event: DeskEvent): String { if (event is Returned) { val item = event.item if (item is Book) { if (item.newRelease) return "reservations desk" return "book trolley" } if (item is Disc) return "disc shelf" } return "nowhere" } Name the shapes you care about, most specific first, and let each label take the event apart. DeskEvent is sealed (Returned, Borrowed) and so is Item, so the switch needs no default. static String shelveTo(DeskEvent event) { return switch (event) { // 1. the special case first case Returned(Book(var format, var isNew), int late) when isNew -> "reservations desk"; // 2. then the general cases, one per kind of item case Returned(Book b, int late) -> "book trolley"; case Returned(Disc d, int late) -> "disc shelf"; // 3. events that need no shelving case Borrowed b -> "nowhere"; }; } fun shelveTo(event: DeskEvent): String = when (event) { is Returned -> when (val item = event.item) { // 1. the special case first is Book if item.newRelease -> "reservations desk" // 2. then the general cases, one per kind of item is Book -> "book trolley" is Disc -> "disc shelf" } // 3. events that need no shelving is Borrowed -> "nowhere" } That doesn't compile, in either language: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values (kotlinc: Add the 'is Magazine' branch). A returned magazine matches no case. The old chain had the same gap and returned "nowhere", so returned magazines were never put back. The compiler found the bug the tests missed. Add the case. case Returned(Magazine m, int late) -> "reading room"; // the case the chain forgot is Magazine -> "reading room" // the case the chain forgot On JDK 22 or newer, replace the bindings you never use with _, so a reader sees at a glance which parts each rule depends on. Kotlin's version already names only what it reads. // JDK 22+ case Returned(Book(_, var isNew), _) when isNew -> "reservations desk"; case Returned(Book _, _) -> "book trolley"; case Returned(Disc _, _) -> "disc shelf"; case Returned(Magazine _, _) -> "reading room"; case Borrowed _ -> "nowhere"; // Kotlin uses _ only for unused lambda parameters and destructured components val (_, daysLate) = returned // skip the item, keep the days late

h: Pattern matching with switch and record patterns · Quiz
x: The switch is case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2)) when x1 == x2 -> "vertical"; case Line(Point from, Point to) -> "other";. What does it return for new Line(null, new Point(1, 1))? It throws NullPointerException "other", with from bound to null It throws MatchException "vertical" The nested record pattern Point(var x1, var y1) never matches null, so the first case is skipped. The type pattern Point from covers the whole component type, so it matches null and binds it. If the second case were also a record pattern, the switch would still compile and would throw MatchException for this line. Which pair of cases, in this order, does javac reject with this case label is dominated by a preceding case label? case Integer i -> ... then case Integer i when i > 0 -> ... case Integer i when i > 0 -> ... then case Integer i -> ... case Integer i when i > 0 -> ... then case 1 -> ... case Book b when b.newRelease() -> ... then case Book b when b.format() == LARGE_PRINT -> ... An unguarded case Integer i matches every Integer, so the guarded case after it can never run. A guarded case never dominates anything, which is why the other three orders compile. The last pair compiles but is probably a bug: new large-print books never reach the large-print rule. Kotlin: data class Book(val title: String, val pages: Int). What does val (pages, title) = Book("Dune", 412) do on Kotlin 2.4 with default settings? It fails to compile because the names don't match the properties It binds by name: pages = 412, title = "Dune" It compiles without a warning and binds pages = "Dune", title = 412 It compiles with a warning about swapped names Destructuring calls component1() and component2() in order, whatever you call the variables. Here the types even differ, but each variable just takes its component's type. Name-based destructuring exists only as an Experimental feature (2.3.20 and later, -Xname-based-destructuring). From lesson 1: record Masked(String phone) overrides phone() to return "****" plus the last four digits. For the number 01614960123, what does switch (m) { case Masked(var p) -> p; } return? 01614960123, because patterns read the field like toString does ****0123, because record patterns call the accessor It doesn't compile: records with overridden accessors can't be taken apart null Record patterns read components through the accessors, while the generated toString and equals read the fields. So this record shows ****0123 to patterns and the full number to toString: one more reason not to mask in the accessor. A switch over String section has case "FIC" -> ... and default -> .... The barcode scanner upstream sometimes passes null. What does the OpenJDK sealed-switch guide prefer? Add case null to every switch that might see it Nothing: default already catches null Wrap the switch in try/catch for NullPointerException Reject null before the switch with Objects.requireNonNull(section) default doesn't match null, so today the switch throws NPE. The guide allows case null but prefers Objects.requireNonNull before the switch: it fails where the bad value enters, with a clear message, instead of spreading null handling into every switch.

h: Pattern matching with switch and record patterns · Key terms
x: Type pattern Book b: matches if the value is a Book, and binds it to b. Record pattern Book(var format, var isNew): matches a Book and binds its components, which can be patterns too. Guard The when condition after a pattern (if in Kotlin). The case matches only if the guard is true. Dominance A case is dominated when an earlier case already matches everything it could. javac rejects it. Remainder The values an exhaustive switch doesn't cover at run time: nested nulls, and subtypes added after compilation. MatchException What Java throws when an exhaustive switch meets a value from its remainder (since JDK 21). Unnamed pattern _ in a pattern: matches anything and binds nothing. Final from JDK 22. Do guarded cases count toward exhaustiveness? No, in Java or Kotlin. End each family of guarded cases with an unguarded case of the same pattern. When does javac say this case label is dominated by a preceding case label? When an earlier unguarded case already matches everything the later case could, such as case String s after case CharSequence cs, or case 1 after case Integer i. What does a pattern switch do with a null selector? It throws NullPointerException unless it has case null (or case null, default). default alone doesn't catch null. case Line(Point from, Point to) and the line's from is null. Does it match? Yes. A nested type pattern that covers the component's type matches null. A nested record pattern such as Point(var x, var y) doesn't. An old program's exhaustive switch meets a subtype added after it was compiled. What happens? Java throws MatchException; a Kotlin when throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException. Recompiling turns it into a compile error. How do you put several patterns in one switch arm? Only with unnamed patterns, from JDK 22: case Return _, Renew _ ->. With named bindings javac says illegal fall-through from a pattern. Kotlin val (a, b) = book: by name or by position? By position, through component1() and component2(). Swapped names compile without a warning. Name-based destructuring is Experimental since 2.3.20.

h: Pattern matching with switch and record patterns · Go deeper
x: Two newer features build on this lesson. Neither belongs in the labs, which compile for JDK 21. Primitive types in patterns have been a preview feature in every JDK from 23 to 27, and they are still a preview in the JDK 28 builds. They let a switch over an int use type patterns and guards, and let instanceof ask whether a value fits another primitive type exactly: Java // JDK 25: java --enable-preview --source 25 preview/PrimitivePatterns.java static String length(int pages) { return switch (pages) { case 0 -> "no pages"; case int p when p < 100 -> "short (" + p + " pages)"; case int p -> "medium or long (" + p + " pages)"; }; } Kotlin // Kotlin has always allowed conditions on any subject fun length(pages: Int): String = when { pages == 0 -> "no pages" pages < 100 -> "short ($pages pages)" else -> "medium or long ($pages pages)" } Without the preview flags, JDK 25 stops with primitive patterns are a preview feature and are disabled by default. Treat the syntax as likely to change until it is final. The second feature is better error messages. JDK 27's javac lists what a non-exhaustive switch is missing, under a missing patterns: line, in the form Rect _ for a type and Pair(Red _,Green _) for a nested record pattern. That one change makes nested exhaustiveness errors much easier to read: on JDK 21 the same Pair switch only says it doesn't cover all possible input values, and you work out the missing combination yourself. One habit to avoid: don't write case _ when .... JDK 25's javac accepts it, but the language specification doesn't allow it, and a fix in JDK 28 development (JDK-8385488) makes javac reject it. Write default or a real type pattern instead.

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Make illegal states unrepresentable
x: One optional-field class allows 48 shapes and 3 make sense; three records under a sealed interface allow only those 3, one parse at the edge lets nothing else in, and the logic lives in functions over the data Here is how the catalogue's answer usually arrives in a program: one class, every field optional. Java public class HoldReplyDto { String status; // "READY", "UNAVAILABLE" or "WAITLISTED" String pickupCode; // only when ready Integer holdShelf; // only when ready String reasonCode; // only when unavailable Integer waitDays; // only when waitlisted } Kotlin data class HoldReplyDto( val status: String?, // "READY", "UNAVAILABLE" or "WAITLISTED" val pickupCode: String?, // only when ready val holdShelf: Int?, // only when ready val reasonCode: String?, // only when unavailable val waitDays: Int?, // only when waitlisted ) A DTO, short for data transfer object, is a class whose only job is to hold the fields of a message as they arrived. Count what this one allows. Three statuses, times four optional fields that are each set or null, gives 48 shapes. Three of them make sense. The other 45, such as ready with no pickup code, or ready with a reason code, can be built, stored and passed around. The comments are the only place that says which fields go together. Every piece of code that reads the DTO has to check that again, and one of them won't. The IllegalStates demo hands a broken reply to the code that prints pickup slips: shapes the DTO allows: 48, shapes that make sense: 3 DTO consumer: print slip: shelf 12, code null A member now holds a slip with no code on it, and the desk can't hand over the book. Model the three outcomes instead, each with only its own fields: Java public sealed interface HoldResult permits Ready, Unavailable, Waitlisted {} public record Ready(PickupCode code, int shelf) implements HoldResult {} public record Unavailable(Reason reason) implements HoldResult {} public record Waitlisted(Duration expectedWait) implements HoldResult {} Kotlin sealed interface HoldResult { data class Ready(val code: PickupCode, val shelf: Int) : HoldResult data class Unavailable(val reason: Reason) : HoldResult data class Waitlisted(val expectedWait: Duration) : HoldResult } Now there are three shapes, and "ready with a reason" can't even be written down. In the paperwork picture, the one form with every box has become three forms, each with only its own boxes. The checks that are left move into the constructors: a pickup code is six letters or digits, and hold shelves start at 1. (The component is expectedWait, not wait; lesson 1's aside showed why Java refuses that name.) That's what "make illegal states unrepresentable" means in practice: the types and the canonical constructors refuse the bad values once, so no reader has to. Brian Goetz calls this style data-oriented programming: model the data as immutable records and sealed types, and write the logic as functions over them. He wrote it up in a 2022 InfoQ article, "Data Oriented Programming in Java". His 2019 design note on records and sealed types gives the vocabulary. A record is a product type: a Ready is a code and a shelf, and its API models "the state, the whole state, and nothing but the state". A sealed interface is a sum type, "a discriminated union of a fixed set of types": a HoldResult is ready or unavailable or waitlisted. Most messages a program handles have exactly this shape, a few alternatives, each a fixed set of fields. A shape that can't be built can't be mishandled. Give each valid combination its own record. Three clean forms help only if every answer from outside is copied onto one of them. That copying needs a place. Count the shapes, then build a bad one Run IllegalStates (or IllegalStatesKt). Read the DTO consumer line: what will the member find on the slip? In the Java demo, try to build a Ready with a reason code. There is no constructor for it: the shape doesn't exist. In the Kotlin twin, change HoldResult.Ready("", 12) to HoldResult.Ready(null, 12) and run. Which tool stopped you this time? IllegalStates.java package workbench.modernjava.l04.demo; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.Objects; /** One class with optional fields, against a sealed model that has only the valid shapes. */ public class IllegalStates { // the "bag of optionals" a JSON mapper gives you for the catalogue's reply to a hold request static final class HoldReplyDto { final String status; // "READY", "UNAVAILABLE" or "WAITLISTED" final String pickupCode; // should be set only when ready final String reasonCode; // should be set only when unavailable final Integer waitDays; // should be set only when waitlisted final Integer holdShelf; // should be set only when ready HoldReplyDto(String status, String pickupCode, String reasonCode, Integer waitDays, Integer holdShelf) { this.status = status; this.pickupCode = pickupCode; this.reasonCode = reasonCode; this.waitDays = waitDays; this.holdShelf = holdShelf; } } // a consumer of the DTO: it trusts that the fields match the status static String pickupSlip(HoldReplyDto r) { if ("READY".equals(r.status)) return "print slip: shelf " + r.holdShelf + ", code " + r.pickupCode; return "no slip"; } // the same information as a closed model: three shapes, each with only its own fields sealed interface HoldResult permits Ready, Unavailable, Waitlisted {} record Ready(String pickupCode, int shelf) implements HoldResult { Ready { Objects.requireNonNull(pickupCode, "pickupCode"); if (shelf < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("hold shelves start at 1"); } } record Unavailable(String reasonCode) implements HoldResult {} record Waitlisted(Duration expectedWait) implements HoldResult {} static String pickupSlip(HoldResult r) { return switch (r) { case Ready(var code, var shelf) -> "print slip: shelf " + shelf + ", code " + code; case Unavailable u -> "no slip"; case Waitlisted w -> "no slip yet"; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { int statuses = 3, optionalFields = 4; System.out.println("shapes the DTO allows: " + statuses * (1 << optionalFields) + ", shapes that make sense: 3"); // ready, but with no pickup code and a reason code: nothing stops it HoldReplyDto broken = new HoldReplyDto("READY", null, "10", null, 12); System.out.println("DTO consumer: " + pickupSlip(broken)); try { new Ready(null, 12); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("sealed model: refused, " + e.getMessage() + " is required"); } System.out.println("sealed consumer: " + pickupSlip(new Ready("K7P2QX", 12))); } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l04.demo.IllegalStates gives you for the catalogue's reply to a hold request data class HoldReplyDto( val status: String?, // "READY", "UNAVAILABLE" or "WAITLISTED" val pickupCode: String?, // should be set only when ready val reasonCode: String?, // should be set only when unavailable val waitDays: Int?, // should be set only when waitlisted val holdShelf: Int?, // should be set only when ready ) // a consumer of the = 3 val optionalFields = 4 println("shapes the DTO allows: ${statuses * (1 shl optionalFields)}, shapes that make sense: 3") // ready, but with no pickup code and a reason code: nothing stops it val broken = HoldReplyDto("READY", null, "10", null, 12) println("DTO consumer: ${pickupSlip(broken)}") // HoldResult.Ready(null, 12) doesn't even compile: the type says the code is there try { HoldResult.Ready("", 12) } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("sealed model: refused, ${e.message}") } println("sealed consumer: ${pickupSlip(HoldResult.Ready("K7P2QX", 12))}") } ./gradlew make sense: 3, then DTO consumer: print slip: shelf 12, code null: nothing stopped a ready reply with no code. The sealed model refuses it (pickupCode is required), and the valid hold prints print slip: shelf 12, code K7P2QX. In Kotlin, Ready(null, 12) doesn't compile at all, because the property is a non-null String: the type system did the constructor's job. Brian Goetz, Data Oriented Programming in Java (InfoQ, 2022) read

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Parse at the edge, then trust the types
x: The sealed model helps only if untrusted data can't get in around it. So the program turns raw input into the model in exactly one place, at its edge: the code that reads the catalogue's message. Everything behind the edge works only with model values. In the picture, letters from outside arrive in any handwriting. One clerk at the door copies each onto the right form, or sends it back with a polite note saying what was wrong. Java static Parsed parse(HoldReplyDto raw) { try { return switch (raw.status) { case "READY" -> raw.pickupCode == null || raw.holdShelf == null ? new Rejected("ready without a code or a shelf") : new Ok(new Ready(new PickupCode(raw.pickupCode), raw.holdShelf)); case "UNAVAILABLE" -> new Ok(new Unavailable(Reason.fromCode(raw.reasonCode))); case "WAITLISTED" -> raw.waitDays == null ? new Rejected("waiting list without a wait") : new Ok(new Waitlisted(Duration.ofDays(raw.waitDays))); case null, default -> new Rejected("unknown status: " + raw.status); }; } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { return new Rejected(e.getMessage()); // a constructor refused a value } } Kotlin fun parse(raw: HoldReplyDto): Parsed = try { when (raw.status) { "READY" -> if (raw.pickupCode == null || raw.holdShelf == null) Rejected("ready without a code or a shelf") else Ok(Ready(PickupCode(raw.pickupCode), raw.holdShelf)) "UNAVAILABLE" -> Ok(Unavailable(Reason.fromCode(raw.reasonCode))) "WAITLISTED" -> if (raw.waitDays == null) Rejected("waiting list without a wait") else Ok(Waitlisted(Duration.ofDays(raw.waitDays.toLong()))) else -> Rejected("unknown status: ${raw.status}") } } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { Rejected(e.message ?: "invalid reply") // a constructor refused a value } Read parse from the top. It switches on the status string. A ready reply needs its code and its shelf, or it's rejected with a reason. An unavailable reply looks up its code in a small table of reasons. A waiting-list reply needs its days. Anything else, null included, is rejected. The tricky part is the try around it all: it catches the IllegalArgumentException a constructor throws when it refuses a value, and turns it into a Rejected too. Two details make this work. The function never throws. A reply the model refuses comes back as Rejected with a reason. The caller decides what that means (log it, ask the catalogue again, tell the member to ask at the desk), and no exception escapes from somewhere deep inside. And the constructors stay the final check: parse doesn't repeat the pickup-code rule, it calls new PickupCode(...) and reports the refusal. Behind the edge, nothing checks again. A method that takes a Ready knows it has a valid code and a real shelf, because no other kind of Ready can exist. Records and sealed types make this cheap: the model is a dozen lines, the edge is one function, and the compiler checks every switch in between. The lab builds exactly this, in Kotlin, including a case the snippets above skip: a ready reply that also carries a reason code contradicts itself, and must be rejected. Check outside data once, at the door. Behind the door, trust the types. Only good forms get in now. The next question is where the rules that read them should live. Predict what the door does The catalogue sends status: "READY " (with a trailing space), pickup code K7P2QX and hold shelf 12. Which arm of parse takes it, and what does the pickup desk see? It sends a waiting-list reply with waitDays: 0. Does parse or a constructor produce the result? A teammate adds if (ready.shelf() < 1) return; inside the code that prints slips. Can that line ever run? The trailing space matches no status string, so case null, default returns Rejected("unknown status: READY "), and the pickup desk never sees the reply: a strict door turns a sloppy reply into a visible rejection instead of a slip with bad data. The zero wait gets past parse, because the field isn't null, and is refused by the Waitlisted constructor once it has the range check (as the lab's does); the catch turns that refusal into Rejected. The teammate's line is dead code: a Ready with a shelf below 1 can't be built, so the check can never be true.

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Keep the rules in one place: operations live outside the data
x: In classic object-oriented design, behavior lives in the classes: result.screenMessage(), result.nextStep(), result.reminderText(), each written three times, across Ready, Unavailable and Waitlisted. Data-oriented code keeps the records plain and writes each operation as one function with a switch. In the picture, the forms stay plain, and the rules live in one binder at the desk: Java static String screenMessage(HoldResult r) { return switch (r) { case Ready(var code, var shelf) -> "Your book is waiting on hold shelf " + shelf + "."; case Unavailable(var reason) when reason == Reason.ACCOUNT_BLOCKED -> "Please ask at the desk."; case Unavailable u -> "This title is not available right now."; case Waitlisted(var wait) -> "You're on the waiting list. Expected wait: " + wait.toDays() + " days."; }; } Kotlin fun screenMessage(r: HoldResult): String = when (r) { is Ready -> "Your book is waiting on hold shelf ${r.shelf}." is Unavailable if r.reason == Reason.ACCOUNT_BLOCKED -> "Please ask at the desk." is Unavailable -> "This title is not available right now." is Waitlisted -> "You're on the waiting list. Expected wait: ${r.expectedWait.toDays()} days." } Everything about the screen at the self-service desk sits in one function. The records don't depend on screen text, and the next operation, say the text message sent to the member's phone, is a new function that touches nothing else. Note the account-blocked line: the screen stands in a public place, so it never says what's wrong with an account. That's one side of the expression problem, which Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento in the patterns track introduced. It says that no design makes both kinds of change cheap: adding a new type, and adding a new operation. With methods on the classes, adding a type is local, and adding an operation means editing every class. With sealed types and switches it's the other way round: a new operation is one function, and a new type breaks every switch until you handle it. The figure shows the grid. Choose by the change you expect more often. For the library's data (hold results, desk events, loans, copy statuses) the set of types changes rarely, and new operations keep arriving: a new report, a new reminder, a new screen. So the data-oriented side wins there. For open hierarchies that others extend, such as the partner libraries' PartnerItem from lesson 2, keep an interface with methods. And behavior that's about the value itself, like Shelfmark.next(), belongs on the record. Keep the library's rules out of the records; small methods that compute with the value itself can stay. The ExpressionProblem demo lets you pay both costs. Its Activity records what happened on a member's account, a book borrowed, returned or renewed, and two functions switch over it: borrowed Dune for 21 days borrowed Emma for 21 days returned Dune renewed Emma for 14 more days books out: 1 Adding a third function changes no existing line. Adding a Lost activity breaks both switches, and the compiler lists each one. Plain data, rules in functions. A new rule then touches one place, and a new type is found by the compiler. Records and sealed types settle how the data is shaped. How the JVM stores that data is the last part of the story. Pay both costs Run ExpressionProblem (or ExpressionProblemKt). Write operation 3 where the comment says: sendsReceipt, true for borrowing and renewing (the member gets the new due date), false for returns. How many existing lines did you change? Add the Lost record (in Java, add it to permits too) and run. List the places the compiler asks you to change. Decide what a lost book does to the count of books out and to the history line, and handle it in each function. ExpressionProblem.java package workbench.modernjava.l04.demo; import java.util.List; /** Data in records, operations in functions. Add an operation, then add a type, and compare the cost. */ public class ExpressionProblem { // what can happen on a member's account sealed interface Activity permits Borrowed, Returned, Renewed {} record Borrowed(String title, int days) implements Activity {} record Returned(String title) implements Activity {} record Renewed(String title, int extraDays) implements Activity {} // Step 3: add Lost to the permits clause, then uncomment this record. // record Lost(String title, int daysOverdue) implements Activity {} // operation 1: how the activity changes the number of books the member has out static int booksOutDelta(Activity a) { return switch (a) { case Borrowed b -> 1; case Returned r -> -1; case Renewed r -> 0; }; } // operation 2: the line in the member's history static String historyLine(Activity a) { return switch (a) { case Borrowed(var title, var days) -> "borrowed " + title + " for " + days + " days"; case Returned(var title) -> "returned " + title; case Renewed(var title, var extra) -> "renewed " + title + " for " + extra + " more days"; }; } // Step 2: write operation 3 here, sendsReceipt(Activity), as one more switch. public static void main(String[] args) { List<Activity> week = List.of(new Borrowed("Dune", 21), new Borrowed("Emma", 21), new Returned("Dune"), new Renewed("Emma", 14)); int booksOut = 0; for (Activity a : week) { booksOut += booksOutDelta(a); System.out.println(historyLine(a)); } System.out.println("books out: " + booksOut); } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l04.demo.ExpressionProblem labs/modernjava/src/demo/java/workbench/modernjava/l04/demo/ExpressionProblem.java ExpressionProblem.kt package workbench.modernjava.l04.demo // what can happen on a member's account sealed interface Activity { data class Borrowed(val title: String, val days: Int) : Activity data class Returned(val title: String) : Activity data class Renewed(val title: String, val extraDays: Int) : Activity // Step 3: uncomment this class. // data class Lost(val title: String, val daysOverdue: Int) : Activity } // operation 1: how the activity changes the number of books the member has out fun booksOutDelta(a: Activity): Int = when (a) { is Activity.Borrowed -> 1 is Activity.Returned -> -1 is Activity.Renewed -> 0 } // operation 2: the line in the member's history fun historyLine(a: Activity): String = when (a) { is Activity.Borrowed -> "borrowed ${a.title} for ${a.days} days" is Activity.Returned -> "returned ${a.title}" is Activity.Renewed -> "renewed ${a.title} for ${a.extraDays} more days" } // Step 2: write operation 3 here, sendsReceipt(Activity), as one more when. /** Data in data classes, operations in functions. Add an operation, then add a type, and compare the cost. */ fun main() { val week = listOf(Activity.Borrowed("Dune", 21), Activity.Borrowed("Emma", 21), Activity.Returned("Dune"), Activity.Renewed("Emma", 14)) var booksOut = 0 for (a in week) { booksOut += booksOutDelta(a) println(historyLine(a)) } println("books out: $booksOut") } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l04.demo.ExpressionProblemKt labs/modernjava/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/modernjava/l04/demo/ExpressionProblem.kt The demo prints four history lines and books out: 1. Adding sendsReceipt changed no existing line. Adding Lost makes javac report each switch over Activity (booksOutDelta, historyLine and your new one) with does not cover all possible input values, and kotlinc asks for the 'is Lost' branch in each when. A new operation cost one function; a new type cost one edit per operation, and the compiler found every one. The expression problem: each style makes one kind of change local and the other kind expensive. Sealed types at least make the compiler find every place to change.

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Project Valhalla: forms printed straight onto the page
x: Records are identity objects, and lesson 1 showed what that means: == compares references, you can lock on a record, and every new makes a separate object. The IdentityDemo shows one more consequence. An array of records is an array of references, each pointing at a separate object on the heap, the memory where Java keeps its objects: equals: true, ==: false shelf[0] == shelf[2]: true, shelf[0] == shelf[1]: false In the paperwork picture, each record is a form in its own envelope, and the array is a list of where the envelopes are. Reading a form means walking to its envelope and opening it. Project Valhalla, a long-running OpenJDK project, wants small forms printed straight onto the page instead, with no envelope. Its first feature lets a class give up identity: Java value record Shelf(short floor, short row) {} // JDK 28 early-access builds, --enable-preview Kotlin @JvmInline value class Isbn(val value: String) // Kotlin today: one property, compiled away The status is often misreported, so here it is precisely. JEP 401, Value Objects (Preview), is the JDK Enhancement Proposal for this feature. Together with JEP 539 (strict field initialization in the JVM), it was integrated into the JDK's main code line on 31 July 2026. JDK 27 had already branched off, so the feature ships in JDK 28, scheduled for 23 March 2027, and early-access builds of JDK 28 have it now. It's a preview: it needs --enable-preview and can still change. JDK 25, 26 and 27 don't have it. The Valhalla docs define value objects as immutable objects that lack identity, "distinguished solely by the values of their fields". == compares two value objects by their fields, and identity operations such as synchronized fail. Two identical printed lines are interchangeable, and you can't seal an envelope that isn't there. In return, the JVM may store them flat. In JDK 28 that means two optimizations. Flattening stores a value's fields directly inside the field or array element that holds it, with no separate object and no reference. Scalarization lets code compiled by the JIT (the part of the JVM that turns busy code into machine code) keep the fields in registers and skip creating the object at all. Here the picture breaks: you don't choose what gets printed onto the page, the JVM does, and only small forms qualify. Flattened values are read and written atomically, in one piece, and must allow null, so value objects with 64 bits or more of field data "cannot normally be flattened". By that rule, a record with a long and anything else is already too big. Scalarization only happens once C2, the JIT's optimizing compiler, has compiled the code, and variables of a general type, including those in generic APIs, aren't flattened. Records whose fields add up to less than 64 bits, such as two short fields, gain first. With the preview on, 28 JDK classes become value classes, among them Integer, Long, Optional, LocalDate, Instant and Duration. Synchronizing on an Integer then throws IdentityException. Null-restricted types, the other thing people expect from Valhalla, are still draft JEPs. Kotlin's @JvmInline value class is an older, different trick. It holds one property and is erased to that property where the compiler can: javap, the JDK's class-file reader, shows that describeIsbn(Isbn) compiles to describeIsbn-3aCjwxg(java.lang.String), a plain String under a mangled name. It's boxed, that is, wrapped in a real Isbn object, when used as a generic T, an interface or a nullable type; the demo prints in a List, the element is a Isbn. Kotlin's design notes say the annotation leaves room for real Valhalla value classes later. No such mode has shipped, so a Kotlin data class on JDK 28 is still an identity object. Don't lean on a record's identity. Then value can be a one-word change later. In practice that means no == between records, no synchronized on them, and no maps keyed on identity. Look at identity, then at a Kotlin value class Run IdentityDemo. Which of its lines would change if Copy were a value record? Run IdentityDemoKt. From labs/, run javap -p modernjava/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/modernjava/l04/demo/IdentityDemoKt.class. What parameter type does describeIsbn take? IdentityDemo.java package workbench.modernjava.l04.demo; /** Records are identity objects today. Here is what that identity looks like. */ public class IdentityDemo { // one physical copy of a book: its ISBN and its copy number record Copy(String isbn, int number) {} public static void main(String[] args) { Copy a = new Copy("9780441013593", 1); Copy b = new Copy("9780441013593", 1); System.out.println("equals: " + a.equals(b) + ", ==: " + (a == b)); System.out.println("identity hash codes differ: " + (System.identityHashCode(a) != System.identityHashCode(b))); synchronized (a) { System.out.println("synchronized on a record: allowed, because it has an identity"); } // the Integer box cache lets identity leak into == for some values and not others Integer x = 127, y = 127, p = 128, q = 128; System.out.println("Integer 127 == 127: " + (x == y) + ", 128 == 128: " + (p == q)); // an array of records is an array of references to separate heap objects Copy[] shelf = { a, b, a }; System.out.println("shelf[0] == shelf[2]: " + (shelf[0] == shelf[2]) + ", shelf[0] == shelf[1]: " + (shelf[0] == shelf[1])); } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l04.demo.IdentityDemo labs/modernjava/src/demo/java/workbench/modernjava/l04/demo/IdentityDemo.java IdentityDemo.kt package workbench.modernjava.l04.demo // one physical copy of a book: its ISBN and its copy number data class BookCopy(val isbn: String, val number: Int) // Kotlin's value class today: one property, erased to that property wherever the compiler can @JvmInline value class Isbn(val value: String) fun describeIsbn(isbn: Isbn): String = "ISBN ending ${isbn.value.takeLast(4)}" /** Data classes are identity objects today; @JvmInline value classes are a compile-time trick. */ fun main() { val a = BookCopy("9780441013593", 1) val b = BookCopy("9780441013593", 1) println("==: ${a == b}, ===: ${a === b}") synchronized(a) { println("synchronized on a data class: allowed, because it has an identity") } val isbn = Isbn("9780441013593") println(describeIsbn(isbn)) // compiled to a call taking a plain String val asAny: Any = isbn // used as another type: boxed println("as Any, the object is a ${asAny::class.java.simpleName}") val inList = listOf(isbn) // used as a generic T: boxed println("in a List, the element is a ${(inList[0] as Any)::class.java.simpleName}") } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l04.demo.IdentityDemoKt labs/modernjava/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/modernjava/l04/demo/IdentityDemo.kt equals: true, ==: false, different identity hash codes, a successful synchronized, Integer 127 == 127: true, 128 == 128: false, and shelf[0] == shelf[2]: true, shelf[0] == shelf[1]: false. With a value record, == would compare fields, so a == b and shelf[0] == shelf[1] would be true, and synchronized would be refused. In Kotlin, javap shows describeIsbn-3aCjwxg(java.lang.String): the value class is erased to a String under a mangled name, and the demo shows it boxed back into an Isbn when stored as Any or in a List. JEP 401: Value Objects (Preview) read Inline value classes (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Java and Kotlin
x: One model and one operation in Java and Kotlin HoldResult.java public record PickupCode(String value) { public PickupCode { if (value == null || !value.matches("[A-Z0-9]{6}")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad pickup code"); } } public sealed interface HoldResult permits Ready, Unavailable, Waitlisted {} public record Ready(PickupCode code, int shelf) implements HoldResult { public Ready { if (shelf < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("hold shelves start at 1"); } } public record Unavailable(Reason reason) implements HoldResult {} public record Waitlisted(Duration expectedWait) implements HoldResult {} static String screenMessage(HoldResult r) { return switch (r) { case Ready(var code, var shelf) -> "Your book is waiting on hold shelf " + shelf + "."; case Unavailable(var reason) when reason == Reason.ACCOUNT_BLOCKED -> "Please ask at the desk."; case Unavailable u -> "This title is not available right now."; case Waitlisted(var wait) -> "You're on the waiting list. Expected wait: " + wait.toDays() + " days."; }; } HoldResult.kt @JvmInline value class PickupCode(val value: String) { init { require(value.matches(Regex("[A-Z0-9]{6}"))) { "bad pickup code" } } } sealed interface HoldResult { data class Ready(val code: PickupCode, val shelf: Int) : HoldResult { init { require(shelf >= 1) { "hold shelves start at 1" } } } data class Unavailable(val reason: Reason) : HoldResult data class Waitlisted(val expectedWait: Duration) : HoldResult } fun screenMessage(r: HoldResult): String = when (r) { is HoldResult.Ready -> "Your book is waiting on hold shelf ${r.shelf}." is HoldResult.Unavailable if r.reason == Reason.ACCOUNT_BLOCKED -> "Please ask at the desk." is HoldResult.Unavailable -> "This title is not available right now." is HoldResult.Waitlisted -> "You're on the waiting list. Expected wait: ${r.expectedWait.toDays()} days." } The design is identical: a closed set of outcomes, each with only its own fields, constructors that refuse bad values, and an operation written as one exhaustive switch outside the data. Two things differ. Java's switch takes Ready and Unavailable apart in the label, while Kotlin tests the type and reads r.shelf after a smart cast. And PickupCode is a record in Java, a full object with identity, while Kotlin's @JvmInline value class is usually erased to a plain String. With JDK 28's preview, Java could write value record PickupCode(String value) and give up identity at the JVM level, which Kotlin's value class doesn't do today.

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Worked example
x: From the delivery van's report to a closed model A van carries crates of books between the branches, and the van company's system sends a report at each stop. Its docs say: a DELIVERED report has an arrival date, a DELAYED report has a reason, and a DAMAGED report says how many books were damaged. The DTO encodes none of that. public record VanReportDto(String type, String crateId, LocalDate arrivalDate, String delayReason, Integer damagedBooks) {} data class VanReportDto(val type: String?, val crateId: String?, val arrivalDate: LocalDate?, val delayReason: String?, val damagedBooks: Int?) Write one record per row of the van company's docs. Every field is required, so a record can't be half a DELIVERED report. // 1. one record per valid combination public sealed interface VanReport permits Delivered, Delayed, Damaged {} public record Delivered(String crateId, LocalDate arrivalDate) implements VanReport {} public record Delayed(String crateId, String reason) implements VanReport {} public record Damaged(String crateId, int books) implements VanReport { public Damaged { if (books <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("a damage report needs at least one book"); } } // 1. one class per valid combination, with non-null properties sealed interface VanReport { data class Delivered(val crateId: String, val arrivalDate: LocalDate) : VanReport data class Delayed(val crateId: String, val reason: String) : VanReport data class Damaged(val crateId: String, val books: Int) : VanReport { init { require(books > 0) { "a damage report needs at least one book" } } } } Write the edge. It's the only code that looks at the DTO, and it checks that each type carries its own field. A null where the docs promise a value becomes a clear error here, not a NullPointerException three methods later. // 2. the edge: DTO in, model out static VanReport toReport(VanReportDto d) { Objects.requireNonNull(d.crateId(), "crateId"); return switch (d.type()) { case "DELIVERED" -> new Delivered(d.crateId(), Objects.requireNonNull(d.arrivalDate(), "arrivalDate")); case "DELAYED" -> new Delayed(d.crateId(), Objects.requireNonNull(d.delayReason(), "delayReason")); case "DAMAGED" -> new Damaged(d.crateId(), Objects.requireNonNull(d.damagedBooks(), "damagedBooks")); case null, default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown van report: " + d.type()); }; } // 2. the edge: DTO in, model out fun toReport(d: VanReportDto): VanReport { val id = requireNotNull(d.crateId) { "crateId" } return when (d.type) { "DELIVERED" -> VanReport.Delivered(id, requireNotNull(d.arrivalDate) { "arrivalDate" }) "DELAYED" -> VanReport.Delayed(id, requireNotNull(d.delayReason) { "delayReason" }) "DAMAGED" -> VanReport.Damaged(id, requireNotNull(d.damagedBooks) { "damagedBooks" }) else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown van report: ${d.type}") } } Now the code that acts on a report. The old version was thirty lines of if ("DELIVERED".equals(type) && arrivalDate != null). The new one is a switch with no default, so a new kind of report from the van company shows up as a compile error, not as a report that is silently ignored. // 3. behind the edge: trust the types static void apply(VanReport r, Catalogue catalogue) { switch (r) { case Delivered(var id, var date) -> catalogue.markArrived(id, date); case Delayed(var id, var reason) -> catalogue.tellBranch(id, reason); case Damaged(var id, int books) -> catalogue.orderReplacements(id, books); } } // 3. behind the edge: trust the types fun apply(r: VanReport, catalogue: Catalogue) = when (r) { is VanReport.Delivered -> catalogue.markArrived(r.crateId, r.arrivalDate) is VanReport.Delayed -> catalogue.tellBranch(r.crateId, r.reason) is VanReport.Damaged -> catalogue.orderReplacements(r.crateId, r.books) }
