h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Quiz
x: The catalogue's DTO has a status and four nullable fields, and its docs list three valid combinations. What does a sealed model with three records give you that careful checks in every reader of the DTO don't? Faster JSON reading Invalid combinations can't be built, so no code behind the edge can receive one Nothing, as long as every reader checks Smaller objects on the heap With the sealed model the bad shapes don't exist, and the constructors refuse bad values once. Checking in every reader works only until one reader forgets, and the DTO keeps letting 45 nonsense shapes travel through the program. Neither the reading speed nor the object size changes. New partner libraries join the regional network every month, each with its own module, and each must answer loanDays() for the items it lends. Which design fits? An enum listing all partner libraries A sealed interface of records, with one switch in the library's own module An interface PartnerItem with a loanDays() method that each partner implements A sealed interface whose switch has a default branch for partners it doesn't know Here the set of types grows and the operation stays the same, and the types live in other modules: the object-oriented side of the expression problem. A sealed hierarchy would force every new partner into the library's module and break its switch each month. A default would just hide the new partners. Which statement about Project Valhalla is accurate? JDK 25 LTS ships value classes as a preview Records became value objects in JDK 27 Null-restricted types such as String! are final in JDK 28 JEP 401 value objects are a preview feature of JDK 28; JDK 25, 26 and 27 don't have them JEP 401 was integrated after JDK 27 branched off, so it ships in JDK 28 (scheduled for March 2027) as a preview. Records are still identity objects; value record is only legal under that preview. Null-restricted types are still draft JEPs. From Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento: you replaced a Visitor over a sealed Expr with switch functions. Now a new node type, Pow, arrives. What does each design make you do? Visitor: add visitPow to the interface and to every visitor. Switches: every switch fails to compile until it handles Pow Visitor: nothing. Switches: nothing, because sealed types accept new records Visitor: one new class. Switches: one new function Both: only add the new record Visitor and sealed switches sit on the same side of the expression problem: adding a type is the expensive change in both. The difference is that the switches need no accept and no visitor interface, and the compiler points at each switch to fix. @JvmInline value class Isbn(val value: String) and fun describe(i: Isbn). What does the JVM see for describe(isbn) and for listOf(isbn)? Two ordinary Isbn objects, like any class A String in both places describe takes a String under a mangled name, and the list holds a boxed Isbn A Valhalla value object, flattened in both places Kotlin erases the value class to its one property where it can, so describe compiles to something like describe-XXXX(String). Used as a generic T, as in a List, it must be boxed into a real Isbn object. None of this uses Valhalla: it's compile-time work, and it runs on any JVM.

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Explain it back
x: Your team lead asks: "Should we move the library's data to records and sealed types now, or wait for Valhalla to make it fast?" Answer in your own words: what the data-oriented style gives you today, where you would and wouldn't use it, and what Valhalla changes.

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Key terms
x: Data-oriented programming Modeling data as immutable records and sealed types, and writing the rules as functions that switch over them. Product type A type whose value is several values together, like a record: a code and a shelf. Sum type A type whose value is one of a fixed set of alternatives, like a sealed interface: ready, unavailable or waitlisted. Illegal state A combination of field values that can't happen in real life, such as ready with a reason code. Expression problem No design makes both new types and new operations cheap; you pick the side that matches how your code changes. Value object Valhalla's object without identity: compared by its fields, and free for the JVM to copy or flatten. Preview in JDK 28. Flattening Storing a value object's fields directly inside the field or array that holds it, instead of a reference to a separate object. What does "make illegal states unrepresentable" mean in Java and Kotlin? Model each valid combination as its own record (or data class) under a sealed type, and check values in the constructors, so an invalid value can't be built. Record and sealed interface, in algebraic terms? A record is a product type: this and that. A sealed interface is a sum type: this or that. Where should untrusted input be checked? Once, at the edge: one parse function turns the DTO into the model or a rejection. Code behind the edge trusts the types. With sealed types and switches, what does adding an operation cost? And a type? An operation is one new function. A type breaks every exhaustive switch over the hierarchy, and the compiler lists each one. When do you keep an interface with methods instead of a sealed type? For open hierarchies that others extend (plug-ins, partner libraries' items), and for behavior about the value itself, like Shelfmark.next(). Which JDK has JEP 401 value objects? JDK 28, as a preview feature (scheduled for March 2027; early-access builds now). Not JDK 25, 26 or 27. Why won't value record Copy(long isbn13, int number) normally be flattened in JDK 28? Flattened values must be read and written atomically and allow null, so values with 64 bits or more of field data aren't normally flattened. The long alone is 64 bits.

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Go deeper
x: Brian Goetz's January 2026 design note, "Data-Oriented Programming for Java: Beyond Records", says where Project Amber, the OpenJDK project behind records and patterns, goes next. It calls records, sealed classes and record patterns "the first feature arc of 'data-oriented programming' for Java", and announces the next arc: carrier classes and carrier interfaces. A carrier class is a normal class with a record-style state description in its header. It would declare its own fields and need not be final, yet still have a canonical constructor, accessors and a deconstruction pattern. So data that is almost a record (one cached field, one derived value) wouldn't force you back to writing everything by hand. The note also describes reconstruction, the with expression from JEP 468, and points out how much its block resembles a compact constructor body: the component variables start with the old values, your block changes some of them, and the canonical constructor builds the new value, so the checks still run. Goetz explains that JEP 468 has been "on hold" until there was a path to extend it beyond records. The note also mentions an upcoming pattern assignment statement, for taking a record apart in an ordinary assignment. None of this is in a JDK or a JEP you can use. The design direction is useful anyway: it says the language will keep making "model the data with records and sealed types, switch over it" cheaper, so code written in that style today is code the platform is moving toward. On the Valhalla side, the next pieces on the project page are null-restricted storage, array improvements, unifying primitives with classes, and a JVM that can specialize generic code for each type it's used with. Only the first piece, value objects, has a JEP that has been integrated, and it's a preview.

h: Advanced Kotlin
x: Inline functions, value classes, delegation, type-safe DSLs, contracts, context parameters and compiler plugins. By the end of this track, the Kotlin features you use every day stop being magic. For each one you can say what the compiler writes into the class file, and so predict how it behaves in a case nobody showed you: what an inline function pastes into its callers, where a value class is a plain long and where it becomes an object again, which hidden fields by creates, how lambdas with receivers become a small language, what a contract promises and why nobody checks it, how context parameters reach a function, and what the all-open, no-arg and serialization plugins add. Each lesson also shows what Java sees when it calls the same Kotlin code, because the two languages meet in the bytecode. You need the basic syntax of Kotlin and Java, and nothing else. One small print shop runs through all six lessons. Its app takes print jobs at the counter, sends them to printers such as laser-1 (which jams now and then), weighs parcels in grams and keeps a logbook for each shift. Every lesson shows the problem first, then the feature that fixes it, then the bytecode as javap (the JDK's class-file printer) shows it, then the trap. The compiler messages quoted in the lessons come from Kotlin 2.4.21. Install JDK 25; the labs compile with release 21. The labs live in labs/kotlin, one package per lesson (workbench.kotlin.l01 to l06). They are in Kotlin, and each lesson adds a Java test that calls your Kotlin code the way a Java module would. Lessons 1 and 5 test inline functions through a Callers.kt file that you don't edit (lesson 1 explains why). The module already applies the kotlinx.serialization, all-open and no-arg plugins; lesson 6 puts them to work. Run ./gradlew :kotlin:test --tests 'workbench.kotlin.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, ./gradlew :kotlin:solutionTest to see the reference answers pass the same tests, and ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=<class> for the Try-it programs. To read bytecode, run javap -c -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo <class> after a demo has compiled. inline pastes a function and its lambdas into each caller: no lambda object and non-local returns allowed, but every caller carries a copy, and a public body stays frozen in compiled callers. crossinline lets an inline function call a lambda from another place, such as a Runnable, by forbidding return in it; noinline keeps a lambda as an object you can store. A value class is its underlying value where it's used as itself and a box everywhere else; functions that take one get mangled names, so give Java a door that checks the value. by on a class forwards to an object stored once; by on a property is a hidden $delegate field plus getValue/setValue calls. lazy costs objects in every instance. A DSL is lambdas with receivers (Function1 on the JVM) and builder classes; @DslMarker on every builder class keeps calls on the nearest receiver. Contracts give callers smart casts and in-place lambdas; they are Experimental and trusted, never checked. Context parameters replaced context receivers and are Stable since Kotlin 2.4.0: arguments the compiler fills by type, and on the JVM ordinary leading parameters. all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization change the class file at compile time: name the exact annotations, mind no-arg's skipped initializers, and pin serial names. When in doubt, run javap: every feature in this track is visible there, and Java sees exactly that.

h: Advanced Kotlin: cheat sheet
x: The one idea Every feature in this track is code the compiler writes for you: a pasted body, an erased wrapper, a hidden field, a function object, an extra parameter, a whole new class. Read it with javap and you can predict how the feature behaves, including what Java sees when it calls the same code. Picture it: one print shop, from the counter to the print line Feature Picture it In the code Where the picture breaks inline (lesson 1) the clerk photocopies the procedure sheet into the job's folder instead of handing the job to a colleague with a slip the body and the lambda are pasted into each caller; no lambda object, and a return in the copy ends the whole job Java can't photocopy: it always hands over the slip, a Function0 noinline, crossinline (lesson 1) a slip kept for the notice board; steps sealed in an envelope for the night shift noinline keeps one lambda as an object; crossinline forbids return in a lambda that runs somewhere else the copy is frozen: it never hears about corrections until the caller is rebuilt Value classes (lesson 2) units on the numbers at the parcel desk, checked by the clerk and gone in the back room Weight is its own type to the compiler and a long at run time pigeonholes that only take envelopes box it; Java comes in by the side door and sees bare numbers Class delegation (lesson 3) the counter clerk passes questions to the expert whose name she wrote down on day one, in ink : Printer by printer forwards every call to $$delegate_0, stored once changing the name on the door doesn't change whom she asks Delegated properties (lesson 3) a cloakroom ticket and its attendant a hidden x$delegate field, and accessors that call getValue and setValue a real cloakroom has one attendant; here every ticket usually comes with its own DSLs (lesson 4) an order form whose sections each offer only their own boxes lambdas with receivers and builder classes; @DslMarker keeps calls on the nearest builder without the marker, a missing box falls through to the section around it; with it, the compiler finds the misfiled box before the form is handed in Contracts (lesson 5) a "checked" stamp that the next clerk trusts without opening the envelope returns() implies ... and callsInPlace give callers smart casts and in-place lambdas nobody checks a stamp, and this one leaves no trace in the running program Context parameters (lesson 5) what every clerk carries for the whole shift: the logbook and the shift's name context(logbook: Logbook, shift: Shift), filled by type at each call on the JVM the logbook is handed over with every call, and Java does it in person Compiler plugins (lesson 6) machines on the print line that change every job as it passes all-open drops final, no-arg adds a constructor, serialization writes a serializer class your source shows none of it; javap does Inline functions You write The compiler Java sees inline fun timed(block: () -> T) pastes the body and the lambda body into each caller an ordinary static method taking Function0 return in a lambda passed to an inline function a non-local return: leaves the enclosing function (Java lambdas can only leave themselves) return@forEach leaves only that lambda call continue in a loop noinline f: () -> Unit keeps f as a real object you can store or pass on Function0 crossinline f: () -> Unit lets you call f inside a Runnable, object or lambda; forbids return in it Function0 @PublishedApi internal fun helper() public in bytecode, so public inline bodies may call it a public method Inline small functions that take lambdas, or need reified or a non-local return. Not functions without lambdas: expected performance impact from inlining is insignificant. A public inline body is copied into callers when they are compiled: a change reaches a caller only when the caller is rebuilt. Not allowed: recursion (cannot be recursive) and local functions inside an inline function. Tests of inline functions must call them through code compiled with the solution, or they keep a copy of the stub. h: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns · What inline does: the compiler pastes the function and its lambda into the caller
x: Kotlin's inline pastes the function body and its lambda into the caller: no Function0, no interface call, no unboxing Start with a helper the print shop's app uses all over the place. It runs one step of a job, such as working out how much ink the job needs, and prints how long the step took. The shop's rule of thumb is 3 ml of ink for every 100 pages: Java static <T> T timed(String label, Supplier<T> block) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return block.get(); } finally { System.out.println(label + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000 + " us"); } } long ink = timed("ink", () -> pages * 3 / 100); Kotlin fun <T> timedNotInline(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println("$label took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } val ink = timedNotInline("ink") { pages * 3 / 100 } The part in braces, { pages * 3 / 100 }, is a lambda: a small function written in place and passed as a value. Count what one call costs. This lambda uses pages, a variable from outside its braces, so it is a closure: a lambda that carries the outside values it needs. To make that work, the JVM builds a small object that holds a copy of pages, and timedNotInline calls that object's invoke method. Kotlin creates the object with invokedynamic, the bytecode instruction Java also uses for its lambdas. (Bytecode is the list of instructions in a .class file that the JVM runs. The lesson "invokedynamic: how lambdas and string concatenation compile", later in the course, takes that instruction apart.) The helper is also generic: it works for any result type T. So the Long result travels back as a plain Object and has to be unboxed, that is, turned from a java.lang.Long object back into a primitive long. That's one object, one call through an interface (a type that only names its methods, here invoke) and one unboxing, on every call. The Kotlin docs name the same three costs. In the print shop, this is the clerk handing the job to a colleague. The lambda is the slip with her own step on it, and invoke is the colleague calling her back to do it. You could skip all of that by hand, by pasting the helper's body into the caller: Java long start = System.nanoTime(); long ink; try { ink = pages * 3 / 100; // the lambda's body, pasted in } finally { System.out.println("ink took " + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000 + " us"); } Kotlin val start = System.nanoTime() val ink = try { pages * 3 / 100 // the lambda's body, pasted in } finally { println("ink took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } Nobody writes that fifty times. The compiler, on the other hand, is happy to. Write inline fun <T> timed(...) with the same body, and the compiler stops making the call. At every call site, each place in the code that calls the function, it copies the function's body and the body of the lambda you passed. That's the photocopy: the whole procedure lands in the job's own folder, with the clerk's step written in place. javap, a tool that comes with the JDK and prints the bytecode in a class file, shows the difference in the demo below. The ordinary call site in inkNotInline is seven instructions long. invokedynamic builds a Function0 (Kotlin's interface for a function with no parameters), invokestatic calls timedNotInline with it, and checkcast java/lang/Number plus longValue unbox the result. The inline call site has none of that. The multiply (lmul) and the divide (ldiv) sit right inside inkInline, between two calls to System.nanoTime, just like the hand-pasted version. Read a little further and you see the price. The finally block appears twice in inkInline, once for the normal exit and once for the exit by exception. Every caller carries its own copy, so the code grows, and the docs say inlining pays off only if you avoid inlining large functions. inline is for small functions that take lambdas. The standard library is full of them: forEach, map, filter, let, apply, use, repeat and require are all inline. That's why jobs.map { it.pages } costs about what a hand-written loop costs. The generics track met inline for one more reason: a reified type parameter works only because the body is copied to a call site where the real type is known. Java is where the picture breaks. A Java caller can't photocopy anything, because javac can't inline Kotlin code. For Java, InlineDemoKt.timed(...) is an ordinary static method that takes a Function0, and the Java lambda becomes an object like any other. Java always hands over the slip. The copy changes more than speed, though. Once the clerk's step sits in her own folder, an instruction like "stop here" means something new. Read the bytecode of an inline call Run InlineDemo (or InlineDemoJava) with the command below. Both print ink = 360 ml twice. From labs/, run javap -c -p kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/InlineDemoKt.class. Find inkNotInline and inkInline. Before you look, predict which one contains invokedynamic and which one contains lmul. Then count the println calls inside inkInline. InlineDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo /** inline: the compiler pastes this body, and the lambda's body, into every caller. */ inline fun <T> timed(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println("$label took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } /** The same function without inline: the caller builds a Function0 object and calls through it. */ fun <T> timedNotInline(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println("$label took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } /** The shop's rule of thumb: 3 ml of ink for every 100 pages. */ fun inkInline(pages: Long): Long = timed("inline") { pages * 3 / 100 } fun inkNotInline(pages: Long): Long = timedNotInline("not inline") { pages * 3 / 100 } fun main() { println("ink = ${inkInline(12_000)} ml") println("ink = ${inkNotInline(12_000)} ml") } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l01.demo.InlineDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/InlineDemo.kt InlineDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo; /** * Java twin of InlineDemo.kt. javac cannot inline Kotlin code, so for Java the inline function * timed() is an ordinary static method on InlineDemoKt that takes a Function0. */ public class InlineDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { // the Java lambda becomes a Function0 object; timed() calls its invoke() like any other method long ink = InlineDemoKt.timed("from Java", () -> 12_000L * 3 / 100); System.out.println("ink = " + ink + " ml"); // the same idea written in plain Java: a Supplier and a call through it long same = timedJava("plain Java", () -> 12_000L * 3 / 100); System.out.println("ink = " + same + " ml"); } static <T> T timedJava(String label, java.util.function.Supplier<T> block) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return block.get(); } finally { System.out.println(label + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000 + " us"); } } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l01.demo.InlineDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/InlineDemoJava.java inkNotInline is short: invokedynamic (a new Function0), invokestatic timedNotInline, then checkcast java/lang/Number and longValue to unbox the result. inkInline holds the arithmetic (lmul, ldiv) and two PrintStream.println calls, because the finally block was copied for both exits. Ignore the microsecond timings: one cold call measures class loading and lambda setup, not inlining. The bytecode is the evidence. The same helper with and without inline. The inline caller has no lambda object and no call, but it carries its own copy of the whole body. Inline functions (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns · Non-local returns: a return in an inlined lambda leaves the whole function
x: Inside an ordinary lambda, a bare return doesn't compile. The error is 'return' is prohibited here. An ordinary lambda is an object with its own invoke method, and code inside that method has no way to make some other function return. An inlined lambda is different. Its body becomes part of the caller, so return can mean exactly what it says. The print shop's printers write one line per job into a log, such as DONE job_1 or JAMMED job_2 in tray 2. Here are two small functions that read such a log: Java static String firstJammed(List<String> log) { for (String line : log) { if (line.startsWith("JAMMED")) return line; // Java needs a real loop to return early } return null; } static int countDone(List<String> log) { int done = 0; for (String line : log) { if (!line.startsWith("DONE")) continue; done++; } return done; } Kotlin fun firstJammed(log: List<String>): String? { log.forEach { if (it.startsWith("JAMMED")) return it } // leaves firstJammed return null } fun countDone(log: List<String>): Int { var done = 0 log.forEach { if (!it.startsWith("DONE")) return@forEach // leaves this lambda call only done++ } return done } The first return is a non-local return: it leaves the function that contains the lambda, firstJammed, not only the lambda. It compiles only because forEach is inline. In the bytecode, firstJammed is a plain loop over an Iterator, with an areturn (the instruction that returns an object) in the middle, and no lambda object exists at all. That's the photocopy at work. The clerk's step is now written in her own folder, so when it says "stop here", she stops the whole job, not just her step. There's no colleague left to stop. To leave only the current call of the lambda, add a label. return@forEach means "return from this call of the lambda passed to forEach", and it behaves like continue in a loop, as in countDone. Since Kotlin 2.2.0, break and continue also work inside a lambda passed to an inline function. The feature is stable, so you need no compiler flag. The demo's pagesUntilEmpty adds up the pages of several batches of jobs, where -1 means the paper ran out. Its break inside batch.forEach { } leaves the outer for loop, the way Java's labeled break outer does. Java has no non-local return. A Java lambda always compiles to a separate method, so return inside forEach(line -> { ... }) only ends that one call, and the loop goes on. The Java twin's firstJammedBroken shows it: it always returns null. That difference sets a trap for anyone who learned Java first. In Java, return inside a forEach lambda skips to the next item, and the habit travels: Java jobs.forEach(job -> { if (job.pages() == 0) return; // Java: skips this job, carries on printer.print(job); }); Kotlin jobs.forEach { job -> if (job.pages == 0) return // Kotlin: leaves the whole function printer.print(job) } The Kotlin version compiles without a warning. The first job with no pages ends the whole function, and every job after it is silently left unprinted. The function simply goes home early. Write return@forEach to skip one item, or use a plain for loop with continue, which reads better anyway. In an inlined lambda, a bare return leaves the whole function. To skip one item, write return@forEach. All of this works because the lambda's body is pasted into the caller's own code. Some functions can't allow that, because they keep the lambda for later or hand it to someone else. Return, label, break Run NonLocalReturnDemo and then NonLocalReturnDemoJava. Before you run the Java one, predict what firstJammedBroken prints. Work out pagesUntilEmpty by hand from the three batches in main, then check your number against the output. Uncomment the wrong move at the bottom of main (a lambda stored in a val). Predict the error, run, then comment it out again. NonLocalReturnDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo /** A bare `return` inside forEach's lambda returns from firstJammed: forEach is inline. */ fun firstJammed(log: List<String>): String? { log.forEach { if (it.startsWith("JAMMED")) return it } return null } /** `return@forEach` leaves only the current lambda call, like `continue` in a loop. */ fun countDone(log: List<String>): Int { var done = 0 log.forEach { if (!it.startsWith("DONE")) return@forEach done++ } return done } /** Since Kotlin 2.2, `break` and `continue` work inside an inlined lambda too. */ fun pagesUntilEmpty(batches: List<List<Long>>): Long { var total = 0L for (batch in batches) { batch.forEach { pages -> if (pages < 0) break // -1 means "out of paper": leaves the for loop, not just the lambda total += pages } } return total } fun main() { val log = listOf("DONE job_1", "JAMMED job_2 in tray 2", "DONE job_3") println("firstJammed = ${firstJammed(log)}") println("countDone = ${countDone(log)}") println("pagesUntilEmpty = ${pagesUntilEmpty(listOf(listOf(1_000L, 250L), listOf(400L, -1L, 900L), listOf(75L)))}") // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // val lookup = { line: String -> if (line.isEmpty()) return; line.length } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l01.demo.NonLocalReturnDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/NonLocalReturnDemo.kt NonLocalReturnDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of NonLocalReturnDemo.kt. A Java lambda is always a separate method, so `return` * inside it only leaves the lambda. To return from the enclosing method you need a real loop. */ public class NonLocalReturnDemoJava { static String firstJammed(List<String> log) { for (String line : log) { if (line.startsWith("JAMMED")) return line; // a loop, so return leaves the method } return null; } static String firstJammedBroken(List<String> log) { log.forEach(line -> { if (line.startsWith("JAMMED")) return; // leaves this lambda call only }); return null; // always reached } static long pagesUntilEmpty(List<List<Long>> batches) { long total = 0; outer: for (List<Long> batch : batches) { for (long pages : batch) { if (pages < 0) break outer; // Java's labeled break: Kotlin's non-local break total += pages; } } return total; } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> log = List.of("DONE job_1", "JAMMED job_2 in tray 2", "DONE job_3"); System.out.println("firstJammed = " + firstJammed(log)); System.out.println("firstJammedBroken = " + firstJammedBroken(log)); System.out.println("pagesUntilEmpty = " + pagesUntilEmpty(List.of(List.of(1_000L, 250L), List.of(400L, -1L, 900L), List.of(75L)))); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l01.demo.NonLocalReturnDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/NonLocalReturnDemoJava.java Kotlin prints firstJammed = JAMMED job_2 in tray 2, countDone = 2 and pagesUntilEmpty = 1650: 1,000 + 250 + 400, then the -1 breaks out of the outer loop, so 900 and 75 are never added. Java's firstJammedBroken prints null. The wrong move fails with 'return' is prohibited here.: a lambda stored in a val is an object, so it can't return from main. What's new in Kotlin 2.2.0: non-local break and continue docs

h: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns · When a lambda can't be copied: noinline and crossinline
x: Inlining works only if the compiler can paste the lambda's body where you call it. Two things get in the way, and each one has its own modifier. The first is using the lambda as a value. An inlined lambda has no object behind it, so you can't store it in a field, add it to a list or pass it to an ordinary function. Try it, and the compiler says illegal usage of inline parameter 'listener: (String) -> Unit'. Add 'noinline' modifier to the parameter declaration. noinline turns that one parameter back into a normal lambda object. The function's other lambda parameters are still inlined. In the print shop, that's a note that has to stay a separate slip, because it gets pinned to the notice board. A photocopy inside one folder would be no use to whoever reads the board later. The second is calling the lambda from somewhere else: from inside an object, a Runnable or another lambda. The docs call this "another execution context". That code may run later, on another thread (a separate path of execution inside the same program), when the caller may have returned long ago. A non-local return from there can't work, so the compiler stops you: cannot inline 'task: () -> Unit' here: it might contain non-local returns. Add 'crossinline' modifier to parameter declaration 'task: () -> Unit'. In the print shop, it's a set of steps sealed in an envelope for the night shift. Nobody may write "stop the whole job" inside, because by the time the night shift opens the envelope, the clerk has gone home. crossinline is that rule, applied to the caller's lambda: no bare return inside it. With the rule in place, the compiler still pastes the lambda's body, now into a Runnable class it generates for that call site. In the demo, javap finds a class called ModifiersDemoKt$main$$inlined$runInBackground$1 with no Function0 field: the body of main's lambda sits inside its run(). Here is the pair. An executor is a JDK object that runs tasks on threads it manages; nightShift has one thread, named night-shift: Java // Java lambdas already behave like crossinline ones: return leaves only the lambda static void runInBackground(Executor executor, Runnable task) { executor.execute(task); } runInBackground(nightShift, () -> System.out.println("printing tomorrow's flyers")); Kotlin inline fun runInBackground(executor: Executor, crossinline task: () -> Unit) { executor.execute { task() } // task runs later, on the executor's thread } runInBackground(nightShift) { println("printing tomorrow's flyers") } // runInBackground(nightShift) { return } // error: 'return' is prohibited here. Here the picture breaks a little. A real night-shift worker who reads "stop the whole job" can shrug and ignore it. The compiler can't shrug, so it refuses to seal the envelope until the lambda promises not to leave early. Both modifiers would make runInBackground compile, so choose by what you do with the lambda. Use crossinline when you call it inside another lambda or object, because its body is still inlined into the new class. Use noinline when the lambda has to exist as a value you keep or hand on. Neither modifier changes the JVM signature: Java sees a Function0 either way. Keep the lambda: noinline. Let someone else call it later: crossinline. You'll need crossinline more often than you might think. Plenty of Java APIs take a callback to run later: Executor.execute(Runnable), CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(Supplier), new Thread(Runnable). Every inline Kotlin wrapper around one of them needs it. So far inline looks like a free upgrade with two small rules. It isn't free, and the next section adds up the bill. Make the compiler ask for each modifier Run ModifiersDemo (or ModifiersDemoJava, which calls the same Kotlin functions with plain Java lambdas). In ModifiersDemo.kt, delete noinline in subscribe. Predict the error, run, read it, then put it back. Delete crossinline in runInBackground, run, and put it back. Uncomment the last line of main and run. Why does the compiler refuse a return that it allowed in forEach? Predict without running: does inline fun once(block: () -> Unit) = run { block() } need crossinline? (run is itself inline.) Then add it to the file and check. ModifiersDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo import java.util.concurrent.Executor import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit val listeners = mutableListOf<(String) -> Unit>() /** noinline: `listener` is stored in a list, so it has to stay a real object. `log` is inlined. */ inline fun subscribe(log: (String) -> Unit, noinline listener: (String) -> Unit) { log("subscribing listener #${listeners.size + 1}") listeners += listener } /** crossinline: `task` runs inside a Runnable on another thread, so it may not return from the caller. */ inline fun runInBackground(executor: Executor, crossinline task: () -> Unit) { executor.execute { task() } } fun main() { subscribe({ println(it) }) { event -> println("listener got $event") } listeners.forEach { it("job-finished") } val pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { Thread(it, "night-shift") } runInBackground(pool) { println("running on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } pool.shutdown() pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // Wrong moves, one at a time. h: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns · When not to inline: code size, frozen copies and visibility
x: inline has three costs, and all three show up in real code. The first is size. The body is copied into every caller, so a 40-line function called from 200 places becomes 200 copies, and every folder in the shop gets thicker. The compiler even warns when you inline a function that takes no lambdas: expected performance impact from inlining is insignificant. Inlining works best for functions with parameters of function types. Without a lambda there is nothing to remove: no object, no call through an interface. And the JIT, the part of the JVM that turns busy code into machine code while the program runs, already inlines small, hot methods by itself. The second is frozen copies. A caller gets its copy of the body when the caller is compiled. In one test, a small app was compiled against version 1 of a library. Then version 2 replaced the library's jar (the zip file a library ships in) without recompiling the app. The app printed inline=v1 plain=v2. The ordinary function ran the new code, and the inline one still ran its old copy. It's the photocopy that never heard about the correction. So if you publish a library that other programs use, treat a public inline body like a public signature. A fix inside it reaches each program only when that program is rebuilt. The third is visibility, and it follows from the second. The body lands in other modules, the separately compiled parts of a program, such as a library and the app that uses it. So it may only use what those modules can use. Call a private function from a public inline one, and you get public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API function. The fix is @PublishedApi internal. internal means visible only inside this module, and @PublishedApi makes the function public in the bytecode anyway, so the pasted copies can reach it. The helper's own body isn't copied anywhere, so it can use private state freely. Here it hands out trace ids, labels that tie the start and end lines of one operation together in the log: Java // Java has no internal or inline. The nearest shape: one public helper that callers reach public final class Tracing { private static final AtomicInteger COUNTER = new AtomicInteger(); public static String nextTraceId() { return "trace-" + COUNTER.incrementAndGet(); } } Kotlin inline fun <T> traced(operation: String, block: () -> T): T { val id = nextTraceId() // must be reachable from every caller's module println("[$id] start $operation") val result = block() println("[$id] end $operation") return result } @PublishedApi internal fun nextTraceId(): String = "trace-" + counter.incrementAndGet() private val counter = AtomicInteger() // fine: nextTraceId is not inline The compiler adds two hard limits. An inline function can't call itself (inline function 'fun recI(n: Int): Int' cannot be recursive.), and it can't contain a local function (local functions are not yet supported in inline functions.). Properties can be inline too, as long as the accessor has no backing field, that is, no stored value of its own. The demo's val Long.asKilos: String inline get() = ... turns 1,999 grams into 1.999 kg. You'll mostly see inline properties when they need a reified type parameter. My rule: inline small functions that take lambdas, or that need reified or a non-local return, and leave everything else ordinary. When an inline body starts to grow, split it. Keep the inline part to a few lines, and move the real work into a @PublishedApi internal function that is compiled once. The lab puts all of this into one small helper: a retry for a printer that sometimes jams, with a non-local return, a crossinline lambda and a @PublishedApi door. Break the visibility rule Run PublishedApiDemo, then PublishedApiDemoJava. In PublishedApiDemo.kt, change @PublishedApi internal fun nextTraceId() to private fun nextTraceId(). Predict the error and run the Kotlin demo. Put it back. Why can the Java twin call nextTraceId() directly, when Kotlin code in another module could not? PublishedApiDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** * A public inline function is pasted into callers, possibly in another module. So its body may * only use declarations those callers could use themselves. */ inline fun <T> traced(operation: String, block: () -> T): T { val id = nextTraceId() println("[$id] start $operation") val result = block() println("[$id] end $operation") return result } /** Not part of the Kotlin API, but public in the bytecode, so the pasted copies can call it. */ @PublishedApi internal fun nextTraceId(): String = "trace-" + counter.incrementAndGet() private val counter = AtomicInteger() // fine: nextTraceId is not inline, so its body is never copied /** An inline property: no backing field, and the getter is pasted into each caller. */ val Long.asKilos: String inline get() = "" + (this / 1_000) + "." + (this % 1_000).toString().padStart(3, '0') + " kg" fun main() { val grams = traced("weigh parcel job_7") { 1_999L } println("parcel weighs ${grams.asKilos}") // Wrong move. Change `@PublishedApi internal` on nextTraceId to `private`, predict, run. } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l01.demo.PublishedApiDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/PublishedApiDemo.kt PublishedApiDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo; /** * Java twin of PublishedApiDemo.kt. `internal` is a Kotlin rule that javac does not know about. * In the bytecode nextTraceId() is public, so Java can call it, and traced() is an ordinary method. */ public class PublishedApiDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { long grams = PublishedApiDemoKt.traced("weigh parcel job_7", () -> 1_999L); System.out.println("parcel weighs " + PublishedApiDemoKt.getAsKilos(grams)); System.out.println("Java can call the internal helper too: " + PublishedApiDemoKt.nextTraceId()); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l01.demo.PublishedApiDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/PublishedApiDemoJava.java Both print [trace-1] start weigh parcel job_7, [trace-1] end weigh parcel job_7 and parcel weighs 1.999 kg, and the Java twin also prints trace-2 from a direct call. With private, the build fails with public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API function. internal is a Kotlin rule. In the bytecode the function is public, and javac doesn't know the rule exists.

h: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns · Java and Kotlin
x: Wrapping a callback API: Java Supplier vs Kotlin inline with crossinline Timing.java import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.Executor; import java.util.function.Supplier; final class Timing { static <T> T timed(String label, Supplier<T> block) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return block.get(); } finally { System.out.println(label + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000 + " us"); } } // the caller's lambda is an object; supplyAsync gets a second lambda that calls it static <T> CompletableFuture<T> timedAsync(String label, Executor executor, Supplier<T> block) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> timed(label, block), executor); } } // call site: Timing.timedAsync("print", nightShift, () -> printer.print(job)); Timing.kt import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.Executor inline fun <T> timed(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println("$label took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } // block runs inside the Supplier, another execution context: crossinline inline fun <T> timedAsync(label: String, executor: Executor, crossinline block: () -> T): CompletableFuture<T> = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ timed(label) { block() } }, executor) // call site: timedAsync("print", nightShift) { printer.print(job) } Both versions time a step on another thread and hand back a future, a placeholder for a result that arrives later. In Java the caller's lambda is always an object, and timedAsync wraps it in a second one for supplyAsync. In Kotlin the compiler pastes both timed and the caller's lambda into one Supplier class that it generates for that call site, so there is one object instead of two, and no call through Supplier.get on the caller's code. The bigger difference is the rule for the caller: inside the Kotlin block, a bare return is a compile error, while a Java lambda simply can't express one. Java code that calls the Kotlin timedAsync gets the ordinary compiled body and passes a Function0.

h: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns · Worked example
x: Write an inline helper over a Java callback API A Java library (invented for this example) lets one job at a time use the shop's printer. You pass the work as a Callable, the JDK's interface for a task that returns a value, and the library runs it while it holds the printer, so two jobs never mix their pages. You want Kotlin callers to write queue.printing { printer.print(job) }. Start with the API and an ordinary Kotlin wrapper. public interface PrinterQueue { <T> T withPrinter(Callable<T> work); } // Java callers write the Callable themselves int pages = queue.withPrinter(() -> printer.print(flyers)); interface PrinterQueue { fun <T> withPrinter(work: Callable<T>): T } // 1. an ordinary wrapper: it works, but each call builds a Function0 and a Callable fun <T> PrinterQueue.printing(block: () -> T): T = withPrinter(Callable { block() }) The wrapper is one line and runs for every job, so make it inline. The compiler refuses, because block() is now called inside the Callable, which the library may run later or on another thread. // 2. add inline: the compiler stops here inline fun <T> PrinterQueue.printing(block: () -> T): T = withPrinter(Callable { block() }) // error: cannot inline 'block: () -> T' here: it might contain non-local returns. // Add 'crossinline' modifier to parameter declaration 'block: () -> T'. // Java has no inline and no non-local return, so the question never comes up: // a return inside the Callable lambda only ends the Callable int pages = queue.withPrinter(() -> { printer.print(flyers); return flyers.pages(); }); Add crossinline. The caller's lambda is now pasted into a Callable class that the compiler generates for each call site. In exchange, callers lose the non-local return: that's the rule crossinline enforces. // 3. crossinline: inlined into the generated Callable, no bare return allowed inline fun <T> PrinterQueue.printing(crossinline block: () -> T): T = withPrinter(Callable { block() }) fun send(job: Job) { queue.printing { printer.print(job) } // queue.printing { if (job.isEmpty) return } // error: 'return' is prohibited here. } void send(Job job) { queue.withPrinter(() -> { printer.print(job); return null; // Callable must return something }); } Check that it earns its place. It does: one line, a lambda parameter, called for every job. If it later grows logging, timing and error handling, keep the inline part to this one line and move the rest into a @PublishedApi internal function, so 300 call sites don't each carry a copy.

h: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns · Quiz
x: What does the compiler say about this function? inline fun onIoThread(pool: Executor, task: () -> Unit) { pool.execute { task() } } Nothing: it compiles as written cannot inline 'task' here: it might contain non-local returns, and it suggests crossinline illegal usage of inline parameter, and it suggests noinline Inline functions can't call Java APIs such as Executor task is called inside the Runnable lambda, which is another execution context. The compiler asks for crossinline, which forbids a return in the caller's lambda and still inlines its body into the generated Runnable. noinline would also make it compile, but the compiler suggests that one when you store or pass the lambda itself, and it gives up inlining the body. What does process(listOf(1, 0, 2)) print? fun process(xs: List<Int>) { xs.forEach { if (it == 0) return print(it) } print(" done") } 1 12 done 1 done 12 forEach is inline, so the bare return leaves process the first time it sees 0. Nothing after that runs, not even print(" done"). 12 done is what the Java habit expects, where return only skips one element; that would be return@forEach in Kotlin. shop-app 2.0 was compiled against the library print-tools 1.4.0, and calls its public inline fun <T> withRetry(block: () -> T). You upgrade print-tools to 1.4.1, which fixes a bug inside withRetry, and keep the shop-app 2.0 you already built. Which withRetry code runs when shop-app calls it? The fixed 1.4.1 code, because the newest jar is on the classpath Neither: the JVM throws NoSuchMethodError The old 1.4.0 code, copied into shop-app's bytecode when it was compiled Whichever version the class loader happens to load first An inline body is copied into the caller at the caller's compile time. shop-app never calls the withRetry method in the jar; it runs its own pasted copy of the 1.4.0 body. The classpath only decides which method exists, and nobody in shop-app calls it. Only rebuilding shop-app against 1.4.1 picks up the fix. Which declaration makes the compiler warn expected performance impact from inlining is insignificant? inline fun <T> timed(label: String, block: () -> T): T inline fun <reified T> Any?.isA(): Boolean = this is T inline fun <T> List<T>.sumPagesBy(selector: (T) -> Int): Int inline fun toSheets(pages: Int): Int = (pages + 1) / 2 toSheets has no function-typed parameter and no reified type parameter, so there is nothing for inlining to remove. The JIT would inline a hot small method like that by itself. isA has no lambda, but it needs inline for its reified T, so the compiler doesn't warn. From the generics track: why does inline fun <reified T> Any?.isA() = this is T need inline? Because reflection is slow, and inlining makes it fast Because the reified type is stored in a hidden field of the lambda object Because the JVM erases T, and only a copy of the body at each call site knows the real class It doesn't: since Kotlin 2.0 reified works on ordinary functions too Type arguments are erased at run time, so an ordinary function can't know what T was. An inline function's body is compiled again at each call site, where the type argument is written in plain sight, and the compiler can put a real instanceof there. Ordinary functions still can't have reified type parameters.

h: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns · Explain it back
x: A teammate asks why the compiler made them write crossinline in inline fun <T> PrinterQueue.printing(block: () -> T) = withPrinter(Callable { block() }). Explain, in your own words, what could go wrong without it and what they give up by adding it.

h: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns · Key terms
x: Inline function A function whose body the compiler copies into each call site, together with the bodies of the lambdas passed to it. Call site A place in the code that calls a function. With inline, this is where the copy of the body ends up. Closure A lambda that uses variables from outside its braces. Unless it is inlined, the JVM keeps those values in a small object. Non-local return A bare return inside an inlined lambda. It leaves the function that contains the lambda, not just the lambda. Labeled return return@forEach: leaves only the current call of the lambda, like continue in a loop. noinline Marks one lambda parameter of an inline function as an ordinary object, so you can store it or pass it on. crossinline Marks a lambda parameter that is called from another execution context. Non-local returns are forbidden in it. @PublishedApi Lets public inline functions use an internal declaration. The declaration is public in the bytecode. What does inline do to a function and the lambdas passed to it? The compiler copies the function body and each lambda body into the call site. No Function object is created and nothing is called through an interface. Inside fun f(), what does the return in list.forEach { if (it == 0) return } leave? The whole function f. It's a non-local return, allowed because forEach is inline. return@forEach would leave only that lambda call. When does the compiler ask for noinline? When you use an inline lambda parameter as a value: store it in a field, add it to a collection, or pass it to a non-inline function. When does the compiler ask for crossinline? When you call the lambda from another execution context, such as an object, a Runnable or another lambda. crossinline forbids non-local returns in the caller's lambda. Why is a public inline function's body part of your library's binary interface? Callers get a copy of the body when they are compiled. Change the body, and an old caller keeps running its old copy until it is recompiled. A public inline function calls a private helper. What happens, and what is the fix? Compile error: public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API function. Mark the helper @PublishedApi internal. What does Java see when it calls a Kotlin inline function? An ordinary static method that takes Function0/Function1 objects. javac inlines nothing. A reified inline function is synthetic, so javac can't see it at all.

h: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns · Go deeper
x: Kotlin's inlining and the JIT's inlining are different tools. Kotlin inlines at compile time, across modules, before the JVM ever sees the code. That is the only kind that can make a non-local return or a reified type work, because both change what the code means. The JIT inlines at run time, only on hot paths, and can undo its choice (deoptimization) when its assumptions break. The lesson "Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics" in the performance track covers that side. The Kotlin docs say inlining pays off "especially at 'megamorphic' call-sites inside loops". The reason is in the profile the JIT keeps for each call site. An ordinary forEach taking a Function1 has one invoke call site inside it. If 30 different lambdas flow through that one call site, the JIT sees 30 receiver classes there and can't inline any of them. With an inline forEach, each caller has its own copy of the loop, with exactly one lambda body pasted in. Nothing is left for the JIT to guess. A crossinline lambda leaves two classes behind. Run javap -p on the ModifiersDemoKt$... classes in kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/: ModifiersDemoKt$runInBackground$1 implements java.lang.Runnable { final kotlin.jvm.functions.Function0<kotlin.Unit> $task; // used when Java calls the compiled body public final void run(); } ModifiersDemoKt$main$$inlined$runInBackground$1 implements java.lang.Runnable { public final void run(); // main's lambda body is pasted in here } The first is the template that the compiled runInBackground method uses when Java (or reflection) calls it: it holds the Function0. The second was generated for the one call site in main, with the lambda's body inside run(). Each inlined call site of a crossinline function gets a class like that, which is one more reason to keep these functions few and small. Finally, a reified inline function has no callable form at all, because its body makes no sense without a concrete type. Kotlin still writes a method into the class file, but marks it ACC_SYNTHETIC, and javac ignores synthetic methods. That's why Java code can't call filterIsInstance<T>()-style functions.

h: Value classes and what they compile to · A value class is its own type to the compiler and a plain long at run time
x: A value class is its own type to the compiler and a plain long at run time, boxed whenever it is used as another type Here are two numbers from the print shop's app: the weight of a parcel in grams, and the number of sheets in it. Both are Long: Java static String ship(long grams) { return "shipped " + grams + " g"; } long grams = 2_500; long sheets = 500; ship(sheets); // compiles: both are long Kotlin fun ship(grams: Long): String = "shipped $grams g" val grams: Long = 2_500 val sheets: Long = 500 ship(sheets) // compiles: both are Long The compiler can't tell them apart, so ship(sheets) happily posts a parcel that weighs 500 sheets. A wrapper class, class Grams(val value: Long), would catch the swap. It works, and every weight is now an extra object on the heap, the memory where the JVM keeps objects. Kotlin's value class keeps the wrapper's type for the compiler and, wherever it can, drops the object. At run time only the wrapped value is left, the underlying type (Long here). In the print shop, the unit on the job sheet is the value class. The clerk, who is the compiler, checks it at the desk. The machines in the back room, which are the JVM at run time, only see the number. Here is the wrapper in both languages: Java // Java's closest shape today: a record. It's a real object, created on every new. record Grams(long value) { Grams { if (value < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative weight: " + value); } } Kotlin @JvmInline value class Grams(val value: Long) { init { require(value >= 0) { "negative weight: $value" } } operator fun plus(other: Grams): Grams = Grams(value + other.value) override fun toString(): String = "$value g" } fun ship(weight: Grams): String = "shipped $weight" ship(sheets) // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Long', but 'Grams' was expected. The rules are short. On the JVM you write @JvmInline value class with exactly one property in the primary constructor. You may add init blocks, functions, secondary constructors, and properties without backing fields, that is, without a stored value of their own (so no lateinit and no delegation). A value class can implement interfaces (types that only name methods and properties), can't extend a class, and is always final. At run time most of it disappears. javap -p, the JDK tool that lists what a class file contains, shows what the compiler built for the demo: public static final java.lang.String ship-P0HeBCA(long); // takes a plain long public static long constructor-impl(long); // Grams(...) runs init here public static final long plus-vak4SgM(long, long); // a member, now static on two longs public static final Grams box-impl(long); // used only when a box is needed Grams(150) compiles to a call to constructor-impl, which runs your init block and hands back the same long. No object is created. plus turned into a static method that adds two longs. The Grams class still exists, with one long field, for the moments when a real object is needed. The odd hash after ship is the compiler's work too, and a later section explains it. Compare a type alias. typealias GramsAlias = Long gives you a second name and nothing else. The docs say aliases are assignment-compatible with their underlying type, and value classes are not. In the demo, sheets: Long goes straight into shipAlias and compiles. Use aliases to shorten long type names. Use value classes where mixing up two values would be a bug. You already use value classes from the standard library. UInt, ULong, kotlin.time.Duration and kotlin.Result are all declared this way, and javap shows the same box-impl and unbox-impl on each. When two values share a type but must never be swapped, give each one its own value class. "Wherever it can" is doing a lot of work in that description, though. Let's find the places where it can't. See what Grams compiles to Run ValueClassDemo with the command below. From labs/, run javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l02.demo.ValueClassDemoKt workbench.kotlin.l02.demo.Grams. Find ship, constructor-impl and plus. Uncomment the wrong move in main, predict the error, and run. Comment it out again. Run ValueClassDemoJava. Before you do, predict its second line: Java calls shipFromJava(-5L). ValueClassDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l02.demo /** A value class: a Grams in your code, a long in the bytecode. */ @JvmInline value class Grams(val value: Long) { init { require(value >= 0) { "negative weight: $value" } } operator fun plus(other: Grams): Grams = Grams(value + other.value) override fun toString(): String = "$value g" } /** A type alias is only a second name. Any Long is accepted where a GramsAlias is expected. */ typealias GramsAlias = Long fun ship(weight: Grams): String = "shipped $weight" @JvmName("shipFromJava") fun shipJava(weight: Grams): String = "shipped $weight" fun shipAlias(weight: GramsAlias): String = "shipped $weight g (alias)" fun main() { val parcel = Grams(150) + Grams(49) println(ship(parcel)) val sheets: Long = 500 println(shipAlias(sheets)) // compiles: a sheet count is a Long, so it is a GramsAlias too try { Grams(-1) } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("rejected: ${e.message}") } // Wrong move. h: Value classes and what they compile to · When the box comes back: generics, nullables, interfaces and collections
x: Value classes do get boxed after all. Boxing means wrapping the value in a real object on the heap, the way Java wraps a long in a Long. The rule fits in one line of the docs: inline classes are boxed whenever they are used as another type. Back in the print shop, some shelves only take envelopes. The shared pigeonholes accept envelopes of any kind, but never a loose number. So a number on its way there goes into an envelope with its unit printed on the front, and comes out again when someone needs the number itself. The demo uses a second value class, Sheets, which implements a small interface, Counted. Here are the four ways it can end up in an envelope: Java // Java's long and Long follow the same rule: a primitive where it can, a box when it must static Object asGeneric(Object x) { return x; } long sheets = 1_999; Object boxed = asGeneric(sheets); // autoboxed into a Long object List<Long> list = List.of(sheets); // another Long object Kotlin fun <T> asGeneric(x: T): Any? = x // used as T: boxed fun asNullable(s: Sheets?): Any? = s // used as Sheets?: boxed fun asInterface(c: Counted): Any = c // used as Counted, an interface: boxed class PrintRun(val sheets: Sheets) // used as Sheets: stored as a long field Four cases box. The first is a generic type parameter such as T. The second is a nullable type: Sheets? must be able to hold null, and a long can't. The third is an interface the class implements, and the fourth is anything typed Any, which includes every collection and println. In the bytecode, each case shows up as a call to Sheets.box-impl(long) right before the call that needs the object. So a List<Sheets> holds one Sheets object per element. The docs draw the comparison you'd draw yourself: it's like Int, which is either a primitive int or a java.lang.Integer. Equality still works by value. s == Sheets(1_999) compiles to equals-impl0(long, long), a comparison of two longs. Identity doesn't exist. Identity asks "is this the very same object?", which is what Java's == asks of two objects and Kotlin's === asks too. For value classes, Kotlin refuses the question: s === t fails with identity equality for arguments of types 'Sheets' and 'Sheets' is prohibited. That's stricter than Java, and for good reason. In Java, Long a = 1_999L, b = 1_999L; a == b is false, while the same code with 100L is true, because the JDK keeps one shared box for each small number. That's a fine way to lose an afternoon. Here the picture breaks a little. A real envelope stays the same envelope wherever it goes. A boxed value doesn't: put the same Sheets into two lists and you get two different boxes. That's one more reason Kotlin won't let you ask whether two of them are the same object. A value class is a plain value only while it's used as itself. Anywhere else, it travels in a box. In practice, a value class saves the allocation (the work of creating an object) wherever it's used as itself: fields, parameters, return values, arithmetic. That covers most of an app's own code. A busy loop that pushes millions of values through a List<Sheets> or a generic Map pays the same boxing as List<Long>. If that shows up when you measure, use a LongArray, as you would in Java. Boxing stays invisible from Kotlin. Java, though, sees the bytecode exactly as it is, and the names in it look strange. Count the boxes Run BoxingDemo and BoxingDemoJava. Predict each line before you look. From labs/, run javap -c -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l02.demo.BoxingDemoKt and count the calls to Sheets."box-impl" in main. Uncomment the wrong move in BoxingDemo.kt and run it. BoxingDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l02.demo interface Counted { val count: Long } @JvmInline value class Sheets(override val count: Long) : Counted class PrintRun(val sheets: Sheets) // used as Sheets: stored as a long fun <T> asGeneric(x: T): Any? = x // used as T: boxed fun asNullable(s: Sheets?): Any? = s // used as Sheets?: boxed fun asInterface(c: Counted): Any = c // used as Counted: boxed fun main() { val s = Sheets(1_999) println("field in PrintRun: ${PrintRun::class.java.getDeclaredField("sheets").type}") println("as generic: ${asGeneric(s)!!.javaClass.simpleName}") println("as nullable: ${asNullable(s)!!.javaClass.simpleName}") println("as Counted: ${asInterface(s).javaClass.simpleName}") println("in a list: ${(listOf(s)[0] as Any).javaClass.simpleName}") println("s == Sheets(1999): ${s == Sheets(1_999)}") // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // println(s === Sheets(1_999)) } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l02.demo.BoxingDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l02/demo/BoxingDemo.kt BoxingDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l02.demo; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of BoxingDemo.kt. Java has the same split for long and Long: a primitive where it can, * a box when the value is used as a generic type, a nullable, or Object. Kotlin forbids === on * value classes; Java lets you compare boxes by identity, and it goes wrong above 127. */ public class BoxingDemoJava { static Object asGeneric(Object x) { return x; } public static void main(String[] args) { long sheets = 1_999; Object boxed = asGeneric(sheets); // autoboxed to Long System.out.println("as Object: " + boxed.getClass().getSimpleName()); System.out.println("in a list: " + List.of(sheets).get(0).getClass().getSimpleName()); Long a = 1_999L, b = 1_999L; System.out.println("a == b (identity): " + (a == b)); // two different Long objects System.out.println("a.equals(b): " + a.equals(b)); Long small1 = 100L, small2 = 100L; System.out.println("100L == 100L: " + (small1 == small2)); // cached box, so true } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l02.demo.BoxingDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l02/demo/BoxingDemoJava.java The field in PrintRun is a long. Every other line prints Sheets, because generic, nullable, interface and list uses all box, and javap shows four box-impl calls in main, one before each of those calls. The equality line prints true through equals-impl0. The wrong move fails with identity equality for arguments of types 'Sheets' and 'Sheets' is prohibited. The Java twin prints false for a == b with 1,999 and true with 100: that's the JDK's shared box for small numbers, a trap Kotlin closes for value classes. Used as itself, a value class is its underlying long. Used as anything else, the compiler puts it in a box first.

h: Value classes and what they compile to · Mangled names keep Java out, and @JvmName lets it back in
x: Look at that name again: ship-P0HeBCA(long). The compiler adds a hash to the name of every function that takes a value class. The docs call this mangling, and it does two jobs. The first job is to prevent clashes. A JobId value class wraps a String, so describe(id: JobId) and describe(text: String) would both be describe(String) in the bytecode. With mangling they become describe-<hash>(String) and describe(String). The second job is to keep Java away from functions that expect a checked value. A - can't appear in a Java method name, so javac can't call ship-P0HeBCA, however nicely you ask. Mangling reaches further than functions. A class with a value-class property gets a private constructor, plus a public one with an extra DefaultConstructorMarker parameter that Java can't sensibly call. It also gets a mangled getter: the demo's PrintRun has getSheets-auOsFv4(). Members that return a value class are mangled too, so the lab's Weight.Companion.parse becomes parse-D9kyZD4(String). A top-level function that only returns one is not: parseWeight(String) hands Java a plain long. This is where the print shop picture breaks. Java comes in by the side door, and it can't read units at all. Either it can't call the function, or, once you open a door for it, it hands over a bare number that nobody checked. For a single function, the quick door is @JvmName, which sets the name the function gets in the bytecode: Java System.out.println(ValueClassDemoKt.shipFromJava(199L)); // shipped 199 g System.out.println(ValueClassDemoKt.shipFromJava(-5L)); // shipped -5 g: init never ran // ValueClassDemoKt.ship(199L); // error: cannot find symbol Kotlin @JvmName("shipFromJava") fun shipJava(weight: Grams): String = "shipped $weight" Read the second Java line again. Java passes a raw long, and nothing runs init on the way in. @JvmName opens a door around your validation, so a function meant for Java must check its input again, for example by building a fresh Grams(weight.value). Kotlin 2.2.0 added a fuller answer, @JvmExposeBoxed. It is still Experimental in Kotlin 2.4, which means it may still change, so you opt in with @OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class). On a class, it adds a public constructor that runs init. On a function, it adds a version that takes and returns the box, describeRun(Copies), next to the mangled describeRun-D2JSnUo(long). The compiler flag -Xjvm-expose-boxed does the same for a whole module: Java Copies copies = new Copies(125); // a real constructor: init runs System.out.println(ExposeBoxedDemoKt.describeRun(copies.doubled())); Kotlin @file:OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class) @JvmExposeBoxed @JvmInline value class Copies(val count: Long) { init { require(count >= 0) { "negative copies: $count" } } fun doubled(): Copies = Copies(count * 2) } @JvmExposeBoxed fun describeRun(copies: Copies): String = "a run of ${copies.count} copies" Libraries see the same bytecode that Java does. Some find getters by name through reflection, that is, by inspecting a class's members while the program runs. A library that turns objects into JSON text, or one that saves them to a database, will meet getSheets-auOsFv4. Check how your libraries handle that before you put value classes into the classes they read. Mangling, boxing and side doors all come from one fact: on today's JVM, a value class is a trick the compiler plays. That trick has a hard limit. Open the door for Java, properly Run ExposeBoxedDemo, then ExposeBoxedDemoJava. Run javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l02.demo.Copies workbench.kotlin.l02.demo.ExposeBoxedDemoKt. Find the two doubled methods and the two describeRun methods. Delete the first line of ExposeBoxedDemo.kt (@file:OptIn(...)) and run. Put it back. ExposeBoxedDemo.kt @file:OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class) package workbench.kotlin.l02.demo /** * @JvmExposeBoxed (Experimental since Kotlin 2.2.0) adds Java-friendly members next to the * mangled ones: a public constructor that runs init, and overloads that take and return the box. */ @JvmExposeBoxed @JvmInline value class Copies(val count: Long) { init { require(count >= 0) { "negative copies: $count" } } fun doubled(): Copies = Copies(count * 2) } @JvmExposeBoxed fun describeRun(copies: Copies): String = "a run of ${copies.count} copies" fun main() { println(describeRun(Copies(125).doubled())) } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l02.demo.ExposeBoxedDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l02/demo/ExposeBoxedDemo.kt ExposeBoxedDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l02.demo; /** * Java twin of ExposeBoxedDemo.kt. With @JvmExposeBoxed, Java gets a real constructor that runs the * init block, and boxed overloads of doubled() and describeRun(). */ public class ExposeBoxedDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Copies copies = new Copies(125); // runs init: validation is back System.out.println(ExposeBoxedDemoKt.describeRun(copies.doubled())); try { new Copies(-1); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage()); } } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l02.demo.ExposeBoxedDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l02/demo/ExposeBoxedDemoJava.java Both print a run of 250 copies, and the Java twin also prints rejected: negative copies: -1, so the public constructor ran init. javap shows doubled-8FQRi2g(long) next to Copies doubled(), describeRun-D2JSnUo(long) next to describeRun(Copies), and a public Copies(long) constructor. Without the opt-in, both annotations fail with this declaration needs opt-in. Its usage must be marked with '@kotlin.ExperimentalStdlibApi' or '@OptIn(kotlin.ExperimentalStdlibApi::class)'.
