h: Value classes and what they compile to · One field only, until Valhalla
x: Give a value class two properties and the compiler stops you: value class must have exactly one primary constructor parameter. So a paper size, PaperSize(widthMm, heightMm), can't be a value class on the JVM in Kotlin 2.4. Neither can a weight that carries its own unit. There is no hidden flag for it either. Even the internal -XXLanguage:+ValueClasses earns only warning: unknown language feature 'ValueClasses'. The limit comes from the JVM. Kotlin can erase a one-field class into its field because the JVM already has a long to erase it into. A value with two fields and no identity needs support from the JVM itself, and that is what Project Valhalla is building. As the last track's Valhalla section said, JEP 401, Value Objects (Preview), was integrated into the JDK's main source tree on 31 July 2026. It ships in JDK 28, scheduled for March 2027, behind --enable-preview, the switch that turns on preview features. JDK 25, 26 and 27 don't have it. Kotlin's design notes explain why @JvmInline is required today. It marks the current compile-time trick, so that a plain value class without the annotation can later compile to real Valhalla value classes. The notes call multi-field value classes before Valhalla "all theoretical", and no Kotlin release has a Valhalla mode yet. For now, the one-field limit shapes your design. A paper size stays a data class, perhaps holding two value classes, a Millimetres for each side. Where do value classes pay off? Anywhere two Strings or two Longs could be swapped by accident: ids (JobId, CustomerId), counts and measures with one fixed unit (Sheets, Grams), and checked strings such as a postcode. Validation runs once, in init, and the type is the proof that it ran. Where don't they? In functions that Java code calls a lot, unless you add @JvmName doors or @JvmExposeBoxed, and in classes that reflection-heavy libraries read. Keep value classes in your Kotlin code, and convert at the edges. A value class holds exactly one value. Anything with two parts stays a data class, for now. In the lab, you'll build two of them, a Weight and a JobId, and give Java a door that still checks. Try a second field In ValueClassDemo.kt, change value class Grams(val value: Long) to value class Grams(val value: Long, val unit: String). Run the demo. Undo it. Which of your own types would you make a value class, and which would stay a data class? The build fails with value class must have exactly one primary constructor parameter. Single-value ideas such as ids, counts and measures in one fixed unit fit. Anything with two parts (a paper size with a width and a height, a weight with its unit) stays a data class for now.

h: Value classes and what they compile to · Java and Kotlin
x: A job id: Java record vs Kotlin value class JobId.java public record JobId(String value) { public JobId { if (value.length() < 8 || value.length() > 64) throw new IllegalArgumentException("job id must be 8 to 64 characters"); if (!value.matches("[A-Za-z0-9_-]+")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad character in job id: " + value); } } // every new JobId(...) is an object with identity static PrintJob findJob(JobId id) { ... } // JVM: findJob(JobId) JobId.kt @JvmInline value class JobId(val value: String) { init { require(value.length in 8..64) { "job id must be 8 to 64 characters" } require(value.matches(Regex("[A-Za-z0-9_-]+"))) { "bad character in job id: $value" } } } // JobId(...) runs init and returns the same String fun findJob(id: JobId): PrintJob? = TODO() // JVM: findJob-<hash>(String) Both validate once, when the value is built, and both compare by value. The record is a real object: each new creates one, and a map keyed by job ids holds those objects. The value class is a String at run time wherever it is used as itself, so findJob costs exactly what a String parameter costs. The price is on the Java side: Java sees findJob-<hash>(String), which it can't call, and it can't construct a JobId at all without @JvmExposeBoxed. JEP 401, a preview in JDK 28, adds value record to Java: a record without identity, which lets the JVM flatten it, that is, store its fields in place with no separate object.

h: Value classes and what they compile to · Worked example
x: Make a swapped argument a compile error, then give Java a safe door The shop can reprint an old job for a customer. The reprint call takes two Strings and a Long. Someone swapped the two ids in a quick fix, and it compiled. static String reprint(String customerId, String jobId, long copies) { ... } reprint(jobId, customerId, 200); // swapped: compiles, reprints the wrong thing fun reprint(customerId: String, jobId: String, copies: Long): String = TODO() reprint(jobId, customerId, 200) // swapped: compiles, reprints the wrong thing Give each idea its own value class. The swapped call now fails to compile, twice, and nothing is allocated: in the bytecode the function still takes two Strings and a long. @JvmInline value class CustomerId(val value: String) @JvmInline value class JobId(val value: String) @JvmInline value class Copies(val count: Long) // 1. one type per idea fun reprint(customer: CustomerId, job: JobId, copies: Copies): String = TODO() reprint(job, customer, Copies(200)) // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'JobId', but 'CustomerId' was expected. // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'CustomerId', but 'JobId' was expected. // Java gets the same safety from records, at the cost of an object each record CustomerId(String value) {} record JobId(String value) {} static String reprint(CustomerId customer, JobId job, long copies) { ... } reprint(job, customer, 200); // error: incompatible types: JobId cannot be converted to CustomerId Check the Java view. javap shows reprint-<hash>(String, String, long), so the older Java program that also reprints jobs can't call it any more. Don't reach for @JvmName here, because Java would pass raw values past every init. Add a Java entry point that takes the raw types and builds the value classes itself, so validation runs. // 2. a door for Java: raw types in, value classes (and their init blocks) inside fun reprintFromJava(customerId: String, jobId: String, copies: Long): String = reprint(CustomerId(customerId), JobId(jobId), Copies(copies)) // javap: reprint-<hash>(String, String, long) and reprintFromJava(String, String, long) // 3. the Java program calls the plain name; a negative count would fail inside Copies' init String result = ReprintsKt.reprintFromJava("c-17", "job-2026-0042", 200L); Java can still swap the two strings in reprintFromJava, so the door is a compromise: it checks values, but it can't check names. That's why the type safety belongs in Kotlin, and the door belongs at the edge, used by as few callers as possible.

h: Value classes and what they compile to · Key terms
x: Value class @JvmInline value class X(val v: T): its own type in Kotlin, its single property T at run time where possible. Underlying type The type of a value class's one property, which is what the JVM actually sees. Boxing Wrapping the underlying value in a real object of the value class, done when it is used as another type. Name mangling The hash suffix, as in ship-P0HeBCA, that the compiler adds to functions with value-class parameters. @JvmName Sets the JVM name of a function, which can remove the mangled suffix so Java can call it. @JvmExposeBoxed Experimental annotation (Kotlin 2.2+) that adds Java-callable boxed constructors and overloads. Type alias A second name for an existing type. It adds no type safety. Project Valhalla The OpenJDK project that adds value objects without identity to the JVM. JEP 401 is a preview in JDK 28. What does @JvmInline value class JobId(val value: String) compile to where it's used as a JobId? A plain String. JobId(...) calls the static constructor-impl, which runs init and returns the same String. When is a value class boxed? Whenever it's used as another type: a generic T, a nullable X?, an interface it implements, or Any (collections, println). Why does fun ship(weight: Grams) compile to ship-P0HeBCA(long)? Mangling. It avoids clashes with overloads on the underlying type, and Java can't call a name with a - in it. What does @JvmName on a value-class function give Java, and what's the catch? A name Java can call. Java passes the raw underlying value, so init never runs: validate again inside. Type alias vs value class? An alias is another name, assignment-compatible with the original type. A value class is a new type: a Long won't go where Grams is expected. How many properties can a Kotlin value class have on the JVM? Exactly one: value class must have exactly one primary constructor parameter. More waits for Valhalla. What does @JvmExposeBoxed add, and what does it need? A public constructor that runs init, and boxed overloads Java can call. It's Experimental: @OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class).

h: Value classes and what they compile to · Go deeper
x: Two details that matter when you design with value classes. A value class can wrap a generic type: @JvmInline value class Box<T>(val value: T). The docs say the underlying type is then mapped to Any?, or to the upper bound of T, so at run time it's an Object field and you rarely save anything. Generic value classes help with type safety, not with speed. The second detail is a compiler bug worth knowing about. In Kotlin 2.4.21 (and 2.3.21) this crashes the compiler with Backend Internal error: Exception during IR lowering and a NoSuchElementException from the string-concatenation lowering: @JvmInline value class W(val grams: Long) { override fun toString() = java.math.BigDecimal.valueOf(grams, 3).toPlainString() } fun label(w: W) = "Parcel $w kg" The trigger is the inferred return type: toPlainString() returns a Java platform type, String!, a type whose nullability Kotlin doesn't know. Write override fun toString(): String = ... and it compiles. It's a small, concrete argument for explicit return types on anything public: they keep platform types from leaking into your API, and here they also keep the compiler alive. Finally, the history of the keyword, which explains old code you'll still meet. Kotlin 1.5.0 made these classes stable with the value modifier plus @JvmInline on the JVM, and deprecated the old inline class spelling with a warning. The design notes give the reason for the split: @JvmInline names today's erasure trick, which leaves the plain value class free to mean a real Valhalla value class one day.

h: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties · Class delegation: every call goes to the object you passed in, captured once
x: An interface lists methods without saying how they work, and a class that implements it fills them in. The print shop's app has one for its printers, Printer, with a print(document) method, and a Laser class that implements it. To wrap such a class, you write a new class that implements the same interface and forwards each call to the wrapped object, changing only the behavior you care about. That's the Decorator pattern, which lesson 5 of the patterns track built by hand. Kotlin writes the forwarding for you. In class FrontDesk(var printer: Printer) : Printer by printer, the part by printer is class delegation. The compiler writes every method of Printer as a call on printer, except the ones you write yourself. In the print shop, FrontDesk is the clerk at the counter, and the Laser is the expert in the back room. You ask the clerk, and the expert does the work. Two details matter once you put by into real classes. The first is that the delegate is captured once. by printer looks as if it forwards to the printer property, but javap shows two fields: private final Printer $$delegate_0; // set from the constructor argument, never changed private Printer printer; // the property you can reassign The generated print calls $$delegate_0. Assign a new printer, and the property changes, but every call still goes to the old one. The demo prints after swap, printer = Laser(laser-2): flyer.pdf printed on laser-1. That's the clerk's notebook: she wrote the expert's name down on her first day, in ink. A hand-written Java decorator reads its field on every call, so swapping works there: Java final class FrontDeskJava implements Printer { private Printer printer; FrontDeskJava(Printer printer) { this.printer = printer; } void setPrinter(Printer printer) { this.printer = printer; } @Override public String print(String document) { return printer.print(document); // the current field, on every call } } Kotlin class FrontDesk(var printer: Printer) : Printer by printer // forwards to the FIRST printer val desk = FrontDesk(Laser("laser-1")) desk.printer = Laser("laser-2") desk.print("flyer.pdf") // "flyer.pdf printed on laser-1": $$delegate_0 still holds laser-1 If the target has to change while the program runs, write the forwarding yourself. Otherwise make the constructor parameter a plain parameter or a val, so nobody expects it to move. by captures the delegate once, when the object is built. If the target must change, write the forwarding yourself. The second detail: equals, hashCode and toString are not forwarded. They come from Any, the root of every Kotlin class, not from the interface. Ask the clerk who she is, and she talks about herself, not the expert. The demo's Tags class delegates MutableSet<String> to an inner set. It prints as workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.Tags@2d209079, a name only a hash function could love, and two Tags with the same elements are not equal. That breaks the contract of Set, which says two sets with the same elements are equal, and a HashSet<Tags> will happily keep both. Override the three, and forward them to the inner set, when the wrapper should behave like what it wraps. With those two details in mind, by is still the best tool for one job: wrapping a wide interface to change one or two methods. Take java.sql.Connection, the JDK's interface for a connection to a database, which has dozens of methods. A wrapper that logs each close() needs one override, and the compiler writes all the others, so none of them can be forgotten. The same keyword does a different job on a property, and it compiles to something quite different. Swap a delegate and watch nothing happen Run ClassDelegationDemo. Before you read the second line, predict which printer prints after the swap. Run javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.FrontDesk from labs/ and find both fields. Run ClassDelegationDemoJava, which swaps a hand-written Java decorator and then the Kotlin class from Java. In Tags, add override fun equals(other: Any?) = other is Set<*> && inner == other and override fun hashCode() = inner.hashCode(). Run again. ClassDelegationDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo interface Printer { fun print(document: String): String } class Laser(private val name: String) : Printer { override fun print(document: String): String = "$document printed on $name" override fun toString(): String = "Laser($name)" } /** `by printer` forwards to the object passed in at construction, stored in a hidden final field. */ class FrontDesk(var printer: Printer) : Printer by printer /** Delegating a Set forwards Set's methods, but not equals, hashCode or toString. */ class Tags(private val inner: MutableSet<String> = HashSet()) : MutableSet<String> by inner fun main() { val desk = FrontDesk(Laser("laser-1")) println(desk.print("flyer.pdf")) desk.printer = Laser("laser-2") // swap the printer... println("after swap, printer = ${desk.printer}: ${desk.print("flyer.pdf")}") val a = Tags().apply { add("rush"); add("colour") } val b = Tags().apply { add("rush"); add("colour") } println("a = $a") println("a == b: ${a == b}, a.size = ${a.size}, \"rush\" in a: ${"rush" in a}") } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.ClassDelegationDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l03/demo/ClassDelegationDemo.kt ClassDelegationDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo; /** * Java twin of ClassDelegationDemo.kt. Java has no `by`, so you write the forwarding yourself. * Written by hand, it reads the field on every call, so swapping the printer works. */ public class ClassDelegationDemoJava { static final class FrontDeskJava implements Printer { private Printer printer; FrontDeskJava(Printer printer) { this.printer = printer; } void setPrinter(Printer printer) { this.printer = printer; } @Override public String print(String document) { return printer.print(document); // reads the current field each time } } public static void main(String[] args) { FrontDeskJava desk = new FrontDeskJava(new Laser("laser-1")); System.out.println(desk.print("flyer.pdf")); desk.setPrinter(new Laser("laser-2")); System.out.println("after swap: " + desk.print("flyer.pdf")); // the Kotlin class, seen from Java: setPrinter changes the property, not the $$delegate_0 field FrontDesk kotlinDesk = new FrontDesk(new Laser("laser-1")); kotlinDesk.setPrinter(new Laser("laser-2")); System.out.println("Kotlin class after swap: " + kotlinDesk.print("flyer.pdf")); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.ClassDelegationDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l03/demo/ClassDelegationDemoJava.java Kotlin prints flyer.pdf printed on laser-1, then after swap, printer = Laser(laser-2): flyer.pdf printed on laser-1: the property moved, the calls didn't. javap lists private final ...Printer $$delegate_0 and private ...Printer printer. The Java decorator prints laser-2 after its swap, and the Kotlin class still prints laser-1 when Java swaps it. a == b is false until you add equals and hashCode, then true. h: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties · A delegated property is a hidden field and two calls
x: A delegated property is a hidden delegate field plus a getter and setter that call getValue and setValue Property delegation shares the keyword by and almost nothing else with class delegation. Start without it. Say every change to an order's status must be logged, and you want the logging written once, in a small helper class you can reuse for any property. By hand, the property forwards its getter and setter to the helper: Java final class OrderJava { private final Box<String> status = new Box<>("NEW"); // the helper holds the value String getStatus() { return status.get(); } void setStatus(String s) { status.set("status", s); } // and logs every change } Kotlin class Order { private val statusBox = Audited("NEW") // the helper holds the value var status: String get() = statusBox.getValue(this, ::status) set(value) = statusBox.setValue(this, ::status, value) // and logs every change } ::status is a reference to the property itself, a KProperty object that knows the property's name. So the helper can log status without a string that could drift out of date. That forwarding is all by does. In the print shop, it's the cloakroom. The property is your ticket. Reading the property is handing in the ticket to get your coat back, and assigning to it is handing in a coat. The attendant is the helper object: it holds the coat, and it may write each swap in a logbook. The helper is called the delegate. It needs only two functions with fixed names, getValue and setValue, and then by writes the getter and setter for you: Java // Java has no `by`: the helper is an ordinary class, and you write the forwarding above yourself final class Box<T> { private T value; Box(T value) { this.value = value; } T get() { return value; } void set(String name, T value) { System.out.println(" " + name + ": " + this.value + " -> " + value); this.value = value; } } Kotlin class Audited<T>(private var value: T) : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, T> { override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): T = value override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: T) { println(" ${property.name}: ${this.value} -> $value") this.value = value } } class Order { var status: String by Audited("NEW") // the same forwarding, written by the compiler var copies: Long by Audited(0L) } getValue receives the owning object (thisRef) and the KProperty, and setValue also gets the new value. A val needs only getValue. You can write the two as operator fun members, as extension functions on any class, or by implementing the standard interfaces ReadOnlyProperty or ReadWriteProperty, as Audited does. The compiler's version matches the hand-written one with one change, shown in the figure. For each delegated property, it adds a hidden field, status$delegate, typed as whatever the expression after by returns. Instead of building a fresh ::status on every call, it builds one static array per class, $$delegatedProperties, with a KProperty object for each property, filled once when the class is loaded. Then getStatus() loads status$delegate, loads $$delegatedProperties[0], calls getValue, and casts the result to String. Java sees none of this. It sees getStatus() and setStatus(String), ordinary methods, and the delegate field is private. That suits libraries that work through getters and setters. It's also a warning: a setter that logs or checks looks exactly like a plain setter from the outside. A few kinds of delegate get no $delegate field: another property (by this::pageCount), a named object, this, or a constant. The docs list the cases. Every other delegated property gets a hidden field in every instance, and usually a new delegate object to put in it. That's where the cloakroom picture breaks. A real cloakroom has one attendant for everybody. Here, every ticket usually comes with an attendant of its own. The two operators don't have to live in the delegate's class. They can be extension functions, and that's how by settings works on a plain Map in the last section. The standard library declares getValue as an extension operator on Map that looks up the key property.name. You can do the same for a class you don't own. ResourceBundle is the JDK class that holds an app's texts in one language. With operator fun ResourceBundle.getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): String = getString(property.name), a class can write val greeting: String by messages. The delegate you'll use most often isn't one you write yourself, though. It's lazy, and it comes with a bill. Find the generated field and array Run PropertyDelegateDemo, then PropertyDelegateDemoJava, which calls the same Order through setStatus and lists its fields by reflection (inspecting the class while the program runs). From labs/, run javap -c -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.Order and read getStatus. Add var note: String? by Audited(null) to Order and set it in main. Predict the new fields before you run. PropertyDelegateDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo import kotlin.properties.ReadWriteProperty import kotlin.reflect.KProperty /** A hand-written delegate: getValue and setValue are all the compiler needs. */ class Audited<T>(private var value: T) : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, T> { override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): T = value override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: T) { println(" ${property.name}: ${this.value} -> $value") this.value = value } } class Order { var status: String by Audited("NEW") var copies: Long by Audited(0L) } fun main() { val order = Order() order.status = "PRINTING" order.copies = 250 println("status = ${order.status}, copies = ${order.copies}") println("fields the compiler generated:") Order::class.java.declaredFields.forEach { println(" ${it.type.simpleName} ${it.name}") } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.PropertyDelegateDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l03/demo/PropertyDelegateDemo.kt PropertyDelegateDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo; import java.lang.reflect.Field; /** * Java twin of PropertyDelegateDemo.kt. Java sees getStatus and setStatus, ordinary methods, * and can't tell that a delegate sits behind them. */ public class PropertyDelegateDemoJava { // the hand-written Java shape: a field holding a helper object, and accessors that call it static final class Box<T> { private T value; Box(T value) { this.value = value; } T get() { return value; } void set(String name, T value) { System.out.println(" " + name + ": " + this.value + " -> " + value); this.value = value; } } static final class OrderJava { private final Box<String> status = new Box<>("NEW"); String getStatus() { return status.get(); } void setStatus(String s) { status.set("status", s); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Order order = new Order(); // the Kotlin class order.setStatus("PRINTING"); // goes through status$delegate.setValue order.setCopies(250L); System.out.println("status = " + order.getStatus() + ", copies = " + order.getCopies()); OrderJava hand = new OrderJava(); hand.setStatus("PRINTING"); System.out.println("fields of the Kotlin Order, seen by reflection:"); for (Field f : Order.class.getDeclaredFields()) { System.out.println(" " + f.getType().getSimpleName() + " " + f.getName()); } } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.PropertyDelegateDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l03/demo/PropertyDelegateDemoJava.java Both print the two changes (status: NEW -> PRINTING and copies: 0 -> 250), then the fields: KProperty[] $$delegatedProperties, Audited status$delegate and Audited copies$delegate. getStatus is getfield status$delegate, getstatic $$delegatedProperties, iconst_0, aaload, invokevirtual Audited.getValue, checkcast String. Adding note adds a note$delegate field and a third array entry, not a second array. What the compiler writes for one delegated property: a field for the delegate, a shared KProperty array, and accessors that call the delegate. Delegated properties (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties · What by lazy costs: objects in every instance and a call on every read
x: by lazy computes a value the first time someone reads the property, then keeps it. The memory model track took it apart in lesson 5. It is double-checked locking (check, take a lock, check again), and SYNCHRONIZED is the default of its three modes, next to PUBLICATION and NONE. A lock lets only one thread at a time run a piece of code, a thread being one path of execution in the program. Here the lock makes sure that only one thread runs the initializer. This section is about the bill. In the cloakroom, lazy is the attendant who fetches your item from the stockroom only the first time anybody asks for it, and keeps it at the counter after that. The demo's PaperSpec looks up how much one sheet of paper weighs, in a paper catalogue that is slow and sometimes times out: Java // Java's per-instance lazy field: volatile double-checked locking, by hand private volatile Double sheetGrams; double sheetGrams() { Double v = sheetGrams; if (v == null) { synchronized (this) { v = sheetGrams; if (v == null) sheetGrams = v = catalogue.weightOf("A4 plain"); } } return v; } Kotlin class PaperSpec(private val catalogue: PaperCatalogue) { val sheetGrams: Double by lazy { catalogue.weightOf("A4 plain") } // SYNCHRONIZED } Each PaperSpec gets a private final kotlin.Lazy sheetGrams$delegate field. The constructor fills it with a new SynchronizedLazyImpl, an object with fields for the initializer, the value and the lock. The initializer lambda is one more object whenever it uses the instance, as this one uses catalogue. Every read then calls Lazy.getValue() through an interface, and for a Double it also unboxes with checkcast Number and doubleValue. There's no $$delegatedProperties array, because lazy never looks at the property. For one settings object, none of that matters. For a class you create for every page or every print job, it's two extra objects each time, for a value you may never read. Use lazy on objects that live long: the app's settings, a cache, one shared catalogue. For short-lived ones, compute the value in the constructor, or make it a function. lazy pays off on objects that live long. On objects you create by the million, compute the value or make it a function. When only one thread can ever touch the object, lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE) drops the lock, and the class becomes UnsafeLazyImpl. The docs say it "doesn't incur any thread-safety guarantees and related overhead". Think of a report builder that lives inside one function call. Don't use it on an object that many threads read at once: NONE gives you no guarantee that they all see one value. One behavior is easy to miss: lazy has a short memory for failures. It doesn't keep an exception. In the demo, the first read throws paper catalogue timed out, the second read runs the initializer again and succeeds, and only then is the value kept. For a slow lookup, that's usually what you want. The standard library has more delegates like lazy, ready to use, and one hook that lets a delegate check its property before anyone reads it. Count the initializer runs Run LazyDemo. Before you do, predict how many times the initializer runs over three reads when the first one throws. Run LazyDemoJava, which does the same with hand-written double-checked locking and then reads the Kotlin class from Java. Run javap -c -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.PaperSpec and read getSheetGrams. LazyDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo var lookups = 0 class PaperSpec { /** Default mode: SYNCHRONIZED. The first reader runs the initializer under a lock. */ val sheetGrams: Double by lazy { lookups++ if (lookups == 1) throw IllegalStateException("paper catalogue timed out") 4.99 // one A4 sheet of 80 g/m2 paper } } fun main() { for (mode in LazyThreadSafetyMode.entries) { println("$mode -> ${lazy(mode) { 0 }.javaClass.name}") } val spec = PaperSpec() try { spec.sheetGrams } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("first read failed: ${e.message}") } println("second read: ${spec.sheetGrams} (initializer ran $lookups times)") println("third read: ${spec.sheetGrams} (initializer ran $lookups times)") println("field: ${PaperSpec::class.java.declaredFields.joinToString { "${it.type.name} ${it.name}" }}") } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.LazyDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l03/demo/LazyDemo.kt LazyDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo; /** * Java twin of LazyDemo.kt. Java has no lazy delegate. For a per-instance lazy field the usual * shape is double-checked locking on a volatile field, which is what Kotlin's SYNCHRONIZED mode does. */ public class LazyDemoJava { static int lookups = 0; static final class PaperSpecJava { private volatile Double sheetGrams; // null means "not computed yet" double sheetGrams() { Double v = sheetGrams; if (v == null) { synchronized (this) { v = sheetGrams; if (v == null) { lookups++; if (lookups == 1) throw new IllegalStateException("paper catalogue timed out"); sheetGrams = v = 4.99; } } } return v; } } public static void main(String[] args) { PaperSpecJava spec = new PaperSpecJava(); try { spec.sheetGrams(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("first read failed: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("second read: " + spec.sheetGrams() + " (initializer ran " + lookups + " times)"); System.out.println("third read: " + spec.sheetGrams() + " (initializer ran " + lookups + " times)"); // the Kotlin class from Java: getSheetGrams() calls Lazy.getValue() on every read PaperSpec kotlinSpec = new PaperSpec(); try { kotlinSpec.getSheetGrams(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("Kotlin PaperSpec from Java, first read failed: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("Kotlin PaperSpec from Java, second read: " + kotlinSpec.getSheetGrams()); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.LazyDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l03/demo/LazyDemoJava.java The three modes map to kotlin.SynchronizedLazyImpl, kotlin.SafePublicationLazyImpl and kotlin.UnsafeLazyImpl. The first read fails with paper catalogue timed out, the second returns 4.99, and the initializer ran 2 times, not 3: once the value is kept, reads stop calling it. The only field is kotlin.Lazy sheetGrams$delegate, and getSheetGrams is getfield, invokeinterface Lazy.getValue, checkcast Number, doubleValue. The Java version behaves the same. h: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties · The standard delegates, and provideDelegate for early checks
x: The standard library ships the delegates you'd otherwise write by hand. Delegates.observable(initial) { property, old, new -> } calls you after every assignment. Delegates.vetoable(initial) { property, old, new -> Boolean } calls you before it, and returning false keeps the old value. In the cloakroom, the first is the attendant who notes every swap in the logbook. The second looks at what you hand in, and may refuse it. A val can also read from a Map: val host: String by settings looks up the key "host", like an attendant who finds your coat on a rack by the name on your ticket. A var does the same with a MutableMap. Delegates.notNull<Int>() covers what lateinit can't. (lateinit marks a var that gets its first value after construction, and it doesn't work for primitive types such as Int.) Reading a notNull property before the first assignment throws Property size should be initialized before get. Here are the first three, by hand in Java and with delegates in Kotlin: Java void setOwner(String owner) { // observable, by hand String old = this.owner; this.owner = owner; System.out.println("owner: " + old + " -> " + owner); } void setCopies(int copies) { // vetoable, by hand if (copies <= 100) this.copies = copies; } int port() { return (Integer) settings.get("port"); } // map-backed, by hand Kotlin var owner: String by Delegates.observable("<none>") { property, old, new -> println("${property.name}: $old -> $new") } var copies: Int by Delegates.vetoable(1) { _, _, new -> new <= 100 } val port: Int by settings // settings["port"], cast to Int The demo prints owner: <none> -> alice, owner: alice -> bob, copies after veto: 1 and copies after ok: 50. The shop's limit of 100 copies per request turned the 500 away. A map-backed property fails only when you read it. A missing key throws java.util.NoSuchElementException: Key port is missing in the map. That's late. For settings, you'd rather fail when the object is built, and that's what provideDelegate is for. If the object after by has an operator fun provideDelegate(thisRef, property), the compiler calls it once per property, while the owning object is being constructed. Then it keeps whatever provideDelegate returns as the real delegate. The docs describe it as the way to get "the necessary validation right away", and PropertyDelegateProvider { thisRef, property -> ... } creates one without writing a new class. In the cloakroom, it's the attendant who checks your ticket as you walk in, not when you come back for your coat. In the demo, binding printerHost prints during ShopSettings(), before anyone reads the property. The lab uses the same trick to register every recorded property up front. Check settings when the object is built, not when they're first read. provideDelegate is the hook for it. Every delegate here adds a hidden field to each instance, usually holding one more object, and puts logic behind a getter or setter that looks plain from the outside. In the lab, you'll write a delegate that earns both: a recorder that logs every real change to a print job. Watch the standard delegates fire Run StdDelegatesDemo (or its Java twin). Predict the order of building ShopSettings..., binding printerHost and built; ... before you look. Change the veto to new <= 40 and run. Predict both copies lines first. Remove "host" to "laser-1.local" from the map. Predict which line fails, and when. StdDelegatesDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo import kotlin.properties.Delegates import kotlin.properties.PropertyDelegateProvider import kotlin.properties.ReadOnlyProperty class PrintRequest { // observable: the handler runs after the assignment var owner: String by Delegates.observable("<none>") { property, old, new -> println("${property.name}: $old -> $new") } // vetoable: the handler runs before the assignment; false keeps the old value var copies: Int by Delegates.vetoable(1) { _, _, new -> new <= 100 } } class PrinterConfig(settings: Map<String, Any?>) { val host: String by settings // reads settings["host"] val port: Int by settings // reads settings["port"] } /** provideDelegate runs once per property, while the object is built: validation happens right away. */ fun requiredSetting(): PropertyDelegateProvider<Any?, ReadOnlyProperty<Any?, String>> = PropertyDelegateProvider { _, property -> println("binding ${property.name}") ReadOnlyProperty { _, _ -> "value of ${property.name}" } } class ShopSettings { val printerHost: String by requiredSetting() } fun main() { val request = PrintRequest() request.owner = "alice" request.owner = "bob" request.copies = 500 println("copies after veto: ${request.copies}") request.copies = 50 println("copies after ok: ${request.copies}") val config = PrinterConfig(mapOf("host" to "laser-1.local")) println("host = ${config.host}") try { println("port = ${config.port}") } catch (e: NoSuchElementException) { println("port failed on access: ${e.message}") } println("building ShopSettings...") val s = ShopSettings() println("built; printerHost = ${s.printerHost}") } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.StdDelegatesDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l03/demo/StdDelegatesDemo.kt StdDelegatesDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo; import java.util.Map; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; /** * Java twin of StdDelegatesDemo.kt. Java writes each behavior into the setter or getter by hand. */ public class StdDelegatesDemoJava { static final class PrintRequestJava { private String owner = "<none>"; private int copies = 1; void setOwner(String owner) { String old = this.owner; this.owner = owner; // observable: assign, then notify System.out.println("owner: " + old + " -> " + owner); } void setCopies(int copies) { if (copies <= 100) this.copies = copies; // vetoable: check, then assign } int getCopies() { return copies; } } static final class PrinterConfigJava { private final Map<String, Object> settings; PrinterConfigJava(Map<String, Object> settings) { this.settings = settings; } String host() { return (String) get("host"); } int port() { return (Integer) get("port"); } private Object get(String key) { if (!settings.containsKey(key)) throw new NoSuchElementException("Key " + key + " is missing in the map."); return settings.get(key); } } // provideDelegate has no Java twin: Java validates in the constructor, which also runs at build time static final class ShopSettingsJava { final String printerHost; ShopSettingsJava() { System.out.println("binding printerHost"); printerHost = "value of printerHost"; } } public static void main(String[] args) { PrintRequestJava request = new PrintRequestJava(); request.setOwner("alice"); request.setOwner("bob"); request.setCopies(500); System.out.println("copies after veto: " + request.getCopies()); request.setCopies(50); System.out.println("copies after ok: " + request.getCopies()); PrinterConfigJava config = new PrinterConfigJava(Map.of("host", "laser-1.local")); System.out.println("host = " + config.host()); try { System.out.println("port = " + config.port()); } catch (NoSuchElementException e) { System.out.println("port failed on access: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("building ShopSettings..."); ShopSettingsJava s = new ShopSettingsJava(); System.out.println("built; printerHost = " + s.printerHost); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.StdDelegatesDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l03/demo/StdDelegatesDemoJava.java building ShopSettings... comes first, then binding printerHost while the constructor runs, then built; printerHost = value of printerHost. With new <= 40 both assignments are vetoed, so both lines print 1: the handler checks assignments, never the initial value. Without host, building PrinterConfig still works, and the program fails on the config.host read with Key host is missing in the map.

h: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties · Java and Kotlin
x: An audited field: Java setters vs a Kotlin delegate PrintJob.java public final class PrintJob { private final ChangeLog log; private String status = "NEW"; private int copies = 1; public PrintJob(ChangeLog log) { this.log = log; } public String getStatus() { return status; } public void setStatus(String s) { if (!s.equals(status)) log.record("status", status, s); // repeated in every setter status = s; } public int getCopies() { return copies; } public void setCopies(int c) { if (c != copies) log.record("copies", copies, c); copies = c; } } PrintJob.kt class Recorded<T>(private var value: T, private val log: ChangeLog) : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, T> { override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): T = value override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: T) { if (value != this.value) log.changes += Change(property.name, this.value, value) this.value = value } } class PrintJob(val log: ChangeLog) { var status: String by Recorded("NEW", log) // the audit is written once, in Recorded var copies: Int by Recorded(1, log) } Both record every real change to a print job, so the shop can see who changed what. In Java the record lives in every setter, and a new field without it is a silent gap that only a careful reviewer can catch. In Kotlin it's written once, in the delegate, and each property opts in with by. The property name comes from the KProperty the compiler passes in, so it can't drift from the field name the way a string literal can. The run-time price is one delegate object per property per instance, plus one static KProperty array per class. Java code calling the Kotlin class can't tell the two apart: it sees getStatus and setStatus either way.

h: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties · Worked example
x: A config object that fails at start-up, not on the first job Start with a map-backed config for the shop's app. It reads nicely, but a missing key is found only when someone reads the property, which may be the first job sent to that printer, late at night. final class ShopConfig { private final Map<String, Object> settings; ShopConfig(Map<String, Object> settings) { this.settings = settings; } String printerHost() { return (String) settings.get("printerHost"); } // null if missing long timeoutMs() { return (Long) settings.get("timeoutMs"); } // NullPointerException if missing } class ShopConfig(settings: Map<String, Any?>) { val printerHost: String by settings // NoSuchElementException, but only when read val timeoutMs: Long by settings } Write a provider. provideDelegate runs once per property while the object is built, so it can check the key right away and hand back a delegate that only returns the value it read. fun <T> Map<String, Any?>.required(): PropertyDelegateProvider<Any?, ReadOnlyProperty<Any?, T>> = PropertyDelegateProvider { _, property -> // 1. check the key while the owning object is constructed require(property.name in this) { "missing config key '${property.name}'" } @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") val value = this[property.name] as T // 2. the real delegate just returns what was read ReadOnlyProperty { _, _ -> value } } class ShopConfig(settings: Map<String, Any?>) { val printerHost: String by settings.required() val timeoutMs: Long by settings.required() } // Java does the same check in the constructor, one line per key ShopConfig(Map<String, Object> settings) { this.printerHost = (String) require(settings, "printerHost"); this.timeoutMs = (Long) require(settings, "timeoutMs"); } private static Object require(Map<String, Object> m, String key) { if (!m.containsKey(key)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("missing config key '" + key + "'"); return m.get(key); } Build one with a key missing. It fails in the constructor, with the property's name in the message, because the name came from the KProperty the compiler passed in. ShopConfig(mapOf("printerHost" to "laser-1.local", "timeoutMs" to 2_000L)) // fine ShopConfig(mapOf("printerHost" to "laser-1.local")) // java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: missing config key 'timeoutMs' new ShopConfig(Map.of("printerHost", "laser-1.local", "timeoutMs", 2_000L)); // fine new ShopConfig(Map.of("printerHost", "laser-1.local")); // java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: missing config key 'timeoutMs' The cast is still unchecked: a "timeoutMs" to "2000" entry passes the check and fails later, with a ClassCastException on the first read. If that matters, pass the expected class into required and check it with isInstance, the class-token trick from the generics track.

h: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties · Quiz
x: What does this print? class FrontDesk(var printer: Printer) : Printer by printer val desk = FrontDesk(Laser("laser-1")) desk.printer = Laser("laser-2") println(desk.print("flyer.pdf")) flyer.pdf printed on laser-1 flyer.pdf printed on laser-2 An IllegalStateException Nothing: it doesn't compile by printer reads the constructor argument once and stores it in $$delegate_0. The generated print calls that field, so the swap changes only the property. laser-2 is what a hand-written decorator that reads its field on each call would print. Which fields does class Order { var status: String by Audited("NEW") } have in the bytecode? private String status private final Audited status$delegate, plus a static KProperty[] $$delegatedProperties One static Audited shared by every Order None: the delegate is inlined into getStatus Each delegated property gets a hidden field holding its delegate, typed as the delegate expression, and each class gets one static array of KProperty objects that the accessors pass to getValue and setValue. Nothing is shared between instances, and nothing is inlined. A PageImage object is created for every page the shop prints, two million a day. It has val summary: String by lazy { describe(this) }, which is read for about 1% of pages. What's the best change? Keep it: lazy costs nothing until it's read Switch to lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION) Mark the property @Volatile Make it a getter without a backing field, val summary get() = describe(this), computed on demand lazy creates the Lazy object and the initializer lambda in the constructor, for every page, read or not. A getter without a backing field costs nothing until it's called. Changing the mode keeps both objects; it only changes the locking. class PrinterConfig(settings: Map<String, Any?>) { val port: Int by settings }, and settings has no "port" key. When does it fail? When PrinterConfig is constructed At compile time Never: port reads as 0 When port is read: NoSuchElementException: Key port is missing in the map. A map-backed property is a lookup in its getter. Building the object only stores the map. To fail at construction, check the key in a provideDelegate, which runs while the object is built. From the memory model track: two threads read val rules by lazy { download() } for the first time at the same moment. What happens? download() may run twice, and each thread keeps its own result download() runs once; the other thread waits and sees the same value Nothing is guaranteed unless the property is @Volatile The second thread gets ConcurrentModificationException The default mode is SYNCHRONIZED: double-checked locking with a lock, so one thread runs the initializer and the other waits for it. The first option sounds like PUBLICATION, but even there every thread ends up seeing the first value stored, not its own.
