h: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties · Key terms
x: Class delegation class A(x: I) : I by x: the compiler writes every method of I as a call on x, except the ones you override. Delegated property A property whose get and set are handed to another object with by. Delegate The helper object behind by. For a property, it has getValue and, for a var, setValue. $delegate field The hidden field, such as status$delegate, that holds a property's delegate. KProperty A run-time description of a property (its name, its type), passed to getValue and setValue. Lazy The standard delegate that computes a value on first read and keeps it. It has three thread-safety modes. provideDelegate An operator the compiler calls once per property at construction, to create or check the real delegate. Map-backed property val host: String by settings: reads settings["host"] each time the property is read. class FrontDesk(var printer: Printer) : Printer by printer. After desk.printer = other, which object gets the calls? The original one. The compiler copied it into a hidden final field, $$delegate_0, at construction. Does class delegation forward equals, hashCode and toString? No. They come from Any, not from the interface. Override them yourself if the wrapper should behave like what it wraps. Which functions does a delegate for a var need? getValue(thisRef, property: KProperty<*>) and setValue(thisRef, property, value), as operators or via ReadWriteProperty. A val needs only getValue. What does the compiler generate for var status by Audited("NEW")? A status$delegate field holding the delegate, a static $$delegatedProperties array of KProperty, and accessors that call getValue/setValue on the delegate. What does by lazy cost per instance? A Lazy object (SynchronizedLazyImpl by default), plus the initializer lambda if it uses the instance, created in the constructor. Every read is an interface call, and primitives are unboxed. observable vs vetoable: when does each handler run? observable runs after the assignment. vetoable runs before it, and returning false keeps the old value. When does provideDelegate run? Once per property, while the owning object is being constructed, before any read. That makes it the place for early validation.

h: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties · Go deeper
x: Delegating to another property is the one case worth knowing that has no $delegate field at all. It is useful when you rename a property and need the old name for a while: Java // Java keeps the old accessor by hand and marks it deprecated public int getPageCount() { return pageCount; } @Deprecated public int getPages() { return pageCount; } Kotlin class PrintJob { var pageCount: Int = 0 @Deprecated("Use pageCount", ReplaceWith("pageCount")) var pages: Int by this::pageCount } javap -p on that class shows getPages and setPages, a private static helper getPages$delegate(PrintJob), and no pages$delegate field: the accessors read and write pageCount directly. The IDE offers the ReplaceWith fix at every call site, so the rename can finish over a few releases. The other cases without a field, from the docs: a delegate that is a named object, this, a constant expression or an enum entry, and "a final val property with a backing field and a default getter in the same module". Everything else pays for a hidden field, and usually a delegate object, per property per instance. One more design note on class delegation, after the aside in the first section. The delegate never calling back into your class can look like a flaw, but it is also what makes by predictable. A subclass of HashSet depends on how HashSet calls its own methods, which a future JDK may change. A by wrapper depends only on the interface, so it behaves the same whatever the inner class does inside.

h: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers · A lambda with a receiver: code that runs inside an object
x: Start with something every Java programmer has written: a StringBuilder that builds a line of text, one append at a time. The print shop's app makes job tickets this way, little slips such as flyer.pdf x 250 that go into each job's folder. Here is a helper that makes one, in both languages: Java // Java has no receiver lambdas. Its idiom: a Consumer that receives the builder as a parameter. static String ticket(Consumer<StringBuilder> block) { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); block.accept(sb); return sb.toString(); } ticket(sb -> sb.append("flyer.pdf x ").append(250)); Kotlin fun ticket(block: StringBuilder.() -> Unit): String = StringBuilder().apply(block).toString() ticket { append("flyer.pdf x "); append(250) } // `this` is the StringBuilder The part in braces is a lambda, a small function written in place and passed as a value. The two calls look almost the same, but one thing is missing in the Kotlin one: the sb.. Inside its braces, append is called on the builder without naming it. The object a call is made on is the call's receiver. In sb.append(x), the receiver is sb. Inside a class's own methods the receiver is this, and you usually leave it out. That's why a method of StringBuilder can call append with no prefix. The parameter type in the Kotlin version, StringBuilder.() -> Unit, is a function type with a receiver. A lambda of that type runs with a StringBuilder as its this, so inside its braces you write code as if you were writing a method of StringBuilder. In the print shop, it's a clerk handed a form already clipped to a clipboard. She writes in the boxes without saying which form, because she's holding it. apply, with and run from the standard library are all built on this one idea. You may wonder what the JVM makes of it. The JVM has no idea what a receiver is. To the JVM, StringBuilder.() -> Unit and (StringBuilder) -> Unit are one and the same: kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1<StringBuilder, Unit>, Kotlin's interface for a function with one parameter. The receiver is simply the first argument. So Kotlin lets you assign one type to the other, and it lets you call a receiver lambda both ways, sb.withReceiver() or withReceiver(sb). Only the compiler cares about the difference, because it decides what this means inside the braces. That is also exactly what Java sees. Java calls the Kotlin ticket with a lambda that gets the builder as a parameter, and the lambda has to end with return Unit.INSTANCE. A Kotlin function with nothing useful to return returns Unit, and to Java, Unit is a real object. Leave the line out, and javac, the Java compiler, says bad return type in lambda expression and missing return value. It's a small toll Java pays on every block. Two more facts turn this into a language. A receiver lambda can take ordinary parameters too: Builder.(Int) -> Unit gets a this and an Int. And an extension function, a function you declare as if it were a member of a class you didn't write, works like a named lambda with receiver. A fun BookletBuilder.folded(...) can be called inside any BookletBuilder.() -> Unit block. The worked example uses that to add a new word to the shop's DSL. A lambda with a receiver is a lambda whose first parameter is this. Inside its braces, you call the receiver's members by name. One clipboard holds one form. A real order has sections inside sections, and for that we need builders. Call a receiver lambda both ways Run ReceiverDemo, then ReceiverDemoJava. In ReceiverDemo.kt, try the reverse assignment: val back: (StringBuilder) -> Unit = withReceiver. Predict whether it compiles, then run. In the Java twin, delete return Unit.INSTANCE; from the first lambda and run. Read javac's complaint. ReceiverDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo // Two function types. Inside the first, the StringBuilder is `this`; in the second it's a parameter. val withReceiver: StringBuilder.() -> Unit = { append("copies: "); append(250) } val withParameter: (StringBuilder) -> Unit = { sb -> sb.append("copies: ").append(250) } /** An ordinary function that takes a lambda with receiver: the smallest possible DSL entry point. */ fun ticket(block: StringBuilder.() -> Unit): String = StringBuilder().apply(block).toString() fun main() { val sb = StringBuilder() sb.withReceiver() // call it like an extension function... withReceiver(sb) // ...or pass the receiver as the first argument println(sb) val swapped: StringBuilder.() -> Unit = withParameter // the two types are interchangeable println(ticket(swapped)) println(ticket { append("flyer.pdf x "); append(250) }) println("JVM type of withReceiver: ${withReceiver.javaClass.interfaces.joinToString { it.name }}") } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l04.demo.ReceiverDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l04/demo/ReceiverDemo.kt ReceiverDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo; import kotlin.Unit; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** * Java twin of ReceiverDemo.kt. Java has no lambdas with receivers. A Kotlin * StringBuilder.() -> Unit is a Function1<StringBuilder, Unit> to Java: the receiver is the first parameter. */ public class ReceiverDemoJava { // Java's own idiom for the same job: a Consumer that gets the builder as a parameter static String ticketJava(Consumer<StringBuilder> block) { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); block.accept(sb); return sb.toString(); } public static void main(String[] args) { String t = ReceiverDemoKt.ticket(sb -> { sb.append("flyer.pdf x ").append(250); return Unit.INSTANCE; // Kotlin's Unit is a real object here }); System.out.println(t); System.out.println(ticketJava(sb -> sb.append("menu.pdf x ").append(40))); StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); ReceiverDemoKt.getWithReceiver().invoke(sb); // a receiver lambda, invoked with the receiver as argument System.out.println(sb); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l04.demo.ReceiverDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l04/demo/ReceiverDemoJava.java Kotlin prints copies: 250copies: 250 (one call as an extension, one with the receiver as an argument), then copies: 250, flyer.pdf x 250 and JVM type of withReceiver: kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1. The reverse assignment compiles too. Without return Unit.INSTANCE, javac stops with incompatible types: bad return type in lambda expression and missing return value: Function1.invoke returns an object, so a Java lambda for it has to return something. Type-safe builders (Kotlin docs) docs Function literals with receiver (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers · Builder classes and an entry function: a booklet order in a few lines
x: Every section of an order needs its own clipboard, and some sections hold smaller ones. Take a booklet, such as a restaurant menu: a cover on thick card, then a few parts on plain paper, say the starters and the mains. The shop makes booklets by folding sheets in half, and one folded sheet gives four pages. So every booklet needs a multiple of 4 pages, or a customer gets blank pages nobody asked for. The pattern Kotlin's docs call a type-safe builder has two pieces. A builder class holds the state and offers the words: properties to set and functions to call. An entry function creates the builder, runs your lambda on it, and returns the finished result. Here is the lab's booklet builder, cut down to its shape: Java // Java: the builder arrives as a parameter, and every line names it static Booklet printBooklet(String title, Consumer<BookletBuilder> block) { BookletBuilder b = new BookletBuilder(title); block.accept(b); return b.build(); } Booklet menu = printBooklet("menu", b -> { b.setNote("staple on the fold"); b.cover(4); b.pages("starters", 4); b.pages("mains", 8); }); Kotlin class BookletBuilder(private val title: String) { var note = "" private val parts = mutableListOf<Part>() fun cover(pages: Int) = add("cover", Paper.CARD, pages) fun pages(name: String, pages: Int) = add(name, Paper.PLAIN, pages) private fun add(name: String, paper: Paper, pages: Int) { /* checks pages > 0, then adds a Part */ } fun build(): Booklet { /* checks the whole booklet, returns a copy of the parts */ } } fun printBooklet(title: String, block: BookletBuilder.() -> Unit): Booklet = BookletBuilder(title).apply(block).build() val menu = printBooklet("menu") { note = "staple on the fold" cover(4) pages("starters", 4) pages("mains", 8) } The Kotlin entry function is one line, BookletBuilder(title).apply(block).build(). It creates a builder, runs the block with that builder as this, and turns the builder into a finished Booklet. The Java version does the same three steps by hand, and its block names the builder, b., on every line. Nesting is the same trick again. The lab's OrderBuilder has a function booklet(title) { ... } that takes another receiver lambda, so an order holds booklets the way a form holds sections. No library is involved: only classes, functions and lambdas with receivers. Where does checking go? Check a single bad value at the call that passes it, so the error points at the wrong line: pages("mains", -4) fails inside pages. Check rules that span several calls in build(), the one place that sees the whole booklet. In the lab, a 4-page cover and a 10-page concert programme make 14 pages, and build() turns it away with booklet programme has 14 pages: a folded booklet needs a multiple of 4. Check one value where it's passed, and the rules between values in build(). The standard library ships three builders of its own that you can use today: Java List<Line> building = new ArrayList<>(); building.add(new Line("flyer.pdf", 250, 1)); building.add(new Line("menu.pdf", 40, 8)); if (building.size() == 2) building.add(new Line("cover-sheet.pdf", 1, 1)); List<Line> lines = List.copyOf(building); // freeze it with a copy String text = new StringBuilder().append("pages to print=").append(571).toString(); Kotlin val lines = buildList { add(Line("flyer.pdf", 250, 1)) add(Line("menu.pdf", 40, 8)) if (size == 2) add(Line("cover-sheet.pdf", 1, 1)) // `this` is a MutableList } val printed = buildMap { for (l in lines) put(l.file, l.copies * l.pages) } val text = buildString { append("pages to print="); append(printed.values.sum()) } Inside buildList { }, this is a MutableList, so add, addAll and even size work. The result is typed List, and it really is read-only. The demo casts it back to MutableList, calls add, and gets an UnsupportedOperationException. That's what you want from a builder: changeable while you build, fixed once you're done. Java gets the same result with List.copyOf, at the price of one copy. buildList, buildMap and buildString are inline, so their lambdas cost nothing at run time (lesson 1 of this track). Your own entry functions can be inline too, though they usually run a few times per order, so it rarely matters. Builders nest nicely. They also nest a little too nicely, and that is where a bug can hide. Use the standard builders Run BuildersDemo and BuildersDemoJava. They print the same four lines. In buildList { }, add println(this::class.simpleName) as the first line. Predict whether you'll see ArrayList, then run. Move the if (size == 2) line above the two add calls and run again. What changed, and why? BuildersDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo data class Line(val file: String, val copies: Int, val pages: Int) fun main() { val lines = buildList { add(Line("flyer.pdf", 250, 1)) add(Line("menu.pdf", 40, 8)) if (size == 2) add(Line("cover-sheet.pdf", 1, 1)) // `this` is a MutableList, so size works here } val printed = buildMap { for (l in lines) put(l.file, l.copies * l.pages) } val text = buildString { append("pages to print=") append(printed.values.sum()) } println(lines.map { it.file }) println(printed) println(text) try { @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") (lines as MutableList<Line>).add(Line("late.pdf", 1, 1)) } catch (e: UnsupportedOperationException) { println("the built list is read-only: ${e.javaClass.simpleName}") } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l04.demo.BuildersDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l04/demo/BuildersDemo.kt BuildersDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * Java twin of BuildersDemo.kt. Java builds a mutable collection, then copies it into an * unmodifiable one. buildList and buildString are inline-only Kotlin functions, so Java can't call them. */ public class BuildersDemoJava { record LineJava(String file, int copies, int pages) {} public static void main(String[] args) { List<LineJava> building = new ArrayList<>(); building.add(new LineJava("flyer.pdf", 250, 1)); building.add(new LineJava("menu.pdf", 40, 8)); if (building.size() == 2) building.add(new LineJava("cover-sheet.pdf", 1, 1)); List<LineJava> lines = List.copyOf(building); Map<String, Integer> printed = new LinkedHashMap<>(); for (LineJava l : lines) printed.put(l.file(), l.copies() * l.pages()); String text = new StringBuilder() .append("pages to print=") .append(printed.values().stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum()) .toString(); System.out.println(lines.stream().map(LineJava::file).toList()); System.out.println(printed); System.out.println(text); try { lines.add(new LineJava("late.pdf", 1, 1)); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("the copied list is read-only: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()); } } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l04.demo.BuildersDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l04/demo/BuildersDemoJava.java Both print [flyer.pdf, menu.pdf, cover-sheet.pdf], {flyer.pdf=250, menu.pdf=320, cover-sheet.pdf=1}, pages to print=571 and a line saying the list is read-only. Inside the block, this is the standard library's own list builder class (it prints ListBuilder), not an ArrayList: that's how the result can become read-only without a copy. With the if first, size is 0, so no cover sheet is added.

h: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers · @DslMarker: each section of the form offers only its own boxes
x: A lambda with receiver runs inside its builder; a bare call goes to the nearest receiver that has it, and @DslMarker stops it there The demo's order form shows the trap best. It has two sections that look alike, the customer and the delivery address. Both take a name and a phone number, so both use one builder class, ContactBuilder. Around them sits OrderFormBuilder, which holds the number of copies and offers the customer { } and deliverTo { } blocks. Inside customer { }, two receivers are in scope: the ContactBuilder for the customer, and the OrderFormBuilder around it. For a call that names no receiver, Kotlin tries each receiver in turn, nearest first. So a deliverTo { } written by mistake inside customer { } compiles. ContactBuilder has no deliverTo, and the compiler, always eager to help, finds one on the outer builder and calls that. On paper, that would be a form where any box missing from your section gets written into the section underneath. The demo's wrong move does exactly that. Without a marker, it compiles, runs, and fails with IllegalArgumentException: phone required for 'oops': the misplaced line built a second, half-filled delivery address. The exception is luck. On a form without a required phone number, the shop would deliver to "oops". @DslMarker closes the hole. It is an annotation, a label in the source that tools can read, and you put it on an annotation class of your own. Then you put your annotation on every builder class. From then on, inside a block, only the nearest marked receiver is implicit. Each section offers only its own boxes: Java // Java needs no marker: each lambda names its builder, so reaching the outer one takes `f.` DslMarkerDemoKt.orderForm("ord-17", f -> { f.customer(c -> { c.setName("Corner Bakery"); c.setPhone("555-0142"); f.setCopies(250); // deliberate, and visible in review return Unit.INSTANCE; }); f.deliverTo(c -> { c.setName("Back door"); c.setPhone("555-0143"); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); Kotlin @DslMarker @Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS, AnnotationTarget.TYPE) annotation class FormDsl @FormDsl class ContactBuilder { /* name, phone, build() */ } @FormDsl class OrderFormBuilder(private val id: String) { /* copies, customer { }, deliverTo { } */ } orderForm("ord-18") { customer { name = "Corner Bakery" deliverTo { name = "oops" } // error: cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver this@orderForm.copies = 250 // an explicit label still works } } The full message is 'fun deliverTo(block: ContactBuilder.() -> Unit): Unit' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver. Use an explicit receiver if necessary. A box from the outer section fails the same way: copies = 5 inside customer { } gets 'var copies: Int' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver. You can still reach the outer section on purpose, by naming it. this@orderForm is a labeled this: it names the receiver of the lambda passed to orderForm, and nobody types it by accident. On the paper form, it's writing "order section, copies: 250" in full. Without a marker, a missing name falls through to the outer builder. Mark every builder class. The rules are narrow, so learn them exactly. A marker counts only where it marks a type. That can be a builder class, or a common superclass of all the builders, which is enough for a DSL with twenty of them. It can be the receiver type of a function type (the TYPE target, as in @FormDsl ContactBuilder.() -> Unit). Or it can be a type alias, a second name for a type. Every builder needs it. Leave ContactBuilder unmarked, and the wrong move compiles again. On a function, the marker does nothing. If your annotation's @Target allows functions, Kotlin 2.4.21 warns applying DSL marker annotation 'FormDsl' to target 'member function' has no effect. With @Target(CLASS, TYPE), as here, it refuses outright: this annotation is not applicable to target 'member function'. Extension functions on a marked builder still work inside its block, because they resolve against the nearest receiver. The paper picture breaks in your favor here. A clerk finds a misfiled box after the form is handed in. The compiler finds it before the program ever runs. The DSL now catches misplaced words in Kotlin. Java callers never had that problem, but they have one of their own. Watch the marker catch a misplaced call Run DslMarkerDemo (or its Java twin). Both print the same OrderForm, with 250 copies. Uncomment the wrong-move block at the end of main. Predict, then run. Now remove @FormDsl from ContactBuilder only, keep it on OrderFormBuilder, and run again. Put the marker back, and inside the working customer { } block add copies = 5. Predict the message before you run. DslMarkerDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo @DslMarker @Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS, AnnotationTarget.TYPE) annotation class FormDsl data class Contact(val name: String, val phone: String) data class OrderForm(val id: String, val copies: Int, val customer: Contact, val deliverTo: Contact) @FormDsl class ContactBuilder { var name = "" var phone = "" fun build(): Contact { require(phone.isNotBlank()) { "phone required for '$name'" } return Contact(name, phone) } } @FormDsl class OrderFormBuilder(private val id: String) { var copies = 1 private var customer: Contact? = null private var deliverTo: Contact? = null fun customer(block: ContactBuilder.() -> Unit) { customer = ContactBuilder().apply(block).build() } fun deliverTo(block: ContactBuilder.() -> Unit) { deliverTo = ContactBuilder().apply(block).build() } fun build() = OrderForm(id, copies, checkNotNull(customer) { "customer missing" }, checkNotNull(deliverTo) { "delivery address missing" }) } fun orderForm(id: String, block: OrderFormBuilder.() -> Unit): OrderForm = OrderFormBuilder(id).apply(block).build() fun main() { val form = orderForm("ord-17") { copies = 100 customer { name = "Corner Bakery"; phone = "555-0142" } deliverTo { name = "Corner Bakery, back door" phone = "555-0143" this@orderForm.copies = 250 // an outer receiver needs an explicit label } } println(form) // Wrong move. Uncomment the block, predict, run. Then remove @FormDsl from both builder // classes and run it again. // orderForm("ord-18") { // customer { // name = "Corner Bakery" // deliverTo { name = "oops" } // phone = "555-0142" // } // } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l04.demo.DslMarkerDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l04/demo/DslMarkerDemo.kt DslMarkerDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo; import kotlin.Unit; /** * Java twin of DslMarkerDemo.kt. Java calls the same Kotlin DSL with Function1 lambdas. It needs no * marker: each block names its builder, so reaching the outer one means typing `f.` on purpose. */ public class DslMarkerDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { OrderForm form = DslMarkerDemoKt.orderForm("ord-17", f -> { f.setCopies(100); f.customer(c -> { c.setName("Corner Bakery"); c.setPhone("555-0142"); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); f.deliverTo(c -> { c.setName("Corner Bakery, back door"); c.setPhone("555-0143"); f.setCopies(250); // the outer builder, named explicitly return Unit.INSTANCE; }); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); System.out.println(form); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l04.demo.DslMarkerDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l04/demo/DslMarkerDemoJava.java With both markers, the build fails with 'fun deliverTo(block: ContactBuilder.() -> Unit): Unit' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver. With ContactBuilder unmarked it compiles, prints the first form, then dies with IllegalArgumentException: phone required for 'oops', thrown while building the misplaced address: the nearest receiver must carry the marker too. copies = 5 fails with 'var copies: Int' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver. With @FormDsl on both builders, only the nearest receiver is implicit inside customer { }. Reaching the outer builder needs an explicit label.

h: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers · Calling the DSL from Java, and what became of context receivers
x: A Kotlin DSL works from Java, though it isn't pretty. Every Builder.() -> Unit parameter is a Function1<Builder, Unit>, so a Java caller writes b -> { b.cover(4); ...; return Unit.INSTANCE; }. The lab's OrderFromJavaTest does just that. If Java callers matter to you, add a thin second entry point that takes a java.util.function.Consumer, Java's own interface for a block that takes one value and returns nothing. Give it a name of its own, so Kotlin callers never have to choose between two kinds of lambda: Java Booklet menu = PrintOrderKt.printBookletJava("menu", b -> { b.cover(4); b.pages("dishes", 8); // a void lambda: no Unit.INSTANCE }); Kotlin fun printBookletJava(title: String, block: Consumer<BookletBuilder>): Booklet = printBooklet(title) { block.accept(this) } // `this` is the BookletBuilder @DslMarker means nothing to Java, and Java doesn't need it. A Java lambda names its parameter, b or c, so reaching an outer builder always means typing its name. The demo's Java twin writes f.setCopies(250) inside the address block, on purpose and in plain sight. DSLs were also the main reason for an experiment you'll still meet in older code and blog posts: context receivers. A context receiver let a function demand a receiver from its surroundings, as in context(Logbook) fun hello(), so a DSL word could only be used inside the right block. Kotlin 1.6.20 shipped them as a prototype behind a compiler flag (an option you pass to the compiler), -Xcontext-receivers, and warned that the result could not be used in production code. Kotlin 2.2.0 replaced them with a new design, context parameters, as a preview. Kotlin 2.3.20 removed the old one: "Experimental context receivers are no longer supported and are replaced by context parameters." Kotlin 2.4.21 tells you so when it meets the old syntax. You get context parameters must be named. Use '_' to declare an anonymous context parameter., then unresolved reference 'write', because a context parameter is not a receiver inside the body. The old flag fails on its own, with experimental context receivers are superseded by context parameters. Remove the '-Xcontext-receivers' compiler argument and migrate to the new syntax. When you see either message, the next lesson has the fix: context parameters, stable since Kotlin 2.4.0. That leaves the limit of today's tool. A DSL and its marker check where a word is written, and only in Kotlin. Rules between values, such as the multiple of 4, still run in build() when the program runs, and Java callers get no marker at all. A check before you move on: a Java caller passes b -> { b.cover(4); b.pages("dishes", 8); } to printBooklet, with no return at the end. Predict what javac says, and why the same lambda is fine for printBookletJava. (The answer follows from the two interfaces: Function1.invoke returns a value, and Consumer.accept returns void.)

h: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers · Java and Kotlin
x: A booklet builder: Java Consumer vs Kotlin lambda with receiver Booklets.java public final class Booklets { public static Booklet booklet(String title, Consumer<BookletBuilder> block) { BookletBuilder b = new BookletBuilder(title); block.accept(b); // the builder arrives as a parameter return b.build(); } } Booklet menu = Booklets.booklet("menu", b -> { b.setNote("staple on the fold"); b.cover(4); b.pages("starters", 4); b.pages("mains", 8); }); Booklets.kt fun printBooklet(title: String, block: BookletBuilder.() -> Unit): Booklet = BookletBuilder(title).apply(block).build() // the builder is `this` inside block val menu = printBooklet("menu") { note = "staple on the fold" cover(4) pages("starters", 4) pages("mains", 8) } Both compile to the same thing: a function object that receives the builder. On the JVM, Kotlin's BookletBuilder.() -> Unit is a Function1<BookletBuilder, Unit>, and Java's Consumer<BookletBuilder> plays the same role. The difference lives only in the source. Kotlin makes the builder this, so the block reads like the booklet it describes, and nested blocks need @DslMarker to stop calls from reaching outer builders by accident. Java names the parameter on every line, which is noisier but can never send a call to the wrong builder.

h: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers · Worked example
x: Add a word to the booklet DSL with an extension function Concert programmes at the shop all have the same shape: a 4-page card cover, the content, then blank pages so the total folds. Written out each time, the padding sum gets copied by hand, and one day it gets copied wrong. Booklets.booklet("concert", b -> { b.cover(4); b.pages("programme", 10); b.pages("blank", 2); // 4 + 10 + 2 = 16, worked out by hand }); printBooklet("concert") { cover(4) pages("programme", 10) pages("blank", 2) // 4 + 10 + 2 = 16, worked out by hand } Write an extension function on the builder. It works even when BookletBuilder lives in a library you can't edit, and inside a block it reads like a word the builder always had. fun BookletBuilder.folded(name: String, contentPages: Int) { // 1. the cover and the content, as before cover(4) pages(name, contentPages) // 2. the padding, worked out once, in one place val blanks = (4 - contentPages % 4) % 4 if (blanks > 0) pages("blank", blanks) } printBooklet("concert") { folded("programme", 10) } // Java's version is a static helper that takes the builder as its first parameter, // which is exactly what the Kotlin extension compiles to static void folded(BookletBuilder b, String name, int contentPages) { b.cover(4); b.pages(name, contentPages); int blanks = (4 - contentPages % 4) % 4; if (blanks > 0) b.pages("blank", blanks); } Check where it can be called. Inside booklet { } it resolves against the nearest receiver, the BookletBuilder. Directly inside printOrder { } it doesn't compile, so nobody can pad an order instead of a booklet. printOrder("ord-17") { booklet("programme") { folded("concert", 10) } // fine folded("recital", 6) // error: candidate 'fun BookletBuilder.folded(name: String, contentPages: Int): Unit' is inapplicable because of a receiver type mismatch. } PrintOrderKt.printOrder("ord-17", o -> { o.booklet("programme", b -> { folded(b, "concert", 10); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); // fine // folded(o, "recital", 6); // error: incompatible types: OrderBuilder cannot be converted to BookletBuilder return Unit.INSTANCE; }); Run it: the programme has a 4-page cover, 10 pages of content and 2 blank pages, 16 in all, and build() accepts it because 16 folds. Whether blank pages go at the end or just before the back cover is a shop rule, and it now lives in one function you can test.

h: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers · Quiz
x: What is the JVM type of a parameter declared as block: ContactBuilder.() -> Unit? kotlin.jvm.functions.Function0<Unit> kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1<ContactBuilder, Unit> java.util.function.Consumer<ContactBuilder> A generated interface named ContactBuilderBlock The receiver becomes the first parameter, so a receiver lambda with no other parameters is a Function1. That's why Java passes c -> { ...; return Unit.INSTANCE; }. Consumer is Java's idiom for the same job, not what Kotlin compiles to. Both builders of the order form carry @FormDsl. Which of these compiles inside customer { }? deliverTo { name = "x" } copies = 5 this@orderForm.copies = 5 None of them With the marker, members of the outer OrderFormBuilder can't be reached implicitly, so deliverTo { } and copies = ... are both errors. An explicit label names the outer receiver on purpose, and that is allowed. You put @FormDsl on OrderFormBuilder but forget it on ContactBuilder. What happens to deliverTo { } written inside customer { }? It compiles and calls the outer builder's deliverTo A compile error: implicit receiver not allowed It always throws at run time, whatever the block contains A compiler warning, then it runs An outer receiver is hidden only when a nearer receiver carries the same marker. ContactBuilder carries none, so the outer deliverTo is still reachable, and the misplaced call builds a second address. Mark every builder class, or one superclass they all share. What does buildList { add(1); if (size == 1) add(2) } return, and can you add to it afterwards? [1, 2], and casting it to MutableList lets you add [1], because size was read before add It doesn't compile: size isn't available inside the block [1, 2], and it's read-only: add after a cast throws UnsupportedOperationException Inside the block this is a MutableList, so size is 1 after the first add and the second element is added. The returned list is read-only even if you cast it, which is the point of a builder: changeable while building, fixed afterwards. From the patterns track: a PrintRequest has six flat fields and no nested parts. What's the best way to build one in Kotlin? A type-safe DSL with @DslMarker A constructor with named and default arguments A Java-style builder with setters and build() A buildMap of field names to values Named and default arguments already give readable, checked construction for flat data. A DSL earns its extra classes only when the data nests, like parts under a booklet or booklets under an order.

h: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers · Key terms
x: Receiver The object a call is made on, such as sb in sb.append(x), or this inside a class. Lambda with receiver A lambda in which one object is this, so its members can be called without a prefix. Function type with receiver A type such as A.() -> B. On the JVM, the receiver is the first parameter of a Function1. Type-safe builder Builder classes plus functions that take receiver lambdas, so nested data can be written as code the compiler checks. @DslMarker Marks an annotation that labels DSL builders. Inside a block, only the nearest labeled receiver is implicit. Labeled this this@orderForm: names an outer receiver by the function that introduced it. Context receivers An experiment from Kotlin 1.6.20 that let a function require a receiver from its surroundings. Replaced by context parameters, removed in 2.3.20. What is A.() -> B? A function type with a receiver: inside the lambda, the A is this. On the JVM it's Function1<A, B>. Are StringBuilder.() -> Unit and (StringBuilder) -> Unit interchangeable? Yes. The receiver is just the first parameter: you can assign one to the other and call either as f(sb). What does @DslMarker change inside a nested block? Only the nearest receiver marked with that annotation is implicit. Outer marked receivers need an explicit this@label. Where must a DSL marker annotation go to have any effect? On every builder class (or a common superclass), on receiver types of function types, or on type aliases. On functions or properties it does nothing. What does buildList { } give you? A MutableList as this while you build, and a read-only List as the result. It's inline, so the lambda costs nothing. How does Java call fun printBooklet(title: String, block: BookletBuilder.() -> Unit)? With a Function1<BookletBuilder, Unit>: b -> { b.cover(4); ...; return Unit.INSTANCE; }. What happened to context receivers? A 1.6.20 prototype behind -Xcontext-receivers, replaced by context parameters in 2.2.0, and no longer supported since 2.3.20.

h: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers · Go deeper
x: Context parameters, the subject of the next lesson, meet implicit receivers in one tricky case, and Kotlin 2.4.21 is strict about it. Here a with block makes one printer the receiver, and a context(...) block brings a second printer into scope as a context value: Java // No Java twin: Java has neither receivers nor context parameters. // The nearest idea is two parameters of the same type, where you must pick one by name. record Printer(String name) {} static void beep(Printer printer) { System.out.println("beep from " + printer.name()); } Kotlin class Printer(val name: String) { fun beep() = println("beep from $name") } with(Printer("laser-1")) { context(Printer("laser-2")) { beep() // which printer? } } A bare beep() would go to the receiver, laser-1, which is probably not what the author meant. Kotlin 2.4.21 reports an error: call to 'fun beep(): Unit' defined in 'Printer' uses an implicit receiver shadowed by a context parameter. Make the receiver explicit using 'this' or 'contextOf<Printer>()'. The type-safe builders page calls this a warning. The compiler you run is what counts, and here it is stricter than the page. The design document for context parameters, KEEP-0367, uses the same shape of example with a cow that moos. A second detail: the TYPE target on the marker lets you mark one block without marking the class, as in fun customer(block: @FormDsl ContactBuilder.() -> Unit). That helps when the builder comes from a library you can't annotate. And when you design a DSL for others, keep each builder's list of members short. The IDE offers every public member inside the block, and every one of them is a word someone will eventually use in the wrong place.

h: Contracts and context parameters · Your own check functions teach the compiler nothing, until they carry a contract
x: The compiler smart-casts only from what it can see and never opens a function you call; a contract writes the guarantee on the outside, and the compiler believes it without checking Start with a check the print shop's app makes all the time. Some printers report their paper size and some don't, so lookupPaper("laser-1") returns a String?: a paper size such as "a4", or null, Kotlin's word for no value at all. Before printing, the app must be sure there is one. The standard library's require(paper != null) does that, and on the next line paper can be used as a plain String. Write the same check as your own function, and the compiler forgets it: Java // Java's type system doesn't track null at all, so the question never comes up static void requirePaper(String paper) { if (paper == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("paper size missing"); } requirePaper(paper); System.out.println(paper.toUpperCase()); // compiles, as everything does Kotlin fun requirePaperPlain(paper: String?) { if (paper == null) throw IllegalArgumentException("paper size missing") } requirePaperPlain(paper) println(paper.uppercase()) // error: only safe (?.) or non-null asserted (!!.) calls are allowed on a nullable receiver of type 'String?'. The feature that fails here is the smart cast: after a check such as if (paper != null), the compiler treats paper as the narrower type, String, without a cast written by you. It does that only for checks it can see in the function it is reading. It never reads the body of a function you call. In the print shop, the compiler is a clerk who trusts her own eyes. She saw the check? Then she knows. A colleague did it at another desk? Then, as far as she is concerned, it never happened. A contract is the stamp on the outside of the envelope. It is a contract { } block, written as the first statement of a function, that states a fact about the function's behavior for callers to rely on. Two kinds matter in practice. returns() implies (paper != null) says: if this function returns normally, the condition holds. callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) says: the lambda runs exactly once, during this call, and is never kept for later. The other counts are AT_MOST_ONCE, AT_LEAST_ONCE and UNKNOWN. Java // Java can't assign a local inside a lambda at all: // "local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final" String[] label = new String[1]; ContractsDemoKt.once(() -> { label[0] = "job-17"; return Unit.INSTANCE; }); Kotlin @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) fun requirePaper(paper: String?) { contract { returns() implies (paper != null) } if (paper == null) throw IllegalArgumentException("paper size missing") } @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) inline fun <T> once(block: () -> T): T { contract { callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) } return block() } val label: String once { label = "job-17" } // allowed: the block runs exactly once With the contract, requirePaper(paper) can be followed by paper.uppercase(), and the demo prints paper = A4. With once, a val declared without a value can be assigned inside the lambda, because the compiler now knows the lambda runs exactly once, before the next line. Take the callsInPlace line out, and being inline (pasted into the caller, as lesson 1 showed) isn't enough. You get 'val' cannot be reassigned. and variable 'label' must be initialized., because an inline function may still call its lambda twice, or not at all. This is how require, check, requireNotNull, run, let and apply work in the standard library. Contracts are still Experimental in Kotlin 2.4, which means the feature may still change and you must agree to use it in writing. The 2.4.0 release notes say so, and without @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) every part of the block fails with this declaration needs opt-in. No compiler flag is needed, only that annotation. The compiler smart-casts only from checks it can see. A contract writes the check on the outside of the function. So the clerk trusts the stamp. The next question is whether she should. Take each contract away Run ContractsDemo (or ContractsDemoJava, which calls the same Kotlin functions). Wrong move 1: call requirePaperPlain(paper) instead of requirePaper(paper). Predict the error, run, undo. Wrong move 2: delete the contract { callsInPlace(...) } line in once. once is still inline. Predict whether that is enough, run, undo. Wrong move 3: delete the @OptIn above isPrinted, run, undo. ContractsDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo import kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts import kotlin.contracts.InvocationKind import kotlin.contracts.contract sealed interface JobEvent data class Printed(val jobId: String, val pages: Int) : JobEvent data class Jammed(val jobId: String, val printer: String) : JobEvent fun lookupPaper(printer: String): String? = if (printer.startsWith("laser-")) "a4" else null /** Checks, but tells the compiler nothing. */ fun requirePaperPlain(paper: String?) { if (paper == null) throw IllegalArgumentException("paper size missing") } /** The same check, plus a promise: if this returns, paper was not null. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) fun requirePaper(paper: String?) { contract { returns() implies (paper != null) } if (paper == null) throw IllegalArgumentException("paper size missing") } /** A promise about the receiver: a true result means this is a Printed. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) fun JobEvent.isPrinted(): Boolean { contract { returns(true) implies (this@isPrinted is Printed) } return this is Printed } /** A promise about the lambda: it runs exactly once, during this call. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) inline fun <T> once(block: () -> T): T { contract { callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) } return block() } fun main() { val paper = lookupPaper("laser-1") requirePaper(paper) println("paper = ${paper.uppercase()}") // smart cast to String val event: JobEvent = Printed("job-7", 12) if (event.isPrinted()) println("printed ${event.pages} pages") // smart cast to Printed val label: String // a val, assigned inside a lambda once { label = "job-17" } println("label = $label") // Wrong moves, one at a time. Predict the error, run, undo. // 1. Call requirePaperPlain(paper) instead of requirePaper(paper). // 2. Delete the line `contract { callsInPlace(...) }` in once. // 3. Delete @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) above isPrinted. } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.ContractsDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l05/demo/ContractsDemo.kt ContractsDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo; import kotlin.Unit; /** * Java twin of ContractsDemo.kt. Java has no contracts. It has no null checks in the type system to * satisfy, its instanceof pattern binds a new variable instead of smart-casting, and a lambda may * not assign a local variable at all. */ public class ContractsDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { String paper = ContractsDemoKt.lookupPaper("laser-1"); ContractsDemoKt.requirePaper(paper); // to Java: a void method, nothing more System.out.println("paper = " + paper.toUpperCase()); JobEvent event = new Printed("job-7", 12); if (event instanceof Printed p) { // the pattern binds p: no promise needed System.out.println("printed " + p.getPages() + " pages"); } // String label; once(() -> { label = "x"; ... }) would not compile: // "local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final" String[] label = new String[1]; ContractsDemoKt.once(() -> { label[0] = "job-17"; return Unit.INSTANCE; }); System.out.println("label = " + label[0]); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.ContractsDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l05/demo/ContractsDemoJava.java The demo prints paper = A4, printed 12 pages and label = job-17. Move 1 fails on paper.uppercase() with the nullable-receiver error. h: Contracts and context parameters · The compiler trusts a contract and never checks it
x: A contract is a promise, and nothing checks the body against it. The design document for contracts, KEEP-139, says the compiler "trusts contracts unconditionally" and that the programmer is "responsible for writing correct and sound contracts". Proving the body right is listed as a non-goal. The demo's job events say what happened to a print job: Printed(jobId, pages) when it came out of the printer, and Jammed(jobId, printer) when it got stuck, which laser-1 does now and then. isPrinted() answers whether an event is a Printed, and its contract lets the caller read event.pages right after a true. The lying version answers true to everything, like a clerk who stamps every envelope unopened. It's very fast work. It also compiles without a single warning: Java // Java's version of the same lie: a check that always says yes, and a cast that believes it static boolean lyingIsPrinted(JobEvent e) { return true; } if (lyingIsPrinted(jammed)) { Printed p = (Printed) jammed; // ClassCastException } Kotlin @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) fun JobEvent.lyingIsPrinted(): Boolean { contract { returns(true) implies (this@lyingIsPrinted is Printed) } return true // the lie } if (jammed.lyingIsPrinted()) println(jammed.pages) // ClassCastException The smart cast to Printed lets jammed.pages compile. At run time the JVM still checks every cast it is given, and a Jammed is not a Printed: class ...Jammed cannot be cast to class ...Printed. A contract can't make a wrong value right. It only moves the cast out of your code, where a reviewer would see it, into a promise inside another function. One level down, the reason is plain. javap -c on the honest isPrinted shows a null check on the receiver, then instanceof Printed and ireturn, with no trace of the contract. The smart cast lands in the caller instead: right after the call, javap shows a checkcast Printed that nobody wrote by hand. The contract itself lives in the Kotlin metadata of the class file, extra data that only the Kotlin compiler reads when it compiles a caller. Java never sees it, and nothing in the running program enforces it. The K2 compiler (the current Kotlin compiler, the default since Kotlin 2.0) does catch some callsInPlace mistakes, as warnings. A block declared EXACTLY_ONCE but called twice gets wrong invocation kind 'EXACTLY_ONCE' for 'block: () -> Unit' specified, the actual invocation kind is 'AT_LEAST_ONCE'. A block declared in place but kept in a list gets leaked in-place lambda 'block: () -> Unit'. Nothing checks returns ... implies. The one firm rule is the position: any statement before the block is an error, contract should be the first statement. A contract is believed, never checked. Keep the body as simple as the promise. So write contracts the way the standard library does: tiny functions whose body is the condition itself, such as if (!condition) throw ..., so that a reader can check the promise at a glance. Kotlin 2.2.20 added more Experimental forms, such as contracts on property getters, returnsNotNull() and holdsIn. The last two need a second opt-in, ExperimentalExtendedContracts. Contracts tell the compiler what a function does. The next feature is about what a function needs, and it changes how arguments get passed. Make a contract lie Run LyingContractDemo. Before you do, predict: compile error, a warning, or a run-time failure? Run LyingContractDemoJava, which tells the same lie in Java with a cast, then calls the Kotlin function. Run javap -c -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.ContractsDemoKt from labs/. Read isPrinted, then find the checkcast in main right after the call to it. The compiler checks neither the promise nor the body. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) fun JobEvent.lyingIsPrinted(): Boolean { contract { returns(true) implies (this@lyingIsPrinted is Printed) } return true } fun main() { val jammed: JobEvent = Jammed("job-8", "laser-1") try { if (jammed.lyingIsPrinted()) println("printed ${jammed.pages} pages") } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("ClassCastException: ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.LyingContractDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l05/demo/LyingContractDemo.kt LyingContractDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo; /** * Java twin of LyingContractDemo.kt. Java's version of the same lie is a helper that answers true * and a cast that trusts it. In both languages the cast is the line that fails at run time. */ public class LyingContractDemoJava { static boolean lyingIsPrinted(JobEvent e) { return true; } public static void main(String[] args) { JobEvent jammed = new Jammed("job-8", "laser-1"); try { if (lyingIsPrinted(jammed)) { Printed p = (Printed) jammed; // Java makes you write the cast yourself System.out.println("printed " + p.getPages() + " pages"); } } catch (ClassCastException e) { System.out.println("ClassCastException: " + e.getMessage()); } // the Kotlin function, seen from Java: just a boolean method, the contract is gone System.out.println("Kotlin lyingIsPrinted from Java: " + LyingContractDemoKt.lyingIsPrinted(jammed)); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.LyingContractDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l05/demo/LyingContractDemoJava.java It compiles cleanly and fails at run time with ClassCastException: class workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.Jammed cannot be cast to class workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.Printed. The Java twin fails the same way, then prints Kotlin lyingIsPrinted from Java: true: to Java it's a boolean method. In javap, isPrinted is a null check on the receiver, then instanceof and ireturn, with no contract in sight. In main, the call to isPrinted is followed by checkcast Printed and getPages: that cast is the smart cast.

h: Contracts and context parameters · Context parameters: what every clerk carries for the whole shift
x: Some values must reach almost every function that handles a job. In the print shop, every decision goes into the shift's logbook, and every line in it starts with the name of the shift on duty, such as [early]. Passed by hand, the logbook and the shift show up in every signature, whether the function uses them or only hands them on: Java static boolean check(Logbook logbook, Shift shift, Job job, String printer) { logbook.write("[" + shift.name() + "] checking " + job.copies() + " copies of " + job.file() + " for " + printer); return job.copies() <= 1_000; } static String takeIn(Logbook logbook, Shift shift, Job job, String printer) { boolean ok = check(logbook, shift, job, printer); // pass both on, by hand remark(logbook, job.file() + (ok ? " accepted" : " refused") + " on the " + shift.name() + " shift"); return ok ? "ACCEPTED" : "REFUSED"; } Kotlin context(logbook: Logbook, shift: Shift) fun Job.check(printer: String): Boolean { logbook.write("[${shift.name}] checking $copies copies of $file for $printer") return copies <= 1_000 } context(logbook: Logbook, shift: Shift) fun takeIn(job: Job, printer: String): String { val ok = job.check(printer) // logbook and shift flow on by themselves remark("${job.file} ${if (ok) "accepted" else "refused"} on the ${shift.name} shift") return if (ok) "ACCEPTED" else "REFUSED" } The Kotlin version declares the two values once per function, in context(...) before fun, and stops passing them. A context parameter is a parameter the caller doesn't write. You declare it with a name and a type, and inside the function you use it by its name, as check does with logbook and shift. At each call, the compiler looks for a value of that type in the caller's surroundings and passes it for you. The value it finds is called the context argument. In the print shop, the context parameters are what every clerk on a shift carries: the shift's logbook and the shift's name. Nobody hands them over with each job. The demo hands them out once, at the start of the shift, with context(console, Shift("early")) { ... }, and inside that block every function that needs them has them. The compiler finds a context argument in one of three places. The first is an enclosing function's own context parameter, as takeIn passes its logbook and shift on to check. The second is a context(a, b) { ... } block from the standard library. The third is an implicit receiver, such as the this of a with(console) { ... } block. If you don't need a name, write _ and read the value with contextOf<Logbook>(), as the demo's remark does. Forget the context altogether, and the call doesn't compile: no context argument for 'logbook: Logbook' found. The docs describe context parameters as dependencies that are "implicitly available in the surrounding context". On the JVM nothing about them is implicit, as the figure shows. They become ordinary leading parameters: the context parameters first, then the extension receiver, then the value parameters. javap prints check(Logbook, Shift, Job, String), and Java calls it by passing all four. That's where the shift picture breaks. On the JVM the clerk is handed the logbook with every single job, and a Java caller hands it over in person, every time. The status changed fast, so here it is plainly. Context parameters replaced context receivers, the experiment from the last lesson. Context receivers arrived in Kotlin 1.6.20 as a prototype behind -Xcontext-receivers. Kotlin 2.2.0 brought context parameters as a preview, a feature you can try but which may still change, behind -Xcontext-parameters. Kotlin 2.3.20 removed context receivers. Kotlin 2.4.0 made context parameters Stable, "except for context arguments and callable references", two parts the next section covers. So in Kotlin 2.4 you need no flag, and an old build file that still passes one earns warning: the argument '-Xcontext-parameters' is redundant for the current language version 2.4. The two designs differ in one way that matters when you read older code. A context receiver had no name and acted like an extra this, so you called its members bare, as in write("hi"). A context parameter has a name, and you write logbook.write("hi"). A context parameter is an argument the compiler finds by type and passes for you. On the JVM, it is a plain leading parameter. Finding a value by type works well while there is exactly one candidate. The next section is about the other cases. Follow a context through two calls Run ContextParamsDemo. Predict the seven lines it prints for the two jobs and the last remark. Run ContextParamsDemoJava, which calls the same functions from Java with every argument spelled out. Run javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.ContextParamsDemoKt and match each parameter to the figure. Uncomment the wrong move at the end of main (a call outside any context). Predict the error, then run. ContextParamsDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo interface Logbook { fun write(line: String) } class Shift(val name: String) data class Job(val file: String, val copies: Int) /** Two context parameters, then an extension receiver, then an ordinary parameter. */ context(logbook: Logbook, shift: Shift) fun Job.check(printer: String): Boolean { logbook.write("[${shift.name}] checking $copies copies of $file for $printer") return copies <= 1_000 } /** Calls check and remark without passing the logbook or the shift: the context flows on. */ context(logbook: Logbook, shift: Shift) fun takeIn(job: Job, printer: String): String { val ok = job.check(printer) remark("${job.file} ${if (ok) "accepted" else "refused"} on the ${shift.name} shift") return if (ok) "ACCEPTED" else "REFUSED" } /** An anonymous context parameter, read with contextOf. */ context(_: Logbook) fun remark(event: String) = contextOf<Logbook>().write("NOTE $event") fun main() { val console = object : Logbook { override fun write(line: String) = println(line) } context(console, Shift("early")) { println(takeIn(Job("flyer.pdf", 250), "laser-1")) println(takeIn(Job("posters.pdf", 5_000), "laser-2")) } with(console) { remark("an implicit receiver works too") } // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict, run. // takeIn(Job("menu.pdf", 40), "laser-1") } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.ContextParamsDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l05/demo/ContextParamsDemo.kt ContextParamsDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo; /** * Java twin of ContextParamsDemo.kt. Java has no context parameters. To Java they are ordinary * leading parameters: context parameters first, then the extension receiver, then the rest. */ public class ContextParamsDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Logbook console = System.out::println; Shift shift = new Shift("java"); // takeIn(Logbook, Shift, Job, String) System.out.println(ContextParamsDemoKt.takeIn(console, shift, new Job("flyer.pdf", 250), "laser-1")); // check(Logbook, Shift, Job receiver, String printer) System.out.println(ContextParamsDemoKt.check(console, shift, new Job("posters.pdf", 5_000), "laser-2")); // remark(Logbook, String) ContextParamsDemoKt.remark(console, "called from Java"); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.ContextParamsDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l05/demo/ContextParamsDemoJava.java Each job prints [early] checking ..., then a NOTE line saying it was accepted or refused (5,000 copies is over the limit of 1,000), then ACCEPTED or REFUSED, and the last line is NOTE an implicit receiver works too. javap lists check(Logbook, Shift, Job, String), takeIn(Logbook, Shift, Job, String) and remark(Logbook, String). The wrong move fails twice: no context argument for 'logbook: Logbook' found. and the same for shift: Shift. On the JVM, context parameters are plain leading parameters, followed by the extension receiver and then the ordinary parameters. h: Contracts and context parameters · Finding values by type: ambiguity, limits, and where context parameters fit
x: The compiler finds context arguments by type, so two values of the same type in the same place are a problem. Take a smaller note that needs only a logbook, context(logbook: Logbook) fun note(line: String). Put the front desk's logbook and the back room's logbook in one block, context(front, back) { note("x") }, and the compiler won't pick one: multiple potential context arguments for 'logbook: Logbook' in scope. The docs give the rule: if several compatible values exist at the same scope level, the compiler reports an ambiguity. A nearer scope still wins over an outer one. In context(front) { context(back) { note("x") } }, the inner back is used, and the line goes to the back room. That's a reason to give context parameters specific types: a Shift class instead of a bare String, a Logbook interface instead of a (String) -> Unit function type. A bare String in a context would match any string in scope. A few things are not allowed. Constructors can't have context parameters: context parameters on primary constructors are unsupported. A property can have them only if it has no backing field, the hidden field that stores a property's value, so it must be a computed getter: property with context parameters cannot be initialized because it has no backing field. And two parts are still not stable in Kotlin 2.4. One is passing a context argument by name, as in note(logbook = front, line = "x"), an Experimental feature behind -Xexplicit-context-arguments. Without the flag, 2.4.21 says it "is only available since language version 2.5". The other is a callable reference, ::note, which fails with callable reference to 'context(logbook: Logbook) fun note(line: String): Unit' is unsupported because it has context parameters. Leave both alone for now. One change in Kotlin 2.3.20 can surprise you if you bring older preview code forward. Overload resolution, the compiler's choice between functions with the same name, used to prefer a function with context parameters over one without. The 2.3.20 notes say that rule no longer applies, so two overloads that differ only by a context may now be ambiguous. The JVM shape has two more consequences. Java can call these functions, as long as it passes every argument itself. And adding a context parameter to a public function changes its JVM signature exactly as adding any parameter does, so code compiled against the old version fails with NoSuchMethodError. Treat it as a change to the function's public API. So where do context parameters fit? Not for the long-lived helpers an object is built with: a paper catalogue or a printer driver belongs in the constructor, passed once. Context parameters suit values that belong to the current piece of work and are needed by many small functions: the shift, its logbook, the id of the job in hand, a clock that tests can stop. They are visible in every signature, and the compiler checks them, which a hidden global value never does. That's also the limit of both tools in this lesson. A contract is believed without checks, and a context argument is found by its type, never by its meaning. Keeping either honest is your job. A check to finish, with the lab's review, which needs a Logbook and a Shift: with(Logbook { println(it) }) { context(Shift("late")) { JobRequest(40, "a3", "poster.pdf").review(1_000) } }. Will it compile, and where does each context argument come from? (It compiles. The Logbook comes from the implicit receiver of with, and the Shift from the context(...) block. Each type has exactly one candidate.)

h: Contracts and context parameters · Java and Kotlin
x: A job review with a logbook: Java parameters vs Kotlin contracts and context parameters Review.java final class Review { static void ensure(boolean condition, String code, Supplier<String> message) { if (!condition) throw new JobRejected(code, message.get()); } static Decision review(Logbook logbook, Shift shift, JobRequest job, int maxCopies) { try { ensure(job.copies() <= maxCopies, "TOO_MANY", () -> "over the limit"); ensure(job.paper() != null, "PAPER_MISSING", () -> "a paper size is required"); logbook.write("[" + shift.name() + "] accepted " + job.paper().toUpperCase()); return Decision.ACCEPTED; } catch (JobRejected e) { logbook.write("[" + shift.name() + "] rejected " + e.code()); return Decision.rejected(e.code()); } } } Review.kt @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) inline fun ensure(condition: Boolean, code: String, lazyMessage: () -> String) { contract { returns() implies condition callsInPlace(lazyMessage, InvocationKind.AT_MOST_ONCE) } if (!condition) throw JobRejected(code, lazyMessage()) } context(logbook: Logbook, shift: Shift) fun JobRequest.review(maxCopies: Int): Decision = try { ensure(copies <= maxCopies, "TOO_MANY") { "over the limit" } ensure(paper != null, "PAPER_MISSING") { "a paper size is required" } logbook.write("[${shift.name}] accepted ${paper.uppercase()}") // smart cast Decision.Accepted } catch (e: JobRejected) { logbook.write("[${shift.name}] rejected ${e.code}") Decision.Rejected(e.code) } The Java version compiles because Java doesn't track null, so job.paper().toUpperCase() is accepted whether or not the check ran. The Kotlin version compiles only because the contract tells the compiler that ensure returns only when its condition holds. Kotlin's ensure is inline, so the message lambda costs nothing when the check passes, while Java builds a Supplier on every call. The logbook and the shift appear in Java's signature as two extra parameters that every caller passes on. In Kotlin they are context parameters, filled in by the compiler, and they still compile to exactly those two leading parameters, so Java can call the Kotlin review as review(logbook, shift, job, maxCopies).

h: Contracts and context parameters · Worked example
x: Replace a ThreadLocal shift name with a context parameter The app keeps the current shift's name in a ThreadLocal, a variable that holds one value per thread, so that deep helpers can write it into the logbook. It works until a helper runs on another thread, or a test forgets to set it, and then the logbook says [null]. The compiler can't help, because nothing in any signature says the value is needed. final class CurrentShift { static final ThreadLocal<String> NAME = new ThreadLocal<>(); } static void note(String line) { System.out.println("[" + CurrentShift.NAME.get() + "] " + line); // null if nobody set it } object CurrentShift { val name = ThreadLocal<String>() } fun note(line: String) { println("[${CurrentShift.name.get()}] $line") // null if nobody set it } Make the need part of the signature. The helper declares a context parameter, and so does every function that calls it, up to the place that knows the shift. class Shift(val name: String) // 1. the helper declares what it needs context(shift: Shift) fun note(line: String) = println("[${shift.name}] $line") // 2. callers in between declare it too, and never pass it by hand context(shift: Shift) fun printJob(jobId: String) { note("printing $jobId") } // Java's honest equivalent: an explicit parameter on every function in the chain record Shift(String name) {} static void note(Shift shift, String line) { System.out.println("[" + shift.name() + "] " + line); } static void printJob(Shift shift, String jobId) { note(shift, "printing " + jobId); } Open the context once, where the job comes in: the function that takes jobs at the counter. Forgetting it is now a compile error, no context argument for 'shift: Shift' found., instead of a [null] in the logbook. // 3. open the context where the shift is known fun onJobArrived(jobId: String, shiftName: String) { context(Shift(shiftName)) { printJob(jobId) } } // printJob("job-7") // error: no context argument for 'shift: Shift' found. void onJobArrived(String jobId, String shiftName) { printJob(new Shift(shiftName), jobId); } Check the price: each function in the chain gets one more JVM parameter, and nothing else. There is no ThreadLocal to look up, and the value follows the call instead of the thread, so it survives a move to another thread or into a coroutine (a task that can pause and resume, from the coroutines track).
