h: Contracts and context parameters · Key terms
x: Smart cast The compiler treating a variable as a narrower type after a check proves it, such as String? to String after != null. Contract A contract { } block that states a fact about a function's behavior for callers to rely on. The compiler trusts it. callsInPlace A contract effect: the lambda runs during the call (it is not kept for later), a given number of times. returns implies A contract effect: if the function returns (or returns a given value), a condition holds. Context parameter A parameter declared in context(...) that callers don't write; the compiler fills it by type from the surroundings. Context argument The value the compiler finds and passes for a context parameter at a call site. Opt-in @OptIn(...): your written agreement to use an Experimental API that may still change. What is a Kotlin contract? A contract { } block, the first statement of a function, that tells the compiler something it can't infer: how a lambda is called, or what a normal return implies. What does returns() implies (x != null) give the caller? A smart cast: after the call returns normally, the compiler treats x as non-null. What does callsInPlace(block, EXACTLY_ONCE) allow in the caller? Assigning a val inside the lambda, because the compiler now knows the block runs exactly once during the call. Does the compiler check a contract against the function body? No. It trusts it. A false returns(true) implies (this is Printed) compiles and fails at run time with ClassCastException. What opt-in do contracts need in Kotlin 2.4? @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class). They are still Experimental. No compiler flag is needed. Where can a context argument come from? From the caller's surroundings, matched by type: an enclosing function's context parameter, a context(a, b) { } block, or an implicit receiver such as with(x) { }. JVM signature of context(logbook: Logbook, shift: Shift) fun Job.check(printer: String): Boolean? static boolean check(Logbook, Shift, Job, String): context parameters, then the receiver, then the value parameters.

h: Contracts and context parameters · Go deeper
x: Kotlin 2.4.0 added one more Experimental contract effect, returnsResultOf(), to help the new checker for unused return values. It needs the flag -Xallow-returns-result-of, and the release notes warn that using it "produces pre-release binaries that earlier Kotlin compiler versions can't read". Keep it out of libraries that other people use. The extended contracts from Kotlin 2.2.20 behave in an interesting way on the 2.4.21 compiler. Their old flags (-Xallow-contracts-on-more-functions and friends) now print the argument '...' is redundant for the current language version 2.4., and a generic returns(true) implies (this is Ok<T>) or a holdsIn contract compiles without any flag. So they appear to be switched on by default from language version 2.3. They still need their opt-ins, though: returnsNotNull() without @OptIn(ExperimentalExtendedContracts::class) is an opt-in error. If you're moving code from context receivers, three differences bite. Context parameters must be named (or _), and a context parameter is not a receiver in the body, so write("x") becomes logbook.write("x"). this@Logbook is gone; use the name or contextOf<Logbook>(). And classes can't declare a context any more, only functions and properties. Finally, a design note. The docs list "simplified dependency injection" as one use, dependency injection being a framework that builds your objects and hands each one the helpers it needs. Treat that with care. A context parameter is resolved when the code is compiled, at each call site, from what is in scope there. A dependency injection framework wires objects when the program starts, from the whole application. They answer different questions: context parameters suit values that belong to one piece of work, and constructors suit helpers that live as long as the object.

h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · Kotlin classes are final, and frameworks that subclass them need them open
x: A proxy must subclass your class, and Kotlin classes are final; a compiler plugin changes what kotlinc emits: all-open drops final, no-arg adds a hidden empty constructor, serialization writes a serializer class Many libraries add behavior to your classes without touching your source. A framework is a library that calls your code, rather than the other way round. Many frameworks do it with a proxy: a class they generate that extends yours and overrides each method. The override does some work before and after calling your original through super. A timing proxy starts a clock, calls your method, and writes down how long it took. Write such a subclass by hand for the shop's PrintQueue, and the problem shows at once: Java class LoggedPrintQueue extends PrintQueue { // error: cannot inherit from final PrintQueue @Override public String print(String job) { return super.print(job); } } Kotlin class TimedPrintQueue : PrintQueue() { // error: this type is final, so it cannot be extended. override fun print(job: String): String = // error: 'print' in 'PrintQueue' is final super.print(job) // and cannot be overridden. } Kotlin classes and their members are final unless you write open: nobody may extend them or override their methods. That default is a good one, because a class then behaves exactly as its author wrote it. But a framework that generates subclasses hits the same wall as your hand-written one, only later, while the program starts. You could write open on every class and every method a framework touches, and nobody keeps that up for long. On the print line, a final class is a job that arrives shrink-wrapped and ready to ship. Nobody can slip a cover sheet in front of it. A compiler plugin is a jar (the zip file a Java library ships in) that the Kotlin compiler loads to change what it writes into class files. The all-open plugin "makes classes and their members open at compile time without requiring the open keyword". It does that for every class that carries an annotation you name in the build, or whose superclass does. It's the machine that takes the shrink-wrap off every job with the right note on its ticket. This lab module names workbench.kotlin.OpenForProxies for all-open, and a second marker for the plugin of the next section: // labs/kotlin/build.gradle.kts (the version, 2.4.21, is set once in the root build file) plugins { kotlin("plugin.allopen") kotlin("plugin.noarg") kotlin("plugin.serialization") } allOpen { annotation("workbench.kotlin.OpenForProxies") } noArg { annotation("workbench.kotlin.NoArgEntity") } javap on the demo's PrintQueue then shows public class and public java.lang.String print(java.lang.String), with no final in sight. What the plugin leaves alone matters just as much. Private members stay private, the field behind traySize stays private final, and the unmarked PlainHelper stays public final class. The plugin matches the annotation by its full name, package included, so an annotation with the same simple name in another package does nothing at all. An annotation is only a note on the ticket. A plugin named in the build is what acts on it. The figure puts the three plugins of this lesson side by side. Each one reads an annotation while the code compiles, and each one changes the class file in its own way: it removes a modifier, adds a constructor, or adds a whole class. The second machine is for frameworks with a different need. Open a class without writing open Run AllOpenDemo, then AllOpenDemoJava, which extends the same Kotlin class from Java. Run javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.PrintQueue from labs/. Which members are still final? Delete @OpenForProxies above PrintQueue. Predict the errors, run, and put it back. AllOpenDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo import workbench.kotlin.OpenForProxies import java.lang.reflect.Modifier /** Marked for all-open: the plugin makes the class and its members open at compile time. */ @OpenForProxies class PrintQueue { val traySize: Int = 500 fun print(job: String): String = "printed $job from a tray of $traySize sheets" private fun secret(): Int = 42 // private stays private, and final } /** Not marked: final, like every Kotlin class by default. */ class PlainHelper { fun help(): String = "help" } /** What a framework generates at build or run time: a subclass that wraps every call. */ class TimedPrintQueue : PrintQueue() { override fun print(job: String): String { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return super.print(job) } finally { println(" print took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } } fun describe(cls: Class<*>) { val methods = cls.declaredMethods.sortedBy { it.name }.joinToString { m -> val kind = when { Modifier.isPrivate(m.modifiers) -> "private" Modifier.isFinal(m.modifiers) -> "final" else -> "open" } "${m.name}:$kind" } println("${cls.simpleName}: ${if (Modifier.isFinal(cls.modifiers)) "final" else "open"} class; $methods") } fun main() { describe(PrintQueue::class.java) describe(PlainHelper::class.java) val queue: PrintQueue = TimedPrintQueue() println(queue.print("flyer.pdf")) // Wrong move. Delete @OpenForProxies above PrintQueue, predict, run. } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.AllOpenDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l06/demo/AllOpenDemo.kt AllOpenDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo; /** * Java twin of AllOpenDemo.kt. Java classes are open unless you write final, so Java can extend the * Kotlin class only because all-open removed its final. Remove the marker and javac says: * "cannot inherit from final PrintQueue". */ public class AllOpenDemoJava { static final class LoggedPrintQueue extends PrintQueue { @Override public String print(String job) { System.out.println(" log: printing " + job); return super.print(job); } } public static void main(String[] args) { PrintQueue queue = new LoggedPrintQueue(); System.out.println(queue.print("flyer.pdf")); AllOpenDemoKt.describe(PlainHelper.class); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.AllOpenDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l06/demo/AllOpenDemoJava.java The demo prints PrintQueue: open class; getTraySize:open, print:open, secret:private, PlainHelper: final class; help:final, a timing line and printed flyer.pdf from a tray of 500 sheets. Ignore the timing: one cold call measures class loading, not the proxy. javap shows public class PrintQueue, private final int traySize and private int secret(): only the field keeps its final. Without the marker, the build fails with this type is final, so it cannot be extended. and 'print' in 'PrintQueue' is final and cannot be overridden., and the Java twin would get cannot inherit from final PrintQueue. Each plugin reads an annotation at compile time and changes the class file: a modifier, a new constructor, or a whole new class. All-open compiler plugin (Kotlin docs) docs Kotlin-spring plugin (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · no-arg: an empty constructor for frameworks that build objects first, minus your initializers
x: Some libraries build your objects in two steps. A library that loads records from a database, for example, first calls a constructor with no parameters to get an empty object. Then it sets each field from the stored record. So it needs every such class to have a constructor with no parameters that isn't private. The shop's JobRow(val id: String, var pages: Int) has none. By hand, you'd add one: Java public class JobRow { private String id; private int pages; private String status = "NEW"; protected JobRow() { } // for the database library public JobRow(String id, int pages) { this.id = id; this.pages = pages; } } Kotlin class JobRow(val id: String, var pages: Int) { var status: String = "NEW" constructor() : this("", 0) // the hand-written version: invented values } The hand-written Kotlin constructor works, but it invents an empty id and zero pages, and now any Kotlin caller can create that half-made row by mistake. The no-arg plugin generates the constructor instead, for classes with an annotation you configure, here workbench.kotlin.NoArgEntity. The docs say it's "annotated with @Deprecated at the HIDDEN level, so you can call it from Java but not from Kotlin". javap -v shows both annotations on it, kotlin.Deprecated with level=HIDDEN and java.lang.Deprecated. The demo shows the two sides: Kotlin's JobRow() fails with no value passed for parameter 'id'., and Java's new JobRow() compiles, with only a deprecation note from javac. On the print line, no-arg is the machine that adds a blank form at the back of every job marked for it, so that a clerk further down can fill it in. Now the trap, and the picture shows it. The blank form is really blank. The generated constructor runs no property initializers: its bytecode is three instructions, aload_0, invokespecial Object.<init> and return, and nothing else. The option that would run them, invokeInitializers, is "disabled by default". So after new JobRow(), status holds null, even though Kotlin declared it a non-null String with the value "NEW". The first status.length in Kotlin code throws a NullPointerException. A paper form would at least have "status: NEW" printed on it. For a database library that's usually fine, because it sets every stored field right afterwards. For anything else, turn invokeInitializers on, or don't rely on initializers in those classes. A no-arg constructor skips your initializers. Don't trust a field of an object you didn't build yourself. Hibernate is the best-known such library for Java, and it follows JPA, the Java standard for mapping classes to database tables. For Hibernate and other JPA libraries, use kotlin-jpa rather than configuring no-arg yourself. It is no-arg with a preset for @Entity, @Embeddable and @MappedSuperclass, in both the javax.persistence and jakarta.persistence packages. Since Kotlin 2.3.20, the Gradle org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.jpa plugin also applies all-open with a JPA preset, so that, in the release notes' words, "lazy associations work as expected instead of causing eager loading". On older Kotlin versions you had to add all-open for those classes yourself. The first two machines change the shape of a class. The third writes code the class never had. Build an object the way a database library does Run NoArgDemo, then NoArgDemoJava. Predict blank.status before you look. Uncomment the wrong move in NoArgDemo.kt, predict, run, and comment it out again. In NoArgDemo.kt, add println(blank.status.length) at the end of main. Predict what happens, then run. NoArgDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo import workbench.kotlin.NoArgEntity /** no-arg adds a zero-argument constructor that only Java and reflection can call. */ @NoArgEntity class JobRow(val id: String, var pages: Int) { var status: String = "NEW" } fun main() { // the way a database library builds an empty object before it fills in the columns val blank = JobRow::class.java.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance() println("blank.pages = ${blank.pages}") println("blank.status is null: ${(blank.status as String?) == null}") // declared String, holds null println("normal status = ${JobRow("job-1", 12).status}") // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict, run. // val direct = JobRow() } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.NoArgDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l06/demo/NoArgDemo.kt NoArgDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo; /** * Java twin of NoArgDemo.kt. Java can call the generated constructor directly: it is hidden from * Kotlin with @Deprecated(level = HIDDEN), which javac doesn't enforce. */ public class NoArgDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { JobRow blank = new JobRow(); // compiles in Java System.out.println("blank.pages = " + blank.getPages()); System.out.println("blank.status = " + blank.getStatus()); // null: the initializer never ran System.out.println("blank.getId() = " + blank.getId()); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.NoArgDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l06/demo/NoArgDemoJava.java Both show pages = 0 and a null status, and the Java twin also prints getId() = null: the generated constructor sets nothing and runs no initializer. The Kotlin call JobRow() fails with no value passed for parameter 'id'. and the same for pages. The added line compiles, because status is declared String, and throws NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "String.length()" because the return value of "...JobRow.getStatus()" is null. No-arg compiler plugin (Kotlin docs) docs Kotlin-jpa plugin (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · kotlinx.serialization writes the serializer while your code compiles
x: The shop's app records what happens to each job as events: a job was queued, printed, jammed or cancelled. To save those events in a file, or send them to another program, the app turns each one into text and back. The usual format for that text is JSON, {"jobId":"job-1","pages":12}: names and values in braces, readable by people and by almost every programming language. Most JSON libraries on the JVM work by reflection, which means inspecting a class while the program runs: they find its constructor and its properties, and guess how to fill them. Kotlin classes make the guessing harder, with default arguments and non-null types that the JVM knows nothing about. kotlinx.serialization doesn't guess. "When you annotate a class with @Serializable, the Kotlin serialization plugin generates a KSerializer for that class." The demo's Queued gets a nested class, Queued$$serializer, that implements GeneratedSerializer<Queued> with real serialize and deserialize methods, plus Queued.serializer() on the companion object. On the print line, it's the machine that clips a slip to each job, listing its fields one by one. With the slip, anyone further down can write the job out as text and read it back. Without the plugin, Queued.serializer() is unresolved reference 'serializer'. Java // Java's usual approach, with Jackson, a JSON library that reads these annotations by reflection @JsonTypeInfo(use = JsonTypeInfo.Id.NAME, property = "type") @JsonSubTypes({ @JsonSubTypes.Type(value = Queued.class, name = "queued"), @JsonSubTypes.Type(value = Cancelled.class, name = "cancelled") }) public sealed interface JobEvent permits Queued, Cancelled { String jobId(); } String json = new ObjectMapper().writeValueAsString(events); Kotlin @Serializable sealed interface JobEvent { val jobId: String } @Serializable @SerialName("queued") data class Queued(override val jobId: String, val pages: Int, val paper: String = "A4") : JobEvent @Serializable @SerialName("cancelled") data class Cancelled(override val jobId: String, val reason: String? = null) : JobEvent private val lenient = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; explicitNulls = false } val text = lenient.encodeToString(events) // events: List<JobEvent> A sealed hierarchy, a base type whose subclasses are all known when the code compiles, is what the docs call "closed polymorphism". The plugin knows every subclass, so it can write and read a "type" field with no registration. That field is the class discriminator: it tells the reader which subclass an object is. Three details decide what the JSON looks like. The discriminator is written only when the static type, the type the compiler sees, is the base. List<JobEvent> gets "type":"queued", while Json.encodeToString(q) with q typed Queued gets none. Its value is the fully qualified class name unless you set @SerialName, so without it, moving a class to another package changes your saved files. And the default Json leaves out properties that equal their default (encodeDefaults is off), writes nulls, and rejects keys it doesn't know: Encountered an unknown key 'tray'. For saved events, that last default matters most. A newer version of the app adds a tray field, and every older reader with the default Json puts the whole file down at the first key it doesn't know. So set ignoreUnknownKeys = true. Build one Json instance and reuse it: the docs say instances "are immutable and thread-safe", and reusing one is faster. The JSON format is Stable; HOCON, ProtoBuf, CBOR and Properties are still Experimental. Pin every subtype with @SerialName, and tolerate unknown keys in data that outlives one version of the app. The generated serializer is plain bytecode, with no reflection while the program runs. Java can call it too, as the demo's twin does with Queued.Companion.serializer(). All three machines so far change the compiler's own output. A second family of tools leaves the class files alone and writes new source files instead. Read the JSON a sealed hierarchy produces Run SerializationDemo. Before you do, predict which lines will contain "type". Remove @SerialName("queued") from Queued and run again. What is the type value now? Run SerializationDemoJava, which uses the generated serializer from Java through Queued.Companion.serializer(). SerializationDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo import kotlinx.serialization.SerialName import kotlinx.serialization.SerializationException import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable import kotlinx.serialization.json.Json @Serializable sealed interface JobEvent { val jobId: String } @Serializable @SerialName("queued") data class Queued(override val jobId: String, val pages: Int, val paper: String = "A4") : JobEvent @Serializable @SerialName("cancelled") data class Cancelled(override val jobId: String, val reason: String? = null) : JobEvent private val lenient = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; explicitNulls = false } fun main() { val events: List<JobEvent> = listOf(Queued("job-1", 12), Cancelled("job-1")) val text = lenient.encodeToString(events) println(text) println("round trip equal: ${lenient.decodeFromString<List<JobEvent>>(text) == events}") val q = Queued("job-2", 1) println("static type Queued: ${Json.encodeToString(q)}") println("static type JobEvent: ${Json.encodeToString<JobEvent>(q)}") val newer = """{"type":"queued","jobId":"job-3","pages":5,"tray":"2"}""" println("lenient: ${lenient.decodeFromString<JobEvent>(newer)}") try { Json.decodeFromString<JobEvent>(newer) } catch (e: SerializationException) { println("default Json: ${e.message?.lineSequence()?.first()}") } println("generated serializer: ${Queued.serializer().javaClass.name}") } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.SerializationDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l06/demo/SerializationDemo.kt SerializationDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo; import kotlinx.serialization.json.Json; /** * Java twin of SerializationDemo.kt. The plugin's output is ordinary bytecode, so Java can use it: * Queued.Companion.serializer() returns the generated KSerializer, and Json.Default does the rest. * Java code normally uses a reflection-based JSON library instead; this shows what the plugin generated. */ public class SerializationDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Queued q = new Queued("job-2", 1, "A4"); String text = Json.Default.encodeToString(Queued.Companion.serializer(), q); System.out.println("Java, static type Queued: " + text); Queued back = Json.Default.decodeFromString(Queued.Companion.serializer(), text); System.out.println("decoded: " + back + ", equal: " + back.equals(q)); System.out.println("generated serializer: " + Queued.Companion.serializer().getClass().getName()); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.SerializationDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l06/demo/SerializationDemoJava.java The list prints [{"type":"queued","jobId":"job-1","pages":12},{"type":"cancelled","jobId":"job-1"}]: no paper (it equals its default) and no reason (null, with explicitNulls = false). The static-type Queued line has no type; the JobEvent line has one. The lenient instance ignores tray, and the default one fails with Encountered an unknown key 'tray'. Without @SerialName the type becomes workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.Queued. The Java twin prints the JSON of one Queued and the class name Queued$$serializer. Serialize polymorphic classes (Kotlin docs) docs Customize the Json instance (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · KSP and kapt write new source files instead
x: The three plugins above change the compiler's output from the inside. A second family of tools generates new source files from your annotations, the way Java's annotation processors do. An annotation processor is a program that runs during compilation, reads the annotations in your code and writes extra source files, which are then compiled with the rest. Libraries use them for code that would be dull to write by hand: mappers that copy fields from one class to another, or the glue that builds your objects and hands each one the helpers it needs. kapt runs Java annotation processors on Kotlin code. The docs say it "generates stub files from Kotlin source code and then runs the Java annotation processors on those stubs". Those stubs are Java declarations of your Kotlin classes, written only so that a Java processor can read them. The migration guide calls them "expensive": they "significantly increase build time" and lose Kotlin-specific features. KSP, Kotlin Symbol Processing, is the Kotlin-native alternative, "a source code generation framework for Kotlin". Its processors read Kotlin declarations directly, and its README says they "can run up to 2x faster" than kapt. The limits are part of the design: KSP processors "can't examine expressions or statements, and they can't modify the source code". They only add new files. On the print line, kapt and KSP aren't machines at all. They are a second shop that prints extra pages from the notes on your tickets, and the extra pages then join the job. kapt first copies every page into another language so that its workers can read it. KSP reads the original. Two version facts matter today. KSP2 "is no longer a compiler plugin" and is built on the same compiler APIs as IntelliJ IDEA. And since KSP 2.3.0, KSP1 is deprecated and "KSP version is no longer tied to the Kotlin compiler version", so a KSP release number no longer has to match your Kotlin version. My rule: use KSP whenever the library ships a KSP processor, and kapt only for processors that exist just for Java. Watch the build time when you add kapt: every module that uses it pays for the stub step on each build. Part 5 of this course is all about KSP: there you'll write processors of your own, from the first one to a small dependency injection tool. That's also the limit of this whole family of tools, plugins included. They change what the compiler writes, and your source doesn't show it. A class that reads as final is open, a constructor nobody wrote exists, and a serializer nobody typed runs. When something surprises you, javap shows what is really there, and the build file says who put it there. A check to end on, and the answer follows from how the serialization plugin works: a module depends on the kotlinx-serialization-json library but doesn't apply kotlin("plugin.serialization"). You mark a class @Serializable and call Queued.serializer(). What happens, and at which stage? (It fails at compile time with unresolved reference 'serializer'.: the annotation compiles because it lives in the library, but nobody generates the companion function.)

h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · Java and Kotlin
x: A proxy-ready service and a database row: Java as written vs Kotlin with plugins Beans.java public class SheetPlanner { // open by default in Java public int sheetsFor(int pages) { return (pages + 1) / 2; } } public class JobRecord { // open by default private String id; private int pages; private String status = "NEW"; // runs in every constructor protected JobRecord() { } // the no-arg constructor, written by hand public JobRecord(String id, int pages) { this.id = id; this.pages = pages; } } Beans.kt @OpenForProxies // all-open is configured for this annotation class SheetPlanner { fun sheetsFor(pages: Int): Int = (pages + 1) / 2 } @NoArgEntity @OpenForProxies // no-arg adds the constructor, all-open the open class JobRecord(val id: String, var pages: Int) { var status: String = "NEW" // skipped by the generated no-arg constructor } Java gets proxy-ready classes for free: classes and methods are open unless marked final, and you write the no-arg constructor yourself, where field initializers run as usual. Kotlin's defaults point the other way, so the plugins put back what frameworks need, at compile time, driven by annotations. The class files end up close to the Java ones, with one difference that bites: Kotlin's generated no-arg constructor skips property initializers unless you enable invokeInitializers, so status is null on a fresh instance, while Java's hand-written constructor runs status = "NEW".

h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · Worked example
x: Add a field to saved job events without breaking older readers Version 1 of the shop's app saves job events to a file, and a second program, the label printer, reads them with the default Json. Here are both sides, with a Java reader that uses Jackson. // Java reader with Jackson: by default it also fails on unknown properties ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper(); Printed p = mapper.readValue(line, Printed.class); @Serializable @SerialName("printed") data class Printed(override val jobId: String, val pages: Int) : JobEvent val event = Json.decodeFromString<JobEvent>(line) // the default Json: strict Version 2 adds a tray field, and the app is updated first. The label printer, still on version 1, now fails on every new line, because unknown keys "result in an error" by default. // version 2 writes {"type":"printed","jobId":"job-7","pages":12,"tray":"2"} Json.decodeFromString<JobEvent>(v2) // SerializationException: ... Encountered an unknown key 'tray' at path: $ mapper.readValue(v2, Printed.class); // Jackson: UnrecognizedPropertyException, unless FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES is turned off Configure the reader once, in one shared instance: tolerate new keys, keep every @SerialName stable, and give new fields defaults so that old lines still decode. // 1. one instance, reused: immutable and thread-safe val events = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; explicitNulls = false } // 2. a new field gets a default, so version 1 lines without it still decode @Serializable @SerialName("printed") data class Printed(override val jobId: String, val pages: Int, val tray: String? = null) : JobEvent ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper() .configure(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, false); Check the other direction. A version-1 reader that doesn't know a new subtype, say "type":"recycled", still fails, and it should: ignoreUnknownKeys covers fields, not types. When you add a subtype, update the readers before the writers.

h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · Lab
x: A serializable event hierarchy and proxy-ready classes labs/kotlin/src/main/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l06/JobEvents.kt labs/kotlin/src/main/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l06/Beans.kt labs/kotlin/src/main/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/Annotations.kt ./gradlew :kotlin:test --tests 'workbench.kotlin.l06.*' Read Annotations.kt and the two plugin lines in labs/kotlin/build.gradle.kts. The annotations do nothing by themselves; the plugins look for their names. Run the tests. All seven fail. In JobEvents.kt, add @Serializable and @SerialName (TODO 1), create the shared Json (TODO 2), and write encodeEvents and decodeEvents (TODOs 3 and 4). In Beans.kt, mark SheetPlanner with @OpenForProxies (TODO 5), and JobRecord with @NoArgEntity and @OpenForProxies (TODO 6). Run until all seven pass, including EventsFromJavaTest. Then run javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/main workbench.kotlin.l06.JobRecord and find the constructor nobody wrote. encodeToString and decodeFromString are extension functions with reified types: json.encodeToString(events) and json.decodeFromString<List<JobEvent>>(text), or let the return type infer it. The "type" field appears because the static type is List<JobEvent>, the sealed base. You don't configure it. Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; explicitNulls = false } covers both rules. Leave encodeDefaults alone: off is the default, and the test expects paper to be left out. The marker annotations live in package workbench.kotlin: import workbench.kotlin.OpenForProxies and workbench.kotlin.NoArgEntity. All seven tests in PluginsTest and EventsFromJavaTest pass. By the end you can say what each of the three plugins changes in the class file, configure all-open for the annotations your framework uses, avoid the no-arg initializer trap, and serialize a sealed event hierarchy with stable type names.

Write a sealed ParcelEvent with two subtypes, ParcelWeighed(parcelId, grams) and ParcelSent(parcelId, sentAtEpochMs), serialized with the stable type names parcel_weighed and parcel_sent, and a shared Json that tolerates new fields. h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · Quiz
x: The build configures all-open with annotation("com.shop.Proxied"). A class is marked with com.shop.legacy.Proxied, an annotation with the same simple name in another package. What does javap show for the class? public class, with open methods public final class: the plugin matches the full name, package included A compile error: the plugin rejects the unknown annotation public class, but every method is still final all-open looks for the fully qualified names listed in the build. com.shop.legacy.Proxied matches none of them, so the plugin leaves the class alone, and it stays final like every Kotlin class. A framework preset that still lists an old package name leaves classes closed in exactly this way. A class built with the default no-arg settings has var status: String = "NEW". What does status hold right after a database library calls the generated constructor, before it sets any field? "NEW" "" null, even though the type is String Nothing: the constructor throws because status isn't set The generated constructor doesn't run property initializers unless invokeInitializers is enabled, and it is off by default. Its bytecode only calls Object.<init>. The library normally overwrites the field from the stored row; any other code that reads it first sees null in a non-null property. Queued is a @Serializable @SerialName("queued") subclass of a sealed JobEvent, and q is typed Queued. What does Json.encodeToString(q) produce? {"jobId":"job-2","pages":1}: no discriminator, because the static type isn't the base {"type":"queued","jobId":"job-2","pages":1} The fully qualified class name in a "type" field A SerializationException: sealed subtypes must be encoded as the base The docs say the class discriminator is included only when the base class is the static type. Encode q as a JobEvent (or inside a List<JobEvent>) to get "type":"queued". The fully qualified name appears only when there is no @SerialName. Your project needs generated mappers from an annotation processor that exists only for Java. Which tool runs it on Kotlin classes? KSP all-open kotlinx.serialization kapt kapt generates Java stubs from your Kotlin sources and runs Java annotation processors on them. KSP runs KSP processors, which a Java-only processor isn't. all-open and kotlinx.serialization change the compiler's output and don't run processors at all. From the patterns track: a framework proxy wraps SheetPlanner, and inside SheetPlanner, plan() calls this.sheetsFor(), which has a timing interceptor. With a proxy that forwards to a separate target object, does the interceptor run for that inner call? Yes, because all-open made sheetsFor open No: this is the target, so the call never goes through the proxy Only if sheetsFor is private Only when the class is written in Java all-open makes the proxy possible; it doesn't route calls through it. A forwarding proxy calls the target, and inside the target this.sheetsFor() is a plain call on the target. That's the self-invocation trap from the Decorator and Proxy lesson, and it's the same in Java and Kotlin.

h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · Explain it back

h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · Key terms
x: Compiler plugin A jar the Kotlin compiler loads to change what it writes into class files, usually driven by annotations. Proxy A class a framework generates that extends yours and overrides methods to add work before and after each call. all-open Compiler plugin that makes marked classes and their members open, without writing open. no-arg Compiler plugin that adds a zero-argument constructor, hidden from Kotlin, for frameworks that need one. kotlin-jpa no-arg with a preset for JPA annotations; since Kotlin 2.3.20 its Gradle plugin also applies all-open for them. Class discriminator The "type" field that tells a JSON reader which subclass an object is. KSP Kotlin Symbol Processing: a framework for processors that read Kotlin declarations and generate new source files. kapt Runs Java annotation processors on Kotlin code by first generating Java stubs of the Kotlin classes. Why does a Kotlin class need all-open (or open) before a framework can proxy it? Kotlin classes and members are final by default, and those proxies are generated subclasses that override your methods. What does all-open leave unchanged? Private members, backing fields (still final), and every class without a configured annotation. How does all-open decide which classes to open? By the fully qualified names of the annotations listed in the build (or in a preset), on the class or one of its superclasses. A same-named annotation in another package doesn't count. What does no-arg generate, and who can call it? A zero-argument constructor marked @Deprecated(level = HIDDEN): Java and reflection can call it, Kotlin code can't. Does no-arg's constructor run property initializers? Not by default (invokeInitializers is off), so a non-null property can hold null on a fresh instance. When does kotlinx.serialization write the "type" discriminator? Only when the static type is the polymorphic base, such as List<JobEvent>. Its value is the @SerialName, or else the fully qualified class name. KSP vs kapt in one line each? kapt runs Java annotation processors on generated Java stubs (slow builds). KSP processors read Kotlin declarations directly, up to 2x faster, and can only add files.

h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · Go deeper
x: The presets inside the 2.4.21 all-open plugin, read from the plugin's own classes, say more than the docs page. spring lists @Component, @Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable, @SpringBootTest and also org.springframework.validation.annotation.Validated, which the docs page leaves out. micronaut lists four of that framework's annotations for adding behavior to methods, jpa lists Entity, Embeddable and MappedSuperclass in both packages, and quarkus lists only the two old javax scopes. When a framework moves its annotations to a new package, presets lag behind, and listing annotations by name is the only setting you control. On the command line the same plugins take -P options, which helps when you test an idea with plain kotlinc: -Xplugin=<allopen jar> -P plugin:org.jetbrains.kotlin.allopen:annotation=workbench.kotlin.OpenForProxies, and for no-arg -P plugin:org.jetbrains.kotlin.noarg:invokeInitializers=true. Maven users add <plugin>all-open</plugin> to the Kotlin Maven plugin with the kotlin-maven-allopen dependency. Since Kotlin 2.3.20, kotlin-maven-noarg also includes kotlin-maven-allopen. kotlinx.serialization has more for data that changes over time. Open polymorphism, where subclasses live in other modules and the compiler can't see them all, needs a SerializersModule that registers each one. classDiscriminator renames the "type" field if your data already uses that name. coerceInputValues turns invalid values, such as an unknown enum constant, into the property's default instead of failing. And @JsonIgnoreUnknownKeys (Experimental) relaxes unknown keys for one class instead of a whole Json instance. Finally, the generated code is plain JVM bytecode, fast and free of reflection while the program runs. That also makes it a good fit for native images, programs compiled ahead of time into a single executable, where reflection needs extra setup. The startup track covers why.

h: Capstone: a typed event library
x: A sealed event model, a typed event bus and an API that reads well from Kotlin and from Java. In three sittings, you build one working library: a small, typed event library for Pedal Post, the bike courier in the small town of the Design patterns track. An event library lets one part of a program announce that something happened, and lets other parts react without the announcer knowing who is listening. A rider's scanner announces "PP-7781 collected, 2.5 kg"; the tracking page, the load board and the text sender each hear it and do their own job. Typed means the compiler knows the kind of every event, so a handler written for deliveries can never be handed anything else. Lesson 1 builds a sealed model of parcel events, with value classes for tracking numbers and weights, behind one parse function at the door that turns raw scanner fields into an event or a note saying why not. Lesson 2 builds the bus: it routes each event to the handlers of its kind and every wider kind, takes one general handler for any subscription, survives a failing handler, and runs a middleware chain and a timing decorator. Lesson 3 adds an API that reads well from both sides, a subscription DSL for Kotlin and overloads, statics and a facade for Java, and ends Part 3 with a design review. The capstone draws on the whole of Part 3 and calls back its pictures as it goes: the fruit shop's storeroom from the Generics track, the recipe book from Functional programming, the small town and its corner shop from Design patterns, the town library's forms from Modern Java data modeling, and the print shop from Advanced Kotlin. There is little new theory. Each design choice names the lesson that taught it, so you can go back when a step doesn't stick. The labs live in labs/events, one package per lesson (workbench.events.l01 to l03), and each lab starts from the previous lab's solution, so you can begin at any sitting. Lessons 1 and 2 are written in Kotlin; lesson 3 adds a Java class, SupportDesk, and a Java test that uses the library the way a Java team would. From labs/, run ./gradlew :events:test --tests 'workbench.events.lNN.*' until it passes, ./gradlew :events:solutionTest to check the reference answers, and ./gradlew :events:demo -Pmain=<class> for the Try-it programs, each in Kotlin and in Java. The tests use kotlin-reflect for two checks (sealedSubclasses and the variance of Handler); the library itself doesn't need it. Install JDK 25; the labs compile with release 21 and Kotlin 2.4.21. Parse raw input once, at the door, into a sealed model; return Ok or Rejected and never throw. Behind the door, handlers trust the types. A when with no else over your own sealed type turns a new event type into a list of compile errors. A sealed middle level lets one branch, or one handler, stand for its leaves. Value classes give ids and weights their own types at no cost where they're used as themselves, and their init blocks make every instance valid. One field only, so a Weight is whole grams, and other units are converted at the door. Route each event to its class and then to its event supertypes, nearest first, from a per-class cache. Declare handlers in, and store them behind casting adapters. The sign-up sheet's rules hold: return a handle, catch and report each handler's exception, and loop over a copy-on-write snapshot. Delivery stays synchronous, so keep handlers fast. Work for every event once is a middleware chain built by a fold, where order is behavior. Work for one handler is a decorator. Test time with a fake ticker. The subscription DSL collects and then commits, uses a reified on<E> with crossinline, and marks its builders with @DslMarker so nested blocks can't reach the wrong one. Give Java Class<E> overloads, @JvmOverloads, @JvmStatic, @JvmField, @file:JvmName and a facade that builds the value classes, and test it all from Java. In the design review, defend forced choices by their mechanism, and write down each judgment call with the condition that would undo it. The bus lives in memory: anything that must survive a crash needs storage of its own.

h: Capstone: a typed event library: cheat sheet
x: The library in one picture A rider's scanner sends raw fields: type=collected, parcelId=PP-7781, grams=2500. At the door, parseEvent turns them into Parsed.Ok(ParcelCollected(PP-7781, 2.5 kg)), or into a note such as Parsed.Rejected("grams is not a whole number: '2.5'"). Then bus.publish(event) calls the handlers of ParcelCollected first, then those of Handover, then those of ParcelEvent, each key in subscription order, and returns how many it called. Picture it: the pictures behind the design Picture it Where it came from What it became in the library a form with a fixed set of boxes to tick Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check sealed interface ParcelEvent, with Handover sealed one level down the clerk working down a printed sheet, one line per box Pattern matching with switch and record patterns a when or switch with no else order slips on a spike, and a note that something happened Observer and Command events named in the past tense: handlers react, never refuse a printed recipe book: new editions, never crossings-out Immutable data and a functional core data classes of vals; copy() runs init again units on numbers at the print shop's parcel desk Value classes and what they compile to ParcelId and Weight: a swapped argument doesn't compile the clerk at the door who copies each letter onto the right form Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla parseEvent(fields): Parsed, the only place raw fields are read a note saying what went wrong, not a thrown pan Errors as values: sealed results, Result and Either Parsed.Rejected(reason): the door never throws a recipe card: same ingredients, same pancakes Pure functions: the idea everything else builds on parseEvent and summary, tested with plain values the board of delivery bells by the back door Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus EventBus, keyed by class, walking each event's supertypes the labelled box "Box of ___" Generics from zero: type parameters Handler<E>, KClass<E>, Subscription the compost bin, a fine apple bin Contravariance with in: consumers Handler<in E>; Java sees Handler<? super E> the travel plug, and the receptionist who checks each call Adapter and Facade; Decorator and Proxy the adapter that stores a narrow handler and casts each event with type.cast the "ring me when the bread arrives" sheet Observer and Command Subscription handles, one try per handler, a copy-on-write snapshot a complaint passed along a line of people State and Chain of Responsibility middleware folded into one chain; order is behavior gift paper around a teapot Decorator and Proxy timed(...): the same Handler<E>, plus timing the print shop's order form, section by section Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers bus.subscriptions { on<E> { }; timed("load") { } } each section offers only its own boxes the same lesson @DslMarker on both builder classes the box whose label wore off Star projection: when you don't know the type List<Pending<*>> inside the builder the clerk who copies the label onto a note before it's torn off Type erasure and reified type parameters subscribe<E> and on<E>; Java gets a Class<E> overload instead steps sealed in an envelope for the night shift Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns crossinline handler: (E) -> Unit in on<E> the hotel reception desk Adapter and Facade Events.collected(String, long): Java's side door, with every check still run Where the pictures break: a paper form can be filled in later, but an event is a fact that already happened. A real clerk at the door may guess what a messy letter meant; parseEvent must never guess, so a missing weight is a rejection, not a zero. And a bell board rings everyone at once, while this bus calls one handler after another on the publisher's thread. The model (lesson 1) [ ] Every event is a past-tense fact in one sealed hierarchy: ParcelEvent, with a sealed Handover in the middle for collections and deliveries. [ ] Leaves are data classes (records in Java): final, compared by value, checked in init. [ ] Ids and weights are value classes with init checks: ParcelId (PP- and 4 to 12 digits) and Weight (whole grams). [ ] Every operation is a when or switch with no else over your own sealed type. [ ] One edge function, parseEvent(fields): Parsed, returns Ok or Rejected and never throws. The rules live in the constructors; the parser turns their IllegalArgumentException into Rejected. [ ] A Rejected scan is set aside with its reason, and never retried. Java sealed interface ParcelEvent permits ParcelBooked, DeliveryFailed, Handover { ParcelId parcelId(); } sealed interface Handover extends ParcelEvent permits ParcelCollected, ParcelDelivered { Weight weight(); } record ParcelCollected(ParcelId parcelId, Weight weight) implements Handover {} Kotlin sealed interface ParcelEvent { val parcelId: ParcelId } sealed interface Handover : ParcelEvent { val weight: Weight } data class ParcelCollected(override val parcelId: ParcelId, override val weight: Weight) : Handover The bus (lesson 2) [ ] Registry keyed by KClass. Dispatch keys are the event's class, then its event supertypes, nearest first, cached per class with computeIfAbsent. Java reflection (getInterfaces, getSuperclass) is enough: no kotlin-reflect. [ ] Delivery order is a promise: the most specific key first, then wider ones; within a key, subscription order. Test it. [ ] fun interface Handler<in E : ParcelEvent>: a consumer, so in. Java sees Handler<? super E>. [ ] Store each handler behind an adapter: Handler<ParcelEvent> { e -> handler.handle(type.cast(e)) }. [ ] subscribe returns a Subscription : AutoCloseable that removes exactly that adapter. Closing twice is harmless. [ ] catch (e: Exception) around each handler, reported to an injected ErrorHandler with the event. [ ] Each key's handlers in a CopyOnWriteArrayList: delivery loops over a snapshot, a handler may unsubscribe itself, and publishers need no lock. [ ] Work for every event once (logging, dropping repeats) is middleware: a chain built once by foldRight over a copy of the list. Order is behavior. [ ] Work for one handler (timing) is a decorator: the same Handler<E>, recorded in finally, with the clock injected as a Ticker. Java <E extends ParcelEvent> AutoCloseable subscribe(Class<E> type, Handler<? super E> handler) { Handler<ParcelEvent> adapter = event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)); List<Handler<ParcelEvent>> list = registry.computeIfAbsent(type, t -> new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>()); list.add(adapter); return () -> list.remove(adapter); } Kotlin fun <E : ParcelEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription { val adapter = Handler<ParcelEvent> { event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)) } val list = registry.computeIfAbsent(type) { CopyOnWriteArrayList() } list += adapter return Subscription { list.remove(adapter) } } The API (lesson 3) [ ] The DSL collects in on and subscribes in commit, after the block: a block that throws subscribes nothing, and one handle closes everything, in reverse. [ ] inline fun <reified E> on(crossinline handler: (E) -> Unit): crossinline because the lambda runs inside a Handler object. [ ] @DslMarker on the builder classes, and a check(!committed) for calls from inside handlers, which the marker can't see. [ ] Every reified or KClass function has a Class<E> overload that delegates with type.kotlin. [ ] @JvmOverloads on constructors with defaults, @JvmStatic on object members, @JvmField on companion constants, @file:JvmName on files of top-level functions. [ ] A facade (Events.collected(String, long)) that builds the value classes, so Java input is checked. Never @JvmName straight past init. [ ] Callbacks are fun interfaces with void or int methods, and the Java DSL entry takes a Consumer: no return Unit.INSTANCE. [ ] One Java test in the Kotlin module's own build. Kotlin as written What Java gets Fix a reified function invisible (synthetic) a Class<E> overload a KClass<E> parameter JvmClassMappingKt.getKotlinClass(X.class) a Class<E> overload default arguments the all-defaults and full constructors only @JvmOverloads an object member, a companion val INSTANCE.f(), Companion.getX() @JvmStatic, @JvmField value classes in a data class a private constructor, mangled getters such as getWeight-RqKWbHU() a facade with plain types Design review questions Question Forced, or a judgment call? No else on sealed whens? forced: Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check Handler<in E>? forced: Contravariance with in: consumers Class<E> overloads? forced: Type erasure and reified type parameters Value classes plus a Java facade? judgment: undo if most callers are Java Weight in whole grams, no unit field? judgment: keep, and convert any other unit at the door Synchronous delivery, in memory? judgment: keep inside one program; events that must survive a crash need storage of their own An unbounded DropDuplicates? judgment: undo; bound it, or let the handler keep its own record

h: Capstone: a typed event library: track quiz
x: A collection arrives as raw fields with grams = "0". Where is it refused, and what does the code that reads scans see? In the load board, which throws, and the reading loop stops In ParcelCollected's init; parseEvent returns Rejected with that message In parseEvent, by its own grams > 0 check, which returns null Nowhere: a zero-gram collection is valid The rule lives in the constructor, once. Weight(0) is a valid weight, but a collection must weigh something, so ParcelCollected's init refuses it. The door calls the constructor and turns its IllegalArgumentException into a Rejected, which is set aside before any handler acts. summary, changesHands and a label for the tracking page are whens over ParcelEvent with no else. Someone adds ParcelLost : ParcelEvent. What finds every place that must change? A NoWhenBranchMatchedException the first time a lost parcel is published A code search for ParcelCollected The compiler: each of those whens fails until it handles lost parcels Nothing: when falls through to the last branch Exhaustiveness is checked at compile time, and with no else the new subtype is missing from each when. An else anywhere would swallow it silently. The exception only happens when code compiled against the old model meets the new type. Why is Weight a value class of whole grams with no unit field? Because a JVM value class can hold exactly one field, and Pedal Post weighs in grams; other units are converted at the door Because value classes can't hold a String Because Java callers can't read two fields Because data classes can't check their values in init Until Valhalla, Kotlin's @JvmInline value class has one property. A weight plus a unit would be a data class, one object per weight. The design review keeps the choice, because the parser can turn pounds into grams once, and nothing behind the door ever sees a pound. Subscribed in this order: tracking under ParcelEvent, handovers under Handover, load then texts under ParcelCollected. You publish a collection. In what order do they run? tracking, handovers, load, texts load, texts, handovers, tracking texts, load, handovers, tracking load, handovers, tracking, texts Keys are visited nearest first: ParcelCollected, then Handover, then ParcelEvent. Within one key, handlers run in subscription order, so load comes before texts. The first option is subscription order across keys, which the bus doesn't use. In a Java class, Handler<ParcelEvent> tracking = e -> ...; and then bus.subscribe(ParcelCollected.class, tracking); compiles. Why? Because Java generics are covariant Because subscribe casts its argument Because ParcelCollected.class is a Class<ParcelEvent> Because Handler is declared in, so kotlinc writes Handler<? super E> into the Java signature Declaration-site in becomes a ? super wildcard in parameter types. A handler of any event can then stand in for a handler of collections, in Java as in Kotlin, like the compost bin that makes a fine apple bin. Java generics are invariant without a wildcard. Of three handlers for a collection, the second throws IllegalStateException. What does publish return, and what happens to the error? 3; the bus reports it, with the event, to its ErrorHandler, and the third handler still runs 1; publish stops at the failure and rethrows 2; the failing handler isn't counted and the error is dropped It throws, after running all three Each call is wrapped in its own try, so one failure can't starve the rest, and publish counts the handlers it called. The bus doesn't decide what an error means: the injected ErrorHandler does. You want to know how long the texts handler takes per event. Where does the timing go? A middleware, first in the list Inside publish, around deliver A decorator around the texts handler: the same Handler<E>, timed in finally In the ErrorHandler Middleware and publish see one delivery to all of an event's handlers, so they'd add the load board's time to the texts' time. A decorator wraps exactly one handler, and with an injected Ticker its numbers are testable. A bus.subscriptions { ... } block declares two handlers and then throws because a setting is missing. How many handlers are subscribed afterwards? Two, and the caller has no handle to remove them One Two, removed again by a finally in the block None: the builder only subscribes after the block returns on only records a pending subscription, and commit runs after the block. So a failing block leaves the bus untouched, and a successful one returns a single handle for everything it declared. Java code needs a delivery event for 2.5 kg on PP-7781. Which line compiles and checks its values? new ParcelDelivered(new ParcelId("PP-7781"), new Weight(2500)) Events.delivered("PP-7781", 2_500) new ParcelDelivered("PP-7781", 2500L) ParcelDelivered.Companion.of("PP-7781", 2500) The value classes' constructors and the data class's constructor are private to Java: javac reports cannot find symbol or has private access. The @JvmStatic facade takes plain values and builds the value classes, so their init checks run. There is no Companion.of in this library. Pedal Post starts taking parcels from a partner courier whose scanners report weights in pounds. Which change comes first? Convert pounds to grams in the parser at the door, and leave Weight as it is Make Weight a data class of an amount and a unit Add an else branch to every when, so the new unit can't break the build Key the bus by unit as well as by class The door is where outside data is turned into the model, so a foreign unit is converted there, once. Every handler behind it keeps working in grams. A unit field would cost an object per weight and push the conversion into every handler, and an else or a new bus key has nothing to do with units.

h: A sealed event model · What we'll build: an event library for a bike courier, starting with the model
x: A tour of the event library: a sealed model behind one parsing edge, a typed bus, and an API for Kotlin and Java Over three sittings, we'll build one small library, a piece of code that other parts of a program call. It's an event library. One part of a program announces that something happened, and other parts react, without the announcer knowing who is listening. The scanner code says "PP-7781 was collected" once. The tracking page, the load board and the text sender each hear it and do their own job. "Typed" means the compiler knows exactly which kind of event each one is, so a handler written for deliveries can never be handed a failed delivery by mistake. And everything happens inside one running program, with no network in between. The three sittings build the library from the inside out. This one writes the model: the types for every event Pedal Post's program can see. The next one builds the bus, the part that carries each event to everyone who signed up for it. It's the board of bells from Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus, grown up. The last one gives the library an API, the set of functions its callers use, that reads well from Kotlin and from Java. Each lab starts from the previous lab's solution, so you can pick up at any sitting. Let's start with what goes wrong without a model. The demo has three handlers, small functions that each react to a scan, and each one reads the scanner's raw fields for itself. Here is the heart of the load board: Java static void loadBoard(Map<String, String> fields) { if ("collected".equals(fields.get("type"))) { long grams = Long.parseLong(fields.get("grams")); // parsing, deep inside a handler onTheBikeGrams += grams; } // ... and the same for "delivered", with a minus } Kotlin fun loadBoard(fields: Map<String, String>) { if (fields["type"] == "collected") { val grams = fields.getValue("grams").toLong() // parsing, deep inside a handler onTheBikeGrams += grams } // ... and the same for "delivered", with a minus } Three scans go in, and the demo printed: tracking collected PP-7781 load +2500 g, on the bike: 2500 g tracking delivered PP-7781 load -2500 g, on the bike: 0 g tracking collected PP-7782 FAILED java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "2.5" texts sent: 0 Two bugs came out of three scans. The third scan says "grams": "2.5", because the rider weighed that parcel in kilograms. The scanner sent it exactly as typed. It always does; the scanner has no opinions. So the load board threw NumberFormatException halfway through its job, and by then the tracking page had already told the world that PP-7782 was on a bike. And no text went out at all, because the text handler compares the type with "deliver", one letter short, and nothing ever complains. Each handler parses and checks for itself, so each one can fail in its own way, and the compiler can't see any of it. The fix comes in three pieces, one per section, and Part 3 has already given us each one. A closed list of event types, so the compiler knows every case: the form with a fixed set of boxes to tick, from Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check. Small types for ids and weights, so a bad value can't even be built: the units on numbers from Value classes and what they compile to. And one function at the door that copies each scan onto the right form, or hands back a note saying what was wrong: the clerk at the door from Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla. Behind that door, no handler ever reads a raw field again. Before you run the demo, predict which scan fails, in which handler, and how many texts go out. Watch the raw-fields version fail Read StringlyDemo.kt (or StringlyDemoJava.java). Write down which scan fails, in which handler, and how many texts go out. Run it with the command below. Find the line that shows the tracking page listed the bad scan before the load board failed. Fix the typo in texts and run again. Then answer: where would a check have to go so that PP-7782 never reaches tracking at all? h: A sealed event model · A sealed interface lists every kind of parcel event
x: Here is the model. Each event is a fact about one parcel, named in the past tense, and that naming is a decision. Observer and Command put requests on order slips, "restock rye bread, 12 loaves", which can wait, be done or be crossed out. An event is a different kind of paper. It says something already happened, so a handler can't refuse it, only react to it. Java sealed interface ParcelEvent permits ParcelBooked, DeliveryFailed, Handover { ParcelId parcelId(); } record ParcelBooked(ParcelId parcelId, Weight weight) implements ParcelEvent {} record DeliveryFailed(ParcelId parcelId, FailReason reason) implements ParcelEvent {} sealed interface Handover extends ParcelEvent permits ParcelCollected, ParcelDelivered { Weight weight(); } record ParcelCollected(ParcelId parcelId, Weight weight) implements Handover {} record ParcelDelivered(ParcelId parcelId, Weight weight) implements Handover {} Kotlin sealed interface ParcelEvent { val parcelId: ParcelId } data class ParcelBooked(override val parcelId: ParcelId, val weight: Weight) : ParcelEvent data class DeliveryFailed(override val parcelId: ParcelId, val reason: FailReason) : ParcelEvent sealed interface Handover : ParcelEvent { val weight: Weight } data class ParcelCollected(override val parcelId: ParcelId, override val weight: Weight) : Handover data class ParcelDelivered(override val parcelId: ParcelId, override val weight: Weight) : Handover Read it from the top. A sender booked a pickup, and nothing has moved yet. A delivery failed, with a reason such as NOBODY_HOME. And a handover is the moment a parcel passes from one pair of hands to another: collected from the sender, or delivered at the door. sealed closes the list of direct subtypes, the types that implement an interface or extend a class directly. Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check pictured it as a request form with a fixed set of boxes to tick. In Kotlin, the subtypes must sit in the same package and the same module, the set of files the compiler builds together; Java names them after permits. Each leaf is a data class in Kotlin and a record in Java: a final class that holds its values and compares by them. Its properties are vals of types that never change, so an event is like a page in the printed recipe book of Immutable data and a functional core: a correction is a new edition, made with copy(), never a crossing-out. That matters in lesson 2, where every handler gets the very same object. So every branch of the tree ends at a leaf, except Handover, which is sealed again one level down. That middle level is a decision we'll use in lesson 2: a handler for Handover will hear about collections and deliveries, and nothing else. The payoff is the exhaustive when: a when, or a Java switch, with a branch for every subtype and no else. The compiler checks it against the list, the way the clerk in Pattern matching with switch and record patterns worked down a printed sheet with one line per box: Java static boolean changesHands(ParcelEvent e) { return switch (e) { case Handover h -> true; // one case covers both leaves case ParcelBooked b -> false; case DeliveryFailed f -> false; }; } Kotlin fun changesHands(e: ParcelEvent): Boolean = when (e) { is Handover -> true // one branch covers both leaves is ParcelBooked, is DeliveryFailed -> false } Now a new kind of event arrives. Parcels get lost now and then, and nobody plans for it, which is exactly why the compiler should. Add ParcelLost to ParcelEvent, and every such when stops compiling: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is ParcelLost' branch or an 'else' branch. State and Chain of Responsibility said it about an order's states: the compiler writes your to-do list. An else throws that list away. The new event quietly takes the else branch wherever nobody went back to look, and the demo's label function files every lost parcel under "other". A sealed type with no else turns a new case into a list of compile errors. Leave the else out. One gap stays open when the program runs. Exhaustiveness is checked when a file is compiled. If code compiled against the old model meets a ParcelLost built by newer code, Kotlin throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException and Java throws MatchException. In our library that can't happen by surprise, because events arrive as raw fields and pass the door first. An old program refuses the unknown type there, as the last section shows. In ExhaustiveDemoJava.java, uncomment the record and add ParcelLost to the permits list of ParcelEvent. Run the Java twin. Put both files back the way they were. h: A sealed event model · Value classes give every number its unit
x: Look at this parcel: RawParcel("PP-7781", 40, 2500). Is it 40 grams and 2,500 centimetres long, or the other way round? The demo's RawParcel takes two Longs, so a swapped call compiles, and the program believes in a 40-gram parcel 25 metres long. Value classes and what they compile to started at the print shop's parcel desk, where every number carries its unit: 500 sheets, 2,500 grams. A value class, a class that wraps exactly one value and is a type of its own to the compiler, puts that unit into code: Java record ParcelId(String value) { ParcelId { if (!value.matches("PP-[0-9]{4,12}")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid parcel id: '" + value + "'"); } } record Weight(long grams) { Weight { if (grams < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("weight must not be negative: " + grams); } } Kotlin @JvmInline value class ParcelId(val value: String) { init { require(PATTERN.matches(value)) { "invalid parcel id: '$value'" } } override fun toString(): String = value companion object { private val PATTERN = Regex("PP-[0-9]{4,12}") } } @JvmInline value class Weight(val grams: Long) { init { require(grams >= 0) { "weight must not be negative: $grams" } } override fun toString(): String = BigDecimal.valueOf(grams, 3).stripTrailingZeros().toPlainString() + " kg" } Now ParcelCollected(Weight(2_500), ParcelId("PP-7781")) fails with Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Weight', but 'ParcelId' was expected. And because init runs on every construction, a ParcelId that exists is a valid one: PP- and 4 to 12 digits. Nothing downstream needs to check it again. You may wonder what all these small types cost. Very little, for the reason that lesson gave. Where a value class is used as itself, the compiler erases it to its one field. That's the print shop's back room, where the units are gone and the machines see plain numbers. The demo prints the fields of ParcelCollected through Java reflection, the JDK's way of asking a class about itself, and they are a java.lang.String and a long. The Java records are separate objects on the heap, the memory where objects live: one for each id and one for each weight. The Kotlin ones become objects too in the places that lesson listed, such as a List<ParcelId>, a nullable Weight? or a generic T. The one-field rule made a decision for this model. A value class holds one field until Project Valhalla arrives, so a Weight is whole grams, and the unit lives in the type's name. That suits Pedal Post, which weighs everything in grams. If a partner courier ever reports pounds, the door converts them, and nothing behind it sees a pound. Lesson 3's design review comes back to that choice. Weight also adds and subtracts, which the load board in lesson 2 will need. plus uses Math.addExact, which throws ArithmeticException instead of wrapping round to a negative number. minus needs no check of its own: a result below zero is a negative Weight, and the constructor already refuses those. h: A sealed event model · Check each scan once, at the door, then trust the types
x: The model refuses bad values, but bad values still arrive. The scanner sends what the rider typed, a partner's program sends what it likes, and a row in a database may have been fixed by hand. So one function turns raw input into the model, in one place, at the edge of the program: the line where outside data comes in. Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla pictured it as a clerk at the door who copies each letter onto the right form, or sends it back. Our clerk never throws: Java static Parsed parse(Map<String, String> fields) { try { String type = field(fields, "type"); return switch (type) { case "collected" -> new Ok(new ParcelCollected(new ParcelId(field(fields, "parcelId")), weight(fields))); // ... one case per type default -> new Rejected("unknown event type: '" + type + "'"); }; } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { return new Rejected(e.getMessage()); // a reader or a constructor said no } } Kotlin fun parseEvent(fields: Map<String, String>): Parsed { // field(name) and weight() are small local readers that throw IllegalArgumentException return try { when (val type = field("type")) { "collected" -> Parsed.Ok(ParcelCollected(ParcelId(field("parcelId")), weight())) // ... one branch per type else -> Parsed.Rejected("unknown event type: '$type'") } } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { Parsed.Rejected(e.message ?: "invalid event") // a reader or a constructor said no } } Parsed is a small sealed type of its own, with two cases: Ok holds a valid event, and Rejected holds the reason a scan was refused. Notice what parse does not do. It doesn't check the tracking number's format or the sign of the weight. It calls ParcelId(...) and Weight(...) and turns their refusal into a Rejected. The rules live in the constructors, once. A second copy of them in the parser would drift the first time someone edits one and not the other. And parseEvent is a recipe card in the sense of Pure functions: the idea everything else builds on: the same fields always give the same result, and nothing outside it changes, so the lab tests it with plain maps and no setup at all. Why return a result instead of throwing? Errors as values: sealed results, Result and Either had two cooks. One hands back a note, "the custard split, let's serve cream", and the other throws the pan across the room. An exception is the thrown pan. The code that reads scans has to decide what a bad scan means, and an exception decides for it: it flies out of the reading loop, and the loop stops at the first bad scan. A Rejected is the note. The loop can set the scan aside with its reason, count it, and carry on with the next one. Don't retry it, though: a malformed scan stays malformed, however often you read it. Behind the door, code trusts the types. A function that takes a ParcelCollected has a valid tracking number and a positive weight, because no other kind of ParcelCollected can exist. There is no !!, no toLong() and no if (type == ...) in any handler you'll write in lesson 2. The door protects us from the future too. When Pedal Post adds ParcelLost, a program that hasn't been updated yet still parses raw fields with its old parser. A lost scan lands in its else branch and becomes Rejected("unknown event type: 'lost'"), and nothing crashes. That's why the edge is the one when that keeps its else. It's a when over strings, and strings can never be listed in full, so the lab's tests do the checking there instead. Parse once, at the door, into an event or a note. Behind the door, trust the types. The demo's parser knows only collections and deliveries. Predict which of its six scans are rejected, and for what reason, before you run it. h: A sealed event model · Java and Kotlin
x: The event model in Java and Kotlin Model.java (Java 21) record ParcelId(String value) { ParcelId { if (!value.matches("PP-[0-9]{4,12}")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid parcel id: '" + value + "'"); } @Override public String toString() { return value; } } record Weight(long grams) { Weight { if (grams < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("weight must not be negative: " + grams); } @Override public String toString() { return BigDecimal.valueOf(grams, 3).stripTrailingZeros().toPlainString() + " kg"; } } sealed interface ParcelEvent permits ParcelBooked, DeliveryFailed, Handover { ParcelId parcelId(); } record ParcelBooked(ParcelId parcelId, Weight weight) implements ParcelEvent { ParcelBooked { if (weight.grams() <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("booked weight must be positive: " + weight); } } record DeliveryFailed(ParcelId parcelId, FailReason reason) implements ParcelEvent {} sealed interface Handover extends ParcelEvent permits ParcelCollected, ParcelDelivered { Weight weight(); } record ParcelCollected(ParcelId parcelId, Weight weight) implements Handover { /* same check */ } record ParcelDelivered(ParcelId parcelId, Weight weight) implements Handover { /* same check */ } static String summary(ParcelEvent e) { return switch (e) { // no default case ParcelBooked(var id, var weight) -> id + " booked, " + weight; case DeliveryFailed(var id, var reason) -> id + " not delivered: " + reason; case ParcelCollected(var id, var weight) -> id + " collected, " + weight; case ParcelDelivered(var id, var weight) -> id + " delivered, " + weight; }; } Model.kt @JvmInline value class ParcelId(val value: String) { init { require(PATTERN.matches(value)) { "invalid parcel id: '$value'" } } override fun toString(): String = value companion object { private val PATTERN = Regex("PP-[0-9]{4,12}") } } @JvmInline value class Weight(val grams: Long) { init { require(grams >= 0) { "weight must not be negative: $grams" } } override fun toString(): String = BigDecimal.valueOf(grams, 3).stripTrailingZeros().toPlainString() + " kg" } sealed interface ParcelEvent { val parcelId: ParcelId } data class ParcelBooked(override val parcelId: ParcelId, val weight: Weight) : ParcelEvent { init { require(weight.grams > 0) { "booked weight must be positive: $weight" } } } data class DeliveryFailed(override val parcelId: ParcelId, val reason: FailReason) : ParcelEvent sealed interface Handover : ParcelEvent { val weight: Weight } data class ParcelCollected(override val parcelId: ParcelId, override val weight: Weight) : Handover { /* same check */ } data class ParcelDelivered(override val parcelId: ParcelId, override val weight: Weight) : Handover { /* same check */ } fun summary(event: ParcelEvent): String = when (event) { // no else is ParcelBooked -> "${event.parcelId} booked, ${event.weight}" is DeliveryFailed -> "${event.parcelId} not delivered: ${event.reason}" is ParcelCollected -> "${event.parcelId} collected, ${event.weight}" is ParcelDelivered -> "${event.parcelId} delivered, ${event.weight}" } Both versions have the same shape: sealed interfaces for the kinds, final carriers for the leaves, the checks in the constructor, and one exhaustive switch per operation. Three things differ. Kotlin's value classes compile to a String and a long wherever they're used as themselves, while Java's ParcelId and Weight records are separate objects until value records arrive with Valhalla. Java names the subtypes in permits (or infers them within one file), while Kotlin requires them to share the package and module. And a data class's copy() runs init, so collected.copy(weight = Weight.ZERO) throws: a new edition of the form goes past the clerk again, and records have no copy at all. kotlinc also writes the same PermittedSubclasses attribute that javac does, so Java code can switch exhaustively over this Kotlin model, which lesson 3 relies on.
