h: A sealed event model · Key terms
x: Event A value that says something already happened, such as a parcel being collected. Sealed hierarchy A type whose list of direct subtypes is closed and known to the compiler. Exhaustive when A when or switch with a branch for every possible subtype and no else, checked at compile time. Value class A one-field wrapper that is its own type in Kotlin and compiles to its field where it can. Edge The one place where raw input from outside the program becomes model values, or is refused. Remainder The cases an exhaustive switch can still meet when the program runs: null, and subtypes compiled after it. Why no else in a when over your own sealed type? Without it, a new subtype is a compile error at every when that must handle it. With it, the new subtype silently takes the else branch. What does a sealed middle level like Handover give you? One branch, is Handover, covers its leaves (collections and deliveries), and code written against it doesn't break when siblings are added elsewhere. @JvmInline value class ParcelId(val value: String): what is a ParcelId field when the program runs? A plain String field. It is boxed only when used as another type: generic, nullable, an interface or Any. Why does Weight hold only grams, with no unit field? A JVM value class holds exactly one field. Pedal Post weighs in grams, so the unit is in the type's name, and any other unit is converted at the door. What does the edge function return for a malformed scan? Parsed.Rejected(reason), never an exception. The caller decides what to do with it: set it aside, count it, and carry on. Where does parseEvent check that a tracking number is well formed? It doesn't. It calls ParcelId(raw), whose init checks, and turns the IllegalArgumentException into Rejected. A program that hasn't been updated gets a scan of a new event type as raw fields. What happens? Its parser's else branch returns Rejected("unknown event type"). Nothing crashes, so update the programs that read events before the ones that send them.

h: A sealed event model · Go deeper
x: Three questions come up once a model like this runs for real. How do events change over time? Adding a field with a default is safe for programs that parse at the door: old scans lack the field and get the default. Renaming a type or a field is not. Keep the old name in the parser for as long as old scans can arrive, and map it to the new type there, so the model itself never carries the history. If you turn the model into JSON with kotlinx.serialization, as Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization showed, pin each type's name with @SerialName for the same reason. Should the door return Either instead of a sealed Parsed? The Either<String, ParcelEvent> from Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus works, and it composes with map and flatMap. A dedicated Parsed reads better where it's used (is Parsed.Rejected), and it leaves room for a third case later, such as Ignored for event types a program deliberately doesn't handle. Kotlin's Result<T> is the wrong fit: its failure side is a Throwable, and a rejected scan is not an exception, as Errors as values: sealed results, Result and Either argued. What about the database? Rows you read back are untrusted input too. A column holding 'collected' and a nullable grams column are a raw map with a schema, and a migration or a fix made by hand can break them. Read rows through the same kind of edge function, or reuse parseEvent by turning each row into its map of fields. Java has one tool here that Kotlin doesn't need: since JDK 21, a pattern switch can take case null explicitly. Kotlin rules null out at compile time by declaring the parameter non-nullable. Both end up with the same guarantee behind the door.

h: A typed event bus · Route each event to its own class, then up through its supertypes
x: One publish looks up the event's class, then each event supertype, nearest first, and a Handler declared in lets one general handler fit any subscription Let's set up the words first. The bus is the object in the middle. A handler, a small object that reacts to one kind of event, subscribes: it signs up with the bus for one type of event. Code that has news publishes an event, and the bus delivers it to every handler that signed up. Inside, the bus keeps a registry, a map from each event type to the list of handlers that signed up for it. Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus keyed that registry by event::class, the event's class when the program runs. That has a hole, the one from the warm-up. A tracking handler subscribed under ParcelEvent::class never runs, because no event's class is the interface ParcelEvent itself. It's always one of the leaves. The same goes for a handler of Handover. Lesson 1 of this track made that middle level on purpose, so the bus has to honor it. There are two honest fixes. The first keeps one flat list of (type, handler) pairs and asks type.isInstance(event) of each pair. It's short and correct, and every publish checks every subscription: forty handlers means forty checks per scan, almost all of them misses. The second keeps the registry keyed by class and works out, for each event class, the list of keys to visit: the class itself, then each supertype that is an event, nearest first. A supertype is a type a class extends or implements, directly or further up. We'll call that list the dispatch keys: Java static List<Class<?>> dispatchKeys(Class<?> type) { LinkedHashSet<Class<?>> found = new LinkedHashSet<>(); ArrayDeque<Class<?>> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of(type)); while (!queue.isEmpty()) { Class<?> c = queue.removeFirst(); if (!ParcelEvent.class.isAssignableFrom(c) || !found.add(c)) continue; queue.addAll(List.of(c.getInterfaces())); if (c.getSuperclass() != null) queue.add(c.getSuperclass()); } return List.copyOf(found); } Kotlin private fun dispatchKeys(type: Class<*>): List<KClass<*>> = keyCache.computeIfAbsent(type) { val found = LinkedHashSet<Class<*>>() val queue = ArrayDeque<Class<*>>().apply { add(type) } while (queue.isNotEmpty()) { val c = queue.removeFirst() if (!ParcelEvent::class.java.isAssignableFrom(c) || !found.add(c)) continue queue.addAll(c.interfaces) c.superclass?.let(queue::add) } found.map { it.kotlin } } Let's read it in order. The queue starts with the event's own class. Each turn takes the next class off the queue and skips it if it isn't an event or was already found. Otherwise it adds the class's interfaces and superclass to the back of the queue. For ParcelCollected the walk gives [ParcelCollected, Handover, ParcelEvent], and publish looks up only those three keys. The order is breadth-first, one level at a time, and it's a promise to callers: the most specific handlers run first, then each wider kind, and within one key, handlers run in the order they subscribed. The walk uses plain Java reflection, getInterfaces() and getSuperclass(), so it needs no extra library. KClass, Class and type tokens kept kotlin-reflect, the 3.8 MB library behind Kotlin's fuller reflection, in a reference book in the other room: naming and casting a class need no trip there, and describing one does. The answer never changes for a class, so computeIfAbsent caches it, once per class. On a ConcurrentHashMap that call is one atomic step, which nothing can interrupt halfway. So two threads, two paths of work running at the same time, can't both fill the cache when they publish the first collection together, as Concurrent collections showed. Before you run the demo, predict the keys it prints for DeliveryFailed. Exact class versus supertypes Read DispatchDemo.kt (or DispatchDemoJava.java). Three handlers subscribe under three types, and the same collection is published to a bus that looks up the exact class only, then to one that walks the supertypes. Add bus.subscribe(Handover::class) { ran += "insurance" } (in Java, bus.subscribe(Handover.class, e -> ran.add("insurance"))) as the last subscription, after the load line. Predict where insurance appears in the second list, then run. h: A typed event bus · A handler only takes events in, so declare it in
x: Handler<E> is the labelled box from Generics from zero: type parameters, "Handler of ___", with a blank that each subscription fills in. A handler only ever takes an event in. It never hands one back. A type that only handed events out would be the apple dispenser of Covariance with out: producers, and it would be out. A handler is the other kind. Contravariance with in: consumers had a compost bin behind the fruit shop: bruised fruit of any kind goes in, nothing comes out, and so the bin for any fruit makes a perfectly good bin for apples. A handler is that bin. One that takes any parcel event makes a perfectly good handler for collections. That lesson's rule says how to write it down: a type parameter that only goes in is declared in. Java @FunctionalInterface interface Handler<E extends ParcelEvent> { void handle(E event); } // Java: no variance on the declaration <E extends ParcelEvent> Subscription subscribe(Class<E> type, Handler<? super E> handler) { ... } Kotlin fun interface Handler<in E : ParcelEvent> { fun handle(event: E) } fun <E : ParcelEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription { ... } Now the tracking handler, written once for every event, fits any subscription: bus.subscribe(ParcelCollected::class, tracking) compiles with tracking: Handler<ParcelEvent>. Delete the in, and the clerk at the storeroom door, the compiler checking every label, turns the same line away: Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Handler<ParcelEvent>', but 'Handler<ParcelCollected>' was expected. Java has no variance on declarations, so the Java version writes ? super E at every use: the "consumer super" half of PECS, Java's rule of thumb "producer extends, consumer super". kotlinc writes that wildcard for us: the Java signature of the Kotlin subscribe is subscribe(KClass<E>, Handler<? super E>). That's why the Java callers of lesson 3 get the same freedom without asking. Why a fun interface, an interface with one abstract method that a lambda can implement, and not the function type (E) -> Unit? A function type is already in on its parameter, so variance would come free. But Java would see a Function1<? super E, Unit>, and every Java lambda would have to end with return Unit.INSTANCE. A fun interface with a void method takes a plain Java lambda. Lesson 3 is all about that Java surface. Inside the bus, handlers for different types share one map, so each one is stored behind an adapter that takes any ParcelEvent: Java Handler<ParcelEvent> adapter = event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)); Kotlin val adapter = Handler<ParcelEvent> { event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)) } The adapter is part travel plug, part receptionist, two pictures from the Design patterns track. Like the plug, it makes a narrow handler fit a list of general ones. Like the receptionist who answers for a busy manager, it checks each call before putting it through. The workshop's receptionist was polite: with safeCast, a call meant for someone else was quietly not put through. Ours is strict. The dispatch keys already guarantee the type, so a wrong event here can only be a bug in the bus, and cast makes that bug loud. The next section makes sure loud doesn't mean fatal. Kotlin callers also get a reified wrapper. It's inline, the print shop's photocopy pasted into each caller, so it can be reified: it's the clerk from Type erasure and reified type parameters who copies the label onto a note before it's torn off: inline fun <reified E : ParcelEvent> subscribe(handler: Handler<E>) = subscribe(E::class, handler). It needs no noinline. Only parameters of a function type are inlined, as Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns showed, and a Handler is an ordinary object. h: A typed event bus · The sign-up sheet's three rules: a way to leave, failures kept apart, a snapshot to walk
x: The bus is the sign-up sheet from Observer and Command, the one by the corner shop's door that says "ring me when the fresh bread arrives". Anyone can sign up, anyone can cross their name off, and one broken phone mustn't stop the shopkeeper from ringing the rest. Those are three rules, and the lab tests each one. First, subscribe returns a handle. Subscription extends AutoCloseable, the JDK interface behind try-with-resources, and closing it removes exactly the adapter that subscribe stored. Closing it twice is harmless. Without a handle, a handler that belongs to a short-lived object stays in the map for ever. That's a lapsed listener: a name nobody can cross off, still rung for every event. It also keeps alive an object the program has finished with, so the garbage collector, the part of the JVM that frees objects nobody uses any more, can never free it. Second, one failing handler must not stop the others. deliver catches Exception around each call and reports it, with the event, to an ErrorHandler, a small callback the bus was given when it was built: Java for (Handler<ParcelEvent> handler : handlers) { // a snapshot: copy-on-write called++; try { handler.handle(event); } catch (Exception e) { onError.onError(event, e); // one failure must not starve the rest } } Kotlin for (handler in handlers) { // a snapshot: copy-on-write called++ try { handler.handle(event) } catch (e: Exception) { onError.onError(event, e) // one failure must not starve the rest } } It catches Exception, not Throwable, because an OutOfMemoryError should still stop the program. And the bus doesn't decide what an error means. The program does, through its ErrorHandler: it can count the failure, log it, or keep the event to try again later. A handler that throws is one bug. Catch it per handler, and report it. Third, delivery walks a snapshot. Each key's handlers live in a CopyOnWriteArrayList, a list that copies its array on every change. A loop over it sees the list as it was when the loop began. A handler may close its own subscription while it runs, like a welcome text that should go out only once, and the loop carries on. With an ArrayList, the loop's next step throws ConcurrentModificationException. Copying the array on every subscribe sounds expensive, and it would be for a list that changed all day. Subscriptions change at start-up; scans arrive all day. Those two collections also make the bus safe for many publishers without a lock of its own, the tool that lets one thread in at a time. ConcurrentHashMap guards the registry, and each list swaps in a new array instead of changing the old one in place, as Concurrent collections described. The lab's load test runs eight publishing threads while another thread subscribes and closes in a loop, and it counts every event. One thing doesn't change: delivery is synchronous. Every handler runs on the publisher's thread, before publish returns. A text that takes 300 ms to send makes every scan 300 ms slower. Keep handlers fast; lesson 3's design review comes back to the slow ones. The demo runs the same three handlers on three buses. Predict what each run prints before you run it. One bad handler, three buses Read IsolationDemo. The first handler unsubscribes itself, the second always throws, the third texts the sender. Each bus gets two collections. Predict the output of each of the three runs. Run it. In the isolated run, change catch (e: Exception) to catch only IllegalArgumentException (in Java, change RuntimeException to IllegalArgumentException). Predict, then run. publish can isolate failures or not. */ class Bus(private val handlers: MutableList<(ParcelEvent) -> Unit>, private val isolate: Boolean) { fun subscribe(handler: (ParcelEvent) -> Unit): AutoCloseable { handlers += handler return AutoCloseable { handlers -= handler } } fun publish(event: ParcelEvent) { for (h in handlers) { if (!isolate) { h(event); continue } try { h(event) } catch (e: Exception) { println(" (error handler: ${e.message})") } } } } fun scenario(title: String, bus: Bus) { println(title) var once: AutoCloseable? = null once = bus.subscribe { println(" welcome text, once"); once?.close() } // unsubscribes itself bus.subscribe { throw IllegalStateException("load board is down") } bus.subscribe { println(" text to sender: ${it.parcelId} is on its way") } try { bus.publish(ParcelCollected("PP-7781", 2_500)) bus.publish(ParcelCollected("PP-7782", 1_200)) } catch (e: Exception) { println(" publish threw $e") } } fun main() { scenario("ArrayList, no isolation:", Bus(ArrayList(), isolate = false)) scenario("CopyOnWriteArrayList, no isolation:", Bus(CopyOnWriteArrayList(), isolate = false)) scenario("CopyOnWriteArrayList, isolated:", Bus(CopyOnWriteArrayList(), isolate = true)) } ./gradlew :events:demo -Pmain=workbench.events.l02.demo.isolation.IsolationDemoKt labs/events/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/events/l02/demo/isolation/IsolationDemo.kt IsolationDemoJava.java package workbench.events.l02.demo.isolation; return () -> handlers.remove(handler); } void publish(ParcelEvent event) { for (Consumer<ParcelEvent> h : handlers) { if (!isolate) { h.accept(event); continue; } try { h.accept(event); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println(" (error handler: " + e.getMessage() + ")"); h: A typed event bus · Work for every event goes in a chain, work for one handler in a wrapper
x: Some extra work belongs to every event, once: logging each one, or dropping a scan that arrives twice. Some belongs to one handler only, such as timing the text sender. The first kind is a chain around publish. The second is a wrapper around one handler. They look alike, and choosing the wrong one gives the wrong numbers. The chain is the one from State and Chain of Responsibility, where a complaint went from the shop assistant to the manager to head office. Each of them answered it or passed it on. Here, each middleware, a link in the chain around delivery, gets the event and next, the rest of the chain. It passes the event on, or returns 0 to stop it. The bus builds the chain once, when it's created, by folding a copy of the list from the right: combining its links one at a time, starting from the last, into a single Next. So the first middleware wraps all the others, and the last one wraps delivery: Java Next pipeline = this::deliver; for (int i = middleware.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { Middleware m = middleware.get(i); Next rest = pipeline; pipeline = event -> m.intercept(event, rest); } Kotlin private val pipeline: Next = middleware.toList() .foldRight(Next(::deliver)) { m, next -> Next { event -> m.intercept(event, next) } } Order is behavior. With [dedupe, logging], a repeated scan is dropped before anything logs it. With [logging, dedupe], it's logged and then dropped, which is what you want if you need to count repeats. Pick one and pin it in a test. Why would a scan arrive twice? A scanner that hears no answer on a weak signal sends the scan again, to be safe. Its caution is admirable, and its arithmetic is terrible: the load board would add 2.5 kg twice. The dedupe middleware is one line, if (seen.add(event)) next.proceed(event) else 0. add is the check and the act in one step, the fix from Race conditions: why count++ lies, so eight threads can't all let the same scan through. Its idea of "the same event" is data-class equality: the same type, the same tracking number, the same weight. The wrapper is the decorator from Decorator and Proxy, the gift paper around a teapot. It implements the same Handler<E>, adds one thing and passes the call on, and the bus handles the wrapped handler exactly as before: Java static <E extends ParcelEvent> Handler<E> timed(Handler<E> inner, String name, Timings timings) { return event -> { long start = timings.ticker().nanos(); try { inner.handle(event); } finally { timings.record(name, timings.ticker().nanos() - start); } }; } Kotlin fun <E : ParcelEvent> Handler<E>.timed(name: String, timings: Timings): Handler<E> { val inner = this return Handler { event -> val start = timings.ticker.nanos() try { inner.handle(event) } finally { timings.record(name, timings.ticker.nanos() - start) } } } It records in finally, so a handler that throws is timed too, and the exception still reaches the bus's try. The clock is a Ticker passed in. Tests use a fake one that moves forward by a fixed step on every read, so they check exact numbers, with no sleeps and no flaky margins. A timing middleware couldn't do this job. It sees one delivery to all of an event's handlers, so it would add the load board's 2 ms to the text sender's 300 ms. In the demo, swap the first two middleware and predict what the repeated scan prints. Reorder the chain Run ChainDemo and read the nesting of the > and < lines. Swap logging("outer") and dropDuplicates() in the list. Predict what the repeated scan prints now, and run. Change tick() to add 90,000 instead of 40,000. Predict the load took line before you run. ChainDemo.kt package workbench.events.l02.demo.chain import workbench.events.l02.demo.ParcelCollected import workbench.events.l02.demo.ParcelEvent // The event model (ParcelEvent and friends) is in DemoModel.kt, one package up. fun interface Next { fun proceed(event: ParcelEvent): Int } fun interface Middleware { fun intercept(event: ParcelEvent, next: Next): Int } fun interface Handler { fun handle(event: ParcelEvent) } /** Chain of responsibility: each middleware passes the event on, or answers 0 itself. */ fun chain(middleware: List<Middleware>, deliver: Next): Next = middleware.foldRight(deliver) { m, next -> Next { e -> m.intercept(e, next) } } fun logging(name: String) = Middleware { event, next -> println("$name > ${event.parcelId}") val called = next.proceed(event) println("$name < ${event.parcelId}: $called handler(s)") called } fun dropDuplicates(): Middleware { val seen = HashSet<ParcelEvent>() return Middleware { event, next -> if (seen.add(event)) next.proceed(event) else 0 } } /** Decorator: the same Handler interface, plus timing. Virtual time keeps the output stable. */ default Handler timed(String name) { return event -> { long start = tick(); try { handle(event); } finally { System.out.println(" " + name + " took " + (tick() - start) / 1_000 + " us"); } }; } } static long clock = 0; static long tick() { clock += 40_000; return clock; } // every read moves the clock by 40 microseconds /** Chain of responsibility: each middleware passes the event on, or answers 0 itself. */ static Next chain(List<Middleware> middleware, Next deliver) { Next next = deliver; for (int i = middleware.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { Middleware m = middleware.get(i); Next rest = next; next = e -> m.intercept(e, rest); } return next; } static Middleware logging(String name) { return (event, next) -> { System.out.println(name + " > " + event.parcelId()); int called = next.proceed(event); System.out.println(name + " < " + event.parcelId() + ": " + called + " handler(s)"); return called; }; } static Middleware dropDuplicates() { Set<ParcelEvent> seen = new HashSet<>(); return (event, next) -> seen.add(event) ? next.proceed(event) : 0; } public static void main(String[] args) { Handler load = ((Handler) e -> System.out.println(" load board adds " + e.parcelId())).timed("load"); Next pipeline = chain( List.of(logging("outer"), dropDuplicates(), logging("inner")), // Step 2: swap the first two e -> { load.handle(e); return 1; }); ParcelCollected scan = new ParcelCollected("PP-7781", 2_500); pipeline.proceed(scan); System.out.println("-- the same scan again (the scanner sent it twice)"); pipeline.proceed(new ParcelCollected("PP-7781", 2_500)); } } ./gradlew :events:demo -Pmain=workbench.events.l02.demo.chain.ChainDemoJava labs/events/src/demo/java/workbench/events/l02/demo/chain/ChainDemoJava.java First run: outer >, inner >, the load board lines, then inner < and outer < in reverse. h: A typed event bus · Java and Kotlin
x: The bus in Java and Kotlin EventBus.java @FunctionalInterface interface Handler<E extends ParcelEvent> { void handle(E event); } @FunctionalInterface interface ErrorHandler { void onError(ParcelEvent event, Exception error); } @FunctionalInterface interface Next { int proceed(ParcelEvent event); } @FunctionalInterface interface Middleware { int intercept(ParcelEvent event, Next next); } final class EventBus { private final Map<Class<?>, List<Handler<ParcelEvent>>> registry = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private final Map<Class<?>, List<Class<?>>> keyCache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private final ErrorHandler onError; private final Next pipeline; EventBus(List<Middleware> middleware, ErrorHandler onError) { this.onError = onError; Next next = this::deliver; for (Middleware m : List.copyOf(middleware).reversed()) { // reversed(): JDK 21 Next rest = next; next = event -> m.intercept(event, rest); } this.pipeline = next; } <E extends ParcelEvent> AutoCloseable subscribe(Class<E> type, Handler<? super E> handler) { Handler<ParcelEvent> adapter = event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)); List<Handler<ParcelEvent>> handlers = registry.computeIfAbsent(type, t -> new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>()); handlers.add(adapter); return () -> handlers.remove(adapter); } int publish(ParcelEvent event) { return pipeline.proceed(event); } private int deliver(ParcelEvent event) { int called = 0; for (Class<?> key : keyCache.computeIfAbsent(event.getClass(), EventBus::dispatchKeys)) { for (Handler<ParcelEvent> h : registry.getOrDefault(key, List.of())) { called++; try { h.handle(event); } catch (Exception e) { onError.onError(event, e); } } } return called; } private static List<Class<?>> dispatchKeys(Class<?> type) { /* breadth-first walk, as above */ } } EventBus.kt fun interface Handler<in E : ParcelEvent> { fun handle(event: E) } fun interface Next { fun proceed(event: ParcelEvent): Int } fun interface Middleware { fun intercept(event: ParcelEvent, next: Next): Int } class EventBus( middleware: List<Middleware> = emptyList(), private val onError: ErrorHandler = ErrorHandler.PRINT, ) { private val registry = ConcurrentHashMap<KClass<*>, CopyOnWriteArrayList<Handler<ParcelEvent>>>() private val keyCache = ConcurrentHashMap<Class<*>, List<KClass<*>>>() private val pipeline: Next = middleware.toList() .foldRight(Next(::deliver)) { m, next -> Next { event -> m.intercept(event, next) } } fun <E : ParcelEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription { val adapter = Handler<ParcelEvent> { event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)) } val handlers = registry.computeIfAbsent(type) { CopyOnWriteArrayList() } handlers += adapter return Subscription { handlers.remove(adapter) } } inline fun <reified E : ParcelEvent> subscribe(handler: Handler<E>): Subscription = subscribe(E::class, handler) fun publish(event: ParcelEvent): Int = pipeline.proceed(event) private fun deliver(event: ParcelEvent): Int { var called = 0 for (key in dispatchKeys(event.javaClass)) { for (handler in registry[key] ?: continue) { called++ try { handler.handle(event) } catch (e: Exception) { onError.onError(event, e) } } } return called } private fun dispatchKeys(type: Class<*>): List<KClass<*>> = keyCache.computeIfAbsent(type) { /* the walk */ } } Both buses work the same way: the same registry, the same walk, the same adapter, the same fold and the same try around each handler. The differences are in who writes what. Java writes Handler<? super E> at the use site; Kotlin declares in once, and kotlinc puts the wildcard into the Java signature. Kotlin gets default arguments on the constructor and a reified subscribe<E> for its own callers; Java callers get neither until lesson 3 adds @JvmOverloads and a Class<E> overload. And Kotlin's Next(::deliver) turns a function reference into a fun interface object, where Java writes this::deliver against its functional interface.

h: A typed event bus · Worked example
x: Wire up delivery texts, and put each concern in its place Every delivery should send the receiver a text: "your parcel is at your door". That's one handler for one event type. Subscribe it under ParcelDelivered, the most specific key, so it never hears about a collection. val texts = Handler<ParcelDelivered> { sms.send(it.parcelId, "your parcel is at your door") } val textsSubscription = bus.subscribe<ParcelDelivered>(texts) // the Java bus from the comparison below Handler<ParcelDelivered> texts = e -> sms.send(e.parcelId(), "your parcel is at your door"); AutoCloseable textsSubscription = bus.subscribe(ParcelDelivered.class, texts); The text service fails about one call in two hundred. Isolation already keeps the load board and the tracking page running when it does. What the program still has to decide is what a failure means. Here the error handler counts it and keeps the event on a list to try again later. val bus = EventBus( middleware = listOf(DropDuplicates()), onError = ErrorHandler { event, error -> failures.incrementAndGet() tryAgainLater += event to error.toString() }, ) ErrorHandler onError = (event, error) -> { failures.incrementAndGet(); tryAgainLater.add(Map.entry(event, error.toString())); }; EventBus bus = new EventBus(List.of(new DropDuplicates()), onError); A scanner on a weak signal sends some scans twice, and nobody wants two texts for one parcel. Dropping repeats applies to every event once, before any handler, so it's middleware, first in the list. A wrapper around the texts handler would drop repeated texts only, and the load board would still add the weight twice. middleware = listOf(DropDuplicates(), logging) // dedupe first: repeats are never logged List<Middleware> middleware = List.of(new DropDuplicates(), logging); // dedupe first: repeats are never logged How long does a text take? That's a question about one handler, so it's a decorator: wrap the handler, not the bus. The timings now show about 300 ms per delivery under texts, all of it spent on the thread that published the scan. That number is the case for handing slow work to another thread, which lesson 3's design review makes. bus.subscribe<ParcelDelivered>(texts.timed("texts", timings)) bus.subscribe(ParcelDelivered.class, timed(texts, "texts", timings)); // the static timed(...) from the last section

h: A typed event bus · Quiz
x: From Contravariance with in: consumers: with fun interface Handler<in E : ParcelEvent>, tracking: Handler<ParcelEvent> and load: Handler<ParcelCollected>, which line compiles? val h: Handler<ParcelEvent> = load val h: Handler<Handover> = load val h: Handler<ParcelCollected> = tracking val h: Handler<ParcelDelivered> = load For a consumer the arrow flips, like the compost bin that makes a fine apple bin: something that takes any event can stand in for something that takes collections. The other three ask a collections-only handler to accept events it can't handle, a delivery or any handover, so the compiler refuses them. From Observer and Command: a RiderScreen object is created each time a rider logs in, and it subscribes to the bus in its constructor. It never closes its Subscription. What happens after a few thousand log-ins? Nothing: the garbage collector removes the old screens once nobody uses them Every old screen is still in the registry, can't be collected, and still reacts to each event The bus throws when the registry grows past a limit Only the newest screen receives events The registry holds a reference to each adapter, and each adapter holds the screen's handler. That's the lapsed listener: memory grows with every log-in, and every scan now runs thousands of stale handlers. The garbage collector can't help, because the bus still reaches every old screen. Closing the handle when the screen closes removes it. From State and Chain of Responsibility: the bus is built with middleware = [dedupe, logging]. A scanner sends a scan the bus has already seen. What does the log show for the repeat? Nothing: dedupe returns 0 before logging runs A log line with 0 handlers A log line with 1 handler, then dedupe drops it Two log lines, one per delivery The first middleware in the list wraps all the others. Dedupe answers 0 without calling next, so logging never sees the event. With [logging, dedupe] you'd get a log line ending in 0 handlers, which is the order to choose if you want to count repeats. From Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns: inline fun <reified E : ParcelEvent> subscribe(handler: Handler<E>) = subscribe(E::class, handler) stores the handler in the registry. Why does it compile without noinline? Because reified makes every parameter noinline Because members of a class are never inlined Because the compiler adds noinline automatically when a lambda is stored Because only parameters of a function type are inlined, and Handler is a fun interface inline pastes in the bodies of lambdas passed to parameters of a function type. A Handler argument is an ordinary object, even when the caller writes it as a lambda, so there is nothing to inline and nothing that needs noinline. With handler: (E) -> Unit it would need noinline, as the generics workshop showed. Subscriptions, in this order: tracking under ParcelEvent, then handovers under Handover, then load under ParcelCollected. You publish a ParcelDelivered. Which handlers run, in what order? tracking, handovers handovers, tracking tracking, handovers, load handovers only The keys for a delivery are [ParcelDelivered, Handover, ParcelEvent], visited nearest first. Nobody subscribed under ParcelDelivered, so handovers runs, then tracking. Subscription order matters only within one key, which is why the first option is wrong, and load sits under a sibling type the walk never visits.

h: A typed event bus · Key terms
x: Dispatch keys The list of types a bus looks up for one event: its class, then its event supertypes, nearest first. Adapter A small wrapper that lets a Handler be stored as a Handler , by casting each event on the way in. Failure isolation Catching each handler's exception so that the other handlers still run. Lapsed listener A handler that was never unsubscribed, so the bus keeps it alive and keeps calling it. Middleware A link in a chain around publish that can pass an event on, change it or stop it. Virtual time A fake clock that tests move forward by hand, so timing can be checked exactly. Why does a bus keyed by event::class never call a handler subscribed under ParcelEvent::class? No event's class is the interface itself. Delivery must also look up each supertype of the event's class. In what order does this bus call handlers? The event's own class first, then each event supertype, nearest first. Within one key, in subscription order. Why is the handler type Handler<in E>? A handler only consumes events. With in, a Handler<ParcelEvent> can stand in for a Handler<ParcelCollected>. What Java signature does kotlinc give fun <E : ParcelEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>) when Handler is in? subscribe(KClass<E>, Handler<? super E>): kotlinc turns declaration-site in into a ? super wildcard in parameters. Why a CopyOnWriteArrayList for each key's handlers? Delivery loops over a snapshot, so a handler can unsubscribe itself, and publishers need no lock. Each subscribe copies the array, which is fine because subscriptions rarely change. Middleware or decorator: timing one handler? Decorator. Middleware wraps one delivery to all of an event's handlers; a decorator wraps one handler and implements its interface. Why does DropDuplicates test seen.add(event) instead of seen.contains(event)? add checks and inserts in one atomic step. Contains-then-add lets two threads pass the same event.

h: A typed event bus · Go deeper
x: Three extensions come up as soon as a bus like this meets real traffic. Asynchronous delivery. Give the bus an Executor and let deliver submit each handler call instead of making it. Two things change. Errors no longer come back to the publisher, so the ErrorHandler becomes the only place they show up. And the order is gone: two scans for the same parcel can run in either order on two pool threads. If the order per parcel matters, and for a load board it does, send each tracking number to one single-threaded lane, for example lanes[abs(id.hashCode() % lanes.size)]. Bound each lane's queue too, or a slow handler turns into an OutOfMemoryError, the lesson of Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection. Generic events. This bus keys by KClass, which is enough because no event has a type parameter. If you ever publish an Envelope<ParcelCollected>, the class key files every envelope under one card, the problem from KClass, Class and type tokens. Key by KType from typeOf<T>() then, and know that the supertype walk gets harder: KType has no cheap "all supertypes" answer without kotlin-reflect. Weak listeners. Some buses hold their handlers through weak references, which Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references covers in Part 4, so that a forgotten handler can be garbage collected. That hides the lapsed-listener bug instead of fixing it: the stale handler keeps running until the collector happens to run, which may be never in a quiet test. A handle the owner must close is the more honest design.

h: An API for Kotlin and Java callers · A subscription DSL: one block declares the wiring, one handle undoes it
x: Wiring by hand looks like this: five subscribe calls, five handles to keep, and a lookup in the program's settings between the third and the fourth. If that lookup throws, three handlers are already live, nobody holds their handles, and the program starts half wired. Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers built the fix at the print shop. A DSL, a small language made for one job, is an order form in code: each section is a block in braces, and inside a block you fill in boxes by name. Behind the form sits a builder that collects what the block declares, and an entry function that runs the block and then acts on all of it at once. Inside a block, the builder is the receiver, the object whose functions the block can call without naming it: Java // Java, through the Consumer entry point Subscription handle = Events.subscriptions(bus, timings, b -> { b.on(ParcelEvent.class, e -> tracking.add(e)); b.on(ParcelCollected.class, Handlers.timed(c -> loadBoard.add(c), "load", timings)); b.on(ParcelDelivered.class, Handlers.timed(d -> loadBoard.remove(d), "load", timings)); }); Kotlin val handle = bus.subscriptions(timings) { on<ParcelEvent> { tracking.add(it) } timed("load") { on<ParcelCollected> { loadBoard.add(it) } on<ParcelDelivered> { loadBoard.remove(it) } } } Each piece of it is a decision. on only adds a Pending(type, handler) to a list, and commit subscribes them all after the block has returned. So a block that throws subscribes nothing, and the caller gets back one Subscription that closes everything, in reverse order, the way nested try-with-resources blocks close. Pending<E> keeps a type and its handler together, so the builder can hold a List<Pending<*>> and still subscribe each entry without a cast. That star is the box whose label wore off, from Star projection: when you don't know the type. We don't know which event type each entry holds, and we don't need to, because each Pending knows its own. on<ParcelCollected> { ... } is inline with a reified E, so it can pass E::class on: the clerk's note from Type erasure and reified type parameters again. Its body is on(E::class, Handler { handler(it) }), and the compiler stops us right there: Cannot inline 'handler: (E) -> Unit' here: it might contain non-local returns. Add 'crossinline' modifier to parameter declaration 'handler: (E) -> Unit'. The lambda is called from inside another object, the Handler, which runs later, long after the function that built it has returned. Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns pictured that as steps sealed in an envelope for the print shop's night shift: nobody may write "stop the whole job" inside, because the clerk has gone home. crossinline is that seal. noinline would compile too, but it keeps a lambda object inside each Handler; crossinline pastes the body into the Handler class the compiler generates. One mistake the DSL can't catch at compile time is calling on from inside a handler. The handler lambda has no receiver of its own, so the builder is still in scope, and the call compiles. When the program runs, it would add to a builder that has already committed, and that subscription would silently never exist. A check(!committed) in on turns the mistake into an IllegalStateException at the first event, which the bus's try catches and reports. Before you run the demo, predict the handler count it prints after the block that fails. Predict the load: line (the fake clock moves 2 ms per read) and the handler count after the failed block. Run it. In SubscriptionsBuilder, make on subscribe at once: replace its body with bus.subscribe(type, handler) and keep nothing. Predict the last two lines, and run. Undo that. h: An API for Kotlin and Java callers · @DslMarker keeps each block inside its own section of the form
x: Inside timed("load") { ... }, two builders are in scope: the TimedGroup nearest to us, and the SubscriptionsBuilder around it. For a call that names no receiver, Kotlin tries each one in turn, nearest first. TimedGroup has no timed function, so this compiles: Java // Java has no implicit receivers: the same mistake must name the outer builder, b b.timed("load", g -> { g.on(ParcelCollected.class, c -> loadBoard.add(c)); b.timed("deliveries", d -> { d.on(ParcelDelivered.class, e -> loadBoard.remove(e)); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); Kotlin timed("load") { on<ParcelCollected> { loadBoard.add(it) } timed("deliveries") { on<ParcelDelivered> { loadBoard.remove(it) } } // reaches the OUTER builder } You meant "time the deliveries inside the load group". What you got is a sibling group: deliveries are timed under deliveries only, and the load group's numbers silently miss them. The demo prints {load=1, deliveries=1}, where you expected the load group to count two. The fix is the one that DSL lesson used to keep each section of the form offering only its own boxes. Mark both builder classes with an annotation, a label in the source that tools can read, which is itself annotated @DslMarker, and the nested call stops compiling: 'fun timed(name: String, block: TimedGroup.() -> Unit): Unit' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver. Use an explicit receiver if necessary. If you really want a sibling group, say so with a label, this@subscriptions.timed("deliveries") { ... }, which nobody types by accident. The marker counts on classes, or on a common superclass, and has no effect on functions. A nested block that can reach an outer builder will one day do it by accident. Mark the builders. Java never had this problem. Every Java lambda names its parameter, so reaching the outer builder takes b.timed, and a reviewer can see it. Java pays elsewhere. timed takes a TimedGroup.() -> Unit, which Java sees as a Function1<TimedGroup, Unit>, so each Java block must end with return Unit.INSTANCE. That cost is why the Java entry point, Events.subscriptions, takes a java.util.function.Consumer instead, and why the lab's Java code times a handler with Handlers.timed(...) rather than a group. In the demo, uncomment the nested timed, run it, then delete @DslMarker and predict the printed map. Reach the outer builder by accident Run MarkerDemo once as it is: timed groups: {load=1}. Uncomment the nested timed("deliveries") line (Step 2) and run. Read the error. Delete @DslMarker above annotation class EventsDsl in DslDemo.kt. Predict the printed map, then run. Put @DslMarker back, comment Step 2 out again and try Step 4, the labelled call. Then run MarkerDemoJava, where the same mistake has to be written out as b.timed. h: An API for Kotlin and Java callers · What Java sees, and a side door that still checks everything
x: Java sees only the class file: default arguments, a reified subscribe, object members and value classes each look odd or go missing there, and Class overloads, @JvmOverloads, @JvmStatic and a facade that still validates fix them javac, the Java compiler, never reads our Kotlin source. It reads the class files kotlinc wrote, and it reads them very literally. Here is what it finds when Java code meets the API as Kotlin developers usually write it. Every error below comes from the demo: Kotlin as written What Java gets The fix inline fun <reified E> subscribe(h) invisible: no suitable method found for subscribe((e)->{ }) a Class<E> overload fun <E> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, h) callable through JvmClassMappingKt.getKotlinClass(X.class) the same overload a constructor with default arguments new PlainBus() and the full one only: no suitable constructor found for PlainBus(String) @JvmOverloads a member of an object Registry.INSTANCE.publish(...) @JvmStatic a companion val SYSTEM Ticker.Companion.getSYSTEM() @JvmField top-level functions in Timing.kt TimingKt.timed(...) @file:JvmName("Handlers") a data class with value-class properties ParcelCollected(String,long) has private access in ParcelCollected, getters such as getWeight-RqKWbHU() a facade Read the table one row at a time with the earlier tracks in mind. A reified function is the clerk's note, and javac can't write one: it can't paste Kotlin code into a Java caller, so kotlinc marks the function synthetic, made by the compiler and hidden from Java source. Type erasure and reified type parameters gave the answer: Java hands over the class itself, ParcelCollected.class, so the bus needs an overload, a second subscribe with the same name that takes Java's Class<E>. The annotations each ask kotlinc for one small thing. @JvmOverloads asks for one Java constructor per default argument. @JvmStatic makes an object's member a real static method. @JvmField exposes a constant as a plain field, and @file:JvmName names the class that holds a file's top-level functions. The facade is the decision that matters, because it touches the checks. A facade, the hotel reception desk from Adapter and Facade, is one small object that gives outsiders a simple way in. Value classes and what they compile to warned that @JvmName on a function that takes a value class lets Java pass a raw long straight past init. Our facade does the opposite. It takes plain values and builds the value classes itself, so every init block runs: Java ParcelCollected c = Events.collected("PP-7781", 2_500); // validates: "7781" throws long grams = Events.grams(c); bus.subscribe(ParcelCollected.class, e -> loadBoard.add(Events.parcelId(e), Events.grams(e))); Kotlin object Events { @JvmStatic fun collected(parcelId: String, grams: Long): ParcelCollected = ParcelCollected(ParcelId(parcelId), Weight(grams)) // the init blocks run @JvmStatic fun grams(event: Handover): Long = event.weight.grams } @JvmExposeBoxed, Experimental in Kotlin 2.4 and switched on with an opt-in, would give Java new ParcelCollected(new ParcelId(...), new Weight(...)) and a boxed getter. In a quick test with its module-wide flag, the getter on the event interface itself stayed mangled, so Java code that knows only ParcelEvent would still need Events.parcelId(e). Keep the facade until that changes. Some of the Java surface came free from earlier decisions. Lesson 2's Handler<in E> shows up as Handler<? super E>, so a Java Handler<ParcelEvent> fits any subscription, and the lab's Java support desk counts failed deliveries with one. kotlinc writes PermittedSubclasses for the sealed model, so a Java switch over a ParcelEvent with one case per leaf compiles with no default. Subscription.close() declares no checked exception, the kind Java forces every caller to catch, so try-with-resources needs no catch. h: An API for Kotlin and Java callers · Design review: defend each choice, or say when you'd undo it
x: A design review is a meeting where you explain each choice in a design while someone sceptical asks why. It's where you find out which decisions you can defend. Here are the questions I'd expect about this library, with the answer I'd give. Disagree where your program differs. "Why value classes, if Java needs a facade?" Keep them. In the Kotlin model, a swapped id and weight don't compile, and an invalid tracking number can't exist. The facade costs one file. If most callers were Java, I'd undo it and use plain records with compact constructors. "A Weight has no unit." Keep it. The one-field rule made that choice cheap, and the door is the right place for any other unit: a partner's pounds become grams in the parser, once. A unit field inside Weight would cost an object per weight and buy nothing. "Supertype dispatch will surprise people." Keep it, and write it down. The sealed hierarchy keeps the set of keys small, fixed and testable, and the order is a tested promise. The surprise to warn about is the other side of that promise: a ParcelEvent handler also hears every event type added next year. "in, adapters, casts: isn't that a lot of machinery?" Keep in: it's what lets one tracking handler serve every subscription, from Kotlin and from Java. The single cast is checked by type.cast and guaranteed by the keys. "Delivery is synchronous and lives in memory." Keep it for connecting the parts of one program. Undo it for anything that must survive a crash or reach another program, because the bus forgets everything when the program stops. Those events need storage that survives a restart, such as a database table written in the same step as the change, or a message broker. Guava's documentation for its own EventBus lists no way to slow a fast publisher, little control over threads and no exception passing among its reasons to look elsewhere. This bus fixes the last one with an ErrorHandler, and not the first two. "DropDuplicates remembers every event for ever." Undo it as written. Bound it to a window of recent events, or let the handler keep its own record of the scans it has seen, which also survives a restart. "The DSL commits after the block. What if commit fails halfway?" Today subscribe can't fail. If it ever can, commit must close what it already opened before it rethrows. Notice the pattern in the answers. A choice is safe when an earlier lesson's mechanism forces it: in for a consumer, no else on a sealed when, a Class<E> overload because Java can't call a reified function. It's a judgment call when it trades cost for safety: value classes with a facade, synchronous delivery, a memory with no limit. Those are the ones to write down, with the condition that would make you undo them. x: Add subscribeOnce, with its Kotlin sugar and its Java door A welcome text must go out for a new sender's first collection only. Start with the core, in Kotlin, taking a KClass. The handle closes itself, and compareAndSet makes sure only one of eight publishing threads runs the handler, the balking idea from Concurrency patterns that tie it all together. One race needs care: an event can arrive before handle.set has run, so the code closes again after setting it. fun <E : ParcelEvent> subscribeOnce(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription { val fired = AtomicBoolean() val handle = AtomicReference<Subscription>() handle.set(subscribe(type) { event -> if (fired.compareAndSet(false, true)) { // 1. only the first event wins try { handler.handle(event) } // 2. do the work finally { handle.get()?.close() } // 3. stop further deliveries } }) if (fired.get()) handle.get().close() // an event won before the handle was set return handle.get() } // What Java sees for the core: a KClass parameter it can only reach the long way round. bus.subscribeOnce(JvmClassMappingKt.getKotlinClass(ParcelCollected.class), c -> sendWelcome(c)); Add the Kotlin sugar: a one-line reified wrapper. It needs no noinline or crossinline: its parameter is a Handler, not a function type, so there is nothing to inline. inline fun <reified E : ParcelEvent> subscribeOnce(handler: Handler<E>): Subscription = subscribeOnce(E::class, handler) bus.subscribeOnce<ParcelCollected> { sendWelcome(it) } // Java can't see the reified wrapper: javac reports "no suitable method found for subscribeOnce" bus.subscribeOnce(c -> sendWelcome(c)); Add the Java door: a Class<E> overload that converts and delegates. Because Handler is declared in, Java sees Handler<? super E>, so a general handler fits too. fun <E : ParcelEvent> subscribeOnce(type: Class<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription = subscribeOnce(type.kotlin, handler) bus.subscribeOnce(ParcelCollected.class, c -> sendWelcome(Events.parcelId(c))); Last, pin it from both sides. Mark handler crossinline: it's called from inside the Handler object, and its body can still be inlined there Remove inline: the function then works without changes Mark the function @PublishedApi Change Handler { handler(it) } to handler as Handler<E> The lambda runs later, from another object, so a non-local return inside it couldn't work, and the compiler asks you to rule it out. noinline would compile too, but it keeps a lambda object inside each Handler. h: An API for Kotlin and Java callers · Key terms
x: DSL A small language made for one job, written as ordinary Kotlin calls and blocks. Entry function The function that creates a builder, runs your block on it and returns the result, such as bus.subscriptions { }. @DslMarker An annotation for your own DSL marker annotation: inside a block, only the nearest marked receiver can be called implicitly. crossinline A modifier for a lambda parameter of an inline function that is called from another object or lambda; it forbids non-local returns. Facade for Java A small object of static functions that takes and returns plain Java types and builds the Kotlin types inside. @JvmOverloads Makes kotlinc generate one Java overload per trailing default parameter. @JvmStatic Makes a member of an object or companion a real static method, so Java needs no INSTANCE or Companion. Design review A meeting where you defend each design choice, say what forces it, and say what would make you undo it. Why does the subscriptions builder collect first and subscribe at the end? A block that throws halfway then subscribes nothing, and the caller gets one handle that closes everything the block declared. Why must the lambda of inline fun <reified E> on(handler: (E) -> Unit) be crossinline? The body calls it from inside another object, the Handler, which runs later. crossinline forbids non-local returns so it can still be inlined there. What does @DslMarker stop, and what can't it stop? It stops implicit calls to an outer marked builder from an inner block. It can't stop a call from inside a handler lambda, which has no receiver: use a runtime check. Java can't call your reified subscribe<E>. What do you add? A Class<E> overload that delegates with type.kotlin. The reified function stays a one-line wrapper for Kotlin. A Kotlin constructor where every parameter has a default: what does Java get without @JvmOverloads? A constructor with no arguments and the full one. @JvmOverloads adds the ones in between. Why a facade like Events.collected(String, long) instead of @JvmName on functions that take value classes? The facade builds the value classes, so their init checks run. @JvmName lets Java pass raw values straight past them. What does a Java caller get for free from Handler<in E> and a Kotlin sealed model? Handler<? super E> in every signature, and an exhaustive switch over the sealed types with no default.

h: An API for Kotlin and Java callers · Go deeper
x: A production version of this library would add, roughly in this order: Asynchronous lanes. An executor per group of handlers, with one single-threaded lane per tracking number so the events for one parcel keep their order, and a bounded queue in front of each lane. That's also where backpressure lives, the idea of a slow receiver slowing a fast sender: when a lane is full, the publisher waits, or the event is kept to try again later. Real metrics. Replace Timings with timers from a metrics library such as Micrometer, named after each subscription, so a slow handler shows up on the same dashboards as the rest of the program. Durability. Events that must survive a crash, or reach other programs, go into a database table in the same transaction as the change that caused them (a pattern often called an outbox), and a separate job sends them on to a message broker. The in-process bus stays for connecting the parts of one program. A shelf for refused scans. Parsed.Rejected goes to a store with its reason, a counter, and a small tool to replay the scans once the bug behind them is fixed. Versioned events. Stable type names with @SerialName if you serialize with kotlinx.serialization, and parser branches that map old names to new types. A checked public API. on<E> and subscribe<E> are public inline functions, so their bodies are compiled into every caller, and the @JvmOverloads overloads are part of what Java callers link against. A binary-compatibility check in the build catches a change that would break callers compiled against the previous version. @JvmExposeBoxed, once it is stable, if it also covers interface members. Until then, the Events facade is the Java door. One thing it should not add is registration by scanning for annotations, Guava style (@Subscribe on methods, found through reflection). Guava's own documentation lists the costs: subscribers are hard to find from the publisher, and reflection breaks under the tools that shrink and rename code for release. Explicit on<E> calls keep every subscription visible in the code that owns it.

x: Class loaders and initialization, reading bytecode, invokedynamic, JDK and generated proxies, the ClassFile API and agents. This track goes backstage in the JVM, with a theatre company as the guide. By the end, you can say which class loader defined a class and exactly when its static initializer runs, the way a props team fetches each prop only when a scene needs it. You can write a JDK dynamic proxy, a stand-in at the stage door, that gets equals, exceptions and default methods right. You can build subclass proxies with Byte Buddy, and predict whether Spring, Quarkus ArC or Hibernate will intercept a call, self-calls and Kotlin's final members included. Then you'll read and print class files with the ClassFile API, and change a loaded class under live objects with an agent. Proxies get the most room, in lessons 4 and 5, because they sit under every annotation a framework honours. You need to read basic Java and Kotlin, and nothing about the JVM's insides. The Decorator and Proxy lesson of the patterns track is a useful warm-up for lesson 4. Install JDK 25. The labs compile with release 21, so they run on JDK 21 or later. The ClassFile API is final only from JDK 24, so lesson 6 keeps that code in single-file programs under labs/bytecode/preview/, which you run with java File.java on JDK 24 or later. The labs live in labs/bytecode, one package per lesson (workbench.bytecode.l01 to l07). Lessons 1, 3, 4 and 6 are in Java, and lessons 2, 5 and 7 in Kotlin. Every sample and demo comes in both languages. The tests read the JVM's own view of your code: class identity and initialization, the members javap would list, call counts through proxies, and a class-file reader checked against ASM. Lesson 7's tests attach an agent to the test JVM, which the build allows with -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading. From labs/, run ./gradlew :bytecode:test --tests 'workbench.bytecode.lNN.*' until it passes. What the frameworks do (Spring, Quarkus, Hibernate) comes from their documentation; the track shows both proxy models with Byte Buddy instead of running the frameworks. A class is (binary name, defining loader). Loaders ask their parent first, and the same bytes defined by two loaders are two classes with separate statics. Loading, linking and initialization are separate and lazy. <clinit> runs once, in source order, under a lock: a throw poisons the class (NoClassDefFoundError from then on), and two initializers that need each other can deadlock. javap shows the JVM's shape: a typed operand stack, a constant pool referenced by number, descriptors like (JI)J, and Kotlin lowered to getters, Companion, INSTANCE, $default and final members. invokedynamic links a call site once, through a bootstrap method. Lambdas become hidden $$Lambda classes, and the call site type shows what they capture. A JDK proxy is a generated final $ProxyN that boxes the arguments and calls one handler. Answer Object methods by identity, run defaults with invokeDefault, unwrap InvocationTargetException, and never retry a default method as a whole. Subclass proxies need non-final classes and methods. Whether self-calls are intercepted depends on whether the proxy is the object (ArC, @SuperCall) or forwards to a target (Spring AOP). The ClassFile API (final in JDK 24) parses class files into lazy models, builds them from lambdas, verifies their types (not their results), and transforms them element by element. The JDK builds its own proxies and lambdas with it. Agents get an Instrumentation: transformers see classes as they load, and retransformation swaps method bodies in place for every caller, never the class's shape. Loading one into a running JVM warns since JDK 21.
