h: Class loading, bytecode and dynamic proxies: track quiz
x: static final Integer CURTAIN_MINUTES = 5; sits in class ShowConfig, which also has a static {} block that reads a settings file. A test only reads ShowConfig.CURTAIN_MINUTES. Does the file get read? No: it's static final, so javac copied the value Yes: Integer isn't a constant variable, so the read initializes ShowConfig and runs its static block Only if the JIT compiled the test Only the first time the test runs on a machine, because the value is cached on disk Only primitives and String with constant initializers are constant variables. The boxed Integer needs Integer.valueOf at run time, so reading it is an ordinary static read that triggers initialization. Make it static final int (or Kotlin const val), and the read no longer touches the class. A theatre app reloads its scene plugins without a restart, through a new class loader each time. After a reload, the log says class theatre.Cue cannot be cast to class theatre.Cue, naming two different loaders. What's the most likely cause? Two versions of the Cue source file The JIT inlined an old version of Cue Cue is missing equals An object created through the previous loader survived the reload, for example in a static cache owned by a loader that outlives it, and met code from the new loader Each reload defines Cue again in a new loader, so the new Cue is a different class from the old one. A reference kept somewhere that outlives the reload still points to an old Cue. The same reference also keeps the old loader, and all its classes, in memory. Java code must call a Kotlin object Lighting { fun fadeSeconds(steps: Long, stepMillis: Int = 32): Long }. Which Java call compiles with no change to the Kotlin side? Lighting.INSTANCE.fadeSeconds(12_500, 32) Lighting.fadeSeconds(12_500) Lighting.fadeSeconds(12_500, 32) Lighting.Companion.fadeSeconds(12_500) An object is a class with a static final INSTANCE, and its functions are instance methods unless marked @JvmStatic. Default values exist only in a synthetic fadeSeconds$default method, so Java passes every argument unless the function has @JvmOverloads. An object has no Companion. javap -c on a class Rehearsal shows invokedynamic #0:accept:(Ltheatre/Rehearsal;J)Ljava/util/function/Consumer; inside the method runAct. What does each call to runAct allocate for that line? Nothing: lambdas are always shared One object per cue the lambda later receives One Consumer object, because the lambda captures this and a long A new hidden class per call The call site type lists the captured values: the Rehearsal (this) and a long. A capturing lambda allocates one object each time its expression is evaluated, so here once per runAct call. The hidden class is built once per call site, not per call. Which handler bug makes listeners.remove(proxy) on an ArrayList return false for a JDK proxy that was just added? Not unwrapping InvocationTargetException Forwarding equals to the target, so proxy.equals(proxy) asks target.equals(proxy) Using invokeDefault for default methods Creating the proxy with the wrong class loader ArrayList.remove(Object) uses equals. A forwarding handler sends it to the target, which doesn't consider the proxy equal to itself. Answer equals and hashCode by the proxy's identity in the handler. Your retry proxy for SeatDesk retries on DeskUnavailableException. holdAndConfirm is a default method that calls hold and then confirm. So that a failed confirmation never holds a second seat, how should the handler treat it? Run it with InvocationHandler.invokeDefault, so its inner calls come back through the handler and each one is retried on its own Retry holdAndConfirm as a whole, like any other method Forward it to the target with method.invoke Skip it: default methods can't be proxied With invokeDefault, the body runs with this as the proxy, so confirm is retried as a confirmation, and the hold that already worked isn't sent again. Retrying the whole method repeats the hold, and forwarding to the target hides the inner calls from the retry logic. You move the box office app from Spring Boot to Quarkus. bookAll() calls this.book(seat), and book is @Transactional. What changes? Nothing: both frameworks use proxies the same way Quarkus refuses to build the bean Under Quarkus, the outer call loses its transaction Under Spring, the inner calls had no transaction of their own (the proxy forwards). Under ArC they're intercepted, so each book call now gets the transactional interceptor Spring's proxy forwards to a separate target, so this.book() bypasses it. Quarkus ArC's intercepted subclass is the bean itself, and the Quarkus documentation says self-interception works. Transaction boundaries, and with them locking and saving, can change without a single edited line. Which tool fits each job? You need to (a) time every method of six seat-desk interfaces you own, (b) add a lazily loaded proxy for a database entity class, and (c) count calls to a method of a final class from a library, including its self-calls, without editing it. (a) agent, (b) JDK proxy, (c) Spring AOP (a) Byte Buddy subclass, (b) agent, (c) JDK proxy (a) JDK proxy, (b) Byte Buddy subclass, (c) agent with Advice All three: a JDK proxy You own interfaces, so one JDK proxy handler covers all six. An entity is a class, so a lazy proxy must be a generated subclass, which is what Hibernate builds with Byte Buddy. A final class with self-calls rules out every proxy; an agent's Advice edits the method itself. A hand-written constant-pool reader works on most classes, but fails on one with unknown constant pool tag 72 near the end. What's the most likely bug? It forgot that Long and Double entries use two pool indexes, so its count is off and it reads past the pool It doesn't handle Kotlin classes The class file is corrupt It reads big-endian instead of little-endian A missed extra index after an 8-byte constant shifts the numbering, so the loop expects one entry more than exists and reads the bytes after the pool as a tag. The symptom shows up far from the cause. Class files are big-endian, which is what DataInputStream reads. An agent attached to a running program adds a field to SoundBoard while retransforming it, so it can count calls. What happens, and what's the fix? It works for objects created after the attach The JVM runs SoundBoard's static initializer again retransformClasses fails and nothing changes: retransformation can't add fields. Keep the counter in a separate public class that the copied advice calls It works, but prints the JEP 451 warning Retransformation may change method bodies, the constant pool and attributes, never the class's fields, methods, signatures, modifiers or superclass. Byte Buddy's disableClassFormatChanges() plus Advice keeps to that rule. The JEP 451 warning is about attaching late, not about what the transformation does.

h: Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization · Three class loaders, and why each asks its parent first
x: Your compiled program is a pile of class files in folders and jars (a jar is a zip file of class files). The JVM reads none of them until some code needs one. The object that finds a class's bytes and turns them into a Class the JVM can run is a class loader. Let's set the theatre up properly before we lean on it. The building has its own store of things every show needs, such as chairs and the curtain. The company has a props department for rarer items. And each production has a stage manager who looks after the props made for that show. A class loader is one of these three people. A class is a prop, and its class file is the drawing the prop is made from. Ask three classes who loaded them, and you get three answers. ShowProgram here is our own main class: Java System.out.println(String.class.getClassLoader()); // null System.out.println(java.sql.Connection.class.getClassLoader()); // ...ClassLoaders$PlatformClassLoader@<hash> System.out.println(ShowProgram.class.getClassLoader()); // ...ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@<hash> Kotlin println(String::class.java.classLoader) // null println(java.sql.Connection::class.java.classLoader) // ...ClassLoaders$PlatformClassLoader@<hash> println(ShowProgram::class.java.classLoader) // ...ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@<hash> The JDK has three built-in class loaders. The bootstrap loader is part of the JVM itself and loads java.base, the module that holds String, List and the other basics. A module is a named group of packages. The bootstrap loader has no Java object of its own, so getClassLoader() returns null. The building's store has no name badge. The platform loader loads the rest of the JDK's modules, such as java.sql for databases: that's the props department. The app loader loads your class path, the list of folders and jars you give the java command: your own code and every library you added, Kotlin's standard library included. That's the stage manager. Each loader has a parent. The app loader's parent is the platform loader, and the platform loader's parent is the bootstrap loader. When code asks a loader for a class, the default loadClass method does three things in order: It checks whether it already loaded that name (findLoadedClass). If not, it asks its parent, which asks its own parent first. Only when every parent says no does it look for the class itself (findClass). That's the stage manager asking the head of props, who asks the building's store, before anyone makes a new crown. It's called parent-first delegation. It's why java.lang.String always comes from the bootstrap loader, even if some jar on your class path holds a class with that very name. A stray jar can't replace a JDK class. The loader that finally builds the class, by calling defineClass, is its defining loader, and it is part of the class's identity. At run time a class is the pair (name, defining loader). The name is the binary name, the full name such as theatre.Scene, or theatre.Scene$Cue for a class nested inside Scene. Two loaders can each define a class with the same name, and the last section shows what that does to a cast. Kotlin adds nothing special here. kotlin.Unit is an ordinary class in an ordinary jar, so the app loader loads it like any other library class. Every loader asks its parent first. That's why the JDK's own classes always win. So far, "loading a class" has sounded like one event. Inside the JVM it's three. Who loaded what Before you run it, write down the loader and the module you expect for String, java.sql.Connection, the demo class itself and kotlin.Unit. Run LoaderTour from the labs/ folder with the command below, then run the Kotlin twin. Compare the two "classes loaded so far" numbers. Why might the Kotlin one be higher? LoaderTour.java package workbench.bytecode.l01; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; /** Which loader defined which class, and the chain a class-loading request walks up. */ public class LoaderTour { public static void main(String[] args) { show(String.class); // java.base show(java.sql.Connection.class); // java.sql, a platform module show(LoaderTour.class); // this program, on the class path show(kotlin.Unit.class); // the Kotlin standard library jar, also on the class path StringBuilder chain = new StringBuilder(); for (ClassLoader l = LoaderTour.class.getClassLoader(); l != null; l = l.getParent()) { chain.append(l.getName()).append(" -> "); } System.out.println("delegation chain: " + chain + "bootstrap (null)"); System.out.println("classes loaded so far: " + ManagementFactory.getClassLoadingMXBean().getLoadedClassCount()); } static void show(Class<?> c) { ClassLoader l = c.getClassLoader(); System.out.printf("%-34s loader=%-9s module=%s%n", c.getName(), l == null ? "bootstrap" : l.getName(), c.getModule().getName()); } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l01.LoaderTour labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l01/LoaderTour.java LoaderTour.kt package workbench.bytecode.l01 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory /** Which loader defined which class, and the chain a class-loading request walks up. */ fun main() { show(String::class.java) // java.lang.String, in java.base show(java.sql.Connection::class.java) // java.sql, a platform module show(TourMarker::class.java) // this program, on the class path show(Unit::class.java) // the Kotlin standard library jar, also on the class path val chain = generateSequence(TourMarker::class.java.classLoader) { it.parent } .joinToString("") { "${it.name} -> " } println("delegation chain: ${chain}bootstrap (null)") println("classes loaded so far: ${ManagementFactory.getClassLoadingMXBean().loadedClassCount}") } private class TourMarker private fun show(c: Class<*>) { val l = c.classLoader println("%-34s loader=%-9s module=%s".format(c.name, l?.name ?: "bootstrap", c.module.name)) } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l01.LoaderTourKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l01/LoaderTour.kt String has the bootstrap loader (printed as null, shown here as bootstrap) in java.base, and java.sql.Connection has the platform loader in java.sql. The demo class and kotlin.Unit both have the app loader and no module name (module=null), because the class path is one unnamed module. The chain is app -> platform -> bootstrap. On JDK 25 one run counted 948 loaded classes for Java and 986 for Kotlin: the Kotlin program touches more of its standard library, and every class it touches is loaded. ClassLoader (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization · Loading, linking and initialization: three steps, and only the last runs your code
x: How a class gets in: parent-first delegation, then loading, linking and initialization Loading a class and running its start-up code are separate events, and they can happen far apart. Chapter 5 of the JVM specification, the document that says how every JVM must behave, splits the work into three steps. HotSpot, the JVM inside the JDK you installed, runs each step as late as it is allowed to. A new prop goes through the same three steps. Someone fetches it. Before any scene uses it, the crew checks it, gives it a labelled spot on the props table and fills in the cue sheet that says where it's needed. Last comes the dress rehearsal, the only step that puts actors on stage. Loading finds the bytes, in a folder, a jar, or made in memory, and turns them into a Class object with defineClass. That's fetching the prop. Linking gets the class ready, in three parts. Verification checks that the bytecode, the instructions the compiler wrote into the class file (the next lesson reads them), is type-safe: no instruction treats a number as a string. Preparation creates the static fields and sets them to their defaults, 0, false or null: an empty, labelled spot on the table. Resolution turns the names the class uses, such as "method fire in class Lights", into direct links. It may do that one name at a time, the first time each is used. Initialization runs the class's static initializer, which javac names <clinit> ("class init"): every static field initializer and static {} block, top to bottom. That's the dress rehearsal. Two small experiments show the gaps between the steps. A generated class with broken bytecode was accepted by defineClass on JDK 25, and the VerifyError came only when code first asked for its methods. A class that referred to a deleted Helper class loaded and ran fine. It failed with NoClassDefFoundError only when the branch that used Helper ran. That second experiment is where the picture breaks. A real crew checks a whole prop before the show. The JVM may fill in the cross-references lazily, one name at a time, and never at all for code that never runs. Initialization is the step your code can see, and its triggers are exact. Section 12.4.1 of the Java Language Specification lists them: creating an instance, calling a static method, assigning a static field, or reading a static field that isn't a constant variable. Initializing a class first initializes its superclass. Reflection counts too: code that looks up classes and their members by name while the program runs, such as Class.forName(name). These do not initialize a class: reading a static final primitive or String whose value the compiler can work out, because javac copied the value into your class file; Limits.class, new Limits[3] and Class.forName(name, false, loader); reading an inherited static field through a subclass: Child.parentValue initializes only Parent, the class that declares the field. The constant rule surprises people most, and it's the warm-up question. static final int MAX_CAST = 12 is a constant variable. static final Integer CAP = 12 is not, because boxing calls Integer.valueOf. Reading the first leaves Limits alone, and reading the second runs <clinit>. Kotlin draws the same line between const val and a plain val. Loading isn't initialization. Only the first real use runs <clinit>. So <clinit> runs late, and it runs once. Those two facts are behind three real bugs, and the call sheet has the first one. The initialization puzzle Read InitPuzzle (or InitPuzzle.kt). For each of the eight steps, write down whether a <clinit> line prints after it, and which one. Run it and check your list. Change CAP to static final int CAP = 12; (in Kotlin, make it const val). Predict step 4, then run it again. InitPuzzle.java package workbench.bytecode.l01; /** Predict which steps run a static initializer. Each <clinit> prints one indented line. */ public class InitPuzzle { static class Parent { static int parentValue = 1; static { System.out.println(" Parent.<clinit>"); } } static class Child extends Parent { static { System.out.println(" Child.<clinit>"); } } static class Limits { static final int MAX_CAST = 12; // a constant variable: javac copies 12 into callers static final Integer CAP = 12; // boxed, so not a constant variable static { System.out.println(" Limits.<clinit>"); } } static class Lazy { static { System.out.println(" Lazy.<clinit>"); } static void touch() {} } interface Step { void run() throws Exception; } static void step(String what, Step s) throws Exception { System.out.println(what); s.run(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { step("1. read Child.parentValue", () -> { int v = Child.parentValue; }); step("2. new Child()", () -> new Child()); step("3. read Limits.MAX_CAST", () -> { int v = Limits.MAX_CAST; }); step("4. read Limits.CAP", () -> { Integer v = Limits.CAP; }); step("5. new Lazy[3]", () -> { Lazy[] a = new Lazy[3]; }); step("6. Lazy.class", () -> { Class<?> c = Lazy.class; }); step("7. Class.forName(name, false, loader)", () -> Class.forName("workbench.bytecode.l01.InitPuzzle$Lazy", false, InitPuzzle.class.getClassLoader())); step("8. Lazy.touch()", Lazy::touch); } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l01.InitPuzzle labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l01/InitPuzzle.java InitPuzzle.kt package workbench.bytecode.l01 // Kotlin has no static fields of its own. An `object` and a companion object compile to a // class with a static initializer, so the same JVM rules decide when the init blocks run. open class KParent { companion object { @JvmField var parentValue = 1 init { println(" KParent.<clinit>") } } } class KChild : KParent() { companion object { init { println(" KChild.<clinit>") } } } object KLimits { const val MAX_CAST = 12 // a constant: kotlinc copies 12 into callers val CAP: Int = 12 // a property: reading it goes through KLimits init { println(" KLimits.<clinit>") } } object KLazy { init { println(" KLazy.<clinit>") } fun touch() {} } private fun step(what: String, s: () -> Any?) { println(what) s() } /** Predict which steps run a static initializer. Each one prints one indented line. */ fun main() { step("1. read KParent.parentValue") { KParent.parentValue } step("2. KChild()") { KChild() } step("3. read KLimits.MAX_CAST") { KLimits.MAX_CAST } step("4. read KLimits.CAP") { KLimits.CAP } step("5. arrayOfNulls<KLazy>(3)") { arrayOfNulls<KLazy>(3) } step("6. KLazy::class.java") { KLazy::class.java } step("7. Class.forName(name, false, loader)") { Class.forName("workbench.bytecode.l01.KLazy", false, KLazy::class.java.classLoader) } step("8. KLazy.touch()") { KLazy.touch() } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l01.InitPuzzleKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l01/InitPuzzle.kt Step 1 prints only Parent.<clinit>, because the field belongs to Parent. Step 2 prints only Child.<clinit>, because Parent is already done. Step 4 prints Limits.<clinit>, step 8 prints Lazy.<clinit>, and steps 3, 5, 6 and 7 print nothing. After the change, step 4 prints nothing too, and Limits is never initialized at all. The Kotlin twin shows the same pattern with KParent, KChild, KLimits and KLazy. Fetch, check and label, then the dress rehearsal: a class can be loaded and linked long before it is initialized. Only the triggers in the bottom box run its static initializer. h: Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization · The dress rehearsal runs once: order, failure and deadlock
x: The show program keeps a call sheet: the list that tells each player how many minutes before curtain-up to arrive. Leads come 90 minutes early and the chorus 45, and anyone else gets a default of 60, read from a setting. Here it is, trimmed from the lab's starting code: Java // Naive: the shared instance is built too early public final class CallSheet { private static final Map<String, Integer> MINUTES_BY_ROLE = Map.of("LEAD", 90, "CHORUS", 45); public static final CallSheet INSTANCE = new CallSheet(); // runs here private static final int DEFAULT_MINUTES = Integer.parseInt(System.getProperty("calls.default.minutes", "60")); private final int fallbackMinutes = DEFAULT_MINUTES; // still 0 here } Kotlin // Naive: the shared instance is built too early class CallSheet private constructor() { val fallbackMinutes = DEFAULT_MINUTES // still 0 here companion object { private val MINUTES_BY_ROLE = mapOf("LEAD" to 90, "CHORUS" to 45) @JvmField val INSTANCE = CallSheet() // runs here private val DEFAULT_MINUTES = System.getProperty("calls.default.minutes", "60").toInt() } } Ask it about the violinist, a role the table doesn't list, and the lab's test reports: CallSheet: an unlisted role gets the 60-minute default, not 0 FAILED expected: 60 but was: 0 Nothing threw. The violinist is now part of the overture. The JVM did exactly what the source says: <clinit> runs top to bottom, and the INSTANCE line builds the object before the next line has set DEFAULT_MINUTES. The constructor reads that field while it still holds the 0 from preparation. Picture a dress rehearsal that plays the scenes in script order, even when scene 2 needs a prop that only scene 3 brings on. With a constant initializer (= 60) the bug would disappear, because javac copies a constant into the code that reads it. That's why this bug tends to arrive on the day someone makes a constant configurable. You'll fix it in the lab. <clinit> has two more properties, and both cause real outages. It runs once, and a failure is permanent. Here's a class that reads a script file while it initializes: Java static class Script { static final String TEXT = load(Path.of("hamlet.txt")); // runs inside <clinit> static String load(Path p) { if (!Files.exists(p)) throw new IllegalStateException("script file missing: " + p); return "To be, or not to be"; } } Kotlin object Script { val TEXT: String = load(Path.of("hamlet.txt")) // runs inside <clinit> fun load(p: Path): String { check(Files.exists(p)) { "script file missing: $p" } return "To be, or not to be" } } With the file missing, a small program touched Script.TEXT three times. On JDK 25 it printed: 1: java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError cause: java.lang.IllegalStateException: script file missing: hamlet.txt 2: java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class Rehearsal$Script cause: java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError: Exception java.lang.IllegalStateException: script file missing: hamlet.txt [in thread "main"] 3: java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class Rehearsal$Script cause: ...the same as 2 The first use gets ExceptionInInitializerError. The JVM marks the class as failed, and every later use, from any thread, gets NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class. Since JDK 21 that error's cause names the first exception and the thread it happened in. A theatre would hold the dress rehearsal again tomorrow. The JVM never tries again, for as long as that class loader lives, and that's where the picture breaks. In a long log you often see the NoClassDefFoundError hundreds of times, and the real cause once, near the top. The third property is that <clinit> runs under a lock. One thread runs it, and every other thread that needs the class waits. That lock is what made the holder idiom in the memory model track safe, and it can also deadlock: two threads each wait for something the other holds, for ever. In the Try it below, Cast's initializer reads Costumes, Costumes's initializer reads Cast, and two threads start one each. Each thread holds one class's lock and waits for the other's. Both threads report RUNNABLE, the most hopeful state a stuck thread can show. ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads(), the JDK's deadlock detector, finds nothing. jstack, a JDK tool that prints every thread's stack, shows this on JDK 25: "cast" #21 ... in Object.wait() java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE at workbench.bytecode.l01.InitDeadlockDemo$Cast.<clinit>(InitDeadlockDemo.java:10) - waiting on the Class initialization monitor for workbench.bytecode.l01.InitDeadlockDemo$Costumes There's no "Found one Java-level deadlock" section. When a program hangs at start-up, search the dump for Class initialization monitor. Keep static initializers boring: constants and small fixed tables only. Reading files, calling other computers and reading other classes' statics belong in ordinary code that runs at start-up, or in a lazy holder. One question from the start is still open: how can a class with a familiar name be a stranger? Deadlock two classes Run InitDeadlockDemo (or the Kotlin twin). It starts two threads, one that needs Cast and one that needs Costumes, and waits one second. Read the state and the top frame it prints for each thread, and what the deadlock detector says. Optional: run it with -Pargs=wait, then run the printed jstack command in a second terminal and search for Class initialization monitor. Fix it: make Costumes.COUNT a constant (static final long COUNT = 36; with no static block, or const val COUNT = 36L in Kotlin) and run it again. InitDeadlockDemo.java package workbench.bytecode.l01; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.util.List; /** Two static initializers that need each other, started from two threads. */ public class InitDeadlockDemo { static class Cast { static final long ACTORS; static { pause(); ACTORS = Costumes.COUNT / 3; } // needs Costumes: 3 costumes an actor } static class Costumes { static final long COUNT; static { pause(); COUNT = Cast.ACTORS * 3; } // needs Cast } static void pause() { try { Thread.sleep(200); } catch (InterruptedException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Thread a = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(Cast.ACTORS), "cast"); Thread b = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(Costumes.COUNT), "costumes"); a.setDaemon(true); // daemon, so the JVM can still exit at the end b.setDaemon(true); a.start(); b.start(); Thread.sleep(1_000); for (Thread t : List.of(a, b)) { StackTraceElement[] stack = t.getStackTrace(); // empty once the thread has ended System.out.printf("%-8s state=%s at %s%n", t.getName(), t.getState(), stack.length > 0 ? stack[0] : "(finished)"); } long[] stuck = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads(); System.out.println("deadlock detector: " + (stuck == null ? "found nothing" : stuck.length + " threads")); if (args.length > 0) { // -Pargs=wait gives you 30 s to run jstack System.out.println("jstack " + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + " (search for 'Class initialization monitor')"); Thread.sleep(30_000); } } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l01.InitDeadlockDemo labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l01/InitDeadlockDemo.java InitDeadlockDemo.kt package workbench.bytecode.l01 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Two objects whose initializers need each other, started from two threads. object KCast { @JvmField val ACTORS: Long init { pausePlease(); ACTORS = KCostumes.COUNT / 3 } // needs KCostumes: 3 costumes an actor } object KCostumes { @JvmField val COUNT: Long init { pausePlease(); COUNT = KCast.ACTORS * 3 } // needs KCast } private fun pausePlease() = Thread.sleep(200) fun main(args: Array<String>) { // daemon threads, so the JVM can still exit at the end val a = thread(name = "cast", isDaemon = true) { println(KCast.ACTORS) } val b = thread(name = "costumes", isDaemon = true) { println(KCostumes.COUNT) } Thread.sleep(1_000) for (t in listOf(a, b)) { val top = t.stackTrace.firstOrNull() ?: "(finished)" // empty once the thread has ended println("%-8s state=%s at %s".format(t.name, t.state, top)) } val stuck = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads() println("deadlock detector: " + (stuck?.let { "${it.size} threads" } ?: "found nothing")) if (args.isNotEmpty()) { // -Pargs=wait gives you 30 s to run jstack println("jstack ${ProcessHandle.current().pid()} (search for 'Class initialization monitor')") Thread.sleep(30_000) } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l01.InitDeadlockDemoKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l01/InitDeadlockDemo.kt Both threads show state=RUNNABLE with a top frame inside a <clinit>, and the detector prints found nothing. The JVM exits only because the threads are daemons, threads it doesn't wait for. In jstack each thread is in Object.wait() and waiting on the Class initialization monitor for the other class. After the fix, Cast reads a constant and no longer needs Costumes to initialize, so the threads print 12 and 36, both show state=TERMINATED at (finished), and the program ends normally.

h: Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization · Same drawing, two stage managers: one class defined twice
x: Because the loader is part of a class's identity, a loader of your own can define a second copy of a class the app loader already has. Programs that load plugins, pieces of code added after the program was built, do this on purpose. Our show program loads each scene as a plugin. If every plugin gets its own copy of its classes, two plugins can't trip over each other's statics. The usual tool is a child-first loader. For names in its own package it calls findClass before it asks its parent, and for everything else it delegates as usual: Java @Override protected Class<?> loadClass(String name, boolean resolve) throws ClassNotFoundException { synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(name)) { Class<?> c = findLoadedClass(name); if (c == null && name.startsWith(prefix)) c = findClass(name); // child-first return c != null ? c : super.loadClass(name, resolve); // parent-first } } Kotlin override fun loadClass(name: String, resolve: Boolean): Class<*> = synchronized(getClassLoadingLock(name)) { var c = findLoadedClass(name) if (c == null && name.startsWith(prefix)) c = findClass(name) // child-first c ?: super.loadClass(name, resolve) // parent-first } Read it as "mine first, then my parent's". The lock from getClassLoadingLock stops two threads from defining the same class twice, and findLoadedClass returns the copy this loader already made. Two such loaders over one class file give you two Class objects. Each has its own statics, and its static initializer runs once per loader. Here the theatre picture breaks, and it's worth saying out loud. Two crowns made from the same drawing are as good as each other: any actor can wear either. Two classes defined from the same bytes are strangers. An object of one can't be cast to the other, even though the names match. TwoLoadersDemo in the Try it loads a small Counter class through two child-first loaders. It calls hit() twice on the copy from plugin-1, then casts that object to the app loader's Counter. On JDK 25 it printed: same name: true c1 == c2: false, c1 == Counter.class: false hits: plugin-1=2, plugin-2=0, app=0 class ...TwoLoadersDemo$Counter cannot be cast to class ...TwoLoadersDemo$Counter (...$Counter is in unnamed module of loader 'plugin-1' @626b2d4a; ...$Counter is in unnamed module of loader 'app') Three classes, and three separate hits fields. The cast message is long, but it's worth learning to read. The same name twice, with two loaders in the parentheses, means two copies, not a missing jar. The two "not found" errors fit the same picture. ClassNotFoundException is a checked exception from a lookup by name that your code asked for, with Class.forName or loadClass: someone asked for a prop that nobody has. NoClassDefFoundError comes from the JVM itself, while it links or initializes code that was compiled against the class. Either the class is missing at run time (the error's cause is then a ClassNotFoundException), or its static initializer already failed, as in the last section. Leaks have the same shape. A loader stays alive as long as anything reachable points at one of its classes or objects. In one experiment for this track, a plugin object was added to a static list in a registry that the parent loader had loaded. That one entry kept the plugin's whole URLClassLoader alive after close() and ten System.gc() calls, along with a 10 MB static array. (URLClassLoader is the JDK's loader for folders and jars, and System.gc() asks the garbage collector, the part of the JVM that frees unused memory, to run.) Without the registration, the loader was collected. The same name with two loaders is two classes. Read both loader names in the message. That's the whole journey of a class, from fetching its bytes to its first run. What we haven't seen yet is what those bytes say. Two Counters that aren't the same class Read TwoLoadersDemo. It loads Counter through two child-first loaders and calls hit() twice on the copy from plugin-1. Predict the three hits values, and whether the cast at the end works. Run it (or the Kotlin twin) and find the two loader names in the exception message. TwoLoadersDemo.java package workbench.bytecode.l01; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.InputStream; /** The same class file defined by two loaders: two classes, two sets of statics. */ public class TwoLoadersDemo { public static class Counter { public static int hits; public int hit() { return ++hits; } } /** Defines Counter itself (child-first); asks the parent for everything else. */ static class ChildFirst extends ClassLoader { ChildFirst(String name) { super(name, TwoLoadersDemo.class.getClassLoader()); } @Override protected Class<?> loadClass(String name, boolean resolve) throws ClassNotFoundException { if (!name.equals(Counter.class.getName())) return super.loadClass(name, resolve); synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(name)) { Class<?> c = findLoadedClass(name); if (c != null) return c; try (InputStream in = getParent().getResourceAsStream(name.replace('.', '/') + ".class")) { byte[] bytes = in.readAllBytes(); return defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.length); } catch (IOException e) { throw new ClassNotFoundException(name, e); } } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String name = Counter.class.getName(); Class<?> c1 = new ChildFirst("plugin-1").loadClass(name); Class<?> c2 = new ChildFirst("plugin-2").loadClass(name); System.out.println("same name: " + c1.getName().equals(c2.getName())); System.out.println("c1 == c2: " + (c1 == c2) + ", c1 == Counter.class: " + (c1 == Counter.class)); Object fromPlugin1 = c1.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance(); c1.getMethod("hit").invoke(fromPlugin1); c1.getMethod("hit").invoke(fromPlugin1); System.out.printf("hits: plugin-1=%s, plugin-2=%s, app=%s%n", c1.getField("hits").get(null), c2.getField("hits").get(null), Counter.hits); try { Counter c = (Counter) fromPlugin1; // checkcast against the app loader's Counter } catch (ClassCastException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); } } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l01.TwoLoadersDemo labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l01/TwoLoadersDemo.java TwoLoadersDemo.kt package workbench.bytecode.l01 class KCounter { fun hit(): Int = ++hits companion object { @JvmField var hits = 0 } } /** Defines KCounter itself (child-first); asks the parent for everything else. */ private class KChildFirst(name: String) : ClassLoader(name, KCounter::class.java.classLoader) { override fun loadClass(name: String, resolve: Boolean): Class<*> { if (name != KCounter::class.java.name) return super.loadClass(name, resolve) synchronized(getClassLoadingLock(name)) { findLoadedClass(name)?.let { return it } val bytes = parent.getResourceAsStream(name.replace('.', '/') + ".class")!!.use { it.readAllBytes() } return defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.size) } } } /** The same class file defined by two loaders: two classes, two sets of statics. */ fun main() { val name = KCounter::class.java.name val c1 = KChildFirst("plugin-1").loadClass(name) val c2 = KChildFirst("plugin-2").loadClass(name) println("same name: ${c1.name == c2.name}") println("c1 == c2: ${c1 == c2}, c1 == KCounter::class.java: ${c1 == KCounter::class.java}") val fromPlugin1 = c1.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance() repeat(2) { c1.getMethod("hit").invoke(fromPlugin1) } println("hits: plugin-1=${c1.getField("hits").get(null)}, plugin-2=${c2.getField("hits").get(null)}, app=${KCounter.hits}") try { val c = fromPlugin1 as KCounter // checkcast against the app loader's KCounter } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println(e.message) } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l01.TwoLoadersDemoKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l01/TwoLoadersDemo.kt same name: true, c1 == c2: false and c1 == Counter.class: false. The hits are plugin-1=2, plugin-2=0, app=0: three classes, three separate static fields. The cast fails with ... cannot be cast to class ...$Counter, and the parentheses name loader 'plugin-1' and loader 'app'. The number after the @ changes from run to run. h: Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization · Java and Kotlin
x: When static initialization runs, in Java and Kotlin Limits.java class Limits { static final int MAX_CAST = 12; // constant: copied into callers, no init static final Integer CAP = 12; // not a constant: reading it runs <clinit> static Limits defaults() { return new Limits(); } static { System.out.println("Limits init"); } } // Limits.MAX_CAST -> nothing // Limits.CAP -> "Limits init" // Limits.defaults() -> "Limits init" (if not done yet) Limits.kt object Limits { const val MAX_CAST = 12 // constant: copied into callers, no init val CAP: Int = 12 // private static field + getCAP() on the object fun defaults() = Limits init { println("Limits init") } } // Limits.MAX_CAST -> nothing // Limits.CAP -> "Limits init" (goes through Limits.INSTANCE) // Limits.defaults() -> "Limits init" (if not done yet) Kotlin has no static, but an object compiles to a class with a public static final INSTANCE field and a static initializer that builds it, so the JVM's rules are the same. Only const val (primitives and String) is copied into callers like a Java constant variable. A plain val in an object becomes a private static field plus a getter, so reading it touches the class and runs its init blocks. Companion objects follow the same rules, and their init code lands in the outer class's static initializer. That's why the Kotlin CallSheet in the section on the dress rehearsal reads 0 exactly like the Java one: a quick run of it printed VIOLIN: 0.

h: Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization · Worked example
x: Read a NoClassDefFoundError back to its cause A test run of the show program prints this forty times. Before you read on, decide: is a jar missing? java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class theatre.ScriptBook at theatre.Rehearsals.start(Rehearsals.java:31) ... Caused by: java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError: Exception java.lang.IllegalStateException: script file missing: hamlet.txt [in thread "main"] No. "Could not initialize class" means the JVM found ScriptBook and already tried its static initializer once. The cause (JDK 21 and later) points at that first failure. Here is the class. Every static field initializer is a line of <clinit>, run once, in order. public final class ScriptBook { // 1. runs inside <clinit>: any exception here poisons the class for good static final ScriptBook CURRENT = load(Path.of("hamlet.txt")); static ScriptBook load(Path p) { if (!Files.exists(p)) throw new IllegalStateException("script file missing: " + p); return new ScriptBook(/* read 4,000 lines */); } } class ScriptBook private constructor() { companion object { // 1. runs inside ScriptBook's <clinit>: any exception here poisons the class for good val CURRENT: ScriptBook = load(Path.of("hamlet.txt")) fun load(p: Path): ScriptBook { check(Files.exists(p)) { "script file missing: $p" } return ScriptBook(/* read 4,000 lines */) } } } Move the file reading out of class initialization, into an ordinary object that the program builds once at start-up. If the file is missing, start-up fails once, with a clear stack trace, and the next run after the file is fixed simply works. The class has no static state left to poison. public final class Scripts { private final ScriptBook current; public Scripts(Path file) { current = ScriptBook.load(file); // 2. ordinary code, ordinary exception } public ScriptBook current() { return current; } // 3. no static state left to poison } // at start-up, once: Scripts scripts = new Scripts(Path.of("hamlet.txt")); class Scripts(file: Path) { private val current: ScriptBook = ScriptBook.load(file) // 2. ordinary code, ordinary exception fun current(): ScriptBook = current // 3. no static state left to poison } // at start-up, once: val scripts = Scripts(Path.of("hamlet.txt")) If the value must stay static, make it lazy with a holder class (memory model track, lesson 5). A failure still poisons the holder, but only callers that need the script see it, and the error appears at the first real use instead of whenever some unrelated code touched ScriptBook.

x: Fix the call sheet, then load one class twice labs/bytecode/src/main/java/workbench/bytecode/l01/CallSheet.java labs/bytecode/src/main/java/workbench/bytecode/l01/IsolatingLoader.java ./gradlew :bytecode:test --tests 'workbench.bytecode.l01.*' Run the tests once. In CallSheet, read the static fields from top to bottom, the way <clinit> runs them. Move one line so the constructor sees the real DEFAULT_MINUTES. Don't change any number. Ask yourself why unit() was right all along. IsolatingLoader is a child-first loader for the show program's scene plugins. In its findClass, read the class file through the parent with getParent().getResourceAsStream(name.replace('.', '/') + ".class"), then call defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.length). Throw ClassNotFoundException when the stream is null. In loadClass, take getClassLoadingLock(name). Return findLoadedClass(name) if it isn't null. For names that start with the prefix, call findClass. For everything else, return super.loadClass(name, resolve). Run the tests until all ten pass. Then read castAcrossLoadersFails and find which loader names appear in the message. Constants such as "minutes" are copied into the code by javac, so their order doesn't matter. Integer.parseInt(...) is a method call, so DEFAULT_MINUTES is 0 until <clinit> reaches its line. If a test fails with LinkageError: attempted duplicate class definition, your loadClass defined the same name twice. Check findLoadedClass first. Don't call super.loadClass for prefix names before findClass: the parent would find the app's copy, and you'd get the same Class from both loaders. All ten tests in ClassLoadingTest pass. By the end you can say which loader defines a class and why, predict exactly when a static initializer runs, and read a NoClassDefFoundError or a class that "cannot be cast to" itself for what it really means.

h: Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization · Quiz
x: class Parent { static int seats = 290; static { log("Parent"); } } and class Child extends Parent { static { log("Child"); } }. In a fresh JVM, your code reads Child.seats. What is logged? Parent then Child Only Child Only Parent Nothing, because seats is static A static field read initializes only the class that declares the field, even when you name it through a subclass. seats is declared in Parent, so only Parent runs its static initializer. Parent then Child is what new Child(), or a static method declared in Child, would log. A program's log shows NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class theatre.SeatPlan on every request since start-up. What do you look for first? A seat-plan jar missing from the class path An earlier ExceptionInInitializerError (or the error's cause) showing what SeatPlan's static initializer threw A second copy of SeatPlan in another jar A bug in the JIT compiler "Could not initialize class" means the JVM found the class and its initializer already failed once. The class stays failed for the life of its loader. The first failure was an ExceptionInInitializerError, and since JDK 21 the later error's cause names it. A missing jar shows up as a NoClassDefFoundError caused by ClassNotFoundException instead. A plugin test fails with class theatre.Scene cannot be cast to class theatre.Scene (theatre.Scene is in unnamed module of loader 'plugin-1' ...; theatre.Scene is in unnamed module of loader 'app'). What happened? Two different versions of Scene were compiled The JVM's class cache is corrupt Scene is missing a no-argument constructor Scene was defined by two loaders, and an object from one copy met a variable typed with the other The same name with two different loaders is two different classes, even from identical bytes. The fix is to make both sides use one copy: for example, share an interface loaded by the parent, and keep the plugin's own classes inside the plugin. Recompiling changes nothing, because the bytes were never the problem. At start-up two threads hang. Both are RUNNABLE with a top frame in a <clinit>, and findDeadlockedThreads() returns null. What is the most likely cause? A class-initialization deadlock: two static initializers that need each other, started from two threads A busy loop, because the threads are RUNNABLE Two threads fighting over a synchronized method A long garbage-collection pause Threads waiting for another thread's class initialization show as RUNNABLE, and the JDK's deadlock detector doesn't report them. jstack gives it away with waiting on the Class initialization monitor for .... Break the cycle so one initializer no longer reads the other class's statics. From Lazy init done right: the holder idiom puts static final Table INSTANCE = new Table(); in a nested Holder class. Why isn't the table built when the outer class Table is initialized? Nested classes are loaded by a different class loader Holder is a separate class, and nothing initializes it until instance() reads Holder.INSTANCE The JIT removes unused static fields static final fields are always initialized lazily A nested class is its own class with its own <clinit>. Initializing the outer class doesn't touch it. The first read of Holder.INSTANCE is a non-constant static read, which runs Holder's initialization once, under the JVM's class-initialization lock. That lock is also why the idiom is thread-safe without volatile.

h: Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization · Key terms
x: Class loader An object that finds a class's bytes and turns them into a Class object. The JDK has bootstrap, platform and app loaders. Parent-first delegation A loader asks its parent for a class before it tries to find the class itself. Defining loader The loader that called defineClass for a class. It is part of the class's identity. Linking Verifying, preparing (static fields set to defaults) and resolving a loaded class, before it is initialized. The static initializer javac builds from static field initializers and static {} blocks, run once per class. Constant variable A final primitive or String whose value the compiler can work out. javac copies the value into the code that reads it. Child-first loader A custom loader that defines certain classes itself before asking its parent, to keep plugins or reloadable code apart. Which loader defines java.lang.String, and how does getClassLoader() show it? The bootstrap loader, built into the JVM. String.class.getClassLoader() returns null. In what order does the default loadClass look for a class? findLoadedClass (already defined here?), then the parent's loadClass, then its own findClass. Does reading static final int MAX = 12; from another class initialize the declaring class? No. It's a constant variable, so javac copied 12 into the caller. static final Integer MAX = 12; is not a constant, and reading it does initialize the class. Your code reads Child.x, where the static field x is declared in Parent. Which classes initialize? Only Parent, the class that declares the field. A static initializer throws. What do the first use and the later uses of the class get? First use: ExceptionInInitializerError. Every later use: NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class .... The JVM never retries. How does a class-initialization deadlock look in a thread dump? Threads in RUNNABLE state, waiting on the Class initialization monitor for ..., and no "Found one Java-level deadlock" section. Two loaders define theatre.Scene from the same bytes. Is b.isInstance(objectFromA) true? No. A class is (name, defining loader), so these are two classes. A cast between them throws ClassCastException naming both loaders.

h: Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization · Go deeper
x: Three details that didn't fit above. Interfaces have their own initialization rule. Initializing a class initializes its superclass, but its superinterfaces only if they declare a default method. In one experiment, new Impl() for a class implementing WithDefault (which has a default method) and NoDefault (which doesn't) printed WithDefault.<clinit> and Impl.<clinit>, and NoDefault stayed uninitialized until code read one of its fields. HotSpot's InstanceKlass::initialize_impl follows the specification's steps one by one, and its comments quote this rule. Lambdas are hidden classes. A lambda's class has a name like InitDeadlockDemo$$Lambda/0x0000000055080210 (a full jstack of the deadlock demo shows two such frames), isHidden() returns true, and Class.forName on that name throws ClassNotFoundException. LambdaMetafactory defines it with Lookup.defineHiddenClass (JDK 15) as a nestmate of the class that contains the lambda, which means it may use that class's private members. Lesson 3 of this track shows the call that creates it. You can watch the steps happen. -Xlog:class+load=info prints a line for each loaded class with where it came from, and -Xlog:class+init=info prints when verification starts and ends and an Initializing '...' line for each class. A Hello World with one lambda loaded 560 classes on JDK 21 and 645 on JDK 25, most of them from the CDS archive (source: shared objects file), a file of JDK classes that were already parsed when the JDK was built. The startup track covers that archive and the AOT cache that JDK 24 and 25 build on it. java -Xlog:class+load=info -Xlog:class+init=info -cp bytecode/build/classes/java/demo workbench.bytecode.l01.InitPuzzle | grep -E 'InitPuzzle|Initializing'

h: Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output · Reading the prompt book: javap turns a class file back into instructions
x: javap comes with every JDK, and it reads .class files and prints what's inside. It's how we read the prompt book. Point it at your build output, from the labs/ folder: javap -c -p bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.class -c prints each method's bytecode, -p includes private members, and -v (verbose) adds everything else: the constant pool, the stack and local sizes, flags and the class-file version. Our running example comes from the theatre's lighting desk, which plays a slow fade as many small steps. How long does a fade of 12,500 steps, 32 ms each, run? Here is the method in Java and its Kotlin twin, both compiled by the labs build. The milliseconds are a long, as time in milliseconds usually is in Java: Java static long seconds(long stepMillis, int steps) { return stepMillis * steps / 1_000; } Kotlin fun seconds(stepMillis: Long, steps: Int): Long = stepMillis * steps / 1_000 And here is what javap printed for each, side by side: javac kotlinc static long seconds(long, int); public static final long seconds(long, int); 0: lload_0 0: lload_0 1: iload_2 1: iload_2 2: i2l 2: i2l 3: lmul 3: lmul 4: ldc2_w #7 // long 1000l 4: sipush 1000 7: ldiv 7: i2l 8: lreturn 8: ldiv 9: lreturn The two compilers agree on almost everything. kotlinc put the top-level function in a class named StackDemoKt, after the file, and made it public static final. For the 1,000, javac loads a ready-made long from a table in the class file. kotlinc pushes it as a small int (sipush) and then widens it to a long (i2l). That's a difference of style. Both leave the same long 1,000 for the next instruction. That's the right way to think of bytecode: it's the contract between your compiler and the JVM. Every tool in this track reads or writes it. The verifier, the JVM's type check from lesson 1, reads it. So does the JIT, the compiler inside the JVM that turns busy bytecode into machine code. java.lang.reflect.Proxy and Byte Buddy, a library that generates classes (lesson 5), write new classes in it, and Java agents, programs that change classes as they load (lesson 7), rewrite it. You'll rarely write bytecode, but you'll read it whenever the source doesn't explain what happens at run time. javap -v also prints the class-file version, which tells you which compiler settings won. The labs compile with release 21, so it says major version: 65. JDK 25's javac with no --release writes 69. kotlinc 2.4.21 run by hand with no -jvm-target writes 52, which is Java 8, and lesson 3 shows how that changes Kotlin's string templates. The prompt book now lies open. Let's follow one cue at a time. Read one method in two languages Run StackDemo once (command below) so Gradle compiles it, and run StackDemoKt for the Kotlin twin. From labs/, run javap -c -p bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.class, then the same for bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemoKt.class. Find describe in both. Which instruction does Kotlin add before it builds the string, and why might it want it? StackDemo.java package workbench.bytecode.l02; /** Small methods to read with javap: run the demo once so Gradle compiles it, then javap -c -p. */ public class StackDemo { /** How long a lighting fade runs: steps of stepMillis milliseconds each, in whole seconds. */ static long seconds(long stepMillis, int steps) { return stepMillis * steps / 1_000; } static String describe(String unit, long amount) { return amount + " " + unit; } public static void main(String[] args) { long fade = seconds(32, 12_500); System.out.println(describe("seconds", fade)); // 400 seconds } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l02.StackDemo labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.java StackDemo.kt package workbench.bytecode.l02 // Small functions to read with javap: run the demo once so Gradle compiles it, // then javap -c -p on StackDemoKt.class (top-level functions live in a class named after the file). /** How long a lighting fade runs: steps of stepMillis milliseconds each, in whole seconds. */ fun seconds(stepMillis: Long, steps: Int): Long = stepMillis * steps / 1_000 fun describe(unit: String, amount: Long): String = "$amount $unit" fun main() { val fade = seconds(32, 12_500) println(describe("seconds", fade)) // 400 seconds } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l02.StackDemoKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.kt Both print 400 seconds. In the Kotlin describe, the first three instructions are aload_0, ldc "unit" and invokestatic Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter: a public Kotlin function checks every non-null reference parameter on the way in, so a Java caller passing null fails right there, with the parameter's name in the message. Both versions then build the string with invokedynamic makeConcatWithConstants. The Kotlin class also has two main methods: your main(), and a main(String[]) that calls it, so the java command can find it. The javap command (JDK 25 tool docs) docs

h: Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output · The operand stack: a stagehand working from a pile of cue cards
x: The JVM is a stack machine: feeMinor's seven instructions push and pop typed values, and a long takes two slots The JVM is a stack machine: its instructions don't name storage places the way a processor's do. Instead, every method call gets a frame with two areas. The local variable slots are a row of numbered places that hold the parameters and local variables. The operand stack is a pile that instructions take their inputs from and put their results on. Picture a stagehand at a small desk. On the wall are numbered hooks, the local slots. On the desk is a pile of cue cards, the operand stack. Every instruction tells the stagehand to take the top card or two off the pile, do one small job, and put the result back on top as a new card. Here is seconds(32, 12_500), one card at a time. The parameters start on the hooks. stepMillis is a long, and a long or a double takes two slots, so it fills slots 0 and 1, and steps hangs in slot 2. lload_0 copies the long from slot 0 onto the pile: 32. iload_2 copies the int from slot 2: 32, 12500. i2l takes the int and puts it back as a long, because lmul only multiplies two longs. lmul takes both and puts back 400000. ldc2_w #7 puts the long constant 1000 on the pile, from entry 7 of the constant pool, the table we'll read next. ldiv takes two longs and puts back 400. lreturn takes the long and hands it to the caller. The first letter of an instruction gives its type: i int, l long, f float, d double, a a reference to an object. iload and lload, iadd and ladd are different instructions. That's how the verifier proves a method type-safe without running it: it follows the cards' types through every instruction. A class whose method put a String on the pile and then ran ireturn loaded fine, then failed with VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack the moment the JVM verified it. That's the linking step from lesson 1, caught in the act. javap -v shows the sizes the compiler worked out for each frame. For seconds it prints stack=4, locals=3. Two longs on the pile at once need four slots, and the hooks need three. Here's where the picture breaks. A stagehand can glance at any card in the pile. An instruction sees only the top ones. And no real cue card takes up two places just because it carries a big number. You've met this pile before. In the first track, count++ on a static field compiled to getstatic, iconst_1, iadd and putstatic. getstatic copies the field onto this thread's pile, and another thread can run between any two of those four instructions. Reading the stack is how you see that one line of source isn't one step. One line of source can be many instructions. Read the bytecode before you count on it. But ldc2_w #7 and invokestatic #15 don't say what they mean. The numbers point somewhere. Predict two instructions Change seconds in StackDemo.java to return stepMillis * steps / 1_000 + 30; (and the same in StackDemo.kt). Before you compile, write down the instructions you expect between ldiv and lreturn, for javac and for kotlinc. Run both demos, then javap -c -p both classes and check. javac adds ldc2_w // long 30l and ladd. kotlinc adds bipush 30, i2l and ladd: it pushes the small int and widens it, as it did with sipush 1000. Both programs now print 430 seconds. The operand stack after each instruction of seconds(32, 12500), drawn as a pile of cue cards. A long counts as one card here, but takes two slots on the stack and on the hooks.

h: Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output · The prompt book's glossary: constant pool entries and descriptors
x: Bytecode never spells out a class name or a method name. invokestatic #15 means "call the method described by entry 15 of the constant pool". The constant pool is a table at the front of the class file that holds every name, type, string and number the bytecode refers to. It's the glossary of the prompt book: the cues say "see entry 15", and the glossary says what entry 15 is. javap -v prints the pool. Here are the entries StackDemo needs to call seconds, trimmed: #7 = Long 1000l #9 = InvokeDynamic #0:#10 // #0:makeConcatWithConstants:(JLjava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/String; #15 = Methodref #16.#17 // workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.seconds:(JI)J #16 = Class #18 // workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo #17 = NameAndType #19:#20 // seconds:(JI)J #18 = Utf8 workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo #19 = Utf8 seconds #20 = Utf8 (JI)J #27 = String #19 // seconds Follow the references. A Methodref points to a Class and a NameAndType, and those point to Utf8 entries, which hold the actual text. Look at entry 27, the string "seconds" that main prints. It points at entry 19, the very Utf8 that also names the method. The compiler is a thrifty clerk: one spelling, used twice. There's no entry 8. A Long or a Double entry uses two pool numbers, a choice the JVM specification itself calls "a poor choice" looking back, and one that every class-file reader must handle. Lesson 6 has you write one. The text (JI)J is a method descriptor: the parameter types in parentheses, then the return type. The rules are short: Descriptor Type B C D F I J S Z byte, char, double, float, int, long, short, boolean Lpkg/Name; a reference type, with / instead of . [ before a type an array of it: [J is long[], [Ljava/lang/Class; is Class[] V void (return type only) So (Ljava/lang/String;J)Ljava/lang/String; is String describe(String, long). The two letters that trip people up are J for long and Z for boolean. A descriptor has no parameter names and no generics. List<String> and List<Scene> are both Ljava/util/List;. Generic types survive only in a separate Signature attribute that reflection reads, which is the type erasure from the generics track, seen from inside the class file. And resolution, the lazy linking step from lesson 1, is the JVM turning an entry like #15 into a direct link the first time an instruction uses it. Entry 9 is a different kind of cue. describe builds its string with invokedynamic, and javap -v shows a BootstrapMethods table at the end of the file, pointing at StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants with the recipe \u0001 \u0001. Lesson 3 is about exactly that. The pool holds the names. The descriptor holds the types. Read both, and #15 turns back into a call. So far we've read code that javac and kotlinc compile almost alike. Kotlin has more to tell us. Walk the constant pool Run javap -v bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.class | less from labs/. Find major version, then the Methodref for describe, and follow it to its Class and NameAndType entries. Decode describe's descriptor by hand, then find stack= and locals= for main. terminal javap -v bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.class | grep -E 'major|Methodref|NameAndType|stack=' major version: 65 (release 21). describe is a Methodref to StackDemo with the NameAndType describe:(Ljava/lang/String;J)Ljava/lang/String;, which reads String describe(String, long). main has stack=4, locals=3: it holds System.out, the string and a two-slot long on the pile at once, and its hooks hold args and the long fade.

h: Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output · What Kotlin wrote for you: getters, Companion, INSTANCE and $default
x: javap shows the JVM's view of a Kotlin class, not the Kotlin you wrote, so it pays to learn the translation. Here is the Actor class from the next Try it, and what a Java caller has to write to use it. The member list in this section is what KotlinShapes printed for kotlinc 2.4.21 in the labs build: Java // what a Java caller writes against the Kotlin class on the right Actor ana = Actor.hire("ana"); // @JvmStatic: a real static method Actor bo = Actor.Companion.guest("bo"); // no @JvmStatic: through the Companion ana.dressingRoom = "Room 4"; // lateinit: a public field int lines = ana.getLines(); // private set: a getter, no setter String stage = Actor.Companion.getHOME_STAGE(); // a plain val: a getter on the Companion int max = Actor.MAX_ROLES; // const val: a real static constant Kotlin class Actor(val name: String) { var lines: Int = 0 private set val isSpeaking: Boolean get() = lines > 0 lateinit var dressingRoom: String companion object { const val MAX_ROLES = 3 val HOME_STAGE = "Main Stage" @JvmStatic fun hire(name: String) = Actor(name) fun guest(name: String) = Actor(name) } } A property becomes a private field plus accessor methods. var lines with private set gives getLines() and no setter at all. A property named isSpeaking keeps its name for the getter: isSpeaking(). And lateinit var dressingRoom becomes a public field, plus a getter and a setter. A companion object becomes a nested class, Actor$Companion, and a field public static final Companion Companion on Actor. Its members land in three places. const val MAX_ROLES becomes public static final int MAX_ROLES on Actor, a real constant that Java can even use in a switch. A plain val HOME_STAGE becomes a private static field on Actor, with the public getter on Companion, plus a synthetic access$getHOME_STAGE$cp() method so the companion can reach it. (A synthetic member is one the compiler made up; it has no line in your source.) A function lives on Companion only, unless you add @JvmStatic, which puts a static copy on Actor as well. object Company becomes a final class with a private constructor and a field public static final Company INSTANCE, built in its <clinit>. Top-level functions become static methods on a class named after the file, here KotlinShapesKt. Default arguments compile to a second, synthetic method. greet(name: String = "Ana", punct: Char = '!') also produces greet$default(String, char, int, Object), and the int is a bitmask, a number whose bits each answer one yes-or-no question. Here each bit says whether the caller left out one argument: 0: iload_2 // the mask 1: iconst_1 2: iand // bit 0 set: name was left out 3: ifeq 9 6: ldc "Ana" 8: astore_0 ... bit 1 the same way for punct, then invokestatic greet(String, char) Java never sees the defaults. It has to say every argument out loud, every time, unless you add @JvmOverloads. A data class Scene adds component1(), component2(), copy, a static copy$default, and equals, hashCode and toString. And every Kotlin class is final unless you write open, which is the root of the proxy trouble in lesson 5. Kotlin keeps its own picture of the class in a @kotlin.Metadata annotation: which types may be null, which methods are really properties, the default values. javap -v shows it as an encoded blob. The Kotlin compiler and kotlin-reflect, Kotlin's reflection library, read it. The JVM ignores it. Java calls what kotlinc generated, not what you wrote. Check it with javap -p. Here's the limit of today's tool. javap reads every instruction except one kind: an invokedynamic names its target nowhere in the class file, and describe already holds one. What Java sees of five Kotlin shapes Read the five declarations at the top of KotlinShapes.kt. For Actor, predict which members Actor has and which Actor$Companion has. Run KotlinShapesKt (command below). It prints each class's fields, constructors and methods. Run the Java twin, KotlinShapesJava, which calls the same classes from Java. Then uncomment ana.setLines(5); and run it again. KotlinShapes.kt package workbench.bytecode.l02 import java.lang.reflect.Modifier // Five Kotlin shapes. main() prints the JVM members of each class, close to what `javap -p` shows. data class Scene(val title: String, val minutes: Int = 0) class Actor(val name: String) { var lines: Int = 0 private set // a getter, and no setter at all val isSpeaking: Boolean get() = lines > 0 lateinit var dressingRoom: String // a public field, plus getter and setter companion object { const val MAX_ROLES = 3 // public static final on Actor val HOME_STAGE = "Main Stage" // private static on Actor, getter on Companion @JvmStatic fun hire(name: String) = Actor(name) // static on Actor AND on Companion fun guest(name: String) = Actor(name) // only on Companion } } object Company { val actors = mutableListOf<Actor>() } fun greet(name: String = "Ana", punct: Char = '!') = "Hello $name$punct" fun main() { val classes = listOf( Scene::class.java, Actor::class.java, Actor.Companion::class.java, Company::class.java, Class.forName("workbench.bytecode.l02.KotlinShapesKt"), ) for (c in classes) { println("${Modifier.toString(c.modifiers)} class ${c.name}") c.declaredFields.sortedBy { it.name }.forEach { println(" field ${Modifier.toString(it.modifiers)} ${it.type.simpleName} ${it.name}") } c.declaredConstructors.forEach { k -> println(" ctor (${k.parameterTypes.joinToString { it.simpleName }})" + if (k.isSynthetic) " synthetic" else "") } c.declaredMethods.sortedBy { it.name }.forEach { m -> println(" method ${Modifier.toString(m.modifiers)} ${m.name}(${m.parameterTypes.joinToString { it.simpleName }})") } } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l02.KotlinShapesKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l02/KotlinShapes.kt KotlinShapesJava.java package workbench.bytecode.l02; /** The Kotlin shapes from KotlinShapes.kt, called from Java: this is the API javap describes. */ public class KotlinShapesJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Scene duel = new Scene("The duel", 12); // Java must pass every argument Scene ball = duel.copy("The ball", 20); // copy() takes all of them too System.out.println(duel.getMinutes() + " " + duel.component1() + " " + ball); Actor ana = Actor.hire("ana"); // @JvmStatic: a real static method Actor bo = Actor.Companion.guest("bo"); // no @JvmStatic: through the Companion ana.dressingRoom = "Room 4"; // lateinit: a public field // ana.setLines(5); // does not compile: private set, no setter System.out.println(ana.getLines() + " " + ana.isSpeaking() + " " + bo.getName()); System.out.println("max=" + Actor.MAX_ROLES + " stage=" + Actor.Companion.getHOME_STAGE()); Company.INSTANCE.getActors().add(ana); // object: a singleton behind INSTANCE System.out.println(KotlinShapesKt.greet("Bo", '?')); // top-level function: static on the file class } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l02.KotlinShapesJava labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l02/KotlinShapesJava.java Actor has public static final int MAX_ROLES, private static final String HOME_STAGE, public String dressingRoom, getLines() with no setter, isSpeaking(), a static hire(String) and the synthetic access$getHOME_STAGE$cp(). Actor$Companion has getHOME_STAGE, guest and hire. Scene has a synthetic constructor ending in DefaultConstructorMarker and the static copy$default. The Java twin prints 12 The duel Scene(title=The ball, minutes=20), then 0 false bo, max=3 stage=Main Stage and Hello Bo?. With the setter line uncommented, the build fails, because the method doesn't exist. Calling Kotlin from Java (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output · Java and Kotlin
x: One performer API, written in Java and generated by Kotlin Performer.java (what you'd write by hand) public final class Performer { public static final int MAX_SHOWS = 8; private final String name; private int shows; public Performer(String name) { this.name = name; } public static Performer sign(String name) { return new Performer(name); } public int getShows() { return shows; } public int book(int count) { return book(count, "Main Stage"); } public int book(int count, String stage) { shows += count; return shows; } } Performer.kt (kotlinc generates the same members) class Performer(val name: String) { var shows: Int = 0 private set @JvmOverloads fun book(count: Int, stage: String = "Main Stage"): Int { shows += count return shows } companion object { const val MAX_SHOWS = 8 @JvmStatic fun sign(name: String) = Performer(name) } } javap -p on the Kotlin class lists the same public members as the Java one, plus a few extras. There's a Companion field and class, sign exists twice (static on Performer, an instance method on Companion), there's a static book$default with the bitmask, and the class carries the @kotlin.Metadata annotation. Two real differences remain. kotlinc inserts Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter for every non-null reference parameter of a public function, so new Performer(null) from Java fails at once with "parameter name". And the class is final by default, so a proxy that works by subclassing can't extend it.

h: Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output · Worked example
x: Translate synthetic names in a Kotlin stack trace A small Java program, ImportCast, reads the cast list from a file and signs each performer through the Kotlin Performer API from the lab's solution. It crashed on JDK 25 with this. Read the trace and name the construct behind each frame before you go on. Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Parameter specified as non-null is null: method workbench.bytecode.l02.Performer$Companion.sign, parameter name at workbench.bytecode.l02.Performer$Companion.sign(Performer.kt) at workbench.bytecode.l02.Performer.sign(Performer.kt) at ImportCast.lambda$main$0(ImportCast.java:10) at java.base/java.util.Arrays$ArrayList.forEach(Arrays.java:4264) at ImportCast.main(ImportCast.java:9) Read it from the bottom. ImportCast.main is Java code that calls forEach with a lambda, and javac compiled the lambda's body into the private method lambda$main$0. The lambda calls the static Performer.sign. That static method exists only because of @JvmStatic, and its whole body forwards to Performer$Companion.sign, where the Kotlin code lives. rows.forEach(r -> { // 1. this lambda body is the method lambda$main$0 Performer p = Performer.sign(r.name()); // 2. the @JvmStatic bridge p.book(r.shows()); }); rows.forEach { r -> // 1. forEach is inline in Kotlin: this body is pasted into the caller, no lambda method val p = Performer.sign(r.name) // 2. Kotlin callers go straight to Companion.sign p.book(r.shows) } The top frame is the null check kotlinc put at the start of Companion.sign. name is a non-null String in Kotlin, but Java passed null, because one row of the file had no name. The message names the method and the parameter, so you don't need a debugger. Fix it at the border, where the null comes in. String name = r.name(); if (name == null) { // 3. decide what a missing name means here, before crossing into Kotlin rejected.add(r); return; } Performer p = Performer.sign(name); // 3. or accept the null in the Kotlin API and decide there companion object { @JvmStatic fun sign(name: String?): Performer = Performer(requireNotNull(name) { "a performer needs a name" }) } The same reading works for every synthetic name: copy$default and greet$default are default arguments, access$...$cp is a companion reaching a private static, INSTANCE is an object, and a lambda$ or $lambda$ in the name is a lambda body. Both Kotlin frames say (Performer.kt) with no line number: each is stopped in code kotlinc added before your first line, a parameter check or a bridge.

h: Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output · Quiz
x: javap shows a static method body: iload_0, iload_1, imul, iconst_1, iadd, ireturn. What source produced it? return a * b + 1; with int a, b return a + b * 1; with int a, b return (a + 1) * b; with int a, b return a * (b + 1); with int a, b Trace the pile: push a, push b, multiply (ab), push 1, add (ab + 1), return. For a * (b + 1) the iconst_1; iadd would come right after iload_1, before imul. Which Java signature has the descriptor (Ljava/lang/String;[JZ)V? void m(String s, long j, boolean z) boolean m(String s, long[] js) void m(String[] s, int j, char z) void m(String s, long[] js, boolean z) Ljava/lang/String; is a String, [J is an array of long (J is long, not int), Z is boolean, and the V after the parenthesis is the void return type. A Kotlin library has fun book(show: String, stage: String = "Main Stage"): Booking. A Java caller writes desk.book("Hamlet"). What happens? It compiles and uses "Main Stage" It compiles, and stage is null at run time It doesn't compile: Java only sees book(String, String) and the synthetic book$default, unless the function has @JvmOverloads It throws NoSuchMethodError at run time Defaults live in the synthetic book$default method with its bitmask, which only kotlinc calls. @JvmOverloads makes kotlinc also emit book(String), which fills in the default for Java callers. Java code must use a Kotlin value in an annotation: @Timeout(Show.CURTAIN_DELAY_MS). In Kotlin it's companion object { val CURTAIN_DELAY_MS = 120L }. What's the right change? Add @JvmStatic to the property Make it const val CURTAIN_DELAY_MS = 120L Add @JvmField to the property Move it to a top-level val Annotation arguments must be compile-time constants. const val emits public static final long CURTAIN_DELAY_MS with a constant value on Show, which javac treats like a Java constant. @JvmField gives a public static field, but not a constant javac can put in an annotation. @JvmStatic gives a static getter, which is still a method call. From Race conditions: count++ on a static int compiles to getstatic count, iconst_1, iadd, putstatic count. Between which instructions can another thread change count and cause a lost update? Only between iadd and putstatic None: one line of Java runs as one step Between any two of them: after getstatic, the value on this thread's operand stack is a private copy Only before getstatic getstatic copies the field onto this frame's operand stack. From then on the thread computes with its own copy, and putstatic writes back whatever it computed. Any write by another thread after the getstatic and before the putstatic is overwritten.
