h: Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output · Key terms
x: javap The JDK tool that prints a class file's members, bytecode and constant pool. Operand stack The per-call pile that bytecode instructions take their inputs from and push their results onto. Local variable slots A per-call row of numbered places holding parameters and locals; long and double take two slots. Constant pool The table in a class file that holds every name, type, string and number the bytecode refers to by number. Descriptor The short type string of a field or method, such as (JI)J for long f(long, int). Class-file version The major version in a class file: 65 for Java 21, 69 for Java 25, 52 for Java 8. @kotlin.Metadata An annotation where kotlinc stores Kotlin-only facts about a class, such as nullability and properties. Which javap flags show private members, bytecode, and the constant pool? -p for private members, -c for bytecode, -v for everything, including the constant pool and the stack and locals sizes. In a method descriptor, what do J and Z mean? J is long and Z is boolean. (I is int, V is void, Lpkg/Name; is a reference type, [ is an array.) How many local variable slots does a long parameter take? Two. So in static long f(long a, int b), a is in slots 0 and 1 and b is in slot 2 (iload_2). Kotlin companion object { val X = 1 }: how does Java read X? And with const val? Plain val: Outer.Companion.getX(). const val: Outer.X, a public static final constant. What does kotlinc generate for fun greet(name: String = "Ana") besides greet(String)? A static greet$default(String, int, Object): the int is a bitmask of the arguments left out. Java can't use the default unless you add @JvmOverloads. What does a Kotlin lateinit var dressingRoom: String look like to Java? A public field dressingRoom, plus getDressingRoom() and setDressingRoom(String). Where does Kotlin keep nullability and property information that the JVM doesn't model? In the @kotlin.Metadata annotation on each class, which kotlinc and kotlin-reflect read and the JVM ignores.

h: Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output · Go deeper
x: Three more things javap shows you. Inline functions are copied, not called. inline fun <T> measure(block: () -> T): T is still emitted as a static method, so Java can call it. But at each Kotlin call site, kotlinc pastes the function body (the System.nanoTime() calls and all) into the caller, and the lambda's code with it, so no Function0 object is created. A non-inline lambda such as val later: (Int) -> Int = { it + 5 } compiles to an invokedynamic that LambdaMetafactory links (Kotlin 2.0 made that the default), with the body in a private static method whose name contains $lambda$. A reified T argument compiles to a plain ldc of the class: typeName<Actor>() becomes ldc class Actor. The JVM target changes the output. With -jvm-target 21, string templates become invokedynamic makeConcatWithConstants. With kotlinc's command-line default, Java 8, the same template becomes new StringBuilder, append, append and toString: a quick check with kotlinc 2.4.21 wrote class-file version 52 and a StringBuilder chain. The Kotlin 1.5.20 release notes describe the switch, and the option -Xstring-concat=inline that turns it off. The labs set jvmTarget = 21 in Gradle, so you see the invokedynamic version. Annotations you never wrote show up too. javap -v on a Kotlin class prints RuntimeVisibleAnnotations: kotlin.Metadata(mv=[2,4,0], k=1, ...) with two encoded arrays. mv is the metadata version, and k=1 means a class. The d1 array is encoded in protobuf, a compact binary format, and the kotlin-metadata-jvm library can decode it. That annotation is how Kotlin reflection knows that a JVM method getShows() is the property shows.

h: invokedynamic: how lambdas and string concatenation compile · invokedynamic: a call whose target is decided once, at first use
x: A lambda is a body method plus an invokedynamic that LambdaMetafactory links once Every other call instruction names its target. invokestatic StackDemo.seconds:(JI)J calls exactly that method, like a cue that says "LX 14 GO". invokedynamic names only a method name, a type, and a bootstrap method: a method that will decide the target the first time the instruction runs. Here is the method reference IndyTour::add in javap -c -p, and its entry from javap -v, on JDK 25: invokedynamic #15, 0 // InvokeDynamic #2:applyAsInt:()Ljava/util/function/IntBinaryOperator; BootstrapMethods: 2: REF_invokeStatic java/lang/invoke/LambdaMetafactory.metafactory:(...)Ljava/lang/invoke/CallSite; Method arguments: (II)I REF_invokeStatic workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour.add:(II)I (II)I Read the type ()IntBinaryOperator from the point of view of the code around it: take nothing off the operand stack, and put an IntBinaryOperator on it. How the instruction gets one isn't written anywhere in your class file. That's the cue that says "ask the director", and the bootstrap method is the director. The first time the instruction runs, the JVM calls the bootstrap method with four things. They are a Lookup for your class (an object that carries your class's access rights), the name, the type, and the static arguments listed above. The bootstrap method returns a CallSite, an object that holds a target of exactly that type. The target is a method handle, a typed reference to a method that the JVM can call directly, much like a function pointer. The JVM links the instruction to the call site. From then on, every run calls the target directly, and the bootstrap method never runs again for that instruction. The answer is in the margin, and the director gets the rest of the run off. LambdaMetafactory, the JDK's bootstrap method for lambdas, and StringConcatFactory, its bootstrap method for string +, both return a ConstantCallSite, whose target can never change. Here the picture needs one correction. A real margin note is in pencil, and a director can change their mind. A ConstantCallSite is written in ink, and that's what lets the JIT compile straight through it, as if the instruction had named its target all along. For languages that do need to relink later, the JDK has MutableCallSite, and the Try it below relinks one by hand. invokedynamic arrived in Java 7, for other languages that run on the JVM, and javac first used it for lambdas in Java 8. It moves a decision out of your class files and into the JDK. The bytecode says "join an int and a String with this recipe". The JDK you run on decides how, so a newer JDK can do it better, and your old class files pick that up without being recompiled. An invokedynamic is linked once, at first use. After that, it's a direct call. So the director is library code in the JDK. Let's see what it builds when the cue is a lambda. Relink a call site by hand Read CallSiteDemo. It builds a MutableCallSite aimed at inSeconds, calls through its dynamicInvoker(), changes the target to inMinutes, and calls again with the same 120. Predict the three lines it prints, then run it (or the Kotlin twin). CallSiteDemo.java package workbench.bytecode.l03; import java.lang.invoke.ConstantCallSite; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles; import java.lang.invoke.MethodType; import java.lang.invoke.MutableCallSite; /** A call site is a slot holding a target method handle. invokedynamic calls through one. */ public class CallSiteDemo { static String inSeconds(long s) { return s + " seconds"; } static String inMinutes(long s) { return s / 60 + " minutes"; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Throwable { MethodHandles.Lookup lookup = MethodHandles.lookup(); MethodType type = MethodType.methodType(String.class, long.class); MethodHandle inSeconds = lookup.findStatic(CallSiteDemo.class, "inSeconds", type); MethodHandle inMinutes = lookup.findStatic(CallSiteDemo.class, "inMinutes", type); MutableCallSite site = new MutableCallSite(inSeconds); MethodHandle invoker = site.dynamicInvoker(); // what an invokedynamic instruction would call through System.out.println("linked to inSeconds: " + (String) invoker.invokeExact(120L)); site.setTarget(inMinutes); // relink: same invoker, new target System.out.println("relinked to inMinutes: " + (String) invoker.invokeExact(120L)); ConstantCallSite fixed = new ConstantCallSite(inSeconds); // what lambdas and string concatenation get try { fixed.setTarget(inMinutes); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("ConstantCallSite.setTarget -> UnsupportedOperationException: linked for good"); } } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l03.CallSiteDemo labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l03/CallSiteDemo.java CallSiteDemo.kt package workbench.bytecode.l03 import java.lang.invoke.ConstantCallSite import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles import java.lang.invoke.MethodType import java.lang.invoke.MutableCallSite // A call site is a slot holding a target method handle. invokedynamic calls through one. object Formats { @JvmStatic fun inSeconds(s: Long) = "$s seconds" @JvmStatic fun inMinutes(s: Long) = "${s / 60} minutes" } fun main() { val lookup = MethodHandles.lookup() val type = MethodType.methodType(String::class.java, Long::class.javaPrimitiveType) val inSeconds = lookup.findStatic(Formats::class.java, "inSeconds", type) val inMinutes = lookup.findStatic(Formats::class.java, "inMinutes", type) val site = MutableCallSite(inSeconds) val invoker = site.dynamicInvoker() // what an invokedynamic instruction would call through println("linked to inSeconds: " + invoker.invoke(120L) as String) site.target = inMinutes // relink: same invoker, new target println("relinked to inMinutes: " + invoker.invoke(120L) as String) val fixed = ConstantCallSite(inSeconds) // what lambdas and string concatenation get try { fixed.target = inMinutes } catch (e: UnsupportedOperationException) { println("ConstantCallSite.setTarget -> UnsupportedOperationException: linked for good") } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l03.CallSiteDemoKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l03/CallSiteDemo.kt linked to inSeconds: 120 seconds, then relinked to inMinutes: 2 minutes through the very same invoker, then a line saying ConstantCallSite.setTarget threw UnsupportedOperationException. An invokedynamic instruction calls through its call site the way the invoker does. Lambdas get the constant kind: written in ink, linked for good. java.lang.invoke package (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: invokedynamic: how lambdas and string concatenation compile · Taking a lambda apart: a body method, plus a hidden class built at first use
x: The theatre's lighting cues run on seconds, and sometimes a whole sequence has to run a little late. delay(5) returns a function that adds 5 seconds to any cue time. javac turns that lambda into two things: a private method that holds the body, and an invokedynamic that produces the object: Java static IntUnaryOperator delay(int extra) { return s -> s + extra; // a lambda that captures extra } Kotlin fun delay(extra: Int): (Int) -> Int = { s -> s + extra } // a lambda that captures extra Here is what javap showed for each compiler on JDK 25, trimmed to the lines that matter: javac, IndyTour.class: 1: invokedynamic #11, 0 // InvokeDynamic #1:applyAsInt:(I)Ljava/util/function/IntUnaryOperator; private static int lambda$delay$1(int, int); // (extra, s): captured value first BootstrapMethods 1: LambdaMetafactory.metafactory (I)I REF_invokeStatic workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour.lambda$delay$1:(II)I (I)I kotlinc, IndyTourKt.class: 1: invokedynamic #44, 0 // InvokeDynamic #1:invoke:(I)Lkotlin/jvm/functions/Function1; private static final int delay$lambda$0(int, int); BootstrapMethods 1: LambdaMetafactory.metafactory (Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/lang/Object; REF_invokeStatic workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTourKt.delay$lambda$0:(II)I (Ljava/lang/Integer;)Ljava/lang/Integer; Read the call-site type as a factory: (I)IntUnaryOperator means "give me the captured int, and I'll give you an operator". To capture is to store a value from the surrounding code inside the lambda, here extra. The body method takes the captured values first, then the lambda's own parameter. Then come the three static arguments. The first is the interface method's type after erasure, the compiler removing generic types, as in the generics track. The second is the body, and the third is the interface method's type as this lambda uses it. Kotlin's Function1.invoke is erased to (Object)Object, so the third argument, (Integer)Integer, tells the factory to insert the boxing and the casts. At link time, LambdaMetafactory generates a class. On JDK 25 the demo printed its name as IndyTour$$Lambda/0x00000000a3080210. It's a hidden class, one defined with Lookup.defineHiddenClass (JDK 15) that no class loader can find by name, so Class.forName on that name throws ClassNotFoundException. It's also a nestmate of IndyTour, a class allowed to use IndyTour's private members, which is how it may call the private body. Since JDK 24, the JDK writes these classes with the ClassFile API that lesson 6 covers. IndyTour shows the allocation rule in two lines of output: captures nothing: same object both times? true captures extra: same object? false, same class? true A lambda that captures nothing is linked to one shared instance, so greeter() == greeter() is true, from the very first call. Two calls, one object. A capturing lambda gets a new object each time the lambda expression is evaluated, and all of those objects share one class. That's one small allocation each time delay(...) runs, not one per call of the operator it returns. Kotlin compiles lambdas the same way, and has done so by default since Kotlin 2.0. The release notes list what you give up: such a lambda isn't serializable, and its toString() is less readable. Function references are different. In the Kotlin demo, ::addSeconds stored as (Int, Int) -> Int compiled to an ordinary generated class, IndyTourKt$main$ref$1, and isHidden printed false. A lambda allocates once per evaluation if it captures, and never if it doesn't. A lambda is one kind of question for the director. String + asks another. Tour the lambdas Run IndyTour, then IndyTourKt. Compare the class names they print. From labs/, run javap -c -p bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour.class | grep -E 'invokedynamic|lambda' and match each invokedynamic to a line of source. Do the same for bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTourKt.class, and run ls on that folder. Which Kotlin construct got a class file of its own? IndyTour.java package workbench.bytecode.l03; import java.util.function.IntBinaryOperator; import java.util.function.IntUnaryOperator; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** Lambdas, a method reference, string concatenation and a record: every one is an invokedynamic. */ public class IndyTour { record Cue(String name, int seconds) {} static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } static Supplier<String> greeter() { return () -> "hello"; } // captures nothing static IntUnaryOperator delay(int extra) { return s -> s + extra; } // captures extra public static void main(String[] args) { IntBinaryOperator ref = IndyTour::add; Class<?> c = ref.getClass(); System.out.println("method ref: " + ref.applyAsInt(90, 30) + ", class " + c.getName()); System.out.println("hidden: " + c.isHidden() + ", nestmate of IndyTour: " + (c.getNestHost() == IndyTour.class)); try { Class.forName(c.getName()); } catch (ClassNotFoundException e) { System.out.println("Class.forName(its name): ClassNotFoundException"); } System.out.println("captures nothing: same object both times? " + (greeter() == greeter())); IntUnaryOperator d5 = delay(5), d10 = delay(10); System.out.println("captures extra: same object? " + (d5 == d10) + ", same class? " + (d5.getClass() == d10.getClass())); Cue cue = new Cue("thunder", 90); System.out.println("concat: " + cue.seconds() + " s to " + cue.name() + ", record: " + cue); } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l03.IndyTour labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour.java IndyTour.kt package workbench.bytecode.l03 // Lambdas, a function reference, a string template and a data class, compiled by kotlinc 2.4.21. data class KCue(val name: String, val seconds: Int) fun addSeconds(a: Int, b: Int) = a + b fun greeter(): () -> String = { "hello" } // captures nothing fun delay(extra: Int): (Int) -> Int = { s -> s + extra } // captures extra fun main() { val ref: (Int, Int) -> Int = ::addSeconds val c = ref.javaClass println("function ref: ${ref(90, 30)}, class ${c.name}") println("hidden: ${c.isHidden}") val lambda = greeter() println("lambda class ${lambda.javaClass.name}, hidden: ${lambda.javaClass.isHidden}") println("captures nothing: same object both times? ${greeter() === greeter()}") val d5 = delay(5) val d10 = delay(10) println("captures extra: same object? ${d5 === d10}, same class? ${d5.javaClass == d10.javaClass}") val cue = KCue("thunder", 90) println("template: ${cue.seconds} s to ${cue.name}, data class: $cue") } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l03.IndyTourKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour.kt Java: IndyTour$$Lambda/0x..., hidden: true, a nestmate of IndyTour, Class.forName fails, same object both times? true for greeter, and same object? false, same class? true for delay. Kotlin: the lambdas print IndyTourKt$$Lambda/0x... and hidden: true, but the function reference prints IndyTourKt$main$ref$1 and hidden: false. That's the IndyTourKt$main$ref$1.class file in the folder. Both programs also contain several makeConcatWithConstants call sites, one for each string they build. The director is asked once per call site. After linking, the instruction calls the target directly. LambdaMetafactory (Java SE 25 API) docs What's new in Kotlin 2.0.0: lambdas via invokedynamic read

h: invokedynamic: how lambdas and string concatenation compile · String concatenation, records and switches ask a bootstrap method too
x: Since JDK 9 (JEP 280), javac compiles + on strings to one invokedynamic per expression, linked by StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants. Before that, javac wrote a chain of StringBuilder calls into every class file, and that choice stayed frozen there. The constant parts now travel as a recipe, a fill-in-the-blanks line in which \u0001 marks each value to be filled in. Here's the last line of IndyTour in both languages: Java "concat: " + cue.seconds() + " s to " + cue.name() + ", record: " + cue Kotlin "template: ${cue.seconds} s to ${cue.name}, data class: $cue" javac, IndyTour.class: 195: invokestatic #97 // Method java/lang/String.valueOf:(Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/lang/String; 198: invokedynamic #103, 0 // InvokeDynamic #7:makeConcatWithConstants:(ILjava/lang/String;Ljava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/String; BootstrapMethods 7, recipe: concat: \u0001 s to \u0001, record: \u0001 kotlinc, IndyTourKt.class: 188: invokedynamic #147, 0 // InvokeDynamic #7:makeConcatWithConstants:(ILjava/lang/String;Lworkbench/bytecode/l03/KCue;)Ljava/lang/String; BootstrapMethods 7, recipe: template: \u0001 s to \u0001, data class: \u0001 The call-site type lists the values in order: an int, the cue's name and the cue. javac first turned the record into a String with String.valueOf, and kotlinc passed the data class object as it is. Kotlin templates compile this way when the JVM target is 9 or newer, which the labs use. With kotlinc's command-line default of Java 8, the same template becomes a StringBuilder chain, as lesson 2 found. Records push the idea further. A record's toString, hashCode and equals are each a couple of instructions around an invokedynamic. The bootstrap is java.lang.runtime.ObjectMethods.bootstrap (JDK 16), and its static arguments describe the record: ObjectMethods.bootstrap Method arguments: workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour$Cue name;seconds REF_getField workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour$Cue.name:Ljava/lang/String; REF_getField workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour$Cue.seconds:I The JDK builds the three methods from that description the first time each is called. A Kotlin data class takes the other road: kotlinc writes the toString body itself, as getfield name, getfield seconds and a concatenation invokedynamic with the recipe KCue(name=\u0001, seconds=\u0001). Both print the same kind of text. The record carries a description, and the data class carries finished code. Pattern-matching switch over a sealed type, one that lists all of its subtypes, compiles to invokedynamic typeSwitch, linked by java.lang.runtime.SwitchBootstraps. javac 21 and later also use a related form, condy (CONSTANT_Dynamic), for enum case labels in such a switch. A condy entry is a constant whose value a bootstrap method works out on first use. Same idea, for a value instead of a call. String +, records and pattern switches all ask a bootstrap method. javap shows the recipe. Every bootstrap method so far was called by the JVM. Nothing stops your code from calling one. A record and a data class, side by side From labs/ (after running IndyTour and IndyTourKt once), run the two javap commands below. In the record, find which bootstrap method its toString uses and the string that lists its components. In the data class, find the recipe that toString passes to makeConcatWithConstants. terminal javap -v 'bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour$Cue.class' | grep -A6 BootstrapMethods javap -v bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/bytecode/l03/KCue.class | grep -A3 BootstrapMethods The record's toString, hashCode and equals all use bootstrap 0, ObjectMethods.bootstrap, with the arguments IndyTour$Cue, name;seconds and two REF_getField handles. The data class has only a StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants bootstrap, with the recipe KCue(name=\u0001, seconds=\u0001). Its hashCode and equals are plain bytecode that kotlinc wrote. h: invokedynamic: how lambdas and string concatenation compile · Calling the bootstrap methods yourself
x: A bootstrap method is an ordinary public static method, so your code can play the JVM and ask the director itself. That's today's lab. LambdaMetafactory.metafactory takes six arguments, and javap -v has already shown you all of them. Here it turns a static method banner(), which returns "curtain up in five minutes", into a Supplier<String>: Java CallSite site = LambdaMetafactory.metafactory( lookup, // 1. caller: must be able to see the body "get", // 2. interface method name methodType(Supplier.class), // 3. factory type: captured values -> interface methodType(Object.class), // 4. interface method type, erased lookup.findStatic(ByHandDemo.class, "banner", methodType(String.class)), // 5. body methodType(String.class)); // 6. interface method type as this lambda uses it Supplier<String> s = (Supplier<String>) site.getTarget().invoke(); Kotlin val site = LambdaMetafactory.metafactory( lookup, // 1. caller: must be able to see the body "get", // 2. interface method name methodType(Supplier::class.java), // 3. factory type: captured values -> interface methodType(Any::class.java), // 4. interface method type, erased lookup.findStatic(Banners::class.java, "banner", methodType(String::class.java)), // 5. body methodType(String::class.java), // 6. interface method type as this lambda uses it ) val s = site.target.invoke() as Supplier<String> The JVM supplies arguments 1 to 3 from the call site, and the static arguments are 4 to 6. getTarget() is the factory. Calling it does what the invokedynamic instruction would do on every run: it takes the captured values and returns a lambda object. For a lambda that captures nothing, call the factory once and keep the result. For one that captures, keep the factory and call it once per object, which is the shape the lab tests for. The generated class is a nestmate of the lookup's class, so the demo printed ByHandDemo$$Lambda/0x..., exactly like a lambda javac compiled. The Kotlin twin printed ByHandDemoKt$$Lambda/0x.... StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants(lookup, name, type, recipe) works the same way. The demo asks it for a (int, long)String handle with the recipe row \u0001 has \u0001 seats, calls it with 12 and 30, and gets row 12 has 30 seats. Both call sites came back as ConstantCallSite. Why would you do this outside a lab? You rarely need to. Code that has a Method in hand at run time can turn it into an interface object once, and then call it as fast as a lambda. A serializer (code that turns objects into text or bytes) and a router (code that picks which method to call by name, while the program runs) are that kind of code. Doing the work once beats paying for Method.invoke, the reflective call, on every call. Every call site in this lesson linked to a method that already existed. The next lesson's tool goes one step further: the JDK writes a whole new class, implementing any interface you name, while your program runs. One lambda and one concatenation, by hand Read ByHandDemo. Match each of the six metafactory arguments to the javap -v listing in the first section. Run it (or the Kotlin twin) and read the class and call-site names it prints. "row " + row + " has " + count + " seats" CallSite concat = StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants( lookup, "concat", methodType(String.class, int.class, long.class), "row \u0001 has \u0001 seats"); MethodHandle mh = concat.getTarget(); System.out.println((String) mh.invokeExact(12, 30L) + " <- call site: " + concat.getClass().getSimpleName()); } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l03.ByHandDemo labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l03/ByHandDemo.java ByHandDemo.kt package workbench.bytecode.l03 import java.lang.invoke.LambdaMetafactory import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles import java.lang.invoke.MethodType.methodType import java.lang.invoke.StringConcatFactory import java.util.function.Supplier object Banners { @JvmStatic fun banner() = "curtain up in five minutes" } // The two bootstrap calls an invokedynamic would make, made by hand from Kotlin. fun main() { val lookup = MethodHandles.lookup() // 1. h: invokedynamic: how lambdas and string concatenation compile · Java and Kotlin
x: Lambdas and function references in Java and Kotlin Cues.java static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } IntBinaryOperator ref = Cues::add; // invokedynamic -> hidden Cues$$Lambda IntUnaryOperator plus5 = s -> s + 5; // invokedynamic, body in lambda$main$0 int extra = 10; IntUnaryOperator later = s -> s + extra; // invokedynamic with type (I)IntUnaryOperator String line = "delay " + extra + " s"; // invokedynamic makeConcatWithConstants Cues.kt fun add(a: Int, b: Int) = a + b val ref: (Int, Int) -> Int = ::add // a generated class (CuesKt$main$ref$1 style) val plus5: (Int) -> Int = { s -> s + 5 } // invokedynamic -> hidden CuesKt$$Lambda val extra = 10 val later: (Int) -> Int = { s -> s + extra } // invokedynamic with type (I)Function1 val line = "delay $extra s" // invokedynamic makeConcatWithConstants (target 9+) Both compilers send lambdas through LambdaMetafactory, so both get hidden $$Lambda classes, a shared instance when nothing is captured, and one class per lambda expression. Two real differences show up in javap. Kotlin's function types are generic interfaces (Function1<P, R>), so an (Int) -> Int boxes its Int through invoke(Object): Object, while Java's IntUnaryOperator stays with plain int. And in this track's kotlinc 2.4.21 build, a function reference such as ::add assigned to a function type compiled to an ordinary generated class instead of an invokedynamic. Kotlin's inline functions such as forEach and map avoid the lambda object entirely, which Java can't do.

h: invokedynamic: how lambdas and string concatenation compile · Worked example
x: What does this lambda capture? The show program fires a list of lighting cues, each shifted by an offset in seconds. lights is the object that talks to the lighting desk. Before you read on: does the lambda capture anything, and how often does it allocate? class CueRunner { private final Lights lights; void run(List<Cue> cues, int offset) { cues.forEach(c -> lights.fire(c.name(), c.seconds() + offset)); } } class KCueRunner(private val lights: KLights) { fun run(cues: List<KCue>, offset: Int) { cues.forEach { c -> lights.fire(c.name, c.seconds + offset) } } } Ask javap. This is what it printed for the Java class, compiled by JDK 25's javac. The call-site type lists the captured values: this, because lights is a field and is read through this, and the int offset. For the same reason, the body became an instance method rather than a static one. // 1. the factory: takes a CueRunner and an int, returns a Consumer invokedynamic #13, 0 // InvokeDynamic #0:accept:(LCueRunner;I)Ljava/util/function/Consumer; // 2. the body: an instance method, the captured int first, then the element private void lambda$run$0(int, CueRunner$Cue); So Java allocates one Consumer per call to run, once per list and not once per cue, and calls it once per element. The Kotlin version compiles to no lambda at all: forEach is an inline function, so kotlinc pasted the loop into run. Its bytecode is Iterable.iterator, hasNext, next and a direct KLights.fire. Store the same lambda in a val first, and Kotlin does what Java does. The comments show what javap printed for this version: fun runStored(cues: List<KCue>, offset: Int) { val fire: (KCue) -> Unit = { c -> lights.fire(c.name, c.seconds + offset) } cues.forEach(fire) } // 3. invokedynamic #92, 0 // InvokeDynamic #0:invoke:(LKCueRunner;I)Lkotlin/jvm/functions/Function1; // private static final kotlin.Unit runStored$lambda$0(KCueRunner, int, KCue); void runStored(List<Cue> cues, int offset) { Consumer<Cue> fire = c -> lights.fire(c.name(), c.seconds() + offset); cues.forEach(fire); } // 3. invokedynamic #23, 0 // InvokeDynamic #1:accept:(LCueRunner;I)Ljava/util/function/Consumer; // Java has no inline functions, so a lambda passed to forEach is always an object The verdict: one small object per list of cues is nothing next to driving the lighting desk, so leave the code as it is. The habit worth keeping is reading the call-site type. When it starts with your own class, the lambda holds this, which also keeps that object reachable for as long as the lambda lives.

h: invokedynamic: how lambdas and string concatenation compile · Key terms
x: invokedynamic A call instruction whose target a bootstrap method chooses the first time it runs. Bootstrap method A static method, named in the BootstrapMethods table, that links an invokedynamic call site and returns a CallSite. CallSite An object holding the method handle an invokedynamic calls. ConstantCallSite can't be relinked; MutableCallSite can. Method handle A typed reference to a method that the JVM can call directly, much like a function pointer. LambdaMetafactory The JDK bootstrap method that turns a lambda's body method into an object implementing a functional interface. Hidden class A class defined with Lookup.defineHiddenClass (JDK 15) that no class loader can find by name. Capture Storing values from the surrounding code inside a lambda, such as a local variable or this. Condy CONSTANT_Dynamic: a constant-pool entry whose value a bootstrap method works out on first use. When does an invokedynamic's bootstrap method run? Once per call site, the first time the instruction runs. It returns a CallSite, and later runs call its target directly. What does the call-site type (I)Ljava/util/function/IntUnaryOperator; on a lambda mean? The lambda captures one int. The call site is a factory: give it the int, get an IntUnaryOperator. () -> "hello" is evaluated twice. Same object? Yes. A non-capturing lambda's call site returns one shared instance. What kind of class is Foo$$Lambda/0x..., and can Class.forName find it? A hidden class defined by LambdaMetafactory as a nestmate of Foo. Class.forName throws ClassNotFoundException. What is \u0001 in a makeConcatWithConstants recipe? A slot for the next value. "\u0001 seconds to \u0001" takes two values. Which bootstrap builds a record's toString, equals and hashCode? java.lang.runtime.ObjectMethods.bootstrap (JDK 16), given the record class, the component names and getter handles. Does Kotlin's list.forEach { ... } create a lambda object? No. forEach is inline, so kotlinc copies the loop and the lambda body into the caller.

h: Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy · Building a stand-in by hand, then reading the one the JDK writes
x: A dynamic proxy: every call becomes one invoke with a Method and an Object array The show program asks the theatre's wardrobe system how many costumes each role has. It talks to it through a small interface, Wardrobe, with one method, costumes(role), and a default method dressed(role) that checks the count is above 0. (A default method is an interface method that has a body.) Let's first write a stand-in by hand, for this one interface. It holds one InvocationHandler: an object with a single method, invoke(proxy, method, args), that receives every call. In the theatre picture, the proxy object is the stand-in, and the handler is the rule the stand-in follows for every request. The real object behind it all, the actor, is called the target. Each request arrives as one note: which method was called (a java.lang.reflect.Method, the object that describes a method) and its arguments, in an Object[]: Java final class HandProxy implements Wardrobe { private static final Method COSTUMES; // 1. looked up once static { try { COSTUMES = Wardrobe.class.getMethod("costumes", String.class); } catch (NoSuchMethodException e) { throw new NoSuchMethodError(e.getMessage()); } } private final InvocationHandler h; HandProxy(InvocationHandler h) { this.h = h; } @Override public int costumes(String role) { try { return (Integer) h.invoke(this, COSTUMES, new Object[]{role}); // 2. box, ask the handler, unbox } catch (RuntimeException | Error e) { throw e; // 3. unchecked: as is } catch (Throwable t) { throw new UndeclaredThrowableException(t); // 4. undeclared checked: wrapped } } // ...the same for dressed, equals, hashCode and toString } Kotlin class HandProxy(private val h: InvocationHandler) : KWardrobe { override fun costumes(role: String): Int = try { h.invoke(this, COSTUMES, arrayOf(role)) as Int // 2. box, ask the handler, unbox } catch (e: RuntimeException) { throw e // 3. unchecked: as is } catch (e: Error) { throw e } catch (t: Throwable) { throw UndeclaredThrowableException(t) // 4. undeclared checked: wrapped } // ...the same for dressed, equals, hashCode and toString companion object { private val COSTUMES = KWardrobe::class.java.getMethod("costumes", String::class.java) // 1. once } } Each method finds its Method object once and puts the arguments into an Object[]. Boxing turns primitive values such as int into objects such as Integer along the way. Then it asks the handler and unboxes the answer. That compiles and works: a test with a handler that always answers 3 printed 3. Writing it by hand for forty methods on six interfaces is the kind of job nobody volunteers for twice, so the JDK writes it for you. In Decorator and Proxy you passed a handler to Proxy.newProxyInstance. At that moment the JDK generated a class like HandProxy, for whichever interfaces you listed. Here's what ProxyAnatomy reports about it, on JDK 21 and JDK 25 alike: class public final jdk.proxy1.$Proxy0 extends java.lang.reflect.Proxy, implements [interface ...ProxyAnatomy$Wardrobe] module jdk.proxy1, hidden: false fields [m0, m1, m2, m3, m4] methods [costumes, dressed, equals, hashCode, proxyClassLookup, toString] The Proxy Javadoc promises most of this. A proxy class is final, extends java.lang.reflect.Proxy, and implements exactly the interfaces you passed, in the same order. Its name isn't specified, but names that start with $Proxy are kept for proxy classes, and Proxy.isProxyClass recognizes it. The module jdk.proxy1 and the counter in $Proxy0 are details of the JDK, free to change. Every generated method looks like HandProxy.costumes, written straight in bytecode. This is costumes(String) as JDK 25 generated it: public final int costumes(java.lang.String) throws ; // JDK 25, names shortened 0: aload_0 1: getfield Proxy.h:InvocationHandler // 1. the handler 4: aload_0 // 2. the proxy itself 5: getstatic m3:Method // 3. Method looked up once, in <clinit> 8: iconst_1 9: anewarray Object // 4. box the arguments into an Object[] 12: dup 13: iconst_0 14: aload_1 15: aastore 16: invokeinterface InvocationHandler.invoke:(Object;Method;[Object;)Object 21: checkcast Integer // 5. unbox the result 24: invokevirtual Integer.intValue:()I 27: ireturn 28: athrow // Error, RuntimeException: rethrow as is 29: new UndeclaredThrowableException // anything else: wrap it ... Exception table: from to target type 0 28 28 Class java/lang/Error 0 28 28 Class java/lang/RuntimeException 0 28 29 any So every call loads the handler and the proxy, and fetches the Method object that the static initializer looked up once. (m0 to m2 are hashCode, equals and toString, then come your interface's methods.) It copies the arguments into a fresh Object[] and calls invoke. The result is cast back and unboxed. A null returned for a primitive return type becomes a NullPointerException at that unboxing step. The exception table, the list at the end of a method that says which instructions each catch guards, is the whole exception contract. Error and RuntimeException pass straight through, and so do checked exceptions that the interface method declares. Anything else gets wrapped in UndeclaredThrowableException. costumes declares nothing, so its last entry is any. The Kotlin twin prints the same shape for a Kotlin interface. Proxies are a JVM feature, and kotlinc's interfaces are ordinary JVM interfaces. Since JDK 23, the JDK writes these classes with the ClassFile API. JDK 21 still used its internal copy of ASM, a library for writing class files, so its bytecode differs slightly in the exception handler. A JDK proxy turns every call into one invoke with a Method and an Object[]. Every call, then, lands in one place. Which calls, exactly, and what must the handler hand back? Take a proxy apart Read ProxyAnatomy (or ProxyAnatomy.kt). Before running it, predict which of the five calls in part 2 reach the handler. Run it. Check the class name, its fields and methods, and the list the handler saw. Look at part 3: why do {Wardrobe, Audited} and {Audited, Wardrobe} get different class names? { int costumes(String role); default boolean dressed(String role) { return costumes(role) > 0; } } public interface Audited { String auditId(); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> seen = new ArrayList<>(); InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, a) -> { seen.add(m.getDeclaringClass().getSimpleName() + "." + m.getName()); return switch (m.getName()) { case "costumes" -> 3; case "hashCode" -> 42; case "equals" -> proxy == a[0]; case "toString" -> "Wardrobe proxy"; default -> null; }; }; ClassLoader app = Wardrobe.class.getClassLoader(); Wardrobe q = (Wardrobe) h: Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy · What reaches the handler, and what the handler owes the caller
x: Three methods of Object reach the handler: hashCode, equals and toString, each with method.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class. The other public Object methods, such as getClass, wait and notify, are final, and the proxy doesn't override them. The stand-in can't lie about which class it is. For hashCode and other methods with no parameters, args is null, not an empty array. What you do with equals matters. The company keeps its big props in a store across town, and the show program reaches it through an interface PropStore. The tempting handler for it forwards everything: Java InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, args) -> m.invoke(target, args); // equals too Kotlin val h = InvocationHandler { _, m, args -> m.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } // equals too Now proxy.equals(proxy) asks target.equals(proxy). The real prop store has never heard of the proxy, so the answer is false. Ask the proxy whether it is itself, and it says no. The ObjectMethodsDemo shows what that costs: p.equals(p): false (target.equals(p) was asked) listeners.remove(p) after listeners.add(p): false, size still 1 HashSet.contains(p): true (HashMap checks == before equals) After listeners.add(p), listeners.remove(p) returns false, and the proxy stays in the list. A HashSet happens to survive, because HashMap compares references with == before it calls equals. That's luck, not correctness. Here the stand-in picture breaks, and it breaks on identity. Ask a human stand-in "are you the one I gave my note to?", and they answer for themselves. A careless handler passes even that question on to the actor. So answer equals and hashCode by the proxy's own identity (proxy == args[0], System.identityHashCode(proxy)), or decide on purpose how two proxies compare. The handler also owes the caller the right exceptions. The generated method rethrows unchecked exceptions and the checked exceptions its interface method declares, and wraps any other checked exception in UndeclaredThrowableException. Method.invoke adds a second layer of its own: whatever the target throws arrives wrapped in InvocationTargetException. A handler must catch that and rethrow e.getCause(). Otherwise the caller sees an UndeclaredThrowableException, wrapping an InvocationTargetException, wrapping the real error. Kotlin makes the first rule easy to trip over. Kotlin has no checked exceptions (exceptions the compiler makes you catch or declare), so a Kotlin interface method declares none unless you write @Throws. A Kotlin implementation may still throw IOException, from a Java library it calls, because Kotlin doesn't check. A handler that unwraps correctly then produces UndeclaredThrowableException, and a Kotlin catch (e: IOException) around the call never matches. The demo's status() shows it. Add @Throws(IOException::class) to interface methods whose implementations can throw checked exceptions. Two more rules from the Javadoc. Only interfaces can be proxied: passing a class fails with IllegalArgumentException: ... is not an interface. And if two interfaces declare the same method, the handler gets the Method from the first interface in your list, whichever one the caller used. Answer equals and hashCode by the proxy's identity, and unwrap InvocationTargetException. Object methods and exceptions are two of the special cases. The third hides in plain sight: default methods. Break equals, then the exception contract Run ObjectMethodsDemo (or the Kotlin twin) and read its five lines. In forwardingEverything, answer equals before the try: if (m.getName().equals("equals")) return proxy == args[0]; (in Kotlin, rename the lambda's first parameter from _ to proxy, then add if (m.name == "equals") return@newProxyInstance proxy === args[0]). Run it again. In the Kotlin twin, remove @Throws(IOException::class) from fetch and predict what the catch (e: IOException) block does now. Run it. java.lang.reflect.UndeclaredThrowableException; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; /** Two handler bugs: forwarding equals to the target, and throwing a checked exception the method doesn't declare. */ public class ObjectMethodsDemo { public interface PropStore { String fetch(String prop) throws IOException; // declares IOException String status(); // declares nothing } static class RealPropStore implements PropStore { public String fetch(String prop) throws IOException { throw new IOException("prop store took longer than 120 ms"); } public String status() { return "OPEN"; } } static PropStore forwardingEverything(PropStore target) { return (PropStore) Proxy.newProxyInstance(PropStore.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{PropStore.class}, (proxy, m, args) -> { try { return m.invoke(target, args); // equals and hashCode go to the target too } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); } }); } HashSet<>(listeners); System.out.println("HashSet.contains(p): " + set.contains(p) + " (HashMap checks == before equals)"); try { p.fetch("crown"); } catch (IOException e) { System.out.println("declared IOException passes through: " + e.getMessage()); } PropStore angry = (PropStore) Proxy.newProxyInstance(PropStore.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{PropStore.class}, UndeclaredThrowableException, cause: " + e.getCause()); } } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l04.ObjectMethodsDemo x: Decorator and Proxy showed the self-invocation trap. The real stockroom's pickBoth called pick through this, and this was the real object, so the proxy never saw the inner calls. Self-invocation is a method calling another method of the same object through this. In the theatre, it's the actor talking to themselves: nothing passes the stage door. Default methods give you a choice about it. Scenes is the interface the show program uses to ask how long a scene runs. It has an abstract minutes(scene) and a default method total(a, b) that calls minutes twice, on this. If the handler forwards total with method.invoke(target, args), the default body runs on the target. Its this is the target, and its two inner calls skip the proxy. DefaultMethodsDemo logs [total]. JDK 16 added InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, args). It runs the interface's default body with this set to the proxy, so every call the body makes comes back through the handler: Java if (method.isDefault()) { return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, args); // the body runs with this = proxy } Kotlin if (method.isDefault) { return@InvocationHandler InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } Now the demo logs [total, minutes, minutes]. The proxy doesn't even need a target. A handler that answers the abstract methods itself, and sends default methods to invokeDefault, is a complete implementation. The demo's target-less proxy answers 5 for every scene, and total comes out at 10. Calling invokeDefault on an abstract method throws IllegalArgumentException, and on a default method your code isn't allowed to reach, it throws IllegalAccessException. Kotlin interfaces work too. With the labs' JVM target 21, kotlinc 2.4.21 compiles an interface function that has a body to a real JVM default method, plus a DefaultImpls class for older callers. method.isDefault is true, and invokeDefault runs the Kotlin body: the Kotlin twin prints the same three calls. This choice decides whether a retry proxy is safe, a proxy that calls again when a call fails. The theatre's seat booking runs on another computer, reached through an interface SeatDesk. hold(show, guest) keeps a seat aside for a guest, confirm(holdId) confirms it, and a default method does both: return confirm(hold(show, guest));. Suppose your handler treats holdAndConfirm like any other method and retries it when it fails. The first attempt holds a seat, then the confirmation fails, so the handler retries the whole method, and the second attempt holds a second seat. Run default methods through invokeDefault and retry only the abstract calls inside them. A failed confirmation is then retried as a confirmation, and the hold that already worked stays at one. The lab tests exactly this. Run default methods with invokeDefault. Never retry one as a whole. That's the handler's logic complete. What's left is the price: of making the class, and of every call through it. Count the handler calls Read DefaultMethodsDemo. Predict the handler saw list for both runs, and the total for the target-less proxy. Run it (or the Kotlin twin). Change RealScenes.minutes to throw IllegalStateException for "duel" and run it again. h: Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy · One class per loader and interface list, and a few nanoseconds per call
x: Generating a class is the expensive part, and the JDK does it only once. Proxy caches proxy classes per class loader, keyed by the ordered list of interfaces. Ten thousand newProxyInstance calls with the same loader and interfaces generate one class and construct ten thousand small objects. Listing the same interfaces in a different order generates a second class, as ProxyAnatomy showed with $Proxy1 and $Proxy2. Each class loader gets one dynamic module for its proxies, a module the JDK creates while the program runs. On the runs for this track, proxies for app-loader interfaces landed in jdk.proxy1, and a Runnable proxy created with the bootstrap loader (null) landed in jdk.proxy2. If any interface isn't public, the proxy class goes into that interface's package instead, and isn't public either (demo.$Proxy8 in one run). Calling Constructor.newInstance on a proxy class in a dynamic module throws IllegalAccessException. Use newProxyInstance, because Proxy.getProxyClass is deprecated. The cost of each call is the bytecode from the first section: an Object[], boxing, a call to the handler, and whatever the handler does. JMH, the JDK project's tool for timing small pieces of code, measured add(3, 4) four ways on JDK 25. This was one run on a shared 4-core machine, with one fork (one separate JVM run) and wide error bars: Call ns per call direct 0.83 Byte Buddy subclass with @SuperCall (lesson 5) 0.88 JDK proxy, handler calls method.invoke(target, args) 4.3 plain Method.invoke with boxing 11.8 Read the order, not the decimals. A few nanoseconds per call is nothing next to a 120 ms call to the seat desk on another computer. It does show up in a loop that calls a proxied interface millions of times, and there a subclass proxy or plain code wins. You can save the generated class and read it yourself. -Djdk.proxy.ProxyGenerator.saveGeneratedFiles=true writes it to jdk/proxy1/$Proxy0.class under the current folder. On JDK 21 that just works. On the JDK 24 to 27 builds tested for this track, JDK 25 included, the JDK writes the first file, and then newProxyInstance throws NullPointerException. The JDK source explains it: a return null; that used to sit inside a doPrivileged block now returns from generateProxyClass itself. The file is still written, so you can read it on any of them. Here's the limit of today's tool, and it's a hard one. A JDK proxy can only implement interfaces. h: Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy · Java and Kotlin
x: A tracing proxy in Java and Kotlin Tracing.java @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") static <T> T tracing(Class<T> iface, T target, List<String> log) { InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, args) -> { if (m.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class) { // 1. identity, not the target's return switch (m.getName()) { case "equals" -> proxy == args[0]; case "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy); default -> "Tracing[" + target + "]"; }; } log.add(m.getName()); if (m.isDefault()) return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, args); // 2. this = proxy try { return m.invoke(target, args); // 3. args is null for no-arg methods } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); // 4. the target's own exception } }; return (T) Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, h); } Tracing.kt inline fun <reified T : Any> tracing(target: T, log: MutableList<String>): T = Proxy.newProxyInstance(T::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(T::class.java)) { proxy, m, args -> val a = args ?: emptyArray() // 3. null for no-arg methods when { m.declaringClass == Any::class.java -> when (m.name) { // 1. identity "equals" -> proxy === a[0] "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy) else -> "Tracing[$target]" } else -> { log += m.name if (m.isDefault) InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, *a) // 2. this = proxy else try { m.invoke(target, *a) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { throw e.cause!! // 4. the target's own exception } } } } as T Same JVM mechanism, same four cases. The Kotlin version is shorter because reified T reads T::class.java itself, so callers write tracing(desk, log). Two Kotlin-specific traps sit in it. args is a nullable Java array, null for methods with no parameters, so spreading it directly (*args) throws NullPointerException on hashCode(). And Kotlin interfaces declare no checked exceptions unless you add @Throws, so an IOException from a Java library, which the handler rethrows correctly, still reaches Kotlin callers as UndeclaredThrowableException.

h: Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy · Worked example
x: A test double for SeatDesk with no implementation class A test needs a SeatDesk that returns canned answers and records what was called, and you don't want to write a class with every method. A test double is a stand-in built for a test. A proxy with no target can be one. Start with the cases every handler needs. static SeatDesk fakeDesk(Map<String, Object> answers, List<String> calls) { InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, args) -> { // 1. Object methods: identity, so the fake behaves in collections if (m.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class) { return switch (m.getName()) { case "equals" -> proxy == args[0]; case "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy); default -> "FakeDesk" + answers.keySet(); }; } // 2. default methods: run the real interface body, which calls back through this handler if (m.isDefault()) return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, args); // 3. abstract methods: record the call and return the canned answer calls.add(m.getName() + Arrays.toString(args)); if (!answers.containsKey(m.getName())) throw new UnsupportedOperationException(m.getName()); return answers.get(m.getName()); }; return (SeatDesk) Proxy.newProxyInstance( SeatDesk.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{SeatDesk.class}, h); } fun fakeDesk(answers: Map<String, Any>, calls: MutableList<String>): SeatDesk = Proxy.newProxyInstance(SeatDesk::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(SeatDesk::class.java)) { proxy, m, args -> val a = args ?: emptyArray() when { // 1. Object methods: identity, so the fake behaves in collections m.declaringClass == Any::class.java -> when (m.name) { "equals" -> proxy === a[0] "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy) else -> "FakeDesk${answers.keys}" } // 2. default methods: run the real interface body, which calls back through this handler m.isDefault -> InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, *a) // 3. abstract methods: record the call and return the canned answer else -> { calls += m.name + a.contentToString() answers[m.name] ?: throw UnsupportedOperationException(m.name) } } } as SeatDesk Use it. The interesting call is the default method: the fake has no code for holdAndConfirm, yet the interface's own body runs, and its two inner calls are recorded in order. A run of this code printed confirmed hold-hamlet [hold[Hamlet, ana], confirm[hold-hamlet]]. That works only because of invokeDefault: forwarding to a target isn't possible here, since there is no target. List<String> calls = new ArrayList<>(); SeatDesk desk = fakeDesk( Map.of("hold", "hold-hamlet", "confirm", "confirmed hold-hamlet"), calls); String result = desk.holdAndConfirm("Hamlet", "ana"); // 4. exercise the default assertThat(result).isEqualTo("confirmed hold-hamlet"); assertThat(calls).containsExactly("hold[Hamlet, ana]", "confirm[hold-hamlet]"); val calls = mutableListOf<String>() val desk = fakeDesk(mapOf("hold" to "hold-hamlet", "confirm" to "confirmed hold-hamlet"), calls) val result = desk.holdAndConfirm("Hamlet", "ana") // 4. exercise the default assertThat(result).isEqualTo("confirmed hold-hamlet") assertThat(calls).containsExactly("hold[Hamlet, ana]", "confirm[hold-hamlet]") Check the edges before you trust it. A canned answer of the wrong type fails at the proxy's checkcast, with a ClassCastException from the generated method rather than from your handler. A missing answer for a method returning int would be null, and the proxy's unboxing would turn that into a NullPointerException, so the handler throws a clear UnsupportedOperationException instead. And this fake works for one interface only. Mocking libraries, which build test doubles for you, grow the same idea with argument matchers and support for classes.

h: Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy · Key terms
x: Dynamic proxy An object of a class generated at run time that implements given interfaces and sends every call to one handler. InvocationHandler The single invoke(proxy, method, args) method that receives every call made on a JDK proxy. UndeclaredThrowableException The unchecked wrapper a proxy throws when its handler throws a checked exception that the method doesn't declare. InvocationTargetException The wrapper Method.invoke puts around whatever the called method threw. Unwrap it with getCause(). invokeDefault InvocationHandler.invokeDefault: runs an interface's default method body on the proxy itself (JDK 16). Self-invocation A method calling another method of the same object through this, which goes straight past any proxy in front of it. Dynamic module A module such as jdk.proxy1 that the JDK creates per class loader, while the program runs, to hold proxy classes. What class does Proxy.newProxyInstance generate for one interface? A public final class such as jdk.proxy1.$Proxy0 that extends java.lang.reflect.Proxy and implements exactly the given interfaces, in order. Which Object methods reach an InvocationHandler? hashCode, equals and toString, with getDeclaringClass() == Object.class. Not getClass, wait or notify. What is args in invoke(proxy, method, args) for a method with no parameters? null, not an empty array. In Kotlin, use args ?: emptyArray() before spreading it. A handler throws a checked exception that the interface method doesn't declare. What does the caller get? UndeclaredThrowableException, with the checked exception as its cause. What does InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, args) do differently from m.invoke(target, args)? It runs the interface's default body with this = the proxy, so the body's inner calls come back through the handler. (JDK 16.) When does Proxy generate a new class? Once per class loader and ordered interface list. {A, B} and {B, A} are two classes. Why must a proxy answer equals itself? Forwarding it makes proxy.equals(proxy) ask target.equals(proxy), which is false, so lists can't find or remove the proxy.

h: Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy · Go deeper
x: Three corners of Proxy that the lesson skipped. Modules and visibility. If every interface is public and in an exported package, the proxy class is public, in an unconditionally exported but non-open package of a dynamic module. If any interface isn't public, the proxy class isn't public either, and goes into that interface's package and module, so all non-public interfaces must share one package. If an interface is in a package its module doesn't export, the proxy goes into a non-exported package of a dynamic module. In every dynamic-module case, Constructor.newInstance on the proxy class throws IllegalAccessException, which is why Proxy.getProxyClass is deprecated. What can fail at creation. newProxyInstance throws IllegalArgumentException when an element isn't a non-hidden, non-sealed interface, when an interface appears twice, when an interface isn't visible by name through the loader you pass (Class.forName(i.getName(), false, loader) != i), when two interfaces have a method with the same signature and incompatible return types, or when you pass more than 65,535 interfaces. The loader rule is the one you'll meet: in a plugin system or a test runner, pass the loader that defined the interface (iface.getClassLoader()), not some other loader that holds a second copy of it (lesson 1). The caches. Proxy keeps the constructors in a ClassLoaderValue, so the cache entry goes away with the loader. A second cache backs isProxyClass. And a ClassValue of ConcurrentHashMap<Method, MethodHandle> holds the method handles behind invokeDefault, so only the first call of each default method pays for the lookup. The saveGeneratedFiles crash from the last section is easy to see in the source. At jdk-21-ga, generateProxyClass wrote the file inside AccessController.doPrivileged(new PrivilegedAction<>() { ... return null; }), and that return null belonged to the inner block. At jdk-24-ga, the release that permanently disabled the Security Manager, the doPrivileged wrapper is gone, and the same return null; now returns from generateProxyClass itself, so defineClass receives null bytes. That matches the message JDK 25 printed: Cannot read the array length because "b" is null.

h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · Sewing the costume: a subclass that overrides every method it can
x: Byte Buddy writes a subclass at run time: its override calls an interceptor that runs code before and after your method, and a final method is never intercepted The theatre's lighting desk is run by a class called CueRunner. Its method run(cue) runs one cue, such as LX-14, and first calls this.check(cue) to make sure the cue exists. A third method, stage(), is final and names the stage. There's no interface anywhere, so the stand-in from the last lesson can't help: Proxy only implements interfaces. A subclass can help. A subclass extends a class and may override its methods, that is, replace them with its own versions. Here is a timing stand-in, written by hand: Java class TimedCueRunner extends CueRunner { @Override public String run(String cue) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { return super.run(cue); // the original body, on THIS object } finally { log("run", System.nanoTime() - t0); } } // check() the same way; stage() is final, so there is nothing to override } Kotlin class TimedCueRunner : KCueRunner() { // needs `open class` override fun run(cue: String): String { // needs `open fun` val t0 = System.nanoTime() try { return super.run(cue) // the original body, on THIS object } finally { log("run", System.nanoTime() - t0) } } // check() the same way; stage() is final, so there is nothing to override } Each override is a place to add work around the original method, and super.run(cue) runs the original body on this same object. That's the costume: every caller sees a CueRunner, because the subclass is one, and it can add a step before and after each method of the role. Writing such a class for every class you own is slow and easy to get wrong. Byte Buddy, a library for writing classes while a program runs, sews the subclass for you. You say which class to extend, which methods to override, and who handles each call: Java Class<? extends CueRunner> sub = new ByteBuddy() .subclass(CueRunner.class) // 1. the class to extend .method(isDeclaredBy(CueRunner.class)) // 2. which methods to override .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration() .filter(named("intercept")) .to(new InSubclass())) // 3. who handles each call .make() .load(CueRunner.class.getClassLoader()) // 4. define it in a new class loader .getLoaded(); Kotlin val sub: Class<out KCueRunner> = ByteBuddy() .subclass(KCueRunner::class.java) // 1. the class to extend .method(isDeclaredBy(KCueRunner::class.java)) // 2. which methods to override .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration() .filter { it.name == "intercept" } .to(KInSubclass())) // 3. who handles each call .make() .load(KCueRunner::class.java.classLoader) // 4. define it in a new class loader .loaded The handler, InSubclass, is an interceptor: an object whose method runs in place of the original and decides when to call it. Byte Buddy chooses what to pass it by the annotations on its parameters. @Origin Method is the method being called. @SuperCall Callable is a small object that runs the original body when you call it. The demo's interceptor logs the method's name, then calls the original. Here's what the demo prints about the class it got back: generated workbench.bytecode.l05.TwoModelsDemo$CueRunner$ByteBuddy$YUk6Nqln declares [check, check$accessor$AJXfCzMY, run, run$accessor$AJXfCzMY] ran LX-14 (checked LX-14), on the main stage The name ends in $ByteBuddy$ and a suffix that is random on every run. The class declares run and check, plus an accessor for each: a helper method that calls super.run(...) for the interceptor's Callable, just as you did by hand. stage() isn't there at all, yet it still answered main stage. A subclass can only intercept what it can override, and that one rule sets the limits of every subclass proxy. A final class can't be extended at all. A final or private method can't be overridden, so it runs as written and no interceptor sees it. And every subclass object is built by a constructor, which runs the superclass constructor too. Kotlin meets the first limit every day, because its classes and their members are final unless you write open. The demo's last line asks for a costume for a plain Kotlin class: Kotlin class without open: Cannot subclass primitive, array or final types: class workbench.bytecode.l05.KotlinCueRunner Kotlin locked the door, and Byte Buddy doesn't pick locks. You can write open on the class and on each method. Or a compiler plugin can do it for you. The Kotlin all-open plugin "makes classes and their members open at compile time without requiring the open keyword". It does that for classes that carry annotations you choose. A subclass proxy can only intercept what it can override. Look for final first. Byte Buddy is the library most Java tools use for this, and the labs use version 1.18.17. You may also meet cglib, an older library for the same job. Its own README says it "is unmaintained and does not work well (or possibly at all?) in newer JDKs, particularly JDK17+", and points to Byte Buddy. Spring still uses cglib, through a copy that the Spring team patches and ships inside Spring, as org.springframework.cglib. So the costume department can sew for any role that isn't locked. The next question is who wears the costume. Generate a subclass, then try a Kotlin class Run TwoModelsDemo (or the Kotlin twin) and read the first three lines and the last line. In TwoModelsDemo.kt, open KotlinCueRunner: open class KotlinCueRunner { open fun run(cue: String) = ... }. Before you run either version again, predict what happens to the last line. From labs/, run javap -p bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/bytecode/l05/KCueRunner.class and find the one method that is still final. TwoModelsDemo.java package workbench.bytecode.l05; import net.bytebuddy.ByteBuddy; import net.bytebuddy.implementation.MethodDelegation; import net.bytebuddy.implementation.bind.annotation.AllArguments; import net.bytebuddy.implementation.bind.annotation.Origin; import net.bytebuddy.implementation.bind.annotation.RuntimeType; import net.bytebuddy.implementation.bind.annotation.SuperCall; import java.lang.reflect.Method; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.Callable; import static net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.isDeclaredBy; import static net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.named; /** The same subclass proxy, two models: the proxy IS the object, or the proxy forwards to a target. */ public class TwoModelsDemo { static final List<String> LOG = new ArrayList<>(); /** Runs one lighting or sound cue. No interface: a JDK proxy can't stand in for it. */ public static class CueRunner { static int constructed; public CueRunner() { constructed++; } public String run(String cue) { return "ran " + cue + " (" + this.check(cue) + ")"; } // self-call public String check(String cue) { return "checked " + cue; } public final String stage() { return "main stage"; } } /** Quarkus ArC style: the generated subclass instance IS the object; @SuperCall runs the original body on it. */ public static class InSubclass { @RuntimeType public Object intercept(@Origin Method m, @SuperCall Callable<?> original) throws Exception { LOG.add("intercepted " + m.getName()); return original.call(); } } /** Spring AOP style: the generated subclass forwards to a separate target object. */ public static class Forwarding { private final Object target; public Forwarding(Object target) { this.target = target; } @RuntimeType public Object intercept(@Origin Method m, @AllArguments Object[] args) throws Exception { LOG.add("forwarded " + m.getName()); return m.invoke(target, args); } } static <T> Class<? extends T> subclass(Class<T> type, Object interceptor) { return new ByteBuddy().subclass(type) .method(isDeclaredBy(type)) .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration() .filter(named("intercept")) // bind to intercept() only, not equals() etc. .to(interceptor)) .make().load(type.getClassLoader()).getLoaded(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Class<? extends CueRunner> sub = subclass(CueRunner.class, new InSubclass()); System.out.println("generated " + sub.getName()); System.out.println("declares " + Arrays.stream(sub.getDeclaredMethods()).map(Method::getName).sorted().toList()); CueRunner runner = sub.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance(); System.out.println(runner.run("LX-14") + ", on the " + runner.stage()); System.out.println("subclass model: " + LOG); LOG.clear(); CueRunner.constructed = 0; CueRunner target = new CueRunner(); CueRunner proxy = subclass(CueRunner.class, new Forwarding(target)) .getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance(); System.out.println(proxy.run("LX-15")); System.out.println("forwarding model: " + LOG + ", constructors run: " + CueRunner.constructed); try { new ByteBuddy().subclass(KotlinCueRunner.class).make(); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("Kotlin class without open: " + e.getMessage()); } } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l05.TwoModelsDemo labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l05/TwoModelsDemo.java TwoModelsDemo.kt package workbench.bytecode.l05 import net.bytebuddy.ByteBuddy import net.bytebuddy.implementation.MethodDelegation import net.bytebuddy.implementation.bind.annotation.AllArguments import net.bytebuddy.implementation.bind.annotation.Origin import net.bytebuddy.implementation.bind.annotation.RuntimeType import net.bytebuddy.implementation.bind.annotation.SuperCall import net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.isDeclaredBy import java.lang.reflect.Method import java.util.concurrent.Callable private val log = mutableListOf<String>() /** Final, like every Kotlin class without `open`. */ class KotlinCueRunner { fun run(cue: String) = "ran $cue" } /** Runs one lighting or sound cue. No interface: a JDK proxy can't stand in for it. */ open class KCueRunner { init { constructed++ } open fun run(cue: String) = "ran $cue (${this.check(cue)})" // self-call open fun check(cue: String) = "checked $cue" fun stage() = "main stage" // final: no `open` companion object { var constructed = 0 } } /** Quarkus ArC style: the generated subclass instance IS the object; @SuperCall runs the original body on it. */ class KInSubclass { @RuntimeType fun intercept(@Origin m: Method, @SuperCall original: Callable<*>): Any? { log += "intercepted ${m.name}" return original.call() } } /** Spring AOP style: the generated subclass forwards to a separate target object. */ class KForwarding(private val target: Any) { @RuntimeType fun intercept(@Origin m: Method, @AllArguments args: Array<Any?>): Any? { log += "forwarded ${m.name}" return m.invoke(target, *args) } } private fun <T : Any> subclass(type: Class<T>, interceptor: Any): Class<out T> = ByteBuddy().subclass(type) .method(isDeclaredBy(type)) .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration().filter { it.name == "intercept" }.to(interceptor)) .make().load(type.classLoader).loaded /** The same subclass proxy, two models: the proxy IS the object, or the proxy forwards to a target. */ fun main() { val sub = subclass(KCueRunner::class.java, KInSubclass()) println("generated ${sub.name}") println("declares ${sub.declaredMethods.map { it.name }.sorted()}") val runner = sub.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance() println("${runner.run("LX-14")}, on the ${runner.stage()}") println("subclass model: $log") log.clear() KCueRunner.constructed = 0 val target = KCueRunner() val proxy = subclass(KCueRunner::class.java, KForwarding(target)).getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance() println(proxy.run("LX-15")) println("forwarding model: $log, constructors run: ${KCueRunner.constructed}") try { ByteBuddy().subclass(KotlinCueRunner::class.java).make() } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("Kotlin class without open: ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l05.TwoModelsDemoKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l05/TwoModelsDemo.kt The generated class name ends in $ByteBuddy$ plus a random suffix, and it declares check, run and an $accessor$ method for each. The last line is Kotlin class without open: Cannot subclass primitive, array or final types: class workbench.bytecode.l05.KotlinCueRunner. After adding open, that line disappears, because make() now succeeds. In javap, run and check are plain public, while stage() is public final: kotlinc keeps a member final unless you mark it open, even inside an open class. h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · Who wears the costume: the proxy is the object, or it forwards to one
x: The costume fits, but it can be worn in two ways. They give opposite answers for run("LX-14"), whose body calls this.check(cue). In the first way, the understudy wears the costume and plays the role. There's no other actor: the generated subclass object is the only CueRunner, and the interceptor runs the original body on it through @SuperCall. When that body calls this.check(...), this is the subclass object. The call goes to its override, and the interceptor runs again. The demo logs both calls: subclass model: [intercepted run, intercepted check] In the second way, a lookalike in the costume stands at the stage door and passes each request to the real actor inside. The subclass object is only a front for a separate object, the target. Written by hand, it looks like this: Java class ForwardingCueRunner extends CueRunner { private final CueRunner target; ForwardingCueRunner(CueRunner target) { this.target = target; } @Override public String run(String cue) { log("run"); return target.run(cue); // the body runs on the target } // check() the same way } Kotlin class ForwardingCueRunner(private val target: KCueRunner) : KCueRunner() { override fun run(cue: String): String { log("run") return target.run(cue) // the body runs on the target } // check() the same way } The demo's Forwarding interceptor does the same with method.invoke(target, args). The body runs on the target, where this is the target. So this.check(...) is an ordinary call inside the target. It's the actor talking to themselves, from the last lesson, and it never comes back out through the door: ran LX-15 (checked LX-15) forwarding model: [forwarded run], constructors run: 2 Here the costume picture breaks. Putting on a costume doesn't create a second actor, but creating a subclass object does create a second object. Java ran CueRunner's constructor twice: once for the target, and once for the proxy, because newInstance builds the subclass the normal way. Two cue runners were built to run one cue. Spring's documentation for its version 3.2 warned about exactly that: "The constructor of your proxied object will be called twice". The second object also has fields of its own, like a costume with empty pockets. Anything the lookalike can't pass on, such as a final method, runs on the lookalike itself, from those empty pockets. The lab tests this with its BoxOffice class. A forwarding proxy answers welcome() from its own venue field, which still says "unset", while the target's says "the Riverside". So "it's a subclass" doesn't settle the question. Ask where the body runs. If the proxy is the object, self-calls are intercepted, and final methods run on the real fields. If the proxy forwards, self-calls skip it, and final methods run on the proxy's own fields. Self-calls are intercepted only when the proxy is the object. Ask where the body runs. Frameworks pick one model or the other, and the code you write rarely shows which. The next two sections take Spring and then Quarkus, from their documentation. This track runs neither framework: the Byte Buddy demo stands in for both models. Watch the two models disagree Run TwoModelsDemo again and compare the subclass model and forwarding model lines, and the constructor count. Predict what the subclass-model log shows if check is final (in Java, add final; in Kotlin, remove open). Run it. Undo that. Then explain in one sentence why no change inside Forwarding.intercept could make it see the target's this.check call.
