With check final, the subclass model logs only [intercepted run], and the class declares only run and its accessor: Byte Buddy can't override check, so the self-call runs the original directly. The forwarding interceptor only sees calls made on the proxy object, and the target's this.check is a call on the target, so nothing the proxy does can see it. If the proxy is the object, a call on this goes through the interceptor again. If the proxy forwards, the target's own calls never leave the target.

h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · Spring AOP: a lookalike at the door, in front of a separate target
x: Spring is a framework that creates your application's objects, which it calls beans, and connects them to each other. Spring AOP, for aspect-oriented programming, is how it adds the same extra work, such as timing or transactions, around many methods without editing each one. Spring calls that extra work advice, and a method that gets it is advised. Spring's reference documentation gives the choice of proxy in one rule: "If the target object to be proxied implements at least one interface, a JDK dynamic proxy is used, and all of the interfaces implemented by the target type are proxied. If the target object does not implement any interfaces, a CGLIB proxy is created which is a runtime-generated subclass of the target type." Spring Boot, the part of Spring that sets up an application with sensible defaults, changes that default. Its AopAutoConfiguration turns on class-based proxies unless you set spring.aop.proxy-target-class=false. So in a Boot application, expect CGLIB subclasses even for beans that have interfaces. Spring Framework 7.0 adds @Proxyable(INTERFACES) and @Proxyable(TARGET_CLASS) to choose for one bean. Either way, the proxy forwards to a separate target bean: the lookalike at the door. The rules follow from the first section, and the documentation lists them for CGLIB proxies: "final classes cannot be proxied", "final methods cannot be advised", "private methods cannot be advised". The constructor no longer runs twice. Spring now creates the CGLIB proxy object through Objenesis, a library that makes objects without running any constructor. The price is the empty pockets: a final method that runs on the proxy sees fields that were never set, often null. The best-known advice is @Transactional. A database transaction is a group of changes that is saved all together or not at all, and this annotation asks Spring to start one around the method. The documentation spells out what proxy mode, the default, means for it. "Only external method calls coming in through the proxy are intercepted", so self-invocation "does not lead to an actual transaction at runtime". Since Spring 6.0, @Transactional also works on protected and package-visible methods when the proxy is class-based. Interface-based proxies need public methods declared in the interface. The documented ways out of self-invocation, best first, are these. Restructure so the call crosses from one bean to another. Inject the bean into itself and call the proxy. Or call AopContext.currentProxy(), which the documentation itself calls "highly discouraged". There's also AspectJ mode, where a tool called AspectJ weaves the advice into your class's own bytecode, so there is no proxy at all. Kotlin adds one requirement. The kotlin-spring compiler plugin is "a preconfigured wrapper around the all-open plugin". It opens classes annotated with @Component, @Async, @Transactional, @Cacheable and @SpringBootTest, and, through @Component, also @Service, @Repository, @Controller, @RestController and @Configuration. Projects made on start.spring.io turn it on by default. Without it, a Kotlin bean is a final class that CGLIB can't extend. Write open class by hand and forget open fun, and you get the quieter failure: methods that are never advised. In Spring, advice runs only on calls that come in through the proxy. Keep advised methods open, and call them from another bean. Spring sews its costumes while the application starts. Quarkus sews them earlier. Read a class the way CGLIB would Open labs/bytecode/src/main/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l05/BoxOffice.kt, the lab's starting point. Compile it with ./gradlew :bytecode:classes from labs/. Run javap -p bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/main/workbench/bytecode/l05/BoxOffice.class. Mark each member: could a CGLIB subclass advise it? Then say what Spring would do with a @Transactional on price. terminal ./gradlew :bytecode:classes javap -p bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/main/workbench/bytecode/l05/BoxOffice.class public final class workbench.bytecode.l05.BoxOffice, and every method public final, the getter and setter of venue included. Nothing can be advised, and the class itself can't be extended, so Spring couldn't build a CGLIB proxy for it at all. With kotlin-spring and a Spring annotation on the class, kotlinc would write the class and its members without final. In the lab you add open by hand. Spring Framework reference: Proxying mechanisms docs kotlin-spring compiler plugin (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · Quarkus ArC: costumes sewn at build time, and self-calls intercepted
x: Quarkus is a framework designed to do as much work as it can while your application is built, so that less is left for start-up. Its container, ArC, is the part that creates beans and runs interceptors around their methods. ArC follows CDI, the Jakarta Contexts and Dependency Injection standard, which defines how a container creates objects, wires them together and intercepts their methods. In CDI, an interceptor is a class that a container runs around each method carrying a matching annotation, such as @Transactional. ArC writes its proxy classes during the build, as ordinary class files, so the costume is sewn before the doors open. Its source names them in comments: "Foo_Subclass extends Foo implements Subclass" for a bean with interceptors, and "Foo_ClientProxy extends Foo implements ClientProxy" for a client proxy. Both are subclasses of your class, playing two different roles. A client proxy is the forwarding model, used for scopes. A scoped bean has one instance per scope, such as one per application (@ApplicationScoped) or one per web request (@RequestScoped). The Quarkus documentation calls a client proxy "an object that delegates all method invocations to a target bean instance". The real instance is created on the first method call. That's why the documentation says to "never read or write a field of a normal scoped bean" from outside: you'd be reading the lookalike's empty pockets. A @Singleton bean has no client proxy. The intercepted subclass is the other model. The Quarkus CDI reference says: "Quarkus supports what is known as intercepted self-invocation or just self-interception - a scenario where CDI bean invokes its own intercepted method from within another method while triggering any associated interceptors." It calls this a non-standard feature, because the CDI specification doesn't say whether self-interception should work. Given Foo_Subclass extends Foo, the natural reading is that the subclass object is the bean itself, the understudy who plays the role, so this.book(seat) reaches the intercepting override. That mechanism is an inference from the documentation and the class names; this track didn't trace it in ArC's source. The behaviour itself is documented. A client proxy in front of an intercepted bean forwards to that subclass object, so both kinds can apply at once. So a class can change behaviour when it moves from Spring to Quarkus, without one edited line. Take a BoxOffice whose bookAll(seats) calls this.book(seat), with @Transactional on book. Under Spring, the inner calls got no transaction of their own. Under ArC, each book call gets one, and the reverse move loses them. ArC also works around Kotlin's final classes. quarkus.arc.transform-unproxyable-classes is true by default and lets Quarkus proxy final classes and classes with final methods. The Quarkus Kotlin guide still sets up the all-open plugin for @Path, @ApplicationScoped and database entity classes. Follow the guide, and check with javap and a test before you assume either one is unnecessary. Every tool in this lesson adds work the same way, by overriding, so they share one limit. A final class from a library you can't recompile stays out of reach, and so does every final method inside it. Quarkus: Contexts and Dependency Injection reference (ArC) docs

h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · Java and Kotlin
x: A timing subclass proxy in Java and Kotlin TimedSubclass.java public class SuperCallTimer { @RuntimeType public Object intercept(@Origin Method m, @SuperCall Callable<?> original) throws Exception { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { return original.call(); // the original body, on this same object } finally { System.out.println(m.getName() + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) + " ns"); } } } // a Java class and its methods are open by default; final methods would be skipped BoxOffice timed = new ByteBuddy() .subclass(BoxOffice.class) .method(isPublic().and(isDeclaredBy(BoxOffice.class))) .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration() .filter(named("intercept")).to(new SuperCallTimer())) .make().load(BoxOffice.class.getClassLoader()).getLoaded() .getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance(); TimedSubclass.kt class SuperCallTimer { @RuntimeType fun intercept(@Origin m: Method, @SuperCall original: Callable<*>): Any? { val t0 = System.nanoTime() try { return original.call() // the original body, on this same object } finally { println("${m.name} took ${System.nanoTime() - t0} ns") } } } // BoxOffice and each method must be `open` (or opened by all-open) val timed: BoxOffice = ByteBuddy() .subclass(BoxOffice::class.java) .method(isPublic<MethodDescription>().and(isDeclaredBy(BoxOffice::class.java))) .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration() .filter(named("intercept")).to(SuperCallTimer())) .make().load(BoxOffice::class.java.classLoader).loaded .getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance() The Byte Buddy calls are the same in both. What changes is what there is to intercept. A Java class and its methods are open unless marked final. A Kotlin class and its members are final unless marked open, so the same builder quietly skips every Kotlin method you didn't open, and refuses the class outright if the class itself is final. Kotlin also needs the type argument in isPublic<MethodDescription>(), because the matcher is generic and nothing else tells the compiler its type. In both, filter(named("intercept")) stops Byte Buddy from treating the interceptor's other methods, such as equals and toString, as candidates, which otherwise fails with "Cannot resolve ambiguous delegation".

h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · Worked example
x: A @Transactional Kotlin method that never starts a transaction A Spring Boot service in Kotlin books seats. SeatRepository is the bean that saves them to a database. Someone added open to the class so Spring could build its proxy, and the application starts fine. Before reading on: does book run in a transaction when a web controller, the class that handles a request, calls it? @Service open class BookingService(private val seats: SeatRepository) { @Transactional fun book(seat: String) { // no `open` seats.save(seat) } } // the Java equivalent of what kotlinc wrote @Service public class BookingService { private final SeatRepository seats; public BookingService(SeatRepository seats) { this.seats = seats; } @Transactional public final void book(String seat) { // final: CGLIB can't override it seats.save(seat); } } Check the JVM's view. javap -p shows the class without final, which is why Spring could build its CGLIB subclass. But book is still public final void book(java.lang.String), and the Spring documentation says "final methods cannot be advised". So the controller calls the proxy, the proxy can't override book, and the inherited body runs on the proxy object, with no transaction. public class BookingService { private final SeatRepository seats; public BookingService(SeatRepository); public final void book(java.lang.String); // 1. final: never advised } It's worse than a missing transaction. The body runs on the proxy, not on the target, and Spring builds CGLIB proxies through Objenesis, which skips constructors. On the proxy, seats was never set: the lookalike's pockets are empty. The forwarding test in this lesson's lab shows the same effect with Byte Buddy, where a final method reads the proxy's own field instead of the target's. Expect a NullPointerException on seats, or quietly wrong data. Fix it in the build, not one method at a time. The kotlin-spring plugin opens classes annotated with @Service or @Transactional, and their members, so book compiles without final. Then keep calls to book coming from outside the bean, because the proxy still forwards, and a self-call would still skip it. // build.gradle.kts plugins { kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.21" kotlin("plugin.spring") version "2.4.21" // all-open preset for Spring annotations }

x: Time a Kotlin class with Byte Buddy, two ways labs/bytecode/src/main/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l05/BoxOffice.kt labs/bytecode/src/main/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l05/TimingProxies.kt ./gradlew :bytecode:test --tests 'workbench.bytecode.l05.*' Run the tests once. Write a SuperCallInterceptor(clock, sink) class with @RuntimeType fun intercept(@Origin method: Method, @SuperCall zuper: Callable<*>): Any?. Read the clock, call zuper.call(), read the clock again and record the call. On an exception, record it with failed = true and rethrow it. Use it in subclassTimed. Run the tests. h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · Quiz
x: A Spring Boot application has class TicketService implements Tickets with a @Transactional method, and no proxy settings. What kind of proxy does Spring Boot put in front of it by default? A JDK dynamic proxy, because the class implements an interface A CGLIB subclass of TicketService, because Boot sets proxyTargetClass=true unless spring.aop.proxy-target-class=false No proxy: @Transactional is applied by an agent A Byte Buddy subclass Spring Framework on its own would pick a JDK proxy for a bean with interfaces. Spring Boot's AopAutoConfiguration turns on class-based proxies by default. Either kind forwards to a separate target, so the self-invocation rules are the same. Kotlin: @Service open class Bookings { @Transactional fun book(seat: String) { repo.save(seat) } }, without the kotlin-spring plugin. A controller calls bookings.book("B12"). What happens? book runs in a transaction Start-up fails: Spring can't proxy the class book is final, so the CGLIB proxy can't advise it. The body runs on the proxy object, without a transaction, where repo may be null Spring builds an interface-based proxy instead open class lets CGLIB extend the class, but each member is still final unless marked open. A final method is inherited unchanged, so calling it on the proxy runs the body on the proxy object, which Spring created through Objenesis without running a constructor. kotlin-spring opens the members as well. In a Quarkus @ApplicationScoped bean, bookAll() calls this.book(seat), and book is @Transactional. Which statement matches the Quarkus documentation? The inner call is intercepted: ArC supports intercepted self-invocation, as a non-standard feature The inner call skips the interceptor, as in Spring It depends on quarkus.arc.transform-unproxyable-classes Quarkus rejects self-invocation at build time The Quarkus CDI reference says ArC supports self-interception: calling an intercepted method from another method of the same bean still triggers its interceptors. It's non-standard because the CDI specification doesn't define it. transform-unproxyable-classes is about final classes and methods, not self-calls. Which change makes an entity class usable for Hibernate's lazy proxies? Mark the entity final so Hibernate can inline it Declare collection fields as ArrayList instead of List Make equals compare getClass() of both objects Keep it non-final and give it a non-private constructor with no parameters Hibernate generates a subclass of the entity, so the class must not be final and needs a non-private constructor with no parameters. Collection fields must use interface types, because Hibernate puts its own collection classes there. A getClass() comparison in equals fails against a proxy, whose class is the generated subclass. From Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy: you call Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[]{BoxOffice.class}, h), where BoxOffice is a class with no interface. What happens? A subclass proxy is generated instead IllegalArgumentException: ... BoxOffice is not an interface It works, but only public methods reach the handler UndeclaredThrowableException A JDK proxy class implements interfaces and extends java.lang.reflect.Proxy, so it can't extend your class. To intercept a class, a library must generate a subclass, which is what Byte Buddy, Spring's CGLIB, ArC and Hibernate do.

h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · Key terms
x: Subclass proxy A generated subclass that overrides methods to add work around them; it works for classes, not only interfaces. Byte Buddy A library for generating and changing classes while a program runs; Hibernate and many tools build on it. Interceptor An object whose method runs in place of an intercepted method and decides when to call the original. CGLIB An older bytecode library, now unmaintained; Spring ships its own patched copy for class-based proxies. Objenesis A library that creates objects without running constructors; Spring uses it for CGLIB proxy objects. Client proxy ArC's Foo_ClientProxy: a subclass that forwards each call to the real bean instance for its scope. Self-interception Intercepting a call a bean makes to its own method. ArC supports it; Spring's proxy mode doesn't. all-open A Kotlin compiler plugin that makes classes with chosen annotations, and their members, non-final. What can a subclass proxy never intercept? Anything it can't override: a final class (no proxy at all), final methods and private methods. Those run as written. Why does a plain Kotlin class fail with Byte Buddy, CGLIB or Hibernate? Kotlin classes and members are final by default. Byte Buddy says Cannot subclass primitive, array or final types. When the proxy is the object (@SuperCall, ArC's _Subclass), is a self-call this.check() intercepted? Yes. this is the generated subclass, so the call goes to its overriding method, and the interceptor runs. On a forwarding proxy (Spring style), where does a final method run? On the proxy object itself, with the proxy's own fields, which Spring's Objenesis-built proxies never set. Which proxy does Spring Boot use by default for a bean that implements an interface? A CGLIB subclass: Boot sets proxyTargetClass=true unless spring.aop.proxy-target-class=false. What does Quarkus ArC do with a bean's call to its own intercepted method? It intercepts it (self-interception), a documented, non-standard CDI behaviour. Spring's proxy mode doesn't. Which Kotlin plugin opens Spring beans, and which opens JPA entities? kotlin-spring (an all-open preset) for Spring annotations; kotlin-jpa for entities, which also adds constructors with no parameters.

h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · Go deeper
x: Byte Buddy can also change a class instead of extending it. rebase(Clock.class) keeps the original method body under a new private name, now$original$..., and generates a new now that can call it. The Javadoc likens it to "creating a subclass where the subclass is later merged with the original class file". redefine(Clock.class) replaces now and throws the original body away. Both produce a class with the original name, so you can only load the result where the original isn't loaded yet, or rename it, or, in a running JVM, use an agent. That's lesson 7, where Byte Buddy's Advice comes in. Advice copies your code into the existing method body instead of adding accessor methods and helper classes, which is what changing an already loaded class requires. The subclass's helpers have a cost you can see. Each intercepted method gets an $accessor$ twin so the interceptor can call the original, and @SuperCall creates a small Callable on every call. In this track's single JMH run on a shared 4-core machine, a Byte Buddy subclass with @SuperCall measured about 0.9 ns per call, against 0.8 ns for a direct call and about 4.3 ns for a JDK proxy. The numbers are noisy and only indicative, but the order is clear. Quarkus can intercept some static methods too. The CDI reference allows an interceptor binding on a non-private static method, with three limits: only bindings on the method itself count, private static methods are never intercepted, and InvocationContext#getTarget() returns null. For producer methods whose result needs interceptors, InterceptionProxy generates, at build time, a subclass that intercepts and forwards. The class must not be final, must not have non-private final methods, and needs a non-private constructor with no parameters. These are the subclass rules once again.

h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · Reading the page by hand: magic number, version and the glossary
x: A class file is bytes with a fixed layout; the ClassFile API parses them into elements, builds classes from builder lambdas, and transforms them as a flatMap: each element in, zero or more out Every tool in this track reads or writes the same format: javap, the verifier (the JVM's check that bytecode is type-safe), Proxy, the lambda machinery, Byte Buddy, and the agents of the next lesson. A class file is an array of bytes with a fixed layout, set out in chapter 4 of the JVM specification. Here are the first ten bytes of java/lang/Object.class on JDK 25, as this section's demo prints them: ca fe ba be 00 00 00 45 00 73 magic minor major constant_pool_count The first four bytes are the magic number, 0xCAFEBABE: the stamp that says "this is a class file". Then come two version numbers. The major version is 0x45, which is 69, and Java 25 wrote it. From Java 5 on, the Java version is the major version minus 44. A JVM refuses a class file whose major version is newer than its own, with UnsupportedClassVersionError. The labs' own classes say 00 41, which is 65, because the build compiles them with release 21. Then comes constant_pool_count, and after it the constant pool itself: lesson 2's glossary, a numbered table of every name and constant the class uses. Every number in the file is big-endian, biggest byte first, which is exactly how DataInputStream reads. So the first four fields take four lines: Java DataInputStream in = new DataInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes)); int magic = in.readInt(); // u4: 0xCAFEBABE int minor = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2 int major = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2: 65 = Java 21, 69 = Java 25 int poolCount = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2: entries are numbered 1 .. poolCount - 1 Kotlin val input = DataInputStream(ByteArrayInputStream(bytes)) val magic = input.readInt() // u4: 0xCAFEBABE val minor = input.readUnsignedShort() // u2 val major = input.readUnsignedShort() // u2: 65 = Java 21, 69 = Java 25 val poolCount = input.readUnsignedShort() // u2: entries are numbered 1 .. poolCount - 1 The glossary is the hard part. Each entry starts with a one-byte tag, and the tag decides how many bytes follow. A Utf8 entry, a piece of text, has a two-byte length and then the text. A Class entry has two bytes: the number of the Utf8 entry that holds the class's name. A Methodref, a reference to a method, has four. And a Long or Double entry takes up two numbers. Remember lesson 2's javap -v listing of StackDemo: #7 = Long 1000l #9 = InvokeDynamic #0:#10 // #0:makeConcatWithConstants:(JLjava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/String; There is no #8, because the 8-byte constant at #7 sits in two seats. After the glossary come the access flags, then this_class, the number of the Class entry that names this class. Then come the superclass, the interfaces, the fields, the methods and the attributes. In the lab, you write this walk yourself and check it against a real class-file library. Each entry's size depends on its tag, so one wrong count shifts everything after it. Count Long and Double twice. That walk is the reason a library helps. Anything that writes or changes classes must get this format exactly right, and the format gains a new major version every six months, sometimes with new kinds of entries. Until JDK 24, the JDK had no public library for it. Frameworks bundled ASM, the long-standing class-file library (Byte Buddy carries its own copy), and needed a new release for each new class-file version. The JDK kept a private copy of ASM too; it's gone from the jdk-25-ga source. Doing the walk by hand once teaches you the format. Doing it for every class, on every JDK, is a job for a press. Read three class-file headers Before you run anything, predict the major version of ClassFileHeader.class (built by the labs), of java.lang.Object on the JDK you're using, and of kotlin.Unit from the Kotlin standard library. Run ClassFileHeader, then its Kotlin twin. If you have both JDK 21 and JDK 25 installed, run the Java version on each, from labs/: java -cp bytecode/build/classes/java/demo:bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.bytecode.l06.ClassFileHeader. ClassFileHeader.java package workbench.bytecode.l06; import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream; import java.io.DataInputStream; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.InputStream; import java.util.HexFormat; /** The first ten bytes of three class files: magic, version and constant pool size. */ public class ClassFileHeader { public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { show(ClassFileHeader.class); // compiled by the labs build with release 21 show(HeaderMarker.class); // compiled by kotlinc in the same build (from ClassFileHeader.kt) show(Object.class); // from the JDK you are running } static void show(Class<?> c) throws IOException { byte[] bytes; try (InputStream in = c.getResourceAsStream(c.getSimpleName() + ".class")) { bytes = in.readAllBytes(); } DataInputStream in = new DataInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes)); int magic = in.readInt(); // u4 int minor = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2 int major = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2 int poolCount = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2: entries are numbered 1 .. poolCount - 1 System.out.printf("%-34s %s magic=%X version=%d.%d (Java %d) pool entries=%d size=%d bytes%n", c.getName(), HexFormat.ofDelimiter(" ").formatHex(bytes, 0, 10), magic, major, minor, major - 44, poolCount - 1, bytes.length); } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l06.ClassFileHeader labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l06/ClassFileHeader.java ClassFileHeader.kt package workbench.bytecode.l06 import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream import java.io.DataInputStream import java.util.HexFormat /** A Kotlin class for the Java twin to read. */ class HeaderMarker /** The first ten bytes of three class files: magic, version and constant pool size. */ fun main() { show(HeaderMarker::class.java) // compiled by kotlinc in the labs build with jvmTarget 21 show(Unit::class.java) // the Kotlin standard library jar show(Any::class.java) // java.lang.Object, from the JDK you are running } private fun show(c: Class<*>) { val bytes = c.getResourceAsStream(c.simpleName + ".class")!!.use { it.readAllBytes() } val input = DataInputStream(ByteArrayInputStream(bytes)) val magic = input.readInt() // u4 val minor = input.readUnsignedShort() // u2 val major = input.readUnsignedShort() // u2 val poolCount = input.readUnsignedShort() // u2: entries are numbered 1 .. poolCount - 1 println("%-34s %s magic=%X version=%d.%d (Java %d) pool entries=%d size=%d bytes".format( c.name, HexFormat.ofDelimiter(" ").formatHex(bytes, 0, 10), magic, major, minor, major - 44, poolCount - 1, bytes.size)) } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l06.ClassFileHeaderKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l06/ClassFileHeader.kt Every line starts with ca fe ba be. The labs' own classes, Java and Kotlin, are version=65.0 (Java 21), because the build uses release 21 and jvmTarget 21. java.lang.Object is 65.0 (Java 21) with 123 pool entries on JDK 21, and 69.0 (Java 25) with 114 on JDK 25, so the same program reports the JDK it runs on. kotlin.Unit is 52.0 (Java 8): the standard library is compiled for Java 8, so it runs everywhere. JVM Specification SE 25, chapter 4: The class File Format docs

h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · Reading it with the ClassFile API: models and elements
x: The package java.lang.classfile is the JDK's own class-file library. It was a preview feature in JDK 22 (JEP 457) and JDK 23 (JEP 466), and became final in JDK 24 (JEP 484). So on JDK 25 you use it with no special flags. A preview feature is a complete design that you can only use with --enable-preview, while the JDK team collects feedback. The labs compile with release 21, which can't see the package, so this lesson's ClassFile API code lives in single-file programs under labs/bytecode/preview/. You run them with java File.java on JDK 24 or later. On JDK 21 they stop at once with package java.lang.classfile does not exist. Everything starts at ClassFile.of(). Its parse method turns bytes into a ClassModel: Java ClassModel cm = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes); System.out.println(cm.thisClass().asInternalName() + " major " + cm.majorVersion()); for (MethodModel m : cm.methods()) { long invokes = m.code() .map(code -> code.elementStream().filter(e -> e instanceof InvokeInstruction).count()) .orElse(0L); System.out.println(m.methodName().stringValue() + m.methodType().stringValue() + " invokes=" + invokes); } Kotlin val cm = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes) println("${cm.thisClass().asInternalName()} major ${cm.majorVersion()}") for (m in cm.methods()) { val invokes = m.code() .map { code -> code.elementStream().filter { it is InvokeInstruction }.count() } .orElse(0L) println("${m.methodName().stringValue()}${m.methodType().stringValue()} invokes=$invokes") } A model is an immutable description of one part of a class file: the class, a field, a method, or a method's code. Picture the press reading a page into a stack of typed cards. The package documentation adds that a ClassModel "is inflated lazily; most parts of the classfile are not parsed until they are actually needed". So a broken method can parse fine, and throw IllegalArgumentException only when you open it. Each model can also be read as a sequence of elements, its cards in order. A class's elements are its methods, fields and attributes. A method's code is a sequence of instructions, labels and other code elements. Each instruction is an object with a type you can test, such as InvokeInstruction, ConstantInstruction or InvokeDynamicInstruction. The rest of the API is built on this one idea. Reading walks the elements, building writes elements, and transforming maps elements to elements. Let's point it at lesson 2's StackDemo, the class with the lighting fade. ClassFileTour parses it, counts the glossary entries by kind, and counts the invoke instructions in each method. On JDK 25 it prints: workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo extends java/lang/Object, major 65 constant pool: {ClassEntry=7, FieldRefEntry=1, InvokeDynamicEntry=1, LongEntry=2, MethodHandleEntry=1, MethodRefEntry=5, NameAndTypeEntry=7, StringEntry=2, Utf8Entry=43} <init>()V invokes=1 seconds(JI)J invokes=0 describe(Ljava/lang/String;J)Ljava/lang/String; invokes=0 main([Ljava/lang/String;)V invokes=3 The two LongEntry cards are the 1000 and the 32 from the fade. seconds(JI)J does arithmetic and calls nothing. describe builds a string with +, and yet its count is 0. Keep that in mind for the Try it. Names and types come back as glossary entries. methodName() is a Utf8Entry, which is why the code calls stringValue(). When you build a class, you go the other way. You pass symbolic descriptions from java.lang.constant, such as ClassDesc.of("Fade") for a class or MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_long, CD_long) for a method type, and the library creates the entries. Reading is half of what a press does. The other half is printing. Tour lesson 2's class with the ClassFile API This needs JDK 24 or later. From labs/, make sure lesson 2's demo was built (./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l02.StackDemo), then run the command below. The Kotlin twin needs kotlinc running on JDK 24 or later. Compare the constant-pool counts with the javap -v listing you read in lesson 2. describe builds a string and calls nothing else, yet its count is 0. Before reading on: which instruction does it contain, and why didn't the filter count it? ClassFileTour.java (JDK 24+) // JDK 24 or later (the ClassFile API is final since JDK 24, JEP 484). From labs/: // java bytecode/preview/ClassFileTour.java [path/to/Some.class] // With no argument it reads StackDemo.class from lesson 2 (run that demo once first), // or java.lang.Integer from the running JDK if the file isn't there. import java.lang.classfile.ClassFile; import java.lang.classfile.ClassModel; import java.lang.classfile.MethodModel; import java.lang.classfile.constantpool.PoolEntry; import java.lang.classfile.instruction.InvokeInstruction; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; public class ClassFileTour { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Path p = Path.of(args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.class"); byte[] bytes = Files.exists(p) ? Files.readAllBytes(p) : Integer.class.getResourceAsStream("Integer.class").readAllBytes(); // 1. parse: an immutable model, inflated lazily as you ask for parts ClassModel cm = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes); System.out.println(cm.thisClass().asInternalName() + " extends " + cm.superclass().map(c -> c.asInternalName()).orElse("-") + ", major " + cm.majorVersion()); // 2. the constant pool, counted by kind of entry Map<String, Integer> kinds = new TreeMap<>(); for (PoolEntry e : cm.constantPool()) { kinds.merge(e.getClass().getInterfaces()[0].getSimpleName(), 1, Integer::sum); } System.out.println("constant pool: " + kinds); // 3. methods, and the invoke instructions inside each one for (MethodModel m : cm.methods()) { long invokes = m.code() .map(code -> code.elementStream().filter(e -> e instanceof InvokeInstruction).count()) .orElse(0L); System.out.println(" " + m.methodName().stringValue() + m.methodType().stringValue() + " invokes=" + invokes); } } } java bytecode/preview/ClassFileTour.java labs/bytecode/preview/ClassFileTour.java ClassFileTour.kt (JDK 24+) // JDK 24 or later, with kotlinc running on that JDK. From labs/: // kotlinc bytecode/preview/ClassFileTour.kt -jvm-target 21 -include-runtime -d build/cftour.jar // java -jar build/cftour.jar [path/to/Some.class] // With no argument it reads StackDemo.class from lesson 2, or java.lang.Integer from the JDK. import java.lang.classfile.ClassFile import java.lang.classfile.instruction.InvokeInstruction import java.nio.file.Files import counted by kind of entry val kinds = cm.constantPool().groupingBy { it.javaClass.interfaces[0].simpleName }.eachCount().toSortedMap() println("constant pool: $kinds") // 3. methods, and the invoke h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · Printing a new class: builders, and a proofreader called verify
x: To print a class, you don't create builder objects yourself. You pass lambdas, and the library hands each one the builder for its level: a ClassBuilder for the class, a CodeBuilder for a method body. A CodeBuilder has one method per instruction, so a method body reads like the javap listings of lesson 2. Here is lesson 2's fade again, as a class of its own. Fade.seconds(steps) says how long a fade of that many 32-millisecond steps runs, in whole seconds: Java byte[] fade = ClassFile.of().build(ClassDesc.of("Fade"), clb -> clb .withFlags(ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_FINAL) .withMethodBody("seconds", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_long, CD_long), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_STATIC, cob -> cob .lload(0) // the number of steps, slots 0 and 1 .ldc(32L) // one step, in milliseconds .lmul() .ldc(1_000L) .ldiv() .lreturn())); Class<?> c = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(fade); // load it next to this class Kotlin val fade = ClassFile.of().build(ClassDesc.of("Fade")) { clb -> clb.withFlags(ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC or ClassFile.ACC_FINAL) clb.withMethodBody("seconds", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_long, CD_long), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC or ClassFile.ACC_STATIC) { cob -> cob.lload(0) // the number of steps, slots 0 and 1 .loadConstant(32L) // one step, in milliseconds (Kotlin: see below) .lmul() .loadConstant(1_000L) .ldiv() .lreturn() } } val c = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(fade) // load it next to this class Read it the way lesson 2's stagehand would. lload(0) puts the number of steps on the pile of cue cards; a long takes local slots 0 and 1. ldc(32L) pushes the step length, and lmul multiplies the top two cards. ldc(1_000L) and ldiv turn milliseconds into seconds, and lreturn hands back the long on top. Then MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass loads the bytes as a class, in the same package and class loader as the class that calls it. (The demo's Fade also gets an empty debugTrace method, for the next section.) The demo prints: built Fade: 198 bytes, verify errors [] Fade.seconds(12500) = 400 That's 400 seconds, the same fade that lesson 2's StackDemo printed. The builder writes what you tell it to, including nonsense. A method declared to return an int that pushes a String builds without a complaint. Lesson 1 showed what happens when such a class loads: defineClass can succeed, and a VerifyError arrives later. ClassFile.of().verify(bytes) runs the verifier's checks on the bytes first and returns a list of errors. The verifier is the JVM's proofreader. It checks that every instruction finds values of the right type, and it never reads the plot: verify(Broken): [java.lang.VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack in Broken::answer() @2 (integer_type is not assignable from java/lang/String)] An empty list proves less than it seems. Delete the ldiv, and the class still verifies. Two long values are left on the stack at lreturn, which is legal, and seconds(12500) returns 1000, the last value pushed. You'll try it in a moment. verify proves that generated code is type-safe, not that it's right. Test what it computes. Kotlin has one trap here. ldc takes a java.lang.constant.ConstantDesc, an interface that Java's String and Long implement. Kotlin's String and Long types don't show that interface, so cob.ldc("forty-two") doesn't compile in Kotlin. Use loadConstant(32L), which has overloads for primitives, or pass a glossary entry: cob.ldc(cob.constantPool().stringEntry("forty-two")). We can print new pages now. The harder job is to edit a page that already exists without smudging the rest. Build, verify, then break it On JDK 24 or later, run ClassFileForge from labs/ (command below), or build and run the Kotlin twin. Read the first three lines: the size of the generated class, its verify result, the fade length, and the verifier's message for Broken. In the seconds body, delete the .ldiv() line, and predict what verify(fade) reports and what seconds(12500) returns. Run it again. h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · Editing a class safely: a transform keeps, drops or replaces each element
x: Changing an existing class is where elements pay off. The package documentation puts it in one sentence: "Transformation can be viewed as a 'flatMap' operation on the sequence of elements; for every element, we could pass it through unchanged, drop it, or replace it with one or more elements." (flatMap is the stream operation that turns each item into zero, one or more items.) Picture copying a page of the prompt book line by line. For each line you can copy it as it is, leave it out, or write something else in its place. A ClassTransform sees a class's elements, and a CodeTransform sees the instructions of one method. Inside a transform, you hand each element to the builder: builder.with(element) passes it through, doing nothing drops it, and calling other builder methods replaces it. This transform drops every method whose name starts with debug, and makes every fade slower, with 40 ms steps instead of 32: Java CodeTransform slower = (cob, element) -> { if (element instanceof ConstantInstruction ci && Long.valueOf(32L).equals(ci.constantValue())) { cob.ldc(40L); // replace } else { cob.with(element); // pass through } }; ClassTransform transform = ClassTransform .dropping(e -> e instanceof MethodModel m && m.methodName().stringValue().startsWith("debug")) .andThen(ClassTransform.transformingMethodBodies(slower)); byte[] v2 = cf.transformClass(cf.parse(fade), ClassDesc.of("FadeV2"), transform); Kotlin val slower = CodeTransform { cob, element -> if (element is ConstantInstruction && element.constantValue().equals(32L)) { cob.loadConstant(40L) // replace } else { cob.with(element) // pass through } } val transform = ClassTransform .dropping { it is MethodModel && it.methodName().stringValue().startsWith("debug") } .andThen(ClassTransform.transformingMethodBodies(slower)) val v2 = cf.transformClass(cf.parse(fade), ClassDesc.of("FadeV2"), transform) The new class, FadeV2, has only seconds left, and the same 12,500 steps now take longer: FadeV2 methods [seconds], seconds(12500) = 500 Everything the transform passed through was copied unchanged. That's also the default: a transform that changes nothing reproduces the class. The JDK prints its own classes on this press. ProxyGenerator moved from its internal ASM to java.lang.classfile in JDK 23, and the lambda class generator, InnerClassLambdaMetafactory, followed in JDK 24. So on JDK 25, the $Proxy0 of lesson 4 and the $$Lambda classes of lesson 3 come from the code you just ran. Who should use it? A tool that only needs to run on JDK 24 or later can drop its ASM dependency, because the API always matches the JDK it runs on. A library that must support older JDKs can't. Byte Buddy's regular jar targets Java 8 and its -jdk5 jar targets Java 5, so it keeps its bundled ASM and bridges to the ClassFile API when it finds one. Its release notes for 1.16.0 say: "Include support for JDK Class File API". To edit a class, copy it element by element. Pass through everything you don't mean to change. Here's the limit of today's tool. Every class in this lesson was new: we printed Fade, then copied it into FadeV2 under a new name. A class that is already loaded, with objects already using it, can't be replaced by defining another class. Changing that one takes an agent. Write your own transform Run ClassFileForge again and read the last line. Change the code transform so it also turns 1_000L into 60_000L, so that the method returns minutes, without touching the 32 branch. Predict the new FadeV2.seconds(12500) before you run it. Undo that, then remove the .andThen(...) part, keeping only dropping. Which number in the last line changes? h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · Java and Kotlin
x: Reading a class's name in Java and Kotlin, by hand and with the API ThisClass.java // by hand (any JDK): walk the pool, then read this_class static String thisClass(byte[] bytes) { return ClassFileFacts.thisClass(bytes); // the lab's DataInputStream walk } // with the ClassFile API (JDK 24+) static String thisClassWithApi(byte[] bytes) { return ClassFile.of().parse(bytes).thisClass().asInternalName(); } ThisClass.kt // by hand (any JDK): walk the pool, then read this_class fun thisClass(bytes: ByteArray): String = ClassFileFacts.thisClass(bytes) // the lab's DataInputStream walk // with the ClassFile API (JDK 24+) fun thisClassWithApi(bytes: ByteArray): String = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes).thisClass().asInternalName() Same bytes, same answer. The API version is one line, because the library walks the pool for you, and only as far as it needs to. The language differences are small but real. Kotlin calls the API through ordinary SAM conversion for its Consumer and CodeTransform parameters, and writes access flags with or instead of |. Kotlin's String and Long types don't show Java's ConstantDesc, so ldc("...") needs a constant-pool entry, or loadConstant for primitives. And compiling Kotlin against the API needs kotlinc to run on JDK 24 or later (or to point -jdk-home at one), whatever -jvm-target you choose.

h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · Worked example
x: Find the jar that broke the start-up The theatre's ticket app starts on JDK 21 and stops at once. A jar is a zip file of class files, and the app is built from several of them. Which part of the message tells you what to look for? Error: LinkageError occurred while loading main class theatre.booking.SeatMap java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: theatre/booking/SeatMap has been compiled by a more recent version of the Java Runtime (class file version 69.0), this version of the Java Runtime only recognizes class file versions up to 65.0 Class file version 69.0 is Java 25 (69 - 44), and the runtime only knows up to 65, Java 21. Something was compiled for JDK 25. Here one class is named, but a jar can mix versions, so check every class. Read each entry's header with the lab's code. try (JarFile jar = new JarFile(path.toFile())) { jar.stream() .filter(e -> e.getName().endsWith(".class")) .forEach(e -> { try (InputStream in = jar.getInputStream(e)) { // 1. read magic, minor, major from the first 10 bytes ClassFileFacts.Header h = ClassFileFacts.header(in.readNBytes(10)); // 2. report anything newer than the runtime if (h.major() > 65) System.out.println(e.getName() + " -> Java " + ClassFileFacts.javaVersion(h.major())); } catch (IOException ex) { throw new UncheckedIOException(ex); } }); } JarFile(path.toFile()).use { jar -> jar.stream() .filter { it.name.endsWith(".class") } .forEach { e -> // 1. read magic, minor, major from the first 10 bytes val h = jar.getInputStream(e).use { ClassFileFacts.header(it.readNBytes(10)) } // 2. report anything newer than the runtime if (h.major() > 65) println("${e.name} -> Java ${ClassFileFacts.javaVersion(h.major())}") } } Two caveats. A multi-release jar, one that carries extra copies of classes for newer JDKs, keeps them under META-INF/versions/25/, and those are allowed: the JVM only loads them on JDK 25. So skip that prefix, or you'll get false alarms. And module-info.class has a version too. When the culprit is your own code, the fix is in the build: compile with --release 21 (in Gradle, options.release.set(21)) and jvmTarget = 21 for Kotlin, as the labs do, so the compilers also refuse APIs newer than JDK 21.

h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · Lab
x: Read the constant pool by hand labs/bytecode/src/main/java/workbench/bytecode/l06/ClassFileFacts.java ./gradlew :bytecode:test --tests 'workbench.bytecode.l06.*' Run the tests once. All seven fail. Read the class-file layout and the tag table in the Javadoc of ClassFileFacts. Write header: wrap the bytes in a DataInputStream, read the int magic and throw IllegalArgumentException (with "magic" in the message) if it isn't 0xCAFEBABE, then read three unsigned shorts. Write javaVersion as major - 44, rejecting anything below 49. Write a private pool walk: for i from 1 to count - 1, read the tag, then either keep the value (readUTF() for tag 1, the name index for tag 7) or skip the right number of bytes. After a tag 5 or 6, add one more to i. Write referencedClasses with the walk: the Utf8 string at each Class entry's name index. Write thisClass: after the walk, read access_flags, then this_class, and look up its name. Run the tests until all seven pass. The expected answers come from ASM, so a pass means your reader agrees with a production library on Java, Kotlin and JDK classes. A wrong byte count anywhere in the walk shifts everything after it, so the symptom is usually unknown constant pool tag far from the bug. Check the table entry for the last tag you handled. DataInputStream.readUTF() reads a two-byte length and then the bytes, in the class file's own "modified UTF-8". That's exactly a Utf8 entry, so you don't decode anything yourself. Forgetting the extra index after Long and Double passes for some classes and fails for Fixture, which has both. All seven tests in ClassFileFactsTest pass. By the end you can read a class file's header and constant pool by hand, and with the ClassFile API (final in JDK 24) parse a class into a model, build a new class from builder lambdas, verify it before loading, and write a transform that drops or replaces elements.

h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · Quiz
x: A class file's major version is 61. Which is the oldest JDK that can load it? JDK 11 JDK 17 JDK 21 JDK 16 From Java 5 on, the Java version is major minus 44, so 61 is Java 17. A JVM loads class files up to its own major version: JDK 17 and later load it, and JDK 16 rejects it with UnsupportedClassVersionError. Your pool walk handles every tag but forgets that Long takes two indexes. What happens on a class with a long constant? Nothing: the second index is empty, so skipping it is optional readUTF throws at once Every index after the long is off by one, and the loop reads one entry too many, past the end of the pool: names come out wrong, or the walk fails on an unknown tag Only the long's own value comes out wrong You skipped the right number of bytes, but the numbering is off by one. Every later entry gets an index one too small, so a Class entry's name index points at the wrong string, and the loop expects one more entry than the file has, so it reads the access flags as if they were a tag. The symptom shows up far from the cause, usually as an unknown tag or garbage names. That's why the lab's Fixture has both a long and a double. ClassFile.of().verify(bytes) returns an empty list for your generated class. What do you know? The class computes the right results The class has already been loaded The class will run on every JDK The bytecode is type-safe for the verifier, for example every return finds the type its descriptor promises, but it may still compute the wrong thing Verification checks types and stack shapes, not meaning. A fade method with a missing ldiv still verifies and returns the wrong number. A class verified today can also fail to load on an older JDK because of its version number. You want a build-time check, running on JDK 25, that fails if any class in the ticket app references java/util/Random (the seat lottery must use SecureRandom). Which tool fits best? ClassFile.of().parse(bytes) over every class file, checking the class entries in each constant pool A JDK dynamic proxy around every class A Java agent that retransforms every loaded class Class.forName on every class, with initialization Every class a class mentions has a Class entry in its constant pool, so parsing the files is enough. No class needs to be loaded, initialized or run. Proxies intercept calls while a program runs, agents change loaded classes, and Class.forName runs static initializers, the last thing a build check should do. From Reading bytecode: javap -v on StackDemo shows #7 = Long 1000l and then #9 = InvokeDynamic ..., with no entry 8. Why? javap hides unused entries The JIT optimized entry 8 away A Long (and a Double) entry takes two constant-pool indexes, so 8 is the second half of 7 Entry 8 is kept for the class's own name The class-file format numbers 8-byte constants as two entries, and the next entry's index skips one. Any reader that walks the pool must add an extra step after each Long or Double, which is the bug the lab's fixture is designed to catch.

h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · Explain it back
