h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · Key terms
x: Magic number The first four bytes of every class file, 0xCAFEBABE. Major version The class-file version number; minus 44, it gives the Java version that wrote it. ClassFile API The JDK's own library for reading, writing and transforming class files, in java.lang.classfile, final in JDK 24. Model An immutable description of part of a class file (class, method, field, code), parsed lazily. Element One item in a model's sequence: a method of a class, or an instruction of a method's code. Transform A function that sees each element and passes it on, drops it, or replaces it while copying a class. ClassDesc A symbolic description of a class (from java.lang.constant) used when building, such as ClassDesc.of("Fade"). What are the first four fields of a class file? u4 magic 0xCAFEBABE, u2 minor version, u2 major version, u2 constant_pool_count. How do you get the Java version from a class file's major version? Subtract 44 (from Java 5 on): 52 is 8, 61 is 17, 65 is 21, 69 is 25. Which constant-pool entries take two indexes? Long (tag 5) and Double (tag 6). Since which JDK is java.lang.classfile a final API, and under which JEP? JDK 24, JEP 484. It was a preview in JDK 22 (JEP 457) and JDK 23 (JEP 466). In a ClassFile API transform, how do you keep, drop and replace an element? Keep: builder.with(element). Drop: don't pass it on. Replace: call other builder methods instead. What does ClassFile.of().verify(bytes) guarantee when it returns an empty list? That the bytecode passes the verifier's type checks. Not that it computes the right result. Why does cob.ldc("x") not compile in Kotlin? Kotlin's String type doesn't show Java's ConstantDesc interface. Use cob.ldc(cob.constantPool().stringEntry("x")), or loadConstant for primitives.

h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · Go deeper
x: Three details from the API's documentation and this track's runs. Models are lazy, and that can surprise you. parse reads little more than the header. A method's code is inflated when you ask for it, so a broken method can parse fine and fail with IllegalArgumentException later, when you iterate its elements. If you run untrusted or generated bytes through the API, iterate or verify them up front. The ClassFile API and Byte Buddy work at different levels. Byte Buddy works with types and methods (extend this class, intercept those methods with that delegate), and it runs on JDK 8. The ClassFile API works with the class file itself (these instructions, that constant), and it needs JDK 24. Byte Buddy's README says that "as of 1.17.0, support will extend to new Java versions unless previously unknown class file features are discovered. This is possible through Byte Buddy's support of the Class File API." So on a new JDK, Byte Buddy can lean on the JDK's own reader and writer. ConstantPool is an Iterable<PoolEntry>, not a collection, so Java needs StreamSupport to stream it, while Kotlin's Iterable extensions work on it directly: Java // JDK 24+: every Class entry a class references, with the API Set<String> names = StreamSupport.stream(ClassFile.of().parse(bytes).constantPool().spliterator(), false) .filter(e -> e instanceof ClassEntry) .map(e -> ((ClassEntry) e).asInternalName()) .collect(Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new)); Kotlin // JDK 24+: every Class entry a class references, with the API val names = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes).constantPool() .filterIsInstance<ClassEntry>() .map { it.asInternalName() } .toSortedSet()

h: Java agents and instrumentation · Before rehearsal: a startup agent watches every class load
x: A Java agent's transformer sees each class's bytes as the JVM defines it; retransformation swaps method bodies in a class already loaded Lessons 4 and 5 added work by wrapping objects. That needs an interface or a class that isn't final, and it misses self-calls whenever the proxy forwards. It also only works on objects that were created through the proxy. Sometimes you need more: timing a method inside a library jar, or tracing a class that a framework creates for you. A Java agent works on the class instead of the object. An agent is an ordinary class with a special entry point. The JVM calls it with a java.lang.instrument.Instrumentation, the JDK's handle for watching and changing classes: the stage manager's key. There are three ways to start one: java -javaagent:agent.jar[=args] calls the agent's premain(String args, Instrumentation inst) before your main. You can repeat the option, and the agents start in the order you list them. An executable jar can name an agent in its manifest with Launcher-Agent-Class. The JVM calls that agent's agentmain before the application's main. A tool can attach to a JVM that is already running and load an agent jar into it. The JVM then calls agentmain(String, Instrumentation). The third section is about this case. The manifest is a small text file inside a jar, META-INF/MANIFEST.MF, that describes the jar. An agent jar's manifest names the agent class with Premain-Class or Agent-Class, and Can-Retransform-Classes: true asks for the right to change classes that are already loaded. The first thing most agents do is register a ClassFileTransformer. From then on, the JVM calls its transform method with the bytes of every class it is about to define. The method returns new bytes, or null, which means "no change". The smallest useful agent changes nothing and only watches: Java public static void premain(String args, Instrumentation inst) { inst.addTransformer(new ClassFileTransformer() { @Override public byte[] transform(ClassLoader loader, String className, Class<?> redefined, ProtectionDomain domain, byte[] bytes) { System.out.println("[agent] loading " + className + " (" + bytes.length + " bytes)"); return null; // null: leave the class as it is } }); } Kotlin @JvmStatic fun premain(args: String?, inst: Instrumentation) { inst.addTransformer(object : ClassFileTransformer { override fun transform( loader: ClassLoader?, className: String?, redefined: Class<*>?, domain: ProtectionDomain?, bytes: ByteArray, ): ByteArray? { println("[agent] loading $className (${bytes.size} bytes)") return null // null: leave the class as it is } }) } The bytes that transform receives are the class files of lesson 6. An agent that wants to change a class rewrites them, with the ClassFile API on JDK 24 and later, or with a library such as Byte Buddy. Notice that the transformer above is an anonymous class, not a lambda. Both of ClassFileTransformer's transform methods are default methods, so it isn't a functional interface. This section's demo builds an agent jar that holds only a manifest, then starts a second JVM with -javaagent:<jar>=opening-night. On JDK 25 it printed: [agent] premain args=opening-night, classes already loaded: 890 [agent] loading workbench/bytecode/l07/AgentTarget (1376 bytes) main: started [agent] loading workbench/bytecode/l07/AgentTarget$Ticket (1667 bytes) main: Ticket[show=Hamlet, seat=B12] [agent] transformer saw 30 class definitions premain ran first, when 890 JDK classes had already loaded. The agent saw AgentTarget before main started, and its Ticket record just before its first use: the lazy loading of lesson 1. That's the note slipped in before rehearsal. Nearly every class of your application loads after premain returns, so a startup agent sees almost all of them. And no warning appeared, because an agent named on the command line is on the guest list. A transformer sees each class once, as the JVM defines it. Register it before the classes you care about load. But what about a class that loaded an hour ago? Watch a startup agent Read CountingAgent and AgentTarget. Predict which workbench/ classes the agent will report, and in which order relative to the two main: lines. Run StartupAgentDemo (or the Kotlin twin). It writes a jar that holds only a manifest with Premain-Class, then starts a second JVM with -javaagent:<jar>=opening-night. Find the arguments string, the number of classes already loaded when premain ran, and the total the transformer saw. StartupAgentDemo.java package workbench.bytecode.l07; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.jar.Attributes; import java.util.jar.JarOutputStream; import java.util.jar.Manifest; /** Builds a one-line agent jar and starts a second JVM with -javaagent, so you can watch premain run. */ public class StartupAgentDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { // 1. an agent jar needs a manifest naming the agent class; the class itself is on the class path Path jar = Files.createTempFile("counting-agent", ".jar"); Manifest manifest = new Manifest(); manifest.getMainAttributes().put(Attributes.Name.MANIFEST_VERSION, "1.0"); manifest.getMainAttributes().putValue("Premain-Class", CountingAgent.class.getName()); try (JarOutputStream out = new JarOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(jar), manifest)) { // no entries needed } // 2. java -javaagent:<jar>=opening-night -cp <this class path> AgentTarget String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); Process child = new ProcessBuilder(java, "-javaagent:" + jar + "=opening-night", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), AgentTarget.class.getName()) .redirectErrorStream(true) .start(); child.getInputStream().transferTo(System.out); System.out.println("child JVM exited with " + child.waitFor()); Files.delete(jar); } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l07.StartupAgentDemo labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l07/StartupAgentDemo.java StartupAgentDemo.kt package workbench.bytecode.l07 import java.lang.instrument.ClassFileTransformer import java.lang.instrument.Instrumentation import java.nio.file.Files import java.security.ProtectionDomain import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.jar.Attributes import java.util.jar.JarOutputStream import java.util.jar.Manifest /** A startup agent: the JVM calls premain before main. It watches classes load and changes nothing. */ object KCountingAgent { @JvmStatic fun premain(args: String?, inst: Instrumentation) { println("[agent] premain args=$args, classes already loaded: ${inst.allLoadedClasses.size}") val seen = AtomicInteger() inst.addTransformer(object : ClassFileTransformer { override fun transform( loader: ClassLoader?, className: String?, classBeingRedefined: Class<*>?, domain: ProtectionDomain?, classfileBuffer: ByteArray, ): ByteArray? { seen.incrementAndGet() if (className?.startsWith("workbench/") == true) { println("[agent] loading $className (${classfileBuffer.size} bytes)") } return null // null means "no change" } }) Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(Thread { println("[agent] transformer saw ${seen.get()} class definitions") }) } } data class KTicket(val show: String, val seat: String) /** The program the startup agent watches. */ object KAgentTarget { @JvmStatic fun main(args: Array<String>) { println("main: started") val t = KTicket("Hamlet", "B12") // KTicket is loaded here, on first use println("main: $t") } } /** Builds a one-line agent jar and starts a second JVM with -javaagent, so you can watch premain run. */ fun main() { // 1. an agent jar needs a manifest naming the agent class; the class itself is on the class path val jar = Files.createTempFile("counting-agent", ".jar") val manifest = Manifest().apply { mainAttributes[Attributes.Name.MANIFEST_VERSION] = "1.0" mainAttributes.putValue("Premain-Class", KCountingAgent::class.java.name) } JarOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(jar), manifest).use { } // no entries needed // 2. java -javaagent:<jar>=opening-night -cp <this class path> KAgentTarget val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") val child = ProcessBuilder(java, "-javaagent:$jar=opening-night", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), KAgentTarget::class.java.name) .redirectErrorStream(true) .start() child.inputStream.transferTo(System.out) println("child JVM exited with ${child.waitFor()}") Files.delete(jar) } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l07.StartupAgentDemoKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l07/StartupAgentDemo.kt [agent] premain args=opening-night, classes already loaded: ... comes first: several hundred JDK classes (819 on JDK 21 and 890 on JDK 25 in the runs for this lesson). Then the agent reports AgentTarget, then main: started, then AgentTarget$Ticket just before it's used, then main: Ticket[show=Hamlet, seat=B12]. At exit, transformer saw N class definitions, a few dozen, because a record's first use also loads some JDK support classes. The Kotlin twin reports KAgentTarget and KTicket. No warning appears: an agent named on the command line is not a dynamic load. java.lang.instrument package (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Java agents and instrumentation · During the run: retransformation swaps method bodies under live objects
x: An agent that arrives late doesn't need a restart, at least for method bodies. Instrumentation.retransformClasses(classes...) runs the registered transformers again on classes that are already loaded, and installs the result in place. The Class object stays the same, so every existing object and every reference to the class sees the new code. It's the correction pasted over one page of the prompt book: the next actor who reaches that cue reads the new version. This section's demo does it to a final class, StageClock, whose now() returns "tick". It creates a clock, attaches an agent to its own JVM, and adds timing code to now(). With its warning lines left out (they're the next section's subject), it printed this on JDK 21: before: tick retransform supported: true [advice] workbench.bytecode.l07.LiveRetransformDemo$StageClock.now took 14176 ns after: tick (the same object, no restart) The same clock, created before the agent existed, ran the new body on its next call. It still says tick; only now someone is timing it. Its class is final, so no subclass proxy from lesson 5 could have touched it. The Instrumentation Javadoc lists what that does and doesn't mean: "If a retransformed method has active stack frames, those active frames continue to run the bytecodes of the original method. The retransformed method will be used on new invokes." "Redefining a class does not cause its initializers to be run. The values of static variables will remain as they were." "If this method throws an exception, no classes have been retransformed." An active stack frame is a call that is still running. So an actor in mid-line finishes the line from the old page, and the next actor reads the new one. And lesson 1's dress rehearsal, <clinit>, isn't held again. There's a hard limit on what may change. JVMTI, the JVM Tool Interface, is the native interface that debuggers and agents are built on, and it says: "The retransformation must not add, remove or rename fields or methods, change the signatures of methods, change modifiers, or change inheritance." Method bodies, the constant pool and attributes may change. You can rewrite what a cue says, but you can't add a character to the cast list. So an agent can add timing code to now(), but it can't add a long calls field to count with. The count must live somewhere else, such as a public class that the new code calls. That's what the lab's CallCounts is for. The same limit explains the other direction. A transformer that wants to add members can only do so when the class is first loaded. That means registering it before the class loads, usually through -javaagent. Retransformation also needs permission. The agent's manifest must say Can-Retransform-Classes: true, and each transformer that should run again must be registered with addTransformer(transformer, true). isRetransformClassesSupported() reports whether this JVM and agent allow it, and it printed true above. Here the prompt-book picture breaks. In a theatre, a correction pasted into one prompt book changes one copy. A class exists once per class loader, so one retransformation changes the code for every object of that class, and for every caller, at once. Retransformation swaps method bodies in place, for every caller at once. It never changes the class's shape. The demo printed four lines of warning before it got that far. The JVM printed them because this agent arrived late. Change a class under a live object Read LiveRetransformDemo (or the Kotlin twin). StageClock is final, and KStageClock is final because it's Kotlin. Before running it: will the after: call on the same clock print an advice line? Will you see a warning? Run it with the command below and read the output from top to bottom. LiveRetransformDemo.java package workbench.bytecode.l07; import net.bytebuddy.agent.ByteBuddyAgent; import net.bytebuddy.agent.builder.AgentBuilder; import net.bytebuddy.asm.Advice; import java.lang.instrument.Instrumentation; import static net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.is; import static net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.named; /** Attach an agent to this running JVM and change a loaded class under a live object. */ public class LiveRetransformDemo { public static final class StageClock { // final: lesson 5's subclass proxies couldn't touch it public String now() { return "tick"; } } public static class TimingAdvice { @Advice.OnMethodEnter static long enter() { return System.nanoTime(); // copied to the start of now() } @Advice.OnMethodExit(onThrowable = Throwable.class) static void exit(@Advice.Origin("#t.#m") String where, @Advice.Enter long t0) { System.out.println(" [advice] " + where + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) + " ns"); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0) { // -Pargs=allowed or -Pargs=blocked relaunch(args[0]); return; } StageClock clock = new StageClock(); System.out.println("before: " + clock.now()); Instrumentation inst = ByteBuddyAgent.install(); // self-attach: JEP 451 warns unless allowed System.out.println("retransform supported: " + inst.isRetransformClassesSupported()); new AgentBuilder.Default() .disableClassFormatChanges() .with(AgentBuilder.RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) .type(is(StageClock.class)) .transform((builder, type, loader, module, domain) -> builder.visit(Advice.to(TimingAdvice.class).on(named("now")))) .installOn(inst); System.out.println("after: " + clock.now() + " (the same object, no restart)"); } /** Runs this demo again in a child JVM with dynamic agent loading explicitly allowed or blocked. */ static void relaunch(String mode) throws Exception { String flag = mode.equals("blocked") ? "-XX:-EnableDynamicAgentLoading" : "-XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading"; String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); Process child = new ProcessBuilder(java, flag, "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), LiveRetransformDemo.class.getName()) .redirectErrorStream(true) .start(); System.out.println("child JVM with " + flag + ":"); child.getInputStream().transferTo(System.out); System.out.println("child exited with " + child.waitFor()); } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l07.LiveRetransformDemo labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l07/LiveRetransformDemo.java LiveRetransformDemo.kt package workbench.bytecode.l07 import net.bytebuddy.agent.ByteBuddyAgent import net.bytebuddy.agent.builder.AgentBuilder import net.bytebuddy.asm.Advice import net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.`is` import net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.named /** Final, like every Kotlin class without `open`: lesson 5's subclass proxies couldn't touch it. */ class KStageClock { fun now() = "tick" } object KTimingAdvice { @JvmStatic @Advice.OnMethodEnter fun enter(): Long = System.nanoTime() // copied to the start of now() @JvmStatic @Advice.OnMethodExit(onThrowable = Throwable::class) fun exit(@Advice.Origin("#t.#m") where: String, @Advice.Enter t0: Long) { println(" [advice] $where took ${System.nanoTime() - t0} ns") } } /** Attach an agent to this running JVM and change a loaded class under a live object. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isNotEmpty()) { // -Pargs=allowed or -Pargs=blocked relaunch(args[0]) return } val clock = KStageClock() println("before: ${clock.now()}") val inst = ByteBuddyAgent.install() // self-attach: JEP 451 warns unless allowed println("retransform supported: ${inst.isRetransformClassesSupported}") AgentBuilder.Default() .disableClassFormatChanges() .with(AgentBuilder.RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) .type(`is`(KStageClock::class.java)) .transform { builder, _, _, _, _ -> builder.visit(Advice.to(KTimingAdvice::class.java).on(named("now"))) } .installOn(inst) println("after: ${clock.now()} (the same object, no restart)") } /** Runs this demo again in a child JVM with dynamic agent loading explicitly allowed or blocked. */ private fun relaunch(mode: String) { val flag = if (mode == "blocked") "-XX:-EnableDynamicAgentLoading" else "-XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading" val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") val child = ProcessBuilder(java, flag, "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.bytecode.l07.LiveRetransformDemoKt") .redirectErrorStream(true) .start() println("child JVM with $flag:") child.inputStream.transferTo(System.out) println("child exited with ${child.waitFor()}") } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l07.LiveRetransformDemoKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l07/LiveRetransformDemo.kt before: tick, then four WARNING: lines about a dynamically loaded agent, then retransform supported: true. On JDK 25, four more WARNING: lines about sun.misc.Unsafe follow. Then comes [advice] ...StageClock.now took ... ns, printed from inside now(), and after: tick (the same object, no restart). The object was created before the agent existed, its class is final, and nothing was restarted. Retransformation changes the method body inside the existing class. Old objects use the new code on their next call. Instrumentation (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Java agents and instrumentation · Arriving mid-run: the warning JDK 21 prints, and the flag behind it
x: The four lines come from JEP 451, "Prepare to Disallow the Dynamic Loading of Agents", which was delivered in JDK 21: WARNING: A Java agent has been loaded dynamically (.../byte-buddy-agent-1.18.17.jar) WARNING: If a serviceability tool is in use, please run with -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading to hide this warning WARNING: If a serviceability tool is not in use, please run with -Djdk.instrument.traceUsage for more information WARNING: Dynamic loading of agents will be disallowed by default in a future release Picture a security desk at the stage door that logs anyone who arrives during a performance with a key. A dynamic load is any agent that arrives after start-up, through the attach mechanism, the JDK's way for one program to connect to a JVM that is already running. ByteBuddyAgent.install() attaches to its own JVM, and so does any library that self-attaches. A serviceability tool, in the warning's words, is a tool for watching or fixing a running program, such as a profiler or a debugger. The java.lang.instrument documentation says "the JVM prints a warning on the standard error stream for each agent that it attempts to start in a running JVM". The documentation also names the switch for HotSpot, the JVM in the usual OpenJDK builds. -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading opts in and hides the warning. -XX:-EnableDynamicAgentLoading refuses the load, and then ByteBuddyAgent.install() throws IllegalStateException: Could not self-attach to current VM using external process. An agent started with -javaagent never warns: the startup demo printed nothing of the kind. Today the default is still "allow, with a warning". In the jdk-25-ga source, the flag is declared product(bool, EnableDynamicAgentLoading, true, ...). Runs for this track on JDK 21, 25, 26 and 27.0.1 all warned and then loaded the agent. The last line says the default will change. When it does, every tool and test that self-attaches without the flag will fail at start-up. So decide on purpose. If a program needs an agent in production, start it with -javaagent, so it's there from the first class. If a test suite self-attaches, add the flag to the test JVM. The labs' Gradle build passes -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading to every test task, which is why the lab runs quietly. To find what would break, run your tests once without the flag and search the output for the warning. On JDK 25, the demo printed four more lines, and they're a different warning: WARNING: A terminally deprecated method in sun.misc.Unsafe has been called WARNING: sun.misc.Unsafe::objectFieldOffset has been called by net.bytebuddy.dynamic.loading.ClassInjector$UsingUnsafe$Dispatcher$CreationAction (...) WARNING: Please consider reporting this to the maintainers of class net.bytebuddy.dynamic.loading.ClassInjector$UsingUnsafe$Dispatcher$CreationAction WARNING: sun.misc.Unsafe::objectFieldOffset will be removed in a future release The security desk has a colleague. These lines come from JEP 498. From JDK 24, the JDK warns by default when code uses the memory-access methods of sun.misc.Unsafe, an old internal class for raw memory access. Byte Buddy's AgentBuilder triggered it. Byte Buddy's release notes show it moving away from Unsafe (1.18.10: "Delay change of default for unsafe use to Java 26"), and in the research runs for this track, JDK 26 and 27 printed no such lines. A late agent works today, with a warning, and will be refused later. Start agents with -javaagent, or allow late ones on purpose. Whichever way the agent arrives, writing its changes by hand is still the hard part. Allow it, then block it Run LiveRetransformDemo with -Pargs=allowed. It starts itself again in a child JVM with -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading. Predict what happens with -Pargs=blocked, which uses -XX:-EnableDynamicAgentLoading. Then run it. Look in labs/build.gradle.kts for the line that keeps the lab tests quiet. terminal ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l07.LiveRetransformDemo -Pargs=allowed ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l07.LiveRetransformDemo -Pargs=blocked With allowed, the child prints the same lines as before, without the four JEP 451 lines (on JDK 25 the Unsafe lines stay, because they're a different warning). With blocked, the child prints before: tick and then dies with java.lang.IllegalStateException: Could not self-attach to current VM using external process, and the demo reports child exited with 1. In labs/build.gradle.kts, the shared test setup has jvmArgs("-XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading", "-Xshare:off"). JEP 451: Prepare to Disallow the Dynamic Loading of Agents read

h: Java agents and instrumentation · Writing the note with Byte Buddy: AgentBuilder and Advice
x: Writing a ClassFileTransformer that edits bytecode by hand means parsing the class, changing it and writing it out again, with lesson 6's tools. Byte Buddy's AgentBuilder does the plumbing, and its Advice does the editing. The lab's SoundBoard is a final Kotlin class whose play(cue) plays one sound cue. This is the lab's solution, which counts every call to play: Java ResettableClassFileTransformer t = new AgentBuilder.Default() .disableClassFormatChanges() // 1. no new members: required to retransform .with(AgentBuilder.RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) // 2. also rewrite classes already loaded .type(is(SoundBoard.class)) // 3. which classes .transform((builder, type, loader, module, domain) -> builder.visit(Advice.to(CountingAdvice.class).on(named("play")))) // 4. what to change .installOn(ByteBuddyAgent.install()); // 5. attach, register, retransform now Kotlin val t = AgentBuilder.Default() .disableClassFormatChanges() // 1. no new members: required to retransform .with(AgentBuilder.RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) // 2. also rewrite classes already loaded .type(`is`(SoundBoard::class.java)) // 3. which classes .transform { builder, _, _, _, _ -> builder.visit(Advice.to(CountingAdvice::class.java).on(named("play"))) // 4. what to change } .installOn(ByteBuddyAgent.install()) // 5. attach, register, retransform now Read it in order. disableClassFormatChanges() promises not to add members, which retransformation requires. RETRANSFORMATION asks Byte Buddy to rewrite matching classes that are already loaded, not only new ones. type(...) picks the classes, and transform says what to change in them. Last, installOn(ByteBuddyAgent.install()) attaches the agent, registers the transformer and retransforms at once. By default, Advice doesn't call your code at all. Byte Buddy copies the body of your @Advice.OnMethodEnter method into the start of the target method, and the body of an @Advice.OnMethodExit method into every exit. It's the stage manager's note written onto the page itself, not a messenger standing next to it. That's why advice methods must be static, and why they may only call public code: the copied code runs inside the target class. It's also why @Advice.Origin("#t.#m") can hand them the method's name as a constant. Nothing new is added to the class, so the result keeps to the retransformation rule. Lesson 5's MethodDelegation adds accessor methods and helper classes, so it only works on new classes, or on classes that aren't loaded yet. The transformer that installOn returns has a reset(inst, RETRANSFORMATION) method, which puts the original bodies back. Because the advice runs inside the method, it sees every call, from anywhere: from other classes, from the class itself through this, and on final classes. Here are the track's three ways to intercept a call, side by side: needs this.method() calls final classes and methods JDK proxy (lesson 4) an interface not seen not relevant subclass proxy (lesson 5) an open class seen only if the proxy is the object can't intercept agent with Advice an agent seen fine Advice copies your code into the method itself, so it sees every call. Keep it static, and call only public code from it. The price is reach, and it's this tool's limit. An agent can rewrite any method body, but never the shape of a class that is already loaded. Every rewrite lands on every caller in that class loader at once, and loading the agent late earns a warning. Use a proxy when you own the call path, and an agent when you must change code you don't control. Check yourself before the lab: SoundBoard.playAll calls play three times on this. With the advice installed on play, how many calls does CallCounts record when you call playAll once? (Three. Each inner call runs play's new body, which begins with the copied advice.) x: The counting advice in Java and Kotlin CountingAdvice.java public class CountingAdvice { @Advice.OnMethodEnter // copied to the start of the method static void enter(@Advice.Origin("#t.#m") String method) { CallCounts.hit(method); // must be public: this code runs in the target class } } // install it new AgentBuilder.Default() .disableClassFormatChanges() .with(AgentBuilder.RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) .type(is(SoundBoard.class)) .transform((b, type, loader, module, domain) -> b.visit(Advice.to(CountingAdvice.class).on(named("play")))) .installOn(ByteBuddyAgent.install()); CountingAdvice.kt object CountingAdvice { @JvmStatic // Advice needs a real static method @Advice.OnMethodEnter // copied to the start of the method fun enter(@Advice.Origin("#t.#m") method: String) { CallCounts.hit(method) // must be public: this code runs in the target class } } // install it AgentBuilder.Default() .disableClassFormatChanges() .with(AgentBuilder.RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) .type(`is`(SoundBoard::class.java)) .transform { b, _, _, _, _ -> b.visit(Advice.to(CountingAdvice::class.java).on(named("play"))) } .installOn(ByteBuddyAgent.install()) Kotlin has no static, so the advice lives in an object with @JvmStatic, which makes kotlinc write a real static method that Byte Buddy can copy. is is a Kotlin keyword, so the matcher must be written `is`(...). The bigger difference is in the target, not in the agent. A Kotlin class is final by default, which blocked every subclass proxy in lesson 5, and an agent doesn't care: Advice edits the existing class instead of extending it. The advice's code is copied into the target class, so anything it calls (CallCounts, println) must be reachable from there, in Kotlin as much as in Java.

h: Java agents and instrumentation · Worked example
x: A transformer that never sees its class An engineer attaches an agent to a running test copy of the ticket app, to log the bytes of SeatMap, which loaded at start-up. transform is never called for it. Read the agent and work out why before reading on. public static void agentmain(String args, Instrumentation inst) { inst.addTransformer(new LoggingTransformer("theatre/booking/SeatMap")); // waits for transform(...) to be called for SeatMap: it never is } @JvmStatic fun agentmain(args: String?, inst: Instrumentation) { inst.addTransformer(LoggingTransformer("theatre/booking/SeatMap")) // waits for transform(...) to be called for SeatMap: it never is } A transformer sees class definitions that happen after it's registered. SeatMap was defined an hour ago, and nothing will define it again. To see it, ask the JVM to run the transformers again for that class. That needs three things: Can-Retransform-Classes: true in the manifest, registering the transformer as able to retransform, and the call itself. public static void agentmain(String args, Instrumentation inst) throws Exception { LoggingTransformer t = new LoggingTransformer("theatre/booking/SeatMap"); inst.addTransformer(t, true); // 1. canRetransform = true for (Class<?> c : inst.getAllLoadedClasses()) { if (c.getName().equals("theatre.booking.SeatMap")) { inst.retransformClasses(c); // 2. run the transformers again for it } } } @JvmStatic fun agentmain(args: String?, inst: Instrumentation) { val t = LoggingTransformer("theatre/booking/SeatMap") inst.addTransformer(t, true) // 1. canRetransform = true inst.allLoadedClasses .filter { it.name == "theatre.booking.SeatMap" } .forEach { inst.retransformClasses(it) } // 2. run the transformers again for it } Now transform is called with the class's current bytes and a non-null classBeingRedefined. If it returns changed bytes, they may only change method bodies, the constant pool and attributes. Returning a class with a new field makes retransformClasses throw, and then, as the Javadoc promises, no class was changed. Calls already inside SeatMap methods finish on the old code, and the next calls run the new code. Byte Buddy packs all of this into the builder. RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION registers the transformer as able to retransform, and retransforms the matching loaded classes. disableClassFormatChanges() stops Byte Buddy from adding members, and Advice changes only method bodies. That's why the lab needs five builder calls and no loop over loaded classes.

h: Java agents and instrumentation · Key terms
x: Java agent A class the JVM starts with an Instrumentation handle, through -javaagent, a launcher manifest or attach. Instrumentation The JDK interface that lets an agent add transformers, list loaded classes and retransform them. ClassFileTransformer A callback that receives each class's bytes before the JVM defines it, and may return changed bytes. Retransformation Running transformers again on a loaded class and swapping in new method bodies, keeping the class's shape. Dynamic attach Loading an agent into a JVM that is already running; warned about since JDK 21 (JEP 451). Advice Byte Buddy's way of copying your enter and exit code into an existing method's body. JVMTI The JVM Tool Interface: the native interface for debuggers and agents, which defines what retransformation may change. Which method does the JVM call for an agent started with -javaagent, and when? public static void premain(String args, Instrumentation inst), before the application's main. What does a ClassFileTransformer.transform return to leave a class unchanged? null. Does retransforming a class run its static initializer again? No. Static fields keep their values, and existing objects are not changed. What may retransformation change, and what not? It may change method bodies, the constant pool and attributes. It may not add, remove or rename fields or methods, or change signatures, modifiers or the superclass. What prints the JEP 451 warning, and how do you silence it? Loading an agent into a running JVM (attach or self-attach). -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading silences it; -XX:-EnableDynamicAgentLoading blocks loading. Why must Byte Buddy advice methods be static and call only public code? Byte Buddy copies their bodies into the target method, so the code runs inside the target class. Which two settings in Byte Buddy's AgentBuilder make a change safe for classes that are already loaded? .with(RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) and .disableClassFormatChanges(), with Advice for the change itself.

h: Java agents and instrumentation · Go deeper
x: Retransformation and redefinition are two different calls. redefineClasses takes new class bytes that you supply. retransformClasses asks the registered transformers to produce them, starting from the class's original bytes. Both follow the same JVMTI rule about the class's shape, and both need permission in the manifest (Can-Redefine-Classes, Can-Retransform-Classes). Byte Buddy's RedefinitionStrategy.REDEFINITION exists too, but RETRANSFORMATION works better alongside other agents, because each transformer sees the result of the one before it. Agent order matters when there is more than one. With several -javaagent options, "the premain methods will be called in the order that the agents are specified", and each registered transformer sees the bytes produced by the ones before it. Two agents that both rewrite the same method, for example a monitoring agent and your own, can conflict. Test them together. This lesson closes the track's "integrity by default" thread: recent JDKs warn before they forbid. Dynamic agents warn since JDK 21 (JEP 451). sun.misc.Unsafe memory access warns since JDK 24 (JEP 498, default --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=warn). Changing final fields through reflection warns since JDK 26 (JEP 500, default --illegal-final-field-mutation=warn). In the runs for this track, none of them had become a hard failure by JDK 27.0.1. To find what will break later, run your test suite once with the stricter settings: test JVM options for a "what will break later" run: --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=deny (JDK 24 and later) --illegal-final-field-mutation=deny (JDK 26 and later) and leave out -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading

h: Memory and garbage collection
x: Heap, stacks and object layout, allocation, references, G1, ZGC and Shenandoah, GC logs, and hunting leaks. By the end of this track you can say where every byte of a JVM process lives, predict what an object costs, measure what a piece of code allocates, and explain how G1 and ZGC find and move the objects still in use. You can read a GC log line by line, choose and configure a collector on JDK 21, 25 or 27, size a heap so a program in a container isn't killed by the kernel, and find a leak: on the heap with a histogram and a heap dump, or outside it with Native Memory Tracking. One picture runs through all seven lessons: a self-storage warehouse. The running program is the building, the heap is the shared storage floor, every object is a box, a reference is a shelf number written on a note, and the garbage collector is the cleaning crew. One example runs through them too: a thumbnail service for a photo site, which makes small preview pictures of uploaded photos and keeps recent ones in memory. You don't need to know anything about garbage collection to start; lesson 1 begins with what the heap is. You do need to read Java and Kotlin, and one idea from the threads track helps: why a ThreadLocal on a pool thread outlives the task. Install JDK 25, the current long-term-support release. Defaults change between JDK 21, 25 and 27 (the collector a small container gets, the size of an object header, the ZGC flags), so the lessons always say which version a fact belongs to. The JDK 26 and 27 details come from reading the JDK source, and the lessons say so. The labs live in labs/memory, one package per lesson (workbench.memory.l01 to l07). Lessons 1, 3, 5 and 7 have Java labs; lessons 2, 4 and 6 are in Kotlin. Run ./gradlew :memory:test --tests 'workbench.memory.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes. The tests give the same answer on every run: they count allocated bytes with generous margins, wait for the GC with bounded loops on a ReferenceQueue, and count live objects with a class histogram. They need System.gc() to work, so never run them with -XX:+DisableExplicitGC. Many demos start a child JVM with the flags they want to show, so ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=... is all you type. Lesson 7's arena demo needs JDK 22 or later and runs outside Gradle, from labs/memory/jdk25. -Xmx caps only the heap, the storage floor. Thread stacks, metaspace, the code cache, the GC's bookkeeping and memory outside the heap come on top: a JDK 25 process with -Xmx256m committed 388 MB. An object costs a 12-byte header plus its fields, rounded up to 8. Compressed oops keep references at 4 bytes below a 32 GB heap; compact headers (a JDK 25 flag, the JDK 27 default) shrink the header to 8, so each object saves 8 bytes or nothing. Allocation is a pointer bump in a thread's TLAB, and the allocation rate is what costs you. Count bytes with getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes, and treat escape analysis as a bonus you show in demos, never one you assert in tests. The GC keeps what the roots can reach. Soft references go before an OutOfMemoryError, weak ones at the next GC, and Cleaner (not finalize()) is the safety net behind close(). Generational collectors copy the few survivors out of eden, and write barriers with card tables keep young collections small. G1 adds equal regions, humongous objects, concurrent marking and mixed collections, but it stops every thread to move objects. ZGC moves objects while the application runs, with colored references and a load barrier, so its pauses stay far below a millisecond. It pays in CPU, headroom and 8-byte references; Shenandoah makes the same trade with another design. With no GC flag, JDK 21 to 26 pick Serial unless the JVM sees 2 CPUs and 1,792 MB; JDK 27 picks G1. Keep G1 for most services, ZGC for tight pause budgets with spare cores, Parallel for batch jobs, Epsilon for allocation-budget tests. A GC log line gives the cause, the heap before and after, and the pause length. A pause line has Pause after GC(id) and ends in ms; the floor of the young pauses and a full GC's after-value show the live set. In a container the default heap is 25% of the memory limit. Size it with MaxRAMPercentage, cap direct memory, and remember that going over the limit is a kernel kill with no Java error. Find heap leaks with a histogram, a heap dump and the dominator tree; find growth outside the heap with NMT's baseline and diff; give off-heap memory a return date with a confined FFM arena.

Sizing a container The process = heap + metaspace and code cache + thread stacks + GC bookkeeping + direct buffers + headroom. Picture it: -Xmx sizes the storage floor, and the whole building must fit inside the plot's fence. After 10,000 warm-up calls, the method allocates exactly 0 bytes The test finishes within 5 ms System.gc() frees less than 1 MB afterwards On one call over 20,000 uploads, after one tiny warm-up call, it allocates no more than its long[500] result plus a small margin Comparing the bytes allocated with what the result itself needs holds in the interpreter, in C1 and in C2, so it doesn't depend on timing. Asserting 0 depends on whether C2's escape analysis has compiled the method yet. Timings and GC results change from run to run. A class wraps a handle from a native image library. Callers should close it, and you want a safety net for the ones who forget. Which tool fits? Override finalize() AutoCloseable plus a shared Cleaner whose action holds only the handle Keep the handle in a WeakHashMap Wrap the object in a SoftReference close() releases the handle at a known point, and a Cleaner action frees it if the object becomes unreachable without being closed. The action must not refer to the object, or it never runs. finalize() is deprecated for removal, and weak or soft references don't release anything themselves. A service has an 8 GB heap with G1. Which object is humongous? A 2.5 MB photo held in one byte[] A 1.5 MB strip of thumbnails held in one byte[] A HashMap with 100,000 entries A 1 MB direct ByteBuffer 8 GB / 2048 is 4 MB, so regions are 4 MB and anything over 2 MB is humongous: the 2.5 MB photo. 1.5 MB is under the threshold. A HashMap is many small objects plus a table array well under 2 MB, and a direct buffer's bytes aren't on the heap at all. A JDK 25 ZGC log says GC(9) Major Collection (Allocation Rate) 258M(25%)->272M(27%) 0.078s. What happened? A 78 ms pause that made the heap grow A failed collection that will be retried A concurrent collection of 78 ms; the heap ended fuller because the application kept allocating while it ran A memory leak of 14 MB ZGC's collection lines show the concurrent work, not a pause; the pauses are separate Pause ... lines of hundredths of a millisecond. The application allocated during the collection, which is why ZGC needs headroom. One line can't show a leak; the trend across many collections can. A small helper program runs on JDK 25 in a container with 1 CPU and a 512 MiB limit, with no GC flag. Which collector does it run, and is that a problem? G1, the default everywhere; fine Serial, because the container isn't server-class; often fine for a small single-CPU program ZGC, because the heap is small Parallel, because it has one CPU On JDK 21 to 26 the JVM picks G1 only with 2 or more CPUs and at least 1,792 MB. This container gets Serial without anyone noticing. With one CPU and a small heap, Serial is a reasonable choice: there's no spare core for concurrent GC threads anyway. JDK 27 would pick G1. A container with a 2 GiB limit runs a service with -Xmx2g. After a few hours under load it restarts with exit code 137 and nothing in the log. What happened, and what is the fix? A heap leak; add -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError The GC pause goal was too long; lower MaxGCPauseMillis Containers restart JVMs after a fixed time The whole process went over the limit and the kernel killed it; size the heap with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage around 60 to 75 and cap direct memory Exit code 137 is SIGKILL from the kernel's OOM killer. Heap plus metaspace, code cache, stacks, GC data and direct buffers outgrew 2 GiB, and it took hours because the heap touches its pages gradually. No OutOfMemoryError was thrown, so no heap dump would be written. Young pauses end at 300, 340, 385, 430 and 470 MB over an hour, and a full GC goes 1400M->1180M(1536M). What do you do first? Take a class histogram and a heap dump, and find the biggest retained size in the dominator tree Turn on Native Memory Tracking Switch to ZGC Lower the pause goal A rising floor and a full GC that frees little mean the live heap is growing: a heap leak. The histogram says which classes pile up, and the dominator tree with its path to a GC root says which field holds them. NMT is for growth outside the heap, with a flat floor. Changing collectors doesn't free reachable objects. An album exporter needs 1 MiB of off-heap memory per album, released as soon as the album is uploaded. Which choice does that without waiting for a GC? ByteBuffer.allocateDirect per album, then drop the reference A segment from Arena.ofAuto() A segment from Arena.ofConfined() in try-with-resources One Arena.global() segment per album A confined arena frees its memory when close() runs at the end of the try block (FFM, final in JDK 22). A direct buffer and an automatic arena are freed only after the GC collects their owner, which a quiet heap may not do for a long time. The global arena never frees.

h: Where objects live: heap, stacks, metaspace and object headers · Where a running program keeps things: heap, stacks and metaspace
x: Let's set up the example for the whole track. A small photo-sharing site runs a thumbnail service. When someone uploads a photo, the service makes a thumbnail, a small preview picture, and keeps recent thumbnails in memory so it can send them again without redoing the work. It's an ordinary program, and the JVM (the Java Virtual Machine, the program that runs your compiled Java and Kotlin) gives it memory in several separate areas. The biggest area is the heap, the shared storage floor. Every object the service creates with new lives there: each thumbnail, its pixels, the strings for its file names. The garbage collector (GC) is the part of the JVM that finds objects nothing uses any more and reuses their memory. It's the warehouse's cleaning crew, and lesson 4 follows it at work. The -Xmx option, given when the program starts, sets the largest size the heap may grow to. A thread is one path of work running through the program, and each thread is a worker with a desk. The desk is the thread's stack: the local variables, and the place to return to, of every method the thread is in the middle of. A local variable never holds an object itself. It holds a reference, the object's address on the heap, like a shelf number on the notepad. An ordinary thread is called a platform thread, because the operating system runs it, and its stack lives outside the heap. The plans live in metaspace: the JVM's description of every class it has loaded, with its fields, its methods and their bytecode (the instructions the compiler wrote into the class file). Next to it sits the code cache. The JIT compilers, the parts of the JVM that turn busy bytecode into machine code while the program runs, keep their output there. It's natural to read -Xmx as the size of the program. It isn't. Here's a JDK 25 program started with -Xmx256m and measured by Native Memory Tracking (NMT), the JVM's own accounting of its memory. The program holds 100 MB of arrays, 50 extra threads and 96 MB of memory outside the heap. Committed means memory the operating system has really handed over, as opposed to addresses only reserved for later: Area Committed What lives there Java heap 216 MB every object you create with new Memory outside the heap 96 MB ByteBuffer.allocateDirect and Arena.allocate (64 MB and 32 MB here) GC bookkeeping 45 MB the collector's own records about the heap (lesson 4) Shared class archive (CDS, class data sharing) 14 MB JDK classes, already parsed, read from a file Code cache 7 MB machine code from the JIT compilers Thread stacks 6 MB one stack per platform thread (71 of them) Metaspace 1 MB the plans for the classes loaded from the program's own jars The process committed 388 MB, and 172 MB of it lives outside the heap, where -Xmx limits none of it. In the warehouse, -Xmx caps the storage floor. The desks (stacks), the filing room (metaspace) and the yard out back (memory outside the heap) come on top. Three rows deserve a sentence each. Each platform thread reserves a 1 MB stack on Linux x64 but commits only the pages it touches, which is why 71 threads committed just 6 MB. Metaspace has no limit by default, so a program that keeps loading new classes keeps growing it. And a direct buffer is memory the program asks for outside the heap, often to read and write files and network data. The heap holds only a small object that points to it. Arena.allocate, from the Foreign Function and Memory API (final since JDK 22), hands out the same kind of memory. (A virtual thread is the one exception to "stacks live outside the heap": while it waits, its frames sit in ordinary objects on the heap, as the virtual threads track showed.) Lesson 6 of this track fits all of these areas into a fixed memory budget, and lesson 7 measures them with NMT. For now, let's step onto the floor and look at one box. List the memory areas of a JVM Read MemoryAreasDemo (or its Kotlin twin). It lists every memory pool the JVM reports, then asks for a 64 MiB direct buffer. Predict: will the buffer show up in one of the heap pools? Run it from the labs/ folder with the command below. Compare the max heap it prints with your machine's memory. When you give no -Xmx, the JVM takes a quarter of it. MemoryAreasDemo.java package workbench.memory.l01; import java.lang.management.BufferPoolMXBean; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.lang.management.MemoryPoolMXBean; import java.nio.ByteBuffer; /** Lists the memory areas this JVM reports, heap and non-heap, then adds a 64 MiB direct buffer. */ public class MemoryAreasDemo { static final long MB = 1024 * 1024; public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.printf("max heap (-Xmx or its default): %,d MB%n", Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() / MB); for (MemoryPoolMXBean pool : ManagementFactory.getMemoryPoolMXBeans()) { System.out.printf("%-9s %-32s used %,6d KB committed %,7d KB%n", pool.getType() == java.lang.management.MemoryType.HEAP ? "heap" : "non-heap", pool.getName(), pool.getUsage().getUsed() / 1024, pool.getUsage().getCommitted() / 1024); } System.out.println("live threads: " + ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().getThreadCount() + ", each with a stack outside the heap"); ByteBuffer direct = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect((int) (64 * MB)); // off-heap: not in any pool above for (BufferPoolMXBean p : ManagementFactory.getPlatformMXBeans(BufferPoolMXBean.class)) { if (p.getName().equals("direct")) { System.out.printf("direct buffers: %d, %,d MB, outside the heap%n", p.getCount(), p.getMemoryUsed() / MB); } } System.out.println("buffer capacity " + direct.capacity()); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l01.MemoryAreasDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l01/MemoryAreasDemo.java MemoryAreasDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l01 import java.lang.management.BufferPoolMXBean import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import java.lang.management.MemoryType import java.nio.ByteBuffer private const val MB = 1024L * 1024 /** Lists the memory areas this JVM reports, heap and non-heap, then adds a 64 MiB direct buffer. */ fun main() { println("max heap (-Xmx or its default): %,d MB".format(Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() / MB)) for (pool in ManagementFactory.getMemoryPoolMXBeans()) { println("%-9s %-32s used %,6d KB committed %,7d KB".format( if (pool.type == MemoryType.HEAP) "heap" else "non-heap", pool.name, pool.usage.used / 1024, pool.usage.committed / 1024)) } println("live threads: ${ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().threadCount}, each with a stack outside the heap") val direct = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect((64 * MB).toInt()) // off-heap: not in any pool above ManagementFactory.getPlatformMXBeans(BufferPoolMXBean::class.java) .filter { it.name == "direct" } .forEach { println("direct buffers: %d, %,d MB, outside the heap".format(it.count, it.memoryUsed / MB)) } println("buffer capacity ${direct.capacity()}") } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l01.MemoryAreasDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l01/MemoryAreasDemo.kt Three heap pools (G1 Eden Space, G1 Survivor Space, G1 Old Gen) and several non-heap ones: Metaspace, Compressed Class Space and three CodeHeap pools for compiled code. The 64 MB buffer appears in none of them, only in the direct buffer pool, because it lives outside the heap. The max heap is 25% of your memory, or of the memory limit the program runs under, if it has one: on the 13.4 GB machine behind this lesson, it printed 3,420 MB. Native Memory Tracking for one JDK 25 process started with -Xmx256m: the heap was 216 MB of the 388 MB the process committed. The java command, JDK 25 manual (source of the man page) docs

h: Where objects live: heap, stacks, metaspace and object headers · The label on every box: a 12-byte header, the fields, then padding
x: The 40 bytes of a Payment: a 12-byte header, fields in the JVM's order, padding to 8, and 4-byte compressed references new Object() has no fields at all, and it still takes 16 bytes of heap. Those bytes are the label. On a 64-bit HotSpot JVM (HotSpot is the JVM inside OpenJDK and most Java downloads), every object starts with a header of two parts. The mark word, 8 bytes, is the housekeeping strip. It holds the object's identity hash code (the one Object.hashCode() returns when a class doesn't override it), once something asks for it. It holds the GC age: how many cleanings the object has survived, in 4 bits, so at most 15. And it holds the bits that synchronized uses when a thread locks the object. The class pointer, 4 bytes by default, says what kind of box this is. It points to the class's plan in metaspace. That's 12 bytes before the first field. After the fields comes padding: every object starts at a multiple of 8 bytes, so its size rounds up to the next multiple of 8. new Object() is 12 bytes of header plus 4 of padding. An Integer puts its 4-byte int where the padding would go, so it's 16 too. A Long needs 8 bytes for its value: 12 + 8 = 20, which rounds up to 24. That was the warm-up. Here the warehouse picture breaks, and it's worth saying out loud. A paper label costs no shelf space. A Java header sits inside the box and takes 12 of its bytes, whether the box holds 4 bytes of data or 4,000. Now the service's own class. A Thumbnail object carries a few facts about one preview picture, and a reference to its pixels: Java class Thumbnail { boolean cached; long createdAtMillis; byte format; // 1 = JPEG, 2 = PNG String name; int width; byte[] pixels; } Kotlin class Thumbnail { var cached = false var createdAtMillis = 0L var format: Byte = 0 // 1 = JPEG, 2 = PNG var name: String? = null var width = 0 var pixels: ByteArray? = null } Kotlin compiles each var to the same JVM field as the Java line above it, so both classes get the same layout. JOL (Java Object Layout), a small OpenJDK tool, prints what the JVM really did with those fields. In its printout, OFF is each part's offset, its distance in bytes from the start of the object, and SZ is its size. This is JOL on JDK 25 with default settings: OFF SZ TYPE DESCRIPTION VALUE 0 8 (object header: mark) N/A 8 4 (object header: class) N/A 12 4 int Thumbnail.width N/A 16 8 long Thumbnail.createdAtMillis N/A 24 1 boolean Thumbnail.cached N/A 25 1 byte Thumbnail.format N/A 26 2 (alignment/padding gap) 28 4 java.lang.String Thumbnail.name N/A 32 4 byte[] Thumbnail.pixels N/A 36 4 (object alignment gap) Instance size: 40 bytes Read it from the top. The header fills offsets 0 to 11. Then the JVM, a tidy packer, did something the source never asked for. It moved width up to offset 12, into the 4 bytes after the header, because a long must start at a multiple of 8 and wouldn't fit there. The long follows at 16, then the two 1-byte fields, a 2-byte gap, and the two references at 4 bytes each. Four bytes of padding end the object at 40. So 6 of the 40 bytes are gaps. They're room for later: a subclass that adds a String and a short still takes 40 bytes, because its fields slide into those gaps. The lab measures exactly that case. You don't need JOL to estimate, though. An object costs its header plus its fields, rounded up to 8. Count objects, not data. Counting objects is where the surprises live. The file extension "jpg" as a String costs 48 bytes, 16 bytes per letter: a 24-byte String object plus a 24-byte byte[] that holds the 3 letters. An ArrayList<Integer> with the numbers 0 to 999 costs 20,976 bytes, because each number is its own 16-byte Integer plus a 4-byte reference in the list. An int[1000] holds the same numbers in 4,016. All of those references took 4 bytes. On a 64-bit machine, that should be impossible. Print real layouts with JOL Before you run anything, write down your guess for a Thumbnail, an Integer, a Long, and the string "jpg" with its array. Run LayoutDemo (Java) or LayoutDemoKt (Kotlin, whose class is called KThumbnail). JOL prints a few warnings first: two about attaching an agent, and on JDK 25 four more about "a terminally deprecated method in sun.misc.Unsafe", because JOL 0.17 dates from 2023. The layouts are still right. Find the padding in the printout. Then read the last line: the JVM's own allocation counter, which measures the same thing without JOL. LayoutDemo.java package workbench.memory.l01; import com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean; import org.openjdk.jol.datamodel.Model64_Lilliput; import org.openjdk.jol.info.ClassLayout; import org.openjdk.jol.info.GraphLayout; import org.openjdk.jol.layouters.HotSpotLayouter; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; /** * Prints real object layouts with JOL. Pass JVM flags to see them change, for example * -Pargs=-XX:-UseCompressedOops (the demo then reruns itself in a child JVM with those flags). */ public class LayoutDemo { /** One thumbnail the service keeps in memory: a small preview picture and a few facts about it. */ static class Thumbnail { boolean cached; long createdAtMillis; byte format; // 1 = JPEG, 2 = PNG String name; int width; byte[] pixels; } public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0) { // flags given: rerun in a JVM that has them Jvm.run(Arrays.asList(args), LayoutDemo.class.getName()); return; } System.out.println(ClassLayout.parseClass(Thumbnail.class).toPrintable()); List<Integer> boxed = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) boxed.add(i); System.out.printf("Object %d, Integer %d, Long %d, String shell %d bytes%n", ClassLayout.parseClass(Object.class).instanceSize(), ClassLayout.parseClass(Integer.class).instanceSize(), ClassLayout.parseClass(Long.class).instanceSize(), ClassLayout.parseClass(String.class).instanceSize()); System.out.printf("\"jpg\" with its byte[]: %d bytes%n", GraphLayout.parseInstance(new String("jpg")).totalSize()); System.out.printf("ArrayList<Integer> of 0..999: %,d bytes, int[1000]: %,d bytes%n", GraphLayout.parseInstance(boxed).totalSize(), GraphLayout.parseInstance((Object) new int[1_000]).totalSize()); // JOL can also simulate a layout: here, an 8-byte compact header with compressed references ClassLayout compact = ClassLayout.parseClass(Thumbnail.class, new HotSpotLayouter(new Model64_Lilliput(true, 8, false), 25)); System.out.printf("Thumbnail with compact headers (JOL simulation): %d bytes%n", compact.instanceSize()); // and the JVM itself can tell you: count the bytes 10,000 new Thumbnail objects take ThreadMXBean threads = (ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); Thumbnail[] keep = new Thumbnail[10_000]; // allocate the array before we start counting long before = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes(); for (int i = 0; i < keep.length; i++) keep[i] = new Thumbnail(); long bytes = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before; System.out.printf("10,000 Thumbnails allocated %,d bytes: %d per object in this JVM%n", bytes, bytes / keep.length); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l01.LayoutDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l01/LayoutDemo.java LayoutDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l01 import com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean import org.openjdk.jol.datamodel.Model64_Lilliput import org.openjdk.jol.info.ClassLayout import org.openjdk.jol.info.GraphLayout import org.openjdk.jol.layouters.HotSpotLayouter import workbench.memory.Jvm import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory /** The same fields as the Java demo's Thumbnail. Kotlin properties compile to the same JVM fields. */ class KThumbnail { var cached = false var createdAtMillis = 0L var format: Byte = 0 // 1 = JPEG, 2 = PNG var name: String? = null var width = 0 var pixels: ByteArray? = null } /** * Prints real object layouts with JOL. Pass JVM flags to see them change, for example * -Pargs=-XX:-UseCompressedOops (the demo then reruns itself in a child JVM with those flags). */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isNotEmpty()) { // flags given: rerun in a JVM that has them Jvm.run(args.toList(), "workbench.memory.l01.LayoutDemoKt") return } println(ClassLayout.parseClass(KThumbnail::class.java).toPrintable()) val boxed = ArrayList<Int>() // List<Int> holds boxed Integers for (i in 0 until 1_000) boxed.add(i) println("Object %d, Integer %d, Long %d, String shell %d bytes".format( ClassLayout.parseClass(Any::class.java).instanceSize(), ClassLayout.parseClass(Int::class.javaObjectType).instanceSize(), ClassLayout.parseClass(Long::class.javaObjectType).instanceSize(), ClassLayout.parseClass(String::class.java).instanceSize())) println("\"jpg\" with its byte[]: %d bytes".format(GraphLayout.parseInstance(String("jpg".toCharArray())).totalSize())) println("ArrayList<Integer> of 0..999: %,d bytes, int[1000]: %,d bytes".format( GraphLayout.parseInstance(boxed).totalSize(), GraphLayout.parseInstance(IntArray(1_000)).totalSize())) // JOL can also simulate a layout: here, an 8-byte compact header with compressed references val compact = ClassLayout.parseClass(KThumbnail::class.java, HotSpotLayouter(Model64_Lilliput(true, 8, false), 25)) println("Thumbnail with compact headers (JOL simulation): %d bytes".format(compact.instanceSize())) // and the JVM itself can tell you: count the bytes 10,000 new Thumbnail objects take val threads = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as ThreadMXBean val keep = arrayOfNulls<KThumbnail>(10_000) // allocate the array before we start counting val before = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes for (i in keep.indices) keep[i] = KThumbnail() val bytes = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before println("10,000 Thumbnails allocated %,d bytes: %d per object in this JVM".format(bytes, bytes / keep.size)) } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l01.LayoutDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l01/LayoutDemo.kt Thumbnail is 40 bytes, with a 2-byte gap in the middle and 4 bytes of padding at the end. Then Object 16, Integer 16, Long 24, String shell 24 bytes, and "jpg" with its array is 48. The ArrayList<Integer> of 0 to 999 costs 20,976 bytes against 4,016 for int[1000]. The last line says 10,000 thumbnails allocated 400,000 bytes, 40 per object: the same answer JOL gave. JOL (Java Object Layout) on GitHub docs

h: Where objects live: heap, stacks, metaspace and object headers · Short shelf numbers: compressed references up to 32 GB
x: A reference on a 64-bit machine should take 8 bytes, the size of a full memory address. On HotSpot it usually takes 4, thanks to compressed oops. ("Oop" is HotSpot's name for an ordinary object pointer, which is what a reference is inside the JVM.) The trick follows from the padding. Every object starts at a multiple of 8, so the lowest 3 bits of every object's address are always zero. The JVM doesn't store them. It stores a 32-bit number instead, and shifts it left by 3 bits (multiplies it by 8) whenever it follows the reference. In the warehouse, it's writing a short shelf number on the notepad instead of the full address, because every shelf slot is 8 bytes wide. A 32-bit number counts about 4 billion slots, and 4 billion slots of 8 bytes reach 32 GB. So while the maximum heap is under 32 GB, every reference field and every slot of an Object[] takes 4 bytes. Give the JVM -Xmx32g or more, and it switches compressed oops off by itself. References go back to 8 bytes. These are JOL's numbers on JDK 25 with -Xmx40g (the JVM only reserves addresses for the maximum heap at start-up, so this runs on a small laptop): Object heap under 32 GB -Xmx40g Thumbnail 40 48 String (the object alone) 24 32 "jpg" with its array 48 56 ArrayList<Integer> of 1,000 20,976 25,920 int[1000] 4,016 4,016 The list grew by 24%. That makes a 40 GB heap a strange deal. Moving from -Xmx31g to -Xmx40g buys 29% more heap, and the same objects grow by about a fifth, so longer references eat most of the new room. Bigger isn't always bigger. The int[] didn't change at all, because it holds numbers, not references. There's a way past the cliff: -XX:ObjectAlignmentInBytes=16. With 16-byte slots, the same 32-bit numbers reach 64 GB. The price is that every object now pads to a multiple of 16, so a Thumbnail is 48 bytes again. I'd rather keep each JVM under 32 GB and run more of them. The class pointer has its own compression, into a separate 1 GB space for class data. That's why the header stays at 12 bytes even when compressed oops are off. And since JDK 25, there's a supported way to make the header itself smaller. Turn compressed oops off Predict the new size of a Thumbnail and of the ArrayList<Integer> once every reference is 8 bytes. Run the demo again with -Pargs=-XX:-UseCompressedOops added to the command. The demo starts a child JVM with that flag. Run it once more with -Pargs=-Xmx40g instead, and compare the two printouts. terminal ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l01.LayoutDemo -Pargs=-XX:-UseCompressedOops ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l01.LayoutDemo -Pargs=-Xmx40g Both runs print the same numbers. References are 8 bytes now, so Thumbnail grows to 48, and its gaps merge into one 6-byte gap before the first reference. The String object is 32, "jpg" is 56 and the list is 25,920 bytes, while int[1000] stays at 4,016. The allocation counter says 48 bytes per thumbnail. -Xmx40g switched compressed oops off all by itself.

h: Where objects live: heap, stacks, metaspace and object headers · A smaller label: compact object headers on JDK 25
x: Project Lilliput, the OpenJDK project working on smaller object headers, shrank the label to 8 bytes. With compact object headers, the class pointer moves into the mark word itself, squeezed into 22 bits, and the separate class word disappears. The flag changed status on the way, each step described in a JEP (a JDK Enhancement Proposal, the document behind each new JDK feature), so the version matters: JDK Compact object headers 21 not there: the JVM stops with Unrecognized VM option 'UseCompactObjectHeaders' 24 experimental (JEP 450): -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders 25 and 26 a product feature, off by default (JEP 519): -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders alone 27 on by default, per the JDK 27 source; -XX:-UseCompactObjectHeaders turns it off On JDK 25, then, it's one flag. Here's the thumbnail with it, printed by JOL and confirmed by the JVM's own allocation counter (10,000 thumbnails took 320,000 bytes): OFF SZ TYPE DESCRIPTION VALUE 0 8 (object header: mark) N/A 8 8 long Thumbnail.createdAtMillis N/A 16 4 int Thumbnail.width N/A 20 1 boolean Thumbnail.cached N/A 21 1 byte Thumbnail.format N/A 22 2 (alignment/padding gap) 24 4 java.lang.String Thumbnail.name N/A 28 4 byte[] Thumbnail.pixels N/A Instance size: 32 bytes The fields now start at offset 8, so the long fits right after the header, and the object ends at exactly 32 bytes with no padding at the end. The JDK 25 manual says the option saves "4 bytes per object (on average)". The word that matters is "average". Objects still round up to a multiple of 8, so each one saves either 8 bytes or nothing. These are JDK 25 measurements, without the flag and with it: Object 12-byte header 8-byte header new Object() 16 8 Thumbnail 40 32 Long 24 16 byte[3] 24 16 Integer 16 16 String (the object alone) 24 24 An Integer was 12 + 4 = 16, and is now 8 + 4 = 12, which rounds right back up to 16. So the ArrayList<Integer> from the last section, a thousand Integers, saved nothing at all: still 20,976 bytes. The saving follows the number of small objects, not the size of the heap. A heap full of small objects, map entries and boxed numbers gains the most; the million-entry map in the worked example below shrinks by 17%. A heap full of large arrays barely notices, because one array saves at most 8 bytes. On JDK 25 it's worth a load test, because it's one flag and you can take it away again. So far we've only measured the boxes. How they get onto the floor, and how fast, is the next question. Turn on compact headers This step needs Gradle running on JDK 25 or later. Check the Daemon JVM line of ./gradlew --version. On JDK 21 the child JVM stops with Unrecognized VM option 'UseCompactObjectHeaders', which proves the first row of the version table. Predict the sizes of Object, Long, Integer and "jpg" with an 8-byte header. Then run the demo with -Pargs=-XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders. Compare the last line, which the JVM measures itself, with the first run of this lesson. terminal (JDK 25) ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l01.LayoutDemo -Pargs=-XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders On JDK 25 the layout starts its fields at offset 8, and Thumbnail is 32 bytes. Then Object 8, Integer 16, Long 16, String shell 24 bytes, "jpg" with its array is 40 bytes, and the list of 1,000 Integers is still 20,976. The counter reports 320,000 bytes for 10,000 thumbnails, 32 per object, against 40 without the flag. The line marked "JOL simulation" says 32 in every run, because it's a model, not a measurement. x: The same two fields in Java and Kotlin Photo.java class Photo { long sizeBytes; // primitive: 8 bytes inside the object Long takenAtMillis; // reference: 4 bytes here, plus a 24-byte Long elsewhere (null when unknown) } Photo.kt class Photo( var sizeBytes: Long, // compiles to a long field: 8 bytes inside the object var takenAtMillis: Long?, // compiles to a java.lang.Long field: a reference plus a 24-byte box ) Both classes compile to the same two JVM fields and the same 24-byte layout, and JOL can't tell them apart. The difference is what the source shows you. Java names the box: Long with a capital L is an object, long is not. Kotlin has one Long type and picks for you: a primitive long when it can, and a boxed java.lang.Long when the type is nullable (Long?) or a type argument (List<Long>). So in Kotlin, a single ? can add an object per value. val versus var changes nothing in size, and data class adds methods, not fields.

h: Where objects live: heap, stacks, metaspace and object headers · Worked example
x: Estimate a million-entry map of upload ids, then check it The thumbnail service remembers which uploads it has already processed, so a photo uploaded twice is only shrunk once. Each upload has an id, a random 36-character string (a UUID written as text), and the map goes from that id to the size of the stored thumbnail in bytes. How much heap does it take at a million entries? // key: the upload's id, value: the thumbnail's size in bytes Map<String, Long> done = new HashMap<>(); done.put(upload.id(), thumbnailBytes); // key: the upload's id, value: the thumbnail's size in bytes val done = HashMap<String, Long>() done[upload.id] = thumbnailBytes List the objects one entry creates, and size each one with the rule: header plus fields, rounded up to 8. The map's table is shared by all entries. A million entries is more than 0.75 of 2^20 slots, so HashMap grows its table to 2^21 slots of 4 bytes, 8 MB in all. String 24 header 12 + byte[] ref 4 + hash 4 + coder 1 + flag 1 = 22 -> 24 byte[36] 56 header 12 + length 4 + 36 bytes of letters = 52 -> 56 Long 24 header 12 + long 8 = 20 -> 24 HashMap$Node 32 header 12 + hash 4 + key, value, next 3 x 4 = 28 -> 32 table slot ~8.4 2,097,152 slots x 4 bytes / 1,000,000 entries ------ ~144 bytes per entry, ~144 MB for the map Check the estimate instead of trusting it. JOL's GraphLayout walks every object the map can reach. On JDK 25 with random ids, it counted 4,000,002 objects and 144,388,672 bytes: 144.4 per entry. The data itself is 36 + 8 = 44 bytes per entry, so two thirds of the map is labels, references and padding. GraphLayout g = GraphLayout.parseInstance(done); System.out.println(g.toFootprint()); // a table: count and bytes per class System.out.println(g.totalSize() / done.size() + " bytes per entry"); val g = GraphLayout.parseInstance(done) println(g.toFootprint()) // a table: count and bytes per class println("${g.totalSize() / done.size} bytes per entry") Shrink it where the bytes are. The key costs 80 bytes as a String plus its array. A UUID object holds the same 128 bits in two long fields and takes 32 bytes. JOL then counts 96,388,672 bytes, 96.4 per entry: a third less. Compact headers on JDK 25 stack on top of that, with 120.4 bytes per entry for the string keys and 72.4 for UUID keys. Putting a limit on the map's size saves even more, and lesson 7 does that. Map<UUID, Long> done = new HashMap<>(); done.put(UUID.fromString(upload.id()), thumbnailBytes); // a 32-byte key instead of 80 val done = HashMap<UUID, Long>() done[UUID.fromString(upload.id)] = thumbnailBytes // a 32-byte key instead of 80

h: Where objects live: heap, stacks, metaspace and object headers · Quiz
x: What is the shallow size (the object alone, without what it points to) of class Size { long bytes; int width; } on JDK 25 with default settings? 12 bytes 16 bytes 24 bytes 32 bytes A 12-byte header + 8 + 4 = 24, which is already a multiple of 8. The JVM puts the int at offset 12, right after the header, and the long at 16. 12 forgets the header. 32 assumes a 16-byte header, which you only get with compressed class pointers switched off. A batch job holds a large in-memory map of photo records. A teammate raises -Xmx from 30g to 36g to fit 20% more records. What happens? Compressed oops switch off, every reference doubles, and the extra 6 GB holds far fewer records than planned It fits 20% more records, because heap size and capacity grow together The JVM refuses to start, because compressed oops can't address 36 GB Nothing changes until the heap is full At 32 GB and above the JVM stops compressing references, so every reference field and array slot grows from 4 to 8 bytes. On JOL's numbers the same objects grow by about a fifth, which eats most of the extra 6 GB. The JVM still starts: it simply picks 8-byte references on its own. Which of these objects gets smaller when you turn on compact object headers on JDK 25? An Integer A Long A String object (without its array) A byte[1_000_000], by a meaningful amount A Long is 12 + 8 = 20, padded to 24. With an 8-byte header it is 8 + 8 = 16 exactly, and the lesson's run measured 16. An Integer is 16 either way (12 + 4 = 16, and 8 + 4 = 12 pads back to 16). A String object stays 24 for the same reason. A one-megabyte array saves at most 8 bytes, which is nothing next to its data. A program started with -Xmx512m calls ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(64 * 1024 * 1024). Where do those 64 MB live? In the young generation In the old generation In metaspace In native memory outside the heap A direct buffer is memory outside the heap. The heap only holds a small DirectByteBuffer object that points to it. That's why the demo showed the buffer in the direct buffer pool and in no heap pool, and why -Xmx does not limit it. Metaspace holds the plans of classes, not buffers. From the virtual threads track: a virtual thread waiting for a slow web service to answer has unmounted from its carrier. Where are its stack frames now? Still on the carrier's stack, which stays reserved for it In a 1 MB thread stack outside the heap In stack chunk objects on the Java heap In metaspace, next to the class data When a virtual thread unmounts, the JDK copies its frames into stack chunk objects on the heap, sized to the frames that exist. The garbage collector manages them like any other object. The carrier's stack is free for the next virtual thread, and only platform threads get a fixed stack outside the heap.
