h: Where objects live: heap, stacks, metaspace and object headers · Key terms
x: Heap The shared memory where every object created with new lives, and that the garbage collector cleans. Thread stack A thread's own memory for the local variables of the methods it is running. Outside the heap for platform threads. Metaspace Memory outside the heap for class metadata: fields, methods, bytecode. Unlimited by default. Object header The bytes at the start of every object: the mark word plus the class pointer, 12 bytes by default. Mark word The first 8 bytes of every object: hash code, GC age and lock bits. Compressed oops 4-byte references that the JVM multiplies by 8 to reach up to 32 GB of heap. Shallow size The bytes of one object alone: header, fields and padding, not the objects it points to. Compact object headers An 8-byte header with the class pointer folded into the mark word. One flag on JDK 25, the default on JDK 27. How big is an object header on a 64-bit JDK 25 with default settings? 12 bytes: an 8-byte mark word and a 4-byte compressed class pointer. What does the mark word hold? The identity hash code (once something asks for it), the GC age in 4 bits, and the lock bits. How many bytes does a Long take by default? 24: a 12-byte header plus 8 bytes of value is 20, rounded up to a multiple of 8. Up to which max heap do compressed oops work by default? Just under 32 GB: about 4 billion 32-bit slot numbers times 8-byte slots. From -Xmx32g up, references take 8 bytes. Does -Xmx limit thread stacks, metaspace or direct buffers? No. It caps only the Java heap. Everything else comes on top of it. How do you turn on compact object headers on JDK 25? -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders on its own. It's a product feature in JDK 25, experimental in JDK 24, and the default in JDK 27. Why can adding a field to a class cost 0 bytes? Objects round up to a multiple of 8. A small new field can fill the padding: the 40-byte Thumbnail plus a String and a short is still 40 bytes.

h: Where objects live: heap, stacks, metaspace and object headers · Go deeper
x: The mark word has an exact bit layout, and it changed between JDK 21 and 25. On JDK 21 a normal object's mark word is unused:25 hash:31 unused_gap:1 age:4 unused_gap:1 lock:2. On JDK 25 it is unused:22 hash:31 unused_gap:4 age:4 self-fwd:1 lock:2, and with compact headers the 22 unused bits become klass:22, the class pointer. 22 bits can name about 4 million classes, which is plenty. The JDK 25 source marks four of the gap bits as reserved for Valhalla, the project that will bring value objects. You can watch the word change with JOL's ClassLayout.parseInstance(obj).toPrintable(). On JDK 25 a fresh object shows 0x0000000000000001 (non-biasable; age: 0). After System.identityHashCode(obj), the hash appears inside the word: 0x000002bc2ae4d001 (hash: 0xbc2ae4d0; age: 0). Inside a synchronized block the word became 0x000002bc2ae4d000: the same bits with the last two changed from 01 to 00. JOL 0.17 labels that a "thin lock" with an address, a name from older JDKs. On JDK 25 the JVM's lightweight locking is the default, so the word keeps its hash and the locking thread records the object on its own small lock stack. With -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders, JOL prints only the mark word, such as 0x0017280000000001 (Lilliput), with the class bits in its top part. Field packing has its own rules since JDK 15. The JVM fills the 4-byte gap after a 12-byte header with an int, a float or a reference, but never with a long, which must start at a multiple of 8. That's why a Long has 4 bytes of padding in the middle and an Integer has none. Subclass fields can fill gaps left by the superclass, as the lab's WatermarkedThumbnail shows. Two practical notes about JOL. On JDK 21 it can't read record field offsets unless you set -Djol.magicFieldOffset=true (the lab's test sets it in code before JOL starts). And without permission to attach to processes it prints warnings and guesses addresses, but the layouts and sizes it prints are still exact.

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · A private stretch of shelf: allocation is a pointer bump in a TLAB
x: Each thread bumps a pointer in its own TLAB, and C2 removes an object that never leaves a hot method New objects go into eden, the part of the heap set aside for new arrivals. (Lesson 4 explains why the heap has a separate area for them.) Every thread shares eden. If each new took its memory straight from eden, every thread would have to update one shared "next free byte" pointer. They'd take turns, like workers queueing at the floor manager's desk. So each thread claims a chunk of eden for itself, its TLAB (thread-local allocation buffer), and allocates inside it with no locking at all. That's the reserved stretch of shelf. In the JDK 25 demo below, each chunk was about 500 KB, room for twelve thousand small arrays. Allocating inside a TLAB means moving a "top" pointer forward, which is called bump-pointer allocation. This is HotSpot's fast path, from the JDK 25 source: HeapWord* obj = top(); if (pointer_delta(end(), obj) >= size) { // does the object fit? set_top(obj + size); // bump the pointer return obj; } return nullptr; // no: take the slow path It's a compare, an add and a store. Then the JVM writes the object's header and zeroes its fields. Once a method is compiled by the JIT (the part of the JVM that turns busy bytecode into machine code), these few instructions sit right inside your code, so a new doesn't even make a call. The slow path runs when the object doesn't fit. Usually the TLAB is simply full, and the thread claims a fresh one from eden with one atomic update, a single step that no other thread can interrupt. That's the only moment two threads' allocations can meet. Objects too big for a TLAB go straight into eden. G1, the JVM's default garbage collector, splits the heap into equal regions of 1 to 32 MB. An object bigger than half a region is humongous: a 3 MB photo in one byte[], on a heap with 2 MB regions, skips TLABs and eden entirely. Lesson 4 shows why that costs more. Here the warehouse picture breaks, and the break teaches something. In a warehouse, carrying a box to its shelf is the hard part. In the JVM, the bump costs a few instructions, and the bill comes later. Every TLAB a thread fills brings eden closer to full, and a full eden is what calls the cleaning crew: a young collection, the GC run that empties eden. So what you pay for is the allocation rate, the bytes allocated per second. A service that allocates 1 GB a second fills a 500 MB eden twice a second, and with G1 each of those is a pause, a moment when the program's threads stop while the collector works. The objects that are already dead cost almost nothing even then, because a young collection copies only the objects still alive. Kotlin compiles to the same new bytecode, so all of this is identical in both languages. The rate, then, is worth measuring. How many bytes does one piece of code allocate? You don't have to guess. Count TLAB refills Read TlabDemo. It allocates 5,000,000 arrays of 40 bytes, 200 MB in all, in a child JVM that logs a TLAB summary at every GC. Predict: how often will the main thread go back to eden for a fresh TLAB? Run it with the command below. Find the GC(1) TLAB totals line. Divide the megabytes that pause found by the number of refills. TlabDemo.java package workbench.memory.l02; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.List; /** * Allocates 5,000,000 small arrays in a child JVM that logs a TLAB summary at every GC. * Each "refills" count is how often a thread went back to eden for a fresh buffer. */ public class TlabDemo { static volatile Object sink; public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length == 0) { for (String line : Jvm.lines(List.of("-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:gc,gc+tlab=debug"), TlabDemo.class.getName(), "allocate")) { System.out.println(line.replaceAll("\\s+", " ")); } return; } for (int i = 0; i < 5_000_000; i++) sink = new byte[24]; // 16-byte header + 24 bytes = 40 bytes each System.out.println("allocated 5,000,000 arrays of 40 bytes: 200,000,000 bytes"); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l02.TlabDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l02/TlabDemo.java TlabDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l02 import workbench.memory.Jvm @Volatile private var tlabSink: Any? = null /** * Allocates 5,000,000 small arrays in a child JVM that logs a TLAB summary at every GC. * Each "refills" count is how often a thread went back to eden for a fresh buffer. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isEmpty()) { Jvm.lines(listOf("-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:gc,gc+tlab=debug"), "workbench.memory.l02.TlabDemoKt", "allocate") .forEach { println(it.replace(Regex("\\s+"), " ")) } return } repeat(5_000_000) { tlabSink = ByteArray(24) } // 16-byte header + 24 bytes = 40 bytes each println("allocated 5,000,000 arrays of 40 bytes: 200,000,000 bytes") } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l02.TlabDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l02/TlabDemo.kt On JDK 25: GC(1) TLAB totals: thrds: 1 refills: 196 ... slow allocs: 0 ... waste: 0.1%, then Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 99M->1M. One thread allocated about 98 MB in 196 refills, so each TLAB held about 500 KB, roughly 12,500 arrays per trip to the shared eden. slow allocs: 0 means no array had to skip its TLAB. JDK 21 uses smaller TLABs (about 305 refills for 61 MB), and the counts change from run to run. Each thread allocates inside its own TLAB by bumping a pointer. Only a refill touches shared eden. threadLocalAllocBuffer.inline.hpp at jdk-25-ga: the fast path read

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · Counting bytes with the thread's allocation counter
x: HotSpot counts every byte each thread allocates. A ThreadMXBean is the JDK's management interface for facts about threads, and com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean, an extension of the standard one, hands you the counter with getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() (since JDK 14). Read it, run the code, read it again: Java var threads = (com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); long before = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes(); byte[] photo = new byte[1 << 20]; long bytes = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before; // 1,048,592 Kotlin val threads = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean val before = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes val photo = ByteArray(1 shl 20) val bytes = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before // 1,048,592 The Javadoc calls the number "an approximation". For code that runs once, it's exact to the byte in practice: 1 MiB of data plus a 16-byte array header gave 1,048,592. That makes it the best way to test your model from the last lesson. A thousand Long boxes for values above the cache allocate 24,000 bytes, exactly 1,000 times 24. The counter has two traps, and the demo below walks into both. The first call to anything pays for one-time setup. The first Long.valueOf builds the JDK's cache of the 256 boxes from -128 to 127, and that cost 7,456 bytes on JDK 25. The first string concatenation sets itself up too: a thousand "img-" + i cost 100,480 bytes the first time and 48,000 the second, 48 bytes per name. Measure twice and trust the second number. The second trap is a virtual thread, the lightweight kind of thread that the JDK runs on top of a few platform threads. There the counter returns -1, its polite way of saying "not here". Measure on a platform thread. In a test, the pattern has three steps. Call the code once on tiny input, so its classes are loaded. Measure one call on real input. Then compare the bytes with what the result itself needs, plus a margin. A method that returns a long[500] needs 4,016 bytes. If it allocates 1.5 MB, something inside it is boxing. That comparison is deterministic, and it's exactly what the lab's tests do. The counter answers questions like "which step of this request allocates?" For the allocation rate of a whole running program, use JFR (Java Flight Recorder, the JDK's built-in recorder) or the GC log. The performance track covers JFR, and lesson 6 of this track reads GC logs. Sometimes, though, the counter reports 0 for code that plainly says new. Predict four allocation counts Read AllocationCounterDemo (or the Kotlin twin). Write down your prediction for each line, for the first run and for the second. Run it with the command below. Explain each difference between the first column and the second. AllocationCounterDemo.java package workbench.memory.l02; import com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; /** Counts the bytes a few small pieces of code allocate, twice each, using the JVM's per-thread counter. */ public class AllocationCounterDemo { static final ThreadMXBean THREADS = (ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); static volatile Object sink; // results escape here, so nothing is optimized away static long bytes(Runnable work) { long before = THREADS.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes(); work.run(); return THREADS.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before; } static void show(String what, Runnable work) { long first = bytes(work); // the first run also pays for one-time setup long second = bytes(work); System.out.printf("%-34s %,10d %,11d%n", what, first, second); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.printf("%-34s %10s %11s%n", "bytes allocated by", "first run", "second run"); show("new byte[1 MiB]", () -> sink = new byte[1 << 20]); show("1,000 x Long.valueOf(i % 128)", () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) sink = Long.valueOf(i % 128); }); show("1,000 x Long.valueOf(1_000 + i)", () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) sink = Long.valueOf(1_000 + i); }); show("1,000 x \"img-\" + i", () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) sink = "img-" + i; }); Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> System.out.println("on a virtual thread the counter says " + THREADS.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes())).join(); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l02.AllocationCounterDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l02/AllocationCounterDemo.java AllocationCounterDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l02 import com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory private val THREADS = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as ThreadMXBean @Volatile private var sink: Any? = null // results escape here, so nothing is optimized away private fun bytes(work: () -> Unit): Long { val before = THREADS.currentThreadAllocatedBytes work() return THREADS.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before } private fun show(what: String, work: () -> Unit) { val first = bytes(work) // the first run also pays for one-time setup val second = bytes(work) println("%-34s %,10d %,11d".format(what, first, second)) } /** Counts the bytes a few small pieces of code allocate, twice each, using the JVM's per-thread counter. */ fun main() { println("%-34s %10s %11s".format("bytes allocated by", "first run", "second run")) show("ByteArray(1 MiB)") { sink = ByteArray(1 shl 20) } show("1,000 x boxing (i % 128).toLong()") { for (i in 0 until 1_000) sink = (i % 128).toLong() } show("1,000 x boxing (1_000 + i).toLong()") { for (i in 0 until 1_000) sink = (1_000 + i).toLong() } show("1,000 x \"img-\$i\"") { for (i in 0 until 1_000) sink = "img-$i" } Thread.ofVirtual().start { println("on a virtual thread the counter says ${THREADS.currentThreadAllocatedBytes}") }.join() } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l02.AllocationCounterDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l02/AllocationCounterDemo.kt On JDK 25, the 1 MiB array costs 1,048,592 bytes both times (the Kotlin twin's first run adds 40 bytes of one-time setup). Long.valueOf(i % 128) costs 7,456 bytes the first time, to build the box cache, and 0 after, because every value comes from the cache. Long.valueOf(1_000 + i) costs 24,000 both times. The string concatenation costs about 100,000 bytes the first time and 48,000 after: 48 bytes per name. On the virtual thread the counter says -1. com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean (JDK 25 API) docs

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · The box that never leaves the desk: escape analysis
x: C2 is the JIT compiler that optimizes a program's hottest methods, and it pays close attention. First it does inlining: it copies the small methods a method calls into the method's own body. Then it runs escape analysis, which checks whether an object can be seen anywhere outside the method it's compiling. If it can't, C2 can skip the object and keep its fields in registers, the processor's own small storage slots. That step is called scalar replacement. In the warehouse, it's a worker noticing that a box never leaves the desk, and writing its contents on the notepad instead. Here's a loop that makes a million short-lived points: Java record Point(long x, long y) {} static long sumPoints(int n) { long s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { Point p = new Point(i, i + 1); // p never leaves the method s += p.x() + p.y(); } return s; } Kotlin data class Point(val x: Long, val y: Long) fun sumPoints(n: Int): Long { var s = 0L for (i in 0 until n) { val p = Point(i.toLong(), i + 1L) // p never leaves the function s += p.x + p.y } return s } A Point is a 12-byte header plus two longs, 28 bytes, padded to 32. So a call with n = 1,000,000 should allocate 32,000,000 bytes. Call it ten times and count each call on JDK 25: round 0: 3,282,776 bytes round 1: 1,572,832 bytes round 2: 262,112 bytes round 3: 0 bytes ... round 9: 0 bytes Same code, same new, zero bytes. With -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis, which switches the analysis off, every round allocated 32,000,000 bytes: a million 32-byte points. Now look at the first rounds. The interpreter (which runs bytecode one instruction at a time) and C1 (the quick JIT compiler that runs first) create every object. The allocation only disappears once C2 has compiled the method, and when that happens depends on timing: one run of the Kotlin twin on JDK 21 reached 0 only at round 5. Here the warehouse picture breaks again. A person would notice the first time that a box never leaves the desk. C2 notices only after it has watched a method run thousands of times, and only inside the code it inlined. Escape analysis is a bonus, not a promise. Never assert "allocates nothing" in a unit test. It can pass on your laptop and fail on a busier machine. The lab asserts only the allocations the code really needs. An object escapes when you store it in a field, an array or a collection, return it, or pass it to a method C2 didn't inline. C2 also won't scalar-replace an array with more than 64 elements (the EliminateAllocationArraySizeLimit flag). So escape analysis helps tight loops. It can't help a design that keeps every size in a HashMap<Integer, Long>, because those boxes live on inside the map. And that's where most of a program's bytes come from. Watch an allocation disappear, then bring it back Run EscapeDemo. It runs the measurement in two child JVMs: one with default flags, one with -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis. Now make p escape. In the Java version add static Point last; to the class and last = p; inside the loop. In Kotlin add a top-level var last: KPoint? = null and last = p. Predict the new numbers, then run it again. Remove the change when you're done. EscapeDemo.java package workbench.memory.l02; import com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.util.List; /** * Sums a million short-lived Points per round and counts the bytes each round allocates. * The demo runs the experiment twice, in child JVMs: with escape analysis, and without it. */ public class EscapeDemo { record Point(long x, long y) {} // 12-byte header + 16 bytes of fields: 32 bytes static long sumPoints(int n) { long s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { Point p = new Point(i, i + 1); // p never leaves this method s += p.x() + p.y(); } return s; } public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length == 0) { System.out.println("== default flags: escape analysis on"); Jvm.run(List.of(), EscapeDemo.class.getName(), "measure"); System.out.println("== -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis"); Jvm.run(List.of("-XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis"), EscapeDemo.class.getName(), "measure"); return; } ThreadMXBean threads = (ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); long checksum = 0; for (int round = 0; round < 10; round++) { long before = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes(); checksum += sumPoints(1_000_000); long bytes = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before; System.out.printf("round %d: %,12d bytes%n", round, bytes); } System.out.println("checksum " + checksum); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l02.EscapeDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l02/EscapeDemo.java EscapeDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l02 import com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean import workbench.memory.Jvm import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory data class KPoint(val x: Long, val y: Long) // 12-byte header + 16 bytes of fields: 32 bytes fun sumPoints(n: Int): Long { var s = 0L for (i in 0 until n) { val p = KPoint(i.toLong(), i + 1L) // p never leaves this function s += p.x + p.y } return s } /** * Sums a million short-lived points per round and counts the bytes each round allocates. * The demo runs the experiment twice, in child JVMs: with escape analysis, and without it. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isEmpty()) { println("== default flags: escape analysis on") Jvm.run(listOf(), "workbench.memory.l02.EscapeDemoKt", "measure") println("== -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis") Jvm.run(listOf("-XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis"), "workbench.memory.l02.EscapeDemoKt", "measure") return } val threads = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as ThreadMXBean var checksum = 0L for (round in 0 until 10) { val before = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes checksum += sumPoints(1_000_000) val bytes = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before println("round %d: %,12d bytes".format(round, bytes)) } println("checksum $checksum") } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l02.EscapeDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l02/EscapeDemo.kt With default flags, the first few rounds allocate megabytes, then the count drops to 0 and stays there (from round 3 in the JDK 25 run behind this lesson). With -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis, every round allocates 32,000,000 bytes. After you add last = p, the default run also allocates 32,000,000 bytes in every round, because the point now escapes into a static field and C2 has to create it.

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · Where the bytes really come from: boxing, strings and copies
x: Most of the allocation in a program doesn't come from the new statements you wrote. It hides in boxing (wrapping a primitive such as a long in an object such as java.lang.Long), in collection helpers and in strings. The lab's upload report is a typical case. It adds up the bytes each user uploaded today: Java Map<Integer, Long> totals = new HashMap<>(); for (int i = 0; i < userIds.length; i++) { totals.merge(userIds[i], sizes[i], Long::sum); // boxes the key, the size and the sum } Kotlin val totals = HashMap<Int, Long>() for (i in userIds.indices) { totals.merge(userIds[i], sizes[i]) { a, b -> a + b } // the same three boxes } For 20,000 uploads from 500 users, this allocates 1,539,040 bytes, about 77 bytes per upload. User ids above 127 become new Integer boxes, and every size and every running sum becomes a new 24-byte Long. The caller only needs one total per user: a long[500] of 4,016 bytes. Index the array by user id and you get the same answer with no garbage at all. These are the usual suspects: Boxed collections: List<Long>, Map<String, Integer>, and in Kotlin anything typed Long? or used as a type argument. Helpers that copy: toList(), map {}, windowed, zip, and streams of boxed values. Strings: each "img-" + i costs 48 bytes (a String and its array). String.format, the most expensive way to glue three values together, cost about 700 bytes per call in the worked example below. Lambdas that capture local variables, which create a new object each time the expression runs. Don't chase every allocation, though. A request that allocates 50 KB is fine. Fix the loops over large batches, and the code behind a young GC that runs several times a second. Measure, change one thing, and measure again. A check before the lab. In Kotlin, sizes.map { it * 2 }.sum(), or in Java, sizes.stream().map(s -> s * 2).toList(), on a List<Long> of 10,000 sizes above 1,000 bytes. Count the objects each one creates and estimate the bytes. (About 10,000 new 24-byte Long boxes and a 40 KB array for the new list, so roughly 280 KB. The same loop over a LongArray creates nothing.) The lab hands you the upload report's two methods. Both give the right answer, and both are wasteful. Your job is to make them allocate only their result.

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · Java and Kotlin
x: A file-size type with and without an object FileSize.java // Java: a record is always an object (escape analysis may remove short-lived ones) record FileSize(long bytes) { FileSize plus(FileSize other) { return new FileSize(bytes + other.bytes); } // a new 24-byte object } FileSize total = new FileSize(0); for (long s : sizes) total = total.plus(new FileSize(s)); FileSize.kt // Kotlin: a value class is a plain long at runtime, unless it has to be boxed @JvmInline value class FileSize(val bytes: Long) { operator fun plus(other: FileSize) = FileSize(bytes + other.bytes) // compiles to long + long } var total = FileSize(0) for (s in sizes) total += FileSize(s) // no objects The Kotlin value class compiles to a raw long in fields, parameters and return types, so the loop allocates nothing, even in the interpreter. The Java record is a real object every time. C2 may scalar-replace the short-lived ones in a hot loop, but you can't count on it. The Kotlin version boxes as soon as the value is used as a type argument, a nullable type or Any: a List<FileSize> or a FileSize? holds boxed objects again, just as List<Long> does.

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · Worked example
x: Take the allocation out of a cache lookup The thumbnail service keeps finished thumbnails in a map, so a second request for the same photo at the same size is served from memory. The first version builds each lookup key with String.format. Measured with the allocation counter over 10,000 lookups in Java on JDK 25, it allocated about 712 bytes per lookup at first, and still 632 to 656 once the code was hot. // Naive: a varargs array, a Formatter, its buffers and the string, per lookup byte[] find(String name, int width, int height) { return cache.get(String.format("%s@%dx%d", name, width, height)); } // Naive: a varargs array, a Formatter, its buffers and the string, per lookup fun find(name: String, width: Int, height: Int): ByteArray? = cache["%s@%dx%d".format(name, width, height)] Build the same string with plain concatenation. The Java version allocated 64 bytes per lookup: a 24-byte String and a 40-byte array for the 19 letters of photo-0.jpg@160x120. Once the code was hot, 40 bytes. byte[] find(String name, int width, int height) { return cache.get(name + "@" + width + "x" + height); } fun find(name: String, width: Int, height: Int): ByteArray? = cache["$name@${width}x$height"] Drop the string. A record key holds the three values as they are, and its equals and hashCode come for free. It's a 12-byte header, one reference and two ints: 24 bytes per lookup. And once C2 had compiled the lookup, the counter read 0, because the key never escapes find, so C2 scalar-replaced it. With -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis it stayed at 24. record ThumbKey(String name, int width, int height) {} final Map<ThumbKey, byte[]> cache = new HashMap<>(); byte[] find(String name, int width, int height) { return cache.get(new ThumbKey(name, width, height)); } data class ThumbKey(val name: String, val width: Int, val height: Int) val cache = HashMap<ThumbKey, ByteArray>() fun find(name: String, width: Int, height: Int): ByteArray? = cache[ThumbKey(name, width, height)] Check that nothing changed but the bytes. In the run behind these numbers, all three versions found all 100 cached thumbnails, and the formatted key equals the concatenated one. Then put the saving in context: at, say, 2,000 lookups a second, the first version makes 1.4 MB of garbage a second and the record at most 48 KB. That's worth a change on a path that runs for every request, and not worth one on a path that runs once a minute.

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · Quiz
x: A test warms up parseSize three times, then asserts that it allocates 0 bytes. It passes on your laptop and fails on the build server. What's the most likely reason? The build server has smaller TLABs The zero depends on C2 having compiled the method with escape analysis, which depends on timing The allocation counter is less accurate on Linux The build server runs the tests on virtual threads The interpreter and C1 create every object. The allocation only disappears once C2 compiles the method, three calls rarely get it there, and when it happens depends on the machine and on what else is running. TLAB size doesn't change how many bytes are allocated. A virtual thread would make the counter return -1, not a small positive number. A service runs G1 with 2 MB regions. Which allocation does NOT happen in a TLAB? new Thumbnail() new byte[1_024] new byte[1_500_000] for an uploaded photo Long.valueOf(1_000_000) In G1, an object bigger than half a region is humongous and never goes in a TLAB: 1.5 MB is more than half of 2 MB. The other three are small and take the bump-pointer fast path. The boxed Long is outside the cache range, so it's a fresh 24-byte object, but still a TLAB allocation. Which of these loops keeps allocating once C2 has compiled it? results.add(new Point(i, i + 1)); Point p = new Point(i, i + 1); sum += p.x(); totals[userIds[i]] += sizes[i]; sum += sizes[i] / 1_024; Adding the point to a list makes it escape: it outlives the loop, so it has to exist on the heap. The local point that only feeds a sum can be scalar-replaced. The last two never create objects at all. In Kotlin, which of these holds 10,000 file sizes without one box per size? List<Long> Array<Long> MutableList<Long?> LongArray LongArray compiles to a JVM long[], with the values stored inline. List<Long>, Array<Long> (a Long[]) and any list of Long? hold references to java.lang.Long boxes, 24 bytes each for values outside the -128 to 127 cache. From the previous lesson: with default settings, how many bytes do 1,000 calls of Long.valueOf(1_000 + i) allocate? 0, because of the Long cache 8,000 16,000 24,000 Values from 1,000 up are outside the -128 to 127 cache, so each call creates a new Long. A Long is a 12-byte header plus 8 bytes of value, rounded up to 24. The allocation counter reports exactly 24,000. 8,000 counts only the values, and 16,000 is what compact object headers would give.

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · Explain it back
x: A colleague says: "Allocation is free on the JVM, so I never think about it." Explain in your own words what is true in that, and what is missing.

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · Key terms
x: Eden The part of the heap where new objects are created. TLAB A chunk of eden that one thread allocates into without locking. Bump-pointer allocation Allocating by moving a 'top' pointer forward by the object's size. Allocation rate Bytes allocated per second. It decides how often young collections run. Escape analysis C2's check for whether an object can be seen outside the method being compiled. Scalar replacement Keeping a non-escaping object's fields in registers instead of creating the object. Boxing Wrapping a primitive in an object, such as a long in a java.lang.Long. What is a TLAB? A thread-local allocation buffer: a chunk of eden owned by one thread. Allocating inside it is a pointer bump with no locking. What happens when an object doesn't fit in the current TLAB? The slow path: the thread claims a fresh TLAB from eden (one atomic update), or a large object goes straight into eden. Which G1 objects never go into a TLAB? Humongous objects: anything bigger than half a region. How do you count the bytes a block of code allocates? Read com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() before and after, on a platform thread. Measure twice to skip one-time setup. What does getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() return on a virtual thread? -1. Measure on a platform thread. What is scalar replacement? C2 replaces an object that never escapes the compiled method with its fields in registers, so the allocation never happens. Why must a unit test never assert that code allocates 0 bytes? The interpreter and C1 create every object. The zero only appears after C2 compiles the method, which depends on timing.

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · Go deeper
x: The TLAB trace has more in it than the summary the demo prints. With -Xlog:gc+tlab=trace, each refill prints a line like this one from JDK 25: TLAB: fill thread: 0x00007f96ec01a030 [id: 20675] desired_size: 512KB slow allocs: 0 refill waste: 8192B alloc: 0.92801 20906KB refills: 44 waste 0.1% gc: 0B slow: 26144B desired_size is the TLAB size the JVM aims for with this thread. It adapts to how fast the thread allocates and how many threads share eden. refill waste is the most free space the JVM is willing to throw away to start a new TLAB. When an object doesn't fit and less than that is left, the thread abandons the rest of its TLAB and claims a new one. When more is left, the thread keeps its TLAB, puts that one object directly in eden, and counts a slow allocation. The abandoned tail of a TLAB is filled with a dummy object so the heap stays easy to walk, and the waste percentage counts those tails. Escape analysis helps with locks too. If an object never escapes, no other thread can ever lock it, so C2 can drop the synchronized blocks on it (the EliminateLocks flag). A local StringBuffer, whose methods are all synchronized, is the classic example. Finally, the counter you used is per thread. getThreadAllocatedBytes(long[] ids) reads it for other threads too. For a whole program, JFR records allocation samples with stack traces, so it can show which code allocates the most. The per-second rate from JFR or the GC log tells you whether allocation is a problem at all; the per-block counter then tells you where the bytes come from.

h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Following the notes: GC roots and the reachability ladder
x: The GC keeps what the roots can reach: strong, soft, weak and phantom holds, and why weak and soft caches forget The garbage collector doesn't free the objects you stopped using. It frees the objects nothing can reach. It starts from the GC roots, the places where a running program holds references directly, not inside another object. The roots are the local variables on every live thread's stack (the desks) and the static fields (the noticeboard by the door). References held by native code (code written in a language such as C, which Java calls through JNI, the Java Native Interface) count as roots too. From the roots the collector follows every reference, and keeps whatever it finds. Everything else is garbage. That rule ignores how many references point at an object. A box that nobody's note leads to is garbage, even if a hundred other forgotten boxes point at it. The package java.lang.ref lets you point at an object without holding it as tightly as an ordinary reference does. A reference object, such as a SoftReference, points at another object, called its referent, and get() returns the referent while it's still there. The package's documentation defines a ladder, from the firmest hold to none: An object is strongly reachable if a chain of ordinary references leads to it. The GC leaves it alone. It is softly reachable if the only way to it goes through a SoftReference: "keep it if there's room". The GC may clear that reference when memory gets tight. It is weakly reachable if the only way goes through a WeakReference: "keep it only while someone else holds it". The next collection that finds it clears the reference. It is phantom reachable if only a PhantomReference is left. Its get() always returns null; it only tells you, afterwards, that the object is gone. Otherwise it's unreachable, and its memory can be reused. Each reference object can carry a ReferenceQueue, a tray where the collector drops the slip. "Some time after" the GC sees the object drop to that rung, it clears the reference and puts it on the queue. That's the specification's own wording, and it promises no deadline: Java ReferenceQueue<byte[]> queue = new ReferenceQueue<>(); WeakReference<byte[]> weak = new WeakReference<>(new byte[1_000], queue); System.gc(); // a request, fine in a demo Reference<?> gone = queue.remove(500); // the same weak reference, once the GC cleared it Kotlin val queue = ReferenceQueue<ByteArray>() val weak = WeakReference(ByteArray(1_000), queue) System.gc() // a request, fine in a demo val gone = queue.remove(500) // the same weak reference, once the GC cleared it Here the warehouse picture breaks, and the break matters for everything in this lesson. A real cleaning crew comes on a schedule. The JVM's crew comes when the heap needs room: many times a second on a busy service, and perhaps not for an hour on a quiet one. Nothing on the ladder says when. The GC frees what the roots can't reach, at a time it chooses. Never plan around that time. That missing "when" is the whole story of the first rung below strong. Climb down the ladder Read ReferenceLadderDemo (or the Kotlin twin). It makes four 1,000-byte arrays: one held strongly, one softly, one weakly and one through a phantom reference. Predict which survive a System.gc(), and which references land on the queue. Run it with the command below. ReferenceLadderDemo.java package workbench.memory.l03; import java.lang.ref.PhantomReference; import java.lang.ref.Reference; import java.lang.ref.ReferenceQueue; import java.lang.ref.SoftReference; import java.lang.ref.WeakReference; /** One object on each rung of the reachability ladder, before and after a GC. */ public class ReferenceLadderDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { ReferenceQueue<byte[]> queue = new ReferenceQueue<>(); byte[] strong = new byte[1_000]; // a plain local: strongly reachable SoftReference<byte[]> soft = new SoftReference<>(new byte[1_000], queue); WeakReference<byte[]> weak = new WeakReference<>(new byte[1_000], queue); PhantomReference<byte[]> phantom = new PhantomReference<>(new byte[1_000], queue); System.out.printf("before GC: soft %s, weak %s, phantom.get() %s%n", soft.get() != null, weak.get() != null, phantom.get()); System.gc(); // a request; fine in a demo, never a guarantee System.out.printf("after GC: soft %s, weak %s, phantom.get() %s%n", soft.get() != null, weak.get() != null, phantom.get()); for (Reference<?> r; (r = queue.remove(500)) != null; ) { System.out.println("enqueued: " + r.getClass().getSimpleName()); } Reference.reachabilityFence(strong); // keep `strong` alive until here System.out.println("strong array still here: " + strong.length + " bytes"); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l03.ReferenceLadderDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l03/ReferenceLadderDemo.java ReferenceLadderDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l03 import java.lang.ref.PhantomReference import java.lang.ref.Reference import java.lang.ref.ReferenceQueue import java.lang.ref.SoftReference import java.lang.ref.WeakReference /** One object on each rung of the reachability ladder, before and after a GC. */ fun main() { val queue = ReferenceQueue<ByteArray>() val strong = ByteArray(1_000) // a plain local: strongly reachable val soft = SoftReference(ByteArray(1_000), queue) val weak = WeakReference(ByteArray(1_000), queue) val phantom = PhantomReference(ByteArray(1_000), queue) println("before GC: soft ${soft.get() != null}, weak ${weak.get() != null}, phantom.get() ${phantom.get()}") System.gc() // a request; fine in a demo, never a guarantee println("after GC: soft ${soft.get() != null}, weak ${weak.get() != null}, phantom.get() ${phantom.get()}") while (true) { val r = queue.remove(500) ?: break println("enqueued: ${r.javaClass.simpleName}") } Reference.reachabilityFence(strong) // keep `strong` alive until here println("strong array still here: ${strong.size} bytes") } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l03.ReferenceLadderDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l03/ReferenceLadderDemo.kt Before the GC: soft true, weak true, and phantom.get() is null (it always is). After it: soft is still true, because memory isn't tight, and weak is false. The queue receives the WeakReference and the PhantomReference. The strong array is untouched. Each kind of reference is a weaker rung on the ladder: the GC clears soft ones under memory pressure, weak ones at the next collection that finds them, and phantom ones only report that the object is gone. java.lang.ref package docs at jdk-25-ga: the reachability definitions docs

h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Keep it if there's room: soft references and memory pressure
x: SoftReference sounds made for caches, and its Javadoc says so: "Soft references are most often used to implement memory-sensitive caches." The contract is thinner than it sounds. The JVM guarantees one thing: every soft reference to a softly reachable object is cleared before it throws an OutOfMemoryError, the error that means the heap has no room left. Otherwise, in the Javadoc's words, "no constraints are placed upon the time" of clearing. HotSpot ties it to a flag, -XX:SoftRefLRUPolicyMSPerMB (default 1000), described as the "number of milliseconds per MB of free space in the heap" that an unused soft referent may live. So let's squeeze one. The thumbnail service decodes photos before it shrinks them, and a decoded photo is big. Here a 64 MB heap keeps one 40 MB decoded photo behind a soft reference, and then the service decodes a second one of the same size. This is the GC log on JDK 25, cut to the lines that matter: beach photo cached: true GC(5) Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 42M->42M(64M) 5.464ms GC(6) Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 42M->1M(64M) 5.325ms after decoding a 40 MB dog photo: beach photo cached: false G1, the JVM's default collector, ran a full GC, a collection of the whole heap with every thread stopped, and it kept the soft referent. There was still no room, so G1 ran a second full GC that cleared the soft reference, and the new photo fit. The cached photo is gone, and the next request for it has to decode it again. That's the trouble with soft caches in a service. A soft cache keeps your things right up to the moment you need them most. It empties in bulk, when the heap is nearly full and the collector is already running full GCs. Then every request that misses the cache rebuilds its entry at the same moment, on a machine that is slow for the same reason. And a heap full of soft references always looks full, so you can't size it by watching it. Use a cache with an explicit size limit and an expiry time instead, and size the heap to hold it. Lesson 7 builds one. I'd keep soft references for data that is truly optional and cheap to rebuild, and decoded photos are neither. Soft references hold on too long and let go all at once. Weak references have the opposite problem, and one job they do perfectly. Squeeze a soft cache Read SoftCacheDemo. It starts a child JVM with -Xmx64m -Xlog:gc, keeps a 40 MB decoded photo behind a soft reference, then decodes a second 40 MB photo. Predict: does the second allocation fail? Run it and read the GC lines between the two printouts. SoftCacheDemo.java package workbench.memory.l03; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.lang.ref.SoftReference; import java.util.List; /** A 40 MB decoded photo behind a soft reference in a 64 MB heap, then another 40 MB allocation. Runs in a child JVM. */ public class SoftCacheDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length == 0) { Jvm.run(List.of("-Xmx64m", "-Xlog:gc"), SoftCacheDemo.class.getName(), "run"); return; } SoftReference<byte[]> beach = new SoftReference<>(new byte[40 << 20]); // a decoded photo, kept "if there's room" System.out.println("beach photo cached: " + (beach.get() != null)); byte[] dog = new byte[40 << 20]; // only fits if the GC clears the soft reference System.out.println("after decoding a 40 MB dog photo: beach photo cached: " + (beach.get() != null) + ", dog " + dog.length + " bytes"); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l03.SoftCacheDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l03/SoftCacheDemo.java SoftCacheDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l03 import workbench.memory.Jvm import java.lang.ref.SoftReference /** A 40 MB decoded photo behind a soft reference in a 64 MB heap, then another 40 MB allocation. Runs in a child JVM. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isEmpty()) { Jvm.run(listOf("-Xmx64m", "-Xlog:gc"), "workbench.memory.l03.SoftCacheDemoKt", "run") return } val beach = SoftReference(ByteArray(40 shl 20)) // a decoded photo, kept "if there's room" println("beach photo cached: ${beach.get() != null}") val dog = ByteArray(40 shl 20) // only fits if the GC clears the soft reference println("after decoding a 40 MB dog photo: beach photo cached: ${beach.get() != null}, dog ${dog.size} bytes") } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l03.SoftCacheDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l03/SoftCacheDemo.kt No OutOfMemoryError. Between the two printouts, on JDK 25, you'll see Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 42M->42M(64M), which kept the soft referent, then a second Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 42M->1M(64M), which cleared it. The last line says the beach photo is no longer cached. Two full GCs to empty one cache is the cost a soft cache hides. SoftReference source at jdk-25-ga: the clearing contract docs

h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Keep it while someone else holds it: weak references and WeakHashMap
x: A weak reference holds nothing up. Once only weak references lead to an object, the next GC that finds it clears all of them at once. In the research behind this course, a short loop of GC requests cleared a weak reference on every run, under every collector it tried. That makes weak references wrong for caches: a weakly held value lasts until the next GC, which on a busy service is milliseconds away. It makes them right for one job: attaching data to an object whose lifetime someone else controls, without making that object live any longer. WeakHashMap is that idea as a map. Its keys are weak and its values are strong. When a key becomes unreachable, its entry disappears the next time you call size(), get() or put(). Here the service keeps a small preview record for each photo it knows about: Java Map<Photo, Preview> previews = new WeakHashMap<>(); previews.put(beach, new Preview(160)); beach = null; // the photo is deleted; after a GC, previews.size() is 0 Kotlin val previews = WeakHashMap<Photo, Preview>() previews[beach] = Preview(160) // once the photo is unreachable, the entry goes after the next GC There's one trap, and the WeakHashMap Javadoc warns about it: a value must not refer to its own key. Suppose the map holds a Thumbnail value that keeps a reference to its source Photo. The map's strong value now holds the weak key strongly, so the key never becomes weakly reachable, and the entry never goes away. The demo below fills two maps and shows one emptying and the other stuck. The same idea gives you a listener registry that doesn't leak. The thumbnail service lets plugins, such as a watermarker or a statistics counter, register to hear about each finished thumbnail. A registry that keeps its listeners in a plain list keeps every plugin alive, plus everything each plugin refers to, until someone remembers to unregister it. Hold them through WeakReference instead, and a plugin whose owner is gone simply disappears from the list. The catch is the mirror image. A lambda registered inline, with no other reference to it anywhere, disappears too, at the next GC. It was a very short registration. Whoever owns a listener must keep a reference to it. The lab builds this registry. The last rung, phantom, holds nothing at all. Its only job is to say when an object is gone, so that something outside the heap can be cleaned up. Watch a WeakHashMap empty, and one that doesn't Read WeakHashMapDemo. Both maps get one entry, and both photos are dropped. Only the Thumbnail value refers back to its key. Predict both sizes, then run it. = KPhoto("beach.jpg") var dog: KPhoto? = KPhoto("dog.jpg") previews[beach!!] = KPreview(160) thumbnails[dog!!] = KThumbnail(dog, 160) beach = null // the photos are deleted: nothing else refers to them dog = null repeat(5) { System.gc(); Thread.sleep(20) } // demo only: ask for a few GCs println("previews left: ${previews.size}") // size also removes cleared entries println("thumbnails left: ${thumbnails.size}") } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l03.WeakHashMapDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l03/WeakHashMapDemo.kt previews left: 0 and thumbnails left: 1. The thumbnail holds its Photo strongly, so the weak key never becomes weakly reachable. That entry will stay for as long as the map does.

h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Tell me after it's gone: Cleaner, phantom references and the end of finalize
x: Some objects own something the GC can't see. The service's image decoder, a native library written in C, hands out buffers of native memory, outside the heap, and each one must be given back exactly once. When the Java object that owns a buffer becomes garbage, the GC frees the object. The native memory stays taken, unless some code runs to free it. finalize() was the first way to run code when an object died. Java 9 deprecated it, and since JDK 18 it has been deprecated for removal (JEP 421, the JDK Enhancement Proposal behind that step). A finalizer can bring its own object back to life. Finalizers run on one JVM thread, in no set order and at no set time. And an object with a finalizer needs at least two collections before its memory is freed. You can check whether your program still depends on one: start it with --finalization=disabled (JDK 18 and later), and no finalizer runs. In the demo on JDK 25, 1,000 objects with a finalizer ran 1,000 finalizers by default and 0 with the flag. The replacement is java.lang.ref.Cleaner, built on phantom references. You register an object with a cleaning action. When the object becomes phantom reachable, the cleaner's thread runs the action. That thread is patient and literal: it runs the action when the slip arrives, and not a moment before. register returns a Cleanable, and its clean() runs the action at most once and unregisters it: Java public final class NativeBuffer implements AutoCloseable { private static final Cleaner CLEANER = Cleaner.create(); // one thread for all buffers private final Cleaner.Cleanable cleanable; public NativeBuffer(NativeMemory memory, int bytes) { long handle = memory.allocate(bytes); cleanable = CLEANER.register(this, new Release(memory, handle)); } private record Release(NativeMemory memory, long handle) implements Runnable { public void run() { memory.free(handle); } // no reference to the buffer } @Override public void close() { cleanable.clean(); } // the normal path, safe to call twice } Kotlin class NativeBuffer(memory: NativeMemory, bytes: Int) : AutoCloseable { private val cleanable: Cleaner.Cleanable init { val handle = memory.allocate(bytes) cleanable = CLEANER.register(this, Release(memory, handle)) } // a nested class has no reference to the outer object; only an `inner` class does private class Release(val memory: NativeMemory, val handle: Long) : Runnable { override fun run() = memory.free(handle) } override fun close() = cleanable.clean() // the normal path, safe to call twice companion object { private val CLEANER: Cleaner = Cleaner.create() } } Read the constructor in order. It takes a handle from the native library, then registers this with the cleaner, together with a small Release object that holds only the library and the handle. close() doesn't free anything itself. It asks the Cleanable to run Release now, and a second close() finds nothing left to run. The cleaning action must not refer to the object it cleans. If it does, the object never becomes phantom reachable, and the action never runs. A lambda that reads a field captures this: in () -> memory.free(handle), handle means this.handle. A non-static inner class in Java captures this too. The Cleaner Javadoc warns about both. And the cleaner is only a safety net. It runs some time after a GC, and maybe not at all before the JVM exits. Release resources with try-with-resources (use {} in Kotlin), and let the cleaner catch the ones somebody forgot. The lab hands you a NativeBuffer that breaks the rule in bold, and a registry that holds on too tightly. Switch finalization off Read FinalizerDemo. It creates 1,000 objects whose class overrides finalize(), asks for 20 GCs, and counts the finalizer calls, once with default flags and once with --finalization=disabled. Run it. Then think of one library your own code uses that might still have a finalizer, and how you'd test without it. FinalizerDemo.java package workbench.memory.l03; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 1,000 objects with a finalize() method, in two child JVMs: default, and --finalization=disabled. */ public class FinalizerDemo { static final AtomicInteger finalized = new AtomicInteger(); static class LegacyHandle { @Override @SuppressWarnings({"removal", "deprecation"}) protected void finalize() { // deprecated for removal since JDK 18 finalized.incrementAndGet(); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { if (args.length == 0) { System.out.println("== default flags"); Jvm.run(List.of(), FinalizerDemo.class.getName(), "run"); System.out.println("== --finalization=disabled"); Jvm.run(List.of("--finalization=disabled"), FinalizerDemo.class.getName(), "run"); return; } for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) new LegacyHandle(); for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) { System.gc(); Thread.sleep(20); } System.out.println("finalized " + finalized.get() + " of 1000"); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l03.FinalizerDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l03/FinalizerDemo.java FinalizerDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l03 import workbench.memory.Jvm import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger private val finalizedCount = AtomicInteger() class KLegacyHandle { // Kotlin has no override for finalize(): you declare it, and the JVM calls it protected fun finalize() { finalizedCount.incrementAndGet() } } /** 1,000 objects with a finalize() method, in two child JVMs: default, and --finalization=disabled. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isEmpty()) { println("== default flags") Jvm.run(listOf(), "workbench.memory.l03.FinalizerDemoKt", "run") println("== --finalization=disabled") Jvm.run(listOf("--finalization=disabled"), "workbench.memory.l03.FinalizerDemoKt", "run") return } repeat(1_000) { KLegacyHandle() } repeat(20) { System.gc(); Thread.sleep(20) } println("finalized ${finalizedCount.get()} of 1000") } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l03.FinalizerDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l03/FinalizerDemo.kt finalized 1000 of 1000 with default flags and finalized 0 of 1000 with --finalization=disabled. The objects were still collected in the second run; only the finalizers were skipped. Running a test suite with that flag shows whether anything depends on them. Cleaner source at jdk-25-ga: the rules for cleaning actions docs JEP 421: Deprecate Finalization for Removal read

h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Java and Kotlin
x: Who holds a reference to the outer object ThumbnailWriter.java class ThumbnailWriter { private final Path tempFile; // inner (the default in Java): holds ThumbnailWriter.this class Cleanup implements Runnable { public void run() { deleteQuietly(tempFile); } } // static nested: holds only what you pass in static class SafeCleanup implements Runnable { private final Path file; SafeCleanup(Path file) { this.file = file; } public void run() { deleteQuietly(file); } } } ThumbnailWriter.kt class ThumbnailWriter(private val tempFile: Path) { // inner (you must ask for it in Kotlin): holds this@ThumbnailWriter inner class Cleanup : Runnable { override fun run() = deleteQuietly(tempFile) } // nested (the default in Kotlin): holds only what you pass in class SafeCleanup(private val file: Path) : Runnable { override fun run() = deleteQuietly(file) } } The defaults are opposite. A class declared inside a class is inner in Java unless you write static, and nested in Kotlin unless you write inner. So a Java cleaning action written as a plain inner class silently holds the object it should clean, while the same code in Kotlin doesn't. Lambdas behave the same in both: one that reads a property or a field captures this. Kotlin also has no override for finalize(): to write one you declare protected fun finalize(), which is one more reason not to.

h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Worked example
x: Find why a WeakHashMap keeps growing The service shows a progress bar for every upload. It keeps the progress in a WeakHashMap keyed by the upload, so finished uploads drop out by themselves once nothing else refers to them. Each entry also holds a callback that tells the photo's owner when the upload is done. The map grows all day and never shrinks. Read the code and look for a strong path back to the key. record UploadProgress(AtomicLong bytesReceived, Runnable onDone) {} static final Map<Upload, UploadProgress> PROGRESS = new WeakHashMap<>(); static void track(Upload upload) { PROGRESS.put(upload, new UploadProgress(new AtomicLong(), () -> notifyOwner(upload.owner()))); } data class UploadProgress(val bytesReceived: AtomicLong, val onDone: () -> Unit) val PROGRESS: MutableMap<Upload, UploadProgress> = WeakHashMap() fun track(upload: Upload) { PROGRESS[upload] = UploadProgress(AtomicLong()) { notifyOwner(upload.owner) } } Follow the references from a GC root. The static field holds the map, the map holds its entries, and each entry holds its value strongly. The value holds the callback, and the callback is a lambda that captured upload, because it calls upload.owner() later. So every finished upload is still strongly reachable from PROGRESS, through its own progress record, and its weak key is never cleared. static PROGRESS -> WeakHashMap -> Entry (weak key, STRONG value) -> UploadProgress -> onDone lambda -> upload <- the key itself Break the strong path. The callback only needs the owner's name, so read it once, before building the lambda, and capture that instead of the upload. static void track(Upload upload) { String owner = upload.owner(); // capture the name, not the upload PROGRESS.put(upload, new UploadProgress(new AtomicLong(), () -> notifyOwner(owner))); } fun track(upload: Upload) { val owner = upload.owner // capture the name, not the upload PROGRESS[upload] = UploadProgress(AtomicLong()) { notifyOwner(owner) } } Prove it with a test that doesn't trust timing. Drop the upload, keep a weak probe on it with its own queue, ask for GCs until the probe arrives (with a limit), then check the map. size() removes cleared entries before it counts. Upload u = newTestUpload(); track(u); ReferenceQueue<Object> q = new ReferenceQueue<>(); WeakReference<Object> probe = new WeakReference<>(u, q); u = null; Reference<?> seen = null; for (int i = 0; i < 50 && seen == null; i++) { System.gc(); seen = q.remove(50); } // bounded wait assertThat(seen).isSameAs(probe); assertThat(PROGRESS).isEmpty(); var u: Upload? = newTestUpload() track(u!!) val q = ReferenceQueue<Any>() val probe = WeakReference<Any>(u, q) u = null var seen: Reference<*>? = null for (i in 0 until 50) { System.gc(); seen = q.remove(50); if (seen != null) break } // bounded wait assertThat(seen).isSameAs(probe) assertThat(PROGRESS).isEmpty()

h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Quiz
x: A WeakHashMap<Album, AlbumView> keeps growing even after albums are deleted everywhere else. AlbumView has a field Album album used for logging. What is the cause? WeakHashMap only removes entries after System.gc() Each value strongly refers to its own key, so the keys never become weakly reachable Album doesn't override equals and hashCode The map needs a ReferenceQueue to remove entries Values in a WeakHashMap are strong. A value that points back to its key gives the key a strong path from the map itself, so the GC never clears it. Normal GCs clear weak keys without any System.gc(), and the map already manages its own internal queue: size(), get() and put() remove stale entries. You need a cache of watermark pictures that the service reloads from disk on a miss. Which choice fits best? Map<String, WeakReference<Picture>> Map<String, SoftReference<Picture>> A cache with a maximum size and an expiry time, and a heap sized for it Map<String, PhantomReference<Picture>> A bounded cache keeps exactly as much as you decided, and expiry keeps its contents fresh. Weak values are gone at the next GC, so the hit rate collapses. Soft values stay until the heap is nearly full and then go in bulk during full GCs, sending all the reloads at once. A phantom reference can't even return its value. A class registers CLEANER.register(this, () -> codec.release(nativeHandle)), where codec and nativeHandle are fields. One code path forgets to call close(). What happens to the native memory? The cleaner frees it at the next GC The cleaner frees it when the JVM exits It is never freed, because the lambda captures this and the object never becomes phantom reachable The JVM throws an exception when the object is collected Reading codec and nativeHandle inside the lambda means this.codec and this.nativeHandle, so the lambda holds this. The cleaner holds the lambda, so the object stays strongly reachable forever: a leak of both the object and its native memory. The Javadoc also makes no promise that cleaners run at exit. A library you use still overrides finalize(). What's the cheapest way to find out whether your program relies on it before finalization is removed? Run the program and its tests with --finalization=disabled Run with -XX:+DisableExplicitGC Search the logs for Finalizer Call System.runFinalization() after each request --finalization=disabled (JDK 18 and later) stops every finalizer from running, which is exactly the world after removal. If the tests and a load run pass, nothing depends on it. DisableExplicitGC only ignores System.gc(), and calling runFinalization makes the dependency worse. From the threads track: a task on a fixed pool of one thread does buffer.set(new byte[1 << 20]) on a ThreadLocal and never calls remove(). The task finishes. When can that 1 MiB array be collected? At the next GC, because the task is done Only when a later task on that same pool thread calls buffer.remove(), or the thread ends When the ThreadLocal object itself is garbage collected Never, while the JVM runs The value lives in the pool thread's own map, and a live thread is a GC root. In the research behind this course, a weak probe on the array stayed set after five System.gc() calls and cleared only after a task called remove() on the same pooled thread. The thread outlives every task, so the value does too.
