h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Key terms
x: GC root A starting point for reachability: a live thread's stack, a static field, a native reference. Strongly reachable Reachable through ordinary references. The GC never frees it. SoftReference A reference the GC clears when memory is short, at the latest before an OutOfMemoryError. WeakReference A reference the GC clears as soon as nothing stronger holds the object. PhantomReference A reference whose get() is always null; it reports that an object is gone. ReferenceQueue Where the GC puts reference objects after clearing them, so your code can react. Cleaner Runs a cleanup action after an object becomes phantom reachable, or when you call clean(). Finalization The old finalize() mechanism. Deprecated for removal since JDK 18. What are GC roots? Where reachability starts: local variables on live threads' stacks, static fields, and references held by native code. When is a SoftReference guaranteed to be cleared? Before the JVM throws an OutOfMemoryError. At any other time, the specification promises nothing. When is a WeakReference cleared? By the next GC that finds its object reachable only through weak references. What does PhantomReference.get() return? Always null. A phantom reference only tells you, through its queue, that the object is gone. In a WeakHashMap, what keeps an entry alive forever? A value that refers to its own key, directly or indirectly. Values are strong. Why might a Cleaner action never run? The action refers to the object it cleans (a lambda reading a field, a Java inner class), so the object never becomes phantom reachable. How do you test whether code still relies on finalizers? Run it with --finalization=disabled (JDK 18 and later): no finalizer runs.

h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Go deeper
x: There's a race the Cleaner pattern can hit even when you follow the rule. The JVM may decide an object is unreachable earlier than the source suggests, even while one of its methods is still running. The Reference.reachabilityFence Javadoc describes it: the JIT can load a field's value early, the object is then no longer needed, and the cleaner's thread can free a resource that the method is about to use. So a method that passes a native handle to native code should keep its object reachable until the call returns: Java public int decode(byte[] input) { try { return Decoder.decode(handle, input); // native call that uses the handle } finally { Reference.reachabilityFence(this); // `this` stays reachable until here } } Kotlin fun decode(input: ByteArray): Int { try { return Decoder.decode(handle, input) // native call that uses the handle } finally { Reference.reachabilityFence(this) // `this` stays reachable until here } } The lab's tests use the same method for the opposite reason: to keep a plugin strongly reachable until the asserts are done. Its Javadoc also states a guarantee in the terms of the memory model track: actions in a thread before reachabilityFence(x) happen-before the garbage collector clears any reference to x, so a cleanup thread sees everything the method wrote. Two more details are useful. Phantom references used to keep their object in memory until you cleared them; since JDK 9 the GC clears them automatically when it enqueues them, which is why Cleaner works without extra steps. And a Cleaner owns a daemon thread, so create one per library (a static final field), never one per object.

h: How garbage collectors work: generations and G1 · Most boxes are thrown out young: why the heap has generations
x: Most objects die young: eden, survivor copies and promotion to the old generation A thumbnail request allocates a lot for a moment: the uploaded bytes, the decoded picture, the small thumbnail, a few strings and the response. All of it is garbage a few milliseconds later. A few objects live much longer: the cache of recent thumbnails, the service's settings, the map of uploads it has already done. That split has a name, the weak generational hypothesis: most objects die young. The lesson's demo shows how lopsided it is. It runs a stand-in for the thumbnail service, with short-lived request objects and a slowly growing cache, and logs each young collection. In one JDK 25 run, the heap held 106 MB before a collection and 8 MB after it: 98 of the 106 MB were garbage. HotSpot's collectors split the heap to match. New objects go into eden, the area where every object starts life. Eden belongs to the young generation, the new-arrivals shelves. When eden fills, a young collection finds the few live objects there and copies them into a survivor space, a small short-stay area. Everything else in eden is reclaimed at once, and the collector never even looks at it. Each time an object survives, its age goes up by one. The age lives in the 4 age bits of the mark word from lesson 1, the housekeeping strip on the label. After enough survivals the object is promoted: copied into the old generation, long-term storage, which is collected much less often. The age at which that happens is the tenuring threshold. It's at most 15 (the MaxTenuringThreshold flag), and G1 lowers it when the survivor space runs short. The demo's age table, trimmed, shows both: GC(0) - age 1: 1755920 bytes GC(1) - age 2: 1754832 bytes GC(2) - age 3: 1754832 bytes GC(3) Desired survivor size 8388608 bytes, new threshold 2 (max threshold 15) GC(3) Old regions: 2->10 The same 1.75 MB of cache entries survived three collections, and its age went up by one each time. By GC(3) the survivors no longer fit the 8 MB of survivor space G1 wanted. So G1 dropped the threshold to 2, and everything that old went to long-term storage: the old generation grew from 2 regions to 10. (G1 counts its heap in regions, equal blocks of memory that a later section explains.) Here the warehouse picture breaks, and the break is the key idea. A real crew leaves a wanted box where it is and carries out the rubbish. A copying collector does the opposite. It carries out every box it keeps, and then declares the whole area empty. That's why a young collection costs time in proportion to what survives, not to what was allocated, which was the warm-up. It also makes medium-lived objects the expensive kind. They survive a few young collections, get copied each time, get promoted, and then die in the old generation, where only a bigger collection can reclaim them. A thumbnail cache whose entries live for ten minutes is exactly that shape. Two questions follow. How does the crew find the boxes to keep? And how can it move a box while a worker is using it? Watch survivors age and move out Read GenerationsDemo. It runs the lesson's stand-in service (ServiceLoad.java: short-lived request objects plus a growing cache of thumbnails) for one second, with G1's age table logged. Run it. For each Pause Young line, compare the heap before and after the arrow. Follow one number through the age table from GC(0) to GC(2). Then find the GC where the threshold drops, and look at Old regions on the same GC. GenerationsDemo.java package workbench.memory.l04; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.List; /** * Runs the service load for one second with G1's age table logged, and prints the first four young * collections: how much of the heap each one freed, how old the survivors are, the age at which G1 * promotes them (the tenuring threshold), and how many old regions they fill. */ public class GenerationsDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0) { ServiceLoad.run(1, 0.30); return; } List<String> flags = List.of("-XX:+UseG1GC", "-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:gc,gc+age=trace,gc+heap=info"); for (String line : Jvm.lines(flags, GenerationsDemo.class.getName(), "load")) { if (line.matches(".*GC\\([0-3]\\) (Pause Young|- age|Desired survivor|Old regions).*")) { System.out.println(line.replaceAll("\\s+", " ")); } } } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l04.GenerationsDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l04/GenerationsDemo.java GenerationsDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l04 import workbench.memory.Jvm /** * Runs the service load for one second with G1's age table logged, and prints the first four young * collections: how much of the heap each one freed, how old the survivors are, the age at which G1 * promotes them (the tenuring threshold), and how many old regions they fill. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isNotEmpty()) { serviceLoad(1.0, 0.30) return } val firstFour = Regex(""".*GC\([0-3]\) (Pause Young|- age|Desired survivor|Old regions).*""") val flags = listOf("-XX:+UseG1GC", "-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:gc,gc+age=trace,gc+heap=info") Jvm.lines(flags, "workbench.memory.l04.GenerationsDemoKt", "load") .filter { firstFour.matches(it) } .forEach { println(it.replace(Regex("\\s+"), " ")) } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l04.GenerationsDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l04/GenerationsDemo.kt Each young pause frees most of what it found: 106M->8M means about 98 of the 106 MB were garbage. In the age table, the same group of cache entries (about 1.75 MB on JDK 25) moves from age 1 to age 2 to age 3. A little later a line says new threshold 2 (max threshold 15), and on that GC Old regions jumps (2->10 in the run behind this lesson): those survivors were promoted. Exact numbers change from run to run, and JDK 21 shows smaller ones because its first eden is smaller.

h: How garbage collectors work: generations and G1 · How the crew works: mark, copy or compact, with every thread stopped
x: A collector needs two steps to be correct, and you can write both in a few lines. Here's a toy one. Its heap is a map, refs, from an object's id to the ids that object's fields point to: Java Set<Integer> mark(Collection<Integer> roots) { Set<Integer> live = new HashSet<>(); for (int root : roots) visit(root, live); return live; } void visit(int id, Set<Integer> live) { if (!live.add(id)) return; // already marked: this also ends cycles for (int next : refs.get(id)) visit(next, live); // follow every reference field } Set<Integer> sweep(Set<Integer> live) { Set<Integer> dead = new HashSet<>(refs.keySet()); dead.removeAll(live); refs.keySet().removeAll(dead); // their memory is free again return dead; } Kotlin fun mark(roots: Collection<Int>): Set<Int> { val live = HashSet<Int>() fun visit(id: Int) { if (!live.add(id)) return // already marked: this also ends cycles refs.getValue(id).forEach(::visit) // follow every reference field } roots.forEach(::visit) return live } fun sweep(live: Set<Int>): Set<Int> { val dead = refs.keys.filterTo(HashSet()) { it !in live } refs.keys.removeAll(dead) // their memory is free again return dead } Marking follows references from the roots and remembers every object it reaches: the crew putting a sticker on each box a note leads to. Sweeping frees the rest. Two things follow from the code. A cycle of objects that point at each other, with no root pointing in, gets freed. Marking asks only whether a root can reach an object, never how many references it has. And the sweep visits every object, dead or alive, so its cost grows with the heap. (The recursion is a toy shortcut. A chain of 200,000 objects would overflow a thread's stack. A real collector keeps its own list of objects still to visit, and so will your lab.) HotSpot replaces the sweep with better moves. Copying, which G1 calls evacuation, moves the live objects into empty space and then treats the whole old space as free. It never touches the dead objects, so its cost follows the live ones, and it leaves the live objects packed together. Mark-compact slides the live objects together inside the space they're already in, which needs no spare room but takes several passes. Young collections copy, and G1 names them evacuation pauses. G1's full GC is a mark-compact of the whole heap, the last resort. Moving an object is only safe while no thread is using it, because every reference to it has to be rewritten with its new address. So these steps run in a stop-the-world pause at a safepoint. A safepoint is a moment when every application thread is stopped at a known place, with its references where the collector can find and update them. It's the crew calling "pens down!" so it can rewrite every note. Compiled code checks for a pending safepoint at method returns and in loops. Getting every thread to stop takes time of its own, and -Xlog:safepoint reports it separately. One line from JDK 25, on a busy 4-core machine: Safepoint "G1CollectForAllocation", Time since last: 109433088 ns, Reaching safepoint: 5101 ns, At safepoint: 2324371 ns, Leaving safepoint: 1536 ns, Total: 2331008 ns, Threads: 0 runnable, 10 total "Reaching safepoint" (5.1 microseconds here) is how long the slowest thread took to put its pen down. "At safepoint" (2.3 ms) is the collector's work. When the first number is large, the collector isn't your problem: some thread ran a long time without reaching a safepoint check. One question from the young collection is still open. How does the crew know which young boxes are kept alive by notes inside long-term boxes, without walking all of long-term storage? Separate stopping from collecting Run SafepointDemo. It logs every safepoint during one second of the stand-in service and prints the first five GC safepoints. For each line, compare "Reaching safepoint" with "At safepoint". Both are in nanoseconds. SafepointDemo.java package workbench.memory.l04; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.List; /** Logs every safepoint during one second of service load and prints the GC ones. */ public class SafepointDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0) { ServiceLoad.run(1, 0.30); return; } Jvm.lines(List.of("-XX:+UseG1GC", "-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:safepoint"), SafepointDemo.class.getName(), "load").stream() .filter(line -> line.contains("G1CollectForAllocation")) .limit(5) .forEach(System.out::println); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l04.SafepointDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l04/SafepointDemo.java SafepointDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l04 import workbench.memory.Jvm /** Logs every safepoint during one second of service load and prints the GC ones. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isNotEmpty()) { serviceLoad(1.0, 0.30) return } Jvm.lines(listOf("-XX:+UseG1GC", "-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:safepoint"), "workbench.memory.l04.SafepointDemoKt", "load") .filter { "G1CollectForAllocation" in it } .take(5) .forEach(::println) } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l04.SafepointDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l04/SafepointDemo.kt Reaching the safepoint takes a few thousand nanoseconds (a few microseconds), and the GC work at the safepoint takes a few million (a few milliseconds; 2.3 to 24 ms in the run behind this lesson, on a busy machine). The threads in this load stop quickly because their loops are short. A long "Reaching safepoint" would point at a thread that runs a long time between safepoint checks.

h: How garbage collectors work: generations and G1 · Notes from old boxes to new ones: write barriers and card tables
x: There's a catch in the young collection story. To decide which young objects are alive, the collector follows references from the roots. But old objects point at young ones all the time: the thumbnail cache sits in the old generation, and every new entry it gets is a young object. If a young collection had to scan the whole old generation to find those pointers, it would cost as much as a full GC, a collection of the whole heap. The fix is to do the bookkeeping at the moment the pointer is written. The heap is divided into cards of 512 bytes (G1 prints CardTable entry size: 512 at start-up on JDK 25), and the card table has one byte per card. Every time your code stores a reference into a field, it also runs a few extra instructions, the write barrier, that mark the card holding that field as dirty. In the warehouse, it's a worker who writes a note inside a long-term box and also ticks that stretch of shelf on the floor plan: cache.entries[i] = thumbnail; // the store you wrote card_table[address_of(field) >> 9] = DIRTY; // what the barrier adds (512 = 2^9) A young collection then scans the roots plus the dirty cards, not the whole old generation. G1 goes a step further. Each of its regions keeps a remembered set, the cards elsewhere in the heap that point into that region. "Merge Heap Roots" in G1's detailed pause log is the step that folds those remembered sets into the roots for the pause. (JDK 26 reworked how G1 processes the cards, in JEP 522; the barrier's job is the same.) G1 has a second barrier, for concurrent marking: marking that runs while the program keeps going, which the last section of this lesson describes. While the program keeps running during marking, it can move a reference out of an object the marker hasn't visited yet into one it already has. To catch that, the barrier records the old value before a reference is overwritten, so the marker still finds every object that was live when marking began. The technique is called snapshot-at-the-beginning (SATB), and the comment on G1's barrier class in the JDK 25 source calls it "a logging barrier to support snapshot-at-the-beginning marking". These barriers are the steady cost of a generational collector that works alongside your code: a few instructions on every reference store, all the time. Lesson 5 shows that ZGC, a collector built for very short pauses, pays at reference loads instead. Reason it through before you move on. The service keeps a long-lived map of each user's latest thumbnail, so the map sits in the old generation. For every new thumbnail it replaces one user's value with the new, young object. Which cards does the barrier dirty, and what does the next young pause scan? (Only the few cards holding the map entries whose value changed. The pause scans those cards and the roots, finds the new thumbnails, and never reads the rest of the old generation.) So far the heap has had fixed parts: eden, survivors, old. G1, the default collector, doesn't keep them fixed at all.

h: How garbage collectors work: generations and G1 · G1 divides the floor into equal regions
x: G1 cuts the heap into equal regions and collects the most garbage first G1 (short for Garbage-First) is HotSpot's default collector. On JDK 25 it's the default on any machine with at least two processors and about 1.8 GB of memory, and from JDK 27 everywhere. G1 doesn't keep one big eden and one big old space. It cuts the heap into equal regions, and each region has a role for a while: eden, survivor, old, humongous or free. The roles move around. After a young pause the evacuated eden regions are free, and next time any of them can become anything. In the warehouse, G1's crew divides the floor into equal bays and labels each bay with its current use. The region size comes from the maximum heap. In the JDK 25 source it's the max heap divided by 2048, held between 1 MB and 32 MB, then rounded up to a power of two. A 1 GB heap gets 1 MB regions, the 3.4 GB default heap on the machine behind this lesson got 2 MB, and -Xmx40g gets 32 MB. Regions explain one of G1's sharp edges. An object larger than half a region is humongous. It skips TLABs (each thread's private chunk of eden, from lesson 2) and eden itself, and gets its own run of whole, contiguous regions, which count as old from the start. A 3 MiB photo in a byte[] is 3 MiB plus a 16-byte header, so with 1 MB regions it takes four regions, and nearly all of the fourth one is wasted. A burst of humongous allocations can start a concurrent marking cycle on its own (the next section's subject; the log gives the cause G1 Humongous Allocation), and each one needs enough free regions in a row. G1 does reclaim dead humongous objects early: in the demo on JDK 25, the first young pause freed Humongous regions: 28->0, seven dead photos at four regions each. For the thumbnail service, the humongous objects are the photos themselves, whenever a whole upload sits in one array. If your log is full of G1 Humongous Allocation, stream those payloads instead of holding them whole (the compare block below shows how), or raise the region size with -XX:G1HeapRegionSize until they're under half a region. G1 also works to a time budget. By default it aims to keep each pause under 200 ms (MaxGCPauseMillis), and it plans how much to collect in each pause to stay inside that budget. Regions are what make the plan possible: G1 can clean part of the old generation without cleaning all of it, and it cleans the messiest bays first, the way anyone tidies a garage with only an hour to spare. To choose the messiest bays, though, G1 first has to know how much garbage each one holds. Count the regions of a humongous photo Read HumongousDemo. It runs a 1 GB G1 heap, so regions are 1 MB, and allocates 3 MiB photos with ordinary garbage in between. Predict how many regions each photo takes, then run it. HumongousDemo.java package workbench.memory.l04; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.List; /** * Allocates 3 MiB photos in a 1 GB G1 heap, where regions are 1 MB, and prints the * region counts G1 logs for the first young pause. */ public class HumongousDemo { static volatile Object sink; public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0) { for (int i = 0; i < 40; i++) { sink = new byte[3 * 1024 * 1024]; // a 3 MiB photo: 3 MiB + a 16-byte header for (int j = 0; j < 20_000; j++) sink = new byte[200]; // some ordinary garbage in between } return; } for (String line : Jvm.lines(List.of("-XX:+UseG1GC", "-Xmx1g", "-Xlog:gc,gc+init,gc+heap=info"), HumongousDemo.class.getName(), "load")) { if (line.contains("Heap Region Size") || line.matches(".*GC\\(0\\) (Pause|.*regions).*")) { System.out.println(line.replaceAll("\\s+", " ")); } } } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l04.HumongousDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l04/HumongousDemo.java HumongousDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l04 import workbench.memory.Jvm @Volatile private var humongousSink: Any? = null /** * Allocates 3 MiB photos in a 1 GB G1 heap, where regions are 1 MB, and prints the * region counts G1 logs for the first young pause. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isNotEmpty()) { repeat(40) { humongousSink = ByteArray(3 * 1024 * 1024) // a 3 MiB photo: 3 MiB + a 16-byte header repeat(20_000) { humongousSink = ByteArray(200) } // some ordinary garbage in between } return } val firstPause = Regex(""".*GC\(0\) (Pause|.*regions).*""") Jvm.lines(listOf("-XX:+UseG1GC", "-Xmx1g", "-Xlog:gc,gc+init,gc+heap=info"), "workbench.memory.l04.HumongousDemoKt", "load") .filter { "Heap Region Size" in it || firstPause.matches(it) } .forEach { println(it.replace(Regex("\\s+"), " ")) } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l04.HumongousDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l04/HumongousDemo.kt Heap Region Size: 1M, then the first young pause reports something like Humongous regions: 28->0 on JDK 25. Every photo took four regions, because 3 MiB plus a 16-byte header doesn't fit in three, so 28 regions held seven photos. All of them were already dead, so the young pause reclaimed them right away. JDK 21 starts with a smaller eden, so its first pause finds fewer photos (12 regions, three photos). G1 gives each equal region a role. Young pauses evacuate every eden and survivor region; mixed pauses also take the old regions with the most garbage. g1HeapRegion.cpp at jdk-25-ga: how G1 picks the region size read

h: How garbage collectors work: generations and G1 · G1's cycle: young pauses, concurrent marking and mixed collections
x: Most of the time G1 runs only young pauses, and each one evacuates every eden and survivor region. Here's the first one from a JDK 25 run of the stand-in service, in a 256 MB heap: GC(0) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 28M->2M(214M) 12.921ms Read it left to right. 28 MB was in use before, 2 MB after, the heap had 214 MB committed (memory the operating system has handed over; G1 grows it toward the 256 MB maximum as needed), and the stop-the-world pause took 12.9 ms on that busy 4-core machine. Your times will differ. The old regions fill up slowly with promoted objects. When old-generation occupancy crosses the initiating heap occupancy percent (IHOP: 45% to begin with, then adapted from what G1 observes), G1 starts a concurrent marking cycle: an inspector who walks the long-term bays while work goes on, noting how full each one is. Here's one from the same run, with the timestamps cut off: GC(21) Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Humongous Allocation) 181M->127M(256M) 4.034ms GC(22) Concurrent Mark Cycle GC(22) Pause Remark 153M->153M(256M) 0.721ms GC(22) Pause Cleanup 163M->163M(256M) 0.021ms GC(22) Concurrent Mark Cycle 25.873ms GC(23) Pause Young (Prepare Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) (Evacuation Failure: Allocation) 253M->202M(256M) 4.001ms GC(24) Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 242M->144M(256M) 3.110ms The cycle starts inside a young pause (Concurrent Start). Marking then runs on a background thread for 26 ms while the program keeps working, with two short pauses to finish (Remark, Cleanup). Now G1 knows how much of each old region is live. The next young pause (Prepare Mixed) is the last young-only one. Then come the mixed pauses: all the young regions plus a few old ones, the ones with the most garbage. That choice is where the name Garbage-First comes from, and the mixed pause freed 98 MB where the young pause before it freed 51. Which old regions? From the JDK 25 source: only regions less than 85% live are candidates (G1MixedGCLiveThresholdPercent). G1 sorts them by efficiency, best first. It drops the cheapest ones as long as the garbage it leaves behind stays within 5% of the heap (G1HeapWastePercent). And each mixed pause takes at least an eighth of the candidates, so the work is done in at most 8 mixed pauses (G1MixedGCCountTarget). The lab has you write these rules. Two phrases in the log mean trouble. (Evacuation Failure: Allocation) means G1 ran out of free regions to copy into, and had to leave objects where they were. (JDK 21 printed only (Evacuation Failure); newer JDKs add the reason.) Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) is the fallback: the whole heap, mark-compact, every thread stopped. Both say the heap is too small for the live data plus the allocation rate. It's tempting to lower -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis to make them go away. The pause goal only steers how much work G1 plans per pause, such as how big eden gets and how many old regions a mixed pause takes. It can't create free regions, and a smaller goal usually means more, smaller pauses on the same full heap. When G1 fails to copy, give it room or keep less alive. A smaller pause goal does neither. Here the warehouse picture breaks for the last time. A real crew can carry boxes while people work around them. G1 marks while the program runs, but it stops every thread before it moves anything, and that stop is your pause. Squeeze G1 until it struggles Read G1CycleDemo. It runs the stand-in service for 3 seconds in a 256 MB heap, with the cache growing to 60% of it. It counts each kind of GC event and prints the first line of each kind, in the order they happened. Run it. Find the cycle from this section among the first lines: Concurrent Start, Remark, Cleanup, Prepare Mixed, Mixed. Run it again and compare the counts. G1CycleDemo.java package workbench.memory.l04; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.regex.Matcher; import java.util.regex.Pattern; /** * Runs the service load for 3 seconds in a child JVM with a tight 256 MB G1 heap, then counts each * kind of GC event and prints the first line of each kind. */ public class G1CycleDemo { // "GC(12) Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) ..." -> "Pause Young (Mixed)" static final Pattern KIND = Pattern.compile("GC\\(\\d+\\) ((?:Pause \\w+(?: \\((?:Normal|Concurrent Start|Prepare Mixed|Mixed)\\))?)|Concurrent \\w+ Cycle)"); public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0) { ServiceLoad.run(3, 0.60); return; } List<String> log = Jvm.lines(List.of("-XX:+UseG1GC", "-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:gc"), G1CycleDemo.class.getName(), "load"); Map<String, Integer> counts = new TreeMap<>(); Map<String, String> firstLine = new LinkedHashMap<>(); // in the order they first happened int evacuationFailures = 0; for (String line : log) { Matcher m = KIND.matcher(line); if (!m.find() || line.endsWith("Cycle")) continue; // skip the "cycle started" half of a pair counts.merge(m.group(1), 1, Integer::sum); firstLine.putIfAbsent(m.group(1), line); if (line.contains("(Evacuation Failure")) evacuationFailures++; // JDK 25 adds a reason: "(Evacuation Failure: Allocation)" } counts.forEach((kind, n) -> System.out.printf("%4d x %s%n", n, kind)); System.out.println(evacuationFailures + " pauses had an evacuation failure"); System.out.println(); firstLine.values().forEach(System.out::println); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l04.G1CycleDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l04/G1CycleDemo.java G1CycleDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l04 import workbench.memory.Jvm // "GC(12) Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) ..." -> "Pause Young (Mixed)" private val KIND = Regex("""GC\(\d+\) ((?:Pause \w+(?: \((?:Normal|Concurrent Start|Prepare Mixed|Mixed)\))?)|Concurrent \w+ Cycle)""") /** * Runs the service load for 3 seconds in a child JVM with a tight 256 MB G1 heap, then counts each * kind of GC event and prints the first line of each kind. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isNotEmpty()) { serviceLoad(3.0, 0.60) return } val log = Jvm.lines(listOf("-XX:+UseG1GC", "-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:gc"), "workbench.memory.l04.G1CycleDemoKt", "load") val events = log.mapNotNull { line -> val kind = KIND.find(line)?.groupValues?.get(1) if (kind == null || line.endsWith("Cycle")) null else kind to line // skip the "cycle started" half } events.groupingBy { it.first }.eachCount().toSortedMap().forEach { (kind, n) -> println("%4d x %s".format(n, kind)) } println("${events.count { "(Evacuation Failure" in it.second }} pauses had an evacuation failure") // JDK 25 adds a reason after a colon println() events.distinctBy { it.first }.forEach { println(it.second) } // in the order they first happened } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l04.G1CycleDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l04/G1CycleDemo.kt About 15 to 35 concurrent mark cycles, each with a Remark and a Cleanup, a dozen or more mixed pauses, and twenty or more pauses with an evacuation failure. Most runs also show one to three Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause). The counts change on every run, and JDK 21 shows more mixed pauses. This heap is too small for its live data on purpose: it's the "bad config" you want to recognize in your own logs. g1CollectionSetChooser.cpp at jdk-25-ga: choosing mixed-collection candidates read

h: How garbage collectors work: generations and G1 · Java and Kotlin
x: Store an upload whole, or stream it StoreUpload.java // holds the whole photo: a 3 MB photo is humongous on any heap with regions of 4 MB or less byte[] photo = in.readAllBytes(); Files.write(target, photo); // streams it: copies through a small buffer, so only small objects are created try (OutputStream out = Files.newOutputStream(target)) { in.transferTo(out); } StoreUpload.kt // holds the whole photo: a 3 MB photo is humongous on any heap with regions of 4 MB or less val photo = input.readBytes() Files.write(target, photo) // streams it: copies through a small buffer, so only small objects are created Files.newOutputStream(target).use { out -> input.copyTo(out) } The GC sees the same thing from both languages. The first version creates one array as big as the photo, which is humongous whenever the photo is over half a region, and the second never holds more than a small buffer. The difference is only in the API. Java's transferTo copies from an InputStream to an OutputStream, and the stream goes in try-with-resources. Kotlin's copyTo is an extension that does the same, and use {} closes the stream when the block ends. Making the thumbnail itself still needs the decoded picture, so streaming helps most where the program only moves bytes along.

h: How garbage collectors work: generations and G1 · Worked example
x: Read a struggling G1 log The stand-in service runs in a 256 MB heap. These are some of the first lines of its -Xlog:gc output on JDK 25, with the timestamps cut off. Before you read on, look at the number after each arrow. GC(0) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 28M->2M(214M) 12.921ms GC(1) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 96M->7M(214M) 7.617ms GC(2) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 110M->13M(214M) 10.765ms GC(4) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 143M->28M(214M) 7.341ms GC(8) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 178M->58M(225M) 8.307ms GC(12) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 217M->88M(240M) 16.690ms Read the floor. The after-values (2, 7, 13, 28, 58, 88 MB) are what's still live after each young pause, and they climb by about 7 MB every pause. Either the service is warming a cache, or something is leaking. Either way the old generation is filling, and the committed heap grows from 214 MB toward its 256 MB maximum. Find the turn. Two pauses later the heap is nearly full and copies start to fail. Humongous photos then start concurrent cycles. The first one that runs to the end tells G1 which old regions to clean, and the mixed pauses begin. GC(14) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) (Evacuation Failure: Allocation) 234M->107M(256M) 16.851ms GC(21) Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Humongous Allocation) 181M->127M(256M) 4.034ms GC(22) Pause Remark 153M->153M(256M) 0.721ms GC(22) Pause Cleanup 163M->163M(256M) 0.021ms GC(23) Pause Young (Prepare Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) (Evacuation Failure: Allocation) 253M->202M(256M) 4.001ms GC(24) Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 242M->144M(256M) 3.110ms GC(28) Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) (Evacuation Failure: Allocation) 249M->156M(256M) 7.027ms Read the verdict. The mixed pauses can't win. The first ones free about 95 MB each and later ones less and less (GC(40) freed 13 MB), and each time the heap is back near 250 MB a few milliseconds later. Then comes the fallback. The full GC brings the heap down to 95 MB, and that number is the live set at that moment: 95 MB of real data in a 256 MB heap, with a high allocation rate on top. GC(44) Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 256M->95M(256M) 19.130ms Decide. G1 copies, so it needs free regions to copy into. As a rule of thumb (mine, not G1's), give it a heap of two to three times the live set, and more when the live data swings, as it does here: this load's cache grows to 60% of the heap before it sheds half. Or keep less alive, by putting a limit on the cache. Then confirm with a new log that the evacuation failures and full GCs are gone. If the floor keeps climbing even then, it's a leak, not a sizing problem, and lesson 7 finds it.

x: A toy collector, then G1 by numbers labs/memory/src/main/kotlin/workbench/memory/l04/ToyHeap.kt labs/memory/src/main/kotlin/workbench/memory/l04/G1Model.kt labs/memory/src/main/kotlin/workbench/memory/l04/OldRegion.kt ./gradlew :memory:test --tests 'workbench.memory.l04.*' Run the tests. Fourteen of fifteen fail; the one that passes tests a helper you're given. Start with the toy: write ToyHeap.mark without recursion. Keep an ArrayDeque of objects still to visit, take one off, mark it, and add its references. Then write sweep. The ToyHeapTest tests should pass, including the unreachable cycle and the 200,000-object chain. Now G1. Write regionSize: divide by 2048, hold the result between 1 MB and 32 MB, then round up to a power of two. In that order. Each KDoc gives the rule from the JDK 25 source. Write isHumongous (strictly more than half a region) and regionsFor (whole regions, rounded up). Write mixedCandidates: filter, sort, then prune from the end, using the given minOldRegionsPerMixedGc. Run the tests until all fifteen pass, then read the test for the 3 MiB photo and explain its numbers to yourself. In mark, skip an object that is already marked when you take it off the deque. That one check ends cycles and avoids scanning anything twice. (a + b - 1) / b rounds a division up, for positive numbers. coerceIn(MB, 32 * MB) clamps. For the power of two, start at 1 MB and double until you reach the wanted size. compareByDescending { regionBytes - it.liveBytes }.thenBy { it.index } sorts the candidates. Pruning: walk back from the last candidate. Stop when you're down to the minimum, or when dropping the next one would push the total dropped garbage past 5% of the heap. All 15 tests in ToyHeapTest and G1ModelTest pass. h: How garbage collectors work: generations and G1 · Quiz
x: A service runs on a 2 GB heap with G1 and default settings. Which of these is a humongous allocation? new byte[400_000] for a thumbnail A HashMap with 30,000 entries new byte[700_000] for a chunk of an uploaded photo A String of 300,000 Latin-1 characters 2 GB / 2048 is exactly 1 MB, so regions are 1 MB and the humongous threshold is 512 KB. 700,000 bytes is over it. 400,000 bytes and a 300,000-character Latin-1 string (a 300 KB array) are under it. A HashMap is many small objects; with 30,000 entries its table has 65,536 slots, a 256 KB array. Why does a young collection not have to scan the whole old generation for pointers into eden? Old objects are never allowed to point to young objects The write barrier marks dirty cards when references are stored, and the collector scans only those The JIT moves such objects into the old generation right away G1 copies the old generation in every young pause Old-to-young pointers are normal, for example a cache in the old generation getting new entries. Every reference store runs a barrier that marks the 512-byte card it wrote to as dirty. A young pause scans the roots plus the dirty cards; in G1, remembered sets track which cards point into which region. A JDK 25 log shows GC(42) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 1210M->1180M(1536M), then (Evacuation Failure: Allocation) on the next pauses, then Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 1490M->1150M(1536M). What does it tell you? The pause goal is too high; set -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=50 The young generation is too small; the old generation is fine The application calls System.gc() About 1.15 GB is really live in a 1.5 GB heap, which leaves G1 too little room to copy The full GC's after-value is the live set: 1,150 MB of 1,536 MB. A young pause that frees only 30 MB, and copies that fail for lack of free regions, say the same thing. A smaller pause goal can't create free regions. A System.gc() call would show (System.gc()) as the cause. In Safepoint "G1CollectForAllocation" ... Reaching safepoint: 48000000 ns, At safepoint: 2100000 ns ..., where would you look first? At the GC settings, because the collection took 48 ms At application code that runs a long time without a safepoint check At the heap size, because the heap is too small At the number of GC worker threads "Reaching safepoint" is the time the slowest thread took to stop: 48 ms here. The GC work itself, "At safepoint", took 2.1 ms. A long time to safepoint means some thread ran far without reaching a safepoint check, which no GC setting fixes. From lesson 2: why is a dead 3 MiB photo cheaper for G1 than a 3 MiB photo that survives several young pauses, even though both are humongous? A dead humongous object can be reclaimed in a young pause without any copying; a live one keeps its contiguous regions and fills the old generation Live humongous objects are copied in every young pause Dead humongous objects go into a TLAB There is no difference; G1 treats all humongous objects alike Humongous objects never go through TLABs or eden, and G1 doesn't copy them in young pauses. The demo showed a young pause freeing Humongous regions: 28->0 because the photos were already dead. A live one keeps its regions as part of the old generation until it dies and a collection finds it.

h: How garbage collectors work: generations and G1 · Explain it back

h: How garbage collectors work: generations and G1 · Key terms
x: Young generation Eden plus survivor space, where new objects live until they die or are promoted. Promotion Moving an object that survived enough young collections into the old generation. Evacuation G1's word for copying live objects out of a region so the region can be freed. Safepoint A moment when every application thread is stopped at a known place, so the GC can move objects. Card table One byte per 512-byte card of heap, marked dirty when a reference in that card changes. Remembered set G1's per-region list of cards elsewhere in the heap that point into the region. Humongous object In G1, an object bigger than half a region, stored in its own contiguous regions. Mixed collection A G1 pause that evacuates the young regions plus some old regions with the most garbage. What does the weak generational hypothesis say? Most objects die young. Collectors use it by collecting a small young generation often and the old generation rarely. What does a young collection's pause time depend on? Mostly on how much survives and must be copied, not on how much garbage there is. What does a write barrier do in a generational collector? On every reference store, it marks the card (512 bytes in G1) that holds the field as dirty, so a young GC scans dirty cards instead of the whole old generation. How does G1 pick its region size by default? Max heap / 2048, held between 1 and 32 MB, rounded up to a power of two. When is an object humongous in G1? When it is bigger than half a region. It gets whole contiguous regions and skips TLABs and eden. Which old regions can a G1 mixed collection take? Regions under 85% live (G1MixedGCLiveThresholdPercent), best first, until the remaining garbage is within 5% of the heap. Two objects point at each other and nothing else points at them. Does a tracing GC free them? Yes. Marking only asks whether a root can reach an object, so an unreachable cycle is never marked and gets freed.

h: How garbage collectors work: generations and G1 · Go deeper
x: The -Xlog:gc* version of a young pause shows where the time goes. From a 1 GB heap on JDK 25: GC(2) Using 4 workers of 4 for evacuation GC(2) Pre Evacuate Collection Set: 0.07ms GC(2) Merge Heap Roots: 0.10ms GC(2) Evacuate Collection Set: 21.05ms GC(2) Post Evacuate Collection Set: 0.22ms GC(2) Other: 0.06ms GC(2) Eden regions: 99->0(116) GC(2) Survivor regions: 8->12(14) GC(2) Old regions: 0->3 GC(2) Humongous regions: 4->0 GC(2) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 110M->14M(214M) 21.701ms Almost all of the 21.7 ms is "Evacuate Collection Set", the copying. "Merge Heap Roots" is the remembered-set work from section 3, tiny here. Eden regions: 99->0(116) means 99 eden regions before, none after, and a target of 116 for the next cycle: G1 resizes eden after every pause to meet its pause goal. Old regions: 0->3 means three regions' worth of survivors were promoted, and Humongous regions: 4->0 is one dead 3 MiB photo reclaimed without copying. The G1 defaults behind this lesson, from the JDK 25 source: InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent 45 with G1UseAdaptiveIHOP on, G1MixedGCCountTarget 8, G1HeapWastePercent 5, G1MixedGCLiveThresholdPercent 85 (an experimental flag), G1ReservePercent 10 (free space G1 tries to keep for copying), and MaxTenuringThreshold 15. h: Low-pause collectors: ZGC, Shenandoah, and choosing a GC · Moving boxes while the workers keep working: how ZGC relocates
x: ZGC moves objects while threads run: colored references and a load barrier that fixes stale ones on the next load In lesson 4, almost all of a G1 young pause, the stop in which G1 cleans the area for new objects, was "Evacuate Collection Set": the collector copying live objects while every thread waited. (The heap is the memory where a Java program keeps its objects, the garbage collector is the part of the JVM that frees the objects nothing uses any more, and a thread is one path of work running through the program.) That pause grows with what survives. Give the thumbnail service a cache of many gigabytes, and every young pause has more to copy. ZGC, the Z Garbage Collector, moves objects while your threads keep running. It has been ready for production since JDK 15. The hard part is easy to state: a thread may be about to follow a reference, an object's address, to an object the collector has just moved. ZGC handles that with two tricks. The first trick is the colored pointer. Every reference stored in the heap carries a few extra bits, its color, which say whether the reference is up to date with the crew's current round of work. Picture a small colored sticker on every note. The bits need room, so ZGC doesn't use lesson 1's compressed 4-byte references: each one takes 8 bytes. Lesson 1's Thumbnail takes 40 bytes under G1 on JDK 25 and 48 under ZGC. The allocation counter says so: 10,000 thumbnails, 480,000 bytes. The second trick is the load barrier: a few instructions added after every load of a reference from the heap. The JIT compiler puts them there; it's the part of the JVM, the program that runs your code, that turns busy bytecode into machine code. Here's what the barrier adds, in spirit: thumb = cache.latest // the load you wrote if (color(thumb) != GOOD) // the barrier: one test and one branch thumb = cache.latest = fix(thumb) // rare: find the new address, repair the field Nearly always the color is good, and the barrier costs a test and a branch. When it isn't, the object may have moved. The barrier looks up the new address, moves the object itself if the crew hasn't got to it yet, and writes the repaired reference back into the field. The next load from that field takes the fast path again. The worker reads the forwarding note once and fixes the shelf number for good. Here the picture bends in two places, and both matter. ZGC doesn't leave its forwarding notes on the old shelves. It keeps them in a small table beside each area it empties, so the old shelves can take new boxes right away. And a real worker reads a forwarding note only after walking to an old shelf. ZGC's check runs on every reference load, all day, whether a move is going on or not. What's left for the pauses is small and fixed: switching the crew from one step to the next. Since JDK 16, ZGC even scans the threads' stacks while they run (JEP 376). The java manual promises "max pause times of a few milliseconds" and says "pause times are independent of what heap size is used", for heaps from 8 MB to 16 TB. The flags changed along the way. JDK 21 added generational ZGC, with lesson 4's young and old generations, as an option (-XX:+ZGenerational, JEP 439). JDK 23 made it the default (JEP 474), and JDK 24 removed the old single-generation mode (JEP 490). On JDK 25, -XX:+UseZGC means generational ZGC, which also has a barrier on reference stores to track notes from old boxes to young ones, the job G1's cards do. Now read one collection from the log. These lines come from a JDK 25 run of the demo's load, logged with -Xlog:gc* and trimmed, on a 4-core machine busy with other work (ZGC's own log reported a load of 26): GC(3) Minor Collection (Allocation Rate) GC(3) y: Pause Mark Start 0.011ms GC(3) y: Concurrent Mark 24.398ms GC(3) y: Pause Mark End 0.015ms GC(3) y: Concurrent Select Relocation Set 0.184ms GC(3) y: Pause Relocate Start 0.020ms GC(3) y: Concurrent Relocate 34.916ms GC(3) Minor Collection (Allocation Rate) 852M(83%)->176M(17%) 0.071s A minor collection cleans only the young generation, and y: marks its lines. The heap went from 852 MB used to 176 MB. The 0.071 s on the last line is the whole collection, which ran beside the application. The pauses are the three Pause lines, 0.046 ms together. Seventy-one milliseconds of cleaning, and the workers lost less than a twentieth of one. So the pauses are nearly gone. The work isn't. Somebody still marks and moves every live box, and somebody runs that barrier. Find the pauses in a ZGC log Read ZgcDemo. It runs two seconds of the stand-in thumbnail service from lesson 4 under ZGC with a 1 GB heap, in a child JVM (it adds -XX:+ZGenerational on JDK 21 and 22). Then it prints every line of the first minor collection and adds up the pauses. Predict before you run: will the pauses be longer than G1's young pauses in lesson 4, about the same, or shorter? And the time on the collection's last line? Run it, and match the three Pause lines to the three red marks in the figure. Change -Xmx1g to -Xmx96m in the demo and run it again. Watch the last line. h: Low-pause collectors: ZGC, Shenandoah, and choosing a GC · What short pauses cost: CPU, headroom and bigger references
x: The java manual is honest about the price: ZGC gives low pauses "at some throughput cost". Throughput is how much useful work a program gets done for each second of CPU. The bill comes in three parts. The first part is CPU. Marking and moving run on GC threads beside your threads, and the barrier's slow path runs on your own threads. A container is a fenced-off part of a shared machine, with its own limits on CPU and memory (lesson 6 looks at one closely). In a container with 2 CPUs, ZGC's threads compete with your request threads exactly when the service is busiest. The second part is headroom: free space for the objects your code creates while the crew works. In the collection above, the application allocated another 100 MB during those 71 ms. One major collection, which cleans the young and old generations together, even ended fuller than it began: GC(9) Major Collection (Allocation Rate) 258M(25%)->272M(27%) 0.078s If the floor fills before the crew finishes, ZGC has one choice left: it makes the threads that want memory wait. The log calls that an allocation stall. Squeeze the demo's load into a 96 MB heap, and JDK 25 printed 22 lines like this in one two-second run and 30 in the next: [2.162s][info][gc ] Allocation Stall (main) 0.895ms A stall hurts more than a pause, because it hits exactly the threads doing the most work. Stalls should be zero. When they aren't, give ZGC more heap or more CPU. The third part is memory. With 8-byte references, every object that holds references grows, like the thumbnail from 40 to 48 bytes. Compact object headers from lesson 1 win that back: with -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders on JDK 25, the same thumbnail took 40 bytes under ZGC. Short pauses move the work; they don't remove it. Check where it went. Shenandoah is OpenJDK's other concurrent collector, a second crew with its own design. It also marks and moves objects while your threads run, and it also has a barrier on reference loads that sends a thread to an object's new copy. One difference shows in its log: after moving, Shenandoah walks the heap and fixes every old reference, in a phase called Concurrent update references. One JDK 25 cycle had four pauses, the longest 0.309 ms. It keeps 4-byte compressed references, so the thumbnail stays at 40 bytes. Its default mode has one generation; a generational mode was experimental in JDK 24 and is a product feature in JDK 25 (-XX:ShenandoahGCMode=generational, JEP 521). Not every vendor's JDK includes Shenandoah, so check that java -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -version starts before you plan on it. Let's put all of them on one load. The demo runs one second of it under five collectors, with a 512 MB heap each. Two JDK 25 runs on the busy machine gave the same shape. Here's the first, in full: collector pauses longest all pauses rounds CPU ms UseSerialGC 31 15.58ms 161.9ms 1550 670 UseParallelGC 13 49.90ms 243.3ms 1299 610 UseG1GC 12 13.49ms 110.4ms 1394 680 UseZGC 58 2.63ms 3.4ms 2311 1010 UseShenandoahGC 30 5.16ms 9.4ms 1522 880 Across both runs, Serial, Parallel and G1 stopped the threads for 110 to 245 ms in total, ZGC and Shenandoah for 1 to 10 ms. In the second run ZGC's longest pause was 0.03 ms, so the 2.63 ms above is the busy machine, where any thread can wait for a core. The two concurrent crews used the most CPU both times: about 1,000 and 900 ms, against 610 to 890 for the rest. Don't judge throughput by the rounds column, though. Serial's jumped from 1,550 to 2,377 between runs. Every crew makes a different trade, then. To choose one, you need to know which part of the bill your program can least afford. Run one load under five collectors Read CollectorCompareDemo. Each collector gets the same second of load with a 512 MB heap, in a fresh child JVM. The child reports the rounds of work it finished and the CPU time the whole process used, GC threads included. Predict the order of the longest pauses, from longest to shortest. Then run it. Run it again and see which columns stay steady and which jump around. h: Low-pause collectors: ZGC, Shenandoah, and choosing a GC · Choosing a crew by what hurts most: the default and a decision table
x: Before you choose, know what you get when you choose nothing. On JDK 21 to 26, the JVM picks G1 only on what it calls a server-class machine: at least 2 CPUs and at least 1,792 MB of memory, both as the JVM sees them inside a container. Anything smaller silently gets Serial, HotSpot's simplest collector: one GC thread does all the work while every application thread waits. (Parallel does the same with many GC threads.) A small helper program next to the thumbnail service, in a container with 1 CPU or a 1 GiB memory limit, has run Serial all along unless someone named a collector. Per the JDK 27 source, JDK 27 picks G1 everywhere. Then ask what hurts most. If long pauses hurt, because a person waits on every request, look at the low-pause crews. If total work per CPU hurts, because a job runs for hours and nobody waits on one step, look at Parallel. If memory hurts, because the container is small, remember that concurrent crews need headroom. These are my starting points, not benchmark results: Collector The crew Pick it when Watch out for Serial one cleaner, pens down 1 CPU and a heap up to a few hundred MB full GCs that grow with the live data Parallel many cleaners, pens down batch jobs, where total time beats any single pause long pauses on big heaps G1 the crew with a stopwatch, from lesson 4 most services: heaps from about 256 MB to tens of GB, pause budgets of tens of milliseconds Evacuation Failure, Pause Full, many arrays over half a region ZGC moves boxes while the workers work pause budgets under about 10 ms, with cores to spare CPU in small containers, Allocation Stall, 8-byte references Shenandoah the same goal, another design the same goals as ZGC, on a JDK that includes it availability; generational mode only from JDK 24 Epsilon never cleans at all tests and benchmarks only the JVM stops when the heap is full, by design The flags change with the JDK: Collector JDK 21 JDK 25 G1, Serial, Parallel -XX:+UseG1GC, -XX:+UseSerialGC, -XX:+UseParallelGC the same Generational ZGC -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -XX:+UseZGC Generational Shenandoah not available -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -XX:ShenandoahGCMode=generational Epsilon -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseEpsilonGC the same When you move a program from JDK 21 to 25, take -XX:+ZGenerational out. JDK 25 starts anyway and says so: Ignoring option ZGenerational; support was removed in 24.0. Pick a collector by the bill you can least afford, then watch the log for that bill. The lab turns both tables into code. One row in the first table looks like a joke: a crew that never cleans. In a test, it's the most honest collector there is. See what the JVM picks with one CPU Run the first command. -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=1 makes the JVM believe it has one CPU, like a container with a 1-CPU limit. Run the second one, without the flag, and compare. Predict what JDK 27 would print for the first command. terminal java -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=1 -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E ' Use(Serial|G1|Parallel|Z|Shenandoah)GC ' java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E ' Use(Serial|G1)GC ' On JDK 25 the first command shows UseSerialGC as true, marked {ergonomic} (the JVM chose it), and UseG1GC as false: one CPU is not a server-class machine. Without the flag, on a machine with 2 or more CPUs and enough memory, UseG1GC is the one that's true and {ergonomic}. JDK 21 to 26 behave the same way. On JDK 27, per its source, both commands select G1. gcConfig.cpp at jdk-25-ga: how the JVM picks a collector read

h: Low-pause collectors: ZGC, Shenandoah, and choosing a GC · A crew that never cleans: Epsilon as an allocation budget
x: Epsilon is a collector that never collects. It hands out memory, and when the heap is full, the JVM stops: Terminating due to java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space Epsilon is a cleaning crew that never shows up. In a running service, that's a short career. In a test, it's a measuring tool, because under Epsilon the heap size becomes an allocation budget: if a piece of code finishes under -Xmx64m, a heap of at most 64 MB, it allocated less than 64 MB in total, a few of which went to starting the JVM. The demo puts lesson 2's upload report on that budget. It adds up the bytes that each of 500 users uploaded, over 5 million uploads, in two versions. Each version runs in its own JVM with Epsilon and a 64 MB heap. The long[] version finishes. The Map<Integer, Long> version dies. It dies even though the JIT's escape analysis (lesson 2's trick of skipping objects that never leave a method) may remove the temporary boxes for the key and the size, because every running sum is a new 24-byte Long that the map stores. Epsilon frees none of the old ones, and 5 million of them need at least 120 MB. Epsilon has two other honest uses: benchmarks that must not be disturbed by GC pauses, and very short jobs that finish before they could fill the heap. It's an experimental option on every JDK from 21 to 27, and the JVM is fussy about the order of its flags. Write -XX:+UseEpsilonGC -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions, and JDK 25 refuses to start: Error: VM option 'UseEpsilonGC' is experimental and must be enabled via -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions. Error: The unlock option must precede 'UseEpsilonGC'. So the experimental switch comes first, and the collector after it. Epsilon makes its bill obvious by failing. The other collectors write theirs into the GC log, quietly, one line at a time. Put the upload report on an allocation budget Read EpsilonDemo. Each version runs in a child JVM with Epsilon and a 64 MB heap. Predict which version finishes, then run it. Change UPLOADS to 1,000,000 and run it again, then to 2,000,000. Does the point where the boxed version breaks match 24 bytes per upload? EpsilonDemo.java package workbench.memory.l05; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * Epsilon never frees anything, so a heap of 64 MB is an allocation budget. Two versions of lesson 2's * upload report (the bytes each user uploaded) run against that budget, each in its own child JVM. */ public class EpsilonDemo { static final int UPLOADS = 5_000_000, USERS = 500; static long boxedTotals() { Map<Integer, Long> totals = new HashMap<>(); // every sum is a new Long stored in the map: at least 24 bytes per upload, even when the JIT // removes the temporary boxes for the key and the size for (int i = 0; i < UPLOADS; i++) totals.merge(i % USERS, 1_000L + i % 9_000, Long::sum); return totals.values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum(); } static long primitiveTotals() { long[] totals = new long[USERS]; for (int i = 0; i < UPLOADS; i++) totals[i % USERS] += 1_000L + i % 9_000; // no objects long sum = 0; for (long t : totals) sum += t; return sum; } public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0) { long sum = args[0].equals("boxed") ? boxedTotals() : primitiveTotals(); System.out.println("finished inside the budget, total " + sum); return; } List<String> epsilon = List.of("-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions", "-XX:+UseEpsilonGC", "-Xmx64m"); for (String version : List.of("primitive", "boxed")) { System.out.println("== " + version); Jvm.lines(epsilon, EpsilonDemo.class.getName(), version).forEach(System.out::println); } } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l05.EpsilonDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l05/EpsilonDemo.java EpsilonDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l05 import workbench.memory.Jvm private const val UPLOADS = 5_000_000 private const val USERS = 500 private fun boxedTotals(): Long { val totals = HashMap<Int, Long>() // every sum is a new Long stored in the map: at least 24 bytes per upload, even when the JIT // removes the temporary boxes for the key and the size for (i in 0 until UPLOADS) totals.merge(i % USERS, 1_000L + i % 9_000) { a, b -> a + b } return totals.values.sum() } private fun primitiveTotals(): Long { val totals = LongArray(USERS) for (i in 0 until UPLOADS) totals[i % USERS] += 1_000L + i % 9_000 // no objects return totals.sum() } /** * Epsilon never frees anything, so a heap of 64 MB is an allocation budget. Two versions of lesson 2's * upload report (the bytes each user uploaded) run against that budget, each in its own child JVM. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isNotEmpty()) { val sum = if (args[0] == "boxed") boxedTotals() else primitiveTotals() println("finished inside the budget, total $sum") return } val epsilon = listOf("-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions", "-XX:+UseEpsilonGC", "-Xmx64m") for (version in listOf("primitive", "boxed")) { println("== $version") Jvm.lines(epsilon, "workbench.memory.l05.EpsilonDemoKt", version).forEach(::println) } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l05.EpsilonDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l05/EpsilonDemo.kt primitive prints finished inside the budget, total 27487500000. boxed prints Terminating due to java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space: five million new Long sums need at least 120 MB, and nothing is ever freed. On JDK 25, the boxed version finished with 1,000,000 uploads (at least 24 MB of sums) and failed every time with 2,000,000 (at least 48 MB, plus the JVM's own start-up and any temporary boxes the JIT didn't remove). A budget test should leave a wide margin for exactly that reason.

h: Low-pause collectors: ZGC, Shenandoah, and choosing a GC · Java and Kotlin
x: Report which collector runs, from inside the program GcReport.java // print once at startup, and on a timer if you like for (GarbageCollectorMXBean gc : ManagementFactory.getGarbageCollectorMXBeans()) { System.out.printf("%s: %d collections, %d ms%n", gc.getName(), gc.getCollectionCount(), gc.getCollectionTime()); } GcReport.kt // print once at startup, and on a timer if you like ManagementFactory.getGarbageCollectorMXBeans().forEach { gc -> println("${gc.name}: ${gc.collectionCount} collections, ${gc.collectionTime} ms") } Both versions call the same JDK API; Kotlin reads the getters as properties and puts the values straight into a string template. What differs is what the beans mean for each collector, as JDK 25 names them. G1 reports G1 Young Generation, G1 Concurrent GC and G1 Old Generation. ZGC reports ZGC Minor Cycles, ZGC Minor Pauses, ZGC Major Cycles and ZGC Major Pauses, and Shenandoah reports Shenandoah Pauses and Shenandoah Cycles. The time of a "Cycles" bean is concurrent work, not stopped time. A chart that adds up every bean's time as "GC pause" makes ZGC look like the slowest collector of all, the same trap as reading the 0.071 s in its log as a pause.

h: Low-pause collectors: ZGC, Shenandoah, and choosing a GC · Quiz
x: A JDK 25 program runs in a container with 2 CPUs and a 1.5 GiB memory limit, with no GC flag. Which collector does it run, and what changes on JDK 27? G1 on both, because G1 is the default collector Serial on JDK 25, because 1,536 MB is under 1,792 MB; G1 on JDK 27 Parallel on JDK 25, G1 on JDK 27 ZGC on JDK 27, because it became the default On JDK 21 to 26, G1 is chosen only on a server-class machine: 2 or more CPUs and at least 1,792 MB as the JVM sees them. 1.5 GiB is 1,536 MB, so this container gets Serial without anyone noticing. Per the JDK 27 source, JDK 27 selects G1 in all environments. ZGC has never been the default. A team moves a service in a 2-CPU container from G1 to ZGC. GC pauses drop below 0.1 ms, but the slowest requests get slower. What is the most likely reason? ZGC's pauses are longer than its log says ZGC can't see the container's CPU limit The heap is now too large for the region size ZGC's GC threads and load barriers take CPU from the request threads, and allocating threads may stall ZGC moves the work out of the pauses, not out of the program. With 2 CPUs, GC threads compete with request threads, every reference load runs a barrier, and if the collection can't keep up with allocation, threads stall waiting for memory. Look for Allocation Stall lines and a busy CPU. The JVM does read the container's CPU limit. Which flags select generational ZGC on JDK 21? -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+UseZGC -XX:ZGCMode=generational -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseZGC On JDK 21, plain -XX:+UseZGC gives the old single-generation ZGC, and -XX:+ZGenerational opts in to the generational one. JDK 23 made generational the default, and JDK 24 removed the old mode, so on JDK 25 -XX:+UseZGC alone is right and -XX:+ZGenerational only earns a warning. ZGC is not experimental, so it needs no extra switch. A test should prove that building one day's upload report from 50,000 lines allocates less than 200 MB in total. Which setup does that most directly? Run it in a child JVM with -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseEpsilonGC -Xmx200m and check that it finishes Run it with -Xmx200m and G1, and check there's no OutOfMemoryError Call System.gc() after it and check Runtime.totalMemory() Run it with ZGC and check the pause times Epsilon never frees anything, so finishing inside a 200 MB heap means the total allocation stayed under 200 MB, minus what the JVM's own start-up used. With G1 the code could allocate gigabytes and still fit in 200 MB, because the GC keeps freeing garbage. totalMemory() after a GC shows what's committed, not what was allocated. From lesson 4: G1's young pauses grow with the amount of live data they copy. Why don't ZGC's pauses grow the same way? ZGC copies live objects while the application runs, and its pauses only switch from one phase to the next ZGC never copies objects; it only marks them ZGC uses bigger regions, so there is less to copy ZGC skips the young generation G1 evacuates inside the stop-the-world pause, so the pause grows with the survivors. ZGC moves objects concurrently, and the load barrier lets application threads find, or even make, the moves. Its pauses do a small, fixed amount of work, and since JDK 16 even the thread stacks are scanned while threads run. ZGC does copy, and it has been generational since JDK 21.

h: Low-pause collectors: ZGC, Shenandoah, and choosing a GC · Key terms
x: ZGC A collector that marks and moves objects while the application runs; its pauses don't grow with the heap. Load barrier A few instructions the JIT adds after each reference load, to catch and repair references to moved objects. Colored pointer A reference with a few metadata bits that tell ZGC's barrier whether it can be used as it is. Concurrent relocation Moving live objects while application threads keep running. Allocation stall An application thread waiting for memory because a concurrent collection hasn't freed enough yet. Throughput How much useful work a program gets done per second of CPU. Server-class machine The JVM's test for picking G1 by default on JDK 21 to 26: 2 or more CPUs and at least 1,792 MB. Epsilon A collector that hands out memory but never frees it. For tests and benchmarks only. In Minor Collection (Allocation Rate) 852M(83%)->176M(17%) 0.071s from ZGC, what is 0.071 s? The whole concurrent collection, not a pause. The pauses are the Pause Mark Start, Pause Mark End and Pause Relocate Start lines. What does ZGC's load barrier do? After every reference load from the heap, it checks the reference's color bits. If they're stale, it finds the object's new address, moving the object if needed, and writes the repaired reference back into the field. What is a ZGC allocation stall? A thread waiting for memory because the heap filled before the concurrent collection finished. It means the heap is too small or the GC is short of CPU. Generational ZGC per JDK version? JDK 21: opt-in with -XX:+ZGenerational. JDK 23: the default. JDK 24 and later: the only mode. Which collector does JDK 25 pick with no GC flag in a 1-CPU container? Serial. G1 needs a server-class machine: 2 or more CPUs and at least 1,792 MB. JDK 27 picks G1 everywhere. How big is lesson 1's Thumbnail under ZGC on JDK 25, and why? 48 bytes instead of 40, because ZGC uses 8-byte references. With -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders it's 40 again. What is Epsilon good for? Tests and benchmarks: it never frees memory, so a heap size becomes an allocation budget. The JVM stops when the heap is full.

h: Low-pause collectors: ZGC, Shenandoah, and choosing a GC · Go deeper
x: The full -Xlog:gc* output of one ZGC minor collection on JDK 25 has more to read than the pause lines. These come from the same run as the lesson's log, trimmed: GC(3) Using 1 Workers for Young Generation GC(3) y: Allocation Stalls: 0 0 0 0 GC(3) y: Load: 26.33 (658%) / 23.99 (600%) / 24.50 (612%) GC(3) y: MMU: 2ms/98.4%, 5ms/99.1%, 10ms/99.4%, 20ms/99.5%, 50ms/99.8%, 100ms/99.9% GC(3) y: Eden 43M (4%) 770M (75%) 375 / 350 2 / 0 0 / 0 GC(3) y: Allocated: - 16M (2%) 22M (2%) 100M (10%) Using 1 Workers means ZGC chose one GC thread for this collection; the count is dynamic. Load is the machine's load average, here over six times its 4 cores: the busy machine this lesson keeps mentioning. MMU is minimum mutator utilization: 2ms/98.4% means that in every 2 ms window of this collection, the application got at least 98.4% of the time. It's a better latency number than pause length alone, because it also catches several pauses close together. The Eden row is lesson 4's generational hypothesis again: 43 MB live against 770 MB of garbage. Allocated is the headroom bill from section 2: 100 MB of new objects by the end of the collection. Allocation Stalls should stay all zeros. A prefix tells you which generation a line is about: y: for the young collection of a minor GC, Y: and O: for the young and old parts of a major GC. ZGC also gives memory back to the operating system on its own. ZUncommit is on by default and returns memory that has been unused for ZUncommitDelay, 300 seconds by default. G1 can shrink its heap after a full GC, and its periodic collection for idle programs is off by default (G1PeriodicGCInterval is 0). That difference can matter in a container: a ZGC program's memory can fall after a busy spell, while a G1 program may keep what it grew to.

h: Reading GC logs and sizing the heap in containers · The crew's logbook: one line per collection with -Xlog:gc
x: Each GC log line is an event on a timeline: pause lines stop every thread, concurrent ones run beside them; in a container the max heap defaults to 25% of the limit One flag makes the garbage collector (GC), the part of the JVM that frees objects nothing uses any more, write a line for every collection. Since JDK 9 the flag is -Xlog:gc, part of the JVM's unified logging system (older guides show -XX:+PrintGCDetails, which JDK 9 replaced). Here's the first line from G1, the default collector, on JDK 25, running the thumbnail service's stand-in load from lesson 4: [0.440s][info][gc] GC(0) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 28M->2M(214M) 8.692ms Read it left to right. [0.440s] is the time since the JVM started, [info] the log level and [gc] the tag, the topic of the line. GC(0) numbers the collection; a concurrent cycle, work the collector does while the program runs, gets a number of its own, and the pauses inside it reuse that number. Pause Young is the event. (Normal) says it's a young-only pause; Concurrent Start, Prepare Mixed and Mixed are the other kinds from lesson 4. (G1 Evacuation Pause) is the cause: eden, the area for new objects, was full. You'll also see G1 Humongous Allocation and System.gc() there. Then come the numbers. 28M->2M(214M) is the heap (the memory where objects live) in use before the pause, the heap in use after it, and the committed heap, the memory the operating system has really handed over. Last, 8.692ms is how long every application thread, every path of work in the program, was stopped. That's the line a person waiting on a request feels. One label changed between versions. When G1 runs out of free regions (lesson 4's equal blocks of heap) to copy into, JDK 21 writes (Evacuation Failure), and JDK 25 adds the reason, as in (Evacuation Failure: Allocation). Search for Evacuation Failure and you'll find both. -Xlog:gc*, with the star, turns on every GC tag: phases, region counts, metaspace and CPU time. That's ten to fifteen lines per pause, the detail lessons 4 and 5 used. For a service, write the log to rotating files with wall-clock times, so it survives a restart and can't fill the disk: -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/app/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m The colons separate the parts: what to log, where to write it, the decorations at the start of each line (time adds the date and time of day), and the rotation, here at most 5 files of 20 MB. A line then looks like this, from the demo below: [2026-11-17T07:31:28.846+0000][1.214s][info][gc ] GC(14) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) (Evacuation Failure: Allocation) 234M->101M(256M) 15.414ms Here a paper logbook and the JVM's part ways. When the current gc.log is full, the JVM renames it to a numbered file such as gc.log.0 and starts a fresh one, and with filecount=5 the oldest file is thrown away. Leave the log on in production. It costs a few lines per collection, and in an incident it's the first thing you'll want. A logbook of three hundred lines is hard to judge by eye, though. Write a GC log the production way Read GcLogFileDemo. It runs two seconds of the stand-in load from lesson 4 in a child JVM with a 256 MB heap, using the rotating-file setting from this section, at 40 KB per file so you can watch it rotate. Predict: will there be more than one file, and will the last young pause leave more or less heap behind than the first? Run it, then open the newest file, labs/memory/build/gc-logs/gc.log, and find a Pause Young line with its date and time. GcLogFileDemo.java package workbench.memory.l06; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import workbench.memory.l04.ServiceLoad; import java.io.IOException; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.List; import java.util.stream.Stream; /** * Runs two seconds of service load in a child JVM that writes its GC log the way a production service * should: to rotating files, with timestamps. Then it does the three checks you do first on any GC log. */ public class GcLogFileDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { if (args.length > 0) { ServiceLoad.run(2, 0.55); return; } Path dir = Files.createDirectories(Path.of("build", "gc-logs")); // labs/memory/build/gc-logs under Gradle try (Stream<Path> old = Files.list(dir)) { for (Path f : old.toList()) if (f.getFileName().toString().startsWith("gc.log")) Files.delete(f); } String logging = "-Xlog:gc*:file=" + dir.resolve("gc.log") + ":time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=3,filesize=40k"; Jvm.lines(List.of("-XX:+UseG1GC", "-Xmx256m", logging), GcLogFileDemo.class.getName(), "load"); System.out.println("last young pause: " + young.get(young.size() - 1).substring(young.get(young.size() - 1).indexOf("GC("))); } System.out.println("logs are in " + dir.toAbsolutePath()); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l06.GcLogFileDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l06/GcLogFileDemo.java GcLogFileDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l06 import workbench.memory.Jvm import workbench.memory.l04.serviceLoad import java.nio.file.Files import java.nio.file.Path import kotlin.io.path.createDirectories import kotlin.io.path.deleteExisting import kotlin.io.path.name import kotlin.io.path.fileSize import kotlin.io.path.listDirectoryEntries import kotlin.io.path.readLines /** * Runs two seconds of service load in a child JVM that writes its GC log the way a production service * should: to rotating files, with timestamps.
