On JDK 25 the run behind this lesson found 2 Pause Full lines and 7 to 13 lines with Evacuation Failure, because this heap is too small for its cache on purpose. The first young pause goes 29M->2M (14M->1M on JDK 21), and the last ones leave 120 to 245 MB behind: the floor rose as the cache filled. JDK 21 shows more evacuation failures, about 20. The counts change from run to run. The java command, JDK 25 man page source: -Xlog docs

h: Reading GC logs and sizing the heap in containers · From three hundred lines to five numbers: what to check first
x: A few numbers say most of what a GC log knows: the number of pauses and their total time; divided by the elapsed time, that's the share of time your threads were stopped; the longest pause, which is what your slowest requests feel; the number of full GCs (collections of the whole heap, with every thread stopped) and evacuation failures, which should be zero in a healthy G1 program; the heap after the last full GC, which is the live set at that moment, the objects really still in use, and the number you size a heap from; the trend of the after-values of young pauses: a floor that keeps rising means the live set is growing. Computing them has two traps. The first is that not every line with a duration is a pause. Concurrent Mark Cycle 25.055ms ran beside the application. G1's Evacuate Collection Set: 21.05ms is one phase inside a pause the log already counted on its Pause Young line. ZGC's Minor Collection ... 0.071s from lesson 5 is a whole concurrent collection. One rule works for every HotSpot collector: a pause line has Pause right after GC(id) and ends with a duration in ms. ZGC puts y:, Y: or O: between the two. The second trap is (System.gc()), which has parentheses inside its parentheses and breaks the obvious regular expression. The lab builds a parser with that rule, and tests it on lines copied from real runs: all five collectors on JDK 21, and G1 on JDK 25. Check yourself on a stretch of the demo's JDK 25 log, with the decorations cut off. It's a G1 cycle like the one in lesson 4: GC(16) Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Humongous Allocation) 205M->158M(256M) 8.143ms GC(17) Concurrent Mark Cycle GC(17) Pause Remark 185M->185M(256M) 0.447ms GC(17) Pause Cleanup 185M->185M(256M) 0.085ms GC(17) Concurrent Mark Cycle 25.055ms GC(18) Pause Young (Prepare Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) (Evacuation Failure: Allocation) 248M->142M(256M) 3.544ms GC(19) Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) (Evacuation Failure: Allocation) 248M->211M(256M) 14.287ms How many pauses are there, how long did they take together, and is this heap healthy? (Five pauses: Concurrent Start, Remark, Cleanup, Prepare Mixed and Mixed, 26.5 ms in all. The two Concurrent Mark Cycle lines are not pauses. Two evacuation failures in a row say the heap is too small for what's live. A full GC a little later in the same log, Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 224M->84M(256M), puts the live set at 84 MB.) The log tells you how full the floor gets. How big the JVM makes the floor in the first place depends on where it runs.

h: Reading GC logs and sizing the heap in containers · How the JVM sizes its heap from the container's memory limit
x: A container is a way to run a program in a fenced-off part of a shared machine. On Linux, the kernel (the core of the operating system) enforces the fence with a feature called cgroups: a memory limit and a CPU limit for a group of processes. In the warehouse, the container is a rented plot on a shared site. The lease says how much ground the building may cover. The JVM reads that lease. UseContainerSupport is on by default in every JDK from 21 to 27, so the JVM sizes itself from the container's limits, not the whole machine's. Without heap flags, the max heap is 25% of the memory limit (MaxRAMPercentage, default 25). A container with a 1 GiB limit gets a 256 MB heap. That's a cautious default: three quarters of the plot stays free unless the program uses it outside the heap. Very small limits get a bigger share: with a 256 MB limit, JDK 25 picked a 126 MB heap, because MinRAMPercentage (50) applies there. -XX:MaxRAMPercentage changes the share. With 75, the same container gets 768 MB. Prefer it over a fixed -Xmx, because the heap then follows the limit when someone gives the container more memory. Watch the top end: in a 64 GB container, 75% is 48 GB, and lesson 1's compressed references switch off, so every reference grows from 4 bytes to 8. -XX:InitialRAMPercentage sets the starting heap. It was 1.5625% on JDK 21 to 25; per the JDK source, it is 0 on JDK 26, where the JVM starts from a small minimum and grows. To see what the JVM detected, run java -XshowSettings:system -version inside the container. On the machine behind this lesson, JDK 25 printed Provider: cgroupv1, Effective CPU Count: 4 and Memory Limit: 13.35G. -Xlog:os+container=debug shows the detection step by step, which helps when the numbers look wrong. The demo can't create a container, so it uses -XX:MaxRAM, which tells the JVM how much memory to plan for, as a stand-in for a limit. That works on JDK 21 to 25. JDK 26 deprecated MaxRAM, and per the JDK source, JDK 27 removed it; there, try the same flags in a real container. Whatever share you pick, though, the heap is only part of the building. Watch the heap follow the limit Predict the max heap for limits of 1, 2 and 4 GiB, with defaults and with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75. Run HeapSizingDemo (JDK 21 to 25). Each line comes from a child JVM started with -XX:MaxRAM as the limit. If you have Docker, a common tool for running programs in containers, run docker run --rm --memory=1g eclipse-temurin:25 java -XshowSettings:system -version and find the memory limit it reports. In a container, -XshowSettings:system reports the limit you gave it, for example Memory Limit: 1.00G. -Xmx equal to the limit leaves no room for the rest of the process. A percentage leaves room for it and for headroom. arguments.cpp at jdk-25-ga: heap sizing from available memory read

h: Reading GC logs and sizing the heap in containers · When -Xmx equals the limit, the kernel ends the whole process
x: Here's the setting that looks right and fails: a container with a 1 GiB limit and -Xmx1g. Lesson 1 already showed why it can't work. The heap is the storage floor, and the building also has desks (thread stacks), a back room with the plans (metaspace), the code cache, the crew's own records, and the yard out back (direct buffers, memory a program asks for outside the heap). In the demo below, a JDK 25 process with a 256 MB heap, one 64 MiB direct buffer and 56 threads had 379 MB in RAM. Scale that to -Xmx1g, and the process needs well over 1 GiB once its heap fills. The failure doesn't look like a Java error. When a process goes over its cgroup limit, the kernel's OOM killer, its out-of-memory guard, ends it at once with SIGKILL, the signal no program can catch. The exit code is 137 (128 plus signal number 9). There's no OutOfMemoryError, no heap dump and nothing in the program's log. The kernel doesn't leave a note. The program can run fine for hours first, because Linux counts only the pages a process has touched, its resident memory, and the heap touches its pages bit by bit as it fills. The demo uses -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch to touch the whole heap at startup. Without it, the same process showed 118 MB resident instead of 379. So budget the whole building: the heap, plus direct buffers, plus metaspace and code cache, plus a stack for each thread, plus the GC's bookkeeping, plus headroom. -Xmx sizes the storage floor, not the building. Leave room for the rest. Direct buffers need a cap of their own. Unless you set -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, the JDK allows direct buffers up to the max heap size, so a program could in theory ask for twice its heap. Network libraries often keep socket data in direct buffers. My starting point for a service is -XX:MaxRAMPercentage between 50 and 75, a -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize that fits what the program's I/O needs, and a bounded number of threads. Then measure under load with Native Memory Tracking, which lesson 7 covers, and adjust. The limit of today's tools shows here too. The GC log sees only the heap, and the kernel's verdict comes with no explanation. To see the rest of the building, you need the JVM's own inventory of it. Compare the heap with the whole process Read FootprintDemo. Its child JVM has -Xmx256m -Xms256m -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch, allocates a 64 MiB direct buffer and starts 50 threads. Then it prints what the JVM reports next to what Linux says is resident in RAM. Predict the resident number before you run it. Run it. Then remove -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch from the demo and run it again. FootprintDemo.java package workbench.memory.l06; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.lang.management.BufferPoolMXBean; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.lang.management.MemoryMXBean; import java.nio.ByteBuffer; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; /** * A child JVM with -Xmx256m that does what services do: a 64 MiB direct buffer (network code often uses * these for socket data) and 50 threads. It then compares what the JVM reports with what the operating system says it uses. */ public class FootprintDemo { static final long MB = 1024 * 1024; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length == 0) { // AlwaysPreTouch touches every heap page at startup, like a service that has run for a while Jvm.run(List.of("-Xmx256m", "-Xms256m", "-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch"), FootprintDemo.class.getName(), "child"); return; } ByteBuffer direct = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect((int) (64 * MB)); CountDownLatch never = new CountDownLatch(1); for (int i = 0; i < 50; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { try { never.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { } }); t.setDaemon(true); t.start(); } MemoryMXBean memory = ManagementFactory.getMemoryMXBean(); long directBytes = ManagementFactory.getPlatformMXBeans(BufferPoolMXBean.class).stream() .filter(p -> p.getName().equals("direct")).mapToLong(BufferPoolMXBean::getMemoryUsed).sum(); System.out.printf("heap committed %,5d MB (-Xmx256m)%n", memory.getHeapMemoryUsage().getCommitted() / MB); System.out.printf("non-heap committed %,5d MB (metaspace, class space, code cache)%n", memory.getNonHeapMemoryUsage().getCommitted() / MB); System.out.printf("direct buffers %,5d MB%n", directBytes / MB); System.out.printf("live threads %,5d (each with its own stack)%n", ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().getThreadCount()); Path status = Path.of("/proc/self/status"); if (Files.exists(status)) { // Linux only Files.readAllLines(status).stream().filter(l -> l.startsWith("VmRSS")).forEach(l -> System.out.printf("resident in RAM %,5d MB (what the container limit counts)%n", Long.parseLong(l.replaceAll("\\D+", "")) / 1024)); } else { System.out.println("resident in RAM not available here (/proc is Linux only)"); } System.out.println("buffer " + direct.capacity()); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l06.FootprintDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l06/FootprintDemo.java FootprintDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l06 import workbench.memory.Jvm import java.lang.management.BufferPoolMXBean import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import java.nio.ByteBuffer import java.nio.file.Path import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.io.path.exists import kotlin.io.path.readLines private const val MB = 1024L * 1024 /** * A child JVM with -Xmx256m that does what services do: a 64 MiB direct buffer (network code often uses * these for socket data) and 50 threads. It then compares what the JVM reports with what the operating system says it uses. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isEmpty()) { // AlwaysPreTouch touches every heap page at startup, like a service that has run for a while Jvm.run(listOf("-Xmx256m", "-Xms256m", "-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch"), "workbench.memory.l06.FootprintDemoKt", "child") return } val direct = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect((64 * MB).toInt()) val never = CountDownLatch(1) repeat(50) { thread(isDaemon = true) { try { never.await() } catch (e: InterruptedException) { } } } val memory = ManagementFactory.getMemoryMXBean() val directBytes = ManagementFactory.getPlatformMXBeans(BufferPoolMXBean::class.java) .filter { it.name == "direct" }.sumOf { it.memoryUsed } println("heap committed %,5d MB (-Xmx256m)".format(memory.heapMemoryUsage.committed / MB)) println("non-heap committed %,5d MB (metaspace, class space, code cache)".format(memory.nonHeapMemoryUsage.committed / MB)) println("direct buffers %,5d MB".format(directBytes / MB)) println("live threads %,5d (each with its own stack)".format(ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().threadCount)) val status = Path.of("/proc/self/status") if (status.exists()) { // Linux only status.readLines().filter { it.startsWith("VmRSS") }.forEach { println("resident in RAM %,5d MB (what the container limit counts)".format(it.filter(Char::isDigit).toLong() / 1024)) } } else { println("resident in RAM not available here (/proc is Linux only)") } println("buffer ${direct.capacity()}") } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l06.FootprintDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l06/FootprintDemo.kt On Linux with JDK 25: heap committed 256 MB, non-heap 8 to 16 MB, direct buffers 64 MB, 56 live threads, and about 379 MB resident, roughly 120 MB more than the heap. Without AlwaysPreTouch the resident number drops to about 118 MB, because most heap pages haven't been touched yet; a running service gets there anyway as its heap fills. On macOS or Windows the demo can't read the resident size and says so.

Kotlin reads getTotalMemorySize() as a property and writes >> as shr. The value of the line is in what it reports. On the machine behind this lesson, JDK 25 printed memory seen 13674 MB, CPUs 4, max heap 3420 MB: 13,674 MB is the container's 13.35 GiB limit, while the machine itself has about 16 GB, and the max heap is a quarter of the limit. availableProcessors() follows the CPU limit the same way. h: Reading GC logs and sizing the heap in containers · Worked example
x: Size the thumbnail service's container from measurements Start from numbers you measured, not from defaults. Suppose a realistic load test of the thumbnail service measured these: the heap left after its full GCs, from the GC log, and everything outside the heap, from Native Memory Tracking (lesson 7). live set (heap after a full GC) 310 MB outside the heap, from NMT: metaspace and class space 95 MB code cache 45 MB thread stacks (140 threads) 35 MB GC bookkeeping 40 MB direct buffers (network I/O) 70 MB Size the heap from the live set. G1 copies, so it needs free regions to copy into: give it two to three times the live set, about 768 MB. Add up the whole building, and leave headroom for what the test didn't hit: a busier hour, a burst of threads, a code cache that grows later in the day. heap 768 MB outside the heap 285 MB (95 + 45 + 35 + 40 + 70) headroom, about 15% 160 MB ------ process ~1,213 MB -> ask for a 1.25 GiB (1,280 MB) limit heap share 768 / 1,280 = 60% Write flags that follow the limit, cap direct memory a little above what NMT showed, and keep the logbook. Then run the load test again and check two things: no Pause Full in the log, and resident memory well under the limit. -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=60 -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=96m -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/app/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m

h: Reading GC logs and sizing the heap in containers · Lab
x: Parse real GC log lines into pause numbers labs/memory/src/main/kotlin/workbench/memory/l06/GcLog.kt labs/memory/src/main/kotlin/workbench/memory/l06/GcPause.kt ./gradlew :memory:test --tests 'workbench.memory.l06.*' Run the tests. All eleven fail. Open GcLogTest.kt: every line in it comes from a real JDK 21 or JDK 25 run. Write parsePause with one regular expression: GC(id), an optional y:, Y: or O:, then Pause and the capitalized words after it, then zero or more ( ... ) labels, then an optional 14M->1M(256M), then the duration in ms at the end of the line. Pull the labels out of their group with a second, smaller regex, and turn missing heap numbers into null. Write summarize: the count, the total, the longest, the full GCs, the evacuation failures (any label that starts with Evacuation Failure, so JDK 25's Evacuation Failure: Allocation counts too), and the after-value of the last full GC. Run the tests until all eleven pass. Then point the parser at the log the first demo wrote, in labs/memory/build/gc-logs. A raw string ("""...""") saves you from doubling every backslash in a Kotlin regex. A label is \((?:[^()]|\(\))*\): an opening parenthesis, then any characters that are not parentheses or the exact pair (), then the closing one. That's what lets (System.gc()) through. Anchor the duration with ms$, so ZGC's 0.071s and the start lines without a duration don't match. Call trimEnd() on the line first. m.destructured gives you the groups as val (id, kind, labels, before, after, committed, ms) = .... An empty optional group comes back as "", and toIntOrNull() turns that into null. For the evacuation failures, p.labels.any { it.startsWith("Evacuation Failure") } matches both versions of the label. All 11 tests in GcLogTest pass. By the end you can read a unified GC log line field by field, turn a log into pause numbers with a small parser, and size the heap of a program in a container so the kernel doesn't kill it.

h: Reading GC logs and sizing the heap in containers · Quiz
x: Which of these log lines is a stop-the-world pause? GC(17) Concurrent Mark Cycle 25.055ms GC(17) Pause Remark 185M->185M(256M) 0.447ms GC(3) Minor Collection (Allocation Rate) 852M(83%)->176M(17%) 0.071s GC(2) Evacuate Collection Set: 21.05ms Remark is one of the two short pauses that finish G1's concurrent marking. The mark cycle itself ran beside the application. ZGC's Minor Collection time is the whole concurrent collection. Evacuate Collection Set is a phase inside a young pause, whose own Pause Young line already counts it. A JDK 25 program runs in a container with a 2 GiB memory limit and no heap flags. What max heap does the JVM pick? 2 GB 1.5 GB 1 GB 512 MB With container support on, the JVM bases the heap on the memory limit and takes MaxRAMPercentage, 25% by default: 512 MB. The demo showed the same arithmetic for 1, 2 and 4 GiB. To use more, set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage, for example 60 or 75. Over ten minutes, a service's young pauses end at 310M, 355M, 402M, 447M and 495M, and a full GC finally goes 1490M->1210M(1536M). What is going on? The live set keeps growing, which points to a leak or a cache with no limit The young generation is too small; make it bigger G1's pause goal is too strict Nothing: G1 always lets the heap fill before collecting The after-values of young pauses are what survives, and their floor rises about 45 MB each time. Even a full GC frees only 280 MB of 1,490 MB: 1.2 GB is really live. A bigger heap only delays the moment it fills; lesson 7 finds what's holding the memory. A container has a 1 GiB limit. The service runs with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 and a network library that keeps socket data in direct buffers, with no other memory flags. Which flag should you add first? -Xmx1g -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=100 -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, with a value that fits what the network code needs -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError, to catch the OOM kill Without MaxDirectMemorySize, direct buffers may grow up to the max heap size, here 768 MB on top of a 768 MB heap in a 1 GiB container. Capping them makes the budget real. -Xmx1g and 100% make the problem worse, and a heap dump is never written when the kernel kills the process. From lesson 5: a ZGC service logs Allocation Stall (main) 0.895ms lines whenever it gets busy. What do they mean? Normal ZGC pauses, which always take about a millisecond Threads waited for memory because the heap filled before the concurrent collection finished The JIT stopped to compile a method A full GC ran ZGC's pauses stay well under a millisecond. A stall means a thread asked for memory and had to wait, because the program allocated faster than ZGC could reclaim. The fixes are more heap headroom, more CPU for the GC threads, or less allocation.

h: Reading GC logs and sizing the heap in containers · Key terms
x: Unified logging The JVM's logging system since JDK 9, configured with -Xlog. Decorations The bracketed fields at the start of each log line: time, uptime, level, tags. Live set The objects that are really still in use. A full GC's after-value shows it. Container A program running in a fenced-off part of a shared machine, with its own memory and CPU limits. MaxRAMPercentage The share of the memory limit the JVM uses as its max heap. Default 25. Resident memory (RSS) The pages of a process that are really in RAM: what a container's memory limit counts. OOM killer The Linux kernel's guard that kills a process that goes over its memory limit. In GC(0) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 28M->2M(214M) 8.692ms, what are 28M, 2M and 214M? Heap in use before the pause, heap in use after it, and the committed heap size. How do you recognize a pause line in any HotSpot GC log? Pause right after GC(id) (ZGC adds y:, Y: or O: in between), and a duration in ms at the end. What GC logging setting suits production? -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m: rotating files with wall-clock times. What max heap does a JVM pick in a container by default? 25% of the container's memory limit (MaxRAMPercentage = 25). Very small limits get up to 50% (MinRAMPercentage). Why does -Xmx equal to the container limit get the process killed? Metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, GC data and direct buffers come on top of the heap, so the process goes over the cgroup limit and the kernel kills it. What does exit code 137 mean for a JVM in a container? The kernel's OOM killer sent SIGKILL (128 + 9). No OutOfMemoryError, no heap dump, nothing in the log. What is the default limit for direct buffers? The max heap size, unless you set -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize.

h: Reading GC logs and sizing the heap in containers · Go deeper
x: Three settings change around the JDK versions this course covers, all read from the JDK source. InitialRAMPercentage was 1.5625 on JDK 21 to 25 and is 0 on JDK 26, where the JVM computes the initial heap from a minimum size instead. A program that used to start with a heap of 1/64 of its limit now starts smaller and grows, so expect a few more young pauses in the first seconds unless you set -Xms or -XX:InitialRAMPercentage yourself. MaxRAM is deprecated on JDK 26 and obsolete on JDK 27, together with the switches that forced or blocked "server-class" behaviour. On 27, test heap sizing in a real container. -XX:+UseContainerSupport is on in every version from 21 to 27, and -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=N overrides the CPU count the JVM detects. That count matters more than it looks. Lesson 5 showed that on JDK 21 to 26 a single CPU silently means Serial GC, and the number of GC worker threads follows the count too. Two flags help with Java's own OutOfMemoryError, the one that happens inside the limit. -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError writes a heap dump (lesson 7 reads one). -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError makes the JVM exit, so whatever started the container can start a fresh one, instead of a program that limps on with threads that died halfway through their work. Both are off by default, and neither helps with a kernel OOM kill.

h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · A box nobody needs, still on a note: what a Java leak is
x: The garbage collector, the JVM's cleaning crew, frees every object on the heap (the memory where objects live) that it can't reach from a GC root. (A GC root is a starting point it trusts: a local variable on a thread's stack, one of the workers' desks, or a static field, the noticeboard by the door.) So in Java, a leak is memory that stays reachable from a root after the program is done with it. The collector is doing its job. Your code still holds the reference. Here's the classic one, a thumbnail cache with no limit. It's a static map from an upload id to its thumbnail, so the service can send the same picture again without redoing the work: Java static final Map<String, CachedThumbnail> THUMBNAILS = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // never evicted static void handle(String uploadId) { THUMBNAILS.computeIfAbsent(uploadId, id -> new CachedThumbnail(id, System.currentTimeMillis(), FORMATS.get(0), new byte[2_048])); } Kotlin private val THUMBNAILS = ConcurrentHashMap<String, KCachedThumbnail>() // never evicted private fun handle(uploadId: String) { THUMBNAILS.computeIfAbsent(uploadId) { id -> KCachedThumbnail(id, System.currentTimeMillis(), FORMATS[0], ByteArray(2_048)) } } FORMATS is a static list of the picture formats the site accepts, and each thumbnail points at one of its strings; that will matter in the next section. Every upload adds an entry, and nothing ever removes one. Lesson 6 showed what that looks like in a GC log: the after-values of young pauses rise pass after pass, full GCs (collections of the whole heap) free less and less, and in the end the JVM throws OutOfMemoryError or spends its time in Pause Full. The same shape turns up in four places, over and over: maps and caches with no limit and no expiry; ThreadLocal values, a separate value per thread, set on the threads of a thread pool and never removed, so each pool thread keeps its last value forever (the threads track showed one); listeners, objects registered to be called back when something happens, that nobody unregisters (lesson 3's weak registry is one fix); class loaders, the parts of the JVM that load a program's classes, that can't be unloaded, which shows up as growth in metaspace, the back room where class plans live, and as collections with the cause Metadata GC Threshold. The first tool is a class histogram: a count of live objects, and their bytes, for every class. jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram prints one after a full GC, so it counts only reachable objects. (jcmd is the JDK's tool for sending commands to a running JVM, and <pid> is its process id.) For the cache above, after 20,000 uploads on JDK 25, the top four rows were: num #instances #bytes class name (module) 1: 52891 43157184 [B (java.base@25.0.5.0.3) 2: 32777 786648 java.lang.String (java.base@25.0.5.0.3) 3: 22654 724928 java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap$Node (java.base@25.0.5.0.3) 4: 20000 640000 workbench.memory.l07.LeakDemo$CachedThumbnail [B means byte[]. Exactly 20,000 thumbnails of 32 bytes each are alive, 20,000 more than anyone meant to keep. That's the clue. The histogram tells you what fills the floor. It can't tell you who holds it. Leak, count, dump Read LeakDemo. Its first child JVM handles 20,000 uploads with the cache above, prints the top of the class histogram, writes a heap dump, and measures what the cache keeps alive. Its second child has -Xmx64m -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError and handles uploads until the heap is full. Predict: which class tops the histogram, and how many CachedThumbnail objects are alive? Run it. h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · A photo of every shelf: heap dumps, retained size and the dominator tree
x: From a heap dump to the leak: retained size and the dominator tree A heap dump is a file with every object on the heap and every reference between them, in a format called HPROF. It's a photograph of every shelf, taken for a detective. You can take one three ways: jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/app.hprof from a running JVM. Its help text says "Impact: High": it runs a full GC first (unless you pass -all) and stops the JVM while it writes. -gz compresses the file, and on JDK 25 -parallel sets how many threads write it. -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError with -XX:HeapDumpPath=..., so the JVM writes one the moment it runs out of heap. It's off by default. It's a manageable flag, so jcmd <pid> VM.set_flag HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError true turns it on in a running JVM. HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean.dumpHeap(path, true) from code, which is what the demo does. You read the photograph with a tool such as Eclipse MAT (Memory Analyzer), a free program from the Eclipse project. It shows two sizes for every object. The shallow size is the object's own bytes: lesson 1's header plus fields. The retained size is everything that would be freed if that one object were gone: the object itself plus everything reachable only through it. You can work out a retained size by hand on a small graph, and doing it once makes MAT's numbers obvious. Look at the figure. The noticeboard's static field holds the map. The map holds a table, the table holds 20,000 nodes, and each node holds a key and a thumbnail with its 2 KB of pixels. Every path from a root to those pixels goes through the map, so the map dominates them, and they're in its retained set. Add it up: 20,000 pixel arrays at 2,064 bytes, keys at 80, thumbnails at 32 and nodes at 32, plus the 128 KB table. That's about 44 MB, held by a 64-byte object. The shared "image/jpeg" string is different. The FORMATS list, another static field, reaches it too, so dropping the map wouldn't free it. It isn't in the map's retained set. Is the arithmetic right? Let's not take my word for it. The demo measures the live heap after a full GC, clears the map, and measures again. On JDK 25 it printed: live heap 47,259,896 bytes with the cache full, 2,763,024 after clear(): it kept 44,496,872 bytes alive That's 44.5 MB, the retained set we added up, give or take a little noise. (clear() keeps the map's table, which the hand count included.) MAT's dominator tree lists objects by retained size, biggest first. For this dump, the map should sit at the top with about 44 MB, and its path to a GC root should name the static field THUMBNAILS. (I couldn't run MAT for this course, so that's what the definition and the measurement predict, not a screenshot.) A histogram says what fills the floor. The dominator tree says who holds it. Fix the holder. Here the photograph picture breaks. A photo shows one moment, while a leak is a habit: the code adds a note on every upload. You find the list in the dump, but you fix it in the code that keeps writing it. And a photograph of the floor can't show what isn't on the floor. Find the holder in Eclipse MAT Download Eclipse Memory Analyzer (MAT) from the Eclipse website, and open labs/memory/build/heapdumps/leak.hprof from the previous demo. Before you click anything, predict the top entry of the dominator tree and its retained size, from the figure and the demo's last line. Open the dominator tree. Then, on the biggest entry, use "Path to GC Roots" to find the field that holds it. From the definition and the measurement, the ConcurrentHashMap should top the dominator tree with a retained size of about 44 MB, almost all of it in 2 KB byte[] pixel arrays. Its path to a GC root should end at the static field THUMBNAILS of LeakDemo. If your top entry is something else, compare its retained size with the histogram's byte counts and follow its path to the root the same way. Everything below the map is reachable only through it, so it is the map's retained set. The shared format string has another root, so the map doesn't retain it. Eclipse MAT help: dominator tree docs Eclipse MAT help: shallow and retained heap docs

h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · The yard out back: Native Memory Tracking finds growth outside the heap
x: Sometimes the heap is fine and the process still grows. The GC log shows a flat floor, a heap dump shows nothing odd, and the container still gets killed. The memory is outside the heap, in the yard out back that the floor plan doesn't show. Native Memory Tracking (NMT) is the JVM's own inventory of the memory it uses, the yard included. It's off by default. Start the JVM with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, then ask the running process: jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary scale=MB In the demo, a JDK 25 process with a 256 MB heap had committed 295 MB at startup (committed means the operating system has really handed it over). Then it allocated one 64 MiB direct buffer, memory outside the heap that ByteBuffer.allocateDirect asks for, and started 100 threads. Now it had committed 370 MB. NMT shows where the difference went. A category called Other appeared with 64 MB, the direct buffer. Thread went from 1 MB to 11 MB committed, with 120 MB reserved (addresses set aside, not yet used), because each new thread reserves about 1 MB for its stack but touches only a little of it. For a slow leak, take a baseline and compare later: jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff scale=MB The diff marks every change. After 100 direct buffers of 1 MiB, JDK 25 printed: - Other (reserved=100MB +100MB, committed=100MB +100MB) (malloc=100MB +100MB #102 +100) A growing Other points at direct buffers or native code, a growing Thread at threads that are started and never stopped, and a growing Class or Metaspace at class loaders. Direct buffers deserve one more level of detail. ByteBuffer.allocateDirect creates a small object on the heap that owns the native memory. When the GC collects that small object, a cleaner frees the memory, the same idea as lesson 3's Cleaner. In the warehouse, each crate in the yard has a tag on the floor, and the crate goes only when the crew throws out its tag. So native memory waits for a collection, and a big, quiet heap may not collect for a long time. Unless you set -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, the limit for all of it is the max heap size. Set it, and a direct-buffer leak fails loudly instead of quietly, with a stack trace that points at the code: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Cannot reserve 67108864 bytes of direct buffer memory (allocated: 0, limit: 33554432) A crate that leaves only when the crew passes by is awkward, though. Sometimes you know exactly when you're done with it. Watch native memory move Read NmtDemo. Its first child runs with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary and prints NMT's summary before and after a 64 MiB direct buffer and 100 threads. Its second child asks for 64 MiB of direct memory under -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=32m. Predict which NMT categories change, and by how much. Then run it. NmtDemo.java package workbench.memory.l07; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import javax.management.ObjectName; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.nio.ByteBuffer; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.regex.Matcher; import java.util.regex.Pattern; /** * Native Memory Tracking from inside a child JVM: the summary before and after a 64 MiB direct buffer * and 100 extra threads. Then a direct buffer that doesn't fit under -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize. */ public class NmtDemo { static final Pattern CATEGORY = Pattern.compile("^-?\\s*(Total|[A-Z][\\w ]+?):? \\(?reserved=(\\d+)MB, committed=(\\d+)MB"); static String nativeMemory() throws Exception { // the same as: jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary scale=MB return (String) ManagementFactory.getPlatformMBeanServer().invoke( new ObjectName("com.sun.management:type=DiagnosticCommand"), "vmNativeMemory", new Object[] {new String[] {"summary", "scale=MB"}}, new String[] {String[].class.getName()}); } static void print(String title) throws Exception { System.out.println(title); for (String line : nativeMemory().lines().toList()) { Matcher m = CATEGORY.matcher(line); if (m.find()) System.out.printf(" %-20s committed %,5d MB (reserved %,5d MB)%n", m.group(1), Long.parseLong(m.group(3)), Long.parseLong(m.group(2))); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length == 0) { Jvm.run(List.of("-Xmx256m", "-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary"), NmtDemo.class.getName(), "track"); Jvm.run(List.of("-Xmx256m", "-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=32m"), NmtDemo.class.getName(), "limit"); return; } if (args[0].equals("limit")) { try { ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(64 * 1024 * 1024); } catch (OutOfMemoryError e) { System.out.println("with -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=32m: " + e); } return; } print("at startup"); ByteBuffer direct = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(64 * 1024 * 1024); // network code often keeps socket data in these CountDownLatch never = new CountDownLatch(1); for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { try { never.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { } }); t.setDaemon(true); t.start(); } print("after a 64 MiB direct buffer and 100 more threads"); System.out.println("buffer " + direct.capacity()); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l07.NmtDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l07/NmtDemo.java NmtDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l07 import workbench.memory.Jvm import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import java.nio.ByteBuffer import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import javax.management.ObjectName import kotlin.concurrent.thread private val CATEGORY = Regex("""^-?\s*(Total|[A-Z][\w ]+?):? \(?reserved=(\d+)MB, committed=(\d+)MB""") // the same as: jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary scale=MB private fun nativeMemory(): String = ManagementFactory.getPlatformMBeanServer().invoke( ObjectName("com.sun.management:type=DiagnosticCommand"), "vmNativeMemory", arrayOf<Any>(arrayOf("summary", "scale=MB")), arrayOf(Array<String>::class.java.name)) as String private fun printNmt(title: String) { println(title) nativeMemory().lines().mapNotNull { CATEGORY.find(it) }.forEach { m -> val (name, reserved, committed) = m.destructured println(" %-20s committed %,5d MB (reserved %,5d MB)".format(name, committed.toLong(), reserved.toLong())) } } /** * Native Memory Tracking from inside a child JVM: the summary before and after a 64 MiB direct buffer * and 100 extra threads. Then a direct buffer that doesn't fit under -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isEmpty()) { Jvm.run(listOf("-Xmx256m", "-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary"), "workbench.memory.l07.NmtDemoKt", "track") Jvm.run(listOf("-Xmx256m", "-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=32m"), "workbench.memory.l07.NmtDemoKt", "limit") return } if (args[0] == "limit") { try { ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(64 * 1024 * 1024) } catch (e: OutOfMemoryError) { println("with -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=32m: $e") } return } printNmt("at startup") val direct = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(64 * 1024 * 1024) // network code often keeps socket data in these val never = CountDownLatch(1) repeat(100) { thread(isDaemon = true) { try { never.await() } catch (e: InterruptedException) { } } } printNmt("after a 64 MiB direct buffer and 100 more threads") println("buffer ${direct.capacity()}") } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l07.NmtDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l07/NmtDemo.kt Java Heap stays at 216 MB committed. Other appears with 64 MB, the direct buffer. Thread grows from about 1 MB to 11 MB committed and from 18 MB to about 120 MB reserved: 100 stacks of about 1 MB each, mostly untouched. Total committed rises by about 75 MB, from 295 to 370 MB on JDK 25. The second child prints Cannot reserve 67108864 bytes of direct buffer memory (allocated: 0, limit: 33554432).

h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · Off-heap memory with a return date: arenas in the FFM API
x: The Foreign Function and Memory API (FFM), final since JDK 22 (JEP 454), gives memory outside the heap a lifetime you control. Memory comes from an arena, and the arena decides when that memory is freed. In the warehouse, an arena is a corner of the yard rented with a return date, handed back all at once. Arena Lifetime Closed by Threads Arena.global() until the JVM exits nobody any Arena.ofAuto() until the GC finds it unreachable the GC any Arena.ofConfined() until you call close() you, from the owner thread the owner only Arena.ofShared() until you call close() you, from any thread any A confined arena in try-with-resources frees its memory at the closing brace. No GC is involved, so there's nothing to wait for. A memory segment is the block of memory an arena hands out: Java try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) { MemorySegment block = arena.allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024); // 32 MiB outside the heap block.setAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 0, 1_999); } // freed here Kotlin Arena.ofConfined().use { arena -> val block = arena.allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024) // 32 MiB outside the heap block.setAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 0, 1_999) } // freed here If code uses a segment after its arena is closed, it gets an IllegalStateException with the message Already closed. In C, the same mistake reads freed memory and may silently corrupt data. The accounting holds a surprise on JDK 25. NMT counts the confined arena's memory under Other: Other (reserved=32MB, committed=32MB) inside the arena, and 0MB after close(). But the JDK's direct buffer pool, and with it -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, counts only automatic arenas. In JDK 25's source, one line decides it: an arena counts its memory as direct memory only when the GC manages the arena's lifetime. That makes sense once you see it. An automatic arena waits for the GC, like a direct buffer, so it shares their limit; a confined arena is freed when you say so. With -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=16m, the demo's confined 32 MiB worked, and its automatic 32 MiB failed with Cannot reserve 33554432 bytes of direct buffer memory. The labs compile for JDK 21, where FFM is still a preview, so this demo is a single file that runs outside Gradle on JDK 22 or later. That's also where today's tools stop. A heap dump is one moment of the floor, NMT counts categories rather than callers, and neither one names the line of code that keeps writing the list. They tell you where to look. Reading that code is still your job. Free 32 MiB at a closing brace (JDK 22 or later) This one runs outside Gradle and needs JDK 22 or later, ideally 25. Check with java -version. From labs/, run java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.java. The Kotlin twin needs kotlinc; its commands are at the top of ArenaDemo.kt. Predict the Other line inside the arena and after close(), then run it. Run it again with -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=16m in place of the NMT flag, and see which of the two arenas the limit stops. ArenaDemo.java (JDK 22 or later) // JDK 22 or later: the Foreign Function and Memory API is final since JDK 22 (JEP 454). Written for JDK 25. // Not part of the Gradle build, because the labs compile for JDK 21, where this API is a preview. From labs/: // java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.java // java -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=16m memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.java import java.lang.foreign.Arena; import java.lang.foreign.MemorySegment; import java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout; import java.lang.management.BufferPoolMXBean; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import javax.management.ObjectName; public class ArenaDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { MemorySegment escaped; try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) { // 1. one owner thread, closed by try-with-resources MemorySegment block = arena.allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024); // 2. 32 MiB outside the heap for (long i = 0; i < block.byteSize() / Long.BYTES; i++) { block.setAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, i, i * 100); // 4 million longs, and no objects } System.out.println("entry 1,000 holds " + block.getAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 1_000)); System.out.println("inside the arena: " + nativeOther()); escaped = block; } // 3. freed here, not by the GC System.out.println("after close(): " + nativeOther()); try { escaped.getAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 0); // 4. use after free is an exception, not a crash } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("reading after close() throws: " + e.getMessage()); } MemorySegment auto = Arena.ofAuto().allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024); // 5. freed only after the GC finds it unreachable, System.out.printf("an automatic arena: %d MiB counted as direct memory%n", // so it counts with direct buffers directBytes() >> 20); System.out.println("segment " + auto.byteSize()); } // Native Memory Tracking's "Other" row, where arena memory shows up (the same as jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary) static String nativeOther() throws Exception { String summary = (String) ManagementFactory.getPlatformMBeanServer().invoke( new ObjectName("com.sun.management:type=DiagnosticCommand"), "vmNativeMemory", new Object[] {new String[] {"summary", "scale=MB"}}, new String[] {String[].class.getName()}); if (!summary.contains("Total")) return "(start java with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary to see it)"; return summary.lines().filter(l -> l.contains(" Other (")).map(l -> l.replaceFirst("^-?\\s*", "")).findFirst() .orElse("Other: under 1 MB, so NMT leaves it out"); } // what the JDK counts against -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize: direct ByteBuffers and automatic arenas static long directBytes() { return ManagementFactory.getPlatformMXBeans(BufferPoolMXBean.class).stream() .filter(p -> p.getName().equals("direct")) .mapToLong(BufferPoolMXBean::getMemoryUsed).sum(); } } java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.java labs/memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.java ArenaDemo.kt (JDK 22 or later) // JDK 22 or later: the Foreign Function and Memory API is final since JDK 22 (JEP 454). Written for JDK 25. // Needs the Kotlin command-line compiler. From labs/: // kotlinc memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.kt -include-runtime -d memory/build/arena-demo.jar // java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary -jar memory/build/arena-demo.jar // java -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=16m -jar memory/build/arena-demo.jar // Not part of the Gradle build, because the labs compile for JDK 21, where this API is a preview. import java.lang.foreign.Arena import java.lang.foreign.MemorySegment import java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout import java.lang.management.BufferPoolMXBean import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import javax.management.ObjectName // Native Memory Tracking's "Other" row, where arena memory shows up (the same as jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary) fun nativeOther(): String { val summary = ManagementFactory.getPlatformMBeanServer().invoke( ObjectName("com.sun.management:type=DiagnosticCommand"), "vmNativeMemory", arrayOf<Any>(arrayOf("summary", "scale=MB")), arrayOf(Array<String>::class.java.name)) as String if ("Total" !in summary) return "(start java with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary to see it)" return summary.lines().firstOrNull { " Other (" in it }?.trim()?.removePrefix("-")?.trim() ?: "Other: under 1 MB, so NMT leaves it out" } // what the JDK counts against -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize: direct ByteBuffers and automatic arenas fun directBytes(): Long = ManagementFactory.getPlatformMXBeans(BufferPoolMXBean::class.java) .filter { it.name == "direct" } .sumOf { it.memoryUsed } fun main(args: Array<String>) { // args unused; one main keeps every launcher happy val escaped: MemorySegment Arena.ofConfined().use { arena -> // 1. one owner thread, closed by use {} val block = arena.allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024) // 2. 32 MiB outside the heap for (i in 0 until block.byteSize() / Long.SIZE_BYTES) { block.setAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, i, i * 100) // 4 million longs, and no objects } println("entry 1,000 holds ${block.getAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 1_000)}") println("inside the arena: ${nativeOther()}") escaped = block } // 3. freed here, not by the GC println("after close(): ${nativeOther()}") try { escaped.getAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 0) // 4. use after free is an exception, not a crash } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("reading after close() throws: ${e.message}") } val auto = Arena.ofAuto().allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024) // 5. freed only after the GC finds it unreachable, println("an automatic arena: %d MiB counted as direct memory".format(directBytes() shr 20)) // so it counts with direct buffers println("segment ${auto.byteSize()}") } kotlinc memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.kt -include-runtime -d memory/build/arena-demo.jar && java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary -jar memory/build/arena-demo.jar labs/memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.kt On JDK 25: entry 1,000 holds 100000, then Other (reserved=32MB, committed=32MB) inside the arena and Other (reserved=0MB, committed=0MB) after close(), then reading after close() throws: Already closed and an automatic arena: 32 MiB counted as direct memory. With -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=16m the confined arena still works (the NMT lines just ask for the NMT flag), and the automatic arena fails with OutOfMemoryError: Cannot reserve 33554432 bytes of direct buffer memory (allocated: 0, limit: 16777216). h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · Java and Kotlin
x: A bounded LRU cache in Java and Kotlin LruCache.java final class LruCache<K, V> { private final Map<K, V> map; LruCache(int maxEntries) { // true = access order: get() moves an entry to the end, so the eldest is the least recently used map = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) { @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) { return size() > maxEntries; } }; } synchronized V get(K key) { return map.get(key); } synchronized void put(K key, V value) { map.put(key, value); } } LruCache.kt class LruCache<K, V>(private val maxEntries: Int) { // true = access order: get() moves an entry to the end, so the eldest is the least recently used private val map = object : LinkedHashMap<K, V>(16, 0.75f, true) { override fun removeEldestEntry(eldest: MutableMap.MutableEntry<K, V>?): Boolean = size > maxEntries } @Synchronized fun get(key: K): V? = map[key] @Synchronized fun put(key: K, value: V) { map[key] = value } } LRU means least recently used: when the cache is full, the entry nobody has asked for the longest goes first. Both versions build on the same JDK class, and both need the lock, because LinkedHashMap isn't thread-safe and in access order even get changes the map. Java overrides removeEldestEntry in an anonymous subclass; Kotlin does it with an object : expression, and its eldest parameter is nullable because the JDK doesn't say whether it can be null. Kotlin returns V? from get, which puts the cache miss in the type. In a real service you'd often use a cache library with size limits and expiry, but the leak fix is the same idea in every form: decide a maximum, and make the structure enforce it.

h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · Worked example
x: From a killed container to the line that leaks Picture an album exporter, a background job of the photo site that packs a user's photos into one download. Suppose it restarts with exit code 137 every two days. Start with the GC log, because it decides which half of memory to look at. Say its young pauses end near the same value day after day: the live heap is flat, so a heap dump would look healthy. Don't start there. Measure the yard. Restart one instance with NMT, take a baseline once it's warm, and diff it a few hours later. Suppose only one category moved: Other, by hundreds of megabytes, with thousands more native allocations. java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary ... -jar album-exporter.jar jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline # a few hours later jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff scale=MB Name the suspect. A growing Other is direct buffers or native code, and the JDK's direct buffer pool confirms it if its count and size keep climbing. Then find who allocates direct buffers for each album. Here it's a map that keeps one buffer per album and never removes them. // 1. the leak: one direct buffer per album, kept forever private final Map<String, ByteBuffer> albumBuffers = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); ByteBuffer bufferFor(String albumId) { return albumBuffers.computeIfAbsent(albumId, id -> ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(1 << 20)); } // 1. the leak: one direct buffer per album, kept forever private val albumBuffers = ConcurrentHashMap<String, ByteBuffer>() fun bufferFor(albumId: String): ByteBuffer = albumBuffers.computeIfAbsent(albumId) { ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(1 shl 20) } Fix the lifetime, then add a guard. Give each album its memory for exactly as long as it's being packed, with a confined arena (JDK 22 or later), or remove the buffer from the map when the album is done. Then cap direct memory, so the next direct-buffer leak fails as an OutOfMemoryError with a stack trace instead of a silent kill. The cap doesn't cover confined arenas; you close those yourself. void packAlbum(String albumId, Album album) { try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) { // 2. memory lives exactly as long as the album is packed MemorySegment buffer = arena.allocate(1 << 20); album.writeInto(buffer); upload(albumId, buffer); } // 3. freed here, no GC needed } // and on the command line: -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=128m fun packAlbum(albumId: String, album: Album) { Arena.ofConfined().use { arena -> // 2. memory lives exactly as long as the album is packed val buffer = arena.allocate(1 shl 20) album.writeInto(buffer) upload(albumId, buffer) } // 3. freed here, no GC needed } // and on the command line: -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=128m

h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · Lab
x: Find and fix the leaks in an upload cache labs/memory/src/main/java/workbench/memory/l07/UploadCache.java labs/memory/src/main/java/workbench/memory/l07/PhotoUpload.java labs/memory/src/main/java/workbench/memory/l07/UploadResult.java ./gradlew :memory:test --tests 'workbench.memory.l07.*' Read UploadCache. A phone on a weak connection often sends the same upload twice, because it never heard the first answer, so the cache remembers the result for each upload id and hands it back on a retry. It also rejects a retry whose photo differs from the original. Run the tests. Four of six fail. The two that pass check behaviour: a retry gets the same result, and a reused upload id with a different photo is rejected. Keep those passing. Read the failing messages. Two tests count live objects with the class histogram, the same one jcmd GC.class_histogram prints: after 20,000 uploads, 20,000 results and 20,000 uploads are still alive. Fix the first leak: bound the cache to maxEntries with an access-ordered LinkedHashMap and removeEldestEntry, and make the methods synchronized. Run the tests again. The upload test still fails, now with about 500. Find out why each entry keeps its whole PhotoUpload, and replace it with what the retry check really needs: a SHA-256 digest of the photo. Run the tests until all six pass. new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) makes the map access-ordered. Override removeEldestEntry to return size() > maxEntries. MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(photo) gives 32 bytes, a fingerprint of the photo. Compare two digests with MessageDigest.isEqual. The entry record is private, so you can change its fields freely, for example to record Entry(byte[] photoDigest, UploadResult result). The leak tests allow 2 stray objects, because the test's own last local variables may still be reachable while it counts. All 6 tests in UploadCacheTest pass. By the end you can tell a heap leak from growth outside the heap, find who holds a leaked object with a histogram, a heap dump and its dominator tree, measure native memory with NMT, give off-heap memory a lifetime with an arena, and fix a leaking cache.

h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · Quiz
x: A class histogram after a full GC shows 2.1 million byte[] instances using 4.3 GB. What does that tell you about the leak? What fills the heap, but not who holds it: you need the dominator tree of a heap dump That byte[] is the leaking class, and the fix is to allocate fewer arrays That the leak is outside the heap Nothing, because the histogram counts garbage too Byte arrays sit under strings, buffers, pixels and file contents alike, so the histogram can't name the owner. GC.class_histogram runs a full GC first and counts only live objects. The dominator tree ranks objects by what they keep alive, and the path to a GC root names the field. In a heap dump, a GalleryIndex object has a shallow size of 24 bytes and a retained size of 1.2 GB. What does that mean? The index object itself is 1.2 GB The index is referenced 1.2 billion times If the index became unreachable, about 1.2 GB would be freed with it The dump is corrupt: retained size can't exceed shallow size by that much Shallow size is the object's own header and fields. Retained size adds everything reachable only through it, its retained set. A small object at the top of a big map routinely retains gigabytes, which makes it exactly the object to look at. The demo's 64-byte map kept 44 MB alive. A program's young pauses end at a flat 400 MB, but NMT's summary.diff after six hours shows Thread (reserved=2150MB +1900MB, committed=210MB +185MB). What is leaking? Heap objects Metaspace Direct buffers Threads: code keeps starting threads, each with its own stack, and never ends them About 1,900 MB more reserved stack is roughly 1,900 new threads at about 1 MB each, with a little of each stack touched. Look for a thread pool created for each request and never shut down, or a thread started per connection. Direct buffers would show in Other, and metaspace in Class and Metaspace. A program needs a 1 MiB off-heap buffer for each album it packs. Which choice frees each buffer as soon as its album is done, without waiting for a GC? ByteBuffer.allocateDirect, then drop the reference A segment from Arena.ofConfined() in try-with-resources A segment from Arena.ofAuto() A segment from Arena.global() A confined arena frees its memory when close() runs, at the end of the try block. A dropped direct buffer and an automatic arena are freed only after the GC finds them unreachable, which on a quiet heap can take a long time. The global arena is never freed. From the threads track: the tasks of a thread pool call CURRENT_USER.set(upload.userId()) on a ThreadLocal and never call remove(). Which leak pattern is this, and what does a heap dump show as the GC root? A cache with no limit; the root is a static map A value kept alive by a long-lived pool thread; the root is the live thread itself A class loader leak; the root is the class loader Not a leak, because ThreadLocal values are weak Each thread keeps its own ThreadLocal values, and a pool thread lives as long as the pool. A started, unfinished thread is a GC root, so the last value each thread saw stays reachable. The ThreadLocal key is weak inside the thread's map, but the value is strong. The fix is remove() in a finally block.
