h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · Key terms
x: Class histogram A count of live objects and their bytes, per class. Heap dump A file (HPROF format) with every object on the heap and every reference between them. Retained size The memory that would be freed if one object became unreachable. Dominator Object X dominates Y if every path from a GC root to Y goes through X. Native Memory Tracking The JVM's own accounting of the memory it uses, including outside the heap. Direct buffer A ByteBuffer whose bytes live outside the heap, freed after its small heap object is collected. Arena In the FFM API, the owner of off-heap memory that decides when it's freed. MaxDirectMemorySize The limit for direct buffers and automatic arenas. Defaults to the max heap. What is a memory leak in Java? Memory that stays reachable from a GC root after the program is done with it, so the GC may not free it. What does jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram show, and what does it miss? Live objects per class, after a full GC: what fills the heap. It doesn't show who holds them. Shallow size vs retained size? Shallow: the object's own bytes. Retained: everything freed if that object went away, the object plus all it alone keeps reachable. How do you get a heap dump at the moment of an OutOfMemoryError? -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=.... It's manageable, so jcmd <pid> VM.set_flag HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError true works on a running JVM. How do you find slow growth outside the heap? Start with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, run jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline, then later jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff. When is a direct ByteBuffer's native memory freed? After the GC collects the small buffer object on the heap and its cleaner runs. On a quiet heap that can take a long time. On JDK 25, which FFM arenas count against -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize? Only automatic ones (Arena.ofAuto()), which wait for the GC like direct buffers. Confined and shared arenas are freed at close() and don't count; NMT shows them under Other.

h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · Go deeper
x: A few details make leak hunting faster. A histogram is cheap enough to take twice. Take one, wait ten minutes under load, take another, and compare instance counts: the class whose count only goes up is your lead, even before you have a dump. jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram -all skips the full GC and counts unreachable objects too, which helps when you can't afford the pause and misleads when you forget the flag. Heap dumps are large: about the size of the live heap, here 52 MB for 44 MB of leak. GC.heap_dump -gz=1 compresses while writing. Writing a dump stops the JVM, so in a group of identical services, take it from one instance after you've stopped sending it traffic. MAT's GC roots have kinds, and the kind is a clue. A System Class root means a static field. A Thread root, "a started, but not stopped, thread" in MAT's words, means something reachable from a live thread: its stack or its thread-locals. JNI Global means native code is holding a reference. Class loader leaks look different from object leaks. Each reload of an application creates a new class loader with new classes. If anything from outside still references one object of an old class, for example a database driver registered in a global list, a ThreadLocal on a shared thread or a static cache in a library, the whole old class loader and every class it loaded stay in metaspace. NMT shows Class and Metaspace growing, and GC logs show collections with the cause Metadata GC Threshold. A service in production rarely reloads, but tools that reload code on every change, and long test suites, do. Finally, jol-cli, JOL's command-line version, can estimate how a heap dump's objects would lay out under other JVM settings. For a similar 50 MB dump full of 2 KB arrays, it estimated 1.3% less with compact object headers and 3.2% more without compressed references. A heap of big arrays gains little from smaller headers, as lesson 1 predicted.

h: JIT, profiling and benchmarking
x: Tiered compilation, inlining and deoptimization, JMH, false sharing, JFR, async-profiler, flame graphs and thread dumps. By the end of this track you can say what the JVM does with your code after javac or kotlinc is done with it: which tier runs a method, what C2 copies into its callers and bets on, and why it sometimes throws compiled code away. You can write a JMH benchmark that measures your code instead of the optimizer, spot false sharing and fix it with padding or LongAdder, record a running JVM with JDK Flight Recorder, read a flame graph from async-profiler without being fooled by it, run an investigation from "it's slow, sometimes" to a fix you can prove to the byte, and read a thread dump to tell a stuck thread from a busy one. You don't need to know anything about compilers or profilers to start: lesson 1 begins with bytecode. The whole track follows one picture, a new cook learning a restaurant's menu, and one program, a small report service that reads documents and reports their word count and reading time. You do need the memory model track's first lesson (why a loop on a plain field can hang) and the first track's lesson on atomics and LongAdder; the memory track's lessons on the garbage collector help in lesson 7. Install JDK 25, the current LTS. The JIT's thresholds and inlining limits are the same from JDK 21 to JDK 27, and every lesson says which JDK a newer feature needs (JFR method timing and CPU-time sampling arrived in JDK 25; compact object headers are on by default in JDK 27). async-profiler is a separate download for lesson 6; this track used version 4.6. The labs live in labs/performance, one package per lesson (workbench.performance.l01 to l08). Lessons 1, 6 and 8 have Kotlin labs; the rest are Java, because JMH benchmarks are Java classes here. The tests never time anything: they parse real JVM output, read class files and object layouts, record and read JFR files, count allocated bytes and read real thread dumps. Run ./gradlew :performance:test --tests 'workbench.performance.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, and ./gradlew :performance:solutionTest to check the reference answers. Demos run with ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=.... Many start a second JVM with the flags the lesson is about, so you see real -XX:+PrintCompilation, -XX:+PrintInlining and JFR output. HotSpot runs every method in the interpreter first, then C1 with profiling (about 200 calls) and C2 (about 5,000 more). OSR compiles long loops while they run. Every new JVM starts cold, so measure after warm-up. C2 inlines within a bytecode budget (35 bytes at sites that aren't hot, 325 at hot ones) and only for one or two receiver types per call site. What it never saw becomes an uncommon trap; when one fires, the code is thrown away and compiled again. A nanoTime loop measures the optimizer. JMH, with returned results, non-final @State inputs, warm-up, forks and a baseline, measures your code. -prof gc B/op is steady once warm; time isn't. Caches move 64-byte lines. Threads writing neighbouring fields can slow each other down (false sharing); pad with a chain of classes, check with JOL, or count with LongAdder. JFR records GC, JIT, locks, samples and your own events on one clock, cheaply enough to leave on. Start it with -XX:StartFlightRecording or jcmd, ask with jfr summary and jfr view, read with RecordingFile, stream with RecordingStream. async-profiler samples stacks without safepoint bias, in cpu, wall, alloc and lock modes. In a flame graph width is samples and left to right is alphabetical; wide bare tops are where the time goes. An investigation goes: the tail and the GC count, allocation by your own line, a flame graph of the callers, one fix, profile again, a JMH proof, and an allocation budget test. A thread dump is a photo of every thread at one safepoint. RUNNABLE doesn't mean busy: compare cpu= across three dumps, follow each wait to its owner, and use Thread.dump_to_file for virtual threads. Every tool here has a blind spot: logs explain one method, benchmarks one piece of code, profiles the seconds you recorded, dumps one moment. Use the one that answers the question in front of you, and check surprising answers with a second.

h: JIT, profiling and benchmarking: cheat sheet
x: Picture it: the kitchen behind each idea Idea Picture it Lesson Bytecode, the interpreter the recipe card, read line by line by a new cook 1 C1 at tier 3, and its profile a quick cheat sheet, plus notes on every order 1 C2 the dish practised by heart, with bets on the usual orders 1, 2 OSR switching technique halfway through a huge pot of soup 1 A restart every new JVM is the cook's first day again 1 Inlining copying the sauce recipe from page 12 into the main recipe 2 Type profile the tally of side dishes; fries kept ready by the stove 2 Uncommon trap, deoptimization the customer who asks for rice 2 Intrinsic the apple corer: one gadget, one job, done in one push 2 JMH a fair taste test: a warm kitchen, a fresh kitchen for each fork, a judge who eats every dish 3 Dead-code elimination the cook who stops making the test bowls nobody eats 3 Cache line, false sharing two cooks sharing one cutting board 4 LongAdder a tally slip per cook, added up at closing time 4 JFR the kitchen's log on one clock, cheap enough to keep all night 5 Your own JFR events the cook's own notes in the same log 5 Sampling profiler the manager's glance through the door every few seconds 6 Safepoint bias a manager who only looks up when a cook puts the knife down 6 Flame graph the tally drawn as towers of blocks, sorted by name, not by time 6 Allocation and GC pauses clean plates, and the whole kitchen stopping to wash up 7 Thread dump a photo of every cook; three photos tell stuck from busy 8 A blocked chain waiters queued for the order book that a cook holds at the back door 8 How HotSpot runs your code (JDK 21 to 27) Tier Runs the code Reached after 0 interpreter, counts calls and loop back-edges start 3 C1 with full profiling (branches, receiver types) about 200 calls (Tier3InvocationThreshold) 4 C2, optimized with the profile about 5,000 more calls (Tier4InvocationThreshold) OSR a running loop compiled and entered mid-loop about 60,000 back-edges (tier 3), 40,000 more (tier 4) Tier 1 is C1 for trivial methods; tier 2 is C1 with counters only, used when C2 has a backlog. Thresholds grow when the compile queues are long. CompileThreshold (10,000) applies only with -XX:-TieredCompilation. Code cache: 240 MB reserved, three parts; check it with jcmd <pid> Compiler.codecache. On JDK 25 an AOT cache (-XX:AOTCacheOutput, then -XX:AOTCache) can carry profiles from a training run. 56 13 % 4 workbench.performance.l01.Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) ms id flags tier method OSR bci bytecode size Flags: % OSR, s synchronized, ! exception handler, b blocking, n native. On JDK 25, made not entrant gets a reason: not used and OSR invalidation of lower level are routine; uncommon trap means a C2 bet failed. Times and ids change on every run. What C2 bets on Rule Value Inline at a call site that isn't hot callee at most 35 bytes of bytecode (MaxInlineSize) Inline at a hot site (25% or more of the caller's calls) at most 325 bytes (FreqInlineSize) Types inlined per call site 2 (TypeProfileWidth); with more, only a type with 90% or more Uncommon trap kinds unstable_if (a branch never taken), class_check (a type never seen) See the decisions with -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining and -Xlog:deoptimization=debug. Keep cold paths out of hot methods: Java static long requireWordCount(long words) { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) throw badWordCount(words); // 21 bytes: inlines anywhere return words; } Kotlin fun requireWordCount(words: Long): Long { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) throw badWordCount(words) // 21 bytes: inlines anywhere return words } final doesn't make calls faster; the number of receiver types at the call does. Prefer JDK intrinsics (Math.addExact, Arrays.equals, Long.bitCount) over hand-written loops. JMH rules Java @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Fork(2) public class ReadingBench { long words = 1_234; // non-final input @Benchmark public long seconds() { return ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words); } // result returned @Benchmark public void baseline() { } // the floor } Kotlin @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Fork(2) open class ReadingBench { // JMH subclasses it var words = 1_234L // non-final input @Benchmark fun seconds(): Long = ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words) // result returned @Benchmark fun baseline() {} // the floor } Return results or Blackhole.consume them; never read inputs from final constant fields; never @Fork(0); compare with a baseline. -prof gc gives gc.alloc.rate.norm (B/op): steady enough for an automatic check once the code is warm, unlike ns/op. Defaults in JMH 1.37: 5 forks, 5 + 5 iterations of 10 s. Caches and false sharing Cache lines are 64 bytes. Two threads writing fields on one line slow each other down (false sharing); how much depends on the hardware and on whether the threads really run at once. Pad hot fields at least 64 bytes apart with a chain of classes, check with JOL (ClassLayout.parseClass(X.class)), and assert distances, not offsets. @Contended needs -XX:-RestrictContended and --add-exports for your own classes. For counters with many writers and rare readers, use LongAdder; when the value drives a decision, use AtomicLong. JFR java -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=rec.jfr,settings=profile -jar app.jar jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=x settings=profile # on a running JVM jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=x filename=x.jfr # copies the data, stops nothing jfr summary rec.jfr # always first jfr view contention-by-site | allocation-by-site | gc-pauses | deoptimizations-by-reason rec.jfr jfr print --events workbench.StoreCall --stack-depth 3 rec.jfr default.jfc stays on ("typically less than 1 % overhead"); profile.jfc for short investigations. Set maxage or maxsize, or the JVM keeps 250 MB. Your own events extend jdk.jfr.Event (begin, end, shouldCommit, commit); fill their fields inside shouldCommit(). Read files with RecordingFile, live events with RecordingStream. A setting for your own event on the command line needs a +: +workbench.StoreCall#threshold=30ms. JDK 25: method-timing=, report-on-exit=, experimental jdk.CPUTimeSample on Linux. Recordings hold environment variables and the command line; JDK 27 can redact them. async-profiler and flame graphs asprof -d 30 -f cpu.html <pid> # CPU (add -e ctimer if perf_events is blocked) asprof -e wall -t -d 30 -f wall.html <pid> # waiting: network, locks, sleep, per thread asprof -e alloc -d 30 -f alloc.html <pid> # who allocates asprof -e lock -d 30 -f lock.html <pid> # contended locks asprof -d 30 -o collapsed -f out.collapsed <pid> # text: "a;b;c 42" Width = samples (inclusive), root at the bottom, left to right is alphabetical, never time. Wide bare tops are self time; follow them down to the first frame in your own code. Profilers built on getStackTrace suffer from safepoint bias; async-profiler doesn't. The investigation loop Symptom: p99.9 and p99.99 and the GC count, per call, not the average. JFR: gc-pauses, then allocation grouped by the first frame in your own code and its line. Flame graph: who calls it. Fix one thing; profile again, because the order of costs changes. Prove it with JMH -prof gc; keep it with an allocation budget test (getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes) with a margin, looked at again on JDK upgrades. Thread dumps jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l > dump-1.txt # platform threads, with java.util.concurrent lock owners for i in 1 2 3; do jcmd $PID Thread.print -l > dump-$i.txt; sleep 5; done jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/threads.json # includes virtual threads Same frames in every dump? CPU grew? Your code in the stack? What it is yes no yes stuck: follow its lock line to the owner, and fix the owner yes yes yes hot: a loop that never leaves that frame no either yes working yes no no idle: a pool or JVM thread waiting for work RUNNABLE only means "not waiting for a Java lock": a thread in a socket read is RUNNABLE with flat cpu=. nid is the PID column of top -H (decimal since JDK 18). A ReentrantLock's owner shows only under Locked ownable synchronizers, with -l.

h: JIT, profiling and benchmarking: track quiz
x: Which compiler produced this line, and why is there an @ 4? 56 13 % 4 workbench.performance.l01.Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) C1, because % marks a profiled compile C2, compiling a running loop (OSR) that is entered at bytecode index 4 The interpreter, at line 4 of the source C2, inlining 4 callees Tier 4 is C2. % marks on-stack replacement: the loop got hot while the method was still running, so C2 compiled a version that is entered at the top of the loop, bytecode index 4. Bytecode indexes aren't source lines. A 49-byte word-count check, most of it the code that builds its error message, is called on 1 in 8 invocations of its caller. Will C2 inline it there? No: below 25% of the caller's calls the limit is 35 bytes, so it's "too big" Yes, everything under 325 bytes is inlined Only if the method is final Only in the interpreter C2 uses the 325-byte limit only when the call runs on at least 25% of the caller's invocations. Otherwise MaxInlineSize (35) applies, and the error path counts too. Moving the cold path into its own method shrank lesson 2's check to 21 bytes. A JMH benchmark reads its input from private final long words = 1_234; and scores the same as an empty benchmark. Why? JMH can't read private fields The benchmark forgot @Fork javac copies the constant into the method, and C2 folds the whole calculation into one number Private fields are always kept in registers A final field with a constant initializer is a compile-time constant in Java, so the method contains ldc2_w 1234, and C2 can compute the result once. Read inputs from a non-final @State field. Two worker threads each update their own volatile long counter in one small object, and the job runs slower with two threads than with one. JOL shows the fields at offsets 16 and 24. What's the first thing to try? Make the fields non-volatile Add synchronized to both updates Use AtomicLong for both fields in the same object Put the counters at least 64 bytes apart (a chain of classes), or use a LongAdder per counter, then measure 8 bytes apart is one cache line, so every write takes the line from the other core: false sharing. Padding or LongAdder's padded cells separate them. Removing volatile changes visibility, not layout, and how much padding helps depends on the machine, so measure. The report service has slow spikes right now, you can't restart it, and you can't install anything on its machine. Which first step gives you GC pauses, lock waits and allocation for the last few minutes? Restart it with -XX:+PrintCompilation Attach async-profiler jcmd <pid> JFR.dump from a recording that's always on, then jfr view gc-pauses, contention-by-site and allocation-by-site Run JMH on the machine JFR is built into the JDK, and a running recording can be dumped without stopping the JVM. Its views answer all three questions from one file. A restart throws away the minutes you wanted, and the other tools need installing or answer other questions. In a flame graph, String.format is drawn to the left of Pattern.compile at the same level. Which statement is true? Their order is alphabetical; only the widths carry information String.format ran first String.format is the slower of the two String.format called Pattern.compile Flame graphs sort frames alphabetically at each level (java/lang/... before java/util/...); left to right is not a timeline. Width is the number of samples, and a callee is drawn above its caller, never beside it. A profiler built on Thread.getStackTrace() charges 29% of the CPU to String.split itself, with nothing ever above it. async-profiler charges most of that time to methods split calls. What's going on? async-profiler skips small methods Safepoint bias: getStackTrace sees a thread only at a safepoint poll, after its inlined callees have returned, so their time is charged to split The JIT inlined split away getStackTrace uses wall-clock time Reading another thread's stack needs that thread at a safepoint, and polls sit at method returns and loop back-edges. async-profiler interrupts the thread with a signal and walks the stack at the exact instruction, inlined frames included. After hoisting a regex into a static final field and guarding a debug log line, the report step's allocation drops from about 2,460 to 832 bytes per call. What does the investigation loop say to do next? Stop: a threefold improvement is enough Give the JVM a bigger heap so the GC runs less Profile again: the remaining bytes have a new top line (here split, then the Matcher), fix the next one if the budget needs it, and stop when what's left fits Rewrite the method in Kotlin Each fix changes the order of costs. In lesson 7, split filled 92% of the profile after round 1, and the Matcher 99.6% after round 2, which left 56 bytes on JDK 25, under the 300-byte budget. In a pull request you must show that a new way of counting words allocates less than the old one, and keep it that way in the automatic build. Which tools fit? A unit test that times 1,000 calls with System.nanoTime() -XX:+PrintCompilation async-profiler in wall mode A JMH benchmark with -prof gc, then an allocation budget test with a margin JMH with -prof gc gives bytes per operation with an error near zero once warm, and a test using the per-thread allocation counter keeps the number from growing. A hand-made timing loop measures the optimizer, and wall mode answers a different question. Three thread dumps, 5 seconds apart. catalog-refresh is RUNNABLE in SocketDispatcher.read0 with cpu=25.09ms in all three, and four other threads are BLOCKED waiting for a lock it holds. What do you fix? The four BLOCKED threads, by giving them a bigger pool catalog-refresh: it holds the lock while it waits for the network, so make the slow call outside the lock, with a timeout Nothing: RUNNABLE means it's working, so it will finish The JIT, because the thread is stuck in native code RUNNABLE in a native socket read with flat CPU means it's waiting for bytes, not working. Every thread that needs its lock queues behind it. Fix the owner, not the queue: call the store without the lock and take the lock only to swap in the result.

h: From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 · Every method starts in the interpreter and climbs to C2
x: From the interpreter to C1 to C2, and back when a bet loses Let's meet the program we'll follow through this track. It's a small report service: a program that takes a document, such as an article or a chapter of a book, and writes a short report about it. How many words does it have? How long does it take to read? Is it made of paragraphs, headings or quotes? One of its jobs is the reading time. At 238 words a minute, rounded up to the next second, it's one line: Java // seconds to read a document at 238 words a minute, rounded up static long readingSeconds(long words) { return (words * 60 + 237) / 238; } Kotlin // seconds to read a document at 238 words a minute, rounded up fun readingSeconds(words: Long): Long = (words * 60 + 237) / 238 WarmupDemo, in the Try it below, fills an array with the word counts of 20,000 documents. Then it times the same batch of 20,000 calls twelve times in a row: same code, same data. One run on JDK 25 printed: batch 1: 1,002 us batch 2: 713 us batch 3: 682 us batch 4: 482 us batch 5: 78 us batch 6: 2,406 us batch 7: 77 us batch 8: 77 us batch 9: 76 us batch 10: 118 us batch 11: 76 us batch 12: 76 us The course machine was busy, with more than 20 programs sharing its four cores, so treat every number as rough. The shape is what matters: four slow batches, then a drop to about 78 µs. Batch 6 is an odd one. A slow batch showed up there in most runs, even with the compiler switched off, so the compiler isn't the culprit; the busy machine is the likely one. Lesson 3 teaches you to distrust a single strange number. The speed-up comes from how the JVM runs code. javac and kotlinc don't produce machine code for your processor. They produce bytecode: compact instructions for the JVM, stored in .class files, such as lload (push a local long onto the JVM's working stack) or lmul (multiply two longs). HotSpot, the JVM in every OpenJDK build, starts every method in the interpreter, a loop inside the JVM that reads one bytecode instruction at a time and carries it out. That's the cook on day one, reading the card line by line. While it reads, the JVM keeps tally marks: how often each method is called, and how often each loop jumps back to its start (a back-edge). When the marks pass a threshold, a compiler thread turns the method into machine code in the background. (A thread is a separate line of work that runs alongside the rest of your program.) The next call runs the machine code instead. This is the JIT (just-in-time) compiler. It compiles while the program runs, so it can see what your code really does. HotSpot has two JIT compilers. C1 compiles quickly and optimizes a little: the cheat sheet. At tier 3 it also takes notes on every order, a profile of what the code really did: which branches ran, which types turned up at each call. C2 compiles slowly and optimizes hard, using those notes. That's the dish practised until it's automatic, with shortcuts that bet on the usual orders. Tiered compilation, on by default, uses all of them in five levels: Tier Runs the code Notes 0 interpreter counts calls and back-edges 1 C1, no profiling for trivial methods such as getters 2 C1 with counters only used in some cases, for example while C2 has a backlog 3 C1 with full profiling records branch counts and the types seen at each call 4 C2 compiles with the profile that tier 3 collected The normal path is 0, then 3, then 4. On JDK 25 a method reaches tier 3 after about 200 calls (Tier3InvocationThreshold) and tier 4 after about 5,000 more (Tier4InvocationThreshold). Loop laps count too. -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal lists these defaults, and they're the same from JDK 21 to JDK 27. When the compile queues are long, the JVM raises the bar on the fly, so treat them as rough sizes. You may have read that a method is compiled after 10,000 calls. That's CompileThreshold, which only applies with -XX:-TieredCompilation. The blog posts weren't wrong, just old: tiered compilation has been the default since JDK 8. Let's check the tiers by taking some away. With -Xint, interpreter only, every batch stayed between 630 and 920 µs, apart from one 2.7 ms batch. With -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1, C1 only, the batches fell to 69 µs from batch 6 on, a touch faster than the default run. On a one-line method, the cheat sheet is already about as good as it gets. C2 earns its slow compile on bigger code, where its bets pay off, as lesson 2 shows. The same code runs at different speeds depending on how long the JVM has watched it. Never trust the first lap. So something compiled our loop around batch 5. But which compiler, and when? The JVM will tell us, if we ask. Watch the same batch get faster Predict: WarmupDemo times the same batch of 20,000 reading-time calculations 12 times. Will batch 12 take as long as batch 1? Write your guess down. Run it from the labs/ folder with the command below, and note the batch where the time drops. Run it again with -Pargs=int, which restarts it with -Xint (interpreter only), then with -Pargs=c1 (-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1, C1 only). Compare the last few batches of the three runs. WarmupDemo.java package workbench.performance.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Times the same batch of 20,000 reading-time calculations 12 times in a row. * No argument: normal tiered JVM. "int": interpreter only (-Xint). "c1": stop at C1 (-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1). */ public class WarmupDemo { static final long[] WORDS = new long[20_000]; // the word counts of 20,000 documents // seconds to read a document at 238 words a minute, rounded up static long readingSeconds(long words) { return (words * 60 + 237) / 238; } static long batch() { long total = 0; for (long w : WORDS) total += readingSeconds(w); return total; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "tiered"; if (mode.equals("int")) { relaunch("-Xint"); return; } if (mode.equals("c1")) { relaunch("-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1"); return; } for (int i = 0; i < WORDS.length; i++) WORDS[i] = 50 + (i * 7919L) % 25_000; long check = 0; for (int round = 1; round <= 12; round++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); check += batch(); long micros = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000; System.out.printf("batch %2d: %,6d us%n", round, micros); } System.out.println("(checksum " + check + ")"); // use the result, so the JIT can't drop the work } // start a second JVM with extra flags and the same classpath, and show its output static void relaunch(String flag) throws Exception { String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, flag, "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), WarmupDemo.class.getName(), "tiered")); System.out.println("running with " + flag); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); try (var out = p.inputReader()) { out.lines().filter(l -> !l.startsWith("Picked up")).forEach(System.out::println); } p.waitFor(); } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l01.WarmupDemo labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l01/WarmupDemo.java WarmupDemo.kt package workbench.performance.l01 // Kotlin twin of WarmupDemo.java: times the same batch of 20,000 reading-time calculations 12 times in a row. // No argument: normal tiered JVM. "int": interpreter only (-Xint). "c1": stop at C1 (-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1). private val words = LongArray(20_000) // the word counts of 20,000 documents // seconds to read a document at 238 words a minute, rounded up fun readingSeconds(words: Long): Long = (words * 60 + 237) / 238 fun batch(): Long { var total = 0L for (w in words) total += readingSeconds(w) return total } fun main(args: Array<String>) { when (args.firstOrNull() ?: "tiered") { "int" -> return relaunch("-Xint") "c1" -> return relaunch("-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1") } for (i in words.indices) words[i] = 50 + (i * 7919L) % 25_000 var check = 0L for (round in 1..12) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() check += batch() val micros = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000 println("batch %2d: %,6d us".format(round, micros)) } println("(checksum $check)") // use the result, so the JIT can't drop the work } // start a second JVM with extra flags and the same classpath, and show its output private fun relaunch(flag: String) { val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") println("running with $flag") val p = ProcessBuilder(java, flag, "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l01.WarmupDemoKt", "tiered").redirectErrorStream(true).start() p.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filterNot { it.startsWith("Picked up") }.forEach(::println) } p.waitFor() } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l01.WarmupDemoKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l01/WarmupDemo.kt With the defaults, the first four batches take several hundred microseconds each, then the time falls below 100 µs once compiled code takes over the loop. On the busy course machine (JDK 25) it went from about 1,000 µs to 78 µs. With int, every batch stays near 700 µs. With c1 it gets fast too, here 69 µs. The drop comes around batch 5, not batch 2: batch() is called only 12 times, so it's the loop inside it that gets compiled, as the section on OSR explains. Your numbers will differ; the shape won't. The Gradle command runs the demo on the JDK that runs Gradle, so java -version tells you which one you measured.

h: From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 · Reading -XX:+PrintCompilation, one column at a time
x: -XX:+PrintCompilation makes the JVM print one line each time a compile finishes, and another when it stops using compiled code. To read the log, we need a program with a story. The Hot demo is a slice of the report service. A document is a list of blocks, and each kind of block knows how long it takes to read: Java interface Block { long millis(); } // one piece of a document: how long to read it? record Paragraph(long words) implements Block { public long millis() { return words * 250; } } static long readingMillis(Block[] blocks) { long sum = 0; for (Block b : blocks) sum += b.millis(); return sum; } Kotlin interface KBlock { fun millis(): Long } // one piece of a document: how long to read it? class KParagraph(private val words: Long) : KBlock { override fun millis() = words * 250 } fun readingMillis(blocks: Array<KBlock>): Long { var sum = 0L for (b in blocks) sum += b.millis() return sum } Hot does three things. It runs longLoop, one method whose loop makes 50 million laps, like one pass over a huge book. Then it adds up the reading time of an article of 1,000 paragraphs, 20,000 times. Finally it switches to a document that mixes paragraphs, headings and quotes. These are real lines from its log on JDK 25, picked from about fifty: 55 11 % 3 workbench.performance.l01.Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) 56 13 % 4 workbench.performance.l01.Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) 67 11 % 3 workbench.performance.l01.Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) made not entrant: OSR invalidation of lower level 252 19 2 workbench.performance.l01.Hot$Paragraph::millis (9 bytes) 252 20 4 workbench.performance.l01.Hot$Paragraph::millis (9 bytes) 271 24 4 workbench.performance.l01.Hot::readingMillis (42 bytes) 309 24 4 workbench.performance.l01.Hot::readingMillis (42 bytes) made not entrant: uncommon trap Read the second line from left to right, with the figure beside you. It finished 56 ms after the JVM started, and its compile id is 13. The % says it's an OSR compile, a loop compiled while it runs, which is the next section's topic. The 4 says C2 did it. @ 4 says the compiled code is entered at bytecode index 4. And (27 bytes) is the size of the method's bytecode, not of the machine code. Lesson 2 shows why that number matters: C2 counts these bytes when it decides what to copy into a caller. The five characters after the id are flags. % marks OSR, s a synchronized method and ! a method with a try/catch. b marks a compile the program had to wait for, and n a wrapper around a native method, one written in C outside Java. A line for a synchronized method looks like 58 25 s 3 Flags::syncInc (9 bytes). The compile id ties lines together. Id 11 shows up twice: once as a compile, and once with made not entrant. That means the JVM stopped using that code, and new calls won't enter it. Most of these lines are housekeeping, because lower-tier code retires as soon as better code takes over. Since JDK 25, the JVM prints the reason after a colon. All three of these came from the same run: made not entrant: OSR invalidation of lower level // C2's OSR code replaced C1's made not entrant: not used // a newer compile of the method took over made not entrant: uncommon trap // one of C2's bets failed (lesson 2) JDK 21 prints a bare made not entrant, with no reason. Now look at id 24 again. C2 compiled readingMillis at 271 ms and threw its work away at 309 ms, just after the headings and quotes arrived. Keep that line in mind; the next section starts to explain it, and lesson 2 finishes the job. Two warnings before you go hunting in logs. First, times and ids change from run to run. In three runs of Hot on JDK 25, the first compile of longLoop landed at 55, 63 and 165 ms. When the JVM compiles depends on how busy its compiler threads are, so never compare two logs line by line. Second, the JDK compiles its own methods too, such as String::hashCode, so filter the log by your package. The % lines are the strangest ones. longLoop is called exactly once, so how did it get compiled at all? Read the log of a running program Read Hot. Predict which of longLoop, readingMillis and Paragraph::millis will reach tier 4, and which will get a % line. Run it. The demo starts a second JVM with -XX:+PrintCompilation and keeps only the lines for this lesson's classes. Find the first tier 4 compile of readingMillis without a %. Then find the later line where its id is made not entrant. What did the program do just before? Run the Kotlin twin and compare the (N bytes) sizes. Add -Pargs=all to either one to see every line the JVM prints. Hot.java package workbench.performance.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Watch HotSpot compile this program. Run without arguments: it starts a second JVM with * -XX:+PrintCompilation and prints only the lines about this lesson's classes. * Pass "all" to see every line, including the JDK's own methods. */ public class Hot { // a document is a list of blocks, and each kind of block knows how long it takes to read interface Block { long millis(); } record Paragraph(long words) implements Block { public long millis() { return words * 250; } } // 4 words a second record Heading(long words) implements Block { public long millis() { return 1_000 + words * 400; } } // a pause, then slower record Quote(long words) implements Block { public long millis() { return words * 300; } } // a little slower static long readingMillis(Block[] blocks) { long sum = 0; for (Block b : blocks) sum += b.millis(); // one call site: first only paragraphs, later three types return sum; } static long longLoop() { // called once, but its loop runs 50 million times, like one pass over a huge book: OSR long acc = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 50_000_000; i++) acc += (i ^ (i >>> 3)); return acc; } static void work() { System.out.println(longLoop()); Block[] article = new Block[1000]; for (int i = 0; i < article.length; i++) article[i] = new Paragraph(i); long r = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 20_000; i++) r += readingMillis(article); // only paragraphs seen so far Block[] mixed = new Block[999]; for (int i = 0; i < mixed.length; i++) mixed[i] = switch (i % 3) { case 0 -> new Paragraph(i); case 1 -> new Heading(i); default -> new Quote(i); }; for (int i = 0; i < 20_000; i++) r += readingMillis(mixed); // two new types reach the same call site System.out.println(r); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("child")) { work(); return; } boolean all = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("all"); // the same as: java -XX:+PrintCompilation -cp <classpath> workbench.performance.l01.Hot child String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, "-XX:+PrintCompilation", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), Hot.class.getName(), "child")); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); try (var out = p.inputReader()) { out.lines() .filter(line -> all || line.contains("l01.Hot") || !line.contains("::")) .filter(line -> !line.startsWith("Picked up")) .forEach(System.out::println); } p.waitFor(); } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l01.Hot labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l01/Hot.java Hot.kt package workbench.performance.l01 // Kotlin twin of Hot.java: the same program, so you can compare what the JIT does with Kotlin bytecode. // Run without arguments: it starts a second JVM with -XX:+PrintCompilation and prints the lines // about this file's classes. Pass "all" to see every line. // a document is a list of blocks, and each kind of block knows how long it takes to read interface KBlock { fun millis(): Long } class KParagraph(private val words: Long) : KBlock { override fun millis() = words * 250 } // 4 words a second class KHeading(private val words: Long) : KBlock { override fun millis() = 1_000 + words * 400 } // a pause, then slower class KQuote(private val words: Long) : KBlock { override fun millis() = words * 300 } // a little slower fun readingMillis(blocks: Array<KBlock>): Long { var sum = 0L for (b in blocks) sum += b.millis() // one call site: first only paragraphs, later three types return sum } fun longLoop(): Long { // called once, but its loop runs 50 million times, like one pass over a huge book: OSR var acc = 0L for (i in 0 until 50_000_000) acc += (i xor (i ushr 3)) return acc } fun work() { println(longLoop()) val article = Array<KBlock>(1000) { KParagraph(it.toLong()) } var r = 0L repeat(20_000) { r += readingMillis(article) } // only KParagraph seen so far val mixed = Array(999) { when (it % 3) { 0 -> KParagraph(it.toLong()); 1 -> KHeading(it.toLong()); else -> KQuote(it.toLong()) } } repeat(20_000) { r += readingMillis(mixed) } // two new types reach the same call site println(r) } fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "child") { work(); return } val all = args.firstOrNull() == "all" // the same as: java -XX:+PrintCompilation -cp <classpath> workbench.performance.l01.HotKt child val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") val p = ProcessBuilder(java, "-XX:+PrintCompilation", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l01.HotKt", "child").redirectErrorStream(true).start() p.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filter { all || it.contains("l01.HotKt") || it.contains("l01.K") || !it.contains("::") } .filterNot { it.startsWith("Picked up") } .forEach(::println) } p.waitFor() } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l01.HotKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l01/Hot.kt longLoop gets % lines at tier 3 and tier 4 before the program prints 1251976370825152. Paragraph::millis reaches tier 4 (through tier 2 on JDK 25, through tier 3 on JDK 21). readingMillis reaches tier 4, then that compile is made not entrant right after the headings and quotes arrive, and a new tier 4 compile with a higher id follows. On JDK 25 each retirement carries its reason. The Kotlin twin compiles to almost the same bytecode: 27 bytes for longLoop and 43 for readingMillis, against 42 in Java, and its OSR entry is @ 14 instead of @ 11. One OSR line from PrintCompilation, column by column. The size is bytecode, not machine code.

h: From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 · OSR: compiling a loop while it is still running
x: longLoop never gets near 200 calls, yet it was the first of our methods to be compiled. If the JVM only counted calls, a method stuck in one long loop would stay in the interpreter forever. So it counts back-edges too. Picture the cook making one enormous pot of soup for a wedding, adding the stock one ladle at a time. Halfway through, they work out a faster way to do it. They don't pour the pot away and start again. They switch technique mid-pot, and the soup carries on. The JVM does the same. When one loop has jumped back about 60,000 times (Tier3BackEdgeThreshold on JDK 25), it compiles a version of the method that starts at the top of the loop. Then it moves the running call, with its local variables, into that code. This is on-stack replacement (OSR): the call's stack frame, the record of its local variables, is swapped for a compiled one while the call is still running. C2 does the same at tier 4 after about 40,000 more back-edges (Tier4BackEdgeThreshold). The @ 4 points at the loop. javap -c, the JDK's class-file printer, shows the bytecode: static long longLoop(); 0: lconst_0 1: lstore_0 2: iconst_0 3: istore_2 4: iload_2 // top of the loop: the OSR code is entered here 5: ldc #13 // int 50000000 7: if_icmpge 25 // the exit test: leave when i reaches 50 million ... 22: goto 4 // the back-edge the JVM counts Here is the rest of longLoop's story, from the same JDK 25 run: 55 11 % 3 ...Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) 55 12 3 ...Hot::longLoop (27 bytes) 56 13 % 4 ...Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) 67 11 % 3 ...Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) made not entrant: OSR invalidation of lower level 246 13 % 4 ...Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) made not entrant: uncommon trap The first retirement is housekeeping: once the C2 OSR code exists, the JVM retires C1's. The second is more interesting. When the loop finishes at 246 ms, the C2 code throws itself away. Running the same program with -Xlog:deoptimization=debug says why: cid= 13 osr level=4 workbench.performance.l01.Hot.longLoop()J trap_bci=7 osr_bci=4 unstable_if reinterpret trap_bci=7 is the exit test. While C1 watched the loop, it never saw the loop end, so C2 didn't compile the exit at all. It put an uncommon trap there instead: a small stub that hands the running call back to the interpreter if a branch C2 never saw ever runs. C2 bet that this loop would never end. It lost exactly once, at the very end, and it cost nothing. That's the JIT's betting habit in miniature, and lesson 2 is all about those bets. The same log has lines for readingMillis with trap_bci=27 class_check, printed the moment the headings and quotes arrived. Bytecode 27 is the b.millis() call. It's the same event as id 24's retirement in the last section, C2 code thrown away when a new kind of block showed up, and lesson 2 picks it up from there. OSR matters to you for one practical reason. A benchmark written as one long loop in main measures OSR code and its quirks, which may not be the code your program runs after warm-up. JMH, the benchmarking tool in lesson 3, avoids that trap. So the JVM compiles loops and methods, and retires code it no longer trusts. All that machine code has to live somewhere, and it doesn't survive a restart. Find the loop and the trap Run the Hot demo once, so Gradle compiles it. From labs/, print the bytecode of longLoop with the first command below. Find index 4 and index 7. Run the second command. It starts Hot directly with the deoptimization log on. h: From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 · The code cache, and why every new JVM starts cold
x: Machine code needs a place to live. HotSpot keeps it in the code cache, a memory area outside the heap (the heap is where your objects live). It's the cook's shelf of cheat sheets. With tiered compilation the JVM sets aside 240 MB for it (ReservedCodeCacheSize), split into three parts. java -XX:+PrintCodeCache -version on JDK 25 prints them as the JVM exits: CodeHeap 'non-profiled nmethods': size=120032Kb used=2Kb max_used=2Kb free=120029Kb CodeHeap 'profiled nmethods': size=120032Kb used=4Kb max_used=4Kb free=120027Kb CodeHeap 'non-nmethods': size=5700Kb used=1256Kb max_used=1256Kb free=4443Kb CodeCache: size=245764Kb, used=1262Kb, max_used=1262Kb, free=244499Kb An nmethod is HotSpot's name for one compiled method. Tier 2 and tier 3 code, which still counts and records, goes in 'profiled nmethods'. Tier 1 and tier 4 code goes in 'non-profiled nmethods'. The third part holds small pieces of glue that the interpreter and compiled code need. After Hot has run, the two method parts hold 10 KB and 18 KB. It's a big shelf. A large program can still fill it. Then the JVM warns CodeHeap 'non-profiled nmethods' is full. Compiler has been disabled., stops starting new compiles and schedules a clean-up so it can start again later. Until then, methods that aren't compiled yet stay in the interpreter. jcmd <pid> Compiler.codecache shows the parts on a running JVM. jcmd is a JDK tool that sends commands to a running JVM, and <pid> is the process id, the number the operating system gives each running program. Look there before you raise the size. The bigger cost for a service is that every JVM starts from scratch, and here the picture breaks. A real cook remembers yesterday's dishes. A JVM forgets everything when its process ends, so every restart is the cook's first day again. After the report service restarts, its first thousands of requests (a request is one user asking for one report) run in the interpreter and in C1. The busy paths reach C2 only after thousands of calls each, and the compiler threads share the machine's cores with the threads serving those requests. So a freshly started service answers more slowly for a while, and a test run against it in its first minute measures day one. There are two usual answers. You can send it made-up warm-up requests before it takes real ones. Or, on JDK 25, you can hand the cook notes from a training day: an AOT cache (ahead-of-time cache), a file recorded during a training run. JEP 514 makes the cache easy to create, and JEP 515 adds method profiles to it: java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=warm.aot -cp warm.jar workbench.performance.l01.WarmupDemo # training run java -XX:AOTCache=warm.aot -cp warm.jar workbench.performance.l01.WarmupDemo # later runs On the course machine, the training run wrote an 11 MB cache. WarmupDemo had to be packed into a jar first: given a folder of classes, the JVM refused with Cannot have non-empty directory in paths. In the next two runs, the batches were fast from batch 2; without the cache, from batch 5. The startup track covers the AOT cache properly. A number from the first seconds of a JVM measures the cook's first day. Measure after warm-up, or say it's a cold start. That rule will follow us through the whole track. Lesson 3 turns it into a tool that does the warm-up for you. Look inside the code cache Run the first command from labs/. It starts a JVM that does nothing and prints the code cache as it exits. Run the second one, which prints the code cache after Hot has run. Compare the used= numbers. Optional: start any demo that runs for a while, find its pid with jcmd -l, and run jcmd <pid> Compiler.codecache against it. terminal java -XX:+PrintCodeCache -version java -XX:+PrintCodeCache -cp performance/build/classes/java/demo workbench.performance.l01.Hot child Three parts of about 117 MB, 117 MB and 5.6 MB, 240 MB in all. With -version, only a few KB of compiled methods are used. After Hot, the two method parts hold more (10 KB and 18 KB on the course machine), because Hot and the JDK methods it called were compiled. That's still a tiny part of 240 MB. JEP 515: Ahead-of-Time Method Profiling read

x: The JIT sees bytecode, not Java or Kotlin Hot.java static long readingMillis(Block[] blocks) { long sum = 0; for (Block b : blocks) sum += b.millis(); return sum; } // PrintCompilation: Hot::readingMillis (42 bytes) // OSR entry: @ 11 Hot.kt fun readingMillis(blocks: Array<KBlock>): Long { var sum = 0L for (b in blocks) sum += b.millis() return sum } // PrintCompilation: HotKt::readingMillis (43 bytes) // OSR entry: @ 14 Both loops compile to an indexed loop over the array with one invokeinterface, a call through an interface that is resolved at run time. So HotSpot treats them the same way: same tiers, same OSR, same throw-away when headings and quotes arrive. The only visible differences are one byte of bytecode and a different loop index. A Kotlin top-level function lives in a class named after its file (HotKt), and that's the name to search for in logs. Where Kotlin really changes what the JIT sees is in inline functions, which come up in lesson 2.

h: From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 · Quiz
x: The report service's rebuildIndex() is called once, and it loops over 3 million lines. What does -XX:+PrintCompilation most likely show for it? Nothing, since it is called only once One tier 4 line after 10,000 calls Lines with % and @ <bci>: OSR compiles of its loop at tier 3, then tier 4 A single tier 1 line, because it is called rarely The JVM counts loop back-edges as well as calls. After about 60,000 back-edges it compiles an OSR version of the method at tier 3, and C2 follows at tier 4. "Called once" only rules out the normal compiles that calls trigger. On JDK 25, which line says that C2 code was thrown away because one of its assumptions failed? 252 19 2 Hot$Paragraph::millis (9 bytes) made not entrant: not used 67 11 % 3 Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) made not entrant: OSR invalidation of lower level 271 24 4 Hot::readingMillis (42 bytes) 309 24 4 Hot::readingMillis (42 bytes) made not entrant: uncommon trap Tier 4 plus uncommon trap means C2 hit a case it had compiled as "never happens" and handed the call back to the interpreter. not used and OSR invalidation of lower level are housekeeping: newer or better code replaced older code. The third line is a compile, not a retirement. What does (42 bytes) at the end of a PrintCompilation line measure? The size of the machine code C2 produced The size of the method's bytecode The stack frame size of the method How much memory one call allocates The JVM prints the length of the method's bytecode. Machine code is usually much larger. The number matters because the inlining limits in lesson 2 are measured in bytecode bytes. A teammate's warm-up script calls the report endpoint exactly 10,000 times "because HotSpot compiles after 10,000 calls". On JDK 25 with default flags, what's wrong with that reasoning? Tiered compilation uses about 200 calls for tier 3 and about 5,000 more for tier 4, loops count too, and the thresholds rise when compile queues are long, so no fixed call count guarantees C2 Nothing, 10,000 is the default threshold HotSpot only compiles methods marked final C2 has been off by default since JDK 21 10,000 is CompileThreshold, which is used only with -XX:-TieredCompilation. With tiered compilation the triggers are different, and they grow with compiler load. Warm up until the timings settle, not to a magic number. In the memory model track, a loop on a plain stop field spun forever, but it stopped when the program ran with -Xint. In this lesson's terms, why? -Xint makes every field volatile -Xint turns off the CPU caches The interpreter re-reads the field on every lap. The hang appears only once C2 (often through OSR) compiles the loop and keeps the value in a register The interpreter runs every thread on one core Under -Xint the method never leaves tier 0, and the interpreter loads the field each time. The JIT is allowed to read a non-volatile field once and lift it out of the loop. A busy loop reaches C2 through OSR even when its method is called once, which is exactly when the hang starts.

h: From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 · Key terms
x: Bytecode The JVM's instructions, written by javac or kotlinc into .class files. Interpreter Tier 0. Runs bytecode one instruction at a time and counts calls and loops. C1 The fast, lightly optimizing JIT compiler. At tier 3 it also collects the profile. C2 The slow, heavily optimizing JIT compiler (tier 4). It uses the profile to make bets. Tiered compilation Using the interpreter, C1 and C2 one after another, on by default. OSR (on-stack replacement) Compiling a running loop and moving the live call into the new code mid-loop. Code cache Memory outside the heap that holds compiled code, 240 MB reserved by default. Made not entrant Compiled code the JVM has retired: new calls no longer enter it. Which compiler runs a method at tier 3, and what does it add? C1, with full profiling: call and loop counters plus branch counts and the types seen at each call. C2 uses that profile. Which compiler runs a method at tier 4? C2, compiling with the profile that tier 3 collected. In a PrintCompilation line, what do % and @ 4 mean? % marks an OSR compile. @ 4 is the bytecode index of the loop where the compiled code is entered. What is the number in (27 bytes) on a PrintCompilation line? The method's bytecode size. Inlining limits are measured in these bytes. Roughly when does a method reach tier 3 and tier 4 on JDK 21 to 27? About 200 calls for tier 3, then about 5,000 more for tier 4. Loop laps count too, and the bar rises when compile queues are long. What does made not entrant mean? The JVM stopped using that compiled version; new calls won't enter it. JDK 25 prints the reason, such as not used or uncommon trap. How big is the code cache by default, and how do you inspect it on a running JVM? 240 MB reserved with tiered compilation, in three parts. jcmd <pid> Compiler.codecache.

h: From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 · Go deeper
x: PrintCompilation is the summary. For the full story, run with -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+LogCompilation, which writes an XML log of every compile decision, and open it in JITWatch, a log viewer for HotSpot's JIT. Its wiki says to add -Xlog:class+load=info so it can build its class model. To see the machine code too, add -XX:+PrintAssembly, which needs the hsdis disassembler library. A few jcmd commands help on a running JVM: Compiler.queue shows what's waiting to be compiled, Compiler.codelist lists the compiled methods, and Compiler.codecache shows the parts of the code cache. The JVM picks the number of compiler threads from the CPU count: -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal showed CICompilerCount = 3 on the 4-core course machine. -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 (C1 only) compiles less and peaks lower on most real code. The HotSpot source describes it as mostly for testing, so keep it out of production. JDK 25 added two JEPs aimed at warm-up, both used in the last section. JEP 514 makes the AOT cache easier to create, with -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot on a training run and -XX:AOTCache=app.aot on later runs. JEP 515 stores method profiles in that cache, so a new JVM can start compiling busy methods with C2 sooner. Compiling the code itself ahead of time is a separate, later step: JEP 544 is in the mainline for JDK 28, which isn't released yet. The startup track goes through all of this. One more thing you may read about: "made zombie". Older JDKs printed that when retired code was finally freed. JDK 25 doesn't print it, so treat articles that show it as describing an older JVM.

h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · Inlining: copying a small method into its caller, within a budget
x: A call is a wall to C2 until it inlines the callee, within a budget of 35 bytes or 325 at a hot site; intrinsics swap JDK methods for hand-written code Start with something you can see. The report service checks every document it receives, and here's one check, written the way most of us would write it the first time: Java static long requireWordCountInline(long words) { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) { throw new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d", MAX_WORDS, words)); } return words; } Kotlin fun requireWordCountInline(words: Long): Long { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) { throw IllegalArgumentException("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d".format(MAX_WORDS, words)) } return words } It looks tiny. C2 disagrees: it's 49 bytes of bytecode, the instructions javac writes into the class file, and that number decides whether C2 will copy it into its callers. Inlining means C2 pastes the body of a called method into the caller and compiles the two as one piece. It's the cook copying the sauce recipe from page 12 into the main recipe. Skipping the call itself is the small win. The big win is that C2's other optimizations can now see both sides of the call. Escape analysis can prove that an object never leaves the method, so it needn't be put on the heap, the memory where objects live, at all. Constant folding can work out results from values known at compile time. Loop optimizations, such as unrolling (copying the loop body a few times so the loop makes fewer laps), can work on the whole loop. A method C2 doesn't inline is a wall it can't see through. C2 decides at each call site, one call instruction in the bytecode, using the callee's bytecode size: the (N bytes) from lesson 1. The rule in HotSpot's bytecodeInfo.cpp is short. If the call runs on at least 25% of the caller's invocations (InlineFrequencyRatio), the site counts as hot, and C2 inlines methods of up to 325 bytes (FreqInlineSize). Otherwise the limit is 35 bytes (MaxInlineSize). C2 also stops 15 levels deep (MaxInlineLevel), and it refuses a callee that is already compiled into more than 2,500 bytes of machine code (InlineSmallCode). These values are the same from JDK 21 to JDK 27. The budget counts every byte, even code that almost never runs. Most of the check's 49 bytes build the error message: two boxing calls, which wrap each long in a Long object, an array for the arguments, and String.format. Move that cold path into its own method and the hot method shrinks to 21 bytes: Java static long requireWordCount(long words) { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) throw badWordCount(words); // hot path: 21 bytes return words; } static IllegalArgumentException badWordCount(long words) { // cold path, its own method return new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d", MAX_WORDS, words)); } Kotlin fun requireWordCount(words: Long): Long { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) throw badWordCount(words) // hot path: 21 bytes return words } fun badWordCount(words: Long) = // cold path, its own function IllegalArgumentException("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d".format(MAX_WORDS, words)) InliningDemo calls both versions from a method called summarize, each on 1 call in 8, so neither call site is hot. This is the real C2 output on JDK 25: @ 15 ...InliningDemo::requireWordCountInline (49 bytes) failed to inline: too big @ 30 ...InliningDemo::requireWordCountSplit (21 bytes) inline (hot) JDK 21 prints the same decisions without the failed to inline: prefix. Don't read too much into inline (hot), by the way. It's simply what C2 prints when it inlines and has nothing more specific to say. The JDK's own code uses this split all the time: a small check, plus a separate method that builds the exception. C2 counts the bytes of the error path too. Give the cold path its own method. This check is a static method, so C2 always knows which code a call to it runs. Most calls in an object-oriented program aren't so simple. See C2 refuse the big check Run InliningDemo. It starts a second JVM with -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining and keeps the lines about summarize and the two checks. Find the decisions under the tier 3 compile (C1 says callee is too large) and under the tier 4 compile (C2 says too big). Run the Kotlin twin. Compare the size of requireWordCountInline in both languages. InliningDemo.java package workbench.performance.l02; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Two versions of the same word-count check. One builds its error message inline, the other moves * the cold path into a helper. Run it: a second JVM starts with -XX:+PrintInlining and the demo * prints what C1 and C2 decided at the two call sites in summarize(). */ public class InliningDemo { static final long MAX_WORDS = 10_000_000L; // the error message is built right here, so its bytecode counts against the inlining budget static long requireWordCountInline(long words) { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) { throw new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d", MAX_WORDS, words)); } return words; } // same check, but the cold path lives in its own method static long requireWordCountSplit(long words) { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) throw badWordCount(words); return words; } static IllegalArgumentException badWordCount(long words) { return new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d", MAX_WORDS, words)); } // a summary is about a tenth of the text; each check runs on 1 call in 8, so neither call site is hot for C2 static long summarize(long words, int i) { long r = words / 10; if ((i & 7) == 0) r += requireWordCountInline(words); if ((i & 7) == 1) r += requireWordCountSplit(words); return r; } static void work() { long s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 2_000_000; i++) s += summarize(1_000 + (i & 1023), i); System.out.println("checksum " + s); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("child")) { work(); return; } String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, "-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions", "-XX:+PrintInlining", "-XX:+PrintCompilation", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), InliningDemo.class.getName(), "child")); } p.waitFor(); } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l02.InliningDemo labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l02/InliningDemo.java InliningDemo.kt package workbench.performance.l02 // Kotlin twin of InliningDemo.java: the same two checks, compiled by kotlinc. // Run it: a second JVM starts with -XX:+PrintInlining and the demo prints the decisions in summarize(). const val MAX_WORDS = 10_000_000L // the error message is built right here, so its bytecode counts against the inlining budget fun requireWordCountInline(words: Long): Long { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) { throw IllegalArgumentException("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d".format(MAX_WORDS, words)) } return words } // same check, but the cold path lives in its own function fun requireWordCountSplit(words: Long): Long { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) throw badWordCount(words) return words } fun badWordCount(words: Long) = IllegalArgumentException("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d".format(MAX_WORDS, words)) // a summary is about a tenth of the text; In Java the sizes are 49 and 21 bytes. In Kotlin the version with the message inline is 66 bytes: "...".format(...) is an inline function, so kotlinc pastes its body (an Arrays.copyOf of the arguments and a null check) into the caller. The split version is 21 bytes in both. On JDK 25 each refusal starts with failed to inline:. bytecodeInfo.cpp: C2's inlining rules (JDK 25) read

h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · C2 bets on the types it has seen at each call
x: Back to the documents. readingMillis from lesson 1 calls b.millis() on every block. That's a call through an interface, so it could go to Paragraph, Heading, Quote or a class nobody has written yet. C2 can only inline it if it knows which one. The object a method is called on is the receiver. At tier 3, C1, the quick compiler from lesson 1, records the receiver types it sees at each call site, and C2 reads that type profile when it compiles. It's the cook's tally of side dishes, and C2 handles three cases: One type seen: C2 inlines that type's method behind a cheap check, "is it a Paragraph?". The site is monomorphic, one shape. That's the basket of fries by the stove. Two types: it inlines both, behind two checks (bimorphic). The profile keeps two types per site (TypeProfileWidth is 2). Three or more: C2 inlines only a type that has at least 90% of the calls (TypeProfileMajorReceiverPercent). Otherwise the site is megamorphic, and C2 emits a plain virtual call, which looks the method up in the receiver's class at run time and jumps to it. Nothing gets inlined. The cook stops keeping sides ready and reads every order. -XX:+PrintInlining shows the bet. This is the real decision for the millis() call in lesson 1's Hot, on JDK 21, while only paragraphs had arrived: @ 27 workbench.performance.l01.Hot$Paragraph::millis (9 bytes) inline (hot) \-> TypeProfile (1408440/1408440 counts) = workbench/performance/l01/Hot$Paragraph Every one of 1,408,440 calls went to a Paragraph, so C2 copied Paragraph::millis into the loop. What happened after the headings and quotes arrived surprised me. The recompiled readingMillis still inlined Paragraph, with TypeProfile (1463420/1572265 counts): 93% paragraphs. The profile is a running tally since the program started, and 20,000 trips through an article of paragraphs had piled up a lot of marks. On JDK 25, the run's last compile did switch to failed to inline: virtual call. The tally remembers the past, and what it says when C2 reads it decides the code. To watch the number of types on its own, MegamorphicBench feeds one call site with 1, 2 or 3 kinds of block, in documents of 1,024 blocks. It's a JMH benchmark (lesson 3 explains JMH), and each case runs in a fresh JVM, so each starts with an empty tally. Two runs on the busy course machine, in nanoseconds per document: types run 1 run 2 1 950 1,170 2 2,093 1,547 3 7,913 5,122 The error bars on that machine were wider than the scores, so read only the shape: three types cost several times more than one or two. With the calls inlined, C2 can optimize the whole loop. With a virtual call per block, it can't. Notice what didn't matter. A record is a final class, so Paragraph can't have subclasses, yet the log says C2 inlined it from the type profile, not from the modifier. Kotlin classes are final by default, and that changes nothing here either. What changes speed is how many types reach one call site. So C2 compiles what its tally shows. What does it do about the orders it has never seen? Count the types at a call site Predict the three numbers before you run: nanoseconds per document with 1, 2 and 3 kinds of block. Run MegamorphicBench. Each case runs in a fresh JVM, so each starts with a clean profile. It takes about 10 seconds. On JDK 24 and later, JMH 1.37 makes the JVM print a few WARNING lines about sun.misc.Unsafe; they're harmless. Run it with -Pargs='1 4'. Does a fourth type cost more than the third? The Kotlin twin runs 1, 3 and 4 types. h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · When a bet loses: uncommon traps and deoptimization
x: C2 compiles what the profile showed and nothing else. A branch that was never taken, or a receiver type that never appeared, gets no compiled code. In its place C2 puts an uncommon trap, the stub from lesson 1. If the "impossible" case ever happens, the trap hands the running call back to the interpreter, the part of the JVM that runs bytecode one instruction at a time. When a trap fires, the JVM deoptimizes: it rebuilds an interpreter frame from the compiled one and carries on in the interpreter. The compiled code is made not entrant, which means retired: no new call will enter it. The method goes back to tier 3 for more profiling, now with the new case in its tally, and is compiled again. In the kitchen, the customer who asks for rice sends the cook back to the recipe card, and soon rice is part of the routine. The figure shows the cycle. DeoptDemo trips both common kinds of trap on purpose. It adds up the reading time of a document in three phases. First come paragraphs only. Then each document gets one folded block, such as a hidden spoiler, which costs the reader only a glance. Finally headings and quotes arrive. The loop body: Java long ms = blocks[i].millis(); // bytecode 16: which types has it seen? if (folded[i]) total += GLANCE_MILLIS; // bytecode 27: has this branch ever been taken? else total += ms; Kotlin val ms = blocks[i].millis() // which types has it seen? if (folded[i]) total += GLANCE_MILLIS // has this branch ever been taken? else total += ms The real log on JDK 25, trimmed to the important lines: phase 2: one folded block per document ... DeoptDemo.readingMillis(...) trap_bci=27 unstable_if reinterpret 224 23 4 ...DeoptDemo::readingMillis (52 bytes) made not entrant: uncommon trap phase 3: headings and quotes arrive ... DeoptDemo.readingMillis(...) trap_bci=16 class_check maybe_recompile 255 26 4 ...DeoptDemo::readingMillis (52 bytes) made not entrant: uncommon trap unstable_if means a branch C2 had compiled as never taken: the folded block. class_check means a type check failed at a call C2 had inlined for paragraphs only. Each time, a new tier 4 compile followed within a few milliseconds, ids 26 and 37 in this run. This is normal, and cheap when it happens a few times. HotSpot also caps how often one method can go around the cycle (PerMethodRecompilationCutoff is 400 recompiles). Expect a burst of deoptimizations just after a program starts, or when a new kind of input gets its first traffic. A steady stream of them in a service that has been up for hours is worth a look. JFR, the recorder built into the JDK, has a ready-made view for that, deoptimizations-by-reason, and lesson 5 uses it. Here the picture breaks a little. A cook who gets burned by a shortcut might grow careful. C2 doesn't: it recompiles with the new facts and bets again, as boldly as before. That's usually right, because most programs settle into the same few cases. C2 compiles only what it has seen. The first unusual input sends the call back to the interpreter. Bets and traps are C2 learning about your code. For a few JDK methods, it doesn't need to learn anything. Trip a branch trap and a type trap Predict: in which phase will the first made not entrant for tier 4 code appear, and with which reason in the deoptimization log? Run DeoptDemo. It starts a second JVM with -XX:+PrintCompilation -Xlog:deoptimization=debug. Match each trap_bci to a line of readingMillis (bytecode 16 is the millis() call, 27 is the if (folded[i]) test). Then run the Kotlin twin: its bytecode indexes differ, the story doesn't.
