h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · Intrinsics: JDK methods the JIT swaps for ready-made machine code
x: Some JDK methods never run as their Java code once they're hot. HotSpot carries hand-written machine code, or hand-written compiler instructions, for them. These are intrinsics, and they're the kitchen gadget that does one job perfectly. The recipe card may say "core the apple with a small knife", in twelve careful steps; a cook with an apple corer does it in one push. In the JDK source, these methods carry @IntrinsicCandidate, whose Javadoc says the method "may be (but is not guaranteed to be) intrinsified". PrintInlining marks the ones that were: java.lang.Long::bitCount (61 bytes) (intrinsic) java.lang.Math::addExact (32 bytes) (intrinsic) java.util.Arrays::equals (43 bytes) (intrinsic) Those are real lines from IntrinsicsDemo, the same on JDK 21 and JDK 25, and the report service has a use for each one. Long.bitCount counts the 1 bits in a long. The service keeps a document's text styles (bold, italic, underline and so on) as one bit each, so the count says how many are switched on. In Java it's 61 bytes of shifts and masks; on x86, C2 replaces it with a single POPCNT instruction. Math.addExact adds up the word counts of many documents and throws ArithmeticException if the total overflows, instead of quietly wrapping around to a negative number. Arrays.equals checks whether two uploaded texts have the same bytes, and ends up in code that compares many bytes per step. The bytecode size doesn't matter for an intrinsic, because that Java code isn't what runs. Those 61 bytes are still there for a reason, though: they're the instructions for a kitchen without the gadget. The interpreter, or a processor without POPCNT, runs the Java version. The practical rule follows. In hot code, call the JDK method instead of writing the loop yourself. A hand-written loop that compares two texts byte by byte gives up the many-bytes-at-a-time path that Arrays.equals gets for free, and it's more code to get wrong. Kotlin gets the same intrinsics, because its standard library calls these JDK methods. ByteArray.contentEquals calls java.util.Arrays.equals, and Long.countOneBits() calls java.lang.Long.bitCount: Java long total = Math.addExact(totalWords, words); // ArithmeticException on overflow boolean same = Arrays.equals(textA, textB); int styles = Long.bitCount(styleBits); Kotlin val total = Math.addExact(totalWords, words) // ArithmeticException on overflow val same = textA.contentEquals(textB) // calls java.util.Arrays.equals val styles = styleBits.countOneBits() // calls java.lang.Long.bitCount That finishes our tour of C2's notebook: it copies small methods, bets on types, loses bets and swaps in gadgets. We've judged every one of those choices with a timing. Which raises a question we've been dodging: how far can a timing taken by hand be trusted? List the intrinsics in a hot loop Run IntrinsicsDemo. It prints the PrintInlining lines for the three JDK methods it calls. Run the Kotlin twin, which uses contentEquals and countOneBits instead of calling Arrays and Long directly. Optional: run the Java demo's second JVM yourself with -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining and search for intrinsic to see how many others the JDK uses on its own. IntrinsicsDemo.java package workbench.performance.l02; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.TreeSet; /** * Calls three JDK methods that HotSpot replaces with hand-written machine code. Run it: a second * JVM starts with -XX:+PrintInlining and the demo lists the intrinsic decisions for them. */ public class IntrinsicsDemo { static long totalWords(long[] words) { long sum = 0; for (long w : words) sum = Math.addExact(sum, w); // throws on overflow instead of wrapping return sum; } static boolean sameText(byte[] a, byte[] b) { return Arrays.equals(a, b); // compares many bytes per step } static int stylesOn(long styleBits) { return Long.bitCount(styleBits); // one POPCNT instruction on x86 } static void work() { long[] words = new long[1_000]; // the word counts of 1,000 documents Arrays.fill(words, 1_999); byte[] t1 = new byte[64], t2 = new byte[64]; // two texts, as bytes long s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) { s += totalWords(words); if (sameText(t1, t2)) s++; s += stylesOn(i); // bold, italic, ...: one bit per style } System.out.println("checksum " + s); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("child")) { work(); return; } String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, "-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions", "-XX:+PrintInlining", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), IntrinsicsDemo.class.getName(), "child")); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); TreeSet<String> seen = new TreeSet<>(); try (var out = p.inputReader()) { out.lines() .filter(l -> l.contains("intrinsic")) .filter(l -> l.contains("Math::addExact") || l.contains("Arrays::equals") || l.contains("Long::bitCount")) .map(l -> l.replaceFirst("^\\s*@ \\d+\\s+", "")) // drop the indent and the call-site index .forEach(seen::add); } p.waitFor(); seen.forEach(System.out::println); } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l02.IntrinsicsDemo labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l02/IntrinsicsDemo.java IntrinsicsDemo.kt package workbench.performance.l02 // Kotlin twin of IntrinsicsDemo.java. The Kotlin standard library calls the same JDK methods, // so the same intrinsics apply: contentEquals calls Arrays.equals, countOneBits calls Long.bitCount. fun totalWordsKt(words: LongArray): Long { var sum = 0L for (w in words) sum = Math.addExact(sum, w) // throws on overflow instead of wrapping return sum } fun sameTextKt(a: ByteArray, b: ByteArray) = a.contentEquals(b) fun stylesOnKt(styleBits: Long) = styleBits.countOneBits() fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "child") { val words = LongArray(1_000) { 1_999 } // the word counts of 1,000 documents val t1 = ByteArray(64) // two texts, as bytes val t2 = ByteArray(64) var s = 0L for (i in 0 until 200_000) { s += totalWordsKt(words) if (sameTextKt(t1, t2)) s++ s += stylesOnKt(i.toLong()) // bold, italic, ...: one bit per style } println("checksum $s") return } val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") val p = ProcessBuilder(java, "-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions", "-XX:+PrintInlining", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l02.IntrinsicsDemoKt", "child") .redirectErrorStream(true).start() val seen = sortedSetOf<String>() p.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filter { "intrinsic" in it } .filter { "Math::addExact" in it || "Arrays::equals" in it || "Long::bitCount" in it } .mapTo(seen) { it.replaceFirst(Regex("""^\s*@ \d+\s+"""), "") } // drop the indent and call-site index } p.waitFor() seen.forEach(::println) } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l02.IntrinsicsDemoKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l02/IntrinsicsDemo.kt Both programs print the same three lines, each ending in (intrinsic): Long::bitCount, Math::addExact and Arrays::equals. Kotlin's standard library functions disappear entirely: they are inline, so the call in the bytecode is already the JDK method.

h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · Java and Kotlin
x: The same check, before and after the split InliningDemo.java // before: 49 bytes, "too big" at a call site that isn't hot static long requireWordCountInline(long words) { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) { throw new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d", MAX_WORDS, words)); } return words; } // after: 21 bytes, inlined static long requireWordCount(long words) { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) throw badWordCount(words); // hot path: 21 bytes return words; } static IllegalArgumentException badWordCount(long words) { // cold path, its own method return new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d", MAX_WORDS, words)); } InliningDemo.kt // before: 66 bytes, "too big" at a call site that isn't hot fun requireWordCountInline(words: Long): Long { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) { throw IllegalArgumentException("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d".format(MAX_WORDS, words)) } return words } // after: 21 bytes, inlined fun requireWordCount(words: Long): Long { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) throw badWordCount(words) // hot path: 21 bytes return words } fun badWordCount(words: Long) = // cold path, its own function IllegalArgumentException("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d".format(MAX_WORDS, words)) After the split, both languages compile requireWordCount to the same 21 bytes, and C2 treats them the same. Before the split, the Kotlin version is 66 bytes against Java's 49, because kotlinc pastes the body of the inline format extension into the caller: an Arrays.copyOf of the arguments and a null check on the result. So the same fix matters a little more in Kotlin. In both languages the cold method still builds exactly the same message, so nobody searching the logs for it will notice the change.

x: Find out why a hot method isn't inlined, and fix it The report handler is slower than expected in a profile. Start the service with the diagnostic flags and look for the check in the inlining log. java -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining -cp report.jar example.report.Main | grep requireWordCount C2's line names the method, its bytecode size and the reason. too big means the call site isn't hot and the callee is over 35 bytes. hot method too big would mean a hot site and a callee over 325 bytes. @ 15 example.report.Guards::requireWordCount (49 bytes) failed to inline: too big Look at what the 49 bytes are. javap -c -p shows the boxing calls, the argument array and the String.format that build the message. All of that is the cold path. javap -c -p -cp report.jar example.report.Guards | grep -A 30 'long requireWordCount' Move the cold path into its own method and return the exception from it, so the hot method still ends in throw. Self-check before reading on: why return the exception instead of throwing it inside the helper? (Answer: with throw badWordCount(words), javac and the next reader can both see that the method ends there. h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · Quiz
x: C2's inlining log shows @ 15 DocumentGuards::requireWordCount (49 bytes) failed to inline: too big inside the report handler. Which change is most likely to get it inlined? Mark requireWordCount as final Move the message building into a separate method so requireWordCount is under 35 bytes Raise the heap size with -Xmx Wrap the call in a lambda too big means the call site isn't hot, so the 35-byte limit applies, and the cold message code is most of the 49 bytes. A static method is already bound to one implementation, so final changes nothing, and the heap has nothing to do with inlining. A call site has seen Paragraph (50%), Heading (30%) and Quote (20%). What does C2 compile there? Three inlined bodies behind three type checks Paragraph inlined, the rest as a virtual call A plain virtual call, with nothing inlined Nothing: the method stays at tier 3 The profile keeps two types per site, and with more than two C2 needs one type with at least 90% of the calls to inline it. 50% isn't enough, so the site is megamorphic and becomes a virtual call. A deoptimization log line reads trap_bci=27 unstable_if reinterpret. What happened? Bytecode 27 is a branch C2 compiled as never taken; it was taken, so the call went back to the interpreter and the method will be compiled again The JVM ran out of code cache at bytecode 27 A class was loaded twice The method threw an exception at bytecode 27 unstable_if is the trap C2 places on a branch the profile never saw taken. When it runs, the JVM deoptimizes the call and the code is made not entrant. class_check would be the type-based version. The inlining log shows java.lang.Long::bitCount (61 bytes) (intrinsic). What does that tell you? The method was too big to inline The method was compiled to 61 bytes of machine code The method runs in the interpreter C2 replaced the call with ready-made code, so the 61 bytes of Java don't run in that compiled code An intrinsic replaces the method body with code HotSpot ships for it, a single POPCNT on x86 for bitCount. The size in the line is still the Java bytecode size, which doesn't matter once the intrinsic applies. PrintCompilation shows DeoptDemo::readingMillis (52 bytes). Using what lesson 1 said about that number, can C2 inline readingMillis into a caller that calls it on only 1 invocation in 10? Yes, 52 bytes of machine code is small No: 52 bytes of bytecode is over the 35-byte limit for a call site that isn't hot Yes, any method under 325 bytes is always inlined No, methods with loops are never inlined (52 bytes) is the bytecode size. A call on 1 invocation in 10 is below the 25% bar, so the 35-byte MaxInlineSize applies and 52 is too big. At a hot site the limit would be 325, and it could be inlined.

h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · Explain it back
x: A colleague asks: "Why did our report loop get slower when we added a third kind of block, even though the new class is tiny?" Explain it in your own words.

h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · Key terms
x: Inlining Pasting a called method's body into the caller so C2 compiles and optimizes them together. Call site One specific call instruction in the bytecode. Profiles and inlining decisions are per call site. Receiver The object a method is called on: b in b.millis(). Monomorphic, bimorphic, megamorphic One, two, or too many receiver types seen at a call site. Uncommon trap A stub in C2 code for a case the profile never saw. Running it deoptimizes the call. Deoptimization Turning a compiled frame back into an interpreter frame and retiring the compiled code. Intrinsic A JDK method that HotSpot replaces with its own ready-made code. Biggest callee (in bytecode) that C2 inlines at a call site it doesn't consider hot? 35 bytes (MaxInlineSize). When does C2 treat a call site as hot, and what's the size limit there? When the call runs on at least 25% of the caller's invocations. Then the limit is 325 bytes (FreqInlineSize). How many receiver types does C2 inline at one call site from the profile? Up to two. With more, only a type with at least 90% of the calls; otherwise it emits a virtual call (megamorphic). What is an uncommon trap? A stub C2 puts where the profile saw nothing, such as an untaken branch or an unseen type. If it runs, the call is deoptimized and the code is made not entrant. Does marking a class final make calls to it faster in C2? Not by itself. C2 inlines from the receiver-type profile. What matters is how many types reach the call site. What does @IntrinsicCandidate on a JDK method mean? HotSpot may replace the method with hand-written machine code or compiler instructions, as it does for Math.addExact and Arrays.equals. Why can a Kotlin function be bigger in bytecode than the same Java code? Calls to Kotlin inline functions, such as "...".format(x), are pasted into the caller by kotlinc, and that bytecode counts against the JIT's inlining budget.

h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · Go deeper
x: Inlining is what makes escape analysis work. C2 can only prove that an object never leaves a method if it can see every method the object is passed to. A small result object created in a hot method and passed to a callee that isn't inlined has escaped, so it gets put on the heap. The memory track looks at escape analysis from the allocation side. For experiments, -XX:CompileCommand=dontinline,example.report.Guards::requireWordCount and -XX:CompileCommand=inline,... force a decision for one method, and the inlining log then says it was forced by CompileCommand. Use them to test a theory, not as a production fix. Not every call through an interface is megamorphic just because many classes pass through it. Take a shared helper such as static long timed(LongSupplier work) that three callers use with three different lambdas. Once C2 has inlined timed into each caller, it can see the exact lambda class at each spot and doesn't need the shared profile. Megamorphic sites come from types C2 can't see at compile time, such as objects read from an array, a field or a collection. Other messages you'll meet in the log: inlining too deep (more than 15 levels, MaxInlineLevel), already compiled into a big method (a callee already compiled into more than 2,500 bytes of machine code), hot method too big (a hot site, over 325 bytes) and no static binding (C1 can't inline a virtual call). JITWatch shows the same information per method if the raw log gets too long.

h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · A nanoTime loop measures the optimizer, not your code
x: A nanoTime loop measures the optimizer: dead code, constant folding, and the loop JMH builds instead Here's the benchmark almost everyone writes first. A benchmark is a small program that measures how long some code takes. This one is as simple as it gets: read the clock, call the code many times, read the clock again. Java long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 100_000_000; i++) { Math.sqrt(x); // result discarded } long t1 = System.nanoTime(); System.out.printf("%.4f ns/op%n", (t1 - t0) / 1e8); Kotlin val t0 = System.nanoTime() for (i in 0 until 100_000_000) { sqrt(x) // result discarded } val t1 = System.nanoTime() println("%.4f ns/op".format((t1 - t0) / 1e8)) NanoLoop, in the Try it, runs that loop five times, next to a second loop that adds every result to a sum and prints the sum. On JDK 25 it printed (with the sum trimmed off): round 1: discarded 0.0678 ns/op, used 3.3919 ns/op round 2: discarded 0.2053 ns/op, used 3.0171 ns/op round 3: discarded 0.0000 ns/op, used 3.3148 ns/op round 4: discarded 0.0000 ns/op, used 3.2549 ns/op round 5: discarded 0.0000 ns/op, used 3.5381 ns/op Zero nanoseconds per square root. That's faster than light, and a little suspicious. The second loop settled at about 3 ns per call, which is believable for a square root and an addition on a busy machine. The first loop measured nothing because, once C2 (the JIT's optimizing compiler) had compiled it, there was nothing left to measure. C2 proved that nobody used the result of Math.sqrt(x), so it deleted the call, and then the empty loop. That's dead-code elimination: work whose result nobody uses can go. It's the cook skipping the bowl nobody eats. Here the picture breaks, and in a useful way. A cook who skips a bowl knows they're cutting a corner. The JIT isn't cheating at all. Removing unused work is exactly its job, and our benchmark gave it permission. Dead code is one of several ways a hand-made loop lies: If the input is a constant, C2 can compute the answer at compile time, and you end up timing the load of one number. That's constant folding: the cook who gets the same order every time makes it before the doors open. The first rounds run in the interpreter, which reads bytecode one instruction at a time, and in OSR code, a loop compiled while it runs, as lesson 1 showed. A benchmark written as one long loop in main keeps measuring OSR code. The JIT unrolls loops and moves work out of them. JMH's own sample on loops reports the measured cost of an addition falling "up to the point we do each addition with 1/20 ns, well beyond what hardware can actually do". A broken benchmark can also print a believable number, which is worse. Change the discarded call to Math.log(x). On JDK 21, that loop was never removed: it reported 10 to 13 ns per call, round after round. On JDK 25, it dropped to 0.0000 by round 3, like the square root. Same source, two JDKs, two stories. Whether the JIT can remove a call depends on what it can prove, and you can't see that from the outside. A timing loop you wrote by hand measures whatever the JIT left behind. Don't trust its number. So we need a loop the JIT can't hollow out, warmed up, in a fresh JVM, timed with care. Writing that by hand is a project of its own. Fortunately, the OpenJDK team already wrote it. Watch the work disappear Read NanoLoop. Predict both columns for round 1 and round 5. Run it. Then run the Kotlin twin. Change the discarded loop to Math.log(x) in either version and run it again. If you have two JDKs installed, try both. NanoLoop.java package workbench.performance.l03; /** * The benchmark everyone writes first: a loop timed with System.nanoTime(). * Round by round it measures the same thing, twice: once with the result thrown away, * once with the result added to a sum that gets printed. */ public class NanoLoop { public static void main(String[] args) { double x = 2.0; for (int round = 1; round <= 5; round++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 100_000_000; i++) { Math.sqrt(x); // result discarded } long t1 = System.nanoTime(); double sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 100_000_000; i++) { sum += Math.sqrt(x + i); // result used } long t2 = System.nanoTime(); System.out.printf("round %d: discarded %.4f ns/op, used %.4f ns/op (sum %.1f)%n", round, (t1 - t0) / 1e8, (t2 - t1) / 1e8, sum); } } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l03.NanoLoop labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l03/NanoLoop.java NanoLoop.kt package workbench.performance.l03 import kotlin.math.sqrt // Kotlin twin of NanoLoop.java: the same naive nanoTime benchmark, with the result // thrown away and with the result used. fun main() { val x = 2.0 for (round in 1..5) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() for (i in 0 until 100_000_000) { sqrt(x) // result discarded } val t1 = System.nanoTime() var sum = 0.0 for (i in 0 until 100_000_000) { sum += sqrt(x + i) // result used } val t2 = System.nanoTime() println("round %d: discarded %.4f ns/op, used %.4f ns/op (sum %.1f)" .format(round, (t1 - t0) / 1e8, (t2 - t1) / 1e8, sum)) } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l03.NanoLoopKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l03/NanoLoop.kt The discarded column starts below 1 ns and reads 0.0000 by round 3; the used column stays near 3 ns. Kotlin does the same. With Math.log, the result depends on the JDK: on JDK 21 the discarded loop reported 10 to 13 ns per call and never reached zero, while on JDK 25 it reached 0.0000 by round 3. Neither loop tells you the real cost of the method.

h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · JMH builds the measuring loop for you
x: That tool is JMH, the Java Microbenchmark Harness: the OpenJDK project's code for running microbenchmarks, benchmarks of small pieces of code. It calls your method, times it and reports the result. Version 1.37, from August 2023, is still the latest release, and it's the version in this course's Gradle build. You write a method and mark it @Benchmark. JMH's annotation processor, a plug-in that runs while javac compiles, generates the measuring loop around it, written to defeat the tricks from the last section. A runner then executes it in fresh JVMs. Think of it as the taste test done fairly. A fair test warms the kitchen up first and throws away the practice dishes. It uses ingredients the cook can't predict, so nothing can be made in advance. A judge eats every dish, so none can be skipped. And it runs in a fresh kitchen each day, so yesterday's habits don't leak into today. JMH gives you each of those. Here's a complete benchmark for the report service's reading time: Java @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1) // 5 x 1 s, results thrown away @Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1) // 5 x 1 s, results kept @Fork(2) // two fresh JVMs public class ReadingBench { long words = 1_234; // input: a non-final field of the state object @Benchmark public long seconds() { return ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words); // returned: JMH consumes it } } Kotlin @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Fork(2) open class ReadingBench { // JMH's generated code extends it, so it can't be final var words = 1_234L // var: an input nobody can predict @Benchmark fun seconds(): Long = ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words) } What each piece does: @State(Scope.Thread): one instance of the class per benchmark thread (a thread is one line of work inside a program, and JMH can run several at once). Its fields are your inputs, the ingredients the cook can't predict. @Setup: a method that prepares the state outside the measured time. Level.Trial, the default, runs it once per fork. @Warmup and @Measurement: how many iterations, and how long each lasts. Warm-up results, the practice dishes, are thrown away. @Fork: how many fresh JVMs to run in, the fresh kitchens. A new JVM starts with a clean profile, the JIT's notes on what the code did, so one benchmark can't skew the next. @Fork(0) runs inside the JVM that launched it, which brings back every problem of the hand-made loop. @BenchmarkMode: Throughput (operations per unit of time, the default), AverageTime, SampleTime or SingleShotTime. @Param: runs the benchmark once per value, as lesson 2's MegamorphicBench did with its number of types. The return value is the judge who eats the dish: JMH consumes it, so the JIT has to compute it. The Kotlin class has to be open, because JMH's generated classes extend it. A Kotlin build also needs a plugin, such as kotlinx-benchmark, to generate the JMH code for Kotlin classes. So this course keeps its benchmarks in Java, and drives them from Kotlin where that helps. The JMH 1.37 defaults are 5 forks, each with 5 warm-up and 5 measurement iterations of 10 seconds: more than eight minutes per benchmark method. JMH is in no hurry, on purpose. The demos in this track use iterations of 100 to 300 ms so they finish quickly. That's fine for seeing a trap, and too short for deciding anything. You can run benchmarks from a main method with JMH's Runner and OptionsBuilder, as the demos do, or from a JMH jar with command-line flags such as -f 2 -wi 5 -i 5 -prof gc. Since JDK 24, JMH 1.37 makes the JVM print a few WARNING lines about sun.misc.Unsafe, an internal JDK class it uses. They don't affect the results. The harness is honest. Our benchmarks still have to give it honest inputs, and that's where most broken benchmarks go wrong. Five ways to measure one square root Read TrapsBench. Predict which of the five benchmarks will score about the same as baseline. Run it (under 10 seconds). Then run the Kotlin twin, which runs two of the five with JMH's full output, so you can watch the warm-up and measurement iterations go by. Change double x = 2.0; to final double x = 2.0; and run the Java version again. Which benchmarks change? TrapsBench.java package workbench.performance.l03; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Benchmark; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.BenchmarkMode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Fork; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Measurement; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Mode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.OutputTimeUnit; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Scope; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.State; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Warmup; import org.openjdk.jmh.infra.Blackhole; import org.openjdk.jmh.results.RunResult; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** The same Math.sqrt measured five ways. The iterations are far shorter than JMH's defaults, so treat the numbers as rough. */ @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 2, time = 100, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Measurement(iterations = 3, time = 100, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Fork(1) public class TrapsBench { double x = 2.0; // input from a non-final @State field static final double CONSTANT = 2.0; // input the JIT knows at compile time @Benchmark public void baseline() { } // the harness on its own @Benchmark public void sqrtDiscarded() { Math.sqrt(x); } // result thrown away @Benchmark public double sqrtReturned() { return Math.sqrt(x); } // JMH consumes the return value @Benchmark public void sqrtBlackhole(Blackhole bh) { bh.consume(Math.sqrt(x)); } @Benchmark public double sqrtOfConstant() { return Math.sqrt(CONSTANT); } // folded before it runs public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { var options = new OptionsBuilder() .include(TrapsBench.class.getName()) .verbosity(VerboseMode.SILENT) .build(); System.out.printf("%-16s %10s %10s%n", "Benchmark", "ns/op", "error"); for (RunResult r : new Runner(options).run()) { var s = r.getPrimaryResult(); System.out.printf("%-16s %10.3f %10.3f%n", r.getParams().getBenchmark().replaceAll(".*\\.", ""), s.getScore(), s.getScoreError()); } } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l03.TrapsBench labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l03/TrapsBench.java TrapsBench.kt package workbench.performance.l03 // JMH benchmarks must be Java classes in this lab (the annotation processor runs on Java only). // This Kotlin twin runs the same Java benchmark through JMH's Runner API, but with JMH's // normal output, so you can see every warm-up and measurement iteration as it happens. import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode fun main() { val options = OptionsBuilder() .include(TrapsBench::class.java.name + ".sqrt(Discarded|Returned)") // a regex: two of the five .verbosity(VerboseMode.NORMAL) .build() Runner(options).run() } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l03.TrapsBenchKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l03/TrapsBench.kt sqrtDiscarded and sqrtOfConstant usually land on top of baseline: 0.4 to 0.9 ns on the busy course machine, with error bars bigger than the scores. sqrtReturned and sqrtBlackhole take about 2 to 5 ns. With final double x = 2.0, javac copies 2.0 into every method, so every benchmark drops to the baseline, sqrtReturned and sqrtBlackhole included: 0.44 and 0.47 ns in the run here. The Kotlin twin's log shows # Blackhole mode: compiler (auto-detected ...) and ends with JMH's "REMEMBER: The numbers below are just data" warning. Each fork is a new JVM. Warm-up iterations are thrown away; measurement iterations from every fork are combined into one score with an error.

h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · Two rules: consume every result, read inputs from non-final fields
x: Two rules fix most broken benchmarks, and the three broken benchmarks in the lab each break one of them. First, every result must reach JMH. The simplest way is to return it, because JMH consumes return values. When there are two results, combine them, or pass each one to a Blackhole, a JMH object whose consume method takes a value and makes sure the JIT has to compute it: Java @Benchmark public void readingAndSpeaking(Blackhole bh) { bh.consume(ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words)); bh.consume(ReadingMath.speakingSeconds(words)); } Kotlin @Benchmark fun readingAndSpeaking(bh: Blackhole) { bh.consume(ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words)) bh.consume(ReadingMath.speakingSeconds(words)) } JMH's sample on Blackholes adds that if you have one result, you should return it: "Do not make your benchmark code less readable with explicit Blackholes!" On JDK 17 and later, JMH uses compiler blackholes, where the JIT itself treats consume as "this value is used, and nothing else". The log header says so, as # Blackhole mode: compiler, and JMH warns that results from different Blackhole modes can't be compared. Second, inputs must come from non-final instance fields of the @State object. A final field with a constant initializer is a compile-time constant in Java, so javac copies the value into your method. javap on the lab's broken ConstantInputBench shows it: public long seconds(); 0: ldc2_w #7 // long 1234l <- the field is gone; the number is baked in 3: invokestatic ReadingMath.readingSeconds:(J)J 6: lreturn From there C2 can fold the whole calculation into one number. JMH's constant-folding sample puts it bluntly: "IDEs will say 'Look, this field could be final'. Don't. Trust. Them." A static final input has the same problem, which is what sqrtOfConstant shows in the Try it above. Even the judge can't help then. With final double x, sqrtBlackhole dropped to the baseline too, because a Blackhole can't stop the cook from making the dish in advance. You can check both rules against a baseline: an empty @Benchmark method that measures the harness alone, 0.6 to 0.9 ns in the busy runs here. A benchmark that scores like the baseline is measuring nothing, whatever its name says. In those runs, the discarded and the constant square roots sat right on it, and the returned and consumed ones took two to seven times as long. The absolute numbers change from run to run on a busy machine. Which benchmarks sit on the baseline doesn't. Check yourself: a benchmark returns ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words * PAGES), where PAGES is a static final long and words is a non-final @State field. Can C2 fold the whole result into a constant? (No. PAGES is known, but words can change between calls, so the calculation has to run.) A benchmark that scores like an empty method is measuring nothing. Put a baseline next to it. Even an honest benchmark has one weak spot, though: look at the error column on any of these runs. There's a steadier number to watch. JMHSample_08_DeadCode read JMHSample_10_ConstantFold read

h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · Count bytes with -prof gc, because they don't wobble
x: Time is the noisiest thing you can measure. On a shared machine, the error bar of a short JMH run is often bigger than the score itself. Allocation is different. Allocation is the memory a method asks for when it creates objects. For the same code and the same input, a method allocates the same number of bytes every time. JMH's GC profiler reports it as gc.alloc.rate.norm, in bytes per operation (B/op). GC stands for the garbage collector, the part of the JVM that frees memory nobody uses. You turn the profiler on with -prof gc on the command line, or addProfiler(GCProfiler.class) in code. The report service counts words all day, so WordCountBench counts the words in 100 lines of text, two ways. One splits each line with String.split(" ") and counts the pieces. The other walks the characters and counts where words start: Java @Benchmark public long wordsBySplit() { // short and clear, and every word becomes a new String long total = 0; for (String line : lines) total += line.split(" ").length; return total; } @Benchmark public long wordsByScan() { // walks the characters and counts where words start long total = 0; for (String line : lines) { boolean inWord = false; for (int i = 0; i < line.length(); i++) { boolean letter = line.charAt(i) != ' '; if (letter && !inWord) total++; inWord = letter; } } return total; } Kotlin fun wordsBySplit(): Long { var total = 0L for (line in lines) total += line.split(' ').size // Kotlin's split returns a List of new Strings return total } fun wordsByScan(): Long { var total = 0L for (line in lines) { var inWord = false for (c in line) { val letter = c != ' ' if (letter && !inWord) total++ inWord = letter } } return total } Two runs on the busy course machine, JDK 25: Benchmark ns/op error B/op error wordsByScan 6906.4 16886.8 0.158 0.387 wordsBySplit 41270.4 301449.2 54400.943 7.286 wordsByScan 7485.8 11955.5 0.173 0.297 wordsBySplit 32185.0 70883.8 54425.122 769.564 Look at the error columns. Every time error is bigger than its score, from one and a half to seven times bigger, so the times say almost nothing. The bytes barely moved: about 54,400 bytes per call, 544 per line, and the same on JDK 21. split builds a new String for each of a line's nine words, plus an array to hand them back in. The scan allocates nothing at all. (The second run's ±770 is the profiler's own sampling showing through, and it's still under 2% of the score.) split is the clear choice for most code. In the report service's busiest loop, though, 54 KB for every 100 lines adds up, and lesson 7 follows an allocation problem like it from start to finish. That steadiness makes B/op the number to check automatically, in CI (continuous integration, the build server that runs your tests on every change). A test can't assert "under 30 µs" without failing at random on a busy build machine. It can assert "under 300 bytes per call", and lesson 7's lab does exactly that. Keep time measurements for quiet, dedicated machines, with several forks. Time wobbles on a busy machine; bytes per operation don't. Put the bytes in your checks. JMH has more profilers. -lprof lists the ones your machine supports. -prof stack samples thread stacks, the chains of method calls each thread is in. The perf family (perfnorm, perfasm) needs the Linux perf tool and shows hardware counters and the generated machine code. Every JMH run ends with a reminder worth reading once: "The numbers below are just data. To gain reusable insights, you need to follow up on why the numbers are the way they are." Everything in this lesson ran on one thread. Programs have many, and two threads can slow each other down even when they never touch the same field. Count the bytes Predict the B/op of each benchmark in WordCountBench, roughly. Run it (about 7 seconds). Compare the error columns for time and for bytes. Run the Kotlin twin. It writes the same two counts in Kotlin and counts bytes with the JVM's per-thread allocation counter instead of JMH. Why might its split number differ from Java's? WordCountBench.java package workbench.performance.l03; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Benchmark; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.BenchmarkMode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Fork; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Measurement; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Mode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.OutputTimeUnit; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Scope; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Setup; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.State; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Warmup; import org.openjdk.jmh.profile.GCProfiler; import org.openjdk.jmh.results.RunResult; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Counts the words in 100 lines of text two ways, String.split and a character scan, with JMH's GC profiler on. */ @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 2, time = 300, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Measurement(iterations = 3, time = 300, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Fork(1) public class WordCountBench { String[] lines; @Setup public void setup() { // built once per fork, outside the measurement lines = new String[100]; for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) lines[i] = "the report counts every word on line number " + i; } @Benchmark public long wordsBySplit() { // short and clear, and every word becomes a new String long total = 0; for (String line : lines) total += line.split(" ").length; return total; } @Benchmark public long wordsByScan() { // walks the characters and counts where words start long total = 0; for (String line : lines) { boolean inWord = false; for (int i = 0; i < line.length(); i++) { boolean letter = line.charAt(i) != ' '; if (letter && !inWord) total++; inWord = letter; } } return total; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { var options = new OptionsBuilder() .include(WordCountBench.class.getName()) .addProfiler(GCProfiler.class) // the same as -prof gc on the command line .verbosity(VerboseMode.SILENT) .build(); System.out.printf("%-14s %12s %10s %14s %8s%n", "Benchmark", "ns/op", "error", "B/op", "error"); for (RunResult r : new Runner(options).run()) { var time = r.getPrimaryResult(); var bytes = r.getSecondaryResults().get("gc.alloc.rate.norm"); System.out.printf("%-14s %12.1f %10.1f %14.3f %8.3f%n", r.getParams().getBenchmark().replaceAll(".*\\.", ""), time.getScore(), time.getScoreError(), bytes.getScore(), bytes.getScoreError()); } } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l03.WordCountBench labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l03/WordCountBench.java WordCountBench.kt package workbench.performance.l03 // WordCountBench.java measures with JMH, which needs Java classes in this lab. This Kotlin twin runs // the same two word counts written in Kotlin and reads the JVM's per-thread allocation counter // around 100,000 calls: the same bytes-per-call idea as JMH's gc.alloc.rate.norm. // Allocation is steady enough to count this way. Time is not (remember NanoLoop). import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory private val lines = Array(100) { "the report counts every word on line number $it" } fun wordsBySplit(): Long { var total = 0L for (line in lines) total += line.split(' ').size // Kotlin's split returns a List of new Strings return total } fun wordsByScan(): Long { var total = 0L for (line in lines) { var inWord = false for (c in line) { val letter = c != ' ' if (letter && !inWord) total++ inWord = letter } } return total } private val threads = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean private var sink = 0L // results go somewhere the JIT can't ignore private inline fun bytesPerCall(calls: Int, block: () -> Long): Double { repeat(50_000) { sink += block() } // warm up first, so C2 code is measured val before = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes repeat(calls) { sink += block() } return (threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before).toDouble() / calls } fun main() { val split = bytesPerCall(100_000) { wordsBySplit() } val scan = bytesPerCall(100_000) { wordsByScan() } println("wordsBySplit: %10.3f B/op".format(split)) println("wordsByScan: %10.3f B/op".format(scan)) println("(checksum $sink)") } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l03.WordCountBenchKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l03/WordCountBench.kt wordsBySplit allocates about 54,400 bytes per call with a small error, while its time error is huge on a busy machine. wordsByScan allocates almost nothing (under 1 byte, which is JMH's own rounding). The Kotlin twin prints exactly 56000.000 and 0.000 B/op. Kotlin's split is a different function from Java's: it returns a List of new strings, not an array, so its count is a little higher. The scan allocates nothing in either language.

h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · Java and Kotlin
x: Constants that get baked into the bytecode Java class Inputs { private final long words = 1_234; // constant initializer: javac copies the value private final long fromCtor; // assigned in the constructor: a real field read long plain = 1_234; // what a benchmark input should be static final long WORDS_PER_MINUTE = 238; // copied by javac, and known to the JIT Inputs(long v) { fromCtor = v; } } Kotlin const val WORDS_PER_MINUTE = 238L // copied by kotlinc; WORDS_PER_MINUTE * 2 becomes 476 open class Inputs(val fromCtor: Long) { // a real field read val words = 1_234L // NOT copied: kotlinc reads the field var plain = 1_234L // what a benchmark input should be } Java copies any final field with a constant initializer into the code that uses it, instance fields included. Kotlin copies only const val. A Kotlin val words = 1_234L compiles to a getfield, as javap shows, so kotlinc doesn't fold it. Use var in a Kotlin benchmark anyway, because it tells the next reader "this is an input". Both compilers also do arithmetic on constants themselves: in Kotlin, WORDS_PER_MINUTE * 2 compiled to ldc2_w 476. In either language, a benchmark that reads only constants measures the JIT's arithmetic, not yours.

h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · Worked example
x: Turn a nanoTime test into a benchmark you can trust A pull request (a proposed change, waiting for review) claims the new word counter is "3x faster", based on this test. Spot the problems before reading on. @Test void newCounterIsFaster() { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) NewCounter.count("the quick report"); // constant input, result dropped long newNs = System.nanoTime() - t0; t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) OldCounter.count("the quick report"); long oldNs = System.nanoTime() - t0; assertTrue(newNs * 3 < oldNs); } @Test fun `new counter is faster`() { var t0 = System.nanoTime() repeat(1_000_000) { NewCounter.count("the quick report") } // constant input, result dropped val newNs = System.nanoTime() - t0 t0 = System.nanoTime() repeat(1_000_000) { OldCounter.count("the quick report") } val oldNs = System.nanoTime() - t0 assertTrue(newNs * 3 < oldNs) } Four problems. The results are dropped (dead code). The input is a constant (folding). The first loop warms up the JVM, so the second inherits a warm JVM and a mixed profile. And a timing assertion in a unit test fails at random on a busy build machine. Move the comparison to JMH, with the input in a non-final field. @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Fork(3) public class CounterBench { String line = "the quick report"; // 1. a non-final input @Benchmark public long oldCounter() { return OldCounter.count(line); } // 2. returned @Benchmark public long newCounter() { return NewCounter.count(line); } @Benchmark public void baseline() { } // 3. the floor to compare with } @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Fork(3) open class CounterBench { var line = "the quick report" // 1. a non-final input @Benchmark fun oldCounter(): Long = OldCounter.count(line) // 2. returned @Benchmark fun newCounter(): Long = NewCounter.count(line) @Benchmark fun baseline() {} // 3. the floor to compare with } Add a @Param so the input isn't one magic line, and turn on -prof gc so you get a steady second number. Self-check: why does @Param take strings? (Answer: JMH sets the field from text, one run per value, so the values also show up in the results table.) @Param({"a", "the quick report", "a much longer line with many more words in it"}) String line; @Param("a", "the quick report", "a much longer line with many more words in it") var line = "" Read the result with the error column, and check the baseline first. If newCounter sits on the baseline, it measures nothing. If the error bars of the two counters overlap, "3x faster" isn't proven. And if newCounter allocates 0 B/op where oldCounter allocates 160, that's a result you can put in the pull request whatever the timer says. Benchmark (line) Mode Cnt Score Error Units CounterBench.newCounter ... avgt 15 ... ... ns/op CounterBench.newCounter:gc.alloc.rate.norm ... avgt 15 ... ... B/op

h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · Quiz
x: A benchmark method is public void seconds() { ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words); }. It scores 0.6 ns/op, the same as an empty benchmark. What is the most likely reason? The reading-time calculation really takes 0.6 ns The result is discarded, so the JIT removed the calculation JMH's timer can't resolve anything under 1 ns The benchmark didn't fork A result nobody uses is dead code, and C2 deletes it. Return the value (JMH consumes return values) or pass it to a Blackhole. Matching the empty baseline is the giveaway. Which input declaration lets C2 fold ReadingMath.readingSeconds(words) into a constant in a Java benchmark? long words = 1_234; in the @State class @Param("1234") long words; private final long words = 1_234; long words; assigned in a @Setup method A final field with a constant initializer is a compile-time constant in Java, so javac writes ldc2_w 1234 into the method and C2 can compute the result once. The other three are real field reads that C2 can't predict. You must compare two word counters in CI and fail the build when the new one gets worse. Which JMH number should the check use? The ns/op score The error column The number of warm-up iterations gc.alloc.rate.norm (bytes per operation) Allocation per operation is the same every time for the same code and input, so its error is tiny. Time on a shared build machine has error bars that can be bigger than the score, so a time threshold fails at random. A colleague's benchmark uses @Fork(0) "to make it faster to run". What do they lose? A fresh JVM: the benchmark now shares the launcher's profile, heap and JIT state, so code that ran earlier can change its result Nothing, forks only matter for benchmarks with several threads The warm-up iterations The ability to use @Setup With 0 forks, the benchmark runs inside the JVM that started JMH. Its type profiles and compiled code are shared with whatever ran before, as lesson 2's MegamorphicBench showed by running each case in its own fork. From lesson 2: MegamorphicBench ran each @Param value (1, 2 and 3 types) in its own fork. What would likely happen to the 1-type result if all three ran in the same JVM, 3 types first? Nothing, each @Param value gets fresh compiled code The 1-type case would likely look slow too, because the call site's profile already holds three types It would get faster, because the JIT is already warm JMH would refuse to run The type profile belongs to the call site in the bytecode, not to the @Param value, and it keeps counting from start-up. After three types have been seen there, C2 compiles a virtual call, and the 1-type run inherits it. Forks give every case a clean profile.

h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · Key terms
x: Benchmark A small program that measures how long some code takes. Dead-code elimination The JIT removing work whose result nothing uses. Constant folding Computing a result at compile time because the inputs are known constants. JMH The Java Microbenchmark Harness: generates and runs correct measuring loops. @State A JMH class whose fields hold benchmark inputs, with a scope such as one instance per thread. Fork A fresh JVM that JMH starts to run a benchmark in. Blackhole A JMH object that consumes values so the JIT must compute them. gc.alloc.rate.norm Bytes allocated per operation, reported by JMH's GC profiler. Why did a nanoTime loop around a discarded Math.sqrt(x) report 0.0000 ns/op? Dead-code elimination: C2 proved the result was unused and removed the call. How do you make sure JMH can't throw a benchmark's result away? Return it from the @Benchmark method, or pass it to Blackhole.consume when there are several results. Why must JMH inputs be non-final @State fields? A final field with a constant initializer is copied into the method by javac (and static final values are known to the JIT), so C2 can fold the computation. What does @Fork(2) give you? Two fresh JVMs per benchmark, each with a clean profile and heap. @Fork(0) runs in the launcher's JVM. What does gc.alloc.rate.norm measure, and why is it useful in CI? Bytes allocated per benchmark operation (-prof gc). It's the same every run for the same code and input, so its error is near zero. In Kotlin, which property is copied into callers as a constant: val x = 5L or const val X = 5L? Only const val. A plain val in a class compiles to a field read. What is a baseline benchmark for? An empty @Benchmark method measures the harness alone. Any benchmark that scores like it is measuring nothing.

h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · Go deeper
x: Three more JMH features are worth knowing before you need them. @State(Scope.Benchmark) shares one state object across all benchmark threads, and @Threads(4) or @Group runs several threads at once. That's how you measure contention, threads getting in each other's way: for example 4 threads incrementing one AtomicLong against one LongAdder. Lesson 4 talks about why those differ. Mode.SampleTime records the times of individual calls and prints percentiles (p50, p99, p99.9), which fits questions about slow requests better than an average does. Mode.SingleShotTime measures one call per iteration, which suits questions about cold starts. JMH pads @State objects automatically against one kind of interference between threads: the JMH false-sharing sample says "@States are automatically padded", but "This padding does not extend to the State internals". Fields inside your state object can still share a cache line, which is lesson 4's topic. If you want to see what C2 really did to a benchmark, -prof perfasm prints the busiest generated machine code next to the hardware counters. It needs Linux perf and the hsdis disassembler. Without it, the cheap check is the one you already know: put an empty baseline next to every benchmark, and be suspicious of anything that scores like it.

h: CPU caches, false sharing and @Contended · Caches move memory in 64-byte lines
x: A processor never reads a single long from memory on its own. Main memory is far away, as distances inside a computer go. So each core, one of the processor's units that runs a thread, keeps small, fast memories close by: its caches (called L1 and L2). They don't hold single variables. They hold cache lines, blocks of 64 bytes on x86 processors. The course machine says so directly: the file /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/index0/coherency_line_size contains 64. A cache line is the cutting board: a fixed-size surface where the work happens. The hardware moves the whole board, never a single onion. Each core keeps its own copy of any line it uses, and the hardware keeps the copies in step. That's cache coherence, which the memory model track met as the reason caches don't serve stale values. Coherence has a price, though. A core that wants to write a line needs the only valid copy of it. Every other core's copy is marked invalid, and the next time one of those cores touches the line, it has to fetch it again. Now look at an ordinary object in memory. The report service works in two stages: a parser reads each document, and a writer produces its report. It counts what each stage has done. JOL (Java Object Layout), a small OpenJDK library, reads the real field offsets from the running JVM. An offset is a field's distance in bytes from the start of the object: Java static final class Adjacent { volatile long parsed; // written only by the parsing thread volatile long written; // written only by the writing thread } // JOL on JDK 21 and JDK 25: 32 bytes; parsed at offset 16, written at offset 24 Kotlin class KAdjacent { @Volatile var parsed = 0L // written only by the parsing thread @Volatile var written = 0L // written only by the writing thread } // JOL on JDK 21 and JDK 25: 32 bytes; parsed at offset 16, written at offset 24 (volatile makes each write visible to other threads at once, as the memory model track showed.) The first 12 bytes are the object header: 8 bytes of bookkeeping and a 4-byte pointer to the object's class. Then come 4 bytes of gap, so the longs start on an 8-byte boundary, and then the two fields, 8 bytes apart. The whole object is 32 bytes. Unless it happens to straddle the edge of a line, both counters sit on the same 64-byte line: the same board. For code that reads, that's good news. Reading parsed brings written along for free, and arrays of numbers are fast to scan for the same reason. For two threads that each write their own field, it's bad news, as the next section shows. Offsets depend on the JVM and its flags. On JDK 25 with -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders (JEP 519), the header shrinks to 8 bytes, and LayoutDemo then shows parsed at 8 and written at 16 in a 24-byte object. JDK 27 turns compact headers on by default (JEP 534). So when you check a layout in a test, check the distance between fields, never their absolute offsets. Memory moves in 64-byte lines, not in fields. Fields 8 bytes apart travel together. Two counters on one line cost nothing while one thread reads them. Let's give each of them a writer of its own. Read real layouts with JOL Before you run anything, predict the offset of written in each of the three classes in LayoutDemo. Run LayoutDemo. Ignore JOL's two # WARNING lines about attaching to the JVM. Look at the last entry: Striped64$Cell, the class LongAdder uses inside. Where is its only field? Run the Kotlin twin and compare. LayoutDemo.java package workbench.performance.l04; import org.openjdk.jol.info.ClassLayout; /** Prints the real field layout of four classes with JOL: where each field sits, in bytes. */ public class LayoutDemo { static final class Adjacent { volatile long parsed; volatile long written; } static final class PaddedInOneClass { // padding fields between the counters volatile long parsed; long p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8, p9, p10, p11, p12, p13, p14, p15, p16; volatile long written; } static class ParsedField { volatile long parsed; } // superclass fields are laid out first static class Pad1 extends ParsedField { long p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8; } static class WrittenField extends Pad1 { volatile long written; } static final class Padded extends WrittenField { long q1, q2, q3, q4, q5, q6, q7, q8; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { print(Adjacent.class); print(PaddedInOneClass.class); print(Padded.class); // the cell behind LongAdder: the JDK pads it with @Contended print(Class.forName("java.util.concurrent.atomic.Striped64$Cell")); } static void print(Class<?> type) { ClassLayout layout = ClassLayout.parseClass(type); System.out.println(type.getSimpleName() + ": " + layout.instanceSize() + " bytes"); layout.fields().stream() .filter(f -> f.name().equals("parsed") || f.name().equals("written") || f.name().equals("value")) .forEach(f -> System.out.printf(" %-7s at offset %3d%n", f.name(), f.offset())); } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l04.LayoutDemo labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l04/LayoutDemo.java LayoutDemo.kt package workbench.performance.l04 import org.openjdk.jol.info.ClassLayout // Kotlin twin of LayoutDemo.java: the same layouts, declared in Kotlin. // @Volatile var compiles to a volatile field, so JOL sees the same thing as in Java. class KAdjacent { @Volatile var parsed = 0L @Volatile var written = 0L } open class KParsedField { @Volatile var parsed = 0L } // superclass fields are laid out first open class KPad1 : KParsedField() { var p1 = 0L; var p2 = 0L; var p3 = 0L; var p4 = 0L; var p5 = 0L; var p6 = 0L; var p7 = 0L; var p8 = 0L } open class KWrittenField : KPad1() { @Volatile var written = 0L } class KPadded : KWrittenField() { var q1 = 0L; var q2 = 0L; var q3 = 0L; var q4 = 0L; var q5 = 0L; var q6 = 0L; var q7 = 0L; var q8 = 0L } fun main() { printLayout(KAdjacent::class.java) printLayout(KPadded::class.java) // the cell behind LongAdder: the JDK pads it with @Contended printLayout(Class.forName("java.util.concurrent.atomic.Striped64\$Cell")) } fun printLayout(type: Class<*>) { val layout = ClassLayout.parseClass(type) println("${type.simpleName}: ${layout.instanceSize()} bytes") layout.fields() .filter { it.name() in setOf("parsed", "written", "value") } .forEach { println(" %-7s at offset %3d".format(it.name(), it.offset())) } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l04.LayoutDemoKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l04/LayoutDemo.kt On JDK 21 and JDK 25: Adjacent is 32 bytes with parsed at 16 and written at 24. PaddedInOneClass is 160 bytes with written at 152. Padded, built from a chain of classes, is 160 bytes with written at 88, 72 bytes after parsed. Cell is 152 bytes, and its value field sits at offset 144: the JDK pads it on purpose. Kotlin's @Volatile var fields get exactly the same layout. With -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders on JDK 25, every offset moves down by 8 and every distance stays the same. On JDK 25, JOL also prints warnings about sun.misc.Unsafe, which it uses internally. h: CPU caches, false sharing and @Contended · False sharing: two threads, two fields, one line
x: False sharing: two threads, two fields, one cache line bouncing between cores The parsing thread now writes only parsed, and the writing thread writes only written. They share no data, so there's nothing to lock and no race, no two threads writing the same variable. But they share a line, and the line can live in only one core's cache for writing at a time. Trace two writes. Core 1 holds the line and adds 1 to parsed. Core 2 wants to add 1 to written, finds its copy invalid, and waits while the line travels over. Now core 1's copy is invalid, so its next parsed++ waits for the line to travel back. Each ++ is a few nanoseconds of work wrapped in a wait. When both threads run at the same moment, the line bounces between the cores on almost every write. This is false sharing: the program shares nothing, and the hardware shares a lot. The figure shows the bounce. FalseSharingDemo runs exactly that, 25 million increments per thread: first with the adjacent fields, then with the fields padded apart. Before you read on, decide what you expect. Here is one run on the busy course machine: round 1: adjacent 994 ms padded 785 ms round 2: adjacent 977 ms padded 784 ms round 3: adjacent 1,124 ms padded 806 ms That's a gap, but a small one, and it wasn't even steady. Across nine runs here, in Java and Kotlin, the padded version lost one round in three. Was the mechanism wrong? No. More than 20 other busy programs were sharing the machine's four cores, so our two threads were rarely running at the same moment. A line can only bounce between two cores that both want it right now. When this lesson was first written, on a quieter day, the same demo on the same machine told the textbook story: adjacent took 957 to 1,387 ms and padded 206 to 247 ms, about five times faster. Where the threads run matters too. Two hyperthreads, two hardware threads that share one physical core, also share that core's L1 and L2 caches. Put the two writers there, and there's no line to bounce at all. So don't promise anyone a speed-up from padding. The mechanism is certain, and the size of the effect isn't. The only way to know is to measure on the hardware you run on, under the load you run with. When it does hit, it hits code that looks perfectly innocent: a stats object with one counter per worker thread, or an array of per-thread totals whose slots sit 8 bytes apart. Separate fields aren't separate memory. Fields that different threads write in a hot loop need lines of their own. The cure, when you need it, is space between the fields. Java makes that a little harder than it sounds. Race two counters on one line Read FalseSharingDemo. Predict: will the adjacent run be slower, the same, or faster than the padded one on your machine? Close other busy programs if you can. Run it, then run it again. Then run the Kotlin twin. If you see a big gap, check how many physical cores your machine has (lscpu on Linux, sysctl -n hw.physicalcpu on macOS). If you see none, check how busy the machine is (uptime shows the load). FalseSharingDemo.java package workbench.performance.l04; /** * Two threads, each incrementing its OWN volatile counter 25 million times: one counts the * documents the report service has parsed, the other the reports it has written. * Run 1: the two counters sit next to each other. Run 2: they are padded apart. * Whether you see a difference depends on your CPU and where the OS puts the threads. */ public class FalseSharingDemo { // the two counters in one 32-byte object: almost certainly on the same 64-byte cache line static final class Adjacent { volatile long parsed; volatile long written; } // superclass fields come first, so the padding class sits between parsed and written static class ParsedField { volatile long parsed; } static class Pad1 extends ParsedField { long p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8; } static class WrittenField extends Pad1 { volatile long written; } static final class Padded extends WrittenField { long q1, q2, q3, q4, q5, q6, q7, q8; } static final int N = 25_000_000; static long run(Runnable a, Runnable b) throws InterruptedException { Thread t1 = new Thread(a), t2 = new Thread(b); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); t1.start(); t2.start(); t1.join(); t2.join(); return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int round = 1; round <= 3; round++) { Adjacent adj = new Adjacent(); long msAdjacent = run(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) adj.parsed++; }, () -> { for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) adj.written++; }); Padded pad = new Padded(); long msPadded = run(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) pad.parsed++; }, () -> { for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) pad.written++; }); System.out.printf("round %d: adjacent %,5d ms padded %,5d ms (counts %d/%d, %d/%d)%n", round, msAdjacent, msPadded, adj.parsed, adj.written, pad.parsed, pad.written); } } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l04.FalseSharingDemo labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l04/FalseSharingDemo.java FalseSharingDemo.kt package workbench.performance.l04 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Kotlin twin of FalseSharingDemo.java: two threads, each incrementing its OWN volatile counter // (documents parsed, reports written). // Run 1: the counters sit next to each other. Run 2: they are padded apart (KPadded from LayoutDemo.kt). // Whether you see a difference depends on your CPU and where the OS puts the threads. private const val N = 25_000_000 private fun timeTwo(a: () -> Unit, b: () -> Unit): Long { val t0 = System.nanoTime() val t1 = thread { a() } val t2 = thread { b() } t1.join(); t2.join() return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 } fun main() { for (round in 1..3) { val adj = KAdjacent() val msAdjacent = timeTwo({ repeat(N) { adj.parsed++ } }, { repeat(N) { adj.written++ } }) val pad = KPadded() val msPadded = timeTwo({ repeat(N) { pad.parsed++ } }, { repeat(N) { pad.written++ } }) println("round %d: adjacent %,5d ms padded %,5d ms (counts %d/%d, %d/%d)" .format(round, msAdjacent, msPadded, adj.parsed, adj.written, pad.parsed, pad.written)) } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l04.FalseSharingDemoKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l04/FalseSharingDemo.kt On a laptop with several physical cores and little else running, the adjacent run is often several times slower than the padded one. On a busy machine you may see a small gap, none, or the reverse, as the course machine did (about 1,000 ms against 800 ms, with some rounds reversed). All four counts always end at exactly 25,000,000: false sharing costs time, never correctness. Adjacent fields share a line, so every write by one core invalidates the other core's copy. Padded apart, each core keeps its own line.

h: CPU caches, false sharing and @Contended · Padding pushes hot fields onto separate lines
x: The fix is to keep at least 64 bytes between fields that different threads write: give each cook a board of their own. Padding means unused bytes placed between fields for exactly that reason. There are three ways to add it. The first is padding fields inside one class: 8 or more unused longs between parsed and written. On today's HotSpot it works (written moved to offset 152), but JMH's false-sharing sample warns that this is "not versatile because JVMs can freely rearrange the field order, even of the same type". The second is a chain of classes. The same sample notes that "superclass fields are usually laid out first". So put each hot field and each block of padding in a class of its own, and chain them, each class extending the one before: Java abstract class ParsedCounter { volatile long parsed; } abstract class PadAfterParsed extends ParsedCounter { long p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8; } abstract class WrittenCounter extends PadAfterParsed { volatile long written; } public final class StageCounters extends WrittenCounter { public void addParsed() { parsed++; } // only the parsing thread calls this public void addWritten() { written++; } // only the writing thread calls this } Kotlin abstract class ParsedCounter { @Volatile @JvmField var parsed = 0L } abstract class PadAfterParsed : ParsedCounter() { @JvmField var p1 = 0L; @JvmField var p2 = 0L; @JvmField var p3 = 0L; @JvmField var p4 = 0L @JvmField var p5 = 0L; @JvmField var p6 = 0L; @JvmField var p7 = 0L; @JvmField var p8 = 0L } abstract class WrittenCounter : PadAfterParsed() { @Volatile @JvmField var written = 0L } class StageCounters : WrittenCounter() { fun addParsed() { parsed++ } // only the parsing thread calls this fun addWritten() { written++ } // only the writing thread calls this } This is the shape the lab asks for. @JvmField in the Kotlin version makes each property a plain public field, which keeps the layout easy to read. The third is @Contended, the JDK's own annotation, jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended, available since JDK 8. The JVM adds ContendedPaddingWidth bytes of padding, 128 by default, around each annotated field. On JDK 25, JOL on a class with both counters annotated showed parsed at offset 144, written at 280, and a 288-byte object. Its Javadoc warns that it "will nearly always add significant space overhead to objects". There are two catches for your own classes. First, the JVM ignores the annotation outside the JDK unless you run with -XX:-RestrictContended. Without that flag, JOL showed the same 16 and 24 as no annotation at all, and the JVM printed no warning. It simply ignores you, politely. Second, the annotation lives in an internal package, so compiling needs --add-exports java.base/jdk.internal.vm.annotation=ALL-UNNAMED. javac refuses that together with --release: "exporting a package from system module java.base is not allowed with --release". This course's labs compile with --release 21, so they can't use it. Every kind of padding costs memory: 160 bytes instead of 32 here, and 288 with @Contended. That's nothing for one counter object and a lot for a million of them. Padding costs memory on every object. Pad the few that several threads write in a hot loop, and check their offsets. Check yourself: a class declares volatile long a;, then seven padding longs, then volatile long b;. JOL shows a at 16 and b at 80. Can they share a line? (No: they're 64 bytes apart. But another JVM may order the fields differently, which is why the lab's test reads the real offsets instead of trusting the source.) Hand padding is fiddly, costs memory and leans on JVM habits. For the most common case, a counter that many threads bump, the JDK has already done all of it. JMHSample_22_FalseSharing read

h: CPU caches, false sharing and @Contended · LongAdder: the padding the JDK already did for you
x: Hand padding is for library authors. For a counter in your own code, use LongAdder. LongAdder (and its sibling LongAccumulator) extends Striped64, whose source explains the design. Its table entries are a "variant of AtomicLong padded (via @Contended) to reduce cache contention", because "Atomic objects residing in arrays will tend to be placed adjacent to each other, and so will most often share cache lines (with a huge negative performance impact) without this precaution". That's the value at offset 144 you saw in LayoutDemo. In the kitchen, it's each cook keeping a tally of dishes on a slip by their own board, and the manager adding the slips up at closing time. The slips are only handed out when needed. The source says: "When there is no contention, all updates are made to the base field." Contention means threads getting in each other's way. Here it's a failed compare-and-set. Compare-and-set is the "update it only if nobody beat me to it" instruction behind AtomicLong, the JDK's thread-safe counter, and it fails when another thread changed the value first. On the first failed compare-and-set, LongAdder creates a table of 2 cells, and it doubles the table under more contention. Each thread then mostly updates its own cell, on its own line. sum() adds up the base and the cells. As "Atomics and compare-and-set" said, sum() is not an atomic snapshot. So use LongAdder for counters you read now and then, such as metrics, and AtomicLong when the value drives a decision. Here's the report service's request counter, the one the lab fixes. Every request thread calls record once per report, and a monitoring program reads the totals every few seconds: Java public final class RequestMetrics { private final LongAdder count = new LongAdder(); private final LongAdder totalWords = new LongAdder(); public void record(long words) { // called by every request thread count.increment(); totalWords.add(words); } public long count() { return count.sum(); } // read by the monitoring program } Kotlin class RequestMetrics { private val count = LongAdder() private val totalWords = LongAdder() fun record(words: Long) { // called by every request thread count.increment() totalWords.add(words) } fun count(): Long = count.sum() // read by the monitoring program } AdderDemo races the two kinds of counter: four threads count 10 million requests each, first into one AtomicLong, then into one LongAdder. On the busy course machine, the race came out backwards: round 1: AtomicLong 705 ms (40,000,000) LongAdder 1,320 ms (40,000,000) round 2: AtomicLong 693 ms (40,000,000) LongAdder 1,144 ms (40,000,000) round 3: AtomicLong 680 ms (40,000,000) LongAdder 1,156 ms (40,000,000) Both counts are exact, as they always are. The speed tells the false-sharing story again. With 20 other programs competing for four cores, our four threads mostly took turns, so their compare-and-sets rarely failed, and LongAdder paid for bookkeeping it didn't need. On the quieter day when this lesson was first written, the same demo gave AtomicLong 640 to 760 ms per round and LongAdder about 200 ms. With four threads really running at once, all four cores fought over the AtomicLong's single line, and LongAdder let each of them work on its own padded cell. This is also where the cutting-board picture breaks. A cook who waits for the board notices, and it costs seconds. A core waits nanoseconds for a line, and nobody notices until it happens a few hundred million times. That's why you measure instead of guessing. Many writers and rare readers: count with LongAdder. When the value drives a decision, use AtomicLong. We can now measure a piece of code carefully, but only a piece we already suspect. A real program has thousands of methods, so the next question is how to catch a running JVM in the act. AtomicLong against LongAdder Predict which one finishes first with four threads, and by how much. Run AdderDemo, then the Kotlin twin. Change THREADS to 1 and run again. Does LongAdder still win? static long time(Runnable perThread) throws InterruptedException { CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] ts = new Thread[THREADS]; for (int i = 0; i < THREADS; i++) { ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } perThread.run(); }); ts[i].start(); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int round = 1; round <= 3; round++) { AtomicLong atomic = new AtomicLong(); long msAtomic = time(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < PER_THREAD; i++) atomic.incrementAndGet(); }); LongAdder adder = new LongAdder(); long msAdder = time(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < PER_THREAD; i++) adder.increment(); }); System.out.printf("round %d: AtomicLong %,5d ms (%,d) LongAdder %,5d ms (%,d)%n", round, msAtomic, atomic.get(), msAdder, adder.sum()); } } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l04.AdderDemo labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l04/AdderDemo.java AdderDemo.kt package workbench.performance.l04 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Kotlin twin of AdderDemo.java: four threads count 10 million report requests each, // into one AtomicLong and then into one LongAdder. private const val THREADS = 4 private const val PER_THREAD = 10_000_000 private fun timeAll(perThread: () -> Unit): Long { val go = CountDownLatch(1) val ts = List(THREADS) { thread { go.await(); perThread() } } val t0 = System.nanoTime() go.countDown() ts.forEach { it.join() } return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 } fun main() { for (round in 1..3) { val atomic = AtomicLong() val msAtomic = timeAll { repeat(PER_THREAD) { atomic.incrementAndGet() } } val adder = LongAdder() val msAdder = timeAll { repeat(PER_THREAD) { adder.increment() } } println("round %d: AtomicLong %,5d ms (%,d) LongAdder %,5d ms (%,d)" .format(round, msAtomic, atomic.get(), msAdder, adder.sum())) } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l04.AdderDemoKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l04/AdderDemo.kt Both always count exactly 40,000,000. With four threads on a machine with free cores, LongAdder usually finishes well ahead. On a busy machine it can lose, as it did on the course machine (about 690 ms against 1,150 ms). With one thread, the counts are 10,000,000 and AtomicLong wins: 103 ms against 181 ms in the last round on the course machine. With no contention, LongAdder only touches its base field, its cells never exist, and its extra checks are pure cost.

h: CPU caches, false sharing and @Contended · Java and Kotlin
x: A padded counter in Java and Kotlin StageCounters.java abstract class ParsedCounter { volatile long parsed; } abstract class PadAfterParsed extends ParsedCounter { long p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8; } abstract class WrittenCounter extends PadAfterParsed { volatile long written; } public final class StageCounters extends WrittenCounter { public void addParsed() { parsed++; } // only the parsing thread calls this public void addWritten() { written++; } // only the writing thread calls this } StageCounters.kt abstract class ParsedCounter { @Volatile @JvmField var parsed = 0L } abstract class PadAfterParsed : ParsedCounter() { @JvmField var p1 = 0L; @JvmField var p2 = 0L; @JvmField var p3 = 0L; @JvmField var p4 = 0L @JvmField var p5 = 0L; @JvmField var p6 = 0L; @JvmField var p7 = 0L; @JvmField var p8 = 0L } abstract class WrittenCounter : PadAfterParsed() { @Volatile @JvmField var written = 0L } class StageCounters : WrittenCounter() { fun addParsed() { parsed++ } // only the parsing thread calls this fun addWritten() { written++ } // only the writing thread calls this } Both compile to the same JVM classes with the same field layout, because the JVM decides the layout, not the language. The differences are in what you write. Kotlin classes are final by default, so the padding classes need abstract or open. A Kotlin var property is a private field plus a getter and a setter; @JvmField exposes the field directly, and @Volatile makes it volatile. In both languages the padding fields are never read, and nothing in either language promises the order of fields within one class, which is why the chain of classes is the safer trick.
