h: CPU caches, false sharing and @Contended · Key terms
x: Cache line The unit a CPU cache moves around: 64 bytes on x86. Cache coherence The hardware keeping every core's copy of a line consistent, by invalidating copies on writes. False sharing Different data on one cache line, written by different cores, making the line bounce between them. Padding Unused bytes placed between fields so they land on different cache lines. @Contended A JDK-internal annotation that makes the JVM pad a field or class, 128 bytes by default. JOL Java Object Layout, a tool that prints the real field offsets and object sizes. LongAdder A counter that spreads contended updates over padded cells and adds them up on read. How big is a cache line on x86? 64 bytes. Caches move whole lines, never single fields. What is false sharing? Threads writing different fields that sit on the same cache line, so the line keeps moving between cores. It costs time, not correctness. How far apart must two hot fields be to avoid sharing a 64-byte line? At least 64 bytes between their offsets. Why is a chain of classes better than padding fields inside one class? HotSpot lays out superclass fields before subclass fields; within one class the JVM may reorder fields, even of the same type. What does @Contended need to work on your own classes? -XX:-RestrictContended at run time (otherwise it's silently ignored) and --add-exports java.base/jdk.internal.vm.annotation=ALL-UNNAMED to compile. How does LongAdder avoid false sharing? Under contention it spreads updates over Striped64.Cell objects, each padded with @Contended (JOL shows the value at offset 144). sum() adds them up. Why should a layout test assert distances, not offsets? Header sizes differ between JDKs and flags: compact object headers (default in JDK 27) move every field.

h: CPU caches, false sharing and @Contended · Go deeper
x: JMH protects you from one source of false sharing automatically. Its false-sharing sample says "@States are automatically padded", but "This padding does not extend to the State internals". Fields inside your @State object can still share a line, which is exactly what that sample demonstrates, with several fixes side by side. To measure it on your own hardware, run that sample with several forks on a machine with real cores and little else running. Why does the JDK pad with 128 bytes when lines are 64? The flag ContendedPaddingWidth only says how many bytes to pad. A common explanation is that some processors also fetch the neighbouring line, so a 64-byte gap can still let two hot fields interfere. This course couldn't check that against a primary source, so treat 128 as "the JDK's safe default" rather than a rule. Two other tools look at the same problem from the hardware side. perf c2c on Linux reports cache lines that bounce between cores (JMH wraps it as -prof perfc2c). And a CPU profiler such as async-profiler, in lesson 6, shows the symptom: lots of samples on a trivial line such as count++. There's also true sharing, which padding can't fix: many threads writing the same field, like an AtomicLong hit by every request. The only fixes there are to write less often or to split the value, which is what LongAdder does.

h: JDK Flight Recorder and Mission Control · JFR records what the JVM did, on one clock, cheap enough to leave on
x: JFR puts timestamped JVM events on one clock; a recording is a ring that keeps the newest within maxage or maxsize, and you read jfr summary first, then a view Start with the hand-made answer. The report service from the earlier lessons fetches each document from a document store, another program that keeps the documents and answers over the network. Some fetches are slow, so we wrap one in a timer and log fetch took 46 ms. That's one number for one call. It can't say whether every thread was paused for a garbage collection at that moment. (The garbage collector, or GC, is the part of the JVM that frees memory nobody uses.) Nor can it say whether the thread waited for a lock, a guard that lets one thread at a time into a piece of code, or whether something allocated a lot of memory that second. JDK Flight Recorder (JFR) is a recorder built into HotSpot, the JVM in every OpenJDK build. It writes events: small records with a start time, often a duration, the thread, and usually a stack trace, the chain of method calls that led there. HotSpot has events for GC pauses, JIT compilations (the JVM turning busy methods into machine code, as lessons 1 and 2 showed), waits for locks, file and network reads, and samples of running threads and of allocation. Your code can add events of its own. All of them go into one timeline, on one clock. That's the kitchen's log for the whole night. A recording is one session of that log, with its settings and limits. It keeps events in memory buffers and moves them to disk in chunks. Picture a log book that tears out its oldest pages when it's full: maxage says how far back to keep, maxsize how many bytes. Set neither, and the JVM keeps 250 MB. You can start a recording when the JVM starts, or on a JVM that's already running: java -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=rec.jfr,settings=profile -jar app.jar jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=reports settings=profile # on a JVM that's already running jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=reports filename=reports.jfr # copy what it has so far to a file jcmd <pid> JFR.stop name=reports jcmd is a tool in the JDK that sends commands to a running JVM, and <pid> is the process id, the number the operating system gives each running program. On JDK 25, the report service answered the first command like this: Started recording 1. No limit specified, using maxsize=250MB as default. Use jcmd 30725 JFR.dump name=reports filename=FILEPATH to copy recording data to file. A dump copies the pages written so far and stops nothing. That's why a recording that's always on pays off: when something goes wrong, the last hour is already in the book. settings picks a configuration file. default.jfc describes itself as "safe for continuous use in production environments, typically less than 1 % overhead". profile.jfc says "typically around 2 % overhead" and records more. In JDK 25, default samples running threads every 20 ms, takes up to 150 allocation samples a second and records lock waits of 20 ms or more. profile samples every 10 ms, takes 300 allocation samples a second and records lock waits from 10 ms. The first question to ask any recording is what's in it. jfr summary, from the JDK's jfr tool, lists every event type with a count. For the Try it below, four threads, lines of work that run side by side inside the program, wrote reports for 4 seconds under profile. Part of the summary: Event Type Count Size (bytes) ============================================================= jdk.GCPhaseParallel 1951 50576 workbench.StoreCall 1361 35305 jdk.ObjectAllocationSample 1207 16978 jdk.ThreadSleep 560 10078 ... jdk.ExecutionSample 40 400 jdk.JavaMonitorEnter 29 667 workbench.StoreCall is ours, one event per call to the document store, and section 3 builds it. Everything else is the JVM's, and only the garbage collector's paperwork outnumbers us. Notice how few execution samples there are. The threads spent most of the time asleep, waiting for the store, and the sampler only counts threads that are running Java code. Keep that 40 in mind for the end of the lesson. A cheap recording that's always on is evidence you already have. Dump it instead of restarting. The summary says what the log holds. Next, we'll ask it a question. Record the busy report service Read JfrDemo and skim ReportWorkload next to it. Four threads each count the words in 2,000 short lines, ask a fake document store for a document (it sleeps a few milliseconds, longer for shelf-7), and on every tenth document hold a shared archive lock for 15 ms. Predict which event type will have the highest count, and roughly how many execution samples 4 seconds will give. Run it from labs/. The demo starts a second JVM with -XX:StartFlightRecording and prints the path of the .jfr file. Run jfr summary on that file (the demo prints the command). JfrDemo.java package workbench.performance.l05; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Runs ReportWorkload for 4 seconds in a second JVM started with * -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=build/perf05.jfr,settings=profile * and tells you where the recording is. */ public class JfrDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("child")) { ReportWorkload.run(4); return; } Path file = Path.of("build", "perf05.jfr").toAbsolutePath(); String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, "-XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=" + file + ",settings=profile", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), JfrDemo.class.getName(), "child")); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).inheritIO().start(); p.waitFor(); System.out.println("recording written to " + file); System.out.println("try: jfr summary " + file); } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l05.JfrDemo labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l05/JfrDemo.java JfrDemo.kt package workbench.performance.l05 import jdk.jfr.Category import jdk.jfr.Description import jdk.jfr.Event import jdk.jfr.Label import jdk.jfr.Name import java.nio.file.Path import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Kotlin twin of JfrDemo.java (with its workload and event in this one file). It runs the workload // for 4 seconds in a second JVM started with -XX:StartFlightRecording and writes build/perf05-kt.jfr. @Name("workbench.StoreCall") @Label("Store Call") @Category("Workbench", "Reports") @Description("A call to the document store while writing a report") class KStoreCallEvent : Event() { @Label("Shelf") var shelf: String? = null // a Kotlin property: JFR records its field @Label("Words") var words = 0L @Label("Found") var found = false } private val archive = Any() fun kCountWords(line: String): Long = line.split(' ').size.toLong() // allocates: a new String for every word fun kCallStore(shelf: String, doc: Int): Long { val event = KStoreCallEvent() event.begin() Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(2, if (shelf == "shelf-7") 40 else 12).toLong()) val found = doc % 17 != 0 val words = if (found) 200L + doc % 3_000 else 0L event.end() if (event.shouldCommit()) { // skip the field work when no recording wants it event.shelf = shelf event.words = words event.found = found event.commit() } return words } fun kRunWorkload(seconds: Int) { val until = System.nanoTime() + seconds * 1_000_000_000L val workers = (0 until 4).map { w -> thread(name = "report-$w") { var sink = 0L var i = 0 while (System.nanoTime() < until) { for (k in 0 until 2_000) sink += kCountWords("page ${(k + i) % 9_000} of the weekly report on rain") sink += kCallStore("shelf-${i % 10}", i) if (i % 10 == w) synchronized(archive) { Thread.sleep(15) } // writing to the shared archive i++ } if (sink == 42L) println() } } workers.forEach { it.join() } } fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "child") return kRunWorkload(4) val file = Path.of("build", "perf05-kt.jfr").toAbsolutePath() val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") ProcessBuilder(java, "-XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=$file,settings=profile", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l05.JfrDemoKt", "child") .inheritIO().start().waitFor() println("recording written to $file") println("try: jfr summary $file") } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l05.JfrDemoKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l05/JfrDemo.kt The JVM prints its "Started recording" lines, then the demo prints the file path; the file was about 440 KB here. In the run above, jfr summary counted 1,951 jdk.GCPhaseParallel, 1,361 workbench.StoreCall, 1,207 jdk.ObjectAllocationSample and 560 jdk.ThreadSleep events, but only 40 jdk.ExecutionSample, because the threads spend most of their time asleep. Your counts will differ from run to run. The java command, JDK 25 (-XX:StartFlightRecording) docs

h: JDK Flight Recorder and Mission Control · Asking the recording questions with jfr view and jfr print
x: Three subcommands of the jfr tool cover most days. You've met jfr summary. jfr view <view> <file> prints a ready-made report: views arrived in JDK 21, and jfr help view lists the dozens there are now. jfr print prints events one by one. Three views answer the questions from the opening. Did threads wait for each other? contention-by-site groups the waits to enter a synchronized block, the lock Java takes with the synchronized keyword, by where they happened: Contention by Site StackTrace Count Avg. Max. -------------------------------------------------------------- ----- ------- ------- workbench.performance.l05.ReportWorkload.reportLoop(int, long) 28 15.5 ms 34.0 ms jdk.jfr.internal.PlatformRecorder.periodicTask() 1 11.0 ms 11.0 ms Twenty-eight waits at the shared archive lock, 15.5 ms on average: about the 15 ms each writer holds it. The second line is JFR's own housekeeping thread, which once got stuck behind a lock of its own. Who allocates? allocation-by-site adds up the allocation samples by the method that did the allocating: Method Allocation Pressure -------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------- java.util.Arrays.copyOfRange(byte[], int, int) 36.56% java.lang.StringLatin1.newString(byte[], int, int) 33.31% jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.allocateUninitializedArray(Class, int) 9.76% java.util.ArrayList.grow(int) 9.51% java.lang.String.split(char, int, boolean) 6.27% Every line is JDK code, and every one is the inside of String.split, which our countWords calls 2,000 times per document. A view names the method that allocated, not the line of yours that asked for it. Lesson 7 walks down the stack traces to find that line. Did the JVM stop every thread? gc-pauses gives the count, the total and the longest pause. And lesson 2 promised a view for the JIT's lost bets, deoptimizations-by-reason: Reason Count ------------------------------------------------------ ------------------------- unstable_if 7 bimorphic_or_optimized_type_check 4 class_check 4 intrinsic_or_type_checked_inlining 1 Sixteen in a program that ran 4 seconds is the burst at start-up that lesson 2 described. A steady stream hours after start is the thing to worry about. Each view is a query over events, and jfr view --verbose shows the query. Pass the name of an event type as the view, such as jfr view workbench.StoreCall rec.jfr, and you get a table of those events. On a running JVM, jcmd <pid> JFR.view hot-methods prints a view without writing a file. jfr print --events workbench.StoreCall --stack-depth 2 rec.jfr prints events one at a time with every field; add --json for a script. JDK Mission Control (JMC) is the desktop app for the same files: timelines, flame graphs of the samples (lesson 6 explains those) and an automatic analysis. It's developed in the openjdk/jmc project and downloaded separately, from builds that several vendors publish. The jfr tool is enough for everything in this lesson, and it's already in your JDK. Read jfr summary first, then ask one question per view. Before you send a recording to anyone, look at what else it holds. The demo's file has 169 jdk.InitialEnvironmentVariable events and the full command line. A recording remembers more than you told it, and environment variables are where programs often keep passwords. JDK 27 adds redaction inside the JVM (JEP 536, -XX:FlightRecorderOptions:redact-argument=...). On older JDKs, check the file first, or share the views instead of the file. The figure shows where all these events go. So far they've been the JVM's, apart from one type we haven't explained yet. Answer three questions from one file Using the file from the last Try it: where do threads wait for locks, and for how long at most? Run jfr view contention-by-site <file>. Which methods allocate the most? Run jfr view allocation-by-site <file>. Which line of ReportWorkload calls all of them? Which shelf has slow store calls? Run jfr view workbench.StoreCall <file> and look at the Duration column, then jfr print --events workbench.StoreCall --stack-depth 2 <file> | head -20. terminal (from labs/) jfr view contention-by-site performance/build/perf05.jfr jfr view allocation-by-site performance/build/perf05.jfr jfr view workbench.StoreCall performance/build/perf05.jfr jfr print --events workbench.StoreCall --stack-depth 2 performance/build/perf05.jfr | head -20 Contention shows reportLoop with a few dozen waits of about 15 ms (28 in the run above, the longest 34 ms). Allocation is all String.split and its helpers, which countWords calls. In the table, shelf-7 calls take up to about 40 ms; on a busy machine some other shelves stretch past their 12 ms too. jfr print shows each event's fields and the two frames that called it, with line numbers. Events go into a recording. A dump makes a .jfr file for the jfr tool, JMC or RecordingFile; RecordingStream reads the same events live. The jfr command, JDK 25 docs

h: JDK Flight Recorder and Mission Control · Your own events add the service's notes to the same log
x: An event of your own is a class that extends jdk.jfr.Event. Its fields are the data, and annotations give it a stable name and labels for the tools. Here's the demo's event for one call to the document store. The demo's store is fake and only sleeps, so the code around the call is shown the way a real service would write it: Java @Name("workbench.StoreCall") @Label("Store Call") @Category({"Workbench", "Reports"}) public class StoreCallEvent extends Event { @Label("Shelf") String shelf; @Label("Words") long words; @Label("Found") boolean found; } StoreCallEvent event = new StoreCallEvent(); event.begin(); // 1. start the clock String text = store.fetch(shelf, title); event.end(); // 2. stop it if (event.shouldCommit()) { // 3. false if no recording wants it event.shelf = shelf; event.words = text == null ? 0 : countWords(text); event.found = text != null; event.commit(); // 4. write it, with a stack trace } Kotlin @Name("workbench.StoreCall") @Label("Store Call") @Category("Workbench", "Reports") class KStoreCallEvent : Event() { @Label("Shelf") var shelf: String? = null @Label("Words") var words = 0L @Label("Found") var found = false } val event = KStoreCallEvent() event.begin() // 1. start the clock val text = store.fetch(shelf, title) event.end() // 2. stop it if (event.shouldCommit()) { // 3. false if no recording wants it event.shelf = shelf event.words = if (text == null) 0 else countWords(text) event.found = text != null event.commit() // 4. write it, with a stack trace } Read it from the top. @Name is the name that recordings and tools use to find the event. @Label and @Category are what JMC and jfr view display. begin() starts the event's clock and end() stops it, so its duration covers the store call. shouldCommit() returns true only if some recording has this event switched on and the duration passes that recording's threshold, the shortest duration it keeps. Only then do we fill in the fields and commit(), which writes the event with the thread and a stack trace taken at that moment. The shouldCommit() check matters because Java works out each field's value before the assignment, and countWords isn't free. When no recording wants the event, the check skips that work, and the event costs almost nothing. In the kitchen, it's a note the cook writes only when somebody is keeping the log. Kotlin needs nothing special. JFR records the field behind each Kotlin property, and a Java annotation such as @Label on a property lands on that field. Compare it with the log line from section 1. The event has fields you can filter, instead of text you have to parse. A recording can also keep only the slow ones: +workbench.StoreCall#threshold=30ms on the command line keeps calls of 30 ms or more. The + is needed because your event isn't listed in the .jfc file. Leave it out, and JDK 25 warns The .jfc option/setting 'workbench.StoreCall#threshold' doesn't exist. and ignores it. Above all, the event sits on the same timeline as the GC pauses and lock waits, with the same thread names. jfr view workbench.StoreCall showed the demo's events like this (trimmed to two rows): Start Time Duration Event Thread Stack Trace Shelf Words Found ---------- -------- ------------ --------------------------------------------------------------- ------- ----- ----- 07:47:36 18.3 ms report-2 workbench.performance.l05.ReportWorkload.callStore(String, int) shelf-1 201 true 07:47:36 46.6 ms report-3 workbench.performance.l05.ReportWorkload.callStore(String, int) shelf-7 207 true Reading events back in code is short. RecordingFile.readAllEvents(path) returns every event in a file. Each RecordedEvent has getEventType().getName(), getDuration(), getString("shelf"), getBoolean("found") and friends. That's the lab. Fill an event's fields inside shouldCommit(). When nobody records, the event costs almost nothing. Check yourself: your event sits in a method that runs 50,000 times a second, and no recording has it switched on. What does shouldCommit() return, and what does it save you? (It returns false, and it saves you the work of computing the fields. commit() would have written nothing anyway.) A recording answers questions after the fact. Sometimes you want the answers while the program is still running. Keep only the slow calls In JfrDemo.java, change the recording option to "-XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=" + file + ",settings=profile,+workbench.StoreCall#threshold=30ms" (note the +). Predict: out of about 1,300 store calls, roughly how many will be recorded now, and from which shelves? Run the demo again, then jfr summary and jfr view workbench.StoreCall on the new file. Only a few dozen workbench.StoreCall events remain, all 30 ms or longer: 50 in one run here, 33 of them from shelf-7, whose fake store sleeps up to 40 ms. The other 17 came from shelves that sleep at most 12 ms; the busy machine stretched those sleeps past 30 ms, which is a finding of its own. The JVM's own events are unchanged, because the threshold is a setting of the recording, not of your code.

h: JDK Flight Recorder and Mission Control · Watching events live, and what JDK 25 added
x: jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingStream, in the JDK since version 14, hands the same events to your own code while the JVM runs: Java try (RecordingStream rs = new RecordingStream()) { rs.enable("workbench.StoreCall").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(35)); // only the slow ones rs.enable("jdk.GarbageCollection"); rs.onEvent("workbench.StoreCall", e -> System.out.printf("slow store call: %s, %d ms%n", e.getString("shelf"), e.getDuration().toMillis())); rs.onEvent("jdk.GarbageCollection", e -> System.out.printf("GC: %s, %.1f ms pause total%n", e.getString("name"), e.getDuration("sumOfPauses").toNanos() / 1e6)); rs.startAsync(); // events arrive on a background thread ReportWorkload.run(3); } Kotlin RecordingStream().use { rs -> rs.enable("workbench.StoreCall").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(35)) // only the slow ones rs.enable("jdk.GarbageCollection") rs.onEvent("workbench.StoreCall") { e -> println("slow store call: ${e.getString("shelf")}, ${e.duration.toMillis()} ms") } rs.onEvent("jdk.GarbageCollection") { e -> println("GC: %s, %.1f ms pause total".format(e.getString("name"), e.getDuration("sumOfPauses").toNanos() / 1e6)) } rs.startAsync() // events arrive on a background thread kRunWorkload(3) } Events reach the callbacks in batches, about once a second, on a background thread. That suits turning JVM events into numbers for a dashboard, such as GC pause time per minute. It's not a hook into the busy path of your code. One run of StreamingDemo printed lines like these: slow store call: shelf-1, 46 ms GC: G1New, 16.3 ms pause total slow store call: shelf-7, 155 ms slow store call: shelf-9, 130 ms Shelf 7 is slow on purpose. The others were slow because the machine was: more than 30 other busy programs shared its four cores that day, so a 12 ms sleep often lasted much longer. A stream can't tell which slowness you meant. That's one more reason to have the CPU and GC events on the same clock as your own. JDK 25 added three profiling features to JFR, and all of these ran here on JDK 25. Method timing and tracing (JEP 520) counts and times chosen methods with no change to the code. -XX:StartFlightRecording:method-timing=workbench.performance.l05.ReportWorkload::countWords,report-on-exit=method-timing printed a table as the JVM exited: 2,024,000 calls of countWords, 0.001160 ms on average, 88.6 ms at most. That maximum is a call that waited out a GC pause or a busy CPU; the average is the cost of the call. The filter can also name a whole class or an annotation. CPU-time sampling (JEP 509), experimental and only on Linux, samples each thread by the CPU time it uses. Switch on jdk.CPUTimeSample (for example jdk.CPUTimeSample#enabled=true,jdk.CPUTimeSample#throttle=10ms) and read it with jfr view cpu-time-hot-methods. On the report workload it took 64 samples in 4 seconds, a quarter of them in String.split. Cooperative sampling (JEP 518) changes how the JVM takes execution samples inside. There's nothing to configure. report-on-exit=<view> prints any view when the JVM exits, so a test run can leave a report in its log. JDK 21 doesn't know the option and says so. Here's where today's tool stops. JFR's classic sampler took 40 execution samples in 4 seconds of a busy program. That's enough to spot a method that takes most of the time, and far too few to see what that method does inside. Lesson 6 brings in a profiler that takes thousands. Watch slow calls and GCs as they happen Run StreamingDemo and watch the output for 3 seconds. Predict before running the Kotlin twin: which shelves will show up, and how slow? On JDK 25 only: run the workload with method timing, using the command in the note below, and compare the table with your guess for one countWords call. h: JDK Flight Recorder and Mission Control · Java and Kotlin
x: A custom JFR event in Java and Kotlin StoreCallEvent.java @Name("workbench.StoreCall") @Label("Store Call") @Category({"Workbench", "Reports"}) public class StoreCallEvent extends Event { @Label("Shelf") String shelf; @Label("Words") long words; @Label("Found") boolean found; } StoreCallEvent event = new StoreCallEvent(); event.begin(); // 1. start the clock String text = store.fetch(shelf, title); event.end(); // 2. stop it if (event.shouldCommit()) { // 3. false if no recording wants it event.shelf = shelf; event.words = text == null ? 0 : countWords(text); event.found = text != null; event.commit(); // 4. write it, with a stack trace } JfrDemo.kt @Name("workbench.StoreCall") @Label("Store Call") @Category("Workbench", "Reports") class KStoreCallEvent : Event() { @Label("Shelf") var shelf: String? = null @Label("Words") var words = 0L @Label("Found") var found = false } val event = KStoreCallEvent() event.begin() // 1. start the clock val text = store.fetch(shelf, title) event.end() // 2. stop it if (event.shouldCommit()) { // 3. false if no recording wants it event.shelf = shelf event.words = if (text == null) 0 else countWords(text) event.found = text != null event.commit() // 4. write it, with a stack trace } The same event, recorded the same way. A Kotlin var compiles to a private field plus a getter and a setter, and JFR records the field. A Java annotation such as @Label placed on a Kotlin property goes to that field, because FIELD is the only one of its targets a property can use. @Category takes an array, written {"Workbench", "Reports"} in Java and as plain arguments in Kotlin. Both versions produce the same event type, workbench.StoreCall, so the same jfr view works on either recording. The Kotlin field for the shelf is a nullable String?, because an event is created empty and filled in later.

h: JDK Flight Recorder and Mission Control · Quiz
x: The report service is misbehaving right now and you can't restart it. How do you get JFR data from the last few minutes? Restart it with -XX:StartFlightRecording If a recording is running, jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=1 filename=now.jfr; otherwise jcmd <pid> JFR.start and wait Read the GC log Attach a debugger and suspend every thread JFR.dump copies a running recording to a file without stopping the JVM, which is why a recording that's always on pays off. Without one, JFR.start begins recording now, so you only see what happens next. A restart throws away the very minutes you wanted. Which jfr view tells you where threads waited to enter a synchronized block, and for how long? hot-methods allocation-by-site contention-by-site gc-pauses contention-by-site groups jdk.JavaMonitorEnter events by stack, with the count, the average and the longest wait. hot-methods shows where threads ran, not where they waited. Your event has @Name("workbench.Lookup"), but jfr summary of a recording shows none of them, although the code calls commit(). What's the most likely cause? Your own events are only recorded with settings=profile Events with a String field can't be recorded commit() needs a call to flush() afterwards The recording's settings switch the event off, or give it a threshold longer than the calls take Your own event types are switched on by default with no threshold, so even a bare new Recording() keeps them, and any .jfc file works. When they're missing although commit() runs, the settings turned them off (+workbench.Lookup#enabled=false) or set a threshold the calls never reach. There's no flush call to make. On JDK 25 you need call counts and timings for one method of the report service. You may restart it with a new flag, but you can't change its code. What fits best? -XX:StartFlightRecording:method-timing=com.example.Reports::render,report-on-exit=method-timing -XX:+PrintCompilation A JMH benchmark of the method jcmd <pid> Thread.print every second JEP 520 (JDK 25) counts and times the methods a filter matches, and report-on-exit prints the table when the JVM exits. PrintCompilation shows compiles, not timings. JMH measures the method on its own, outside the running service. From lesson 2: hours after start-up, a service still keeps throwing away C2 code because a type check fails. Which JFR view helps you confirm it? jfr view gc-pauses jfr view allocation-by-site jfr view deoptimizations-by-reason jfr view hot-methods JFR records a jdk.Deoptimization event each time compiled code hits an uncommon trap, and this view groups them by reason, such as class_check or unstable_if. The demo showed 16 in its first 4 seconds, the normal start-up burst. A count that keeps growing hours later is the signal lesson 2 described.

h: JDK Flight Recorder and Mission Control · Explain it back
x: A teammate asks why you'd add a JFR event around the call to the document store when there's already a log line with the duration. Explain the difference in your own words.

h: JDK Flight Recorder and Mission Control · Key terms
x: JFR (JDK Flight Recorder) A recorder built into HotSpot that writes timestamped events about the JVM and your code. Event One timestamped record, such as a GC pause, a lock wait or one call to the document store. Recording A running JFR session with its settings and limits, which you dump to a .jfr file. Execution sample A snapshot of a running thread's stack, taken every 10 or 20 ms, used to find busy methods. Threshold The shortest duration a recording keeps for an event; shorter ones are dropped. JMC (JDK Mission Control) The desktop app for reading .jfr files, downloaded separately from the JDK. RecordingStream An API that hands JFR events to your code while the JVM runs, in batches. How do you start a JFR recording on a JVM that's already running, and get the data out? jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=x settings=profile, and later jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=x filename=x.jfr. The dump stops nothing. default.jfc or profile.jfc for a recording that stays on all the time? default.jfc ("typically less than 1 % overhead"). profile.jfc samples twice as often; use it for short investigations. What's the first command to run on a .jfr file you've never seen? jfr summary file.jfr: every event type with its count and size. Then ask one question per jfr view. What does event.shouldCommit() tell you? Whether some recording has this event switched on and the duration passes its threshold. If it's false, skip filling in the fields. How do you read events from a .jfr file in Java? RecordingFile.readAllEvents(path), then filter on e.getEventType().getName() and read fields with getString, getLong, getBoolean, getDuration. Your event's threshold on the command line is ignored with a warning that the setting doesn't exist. What's missing? The +: +workbench.StoreCall#threshold=30ms. Your event isn't in the .jfc file, so the setting must be added. Why check a .jfr file before sharing it? It holds environment variables and the command line, where secrets often live. JDK 27 adds redaction (JEP 536).

h: JDK Flight Recorder and Mission Control · Go deeper
x: JFR's views are queries, kept in the JDK source in a file called view.ini. For example, hot-methods counts ExecutionSample events grouped by their top frame, and deoptimizations-by-reason counts Deoptimization events grouped by reason. jfr view --verbose prints the query a view runs, which helps when you build your own analysis with RecordingFile. The demo got only 40 execution samples in 4 seconds. Its threads sleep most of the time, and the classic sampler records threads that are running Java code, not sleeping ones. On a machine shared with many busy programs, a running thread may also be waiting for a CPU core when the sampler looks. That's one reason lesson 6 brings in async-profiler, which samples with signals and timers, and why JDK 25 added the CPU-time sampler. jfr has more subcommands: jfr configure builds a custom .jfc file from options, jfr scrub writes a copy of a recording without chosen events, jfr assemble and jfr disassemble join and split chunk files, and jfr metadata lists every event type and field. To record a whole test run, add -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=build/test.jfr to the test JVM's arguments. On JDK 25, adding report-on-exit=allocation-by-site prints the allocation report straight into the build log, so a reviewer can see it without opening any file.

h: async-profiler and flame graphs · A sampling profiler is a loop that counts stacks
x: Here's the code we'll profile in this lesson and the next. It's the report service's busiest step. It checks a document's language, counts its words and works out the reading time. Then it writes a line for the debug log, a level of logging that's usually switched off. The result is right, and the code looks harmless: Java static long readingSeconds(Document d) { if (!Pattern.compile("^[a-z]{2}$").matcher(d.language()).matches()) // a regex compiled per call throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad language"); long words = d.text().split(" ").length; // a new String for every word long seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238; // 238 words a minute, rounded up debug(String.format("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d", // formatted, then thrown away d.id(), d.language(), words, seconds)); return seconds; } Kotlin fun kReadingSeconds(d: KDocument): Long { require(Regex("^[a-z]{2}$").matches(d.language)) { "bad language" } // a regex compiled per call val words = d.text.split(' ').size.toLong() // a new String for every word val seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238 // 238 words a minute, rounded up kDebug("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d" // formatted, then thrown away .format(d.id, d.language, words, seconds)) return seconds } We want to know where its CPU time goes, call by call, without changing it. We could put timers around every line, but timers change what they measure, and we'd need to know where to put them first. A sampling profiler does something simpler. Every few milliseconds it looks at what each thread is running, writes down the thread's whole call stack, and counts how often each stack turns up. A thread is one line of work inside a program. Its call stack is the chain of methods it's inside right now, from Thread.run at the bottom to the running method at the top. If a method is on top in 20% of the samples, the thread spent about 20% of its time there. That's the manager's tally: one glance is a sample, and "Ana, soup, chopping onions" is a stack, read from the bottom up. You can build one in a dozen lines: Java Map<String, Long> stacks = new HashMap<>(); while (worker.isAlive()) { Thread.sleep(10); // 1. wait one sampling interval StackTraceElement[] st = worker.getStackTrace(); // 2. snapshot the thread's stack List<String> frames = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = st.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) // 3. root first frames.add(st[i].getClassName() + "." + st[i].getMethodName()); stacks.merge(String.join(";", frames), 1L, Long::sum); // 4. count identical stacks } Kotlin val stacks = HashMap<String, Long>() while (worker.isAlive) { Thread.sleep(10) // 1. wait one sampling interval val st = worker.stackTrace // 2. snapshot the thread's stack val key = st.reversed() // 3. root first .joinToString(";") { "${it.className}.${it.methodName}" } stacks.merge(key, 1L, Long::plus) // 4. count identical stacks } The output is called collapsed stacks, the text format that flame-graph tools read. Each distinct stack gets one line: its frames from the root to the top, separated by ;, then the number of samples. A frame is one method call on the stack. Here's a real line: java.lang.Thread.run;workbench.performance.l06.SlowReport.lambda$hammer$0;workbench.performance.l06.SlowReport.readingSeconds;java.lang.String.split;java.lang.String.split;java.lang.String.split 60 Two words come up all the time. A frame's self time is the samples where it was on top of the stack, doing the work itself. Its inclusive time adds everything it called. readingSeconds has little self time and a large inclusive time: it does little on its own and calls expensive things. PoorMansProfiler runs the step on two threads for 4 seconds and samples them this way. One run on the busy course machine took 238 samples. That's fewer than the 800 the arithmetic promises, because the sampler's own thread didn't always get a CPU core on time. Its top frames: 238 samples; top frames: 29.4% java.lang.String.split 13.4% java.util.Formatter.format 12.6% java.util.Formatter.parse 7.1% java.util.regex.Pattern.sequence 5.9% java.util.regex.Pattern.clazz 5.9% java.util.regex.Pattern.compile That looks like a usable answer: splitting the text is the biggest cost. Is it really? The next section says no. Run a profiler you can read in one screen Read PoorMansProfiler and SlowReport.readingSeconds. Predict the three methods that will be on top most often. Run it. It prints the top frames and writes build/poor-man.collapsed (inside labs/performance). Open the collapsed file and find the line with the biggest count. How many frames deep is it, and what's on top? Then run the Kotlin twin and compare its top frames. PoorMansProfiler.java package workbench.performance.l06; import java.io.IOException; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * A sampling profiler in 40 lines: every 10 ms, take the stack of each worker thread with * Thread.getStackTrace() and count it. Writes the samples as collapsed stacks, the text format * flame graph tools read, to build/poor-man.collapsed. */ public class PoorMansProfiler { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { long until = System.nanoTime() + 4_000_000_000L; Thread work = new Thread(() -> { try { SlowReport.hammer(2, until); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); work.start(); Map<String, Long> stacks = new HashMap<>(); // "frame;frame;frame" -> samples while (work.isAlive()) { Thread.sleep(10); for (Thread t : Thread.getAllStackTraces().keySet()) { if (!t.getName().startsWith("report-")) continue; StackTraceElement[] st = t.getStackTrace(); // the JVM must pause t to walk its stack if (st.length == 0) continue; List<String> frames = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = st.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) // root first, as flame graphs want frames.add(st[i].getClassName() + "." + st[i].getMethodName()); stacks.merge(String.join(";", frames), 1L, Long::sum); } } write(stacks, Path.of("build", "poor-man.collapsed")); Map<String, Long> self = new HashMap<>(); // top frame = where the thread was stacks.forEach((k, v) -> self.merge(k.substring(k.lastIndexOf(';') + 1), v, Long::sum)); long total = self.values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum(); System.out.println(total + " samples; top frames:"); self.entrySet().stream().sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed()).limit(6) .forEach(e -> System.out.printf(" %5.1f%% %s%n", 100.0 * e.getValue() / total, e.getKey())); } static void write(Map<String, Long> stacks, Path file) throws IOException { Files.createDirectories(file.getParent()); List<String> lines = new ArrayList<>(); stacks.forEach((k, v) -> lines.add(k + " " + v)); Files.write(file, lines); System.out.println("collapsed stacks written to " + file.toAbsolutePath()); } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l06.PoorMansProfiler labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l06/PoorMansProfiler.java PoorMansProfiler.kt package workbench.performance.l06 import java.nio.file.Files import java.nio.file.Path import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Kotlin twin of PoorMansProfiler.java: every 10 ms, take the stack of each worker thread with // Thread.getStackTrace() and count it. Writes collapsed stacks to build/poor-man-kt.collapsed. fun main() { val until = System.nanoTime() + 4_000_000_000L val work = thread { kHammer(2, until) } val stacks = HashMap<String, Long>() // "frame;frame;frame" -> samples while (work.isAlive) { Thread.sleep(10) for (t in Thread.getAllStackTraces().keys) { if (!t.name.startsWith("report-")) continue val st = t.stackTrace // the JVM must pause t to walk its stack if (st.isEmpty()) continue val key = st.reversed().joinToString(";") { "${it.className}.${it.methodName}" } // root first stacks.merge(key, 1L, Long::plus) } } val file = Path.of("build", "poor-man-kt.collapsed") Files.createDirectories(file.parent) Files.write(file, stacks.map { (k, v) -> "$k $v" }) println("collapsed stacks written to ${file.toAbsolutePath()}") val self = stacks.entries.groupBy({ it.key.substringAfterLast(';') }, { it.value }).mapValues { it.value.sum() } val total = self.values.sum() println("$total samples; top frames:") self.entries.sortedByDescending { it.value }.take(6) .forEach { (frame, n) -> println(" %5.1f%% %s".format(100.0 * n / total, frame)) } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l06.PoorMansProfilerKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l06/PoorMansProfiler.kt A few hundred samples in 4 seconds (2 threads, one sample each every 10 ms if the machine keeps up; 238 in a busy run here). The top frames are String.split (19 to 29% in two runs), then Formatter and regex methods. The biggest line ends in String.split;String.split;String.split: three split frames and nothing above them. The Kotlin twin shows kotlin.text.StringsKt__StringsKt.split$StringsKt__StringsKt on top, Kotlin's own split. Remember that nothing ever sits above split for the next section.

h: async-profiler and flame graphs · Safepoint bias: the hand-made sampler only sees threads where they can stop
x: Thread.getStackTrace() on another thread can't read that thread's stack at just any instruction. Compiled code keeps values in the processor's registers, and it has small methods inlined, copied into their callers (lesson 2). So the JVM can only describe a thread's stack at a safepoint: a place in the code where it has written down the full state of every frame. Compiled code checks for a request to stop at safepoint polls, which sit mostly at method returns and at the jumps back to the top of a loop. So when the sampler asks, the thread runs on to its next poll and reports its stack from there. That's the manager who only glances when a cook puts the knife down. Samples pile up at the polls instead of where the CPU spends its time. A tight inlined loop with no poll looks free, and the method that holds the next poll gets the blame. This is safepoint bias, and every profiler built on getStackTrace, or on the JVM's tool interface call GetAllStackTraces, has it. Our sampler shows it. String.split came top with 29.4%, and every one of its stacks ended at split itself, three frames deep. Not one sample caught the methods that split calls to find each space and copy each word. They're inlined, and by the time the thread reached a poll, they had returned. A second run put 19.3% on split and 15.8% on Formatter.parse, the same pattern. async-profiler is an open-source profiler for the JVM, and version 4.6 is the one used here. It samples without the bias. It interrupts each thread with a signal from the operating system, driven by Linux perf_events or by a timer. Then it walks the stack at the exact instruction where the signal landed. To make sense of compiled frames there, it reads HotSpot's internal structures, including the records of which methods were inlined where. The same code under async-profiler 4.6 on JDK 25, four threads for 10 seconds, gave 3,569 samples. Its top self frames were readingSeconds 7.2%, String.split 5.8%, StringLatin1.indexOf 5.1% and Pattern.compile 4.0%. So split itself does about a fifth of what our sampler claimed. The rest is spread over indexOf (searching for the next space), ArrayList.add and StringLatin1.newString (building each word), exactly the frames the hand-made profiler never saw. Because it works below the JVM, async-profiler also shows native code, the JVM's own threads and the operating system's kernel. In this run, the threads of the JIT, the part of the JVM that compiles busy methods, took 21.8% of all samples, and the garbage collector, which frees memory nobody uses, took 2.7%. JFR, from lesson 5, doesn't have the bias in its old form either. On JDK 25 its sampler records where the thread was at the moment of the sample. Then it lets the thread finish the stack walk at its next safepoint (cooperative sampling, JEP 518). A profiler that waits for safepoints reports where threads can stop, not where they spend their time. Check a surprising answer with async-profiler. Check yourself: a method has one hot inlined loop and returns once, at the end. Which method would a getStackTrace profiler blame for the loop's time? (Whichever frame reaches the next safepoint poll, often the loop's own jump back or the caller after the return, not the instructions that burned the CPU.) Thousands of honest samples are still just a long list of stacks. A flame graph turns them into a picture. Profile the same code with async-profiler Download async-profiler from its GitHub releases page (Linux x64 or arm64, or macOS) and unpack it. bin/asprof is the launcher. Run ProfileMe. It prints its process id and keeps four threads busy for 8 seconds. In a second terminal, within those 8 seconds: asprof -d 5 -f cpu.html <pid>. Open cpu.html in a browser. Find String.split and look at what sits on top of it. Compare with PoorMansProfiler's list. ProfileMe.java package workbench.performance.l06; /** * A target for async-profiler: four threads run SlowReport.readingSeconds for 8 seconds. * While it runs, attach from another terminal: asprof -d 5 -f cpu.html <pid> */ public class ProfileMe { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int seconds = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 8; System.out.println("pid " + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + ", running for " + seconds + " s"); System.out.println("attach with: asprof -d 5 -f cpu.html " + ProcessHandle.current().pid()); SlowReport.hammer(4, System.nanoTime() + seconds * 1_000_000_000L); System.out.println("done"); } } ./gradlew :performance:demo h: async-profiler and flame graphs · Reading a flame graph: width is samples, left to right is the alphabet
x: Reading a flame graph: counted stacks where width is samples, left to right is the alphabet, and the tops are where the CPU was A flame graph is the collapsed stacks drawn as boxes. In the kitchen, it's the manager's tally drawn as towers of blocks. The bottom block is the whole evening, every glance. On top of it sits a block for each dish, as wide as the number of glances that caught someone cooking it. On top of those sit the steps of each dish. Three rules make it readable. Width is samples. A box's width is the number of samples that had that frame at that place in the stack: its inclusive time there. Identical frames at the same depth, under the same parent, merge into one box. Left to right is not time. Boxes at the same level are sorted alphabetically by name. The header of flamegraph.pl, the original drawing script, says "The ordering on the x-axis has no meaning". async-profiler's guide says a flame graph "does not preserve information on when a particular stack trace was taken". A box on the left didn't run first. That's where the picture breaks: the manager's blocks for the evening would line up by clock time, and these never do. Look at the tops. The part of a box with nothing on top of it is self time: the CPU was in that frame's own code. Wide tops are where to start. A wide box covered by its children is a caller, and the fix is usually in one of those children, or in the decision to call them. The figure is drawn from the 3,569-sample profile of the last section. readingSeconds covers 2,546 samples, 71.3% of the total. Its widest children are String.split (24.2% of all samples), String.format (22.3%) and Pattern.compile (13.6%). Notice String.format on the far left. It isn't first because it ran first. It's first because java/lang/String.format sorts before java/lang/String.split, and both sort before java/util/regex. Two smaller towers sit beside readingSeconds. One is os::javaTimeNanos: the demo's own loop calls System.nanoTime() before every call to check its deadline, and 64 samples landed in reading the clock. The measuring shows up in the measurement. The other tall towers belong to the JIT's compiler threads, busy for a fifth of the run, because 10 seconds is a short life for a JVM, as lesson 1 showed. async-profiler's HTML colours frames by type: green for compiled Java, aqua for inlined Java, light green for interpreted Java, yellow for the JVM's own C++ code, red for native code and orange for the kernel. Clicking a box zooms in, and the search field highlights every frame that matches. Two variants are useful too. A reversed graph (--reverse) merges stacks from the top frame down, which gathers all the callers of one busy method. An icicle graph (--inverted) hangs from the top. Width is time, left to right is the alphabet. Start at the widest top and walk down to your own code. So the flame graph says split, format and the regex. Each of those questions came from a CPU profile. Some questions aren't about the CPU at all. Read your flame graph like a profile Open cpu.html from the previous Try it. Type Pattern into the search field: what share of the samples matches? Click readingSeconds to zoom in. Find the widest box that has nothing above it. Predict before checking: if you moved Pattern.compile(...) into a static final field, which boxes would disappear, and roughly how much narrower would readingSeconds get? The search shows the matching share in the bottom-right corner; in the profile the figure comes from, Pattern.compile alone was 13.6% of all samples, and Pattern.matcher about 1.5% more. The widest bare tops sit inside split (searching for spaces, copying words) and Formatter. Hoisting the pattern removes the Pattern.compile tower but keeps Pattern.matcher, which still creates a Matcher on every call. Lesson 7 runs exactly that experiment. The readingSeconds part of a real 3,569-sample CPU profile. Widths are sample counts; small frames are grouped in this drawing. Interpreting a flame graph (async-profiler docs) read

h: async-profiler and flame graphs · Pick the mode for the question: cpu, wall, alloc or lock
x: A flame graph shows samples of something, and the mode decides what. async-profiler's main modes: Mode A sample means Use it for cpu (default) the thread was running on a CPU where CPU time goes wall the thread existed, running or not where a request waits: the network, a lock, a sleep alloc the thread allocated memory who creates the garbage lock the thread waited to enter a lock contention cpu mode takes its samples from Linux perf_events. Those can be blocked, for example when the file /proc/sys/kernel/perf_event_paranoid holds 2 or more, or inside some containers. Then -e ctimer gives similar results from a timer, without the kernel frames. wall mode samples every thread at the same rate, whether it runs, sleeps or waits, and the docs recommend it per thread: asprof -e wall -t -i 50ms -f wall.html <pid>. Remember the document store from lesson 5. A report that's slow because it waits for the store spends no CPU while it waits, so a cpu profile barely shows it, and wall shows exactly where it waits. In alloc mode, "the top frame of every call trace is the class of the allocated object, and the counter is the heap pressure". It hooks into HotSpot when an object needs a fresh TLAB, the private stretch of heap each thread fills on its own, or has to be placed outside one. It doesn't disturb escape analysis, the JIT's trick of skipping objects that never leave a method: those never show up, because they were never made. An alloc profile of the report step put 34.1% of the allocated bytes under String.format, 33.3% under Pattern.compile and 28.2% under String.split. The top frames were byte[] 26.2%, java.lang.String 13.0% and boolean[] 11.0%: text being built and copied, and the regex's own tables. (Each class name ends in a short marker such as _[i], which the drawing uses to pick a colour; you can ignore it.) lock mode puts the class of the lock on top, and the counter is the nanoseconds spent waiting to enter it: asprof -e lock -t -i 5ms -f lock.html <pid>. You can also load the profiler when the JVM starts instead of attaching later, which helps inside a container: -agentpath:/path/to/libasyncProfiler.so=start,event=cpu,file=cpu.collapsed,collapsed. -o collapsed (or collapsed in the agent's options) writes collapsed stacks instead of HTML, which is what the lab reads. --all switches on every mode at once, and the docs say it's not recommended for production. Here's where today's tool stops. A profile shows where the time and the bytes go, during the seconds you recorded. It doesn't say which cost you can remove, whether removing it helps the slow requests, or what the next problem will be once this one is gone. Those questions need a whole investigation, and that's the next lesson. Who allocates, and who waits Start ProfileMe again. Attach in alloc mode: asprof -e alloc -d 5 -f alloc.html <pid>. Before opening it, predict the three widest children of readingSeconds in the allocation graph. Start ProfileMe once more and attach with asprof -e wall -t -d 5 -f wall.html <pid>. How does it differ from cpu.html? terminal asprof -e alloc -d 5 -f alloc.html <pid> asprof -e alloc -d 5 -o collapsed -f alloc.collapsed <pid> # the same, as text asprof -e wall -t -d 5 -f wall.html <pid> In the allocation graph, String.format, Pattern.compile and String.split are the three wide children of readingSeconds, about a third each, and the top frames are classes such as byte[], java.lang.String and boolean[]. The wall graph is split by thread (-t). The four report- threads look much like the CPU profile, because they never wait, while main sits in Thread.join the whole time. In a 3-second run here, every thread got about 60 samples, one per 50 ms, the JVM's sleeping threads included: wall mode samples every thread equally, and a CPU profile would ignore main completely.

h: async-profiler and flame graphs · Worked example
x: From a profile to the line to change The report service runs hot. h: async-profiler and flame graphs · Quiz
x: A report is slow because each one waits 120 ms for the document store to answer. The CPU flame graph of the service barely shows the report path. Which mode shows the wait? -e cpu with a shorter interval -e wall -t -e alloc -e lock wall samples every thread at the same rate whether it runs, sleeps or waits, so a thread waiting on a network socket shows up. CPU sampling only sees threads that are running. Waiting for a socket isn't a Java lock, so lock won't show it either. In a flame graph, SlowReport.readingSeconds is a very wide box, almost completely covered by String.split, String.format and Pattern.compile above it. Where is the time? In readingSeconds's own code Spread evenly over the graph In the frames above it: readingSeconds has little self time, so its callees do the work In the frames below it Width is inclusive. A box that's covered has little self time. The fix is still in readingSeconds, because it's the frame in your code that calls split, format and Pattern.compile, but the CPU is in those callees. A profiler built on Thread.getStackTrace() charges 29% of the CPU to String.split itself and never shows a frame above it. async-profiler charges most of that time to methods split calls, such as StringLatin1.indexOf. Which is closer to the truth, and why? The hand-made profiler: getStackTrace is exact async-profiler: getStackTrace only sees a thread at a safepoint poll, after the inlined callees have returned, so their time is charged to split Neither: the two runs used different threads The hand-made profiler, because async-profiler can't see inlined methods Reading another thread's stack with getStackTrace needs that thread at a safepoint, and polls sit at method returns and loop back-edges. Inlined callees such as indexOf have finished by then, so their time lands on split. async-profiler interrupts the thread wherever it is, and it does show inlined frames. You profile with asprof -e alloc and see no Summary objects, although the code creates one for every document. What could explain it? Alloc mode only shows arrays Allocation profiles only cover the main thread async-profiler can't see your own classes The JIT's escape analysis proved the Summary never leaves its method and replaced it with plain local values, so it was never made on the heap async-profiler's docs say alloc mode doesn't disturb escape analysis and measures only real heap allocations. An object that never escapes its compiled method can be broken into its fields, kept in registers, so there's nothing to sample. From lesson 5: you need to know which methods allocate the most in a running service, but you can't install async-profiler there. What's the closest built-in answer? jfr view allocation-by-site on a recording dumped with jcmd <pid> JFR.dump -XX:+PrintCompilation jcmd <pid> Thread.print A JMH benchmark with -prof gc JFR samples allocations as jdk.ObjectAllocationSample events with stack traces, and the allocation-by-site view adds them up by method. It's built into the JDK, so nothing needs installing. JMH measures a piece of code on its own, not the running service.

h: async-profiler and flame graphs · Key terms
x: Sampling profiler A profiler that writes down stacks at intervals and counts them, instead of timing every call. Collapsed stacks Text format: one line per distinct stack, frames joined by ;, then a count. Self time Samples where a frame was on top of the stack, running its own code. Inclusive time Samples where a frame was anywhere on the stack, including the time in what it called. Safepoint A place in the code where the JVM knows a thread's full state, so it can stop the thread or read its stack. Safepoint bias The error a profiler makes when it can only see threads at safepoint polls. Flame graph Stacks drawn as boxes: root at the bottom, width = samples, alphabetical from left to right. What does a line of collapsed stacks look like? root;caller;callee 42: frames from the root to the top separated by ;, then the number of samples. Self time vs inclusive time of a frame? Self: samples with the frame on top of the stack. Inclusive: samples with the frame anywhere on the stack. What is safepoint bias? Profilers that use getStackTrace or JVMTI only see threads at safepoint polls, so samples land on the next poll instead of where the CPU was. In a flame graph, what does left to right mean? Nothing about time: frames at the same level are sorted alphabetically. Width is the number of samples. Which async-profiler mode shows where requests wait for the network? wall (ideally with -t), which samples threads whether they run, sleep or wait. What's on top of each stack in async-profiler's alloc mode? The class of the allocated object, such as byte[]; the counter is the heap pressure. What do you do when async-profiler can't use perf_events (containers, perf_event_paranoid of 2 or more)? Use -e ctimer, which samples CPU with a timer, without kernel frames.

h: async-profiler and flame graphs · Go deeper
x: Before version 4.2, async-profiler took Java stacks with AsyncGetCallTrace, a HotSpot function that isn't part of any standard API and that the profiler is named after. Its docs say it "was broken several times even in minor JDK updates" and could crash the JVM. That's why 4.2 made its own walker over HotSpot's internal structures the default (--cstack vm). vmx mode goes further and mixes Java and native frames in one stack. -a (or --ann) marks frames by how they were compiled: _[j] for JIT-compiled methods, _[i] for inlined ones, _[0] for interpreted and _[1] for C1-compiled. That connects a profile back to lessons 1 and 2: a busy method stuck at _[0] or _[1] deserves a look with PrintCompilation. Lesson 4 promised a symptom of false sharing: in a CPU profile, it shows up as a wide top on a line that does almost nothing, such as count++, because the thread spends its time waiting for the cache line. Differential flame graphs compare two profiles. Brendan Gregg's FlameGraph tools colour frames "red for more, and blue for less", which is a quick way to see what a change did. Make both profiles the same length and under the same load, or the comparison measures the traffic instead of the code. async-profiler can also write JFR files (-o jfr) that JDK Mission Control opens, and convert them later with jfrconv. With JMH, -prof async:libPath=<path to libasyncProfiler.so> runs it around a benchmark, so you get a flame graph of exactly the code you measured.

h: A performance investigation, start to finish · Start from the symptom: the slowest calls and the GC count, not the average
x: One loop from symptom to proof: read the tail and the GC count, group JFR by your own line, fix one thing, profile again, then prove it with JMH and keep it with an allocation budget Here's the code under suspicion, the report step from lesson 6, now in a class called ReportVariants that also holds each round of the fix. It checks the two-letter language with a regex, a small pattern language for matching text. It counts the words with split, and it formats a line for the debug log, which is switched off: Java static long slow(Document d) { if (!Pattern.compile("^[a-z]{2}$").matcher(d.language()).matches()) // line 17 throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad language"); long words = d.text().split(" ").length; // line 19 long seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238; debug(String.format("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d", // line 21 d.id(), d.language(), words, seconds)); return seconds; } Kotlin fun ktSlow(d: KtDocument): Long { require(Regex("^[a-z]{2}$").matches(d.language)) { "bad language" } // a regex per call val words = d.text.split(' ').size.toLong() // a new String per word val seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238 ktDebug("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d" // formatted, then dropped .format(d.id, d.language, words, seconds)) return seconds } ReportInvestigation runs it on four threads, four lines of work side by side, for 3 seconds. It does that in a second JVM, with a 256 MB heap (-Xmx256m: the most memory the JVM may use for objects) and a JFR recording, lesson 5's log of what the JVM did. It times every call into a histogram, a fixed array of counters by duration. Then it prints the percentiles. Sort all the calls by time: p50 is the one in the middle, p99 is the one that 99% of calls beat, and only one call in ten thousand is slower than the p99.99. Those rare slow calls are the tail. Here's one run on JDK 25, on the busy course machine: slow: 218,239 calls/s p50 <1500ns p99 <27300ns p99.9 <110800ns p99.99 <36700us GCs 14 (235 ms) Half the calls take under 1.5 µs. The p99.99 is over 36 ms, more than 20,000 times longer. The JVM collected garbage 14 times in 3 seconds, and jfr view gc-pauses on the same recording agrees: 14 pauses, 236 ms in total, the longest 53.2 ms. That's our first suspect, and the kitchen explains it. Every object a call creates is a clean plate taken from the shelf. When the young part of the heap, where new objects start out, fills up, the garbage collector stops every thread of the program while it clears the dead objects away: the whole kitchen washing up. A call that's running when a pause starts waits for the pause to end. So the slowest calls are probably the ones that met a pause, and the pauses come often because the code allocates a lot. Here the picture breaks a little. G1, the JVM's default collector, does some of its work while the program runs, like a kitchen porter washing in a corner. But the young collections, the frequent ones here, stop everyone. One caution before we change anything. This machine shared its four cores with more than 30 busy programs, so some slow calls simply waited for a core, and the p99.9 of 110 µs is probably that. The longest call of a run is mostly that noise too. Don't present it as the effect of a fix. The percentiles and the GC counts are the evidence. A good median can hide calls that wait for the garbage collector. Measure the tail and count the GCs. The figure shows the loop this lesson follows. The step people skip is the dashed one. So the GC is the suspect, and allocation is the motive. Which lines allocate? Reproduce the symptom Read ReportVariants.slow and ReportInvestigation. The demo starts a second JVM with -Xmx256m and a JFR recording, runs 4 threads for 3 seconds, then reads the recording. Predict: which line of slow allocates the most? Run it with -Pargs=slow. Write down the p50, the p99.99, the GC count and the calls per second. ReportInvestigation.java package workbench.performance.l07; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedEvent; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedFrame; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile; import java.lang.management.GarbageCollectorMXBean; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.function.ToLongFunction; /** * Runs one version of the report step (slow, hoisted, scanned or noregex) on 4 threads for 3 seconds in a * second JVM with -Xmx256m and a JFR recording, prints latency percentiles and GC counts, then reads the * recording and prints allocation by source line in this package. Usage: -Pargs=slow (or hoisted, ...). */ public class ReportInvestigation { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "slow"; if (args.length > 1 && args[1].equals("child")) { load(mode); return; } Path file = Path.of("build", "report-" + mode + ".jfr").toAbsolutePath(); String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(java, "-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:jfr+startup=warning", "-XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=" + file + ",settings=profile", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), ReportInvestigation.class.getName(), mode, "child") .inheritIO().start(); p.waitFor(); allocationByLine(file); } // the load: 4 threads, each timing every call into a fixed histogram (no allocation of its own) static void load(String mode) throws Exception { ToLongFunction<ReportVariants.Document> step = switch (mode) { case "slow" -> ReportVariants::slow; case "hoisted" -> ReportVariants::hoisted; case "scanned" -> ReportVariants::scanned; default -> ReportVariants::noRegex; }; ReportVariants.Document[] ds = ReportVariants.documents(4_096); long end = System.nanoTime() + 3_000_000_000L; long[][] hist = new long[4][]; List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int t = 0; t < 4; t++) { int id = t; Thread th = new Thread(() -> { long[] h = new long[20_001]; // 100 ns buckets up to 1 ms, then 100 us buckets up to 1 s long sink = 0; for (int i = id; System.nanoTime() < end; i++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); sink += step.applyAsLong(ds[i & 4095]); long d = System.nanoTime() - t0; h[d < 1_000_000 ? (int) (d / 100) : (int) Math.min(20_000, 10_000 + (d - 1_000_000) / 100_000)]++; } hist[id] = h; if (sink == 42) System.out.println(); }); th.start(); threads.add(th); } for (Thread th : threads) th.join(); long[] h = new long[20_001]; for (long[] x : hist) for (int k = 0; k < h.length; k++) h[k] += x[k]; long total = 0; for (long n : h) total += n; long gcs = 0, gcMs = 0; for (GarbageCollectorMXBean gc : ManagementFactory.getGarbageCollectorMXBeans()) { gcs += gc.getCollectionCount(); gcMs += gc.getCollectionTime(); } System.out.printf("%s: %,d calls/s p50 %s p99 %s p99.9 %s p99.99 %s GCs %d (%d ms)%n", mode, total / 3, pct(h, total, 0.5), pct(h, total, 0.99), pct(h, total, 0.999), pct(h, total, 0.9999), gcs, gcMs); } static String pct(long[] h, long total, double q) { long target = (long) Math.ceil(total * q), acc = 0; for (int k = 0; k < h.length; k++) { acc += h[k]; if (acc >= target) return k < 10_000 ? "<" + (k + 1) * 100 + "ns" : "<" + ((k - 10_000 + 1) * 100 + 1_000) + "us"; } return "?"; } // what `jfr view allocation-by-site` can't tell you: the line in YOUR code each sample came from static void allocationByLine(Path file) throws Exception { Map<String, Long> weight = new HashMap<>(); long total = 0; for (RecordedEvent e : RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) { if (!e.getEventType().getName().equals("jdk.ObjectAllocationSample") || e.getStackTrace() == null) continue; for (RecordedFrame f : e.getStackTrace().getFrames()) { if (f.getMethod().getType().getName().startsWith("workbench.performance.l07.ReportVariants")) { weight.merge(f.getMethod().getName() + " line " + f.getLineNumber(), e.getLong("weight"), Long::sum); total += e.getLong("weight"); break; // the first frame in our code is the one to change } } } long sum = total; System.out.println("allocation by line in ReportVariants.java (from " + file.getFileName() + "):"); weight.entrySet().stream().sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed()).limit(5) .forEach(en -> System.out.printf(" %5.1f%% %s%n", 100.0 * en.getValue() / sum, en.getKey())); } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l07.ReportInvestigation -Pargs=slow labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l07/ReportInvestigation.java ReportInvestigation.kt h: A performance investigation, start to finish · JFR names the allocation, and the first frame in your code names the line
x: jfr view allocation-by-site on the slow run answers "what allocates" in the JDK's words: Method Allocation Pressure ---------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------- java.util.Formatter.parse(String) 16.09% java.lang.Long.toString(long) 14.19% java.util.regex.Pattern.compile(String) 9.65% java.util.Arrays.copyOfRange(byte[], int, int) 7.79% java.util.regex.Pattern$BitClass.<init>() 7.33% java.lang.StringLatin1.newString(byte[], int, int) 6.83% That's real, and not yet useful: you can't change Formatter.parse. The view groups by the top frame, the JDK method that did the allocating. What we want is the first frame in our own code below it. Each jdk.ObjectAllocationSample event carries a stack trace and a weight, the number of bytes the sample stands for. So a few lines of RecordingFile, as in lesson 5's lab, can group the samples by our file and line instead: Java for (RecordedEvent e : RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) { if (!e.getEventType().getName().equals("jdk.ObjectAllocationSample")) continue; for (RecordedFrame f : e.getStackTrace().getFrames()) { if (f.getMethod().getType().getName().startsWith("workbench.performance.l07.ReportVariants")) { weight.merge(f.getMethod().getName() + " line " + f.getLineNumber(), e.getLong("weight"), Long::sum); break; // the first frame in our code is the one to change } } } Kotlin for (e in RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) { if (e.eventType.name != "jdk.ObjectAllocationSample") continue val frame = e.stackTrace?.frames ?.firstOrNull { it.method.type.name == "workbench.performance.l07.ReportInvestigationKt" } ?: continue // the first frame in our code is the one to change weight.merge("${frame.method.name} line ${frame.lineNumber}", e.getLong("weight"), Long::plus) } ReportInvestigation does exactly that after each run. For the run above: allocation by line in ReportVariants.java (from report-slow.jfr): 49.1% slow line 21 String.format(...) for a log line nobody reads 32.3% slow line 17 Pattern.compile(...) on every call 18.5% slow line 19 split(" "), a new String for every word A second run put the same three lines on top in another order: line 17 first with 46.5%, then 19 and 21. JFR samples allocations instead of counting every byte, so read its shares as rough. A big share is big, and the order of near-equals means little. Measured one at a time, with the per-thread counter we'll meet at the end, the regex cost about 800 bytes per call, the log line 810 and split 690, out of 2,460. A flame graph answers the next question, who calls the allocating code. Lesson 6's allocation profile of the same code put 34.1% of the bytes under String.format, 33.3% under Pattern.compile and 28.2% under split. Two different tools agree, which is the point of using both. JFR is built in and cheap enough to leave running. async-profiler shows the whole picture, native frames included, when you can attach it. So the three costs have names. The regex is compiled again on every call. split builds a String for every word, only so that we can count them. And a third of all the bytes is a sentence written for the debug log, which is switched off, so nobody ever reads it. The view names the JDK method that allocated. The first frame in your own code names the line to change. Three costs, three fixes. The temptation is to make all of them at once. In jfr print, each sample shows objectClass, weight and a stack where, a few frames down, ReportVariants.slow appears with its line number: 21 under the Formatter frames, 17 under the Pattern frames and 19 under String.split.
