h: A performance investigation, start to finish · Fix one thing, then profile again
x: Round 1 removes the two costs that are pure waste, work done for nothing. They're the same kind of fix, so we'll make them together and count them as one round. The pattern becomes a static final field, compiled once, and the log line is formatted only when DEBUG is on. Moving work that doesn't change out of the path that runs on every call is called hoisting. Java static final Pattern LANGUAGE = Pattern.compile("^[a-z]{2}$"); // compiled once static long hoisted(Document d) { if (!LANGUAGE.matcher(d.language()).matches()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad language"); // line 30 long words = d.text().split(" ").length; // line 31 long seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238; if (debugEnabled) debug(String.format("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d", // only when DEBUG is on d.id(), d.language(), words, seconds)); return seconds; } Kotlin val KT_LANGUAGE = Regex("^[a-z]{2}$") // compiled once fun ktHoisted(d: KtDocument): Long { require(KT_LANGUAGE.matches(d.language)) { "bad language" } val words = d.text.split(' ').size.toLong() val seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238 if (ktDebugEnabled) ktDebug("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d" // only when DEBUG is on .format(d.id, d.language, words, seconds)) return seconds } The same harness, on the same busy machine: hoisted: 767,348 calls/s p50 <300ns p99 <4200ns p99.9 <23500ns p99.99 <12400us GCs 15 (161 ms) Three and a half times the throughput, and the p99.99 down from 36.7 ms to 12.4 ms. But the GC count went up, from 14 to 15. Did the fix fail? No. The faster version made 3.5 times as many calls in the same 3 seconds, so count collections per call: about 21 per million calls before, about 6.5 now. Then profile again, because the picture has changed: allocation by line in ReportVariants.java (from report-hoisted.jfr): 91.5% hoisted line 31 split(" ") 8.4% hoisted line 30 LANGUAGE.matcher(d.language()).matches() split was about a quarter of the problem before. Now it's nearly all of it. We already know the cure from lesson 3: count where words start, without building any words. That's round 2: Java static long countWords(String text) { // round 2: count where words start, make nothing long words = 0; boolean inWord = false; for (int i = 0; i < text.length(); i++) { boolean letter = text.charAt(i) != ' '; if (letter && !inWord) words++; inWord = letter; } return words; } static long scanned(Document d) { if (!LANGUAGE.matcher(d.language()).matches()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad language"); // line 51 long words = countWords(d.text()); long seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238; if (debugEnabled) debug(String.format("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d", d.id(), d.language(), words, seconds)); return seconds; } Kotlin fun ktCountWords(text: String): Long { // round 2: count where words start, make nothing var words = 0L var inWord = false for (c in text) { val letter = c != ' ' if (letter && !inWord) words++ inWord = letter } return words } fun ktScanned(d: KtDocument): Long { require(KT_LANGUAGE.matches(d.language)) { "bad language" } val words = ktCountWords(d.text) val seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238 if (ktDebugEnabled) ktDebug("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d" .format(d.id, d.language, words, seconds)) return seconds } scanned: 2,066,071 calls/s p50 <200ns p99 <800ns p99.9 <6100ns p99.99 <51200ns GCs 4 (75 ms) The p99.99 fell from milliseconds to 51 µs, and the GCs to about 0.65 per million calls. Profile once more, and 99.6% of what's left is on line 51. A precompiled Pattern still creates a new Matcher object, its working state for one match, on every call. That cost was there from the start, a few percent hidden under bigger ones. It only rose to the top once they were gone. Do we fix it too? The answer depends on a budget: the number of bytes per call you've agreed the step may cost. This one's budget is 300 bytes, and the Matcher costs 56, so round 2 is enough. A third round could check the two letters by hand, and noregex in the demo does: 3.8 million calls a second and no GCs at all. For a two-letter rule, that's a small, safe change. For a rule with ten cases, the regex may be worth its bytes. Fix one thing, then profile again. The order of costs changes after every fix. Check yourself: in round 1 you hoist the Pattern but forget to guard the log line. Which line leads the next profile? (Line 21, the String.format: about 810 bytes per call, now the biggest cost left.) The harness tells us the fix helped. It can't yet tell us by exactly how much. Run every round Run ReportInvestigation with -Pargs=hoisted, then -Pargs=scanned, then -Pargs=noregex. For each, write down the top line, the p99.99 and the GC count next to your numbers for slow. Work out GCs per million calls, too. Run the Kotlin twin with -Pargs=scanned. What's left, and in which function? "<" + (k + 1) * 100 + "ns" : "<" + ((k - 10_000 + 1) * 100 + 1_000) + "us"; } return "?"; } // what `jfr view allocation-by-site` can't tell you: the line in YOUR code each sample came from static void allocationByLine(Path file) throws Exception { Map<String, Long> weight = new HashMap<>(); long total = 0; for (RecordedEvent e : RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) { if (!e.getEventType().getName().equals("jdk.ObjectAllocationSample") || e.getStackTrace() == null) continue; for (RecordedFrame f : e.getStackTrace().getFrames()) { if h: A performance investigation, start to finish · Prove it with JMH, then keep it with an allocation budget
x: JMH, the OpenJDK benchmark tool from lesson 3, gives the exact answer, with -prof gc and its bytes per operation. ReportBench runs each round on one document of 12 words (one fork, 5 warm-up and 3 measured rounds of 0.3 s each): Benchmark ns/op error B/op error after1Hoisted 856.5 7035.0 832.020 0.165 after2Scanned 311.6 2163.9 56.007 0.047 after3NoRegex 136.9 424.4 0.003 0.010 before 1776.1 6654.6 2464.040 0.128 The time column says the fixes helped, with errors bigger than the scores on this machine. The bytes column says how much, to a fraction of a byte: 2,464, then 832, then 56, then nothing. One run earlier, before showed 2499.551 ± 907.021 instead. On a machine this busy, five short warm-up rounds weren't always enough for the JIT to finish compiling the regex code, so one measured round still ran slower code that allocated more. Once the code is warm, bytes don't wobble. Before it's warm, they can. A benchmark proves the fix today. A test keeps it fixed. The JVM counts the bytes each thread allocates, and com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() reads that counter: Java var threads = (com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); long before = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes(); for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) sink += report.readingSeconds(ds[i & 1023]); double perCall = (threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before) / 100_000.0; assertThat(perCall).isLessThan(300); // the budget Kotlin val threads = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean val before = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes repeat(100_000) { sink += report.readingSeconds(ds[it and 1023]) } val perCall = (threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before) / 100_000.0 assertThat(perCall).isLessThan(300.0) // the budget That's an allocation budget test: it fails the build when the code allocates more than the agreed bytes per call, which is the check lesson 3 promised. Measure after warm-up, because allocation only settles once C2 has compiled the method and its escape analysis, the trick of skipping objects that never leave a method, has done its work. The lab's test runs 10 rounds of 100,000 calls and judges the best one. Measured that way, the slow version settles at about 2,400 bytes per call. Round 1 settles at about 750 on JDK 25 and 820 on JDK 21, and round 2 at 56 on JDK 25 and 128 on JDK 21. The numbers move with the JDK and with the shape of the loop, so set the budget with a margin, and look at it again when you upgrade. Here's where this loop stops. It finds code that burns CPU or makes garbage. Some programs are slow, or frozen, because their threads are waiting for each other, or for something outside the JVM. A profile of a waiting thread shows almost nothing, so that needs a different look. The proof, in bytes Predict the B/op of each benchmark in ReportBench, using what the investigation showed. Run it (about 20 seconds with Gradle). Compare the error columns for time and for bytes. Run the Kotlin twin, which measures the Kotlin versions with the per-thread allocation counter, like the lab's test. x: The fixed report step in Java and Kotlin ReportVariants.java static long countWords(String text) { // round 2: count where words start, make nothing long words = 0; boolean inWord = false; for (int i = 0; i < text.length(); i++) { boolean letter = text.charAt(i) != ' '; if (letter && !inWord) words++; inWord = letter; } return words; } static long scanned(Document d) { if (!LANGUAGE.matcher(d.language()).matches()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad language"); // line 51 long words = countWords(d.text()); long seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238; if (debugEnabled) debug(String.format("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d", d.id(), d.language(), words, seconds)); return seconds; } ReportInvestigation.kt fun ktCountWords(text: String): Long { // round 2: count where words start, make nothing var words = 0L var inWord = false for (c in text) { val letter = c != ' ' if (letter && !inWord) words++ inWord = letter } return words } fun ktScanned(d: KtDocument): Long { require(KT_LANGUAGE.matches(d.language)) { "bad language" } val words = ktCountWords(d.text) val seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238 if (ktDebugEnabled) ktDebug("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d" .format(d.id, d.language, words, seconds)) return seconds } After round 2 both versions allocate 56 bytes per call on JDK 25, all of it the Matcher behind the language check: Kotlin's Regex.matches creates one, just like Pattern.matcher. Round 1 cost 832 bytes in Java and 840 in Kotlin, where split(' ') returns a List<String> instead of an array. One Kotlin detail is worth knowing. The harness calls each version through a function type, (KtDocument) -> Long, whose invoke returns an object, so every result is boxed into a Long. Here that costs nothing, because Long.valueOf keeps ready-made objects for -128 to 127 and reading times are small. A function returning bigger numbers would allocate on every call. In hot Kotlin code, call the function directly, pass it to an inline function, or use a fun interface with a primitive return type, the Kotlin counterpart of Java's ToLongFunction.

h: A performance investigation, start to finish · Worked example
x: Write up the investigation for the pull request A pull request is the proposed change that reviewers read before it's merged. Start with the symptom and how you measured it, with the conditions. Without the conditions, the numbers mean nothing to a reviewer. Symptom: report step p99.99 < 36.7 ms (p50 < 1.5 us); 14 GCs in 3 s. Setup: 4 threads, 3 s, -Xmx256m, JDK 25, 4 shared cores, a latency histogram per call. Then the evidence for the cause, from two tools, with the lines named. JFR jdk.ObjectAllocationSample, first frame in our code (two runs): line 21 String.format for a disabled DEBUG line 49.1% / 24.4% line 17 Pattern.compile on every call 32.3% / 46.5% line 19 split(" "), a String per word 18.5% / 28.8% async-profiler alloc: format 34.1%, Pattern.compile 33.3%, split 28.2% of bytes Then each round on its own, with the profile that justified the next one. Self-check: why list round 1, even though round 2 includes it? (So the reviewer sees what each change bought, and that the next cost was found by measuring, not guessed.) Round 1 (hoist the pattern, guard the log line): p99.99 < 12.4 ms, 6.5 GCs per million calls. Profile again: 91.5% of allocation now at split(" "). Round 2 (count words without split): p99.99 < 51.2 us, 0.65 GCs per million calls. Profile again: 99.6% at LANGUAGE.matcher(...). 56 B/call, under the 300 B budget. Stopping. End with the proof and the guard: the JMH numbers with their errors, and the test that keeps it fixed. JMH -prof gc (1 fork, 5 warm-up + 3 x 0.3 s): before 2,464.040 +/- 0.128 B/op, after 56.007 +/- 0.047 B/op. DocumentReportTest.allocationBudget: < 300 B/call after warm-up (JDK 25: 56, JDK 21: 128).

x: Bring the report step under its allocation budget labs/performance/src/main/java/workbench/performance/l07/DocumentReport.java ./gradlew :performance:test --tests 'workbench.performance.l07.*' Open DocumentReport. Its readingSeconds checks the language, counts the words, works out the reading time and writes a DEBUG line through DebugLog, a tiny logging interface. Run the tests. Three pass (reading times, language check, DEBUG message) and one fails: the slow version settles at about 2,400 bytes per call, against a budget of 300. Optional but worth it: run ReportInvestigation -Pargs=slow and read the allocation by line. DocumentReport has the same three costs. Round 1: make the pattern a static final field, and format the DEBUG line only when log.isDebugEnabled(). Run the tests. The budget test still fails, now at about 750 bytes (820 on JDK 21). Its failure message lists every round it measured. Round 2: count the words without split, by walking the characters and counting where words start, as in lesson 3. Run the tests until all four pass. Keep the reading times, the bad language message and the exact DEBUG text: the other three tests guard them. Optional round 3: replace the regex with a check for exactly two letters from a to z. Pattern.compile(...) in a static final field stops the compile, but matcher() still creates a Matcher on every call. That's what's left after round 2: 56 bytes on JDK 25, 128 on JDK 21, both under the budget. The budget test measures 10 rounds of 100,000 calls and judges the best one, so a slow start while the JIT warms up won't fail it. For the words: keep a boolean inWord. A character that isn't a space, after a space or at the start, begins a new word. The texts have single spaces and at least one word, so this count equals split(" ").length. By the end you can take a complaint about slow calls from symptom to proof: read the tail and the GC count, find the allocating lines with JFR, confirm the callers with a flame graph, fix one thing at a time, and keep the result with JMH and an allocation budget test.

A pull request changes three things and reports "average latency down 40%". What should you ask for before approving? A bigger heap for the benchmark Nothing: 40% is a clear win The percentiles and GC numbers before and after, and the effect of each change on its own A flame graph of the test suite The average can improve while the tail stays bad, and with three changes at once nobody knows which one helped. Numbers per change, including the p99.9 or p99.99 and the GC count, are what make the claim checkable. jfr view allocation-by-site shows Formatter.parse and Long.toString on top. The fix made allocation worse The faster version made 3.5 times as many calls in the same 3 seconds, so collections per call fell, from about 21 to 6.5 per million GC counts are random The heap shrank A run of fixed length counts collections per second, and a faster program does more work in that time. What the fix changes is the garbage per call, so compare GCs per call, or use JMH's bytes per operation. h: A performance investigation, start to finish · Key terms
x: Percentile The time that a given share of calls beat: p99.99 is slower than all but one call in ten thousand. Tail latency The slowest calls, measured by high percentiles such as p99.9 and p99.99. GC pause A moment when the garbage collector stops the program's threads to clear dead objects away. Allocation sample weight How many bytes a JFR allocation sample stands for; adding them up gives allocation pressure. Hoisting Moving work that doesn't change, such as compiling a pattern, out of the path that runs on every call. Allocation budget A test that fails if a method allocates more than an agreed number of bytes per call. Which numbers show GC pauses hurting a few calls? The tail percentiles (p99.9, p99.99) together with the GC count and pause times, not the average. jfr view allocation-by-site shows JDK methods. How do you find your line? Walk each allocation sample's stack trace to the first frame in your own package and group by its method and line number, adding up weight. Why profile again after each fix? The order of costs changes. Smaller costs, such as the Matcher behind a hoisted Pattern, only rise to the top after the bigger ones are gone. When do you stop cutting an allocation hot spot? When what's left fits the agreed budget, or is the work the code exists to do. How do you measure allocation per call in a unit test? Warm up, then read com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() before and after N calls and divide by N. A fix makes the code faster, and the GC count in a 3-second run goes up. Is that bad? Not by itself: the faster code made more calls. Compare GCs per call, or bytes per operation.

h: A performance investigation, start to finish · Go deeper
x: The harness in this lesson measured latency without adding garbage of its own. Its histogram is a fixed array of counters (100 ns buckets up to 1 ms, then 100 µs buckets up to 1 s), filled in place. A latency recorder that allocated an object per call would add exactly the garbage you're trying to measure. HdrHistogram is the usual library for this in real services. Measuring still costs something. Lesson 6's CPU profile showed 64 of 3,569 samples in reading the clock, because the demo calls System.nanoTime() on every lap, and this harness calls it twice per call. On an operation of a few hundred nanoseconds, that's a real share. It's one more reason the final proof is a JMH benchmark rather than the load harness. Many logging libraries take a message pattern and its arguments separately, for example log.debug("document {} words={}", id, words) in SLF4J, a common logging library, and build the text only when the level is on. That removes the formatting, but the arguments are still computed, numbers are still boxed, and a call with many arguments still builds an array for them. In a hot path, the explicit if (log.isDebugEnabled()) guard is the version you can reason about. A profile will tell you if it matters. The cost of split grows with every word, while the scan's stays at zero. The documents here have 8 to 14 words. Lesson 3 counted 544 bytes per line of nine words, so a 2,000-word chapter split this way would make about 120 KB of short strings, just to be counted.

h: Reading thread dumps: stuck, blocked and hot threads · A thread dump is every stack, printed at one safepoint
x: Meet the patient. FrozenService is the report service on a bad day, stuck in five ways at once. A thread refreshes the catalog, the service's list of every document and the shelf it's on, while holding the catalog's lock. It asks the document store for the new list, and the store never answers. Four report workers need the same lock. There's also an idle pool, a busy loop, a second kind of lock, and 10,200 virtual threads. Run it, and it waits for you to look. A thread dump is a printout of every thread in the JVM at one moment. (A thread is one line of work inside a program.) For each one it shows the name, the state, the stack of method calls it's in, and the locks it holds or wants. jcmd <pid> Thread.print asks the JVM for one. jcmd is the JDK tool that sends commands to a running JVM, and <pid> is the process id the operating system gave it. The JVM stops every Java thread at a safepoint, a point where it knows the full state of each frame (lesson 6 showed why profilers need one). While the threads stand still, it walks each stack and prints it, and then they all run on. That pause is the photo's flash. With -Xlog:safepoint on JDK 25, the safepoint called PrintThreads took 36 to 74 ms for 28 threads on this busy 4-core machine. That's fine a few times on a live service. jstack <pid> prints the same dump. jcmd # lists Java processes and their PIDs jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l > dump-1.txt # every platform thread, plus the java.util.concurrent locks each one owns Take the dump before anyone restarts a frozen service, because a restart throws the evidence away. If jcmd can't attach (it must run as the same operating-system user as the JVM), kill -3 <pid> sends the signal SIGQUIT, and the JVM prints the same dump to its own standard output. Here's one thread from a real dump of the demo on JDK 25: "report-worker-3" #24 [25043] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=0.36ms elapsed=11.19s tid=0x00007ff4242e2bc0 nid=25043 waiting for monitor entry [0x00007ff40888d000] java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor) at workbench.performance.l08.FrozenServiceKt.writeReport(FrozenService.kt:54) - waiting to lock <0x0000000735c08070> (a java.lang.Object) at workbench.performance.l08.FrozenServiceKt.main$lambda$1$0(FrozenService.kt:32) at workbench.performance.l08.FrozenServiceKt$$Lambda/0x000000001e083000.run(Unknown Source) at java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor.runWorker(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/ThreadPoolExecutor.java:1090) at java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker.run(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/ThreadPoolExecutor.java:614) at java.lang.Thread.runWith(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/Thread.java:1487) at java.lang.Thread.run(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/Thread.java:1474) Read each thread in this order. The name. report-worker-3 says which pool and which job, which is why the executors track had you name your threads. Unnamed threads all look like pool-3-thread-7. The state line. BLOCKED (on object monitor) means it wants to enter a synchronized block that another thread is inside. A monitor is the lock behind synchronized. The frames, top first, down to the first line of your own code: FrozenService.kt:54. That's where it is now. The frames below say how it got there. The lock lines, which start with -. - locked <a> means it holds the monitor of object a. - waiting to lock <a> means it wants it. - parking to wait for <a> means a java.util.concurrent lock, condition or queue has parked it, put it to sleep until someone wakes it. - waiting on <a> means it's inside Object.wait() and has given a back. The number in <0x0000000735c08070> is the object's address in the heap at that moment. Inside one dump, the same address means the same object. Between dumps, a garbage collection, the JVM's clean-up of unused memory, may have moved the object. So don't match addresses across dumps. Take the dump before you restart. Read each thread by name, state, first frame of your code, then its lock lines. Check yourself: in one dump, four threads show - waiting to lock with the same address, and no thread shows - locked with it. What does that mean? (A thread holding it would show - locked. If none does, the lock was released a moment ago, and the next dump will tell.) The demo's busiest-looking threads say RUNNABLE. That word deserves a closer look. Take your first dump Run the demo. It prints its PID and stays frozen for 120 seconds (pass -Pargs=300 for longer). In a second terminal, run jcmd to confirm the PID, then jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l > dump-1.txt. h: Reading thread dumps: stuck, blocked and hot threads · RUNNABLE doesn't mean busy: compare cpu= between dumps
x: Both of these threads are RUNNABLE. One is burning a CPU core, and the other is asleep: "catalog-refresh" #21 [25040] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=25.09ms elapsed=11.41s tid=0x00007ff4242d8600 nid=25040 runnable [0x00007ff408b8d000] java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE at sun.nio.ch.SocketDispatcher.read0(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/Native Method) "index-rebuild" #28 [25047] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=4089.43ms elapsed=11.18s tid=0x00007ff4242e7ac0 nid=25047 runnable [0x00007ff40848c000] java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE at workbench.performance.l08.FrozenServiceKt.rebuildIndex(FrozenService.kt:61) The state is what the JVM knows, and the JVM can't see inside native code, code that runs outside Java in the operating system. When a thread calls a native method like read0, the JVM marks it "in native" and reports RUNNABLE, because that native code could be computing. Here the kernel, the core of the operating system, has the thread asleep until bytes arrive from the network. That's the cook at the back door: standing at his post, doing nothing. RUNNABLE means "not waiting for a Java lock", not "using the CPU". The cpu= field tells them apart. It's the CPU time the operating system has charged to that thread since it started, the cook's step counter. One value means little. The change between two dumps says what the thread did in between. In the second dump, 5.6 seconds later, catalog-refresh still shows cpu=25.09ms: it used nothing. index-rebuild went from 4,089.43 ms to 6,288.02 ms while elapsed went from 11.18 s to 16.82 s. That's 2.2 seconds of CPU in 5.6 seconds, about 39% of one core. On a quiet machine it would be close to 100%. This one was shared with more than 30 busy programs. On Linux, top -H -p <pid> shows the same thing per thread, live: PID USER PR NI VIRT RES SHR S %CPU %MEM TIME+ COMMAND 25047 root 20 0 7219012 186784 23404 R 80.0 1.1 0:12.57 index-rebuild 25014 root 20 0 7219012 186784 23404 S 0.0 1.1 0:00.00 java The PID column of top -H is the Linux thread id. It's the same number as nid= and the number in brackets in the dump, so you can search the dump for nid=25047. Since JDK 18 the dump prints nid in decimal (change JDK-8268425). JDK 17 and older print it in hex, nid=0x61d7, so convert first with printf '%x\n' 25047. The JVM also gives each operating-system thread its Java name, cut to 15 characters, so top often shows the name straight away. Inside a container you may not have top. Two dumps and cpu= work everywhere. Check yourself: a thread shows the same stack in two dumps 5 seconds apart, and its cpu= grew by 4,900 ms. Is it stuck? (No. It's hot: a loop that never leaves that frame.) catalog-refresh isn't stuck in the usual sense, then. It's waiting, and it's holding something while it waits. Find the hot thread two ways With the demo still running, take a second dump about 5 seconds after the first: jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l > dump-2.txt. Predict: which of catalog-refresh and index-rebuild will show more CPU in the second dump? Run the two grep lines below and work out how much CPU each thread used between the dumps. In top -H, the top line is index-rebuild, and its PID equals its nid= in the dump. ThreadMXBean: per-thread CPU time from inside the JVM docs

h: Reading thread dumps: stuck, blocked and hot threads · Follow the lock to the thread that holds everyone up
x: Four report-worker threads waiting to lock <0x0000000735c08070> are a queue at one door. The question is who's inside. Search the same dump for that address with - locked: "catalog-refresh" #21 [25040] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=25.09ms elapsed=11.41s tid=0x00007ff4242d8600 nid=25040 runnable [0x00007ff408b8d000] java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE at sun.nio.ch.SocketDispatcher.read0(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/Native Method) ... at java.net.Socket$SocketInputStream.read(java.base@25.0.5.0.3/Socket.java:958) at workbench.performance.l08.FrozenServiceKt.main$lambda$0(FrozenService.kt:26) - locked <0x0000000735c08070> (a java.lang.Object) The - locked line sits under the frame that entered synchronized. So catalog-refresh took the catalog lock in its own code, then called the document store, and is waiting for an answer with the lock still held. Every report that needs the catalog now waits for the store. That's the cook at the back door with the order book under his arm. The fix isn't in the four blocked threads. Make the slow call outside the lock, give the socket a read timeout, and take the lock only to swap in the result. A ReentrantLock, the JDK's other kind of lock, shows up differently. The waiter says - parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync), but its owner prints no - locked line, because a ReentrantLock isn't tied to a stack frame. That's what -l is for: it ends each thread with the java.util.concurrent locks it owns. "archive-writer" #29 [25048] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=0.19ms elapsed=11.18s ... waiting on condition java.lang.Thread.State: TIMED_WAITING (sleeping) ... Locked ownable synchronizers: - <0x0000000735c10a88> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync) Without -l, you can see that archive-reader waits, but not for whom. catalog-refresh lists one too: the socket's own read lock inside NioSocketImpl. A thread can hold several locks. Keep following. The owner may itself wait for another lock, and so on. If the chain comes back to a thread you already passed, it's a deadlock, two cooks each holding the pan the other needs. The JVM checks for that while it prints, and adds Found one Java-level deadlock at the end of the dump, with both threads. Not every parked thread is stuck. An idle pool thread, such as export-worker-1, shows - parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.AbstractQueuedSynchronizer$ConditionObject) under LinkedBlockingQueue.take and ThreadPoolExecutor.getTask. A condition has no owner, so the chain ends there. It's a worker waiting for a task, leaning on the wall, and none of your code is in its stack. Follow every wait to its owner, and fix the owner. The queue is only the symptom. Check yourself: 30 threads are parked inside your connection pool's getConnection, and no thread holds a lock they want. What doesn't the dump show you? (Who holds the 20 connections. Look for the threads whose stacks show they're using one, for example inside a database call.) A photo shows where everyone stands. It can't show who's moving. Find archive-reader, copy the address on its parking to wait for line, and search plain.txt for that address. Can you find the owner? Now search dump-1.txt (taken with -l) for the same address. Run the awk line below on dump-1.txt, with the address the report-worker threads wait for. It prints the name of the thread that holds it. terminal 2 jcmd <pid> Thread.print > plain.txt grep -n 'ReentrantLock' plain.txt dump-1.txt # who holds a monitor? print the thread whose stack has "- locked <address>" awk '/^"/ { name = $1 } /- locked <0x0000000735c08070>/ { print name }' dump-1.txt In plain.txt the address appears only under archive-reader: nothing says who owns it. In dump-1.txt it also appears under archive-writer's Locked ownable synchronizers. The awk line prints "catalog-refresh". Use the address from your own dump; it changes on every run. Four BLOCKED workers, one lock, one owner. The owner is RUNNABLE but uses no CPU: it's waiting on a socket with the lock held. JEP 444: Virtual Threads (the new thread dump format) read

Take three, a few seconds apart, and compare each thread across them: for i in 1 2 3; do jcmd $PID Thread.print -l > dump-$i.txt; sleep 5; done Same frames in every dump? CPU grew? Your code in the stack? What it is yes no yes Stuck: waiting for a lock, a socket or a queue. Follow its lock line. yes yes yes Hot: a loop that never leaves that frame no either yes Working: it moves through the code yes no no Idle: a pool or JVM thread waiting for work This lesson's lab turns that table into code. One caution about hot threads. The dump stops threads at safepoints, so a hot thread's top frame is where it reached the next safepoint poll, not always the line that costs the most. That's the safepoint bias from lesson 6. In index-rebuild the whole loop is one line, so the dump is right. In a big method, confirm with async-profiler. Now the virtual threads, the JDK's lightweight threads that run on a few ordinary ones. The demo started 10,000 virtual threads that wait for a permit and 200 that sleep. Thread.print shows none of them, only the four idle carrier threads, ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1 to -4, that would run them. In the kitchen, the photo shows the cooks and not the order tickets pinned on the rail. Virtual threads need the newer dump format that came with them (JEP 444): jcmd $PID Thread.dump_to_file /tmp/threads.txt # plain text, includes virtual threads jcmd $PID Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/threads.json # the same, for tools On JDK 25 each virtual thread looks like this. h: Reading thread dumps: stuck, blocked and hot threads · Java and Kotlin
x: The cpu= column from inside the process, with ThreadMXBean HotThreadsJava.java package workbench.performance.l08; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.lang.management.ThreadInfo; import java.lang.management.ThreadMXBean; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; // The "cpu=" column of a thread dump, read from inside the process: which platform threads used CPU in the last interval? public class HotThreadsJava { record Hot(String name, long cpuNanos) { } static List<Hot> hottest(long millis, int n) throws InterruptedException { ThreadMXBean mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); Map<Long, Long> before = new HashMap<>(); for (long id : mx.getAllThreadIds()) before.put(id, mx.getThreadCpuTime(id)); // platform threads only Thread.sleep(millis); List<Hot> hot = new ArrayList<>(); for (long id : mx.getAllThreadIds()) { Long then = before.get(id); long now = mx.getThreadCpuTime(id); // -1 once a thread has died ThreadInfo info = mx.getThreadInfo(id); if (then != null && info != null && now > then) hot.add(new Hot(info.getThreadName(), now - then)); } hot.sort(Comparator.comparingLong(Hot::cpuNanos).reversed()); return hot.subList(0, Math.min(n, hot.size())); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread spinner = Thread.ofPlatform().daemon().name("index-rebuild").start(() -> { long x = 1; while (true) x = x * 31 + 7; }); for (Hot h : hottest(500, 3)) System.out.printf("%-20s %6.1f ms%n", h.name(), h.cpuNanos() / 1e6); } } HotThreads.kt package workbench.performance.l08 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory // The "cpu=" column of a thread dump, read from inside the process: which platform threads used CPU in the last interval? data class Hot(val name: String, val cpuNanos: Long) fun hottest(millis: Long, n: Int): List<Hot> { val mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() val before = mx.allThreadIds.associateWith { mx.getThreadCpuTime(it) } // platform threads only Thread.sleep(millis) return mx.allThreadIds.toList().mapNotNull { id -> val then = before[id] ?: return@mapNotNull null val now = mx.getThreadCpuTime(id) // -1 once a thread has died val name = mx.getThreadInfo(id)?.threadName ?: return@mapNotNull null if (now > then) Hot(name, now - then) else null }.sortedByDescending { it.cpuNanos }.take(n) } fun main() { Thread.ofPlatform().daemon().name("index-rebuild").start { var x = 1L while (true) x = x * 31 + 7 } for (h in hottest(500, 3)) println("%-20s %6.1f ms".format(h.name, h.cpuNanos / 1e6)) } Both read the same JVM counters that a dump prints as cpu=: sample every thread's CPU time, wait, sample again, and sort by the difference. That's a cheap health check that answers "which thread is hot" without top. The behavior is the same. Kotlin's associateWith and mapNotNull replace the two loops, and since LongArray has no mapNotNull, the Kotlin version calls toList() first. One limit applies to both, checked on JDK 21 and 25: getAllThreadIds() lists only platform threads, and getThreadCpuTime returns -1 for a virtual thread. For virtual threads, look at the carrier threads' CPU, or use a profiler.

x: Three dumps of a frozen service, read in five minutes Capture the evidence before anyone restarts anything: three dumps, 5 seconds apart, each in its own file. PID=$(pgrep -f FrozenService | head -1) for i in 1 2 3; do jcmd $PID Thread.print -l > dump-$i.txt; sleep 5; done Count the states to see the shape. Four BLOCKED threads in a service that should never wait long for a monitor is the first lead. The 12 RUNNABLE ones include JVM threads and threads in native calls, so they prove nothing yet. grep -h 'java.lang.Thread.State' dump-1.txt | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn # 12 java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE # 6 java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking) # 4 java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor) # 3 java.lang.Thread.State: TIMED_WAITING (parking) # ... Ask what the BLOCKED threads want. One address four times means one door and one queue. grep -h 'waiting to lock' dump-1.txt | sort | uniq -c # 4 - waiting to lock <0x0000000735c08070> (a java.lang.Object) Find who holds it, then check whether the owner is working or waiting. Its stack ends in a socket read, and its CPU time is the same in all three dumps: it's waiting for the network with the lock held. awk '/^"/ { name = $1 } /- locked <0x0000000735c08070>/ { print name }' dump-1.txt # "catalog-refresh" grep -h '^"catalog-refresh"' dump-*.txt | grep -o 'cpu=[0-9.]*ms' # cpu=25.09ms # cpu=25.09ms # cpu=25.09ms Fix the owner, not the queue. Make the slow call with a deadline and no lock held, then take the lock only to swap in the result. Now a slow store delays one refresh, not every report. CatalogData fresh = store.fetchCatalog(Duration.ofSeconds(2)); // 1. slow call: no lock held, with a deadline synchronized (catalog) { // 2. lock only to swap the data catalog.replace(fresh); } val fresh = store.fetchCatalog(Duration.ofSeconds(2)) // 1. slow call: no lock held, with a deadline synchronized(catalog) { // 2. lock only to swap the data catalog.replace(fresh) }

h: Reading thread dumps: stuck, blocked and hot threads · Quiz
x: A dump shows 30 threads WAITING (parking) with - parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync), all the same address. No thread's stack shows - locked with that address. What do you do next? Conclude the lock is free and the dump caught a hand-over Take the dump again with -l and look for the address under some thread's Locked ownable synchronizers Restart the service, since parked threads can't be diagnosed Look for Found one Java-level deadlock, because parked threads always mean a deadlock A ReentrantLock isn't tied to a stack frame, so its owner never prints - locked. With -l, each thread lists the java.util.concurrent locks it owns, and that's where the owner shows up. A free lock wouldn't keep 30 threads parked, and parked threads are often queued behind a slow owner, not deadlocked. top -H -p 4100 on a JDK 25 service shows thread PID 4187 at 100% CPU. How do you find it in the dump? Convert 4187 to hex and search for nid=0x105b Search for #4187, the Java thread number Search for nid=4187 or [4187] in the header lines You can't: top's thread ids aren't in thread dumps The top -H PID is the Linux thread id, which the dump prints as nid= and in brackets. Since JDK 18 it's printed in decimal, so search for it as it is. Converting to hex was needed on JDK 17 and older. #N is the Java thread id, a different number. Three dumps 5 seconds apart. Thread export-worker-2 is in LinkedBlockingQueue.take under ThreadPoolExecutor.getTask in all three, with the same CPU time, and no frame from your code. What is it? Stuck: same frames and flat CPU in every dump Hot: it never leaves that frame Deadlocked with the thread that should put work on the queue Idle: a pool worker waiting for a task, which is normal Same frames and flat CPU fit both stuck and idle. What decides it is whose code is waiting. With no frame of yours, it's the pool's own loop waiting for the next task. It parks on a condition object, which has no owner, so there's nobody to follow. Stuck threads have your code in the stack, waiting for something your code asked for. Your service runs 8,000 requests on virtual threads. jcmd <pid> Thread.print shows about 40 threads and none of your request code. Why? Thread.print lists platform threads only. Use jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file, which includes virtual threads The requests already finished Virtual threads have no stacks until they run You need -l to see virtual threads The classic dump lists platform threads, so you see the carrier threads but not the virtual threads on them. JEP 444 added Thread.dump_to_file (plain or JSON), which includes virtual threads, running or parked. -l only adds lock ownership to the classic dump. A hot thread's dump shows its top frame at the end of a short loop in buildSummary, but async-profiler puts most of its CPU in String.split, which buildSummary calls inside that loop. Which is right, and why? The dump: it's taken from the real thread, so its top frame is exact Neither: both tools sample at random async-profiler: a thread dump stops threads at safepoint polls, such as the jump back in a loop, so it reports where the thread reached the next poll The dump, because async-profiler can't see inlined methods A thread dump is taken at a safepoint, so it has the safepoint bias from lesson 6: a hot thread is caught at its next poll, often a loop's jump back or a method return, not at the instruction that costs the most. async-profiler interrupts the thread wherever it is, and it does show inlined frames. h: Reading thread dumps: stuck, blocked and hot threads · Key terms
x: thread dump A printout of every thread's name, state, stack and locks at one moment. safepoint A point where the JVM knows the full state of every frame, so it can stop a thread there and read its stack. nid The operating system's thread id in a dump header. It's the PID column of top -H. monitor The lock that synchronized takes on an object. A dump shows it as - locked <address>. ownable synchronizer A java.util.concurrent lock, such as ReentrantLock, that a thread owns. Thread.print -l lists them per thread. carrier thread A platform thread that runs virtual threads. A classic dump shows the carriers but not the virtual threads. A thread is RUNNABLE in SocketDispatcher.read0 and its cpu= doesn't change between dumps. What is it doing? Waiting for bytes from the network. The JVM reports threads in native code as RUNNABLE; the operating system has it asleep. How do you tell a hot thread from a stuck one, with only thread dumps? Take two dumps a few seconds apart and compare cpu=. Same frames and rising CPU is hot; same frames and flat CPU is stuck. top -H shows thread 25047 busy. Where is it in a JDK 18+ dump? Search for nid=25047. Since JDK 18 the nid is decimal; JDK 17 and older print it in hex. Which jcmd option shows who owns a ReentrantLock? Thread.print -l. It lists each thread's Locked ownable synchronizers. Without it, only the waiters show. What does - waiting on <a> mean, compared with - waiting to lock <a>? waiting on: inside Object.wait(), with the monitor given back. waiting to lock: BLOCKED, trying to enter synchronized on a. Your virtual threads don't appear in jcmd <pid> Thread.print. What do you run instead? jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file <file> (add -format=json for tools). Then group the threads by their first frame of your code. Why can't you match a lock address like <0x0000000735c08070> across two dumps? It's the object's heap address at that moment, and a GC can move the object between dumps. It's reliable only within one dump.

h: Reading thread dumps: stuck, blocked and hot threads · Go deeper
x: The JSON format is what you'd feed a tool. On JDK 25 each thread has tid, name, state, stack, and lock fields: parkBlocker with the parked-on object and its owner thread id, blockedOn for a monitor a thread wants, waitingOn, and monitorsOwned. On JDK 21 a thread has only tid, name and stack. The JSON also groups threads by thread container: <root>, each thread pool, and each executor made by Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). In this lesson's demo, <root> holds 10,212 threads, because the demo starts its virtual threads with Thread.ofVirtual() directly, and each ThreadPoolExecutor holds its own workers. With virtual threads, that grouping often says more than the stacks do. The JSON also names owners: in the demo's file, archive-reader's parkBlocker gives its owner as thread 29, archive-writer, with no -l needed. jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/threads.json jq '.threadDump.threadContainers[] | {container, threadCount}' /tmp/threads.json Thread.print -e adds allocated= and defined_classes= to each header. That's another cheap way, besides JFR, to find the thread that allocates the most. If the JVM is so stuck that it can't reach a safepoint, jcmd and kill -3 both hang, because both need one. The last resort is jhsdb jstack --pid <pid>. It reads the process from outside, like a debugger, so it needs permission to attach to the process (ptrace on Linux) and pauses the whole JVM while it reads. Use it only when the normal dump won't come. In code, ThreadMXBean.dumpAllThreads(true, true) returns the same information as Thread.print -l as ThreadInfo objects, and findDeadlockedThreads() runs the deadlock check. Both cover platform threads only. A health check that runs findDeadlockedThreads() every minute costs a safepoint each time. On this busy machine one Thread.print safepoint took 36 to 74 ms, so measure before you add one to a service where every millisecond counts.

h: Startup and footprint
x: Why the JVM starts slowly, class data sharing, Project Leyden's AOT cache, GraalVM native image and CRaC. By the end of this track you can say where a JVM's start-up time and memory go, and measure both the way your users and a memory limit see them: time to first request from outside the process, and RSS from the operating system. You can build and check a class data sharing archive on JDK 21 and a Project Leyden AOT cache on JDK 25, and you know the traps that quietly make them useless or, on JDK 25 builds before 25.0.4, run stale code. You can explain what GraalVM native image's closed world costs, write its reachability metadata, and spot static initializers that break when the build runs them. You can write CRaC checkpoint hooks in the right order, and choose between doing nothing, AppCDS, the AOT cache, native image and CRaC for a given service. One picture runs through the whole track, a corner shop that has to open every morning, and so does one program, a small parcel-tracking service. You need no background in any of this: lesson 1 starts from what happens between typing java and the first line of main. Install JDK 25, at least 25.0.4, because earlier JDK 25 builds can run old classes from an AOT cache after the JAR changes. The Leyden flags need JDK 24 or 25 and say so wherever they appear. Native image needs GraalVM or Mandrel, and CRaC needs a CRaC-enabled vendor JDK, such as Azul's Zulu CRaC builds on Linux. Those steps are marked optional, and everything else runs on a plain JDK. The labs live in labs/startup, one package per lesson (workbench.startup.l01 to l04). Lessons 1 and 3 are in Java, lessons 2 and 4 in Kotlin, and every sample and demo comes in both languages. Start-up numbers are noisy, so no test measures time or counts all loaded classes. The tests load your classes in fresh class loaders and compare exact sets of class names, check JSON metadata against the GraalVM schema and against what the code really does, and drive a simulated checkpoint. Many demos start a second JVM with the flags you pass in -Pargs, because start-up has to be measured on a fresh process, and Gradle runs them on the JDK that runs Gradle. A few Try-its run java directly on a JDK 25 against startup/build/classes/java/demo. Run ./gradlew :startup:test --tests 'workbench.startup.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, and ./gradlew :startup:solutionTest to run the same tests on the reference answers. Start-up repeats the same work on every launch: create the VM, load, parse and verify each class on first need (818 for a one-class demo on JDK 25, about 1,500 for a 300-class app), run static initializers, interpret until the JIT has profiles, and run any framework's start-up. Measure what users see: time to first request from outside, and RSS from ps or /proc. Create VM, the program's own started in, NMT's committed memory and docker stats each miss part of it. <clinit> runs on first active use. The holder idiom (a nested class, or a Kotlin nested object) keeps expensive static work off the start-up path; a Kotlin companion object does not. CDS maps ready-made classes from an archive: the default one for the JDK's classes, AppCDS for yours. It saves loading and verification, not initialization or JIT warm-up. The AOT cache (final in JDK 24, one step on JDK 25) adds linked classes, resolved lambdas and profiles from a training run. Require JDK 25.0.4+, rebuild it with every JAR, check it in your build, and run production in the default mode. A training run, an AOT cache and the native-image tracing agent all see only the code paths you exercise, so drive them with production-like traffic. Native image starts in milliseconds and uses less memory, but has no JIT (lower peak), needs metadata for reflection and proxies, needs GraalVM or Mandrel to build, and runs static initializers at build time in Quarkus. CRaC restores a warm process from an image, on a CRaC-enabled vendor JDK. Close sockets and files before the checkpoint, reopen them after, mind the hook order and the weak references, and recreate per-copy state. Default to the JVM with an AOT cache or AppCDS; choose native or CRaC only when start-up or memory per copy is the real limit and you accept their costs.

A companion object's properties are static fields of the outer class, and they are built with it.
