Quarkus initializes all classes at build time. Fix one with quarkus.native.additional-build-args=--initialize-at-run-time=a.B\\,c.D. Quarkus: @RegisterForReflection (targets for a library's classes, ignoreNested, serialization), @RegisterForProxy(targets = ...) in order, quarkus.native.resources.includes. CRaC java -XX:CRaCCheckpointTo=cr -jar tracker.jar # start, then warm it up jcmd tracker.jar JDK.checkpoint # read the app's console: jcmd always says success java -XX:CRaCRestoreFrom=cr # restore, already warm Hooks: org.crac.Resource (beforeCheckpoint, afterRestore), Core.getGlobalContext().register(r) in org.crac 1.5.0. Keep r in a field: the context holds weak references. Order: checkpoint in reverse registration order, restore in registration order. Everyone is told even if one throws; failures arrive as suppressed exceptions on a CheckpointException. Open files and sockets fail the checkpoint (policy error). Socket reopen isn't implemented. Recreate per-copy ids and tokens after the restore. Builds: Azul Zulu 17, 21 and 25 Linux -crac- builds; BellSoft Liberica 17 and 21 CRaC builds. Not in mainline OpenJDK. AWS Lambda SnapStart uses the same hooks. Choosing Constraint Pick Picture it Long-running, rarely restarted, nobody waits on start-up nothing unpack every morning, it's fine JDK 21, no code changes dynamic AppCDS built with the program shelves kept in the back room JDK 25.0.4+, no code changes, full peak throughput AOT cache trained by integration tests the shelves plus the notebook Milliseconds to start, or memory per copy, is the limit native image (about 59% lower peak in Quarkus's benchmark) the pop-up stall Must start fast and warm, runtime under your control CRaC or Lambda SnapStart, with hooks the photo of the busy shop

h: Startup and footprint: track quiz
x: A new copy of your service logs started in 0.9s, but the load balancer only sends it traffic 2.4 s after the process was launched. Which number should you work on, and how do you measure it? The 0.9 s from the log, because it is the service's start-up The Create VM time from -Xlog:startuptime Time from launch to the first 200 from the health check, measured from outside The time until C2 has compiled the hot methods Only the outside clock includes everything the load balancer waits for: the launcher, VM creation, class loading, the program's own start-up and the first request. The service's log line starts late and stops early, and Create VM stops before your code runs. In Kotlin, class DeliveryCalendar { companion object { val holidays = loadHolidays(); fun source() = "national" } }. A health check calls DeliveryCalendar.source(). Is loadHolidays() called? No, companion objects are lazy Yes: holidays is a static field of DeliveryCalendar, filled when the class is initialized, which this first call triggers Only on the first access to holidays Only if holidays is declared const Kotlin compiles companion properties to static fields of the outer class and fills them in its <clinit>. Use a private nested object holding holidays, or by lazy, to build them only when needed. NMT reports 296 MB committed, 216 MB of it heap, while VmRSS is 60 MB. What explains the gap? NMT counts the heap twice The JVM leaked native memory RSS doesn't include the Java heap Committed memory has been requested from the operating system, but most of it, such as a fresh heap, has never been touched, so it isn't resident Pages become resident only when something touches them. A memory limit counts resident memory, so RSS is the footprint; NMT tells you which part of the JVM asked for what. On JDK 25, java -Xshare:off -version loads 411 classes and none comes from an archive; without the flag, 396 load and 393 are shared. Why does start-up get slower with sharing off? Each class now has to be found, parsed and verified by the JVM instead of being mapped ready-made from classes.jsa The JIT is turned off along with sharing The heap is smaller The JVM runs every static initializer twice The default CDS archive holds the JVM's internal form of about 1,300 JDK classes. Without it every class goes the full way, and the JVM also generates on the spot some classes the archive would have supplied, hence 411 instead of 396. A build rebuilt tracker.jar with a fix and reused last week's app.aot. The server runs JDK 25.0.2. What do you expect? A warning, then the fixed code without the cache The JVM refuses to start Possibly last week's classes, served from the cache with no error (JDK-8377932) The fixed code, with the full speed-up JDK 25.0.0 to 25.0.3 (and 26.0.0 to 26.0.1) didn't check the application's JARs against the cache. 25.0.4 and later warn and run without the cache. Pin 25.0.4 or later, and rebuild the cache with every JAR. Someone adds -XX:AOTCache=/srv/app.aot to every server's JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, but the file isn't there. What happens to start-up? Nothing changes: the JVM ignores the flag It gets slower than with no flag: the JVM runs with no archive at all, not even the default CDS archive The JVM refuses to start The JVM writes the cache when it exits In the default auto mode the JVM prints an error and carries on, but with zero archived classes; in this track's run, a one-class program went from 542 shared classes to 0. Only -XX:AOTMode=on or required makes it stop, and only -XX:AOTCacheOutput writes a cache. Which entry correctly registers a JDK dynamic proxy over tracker.DepotClient and java.io.Closeable in schema v1.2.0? {"proxy": [["tracker.DepotClient", "java.io.Closeable"]]} at the top level {"reflection": [{"type": "tracker.DepotClient", "allPublicMethods": true}]} A proxy-config.json next to the file {"reflection": [{"type": {"proxy": ["tracker.DepotClient", "java.io.Closeable"]}}]} In v1.2.0 a proxy is a reflection entry whose type is an object with an ordered proxy list. The top level allows only reflection, resources, foreign and comment, and Quarkus 4.0 doesn't support the legacy separate files. Registering the interface itself doesn't define the proxy class. A Quarkus native service has static final String NODE_ID = UUID.randomUUID().toString().substring(0, 8); in an ordinary class, used to start every event id it writes. Assuming the build succeeds, what do copies started from the same binary see? The same NODE_ID in every copy, computed once during the build A different NODE_ID in each copy null A different value on every read Quarkus initializes all classes at build time by default, so the initializer runs once in the build and its result is stored in the image heap. Per-copy values belong in code that runs at start-up, or in a class marked --initialize-at-run-time. A service registers its database pool first and its scan listener second with the CRaC global context. The listener forgets to close its queue connection. What happens on jcmd tracker.jar JDK.checkpoint? jcmd reports an error and the JVM exits The checkpoint fails under the default error policy; the restore hooks run in registration order, and the app's console, not jcmd, shows the error The image is written, and the connection is reopened after the restore Only the listener's hooks run Open sockets fail the checkpoint by default. The context still tells everyone (listener, then pool, before; pool, then listener, after), collects the problems in a CheckpointException, and the process keeps running. jcmd prints success either way. A company runs 120 small, lightly loaded services on each machine, and memory per copy is what limits how many fit. Slower builds are acceptable. Which option fits best? The JVM with no changes An AOT cache on JDK 25 A native image for each service CRaC for each service Density is native image's strongest case: in Quarkus's benchmark, 95 MiB of RSS against 304 MiB on the JVM and 240 MiB with the AOT cache. Its lower peak throughput matters little for lightly loaded services. CRaC restores a full warm JVM, so it doesn't cut memory.

h: Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it · Start-up is work the JVM repeats on every launch
x: Every launch repeats the same work: create the VM, load, parse and verify about 1,500 classes, interpret until the JIT has profiles, then the framework's own start-up Let's count the boxes first. ClassSourcesDemo, in the Try it below, has exactly one class of its own. It starts a second JVM, has it read three lines of settings, format a date and join a few strings, then counts the classes that JVM loaded. On JDK 25.0.5 it printed this: JDK 25.0.5.0.3+1-1-24.04.1-Ubuntu, flags []: 818 classes loaded 1 file: (your classes and JARs) 19 jrt:/ (the JDK's modules file, parsed now) 5 other (hidden classes: lambdas, method handles) 793 shared objects file (the CDS archive) One class was ours. The other 817 belong to the JDK and to the machinery that runs Java. A bigger program tells the same story: a generated app with 300 classes of its own loaded 1,537 classes on JDK 21 with the JDK's archive turned off. Its own classes were a fifth of the total. Here's the morning routine, step by step. When you type java, a small native program called the launcher starts first. (Native means compiled for your machine, as C programs are, rather than for the JVM.) The launcher loads the JVM and asks it to create a VM, which is the shopkeeper unlocking the door and switching on the lights. The JVM reserves memory for the heap, the area where your objects will live. It generates its interpreter, starts its own helper threads, and sets up the core java.lang classes and the module system. Only then does it look for your main class. From there, each class goes through the same steps the first time something needs it. The JVM finds the class file and parses it into its own internal form, in metaspace, memory the JVM keeps for class data outside the heap. That's unpacking a box. Then it verifies the bytecode, the instructions javac and kotlinc write into class files: it checks that every instruction is type-safe before any of them runs. That's the delivery note, checked item by item. Later it runs the class's static initializer, which the next section is about. Your code then runs in the interpreter, which executes bytecode one instruction at a time, like a shopkeeper looking up every price in the catalogue. The JIT compilers turn hot methods, the ones that run often, into machine code while the program runs. First, though, they wait for profiles: counts of which methods, branches and types the code really uses. That's the shopkeeper learning the popular items by heart, and it takes a while. A framework, a library that starts and wires your program for you, adds work of its own. It scans classes for annotations, creates objects by reflection (code that finds classes and calls them by name) and reads configuration. Nothing of this survives the process. Stop the JVM, and the next launch unpacks, checks and learns it all again, with exactly the same care. There's one exception, and it's in the output above. A JDK build ships an archive of about 1,300 of its own classes, already parsed, and the JVM maps them from disk instead of unpacking them. Those are the 793 shared objects file lines. Lesson 2 of this track is about that archive and the bigger ones you can build. You can watch the unpacking yourself. -Xlog:class+load prints one line per class, and the end of each line says where the class came from. Four real lines from a run of the same work, with the folder shortened: [0.063s][info][class,load] java.lang.Object source: shared objects file [0.078s][info][class,load] sun.util.PreHashedMap source: jrt:/java.base [0.124s][info][class,load] workbench.startup.l01.demo.ClassSourcesDemo source: file:.../classes/java/demo/ [0.171s][info][class,load] workbench.startup.l01.demo.ClassSourcesDemo$$Lambda/0x000000006f040210 source: workbench.startup.l01.demo.ClassSourcesDemo shared objects file means the class came ready-made from the archive. jrt:/ means the JVM read it from the JDK's modules file, where the JDK keeps its classes, and parsed it on the spot. file: is your own class path, the list of folders and JAR files (zip files of classes) where the JVM looks for your code. A class name as the source marks a hidden class, a class the JVM generates in memory while the program runs, with no class file behind it. Each lambda gets one. Here the shop picture breaks, and the break matters. Our shopkeeper unpacks everything before she opens. The JVM doesn't: it unpacks a box only when someone first asks for something inside it. Check yourself before the Try it: a hidden class has no class file. Why can its source never start with file:? (Because file: names the place its bytes were read from, and a hidden class's bytes were made in memory.) So the JVM unpacks lazily. The next question is when it runs the static code inside a class, and that decides how much of your own work lands on the start-up path. Count where your classes come from Read ClassSourcesDemo. It starts a second JVM with -Xlog:class+load, runs a little start-up work there (settings, a regular expression, a date, a stream), and groups the log lines by source:. Predict: out of roughly 800 classes, how many come from the JDK's archive? Then run it from labs/ with the command below. Run it again with -Pargs=-Xshare:off added. That turns the archive off in the second JVM. Predict the jrt:/ line first. Run the Kotlin twin (ClassSourcesDemoKt) once, and look at the file: line. ClassSourcesDemo.java package workbench.startup.l01.demo; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.time.LocalDate; import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.regex.Pattern; import java.util.stream.Collectors; /** * Starts a second JVM with -Xlog:class+load, runs a little start-up work in it, and counts * where each loaded class came from. Extra arguments are passed to that JVM as flags. */ public class ClassSourcesDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("--work")) { work(); return; } List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(); cmd.add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()); cmd.addAll(List.of(args)); // e.g. -Xshare:off cmd.addAll(List.of("-Xlog:class+load", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), ClassSourcesDemo.class.getName(), "--work")); Process child = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); Map<String, Integer> bySource = new TreeMap<>(); try (var lines = child.inputReader().lines()) { lines.filter(l -> l.contains(" source: ")) .forEach(l -> bySource.merge(bucket(l), 1, Integer::sum)); } child.waitFor(); int total = bySource.values().stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum(); System.out.printf("JDK %s, flags %s: %,d classes loaded%n", Runtime.version(), List.of(args), total); bySource.forEach((source, n) -> System.out.printf("%7d %s%n", n, source)); } /** Groups the "source:" field of a class+load line into a few buckets. */ static String bucket(String line) { String source = line.substring(line.indexOf(" source: ") + 9); if (source.equals("shared objects file")) return "shared objects file (the CDS archive)"; if (source.startsWith("jrt:/")) return "jrt:/ (the JDK's modules file, parsed now)"; if (source.startsWith("file:")) return "file: (your classes and JARs)"; return "other (hidden classes: lambdas, method handles)"; } /** A small taste of what services do at start-up: config, regex, dates, streams, lambdas. */ static void work() { Map<String, String> config = new TreeMap<>(); Pattern line = Pattern.compile("(\\w+(?:\\.\\w+)*)\\s*=\\s*(.*)"); for (String l : List.of("depot.url = https://depot.example", "pool.size = 20", "timeout.ms = 120")) { var m = line.matcher(l); if (m.matches()) config.put(m.group(1), m.group(2)); } String today = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 15).format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE); String summary = config.entrySet().stream() .map(e -> String.format("%s=%s", e.getKey(), e.getValue())) .collect(Collectors.joining(", ")); if (summary.isEmpty() || today.isEmpty()) throw new AssertionError(); } } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l01.demo.ClassSourcesDemo labs/startup/src/demo/java/workbench/startup/l01/demo/ClassSourcesDemo.java ClassSourcesDemo.kt package workbench.startup.l01.demo import java.nio.file.Path import java.time.LocalDate import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter import java.util.TreeMap /** * Starts a second JVM with -Xlog:class+load, runs a little start-up work in it, and counts * where each loaded class came from. Extra arguments are passed to that JVM as flags. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "--work") { work() return } val cmd = buildList { add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()) addAll(args) // e.g. -Xshare:off addAll(listOf("-Xlog:class+load", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.startup.l01.demo.ClassSourcesDemoKt", "--work")) } val child = ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start() val bySource = TreeMap<String, Int>() child.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filter { " source: " in it }.forEach { bySource.merge(bucket(it), 1, Int::plus) } } child.waitFor() println("JDK ${Runtime.version()}, flags ${args.toList()}: %,d classes loaded".format(bySource.values.sum())) bySource.forEach { (source, n) -> println("%7d %s".format(n, source)) } } /** Groups the "source:" field of a class+load line into a few buckets. */ private fun bucket(line: String): String { val source = line.substringAfter(" source: ") return when { source == "shared objects file" -> "shared objects file (the CDS archive)" source.startsWith("jrt:/") -> "jrt:/ (the JDK's modules file, parsed now)" source.startsWith("file:") -> "file: (your classes and JARs, kotlin-stdlib too)" else -> "other (hidden classes: lambdas, method handles)" } } /** A small taste of what services do at start-up: config, regex, dates, collections, lambdas. */ private fun work() { val line = Regex("""(\w+(?:\.\w+)*)\s*=\s*(.*)""") val config = listOf("depot.url = https://depot.example", "pool.size = 20", "timeout.ms = 120") .mapNotNull { line.matchEntire(it)?.destructured } .associate { (key, value) -> key to value } .toSortedMap() val today = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 15).format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE) val summary = config.entries.joinToString(", ") { (k, v) -> "%s=%s".format(k, v) } check(summary.isNotEmpty() && today.isNotEmpty()) } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l01.demo.ClassSourcesDemoKt labs/startup/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/startup/l01/demo/ClassSourcesDemo.kt Gradle runs the demo on the JDK that runs Gradle. On JDK 25.0.5: 818 classes, 793 from the shared objects file, 19 from jrt:/, 5 hidden and 1 from file:, the demo itself. With -Xshare:off: 831 classes, 816 parsed from jrt:/, 14 hidden, none shared. On JDK 21 the same runs gave 734 (718 shared) and 767 (747 from jrt:/). The Kotlin twin loads 929 on JDK 25 and 876 on JDK 21, with 63 from file: both times, because the Kotlin standard library is a JAR on your class path like any other. The java command (JDK 25 man page source): -Xlog and class data sharing docs

h: Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it · Loading is lazy, and initialization is lazier
x: The tracking service has to know which depot delivers to each postcode. The lab class PostcodeTable keeps that as a map of 200,000 rows, which a real service would build from a big file. It also has a version() method, and the service's health check calls it. A health check is a tiny request that another program sends every few seconds to ask "are you up?", and this one also reports which postcode data is loaded. Here's the first version, as the lab hands it to you: Java // Naive: the health check pays for the whole table (trimmed) public final class PostcodeTable { private static final Map<String, String> TABLE = build(); // runs in <clinit> public static String version() { return "postcodes-2026.11"; } public static String depotOf(String postcode) { return TABLE.get(postcode); } } Kotlin // Naive: the health check pays for the whole table class PostcodeTable { companion object { private val table = build() // also runs in PostcodeTable's <clinit> fun version() = "postcodes-2026.11" fun depotOf(postcode: String) = table[postcode] } } To see what's wrong, separate two events that sound alike. The JVM loads a class when something needs its definition. It initializes the class, which means it runs the class's static initializer, only on the class's first active use. The static initializer is a hidden method that the bytecode calls <clinit>. It holds every static field initializer and static {} block, in source order. Active uses are new, a call to a static method, a read or write of a static field that isn't a compile-time constant, and reflection that asks for initialization. Initializing a class initializes its superclass first. Declaring a variable of the type doesn't count, and neither does PostcodeTable.class, which loads the class but runs nothing. Now the problem is plain. The health check calls version(), a static method, so it initializes PostcodeTable, and the initializer builds the table. The health check asked for one line of text and paid for 200,000 rows. The Kotlin version has the same problem, and that one surprises people. A companion object's properties compile to static fields of the outer class, and the outer class's <clinit> fills them. The worked example below shows it in javap output, the JDK's tool for reading class files. In the shop, the fix is a sealed box in the back room, opened only when a customer asks for what's inside. In code, it's the holder idiom: give the expensive field a small class of its own. Java // Fixed: the table waits in a class of its own public final class PostcodeTable { private static final class Holder { static final Map<String, String> TABLE = build(); // runs on first use of Holder } public static String version() { return "postcodes-2026.11"; } public static String depotOf(String postcode) { return Holder.TABLE.get(postcode); } } Kotlin // Fixed: the table waits in a class of its own object PostcodeTable { fun version() = "postcodes-2026.11" fun depotOf(postcode: String) = Holder.table[postcode] private object Holder { val table = build() // a nested object is its own class } } Now version() touches only PostcodeTable. The JVM loads and initializes Holder the first time depotOf reads Holder.TABLE. Two things changed in Kotlin: the class with a companion became an object, and the table moved into a private nested object, which is a class of its own with its own <clinit>. You may wonder what happens if eight requests arrive at once and all call depotOf first. The table is still built once. The JVM initializes each class under its own lock (JLS 12.4.2, the language rules for initialization): one thread runs the initializer, and the others wait, then see the finished table. In Kotlin, val table by lazy { build() } gives the same laziness with a lock you can see. The memory model track's lesson "Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders" shows why the holder is safe. Lazy isn't always better, though. Moving the cost to the first lookup makes the first customer wait instead. Be lazy about work that many starts never need, such as a rarely used report. Do the work early, on purpose, when every request needs it. Work that every start pays for should be work that every start needs. Move the rest behind a holder. Check the rule on a case we didn't show. PostcodeTable gets public static final String VERSION = "postcodes-2026.11";, and the health check reads PostcodeTable.VERSION instead. Is the table built? (No. javac copies a compile-time constant into the caller's class file, so reading it doesn't touch PostcodeTable at all.) We can now take work off the start-up path. To know whether that helped, we need a clock, and there are three to choose from. Predict the order of static initializers Open InitOrderDemo. main calls Eager.version(), then Lazy.version(), then Lazy.table() twice. Each static initializer adds a line to a log. Write down the order of the log lines before you run it. Which call adds no line at all? Run it. Then run the Kotlin twin, InitOrderDemoKt, which compares a companion object (Postcodes), a nested object (Depots) and by lazy (Routes). InitOrderDemo.java package workbench.startup.l01.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** Prints the moment each static initializer runs. Predict the order before you run it. */ public class InitOrderDemo { static final List<String> LOG = new ArrayList<>(); static Map<String, String> build(String who) { LOG.add(who); // the expensive part would go here return new HashMap<>(Map.of("411111", "North depot")); } /** The table is a static field of the class itself: built on first use of Eager. */ static class Eager { static final Map<String, String> TABLE = build("Eager.<clinit> builds the table"); static String version() { return "eager-v1"; } static Map<String, String> table() { return TABLE; } } /** The table lives in a nested holder: built on first use of Holder. */ static class Lazy { static { LOG.add("Lazy.<clinit> (no table here)"); } static String version() { return "lazy-v1"; } static Map<String, String> table() { return Holder.TABLE; } private static class Holder { static final Map<String, String> TABLE = build("Lazy.Holder.<clinit> builds the table"); } } public static void main(String[] args) { LOG.add("main starts"); Eager.version(); Lazy.version(); LOG.add("-- both versions read --"); Lazy.table(); LOG.add("-- Lazy.table() called --"); Lazy.table(); LOG.forEach(System.out::println); } } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l01.demo.InitOrderDemo labs/startup/src/demo/java/workbench/startup/l01/demo/InitOrderDemo.java InitOrderDemo.kt package workbench.startup.l01.demo /** Prints the moment each initializer runs. Predict the order before you run it. */ private val log = mutableListOf<String>() private fun build(who: String): Map<String, String> { log += who // the expensive part would go here return mapOf("411111" to "North depot") } /** A companion's properties are static fields of Postcodes: built when Postcodes is initialized. */ class Postcodes { companion object { val table = build("Postcodes companion: table built with the outer class") fun version() = "postcodes-v1" } } /** A nested object is its own class, with its own initializer: the Kotlin holder idiom. */ object Depots { fun version() = "depots-v1" fun table() = Holder.table private object Holder { val table = build("Depots.Holder: table built") } } /** by lazy: built on the first get, under a lock by default (LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED). */ object Routes { fun version() = "routes-v1" val table by lazy { build("Routes lazy: table built") } } fun main() { log += "main starts" Postcodes.version() Depots.version() Routes.version() log += "-- all three versions read --" Depots.table() Routes.table log += "-- Depots.table() and Routes.table read --" log.forEach(::println) } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l01.demo.InitOrderDemoKt labs/startup/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/startup/l01/demo/InitOrderDemo.kt Java prints main starts, Eager.<clinit> builds the table, Lazy.<clinit> (no table here), -- both versions read --, Lazy.Holder.<clinit> builds the table, -- Lazy.table() called --. Calling Eager.version() built a table nobody asked for. The second Lazy.table() adds nothing, because a class is initialized once. Kotlin prints Postcodes companion: table built with the outer class before -- all three versions read --, and Depots.Holder: table built and Routes lazy: table built only after it. JLS 12.4: Initialization of classes and interfaces docs

h: Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it · Three clocks, and only one is what users see
x: The tracking service from the opening printed two numbers that disagreed. There's a third one, and the three are easy to mix up. The first is the JVM's own. -Xlog:startuptime prints the phases of creating the VM, and its last line reads like Create VM, 0.0550112 secs. That's the lights going on: the JVM is ready to run main. It says nothing about your code. The second is the program's own log line, such as started in 0.151s. It's the shop turning its sign to OPEN. The program measures it from the inside, and every framework starts its clock at a slightly different place. Our demo service prints the JVM's uptime at the moment its server is ready to accept connections. The third is time to first request: the time from launching the process to the first successful answer, measured from outside. A request is a message another program sends to ask for something, and a successful answer on the web carries status 200, the code for "OK". This is the first customer walking out with what they came for, and it's the only clock the street sees. A load balancer, a program that spreads incoming requests over several copies of a service, waits for it. So do your users. FirstRequestTimer, in the Try it below, reads all three. It starts the tracking service in a second JVM, asks /track every 2 ms from outside, and stops its clock at the first 200. On JDK 25.0.5, on a busy machine with 4 cores (a core is one of the processor's independent workers), one run printed: log : [0.056s][info][startuptime] Create VM, 0.0550112 secs log : started in 0.151s. Listening on: http://127.0.0.1:40931 first 200: 429 ms after launch, measured outside (19 attempts) That's 55 ms, 151 ms and 429 ms. The service's own clock is honest; it simply starts late and stops early. The gap after it holds the launcher, the creation of the process and the first request itself. That request loads more classes again: the code that reads it, builds the answer and writes it out. On a machine this busy, some of the gap is plain waiting for a free core. Over nine runs in a row, the medians were 62, 255 and 529 ms. Even the first 200 isn't the end of the story. HotSpot, the JVM in most JDK builds, has two JIT compilers: C1 compiles quickly with simple optimizations, and C2 compiles slowly into much faster code. h: Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it · Footprint is RSS, and the heap is only part of it
x: The same demo can also ask how much memory the service takes, and two honest answers differ by a factor of five. Run it with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, and on JDK 25.0.5 it printed: RSS : VmRSS: 60376 kB, RssAnon: 33056 kB, RssFile: 27320 kB NMT : Total: reserved=4904MB, committed=296MB NMT : Java Heap (reserved=3420MB, committed=216MB) Footprint is how much memory a running program really takes. Native Memory Tracking (NMT) is the JVM's own accounting of its memory, and it says the JVM has committed 296 MB, 216 MB of it for the heap. Committed memory is memory the JVM has asked the operating system for. The operating system says the process has about 60 MB resident. RSS, the resident set size, is the memory of a process that is really in RAM. Both are right, and the shop explains why. Committed is the floor space you've booked; resident is the floor you've actually put shelves on. Memory comes in pages, small blocks of usually 4 KB, and a page becomes resident only when the program first touches it. A fresh heap is mostly untouched pages. Reserved is larger still: 4,904 MB of addresses set aside, most of them never even booked. RSS is the number a memory limit cares about, and it holds much more than the heap. It counts the touched heap pages and metaspace, the code cache where the JIT keeps its machine code, and the tables of the garbage collector, the part of the JVM that frees memory no object uses anymore. It also counts every thread's stack, the mapped archive from the first section, the JDK's modules file and the JVM itself. RssAnon is memory the process made for itself. RssFile is pages read from files, such as the modules file, which processes that map the same file can share. You can read all of it with three commands: ps -o pid,rss,args -p <pid> # RSS in kB, on Linux and macOS grep -E 'VmRSS|RssAnon|RssFile' /proc/<pid>/status jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary # only if started with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary <pid> is the process id, the number the operating system gives each running program, and jcmd is a tool that comes with the JDK. Many services run in a container, a box the operating system builds around a program to cap its memory and CPU. When the program goes over the memory limit, the operating system stops it, and it judges by resident memory. So "heap used" on a monitoring dashboard isn't your footprint either. It leaves out everything in the list above, and it counts live objects, not the heap pages the collector has already touched. A memory limit counts resident pages. Measure RSS, then ask NMT where it went. Check yourself: the service starts with -Xms2g, which makes the JVM commit a 2 GB heap at once. Right after start-up, is its RSS about 2 GB? (No. The JVM books 2 GB of floor, but RSS grows only as the program and the collector touch those pages.) Every number in this lesson comes back on the next launch, because the JVM keeps nothing between runs. Almost nothing, that is: those 793 classes from the archive were unpacked before the shop ever opened. Committed is not resident Run FirstRequestTimer again with -Pargs=-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary. Before it stops the service, the demo asks it for its NMT summary with jcmd. Compare the Total: committed line with VmRSS. Which one would a 512 MiB memory limit compare against? On Linux, run grep Rss /proc/self/status in a shell to see the same fields for grep itself. x: A lazy table in Java and in Kotlin DepotDirectory.java public final class DepotDirectory { // eager: built in DepotDirectory.<clinit>, on the first use of the class private static final Map<String, String> ALIASES = loadAliases(); // lazy: built in Holder.<clinit>, on the first read of Holder.POSTCODES private static final class Holder { static final Map<String, String> POSTCODES = loadPostcodes(); } public static String version() { return "dir-v7"; } public static String depotOf(String postcode) { return Holder.POSTCODES.get(postcode); } } DepotDirectory.kt object DepotDirectory { // eager: built in DepotDirectory.<clinit>, on the first use of the object private val aliases = loadAliases() // lazy: Holder is its own class with its own <clinit> private object Holder { val postcodes = loadPostcodes() } // also lazy, with a visible lock (LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED by default) val routes by lazy { loadRoutes() } fun version() = "dir-v7" fun depotOf(postcode: String) = Holder.postcodes[postcode] } Both versions compile to the same JVM mechanism: a static field filled in a class initializer, which runs once, on first active use, under the JVM's initialization lock. What differs is where Kotlin puts the fields. Properties of an object live in the object's own class. Properties of a companion object live as static fields of the outer class, so touching the outer class at all builds them. A private nested object is the exact twin of Java's holder class. by lazy is a library feature, not a JVM one: it creates a small Lazy object and takes a lock on first access. That costs a little, but it also works for instance properties, where a holder class can't help.

Create VM stops before your code runs, and the service's own line is measured inside the process, from wherever its framework starts counting, and before the first request loads its own classes. h: Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it · Key terms
x: Class loading Finding a class's bytes and turning them into the JVM's internal form in metaspace. Verification The check, before a class runs, that its bytecode is type-safe. Static initializer (<clinit>) The method that sets a class's static fields and runs its static blocks, once, on first active use. Holder idiom Putting an expensive static field in a small nested class, so it is built on first use of that field only. Hidden class A class the JVM generates in memory while the program runs, with no class file, for example for a lambda. Time to first request From launching the process to the first successful answer, measured from outside. RSS Resident set size: the memory of a process that is really in RAM. NMT Native Memory Tracking: the JVM's own breakdown of the memory it has reserved and committed. What does each line of -Xlog:class+load tell you? The class name and its source:: shared objects file (the archive), jrt:/... (parsed from the JDK's modules file), file:... (your class path), or a defining class name for a hidden class such as a lambda. When does the JVM run a class's <clinit>? On first active use: new, a static method call, a read or write of a non-constant static field, reflection that initializes, or initializing a subclass. Loading alone doesn't run it. Why is the holder idiom thread-safe with no lock in your code? The JVM initializes each class under its own lock (JLS 12.4.2). One thread runs Holder.<clinit>; the others wait, then see the finished field. Is a Kotlin companion object property initialized lazily? No. It compiles to a static field of the outer class, filled by the outer class's <clinit>, so any first use of the outer class builds it. Use a private nested object or by lazy. What does the Create VM line of -Xlog:startuptime measure? Only the JVM creating itself, before main runs: not your classes, not the framework, not the first request. NMT says 296 MB committed and RSS is 60 MB. Which one is resident memory? RSS. Committed memory has been requested from the operating system, but untouched pages (most of a fresh heap) aren't resident. Which start-up number does a load balancer see? Time to first request: from launching the process to the first successful answer, measured from outside the process.

h: Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it · Go deeper
x: Loading is lazy, but not quite as lazy as the rule in this lesson suggests. Two things load classes you never called. The first is the verifier. To check that a method is type-safe, it sometimes needs to know whether one class is a subtype of another, for example when two branches produce different classes that meet in the same variable. To answer that, it loads both. A prototype of lesson 2's lab hit this: a test class whose static initializer read a field of its outer class pulled in the outer class, and verifying that class pulled in more. That's why the lab compares the exact set of classes your own loader defined, taken from a run of the reference answer, and never a count of all loaded classes, which changes from one JDK build to the next. The second is the framework. Scanning for annotations reads class files, and wiring objects by reflection loads every class it wires, all at start-up. Some frameworks, Quarkus among them, move that work into the build: they index the classes, decide the wiring and generate plain code that does it, so a start has nothing to scan. Lesson 3 of this track, and the capstone after it, come back to that idea. If you want to see where a large program spends its start-up, pipe -Xlog:class+load through sed -E 's/.*source: //' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head for the same histogram as the demo. The JDK Flight Recorder's jdk.ClassLoad event, off by default, records a stack trace for each class load once you enable it, so you can see who asked for each box. Measure first, then pick a fix from lessons 2 to 4.

h: Class data sharing and Project Leyden's AOT cache · The archive every JDK already ships
x: Start with the cost of an empty back room. Turn the JDK's archive off with -Xshare:off, and java -version alone makes the JVM find, parse and verify 411 classes before it prints a line. With the archive on, it loads 396, and 393 of them come ready-made. Lesson 1's tracking service felt the difference. Over nine runs on JDK 25.0.5, Create VM took 173 ms instead of 62, and the first answer came at 731 ms instead of 529. That archive is class data sharing, CDS for short: a file of classes the JVM has already parsed and verified, stored in the JVM's own internal form. Every JDK build since JDK 12 ships one, in lib/server/classes.jsa, with about 1,300 core JDK classes. (It came with JEP 341; a JEP, or JDK Enhancement Proposal, is the document that describes a new JDK feature.) In the shop, these are the shelves that came with the shop: the JDK's makers unpacked them before you ever opened. The file doesn't hold class files. It holds the structures the JVM would otherwise build in metaspace, laid out the way they sit in memory. At start-up the JVM memory-maps the file: it asks the operating system to make the file part of the program's memory. Each page is then read from disk only when it's first touched. The JVM fixes up a few pointers and uses the classes as they are. All of that happens by default; -Xshare:off turns it off, which is mostly useful for lessons like this one. There's more than one file in that folder, and the JVM picks the one that matches its settings. JDK 25 ships four. classes_nocoops.jsa is for a JVM running without compressed object pointers, the 32-bit object references it uses by default for heaps below 32 GB. The two _coh files are for compact object headers, a smaller layout for the hidden header every object carries. JEP 519 made them a product feature in JDK 25, still off by default. That tells you what CDS can save and what it can't. It saves finding, parsing and verifying the archived classes: the unpacking and the checking. It doesn't run static initializers. Those still run on first use, in the same order, so lesson 1's 200,000-row table takes just as long with any archive. The research behind this course logged a program's initializer order with and without a JDK 21 archive and a JDK 25 AOT cache, and the output was identical. And an archive does nothing for the JIT, which still starts cold. An archive saves the unpacking and the checking. Your static initializers and the JIT still run on every start. Check yourself: with the archive on, java -version loaded 396 classes, and with it off, 411. Why would turning the archive off make the JVM load more classes? (Without the archive, the JVM must generate some classes on the spot that the archive would have supplied ready-made. On JDK 21 the gap is 35: 405 against 440.) The JDK's shelves arrive ready-made. The tracking service's own classes still come out of boxes, one by one, from file:. Look at the default archive List the archives your JDK ships, with the first command. h: Class data sharing and Project Leyden's AOT cache · AppCDS puts your own classes in the archive
x:
The default archive covers the JDK. AppCDS, application class data sharing, adds your own classes to an archive. It has been part of OpenJDK since JDK 10 (JEP 310), and it's the start-up gain you can have on JDK 21 without touching your code. There are three ways to build one. The dynamic archive (JDK 13 and later, JEP 350) needs one training run: an ordinary run of the program whose extra job is to write down what it loaded. The JVM writes the archive when that run exits: java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main # training run java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main # every start after A dynamic archive stores only what the default archive lacks, so it's small: 221,184 bytes for the demo below. The static archive takes three steps: record the list of classes, dump them into an archive, then use it. java -Xshare:off -XX:DumpLoadedClassList=app.classlist -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main java -Xshare:dump -XX:SharedClassListFile=app.classlist -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp tracker.jar java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main -XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive (JDK 19 and later), used with -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa, folds all this into your normal start command. If the file exists and came from the same JDK, the JVM uses it; if not, it writes one at exit. That's handy on a laptop and wrong for a server that starts from a read-only disk, or one that's thrown away after every run. There, build the archive when you build the program. ArchiveLadder, in the Try it below, packs a small workload into a JAR and starts it under each setup. On JDK 25.0.5, one run printed: setup loaded from archive wall ms no sharing 909 0 388 default CDS 897 868 187 AppCDS (dynamic) 826 794 153 AOT cache 959 959 86 Read the counts first, because they don't change from run to run. With AppCDS, the demo's own classes join the JDK's on the ready-made shelves, and the JVM generates fewer classes on the spot. The times come from one run on a busy machine, so treat them as a direction. The research behind this course measured more carefully, with 30 interleaved runs of a 300-class app on JDK 21. AppCDS cut its start-up CPU time about in half, from 349 ms to 171 ms. Leave the last row for the next section. The archive comes with rules, and the JVM checks them like a strict stock clerk. The class path must hold JAR files, not folders of class files. It must be the same as when the archive was made, or start with it. And if a JAR changed after the archive was made, the JVM refuses the archive. Here's JDK 21 starting a rebuilt JAR with its old archive, trimmed: [0.020s][warning][cds] hello.jar timestamp has changed. [0.020s][warning][cds] hello.jar size has changed. [0.020s][warning][cds,dynamic] Unable to use shared archive. The top archive failed to load: hello.jsa version TWO, rebuilt It warned, ran the new code from the JAR, and kept the default archive for the JDK's own classes. Remember that last detail, because the AOT cache behaves differently. Build the archive with the program, from the same JARs, and ship the two together. Check yourself: you add -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa while the class path is a folder of compiled classes. What happens at exit? (JDK 25 refuses with Cannot have non-empty directory in paths. Pack the classes into a JAR first, as ArchiveLadder does.) AppCDS saves the unpacking. But a class taken from the shelf still has to be linked, every lambda is still built on the spot, and the JIT still learns everything from scratch. That's the work Project Leyden goes after. h: Class data sharing and Project Leyden's AOT cache · Leyden's AOT cache: train, assemble, then run
x: Leyden's AOT cache: train, assemble, then start with the classes already loaded and linked Project Leyden is the OpenJDK project that moves start-up work out of production runs, the real runs that serve your users. Its first result is the AOT cache, where AOT means ahead of time. It arrived one JEP at a time, and every piece of it is a final, standard feature: no preview flag and no special switch. JDK What arrived 24 JEP 483: the AOT cache, with classes already loaded and linked; flags -XX:AOTMode, -XX:AOTConfiguration and -XX:AOTCache 25 (LTS) JEP 514: one command, -XX:AOTCacheOutput, to create it. JEP 515: method profiles from training, for faster warm-up 26 JEP 516: the full cache works with every garbage collector, ZGC included 27 no Leyden JEP; -XX:AOTMode=required becomes the name for on 28, in development JEP 544: compiled machine code in the cache LTS means a long-term-support release, the kind most teams run in production, and JDK 25 is the current one. The java manual names three phases, and the shop has all three. In training, you run the program on a realistic workload, and the JVM writes what it loaded and linked into an AOT configuration file. That's an ordinary day, with a notebook on the counter. In assembly, the JVM turns that file into the cache, and your program doesn't run: the evening, spent writing up the notes. In production, every start uses the cache. On JDK 25, one command does the first two: java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main # training and assembly, JDK 25+ java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main # production When training and assembly run at different times, use the two-step form from JDK 24: java -XX:AOTMode=record -XX:AOTConfiguration=app.aotconf -cp tracker.jar tracker.Main java -XX:AOTMode=create -XX:AOTConfiguration=app.aotconf -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp tracker.jar The one-step command does the same underneath: when the training run ends, it starts a second JVM with -XX:AOTMode=create, as the Try it below shows. The cache holds more than an AppCDS archive. Normally the JVM links a class lazily. The first time an instruction runs, the JVM turns a symbolic name in the class file, such as java/util/Map.get, into a pointer to the real method. The first run of a lambda costs more. Its invokedynamic instruction, the bytecode that asks a helper method how to make a call, builds the lambda's hidden class on the spot. The AOT cache stores the results of that work from the training run. It holds classes already linked, names and lambda call sites already resolved, and Java objects the JVM would otherwise build at every start, such as its map of modules. On JDK 25 it also stores the method profiles that tell the JIT what's hot. Look back at the ladder. The AOT cache row loaded 959 classes, more than any other row, and all 959 came from the archive: the JVM loads and links every cached class before main runs. Code the training never ran gets none of this. It loads the usual way, as the lab shows. The research behind this course measured the gain carefully on JDK 25. For a 300-class app, start-up CPU time fell from 504 ms to 81 ms, wall time from 431 ms to 98 ms, and peak memory from 64 MiB to 42 MiB. A small web service's median time to first request fell from 218 ms to 136 ms. None of that needed a code change. Train on work that looks like production. The cache only knows the shelves you used. A cache built from one day's notes fits that day's shop exactly. Change the stock, the supplier or the layout, and it no longer fits. Make an AOT cache by hand (JDK 25+) Run ArchiveLadder once (previous Try it), so startup/build/boot02/app.jar exists. Then cd labs/startup/build/boot02 and use a JDK 25 java. Run the first command: training and assembly in one go. Find the Launching child process line and the second Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS line, which hands the child its settings. Run the second command and look for Opened AOT cache. Predict the count the third command prints. It names a cache file that doesn't exist. Then run it. terminal (JDK 25+) java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=track.aot -cp app.jar workbench.startup.l02.demo.ArchiveLadder --work java -XX:AOTCache=track.aot -Xlog:aot -cp app.jar workbench.startup.l02.demo.ArchiveLadder --work | grep Opened java -XX:AOTCache=nope.aot -Xlog:class+load -cp app.jar workbench.startup.l02.demo.ArchiveLadder --work | grep -c 'shared objects file' On 25.0.5 the first command printed Temporary AOTConfiguration recorded: track.aot.config, then Launching child process ... to assemble AOT cache track.aot using configuration track.aot.config, a Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: ... -XX:AOTMode=create line, and AOTCache creation is complete: track.aot 11010048 bytes. The second printed [0.020s][info][aot] Opened AOT cache track.aot. The third printed errors ending in Unable to map shared spaces, still ran the program, and counted 0 shared classes: a bad cache path loses the default archive too. Training writes down what the program loaded and linked, assembly turns those notes into the cache without running the program, and every production start maps it. x: A training entry point in Java and Kotlin TrainingMain.java /** Starts the service, sends it every kind of request real users send, then exits so the JVM writes the cache. */ public final class TrainingMain { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { TrackingService service = TrackingService.start(); // the same wiring as production for (String request : List.of("track PX-1042", "track PX-2001", "redirect PX-1042", "history PX-2001")) { service.handle(request); // real code paths, test depots } service.stop(); System.exit(0); // JDK 24 and 25 write the training data when the JVM exits } } TrainingMain.kt /** Starts the service, sends it every kind of request real users send, then exits so the JVM writes the cache. */ fun main() { val service = TrackingService.start() // the same wiring as production listOf("track PX-1042", "track PX-2001", "redirect PX-1042", "history PX-2001") .forEach { service.handle(it) } // real code paths, test depots service.stop() exitProcess(0) // JDK 24 and 25 write the training data when the JVM exits } Both versions do the same three things: start the service exactly as production does, drive every kind of request through it, and exit. The cache doesn't care which language produced the bytecode. What differs is the class path and the entry point. A Kotlin service has kotlin-stdlib as a JAR on its class path, and it must be there, in the same order, in training and in production, or the cache is refused. The Kotlin entry point is the class TrainingMainKt, not TrainingMain. Kotlin 2.x compiles lambdas to invokedynamic, like Java, so the cache can resolve those call sites ahead of time in both languages. Before JDK 26 a training run has to exit to write its data, which is why both versions end the process; JDK 26 adds jcmd <pid> AOT.end_recording for servers that should keep running.

x: Add the AOT cache to your build Pin the JDK, and use the same build of it where you train and where you run. The cache records the exact JDK build and is refused by any other. Pick 25.0.4 or later, so a changed JAR can never run stale classes. # the build machine and the server must print the same line java -version 2>&1 | head -1 # openjdk version "25.0.5" ... must be 25.0.4 or later In the build, put the JAR at the path it will have on the server, then train and assemble in one step. Use the training entry point from the compare block, so the run goes through every kind of request and then exits. cp build/libs/tracker.jar /srv/tracker.jar java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=/srv/app.aot -cp /srv/tracker.jar tracker.TrainingMain # ... AOTCache creation is complete: /srv/app.aot <size> bytes Add a check to the build: start the real entry point with -XX:AOTMode=on and -Xlog:aot, and fail if the cache doesn't open. A wrong path, a different JDK or a changed JAR all make this check fail, loudly, before any user is affected. java -XX:AOTMode=on -XX:AOTCache=/srv/app.aot -Xlog:aot -cp /srv/tracker.jar tracker.SmokeMain \ | grep -q 'Opened AOT cache' || { echo 'AOT cache not used'; exit 1; } # JDK 27+: AOTMode=required Ship tracker.jar and app.aot together, as one unit, and start production without AOTMode. If someone later adds an agent the cache can't work with, the service starts slower instead of not at all. java -XX:AOTCache=/srv/app.aot -cp /srv/tracker.jar tracker.Main

x: You add -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa, a dynamic archive, and run with -Xlog:class+load on JDK 21. Most JDK classes log source: shared objects file, but your own classes log source: file:/srv/tracker.jar. What does that tell you? The JVM rejected your dynamic archive and kept only the default one, so look for the warning that says why Everything works: your classes are always logged with their JAR Your classes are archived, but -Xlog:class+load can't see that The default archive failed, and your archive replaced it Archived classes log source: shared objects file, yours included. When JDK 21 rejects a dynamic archive (a changed JAR, a different class path), it warns and keeps the default archive underneath, so the JDK's classes stay shared and only yours come from the JAR. The warnings at the start of the output say which check failed. The runs that train your AOT cache only ever track parcels. In production, someone redirects a parcel. What happens on the redirect path? The redirect fails with ClassNotFoundException The JVM throws the whole cache away Its classes load the usual way, from the JAR, parsed and verified at that moment, so the first redirect is a little slower The JVM retrains the cache in the background The cache holds what the training run loaded. Anything else loads the usual way, so the program stays correct, but those classes get no head start. That's why training should look like production traffic, which is what the lab's missing function measures. A service runs ZGC on JDK 25. Its AOT cache was trained with the default G1. What do you get? The full speed-up, because the cache doesn't depend on the GC Only the method profiles A crash at start-up Nothing: the JVM can't use the G1-trained cache under ZGC and runs with zero archived classes On JDK 25.0.5 a G1-trained cache gave 0 archived classes under -XX:+UseZGC, and the JVM ran on without any archive. Training under ZGC helps only partly on JDK 25. JDK 26's JEP 516 stores the cache's heap objects in a form every GC can load. Your company adds a monitoring agent to every server through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS. Your service starts with -XX:AOTMode=on -XX:AOTCache=app.aot. What's the risk? None: on only means the cache is enabled If the agent's options don't work with the cache, the JVM stops at start-up instead of running without the cache The agent's classes get added to the cache The cache is rebuilt on every start on (required from JDK 27) is a fail-fast setting: if the cache can't be used, the JVM stops with Unable to use AOT cache. The manual lists certain JVMTI options, which agents use, among the incompatible ones, and the JDK 27 manual warns about exactly this case. In production leave the mode at the default, auto, which runs without the cache instead. A JDK 21 service starts from a read-only disk, and each copy of it is thrown away when it stops. You want AppCDS with no code change. Which setup fits? -XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive -XX:SharedArchiveFile=/app/app.jsa in the start command -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot in the start command A dynamic archive made during the build with -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit, shipped with the program and used with -XX:SharedArchiveFile -Xshare:off, for a predictable start-up AutoCreateSharedArchive writes the file at the exit of a run that had none, which fails on a read-only disk and is lost with the copy anyway. Building the archive during the build gives every copy the same archive from its first start. -XX:AOTCacheOutput needs JDK 25.
