h: Class data sharing and Project Leyden's AOT cache · Key terms
x: CDS Class data sharing: classes stored ready-made in a .jsa file that the JVM maps into memory at start-up. Default CDS archive The archive of about 1,300 JDK classes in lib/server/classes.jsa, used unless you pass -Xshare:off. AppCDS A CDS archive that also holds your application's classes. AOT cache Leyden's archive (JDK 24+): classes loaded and linked ahead of time, heap objects and, from JDK 25, method profiles. Training run A run of the program on a realistic workload that records what to put in the archive or cache. Assembly The step that turns the training notes into the AOT cache; the program itself doesn't run. AOTMode The flag that says how the JVM treats the cache: auto (the default), record, create, on (required on 27+) or off. What work does a CDS archive save at start-up? Finding, parsing and verifying the archived classes: the JVM maps them ready-made from the .jsa file. Static initializers still run on first use. The two commands for a dynamic AppCDS archive (JDK 13+)? java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa -cp app.jar Main, then java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp app.jar Main. The two commands for an AOT cache on JDK 25? java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot -cp app.jar Main (training and assembly), then java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp app.jar Main. Which JDK builds can run stale classes from an AOT cache after the JAR changed? 25.0.0 to 25.0.3 and 26.0.0 to 26.0.1 (JDK-8377932). Fixed in 25.0.4, 26.0.2 and 27. -XX:AOTCache= names a missing or stale file, in the default mode. What do you get? The program runs with no archive at all, not even the default CDS archive, so it starts slower than with no flag. Where does -XX:AOTMode=on (JDK 27: required) belong? In your build's checks, to fail fast when the cache doesn't open. Not in production, where an incompatible agent would stop the JVM from starting. From which JDK does the full AOT cache work with ZGC? JDK 26 (JEP 516). On JDK 25 a G1-trained cache gives nothing under ZGC.

h: Class data sharing and Project Leyden's AOT cache · Go deeper
x: A few details that matter once you run this for real. The static archive is dumped in interpreter-only mode, as if -Xint were set, so the output is the same bit for bit every time. For long class lists you can add -Xmixed to speed up the dump when you don't need that. You can also take an archive from a running process: jcmd <pid> VM.cds dynamic_dump app.jsa, if the process was started with -XX:+RecordDynamicDumpInfo, or jcmd <pid> VM.cds static_dump app.jsa. That suits a service whose real warm-up needs real traffic. To try flags without editing start scripts, JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa works, because the JVM reads that variable at start-up. In AOT cache file names, %p and %t are replaced by the process id and the start time, as in -XX:AOTCacheOutput=tracker%p.aot, so parallel training runs don't overwrite each other. Old articles sell CDS as a way for many JVMs on one machine to share memory. Count on start-up time instead. Modern JDKs map each archive at a different, random address by default and then patch its pointers, which writes to most of its pages and makes them private to the process. In one JDK 25 process, 11.5 MiB of the 14.4 MiB resident in the AOT cache's mapping were private. The manual lags behind the code in one place: the JDK 25 page still says the cache holds "Java classes and heap objects" and that profiles will come in a future release, although JEP 515 shipped them in JDK 25. What's next, as of the JDK 28 development line: JEP 544 moves JIT compilation into the training run and ships the machine code in the cache, while the JIT can still recompile in production, and JEP 545 targets start-up and warm-up with ZGC. Neither is in a released JDK yet, so treat them as previews of where this is going, not as flags to use.

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · Native image builds a closed world
x: Native image builds a closed world: only code reachable from main gets in, so a class named at run time needs a metadata entry Lesson 2's best result still started a JVM. Even with a perfect AOT cache, the JVM maps its classes, links what training missed, interprets, and waits for the JIT. In a benchmark that the Quarkus project publishes for one of its sample services, the first request still took 1,859 ms with the cache. (Quarkus is a framework for Java services, and we'll meet it properly in the last section.) Native image removes that work from every start by doing it once, in the build. The tool is called native-image. It comes with GraalVM, a JDK from Oracle with extra tools, or with Mandrel, a build of the same tool that the Quarkus project tailors for its framework. A plain OpenJDK doesn't have it. GraalVM comes in two editions, the open-source Community Edition and Oracle GraalVM, and the difference matters below. native-image takes your class path and builds one executable file for one operating system and one kind of CPU, in three steps. First it analyzes the program. Starting at main, it follows every method call and field access it can see, and works out which classes can show up at each call. Second, it runs static initializers where it can. It saves the objects they create into the image heap, a part of the executable that is mapped straight into memory at start-up. Third, it compiles every method it reached to machine code. Code the analysis never reached is left out, and so are the JDK classes nothing uses. That's the closed-world assumption: everything the program will ever run is known when you build it. In the shop picture, the factory packs the stall by following the shop's own catalogue. Every item a page points to goes in the van, and nothing else does. The finished binary runs on a small runtime called Substrate VM, with no class loading, no bytecode verification, no interpreter and no JIT. That's why it starts in milliseconds and stays small. The Quarkus benchmark (Quarkus 3.34.3 on JDK 25.0.2, tuned by its authors) puts numbers on it: JVM JVM + AOT cache Native image (Mandrel) Time to first request 4,417 ms 1,859 ms 581 ms Peak throughput 13,265 requests/s 12,389 requests/s 5,411 requests/s RSS 304 MiB 240 MiB 95 MiB Build about 30 s build plus a training run 3 to 10 min, 4 to 8 GB of RAM Peak throughput, the most requests per second a service handles once it's busy, is 59% lower as a native image. With no JIT, there are no profiles from the real run. GraalVM's own docs say that "without profiling information, it is difficult to generate machine code of the same quality as a JIT compiler". The stall's staff follow a printed script, and they never learn shortcuts. Profile-guided optimization (PGO), building again with profiles recorded from a test run, narrows the gap, but "PGO is not available in GraalVM Community Edition", only in Oracle GraalVM. The default garbage collector is Serial, a single-threaded collector "optimized for low footprint and small Java heap sizes". G1 is available only in Oracle GraalVM, on Linux. The other price is everything the analysis can't see. Reflection is code that looks up classes and methods by name while it runs. The analysis can't follow reflection, and it can't follow dynamic proxies, resources (files packed in a JAR) loaded by name, JNI (calls into native C code) or serialization (turning objects into bytes and back) either. The analysis is clever, not psychic. It works out reflective calls at build time "given that all the call arguments are constant", so Class.forName("tracker.ParcelScanned"), with the name written in the code, just works. The tracking service isn't that lucky. It reads messages from its depots, and each message names its event class in a header: Class.forName(message.header("type")). The build can't know that name. You have to tell it, or the call fails at run time. Current GraalVM throws MissingReflectionRegistrationError, which "extends java.lang.Error and should not be handled". Here the stall picture breaks, and the break costs real time. Changing one price tag on a real stall takes a minute. Changing one line of your code means building the whole stall again at the factory, which takes minutes and gigabytes of memory, every time. A native image runs only what the build could see. Anything your code finds by name must be on a list. GraalVM calls that list reachability metadata, and the next section writes one. A class name that only exists at run time Read DynamicLookupDemo. It calls a static method with no arguments, chosen by two strings. Run it as it is, then with -Pargs='java.util.UUID randomUUID'. On the JVM, any class on the class path works. Ask yourself which classes a build would have to keep to support every possible argument. That's why the build needs a list. Optional, with a GraalVM JDK: run the class with java -agentlib:native-image-agent=config-output-dir=build/ni -cp startup/build/classes/java/demo workbench.startup.l03.demo.DynamicLookupDemo java.util.UUID randomUUID, and read the JSON the agent wrote into build/ni. DynamicLookupDemo.java package workbench.startup.l03.demo; import java.lang.reflect.Method; /** * Calls a static, no-argument method chosen at run time, by class name and method name. * On the JVM any class on the class path works. A native image can only do this for the * classes and methods listed in its reachability metadata, so the demo prints that entry too. */ public class DynamicLookupDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String className = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "java.time.LocalDate"; String methodName = args.length > 1 ? args[1] : "now"; Class<?> type = Class.forName(className); // a name from data: the analysis can't see it Method method = type.getMethod(methodName); System.out.println(className + "." + methodName + "() = " + method.invoke(null)); System.out.println("A native image needs this in reachability-metadata.json:"); System.out.printf("{ \"reflection\": [ { \"type\": \"%s\", \"methods\": [ { \"name\": \"%s\", \"parameterTypes\": [] } ] } ] }%n", type.getName(), method.getName()); } } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l03.demo.DynamicLookupDemo labs/startup/src/demo/java/workbench/startup/l03/demo/DynamicLookupDemo.java DynamicLookupDemo.kt package workbench.startup.l03.demo /** * Calls a static, no-argument method chosen at run time, by class name and method name. * On the JVM any class on the class path works. A native image can only do this for the * classes and methods listed in its reachability metadata, so the demo prints that entry too. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val className = args.getOrElse(0) { "java.time.LocalDate" } val methodName = args.getOrElse(1) { "now" } val type = Class.forName(className) // a name from data: the analysis can't see it val method = type.getMethod(methodName) println("$className.$methodName() = ${method.invoke(null)}") println("A native image needs this in reachability-metadata.json:") println("""{ "reflection": [ { "type": "${type.name}", "methods": [ { "name": "${method.name}", "parameterTypes": [] } ] } ] }""") } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l03.demo.DynamicLookupDemoKt labs/startup/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/startup/l03/demo/DynamicLookupDemo.kt The first run prints today's date, such as java.time.LocalDate.now() = 2026-11-17, and the entry { "reflection": [ { "type": "java.time.LocalDate", "methods": [ { "name": "now", "parameterTypes": [] } ] } ] }. The second prints a random UUID and the same entry for java.util.UUID and randomUUID. On the JVM both just work. A native image would work only for the class and method its metadata listed. The analysis follows calls from main. A class reached only through a name in a message is in the binary only if the metadata lists it. GraalVM: Reachability Metadata docs

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · Reflection and proxies need reachability metadata
x: You tell the build in a file named reachability-metadata.json, in the folder META-INF/native-image/<groupId>/<artifactId>/ on the class path. (A group id and an artifact id are the two names that identify a library, such as com.example and tracker.) The current schema, version 1.2.0, allows four keys at the top level: reflection, resources, foreign and comment. Proxies, serialization and JNI all live inside reflection entries. In the shop, this file is the packing list for the items customers ask for by name. A reflection entry names a type, and the members your code uses on it: { "reflection": [ { "condition": { "typeReached": "tracker.EventDecoder" }, "type": "tracker.ParcelScanned", "methods": [ { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] }, { "name": "parcelId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] } ] } A constructor is named <init>, the JVM's own name for it. Parameter types are fully qualified, primitives go by name (long, int), and every method needs parameterTypes, even an empty one. Instead of listing members, you can set allDeclaredConstructors or allPublicMethods, which keeps more code in the binary. The optional condition switches the entry on only once EventDecoder is reached at run time, which means just before its static initializer starts. Writing EventDecoder.class on its own doesn't count. A dynamic proxy is an object the JDK builds while the program runs: it implements a list of interfaces and sends every call to one handler method. Web client libraries use them a lot. The tracking service's DepotClient, which asks a depot where a parcel is, is one. In the metadata, a proxy is a reflection entry whose type is the ordered list of its interfaces: { "reflection": [ { "type": { "proxy": ["tracker.DepotClient", "java.lang.AutoCloseable"] } } ] } The order is part of the proxy's identity: a proxy for (A, B) is a different class from one for (B, A), as the Try it below shows. If the proxy gets serialized, add "serializable": true; the docs say proxies "can only be registered for serialization via the JSON files". Two warnings about what you'll find online. The older schema, v1.1.0, had separate top-level jni and serialization sections, and some GraalVM pages still show a top-level jni array, which v1.2.0 rejects. The current Quarkus development docs tell you to use "a proxy section", which v1.2.0 rejects too. Check your file against the schema of the GraalVM you build with. You rarely write all of it by hand. The tracing agent watches a run on a normal JVM and writes down every reflective call it saw: java -agentlib:native-image-agent=config-output-dir=build/ni-config -jar tracker.jar Like an AOT training run, the agent sees only the code paths you exercise, so drive it with real tests, then read what it wrote. To make a missing entry fail loudly, build with --exact-reachability-metadata, and run your tests with -XX:MissingRegistrationReportingMode=Exit. Write the list from what the code really does, then let a test prove it's complete. The list covers what the analysis can't see. But the factory also runs some of your code while it builds, and that has a surprise of its own. The order of proxy interfaces Read ProxyOrderDemo. It builds three proxies: (DepotApi, AutoCloseable), (AutoCloseable, DepotApi), and the first pair again. Predict the two same class lines before you run it. Run it, then the Kotlin twin. ProxyOrderDemo.java package workbench.startup.l03.demo; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.Arrays; /** Builds two JDK dynamic proxies from the same two interfaces, in opposite orders. */ public class ProxyOrderDemo { public interface DepotApi { String locate(String parcelId); } public static void main(String[] args) { InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, a) -> method.getName().equals("locate") ? "OUT FOR DELIVERY " + a[0] : null; ClassLoader loader = ProxyOrderDemo.class.getClassLoader(); Object first = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[] {DepotApi.class, AutoCloseable.class}, handler); Object second = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[] {AutoCloseable.class, DepotApi.class}, handler); Object again = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[] {DepotApi.class, AutoCloseable.class}, handler); System.out.println("first : " + first.getClass().getName() + " " + names(first.getClass())); System.out.println("second: " + second.getClass().getName() + " " + names(second.getClass())); System.out.println("same class for (A, B) and (B, A)? " + (first.getClass() == second.getClass())); System.out.println("same class for (A, B) twice? " + (first.getClass() == again.getClass())); System.out.println(((DepotApi) first).locate("PX-1042")); } static String names(Class<?> c) { return Arrays.toString(Arrays.stream(c.getInterfaces()).map(Class::getSimpleName).toArray()); } } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l03.demo.ProxyOrderDemo labs/startup/src/demo/java/workbench/startup/l03/demo/ProxyOrderDemo.java ProxyOrderDemo.kt package workbench.startup.l03.demo import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler import java.lang.reflect.Proxy /** Builds two JDK dynamic proxies from the same two interfaces, in opposite orders. */ interface DepotApi { fun locate(parcelId: String): String } fun main() { val handler = InvocationHandler { _, method, a -> if (method.name == "locate") "OUT FOR DELIVERY ${a[0]}" else null } val loader = DepotApi::class.java.classLoader val first = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, arrayOf(DepotApi::class.java, AutoCloseable::class.java), handler) val second = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, arrayOf(AutoCloseable::class.java, DepotApi::class.java), handler) val again = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, arrayOf(DepotApi::class.java, AutoCloseable::class.java), handler) fun names(c: Class<*>) = c.interfaces.map { it.simpleName } println("first : ${first.javaClass.name} ${names(first.javaClass)}") println("second: ${second.javaClass.name} ${names(second.javaClass)}") println("same class for (A, B) and (B, A)? ${first.javaClass == second.javaClass}") println("same class for (A, B) twice? ${first.javaClass == again.javaClass}") println((first as DepotApi).locate("PX-1042")) } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l03.demo.ProxyOrderDemoKt labs/startup/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/startup/l03/demo/ProxyOrderDemo.kt The first two proxies are different classes, jdk.proxy1.$Proxy0 and jdk.proxy1.$Proxy1, so same class for (A, B) and (B, A)? prints false. The repeat of the first pair reuses $Proxy0 and prints true, and the last line is OUT FOR DELIVERY PX-1042. The JVM keeps one proxy class per ordered list of interfaces, which is why the metadata lists them in order. Reachability metadata schema v1.2.0 (JSON schema) docs

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · The build is your program's first run
x: Class initialization is the other half of the story. GraalVM's docs give the numbers: "the simple 'Hello, World!' application requires more than 300 classes to be initialized". In code compiled ahead of time, checking "is this class initialized yet?" on every access "can reduce performance by more than twofold". So the builder runs static initializers at build time wherever it can, and stores what they produced in the image heap. The stall's displays are built at the factory. Plain GraalVM initializes most JDK classes at build time, and your own classes only when it can prove that's safe. An initializer that calls native code (System.out.println counts) or makes a call it can't pin to one target stays at run time. Quarkus goes further: "By default, Quarkus initializes all classes at build time." So your static initializer runs on the build machine, once, and its results are frozen into the binary: Java static final Instant STARTED_AT = Instant.now(); // the build's clock, on every start static final Random JITTER = new Random(); // the builder refuses this one Kotlin val startedAt: Instant = Instant.now() // the build's clock, on every start val jitter = Random() // the builder refuses this one These two lines come from BuildTimeInitDemo, in the Try it below. The second one is a retry jitter: a small random delay before trying again, so that many copies of a service don't all retry at the same moment. On a JVM, each run prints a new start time and a new delay. In a native image with build-time initialization, STARTED_AT would tell every user, for months, the moment the factory built the stall. The builder catches some of these. Quarkus lists two errors you're likely to meet: "Detected an instance of Random/SplittableRandom class in the image heap. Instances created during image generation have cached seed values", and "No instances are allowed in the image heap for a class that is initialized or reinitialized at image runtime: sun.security.provider.NativePRNG". A seed is the starting value of a random number generator, and the same seed gives the same "random" numbers. Don't count on the builder for anything else. A timestamp, the computer's name, a token fetched at start: whatever an initializer computes, every copy started from that binary sees the build's value. The fix is to initialize that class at run time instead: quarkus.native.additional-build-args=--initialize-at-run-time=tracker.InstanceInfo\\,tracker.RetryJitter Quarkus needs the comma escaped like that. With plain native-image, the options are --initialize-at-run-time= and --initialize-at-build-time=, and -H:+PrintClassInitialization reports which classes were initialized where. Better still, keep per-copy values out of static initializers altogether, and compute them in a method that runs when the program starts. Whatever a static initializer computes, the build computes once. Keep per-run values out of it. Writing these lists by hand is fine for one decoder. For a whole service, you'd want the framework to write them for you. Values that would be frozen at build time Read BuildTimeInitDemo. Two static fields are set in a class initializer. Run it twice and compare the two outputs. Now imagine the class was initialized at build time, the Quarkus default. Which line would be the same on every start of every copy, and which one would stop the build? BuildTimeInitDemo.java package workbench.startup.l03.demo; import java.time.Instant; import java.util.Random; /** * Static state computed in a class initializer. On the JVM it is computed again on every start. * In a native image built with build-time initialization (the Quarkus default), the initializer * runs once, inside the build, and every start of the binary sees the build's values. */ public class BuildTimeInitDemo { static final class InstanceInfo { static final Instant STARTED_AT = Instant.now(); // build-time init: the build's time, forever static final Random JITTER = new Random(); // build-time init: the native builder rejects it } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("started at: " + InstanceInfo.STARTED_AT); System.out.println("retry jitter ms: " + InstanceInfo.JITTER.nextInt(250)); } } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l03.demo.BuildTimeInitDemo labs/startup/src/demo/java/workbench/startup/l03/demo/BuildTimeInitDemo.java BuildTimeInitDemo.kt package workbench.startup.l03.demo import java.time.Instant import java.util.Random /** * Static state computed in a class initializer. On the JVM it is computed again on every start. * In a native image built with build-time initialization (the Quarkus default), the initializer * runs once, inside the build, and every start of the binary sees the build's values. */ object InstanceInfo { val startedAt: Instant = Instant.now() // build-time init: the build's time, forever val jitter = Random() // build-time init: the native builder rejects it } fun main() { println("started at: ${InstanceInfo.startedAt}") println("retry jitter ms: ${InstanceInfo.jitter.nextInt(250)}") } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l03.demo.BuildTimeInitDemoKt labs/startup/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/startup/l03/demo/BuildTimeInitDemo.kt On the JVM each run prints a new started at time and a new jitter value, because the initializer runs at every start: one run printed started at: 2026-11-17T07:11:25.498913321Z and retry jitter ms: 148. Initialized at build time, started at would print the build's moment forever, in every copy. The Random in the image heap is one of the cases the builder refuses, with the "cached seed values" error. GraalVM: Class Initialization in Native Image docs

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · Quarkus writes most of the metadata for you
x: Quarkus is an open-source framework for writing services in Java and Kotlin, and it's the second half of this lesson's title. Its main idea is the one this track keeps coming back to: do at build time what other frameworks do at every start. It scans and wires your program while it builds, and it treats native image as a first-class target, which it calls Quarkus native. Quarkus is made of extensions, add-on modules that each bring one library, such as a JSON library or a database driver. Each extension knows what its library reflects on, and Quarkus generates reachability-metadata.json itself. Your part is the classes only your own code knows about, and you declare them with annotations: Java @RegisterForReflection public record ParcelScanned(String parcelId, String depot, long weightGrams) { } @RegisterForReflection(targets = {DepotReply.class, DepotError.class}) // a library's classes public class DepotReflectionConfig { } @RegisterForProxy(targets = {DepotClient.class, AutoCloseable.class}) // order matters public class DepotProxyConfig { } Kotlin @RegisterForReflection data class ParcelScanned(val parcelId: String, val depot: String, val weightGrams: Long) @RegisterForReflection(targets = [DepotReply::class, DepotError::class]) // a library's classes class DepotReflectionConfig @RegisterForProxy(targets = [DepotClient::class, AutoCloseable::class]) // order matters class DepotProxyConfig @RegisterForReflection registers methods and fields by default, plus any nested classes unless you set ignoreNested = true. With targets, it registers the listed classes and not the class it sits on, which is how you cover a library's classes that you can't annotate. serialization = true adds Java serialization. @RegisterForProxy takes the interfaces in order, and the Quarkus docs repeat that "the order of the specified proxy interfaces is significant". Resources go in application.properties, Quarkus's settings file: quarkus.native.resources.includes=templates/**,postcodes/*.csv. When you do need JSON, put it in src/main/resources/META-INF/native-image/<group-id>/<artifact-id>/. The current docs warn that Quarkus overwrites a file placed directly in META-INF/native-image/. Versions matter here too. The latest 3.x release is 3.40.1.1, and its guides still show the older separate files, reflect-config.json and proxy-config.json, while the 4.0 guides say those legacy files "are not supported". Write the unified reachability-metadata.json, and the file survives the upgrade. ./mvnw verify -Dnative (mvnw runs Maven, a build tool) builds the binary and runs your integration tests against it. Integration tests start the whole program and talk to it from outside. Because a native build takes minutes and gigabytes, most teams build it in a shared build, not after every change, and develop in JVM mode. Quarkus's own advice is "Start with JVM mode. Move to native when you have a concrete need." Lesson 4 of this track turns that into a decision table. Check before the lab: your scan events live in a shared JAR that another team owns, so you can't annotate them. Which annotation do you add, and on which class? (@RegisterForReflection(targets = {...}) on any class in your own code, listing their classes. The class carrying the annotation isn't registered itself.) A native image wins the start and the memory, and pays at peak speed and in the build. The next lesson keeps the full JVM, JIT and all, and skips the warm-up instead. Quarkus 3.40: Tips for writing native applications docs

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · Java and Kotlin
x: The same event class registered from Java and from Kotlin ParcelScanned.java @RegisterForReflection public record ParcelScanned(String parcelId, String depot, long weightGrams) { } // the same thing by hand in reachability-metadata.json: // { "type": "tracker.ParcelScanned", // "methods": [ // { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] }, // { "name": "parcelId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] } ParcelScanned.kt @RegisterForReflection data class ParcelScanned(val parcelId: String, val depot: String, val weightGrams: Long) // the same thing by hand: the accessor is a getter on the JVM // { "type": "tracker.ParcelScanned", // "methods": [ // { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] }, // { "name": "getParcelId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] } The annotation is the same, and Quarkus reads it the same way from both languages. What differs is the bytecode it describes. A Java record has an accessor named parcelId(). A Kotlin val parcelId compiles to a private field and a method named getParcelId(). Hand-written metadata names JVM members, so the two entries differ even though the sources look alike. A non-null Kotlin Long is the primitive long in the constructor's signature; Long? would be java.lang.Long. Annotation arrays are {...} with .class in Java and [...] with ::class in Kotlin.

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · Worked example
x: Write the metadata for a scan decoder Here is the tracking service's decoder: each message from a depot names its event class in a header. Find every reflective call and, for each one, the exact member it needs. Ignore code that names a class in the source, such as new or a direct method call: the analysis sees those. Object decode(Message msg) throws ReflectiveOperationException { Class<?> type = Class.forName(msg.header("type")); // 1 Object event = type.getConstructor(String.class, String.class, long.class) // 2 .newInstance(msg.parcelId(), msg.depot(), msg.weightGrams()); log.info(type.getMethod("parcelId").invoke(event)); // 3 return event; } fun decode(msg: Message): Any { val type = Class.forName(msg.header("type")) // 1 val event = type.getConstructor(String::class.java, String::class.java, Long::class.javaPrimitiveType) // 2 .newInstance(msg.parcelId(), msg.depot(), msg.weightGrams()) log.info(type.getMethod("parcelId").invoke(event)) // 3 return event } There are three needs: (1) the class by name, for every event type a depot can send; (2) its (String, String, long) constructor; (3) its parcelId() method. Say the depots send ParcelScanned and ParcelDelivered. Each gets one entry, and the condition limits them to binaries where the decoder is used. { "reflection": [ { "condition": { "typeReached": "tracker.EventDecoder" }, "type": "tracker.ParcelScanned", "methods": [ { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] }, { "name": "parcelId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] }, { "condition": { "typeReached": "tracker.EventDecoder" }, "type": "tracker.ParcelDelivered", "methods": [ { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] }, { "name": "parcelId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] } ] } Put the file at src/main/resources/META-INF/native-image/com.example/tracker/reachability-metadata.json, the <groupId>/<artifactId> folder. In a Quarkus service, the annotation does the same job, and it moves with the class when someone renames it. That's the version to prefer. @RegisterForReflection public record ParcelScanned(String parcelId, String depot, long weightGrams) { } @RegisterForReflection public record ParcelDelivered(String parcelId, String depot, long weightGrams) { } @RegisterForReflection data class ParcelScanned(val parcelId: String, val depot: String, val weightGrams: Long) @RegisterForReflection data class ParcelDelivered(val parcelId: String, val depot: String, val weightGrams: Long) Prove it in the shared build. Build the native binary and run the integration tests against it, with missing registrations turned into a hard exit. A new event type that nobody registered now fails the build, not a parcel at three in the morning. ./mvnw verify -Dnative \ -Dquarkus.native.additional-build-args=--exact-reachability-metadata # and start the binary under test with -XX:MissingRegistrationReportingMode=Exit

x: Write reachability metadata for a class and a proxy labs/startup/src/main/resources/META-INF/native-image/workbench/startup/reachability-metadata.json labs/startup/src/main/java/workbench/startup/l03/MetadataWriter.java ./gradlew :startup:test --tests 'workbench.startup.l03.*' Run the tests once. Write down every reflective call: which class, which constructor (with its parameter types), which methods, and which proxy interfaces in which order. Edit reachability-metadata.json by hand. Add one reflection entry for workbench.startup.l03.ParcelScanned with its <init> and the three accessors from EventDecoder.ACCESSORS, and one entry whose type is {"proxy": [...]}. Run MetadataFileTest until it passes. Implement MetadataWriter.reflection and MetadataWriter.proxy, so the same entries can be generated from Class objects. Run all ten tests. A method entry needs both keys, even with no parameters: {"name": "depot", "parameterTypes": []}. Class.getName() gives exactly the names the schema wants: java.lang.String for a class, long for a primitive. m instanceof Constructor<?> tells a constructor from a method. Class.isInterface() and a HashSet cover the two proxy rules. All ten tests in MetadataFileTest and MetadataWriterTest pass. By the end you can explain what the closed-world assumption costs, write reachability metadata for reflection and proxies by hand, use Quarkus's annotations instead, and spot static initializers that break when the build runs them.

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · Quiz
x: Code calls Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[] {A.class, B.class}, h), and elsewhere the same with {B.class, A.class}. On a normal JVM, how many proxy classes exist, and what does that mean for native-image metadata? One class, so one proxy entry covers both Two classes, so you need two proxy entries, each with its own interface order None until the first method call Two classes, but the metadata only needs the set of interfaces, not their order The JDK defines one proxy class per ordered list of interfaces, so (A, B) and (B, A) are different classes; the demo prints $Proxy0 and $Proxy1. Native-image metadata describes proxy classes the same way, as ordered lists, so each order needs its own entry. Which of these calls needs a reachability metadata entry in a native image? Class.forName("tracker.ParcelScanned"), with the name written in the code new ParcelScanned(...) Class.forName(msg.header("type")) in a message decoder A lambda passed to stream().map(...) The analysis handles reflective calls whose arguments are constants, and it sees new and lambdas directly. A class name that arrives in a message header can't be known at build time, so the class, and the members used on it, must be listed. A Quarkus native service has static final Instant BOOTED = Instant.now(); in an ordinary class, with default settings, and its health check reports BOOTED. What do copies started on different days show? The same time in every copy: the moment the native binary was built Each copy's own start time The build fails with an image-heap error null, because static fields aren't set in native images Quarkus initializes all classes at build time by default, so the initializer runs once, inside the build, and the Instant is stored in the image heap. The builder rejects some objects, such as a Random, but a timestamp is an ordinary value. Mark the class with --initialize-at-run-time, or compute the value when the program starts. A colleague's reachability-metadata.json has a top-level "proxy": [["tracker.DepotClient", "java.io.Closeable"]], copied from an old example. With GraalVM's schema v1.2.0, what's the fix? Nothing, proxy is a valid top-level section Rename the file to proxy-config.json Replace it with allPublicMethods: true Move it into reflection, as {"type": {"proxy": ["tracker.DepotClient", "java.io.Closeable"]}} Schema v1.2.0 allows only reflection, resources, foreign and comment at the top level. A proxy is a reflection entry whose type is an object with a proxy list. Legacy files such as proxy-config.json aren't supported in Quarkus 4.0, and allPublicMethods on an interface doesn't define a proxy class. A service reads messages all day at high load. It restarts about once a week, and a six-second start hurts nobody. Which runtime fits best? A native image, for the smallest RSS The normal JVM, with an AOT cache if you want a shorter start A native image with build-time initialization of everything A native image with profile-guided optimization in GraalVM Community Edition This service lives on peak throughput and barely restarts, which is where the JIT wins: Quarkus's benchmark shows native at 59% lower peak. An AOT cache shortens the start with no code change and cost about 7% of peak in the same benchmark. Profile-guided optimization isn't available in GraalVM Community Edition at all.

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · Key terms
x: Native image A standalone executable built ahead of time from your class path by GraalVM or Mandrel. Closed-world assumption The rule that all code a native image will run is known at build time. Reflection Code that looks up classes, methods and fields by name while the program runs. Reachability metadata The list of classes, members, proxies and resources the build must keep because only dynamic code uses them. Image heap Objects created at build time, stored in the executable and mapped into memory at start-up. Build-time initialization Running a class's static initializer during the build instead of at each start. Tracing agent A JVM agent (-agentlib:native-image-agent) that records the reflection, proxies and resources a run uses. Mandrel A GraalVM-based distribution of native image tailored for Quarkus. What is native image's closed-world assumption? All code is known at build time. The analysis keeps only what it can reach from main; anything used only through reflection, proxies or resource names must be listed in metadata. Where does reachability-metadata.json go? In META-INF/native-image/<groupId>/<artifactId>/ on the class path. How do you list a JDK dynamic proxy in schema v1.2.0? As a reflection entry: {"type": {"proxy": ["tracker.DepotClient", "java.io.Closeable"]}}, with the interfaces in the order the code uses. How is a constructor written in a methods entry? {"name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "long"]}: fully qualified class names, primitives by name. What does Quarkus do with static initializers in native mode by default? It runs them at build time. The values they compute are stored in the image heap, and every start sees the same ones. What do you need to build a native image? GraalVM (Oracle GraalVM or GraalVM Community Edition) or Mandrel. A plain OpenJDK has no native-image tool. @RegisterForReflection(targets = {X.class}) on class Config: which class gets registered? X, not Config. That's how you register a library's classes you can't annotate.

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · Go deeper
x: Some details for when you go native for real. Conditions are precise. "condition": {"typeReached": "tracker.EventDecoder"} makes an entry active when that type is reached at run time, which the docs define as "right before the class-initialization routine starts for that type", or when one of its subtypes is reached. Writing EventDecoder.class doesn't reach it. Conditions mostly help library authors ship metadata that costs nothing in programs that never use the feature. Resources use globs: {"resources": [{"glob": "META-INF/**/*.properties"}, {"bundle": "tracker.Messages"}]}. In Quarkus, use quarkus.native.resources.includes instead. The heap needs a limit. Without an explicit maximum, a native image sets the maximum Java heap to 80% of the physical memory, according to the GraalVM memory docs. In a container, pass -Xmx (or -XX:MaximumHeapSizePercent) yourself. The default collector is Serial. --gc=G1 needs Oracle GraalVM on Linux, and --gc=epsilon never frees memory, which only makes sense for short jobs. PGO, in Oracle GraalVM only, is a three-step build: native-image --pgo-instrument ... builds an instrumented binary, you run it on a real workload so it writes a .iprof profile when it exits, and native-image --pgo=app.iprof ... builds the optimized binary. That's the same idea as Leyden's training run, applied to compiled code. The JDK is moving toward some of these gains without leaving the JVM. Lesson 2's AOT cache already ships linked classes and profiles, and JEP 544, in development for JDK 28, adds compiled code to the cache while keeping the JIT. Native image stays the option when the binary's size and start time, not the JVM's, are the limit.

h: CRaC, and choosing a startup strategy · A started JVM is still cold
x: Lessons 1 to 3 were about reaching the first request. There's a second wait after it. WarmupDemo, in the Try it below, starts a fresh JVM and runs the same work ten times: 20,000 check-digit tests on 16-digit tracking numbers. (A check digit is the last digit of a number, chosen so that a simple sum catches most typing mistakes.) On JDK 25.0.5, on a busy machine, one run printed: round 1: 124,855 us round 2: 6,307 us round 3: 6,440 us round 4: 5,474 us round 5: 5,449 us round 6: 4,710 us round 7: 4,760 us round 8: 4,635 us round 9: 4,516 us round 10: 5,141 us Round 1 took 125 ms, and every round after it about 5 ms. Nothing in the code changed between rounds. The JVM did. A fresh JVM runs every method in the interpreter, which executes bytecode one instruction at a time, and counts how often each method runs and each loop turns. When a method gets hot, C1, the JIT's quick compiler, compiles it with light optimization and keeps counting. When it stays hot, C2, the slow and thorough one, compiles it again using the profile: which branches were taken, and which classes arrived at each call. That climb is called warm-up, and every new JVM climbs it again. In the shop, it's the shopkeeper learning the popular items by heart, and forgetting them all every night. The demo can switch parts of the climb off. With -Xint, the interpreter alone, every round took 164 to 323 ms and never got faster. With -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1, C1 alone, round 1 took 28 ms and the rounds from 5 on about 5 ms. That looks odd at first: C1 alone beat the default on round 1. In the default setup, C1's first versions also count branches and types for C2, which slows them down, and C2's own compiling competes for the machine's four busy cores, the processor's independent workers. The default pays early and catches up later. From round 6 on, both settled at about 4.5 to 5 ms, because a loop this simple gives C2 little to add. The tools in this track each attack part of the wait. AppCDS and the AOT cache get classes ready sooner. On JDK 25, the AOT cache also hands the JIT the profiles from its training run (JEP 515), so it can start compiling sooner. The compiling still happens inside each new JVM, though; compiled code in the cache is JEP 544, still in development for JDK 28. A native image is compiled before it runs, so it never warms up, and it never reaches C2's profile-driven code either. A JVM that has started isn't yet a JVM that's fast. Warm-up repeats in every new process. Before the Try it, sketch the ten round times you expect with -Xint, and with C1 only. CRaC takes a different route from all of them. It lets one JVM warm up, saves the whole running process to disk, and starts copies of it later, already warm. Watch a JVM warm up Read WarmupDemo. It starts a fresh JVM and runs ten rounds of 20,000 check-digit tests on 16-digit tracking numbers, printing each round's time. Run it as it is. Note round 1 and round 10. Run it with -Pargs=-Xint, then with -Pargs=-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1, after writing down your prediction for each. Explain the three shapes with what the interpreter, C1 and C2 do. WarmupDemo.java package workbench.startup.l04.demo; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Runs the same work in 10 rounds in a fresh JVM and prints how long each round took. A fresh * JVM starts in the interpreter, then the JIT compiles the hot code. Extra arguments are passed * to that JVM as flags, for example -Xint (interpreter only) or -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 (C1 only). */ public class WarmupDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("--work")) { work(); return; } List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(); cmd.add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()); cmd.addAll(List.of(args)); cmd.addAll(List.of("-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), WarmupDemo.class.getName(), "--work")); System.out.println("fresh JVM, flags " + List.of(args)); Process child = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).inheritIO().start(); child.waitFor(); } /** Ten rounds of 20,000 check-digit tests on 16-digit tracking numbers, the test every typed-in number gets. */ static void work() { long checksum = 0; for (int round = 1; round <= 10; round++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 20_000; i++) { String digits = Long.toString(1_000_003L * i + round); String number = "7000" + "0".repeat(12 - digits.length()) + digits; // a 16-digit tracking number if (checkDigitOk(number)) checksum += i; } long us = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000; System.out.printf("round %2d: %,7d us%n", round, us); } if (checksum == 42) System.out.println(); // keeps the JIT from dropping the work } /** The Luhn check: the last digit makes the weighted sum a multiple of 10, so most typos show. */ static boolean checkDigitOk(String number) { int sum = 0; boolean twice = false; for (int i = number.length() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { int d = number.charAt(i) - '0'; if (twice) { d *= 2; if (d > 9) d -= 9; } sum += d; twice = !twice; } return sum % 10 == 0; } } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l04.demo.WarmupDemo labs/startup/src/demo/java/workbench/startup/l04/demo/WarmupDemo.java WarmupDemo.kt package workbench.startup.l04.demo import java.nio.file.Path /** * Runs the same work in 10 rounds in a fresh JVM and prints how long each round took. A fresh * JVM starts in the interpreter, then the JIT compiles the hot code. Extra arguments are passed * to that JVM as flags, for example -Xint (interpreter only) or -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 (C1 only). */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "--work") { work() return } val cmd = listOf(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()) + args + listOf("-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.startup.l04.demo.WarmupDemoKt", "--work") println("fresh JVM, flags ${args.toList()}") ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).inheritIO().start().waitFor() } /** Ten rounds of 20,000 check-digit tests on 16-digit tracking numbers, the test every typed-in number gets. */ private fun work() { var checksum = 0L for (round in 1..10) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() for (i in 0 until 20_000) { val number = "7000" + (1_000_003L * i + round).toString().padStart(12, '0') // a 16-digit tracking number if (checkDigitOk(number)) checksum += i } val us = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000 println("round %2d: %,7d us".format(round, us)) } if (checksum == 42L) println() // keeps the JIT from dropping the work } /** The Luhn check: the last digit makes the weighted sum a multiple of 10, so most typos show. */ private fun checkDigitOk(number: String): Boolean { var sum = 0 var twice = false for (i in number.indices.reversed()) { var d = number[i] - '0' if (twice) { d *= 2 if (d > 9) d -= 9 } sum += d twice = !twice } return sum % 10 == 0 } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l04.demo.WarmupDemoKt labs/startup/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/startup/l04/demo/WarmupDemo.kt Three runs of each on JDK 25.0.5, on a busy machine: the default went from 75 to 128 ms in round 1 to about 3 to 7 ms from round 3 on, with an occasional spike to 10 or 30 ms when another program grabbed the cores. With -Xint every round took 150 to 360 ms and never got faster, because nothing is compiled. With C1 only, round 1 took 22 to 28 ms and later rounds about 5 ms: faster than the interpreter at once, and about as fast as C2 for a loop this simple. Your numbers will differ; the shapes won't. h: CRaC, and choosing a startup strategy · CRaC saves a warm JVM to disk and brings it back
x: A started JVM is still cold: CRaC saves a warm process to disk and restores it, once your resources let go CRaC stands for Coordinated Restore at Checkpoint. A checkpoint writes a running JVM to disk, and a restore starts a new process from that image. In the shop, the checkpoint is a photo of the busy shop, and the restore is stepping into that photo the next morning, with everything exactly as it was. Under the hood, the OpenJDK implementation uses CRIU (Checkpoint/Restore In Userspace), a Linux tool that freezes a process. CRIU writes the process's memory pages, each thread's CPU registers (the processor's own small storage slots) and the state the operating system keeps for the process into a folder of image files. A restore builds a new process from those files, and the new process carries on at the instruction where the old one stopped. The heap, the loaded classes and the JIT's compiled code all come back as they were. The CRaC docs put it this way: "After the restore, Java runtime performance is also on-par with the one at the checkpoint." The same mechanism tells you what can't come back. A network connection lives partly in the operating system and partly on the other computer, and the database at the other end dropped its side long before your restore. A file may have changed or moved. So the JVM tells your code before the checkpoint and after the restore, which is the "coordinated" part, and CRaC refuses to checkpoint while files or sockets are still open. (A socket is one end of a network connection, as your program sees it.) The whole flow is three commands: java -XX:CRaCCheckpointTo=cr -jar tracker.jar # start; allows a checkpoint into the folder cr jcmd tracker.jar JDK.checkpoint # after warm-up traffic: write the image, end the process java -XX:CRaCRestoreFrom=cr # later, as often as you like: carry on from the image There's one trap in those three lines, and jcmd is the cheerful culprit. The docs say "success is always reported in jcmd output, problems are reported in the console of the application". So jcmd prints "Command executed successfully" whatever happened, and only the application's own log tells you the truth. The CRaC project published these "time to first operation" numbers in 2020. They come from an early CRaC build of JDK 14 on a laptop, for services written with three popular frameworks: Service built with Normal start Restored Spring Boot 3,898 ms 38 ms Micronaut 1,001 ms 46 ms Quarkus 980 ms 33 ms Now the catch. CRaC isn't part of mainline OpenJDK: there's no JEP, and the main repository has no CRaC commits. You need a CRaC-enabled JDK build from a vendor. Azul ships CRaC in its Zulu builds of JDK 17, 21 and 25 for Linux on x64 and ARM64, in the files with "-crac-" in the name. BellSoft ships CRaC builds of Liberica JDK 17 and 21. CRIU needs extra rights from the operating system. Restoring on a computer with a different CPU can fail, unless you pin the CPU features with -XX:CPUFeatures when you take the checkpoint. And the image holds the whole heap, secrets included, so store it as carefully as a heap dump, a file of every object in memory. Here the photo picture breaks, and the break matters. You can't step into the same photo twice, but you can restore one CRaC image into ten processes, and all ten wake up with exactly the same memory. A checkpoint saves everything inside the process, and nothing outside it. So before the checkpoint, everything that reaches outside the process has to let go, and after the restore it has to reach out again. Your code does that through two hooks. Checkpoint and restore (optional, needs a CRaC JDK on Linux) If you have a CRaC-enabled JDK (for example a Zulu build with -crac- in its name), build any small service JAR and start it with the first command. Send it some requests. Run the jcmd command. Look at both terminals: jcmd's and the application's. Run the restore command and send a request at once. Compare how fast it answers with a normal start. Without a CRaC JDK, answer this from the mechanism instead: your service opened a log file for appending and keeps it open. What does the checkpoint do, and why? terminal (CRaC JDK on Linux) java -XX:CRaCCheckpointTo=cr -jar tracker.jar # in a second terminal, after some traffic: jcmd tracker.jar JDK.checkpoint # later, as often as you like: java -XX:CRaCRestoreFrom=cr jcmd prints Command executed successfully whatever happened; the application's console shows any problem. If the checkpoint worked, the original process ends and cr is a folder of image files. The restore carries on from the checkpoint and answers like a warm JVM. The open log file fails the checkpoint under the default error policy, because an open file can't safely go into the image: the file might change or vanish before a restore. h: CRaC, and choosing a startup strategy · Resources must let go before the checkpoint
x: Your code takes part through two methods. In the org.crac library (1.5.0 is the latest release), a resource, anything that must hear about checkpoints, looks like this: Java public final class DepotDbPool implements Resource { public DepotDbPool() { Core.getGlobalContext().register(this); // the context only holds a weak reference } @Override public void beforeCheckpoint(Context<? extends Resource> c) { closeAllConnections(); } @Override public void afterRestore(Context<? extends Resource> c) { reconnect(); } } Kotlin class DepotDbPool : Resource { init { Core.getGlobalContext().register(this) // the context only holds a weak reference } override fun beforeCheckpoint(c: Context<out Resource>) = closeAllConnections() override fun afterRestore(c: Context<out Resource>) = reconnect() } The two versions match line for line; Kotlin writes Java's Context<? extends Resource> as Context<out Resource>. org.crac mirrors the jdk.crac API of CRaC JDKs, and finds the real implementation by reflection, looking it up by name, when the program runs. On a JDK without CRaC you can still register resources, and only a checkpoint request fails. So the same JAR runs everywhere. The global context, the list of resources the JVM tells, follows documented rules. It calls beforeCheckpoint in the reverse order of registration, and afterRestore in registration order. Components created later usually use the earlier ones. The tracking service's scan listener, which reads scan messages from the depots, saves them through the database pool, so it must stop first and start last. In the shop, it's the closing routine: the last thing switched on in the morning is the first thing switched off at night. Every resource is told, even when another one throws. The context collects the exceptions as suppressed exceptions on one CheckpointException. (A suppressed exception is an extra exception attached to the one that's thrown, so that none gets lost.) If the checkpoint fails, the restore notifications run at once, without an image, and the process carries on. Open files and sockets fail the checkpoint by default. Their policy is error, which the CRaC docs describe as "just print error and fail the checkpoint". You can set other policies (ignore, close, reopen) in a file named by -Djdk.crac.resource-policies. For sockets, though, "the reopening part is not implemented, therefore will result in a runtime exception after restore". Close them yourself. The image is one copy of memory, and every restore starts from it. Restore ten copies of the shop from one photo, and every till starts at ticket number 42. Anything generated before the checkpoint is the same in all ten: an instance id, a counter, a cached access token. Recreate those in afterRestore. One more trap hides in that comment about weak references. The global context holds each resource weakly, so the garbage collector, the part of the JVM that frees unused memory, may remove a resource that nothing else refers to. Then its hooks never run. Keep the resource in a field of the component it belongs to, as the compare block below does. Close what reaches outside before the checkpoint. Rebuild what must be unique after the restore. That completes the toolbox. The last step is choosing from it. Hook order, and a forgotten socket Read HookOrderDemo. Three components register in the order the tracking service creates them: the database pool, the scan listener, the stats reporter. Predict the order of the six hook lines, then run it. Run it with -Pargs=leak, where the reporter forgets to close its socket. Predict whether the restore hooks still run. HookOrderDemo.java package workbench.startup.l04.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * A toy checkpoint: three components register hooks in the order the service creates them. * Pass "leak" as an argument and the stats reporter forgets to close its socket. */ public class HookOrderDemo { /** org.crac.Resource has the same two methods, each taking a Context argument. */ interface Resource { void beforeCheckpoint(); void afterRestore(); } static final List<Resource> registered = new ArrayList<>(); static final List<String> openSockets = new ArrayList<>(); static final class Component implements Resource { final String name; final boolean leaks; Component(String name, boolean leaks) { this.name = name; this.leaks = leaks; openSockets.add(name); // every component holds a connection registered.add(this); // and registers itself when it is created } public void beforeCheckpoint() { System.out.println(" beforeCheckpoint: " + name); if (!leaks) openSockets.remove(name); } public void afterRestore() { System.out.println(" afterRestore: " + name); if (!openSockets.contains(name)) openSockets.add(name); } } public static void main(String[] args) { boolean leak = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("leak"); new Component("database pool", false); // created first: the others use it new Component("scan listener", false); new Component("stats reporter", leak); System.out.println("checkpoint requested"); for (Resource r : registered.reversed()) r.beforeCheckpoint(); // last registered first if (openSockets.isEmpty()) { System.out.println(" -- snapshot written --"); } else { System.out.println(" -- checkpoint refused, still open: " + openSockets + " --"); } for (Resource r : registered) r.afterRestore(); // first registered first } } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l04.demo.HookOrderDemo labs/startup/src/demo/java/workbench/startup/l04/demo/HookOrderDemo.java HookOrderDemo.kt package workbench.startup.l04.demo /** * A toy checkpoint: three components register hooks in the order the service creates them. * Pass "leak" as an argument and the stats reporter forgets to close its socket. */ private interface Hooks { // org.crac.Resource: the same two methods, plus a Context argument fun beforeCheckpoint() fun afterRestore() } private val registered = mutableListOf<Hooks>() private val openSockets = mutableListOf<String>() private class Component(val name: String, val leaks: Boolean) : Hooks { init { openSockets += name // every component holds a connection registered += this // and registers itself when it is created } override fun beforeCheckpoint() { println(" beforeCheckpoint: $name") if (!leaks) openSockets -= name } override fun afterRestore() { println(" afterRestore: $name") if (name !in openSockets) openSockets += name } } fun main(args: Array<String>) { val leak = args.firstOrNull() == "leak" Component("database pool", false) // created first: the others use it Component("scan listener", false) Component("stats reporter", leak) println("checkpoint requested") registered.asReversed().forEach { it.beforeCheckpoint() } // last registered first if (openSockets.isEmpty()) { println(" -- snapshot written --") } else { println(" -- checkpoint refused, still open: $openSockets --") } registered.forEach { it.afterRestore() } // first registered first } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l04.demo.HookOrderDemoKt labs/startup/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/startup/l04/demo/HookOrderDemo.kt beforeCheckpoint runs for the stats reporter, the scan listener, then the database pool; then -- snapshot written --; then afterRestore runs for the pool, the listener, then the reporter. With leak, the checkpoint is refused (-- checkpoint refused, still open: [stats reporter] --), and the restore hooks still run in the same order, so the service keeps working. That's what the real global context does when a checkpoint fails. The global context tells the newest component first at the checkpoint, and the oldest first at the restore. h: CRaC, and choosing a startup strategy · Choosing a start-up strategy
x: Here's the whole track in one table. The numbers come from the lessons: this track's own runs on a busy machine, the research behind the course, the Quarkus benchmark from lesson 3, and CRaC's 2020 results. Read them as directions, not promises. Nothing AppCDS AOT cache Native image CRaC or SnapStart In the shop unpack every morning yesterday's shelves in the back room the shelves, plus the notebook a pop-up stall from the factory a photo of the busy shop Needs any JDK JDK 13+ for a dynamic archive JDK 24+; 25.0.4+ to be safe GraalVM or Mandrel a vendor CRaC JDK on Linux, or Lambda Code changes none none none metadata, build-time initialization fixes hooks for sockets, files and pools Start-up gain seen baseline about half the CPU about a sixth of the CPU; first request 218 to 136 ms first request 581 ms instead of 4,417 ms first operation 33 ms instead of 980 ms Peak throughput baseline the same about 7% lower about 59% lower a warm JVM's Memory (RSS) baseline a little lower 240 instead of 304 MiB 95 instead of 304 MiB a warm JVM's What it costs nothing an archive step in the build a training run; the same JDK build, flags and JAR builds of 3 to 10 minutes and 4 to 8 GB CRIU rights, image storage, per-copy ids Start with the JVM and measure, the way lesson 1 did: time to first request from outside, and RSS from ps. On JDK 25.0.4 or later, add the AOT cache, trained by your integration tests. It's the cheapest gain in the table, and it changes no code. On JDK 21, build a dynamic AppCDS archive when you build the program. For a service that rarely restarts and that nobody waits on, do nothing more. Move to a native image when start-up in milliseconds, or memory per copy, is the real limit. Think of small tools people run from a terminal, functions that start on demand and stop when idle, or many small services packed onto one machine. The team must accept slow builds, metadata upkeep and lower peak throughput. Move to CRaC or SnapStart when new copies must be fast and warm at once, and you control the runtime: Lambda, or a CRaC JDK on Linux with CRIU rights. You also need to make every connection pool, listener and open file checkpoint-safe. Measure first. Then pick the cheapest column that meets the need. Check yourself with a case the table doesn't list. A nightly batch job on JDK 25.0.5 runs for 40 minutes, starts once a night, and keeps the CPU busy the whole time. Which column wins? (Nothing, or at most the AOT cache. Its start-up is a rounding error next to 40 minutes, and a native image would cost it peak throughput in every minute of the run.)

h: CRaC, and choosing a startup strategy · Java and Kotlin
x: A checkpoint-safe pool with org.crac in Java and Kotlin DepotClientPool.java public final class DepotClientPool { private final List<DepotConnection> connections = new ArrayList<>(); // a field keeps the handler reachable: the global context only holds a weak reference private final Resource cracHandler = new Resource() { @Override public void beforeCheckpoint(Context<? extends Resource> c) { closeAll(); } @Override public void afterRestore(Context<? extends Resource> c) { openAll(); } }; public DepotClientPool() { openAll(); Core.getGlobalContext().register(cracHandler); } private synchronized void openAll() { for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) connections.add(DepotConnection.open()); } private synchronized void closeAll() { connections.forEach(DepotConnection::close); // nothing open in the image connections.clear(); } } DepotClientPool.kt class DepotClientPool { private val connections = mutableListOf<DepotConnection>() // a property keeps the handler reachable: the global context only holds a weak reference private val cracHandler = object : Resource { override fun beforeCheckpoint(c: Context<out Resource>) = closeAll() override fun afterRestore(c: Context<out Resource>) = openAll() } // after cracHandler: Kotlin runs property initializers and init blocks top to bottom init { openAll() Core.getGlobalContext().register(cracHandler) } @Synchronized private fun openAll() = repeat(20) { connections += DepotConnection.open() } @Synchronized private fun closeAll() { connections.forEach { it.close() } // nothing open in the image connections.clear() } } The JVM sees the same thing from both: an object implementing org.crac.Resource, held strongly by the pool and weakly by the global context. Java's anonymous class and Kotlin's object : expression both compile to a small inner class, and Resource has two methods, so neither language can use a lambda for it. The Kotlin trap is order. Properties and init blocks run top to bottom. With the init block above cracHandler, a direct reference fails to compile ("variable 'cracHandler' must be initialized"), but the same reference made through a helper method compiles and registers null. Java runs all field initializers before the constructor body, so the Java version has no such trap. Kotlin also writes the parameter as Context<out Resource>, which is Java's Context<? extends Resource>.

h: CRaC, and choosing a startup strategy · Worked example
x: Make the scan listener checkpoint-safe List what the tracking service holds that lives outside the process. There's a database pool, and a scan listener that reads messages from a message queue (a server that holds messages until a reader takes them) and saves them through the pool. There's also an instance id that starts every event id the service writes. The pool and the listener hold sockets. The instance id is plain memory, and that's its problem: every restored copy would get the same one. Give the listener its hooks. It's created after the pool, so it's registered later, which makes the context stop it before the pool closes and start it after the pool is back. Keep the handler in a field. final class ScanListener { private volatile QueueReader reader = newReader(); private final Resource cracHandler = new Resource() { // 1. stop reading, finish the message in hand, and close the queue connection @Override public void beforeCheckpoint(Context<? extends Resource> c) { stopReading(); reader.close(); } // 2. a new reader connects again after the restore @Override public void afterRestore(Context<? extends Resource> c) { reader = newReader(); startReading(); } }; ScanListener() { Core.getGlobalContext().register(cracHandler); } } class ScanListener { @Volatile private var reader = newReader() private val cracHandler = object : Resource { // 1. stop reading, finish the message in hand, and close the queue connection override fun beforeCheckpoint(c: Context<out Resource>) { stopReading(); reader.close() } // 2. a new reader connects again after the restore override fun afterRestore(c: Context<out Resource>) { reader = newReader(); startReading() } } init { Core.getGlobalContext().register(cracHandler) } } Make per-copy state after the restore. The instance id moves out of a final field and into something afterRestore can replace, so two copies restored from one image never write the same event id. final class InstanceId implements Resource { private volatile String value = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); InstanceId() { Core.getGlobalContext().register(this); } // kept alive by whoever holds InstanceId String get() { return value; } @Override public void beforeCheckpoint(Context<? extends Resource> c) { } // 3. every restored copy gets its own id @Override public void afterRestore(Context<? extends Resource> c) { value = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); } } class InstanceId : Resource { @Volatile var value: String = UUID.randomUUID().toString() private set init { Core.getGlobalContext().register(this) } // kept alive by whoever holds InstanceId override fun beforeCheckpoint(c: Context<out Resource>) {} // 3. every restored copy gets its own id override fun afterRestore(c: Context<out Resource>) { value = UUID.randomUUID().toString() } } Test the checkpoint for real on a CRaC JDK, and read the application's console, because jcmd reports success either way. A refused checkpoint names what was still open. java -XX:CRaCCheckpointTo=cr -jar tracker.jar & # send some traffic, then: jcmd tracker.jar JDK.checkpoint # prints "Command executed successfully" in any case # check the service's own log for errors, then restore and track a parcel: java -XX:CRaCRestoreFrom=cr

h: CRaC, and choosing a startup strategy · Quiz
x: On JDK 25, which of these brings back JIT-compiled machine code from an earlier run, so hot methods are fast from the first request? An AOT cache made with -XX:AOTCacheOutput A dynamic AppCDS archive Restoring a CRaC checkpoint The default CDS archive A CRaC image holds the whole process memory, code cache included, so a restored JVM is as warm as it was at the checkpoint. Compiled code in the AOT cache is JEP 544, in development for JDK 28. A service registers, in this order, a database pool, a scan listener and a stats reporter. In which order does the global context call beforeCheckpoint? Pool, listener, reporter Reporter, listener, pool All at once, on separate threads In no defined order Checkpoint notification runs in reverse registration order, and restore notification in registration order. Components created later tend to use earlier ones: the listener saves through the pool, so it must stop before the pool closes and start after it reopens. Nobody wrote hooks for the web client's open connection to a depot server. With the default settings of a CRaC JDK, what does a checkpoint request do? Saves the connection in the image, and it works after the restore Closes it silently, and reopens it after the restore Exits the JVM Fails the checkpoint with an error, runs the restore hooks, and leaves the process running The default policy for open files and sockets is error, which prints an error and fails the checkpoint. Restore notification then starts at once, without an image, and the service carries on. Even the reopen policy can't help a socket: the docs say reopening sockets isn't implemented. One CRaC image is restored into 20 copies. Each copy builds event ids from a random prefix chosen in a constructor before the checkpoint. What happens? All 20 copies use the same prefix, so their ids can collide Each copy gets its own prefix, because the restore reseeds memory The checkpoint fails, because random numbers can't be saved The prefix is lost and becomes null A restore copies the image's memory as it was, so every copy starts with the same prefix. Recreate per-copy values like this in afterRestore. A web service runs JDK 25.0.5, is deployed several times a day, and peak throughput matters. The team wants faster starts without changing code. Which option fits best?
