h: CRaC, and choosing a startup strategy · Key terms
x: Warm-up The time after start-up while the JIT is still compiling hot code, so the program runs slower than it will later. CRaC Coordinated Restore at Checkpoint: save a running JVM to disk, and start copies of it later, already warm. Checkpoint The moment a running process is written to an image on disk. Restore Starting a new process from a checkpoint image; it carries on where the old one stopped. CRIU Checkpoint/Restore In Userspace, the Linux tool CRaC uses to save and rebuild a process. Resource (org.crac) An object with beforeCheckpoint and afterRestore hooks, registered with a CRaC context. File descriptor policy The rule for an open file or socket at checkpoint time; the default, error, fails the checkpoint. Lambda SnapStart AWS Lambda's snapshot and restore of initialized Java functions, using the same org.crac hooks. What does CRaC do? Coordinated Restore at Checkpoint: it writes a running JVM's whole process to an image (with CRIU, on Linux), and later starts new processes from it, warm, with heap, classes and compiled code as they were. In which order are CRaC hooks called? beforeCheckpoint in reverse registration order; afterRestore in registration order. What does CRaC do by default with an open file or socket at checkpoint time? Its policy is error: it prints an error and fails the checkpoint. The process keeps running. Why must you keep your org.crac Resource in a field? The global context holds only a weak reference. A resource nothing else refers to can be garbage-collected, and then its hooks never run. Is CRaC part of mainline OpenJDK? No. There's no JEP. You need a CRaC-enabled vendor build, such as Azul Zulu (17, 21, 25 on Linux, the -crac- files) or BellSoft Liberica (17, 21). jcmd tracker.jar JDK.checkpoint prints "Command executed successfully". Did the checkpoint work? You don't know yet. jcmd always reports success; problems appear in the application's own console. What do copies restored from one image share? Everything in memory at the checkpoint: ids, counters, random seeds, cached tokens. Recreate per-copy values in afterRestore.

h: CRaC, and choosing a startup strategy · Go deeper
x: Three details for when you try CRaC for real. First, the threads. A resource can be called while other threads still use the component. The CRaC best-practices guide sorts components by how threads reach them: an unknown number of threads arriving at random, a known number of threads arriving now and then, or an event loop. For the first case it suggests a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReadWriteLock: borrowers take the read lock, and beforeCheckpoint takes the write lock and keeps it until afterRestore, so callers wait during the checkpoint instead of failing on a closed connection. Second, the policies. If a library holds a file you can't close, -Djdk.crac.resource-policies=<file> points at a policy file. Rules are separated by ---, match by type (file, pipe, socket, filedescriptor) and by fields such as the path or port, and the first matching rule wins. ignore leaves the descriptor to CRIU, close closes it ("an attempt to use it after restore will fail"), and reopen reopens a file at the same position. Use policies as a stopgap; hooks in your own code are clearer. Third, the warm-up you capture. The CRaC docs describe the intended flow as a canary deployment: a new version first serves a little real traffic, which triggers class loading and JIT compilation, then you checkpoint it, and the image becomes part of the release. A checkpoint taken after a made-up warm-up only contains what that warm-up exercised, the same lesson as lesson 2's training run. For Lambda, the Quarkus SnapStart guide also suggests -XX:+TieredCompilation -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, which trades peak speed for less compiling right after a restore. The C1-only run in this lesson's first Try it shows that trade.

h: Capstone: a tiny dependency injection container
x: Wire classes by reflection, add interceptors with proxies, then measure it and move the wiring to build time. Across three sittings you build one small program: a dependency injection container, a small program that builds your objects and hands each one the other objects it needs, so classes don't build their own helpers. It wires the box office of the theatre company from the Class loading track: a seating plan, a price list, a sales book and a link to the city's booking service. Lesson 1 wires the parts by reflection, the way a front-of-house manager reads each desk's card before the doors open. It finds the components from a list or a class path scan, picks each constructor, puts the parts in order with a readable error for a loop, and builds each shared part once, even when eight threads ask at the same moment. Lesson 2 adds @Timed and @Retry through stand-ins, a JDK proxy for parts with an interface and a Byte Buddy subclass for the rest, and refuses at start-up what Kotlin's final classes would otherwise break in silence. Lesson 3 measures the result per call with JMH and at start-up with -Xlog:class+load, looks inside the running container with a class histogram and a heap dump, then generates the same wiring as plain Java at build time and archives what is left. At the end you can defend, with numbers you measured, why some frameworks wire at run time and others moved the work to the build. The capstone draws on every track of this part and calls back its pictures: the theatre of Class loading, bytecode and dynamic proxies (the props team, the dress rehearsal, the stand-in at the stage door, the costume department, the printing press); the warehouse of Memory and garbage collection (the box that never leaves the desk, the cleaning crew's notes); the kitchen of JIT, profiling and benchmarking (the cook's first day, the fair taste test); and the corner shop of Startup and footprint (unpacking every box each morning, yesterday's shelves in the back room). The holder idiom and double-checked locking come from the memory model track. Each lesson names the earlier lesson it leans on, so you can go back for a mechanism when you need it. The labs live in labs/container, one package per lesson (workbench.container.l01 to l03). Lessons 1 and 3 are Java; lesson 2 is Kotlin, on top of lesson 1's Java container. Each lesson's starter code contains the previous lesson's solution, so you can start any sitting fresh. The tests check behaviour, never time: creation order, the messages for loops, one instance under concurrent first access, retry counts, proxy identity, and a generated registry that wires the same graph as the reflective container. Run ./gradlew :container:test --tests 'workbench.container.lNN.*' from labs/, and ./gradlew :container:solutionTest for the reference answers. The demos run the reference container from src/solution, so they work before you finish a lab. Lesson 3's demos start child JVMs and take ten to twenty seconds; its AOT cache commands need JDK 25.0.4 or later and say so. A container automates the wiring block of main, like a front-of-house manager reading each desk's card: find the components, build each one from its constructor, and decide how many instances exist. Scan with getResources and Class.forName(name, false, loader); @Component needs RUNTIME retention, and every scanned class is loaded on every start. Pick the @Inject or only public constructor, skip Kotlin's synthetic ones, match by type, and order the graph depth-first post-order with a path that names any loop. A singleton cell with double-checked locking on a volatile field builds one instance under concurrent first access; check-then-act and recursive computeIfAbsent don't. Interfaces get a JDK proxy (identity equals, invokeDefault, unwrapped exceptions, annotations on the interface); classes get a Byte Buddy subclass that intercepts self-calls but not final members. Kotlin is final by default: open the class and methods, use all-open, or add an interface, and let the container refuse what it can't intercept instead of skipping it. Per call, proxies cost a few hundred bytes at most, and B/op is far steadier than time; at start-up the reflective container loaded 2,207 classes against 991 for generated wiring. Generated wiring does the graph work in the build and wires with holders and new; it gives up run-time flexibility, and a failed holder stays failed until restart. A class histogram says what is alive, a heap dump says who holds it; the container held its parts and Byte Buddy's loader, while the JDK proxy class and annotation instances stay for the life of the application class loader. Archives and caches help most when little is made at run time: AppCDS skips proxies and custom-loader classes, so build-time wiring and an AOT cache work best together.

Generated wiring leaves almost nothing to make at start-up, and suits native image. Review questions for any container What does it do at start-up that depends only on the classes? Which of my methods are really intercepted, and how did I check? What allocates per call on the hot path, in B/op? How many classes does a cold start load, and how many are made at run time? h: Capstone: a tiny dependency injection container: track quiz
x: A teammate's scanner finds no components in production, though the same code finds twelve in the IDE. Production runs from a JAR built by a custom packaging step. What do you check first? Whether @Component has @Retention(RUNTIME) Whether the JAR has directory entries for the package Whether the classes are compiled with -parameters Whether the JIT has compiled the scanner getResources("com/acme/theatre") finds a package in a JAR only through the directory's own entry. The IDE runs from a build directory, where every package is a real directory. A retention problem, the tempting first option, would fail in the IDE too. Kotlin: class PriceRules @Inject constructor(val feePercent: Int = 3, val currency: String = "EUR"). What does the lab's Constructors.pick do? Picks the primary constructor Picks the no-argument constructor Refuses: there are two @Inject constructors Picks the synthetic DefaultConstructorMarker constructor When every parameter has a default, kotlinc adds a public no-argument constructor, and it copied @Inject onto it. The synthetic one is filtered out, but two real marked constructors remain. Don't give injected parameters defaults. Eight threads call get(SeatingPlan.class) on a fresh container at the same moment. Which implementation builds exactly one SeatingPlan? if (map.get(t) == null) map.put(t, create(t)) on a ConcurrentHashMap A recursive map.computeIfAbsent(t, this::create) A per-component cell: volatile read, then lock, read again, create synchronized only around map.put Check-then-act lets every thread that saw null create one, and a lock around put alone keeps that gap open. A recursive computeIfAbsent may throw Recursive update when keys share a bin. The cell checks again under its lock, so only the first thread runs the factory. BookingClient is implemented by a final Kotlin class RemoteBookingClient, with @Retry on the interface method reserve. What does the lab's container do? A subclass can't override a final method, so Byte Buddy leaves it alone and the annotation does nothing. The lab's container checks intercepted methods for final and refuses at start-up. Which number from ProxyCallBench belongs in a CI check that the booking stand-in hasn't become more expensive? ns/op of the JDK proxy row The ratio of the JDK proxy time to the direct time B/op (gc.alloc.rate.norm) with a small margin The number of JIT compilations On a shared machine, the time error was larger than most scores and the JDK proxy's time ranged from about 110 ns to over 3,000 across runs, while its bytes per call stayed at 208 to 213. Classes from JARs, Byte Buddy's own included, do come from the archive, so the third option is wrong. After the reflective container is dropped and a GC runs, which of these is still loaded? The Byte Buddy subclass Byte Buddy's ByteArrayClassLoader The JDK proxy class for BookingClient The SingletonCell objects Nothing outside the container pointed at the Byte Buddy object, its class or its loader, so the whole chain was collected. The JDK proxy class was defined in the application class loader and is cached by Proxy for that loader, so it stays as long as the application runs. Design review: a program starts once a week, runs for days, and loads plugins (extra parts in separate JAR files) from a directory chosen at start-up. Which wiring fits best? Run-time wiring: the component set isn't known until start-up, and one slow start a week costs little Build-time wiring: it is always faster Native image: it starts fastest No container: wire everything by hand in main Build-time wiring needs the component set when you build, and plugins chosen at start-up break that. h: Wire classes by reflection · What we'll build: a container for the box office, starting with ten lines of reflection
x: A tour of the container: wiring by reflection, interceptors through proxies, then the same wiring generated at build time Most programs start with a block like this somewhere near main. Here it sets up the box office: Java BookingConfig config = new BookingConfig(); SeatingPlan plan = new SeatingPlan(); BoxOffice office = new BoxOffice( new RemoteBookingClient(config), // talks to the city's booking service new PriceList(plan), new SalesBook()); Kotlin val config = BookingConfig() val plan = SeatingPlan() val office = BoxOffice( RemoteBookingClient(config), // talks to the city's booking service PriceList(plan), SalesBook()) That block is dependency injection done by hand. A dependency is an object that another object needs to do its job, and injecting it means handing it in from outside, here through the constructor. BoxOffice never calls new on its helpers, so a test can hand it a fake booking service and never touch the network. The block has two jobs, and both get harder as the program grows. It must build things in the right order: config before the booking client that reads it. And it must share the right objects: one plan for everyone. With six classes you do that in your head. With eighty, someone adds a constructor parameter, and the block stops compiling in three places. Picture the theatre's front-of-house manager an hour before the doors open. Every desk in the foyer has a card that says what it needs before it can open. The box office card says "the booking link, the price list, the sales book", and the price list's card says "the seating plan". The manager reads every card, sets things out so that nothing opens before what it needs, and puts a single seating plan where everyone can reach it. A container is that manager, written in code, and the cards are the constructors. The manager makes three decisions for each desk, and so does a container. Which classes take part? We'll call them components. How do you build one? Its constructor says what it needs. How many of each should exist? That's its scope. Over three sittings, we'll build a container that makes all three decisions, as the figure shows. This sitting wires the parts by reflection, the JDK's way of asking a class about itself while the program runs. The next one wraps some parts in proxies, the stand-ins from the Class loading track, to time and retry their calls. The last one measures what all of it costs, then writes the same wiring out before the program starts. Each lab begins with the previous lab's solution, so you can pick up at any sitting. The smallest container fits in ten lines. type.getConstructors() returns a class's public constructors as Constructor objects. getParameterTypes() lists what one needs, and newInstance(args) calls it, which creates the object and runs the constructor exactly as new would. Build each parameter first, the same way, and you have a container: Java static Object build(Class<?> type) throws ReflectiveOperationException { Constructor<?> c = type.getConstructors()[0]; // the card: what it needs Object[] args = new Object[c.getParameterCount()]; for (int i = 0; i < args.length; i++) args[i] = build(c.getParameterTypes()[i]); // build those first return c.newInstance(args); // then the part itself } Kotlin fun build(type: Class<*>): Any { val c = type.constructors[0] // the card: what it needs return c.newInstance(*c.parameterTypes.map { build(it) }.toTypedArray()) // those first, then the part } Read it as one sentence: to build a part, build everything its constructor asks for, then call the constructor. The demo hands it a box office whose PriceList and SeatFinder both need a SeatingPlan. By hand, new SeatingPlan printed once. By reflection it printed twice: by reflection: new SeatingPlan new PriceList new SeatingPlan new SeatFinder new BoxOffice Two seating plans for one hall, and each of them is sure it's the real one. Our ten lines have no memory, so they build a fresh plan for every constructor that asks. That's one of four flaws, and this lesson fixes all of them. The code takes "the first" constructor, when a class may have several. It has no list of the classes that take part. It would loop forever if two cards needed each other. And it builds a shared part once per request instead of once. Let's start with the list. Count the seating plans Read TinyContainerDemo (or the Kotlin twin). PriceList and SeatFinder both need a SeatingPlan. Predict how many times new SeatingPlan prints in each half. Run it from labs/. Give build a memory: add static final Map<Class<?>, Object> made = new HashMap<>();, return made.get(type) when it's there, and call made.put(type, result) before returning. In Kotlin, made.getOrPut(type) { ... } does both. Run it again. TinyContainerDemo.java package workbench.container.l01.demo; import java.lang.reflect.Constructor; /** The smallest container that works: read a constructor, build its parameters first, then call it. */ public class TinyContainerDemo { public static class SeatingPlan { public SeatingPlan() { System.out.println(" new SeatingPlan"); } } public static class PriceList { public PriceList(SeatingPlan plan) { System.out.println(" new PriceList"); } } public static class SeatFinder { public SeatFinder(SeatingPlan plan) { System.out.println(" new SeatFinder"); h: Wire classes by reflection · Find the parts: a list you write, or a scan through a class loader
x: The simplest way to tell a container which classes take part is a list you write: new Container(List.of(BoxOffice.class, SalesBook.class, ...)). A list is fast and plain, and it's one more file to keep in step with the code. The usual alternative is to mark each component with an annotation, a label in the source that tools can read, such as @Component, and then to search for the label. That search goes through a class loader. A class loader is the props team from Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization. It fetches each class only when a scene first needs it, and asks its senior first. loader.getResources("workbench/container/l01/demo/app") asks the team where a package's directory is. It answers with one URL for every place on the class path (the list of directories and JAR files the JVM loads classes from) that holds the package. For a build directory it's a file: URL; inside a JAR it's a jar:file:...!/workbench/... URL. You list the .class files there and turn each file name into a class name. Then you load each class, and one argument decides what runs: Java Class<?> c = Class.forName(name, false, loader); // load and link, no <clinit> if (c.isAnnotationPresent(Component.class)) components.add(c); Kotlin val c = Class.forName(name, false, loader) // load and link, no <clinit> if (c.isAnnotationPresent(Component::class.java)) components += c false means "fetch the prop and check it, but don't hold its dress rehearsal". The rehearsal is <clinit>, a class's static initializer, the code that sets its static fields, and the JVM runs it once, on the class's first real use. The one-argument Class.forName(name) holds the rehearsal on the spot. In a scan, that runs every static initializer in the package, components or not, before anyone has asked for anything. The demo's package has two classes whose initializers print a line, and with true both lines appear in the middle of the scan: AttendanceLog.<clinit>: opening the attendance file TicketArchive.<clinit>: loading 40,000 old tickets The annotation needs one setting too. @Component must carry @Retention(RUNTIME). With the default, CLASS, javac writes the label into the class file, but the JVM never shows it to reflection, so isAnnotationPresent says false and the scan finds nothing. Nothing fails, either. The container just starts empty. A scan has a price that a list doesn't. It loads every class in the package, including the ones that turn out not to be components. In the demo, scanning an 11-class package loaded 272 classes: the 11, plus the JDK code for listing directories, reading streams and checking annotations. Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it pictured the JVM as a corner shop that unpacks and checks every box each morning: every class it loads is found, read and checked again on every launch. A large program that scans thousands of classes pays for all of them at every start, even for the ones it throws away. One more trap hides in JAR files. getResources finds a package inside a JAR only when the JAR has an entry for the directory itself. Most build tools write those entries, but a JAR packed with files only gives the scan zero roots. Again nothing fails: the props team simply reports an empty store. So the lab's container takes a list, and a ClassScanner (given complete) can build that list with forName(name, false, loader). Next, the container must read each card. Scan a package, then hold every dress rehearsal by accident Read ScanDemo (or ScanDemo.kt). TicketArchive and AttendanceLog in the app package print a line from their static initializers. Predict: does either line print during the scan? Then run it. Set INITIALIZE = true and run it again. Then read the last two lines: the same package packed into two JAR files. Set INITIALIZE back to false. h: Wire classes by reflection · Read each card: pick one constructor, then put the parts in order
x: Every card must be readable, and in code a card is a constructor. A class can have several, and reflection hands them back in no order you can rely on, so "the first" is a coin toss. The lab's rule is the one most containers use. If exactly one public constructor carries @Inject, use it. If the class has only one public constructor, use that. Otherwise refuse, with a message that says what to do: TwoDoors has 2 public constructors; mark the one to use with @Inject. Kotlin makes "only one public constructor" harder than it looks. Write class PriceList(val plan: SeatingPlan, val feePercent: Int = 3), and the JVM sees two public constructors: yours, and a synthetic one, made by the compiler rather than by you, that takes an extra int and a DefaultConstructorMarker. Kotlin callers use it when they leave feePercent out. It's the $default trick that Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output found in the prompt book's shorthand, applied to a constructor. The container skips it with isSynthetic(). When every parameter has a default, kotlinc adds a third, a real no-argument constructor, and in this track's run it copied @Inject onto that one too. The container then sees two marked constructors and refuses. The cure is simple: don't give injected parameters defaults. Each parameter is matched by its type, never by its name. A class file keeps parameter names only when javac runs with -parameters (-java-parameters for kotlinc), so reflection usually reports arg0 and arg1. The type is always there. A parameter of interface type, such as BookingClient, goes to the one component that implements it, here RemoteBookingClient. None, or two, is an error. Now the order. Visit a component, visit everything its constructor needs, and only then add the component to the list. That's a depth-first, post-order walk: depth first because it follows one card's needs all the way down before it moves on, and post-order because a component joins the list after its needs. The result is a creation order, a list in which every component comes after everything it depends on. A shared part joins once, because the walk skips anything already done. The figure numbers the box office's parts in the order the walk adds them. The same walk finds loops. Keep a path: the components you're inside right now. If you reach one that's already on the path, you've come back to a card that is still waiting for its own needs. Picture three cards that point in a circle: the rota of who works which night needs the cast list, the cast list needs the rehearsal plan, and the rehearsal plan needs the rota. The container reports the slice of the path from the repeated class back to itself: Dependency cycle: Rota -> CastList -> RehearsalPlan -> Rota Here the manager picture breaks, in a useful way. A manager can improvise when a card is unclear or two cards point at each other, and often gets away with it. A container that improvises, picking a constructor or breaking a loop by guessing, builds a program nobody wrote. So the lab's container reads every card in its own constructor, before it builds a single part. A container should refuse a card it can't read, before the doors open. Check the whole graph when the container is created. A missing part, a doubtful constructor or a loop then stops the program as it starts, with a message, instead of at the first ticket of the night. Building the parts can still wait until someone asks for them, and that's where the last flaw lives. Predict the order, then make a loop Read GraphDemo. The scan returns the components in name order, and the walk starts from each one in turn. Write down the creation order you expect for all nine. Run it and compare. Then run the Kotlin twin, which ends with two refusals. In app/SalesBook.java, change the constructor to public SalesBook(BoxOffice office) {}. Predict the message, then run GraphDemo again. Undo the change afterwards. h: Wire classes by reflection · Build each shared part once, even when eight threads ask first
x: A singleton component has one instance per container, created the first time someone asks for it: the one seating plan. A prototype component is created again on every request, like a fresh basket for each customer at the box office. Singleton is the default, and it's where the bugs live, because the first request often arrives on several threads at once. (A thread is one path of work running beside others in the same program.) When the doors open, eight customers can reach the box office in the same second. The obvious memory for our ten lines is a map from class to instance: look the class up, and build the part only if it's missing. That's check-then-act, the race from Race conditions: why count++ lies. Every thread that reads null before the first put builds a plan of its own. The demo releases eight threads at once on a SeatingPlan that takes 20 ms to read the hall's map: check-then-act on a map constructor ran 8 times, threads saw 8 instance(s) Eight customers, eight seating plans. ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent looks like the fix, because it builds a missing value atomically, in one step that no other thread can split. But a container calls it recursively: building BoxOffice means building SalesBook first, from inside the function that builds BoxOffice. The Javadoc forbids that; the function must not change the map. In practice the result depends on luck. The map keeps its entries in numbered buckets called bins, chosen from each key's hash code. Two keys in different bins work. Two in the same bin throw: computeIfAbsent, boxOffice needs priceList: worked computeIfAbsent, boxOffice needs salesBook: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Recursive update With Class keys, the hash code changes from run to run, so the same container would fail on some starts and not on others. Nobody wants to debug that on opening night. The JVM has a lazy singleton of its own: the holder idiom from Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders. A nested class keeps the instance in a static final field, and the JVM sets that field in the class's dress rehearsal, once, under the class initialization lock. It's the best tool when you can write one holder class per singleton before you compile. A reflective container can't, because it learns its components only when the program runs. Lesson 3 of this track generates those holder classes. So the lab gives each singleton a small cell that uses double-checked locking. In that lesson's shop, two assistants saw the stockroom door shut and both went to open it. The fix was to look, and only if the door is shut, take the key and look again: Java T value = instance; // volatile read: no lock once it's built if (value == null) { synchronized (this) { value = instance; // someone may have built it while we waited if (value == null) instance = value = factory.get(); } } return value; Kotlin var value = instance // @Volatile var instance: T? = null if (value == null) { synchronized(this) { value = instance // someone may have built it while we waited if (value == null) { value = factory(); instance = value } } } return value!! volatile is what makes the first, unlocked read safe. A thread that reads a non-null reference also sees every write the constructor made before the reference was stored. Without it, a thread could see the reference and still read the new object's fields as zero: the stockroom door open, the lights still off. In the demo, the cell ran the constructor once, and all eight threads saw one instance. You may worry about the locks. Building BoxOffice holds its cell's lock while it builds PriceList, which takes another cell's lock. Nested locks usually bring a risk of deadlock: two threads each waiting for a lock the other holds. Deadlock, livelock and starvation showed that such a freeze needs the waits to form a loop. Here every lock is taken along an arrow of the graph, from a component to something it needs, and the container has already refused loops. One more difference from a holder: if the constructor throws, the cell stays empty and the next get tries again. A dress rehearsal that fails is a failure for good, and the class answers NoClassDefFoundError from then on. Race for the first seating plan Read SingletonRaceDemo (or the Kotlin twin). Each row releases eight threads at the same moment, and SeatingPlan takes 20 ms to build. Predict the two numbers on each of the first two rows, and which computeIfAbsent line fails. Run it twice. Do the numbers change? h: Wire classes by reflection · Worked example
x: Break a loop the container reported The container refuses to start with Dependency cycle: BoxOffice -> SeatFinder -> BoxOffice. Here are the two classes. Read them and ask what each one needs while it's being built, and what it only needs later, inside a method. @Component public class BoxOffice { private final SoldSeats sold = new SoldSeats(); // hidden inside private final SeatFinder finder; public BoxOffice(SeatFinder finder) { this.finder = finder; } public String sellBestSeat() { String seat = finder.bestFreeSeat(); sold.add(seat); return seat; } public boolean isSold(String seat) { return sold.contains(seat); } } @Component public class SeatFinder { private final BoxOffice office; public SeatFinder(BoxOffice office) { this.office = office; } public String bestFreeSeat() { return SEATS.stream().filter(s -> !office.isSold(s)).findFirst().orElseThrow(); } } @Component class BoxOffice(private val finder: SeatFinder) { private val sold = SoldSeats() // hidden inside fun sellBestSeat(): String = finder.bestFreeSeat().also { sold.add(it) } fun isSold(seat: String): Boolean = sold.contains(seat) } @Component class SeatFinder(private val office: BoxOffice) { fun bestFreeSeat(): String = SEATS.first { !office.isSold(it) } } SeatFinder doesn't need a BoxOffice at all. It needs to know which seats are sold, and that list lives in SoldSeats, hidden inside BoxOffice. BoxOffice needs the list to write to and the finder to ask. The loop exists only because the list is hidden. Give the list its own component. Both classes depend on it, and the arrows no longer close a loop: SoldSeats is created first, then SeatFinder, then BoxOffice. @Component public class SoldSeats { private final Set<String> seats = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); public void add(String seat) { seats.add(seat); } public boolean contains(String seat) { return seats.contains(seat); } } @Component public class SeatFinder { private final SoldSeats sold; public SeatFinder(SoldSeats sold) { this.sold = sold; } public String bestFreeSeat() { return SEATS.stream().filter(s -> !sold.contains(s)).findFirst().orElseThrow(); } } @Component public class BoxOffice { private final SoldSeats sold; private final SeatFinder finder; public BoxOffice(SoldSeats sold, SeatFinder finder) { this.sold = sold; this.finder = finder; } public String sellBestSeat() { String seat = finder.bestFreeSeat(); sold.add(seat); return seat; } } @Component class SoldSeats { private val seats = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet<String>() fun add(seat: String) { seats += seat } fun contains(seat: String): Boolean = seat in seats } @Component class SeatFinder(private val sold: SoldSeats) { fun bestFreeSeat(): String = SEATS.first { !sold.contains(it) } } @Component class BoxOffice(private val sold: SoldSeats, private val finder: SeatFinder) { fun sellBestSeat(): String = finder.bestFreeSeat().also { sold.add(it) } } If two parts really do need each other at call time, real containers offer a lookup instead of an object: jakarta.inject.Provider<BoxOffice> in the Jakarta standard, ObjectProvider<BoxOffice> in Spring. The constructor then receives something that finds the BoxOffice later, inside a method. The lab's container doesn't offer that, on purpose. Reach for it after you've tried the split, not before.

h: Wire classes by reflection · Quiz
x: Your scanner calls Class.forName(name), with one argument, for every class in com.acme.theatre. TicketArchive has static final List<Ticket> OLD = loadFromDisk(); and nobody ever asks the container for it. When does loadFromDisk() run? Never, because nothing asks for TicketArchive During the scan, because the one-argument forName initializes every class it loads When the JIT compiles TicketArchive Only if TicketArchive is annotated @Component The one-argument Class.forName loads, links and initializes, so <clinit> runs during the scan for every class in the package, component or not. Class.forName(name, false, loader) loads and links without initializing. Being a component doesn't matter either way, which is why the last option tempts: the scan checks the annotation only after the class is loaded. A container matches constructor parameters by name with Parameter.getName(). Gradle compiles BoxOffice(BookingClient booking, SalesBook book) with javac's default options. What names does the container see? arg0 and arg1 booking and book BookingClient and SalesBook A NoSuchFieldException, because the names are private A method's descriptor in the class file carries types, not names, and javac writes a MethodParameters attribute only when you pass -parameters (-java-parameters for kotlinc). Without it, reflection makes up arg0 and arg1. The second option is what the source says, and that's the trap. It's also why the lab matches by type: the type is always in the descriptor. A program's container scans 4,000 classes at start-up, though only 300 are components, and none of the 4,000 has a static initializer. What does the scan add to every start? Nothing, because classes without static initializers are free Only the cost of calling 300 constructors Finding, parsing and verifying 4,000 classes, and reading their annotations A garbage collection to unload the 3,700 non-components Loading is the expensive part even without initialization: the JVM finds each class file, parses it into metaspace and verifies its bytecode, on every launch. The 3,700 non-components stay loaded, because nothing unloads classes of the application class loader. Initialization would add the static initializers on top. A teammate's SingletonCell uses double-checked locking, but the instance field is a plain field, not volatile. What can go wrong? Two threads can both run the factory The nested locks can deadlock Nothing on x86, so it's fine in production A thread can see a non-null reference and still read the new object's fields as zero The lock still makes the factory run once, so the first option doesn't happen. What the unlocked first read lacks is a happens-before edge to the constructor's writes: without volatile, the reference can become visible before the fields behind it, the stockroom door open with the lights still off. "It works on x86" describes one processor and one JIT, not what the memory model allows. SalesBook needs AttendanceLog, AttendanceLog needs BoxOffice, and BoxOffice needs SalesBook. The container is built with the list [SalesBook, BoxOffice, AttendanceLog]. What message does the lab's creationOrder throw? Dependency cycle: SalesBook -> AttendanceLog -> BoxOffice -> SalesBook Dependency cycle: BoxOffice -> SalesBook -> AttendanceLog -> BoxOffice A StackOverflowError, because the walk never ends Dependency cycle: SalesBook -> BoxOffice -> AttendanceLog -> SalesBook The walk starts at the first component in the list, SalesBook, follows its constructor to AttendanceLog, then to BoxOffice, and then reaches SalesBook, which is still on the path. The message is the path from the repeated class back to itself, in the order the walk went. Without a path, the recursion would overflow the stack, which is what the ten-line container from section 1 does.

h: Wire classes by reflection · Key terms
x: Dependency injection Handing a class the objects it needs, usually through its constructor, instead of letting it create them itself. Dependency injection container A small program that builds your objects and hands each one the other objects it needs, so classes don't build their own helpers. Component A class the container creates and hands to others. Spring and other frameworks call the instances beans. Scope How many instances of a component exist: one per container (singleton) or a new one per request (prototype). Creation order A list of all components in which each one comes after everything it depends on. Also called a topological order. Class path scan Finding classes by asking a class loader for a package's directory and loading every class file in it. Double-checked locking Read a volatile field without a lock; only if it is empty, lock, read it again, and build. Fast after the first call. What does Class.forName(name, false, loader) do that Class.forName(name) doesn't? It loads and links the class without initializing it, so no static initializer runs. A scanner should always pass false. Why does @Component need @Retention(RUNTIME)? With the default CLASS retention the annotation is in the class file, but reflection can't see it, so isAnnotationPresent returns false. Kotlin class Prices(val plan: SeatingPlan, val feePercent: Int = 3): how many public constructors does getConstructors() return? Two: (SeatingPlan, int) and a synthetic (SeatingPlan, int, int, DefaultConstructorMarker) for the default argument. Filter with isSynthetic(). In what order does a container create components? Depth-first post-order: each component after everything its constructor needs. Shared dependencies appear once. How does a depth-first walk detect a dependency loop? It keeps a path of the components it is still inside. Reaching one of them again is a loop; the path from that component back to itself is the message. Why not build a container's singletons with a recursive ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent? The mapping function must not change the map. If the inner key lands in the same bin, it throws IllegalStateException: Recursive update, and with Class keys that depends on identity hash codes. Why can nested SingletonCell locks not deadlock? Each lock is taken along a dependency arrow, from a component to what it needs. A deadlock would need the arrows to form a loop, and the container rejects loops at start-up.

h: Wire classes by reflection · Go deeper
x: Spring creates its singletons eagerly at the end of start-up by default, after the scan and the graph work, so that a constructor that throws stops the start too. The lab's container is lazy, like a CDI client proxy (CDI is the Jakarta standard for dependency injection), which creates its bean on the first method call. Neither is wrong; they put the same failure at different times. Spring can also resolve some loops that the lab refuses. With field or setter injection, it can hand out a reference to an object whose constructor has finished but whose fields aren't all set yet, from a cache of "early" singleton references. Constructor injection can never do that, because the object doesn't exist until its constructor's arguments do. That's one reason constructor injection is the recommended style: an impossible graph fails loudly. Since Spring Boot 2.6, even the setter-injection kind of loop is refused unless you set spring.main.allow-circular-references=true. Three things a production container adds to this lesson's graph. Qualifiers, for when two components implement the same interface and the injection point must say which (@Named, @Qualifier). Generic types, so that Repository<Show> and Repository<Seat> are different dependencies (the lab compares erased classes only). And lookups such as Provider<T>, which turn a hard edge into one that is followed at call time. Each one makes the graph work harder, and each one is easier to check at build time than at start-up, which is where lesson 3 of this track ends up.

h: Add interceptors with proxies · An interceptor runs around a call, and proceed() passes it on
x: An interceptor runs around a call and proceed() hands it on: a JDK proxy for a component with interfaces, a Byte Buddy subclass for one without, and retry only the smallest call that is safe to repeat Here is what timing and retries look like when a method does them itself: Java public String reserve(String seat, long priceCents) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) { try { return remote.reserve(seat, priceCents); } // the one line of real work catch (BookingUnavailableException e) { if (attempt == 3) throw e; } } } finally { timings.record("reserve", System.nanoTime() - t0); } } Kotlin fun reserve(seat: String, priceCents: Long): String { val t0 = System.nanoTime() try { var attempt = 1 while (true) { try { return remote.reserve(seat, priceCents) } // the one line of real work catch (e: BookingUnavailableException) { if (attempt++ == 3) throw e } } } finally { timings.record("reserve", System.nanoTime() - t0) } } One line of real work and a dozen lines of plumbing, copied into confirm, cancel and every method the booking service will ever grow. Decorator and Proxy moved that plumbing into a class that wraps the real one, but you still write one wrapper per interface. And the timer and the retry are tangled together, so changing one means reading both. An interceptor is the plumbing written once, for any method. Think of the stand-in at the stage door with one routine: note the time, pass the request on, note the time again. The container hands each interceptor an Invocation, which carries the method's name, its arguments, and proceed(), which means "pass it on". Here is the lab's timer: Java public Object intercept(Invocation inv) { long start = clock.getAsLong(); boolean failed = true; try { Object result = inv.proceed(); // pass it on failed = false; return result; } finally { log.record(inv.getName(), clock.getAsLong() - start, failed); } } Kotlin override fun intercept(inv: Invocation): Any? { val start = clock.asLong var failed = true try { return inv.proceed().also { failed = false } // pass it on } finally { log.record(inv.name, clock.asLong - start, failed) } } Read it in order. First it notes the start time and assumes the worst. Then it passes the call on and, if nothing was thrown, marks it a success. Finally, whatever happened, it records the name, the time taken and the outcome. The finally is the tricky line: it runs on success and on failure, so a call that throws is timed too. Several interceptors make a chain, like helpers standing in a row at the door. proceed() hands the call to the next helper, and after the last one it runs the real method. A retry interceptor is a loop that calls proceed() again after a failure it was told to retry. Real frameworks have the same shape: InvocationContext.proceed() in Jakarta, the standard set of Java server libraries, and MethodInvocation.proceed() in Spring are this method under other names. The order of the chain changes what you measure. With the timer outside the retry, it sees one call that took as long as all the attempts together. With the timer inside, it records every attempt on its own. The demo sends one booking call that fails twice through both orders, with a fake clock that moves 10 ms per read. Its two result lines: result hold-C12 after 3 calls, log [Call(name=Booking.reserve, nanos=10000000, failed=false)] result hold-C12 after 3 calls, log [Call(name=Booking.reserve, nanos=10000000, failed=true), Call(name=Booking.reserve, nanos=10000000, failed=true), Call(name=Booking.reserve, nanos=10000000, failed=false)] The lab puts @Timed first, outside, because the customer waited for all of it. The annotations themselves only mark methods. Like @Component in lesson 1, they need @Retention(RUNTIME) so the container can read them with getAnnotation. Now the container has to put the chain in front of the real object, and how it does that depends on whether the part has an interface. Swap the order of two interceptors Read ChainDemo (or the Kotlin twin). The "booking service" fails twice and then answers. A third interceptor prints each time the chain reaches it. Predict, for each order: how many -> lines, and how many entries in the log? Run it. Then change RetryInterceptor(3, ...) to RetryInterceptor(2, ...) and predict what the first order prints. ChainDemo.java package workbench.container.l02.demo; import workbench.container.l02.CallLog; import workbench.container.l02.Interceptor; import workbench.container.l02.Invocation; import workbench.container.l02.RetryInterceptor; import workbench.container.l02.TimedInterceptor; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; import java.util.function.LongSupplier; /** One booking call that fails twice, sent through the same two interceptors in both orders. */ public class ChainDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { AtomicLong ticks = new AtomicLong(); LongSupplier clock = () -> ticks.addAndGet(10_000_000); // a fake clock: 10 ms per read Interceptor shout = inv -> { // a third interceptor, to watch proceed() System.out.println(" -> " + inv.getName()); try { return inv.proceed(); } finally { System.out.println(" <- " + inv.getName()); } }; for (String order : List.of("timed, retry", "retry, timed")) { CallLog log = new CallLog(); Interceptor timed = new TimedInterceptor(log, clock); Interceptor retry = new RetryInterceptor(3, List.of(IllegalStateException.class)); List<Interceptor> chain = order.startsWith("timed") ? List.of(timed, retry, shout) : List.of(retry, timed, shout); AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); System.out.println(order + ":"); Object result = new Invocation("Booking.reserve", new Object[] {"C12"}, chain, () -> { if (calls.incrementAndGet() < 3) throw new IllegalStateException("booking service timed out"); // fails twice return "hold-C12"; }).proceed(); System.out.println(" result " + result + " after " + calls.get() + " calls, log " + log.calls()); } } } ./gradlew :container:demo -Pmain=workbench.container.l02.demo.ChainDemo labs/container/src/demo/java/workbench/container/l02/demo/ChainDemo.java ChainDemo.kt package workbench.container.l02.demo import workbench.container.l02.CallLog import workbench.container.l02.Interceptor import workbench.container.l02.Invocation import workbench.container.l02.RetryInterceptor import workbench.container.l02.TimedInterceptor import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import java.util.function.LongSupplier // One booking call that fails twice, sent through the same two interceptors in both orders. fun main() { val ticks = AtomicLong() val clock = LongSupplier { ticks.addAndGet(10_000_000) } // a fake clock: 10 ms per read val shout = Interceptor { inv -> // a third interceptor, to watch proceed() println(" -> ${inv.name}") try { inv.proceed() } finally { println(" <- ${inv.name}") } } for (order in listOf("timed, retry", "retry, timed")) { val log = CallLog() val timed = TimedInterceptor(log, clock) val retry = RetryInterceptor(3, listOf(IllegalStateException::class.java)) val chain = if (order.startsWith("timed")) listOf(timed, retry, shout) else listOf(retry, timed, shout) var calls = 0 println("$order:") val result = Invocation("Booking.reserve", arrayOf("C12"), chain) { if (++calls < 3) throw IllegalStateException("booking service timed out") // fails twice "hold-C12" }.proceed() println(" result $result after $calls calls, log ${log.calls()}") } } ./gradlew :container:demo -Pmain=workbench.container.l02.demo.ChainDemoKt labs/container/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/container/l02/demo/ChainDemo.kt Both orders print three ->/<- pairs, because the retry calls proceed() three times. With the timer outside, the log has one entry, failed=false, 10 ms on the fake clock. With the retry outside, it has three: two failed=true, one failed=false. With two attempts, the call throws IllegalStateException: booking service timed out after two pairs, and the one log entry is recorded with failed=true on the way out.

h: Add interceptors with proxies · A part with an interface gets a stand-in at the stage door: a JDK proxy
x: For each component, the container now decides how its interceptors will run. If the component implements an interface, it gets a JDK proxy. Proxy.newProxyInstance writes a class that implements the interfaces and sends every call to one InvocationHandler, as Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy showed: the stand-in at the stage door, with the actor behind it. The container creates the real object first, the target, and the proxy holds it. Spring Framework documents the same rule for its own proxies: if the target implements at least one interface, it uses a JDK proxy. (Spring Boot, its quick-start layer, switches the default to subclasses, as Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors showed.) That lesson's rules for the handler come back as the four cases you write in the lab, in this order: equals, hashCode and toString arrive with method.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class. Answer them on the proxy itself, by identity. A handler that sends equals to the target makes proxy.equals(proxy) false, and list.remove(proxy) quietly fails. A default method, an interface method with a body, goes to InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, args). Its body then runs with this being the proxy, so the calls inside it come back through the handler. Every other method gets an Invocation with that method's chain, ending in method.invoke(target, args). That last call catches InvocationTargetException and throws its cause, so the caller sees the booking service's own BookingUnavailableException, not a wrapper around it. The demo puts the container's proxy next to one whose handler forwards every method, equals included: bean class: jdk.proxy2.$Proxy5 implements [BookingClient] container's handler p.equals(p)=true listeners.remove(p)=true hashCode is identity=true forward everything p.equals(p)=false listeners.remove(p)=false hashCode is identity=false The forwarding stand-in asked the actor whether the actor was the stand-in, and the actor said no. Fair enough. Two consequences follow from "the proxy implements the interfaces", and both surprise people. First, the object you get back isn't a FlakyBooking. It's a $Proxy5 that implements BookingClient. get(BookingClient.class) works, but get(FlakyBooking.class) can't return it, so the lab's container refuses with a message that names the interface to ask for: FlakyBooking is behind a JDK proxy that implements [BookingClient]; ask for one of those, not for the class Second, the handler only ever sees the interface's Method, so the annotations must sit on the interface. @Timed on the class's method would never be read, and nothing would say so. The container refuses that case when it starts, rather than skip the timer in silence. Kotlin's final classes don't matter on this path. FakeBooking in the tests is a plain, final Kotlin class, and that's fine: the JDK needs only the interface. A part without an interface is a different story. Ask two proxies whether they equal themselves Read ProxyIdentityDemo (or the Kotlin twin). It compares the container's proxy with one whose handler forwards every method to the target. Predict the three booleans on each line. Run it, and read the last line. h: Add interceptors with proxies · A part without an interface gets a costume copy: a Byte Buddy subclass, so final is fatal
x: ShowCloser closes the box office after the last show of the night. It checks the night's code, files the night in the archive, and returns a short note. It has no interface, so there is no job card for a stand-in to copy. Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors had the answer: the costume department sews a full copy of the costume, a subclass that extends the class and replaces some of its methods. Byte Buddy, a library that writes classes while your program runs, does the sewing. Byte Buddy's subclass(type) copies the class's public constructors. The container calls the generated ShowCloser$ByteBuddy$... constructor with the ShowArchive it resolved, and the original class is never created on its own. There is one object. Each intercepted method becomes an override whose @SuperCall callable, a small object that runs super.close(...), sits at the end of the chain. A retry simply calls it again. Because the subclass is the object, a self-call, a call from one of the object's methods to another through this, goes through it too. close calls this.verify(night). this is the subclass, so verify's override runs its own chain. The Class loading track called this the understudy who plays the role, as against the lookalike at the door who passes requests to the actor. The figure shows both: the JDK proxy is the lookalike, and the actor's own calls never pass the door. The lab's test closes night N-17 and reads the log: [ShowCloser.verify, ShowCloser.close]. verify comes first because each timer records when its call ends, and verify ends inside close. A subclass can only intercept what it's allowed to override, and Kotlin makes that a daily problem. A Kotlin class is final unless you write open, and so is each of its members: a role nobody may copy. On a final class, Byte Buddy fails loudly: Cannot subclass primitive, array or final types. On an open class with a plain fun, it succeeds and simply leaves the method alone. @Timed sits on it and does nothing. That silent case is why the lab's container calls check(component) for every component when it starts. It refuses a final class, or a final or private intercepted method, with a message that says what to change. The demo tries two Kotlin classes with the same @Timed method, and the build opens only the second: KFinalPrices: class final=true, feeCents final=true refused: KFinalPrices is final, so no subclass can intercept it: make it open, or give it an interface KOpenedPrices: class final=false, feeCents final=false wired as KOpenedPrices$ByteBuddy$w7Szn3cT, timed calls [KOpenedPrices.feeCents] There are three fixes. Write open on the class and on each intercepted method. Or let the all-open compiler plugin do it for classes that carry an annotation you choose; this lab's build opens classes marked @OpenForProxies: // container/build.gradle.kts plugins { kotlin("plugin.allopen") } allOpen { annotation("workbench.container.l02.demo.OpenForProxies") } kotlin-spring is the same plugin, preset to open the classes Spring creates. The third fix is an interface, which moves the part to the JDK proxy path, where finality doesn't matter. (Quarkus goes a fourth way: by default it rewrites final classes while the program is built, so that it can subclass them.) An annotation only works if a proxy can reach the method. Make the container refuse what no proxy can reach. Each class Byte Buddy writes also gets a class loader of its own, a ByteArrayClassLoader, unless you choose another loading strategy. Lesson 3 counts what that leaves behind. Watch a Kotlin class get refused, then opened Read FinalClassDemo.kt: two identical classes with a @Timed method, one marked @OpenForProxies. The Java twin, FinalClassDemoJava, does the same with a Java final class. Predict the final= flags on each line, and which class the container refuses. Run it. From labs/, run javap -p container/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/container/l02/demo/KOpenedPrices.class and compare it with KFinalPrices.class. h: Add interceptors with proxies · Retry the smallest call that is safe to repeat
x: A retry interceptor makes three promises. It only retries the failures the annotation lists: a BookingUnavailableException is worth another try, a seat that doesn't exist is not. It counts attempts in total, so attempts = 3 means at most three calls. And when it gives up, the caller gets the original exception, not an UndeclaredThrowableException or an InvocationTargetException wrapped around it. The hard part is choosing which call to repeat. Selling a ticket takes two calls to the booking service: reserve holds the seat, and confirm turns the hold into a ticket. reserveAndConfirm is a default method that makes both: Java default String reserveAndConfirm(String seat, long priceCents) { return confirm(reserve(seat, priceCents)); } Kotlin fun reserveAndConfirm(seat: String, priceCents: Long): String = confirm(reserve(seat, priceCents)) Say the first confirm times out. A handler that forwards the default method to the target, and retries it as a whole, repeats the reservation too. The demo's booking service keeps a list of every call it saw: container's proxy: ticket-hold-C12, booking service saw [reserve, confirm (timed out), confirm] timed calls: [BookingClient.reserve, BookingClient.confirm] retry the shell: ticket-hold-C12, booking service saw [reserve, confirm (timed out), reserve, confirm] Both halves print a ticket, and the second also held a second seat: one customer, two seats, and an empty one on the night that nobody else can buy. Through the container, invokeDefault runs the default body on the proxy, so each inner call carries its own @Retry, and the confirmation is retried as a confirmation. That's the rule for default methods from Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy, and the lab tests it. Even a single call is only safe to repeat if the other side can spot the repeat. A timeout doesn't tell you the booking service didn't confirm. It tells you that you don't know. So retry confirm only if it carries a booking reference, the same one on every attempt, which the service uses to recognize a repeat and do the work once. The general name for such a reference is an idempotency key. The interceptor can't know whether a call carries one; the person who writes @Retry on the method has to. Retries also multiply when they nest. With a subclass proxy, a retried close that calls a retried verify runs verify's body up to 3 x 3 = 9 times, as the warm-up asked. A retry repeats whatever you annotate, harmful or not. Put @Retry on the smallest call that is safe to repeat, and only once along a chain of calls. Here the stand-in picture breaks. A real stand-in would notice the same customer coming back twice for the same seat. An interceptor notices nothing. It does exactly what the annotation says, as many times as it says. Retry the confirmation, not the reservation Read RetryDemo (or the Kotlin twin). The booking service's first confirmation times out. The first half uses the container's proxy; the second uses a handler that retries every method as a whole. Predict the list of calls the booking service sees in each half. Run it. RetryDemo.java package workbench.container.l02.demo; import workbench.container.l02.Container; import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingClient; import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.FlakyBooking; import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingScript; import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingUnavailableException; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.List; /** reserveAndConfirm, with one confirmation timing out: what does the booking service see? */ public class RetryDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { Container c = new Container(List.of(BookingScript.class, FlakyBooking.class)); BookingScript script = c.get(BookingScript.class); script.confirmFailures.set(1); String result = c.get(BookingClient.class).reserveAndConfirm("C12", 12_000); System.out.println("container's proxy: " + result + ", booking service saw " + script.seen); System.out.println(" timed calls: " + c.callLog().names()); BookingScript naiveScript = new BookingScript(); naiveScript.confirmFailures.set(1); FlakyBooking target = new FlakyBooking(naiveScript); InvocationHandler retryEverything = (proxy, method, a) -> { // retries any method, default ones too for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) { try { return method.invoke(target, a); // the default body runs on the target } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { if (attempt == 3 || !(e.getCause() instanceof BookingUnavailableException)) throw e.getCause(); } } }; BookingClient naive = (BookingClient) Proxy.newProxyInstance( BookingClient.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[] {BookingClient.class}, retryEverything); System.out.println("retry the shell: " + naive.reserveAndConfirm("C12", 12_000) + ", booking service saw " + naiveScript.seen); } } ./gradlew :container:demo -Pmain=workbench.container.l02.demo.RetryDemo labs/container/src/demo/java/workbench/container/l02/demo/RetryDemo.java RetryDemo.kt package workbench.container.l02.demo import workbench.container.l02.Container import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingClient import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.FlakyBooking import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingScript import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingUnavailableException import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException import java.lang.reflect.Method import java.lang.reflect.Proxy // reserveAndConfirm, with one confirmation timing out: what does the booking service see? fun main() { val c = Container(listOf(BookingScript::class.java, FlakyBooking::class.java)) val script = c.get(BookingScript::class.java) script.confirmFailures.set(1) val result = c.get(BookingClient::class.java).reserveAndConfirm("C12", 12_000) println("container's proxy: $result, booking service saw ${script.seen}") println(" timed calls: ${c.callLog().names()}") val naiveScript = BookingScript().apply { confirmFailures.set(1) } val target = FlakyBooking(naiveScript) val retryEverything = InvocationHandler { _, method, a -> callWithRetry(target, method, a) } // any method, defaults too val naive = Proxy.newProxyInstance(BookingClient::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(BookingClient::class.java), retryEverything) as BookingClient println("retry the shell: ${naive.reserveAndConfirm("C12", 12_000)}, booking service saw ${naiveScript.seen}") } private fun callWithRetry(target: Any, method: Method, a: Array<Any?>?, attempt: Int = 1): Any? = try { method.invoke(target, *(a ?: emptyArray())) // the default body runs on the target } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { if (attempt == 3 || e.cause !is BookingUnavailableException) throw e.cause!! callWithRetry(target, method, a, attempt + 1) } ./gradlew :container:demo -Pmain=workbench.container.l02.demo.RetryDemoKt labs/container/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/container/l02/demo/RetryDemo.kt Both halves return ticket-hold-C12. h: Add interceptors with proxies · Java and Kotlin
x: A part a subclass can intercept, in Java and in Kotlin ShowCloser.java @Component public class ShowCloser { // open unless you write final private final ShowArchive archive; public ShowCloser(ShowArchive archive) { this.archive = archive; } @Timed public String close(String night) { // overridable verify(night); // self-call: intercepted in a subclass archive.file(night); return "closed " + night; } @Timed public void verify(String night) { /* ... */ } public final String hall() { return "Main hall"; } // final on purpose: not intercepted } ShowCloser.kt @Component open class ShowCloser(private val archive: ShowArchive) { // final without open @Timed open fun close(night: String): String { // final without open verify(night) // self-call: intercepted in a subclass archive.file(night) return "closed $night" } @Timed open fun verify(night: String) { /* ... */ } fun hall(): String = "Main hall" // final by default: not intercepted } The two classes compile to the same shape only after you add open in Kotlin. Java's default is overridable, so final is the exception you write; Kotlin's default is final, so open is. That single difference decides whether a subclass proxy can work, and on an open class with a plain fun it fails silently. The all-open plugin flips Kotlin's default for classes with an annotation you choose. Nothing differs for JDK proxies: both languages compile interfaces to ordinary JVM interfaces, and Kotlin interface functions with a body become JVM default methods that invokeDefault can run.

h: Add interceptors with proxies · Worked example
x: Add a third interceptor: @Recorded The theatre wants every cancellation written down with its arguments, so that a customer's complaint can be checked later. Start with the marker. It needs RUNTIME retention and targets methods, like @Timed. @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) @Target(ElementType.METHOD) public @interface Recorded { } @Retention(AnnotationRetention.RUNTIME) @Target(AnnotationTarget.FUNCTION) annotation class Recorded Write the interceptor. It writes the call down before it passes it on, so an attempt that throws is on the record too. It doesn't catch anything: failures are the retry's business, or the caller's. public final class RecordInterceptor implements Interceptor { private final List<String> record; public RecordInterceptor(List<String> record) { this.record = record; } @Override public Object intercept(Invocation inv) { record.add(inv.getName() + Arrays.toString(inv.getArgs())); // 1. write it down first return inv.proceed(); // 2. then pass it on } } class RecordInterceptor(private val record: MutableList<String>) : Interceptor { override fun intercept(inv: Invocation): Any? { record += inv.name + inv.args.contentToString() // 1. write it down first return inv.proceed() // 2. then pass it on } } Decide where it goes in the chain. Outside @Retry, it writes one entry per cancellation the customer asked for. Inside, it writes every attempt. The theatre asked for every request sent to the booking service, so it goes inside: after the timer and the retry. List<Interceptor> chainFor(Method m) { List<Interceptor> chain = new ArrayList<>(); if (m.isAnnotationPresent(Timed.class)) chain.add(new TimedInterceptor(log, clock)); Retry r = m.getAnnotation(Retry.class); if (r != null) chain.add(new RetryInterceptor(r.attempts(), List.of(r.on()))); if (m.isAnnotationPresent(Recorded.class)) chain.add(new RecordInterceptor(record)); // 3. innermost return chain; } fun chainFor(m: Method): List<Interceptor> = buildList { if (m.isAnnotationPresent(Timed::class.java)) add(TimedInterceptor(log, clock)) m.getAnnotation(Retry::class.java)?.let { add(RetryInterceptor(it.attempts, it.on.map { k -> k.java })) } if (m.isAnnotationPresent(Recorded::class.java)) add(RecordInterceptor(record)) // 3. innermost } Teach the container that @Recorded counts as intercepted, in isIntercepted, so check refuses a final recorded method too. Then test through the container: a cancellation that times out once leaves two entries with the same booking reference. If it leaves one, the interceptor sits outside the retry; if it leaves none, the method was never overridden.
