h: Add interceptors with proxies · Quiz
x: A handler has no isDefault branch, so the default method reserveAndConfirm goes through an empty chain to method.invoke(target, args). confirm is @Retry(attempts = 3) on the interface, and its first call times out. What happens? One reservation, two confirmations: the retry still works One reservation and one confirmation, then the timeout reaches the caller Two reservations and two confirmations invokeDefault throws IllegalArgumentException Forwarded to the target, the default body runs with this being the target, so its call to confirm is an ordinary call that never reaches the handler. No interceptor sees it, nothing retries it, and the timeout goes straight out. The first option is what you'd expect if annotations worked by themselves; only invokeDefault makes the inner calls pass through the proxy. Kotlin, no compiler plugins: open class Ushers { @Timed fun assign(seat: String) { ... } }. A container without a start-up check builds a Byte Buddy subclass of it. What happens when a caller runs assign("C12")? Byte Buddy throws Cannot subclass primitive, array or final types The call is timed, because the subclass overrides every method assign runs normally and is never timed, with no error anywhere The JVM throws VerifyError when the subclass loads The class is open, so subclassing works, and the first option doesn't happen. assign has no open, so kotlinc made it final, and Byte Buddy can't override a final method; it leaves it alone. The subclass inherits the original assign, which runs untimed. That silent case is why the lab's container checks intercepted methods for final when it starts. You want to build this container into a GraalVM native image, a program compiled ahead of time into one machine-code file. Which part is the real obstacle? The JDK proxies: native image can't run java.lang.reflect.Proxy at all The singleton cells, because native image has no volatile Nothing: native image supports any code that runs on HotSpot The Byte Buddy subclasses: they are classes defined from bytes at run time, which a closed world can't contain Native image builds a closed world, so every class must exist when the image is built. JDK proxies work if the reachability metadata lists each proxy's interfaces in order, so the first option is wrong. Classes that Byte Buddy writes while the program runs have no place in that world. That's one reason Quarkus generates its intercepted subclasses while the application is built. Every Byte Buddy subclass in the lab is defined by its own ByteArrayClassLoader. After a test drops its last reference to the container, what keeps one of those loaders alive? Nothing it created: the loader can be collected with its class once no instance and no reference to the class is reachable The application class loader, which holds every child loader forever The JIT's code cache, which pins every class it compiled Metaspace, which is never collected A class keeps its loader alive and an object keeps its class alive, so the chain is: container, cell, part, subclass, loader. Remove the root and the whole chain is unreachable, and a full GC can unload the class and free its metaspace. A class loader leak is the same chain with something long-lived, such as a static map or a thread local, still holding one link. A part is intercepted by a subclass. close is @Timed and calls this.verify(), which is also @Timed. In what order does the lab's CallLog record them? close, then verify verify, then close Only close, because self-calls skip the proxy Only verify The subclass is the object, so this.verify() runs verify's override and its timer. Each timer records in its finally, when its call ends, and verify ends first, inside close. With a JDK proxy over a separate target, only close would be recorded, which is the third option's model.

h: Add interceptors with proxies · Explain it back
x: A teammate asks why the container uses two kinds of proxy instead of always generating a subclass with Byte Buddy. Explain what each kind gives up, and how the container decides.

h: Add interceptors with proxies · Key terms
x: Interceptor Code written once that runs around many method calls, such as a timer or a retry. Interceptor chain The interceptors for one method, in order; each calls proceed() to hand on to the next, and the last hands on to the method. Target The real object behind a forwarding proxy, which the handler calls when the chain ends. Subclass proxy A generated subclass that overrides the intercepted methods and is itself the object, so self-calls are intercepted. all-open A Kotlin compiler plugin that makes classes with chosen annotations, and their members, open instead of final. Idempotency key An ID sent with a request, such as a booking reference, so the receiver can recognize a repeat and not do the work twice. What does proceed() do in an interceptor chain? It runs the next interceptor, or after the last one, the real method. A retry interceptor calls it again after a listed failure. Why put @Timed outside @Retry in the chain? Then it records one call that includes every attempt: the time the caller really waited. Inside, it records each attempt separately. The four cases of a decorating InvocationHandler, in order? Object methods by identity; default methods with invokeDefault; the chain ending in method.invoke(target, args); unwrap InvocationTargetException. Why can't a container return a JDK proxy for get(FakeBooking.class)? The proxy class extends java.lang.reflect.Proxy and implements only the interfaces, so it is not a FakeBooking. Ask for the interface. Kotlin open class S { @Timed fun close() }: does a Byte Buddy subclass time close? No, silently. close is final because it isn't open, so the subclass can't override it. Three ways to make a Kotlin class interceptable by a subclass proxy? Write open on the class and the intercepted methods; use the all-open plugin (or kotlin-spring); or give it an interface and use a JDK proxy. When is it safe for an interceptor to retry a booking call? When the failure is listed as worth retrying and the call carries a booking reference (an idempotency key), the same on every attempt, so the service can spot a repeat.

h: Add interceptors with proxies · Go deeper
x: Jakarta Interceptors, the standard behind CDI and Quarkus, has the same pieces under other names. An interceptor binding is an annotation like @Timed that is itself annotated @InterceptorBinding. The interceptor is a class with an @AroundInvoke method that takes an InvocationContext and calls ctx.proceed(). The order of the chain comes from @Priority on each interceptor class, with lower numbers running first. Spring AOP's equivalent is an AOP Alliance MethodInterceptor, whose invoke(MethodInvocation) also ends in proceed(), ordered by @Order or the Ordered interface. Annotations and proxies have a quieter interaction too. Java annotations are not inherited from interfaces: @Timed on BookingClient.reserve is not visible through FakeBooking.class.getMethod("reserve", ...). A JDK proxy hands the handler the interface's Method, so the lab's container sees it. A subclass proxy looks at the class's methods, so an annotation that lives only on an interface method would not be found there. Spring papers over this with its own annotation search, which walks interfaces and superclasses. The lab refuses the doubtful case instead: annotations on the class of an interface-proxied component are an error. Byte Buddy can also load a generated class without a new class loader. ClassLoadingStrategy.UsingLookup, with a MethodHandles.Lookup from the part's package, defines the subclass in the same loader and package as its superclass. That lets it override package-private methods and avoids one loader per class. The lab uses the default, the simplest strategy, and lesson 3's histogram shows what it leaves behind.

h: Measure it, then make it start fast · One call through a stand-in: nanoseconds and a couple of hundred bytes
x: Start with the cost of one call. Measuring a single call needs care. From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 pictured the JVM as a new cook. A fresh JVM reads every method from its recipe card, line by line, and cooks the busy ones from memory only later, with shortcuts. Time the first calls, and you've measured the cook's first day. So ProxyCallBench uses JMH, the OpenJDK project's benchmark harness. JMH runs a small piece of code in a fresh JVM and measures it only after the JIT compiler has done its work. (The JIT compiler is the part of the JVM that turns busy methods into machine code.) Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from called it the fair taste test: a warmed-up kitchen, a fresh JVM for each round, ingredients the cook can't predict, and a judge who eats every result. Here we return each result and read the input from a non-final field, so the JIT can neither throw the work away nor fold it into a constant. JMH's -prof gc option adds a second number: the bytes each call allocates, B/op. The benchmark makes one booking-fee calculation four ways. Each chain holds a single interceptor that only calls proceed(), so the numbers are the stand-ins' own cost, and the direct call is the baseline. One run on this course's 4-core machine, which was busy with other builds at the time: Call ns/op B/op direct 1.4 0 generated forwarding class (this lesson) 2.3 0 Byte Buddy subclass (lesson 2) 69 160 JDK proxy (lesson 2) 239 208 Every error bar was larger than its score, so read the time column for its order only. The bytes held up better. Over four runs, the direct and generated rows stayed at 0, and the JDK proxy at 208 to 213 B/op, while its time went from about 110 ns to over 3,000. Byte Buddy's row moved between 64 and 160 B/op: these runs are short, and the JIT didn't remove the same objects on that path every time. Where do 208 bytes come from? The JDK proxy's generated method boxes the long argument, wrapping it in a Long object, and puts it in an Object[]. The handler builds an Invocation for each step of the chain and a lambda for the target call, and Method.invoke boxes the result. The generated forwarding class does the same things in its source: new Object[] {p0}, new Invocation(...), a lambda. But its whole call is plain code that C2, the JIT's optimizing compiler, can inline: it copies each method the call reaches into the caller. Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics pictured that as the cook who copies the sauce from page 12 into the main recipe. Once inlined, none of those objects leaves the compiled method, and escape analysis, C2's check for objects that never leave the code it compiled, removes them all. Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis put it in the warehouse's words: a box that never leaves the desk is never made. On the two reflective paths, C2 couldn't see the whole call, so the objects stay. Don't build on that zero. As the Try it shows, one more interceptor is enough to lose it. The Kotlin twin counts the same calls in a plain loop and gets 0, 208, 192 and 48 bytes: the same order, with less of the generated class's allocation removed. Does any of it matter? At 2,000 booking calls a second, 208 bytes each is 400 KB of short-lived garbage a second, next to a network call that takes milliseconds: nothing. In a loop that prices 10,000 seats through a proxied PriceList, it's 2 MB for every pass. Put the stand-in in front of the booking service, not in front of the arithmetic. Per call, then, the stand-ins are cheap. The start is another matter. Count the bytes per call Read ProxyCallBench. Predict the B/op of each of the four benchmarks before you run it. Run it (it forks four JVMs, about 10 seconds on a quiet machine). Then run the Kotlin twin, which counts bytes with the per-thread allocation counter instead of JMH. In ProxyCallBench, add a second PASS to CHAIN (List.of(PASS, PASS)) and run it again. Which rows change? Change it back afterwards. h: Measure it, then make it start fast · At start-up, the reflective container loads Byte Buddy and writes classes
x:
A reflective start finds components, reads annotations, orders the graph and has Byte Buddy write a subclass: 2,207 classes and 1,029 ms; the same wiring generated at build time leaves only holders: 991 classes and 266 ms StartupLadder packs the demo box office into a JAR and starts it in fresh JVMs. It counts the lines that -Xlog:class+load prints, one per class the JVM loads, grouped by the source: each line names, as Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it did. On JDK 21: setup loaded archived run-time ready ms wall ms reflective + Byte Buddy 2207 953 156 1029 1307 parsed from byte-buddy.jar 814, JDK proxies 30, defined from bytes 3, hidden 123 generated registry 991 834 51 266 418 The 1,216 extra classes are all machinery. 814 come from byte-buddy-1.18.17.jar: the library loads its own model of types, its matchers and its class writer before it can write one subclass. The costume department unpacks its whole sewing room to sew one costume. The 3 classes defined from bytes (source: __JVM_DefineClass__) are what it sewed: ShowCloser$ByteBuddy$... and two $auxiliary$ helper classes, the @SuperCall callables for close and verify. Then come 30 JDK proxy classes (__dynamic_proxy__), and only one of them is the booking stand-in. Every annotation you read through reflection is an object of a proxy class that the JDK writes for that annotation's type. So getAnnotation(Component.class) and isAnnotationPresent(Timed.class) make stand-ins too, and Byte Buddy uses a few proxies of its own inside. The 123 hidden classes are lambdas and method handles. A hidden class is one the JVM makes for its own use, which no class loader can find by name, and a method handle is a small JDK object that points at a method. Each lambda becomes a hidden class the first time its "ask the director" cue runs, as invokedynamic: how lambdas and string concatenation compile showed. Since JDK 18, core reflection itself runs on method handles, so every reflective call path adds a few more. Each of those classes is found, parsed and verified, the corner shop unpacking and checking every box again, then run in the interpreter, because nothing is hot yet. Every start is the cook's first day again. That's why ready, from the first line of main to the first ticket sold, was 1,029 ms against 266 ms. The machine was busy, and the times moved by a factor of two between runs. The reflective start was always several times slower, though, and the class counts barely moved: a later run gave 2,208 and 991. None of this means Byte Buddy is slow. It does at every start what a compiler could have done once. So let's give that work to the compiler. Count what each start loads Read StartupLadder (the Kotlin twin runs the first two rows). h: Measure it, then make it start fast · Write the wiring out at build time: generate the registry
x: Everything the reflective container works out at start-up depends only on the classes, and the classes are fixed when the program is built. So do the work then. Picture the front-of-house manager from lesson 1 writing the evening's running order the afternoon before. On the night, nobody reads a single card; the crew follows the sheet. RegistryGenerator is that afternoon. It runs the same BeanGraph from lesson 1 at build time: it picks the constructors, orders the graph and checks for loops, and a loop now fails the build instead of the start. Then it prints a Java class that does the wiring with plain new calls, and the lab's test compiles that class with javac, the way a build would. It prints source rather than class files on purpose. Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API showed the theatre's own printing press for class files, but source is easier to read, and javac checks it for us. Each singleton gets a holder class, as lesson 1 promised: Java private static final class PriceList_Holder { static final PriceList INSTANCE = new PriceList(SeatingPlan_Holder.INSTANCE); } Kotlin private object PriceListHolder { val INSTANCE = PriceList(SeatingPlanHolder.INSTANCE) // a Kotlin object is a holder class too } The JVM initializes PriceList_Holder the first time get touches it: one dress rehearsal, under the class initialization lock from Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization. Its dependency is another holder, which the JVM initializes first. There is no volatile, no lock after the first call, and no map: get is a list of checks like if (type == PriceList.class). A prototype gets a factory method instead. Interceptors become source too. For BookingClient, the generator writes RemoteBookingClient_Proxy implements BookingClient, and for ShowCloser it writes ShowCloser_Intercepted extends ShowCloser: the same stand-in and costume copy as lesson 2, printed in advance. The generator reads @Timed and @Retry while it runs and writes their values into the code, as in INTERCEPTION.chain(true, 3, BookingUnavailableException.class), so nothing reads an annotation when the program starts. Real frameworks do the same. Quarkus's container, ArC, generates subclasses like these while the application is built; Micronaut does the graph work while javac compiles; and Spring can generate its wiring as code ahead of time. You give up two things. The set of components is fixed when you build: nothing can scan a plugin directory at start-up, or choose a part from a setting, unless the generator wrote code for it. And a holder fails for good. If BoxOffice's constructor throws on first use, the JVM marks BoxOffice_Holder as failed, and every later get throws NoClassDefFoundError until the program restarts. Lesson 1's cell would simply have tried again. What depends only on your classes can be worked out once, when you build. Do it there, and leave the start only what's left. Before we archive what's left, let's look inside a running container and count what it keeps. Read the class the generator writes Run GenerateDemo (or the Kotlin twin). It prints the registry the generator writes for the demo box office, then tries a graph with a loop. Find BoxOffice_Holder. Which holders must the JVM initialize before it, and in what order? Find ShowCloser_Intercepted.verify. Which line makes close's self-call go through the chain? h: Measure it, then make it start fast · Look inside the running container: a histogram and a heap dump
x: Measure the running container from outside. Picture the warehouse from the Memory and GC track: the heap is its shared floor, and each object is a box with a label that names its class. jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram runs a full GC and then counts the boxes on the floor by label. (jcmd is the JDK's tool for sending commands to a running JVM, and <pid> is that JVM's process id.) Here is the reflective container after one sale, one return and one closing, trimmed: num #instances #bytes class name (module) 99: 42 672 jdk.proxy2.$Proxy8 (jdk.proxy2) 138: 13 312 workbench.container.l03.SingletonCell 167: 14 224 jdk.proxy2.$Proxy2 (jdk.proxy2) 247: 1 112 net.bytebuddy.dynamic.loading.ByteArrayClassLoader 523: 1 32 workbench.container.l03.Container 866: 1 16 jdk.proxy2.$Proxy6 (jdk.proxy2) 910: 1 16 workbench.container.l03.ShowCloser$ByteBuddy$3cYlOLuY Read it like a stock list. The 13 SingletonCells are the 14 components minus the one prototype, Basket. One $Proxy6 is the booking stand-in. One ByteArrayClassLoader holds the Byte Buddy subclass and its two helper classes, and one ShowCloser$ByteBuddy$... is the closer itself. The other proxy objects are not parts of the box office at all. In this run, $Proxy2, with 14 instances, is the @Component annotation, one instance per component class. $Proxy8, with 42, is a proxy Byte Buddy uses to call JDK methods that don't exist on every Java version it supports. There were 119 proxy objects in all, and one of them was a part of the box office. The histogram says what is alive, not who holds it. jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump <file> writes every object and every reference between them to a file, 8 MB here, in the HPROF format that heap tools read. The JVM pauses while it writes, so on a busy program, take one only when you can afford a pause. Eclipse MAT, a free tool for reading heap dumps, can then show any object's path to GC roots. That's the cleaning crew's route from the Memory track: the notes it follows from the workers' desks and the noticeboard to the box. For the ShowCloser$ByteBuddy$... object, the path should run through SingletonCell.instance and the container's singletons map to the Container, held by a local variable of the main thread. The demo also proves it by letting go. It drops its only reference to the container and asks for a GC. Byte Buddy's class loader is collected, and with it the generated class. A class keeps its loader alive and an object keeps its class alive, so once the container was unreachable, the whole chain was. The plan for that box left the filing cabinet once no box made from it remained. The JDK proxy class stays loaded, because it was defined in the application class loader, which lives as long as the program, and Proxy caches it there. The annotation instances stay too, cached with the classes and methods they label. The generated registry has a different root. Its singletons sit in static fields of holder classes, so they live as long as the class loader that loaded the registry. That's why the lab's tests load a fresh copy of the class for every test. And that registry leaves very little to make at start-up, which is exactly what an archive wants. Take a histogram and a heap dump of the container Run RunningContainer with -Pargs=wait added to the command below. It wires the box office, makes three calls, prints its pid and two jcmd commands, and waits. In a second terminal, from labs/, run the two commands it printed. Count the SingletonCells, the ByteArrayClassLoaders and the $ByteBuddy$ instances before you look at the answer. Optional: open container/build/heapdumps/container.hprof in Eclipse MAT and use "Path to GC Roots" on the ShowCloser$ByteBuddy$... object. Press Enter in the first terminal. It drops the container. Run the histogram command again, then press Enter to end. Without -Pargs=wait, the demo (and its Kotlin twin) runs both jcmd commands itself and prints a shorter, grouped histogram. h: Measure it, then make it start fast · Archive what's left: AppCDS on JDK 21, the AOT cache on JDK 25
x: Class data sharing and Project Leyden's AOT cache showed how to skip part of a start. Its shopkeeper keeps yesterday's filled shelves in the back room and wheels them out at opening time. An archive is a file of classes the JVM has already parsed and checked; at the next start, the JVM maps the file into memory instead of reading each class again. AppCDS, application class data sharing, puts your own classes in such an archive, and on JDK 21 one flag on a training run writes it. Apply it to both containers, and the last two rows of StartupLadder appear: reflective, AppCDS 2145 2037 108 544 858 parsed from byte-buddy.jar 0, JDK proxies 30, defined from bytes 3, hidden 75 generated, AppCDS 882 847 35 143 362 parsed from byte-buddy.jar 0, JDK proxies 0, defined from bytes 0, hidden 35 AppCDS took Byte Buddy's 814 classes from the archive and nearly halved the reflective start. It couldn't take the classes made while the program runs. When the archive was written, JDK 21 printed Skipping jdk/proxy2/$Proxy3: Unsupported location for each of the 30 proxy classes. And the archived run still logs Byte Buddy's three classes as __JVM_DefineClass__: defined from bytes by its own class loader, at every start. So every start still writes and verifies them, and still runs the code that writes them. The generated registry has nothing of the kind. Its only classes made at start-up are 35 hidden ones for lambdas. The AOT cache, Project Leyden's newer archive, goes further for the classes it can store. They arrive already loaded and linked, with the shopkeeper's notes from the training run about which code was busy. JEP 483 brought it in JDK 24, and JDK 25 made it a single step with -XX:AOTCacheOutput. Use JDK 25.0.4 or later, as that lesson explained. The limit on custom class loaders stays: the cache doesn't store the classes they define, so Byte Buddy's classes are made at every start either way. The registry is also the shape GraalVM native image wants. GraalVM native image and Quarkus native pictured it as a pop-up stall built at a factory, which sells only what the factory packed. The registry has no reflection to declare and no classes defined at run time, which a closed world can't contain. (CRaC, the photo of the warm shop, sidesteps the question: a restored JVM already holds the classes Byte Buddy made before the photo.) That is the whole argument for build-time wiring in one sentence: the less a start has to discover, write and verify, the more of it a cache, an archive or a native build can do for you. Archive both starts Run StartupLadder once (section 2), so app.jar and classpath.txt exist in container/build/cap4. Run the two JDK 21 commands. Predict both answers first: how many classes does the archive refuse, and which classes made at start-up remain? If you have JDK 25.0.4 or later, run the last two commands with its java. terminal (from labs/) # from labs/, after StartupLadder has run once: it wrote app.jar and classpath.txt cd container/build/cap4 CP=$(cat classpath.txt) MAIN=workbench.container.l03.demo.StartupLadder # JDK 21 or later: a dynamic AppCDS archive for the reflective start java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=reflective.jsa -cp "$CP" $MAIN --reflective 2>&1 | grep -c 'Unsupported location' java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=reflective.jsa -Xlog:class+load -cp "$CP" $MAIN --reflective \ | grep -o 'source: __[A-Za-z_]*' | sort | uniq -c # JDK 25.0.4 or later: the one-step AOT cache for the generated registry java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=generated.aot -cp "$CP" workbench.container.l03.demo.gen.GeneratedStart java -XX:AOTCache=generated.aot -Xlog:aot -cp "$CP" workbench.container.l03.demo.gen.GeneratedStart | grep Opened On JDK 21 the first command prints 30: one Unsupported location warning per proxy class. The second prints 3 source: __JVM_DefineClass__, 75 source: __JVM_LookupDefineClass__ and 30 source: __dynamic_proxy__: the Byte Buddy classes, hidden classes and proxies that every start still makes, even with the archive. On JDK 25.0.4 or later the AOT cache commands should end with Opened AOT cache generated.aot. (this course's machine had only JDK 21, so that line comes from the Startup track's runs, not from this app). JEP 483: Ahead-of-Time Class Loading & Linking read

h: Measure it, then make it start fast · Java and Kotlin
x: A generated registry in Java, and the same idea written by hand in Kotlin AppRegistry.java (generated, trimmed) public final class AppRegistry implements Registry { private static final class SeatingPlan_Holder { static final SeatingPlan INSTANCE = new SeatingPlan(); } private static final class PriceList_Holder { static final PriceList INSTANCE = new PriceList(SeatingPlan_Holder.INSTANCE); } private static Basket new_Basket() { // a prototype return new Basket(PriceList_Holder.INSTANCE); } @Override public <T> T get(Class<T> type) { if (type == SeatingPlan.class) return type.cast(SeatingPlan_Holder.INSTANCE); if (type == PriceList.class) return type.cast(PriceList_Holder.INSTANCE); if (type == Basket.class) return type.cast(new_Basket()); throw new ContainerException("No component provides " + type.getSimpleName()); } } AppRegistry.kt (by hand) object AppRegistry { private object SeatingPlanHolder { val INSTANCE = SeatingPlan() } private object PriceListHolder { val INSTANCE = PriceList(SeatingPlanHolder.INSTANCE) } private fun newBasket() = Basket(PriceListHolder.INSTANCE) // a prototype @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") fun <T> get(type: Class<T>): T = when (type) { SeatingPlan::class.java -> SeatingPlanHolder.INSTANCE PriceList::class.java -> PriceListHolder.INSTANCE Basket::class.java -> newBasket() else -> throw ContainerException("No component provides ${type.simpleName}") } as T } Both compile to the same mechanism: one class per singleton whose static initializer builds it on first use, under the JVM's class initialization lock. A Kotlin object is that holder class, with its instance in a static INSTANCE field. The difference is who writes it. The Java one comes from a generator and is never edited; the Kotlin one is the kind of code Dagger, a build-time container, generates, written here by hand, which is fine for ten components and painful for eighty. You don't need by lazy here: it would work, but it adds a Lazy object per part and a volatile read per access to do what the class initialization lock already does.

h: Measure it, then make it start fast · Worked example
x: Design review: where does a setting go? A new requirement: on the theatre's test machine, the box office must use MockBookingClient instead of RemoteBookingClient, chosen by the property booking=mock (a setting passed on the command line as -Dbooking=mock). In the run-time container it's one filter before the graph is built, because the container learns its components at start-up anyway. List<Class<?>> components = new ArrayList<>(DemoApp.COMPONENTS); if ("mock".equals(System.getProperty("booking"))) { components.remove(RemoteBookingClient.class); // decided at start-up components.add(MockBookingClient.class); } Registry registry = new Container(components); val components = DemoApp.COMPONENTS.toMutableList() if (System.getProperty("booking") == "mock") { components -= RemoteBookingClient::class.java // decided at start-up components += MockBookingClient::class.java } val registry: Registry = Container(components) The generated registry has no start-up graph to change. One option is to generate one registry per setup and choose at the edge of the program, where it starts. Each registry stays plain code, and the setting picks a class, not a graph. String source = RegistryGenerator.generate("theatre.gen", "TestRegistry", testComponents); // ...and LiveRegistry from the live list, both at build time Registry registry = "mock".equals(System.getProperty("booking")) ? new TestRegistry() : new LiveRegistry(); val source = RegistryGenerator.generate("theatre.gen", "TestRegistry", testComponents) // ...and LiveRegistry from the live list, both at build time val registry: Registry = if (System.getProperty("booking") == "mock") TestRegistry() else LiveRegistry() Check the costs. Two registries double the generated code and ship the mock inside the real program. If the choice really is fixed per machine, a build-time setting is cleaner: build the test copy from the test list. Quarkus draws exactly this line between build-time configuration, fixed in the built program, and run-time configuration, read at start-up. Write the decision down in one sentence a reviewer can check: "The booking implementation is chosen per build, so each build wires one graph; a run-time property may change the booking service's address and timeouts, never which class is wired." That sentence is the design review's answer, and the test that proves it is the lab's: the generated registry wires the same graph as the reflective one, for each list.

h: Measure it, then make it start fast · Quiz
x: You want CI, the build server that checks every change, to fail when someone makes the booking stand-in more expensive. Which number from ProxyCallBench should the check use? ns/op, with a 10% margin gc.alloc.rate.norm (B/op), with a small margin The score error, which must stay below 1 ns The number of forks Over four runs on a busy machine, the JDK proxy's bytes per call stayed between 208 and 213 while its time went from about 110 ns to over 3,000, so a 10% margin on time fails at random. Keep a margin on the bytes too, because B/op can shift with the JDK version, the length of the chain and what the JIT manages to remove. The generated Prices_Proxy allocates new Object[] {p0}, a boxed Long and an Invocation on every call, in its source. JMH reports 0 B/op for it. Why? JMH doesn't count objects smaller than 64 bytes The TLAB hides allocations from the GC profiler C2 inlined the whole call, and escape analysis removed the objects because none of them leaves the compiled method The objects are allocated off-heap Allocation in a TLAB is still allocation and is still counted, so the second option fails. What removed it is escape analysis after inlining: when every use of an object stays inside one compiled method, C2 can replace the object with its fields in registers. It only works once C2 has compiled the code and can see the whole call, which is why the reflective paths keep their 160 to 208 bytes. On JDK 21 you add a dynamic AppCDS archive to the reflective container's start. Which classes does every start still create at run time? None: the archive stores every class the training run loaded Only the application's own classes Byte Buddy's own classes from its JAR The JDK proxy classes, the classes Byte Buddy generates, and some hidden classes An archive holds classes the JVM can find again at a known location, such as a JAR on the class path. At dump time JDK 21 skips each proxy class with Unsupported location, and Byte Buddy's subclass is defined from bytes by its own class loader. Byte Buddy's JAR classes do come from the archive, so the third option is wrong, and that's why AppCDS still nearly halved this start. A generated holder's constructor throws on first use because the booking service key is missing. Someone fixes the configuration, and the next sale calls get(BoxOffice.class) again on the same JVM. What happens? NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class ...BoxOffice_Holder, until the JVM restarts The holder retries, and the sale succeeds get returns null The JVM retries the static initializer after a pause A static initializer runs once: the dress rehearsal can't be held twice. When it throws, the JVM marks the class as failed, and every later use gets NoClassDefFoundError for the life of its class loader. Lesson 1's SingletonCell stores nothing when its factory throws, so it retries, which is what the second option describes. That's one real cost of build-time holders: keep their constructors free of input, output and configuration lookups. In a heap dump of the generated registry, what holds the BoxOffice singleton? A SingletonCell in the registry's map The static field INSTANCE of the class BoxOffice_Holder, which lives as long as its class loader Nothing: the JVM keeps holder instances off the heap The thread that first called get A holder's instance is a static field, and static fields belong to their class, which stays loaded while its class loader is reachable. The registry has no map and no cells, so the first option describes the reflective container instead. That's why the lab loads the registry in a new class loader for each test: the only way to get fresh singletons is a fresh copy of the classes.

h: Measure it, then make it start fast · Key terms
x: Build-time wiring Working out the dependency graph while the application is built, and writing plain code that creates the components. Holder class A nested class whose static field holds one singleton; the JVM builds it on first use, once, under its class initialization lock. Class histogram A count of live objects and bytes per class, taken after a full GC: jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram. Heap dump A file with every object on the heap and every reference between them, read with a tool such as Eclipse MAT. Path to GC roots The chain of references that keeps an object alive, from a root such as a thread's local variable or a static field. B/op Bytes allocated per benchmark operation, from JMH's GC profiler: far steadier than time, so it is the number to compare and to check in CI. Which JMH number should a CI check on proxy cost use? gc.alloc.rate.norm, bytes per operation, with a small margin. Time is too noisy on shared machines. Why can generated interceptor code show 0 B/op although its source allocates? C2 inlines the whole call, and escape analysis removes objects that never leave the compiled method. Name the -Xlog:class+load sources for classes made at run time. __dynamic_proxy__ (JDK proxies), __JVM_DefineClass__ (defined from bytes, as Byte Buddy does), and hidden classes such as lambdas. Why does reading annotations by reflection create classes? Each annotation instance is an object of a JDK proxy class generated for that annotation type. What makes a generated holder thread-safe without a lock in your code? The JVM runs a class's static initializer once, under the class initialization lock; other threads wait for it. What happens when a holder's constructor throws? ExceptionInInitializerError once, then NoClassDefFoundError on every later use until the JVM restarts. A SingletonCell would retry. Why can't AppCDS on JDK 21 archive a JDK proxy class? The class has no location an archive can check (Unsupported location); it is generated at run time.

h: Measure it, then make it start fast · Go deeper
x: What a production container adds to the one you built, roughly in the order you would need it: Lifecycle callbacks: @PostConstruct after injection, and @PreDestroy at shutdown, run in reverse creation order so a SalesBook closes after the BoxOffice that writes to it. Qualifiers (@Named, @Qualifier) for two implementations of one interface, and matching by generic type, so Repository<Show> and Repository<Seat> are different dependencies. More scopes: one instance per request or per user session, with a client proxy that forwards each call to the right instance for the current scope. Configuration injection, with type conversion and checks, split into build-time and run-time settings. Interceptor ordering by priority, decorators, and events between components. Lookups (Provider<T>, Instance<T>) for edges that must be followed at call time. Test support: swapping one component for a fake without rewriting the graph. Error messages that print the whole dependency path, not only the loop. The way the generator runs matters too. This lab runs it as a separate step on compiled classes, which is close to what Quarkus does during its build. Dagger and Micronaut run theirs as annotation processors inside javac, so the generated classes are compiled with your code and IDEs can show them, but the processor sees source-level elements instead of loaded classes. Spring's AOT processing starts the application's wiring during the build and writes what it found as code. For the start itself, the next levers after this lesson are the ones the Startup track covered: an AOT cache trained on representative work, then native image if memory per copy or start time is still the limit. Generated wiring makes both easier, because there is less left for the JVM to discover.

h: Kotlin Symbol Processing (KSP)
x: Generate Kotlin code during the build: processors, the symbol model, KotlinPoet, errors, rounds, incremental builds and testing. By the end of this track you can write a KSP processor for Kotlin code from an empty file and know why each line is there. You'll find the classes that carry an annotation, refuse the ones you can't handle with a message on the exact file and line, read their declarations and types, write new code with KotlinPoet, survive several rounds and incremental builds, test the processor the way a library author does, and decide when KSP is the wrong tool. KSP, Kotlin Symbol Processing, is Kotlin's own way to do what Java's annotation processors have done since Java 6: read your code during the build and write new code next to it. One picture runs through all nine lessons: a family moving house. Your source files are sealed boxes. The label on top lists what's inside, the declarations, and the packing stays sealed. An annotation is a sticky note on a box. A processor is a helper with a clipboard, and the clipboard is the Resolver: "show me every box with this note". The helper reads labels, never opens or repacks a box, and writes new cards and lists that travel with the move. The running example is MoveMate, a small app that helps the family, with the same four classes everywhere: Box, Lamp, Bookshelf and Plant, and the same card, Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null. You need basic Kotlin and Java, and nothing else: every term is defined where it first appears. The versions are Kotlin 2.4.21, KSP 2.3.14 (KSP2), KotlinPoet and kotlinpoet-ksp 2.4.0, kctfork 0.14.0 for the in-memory tests, Gradle 9.8.2, JUnit 6.1.3 and AssertJ 3.27.7. Install JDK 25; the labs compile with release 21. The outputs quoted in the lessons were copied from real runs of these versions. The labs live in labs/ksp. You write each lesson's processor in src/main/kotlin/workbench/ksp/lNN, and every lab follows the same five moves: Find, Check, Read, Write, Prove. From labs/, run your lab's tests with ./gradlew :ksp:test --tests 'workbench.ksp.lNN.*', and the reference answers with ./gradlew :ksp:solutionTest --tests 'workbench.ksp.lNN.*'. Demos run with ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=<class>, using the reference processors until you add -Pmine=lNN. The real build is labs/ksp/app, one source set per lesson: ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspLNNKotlin -Pmine=lNN runs your processor in it, its output lands in labs/ksp/app/build/generated/ksp/lNN/, and -Pksp.incremental.log=true writes KSP's incremental logs to labs/ksp/app/build/kspCaches/lNN/logs/. An unfinished processor only prints a warning, so the real build always runs. An annotation processor runs during the build, reads declarations and writes new source files that compile with yours. KSP is Kotlin's own, running as a Gradle task (kspKotlin) before the compiler; Java has had javac processors since Java 6. KSP's two limits shape everything: it never sees bodies or expressions, and it only adds files. Anything that must change a class you wrote is a compiler plugin's job. A processor is a provider, a processor and a services file. Find symbols by the annotation's full name, check each one and report problems with logger.error(message, symbol) on the declaration's line, then read and write. Read types through KSTypeReference.resolve() once, keep every ? and type argument, and write code with KotlinPoet's %T %N %S %L and kotlinpoet-ksp's toTypeName(), never with string templates. process() runs once per round and returns what to defer; rounds go on while they write files, and in KSP 2.3.14 a symbol deferred to the end is dropped silently, so check in finish(). Every output names its source files in Dependencies: isolating for one class's file, aggregating for a list of many. A wrong choice is silent until an incremental build, where a list shrinks or vanishes. Test like a library author: compile in memory with kctfork, then check the exit code, the generated text, the messages by file and line, and a call into the generated code. Real builds test the wiring. Choose with evidence: reflection for a few calls on a few classes, KSP for repeated work and build-time checks, a compiler plugin to change classes, kapt only for Java-only processors, and per-target configurations in multiplatform modules.

h: Kotlin Symbol Processing (KSP): cheat sheet
x: The one idea A processor runs during the build, before the Kotlin compiler. It reads declarations (names, types, annotations, signatures, never bodies), and it adds new files that are compiled with yours. It never changes a file you wrote. Everything else in the track is how to do those two things correctly, quickly and testably. Picture it: a family moving house Mechanism Picture it In the code Where the picture breaks Source file, declarations (lessons 1, 3) a sealed box, and the label on top KSFile, KSClassDeclaration, KSPropertyDeclaration, KSFunctionDeclaration the label also lists named things packed inside; only the how (expressions, default values) stays sealed Annotation (1, 2) a sticky note: "make a card for this one" @Inventory, found by its full name notes go on label lines too (properties, parameters), and carry values with defaults Processor and provider (2) the helper, and the moving company that sends the helper SymbolProcessor, created once by SymbolProcessorProvider KSP finds the company through a services file, or not at all Resolver (2, 3) the clipboard: "every box with this note" resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation(fqName) a fresh clipboard each pass; an old one is no good Generated file (1, 2, 4) a new card or list that travels with the move codeGenerator.createNewFile(...), or KotlinPoet's writeTo the cards are boxes too: next pass, every helper reads them Logger message (2, 5) the helper's note: "box 7 has a note but no label" logger.error(message, symbol) a thrown exception is the helper dropping everything: no note, no onError() KotlinPoet (4) a label printer instead of handwriting FileSpec, TypeSpec, %T %N %S %L it prints declarations; bodies are still format strings Rounds (6) another walk through the house for the new cards process() once per round a walk happens only if the last one wrote something Deferral (5, 6) a box set aside: its label mentions something not packed yet return it from process(); validate(apiFeatures = apiFeatures) the pile is shared by every helper, and in 2.3.14 a box left there at the end gets no word at all Isolating output (7) one box's own card, redone when that box is repacked Dependencies(aggregating = false, file) KSP knows a box was repacked only from what you declared Aggregating output (7) the master list on the fridge Dependencies(aggregating = true, *files) the whole list is rewritten from every box, never patched Processor options (7) the job sheet the company hands the helper ksp { arg(k, v) }, environment.options one sheet for every helper in the module Testing (8) a practice pack in an empty room kctfork, four checks the room is emptied after each pack, so it never sees an incremental build Reflection (1, 9) unpacking and checking boxes at the new house, every time javaClass.declaredFields it costs a fifth of a microsecond, not an afternoon Compiler plugin (9) the mover who repacks boxes all-open, no-arg, kotlinx.serialization more power, and the class you read is no longer the class that runs kapt (9) a helper who reads only Java, so every label is copied out in Java first kapt(...), Java stubs the copies lose words, such as default values Multiplatform (9) moving into several houses on one day kspJvm, kspJs, kspCommonMainMetadata a shared box gets a card in every house The five moves Move KSP Lesson 1. Find resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory"): the full name; a short name finds nothing 2 2. Check keep symbol is KSClassDeclaration && symbol.classKind == ClassKind.CLASS, else logger.error("...", symbol); check every symbol, report every problem 2, 5 3. Read primaryConstructor?.parameters, type.resolve(), isMarkedNullable, annotations and their arguments 3 4. Write KotlinPoet FileSpec, then writeTo(codeGenerator, Dependencies(...)) with the right files and category 4, 7 5. Prove kctfork tests (exit code, text, messages, a call), then the real build 8 The KSP API on one page class CardProcessorProvider : SymbolProcessorProvider { // listed in the services file override fun create(environment: SymbolProcessorEnvironment): SymbolProcessor = CardProcessor(environment.codeGenerator, environment.logger, environment.options) } class CardProcessor( private val codeGenerator: CodeGenerator, private val logger: KSPLogger, private val options: Map<String, String>, // ksp { arg("k", "v") } ) : SymbolProcessor { override val apiFeatures = buildApiFeatures { enableBackingFields = true; enableContextParameters = true } override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { // once per round val (ready, later) = resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory") .partition { it.validate(apiFeatures = apiFeatures) } for (symbol in ready) { if (symbol !is KSClassDeclaration || symbol.classKind != ClassKind.CLASS) { logger.error("@Inventory goes on a class, but ...", symbol) // file and declaration line continue } cardFile(symbol).writeTo(codeGenerator, Dependencies(aggregating = false, symbol.containingFile!!)) } return later // deferred to the next round } override fun finish() { /* after the last round: report anything still deferred */ } } Services file: src/main/resources/META-INF/services/com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessorProvider, one provider class per line. Missing: e: [ksp] No providers found in processor classpath. Symbols: KSFile, KSClassDeclaration (classKind, modifiers, primaryConstructor, getDeclaredProperties()), KSPropertyDeclaration, KSFunctionDeclaration, KSValueParameter (name, type, isVal, hasDefault). origin is KOTLIN, JAVA, KOTLIN_LIB, JAVA_LIB or SYNTHETIC. Types: a KSTypeReference is the type as written; resolve() gives the KSType (declaration, arguments, isMarkedNullable, isError). Resolving is expensive: once per reference. A Java type can be a platform type, (String..String?). Annotation arguments: annotation.arguments, by name. A String or Boolean arrives as itself, a class as a KSType, an enum value as the entry's KSClassDeclaration. Unwritten arguments are there with their defaults, and isDefault() is true. Visitors: KSVisitorVoid(apiFeatures), not the deprecated KSVisitorVoid(). The same goes for validate(apiFeatures = apiFeatures). KotlinPoet: %T a type (imported), %N a name (escaped), %S a string (quoted, $ escaped), %L a literal (as is), %M a member (imported), %P a string template. kotlinpoet-ksp: toClassName(), toTypeName(), copy(nullable = true), addOriginatingKSFile(file), writeTo(codeGenerator, aggregating = ...). Rounds: a round runs only if the last one wrote a file; process() returns what to defer; finish() runs once at the end, onError() after a logger.error. A file written twice: kotlin.io.FileAlreadyExistsException. Dependencies: Dependencies(false, file) for an output from one file, Dependencies(true, *files) for one that any file can change, Dependencies.ALL_FILES to turn incremental processing off for it. KSP and javac's annotation processing, side by side KSP javac (javax.annotation.processing) SymbolProcessorProvider.create(environment) a public no-argument constructor, then init(ProcessingEnvironment) process(resolver): List<KSAnnotated>: returns symbols to defer process(annotations, roundEnv): boolean: returns whether it claims them every processor sees every symbol @SupportedAnnotationTypes, and claiming resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation(fqName) roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(type) KSClassDeclaration, KSPropertyDeclaration, KSFunctionDeclaration, KSValueParameter TypeElement, VariableElement, ExecutableElement classKind == ClassKind.CLASS getKind() == ElementKind.CLASS KSTypeReference.resolve() gives a KSType; a.isAssignableFrom(b) TypeMirror, already resolved; types.isAssignable(b, a), the other way round KSAnnotation.arguments element.getAnnotation(Room.class) or AnnotationMirror codeGenerator.createNewFile(Dependencies(...), pkg, name, ext) filer.createSourceFile(name, originatingElements...), createResource(...) logger.error(message, symbol) messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, message, element) environment.options, from ksp { arg(k, v) } processingEnv.getOptions(), from -Ak=v, declared in @SupportedOptions rounds end when one writes nothing; finish() an extra last round with processingOver() true isolating or aggregating per output, in Dependencies isolating or aggregating per processor, in META-INF/gradle/incremental.annotation.processors META-INF/services/com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessorProvider META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor KotlinPoet JavaPoet kctfork Google's compile-testing What the build prints A processor error: e: [ksp] /abs/path/Shape.kt:6: @Builder goes on a class, but Shape is an interface: an absolute path, the declaration's line (not the annotation's), no column. The task then fails with KSP failed with exit code: PROCESSING_ERROR. Follow-on errors such as e: [ksp] MovingDay.kt:14: Unresolved reference 'MovingDayList'. come after a failed run: fix the first error. A compiler error in generated or user code: e: file:///.../Use.kt:5:16 ..., with a column. logger.warn shows at Gradle's default level; logger.info only with --info. Where KSP 2.3.14 disagrees with its own docs A symbol still deferred when processing ends gets no error and no warning: check in finish() and report it yourself. onError() runs after logger.error, not after a thrown exception; logger.exception(e) prints e: [ksp] and doesn't fail the build. The quickstart's KSVisitorVoid() and validate() are deprecated since 2.3.12: use apiFeatures everywhere. KSP1 is gone: ksp.useKSP2=false fails the build. KSP2 runs in the Gradle daemon, and its version isn't tied to Kotlin's. "Up to 2x faster than kapt" is a 2021 Room benchmark, not a law. A lambda CommandLineArgumentProvider isn't a tracked task input, and option values from one can't contain spaces. Testing a processor: the four checks Check Catches Bench call 1. exit code a crash (INTERNAL_ERROR) or a reported error (COMPILATION_ERROR) run.exitCode 2. generated text any change, through a golden file (UPDATE_GOLDEN=true to rewrite on purpose) checkGolden(run.generated(path), file) 3. messages the wrong text or the wrong line run.errors as Message(severity, file, line, text) 4. call the code code that compiles and is still wrong run.newInstance(...), run.call(...) In-memory tests never see incremental builds, the services file or option wiring: those need a real build or Gradle TestKit.
