h: Kotlin Symbol Processing (KSP): track quiz
x: Which of these can a KSP processor do? Read the expression inside fun totalWeight(): Int Add a member function to an existing class Write a new file with an extension function for that class Change the default value of a constructor parameter KSP reads declarations and adds new files; it never sees bodies or default values, and it never changes existing code. An extension function in a new file is how a processor gives a class new behaviour. Adding a member needs a compiler plugin. A processor calls resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation("Inventory"), and the project has @Inventory classes. What does it get? Every class with an annotation named Inventory Nothing: the call needs the fully qualified name An error that the name is ambiguous Only the classes in the default package The lookup takes the annotation's fully qualified name, here workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory. A short name silently finds nothing, and the trouble shows up later as Unresolved reference errors for cards that were never written. A property is declared val shade: String?. Which call tells the processor it is nullable? property.type.toString() property.hasDefault property.isMutable property.type.resolve().isMarkedNullable type is a KSTypeReference, the type as written; resolve() gives the KSType, which knows its nullability and arguments. Resolving costs time, so do it once per reference. toString() is a display form, not reliable code. In a KotlinPoet format string, which placeholder writes a type and adds its import? %S %L %T %N %T emits a type and imports it if it can. %N is for names and escapes keywords, %S quotes and escapes a string, and %L writes a literal as it is. A processor finds an interface where it needs a class. What should it do? logger.error("@Builder goes on a class, but Shape is an interface", symbol) and carry on with the other symbols throw IllegalStateException("not a class") logger.exception(e), so the build fails Skip the symbol without a word logger.error on the symbol points at the user's file and the declaration's line, lets the processor report every problem in one build, and fails the build at the end. A thrown exception points into the processor, skips onError() in KSP 2.3.14, and stops everything. logger.exception doesn't fail the build at all. A processor returns the same symbol from process() in every round, because its type never becomes valid. What does KSP 2.3.14 do at the end? Logs an error for the symbol, as the docs say Logs a warning Drops it silently, calls finish(), and the build can pass Keeps running rounds until a timeout Processing stops when a round writes no file, and 2.3.14 reports nothing about symbols still deferred, although the multi-round docs promise an error. A careful processor checks in finish() and reports each leftover with logger.error on the symbol. A processor writes one Index.kt naming every @Indexed class, with Dependencies(aggregating = false, *files). What happens after a new @Indexed class is added in a new file? The index lists every class, the new one too The index is rewritten with only the new class, and the build passes KSP fails with a Dependencies error The index keeps the old classes until a clean build adds the new one A new file is tied to no output, so only that file is dirty, and the processor sees one class. Only an aggregating output, Dependencies(aggregating = true, ...), is redone for new files. Clean builds and in-memory tests never show the mistake. A builder test checks that the compile succeeded and that the text contains class LampBuilder. The processor drops the ? from shade: String?. Which check would catch it? Checking the exit code again with --info Checking that the text contains fun build() Running the test twice Calling shade(null) on the generated builder through the class loader The broken builder is valid code, so it compiles and contains its class and build(). Calling the code with null fails with NullPointerException: Parameter specified as non-null is null. A golden file would catch it too, by the changed line. A team wants each @Serializable class to contain its own generated serializer. Which tool does that? A compiler plugin, kotlinx.serialization A KSP processor kapt Reflection at start-up The serializer goes inside the class, with a serializer() function on its companion, which changes a class you wrote. Only a compiler plugin can do that. A KSP processor could write a separate serializer class next to it, which is a different design. A module runs Moshi's codegen with KSP and one Java-only processor with kapt. Why is the build still slow? KSP and kapt can't run in one module KSP processes kapt's stubs again kapt still writes Java stubs of every class in the module for the one processor left Moshi runs twice kapt runs Java processors on Java stubs of the module's Kotlin classes, and writing the stubs is the cost. As long as one kapt processor remains in a module, the stubs are written there. KSP and kapt can run side by side, which is how a migration goes one library at a time.

h: Code that writes code: what KSP is and where it runs · Four cards written by hand, and the one that went stale
x: MoveMate has four kinds of thing to move: boxes, lamps, bookshelves and plants. Each one is a small class, and each class has a matching card function that we wrote by hand. Here is the lamp's, in both languages: Java record Lamp(String name, int bulbs, String shade) {} static String inventoryCard(Lamp lamp) { return "Lamp: name=" + lamp.name() + ", bulbs=" + lamp.bulbs() + ", shade=" + lamp.shade(); } Kotlin data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?) fun Lamp.inventoryCard(): String = "Lamp: name=$name, bulbs=$bulbs, shade=$shade" Both versions do the same two things. The class lists the properties, and a separate function repeats that list as text. Two Kotlin features carry the weight. A data class writes its constructor, getters and toString for you, as Java's record has done since Java 16. And an extension function, fun Lamp.inventoryCard(), is called like a member, lamp.inventoryCard(), without changing the class. Java's version stays a static method that takes the lamp. The hand-written card has real strengths. It's plain code that anyone can read, it runs as fast as code can, and the compiler checks every name in it. Rename bulbs and the card stops compiling, so you fix it at once. Adding a property is a different story. The lamps gained watts, and the DriftDemo in the Try it runs the new Lamp with the old card: the lamp: Lamp(name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null, watts=40) its card: Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null The lamp knows it draws 40 watts, and its card keeps that a secret. The build passed, the program ran, and nothing printed a warning. The compiler checks that every name in the card exists, and all three still do. It cannot check that the card says everything, because nothing in the code says that it should. That gap has a name: the card has drifted from its class. Drift happens to any code that repeats information kept somewhere else, and every class you add is one more chance. MoveMate has four classes today; a real program may have forty. Code that repeats a class's shape by hand drifts from it. Something has to keep the copy in step. The question is who. One answer is to stop writing the card at all, and let the program work it out from the object while it runs. Watch a card drift Read DriftDemo: the new Lamp has watts, the card is the old one. Predict both printed lines, then run it from labs/. Run the Java twin, DriftDemoJava, where a record gained a component the same way. In DriftDemo.kt, rename bulbs to bulbCount in the class only. Predict what the build says this time, then undo it. DriftDemo.kt package workbench.ksp.l01.demo // MoveMate's lamps now record how many watts they draw, so Lamp gained a property. Nobody remembered the // hand-written card, which was written before watts existed. Predict what the two lines print. // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l01.demo.DriftDemoKt data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?, val watts: Int) // the card, exactly as it was written for the old Lamp fun Lamp.inventoryCard(): String = "Lamp: name=$name, bulbs=$bulbs, shade=$shade" fun main() { val lamp = Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null, 40) println("the lamp: $lamp") println("its card: ${lamp.inventoryCard()}") } ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l01.demo.DriftDemoKt labs/ksp/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/ksp/l01/demo/DriftDemo.kt DriftDemoJava.java package workbench.ksp.l01.demo; // The Java twin of DriftDemo.kt: a record gained a component, watts, and the hand-written card didn't. // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l01.demo.DriftDemoJava public class DriftDemoJava { record Lamp(String name, int bulbs, String shade, int watts) {} // the card, exactly as it was written for the old Lamp static String inventoryCard(Lamp lamp) { return "Lamp: name=" + lamp.name() + ", bulbs=" + lamp.bulbs() + ", shade=" + lamp.shade(); } public static void main(String[] args) { Lamp lamp = new Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null, 40); System.out.println("the lamp: " + lamp); System.out.println("its card: " + inventoryCard(lamp)); } } ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l01.demo.DriftDemoJava labs/ksp/src/demo/java/workbench/ksp/l01/demo/DriftDemoJava.java the lamp: Lamp(name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null, watts=40) and its card: Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null, and the Java twin prints the same card after Lamp[name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null, watts=40]. The build is green and nothing warns. The rename is different: the card no longer compiles, because bulbs no longer exists. The compiler catches a name that disappears, never a name that's missing.

h: Code that writes code: what KSP is and where it runs · Reflection: working out the card while the program runs
x: Reflection is a program looking at its own classes while it runs. It asks an object for its class, the class for its fields, and each field for its value. Every JVM has it built in, in the java.lang.reflect package. Here is the whole card, by reflection: Java static String reflectionCard(Object thing) throws IllegalAccessException { Class<?> type = thing.getClass(); if (!type.isAnnotationPresent(Inventory.class)) throw new IllegalArgumentException(type.getSimpleName() + " has no @Inventory note"); StringJoiner pairs = new StringJoiner(", "); for (Field field : type.getDeclaredFields()) { if (Modifier.isStatic(field.getModifiers()) || field.isSynthetic()) continue; field.setAccessible(true); // the fields are private pairs.add(field.getName() + "=" + field.get(thing)); } return type.getSimpleName() + ": " + pairs; } Kotlin fun reflectionCard(thing: Any): String { val type = thing.javaClass require(type.isAnnotationPresent(Inventory::class.java)) { "${type.simpleName} has no @Inventory note" } val pairs = type.declaredFields .filter { !Modifier.isStatic(it.modifiers) && !it.isSynthetic } .joinToString(", ") { field -> field.isAccessible = true // the fields behind properties are private "${field.name}=${field.get(thing)}" } return "${type.simpleName}: $pairs" } The two versions match almost line for line, because Kotlin uses the same Java reflection here. Read the Kotlin one aloud: "check that the class carries the @Inventory note, then for every field that isn't static, open it up, and print its name and its value." That sentence uses a word that needs a plain meaning. An annotation is a note you attach to a class, a function or a property, written with @, such as @Inventory. By itself it does nothing at all. It waits for a tool that reads it. @Inventory is MoveMate's sticky note on a box: "make an inventory card for this one." Here the tool is our own function, which reads the note while the program runs. So @Inventory is declared with RUNTIME retention, which keeps it in the class file for that purpose. Reflection fixes the drift. A class that gains a property gets it on its reflection card at once, with no card to update. The lab's tests check that with a Rug nobody wrote a card for, Rug: colour=red, metres=2.0, and check that reflection gives the same four cards as the hand-written ones. That's its honest credit: it never forgets a property. Now the price. The ReflectionCostDemo gives both versions the same lamp, checks that the two cards match, then times them. On the course's build machine, four cores busy with other builds at the time, it printed: the same card: true first call: hand-written 18,045,284 ns reflection 47,526,401 ns round 1 per call: hand-written 64 ns reflection 395 ns round 2 per call: hand-written 27 ns reflection 217 ns round 3 per call: hand-written 24 ns reflection 241 ns Correct first: the same card both ways. The first call of each pays for one-time setup inside the JVM, and reflection's setup costs more, about 48 ms against 18 ms here. Once the JVM has warmed up, a reflection card costs about 220 ns against about 25 ns by hand. That's roughly nine times as much, on every call, for as long as the program runs. A few hundred nanoseconds won't hurt MoveMate. A program that prints a million cards, or starts on a small phone, feels it. Cost is the first flaw. The second is timing. Hand reflectionCard a Wardrobe without the note and it fails with Wardrobe has no @Inventory note, but only when that line runs, perhaps on moving day itself. The third is quieter. The Javadoc, Java's official API documentation, says that getDeclaredFields() returns fields that "are not sorted and are not in any particular order". HotSpot, the usual JVM, returns them in declaration order today, so our cards come out right by habit, not by promise. In the moving-house picture, reflection means unpacking every box at the new house and checking what's inside, each time someone asks for a list. It works. It's slow, and a box with a missing note turns up only when you open it. A third way keeps the speed of the hand-written card and the memory of reflection. Let a program write the cards for us, once, while the program is built. Time the card both ways Run ReflectionCostDemo. It uses the reference reflectionCard until you finish the lab; add -Pmine=l01 afterwards to time yours. Check the third line first: are the two cards the same? Then compare the per-call times in round 3. Run it twice more, and the Java twin ReflectionCostDemoJava once. Which numbers stay about the same, and which jump around? ReflectionCostDemo.kt package workbench.ksp.l01.demo import workbench.ksp.l01.Lamp import workbench.ksp.l01.inventoryCard import workbench.ksp.l01.reflectionCard // The hand-written card against the reflection card: the same text, then what each costs. It uses your // reflectionCard with -Pmine=l01, the reference one otherwise. // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l01.demo.ReflectionCostDemoKt // The timings are for teaching, from a single run: expect different numbers on your machine. fun main() { val lamp = Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null) "warm up string building: ${lamp.name}".length // so neither first call pays for it // correctness first: the same card both ways var start = System.nanoTime() val byHand = lamp.inventoryCard() val firstByHand = System.nanoTime() - start start = System.nanoTime() val byReflection = reflectionCard(lamp) val firstByReflection = System.nanoTime() - start println("hand-written: $byHand") println("reflection: $byReflection") println("the same card: ${byHand == byReflection}") // then the cost: the very first call, and the average over many calls once the JVM has warmed up println("first call: hand-written %,9d ns reflection %,9d ns".format(firstByHand, firstByReflection)) val calls = 2_000_000 repeat(3) { round -> val hand = timePerCall(calls) { lamp.inventoryCard() } val reflection = timePerCall(calls) { reflectionCard(lamp) } println("round ${round + 1} per call: hand-written %,9.0f ns reflection %,9.0f ns".format(hand, reflection)) } } /** Average nanoseconds per call of [card] over [calls] calls (the lengths are summed so the JIT keeps the work). */ private fun timePerCall(calls: Int, card: () -> String): Double { var sink = 0L val start = System.nanoTime() repeat(calls) { sink += card().length } val elapsed = System.nanoTime() - start if (sink == 42L) println("unlikely") // uses sink return elapsed.toDouble() / calls } ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l01.demo.ReflectionCostDemoKt labs/ksp/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/ksp/l01/demo/ReflectionCostDemo.kt ReflectionCostDemoJava.java package workbench.ksp.l01.demo; import java.util.function.Supplier; import workbench.ksp.l01.HandCardsKt; import workbench.ksp.l01.Lamp; import workbench.ksp.l01.ReflectionCardsKt; // The Java twin of ReflectionCostDemo.kt: Java calling the same two Kotlin functions. HandCards.kt compiles to // the class HandCardsKt, and the extension function Lamp.inventoryCard() becomes a static method taking the lamp. // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l01.demo.ReflectionCostDemoJava // The timings are for teaching, from a single run: expect different numbers on your machine. public class ReflectionCostDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Lamp lamp = new Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null); ("warm up string building: " + lamp.getName()).length(); // so neither first call pays for it long start = System.nanoTime(); String byHand = HandCardsKt.inventoryCard(lamp); long firstByHand = System.nanoTime() - start; start = System.nanoTime(); String byReflection = ReflectionCardsKt.reflectionCard(lamp); long firstByReflection = System.nanoTime() - start; System.out.println("hand-written: " + byHand); System.out.println("reflection: " + byReflection); System.out.println("the same card: " + byHand.equals(byReflection)); System.out.printf("first call: hand-written %,9d ns reflection %,9d ns%n", firstByHand, firstByReflection); int calls = 2_000_000; for (int round = 1; round <= 3; round++) { double hand = timePerCall(calls, () -> HandCardsKt.inventoryCard(lamp)); double reflection = timePerCall(calls, () -> ReflectionCardsKt.reflectionCard(lamp)); System.out.printf("round %d per call: hand-written %,9.0f ns reflection %,9.0f ns%n", round, hand, reflection); } } /** Average nanoseconds per call over {@code calls} calls (the lengths are summed so the JIT keeps the work). */ private static double timePerCall(int calls, Supplier<String> card) { long sink = 0; long start = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < calls; i++) sink += card.get().length(); long elapsed = System.nanoTime() - start; if (sink == 42) System.out.println("unlikely"); return (double) elapsed / calls; } } ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l01.demo.ReflectionCostDemoJava labs/ksp/src/demo/java/workbench/ksp/l01/demo/ReflectionCostDemoJava.java the same card: true, then a first call of a few to a few tens of milliseconds for each, reflection's the larger, and warm per-call times of roughly 15 to 60 ns by hand against roughly 200 to 400 ns by reflection. The first-call numbers jump around from run to run, because they measure one-time setup inside a busy machine. The warm ratio, about eight to ten times, stays steady. Your machine will give its own numbers. Class.getDeclaredFields (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Code that writes code: what KSP is and where it runs · Code that writes code: a processor writes the cards during the build
x: Code that writes code: a helper reads each box's label during the build and writes the card, so it can't drift First, two moments in a program's life. Compile time is when the compiler turns your source files into class files, the bytecode the JVM runs. Run time is later, when the JVM runs those class files. The build is everything a tool such as Gradle does to get from source files to a program you can run, and compiling is one step of it. The hand-written card was written before the build, by a person. The reflection card is worked out at run time, by the program. The third way does the work during the build, by a program. That's code generation: one program writes source code, which is then compiled together with yours. The program that writes the code is an annotation processor. It runs during the build, finds the declarations that carry a given annotation, and writes new source files from what it reads. A declaration is a named thing you declared in the code: a class, a property, a function, a parameter. MoveMate's processor looks for @Inventory and writes one card per class. KSP, short for Kotlin Symbol Processing, is an open-source tool from Google that runs such processors on Kotlin code. (A symbol is any named thing in your code, which is what a processor reads.) Its docs call it "a source code generation framework for Kotlin". With it, "you can create processors that inspect static information about your source code and generate new code from it". Static information is what you can know without running the code: names, types and annotations. Here is the moving-house picture, part by part. Your source files are sealed boxes. The label on top lists what's inside: the class name, the properties with their types, the functions and their parameters. Those are the declarations. The annotation is the sticky note on a box. The processor is a helper with a clipboard who walks through the house, finds every box with that note, reads its label, and writes a new card. The cards travel with the move: they're compiled together with your code. The picture breaks in one place, and it matters. A real helper could lift a flap and peek inside a box. KSP truly can't, as the next section explains. Let's watch a ready-made processor at work. The lab's real-build playground, labs/ksp/app, is an ordinary Gradle project with KSP switched on. Its lesson 1 folder holds the four MoveMate classes, each marked @Inventory, and no card functions at all. From labs/, run KSP on it alone with ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL01Kotlin. The task runs the processor you'll write yourself in the next lesson, and it writes four new files. Open labs/ksp/app/build/generated/ksp/l01/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l01/LampInventoryCard.kt: // Generated by InventoryProcessor from Lamp. Do not edit. package workbench.ksp.app.l01 fun Lamp.inventoryCard(): String = "Lamp: name=$name, bulbs=$bulbs, shade=$shade" That's the hand-written card, line for line, written by a program that has no way to forget a property. Add watts to Lamp and run the task again, and the card gains watts=$watts, because the helper reads every label afresh on each build. Generated code is checked like hand-written code and runs as fast. Only the writing moves, from a person to the build. You may wonder whether the generated card is somehow special. It isn't. It's an ordinary Kotlin file, so Java can call it like any other Kotlin code: Java // Java calling the card that KSP generated in Kotlin Lamp lamp = new Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null); System.out.println(LampInventoryCardKt.inventoryCard(lamp)); Kotlin // Kotlin calling the same generated card val lamp = Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null) println(lamp.inventoryCard()) So where exactly in the build does the helper work, and what is it not allowed to touch? Run a ready-made processor in a real build From labs/, run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL01Kotlin. Then list labs/ksp/app/build/generated/ksp/l01/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l01/. Predict how many files you'll find, and why that many. Open PlantInventoryCard.kt and compare it with the given Box card in labs/ksp/src/main/kotlin/workbench/ksp/l01/HandCards.kt. Run the app's MoveMate.kt below with ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l01.MoveMateKt, then the Java twin with -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l01.MoveMateJava. Add val watts: Int = 60 to Lamp in labs/ksp/app/src/l01/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l01/MoveMate.kt, run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL01Kotlin again and reopen LampInventoryCard.kt. Then undo the change. MoveMate.kt package workbench.ksp.app.l01 import workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory // Lesson 1, the real build. Nobody wrote a card for these classes. Before the Kotlin compiler runs, KSP runs a // ready-made card processor (lesson 2's, named in labs/ksp/app/src/l01/processors.txt), and it writes one new // file per class into labs/ksp/app/build/generated/ksp/l01/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l01/. // ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL01Kotlin run KSP alone, then open that folder // ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l01.MoveMateKt compile everything and print the cards @Inventory data class Box(val label: String, val room: String, val weightGrams: Int, val fragile: Boolean = false) @Inventory data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?) @Inventory class Bookshelf(val shelves: Int, val books: List<String>) @Inventory data class Plant(val kind: String, val potLitres: Double, val waterEveryDays: Int = 7) fun main() { // inventoryCard() is defined nowhere in src/l01: KSP generated it during this build println(Box("kitchen 1", "kitchen", 5200, fragile = true).inventoryCard()) println(Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null).inventoryCard()) println(Bookshelf(3, listOf("atlas", "cookbook")).inventoryCard()) println(Plant("fern", 2.5).inventoryCard()) } ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l01.MoveMateKt labs/ksp/app/src/l01/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l01/MoveMate.kt MoveMateJava.java package workbench.ksp.app.l01; import java.util.List; // The Java twin: Java calling the cards that KSP generated in Kotlin. Each generated file compiles to an // ordinary class (LampInventoryCard.kt becomes LampInventoryCardKt) with a static method that takes the object. // ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l01.MoveMateJava public class MoveMateJava { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(BoxInventoryCardKt.inventoryCard(new Box("kitchen 1", "kitchen", 5200, true))); System.out.println(LampInventoryCardKt.inventoryCard(new Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null))); System.out.println(BookshelfInventoryCardKt.inventoryCard(new Bookshelf(3, List.of("atlas", "cookbook")))); System.out.println(PlantInventoryCardKt.inventoryCard(new Plant("fern", 2.5, 7))); // Java passes the default } } ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l01.MoveMateJava labs/ksp/app/src/l01/java/workbench/ksp/app/l01/MoveMateJava.java Four files, one per class with @Inventory: BookshelfInventoryCard.kt, BoxInventoryCard.kt, LampInventoryCard.kt and PlantInventoryCard.kt, each written exactly like the given Box card. Both demos print the same four cards, starting with Box: label=kitchen 1, room=kitchen, weightGrams=5200, fragile=true. With watts added, the generated card ends shade=$shade, watts=$watts with no card written by anyone. If you run the Java twin before undoing, javac stops at new Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null): Java has no default arguments, so a Java call must pass watts too. The compiler checks calls; it was never checking cards. KSP overview (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Code that writes code: what KSP is and where it runs · Where KSP runs in the build, and the two things it cannot do
x: KSP runs as its own Gradle task, one step of the build, just before the Kotlin compiler. For the lesson 1 folder the task is kspL01Kotlin, and the compile task is compileL01Kotlin; in an ordinary project with one source folder they're called kspKotlin and compileKotlin. Gradle calls such a group of source folders a source set: an ordinary project has one, main, and this playground has one per lesson, l01 here. Gradle's -m flag lists the tasks a command would run, in order, without running them: $ ./gradlew :ksp:app:compileL01Kotlin -m :ksp:compileSolutionKotlin SKIPPED :ksp:l02SolutionJar SKIPPED :ksp:app:kspL01Kotlin SKIPPED :ksp:app:compileL01Kotlin SKIPPED Read it from the top. Gradle first compiles the processor and packs it into a jar, the zip file a Java library ships in (l02SolutionJar), because a processor is a program that must exist before it can run. Then KSP runs it on your files, and only then does the Kotlin compiler start. The figure draws the same order. KSP writes its files into build/generated/ksp/l01/kotlin, a folder it adds to the compile's inputs, and the compiler compiles them together with yours. That's why MoveMate.kt can call inventoryCard() although no file in src/l01 defines it. (An IDE, the editor you write code in, marks that call red until the first build has run KSP.) KSP isn't part of the Kotlin compiler. Its KSP2 notes say it "is no longer a compiler plugin", and that it "runs in Gradle daemon", the background process Gradle keeps alive between builds. KSP's version numbers no longer follow Kotlin's either: these labs run KSP 2.3.14 with Kotlin 2.4.21. Now the two limits, in the docs' own words: KSP-based processors "can't examine expressions or statements, and they can't modify the source code." The first limit means the helper reads labels and never what's packed. It sees fun areaCm2(): Int, a function's name and its return type, but not the multiplication inside it. It sees that a parameter has a default value, but not what the value is. Lesson 3 of this track proves this with a demo. The second limit means the helper never relabels or repacks a box. A processor can't add a function to Lamp; it can only write a new file. That's why the card is an extension function in a file of its own, and not a member of Lamp. KSP reads declarations, never bodies, and it adds new files, never edits yours. Java has had this idea for a long time. Since Java 6, javac has run annotation processors written against javax.annotation.processing, and many Java libraries generate code that way. KSP is Kotlin's own, faster way to do the same job for Kotlin code. It reads Kotlin's features, such as nullable types and default values, directly. An older bridge, kapt, runs Java's processors on Kotlin by first writing Java copies of your classes, which is slow; lesson 9 of this track returns to it. Both kinds of processor have the same shape: Java // Closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor (javax.annotation.processing, since Java 6) @SupportedAnnotationTypes("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory") @SupportedSourceVersion(SourceVersion.RELEASE_21) public class InventoryProcessor extends AbstractProcessor { @Override public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment roundEnv) { TypeElement inventory = processingEnv.getElementUtils().getTypeElement("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory"); for (Element element : roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(inventory)) { // read the element's label, then write a file with processingEnv.getFiler() } return false; } } Kotlin // A KSP processor, the shape lesson 2 builds class InventoryProcessor(private val codeGenerator: CodeGenerator) : SymbolProcessor { override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { for (symbol in resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory")) { // read the symbol's label, then write a file with codeGenerator.createNewFile(...) } return emptyList() } } Lesson 2 builds the Kotlin one, line by line. Put the three ways side by side in the picture, with one more. A hand-written card is a person keeping a list. Reflection is unpacking every box at the new house, each time. A processor is the helper who writes the cards before the van leaves. A compiler plugin, from the last lesson of Advanced Kotlin, changes what the compiler writes into a class. It's a mover who repacks boxes: more power, and more risk. KSP stays a helper on purpose. Next, you'll stop watching the helper and write one. Change the label, watch the card follow Run GeneratedCardDemo. It compiles the new Lamp in memory with the ready-made processor and prints the card file it wrote. In the demo's source string, give Lamp one more property, val colour: String, and pass "white" to it in deskLampCard(). Predict the new card, then run it. Now add val heat = watts * 2 inside the class body instead, as a property that isn't in the constructor. Predict whether the card shows it, then run. GeneratedCardDemo.kt package workbench.ksp.l01.demo import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.KotlinCompilation import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.SourceFile import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.configureKsp import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.kspSourcesDir import java.io.File import java.io.OutputStream import workbench.ksp.l01.ReadyMadeInventoryProcessorProvider // The third way, in memory: compile the new Lamp (with watts) together with the ready-made card processor, // print the card file the processor wrote, then call it. Nobody writes a card, so nobody can forget one. // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l01.demo.GeneratedCardDemoKt fun main() { val lamp = SourceFile.kotlin( "Lamp.kt", """ package movemate import workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory @Inventory data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?, val watts: Int) fun deskLampCard() = Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null, 40).inventoryCard() """, ) val compilation = KotlinCompilation().apply { workingDir = File("build/kctfork/demo").apply { deleteRecursively() } sources = listOf(lamp) inheritClassPath = true jvmTarget = "21" messageOutputStream = OutputStream.nullOutputStream() configureKsp { symbolProcessorProviders += ReadyMadeInventoryProcessorProvider() } } val result = compilation.compile() println("exit code: ${result.exitCode}") val generated = compilation.kspSourcesDir.resolve("kotlin") generated.walk().filter { it.isFile }.forEach { file -> println("--- ${file.relativeTo(generated).invariantSeparatorsPath}") print(file.readText()) } val card = result.classLoader.loadClass("movemate.LampKt").getMethod("deskLampCard").invoke(null) println("--- deskLampCard() returns: $card") } ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l01.demo.GeneratedCardDemoKt labs/ksp/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/ksp/l01/demo/GeneratedCardDemo.kt First exit code: OK, the file movemate/LampInventoryCard.kt with watts=$watts in the template, and deskLampCard() returns: Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null, watts=40. With colour, the card gains colour=$colour and prints colour=white. The property in the body doesn't appear: the card lists the primary constructor's properties only, because that's the label the processor reads. The demo takes about 10 s, most of it starting the compiler. KSP runs as its own task before the Kotlin compiler; the files it writes are compiled together with yours. h: Code that writes code: what KSP is and where it runs · Java and Kotlin
x: The lamp's card three ways, in Java and Kotlin Cards.java // 1. by hand: fast, checked by the compiler, and it drifts static String inventoryCard(Lamp lamp) { return "Lamp: name=" + lamp.name() + ", bulbs=" + lamp.bulbs() + ", shade=" + lamp.shade(); } // 2. by reflection, at run time: a record promises its components' order static String reflectionCard(Record thing) throws ReflectiveOperationException { StringJoiner pairs = new StringJoiner(", "); for (RecordComponent c : thing.getClass().getRecordComponents()) { pairs.add(c.getName() + "=" + c.getAccessor().invoke(thing)); } return thing.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + pairs; } // 3. by a javac annotation processor during the build: it writes // LampInventoryCard.java, and the program calls LampInventoryCard.inventoryCard(lamp) Cards.kt // 1. by hand: fast, checked by the compiler, and it drifts fun Lamp.inventoryCard(): String = "Lamp: name=$name, bulbs=$bulbs, shade=$shade" // 2. by reflection, at run time: fields in whatever order getDeclaredFields() gives fun reflectionCard(thing: Any): String = thing.javaClass.simpleName + ": " + thing.javaClass.declaredFields .filter { !Modifier.isStatic(it.modifiers) } .joinToString(", ") { it.isAccessible = true; "${it.name}=${it.get(thing)}" } // 3. by a KSP processor during the build: it writes LampInventoryCard.kt holding // the same function as 1, and the program calls lamp.inventoryCard() The three ways line up in both languages. One real difference sits in the middle. A Java record promises the order of its components: getRecordComponents() returns them in the order they're declared in the record header. A Kotlin data class is an ordinary class to the JVM, so reflection falls back on getDeclaredFields(), whose Javadoc promises no order at all. The other difference is in the third way. A javac processor writes a Java helper class that you call with the object as an argument. A KSP processor can write an extension function, so the generated card reads like a member, lamp.inventoryCard(). Neither tool can add a real member to the class.

h: Code that writes code: what KSP is and where it runs · Worked example
x: Guard the hand-written cards with a test, and see why it isn't enough Before reaching for a processor, a careful team might guard the hand-written cards with a test: for each class, build one sample object and compare its hand-written card with the reflection card. Reflection becomes the referee. // 1. one sample per class private val samples = listOf( Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null, 40), Plant("fern", 2.5), ) @Test fun `every hand-written card lists every property`() { // 2. the referee: the same card, worked out by reflection assertThat(samples[0].inventoryCard()).isEqualTo(reflectionCard(samples[0])) assertThat(samples[1].inventoryCard()).isEqualTo(reflectionCard(samples[1])) } // 1. one sample per class private final Lamp lamp = new Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null, 40); private final Plant plant = new Plant("fern", 2.5, 7); @Test void everyHandWrittenCardListsEveryProperty() throws Exception { // 2. the referee: the same card, worked out by reflection assertThat(Cards.inventoryCard(lamp)).isEqualTo(Cards.reflectionCard(lamp)); assertThat(Cards.inventoryCard(plant)).isEqualTo(Cards.reflectionCard(plant)); } With the stale lamp card, the first assertion fails, and AssertJ prints both cards, the one with watts=40 and the one without. The drift is caught by the tests, before moving day. That's a real improvement, and a cheap one. Now MoveMate gains a fifth class, Rug, and whoever adds it forgets to add a sample to this test. The test passes, and the rug's card can drift as freely as the lamp's did. The drift has moved from the card into the test: the list of samples is one more thing a person must keep in step. A processor ends the chase. It finds every class with @Inventory itself, on every build, so there is no list for anyone to forget. The cards follow the labels because nobody writes them. That's the job the rest of this track teaches, starting with the next lesson.

h: Code that writes code: what KSP is and where it runs · Quiz
x: Which parts of this class can a KSP processor read? class Mirror(val widthCm: Int, val heightCm: Int) { fun areaCm2(): Int = widthCm * heightCm } Only the class name: types are worked out later by the compiler The class, both properties with their types, and areaCm2(): Int, but not widthCm * heightCm Everything, including the multiplication, as a tree of expressions Nothing until compileKotlin has turned it into class files KSP sees declarations: names, types, parameters, annotations. It can't see expressions or statements, so the body of areaCm2 is closed to it. It runs before the compiler, on source files, so the last option has the order backwards. The third is what a compiler plugin can see, and KSP deliberately can't. MoveMate needs a card() function that reads like a member of Lamp. What does a KSP processor do? It adds fun card() inside class Lamp in Lamp.kt It edits the compiled Lamp.class after compileKotlin It asks the compiler to add the member while it compiles It writes a new file with an extension function, fun Lamp.card() KSP can't modify existing code; it only creates new files, which are compiled with yours. An extension function in a new file is the usual way to make generated code read like a member. Changing a class or its class file is a compiler plugin's job. After ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL01Kotlin, where is the generated LampInventoryCard.kt? labs/ksp/app/build/generated/ksp/l01/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l01/ labs/ksp/app/src/l01/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l01/, next to MoveMate.kt labs/ksp/app/build/classes/kotlin/l01/ Nowhere on disk: KSP hands it to the compiler in memory KSP writes generated sources under build/generated/ksp/<source set>/kotlin/, in the package's folders, and adds that folder to the compile. It never writes into src, which belongs to you, and class files come later, from the compiler. Pick the tool. A test helper prints every property of whatever object a test hands it, a few dozen times per test run, including objects from libraries you can't annotate. A KSP processor, because generated code is faster A hand-written card for each class Reflection: it works on any object at run time, and a few dozen calls cost almost nothing A compiler plugin that adds a card to every class A processor only sees source code it is run on, marked with its annotation, so library classes are out of reach, and hand-written cards can't cover unknown classes. At a few dozen calls, reflection's few hundred nanoseconds are invisible. Reflection's costs matter in hot paths and at start-up, not in a test helper. From Part 4's capstone: the container moved its wiring from reflection at every start to a registry generated during the build. What did that trade give up? Speed: generated wiring is slower on every call Choosing parts at start-up: the set of components is fixed when you build Type checking: generated code isn't checked by the compiler Thread safety: the generated holders can't be shared between threads Work that depends only on the classes can move to the build, but then the set of parts is fixed when you build; nothing can pick a component from a setting or a plugin folder at start-up unless the generator wrote code for it. Generated code is compiled and checked like any code, and it's faster, which is why the move was worth it.

h: Code that writes code: what KSP is and where it runs · Key terms
x: Annotation A note attached to a class, function or property with @. It does nothing until a tool reads it. Build Everything a tool such as Gradle does to turn source files into a program you can run; compiling is one step. Compile time When the compiler turns source files into class files, before the program runs. Run time When the JVM runs the compiled program. Reflection A program inspecting its own classes, fields and annotations while it runs, through java.lang.reflect. Code generation One program writing source code that is then compiled together with yours. Annotation processor A program that runs during the build, reads annotated declarations and writes new source files. KSP Kotlin Symbol Processing: the tool that runs annotation processors on Kotlin code, as a Gradle task before the Kotlin compiler. What is an annotation processor? A program that runs during the build, finds declarations that carry a given annotation, and writes new source files that are compiled together with yours. What does KSP stand for, and what does it run? Kotlin Symbol Processing. It runs annotation processors written against its own API on Kotlin (and Java) source code during the build. Which Gradle task runs KSP, and when? kspKotlin for the main source set (kspL01Kotlin in the lab), before compileKotlin, which then compiles your files and the generated ones together. Where do KSP's generated Kotlin files go? build/generated/ksp/<source set>/kotlin/<package folders>/, for example build/generated/ksp/main/kotlin/... in an ordinary project. What are KSP's two limits? It can't see expressions or statements (function bodies, default values), and it can't modify existing code: it only adds new files. Why does the reflection card need @Inventory with RUNTIME retention, while KSP doesn't? Reflection looks for the annotation while the program runs, so it must survive into the class file. KSP reads source files, so SOURCE retention is enough for it. Hand-written card vs reflection card: one cost each? The hand-written card drifts when the class changes. The reflection card costs on every call (here about 220 ns against 25 ns) and finds mistakes only when it runs.

h: Code that writes code: what KSP is and where it runs · Go deeper
x: Three facts for a curious day. First, the Java side changed recently. Since JDK 23, javac no longer runs annotation processors that it merely finds on the class path. The release notes say processing "is only run with some explicit configuration of annotation processing or with an explicit request to run annotation processing on the javac command line", and -proc:full restores the old behavior. Gradle passes processors explicitly through its annotationProcessor configuration, so Gradle builds don't notice. Plain javac scripts that relied on discovery do. Second, kapt. It lets Kotlin projects run Java annotation processors by first generating Java stubs, Java copies of your Kotlin classes with the bodies replaced, so the Java processor has something it can read. The migration guide calls that step "expensive": it "significantly increases build time" and loses Kotlin details such as nullability. KSP's README says KSP processors "can run up to 2x faster" than kapt. That figure comes from early benchmarks with Room, a database library, when KSP was announced in 2021, so read it as one measurement, not a law. Lesson 9 of this track weighs the two in a real build. Third, treat generated files as output, not source. Each one says Do not edit because KSP rewrites it whenever the class it came from changes, and a clean build deletes it. If a generated file is wrong, fix the processor or the annotated class. Read generated files often, though: they're the quickest way to see what a processor really does, and lesson 8 turns that habit into tests.

h: Your first processor · The smallest processor KSP will run: a provider, a processor and a services file
x: An annotation is a note in the code written with @, such as @Inventory, MoveMate's sticky note for "make an inventory card for this one". An annotation processor is a program that runs during the build (the steps Gradle takes to turn your source files into a program), reads the annotated classes, and writes new source files. KSP, Kotlin Symbol Processing, runs such processors on Kotlin code. A KSP processor is two small classes and one text file. The processor is the helper: a class that implements SymbolProcessor, whose process function KSP calls during the build. The provider is the moving company that sends the helper: a class that implements SymbolProcessorProvider, whose one job is to create the processor and hand it its tools. The services file is how KSP finds the company: a text file inside the processor's jar (the zip file a Java library ships in) that names the provider class. Here's the first rung, a processor that only reports each pass it makes, with the closest Java equivalent first: Java // Closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor (javax.annotation.processing) @SupportedAnnotationTypes("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory") @SupportedSourceVersion(SourceVersion.RELEASE_21) public class RoundLogger extends AbstractProcessor { // javac creates it with new RoundLogger() private int round = 0; @Override public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment roundEnv) { round++; processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.WARNING, "round " + round); return false; // don't claim @Inventory for this processor alone } } Kotlin class RoundLoggerProvider : SymbolProcessorProvider { // KSP finds this through the services file override fun create(environment: SymbolProcessorEnvironment): SymbolProcessor = RoundLogger(environment.logger) } class RoundLogger(private val logger: KSPLogger) : SymbolProcessor { override val apiFeatures = buildApiFeatures { enableBackingFields = true; enableContextParameters = true } private var round = 0 override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { round++ logger.warn("round $round") return emptyList() // nothing set aside for a later round } } Let's walk through the Kotlin version from the top. KSP calls the provider's create once per build and passes it an environment, a bag of tools. codeGenerator writes files, logger prints messages, and options holds settings from the build file (lesson 7). Our processor keeps only the logger. KSP then calls process with a Resolver, the helper's clipboard: it answers questions such as "which symbols carry this note?" process returns the symbols it couldn't handle yet, and an empty list means "all done". The apiFeatures line opts in to newer KSP behavior; without it, KSP 2.3.14 prints three notes on every run asking you to. Java has had annotation processors like this one since Java 6, and KSP is Kotlin's own, faster way to do the same job for Kotlin code. Two things differ in the Java twin. Java has no provider: javac creates the processor itself, through a public constructor with no parameters. And @SupportedAnnotationTypes tells javac which annotations the processor wants, while every KSP processor simply sees every file. The services file is one line, the provider's full class name: workbench.ksp.l02.InventoryProcessorProvider In an ordinary project it lives at src/main/resources/META-INF/services/com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessorProvider. In this lab each lesson keeps its own copy, at src/main/resources/workbench/ksp/l02/SymbolProcessorProvider, and the build moves it to that path inside lesson 2's jar. Java's file has a different name, META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor, and the same job. What happens without it? Empty the lab's file, keep it, and run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL02Kotlin -Pmine=l02: > Task :ksp:app:kspL02Kotlin FAILED e: [ksp] No providers found in processor classpath. Misspell the class name instead, and the build names the typo: Provider workbench.ksp.l02.InventoryProcessorProvidr not found. KSP is strict about this file, and that's a kindness: it fails at once, not three steps later. Why does the processor live in its own module, a project of its own within the build (labs/ksp), and not next to MoveMate's classes in labs/ksp/app? Because it's a program that must be compiled before it can run on your code. If the app's KSP task needed the app's own compiled classes, each would wait for the other, and Gradle refuses such a loop with Circular dependency between the following tasks. So the processor sits in a module of its own, and the app adds it through the ksp configuration, a named list of dependencies that only KSP uses: // app/build.gradle.kts in an ordinary project: the processor lives in a module of its own plugins { kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.21" id("com.google.devtools.ksp") version "2.3.14" } dependencies { implementation(project(":annotations")) // the sticky notes: your code uses them ksp(project(":processor")) // the helper: only the build uses it } A processor is a provider, a processor and a services file. If KSP can't find all three, nothing runs. Every processor in this track makes the same five moves, named the same way each time. Find the symbols with the note. Check that each one is something you can handle. Read the parts of its label you need. Write the new file. Prove it works, in tests and then in a real build. Rung one makes none of them yet; it only shows that KSP found the helper. Next, the helper should notice the sticky notes. Run your processor in a real build, then break the services file From labs/, run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL02Kotlin -Pmine=l02. -Pmine=l02 uses your processor from src/main, still the lab's stub. Read the one w: [ksp] line it prints. (If the task says UP-TO-DATE and prints nothing, Gradle reused its last result: add --rerun.) Open labs/ksp/src/main/resources/workbench/ksp/l02/SymbolProcessorProvider, delete its one line (keep the empty file), and run the same command. Then type the class name back with one letter missing and run it again. Put the correct line back. Run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL02Kotlin without -Pmine, so the reference processor runs, and list labs/ksp/app/build/generated/ksp/l02/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l02/. The MovingDay.kt below calls those files, and so does its Java twin. MovingDay.kt package workbench.ksp.app.l02 import workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory // Lesson 2, the real build: your @Inventory processor (with -Pmine=l02) or the reference one runs on this file. // ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL02Kotlin -Pmine=l02 run KSP alone with yours; it works even on the stub // then open labs/ksp/app/build/generated/ksp/l02/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l02/LampInventoryCard.kt // ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l02.MovingDayKt -Pmine=l02 once your lab passes @Inventory data class Box(val label: String, val room: String, val weightGrams: Int, val fragile: Boolean = false) @Inventory data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?) @Inventory class Bookshelf(val shelves: Int, val books: List<String>) @Inventory data class Plant(val kind: String, val potLitres: Double, val waterEveryDays: Int = 7) fun main() { val van = listOf( Box("kitchen 1", "kitchen", 5200, fragile = true).inventoryCard(), Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null).inventoryCard(), Bookshelf(3, listOf("atlas", "cookbook")).inventoryCard(), Plant("fern", 2.5).inventoryCard(), ) van.forEach(::println) } ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l02.MovingDayKt labs/ksp/app/src/l02/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l02/MovingDay.kt MovingDayJava.java package workbench.ksp.app.l02; import java.util.List; // The Java twin: Java calling the cards your processor generated. LampInventoryCard.kt compiles to the class // LampInventoryCardKt, and the extension function becomes a static method that takes the lamp. // ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l02.MovingDayJava -Pmine=l02 public class MovingDayJava { public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> van = List.of( BoxInventoryCardKt.inventoryCard(new Box("kitchen 1", "kitchen", 5200, true)), LampInventoryCardKt.inventoryCard(new Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null)), BookshelfInventoryCardKt.inventoryCard(new Bookshelf(3, List.of("atlas", "cookbook"))), PlantInventoryCardKt.inventoryCard(new Plant("fern", 2.5, 7))); van.forEach(System.out::println); } } ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l02.MovingDayJava labs/ksp/app/src/l02/java/workbench/ksp/app/l02/MovingDayJava.java Step 1 prints w: [ksp] l02 not done yet: 1. Find: ask the resolver for every symbol annotated @Inventory, by its fully qualified name and BUILD SUCCESSFUL: KSP found your provider, created your processor and called process, which is rung one. The empty file gives e: [ksp] No providers found in processor classpath. and a failed task; the typo gives Provider workbench.ksp.l02.InventoryProcessorProvidr not found. Step 3 lists four files, one per class, such as LampInventoryCard.kt. KSP quickstart (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Your first processor · Finding the sticky notes: getSymbolsWithAnnotation and the annotation's full name
x: Rung two asks the clipboard its first question. A symbol is anything in your code with a name: a class, a function, a property, a parameter. A declaration is a symbol you declared yourself, and a class declaration arrives as a KSClassDeclaration. KSP calls everything that can carry an annotation a KSAnnotated, and getSymbolsWithAnnotation returns those that carry the one you name: Java // Closest Java equivalent: javac's RoundEnvironment @Override public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment roundEnv) { Messager messager = processingEnv.getMessager(); TypeElement inventory = processingEnv.getElementUtils().getTypeElement("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory"); Set<? extends Element> found = roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(inventory); messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.WARNING, "found " + found.size()); for (Element element : found) { messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.WARNING, "found " + element.getSimpleName(), element); } return false; } Kotlin override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { val found = resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory").toList() logger.warn("found ${found.size}") for (symbol in found) { if (symbol is KSClassDeclaration) logger.warn("found ${symbol.simpleName.asString()}", symbol) } return emptyList() } Both versions ask by the annotation's identity. Java looks up the annotation's TypeElement and passes it in. KSP takes the annotation's fully qualified name, its package and class name together, as a plain string. The second argument to logger.warn is the symbol itself, and that's worth making a habit: KSP then prints where the symbol is, its file and line. RungsDemo runs rung one, this rung, and a variant that asks for the short name "Inventory", all on one MoveMate file. The file has two @Inventory classes and a Wardrobe without the note. x: The same first processor, as a javac processor and as a KSP processor InventoryProcessor.java // Closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor @SupportedAnnotationTypes("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory") @SupportedSourceVersion(SourceVersion.RELEASE_21) public class InventoryProcessor extends AbstractProcessor { @Override public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment roundEnv) { Elements elements = processingEnv.getElementUtils(); TypeElement inventory = elements.getTypeElement("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory"); for (Element element : roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(inventory)) { // 1. Find if (element.getKind() != ElementKind.CLASS) { // 2. Check processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, "@Inventory goes on a class", element); continue; } TypeElement cls = (TypeElement) element; String pkg = elements.getPackageOf(cls).getQualifiedName().toString(); String name = cls.getSimpleName().toString(); try (Writer out = processingEnv.getFiler() // 4. Write .createSourceFile(pkg + "." + name + "InventoryCard", cls).openWriter()) { out.write("package " + pkg + ";\n..."); } catch (IOException e) { processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, e.toString(), cls); } } return false; } } // registered in META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor InventoryProcessor.kt class InventoryProcessorProvider : SymbolProcessorProvider { override fun create(environment: SymbolProcessorEnvironment): SymbolProcessor = InventoryProcessor(environment.codeGenerator, environment.logger) } class InventoryProcessor( private val codeGenerator: CodeGenerator, private val logger: KSPLogger, ) : SymbolProcessor { override val apiFeatures = buildApiFeatures { enableBackingFields = true; enableContextParameters = true } override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { for (symbol in resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory")) { // 1. Find if (symbol !is KSClassDeclaration || symbol.classKind != ClassKind.CLASS) { // 2. Check logger.error("@Inventory goes on a class", symbol) continue } val names = symbol.primaryConstructor?.parameters.orEmpty() // 3. Read .filter { it.isVal || it.isVar }.map { it.name!!.asString() } codeGenerator.createNewFile( // 4. Write Dependencies(false, symbol.containingFile!!), symbol.packageName.asString(), "${symbol.simpleName.asString()}InventoryCard", ).use { it.write(cardSource(symbol, names).toByteArray()) } } return emptyList() } } // registered in META-INF/services/com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessorProvider The two processors make the same moves in the same order, and most of the API maps one to one: getElementsAnnotatedWith to getSymbolsWithAnnotation, Messager.printMessage(ERROR, ..., element) to logger.error(..., symbol), Filer.createSourceFile(name, element) to createNewFile(Dependencies(...), package, name). Three differences are real. javac creates its processor through a no-argument constructor, while KSP asks a provider, so a KSP processor can take its tools as constructor parameters. javac returns true or false to "claim" annotations from other processors; KSP has no claiming, and process returns the symbols it set aside for a later round. And the Java version needs a read step of its own to find a constructor, because Java has no primary constructor; lesson 3 shows how much more of the Kotlin label KSP can read.

A processor writes LampInventoryCard.kt in round 1, and in every round asks getSymbolsWithAnnotation for @Inventory. What does round 2 return? Lamp again, so the processor must remember which cards it wrote Every symbol in the generated card file Nothing: only symbols from round 2's new files, and the card carries no @Inventory There is no round 2, because the processor returned an empty list From round 2 on, getSymbolsWithAnnotation returns symbols from the files the last round created, plus symbols set aside for later. The card has no @Inventory, so the answer is empty. Round 2 happens because round 1 wrote a file; the returned list only says what was set aside. Walking getAllFiles() instead would find Lamp again and fail with FileAlreadyExistsException. @Inventory is on line 5 and interface Shape on line 6, and the processor calls logger.error(message, symbol). Which line does the error name? Line 6, the declaration Line 5, the annotation Line 1, the package line No line: only the file name KSP reports a symbol's own location, and a class declaration's location is its interface or class line, not the line of its annotation. That's why the lab's test looks for Shape.kt:6. Only the follow-on errors after a failed run name a file without its folder. Why does the processor live in its own module instead of next to the classes it reads? KSP only reads files from other modules The services file must sit in a separate jar for licensing reasons Kotlin can't compile two kinds of class in one module It must be compiled before it can run, and the module's KSP task runs before that module's own compile The processor is a program. Gradle compiles and packs it first, then KSP runs it on the app's sources before the app is compiled. If the processor were part of the app, the app's KSP task would need the app's classes, which need the KSP task: Gradle reports that loop as a circular dependency. From lesson 1 of this track: you build the lesson 1 playground. Which of these runs first? compileL01Kotlin, so that KSP can read class files kspL01Kotlin, so that its files can join the compile compileL01Java They run at the same time KSP reads source files, not class files, and its output must exist before the Kotlin compiler starts, because your code calls it. So kspL01Kotlin runs first and compileL01Kotlin compiles your files and the generated ones together; compileL01Java comes after, and sees the Kotlin classes.
