h: Your first processor · Key terms
x: Processor A class implementing SymbolProcessor; KSP calls its process function during the build. Provider A class implementing SymbolProcessorProvider that creates the processor and hands it its tools. Services file A text file in the processor's jar, under META-INF/services/, that names the provider class. Resolver What KSP passes to process: it answers questions such as which symbols carry an annotation. Symbol Anything in the code with a name: a class, a function, a property, a parameter. Fully qualified name A name with its package, such as workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory. Round One pass of every processor over the files; a round that writes files earns another one. Dependencies The createNewFile argument naming the source files an output came from, so incremental builds redo the right files. Which interface does KSP call to create your processor, and how often? SymbolProcessorProvider.create(environment), once per build. KSP finds the provider through the services file. Where does a KSP services file live, and what's in it? META-INF/services/com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessorProvider, with one fully qualified provider class name per line. What does getSymbolsWithAnnotation("Inventory") return when the annotation is workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory? Nothing, and without a warning. It needs the fully qualified name. What does process() return? The symbols it couldn't process yet, to try again next round. emptyList() means everything was handled. What happens when a processor creates the same file twice in one build? KSP throws kotlin.io.FileAlreadyExistsException and the build fails. javac's Filer throws a FilerException for the same mistake. When does KSP run another round? Only when the last round created at least one new file. The new files are read in that next round. Which line does logger.error(msg, symbol) name for an annotated class? The declaration's line (class or interface), not the annotation's, as e: [ksp] <path>:<line>: msg.

h: Your first processor · Go deeper
x: Where do a processor's messages show up? KSP's levels follow Gradle's. At the default level you see warn and error lines; info appears with --info, logging only with --debug, and -q hides even warnings. A message logged on a symbol from source gets <absolute path>:<line>: in front of it, with no column. That's why the lab's round lines use logger.info: they're there when you ask, and quiet when you don't. javac's rounds work almost the same way, with one extra step. javac keeps calling a processor in every later round once it has been asked to process, and it ends with a final round in which roundEnv.processingOver() returns true and no new files will be read. KSP has no such empty round; its end hook is finish(), which lesson 6 uses. javac also lets a processor claim annotations by returning true, so that no other processor sees them. KSP has no claiming at all. Writing the services file by hand is fine for one provider, but easy to forget when classes are renamed. Many Java libraries use AutoService, which generates META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor from an annotation on the processor class, and a KSP port of it, auto-service-ksp, does the same for KSP providers. A typo in the class name is still possible either way, and the build still names it: Provider ... not found. One trap from the Java side: since JDK 23, javac no longer runs a processor just because its jar is on the class path. Gradle's annotationProcessor configuration passes processors explicitly, so Gradle builds don't notice, but a plain javac -cp processor.jar command quietly generates nothing until you add --processor-path or -proc:full.

h: Reading declarations, types and annotations · The label from top to bottom: a file, its classes and their members
x: A processor is the program that KSP, Kotlin Symbol Processing, runs during the build: it reads the classes that carry an annotation and writes new files. Everything KSP knows about your code comes as a tree of symbols, one node for each named thing. A declaration is a symbol you wrote yourself, such as a class or a function. Each file is the root of its own small tree. A KSFile holds KSClassDeclarations. Each class holds its properties (KSPropertyDeclaration), its functions (KSFunctionDeclaration) and any classes nested inside it, and each function holds its parameters (KSValueParameter). In the moving-house picture, the file is a box, and this tree is everything written on its label. TreeDemo prints that tree for a small Kotlin file with Plant and Mirror, and for a Java file we'll meet in the last section: file Rooms.kt package=movemate class Plant kind=CLASS modifiers=[DATA] origin=KOTLIN property kind: String property potLitres: Double property waterEveryDays: Int function component1(): String origin=SYNTHETIC function component2(): Double origin=SYNTHETIC function component3(): Int origin=SYNTHETIC function copy(kind: String (hasDefault), potLitres: Double (hasDefault), waterEveryDays: Int (hasDefault)): Plant origin=SYNTHETIC function <init>(kind: String, potLitres: Double, waterEveryDays: Int (hasDefault)): Plant origin=KOTLIN class Mirror kind=CLASS modifiers=[] origin=KOTLIN property widthCm: Int property heightCm: Int property glass: String function areaCm2(): Int origin=KOTLIN property area: Int function <init>(widthCm: Int, heightCm: Int, glass: String): Mirror origin=KOTLIN Let's read it from the top. kind=CLASS comes from classKind, which tells a class from an INTERFACE, an OBJECT or an ENUM_CLASS; lesson 2's Check move used it. modifiers=[DATA] lists only the modifiers written in the source. Plant is public and final too, but nobody wrote those words, so they're not on the list. origin=KOTLIN says the symbol came from Kotlin source. The functions hold two surprises. The constructor is a function named <init>; for a class with a primary constructor, primaryConstructor gives you the same node directly. And component1 to component3 and copy are listed too, marked origin=SYNTHETIC. Nobody wrote them, but a data class will have them, so KSP shows them. Now look for what's missing. waterEveryDays: Int (hasDefault) says the parameter has a default value, and nothing more: the 7 is an expression, and KSP shows no expressions. areaCm2(): Int is there with its name and return type, and inside it property area: Int, because a local val is a named declaration too. The multiplication widthCm * heightCm is nowhere. That's lesson 1's limit, now proved: the helper reads labels, never what's packed. Java has had annotation processors since Java 6, and KSP is Kotlin's own, faster way to do the same job for Kotlin code. javac builds the same kind of tree for them, from Elements: a TypeElement for a class, an ExecutableElement for a method or constructor, and a VariableElement for a field or parameter. Walking a class's members looks much the same in both: Java // Closest Java equivalent: a class's members in a javac processor for (Element member : cls.getEnclosedElements()) { switch (member.getKind()) { case FIELD -> messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.NOTE, "field " + member.getSimpleName() + ": " + member.asType()); case CONSTRUCTOR, METHOD -> messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.NOTE, "method " + member.getSimpleName() + ((ExecutableElement) member).getParameters()); default -> { } } } Kotlin for (member in cls.declarations) { when (member) { is KSPropertyDeclaration -> logger.warn("property ${member.simpleName.asString()}: ${member.type}") is KSFunctionDeclaration -> logger.warn("function ${member.simpleName.asString()}" + member.parameters.map { it.name?.asString() }) else -> {} } } One difference shows already. Java has no primary constructors and no data classes, so the Kotlin label says more than any javac processor could ever read from Java code. KSP gives you every declaration and its type, and never an expression. Plan your processor around what the label says. The tree prints types as text, such as Int and String. Printing them right is harder than it looks. Print a file's symbol tree Run TreeDemo from labs/. It takes about 10 s. The walk is written as a visitor, which the last section explains; read the output first. Find the line for areaCm2. Which of its parts appear, and which part of its body appears at all? In the Kotlin source string, give Mirror a default, val glass: String = "plain", and make Plant an ordinary class instead of a data class. Predict both changes in the output, then run it again. TreeDemo.kt package workbench.ksp.l03.demo import com.google.devtools.ksp.ApiFeatures import com.google.devtools.ksp.buildApiFeatures import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.Resolver import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessor import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessorProvider import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSAnnotated import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSClassDeclaration import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSFile import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSFunctionDeclaration import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSPropertyDeclaration import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSVisitorVoid import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.KotlinCompilation import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.SourceFile import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.configureKsp import java.io.File import java.io.OutputStream // Everything KSP shows a processor about one Kotlin file and one Java file: the label on each box, printed as a // tree. Look for what is there (names, types, hasDefault, a local val) and what is not (any expression). // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l03.demo.TreeDemoKt /** A processor that prints the symbol tree of every source file once, in round 1. */ class TreeProcessor(private val lines: MutableList<String>) : SymbolProcessor { override val apiFeatures: ApiFeatures = buildApiFeatures { enableBackingFields = true; enableContextParameters = true } private var round = 0 override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { if (++round == 1) resolver.getNewFiles().forEach { it.accept(TreePrinter(), Unit) } return emptyList() } /** A visitor: KSP calls the visit function that matches each node; each one decides where to go next. */ inner class TreePrinter : KSVisitorVoid(apiFeatures) { private var depth = 0 private fun line(text: String) { lines += " ".repeat(depth) + text } private fun children(nodes: Sequence<KSAnnotated>) { depth++ nodes.forEach { it.accept(this, Unit) } depth-- } override fun visitFile(file: KSFile, data: Unit) { line("file ${file.fileName} package=${file.packageName.asString()}") children(file.declarations) } override fun visitClassDeclaration(classDeclaration: KSClassDeclaration, data: Unit) { line("class ${classDeclaration.simpleName.asString()} kind=${classDeclaration.classKind} " + "modifiers=${classDeclaration.modifiers} origin=${classDeclaration.origin}") children(classDeclaration.declarations) } override fun visitFunctionDeclaration(function: KSFunctionDeclaration, data: Unit) { val parameters = function.parameters.joinToString(", ") { p -> "${p.name?.asString()}: ${p.type}" + if (p.hasDefault) " (hasDefault)" else "" } line("function ${function.simpleName.asString()}($parameters): ${function.returnType} origin=${function.origin}") children(function.declarations) // a function's own named declarations, such as a local val } override fun visitPropertyDeclaration(property: KSPropertyDeclaration, data: Unit) { line("property ${property.simpleName.asString()}: ${property.type}") } } } fun main() { val kotlin = SourceFile.kotlin( "Rooms.kt", """ package movemate data class Plant(val kind: String, val potLitres: Double, val waterEveryDays: Int = 7) class Mirror(val widthCm: Int, val heightCm: Int, val glass: String) { fun areaCm2(): Int { val area = widthCm * heightCm return area } } """, ) val java = SourceFile.java( "MovingCrate.java", """ package movemate; public class MovingCrate { private final String label; public MovingCrate(String label) { this.label = label; } public String getLabel() { return label.trim(); } } """, ) val lines = mutableListOf<String>() val compilation = KotlinCompilation().apply { workingDir = File("build/kctfork/demo").apply { deleteRecursively() } sources = listOf(kotlin, java) inheritClassPath = true jvmTarget = "21" messageOutputStream = OutputStream.nullOutputStream() configureKsp { symbolProcessorProviders += SymbolProcessorProvider { TreeProcessor(lines) } } } val result = compilation.compile() println("exit code: ${result.exitCode}") lines.forEach(::println) } ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l03.demo.TreeDemoKt labs/ksp/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/ksp/l03/demo/TreeDemo.kt The output in this section, then the Java file. areaCm2(): Int shows its name and return type, and property area: Int under it, because a local val is a declaration; the multiplication never appears. With the default, Mirror's constructor line shows glass: String (hasDefault), without the value. Without data, Plant's modifiers becomes [], and component1 to component3 and copy disappear, because only a data class gets them.

h: Reading declarations, types and annotations · Printing a type correctly: references, resolved types, nullability and arguments
x: Reading a label: a type reference, the resolved type, nullability and type arguments, level by level Each parameter's type arrives as a KSTypeReference, the type as it's written in the source: String?, or Litres, not yet looked up. Calling resolve() turns it into a KSType, the type the compiler means, with its declaration (the class it names), its nullability and its type arguments. Resolving is a real lookup through imports, packages and type aliases. KSP's docs call it "one of the most expensive operations in the KSP API", so KSP resolves nothing until you ask. In the picture, resolve() is the helper looking up a word on the label to see what it refers to: is Litres a box in this house, or shorthand for something else? Each lookup takes time. Here the picture breaks a little, too: unlike a person, KSP writes down every lookup a processor makes, because a later build needs to know which boxes each card depended on (lesson 7). The label we want is the class's typed shape, Lamp(name: String, bulbs: Int, shade: String?). Two quick attempts come to mind: print the reference with toString(), or resolve it and print the declaration's name. ShapeDemo tries both, on a crate with tricky types and on a small Java class, next to the lab's typeText: parameter toString() name only typeText Crate.shade String? String String? Crate.books List<String> List List<String> Crate.water [typealias Litres] Litres Litres Crate.sizes Map<String, List<Int?>>? Map Map<String, List<Int?>>? Crate.odds List<*> List List<*> Crate.onDrop Function1<Int, Unit> Function1 Function1<Int, Unit> MovingCrate.label (String..String?) String String! MovingCrate.weightGrams Int Int Int The name-only column fails at once. It drops every ? and every <...>, so shade becomes a String that can never be empty, which the first lamp without a shade will quickly disprove, and sizes loses its key and value types along with its ?. The toString() column looks right on easy types, and that's what makes it a trap. On the type alias, a second name for a type (typealias Litres = Double), it prints [typealias Litres]. On the Java class it prints (String..String?). KSP's toString() is a display form for people reading logs, not a promise about Kotlin syntax. So we build the text ourselves from what KSType says, in three steps. First the name, type.declaration.simpleName. Then the type arguments, each printed the same way, because List<Int?> holds a type that needs exactly the same treatment: a recursive function. Then the nullability mark. Here is the core of it, with javac's closest equivalent first: Java // Closest Java equivalent: printing a javac TypeMirror (javax.lang.model.type) static String typeText(TypeMirror type) { if (type instanceof DeclaredType declared) { // a class type, maybe with arguments String name = declared.asElement().getSimpleName().toString(); List<? extends TypeMirror> arguments = declared.getTypeArguments(); if (arguments.isEmpty()) return name; return name + arguments.stream().map(Labels::typeText).collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "<", ">")); } return type.toString(); // int, boolean and the other primitives } Kotlin // the core of typeText; the lab adds the * and ! cases fun typeText(ref: KSTypeReference): String { val type = ref.resolve() // the expensive step val name = type.declaration.simpleName.asString() val arguments = if (type.arguments.isEmpty()) "" else type.arguments.joinToString(", ", "<", ">") { typeText(it.type!!) } // the same, all the way down val mark = if (type.nullability == Nullability.NULLABLE) "?" else "" return name + arguments + mark } Two cases are left for the lab. A star projection, List<*> (a list of something unknown), has a type argument with no type at all: its type is null, so it.type!! would crash, and the argument's variance says STAR. And a platform type is a type from Java, where nothing says whether null is allowed; its nullability is PLATFORM, and Kotlin writes it String!. Printing Function1<Int, Unit> for (Int) -> Unit is fine for a label: both name the same type, and Kotlin simply has a shorter way to write it. The Java twin can't print ? at all. A javac TypeMirror knows nothing about nullability, because Java's type system has none; Java code marks it with annotations such as @Nullable instead. That's one of the Kotlin facts a KSP processor keeps and a Java processor never sees. Resolve each reference once, then build the text from the resolved type: name, arguments, mark. toString() is for your eyes, not for your output. Each line of the label now prints right. Some boxes also carry notes with values written on them. Print a type three ways Run ShapeDemo. It prints the table in this section, using the reference typeText; with -Pmine=l03 it uses yours, or prints (not done yet). Add a parameter val spare: Crate? to Crate in the source string. Predict all three columns for it, then run again. Once your lab passes, run it with -Pmine=l03 and check that your column matches the reference one, row for row. ShapeDemo.kt package workbench.ksp.l03.demo import com.google.devtools.ksp.ApiFeatures import com.google.devtools.ksp.buildApiFeatures import com.google.devtools.ksp.getConstructors import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.Resolver import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessor import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessorProvider import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSAnnotated import com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSClassDeclaration import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.KotlinCompilation import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.SourceFile import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.configureKsp import java.io.File import java.io.OutputStream import workbench.ksp.l03.typeText // Three ways to print a parameter's type, side by side, for every constructor parameter of the @Label classes: // toString() what the type reference prints by itself // name only the resolved type's declaration name, the first thing people try // typeText lesson 3's typeText (the reference one, or yours with -Pmine=l03) // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l03.demo.ShapeDemoKt class ShapeTable(private val rows: MutableList<List<String>>) : SymbolProcessor { override val apiFeatures: ApiFeatures = buildApiFeatures { enableBackingFields = true; import workbench.ksp.annotations.Label; @Label public class MovingCrate { public MovingCrate(String label, int weightGrams) { } } """, ) val rows = mutableListOf(listOf("parameter", "toString()", "name only", "typeText")) val compilation = KotlinCompilation().apply { workingDir = File("build/kctfork/demo").apply { deleteRecursively() } sources = listOf(kotlin, java) inheritClassPath = true jvmTarget = "21" messageOutputStream = OutputStream.nullOutputStream() configureKsp { symbolProcessorProviders += SymbolProcessorProvider { ShapeTable(rows) } } } val result = compilation.compile() println("exit code: ${result.exitCode}") val widths = (0..3).map { column -> rows.maxOf { it[column].length } + 2 } rows.forEach { row -> println(row.mapIndexed { i, cell -> cell.padEnd(widths[i]) }.joinToString("").trimEnd()) } } ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l03.demo.ShapeDemoKt labs/ksp/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/ksp/l03/demo/ShapeDemo.kt The table in this section. spare prints Crate?, Crate and Crate?: a class can name itself, and only the name-only column loses the ?. With your finished lab, the typeText column is identical, including List<*> and String!. A class's label as KSP models it: declarations down to a type reference, which resolve() turns into the type it names. Kotlin model and type resolution (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Reading declarations, types and annotations · Reading the values on a sticky note: annotation arguments and their defaults
x: An annotation, a note written with @ on a declaration, can carry values, called its arguments: @Room("study") says which room a box goes to. MoveMate's lesson 3 note, @Handling, has three, each of a different kind and each with a default: Java public enum Care { NORMAL, GENTLE, UPRIGHT } @Target(ElementType.TYPE) @Retention(RetentionPolicy.SOURCE) public @interface Handling { Care care() default Care.NORMAL; boolean stackable() default true; Class<?> packWith() default Object.class; } Kotlin enum class Care { NORMAL, GENTLE, UPRIGHT } @Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS) @Retention(AnnotationRetention.SOURCE) annotation class Handling( val care: Care = Care.NORMAL, val stackable: Boolean = true, val packWith: KClass<*> = Any::class, ) The two declarations line up closely. Java writes each argument as a method with a default; Kotlin writes it as a constructor property with a default value. One difference: Java's "no particular class" is usually Object.class, and Kotlin's here is Any::class. KSP gives each annotation on a symbol as a KSAnnotation, and its arguments as a list of KSValueArgument, each with a name and a value. What kind of object the value is depends on the argument's type. A String or a Boolean arrives as itself. A class argument (KClass) arrives as a KSType. An enum value arrives as a KSClassDeclaration, the declaration of the enum entry, so its simpleName is UPRIGHT. Running it showed two details worth remembering. The list holds every parameter of the annotation, including the ones the source didn't write, filled in with their defaults; such an argument has origin=SYNTHETIC, which isDefault() checks. And the list isn't in declaration order. KSP lists the written arguments first, in the order they were written, and the defaults after them. So look arguments up by name, never by position: Java // Closest Java equivalent: reading annotation values in a javac processor Map<? extends ExecutableElement, ? extends AnnotationValue> written = handling.getElementValues(); Map<? extends ExecutableElement, ? extends AnnotationValue> all = processingEnv.getElementUtils().getElementValuesWithDefaults(handling); for (var entry : all.entrySet()) { String name = entry.getKey().getSimpleName().toString(); // care, stackable, packWith Object value = entry.getValue().getValue(); // an enum: a VariableElement; a class: a TypeMirror boolean isDefault = !written.containsKey(entry.getKey()); } Kotlin val handling = annotationNamed(cls, "workbench.ksp.annotations.l03.Handling") ?: return null fun argument(name: String) = handling.arguments.first { it.name?.asString() == name } // by name val care = argument("care").value as KSClassDeclaration // an enum value: the entry's declaration val stackable = argument("stackable").value as Boolean // a Boolean: itself val packWith = argument("packWith").value as KSType // a class: a KSType val chosen = !argument("stackable").isDefault() // false when the source didn't write it javac draws the same line differently: getElementValues() holds only what was written, and getElementValuesWithDefaults fills in the rest, so a default is whatever the first map lacks. Finding the annotation itself needs one more bit of care. Its shortName is the name as written, Room, and another package could have a Room of its own. The lab's given annotationNamed compares the short name first, which costs nothing, and resolves annotationType to its full name only when the short name matches: the cheap check first, then the expensive one, as KSP's docs advise. LabelDemo runs the whole lesson 3 processor on a lamp and on a bookshelf marked @Room("study") @Handling(care = Care.UPRIGHT, packWith = Lamp::class). Here is the bookshelf's label: --- movemate/BookshelfLabel.kt // Generated by LabelProcessor from Bookshelf. Do not edit. package movemate object BookshelfLabel { const val SHAPE: String = "Bookshelf(shelves: Int, books: List<String>)" const val ROOM: String = "study" const val HANDLING: String = "care=UPRIGHT, stackable=true (default), packWith=Lamp" } stackable wasn't written, so it says true (default). The lamp's label has a SHAPE line and nothing else, because the lamp carries neither note. Look annotation arguments up by name, and ask isDefault() before you assume the user chose a value. So far every label was written in Kotlin. MoveMate also has one box from a Java team. Read the notes' values Run LabelDemo and read the two label files it prints. In the source string, change the bookshelf's note to @Handling(stackable = false). Predict the HANDLING line, then run it. Now remove @Room("study") from the bookshelf. Predict which lines its label keeps. h: Reading declarations, types and annotations · A Java box, and a visitor that walks any box
x: KSP reads Java source files in the same module too, through the same API. Their symbols say origin=JAVA. Here is the rest of TreeDemo's output, for a small Java class: file MovingCrate.java package=movemate class MovingCrate kind=CLASS modifiers=[PUBLIC] origin=JAVA property label: (String..String?) function getLabel(): (String..String?) origin=JAVA function <init>(label: (String..String?)): MovingCrate origin=JAVA Three things differ from a Kotlin class, and the label meets two of them. Java has no primary constructor, so primaryConstructor is null, and the label falls back to the first constructor that getConstructors() finds. Java fields come back as properties, even the private label. And a Java String is a platform type, (String..String?): Kotlin can't tell whether it may be null, so the label prints String!. A Java int, which can never be null, comes back as a plain Int. In the picture, this is a box labeled in another language. The same helper can read it, but a few words are fuzzy, and the helper says so with a ! instead of guessing. The real build needs no extra setup for it. The lesson 3 playground keeps MovingCrate.java next to the Kotlin classes, and ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL03Kotlin writes MovingCrateLabel.kt for it: a Kotlin file describing a Java class, which Java code then reads as MovingCrateLabel.SHAPE. Now the visitor that TreeDemo used. A visitor is an object with one function per kind of node: visitFile, visitClassDeclaration, visitFunctionDeclaration and so on. Calling node.accept(visitor, data) makes KSP call the function that matches the node's kind, so the visitor never needs a chain of is checks. Both compilers offer the same pattern: Java // Closest Java equivalent: a javac element visitor (javax.lang.model.util, JDK 16+) class TreePrinter extends SimpleElementVisitor14<Void, Void> { @Override public Void visitType(TypeElement type, Void unused) { line("class " + type.getSimpleName()); type.getEnclosedElements().forEach(child -> child.accept(this, null)); // go to the children yourself return null; } @Override public Void visitVariable(VariableElement field, Void unused) { line("field " + field.getSimpleName() + ": " + field.asType()); return null; } } // start the walk: element.accept(new TreePrinter(), null) Kotlin inner class TreePrinter : KSVisitorVoid(apiFeatures) { override fun visitClassDeclaration(classDeclaration: KSClassDeclaration, data: Unit) { line("class ${classDeclaration.simpleName.asString()}") classDeclaration.declarations.forEach { it.accept(this, Unit) } // go to the children yourself } override fun visitPropertyDeclaration(property: KSPropertyDeclaration, data: Unit) { line("property ${property.simpleName.asString()}: ${property.type}") } } // start the walk: file.accept(TreePrinter(), Unit) KSVisitorVoid does nothing by default. Each of its functions has an empty body, so the visitor goes only where your code sends it, by calling accept on the children. javac's SimpleElementVisitor14 behaves the same way; its sibling ElementScanner14 is the one that visits every child for you. Write it as KSVisitorVoid(apiFeatures), passing the processor's apiFeatures. The official quickstart still writes KSVisitorVoid(), and that spelling has been deprecated since KSP 2.3.12. On 2.3.14 it compiles with the warning 'constructor(): KSVisitorVoid' is deprecated. The same goes for validate() without arguments, which lesson 5 meets. A visitor earns its keep when one walk must handle many kinds of node, as TreeDemo does. The lab's labels only ever look at a class and its constructor, so plain functions read better there. A visitor sends each node to the function for its kind. Use one when the walk is the job, and plain functions when you know where you're going. That's the whole label read: the tree, the types, the notes, and the boxes from Java. Read a Java class in the real build From labs/, run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL03Kotlin and open labs/ksp/app/build/generated/ksp/l03/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l03/MovingCrateLabel.kt. Run ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l03.MoveMateKt, then the Java twin with -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l03.MoveMateJava. h: Reading declarations, types and annotations · Java and Kotlin
x: Reading a parameter's type and an annotation's values: javac and KSP LabelProcessor.java // Closest Java equivalent: javac's model (javax.lang.model) ExecutableElement constructor = ElementFilter.constructorsIn(cls.getEnclosedElements()).get(0); for (VariableElement parameter : constructor.getParameters()) { TypeMirror type = parameter.asType(); // already resolved, no nullability at all line(parameter.getSimpleName() + ": " + typeText(type)); } for (AnnotationMirror note : cls.getAnnotationMirrors()) { var all = processingEnv.getElementUtils().getElementValuesWithDefaults(note); for (var entry : all.entrySet()) { Object value = entry.getValue().getValue(); // enum: VariableElement, class: TypeMirror line(entry.getKey().getSimpleName() + "=" + value); } } LabelProcessor.kt val constructor = cls.primaryConstructor ?: cls.getConstructors().first() for (parameter in constructor.parameters) { val type = parameter.type.resolve() // resolved on request, with its nullability line("${parameter.name!!.asString()}: ${typeText(parameter.type)}") } for (note in cls.annotations) { for (argument in note.arguments) { // defaults included, after the written ones val value = argument.value // enum: KSClassDeclaration, class: KSType line("${argument.name?.asString()}=$value" + if (argument.isDefault()) " (default)" else "") } } The two models match almost one to one: TypeElement to KSClassDeclaration, ExecutableElement to KSFunctionDeclaration, VariableElement to KSValueParameter or KSPropertyDeclaration, AnnotationMirror to KSAnnotation. Three differences are real. A javac TypeMirror arrives already resolved, while KSP hands you a reference and resolves it only when you call resolve(), because resolving is expensive. A TypeMirror has no nullability, because Java has none, while a KSType says NULLABLE, NOT_NULL or, for Java types, PLATFORM. And the value kinds differ: javac gives an enum constant as a VariableElement, KSP 2 gives the enum entry's KSClassDeclaration; both give a class as a type (TypeMirror, KSType). Kotlin's version also gets the primary constructor directly; Java has to pick one.

h: Reading declarations, types and annotations · Worked example
x: Print Map<String, List<Int?>>? by hand, the way typeText does Start at the outside. Resolve the reference once and read the three facts the label needs: the declaration's name, the type arguments, and the nullability. // 1. the outer type val type = ref.resolve() type.declaration.simpleName.asString() // "Map" type.arguments // [String, List<Int?>], both INVARIANT type.nullability // NULLABLE // 1. the outer type (javac: already resolved) DeclaredType type = (DeclaredType) parameter.asType(); type.asElement().getSimpleName(); // Map type.getTypeArguments(); // [java.lang.String, java.util.List<java.lang.Integer>] // no nullability: Java's types don't carry any The first argument is simple: String, no arguments, NOT_NULL, so it prints String. The second is a List with one argument, Int, whose nullability is NULLABLE, so the inner call prints Int? and the list prints List<Int?>. Each argument goes through the same function, which is why it's recursive. // 2. each argument, with the same function typeText(stringRef) // "String" typeText(listRef) // "List" + "<" + typeText(intRef) + ">" = "List<Int?>" // 2. each argument, with the same function typeText(stringMirror) // "String" typeText(listMirror) // "List" + "<" + typeText(integerMirror) + ">" = "List<Integer>" Put the outer parts back together: the name, the arguments joined with , inside < and >, and the mark for the outer nullability. The result is Map<String, List<Int?>>?, the type exactly as written. The Java twin prints Map<String, List<Integer>>, with no marks, because javac never had them to give. // 3. assemble "Map" + "<String, List<Int?>>" + "?" // "Map<String, List<Int?>>?" // 3. assemble "Map" + "<String, List<Integer>>" // "Map<String, List<Integer>>" Count the resolutions: four, one per reference, for Map, String, List and Int. Each is a lookup, and KSP records each one, because an incremental build, one that redoes only what changed, must know which files this label read (lesson 7). That's the reason for the rule: resolve each reference once, and only the ones you need.

h: Reading declarations, types and annotations · Quiz
x: fun areaCm2(): Int { val area = widthCm * heightCm; return area }. What does a processor see under areaCm2 when it walks its declarations? Nothing: a function's insides are invisible A property area: Int, but not widthCm * heightCm val area = widthCm * heightCm as an expression tree The return area statement A local val is a named declaration, so it shows up in the function's declarations, with its type. Its initializer is an expression, and KSP shows no expressions or statements, so the multiplication and the return stay out of reach. A parameter is declared val water: Litres, with typealias Litres = Double. What does parameter.type.toString() print in KSP 2.3.14? Double Litres kotlin.Double [typealias Litres] toString() is a display form, and for a type alias it prints [typealias Litres]. Resolving and reading declaration.simpleName gives Litres, the name as written, which is what a label wants; following the alias to Double is a separate step. Never generate code from toString(). @Handling(stackable = false) sits on a class. What does annotation.arguments hold? Only stackable, because the others weren't written stackable first, then care and packWith with their defaults and isDefault() true care, stackable, packWith in declaration order, all with isDefault() false care and packWith only, because false is a default KSP fills in every parameter, so defaults are in the list, marked with origin=SYNTHETIC, which isDefault() checks. The written arguments come first, then the defaults, which is why the lab looks arguments up by name. stackable = false was written, so it isn't a default, even though it differs from the declared default only in value. A Java constructor parameter is declared String label. What is the nullability of its resolved KSType? NOT_NULL, because it has no ? NULLABLE, because Java objects can be null PLATFORM: Kotlin can't know, and writes it String! KSP can't read Java parameters A type from Java carries no nullability, so KSP reports PLATFORM, and its toString() shows (String..String?), a range from not-null to nullable. Kotlin writes such a type String!. A Java int is different: it can never be null, so it arrives as a plain Int. From lesson 2 of this track: @Label is on line 8 and class Mirror(...) on line 9, and the processor calls logger.error(message, symbol) for Mirror. Which line does the message name? h: Reading declarations, types and annotations · Key terms
x: Symbol A node in KSP's model of the code, one for each named thing: a file, a class, a function, a parameter. Declaration A symbol you wrote yourself, such as a class (KSClassDeclaration) or a function (KSFunctionDeclaration). KSTypeReference A type as written in the source, before it is looked up. KSType A resolved type: the class it names, its type arguments and its nullability. Platform type A type from Java, whose nullability Kotlin can't know; written String!. Annotation argument A value written on an annotation, such as the "study" in @Room("study"), or its default when not written. Type alias A second name for an existing type, such as typealias Litres = Double. Visitor An object with one function per kind of node; node.accept(visitor, data) calls the matching one. KSTypeReference vs KSType? A reference is the type as written in the source. resolve() turns it into a KSType, the type it means, with its declaration, arguments and nullability. Why doesn't KSP resolve types for you? Resolving is one of the most expensive operations in its API, and KSP records each one for incremental builds, so it waits until you call resolve(). What does KSP tell you about the default in val waterEveryDays: Int = 7? hasDefault == true, and never the value 7: a default value is an expression, and KSP shows no expressions. In KSP 2, what is an enum annotation argument's value? And a class argument's? An enum value is the entry's KSClassDeclaration (classKind == ENUM_ENTRY). A KClass argument is a KSType. How do you tell a default annotation argument from a written one? argument.isDefault(), true for origin == SYNTHETIC. Defaults come after the written arguments in the list, so look arguments up by name. What does a Java String parameter look like to KSP? A platform type: nullability PLATFORM, toString() (String..String?), written String! in Kotlin. A Java int is a plain Int. Does KSVisitorVoid visit a node's children by itself? No: every visit function is empty, so you call accept on the children yourself. Build it as KSVisitorVoid(apiFeatures); KSVisitorVoid() is deprecated since 2.3.12.

h: Reading declarations, types and annotations · Go deeper
x: A few more facts about the label, for the day you need them. getDeclaredProperties() lists only the class's own properties, while getAllProperties() includes inherited ones too, and needs type resolution to find them, so it costs more. The same split exists for functions. Both getDeclared... helpers are extension functions in com.google.devtools.ksp that filter declarations. You can often avoid resolving at all. A reference's element is the type as written, and for a class name, (ref.element as? KSClassifierReference)?.referencedName() gives the written name without a lookup. KSP's docs suggest filtering that way first, and resolving only the references you still care about, because every resolution is both slow and recorded as a dependency for incremental builds. Nested classes need care. simpleName of Kitchen.Drawer is just Drawer, and splitting qualifiedName at dots can't tell a package from an outer class. For a label, drop the package from the qualified name; for generated code, lesson 4's KotlinPoet does it properly. Comparing types has a trap for Java hands. KSP's a.isAssignableFrom(b) asks whether a b can be stored in an a, so Any.isAssignableFrom(String) is true. javac's Types.isAssignable(t1, t2) asks whether a t1 can be stored in a t2, so the arguments come in the opposite order. And == on KSType includes nullability: String? is not equal to String. Finally, getAnnotationsByType(Room::class) looks convenient, because it hands you a real annotation instance. But it's marked experimental, and reading a class argument through it throws KSTypeNotPresentException, because the class it names may not be compiled yet. Read KSAnnotation.arguments, as this lesson does.

h: Generating code with KotlinPoet · A builder from a string template, and four classes that break it
Generating code with KotlinPoet · KotlinPoet builds the file from specs and four placeholders
x: KotlinPoet as a label printer: specs build LampBuilder.kt, and %T writes the import the template forgot KotlinPoet is a library from Square, here in version 2.4.0, that writes Kotlin source files from objects instead of strings. You describe what the file holds, such as a class with these properties and these functions. KotlinPoet prints it, with the imports, the indentation and the escaping done for you. In the picture, it's the label printer that replaces handwriting. Each piece of code has its own description, called a spec. FileSpec describes a whole file, TypeSpec a class, PropertySpec a property, FunSpec a function, and ParameterSpec a parameter. You make each one with its builder and finish it with build(). Here is the smallest useful spec, one function, in both libraries: Java // Closest Java equivalent: JavaPoet, KotlinPoet's older sibling for Java MethodSpec greet = MethodSpec.methodBuilder("greet") .addModifiers(Modifier.PUBLIC) .returns(String.class) .addStatement("return $S", "Hello from Lamp") .build(); // prints: public String greet() { // return "Hello from Lamp"; // } Kotlin val greet = FunSpec.builder("greet") .returns(STRING) .addStatement("return %S", "Hello from Lamp") .build() // prints: public fun greet(): kotlin.String = "Hello from Lamp" KotlinPoet's single line of output shows three habits. KotlinPoet writes public itself; its docs say it generates "explicit visibility modifiers" to maximize portability. It turned a body of one return into an expression body. And printed on its own, a spec spells out kotlin.String. Inside a FileSpec, the same type prints as String, with import kotlin.String at the top of the file. The string "return %S" is a format string: code text with placeholders, which KotlinPoet fills from the arguments that follow it. Four placeholders do nearly all the work in this lesson: Placeholder Takes Prints %T a type: ClassName, TypeName its name, and adds the import %N a name: a string or a spec the name, with backticks if it needs them %S a string a string literal, quoted, with " and $ escaped %L anything the value as it is, with no escaping %S given Write $room on each "fragile" box prints "Write ${'$'}room on each \"fragile\" box", which is the same text as a Kotlin string, $ and all. %L would paste it raw and break the file, and an unescaped $room would quietly read a variable named room. Each placeholder knows the one rule its kind of value needs, which is exactly what the handwriting kept forgetting. Pass types with %T and names with %N. Never paste them into the format string. The figure shows the whole builder as specs: five calls on the left, the part of LampBuilder.kt each one prints on the right. KotlinPoet, though, speaks in ClassName and TypeName, while our processor holds KSP symbols. The next step joins the two. Print the same classes with KotlinPoet Open PoetBuilderDemo.kt, next to the template demo. It compiles the same classes with the lab's reference processor, prints each generated file, then calls every builder from a small Use.kt. With the new property, KotlinPoet writes public fun `fun`(`fun`: String): CrateBuilder: %N met a keyword and added backticks. Each spec the processor builds becomes one part of the printed file; the originating file and writeTo connect the result to KSP.

h: Generating code with KotlinPoet · kotlinpoet-ksp turns KSP symbols into KotlinPoet names
x: kotlinpoet-ksp is KotlinPoet's small companion for processors, also version 2.4.0. It adds extension functions that turn KSP symbols into KotlinPoet names, and a writeTo that hands a finished file to KSP. The builder processor uses four of them. cls.toClassName() turns a KSClassDeclaration, the symbol for a class, into a ClassName: a package plus one or more simple names. For the nested drawer that's package movemate with the names Kitchen and Drawer, and %T prints Kitchen.Drawer. String surgery on movemate.Kitchen.Drawer can't tell you whether Kitchen is a package or a class. ClassName knows. The builder's own name comes from the same parts, simpleNames.joinToString("") plus Builder, so the drawer gets KitchenDrawerBuilder. param.type.toTypeName() turns a KSTypeReference, the type as written in the source, into a TypeName, with every type argument and every ? in place: List<Box?>?. To do that it resolves the type, the step lesson 3 called expensive, and if the type can't be resolved it throws (lesson 5 deals with that). The field needs the same type made nullable, and copy(nullable = true) does it without doubling anything: String becomes String?, and String? stays String?. That's the smudge from the template, gone. Here is the setter in both languages: Java // Closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor with JavaPoet MethodSpec setterMethod(VariableElement param, ClassName builder) { String name = param.getSimpleName().toString(); return MethodSpec.methodBuilder(name) .addModifiers(Modifier.PUBLIC) .addParameter(TypeName.get(param.asType()), name) .returns(builder) .addStatement("this.$N = $N", name, name) .addStatement("return this") .build(); } Kotlin fun setterFunction(param: KSValueParameter, builder: ClassName): FunSpec { val name = nameOf(param) return FunSpec.builder(name) .addParameter(name, param.type.toTypeName()) .returns(builder) .addStatement("this.%N = %N", name, name) .addStatement("return this") .build() } Read the Kotlin version aloud: a function named after the parameter, taking one parameter with the same name and type, and returning the builder. Its body sets the field and returns this. Both names go through %N, so in comes out as `in` in all three places. The last two calls hand the file to KSP: Java // javac: the class is the originating element, and the Filer writes the file TypeSpec builderType = TypeSpec.classBuilder(builder) // ... fields, setters, build() .addOriginatingElement(type) .build(); JavaFile.builder(packageName, builderType).build().writeTo(processingEnv.getFiler()); Kotlin // KSP: the class's source file is the originating file, and writeTo hands it to the CodeGenerator val builderType = TypeSpec.classBuilder(builder) // ... properties, setters, build() .addOriginatingKSFile(cls.containingFile!!) .build() FileSpec.builder(builder).addType(builderType).build().writeTo(codeGenerator, aggregating = false) The originating file is the source file an output was made from, here Lamp.kt. aggregating = false says that this output depends on its originating files and nothing else. Together they are KotlinPoet's way of writing lesson 2's Dependencies(false, file): writeTo collects the originating files from the file's top-level specs and builds the Dependencies itself. aggregating has no default, so you decide every time. A wrong decision doesn't show on a clean build or in a test. It shows later, after an ordinary edit, as a generated file that has quietly disappeared. Lesson 7 makes that happen on purpose. In the picture, the originating file is the note clipped to each card that says which box it came from. When that box is repacked next weekend, the helper knows exactly which card to redo. h: Generating code with KotlinPoet · Reading the generated builder aloud, and where it stops
x: Here is LampBuilder.kt exactly as the lab's processor writes it, next to the builder a Java developer would write for a Java Lamp: Java // The same builder for a Java record Lamp(String name, int bulbs, String shade) public class LampBuilder { private String name; private Integer bulbs; private String shade; public LampBuilder name(String name) { this.name = name; return this; } // bulbs(...) and shade(...) have the same shape public Lamp build() { if (name == null) throw new IllegalStateException("LampBuilder: name was not set"); if (bulbs == null) throw new IllegalStateException("LampBuilder: bulbs was not set"); return new Lamp(name, bulbs, shade); } } Kotlin // Generated by BuilderProcessor from Lamp. Do not edit. package movemate import kotlin.Int import kotlin.String public class LampBuilder { private var name: String? = null private var bulbs: Int? = null private var shade: String? = null public fun name(name: String): LampBuilder { this.name = name return this } public fun bulbs(bulbs: Int): LampBuilder { this.bulbs = bulbs return this } public fun shade(shade: String?): LampBuilder { this.shade = shade return this } public fun build(): Lamp = Lamp( name = name ?: error("LampBuilder: name was not set"), bulbs = bulbs ?: error("LampBuilder: bulbs was not set"), shade = shade, ) } Read it from the top. The file says where it came from and which package it's in, then imports kotlin.Int and kotlin.String, which KotlinPoet always writes although Kotlin would find them anyway. LampBuilder holds three empty slots. Each setter fills one slot and hands the builder back, so the calls chain. build() calls Lamp with named arguments. A slot that must be filled either has a value or stops the program with a message that names the builder and the slot. shade, which may be null, goes in as it is. The two-space indent and the blank line between members are KotlinPoet's house style, which is why the lab's first test compares the whole text. Is it worth a library? The template's text took 23 lines and got one of five cases clean. The KotlinPoet functions take 48 lines, twice as many, and get all five right, plus the Bag and fun cases from the Try its. The gain isn't fewer lines. It's the cases you never had to think of. Now the limits. KotlinPoet models declarations, not expressions. Its docs put it plainly: "the body of methods and constructors is not modeled." A body is a format string such as "%N = %N ?: error(%S),\n". KotlinPoet checks the names and types you pass in, and nothing about what the code means. If build() passed the arguments in the wrong order, KotlinPoet would print it faithfully and the compiler would object. That's why every test in this lesson's lab compiles the generated code and calls it. This is also where the picture breaks. A label printer prints exactly the words you type. KotlinPoet edits as it prints: it adds imports, public and backticks, and turns a one-line return into an expression body. So read its output at least once before you trust it. The second limit is KSP's, and our builder inherits it. Lesson 3 showed that a parameter's hasDefault says that a default exists, never what it is. So PlantBuilder can't fill in waterEveryDays = 7, and it asks you instead: PlantBuilder().kind("fern").potLitres(2.5).build() stops with PlantBuilder: waterEveryDays was not set. The label says "spare bulb included", and the helper can't open the box to see which bulb. KotlinPoet checks the shape of the code, not its meaning. Compile and call what you generate. There's one thing this builder can't do yet: say no. Give it an interface, and the !! in constructorParameters is waiting for it.

h: Generating code with KotlinPoet · Java and Kotlin
x: The builder class, assembled with JavaPoet and with KotlinPoet BuilderProcessor.java (javac, JavaPoet) // Closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor with JavaPoet TypeSpec builderType(TypeElement type, List<? extends VariableElement> params) { String pkg = processingEnv.getElementUtils().getPackageOf(type).getQualifiedName().toString(); ClassName builder = ClassName.get(pkg, type.getSimpleName() + "Builder"); TypeSpec.Builder spec = TypeSpec.classBuilder(builder).addModifiers(Modifier.PUBLIC); for (VariableElement p : params) { TypeName empty = TypeName.get(p.asType()).box(); // int becomes Integer, which can be null spec.addField(FieldSpec.builder(empty, p.getSimpleName().toString(), Modifier.PRIVATE).build()); spec.addMethod(setterMethod(p, builder)); } return spec.addMethod(buildMethod(type, params, builder)) .addOriginatingElement(type) .build(); } // then: JavaFile.builder(pkg, builderType(type, params)).build().writeTo(processingEnv.getFiler()); BuilderProcessor.kt (KSP, KotlinPoet) fun builderType(cls: KSClassDeclaration): TypeSpec { val builder = builderName(cls) val params = constructorParameters(cls) return TypeSpec.classBuilder(builder) .addProperties(params.map(::builderProperty)) // private var name: String? = null .addFunctions(params.map { setterFunction(it, builder) }) .addFunction(buildFunction(cls, builder)) .addOriginatingKSFile(cls.containingFile!!) .build() } // then: builderFile(cls).writeTo(codeGenerator, aggregating = false) The plan is the same call for call: a class, one field and one setter per parameter, build(), and the input the output came from. Three differences matter. JavaPoet needs addModifiers(Modifier.PUBLIC), while KotlinPoet writes public itself. To let a Java field start empty, box() turns int into Integer; Kotlin says the same with copy(nullable = true), and its TypeName keeps the ? right on every type argument too. And the originating input differs in size: javac's Filer takes elements (the class), KSP takes files (Lamp.kt). Gradle's incremental Java processing sorts whole processors into isolating and aggregating, while KSP decides per output, which lesson 7 takes apart.

h: Generating code with KotlinPoet · Worked example
x: Generate one more function: Lamp.toBuilder() A user of LampBuilder asks for the other direction: start from an existing Lamp, change one value, build again. Start, as always, from the text you want KotlinPoet to print. public fun Lamp.toBuilder(): LampBuilder = LampBuilder().name(name).bulbs(bulbs).shade(shade) // in use: copy a lamp with two bulbs val brighter = Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null).toBuilder().bulbs(2).build() public static LampBuilder toBuilder(Lamp lamp) { return new LampBuilder().name(lamp.name()).bulbs(lamp.bulbs()).shade(lamp.shade()); } // in use: copy a lamp with two bulbs Lamp brighter = toBuilder(new Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null)).bulbs(2).build(); The function first: its name, a receiver and the return type. The receiver makes it an extension function, which Java doesn't have, so the Java twin is a static method that takes the lamp as a parameter. // 1. the function: name, receiver, return type val toBuilder = FunSpec.builder("toBuilder") .receiver(cls.toClassName()) .returns(builder) // 1. the method: name, modifiers, parameter, return type MethodSpec.Builder toBuilder = MethodSpec.methodBuilder("toBuilder") .addModifiers(Modifier.PUBLIC, Modifier.STATIC) .addParameter(ClassName.get(type), "lamp") .returns(builder); Then the body: one chained call per property. %T writes the builder's type, and %N writes each name, backticks included when a name needs them. // 2. the body: start a builder, then one setter call per property val body = CodeBlock.builder().add("return %T()", builder) for (param in constructorParameters(cls)) { body.add(".%N(%N)", nameOf(param), nameOf(param)) } toBuilder.addCode(body.build()) // 2. the body: start a builder, then one setter call per record component CodeBlock.Builder body = CodeBlock.builder().add("return new $T()", builder); for (VariableElement p : params) { String name = p.getSimpleName().toString(); body.add(".$N(lamp.$N())", name, name); } toBuilder.addStatement(body.build()); Add it to the file with addFunction(toBuilder.build()) and run. KotlinPoet prints exactly the line from step 1, and brighter comes out as Lamp(name=desk lamp, bulbs=2, shade=null). This works only because every parameter of Lamp is also a property (val), so name can be read back. A plain constructor parameter has nothing to read: that is one more thing a careful processor checks before it writes, the subject of the next lesson.

In setterFunction, addParameter(name, type) adds the parameter, returns(builder) the return type, and two addStatement calls the body. Use %N for both names in "this.%N = %N". builderType is TypeSpec.classBuilder(builder), then addProperties, addFunctions, addFunction(buildFunction(cls, builder)), addOriginatingKSFile(cls.containingFile!!) and build(). h: Generating code with KotlinPoet · Quiz
x: In CodeBlock.of("return %? (", cls.toClassName()), the class is the nested Kitchen.Drawer from another package. Which placeholder belongs in place of %?? %T: it prints the type's name and adds the import %N: it prints a name with backticks if needed %S: it quotes the value %L: it pastes the value as it is %T is the type placeholder: it prints Kitchen.Drawer and adds import movemate.Kitchen to the file when needed. %L would paste the ClassName's text without arranging the import, so the code might not compile in another package. %N is for names of properties, functions and parameters, and %S would turn the type into a string literal. A constructor parameter is declared val tags: List<String>?. What does param.type.toTypeName().copy(nullable = true) print as a field type? List<String>?? List<String?>? List<String>? List<String> toTypeName() keeps the type as declared, List<String>?, and copy(nullable = true) sets the outer type's nullability, which is already on, so nothing doubles. It doesn't touch the type argument, so String stays non-null. The first option is what the string template printed for Lamp.shade: String??, which the compiler flags as Redundant '?'. A processor tags its builder with addOriginatingKSFile(...) but calls writeTo(codeGenerator, aggregating = false) for a file that lists every @Builder class in the module. Where does the mistake show first? The processor doesn't compile: aggregating is checked against the content In the kctfork tests, which compile in memory Nowhere: KSP corrects the flag from the content On a later incremental build, as a list that silently misses classes aggregating describes what the output depends on, and nothing checks it against what the file contains. A list of every class depends on every file, so it must be aggregating. Declared isolating, it is regenerated only from the files that changed, and the other classes drop out. A clean build and kctfork (which starts fresh each time) both look fine; lesson 7 reproduces the failure. What does %S print for the Kotlin string Write $room on each "fragile" box? "Write ${'$'}room on each \"fragile\" box" Write $room on each "fragile" box, unquoted "Write $room on each \"fragile\" box", so $room becomes a template It throws, because $ isn't allowed in %S %S writes a string literal that means exactly the text you passed: it adds quotes and escapes " and $, which in Kotlin source would otherwise start a template. Unquoted output is what %L gives. If you want a real string template in the generated code, KotlinPoet has %P, which doesn't escape $. From lesson 3: toTypeName() on a parameter's KSTypeReference resolves the type before it converts it. What does resolving do, and why did lesson 3 call it the expensive step? It reads the type's name as written, which is free It loads the class with reflection while the processor runs It asks the compiler what the written name refers to, possibly across other files, and KSP records that lookup for incremental builds It compiles the generated file early to check the type A KSTypeReference is the type as written; resolve() finds the declaration it refers to, including type arguments and nullability, which can mean analysing other files. KSP's docs call type resolution one of the most expensive operations in its API, and each resolution adds a dependency that incremental builds track. Nothing runs or loads with reflection: KSP only reads declarations.

h: Generating code with KotlinPoet · Key terms
x: Builder A small class that collects an object's values one call at a time, then creates the object with build(). String template Text with values pasted in, here used to write source code by hand. KotlinPoet A library that writes Kotlin source files from descriptions (specs), with imports, escaping and formatting done for you. Spec KotlinPoet's description of one piece of code: FileSpec, TypeSpec, PropertySpec, FunSpec, ParameterSpec. Placeholder A marker in a format string, such as %T or %N, that KotlinPoet replaces with a correctly written argument. kotlinpoet-ksp KotlinPoet's companion library that turns KSP symbols into KotlinPoet names and writes files through KSP. Originating file The source file a generated output was made from; KSP uses it to know which outputs to redo when a file changes. JavaPoet The Java counterpart of KotlinPoet for javac annotation processors; Square's original is deprecated, Palantir's fork carries on. %T, %N, %S, %L: what does each take? %T a type (adds the import), %N a name (adds backticks when needed), %S a string (quoted and escaped), %L any value, pasted as it is. What does toClassName() give for the nested class movemate.Kitchen.Drawer? A ClassName with package movemate and simple names Kitchen and Drawer, printed as Kitchen.Drawer. Why make a field nullable with copy(nullable = true) rather than by adding ? to the text? copy sets nullability, so an already nullable type stays String?. Adding ? to the text doubles it: String??. Who reports an error inside generated code, KSP or the compiler? The Kotlin compiler, after KSP has written the file: e: file:///.../LoadBuilder.kt:4:24 ..., with a column and no [ksp]. What does writeTo(codeGenerator, aggregating = false) use for the output's Dependencies? The originating files tagged with addOriginatingKSFile on the file's top-level specs, plus your aggregating choice, which has no default. Does KotlinPoet check the code inside a function body? No. Bodies are format strings; KotlinPoet checks names and types, and the compiler checks the meaning later.

h: Generating code with KotlinPoet · Go deeper
x: Three more placeholders and behaviours are worth knowing. %P writes a string template: like %S, but it leaves $ alone, so $name stays a template in the generated code. %M writes a member reference from a MemberName, for example MemberName("kotlin.collections", "mutableMapOf"), and adds the import for it. When two types share a simple name, say move.Box and storage.Box in one generated file, KotlinPoet 2.4.0 imports both under aliases (import move.Box as MoveBox) instead of guessing. Generic classes need one more step. A class such as Shelf<T : Comparable<T>> uses its type parameter in its properties, and KotlinPoet has to know which T is meant. The tool is a TypeParameterResolver, made with toTypeParameterResolver() on the class's type parameters and passed to toTypeName(...). Since 2.4.0 the default resolver also finds type parameters from the enclosing declarations instead of throwing, so older blog posts that say it throws describe an earlier version. KotlinPoet 2.0 changed how long lines wrap: spaces no longer wrap by default, ♢ marks a space where a line may break, and · is now an ordinary space. Golden-file tests, which compare a whole generated file with a stored copy, will notice such changes across KotlinPoet upgrades. Pair each golden test with one that compiles and calls the generated code, as this lesson's lab does.

h: Errors, validation and helpful messages · Lesson 4's builder meets an interface and crashes
x: Let's give lesson 4's processor something it didn't expect. A symbol is KSP's object for one declaration in your code: a class, a property, a function or a parameter. The @Builder annotation may go on any class-like declaration, and to Kotlin an interface, an object and an enum class are all class-like. So this compiles, and the processor gets its symbol: @Builder interface Wardrobe KSP hands the processor a KSClassDeclaration whose classKind is INTERFACE. An interface has no constructor at all, so primaryConstructor is null. Lesson 4 read it without looking: Java // Closest Java equivalent: a javac processor that assumes every element is a class with a constructor TypeElement type = (TypeElement) element; ExecutableElement constructor = ElementFilter.constructorsIn(type.getEnclosedElements()).get(0); // an interface has no constructor, so get(0) throws, deep inside the processor Kotlin // Naive: lesson 4 assumed every @Builder class has a primary constructor fun constructorParameters(cls: KSClassDeclaration): List<KSValueParameter> = cls.primaryConstructor!!.parameters Here is the real build, ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL04Kotlin, with that interface added to lesson 4's playground: > Task :ksp:app:kspL04Kotlin FAILED e: [ksp] java.lang.NullPointerException * What went wrong: Execution failed for task ':ksp:app:kspL04Kotlin' (registered by plugin 'org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm'). > A failure occurred while executing com.google.devtools.ksp.gradle.KspAAWorkerAction > java.lang.NullPointerException (no error message) No file, no line, no class name. Run it again with --stacktrace, and well over a hundred lines into the output you find the cause, at workbench.ksp.l04.BuilderProcessorKt.constructorParameters(BuilderProcessor.kt:88). A stack trace is the list of method calls that were running when an exception was thrown, newest first. Every frame in it points into the processor, the helper's own code, and none of them at Wardrobe.kt, where the user made the mistake. A thrown exception does more harm than a bad message. It stops KSP on the spot: the rest of the round doesn't run, other processors in the build never get their turn, and none of them is told. KSP's docs say onError(), the method a processor overrides to clean up after a failed run, is called after an error or an exception. In KSP 2.3.14 a thrown exception skips it. In the picture, the helper dropped the clipboard in the hallway. The move is over, and the only clue is where the clipboard landed. A crash shows where the processor broke, not where the user went wrong. Check before you read. The first fix, then, is a check. The harder question is what the check should say. Crash the lesson 4 processor in a real build Create labs/ksp/app/src/l04/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l04/Wardrobe.kt with package workbench.ksp.app.l04, import workbench.ksp.annotations.Builder, and @Builder interface Wardrobe on two lines. Predict what the build will tell you. Then run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL04Kotlin from labs/. Run it again with --stacktrace and search the output for Caused by: java.lang.NullPointerException. Which file do the frames below it name? Then delete Wardrobe.kt. The task fails with e: [ksp] java.lang.NullPointerException and > java.lang.NullPointerException (no error message): no file, no line, no class. With --stacktrace, the Caused by block lists constructorParameters(BuilderProcessor.kt:88), then builderType, builderFile and processBuilders, all inside the processor. Wardrobe.kt appears nowhere in the stack trace. Once the file is gone, the task passes again.

h: Errors, validation and helpful messages · From a vague error to the exact file and line
x: From a crash to a note on the exact box: errors that name the file and line A processor talks to you through KSPLogger, which KSP passes in when it creates the processor. It has error, warn, info and logging, from loudest to quietest, and each takes a message and, optionally, a symbol. Gradle shows warn and error by default; info needs --info. Java's annotation processors, which javac has run since Java 6, have the same tool, the Messager, with printMessage(kind, message, element). KSP is Kotlin's own, faster way to do their job for Kotlin code. Here are two rungs of the ladder in both languages: Java // Closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor reporting through the Messager Messager messager = processingEnv.getMessager(); // rung 2, vague: no element, so javac can't say where messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, "@Builder can't build this"); // rung 3, precise: what is wrong and how to fix it, on the element itself messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, "@Builder needs a class to build, but " + element.getSimpleName() + " is an interface. " + "Put @Builder on a class.", element); Kotlin // rung 2, vague: no symbol, so KSP can't say where logger.error("@Builder can't build this") // rung 3, precise: what is wrong and how to fix it, on the symbol itself logger.error( "@Builder needs a class to build, but ${describe(cls)}. Put @Builder on a class with a primary constructor.", cls, ) The vague rung is already better than the crash: the build fails with a sentence instead of an exception. But the Try it shows what that sentence looks like with three bad classes in the build: === 2. a check with a vague message: COMPILATION_ERROR e: [ksp] @Builder can't build this === 3. a precise message on the symbol: COMPILATION_ERROR e: [ksp] Crate.kt:6: Crate has no primary constructor "This" could be any of them. Give the logger the symbol, and KSP adds the where: the file and the line, in front of your message. In a real Gradle build the path is absolute, e: [ksp] /…/labs/ksp/app/src/l05/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l05/Wardrobe.kt:6: ..., and there's no column. A good editor turns that path into a link. Look closely at the line number. In the lab's test, @Builder sits on line 5 and interface Wardrobe on line 6, and KSP reports line 6. The location of a symbol is its declaration's line, not its annotation's. In the picture, the helper's note goes on the box itself, not on the sticky note. Tests that expect the annotation's line fail, and the lab's tests count from the declaration. The symbol says where, so your words only have to say two things: what is wrong, and how to fix it. "@Builder needs a class to build, but Wardrobe is an interface. Put @Builder on a class with a primary constructor." Read it as the user would, with no idea how the processor works. It names the annotation, the class and its kind, and the next step, and it uses no word from KSP's API. Every error names its symbol. The symbol is the where; your sentence is the what and the how. Rung 3 still has a flaw, and the output shows it: it reported Crate and stopped, though Wardrobe and Settings were just as wrong. Climb the ladder in one run Open labs/ksp/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/ksp/l05/demo/ErrorLadderDemo.kt. Rungs 1 to 3 are small processors in that file (Crashing, Vague, Precise); rung 4 is the lab's processor. All four get the same three bad classes and a Plant with a default value. Predict what each rung prints. Then run ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l05.demo.ErrorLadderDemoKt. In Vague, pass cls as a second argument to logger.error and run again. What does the message gain, and what does it still lack? Rung 1 ends with INTERNAL_ERROR and java.lang.NullPointerException plus frames inside BuilderProcessor.kt. Rung 2 prints e: [ksp] @Builder can't build this, rung 3 e: [ksp] Crate.kt:6: Crate has no primary constructor, and both stop there. Rung 4 prints a warning for Plant.kt:9 and three errors, Crate.kt:6, Wardrobe.kt:6 and Wardrobe.kt:9, each saying what is wrong and how to fix it. With cls added, rung 2 gains Crate.kt:6: but still doesn't say what is wrong. The demo shortens the paths to file names; the run takes about 10 seconds. The ladder this lesson climbs: each rung changes one thing about how the processor reports a problem.

h: Errors, validation and helpful messages · Every problem in one build, and warnings for what you can't do
x: A processor that stops at the first problem makes the user play a slow game: fix one class, rebuild, meet the next error, fix that, rebuild again. Three bad classes cost three builds. Stopping early was our choice, though, not KSP's. logger.error doesn't stop anything: it marks the run as failed, and the round goes on. Every processor finishes the round, and then KSP starts no new one. It calls onError() on each processor instead of finish(), and Gradle fails the task with KSP failed with exit code: PROCESSING_ERROR. So the fix for rung 3 is one word, continue instead of return: Java // Closest Java equivalent: report each bad element, then keep going for (Element element : roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Builder.class)) { if (!check(element)) continue; // reported; the next element still gets its turn writeBuilder((TypeElement) element); } return false; Kotlin fun processBuilders(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { val symbols = resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation(Builder::class.qualifiedName!!).toList() val (ready, later) = symbols.partition { it.validate(apiFeatures = apiFeatures) } for (symbol in ready) { if (!check(symbol)) continue // reported; the next symbol still gets its turn builderFile(symbol as KSClassDeclaration).writeTo(codeGenerator, aggregating = false) } return later } javac works the same way: its RoundEnvironment docs say that if a processor raises an error, the current round runs to completion. Here is lesson 5's processor in the real build, with Wardrobe and Crate added to the playground (paths shortened): > Task :ksp:app:kspL05Kotlin FAILED e: [ksp] /…/l05/Wardrobe.kt:6: @Builder needs a class to build, but Wardrobe is an interface. Put @Builder on a class with a primary constructor. e: [ksp] /…/l05/Wardrobe.kt:9: Crate has no primary constructor, so CrateBuilder doesn't know what to pass. Declare the properties in one: class Crate(val label: String). > A failure occurred while executing com.google.devtools.ksp.gradle.KspAAWorkerAction > KSP failed with exit code: PROCESSING_ERROR Two problems, one build. The good classes still got their builders in that round, as the lab's test checks, even though the build failed. In the picture, the helper walks the whole house and leaves a note on every bad box before calling you, instead of calling you once per box. Not every problem should fail the build. That calls for a warning, logger.warn(message, param), on the parameter's own line: w: [ksp] /…/l05/MoveMate.kt:21: PlantBuilder can't see the default value of waterEveryDays, so build() will require it. Set it on the builder. The build goes on. Use an error when the output would be wrong or missing, and a warning when it works but surprises. Two cautions: -q hides warnings completely, and ksp { allWarningsAsErrors = true } turns them into errors. One quiet trap sits in logger.exception(e), which sounds like the polite way to report a caught exception. In KSP 2.3.14 it prints e: [ksp] and the exception's text, and the build passes. If you mean "fail", call logger.error. Report every problem you can see, then let the build fail once. Every check so far looked at things KSP can see right away.
