h: Errors, validation and helpful messages · Setting aside what can't be read yet with validate()
x: Here is a class whose label mentions a type that doesn't exist. It may be a typo, or a type that another processor hasn't written yet: @Builder class Parcel(val label: String, val sticker: Sticker) KSP doesn't stop at the unknown Sticker; it hands the processor a type it calls an error type, one the compiler can't resolve. The checks pass, because Parcel is a class with a public primary constructor. Then KotlinPoet's toTypeName() meets the error type and throws: === without validate(): lesson 4's processor: INTERNAL_ERROR java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Error type '<ERROR TYPE: Sticker>' is not resolvable in the current round of processing. It's a crash again, inside our processor, and the message even says what to do: wait. validate() is KSP's check for exactly this. It walks every type a declaration mentions (its supertypes, its properties' types, its functions' parameters) and returns false if any of them can't be resolved yet. The symbols that fail go back to KSP as the return value of process(), and KSP offers them again in the next round. Setting a symbol aside like this is called deferral: Java // Closest Java equivalent: javac has no validate(); look for error types yourself boolean ready = ElementFilter.fieldsIn(type.getEnclosedElements()).stream() .noneMatch(field -> field.asType().getKind() == TypeKind.ERROR); if (!ready) waiting.add(type.getQualifiedName().toString()); // look it up again next round Kotlin val symbols = resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation(Builder::class.qualifiedName!!).toList() val (ready, later) = symbols.partition { it.validate(apiFeatures = apiFeatures) } // ... check and write the ready ones, as before return later // KSP offers these again in the next round In KSP 2.3.14, write validate(apiFeatures = apiFeatures), passing the processor's own apiFeatures. Plain validate(), the spelling in the official quickstart, has been deprecated since 2.3.12 and compiles with a warning. With validation in place, the same input gives: === with validate(): the lab's processor: COMPILATION_ERROR e: Parcel.kt:6:46 Unresolved reference 'Sticker'. That's no crash. The error comes from the compiler, on the user's own line, about the user's own typo. In the picture, the helper set the box aside, because its label mentions something that isn't packed yet. The picture breaks a little here: a real helper could open the box and look. KSP can't, so it can only wait for the missing type to appear. validate() resolves the whole declaration tree, so it costs something; KSP's docs advise checking only what your output needs. Our builder needs a second round only when someone else writes Sticker. Lesson 6 builds exactly that case, and finds a catch in what KSP 2.3.14 does with a symbol that stays set aside to the end. Checks catch only what you thought of. Put @Builder on abstract class Furniture(val legs: Int): it is a class, its constructor is public, and every check passes. Then the compiler rejects the generated code, e: FurnitureBuilder.kt:14:35 Cannot create an instance of an abstract class., pointing at a file the user never wrote. Each such case is one more check, written before you read. Crash on an unknown type, then set it aside Open SetAsideDemo.kt next to the ladder demo. It compiles Parcel(val label: String, val sticker: Sticker) twice: with lesson 4's processor, then with the lab's. Predict both outcomes. Then run ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l05.demo.SetAsideDemoKt. In the demo's source string, add class Sticker(val text: String) below Parcel and run again. What changes for each processor? Without validate(), the run ends with INTERNAL_ERROR and IllegalArgumentException: Error type '<ERROR TYPE: Sticker>' is not resolvable in the current round of processing. With it, there is no crash: KSP sets Parcel aside, processing ends, and the compiler reports e: Parcel.kt:6:46 Unresolved reference 'Sticker'. on the user's line. Once Sticker exists, both processors write ParcelBuilder and both runs end OK.

h: Errors, validation and helpful messages · Java and Kotlin
x: Checking a symbol and reporting on it: javac's Messager and KSP's KSPLogger BuilderProcessor.java (javac) // Closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor boolean check(Element element) { Messager messager = processingEnv.getMessager(); if (element.getKind() != ElementKind.CLASS) { messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, "@Builder needs a class to build, but " + element.getSimpleName() + " is not a class. " + "Put @Builder on a class.", element); return false; } List<ExecutableElement> constructors = ElementFilter.constructorsIn(element.getEnclosedElements()); if (constructors.stream().allMatch(c -> c.getModifiers().contains(Modifier.PRIVATE))) { messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, element.getSimpleName() + "Builder can't call a private constructor. Make one public.", constructors.get(0)); return false; } return true; } BuilderProcessor.kt (KSP) fun check(symbol: KSAnnotated): Boolean { if (symbol !is KSClassDeclaration || symbol.classKind != ClassKind.CLASS) { logger.error("@Builder needs a class to build, but ${describe(symbol)}. " + "Put @Builder on a class with a primary constructor.", symbol) return false } val name = symbol.simpleName.asString() val builder = builderName(symbol).simpleName val constructor = symbol.primaryConstructor if (constructor == null) { logger.error("$name has no primary constructor, so $builder doesn't know what to pass. " + "Declare the properties in one: class $name(val label: String).", symbol) return false } if (constructor.isPrivate()) { logger.error("$builder can't call $name's constructor, because it is private. " + "Make it internal or public, or remove @Builder.", constructor) return false } for (param in constructor.parameters.filter { it.hasDefault }) { logger.warn("$builder can't see the default value of ${nameOf(param)}, so build() will require it. " + "Set it on the builder.", param) } return true } Both report on an element, both land on the declaration's line, and both let the round finish after an error. The differences are in the details. javac prints Wardrobe.java:4: error: ... followed by the source line and a caret under the declaration; KSP prints the absolute path and the line, with no column and no source line. Java has no primary constructor, so the Java check looks through every constructor, where Kotlin asks for exactly one. And Kotlin's default values give the KSP version a warning with no Java twin: a Java constructor parameter can't have a default at all.

h: Errors, validation and helpful messages · Worked example
x: Turn an unhelpful message into a good one, and pin it with a test A teammate's processor reports a private constructor like this. Read it as a user who has never seen the processor's code, and list what's missing. // before: true, but no class, no line, no next step if (constructor.isPrivate()) { logger.error("constructor is private") return false } // before: true, but no class, no line, no next step if (constructor.getModifiers().contains(Modifier.PRIVATE)) { messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, "constructor is private"); return false; } Ask the three questions. Where? Pass the constructor as the symbol, so KSP adds the file and line. What? Name the builder and the class. How to fix it? Give the user a choice of next steps. if (constructor.isPrivate()) { logger.error( "$builder can't call $name's constructor, because it is private. " + "Make it internal or public, or remove @Builder.", constructor, // where: Crate.kt:11 ) return false } if (constructor.getModifiers().contains(Modifier.PRIVATE)) { messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, builder + " can't call " + name + "'s constructor, because it is private. " + "Make it public, or remove @Builder.", constructor); // where: the constructor's line return false; } Now pin it with a test, so the message never drifts back. The test compiles a small source in memory and checks the end of the path, the line and the text. The Java twin uses Google's compile-testing library, which has the same three checks built in. val safe = SourceFile.kotlin("Crate.kt", """ package movemate import workbench.ksp.annotations.Builder @Builder class Crate { constructor(label: String) } @Builder class Safe private constructor(val code: String) """) val run = compileWithKsp(safe, processors = listOf(BuilderProcessorProvider())) assertThat(run.messages).containsPattern( """e: \[ksp] \S*/Crate\.kt:11: SafeBuilder can't call Safe's constructor, because it is private\.""") JavaFileObject safe = JavaFileObjects.forSourceString("movemate.Safe", """ package movemate; import workbench.ksp.annotations.Builder; @Builder public class Safe { private Safe(String code) {} } """); Compilation compilation = javac().withProcessors(new BuilderProcessor()).compile(safe); assertThat(compilation).failed(); assertThat(compilation).hadErrorContaining("can't call a private constructor").inFile(safe).onLine(5); Run it and watch it pass. Then change :11: to :10:, the line of @Builder, and watch it fail: KSP reports the declaration's line, not the annotation's. Put it back. h: Errors, validation and helpful messages · Quiz
x: In a source file, line 5 is @Builder and line 6 is interface Wardrobe. The processor calls logger.error(message, symbol) with Wardrobe's symbol. Which location does KSP print? Wardrobe.kt:5, the annotation's line Wardrobe.kt:6, the declaration's line Wardrobe.kt:5:1, with a column No location: interfaces have none A symbol's location is its declaration's line, so the error lands on interface Wardrobe. KSP prints a path and a line but never a column. The first option is the common guess, and the reason tests written for the annotation's line fail. A processor throws IllegalStateException for the first bad class it meets. A second processor runs after it in the same build. What happens? Both processors finish the round, then the build fails The second processor runs, then onError() is called on both KSP stops at once: the second processor never runs, and in 2.3.14 no onError() is called KSP turns the exception into a warning and goes on A thrown exception escapes KSP's round loop, so processing ends on the spot: later processors in that round don't run, and KSP 2.3.14 skips onError(), although its docs say it is called after an exception too. Gradle fails with the exception's message. logger.error is what lets the round finish, which is the first two options. A processor catches an exception and reports it with logger.exception(e). What does the build do in KSP 2.3.14? It prints e: [ksp] and the exception's text, and the build passes It fails with PROCESSING_ERROR, like logger.error It hides the message unless Gradle runs with --info It rethrows the exception and fails with its stack trace logger.exception only prints. It doesn't mark the run as failed, so finish() runs and the build passes. The e: prefix makes it look like an error, which is the trap. If the problem should fail the build, call logger.error(message, symbol). @Builder class Parcel(val label: String, val sticker: Sticker), and no Sticker exists anywhere. The processor sets invalid symbols aside with validate(). What does the user see? IllegalArgumentException: Error type '<ERROR TYPE: Sticker>' ... from inside the processor Nothing: the build passes and ParcelBuilder is generated A KSP error that says Parcel is invalid No KSP message; the compiler reports Unresolved reference 'Sticker' on Parcel's line validate() returns false, so Parcel is returned from process() and never reaches KotlinPoet. No new file appears, so processing ends after that round, and the compiler then reports the unknown type in the user's own source. The first option is what happens without validate(). Lesson 6 looks at what KSP itself says about a symbol that is still set aside at the end. From lesson 4: PlantBuilder requires waterEveryDays although Plant declares waterEveryDays: Int = 7. Why can't the processor use the default? KotlinPoet can't write default values KSP reads declarations, not expressions: it shows that a default exists, never its value Defaults exist only while the program runs, so no build tool can see them The builder could, but only with a @Default annotation A default value is an expression, and KSP doesn't model expressions: hasDefault is all a processor learns. KotlinPoet could print a default if the processor knew one. The compiler does see the expression; KSP's model leaves it out on purpose. That is why lesson 5 reports the default as a warning on the parameter's line.

h: Errors, validation and helpful messages · Key terms
x: Symbol KSP's object for one declaration in your code: a class, a property, a function or a parameter. Stack trace The list of method calls that were running when an exception was thrown, newest first. KSPLogger The processor's way to report: error, warn, info and logging, each optionally on a symbol. Location Where a symbol is declared: a file and the declaration's line, which KSP prints before a message. Error type A type the compiler can't resolve, such as a typo or a type another processor hasn't written yet. validate() KSP's check that every type a declaration mentions can be resolved; false means the symbol isn't ready. Deferral Returning a symbol from process() so that KSP offers it again in the next round. onError() The method KSP calls on every processor after a round in which logger.error was used, instead of finish(). What does a processor that throws an exception do to a KSP build? Processing stops at once; later processors don't run, onError() is skipped (KSP 2.3.14), and Gradle fails with the exception's message, with no file or line. What does logger.error("...", symbol) print in a Gradle build? e: [ksp] <absolute path>:<line>: ...: an absolute path and the declaration's line, with no column. Does logger.error stop the round? No. The round finishes and files are still written; then no new round starts, onError() runs instead of finish(), and the build fails with PROCESSING_ERROR. Error or warning for "this works, but the builder can't use the default"? A warning (logger.warn on the parameter): the output is correct, just surprising. Errors are for output that would be wrong or missing. What makes validate() return false? A type somewhere in the declaration (supertypes, property types, parameter types) that can't be resolved yet, an error type. How do you call validate() without a deprecation warning in KSP 2.3.14? symbol.validate(apiFeatures = apiFeatures), passing the processor's own apiFeatures. Plain validate() is deprecated since 2.3.12. What does logger.exception(e) do to the build in KSP 2.3.14? Nothing: it prints e: [ksp] and the exception's text, and the build passes.

h: Errors, validation and helpful messages · Go deeper
x: When a run fails, KSP 2.3.13 and later also print follow-on errors from a quick type check of the round's new files, for example e: [ksp] Greeter.kt:11: Unresolved reference 'helloFromGreeter'. from the lab's smoke example, with a file name only and no folder. They are not your bug: code that uses a generated declaration was checked before the declaration existed. Fix the first error with a full path, and the follow-ons disappear. The log levels map to Gradle's own. At the default level you see warn and error; --info adds info, and --debug adds logging. With -q, warnings disappear completely, so a processor that warns about something important should consider an error, or the ksp { allWarningsAsErrors = true } switch for teams that want warnings to stop the build. When a processor looks at things outside its own source set, the location can be missing. A class that comes from a compiled library has no file, so its location is NonExistLocation and its containingFile is null. A message logged on such a symbol has no path in front, and code that writes containingFile!! on a library class crashes. Check symbol.origin (KOTLIN and JAVA mean source code) before you rely on a file. On the Java side, javac's Messager can also report on an annotation or one of its values, with the overloads printMessage(kind, message, element, annotationMirror) and printMessage(kind, message, element, annotationMirror, annotationValue). Its Javadoc warns that such location hints "may be unavailable or only approximate".

h: Rounds, generated code and deferral · A receipt that needs its own card: rounds made visible
x: Rounds made visible: a receipt written in round 1 gets its card in round 2, and a box set aside waits its turn This lesson's lab has two processors. The receipt processor is new: for each class marked @Moving, it writes a <Name>Receipt data class with the same properties plus signedBy, and a receipt(signedBy) function to make one. The receipt carries @Inventory, the sticky note that asks for an inventory card. The second processor is lesson 2's card processor, copied into the lab and rewritten with KotlinPoet, which writes inventoryCard() for every @Inventory class. Used from code, the two outputs look like this: Java // Java calling the same generated Kotlin: extension functions are static methods of their file's class LampReceipt lampReceipt = LampReceiptKt.receipt(new Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null), "Ana"); System.out.println(LampReceiptInventoryCardKt.inventoryCard(lampReceipt)); Kotlin val lampReceipt = Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null).receipt(signedBy = "Ana") println(lampReceipt.inventoryCard()) // LampReceipt: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null, signedBy=Ana The card processor must write a card for a class that the receipt processor writes during the same build. How can it see that class? The answer is rounds. A round is one pass in which KSP calls process() on every processor, one after another, in the order of the services file. Each call gets a new Resolver, the object a processor asks for symbols. In round 1, the Resolver offers the source files. When a round is over, KSP reads the files written during it, and the next round offers those, plus the symbols set aside the round before. A new round starts only if the previous one wrote at least one file. javac, which has run Java's annotation processors since Java 6, works in rounds too. KSP is Kotlin's own, faster way to do the same job for Kotlin code. To watch the rounds, count them. KSP's docs say it "creates a processor instance only once", so a field lives from round to round. The Resolver must not be kept: each round brings a new one. Both lab processors log each round with logger.warn, so it shows at Gradle's default log level: Java // Closest Java equivalent: javac calls process() once per round, on the same processor object private int round = 0; @Override public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment roundEnv) { round++; processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.WARNING, "[receipts] round " + round + ", processingOver=" + roundEnv.processingOver()); // ... find, check, read, write return false; } Kotlin private var round = 0 // KSP creates the processor once, so the field lives across rounds fun processReceipts(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { round++ // ... find, check, read, write logger.warn("[receipts] round $round: wrote $written, set aside ${later.map(::nameOf)}") return later } Here is ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL06Kotlin on the lab's playground, with @Moving on Lamp and Van, and @Inventory on Box: w: [ksp] [receipts] round 1: wrote [LampReceipt], set aside [Van] w: [ksp] [cards] round 1: wrote cards for [Box] w: [ksp] [receipts] round 2: wrote [VanReceipt], set aside [] w: [ksp] [cards] round 2: wrote cards for [LampReceipt] w: [ksp] [receipts] round 3: wrote [], set aside [] w: [ksp] [cards] round 3: wrote cards for [VanReceipt] w: [ksp] [receipts] round 4: wrote [], set aside [] w: [ksp] [cards] round 4: wrote cards for [] w: [ksp] [receipts] finish() after 4 rounds Read it as a story. In round 1 the receipts processor wrote LampReceipt, and the cards processor, running right after it, still didn't see it: it found only Box. In round 2 the new file was offered to everyone, and LampReceipt got its card. Each round wrote something, so another followed, until round 4 wrote nothing and KSP ended with finish(). Four rounds for three classes. In the picture, each round is a walk through the house, and the cards written on one walk are new boxes for the next. The picture breaks in one way. Real helpers work side by side, while KSP's take turns, and a card that helper A writes is invisible to helper B until the next walk. What a round writes, the next round reads. That leaves Van, set aside in round 1. Why it had to wait is the next step. Watch the rounds in a real build From labs/, run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL06Kotlin and read the nine w: [ksp] lines. Before you look at the figure, mark for each line which file it saw for the first time. h: Rounds, generated code and deferral · A label that mentions a card not written yet: setting Van aside
x: Van is a moving van whose label mentions the last receipt it carried: @Moving data class Van(val plate: String, val lastLoad: LampReceipt) A receipt copies its class's property types, so VanReceipt needs the type LampReceipt, and in round 1 that type doesn't exist yet. Let's first see what happens if the processor doesn't care. The Try it's first run writes every receipt at once, ready or not: === 1. eager, no validate(): INTERNAL_ERROR java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Error type '<ERROR TYPE: LampReceipt>' is not resolvable in the current round of processing. That's the crash from lesson 5, and this time the missing type isn't a typo. It's on its way, written by the same build one round from now. An error type is a type the compiler can't resolve; KSP shows it as <ERROR TYPE: LampReceipt>. So the processor sets Van aside: validate() returns false for it, and process() returns it to KSP. Setting a symbol aside for a later round is called deferral. Here is the lab's whole round, with the Java version for comparison: Java // Closest Java equivalent: javac has no deferral; keep the names and look them up next round for (TypeElement type : candidates) { boolean ready = ElementFilter.fieldsIn(type.getEnclosedElements()).stream() .noneMatch(f -> f.asType().getKind() == TypeKind.ERROR); if (ready) writeReceipt(type); else waiting.add(type.getQualifiedName().toString()); // next round: elements.getTypeElement(name) } Kotlin fun processReceipts(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { round++ val symbols = resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation(Moving::class.qualifiedName!!).toList() val (ready, later) = symbols.partition { it.validate(apiFeatures = apiFeatures) } val written = mutableListOf<String>() for (symbol in ready) { if (!check(symbol)) continue val file = receiptFile(symbol as KSClassDeclaration) file.writeTo(codeGenerator, aggregating = false) written += file.name } waiting = later logger.warn("[receipts] round $round: wrote $written, set aside ${later.map(::nameOf)}") return later } Walk through it in order. Count the round. Ask for the @Moving symbols. Split them into the ones whose types all resolve and the rest. Check, read and write the ready ones. Remember the rest in waiting for later, log the round, and hand the rest back. What KSP does with that list is the second half of the mechanism. Its docs say that in later rounds getSymbolsWithAnnotation returns "only deferred symbols from the last round and symbols from newly generated files". So in round 2 the receipt processor asks for @Moving again and gets Van back, now with a LampReceipt to point at. validate() says yes, and VanReceipt is written. javac has no such list: a Java processor keeps the class names itself and looks them up again with Elements.getTypeElement, as the Java twin's comment says. Why return the symbol, rather than keep it in a field and reuse it? Because KSP drops its caches between rounds, and its docs warn that "not all KSP symbols can be reused across rounds". The symbol you get back from the next Resolver is the safe one. In the picture, Van is a box set aside because its label mentions a receipt that isn't written yet. On the next walk, the receipt is there, and the box goes on the van. The set-aside pile has one more property, and it's easy to miss. Crash, then wait a round Open labs/ksp/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/ksp/l06/demo/RoundsDemo.kt. Eager writes every receipt at once; Quiet sets aside what isn't valid yet. Each run also has the card processor. Predict the first two runs, then run ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l06.demo.RoundsDemoKt. Look only at runs 1 and 2 for now. In the demo's move source, add @Moving data class Truck(val plate: String, val towing: VanReceipt). How many rounds will run 2 need now? Predict, then run. Run 1 ends INTERNAL_ERROR with Error type '<ERROR TYPE: LampReceipt>' is not resolvable in the current round of processing. Run 2 ends OK with the same eight round lines as the real build: Van is set aside in round 1 and written in round 2. With Truck added, Truck waits two rounds (round 1 for LampReceipt, round 2 for VanReceipt), TruckReceipt is written in round 3, its card in round 4, and round 5 is the empty one. Runs 3 and 4 belong to the last section of this lesson.

h: Rounds, generated code and deferral · The set-aside pile is shared by every processor
x: Suppose Van deserves an inventory card too, so it carries both notes, @Moving @Inventory. In round 1 the receipt processor sets it aside, and the card processor writes VanInventoryCard.kt, since a card needs only names, never types. Now remove one line from the card processor, the guard that remembers which classes have a card, and run the real build again: w: [ksp] [receipts] round 1: wrote [LampReceipt], set aside [Van] w: [ksp] [cards] round 1: wrote cards for [Box, Van] w: [ksp] [receipts] round 2: wrote [VanReceipt], set aside [] e: [ksp] kotlin.io.FileAlreadyExistsException: /…/build/generated/ksp/l06/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l06/VanInventoryCard.kt The card processor set nothing aside, and yet in round 2 it got Van again. KSP keeps one pile of set-aside symbols for all processors, and a symbol on the pile comes back in every processor's lookup, for every annotation it carries. The card processor wrote the same file a second time, and KSP refuses that, in round 2 just as in round 1. The fix is to remember what you've written, keyed by the class's full name: Java // Closest Java equivalent: javac's Filer refuses a second file with the same name, // so a processor that may meet an element twice keeps its own list private final Set<String> carded = new HashSet<>(); if (!carded.add(type.getQualifiedName().toString())) continue; writeCard(type); // a second createSourceFile for the same name throws FilerException Kotlin /** Classes that already have a card. A symbol another processor set aside comes back here too. */ private val carded = mutableSetOf<String>() if (!carded.add(cls.qualifiedName!!.asString())) continue cardFile(cls).writeTo(codeGenerator, aggregating = false) With the guard in place, the same build prints [cards] round 2: wrote cards for [LampReceipt] and carries on to round 4. In javac the problem has a different source, since nothing is ever handed back. A Java processor meets an element twice only when it looks up its own saved names again, and its Filer refuses the second file with a FilerException. This is where the picture breaks again. In a real house each helper keeps their own pile of boxes to come back to. In KSP the pile is shared, and every helper on the next walk trips over every box on it. A set-aside symbol comes back to every processor. Never write a file twice for one symbol. So far every set-aside box found its type a round later. The last case is the one the docs and KSP 2.3.14 disagree about. h: Rounds, generated code and deferral · A box set aside forever, and the check in finish()
x: Here is a trailer that will wait forever, because nobody put @Moving on Piano, so no round will ever write PianoReceipt: data class Piano(val keys: Int) @Moving data class Trailer(val plate: String, val load: PianoReceipt) KSP's docs say what should happen: "If deferred symbols remain unprocessed, KSP logs an error for each processor with remaining deferred symbols." Let the build be the referee. Here is the KSP task with a receipt processor that sets Trailer aside each round and checks nothing at the end: > Task :ksp:app:kspL06Kotlin w: [ksp] [receipts] round 1: wrote [LampReceipt], set aside [Van, Trailer] ... w: [ksp] [receipts] round 4: wrote [], set aside [Trailer] w: [ksp] [cards] round 4: wrote cards for [] w: [ksp] [receipts] finish() after 4 rounds BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 2s Not a word. KSP 2.3.14 has no code that reports leftovers. When a round writes nothing, the loop stops, finish() runs, and the set-aside symbols are dropped. The lab has a test that proves it with a processor that sets every symbol aside forever: the exit code is OK, and there is no error. Here the compiler trips over PianoReceipt later, e: …/Trailer.kt:9:49 Unresolved reference 'PianoReceipt'., because Trailer's own label mentions it. That error names the type but not the reason, and a processor that sets symbols aside for any other reason gets a green build and a missing file. So the careful processor checks at the end itself. finish() is the method KSP calls on every processor once, after the last round, when no error was logged (after an error it calls onError() instead). Our processor still holds the last round's set-aside list in waiting, and its symbols are still good for a location: Java // Closest Java equivalent: javac's last round, where processingOver() is true if (roundEnv.processingOver()) { for (String name : waiting) { processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, name + "Receipt was never written: a type it needs was never generated", processingEnv.getElementUtils().getTypeElement(name)); } } Kotlin fun reportLeftovers() { // called from finish(), after the last round logger.warn("[receipts] finish() after ${rounds(round)}") for (symbol in waiting) { val cls = symbol as KSClassDeclaration val missing = missingTypes(cls).joinToString(", ") logger.error( "${receiptName(cls).simpleName} was never written: ${nameOf(cls)} still needed $missing " + "when processing ended after ${rounds(round)}. Check the spelling, or the annotation that should generate $missing.", cls, ) } } Now the same build fails where the cause is: e: [ksp] /…/l06/Trailer.kt:9: TrailerReceipt was never written: Trailer still needed PianoReceipt when processing ended after 4 rounds. Check the spelling, or the annotation that should generate PianoReceipt. An error logged in finish() still fails the build. javac's twin is its last round: javac runs one more round in which processingOver() returns true, and leftovers are checked there. In the picture, finish() is the last walk through the empty house before the van leaves, and the careful helper counts the set-aside pile. KSP 2.3.14 forgets what you set aside. Check in finish(), and report each symbol still waiting. Rounds have limits worth knowing. Every round costs a new Resolver and a new validate() pass, so a chain of receipts that need receipts adds a round per link. A file written in finish() is compiled, but no round reads it, so its sticky notes are ignored. And none of this lets a processor see more of a box: each round still reads labels, never bodies. Leave a trailer waiting forever Look at runs 3 and 4 of the demo from the second Try it. Run 3 uses Quiet, run 4 the lab's processor, on the same Trailer. Create labs/ksp/app/src/l06/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l06/Trailer.kt with package workbench.ksp.app.l06, import workbench.ksp.annotations.Moving, data class Piano(val keys: Int), and @Moving data class Trailer(val plate: String, val load: PianoReceipt). h: Rounds, generated code and deferral · Java and Kotlin
x: Rounds and leftovers: javac's processingOver() and KSP's finish() ReceiptProcessor.java (javac) // Closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor private final Set<String> waiting = new LinkedHashSet<>(); private int round = 0; @Override public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment roundEnv) { round++; Elements elements = processingEnv.getElementUtils(); List<TypeElement> candidates = new ArrayList<>(); for (Element e : roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Moving.class)) candidates.add((TypeElement) e); for (String name : waiting) candidates.add(elements.getTypeElement(name)); // no deferral: look up again waiting.clear(); for (TypeElement type : candidates) { if (hasErrorTypes(type)) waiting.add(type.getQualifiedName().toString()); else writeReceipt(type); } if (roundEnv.processingOver()) { // javac's extra, final round for (String name : waiting) { processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, name + "Receipt was never written", elements.getTypeElement(name)); } } return false; } ReceiptProcessor.kt (KSP) private var round = 0 private var waiting: List<KSAnnotated> = emptyList() override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { round++ val symbols = resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation(Moving::class.qualifiedName!!).toList() val (ready, later) = symbols.partition { it.validate(apiFeatures = apiFeatures) } for (symbol in ready) { if (check(symbol)) receiptFile(symbol as KSClassDeclaration).writeTo(codeGenerator, aggregating = false) } waiting = later return later // KSP hands these back next round } override fun finish() { // once, after the last round for (symbol in waiting) { logger.error("${receiptName(symbol as KSClassDeclaration).simpleName} was never written", symbol) } } Both run in rounds, and in both a file written in one round is read in the next. The bookkeeping differs. javac has no deferral, so the Java processor keeps class names itself and looks them up again each round with Elements.getTypeElement; KSP takes the symbols back from process() and returns them, pooled across all processors. javac ends with one extra round in which processingOver() is true and nothing new is processed; KSP has no extra round and calls finish() instead (or onError() after an error). And in KSP 2.3.14, unlike its docs, nothing reports what is still set aside: the Kotlin version must do it in finish().

h: Rounds, generated code and deferral · Worked example
x: Predict the rounds for a truck that tows a van Add one class to the lab's move: a truck whose label mentions the van's receipt. Before you run anything, decide in which round TruckReceipt will be written. @Moving data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?) @Moving data class Van(val plate: String, val lastLoad: LampReceipt) @Moving data class Truck(val plate: String, val towing: VanReceipt) // The same chain in Java, using the generated Kotlin receipts as ordinary types @Moving public record Truck(String plate, VanReceipt towing) {} // VanReceipt needs LampReceipt, which needs Lamp: three links, one per round Trace it like a helper. Round 1 offers all three classes: only Lamp is valid, so LampReceipt is written and Van and Truck are set aside. Round 2 offers the set-aside pair plus LampReceipt.kt: Van is valid now, Truck still isn't, and the cards processor meets LampReceipt. Round 3: Truck at last, and VanReceipt's card. Round 4: TruckReceipt's card. Round 5 writes nothing, so it's the last. Now the referee. This is the real log from the lab's processors: w: [ksp] [receipts] round 1: wrote [LampReceipt], set aside [Van, Truck] w: [ksp] [cards] round 1: wrote cards for [] w: [ksp] [receipts] round 2: wrote [VanReceipt], set aside [Truck] w: [ksp] [cards] round 2: wrote cards for [LampReceipt] w: [ksp] [receipts] round 3: wrote [TruckReceipt], set aside [] w: [ksp] [cards] round 3: wrote cards for [VanReceipt] w: [ksp] [receipts] round 4: wrote [], set aside [] w: [ksp] [cards] round 4: wrote cards for [TruckReceipt] w: [ksp] [receipts] round 5: wrote [], set aside [] w: [ksp] [cards] round 5: wrote cards for [] w: [ksp] [receipts] finish() after 5 rounds Read the shape, not just the numbers. Each link in a chain of generated types costs one round, and the cards trail one round behind the receipts they describe. The last round always writes nothing, because that is how KSP knows to stop. Each round also means a fresh Resolver and another validate() pass over everything set aside, which is why a processor should validate only what its output needs.

h: Rounds, generated code and deferral · Quiz
x: In a build, the last file any processor writes is TruckReceiptInventoryCard.kt, in round 4. How many rounds run in total? 4: the round that wrote the last file is the last round 5: round 5 runs because round 4 wrote a file, finds nothing to do, and ends the loop As many as there are annotated classes Until every symbol has been set aside at least once KSP starts a new round whenever the previous one wrote at least one file, so round 4's card triggers round 5. Round 5 writes nothing, and only then does KSP stop and call finish(). The lab's log shows the same shape: the last line before finish() is always a round that wrote nothing. The receipt processor sets aside Van, which carries @Moving and @Inventory. In round 2, what does the card processor get from getSymbolsWithAnnotation("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory")? Only LampReceipt, from the new file Nothing: the card processor deferred nothing LampReceipt and Van: set-aside symbols return to every processor, for every annotation they carry Only Van, because deferred symbols come first KSP keeps one pool of set-aside symbols and merges it into every processor's lookup. So Van comes back to the card processor even though the receipt processor set it aside, and a card processor without a guard writes VanInventoryCard.kt a second time and fails with FileAlreadyExistsException. A processor returns the same perfectly valid symbol from every process() call and never reports anything. What does KSP 2.3.14 do at the end? Logs an error for that processor, as the docs say Logs a warning and passes the build Keeps starting rounds until a timeout Nothing: no file was written, so the loop stops, finish() runs, the symbol is dropped, and the build passes A round that writes no file ends processing, whatever is still set aside. KSP's docs say it logs an error for each processor with deferred symbols left; 2.3.14 has no code that does, and the lab's test shows exit code OK with no error. That's why the lab's processor checks waiting in finish() itself. Where should a processor report the symbols that are still set aside when processing ends? In finish(), which KSP calls once after the last round In process(), when it notices that this is the last round In onError(), which KSP calls when processing ends In the provider's create() process() can't know a round is the last one: KSP decides that only after the round, when it sees no new files. finish() runs exactly once afterwards, and an error logged there still fails the build. onError() runs only after an error was already logged, and create() runs before the first round. From lesson 5: the receipt processor skips validate() and calls KotlinPoet's toTypeName() on Van's property lastLoad: LampReceipt in round 1. What happens? KotlinPoet writes LampReceipt anyway, and the build passes The processor throws IllegalArgumentException: Error type '<ERROR TYPE: LampReceipt>' is not resolvable in the current round of processing., and KSP stops with an internal error KSP sets Van aside by itself The compiler reports Unresolved reference 'LampReceipt' In round 1, LampReceipt is an error type, because it is only being written in this round. toTypeName() refuses error types and throws, which ends processing at once, as lesson 5's crash did. KSP never sets symbols aside by itself: a processor must check with validate() and return the symbol, and then Van is written in round 2.

h: Rounds, generated code and deferral · Key terms
x: Round One pass in which KSP calls process() on every processor; files written in it are read in the next round. Resolver The object a processor asks for symbols; KSP gives it a new one each round. Deferral Returning a symbol from process() so that KSP offers it again in the next round. Error type A type the compiler can't resolve yet, shown by KSP as <ERROR TYPE: LampReceipt>. finish() The method KSP calls on every processor once, after the last round, when no error was logged. processingOver() javac's signal, on RoundEnvironment, that this is the final round of annotation processing. When does KSP start another round? When the round that just ended wrote at least one file. A round that writes nothing ends processing. In round 2, what does getSymbolsWithAnnotation return? Symbols from the files written in round 1, plus the symbols set aside in round 1, by any processor. Can a processor keep state from one round to the next? Yes, in fields: KSP creates each processor once. But never keep the Resolver; each round brings a new one. What does KSP 2.3.14 report about symbols still set aside at the end? Nothing: no error, no warning. The docs say it logs an error; check in finish() yourself. finish() or onError(): which runs when? Exactly one runs, once, after the last round: onError() if an error was logged, otherwise finish(). A thrown exception skips both. Why can a symbol set aside by processor A crash processor B? The set-aside pile is shared: the symbol returns to B for every annotation it carries, and B may write the same file twice (FileAlreadyExistsException). What is javac's counterpart of KSP's finish()? The final round, in which RoundEnvironment.processingOver() returns true.

h: Rounds, generated code and deferral · Go deeper
x: Processors run in the order the services file lists them: swap two lines, and the order swaps in every round. KSP's docs make no promise about order, though, and across several jars it depends on the classpath, so write processors that don't care who runs first. In round 1, resolver.getNewFiles() returns the source files themselves, not an empty list. On an incremental build, a later lesson's subject, it returns only the files KSP decided to reprocess, and getSymbolsWithAnnotation likewise offers only symbols from those files. A processor that expects to see every annotated class in round 1 will be surprised on the second build. Files are parsed for the next round only if they are Kotlin or Java. A processor can also write other files, such as a text resource with createNewFile(..., extensionName = "txt"), and those don't start a new round's processing of their own content. Everything a processor writes in finish() is still compiled and packed, but no round reads it, so its annotations are never seen. getSymbolsWithAnnotation(name, inDepth = true) also finds annotated declarations nested inside function bodies, such as a local class, at a higher cost. The notes on what a round offers apply to it in the same way.

h: Incremental builds and processor options · Repacking one box: which files KSP reads again after an edit
x: A build turns your source files into a program you can run, and on a real project it runs dozens of times a day. Most of those runs follow a small edit. An incremental build redoes only the work that edit can affect and reuses the rest from the last run. Gradle does this one task at a time. A task's inputs are the files and settings it reads. Before running a task, Gradle compares them with the last run, and if nothing changed, it skips the task and marks it UP-TO-DATE. It compares contents, not dates: touch Lamp.kt changes the file's time, and the KSP task stays UP-TO-DATE. Touching a file fools nobody. KSP goes one level further, inside its own task. When a source file did change, KSP works out which files must be processed again. Those are the dirty files, and the processors see only them in round 1. Every output of a clean file comes back from a copy KSP keeps under build/kspCaches/. Let's watch it decide. The playground gives each lesson its own source set, a group of source folders that Gradle compiles together. Lesson 7's, labs/ksp/app/src/l07, holds the four MoveMate classes, one per file, each with @Inventory, plus MovingDay.kt, which prints the cards, and its Java twin. The lesson's processor writes two kinds of output: a card per class, as in lesson 2, and one master list of every class, which we'll meet in the next section. The Gradle property ksp.incremental.log makes KSP write what it decided into labs/ksp/app/build/kspCaches/l07/logs/. After a first build, we added one comment line to Lamp.kt and built again: ./gradlew :ksp:app:compileL07Kotlin -Pksp.incremental.log=true kspDirtySet.log then read like this (empty sections trimmed): Modified src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Lamp.kt Dirty: src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Bookshelf.kt src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Lamp.kt src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Plant.kt src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Box.kt Dirty / All: 66.67% One file was modified, and four were read again. MovingDay.kt and the Java file were not. That's the first thing to notice: KSP doesn't reprocess everything, and it doesn't reprocess only the edited file either. It follows the outputs back to their sources. The card is the easy half. Lamp's card was written with these Dependencies: Java // Closest Java equivalent: a javac processor writing one card per class JavaFileObject card = processingEnv.getFiler() .createSourceFile(pkg + "." + name + "InventoryCard", cls); // cls: the one element it came from // META-INF/gradle/incremental.annotation.processors: workbench.ksp.l07.CardProcessor,isolating Kotlin // lesson 2's card, written with KotlinPoet: it came from this class's own file, and nothing else inventoryCardFile(cls).writeTo(codeGenerator, Dependencies(aggregating = false, cls.containingFile!!)) Read the Kotlin line aloud: "this card came from this class's file, and from nothing else." KSP calls that an isolating output: it depends only on the source files you name. Java has had annotation processors, programs that javac runs while it compiles, since Java 6, and KSP is Kotlin's own way to do that job for Kotlin code, without going through Java. The Java side has the same idea one level up. Gradle sorts whole javac processors into categories, and an isolating one must give exactly one originating element, the element the file came from, for each file it writes. In the moving-house picture, Lamp.kt is the repacked box, and its card is the only card that must be redone because of it. The cards of the untouched boxes come back from storage. The picture breaks in one place: a real helper sees which box was repacked. KSP sees only what your Dependencies say, plus the types your processor looked up. It doesn't open boxes to check. So why were Box, Bookshelf and Plant read again for one bulb? Because of the master list. Edit one box and read what KSP read again From labs/, build lesson 7's source set once: ./gradlew :ksp:app:compileL07Kotlin -Pksp.incremental.log=true. Keep that flag on every command in this lesson. Gradle counts it as part of the task's setup, so a run without it makes the next run start over. Run touch ksp/app/src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Lamp.kt, then the same build. Predict the status of kspL07Kotlin before you look. Add a comment line at the end of Lamp.kt and build again. Open labs/ksp/app/build/kspCaches/l07/logs/kspDirtySet.log. Which files are under Dirty:, and which aren't? Run the program with the command below, or its Java twin. Then remove your comment. MovingDay.kt package workbench.ksp.app.l07 // Prints the master list and one card per thing, through code KSP generated in this build: // MovingDayList (aggregating) and the inventoryCard() functions (isolating). // ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l07.MovingDayKt // ./gradlew :ksp:app:compileL07Kotlin -Pksp.incremental.log=true then read build/kspCaches/l07/logs/ fun main() { val things = listOf( Box("books", "study", 12_000), Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null), Bookshelf(3, listOf("Dune", "Emma")), Plant("fern", 2.5), ) println("MovingDayList: ${MovingDayList.names}") for (thing in things) println(MovingDayList.cardFor(thing)) } ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l07.MovingDayKt -Pksp.incremental.log=true labs/ksp/app/src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/MovingDay.kt MovingDayJava.java package workbench.ksp.app.l07; import java.util.List; // The Java twin of MovingDay.kt: Java calling the master list KSP generated in Kotlin. MovingDayList is a Kotlin // object, so Java reaches it through its INSTANCE field; the names property is the getter getNames(). // ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l07.MovingDayJava public class MovingDayJava { public static void main(String[] args) { List<Object> things = List.of( new Box("books", "study", 12_000, false), new Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null), new Bookshelf(3, List.of("Dune", "Emma")), new Plant("fern", 2.5, 7)); System.out.println("MovingDayList: " + MovingDayList.INSTANCE.getNames()); for (Object thing : things) System.out.println(MovingDayList.INSTANCE.cardFor(thing)); } } ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l07.MovingDayJava -Pksp.incremental.log=true labs/ksp/app/src/l07/java/workbench/ksp/app/l07/MovingDayJava.java touch leaves kspL07Kotlin UP-TO-DATE: Gradle compares contents, not dates. After the comment, Modified lists only Lamp.kt, and Dirty: lists the four files with an @Inventory class (Dirty / All: 66.67% on our run), but not MovingDay.kt or MovingDayJava.java. The program prints MovingDayList: [Bookshelf, Box, Lamp, Plant] and one card per thing, such as Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null. Incremental processing (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Incremental builds and processor options · The master list: an aggregating output that every box feeds
x: The master list is one file, MovingDayList.kt, that names every @Inventory class and hands out the right card for any of them: public object MovingDayList { public val names: List<String> = listOf("Bookshelf", "Box", "Lamp", "Plant") public fun cardFor(thing: Any): String = when (thing) { is Bookshelf -> thing.inventoryCard() is Box -> thing.inventoryCard() is Lamp -> thing.inventoryCard() is Plant -> thing.inventoryCard() else -> error("MovingDayList has no card for ${thing::class.simpleName}") } } That's generated code, shown as KotlinPoet printed it. A list like this can't belong to one box. Change any class on it, and the list may change. Add a new class anywhere in the source set, and the list must change, though no file on the list was touched. KSP's docs call such an output aggregating: it "can be affected by changes in any source file". The opposite, isolating, depends "only on their specified sources". Here is how the processor says so, and what the Java side writes: Java // Closest Java equivalent: one file made from many classes JavaFileObject list = processingEnv.getFiler() .createSourceFile(pkg + ".MovingDayList", classes.toArray(new Element[0])); // Gradle can only mark the whole processor, in META-INF/gradle/incremental.annotation.processors: // workbench.ksp.l07.MasterListProcessor,aggregating Kotlin fun listDependencies(classes: List<KSClassDeclaration>): Dependencies = Dependencies(aggregating = true, *classes.mapNotNull { it.containingFile }.distinct().toTypedArray()) masterListFile(classes, listOptions).writeTo(codeGenerator, listDependencies(classes)) Read listDependencies aloud: "this list came from the file of every class on it, each file once, and new files can change it too." aggregating = true is the second half of that sentence. The two languages split the work differently. Gradle puts its category on a whole javac processor, and its isolating processors need exactly one originating element per file. KSP puts the category on each output, and an isolating output may name several files. If you build files with KotlinPoet, addOriginatingKSFile(file) on the top-level TypeSpec and writeTo(codeGenerator, aggregating = true) do the same job. KotlinPoet collects originating files only from top-level members, though, not from nested types. The second log, kspSourceToOutputs.log, shows what KSP recorded. Each annotated file maps to its card and to the list, and one more key stands alone: src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Lamp.kt: build/generated/ksp/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/LampInventoryCard.kt build/generated/ksp/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/MovingDayList.kt <AnyChanges is a virtual file; DO NOT USE.>: build/generated/ksp/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/MovingDayList.kt That virtual key is how "any change" reaches the list: every edit dirties it, and a dirty list makes every file it came from dirty. KSP's label, DO NOT USE, is fair, because you never name the key yourself; aggregating = true does it for you. That explains the 66.67%: one edit, the whole list, and with it all four of its boxes. Now add a fifth box. We created Rug.kt with @Inventory data class Rug(val size: String) and built again. The dirty set held all five annotated files (71.43%), and the program printed MovingDayList: [Bookshelf, Box, Lamp, Plant, Rug]. In the picture, the master list on the fridge is rewritten after any change to the house, from every box on it. The picture breaks here: a family would add one line for the rug. KSP rewrites the whole list, from scratch, from every file it came from. An output that lists many boxes depends on all of them, and on boxes not packed yet. Mark it aggregating. The price is visible in the log: every edit re-reads every box on the list. Still, MovingDay.kt stayed clean, and on a real project the cards of classes outside the list stay clean too. That's the right Dependencies. Let's see the wrong ones. Add a box and watch the list follow Create labs/ksp/app/src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Rug.kt with package workbench.ksp.app.l07, import workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory and @Inventory data class Rug(val size: String). Predict which files will be dirty, then build with ./gradlew :ksp:app:compileL07Kotlin -Pksp.incremental.log=true. Open kspDirtySet.log, then kspSourceToOutputs.log. Find Rug.kt's two outputs, and the line under <AnyChanges is a virtual file; DO NOT USE.>. Run ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l07.MovingDayKt -Pksp.incremental.log=true. Keep Rug.kt for the next Try-it. All five annotated files are dirty (Dirty / All: 71.43% on our run), and MovingDay.kt is not. Rug.kt maps to RugInventoryCard.kt and MovingDayList.kt, and the virtual key maps to MovingDayList.kt alone. The program prints MovingDayList: [Bookshelf, Box, Lamp, Plant, Rug], and its four cards as before, because MovingDay.kt doesn't make a rug. Each card comes from one file, an isolating output; the master list comes from every annotated file and from any change, an aggregating output, so one edit makes all four annotated files dirty. Incremental annotation processing (Gradle Java plugin docs) docs

h: Incremental builds and processor options · Wrong Dependencies on purpose: a list that shrinks, and a list that vanishes
x: Wrong Dependencies on purpose: the master list shrinks to one mirror, then vanishes, and only an incremental build shows it A wrong Dependencies doesn't fail the build. It fails a later build, after an ordinary edit, and only sometimes. So let's make the mistakes on purpose and watch. The lab's processor has a teaching switch that no real processor has: the option movemate.listDependencies in labs/ksp/app/src/l07/ksp.properties replaces your Dependencies for the list with one of three wrong ones. Java // Closest Java equivalent: what Gradle does with a javac processor's originating elements filer.createSourceFile(pkg + ".MovingDayList"); // isolating processor, no element: // Gradle recompiles every source file (slow, safe) filer.createSourceFile(pkg + ".MovingDayList", lamp); // isolating, one element: Gradle trusts it Kotlin // Naive: three Dependencies for the master list, each wrong in its own way Dependencies(false, *files) // isolating: right after an edit, wrong after a new box Dependencies(false) // no file at all: the list belongs to nobody Dependencies.ALL_FILES // safe, but every edit dirties every file The first one deserves a word of credit. Dependencies(false, *files) names every file the list came from, so an edit to an existing box still redoes it: a dirty list makes all its files dirty, whatever its category. Its flaw is the new box. We set the switch to isolating and built once. A changed option is a changed input, so that build ran KSP over every file (Dirty / All: 100.00%), and the list's AnyChanges key was gone. Then we added Mirror.kt with one more @Inventory class: Modified src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Mirror.kt Dirty: src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Mirror.kt Dirty / All: 12.50% A new file is tied to no output yet, so nothing marked the list as dirty. The processor saw one class and wrote a list of one, right over the old one. The build passed. Then the program ran: MovingDayList: [Mirror] Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalStateException: MovingDayList has no card for Box at workbench.ksp.app.l07.MovingDayList.cardFor(MovingDayList.kt:13) A move with one mirror in it. That's the warm-up's answer: only Mirror. The second one is lesson 2's promise, paid. With Dependencies(false) and no file, the list belongs to no box. We switched to none, built once, and added one comment to MovingDay.kt, a file with no annotation at all. Only MovingDay.kt was dirty (12.50%), the processor found no @Inventory class to list, and KSP filed the list under <This is a virtual key for removed outputs; DO NOT USE> and deleted it. The compiler had the last word: e: file:///.../labs/ksp/app/src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/MovingDay.kt:14:31 Unresolved reference 'MovingDayList'. The third one is the safe retreat. With Dependencies.ALL_FILES, one comment in Lamp.kt made every file dirty, MovingDay.kt and the Java file included: Dirty / All: 100.00%. KSP's own KDoc says it "essentially disables incremental processing". It's correct, and slow. Notice what all three have in common. A clean build, ./gradlew clean or --rerun on the KSP task, puts them right, because it reprocesses everything. The kctfork tests from lesson 2 pass too, because kctfork deletes its caches and runs a clean build every time. Only an incremental build shows the mistake. The Java side has one safety net here that KSP lacks: when an isolating javac processor gives no originating element, Gradle recompiles every source file, slowly but correctly. KSP believes you. A generated file that is right after a clean build and wrong after an edit has the wrong Dependencies. Fix them; don't make cleaning a habit. In the picture, these are helpers who didn't write down which boxes a card came from: the master list goes stale, or gets thrown out with the packing paper. The switch we flipped lives in a file of options, and options have a trap of their own. Break the master list, then mend it Add the line movemate.listDependencies=isolating to labs/ksp/app/src/l07/ksp.properties and build: ./gradlew :ksp:app:compileL07Kotlin -Pksp.incremental.log=true. The option changed, so kspDirtySet.log shows every file dirty. Create Mirror.kt like Rug.kt, with @Inventory data class Mirror(val widthCm: Int). Predict the list, then build with ./gradlew :ksp:app:compileL07Kotlin -Pksp.incremental.log=true and run the program. Change the switch to none and build once. Then add a comment to MovingDay.kt and build again. Which file does the compiler complain about? Mend it: delete the switch line, remove your comment, delete Rug.kt and Mirror.kt, build, and run the program once more. With isolating, only Mirror.kt is dirty (12.50% on our run), the build passes, and the program prints MovingDayList: [Mirror], then fails with IllegalStateException: MovingDayList has no card for Box. With none, only MovingDay.kt is dirty, kspSourceToOutputs.log files the list under the virtual key for removed outputs, and the compile fails with MovingDay.kt:14:31 Unresolved reference 'MovingDayList'. After the mending, the program prints the four names again. KSP README: Gradle properties such as ksp.incremental and ksp.incremental.log docs

h: Incremental builds and processor options · Processor options: the job sheet you hand the helper
x: The master list needs a name, and the processor can't guess it: one family calls it MovingDayList, another PackingList. A processor option is a key and a text value that the build passes to every processor. It's the job sheet the moving company hands the helper, with the address on it. In Gradle you write them in the module's build file: // build.gradle.kts of a Kotlin module that uses the processor ksp { arg("movemate.listName", "MovingDayList") arg("movemate.listPackage", "movemate.lists") } // the same options for a javac processor in a Java module tasks.withType<JavaCompile>().configureEach { options.compilerArgs.add("-Amovemate.listName=MovingDayList") } In this lab, each lesson's source set has its own job sheet instead, labs/ksp/app/src/l07/ksp.properties, with lines such as movemate.listName=MovingDayList. The processor gets every option as one Map<String, String>, environment.options, and reads two kinds: Java // Closest Java equivalent: a javac processor's options, passed as -Amovemate.listName=MovingDayList @SupportedOptions({"movemate.listName", "movemate.listPackage"}) public class MasterListProcessor extends AbstractProcessor { ListOptions readListOptions() { String listName = processingEnv.getOptions().get("movemate.listName"); if (listName == null) { processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, "MasterListProcessor needs the processor option movemate.listName, the name of the list it generates. " + "Add -Amovemate.listName=MovingDayList to the compiler arguments."); return null; } return new ListOptions(listName, processingEnv.getOptions().getOrDefault("movemate.listPackage", "movemate")); } } Kotlin fun readListOptions(options: Map<String, String>, logger: KSPLogger): ListOptions? { val listName = options[LIST_NAME] // "movemate.listName", null when missing if (listName == null) { logger.error( "MasterListProcessor needs the processor option $LIST_NAME, the name of the list it generates. " + "Add ksp { arg(\"$LIST_NAME\", \"MovingDayList\") } to the build file.", ) return null } if (!listName.matches(Regex("[A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*"))) { logger.error("$LIST_NAME must be a class name such as MovingDayList, but it is '$listName'") return null } return ListOptions(listName, options[LIST_PACKAGE] ?: "movemate") // optional, with a default } movemate.listPackage has a sensible default, so a missing value is fine. movemate.listName has none, so a missing value is an error. Lesson 5's rule holds: say what is wrong and how to fix it. An option isn't on any box, though, so there's no symbol to say where, and the words name the place instead: the build file. We deleted the line from ksp.properties and ran KSP: > Task :ksp:app:kspL07Kotlin FAILED e: [ksp] MasterListProcessor needs the processor option movemate.listName, the name of the list it generates. Add ksp { arg("movemate.listName", "MovingDayList") } to the build file. e: [ksp] MovingDay.kt:14: Unresolved reference 'MovingDayList'. The second line is a follow-on: the list was never written, so the code that uses it can't resolve. Fix the first line. The two sides differ in one more way. javac warns about an -A option that no processor declared in @SupportedOptions. KSP passes every option to every processor without a word. Now the trap. An option changes the output, so it must be one of the KSP task's inputs, or Gradle skips the task after you change it. In KSP 2.3.14, ksp { arg(key, value) } fills two settings of the KSP task. processorOptions is what the processors read, and it's marked @Internal, so Gradle doesn't compare it. apOptions is an @Input, and Gradle does. Change the value, and KSP runs again, over every file. This lab's ksp.properties fills the same two settings, and the build showed it: we changed movemate.listName to moving-day and ran kspL07Kotlin with no extra flag. It ran, and failed with movemate.listName must be a class name such as MovingDayList, but it is 'moving-day'. Not every way of passing an option is compared, though. A lambda CommandLineArgumentProvider, arg(CommandLineArgumentProvider { listOf("movemate.listName=$name") }), isn't: in the research behind this lesson, changing the lambda's value left the task UP-TO-DATE, with the old option. A provider class with an @get:Input property is compared. And a provider's values can't contain spaces: Processor arguments not in the format \S+=\S+. An option that changes the output must be a tracked input of the task. Check it by changing the value and watching the task run. In the picture, the job sheet goes to every helper the company sends to this house, and to no other house. The picture breaks a little: one sheet serves every processor in the module at once, so name your keys with a prefix, as movemate. does here. Run the list without its job sheet Run MasterListDemo. It compiles two classes in memory twice: once with movemate.listName, once with no options at all. In labs/ksp/app/src/l07/ksp.properties, change movemate.listName to moving-day. Predict whether ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL07Kotlin runs, then run it. Change it to PackingList, run the same task, and look in labs/ksp/app/build/generated/ksp/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/. Then put MovingDayList back. MasterListDemo.kt package workbench.ksp.l07.demo import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.KotlinCompilation import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.SourceFile import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.configureKsp import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.kspSourcesDir import java.io.File import java.io.OutputStream import workbench.ksp.l07.MasterListProcessorProvider // Runs the master list processor twice in memory: once with the job sheet (the processor options), once // without it. Uses the reference processor; add -Pmine=l07 for yours. // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l07.demo.MasterListDemoKt fun main() { val things = SourceFile.kotlin( "Things.kt", """ package movemate import workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory @Inventory data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?) @Inventory data class Plant(val kind: String, val potLitres: Double, val waterEveryDays: Int = 7) """, ) println("=== with ksp { arg(\"movemate.listName\", \"MovingDayList\") }") val withSheet = compile("with-options", things, mapOf("movemate.listName" to "MovingDayList")) println("exit code: ${withSheet.first.exitCode}") print(withSheet.second.resolve("movemate/MovingDayList.kt").readText()) val list = withSheet.first.classLoader.loadClass("movemate.MovingDayList") val instance = list.getField("INSTANCE").get(null) val lamp = withSheet.first.classLoader.loadClass("movemate.Lamp") .getConstructor(String::class.java, Int::class.java, String::class.java).newInstance("desk lamp", 1, null) println("--- MovingDayList.cardFor(lamp) returns: ${list.getMethod("cardFor", Any::class.java).invoke(instance, lamp)}") println() println("=== with no options at all") val without = compile("without-options", things, emptyMap()) println("exit code: ${without.first.exitCode}") without.first.messages.lines().filter { it.startsWith("e: ") }.forEach(::println) println("generated files: ${without.second.walk().filter { it.isFile }.map { it.name }.toList()}") } private fun compile(name: String, source: SourceFile, options: Map<String, String>) = KotlinCompilation().run { workingDir = File("build/kctfork/demo/l07-$name").apply { deleteRecursively() } sources = listOf(source) inheritClassPath = true jvmTarget = "21" messageOutputStream = OutputStream.nullOutputStream() configureKsp { symbolProcessorProviders += MasterListProcessorProvider() processorOptions += options } compile() to kspSourcesDir.resolve("kotlin") } ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l07.demo.MasterListDemoKt labs/ksp/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/ksp/l07/demo/MasterListDemo.kt The demo prints exit code: OK, the generated list for Lamp and Plant and Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null, then exit code: COMPILATION_ERROR, the needs the processor option movemate.listName error and generated files: []. In the app, the task runs, because the option is a tracked input, and fails with e: [ksp] movemate.listName must be a class name such as MovingDayList, but it is 'moving-day', plus follow-on errors for code that uses the list. With PackingList, it succeeds and writes PackingList.kt instead of MovingDayList.kt; putting the old name back may come FROM-CACHE. ProcessingEnvironment.getOptions (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Incremental builds and processor options · Java and Kotlin
x: One master list from many classes: a javac processor and a KSP processor MasterListProcessor.java // Closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor @SupportedAnnotationTypes("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory") @SupportedOptions({"movemate.listName", "movemate.listPackage"}) public class MasterListProcessor extends AbstractProcessor { private boolean written; @Override public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment roundEnv) { if (written || roundEnv.processingOver()) return false; String listName = processingEnv.getOptions().get("movemate.listName"); // the job sheet String pkg = processingEnv.getOptions().getOrDefault("movemate.listPackage", "movemate"); List<Element> classes = new ArrayList<>(roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Inventory.class)); if (listName == null || classes.isEmpty()) return false; try (Writer out = processingEnv.getFiler() .createSourceFile(pkg + "." + listName, classes.toArray(new Element[0])) // every origin .openWriter()) { out.write(listSource(pkg, listName, classes)); } catch (IOException e) { processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, e.toString()); } written = true; return false; } } // META-INF/gradle/incremental.annotation.processors: // workbench.ksp.l07.MasterListProcessor,aggregating MasterListProcessor.kt class MasterListProcessor( private val codeGenerator: CodeGenerator, private val logger: KSPLogger, private val options: Map<String, String>, ) : SymbolProcessor { override val apiFeatures = buildApiFeatures { enableBackingFields = true; enableContextParameters = true } private var listWritten = false override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { if (listWritten) return emptyList() val listOptions = readListOptions(options, logger) ?: return emptyList() // the job sheet val classes = resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory") .filterIsInstance<KSClassDeclaration>().toList() if (classes.isEmpty()) return emptyList() masterListFile(classes, listOptions) .writeTo(codeGenerator, Dependencies(aggregating = true, *classes.mapNotNull { it.containingFile } .distinct().toTypedArray())) // every origin listWritten = true return emptyList() } } Both write one file from many classes, once, and both name every class's source as an origin: javac through createSourceFile's originating elements, KSP through Dependencies. The difference is where the category lives. Gradle marks a whole javac processor isolating or aggregating, in a file inside the processor's jar, and falls back to a full recompile when an isolating processor gives no origin. KSP marks each output, so one processor can write isolating cards and an aggregating list, and it trusts what you declare: there's no fallback when it's wrong. Options travel the same way in both, as text keys (-A for javac, ksp { arg(...) } for KSP), but only javac warns about a key no processor declared.

h: Incremental builds and processor options · Worked example
x: A list that's right after a clean build and wrong after an edit: find the cause The report: a teammate added a class with the @Registered annotation, and the generated Registry lost every older entry. ./gradlew clean build fixed it, so the team now cleans before each release. That's the shape of a Dependencies bug: right on a clean build, wrong on an incremental one. Turn the logs on, add a throwaway annotated file, and build. Then read kspSourceToOutputs.log for the registry's file. Declared isolating, the index shrinks to the new file; with no file it can be deleted; ALL_FILES works but makes every edit reprocess everything. A team's generated file is right after ./gradlew clean and sometimes missing after an ordinary edit, with a green build. What do you suspect first? A KSP bug in the incremental caches The output's Dependencies: it was written without naming the file it came from The build cache restored an old copy The processor throws in round 2 An output that names no source file belongs to no box: when the processor doesn't write it again, KSP files it under removed outputs and deletes it.
