h: Incremental builds and processor options · Key terms
x: Incremental build A build that redoes only the work an edit can affect and reuses the rest from the last run. Task input A file or setting a Gradle task reads; when none changed, Gradle skips the task as UP-TO-DATE. Dirty file A source file KSP must hand to the processors again on this build. Isolating output A generated file that depends only on the source files it names, such as one card per class. Aggregating output A generated file that any source file can change, new files included, such as one list of every class. Dependencies What a processor tells KSP about each output: which files it came from, and whether it's aggregating. Processor option A key and a text value the build passes to every processor: ksp { arg(...) } for KSP, -A for javac. What does Dependencies(aggregating = false, file) tell KSP about an output? It depends only on that file: redo it when that file is dirty, restore it from the caches otherwise. When is an output aggregating? When a new file or a change in any file can change it, such as one list of every annotated class. Mark it aggregating = true. A master list is declared isolating, with every file named. You add a new annotated file. What does the next incremental build write? A list of one: only the new file is dirty, so the processor sees one class. The build stays green. What happens to an output written with Dependencies(false) and no file? It belongs to no source file. On a later incremental build where nothing writes it again, KSP files it under removed outputs and deletes it. What does Dependencies.ALL_FILES cost? Any change makes every file dirty, so incremental processing is effectively off. Safe, and slow. How do you see what KSP reprocessed, and where? Build with -Pksp.incremental.log=true, then read build/kspCaches/<source set>/logs/kspDirtySet.log and kspSourceToOutputs.log. Each build rewrites them. How does a processor read ksp { arg("k", "v") }, and what's the javac twin? environment.options["k"], which is null when missing. javac: processingEnv.getOptions().get("k"), passed as -Ak=v.

h: Incremental builds and processor options · Go deeper
x: Dependencies aren't the only thing KSP tracks. Every time a processor resolves a type, KSP records the lookup, and kspLookupGraph.log lists them. On lesson 7's first build it held lines such as src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Lamp.kt -> workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory and src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Lamp.kt -> workbench.ksp.app.l07.String. The second looks odd until you remember how Kotlin resolves a name: String in Lamp.kt could mean a class called String in Lamp's own package, so a new file in that package could change what the processor saw. KSP's docs call this resolution tracing: a file that resolved a type depends on the files that could change the answer. It's also why resolving types you don't need costs incremental builds, not just time. A few more switches and facts, from the KSP README and the research behind this lesson. ksp.incremental=false turns incremental processing off and deletes the caches. ksp.incremental.log.graph.origin=<a fully qualified name> writes a kspLookupGraphOrigin.dot graph for one symbol. A file that calls getSealedSubclasses() is dirty on every build, because any file could add a subclass. Since 2.3.14, when nothing at all is dirty, KSP restores the outputs and returns without creating any processor. Two traps come from Gradle rather than KSP. The labs turn on the build cache, and the KSP task is cacheable: undo an edit, and Gradle may restore the outputs FROM-CACHE without running KSP, so the logs describe an older run. Make a fresh edit, or add --no-build-cache. And processor jars are a classpath input: change the processor itself, and Gradle runs the KSP task again in full, which is why switching between -Pmine=l07 and the reference jar always starts with a 100% dirty set.

h: Testing a processor · A practice pack in an empty room: compiling a few lines in memory
x: A processor test needs four things. It needs a few lines of source code, and KSP to run the processor on them. It needs the Kotlin compiler, to compile the sources together with whatever was generated. And it needs a way to look at the results. A real Gradle build does all four, and takes seconds and a whole project per test. So processor tests run the compiler in memory instead, inside the test's own JVM. The library that does it here is kctfork, a community fork of Kotlin Compile Testing. It runs KSP2 and the Kotlin compiler on source code held in strings, in a fresh folder per compile, and hands back what happened. Its Maven group, the first part of the name a build uses to download it, is dev.zacsweers.kctfork, and its classes still live in the old package, com.tschuchort.compiletesting. Java has had annotation processors, programs that javac runs while it compiles, since Java 6, and KSP is Kotlin's own way to do that job for Kotlin code. Java's processors have a test library of the same kind, Google's compile-testing, and kctfork describes itself as "in the spirit of" it. Every test that calls kctfork by hand repeats the same dozen lines. A test harness is the reusable code around a test that does the setting up, the running and the collecting, so that each test states only what's special about it. This lesson's lab is one, ProcessorBench, and its tests use it on two processors from earlier lessons: Java // Closest Java equivalent: Google's compile-testing runs javac with your processor, in memory JavaFileObject lamp = JavaFileObjects.forSourceString("movemate.Lamp", """ package movemate; @Builder public class Lamp { ... } """); Compilation compilation = Compiler.javac() .withProcessors(new BuilderProcessor()) // passed directly: no services file .compile(lamp); Kotlin val bench = ProcessorBench(KctforkCompiler) // kctfork, plugged in from src/test val run = bench.run( Source( "Lamp.kt", """ package movemate import workbench.ksp.annotations.Builder @Builder data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?) """, ), processors = listOf(BuilderProcessorProvider()), // passed directly: no services file ) Both versions hand the processor over directly, so the services file from lesson 2 plays no part in a test. The bench does one quiet favour first: it trims each source's indent. Then line 1 is the package line, and a message's line number matches what you count in the test. The result carries what the four checks need. One part is a class loader, the JVM object that finds compiled classes and loads them into the running program. kctfork's class loader sees your source classes and the generated ones, and that's how a test can call LampBuilder although the test itself was compiled long before LampBuilder existed. You may wonder why the compiler is a parameter of the bench. The plain reason is the build: kctfork is on this project's test and demo class paths only, and the bench lives in src/main, so it can't create a kctfork compile itself. Instead the bench asks for the one thing it needs, any InMemoryCompiler, and the tests hand it one. Giving an object what it needs, instead of letting it build its own, is called dependency injection, and this is it in miniature; the capstone after this track builds it at full size. That split pays for itself: the bench's message parsing and golden files are tested with no compiler at all, in milliseconds. A compile costs more. The first one in a test JVM takes 4 to 7 seconds while the compiler loads, and later ones under a second. In the picture, this is the practice pack: a few boxes in an empty room, the same helper, and a look at the cards. The picture breaks in one useful place. kctfork tidies the room after every practice pack, deleting its caches, so it never sees a second build. A compile that ran tells you almost nothing yet, though. The checks do the work. Read what a test generated From labs/, run the reference bench's tests: ./gradlew :ksp:solutionTest --tests 'workbench.ksp.l08.*'. Open labs/ksp/build/kctfork/solutionTest/. Each compile left a folder named l08-<nnn>. Find the one whose ksp/sources/kotlin/movemate/ holds BookshelfBuilder.kt and read it. In the same folder, find sources/Bookshelf.kt. Its first line is package movemate: that's line 1 when you count lines in a message. Ten tests pass. The work folders keep every source the tests compiled and every file KSP generated, so BookshelfBuilder.kt is there with private var books: List<String>? = null and public fun boughtOn(boughtOn: LocalDate?): BookshelfBuilder. The folders are cleared at the start of the next test run. kctfork README (Kotlin Compile Testing fork) docs

h: Testing a processor · Four checks, weakest first: a builder bug that two of them miss
x: Four checks, weakest first: a dropped question mark that the exit code and a contains miss, and a golden file and a call catch Every processor test makes some of four checks. The exit code says how the compile ended: OK, COMPILATION_ERROR when a processor called logger.error or the code didn't compile, or INTERNAL_ERROR when a processor threw. The generated text is what the processor wrote. The messages are what it and the compiler printed. Last, calling the generated code runs it through the class loader. Which of them does a test really need? Let's plant a bug and find out. The lab's builder processor turns each parameter's type into KotlinPoet's TypeName through one function, and the demo passes it a broken one that drops the question mark: typeOf = { it.toTypeName().copy(nullable = false) }. For Lamp, that turns shade(shade: String?) into shade(shade: String). WeakTestsDemo runs that builder through the four checks, weakest first: check 1, the exit code is OK: passes (OK) check 2, the text contains LampBuilder: passes check 3, the golden file: FAILS at line 18 expected: public fun shade(shade: String?): LampBuilder = apply { this.shade = shade } actual: public fun shade(shade: String): LampBuilder = apply { this.shade = shade } check 4, call shade(null): FAILS with NullPointerException: Parameter specified as non-null is null: method movemate.LampBuilder.shade, parameter shade The first two checks pass, and they pass honestly: the broken builder compiles, and it does contain class LampBuilder. A test made of those two proves that the processor didn't crash. The bug would reach the first family whose lamp has no shade. The third check is a golden file: a stored copy of the output you expect, compared with the real output on every run, with a way to rewrite it on purpose. The bench's checkGolden writes a missing golden file and fails once, so a person reads the new text before it becomes the standard. It reports the first line that differs, counting from 1, and UPDATE_GOLDEN=true ./gradlew :ksp:test ... rewrites every file it checks. A golden file is a proofreader with no sense of proportion: it flags a moved space as loudly as a lost question mark. A KotlinPoet upgrade that changes how it formats code will fail every golden file you have, as KotlinPoet 2.4.0 did when it changed how annotation arrays are written. The fourth check calls shade(null) through the class loader and gets the generated code's own exception. That one checks behaviour, and formatting can't fool it. Here are the four checks in one test, for KSP and for javac: Java // Closest Java equivalent: the same checks with compile-testing and Truth Compilation compilation = javac().withProcessors(new BuilderProcessor()).compile(lamp); assertThat(compilation).succeededWithoutWarnings(); // 1 and 3 assertThat(compilation).generatedSourceFile("movemate.LampBuilder") // 2, against a stored file .hasSourceEquivalentTo(JavaFileObjects.forResource("golden/LampBuilder.java")); // 4: compile-testing's checks stop at the compile; call the generated builder // from a test in a module whose own build runs the processor Kotlin val run = bench.run(lamp, processors = listOf(BuilderProcessorProvider())) assertThat(run.exitCode).isEqualTo("OK") // 1. the exit code assertMatchesGolden(run.generated("movemate/LampBuilder.kt"), // 2. the text goldenDir.resolve("LampBuilder.kt.golden")) assertThat(run.messages).isEmpty() // 3. the messages val builder = run.newInstance("movemate.LampBuilder") // 4. call the code run.call(builder, "name", "desk lamp") run.call(builder, "bulbs", 1) run.call(builder, "shade", null) assertThat(run.call(builder, "build").toString()).isEqualTo("Lamp(name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null)") A test that only compiles proves the processor didn't crash. Call the code it wrote. Pair each golden file with at least one call into the generated code. The golden file catches any change; the call tells you whether the change matters. The two tests left are the unhappy ones, the inputs your processor must refuse. Plant a bug and see which checks notice Run WeakTestsDemo and read the four verdicts. Which two would a quick test have stopped at? In WeakTestsDemo.kt, change copy(nullable = false) to copy(), so the builder keeps its question marks. Predict the four verdicts, then run it again. Change it back. Once your bench passes the lab, run the demo with -Pmine=l08: it uses your checkGolden and your call. WeakTestsDemo.kt package workbench.ksp.l08.demo import com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessorProvider import com.squareup.kotlinpoet.ksp.toTypeName import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.KotlinCompilation import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.SourceFile import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.configureKsp import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.kspSourcesDir import java.io.File import java.io.OutputStream import workbench.ksp.l08.BuilderProcessor import workbench.ksp.l08.Compiled import workbench.ksp.l08.GoldenResult import workbench.ksp.l08.InMemoryCompiler import workbench.ksp.l08.ProcessorBench import workbench.ksp.l08.Source import workbench.ksp.l08.checkGolden // A builder processor with one planted bug: it drops the '?' from every parameter type, so shade(shade: String?) // comes out as shade(shade: String). Then the four checks, weakest first. Which ones notice? // Uses the reference bench; add -Pmine=l08 for yours. // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l08.demo.WeakTestsDemoKt fun main() { val buggy = SymbolProcessorProvider { env -> BuilderProcessor(env.codeGenerator, env.logger, typeOf = { it.toTypeName().copy(nullable = false) }) } val lamp = Source( "Lamp.kt", """ package movemate import workbench.ksp.annotations.Builder @Builder data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?) """, ) val run = ProcessorBench(DemoCompiler).run(lamp, processors = listOf(buggy)) val text = run.generated("movemate/LampBuilder.kt") println("check 1, the exit code is OK: ${verdict(run.exitCode == "OK")} (${run.exitCode})") println("check 2, the text contains LampBuilder: ${verdict("class LampBuilder" in text)}") val golden = File("src/test/resources/workbench/ksp/l08/golden/LampBuilder.kt.golden") when (val g = checkGolden(text, golden, update = false)) { is GoldenResult.Differs -> { println("check 3, the golden file: FAILS at line ${g.line}") println(" expected: ${g.expected.trim()}") println(" actual: ${g.actual.trim()}") } else -> println("check 3, the golden file: $g") } val builder = run.newInstance("movemate.LampBuilder") run.call(builder, "name", "desk lamp") run.call(builder, "bulbs", 1) try { run.call(builder, "shade", null) println("check 4, call shade(null): passes") } catch (e: NullPointerException) { println("check 4, call shade(null): FAILS with ${e.javaClass.simpleName}: ${e.message}") } } private fun verdict(ok: Boolean) = if (ok) "passes" else "FAILS " /** The demo's own copy of the bench's compiler (the tests' copy lives in src/test, which demos can't see). */ private object DemoCompiler : InMemoryCompiler { override fun compile(sources: List<Source>, processors: List<SymbolProcessorProvider>, options: Map<String, String>): Compiled { val compilation = KotlinCompilation().apply { workingDir = File("build/kctfork/demo/l08").apply { deleteRecursively() } this.sources = sources.map { SourceFile.kotlin(it.fileName, it.text, trimIndent = false) } inheritClassPath = true jvmTarget = "21" messageOutputStream = OutputStream.nullOutputStream() configureKsp { symbolProcessorProviders += processors processorOptions += options } } val result = compilation.compile() return Compiled(result.exitCode.name, result.messages, compilation.kspSourcesDir.resolve("kotlin"), result.classLoader) } } ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l08.demo.WeakTestsDemoKt check 4 fails with NullPointerException: Parameter specified as non-null is null: method movemate.LampBuilder.shade, parameter shade. With copy(), checks 1, 2 and 4 pass, and check 3 prints Matches. The bench: source strings in, a compile in memory, and four checks on what came out. Gradle TestKit (Gradle docs) docs

h: Testing a processor · Errors by file and line: pinning down what the processor refuses
x: Lesson 5 taught the builder to refuse bad input with an error on the exact box. A test of that has three things to pin down: the compile failed, the message says the right thing, and it points at the right file and line. The last part is the one people skip, and it's the one users feel. Here is what kctfork printed for @Builder interface Shape, with the interface on line 6: e: Error occurred in KSP, check log for detail e: [ksp] /…/sources/Shape.kt:6: @Builder goes on a class, but Shape is an interface And here is the Kotlin compiler on a user's file that passes an Int to shade: e: file:///…/sources/Use.kt:5:16 Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'String?' was expected. Three shapes of message, then. KSP's own has [ksp], an absolute path, a line and no column. The compiler's has file://, a line and a column. And a line with no location at all, like kctfork's summary Error occurred in KSP. The paths point into a temporary folder that changes with every run, so a test must never compare them. The bench's parseMessage splits each line into a Message: the severity, the file name only, the line and the text. It skips lines that aren't messages, such as a stack trace. Then a test can say exactly what it means: Java // Closest Java equivalent: compile-testing finds an error by its text, file and line assertThat(compilation).failed(); assertThat(compilation).hadErrorContaining("@Builder goes on a class, but Shape is an interface") .inFile(bad) .onLine(6); Kotlin assertThat(run.exitCode).isEqualTo("COMPILATION_ERROR") assertThat(run.errors).contains( Message('e', "Bad.kt", 6, "@Builder goes on a class, but Shape is an interface"), Message('e', "Bad.kt", 9, "@Builder goes on a class, but Van is an object"), Message('e', "Bad.kt", 12, "SafeBuilder can't call Safe's private constructor. Make the constructor public or internal."), ) That Kotlin test compiles one file with three bad classes and expects three errors in one build, each on its own line. The lines are 6, 9 and 12, the lines of interface Shape, object Van and class Safe, not the lines of their @Builder notes. KSP reports a declaration's own line, and so does javac, which is why compile-testing's onLine(6) finds the same line. Count from the package line, which is line 1 because the bench trimmed the indent. An error test checks the text and the line. A message on the wrong line is a bug the user feels. In the picture, the helper's note must say which box, not "somewhere in the hall". The same note in a real build points at your real file. The practice room, though, can't show everything about moving day. Read the same error in a real build Run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL08Kotlin and open labs/ksp/app/build/generated/ksp/l08/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l08/LampBuilder.kt. Compare it with labs/ksp/src/test/resources/workbench/ksp/l08/golden/LampBuilder.kt.golden: only the package differs. Run the program below, or its Java twin. Create labs/ksp/app/src/l08/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l08/Shape.kt with the package line, import workbench.ksp.annotations.Builder, a blank line, @Builder and interface Shape, so the interface is on line 6. h: Testing a processor · What a practice pack can't show: the real build, TestKit and debugging
x: An in-memory test is fast because it skips the build, and so it can't see anything that lives in the build. Lesson 7's bugs are the clearest case. kctfork deletes its caches and runs a clean pass on every compile, so a wrong Dependencies passes every kctfork test you can write. The services file is another: tests hand the provider over directly, so a missing services file passes them all, and the real build then fails with e: [ksp] No providers found in processor classpath. Options come through the real build too, and lesson 7 showed that a new value reaches the processor only when it's a tracked input of the task. And a multiplatform project's per-target KSP tasks exist only in Gradle. For those, there's Gradle TestKit: Gradle's own library for running a real build from a test. In the Gradle docs' words, "builds run in a separate process from your tests". A TestKit test writes a tiny project to a folder, runs Gradle on it, and checks the tasks and the files: Java // A TestKit test, sketched (this lab has no TestKit dependency) BuildResult result = GradleRunner.create() .withProjectDir(projectDir) // a tiny build the test writes on disk .withArguments("compileKotlin", "-Pksp.incremental.log=true") .build(); assertEquals(TaskOutcome.SUCCESS, result.task(":kspKotlin").getOutcome()); Kotlin // A TestKit test, sketched (this lab has no TestKit dependency) val result = GradleRunner.create() .withProjectDir(projectDir) // a tiny build the test writes on disk .withArguments("compileKotlin", "-Pksp.incremental.log=true") .build() assertThat(result.task(":kspKotlin")?.outcome).isEqualTo(TaskOutcome.SUCCESS) Each such test costs a Gradle daemon and a real KSP run: seconds, where kctfork costs a fraction of one. So a library keeps a handful of them, for the services file, one edit-and-rebuild for each aggregating output, and the options. This course's lab has no TestKit dependency. The playground in labs/ksp/app plays that part by hand, as lesson 7's Try-its did. When a test fails and you don't know why, debug in this order. First, read the generated file: the kctfork work folder keeps it, under ksp/sources/kotlin/, and most surprises are visible there. Second, add a temporary logger.warn("..."): a warning shows at Gradle's default log level, and logger.info only with --info. Third, a debugger. A kctfork test is an ordinary JUnit test, so debug it like one. In a real build, KSP2 runs inside the Gradle daemon, so KSP's docs suggest starting Gradle with -Dorg.gradle.debug=true and attaching to it. Test a processor's logic in memory, and its wiring in a real build. In the picture, the practice pack checks the helper's cards; only moving day checks that the van turns up. Together they cover the move. Check the wiring that tests skip Build lesson 8's processor jar: ./gradlew :ksp:l08SolutionJar. List it with unzip -l ksp/build/processors/ksp-l08-solution.jar and print its services file with unzip -p ksp/build/processors/ksp-l08-solution.jar META-INF/services/com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessorProvider. Run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL08Kotlin --rerun --info and look for the lines that start with i: [ksp]. The jar holds the lesson's classes and META-INF/services/com.google.devtools.ksp.processing.SymbolProcessorProvider, with two lines: workbench.ksp.l08.InventoryProcessorProvider and workbench.ksp.l08.BuilderProcessorProvider. With --info, KSP prints i: [ksp] loaded provider(s): [workbench.ksp.l08.InventoryProcessorProvider, workbench.ksp.l08.BuilderProcessorProvider]. None of this exists in a kctfork test. h: Testing a processor · Java and Kotlin
x: One error test: compile-testing for a javac processor, the bench for a KSP processor BuilderProcessorTest.java // Closest Java equivalent: Google's compile-testing with Truth import static com.google.testing.compile.CompilationSubject.assertThat; import static com.google.testing.compile.Compiler.javac; class BuilderProcessorTest { @Test void reportsAnInterfaceOnItsOwnLine() { JavaFileObject bad = JavaFileObjects.forSourceString("movemate.Shape", """ package movemate; import movemate.annotations.Builder; @Builder interface Shape {} """); Compilation compilation = javac().withProcessors(new BuilderProcessor()).compile(bad); assertThat(compilation).failed(); // 1. the outcome assertThat(compilation) .hadErrorContaining("@Builder goes on a class, but Shape is an interface") // 3. the text .inFile(bad) .onLine(6); // and the line // 2 and 4: generatedSourceFile(...) for the text; calling the code is not among its checks } } BuilderProcessorTest.kt class BuilderProcessorTest { private val bench = ProcessorBench(KctforkCompiler) @Test fun `reports an interface on its own line`() { val run = bench.run( Source( "Shape.kt", """ package movemate import workbench.ksp.annotations.Builder @Builder interface Shape """, ), processors = listOf(BuilderProcessorProvider()), ) assertThat(run.exitCode).isEqualTo("COMPILATION_ERROR") // 1. the outcome assertThat(run.errors) // 3. text and line .contains(Message('e', "Shape.kt", 6, "@Builder goes on a class, but Shape is an interface")) assertThat(run.generated).isEmpty() // 2. nothing written } } The two tests have the same shape: source in a string, the processor passed directly, then the outcome, the text and the line. compile-testing came first and kctfork follows its spirit. The differences are in the details. compile-testing works through Truth subjects (failed(), hadErrorContaining(...).inFile(...).onLine(...)), while the bench parses messages into plain Message values that any assertion library can compare. Both report the declaration's line, 6 here, not the annotation's. And the kctfork result carries a class loader, so a Kotlin test can call the generated code in the same test, the fourth check; compile-testing's documented checks stop at the compile.

h: Testing a processor · Worked example
x: Turn a bug report into a test that fails first The report: "The builder breaks for my class with a private constructor: the build fails, but the message points at line 1." Before touching the processor, reproduce it on the bench, with the class on a line you can count. val safe = Source( "Safe.kt", """ package movemate import workbench.ksp.annotations.Builder @Builder class Safe private constructor(val code: String) """, ) val run = bench.run(safe, processors = listOf(BuilderProcessorProvider())) JavaFileObject safe = JavaFileObjects.forSourceString("movemate.Safe", """ package movemate; import movemate.annotations.Builder; @Builder public class Safe { private Safe(String code) {} } """); Compilation compilation = javac().withProcessors(new BuilderProcessor()).compile(safe); Write the assertion the user wanted: the error, its text, and line 6, the line of class Safe. Run it and watch it fail with the processor as it is. A test that has never failed hasn't proved anything yet. assertThat(run.exitCode).isEqualTo("COMPILATION_ERROR") assertThat(run.errors).contains( Message('e', "Safe.kt", 6, "SafeBuilder can't call Safe's private constructor. Make the constructor public or internal."), ) assertThat(compilation).failed(); assertThat(compilation) .hadErrorContaining("SafeBuilder can't call Safe's private constructor") .inFile(safe) .onLine(6); Fix the processor: the error must be logged on the class symbol, logger.error(message, symbol), not without a node and not on a file. The javac twin passes the element to printMessage. if (constructor.isPrivate()) { logger.error("${name}Builder can't call $name's private constructor. Make the constructor public or internal.", symbol) return null } if (constructor.getModifiers().contains(Modifier.PRIVATE)) { messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, name + "Builder can't call " + name + "'s private constructor. Make the constructor public or internal.", type); return; } Run the test until it passes, and keep it. The bug can't come back without a red test, and the next reader of the suite learns what a private constructor should produce, on which line.

You won't change them; you'll test them. Read ProcessorBench.kt. Given: Source, the InMemoryCompiler interface, Compiled, Message, newInstance, the three Regex values and GoldenResult. Five functions are yours. Then read KctforkCompiler.kt in src/test: the compiler the tests plug in. Run the tests: all ten fail with NotImplementedError. This lab is the fifth move, Prove. Each check you build proves one of the other four moves: the messages prove Check, the generated text proves Read and Write, a call into the code proves Write from end to end, and the exit code proves the processor finished. Write run (trim each source, compile, wrap) and generated (walk the folder; paths with /). Then parseMessage: try the three Regex values in order, and keep only the file name of a path. Write call, modelled on newInstance: find the method by name and parameter count. A String target is a class name: call a static method with no receiver, or a Kotlin object's method on its INSTANCE field. Then compare it with the drill's answer. Source.copy(text = text.trimIndent()) keeps the file name. The Compiled from the compiler goes straight into BenchRun(...). compiled.generatedDir.walk().filter { it.isFile }, then relativeTo(generatedDir).invariantSeparatorsPath gives movemate/LampBuilder.kt on every system. Regex.matchEntire(line)?.destructured gives the groups. In the KSP pattern the location group is optional, so an empty path means no file and no line. Modifier.isStatic(method.modifiers) tells a top-level function from an object's method. Wrap the call in unwrapped { ... }, so a test sees the generated code's own exception. String.lines() keeps a last empty line after a final newline, so a missing last line compares "line two" with "". getOrNull handles files of different lengths. h: Testing a processor · Quiz
x: A builder test checks exitCode == OK and that the generated text contains fun build(). Which bug can it catch? A builder whose shade setter takes String instead of String? A processor that throws while it reads the class A builder that sets the wrong property in build() A missing services file A processor that throws ends the compile with INTERNAL_ERROR, so the exit-code check fails. The wrong nullability and the wrong property both compile and contain fun build(): only a golden file or a call into the code catches them. Tests pass the provider directly, so no in-memory test sees the services file. After a KotlinPoet upgrade, every golden-file test fails. Each diff is one moved line break, and all the call-the-code tests pass. What do you do? Delete the golden files: they are too brittle to keep Pin KotlinPoet to the old version for good Read the diffs, confirm only formatting changed, and rewrite the files with UPDATE_GOLDEN=true Change the processor until the old text comes back Golden files fail on any change, which is their job; the behavioural tests tell you whether it matters. Here nothing a user would notice changed, so review the diff once and accept it on purpose. Deleting them throws away the check that caught the lost question mark. In a kctfork test, @Builder is on line 5 and interface Shape on line 6, counted from the package line. The processor logs logger.error(message, symbol). Which line does the message carry? 5, the line of the annotation 6, the line of the declaration 1, the start of the file No line: kctfork removes locations KSP reports a declaration's own line, and javac does the same, which is why compile-testing's onLine(6) would match. kctfork keeps the location; only the folder is temporary, so a test compares the file name and line, not the path. Yes, with kspIncremental = true and two compiles Yes, if the test compiles the new file in a second SourceFile No: every kctfork compile deletes its caches and runs a clean build, which writes a correct list No, because kctfork ignores Dependencies, though a second compile would show it kctfork wipes its KSP caches and outputs on every compile and passes no changed-file sets, so each compile is a clean build, and a clean build lists every class. A test calls a generated builder's shade(null) through reflection, and the parameter is non-null. Without the bench's unwrapping, what does the test see? h: Testing a processor · Explain it back
x: A teammate's processor tests all look like this: compile a class, assert the exit code is OK, assert the output contains the class name. They say the processor is well tested. Explain what those tests prove, what they miss, and what you would add.

h: Testing a processor · Key terms
x: Test harness Reusable code around tests that sets up, runs and collects, so each test states only what's special about it. kctfork A library that runs KSP2 and the Kotlin compiler inside a test, on source code held in strings. compile-testing Google's library that runs javac with your annotation processors inside a test, and checks the result. Class loader The JVM object that finds compiled classes and loads them into the running program. Golden file A stored copy of the expected output, compared with the real output on every test run. Exit code How a compile ended: OK, a compilation error, or an internal error from a processor that threw. Gradle TestKit Gradle's library for running a real build from a test, in a separate process. What does kctfork do in a processor test? It runs KSP2 and the Kotlin compiler in the test's JVM on source code in strings, and returns the exit code, the messages, the generated files and a class loader. What are the four checks a processor test makes? The exit code, the generated text (often a golden file), the messages by file and line, and a call into the generated code. What do COMPILATION_ERROR and INTERNAL_ERROR mean in a kctfork result? COMPILATION_ERROR: a processor called logger.error, or the code didn't compile. INTERNAL_ERROR: a processor threw. What is a golden file? A stored copy of the expected output, compared with the real output on every run, with a way to rewrite it on purpose after you've read the diff. Why must a test call the generated code and not only read it? Code can compile and look right and still be wrong: a builder that lost a ? compiles, and only shade(null) shows the bug. What can't an in-memory processor test see? Anything in the build: incremental behaviour and wrong Dependencies, the services file, how options are wired, multiplatform tasks. Use a real build or Gradle TestKit. What's the javac twin of asserting an error's line in kctfork? compile-testing: assertThat(compilation).hadErrorContaining("...").inFile(file).onLine(6).

h: Testing a processor · Go deeper
x: The bench splits the compiler from the checks, and the same idea works inside a processor. Split it in two: one half turns KS symbols into a plain data model (the class name, the parameters and their types), the other turns that model into a FileSpec. The second half can then be tested with fileSpec.toString() and no compiler at all, in milliseconds, and the compile tests shrink to a few that check the wiring. A few kctfork details are worth knowing before you read older blog posts. Since version 0.10.0 it supports KSP2 only, and configureKsp(useKsp2 = true) no longer compiles: write configureKsp { symbolProcessorProviders += ... }. Setting providers before KSP is configured throws IllegalStateException: KSP not configured, which is exactly what the README's snippet does. kspWithCompilation does nothing on KSP2. kctfork compiles with its own Kotlin compiler, 2.4.20 in version 0.14.0, while this course builds with 2.4.21, and it was built against KSP 2.3.12, which is why the lab's build pins every KSP artifact to 2.3.14. Without that pin, any source with a property fails with a NoSuchMethodError. On the Java side, compile-testing's documented examples live in its package-info.java, and its checks cover the outcome (succeeded(), failed()), the messages (hadErrorContaining(...).inFile(...).onLine(...), also atColumn and onLineContaining) and the generated files (generatedSourceFile(...), hasSourceEquivalentTo(...)). It passes processors to javac directly, so JDK 23's change, which stopped javac from running processors it merely finds on the class path, doesn't affect it.

h: Choosing the tool: KSP, reflection, kapt or a compiler plugin · Reflection or generated cards: what the numbers say
x: Reflection is a program inspecting its own classes while it runs: finding a class's fields, reading their values, calling methods by name. Lesson 1 wrote MoveMate's card that way, and lesson 7 generated the same card during the build. Lesson 9's playground puts the two side by side, plus a third version that gives reflection its best shot by looking up each class's fields once and keeping them. Here is the plain reflection card: Java static String reflectionCard(Object thing) throws IllegalAccessException { Class<?> type = thing.getClass(); if (!type.isAnnotationPresent(Inventory.class)) throw new IllegalArgumentException(type.getSimpleName() + " has no @Inventory"); StringJoiner pairs = new StringJoiner(", "); for (Field field : type.getDeclaredFields()) { if (Modifier.isStatic(field.getModifiers()) || field.isSynthetic()) continue; field.setAccessible(true); // open the box pairs.add(field.getName() + "=" + field.get(thing)); } return type.getSimpleName() + ": " + pairs; } Kotlin fun reflectionCard(thing: Any): String { val type = thing.javaClass require(type.isAnnotationPresent(Inventory::class.java)) { "${type.simpleName} has no @Inventory" } val fields = type.declaredFields.filter { !Modifier.isStatic(it.modifiers) && !it.isSynthetic } return type.simpleName + ": " + fields.joinToString(", ") { field -> field.isAccessible = true // open the box "${field.name}=${field.get(thing)}" } } The generated card is what lesson 7's processor wrote: MovingDayList.cardFor(thing), a when with one branch per class and a string template per card. The program CardTiming checks correctness first, then measures. It times the first call of each way in a fresh JVM, with the classes the JVM loaded for it, then a million calls of each after a warm-up. On our machine, four cores busy with other builds, it printed: first call, generated: 34.55 ms, 116 classes loaded -> Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null first call, reflection: 25.45 ms, 114 classes loaded -> Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null all three ways agree on all 4 cards: true generated 119 / 38 / 47 ns per card reflection 313 / 273 / 267 ns per card cached 197 / 192 / 178 ns per card And with the first calls the other way round, -Pargs=reflection-first: first call, reflection: 33.17 ms, 136 classes loaded -> Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null first call, generated: 23.46 ms, 95 classes loaded -> Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null The first calls surprised me. I expected reflection to pay a lot at its first call. It pays a little: in the same position, about 20 more classes and a few more milliseconds. Both ways pay 20 to 35 ms and about a hundred classes for their first card, whichever goes first. The class log says what most of them are: java.lang.invoke classes, the machinery the JVM uses to link a string template the first time it runs. The way that goes second still loads about a hundred, so each new kind of template seems to pay for its own. With four small classes, the first call can't tell the two ways apart. The Part 4 capstone showed where start-up does tell. Its container wired a program's objects by reflection, and it loaded more than twice as many classes as the same wiring written out as plain code. The warm numbers are steady across runs. A generated card costs about 45 ns; reflection's best shot about 190 ns, four times as much; plain reflection about 280 ns, six times. Lesson 1 saw the same gap between its hand-written card and reflection. Either way, it's a fifth of a microsecond. Nobody at the new house waits for that, unless the program prints a million cards. So reflection is fine for work that runs a few times, on a few classes: a debug screen, a test helper, a small tool reading settings once at start. It also reaches what a processor can't: classes that arrive while the program runs. Generated code wins when the work repeats, and it brings two things the stopwatch doesn't show. A mistake stops the build with a file and line, as in lesson 5, instead of failing on moving day. And programs compiled ahead of time into a single executable need extra setup for every class they reach by reflection, and none for plain code. Reflection that runs a few times on a few classes is fine. Generate code when the work repeats, or when a mistake should stop the build. In the picture, reflection is unpacking a box at the new house to see what's inside. The picture breaks on the size of the cost: unpacking takes an afternoon, and reflection a fifth of a microsecond. Speed, though, was never the only question. Some jobs aren't cards at all. Time the cards, both ways round From labs/, run CardTiming with the command below. Before you look, write down which first call you expect to be slower. Run it again with -Pargs=reflection-first. Which numbers moved with the order, and which stayed with the way? Run the Java twin, CardTimingJava, once. It calls the cards KSP generated in Kotlin, through MovingDayList.INSTANCE. CardTiming.kt package workbench.ksp.app.l09 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory // Generated cards (lesson 7's MovingDayList.cardFor, written by KSP in this build) against reflection. // The first call of each way, in this order, then many calls. Run it twice, the second time with the order // swapped, and see which cost moves with the order: // ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l09.CardTimingKt // ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l09.CardTimingKt -Pargs=reflection-first fun main(args: Array<String>) { val ways: Map<String, (Any) -> String> = linkedMapOf( "generated" to MovingDayList::cardFor, "reflection" to ::reflectionCard, "cached" to CachedReflectionCards::card, ) val things = movingDayThings() val lamp = things[1] // 1. the first call of each way: time, and the classes the JVM loaded for it val order = if (args.firstOrNull() == "reflection-first") listOf("reflection", "generated") else listOf("generated", "reflection") val classes = ManagementFactory.getClassLoadingMXBean() for (name in order) { val loadedBefore = classes.totalLoadedClassCount val start = System.nanoTime() val card = ways.getValue(name)(lamp) val ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1e6 println("first call, %-10s %6.2f ms, %3d classes loaded -> %s".format(name + ":", ms, classes.totalLoadedClassCount - loadedBefore, card)) } // 2. correctness before speed: every way writes the same four cards val agree = things.all { thing -> ways.values.map { it(thing) }.distinct().size == 1 } println("all three ways agree on all ${things.size} cards: $agree") // 3. many calls, after a warm-up: nanoseconds per card, three rounds each val calls = 1_000_000 for ((name, f) in ways) { repeat(200_000) { f(things[it % 4]) } val rounds = (1..3).map { var length = 0L val t0 = System.nanoTime() for (i in 0 until calls) length += f(things[i % 4]).length check(length > 0) (System.nanoTime() - t0).toDouble() / calls } println("%-12s %s ns per card".format(name, rounds.joinToString(" / ") { "%.0f".format(it) })) } } ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l09.CardTimingKt labs/ksp/app/src/l09/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l09/CardTiming.kt CardTimingJava.java package workbench.ksp.app.l09; import java.lang.management.ClassLoadingMXBean; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.function.Function; // The Java twin of CardTiming.kt: Java code calling the cards KSP generated in Kotlin. They compiled to ordinary // classes, so Java sees MovingDayList as a class with an INSTANCE field, and the reflection cards as static methods. // ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l09.CardTimingJava // ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l09.CardTimingJava -Pargs=reflection-first public class CardTimingJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Map<String, Function<Object, String>> ways = new LinkedHashMap<>(); ways.put("generated", MovingDayList.INSTANCE::cardFor); ways.put("reflection", ReflectionCardsKt::reflectionCard); ways.put("cached", CachedReflectionCards.INSTANCE::card); List<Object> things = MoveMateKt.movingDayThings(); Object lamp = things.get(1); List<String> order = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("reflection-first") ? List.of("reflection", "generated") : List.of("generated", "reflection"); ClassLoadingMXBean classes = ManagementFactory.getClassLoadingMXBean(); for (String name : order) { long loadedBefore = classes.getTotalLoadedClassCount(); long start = System.nanoTime(); String card = ways.get(name).apply(lamp); double ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1e6; System.out.printf("first call, %-10s %6.2f ms, %3d classes loaded -> %s%n", name + ":", ms, classes.getTotalLoadedClassCount() - loadedBefore, card); } boolean agree = things.stream().allMatch(t -> ways.values().stream().map(f -> f.apply(t)).distinct().count() == 1); System.out.println("all three ways agree on all " + things.size() + " cards: " + agree); int calls = 1_000_000; for (var entry : ways.entrySet()) { Function<Object, String> f = entry.getValue(); for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) f.apply(things.get(i % 4)); StringBuilder rounds = new StringBuilder(); for (int r = 0; r < 3; r++) { long length = 0; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < calls; i++) length += f.apply(things.get(i % 4)).length(); if (length == 0) throw new IllegalStateException(); rounds.append(r == 0 ? "" : " / ").append(String.format("%.0f", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / (double) calls)); } System.out.printf("%-12s %s ns per card%n", entry.getKey(), rounds); } } } ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l09.CardTimingJava labs/ksp/app/src/l09/java/workbench/ksp/app/l09/CardTimingJava.java Every run prints all three ways agree on all 4 cards: true. The first calls cost tens of milliseconds and about a hundred classes each; reflection loads about 20 more than the generated card in the same position (on our run, 136 against 116 when first, 114 against 95 when second). After warm-up, the generated card takes roughly 40 to 70 ns, the cached reflection card roughly 160 to 250 ns, and plain reflection roughly 220 to 400 ns. Your numbers will differ, and the ratios should not move much. KSP overview (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Choosing the tool: KSP, reflection, kapt or a compiler plugin · Jobs a helper can't do: when the class itself must change
Choosing the tool: KSP, reflection, kapt or a compiler plugin · When the only helper reads Java: kapt, and moving a library to KSP
x:
Java has had annotation processors, programs that javac runs while it compiles, since Java 6, and the Java world has written many of them. KSP is Kotlin's own way to do that job for Kotlin code. Between the two sits kapt, Kotlin's bridge to Java's processors. The docs say it "generates stub files from Kotlin source code and then runs the Java annotation processors on those stubs". A stub is a Java copy of a Kotlin class's declarations with the bodies emptied out: methods return null; or return 0;, nullability turned into @NotNull annotations, default values gone. In the picture, kapt is the older helper who reads only Java, so every label in the room is first copied out in Java for that helper. That copying is the slowness. The picture breaks in one place: a person copying labels would keep every word, and stubs lose some, such as default values. The migration guide calls it "expensive" and says it "significantly increases build time". Android's guide adds a detail that matters when you migrate one library at a time: "If a module has any kapt processors remaining, stubs are still generated in that module." The often-quoted "up to 2x faster" comes from the KSP alpha announcement in 2021, where "initial benchmarks with the Room library show that KSP is approximately 2x faster than KAPT". It's one benchmark, from KSP1 days, not a law. kapt is still the answer for a processor that exists only for Java. Android's Data Binding is one: "KSP support for Data Binding is not planned". When a library ships both, moving to KSP is mostly a change to the build file. The migration guide says: "For most libraries, this replacement is enough": // build.gradle.kts, before: kapt runs a javac processor on Java stubs of your Kotlin classes plugins { kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.21" kotlin("kapt") version "2.4.21" } dependencies { kapt("com.squareup.moshi:moshi-kotlin-codegen:1.15.2") } kapt { arguments { arg("movemate.household", "Okafor") } } // after: KSP reads the Kotlin declarations directly plugins { kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.21" id("com.google.devtools.ksp") version "2.3.14" } dependencies { ksp("com.squareup.moshi:moshi-kotlin-codegen:1.15.2") // the same artifact serves kapt and KSP } ksp { arg("movemate.household", "Okafor") } KSP and kapt can run side by side, so a project can move one library at a time. Many libraries ship both processors in one jar: Moshi's codegen jar holds a javac services file, a KSP services file and the Gradle incremental descriptor. When the library is your own, migrating means porting the processor, and this lesson's lab does exactly that. The Java team's JavacPackingSlipProcessor writes META-INF/movemate/packing-slip.txt, one line per @Inventory class with its room and its fields. You port it to KSP, move by move, until the two outputs match byte for byte. Each javac line has a KSP line: Java // Closest Java equivalent: the given javac processor, Find and Write for (Element element : roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Inventory.class)) { ... } var slip = processingEnv.getFiler().createResource(StandardLocation.CLASS_OUTPUT, "", "META-INF/movemate/packing-slip.txt", classes.toArray(new Element[0])); try (Writer out = slip.openWriter()) { out.write(text); } Kotlin // The KSP port, Find and Write (the Write is given in the lab) val found = resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation(Inventory::class.qualifiedName!!).toList() codeGenerator.createNewFile(slipDependencies(classes), "META-INF/movemate", "packing-slip", "txt") .use { it.write(text.toByteArray()) } The rest of the mapping is the same kind of swap. element.getKind() != ElementKind.CLASS becomes classKind != ClassKind.CLASS, and messager.printMessage(ERROR, text, element) becomes logger.error(text, symbol). Fields in source order become the primary constructor's properties. type.getAnnotation(Room.class) becomes a KSAnnotation and its arguments, and getOptions() becomes environment.options. Two javac ideas have no twin. Claiming an annotation by returning true doesn't exist in KSP, where every processor sees every symbol. And Gradle's aggregating category for the whole processor becomes Dependencies(aggregating = true, ...) on the one output, as in lesson 7. Use KSP for every processor that has a KSP version, and keep kapt only for the ones that don't. One kapt processor left in a module keeps the stubs in that module. One port detail catches people. Kotlin has a kind of class javac never sees, the object, so the port needs an answer for it that the Java processor never needed. KSP's own story, meanwhile, has moved on from the days of that 2021 benchmark. Compare the port's slip with javac's Read JavacPackingSlipProcessor.java, the Java twin below. Find its four moves. Run PortDemo. It runs the reference KSP port on Kotlin twins of the four classes and prints its slip next to the one javac wrote for the Java twins. Open labs/ksp/src/test/resources/workbench/ksp/l09/java-twins.txt to see how javac's slip was made. Once your port passes the lab, run PortDemo with -Pmine=l09. PortDemo.kt package workbench.ksp.l09.demo import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.KotlinCompilation import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.SourceFile import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.configureKsp import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.kspSourcesDir import java.io.File import java.io.OutputStream import workbench.ksp.l09.HOUSEHOLD import workbench.ksp.l09.PackingSlipProcessorProvider // Runs the KSP port of the javac packing slip processor on Kotlin classes, then puts its slip next to the one // javac wrote for the Java twins (stored in src/test/resources/workbench/ksp/l09/). Reference port by default; // add -Pmine=l09 for yours. // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l09.demo.PortDemoKt fun main() { val things = SourceFile.kotlin( "Things.kt", """ package movemate import workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory import workbench.ksp.annotations.Room @Inventory @Room("hall") data class Box(val label: String, val room: String, val weightGrams: Int, val fragile: Boolean = false) @Inventory @Room("living room") data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?) @Inventory @Room("study") class Bookshelf(val shelves: Int, val books: List<String>) @Inventory data class Plant(val kind: String, val potLitres: Double, val waterEveryDays: Int = 7) """, ) val compilation = KotlinCompilation().apply { workingDir = File("build/kctfork/demo/l09").apply { deleteRecursively() } sources = listOf(things) inheritClassPath = true jvmTarget = "21" messageOutputStream = OutputStream.nullOutputStream() configureKsp { symbolProcessorProviders += PackingSlipProcessorProvider() processorOptions += mapOf(HOUSEHOLD to "Okafor") } } val result = compilation.compile() println("exit code: ${result.exitCode}") result.messages.lines().filter { it.startsWith("w: [ksp]") || it.startsWith("e: [ksp]") }.forEach(::println) val ksp = compilation.kspSourcesDir.resolve("resources/META-INF/movemate/packing-slip.txt") val javac = File("src/test/resources/workbench/ksp/l09/javac-packing-slip.txt") println("--- KSP wrote ${ksp.relativeTo(compilation.kspSourcesDir).invariantSeparatorsPath}:") print(if (ksp.exists()) ksp.readText() else "(nothing yet)
") println("--- javac wrote META-INF/movemate/packing-slip.txt for the Java twins:") print(javac.readText()) println("--- the same, byte for byte: ${ksp.exists() && ksp.readBytes().contentEquals(javac.readBytes())}") } ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l09.demo.PortDemoKt labs/ksp/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/ksp/l09/demo/PortDemo.kt JavacPackingSlipProcessor.java package workbench.ksp.l09; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.Writer; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import javax.annotation.processing.AbstractProcessor; import javax.annotation.processing.Messager; import javax.annotation.processing.RoundEnvironment; import javax.annotation.processing.SupportedAnnotationTypes; import javax.annotation.processing.SupportedOptions; import javax.lang.model.SourceVersion; import javax.lang.model.element.Element; import javax.lang.model.element.ElementKind; import javax.lang.model.element.Modifier; import javax.lang.model.element.TypeElement; import javax.lang.model.element.VariableElement; import javax.lang.model.util.ElementFilter; import javax.tools.Diagnostic; import javax.tools.StandardLocation; import workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory; import workbench.ksp.annotations.Room; /** * Lesson 9, given and read-only: the Java team's packing slip processor, a javac annotation processor * (javax.annotation.processing, part of the JDK since Java 6). For every class annotated @Inventory it writes one * line into META-INF/movemate/packing-slip.txt: the class name, its room from @Room, and its fields in order. * Your job in PackingSlipProcessor.kt is to port it to KSP, move by move, so Kotlin classes get the same slip. * * In a Java build it would run through Gradle's annotationProcessor configuration, registered in * META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor, and declared aggregating for Gradle's incremental * compile in META-INF/gradle/incremental.annotation.processors: * workbench.ksp.l09.JavacPackingSlipProcessor,aggregating */ @SupportedAnnotationTypes("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory") @SupportedOptions("movemate.household") public class JavacPackingSlipProcessor extends AbstractProcessor { private boolean slipWritten = false; @Override public SourceVersion getSupportedSourceVersion() { return SourceVersion.latestSupported(); } @Override public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment roundEnv) { if (slipWritten || roundEnv.processingOver()) return false; Messager messager = processingEnv.getMessager(); String household = processingEnv.getOptions().getOrDefault("movemate.household", "MoveMate"); // 1. Find: every element annotated @Inventory in this round List<TypeElement> classes = new ArrayList<>(); for (Element element : roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Inventory.class)) { // 2. Check: only classes, with an error on the exact element if (element.getKind() != ElementKind.CLASS) { messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, "@Inventory goes on a class, but " + element.getSimpleName() + " is " + kindWords(element.getKind()), element); continue; } classes.add((TypeElement) element); } if (classes.isEmpty()) return false; classes.sort(Comparator.comparing(c -> c.getSimpleName().toString())); // 3. Read: one line per class, its fields in source order List<String> lines = new ArrayList<>(); for (TypeElement type : classes) lines.add(slipLine(type)); // 4. Write: one resource for all of them; the originating elements tell an incremental build where it came from try { var slip = processingEnv.getFiler().createResource(StandardLocation.CLASS_OUTPUT, "", "META-INF/movemate/packing-slip.txt", classes.toArray(new Element[0])); try (Writer out = slip.openWriter()) { out.write("# " + household + " packing slip. Generated, do not edit.
"); for (String line : lines) out.write(line + "
"); } } catch (IOException e) { messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, "could not write the packing slip: " + e.getMessage()); } slipWritten = true; return false; // don't claim @Inventory: other processors may want it too } /** "Lamp [living room]: name, bulbs, shade" */ static String slipLine(TypeElement type) { Room room = type.getAnnotation(Room.class); List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); for (VariableElement field : ElementFilter.fieldsIn(type.getEnclosedElements())) { if (!field.getModifiers().contains(Modifier.STATIC)) names.add(field.getSimpleName().toString()); } return type.getSimpleName() + " [" + (room == null ? "no room" : room.name()) + "]: " + String.join(", ", names); } /** The same words the KSP port uses for each kind of declaration. */ static String kindWords(ElementKind kind) { return switch (kind) { case INTERFACE -> "an interface"; case ENUM -> "an enum"; case ANNOTATION_TYPE -> "an annotation"; case RECORD -> "a record"; default -> "a " + kind.name().toLowerCase(); }; } } labs/ksp/src/main/java/workbench/ksp/l09/JavacPackingSlipProcessor.java Both slips read # Okafor packing slip. Generated, do not edit., then Bookshelf [study]: shelves, books, Box [hall]: label, room, weightGrams, fragile, Lamp [living room]: name, bulbs, shade and Plant [no room]: kind, potLitres, waterEveryDays, and the last line is --- the same, byte for byte: true. With an unfinished port, the demo prints w: [ksp] l09 not done yet: ..., (nothing yet) and false. Migrate from kapt to KSP (Kotlin docs) docs Migrate from kapt to KSP (Android Developers) docs

h: Choosing the tool: KSP, reflection, kapt or a compiler plugin · Several houses at once: KSP2, versions and multiplatform
x: The KSP in this track is KSP2, and it differs from older articles in ways that matter. Since KSP 2.3.0, KSP2 is the only kind: setting ksp.useKSP2=false fails the build with "KSP1 is no longer available. Please use KSP2 instead". KSP2 "is no longer a compiler plugin". It runs inside the Gradle daemon, the long-lived Gradle process, so a big project may need more heap there, and KSP's docs suggest settings such as org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx4096M. Its version number is no longer tied to Kotlin's: this track builds with Kotlin 2.4.21 and KSP 2.3.14. A version written like 2.2.21-2.0.5, Kotlin's number and then KSP's, is the old scheme. The API moved too. KSP 2.3.12 deprecated KSVisitorVoid() and validate() without arguments, the spelling of the official quickstart, and 2.3.14 added the apiFeatures property that every lab in this track overrides. The last setting is several houses at once. Kotlin Multiplatform is one project compiled for several platforms, such as the JVM, JavaScript and native code, from shared code and code for each platform. Each platform is a target, and each target compiles separately. So KSP runs once per target, with a task and a configuration each: // build.gradle.kts of a multiplatform module: one KSP configuration per target kotlin { jvm() js { browser() } } dependencies { add("kspCommonMainMetadata", project(":processor")) // the shared code add("kspJvm", project(":processor")) // the JVM target: task kspKotlinJvm add("kspJs", project(":processor")) // the JavaScript target: task kspKotlinJs // ksp(project(":processor")) here fails the build: // The 'ksp' configuration is deprecated in Kotlin Multiplatform projects. // Please use target-specific configurations like 'kspJvm' instead. } The plain ksp(...) configuration is right in the single-platform builds of this track. In a multiplatform module it's an error since KSP 2.3.12: you name the targets that need the processor. Each target's output goes to its own folder, such as build/generated/ksp/jvm/jvmMain/kotlin. A class in the shared code gets its card once per target: a run with a JVM and a JavaScript target wrote one in each of metadata/commonMain, jvm/jvmMain and js/jsMain. Koin names "a KSP configuration per Kotlin Multiplatform target" among its reasons for moving to a compiler plugin. In the picture, it's a family moving into two houses on the same day. Each house gets its own helper, its own pass through the boxes, and its own set of cards, even for the boxes both houses share. The picture breaks only in the counting: in a build, the shared boxes are read once more for the shared code itself. In a multiplatform module, add the processor to each target that needs it. Plain ksp(...) is for single-platform modules. That's the last piece of the toolbox. What's left is to use it on a job big enough to need all of it. KSP with Kotlin Multiplatform (Kotlin docs) docs KSP2 introduction (google/ksp docs) docs

h: Choosing the tool: KSP, reflection, kapt or a compiler plugin · Java and Kotlin
x: The packing slip processor: the javac original and its KSP port, move by move JavacPackingSlipProcessor.java (excerpt) // The given javac processor (javax.annotation.processing) @SupportedAnnotationTypes("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory") @SupportedOptions("movemate.household") public class JavacPackingSlipProcessor extends AbstractProcessor { private boolean slipWritten = false; @Override public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment roundEnv) { if (slipWritten || roundEnv.processingOver()) return false; String household = processingEnv.getOptions().getOrDefault("movemate.household", "MoveMate"); List<TypeElement> classes = new ArrayList<>(); for (Element element : roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Inventory.class)) { // 1. Find if (element.getKind() != ElementKind.CLASS) { // 2. Check messager.printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, "@Inventory goes on a class, but ...", element); continue; } classes.add((TypeElement) element); } // 3. Read: slipLine(type) reads the fields and @Room // 4. Write: filer.createResource(CLASS_OUTPUT, "", "META-INF/movemate/packing-slip.txt", elements) slipWritten = true; return false; // claim nothing } } PackingSlipProcessor.kt (the given part) class PackingSlipProcessor( private val codeGenerator: CodeGenerator, private val logger: KSPLogger, private val options: Map<String, String>, ) : SymbolProcessor { override val apiFeatures = buildApiFeatures { enableBackingFields = true; enableContextParameters = true } private var slipWritten = false fun processSlip(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { if (slipWritten) return emptyList() // javac: if (slipWritten || processingOver()) val household = options[HOUSEHOLD] ?: "MoveMate" // javac: getOptions().getOrDefault(...) val classes = findInventory(resolver) // 1. Find .mapNotNull { checkKind(it, logger) } // 2. Check .sortedBy { it.simpleName.asString() } if (classes.isEmpty()) return emptyList() val lines = classes.map(::slipLine) // 3. Read val text = "# $household packing slip. Generated, do not edit.\n" + lines.joinToString("") { "$it\n" } codeGenerator.createNewFile(slipDependencies(classes), "META-INF/movemate", "packing-slip", "txt") .use { it.write(text.toByteArray()) } // 4. Write slipWritten = true return emptyList() // deferred symbols: none } } The two processors make the same moves in the same order, which is what makes a port a matter of swapping lines rather than redesigning. The differences are in the contract around them. javac creates the processor with a no-argument constructor and calls process with the annotations it may claim; returning true claims them, and KSP has no claiming at all. KSP creates the processor through a provider and gets back a list of symbols to defer, which javac has no word for. javac runs one more, empty round with processingOver() true; KSP calls finish() instead. And the incremental category moves from the processor (Gradle's descriptor file) to the output (Dependencies).

h: Choosing the tool: KSP, reflection, kapt or a compiler plugin · Worked example
x: Pick the tool for MoveMate's next four jobs Job 1: a debug screen that prints every field of whatever object a tester taps, a few times a day. It runs rarely and must work for classes nobody annotated. Reflection is fine, and a processor would only add a module and a test suite. static String debugPrint(Object thing) throws IllegalAccessException { StringJoiner parts = new StringJoiner(", ", thing.getClass().getSimpleName() + "(", ")"); for (Field f : thing.getClass().getDeclaredFields()) { if (Modifier.isStatic(f.getModifiers())) continue; f.setAccessible(true); parts.add(f.getName() + "=" + f.get(thing)); } return parts.toString(); } fun debugPrint(thing: Any): String = thing.javaClass.declaredFields .filter { !Modifier.isStatic(it.modifiers) } .onEach { it.isAccessible = true } .joinToString(", ", "${thing.javaClass.simpleName}(", ")") { "${it.name}=${it.get(thing)}" } Job 2: save every box to a file as JSON and read it back, thousands of times a day. The serializer belongs inside each class, with a serializer() function on its companion: that changes classes you wrote, so it's the kotlinx.serialization compiler plugin from the Advanced Kotlin track. In Java you'd reach for a library that reads annotations by reflection. @Serializable data class Box(val label: String, val room: String, val weightGrams: Int, val fragile: Boolean = false) val json = Json.encodeToString(Box("books", "study", 12_000)) // the plugin wrote Box's serializer // Java's usual approach: a JSON library such as Jackson, which reads the class by reflection String json = new ObjectMapper().writeValueAsString(new Box("books", "study", 12_000, false)); Job 3: wire the moving-day crew, where each class asks for what it needs in its constructor, and a missing part should stop the build. The wiring is new code next to your classes, written from their constructors: a KSP processor, and the next capstone builds it. class Truck @Inject constructor(val driver: Driver) // the processor writes a factory for Truck // and a component that builds Driver before Truck, checked during the build public class Truck { private final Driver driver; @Inject public Truck(Driver driver) { this.driver = driver; } // a javac processor writes the factory } Job 4: a module uses a processor that exists only as a javac processor, with no KSP artifact. Keep it on kapt for now, move every other library in the module to ksp(...), and remember that the stubs stay until the last kapt processor leaves the module.

h: Choosing the tool: KSP, reflection, kapt or a compiler plugin · Lab
x: Port a javac annotation processor to KSP labs/ksp/src/main/kotlin/workbench/ksp/l09/PackingSlipProcessor.kt labs/ksp/src/main/java/workbench/ksp/l09/JavacPackingSlipProcessor.java labs/ksp/src/test/resources/workbench/ksp/l09/javac-packing-slip.txt labs/ksp/src/test/resources/workbench/ksp/l09/java-twins.txt ./gradlew :ksp:test --tests 'workbench.ksp.l09.*' Read JavacPackingSlipProcessor.java: the Java team's processor, given and read-only. Its process method makes four moves, and java-twins.txt shows the Java classes javac ran it on and the command. javac-packing-slip.txt is what it wrote: your target, byte for byte. Read PackingSlipProcessor.kt. The provider, apiFeatures, the process wrapper and processSlip are given, in the same order as the Java process, and each comment names the javac line it replaces. Four functions are yours, one per move. Run the tests: all five fail. Run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL09Kotlin -Pmine=l09: your port already runs in the real build and warns w: [ksp] l09 not done yet: 1. Find: .... Find: write findInventory, the KSP line for roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Inventory.class). Check: write checkKind. A class passes; anything else gets logger.error on the symbol with the javac processor's words, @Inventory goes on a class, but Shape is an interface, plus one kind javac never sees: Van is an object. Read: write slipLine. javac read the fields in source order and getAnnotation(Room.class); you read the primary constructor's properties in order, and the name argument of the @Room annotation. Check shortName first, then resolve the annotation type to be sure. Write: write slipDependencies, aggregating, with the file of every class on the slip: the KSP form of the originating elements and of Gradle's aggregating category. Prove: run the tests until all five pass. Run PortDemo with -Pmine=l09 and look for byte for byte: true. Then run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL09Kotlin -Pmine=l09, open labs/ksp/app/build/generated/ksp/l09/resources/META-INF/movemate/packing-slip.txt, and print it from the class path with ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l09.PackingSlipKt -Pmine=l09. From memory: close both files and write, on paper, the KSP line for each of these javac calls: getElementsAnnotatedWith, printMessage(ERROR, text, element), getAnnotation(Room.class).name(), getOptions().get(key) and createResource(...). The drill below has the answer. Inventory::class.qualifiedName!! gives the full name that getSymbolsWithAnnotation needs; the short name finds nothing. ClassKind.INTERFACE, ENUM_CLASS, ANNOTATION_CLASS and OBJECT match the Java processor's kindWords when you use the same words: an interface, an enum, an annotation, and an object for the new one. cls.primaryConstructor?.parameters.orEmpty().filter { it.isVal || it.isVar } gives the properties in order. For @Room: annotations.firstOrNull { ... }?.arguments?.firstOrNull { it.name?.asString() == "name" }?.value as String?. The first test compares bytes: a missing trailing newline or an extra space fails it. processSlip already writes the header and one \n per line; slipLine returns the line without its newline. If the test that expects Shape.kt:6 fails, check that the error is logged on the symbol, not without one: a message without a symbol has no file and line. All five tests in PackingSlipProcessorTest pass, and PortDemo -Pmine=l09 prints the same, byte for byte: true. By the end you can choose between reflection, a KSP processor, a compiler plugin and kapt for a job, with evidence; move a library from kapt to KSP in Gradle; port a javac processor to KSP move by move; and set up KSP in a multiplatform module.
