h: Choosing the tool: KSP, reflection, kapt or a compiler plugin · Quiz
x: A settings screen reads a @MenuEntry annotation on 12 classes once when the program starts, to build a menu. Which tool fits best? A KSP processor that generates the menu Reflection while the program runs A compiler plugin that adds a label() member to each class kapt, because the annotation is read at start-up Twelve classes, once at start: a few milliseconds and a few dozen classes loaded, which nobody notices. A processor would add a module, a test suite and build time for no visible gain. The annotation needs RUNTIME retention for this, as @Inventory has, so it's still there while the program runs. A library needs each annotated class to gain a companion object with generated functions on it. What does KSP let it do? Generate the companion object in a new file Add functions to a companion only if the user already wrote one, even an empty one Nothing: KSP can't see companions Generate a second class with the same name that contains the companion A processor can write extension functions on an existing companion, in a new file, but it can't add the companion to your class: that changes the class. That's why Arrow Optics' KSP version needs "a companion object declaration in each class, even if it's empty", and why Arrow now recommends its compiler plugin. A second class with the same name is a Redeclaration error. A module uses Moshi's codegen and one Java-only processor through kapt. You move Moshi to ksp(...). What happens to the stubs? They are no longer generated They are still generated, because one kapt processor remains in the module KSP generates them instead They are generated only for Moshi's classes kapt makes Java stubs for the whole module whenever it runs any processor there. Android's guide: "If a module has any kapt processors remaining, stubs are still generated in that module." The build gets fast only when the last kapt processor leaves. In a Kotlin Multiplatform module with a JVM and a JavaScript target, someone writes ksp(project(":processor")). What happens with KSP 2.3.14? KSP runs on every target KSP runs on the JVM target only The build fails: use target configurations such as kspJvm and kspJs KSP runs only on the shared code Since KSP 2.3.12 the plain configuration is an error in multiplatform modules: "The 'ksp' configuration is deprecated in Kotlin Multiplatform projects. Please use target-specific configurations like 'kspJvm' instead." Each target has its own KSP task, such as kspKotlinJvm. From the Advanced Kotlin track: a framework must subclass your Kotlin classes to wrap their methods. Which tool removes final from them? A KSP processor The all-open compiler plugin kapt Reflection at start-up all-open changes what the compiler writes for marked classes: no final on the class or its members. A processor can't change an existing class, kapt only runs Java processors, and reflection can't make a final class subclassable.

h: Choosing the tool: KSP, reflection, kapt or a compiler plugin · Explain it back
x: A colleague says: "KSP is up to twice as fast as everything, so let's generate code for all our reflection and move every annotation library to KSP." Explain what you'd agree with, what you'd push back on, and how you'd decide each case.

h: Choosing the tool: KSP, reflection, kapt or a compiler plugin · Key terms
x: Reflection A program inspecting its own classes while it runs: their fields, values and methods. Compiler plugin A jar the Kotlin compiler loads to change what it writes into class files, for example all-open. kapt Kotlin's bridge to Java annotation processors: it writes Java stubs of Kotlin classes and runs the processors on them. Stub A Java copy of a Kotlin class's declarations, with empty bodies, made only for Java processors to read. KSP2 The current KSP, the only one since 2.3.0: not a compiler plugin, run in the Gradle daemon. Kotlin Multiplatform One project compiled for several platforms, such as the JVM and JavaScript, from shared and per-platform code. Target One platform a multiplatform project compiles for, with its own compilation and its own KSP task. When is reflection the right tool instead of a processor? When the work runs a few times on a few classes, or the classes arrive while the program runs: a debug screen, a test helper, settings read once at start. Generated card against reflection card, once warm: roughly how far apart? On this course's loaded machine, about 45 ns against about 190 ns cached and 280 ns plain: four to six times. The first calls were close. What happens when a processor writes a class with the same name as one of yours? The compiler reports Redeclaration: in both files. A processor can only add new declarations, never change yours. Which kind of job needs a compiler plugin rather than KSP? One that must change a class you wrote: remove final (all-open), add a constructor (no-arg), or add a serializer inside it (kotlinx.serialization). What does kapt do, and why is it slow? It writes Java stubs of your Kotlin classes, then runs Java annotation processors on them. Writing the stubs is the cost. How do you move a library from kapt to KSP in Gradle? Apply com.google.devtools.ksp, replace kapt(...) with ksp(...) and kapt { arguments { ... } } with ksp { arg(...) }, and remove the kapt plugin when no kapt processor is left. How do you add a KSP processor in a multiplatform module? Per target: add("kspJvm", ...), add("kspJs", ...), add("kspCommonMainMetadata", ...). Plain ksp(...) is a build error since KSP 2.3.12.

h: Choosing the tool: KSP, reflection, kapt or a compiler plugin · Go deeper
x: Why are the first calls so close? Each first card makes the JVM link the card's string template: Kotlin compiles a template to a call through java.lang.invoke, and the JVM builds the code for each new kind of template the first time it runs. In the class log of the generated run, most of the hundred-odd classes loaded around the first card were java.lang.invoke classes, and reflection's first card needs the same machinery for its own templates, plus about twenty classes for reading annotations and fields. On a real program, reflection's start-up cost grows with the number of classes it inspects and with the libraries it drags in, which is what the Part 4 capstone measured. Moshi offers both paths in one library and says when to pick which: "Prefer codegen for better performance and to avoid the kotlin-reflect dependency; prefer reflection to convert both private and protected properties." Its reflection adapter depends on kotlin-reflect, "a 2.5 MiB .jar file". This course's reflection cards avoid that by using plain Java reflection, which works for Kotlin classes because they compile to ordinary JVM classes, but sees only JVM facts: fields and their order, not Kotlin's nullability or default values. The ecosystem moves both ways at once, and the reasons are the same picture. Libraries whose job is new code next to yours (Room's database code, Dagger's factories, kotlin-inject's components) went KSP-first or KSP-only. Libraries whose job is to change or extend your classes from the inside (Koin's wiring rewrites calls such as single<UserRepository>(), Arrow Optics needs companions, DataFrame adds properties) moved to compiler plugins, which also skip the per-target KSP configurations of multiplatform modules. Before you pick a library, read which of the two it has become.

h: Capstone: dependency injection at compile time
x: Generate the wiring with KSP: factories, a component, and wiring mistakes caught as compile errors. Across three sittings you build a dependency injection container that does its work during the build. Dependency injection means that each class says in its constructor what it needs, and something else builds the objects in the right order and hands them over. Part 4's capstone did that by reflection while the program ran. Here a KSP processor writes the same wiring as ordinary Kotlin, so a wiring mistake becomes a compile error with a file and a line, and nothing is looked up when the program starts. Lesson 1 generates a factory for each @Inject class and a component that builds the whole graph in dependency order. Lesson 2 makes the processor report missing bindings with their whole path, cycles and duplicate bindings, all in one build, and adds @Named qualifiers and @Module objects with @Provides functions. Lesson 3 races the result against a reflection container from a cold start, lets an expensive part wait with Lazy<T> and () -> T, reads KSP's incremental log after one edit, and sets the processor next to Dagger, Hilt, kotlin-inject and Koin. The picture continues the KSP track's moving house: the moving-day plan. The truck needs a driver, the driver needs the route, every packer needs a roll of tape, and the crew can't start until all of them are ready. Someone writes the plan the night before: who comes first, who waits for whom, what is shared (one truck for the whole day) and what is new each time (a roll of tape per packer). Writing the plan the night before is compile-time wiring; working it out on the street in the morning is reflection. A driver waiting for the truck that waits for him is a cycle, and it's far better to find it the night before. You need the KSP track first, and Part 4's capstone helps; each lesson reminds you of what it uses. The labs live in labs/injector. :injector holds the processors you write (packages workbench.injector.l01 to l03), :injector:annotations the six annotations, and :injector:app a real Gradle build that runs your processors on the full MoveMate crew, one source set per lesson. Each lesson's package is self-contained and starts from the previous lesson's solution as given code. Run ./gradlew :injector:test --tests 'workbench.injector.lNN.*' from labs/ for your processor and ./gradlew :injector:solutionTest for the reference answers; the tests compile small graphs in memory with kctfork and check the generated text, the messages with their file and line, and calls into the generated component. ./gradlew :injector:app:kspLNNKotlin -Pmine=lNN runs your processor in the real build, and the demos run the reference processors, so every Try it works before you finish a lab. Versions: Kotlin 2.4.21, KSP 2.3.14, KotlinPoet 2.4.0, kctfork 0.14.0, Gradle 9.8.2, JDK 25 running a build with release 21. Dependency injection hands each object what its constructor asks for. A binding says how to get one type; a singleton exists once per component, and anything else is built for each request. The factory processor writes one <Name>Factory per @Inject class, an isolating output tied to that class's file. The component processor walks the graph depth first from the @Component functions and writes the plan in post-order: a private val per singleton, a new...() function for the rest. The order is what makes it compile. The component is aggregating: built from the component's file and every module's file, and redone whenever any file changes. A missing binding is reported on the parameter that asks, with the path joined by "needs"; a cycle is a dependency that is still on the path; a duplicate is reported on the second binding. One build reports them all. A reflection container meets the same mistakes only on the day: an exception from its own code, a 1,024-frame StackOverflowError, or a silent winner between two routes. @Module objects with @Provides functions bind classes you can't annotate, and @Named qualifiers tell two bindings of one type apart; a misspelt name is a missing binding. Lazy<T> builds once on first use and () -> T gives one more per call; laziness moves a cost rather than removing it. From cold, the generated component wired the crew two to three times faster and loaded 817 classes against 1,059, with no proxies and no annotation classes at run time. Dagger, Hilt and kotlin-inject generate wiring with KSP as we did; Koin moved to a compiler plugin because rewriting your calls is a job KSP can't do.

h: Capstone: dependency injection at compile time: track quiz
x: A generator writes private val truck: Truck = TruckFactory.create(driver) on the line above private val driver: Driver = DriverFactory.create(route). What happens? It compiles, and the truck's driver is null at run time It doesn't compile: Variable 'driver' must be initialized. Kotlin reorders the properties KSP reports a cycle Kotlin initializes properties from top to bottom and rejects an initializer that reads a property declared below it. That's why the component must be written in post-order. Nothing loops here, so it isn't a cycle. Which generated file must be declared aggregating, and why? DriverFactory.kt, because the driver is shared Every factory, because they're all used by the component GeneratedMovingDayComponent.kt, because a new file, such as a new @Module, can change the plan None: KSP works it out from the imports A factory depends on its own class's file, so it's isolating. The component is built from many files and every module, and a brand-new file can add a binding or a duplicate, which only an aggregating output notices. A test creates two GeneratedMovingDayComponent objects. How many trucks exist? One: @Singleton means one per program Two: a singleton is one per component object None until truck() is called It depends on the order of creation Each component holds its singletons as its own fields, so each component builds its own truck. One per component is usually what tests want: each test gets a fresh plan. The walk is inside MovingDay, Crew, Truck and Driver, and the driver asks for Crew. What is reported? Dependency cycle: Crew needs Truck needs Driver needs Crew. Dependency cycle: MovingDay needs Crew needs Truck needs Driver needs Crew. Nothing: Crew is shared A missing binding for Crew Crew is still on the path, so this is a loop, and the loop starts at the repeated binding. Crew isn't finished yet, so it isn't shared. The real build reported exactly this line when val crew: Crew was added to the driver. Crew needs Route and MovingDay needs the same singleton Route. Why does the walk not report a cycle when it meets Route again? Because Route comes from a module Because it checks the finished set before the path, and Route is finished Because it only checks for cycles at entry points Because singletons can't be in cycles Two arrows into one finished binding are sharing, not a loop. Checking the finished set first is what keeps a diamond-shaped graph from looking like a cycle. Route has an @Inject constructor, and a module also has @Provides fun route(): Route. What does the build say, and where? Nothing: the module wins Nothing: the constructor wins A cycle between Route and the module Route is provided twice: by Route's @Inject constructor and by RouteModule.route()., on the @Provides function Both bindings answer the key Route, so the plan can't choose. The @Inject constructor counts as the first, and the error lands on the second binding's own line, the line you would edit. A reflection container is given two unqualified @Provides functions for Route. What did the lesson's container do? It refused when it was created It threw when the driver asked for a route It kept one of them without a word It gave the driver both It stored providers in a map by key, so the second one replaced the first, and getDeclaredMethods() promises no order. The driver took the back roads and nothing was printed. The processor turns the same mistake into a compile error. Which request fits each part: the truck's GPS, slow to switch on and not needed every day; a fresh label sticker for every box? Lazy<GpsUnit> and () -> Sticker () -> GpsUnit and Lazy<Sticker> GpsUnit and Sticker, both direct Lazy for both Lazy<GpsUnit> builds the GPS on first use and keeps it. () -> Sticker returns one more sticker on every call, as long as Sticker isn't a singleton. Lazy<Sticker> would give every box the same sticker. The milliseconds to wire the crew The whole JVM run time The count of classes loaded The second request's microseconds Timings move with whatever else is running; ours moved by a third between runs. The classes a program loads depend only on the code it runs, so 817 against 1,059 held in every run. Count first, then time with many runs. Why did Koin move its annotations from a KSP processor to a compiler plugin? KSP can't read annotations on classes Its plugin rewrites single<T>() calls in your code into constructor calls, and KSP can only add new files KSP is deprecated Compiler plugins run while the program runs KSP reads declarations and writes new files; it can't change an expression in your code. Rewriting a call is a compiler plugin's job, as the compiler plugins lesson showed. KSP itself is alive and well: Dagger, Hilt and kotlin-inject use it.

h: Factories and a component, generated at build time · The moving-day plan, written by hand: dependencies, bindings and one shared truck
x: Moving day has a plan even when nobody writes it down. In MoveMate, our small app for a family's move, each person and thing on the crew is a class, and each class says in its constructor what it needs. Here is the plan written by hand, the way most programs do it near main: Java Route route = new Route(); Driver driver = new Driver(route); Truck truck = new Truck(driver); Crew crew = new Crew(truck, new Packer(new TapeRoll()), new Packer(new TapeRoll())); MovingDay day = new MovingDay(crew, route); Kotlin val route = Route() val driver = Driver(route) val truck = Truck(driver) val crew = Crew(truck, Packer(TapeRoll()), Packer(TapeRoll())) val day = MovingDay(crew, route) An object that another object needs is a dependency: the route is a dependency of the driver. Handing dependencies in from outside, instead of letting each class build its own, is dependency injection. Doing it through the constructor, as here, is constructor injection. Notice what those five lines get right. The driver and the moving day share one route. There is one truck. Each packer gets its own roll of tape. And every object is built after the objects it needs. Five lines are easy to keep right by hand, but eighty are not. Someone adds a parameter to Truck, and the block breaks in three places, or still compiles and quietly builds a second truck. So let's give the block a picture. The night before the move, someone writes the plan for the day on a sheet of paper. Each line of the plan says how to get one kind of thing: "the route: print it from the map", "a driver: call Sam and hand him the route". In code, such a line is a binding: what the plan does when someone needs a Driver. Some things are shared for the whole day, like the one truck. A thing that exists once per plan is a singleton. Others are new each time someone asks, like a roll of tape for each packer. Draw an arrow from each person to what they wait for, and you have the graph of the day. The picture breaks in one place, and it matters. A real planner can improvise in the morning, when a neighbour turns up with a ladder. A plan written by the build can't. Everything it will ever build must be in it when the build runs. Part 4's container worked the plan out on the street: it read your classes while the program ran. This capstone writes it the night before, with KSP. MoveMate's classes get sticky notes: annotations, labels in the code that tools can read. Three come from labs/injector/annotations: Java @Singleton public class Truck { private final Driver driver; @Inject // "build me with this constructor" public Truck(Driver driver) { this.driver = driver; } } @Component // "what the app asks the plan for" public interface MovingDayComponent { MovingDay movingDay(); Truck truck(); } Kotlin @Singleton class Truck @Inject constructor(val driver: Driver) // "build me with this constructor" @Component // "what the app asks the plan for" interface MovingDayComponent { fun movingDay(): MovingDay fun truck(): Truck } @Inject marks the constructor the plan should call. Put on the class instead, as in @Inject class Packer(val tape: TapeRoll), it means the primary constructor. @Singleton asks for one per plan, and @Component marks the interface that lists what the app will ask for. Our processors read those notes and write the plan as ordinary Kotlin. The first thing they write is the smallest piece: a card for each member of the crew.

h: Factories and a component, generated at build time · One card per class: a factory for each @Inject constructor
x:
A factory is a small piece of code whose only job is to build one class. The factory for Driver takes a route and calls the constructor. On paper, it's the card the plan keeps for Sam: what he needs, and how to bring him. It's dull code on purpose, and nobody should have to write eight of these by hand. A processor writes them. A processor is a plug-in for the build that reads your declarations and writes new source files. KSP, Kotlin Symbol Processing, runs processors during the build, before the Kotlin compiler compiles your code, and then compiles what they wrote along with it. In the KSP track's picture, a processor is the helper with a clipboard. It reads the labels on the boxes, never opens one, and writes new cards that travel with the move. Java has had the same idea since Java 6, as annotation processors that javac runs. KSP is Kotlin's own, faster way to do that job for Kotlin code. Our factory processor follows the five moves of the KSP track. Find: ask the Resolver, KSP's view of your code, for every symbol, that is, every declaration it can see, that carries @Inject. Check: refuse what the plan can't build, such as an interface, with an error on its line. Read: the constructor's parameters. Write: one file per class. Prove: tests, then a real build. Here is the loop, next to the closest Java equivalent: Java // Closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor (FactoryDemoJava in the demos) for (Element element : round.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Inject.class)) { // 1. Find if (element.getKind() != ElementKind.CONSTRUCTOR) { /* error */ continue; } // 2. Check ExecutableElement constructor = (ExecutableElement) element; TypeElement type = (TypeElement) constructor.getEnclosingElement(); for (VariableElement p : constructor.getParameters()) { /* ... */ } // 3. Read Writer out = processingEnv.getFiler() // 4. Write .createSourceFile(pkg + "." + name + "Factory", type).openWriter(); } Kotlin val (ready, later) = resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation(INJECT).toList() // 1. Find .partition { it.validate(apiFeatures = apiFeatures) } for (symbol in ready) { val binding = checked(symbol) ?: continue // 2. Check factoryFile(binding) // 3. Read, 4. Write .writeTo(codeGenerator, Dependencies(aggregating = false, binding.declaration.containingFile!!)) } return later Find has one surprise. @Inject on a constructor gives you a KSFunctionDeclaration, while @Inject on the class gives you a KSClassDeclaration. The given checked function turns both into a Binding: the class, plus the constructor the plan will call. factoryFile then reads that constructor's parameters and builds the file with KotlinPoet, a library for writing Kotlin source from code, one ParameterSpec per parameter, as in the KSP track. The demo prints what it wrote: --- movemate/DriverFactory.kt // Generated by FactoryProcessor from Driver. Do not edit. package movemate public object DriverFactory { public fun create(route: Route): Driver = Driver(route) } create takes what the constructor takes and passes it straight on. KotlinPoet wrote the public modifiers and turned the one-statement body into an expression body: = Driver(route) instead of a block with return. The last argument of writeTo matters most. Dependencies(aggregating = false, driverFile) tells KSP that this card depends on Driver.kt and on nothing else. That makes it an isolating output: when Truck.kt changes, KSP has no reason to redo the driver's card. Lesson 3 watches that happen in KSP's own log. A factory knows one class. Tie it to that class's file only. Eight cards now sit in build/generated/ksp, and none of them says when to call it. Sam can't drive before someone has printed the route. Watch the factory processor write its cards Run FactoryDemo from labs/. It compiles three small classes in memory with lesson 1's reference processor and prints every card it wrote. Run FactoryDemoJava, which does the same job with a javac annotation processor on three Java classes. Compare the two DriverFactory files line by line. In FactoryDemo.kt, give the truck a second parameter: class Truck @Inject constructor(val driver: Driver, val route: Route). Predict TruckFactory, then run again. FactoryDemo.kt package workbench.injector.l01.demo import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.KotlinCompilation import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.SourceFile import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.configureKsp import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.kspSourcesDir import java.io.File import java.io.OutputStream import workbench.injector.l01.FactoryProcessorProvider // Runs lesson 1's factory processor in memory on three classes and prints the cards it writes. // ./gradlew :injector:demo -Pmain=workbench.injector.l01.demo.FactoryDemoKt fun main() { val sources = listOf( "Route" to "class Route @Inject constructor()", "Driver" to "class Driver @Inject constructor(val route: Route)", "Truck" to "class Truck @Inject constructor(val driver: Driver)", ).map { (name, line) -> SourceFile.kotlin("$name.kt", "package movemate

h: Factories and a component, generated at build time · The plan for the whole day: a component that builds the crew in order
x: The plan for the whole day: a depth-first walk writes the crew in dependency order, and a swapped line won't compile The cards say how to bring each member of the crew. The plan for the day says in which order, and what is shared. A component is that plan in code: a generated class that implements your @Component interface and builds everything the interface hands out. Ours is called GeneratedMovingDayComponent. To write it, the second processor walks the graph. It starts at each function of the interface, movingDay() and truck(), and follows the constructors down. MovingDay needs Crew and Route, Crew needs Truck and two packers, and so on, as the figure draws it. The rule fits in one sentence: a binding joins the plan when the walk leaves it, after everything it needs. That order is called post-order, and the walk is depth first: Java // The same walk in Java, over a map from each class to what its constructor needs void visit(String name, Map<String, List<String>> needs, LinkedHashSet<String> order) { if (order.contains(name)) return; // already in the plan: shared for (String dependency : needs.get(name)) visit(dependency, needs, order); order.add(name); // after everything it needs } Kotlin fun visit(binding: Binding) { if (binding.key in order) return // already in the plan: shared for (p in binding.parameters) need(p.type.resolve(), binding.name, p)?.let(::visit) order[binding.key] = binding // post-order: after everything it needs } need finds the binding for a parameter's type, or reports that nobody provides it. Then the processor writes the plan: a private val for each singleton, in the order the walk found, and a new...() function for everything else. Read the result aloud. It is the code you'd write by hand, in the right order: Java // The same plan as a javac annotation processor would write it in Java public final class GeneratedMovingDayComponent implements MovingDayComponent { private final Route route = RouteFactory.create(); private final Driver driver = DriverFactory.create(route); private final Truck truck = TruckFactory.create(driver); private final Crew crew = CrewFactory.create(truck, newPacker(), newPacker()); private final MovingDay movingDay = MovingDayFactory.create(crew, route); private TapeRoll newTapeRoll() { return TapeRollFactory.create(); } private Packer newPacker() { return PackerFactory.create(newTapeRoll()); } @Override public MovingDay movingDay() { return movingDay; } @Override public Truck truck() { return truck; } } Kotlin // Generated by ComponentProcessor from MovingDayComponent. Do not edit. (blank lines removed) public class GeneratedMovingDayComponent : MovingDayComponent { private val route: Route = RouteFactory.create() private val driver: Driver = DriverFactory.create(route) private val truck: Truck = TruckFactory.create(driver) private val crew: Crew = CrewFactory.create(truck, newPacker(), newPacker()) private val movingDay: MovingDay = MovingDayFactory.create(crew, route) private fun newTapeRoll(): TapeRoll = TapeRollFactory.create() private fun newPacker(): Packer = PackerFactory.create(newTapeRoll()) override fun movingDay(): MovingDay = movingDay override fun truck(): Truck = truck } First the route, then the driver who needs it, then the truck. The crew's line calls newPacker() twice, and each call makes a new packer with a new roll of tape. So the app prints one truck for the whole day: true and tape rolls made: 2. The one truck is a field, built once. The tape rolls come from a function, built on every call. Remember the warm-up? Kotlin runs those initializers from top to bottom, as Java runs field initializers. Write the driver's line above the route's, and the compiler, a stickler for order, refuses: Variable 'route' must be initialized. javac says illegal forward reference for the same line in Java. The order isn't decoration. It's what makes the class compile. The component's text depends on many files, so the processor writes it with Dependencies(aggregating = true, componentFile). In the KSP track's words, it's the master list, an aggregating output, redone whenever any file changes. KSP also records each type the walk looks up, so it would notice a changed constructor anyway. Aggregating covers new files too, which matters in the next lesson, where a new module can add a line to the plan. One caution before we move on. The walk remembers what it has finished, but not the path it is on right now. Give it a driver who waits for the truck, and it walks in circles until the stack runs out. The next lesson gives it that memory. We have the plan, in a file you can open and read. How does it compare with working it out on the street? Build the plan in a real Gradle build From labs/, run ./gradlew :injector:app:kspL01Kotlin and open injector/app/build/generated/ksp/l01/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l01/GeneratedMovingDayComponent.kt. Find the line that builds the truck. Which lines must come before it? Run MovingDayApp with the command below, then its Java twin, MovingDayAppJava. Delete @Singleton above class Truck in app/src/l01/.../Truck.kt. Predict how the component changes and what one truck for the whole day prints. Run MovingDayApp again, then put the annotation back. MovingDayApp.kt package workbench.injector.app.l01 // Uses the component KSP wrote during the build: // build/generated/ksp/l01/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l01/GeneratedMovingDayComponent.kt // ./gradlew :injector:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.injector.app.l01.MovingDayAppKt fun main() { val plan: MovingDayComponent = GeneratedMovingDayComponent() val day = plan.movingDay() day.plan().forEach(::println) println("one truck for the whole day: ${plan.truck() === day.crew.truck}") println("tape rolls made: ${TapeRoll.made}") } ./gradlew :injector:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.injector.app.l01.MovingDayAppKt labs/injector/app/src/l01/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l01/MovingDayApp.kt MovingDayAppJava.java package workbench.injector.app.l01; // Java calling the same generated Kotlin component: once compiled, it is an ordinary class. // ./gradlew :injector:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.injector.app.l01.MovingDayAppJava public class MovingDayAppJava { public static void main(String[] args) { MovingDayComponent plan = new GeneratedMovingDayComponent(); MovingDay day = plan.movingDay(); day.plan().forEach(System.out::println); System.out.println("one truck for the whole day: " + (plan.truck() == day.getCrew().getTruck())); System.out.println("tape rolls made: " + TapeRoll.Companion.getMade()); } } ./gradlew :injector:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.injector.app.l01.MovingDayAppJava labs/injector/app/src/l01/java/workbench/injector/app/l01/MovingDayAppJava.java Both languages print Sam drives truck MOVE-1 on the highway (42 min), tape rolls #1 and #2, one truck for the whole day: true and tape rolls made: 2. Without @Singleton, the truck's val becomes private fun newTruck(): Truck, the crew's line calls newTruck(), truck() returns newTruck(), and the line prints false: the crew drives one truck and truck() builds another. The crew's graph: each arrow means "needs". The plan builds every box after the boxes it points at, so the numbers are the order of the lines in the generated component. h: Factories and a component, generated at build time · The night before or on the street: generated wiring next to the reflection container
x: Both ways build the same crew. They differ in when the work happens and in what you see when it goes wrong. Here's the generated component next to Part 4's reflection container: Reflection container (Part 4) Generated component (this lesson) When the wiring is checked When the program first asks for a part When the build runs What runs at start Reading annotations, getConstructors() and newInstance for every part One constructor call per part, in order What you can read Nothing: the plan exists only in memory A Kotlin file in build/generated/ksp A mistake looks like An exception thrown from inside the container An error on the file and line of your class Can it change its mind at run time? Yes: it can scan for parts and choose No: the plan is fixed when you build Let the build settle the fourth row. Delete @Inject from Driver in app/src/l01 and run ./gradlew :injector:app:kspL01Kotlin: e: [ksp] .../labs/injector/app/src/l01/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l01/Truck.kt:8: Truck needs Driver, but nobody provides Driver. Add @Inject to its constructor. > Task :injector:app:kspL01Kotlin FAILED > KSP failed with exit code: PROCESSING_ERROR The program never ran. The error points at line 8 of Truck.kt, where the truck asks for a driver, and not at a line of the processor. In a reflection container, the same mistake would surface only when the app first asked for the crew, as an exception from the container's own code. The next lesson shows that stack trace. A stack trace from a reflection container is mostly the container talking about itself. Using the generated component is ordinary code in either language. It compiles to a plain class, so Java calls it like any other: Java MovingDayComponent plan = new GeneratedMovingDayComponent(); MovingDay day = plan.movingDay(); System.out.println(plan.truck() == day.getCrew().getTruck()); // true: one truck Kotlin val plan: MovingDayComponent = GeneratedMovingDayComponent() val day = plan.movingDay() println(plan.truck() === day.crew.truck) // true: one truck Wiring that depends only on your classes can be checked when you build. Check it there. The last row of the table is the price. The generated plan can't discover a part while the program runs, or choose one from a setting, unless the build wrote code for it. Today's processor has three gaps of its own, too. Its message names only the last step ("Truck needs Driver"), which helps little when ten classes need a driver. It has no answer to a cycle. And it has no way to bind a class you can't put a note on, such as one from a library. Those three are the next lesson. Forget a note, and see who complains In labs/injector/app/src/l01/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l01/Driver.kt, delete @Inject. From labs/, run ./gradlew :injector:app:kspL01Kotlin. Which file and line does the error name, and why that one? Now put the note on the class instead (@Inject class Driver(val route: Route) { ... }, keeping @Singleton above it) and run the task again. Open GeneratedMovingDayComponent.kt once more. Did anything in it change? The first run fails with e: [ksp] .../Truck.kt:8: Truck needs Driver, but nobody provides Driver. Add @Inject to its constructor. and KSP failed with exit code: PROCESSING_ERROR: the error names the truck's parameter, where a driver is asked for. With @Inject on the class, the build passes, DriverFactory.kt is back, and the component is the same as before, because a note on the class means its primary constructor.

h: Factories and a component, generated at build time · Java and Kotlin
x: One card, two helpers: the factory javac's processor writes and the one KSP writes DriverFactory.java (from FactoryDemoJava) // Generated by FactoryAnnotationProcessor from Driver. Do not edit. package movemate; public final class DriverFactory { private DriverFactory() {} public static Driver create(movemate.Route route) { return new Driver(route); } } // a caller Driver driver = DriverFactory.create(new Route()); DriverFactory.kt (from FactoryDemo) // Generated by FactoryProcessor from Driver. Do not edit. package movemate public object DriverFactory { public fun create(route: Route): Driver = Driver(route) } // a caller in Kotlin, then in Java val driver = DriverFactory.create(Route()) // Driver driver = DriverFactory.INSTANCE.create(new Route()); Both helpers read the same constructor and write a card that takes what it takes and calls it. The Java card is a final class with a static method and a private constructor, so nobody can build the factory itself; the Kotlin card is an object, which Java reaches through INSTANCE. The javac processor wrote its text with a string template, so it spells movemate.Route in full; KotlinPoet manages imports and would add one for a type from another package. Neither card uses reflection, and both are ordinary source that the compiler checks like your own.

h: Factories and a component, generated at build time · Worked example
x: Add a moving blanket to the plan The family's piano needs wrapping, so a packer now needs a moving blanket. Start with the class, and give it an @Inject constructor. class Blanket @Inject constructor() public class Blanket { @Inject public Blanket() {} } Ask for it where it's needed: in the packer's constructor. That's the only change you make by hand. @Inject class Packer(val tape: TapeRoll, val blanket: Blanket) public class Packer { @Inject public Packer(TapeRoll tape, Blanket blanket) { /* ... */ } } Build. KSP writes BlanketFactory, PackerFactory.create gains a parameter, and the packer's line in the component changes. The walk put the blanket before the packer, as post-order must. private fun newBlanket(): Blanket = BlanketFactory.create() private fun newPacker(): Packer = PackerFactory.create(newTapeRoll(), newBlanket()) private Blanket newBlanket() { return BlanketFactory.create(); } private Packer newPacker() { return PackerFactory.create(newTapeRoll(), newBlanket()); } Decide whether it's shared. Without @Singleton, each packer gets its own blanket, like its own roll of tape. Add @Singleton only if one blanket for the whole day is what you mean, because then every packer wraps with the same one.

h: Factories and a component, generated at build time · Key terms
x: Dependency An object that another object needs in order to do its job. Dependency injection Handing an object its dependencies from outside, instead of letting it build them itself. Constructor injection Dependency injection through constructor parameters: the class says what it needs, and someone else passes it in. Binding One line of the plan: how to get one type, such as "call the @Inject constructor of Driver". Singleton A binding that exists once per component and is shared by everyone who asks for it. Graph The bindings and the arrows between them: who needs whom. Factory Generated code whose only job is to build one class from what its constructor takes. Component The generated class that implements a @Component interface and builds the whole graph in dependency order. What is a dependency? An object another object needs to do its job. The driver is a dependency of the truck. What is constructor injection? A class lists what it needs as constructor parameters, and something outside builds those and passes them in. Isolating or aggregating: a factory for one @Inject class? Isolating. It depends only on that class's file: Dependencies(aggregating = false, file). Isolating or aggregating: the generated component? Aggregating. It's built from many files and is redone whenever any of them changes. In what order does the component build its singletons, and why does it matter? Depth-first post-order: each one after everything its constructor needs. Kotlin initializes properties top to bottom and rejects a forward read with Variable '...' must be initialized. How does the generated component handle a binding without @Singleton? As a private new<Name>() function, so every request builds a new object.

h: Factories and a component, generated at build time · Go deeper
x: Why generate factories at all, when the component could call each constructor directly? In a single module, it could. The factory earns its keep when classes live in several modules. A library module compiled earlier ships its factories with it, and the component in the app module only calls them. Each factory is compiled once, in the module that owns the class, so the app's build never needs to look inside that class's constructor again beyond its signature. Our component builds its singletons eagerly, in the constructor. That keeps the generated text in plain dependency order, and it's thread-safe for a simple reason: each private val compiles to a private final field, and the memory model guarantees that final fields set in a constructor are visible to any thread that sees the finished object (the memory model track has the rule). The cost is that creating the component builds everything, even parts nobody asks for. Lesson 3 adds Lazy<T> for the one expensive part. A singleton here is one per component object, not one per program. Create two GeneratedMovingDayComponents and you get two trucks. That's usually what you want in tests: each test builds its own plan. The javac twin of the factory processor has a trap of its own. Since JDK 23, javac doesn't run processors it merely finds on the class path; it needs --processor-path, -processor or -proc:full. Gradle's annotationProcessor configuration passes the processor path explicitly, and FactoryDemoJava hands the processor to the compiler task directly, so neither is affected.

h: Wiring mistakes as compile errors · Three mistakes, met on the day: what a reflection container does with them
x: First, the words, since all of them are in play today. A dependency is an object another object needs, and dependency injection hands it in from outside, here through the constructor, which is constructor injection. A binding is one line of the plan: how to get one type. A singleton is built once per plan, and anything else is built new for each request. The graph is all the bindings, with an arrow for each "needs". Our KSP processor is a plug-in for the build that reads declarations and writes code. The component is the class it generates to build that graph, calling one generated factory, a small object that builds one class, for each. Three mistakes in bindings are common enough to have names. A missing binding: somebody needs a type that nobody provides. A cycle: the "needs" arrows lead back to where they started. A duplicate binding: two bindings answer the same request, and the plan can't say which one is meant. Here they are, one small crew each: Java // missing: Driver forgot its @Inject class Driver { Driver(Route route) { } } // cycle: the driver waits for the truck, and the truck for the driver class Driver { @Inject Driver(Route route, Truck truck) { } } class Truck { @Inject Truck(Driver driver) { } } // twice: two routes, and nothing says which one the driver means @Module public final class RouteModule { @Provides public Route highway() { return new Route("highway"); } @Provides public Route backRoads() { return new Route("back roads"); } } Kotlin // missing: Driver forgot its @Inject class Driver(val route: Route) // cycle: the driver waits for the truck, and the truck for the driver class Driver @Inject constructor(val route: Route, val truck: Truck) class Truck @Inject constructor(val driver: Driver) // twice: two routes, and nothing says which one the driver means @Module object RouteModule { @Provides fun highway(): Route = Route("highway") @Provides fun backRoads(): Route = Route("back roads") } Let's meet them the way a container that works things out on the street would. ReflectionContainer in this lesson's demos is about forty lines. It reads the sticky notes, the annotations, while the program runs. Ask it for a type, and it builds that type's constructor arguments first, then the type. It checks nothing in advance, on purpose. Asked for each crew's MovingDay, it printed: --- missing: Driver has no @Inject java.lang.IllegalStateException: no @Inject constructor on workbench.injector.l02.demo.missing.Driver 19 stack frames, the first three: at workbench.injector.l02.demo.ReflectionContainer.construct(ReflectionContainer.kt:47) at workbench.injector.l02.demo.ReflectionContainer.get(ReflectionContainer.kt:37) at workbench.injector.l02.demo.ReflectionContainer.argumentsFor(ReflectionContainer.kt:52) --- cycle: the driver waits for the truck java.lang.StackOverflowError 1024 stack frames, the first three: at java.base/java.lang.Class.privateGetDeclaredConstructors(Class.java:3540) at java.base/java.lang.Class.getConstructors(Class.java:2229) at workbench.injector.l02.demo.ReflectionContainer.construct(ReflectionContainer.kt:45) --- twice: two routes, no names no error: the driver takes the back roads Three mistakes, three different failures, and every one of them at run time. The first names the class but not who asked for it, and its top frames are the container's own lines. The second is 1,024 frames of the container asking itself for a truck, which is as many frames as the JVM keeps in a stack trace by default. The third is the worst, because it isn't a failure at all. The container stored both routes under one key, and the second one it read quietly replaced the first. getDeclaredMethods() returns methods "not in any particular order", in the Javadoc's words, so which route wins is luck. And lesson 1's processor? As promised, its walk has no memory of the path it is on, so it fails on the cycle the same way, only earlier. In a test compile it stopped with INTERNAL_ERROR, the exit code a test compile gives when a processor crashes, and a java.lang.StackOverflowError whose top frames are inside KotlinPoet. Earlier is better. But a stack overflow says nothing about which classes are to blame, at either time. So the night-before check needs two things lesson 1's walk lacks: the path it's on, and the patience to report a problem and carry on. Run the three broken crews by reflection Read the three files in labs/injector/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/injector/l02/demo/ named missing/Missing.kt, cycle/Cycle.kt and twice/Twice.kt. Predict which crew fails loudest, and which fails quietest. Run RunTimeMistakesDemo, then its Java twin, which asks the same Kotlin container for the same crews. In missing/Missing.kt, give Driver its note back (class Driver @Inject constructor(val route: Route)), predict, and run the Kotlin demo again. Then take the note off once more: the next Try it compiles this file and expects the mistake in it. h: Wiring mistakes as compile errors · Nobody provides Driver: a missing binding named with its whole path
x: Lesson 1's message said Truck needs Driver, but nobody provides Driver. That's true, and it's enough when one class needs a driver. When ten classes do, you want to know how the plan got there. The walk already knows: it just has to keep the path it's on, the bindings it has entered and not yet left. So lesson 2's walk carries a list called path. It adds a binding on the way in and removes it on the way out. When a dependency has no binding, the message is the path plus the missing type, joined with "needs". Here is the KSP walk next to the javac processor that does the same check: Java // Closest Java equivalent: the javac processor in CompileTimeMistakesDemoJava ExecutableElement constructor = ElementFilter.constructorsIn(cls.getEnclosedElements()).stream() .filter(c -> c.getAnnotation(Inject.class) != null).findFirst().orElse(null); if (constructor == null) { // nobody provides it List<String> needs = new ArrayList<>(path); needs.add(name); processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, String.join(" needs ", needs) + ": nobody provides " + name, askedBy); return; } path.add(name); // on the way in for (VariableElement p : constructor.getParameters()) walk(p.asType(), path, done, p); path.remove(path.size() - 1); // on the way out done.add(name); Kotlin fun visit(binding: Binding) { path += binding // on the way in for (dependency in binding.dependencies) { val target = bindingFor(dependency.key, dependency.type) when { target == null -> error( // nobody provides it (path + dependency.key).joinToString(" needs ") + ": nobody provides ${dependency.key}. ${hint(dependency.key)}", dependency.node, // the parameter that asks ) target.key in done -> Unit // already built: shared // ... the cycle check comes here, in the next section else -> visit(target) } } path.removeAt(path.lastIndex) // on the way out done[binding.key] = binding } Two details make the message useful. The error goes on dependency.node, the parameter that asks, so logger.error prints that parameter's file and line. And the walk doesn't stop there. It reports, skips the missing piece and carries on, so one build can list every problem. The demo compiles the three broken crews from the last section, the very same files, in one build: exit code: COMPILATION_ERROR e: [ksp] Twice.kt:13: Route is provided twice: by RouteModule.highway() and by RouteModule.backRoads(). Give each one its own @Named qualifier and ask for the one you mean. e: [ksp] Missing.kt:8: MovingDay needs Crew needs Truck needs Driver: nobody provides Driver. Add @Inject to its constructor, or a @Provides function in a @Module. e: [ksp] Cycle.kt:7: Dependency cycle: Truck needs Driver needs Truck. Nothing in a cycle can be built first: change one of these constructors. Missing.kt:8 is the truck's constructor, where the driver is asked for. (KSP prints the absolute path; the demo shortens it to the file name.) The javac twin finds the first two mistakes the same way. It reports through the Messager, javac's channel for a processor's messages, and prints Missing.java:7: error: MovingDay needs Crew needs Truck needs Driver: nobody provides Driver. Java has had annotation processors that javac runs since Java 6; KSP is Kotlin's own, faster way to do the same job for Kotlin code. A good message says what is wrong, where, and how to fix it. In a graph, "where" has two halves. The file and line tell you which parameter asked, and the path tells you why the plan needed it at all. The hint at the end covers "how": add @Inject, or a @Provides function in a @Module, which the last section brings in. A missing binding is reported where it's asked for, with the path that led there. Report it there, and keep walking. The other two lines in that output come from checks we haven't built yet. The cycle comes first, because the path makes it almost free. Catch all three mistakes in one build Run CompileTimeMistakesDemo. It reads the same three files from disk, compiles them in one build with lesson 2's reference processors, and prints every error. Run CompileTimeMistakesDemoJava: a javac annotation processor doing the first two checks on the same crews, written in Java. Match each error to its run-time failure in the last Try it. Which mistake did the reflection container not report at all? import javax.lang.model.element.VariableElement; import javax.lang.model.type.TypeMirror; import javax.lang.model.util.ElementFilter; import javax.tools.Diagnostic; import javax.tools.DiagnosticCollector; import javax.tools.JavaCompiler; import javax.tools.JavaFileObject; import javax.tools.SimpleJavaFileObject; import javax.tools.ToolProvider; import workbench.injector.annotations.Component; import workbench.injector.annotations.Inject; // The closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor that walks each @Component's graph and reports a // missing binding or a cycle with its path, on the exact parameter, through the Messager. (It does the first // two checks only; the duplicates need modules.) main() runs javac in memory on two broken Java plans. // ./gradlew :injector:demo -Pmain=workbench.injector.l02.demo.CompileTimeMistakesDemoJava public class CompileTimeMistakesDemoJava { @SupportedAnnotationTypes("workbench.injector.annotations.Component") public static class GraphCheckProcessor extends AbstractProcessor { @Override public SourceVersion getSupportedSourceVersion() { return SourceVersion.latestSupported(); } @Override public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment round) { for (Element component : round.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Component.class)) { // 1. h: Wiring mistakes as compile errors · The driver waits for the truck: finding a cycle before anyone moves
x: The driver waits for the truck: keep the path the walk is on, and the build names the loop before anyone moves A cycle is a path of "needs" arrows that comes back to where it started: the truck needs a driver, and the driver needs the truck. Nothing in a cycle can be built first, because each constructor needs the other object already built. With the path in hand, finding one takes a single check. Before visiting a dependency, ask whether it's already on the path. If it is, the walk has come back to a binding it's still inside. The loop is the part of the path from that binding on, plus the binding once more: Java if (path.contains(name)) { // we are inside it already List<String> loop = new ArrayList<>(path.subList(path.indexOf(name), path.size())); loop.add(name); processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, "Dependency cycle: " + String.join(" needs ", loop), askedBy); return; } Kotlin path.any { it.key == target.key } -> { // we are inside it already val loop = path.dropWhile { it.key != target.key } + target error( "Dependency cycle: ${loop.joinToString(" needs ")}. " + "Nothing in a cycle can be built first: change one of these constructors.", dependency.node, ) } Let's trace the broken crew from the walk's point of view. It enters MovingDay, then Crew, then Truck, then Driver, so the path is [MovingDay, Crew, Truck, Driver]. The driver's first parameter, the route, is fine. His second asks for Truck, which is on the path. Drop everything before Truck, add Truck again, and the loop reads Truck needs Driver needs Truck. The error goes on the driver's truck parameter, the arrow that closes the loop, as the figure shows. The order of the checks matters. A binding that is finished is shared, not a loop, even when two classes need it: the driver and the moving day both need a route. So the walk checks done before it checks the path. Part 4's container made the same choice for the same reason. In the real build it looks like this. Uncomment val truck: Truck in app/src/l02/.../Driver.kt and run ./gradlew :injector:app:kspL02Kotlin: e: [ksp] .../labs/injector/app/src/l02/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l02/Driver.kt:12: Dependency cycle: Truck needs Driver needs Truck. Nothing in a cycle can be built first: change one of these constructors. > Task :injector:app:kspL02Kotlin FAILED Here the picture breaks again. On a real street, the driver and the truck company would sort it out with a phone call. Code can't negotiate. Someone has to change a constructor, and the message lists the constructors to look at. Lesson 3 meets Lazy, which delays building something until it's first used, but our processor still calls a loop through a Lazy a cycle. It's the safe answer. A cycle is a request for something you're still building. Check the path before you visit. Missing bindings and cycles are about too few answers. The last mistake is one answer too many. Make the driver wait for the truck in the real build In labs/injector/app/src/l02/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l02/Driver.kt, uncomment the line val truck: Truck,. Write down the loop you expect, then run ./gradlew :injector:app:kspL02Kotlin from labs/. Comment that line out again, and on the same line write val crew: Crew, instead. Predict the loop now, and run the task again. Put Driver.kt back as it was, and run the task once more to see it pass. The first run fails with Driver.kt:12: Dependency cycle: Truck needs Driver needs Truck. The second fails with Dependency cycle: Crew needs Truck needs Driver needs Crew., again on line 12 of Driver.kt, because that parameter still closes the loop; the loop just starts further up the path. The last run is BUILD SUCCESSFUL. The walk keeps the path it is on. When Driver asks for Truck, Truck is still on the path, so the loop is Truck needs Driver needs Truck, reported on the driver's parameter.

h: Wiring mistakes as compile errors · Two routes: duplicate bindings, @Named, and a @Module for a class you can't annotate
x: So far every binding came from an @Inject constructor. That works for your own classes. But MoveMate's Route now comes from a maps library, and you can't put a sticky note on a class you can't edit. A module fills that gap: an object whose functions say how to get such things. Each function marked @Provides is a binding, and its parameters are its own dependencies: Java // The same module in Java: a Kotlin object compiles to a final class with one INSTANCE @Module public final class RouteModule { public static final RouteModule INSTANCE = new RouteModule(); private RouteModule() { } @Provides @Singleton @Named("highway") public Route highway() { return new Route("highway", 42); } @Provides @Singleton @Named("back roads") public Route backRoads() { return new Route("back roads", 51); } } Kotlin @Module object RouteModule { @Provides @Singleton @Named("highway") fun highway(): Route = Route("highway", 42) @Provides @Singleton @Named("back roads") fun backRoads(): Route = Route("back roads", 51) } Take the names away first, as in the third broken crew, and the plan has two answers to one question. The reflection container shrugged and kept whichever one it read last. The processor's duplicate check groups every @Provides function by its key, the type plus any qualifier. Then it reports every binding after the first on its own line: Twice.kt:13: Route is provided twice: by RouteModule.highway() and by RouteModule.backRoads(). An @Inject constructor counts too. Provide a Route from a module while Route also has an @Inject constructor, and the message says by Route's @Inject constructor and by RouteModule.route(). The fix is a qualifier: a name that tells two bindings of the same type apart. @Named("highway") on a @Provides function marks one binding, and @Named("highway") on a parameter asks for exactly that one: Java public class Driver { @Inject public Driver(@Named("highway") Route route) { /* ... */ } } public class MovingDay { @Inject public MovingDay(Crew crew, @Named("back roads") Route familyRoute) { /* ... */ } } Kotlin @Singleton class Driver @Inject constructor(@Named("highway") val route: Route) @Singleton class MovingDay @Inject constructor(val crew: Crew, @Named("back roads") val familyRoute: Route) Now the truck takes the highway, and the family follows in their own car on the back roads. The generated plan names each route after its qualifier, so the two never mix: private val highwayRoute: Route = RouteModule.highway(), private val backRoadsRoute: Route = RouteModule.backRoads(), and the driver's line reads DriverFactory.create(highwayRoute). A qualifier is part of the key, so a misspelt one is simply a missing binding. Ask for @Named("hihgway"), a road no map has heard of, and the walk says so, path and all: MovingDay needs Crew needs Truck needs Driver needs @Named("hihgway") Route: nobody provides @Named("hihgway") Route. Duplicates belong to the modules, not to one component, so the processor checks them once per build, before it walks any component. Then each component's walk adds what it finds. Missing, circular or doubled, every mistake gets its own line in one build, and a component is written only when its plan is clean. When a component isn't written, the app code that uses it can't compile either. So KSP adds follow-on lines such as MovingDayApp.kt:6: Unresolved reference 'GeneratedMovingDayComponent'. Fix the first errors; those go away with them. That leaves the limit of today's checks. They see what the plan is made of: types, names and constructors. They can't tell you that a route of 42 minutes is a bad one, or that a constructor will throw on the day. Those stay run-time problems. Send the truck and the family down different roads Run MovingDayApp and its Java twin. Which road does the truck take, and which does the family take? Open injector/app/build/generated/ksp/l02/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l02/GeneratedMovingDayComponent.kt and find the two route lines and the driver's line. In RouteModule.kt, change @Named("back roads") to @Named("highway"). Predict every error, run ./gradlew :injector:app:kspL02Kotlin, then change it back. MovingDayApp.kt package workbench.injector.app.l02 // Uses the component KSP wrote: build/generated/ksp/l02/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l02/GeneratedMovingDayComponent.kt // ./gradlew :injector:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.injector.app.l02.MovingDayAppKt fun main() { val plan: MovingDayComponent = GeneratedMovingDayComponent() plan.movingDay().plan().forEach(::println) println("one truck for the whole day: ${plan.truck() === plan.movingDay().crew.truck}") } ./gradlew :injector:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.injector.app.l02.MovingDayAppKt labs/injector/app/src/l02/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l02/MovingDayApp.kt MovingDayAppJava.java package workbench.injector.app.l02; // Java calling the same generated Kotlin component. // ./gradlew :injector:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.injector.app.l02.MovingDayAppJava public class MovingDayAppJava { public static void main(String[] args) { MovingDayComponent plan = new GeneratedMovingDayComponent(); plan.movingDay().plan().forEach(System.out::println); System.out.println("one truck for the whole day: " + (plan.truck() == plan.movingDay().getCrew().getTruck())); } } ./gradlew :injector:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.injector.app.l02.MovingDayAppJava labs/injector/app/src/l02/java/workbench/injector/app/l02/MovingDayAppJava.java Both languages print Sam drives truck MOVE-1 on the highway (42 min), the family takes the back roads (51 min), two tape-roll numbers and one truck for the whole day: true. With two highways, one build reports both real problems: RouteModule.kt:16: @Named("highway") Route is provided twice: ... and MovingDay.kt:12: MovingDay needs @Named("back roads") Route: nobody provides @Named("back roads") Route., followed by two follow-on Unresolved reference 'GeneratedMovingDayComponent' lines from the app code.

h: Wiring mistakes as compile errors · Java and Kotlin
x: One mistake, two messengers: javac's Messager and KSP's logger GraphCheckProcessor (javac) // in the processor: the message, and the element it is about processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, "MovingDay needs Crew needs Truck needs Driver: nobody provides Driver", parameter); // what the demo's DiagnosticCollector gives back: the file, the line, the message // Missing.java:7: error: MovingDay needs Crew needs Truck needs Driver: nobody provides Driver Graph (KSP) // in the processor: the message, and the symbol it is about logger.error( "MovingDay needs Crew needs Truck needs Driver: nobody provides Driver. " + hint(key), dependency.node, ) // what the build prints: the absolute path and the line, no column // e: [ksp] /.../Missing.kt:8: MovingDay needs Crew needs Truck needs Driver: nobody provides Driver. ... Both APIs take a message and the symbol it is about, and both report the declaration's line, which for a parameter is the parameter's own line. A javac diagnostic also carries a column, and javac's default printer shows the source line with a caret; KSP prints e: [ksp], the absolute path and the line, with no column. In both, an error lets the current round finish, so a processor that reports and carries on gets every mistake into one build. The difference is in the model, not the messenger: our KSP processor reads Kotlin types such as Lazy<T> and nullability as Kotlin sees them, where javac sees the Java view of them.

h: Wiring mistakes as compile errors · Quiz

Dependency cycle: MovingDay needs Crew needs Truck needs Driver needs Truck Dependency cycle: Truck needs Driver needs Truck Nothing: Truck is already built, so it's shared A missing binding for Truck The loop starts at the binding that repeats, so the processor drops MovingDay and Crew, which lead into the loop but aren't part of it. Truck isn't finished yet, because the walk is still inside it, so it isn't in done and isn't shared. Crew and MovingDay both need the same singleton Route. What happens when the walk reaches Route for the second time? The processor reports a cycle, because Route was visited before The processor reports a duplicate binding Nothing: Route is in done, so it's shared The component builds a second route Route was finished on the first visit, so it's in done, and the walk checks done before the path. Two arrows into one binding are sharing, not a loop. A duplicate would be two bindings for one key, which isn't the case here. A module has @Provides @Named("highway") fun highway(): Route, and the driver asks for @Named("Highway") route: Route. What does the build say? A missing binding: nobody provides @Named("Highway") Route Nothing: qualifiers are compared without case A duplicate binding for Route It compiles, and the driver gets the highway at run time A qualifier is part of the key, and Highway and highway are different strings. So the request has no binding, and the walk reports it with the whole path, on the driver's parameter. From Errors, validation and helpful messages: your processor throws an IllegalStateException with a clear message when it finds a mistake, instead of calling logger.error. What changes? Nothing: KSP turns the exception into the same error The message gains the file and line of the symbol KSP calls onError() first, then stops Processing stops at the first mistake, and kctfork reports INTERNAL_ERROR instead of COMPILATION_ERROR A thrown exception stops processing at once: later checks and processors don't run, and KSP 2.3.14 doesn't call onError() for it. logger.error(message, symbol) lets the round finish, points at the symbol's file and line, and gives COMPILATION_ERROR in kctfork, so one build can list every mistake. Refuses when it's created Throws when the driver first asks for a route Keeps one of them without a word, and which one depends on method order Gives the driver a list of both routes It stores providers in a map by key, so the second put replaces the first. getDeclaredMethods() returns methods in no particular order, so the winner isn't something you chose. h: Wiring mistakes as compile errors · Key terms
x: Binding One line of the plan: how to get one type, from an @Inject constructor or a @Provides function. Missing binding A request for a type that no binding provides. Cycle A chain of "needs" that leads back to where it started, so nothing in it can be built first. Duplicate binding Two bindings for the same type and qualifier, so the plan can't tell which one is meant. Module An object whose @Provides functions are bindings for types you can't annotate. Qualifier A name, such as @Named("highway"), that tells two bindings of the same type apart. What is a missing binding? A type someone needs that no binding provides: no @Inject constructor and no @Provides function. How does the walk detect a cycle? Before visiting a dependency, it checks whether that binding is on the current path: entered, and not yet left. Why check the finished set before the path? A finished binding is shared, not a loop. The crew and the moving day can both need one route. What is a qualifier? A name such as @Named("highway") that's part of a binding's key, so two bindings of one type can be told apart. What does a @Module give the plan? Bindings for types you can't annotate: each @Provides function says how to get its return type, and its parameters are dependencies. Why logger.error(message, node) and carry on, instead of throwing? The error lands on that symbol's file and line, the round finishes, and one build reports every mistake. A thrown exception stops at the first one. Where should a missing-binding error point? At the parameter that asks for the type, with the path from the entry point in the message.

h: Wiring mistakes as compile errors · Go deeper
x: When the component isn't written, every line of your code that uses it breaks too, and KSP adds follow-on messages after the real ones, with the file name only: e: [ksp] MovingDayApp.kt:6: Unresolved reference 'GeneratedMovingDayComponent'. They come from a type check KSP runs on a failed build, and they disappear when the first errors are fixed. Read the messages from the top. Where an error points is a choice the processor makes. Ours puts a missing binding on the parameter that asks, a cycle on the parameter that closes the loop, and a duplicate on the second binding. Each is the line you would edit. javac's Messager has overloads that take an AnnotationMirror or an AnnotationValue too, so a Java processor can point at a single annotation argument, such as a misspelt @Named value. KSP's logger takes any KSNode, and its location is the line of the declaration. The checks are cheap because the graph is small and each binding is visited once. Resolving types is the expensive part of KSP, and the walk resolves each parameter's type once per binding. A much larger graph would want each resolved type cached in the binding, which ours does with by lazy. Our checks stop at what the plan is made of. They don't warn about a binding nobody uses, or a singleton that depends on something built fresh each time and so keeps one copy for good. Real tools add checks like those; once you have the graph and the path, each one is a few lines in the same walk.

h: Measure the payoff, then meet the real tools · Race them from cold: wiring time, start-up and classes loaded
x: First, the words in one breath. KSP, Kotlin Symbol Processing, runs processors, plug-ins for the build that read your declarations and write new code. Java has had the same kind of plug-in since Java 6, the annotation processors that javac runs, and KSP is Kotlin's own, faster way to do that job for Kotlin code. Our component is the class our processor generates to build the graph: every object of the moving day, and who needs whom. It hands each object its dependencies, the objects it needs, through its constructor, which is dependency injection by constructor injection. Each line of the plan is a binding. A singleton is built once per component, anything else on each request, and each class has a generated factory that calls its constructor. Now the race. StartupRace in the lesson 3 app starts a fresh JVM for every run, seven runs for each way of wiring the same crew. In each JVM, WiringProbe wires the crew one way and asks for the moving day twice, timing each step with System.nanoTime(): Java long t0 = System.nanoTime(); MovingDayComponent plan = new GeneratedMovingDayComponent(); // builds every singleton, in order long t1 = System.nanoTime(); MovingDay day = plan.movingDay(); // returns a field long t2 = System.nanoTime(); // the other way: ReflectionContainer c = new ReflectionContainer(RouteModule.INSTANCE); // MovingDay day = c.get(MovingDay.class); // reads the notes, builds everything Kotlin val t0 = System.nanoTime() val plan = GeneratedMovingDayComponent() // builds every singleton, in order val t1 = System.nanoTime() val day = plan.movingDay() // returns a field val t2 = System.nanoTime() // the other way: val c = ReflectionContainer(RouteModule) // val day = c.get(MovingDay::class.java) // reads the notes, builds everything The parent times the whole JVM run, and -Xlog:class+load, a JVM switch that logs every class as it's loaded, counts the classes. Both ways build the same crew: each probe's line ends with the plan's first line, Sam drives truck MOVE-1 on the highway. Make your guess for the wiring ratio before you read on. On this machine, four cores with a load average around 5 from other builds, the race printed: 7 cold starts each, medians (a busy machine: compare the two rows, not the numbers with yours) create first get second get JVM run classes proxy classes annotations generated 25.53 ms 0.00 ms 0.000 ms 181 ms 817 0 0 reflection 50.92 ms 21.02 ms 0.002 ms 256 ms 1059 6 4 The generated component does all its work in create: its constructor builds every singleton in order, so the first movingDay() only returns a field. Add create and first get together, and it's 25.5 ms against 71.9 ms, about 2.8 times faster. The whole JVM run was 75 ms shorter. An earlier run, at a higher load, gave 17.6 against 46.3 ms and 139 against 192 ms, and the Java twin's run gave 32.1 against 66.6 ms. So the times moved by a third from run to run, and the ratio stayed between 2 and 3. The class counts didn't move at all. What are the 242 extra classes? About forty come from java.lang.reflect, much of it the JDK's proxy machinery. Six are proxy classes it generated while the program ran, jdk.proxy1.$Proxy0 to jdk.proxy2.$Proxy5, to stand for annotations being read. Others parse the generic signature Lazy<GpsUnit> out of the class file. And four are the annotation classes themselves. The generated component never loads Inject, Singleton, Named or Provides at all. The sticky notes did their job in the build and stayed there. Once wired, the two are equally quick: the second request costs a few microseconds or less either way. Fifty milliseconds won't matter to a program that starts once a week. They matter to one that starts often, like a command-line tool, or a test suite that builds a fresh component for every test. And this crew has eight classes, where a real program has hundreds. Reflection pays for the wiring at every start. Generated wiring pays once, in the build. Look at the generated create time again. It builds everything at once, including parts nobody needs at seven in the morning. The truck's GPS is one of them. Run the cold-start race Write down your guess: how much faster will the generated component wire the crew, and how many extra classes will reflection load? Run StartupRace from labs/. It starts fourteen small JVMs, one after another, and prints one row per way of wiring. Run StartupRaceJava, the same race with Java calling the same generated component and the same container. Run StartupRace again with -Pargs=3 added (three starts each). Which columns moved, and which didn't?
