h: Measure the payoff, then meet the real tools · The GPS can wait: Lazy and () -> T
x: The truck's GPS takes a while to switch on, because it has to find the satellites first. In the demo app, GpsUnit's constructor sleeps for 300 ms to stand in for that wait, a delay chosen for teaching. With the plan as it was, the component's constructor would build the GPS along with the truck. Every start would pay those 300 ms, even on a day the truck never asks for directions. Lazy injection fixes that. The truck asks for Lazy<GpsUnit> instead of GpsUnit. That's a box that builds its contents the first time someone opens it with .value, and hands back the same contents after that. Provider injection is its sibling. The packer asks for () -> TapeRoll, a function that hands out one more roll on every call. In the moving-day picture, the GPS is on call and comes when it's first needed, and every room gets a fresh roll of tape: Java // Closest Java equivalent: a Supplier, which the component makes build the GPS only once public class Truck { private final Supplier<GpsUnit> gps; @Inject public Truck(Driver driver, Supplier<GpsUnit> gps) { this.gps = gps; /* ... */ } public String directions() { return gps.get().directionsTo("the new house"); } } public class Packer { private final Supplier<TapeRoll> newTape; // one more roll on every get() @Inject public Packer(Supplier<TapeRoll> newTape) { this.newTape = newTape; } public String pack(String room) { return room + " packed with tape roll #" + newTape.get().getNumber(); } } Kotlin @Singleton class Truck @Inject constructor(val driver: Driver, private val gps: Lazy<GpsUnit>) { fun directions(): String = gps.value.directionsTo("the new house") // switched on here, once } class Packer @Inject constructor(private val newTape: () -> TapeRoll) { // one more roll on every call fun pack(room: String): String = "$room packed with tape roll #${newTape().number}" } The processor changes in two of the KSP track's five moves. In the Read move, requestOf unwraps the type a parameter asks for: Lazy<GpsUnit> becomes (LAZY, GpsUnit), and () -> TapeRoll, whose class is kotlin.Function0, becomes (PROVIDER, TapeRoll). The key is the type inside, so every check from lesson 2 still works. Forget the GPS's @Inject, and the build says MovingDay needs Crew needs Truck needs GpsUnit: nobody provides GpsUnit., on the truck's gps parameter. In the Write move, a singleton that someone asks for lazily is held in a Lazy of its own, and each request gets the expression for its kind: Java // The same lines in Java, written by a javac processor; memoize() is a small generated helper private final Supplier<GpsUnit> gpsUnit = memoize(GpsUnitFactory::create); // built on the first get() private final Truck truck = TruckFactory.create(driver, gpsUnit); private Packer newPacker() { return PackerFactory.create(this::newTapeRoll); } Kotlin private val gpsUnit: Lazy<GpsUnit> = lazy { GpsUnitFactory.create() } // built on the first .value private val truck: Truck = TruckFactory.create(driver, gpsUnit) private fun newPacker(): Packer = PackerFactory.create({ newTapeRoll() }) asked for as gpsUnit (singleton, held in a Lazy) truck (singleton, built at once) newTapeRoll (no @Singleton) the type itself gpsUnit.value truck newTapeRoll() Lazy<T> gpsUnit lazyOf(truck) lazy { newTapeRoll() } () -> T { gpsUnit.value } { truck } { newTapeRoll() } Kotlin's lazy { } is safe with threads by default: its mode is SYNCHRONIZED, so the body runs once even if two threads open the box at the same moment. The app shows the result: crew ready after 109 ms, GPS switched on: 0 Sam drives truck MOVE-1 on the highway the family takes the back roads kitchen packed with tape roll #1 pantry packed with tape roll #2 bedroom packed with tape roll #3 GPS: turn left at the bakery for the new house first directions after 488 ms, GPS switched on: 1 GPS: turn left at the bakery for the new house second directions after 489 ms, GPS switched on: 1 The crew was ready with the GPS still off. The first request for directions paid for the GPS, and the second paid nothing: the same GPS, still on. Three rooms, three rolls of tape. Ask for GpsUnit directly instead, and the generated line becomes private val gpsUnit: GpsUnit = GpsUnitFactory.create(); the crew is then ready after 327 ms, with the GPS already on. Laziness moves a cost; it doesn't remove one. The first caller who needs directions waits the 300 ms, perhaps at a worse moment than seven in the morning. And a cycle, a chain of "needs" that comes back to where it started, is still a cycle to our processor when one link is a Lazy. Nothing would actually be built twice there, but we chose to keep the check simple and strict. Make a part lazy when it's expensive and not always needed. Build the rest with the plan. The plan is fast now, and patient. But two claims about it still rest on our word: that the generated code uses no reflection, and that one edit doesn't redo everything. Let's check both. h: Measure the payoff, then meet the real tools · Proof, not promises: no reflection in the generated code, and what one edit rebuilds
x: Proof, not promises: a test reads the generated code, the class log agrees, and KSP's log shows what one edit redoes The first claim is that the generated code uses no reflection, a program inspecting its own classes while it runs. The lab doesn't take that on trust. One test reads every file KSP generated and fails if any of them reaches for reflection: Java // The same check in Java, with AssertJ, calling the Kotlin test helper for (Map.Entry<String, String> file : run.getGenerated().entrySet()) { assertThat(file.getValue()).as(file.getKey() + " uses reflection") .doesNotContain("java.lang.reflect", "kotlin.reflect", "::class", "Class.forName", "javaClass", "getDeclared"); } Kotlin for ((path, text) in run.generated) { // every file KSP wrote assertThat(text).withFailMessage("$path uses reflection:\n$text") .doesNotContain("java.lang.reflect", "kotlin.reflect", "::class", "Class.forName", "javaClass", "getDeclared") } The race's class log agrees from the other side: no proxy classes, and not one annotation class loaded. That test is a cheap habit to keep. It fails on the day someone "just quickly" reads an annotation at run time. The second claim is about the build. Incremental processing means KSP reprocesses only the files a change can affect. In the KSP track's picture, you repack one box, redo its card, and redo the master list. Let's watch it in lesson 3's source set. Build once with KSP's log switched on, add one comment line to Truck.kt, and build again: ./gradlew :injector:app:compileL03Kotlin -Pksp.incremental.log=true echo "// a comment, so the file's text changes" >> injector/app/src/l03/kotlin/workbench/injector/app/l03/Truck.kt ./gradlew :injector:app:compileL03Kotlin -Pksp.incremental.log=true KSP rewrites its logs on every run, in injector/app/build/kspCaches/l03/logs/. h: Measure the payoff, then meet the real tools · The real tools: Dagger and Hilt, kotlin-inject, and Koin
x: Everything in this capstone has full-sized relatives. Now that the idea is clear, here they are, each in a few plain sentences, as of November 2026. Dagger generates component implementations and factories, the same two kinds of output as ours. Its KSP processor is dagger-compiler, and its docs say "Dagger's KSP support is stable as of Dagger 2.60+ and KSP 2.3.9+". Hilt, built on Dagger for Android phone apps, ships its own KSP processor, hilt-compiler, at the same version. Two warnings from Dagger's docs matter when you move a project over. Plugins written against Dagger's SPI, the interface its plug-ins use, must move to its new SPI. And "KSP processors are not able to resolve types generated by other Javac/KAPT processors". kotlinlang's list of supported libraries, on a page dated November 2026, still says "Dagger: Alpha" and "Hilt: In progress". Dagger's own docs are the ones to trust. kotlin-inject is closer to what you wrote. It runs only on KSP, and its 0.9.0 release removed KSP1 support. In its README's words, "An implementation of this component will be generated for you". You reach it through a generated .create() extension, instead of a class name like our GeneratedMovingDayComponent. Koin moved the other way. Its annotations used to go through a KSP processor that generated visible source files and extensions such as AppModule().module. Its docs now say "koin-ksp-compiler is deprecated and will be removed in a future Koin version". The annotations stay, and the Koin Compiler Plugin, koin-compiler-plugin, now processes them (1.2.3 on Maven Central, November 2026). They keep KSP only for projects that "can't move to Kotlin 2.3.20 or later yet". The plugin "replaces single<UserRepository>() (or the @Singleton class) with the equivalent of single { UserRepository(get(), get()) }" during compilation. That's a change to your own code. In the KSP track's picture, it's a job for the mover who repacks the box, not for the helper who can only add new cards. Each get() in that line asks Koin's container for an argument, so that part of the lookup still happens while the program runs. Adding either of the first two to a real build is one line, as our app's processors are: // build.gradle.kts of an app module: one of these, not both dependencies { ksp("com.google.dagger:dagger-compiler:2.60.1") // Dagger ksp("me.tatarka.inject:kotlin-inject-compiler-ksp:0.9.0") // kotlin-inject } What you built has the same bones. There's a factory per class and a component per interface, checks fail the build on the exact line, and parts can be asked for lazily or through a provider. The real tools add years of cases you can now recognise when you meet them. Dagger: KSP (dagger.dev) docs kotlin-inject (GitHub) read Koin Annotations with KSP (Koin docs) docs

h: Measure the payoff, then meet the real tools · Java and Kotlin
x: A part that waits: Supplier in Java, Lazy in Kotlin Truck.java public class Truck { private final Supplier<GpsUnit> gps; @Inject public Truck(Driver driver, Supplier<GpsUnit> gps) { this.gps = gps; } public String directions() { return gps.get().directionsTo("the new house"); // builds once only if the Supplier remembers } } // a Supplier that remembers, written by hand static <T> Supplier<T> memoize(Supplier<T> make) { return new Supplier<>() { private volatile T value; public synchronized T get() { if (value == null) value = make.get(); return value; } }; } Truck.kt @Singleton class Truck @Inject constructor(val driver: Driver, private val gps: Lazy<GpsUnit>) { fun directions(): String = gps.value.directionsTo("the new house") // builds once, then remembers } // the component's side: the standard library's lazy {}, SYNCHRONIZED by default private val gpsUnit: Lazy<GpsUnit> = lazy { GpsUnitFactory.create() } Java's Supplier<T> only promises a get(): whether it builds once or every time is up to whoever wrote it, so a component that wants "once, on first use" has to wrap it, as memoize does. Kotlin's Lazy<T> makes the promise part of the type: .value builds on first use and returns the same object afterwards, and lazy { } is thread-safe by default. For a fresh object on every call, the two languages meet in the middle: Java's Supplier<TapeRoll> and Kotlin's () -> TapeRoll are both just functions with no parameters.

h: Measure the payoff, then meet the real tools · Worked example
x: Choose how each part asks for what it needs The driver is cheap to build and needed every day: ask for him directly. The component builds him with the plan and passes the object. class Truck @Inject constructor(val driver: Driver /* ... */) // generated: TruckFactory.create(driver, ...) @Inject public Truck(Driver driver /* ... */) { /* ... */ } // generated: TruckFactory.create(driver, ...) The GPS is slow to start and not needed on every day: ask for Lazy<GpsUnit>. Because it's a singleton asked for lazily, the component holds it in a Lazy and passes that. class Truck @Inject constructor(val driver: Driver, private val gps: Lazy<GpsUnit>) // generated: private val gpsUnit: Lazy<GpsUnit> = lazy { GpsUnitFactory.create() } @Inject public Truck(Driver driver, Supplier<GpsUnit> gps) { /* ... */ } // generated: private final Supplier<GpsUnit> gpsUnit = memoize(GpsUnitFactory::create); Tape runs out room by room: the packer asks for () -> TapeRoll and calls it once per room. TapeRoll has no @Singleton, so each call builds a new roll. class Packer @Inject constructor(private val newTape: () -> TapeRoll) // generated: PackerFactory.create({ newTapeRoll() }) @Inject public Packer(Supplier<TapeRoll> newTape) { /* ... */ } // generated: PackerFactory.create(this::newTapeRoll) Check the choice with the app, not with your intuition: MovingDayApp prints when the crew is ready and when the GPS switched on. If a part is needed on every start anyway, Lazy only adds a lock and a box; ask for it directly.

h: Measure the payoff, then meet the real tools · Quiz
x: In the race, the generated component's first get was 0.00 ms, while its create took about 25 ms. Why? The JIT compiled movingDay() away Its constructor builds every singleton in order, so movingDay() only returns a field The timer can't measure below a millisecond It cached a reflection result from the build The generated plan is eager: every singleton is a private val set in the constructor, so all the work lands in create. The fair comparison is create plus first get on both sides, which is why the lesson adds them. There is no reflection in the generated code to cache. Truck asks for Lazy<GpsUnit>, and GpsUnit is a @Singleton. What does the generated component hold for the GPS? private val gpsUnit: Lazy<GpsUnit> = lazy { GpsUnitFactory.create() } private val gpsUnit: GpsUnit = GpsUnitFactory.create() private fun newGpsUnit(): GpsUnit Nothing: the truck builds its own GPS A singleton that someone asks for lazily is held in a Lazy, and the truck gets that Lazy itself, so the GPS is built on the first .value and shared afterwards. A plain val would build it with the plan; a new...() function would make a new GPS per request, which is what you get without @Singleton. A packer asks for newTape: () -> TapeRoll, and TapeRoll has no @Singleton. The packer packs three rooms, calling newTape() once per room. How many rolls does it use? One, built on the first call None until the component is closed Three, one per call It depends on how many threads pack The generated argument is { newTapeRoll() }, and newTapeRoll() builds a new roll every time because TapeRoll isn't a singleton. One roll for every call is the point of provider injection; Lazy<TapeRoll> would have given one roll, built on first use. From Compiler plugins: Koin's compiler plugin replaces single<UserRepository>() with the equivalent of single { UserRepository(get(), get()) } while your code compiles. Why couldn't a KSP processor do the same job? KSP is too slow for Koin's users KSP can't read annotations on classes KSP runs after the Kotlin compiler, too late to change anything KSP can only add new files: it can't change an expression in your code KSP processors read declarations and write new files; they can't see expressions or change existing code, as the compiler plugins lesson put it. Rewriting a call inside your function is a compiler plugin's job. KSP actually runs before the Kotlin compile, and it reads annotations well, which is how Koin's older KSP processor worked. You add one comment to Truck.kt and rebuild lesson 3's app with -Pksp.incremental.log=true. Which output does KSP restore from its backup instead of regenerating? GpsUnitFactory.kt TruckFactory.kt GeneratedMovingDayComponent.kt CrewFactory.kt GpsUnit.kt neither changed nor looked up anything in Truck.kt, so its isolating card is restored. TruckFactory.kt comes from the edited file, CrewFactory.kt from a file that looked up Truck, and the component is aggregating, so it's redone on every change.

h: Measure the payoff, then meet the real tools · Key terms
x: Reflection A program inspecting its own classes, constructors and annotations while it runs. Cold start A start in a fresh JVM, before anything is loaded or compiled, the way a program really starts. Lazy injection Asking for Lazy : the object is built on the first .value and shared after that. Provider injection Asking for () -> T: a function that hands out one more object on every call. Incremental processing KSP reprocessing only the files a change can affect, and restoring the other outputs from its backups. Aggregating output A generated file built from many sources, which KSP redoes whenever any file changes. Compiler plugin A jar the Kotlin compiler loads to change the code it compiles, which KSP can't do. What does Lazy<T> injection give a class? A box that builds its T on the first .value and returns the same one after that. What does provider injection, () -> T, give a class? A function that returns one more T on every call, or the shared one if T is a singleton. Which number in the cold-start race stayed the same from run to run? The classes loaded: 817 for the generated component, 1,059 for reflection. The times moved with the machine's load. Why does the generated path load no annotation classes? KSP read the annotations during the build. The generated code only calls constructors and factories. Why is the component redone after any edit? It's an aggregating output: KSP files it under <AnyChanges is a virtual file; DO NOT USE.>, so any change redoes it. Why did Koin move its annotations from a KSP processor to a compiler plugin? The plugin rewrites single<T>() calls in your code into constructor calls. KSP can only add new files.

h: Measure the payoff, then meet the real tools · Go deeper
x: Why count classes at all? Loading a class means finding its bytes, checking them and linking them, and every class costs the start a little. A count is also the honest number on a busy machine: it doesn't depend on what else is running. -Xlog:class+load prints one line per class with its source, so you can tell your own classes from the JDK's and from classes made while the program ran, such as jdk.proxy2.$Proxy1. Wiring generated at build time also suits the start-up tools of Part 4. A class data sharing archive or an AOT cache stores classes loaded from jars; classes defined while the program runs, such as dynamic proxies, can't be archived the same way, as the Part 4 capstone found. A generated plan leaves almost nothing to be made at run time, so more of the start can come from the archive. Our component is eager except where you ask for Lazy. An eager plan is simple to read and fails fast: if a constructor throws, it throws when the component is created. A fully lazy plan, with every singleton in a lazy { }, would start faster still and build only what's used, but a broken constructor would then surface later, on first use. Both are reasonable; pick the failure time you'd rather have. In KSP's incremental logs, kspLookupGraph.log lists what each reprocessed file looked up, so you can see exactly why Crew.kt became dirty when Truck.kt changed. With -Pksp.incremental.log.graph.origin= and a fully qualified name, KSP also writes a .dot file of the lookups around that symbol.
